## Volume Front Matter

### Series Title Page

**COMPLETE COURSE OF PATROLOGY, OR UNIVERSAL, COMPLETE, UNIFORM, CONVENIENT, AND ECONOMICAL LIBRARY**

of all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprinting of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have survived through the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, carefully collated both with one another and with numerous manuscript codices, and corrected with the greatest diligence; continuously illustrated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by all works discovered after the extensive editions produced during the last three centuries had been completed; supplied with particular analytical indexes following each volume or each author of importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of every page and indicating the subject treated; augmented by works both doubtful and apocryphal, and by others possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any theme may be surveyed at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, by which it is immediately evident to the reader which Fathers have commented on the individual texts of each book of Scripture and in which places of their works they have done so.

An exceptionally accurate edition, and one that can easily be preferred to all others if the following are taken into account: the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the thoroughness of the correction, the variety and number of the works reprinted, the highly convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the entire work, and the low price. Above all, this collection is a single, methodical, and chronological gathering of six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, but collected for the first time in our library from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.

### FIRST SERIES

In which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church from Tertullian to Gregory the Great.

Under the direction of J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or of the complete courses in each branch of ecclesiastical learning, Patrology has been issued in two editions: one Latin, the other Greek-Latin. The Latin edition is sold for 1,200 francs; the Greek-Latin edition for 1,300 francs. The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the latter, however, are presented in it only in Latin translation.

# The Complete Works of Saint Eusebius Jerome, Presbyter of Stridon

After the recension of the monks of the Order of St. Benedict of the Congregation of St. Maur, and especially that of Jean Martianay of the same order, once again corrected against Roman, Ambrosian, Veronese, and many other manuscripts, as well as against all French and foreign editions; enlarged by very numerous monuments previously entirely unpublished and by other writings of the holy Doctor previously issued only separately; and illustrated by innumerable notes, observations, and corrections through the study and labor of Vallarsi and Maffei, priests of Verona, with the assistance of other learned men in that same city.

The latest Paris edition, revised from the second edition by the Veronese editors themselves through their later labors, and so enriched by more recently discovered material that the present edition, solely in its extent and apart from its other omitted emendations, materially surpasses all preceding editions, including the Benedictine editions, by a third, or one-third.

# [The Complete Works of St. Jerome]

## [Col. V]

### To Our Most Holy Lord Clement XII, Supreme Pontiff

Most Holy Father,

As this greatest teacher of the Churches, Jerome, enjoyed during his lifetime an exceptionally distinguished reputation and fortunate position among your most holy predecessors, the Roman pontiffs, so today his remarkable intellectual offspring—these writings through which, commended in some way to Your most exalted name, he comes to life again and appears more eagerly before the gaze of mankind—enjoy a prosperous destiny with You.

For when, in Rome, the seat of the Catholic religion, he had put on the garment of Christ (Letter XV) as a young man, almost still a boy, he thereafter won such love and favor from the most holy pontiff Damasus that, having been appointed by him as an assistant in ecclesiastical correspondence (Letter CXXIII), he also replied in Damasus’s own name to the synodal consultations of the East and West. He then so earned the esteem of the Roman Church and so bound its affection to himself that, after Damasus had been summoned to heaven, he himself was regarded as worthy of the supreme priesthood (Letter XLV), with the whole city joining in his praise.

Although he preferred to place this greatest honor and dignity among men below the silence and hiding places of the desert, he could not altogether escape the esteem or lack the favor of those who subsequently held the office; this is shown in Books II and III Against Rufinus and in Letters CXXVII and CXXX. He experienced the goodwill of Anastasius, whose praises he often celebrates, as so favorable to his cause that, when Anastasius merely conveyed it through his friends (Letters XCV and XCVII), the patrons of the Origenist cause—namely, Jerome’s enemies—were condemned (Letters CXXXV, CXXXVI, and CXXXVII).

I pass over Innocent’s very extensive goodwill toward him, the most friendly letters exchanged on both sides, the protection he received against factious men, the violent hands driven away from the place which he occupied at Bethlehem by the highest authority, and, finally, the praises that were proclaimed throughout the ends of the earth. These were of such a kind (Letter to Innocent I) that the Fathers of the Council of Milevis, writing to the holy pontiff, named Jerome alone, in honor, as Innocent’s son; while Gelasius, when Jerome had recently departed to heaven, proclaimed in the Roman council to the whole world: “We hold those things which we know blessed Jerome to have held” (Decree, chapter III).

And now, Most Blessed Father, what is the character of Your devotion to Jerome’s name, by which, if I interpret Your mind correctly, You do not so much rival Your predecessors as surpass them? Surely it is this: You have caused the outstanding monuments of his mind, by whose virtue the Christian cause once stood, to be brought forth for publication adorned with new care. I do not know whether I should call this the greatest of all reasons for their being brought forth.

Now, Most Blessed Father, I recall an event most pleasing to me and glorious to Jerome. At the beginning of Your pontificate, to which You were divinely appointed, when I was about to depart from Rome so that, after gathering materials there—especially from the Vatican Library—I might more conveniently undertake this edition in my homeland, and might throw myself at Your feet and receive Your apostolic blessing, You encouraged me with such kindness to undertake this labor that You did not wish me to omit any means of bringing the work to completion more quickly.

I shall speak truly—not because I think I have done anything worthy of Your commands, but so that, wherever the undertaking may seem to have succeeded somewhat according to my wishes, I may ascribe the whole to Your benevolence: awakened by the memory of Your auspicious encouragement, in attempting this arduous task I ventured with a confident spirit whatever I seemed capable of doing.

Yet, Most Blessed Father, even if I had not applied my mind to these things, there is another kind of patronage which You extend to Jerome’s labors and which renews my courage as I adorn them. I mean the most holy manner and discipline of life by which, through a certain immediate and supreme testimony, You command that the precepts which Jerome gives for destroying the roots of vices and raising minds toward virtue be believed, so that those precepts cannot in the future appear burdensome to anyone, since You reproduce their image in Yourself in every respect with the greatest perfection.

For since everything treated by Jerome concerns knowledge and piety—the two weapons of priests—nature itself formed You, Most Clement Father, to enlarge the glory of wisdom, to extend the boundaries of the liberal arts, and to bestow honors and rewards upon virtue; and especially to cultivate prudence in the conduct of affairs, seriousness, justice, and the other virtues worthy of a prince of sacred things.

Through Your counsel, the majesty of the sacred laws, formerly diminished, is being restored to its original dignity and splendor. The several parts of the Church are returned to their proper order; those that had collapsed or been weakened are restored; and the difficulties of the times are softened. Your supreme skill in resolving the gravest disputes, and the equal greatness of Your spirit in conducting the affairs of the Christian commonwealth, are on everyone’s lips together with the grandeur of Your supreme authority.

If I turn to the subject of pious devotion, it is almost the unique distinction of Your noble Corsini family to excel in the glory of piety. Long distinguished by splendid examples, from that Andrew who fills heaven with the honors of the saints onward, it is now most abundantly adorned by the present zeal of Your most illustrious nephew through Your brother, the most eminent Cardinal Nerio.

## [Col. VII]

But the qualities that are peculiarly Your own, Most Holy Father, in this praise easily surpass every power not only of ornament but even of speech: deeds of distinction, to be committed to monuments that will never perish. They include the awakened vigor of Your religious spirit in performing the duties of the supreme pontificate; the generosity displayed in relieving the distress of the needy; the magnificence shown in repairing sacred buildings, and especially in raising them anew from the foundations; Your excellent resolve to benefit everyone; Your benevolence, humanity, equity, and the nearly countless other praises of this kind, which, if You should at some time turn Your eyes from the very weighty concerns of Christian affairs toward these labors of the great Jerome, You must necessarily behold in them as in a kind of mirror.

For this reason, insofar as the weakness of my talent allowed, I have earnestly striven to present Jerome himself before Your throne in his native appearance; to cover with a scar or a bandage the ulcers that flowed so abundantly from the injury of the ages; and, wherever many limbs were missing from that noble body, either to gather together those long scattered or to rescue from the final collapse those already tottering under the injuries of fortune.

You, Most Blessed Father, clearly understand that it is not the divine monuments themselves—which You embrace spontaneously and regard with admiration for the sake of imitation—but rather the labor which I have expended in polishing them, that is being commended specifically to Your name and patronage. You will therefore, if I am not mistaken, receive this labor itself with a kindly spirit, and You will not deny me and my studies the assistance which I am permitted to hope for from Your benevolence, with Jerome making the request worthy.

Thus he vows, humbly imploring Your apostolic blessing,

Your Holiness’s most humble and obedient servant and son,

**Dominicus Vallarsius, Priest of Verona**

## [Col. VII]

# General Preface

## 1. The Excellence of Jerome’s Works

If you consider Jerome’s discipline of life, examples of virtue, and the glory of his achievements, this greatest teacher of the Churches filled the whole world far and wide with admiration and veneration for himself. If you consider the distinction of his learning and the monuments of an almost divine intellect, there is scarcely any other among the Fathers of the Latin Church who left to posterity as great a reputation for wisdom as he did.

From the fourth century of Christ, during which, as it passed midway, he began to set pen to paper and submit the offspring of his mind to human judgment, down to the present age, after the passage of nearly fifteen centuries, he has been regarded as pre-eminent in the exposition of Scripture, so that no one has surpassed his excellence in the other disciplines related to Scripture—though all the more illustrious disciplines do relate to it—and very few have even approached it.

For, unlike what generally happens with others, he was not content with the learning of a single nation, nor did he cultivate only the field upon which he had first labored. After his industry in Latin literary studies, he embraced whatever Greece, the mother of the liberal arts, had taught; whatever had been handed down in the languages of the Hebrews and of the other most ancient peoples of the East. Having diligently mastered in all these fields not only sacred doctrines but also human learning, he always combined them and adorned them with extensive monuments.

Accordingly, in the works of all those who later became especially famous in sacred letters, there are testimonies to his extraordinary learning so clear and distinguished that it is not easy to find more brilliant testimonies concerning anyone else; and they are so numerous, indeed almost countless, that I do not think there was anyone in any century who attained some reputation for learning without seeking fame for himself through the splendor of Jerome’s name.

If I wished to review each of these authorities individually, I should exceed all measure and accomplish nothing. On the other hand, if I myself undertook, after men of such renown, to recommend this most industrious author to learned readers, I might perhaps seem to be claiming too much for myself. For who, after all, could suppose himself able either to follow with the sharpness of his mind Jerome as he rises in a kind of impulse toward sublime heights, or to comprehend him as he penetrates profound mysteries; to explain him as he continually overflows with such a variety of disciplines; or to portray him as cultivated with an almost unique dignity and elegance of speech?

## 2. The Necessity of a New Edition

But this is not my present purpose. I have touched upon the matter only superficially, in order to clear a path toward what must be said.

For if, in proportion as the works or teachings of any writer surpass those of others in merit or renown, one must continually strive with greater zeal to bring them to light as perfectly as human effort permits, then surely no learned person who desires knowledge can fail to acknowledge with equanimity that this labor ought above all to be expended upon the great Jerome.

Let the man, therefore, be regarded as having deserved well of the holy Doctor and especially of ecclesiastical learning who has returned his works to the anvil, even if they may previously have been polished without complete inadequacy. But if the situation is otherwise, and if, whether through the fault of the times or through the fault of those otherwise learned men who first set foot upon the task of publishing or even explaining them—or, as I think, through the fault of both—they are very far from that perfection which is fitting for them, lest the benefit due from reading them be obstructed, then the man should be considered to have produced a fruit of labor not a little useful who has devoted all his strength to preparing an entirely new edition. Indeed, he should be considered to have accomplished something that will serve the uses and advantage of learned people and is of the greatest necessity.

Now anyone who does not approach the matter with a completely inattentive mind will easily understand that the editions prepared down to the present time are generally unattractive and incomplete. It is especially useful and convenient to possess together all the writings produced by one and the same author. Yet, by contrast, many works are missing from the Jerome collections, and these are nearly all the most important ones; it is necessary to recover them from other books of different kinds, at the cost of considerable loss of time, and to obtain them only through great expense.

I say nothing about several works previously unpublished, of which, from the collection of Erasmus down to the present day, nothing at all has been added—whether because they were not diligently sought in the libraries where they lay hidden at enormous cost to ecclesiastical and literary studies, or because they escaped the investigators’ diligence.

Indeed, even the works that have been reprinted most often and are worn by the hands of students are disfigured by very numerous blemishes. False readings and errors occur, some originating with ancient copyists and others with recent critics; those who are engaged in such studies know well how much these impede the progress of readers.

Moreover, many of the more difficult passages remain shrouded in darkness to this day, while many others lead the reader astray—especially since, in this latest age, there have been and still are not a few men who are by no means unlearned, yet dare to charge Jerome with errors which he least of all people committed. Before the fault has been cleared away, or rather before the calumny has been removed, they may perhaps deceive the learned public.

## 3. The Reasons for Undertaking a New Edition

I have learned these matters through personal experience—not so that anyone may think I am repeating these defects in order to diminish the praise owed to the most learned men who labored over the revision of Jerome’s writings. Nearly seven years ago, when I was still very young, I devoted myself entirely to their study.

I also often discussed the matter with learned men living in this very city, men closely joined to me by a great partnership in study. I pointed out, not unsuccessfully as it seemed to them, how quite a few passages could be restored and how deficiencies could be supplied.

They therefore encouraged me to undertake a new edition and to gather the materials necessary for it, especially after they had discovered that copies of those works which had not been reprinted anywhere for nearly forty years after the Paris edition of the Benedictine Fathers were lacking in libraries throughout Italy. Yet they would not tolerate having even those works copied without examination and study, as had been done through the sordid negligence of certain printers.

While I was hesitating and inventing one reason after another for not undertaking the task, the most illustrious archpriest of the Church of Verona, Giovanni Francesco Muselli, came forward. In addition to his other praises, he possessed an exceptional enthusiasm for promoting learning and a favorable generosity toward learned men. He would not permit so useful a plan to dissolve into nothing. He immediately began to provide whatever was necessary, whether by advice, resources, books, or authority, freely promising that he would do so.

He ordered me—and, with his characteristic humanity, earnestly urged me—to undertake the entire responsibility of preparing a new edition. Those who had an interest in Jerome’s appearing in splendid attire, or who were in some way concerned with my affairs, also strongly urged me not to reject the province entrusted to me.

Thus, encouraged by their exhortations, and especially attracted by the hope of assistance, through which I confidently expected that some considerable benefit might accrue to the Church and to good letters, and that light and adornment might be added to the teaching of the holy Father, I did not hesitate to undertake so great a burden, though it was certainly not proportionate to my shoulders.

Indeed, I am resolved to do everything in my power for the benefit of students. If through this little work of ours we have been able to help them in any way, we gladly dedicate ourselves to that purpose; if not, at least we may have stimulated the minds of more learned men to contribute something better.

## 4. The Threefold Division of This Preface

Before I explain what labor I have proposed to undertake in adorning this neglected *Sparta*, certain matters must first be discussed more fully concerning the earlier collections, both those preserved in manuscripts and the much more distinguished collections that appeared after the invention of printing. We must briefly note what others accomplished before us.

Next, the character of Jerome’s works themselves must be explained, and some knowledge must be gained of those that have genuinely perished. Several others, however, which are commonly thought to have suffered the same fate, must be discussed at somewhat greater length, since they do not seem to us to have been composed at all.

This will perhaps bring greater light and usefulness to our edition, which examines and embraces everything that belongs to Jerome. Finally, we must briefly explain what assistance we used, what purpose and order we followed, and by what method we proceeded in establishing the text and notes.

# PART ONE

## Concerning Manuscript and Printed Collections, Considered Individually

## 5. Manuscript Collections of Jerome’s Works

There is something almost peculiar to Jerome’s writings: because they were received with the greatest eagerness, learned men, at the very time when they were being written and without the author’s knowledge, took great care to publish them publicly.

The forty-eighth letter in our recension, addressed to Pammachius, which the holy Doctor titled *Against Jovinianus* in defense of his own books, bears the clearest witness to the fame of his works among the public. Jerome attributes this fame partly to the zeal of his friends and partly to the envy of his rivals:

> “I am not as fortunate as most writers of our time, so that I can correct my trifles whenever I wish. As soon as I have written something, either my admirers or my envious opponents, moved by different purposes but engaged in an equal contest, spread my writings among the public.”

Elsewhere he expresses the same idea, which occurs not infrequently: sometimes he approves of what he has written being made public, while at other times—using the phrase and words of Quintilian in the preface to Book I—he laments that it has been published with the rash honor of an edition. On this subject, see Letter XLVII to Desiderius in the present edition.

More famous than the others, and also more extensive, is the recension which he himself permitted to be made by the copyists of Lucinius of Baetica. Writing in response to Lucinius, he says:

> “I have given my minor works, which you say you desire not because of their own merit but because of your kindness, to your men for copying, and I saw them copied into paper codices. I frequently urged them to collate them more carefully and correct them. For, because of the constant crowds of visitors and travelers, I was unable to reread such extensive volumes.”

Hence manuscripts still exist today that approach Jerome’s own age very closely, namely those assigned to the sixth century or the beginning of the seventh. Two certainly of this antiquity are preserved in the Veronese library. They contain minor works of the same, so to speak, institution, arranged with such care and order and with such discrimination in matters and readings that, in this age of letters, the diligence of a modern editor could scarcely surpass them.

At times we also find in them the inscription of the calligrapher or scholar who had displayed his industry in correcting them, especially one belonging to a monastic community, whose usual practice it was to copy the books of the holy Fathers and prepare editions of them.

I should like to present one among many, and the oldest of all that have come to our notice. It belongs to a certain Ursicinus, a lector of our own Veronese Church. He added it to a small codex containing the life of St. Paul, the first hermit, from Jerome’s works, together with a consular date designating the year 517.

Thus fewer than one hundred years had elapsed since the death of the holy Doctor. I do not know whether another manuscript of such antiquity can be found anywhere in the world.

The note is as follows; in deference to the taste of the learned age, I reproduce it most faithfully as it stands:

> **PER SCRIBTVS. CODIX HEC SVB DIE KAL. AVG. AGAPITO VCC INDI DECIMAE PER VRSICINUM LECT. ECCLESIAE VERONENSIS.**

“This codex was written on the Kalends of August, under Agapitus, vir clarissimus, in the tenth indiction, by Ursicinus, lector of the Church of Verona.”

Among those who deserved well above others for collecting and correcting Jerome’s writings, first place belongs to Cassiodorus, who readily reviewed each work and stored them with the greatest care in the library cabinets. Almost nothing else is said throughout that entire book on the instruction of divine letters, which he composed as if to equip a library of the Fathers.

In the later age, many *Jerome-centonists*—as they may be called—earned great gratitude from us, especially Rabanus Maurus, who copied Jerome’s complete books word for word and, through that industry, often preserved a better reading.

Passing over other examples of learned men, there is the remarkable case of Guigo, the fifth prior of the Great Charterhouse near the end of the eleventh century. He relates the following in his letter to the brothers of Durbon:

> “We gathered into one large volume all the letters of blessed Jerome that we were able to seek out from every source and, with the ability granted by God, cleanse of falsehoods. From them we removed certain letters which we discovered, either from the writings of other teachers or from their difference in style and thought, to be unworthy of the title of so great a man.”

So that he might not appear to the unlearned to have reduced Jerome’s writings without reasonable cause, he ordered this very letter to be placed at the front of the volume.

In subsequent times, many other manuscript editions of this kind, as they may properly be called, are found scattered throughout libraries. It is certain that, after the twelfth century, the manuscripts of no author were so widely available as those of Jerome, since almost the entire world poured itself into the study of him.

Would that copyists and critics had not taken some liberties for themselves in transcribing them; that they had not occasionally substituted their own words for a more hidden meaning, or appended glosses in the blank space of the book, which later prevailed after the true readings had been deleted.

## 6. The First Edition at Rome

But to come to those editions that were properly printed, from the very beginnings of the printing art one finds several outstanding men who labored greatly to prepare them.

Since countless editions appeared at various times, especially of the letters into which minor works were inserted, it is neither my inclination nor worth the effort to review each one tediously. I shall discuss only those which, prepared with some regard for sacred letters and learning, were produced according to the reliability of manuscripts or were newly reviewed rather than copied from earlier editions.

First place belongs to the Roman edition. In the year 1470, Andreas, Bishop of Aleria and custodian of the Vatican Library, most elegantly prepared it under Paul II, the Venetian, after it had recently been collected by Theodorus Laelius of Terni, later Bishop of Treviso.

Some catalogues even record the same edition as having been issued two years earlier—a circumstance that occurs only very rarely. We saw such a copy in the Novara library, and Simonius reports that one is preserved in the Colbert Library.

The editor, who had deserved exceptionally well of literary scholarship and had previously practiced himself in revising the works of other authors, explains in the letter prefixed to the pope what task he had undertaken in this Jerome edition and what plan he had adopted:

> “Recently certain friends asked me to receive and correct the little books and numerous letters of the divine Jerome, written with considerable error and previously collected from very different codices, which had been arranged in a definite order by the most learned and excellent father, the Bishop of Treviso. While he lived among mortals, he had always performed with great distinction before Your Holiness the office of referendary and apocrisarius. They asked that, through my diligence, these works might be returned somewhat more accurately, so that they could be read with less difficulty.”

He declares that he accomplished this in the Latin text with great fidelity and diligence. Concerning the Hebrew words that occur frequently, he says:

> “I left aside the Hebrew words, considering that each person, if able and willing, might supply them in his own volume.”

Concerning the Greek, he immediately adds:

> “There remained above all the Greek matters necessary for understanding, without which it was entirely impossible to read the writings of this most sacred Doctor for the sake of understanding, since these Greek materials are found in nearly all the principal volumes of the Latins. In these matters, therefore, I consulted not only certain other men worthy of praise and remembrance, but especially my most learned and most humane Theodorus Gaza.”

A little later he adds:

> “Without my Theodorus I undertake nothing more than I would without my genius.”

Finally, he excuses the fact that he tolerated, rather than approved, the insertion of many works that did not have Jerome as their author, allowing them to pass under his eyes in order to oblige certain friends.

The edition was issued from the house of the Maximi, whose work is certainly deserving of the highest praise.

Many other editions followed immediately. Indeed, in the same year, 1470, one appeared at Mainz through Peter—or, as some read it, Father—Schaeffer of Gernsheim. Six years later came another at Venice, prepared through the efforts of Antonio Bartholomeo. Three years afterward it was followed by another highly elegant edition at Rome, once again revised by the venerable Georgius Laurentius of Würzburg.

The following year there appeared the Parma edition, the most splendid of all, enlarged by several treatises and letters. Five years later came an edition at Nuremberg. Finally, there were countless others, the diligent collection of which is of no interest to us.

We shall add only one edition, dated 7 January 1496, without the name of its place or editor, which is in our possession. We often use it because it appears to have been reproduced directly from manuscripts, although it teems with innumerable errors.

## 7. Ancient Editions of the Commentaries and Other Works

The editions just mentioned contain only the letters and treatises. The commentaries on Sacred Scripture—for that is how they are entitled—were first rescued from neglect and squalor by the Nuremberg edition of 1477, followed two years later by another at Cologne and then by the Venetian edition of 1498, printed by Giovanni and Gregorio de Gregori.

There are also two folio volumes recorded under the title *Expositions on the Old and New Testament*, but without the printer’s name, the place, or even the year in which they were printed.

Other parts of Jerome’s works may also be added, works that appeared separately or again in other places.

Such are several homilies from Origen and the commentary *On the Song of Songs*, published, as I believe, at Basel in 1475 and at Nuremberg the following year.

There are also the *Lives of the Holy Fathers of Egypt* and of those who lived in Scythia, the Thebaid, and Mesopotamia. Of these, however, only the three most famous—those of Paul, Malchus, and Hilarion—came from the pen of our author. An edition of these appeared again five years later, and another seems to be much older, without the name of printer, year, or place.

Achilles Statius first published the Rule of St. Pachomius at Rome in 1575.

Many other works of this kind, whether separately or mixed into the writings of other authors, are found as the fifteenth century was drawing to a close.

Nor have we yet touched upon the editions of the *Chronicle*, all of which, from that of Boninus Mombritius down to the latest, we shall review in the preface to that work.

## 8. The Editions Are All Imperfect

It is neither possible in the time available nor worthwhile to examine these editions and submit them to detailed accounting.

I would not wish to deny learned men, or the printers themselves who undertook this task, the praise they deserve. But I say that it would have been desirable that, just as they did not spare expense in order to serve the students of sacred letters as well as they could, so they should have drawn their readings from various archetypes, rather than imagining that the only task assigned to them was to take in hand one old copy they happened to obtain and reproduce it accurately—or, if something seemed to be less correct, to alter it according to private judgment and, worse still, without the reader’s knowledge.

This is what generally occurred in the Latin text. In the Hebrew words, where space has been left for supplementation, the error is less serious than in the other words—which occur only rarely—that are represented in Latin letters, indeed with good intention but with corrupt readings.

Greek terms, too, have frequently been fabricated and distorted.

### 9. The Edition of Desiderius Erasmus

But perhaps nothing better was to be expected from the intellectual temper of that age, which not long afterward—namely, in 1516—was supplied by Erasmus of Rotterdam. He was the first to undertake not merely one book or another, but the preparation of a complete collection of all the works. Long practiced in polishing the writings of the ancients, he reviewed each work by consulting manuscripts gathered from every quarter, weighed them with keen judgment, prefixed summaries to shed light upon the treatises and letters, and finally illustrated them with sufficiently learned scholia and notes.

Indeed, he was the first to remove the innumerable writings of others which, falsely attributed to Jerome, had been mixed in with his genuine works, to the extraordinary detriment of scholarship. He did so only after sharp examination, briefly and learnedly touching upon and censuring nearly every little work; then he identified the pseudonymous writers by name, or at least forbade those works to come forward under the same auspices as Jerome or to bear his title.

He arranged the whole work in nine folio volumes. He assigned the genuine letters and minor works to the first three, and the spurious additions to the fourth. To two further volumes he appended commentaries on all the prophets. The seventh and eighth were enlarged by a mass of spurious material, apart from the commentaries on Ecclesiastes and the Psalter according to the Hebrew truth. Finally, in the last volume he mixed together the false and the genuine works relating to the exposition of the New Testament.

The brothers Bruno and Basilius Amerbach, together with their father Johannes, contributed their share to so great a work. They themselves again confess that they completed this task, as they say, οὐκ ἄνευ θέσεως (“not without effort”); but they acknowledge that they were assisted by the work of very learned men whom Johannes had summoned from throughout Germany, especially Johannes Reuchlin, who restored certain passages in the Hebrew; Conon of Nuremberg, who corrected most things in the Greek and Latin; Gregorius Reisch; and finally Conrad Pellican of Rouffach, under whose direction the undertaking was chiefly carried out.

This edition first appeared at Basel from the Froben press. It was received with the applause of scholars, especially of those who had departed from the Roman Church, so warmly that ten years later it was revised by Erasmus himself and repeatedly reprinted: at Basel and at Lyons and Paris, and for a third time at Basel, as well as elsewhere, down to the year 1565. Indeed, about fifty years ago it was reprinted at Leipzig, although it bears the imprint of Frankfurt am Main.

No one would begrudge Erasmus the praise due to that labor, had he abstained from that unrestrained and recklessly audacious disease of attacking the holiest Fathers in order to hunt down glory for himself. Whenever he praises them enthusiastically, he does so deliberately, so that afterward he may bite them with less resentment directed against him and with greater credit to himself. Had he restrained himself from insulting sacred matters when issuing his censures, and had he not so often mingled empty conjectures with the writings both of other ancient Fathers and of Jerome, then—unless the efforts of later theologians had opposed him—scarcely anything certain concerning ecclesiastical tradition could have been established from his judgment.

### 10. The Edition of Marianus Victorius

Moreover, the Erasmian edition so plainly seemed not to have attained legitimate perfection in the eyes of learned men that Marianus Victorius of Ameria, a priest and afterward bishop of Rieti, judged it in the interest no less of ecclesiastical doctrine than of scholarship to undertake a new one.

Having once again diligently gathered manuscript copies throughout Italy, especially at Florence and Brescia—not to mention the Roman manuscripts that were available—and acting with the support and patronage of the immortal-memory cardinal Morone, to whom he gives first place among the sponsors of his undertaking, he produced a sufficiently improved edition. In 1565 he issued the first three volumes from the elegant press of the Manutii, dedicating them to Pius IV.

In these volumes, covering the portion of Jerome’s works that Erasmus had specifically revised, he removed so many errors and hallucinations—introduced partly through incompetence and partly through carelessness—that he does not hesitate to claim that he restored approximately fifteen hundred passages which Erasmus had either marred with his own hand or, because of his ignorance of the subject, had been unable to restore after they had become corrupt through time.

In the scholia that he added at the end, he explains at considerable length the grounds for the readings he restored and their variation according to the manuscripts; he also elucidates many passages that seemed to him to require illumination.

He pursued the remaining volumes with no less diligence, publishing them in 1567 and the following year from the same Manutian press, and dedicating them to the succeeding pontiffs, Pius V and Gregory XIII. He professes to have removed an equal multitude of errors from them and to have refuted an equal number of instances of ignorance—whether because the Amerbach brothers had not possessed sufficiently refined judgment, or because those who assisted them, being unable to depart from Erasmus’s thread and conception, had handled the matter perfunctorily, as often happens in works carried out under another person’s name.

This edition, then, although it is not more extensive than the Erasmian recension and departs scarcely at all from its arrangement, is nevertheless far more accurate than that one, as even the remaining defenders of Erasmus are forced to admit. As soon as it was completed, it gained acceptance everywhere and was repeatedly reissued in various places: especially at Antwerp in 1578, revised by Victorius himself in a second edition; then at Paris the following year and again in 1602; and at Cologne in 1616. I do not intend to gather all the editions into a complete catalogue.

### 11. Enlarged by Additions from Several Learned Men

The second Paris edition of 1623 deserves brief consideration, since various observations and emendations by other learned men were added to it. They are as follows:

- Difficult passages in Jerome elucidated by Franciscus of Messana.
- The theological observations of Ferdinand Velosillo, bishop of Lucca, or scholastic-theological remarks upon the works of the holy Father.
- A dissertation of Frederic Morellus containing observations and emendations.
- A notable correction of a passage in Jerome by Laelius, bishop of Bagnoregio.
- The learned notes of Henri Gravius on the 102 letters and on the book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*.
- The notes of Fronto Ducaeus, which are said to deal especially and successfully with philological matters.
- Finally, the emendations and conjectures of Latinius Latinius, taken from his library.

Other editions reprinted at Paris and Venice within twenty years repeated these commentaries by learned men, which seemed in some measure to supply what was lacking in Victorius’s diligence. But the Frankfurt—or Leipzig—edition prepared about fifty years ago, which we mentioned above, appended to the Erasmian text his notes and scholia; Fridericus Ulricus Calixtus and Adamus Tribbechovius, who contributed their labor, divided the whole into twelve volumes.

### 12. Nevertheless, Especially False in the Hebrew Material

After the labors of so many learned men had been compared, if anyone should persuade himself that an edition of these works had at last been completed in every respect, he would be as far as possible from the truth. Even if everything else had been sound—and much of it is faulty—the chief benefit of reading Jerome, one that is readily accessible to the reader, was nevertheless intercepted by misguided editorial care.

I mean the reading of the Hebrew words by which Jerome’s entire work is marked at every third word: the ancient reading, expressed in Latin letters, in place of which the editors continually imposed the more recent Masoretic form.

It is well known how great the difference is between the two, and how great a loss to deeper learning and sacred doctrine results from this alteration. For it thereby became frequently impossible to understand either the holy Doctor’s judgment concerning various Hebrew words and passages of Scripture, or the agreement of the ancient Greek translations whose fragments he appends, or finally the Jewish traditions and opinions concerning the meaning of Hebrew words and the sense of scriptural passages.

The very learned Drusius and Morinus had long ago lamented this. The former writes in *Hebrew Questions*, book III, chapter 75:

> “The recent correctors have erred in Jerome in two ways: first, in writing with Hebrew characters what Jerome had written in Latin letters; and second, in changing the ancient reading and putting in its place a new one unknown to Jerome.”

The latter, in *Biblical Exercises*, p. 108, complains that Hebrew names written in Latin letters were removed with extraordinary thoughtlessness, and that Hebrew names written in Hebrew characters and supplied with rabbinic points were substituted in their place.

Isaac Vossius says the same in *On the Sibylline Oracles*, chapter 16, as do many others whose judgment is more sound.

### 13. The Edition of the Benedictine Fathers, or of Dom Jean Martianay

To remedy this evil above all, the celebrated Parisian Benedictine monks of the Congregation of Saint-Maur—whose industry in restoring the writings of the holy Fathers can never be praised enough—entrusted the task of revising and restoring Jerome’s works to two distinguished members of their community, Dom Jean Martianay and Dom Antoine Pouget.

To put the proposed new edition before the learned world, Martianay published in 1690 Jerome’s *Prodromus*. In it he restored the letter to Sunnia and Fretela in quite a few passages, but above all he reproduced from manuscripts the genuine ancient spelling of the Hebrew words. The first volume of the works appeared in 1693. It was a large volume entitled *Divine Library*, containing previously unpublished Latin translations of the Old and New Testaments derived by Jerome both from Hebrew and from Greek sources.

If one excepts the Psalter according to the Hebrew truth, this was indeed a new mass added to the complete collection of the works. I think, however, that the earlier editors did not consider this Latin version worth joining to Jerome’s works because in relatively few passages it differs from the Vulgate edition of the Bible, which is already in everyone’s hands. Much will have to be said about this matter, and about the work itself, in the preface to that volume; there is no need now to digress farther from our purpose.

Six years later, namely in 1699, the second volume appeared, prepared by Martianay alone, for it makes no mention of Pouget or anyone else. It contains the books of Hebrew names and places, as well as the Hebrew Questions on Genesis. To these are appended eighteen letters from those called *Critical Letters*, a commentary on Ecclesiastes, and two homilies of Origen on the *Song of Songs*, which Jerome translated into Latin. Finally, it contains an appendix comprising certain spurious writings, such as the questions on the books of Kings and Chronicles, commentaries on Job, and a summary of the Psalter, not to mention other minor writings and letters.

In the *Prolegomena*, the editor attempts to justify the new and plainly incongruous arrangement of the works on the grounds that, since Scripture occupies the first volume, it is preferable for the remaining writings of Jerome to correspond to it and to be referred back to that order. But is there anyone who does not know that those letters absurdly take the place of a commentary, and indeed that, with incredible confusion, the natural order of the letters and commentaries is reversed? But this too will be discussed elsewhere.

The third volume appeared after five years, in 1704. It contains commentaries on the sixteen major and minor prophets, as they are called, together with the letter on the Seraphim and the coal addressed to Damasus. It deserves special praise because it restored in their proper places, from manuscripts, many of the asterisks and obeli with which the holy Doctor had occasionally marked his work and which were missing from the other editions.

The fourth volume appeared two years later and is divided into two parts. One presents the commentaries on the New Testament, interspersed with nine critical letters; the other presents the remaining letters and treatises, in a supposedly chronological order, though often in no order at all. The fifth volume belongs to the same year. It contains the spurious works, apart from a few additions, and was copied in its entirety from the Erasmian text; with it the whole collection was completed.

### 14. The Principal Defects of That Edition

I shall not repeat the books which the heterodox Jean Le Clerc and the Catholic Richard Simon brought against it. Rather, I wish once again to say that praise and gratitude are due to the labors of Martianay, a most devout man sufficiently learned in Greek and Hebrew letters.

I would myself willingly consign even the errors for which I excuse him to silence, were I not compelled by the necessity of the recension I have undertaken, and by that perverse partisan zeal afflicting a certain class of people, who consider it sacrilegious in any way to tear down whatever has been committed to writing by one particular group.

“Abundant are the doors of the Muses” [Ἄφθονοι Μουσῶν θύραι].

The errors that beset Martianay’s edition, so far as they concern the undertaking as a whole, may be reduced to roughly the following points.

He copies the Erasmian edition almost continuously, neglecting—and often not even mentioning—the industry of Victorius, who is known to have corrected a great many errors that are once again imposed upon the reader without his knowledge.

He did not diligently collate manuscript copies throughout each work from beginning to end, but consulted them only in a few disputed passages. It is altogether impossible that he was never, or only very rarely, warned by the manuscripts—or that he himself warned his readers—of the many false readings that deform the older editions. Yet he encountered so few variants that more of them have come before us in a small booklet than he records as rejected by himself in some very large volume. I mean variants whose selection must be left to the reader’s judgment, not manifest scribal errors.

One also rarely finds difficult passages explained. Indeed, apart from the summaries of the letters composed by Erasmus, the works are almost entirely deprived of notes and prefaces intended to shed light upon them.

Conversely, the annotations themselves—which, except for the critical letters and the two lexicons of names and places, he added to the other books in very small and meager number—are for the most part occupied with false judgments, and often with personal controversies, so to speak, in which he takes the opportunity to sneer at very learned men; but he scarcely interprets Jerome’s text at all.

Finally, there is the perverse order, and the false order wherever he took chronology into account, along with many other matters of the same kind which we conceal in order to avoid incurring hostility.

## PART TWO

### In Which, Having Explained the Character of Jerome’s Works, We Discuss Those That Have Perished or Are Thought to Have Perished

### 15. Two Kinds of Jerome’s Works

The works of so great a Father, reprinted by so many presses and revised in so many editions, are shown even by this simple account to require another restoration, so that they may be returned to their original and native splendor.

Since I have earnestly resolved to undertake this labor, I must now prepare the way for my purpose, so that from the outset it may be placed before the reader’s eyes whose memory of the Father must be recalled, and so that his teaching may be more easily understood and more conveniently retained.

First, then, the character and nature of these writings must be explained; afterward, some knowledge must also be supplied concerning those that no longer exist. Since we are not merely following the traces of the old editions, but are bringing many absent works together into a single body, we shall embrace, both by displaying the monuments themselves and by reporting what has been lost, something like the whole circle of Jerome’s works.

They fall, as it were, into two classes or kinds. Some he composed from his own understanding and in the Latin language; others he gave to Latin-speaking people by translating from other authors, chiefly Greek ones.

To give a few examples, such works include the immense labor of interpreting Scripture: the Old and New Testaments, of which he rendered one according to the Greek text and translated the other according to the Hebrew. Then there are the noblest portions of Origen’s works, nearly seventy homilies, as his enemy Rufinus alleges; the book of Hebrew names; another book, *On First Principles* (περὶ Ἀρχῶν), whose Latin translation, together with the Greek exemplar itself, the passage of time has denied us; and many other excerpts from the products of that intellect in which he took especial delight, ἀποσπασμάτια (“extracts” or “fragments”).

From Didymus also he translated into Latin the book *On the Holy Spirit*, whose original the passage of many years has not preserved. From Theophilus of Alexandria he translated the Paschal writings, especially that outstanding synodical letter against Origen which we have ourselves been the first to discover, as well as several other letters and books against John Chrysostom.

From Eusebius of Caesarea he likewise translated the *Chronicle* of universal history—that treasure, by far the most illuminating account of all preceding ages and supremely necessary to sacred as well as secular studies. He also translated the book of the places of divine Scripture and their locations and distances, a distinguished portion of ancient geography, together with many other works of the same kind excerpted from highly approved authors, such as Epiphanius, Theodore, Gregory of Nazianzus, and Apollinarius, whose more outstanding doctrines he inserted into his own commentaries.

It is entirely true that, among Greek writers distinguished for eloquence and learning, no one was unknown to Jerome. Thus, if his adversaries noted or charged him with some fault in his books, he often excused himself by this one argument: that he had spoken according to the judgment of the Greek interpreters, and that he was ready to acknowledge and apologize for it as his own if they did not find it in their commentaries.

### 16. The Second Kind

The writings which he himself produced from his own intellect, and which I prefer to call original works, deal for the most part with the interpretation of sacred Scripture.

Among the works that survive, the first place belongs to the Questions on Genesis, filled with Hebrew traditions and opinions. Closely following them in subject are the commentaries on Ecclesiastes and on the prophets.

There are also the remarkable books on Matthew, which he produced for the most part αὐτοσχεδιασίᾳ (“improvisationally”), and those which he composed on four of Paul’s Epistles with such varied and manifold learning.

Other works were written either to defend the Christian cause against heretics or to advance it among the faithful. The former attack Helvidius, Jovinianus, Vigilantius, and such groups as the Luciferian and Pelagian sects. The latter, by narrating the deeds of the holiest monks, offer examples of piety, or by means of letters invite their readers to order their lives rightly.

This is, in general, an overview of Jerome’s works, set out in much the same way as someone might measure the immense spaces of the heavens and the locations of the lands on a small chart.

One or two points about each kind of writing should be noted. The Greek works which he undertook to explain in Latin were among those that held first place among the most learned Fathers. When he gave them to Roman ears, he made excellent Latin works out of good Greek ones. In this matter, his greatest praise seems to me to be that, thanks to his industry, we enjoy the writings of several men of outstanding distinction whose ancient Greek originals have perished through the violence of time.

As for the original works, they have received such universal approval from successive ages and from all learned men that, among the immense choir of the Latin Fathers, Jerome was granted by the judgment of the Church—than which no judgment is more genuine or secure—the prerogative of being called the Doctor par excellence.

### 17. Concerning the Works That No Longer Exist, and First the Emendation of Scripture from the Greek

Some account must also be given of the works that no longer exist, so that they may nevertheless be identified. I divide them once again into two classes: the first comprising those that certainly perished, the second those concerning which it is permissible to doubt whether they ever existed.

I say nothing about the spurious works, of which there are far too many; their examination belongs to the preface of the final volume, to which they are being assigned.

Here the first work to present itself, on account of its importance, is the labor he expended in correcting from the Greek the ancient Latin translation of the LXX.

“I remember,” he says near the end of the preface to the book of Chronicles, “that I once gave our people the edition of the Seventy Translators corrected from the Greek.”

And in Letter 71 to Lucinus:

> “I do not doubt that you possess the edition of the Seventy Translators, and many years ago I carefully corrected it and delivered it to students.”

What this correction was like, and how it was carried out, we learn from Letter 112 in our recension, addressed to Augustine, where he explains why it was marked with asterisks and obeli.

Examples of this work are also supplied by the commentaries on Ecclesiastes and especially on the major and minor prophets, as they are called. In them he often compares the Latin version he had revised with the version he later prepared according to the Hebrew exemplar.

Moreover, two complete books of this work survive—Job and the Psalter—which we shall place after Martianay in the second part of the *Divine Library*. They will provide sufficient evidence, so that there is no need to digress farther, concerning what use he made of those signs.

The remaining books perished long ago. For while Jerome himself was still alive, he complains that he had lost most of his earlier labor through the fraud of a certain person. It may also easily have happened, as often happens elsewhere, that the far more accurate Latin version according to the Hebrew truth, which subsequently prevailed, gradually displaced that earlier correction, encumbered as it was by the difficulties associated with the signs.

It is therefore surprising that Cassiodorus reports in *Divine Institutes*, chapter 13, that he had preserved the whole work in the *Armarium*:

> “The third division is contained, among the others, in a larger codex written in clearer letters. It has ninety-five gatherings, and contains the translation of the Old Testament by the Seventy Interpreters in forty-four books. To these are joined the twenty-six books of the New Testament, making seventy books in all . . . This text, altered by the translations of many persons, was corrected through the diligent care of Father Jerome and left in an ordered form.”

It is fortunate that we learn from this that the work could have been preserved intact down to that age through the care of so diligent a scholar—provided we are willing to place enough confidence in the report that the codex was not misidentified.

### 18. The Gospel According to the Hebrews

The Gospel according to the Hebrews likewise suffered an equally adverse fate long ago. It was written in the Chaldaic language but in Hebrew letters. When the holy Doctor was granted permission to copy it from the Nazarenes living in the Syrian city of Beroea, he translated it into Greek and Latin, as he himself states most clearly both in chapter 2 of *On Illustrious Men* and in his Commentary on Matthew, book XII, chapter 13.

I am not arguing here whether he believed it to be the authentic Gospel of Matthew, which he says had been preserved in the Caesarean library down to his own time—as may be suspected from other statements of his—or whether, as Bede teaches at the beginning of his Commentary on Luke, he understood the Gospel according to the Hebrews to be one thing and the Gospel according to the Apostles another.

What surprises me more is why, or with what purpose, he translated the book from the Chaldaic language into Greek, since a Greek translation of it already existed, a fact which Jerome himself by no means denies when, speaking of Origen—whom I have no doubt read it only in Greek—he says that Origen repeatedly used testimonies from that book.

Nevertheless, since the matter itself cannot be doubted, both on the testimony of the author himself and with the added support of writers of a later age, such as the venerable Bede and Freculphus, I would have it understood in this way: Jerome undertook the work not in order to publish whatever it was that he had produced, but to test through Greek how far he had advanced in Chaldaic, and then to demonstrate in Latin how much Greek he knew.

In fact, although elsewhere, and especially in the catalogue of his works, he diligently calls attention to this labor, when he reaches the catalogue’s final chapter, where he gives a particular enumeration of his writings, he plainly conceals it.

Nevertheless, he had completed it approximately two years earlier, or around the year 390, as may be inferred from the recent chronological indication he uses.

A few small fragments of the Latin translation have been preserved by Jerome himself in other books. One such fragment occurs in his Commentary on Matthew 7:6, spoken in the person of the Savior:

> “Just now my mother, the Holy Spirit, took me by one of my hairs.”

Another occurs in the Commentary on Isaiah 11:2:

> “But when the Lord had ascended from the water, the fountain of the whole Holy Spirit descended and rested upon him, and said to him: ‘My son, in all the prophets I was waiting for you to come, so that I might rest in you. For you are my rest; you are my firstborn son, who reigns forever.’”

Likewise, in book 3 against the Pelagians, chapter 1:

> “Behold, the mother of the Lord and his brothers were saying to him: ‘John the Baptist baptizes for the remission of sins. Let us go and be baptized by him.’ But he said to them: ‘What sin have I committed, that I should go and be baptized by him? Unless perhaps this very statement I have made is ignorance.’”

And in the same volume:

> “‘If your brother has sinned in word,’ he says, ‘and has satisfied you, receive him seven times a day.’ His disciple Simon said to him: ‘Seven times a day?’ The Lord answered and said to him: ‘I also say to you, seventy times seven.’”

And in book 2 on Matthew, at Matthew 12:13, concerning the man who had a withered hand, who is recorded in that Gospel as having been a mason:

> “I was a mason, earning my living with my hands. I beg you, Jesus, to restore my health, lest I shamefully beg for food.”

Finally, there is this very brief passage in the Commentary on Ephesians 5:4, spoken by the Lord to his disciples:

> “‘And never be joyful,’ he says, ‘except when you see your brother in charity.’”

We have brought all these passages together so that, since the work itself has perished through the antiquity of time, we would not deprive the reader of some small specimen—whatever its worth—of Jerome’s labor.

### 19. What Theodore of Mopsuestia Falsely Alleged about That Translation

It must not be omitted that Theodore of Mopsuestia, whose allegation Photius reports in codex 177, fabricated a slander concerning this book.

When this heretic wished to attack the holy Doctor’s dialogues against the Pelagians, he produced a volume divided into five books under the title *Against Those Who Assert That Human Beings Sin by Nature, Not by Will*.

In it he accuses Jerome—whom he calls Aram or Aramus, not as a name or surname, as Photius hesitates to interpret it, but in order to turn it into an insult—of committing the chief offense of fabricating a fifth Gospel and pretending that he had found it in the libraries of Eusebius of Palestine.

Jerome had said that this Gospel according to the Hebrews was preserved at that time in the Caesarean library, both elsewhere and especially near the beginning of the third book of the dialogues against the Pelagians. The bishop of Mopsuestia partly turns this into a reproach and partly accuses him of lying.

In reality, Theodore acts wrongly and most calumniously. It is perfectly clear that the holy Doctor did not lie, and the examples of the ancient Fathers—Papias and Hegesippus as cited by Eusebius, as well as Clement of Alexandria, Origen, and others—demonstrate that, if testimonies were repeatedly produced from that history, this could be done not to establish its authority but to affirm the antiquity of an ecclesiastical opinion. The translation itself therefore deserves praise, not blame.

Accordingly, Julian, a bishop cut from the same Pelagian cloth as Theodore, is rightly reproved by Augustine in book 4, chapter 87, of the *Unfinished Work*, because he treated that labor as a crime committed by Jerome.

But I do not at all see by what right my most learned countryman Norisius, in *Pelagian History*, book 1, chapter 9, while transferring to Julian the charge of lying and reckless audacity, denies that Jerome undertook this translation. For although Jerome says nothing in that dialogue—which alone the Pelagians strained every nerve to attack—about the labor he had begun, the testimonies cited above establish the matter so certainly and firmly that no room for doubt remains.

### 20. A Specimen of the Commentary on Obadiah

In third place comes the specimen of a commentary on Obadiah. What it was, what its value was, and at what age it was composed, may be learned from Jerome himself, when he unraveled this web. Returning once more to his old tracks, correcting where possible the crooked strokes of the letters, or at least pleading for pardon on the grounds of his age, he prefaced it to Pammachius as follows:

> “I ought to receive pardon because, in my youth, provoked by ardor and enthusiasm for the Scriptures, I interpreted the prophet Obadiah allegorically, although I did not know his history. My spirit burned for mystical knowledge; and because I had read that all things are possible for believers, I did not know that spiritual gifts are diverse. I knew the literature of the world, and for that reason thought that I could read a sealed book.”

After inserting other excuses of this kind, he continues:

> “I hoped that what I had written would remain hidden, and I had devoted the first rash work of my little talent to the flames, when suddenly a copy was brought from Italy by a certain young man who was as many years old as I had once been when I wrote it, and who praised my little work. I confess that I was amazed: however badly someone may write, he finds a reader like himself. He praised it; I was ashamed. He carried its mystical meanings to heaven, as it were; I, with lowered head, was prevented from confessing my shame. What, then? Shall we condemn the things in which we played as children? Certainly not. For we know that both gold and goats’ hair are offered alike in the tabernacle of God. We read in the Gospel that the two mites of the poor widow were approved above the wealth of the rich. Then we gave what we had, and now, if indeed we have produced anything, we return to the Lord what belongs to him. By his grace I am what I am. Nor do I deny that for these thirty years I have labored and sweated in his work.”

I have copied this passage at somewhat greater length because from it we learn what judgment may be formed concerning that work.

From this it may be inferred that he seems to indicate that he undertook the same labor again after thirty years, and that this second effort belongs to the year 396. The earlier work must therefore be assigned, by calculation, to the year 366 or thereabouts, when he had not yet reached his thirtieth year. For he says that he had not yet attained the age of a mature man or the measure of Christ.

From this one may reasonably conclude that he wrote these words around the year 396. See the preface itself to the end.

It happened, however, according to his own account, that a later age entirely destroyed the work he had committed to the flames. No fragment of it has appeared, nor is it mentioned by any other ancient writer.

Yet the possibility that it may lie hidden somewhere is suggested by the heading of a very ancient manuscript in the Gotha library, no. 34, in which, after the Commentaries on Jeremiah, a *Treatise on Obadiah* is contained. The commentary on that prophet which survives is not properly designated by this title.

Learned men who pore over those treasures either know, or can discover, the truth of the matter. If that work truly is the one in question, although it should not be assigned a number other than the one given to it by the author himself—who did not include it in the catalogue among the enumeration of his writings—we nevertheless judge that, if it exists anywhere, we may profitably use it and should not, without injustice, deprive the public of it.

### 21. Seven Treatises on the Psalms

We must now speak of the commentaries on the Psalms.

There is an old and stale controversy, debated in the discussions of many more recent interpreters ever since Erasmus, whether the holy Doctor composed commentaries on all the Psalms or only on certain ones mentioned in his writings.

Certainly, it is not the place or purpose here to prove the work entitled *Summary of the Psalms* to be of notorious spuriousness, since this discussion concerns only genuine works that have perished.

Such works include the seven treatises on Psalms 10 through 16, by which words the author himself lists them in the catalogue of his works. Not even a fragment of these survives, nor any trace—unless, as most learned men have thought, they are concealed in the work just mentioned, the *Summary*, after much has been sewn into it and other material interpolated.

Meanwhile, so that something may be determined concerning their character, learned men—and Tillemont above all—observe that these seven works should be understood not as an original production of Jerome, but as excerpts from Origen’s work of homilies on the entire Psalter, which Jerome translated and explained in Latin.

There are two arguments for this assertion. First, in the catalogue he immediately places them after the thirty-nine homilies on Luke, which he certainly and unquestionably expressed in Latin words from Origen. Second, he calls them “treatises,” the term by which the ancients designated homilies addressed to the people. But Jerome, who held neither the office of bishop nor that of a presbyter serving as a κατηχητής (“catechist”), composed no discourses of that kind.

## 22. Whether They Were Rendered into Latin from Origen

If I were to reply to these points, I might seem intent on overturning a moderately well-established conclusion; nevertheless, a reply is necessary so that the matter may become clearer. First, the argument based on proximity in the recension does not seem to me to deserve so much weight. For if whatever is appended immediately after a work cited under someone’s name belongs to that person, even though the author’s name is nowhere added, why should we not say that Origen was the author of the work likewise appended after these treatises, and that Jerome was its translator—namely, the Life of Malchus? Moreover, the name *treatise* (*tractatus*) is not so peculiar to the homiletic mode of discourse that, according to the usage of the ancient Fathers, it could not often be transferred to other writings. Indeed, in Jerome himself one finds it used for the explanation of some particular passage of Scripture: a briefer exposition, certainly, but separately worked out in the manner of a commentary.

Certainly, the letter or little book on the Seraphim and the coal which he wrote to Damasus was translated neither from Origen nor from any other Greek writer. Indeed, he argues against Origen’s very opinion, and plainly contains nothing that resembles a homily; yet at the beginning of his *Commentary on Isaiah*, chapter 6, he calls it a brief and hastily composed *treatise*. Therefore, to leave aside other examples, I think that at first the name did not signify sermons, as learned men commonly suppose, but rather an exposition, as I have said, of some passage of Scripture. Then, since in sacred addresses some matter from Scripture would continually have to be discussed, the name was also extended to those addresses in a broader sense.

The word *tractator* likewise, according to the usage of the more ancient ecclesiastical writers, properly designates those who excelled in knowledge of the Scriptures and devoted their labor to explaining them—those whom the Greeks call *ἐξηγηταὶ τοῦ λόγου*, “interpreters of the Word of God.” Jerome himself, in Letter 82 to Theophilus, section 7, contrasts *tractatores* with the canonical and God-inspired (*θεοπνεύστοις*) Authors, and does not deny that he himself is a *tractator*. Thus we restore the passage from the manuscripts [Col. XXV]:

> “Am I introducing Origen into the crowd, or associating myself with the other *tractatores*? I know that the apostles are one thing, and the *tractatores* another.”

He confirms something of this sort about himself in many other passages. But how, according to the opinion of his opponents, could he call himself a *tractator* if he had never composed treatises, or if, by the circumstances of his life, he had not been permitted to compose them?

Add to this the argument from Rufinus’s silence. Jerome never translated anything from Origen—*Adamantius*—which Rufinus does not continually attack and examine in his books of invective. It is well known with what subtlety he probes and drags into disrepute the prefaces to the homilies on Luke, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and the Song of Songs—works of Origen which, as they say, the holy Doctor expounded in Latin from beginning to end. Nor does he spare the fragments of other statements which were transferred from there, especially into the *Commentaries on the Epistle to the Ephesians* and on *Ecclesiastes*. I say nothing of the private letters themselves, in which, if any mention of Origenist doctrine—or even of Origen’s name—lies hidden, he diligently investigates, brings it forth, and tears it to pieces.

How, then, does Rufinus entirely pass over seven complete treatises, in whose preface Jerome could not fail to praise the genius of Adamantius, with whom he was extraordinarily delighted, and to offer reasons for his translation? And this in such lengthy and *διασυρτικοί*—ridiculing or sarcastic—discussions, in which he set himself almost one task: by arguments gathered from every quarter, to ensure that nothing favorable to Origen in any of our holy Doctor’s writings should pass unchallenged?

These remarks are offered, nevertheless, merely to cast doubt upon the commonly accepted opinion, so that the nature of the work may be investigated; they are not advanced as established certainties. We recognize the weakness of a negative argument, and someone might reply that Rufinus says in the preface which he prefixed to the books *Περὶ ἀρχῶν* (*On First Principles*) that more than seventy of Origen’s homiletic booklets were translated into Latin by Jerome. That number would be entirely accounted for if the treatises on the Psalms were included; if they are excluded, one scarcely reaches seventy.

But the very testimony in question shows how much Rufinus’s troublesome reliability must be doubted. Immediately afterward he speaks of volumes on the Apostle rendered into Latin by the same Jerome—something Jerome certainly did not do, as we shall show below in its proper place. It therefore seems preferable to establish something from Rufinus’s concealment than to argue from his calumny.

## 23. Exposition of Psalm 93

Besides those seven treatises, the fact that Jerome also expounded Psalm 93 is attested by Augustine, a most authoritative witness beyond all objection, in his *Memorandum to Fortunatianus*, section 14. The passage is as follows:

> “When that man”—Jerome—“most learned in the Scriptures, was expounding the Psalm in which it is said, ‘Understand, therefore, you who are foolish among the people, and you who are senseless, become wise at last: he who planted the ear, will he not hear? Or he who formed the eye, does he not observe?’ among other things he said:
>
> “‘This passage is directed especially against those who are anthropomorphites, who say that God has what we also have. For example, God is said to have eyes because “the eyes of the Lord look upon all things”; “the hand of the Lord makes all things.” And Adam, it says, heard the sound of the feet of the Lord walking in Paradise. They hear these things literally, and refer human weaknesses to God’s majesty.
>
> “‘But I say that God is entirely eye, entirely hand, entirely foot. He is entirely eye because he sees everything; entirely hand because he accomplishes everything; entirely foot because he is everywhere.
>
> “‘Therefore consider what he says: “He who planted the ear, will he not hear? Or he who formed the eyes, does he not observe?” He did not say, “He who planted the ear therefore does not himself have an ear”; he did not say, “therefore he himself does not have eyes.” What did he say? “He who planted the ear, will he not hear? He who formed the eyes, does he not observe?” He removed the bodily members and granted their functions.’”

This same passage, word for word, is found in the *Breviary* attributed to Jerome for the whole Psalter. Accordingly, it might seem that we do not properly need to list this exposition among the lost works. But since it is entirely clear that that work is not a product of Jerome, but of a diligent man who gathered various people’s statements and commentaries into one collection and added much of his own, and since it is also readily apparent that almost all the commentary on this Psalm did not proceed from the holy Doctor’s pen, we have no doubt that the passage quoted was extracted from another lost work.

What that work may have been, however, is not easy to determine. For the holy Father never states that he completed *Commentaries on the Psalms*. Indeed, when, around the year 410, he was explaining Isaiah, chapter 63, he promises that, if life should accompany him and the Lord should grant it, he would explain those two Psalms entitled *For the Winepresses*, Psalm 8 and Psalm 83. And near the end of his life, while commenting on Jeremiah—a labor interrupted by death—he says, concerning chapter 2, that in its proper place he will discuss more fully the Gates mentioned in Psalm 23.

From this it is easily gathered that he did intend to compose the proposed work, but, first interrupted by other causes and then cut off by death itself, was unable to complete it. Nor do we include among *Commentaries on the Psalms*, as others do, those three letters: one on Psalm 44 to Principia, another on Psalm 89 to Cyprian, and finally one on Psalm 126 to Marcella. We exclude them for much the same reasons that neither the letter to Hedibia, nor that to Algasia, nor finally the letter to Damasus concerning the frugal and the luxurious sons can be regarded as any part of a commentary on the Apostle or on Matthew.

I would therefore also maintain that the fragment on Psalm 93 which we quoted from Augustine was taken from some letter that has perished—a letter which Jerome wrote against the Egyptian monks who, at that time, had attempted to revive the heresy of the anthropomorphites. This is known from Socrates, *Ecclesiastical History*, book 6, chapter 7. We too have touched on the matter in part, when we said that, while Theophilus governed the Church of Alexandria, this question was debated there in many controversies: whether God was corporeal and possessed a human form, or incorporeal. When Theophilus defended the latter opinion, he was brought into the gravest danger to his life by the faction of those same monks.

## 24. Shorter Commentaries on the Psalms

There are still other works to be added to the lost writings: *Commentarioli*—“shorter commentaries”—on the Psalms, as Jerome himself calls them more than once in Book 1 of his *Apology against Rufinus*. For when he was interpreting Psalm 2, in place of the Latin reading *Apprehendite disciplinam*—“Embrace instruction”—he had explained, from the ambiguity of the Hebrew language, *Adorate Filium*—“Worship the Son.” Rufinus dragged this into a slanderous accusation, as though it harmed the faith of the Church. Jerome, in response, first excuses himself learnedly, then says:

> “What have I done wrong if I have rendered an ambiguous word by a different interpretation?
