And when, in the shorter commentaries, where there is freedom to discuss matters, I had said, ‘Worship the Son,’ lest I should seem a violent translator in the text itself and give occasion for Jewish calumny, I said, ‘Worship purely,’ or ‘Worship the Chosen One’!”

Who could doubt, on the strength of this exceptionally clear testimony, that Jerome worked out some shorter commentaries on at least certain Psalms, and that these differed considerably from the treatises? Nevertheless, if one examines the chronology, one encounters extremely serious difficulties and perplexities.

Certainly he must have composed these commentaries before he produced the Latin Psalter from the Hebrew text. Rufinus draws the occasion for his contradiction from this fact, and Jerome does not deny it in the passage cited:

> “And again, when translating the whole Psalter into the Roman idiom, as though forgetful of my earlier exposition, I wrote, ‘Worship purely’—something plainly contrary to it.”

He prepared this version of the Psalter before the year 392, that is, before the book *On Illustrious Men* and the catalogue of his works. This is also established from chapter 134, concerning Sophronius, who reissued it in Greek.

For what reason, then, does Jerome not acknowledge these *Commentarioli* in his catalogue of works, when he carefully records even much shorter books, as one must believe, and his letters as well? The reason is surely the one we indicated above: he had resolved to write on all the Psalms in their entirety, but at that time had scarcely touched upon some portion of them, and perhaps not in order, but at will or according to the occasion that supplied material for discussion. He therefore does not mention an unfinished work in his catalogue, intending to account for it if he completed what he had planned.

## 25. Translation of the Book *Περὶ ἀρχῶν*

Let us continue with the remaining works. We encounter the notable Latin version of the Origenist book *Περὶ Ἀρχῶν*, that is, *On First Principles*. As everyone knows, Origen had intended in that book to set forth the precepts of the Christian religion and of true philosophy. In reality, however, he enveloped true doctrines in many difficulties and mixed in numerous errors and absurdities.

Rufinus, daring to present this book to Latin ears, and thinking himself permitted to do anything lest the reader be offended by blasphemies and other errors of *ψευδώνυμος γνῶσις*—“falsely named knowledge”—offers it in Latin after inserting and removing whatever he wished, and expounding it with the most deplorable lack of fidelity.

Jerome, understanding clearly that this unfaithfulness threatened Christian faith and piety with many dangers, prepared a new translation without altering anything, so that readers might more easily guard themselves against the errors, which were concealed by no devices and covered by no disguise of false translation, but left exposed in the open.

Small but notable fragments of this work survive in Letter 124 in our recension, fragments which more clearly reveal the poisonous elements of Origenist doctrine. We have distinguished them from Jerome’s own text so that they may be more easily recognized, and have examined them in various places in the notes.

The entire book, like the Greek original, was long ago destroyed through the misguided zeal of men, whereas the Rufinian version—which ought rather to be called a foul interpolation—has survived to the present age. For ecclesiastics who, from those times onward, raged against Origen’s teaching with such zeal strove above all to destroy that book and abolish it by every means, by means of synodal and episcopal anathemas. They considered it unlawful to copy one who reported it faithfully, since it was filled with the same errors.

## 26. Translation of the Book against Saint John Chrysostom

Something similar happened with the book of invectives, as it is called, against Saint John Chrysostom. Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, a man of unrestrained temper, wrote it in Greek and persuaded Jerome to render it into Latin.

Very few fragments of it survive, and these once again contain nothing but sheer insults and reproaches against that most holy prelate—material more likely to win envy for its most holy translator among deeply religious people than praise.

The order of our discussion does not allow us to digress into Jerome’s defense; the history of those times sufficiently clears him. When Chrysostom had fallen under the gravest suspicion of Origenism, he was already commonly regarded as a heretic, was deprived of office by the votes of the bishops, and was driven into exile.

Moreover, it is by no means established that Jerome was aware of Theophilus’s intentions, contrary to what Huet and other learned men have inferred from the false superscription of Letter 113. Accordingly, because those very fragments seemed likely to contribute no small light to the Origenist controversy and its history, we append them to Letter 114 in our recension—the letter which Jerome joined to his translation in order to avoid incurring odium—after excerpting them from *Facundus of Hermiane*, book 6, at the end of the final chapter.

If anyone finds this addition less acceptable, I would ask him to consider that, just as in the workshops of goldsmiths even the refuse is valuable, so among the golden remains of the great Jerome it is of the greatest importance to investigate in what spirit even those things were written which may appear otherwise.

There were, moreover, many other matters in that work which, as the holy translator says, would contribute to the benefit of all the churches. From it one could learn with what reverence holy things ought to be received and how one should serve the ministry of Christ’s altar; and that sacred chalices, holy veils, and the other things pertaining to the worship of the Lord’s Passion should not be regarded as empty and devoid of sense, without sanctity, but should be venerated with the same majesty as his Body and Blood, because of their participation in the Body and Blood of the Lord.

These points, to be sure, served as a pretext for disparagement of a deeply religious man whose faith and piety, as we have said, were nevertheless suffering under suspicion of Origenism at that time. But once his integrity had finally been recognized, a later age, unwilling to admit any stain upon him, consigned the book to oblivion and easily allowed it to perish completely.

## 27. Several Lost Letters

Among the number of Jerome’s works upon which the harshness of time inflicted the greatest damage, his letters suffered injury above all. Some of them disappeared so completely that at times it is scarcely possible to discover that they had ever been written. We are therefore compiling a catalogue of them rather than a full account, so that, if anyone should someday extract one from the hiding places of libraries, it may at least be identified from its superscription.

Accordingly, preserving as far as possible the order of the times in which they were sent, the first that appear are the letters to his maternal aunt Castorina. He himself mentions them again after the year had passed, in the one letter to her that survives. In them he earnestly begged her to keep with her the peace which the Lord had left, after laying aside an old resentment, although we do not know its causes.

The ten letters which he wrote at approximately the same time—or while preparing to undertake his solitary life—to Antony, a monk of Emona—this was formerly a town near his native place—must have had much the same purpose. “I have sent,” he says in Letter 12 to the same man, “if I am not mistaken, ten letters full both of duty and of entreaty.”

I do not know whether the letters which he says he wrote to the virgins of the same place, or to the Aemonenses—over whom Antony could easily have presided—should be counted among the same group. He laments that he had received no return from them:

> “You have not performed for me even the smallest service, although I have so often paid you the tribute of my attention.”

Certainly, if they had escaped the violence of time, we could no doubt recover from them excellent examples for restoring and renewing peace and friendship.

He also sent a letter to his teacher Didymus, whom he had not long before heard teaching in the Alexandrian school; that letter is not extant. His rivals repeatedly paraded it invidiously, because it had been addressed to a man, learned though he was, who was strongly devoted to Origen’s doctrine. The holy Doctor clears himself of this charge in Letter 84 to Pammachius and Oceanus in these words:

> “Someone dares to produce my letter to Didymus, as though it had been addressed to a teacher. What a great crime for a pupil, if I called a learned and elderly man my teacher! And yet I wish to see the letter itself, which has been kept for so long as material for calumny. It contains nothing beyond honor and a greeting.”

The loss of a letter containing nothing more than a customary courtesy might seem less painful. Yet I would read no letter with greater pleasure if it survived.

Rufinus said that he possessed another letter of some sort in which Jerome reproached Saint Ambrose. When Jerome was translating into Latin the forty homilies of Origen on Luke, he said in the preface that a certain expositor—whose name he conceals—played with words and nodded off over his thoughts in a similar work.

Rufinus claims in the second book of his *Invectives* that these remarks were directed against Ambrose, bishop of blessed memory:

> “He”—Jerome—“knows that I possess a letter of his in which, while excusing this very thing in others, he turns the suspicion against that man”—Ambrose.

“But because that letter also contains certain more private matters, which for the present I do not wish to publish before the proper time, I shall establish the point from other similar evidence.”

Indeed, if he had produced it, we would have been grateful; but I believe it was more in his interest to suppress it in silence in order to construct his calumny.

Augustine himself praises the earlier letter to Augustine—one that he presented as a complete letter, not among the accepted letters but under the heading of a greeting, around the year 397—in his Letter to Jerome, Letter 67 in our recension. He indicates its contents clearly enough, although he regrets that it was much shorter than he would have wished to receive from such a man, from whom, however occupied he might be, no discourse is ever too long.

Some maintain that other letters exchanged between the two men have perished, but I think they are mistaken because they have not properly arranged or considered the chronology in which the individual letters were written. In any case, several letters to Theophilus seem not to have survived, as is evident from their sequence.

To Paulinus, I think, only one letter is indicated: in Letter 85 he complains that Jerome sends him little letters that are short and unadorned. Yet the surviving Letters 53 and 58 can in no way be called either short or unadorned. One of them discusses the books of Scripture at great length; the other sets forth a rule for the establishment of a most holy life and invites him to the study of the divine writings by the examples of the ancient Fathers.

We must therefore suppose that another letter is meant—one in which Paulinus complains about his friend and our Jerome begs forgiveness for his fault.

It is also extremely likely that Jerome joined a letter to Pammachius and Marcella when he sent them a Latin explanation of Theophilus’s first Paschal letter of the year 401. For in the preface to the Paschal letter of the following year, likewise addressed to them, he says:

> “Again I enrich you with merchandise from the East.”

And below:

> “Receive this year also both a Greek and a Latin letter.”

If that earlier letter survived, I have no doubt that we could understand the beginnings of the Origenist controversy and the factions which arose from it.

Only one letter to Marcellinus and Anapsychia survives in our recension, Letter 126. From it, however, it is perfectly clear that Jerome had written several others to them, since at the very beginning he says:

> “I do not regret the boldness with which, while you remained silent, I repeatedly thrust my letters upon you in order to deserve a reply.”

By a similar argument, from the three letters of Pope Innocent which we first transferred into the catalogue of Jerome’s works, we have no doubt that several others were sent to Innocent himself and to Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, concerning the violence of the Pelagians and the killings inflicted upon Jerome and his companions—letters sent in Jerome’s own name and in the names of Eustochium and the younger Paula.

Their principal subject must have been the plundering and burning of the monastery. Jerome first disclosed these events to Aurelius, whom he used as an intercessor with the pontiff, and through whose agency the letters were carried back and forth.

He also made known to Innocent that Aurelius had conceived the desire to visit him and consult him in person. Yet he lamented with such restraint the very grave evils inflicted upon his own people by the agents of the heretics, as well as the still worse things he feared for himself, that although he knew perfectly well who had caused the persecution, he preferred to conceal the persecutor entirely rather than appear to seek retaliation against him.

Finally, we understand from Letter 124 to Augustine that a letter to Firmus had been written, although the Ambrosian manuscript makes no mention of it.

These, then, are Jerome’s letters—or rather, his writings in general—the certain loss of which greatly diminishes the sum of the very great benefit that could have been gained from reading the holy Father.

[Col. XXXI]

## 28. Hebrew Questions on the Old Testament

It remains for us now to discuss those works which, according to the received judgment of learned men, are considered lost, but which I by no means believe were ever completed.

The first that appear are the *Hebrew Questions*. Apart from Genesis, for which the sole surviving book remains, Jerome himself mentions them not only once or twice but in fully nineteen passages, and in words that are, as can be seen, exceptionally clear, in the book which he translated from Eusebius, *On the Topographical Questions of Scripture*.

Learned men therefore commonly lament their loss; Martianay above all, whenever mention of them occurs, magnifies the irreparable damage to the Church and to scholarship caused by their disappearance.

Tillemont still remains uncertain, and would like the question examined with the utmost care: whether what is cited as having been explained concerning the other books of Scripture can be found in the surviving work on Genesis. If each item should be found there, he thinks that the one book must be indicated throughout.

But first, Jerome calls the books by a plural name; and he praises them in Numbers, Deuteronomy, Judges, and especially Kings, as well as in the Prophets themselves. Moreover—and this is the heart of the matter—the passages are not found in the commentary on Genesis. Thus even the distinguished scholar’s opinion must be that they have perished.

I, however, reach a different conclusion. I do not deny that Jerome had prepared the warp and woof of that work, and perhaps even arranged some material in notebooks, which he could easily have completed if he had possessed sufficient leisure. In the preface he himself says:

> “I have arranged to write books of Hebrew Questions on the whole of Holy Scripture.”

Not much later, however, in another preface—that of the homilies on Luke addressed to Paula and Eustochium—he says:

> “I have set aside for a little while the books of Hebrew Questions, so that I might dictate these whatever they may be, according to your wishes.”

Nor will I deny that he expounded the remaining books of Scripture to Paula and Eustochium, at least orally. This is established by his own testimony in the *Commentary on the Epistle to Titus*, chapter 2:

> “In the law of Moses, thieves are sometimes compelled to repay sevenfold, sometimes fourfold; at times the thief himself is executed, at times he is sold on account of the theft. I remember having recently explained these matters to you in Leviticus.”

But for what reason, then, should he have completed only the book explaining Genesis and published no other? I shall demonstrate this by a simple explanation.

At the time when the holy Doctor was preparing the *Hebrew Questions*, he had also undertaken to translate from Eusebius the book *On Hebrew Places*, because of a certain correspondence between the work and his studies; indeed, one work interrupted the other.

This is made perfectly clear in the preface to the other book, entitled *On Hebrew Names*. He says:

> “I now have in hand the books of Hebrew Questions.”

And shortly afterward:

> “The book of places, which I am about to publish, if anyone wishes to possess it.”

He therefore reworked this Eusebian work in Latin. Although he was still planning the books of Questions—for he had already completed the Questions on Genesis—he occasionally instructed the reader concerning what he intended shortly to pour out on the remaining books, as though he had already completed it.

In reality, it is only in that one book that one finds these Questions praised with reference to the remaining parts of Scripture by name. For after he abandoned the project, he nowhere afterward mentions them.

Indeed, nearly six years later, when he himself composed the catalogue of his works and listed the *Hebrew Questions*, he acknowledges only one book of them, on Genesis. That he later reworked them is wholly improbable. Certainly, in the books which he composed afterward, there is not even a trace of them, although occasions arose on which he could not have failed to recall them had they existed.

On the contrary, he acts in the opposite manner. If any of the difficulties which he had already said he had resolved in his interpretation of *On the Places* occurs again in another work, he explains it as though he had never touched upon it before.

Let us confirm the point by an example. Concerning the word *Ariel* in Isaiah, he had said, with his customary concluding formula:

> “This has been discussed more fully in the books of the Hebrew Questions.”

About twenty-four years later, listen to what he says in his *Commentaries*:

> “Ariel is interpreted as ‘lion of God.’ For the city, which Aquila rendered *πολίχνην*, that is, ‘a little town’ or ‘village,’ the Hebrew reads *CARIATH*, which properly means ‘village,’ and in the Syriac language is called *cartha*. Hence the village of the forests is also called *Cariath-jarim* . . . Therefore Ariel, that is, ‘lion of God,’ is the name given to Jerusalem, once exceedingly strong; or, as others think, of the temple and altar of God which was in Jerusalem.”

Does he really expound at greater length, while concealing his earlier work, a passage which he had previously explained according to a definite plan? Anyone who persuades himself of this must surely be a stranger to Jerome’s writings.

For, on the contrary, near the beginning of the same chapter of Isaiah, chapter 54, after saying indefinitely that the number seven, the Sabbath, and several other things are signified by the ambiguity of the Hebrew language—and although he had also touched upon these matters in Genesis 21—he immediately adds:

> “This has been discussed more fully in the book of Hebrew Questions which we wrote on Genesis.”

## 29. Shorter Commentaries on the Twelve Prophets

Let us hasten to other matters. Several learned men, especially Father Martianay, confidently assert and lament that *ὑπομνήματα*, or shorter commentaries on the Twelve Prophets, distinct from those that survive, perished through the violence of time.

The occasion for this complaint was provided by Jerome’s words in Letter 49 to Pammachius, section 4, near the end:

> “I have sent to the holy Father Domnio some of the *ὑπομνήματα* on the Twelve Prophets . . . If you wish to read them, you will recognize how difficult it is to understand divine Scripture, and especially the Prophets,” etc.

These words seem to indicate commentaries on all twelve of the prophets whom they call the Minor Prophets. Since the holy Doctor did not complete his commentaries on all of them until after the year 406, while this letter is certainly dated to 393, it follows that works other than those which survive must be indicated.

The word *ὑπομνήματα* itself also contributes to the opinion that those commentaries designated another work or written memorial.

But, if I may say so with due respect for learned men, I believe they are mistaken. I think that the holy Doctor was referring altogether to the portion of the surviving commentaries which he had completed by that time.

First, when he mentions a work on the Twelve Prophets, he does not designate the individual books of the Prophets which he had undertaken to explain. Rather, just as in the canon of Scripture, he simply indicates one book entitled *The Twelve Prophets*. From this it does not follow that he explained each of the twelve prophets, merely because he wrote something on the book of the Twelve Prophets.

Thus Jerome himself says in the *Dialogue against the Luciferians*, section 5, when quoting a passage from Hosea:

> “It is written in the Twelve Prophets that their sacrifices are like . . .”

Furthermore, Jerome did not simply say *ὑπομνήματα*, but rather *quaedam τῶν ὑπομνημάτων*—“some of the *ὑπομνήματα*”—thus indicating very plainly that at that time he had explained not all twelve, but only some of them.

In fact, he had expounded Micah from the year 392 into the following year, as well as Nahum and the prophets who followed it: Habakkuk, Zephaniah, and Haggai. These are surely the commentaries which he indicates to Pammachius that he had sent to Domnio. There is no need to invent shorter works, or others different in kind, which the passage of time supposedly deprived us of.

To add this argument as well: who could persuade himself that, if Jerome interpreted the same prophets twice, he would conceal from the diligent reader the commentaries which he had already composed, when he was reweaving the same fabric a second time?

The surviving commentaries are later than those which the learned men who hold the contrary view imagine to have perished; and those learned men themselves scarcely deny this. Take the example of Obadiah, whom Jerome revised in a second edition, entirely rejecting the earlier one; or the *Visions of Isaiah* addressed to Amabile, which he had once explained separately and later attached to the commentaries themselves.

### 30. Fourteen Books on Jeremiah

I consider the complaint of both ancient and modern writers concerning the fourteen books of Commentaries on Jeremiah, long since lost, to be no less absurd or reasonable than the one we have shown to arise from sheer hallucination. Cassiodorus says in *Institutes*, chapter 3, concerning the prophets:

> “The holy Jerome is also shown to have commented on Jeremiah in twenty books. Of these we have been able to find only six; we are still searching for the rest, with the Lord’s help.”

Thus the ancient author of the sermon *On the Nativity of St. Jerome*, whom we present in the final volume, says that the holy Doctor commented on all the prophets in seventy-four books. There can therefore be no doubt that, by his reckoning, he counts twenty complete books on Jeremiah.

Rabanus laments the loss even more vehemently. After inserting the first six books into his own work, he nowhere found the exposition of Jeremiah by the aforesaid commentator, and therefore thought it necessary to extract from expositions of the other prophets whatever Jerome appeared to have mentioned concerning this prophet. Writers of the later age say similar things; indeed, more than one of them seemed to himself to have found one or another of those books which he supposed lost.

In a certain manuscript of the Abbey of St. Laurence, cited by two Benedictine fathers of the Congregation of St. Maur in their *Literary Journey*, the following note is added after the six books on Jeremiah:

> “Note that the glorious Doctor Jerome wrote twenty books on the prophet Jeremiah. The first six books are contained in this volume; the three last are found among the Canons Regular of the Seven Fountains in Brabant. But the eleven middle books are not found—a loss lamented by Cassiodorus, Rabanus, and John Andreas (the author of the sermon on the Nativity of St. Jerome cited above).”

Among more recent scholars, some, being almost certain that those Commentaries were never completed because death intervened, attempt to diminish the authority and testimony of the ancient writers who appear to contradict them. The most distinguished Tillemont preferred to tamper with Cassiodorus’s passage and, by some means unknown to me, substituted *nine* for *twenty-nine*—a plainly violent alteration, supported by no testimony whatever from manuscripts or even printed editions, and indeed wholly contrary to the author’s meaning and to the context. Once Cassiodorus’s manuscripts have been rashly altered, one would also have to invade the books of the other writers with the same license and oppose the most consistent authority.

I shall therefore explain briefly what the matter is and how the opinions may be reconciled. Jerome had formerly translated into Latin from Origen’s Greek fourteen *tractatus*, or [Col. XXXV] homilies, on Jeremiah. Afterwards he commented on the same prophet in six books according to his own judgment. If these two kinds of Commentaries on the same subject are joined together, so to speak, by the number of chapters or books—namely, six and fourteen—the total is twenty, precisely the number said to have been elaborated on Jeremiah.

I therefore suppose that, in some very ancient copy predating Cassiodorus—and with good reason—fourteen other treatises were appended to those six books of Commentaries, and that from this arose the opinion concerning twenty books on Jeremiah. Certainly, whoever first counted twenty must have been that person who, by adding the numbers together, joined the treatises to the Commentaries. In nearly all other copies, and with better judgment, these works were easily transcribed separately, since they did not serve as substitutes for Commentaries in Jerome’s own sense, but were regarded as Origenian offspring.

Afterwards, when the six proper books of Commentaries did not complete the prophet’s exposition and were plainly recognized as parts of an unfinished work, those who had accepted that Jerome had commented in twenty books grieved that the fourteen later books had not survived the injuries of time. It was not easy to suspect that the number established by the ancients was fulfilled by those treatises. Meanwhile, this single observation could have consoled that imaginary longing and untied the question, which has been agitated by so many disputes.

To make this absolutely clear and leave no room for doubt, one further point must be observed. Of the fifty-two chapters that make up the whole of Jeremiah, the first thirty-three are fully expounded by Jerome in those six books of Commentaries. The remaining nineteen, which consist almost entirely of a historical narrative, and which he himself promised in his preface to explain in a much more abbreviated style, if he had been able to pursue the work despite his death—or the illness that preceded it—could have been adequately treated in three or four books at most, perhaps even fewer. They certainly would not have required the full fourteen books which some absurdly dream of.

That, nevertheless, they obstinately assert fourteen is the result of sheer hallucination: no one after Cassiodorus, who dragged the others along in his wake, understood that those same fourteen treatises, or homilies, had to be divided into sections in order to complete the number.

### 31. The Latin Translation of the Commentaries of Alexander of Aphrodisias

There is another, much less serious hallucination among learned men concerning the Commentaries of Alexander of Aphrodisias, supposedly explained in Latin by Jerome—for example, Tillemont in *Life*, article 10, and Albert Fabricius in *Greek Library*, book IV, chapter XXV.

All of them have essentially one argument for the loss of that work, drawn from the testimony of the holy Doctor in Letter 50 to Domnion, section 1. There, after declaring that he had long occupied himself with the writings of the philosophers Aristotle and Cicero in order to overcome the crude presumption of his opponents, who despised philosophical learning, Jerome says:

> “Why, then, did I translate the Commentaries of Alexander? Why did my learned teacher introduce me to logic through Porphyry’s *Introduction* (*εἰσαγωγή*, *Eisagōgē*) in vain?”

They do not doubt that the verb “to translate” must be understood in the sense in which it denotes interpretation from one language into another—namely, into Latin from Greek. But Jerome added nothing about languages, neither the language into which nor the language out of which he was translating. I am convinced that, without specifying one or the other, examples of this meaning can scarcely be found in any Latin writer, and scarcely even in Jerome.

When Cicero says in *On Ends*, book I, “If I were translating Plato or Aristotle, as our poets translated plays,” the preceding context makes it perfectly clear that Greek works are understood. Accordingly, it must be certain and established that when someone is said simply to “turn over” books (*ἀπλῶς*), nothing else is meant than handling or leafing through them—Italian *scartabellare*, “to rummage through.” In this sense Horace says:

> “Turn over your Greek exemplars by night, turn them over by day.”

I could prove by very many passages that Jerome understood the word in no other sense. First of all, the context immediately preceding the passage in that letter—from which alone this whole story was imported into the republic of letters—speaks of nothing except diligence and devotion in reading and studying the books of the philosophers.

Why, then, did the holy Doctor not specify which book he had actually interpreted? Instead he spoke indistinctly of “the Commentaries,” a title by which at least ten enormous volumes are designated—not to mention the complete works of that author, including even those that have perished—which are called *ὑπομνήματα* (*hypomnēmata*), or Commentaries. Moreover, why would he have undertaken so great and burdensome a task: translating writings that learned people generally understood in Greek, especially those who had devoted themselves most intensely to philosophical studies?

I would rather have the matter determined by the opinion of Rufinus, than by anyone else, for no one was ever more hostile to Jerome’s works than he. When Rufinus, in book II of his *Invectives*, attacked those words addressed to Domnion as spitefully as possible, he never accused Jerome of translating Alexander’s Commentaries, which would have been the chief point of the charge. Instead, he charged Jerome with perjury merely for having read that book. According to Rufinus, Jerome had said to Christ in that much-vexed vision:

> “I denied you, if I should possess or read the books of the Gentiles.”

If Rufinus had understood—or could in any way have suspected—that the Commentaries of Aphrodisias were said to have been translated into Latin, who could believe that he would have attacked the reading and study while concealing the labor of so great a work, only to present it again, when convenient for calumny, as something most harmful even to Latin ears? And who would believe that, in the entire accusation concerning listening to Porphyry’s *Introduction* (*εἰσαγωγή*), he would find nothing to object to in Alexander’s books translated from Greek except that syllogisms from his Commentaries were not woven into Jerome’s discourse before God?

How cleverly could he have brought the same charge against Jerome, who was so severely accused for himself interpreting Origen’s book *On First Principles* (*περὶ ἀρχῶν*)! Furthermore, Rufinus himself appropriately records for our purpose that, before his conversion, the holy Doctor was completely ignorant of Greek letters and language. This also disposes of the *problem* (*πρόβλημα*) that someone might easily have proposed: that the translation was produced in Jerome’s early youth, before he had given his name to the Christian religion.

For if at that time he was ignorant of Greek letters, and, when he learned them, understood that he was no longer free to occupy himself in translating pagan writings into Latin, there is no period to which that supposed translation can properly be assigned.

### 32. The Book Addressed to Abundantius

Two more books must be considered briefly, so that none of this kind may be overlooked.

The first is the exegetical work addressed to Abundantius—or, as the older editions report, to Antius—which Cassiodorus mentions in *Institutes*, chapter 2, in these explicit words:

> “The blessed Jerome, writing to Abundantius, explained three other extremely obscure questions. The first is why David, who was voluntarily coming with Achish, king of the Philistines, to attack Saul, killed the man who afterwards reported Saul’s death. The second is why, when dying, David commanded his son Solomon to kill Joab, the commander of his army. The third question concerns Shimei, who, while David was fleeing, inflicted intolerable insults of cursing upon him, even throwing stones.”

There is no mention or trace of this writing in Jerome’s works or in those of other writers from which anything certain can be extracted. I can easily believe that some ancient book was imposed upon Cassiodorus in which this Epistle or little book was attributed to Jerome. But since the monument itself did not survive to our time, it is not easy to pronounce a definite judgment.

The other work is praised by St. Agobard in book 39 of his treatise *Against Felix* (*On the Likeness of Sinful Flesh*). He calls it a brief and most elegant Treatise *On the Likeness of Sinful Flesh* against the Manichaeans. Nor should one suppose that he could have mistaken the author’s name through carelessness or haste in writing. The whole discussion that he conducts in that chapter concerns Jerome’s view of the term “adoption.” He was so confident that the book was genuinely Jerome’s that he believed neither opponents nor anyone else could doubt its author or reply to it. He therefore transcribes a fairly long extract from it, twice and even three times introducing Jerome’s name and pressing the authority of the Doctor upon his adversary.

[Col. XXXVII]

Baluzius, who most recently edited Agobard and supplied notes to him, left this passage untouched. Yet I easily imagine that learned men of our own age will find it difficult to persuade themselves that Jerome was the author of such a work.

For my part, I would rather attribute it to Audentius, a Spanish bishop said to have lived around the year 360. Gennadius, chapter 14, reports that he wrote a book against the Manichaeans in which he showed that the antiquity of the Son of God was eternal with the Father, and that he did not then receive the beginning of his divinity from God the Father when, through God’s agency, he was conceived and born as man from the Virgin Mary.

Or, if this attribution seems less suitable, I would assign it to Sabbatius, a bishop of the Gallican Church around the year 440. According to Gennadius, chapter 25, he composed a book on a similar subject and showed that Christ had true flesh, by which, through eating, drinking, becoming weary, weeping, dying, and rising again, he was proved to be truly human.

In reality, since nothing can be established with certainty, and since no conclusive arguments are available for denying the work to Jerome, lest we appear rashly to diminish Agobard’s authority or pass over something Jerome may have written without due consideration, we transcribe the entire passage.

The very argument proposed confirms this. It testifies that the first Adam was made a living soul, and the last Adam a life-giving spirit:

> “Behold why, after so many innumerable years and immeasurable courses of ages, the last is set apart from all mortals, from whom he is distinguished even as one born according to the flesh: the former is first, living; the latter last, life-giving. The former scarcely possessed what had been given to him; the latter bestows what is to be possessed.
>
> “The Psalmist explained this in two verses when he said: ‘What is man, that you are mindful of him, or the son of man, that you visit him?’ ‘Man’ must be understood as Adam; ‘the son of man’ must be understood as the Lord. He is visited in remembrance of the old man and filled with the spirit of salutation in remembrance of the dead.
>
> “The very words express this, so that it is not surprising to see the remembrance joined to man and the visitation joined to the son of man. What else could remain for that mortal one? What else had to be infused into this life-giving one? Remembrance is owed to the dead; visitation is offered to the living.
>
> “Both are shown to have been fulfilled in the Lord through the Incarnation: on account of the remembrance of the first, the last is visited, and through the visitation of the last, the first is saved.
>
> “This meaning is closely related to the statement: ‘The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second from heaven, heavenly.’ Who is this heavenly one? Without doubt, he who caused the one whom he bore in baptism to hear what no one before him had heard: ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you.’
>
> “And how is it said to be ‘today,’ if ‘in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word’? Because it is not that Word who must be believed to have always existed in the Father, and with the Father, and beside the Father; rather, the man whom God the Word had taken up into the grace of salvation heard it.
>
> “This son of man, through the Son of God, merits being the son of God in the Son of God. Adoption is not separated from nature; rather, nature is joined to adoption. For when the Word became flesh, the one who assumed did not diminish through what was assumed; rather, the assumption grew in the one assuming.
>
> “The substance of weakness could be changed in a creature through the Creator; but the nature of eternity in the Creator could not be changed into a creature. Therefore, when it is said, ‘The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second from heaven, heavenly,’ it is not the material of the body that is separated, but its living form. The flesh is not removed; rather, the receiver of flesh is revealed—he, I say, who says in the Gospel: ‘You are from below; I am from above.’
>
> “He says ‘from above,’ not, of course, because of a starry flesh, but because of divine power.”

### 33. Two Books Against Helvidius, and Other Matters

I deliberately pass over certain other things which, in the revision of Jerome’s writings, are merely human mistakes. Such is the statement of the author of *Predestination*, who mentions two books against Helvidius rather than one:

> “The distinguished Doctor Jerome wrote two books against the Helvidians; when read at the proper time, they will anathematize them with a fitting curse.”

Nor should we include here those works which Jerome promised that he would compose but never actually completed. Among these are the Commentaries on the *Song of Songs*, which he promised to Principia when he was explaining Psalm 44 to her, in Letter 75, at the end. But, as he says in the Commentaries on Matthew, prolonged illness prevented him from undertaking that work, and he postponed his hope to the future. Afterwards no opportunity arose for completing it.

Likewise there is the ecclesiastical history which, at the very beginning of the *Life of Malchus*, he openly professes that he was preparing to write, in these remarkable words:

> “I have decided to write, if the Lord grants me life and if my detractors at least cease pursuing me while I flee and remain shut away: from the coming of the Savior down to our own age—that is, from the apostles to the dregs of our present time—how and through whom the Church of Christ was born, grew to maturity through persecutions, and was crowned with martyrdoms; and, after it came under Christian emperors, how it became greater in power and riches but less in virtues.”

It cannot, however, be clearly concluded from the catalogue or from any other work that he fulfilled this intention. When he says in the first book against Rufinus, “I praised Eusebius in his ecclesiastical history, in his arrangement of periods, and in his description of the Holy Land; and, translating these little works into Latin, I gave them to people who speak my language,” it is better understood to mean that the praise refers to the ecclesiastical history, while the translation refers to the other two little works.

## PART THREE

In which what has been accomplished in this new edition is explained.

### 34. The Division of the Works

Let us now finally say what we have accomplished in preparing this edition. First, the arrangement and division by which we have organized Jerome’s complete works must be briefly explained, and the entire plan of our edition must be set forth.

Everything from Jerome’s writings that we were able to gather has been distributed among ten volumes in such a way that primary consideration was given to the nature of the subjects and matters he treats, and so that each volume might in some fashion draw the reader onward to the next.

The first volume contains the letters. The second contains the treatises or little books dealing with particular subjects and definite material of whatever kind [Col. XXXIX], but especially works directed against heretics. The third presents, first, two kinds of apparatus concerning Sacred Scripture and then the Commentaries themselves, through the *Song of Songs*. The next two explain the prophets. The sixth contains the most distinguished parts of the New Testament. The seventh is filled by the Latin translation and supplement of the Eusebian Chronicle. The eighth and ninth contain the Hebrew truth—that is, Jerome’s Latin translation of the books of the Hebrew canon—together with what he translated from the Greek Old Testament and what he restored in the New Testament to fidelity to the Greek.

Finally, in the last volume we give works that claim the name of Jerome but belong to someone else, whether the author is known or unknown. We have admitted them into the family of the holy Father as foster offspring, lest, if we completely rejected them, they should be forced to wander homeless and perish.

A preface will stand at the beginning of each volume, explaining the reasons and principles of everything belonging to that volume, and especially of the considerable number of works by which each volume has been enriched. Where these are previously unpublished excerpts from autograph manuscripts, we shall indicate this; where they have been taken from elsewhere, we shall state for what reasons and in what order. The chronology will also be explained, and many other matters discussed, so that the character of the books may be evident immediately at the threshold to anyone who is not indifferent to them.

### 35. The Libraries and Manuscripts We Use, and How We Use Them

After arranging everything in this way, as seemed sufficiently suitable, I turned to emending the text itself and devoted all my attention to this task insofar as possible.

My first concern was to search the shelves of the libraries and carefully compare and transcribe everything in the manuscripts relevant to our purpose. I did not, as is commonly done, entrust this labor to the reliability or diligence of others, because I discovered that those who had not previously spent a long time practicing either the reading of ancient codices or the text of the author whom they were collating performed this task neither very carefully nor usefully.

However unpleasant this labor may be, I personally performed the greater part of it with my own eyes and diligence. I did not lose heart because of the length of the work or the tedium that almost inevitably creeps in; the abundance of variant readings and highly certain emendations repeatedly restored my spirits.

The most celebrated libraries I examined were, first of all, the Vatican Library at Rome, extraordinarily rich in an immense store of excellent manuscripts and enriched beyond description by the additions of the libraries of Urbino, the Palatine, and Queen Christina of Sweden. Then there was the other library of the Cistercian monks, formerly Nonantulan and now that of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme, from which I had quite a number of venerably ancient copies.

Next came the Milanese library, commonly called the Ambrosiana, equally well supplied, but especially rich in the very ancient and generally superior copies transferred there from St. Columbanus of Bobbio. Finally there was our Veronese library, or that of the most extensive cathedral chapter. Although it is far inferior to the others in the number of books, it surpasses them almost all in antiquity and excellence.

The libraries of Parma and Vercelli may also be added. From the former I had, in particular, an elegant and emended manuscript of the Eusebio-Jerome Chronicle at my disposal; the latter is much more richly supplied. There are also various others which I would call private libraries. It is not possible, in the time available, to list every codex in an organized catalogue or discuss their dates, especially since I have referred to each one by name in the notes wherever this was necessary to establish the reliability of a reading.

Since I encountered an enormous number of manuscripts in these libraries, I decided to use their authority in a way different from the usual practice. Before reading them from beginning to end, as the saying goes, I tested their reliability. For many appear, not without reason, to have been copied from one and the same exemplar, since they agree in precisely the same critical conjectures and the same scribal errors. I therefore judged that they were worth no more than a single codex.

From time to time I brought into consultation others which I judged to have flowed from a different source. When these agreed on a reading of no slight importance, only then did they prevail by their authority. When there was conflict and variation, their disagreements could either cast suspicion upon the soundness of a passage or teach the means of curing it.

Following this principle, I nevertheless preferred those manuscripts to the others which approached their source—that is, Jerome’s own age—more closely. No one should think the claim rash if I wish many of those I use to precede the seventh century, and nearly all of them to precede the tenth.

### 36. The Method by Which the Text Was Emended

In reconstructing the text from these copies (*ἀντίγραφα*, *antigraphai*), I observed the following additional rule: I would not dare to alter anything unless an error arising plainly from the ignorance of ancient scribes or from the boldness of critics clearly revealed itself.

Nor did I assign such authority even to the most approved parchment manuscripts that I would expel the received reading solely on their evidence. I also examined and weighed the context of the discourse, the deeper meaning, Jerome’s usage in writing, and his character.

When new readings were supported by these qualities, by the argument of sound reason, and by the testimony of ancient books, I introduced them into the text. There are indeed quite a number which had escaped the prudent diligence of earlier editors, and many others commonly received which I abandoned, although no one had doubted them any more than if they had been found in every manuscript.

I often suppressed at the outset conjectures that arose in my own mind, lest I disturb passages that were moderately well established. Yet whenever the sense itself indicated that a passage was corrupt, and I could restore it by conjecture despite the silence of the manuscripts, and when I could demonstrate the causes of the error most clearly in the notes, why should I continue to burden learned readers or expose an error to the unlearned?

Even so, I did this very rarely and cautiously, especially where the defective writing of the ancient codices was not merely an indication but an argument. I therefore do not doubt that prudent men will find in it more material for criticizing timidity than recklessness.

For, with a kind of religious diligence, we have sometimes preferred to place even an obvious truth before the judgment of the reader rather than endanger the author’s meaning.

### 37. Variant Readings

I append variant readings, and in selecting and arranging them I generally followed this method.

First, I ordered to be completely excluded [Col. XLI] those which are mere scribal jeux d’esprit and a vast mass of idle variations—readings which, whether rejected or placed in the text of the printed editions, would cause the prose no harm whatever and could do nothing except add bulk to the volume. If I present any of this kind, it is only when they may have some use: either because genuine readings can be better established by comparison with false ones, or because the sons of critics may be able to extract something sound from corrupt readings. If I had indiscriminately cut them all away, they might justly have complained that I had rejected what they themselves valued according to their own judgment.

I have placed the rest continuously, and in this respect I preferred to err on the side of inclusion, admitting some that contained nothing of value rather than risk cutting away something useful.

Finally, readings that appeared to be of lesser importance, most of them extracted from the books of older editions, I did not defer to the bottom margin. Instead, I marked them with an asterisk opposite the relevant passage, so that the words to which they refer might be recognized at a glance and the reader would not be troubled to turn elsewhere without good reason.

Learned men know the usefulness of all these things well. I do not think I need labor in this area to overcome the crude disdain of certain people who almost despise variant readings, since I know that many others judge the excellence of an edition principally from its treatment of variants.

### 38. Observations and Notes

The remaining task was to illuminate the holy Doctor’s text with our observations wherever the matter required it, and I pursued this through continuous notes.

When I have removed an old reading and substituted a new one from manuscripts in a defective passage, or restored one that had long ago been eliminated, I append the reasons for the emendation and show the arguments that led me to it.

In other passages that are not corrupt but more difficult to understand, I spend somewhat more labor and words if my efforts can contribute anything toward diminishing their obscurity.

It was first necessary to explain the author’s native meaning, whatever that may be. I have always kept before my eyes the wise maxim of Jerome himself, in Letter 48 to Pammachius, section 17:

> “It is the commentator’s task to explain not what he himself wishes, but what the person whom he interprets means. Otherwise, if he says the opposite, he will be not so much an interpreter as an adversary.”

I have either not touched at all upon lesser difficulties—those which might trouble someone among the general body of readers but can be explained from other books, especially lexicographers, and which have already been explained fully and systematically by others—or I have briefly indicated from which sources they should be sought.

In passages that have been wrongly understood or maliciously misrepresented, whenever it can be done without injury to the most holy Doctor and with some appearance of truth, I have omitted almost no charge or suspicion without attempting to clear it.

Finally, since Jerome was especially fond of the literary device which the Greeks call *παρῳδικόν* (*parōidikon*, parody or adaptation), I generally indicate what he took, or appears to have taken, from other writers, especially Greek ones. Sometimes I mention only the names of the Fathers, when it did not seem to matter greatly; sometimes I cite entire passages, especially when they have been transferred almost word for word and the meaning of both writers may thereby be illuminated.

At times I have also noted passages which later Fathers copied from our author. I have done this very sparingly and only where the cited opinion gains either clarity or authority from them. If I had wished to pursue everything, I could scarcely have made the labor worthwhile despite immense effort.

For the same reason—namely, to spare both the work and the time—I have generally ordered the testimonies to be excluded entirely which editors of ancient writers commonly use to burden the margins of books when they collect similar opinions from other sources and call the passages *παράλληλα* (*parallēla*, parallels).

In short, I do not claim to have neglected any means of securing brevity. I have restrained my pen in such a way that, in accordance with the opinion of a most learned recent editor, I have judged that my reader neither knows everything nor, again, knows nothing.

### 39. The Notes of Other Editors, Especially the Benedictines, at the End of the Volume

So much, then, concerning the notes I have added.

For a long time I had intended to append to the end of each volume notes and observations by all the editors who preceded me. But I was recalled from that plan by the judgment both of myself and of prudent men, who thought it would result in useless labor and the waste of better hours.

The older editors often wander at great length over passages worn smooth by everyone’s discussion. Frequently, too, they repeat what earlier writers have said, following one another with only slightly altered wording. Finally, they rely upon false readings and labor in vain to explain them.

I do not deny that some material is occasionally mixed in which may contribute to the reader’s learning. Nevertheless, such material is extremely limited. Without diminishing their praise, we could have treated it much more fully in this light of letters, and these matters have in fact been discussed.

The notes of Henri de Gravii are certainly more learned. But because he wished the principal and almost exclusive purpose of his work to be the comparison of Jerome—comparing opinions with opinions—and devoted his labor only to the letters and treatises, their usefulness is sufficiently served by a careful index. That is the better course.

Nevertheless, I append the fewer notes that clarify the text, as well as the eight or ten most select notes of Fronto Ducaeus, so that nothing may appear to be lacking.

The commentaries of the Benedictine editor, however, had to be treated differently. Although they could have been entirely omitted without detriment to our edition, I have appended them complete to the end of each volume in order to avert the resentment of certain people who might complain that they had been deprived either of the advantages or of the disadvantages of that labor.

### 40. Praise of the Men Named

I have also undertaken many things for the elegance of the work and many for the benefit of the reader. I ask that earnest students receive them with an even temper.

If I do not obtain this favor from some one person, I know Jerome’s judgment in Letter 66 to Pammachius:

> “One must stand by the judgment of the crowd; and he is to be feared in the crowd whom, when you see him alone, you would despise.”

It is now my duty to praise with grateful remembrance the outstanding men who supplied me with the assistance of manuscript codices.

I do not list their names here in an organized catalogue, lest, since there are many of them from many cities of Italy, I inadvertently pass over anyone without praise. I give thanks to all of them, individually and collectively, and wish benevolent readers to recognize how greatly they are indebted to them when they read the names of the libraries over which those men preside.

But I cannot, without incurring the guilt of ingratitude, remain silent about the most illustrious man, the Marquis Scipione Maffei, a singular ornament of our homeland. He first advanced all this labor of mine through his immediate assistance, and, although far away and prolonging his absence from us in Gaul, he continues to support it with constant favor—a new *ἔργοδιώκτης* (*ergodiōktēs*), a pursuer of labor.

[Col. XLIII]

## Preface to This Volume

### 1. The Qualities of the Letters of St. Jerome

Among the writings of illustrious men, letters are judged by prudent people to be far superior to the rest, chiefly because in them the person of the writer stands so closely before the reader’s eyes that we seem almost to embrace a man restored to life and to gaze upon his very face.

If this is the privilege of letters in the case of any other writer, it is certainly the privilege of Jerome’s letters. Their mute lines reproduce the image of his intellect and virtues, and represent the hidden disposition of his mind and that fire of his breast which his living body itself, if present, would not display.

But their dignity is much greater for another reason. The most holy Doctor, having held the highest offices in the Christian commonwealth, had, almost from his youth, assisted Damasus, bishop of the city of Rome, in ecclesiastical documents and had responded to the synodal consultations of East and West (Letter 123). Afterwards he was consulted, as it were, as the common oracle of his age concerning the gravest and most difficult matters—and, what is most important, by those who at that time held the first place in holiness, learning, or dignity, even in regions far removed from one another.

Examples include the great Augustine from Africa, whose name alone would suffice; Lucinius and Exsuperius from Spain; Minervius, Alexander, Riparius, and Rusticus from Gaul; Sunnia and Fretella from more distant Germany; Epiphanius from the East; and Theophilus from Egypt and from Alexandria itself. I say nothing meanwhile of the countless and often even more august names from Italy and from the leading men of Roman nobility.

Therefore his letters embrace not merely the learned concerns of a private individual, but nearly all the more notable questions: outstanding monuments for the explanation of Scripture, and indeed almost the entire ecclesiastical history, doctrines, and events of his age. Anyone eager to learn these matters from the purest sources must diligently examine the letters.

## 2. Confusion among the old editions in reviewing them

I therefore devoted my efforts so that the reader might return with the fullest possible benefit, not only by carrying out what I set forth in the preceding Preface, but also by reviewing each Letter, so that they might be arranged in proper chronological order. The old Editors, in fact, present a sequence of Letters arranged more according to subject matter than according to time; and since they reduce Letters of such varied content to only three classes, and do not do so with sufficient accuracy, the arrangement itself suffers from the defect of confusion, so that polemical letters are often mixed with laudatory ones, moral with critical, theological with personal.

The Benedictine edition, while attempting to remedy this fault—let there be no ill will in saying so—confuses everything still further. For it forcibly removed a number of Letters that it calls critical from their native setting and transferred them to a foreign one; moreover, throughout the entire corpus of Jerome’s works it inserted and scattered them here and there among the commentaries in the several volumes. If one wishes to take an example of this intolerable confusion from several Letters addressed to one and the same Damasus, the Letter explaining Cain’s vengeance appears in the second volume after the *Questions on Genesis*; the one concerning the Seraphim in the third, after the *Commentaries on Isaiah*; and the one explaining the word *Hosanna* in the first part of the fourth volume, where it is appended to the exposition of Matthew. Other Letters of this kind have been omitted, and others placed outside their proper setting, so that it is clear that even in arranging the material according to its own judgment he was not especially successful.

In all the remaining Letters, which he collected together in the second part of the fourth volume, he certainly employed an excellent plan, since he sought to arrange each according to the rules of chronology; nevertheless, the result was not equally successful. The first Letter encountered there, addressed to Rufinus and concerning seven years of labor, contains an anachronism; and Innocentius, who is presented as Jerome’s companion on his journey, is said to have died, while after sixteen intervening Letters he is addressed as still alive.

When the Editor attempts to correct this error in his prolegomena and moves the Letter to Innocentius back to the year 364, he compounds it with a new error. From that point onward he adapted the remaining Letters of this First Class to the hypothesis he had conceived on the basis of a preconceived opinion. The other Classes are no less faulty: often earlier Letters follow later ones; some are placed ahead of, or behind, others by one, two, or three years, and sometimes even more, contrary to what is proper. Thus, whenever he confuses chronological calculations, he drags the reader along with him into the same disorder.

## 3. The necessity and method of a new arrangement

Since, therefore, I could neither repeat the inconvenient arrangement of the old editions nor continue too often in the misguided footsteps of the Benedictine monk—although I wished not to depart from either of the published arrangements, lest an alteration create some difficulty for students—it was nevertheless wholly necessary to inaugurate a better arrangement, or to reform the chronological one completely and as accurately as possible.

For it was necessary both to remove many items from the published collections of the Letters and to supply many others that were lacking in our own; and once it had become necessary either to increase, diminish, or alter the old numbering, it was impossible to preserve the prescribed sequence everywhere except at the cost of greater inconvenience to readers. Accordingly, in some places I inverted it, introducing detours where the subject itself required them.

I therefore judged—having also been instructed by the examples of other Editors—that it would be useful if students could continue to use the customary citations of earlier times; and, so that they might not be deprived of the convenience of that arrangement, whatever its ultimate character, I noted at the beginning of each Letter what number it had held in the old recension. I also had a table prepared at the front of the work, comparing the new order with the old and with the Benedictine edition itself, whose sequence I placed alongside it, so that at a single glance one might understand how the several arrangements correspond and in what order each Letter has proceeded.

Furthermore, lest I appear to have undertaken a new arrangement rashly and on slight grounds, I append below, separately, the considerations that led me to establish this sequence, as is customary in more accurate recensions of the Fathers. This is especially necessary because I have restored many Letters that had wandered far from their proper places to definite locations and years, and most of them to dates other than those ordinarily assigned to them by the Chronologists.

Only three Letters preserve neither such a certain chronological indication nor the memory of any historical event that they can be assigned to a definite year. I have therefore placed them at the end of the others, prefacing the page with the heading *of uncertain date*, so that no one may suppose them more recent merely because they are placed after the rest. Yet they contribute almost nothing to history, so that ignorance of their date is less burdensome.

## 4. Treatises and longer works, together with prefaces to other works, are excluded

Now, in order to prepare a collection properly of the Letters—a notion that had occurred to no one before—I first removed from this place the treatises and longer works that Jerome himself counts among his books in the *Catalogue*, and elsewhere whenever they are mentioned, reserving them for another volume.

For what do the Lives of the three monks Paul, Hilarion, and Malchus have in common with the Letters, so that they should be included in their sequence? Or the *Book on Illustrious Men*; the work against Helvidius; the two much longer works against Jovinian; the *Dialogue between an Orthodox Christian and a Luciferian*; the three books bearing the same title against Pelagius; and many other works of the same kind, which by the very nature of their composition demand a different place?

I likewise excluded from this series those Letters that serve as prefaces to other books, since they do not preserve the character of the other Letters and are adorned with a different purpose. Of this kind are the twenty prefaces that the holy Doctor composed for as many books of Sacred Scripture and placed before them when he wished to forewarn the reader about his translation and work. Erasmus and Victorius, however, counted them among the remaining Letters in their editions, either because they did not intend to print those books or because they did not think that complete copies of them existed.

The same applies to the prefaces to several books that Martianaeus reviewed in his Eighth Class, although he omitted those books from his collection of the works. In reviewing them, he committed the additional fault of passing off one as a work of Jerome, although it is manifestly Rufinus’s preface to Origen’s *Homilies on Paul’s Epistle to the Romans*, as is clear from the translator’s own conclusion at the end of those expositions.

I therefore judged that all these had been forcibly torn from their proper places; if they were transferred here, each ought to be attached to its own book. Just as Martianaeus did not receive the prefaces to Scripture that the old Editors had included, because, when printing Scripture itself, he represented them in their proper places, so I wished to exclude from this series the prefaces that Martianaeus himself had exhibited, in one way or another, with various other books, since, when I present the books themselves, I shall restore them, as it were, as heads to their own bodies.

## 5. Five Letters not previously published are added

Conversely, I added many items that had hitherto been lacking in the published editions, and I thought this effort worthwhile. In all, there are eleven of them: five had never before seen the light, while the others are taken from different books.

Let us speak first of the *anekdota* (ἀνέκδοτα, unpublished pieces). I transcribed the four contained under numbers XCII–XCV from a manuscript in the Ambrosian Library at Milan, formerly belonging to Saint Columbanus of Bobbio, numbered 59 and marked with the letter H. I trust that such value has thereby been added to our edition that, even if I had accomplished nothing else, I might still believe that I had deserved well enough of the lovers of Jerome’s works.

The first is the celebrated Synodical Letter of Theophilus against Origen and his followers, from which we learn almost the whole history of the Origenist cause, much of it otherwise unknown: the grave accusations brought against Isidore; the disturbances of the Nitrian monks; the exiles of the brothers commonly called the Longi; and other matters of this kind. Some of these are indispensable for properly understanding the positions of the heretics, others for assigning to their proper time the events that took place on both sides. Learned men have occasionally gone wrong in explaining these matters because they were ignorant of them.

The second is the response of the Jerusalem Synod to this Letter of Theophilus, following almost the same course; and the third is the Letter of Dionysius of Lydda to Theophilus himself. From these we learn how much confidence the Origenists placed in themselves, what regions they traversed, and by what devices they ultimately deceived people.

These works properly belong to the catalogue of Jerome’s writings because they were translated into Latin by Jerome and are therefore properly his. So that no one who has merely read them may dare to question this, so that the elegance of the style itself may immediately reveal it, so that the sequence of the matters discussed may agree with it, and so that the authority of the manuscript may also support it, Jerome himself stands forth as a sure witness to his own fidelity. In disputing against Rufinus, he explicitly professes that he translated them into Latin, in these words, *Book 3*:

> “For nearly two years I have translated the two Letters of Theophilus—the Synodical and the Paschal—against Origen and his disciples, and I have made them available in our language for our people to read for the edification of the Church.”

He says the same concerning the others at the beginning of *Book 1*:

> “If you think that whatever is said against Origen and his followers is said against you, then the Letters of Pope Theophilus, Epiphanius, and the other Bishops, which I recently translated at their command, attack you and tear you to pieces.”

When he adds “the other Bishops” besides Epiphanius, if Jerome did not mean the Fathers of the Jerusalem Synod and Dionysius of Lydda—whose Letters to Theophilus against Origen we are publishing—it would be pointless to devise another kind of argument for proving the *identity* (ταυτότητα) of these Letters with those Jerome mentions.

The Letter that follows these, number XCV, from Pope Anastasius to Simplicianus, seemed rightly to demand a place among Jerome’s works because it is closely connected and intertwined with those preceding it. I have perhaps discussed its authenticity and character at greater length than necessary in the Notes.

I added another in Class V, under number CXLIX, transcribed from Vatican Codex 642. It is not of great value, but because it was distinguished by the prestige of Jerome’s name, although falsely attributed to him, it ought not to be omitted after the two other apocryphal pieces.

## 6. Six other Letters added here for the first time

Of the six other Letters that we count among Jerome’s works because they were either written to Jerome himself or concerning questions proposed to him, or because they wholly concern his history, three belong to Innocentius—CXXXV and the two following—and three to Augustine, namely CXXXI, CXXXII, and CXLIV.

It is important to preface the last of these with a few remarks; the others are better known and do not require the assistance of our work. It is addressed to Optatus concerning the nature and origin of the soul, and about halfway through it speaks of Jerome as the arbiter of the question.

When the Benedictines were preparing the Augustinian edition, this Letter had not yet been published. Not long ago it was discovered in the monastery of Göttweig, in a manuscript dating approximately from the thirteenth century, together with another Letter addressed to Peter and Abraham, and was first printed at Vienna in Austria in the preceding year, 1732.

Its authenticity (γνησιότης), which several learned men had, in letters addressed to me, suspected without sufficient reason, is proved above all by the very structure of the document. The history of the question agrees with it in a remarkable way, as does the sequence of the writings on the matter by Jerome, Augustine, and Optatus; and the testimonies of Possidius and Fulgentius establish it most clearly.

For while only one Letter of Augustine to Optatus survives in the published books, bearing the number CXC, Possidius lists two in his *Index*, whereas Fulgentius, in *On the Truth of Predestination*, Book 3, chapter 18, cites three. I do not dispute which authority deserves greater confidence; but, as far as the present matter is concerned, I insist on this one point: not only Fulgentius, but Possidius himself, whose number is smaller, knew this Letter, since he says that the Letters were written against the Priscillianists, or concerning the question of souls.

But, so that no further reason for doubt might remain, the authority of the Abbot Eugyppius settles the matter. He was the man who, toward the end of the fifth century, collected into a single work, to use Cassiodorus’s words, questions, opinions, and various matters extracted from the works of Saint Augustine. In this work—called *The Treasury*, chapter 345, in the Basel and Venetian editions, although the Cassiodorus just mentioned says that the entire work was contained in 338 chapters—Eugyppius discusses whether the features of human beings are formed individually by God the Creator and the question of the soul. From this very Letter he transcribes a substantial passage, from number eight to the end, in exactly the same words. Thus it is most manifestly established that the Göttweig manuscript is truly the very Letter that the Bishop of Hippo sent to Optatus.

Indeed, there are two or three passages in that archetype, and in the Viennese edition, that have been somewhat corrupted through the carelessness of scribes and that can easily be restored from Eugyppius’s work. I recommend that they be restored here. When I gave that Letter to the printers for publication, I had not yet consulted Eugyppius’s book with my own eyes.

The corrections are as follows. In column 1070, line 11, instead of *Utrum horum vis ut confirmem?* (“Which of these do you wish me to confirm?”), I prefer Eugyppius’s *unum horum* (“one of these”), without a question mark. Below, in the fourth line from the end, after the parenthesis and following the words *initium meum* (“my beginning”), add *utinam tamen non initium* (“yet would that it were not a beginning”), although the Abbot incorrectly reads *nunc* in place of *non*. Finally, in column 1072, line 10, replace *intuens* (“observing”) with *metuens* (“fearing”). The remaining places in which Eugyppius differs from our reading, and therefore from that of the manuscript, are either insignificant or are scribal errors—*sphalmata* (σφάλματα).

## 7. The five Classes of Letters, their Contents, Capitulations, and so forth

I shall now explain what else I have accomplished. I divided all the Letters, thus collected, into five Classes, beginning from the principal stages of Jerome’s life and maintaining an uninterrupted sequence of events.

The First Class presents the Letters that Jerome wrote from the year 370, before he sought the desert, but chiefly while he was in the desert, through the year 381, when, having long since left his solitude, he went to Rome.

The Second contains those that he wrote at Rome from the year 382 to beyond the middle of 385, when, weary of residence in Rome, he departed and sailed to Jerusalem.

The Third contains those that he wrote from the monastery at Bethlehem from the year 386 through 400, when Origen was finally condemned at the Synod of Alexandria. This chronological indication is, in fact, almost the most useful of all for properly understanding Jerome’s Letters, which for the most part are occupied with attacking the errors of Adamantius and his supporters.

The Fourth represents those that he wrote from that time, namely from the year 401, until the holy Doctor’s death, that is, until the year 420.

Finally, in the Fifth Class I placed the three Letters whose date is less certain, and beneath them I added three others, distinguished by smaller type, whose author is uncertain.

Lastly, I either printed anew or corrected for the most part the contents of the individual Letters. Erasmus had copied most of these, and the Benedictine Editor had copied them from Erasmus, but they were full of errors and often contradicted the history. I introduced new capitulations almost everywhere, adding numerical markers by which the reader’s memory is supported and the use of citations is made much easier.

Finally, lest I appear arrogantly to claim credit for my own labor, two of our friends diligently prepared the two Indices, one of Scripture and the other of subjects.

What remains is to present the chronological arguments that I promised.

---

# THE CHRONOLOGICAL ORDER OF THE LETTERS DEMONSTRATED BY THEIR CONTENTS

## FIRST CLASS OF LETTERS, WHICH JEROME WROTE CHIEFLY FROM THE DESERT OF CHALCIS, FROM THE YEAR 370 TO 380

### I. Written about the year 370 or 371

We assign the first place in the sequence of the Letters to this one, which seems to claim the same place among Jerome’s other writings as well—at least among those that the author wished to be read by posterity and that have come down to us.

At the beginning he immediately declares that idleness had dried up, as it were, a little rust of his intellect and the power of his former eloquence; and shortly afterward he complains that a man who has not yet steered a skiff on a lake is being exposed to the roar of the Euxine Sea. By these words he clearly hints at the leisure that followed his Roman studies and at the rust brought on by the long duration of his travels; and because he had not yet tested his abilities in any other work, he distrusts himself in adorning this one.

The year in which the Letter itself was written is investigated as follows. Near the end of the Letter he says that Auxentius, who was lingering at Milan, was buried beneath the vigilance of Evagrius almost before he was dead. By this he clearly indicates the Roman Synod convened chiefly through the efforts of Evagrius, at which Auxentius was condemned by the judgment of ninety-three Bishops from Italy and Gaul.

Baronius and Holstenius assign this Synod to the year 369; Valesius to 370, followed by the Benedictine Monks in the *Life of Saint Athanasius*, although, with Pagius, they hesitate over whether it may have taken place later. But there is truly no necessity for postponing it, and such a delay is not supported by Saint Basil’s Letter 220 to Damasus concerning the convocation of a Synod against the Arians, which is usually assigned to the end of the year 371. For when Basil wrote, he was unaware of the Roman Synod that had already taken place.

Accordingly, since it must be assigned to the year 370, this Letter of Jerome cannot be dated earlier than that year. From what follows, however, it cannot conveniently be attached to any later date unless one chooses the beginning of 371.
