From that year through the whole of 373 Jerome traveled through the regions of the East; for a long time, to use his own words in Letter III, he wandered uncertainly through Thrace, Pontus, and Bithynia, through the whole of Galatia and Cappadocia, and through the lands of Cilicia, until he settled in Syria as in a most secure harbor.

Moreover, Innocentius, to whom the Letter is addressed, had already been carried from the living by a sudden fever around the middle of the year 374, as we shall show shortly below from Letter III. I do not say that it could not have happened that, during his travels, Jerome wrote a brief historical account in a Letter to Innocentius, his companion on the journey. But I consider it much more probable that Jerome wrote it when, returning from his journey in the West, he found leisure in Italy; and therefore it should be assigned either to the year 370 itself or to the beginning of the following year.

Once these points have been established, one cannot conceal the opinion of certain learned men who wish those words about Auxentius—“buried almost before he was dead”—to indicate Auxentius’s actual death. Since they maintain that he died in the year 374, they therefore believe that the Letter must be dated after that time.

This opinion had also persuaded the distinguished Tillemont, and it has the appearance of truth. Nevertheless, the following consideration chiefly prevented me from accepting it. It seemed wholly improbable that seven or eight months intervened between the death of Auxentius and the election of Saint Ambrose, who succeeded him in the episcopate; no ancient writer who carefully followed the circumstances of the history has reported such a delay.

Indeed, an even longer interval might have to be supposed if we wished to place this Letter at Antioch in the year 374. Jerome could not have learned of Auxentius’s death earlier than at least two months afterward, since that much time would necessarily have been required for the news to travel from Milan to Antioch. When he wrote, moreover, he must have been writing no earlier than May, or at the latest June, if one wishes to date it late; for by the following July the same Innocentius to whom the Letter is addressed had already died, while Ambrose was ordered to become bishop on the seventh day before the Ides of December. Thus, if one calculates the interval, nearly ten months—not merely eight—would have elapsed between the death of Auxentius and the election of Ambrose, something that neither the sequence of events nor the evidence of the ancient writers seems to permit.

### II. Written about the year 374

We assign the Letter that follows, addressed to Theodosius, to the year 374, because it was written at Antioch and because Jerome had not yet fulfilled his intention of undertaking a life of solitude but was still wavering uncertainly.

### III. Written in the summer of 374

The Letter that stands third in the sequence, addressed to Rufinus, cannot have been written before this same year 374, since in number 3 Jerome laments that Innocentius—whom we understand to be addressed as alive in the First Letter—had been carried off from the living by a sudden fever.

This is demonstrated even more clearly by the mention in number 2 of the Alexandrian monk who is said to have been sent long before, through the pious service of the people, to the Egyptian confessors and those already martyrs in intention. No other Egyptian confessors can possibly be meant than those whom the Emperor Valens, in this very year 374, certainly after the death of the great Athanasius—which occurred in the middle of 373—had driven into exile because of their confession of Christ’s divinity.

The Letter therefore cannot in any way have been written later, since Jerome notes that he had not yet entered the desert but was still living at Antioch, and says that the middle of his life was in turmoil. This cannot be understood as referring to any other time than the year 374. In the preceding year the Egyptian confessors had not yet been driven into exile; in the following year Jerome himself was no longer at Antioch but in the desert.

### IV. Written at the same time

This Letter was attached to the preceding one and was written and sent at the same time.

### V. Written several months after the preceding one

The entire context proves that this Letter was written several months after the preceding one, but still in the year 374. Jerome was no longer at Antioch but in that part of the desert that borders Syria and the Saracens.

See the Preface to *Obadiah*, near the end.

### VI, VII, VIII, IX, X, XI, XII, XIII. Written about the year 374

Having undertaken the solitary life during the course of the year 374 and for some time thereafter, Jerome sent these eight Letters to his friends, especially to the Aquileians. The same chronological indication is evident in each: either the solitude that had recently begun or the arrival of Heliodorus in his homeland.

Their order among themselves is easily established from the relationship they bear to one another. We have merely moved the Letter to Antonius, which is number twelve, from its place. Although it is not easy to determine the exact time at which it was sent, it is nevertheless reasonable to believe that an interval of several months intervened, since Jerome had previously written several other Letters to the same monk that have been lost.

### XIV. Written in the year 374

The description of the desert life recently begun, together with the entire context in which Jerome attempts to draw Heliodorus into fellowship with the solitary life—as he had promised to do when Heliodorus, departing from Jerome, asked him to send an invitation after he had migrated to the wilderness—causes us to assign this Letter to the same year 374.

The reason for placing it last after the Letters just reviewed is the chronological order in which Jerome himself enumerates his works in the *Catalogue*. He says:

> “I wrote the life of Paul the Monk, one book of Letters to various persons, and an exhortation to Heliodorus.”

It appears, then, that he forms a book from the preceding Letters and places it, according to chronology, before this other Letter.

### XV, XVI, XVII. Written from the end of the year 376 to the beginning of 379

We join these three Letters together because they support one another in determining their date and differ from each other by no more than a few months.

Jerome had written to Damasus asking with which of the three bishops then serving at Antioch he ought to be in communion and requesting that Damasus inform him whether three hypostases should be affirmed in God. When the Roman Pontiff did not answer this request, Jerome urged him again in another Letter, after an interval of at least three or four months, as it is reasonable to believe.

On the other hand, when factional men were pressing him to accept the expression “three hypostases,” a new term for a Roman, he preferred to escape their violence. Writing to Marcus, he states that he would depart from the desert at the latest when winter was over.

The year of each Letter can easily be inferred from the fact that in both Letters to Damasus he plainly affirms that Vitalis had already been established in the see of Antioch. In the first, however, he says that he is in Syria, and that, despite the great distances between them, he cannot seek from the Roman Pontiff the holy thing of the Lord, follow in those regions the exiled associates of the Egyptian confessors or Bishops, or adhere to their faith.

Vitalis, as no one can rightly deny, was appointed bishop of the Church of Antioch in the year 376 by his teacher Apollinarius, or was added to the two others, Meletius and Paulinus. The Egyptian confessors, however, were recalled from exile and restored to their churches by Gratian’s decree at the beginning of the year 379. From that time onward Jerome could no longer use their communion or receive the holy thing of the Lord from them.

These Letters must therefore be assigned to the two-year period intervening between those events, namely, the years 377 and 378. Their order should be established as follows: the first Letter to Damasus should be assigned either to the latter part of 376 or the beginning of the following year; the second, which was sent several months after the first, to the year 377; and the third, addressed to Marcus, which was written in winter and at a time when Jerome appeared confident that he had received the Roman Pontiff’s judgment, either to the end of 378—say, December—or to the beginning of the following year.

The name *Campenses*, by which he calls the Meletians in number 3 of the first of these three Letters, also prevents the Letters from being dated much later. The Meletians had been expelled from the Antiochene churches and were therefore compelled to hold their gatherings in the fields.

Theodoret, in Book V, chapter 3, reports that immediately after Gratian issued the law ordering those who had been driven into exile to return, be restored to their flocks, and have the sacred buildings handed over to them, he sent Sapor, master of the soldiers, to Antioch to decide between the leaders of the parties. Each group claimed to adhere to Damasus and to represent the true communion of the Roman Pontiff, and the question was which Church should receive the buildings.

The matter turned out favorably for Meletius, who took possession of the churches assigned to him by the judgment. Those who followed him therefore no longer held assemblies outside the city in the fields and could no longer in any way be called *Campenses*, since from that year 379 onward they possessed all the churches in the city.

### XVIII. Written in the year 381

After Jerome departed from the desert of Chalcis, he easily proceeded to Antioch, where he spent a considerable number of months with Paulinus, with whom he understood that he ought to communicate in accordance with Damasus’s judgment.

There he heard and frequently honored Apollinarius of Laodicea, as he testifies in the Letter to Pammachius and Oceanus. He was carried along by an extraordinary desire to learn, and his exceptional integrity both in doctrine and in conduct provided Paulinus with no slight test, so that Paulinus himself ordained him a presbyter at Antioch.

Although others doubt whether the man who had Paulinus ordain Jerome a presbyter was truly the Bishop of Antioch, I do not see on what grounds they do so. Jerome’s Letter to Pammachius against the errors of John of Jerusalem plainly establishes that Paulinus ordained him at Antioch and during this period. “Paulinus, the bishop of holy memory,” he says, “heard the question: ‘Did I ask you to ordain me?’” and he says other things that are discussed more fully in the *Life*.

In the meantime, Jerome departed from there either in the following year, 380, or at the beginning of 381, and traveled through the cities of the East to Constantinople. There he heard and honored Gregory during the period in which Gregory held the episcopate of the imperial city—from May, after Maximus the Cynic had been deposed, until July, when Gregory voluntarily resigned at the ecumenical council.

These points being established, the final Letter of this Class, addressed to Damasus concerning the Seraphim, must be assigned to the year 381, since Jerome himself clearly indicates this in chapter 6 of Isaiah.

> “Concerning this vision,” he says, “about thirty years ago, when I was at Constantinople and was being instructed in the study of the Sacred Scriptures by the most eloquent man Gregory of Nazianzus, then bishop of that same city, I know that I dictated a brief and spontaneous treatise, both to test my modest talent and to obey the command of my friends.”

Again, in Letter 84 to Pammachius and Oceanus:

> “In the reading of Isaiah in which the two Seraphim are described as crying out, when he [Origen] interpreted them as the Son and the Holy Spirit, did I not change that detestable interpretation into the two Testaments? The book is in people’s hands; it was published twenty years ago.”

Moreover, Jerome may have remained at Constantinople for the greater part of the following year, finding a suitable opportunity for his studies, until he sailed to Rome for the council with the aforementioned Paulinus and Bishop Epiphanius.

---

# SECOND CLASS OF LETTERS, WHICH JEROME WROTE AT ROME FOR ALMOST THREE YEARS, FROM THE END OF THE YEAR 382 OF CHRIST TO BEYOND THE MIDDLE OF 385

### XIX and XX. Written in the year 383

When the affairs of the Church of Antioch were being thrown into disorder by schism, and the disturbance was increased by the ordination of Flavian at the Synod of Constantinople, imperial letters summoned the Bishops of East and West to Rome, so that they might attend the great Synod being prepared there, as Theodoret explains.

Jerome himself, compelled by ecclesiastical necessity—as he relates in the *Epitaph of Marcella* to Principia—came to Rome with the holy Pontiffs Paulinus and Epiphanius, the former governing the Church of Antioch and the latter that of Salamis in Cyprus.

Jerome himself also makes it clear that they arrived and that the Synod was held only toward the end of the year 382. In Letter 108 he writes that the Eastern Bishops who had assembled for it were unable to depart before the winter of the following year, namely 383, had ended and the sea had opened. This will become clearer when the calculation is drawn from the Letter to Asella.

Meanwhile, Damasus retained Jerome, whom he knew from experience to be highly learned, so that he might assist him in ecclesiastical matters and answer in his name the consultations of the whole world. From time to time Damasus proposed various questions to him.

First he asked about *Hosanna*, in Letter XIX. Jerome immediately satisfied him with Letter XX, which he also lists in this order in the *Catalogue*. Its assignment to the year 383 is confirmed by the sequence of events that we have described.

### XXI. Written in the same year

Not long afterward, Damasus made useful use of Jerome’s learning in resolving difficulties in Sacred Scripture. He asked Jerome to explain the parable of the two sons, the prudent and the prodigal. Jerome expounded it in a sufficiently elegant and lengthy Letter.

This Letter follows immediately after the preceding one in the *Catalogue*. Although more precise evidence concerning the date of its subject is lacking, it does not appear possible in any way to transfer it to the following year.

### XXII. Written in the year 384

The book against Helvidius makes the date of this Letter to Eustochium more certain. Jerome could not have written it earlier than the end of the year 383, since he uses language in which he professes that he had recently arrived at Rome and had long delayed writing.

Nevertheless, in this Letter he says that the book had already been widely circulated, so that one must understand that at least several months had passed since it reached the hands of the public. The year 384 had therefore already begun when he wished to instruct Eustochium, in this notable work, concerning the preservation of virginity.

For when he was living at Rome, he did not immediately become acquainted with the household of Saint Paula, whose daughter Eustochium was. Indeed, so much time had passed before he came to know it that, in the judgment of almost everyone, he could have been deemed worthy of the highest priesthood through the evidence of his virtues, as he himself relates in the Letter to Asella.

He also mentions Blaesilla, Eustochium’s sister, whom he indicates had already been a widow for seven months and was seeking the perfection of that way of life. She died at the beginning of the following year, as we shall show shortly below.

Furthermore, when Jerome wrote to Nepotianus in the year 394, as will be clearly established in its proper place, he reckoned ten years from that time and said that, after the little book on virginity that he had written for Saint Eustochium at Rome had been stoned, he was opening his mouth again at Bethlehem after ten years. From this calculation there can be no doubt about the date prefixed to this Letter.

Nevertheless, the sequence of events and the order of the *Catalogue* seem to require that it be placed immediately after the following Letter.

### XXIII. Written in the same year, 384

Of the several letters which he composed to Marcella, and of which he cites an entire book in the Catalogue, since we can scarcely doubt the year in which each was written, we have judged that this one, entitled *On the Death of Lea*, ought to be placed first—not, to be candid, on the basis of any entirely conclusive evidence, but on a conjecture supported by the order of events.

When Hieronymus was staying with Marcella and the other holy virgins—the community of women whom he calls Paula’s domestic church—he had undertaken to explain the Book of Psalms to them orally. Hence letters are found throughout his correspondence which he wrote on the occasion of some psalm, or in which he expounds at greater length what he had conveyed orally, so that it might take deeper root in them. Examples are, above all, this very letter before us, as well as another on the ten names of God, another on the Hebrew alphabet, and one which explains certain passages of Psalm 126.

It is hardly credible that Hieronymus interpreted the psalms in reverse or confused order, according as one or another happened to come to hand,

[Col. LV]

rather than proceeding, as was proper, from the earlier ones to the later—especially since there is almost nothing in the letters themselves that contradicts this. Accordingly, since this letter to Marcella precedes the others in the order and numbering of the psalms, it seemed convenient to place it before them also in the sequence. The same consideration has been observed in the case of the remaining letters, which, when the chronological calculations are fully taken into account, follow one another more suitably in their respective places.

The year is in fact nearly the same for all of them, namely 384, which is established most clearly from this first letter. In it he compares Lea’s death with the death of the designated consul, Praetextatus, who had died at about the same time. It is certain from a letter of Symmachus, in which he petitions the emperors to permit a statue to be erected in memory of that deceased senator, that Praetextatus died in this year.

### XXIV. Written two days after the preceding letter

The letter which follows, on the praises of Asella, was written two days after the preceding one. “The day before yesterday,” he says, “we said something about the blessed Lea. Immediately it touched my heart, and it came to mind that we ought not to remain silent about a virgin, since we have spoken of the second order of chastity.”

### XXV, XXVI, XXVII, XXVIII, and XXIX. Written in 384

The five letters to Marcella which follow together derive their date and order from the preceding Letter 25. The next one, entitled *On Certain Hebrew Words*, in which he explains the word *Alleluia*, assumes that the name of God *Ia*, from which that word is formed, had already been made known in the preceding letter.

The second is written in defense of that letter, *Against Detractors*. “For,” he says, “after the preceding letter, in which I had briefly touched upon Hebrew words, it was suddenly reported to me that certain little men were assiduously disparaging me.”

The remaining two, Letters 28 and 29—the former dealing with the *diapsalma*, the latter with the *ephod* and *teraphim*—had been promised in the same letter on the Hebrew words, in which he said that he would write about them. It is immediately evident from the context of both that he fulfilled this promise. Thus they follow one another with intervals of only a few days or so; yet you should understand that the earlier letter, which interprets the ten names of God and on which the others depend, was written on the occasion of Psalm 90 and, in accordance with the conjecture we explained above, has been restored by us to that place and to its proper order, the other chronological indications agreeing entirely with it.

### XXX, XXXI, and XXXII. Written in 384 or 385

We place here, on the same grounds, the letter to Paula on the Hebrew alphabet, since it was dictated while Hieronymus was attempting to explain Psalm 118.

The letter which follows, to Eustochium, *On Little Gifts*, was written toward the end of June of this year, on the feast day of the Nativity of Saint Peter, prince of the Apostles. Since he added that Marcella had asked him for both this letter and the preceding one—so that she had not asked him for letters in vain—you understand that the three letters were separated from one another by only a very few days. For unless the matters contained in them had been very recent, letters written to persons living in one and the same house would not have been sent to Marcella as though she had not previously heard them and might therefore think that they too had been written especially for her. [Col. LVI]

We pass over other arguments of this kind, for the sake of brevity, although the matter is quite certain.

### XXXIII. Perhaps written at the same time

The thirty-third letter to Paula appears to belong to the same period. Only a fragment of it survives, which has been included here from the second book of Rufinus’ *Invectives*.

### XXXIV. Written about the same time

No one will readily doubt that this letter to Marcella on Psalm 126 belongs to this period. Its position in the sequence is determined by the order of the psalm.

If Rufinus, as is probable, preserved the exact chronological order in which he reviewed these Hieronymian letters—XXXIII, XXXIV, and XLIII—in *Apology*, Book II, chapters 17 and 18, then, although all belong to the same year, he proceeded here in the reverse order: this letter must be placed before the preceding one, and Letter XLIII must be placed before both.

### XXXV and XXXVI. Written about 385

When Hieronymus received Damasus’ letter, he had undertaken to explain Didymus’ book *On the Holy Spirit* in Latin, intending to dedicate it to that pontiff, as he himself bears witness in the preface to the work. But the Roman pontiff who had first urged the holy Doctor to translate that little work into Latin died before the translation then being prepared was completed. From this it may reasonably be inferred that Hieronymus had begun the work shortly before Damasus’ death.

For a man thoroughly trained in translating books from Greek and, as usual, working rapidly, the labor would have required only a few days, unless he had been detained by other studies and interrupted it, or, pleading the illness that preceded Damasus’ death, had postponed the matter for the future.

Damasus died this year, according to the testimony of the most ancient martyrologies, on December 10 or 11. Thus both Damasus’ letter and Jerome’s letter, in which Jerome says, “I have in hand the book of Didymus *On the Holy Spirit*, which I wish to translate and dedicate to you,” must easily have preceded his death by one or two months. If anyone prefers to posit a longer interval and assign it to 384, he may support that view with an equally plausible argument.

### XXXVII. Written about the same time

Hieronymus had recently read Rheticius’ commentary on the *Song of Songs* when he gave Marcella this letter, which is entitled *On the Same Subject*. He could easily have read it at about the time when he translated two homilies of Origen on the *Song of Songs* into Latin and dedicated them to Damasus, namely, so that he might compare the meaning, learning, and skill in interpreting Scripture displayed by the two authors.

Certainly he produced those Latin homilies in 384, for in the preceding Catalogue he places them immediately after the letter to Damasus. Nor can this letter to Marcella conveniently be assigned to another year, since it was written in Rome, a point no one has ever doubted. Since both works therefore belong to a single year, and stand in such a relation to each other that one may have furnished the occasion for composing the other, this letter may, by a plausible conjecture, be assigned to the latter part of the year to which the former is attributed.

[Col. LVII]

### XXXVIII. Written about 385

The following considerations chiefly lead us to place the thirty-eighth letter to the same Marcella—although we review it later—at the beginning of 385. In the preface to his commentaries on Ecclesiastes, Hieronymus himself relates the following concerning Blaesilla:

“I remember that nearly five years ago, when I was still at Rome and was reading Ecclesiastes to the holy Blaesilla in order to urge her to despise this age [lacuna], I was asked by her to discuss all obscure matters in the manner of a little commentary, so that she might understand without me what she was reading. And so, since she was taken from us by sudden death as our work was being prepared, etc.”

These words make clear both the final period of his residence in Rome—the adverb still explains this sufficiently plainly—and the fact that Blaesilla had not yet begun her more perfect way of life.

It is known from other evidence that Hieronymus published these commentaries on Ecclesiastes toward the end of 389 or at the beginning of the following year, as will be established by certain arguments in its proper place. We have therefore judged that Blaesilla’s illness, which was immediately followed by her conversion, and then the sudden death by which she completed her life—which all occurred within an interval of only two months and are said there to have taken place nearly five years earlier—should be assigned to the beginning of the same year, 385.

We do not deny that, if someone prefers to calculate by other methods, that illness could be placed somewhat earlier and moved back to the end of the preceding year. Indeed, we consider that this can be done quite appropriately, provided that the letter itself, which is entitled *On Her Illness*, was written not merely thirty days later, during which she had continually burned with fever, but also after she had recovered her health and adopted the stricter way of life. By then it was necessary to excuse before worldly people those practices that might scandalize others: harsher food, a dark-colored tunic, and a cheaper shoe.

### XXXIX. Written shortly after the preceding letter

The same arguments used above support the proper placement of this letter, a consolatory letter to Paula on the death of Blaesilla. It was written approximately four months after Blaesilla had, in a certain sense, washed herself in a second baptism of her purpose—that is, had turned from worldly adornment to the Lord.

Again, toward the end of the letter, when she is introduced speaking of herself, she says: “I have attained in three months the labors of so many years”—that is, the reward of eternal life. From this, when the calculations are made, you may understand that approximately one month elapsed between her death and the date of the letter, and at the same time that this letter was written no more than three months, or perhaps only a few days, after the preceding one.

### XL, XLI, and XLII. Written about 385

These three letters were written in Rome, at a time when a very close relationship had long existed between Marcella and Hieronymus. They are not connected with one another, nor do they refer back to the preceding letters, so that it is possible to establish neither their order nor a distinct period.

Since they may be assigned no less suitably to the preceding period than to this year, we have nevertheless thought it preferable to attach them to this year—both so that the sequence of letters following one another should not be interrupted, and because they seem to belong more closely to the time when

[Col. LVIII]

Hieronymus incurred great unpopularity, to the point of being forced to leave Rome, after he had begun to criticize and attack the city’s vices and the perverse opinions of certain people.

### XLIII. Written in 385

The forty-third letter to Marcella is usually assigned to the period when Hieronymus, having already escaped from Rome and traveled through many distant regions, had recently settled in the cave at Bethlehem. This opinion does not please us. For when he compares the quiet of the countryside with the disturbances and inconveniences of the city, he is encouraging not so much Marcella as himself to seize some secluded solitude, so that they might be free from the present concerns and hindrances of Rome, which he sets before their eyes.

These words seem more readily understood as having been written when he had grown weary of his residence in Rome—which is also clear from the rest of the context—and was already planning in his mind to depart. These are unmistakable indications of this year.

Nor do I think that learned men postponed this letter beyond 388 for any other reason than that in ancient editions an account of Bethlehem, copied in exactly the same words from the letter of Paula and Eustochium to Marcella, was wrongly appended to this letter, contrary to the testimony of the manuscripts.

### XLIV. Written about the same time

If anyone considers attentively this letter, the shortest of all those written by Hieronymus, consisting of only a few lines, he will never persuade himself that it was sent from the desert, from so distant a region, in order that the absence of their bodies might be relieved by conversation of the spirit—as the author immediately states at the beginning. It was neither worthwhile to write so little for that purpose, nor credible that the small gifts which he interprets allegorically in jest could have been sent from so great a distance.

Among these gifts are chairs, which could indeed be given as presents by people who were present, but which no one can reasonably believe Marcella wished to send from so far away—from Rome to Palestine—with such a heavy and entirely useless expense.

The remaining clauses of this little letter also indicate to us that it was written to people absent from one another in the sense that they were not together at the moment, but who nevertheless lived in the same city, namely Rome. We have therefore restored this letter, like the preceding one, to its proper class and place by right of return—places from which Martianaeus and other learned men had unjustly expelled them.

### XLV. Written in August 385

Letter XLV to Asella occupies the final place in the second class. Its date is among the most certain of all, and its calculation is the simplest.

Hieronymus composed it hastily, weeping and grieving, when he was already boarding the ship from Babylon—as he likes to call Rome—on his return to Jerusalem, that is, from Rome to the desert.

As he himself relates in the same order in *Against Rufinus*, Book 3: “In the month of August, when the Etesian winds were blowing, he safely boarded a ship in the Roman harbor with the presbyter Saint Vincentius, his young brother Paulinianus, and other monks.”

There can therefore be no reasonable doubt that this letter belongs to that same month of August. That the August in question was August of the year 385 is made perfectly clear by other words in the letter.

[Col. LIX]

It cannot possibly be assigned to the preceding year, 384, since it is certain that Hieronymus departed only after the death of Damasus, whom he here calls and praises as “of blessed memory,” and who did not die before December

[Col. LX]

of that year.

Nor can it be assigned to the following year, 386, since he expressly testifies that he had lived with them—that is, with the Romans—for scarcely three years.

## LETTERS OF THE THIRD CLASS, WHICH HIERONYMUS WROTE FROM THE MONASTERY AT BETHLEHEM FROM THE YEAR 386 UNTIL THE END OF THE FOURTH CENTURY, AND ORIGEN WAS CONDEMNED AT THE SYNOD OF ALEXANDRIA IN THE YEAR 400

[Col. LIX]

### XLVI. Written in 386

We begin the third class with a letter belonging to someone else—namely Paula and Eustochium—which nevertheless has been accepted in both the printed editions and the manuscripts, and for which Hieronymus may seem to have supplied the occasion for writing.

It cannot in any way be assigned to a date before 386, since Paula sailed to Jerusalem in the preceding year. Nor can it conveniently be placed later, since the beginning of the letter makes it easy to see that the holy women seized the first opportunity to write, so that they might draw Marcella as quickly as possible to the holy places which they themselves had just visited and to the solitudes into which they had withdrawn.

“Love,” they say, “has no measure; impatience knows no limit; and desire cannot endure.”

### XLVII. Perhaps written in 393

From the preceding year until this one, 393, no letters of Hieronymus can be found that fill the gap of nearly seven years. Perhaps the holy Doctor, occupied in composing commentaries and other works at the cave of Bethlehem, interrupted his epistolary activity for a long time.

Accordingly, in his Catalogue of his works—which he compiled down to the fourteenth year of the reign of the emperor Theodosius—he records no letters from this period that he gave to others, except for those which he says were written daily to Paula and Eustochium.

Those letters, however, are either among the pieces placed before commentaries and other works as prefaces, or, if they are identified as different from them, they have not survived to our own age.

The first letter that appears from this period is therefore this one to Desiderius, whose date can be gathered with reasonable clarity in the following way.

Desiderius had asked Hieronymus to have copies made for him of the works he had composed. Since most of them had already been published with the rash distinction of an edition, Hieronymus sent him nothing, lest he perhaps send works Desiderius already possessed. Instead, he advised him to read the book *On Ecclesiastical Writers* at Marcella’s house or Domnio’s.

At the end of that volume, since the works he had composed down to the fourteenth year of the reign of Theodosius were briefly listed, Hieronymus told him to have copied whatever he lacked from the Index.

For Hieronymus assumes that nearly everything he had written up to that day was contained in that Catalogue. If any further writings had existed, he would certainly have added them or mentioned them. Since he did neither, it is evidence that he had scarcely anything beyond the Catalogue to point out to his anxious friend.

The letter should therefore reasonably be assigned to the year immediately following the composition of *On Illustrious Men*, namely 393. We do not deny, however, that

[Col. LX]

Desiderius may have been warned that Hieronymus possessed more recent little works and might therefore have asked him for other writings on that account.

There is no trace of this in the letter. Moreover, Desiderius was, unless we are mistaken, a man who can conveniently be understood to have been living in Rome at that time. For he is the same person as the famous Aquitanian who not long afterward migrated to Palestine, and who, when leaving in 398, carried certain gifts in Hieronymus’ name to Vitalis. Later, after being made a presbyter, he urged Hieronymus to write against Vigilantius. We have assembled elsewhere, in its proper place, arguments that seem to us substantial in support of this identification.

### XLVIII. Written in 393 or at the beginning of the following year

After the books written against Jovinian, this letter to Pammachius follows. As Hieronymus himself says, in it he “made my defense” (*ἀπελογησάμην*, “I defended myself”) as best I could and discussed the matter in a longer letter.

It is established that Hieronymus sharpened his pen against Jovinian—whom he here notes as already condemned through Pammachius’ efforts—either toward the end of the preceding year or at the beginning of 393. Nothing compels us to think that the letter itself was written later than that year.

To support this with other arguments, we may first cite what emerges from the preface to the commentaries on Jonah, since the dates of several letters that follow are determined by the order in which they are reviewed there.

“About three years have passed,” he says, “since I interpreted five prophets—Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, and Haggai—and, detained by another work, I could not complete what I had begun. For I wrote a book *On Illustrious Men*, two volumes against Jovinian, an *Apology*, also *On the Best Kind of Translation* to Pammachius, and two books to Nepotianus, or *On Nepotianus*, besides other works which it would take too long to enumerate.”

This approximate three-year period must be reckoned from 392, by the end of which year he had written both *On Ecclesiastical Writers* and the works against Jovinian, through the beginning of 396. We shall demonstrate that Tillemont is entirely removed from the appearance of truth when he tries to force Hieronymus’ passage and thinks that “four years” should be substituted for “three.”

Meanwhile, since this letter—which he there calls the *Apology*—and the one joined to it, Letter XLIX, were written after such an interval that Hieronymus could say that he had long been concealing the complaints of his opponents, and since the books had been circulated so widely that people arriving from the city would repeatedly read to him what they reported having heard at Rome, we reasonably conclude that approximately one year had elapsed. The letter should therefore be assigned to the end of 393 or the beginning of the following year.

[Col. LXI]

### XLIX. Joined to the preceding letter

As we have just noted, this letter was joined to the preceding one, was written at the same time, and was sent together with it to Pammachius.

### L. Written about 394

Hieronymus is distressed that a certain rumor-mongering monk still disparages him on account of his books against Jovinian. “He ought,” he says, “either to have reproved me or to have questioned me by letter, as the learned and noble Pammachius did, to whom I made my defense (*ἀπελογισάμην*, ‘I defended myself’) as best I could and discussed the matter in a longer letter.”

Therefore, if the date of the earlier letter to Pammachius is correct, it is clear that this one should be assigned not long afterward, either to the beginning of 394 or very near it.

### LI. Written about the same time

Hieronymus translated into Latin, for the benefit of Eusebius of Cremona, a letter which Epiphanius had written in Greek shortly before. This he did in the same year, 394.

This is established clearly enough by the fact that Letter LVII, which we shall show below belongs to the earlier part of 395, was written one year and six months after this one.

### LII. Written in this year, 394

When Hieronymus wrote this letter to Nepotianus on the life of the clergy, he himself explicitly indicated the year, 394. At the end he said that, after ten years, he was compelled once again to open his mouth at Bethlehem, after the little book on virginity which he had written at Rome to Saint Eustochium had already been stoned—that is, attacked.

That little book is Letter 22, which we stated belonged to 384. Again, as we observed above from the preface to Jonah, its position in the sequence is such that it can conveniently be assigned only to this year.

### LIII. Written about the same time

Hieronymus had received from Paulinus a most gracious letter which, from the beginning of their friendship—an indication that neither had previously written to the other—bore witness to a friendship already tested and longstanding.

He replies to it in this letter. After praising Paulinus’ studies and eagerness for knowledge at length, he especially urges him to renounce the world completely and to cut, rather than loosen, the rope of riches that still held him back, like a little boat stuck fast on the shore.

In other words, he urges him to abandon entirely the small properties that remained to him and not to concern himself with how wisely he might sell them for the use of the poor, since they could become an impediment while he cautiously and gradually postponed the matter and kept putting off the day.

Since the life and third and fourth letters of Saint Paulinus establish that in 394 he had already begun selling part of his property and renouncing earthly possessions, it is easy to infer from the foregoing that Hieronymus’ letter should be assigned to that same year.

### LIV. Written toward the end of 394

Hieronymus himself indicated the date of this letter, which he wrote to Furia, when he said: “I know that nearly two years ago I published books against Jovinian.”

As we have stated more than once elsewhere from the preface to the commentaries on Jonah, and as will be established more fully in its proper place, the holy Doctor composed those books against Jovinian at the beginning of 393. If nearly two years are added to that date, one arrives at the end of 394, which we assign to this letter.

### LV. Written about the same time

In this letter he explains three questions from the New Testament. The first is drawn from Matthew’s Gospel,

[Col. LXII]

the other two from Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians.

But since he neither lists this letter in the Catalogue nor cites his commentaries on Matthew in it, this indicates that it was written after he had composed *On Illustrious Men*, that is, after 392, and before he explained Matthew, namely before 398.

According to Hieronymus’ usual practice, it is scarcely credible either that he would fail to count an exegetical letter on Holy Scripture among his other works if he had composed it at that time, or that, if he had explained the same question in its proper place, he would have made no mention of that work.

That nearly five-year period, therefore, bounded by these dates, is the certain chronological framework of the letter. Nevertheless, we shall say that it more probably belongs to 394, because of the authority of learned men and the following conjecture.

When Hieronymus discusses the resurrection of bodies near the end of the letter, and the sense in which Christ is said to subject everything, and finally himself, to God the Father, he introduces nothing against Origen on the occasion, but rather employs almost the same method of interpretation by which he shows himself less concerned to guard against Origen’s doctrine—a doctrine which he later began to condemn.

### LVI. Written about 394

It has not been sufficiently established to which of the two years, 394 or 395, this letter of Augustine to Hieronymus should be assigned.

The inclination would easily be toward 394, since Augustine was still serving in the office of presbyter. But, so that we may not delay the reader or appear to repeat what has already been done, we append the arguments of the Benedictine editors of Saint Augustine on this matter.

“At the beginning of this letter,” they say, “Alypius is praised, having already attained episcopal dignity after his return from Hieronymus. Baronius assigns Alypius’ journey to Palestine to 394 and his promotion to the episcopate to 394. Therefore the letter was written in 394 or certainly in 395, but not later, since Augustine wrote it while he was not yet a bishop, according to Letter 104, section 2.

“This is supported by the fact that Augustine likewise attacks—though without naming the author—Hieronymus’ opinion concerning Peter’s rebuke by Paul, which he here rejects, in *On Lying*, chapters 5 and 20. In the *Retractions*, Book 1, he places that work last among those he wrote while he was not yet a bishop.”

### LVII. Written toward the end of 395

Since not only the letter of Epiphanius which we reviewed above, but also most of the important stages of the Origenist controversy depend upon this letter, the authority of learned men makes it difficult to establish its date with certainty. We have not examined that authority elsewhere, lest we delay the diligent reader.

Tillemont and Martianaeus assign it to 396, while our fellow countryman Cardinal Norisius thinks it was written two years later.

As for Norisius, I believe that he was led into error by the fact that, twenty years earlier, he had read Jerome’s Latin translation of Eusebius’ *Chronicle*, deceived by a corrupt reading. There one must certainly read fifteen instead of twenty—or XV for XX, Roman numerals which are easily confused in writing and can mislead.

That Hieronymus undertook this work when he was at Constantinople in 380 is established by so many and such certain

[Col. LXIII]

testimonies that no one has ever called it into question.

But if we retain the corrupt reading of the letter, we would have to assign it not merely to 398 but to the very end of the century—something immensely contrary to every appearance of truth.

The arguments that follow also draw us away from the other opinion. When Hieronymus wrote this letter, Theodosius had some time earlier condemned Hesychius, a man of consular rank, to capital punishment. But Theodosius himself died on January 17, 395, and the sentence against Hesychius cannot be understood as having been imposed later than the beginning of that month.

This letter therefore belongs to approximately the same period, certainly to the same year, indeed to the first part of the year. For the adverb *dudum* (“some time ago”) is used of a short interval, especially according to Hieronymus’ meaning and usage, so that it denotes something scarcely past or just recently past. Even when it extends more broadly in writers of inferior quality, it can never be taken to signify an interval of a full year or more.

[Note: [Col. LXIII] Some maintain that *Dudum* was Hesychius’ praenomen, in which case he is called *Dudus Hesychius*. See Basnage, *History of the Jews*, Book III, chapter II, p. 54. This is in volume V as it is entitled, or volume III, part I.]

Furthermore, the remaining features of the letter fit this period extremely well. In the much-praised preface to the commentaries on Jonah, it is placed immediately after the *Apology* to Pammachius and counted among the works composed during the three years beginning in 393. On our hypothesis, therefore, there is no need to do violence to the holy Doctor’s text, as Tillemont does when he says that “four years” should be read instead of “three,” despite the unanimous opposition of all the manuscripts and printed books, as well as the correct reckoning of the dates.

Again, if, where this letter mentions the translation of the *Chronicle*, we recognize a slip in the word “twenty,” as we contend we must, and correct the passage at our own risk, this date too will agree perfectly with the argument. For if fifteen years are added to 380, the result is 395, the year we assign to the letter.

Finally, the year and a half during which Epiphanius’ earlier letter remained hidden in Greek at Eusebius’ house, from which this letter of Hieronymus begins, can be calculated with complete propriety. It is therefore entirely unjust that Tillemont, as he often does, accuses the holy Doctor of carelessness in reckoning the years.

### LVIII. Written about the same year, 395

When Hieronymus had read the panegyrical oration of Theodosius which Paulinus had just composed, he praised it highly in this letter, which he sent to its author, Paulinus.

From the date of that oration it is not difficult to determine the date of the letter itself, since Gennadius, chapter 48, states that Paulinus dedicated the oration to Theodosius, who, as we noted above, died in the preceding month of January, 395.

The subject of the panegyric itself proves that it was not written before September of the preceding year, 394: it celebrated Theodosius’ victory over the tyrants Maximus and Eugenius, and Eugenius was not defeated and killed before that month.

This letter, therefore, in which Hieronymus congratulates Paulinus on the brilliance of his talent in adorning that

[Col. LXIV]

work and gives him thanks, may perhaps be assigned to the end of 395.

Several other arguments support this, especially one usually drawn from Vigilantius, who is praised toward the end of the letter. He is said here to be leaving Palestine, and perhaps carried the letter to Paulinus; yet he was still there toward the end of the preceding year, 394. At that time, suddenly terrified by an earthquake in the middle of the night, he leapt out naked and without a tunic and prayed in the sight of others. Hieronymus reproaches him for this disgrace in the little work he entitled *Against Vigilantius*.

### LIX. Written in 395 or 396

Among the questions from the New Testament which Marcella had proposed for Hieronymus to solve was the second in order, which she said she had read incidentally in his works: that the sheep standing on the right and the goats standing on the left represented Christians and Gentiles, rather than the good and the wicked.

Hieronymus professes that he does not remember ever having said this, but he does not deny that, as much as occurred to him suddenly while dictating, he had discussed the matter in the second book against Jovinian—or had discussed a related question, namely the passage in which bad fish are separated from good fish.

From this it may be argued without difficulty that the letter was written at least one or two years after the books against Jovinian. For Marcella seems to have had before her no works other than those mentioned in the preface to Jonah and composed between 392 and 395; nor does Hieronymus indicate that the books against Jovinian had only then been published, but rather that they had been circulated not long before, so that the passage might have come to mind when he recalled the matter.

### LX. Written at the beginning of 396

We assign this letter to Heliodorus on the death of Nepotianus to the beginning of 396. We are convinced by firm arguments that it can neither be postponed further, as many learned men do, nor placed earlier.

First, it is absolutely certain that it must fall within approximately the three-year period which Hieronymus himself reckons from the end of 392 in the preface to the commentaries on Jonah. For if it is extended with Tillemont to 397, four years rather than three will have elapsed.

It is no less certain that the letter could not have appeared before 396, since it recounts the miserable ends of three men of consular rank—Timasius, Rufinus, and Abundantius—which occurred toward the end of the preceding year, 395. It notes that Abundantius was an exile not at Sidon, where he had first been banished, but at Pityus. Rufinus, whom historians report to have been the first to fall from the highest rank of fortune, was not overthrown and killed until November 27.

A well-known error must therefore be avoided here, into which many learned men fall because they do not properly understand the words of Saint Hieronymus. They think that he says these calamities of illustrious men occurred two years earlier. He says nothing of the kind. Rather, after lamenting the condition of the emperors and wishing to cite private ruin as well, he declares that he will omit cases extending beyond two years. To support his point, he says that it is enough to mention the different fates of

[Col. LXV]

three men of consular rank who had recently fallen.

Finally, there seems to be an argument of the greatest weight in our favor in this passage. After Hieronymus had stated that the East had previously been free from the evils weighing upon other parts of Roman territory, he immediately adds:

“Behold, last year, wolves sent against us from the furthest rocks of the Caucasus—no longer wolves of Arabia but of the North—traversed such great provinces in a short time.”

By these words he most clearly indicates the Hunnic peoples whom Rufinus admitted into the territories of the Empire in 395 to aid his rebellion. There can therefore be no further doubt that the letter, said to belong to the following year, must be assigned to 396.

On the contrary, it is impossible to explain this passage according to those who postpone the letter until 397. How could the holy Doctor have said that in the preceding years the East had scarcely experienced battles and incursions by barbarian peoples, when Claudian, in *Against Eutropius*, Book 1, and other authors establish that the barbarians had already widely devastated Asia and Syria from 395 onward?

### LXI. Written around the end of 396.—

Jerome’s entire concern is to drive as far from himself as possible the slander of Origenist heresy, and to rebuke Vigilantius sharply—a most cunning and abusive man who, after recently departing from Palestine under a feigned reconciliation of friendship, dared, on the very journey by which he was making for his homeland, amid the waves of the Adriatic Sea and the Cottian Alps, once again to open his foul mouth against Jerome and to spread his name far and wide in disgrace. Hence the generally accepted opinion—which we also share—is that this letter should be assigned to the year 396, since it is established that Vigilantius escaped from Palestine only in the preceding year, 395, and toward its end. We indicated this shortly above in the other letter to Paulinus.

### LXII. Written in 396 or 397.—

We believe that we have extracted the year assigned to this letter to Tranquillinus from almost the entire context, on grounds that are not inappropriate. The Origenist controversy was then beginning to stir disturbances in the Church, and at Rome the question concerning Origen was finally being debated: whether he should be wholly rejected—a view for which only a certain Faustinus is cited as a witness—or whether, as some held, he should be read in part. Jerome, who does not hesitate to prefer the latter opinion, asserts that those who are led either into excessive love of Origen or into hatred through the perversity of their own stomachs are subject to the prophetic curse: “Woe to those who call good evil and evil good.”

He rejoices to learn from Tranquillinus that Oceanus opposed the madness of those who allowed themselves to be deceived by Origenist errors, and that this was happening for the first time, while an educated man was coming to the aid of those who were in error. Oceanus, however, had already left Bethlehem with Saint Fabiola in the preceding year, 395, and, having returned to Rome, explained to those whom he had instructed Jerome’s views and teaching.

Nothing, moreover, appears anywhere in the letter that indicates factions organized around Origen’s name, or repeats complaints against Rufinus, or introduces the other matters that are mentioned at every third word in the letters that immediately follow.

### LXIII. Written around 397.—

Among Jerome’s surviving letters to Theophilus—for many have perished, as we have noted in their proper places—this very brief letter appears to hold the first position. It cannot conveniently be assigned either before 396 or after 399, but is bounded on either side by that approximate three-year period. Nevertheless, in view of the calculations of other learned men, we judge that it should more readily be assigned to the end of 396 or to the following year, 397.

At that time there was a disagreement between John of Jerusalem and Jerome, which had begun on the occasion of Epiphanius’ letter. For a long time our author endured Theophilus’ silence toward him, although Theophilus was the person by whom the disagreements were to be settled; he regarded that silence as a form of administrative discretion. Yet he did not cease from his duties, and imitated the widow in the Gospel who persistently appealed to the harsh judge.

Now, however, having at last received letters from Theophilus, he is indignant that he should be admonished concerning ecclesiastical canons, since nothing was more important to him than to preserve Christ’s rights and not to transfer the boundaries established by the Fathers. By these words he is not, as might appear at first glance, defending the ordination of his brother Paulinianus, which John had put forward as the cause of the dispute—namely, that Paulinianus had been consecrated in John’s diocese by a foreign bishop, contrary to the canons. Rather, he wishes more truly to defend himself: since 394 he had not been in communion with the bishop of Jerusalem, and in this matter he claims that the Roman faith, praised by apostolic speech, is sufficient for him—the faith of which the Church of Alexandria boasts that it shares.

As for his disapproval of Theophilus’ policy, by which he was conducting himself too leniently and with excessive patience toward the Origenists, and his assertion that this displeased many holy men lest, while waiting for the repentance of a few, Theophilus should foster the boldness of the wicked and allow the faction to grow stronger: once these statements are compared with the preceding material, anyone can easily persuade himself that they cannot be understood more suitably than as belonging to 396 or the following year.

### LXIV. Written in 396 or 397.—

This letter to Fabiola is commonly and justifiably assigned either to this year or the preceding one, after she had abandoned Bethlehem, where she had stayed for some time, in the face of the devastation brought on by the Huns, and had returned to Rome. That she was then living in the City is indicated by these words at the end of the letter. After saying that he had seen a certain book of Tertullian, *On the Garments of Aaron*, only in the catalogue, he adds: “If, because of the fame of the City, it has been found among you, I beg you not to compare my little stream with that river.”

### LXV. Written in the middle of 397.—

The following words in the Preface to the Commentaries on Matthew, addressed to Eusebius, persuade us that this letter to Principia was written before Jerome composed those commentaries:

“I beg you, when you come to Rome, to give a copy to Christ’s virgin Principia, who asked me to write on the Song of Songs. Excluded from that work by a prolonged illness, I have deferred the hope of completing it to the future.”

For at the end of this letter he had promised that, if life permitted, he would explain the entire Song of Songs to her. Since he had been prevented from completing it by an illness lasting five months—elsewhere he says three—he later asked Eusebius to excuse him to Principia.

From this we also learn that the letter was not, as others, especially Martianaeus, think, entrusted to Eusebius when he was setting out for Rome and then returned by him to Principia. For in that case, since Jerome had not written on the Song of Songs as she had requested, he ought to have attributed the failure to that same illness; yet he does nothing of the kind. Rather, it had been sent through someone else before Eusebius departed and had therefore been written at least several months before the illness, perhaps around the middle of 397.

### LXVI. Written around the end of 397.—

The entire chronology by which the true date of this letter is established must be derived from Letter LXXVII, entitled *On the Death of Fabiola*. There Jerome testifies that nearly two years earlier he had given this letter to his friend Pammachius on account of Paulina’s sudden journey.

Since it is absolutely certain—as we shall show in its proper place—that the letter on Fabiola’s death belongs to the summer of 399, it will be sufficient to assign this letter on Paulina’s death to the final months of 397, if nearly two years are understood to have elapsed—say, ten months beyond the year. Everything else fits this hypothesis exceedingly well; it is also supported by the fact that there is not yet any mention of Jerome’s illness.

### LXVII. Written in 397.—

These are Augustine’s second letters to Jerome. At the very beginning he expresses his gratitude that Jerome had returned a full letter to him in place of the salutation written beneath another letter.

The situation was this: in the preceding year the bishop of Hippo, while subscribing a letter belonging to someone else from Africa, had courteously greeted Jerome. Jerome, through a certain deacon named Asterius, who was then sailing toward the West, promptly returned the courtesy of the greeting in a separate and complete letter—the one alluded to here—and Augustine’s present response was sent in reply to it.

Jerome’s letter cannot now be found, and some infer only from section 9 of this response that it dealt with Origen and his errors. Just as Profuturus did not deliver the earlier letter of Augustine to Jerome, which we reviewed above—for, while preparing for his journey, he was made bishop—so Paul did not deliver this second one, since he changed his plan to sail to Palestine. As a result, the letter was circulated through Italy before it reached Jerome. Jerome received it through another bearer, the deacon Sisinnius, and thought that it had been written against him with the intention of offending him and had been published to the general public.

Its date can therefore be investigated with ease. According to Letter CV, Sisinnius had found it, among Augustine’s other treatises, not in Africa or with Augustine himself, but on the island of Adria, at the latest in 398—that is, approximately five years before Jerome wrote Letter CV, which belongs to 403, as we shall demonstrate more fully in its proper place.

For Paul to change his plan and cross into Italy, for the letter to be published, and for it to be issued together with Augustine’s other treatises, scarcely allows a shorter interval than this. Thus the letter cannot reasonably be assigned much later than 397.

We infer the same again from another letter of Augustine, numbered here CIV, which cannot conveniently be placed before this one. It was dictated when Augustine was already a bishop, as he makes sufficiently clear when he says that he had prepared the first letters—those counted here as CI—while he was still a presbyter, so that the later letters may be understood to have proceeded from him as bishop. It is established that he was not ordained bishop before the end of the preceding year, 396, close to the Nativity of the Lord.

The Benedictine editors place before these letters of Augustine the letters of Jerome beginning, “Last year, through our brother Asterius,” and likewise assign them to 397. Since, however, their conjecture does not sufficiently persuade us, we have moved that letter from its place and postponed it to number CIII and as far as the year 402. When we reach that point, we shall offer what seem to us firmer arguments, which led us to establish a different order. See also below, Letter CXI.

### LXVIII. Written in 397.—

Heraclius the deacon was the bearer of this letter to Castrucius. Through Heraclius, Jerome had learned that Castrucius, eager to see him, had come as far as Cissa while returning from Palestine to Pannonia.

In this year, 397, a certain Amabilis, apparently a bishop of Pannonia, had sent that deacon from Bethlehem so that, by appearing in person, he might obtain from Jerome an explanation of the Ten Visions of Isaiah, which he had previously requested from him. Saint Jerome explains the matter in the Preface to those interpretations, addressed to Amabilis:

“This year you sent our son Heraclius the deacon, who summoned me to court with hand joined to hand and demanded the work that had been promised from moment to moment.”

It therefore seems rightly established that the letter to which the interpretation of the Visions is attached belongs to that same year, since the same person obtained both works and undertook to carry them at the same time.

The fact that Heraclius came to Bethlehem again in the following year, as we shall explain in its proper place when reviewing the letter to Vitalis, cannot possibly refer to this letter addressed to Castrucius. Jerome writes to Castrucius that he will gladly receive him if, when the holy deacon comes again to Palestine, Castrucius accompanies him and acts as his guide. Jerome had been made to hope by Heraclius, as he departed from the East, that the latter would return there.

As for the commentary on the Ten Visions of Isaiah, there is no room for doubt that it must be assigned to the same period in which Heraclius first returned from Palestine. For when he sailed once more from Pannonia to the East and brought the letters of the presbyter Vitalis to Jerome, Jerome, in answering him, mentions Isaiah’s prophecy, which he says he had recently interpreted among the Ten Visions.

Moreover, in another letter to Lucinius—which, as we shall establish by firm arguments, must be assigned to 398—he testifies that he had recently discussed Isaiah’s extremely obscure Visions in a historical exposition.

Therefore, if the proper date of the letters to Vitalis and Lucinius is 398, as we establish both by other arguments and especially by Jerome’s prolonged illness during that period, it follows with certainty that the Book of the Ten Visions, said there to have been recently explained, must be assigned to the preceding year, 397. Consequently, the letter to Castrucius itself—the purpose for which all the preceding discussion has been offered—must also be assigned to that year, since we have shown that it belongs entirely to the same period.

### LXIX. Written around 397.—

This letter was certainly written after Oceanus’ return from the East to Rome with Fabiola, which occurred in 396, and before the first book of the *Apology against Rufinus*, which is assigned to the beginning of 402.

The first point is proved by the inscription itself. The second follows from these words in that book of the *Apology*:

“I hear that Chrysogonus, a follower of his [Rufinus], objects to me why, at baptism, I said that all sins are forgiven, and that when a woman’s second husband has died she rises again to a new husband in Christ . . . I shall answer him briefly. Let them produce the little book which they accuse; let him answer it, let him overthrow it in his own discussion, and let writings refute writings.”

Since it is not entirely easy to determine to which of the intervening years the letter properly belongs, we assigned it to the earlier part of 397, persuaded by the authority of learned men, since almost everything fits this hypothesis reasonably well.

### LXX. Probably written in 398.—

Magnus had asked Jerome why he inserted examples from secular literature in his little works, as though he were polluting the purity of the Church with pagan filth. Jerome answered him throughout this letter, yet he perceived that the question had been proposed to him by Calpurnius Sallustianus—a name by which he designates Rufinus—and he confirms that suspicion quite openly in the first book against Rufinus:

“Clearly this is Calpurnius Sallustianus, who through Magnus the orator—though not a great one—had raised a question for us.”

For this suspicion to have entered Jerome’s mind, and for him to have stated it, if not with certainty, at least with plausible justification, it is necessary—or at least highly probable—that Rufinus, whom Magnus was believed to have prompted to raise the question, was already living at Rome when the letter was delivered.

Of the two years, 397 and the following year, 398, during which Rufinus remained at Rome under Siricius after his return from Palestine, the latter appears the more suitable for assigning this letter concerning the question at issue.

### LXXI. Written in 398.—

We assign the letter to Lucinius to the period around Lent of this year, 398, because of Jerome’s own words about himself:

“Held by a prolonged illness, I scarcely began to breathe again during the days of Lent, when the notaries were departing.”

This illness is marked by the same chronological indications as the one he mentions in the Preface to the Commentaries on Matthew, when he says:

“With Easter already approaching, you compel me to dictate, although you know that I have been so ill for three months that only now am I beginning to walk again.”

A little later, or toward the end of the same year, while writing to Evangelus about Melchizedek, he says:

“After a prolonged illness, I could scarcely be free of fever during the days of Lent, and, while preparing myself for another work, I used up the few days that remained in the exposition of Matthew.”

It is established from the Preface to the work on Matthew itself that Jerome dedicated those commentaries to Eusebius of Cremona when Eusebius was departing from the East for Rome and wanted him to provide this work, as though a traveling ration, for his sudden voyage.

It is no less certain from the third book of the *Apology against Rufinus* that Eusebius’ departure for Rome occurred in 398, since it must be placed one year after Rufinus had arrived there.

Accordingly, the Commentaries on Matthew must be assigned to April of 398—for Easter fell on April 18 in that year—and the three months during which Jerome suffered from continual weakness must be reckoned from approximately December of the preceding year.

Since this is so, the letter to Lucinius itself, which bears the same marks and mentions the same illness that allowed him to breathe again, however briefly, during Lent, should reasonably be assigned to the first part of 398, perhaps to April. Moreover, he sends Lucinius here the extremely obscure Ten Visions of Isaiah, which he says he had recently discussed in a historical exposition. This provides a further chronological indication, as will be abundantly clear from the chronological reasoning in Letter LXVIII above.

### LXXII. Written in the same year, 398.—

Just as the preceding letter, written after the Ten Visions of Isaiah had recently been presented in a historical exposition, is nevertheless established as belonging to 398, so this letter, which Jerome sent to Vitalis, must be assigned to the same period, since Jerome says that he had recently interpreted that same prophecy of the Ten Visions—unless the arguments by which we establish the preceding date deceive us.

Vitalis’ question was brought to Jerome by Heraclius the deacon, the same man about whom much was said in the discussion of the letter to Castrucius. Jerome, in replying to Vitalis, mentions that he had recently explained the Ten Visions of Isaiah. Above we showed that Heraclius had carried those Visions, which had been entrusted to him, to Amabilis.

It follows clearly that this letter refers to a second journey by that deacon to Palestine, which took place in 398.

### LXXIII. Written in the same year, 398.—

This letter to Evangelus appeared not long after the Commentaries on Matthew had been written. Jerome himself makes this sufficiently clear in the following words:

“After a prolonged illness, I could scarcely be free of fever during the days of Lent, and, while preparing myself for another work, I used up the few days that remained in the exposition of Matthew. Then I resumed my neglected studies with such eagerness that what benefited the exercise of my tongue harmed the health of my body.”

There is therefore no need to determine the letter’s true date beyond adding several months to the Commentaries on Matthew, during which Jerome, in taking up his neglected studies with the greatest eagerness, relapsed into the illness from which he had only just begun to recover.

Since above we assigned those commentaries to April of 398 on the basis both of their Preface and of Eusebius of Cremona’s departure for the West, it is easy to understand that the letter belongs to the middle of the year.

### LXXIV. Written toward the end of 398.—

Jerome dictated this letter while lying in bed, exhausted by a prolonged illness, and scarcely able to dictate it rapidly to his notary. Again, near the end of the letter, he counts twelve months during which he had been worn down by continual weakness.

It will easily be clear that these months must be reckoned from December of the preceding year, 397, if one observes that this is the same illness which, in the Preface to the Commentaries on Matthew, he says had lasted three months when he wrote during the days of Lent—that is, counting back again from March—and which he immediately mentions in the letter to Evangelus and in the preceding letter to Lucinius.

The holy Doctor, then, having begun to breathe again somewhat during the days of Lent in this year, quickly interpreted Matthew. He then took up his neglected studies with such eagerness that, as he himself testifies in the letter to Evangelus, what benefited the exercise of his tongue harmed the health of his body. He immediately relapsed into fever and weakness, from which he had not properly recovered, and suffered continuously until the end of the year. Thus he now counts the month of Lent itself and the period extending beyond it among the months during which he was exhausted by continuous illness. Accordingly, we believe that this letter was written in November of 398, and that he very truthfully said that he had been ill for twelve months.

But lest this appear to have been established by a slight conjecture—especially since we know of no one who has hitherto assigned a definite date to this letter or properly distinguished Jerome’s illness during this period—we propose a new argument of the following kind.

This letter was certainly written while Eusebius of Cremona was at Rome, and while he and Rufinus, the presbyter of the Roman Church, were making Jerome’s name widely celebrated. This is plainly evident from Jerome’s words at the very beginning:

“I rejoice, indeed, in the testimony of your holiness toward me and in the love of the holy presbyter Eusebius, and I do not doubt that you proclaim me publicly.”

This Eusebius, who, as was established above, arrived at Rome around the middle of 398, remained there for approximately two years. For it is established by various arguments, and especially by a certain letter of Anastasius to Simplicianus—which by good fortune we found in a Milanese manuscript and shall count among Jerome’s letters in its proper place—that he went to Milan around the middle of 400.

Since the matters we have related concerning his association with Rufinus cannot be extended beyond the approximate two years during which the presbyter of Cremona lived at Rome, one thing remains: we must prove that Jerome’s prolonged illness, which is the principal mark of this letter, cannot belong to 399 or 400, and therefore must be referred entirely to the preceding year, 398, to which it fits perfectly.

This can easily be established by examining the many works that Jerome wrote during that period. None of them ever mentions his illness or gives any indication of it. How could it have happened—or how is it reasonable to believe—that a man who had lain exhausted in bed for a full year under continual weakness nevertheless continued to send letters, without ever assigning his illness as the reason; without ever mentioning that he was not writing with his own hand but dictating to notaries; and without ever saying that he had obtained even a little time for rest in which to write?

Anyone who entertains such a notion would be a stranger to Jerome’s writings and would not know—among six hundred other examples—the earlier cases in which, in each of his letters to Eusebius, Evangelus, and Lucinius, he does not allow the matter to remain hidden and wisely explains the inconvenience of the three months during which he had been ill.

Moreover, during this period Jerome produced certain works that he could not possibly have pursued if he had been burning with fever and detained by such an illness. Among these are Origen’s books *Περὶ Ἀρχῶν* (*On First Principles*), which he translated into Latin for Pammachius and Oceanus, either toward the end of 399 or at the beginning of 400, at their earnest request. He rendered the author’s meaning and words with the utmost care, so as to answer the version of those same books that Rufinus had prepared shortly before, and so that, once the dispute had been joined, a reliable judgment might be made concerning Origen’s thought and errors.

On the other hand, these facts, as well as almost everything else, fit our hypothesis exceedingly well. On that hypothesis we have shown by a straightforward argument that Jerome’s letters throughout that year—which he wrote in smaller number, as his health permitted—continually mention the illness, and that it extended through the twelfth month, with no writings intervening. Thus we do not hesitate to assign this letter to the end of 398, the period when the holy Doctor was also restored to health.

### LXXV. Written around 399.—

Among the other matters over which Jerome grieves in this letter on account of the death of Theodora’s husband Lucinius, he particularly complains that he had not deserved to see the face of that man whom he believed would soon come to Bethlehem.

Although these words are few and may not seem to indicate a definite date, we can nevertheless reasonably conclude that this letter is separated by approximately one year from the one sent to Lucinius and cannot easily be placed later.

Jerome and Lucinius had exchanged letters only once, and that in the preceding year. Therefore, unless Lucinius had given Jerome hope of visiting Jerusalem in that letter, it is not to be believed that Jerome could now say that he had hoped shortly to embrace him in the holy places. It is readily understood as having been said a year later, namely in the following year, 399, to which we assign the letter.

### LXXVI. Written at the same time.—

This letter to Abigaus was written around the same period. In it Jerome says that he commends in his own words “my holy daughter Theodora, sister of Lucinius of blessed memory, who has commended herself to me,” so that she would not grow weary on the journey she had begun but would reach the Holy Land through the wilderness after much labor, together with other statements of the same kind. These indicate that she had entered upon the path of perfection not long before.

### LXXVII and LXXVIII. Written around the end of 399.—

That these two letters belong to the part of the year 399 that was moving toward its end, and that they have the order we have established between them, is confirmed by Jerome himself.

When writing the earlier letter on Fabiola’s death, he says that he had completed the fourth cycle of summer from the time when, while composing the *Epitaph of Nepotianus*, he had expended whatever strength he possessed in the grief he was then suffering.

We have proved by sufficiently firm arguments that this *Epitaph* must be dated precisely to the beginning of 396 and cannot be postponed even slightly. Therefore, if the summers are to be counted from that point, the summer of that year must be counted first, and this fourth summer must be the summer of 399, to which we assign this letter.

Jerome does not imply that he wrote of Fabiola’s death, as he had in fact written of Nepotianus’ death, during the summer. He merely says that the fourth cycle of summer had passed since he composed that work, although he had actually written it in the very first days of that year.
