Again, he indicates that approximately two years earlier he had given Pammachius a letter concerning Paulina’s sudden journey. Since this can be assigned quite suitably to the end of 397, it is necessary to assign this letter to 399 so that it may correspond to that chronological indication.

As for the other letter addressed to Fabiola herself, we append it here because, although it may perhaps have begun to be written long ago, when Fabiola herself was at Bethlehem, it was nevertheless postponed by God’s will until the present time, after her death, as Jerome states. In section 8 he dedicates it to her memory, so that, clothed in the priestly garments of the earlier volume addressed to him, she might rejoice that she had at some time come through the solitude of this world to the promised land.

### LXXIX. Written in 399 or 400.—

Although this letter lacks any clear chronological markers, it is nevertheless not rashly assigned by the common judgment of learned men to approximately 400.

It cannot conveniently be placed after 401. For this is the Salvina who carried letters to Chrysostom and was joined to him by the closest bond in Christ. When he was forced to leave the see of Constantinople, he entered the baptistery and, as Palladius reports, called Salvina to him—Salvina, the wife of the blessed Nebridius, who adorned her widowhood with exceptional virtue and propriety.

But Chrysostom had received the monks of Nitria who were Origenists, and from that time onward he was already poorly regarded by Jerome, who supported Theophilus and had been imbued with a preconceived opinion against him. It is therefore hardly credible that letters were sent to Salvina during that period, when she might reasonably have been suspected of sharing John’s views concerning Origen.

Nor can the letter be assigned before 395, since in his letter to Hedibia Jerome says:

“How a widow ought to live . . . we believe that we have discussed more fully in the two little books that we wrote to Furia and Salvina.”

We have already shown above that the letter to Furia, which precedes this one, belongs to the end of 394.

Of the approximately five years within which this letter to Salvina could fall, the last seems by far the most suitable. It is indicated that Salvina’s mother was at Constantinople with her daughter when Jerome wrote:

“Certainly, when a holy mother is with you and a perpetual virgin clings to your side,” and so forth.

She must not be thought to have crossed to Constantinople before the death of her husband Gildo in 398, although from the same words it is easy to suppose that she had already been there for one or two years.

### LXXX. Written, indeed, in 398, but delivered to Jerome somewhat later.—

The Preface of Rufinus to Origen’s book *Περὶ Ἀρχῶν* (*On First Principles*), which he translated into Latin, cannot properly be regarded as a letter to Jerome. Nevertheless, it is placed here because Jerome, perceiving that it adorned him with flattering and figurative praise and brought him forward as a witness in support of Origen, was compelled to respond to it in order to clear himself of people’s suspicions. He did so in letters sent to Rufinus himself.

Rufinus had therefore arrived at Rome from the East in 397. No one should doubt this, since we have shown by other arguments that Eusebius of Cremona left Palestine for Rome around Easter of the following year, 398, and in the third book of the *Apology* is said to have departed one year after Rufinus’ journey.

Rufinus remained there for nearly two years, from approximately April 397 until September of the following year, 398. First he translated Pamphilus’ *Apology for Origen* into Latin; then he likewise translated Origen’s own work *On First Principles* into Latin. From this arose the entire occasion of the dispute and the great conflagration in the Church.

He rapidly translated the first two books of that work during the days of Lent and explained the remaining books somewhat more slowly. This indicates that the translation belongs to the year 398, since it is not reasonable to believe that he sailed to Rome during the winter, before Lent of the preceding year, over an impassable sea, and then completed that work.

Meanwhile, by divine providence, these books—which Rufinus cautiously kept within the walls of his house—came into the hands of Eusebius. Eusebius attacked the blasphemies with all his strength, exposed the hidden poison to the public so that the simple might beware, and warned Jerome to clear himself of the suspicion into which that Preface had drawn him.

These things could have been accomplished quickly, toward the end of the year. Rufinus, who had cautiously obtained letters of communion from Pope Siricius before the latter’s death in November, went to Aquileia. In the first book of his *Invectives* he complains about Eusebius, because Eusebius had chosen to attack him in his absence, when he could have refuted him more forcefully in person.

### LXXXI. Written in 399.—

This letter belongs to 399. The principal arguments for this date are as follows.

First, Jerome does not seem able to have received copies from Rome of Rufinus’ Preface—the Preface to which this response was directed—any earlier in that year, or certainly not until the final months of the preceding year, as is clear from the sequence of events involving Eusebius, which we explained above.

Second, Jerome now does not hesitate to say that Rufinus had been recalled to his homeland by longing for his spiritual fathers, Chromatius and Eusebius. Jerome himself could not have learned this before the end of the preceding year, because of the distance between the places from which the information was sent; nor could he have affirmed it with certainty until at least several months after Rufinus’ return.

We therefore calculate that Rufinus did not depart before September of that year, and that Jerome was speaking accurately of Eusebius when he said that Eusebius could have refuted him more forcefully in person, but had preferred to attack him in his absence.

Moreover, if the calculation by which we established Jerome’s illness in the preceding year is correct, he must have been recovered for several months when he wrote this letter to the presbyter of Aquileia, since he makes no mention either of his illness or of his restored health.

### LXXXII. Written around 399.—

The entire context makes it clear that this letter was written shortly afterward, though still in the same year in which Jerome sent Pammachius the longer treatise on the same subject—that is, against John of Jerusalem. When we publish that treatise in the series of his shorter works, we shall show that it belongs to 399 and shall answer the arguments of learned men who have postponed it to one period or another.

In the meantime, however, it seems worthwhile to bring forward two considerations, so that the date we require to be established with certainty may not lack reasons of its own.

First, Jerome says that he had prepared the Commentaries on Ecclesiastes and the exposition of the Letter to the Ephesians approximately ten years earlier. As far as the Commentaries are concerned, he himself testifies elsewhere, and especially in their Preface addressed to Paula and Eustochium, that he composed them around 390. There he clearly indicates that he undertook the work approximately five years after he had escaped from Rome.

If nearly ten years are added to that date, the year 399 results.

The second argument by which we establish the same year is drawn from the fact that, near the end of the short work, Jerome says that thirteen years earlier he had abandoned Antioch, that most celebrated city, so that, in the fields and solitude, mourning the sins of his youth, he might turn Christ’s mercy toward himself.

These thirteen years cannot in any way be reckoned except from the completion of the year 386, since it is established that he remained at Rome until August of the preceding year, 385. At that time he sailed to the East and, after traveling through various regions, finally settled at Antioch.

He says that he abandoned that city because, although he could have discharged the office of a priest splendidly in its Church, to which he appeared to belong on account of his ordination, he preferred to seek the fields and solitude, so that he might wipe away the sins of his youth through repentance.

Thus, when thirteen years are added to 386, the year 399 emerges. That is the year to which the treatise must be assigned. The same date must be assigned to the letter to Theophilus, which was written shortly afterward, as the entire sequence and context of the discourse prove. The references there to Isidore, the Alexandrian presbyter, also persuade us that it had not yet reached the year 400, since we shall understand Isidore to have been condemned at the beginning of the following year.

Nevertheless, this letter appears to deserve chronological precedence over the two preceding ones, still within the same year, 399.

### LXXXIII and LXXXIV. Written in the year 400

The earlier letters of Pammachius and Oceanus to Jerome, since it is natural to suppose that they were sent a few months before Jerome’s reply, which we append below, must be dated from that reply itself. This reply, moreover, must be assigned to the year 400, for what seems to us an irresistible reason: here he cites, as number 3, the letter to Damasus concerning the Seraphim and the “Cal­culus,” and states that it had been published twenty years earlier. Now, I think, no one will call into question what we have demonstrated in its proper place by such definite arguments—namely, that this letter must be assigned to the middle of the year 381, when Jerome was living at Constantinople with Saint Gregory, bishop of that city [Col. LXXVI].

But the twenty years that he counts should properly be understood as begun, not completed: partly because he reckons from the middle of 381, and partly because he uses a round number. For it is absolutely certain from the sequence of events and from the very context of the letter that it appeared before Origen was condemned in the Alexandrian Synod, in this same year. This, however, is why we would prefer to assign the letters of Pammachius and Oceanus to the end of the preceding year, 399, so that several months may be understood to have intervened before Jerome’s reply, during which he could have translated Origen’s books *On First Principles* (*περὶ Ἀρχῶν*) into Latin and sent them to Rome together with this letter.

### LXXXV. Written in the year 400

Of the letters said to have been written to Paulinus, this is the last in order. Jerome excuses himself to the holy presbyter because he had not been able, in the meantime, to explain Daniel as he had promised to do:

> “Recently, at the command of our Pammachius, I translated the books *On First Principles* (*περὶ Ἀρχῶν*) . . . . Detained by this work, I was unable to fulfill what I had promised you, and I postponed our Daniel yet again.”

Then, toward the end of number 4:

> “The necessity mentioned above drew me back from the very preparation and beginning of the translation.”

No one, therefore, can deny that this Letter followed the books of Origen at a very short interval. We have just said that those books were translated into Latin at the beginning of this year, 400, and that this translation was sent to Pammachius together with the preceding letter.

### LXXXVI, LXXXVII, LXXXVIII, LXXXIX, XC, and XCI. Written in the year 400

Although the same year of composition can easily be assigned to all six of the following letters—whether they belong to the period between 400 and 401—their order is reversed in one respect, since Letter LXXXIX appears to deserve precedence over the others.

All six letters have the same chronological mark and characteristic: the condemnation, in the Alexandrian Synod convened chiefly through Theophilus’s efforts at the beginning of this year 400, of Origen and of the frenzied men who wished to sow and establish Origen’s heresy in the monasteries of Nitria.

Moreover, all were sent—as is plainly evident from their context—before Jerome translated into Latin the synodical letter of that Council, written in Greek by Theophilus. He completed this a little after the middle of the year, as we shall show by definite arguments shortly, in the note to the following letter. The six letters are therefore comprised within at most seven or eight months. We have consequently established the order given here, judging it more coherent in view of their mutual relationships and as the circumstances themselves seemed to require.

### XCII. Rendered into Latin after the middle of the year 400

We have said that this synodical letter of Theophilus to the bishops of Palestine and Cyprus, which until now was believed to have perished through the ravages of time, was rendered into Latin by Jerome after the middle of the year 400.

The principal argument for this assertion is drawn from the third book of the holy Doctor against Rufinus, which unquestionably was written around the middle of the year 402. There Jerome, while recounting in order what he had translated from Theophilus over nearly two years, places the synodical letter first, then the Paschal letter of the year 401 against Origen and his disciples, and finally another letter from the following year against Apollinarius and the same Origen. He claims to have translated no other work of Theophilus.

Thus, to make it perfectly clear from the order in which the individual works are listed that this letter belongs to the year 400, which precedes the others in position, the matter is more conveniently understood on the assumption that nearly two years had elapsed—a fact that cannot otherwise be established.

### XCIII, XCIV, and XCV. Rendered into Latin or written shortly after the preceding letter

We gave, in the earlier part of the preface, the reasons why we count these three letters among Jerome’s letters, although only the first two have Jerome as their translator. There is no room to recall them here.

As for the chronological date of each, however, they fit and connect with the preceding synodical letter so neatly, and with one another, that there can be no doubt that they should be assigned approximately to the same year, 400.

The first two respond directly to Theophilus and his letter. There is no reason to doubt that Dionysius and the fathers of the Jerusalem Synod did so after a short interval, indeed as quickly as possible—both because of the importance of the matter at issue and because their context shows that they acted with great anxiety.

The letter that Pope Anastasius sent to Simplicianus, certainly the bishop of Milan, requires fuller proof before it can be shown to belong to the same period. Summoned by the letter of the aforementioned assembly—Theophilus’s—Anastasius wrote it and entrusted it for delivery to the presbyter Eusebius, who had brought him certain chapters of blasphemy excerpted from Origen’s books.

This Eusebius is none other than the famous Cremonese friend of Jerome, bitterly hostile to Origen’s supporters. We have seen that he remained in Rome from the middle of the year 398 and understand that he left after nearly two years, both from other arguments and especially from the first book of Rufinus’s *Invectives*, where Jerome says that, when Eusebius was at Milan, he attacked him over a certain fictitious opinion of Origen.

Anastasius therefore entrusted the letter to Eusebius when he was setting out from Milan, and for that reason it must be assigned to the year 400.

The same date, however, may perhaps be established more clearly from the person of Simplicianus himself, to whom the letter was addressed. For, as has been ascertained from the records of the Church of Milan, he died on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of September. Learned men have demonstrated by a straightforward argument that this was in the month of the present year 400.

For in the following year, 401, after the consulship of the most illustrious Flavius Stilicho, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July, Venerius, who succeeded Simplicianus, is mentioned as bishop of Milan in the canonical code of the African Church, chapter 56, where a delegation is sent to him from the Fifth Council of Carthage.

Accordingly, Anastasius could not have written to Simplicianus later than this year 400; nor, on the other hand, could he have sent this letter before that same year, since he says that he was writing in response to Theophilus’s letter concerning the condemnation of Origen.

## CLASS IV OF THE LETTERS THAT JEROME WROTE FROM THE BEGINNING OF THE YEAR 401 UNTIL 420, THE END OF HIS LIFE

[Col. LXXVII]

### XCVI. Written and rendered into Latin in the year 401

The first in the order of this fourth class of letters is this Paschal letter of Theophilus against Origen and his disciples, which Jerome rendered into Latin.

At its end, Easter is announced for the nineteenth day of the month Pharmuthi, which plainly indicates the year 401, as Cardinal Noris correctly observed. That day of Pharmuthi corresponds among the Latins to 14 April. For, as Saint Ambrose most accurately states in his letter to the bishops of Emilia, Pharmuthi, which is the first month among the Egyptians, begins on the sixth day before the Kalends of April and ends on the seventh day before the Kalends of May.

On 14 April of the year 401, the Paschal feast was celebrated in the Roman Church, in the eighteenth solar cycle, the third lunar cycle, and letter F. After Noris’s arguments, this cannot reasonably be called into doubt.

Accordingly, we had to correct the error of Martianay and the other editors, who reverse the order of these letters and place first the one announcing the Paschal cycle of the following year, 402. The Paschal indicators, which are the most certain signs of the years, and the Milanese manuscript from which we have borrowed the unpublished documents of the Origenist controversy, provide excellent safeguards against that error.

There is no doubt that Jerome gave this letter to Latin readers in this same year, as is perfectly clear from the third book of his work against Rufinus, where he appends it to his translation of the synodical letter, and from various other testimonies.

### XCVII and XCVIII. Written in the year 402

These two letters appeared together and are connected with each other. In the first, he dedicates the translation of the Paschal letter to Pammachius and Marcella, as he had done the preceding year:

> “Receive the Greek letter, and also the Latin one for this year, lest the heretics again claim that many things have been added or altered by us.”

A little farther on he says:

> “If anything has been said here less fully against Origen, it is contained in the letter of the preceding year.”

The date of the letter is sufficiently clear when he says that the blessed Pope Anastasius was persecuting the heretics and wishes him many years, so that through his zeal the resurgent shoots of heresy might wither and die over a long period.

For the death of Anastasius, as late a date as possible, must be assigned to 27 April of this year 402, as is attested by the chronicles of Prosper and Marcellinus Comes, as well as by many ancient martyrologies.

When he says that, in early spring, he is sending Theophilus’s second Paschal letter from Alexandria, it is clear that he is not speaking of any other Paschal letter than the one appended below. As Jerome notes, it is divided into four parts: the first exhorts the faithful to celebrate the Paschal feasts with the utmost holiness; the second attacks the disciples of Apollinarius; the third attacks Origen; and finally, after inviting the heretics to repentance, it announces Easter for the eleventh day of the month Pharmuthi.

This corresponds among the Latins to the eighth day before the Ides of April, on which day, in the year 402, with the nineteenth solar cycle, the fourth lunar cycle, and letter E, the Lord’s Paschal feast was celebrated in the Roman Church [Col. LXXIX].

### XCIX and C. Written in the year 404

Here, for once, we have anticipated the chronological order so that Paschal letters of the same subject and author might follow one another continuously. The two that follow belong to the year 404, after the death of Saint Paula, which occurred on the seventh day before the Kalends of February of that year.

For, as Jerome says in the first letter to Theophilus, number 2:

> “I have been so overwhelmed by the falling asleep of the holy and venerable Paula that, apart from translating this book”—that is, the Paschal letter—“I have written no other work of God up to the present.”

Both appeared together: first, the letter to Theophilus, by which Jerome sent him the translation of the Paschal letter and explained the labor he had undertaken in giving it to Latin readers; and second, the Paschal letter itself of the Alexandrian bishop, which he sent to him at the same time in Latin translation, joining it to the earlier letter.

That there may be no doubt about the date of the letters, which is plainly established by Paula’s death, will be made still more certain by the Paschal indication. Easter is announced for the twenty-second day of the month Pharmuthi, that is, among the Romans, 17 April. On that day, as our Noris notes, Easter was celebrated in the leap year 404, with the twenty-first solar cycle, the sixth lunar cycle, and letter C.B.

### CI and CII. Written around the year 402

The Benedictine monks, to whom we owe the edition of Saint Augustine, assign these two letters to the year 402, guided by the following conjectures.

They suppose that they were written after Paulinianus’s return from the West to Palestine, since Augustine greets him and is in turn greeted by him through Jerome. They say that Paulinianus was sent by his brother Jerome to the West in the year 398 to sell their common patrimony, as Jerome says in Letter 56 to Pammachius, and did not return to Bethlehem until the end of the year 401.

Moreover, Jerome now sends Augustine his *Apology against Rufinus*, either the first or the second; Augustine quotes some of its words in Letter CLXVI, number 15.

Rufinus had certainly already sent his curses to Jerome, as is stated in this letter, number 30. He did so after the first *Apology*, thereby providing the occasion for the second, as is clear from that later *Apology*, which belongs to the year 402.

These are the arguments of the Benedictines. Without offering any reply to them, we omit here the additional points they make concerning Asterius, the bearer of the letter, and the conjectures they draw from them, because we think the matter must be arranged and explained in another sense and order.

### CIII. Written in the year 403

As we noted above [Col. LXXX], the Benedictines believe that this letter of Jerome to Augustine was sent six years earlier, namely in 397. They advance the following arguments for their view.

They maintain that Asterius the subdeacon, who carried Jerome’s preceding letter and is praised at once at the beginning of this one, sailed twice from the East to Africa and back from Africa to the East. They cannot be persuaded that the letter which Jerome here recalls as having been entrusted to the same Asterius in the preceding year—one in which he would readily perform the service of conveying greetings—is the very letter now under consideration, whose beginning is:

> “At the very moment of the departure of our holy son Asterius the subdeacon.”

Furthermore, since Jerome here indicates that he was established in a monastery but was nevertheless shaken by various waves from every side, they do not think that this could have been written after 397, but rather before he had been reconciled with John of Jerusalem. They apparently had not read that, from the time of that reconciliation until the persecutions stirred up against him by the Pelagians, Jerome had ample occasion to complain in this way.

Accordingly, the letters of Jerome that we are discussing, which we count as the third of those addressed to Augustine, they make the second. As for the first letters, which have perished and to which Augustine replied, “I give thanks that …,” there is no disagreement on either side.

Yet in the first place, Asterius’s supposed repeated journey from Africa back to the East seems to us wholly fictitious; there is neither the slightest trace nor any indication of it in Jerome’s or Augustine’s letters. Indeed, it is to be understood from them that he undertook only one journey, which is also by far the most probable explanation.

Next, Jerome’s description of the preceding letter as a ready service of greeting is so far from inappropriate that he could scarcely have recalled it in more fitting words. It is shorter and breathes Jerome’s affection for Augustine throughout:

> “See how much I love you: though provoked, I did not wish to reply, nor do I believe that what I might otherwise have criticized belongs to you.”

But the principal point is that he calls the greeting-service “ready” because the letter was sent at the very moment when Augustine’s letters were delivered to him:

> “At the very moment of the departure of our holy son Asterius the subdeacon, my intimate friend, your letters, Your Blessedness, reached me.”

It also fits perfectly with what Jerome says about being shaken by various waves from every side. At that time he was in Jerusalem, where there was Rufinus’s faction; there were the Origenists, who attacked Jerome with insults, slanders, and other persecutions, thus giving the holy Father occasion to complain.

Since there is therefore no reason to twist Jerome’s words in another direction or to overturn the order they naturally indicate, we append this letter to the preceding one and assign it to the following year, 403, since he expressly states in the very first words that it was sent by him from that time.

### CIV. Written in the same year, 403

The entire context of this letter makes clear that Augustine had not yet received either Jerome’s letter entrusted to Asterius in the preceding year or the more recent one to be carried by Praesidius [Col. LXXXI], when Jerome took advantage of the very timely opportunity provided by the deacon Cyprian and entrusted this letter to his diligence and fidelity.

For, as the most learned Benedictine editors say, Jerome makes no mention of his disagreement with Rufinus. He also speaks openly here about his opinion of Augustine’s labor in translating the books of the Old Testament from Hebrew—something he certainly would not have done if he had understood that Augustine had been disturbed and offended by his earlier letters.

Again, Augustine joins together three other letters written earlier. Of these, he believed that the later two, namely LXVII and CI, had not reached Jerome, while he knew that the earlier one, LVI, had not been delivered. From the sequence of events that we have set out, it therefore follows that the letter under discussion belongs to the year 403.

### CV. Written in the same year, 403

This letter responds to Augustine’s letters—not those carried by Cyprian, but two that had been delivered to Jerome shortly before, namely LXVII and CI, as is clear from number 4. There he repeats certain words from those same letters, which had been sent to him in the preceding year. This letter, therefore, is readily assigned to the year 403.

The same conclusion follows from number 1, where Jerome says that Augustine’s Letter LXVII, about which he is here complaining, had been found by Sisinnius on the island of Adria nearly five years earlier. We have shown that this occurred around the year 398.

The frequently mentioned Benedictine editors, from whom these arguments are largely taken, add that Jerome responds partly to the preceding letters, but partly also to another letter that has not been found. In that letter Augustine supposedly indicated that a certain letter requiring a reply had first been handed by him to Profuturus, then sent through someone else; that this person had feared the dangers of the sea and changed his plans for the voyage.

They then add that Jerome did not send this reply before Cyprian’s return. Cyprian was both the bearer of this reply, according to Augustine’s Letter CXVI, number 30, and the bearer of another letter of Jerome’s, Letter CXII, written at the end of the year 404 or later.

### CVI. Probably written in the year 403

This outstanding letter to Sunnias and Fretela is usually counted among those whose date is less certain and is not assigned to a definite period. We think otherwise and believe that we have found unmistakable indications by which it may conveniently and readily be assigned to the year 403.

The first point is generally admitted and was also properly noted by Martianay: Jerome would never have passed over this eloquent letter in silence if he had composed it at the time when he was writing his *Apology* on his own behalf against Rufinus.

Since the presbyter of Aquileia was then chiefly attacking Jerome with slander over his undertaking to revise the translation of the Old Testament by the Seventy, it is scarcely credible that Jerome, in order to repel his adversary’s slander, would have gathered examples here and there while suppressing this one letter in silence—a letter in which the Seventy are consistently praised and which could have supplied him with the most eloquent testimony on his own behalf.

He had therefore not yet prepared it. It must consequently be placed after the middle of the year 402, to which Jerome’s later *Apology* is assigned.

But it does not seem possible to postpone it beyond the following year, 403, if we are not mistaken in being persuaded that it is mentioned in Jerome’s Letter CVII to Laeta, which we shall append shortly.

There Jerome, enumerating the advances that had accrued to the Christian religion at that time, says:

> “From India, Persia, and Ethiopia we daily receive crowds of monks; the Armenian has laid down his quivers; the Huns are learning the Psalter”—

and so forth.

By these last words we believe that no others are meant than the Huns Sunnias and Fretela, or Huns living near them, whom Jerome had just taught the Psalms in the letters now under discussion, bringing their Greek and Latin variant readings closer to the Hebrew truth.

For why, unless he had this letter in mind and was referring to it in writing, would he attribute the Psalter to them and say that they had long been instructed in it? Why would he not instead speak of laid-down arrows, warlike breasts converted to Christian gentleness, and other such qualities more suited to their character?

Since the letter to Laeta must certainly be placed in the year 403, as we shall soon show, before the death of Saint Paula—which occurred on the seventh day before the Kalends of February in the year 404—this letter to Sunnias and Fretela, which is understood to have preceded it, may very suitably be assigned to the preceding year, 403, after the books of apology against Rufinus had been written.

[Note: [Col. LXXXI] See this very letter to Sunnias and Fretela, number 12. From that passage it seems that the holy Father wrote it before he corrected the other translation from the Greek, or the Gallican translation, as it is called. See also the notes on that passage of the Psalter.]

### CVII. Written in the year 403

If what we have just explained in assigning the letter to Sunnias and Fretela to this year is sound, this letter to Laeta, dictated at least several months after it, must belong to the end of the year.

It certainly cannot be transferred to the following year, 404, since it repeatedly mentions Paula, Laeta’s mother, who was still alive and could hold her granddaughter, Laeta’s daughter, in her arms and mold her tender spirit toward virtue, whereas it is established that Paula died at the beginning of that year.

There is also no less clear an indication in number 2, where Jerome says that the red-haired and blond army of the Getae was carrying its tents around the churches, and perhaps was therefore fighting against us in an equally balanced battle line because they professed the same religion.

The Goths, whom he calls Getae, had invaded Italy in the year 400. Two years later, in the consulship of Arcadius V and Honorius V, they fought bravely in an evenly matched battle against the Roman army. Prosper said in his chronicle that the battle was fought at Pollentia with the severe slaughter of both sides.

Jerome plainly refers to this battle when he writes in the following year, 403—

### CVIII. Written in the year 404

To console himself and Eustochium over the grief with which he was overwhelmed by Saint Paula’s falling asleep, Jerome dictated this letter on her praises and life in two short compositions. It is easy to gather from the whole sequence of the discourse that he did so a few months after her death.

At the end of the letter, he explained by the following indications when she had departed this life:

> “The holy and blessed Paula fell asleep on the seventh day before the Kalends of February, on the third day of the week, after sunset. She was buried on the fifth day before the Kalends of the same month, in the sixth consulship of the Emperor Honorius and the consulship of Aristaenetus.”

This was in the year 404.

### CIX. Written in the same year, 404

Jerome himself states in his book against Vigilantius that he had sent this letter to Riparius of Tarragona two years before deliberately composing the treatise against Vigilantius. Speaking of the vigils and all-night services often celebrated in the basilicas of the martyrs, he says:

> “I replied briefly in another letter, which I had written nearly two years earlier to the holy presbyter Riparius.”

As Jerome himself notes, he dictated that treatise because the brother Sisinnius was in great haste and was preparing to travel to Egypt for the sake of the shrines of the saints.

From the preface to the second book of the *Commentaries on Zechariah* and partly from another passage in the third book on Amos, this Sisinnius is understood to have been hurrying to Egypt in the year 406, when he had received from the holy Doctor the commentaries on Zechariah to be delivered to Exuperius of Toulouse. Jerome testifies that he had composed them in that same year 406, which was designated in the consular records by the sixth consulship of Arcadius Augustus and the consulship of Anicius Probus.

Thus, when the calculations are made, this letter to Riparius, which was sent nearly two years earlier, belongs to the year 404.

### CX. Written around the year 404

This is what the Benedictines say about the date of this letter:

> “After Cyprian’s departure for Palestine, when Augustine, having received through Asterius Letter CII of this collection, realized that Jerome had been somewhat offended by his letters—which he complained had been circulated throughout Italy but had nevertheless not reached the person to whom they were written—he did not delay, but immediately wrote this letter in reply. While endeavoring to satisfy Jerome’s complaints, Augustine testifies that he had received the *Apology against Rufinus*. He says that he had been frightened by the example of the disagreement that had arisen between them, since he had read in Jerome’s letter certain indications of Jerome’s own indignation.

> “This letter therefore belongs approximately to the year 404, by which time Augustine had reached his fiftieth year of age. He declares himself to be an old man in number 5, not using the word ‘old’ there, as he sometimes does, to indicate the final period of life, which begins at the age of sixty-one; otherwise the letter would have to be postponed beyond the year 414.”

### CXI. Written in the same year, 404

Although Praesidius is called a fellow priest—that is, a bishop—in the heading of this letter, he nevertheless seems entirely to be the same man whom, at the beginning of the preceding year, Jerome strongly commended to Augustine in Letter CIII, calling him a deacon and especially dear to him.

From this, and still more from the present letter itself, it may again be understood that the letter in which Praesidius was commended to Augustine was more suitably assigned by us to 403 than, as is commonly done, to 397.

This letter, which we are discussing, was written on the occasion of the preceding one, as the Benedictines correctly observed. Augustine requests that the preceding letter be sent to Jerome through Praesidius and even asks Jerome to be reconciled to him through Praesidius’s letters. It is therefore easily understood to belong to the same period, namely the year 404 [Col. LXXXIV].

### CXII. Written around the end of the year 404

The Benedictines argue for the date of this letter as follows:

> “When Cyprian was returning to Africa, Jerome gave him two letters for Augustine, namely Letter CV and this Letter CXII, according to Augustine’s Letter CXVI, number 36. In this Letter CXII Jerome responds to three of the letters brought to him by Cyprian, namely LVI, LXVII, and CIV. He says nothing about Letter CX, which he had certainly not yet received.

> “He was therefore writing toward the end of the year 404. Certainly not earlier, since John Chrysostom had already been deposed, as he indicates rather clearly in this same letter, number 6.”

### CXIII. Rendered into Latin, and CXIV. Written in the year 405

We have established in the notes, by definite arguments, that these are to be regarded not as one letter, as has hitherto been maintained, but as two. One of them, truncated through most of its more important portion, had Jerome as its translator; the other, which appears to be complete, presents him as its author.

We therefore infer that both proceeded from the holy Doctor’s pen at approximately the same time. In the latter, namely Letter CXIV, by which he returned to Theophilus the Theophilian book together with his accompanying letter—of which only this brief fragment survives—he gives as excuses for the delay in translating the work the sudden eruption of the Isaurians, the devastation of Phoenicia and Galilee, the severity of winter, and intolerable famine.

These circumstances indicate the year 405, when the Isaurians, after laying waste the regions of Phoenicia and Galilee, brought terror upon Palestine and especially Jerusalem; from this also arose the intolerable famine.

The winter of this year is likewise described as unusually severe in several letters written after Chrysostom’s deposition.

The letters of Jerome should therefore preferably be dated approximately to the middle of that year, because, when excusing his delay in translating Theophilus’s writings, he says that during the days of Holy Lent he was seized by the gravest illness and had almost crossed the threshold of death.

[Note: [Col. LXXXIV] I fear that this may be the very grave illness which he mentions in the preface to the third book on Amos, and which unquestionably befell the holy Doctor in the year 404, the sixth consulship of Arcadius Augustus and the consulship of Anicius Probus.]

See the notes on Letters CXIII and CXIV.

### CXV. Written in the same year, 405

The Benedictine editors investigate the date of the letter in this way:

> “Jerome sends this through Firmus, excusing himself for having finally replied, though unwillingly, when provoked and compelled to do so by Augustine—namely, in Letter CXII, which therefore shortly preceded this Letter CXV.

> “In the following letter, number 1, Augustine also seems to suspect that his Letter CX had already been delivered to Jerome before Jerome dictated this one to him.

> “This letter is therefore not rashly assigned to approximately the year 405.”

### CXVI. Written at approximately the same time

The Benedictines again say:

> “After reading the preceding letter, Augustine immediately wrote this Letter CXVI to Jerome. In it he responds both to that last letter, brought by Firmus, and to the other two carried by Cyprian, namely Letters CV and CXII.”

### CXVII. Probably written in the year 405

Jerome mentions this letter in his book against Vigilantius, which unquestionably belongs to the year 406:

> “Lest the malicious interpreter again say that I invented material to which I could reply with rhetorical declamation, as I did in the letter I wrote to the Gauls who were quarreling with one another, mother and daughter” [Col. LXXXV].

We have conjectured that this refers to Jerome’s most recent work and that it was separated by only a short time from the work against Vigilantius. For why would he then recall an old slander?

Perhaps the malicious interpreter was also Rufinus. Since Rufinus made no such accusation against Jerome in the books of the *Invectives*, he must be thought to have brought it out of his mouth later.

These conjectures readily indicate the year 404 or the following year, 405.

### CXVIII. Written in the year 406

To Julianus, who was bidding a final farewell to the world, Jerome proposes for imitation the holy man Pammachius and Paulinus the presbyter, a man of the most fervent faith. They offered to the Lord not only their wealth but themselves.

From this it is properly established that the letter cannot be reviewed before the year 397 or 398, when Pammachius embraced the monastic life after the death of his wife Paulina; nor after 409, when Paulinus was raised to the episcopate.

Meanwhile, Jerome mentions among Julianus’s trials the devastation of the entire province by a barbarian enemy; the destruction of his private estates amid the general devastation; the driving away of herds of cattle and flocks of sheep; enslaved servants who were bound and killed; and other events of this kind. It is therefore not obscure that he indicates the year 406 as the time when he wrote.

The eruption of the barbarians that swept through those regions must be understood as none other than the invasion that occurred under Rhadagaisus in the year 405, during the consulship of Stilicho II and Anthemius, as recorded in Prosper’s chronicle.

This letter may therefore quite suitably be assigned to the following year, 406, perhaps even to its end.

### CXIX. Written toward the end of the year 406

The holy Exuperius, bishop of Toulouse, had sent the monk Sisinnius to the East in this year 406 with a large sum of money, in order to relieve the poverty of the monks of Palestine and Egypt. Sisinnius also brought to Jerome the questions of Minervius and Alexander, as is clear from the preface to the *Commentaries on Zechariah*.

He reached Bethlehem when autumn was already ending, as is known from that preface. After delivering his letters to Jerome, he promised to remain there until the day of Epiphany, as is clear from number 1 of the letter under discussion.

Jerome says:

> “With so generous a period of time before me, I thought I would answer each of them. While I was dictating to most of them in the stolen hours of the night, and, after completing the others, was reserving yours—those of Minervius and Alexander—as though the most difficult of all, he suddenly appeared and said that he was about to depart immediately.”

There can therefore be no doubt that Jerome was forced to reply hastily before the days of Epiphany, and thus before the month of January of the following year. The letter may most conveniently be assigned to December of this year 406.

### CXX and CXXI. Written at approximately the same time

Jerome nowhere mentions in these letters the devastation inflicted on Gaul by the invasion of the Goths and Vandals, which occurred toward the end of the year 406. Yet he certainly would not have passed it over in silence had he written after that disaster, when the cities of Aquitaine, Narbonensis, and the other provinces were being ravaged from without by the sword and from within by famine.

Hedibia belonged to those regions, as is clear from the very first words of this letter. On the other hand, the questions that this letter proposed for solution were brought to Jerome by the same Apodemius through whom, apparently from those same regions of Gaul, Algasia had entrusted her questions to be delivered to the same holy Doctor, as is clear from the beginnings of both letters.

It is therefore natural to believe that both of Jerome’s replies were sent at approximately the same time, perhaps also through the same Apodemius as he returned to his homeland.

This is made especially probable by the fact that the latter letter, to Algasia, likewise makes no mention of the Vandals, although it was certainly not sent until at least several months after the year 406.

For when Remphas is mentioned in Question 10, Jerome says:

> “We discussed him more fully in the prophet Amos.”

There can be no doubt that he composed those commentaries in this same year, which was designated in the consular records by the sixth consulship of Arcadius Augustus and the consulship of Anicius Probus.

Accordingly, if these two letters, joined together, are not assigned to the end of this year—on nearly the last day of which a barbarian army invaded Gaul—they may suitably be brought forward to the beginning of the following year, 407, on the understanding that Jerome had not yet heard of the disaster in so distant a region, although its report soon spread throughout the world.

## CXXII. Written in A.D. 407

This letter, which for that reason we have assigned to A.D. 407, is the one in which Jerome recalls the invasion and devastation of Gaul by the barbarians. In order to stir Rusticus, to whom the letter is addressed, to repentance by the example of his converted wife Artemia, and to remind him of the oath by which he had promised that he would follow his wife when she departed for the holy places, either immediately or later, he sets before his eyes the wretched condition of his province—an event which, as we have shown above, points to the year 407.

“If,” he says, “the remnants of your property hold you back, so that you may see both the deaths of your friends and fellow citizens and the ruins of cities and villages, at least amid the evils of captivity, the savage faces of the enemy, and the boundless shipwreck of your province, hold fast to the tablet of repentance.”

## CXXIII. Written in A.D. 409

To dissuade Ageruchia from entering a second marriage, he exaggerates, besides the disadvantages of bigamy, those calamities which were being inflicted at that time. Among them are Spain, already on the point of perishing, and Rome herself, fighting within her own bosom not for glory but for safety—or rather not even fighting, but purchasing life with gold and all her possessions. These are sufficiently clear indications of the year 409, when Rome was besieged by Alaric toward the end of the preceding year, through the crime of the half-barbarian traitor Stilicho, sprung from the Vandals; and when, in order to buy safety by whatever means, she paid the barbarian commander an enormous quantity of gold.

## CXXIV. Written in A.D. 409 or 410

The first words of the letter themselves plainly reveal the time at which it was written:

“About ten years ago,” he says, “the holy man Pammachius sent me some notes of a certain person containing translated volumes of Origen’s *On First Principles* (*περὶ Ἀρχῶν*), etc.”

Indeed, we showed in its proper place that Pammachius’s Letter LXXXIII, which Jerome recalls here, must be assigned to A.D. 399. Accordingly, this letter to Avitus, written about ten years later, will belong to A.D. 409 or 410.

## CXXV. Written in A.D. 411

We cannot avoid referring to the already deceased Rufinus what is said about Grunnius in section 18 of this letter:

“Grunnius proceeded in a tortoise-like pace when he spoke, and at certain intervals would barely snatch out a few words, so that you would think he was sobbing rather than speaking. Yet when, after the table had been set, he had displayed a heap of books, etc.”

This extends to the end of that section.

By this single argument, we think, the conjectures of learned men are overturned—those who unhesitatingly assign the letter to A.D. 406 and wish it to be one of the letters which Sisinnius, returning from Palestine at that time, carried into Spain. For what he says near the end of the letter about Exuperius, bishop of Toulouse, and his almsgiving, refers to an earlier period. He does not here indicate those alms which Exuperius had sent through Sisinnius to be distributed among the monasteries of Egypt, but others which he was dispensing at that same period.

Since it is clear that Rufinus died toward the end of A.D. 410, the mention made here of him as already dead compels us to assign the letter at least to the following year, 411. That year also suits very well the extremely sorrowful picture of the whole world described near its end: after the City had been captured and plundered, amid the miseries of that time and swords raging everywhere, a man was sufficiently rich if he did not lack bread, and excessively powerful if he was not compelled to serve.

## CXXVI. Written in A.D. 412

When this letter was sent to Marcellinus, the tribune, in Africa, Jerome had interrupted his commentary on Ezekiel—as is clear from section 2, at the very beginning of the dictation—because his mind was too deeply distracted by the devastation of the Western provinces, and especially of the City of Rome.

In this year, after he had explained three books, a sudden assault of the barbarians swept across the frontier of Egypt, Palestine, Phoenicia, and Syria . . . so that scarcely anyone could escape their hands except through Christ’s mercy. Therefore this letter must be dated to a year other than that in which Rome was captured, as Jerome himself most plainly declares by his words, “in this year.”

This can conveniently be understood only as the second year after the devastation of the City, namely 412, since it is not desirable to defer to the following year, 413, the commentaries on Ezekiel, which in this same year he again carried from the beginning as far as the third book.

I nevertheless think that from Letter CXXXI here, section 8, together with Augustine’s Letter 190, section 6, no. 20, it may be inferred that Marcellinus did not inquire of Jerome about the origin of souls until he had received Augustine’s reply on this matter. That reply, however, is none other than Augustine’s Letter 143, which belongs to August of the year 412; accordingly, Jerome’s response might seem to have to be transferred to the following year, 413.

## CXXVII. Written in the same year, A.D. 412

A few days after Rome had been captured and plundered by Alaric in 410—perhaps in September—Marcella died. Jerome narrates this at length near the end of the present letter.

At the beginning of the same letter he explains that he had postponed praising the memory of the holy woman from the time of her death until then, and that two years had passed in silence because of the incredible grief with which the captivity of the Roman Empire had overwhelmed him—indeed, because the whole world had been afflicted by disasters—so that he judged that nothing worthy of Marcella’s praises could then be said.

When that interval of time had therefore elapsed, namely in 412, he dedicated her epitaph to her memory under better auspices, addressing it to the virgin Principia.

## CXXVIII. Written in A.D. 413

He plainly indicates near the end of this letter that Pacatula, whom he undertakes to instruct by these letters, which she would read later, had been born two or three years before he wrote them. While lamenting the calamities of his time, he says:

“The world is falling . . . the famous City, the capital of the Roman Empire, has been consumed in a single conflagration; there is no region that does not contain Roman exiles.”

A little farther on:

“In such times our Pacatula was born; amid these childish rattles she passed through the first stage of life, destined to know tears before laughter.”

This exceedingly sorrowful picture of affairs, which he describes after the City had already been captured and the head of the Roman Empire severed, does not seem to fit any year more suitably than 413. Nor, likewise, should the little girl herself be thought to have exceeded three years of age if she was born at the same time as Rome fell. For, according to the whole preceding context, she was still babbling with a childish voice in her mother’s lap and, even if she had begun to learn the elements of letters, could have done no more than join syllables together.

## CXXIX. Written in A.D. 414

Dardanus had already completed the honor of two prefectures when Jerome sent this letter to him, as is clear near its end.

First, he was prefect of the Gauls in A.D. 409, as Gothofredus records in the *Theodosian Code*, book XII, title 1, *Concerning Centurions*, law CLXXI. He held the same prefecture again in A.D. 413, as may be gathered from the chronicle of Prosper of Tiro, where it is reported that the tyrant Jovinus was overthrown chiefly through Dardanus’s efforts, after King Athaulf had withdrawn from Jovinus’s alliance. Olympiodorus confirms this.

These facts sufficiently demonstrate that the letter was not written before A.D. 414. But when Jerome says that he had recently published the first book of his commentaries on Jeremiah, and since that book might, at the latest, be assigned to the following year, 415, as we show in its proper place, it becomes clear that the letter appeared in the preceding year, namely 414.

## CXXX. Written in A.D. 414

Jerome himself indicated the time at which he was writing to Demetrias by three unmistakable signs.

The first is in section 2, where he says that he was occupied in explaining Ezekiel’s temple . . . and, in that part of the sanctuary in which the Holy of Holies and the altar of incense are described, he preferred to use this brief digression, so that he might pass from one altar to another—namely, to Demetrias.

A letter dictated during the interruption of that work should certainly not be placed after A.D. 414, since the three final books of the commentaries on Ezekiel can scarcely be carried beyond that year.

The second indication appears when he describes Heraclianus, the count of Africa, in terms that make it entirely clear that he is speaking after Heraclianus’s death:

“You do not know,” he says, “whether he was more avaricious or more cruel; nothing was sweet to him except wine and money, and under the pretext of supporting the most merciful Emperor, he proved himself the most savage of tyrants, etc.”

In A.D. 413, when he was consul with Lucianus, a man of senatorial rank, Heraclianus, as Prosper says, lost both his office and his life in August, having been held responsible for the new disturbances in Africa. It is therefore easy to understand that Jerome could not have written the account of his utterly wicked character before the end of that year.

Finally, near the end of the letter—the third indication—Jerome notes that he had published his book *On the Preservation of Virginity* about thirty years earlier. Since that book, namely Letter XXII, certainly belongs to A.D. 384, this more nearly shows that the present letter should be assigned to 414 itself.

## CXXXI–CXXXII. Written in A.D. 415

We assign the date of these letters to A.D. 415, together with the Benedictine editors, because the first was dictated on the occasion of the presbyter Orosius’s voyage to Palestine in the spring of that year, as is clear from section 2.

Orosius is demonstrably shown to have arrived in Palestine before July of that year, since no one denies that in that month he entered into public debate at Jerusalem against Pelagius.

The other letter, which Orosius received at the same time to deliver together with the first, was written at that same period. This is indicated not only by Augustine, here in section 1, in another letter, CLXIX, chapter 4, no. 13, and in book 2 of the *Retractations*, chapter 45, but also by Jerome himself in his reply, which is Letter CXXXIV here.

## CXXXIII. Written in the same year, A.D. 415

Orosius, who had received the preceding letters for delivery to Jerome, indicates the time of this letter with reasonable clarity in his *Apology*, chapter 4.

Discussing the assembly at Jerusalem and Pelagius’s error—that a person could keep God’s commandments by his own strength if he wished—he says:

“This the blessed Jerome . . . condemned in his letter which he recently published to Ctesiphon; likewise, in the book which he is now writing, he refutes it in the form of a dialogue by setting out the dispute.”

That assembly was held under John, bishop of that region, near the end of July in A.D. 415, as may be gathered from Orosius himself, who then notes that it was the forty-seventh day before the first day of the Encaenia.

The first day of the Encaenia was September 14, as we have noted elsewhere, according to Nicephorus, *History*, book 8, chapter 10.

Accordingly, the letter to Ctesiphon, which Orosius says had recently been written before the assembly at Jerusalem, may perhaps be assigned, if one prefers to carry it farther back, to the beginning of that same year, 415. Certainly it cannot have preceded that assembly by a longer period if Orosius is to have spoken truthfully.

Nor should anyone be influenced by the opinion of a recent chronologer who thinks that it was written three years earlier, namely in 412. That would make Jerome the very first to confront Pelagius in writing and would suggest that he did so at the very beginnings of the Pelagian heresy.

## CXXXIV. Written in A.D. 416

It is reasonably believed that this letter was delivered to Augustine through Orosius, whom Jerome immediately praises enthusiastically and who returned from Palestine to Africa in the spring of A.D. 416.

Certainly it was written after the completion of the three books of the *Dialogues* against the Pelagians, for Jerome cites the third book in section 1, in which he had praised Augustine:

“Certainly, in the *Dialogue* which I recently published, I remembered your blessedness as was fitting.”

From Orosius’s testimony we understand that these books belong to the latter part of the preceding year, 415. Since the letter itself was dictated soon after those books, we have judged that it must be assigned to the immediately following year, 416.

## CXXXV–CXXXVII. Written in A.D. 417

The occasion of these letters may be understood from Augustine’s book *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, near its end; from the same passage their date may also be correctly inferred.

“Concerning what is said to have been perpetrated there after this judgment”—that is, the Synod of Diospolis—“by some band of wretched men, who are reported to be strongly inclined to support Pelagius in his perversity, with incredible boldness: that servants of God and women belonging to the care of Saint Jerome were subjected to a most wicked massacre, that a deacon was killed, that the monastery buildings were burned, and that only a stronger fortified tower, by God’s mercy, protected Jerome himself from this attack and assault of the impious—I think it is better for us to remain silent and await what our brother bishops there judge should be done concerning such great evils. Who could believe that they could disregard these things?”

In these letters Innocent condemns these very evils.

From that account it is clear that after the Synod of Diospolis, which was held in December of A.D. 415, the band of wicked men inflicted these injuries on Jerome in the following year, 416, and not until at least several months of that year had passed.

Nevertheless, learned men, especially the distinguished Father Constantius, argue from the first of these letters, which is addressed to Aurelius, that the letters themselves should be assigned to the beginning of the following year, 417.

Aurelius appears to have taken care that Jerome’s letters, which have now been lost, should reach Innocent; and Innocent in turn orders him to see that these letters are delivered to Jerome. He was the bishop of Carthage who, writing with the colleagues of the Synod of Milevis to Innocent against Pelagius and Caelestius toward the end of A.D. 416, was unaware that Jerome had suffered anything from the Pelagian faction. This is correctly inferred from the synodical letter, where Jerome’s zeal for the Catholic faith is mentioned.

Again, from Innocent’s familiar reply to Aurelius and from the entire sequence of that pope’s letters, it is inferred that Innocent had no knowledge of so atrocious a crime before this same year, 417. Nor do the letters under discussion seem to have been known to Augustine, who, while writing his book *On the Proceedings of Pelagius* at the beginning of that year, said in the passage cited above that it was necessary to await what the bishops would judge should be done about such great evils, since he did not believe that they could disregard them.

Moreover, since ancient records assign Innocent’s death to March 12 of this year, everyone will judge that the letters should be assigned, at the latest, to the month of February.

## CXXXVIII–CXXXIX. Written about A.D. 417

These letters appear to report the same crime committed against Jerome by the agents of the heretics: the burning of the monastery and the destruction of the house. For that reason we have judged that they belong to approximately the same period.

In the first, Jerome indicates that Catilina had been driven not only from the city but also from the boundaries of Palestine. It is not likely that by this name he intended anyone other than Pelagius.

Soon afterward he says that he considered it better to change his place than the truth of the faith, and better to lose the beauty of the buildings and dwelling than to stain himself by their fellowship—those with whom at that time he had either to yield or, at any rate, to fight daily not with the tongue but with swords.

In the other letter, addressed to Apronius, he does not so much grieve that his house, in respect of worldly goods, had been utterly destroyed by the persecutions of the heretics as rejoice that, by Christ’s favor, it was being filled with spiritual riches.

For the rest, he declares that everything is peaceful in the Holy Places and that the heretics do not dare to open their impious mouths. This indicates that the letter must be placed somewhat later than the preceding one, although it refers to the same disturbances and upheavals.

## CXL. Written about the same time

This letter was given to Cyprian while Jerome was in the Holy Places. Although he attacks the Pelagian doctrine in more than one passage, he does so without bitterness. It may therefore reasonably be argued that it too was written after Pelagius had already been expelled from the boundaries of Palestine and everything was peaceful, as he notes in the preceding letter.

We do not deny that it could be placed two years earlier, before the heretics laid violent hands upon Jerome. But, we hope, no one will be displeased that we have assigned it this position on the basis of other conjectures, since most of its features seemed to fit better here.

## CXLI–CXLII. Written about A.D. 418

We long ago formed the view that these are not, as is commonly believed, two letters of Jerome to Augustine, but one letter, of which the shorter piece after the subscription should be regarded as a kind of appendix to the other.

The very brief sequence of the discourse in both, the character of the later little piece, and especially the authority of the manuscript of the monastery of Vendôme persuaded us of this, as we stated in the notes to Letters CXLI and CXLII themselves.

Although we did not dare to list them as only one letter, we nevertheless changed the order in which they also appeared in Saint Augustine, and instead of separating them by nearly a decade, we wish to assign both to one and the same period.

That period is approximately A.D. 418, since they speak chiefly of the condemnation of the Pelagians in Palestine, of their agents, and of the disturbances—although in riddles, such as that of Jerusalem captured by Nebuchadnezzar, which refused to heed Jeremiah’s counsels. They also praise Augustine, who stood firm against the blowing winds through the fervor of his faith.

## CXLIII. Apparently written toward the end of A.D. 419

The Benedictine Fathers argue as follows concerning the date of this letter.

Baronius considers it the latest of all the letters written by Jerome and assigns it to A.D. 420, the year to which Jerome’s death belongs according to Prosper’s chronicle.

Certainly the death of the virgin Eustochium, whose loss Jerome here declares to have occupied him with intense grief, can be placed not long before the aforementioned year 420. For Palladius, writing his *Lausiac History* in A.D. 419 or 420, believed that she was still alive in chapter 125.

As for the bearer of the letter, the presbyter Innocentius, he was sent by the African Fathers to Cyril in A.D. 419 to investigate the Nicene Canons and returned from there to Africa in the same year, before November 26, as is clear from the *Code of the Canons of the African Church*, title, chapter 137.

Without doubt, on that occasion he saw Jerome and received the letter in question for delivery—within this very year, not the following one. For at the beginning of the letter, when Jerome excuses himself because Innocentius, in the preceding year, as though he had not returned to Africa at all, had not carried his writings to Augustine, he indicates one or another of Innocentius’s journeys to the East.

The first of these, since Innocentius was uncertain about his return to Africa, is not the same as the journey which he undertook in A.D. 419 on the authority of the African Synod. Nor does Baronius correctly infer from Jerome’s words that the letter was sent in the year following Innocentius’s embassy.

## CXLIV. Written at the beginning of A.D. 420

Finally, we infer that this letter of Augustine was sent at the beginning of the year 420 because in section 1 he notes that he is writing after nearly five full years had elapsed since he sent to Jerome in the East his book, not of presumption but of consultation.

That book is the very letter which, in our numbering, is Letter CXXXI, sent to Palestine through Orosius in A.D. 415, as we have shown from Orosius’s departure and from the debate held at Jerusalem against Pelagius.

If five further years are added to 415, the result is 420, to which we assign the letter.

## The three remaining letters, whose date is less certain

[Col. XCI]

We have deferred three letters of Jerome to Class V because it was not expedient to assign them a definite chronological epoch either on the basis of probable reasoning or of the consistent authority of learned men.

The first, Letter CXLV, addressed to Exuperantius, is more easily understood as having been written after A.D. 386 from Bethlehem than earlier from the desert of Chalcis. See what we observe from Palladius in the notes.

The following letter, CXLVI, addressed to Evangelus, should, I think, be assigned after the same year because in section 2 he says that he saw at Rome, “among the presbyters, in the bishop’s absence, a deacon sitting.”

CXLVII. The last, addressed to Sabinianus, is customarily assigned to the period when the barbarians had invaded the lands of the Empire. Certainly section 11 indicates that the husband of the woman whom Sabinianus had corrupted was a barbarian and that he was a soldier.

[Col. XCI]

Thus, in properly arranging Jerome’s letters—a task that is almost the editor’s greatest labor and from which students derive the greatest benefit—we have contributed everything we could to the common effort. Now let us contribute the remaining matters that belong to our part.

[Col. 0005]

# THE LIFE OF SAINT EUSEBIUS HIERONYMUS, PRESBYTER OF STRIDON, COMPOSED CHIEFLY FROM HIS OWN WRITINGS, ADDRESSED TO HIS EMINENCE, DOMINICUS RIVIERA, CARDINAL OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH

## CHAPTER ONE

I. Jerome’s homeland.  
II. The year of his birth.  
III. His name.  
IV. His parents and relatives.

### I

Eusebius Hieronymus, the greatest Doctor of the Churches, ennobled Stridon, an obscure town which, as he himself says, was once situated on the boundary of Dalmatia and Pannonia and was destroyed by the Goths (*On Illustrious Men*, final chapter).

But this honor, since the former traces of the place had already almost entirely disappeared in his own age, is now claimed by several cities and by different provinces. Recent scholars also assign it to different locations in Dalmatia. The writer Palladius, who lived not long after Jerome, called Jerome a Dalmatian. The same view is also commonly held—without delaying to cite the names of its supporters—and rests on the authority of witnesses of great reputation.

Yet first, Saint Jerome himself never calls himself a Dalmatian. Rather, he indicates that he was born beneath another sky, both elsewhere and especially in the testimony quoted below from the first chapter of Sophonias.

Nor is it possible to find within the boundaries of Dalmatia any place which suitably resembles ancient Stridon either in the similarity of its name or in the situation of its land. Lucius, that great defender of this opinion and a recent historian of Dalmatian affairs, does not assign any such place by name. Those who refer the Sidrona of Ptolemy to this matter will soon be shown, when we speak of Liburnia, how far they have strayed from every appearance of truth.

Others prefer to assign Stridon to Pannonia. For in the Nicene subscriptions a certain Domnus, bishop of Stridon in Pannonia, is mentioned, and he is distinguished from the bishop of Dalmatia who immediately precedes him there.

Although it has been disputed whether those subscriptions are Nicene or should be assigned to some later synod, they nevertheless sufficiently persuade us that Stridon was formerly reckoned among the towns of Pannonia.

Nor is it credible, as a learned man maintains, that it was later transferred from Dalmatia to the jurisdiction of Pannonia, since ecclesiastical provinces often adhere to an older division. Saint Jerome himself also gives some indication that he was a Pannonian when he calls his homeland “the native rusticity” (*Letter VII*), and when he calls Castrucius, perhaps an old friend and fellow countryman, “a Pannonian man, that is, an earthly animal” (*Letter LXVIII*). He would not, it seems, have cast this insult at his friend unless it were likewise applicable to himself through the character of their people.

But those who take this side say that Stridon was situated on the river Mura, somewhere in Upper Pannonia, today in Styria, fifteen thousand paces below Rakeltburg toward the southeast, in the direction of the confluence of the Mura and the Drava—or, which amounts to the same thing, near the fortress of Csan Tornga, and no more than a day’s journey from Sabaria, a town of well-known name in Hungary.

These people, I say, make an incredible claim. If there is no other place to which they can assign the claims of Jerome’s homeland, they completely destroy the very position they had proposed. For that place lies almost in the middle of Pannonia, not at its boundaries; nor could it ever have been, as Jerome says, adjacent to Dalmatia. Accordingly, it was not his homeland at all.

Those seem to speak more nearly to the truth who locate Stridon in Liburnia. That province bordered both Pannonia and Dalmatia: it was separated from Dalmatia by the Bebian Mountains mentioned by Strabo, and from Pannonia by the river Tisza.

There Ptolemy, in book II, chapter 17, lists among the inland cities a town almost identical in name, Sidrona, and assigns it to Liburnia, though in such a way that it falls upon the boundary of Dalmatia, slightly above the sources of the river Titius, which borders Liburnia.

This discovery seemed to preserve the argument. For although Jerome mentions Pannonia and Dalmatia, not Liburnia, it is possible that in his age, when the boundaries of the provinces were repeatedly altered, that city had passed from Liburnia into Dalmatia or Pannonia. Indeed, it is sufficient, as I think, if it bordered both provinces without itself being assigned to either.

This opinion has therefore persuaded many, although they dispute among themselves either for the honor of Pannonia or for that of Dalmatia; and for a long time critics of great reputation have been unable to embrace any better view.

Yet that city is much too far removed from the tract of land indicated by the sequence of Jerome’s life and circumstances. It is not likely that he originated at a greater distance from the soil on which he evidently spent his childhood and formed friendships from his earliest years.

I mean the tract lying between Aemona and Aquileia, or in their vicinity. Ptolemy’s Sidrona is separated entirely from this region, lying on the opposite boundary, with the intervening province of Liburnia between them.

Furthermore, Liburnia, like Dalmatia, was contained within Illyricum; they were, as it were, two parts of that region. Although the whole tract was sometimes also called Dalmatia in place of Illyricum, Liburnia is never understood except as a part of Illyricum—or, if one prefers, of Dalmatia.

Saint Jerome himself bears witness in explicit words that he was born in a land other than the soil of Illyricum:

“Illyricum is my witness,” he says in the first chapter of Sophonias, verse 2; “Thrace is my witness; the land in which I was born is my witness.”

Therefore he was not born in Liburnia, which was included within Illyricum; and certainly not in Ptolemy’s Sidrona, which borders Liburnia to the east and, according to Ptolemy himself—who extends the boundaries of Illyricum from Istria as far as Mount Scardus and Upper Moesia—lies almost in the middle of Illyricum, behind it.

“But then,” you will say, “where and among what peoples shall we finally seek the birthplace of the holy Father?”

If I may repeat the opinion which Erasmus long ago and Lucius more recently accused of misguided zeal and an affectation unworthy of serious men, I would prefer, together with highly learned writers—including Thomas the Archdeacon of Split, who lived at the beginning of the thirteenth century, Blondus, and Marianus Victorius—to place it in Istria, which indeed belongs to our Italy.

They now call the place Sdrigna, or Sdrin, a small town in the diocese of Trieste, situated between Petra Pilosa, Portula, and Primont, scarcely forty thousand paces distant from Aquileia.

Jerome himself seems plainly to indicate this to us in the passage quoted above, if we have correctly understood his meaning.

For when he says that the city was once on the boundary of Dalmatia and Pannonia, he shows that he is recalling an ancient memory, not describing the boundaries of his own time. By mentioning two neighboring provinces, he also suggests that the place, in his judgment, properly belonged to neither.

Moreover, you may learn from the ancient geographers that Dalmatia once extended as far as the boundary of Istria—especially from those who describe it under the name Illyricum and who never call it Dalmatia by name, notably Pomponius Mela, Scymnus of Chios, Scylax, and others.

Nor does the previously mentioned Lucius deny this, when he says that, once the name “maritime Illyricum” began to fall out of use and the name Dalmatia became common in its place, Dalmatia included not only its ancient boundaries but also neighboring Liburnia.

The boundary of Dalmatia, therefore, at which Saint Jerome notes that his homeland, Stridon, was situated, must be sought at the extreme western limit of Liburnia. There the boundaries of Upper Pannonia, which turns northward from that point, run into it.

Istria, moreover, is adjacent to both regions. Stridon should consequently be placed at the beginning of Istria, toward Mount Ocra—so that the account given by Jerome concerning that very obscure boundary between ancient Dalmatia and Pannonia may retain its proper coherence, since otherwise, as has been shown, it can scarcely be understood or explained.

Thus Jerome could be called both a Pannonian and a Dalmatian—or perhaps more truly an Italian, since Istria had been assigned to Italy from the time of Augustus and Tiberius—according to the ancient division.

None of the objections by which the other opinions recited above are refuted applies here.

As for our statement that this is the place now called Sdrigna, we base it partly on the opinion of the ancients, partly on a certain similarity of name, and finally on the widespread tradition of the inhabitants, who, as proof of the matter, display there a monument of Jerome’s father Eusebius, with an epitaph engraved on plates.

In any case, it is sufficient for our purpose if we have established that Jerome’s homeland should be located in this region of Istria, even if the small town, destroyed by the Goths during the lifetime of that same holy Father, was then called by another name unknown to us.

Certainly—and this is a second argument in the matter—nearly all the circumstances of his life and the testimonies in his writings confirm that it stood not far from the territory of Aquileia.

Such is the passage in *Letter VII*, where he commends his sister to Chromatius, Eusebius, and Jovinus, presbyters of Aquileia, because she did not have good teachers of life in her homeland. He calls her the fruit of the deacon Julian—who, according to the manuscript books, was an Aquileian—and asks that they support her in her holy purpose by frequent letters and obtain from Pope Valerian, then bishop of Aquileia, letters to encourage her.

If Stridon lay farther away—or, indeed, unless it was neighboring Aquileia—it is scarcely credible that his sister, living in her homeland and at home, could have been strengthened in the stricter discipline of life by the exhortations of Julian, who was present; or that Jerome would have asked his Aquileian friends to nourish her through the frequent consolation of letters and would have sought letters for that purpose from the bishop of Aquileia himself.

On the other hand, he addresses the virgins of Aemona—not Hermona, as has hitherto been incorrectly read—and Antonius, a monk in that same city, through letters in such a way as to indicate that his homeland lay nearby.

This is especially clear where he complains to them about a detractor of his name; it is evident that this was one and the same person as the man who was attacking him with malicious speech among the Aquileians.

Aemona is the city now called Ljubljana, commonly Laubac. It was formerly a frontier city of Italy and, according to Ptolemy, lay between Italy, Noricum, and Pannonia, about fifty thousand paces from Aquileia.

What could be more plausible, then, than what we have proposed: that in the tract between Aquileia and Aemona, toward the Julian Alps, at the place where, according to the ancient division, Pannonia and Dalmatia—or Liburnia, which at that time was called a part of Dalmatia—met at the same boundaries, Stridon, Jerome’s birthplace, was situated?

[Col. 0009] **II.** There is another question concerning the year in which he came into the world, and among scholars the dispute over it is no less uncertain and obscure.
