Prosper, in the *Chronicon Integrum*, as it is called—the work first published by Philippe Labbe from the Lodunensis manuscript and recently reviewed by the editor of Canisius’s *Antiquae Lectiones*—provided the occasion for the question and for the various opinions of scholars on the matter. For in the year of Christ 331, when Bassus and Ablavius were consuls, he assigns the birthdate of Saint Jerome. Although he is not sufficiently consistent in his calculations of the years, when he places Jerome’s death in the year 420, under the consulship of Theodosius IX and Constantius III, yet in this error—for he assigns him ninety-one years of life—he shows that he preferred to place Jerome’s birth earlier rather than later. Some, indeed, lessen that error by a convenient interpretation and reconcile Prosper with himself, and with the ancient author of Jerome’s *Life*, commonly thought to be Gennadius, who assigns him only eighty-eight years; finally, they reconcile him also with Augustine, whom our author repeatedly addresses in his letters as his father in dignity but his son in age.

But since Prosper’s notice continually conflicts with historical truth and with the sequence of Jerome’s life, and places the birth of the holy Father far too early, we who are composing his life from his own writings may properly prefer the testimonies that he himself gives concerning his age to Prosper’s authority and to all the opinions that critics have held or now hold on the matter.

Let this first be taken as established and certain: when Jerome calls himself an infant, a boy, a young adolescent, or a young man, and connects that designation with some indication of an event in his life, he follows the Pythagorean method of reckoning human life by periods of twenty years, as Laërtius reports (*Book* VIII, sections 9–10), a method that was also commonly followed at that time.

> “A boy,” he says, “completes twenty years; a young man, twenty; an old man, twenty.”

Only infancy was not distinguished from childhood; rather, it was extended as a part of childhood up to the fifteenth year, as Censorinus teaches concerning Varro (*On the Birthday*, chapter XIV). Thus also the Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter LXX:

> “For infants up to the fifteenth year of age, all are to provide diligent discipline and supervision.”

Once this rule has been properly established, if we weigh Jerome’s words, it will become clear that he was born about the year 346, approximately fifteen years later than Prosper reports. Let us therefore examine at least some of the more significant passages according to the stages of life.

In Letter LXVIII to Castrucius, section 2, he says:

> “I shall relate to you a brief story that occurred in the time of my infancy. When blessed Antony had been summoned from Alexandria to the city by Saint Athanasius, Bishop of Alexandria, for the refutation of the heretics, Didymus went to him, etc.”

The more accurate chronologers assign this event to the year 355. At that time, according to our hypothesis, Jerome was about ten years old; according to those who follow Prosper’s calculations in whatever way they can, he had passed his twenty-fourth year and was not merely no longer an infant or a boy, but had already entered adolescence.

Later, in *Commentary on Isaiah*, book V, chapter 15, he extends the span of this age, where he refers to the great earthquake to the time of his infancy:

> “When the seas crossed the shores of the whole world, and on that same night the walls of Areopolis collapsed.”

If he is speaking of the earthquake concerning which Ammianus Marcellinus likewise reports that the sea overflowed its boundaries (*Book* XXVI, chapter 10), and if Idatius understands it as referring to August of the year 365, while Jerome himself in the *Chronicle* relates that the sea went beyond the shore, then Jerome had already completed his nineteenth year. There is nothing impossible in extending infancy up to that age if, as noted above, the word is being used for childhood; strictly speaking, however, that age does not seem to have exceeded the fifteenth year.

Yet other terrible earthquakes occurred around that time, and someone may prefer to refer this passage to one of them. Formerly we ourselves said that the year 344 was indicated there; now, however, we withdraw that view and correct it. Whatever the case may be, the opinions of those who place the birth of the holy Father earlier cannot in any way be reconciled with this testimony.

Still more decisive than the others is the passage in the book *On Places*, under the heading *Drys Mambre* from Genesis:

> “Up to the time of my infancy, and the reign of King Constantius, the terebinth was shown as extremely ancient and, by its size, indicating its age.”

As I understand it, both endpoints are designated here: the final period of his infancy and the end of Constantius’s reign. Constantius ceased to rule in the year 361; at that time the holy Father was entering his fifteenth year, which, as we showed earlier, was precisely the point at which infancy ended. If this is true, as it has every appearance of being, Jerome could not have given a more exact indication of the year of his birth, which we have identified as 346.

He had certainly passed beyond infancy when he calls himself a boy; for example, in Habakkuk, book I, chapter 10: “While I was still a boy and being trained in the school of grammar, and all the cities were being polluted with the blood of victims, the death of Julian was suddenly announced in the very heat of the persecution; one of the pagans aptly said, etc.” Julian was killed in 363, the seventeenth year of Jerome’s life.

Elsewhere he reckons the full twenty years assigned to that stage of life. Such is the statement in the Preface to the *Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians*: “Not that I am unaware that Gaius Marius Victorinus, who taught rhetoric at Rome when I was a boy, published commentaries on the Apostle, etc.” Its counterpart is found in book XII on Ezekiel, chapter 40: “When I was a boy at Rome and was being trained in the liberal studies, I used, with others of the same age and purpose, etc.” For when he was applying himself at Rome to learning letters, already somewhat older but still a boy, he had completed twenty years.

Thereafter he so joins adolescence to boyhood, and thereby indicates still more clearly for our purpose the year in which he was born, as he comes nearer to the boundaries of each age from which we may draw more certain calculations. In Letter LII to Nepotianus he says: “While I was an adolescent—indeed, almost a boy—and was restraining the first impulses of a wanton age by the rigour of the desert, I wrote an exhortatory letter to your uncle Heliodorus.” That letter was written, as we have shown more fully in its proper place, in 373, when he was already entering upon adolescence, that is, when he was twenty-seven years old. This fits our calculation so exactly that from this testimony alone the true year of his birth, which we have given, is virtually established.

Indeed, he used precisely the same words in marking the age of the Emperor Valentinian when he met his death, in Letter LX, or the *Epitaph of Nepotianus*: “Valentinian, an adolescent and almost a boy, after flight, after exiles . . . was killed.” The histories of those times establish that Valentinian was then in his twenty-sixth year—just as many years, or one fewer, as Jerome had indicated when speaking of himself. Nor is it likely that he used the same words in one sense of himself and in another of others.

Nearly the same indication of years occurs when he calls himself *adolescentulus* “diminutively” (ὑποκοριστικῶς), in book I *Against Jovinianus*, chapter 36: “When I myself, as a young adolescent, saw in Gaul the Attacotti, a British people, feed on human flesh.” At that time he was in the twenty-fourth or twenty-fifth year of his life, as will appear from what is said below. In Letter CXX to Hedibia: “Your elders, Patera and Delphidius, of whom the former taught rhetoric at Rome before I was born, while the latter, when I was already an adolescent, made all Gaul illustrious by his talent in prose and verse.”

This passage has troubled many, who, reading in the *Chronicle* that Delphidius is mentioned under the year of Christ 355, argue that Jerome—who even on our view was then at most ten years old—was still a full decade away from the beginning of adolescence. But the notation in the *Chronicle* follows another principle: it records, as is customary, not the time when Delphidius had already filled Gaul with the fame of his name and works, but the year in which he first began to flourish. If the occasion required it, this could readily be demonstrated by other and almost countless examples. Who, moreover, would not see that after at least another twenty years and more, through continually renewed literary labours, he would at last have attained such celebrity that the holy Father could truly say that, when he was an adolescent, Delphidius had made Gaul illustrious by his talent?

Nor should anyone be troubled that in Letter XXXIX he calls Blesilla, who was twenty years old, an *adolescentula*, though one might perhaps have preferred to call her a girl for that reason; for when such expressions are applied to the weaker sex, they do not have precisely the same force or appropriate meaning. Finally, it is sufficiently clear how faithfully he himself followed the stages of life according to that rule when he calls himself in adolescence, or simply an adolescent—a term which might be extended as far as his fortieth year. In Commentary XIII on Ezekiel, chapter 44, he says: “On this little question, I know that at Rome, in my adolescence, I wrote against Helvidius, the heretic of that time, a book that was not large.” He was then about thirty-seven years old, since that book was written in 383, as we shall show in its proper place.

We pass over other testimonies of this kind, all of which fit together and agree excellently under our hypothesis, but which under every other view that follows the calculations of Prosper’s *Chronicle* can neither be understood nor explained in any way. I shall add only one noteworthy observation, which more firmly establishes what has so far been argued. In the Preface to the *Commentary on Obadiah*, the holy Father declares that formerly, while he had not yet attained the age of the perfect man and the measure of Christ, he had, in adolescence, been stirred by zeal and devotion to the Scriptures to interpret this same prophet allegorically. This exposition—which his age could least of all sustain—was repudiated by its author; it belongs, as has been shown elsewhere and will appear more clearly below, to 374 or the following year. At that time he himself states that he had not yet attained the perfect age of the fullness of Christ.

The perfect age of Christ comprises the span of thirty years, as Jerome himself interprets his meaning. Writing in Letter LXXXII to Theophilus on behalf of his brother Paulinian, whose premature ordination John was accusing, he says: “His age is known to Your Blessedness; and since he has now reached the span of thirty years, I think that it ought not to be reproved in this respect, since, according to the mystery of the assumed man, it is perfect in Christ.” If, then, he himself had not yet attained that age, that is, thirty years, when he wrote that specimen of a commentary on Obadiah, in 374, it is clearer than the noonday light that his birth cannot possibly be placed earlier than 345.

That the date should instead be moved forward to 346 is easily suggested both by the arguments already offered and by that passage in the cited Preface to *Commentary on Obadiah*, where he calls himself a boy. By that term he seems to have wished to temper what he had said shortly before about being in adolescence, so as to indicate that he was then at the beginning rather than the middle of that period and was still a considerable distance from thirty years of age.

**III. On the Name of the Holy Father**

There is also controversy among scholars concerning the name of the holy Father, so that no point might be lacking from the disputes on either side. *Hieronymus*, which was his cognomen, signifies for some, with Victorius, “sacred law”; for others, with Erasmus—and much more probably—“the designation of a sacred name.” Some have even wished the name Eusebius to be entirely removed from Hieronymus, although he himself indicates in the *Catalogue of Illustrious Writers* that it was his father’s name, while the very structure of the names and the ancient custom of the nation persuade us that he received it from his father. Indeed, there are some who maintain that he acquired it from Eusebius of Caesarea through a Latin translation that Eusebius himself prepared from several of his own Greek books, as Menagius argues in his notes on Laërtius. As we have said elsewhere, these men seem to us to be indulging in nonsense rather than speaking seriously.

Another name or forename, *Sophronius*, is also found added to his name in ancient books. The matter seemed worthy of careful investigation. Martianaeus found it written at the beginning of only one or two books falsely attributed to the holy Father, and therefore judged that their testimony was not sufficient to establish the fact. We, however, have been more fortunate, for we have found it inscribed also in genuine works, although, to conceal nothing, in manuscripts that are not extremely ancient and that, as far as could be conjectured, do not go back beyond the twelfth century.

The Ambrosian Library at Milan possesses two such manuscripts. One is marked number 88 and contains the book *Hebrew Names*, which is entitled:

> “Of Eusebius Sophronius Hieronymus.”

Although this title seems to have been prefixed by some learned person—not by Jerome—to the very brief letter on the forms of the Hebrew letters that serves as the Preface to that book, we are the first to append that letter to this volume.

The other manuscript contains the book *On the Places of the Holy Land*, and bears this very clear inscription:

> “Here begins the Preface of Lord Eusebius Sophronius Hieronymus to the book of Places, previously published in Greek by Eusebius Pamphili, Bishop of Caesarea, but afterward carefully translated into Latin style by the aforesaid Hieronymus.”

On the strength of this testimony I am readily persuaded to believe that *Sophronius* was also his name, whether he received it as an infant from the very beginning of his life or later, when he began to be celebrated throughout the world for the merit of his life and learning.

**IV. Summary of the Matters Hitherto Discussed**

Thus, to gather briefly what it has so far been necessary to discuss at greater length concerning the manner of composing his life: Eusebius Sophronius Hieronymus was born at Stridon, a city that seems to have belonged rather to the boundary of Italy, though it once lay on the border of Dalmatia and Pannonia. In any event, it was not far from Aquileia and Aemona, the most distinguished cities of Italy. He was born, apparently, in the year of Christ 346, when Constantius and Constans, the Augustan brothers, had already been ruling for eleven years, and when Pope Julius was administering the Christian commonwealth.

Jerome himself states in more than one place, and especially in the Preface to *Job*, that both his parents were devoted to the Christian religion; he also indicates that he was religiously brought up by them. From Letter LXXXII to Theophilus, section 2, one may rightly infer that they never lent their minds or ears to the Arians who were spreading through those regions, since Jerome boasts that he was nourished by them, from what I may call his very cradle, on Catholic milk:

> “For no one is more ecclesiastical than he who has never been a heretic.”

Some assert that his parents were also of the noblest rank. On the other hand, someone may hesitate over their having belonged to a servile family because of the Greek, rather than Roman, origin of the name. A passage in the letter cited above, section 3, once caused me some difficulty. In response to John of Jerusalem’s accusation that his brother Paulinian had been made a cleric from a slave, Jerome says nothing more than that John himself had some clerics of that sort and that Onesimus is read among Paul’s converts, having begun, from being a slave, to become a deacon.

But if Jerome himself had belonged to that condition, it does not seem likely that he would have called Palladius, in the *Prologue against the Pelagians*, “a man of servile wickedness,” since his adversaries could easily have charged Jerome with the same servile mark. Still less would he have added jokingly that he did not envy Palladius his nobility.

Moreover, it is generally agreed among writers that his parents were wealthy and honored by a substantial patrimony. The familiar passage from book I *Against Rufinus* is commonly cited to prove that they had a large household of slaves:

> “I remember that as a boy I used to run through the little rooms of the household servants and spend holidays in play, etc.”

I fear, however, that this passage is not always understood and interpreted quite appropriately. Certainly, the patrimony left by his father, which Jerome eventually arranged to sell so that the money returned from it could be spent on receiving the crowds of monks flocking from every direction, must have been far from insignificant, although he modestly calls it in Letter LXVI:

> “Half-ruined little estates that escaped the hands of the barbarians, and the common property of our parents.”

Finally, when he describes the customs of his native land in Letter VII—a place where the belly was god and the holier person was the richer—and in Letter XXII says that, among the other comforts of life, he had cut himself off from the habitual enjoyment of richer food for the sake of the kingdom of heaven, and in several other passages, as when he speaks of Bonosus’s companionship, of the long journeys he traversed, and of the very well-stocked library he had acquired for himself (Letter III), he plainly indicates that he was born into a sufficiently prosperous fortune.

His father’s name was Eusebius, as we have already suggested, and this name passed to the son according to Roman custom. His mother’s name is not reported. His maternal aunt—that is, his mother’s sister—was called Castorina. For some unknown reasons, Jerome, who bore her ill will, invited her once and again to peace and reconciliation in the most humane letters, as appears from Letter XIII.

He also had a sister whose name is unknown, of whom he speaks more than once in Letters VI and VII. It seems that, after she had fallen away from her intention of serving Christ, she persevered in it at the urging of the deacon Julian.

Finally, he had a younger brother named Paulinian, about whom we shall speak more than once later.

# CHAPTER II

**I.** Well educated at home together with Bonosus, he is sent to Rome to study.  
**II.** He attends the schools of grammarians, rhetoricians, and philosophers.  
**III.** He falls into certain vices of youth.

**I.** There can be no doubt that, when Jerome says—as we observed above—that he was nourished on Catholic milk from his very cradle, he was still an infant when he was formed through holy instruction and precepts by the efforts of his parents, who imbued his inexperienced mind with the first elements of Christian piety and faith.

His foster-brother and companion in life was a certain Bonosus, born of a distinguished and wealthy family. Jerome praises him warmly and more than once, but especially in Letter III, where he says:

> “The same nurses’ bosoms nourished us, the same embraces of our bearers cherished us.”

As for literary studies, he learned in his native land the rudiments of learning—the first elementary education, as it were the infancy of grammar—from a teacher whom he nicknames Orbilius after the famous Beneventan grammarian mentioned by Suetonius, a harsh and flogging master. Jerome says that he was dragged away as a captive from his grandmother’s bosom to face that raging teacher.

**II.** When he had grown older, though he was still a boy, and when, strengthened by domestic instruction, he began to seek the wider world, he was sent to Rome to be educated in the liberal arts. He must have been about eighteen years old, for it is most probable that he was then living in Rome when he heard the saying of the pagan concerning the sudden death of Julian. That was the year 363, as we noted above, and Jerome testifies that he was then a boy studying in the school of grammar.

There he attached himself to the grammarian Donatus, then the most celebrated teacher, the same Donatus who left commentaries on Terence and Virgil. In his school Jerome acquired such mastery and elegance in the Latin language that he easily surpassed all the writers of his time in this distinction.

The holy Father mentions Donatus in his *Commentaries on Ecclesiastes* and in several other places. One passage from book II *Against Rufinus* will suffice:

> “I suppose that as a boy you read the commentaries of Asper on Virgil and Sallust . . . those of Vellius on Cicero’s speeches, those of Victorinus on his dialogues, and those of my teacher Donatus on the comedies of Terence, likewise on Virgil, and those of others on other authors.”

Some say that Jerome was also a pupil of Victorinus, an exceptional teacher of eloquence during the same period. But since Jerome himself never reports this—although he frequently mentions Victorinus, both elsewhere and in the passage just cited, as well as in the *Catalogue of Illustrious Writers*, chapter CI, and in the Preface to the *Epistle to the Galatians*—and does not note it even in a single word, no arguments compel us to agree with them.

Indeed, his very silence argues against the claim, especially in the *Chronicle* and in the testimony just cited. In those passages, when he mentions that rhetorician together with Donatus, he calls Donatus alone, in the singular, “my teacher”; Victorinus he calls neither teacher nor friend.

Nor should you conclude from this that Jerome kept away from the platforms of the rhetoricians. On the contrary, he devoted himself to the first principles of eloquence and testifies in book I *Against the Pelagians* that, as a boy, he played at composing *Controversiae*. In chapter 2 of the *Commentary on Galatians* he says:

> “Sometimes, when as a young man I was declaiming *Controversiae* at Rome and training myself for real contests with imaginary soldiers, etc.”

He also attended the Forum and the tribunals of the judges in order to hear the most eloquent orators.

Finally, he played with the tricks of derisive preaching—that is, with a feature of the oratorical art, almost its chief one—when difficult things to answer are made light of.

Nor was he worn out only among grammarians and rhetoricians. He also studied dialectic and says that he spent a considerable part of his life among philosophers (Letter L). He read Porphyry’s *Isagoge* and translated the commentaries of Alexander of Aphrodisias—“translated,” I say, meaning that he handled and studied them day and night, not, as has hitherto been falsely believed, that he rendered them from Greek into Latin.

In Letter LX to Heliodorus he also says that he had read the little works of Plato, Diogenes, Clitomachus, Carneades, and Posidonius. Elsewhere he repeatedly shows that he had acquired distinguished knowledge of philosophy through the doctrines and opinions of the ancient philosophers that he weaves into his writings.

He also gathered an immense store of knowledge about antiquity. To master this, and likewise the other branches of learning, he followed an excellent plan: at great effort and expense he furnished himself with a library abundantly stocked with books of every kind of learning.

Finally, he left no branch of knowledge untouched except the discipline of sacred studies, toward which all his reflections already seem to have been directed. He cultivated piety to such a degree that one could understand those studies to have been pursued chiefly for the advancement of the Church and religion.

Thus he writes of himself in chapter XL of *Ezekiel*:

> “When I was a boy at Rome and was being trained in the liberal studies, I used to go around on Sundays with others of the same age and purpose—among them was Pammachius, of whom we shall speak frequently below—the tombs of the Apostles and Martyrs, and often enter the crypts, which, dug deep into the earth, had on both sides along the walls the bodies of those who had been buried there. Everything is so dark that the prophetic saying is almost fulfilled: ‘They descend alive into the underworld,’ etc.”

**III.** Although he had not yet been initiated through Baptism and was already entering adolescence—a period that, according to his method of reckoning, follows the twentieth year—he did not sufficiently guard himself on the slippery path of adolescence. In Letter VII to Chromatius he humbly confesses that he had fallen.

Writing to Heliodorus in Letter XIV, he identifies the kind of sin with which he polluted his conscience, lamenting the virginity he had lost:

> “I do not give this warning as one whose vessel or cargo is intact, nor as someone ignorant of the dangers of the sea, but as one who has recently been cast upon the shore after a shipwreck; in a timid voice I warn those preparing to sail: in that heat the Charybdis of lust devours salvation. There, with a virgin’s mouth, desire smiles like Scylla and beguiles one toward the shipwrecks of chastity, etc.”

He speaks still more plainly in Letter XLVIII to Pammachius, where, having lost the first virginity that belongs to birth, he scarcely preserves the second, which belongs to Baptism:

> “I carry virginity into heaven, not because I possess it, but because I marvel all the more that I do not possess it. It is an ingenuous and modest confession that you preach in others what you yourself lack . . . . . . . . Let no one deceive himself; let no one hurl himself into ruin through a flattering admirer. The first virginity is from the first birth; the second virginity is from the second birth.”

Some excuse such lapses at greater length. To me, however, it sometimes seems preferable that some offense should be acknowledged in the saints as a scar, so that the examples of those who turn back from vices to piety may move us more powerfully.

For that reason I will add that it may be possible that he sinned and polluted himself again even after Baptism, so that, just as he needed the waters of Baptism to assume the second virginity, he might need a second baptism of fire to cleanse other impurities.

His words are in Letter XVIII to Damasus, section 11:

> “Because I see with my eyes for the purpose of desiring, and am scandalized by my hand and my foot, and sin with every part of my members, I have everything unclean. And because, though baptized in spirit, I have again polluted my garment, I need the cleansing of a second baptism, that is, of fire.”

Yet there is nothing unusual in these statements, nor anything contrary to the customary language of holy men who humble themselves for the sake of modesty.

# CHAPTER III

**I.** He receives Baptism at Rome.  
**II.** Under Pope Liberius, at about the twentieth year of his age.

**I.** We are so certain that Jerome was cleansed by the washing of Baptism nowhere other than at Rome that we completely reject the view of those who think otherwise and place the event at Aquileia, even though they produce as evidence an inscription formerly attributed to a stone—though falsely.

The holy Father himself is a witness beyond all objection in two letters to Damasus, Letters XV and XVI:

> “From there, I now ask food for my soul, from where I once received the garments of Christ.”

And:

> “I, therefore, as I have already written, having received the garment of Christ in the city of Rome, am now held on the barbarous frontier of Syria.”

There is no way that any other garments of Christ can be understood here than those which, according to the Apostle, we put on through the washing of grace and faith, apart from the allusion in these words to the white garments with which Christians were formerly accustomed to be clothed at the time of Baptism.

It is also certain—indeed, it follows from this conclusion—that he did not receive Baptism immediately after birth or in the first years of infancy, but at an adult age, namely, while he was at Rome.

A very difficult question nevertheless arises: whether he received Baptism when he first came to Rome to be educated in literary studies, or later, when, after traveling through Gaul and considering entering the desert, he returned there and washed himself in the sacred waters.

The most learned among modern writers defend the latter opinion, chiefly because in former times those who had not been baptized as infants commonly postponed Baptism until they had passed through the dangers of youth and its sharper impulses. This would have been especially appropriate to Jerome’s ardent temperament.

They say that it seems an injury to his piety and religion to suppose that the purpose of serving God—which, as we shall soon explain, he began to entertain when he traveled in Gaul—came after his Baptism, and not by a small interval of time, if the Baptism is to be referred to his earlier residence in the city.

But these considerations do not move us. It was not customary for all Christians who had advanced somewhat in age without Baptism to postpone it until so late a time. Nor does Jerome’s later purpose of serving God imply any deficiency in his earlier piety. Rather, it greatly increases it, since his purpose was not then to begin the Christian life, but to live a much more perfect one—a purpose that he afterward fulfilled in the desert.

Moreover, the claim that the holy Father returned to Rome from Gaul rests on no foundation anywhere in the sequence of his life; indeed, it is entirely contrary to probability. These matters, however, will become clearer from what follows.

**II.** Let it therefore be established that, before leaving Rome, Jerome was washed in the sacred waters when he first came there to study secular literature—at the time to which the order of the life we are composing has now brought us—under Pope Liberius, not Damasus, and apparently before he had completed his twentieth year.

If, as we showed earlier, he did not postpone Baptism until he returned from his journey through Gaul, it follows that he received it earlier, when he came to Rome to be educated, since he was baptized nowhere else. If we have rightly refuted the former opinion, this alternative must necessarily be the true one.

It is also possible to prove this through particular arguments. The holy Father himself gives a fairly clear indication that he was baptized while Liberius, Damasus’s predecessor, was administering the Roman Church, not under Damasus.

When writing to Damasus in the letters just cited, Jerome insists that he received the garments of Christ at Rome, so that he might more justly seek advice from Damasus concerning the faith. If he had received Baptism from Damasus, or while Damasus held the See, he would certainly have added that fact, since it would have been the strongest point in his case. Yet he says nothing of the sort in either letter.

Indeed, in the first letter he suggests the contrary through the adverb “formerly”:

> “From there,” he says, “I formerly received the garments of Christ,”

as though he were saying, “before you obtained the governance of this Church.” Damasus began his pontificate toward the end of the year 366, when Jerome was about twenty years old.

The same conclusion may be drawn from the date at which his friend Rufinus received Baptism—at the latest in 371, as is clear from Rufinus’s letter to Pope Anastasius and from book II of Jerome’s *Invectives*. Both the unanimous opinion of learned men and several testimonies of the same holy Father confirm that Jerome had received this sacrament several years before Rufinus.

Consider the passage from Letter IV to Florentius:

> “He”—Rufinus—“has just washed himself and is clean, and has been made white like snow; while I, stained with all the filth of sins, wait day and night in fear to pay the last farthing.”

But if Jerome was baptized only after his journey through Gaul, the difference in time would scarcely have been worth noting; certainly it would not have been so great that one could establish a comparison between innocence received long before and the filth contracted over the course of time.

He therefore received Baptism before departing from the city after completing the course of his studies, approximately four years before Rufinus.

I would also refer here to the passage cited earlier, in book XII of the *Commentary on Ezekiel*, where the holy Father says that, when he was a boy at Rome and was being educated in the liberal studies, he used to go around on Sundays with others of the same age and purpose to the tombs of the Apostles and Martyrs.

What else can be understood here by “purpose” more appropriately than the Christian religion, to which he had given his name through Baptism?

Finally, the ancient author of Jerome’s *Life*, known as Gennadius, also testifies that Jerome received Baptism while he was still a boy—which, according to the understanding of the ancients, means that he had not yet passed his twentieth year.

Although for other reasons we attach little weight to an author who even falsifies his name, there is nevertheless no testimony either older or more closely positioned to establish the truth. But enough of this.

# CHAPTER IV

**I.** After his studies at Rome, he returns home.  
**II.** He remains for a short time at Aquileia.  
**III.** He sets out for Gaul.

**I.** Having been thoroughly educated at Rome in secular literature and having spent a long time practicing in the schools of the rhetoricians, Jerome resolved to leave the city and travel to Gaul, which at that time flourished in the glory of learning. He went together with Bonosus, his constant companion in study and life.

Jerome was then approximately twenty-three years old, in the year 369 after the restoration of salvation.

[Col. 0019] This may be gathered from his own testimony in book II *Against Jovinianus*, where he calls himself a young man when, during his travels in Gaul, he saw certain Attacoti, a British people, eating human flesh.

The same designation of age appears when he notes that, while he was already a young man, Delphidius had illuminated all Gaul by his talent in prose and verse. The reason for this is plainly that Jerome himself was at that time living in Gaul.

**II.** Nothing is more probable than that, when Jerome left Rome, he first returned to Stridon, from which he could both proceed directly to Gaul and obtain in his father’s house the expenses of a more distant journey.

But he stayed only briefly in his native land, which was not suited to his temperament. As we showed in chapter I, Stridon was close to Aquileia. Aquileia was also a much more distinguished city and, what would have attracted and detained Jerome even more, was rich in holy and learned men, especially those who lived in the very famous monastery there. Many of their distinguished names still survive among Jerome’s friends.

One of these was Rufinus. Perhaps because of his superior talent, Jerome associated with him more frequently than with the others and conversed with him about his studies.

It is apparently in this sense that, writing to him several years later in Letter III, Jerome said:

> “How I wish I could fix those lips with my own, those lips that once either erred with me or spoke wisely!”

It was certainly at this first period that the friendship between Jerome and Rufinus began to become known. There is no equal reason to believe that they first became acquainted anywhere other than Aquileia. Those who wish to place the beginning of their friendship much earlier, at Rome, describe an entirely new circumstance for which no evidence can be found either in Jerome’s writings or in the sequence of events.

III. It is therefore established that Jerome remained at Aquileia for no very short time. Yet his innate zeal for learning, and his desire to visit men distinguished among foreign peoples for their reputation in scholarship, did not allow him to stay there longer. He therefore set out for Gaul, and did not visit merely one or two parts of it, but, as far as he was able, traversed all the regions of Gaul, so that from all its learned men and libraries he might gather for himself a treasury of knowledge.

This is especially clear from the fact that he frequently recalls particular places, and not without a distinctive emotional attachment, as in Letter 123 to Ageruchia, where he laments in a deeply moving manner whatever lies between the Alps and the Pyrenees, enclosed by the Ocean and the Rhine, after it had been ravaged by the barbarians:

> Mainz, he says, once a noble city, has been captured and destroyed, and many thousands of people have been massacred in the church. The Vangiones have been wiped out by a long siege. The very powerful city of the Remi, Amiens, the Atrebates, the Morini—at the farthest edge of humankind—Tournai, the Nemetes, and Strasbourg have been transferred into Germany. All of Aquitaine, the province of the Nine Peoples, and the provinces of Lugdunensis and Narbonensis have been laid waste, except for a few cities; and even these are devastated from without by the sword and within by famine. I cannot mention Toulouse without tears; that it has not yet fallen is due to the merits of Saint Bishop Exuperius.

Yet he seems not to have lived longer in any region of Gaul than at Trier. As he was just about to depart, Ruffinus had asked him to copy out Saint Hilary’s books for him; when Jerome himself reached Trier, he carried this out with great diligence. Thus, as he later says in Letter 6, writing to Florentius:

> I myself copied out for him [Ruffinus] at Trier, in my own hand, Saint Hilary’s very lengthy book On the Synods.

And indeed that transcription of the Hilary manuscript could not have been completed in a very short time. Moreover, he indicates in the Preface to the second book of his Commentaries on the Epistle to the Galatians that he knew the language of the people of Trier well. There he says that, apart from the Greek language, they had a language of their own, and that it was almost the same as that spoken by the Treveri in Gaul. He could certainly not have learned this so well without spending a considerable period of time among them.

Elsewhere also, when he recalls his travels with Bonosus, he immediately names the region through which they had passed: the half-barbarous banks of the Rhine, where, after their Roman studies, he and Bonosus were to enjoy the same food and equal hospitality together (Letter 3). Finally, it was there that he first began to wish to serve God (ibid.), that is, to consider undertaking a new way of life and perhaps even entering the desert, and to encourage Bonosus to adopt the same calling.

# CHAPTER V

I. He returns from Gaul to Stridon and Aquileia.  
II. He writes a Letter to Innocentius concerning a woman struck seven times.

## I.

Since the purpose of serving Christ that he had conceived in Gaul was to be fulfilled by action as soon as possible, Jerome understood that he must return to Italy and to his native land. This was not because he wished to profess himself a monk in his father’s house, among his relations and kinsmen (Letter 15)—indeed, he could not calmly tolerate the presence of monks even in cities—but because, in some way, responsibility for the family property, as well as for his sister and for his brother Paulinianus, who was then in the earliest years of childhood, seemed to rest upon him.

Certainly, several matters stood in the way of his immediately carrying out that purpose. He himself excuses these to Christ in Letter 3 to Ruffinus with the words “because I could not fulfill it.” He therefore remained in his homeland, or rather at Aquileia because of its proximity and his friendships there. For it is apparently to this period that the principal examples of his friendships with Valerianus, Chromatius, Jovinus, Eusebius, Julianus, Nicaea, Chrysogonus, Ruffinus, and others belong—friendships whose examples we have already reviewed above.

During the same period—or, if one prefers, while he was traveling toward Gaul—at Concordia, which is near Aquileia (not, as Victorius thinks, another town near Mirandola), he met the old man Paulus and made him his friend. Paulus was one hundred years old and had served as Saint Cyprian’s secretary at Rome.

There are also those who report that Jerome wished to enroll himself among the monks of Aquileia, or among those who, under Bishop Valerianus, were living a life modeled on that of monks. But this is established by no certain testimony, nor can it be inferred from the passage that they cite in support of it, from Letter 82 to Theophilus. There the holy Father says that “from adolescence he had preferred to be shut up in the cells of a monastery rather than to appear to be something.” For the passage must be understood entirely of the solitude of Syria, which he entered while still a young man, not of the monastery at Aquileia.

Those are still more mistaken, and reverse the sequence of Jerome’s life, who maintain that he went from Gaul first to Rome and then from Rome to Aquileia. They invent this account to serve their hypothesis and to transfer to this period the baptism of the holy Father, which they believe he received nowhere but at Rome.

But there is no evidence in Jerome’s writings or in his entire history by which they can establish this. As for the one passage they produce from Letter 43 to Marcella, where Jerome indicates that he was unwillingly living at Rome amid such a great crowd of citizens and foreigners, and further says that he would rather move elsewhere—that passage, I say, has nothing to do with the matter. For the letter was written much later than they suppose: it was written after he had left the solitude of Chalcis, come to Rome, spent a long time there with Damasus, and formed a friendship with Marcella. This belongs approximately to the year 385.

Nor can anything less be gathered from the context than that he had Aquileia in mind. While exaggerating how many troubles Rome contained, he was discouraging not so much Marcella as himself from the tumult of cities and inviting them to the seclusion of the countryside.

I add that, given the geographical situation and the character of Jerome’s travels, it is wholly implausible that he came from Gaul to Rome in order later to withdraw again to his homeland or to Aquileia. Moreover, we have already shown in Chapter III above that he had previously received baptism, namely when he was first studying literature at Rome. Thus the supposed reason for his returning there is entirely fabricated, and the whole account of the otherwise highly learned men has the appearance of an invention.

The holy Father therefore came directly from Gaul to Stridon, but spent most of his time at Aquileia, for the reasons we have mentioned.

## II.

It seems that he also began his literary work there with the account of the woman struck seven times, which he addressed to Innocentius and to which we assigned the first place in our sequence of the Letters, as it also occupies the first place among his other writings.

This Innocentius is the same man who shortly afterward accompanied Jerome when he migrated to the East. We must not invent, as some do, other men of the same name who were equally close friends of his.

As for the date, one may consult the chronological notes on that Letter, where we have set out the arguments that persuaded us to assign it to this period, or to the year 371. It would now be preferable to place it a year later, after Auxentius had been condemned through the efforts of Evagrius at the Roman Synod of 372.

Nevertheless, the arguments of those who place it still later are not without probability, assigning it as late as the year 374, when the holy Father was staying at Antioch after his long journey in the East. The principal argument they derive from the death of Auxentius, where Evagrius is said to have buried him almost before he was dead, does not have the same force for us. For they insist that those words truly indicate death; we understand “buried” to be used metaphorically (*μεταφορικῶς*), when he was struck with an anathema. Dead, but not in the literal sense.

# CHAPTER VI

I. He incurs various hostilities at Aquileia.  
II. Suddenly torn away from there, he sails to the East.

## I.

Jerome would very gladly have remained at Aquileia, and perhaps would even have fulfilled there, in the monastery that existed in that place, his purpose of serving God more perfectly—a purpose by which he was possessed with extraordinary ardor—had he not been driven away by a sudden storm, as he himself says, and by an impious separation.

What exactly happened is unknown; but several things seem to have combined to create hostility toward him. Some lapse on the part of his sister aroused great hatred against him. From this perhaps also arose his disagreement with Lupicinus, the priest of Stridon, whom he sharply attacks in Letter 7, calling him “a lid worthy of a pot”—that is, as though a blind man were leading the blind into a pit, and as though the ruler were like those whom he ruled.

There are also those who think that Jerome refers to him under the name of the Iberian viper, by whose evil tongue the holy Father complains in the preceding Letter that he had been savaged. He also incurred the hostility of his maternal aunt Castorina, which he later attempted to soften by the most gracious letters.

## II.

At that time other quarrels of this kind could have arisen through the devil’s art, as he himself suggests. Since he was unable to endure them calmly, he suddenly resolved to say farewell to his homeland, parents, relations, and friends, and to cross into the East, so that he might find a region more suitable both to the purpose of a solitary life and to the sanctity of the places, as well as to the proximity of the monks who lived there, and thus be farther removed from the hatred of his enemies.

We assign this journey to the year 372, and do not think that our calculations mislead us. But because the matter is complicated, and many points in Jerome’s life depend upon this date, it must be supported by arguments of its own.

The entire sequence of events that we have related so far forbids placing it earlier. To place it later is even more strongly forbidden by the argument drawn from Ruffinus’s journey. It is clear to everyone that Jerome had set out before him; and Jerome himself is the most explicit witness to this in the frequently cited passage of Letter 3: “After a sudden storm tore me away from your side,” and so forth.

It is established from Ruffinus’s own words that in this very year 373, perhaps several months after Jerome, Ruffinus left the monastery at Aquileia in order to travel to Egypt with Saint Melania. Writing to Pope Anastasius in the year 400 or the following year, he says that he had been restored to his parents after nearly thirty years.

“Nearly,” he says, so that one should not understand him to mean a full thirty years, but rather infer from that expression and the round number that it is sufficient if the twenty-ninth year had only just begun. Now, from 372 to 401 there are precisely that many years. There is certainly no clearer passage for establishing the date of Jerome’s journey as well as Ruffinus’s.

Nevertheless, there will perhaps be those who conclude from the same evidence that the journey must be postponed to the following year, 373, and who will wish to calculate the thirty years mentioned by Ruffinus from the time when he had ceased to live with his parents—not from the time when he sailed to Egypt, but from approximately three years earlier, when he left his native town of Tora and withdrew to Aquileia.

Although this is contrary to probability—for Tora, or Tyra or Tura, was a small town very near Aquileia, so that Ruffinus would not seem to have been away from his family while he was at Aquileia, and in fact, when he says that he was restored to his parents, Jerome testifies at the beginning of his second book against Ruffinus that he was living at Aquileia—there are nevertheless other arguments that can be raised in support of the year 373, and it is our responsibility to answer them.

First, Evagrius, who is mentioned so frequently in Jerome’s letters, appears to have been his companion on the journey. He, however, had come from the East to the West with Saint Eusebius of Vercelli in order to assist the churches in their gravest affairs. After Auxentius, condemned chiefly through his efforts, he is believed to have returned to the East only in the year 373. Certainly, before reaching Antioch, he passed through Cappadocia and discussed certain matters with Saint Basil; Basil records these in Letter 8, written after the autumn of that year, 373. Therefore Jerome, who seems to have accompanied Evagrius, cannot have set out before that year.

Furthermore, Ruffinus himself could not have undertaken the journey earlier. It is established and indisputable that he was in Alexandria in this very year 373, before Saint Athanasius’s death. Jerome’s third Letter to him makes the same point. Since, as we shall show more fully in its proper place, it was written in the summer of 374, it nevertheless indicates that the first news he received of Ruffinus’s arrival in Egypt became for him the occasion of unexpected joy. If Ruffinus had traveled to those regions two years earlier, it scarcely seems plausible that news of it should have reached his friend Jerome so late.

To answer these points, we say first that Evagrius was indeed among Jerome’s earliest friends, but was by no means his companion on this journey. Certainly, nowhere in the entire history of Jerome’s life are we led to believe this. The many praises that the holy Father offers of Evagrius are simply testimonies to their familiar association, especially when they were together at Antioch. This includes the passage in the already cited Letter 3, where he compares Innocentius, who had certainly been his companion in travel, with Evagrius as one eye with another. After Innocentius had been taken from him by an unexpected death, he says: “Now I enjoy our Evagrius as my one and complete light.”

Even if we grant that Evagrius was his companion on the journey, he was certainly not so when Jerome first departed from Aquileia. Perhaps Evagrius encountered him while Jerome had already been traveling through various provinces for some time, in Cappadocia, and completed the remainder of the journey with him toward Syria.

We can dispose of the second argument, drawn from Ruffinus’s departure, more easily. Ruffinus did not proceed directly to Egypt, but first visited Jerusalem and the Holy Places. Considering the religious care with which these places had to be explored, and especially the great distance by land and sea that had to be covered, the interval between the year 372—probably in its final months—and March or April of the following year, 373, when he was in Alexandria before Athanasius’s death, should certainly not seem excessively short.

Moreover, it is false that Jerome received news of Ruffinus’s stay in Egypt only around the middle of the following year, 374. He could easily have heard of it much earlier from Heliodorus, his companion on the journey, who had gone to Jerusalem, when Heliodorus returned to Alexandria.

The same news was confirmed shortly afterward, still in the preceding year, 373, by an Alexandrian monk sent to the confessors whom the Emperor Valens ordered to be exiled in Egypt immediately after Athanasius’s death. But the holy Father was not satisfied by these and subsequent reports until, in the year 374, he finally gave credence to the large number of travelers who came from there and reported the matter with more certain testimony.

He himself bears witness to all this in detail in that Letter 3 to Ruffinus. It will be useful to transcribe a few passages:

> The first report of this unexpected joy, this happiness, was brought to me by the brother Heliodorus. I did not believe what I wished to be certain, especially since he said that he had heard it from someone else, and the novelty of the matter deprived the report of credibility.  
>   
> Again my hopes were suspended and my mind wavered, until an Alexandrian monk, who had long before been sent to the Egyptian confessors—already martyrs in intention—through the devout service of the people, compelled me to believe the report by his evident authority. I confess that even then my conviction faltered. For although he did not know your homeland or your name, he seemed to offer greater confirmation because he asserted the same things that another had already reported.  
>   
> At last the full weight of truth burst forth: a large number of travelers reported that Ruffinus was at Nitria and had gone to the blessed Macarius. Then I completely loosened the reins of my credulity, and so forth.

Nothing, therefore, prevents us from assigning Jerome’s journey to the East to the year 372, despite the arguments that seemed most strongly to oppose it.

# CHAPTER VII

I. The journey of the holy Father is described.  
II. Did he visit Jerusalem at that time?  
III. He remained at Antioch.

## I.

Some are convinced that Jerome undertook the journey by land through Illyricum, and traveled through Thrace, Pontus, Bithynia, Galatia, Cappadocia, and finally Syria. This opinion seems to us wholly implausible. Indeed, the holy Father himself appears to indicate quite clearly that, having embarked at once from the Aquileian coast, he reached Thrace by ship and initially suffered the violence of the sea.

Let us give his own words, which explain the entire matter admirably in the frequently cited Letter 3 to Ruffinus:

> After a sudden storm, he says, tore me away from your side; after an impious separation tore me away from the bond of love to which I clung,
>
> then the blue rain stood above my head,
>
> [lacuna]
>
> then sea everywhere and sky everywhere.
>
> At last, as I wandered uncertainly in my exile, when Thrace, Pontus, and Bithynia, and the entire journey through Galatia and Cappadocia, and the land of the Cilicians with its burning heat had broken me, Syria appeared to me as a most faithful harbor for a shipwrecked man.

Elsewhere also he mentions other regions and cities through which he passed. Thus, in his Commentary on chapter 12 of Zechariah, he reveals that he had been at Athens:

> On the Acropolis of the Athenians, he says, beside the statue of Minerva, I saw a bronze sphere of enormous weight, which I could scarcely move because of my feeble little body, and so forth.

And in the Preface to the second book of his Commentaries on the Epistle to the Galatians:

> He who saw Anchyr[a], the metropolitan city of Galatia, knows with me how many schisms have torn it apart even to this day and with how many varieties of doctrines it has been defiled.

He examined other places of this kind elsewhere. It can also be gathered from Letter 121 to Algasi[a], Question 2, that he spent some time at Tarsus in Cilicia, where he shows that he knew very well the peculiarities of the Cilician language used by the Apostle Paul in his Letters.

Likewise, it is clear from Letter 2, addressed to Theodosius, that he met Theodosius—who is believed to have established a monastery at Rhossus in Cilicia on the seacoast—and investigated his way of life, as well as that of the other anchorites under him, and was inflamed with love for a similar life.

For he wished to observe with his own eyes whatever seemed especially noteworthy, above all the more celebrated communities of monks, whose institutions he traveled in particular to learn and imitate.

His constant companions on the journey were, besides Innocentius and Heliodorus, whom we mentioned above, Nicaeas, a subdeacon of Aquileia, and Hyla, the servant of Saint Melania, who had washed away the stain of slavery through the purity of his conduct (Letter 3).

Bonosus, with whom he had been raised from infancy and educated in the honorable arts of the world, and who had accompanied him on his journey through Gaul, had already sought solitude on an island surrounded, apparently, by the sea of Dalmatia—a shipwrecked place where everything was terrifying.

## II.

Whether he visited Jerusalem on this first journey to the East has been disputed among scholars. The holy Father himself, writing to Eustochium in Letter 22, testifies that he had left his people with the intention of going to Jerusalem to serve as a soldier. In Letter 45 to Asella, when he was at Rome, he also asks her to pray that he may one day be permitted to return from Babylon to Jerusalem. These words indicate that he had previously been at Jerusalem.

Likewise, in the Preface to Didymus’s book On the Holy Spirit, which he translated from Greek into Latin, he says that from Babylon—that is, Rome—he had returned to Jerusalem as though by right of return, and that after Romulus’s hut and the Lupercalia festival he had entered the lodging of Mary and the cave of the Savior.

Furthermore, Baronius, Victorius, and other men of great reputation hold the opinion that he came to Jerusalem twice: once on this first journey to the East, before entering the desert of Chalcis; and no one doubts the second arrival, namely when he departed from Rome after the death of Damasus.

Yet whatever others may think, more compelling testimonies from the holy Author himself persuade us that he went to Jerusalem only once, and not on the journey we are discussing, but on another journey to the East undertaken long afterward.

Indeed, if he had gone there at that time, how could it be that, after enduring the hardships of his long journey, while staying at Antioch and writing from there the frequently mentioned Letter to Ruffinus, he would omit, among the many details he relates to his friend about his travels, the one matter that surpassed all the others? Why would he not mention the holy city, where he knew that his friend had long before been?

He omitted it because he had not yet visited it.

And indeed, in Book 3 against the same Ruffinus, speaking of his second journey through the regions of the East, he declares that he visited the Holy Places as though he had previously heard something about them only by report and had never seen them:

> I entered Jerusalem, I saw many miracles, and I confirmed by the judgment of my eyes what report had previously brought to me.

As far as I can see, nothing can be set against this argument. The points brought forward above in opposition admit of an easy answer.

First, the holy Doctor truly migrated to the East with the intention and desire of visiting Jerusalem, but afterward was led to Syria for other reasons and changed his plan or postponed it to another time. He himself indicates this when, having already entered the desert of Chalcis and writing from there Letter 5 to Florentius, he reveals that, after reading Florentius’s letter, his desire to travel to Jerusalem had been rekindled.

There is therefore no reason to alter anything in that passage of the Letter to Eustochium, as Tillemont thought necessary. He judged that “Jerusalem” should there be read as “Antioch” or “the East.”

The other two passages trouble us much less, indeed scarcely at all. Since it is certain that he calls Rome Babylon metaphorically (*μεταφορικῶς*), the nature of the matter itself requires us to understand the Jerusalem that he sets against it in the same sense: as a place of solitude and peace. Thus he signifies once again that he had passed from the tumult of cities and the world to a solitary life.

We therefore do not agree with those who deny that the holy Father went to Jerusalem at this time, before withdrawing to Chalcis, but maintain that he went there on his first visit only after leaving the desert of Chalcis, around the year 378, before returning to Rome.

The arguments presented above prove, in fact, that he did not move there until much later, when he again departed from Rome after the death of Damasus, intending to spend the rest of his life in the Holy Places and in the cave at Bethlehem.

## III.

At that time, therefore, he appears to have traveled no farther than Antioch. In that city he was obliged to remain for some time with Evagrius, to whom he was especially dear, for reasons that we shall soon explain, and also because his bodily strength, weakened by so long a journey, was no longer sufficient and he had begun to suffer from poor health.

Of the entire journey, however, nothing seems so remarkable to us as this: although he could calmly endure, as he himself testifies, being without his homeland, home, parents, sister, relations, the custom of more refined food (Letter 22), and all the other conveniences of life, he nevertheless carried with him a single library, furnished with carefully selected books, which he had assembled at Rome with immense labor and expense, because he could not endure being without it.

So great was his love of letters and learning.

# CHAPTER VIII

I. He stays as a guest at Antioch, where he considers entering solitude.  
II. He writes Letters to his friends on this subject.  
III. He listens to Apollinarius of Laodicea and guards against his heresy.  
IV. He stays at Maronia and hears from Malchus himself the story of the monk.

## I.

The year 373 was drawing to an end, if our calculations are correct, when Jerome came to Antioch. He remained there as Evagrius’s guest until well into the middle of the following year.

We have already indicated that the principal reason for his delay was the illness into which he had fallen. For he himself says that, being always ill, he had added a burden to the labor of his friend Evagrius and had experienced every kind of disease that could exist.

Other struggles with harsher fortune were added to these. Of his four companions on the journey, Innocentius and Hyla were carried off by sudden death, one after the other. The former was taken by a sudden attack of fever; the latter did not wait until the wound left by Innocentius’s death had healed before his own death reopened it.

Heliodorus, and perhaps Nicaeas with him, had already gone to Jerusalem. They did not soon return from there to Antioch to remain with their Jerome, but were considering a return to their homeland, each for a different reason.

Heliodorus had a fair claim: having been informed unexpectedly of the death of a relative, he was compelled to return to his homeland in order to attend to the affairs of his widowed sister and her small child, his nephew Nepotianus.

Yet he did not entirely abandon his plan of entering solitude. Rather, he asked Jerome to send him an invitation once Jerome had withdrawn to the desert. We shall explain in its proper place that this was done shortly afterward.

## II.

Meanwhile, as the holy Father burned ever more intensely with the desire to enter solitude, and turned no other matter over in his mind, he wrote on the subject to Theodosius, whom we mentioned shortly above and whom Theodoret mentions in Chapter 10 of the *Lives of the Fathers* as the superior of the monastery at Rhossus in Cilicia. Jerome indicates that he had visited him shortly before while passing through that province.

From this one may conclude that those are mistaken who regard this Theodosius as another man, one who lived in the desert of Chalcis. For Jerome had not yet gone there when he wrote this letter.

He asks Theodosius and the other anchorites with him to obtain from God that he may at last wish and be able to carry out his purpose of serving God more perfectly.

That Letter occupies the second place in our recension. During the same period of his stay at Antioch he wrote two others, one to Ruffinus and the other to Florentius; in this same edition of ours they follow under numbers 3 and 4.

It does not seem necessary for our present purpose to repeat what they contain or for what reasons we assign them to this period, especially since these matters have been treated sufficiently and at length in the chronological notes on them. We merely point out that the year 373 is marked in some places through a printer’s error instead of the year 374, to which we assign them. In certain copies this error continues as far as Letter 14. We are taking care to correct it.

## III.

To return to the sequence of his life: the holy Father did not remain with Evagrius in such a way that he never left Antioch. Rather, inflamed by his devotion to sacred literature, and, as he elsewhere testifies of himself, having no confidence at all in his own intellectual powers and wishing to teach himself by learning from learned and distinguished men, he frequently visited Apollinarius, Bishop of Laodicea, a city not far from Antioch, and placed himself under his instruction.

He relates the matter in Letter 84 to Pammachius and Oceanus. There he also professes that he owed Apollinarius much, since, although he had previously scarcely saluted the threshold of scriptural learning, he had made considerable progress by becoming accustomed to reading foreign authors.

More remarkable is what he adds: that he had never accepted Apollinarius’s contentious doctrine concerning the sense. That is, he never accepted, nor allowed himself to be deceived by, that heretical teaching of Apollinarius, drawn from the muddy springs of the Platonists: namely, that the soul is a certain separable substance; consequently he maintained that the man whom the Lord had assumed was deficient in the part by which he is rational, and transferred that part’s functions to the Word, so that, in his delusion, Christ might be called one.

This also confirms what we said: that during this period Jerome had studied under the teacher of Laodicea. For Apollinarius had concealed his poisonous doctrine by craft for a long time and did not break into open heresy until the year 376.

Nor does it have any appearance of truth that Jerome used as his teacher a man who openly corrupted the Church’s doctrines with Platonic sophistries and who already bore the manifest mark of heresy.

## IV.

But during this period the holy Father also occasionally went elsewhere. Maronia, a village situated about thirty miles from Antioch, had come into the possession of the priest Evagrius after passing through many owners or patrons.

Because of his friendship with Evagrius, Jerome came there and stayed for some time. This happened before he withdrew to the desert, as nearly everything provides evidence. There lived an old man of great renown named Malchus. The holy Father visited him and wished to receive from his own mouth the account of his life, which he later, before the year 392, as we shall explain in its proper place, committed to writing on the authority of Malchus’s own words.

# CHAPTER IX

I. He withdraws into the desert of Chalcis and devotes himself to penance.  
II. He gives himself over to the study of Hebrew in order to subdue the flesh more completely.  
III. Did he also learn Greek at that time?  
IV. Warned in a dream, he sends pagan authors away.

## I.

At last Jerome entered the solitude toward which he had been carried with all his zeal. From what has been discussed so far, it is clear that this occurred toward the end of the year 374 or at the beginning of the following year.

To grasp this more clearly here, and almost with evident proof, calculate the chronology as follows. The year 374 was in progress and summer had reached its midpoint when, after receiving news of Ruffinus’s arrival in Palestine, the holy Father sent him a Letter, attaching it to another addressed to Florentius so that it might be delivered more securely.

At that time Jerome himself was still at Antioch, or had not yet withdrawn to the desert; this is clear from the context of both Letters. He had recently withdrawn there when he received Florentius’s reply. He says that the letter was delivered to him “while I was staying in that part of the desert which adjoins the Saracens beside Syria,” and “while I was confined within the boundaries of the solitude I had undertaken.”

Therefore, unless we assign to Florentius’s letter to Jerome a longer interval than it is reasonable to suppose, it is evident that Jerome withdrew into the desert toward the end of the year 374 or, at the latest, at the beginning of the following year. So much may be said about the date.

As for the solitude itself, it was situated in Chalcis of Syria, that is, where the Syrians are separated from the barbarous Hagarenes, in a vast tract of land extending in every direction. Scorched by the heat of the sun, it provided the monks with a dreadful dwelling.

There the holy young man sat alone, accompanied only by scorpions and wild beasts. Out of fear of Gehenna he had condemned himself to such a prison. His emaciated limbs bristled beneath sackcloth, and his filthy skin was covered with the squalor of Ethiopian flesh. Every day there were tears, every day groans; and whenever approaching sleep overcame him despite his resistance, he struck his barely attached bones against the bare earth.

His face grew pale through fasting, along with the other details that you may read for yourself in the Letter to Eustochium, Letter 22, from which these words have been taken.

In addition, he was very frequently, almost continually, tested by illness and suffered from his stomach. Yet even when he was weak, he was extraordinarily abstinent from wine, oil, and other foods by which strength is restored and people are refreshed for labor. He used only cold water and considered it luxury to have eaten anything cooked.

He also seems to have devoted part of the day to manual labor, namely to copying books. He revealed in Letter 5 to Florentius that he had assistants who practiced the art of the copyist; everyone knows that by this term amanuenses are meant.

For the rest, he divided his whole life between prayer and reading in such a way that, although he possessed an abundance of many excellent books of the sacred library, reading followed prayer, and prayer sustained reading.

II. He devoted his mind especially to understanding the Scriptures and investigating divine matters, and in this study he disciplined himself with daily exercises, applying himself with the utmost diligence, beyond anything that can be expressed. But when he realized that his efforts were being spent less profitably without knowledge of Hebrew, and when he also wished to employ some new torment to restrain the daily increasing impulses of the flesh, he gave himself over to this study—or, as he himself calls it, to this “mill” (pistrinum).

He himself relates the story in Letter 125 to Rusticus:

> “When I was a young man,” he says, “and the deserts of solitude enclosed me, I could not endure the incentives to vice and the ardor of nature. Although I broke these by frequent fasts, my mind nevertheless seethed with thoughts. To tame it, I placed myself under the instruction of a certain Brother who had converted from the Hebrews, so that, after the refinements of Quintilian, the flowing eloquence of Cicero, the gravity of Fronto, and the gentleness of Pliny, I might learn the alphabet and practice hissing, breathless words. My conscience bears witness to how much labor I expended there, how much difficulty I endured, how often I despaired, how often I stopped, and how, through the intensity of my desire to learn, I began again—my own conscience, which suffered these things, as well as the consciences of those who shared my life. And I give thanks to the Lord that I now reap sweet fruits from the bitter seed of letters.”

The same purpose also seems to be indicated by what he relates in chapter 3 of *On Illustrious Men*: namely, that when the Nazarenes who used it in the Syrian city of Beroea gave him the opportunity, he copied what was said to be a Hebrew copy of Matthew.

As time passed, having learned by experience the usefulness of this study, he cultivated it through constant practice and mentions elsewhere the other teachers through whom he advanced. “With what labor,” he says in Letter 84, “at what price I acquired Baranina as a teacher by night! For he feared the Jews and provided me with another Nicodemus.” This appears to be the same man whom he calls “my Hebrew” in his Commentary on chapter 3 of the Epistle to the Galatians, and from whom he quotes several statements, although others—including Morinus—maintain that he was a Christian converted from Judaism.

Finally, when he undertook to emend the Book of Chronicles according to the Septuagint from the Hebrew original and to translate it into Latin, he consulted another teacher of that language, as he testifies in the Preface:

> “From Tiberias I obtained a former teacher of the Law, who was held in admiration among the Hebrews, and I compared [the text] with him from the top, as they say, to the very last fingernail.”

But these matters belong elsewhere.

III. There are some who maintain that he first applied himself to the Greek language in the solitude of Chalcis. They infer this from Rufinus, who testifies that before his conversion he was entirely ignorant both of Greek literature and of the language itself. But if Rufinus wrote this truthfully, without being driven by a malicious desire to disparage him, he intended by the word “conversion” not the beginning of Jerome’s withdrawal into solitude, as it is commonly understood, but his reception of baptism. The entire context of the passage also strongly favors this interpretation.

This confirms once again what we stated earlier in its proper place: that Jerome was educated in the liberal studies while he was at Rome, and was not, as some hold, washed in the waters of baptism only afterward. Otherwise, I can hardly bring myself to believe that, when he traveled to the East, he knew no Greek at all. In order to become increasingly proficient in the language, he was able to acquire it through his regular contact with Greeks. Indeed, while he was staying at Tarsus, he knew it well enough to distinguish from the rest of Greek the particular features of the Cilician dialect that Paul used in his Epistles.

Moreover, when he shortly afterward came to Antioch, he frequently visited Apollinarius, as we have said, and listened to him expound the Scriptures in Greek—for he could scarcely have been instructed by his teaching unless he already understood the language thoroughly. He had therefore added this further accomplishment to the other distinctions of his learning before he entered the desert of Chalcis.

IV. There is, however, another matter that should be assigned to that place and approximately that period, and that likewise concerns his literary studies. I mean the vision or dream that has become especially famous and that the holy Father himself recounts at length in Letter 22 to Eustochium.

In the middle of Lent—perhaps in the year 275 or the following year, as may be inferred from the sequence of events—he was seized by a very violent fever. His body was so exhausted that his bones scarcely held together, and he came very near actually giving up his spirit; funeral preparations were already being made as though he were on the point of death. Suddenly he was carried in spirit before the tribunal of Christ. Because he had devoted himself to reading Cicero, the presiding judge ordered that he be beaten with the utmost severity.

While he was crying out amid the blows and pleading for mercy, and while those standing nearby fell at the President’s knees and begged him to pardon his youth and grant his error an opportunity for repentance, Jerome, constrained by the extremity of his situation, promised under oath that he would never again read the writings of pagan authors:

> “Lord,” he said, “if I ever possess secular books, if I read them, I have denied you.”

To confirm the reality of the event, he adds that, after being dismissed upon this oath, he awoke and found his shoulders bruised and felt the marks of the blows after his sleep.

Thus he was terrified by the appearance of reality in something that was nothing but a dream. Yet no one who repeatedly observes the testimonies and historical material scattered throughout the works he later composed can persuade himself that from that time onward he entirely renounced the reading of pagan authors. Accordingly, when Rufinus charged him with violating his religious commitment, Jerome most emphatically mocks the man’s curiosity in observing the deceptions of the night and demanding from a waking person what he had dreamed while asleep (*Against Rufinus*, Book II).

In the same way, when his rival objected that Jerome had had Cicero’s *Dialogues* copied by the brothers on the Mount of Olives at great expense, and that he read poets aloud to boys, Jerome mocks the charge more than he refutes it, thereby indicating that it deserved laughter rather than defense.

The account of the vision or dream therefore signifies nothing other than that, having from that time set aside the memorials of pagan authors—authors in whose works he had previously taken the greatest pleasure—he devoted himself entirely to the study of the Sacred Scriptures, whose language had previously seemed to him uncultivated and crude. He was no longer eager for secular learning, although, as he himself replies to Rufinus (*ibid.*), he continued to draw from the writings of those authors what he had formerly read, on account of his memory, while making all of it serve the exposition of divine matters as a handmaid serves her mistress.

We have said that no period can more suitably be assigned than this one for his renunciation of pagan literature and his transition to ecclesiastical studies.

# CHAPTER X

I. He writes the Life of Saint Paul the Hermit.  
II. He also writes letters to various persons.  
III. And an exhortation to Heliodorus.

[Col. 0032]

I. As soon as he had undertaken his life in solitude, Jerome thought that nothing was more consistent with his purpose than to stimulate his mind to imitation by recounting examples from the lives of its more distinguished practitioners. He therefore began by narrating the Life of Saint Paul, the first person to inhabit the desert and, by right and justice, its most eminent founder and exemplar.

Among all his writings he assigned this work the first place in his catalogue of writings. I have no doubt that, in compiling the catalogue, he took chronological order into account. Indeed, he places it before the Letter to Heliodorus, which was plainly written at the beginning of his life in solitude, and before the little book of letters to various persons, of which we shall speak presently.

It is thus entirely clear that those who think the work was written considerably later, after the holy author had left the Syrian desert, are mistaken. They were misled by a corrupt reading of the passage, which we long ago corrected with the help of excellent manuscripts.
