Where some editions had *vidisse me, et vixit, et sustentabatur* (“that I had seen, and he lived, and he was sustained”), we restored *videre, vivit et sustentatur* (“to see; he lives and is sustained”).

The holy Father also mentions the work in his *Chronicle* under the nineteenth year of Constantius, where he says that he explained the death of Paul of Thebes in a brief work. We shall mention it again shortly, when we review the Letter to Paul of Concordia.

II. Meanwhile, when Heliodorus had returned to Aquileia and informed his friends more fully about Jerome’s circumstances and holy purpose, they sent letters to him. Among the first were Chromatius and his brother Eusebius, together with their friend Jovinus, who also reported certain matters concerning Jerome’s sister—though Jerome himself had already learned these things somewhat earlier from Julian the Deacon of Aquileia.

These letters were carried to Antioch and, through the diligence of Evagrius, forwarded to Jerome, who was already living in solitude. He therefore wrote first to Julian, who had earlier written concerning his sister’s return to a better way of life. In our recension this is Letter 6. He earnestly asks Julian to assist her by whatever means he can and to make him happier through frequent conversations about their common glory in Christ.

Then, writing to Chromatius, Jovinus, and Eusebius in Letter 7, he adds praise of Bonosus, about whom they too had written, and commends to them his own sister, who had no good teachers in her homeland.

He appears to have added Letter 8, addressed to Nicaea, a former companion and fellow traveler from Aquileia who was now a subdeacon and had returned to his homeland—“You,” he says, “who have just departed from us,” and so forth. He urges him to write to him at some point, following the example of the brothers Chromatius and Eusebius. From this one may infer that the letter was written after Jerome had received their letters, and that it was composed on the same occasion on which he replied to them.

At the same time he also wrote Letter 9 to Chrysogonus, a monk of Aquileia, likewise encouraging him to write to him; and Letter 10 to Paul, an old man of Concordia—which, as we have said elsewhere, should not be confused with any place near Victorius, but was an important Italian town between Aquileia and Altinum [Col. 0033]. To Paul he sent as a gift the recently completed Life of Saint Paul the Hermit, which we have just reviewed.

The three letters that follow—to the Aemonian virgins, to Antonius, and to Castorina—may perhaps have been written in the same year, but on another occasion and somewhat later than the preceding letters. Jerome had previously sent them several other letters. Since they had neglected to reply, he complains bitterly and again urges them to write back at last.

With regard to the first two, we must first point out an old error, one that has prevailed among editors and among all writers of Jerome’s life. These virgins were called “Hermonian,” as was Antonius the monk; and it was commonly believed that they had lived on Mount Hermon in Palestine.

We have shown, however, as clearly as daylight—and have established the matter with the authority of manuscripts of the highest quality—that the reading should be *Aemonenses*, “Aemonian,” and that the reference is not to a mountain in Palestine, where the holy Father had not yet been, but to a notable city within the boundaries of Italy, Aemona or Haemona, praised by ancient geographers. It lay in Noricum, beneath Pannonia, and Jerome himself lived there for some time, since it appears to have bordered his native Stridon.

The other letter, namely Letter 13, addressed to his maternal aunt Castorina, was written a year after an earlier letter that he had sent her—which has been lost—in order to settle some disagreement he had had with her and to invite her once again to the peace and harmony for which he now prayed. It therefore appears to have been the last of the surviving letters that constituted the collection of letters to various persons, as Jerome himself calls it in his catalogue.

III. These letters are followed, in a separate recension, by the exhortation to Heliodorus, which carried off every prize for piety and learning. In chronological precedence it seems to deserve priority over some of the letters just reviewed, since it declares itself to have been written immediately after Jerome undertook his life in solitude. But its distinctive title and the order it occupies in the catalogue compel us to place it here.

When Heliodorus departed from Jerome, as we indicated a little earlier, he left him hope that, after arranging his domestic affairs in his homeland, he would return to the solitude in which he had not then been able to remain as a companion in the undertaking. He had even asked Jerome to write him an exhortatory letter on the subject once he had entered the desert.

Accordingly, as soon as the holy Father had entered the desert of Chalcis, he sent Heliodorus the eloquent exhortation he had promised him at his departure. In it, praising the blessedness of the hermit’s life, he left nothing unused in support of his case, whether from rhetorical art, the cultivation of piety, or the divine Scriptures.

It was valued so highly when it reached Aquileia and became publicly known that everyone competed to make copies of it; there were even people in Rome who learned it by heart. The holy author himself mentions it elsewhere more than once.

When Heliodorus received it, although he had not yet held office in the clergy, he could not bring himself to return to Syria, despite being called to that way of life. Instead, devoted to the service of the Church and later initiated into sacred orders, he advanced through a succession of Christian and especially distinguished virtues even to the dignity of bishop of Altinum [Col. 0034].

# CHAPTER XI

I. The Church of Antioch is disturbed by the factions of three bishops at once.  
II. Each faction attempts to draw Jerome to itself.  
III. The Meletians demand from him a profession of three hypostases.  
IV. He writes to Damasus once and again on this matter.  
V. The date of the first letter is asserted and defended.  
VI. Forced to yield to the arrogance of the factions, the holy young man considers abandoning the desert.  
VII. He writes to Marcus.

I. Jerome had hidden himself in that desert of Syria with the intention of remaining far from the snares of the world, washing away by the rain of tears and the harshness of his life the stains contracted through the heedlessness of youth. But, as he himself testifies concerning his situation (Letter 17), the relentless enemy followed him even there, so that he now suffered greater battles in solitude. Harassed by so many factions of the Church of Antioch, under whose jurisdiction he was, he thought it preferable to live among wild beasts than with such Christians.

For the history of the matter to be properly understood, we must go back somewhat further. Meletius had been transferred from the see of Sebaste to Antioch through the efforts of the Arians, though not without the considerable agreement of the Catholics. In his first sermon to the people in that Church he had argued against Arian doctrine, and was consequently rejected by the heretics, who appointed Euzoius as bishop in his place.

The Catholic party also separated itself from his communion, since its members knew that he had once communicated with the Arians and had been elected especially through Arian favor. This was particularly true of the Eustathians, that is, the body of more prominent Catholics who, from the time of Eustathius until Meletius, had adhered to none of the Arian bishops of Antioch.

To remedy this evil, Lucifer of Cagliari, a bishop then of great reputation and authority, created Paulinus a new bishop of Antioch in the year 372. His intention was certainly good, namely, to remove the schism, but the result was entirely contrary to what he intended.

At that point, apart from the Arian faction, the whole Church was divided into what were virtually two parties. The East joined the communion of Meletius, especially after the Council of Alexandria. That council had rejected the leaders and principal figures of the Arian heresy, but had determined that others should be received into Catholic communion—men who had either formerly communicated with the Arians or had been promoted through their influence to ecclesiastical offices.

The West and Egypt followed the party of Paulinus. But the evil did not stop there. Apollinarius of Laodicea seized this opportunity of dissension as a favorable occasion for bringing into the open the heresy he had long concealed. In the year 376 he sent another bishop to the Church of Antioch, a certain Vitalis, his own disciple, who was to uphold the unsound doctrines entrusted to him by the authority of the episcopal chair.

II. There were therefore four bishops of the same Church at one time. Three in particular—Meletius, Vitalis, and Paulinus [Col. 0035]—hurried, as Jerome says, to draw him to themselves. Each intended that Jerome should follow his own party and communion.

Since Jerome was uncertain about their orthodoxy, he answered: “If anyone is joined to the Chair of Peter, he is mine.” He considered only that person to be Catholic who was in communion with Peter’s successor and rested upon that rock on which the Church was built.

He knew well enough that Paulinus was in communion with Rome. Yet when the adherents of the other parties replied that they too differed in nothing from the Roman Pontiff—for, in writing to Damasus, Jerome says, “Meletius, Vitalis, and Paulinus claim that they adhere to you”—he was again left in doubt.

“I could believe it,” he said, “if only one person asserted this. Now either two are lying, or all of them.”

Indeed, almost the whole point of the controversy turned on this: all of them arrogated to themselves communion with Damasus, but which of the three had the right to do so? For this purpose, Gratian also sent Sapores, *magister militum*, to Antioch to hear the parties contend over that prerogative, as we learn from Theodoret.

Meanwhile, the holy Father adhered to none of them. Following no one as his leader except Christ, as he himself says, he joined himself in spirit to Damasus alone—that is, to the Chair of Peter. For this reason he would also have wished to seek the Lord’s sacrament, or the Eucharist, if the great distances of sea and land lying between them had not prevented it.

In the meantime, he followed only the Egyptian Confessors, Damasus’s most reliable colleagues in those regions, and would not allow himself to be defiled by communion with either faction.

III. The Meletians, more than the others, tried to draw him into their party. Unless he professed himself one of them, they terrified him with the suspicion and accusation of heresy, questioning him about the faith every day.

The source of the dispute—or rather, the stumbling block—was the word *hypostasis* (Greek: ὑπόστασις). The Greeks used it to signify a person and therefore did not hesitate to speak of three hypostases in the Trinity. The Latins, however, understood the word to mean “substance” and shrank in word and thought from speaking of three substances in the Trinity.

Yet Saint Athanasius had defined at the Council of Alexandria in the year 372 that either “one” or “three” could be said in an equally Catholic sense, since those who asserted one understood “substance,” whereas those who asserted three signified “persons” by that term.

Nevertheless, an incurable morbid passion for dispute had so invaded the minds even of learned bishops that it prevented them from recognizing the reality of the matter. They looked for a knot in a reed, twisting the word itself into an accusation of heresy according to the ideas of those who used it.

The Meletians were accused of defending three hypostases because, having once been joined in communion with the Arians, they were thought not yet to have completely abandoned their heretical mind. In turn, they accused the supporters of Paulinus, who asserted one hypostasis, as though they favored Marcellus and Sabellius.

Jerome therefore fell under the same suspicion, about which he complains at length in his Letter to Marcus:

> “I am called a heretic while proclaiming the Trinity as *homoousian* [ὁμοούσιον, ‘of one substance’]. I am accused of Sabellian impiety while proclaiming in an unwearied voice three true, complete, and perfect subsisting persons.”

And in the first letter to Damasus:

> “From the offspring of the Arians, the Campenses, a novel name is demanded of me, a Roman man: three hypostases . . . . . . We ask what they think can be understood by three hypostases. ‘Three subsisting persons,’ they say. We reply that we believe this. The meaning is not enough; they demand the word itself, because I do not know what poison lies hidden in the syllables . . . . . . and because we do not utter the terms, we are judged heretics.”

The holy young man could never be brought to make this profession of the three hypostases, unless it was explained in terms of the words themselves. He held that *hypostasis* properly signified “substance,” and that to speak absolutely of three hypostases in God was entirely impossible without sacrilege.

“The entire school of secular literature,” he says, “knows no meaning for *hypostasis* other than *ousia* [οὐσία, ‘substance’]. Who, I ask, will proclaim three substances with sacrilegious lips?”

IV. Thus, constrained on every side by such difficulties, the holy Father took refuge in the Roman Church. Before consulting its oracle, he thought that he had to withhold assent from everyone.

He therefore wrote Letter 15 in our recension to Damasus, earnestly imploring him to decide what he ought to believe and with which of the three bishops at Antioch he ought to communicate. After waiting a long time in vain for an answer, while the heretics continued to harass him more intensely each day, he wrote again to the same Pontiff, asking even more insistently the question of his communion.

If the reading of the first letter were the true and genuine one—“from the Arian bishop and the Campenses,” as some printed books and learned men prefer—then, since according to Jerome the only Arian bishop was Meletius, it would be certain that these events belonged to the year 378 or the following year. Meletius was not recalled from exile until the year 378, and only then could he have compelled Jerome, face to face, to confess the three hypostases.

We, however, have judged another reading to be more genuine: “from the offspring of the Arians, the Campenses.” This is the reading found in most manuscripts of better quality, examined both by us and by the Benedictine editor.

The meaning of the name also agrees with this reading. There is no reason to think that the Campenses were called by that name except that they held their sacred gatherings in the fields. In the same way, among others, Jerome himself calls the Donatists near Rome “Campenses” toward the end of his *Dialogue against the Luciferians*: since they were forbidden to remain in the city, they assembled in the countryside to perform their sacred rites.

In the same sense Jerome designated the followers of Meletius as the “offspring of the Arians,” because they had as their father a bishop whom the Arians had especially chosen; and he called them “Campenses” because, having been expelled from the city’s churches, they gathered in the fields and conducted their worship there for as long as Meletius remained in exile.

Meletius, therefore, had not yet been restored to the Chair of Antioch by Gratian’s decree. Once that had happened, he and the members of his communion regained the city churches and could no longer be called Campenses.

The same chronological indication is evident—and places the events somewhat before Gratian’s law of the year 378—from the passage in which the holy Father says that meanwhile he was following the Egyptian Confessors, Damasus’s colleagues.

These are the same Confessors whom we said were praised in Letter 3 to Rufinus: Egyptian bishops and colleagues of Damasus in the priestly rank, whom the emperor Valens had ordered to be exiled to Caesarea in Palestine.

If Jerome was receiving the Lord’s sacrament from them, he himself was certainly not far away, and they were still living in exile. For if they had already returned to Egypt through Gratian’s pardon, he would not have said that he was following merely those Confessor-bishops, but all the Egyptian Catholics, and especially Peter, the bishop of Alexandria himself.

They returned to their own people in that same year, 378, by the law of Gratian through which Meletius was restored to the Church of Antioch. The disputes about *hypostasis*, and the disturbances that so greatly tormented Jerome, therefore belong to the immediately preceding year, 377.

His first letter to Damasus must consequently be assigned to that period. The preceding events and the entire sequence of Jerome’s life do not permit us to place it earlier. Nor can it be postponed to a later time, because of the indication that Meletius was still in exile, from which we have argued above.

The other letter, Letter 13 to the same Damasus, appears to belong to the following year, 378. It was certainly written long enough after the first for Jerome to have been waiting patiently—and more than once—for the response of the Roman Pontiff.

It also appears to us to have been written after Gratian’s decree, or after the Meletians had regained their churches through the judgment of Sapores, the *magister militum*, if we correctly understand the sense of these words:

> “Here the Arian madness, supported by the defenses of the world, rages.”

By this name the holy Father can have meant no other party than the one that troubled him most. Of the three factions dividing the Church, it was the Meletian party that so insistently demanded from him a profession of the three hypostases.

It is called “Arian” in the sense explained above: Meletius had ascended the Chair of Antioch chiefly through the efforts of the Arians.

V. The learned Father Constantius, who reprinted these two letters of Jerome in his edition of the letters of the Roman Pontiffs, argues that both must be assigned much later, as late as the year 381. Since there is no time to pursue all the consequences of his argument, his chief evidence is that a synodal document, published by Labbeus in volume 2, seems to persuade us that Vitalis was appointed bishop of Antioch only after the death of Valens, that is, after the year 378.

Even if we do not now wish to diminish the authority of that book, it is not sufficiently authoritative to outweigh the Letter of Peter of Alexandria to the bishops, presbyters, and deacons who were in exile for the true faith. That letter is preserved by Facundus of Hermiane and belongs to the year 378 itself, when Valens was still alive.

There Peter, speaking of Timothy, whom Apollinarius had appointed bishop of Alexandria, says:

> “He also wanted me to anathematize Basil of Caesarea, Paulinus, Epiphanius, and Diodorus, the bishops, and to communicate with Vitalis.”

Vitalis, therefore, had long since been appointed bishop by Apollinarius.

Saint Ephrem confirms the same point. According to Jerome’s testimony in *On Illustrious Men*, Ephrem died during the reign of Valens; in his testament he mentions the “Vitalian” heretics—that is, the Apollinarians, whose doctrine Vitalis, already a bishop, represented by virtue of his office.

Finally, when Saint Epiphanius had dated the thirteenth year of Valens, corresponding to the conventional year 376, in the sixty-sixth heresy of the *Panarion*, he mentioned Vitalis as a bishop among the Apollinarians in the following, sixty-seventh heresy, which belongs to that same year or, at the latest, the next.

His ordination therefore cannot be postponed until after the death of Valens. There is no basis for the argument that the learned Constantius derives from the author of the *Synodicon*, a man whose reliability is not especially great. Rather, the common opinion should be retained: Vitalis was ordained around the year 376. This fits exceptionally well with the sequence of Saint Basil’s letters and the events related in them.

VI. Nothing is more probable, nor more consistent with Jerome’s history, than what we have stated: beginning in the year 377, he was harassed by the disturbances and demands of the factions, and was not thereafter permitted to remain in peace for a full two years and more.

They pressed, attacked, and demanded a declaration of faith from him every day, so that they seemed genuinely intent on driving the holy young man from the desert by these annoyances.

“Every day,” he says, “I am asked for my faith, as though I had been reborn without faith. I confess as they wish, but they are not satisfied. I subscribe, but they do not believe. They desire only one thing: that I leave this place.”

At last he was actually compelled to do so:

> “Now, now I yield. They have torn from me a part of my soul—my dearest brothers. Behold, they wish to depart—indeed, they are departing. I myself would already be fleeing, were I not held back by the weakness of my body and the severity of winter. Nevertheless, until spring arrives, I beg that I be granted the hospitality of the desert for a few months; or, if this seems too long to wait, I shall depart.”

Before leaving, he thought these words should be written to Marcus, a presbyter of Teleda, in Letter 17 of our recension. He did not so much answer Marcus’s demand for a profession of faith as complain about the utterly unjust harassment of the factions.

When he wrote this, he had already received from Damasus the answer he had so greatly desired, namely, with whom he should communicate at Antioch. He says:

> “They condemn me as a heretic with the West, as a heretic with Egypt—that is, with Damasus and Peter.”

The severity of winter of which he complains is an unmistakable indication of the end of the year 378, unless one prefers to think that he is referring to the beginning of the following year, 379.

It was certainly not the weather at the beginning of the year 378, as some have persuaded themselves. In that very year Jerome had written the second letter to Damasus, as has been shown, and in the letter to Marcus he indicates that he had already received Damasus’s answer.

Even if we grant that the letter was written in the preceding year, or in the same year as the first letter, the sequence of events and the interval of time between the first letter and this one, and then between this one and the response of the Roman Pontiff [Col. 0039], absolutely prevent us from thinking that the winter mentioned in the letter to Marcus belonged to the end of that same year or the beginning of 378.

If, on the other hand, one insists that these events occurred later, after the year 381, the same arguments by which we have just refuted the opinion of Father Constantius will easily disprove that view.

That winter, therefore, was the winter of the year 379. Jerome appears to have remained in the desert until the spring of that year, enduring the troubles we have described.

VII. With regard to Marcus himself, we noted long ago that in ancient manuscripts he is called “presbyter” or “bishop of Chalcis,” whereas some older printed editions call him “Celedensis.” It therefore seemed much more probable that, following other manuscripts, the name should be restored as “Teledensis,” after the town of Teleda in the region of Chalcis.

We learn from Theodoret’s *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 4, that the monastery of Saint Eusebius was not far from that place. Marcus could therefore readily have been the presbyter of that place to whom it belonged to learn about the faith of the people of Chalcis.

Near the end of the letter Jerome says that he had given Saint Cyril a written profession of faith. Since that writing was lost long ago, whatever it may have been, it nevertheless provided an opportunity for an impostor to fabricate a work under the holy Doctor’s name with the title *Explanation of the Faith to Cyril*. We have rejected it to the final volume among the falsely attributed works.

Those words also gave rise to a conjecture that we do not at all approve: learned men have thought that Saint Cyril of Jerusalem is being indicated there, and they claim that this fits because at that time Cyril had been expelled from his episcopal see and was wandering through the deserts of Syria.

But Jerome seems elsewhere to have been almost hostile to that Father’s name. In the *Chronicle*, composed shortly afterward, he attacks his ordination in harsh language and marks him as impious. It is therefore highly improbable that Jerome would entrust him with his profession of faith or call him “Saint.”

But enough of this.

# CHAPTER XII

I. He leaves the desert and returns to Antioch.  
II. He writes the *Dialogue between a Luciferian and an Orthodox Christian*.  
III. He is ordained presbyter by Paulinus.  
IV. The date of his ordination is established.

I. Since the Meletians continued their harassment without end, it is reasonable to believe that Jerome left the desert as soon as the season allowed—namely, in spring, as he had promised. He could no longer remain peacefully in a place where, contrary to the disposition both of his mind and of the region, he had not been permitted to live in quiet.

The year was 379, as is established by the arguments set out in the preceding chapter. This coincided approximately with the thirty-third year of his life and with the fourth, or at most the fifth, year from the beginning of his life in the solitude of Chalcis.

His love of that solitude had been deeply fixed in his mind. Whenever circumstances allowed, he had experienced so many spiritual delights there that, when he was forced to leave, he was almost consumed with grief, and afterward often regretted his departure.

“I was not at Rome,” he says in a letter to Pammachius, “and at that time the desert held me—and would that it had held me forever!”

Having left—or, more accurately, having been driven out by the persecutions of the heretics [Col. 0040]—he returned to Antioch and readily lodged with Evagrius, who, as before, generously supplied all his needs.

There, following the example of the Westerners, but especially instructed by the response of Damasus, he may be believed to have communicated with Bishop Paulinus, if ever he came close to the truth. Yet he did not do so in order to involve himself in the conflicts of the parties. Rather, since an opportunity for peace had been offered him and the most generous friend was providing for him, he used that opportunity for the benefit of the studies to which he remained constantly devoted.

## II.

As we stated in its proper place, Bishop Paulinus had been appointed by Lucifer of Caralis to succeed Meletius, who was then living in the Church of Antioch—a well-intentioned arrangement, certainly, but one that by no means turned out as intended. Jerome, however, although he adhered to Paulinus, Lucifer’s disciple, nevertheless strongly detested the sect of those who took their name from him, the Luciferians, and even attacked them in his writings.

It happened, in fact, in this very year, during which he stayed at Antioch, that a certain Luciferian named Elladius held a disputation in the city with an Orthodox Christian—for he calls the place a street and a portico. The holy Father recorded it in writing and even made it publicly available for the praise of Catholic doctrine. The affair lasted two days. At first, indeed, both sides proceeded more by insults than by arguments. When the lamps, already lit in the streets, dispersed the audience and the circle of listeners, and night interrupted the disorderly debate, they withdrew after having almost spat in each other’s faces. Nevertheless, those who had been present decided that they would meet early the next morning in a secluded portico. The disputation was taken down by notaries, and finally ended so successfully for the Orthodox side that the Luciferian, advancing toward better things, abandoned the position he had wrongly maintained.

Jerome represents this contest of the following day—or rather, the victory of the Catholic party—after prefacing it with a short introduction explaining the history, in the form of a dialogue. It may quite reasonably be believed that he copied it almost entirely from the official records, occasionally adding only a few details of his own, although to others the work appears to have been deliberately composed and polished in support of Catholic truth. Certainly, the events of the Council of Rimini, which are recounted in a sufficiently careful sequence, were copied from the council’s own records. These fragments, to be valued like gold and gems, survive today nowhere else and in no other place than in this book.

We must now demonstrate that we refer these events to this same year, 379. They cannot be assigned to a date earlier than Jerome’s return from the desert to Antioch. For Euzoius is already mentioned as dead—he died in the year 376 under Valens—and the disputation took place at Antioch. It was immediately after this disputation that the holy Father professes to have written the work, and, as we have shown, he came there in this very year.

Nor can his departure from that city for Constantinople be placed later. This book preceded Jerome’s work on the *Chronicle*, as the saint himself testifies in his catalogue of works; and it is generally agreed among chronologists that the *Chronicle* was published at Constantinople in the following year, that is, 380. Therefore, even if someone insists that the disputation was held somewhere other than Antioch—whether at Constantinople [Col. 0041] or in another city—he must place it before the composition of the *Chronicle*, which is assigned to the year 380, and can scarcely differ from our reckoning by more than a few months.

If anyone is still troubled by the fact that Lucifer is mentioned with considerable praise in the *Chronicle*, and finds it implausible that the constancy and faith of a man whose opinion—indeed, whose error—this dialogue attacks should there be celebrated, unless this book, in which he receives a bad report, was written after the one in which he is praised, let him know that even in this dialogue Lucifer is treated with sufficient restraint. Jerome says there: “I am compelled to think something different about the blessed Lucifer from what both his merit and my humanity require.” Conversely, in the *Chronicle* the man is not praised in such a way that his harshness and conduct are exempted from blame. There is therefore nothing here that should trouble anyone.

We now prefer to withdraw what we formerly judged in the note to this book—namely, that it should be referred to the immediately preceding year, 378—and to assign it instead to the subsequent year, about which we have been speaking.

## III.

Such studies, a mind naturally formed for handling divine matters, and, above all, extraordinary moral integrity established Jerome in the great esteem of men. They were so highly approved by Paulinus, the bishop of his party, that he wished to enroll him among the clergy and advance him to the sacred order of the presbyterate.

Jerome accepted this only very nearly against his will, allowing himself to be persuaded by the judgment and exhortations of so great a prelate. He imposed, however, the condition that this should in no way prevent him from returning to the desert if he wished, and that he could never be compelled to exercise the order he had received while bound to any particular church.

At the end of his book against John of Jerusalem, he himself reports what Bishop Paulinus heard from him, “a wretched man,” as he calls himself:

> “Did I ask you to ordain me? If you confer the presbyterate in such a way that you do not take away the monk from us, you must answer for your own judgment. But if, under the name of presbyter, you take from me that for which I abandoned the world, I have what I always had; you have suffered no loss in ordaining me.”

He consistently remained of this opinion, as may be gathered from the whole course of his life, and especially from the testimony of Saint Epiphanius in Letter 51 among the Hieronymian letters. There Epiphanius says that even in the year 394, out of modesty and humility, Jerome was unwilling to perform the sacrifices required by his office and was reluctant to undertake that part of the ministry which is the principal salvation of Christians.

In Jerome this was, as it was also in the presbyter Vincentius—of whom there will be occasion to speak later—an impulse that was by no means blameworthy, though it arose from a motive of piety toward God and religion different from the one usually assumed. From this we may infer for our present purpose that he was initiated into the presbyterate by a single χειροτονία (*cheirotonia*, ordination), in accordance with a practice that sometimes occurred in those ecclesiastical times on account of the exceptional merits of certain persons. Certainly he had not previously served as a deacon or received the earlier orders.

## IV.

We must now investigate the time at which this event took place. The sequence of the narrative that we have followed clearly shows that it occurred in this year, 379, or in the following year.

If the holy Father [Col. 0042] was ordained at Antioch—as we have no doubt, and as he himself explicitly testifies at the end of the already-mentioned book against John of Jerusalem:

> “For this reason I too left Antioch, and he [Vincentius] Constantinople, those most illustrious cities—not in order to praise you while you preached before the crowds, but to lament the sins of our youth in the fields and in solitude, and to turn Christ’s mercy toward us”—

then he was certainly not ordained on the first occasion when he stopped there during his journey from the East, but when he came there again from the desert of Chalcis. There is no doubt that he had not yet been initiated into sacred orders when he withdrew into that Syrian desert. Indeed, Paulinus’s words themselves make this clear:

> “If you confer the presbyterate in such a way that you do not take away the monk from us.”

That is, Jerome had already professed his name among the solitaries and wished to continue professing it in the future, even if he were advanced to the priestly rank.

He was therefore not ordained earlier than his second arrival at Antioch. Nor could it have been later. Since he was ordained nowhere but Antioch, and by no one other than Paulinus, bishop of that same Church—for those who regard this as uncertain are simply deceiving themselves—he nevertheless counts himself among the presbyters when he was living at Rome shortly afterward:

> “There are others,” he says, “and I am speaking of men of my order, who seek the presbyterate and the diaconate in order to look more freely upon women” (*Letter 22.28*).

It follows directly that the ordination in question cannot conveniently be assigned to any other period than that during which he stayed at Antioch for the second time, from the year 379 until approximately the middle of the following year.

Yet I see that these arguments conflict with a very clear testimony of Jerome himself in the book against John of Jerusalem, from which we have been arguing. There, in reply to an opponent who maliciously accused him of seeking primacy in the Church of God, he says:

> “If you speak of me and the presbyter Vincentius, you have slept for a very long time, since, after thirteen years, you now raise these accusations. For this reason I too left Antioch, and he Constantinople, those most illustrious cities … so that, while lamenting the sins of our youth in the fields and in solitude, we might turn Christ’s mercy toward us.”

Although it is not entirely certain in what precise year he wrote these words, we maintain, on good grounds, that they refer to the year 399; and if the arguments of others are preferred—as we shall discuss more fully in its proper place—they may be placed two years earlier.

However the matter may stand, if the thirteen years mentioned by the holy Father are to be reckoned from his ordination to the presbyterate—as the context at once seems to indicate, and as scholars generally do—then it follows that he was initiated into sacred orders considerably later, either in the year 386 or, at the very least, according to the opinion of others, in 384. This cannot in any way be reconciled either with the arguments given above or with the rest of his life.

Our own interpretation is different, and, unless we are very much mistaken, it is the only one consistent with the mind of the holy Doctor: namely, that those years are to be subtracted from 386, when Jerome himself returned to Antioch for the third time, after the death of Damasus, together with Vincentius, shortly before he hid himself in the cave at Bethlehem.

The words [Col. 0043] can mean nothing else than this: after returning to Antioch, where he could have remained in the Church to which he belonged by virtue of his earlier ordination, and where he may perhaps even have been attracted by the exhortations of the bishop and his friends to discharge the office of presbyter with greater distinction, he preferred to seek the fields and solitude.

He cannot have been referring to the time of his ordination. Since he joins his own conduct with that of Vincentius under the same reckoning of thirteen years, Vincentius certainly had not yet attained the same dignity at the time when Jerome was ordained. This is established by the holy Father’s own preface to the *Chronicle*, addressed to that same Vincentius. Although it was given in the following year, 380, while Jerome was living at Constantinople, he never addresses Vincentius as a presbyter, either at the beginning of the letter or in its body. He always adds that title in other books whenever he later mentions him, after Vincentius had received it.

There may also be someone who thinks that Vincentius was not ordained until after the middle of the year 385, when he returned once again to Constantinople—the period to which we argue that Jerome was referring. Yet in Book 3 against Rufinus, paragraph 22, when Vincentius boards a ship together with Jerome in the Roman harbor in order to return to the East, he is called “the holy presbyter.”

He could easily have been named so by πρόληψις (*prolepsis*, anticipation), because by the time these words were written he had long since been made a presbyter, even though he had not yet been one when the event narrated actually occurred.

However the matter may stand, it is clear that the thirteen years should not be reckoned from the date of ordination, when Jerome had no thought in mind other than being a monk, but from his second renunciation of the presbyterate, when he left Antioch for the third time. He even boasts that he was then in that city, enjoying communion with the pontiff and confessor Paulinus, and that, having been escorted by him in midwinter, he entered Jerusalem.

Nor does the holy Father indicate any other opportunity offered to him for earning advancement in an ecclesiastical rank. Nothing is more probable than that he was invited, with the greatest urgency and insistence, and almost compelled, to allow himself to be enrolled among the clergy and to perform the duties of his order.

On this interpretation, his statement is perfectly coherent: thirteen years earlier he had preferred to seek the fields and solitude rather than be devoted to the ministry of the Church and live amid the crowds, even with great dignity. Those, by contrast, who think that the reckoning refers to the ordination itself have no means of reconciling the events with one another and depart in every other direction.

Finally, those who dare to lay hands on the holy Father’s text and wish to have “sixteen” written in place of “thirteen” deserve to be admonished, so that they may learn to approach the records of the ancients, and especially of the Fathers, with greater caution and reverence.

# Chapter VI

[Col. 0044]

I. He travels from Antioch to Constantinople, where he hears Gregory of Nazianzus. II. There he translates Eusebius’s *Chronicle* into Latin and continues it. III. He also translates twenty-eight homilies of Origen. IV. He writes a treatise on the Seraphim.

What prevented Jerome, inflamed by his longing for the solitary life, from devoting himself to the services of the Church was also the fact that he was driven each day more strongly by a love of learning and wished to visit and adopt as his teachers those who were especially distinguished for their reputation in ecclesiastical learning.

For this reason he left Antioch, which was being miserably agitated by party disputes, and traveled to Constantinople. There he placed himself under the instruction of Saint Gregory of Nazianzus, whose eloquence and knowledge of Scripture he greatly admired. He boasts in several places that he had Gregory as his catechist (*Letter 50*, and elsewhere). He also professes that, under this teacher, he made great progress in the knowledge of divine matters—the reason Gregory was given the title “the Theologian” (*Against Jovinianus*, Book 1; *Against Rufinus*, Book 1)—and he sometimes cites conversations that he had with him.

He considered it a great benefit that, during the same period, he also came to know Saint Gregory of Nyssa at Constantinople (*Commentary on Ephesians*, chapter 5). Gregory of Nyssa read aloud to him, and to his namesake of Nazianzus, the books he had written against Eunomius, works full of learning and doctrine.

It is easy to suppose that Jerome went to Constantinople for the Second Ecumenical Synod, held in the year 381, and that he arrived before it was celebrated, specifically so that he might confer with Nazianzenus about certain matters. Gregory held the episcopate of the imperial city only during this period, from May of that year, after Maximus the Cynic had been deposed, until July, when he voluntarily resigned at the Ecumenical Council.

Yet he was acting as bishop when Jerome enjoyed his company, as the latter testifies in his commentary on Isaiah, chapter 6:

> “About thirty years ago, when I was at Constantinople and was being instructed in the studies of the holy Scriptures by the most eloquent man Gregory of Nazianzus, then bishop of that same city, I know that I dictated a brief and impromptu treatise …”

Nor does it seem proper to call Gregory bishop of that city for the period when he arrived to administer its Church, at the beginning of the year 379 or in the following year, when he was sent by the Emperor Theodosius to take possession of its basilicas.

Whatever the precise circumstances may have been, it may nevertheless properly be concluded from this that the sequence of the narrative places Jerome at Constantinople from the year 380 until approximately the middle of the following year.

## II.

Among the monuments of his intellect that he committed to writing while he was there, the first place belongs to the *Chronicle* of universal history. He translated into Latin the work written in Greek by Eusebius of Caesarea, enlarged it in many places, especially where Roman affairs were concerned, from the histories of Suetonius and other Latin writers, and finally continued it entirely on his own from the twentieth year of Constantine—where Eusebius’s work ends—up to the death of Valens, that is, the year 378.

It is astonishing, almost beyond belief, that he composed by rapid dictation a work of such magnitude. In the preface, which he addressed to Vincentius, of whom enough has been said above [Col. 0045], and to Gallienus, whom we do not know, he indicates near the end that he is reserving the history of Theodosius for another work. From this one understands that some time had already elapsed in his reign, which began in the year 379, and that the *Chronicle* itself can conveniently be assigned no earlier than the following year.

On the other hand, it cannot be postponed to a later date because of its mention in Letter 18 to Damasus, concerning the Seraphim, which we shall soon show was written at the beginning of the year 381.

I know that Jerome’s own testimony in Letter 57.5 appears to conflict with these arguments. There he says that he translated this *Chronicle* into Latin “about twenty years ago,” although everyone agrees that the letter itself was written in the year 395. I have long ago pointed out, however, that an error entered the numerical notation through the carelessness of the copyists, who wrote the Roman numeral XX by an obvious slip in place of XV. Although this is entirely clear from what has been said above and from other arguments that will be presented in their proper places, I nevertheless thought it improper to alter the text without the support of manuscripts. Yet a man of such great wit was found who, for this very reason, disparaged our studies.

## III.

Immediately after the *Chronicle*, in his catalogue of works, the holy Father lists twenty-eight homilies of Origen on Jeremiah and Ezekiel, which, he says, “I translated from Greek into Latin.” He then adds: “On the Seraphim.”

There is no doubt that he composed these works during this period, while he was still at Constantinople. Some, however, have thought otherwise concerning the homilies on Ezekiel. They argue that Jerome rendered them into Latin much later because, in their preface, he praises the opinion of Didymus, whom he heard only when he went to Egypt, almost six years afterward. But it is not necessary to suppose that he received this opinion from Didymus’s own mouth; it is more reasonable to believe that he took it from one of his books.

## IV.

The treatise on the Seraphim—which for good reasons, as may be seen in its proper place, we have listed among the letters under number 18, addressed to Damasus—was dictated at the imperial city at the request of friends.

He dictated it intermittently because he was suffering from pain in his eyes. Later, when he came to Rome, he gave it to Damasus, to whom it is now addressed, for reading.

The holy Father mentions it in Letter 84, which belongs approximately to the year 400, and there says that it was published twenty years earlier. If this passage is compared with the treatise itself, where he mentions the *Chronicle*—“the book of the times, which we translated into Latin from the Greek”—and also with his commentary on Isaiah, chapter 6, where he reckons about thirty years from that composition, saying that he was then being instructed at Constantinople by Saint Gregory, at that time bishop of the same city, a careful reckoning makes it clear that the treatise was written approximately in the middle of the year 381.

It is not our task to pursue these matters at greater length; we have explained them sufficiently in their proper places. The other questions concerning the character of that writing, and especially the Addition which Baronius supposes was appended in the following year, after the holy Father had come to Rome, have likewise been discussed in their proper places.

# Chapter XIV

[Col. 0046]

I. He travels from Constantinople to Rome for the Synod. II. There he is appointed Damasus’s secretary and responds in his name to consultations from the East and the West. III. Whether he was a cardinal presbyter. IV. He answers Damasus’s questions concerning “Hosanna” and the two sons, the frugal and the prodigal. V. At Damasus’s request he restores the Gospels according to the Greek text. VI. He also hastily corrects the Psalter according to the Septuagint.

While these events were taking place, imperial letters summoned the bishops of the East and the West to Rome on account of certain disputes among the Churches, as the holy Father himself says in Letter 108 to Eustochium. It was the great Synod, as Theodoret calls it (*History*, chapter 8), which was to be held at Rome after the middle of the year 382.

Among those summoned from the East, Paulinus of Antioch and Epiphanius, bishop of Salamis in Cyprus, went to Constantinople so that they might sail directly from there to Rome together. Jerome, who was waiting for a suitable opportunity to travel there, was still detained in that imperial city. He joined these bishops, his fathers and friends, and crossed over to the West with them.

It is true, or at least highly probable, that Baronius was formerly correct in thinking that Jerome too had been summoned to Rome by Pope Damasus, so that he might attend the Synod and assist the Church in its most difficult affairs by his learning.

## II.

This may perhaps have been the ecclesiastical necessity that, as he testifies in the letter mentioned above, drew him to Rome. His having served as Damasus’s secretary is also established beyond doubt by Letter 122 to Ageruchia:

> “Many years ago, when I was assisting the bishop of the city of Rome with ecclesiastical documents and responding to the synodal consultations of the East and the West …”

It is not at all unlikely that he was honored with this office as soon as he arrived in the City, and that he performed it at the Roman Synod held shortly afterward, still in the year 382.

I am also easily persuaded that he received from the Synod the task of composing the formulas of faith to be imposed upon heretics who were to be received into the Church. I do not think that he denies this elsewhere, as some maintain, by wrongly interpreting a passage from Book 2 against Rufinus, paragraph 20.

He says there:

> “When my little story is brought against me—by the Synod, that is—and I am challenged under the name of a certain friend of Damasus, bishop of the city of Rome, to whom he entrusted the dictation of ecclesiastical letters …”

He then describes the cunning of the Apollinarists: they had received for reading a book of Athanasius in which “the Dominical man” was written, and corrupted it in such a way that, after scraping away the text, they wrote it again in the erasure, so that it would appear not to have been falsified by them but added by Jerome.

These words do not mean that he had been chosen by the Roman Synod, and above all by Damasus himself, to write ecclesiastical documents. Rather, he assigns to his “little story” the other matter that occurred on that occasion, namely, the deceit of the Apollinarists.

He assigns it in the following response:

> “Even if you have heard the truth from me, someone else who is ignorant of the matter may say that you composed it yourself” (*Against Rufinus*, Book 2).

By these words he is far from denying the event. [Col. 0047] Rather, he seems to admit that he had previously related it to Rufinus in his presence, and merely says that others who did not know the facts might think that Rufinus himself, as his enemy, had invented it.

Jerome rejects the story because he wishes the gravest authority to be presented in ecclesiastical treatises, where the truth of doctrines is at issue, and wishes that people abstain from such anecdotes—which, even when true, he habitually calls “stories.”

We are not unaware of the further objection offered by P. Constantius, a man learned in ecclesiastical antiquity, for counting this among stories: namely, that there was no need to compose a formula of faith for the Apollinarists to sign, since Damasus had already sent Paulinus of Antioch, several years earlier, a statement of belief against their heresy.

But since Saint Ambrose testifies in a letter written in this same year that the Apollinarists were again discussed at that Synod, it was easy, and indeed appropriate, for a new formula to be composed. We may infer that one was actually composed from the fact that in the earlier statement sent to Paulinus of Antioch Christ is never called “the Dominical man.”

Finally, there is no reason to deny this distinction to Jerome, whose exceptional learning had already been put to some use by the Fathers and by Damasus.

## III.

Some people formerly argued with great effort that Jerome, as soon as he came to Rome, was enrolled among the Roman clergy and should consequently be counted among the cardinals, as they are now called.

Pelagius II even calls him bishop of the Roman Church (*Collection of Councils*, vol. 4, B, p. 314), while Anastasius gives him the same title and office that he himself held, that of Librarian (*Mabillon, Museum Italicum*, vol. 1, p. 82).

But since Jerome himself never mentions such honors, not even once, and especially since it would have served his interests to do so—indeed, when he justly freed himself from John of Jerusalem, he recalls only the presbyterate, which, as we have said, he had accepted at Antioch on the condition that he would not be bound to any church—these claims are refuted with the same ease with which they were proposed.

Surely no one today should still be held by that distorted popular opinion, now that Baronius, the greatest defender of Jerome’s reputation, did not hesitate to refute it deliberately. Nothing could have been imagined more contrary to the holy Father’s character and conduct than that he should have wished to bind himself to ecclesiastical ranks and titles—a man who either continually lived in deserts or never entertained any other desire in his mind.

## IV.

He was certainly dear and intimate to the pontiff among his close associates. He especially demonstrated his talent and learning in explaining the Scriptures, so that Damasus not only read his works with great pleasure but often copied them out with his own hand.

He also frequently consulted Jerome about the meaning of passages that appeared more difficult. Since Damasus was more occupied with reading through the sacred books than with composing new works, he invited Jerome to write and provoked him by his requests.

Among the questions he proposed for Jerome to solve were the meaning of the word “Hosanna” in Matthew, from the Hebrew source, and the matter of the two sons in Luke, the frugal son and the luxurious one [Col. 0048]. Jerome answered and satisfied these requests in two letters, numbered 20 and 21 in our edition.

In his catalogue he lists them immediately after the letter on the Seraphim, one after the other, because both belong to the same period, namely the year 383, as the sequence of this history indicates and as has been established in their proper places. He later wrote other works to the same pontiff at his request; these must be assigned to the following year and somewhat later.

## V.

Far more serious, and filled with greater difficulty and danger, was the work that Damasus asked of him during this period—for it cannot conveniently be assigned to another time: that he correct and restore the Gospels against the Greek manuscripts.

At that time there were almost as many copies of the Latin Vulgate version, which the Churches used everywhere, as there were manuscripts (*Preface to the Gospels*). Many passages had been badly rendered by incompetent translators; others had been perversely corrected by ignorant presumers; and most had been added or altered by careless copyists.

There was also a deeply established confusion in the Evangelists’ text, so that in Mark many passages belonging to Luke and Matthew were found, and again in Matthew many passages belonging to John and Mark, and similarly elsewhere: passages proper to one Evangelist appeared in the books of others.

Thus, when the holy Father allowed himself to be entrusted with this task, it was necessary for him to sit as a kind of arbiter among the various and mutually conflicting Latin copies already scattered throughout the whole world. He had to distinguish, amid so many disagreements of readings, transpositions, and additions—where everything was serious and of very great importance for the integrity of the divine meanings—what was genuine, and from it produce a single text, even if only every third word had to be struck anew, one that was measured against the authority of the most carefully corrected Greek exemplar and agreed uniquely with the truth.

He nevertheless undertook the task of embellishing the work and endured the labor with unconquered courage. After correcting almost countless passages, he produced the genuine text of the Evangelists and dedicated to Damasus the preface in which he explained the purpose of his work.

He further appended the Canons that Eusebius of Caesarea had prescribed in Greek, following Ammonius of Alexandria, translated into Latin, so that at a glance it might be distinguished what was peculiar to each Evangelist and what they shared with one another.

Whether he later polished the remainder of the New Testament with the same light touch of the file, according to the Greek authority—as he himself suggests in Letter 27 and in his catalogue—is discussed in our preface placed at the beginning of the tenth volume of his works.

## VI.

After removing the errors of the Gospels, Jerome likewise undertook at Rome to correct the Psalter according to the Septuagint translators, though hastily and only in large part (*Preface to the Psalter from the Greek*).

This recension is now called the Roman Psalter. Whether at the request of Damasus or of other friends in the City, Jerome certainly prepared it for the benefit and use of that Church. The Vatican Basilica at Rome still uses it.

We shall speak in their proper places of the other, much more accurate edition that he later prepared according to the Greek Hexapla, with obeli and asterisks, which is called the Gallican Psalter, and also of the entirely new translation from the Hebrew archetype.

# Chapter XV

[Col. 0049]

I. He is compelled to instruct certain Roman virgins and matrons in the sacred writings. II. He writes several letters to them. III. Some separate remarks on that celebrated letter to Eustochium. IV. Asked by Damasus about five questions, he replies. V. He compares Aquila’s edition with the Hebrew exemplar and also translates Origen’s homilies on the Song of Songs. VI. He writes against Helvidius. VII. Certain other writings and actions of his.

## I.

Amid all these studies—and, what is more remarkable, amid the great crowds of the City and the favor of the Supreme Pontiff—Jerome relaxed nothing of the austerity of life that he had formerly adopted in the desert of Chalcis.

He declares in more than one place that he was accustomed to sustain his little body on beans and that he took pleasure in emaciation and pallor (*Letter 45*). If anyone considered such a life miserable, he regarded them as much more miserable.

For this reason he was so highly esteemed by many that everywhere he was called a holy, humble, and forsaken man, and, in the judgment of almost everyone, worthy of the highest priesthood.

This very high opinion of him so stimulated the zeal of several matrons to undertake such a life and such disciplines that, although he never ceased carefully avoiding the company of women, he was nevertheless compelled to make himself their teacher in understanding the Scriptures when certain exceptionally holy women sought this of him with their most earnest prayers.

“There was no other matron at Rome,” he says, “who could subdue my mind, except one who mourned and fasted, was squalid with filth, and almost blinded by tears; one whom the Sun repeatedly found, through unbroken nights, imploring the Lord’s mercy.”

Among these were Paula, a glory of Roman nobility and piety; her daughter Eustochium, than whom no woman is more celebrated in Jerome’s writings; her sister Blaesilla, who, after her husband’s death, had turned her whole self toward God; then Lea, a woman of profound religious devotion; and the virgin Asella, who lived at Rome a solitary life as though in the desert.

Finally there was Marcella, a widow of the highest nobility. Into her house those women, together with other matrons and virgins, gathered in order to hear Jerome explain the Scriptures.

Besides these there were Albina, Marcellina, and Felicitas, whom he greets in Letter 45; Principia, whom he praises warmly in many places; and Feliciana, whom he mentions in Letter 30. The lives and examples of all of them greatly adorned the Christian cause.

Some of these women excelled so greatly in knowledge of Scripture under his instruction that Paula spoke Hebrew fluently; her daughter Eustochium knew how to copy Hebrew books with particular elegance; and Blaesilla, her sister, had already overcome the difficulties of the language in a short time and competed with her mother in learning and singing the Psalms in Hebrew.

Marcella, however, drew so much knowledge of sacred disciplines from his instruction that the holy Father confesses he had scarcely acquired as much through his own long study and labor. He says:

> “I shall say only this: whatever had been gathered in us through long study and transformed, as it were, into nature through prolonged meditation, she [Col. 0050] tasted, learned, and possessed. Thus, after our departure, whenever a dispute arose about some testimony of Scripture, people went to her as judge” (*Letter 127*).

The disposition, character, and progress of the others were by no means inferior—for he raised them all toward virtue and, through many exercises, taught them such knowledge of the sacred Scriptures as would be useful for their perfect interpretation.

## II.

The fruit of this labor has come down to us in such a way that many letters to these women still survive, in which certain more difficult passages of Scripture are explained. For the present, I shall mention only those that he wrote at Rome and during this period in response to their requests.

We possess three letters to Paula, two to Eustochium, and approximately sixteen to Marcella. He sent all of these from the end of the year 384 until approximately the middle of the following year.

The chronological notes to these letters contain considerable discussion of the period to which each belongs and of the order they occupy among themselves by reason of the precedence of their dates. To repeat that discussion here, although it contains part of the particular history of these women, is neither our task nor within our available time.

We also know that another order could be established among them, perhaps even one closer to the truth. The earlier letter to Eustochium, which bears number 22 in our recension, could be assigned to October or November of the year 384.

But since they cannot be assigned to a period other than the one we have indicated, and since they all fall within scarcely ten months, it does not seem useful either for us or for the reader to linger over arguments of such slight importance.

It is more valuable to infer from this dating—something of considerable importance for praising Jerome’s modesty—that he did not allow women to come to him for the sake of learning until very late; and properly speaking, they did not come to him, but to the house of Marcella, the most noble and most holy widow, where he was staying.

Nor did he receive them into instruction before he had tested the virtue of each one. In earlier days, perhaps through personal experience, he feared that frequent association with women might lead a man to pleasure, although he placed everything beneath his devotion to chastity.

He became acquainted with Saint Paula’s household much later still, as is established by Letter 45.

### III.

We learn the same thing from Letter XXII to Eustochium, which was the principal cause of Jerome’s changing fortunes and therefore deserves to be recalled in detail. There the holy Father omitted nothing that pertains to the instruction of a virgin and the preservation of virginity: admonitions concerning flight from the world; frugal food and clothing; avoidance of certain vices among clergy and monks, especially avarice and gluttony; the examples of the saints; devotion to the Scriptures; and other matters that he discusses there at length and with great elegance. It seemed so learned and polished, and so weighty in its subject matter and thought, that Sophronius, Jerome’s friend, considered it worthy of translation into Greek. [Col. 0051]

Nevertheless, how much hatred he aroused against himself from it and from his association with women in that malicious city, that city which had once contained the population of the whole world and was the chief seat of vice, and what enmities he incurred, we shall explain shortly, in the proper sequence of events. Meanwhile, we add that he was accustomed to be surrounded not only—as he says—by frequent throngs of virgins who questioned him about the Scriptures and wished to undertake more sacred studies, but also by certain men whom he compares to Daniel, Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael in Babylon: men eager for sacred learning who often made use of his assistance and companionship for that purpose. Besides Damasus, the supreme pontiff, who abounded in every literary accomplishment, the more distinguished among them were Pammachius, Marcellinus, Domnio, Rogatianus, and Oceanus, as is evident from the letters that he later wrote to them. We shall return to these men later.

### IV.

The time that remained after instructing the women Jerome devoted to reading, to which he had given himself entirely. Thus, apart from Didymus’s treatise *On the Holy Spirit*, which he had begun to render into Latin (but, as we shall say, was forced to postpone to another time), he was now laboring over nothing else by dictation or writing. When Damasus found this difficult to bear—for he was extraordinarily delighted by the monuments of Jerome’s intellect—he asked him, as though to awaken someone who had long been asleep, to give him for reading whatever work he might have at hand. Jerome replied that he had nothing available except letters formerly written in the desert; nevertheless, he promised that, if Damasus wished, he would compose something new by the stolen labor of his nights.

Damasus received this graciously and, sending a letter through a courier-deacon, proposed to the holy Father five questions from the Old Testament. Of these Jerome solved only three, and did so with remarkable learning; he omitted the other two because Tertullian, Novatian, and Origen had long since discussed and resolved them.

From this entire account it is quite clear that the two letters—Damasus’s to Jerome and Jerome’s to Damasus—ought to be placed before the other letters of that same year to Eustochium and Marcella, which in our edition are placed first in sequence. I would now restore them in that order. For if those letters had already been produced by Jerome, Damasus would not have called him one who had been asleep for a long time and who was reading rather than writing; nor would our author have replied that he no longer had any letters except those that he had once dictated in the desert, and which the holy pontiff had already read and copied with the greatest eagerness.

Moreover, in his catalogue of his own works the holy Father places this work on the three Questions of the Old Law before those celebrated letters to Eustochium and Marcella, indeed even before the Homilies on the Song of Songs and the book against Helvidius. It is preferable to preserve this order rather than to rely on arguments of any other kind.

After Jerome had summoned a notary and begun dictating his answers, a certain Hebrew arrived and brought Hebrew codices that Jerome had long and diligently sought. Interrupted in his writing by this unexpected event, and wholly absorbed in those books, he refrained from answering. These Hebrew codices seem indeed to have been the same ones with which, as he testifies in Letter XXXII to Marcella, he had previously compared the edition of Aquila. This makes it still clearer that this response to Damasus was composed before that letter and the preceding letters to Marcella.

It will be sufficient to correct the disorder in our edition if you place before Letter XXII to Eustochium the two letters numbered XXXV and XXXVI. At about the same time, and at the urging of that same Damasus, he translated two of Origen’s Homilies on the Song of Songs into Latin and dedicated them to Damasus by name.

### V.

Not long afterward, at the request of the brothers, Jerome sharpened his pen against Helvidius, whom he had long refused to refute, lest by answering him he should make him worthy of being defeated (*Book against Helvidius*). Helvidius was a common man from the people, rustic, a layman, and scarcely instructed in the rudiments of letters; his name was so obscure that although he lived in the same city as Jerome, Jerome says that he never knew him by sight and did not know whether he was fair or dark. Yet Gennadius calls him a disciple of Auxentius, and the holy Father bears witness that he had written against a certain brother, Craterius or Carterius—perhaps *Craterius* is the correct form—in whom even this utterly uneducated man sought eloquence and polish of language.

That fool tried to prove, by several passages of Holy Scripture wrongly understood and by the authority of two ancient writers, namely Tertullian and Victorinus of Pettau, that after giving birth to Jesus Christ through no human agency but by the work of the Holy Spirit, Mary had borne other children from Joseph in the ordinary human manner—those, namely, who are called the Lord’s brothers in the Gospels. Nor did the evil stop there, for he also attempted, with whatever empty arguments he could devise, to prove that marriage should be placed on an equal footing with virginity.

Eunomius had long before been the teacher of this error concerning Mary as the mother of several children from Joseph, as we understand from Philostorgius (*History*, book V, chapter 2); and the same doctrine had once spread widely through Apollinarius, as Epiphanius testifies. Moreover, around the time when Helvidius was writing, that most foolish error had invaded the minds of other men in Italy as well, as is shown by the bishop whom Saint Ambrose refuted in his book *On the Institution of the Virgin*, addressed to Eusebius.

We have pursued these matters at somewhat greater length than usual because a more thorough understanding of the history and causes of Jerome’s dispute with that heretic seems likely to contribute something to the sequence of his life. The holy Father wrote this book, as he testifies in Letter XLVIII to Pammachius, while Damasus of holy memory was still alive; and he indicates that the work had received Damasus’s approval in the words that follow: “Did that distinguished man, learned in the Scriptures, and virgin, teacher of the Church’s virgin, find anything to criticize in that discourse?”

He also mentions the book in Letter XXII to Eustochium, which was sent a few months later in this same year: “How many troubles marriage has … I think I have expressed briefly in the book that we published against Helvidius concerning the perpetual virginity of Blessed Mary.” Therefore, if we have correctly maintained that this letter should be assigned to the final months, or nearly the final months, of the year 384, it is still much closer to the truth to suppose that this book itself was written in that same year, and not much before its midpoint, as we formerly conjectured in the preface to the work. [Col. 0053]

### VI.

There are, moreover, other writings of the holy Father that were either merely sketched and begun, but completed only later; or prepared for private, so to speak, schoolroom use, rather than for public circulation; or finally promised and conceived in his mind, but later abandoned and never brought to completion. If anyone wishes to assign all these works to this period, since they can scarcely be referred to another, I shall favor the conjecture, although the year—or, more accurately, the portion of the year—is not established with complete certainty. I do so, however, in such a way that each person may retain his own judgment intact and, if circumstances require, adopt other explanations at will.

Among these works, the first to be mentioned is the translation of Didymus, which we have already touched upon. Next comes the Exposition of the Psalms to Marcella, of which a small portion survives in the letters addressed to her. There is also a brief commentary on Ecclesiastes, prepared for Blaesilla’s instruction and private use, so that she might understand the more difficult passages even without the voice of her teacher.

There was also that comparison of the Hebrew codices with Aquila’s edition. This study certainly did not lack the value of its labor, nor was it completed within so brief a period. Finally, there was the work that he had undertaken in Letter XXII to Eustochium to write, *Against Avarice*, and, if he approved, concerning the manner of life of the Egyptian hermits. Although he may perhaps have prepared the threads for weaving that work at the time, he never afterward laid his hand to it.

It is also appropriate to refer here to the discussion that he reports in Letter LXIX to Oceanus as having held at Rome with a most eloquent man on the question whether someone who had married one wife before baptism and another after baptism, the first having died, should be considered a bigamist and could be promoted to the sacred orders. Jerome held—and, as we shall say in its proper place, committed to writing nearly twelve years later—that a wife taken before baptism should in no way be counted against a man who was to be ordained. From the aforementioned letter to Oceanus you will learn what arguments he then used and how he answered his opponent, for there he recounts the history of the discussion in detail.

## CHAPTER XVI

**I. Damasus dies, and Siricius, not especially devoted to Jerome, succeeds him. II. Jerome incurs the enmity of many. III. He is cleared of a most serious calumnious accusation. IV. He decides to leave Rome. V. He writes to Asella.**

### I.

While Jerome’s mind was occupied with these studies, the supreme pontiff died—also the supreme support of his works and life—Damasus, after administering the Christian commonwealth for eighteen years with singular innocence and holiness. He died at nearly eighty years of age, as our author says in his book *On Illustrious Men* (chapter 4, p. 130), and as the most ancient martyrologies testify, toward the end of the year 384, on the tenth or eleventh day of December.

In that same year, a few days later, Siricius was appointed in his place: a man who undertook to govern the people more through affection than authority, of a very mild and simple character, and one who, as our author says again (*Against Rufinus*, book III), judged others by his own abilities.

Those who had secretly disparaged Jerome while Damasus was alive—under whom Jerome possessed very great influence and was honored with every sign of distinction—now that Siricius was in power, a man who did not know how to suspect anyone of wrongdoing and who does not seem to have protected the holy Doctor very vigorously by his support, dared to rise openly against him and wage undisguised war.

Indeed, some people, among them Baronius, even draw Siricius into the share of the complaints, because he allegedly exposed Jerome—deprived of the honor of secretary for sacred letters—to the slanders of his enemies. It should also be noted that about a month after his ordination, or on the third day before the Ides of February in the year 385, in the decretal letter addressed to Himerius, chapter II, he passed judgment against the opinion of Jerome that we have explained above—namely, that a wife taken before baptism should not be counted against one who wished to be admitted to the clergy. He decreed that clerics who had taken a second wife should be deposed, and established by his supreme authority that bigamy could also arise from marriages contracted before baptism.

Yet no one should therefore imagine that he did anything against the holy Doctor by which Jerome fell into the accusations and hatred of others. This can be proved from Jerome himself. When Rufinus rashly reproached him with the judgment that had then been held about him at Rome and with what had subsequently been written, Jerome firmly replied that he feared none of these things, since he could be convicted only by ecclesiastical writings (*Against Rufinus*, book III, chapter 7). He immediately added: “See how much I fear you. If you produce even a small sheet written against me by the Roman bishop or by another Church, I shall confess as my crimes everything that has been written against you.”

Thus he complains nowhere, either here or elsewhere, about Siricius; nor should the cause of the holy Father’s conflicts with his rivals and evil men be sought in him.

### II.

Jerome himself, however, knew and admitted what the cause had been, in Letter XL: “By censuring vices,” he says, “we have offended many.” The origin of the complaints was the letter, or little book, on the preservation of virginity addressed to Eustochium. Writing later to Nepotianus, Jerome himself relates that it had been stoned by the hand of his detractors at Rome.

There he had especially criticized monks who, living a life contrary to their profession, indulged their appetite and their belly, frequented the houses of the wealthy, pursued avarice, and grew arrogant through pride and superstition. “Among them,” he says, “everything is affected: loose sleeves, puffed-out boots, coarser clothing, frequent sighs, visits to virgins, and slander of the clergy.”

He also burned against the clergy who sought the presbyterate and diaconate so that they might look at women more freely. “Their whole concern,” he says, “is with their clothes—whether they smell good, whether their foot bulges beneath loose leather; hair curled by the mark of the curling iron; fingers shining with rings.” Among these he briefly and concisely describes one whom he calls the chief of the profession and the city’s courier.

Nor did he spare virgins who did not avoid the company of men. When he had commanded—or rather stated—that virgins should more often be with women than with men, he offended the eyes of the entire city and became the object of everyone’s pointing finger (Letter XXVII).

Among the many who were offended by these things was a certain Onasus of Segesta, whether he was from Pannonia or Sicily—for there is a city of that name in each province. Living at Rome at that time, and perhaps sensing that he was guilty of the vices Jerome was censuring generally, he took Jerome’s words and writings as an insult directed at himself. From Letter XL to Marcella, in which the holy Father refutes and mocks the man’s shamelessness with complete falsity, one may learn how much turmoil he stirred up.

With each passing day the force and recklessness of the detractors increased, until Jerome was commonly called a satirical writer, a turncoat, and a criminal, and, being repeatedly attacked by the most unjust slanders, began to be publicly spread about and abused. Yet when he wrote, he had already warned that the weapons of all his slanderers would be turned back upon themselves. “I beg them,” he said, “to be quiet and cease their abuse. For we wrote not as enemies but as friends; we did not attack those who sin, but warned them not to sin.”
