Nor was Jerome’s freedom in censuring vices the only thing that created envy against him. His counsels toward virtue and his holy way of life—by which he called the noblest women away from the allurements and displays of the world to the duties of Christian piety and meditation on the Scriptures—also sharpened the hatred of his fellow citizens and aroused the hostility of the powerful.

Because he had encouraged Blaesilla, a recently widowed woman, to undertake a holier manner of life and even to profess herself a nun, he wounded the feelings of many so deeply that when she died shortly afterward in the heat of a fever, she was said to have been killed by the harshness of her way of life. At her funeral, while her mother Paula was almost lifeless with grief, the people muttered:

“Is this not what we often said? She grieves because her daughter was killed by fasts, since she did not preserve grandchildren for her from a second marriage.”

“How long,” they added, “will this detestable race of monks not be driven from the city? Not buried under stones? Not thrown into the waves? They have seduced a pitiable matron, who clearly did not wish to be a nun, since no pagan woman ever mourned her children in this way.”

In the preface to Didymus’s book Jerome himself relates that, while he was still in Babylon—that is, Rome—as is clear from the sequence of events, after Damasus’s death, he had endured the hatred of that malicious city and purple-clad harlot to such a degree. “Behold,” he says, “the Senate of the Pharisees cried out, and no scribe, whether counterfeit [perhaps *velificatus* should be read as a single word], but the whole faction of ignorance, as though a battle of doctrines had been declared against itself, conspired against me.” It is clear that by these words he was pointing to leading men, both from the clergy and perhaps also from the patrician order, among whom he was greatly hated.

### III.

Amid the great loss of reputation and good name that the holy Father had suffered among so many—so that he was called disgraceful, deceitful, slippery, and one who deceived others by Satan’s art, although Christian piety had received and would continue to receive great increase through him—he was also treated as guilty of some particular and extremely serious crime.

A certain rumor-mongering man was found, so shameless and brazen that, having been appointed as a witness, he asserted that he had seen or heard some unspecified crime, in order to lend credibility to his most wicked accusation by his testimony. But when brought to examination, he did not hesitate to confess the fabricated calumny and to remove from an innocent man the offense that he had imposed upon him.

Regarding this matter the holy Father wrote to Asella: “Granted that they believed the liar: why do they not believe the man who denies it? The man is the same as he was before; he now confesses innocent the one whom he had earlier declared guilty. Certainly torments express the truth more clearly than laughter—unless what is invented and willingly heard is more easily believed, or unless what is not invented is driven to appear invented” (Letter XLV).

Even here, however, he gives no indication of the precise offense of which he was accused. What some people report, and what the ancient author of Jerome’s Life suggests—namely, that a woman’s garment had been planted, which Jerome imprudently put on as though it were his own, and that, appearing at night in an ecclesiastical gathering dressed in it, he had brought upon himself both laughter and suspicion of sexual misconduct—has no appearance of truth.

For Jerome could easily have done so, and indeed would have had to do so, in order to defend the reputation of his innocence once his enemy’s stratagem had been exposed. He would not have kept entirely silent about it, nor would he have made no mention of it in the aforementioned letter, in which he responds to various slanders of his envious enemies.

It is far more plausible that he was accused of having deceived noble and wealthy matrons, under the pretext of a holier life, for the sake of profit and illicit companionship, and that he wished to take Paula to Jerusalem in order to satisfy his lust. For he says there: “Nothing else is charged against me except my sex, and this is never charged except when Paula departs for Jerusalem.”

### IV.

Finally, when matters had reached such a degree of madness that everything the holy Father did was counted as a crime—“one man,” he says, “slandered my walk and my laughter; one seemed to disparage me, another suspected something else in my simplicity”—he deliberated with himself about leaving that malicious city. There was no other way of avoiding the most pestilential plotters.

He therefore first withdrew from them by fleeing to a solitary place and retiring to the countryside. From there he seems to have sent Letter XLIII in our recension to Marcella, in which he also urges her, after leaving behind the troubles and tumult of the city, to withdraw to the country, where she might enjoy peace in solitude.

But Jerome, weary not only of the city but also of its surrounding districts, was now preparing his departure not merely in intention but in deed. At last, in the month of August, when the Etesian winds were blowing, he found a favorable opportunity for sailing eastward and said his final farewell to Rome, which had shown itself so unworthy of his companionship.

### V.

Before he nevertheless spread his sails to the winds, after he had already boarded a ship in the Roman harbor, he hurriedly wrote, weeping and grieving, Letter XLV to Asella. From it we have already extracted a few passages above, and it is worthwhile to transcribe here several others relevant to our subject.

“For nearly three years,” he says, “certainly, I lived among them—the Romans. A frequent crowd of virgins often surrounded me. I explained the divine books to some of them as best I could. Reading produced regular attendance, regular attendance familiarity, and familiarity confidence. Let them say what they ever perceived in me that was unbecoming to a Christian. Did I receive anyone’s money? Did I refuse gifts, whether small or great? Did any person’s coin jingle in my hand? Was there an oblique word, a wanton eye? Nothing else is charged against me except my sex, and this is never charged except when Paula departs for Jerusalem,” and so forth.

A little later he writes:

“Did I ever enter the house of any more wanton woman? Did silken garments, gleaming jewels, painted faces, or the ambition for gold ever captivate me? There was no other matron who could conquer my mind except one who mourned and fasted … Her song was the Psalms, her speech the Gospel, her delights self-restraint, her life fasting. No other woman could please me except one whom I never saw eating.

“But after I began to venerate, honor, and admire her for the merit of her chastity, all my virtues immediately deserted me. O first-biting envy of you! O cunning of Satan, always persecuting holiness! No other women furnished a spectacle for the city of Rome except Paula and Melanium, who, after despising their possessions and abandoning their children, raised the Lord’s Cross like a kind of banner of piety.

“If they sought the baths, chose perfumes, and possessed wealth and widowhood as the material of luxury and freedom, they would be called ladies and saints. Now they wish to appear beautiful in sackcloth and ashes and to descend into the fire of Gehenna with fasting and foulness. Evidently they are not permitted, while the people applaud, to perish with the crowds.

“If pagans criticized this way of life, or Jews, they would have the consolation of not pleasing those whom Christ displeases. But now—shameful to say—Christian men, neglecting the beam in their own eye, search for the speck in another’s eye. They tear apart a holy resolve and consider it a remedy for their own punishment if no one is holy, if everyone is slandered, if there is a crowd of the perishing, if there is a multitude of sinners.”

Finally, after inserting several passages of this kind, he says:

“I give thanks to my God that I am worthy for the world to hate me. But pray that I may return from Babylon to Jerusalem, so that Nebuchadnezzar may not rule over me, but Jesus the son of Josedech … Fool that I was, wanting to sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land, and, having abandoned Mount Sinai, seeking aid from Egypt. I did not remember the Gospel: that the one who departs from Jerusalem immediately falls among thieves, is stripped, wounded, and killed. But although the priest and the Levite despise him, that merciful Samaritan …”

“Some babble that I am a sorcerer: I acknowledge the title as a servant of the faith. They call me great: so did the Jews call my Lord. A seducer: the Apostle was called that as well. May no temptation seize me except what is human. What part of the anguish have I suffered, since I serve the Cross? They charged me with the disgrace of a false crime; but I know that through good report and bad report one reaches the kingdom of heaven. It would take too long to pursue the rest.”

The time could scarcely be indicated more clearly. He notes that he was writing these things while the Etesian winds were blowing, on the point of setting sail from the harbor. This was in August of the year 385, by which time Damasus had already died; Jerome calls him “of blessed memory,” and we have shown that Damasus died in December of the preceding year. Jerome adds, lest anyone think these events occurred later, that he had lived among the Romans for nearly three years. He arrived at Rome, as we have established by certain arguments, around September of the year 382.

## CHAPTER XVII

**I. Jerome sails to the East. II. Saint Paula and Eustochium also depart. III. Together they visit all Palestine and the Holy Places. IV. They also tour Egypt and the monasteries of Nitria. V. They settle in Bethlehem and establish their residence there.**

### I.

The history of Jerome’s voyage to the East cannot be understood more effectively in its several parts than from Jerome himself, who remembers it with great care and recounts it in the clearest language in Book III against Rufinus, in order to blunt the quibbles of his rival:

“Do you wish to know the sequence of my withdrawal from the city and my attainment of perfection? In the month of August, when the Etesian winds were blowing, I confidently boarded a ship in the Roman harbor with the presbyter Saint Vincentius, my adolescent brother, and other monks who now live in Jerusalem, while a great crowd of saints accompanied me.

“I came to Rhegium and stayed for a short time on the shore of Scylla, where I learned the ancient tales: the precipitous course of deceptive Ulysses, the songs of the Sirens, and the insatiable whirlpool of Charybdis. When the inhabitants of that place told me many things and advised me to sail not to the pillars of Proteus but to the harbor of Jonah—the former being the route of fugitives and troubled men, the latter that of a secure man—I preferred to proceed through Malea and the Cyclades to Cyprus.

“There I was received by the venerable Bishop Epiphanius, whose testimony you boast of. I came to Antioch, where I enjoyed communion with the pontiff and confessor Paulinus. Led onward by him in midwinter and in the severest cold, I entered Jerusalem. I saw many miracles and confirmed by the judgment of my eyes what rumor had previously reported to me.

“From there I hastened to Egypt, visited the monasteries of Nitria, and saw aspics lurking among the choirs of the saints. Immediately, with quickened step, I returned to my Bethlehem, where I adored the manger and the cradle of the Savior. See also the most famous lake. I did not surrender myself to idle leisure, but learned many things that I had previously not known.”

In these words the holy Father embraces the whole history of his journey from Rome to Bethlehem. We shall now describe it more fully and in its separate parts.

But first, something should be said about Paulinianus, Jerome’s brother. Vincentius, whom he names as his other companion on the journey, has already become sufficiently known from what precedes. The holy Father seems to have summoned Paulinianus from his homeland of Stridon to share his lodging shortly before, when Jerome had arrived at Rome. We attribute the fact that Paulinianus is never mentioned while they were living together in the city to his youth; unless our calculations are mistaken, he does not seem even to have reached the age of twenty in the year when Jerome sailed from Rome to the East.

It is therefore futile to debate whether he had then embraced the monastic way of life or not. Those are seriously mistaken who think that he had accompanied Jerome much earlier, when Jerome first went to Syria, and had served Christ with him there in the desert. We shall speak of him again, and more than once. Let us continue with the rest.

### II.

Saint Paula, who had long before been seized by a desire to visit Jerusalem—for when Epiphanius and Paulinus departed from the Roman Synod, she had wished to sail with them to the East—immediately after Jerome had gone there, set out on the journey together with her daughter Eustochium.

I say immediately, for if the circumstances established earlier had permitted, she ought to be said to have undertaken the journey before Jerome. If she had already lived twenty years in Bethlehem when she died at the beginning of the year 404, during the consulship of Augustus for the sixth time and Aristenetus, as the holy Father himself testifies in her epitaph, she must have left Rome before 385, and therefore before Jerome himself.

Yet since both termini are included and the number is also rounded—something the holy Doctor often does in such matters—another passage compels us to believe that Jerome used the figure twenty there. At the end of the letter to Asella mentioned above, where, as he was departing from the Roman harbor, he sends greetings among the other holy women to Paula and Eustochium as well.

Indeed, they may seem to have sailed together with him, since the order of their journey described in Letter CVIII is one and the same as that which Jerome himself followed: through Malea and Cythera, across the Cyclades scattered over the sea, to Cyprus, Seleucia, and finally Antioch.

There can be no doubt that they were together in that city, and that from there they completed the rest of the journey together through Palestine and Egypt. They are said to have been led to Jerusalem in midwinter by Paulinus just as Jerome was, and the holy Father himself testifies that he arrived at Bethlehem with Paula and then, at her request, proceeded to Alexandria—one statement occurring in the preface to Hosea, the other in the aforementioned letter.

In that letter, too, he gives an extremely precise description of the places through which they passed, the things that Paula admired, and what was done and said at each place according to the circumstances. He reveals himself everywhere as her companion at her side. Therefore, the journey that he describes there under Paula’s name, from Antioch through the cities and monasteries of Palestine and Egypt, was also his own journey; and we shall report it here as though he were recounting it about himself.

He names only those places that are contained in the Sacred Volumes. Beginning from the shore of Sarepta, he came through the sands of Tyre to Acco, and through the plains of Megiddo to the land of the Philistines. He then entered Dor, or the Tower of Strato, and Antipatris and Lydda, as well as Arimathea and Nob, reaching as far as Joppa, the harbor of the fleeing Jonah.

From there, taking the road toward Nicopolis, or Emmaus, he went up to Beth-horon, looking to the right toward Aijalon and Gibeon. In the city of Gibeah itself, reduced completely to ruins, he stopped for a short time.

Finally, he entered Jerusalem. The proconsul of Palestine, who knew Paula’s family very well, had sent attendants ahead and ordered the praetorium to be prepared. But she—and Jerome himself, who clung to her side—chose a humble cell. She visited all the places with such ardor and devotion that, unless she hurried on to the remaining sites, she could not have been drawn away from the first.

It would be far too long to pursue the nearly countless mysteries that she gathers from each individual place. She examined everything so carefully that she even took along as companions the wisest men from among the Jews, especially to identify more deeply the sites mentioned in Scripture and the names in which the meaning of each place was contained. This was particularly necessary because, concerning the ancient names, they had often established that most of them had been given other names after the region was subjected to Roman rule, and that almost all traces of the former names had been erased.

Anyone who wishes to have all these matters reviewed should consult the letter itself. But we should not omit the fact that Jerome seems on this occasion to have copied all the books of the Old Testament from Origen’s *Hexapla*, whose ancient exemplars he had found in the Caesarean Library. With their aid he later prepared that emendation from the Greek which, although it had already largely perished long ago, even during Jerome’s lifetime, nevertheless immediately enjoyed great esteem among the Churches, insofar as it surpassed other versions and abounded in every commendation of a sound recension. We shall return to it below.

## IV.

After thoroughly and diligently examining Palestine, Jerome proceeded to Egypt, Paula accompanying him as his fellow traveler, in order to visit the monasteries of Nitria, whose fame had spread far and wide and toward which both were being drawn with nearly every effort. They were met by the holy and venerable Isidore, Bishop of Hermopolis, and by countless crowds of monks. At the sight of these men they greatly rejoiced in the glory of the Lord, yet confessed themselves unworthy of so great an honor. They saw the Macarii, the Arseniuses—or Arsisii—the Serapions, and the other names of Christ’s columns; they entered their individual cells, believing that in each of them they were seeing Christ.

Yet Jerome did not go to Egypt solely to survey the monasteries of Nitria. He gives another reason in the Preface to his Commentaries on the Epistle to the Ephesians:

> “For this reason above all,” he says, “I went to Alexandria, that I might see Didymus and ask him about all the difficulties in the Scriptures that I encountered.”

Elsewhere, in the Preface to Hosea, he says that he undertook the journey at Paula’s request:

> “About twenty-two years ago, when at the request of the holy and venerable mother—indeed, of your mother, Paula—I was in Alexandria, I saw Didymus and frequently heard him, a man of the greatest learning of his age. I asked him to complete what Origen had not done and to write Commentaries on Hosea; at my request he dictated three books.”

He himself testifies that these books were inscribed to him by Didymus, in *On Illustrious Men*, chapter CIX, and in his final *Apology against Rufinus*. Those who believe that another five books on Zechariah and three on Micah were likewise dedicated to him are deceived by a faulty reading, as has been noted in the appropriate places.

But to return to the subject: in Letter 84 to Pammachius he likewise says:

> “I went to Alexandria, saw Didymus, and in many things I thank him: what I did not know, I learned; what I knew, while he taught me, I did not lose.”

Clearly he did not allow himself to be persuaded in the least by [lacuna] his doctrines, which tended to confirm Origen’s errors, errors that he had already detected with care. Shortly afterward he even boasts that he was a disciple of the living Didymus; and from Rufinus we gather that he sent him a letter full of respect.

Yet if we believe Rufinus—and there is nothing that forbids this—he “did not remain for a full thirty days in Alexandria, where Didymus was” (*Invective*, book II). Nor does the holy Father himself contradict this; rather, he agrees with it in these words:

> “Immediately, with hurried steps, I returned to my Bethlehem” (*Against Rufinus*, book II).

By these words he also indicates that he visited the monasteries of Nitria before approaching Didymus, not after leaving him, as some maintain.

Whatever the precise circumstances may have been, it is evident that, in traversing the regions, he never spared himself any labor—whether in order to gather examples of piety from many sources or to listen to outstanding teachers of divine matters. His statement on this subject in the Preface to the Book of Chronicles according to the Septuagint is remarkable; we have already alluded to part of it:

> “Just as those who have seen Athens understand Greek histories better, and those who have sailed from Troy through Leucas and the Acroceraunian Mountains to Sicily, and from there to the mouths of the Tiber, understand the third book of Virgil more fully, so will he contemplate Holy Scripture more clearly who has observed Judea with his own eyes and has learned the memories of ancient cities and places, whether they retain the same names or have changed them. For this reason, we took care to undertake this labor with the most learned Hebrews, so that we might travel through the province celebrated throughout all the Churches of Christ.”

## V.

After returning from this journey, he immediately went back to his Bethlehem, where he first venerated the Savior’s manger and cradle. Captivated by the holiness of the place, he decided, together with the most holy monks who were there, to establish his residence there.

This place was formerly called Ephrata, as Jerome himself testifies in the *Hebrew Questions* and, from Eusebius, in the *Book of Places*:

> “Ephrata, the region of the city of Bethlehem of David, in which Christ was born … beside the road where Rachel was buried, five miles from Jerusalem” (*Dialogue*, book I).

Severus Sulpicius, who is said to have visited that region at some time and to have spent six months there with Jerome, says that it was one mile farther away—that is, six miles from Jerusalem. Bethlehem, however, was situated altogether in the southern region, beside the road leading to Hebron, and was counted as belonging to the tribe of Judah, not Benjamin. It was sixteen stages from Alexandria and forty-six miles from Joppa (*Letter* 129).

Nor was it then included in the census of cities. It was an obscure village, beyond which stretched an immense wilderness filled with savage barbarians. But because it had been ennobled by the birth of our Savior Jesus Christ, and because it was therefore made famous by the devotion of those who flocked there, it was preferred to all the other cities of the world and was itself called more august than Rome.

A church had been built over the very cave from which the salvation of the world emerged, and over the very manger in which the Lamb of God had lain an altar had been erected. Saint Jerome’s cell was situated immediately beside that cave. Although he was once forbidden to enter it, he was nevertheless able to see it conveniently from his cell.

It was, however, some distance from the public road, on a side path whose route began at the tomb of Archelaus, formerly king—or, more accurately, ethnarch—of Judea (*Book of Places*). Three years later Paula constructed there a double monastery and several lodgings for receiving pilgrims.

One monastery was inhabited by virgins whom Paula had gathered from various provinces, both those of noble rank and those of middle and lowest status. According to the editions commonly published, she divided them into three groups and monasteries. Their manner of life was such that, though separated in their work and food, they were united in psalmody and prayer. Only on Sunday did they proceed to the church, beside which they lived; and each group followed its own mother-superior.

They all wore the same clothing. They used linen only for wiping their hands. Their separation from men was so strict that they were separated even from eunuchs. She entrusted the other monastery to men for its administration, and there is no doubt that she chiefly left its care to Jerome. Their administration was more or less the same as that of the women.

We have already touched on some matters concerning them, so that they may be related here also according to the distinction of sex and manner of life, together with the other matters that the holy Father discusses at length in Letter 108 to Eustochium. I should like that passage to be consulted.

Nothing, however, contributes more to understanding the character of Jerome’s solitude than the letter sent by Paula and her daughter Eustochium to Marcella, numbered 46 in our recension. Jerome may seem to have supplied both its sentiments and, repeatedly, its very words. It was certainly written with one and the same spirit as soon as they had settled together at Bethlehem and decided to establish their permanent residence there.

They mention every possible praise of the place and every advantage of its retreats for living a most holy life, in order to inflame Marcella’s desire to migrate there. If, at last, she should leave Rome and go to Bethlehem, she would enjoy all the memorials of Christ in the places where most of the mysteries of our religion had been accomplished.

This cannot in any way be thought to have taken place before the year 386, since Paula sailed to Jerusalem toward the end of the immediately preceding year. Nor can it conveniently be placed later, since the beginning of the letter makes it sufficiently clear that it was written as soon as the opportunity to send a letter arose.

Yet I admit that it may seem scarcely credible that Marcella was invited by them to withdraw to Bethlehem before the death of her mother Albina. They would have appeared to be urging her to abandon the woman whose companionship and assistance they knew she needed most on account of her old age.

There is also an indication that Albina had already died when this letter was sent. Paula and Eustochium do not tell her daughter to convey their greetings to her; and if she had still been alive, it is reasonable to believe that they would not have omitted this, at least near the end of the letter.

Albina died, as will be established below, in the following year, 387. Thus the letter seems to have been written after some interval following her death and, at the latest, during the subsequent year. Yet I can hardly be persuaded, from the sequence of events, to believe that Paula and Eustochium, the spiritual daughters, so to speak, of Marcella, allowed at least two years to pass before writing to one from whom they had been so painfully separated, or that they suppressed for so long the longing that they bore impatiently to enjoy her companionship.

Nor do the very first words of the letter permit such an opinion:

> “Love has no measure, impatience knows no limit, and longing cannot endure.”

A little later she says:

> “The only thing we can do while absent is to pour forth complaining prayers; and we express our longing not so much with tears as with cries of lamentation,”

and so forth—passages that the reader may himself refer here.

# CHAPTER VIII

I. Jerome’s manner of life at Bethlehem.  
II. Whether he was rector of its church, as Sulpicius says.  
III. He writes Commentaries on four of Paul’s Epistles.  
IV. Whether he also expounded all the others.  
V. The general character of his writing according to Jerome’s own understanding.

## I.

Having finally been restored at Bethlehem to the tranquility that he had once tasted in Syria, the holy Father devoted himself entirely to the worship of God and to the contemplation and study of divine things—the two weapons of priests. Desiring to be something rather than merely to seem something, he shut himself within his cell (*Letter* 82); and he labored daily to advance by stages of virtue in the man within, not in the man without.

In one place he himself testifies that he shut himself within the hiding places of the desert in order, while mourning the sins of his youth, to draw Christ’s mercy toward himself (*Against John of Jerusalem*). Elsewhere he says that he did so either to lament past vices or to strive to avoid present ones; likewise, so that he might await the day of the Lord, or the day of judgment, in greater readiness.

His food was a poor vegetable dish and bread, and even that was exceedingly sparse and moderate. As Palladius testifies (*Lausiac History*, chapter 10), he received it, together with the other necessities of life, from Paula’s generosity. His fasts were long, his sleep brief, and he slept either on the ground or on a mat, wherever he could lie down.

He wore clothing that was despised, although in one place he indicates that he used cleaner garments (*Against John of Jerusalem*). For one who was then living as a monk was not required to profess this by an outward bodily appearance, provided that he displayed Christian simplicity in his dress.

To these things was added—or rather, these things were animated in his soul and life by—the constant practice of all the virtues worthy of a Christian and of one professing a more perfect imitation of Christ. Whatever time remained after prayer he spent during the day teaching and at night reading.

He was wholly absorbed in meditation on the Scriptures, which every day he explained, especially to Paula and Eustochium (*Invective*, book II). Rufinus reports—although with the intention of disparaging him—that he also instructed the sons of noble families entrusted to him in the literature of poets and rhetoricians.

The holy Father feared this accusation so little that he did not even consider it worthy of refutation. By this silence he indicated that, like Paul, he gloried in having become all things to all people in order to win all people for Christ, adapting himself to every sex and every age.

Indeed, people of different ages increasingly flocked to him from every part of the world, drawn not so much by the holiness of the place as by the fame of his name and the wonder of his learning, and by the desire to acquire a greater knowledge of divine matters.

## II.

Yet it is astonishing—indeed, almost unbelievable—that Postumianus reports about Jerome in the dialogue of Sulpicius Severus: namely, that although he was occupied with such great and varied duties of solitary life, he also governed the church that was at Bethlehem.

> “Jerome the Presbyter governs the church of that place,” he says, “for it is a parish belonging to the bishop who holds Jerusalem.”

Nor does he seem capable of having been mistaken in this matter, since the other things he reports about Jerome agree with the truth, and since he testifies that he had stayed with him for six months.

Nevertheless, that he was mistaken is clear from a letter among the Hieronymian letters, namely the letter of Saint Epiphanius to John of Jerusalem that we cited above. From it it is evident that, from the time of his ordination until the year 394, Jerome never wished, even in the monastery, to perform the office of a presbyter because of his modesty and humility, or to carry out the sacrifices owed to his name, or to labor in that part of the ministry which is the chief salvation of Christians—namely, the care of souls.

Furthermore, when John formerly stirred up conflicts and hatred against Jerome, as we learn from the holy Father himself, Jerome and his brethren were for some time forbidden to enter John’s church.

Some think that these facts can be reconciled if one supposes that Sulpicius was speaking of the time after reconciliation had been restored on both sides—that is, in the year 398, as they maintain—when Sulpicius came there and Jerome had already undertaken that office together with his brother Paulinianus.

But this cannot be established, nor does it possess any plausibility. If the holy Father could not then be moved from what he had proposed at his ordination, and could not be persuaded to perform sacred duties even in the monastery when he was barred from entering the public church, who could persuade himself that, after his friendship with John had been restored, when he was able to participate in sacred functions in that church at will and his ministry was not needed there, he abandoned his purpose?

This is especially unlikely since several other presbyters had long since been placed over that church, and since we understand that no necessity for such a thing arose after the time when the holy Father had fallen out with John.

Let us grant—even though I certainly will not grant it—that Sulpicius once went to Bethlehem, and that this happened in 398. Let us also grant that peace with John had then been made, though, unless our calculations deceive us, it was not fully restored until two years later. Jerome nevertheless lived there for a long time after that, and whenever he mentions his life, he continually declares that he was living a wholly solitary life with the monks.

Thus in Letter 117, written in the year 409, he says that he was shut up in his cell and far removed from crowds—circumstances that certainly cannot belong to the prefect of a parish church.

Moreover, how great was his reverence for what was just, and how carefully he took care not to violate parochial rights, he himself declares in the book against John that we have so often cited, in words and by an example especially rich for our purpose:

> “Who is dividing the Church? Is it we, whose entire household at Bethlehem communicates in the Church? Or is it you, who …? Are we dividing the Church, we who a few months ago, around the days of Pentecost, when the sun had been darkened and the whole world feared that the coming Judge was just about to arrive, presented forty persons of different ages and sexes to your presbyters to be baptized?  
>   
> “Certainly there were five presbyters in the monastery who could lawfully baptize, but they did not wish to do anything against your displeasure, lest you should be given this further opportunity to keep silent about the faith. Or do you not rather divide the Church, you who ordered your presbyters at Bethlehem not to give baptism at Easter to our catechumens, whom we sent to Diospolis to be baptized by the confessor and bishop Dionysius?  
>   
> “We are said to divide the Church, we who have no place outside our cells that belongs to the Church.”

But, you will say, these events preceded the restoration of their friendship. Let it be so, according to your preconceived opinion. Nevertheless, they are certainly matters from which one may rightly infer the character of the rest of his life and may discern what kind of disposition the holy Father possessed and what spirit animated him.

Sulpicius therefore needs a benevolent reader and a sympathetic interpreter. I understand him to have meant that Jerome administered the private church of the monastery—or, if you prefer the Latin term used in ecclesiastical language, the assembly. In this sense he would have spoken truly. Jerome held the first place there, and nothing is more consistent with the facts than that he was placed over the assemblies of the brethren by reason both of his virtue and of the honor of his priesthood.

They gathered daily in one place for prayers and psalmody, and this was a private church. It is certainly impossible to believe that, when Jerome and his companions were forbidden to enter the public church, he ceased this act of devotion to God and allowed the monks to pass so long a period without common prayer.

There the holy Father instructed the entire gathering of monks in the teaching of the sacred Scriptures and explained, day after day, the difficulties that arose from their reading, in the manner of a catechist (Κατυιστοῦ).

For this reason, in the Preface to his translation of the Book of Chronicles from the Hebrew, he says:

> “I always expound the interpreters of the Seventy in the assembly of the brethren.”

And at the end of Letter 112 to Augustine, written in the year 404:

> “You, who are young and have been placed at the summit of the episcopate, teach the peoples, and so forth. For me it is enough to whisper with a poor hearer and reader in a corner of the monastery.”

You will find several other such testimonies in Jerome’s writings. It would be tedious, and perhaps contrary to the purpose of this account, to report them individually. We have cited these two chiefly to show that, contrary to what Sulpicius seems to have thought, and long after the time he indicated, the only church administered by Jerome was the private one that assembled in the monastery, more properly called an assembly (*Book against John of Jerusalem*).

You will also find passages attesting that the number of monks living there, and of others flocking there, was immense. Paula’s monastery was no longer sufficient, and it became necessary to construct a lodging house for receiving pilgrims. Jerome presided over all of them.

Among these were four or five men adorned with the rank of presbyter—although they never performed its duties because of their humility—as we understand from the testimony cited above against John.

From the same passage one may also infer how great was the crowd of those who came there, drawn by their love of Jerome’s way of life. At times as many as forty people of different ages and sexes, either still unbaptized or recently converted, are said to have been there.

We also infer from the third book against Rufinus that a certain bishop named Paul, whom Theophilus was persecuting, had been incorporated among the monks there. The holy Father himself concludes the passage with these words:

> “In the monastery hospitality is dear to us, and we receive all who come to us with a joyful face of kindness,”

and so forth.

He says still more clearly earlier, in Letter 66 to Pammachius:

> “In this province, after building a monastery and constructing a lodging house beside it … we are overwhelmed by such crowds of monks flocking from the whole world that we can neither abandon the work we have begun nor bear what exceeds our strength.  
>   
> “Since almost what is said in the Gospel about the tower has happened to us—that we did not first calculate the expense of the tower that was to be built—we have been compelled to send our brother Paulinianus to our homeland, so that he might sell the half-ruined little estates that escaped the hands of the barbarians, together with the estates of our common parents. Otherwise, if we abandoned the ministry begun for the saints, we would provide laughter for slanderers and rivals.”

But enough of this.

## III.

It was characteristic of monks, as the holy Father himself often admits, to seek their livelihood by the labor of their hands. He nevertheless judged that he would be acting more wisely for himself and more usefully for the whole Church if he substituted the study of Scripture for manual labor.

> “I judged that more useful things would come to the Church of Christ from my leisure than from the business of others” (*Preface to Job from the Septuagint*).

Accordingly, he first devoted himself to the Hebrew language. Although he knew it well, he nevertheless wished to pursue it as deeply as possible.

At that time he used as his teacher a certain Barabbas, or Baranina—he calls him by both names—who, fearing that he would incur the hatred of his own people on this account, came to Jerome only at night. For this reason Jerome calls him his “nighttime teacher.”

Much later he himself reports that he never abandoned this language, which he had learned from adolescence through great labor and sweat, by means of tireless meditation, lest it abandon him (*Letter* 118).

From this study he advanced to the interpreters of Scripture. He diligently read not merely one or two of them, but as many as had existed before him, so that no one among either the Greek or Latin Fathers seems to have read more authors than Jerome.

He then added writing to his reading. In writing he had acquired from nature such an easy style and such naturally flowing expression that, as one might say, in a single night’s labor he sometimes wrote a thousand verses, or lines, in composing Commentaries on Scripture, and translated from Hebrew an entire book of the Old Testament each day.

He was so constant in this work also that every day was occupied with the study of sacred literature. Postumianus testifies to this in an outstanding eulogy in the dialogue of Sulpicius Severus, about which much has already been said:

> “He is wholly absorbed in reading, wholly absorbed in books. He rests neither by day nor by night. He is always either reading something or writing” (*Dialogue*, book II).

## IV.

Let us now review his individual writings in chronological order.

Paula and Eustochium had asked him to write Commentaries on Paul’s Epistles, which no Latin author before him had interpreted. To satisfy them, he began with the shorter and more readily handled Epistle to Philemon.

After a few days he undertook the exposition of the Epistle to the Galatians, which he completed in three books. Following Origen in these books, he stirred up a new controversy concerning the dispute between Saint Peter and Paul. Jerome himself and Augustine later argued the matter at length in their letters, each in support of the opposing side.

In his Prefaces he frequently excuses himself, saying that he had been compelled to dictate these works quickly, and that the result should not be expected to appear as a fully considered work or as highly polished prose.

A few passages from the third Preface deserve to be recalled:

> “All elegance and the beauty of Latin eloquence have been sullied by the harshness of reading Hebrew. You yourselves know—for more than fifteen years have passed since Cicero, Virgil, or any author of pagan literature has entered my hands—that if something happens to slip out while we speak, we remember it as though through the mist of a dream from long ago.  
>   
> “What progress I have made through tireless study of that language I leave to the judgment of others; I know what I have lost in my own language. Moreover, because of the weakness of my eyes and of my entire body, I do not write with my own hand, and I cannot compensate through labor and diligence for the slowness of my speech. They say that Virgil likewise shaped his books by licking them into form, like bear cubs.  
>   
> “But when I summon a secretary, I either dictate immediately whatever comes into my mouth, or, if I wish to think for a little while so as to produce something better, that silent man rebukes me, draws back his hand, wrinkles his forehead, and by the whole gesture of his body protests that he is present in vain.”

A matter relevant to the history of Jerome’s writings must not be passed over. When he had begun to devote himself to composing these Commentaries on the Epistle to the Galatians, he was informed that the venerable old woman Albina, Marcella’s mother, had died.

Principia, who had succeeded Marcella in her place after Jerome’s departure from the City, immediately joined Marcella, who had been deprived of her mother’s companionship. Together they withdrew to a suburban estate as though into a wilderness. The holy Father himself relates the event partly in the Preface to the first Commentary and partly in Letter 127, which is Marcella’s epitaph.

Having carefully continued the work he had begun, he next undertook the exposition of the Epistle to the Ephesians, as he had done with the others, and likewise completed it in three books.

He inscribed it, as usual, to Paula and Eustochium, but in the first Preface he also names Marcella, whom he calls the unique model of widowhood. He wishes the work to be sent to her as well, while taking the precaution that she not hand it over for reading to slanderers and envious people.

In the second Preface he indicates that she herself had urgently requested this from him through letters, and he says that he is preparing it for her benefit, with new little gifts to be sent to Rome from time to time.

Finally, shortly afterward he explained the Epistle to Titus in a singular and brief Commentary. He made no remark in its Preface relevant to our purpose.

In the eleventh verse of the first chapter, however, he says that a few months earlier he had dictated three volumes in his exposition of the Epistle to the Galatians. From this it is clearer than daylight that all these Commentaries on the four Epistles of Paul were composed not merely within one year, but within a part of a year—that is, in the space of a few months.

We have elsewhere said that no other year seems possible than 387 or the following year. Two further arguments may conveniently confirm this.

First, the holy Father says that for more than fifteen years he had not taken any author of pagan literature into his hands. This must refer, without doubt, to the time when, after withdrawing into the desert of Chalcis, he was warned in a dream and renounced by oath the reading of profane writers.

If fifteen years are added to that date, one arrives at the year we have mentioned, namely 387.

The testimony of Rufinus confirms the same point in the second book of his *Invectives*, which was written, as you know, in the year 401. There he states that Jerome’s Commentary on the Epistle to the Ephesians had been written about fifteen years earlier. Jerome, of course, counted completed years, whereas Rufinus counted years that had scarcely begun.

Finally, the same chronological indication appears in the Preface to the Commentary on Ecclesiastes, which will be discussed in the following chapter.

When the holy Father therefore says in the first book against Rufinus, concerning his exposition of the Epistle to the Ephesians, “It is almost eighteen years since I dictated these books, at the time when Origen’s name flourished in the world,” the numerical figure is either corrupted by the copyists—or, since there is no doubt that he wrote this against his rival in the year 401, “almost fifteen,” or XV, must be read in place of “eighteen,” or XVIII.

Or, what I prefer to think, Jerome must be understood as speaking of the time when he first laid his hand to translating Origen’s writings into Latin.

## IV.

No other Commentaries on the Apostle were composed by him. He himself indicates this in his catalogue of works, where he lists only the four Epistles just mentioned as having been explained by him. Although he places Philemon, with which he began his exposition, last, he follows the order of the Scriptures rather than the order of time.

Those therefore are very far from the truth who have believed, from the age of Cassiodorus onward, that the whole Apostle had been illuminated by Jerome’s Commentaries.

I think that a deception was perpetrated upon learned men by that passage in the second Prologue to the book on the Epistle to the Ephesians, where the holy Father says simply:

> “We are attempting to expound Paul’s Epistles.”

They understood this as referring to all of them, although it refers either only to these four or at least merely expresses the plan and intention he had of writing on the others, an intention that he never fulfilled.

Nor did the evil stop there. In ancient books one can subsequently find a Commentary attributed to Jerome on all Paul’s Epistles except the one to the Hebrews.

Copyists once dared to perpetrate such a great fraud for the sake of profit: they attributed to Jerome a work composed by a most wicked heretic and, if heaven permits the expression, the most bitter enemy of Jerome’s name.

It has long since been relegated among the spurious works, and we have placed it in the volume of that class of Jerome’s writings. We have said enough about this matter in the Admonition prefixed to it.

## V.

Some preliminary observations must now be made about the method the holy Father used in composing his Commentaries. They must be made here at the first opportunity, so that it will not be necessary to repeat them continually as we review the remaining works.

Because he distrusted his own ability to expound the Scriptures—knowing that they were to be interpreted not according to one’s own judgment but according to the traditions of the Fathers—he turned to those who had previously published something on the book he had undertaken to explain.

He searched through all of them so diligently that no one seems to have escaped his attention. He read them with such careful remembrance of his purpose that he passed over nothing relevant to his subject and transferred everything into his own work.

At the beginnings of his Commentaries he often praised by name those whom he followed. Yet he also frequently omitted their names when this seemed more convenient, while nevertheless inserting their opinions into the fabric of his own work.

He says that he did this according to a certain law of Commentaries, as he himself explains: in Commentaries, many different opinions are set forth, with the authors’ names either concealed or stated, so that it remains for the reader to decide what should chiefly be chosen.

For this reason he sometimes professes in his Prefaces to dictate his own words and sometimes those of others. Yet it is difficult to distinguish the borrowed material from his own unless one has read all the authors from whom he excerpted and has their statements and opinions fully at hand.

He was often accused—by Rufinus in particular, who made a lengthy accusation against him on this subject, and by others—of the fickleness and occasional impropriety of opinions that he had reported while concealing their authors, as though he had advanced them as his own or at least as opinions supported by an authority he approved.

He answered all such accusations with one consistent reply, by which he also defended himself against Augustine’s demands:

> “If you thought that something in our exposition deserved criticism, it was the duty of your learning to ask whether what we wrote was found among the Greeks. If they had not said it, then you might condemn it as properly my own opinion, especially since I openly confessed in the Preface that I had dictated either my own words or those of others.”

His replies to Rufinus are similar, and I have referred you to them so that you may recall them. The order of the account we have undertaken does not permit us to reproduce them here.

Certainly it would have been greatly in the interest of his own work, and of our instruction in Scripture, if he had identified each author of every opinion by name, or had transferred into his Commentaries only the most probable opinions from those authors, or, finally, had consistently observed the rule that he says he had established for himself: openly to acknowledge what was heretical and what was Catholic.

But since for other reasons he judged it preferable to spare the authors’ names, lest he appear to tear anyone apart, we have undertaken, for the benefit of readers, to restore to their authors in the Notes the passages that the holy Father drew from others, especially from Origen and Eusebius—either by adding the Greek text itself whenever possible, or at least by indicating the author’s name and the book from which it was taken.

# CHAPTER XIX

I. He writes Commentaries on Ecclesiastes.  
II. He also writes individual books of Hebrew Questions on Genesis, of Places, and of Hebrew Names.  
III. He translates Didymus’s book on the Holy Spirit into Latin.  
IV. He also translates thirty-nine Homilies of Origen on Luke.  
V. He writes seven Treatises on the Psalms, from the tenth through the sixteenth.  
VI. Finally, the life of Malchus the captive monk and of the blessed Hilarion.

## I.

Enjoying both the tranquility of his solitary life, than which nothing is more suitable for literary studies, and the most beneficent liberality of mother Paula, Jerome—whose works of genius had already begun to redound to the benefit of the Churches—devoted himself ever more completely, in mind and strength, to producing those works.

Immediately after his Epistle to the Ephesians, he undertook to write on Ecclesiastes. The interval between the two works was so short and slight that he himself joins them under a single chronological indication in his book against John of Jerusalem.

Indeed, he seems to place Ecclesiastes before the Epistle in an order that is reversed from the actual sequence:

> “Almost ten years ago,” he says, “in my Commentaries on Ecclesiastes and in my exposition of the Epistle to the Ephesians, I believe that I explained the thoughts of my mind to prudent people.”

The sequence of events, however, and the matters discussed above, clearly prove that the Commentaries on that Epistle of the Apostle preceded those on Ecclesiastes. The former were composed in the year 388, as that year was drawing to a close; the latter should be assigned to the beginning of the following year, 389.

The history of the composition and the most authoritative passage from the holy Author himself in the Preface bear witness to the same conclusion:

> “I remember that nearly five years ago, while I was still at Rome and was reading Ecclesiastes to Saint Blaesilla … she asked me to discuss whatever was obscure in the manner of a brief Commentary, so that afterward she might understand without me what she was reading.  
>   
> “And so, when I was at the threshold of my work, she was taken away by a sudden death … and, struck then by so great a wound, I fell silent. Now, situated at Bethlehem, a more exalted city, I return to her memory and to you—Paula and Eustochium—what I owe.”

We showed in its proper place that Blaesilla died toward the end of the year 384, after having spent nearly three months under Jerome’s instruction. If nearly five years are added to that date, one arrives at the year 389, or at least at its beginning, in which we believe Jerome composed these Commentaries.

Some matters concerning the nature and character of his exposition have already been touched on above; others must be recovered from the Preface itself and from the structure of the work.

## II

In the course of this same year—or, if one prefers, down to the beginning of the following year—the Holy Father appears to have published three other individual books, differing somewhat in subject, which he lists in this order in his catalogue of works:

> One book of *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*. One book *On Places*. One book *of Hebrew Names*.

In the first he mentions the second of these, in the second the first and third, and in the third the two earlier ones; so that from this very enumeration one may understand that he had all three in hand at the same time. Indeed, he first published the one which he places last in the catalogue: while he was still laboring over the Hebrew Questions and had not yet published the book *On Hebrew Places*, he brought out the third book, *On Names*.

This book had long been said to have been first roughly composed in Greek by Philo and then enlarged through Origen’s efforts, but it had become so disordered and confused that Jerome thought its usefulness could scarcely be preserved merely by translating it into Latin; rather, he undertook almost entirely to restore it anew. It was an example and test of the progress he had made in Hebrew letters. For this reason, at the urging of the brothers Lupulianus—or Lupulus, as some manuscripts read—and Valerianus, he undertook to write it, moved by the usefulness of the work itself and by the desire, as he boasts, to have done something which even the Greeks might seek.

Although he retained almost all the etymologies of the names found in the Greek exemplar—including, indeed, several Greek names that had formerly been intruded through misguided diligence—he nevertheless frequently added others from his own resources. He acknowledged that some of these appeared rather absurd and were explained by a forced interpretation contrary to the character of the Hebrew language. Thus he sometimes calls the book his own, sometimes Philo’s or Origen’s; and he says that he found certain things elsewhere in a book of *Hebrew Names* which are by no means found in this work of his.

The honor of this edition was followed by the *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*, an entirely new work, previously unknown to both Greeks and Latins. In it he proposed either to refute the errors of those who had made various conjectures about the Hebrew books, or to restore to their authority those readings which seemed to be swarming with corruptions in Greek and Latin manuscripts.

He intended to prepare questions of this kind on the other books of Scripture as well, and perhaps even began the task. He himself occasionally hints at this, as when he undertakes to discuss some matter “when he explains the Questions on Joshua.” But, as we showed in our General Preface, either he did not subsequently complete what he had begun to sketch, or—and this seems closer to the truth—after changing his plan, he made useful use, while composing his Commentaries, of those materials which he had hastily gathered; or finally, whatever the work may have been, he kept it confined within the walls of his own household.

Certainly, in the catalogue of his works, which he wrote approximately two years later, he lists no other *Hebrew Questions* besides those on Genesis and admits no others into the reckoning of his productions.

Finally, he published the book *On Places*, which he translated from the Greek text set forth by Eusebius into Latin; in some places he also altered it and enlarged it somewhat, as is clear from a comparison with the Greek text which we published in the section devoted to Jerome’s interpretation. In his Preface he excuses this freedom in the following words:

> For I have already stated, in the book of the *Chronicle*, that I am either a translator or the founder of a new work.

He set this translation of his against another which someone scarcely trained in letters had dared to publish, so that the prudent reader might judge by comparing the two.

## III

After these works he appends Didymus’s book in the catalogue, a work on which he had now been engaged for nearly five years, since he had begun translating it at Rome, while Damasus was still alive—that is, toward the end of the year 384, as we noted in its proper place.

He therefore took it up again and, whether he revised the whole work in a second edition or merely translated into Latin the remaining portion which he had previously omitted, he certainly did not allow it to remain hidden any longer within the walls of his cell. Rather, in the manner of speaking which he particularly favored, he permitted it to receive the honor of publication as the year 389 was drawing to a close, and dedicated it to his brother Paulinianus.

He relates the whole matter himself in the Preface:

> When I was living in Babylon, when I was a tenant of the purple-clad harlot and was living according to the rights of Roman citizens, I wished to prattle somewhat about the Holy Spirit and to dedicate the work I had begun to the bishop of that same city.

After inserting a few words about the hatred under which he suffered at Rome, he adds:

> At once, as though by a restoration of citizenship, I returned to Jerusalem; and after Romulus’s hut and the Lupercalian games, I looked upon Mary’s lodging and the cave of the Savior. Therefore, my brother Paulinianus, since the aforementioned Bishop Damasus, who had first urged me to this work, has fallen asleep in Christ, and since I am now aided by the prayers both of you and of Christ’s venerable handmaids Paula and Eustochium, here in Judaea, at your prompting, I murmur the song which I could not sing in a foreign land . . .

And, in order to acknowledge the author in the title, he says:

> I preferred to be the translator of another’s work rather than, as certain people do, adorn myself like a misshapen jackdaw with another’s colors.

Rufinus maintains that these last words, and especially those that follow, were directed as a taunt against Saint Ambrose; for that reason he brings a most serious accusation against Jerome. We have spoken of this matter elsewhere, in its proper place.

## IV

The thirty-nine Homilies of Origen on Luke follow. Learned men have been persuaded that Jerome translated these into Latin before he published the *Hebrew Questions on Genesis* and the book *On Places*, and therefore still earlier than the work on the Holy Spirit which we have just mentioned.

The principal basis for their view is a substantial passage from the Holy Father’s own Preface to those Homilies:

> I set aside for a little while the books of the Hebrew Questions, so that, for your pleasure, I might dictate these works, whatever they may be, as profitable labor—works not my own but another’s.

I, however, hold a very different opinion and think that they misunderstood the Holy Doctor’s meaning and the sense of his words. For he does not say that he interrupted the *Questions on Genesis*, but simply the *Questions*—ἁπλῶς, “Questions” without qualification. It is much more probable, and equally reasonable to believe, that when he speaks of other Questions he means those which he was preparing on the remaining books of Scripture—Questions which, once interrupted at that time, he subsequently abandoned altogether, as we have said—rather than a single book on Genesis, which the entire sequence of events and the order maintained in his catalogue persuade us had already been completed and published.

If this is true, as it appears wholly plausible, he undertook to translate these Homilies from Greek into Latin only in the year 390.

In the Preface addressed to Paula and Eustochium, the Holy Father attacks a certain interpreter of Luke whom they had read but had not sufficiently approved. Rufinus contends that this person was Saint Ambrose, who had published his Commentaries on Luke almost four years earlier (*Invective* II).

He attempts to establish this both from the fact that, up to that time, no Latin author besides Ambrose had written on Luke, and from the fact that he could produce Jerome’s own letter in which, while excusing himself in this very matter with regard to others, Jerome turns suspicion against Ambrose.

But Rufinus neither published this letter, because it contained certain more private matters, nor had anyone seen it, so that no argument can legitimately be drawn from it. Nor will it be easy to induce anyone to place confidence in a man who exercised against Jerome hatred more than Vatinian in its intensity.

The remaining matters concerning his accusations, which he directs against Jerome’s Latin translation of these Homilies of Origen, have been sufficiently and abundantly examined and refuted by us in the Preface to Volume Seven. If these matters are of sufficient interest, the reader may return to that discussion.

## V

A little later—apparently in this same year—the Holy Father also composed the seven Treatises which he places below the Psalms, from the tenth through the sixteenth.

Learned men, among whom are Sixtus of Siena and Daniel Huetius, think that these were nothing other than seven Homilies of Origen, translated by Jerome from Greek into Latin.

We prefer to make no definite assertion on this matter, especially since the entire work has perished, and therefore the evidence from which an argument for either view might be drawn is lacking. Indeed, if one may conjecture anything from the manner in which Jerome himself lists them, I would rather regard them as the first fruits of the Holy Doctor, although I readily acknowledge that most of their material was drawn from Greek writers, especially Origen, as was then his customary practice.

We have added the reason why they disappeared—or, at any rate, why they have survived neither in their entirety nor in a form sufficiently pure to distinguish them from the interpolations of others—in our *Admonition to the Breviary on the Psalms*, which we append to Volume Seven as an Appendix.

## VI

After completing these writings, the Holy Father appears to have imposed silence upon himself for a time. “He made me keep silent,” he says, “for whom my speech is punishment” (*Prologue to the Life of Malchus*).

Meanwhile, however, he was already planning a more serious work, one requiring much longer labor: namely, to commit the entire history of Christian affairs to writing. For he says:

> I have resolved to write—if only the Lord grants me life, and if my detractors cease pursuing me, even as I flee and shut myself away—from the coming of the Savior down to our own age, that is, from the Apostles to the dregs of our own times: how and through whom the Church of Christ was born, grew to maturity, increased through persecutions, and was crowned with martyrdoms; and how, after it came to Christian rulers, it became greater in power and wealth but lesser in virtues.

Whether he later composed this work has been debated among the learned. Although nothing of the kind has come down to us, and although no trace or vestige of it has ever appeared among the ancients, Jerome himself nevertheless seems to affirm that he did so—indeed, some ten years later, in Book I *Against Rufinus*, where he says that he translated Eusebius’s *Ecclesiastical History* into Latin, though he could have incorporated it into his own.

> I praised Eusebius in the *Ecclesiastical History*, in the arrangement of the chronology—this is the Latin version of the *Chronicle*—and in the description of the Holy Land—this is the book *On Places*; and, by translating these little works into Latin, I gave them to the speakers of my language.

We have elsewhere indicated that the Holy Doctor intended that passage differently from the interpretation commonly assigned to it, and from what appears at first sight. His words should be understood so that what he says “I praised” refers exclusively to the *Ecclesiastical History*; while, with regard to the other two little works, the statement that he gave them to speakers of his language refers to the fact that he translated them.

This still appears to be the genuine explanation of his meaning, and it could easily be confirmed by similar examples in his writings, should the occasion arise.

If anyone finds this less convincing, it may also be supposed that he was referring to a portion of Eusebius’s history—not a very large portion, certainly, but the literal, κατὰ λέξιν, “word-for-word,” account of Eusebius which lists ecclesiastical writers and which Our Author inserted word for word, translated into Latin, in his book *On Illustrious Men*.

Certainly, those who think that Jerome actually composed a universal ecclesiastical history have departed very far from every appearance of truth.

## VII

In any event, when he first ceased to remain silent, apparently in the year 391, the Holy Father composed the *Life of Malchus the Captive Monk* and the *Life of Blessed Hilarion*. In his catalogue he lists them together, as it were in a single breath, connecting them in this fashion.

The first history, as we said in its proper place, he had heard at Maronia in Syria from Malchus’s own mouth; the second he arranged from an account narrated by Egyptian monks.

The book entitled *The Life of the Fathers* adds that Jerome dedicated it under the name of Asella. Yet no trace or vestige of this claim is found either in the printed or handwritten Jerome manuscripts.

The only fact which the Holy Father himself reveals is that Sophronius translated it into Greek in an elegant style. From this it is clear that Vossius is mistaken when, in his work *On Greek Historians*, he makes Sophronius the author rather than the translator of the *Life of Hilarion*.

## CHAPTER XX

I. The books which Jerome corrected from the exemplar of the Septuagint in the Latin edition then current are reviewed. II. The books which now survive from that labor.

### I

The Holy Father seems to have made no entry in his Catalogue—at least none bearing on chronology—of that exceedingly useful and difficult labor by which he reviewed the books of Holy Scripture according to the most accurate exemplars of the Septuagint, correcting the old Latin translation and restoring it in innumerable places. Nor indeed does he there make any mention of it as a work composed by himself, though he includes among his productions all the rest, even those of less importance if one wishes. Yet it is clearly established that, when he wrote that Catalogue, or book *On Illustrious Men*, namely in the year 392, he had already completed the greater part of this labor and had allowed no small part of it to appear publicly. In Book II *Against Rufinus* he says: “Have I spoken anything against the Seventy Translators, whom, most carefully corrected, I gave many years ago to students of my language?” And in nearly the same words in Book III: “The edition of the Seventy, most carefully corrected, I gave many years ago to speakers of my language.” Likewise, in the Prologue to the books of Solomon translated from Hebrew: “If anyone indeed prefers the edition of the Seventy Translators, he has it corrected by us.” Finally, to omit much else, in Epistle LXXI to Lucinius: “I do not doubt that you possess the edition of the Seventy Translators; many years ago I handed it down, most carefully corrected, to students.” These more than sufficient testimonies of the Translator himself prove that he not only undertook this work but also allowed it, at least in good part, to receive the honor of publication, as he elsewhere puts it.

### II

These passages also sufficiently establish, contrary to the opinion of certain critics, otherwise not unlearned, that Jerome reviewed according to the Greek exemplar not merely those books of Scripture which still survive or which he expressly names, and no others besides. For when he says simply that he corrected the edition of the Septuagint in Latin from Greek exemplars, and compares it with his other translation from Hebrew, it is manifest that he denotes as polished by this labor not merely a few little books—at most six, as they would have it—but the entire Canon. There are other arguments for this, set out more fully in our Preface to Volume Ten; consult them again, if you think it worthwhile, and refer them here. Most striking, surely, is the testimony of the Interpreter himself in Epistle CXXXIV to Augustine, where he laments that the greater part of this correction had already been appropriated by somebody or other. “In the edition,” he says, “of the Seventy . . . we have lost through the fraud of someone the greater part of our earlier labor.” Therefore, there were many other things besides those then commonly available and still surviving today; these could be called the greater part of the work and readily filled out the entire Canon of Scripture. Augustine, having at last learned this fact more certainly, asks Jerome for the complete recension in Epistle CXVI among Jerome’s letters: “Please send me your translation of the Septuagint, which I did not know you had published.”

### III

It remains to explain how great this labor cost the Holy Doctor, and what precisely its nature and scope were. There was an old translation, the ancient Latin Vulgate of the Old Testament, which at that time prevailed everywhere in the churches. It had been rendered into Latin from another Greek version of the Septuagint, but had been so disfigured by copyists’ errors of every sort—gaps, transpositions, and additions—that it sometimes conveyed a sense other than the true one and made the words and meanings of divine authority uncertain through variant readings. The chief cause of the errors was that it had originally been derived from the Greek κοινή, that is, the Common Edition, which teemed with countless corruptions of this kind. The difficulty was further increased because the other Greek editions then in circulation differed greatly from one another according to regional variation and the practice of churches. “Alexandria and Egypt,” he says, “commend Hesychius as the author of their Septuagint; Constantinople as far as Antioch approves the exemplars of Lucian the martyr. The provinces lying between read the Palestinian codices, prepared by Origen and published by Eusebius and Pamphilus; and the whole world contends against itself in this threefold diversity.”

And indeed Origen not only set out exemplars of four editions, writing the individual words opposite one another so that one differing reading might immediately be convicted by the agreement of the others; but, in a bolder undertaking, he mixed the edition of Theodotion into the edition of the Septuagint, marking with asterisks what had previously been lacking and with obeli what seemed superfluous (*Preface to the Books of Paralipomena from Hebrew*). I pass over the editions and exemplars which he mentions elsewhere. The one that alone approached the truth, or at least came far closer to it than all the others, was that prepared long before by Origen’s industry in the *Hexapla* (Ἑξαπλοῖς), with obeli and asterisks. It was this, surely, that our author used amid such a diversity of editions, having found a very accurate exemplar of it in the library at Caesarea. Moreover, in restoring the Latin version he employed that same system of signs, namely the obelus and the asterisk. Hence in Epistle CXII to Augustine he says: “What you ask, why my earlier translation of the canonical books has asterisks and obeli prefixed . . . that translation is the translation of the Seventy interpreters; and wherever the marks called obeli occur, it is indicated that the Seventy said more than is found in the Hebrew. But where there are asterisks, that is, shining little stars, something has been added by Origen from Theodotion’s edition: there we translated the Greek; here we expressed from the Hebrew itself what we understood.” And elsewhere, in Epistle CXXXIV to the same man: “I cannot comply with your commands, especially in the edition of the Septuagint, which is distinguished by asterisks and obeli.” Finally, most clearly of all, in Epistle CVI to Sunnia and Fretela, he teaches also how much difference there is between the Common and the Hexaplar Edition, and testifies that he translated the latter faithfully into Latin. A little later he says: “But that which is found in the *Hexapla*, and which we translated, is precisely that incorrupt and undefiled translation of the Seventy interpreters which is preserved in the books of the learned.”

### IV

As regards the date, since the same year cannot be assigned to every individual book, nor a certain year to each, it is nevertheless highly probable that all were completed before the year 391. For it is not reasonable to believe that, after the Holy Father had from that time begun a new translation from the Hebrew text, he gave further thought to that earlier correction. Thus whatever this work amounted to was evidently already finished and for the most part kept within the walls of his cell for the private use of the monastery; or at least it had not pleased its author so thoroughly that he thought the needs of the churches sufficiently provided for by it. For he would not have undertaken a wholly new translation from Hebrew if that edition, however exact in its fidelity to the Greek codices, had sufficed. The entire labor was completed in roughly five years. For in 392, when he was composing the Catalogue of his works, he had already begun translating certain books from Hebrew; this is an indication that he had already ceased working from Greek. Yet he did not begin translating these—or bringing the Latin into conformity with them—until the year 387, after he had withdrawn to Bethlehem. He had, however, prepared the way for so great a work by that almost hasty recension of the Psalms which, as he says, while living at Rome he had completed rapidly and in large part. When this first attempt succeeded well and was especially approved by the practice of the Roman Church—for it is still called the Roman Psalter—it encouraged him, after he soon moved to Bethlehem and expounded the Septuagint edition daily in the community of brothers, to recast that version completely according to the Greek text, specifically the very accurate Hexaplar text. There seems to be no doubt that by this continuous comparison with Greek he polished the entire Canon; we have discussed this more fully in the Preface to Volume Ten, to which refer.

### V

But only two complete books now survive from that whole recension, Job and the Psalter, together with two Prologues to the books of Solomon and Paralipomena. These are scarcely any evidence of so great a work; they afford us more cause to long for and lament what has perished than to enjoy what remains. Although the books of all the Prophets also—a by no means small portion of Scripture—may be reconstructed from that version or correction which the Holy Father immediately appends in his Commentaries to his translation from Hebrew, according to the Septuagint. Yet I do not know whether it can be printed continuously and entire from this source in such a way that, what is the main point, the Holy Doctor’s great diligence in the marks of obeli and asterisks may be apparent. These could easily have fallen out through copyists’ carelessness and because they occurred, as it were, in foreign places; and it is established that they have in fact fallen out in some places. The greatest part of the rest of his work perished long ago, even during the lifetime of the holy Interpreter himself. We have noted this before from the end of his Epistle CXXXIV to Augustine, where he says: “I cannot comply with your commands, especially in the edition of the Septuagint, which is distinguished by asterisks and obeli; for through the fraud of someone we have lost the greater part of our earlier labor.” We have said enough in the Preface to Volume Ten concerning this loss and the two books which survive.

## CHAPTER XXI

I. He translates the Old Testament from Hebrew. II. Beginning with the books of Kings and proceeding in an inverted order, he published the greater part of that version before the year 392. III. He also kept some part of it by him for a time. IV. In subsequent periods he completed what remained of the Hebrew Canon.

### I

Yet Jerome, not fully satisfied with that recension and correction of Scripture, turned his mind to preparing a wholly new Latin translation from the Hebrew exemplar itself, as superior to all the others and more faithful. [Col. 0078] He had certainly completed the greater part of it by the year 392; for when, plainly and without qualification (ἁπλῶς), he then composed the Catalogue of his works, he stated that he had translated the Old Testament according to the Hebrew. This is why it seems more consistent with the history of Jerome’s affairs to assign the whole labor here at once, although he translated what remained of that work in subsequent times—some parts nearly two years later, others much later—so that the entire translation of the Canon according to Hebrew was not completed until about twelve years afterward. But let us explain the date and order of each book.

### II
