He did not undertake to translate the books in the order in which they are contained in the Hebrew Canon, from first to last; rather, as he could and as he was asked by the brethren, he set himself to translate them. He began with the books of Kings, which the Hebrews divide into only two volumes, calling them Samuel and Malachim. In the Prologue, which for this reason he calls a “helmeted beginning,” and which, he says, applies to all the books he intended to translate from Hebrew into Latin, he plainly states that this was his first attempt. For he wished to prepare a defence against those whom he foresaw would be all the more hostile to his endeavor because it was an undertaking of greater importance and labor than what he had previously achieved in reviewing and correcting the version of the Septuagint. It was indeed the work of a man endowed with a certain divine intellect and trained in almost every kind of learning beyond the ordinary human condition, to reach sources of Scripture long inaccessible to all and to desire to teach the churches from them meanings and words not previously heard. Accordingly, being about to offer these books first as a specimen of his learning, he asks that they be read, lest he seem to claim too much for himself; and in that very respect he indicates that they were the first, or before all others, translated by him from Hebrew.

He then sent them to Rome to Father Domnio, as he relates in Epistle XLIX to Pammachius, written in 393. In that letter he also testifies that he had by then translated the sixteen books of the Prophets from Hebrew into Latin, and indeed says that they were available for Pammachius to read. He adds that, if these please him and he finds that he takes delight in this work, he will be prompted not to keep the remaining books shut up in his bookcase. Immediately thereafter he names his version of Job. For he had already gathered courage for that exceedingly difficult book, which had to be translated not only from Hebrew but also from Arabic and Syriac; for this purpose he had previously engaged for himself a Jewish teacher from Lydda. He recounts this more fully in the Preface; but he indicates the date in the letter to Pammachius just cited, in these words: “I have recently translated Job into our language; you may borrow an exemplar of it from your cousin Saint Marcella.” Therefore that translation had not only long since been completed, but had also been publicly issued and sent to Rome; thus, from that adverb “recently,” you may infer that no insignificant interval of time had preceded it.

The argument has still more force if, as is also highly probable, all these volumes were translated into Latin in a more or less continuous course of work and sent to Rome on the same occasion. For it is clear from the book *On Illustrious Men*, which the Holy Father composed in that very year, that they had appeared much earlier, and before 392. From it we likewise learn that he had already long before given the Psalter to speakers of his language, and that he did so before translating the Prophets, whom we have listed second. For among his other little works, which he there lists in the one hundred and thirty-fourth chapter, he mentions also the Psalter and the Prophets as having been translated into Greek by his friend Sophronius: “we,” he says, “translated them from Hebrew into Latin.” And there must indeed have been a fairly considerable interval of time, so that they could be rendered into Greek by Sophronius and listed by our author as works already completed and published.

### III

Thus, before the year 392, the Holy Father had completed the volumes which we have expressly named, and these contain a part of all Scripture greater by half again than the remainder. He published the rest in subsequent times; but from these too I am readily led to believe that he then had some ready at hand, from the passage cited above in which he says that he was keeping the rest shut up in his bookcase. Whether Daniel was among their number, or should be reckoned as the fourth among the Major Prophets, may not inappropriately be asked. For when the holy Interpreter himself, in the cited letter to Pammachius, states that he had translated sixteen Prophets from Hebrew into Latin, he surely counts Daniel among them; otherwise he should have counted only fifteen. In fact, elsewhere too, as in Epistle LIII to Paulinus, he includes Daniel among the Major Prophets and joins him to the other three.

On the other hand, that book is not counted among the Prophets in the Hebrew Canon, but among the Hagiographa; nor does it occupy any other place in Jerome’s version itself, in accordance with the arrangement of the ancient exemplars. In the Helmeted Prologue and elsewhere, the Doctor himself counts Daniel among the Hagiographa, and he seems not to have wished to invert in preparing his translation the order of the Canon which he had adopted. Finally, in the Preface he indicates that he separated this work by a long interval from the prophetic books, especially in these words: “I came at last upon Daniel and was so overcome with weariness that, in sudden despair, I wished to despise all my previous labor. But encouraged by a certain Hebrew, who kept repeating to me more than once in his own language, ‘Persistent labor conquers all’ (*Labor omnia vincit improbus*), I, who had seemed a smatterer among the Hebrews, began again to be a pupil in Chaldee. And, to tell the truth, to the present day I can read and understand the Chaldean language better than pronounce it.”

However the matter may stand—for it seems possible to argue either side—I would nevertheless prefer to think that Jerome rendered Daniel into Latin from Hebrew before at least the year 393. Nor do I doubt that by that time he had attained such knowledge of the language as was required for properly composing his translation of that book. But from this I would draw a different inference concerning other books written in the Chaldean dialect, such as Tobit. For if, when Jerome translated Daniel before the year 393, as we have said, he did not yet know the Chaldean language perfectly, he nevertheless knew it; whereas, when he translated Tobit, he confessed himself so ignorant of that language that he could not understand for himself what was written there in Chaldee unless it had first been rendered into Hebrew. It follows that he undertook the Latin translation of this book much earlier than that one. For, in the Preface to Chromatius and Heliodorus, he says: “Because the language of the Chaldeans is akin to Hebrew speech, finding a speaker most skilled in both languages, I took up the labor of one day; and whatever he expressed to me in Hebrew words, I set forth in Latin speech through a summoned secretary.”

Thus this translation had certainly been completed long before he wrote the letter to Pammachius so often cited; and since it is not mentioned there, it must certainly be counted among the books which he says he kept shut up in his bookcase. For although that book was not of the earlier Hebrew Canon, which included only books written in Hebrew, it nevertheless possessed divine authority both among that people and among the Fathers of the Church, and Jerome immediately received it into the reckoning of sacred Scripture. Judith was a book of the same kind; Jerome, apparently already thoroughly acquainted with the Chaldean language, and therefore after Daniel himself, translated it into Latin. Perhaps one or another additional book might be added to these, which he had given Roman dress during that period but had not yet brought out publicly; but this is less certain.

On the other hand, these considerations are enough to establish the truth of his statement: namely, that from the year 392 the Old Testament had been translated by him according to Hebrew fidelity. For the items then lacking for the completion of the work, though he does not enumerate them individually in the letter to Pammachius, he was already keeping for the most part shut up in his bookcase; and although he brought them out in succeeding years, he nevertheless indicated that they should be dated simply from that beginning and time, unless he expressly directed otherwise.

## IV

The volumes, then, which Saint Jerome had either not yet taken up from the entire Hebrew canon, or at least had not yet made publicly available, appear to have been the Octateuch, the Books of Chronicles, the books of Solomon, and those of Ezra. The latter he published, together with Nehemiah, not much later—at most, two years after the publication of *On Illustrious Men*, that is, in the year 394—dedicating it to Domnio and Rogatianus, by whom he had continually been urged for the preceding three years to undertake this labor. In the Prologue he in turn asks them to be content with private reading, not to bring the book out into public view, and not to force food upon the fastidious; they should avoid the disdain of those who know only how to judge others and themselves know how to do nothing.

“If there are any of the brethren,” he adds, “to whom our work is not displeasing, give them a copy, admonishing them to transcribe the Hebrew names, of which there is a great abundance in this volume, distinctly and with intervals between them.” From this you understand once more, to our present purpose, with what zeal he avoided the public light, and wished everything except what he entrusted to his friends to remain hidden from everyone. This is why certain works seem to have to be dated not from the time when they were composed, but from the time when they were made public. [Col. 0081]

The year of this translation, 394 as we have said, is clearly apparent from that same Preface, where he says that he is reserving for a more extensive work the discussion of many passages which are praised in the Gospels as coming from the Old Testament but are not found in the Septuagint. By the name “more extensive work” he intended nothing other than Epistle LVII in our recension, or the little book *On the Best Kind of Translation*, in which, according to its purpose, he discusses the comparison of that Septuagint translation with the Hebrew text and resolves the question, traced from the Gospels, which it raises. Moreover, there is now no doubt that this little book, or Epistle, was written in the year 395, as we have shown in its proper place.

Saint Jerome appended to Ezra his translation of Chronicles in that same year, as it appears. For in the Prologue to Chromatius he called that same little book *On the Best Kind of Translation* a work “recently published” by him. You will learn from the sequence of events above all, and then from many other examples in his writings, how short an interval of time he denotes by that adverb. Therefore those who assert that these works were published last of all depart rather far from the truth, as will become clearer from the testimony cited and from what will be said below.

Some add the Book of Esther to these works. But Saint Jerome appears to have included it among the books of the Octateuch, which we shall discuss presently, in accordance with the form of the Hebrew canon he had adopted, in which the books of Judges and Ruth are combined into one. It is therefore more probable that, after Chronicles, he translated the three little books of Solomon—Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Songs—into Latin in no more than three days’ work, and dedicated them to the bishops Chromatius and Heliodorus, who daily demanded from him memorials of his talent.

“I did this,” he says, “so that, broken by a long illness, I might not be altogether silent this year and remain mute before you.” By this illness he seems to us to indicate the one into which he elsewhere also complains of having fallen, as in the Preface to the Commentaries on Matthew, Epistle LXXI to Lucinius, and much more fully Epistle LXXIII to Evangelus. From it he indicates that he had only recently recovered in the Prologue to the Third Commentary on Amos.

We have shown by certain arguments, especially from the sequence of events in the chronological notes attached to those Epistles and Commentaries, that Saint Jerome’s illness began at the start of the year 398—or, if one prefers, at the end of the preceding year. After recovering somewhat only a few months later, he resumed his interrupted studies with excessive eagerness and consequently fell ill again, more seriously. Thus, after the middle and nearly at the end of that year—as he himself seems to indicate by the words “so that I might not be altogether silent this year”—he translated those three little books from Hebrew into Latin.

The Octateuch remained: that is, the first eight books of the sacred text, or seven, as some maintain, completing the number eight by adding Esther as the eighth book. For, as we have said, according to the Hebrew recension Ruth is counted as one with Judges. Certainly Saint Jerome himself calls it the Octateuch in Epistle LXXI to Lucinius, the passage from which we shall shortly cite, although certain older editions of that passage read *Heptateuch*, that is, “seven books only.” If that reading were retained, even if one followed the reckoning of the Hebrew codex, Esther would necessarily be excluded.

Nevertheless, *Octateuch* is unquestionably the correct reading, and the fact that Saint Jerome counted the Book of Esther among it will be demonstrated by a passage from his Preface to Joshua, which will be cited below. We are therefore not influenced by the strenuous insistence of some who claim that it is clear from the Preface to the book that it was translated into Latin while Paula the mother was still alive, since it is dedicated to her and to her daughter Eustochium. For, on the contrary, if this was, as it should have been, the last book of the Octateuch to be translated into Latin, Paula had already died at least two years earlier.

Cleverly, however, this argument has been answered both by others and by the Benedictine editor himself: Paula, the mother of Eustochium, should not be understood there, but another and younger Paula, the daughter of Laeta and, through her brother, Eustochium’s niece. The matter should be attributed to the carelessness of scribes and to the custom that had become established in the placement of these names, by which the younger niece is put before the older aunt.

But enough of this.

Jerome testified in that Epistle to Lucinius that the Octateuch was the only part remaining to him, since he had already assigned all the other books of the Hebrew canon to Lucinius’s boys and secretaries for copying:

> “I have given the canon of Hebrew truth, except for the Octateuch, which I now have in hand, to your boys and secretaries to copy.”

The year was 398 when he wrote this, as has been demonstrated in its proper place by firm arguments, and as the order of the events we have discussed proves.

It appears, however, that he had undertaken the translation of the Pentateuch—that is, the five books of Moses—some time earlier at the urging of Desiderius, a presbyter of Aquitaine, the same man to whom he had previously sent Epistle XLVII in our recension and at whose later urging he wrote against Vigilantius. He subsequently dedicated this work to him. Yet some part of it—Genesis and Exodus at least—he had already completed before that year, when he truly said that he was laboring over the other books of the Octateuch.

The remaining books he postponed, being hindered by certain cares—I do not know what they were—and putting off the day from one day to the next. He did not complete them until after the death of Paula the mother, that is, after the year 404. This is established beyond all doubt by the Preface to Joshua, Judges, and Ruth, whose translation he prepared at the earnest request of Eustochium and gave to her alone as a gift.

“At last,” he says, “the Pentateuch of Moses being finished, as though released from a great debt, we lay our hand upon Jesus the son of Nave, whom the Hebrews call Joshua ben Nun, that is, Joshua son of Nun; and upon the Book of Judges, which they call *Sophtim*; and also upon Ruth and Esther, which they designate by the same names.”

And near the end:

> “Moreover, after the dormition of Saint Paula, whose life is an example of virtue, we resolved to complete these books, which I could not deny to the virgin of Christ Eustochium,” and so forth.

Paula died, as has been shown elsewhere, and as her own epitaph confirms, during the consulship of Honorius Augustus for the sixth time and Aristaenetus, which is the date of the year 404. [Col. 0083]

This translation can therefore appropriately be assigned to the following year, in which the entire Hebrew canon was completed. As we have said, he began with Samuel, or the Books of Kings, and ended with Esther, bringing to a close, after nearly fifteen years of such labors, the work of Saint Jerome.

As for what concerns, so to speak, the fortunes of that edition among the Latin Churches, and its history, we have touched upon it in part in the Preface to Volume X, while other highly learned critics have already discussed it, some of whom we name there. Finally, these matters have little or nothing to do with the Life of the Saintly Doctor that we are writing.

# CHAPTER XXII

I. Meanwhile Jerome writes various Epistles to Paula and Eustochium.  
II. He also writes Commentaries on Micah, Zephaniah, Nahum, Habakkuk, and Haggai.  
III. Whether he had earlier expounded Jonah, and whether he had composed shorter Commentaries on each of the twelve Minor Prophets.  
IV. He continues to elucidate the other Prophets in the same work.  
V. He publishes *On Illustrious Men*.

## I

The sequence of the books of Scripture compelled us for a while to stray from the chronological path of our subject. We now return to the order of Jerome’s life and history.

Immediately after reporting the translation of the Old Testament according to the Hebrew, Saint Jerome, in his Catalogue of his works addressed to Paula and Eustochium, mentions Epistles to them, saying that their number is uncertain because they are written every day. It seems to us that he is indicating, for the most part, those very Epistles in which he dedicated to the same holy women various translations from Hebrew or Commentaries on several books of Scripture.

Of this kind are the Prefaces to the Books of Kings, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel, as well as to the twelve Minor Prophets, Job, Daniel, and Chronicles; their dates are already established from the chronological notices of the books to which they are prefixed.

Eight other Epistles may be added to these, by which he had long before dedicated to the same women his Commentaries on four of Paul’s Epistles. Again, other Epistles are those by which he dedicated to them his exposition of Ecclesiastes and his translation from Greek of Origen’s Homilies on Luke.

If any others existed, or if they were of another kind, they have not reached us, or at least remain entirely unknown to us, as to the other most diligent critics who preceded us.

## II

As we have said, Saint Jerome had interrupted his translation of Scripture from Hebrew in order to labor over other works as he was requested. He was first interrupted by the writing of several Commentaries on the Minor Prophets. When he began this work, the year 391 or the following year was certainly still in progress. He had already completed nearly half of the labor when, in that same year, while composing his Catalogue of his works, he listed those Prophets by name:

> “Moreover, I wrote two books of explanations on Micah, one book on Zephaniah, one book on Nahum, two books on Habakkuk, and one book on Haggai.” [Col. 0084]

He relates the matter in still clearer words in the Preface to the Third Commentary on Amos, except that he gives the order differently, excludes Habakkuk from this group, and seems to assign it to another period:

> “We both began and, with Christ’s help, shall complete the work on the twelve Prophets in a disorderly and confused sequence. For we did not discuss them from the first to the last according to the order in which they are read, but as we were able and as we were asked. I first addressed Nahum, Micah, Zephaniah, and Haggai to the industrious Paula and her daughter Eustochium; secondly, I assigned two books on Habakkuk to Chromatius, Bishop of Aquileia.”

## III

It is difficult to explain what Saint Jerome intended when, in the second chapter of his Commentary on Zephaniah, he says that he interpreted Nineveh in Jonah—that is, “the beautiful one”—as the Church gathered from the Gentiles, which had done penance at the preaching of Jonah, that is, “the Dove.” At that time he was expounding Zephaniah, and yet he was so far from having already explained Jonah that in the Preface to Amos which we have just cited, where he accounts for the course of his work, he indicates that he had undertaken Zephaniah in the first group, but Jonah in the third, and long afterward:

> “Third, after a long silence, I explained Obadiah and Jonah to you at your command.”

Again, in the Preface to Jonah itself:

> “After so long a time I take Jonah as the beginning of my interpretation.”

Scholars commonly resolve this difficulty in the following way. They maintain that Saint Jerome devoted himself twice to explaining the Minor Prophets. First, they say, he composed brief observations on each of the twelve, of a different kind from Commentaries, which do not now exist but had already been completed before the year 393. To these, they claim, he referred in that passage on Zephaniah.

To make this seem more plausible, they cite Jerome himself as a guarantor in Epistle XLIX to Pammachius, section 4, where he says:

> “I sent Saint Domnio some of the *hypomnemata* [ὑπομνήματα] on the twelve Prophets, which, if you wish to read them,” and so forth.

This Epistle was delivered in the year 393, and therefore the *hypomnemata* on the twelve Prophets mentioned there must necessarily be earlier and different from those now extant, since the latter were not completed until after the year 406.

But we have shown in its proper place, and have further refuted at length in the General Preface, that this is a sufficiently foolish error on the part of learned men, resulting from a mistaken understanding of Saint Jerome’s testimony. In the first place, Jerome did not say that he had composed a work on all twelve Prophets, nor did he designate each of the prophetic books on which he had exercised his efforts. He simply praises a book entitled “The Twelve Prophets” and says that he had written some commentary on it.

Thus, in the *Dialogue against the Luciferians*, he said that it was written “in the twelve Prophets” that their sacrifices were “like the bread of mourning,” and so forth; yet this is a passage belonging to Hosea alone.

Moreover, he does not say absolutely *hypomnemata*—“Commentaries”—but “some of the *hypomnemata*,” indicating not all twelve but only some of them, which he had already explained at that time. These are the Prophets we have listed: Nahum, Micah, and Zephaniah; if you wish, add one or two more, namely Haggai and Habakkuk.

## IV

“But how did it happen,” you will ask, “that, when writing on Zephaniah, Saint Jerome mentions Commentaries on Jonah which he composed nearly five years later?”

I think that there he is indicating certain notes of his on that book of the Twelve Prophets, which he had prepared earlier, before undertaking to elucidate any one of them in a continuous exposition. Although he explained Jonah so long after Zephaniah, he could nevertheless, while writing on it, praise that allegory as having been previously expounded by him, since he already had at hand certain threads and woof for weaving its Commentary.

Nor is it implausible that the words “Nineveh, which at the preaching of Jonah—that is, the dove—did penance, we have interpreted as the Church gathered from the Gentiles” were later added by the Saint himself when, after completing the entire work, he arranged the book and revised it in his customary final editing.

Choose whichever of the two alternatives you find more probable.

It is certain that Saint Jerome did not abandon what he had begun. During the period in which he said that he had explained the five Prophets named above in Commentaries, he was also pursuing many others in the same work, while laboring meanwhile to bring them to completion and polish them.

He himself testifies to this in the explicit words that he immediately adds and with which he concludes his list of books:

> “And many other things from the prophetic work, which I now have in hand and which have not yet been completed.”

We must carefully observe once more what we have proposed: namely, that he had previously drafted certain observations on all, or at least on most, of the twelve Prophets before undertaking to expound any one of them in full. He placed these in his notes so that they might provide a suitable connection between his interpretation and the whole prophetic work, and so that he himself could examine the arrangement should circumstances require it.

Indeed, he does not say that he then had one or two specific works—Obadiah or Jonah, for example—in hand, but “many other things, and from the prophetic work as a whole,” which, he says, “have not yet been completed.”

## V

With this the Catalogue of the works which Saint Jerome himself listed as having been composed up to the fourteenth year of the reign of the Emperor Theodosius—that is, up to A.D. 392—comes to an end.

Other editions of his Catalogue append the two books *Against Jovinian*, together with the *Apology* and *Epitaph* addressed to Pammachius. But these are not found in the older and better manuscripts; they reveal themselves as additions inserted by another hand, as we have shown in its proper place from the Preface to the Commentaries on Jonah.

They certainly had not yet been composed by Jerome when he wrote *On Illustrious Men*. This, therefore, is the last book in this sequence, which he published immediately after his interpretation of the five Prophets—or rather, the book with which he interrupted that prophetic work, as the Preface to Jonah testifies:

> “After I had interpreted five Prophets—Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, and Haggai—I was detained by another work and could not complete what I had begun. For I wrote the book *On Illustrious Men*,” and so forth.

To remove any doubt about the year, he mentions the fourteenth year of the Emperor Theodosius both at the beginning and near the end of the book. The emperor began that year on the Kalends of February, and we showed long ago that it corresponds to the Christian year 392.

The author and instigator of this work was Dexter, whom Baronius indeed considers to have been the son of Saint Pacianus of Barcelona. He was certainly a man of the highest rank and served as Prefect of the Praetorium, as Saint Jerome himself reveals in Book II against Rufinus; this is especially clear from the prosopography of the Theodosian Code.

Our author accepted this task—the *sparta* [σπάρτα], or assignment—all the more willingly because he perceived that it opened a clearer path for blunting the reproaches of the pagans against Christians, especially those of Celsus, Julian, and Porphyry, whom he calls rabid dogs against Christ. He could refute the insults and writings of their followers, who recklessly clamored that the Church had possessed no philosophers, eloquent men, or learned teachers.

How admirably he pursued his purpose, and how many volumes of writers—not only almost all who had preceded him but also some who were still living—he had either examined with his own eyes or at least knew sufficiently well to judge them, you will learn from that book of almost immeasurable learning. He completed it in 135 sections, or chapters, arranged under the individual names and writings of the authors.

His omission of certain figures, such as Athenagoras, Hermas, and perhaps another, seems to have arisen from his preference for remaining silent about those whom he did not know sufficiently well rather than pronouncing rashly upon them.

But lest we seem too long-winded in pursuing matters which we once discussed in detail in the notice prefixed to that book, receive what the holy Author himself teaches, in his reply to Augustine in Epistle CXII, about the title he had given the work and, so to speak, its character and nature:

> “You say that you received my book from a certain brother who did not have its title, in which I listed ecclesiastical writers, both Greek and Latin. When you asked him—for I use your own words—why the title had not been written on the title page, or by what name the work should be known, he replied that it was called an *Epitaph*. You argue that it would rightly be so called if you had read there only the lives or writings of those who were already dead; but since the little works of many who were alive both at the time it was written and still are today are mentioned, you wonder why I gave it this title.
>
> “I think that your prudence can understand the title from the work itself. For you have read both Greek and Latin authors who described the lives of illustrious living men; yet they never gave such a work the title *Epitaph*, but rather *On Illustrious Men*—for example, generals, philosophers, orators, historians, epic, tragic, and comic poets.
>
> “An *epitaph*, properly speaking, is written for the dead. I know that I once composed such a work on the death of Nepotianus, a presbyter of blessed memory. Therefore this book should be called either *On Illustrious Men* or, more properly, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, although most unskilled editors have entitled it *On Authors*.”

# CHAPTER XXIII

I. Saint Jerome attacks the heresy of Jovinian in two books.  
II. While extolling virginity, he seemed to disparage marriage.  
III. He therefore writes an *Apology* to Pammachius in defense of those books.  
IV. Likewise to Domnio on the same subject.  
V. He also replies to the letter of Desiderius and to the questions posed to him by Amando.

## I

Jerome had scarcely satisfied the calumnies of the pagans with that learned book *On Illustrious Men* when, in the same year 392—or at the beginning of the following year, as we infer from the frequently cited Preface to Jonah—he was compelled to undertake a far more difficult labor and to engage with a heretical opponent.

Jovinianus was a wealthy monk—enough said to make you understand what a wretched man he was—so devoted and abandoned to luxury that he deserved to be called the Epicurus of the Christians. Whether he introduced a heresy that appeared to excuse his manner of life, or revived one long since extinguished after Basilides, he strove to insinuate it into Roman ears by publishing Commentaries so that it might spread more widely. He was an entirely ordinary man, neither eloquent nor learned, but second to no one in wit and arrogance.

The main points of his wicked doctrine were these.

First, virgins, widows, and married women who had once been washed in Christ were, if they did not differ from others in their works, of equal merit.

Second, those who had been reborn in Baptism with complete faith could not be overthrown by the Devil.

Third, there was no difference between abstaining from food and receiving it with thanksgiving.

Finally, all those who had preserved their Baptism would receive one and the same reward in the kingdom of heaven.

Saint Augustine further attributes to him two blasphemies, almost more destructive than these: one, that all sins are equal; the other, that the Virgin who bore God, the mother of Christ, had not been violated in conception but had been violated in giving birth.

Some, however, think that these two charges were circulated against Jovinianus only by popular rumor, especially since Jerome does not refute them in a specific response. Nevertheless, the first appears to be a consequence of the equality of merits that the heretic asserted. The second is also established by a reply of Saint Ambrose, according to which Jovinianus and his followers impiously asserted: “The Virgin conceived, but the Virgin did not give birth.”

Such poisons this new teacher of the Churches was administering to the Romans. And, as commonly happens when the reins are loosened on vices, to use Augustine’s words, he gained such influence in the city of Rome that he was said to have brought some nuns into marriage, although no suspicion had previously touched their chastity; he even weakened the holy celibacy of holy men by invoking and comparing brothers (*Retractations*, Book II).

He also acquired a number of Roman followers, as is written in the Epistle of Siricius, as well as others whom Jerome mentions in the passage where he says:

> “Do not boast that you have many disciples,”

although, as Augustine testifies, he was never able to draw to himself any of the priests or any clergy of distinction.

## II

With Pammachius taking the leading role—“the noblest of Christians, and the most Christian of the nobles,” as Jerome calls him—and with other men, whom Siricius calls “most faithful Christian men, of excellent birth and distinguished in religion,” Jovinianus had been condemned by the judgment of the Roman Pontiff. His dreadful writing had been exposed by sacerdotal judgment as contrary to the divine law and erased by a spiritual sentence.

When he was expelled from Rome and withdrew with his followers to Milan, a synod gathered there and drove them out of Milan as fugitives, condemned by the execration of all.

Finally, it seems that imperial action was also taken against him in Law 53 of Title V of the Theodosian Code, *On Heretics*. We have discussed this matter more fully in the notice prefixed to Jerome’s books.

Nevertheless, since the provocations of his wickedness—by which I mean Jovinianus’s writings—were publicly available and perhaps read with even greater eagerness because they removed the restraints from vice, the holy brothers from Rome, and Pammachius above all, sent these little Commentaries of the heretic to Jerome. They asked him to answer their absurdities and crush the Epicurus of the Christians with evangelical and apostolic vigor (*Book I*).

He undertook this only a few days later. At the very beginning he declared that it was far more difficult for him to understand that writing, whose barbarism was so great and whose language was so foully confused by so many defects, than to defeat it.

He overcame it in two books. In the first he attacks Jovinianus’s first proposition; in the second, the three remaining ones. He overwhelms and routs the man with innumerable passages of divine Scripture, as well as with the testimony of histories and the judgments of philosophers, leaving him no avenue of escape.

This, however, was an exceedingly difficult work, as Augustine himself later observed: Jerome had to refute the claim that marriage was equal to virginity without seeming to condemn marriage, since he wished to award virginity its deserved crown (*Retractations*, Book II, chapter 22).

It was also commonly asserted at the time—for the slippery heretic had fascinated many minds with such seductive allurements—that Jerome could not answer him with praise but only with criticism of marriage. In addition, the Manichaeans condemned marriage, and there was great danger that, while Saint Jerome devoted himself entirely to praising virginity, he might arouse suspicion of favoring that sect.

## III

Accordingly, with sufficient skill and wisdom—more than on almost any other occasion—and in no few words at the very beginning of the first book, Jerome guarded himself against the suspicion that he condemned marriage. He openly professed that, with the Apostle, he knew marriage to be honorable and the marriage bed undefiled.

Nevertheless, when the books reached Rome, because he had argued at greater length in favor of virginity, he easily appeared too harsh toward marriage. He was attacked not only by laymen and the unlearned but also by clergy, monks, and educated men, and was everywhere branded with this accusation.

Among the others was some rumor-mongering monk who, in the circles of the ignorant and at the *symposia* [συμπόσια] of little women, preached against him and gnawed, tore apart, and mangled his books with a dog’s tooth.

Pammachius opposed these attacks as far as he could and endured the insults with which the men of the opposing party loaded his friend. At last, when he saw that these measures were achieving little even for himself, he carefully withdrew as many copies of Jerome’s work as he could find, wherever he found them, and sent a letter to Jerome himself—either asking him to explain more clearly what seemed obscure, as may be gathered from Epistle XLVIII, or, as appears from the following Epistle, reproaching him for what he found less satisfactory. For he indicates in one place that he himself had also been somewhat offended.

He also sent back the withdrawn little books so that the marked passages might be corrected. Domnio did nearly the same somewhat later; he added the criticisms of the abusive monk mentioned above and extracted and arranged in order from the volume those passages which seemed to cause scandal to some people, asking Jerome either to correct or to explain them.

## IV

It seems that Saint Jerome himself would also have preferred to accommodate his friends and alter the passages that troubled them according to their understanding. But this was no longer possible, because copies of the work had already spread far and wide among friends and enemies alike.

Therefore, writing back to Pammachius, he says:

> “I know very well what you have done, both wisely and affectionately, in withdrawing copies of my little books against Jovinianus. But this diligence achieved nothing, since some who came from the City read me the very passages which they said they had received at Rome. In this province too the books had already been circulated, and, as you yourself have read, ‘The word once sent out does not know how to return.’ I do not possess the good fortune enjoyed by most writers of our time, that I can correct my trifles whenever I wish. As soon as I have written something, either my admirers or my envious opponents—though with different motives, they compete with equal zeal—scatter our writings among the public. They are excessive both in praise and in blame, following not the merit of the style but their own irritation.
>
> “Therefore the only thing I could do was to dedicate to you an *Apology* for the work itself [προσεφώνησα]. When you have read it, you yourself will satisfy people on our behalf. Or, if you too wrinkle your nose, you will be compelled to discuss differently that apostolic *pericope* [περικοπή] in which he treats of virginity and marriage.”

Speaking also to Domnio about that slanderous monk, he says:

> “Certainly, if he thought that I was in error . . . he ought either to have reproved me or to have questioned me by letter, as the learned and noble Pammachius did. To him I made my defense [ἀπελογισάμην], as best I could, and discussed the matter in a longer Epistle, explaining what I had meant in each passage.”

The immediately preceding Epistle, numbered XLVIII in our recension and addressed to Pammachius, is where he made his defense [ἀπελογίσατο], that is, defended his books against Jovinianus. His rivals had maliciously accused him of being excessive in praising virginity and unjust toward marriage. For that reason the book is also entitled *Apology*.

Some wish to count Pelagius among those who attacked him and against whom Jerome principally directed his mind and intention in writing this *Apology*. Jerome certainly calls him a disciple of Jovinianus in explicit terms in the Preface to the First Commentary on Jeremiah:

> “I pass over the volumes against Jovinianus, in which he grieves”—Pelagius, clearly, as is evident from what precedes—“that virginity has been preferred to marriage, marriage to digamy, and digamy to polygamy. Nor does the most foolish man, weighed down by Scottish porridge, remember that we said in that very work: ‘I do not condemn those married twice, nor even those married three times; if possible, I would admit those married eight times. I shall go further: I also receive the fornicator who repents. Whatever is equally permitted must be weighed in an equal balance.’
>
> “Let him read the *Apology* of that same work, which rejoicing Rome once received many years ago against his master. Then he will perceive that he blasphemes with another’s voice,” and so forth.

Jerome also counts Jovinianus among the forerunners of the Pelagian heresy in the Prologue to the *Dialogue against the Pelagians*, and near the beginning of Book III he says:

> “Are you not ashamed to follow the opinion of Jovinianus, which was rejected and condemned? For he too relies upon these testimonies and upon your arguments; indeed, you follow his inventions.”

From this, however, one must not conclude that Pelagius belonged to the school of Jovinianus, or that Jerome wrote this *Apology* chiefly against him. If the person who embraces another’s opinion in some particular and to some extent is to be called his disciple, then all of us who devote ourselves to literature are mutually one another’s disciples.

It is nevertheless a useful fact that from the passage cited we learn that Saint Jerome enjoyed much better fortune in composing this book, which rejoicing Rome received, and by which he removed all the blemishes with which his books against Jovinianus had been sprinkled, together with all the calumnies of his opponents.

Indeed, Rufinus extracted nothing from those books that he could use as an accusation, although he eagerly seized every possible opportunity to disparage Jerome from almost all his other writings.

The second point which we should infer from Jerome’s testimony is the date, considered together with the history of the events we have described. There is no doubt that the books against Jovinianus were composed in the year 393, or toward the end of the preceding year. We established this long ago from the fact that Jerome does not list them in the Catalogue of his works, which he extended to the fourteenth year of the reign of Theodosius, A.D. 392, but mentions them in other books as works composed immediately afterward.

In the Preface to the Commentaries on Jonah he says:

> “I wrote the book *On Illustrious Men*, two volumes against Jovinianus, also an *Apology*, and *On the Best Kind of Translation* to Pammachius.”

One should not suppose, however, that the *Apology* was written immediately after the books against Jovinianus. The Epistle joined to it, XLIX to Pammachius, indicates how much time intervened. Jerome says that he had long concealed the complaints of his rivals and that his books had spread so widely that some people coming from the City read to him the passages they claimed to have received at Rome.

This appears to us to indicate an interval of approximately one year. We therefore assigned the *Apology* either to the end of the year 393 itself or to the beginning of the following year. [Col. 0091]

The Epistle to Domnio followed shortly afterward.

### V.

But during the same period he also sent other letters to various persons. One of these is Letter XLVII, to Desiderius, which we believe was written somewhat earlier, before he sharpened his style against Jovinian. This appears to have been the same presbyter whom we mentioned long ago as having asked Jerome to translate the Pentateuch from the Hebrew language into Latin, and to whom the Preface to Genesis is in fact addressed. When he happened to be staying in Rome for some reason, he again asked the holy Doctor to send him some copy of his works. Our author replied that, since nearly everything had already been published, he did not know what he could send, lest he perhaps send the same works that Desiderius already possessed. Concerning the book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, however, he advised him to read it at Marcella’s or Domnion’s house:

> At the end of this volume I have placed myself, as it were, an aborted and least of all Christians, where it was necessary for me briefly to record what I had written up to the fourteenth year of the Emperor Theodosius. When you have obtained the book from the persons mentioned above, whatever you find lacking in the catalogue, I shall gradually have written out, if you wish.

He added nothing further about the books against Jovinian or about the *Apology* on their behalf. From this it may reasonably be inferred that these little works had not yet been completed. Nevertheless, we do not deny that Desiderius may have indicated in his own letter that he already had these works with him—as recently written works, and ones especially on everyone’s lips at Rome—and that on this account he requested other writings from Jerome. However the matter may stand, both the argument itself and the entire sequence of events persuade us that this Letter was written neither before the year 393 nor after the following year.

### VI.

It is nevertheless reasonable to believe that Jerome wrote six other letters in the following year, that is, in 394. Among these Letter LV, to Amandus, a presbyter of Bordeaux and later a bishop, seems to claim some sort of precedence of age—though I do not know precisely what kind. In it Jerome answers three questions proposed by Amandus from the New Testament, and also answers the question which Amandus had enclosed on a short sheet of paper:

> Whether a woman who has left an adulterous and sodomitical husband, and has taken another by force, may, without penance, communicate with the Church while the man whom she previously left is still alive.

Since Jerome makes no mention of this letter in his *Catalogue*, it is clear that it was written after the year 392, when that book was published. For he would not have omitted to count among the others a letter of such importance, and especially one so exegetical in its treatment of Sacred Scripture. On the other hand, in the third question—which some codices title “the second Letter to Amandus”—he discusses the resurrection of bodies and the meaning in which Christ is said to subject all things, and finally himself, to God the Father. He explains his view in such a way that he appears to approach Origen’s dangerous interpretation. It is therefore sufficiently evident that he dictated this letter before he set himself against Origen, namely after Epiphanius’s arrival, of which there will soon be occasion to speak, and thus around the middle of the year 394.

We have said that the remaining letters were written during this same period. I mean the learned—good God, how learned and laborious—Letter to Nepotian on the life of the clergy, the year of which Jerome himself indicates, as though with a finger, near the end, when he says:

> You compelled me, now that the little book on virginity which I had written at Rome for Saint Eustochium had been stoned, after ten years once again to open my mouth at Bethlehem.

Then there are the two following letters, numbered LIII and LIV. One, addressed to Paulinus, praises the beginnings of his conversion, or of the more perfect life which he had undertaken—an event assigned to this year, 394. The other, addressed to Furia, records that Jerome had published his books against Jovinian nearly two years earlier. This is a sign that the same year was already drawing toward its end.

## CHAPTER XXIV

I. He temporarily withdraws from Rufinus’s friendship by a certain declaration concerning Origen.  
II. This develops into open hostility on the occasion of Saint Epiphanius’s arrival at Jerusalem.  
III. Hence the beginnings of the Jerusalem schism, whose history is briefly outlined.  
IV. Our author takes the side of Epiphanius against the Origenists, while Rufinus adheres to John of Jerusalem.  
V. The occasion of the disagreement is increased by Epiphanius’s ordination of Paulinian, Jerome’s brother.  
VI. The conflict becomes sharper because of the same Epiphanius’s letter to John, written in Greek, which Jerome translated into Latin and defended in another letter to Pammachius.

### I.

Up to this time, or at least until shortly before it, the relationship between Jerome and Rufinus had been such as to serve as an example to all Christians. Everyone admired those most intimate friends—“dear and familiar persons,” as Augustine calls them—united by the bond of friendship and known to nearly all the Churches (*Letter* CX). In addition to the other circumstances that bind a friendship together—especially the fact that their association had begun in early youth and had been nourished by great virtues on both sides—there was the closeness of their residence. Rufinus had long been living at Jerusalem, where he had also received the presbyterate, so that they could meet frequently and enjoy nearly the same way of life and course of study.

What is more, both men took great delight in Origen’s genius, although, as we shall soon explain, their understanding and attitude toward him were different. It happened, however, in the year 393, that a certain Aterbius, arriving at Jerusalem with others, said—I shall state the matter as it was—that Rufinus was gravely suspect because he followed Origen. By this accusation he also implicated Jerome, since Jerome was Rufinus’s intimate friend and had once been a herald of the Adamantine.

Here was the first stain of the evil and the beginning of the storm of discord. Jerome had not been so captivated by admiration for Origen’s teaching that he did not occasionally perceive that he had reason to fear Origen’s errors. He therefore did not hesitate publicly to repudiate Origen’s authority and to dismiss him in his error. Rufinus, by contrast, not knowing how sufficiently to restrain his zeal, shut himself up at home and did not even dare to see Aterbius. He took it very badly that his friend had condemned Adamantius.

The holy Father himself recounts the matter in very clear words in Book III of his *Apology*:

> Who stirred up against you the fury of Aterbius and the others? Was it not the man who also judged me a heretic on the basis of your friendships, although I had satisfied him by condemning Origen’s doctrines? You, shut up at home, never dared to see him, lest you either condemn what you did not wish to condemn or, by openly resisting, incur the odium of heresy. Can he therefore be a witness against you because he is your accuser?

A little later he adds:

> He barked against you more fiercely at Jerusalem; and if he had not quickly departed, he would have felt the staff—not of literature, but of your right hand—with which you are accustomed to drive away dogs.

### II.

This first declaration by Jerome against Origen consequently turned Rufinus’s mind away from him to no small degree. Rufinus thought that Jerome had thereby especially injured their mutual friendship, because, in order not to incur the charge of heresy through his friendship with Rufinus, Jerome had professed to avoid it by condemning Origen’s doctrines.

The trouble did not long remain at this stage. In the following year, 394—the year to which the course of Jerome’s life has now brought us—it developed into open hostility, and both sides were inflamed with quarrels and the most serious hatred.

The occasion and history of the event are as follows. Saint Epiphanius, bishop of Salamis in Cyprus, was extremely distressed that Origen’s partisans were spreading more widely. He already knew that John, the bishop of the Jerusalem Church, had been drawn over to their side. In order to confront the growing evil before it became more serious, Epiphanius came to Jerusalem around Easter of that year.

John received him as a guest at his table and in his house. Epiphanius gently reminded him, as he ought, of his error. John, however, seems to have paid so little attention to this that he did not even notice it (*from Letter* LXXXII and the book *Against John*). In this way, I believe, the following statements can be reconciled. Later, when John was publicly corrected in the Church, he grieved deeply and affirmed under oath that Epiphanius had said nothing to him about the matter at their first meeting. Jerome proves that this was false, asserting that he could establish the contrary by witnesses, unless he thought it wrong to charge a bishop with perjury.

Epiphanius next visited our Jerome, with whom he also stayed, as we shall say later. He then visited Rufinus with considerable care. Epiphanius knew that Rufinus was deeply entangled in Origen’s errors, and, in order more easily to disabuse him and draw him back to a sounder mind, he received him with the kiss of peace and with prayers.

But either he achieved nothing, or at least very little, through such private exhortations. At last, publicly and before a large crowd, in the Anastasis, or Church of the Resurrection, he inveighed against Origen with great force of spirit. He also obliquely reproached John, who was present as a disciple of the same teaching, warning him not to praise Arius’s father—namely Origen, the root and parent of other heresies.

John became so enraged that he immediately sent the archdeacon to silence Epiphanius and ordered him to desist from the public sermon he had begun. Not long afterward, on another occasion in the Church of the Holy Cross, John gathered into a single address all the sermons he had delivered during Lent—at its end, or at least not long after Easter. For this reason we assign Epiphanius’s arrival at Jerusalem to that period. In this address John argued at length not only in defense of Origen, and therefore also of himself, but dared publicly to accuse Epiphanius of the heresy of the Anthropomorphites, who attribute human form to God and who are diametrically opposed to Origen’s teaching.

Epiphanius immediately rejected the charge of heresy. He openly declared that he approved John’s sermon and wished the heresy condemned by John to be condemned, but that, in turn, John ought to reject Origen’s doctrines. John, however, eager for quarrels, looked for nothing but grounds for revenge. He harassed the holy bishop so severely that Epiphanius was forced to withdraw from there to his monastery at Bethlehem.

He did return to Jerusalem at the urging and entreaties of the monks, so that he might once again confer with John about the faith. But scarcely had he reached John in the evening when he was forced to flee in the middle of the night. He again took refuge with Jerome and the other solitaries. At that time he also declared that he greatly regretted the communion he had maintained with John and his other partisans.

### III.

Through this storm of discord the way was being prepared for the Jerusalem schism. Jerome stood on Epiphanius’s side—that is, on the Catholic side—together with the numerous monks who lived with him at Bethlehem. Rufinus eagerly seized this opportunity to attack Jerome, since he was permitted to defend himself and his preconceived opinion concerning Origen by the judgment of the Church to whose clergy he belonged.

He therefore immediately adhered to John. He also seems to have supplied John with Origenist doctrines and to have entrusted to him the advancement of the cause with all the dignity and authority of the see that John occupied. Epiphanius certainly knew this. As we have said, he had met Rufinus in particular and thought that he would have achieved everything if he had deterred Rufinus from his rash sponsorship of Origen.

This was also repeatedly pointed out to Jerome, especially in his book against John. Jerome reproaches John for complaining that Epiphanius had not privately accused him, before the public sermon, of supporting Adamantius, although Epiphanius later accused him openly:

> He says that he accused you; you deny it. He produces witnesses; you refuse to hear those who have been produced. He also states that another person was present at the meeting; you conceal the matter for both reasons.

Jerome explains that this “other person” was none other than Rufinus in Book III of his *Apology*:

> So Epiphanius will be polluted, the man who offered you peace while keeping deceit in his heart. Why should it not be truer that he warned you first?

Rufinus was also among those who mocked Epiphanius during that public sermon. The holy Father reproaches him for this in the book against John mentioned above:

> When Pope Epiphanius was speaking against Origen in your Church; when, under his name, javelins were being hurled against you; you and your chorus, with doglike grimaces and contracted nostrils, scratching your heads, spoke to one another by gestures about the old man’s madness, and so forth.

Jerome again reproaches Rufinus for the same conduct in Book III of his *Apology*:

> I cannot restrain my laughter when, after someone had prudently admonished him, he turned to praise Epiphanius. “This is the mad old man; this is the Anthropomorphite,” and so forth.

Finally, to pass over many other matters of the same kind, Rufinus himself, near the end of the *Prologue to the Apology of Pamphilus*, claims not only to follow John’s party but also to hold no other faith than that which John proclaimed to the Jerusalem Church:

> These things are proclaimed at Jerusalem in the Church of God by its holy priest, John. These things we both say and hold together with him.

### IV.

It is difficult to say how much distress this close alliance of Jerome’s enemies caused the holy Doctor. One was driven on by an authority that inflamed him beyond the control of anger; the other was embittered by suspicion of a recently injured friendship and by the opportunity he had sought for revenge.

There was, however, another circumstance that seemed to give them a legitimate reason to attack Epiphanius and Jerome, or at least a means of evading their demands concerning the true faith and of shifting the whole cause and blame of the quarrels onto them. I mean the ordination of Paulinian, Jerome’s brother, by Epiphanius, without consulting John, to whose parish Paulinian had until then belonged.

The matter took place as follows. After leaving Jerusalem—or rather, fleeing from it by night—for the reasons we have described, Epiphanius withdrew to his monastery at Bethlehem. There he complained at length about the disturbances caused by John and about John’s suspect communion. In turn, he heard many of the monks complaining that they had no presbyter to perform the sacred rites. If circumstances required them to separate themselves from communion with the bishop of Jerusalem, there was no one among them who could celebrate the Sacraments.

As has been noted elsewhere, Jerome and Vincent, although the former had been ordained a presbyter at Antioch and the latter at Constantinople, could never be persuaded, out of reverence and humility, to perform that office. This was especially true of our author, who had accepted ordination on that condition. All the monks, however, spoke with one voice in favor of Paulinian. They declared that, if he would ever allow himself to be ordained a presbyter, he would bring the greatest benefit to the whole monastery.

He had often been urged in vain on other occasions, as he had been then—for at one point he even escaped such an ordination by fleeing—or perhaps Epiphanius had been waiting for a more suitable opportunity. In the following year, therefore, when some men from the same monastery had been sent as envoys to him while he was then, apparently, acting as bishop at Eleutheropolis, to satisfy him concerning certain matters, Paulinian was among them.

Epiphanius considered both Paulinian’s merit, which had long been attested to him by the testimony of all the monks, and the monastery’s need. By exhortations and commands alike he overcame the holy young man’s resolve, and, although Paulinian was almost unwilling and reluctant, he first ordained him a deacon and, after he had served, ordained him a presbyter.

He did not dare perform this act within the boundaries of the Jerusalem jurisdiction. Instead, he did it in the monastery of the brothers—of the foreign brothers, who owed nothing to John’s province. I mean the monastery called Vetus, situated between Jerusalem and nearby Eleutheropolis and originally built by Epiphanius himself.

Nevertheless, John considered himself gravely offended and believed that the rights of his parish had been violated. He erupted in anger and complained repeatedly, both privately and publicly, threatening to publish the matter to everyone, especially to the Westerners, by letter. He used this as a pretext for his disagreement with Epiphanius and Jerome, and transferred the odium of all the complaints onto them.

He even wrote to Theophilus of Alexandria that, before Paulinian had become a presbyter, Pope Epiphanius had never conferred with him concerning Origen’s error. Jerome reports this again, not without irritation, in Letter LXXXII to the same Theophilus:

> Before my brother Paulinian was ordained, John said that there had never been any discussion between himself and the holy Pope Epiphanius about doctrines. What reason compelled him, as he finally writes, to dispute among the people about a matter which no one was asking about?

John complained not only—however rashly and falsely—of the violation of his parish rights, but also that Paulinian was not yet of an age suitable for the priesthood. The holy Father dismisses these two charges as follows:

> He says that my brother is the cause of the discord—a man who rests in the cell of a monastery and interprets the clerical state not as an honor but as a burden. Although he has deceived us up to the present day by a pretended display of peace, he has stirred up the ears of the Westerners, saying that a young man, almost a boy, had been made presbyter in his parish at Bethlehem. If this is true, all the bishops of Palestine know it. The monastery of the holy Father Epiphanius, called Vetus, in which my brother was ordained presbyter, is situated in the territory of Eleutheropolis, not in the territory of Aelia. Moreover, his age is known to Your Beatitude; and since he has already reached nearly thirty years, I think it ought not to be criticized in this matter, for it is perfected according to the mystery of the humanity assumed in Christ, and so forth.

Finally, to make these objections seem defensible, John especially charged Epiphanius with having failed to keep his promise. He claimed that he had sent word through the holy presbyter and abbot of the monks, Gregory, that Epiphanius should ordain no one, and that Epiphanius had promised this, saying:

> “Am I perhaps a young man, or do I not know the canons?”

### V.

These were the crimes John laid against Epiphanius. Epiphanius immediately endeavored to refute them in the mild letter now numbered LI among Jerome’s letters.

First, concerning the alleged violation of the rights of the Jerusalem parish, Epiphanius refutes the charge in almost the same words that we have just taken from Jerome—for that is the only truly valid answer. The second charge, that Paulinian was not yet of suitable age for the presbyterate, he entirely disregards, since it was plainly false and already appeared to have been rejected.

The third charge was more serious: Epiphanius was said not to have kept an agreement. He removes this accusation from himself under the solemnity of an oath:

> Hear the truth in the word of God: I neither heard nor knew this, nor do I remember this statement at all.

He then suspected that he might perhaps have forgotten it amid many other matters, since he was human. For this reason he summoned the holy Gregory and the presbyter Zeno, who was with him. Abbot Gregory replied that he knew nothing whatever about it. Zeno, however, said that when the presbyter Rufinus was speaking with them briefly about something else, he had also said:

> “Do you suppose that the holy bishop is going to ordain anyone?”

And that the conversation had ended there. Epiphanius added:

> I neither heard anything nor gave any answer.

Finally, in milder words, he calms the man eager for quarrels and shows that John had attacked him not because Paulinian had received the character of the presbyterate, but because John had been reproved for his devotion to Origen’s doctrines. Epiphanius earnestly urges John once again to beware of those doctrines:

> May God deliver you, brother, and the holy people of Christ entrusted to you, and all the brothers who are with you, and especially the presbyter Rufinus, from the heresy of Origen, from other heresies, and from their destruction.

The letter was sent by a member of the clergy, or a reader. In Book III against Rufinus, the holy Doctor proved that the original letter had come into Rufinus’s hands, although Rufinus at one point pretended that he knew nothing of it.

Such an act by the bishop of Jerusalem ought certainly to have recalled John to a better frame of mind and restored peace and concord between him and Epiphanius, as well as with Jerome, who stood on Epiphanius’s side. The opposite, however, occurred.

The letter was received with the greatest applause by everyone except John and his partisans. Copies of it were eagerly carried throughout Palestine, whether because of the author’s reputation or because of the elegance of its language. This only further inflamed John’s feelings. He turned those praises, and the favor shown to Epiphanius, into an insult against himself.

The letter was passed from mouth to mouth, and learned and unlearned alike admired it. John, meanwhile, searched for a knot in a reed, seized on rumors, and stirred up sadness and quarrels among the brothers. He complained, with the utmost injustice, that his doctrine and faith were being branded with heresy, even though they were so far from departing from Orthodox truth that, as he claimed, they rather asserted and defended it against the rusticity of its adversaries.

The situation was worse because he had persons readily available from whom he could demand satisfaction and against whom he could vent and discharge his anger: Jerome, especially, since he wished to make him the principal cause of the disturbances, and the brothers under Jerome’s authority, as men formed by the same doctrines and studies.

### VI.

The bond of communion between the two sides had not yet, however, been broken. The whole of Epiphanius’s letter shows that he had preserved it up to that time. He declares that he had retained affection for John, although John was deliberately trying to tear it apart, and that he had been accustomed to pray publicly for him.

This is shown even more clearly by the passages in which Epiphanius warns John to withdraw from Origen. If John would not obey him, Epiphanius threatens to cut off from himself, according to the command of the Gospel, whatever was a stumbling block—foot, eye, or hand:

> And you, whether you are eyes or feet, will suffer the same things.

Epiphanius does not say, “You have suffered” or “You are suffering,” but “You will suffer.” He therefore indicates that, when he wrote this, he had not yet separated himself from John’s communion. If Epiphanius himself had not yet separated from John, it is even less likely that he then wished the monks of Bethlehem to separate themselves from the affection of their bishop.

Indeed, Jerome’s book against John indicates that Epiphanius had written to the monks, advising them to remain, as far as possible, in communion with John. Somewhat later, however, when John gave no answer to Epiphanius’s letter, did not appear capable of being recalled to a better way of life, and instead stirred up greater disturbances day by day and hardened himself in his defense of Origen, Epiphanius advised them not to communicate rashly with John thereafter. Unless John first gave satisfaction concerning the faith, they were to abstain entirely from his communion.

Since John refused to give satisfaction concerning the faith, they separated from him at Epiphanius’s direction and, to conceal nothing, under Jerome’s leadership. When the faith was at issue, Jerome allowed no place for dissimulation. He could not persuade himself to maintain sincere peace and concord in Christ with a heretic, or with anyone burdened by suspicion of such a stain.

### VII.

It is impossible to say how much odium John then created for Jerome among everyone through his venomous slanders, or how much distress he caused Jerome’s followers. John continually accused them of dividing the Church of God and of making a principality for themselves. He treated them so harshly that he even denounced them as sacrilegious and prohibited them from every sacred activity and from entering the Bethlehem church itself.

The holy Father briefly recounts some of the evils John plotted against them or actually inflicted upon them near the end of the book he wrote against John to Pammachius. It is best to hear the matter from Jerome himself:

> Are you not rather the one who divides the Church, since you ordered your presbyters at Bethlehem not to give Baptism at Easter to our catechumens, whom we had sent to Diospolis to be baptized by the confessor and bishop Dionysius? We are said to divide the Church, although outside our cells we have no place in the Church? Are you not the one who divides the Church, since you ordered your clergy that, if anyone called Paulinian a presbyter consecrated by Bishop Epiphanius, he should be forbidden to enter the Church? From that time until the present day, we have seen only the Lord’s cave, and, standing at a distance, we sigh while heretics enter. Are we the ones dividing the Church, or is it the man who denies the living a dwelling place and the dead a tomb? Who stirred that most powerful beast, hanging over the necks of the whole world, especially against our necks? Who allows the bones of the saints and their innocent ashes to be beaten by the rains even now?

Concerning the exile which John had worked to procure for Jerome and the brothers, Letter LXXXII speaks again to the same Theophilus:

> Recently he requested and obtained exile for us. Would that he had been able to carry it out, so that just as his intention is counted as the deed, we too might have been crowned with the crown of exile not only in intention but also in effect.

We have said that the “most powerful beast” mentioned here appears to be Rufinus, the guardian of Arcadius, that traitor who summoned Alaric, leader of the Goths, against Arcadius in order to seize the imperial power for himself. This becomes still more probable from Jerome’s addition that John was unable to accomplish what he wished. For after Alaric was repelled, Rufinus was murdered toward the end of the year 395, and his rescript ordering Jerome to be carried into exile consequently came to nothing.

### VII.

These examples of savagery and harshness in John’s ferocious spirit, deeply infected with the disease of Origenism, were provoked by Epiphanius’s letter, which was suited to draw him away from error and restore him to favor. On Jerome’s side, however, an event occurred shortly afterward, once the letter had reached the hands of the common people, that sowed the seeds of still more serious quarrels. These quarrels broke out about a year and six months later, as we shall explain in their proper place.

It is appropriate, as we customarily do, to let the holy Father himself tell this matter in his own words:

> There was in our monastery a man of no little standing among his own people, Eusebius of Cremona. When this letter of Epiphanius was circulating through many mouths, and learned and unlearned alike admired it for its teaching and purity of expression, Eusebius began earnestly to ask me to translate it for him into Latin and to explain it more openly for ease of understanding. For he was entirely ignorant of the Greek language. I did what he wished. Calling in a secretary, I dictated it rapidly and quickly, briefly noting in the margin of the page what inner meaning each chapter contained. He had especially insisted that I do this for him alone. I also asked him in return to keep the copy at home and not readily to publish it to the people. The matter remained thus for a year and six months, until the aforementioned translation migrated from his chests to Jerusalem by a new trick. For, as can be clearly understood, whether through money or through gratuitous malice—as the corruptor vainly tries to persuade us—after Eusebius’s papers and expenses had been gathered together, Judas became a traitor and gave my adversaries an opportunity to bark against me. They proclaimed among the ignorant that I was a falsifier; that I had not rendered word for word; that I had translated *carissimum* as “dearest” instead of “most honorable”; and, by a malicious translation, that I had refused to render—an unspeakable charge—the words **αἰδεσιμώτατον πάππαν**, “the most reverend pope.”

All these disturbances had been stirred up by Rufinus. His anger and hostility were all the greater because he did not dare come forward openly but struck secretly, like a scorpion—as Jerome calls him—and supplied others with occasions and weapons for quarrelling.

The holy Father attributes to Rufinus’s “new trick” the fact that this letter traveled from Eusebius’s chests to Jerusalem and came into the hands of Rufinus and his other enemies. He openly lays the guilt for the theft upon the monk who had been induced to commit it:

> This is the letter which you brought out of our brother Eusebius’s room for gold coins.

Some, however, consider it more plausible that the theft was committed through gratuitous malice, since the pseudo-monk is said to have laid his criminal hands not only on the papers but also on the “expenses.” It would not be reasonable to believe that he had been hired for money to take anything other than the papers from Eusebius’s chests.

Nevertheless, since it is not sufficiently clear what the word *expenses* means in this passage, and since it may refer to other papers or objects on which Eusebius had spent money, that explanation seems a rather weak defense—one scarcely capable of clearing Rufinus, a cunning and formidable adversary.

Indeed, elsewhere Rufinus seems almost to admit to Jerome that he was the monk’s corruptor:

> And one of them—for clearly Rufinus is meant—dares, with raised eyebrows and snapping fingers, to belch out and say: “What if he bought him? What if he solicited him? He did what benefited him.”

Jerome continues his attack:

> A remarkable defense of crime—as though robbers, thieves, and pirates did not do what benefits them. Certainly Annas and Caiaphas, when they led the wretched Judas astray, did what they thought useful to themselves.

Jerome presses the same point in Book III of his *Apology*. He attributes to Rufinus’s devices and deceptions the secret placement of a certain codex from Bethlehem in the rooms of the elder Saint Fabiola and of Oceanus, without either of them knowing it:

> Who stole from Bethlehem, from our brother Eusebius’s room, the letter praising you? Through whose contrivance, and by whose agents, was the codex found in the house of Saint Fabiola and of the Christian and prudent man Oceanus, although they had never seen it? Do you therefore think yourself innocent if you transfer whatever belongs to you onto others?

I believe that Rufinus had long suspected certain features of that letter which could easily be twisted into a charge. This may have been why he prompted the wicked monk to rifle Eusebius’s chests. In fact, once the letter finally came into his hands, Rufinus celebrated so many triumphs and raised such clamors as though he had at last obtained something long and eagerly desired.

There was then no end to his more freely insulting Jerome and raging against him, attacking not so much Jerome’s lack of skill as his fidelity, since Jerome had translated the letter into Latin with sentences and words different from those in the Greek.

Nor is it our task here to judge that translation or defend the holy Doctor’s cause against the attacks of his rivals. Rather, we should admit that, if Epiphanius addressed John with the honorific **αἰδεσιμώτατον πάππαν**—“the most reverend pope”—Jerome did badly in either completely omitting this expression of respect or weakening it by substituting some less forceful formula.

This was especially serious given the circumstances and the time. Since feelings and hatred were growing on both sides, what Jerome had done accidentally and while occupied with something else in John’s honor could scarcely, or perhaps not at all, be attributed to carelessness.

I would also readily grant that the translation suffers from defects neither trivial nor few, if the surviving Greek words are to be weighed—the words from which Epiphanius’s letter began:

> **Ἔδει γὰρ ἡμᾶς, ἀγαπητέ, μὴ τῇ οἵήσει τῶν κλήρων φέρεσθαι γὰρ**  
> “For it was necessary for us, beloved, not to be borne along by the conceit of clerical offices, for …”

Jerome rendered it:

> *Oportebat nos, dilectissime, Clericatus honore non abuti in superbiam*  
> “It was necessary for us, most beloved, not to abuse the honor of the clergy into pride.”

The initial **γάρ** (“for”) was not justifiably omitted; nor was **ἀγαπητέ** correctly rendered as *dilectissime* (“most beloved”) instead of *dilecte* (“beloved”). Jerome also added *honore* (“honor”), which is not present in the Greek. Finally, *abuti in superbiam* (“to abuse into pride”) seems even more remote from **οἵήσει φέρεσθαι** (“to be carried away by conceit/pride”).

I could easily cite other defects of this sort in the remaining context and believe that they occurred in a translation dictated in haste. Yet far be it from me to think that the holy translator deserved the punishments Rufinus inflicted upon him for this reason. I omit the fact that there is no loss of meaning in these matters, even though the phrases and words sometimes diverge considerably.

One consideration excuses Jerome and strongly safeguards his entire case: he prepared the translation for the private use of a friend and intended it to remain permanently within the household walls. His only concern was that a student ignorant of Greek might understand the author’s mind and meaning more clearly.

Jerome himself sufficiently defends this purpose in Letter LVII:

> I wish to write any nonsense I please on my little sheets of paper, to comment on the Scriptures, to bite back at those who injure me, to digest my anger, to exercise myself in commonplaces, and, as it were, to store up polished arrows for battle. As long as I do not publish my thoughts, they are curses, not crimes; indeed, they are not even curses if the public ears do not hear them. You corrupt little slaves, solicit clients, and, as we read in the stories, penetrate with gold to Danaë; then, concealing what you have done, you call me a falsifier, although by accusing me you confess against yourself a much worse crime than the one you charge against me.

Moreover, that translation was not regarded as worthless, nor did it lack the praise of good interpretation in many other places. We also know that it was praised by Álvaro, a not inconsiderable writer of the ninth century, in the *Life of Saint Eulogius*, to pass over the many others who followed him in later times.

### VII.

The literary outcome was also advantageous to us.
