Provoked by that controversy to repel the calumnies of his adversaries and to establish his method of explaining Greek writers, especially, in Latin, the holy Father composed a new letter to Pammachius, *On the Best Method of Translation*. In it, by the testimonies and examples both of all the ancient learned writers and of the interpreters of Sacred Scripture, he teaches what constitutes the best method of that art. He shows that it is the method by which meaning is translated from meaning, not word from word:

> Let others hunt for syllables and letters; seek out the sense.

In our recension this letter is numbered LVII. The chronological notes attached to it have demonstrated sufficiently and at length that it properly belongs to the year whose history we are examining—395. Let us pursue the remaining matters that concern the life of the holy Doctor.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

I. Count Archelaus unsuccessfully strives to reconcile the dissenting parties.  
II. The same thing is unsuccessfully attempted by Theophilus, Bishop of Alexandria.  
III. The chief fault lies with the Origenist priest Isidore, whom he had sent as envoy for this purpose.  
IV. Hence Theophilus’s benevolence toward Jerome grows cold.  
V. Nevertheless, the holy Father writes to him repeatedly.  
VI. He also writes to Marcella and composes Nepotian’s Epitaph.  
VII. He also writes commentaries on Jonah.  
VIII, IX, X. Then other letters to other persons, containing various matters concerning the Origenist controversy.

### I

Count Archelaus endeavored to restrain the movements of hostility, which grew more intense day by day between John and Epiphanius, or between those who supported either side. Jerome adorns him with the praises of a most eloquent and Christian man (*Against John*, Book I). Through his intervention as a mediator of peace, since suspicion of violated faith had given rise to the quarrels, it was determined that a way toward concord should be secured by first establishing a confession of faith.

“The foundation of future concord was requested,” says the holy Father. At an agreed place where both parties were to meet, John himself also promised that he would come. The days of Easter were approaching; a large crowd of monks had assembled; only he was awaited at the appointed place, and no one knew what he would do. These are Jerome’s words [Col. 0102], whose footsteps we are carefully following.

Suddenly he sent word that some woman or other was ill and that he could not come that day. “Is it as a jester or as a bishop,” Jerome adds, “that you speak thus? Suppose that what you say is true: on account of the comforts of a single little woman, lest in your absence she should suffer a headache, experience nausea, or become chilled in the stomach, do you neglect the cause of the Church? Do you disdain the dignity of so many men, Christians, and monks? We did not wish to provide an occasion [for conflict], for we saw through the trick of your delay; we overcame the insult by patience.”

Archelaus writes back, advising him to remain for a second and third day, if he wished to come. But John, occupied—for the little woman did not cease vomiting—once he had escaped the nausea, completely forgot us. Although Archelaus repeatedly admonished him and invited him to make an agreement, he continually used the same excuse and paid no attention.

### II

At last, after two months, Isidore arrived (ibid.), that celebrated Alexandrian priest and monk, sent as an envoy to John and the others by Theophilus, Bishop of Alexandria, with letters in which he attempted to calm those disputes and restore mutual goodwill between the opposing parties.

Whether Theophilus judged that this was part of his duty because of the eminence of the see he held, or whether—as Jerome reports—he was stirred by John’s entreaties and complaints to oppose these disputes, he offered himself as arbiter between the two sides. Yet at that very time he favored Origen, since he was wholly committed against the Anthropomorphites, who opposed Origen’s doctrine.

Palladius also records in his *Life of Chrysostom* that Isidore wrote letters to Siricius at Rome, in which he denounced Epiphanius as a heretic and author of schism, on account, namely, of the ordination of Paulinian. Moreover, Theophilus himself was joined to John and to Rufinus, formerly his disciple, by friendship, and had long since been won over to their opinion.

For this reason the holy Father justly complains, among other things, that John had sent his letters to the Alexandrian bishop, to whom nothing concerning Palestine belonged, rather than to the bishop of Caesarea, to whom he was subject as metropolitan and with whom, Jerome says, “you knew that we were in communion, having spurned your own communion” (ibid.), or to the Patriarch of Antioch, the head of the whole East.

“But I know,” he continues, “why you did not wish to send them to Caesarea or Antioch. You knew what you were fleeing and avoiding. You preferred to trouble occupied ears rather than render the honor due to your metropolitan. Nor do I say this because, apart from the friendships that generate suspicion, I find anything else to criticize in the embassy.”

Finally, Rufinus had often incited Theophilus against Jerome, because Jerome had received in his monastery a certain Paul, a bishop of uncertain see in Egypt, expelled by Theophilus, and, as that rival loudly alleged, had defended him with all his strength and every effort, and had encouraged him to recover through an imperial rescript the priesthood which he had lost by episcopal judgment.

Rufinus exaggerated and distorted these matters into an insult against Theophilus to such an extent that he even sometimes prevented Theophilus’s letters to Jerome from being delivered.

“As for my communion,” the holy Father replies [Col. 0103] in Book III of his *Apology*, “and that of Pope Theophilus, I shall call no other witness than the very man whom you pretend was injured by me. You know that his letters were always sent to me, even at the time when you forbade them to be delivered to me; and that, by sending messengers daily, you kept proclaiming that his enemy was our friend and closest associate. You lied about the things you now write shamelessly, in order to stir up his hatred against us, so that the pain of the injury might become an oppression of faith.”

### III

Such was Theophilus’s character, and such was his disposition at that time, although in other respects he was especially distinguished by the praises of piety and learning.

But that Isidore whom he had sent to John, and whose services he wished to use in soothing the inflamed passions, was a thoroughgoing Origenist, strongly devoted to the party of John and Rufinus, and ultimately more suited to disturbing affairs than to settling them.

Three months before he came to Jerusalem, Isidore sent a letter which, through an error on the part of the bearer—unless, as Vastelius thinks, it should be read *portantes terrorem* (“bringing terror”), for *portantes errorem* (“bringing error”) is not entirely satisfactory [*Against John*], although all the books have the latter reading—was delivered to the priest Vincent. In it he exhorted the leader of his army to stand firmly upon the rock of faith—for by this name he designated Origenism—and not to be frightened by the threats of Jerome and his followers. Even before there was any suspicion of an embassy, he promised that he would soon be present to crush the ranks of his adversaries.

“As smoke,” he said, “is dissolved in the air and wax melts in the vicinity of fire, so those who have always resisted the faith of the Church and now attempt to disturb that same faith through simple people—meaning monks—will be scattered.”

That Rufinus is designated by the expression “leader of the army” is manifest from what Jerome says in almost the same words in Book III of his *Apology*, where he discusses Isidore’s letter:

“Let him not be angry with you who, sending letters to you against Pope Epiphanius, exhorted you to remain in the truth of the faith and not to alter your judgment through any terror. This letter is held in the handwriting of the author by those to whom it was delivered,” namely, by the priest Vincent.

Thus disposed, that distinguished mediator of peace arrived, approached John and his followers, and announced his embassy. He also approached Jerome a second and third time in Theophilus’s name, but he never wished to deliver the letters entrusted to him for Jerome.

When the holy Father said, “If you are an envoy, deliver the letters of your embassy; if you have no letters, how will you prove that you are an envoy?”, Isidore replied that he did indeed have letters, but that he had been placed under oath by the bishop of Jerusalem not to deliver them (ibid.).

By thus openly showing himself devoted to John, he destroyed every hope of peace and departed with nothing accomplished. As John was leaving, he gave Isidore an *Apology* for his cause, to be carried to Theophilus. Isidore himself had assisted in composing it, so that, as Jerome reproaches him, he was both the author and the bearer of the letter (ibid.).

The bishop of Jerusalem then sent this letter in every direction and took the greatest pains to have it disseminated throughout the entire world, especially to stir the ears of the Western bishops [Col. 0104]. In it he declared that he had been attacked by Epiphanius with the greatest injustice, not at all because he had violated the doctrines of Origen, as was shown above all by the fact that he had never rejected Epiphanius’s communion. Accordingly, he denounced Jerome and the numerous choirs of monks who stood with him as seditious men and public enemies.

### IV

Nor did the affair turn out badly according to John’s intentions. Theophilus’s mind, occupied by John’s letters and by Isidore’s insinuations, seemed to take offense that Jerome had rejected the conditions of peace to which Theophilus had invited him through his envoy.

For a long time, therefore, he gave Jerome no letters and did not deign to answer any that Jerome sent to him. Nevertheless, the holy Father never ceased performing his duties. He never stopped trying, by voice and by writing, to soothe the man—otherwise endowed with outstanding virtues and formerly well disposed toward him—who had been angered against him by the evil instigations of his adversaries.

At last, by his repeated services, he won over the man who broke his prolonged silence and sent the holy Doctor letters that were indeed somewhat bitter, but nevertheless letters. In them he first admonished him concerning the observance of the sacred canons: Jerome, he said, did not obey his bishop of Jerusalem, remained in communion with him, and insisted that his brother Paulinian had been properly ordained.

Then Theophilus appears to complain that Jerome conducted himself with such hostility toward the name of Origen and toward those who admired Origen’s genius, even where no loss of faith was involved.

We interpreted these words as signs of complaint rather than of friendship and benevolence from the holy Father’s own reply to Theophilus, which occupies place LXIII in our recension of the letters, and which it is worthwhile to reproduce here.

“Your Beatitude remembers that, during the time when you were silent toward us, my speech never ceased to perform its duties. I did not consider what you were then doing in the exercise of your office, but what it was fitting for me to do.” And now, having received the letters of Your Dignity, I see that I have gained some fruit from evangelical reading.”

A little later he writes:

“We give thanks for your admonition concerning the ecclesiastical canons; for ‘the Lord chastens him whom he loves, and scourges every son whom he receives.’ Nevertheless, know that nothing is more important to us than to preserve the rights of Christ, not to move the boundaries of the Fathers, and always to remember the Roman faith, praised by the apostolic mouth, of which the Church of Alexandria glories in being a participant.”

Finally:

“As for the wicked heresy”—certainly the Origenist heresy—“that you show such great patience and think that those who cling to the vitals of the Church can be corrected by your gentleness, this displeases many holy men. While you await the repentance of a few, you may be nurturing the audacity of the lost and strengthening the faction.”

This letter was sent about the year 397, namely within the period whose history we are describing, as we have shown clearly enough in the chronological notes attached to it.

### V

A little earlier, however, namely from the year 395, during the midst of the disputes, the holy Father had written other works which the sequence and order of the history require us to gather here in one place.

First comes the letter to Marcella, numbered LIX [Col. 0105] in advance, in which he answers the holy woman when, among other things, she asked what he meant by something she said she had read in passing in his works: that the lambs standing on the right and the goats standing on the left were Christians and Gentiles, rather than the good and the wicked.

He replies that he does not at all remember having written this at any time; nevertheless, insofar as something came suddenly to his memory while dictating, he had argued something similar in the second volume *Against Jovinian*.

For this reason we assigned the holy Father’s letter—since no arguments closer to the truth were available—to several years later, perhaps two or three after the books *Against Jovinian* had been written. For Marcella seems to have had before her eyes no works other than those mentioned in the Preface to the *Commentary on Jonah*, which were composed between 392 and 395; nor does Jerome describe the books he had written against Jovinian as so recently published that, upon recalling the matter, that passage would only then have occurred to him.

At about the same time, or at the end of the year 395 itself, Nepotian died, struck by a sudden fever. He was that distinguished ornament of the Church of Altinum, in whom all the adornments of clerical life seemed to reside alone.

As has often been related above, Jerome had been devoted to him with his whole heart from childhood. To the other praises of the holy youth—which would have compelled love even from the unwilling—was added his uncle Heliodorus’s long-standing friendship with the holy Doctor, which doubled the reasons for affection.

Finally, when Nepotian was already uttering his last words, his soul struggling, he grasped his uncle’s hand and, remembering his relationship with Jerome, said:

“Send this tunic, which I wore in the service of Christ, to him who is most dear to me, my father in age, my brother in fellowship; and transfer to him whatever affection you owed your nephew.”

With these words he failed, touching his uncle’s hand while remembering me, Jerome.

After he had thus been taken to heaven, the holy Father could not help mourning both his own loss and that of his friend Heliodorus. Wishing to console both himself and Heliodorus as far as possible, he found some relief in celebrating the praises of the deceased.

He therefore took up his pen and wrote the letter to Heliodorus numbered LX in our recension. Just as the chronological notes attached to it show, it must be assigned to the beginning of the year 396. It cannot rightly be postponed any further, as learned men commonly do, nor can it be placed earlier.

The arguments by which we think this has been established must be recalled and transferred here, lest we become unduly long by repeating them elsewhere and be forced to break the thread of the history we are weaving.

### VI

From this panegyric letter, so to speak, the holy Father turned to composing a commentary on Jonah. We place this work within the limits of the year 396, although we ourselves were once persuaded, and the reasons which the holy Father gives in his Prologue seem to indicate, that it reached the beginning of the following year.

“About three years have passed,” he says, “since I interpreted five prophets—Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, and Haggai—and, occupied with other work, I could not complete what I had begun. For I wrote a book *On Illustrious Men*, two volumes *Against Jovinian*, an *Apology* as well, and *On the Best Kind of Interpretation* to Pammachius, and two books to Nepotian, or *On Nepotian*, as well as other works which it would take too long to enumerate” [Col. 0106].

He means Nepotian’s *Epitaph*, the book or letter which is indicated by the words “to Nepotian,” and which we have said must be assigned to the beginning of the year 396, so that it cannot in any way be either postponed or placed earlier.

Since more than three years elapsed between the interpretation of the first five prophets and the composition of this *Epitaph*—which falls somewhere between the end of 392 and 396—and since Jerome may be understood to have used the word “about” (*circiter*), it is nevertheless not permissible to extend the period as far as 397, so that the chronological indication may remain consistent. Otherwise the holy Father should no longer have said “three years,” but “four.”

The otherwise very learned man who dared to tamper with Jerome’s passage in favor of this reading acted rashly and contrary to the testimony of all the books, as we have shown in its proper place.

Accordingly, in this year, as late as possible within the limits allowed, after an interval of about three years during which his commentaries on the Minor Prophets had been interrupted, the holy Father, overcome by Pammachius’s entreaties, turned to expounding Jonah.

He readily dedicated the work to Pammachius, who was especially close to him. Yet in the printed books, and in the manuscripts which we have been able to use down to the present day, Pammachius is not addressed in the Preface; instead, the venerable Pope Chromatius is addressed.

We discussed this matter in the notes on that passage. Now another explanation occurs to us, and it is by no means implausible. In some copy, *Chromati* may once have been written, whereupon an ancient copyist may have noted in the margin that *Pammachi* should be restored. Another person, who undertook to copy that exemplar but failed to understand the letters and intention of the corrector, may have thought that the abbreviated notation indicated not Pammachius—for Chromatius was what he read in the text—but “the Venerable Pope,” which is also an appropriate expression of honor and has a certain similarity of letters. He then inserted these words in place of the name.

Whatever the truth of the matter, the holy Father himself elsewhere seems to assert that this Commentary had been dedicated by him to Pammachius. Addressing his friend, he says: “Third, after a long period of silence, I expounded Obadiah and Jonah for you, who had commanded me to do so” (Preface to Book III on Amos).

Yet this passage is subject to several difficulties. As we have often said, and shall say again below, it requires a competent interpreter; otherwise the entire history of the Commentary on Jonah cannot be reconciled if the testimonies have been corrupted in places through the fraud of interpolators.

For our present purpose, however, a notable passage occurs in Chapter II. From it it is clear that, when the holy Father wrote about the corruption and incorruption of bodies, the Church of Jerusalem was still being troubled by the factions of Origenism.

“This,” he says, “they”—the Origenists—“take as an occasion for their heresy: under the person of Christ they lie about the Antichrist, they seize the churches so that they may fatten their very fat bellies, and, living carnally, they argue against the flesh” [Col. 0107].

The words “so that they may seize the churches” clearly designate John and his followers, defenders of Origen—for they indicate no one other than the bishop. The words “argue against the flesh” refer to men entangled in Origenist errors. It is well known that, when they were forced to confess the resurrection of bodies, they avoided using the word “flesh.”

Against John, Jerome says: “To deceive the ears of the ignorant, you mention the body nine times and do not mention the flesh even once.”

Finally, the words “so that they may fatten their very fat bellies” strike more closely at Rufinus, whom the holy Father often elsewhere mocks as a fat, sleek man with well-tended skin.

### VII

During this period Jerome also sharpened his pen against Vigilantius. Nearly two years earlier, Vigilantius had been with him in Palestine, apparently commended by letters from Paulinus, but he had failed to benefit from that association or from the example of the monks. Consequently, either in the very year in which he had arrived or immediately afterward, he grew weary of their life and departed.

He was a Gaul by birth and a man of crafty mind—Baronius considers him a Spaniard. He had carried letters from Sulpicius Severus to Paulinus of Nola and from Paulinus to Jerome; perhaps inflated by the authority of these endorsements, he had deceived others and had even been raised to the rank of priest.

While staying at Bethlehem with the holy Doctor, he is said to have lent his ears to Rufinus and, on Rufinus’s advice, to have held Jerome in contempt because Jerome dared both to read Origen’s books publicly and to follow his errors.

Although the holy Doctor had attempted by many arguments to satisfy him, he did not persuade him or succeed in curbing the unbridled license of his mind. Rather, Vigilantius accused Jerome of heresy with the utmost injustice and dragged his friend Oceanus, who had then moved from Rome to Palestine, into the same charge and slander.

Nor was he satisfied by the testimony of the priests Vincent and Paulinian—for the latter had perhaps then come from Cyprus to visit his brother Jerome—nor did he fear the judgment of Eusebius of Cremona concerning the holy Father’s orthodox faith.

At last, however, Vigilantius withdrew, repented of his conduct, and asked Jerome’s pardon. When Jerome spoke about the Resurrection and the reality of the flesh, Vigilantius applauded him with hands and voice.

Thus, whether genuinely reconciled or merely pretending reconciliation, he departed from Palestine. When writing about him to Paulinus, who had commended Vigilantius to him, Jerome preferred to pass over the reason for his departure in silence rather than state it.

“Why Vigilantius left us so quickly and abandoned us,” he says, “I cannot say, lest I seem to injure anyone. Nevertheless, as he was passing by and hurrying on, I detained him for a little while,” and so forth.

After returning to the West and passing through this particular part and region of Italy, between the waves of the Adriatic and the Alps of King Cottius, he began once again to criticize Jerome and his friends and to denounce them as heretics. After returning to his homeland, he did not hesitate to attack the holy Doctor in writing and overwhelm him with his books.

The holy Father therefore considered it his duty [Col. 0108], although Vigilantius was not a man who deserved a reply, to clear away the accusations and slanders of this most shameless detractor. He sent him the letter numbered LXI in our recension, in which he refutes each of his malicious objections and exhorts him finally to repent sincerely and perform penance.

It is clear from what has been said that Jerome wrote this letter near the end of 396 or at the beginning of the following year. Vigilantius had already returned to the West and was diminishing the reputation of the holy Doctor both on his journey and in his homeland. Yet he had departed from Palestine, or from the monastery at Bethlehem, while Vincent was still living there. From Book III of the *Apology* we learn that Vincent came to Rome in the year 397—or, if one prefers, near the end of the preceding year—and certainly a considerable time before Rufinus.

### VIII

The letter which the holy Father wrote to Tranquillinus, numbered LXII in our recension, belongs to the same period and concerns nearly the same subject. Tranquillinus had asked him whether the reading of Origen’s books should be avoided altogether, as a certain Faustinus maintained, or whether it should be permitted in part, as many others generally believed.

The holy Father does not hesitate to prefer this second position. He asserts that those who are led either into excessive love of Origen or into hatred of him by the perversity of their own temper are subject to the prophetic curse: “Woe to those who call good evil and evil good.”

Nevertheless, he advises Tranquillinus to proceed cautiously through the writings of that author, approving the better passages and rejecting the worse.

The chronological indication is therefore quite clear. The notoriety of the Origenist name had already spread from the East into the West, and there, amid the zeal of various parties, had begun to stir up disturbances. These circumstances designate no year other than 396 or the beginning of the following year.

### IX

The chronology becomes still clearer from the mention of Oceanus, who was then living at Rome, which the holy Father introduces in the same letter and through which he preserves a noteworthy memory of those times.

Let us recall what we said shortly before: Oceanus had been at Jerusalem, or in the monastery at Bethlehem, during the immediately preceding year, where he was accused of heresy in the presence of Vigilantius, who was likewise living there at the time.

After some time had passed, although the same year was hastening toward its end, while disputes about Origenist doctrine were taking place on both sides, a sudden barbarian invasion either devastated several provinces of the Roman Empire—including Palestine—or at least terrified them by the proximity of disaster.

“Behold,” says the holy Father in Letter LX to Heliodorus, “last year”—that is, 395—“wolves sent against us from the furthest rocks of the Caucasus, no longer of Arabia but of the North, traversed so many provinces in a short time. How many monasteries were captured! How many waters of rivers were changed by human blood! Antioch was besieged, as were the other cities through which the Halys, Cydnus, Orontes, and Euphrates flow. Flocks of captives were dragged away. Arabia, Phoenicia, Palestine, and Egypt were held captive by fear.”

He had scarcely written these words when Palestine itself seemed to flash its barbarian swords before his eyes and to threaten their necks.

“Swarms of Huns,” he says in Letter LXXVII [Col. 0109], “flying here and there on swift horses filled everything alike with slaughter and terror . . . They were unexpectedly present everywhere; surpassing rumor in speed, they spared neither religion, rank, nor age, and had no pity on the wailing infancy of children . . . A common report circulated among all: they were making for Jerusalem and, out of excessive desire for gold, were rushing toward that city . . . Then we too were compelled to prepare ships, remain on the shore, and guard against the enemy’s arrival; amid raging winds we feared the barbarians more than shipwreck, providing not so much for our own safety as for the chastity of virgins.”

“At that time there was a certain dissension among us”—the dispute over Origen’s doctrine with John of Jerusalem, Rufinus, and the other Origenists—“and domestic conflicts surpassed the warfare of the barbarians.”

Struck by these difficulties and the terror of war, Oceanus, who had come to Jerusalem with the holy Fabiola—and who had wished to spend the rest of his life in the holy places—lost heart and returned with the holy woman to his homeland, namely Rome.

“We,” Jerome adds, “were held in the East by our already established residence and our long-standing longing for the holy places. She”—Fabiola, together with Oceanus, her constant companion on the journey—“who was entirely occupied with her baggage and a stranger in every city, returned to her homeland.”

The year 396 had therefore already begun and had advanced considerably, as will become clear from what follows. John of Jerusalem had already sent his *Apology* against Jerome to Rome, as he had sent it to many other parts of the world, and there it had already stirred the minds of many.

On the other hand, Oceanus had already resisted vigorously the disturbances which that document had caused in the City and had confronted the foolishness of those who allowed themselves to be deceived by the arts of the Origenists.

The holy Father indicates, in replying to Tranquillinus, that he first learned all these matters from Tranquillinus himself. This is by no means an insignificant indication of the intervening period following Oceanus’s return to his homeland.

“What you say,” Jerome writes, “that many have been deceived by Origen’s error, and that my holy son Oceanus resists their madness, both grieves and rejoices me: I grieve that the simple have been overthrown, but rejoice that an educated man comes to the aid of those who are in error.”

### X

At about the same time, or roughly in the middle of the year 397, Jerome wrote to Principia on Psalm 44 and, somewhat later, to Pammachius also concerning Paulina’s death. Since the chronology of these letters has been established sufficiently fully in the chronological notes attached to them, there is no reason to linger over them by explaining them at greater length.

The letters of Augustine to Jerome should also be assigned to this period. In them Augustine thanks Jerome for having sent him a full letter in place of a salutation appended beneath the subscription.

That letter has long since perished. Beyond conjecture, it can only be gathered that learned men believe Jerome used the opportunity to speak in it about Origen and his errors, and wished to warn the bishop of Hippo—already flourishing in piety and learning, and with whom he had some acquaintance—that he should beware of the Origenist plague, which was becoming more virulent day by day.

Indeed, this reply of Augustine—which is his second letter to our author—speaks especially about Origen, whose errors Augustine nevertheless asks to have explained, since they were little known to him.

“I desired,” he writes, “and still desire from your prudence and learning that you make known to us those very errors of his—Origen’s—by which it is proved that so great a man departed from the faith of the truth.”

Although this letter was sent in this very year, it was nevertheless delivered much later, after an interval of at least half a year.

Finally, the holy Father wrote to Castrucius, a Pannonian, whose love and devotion toward him were truly remarkable. Although Castrucius suffered from weak eyesight, he had set out for Palestine from a desire to visit Jerome and had come as far as Cissa, fearing neither the storms of the Adriatic nor the dangers of the Aegean and Ionian seas. Had the affectionate devotion of his brethren not detained him, he would have fulfilled his intention in deed.

Jerome had learned of Castrucius’s extraordinary devotion toward him from the deacon Heraclius. A certain Amabilis, bishop of the same region, namely Pannonia, had sent Heraclius to Bethlehem so that, in person, he might obtain from the holy Doctor an explanation of the ten visions of Isaiah, which Amabilis had often previously requested.

When Heraclius had obtained this, he also received a letter from the holy Father to deliver to Castrucius. From this it may be understood that both writings belong to one and the same period.

### XI

This second work concerning the ten visions of Isaiah is both more significant as a chronological indication and much more distinguished in its literary character.

Although the holy Father says that, given the pressure of the time, he briefly touched upon what he thought concerning each vision, in fact he explained only the historical sense, which was what Amabilis had requested.

Later, however, when he was writing commentaries on the Prophet as a whole and had reached that passage, he judged it superfluous either to repeat the same material or to set forth different opinions in a single work. He therefore made this the fifth book on Isaiah, which was once published by itself.

These are Jerome’s words in the Preface to that book, addressed to Eustochium, whose footsteps we are carefully following.

In the earlier Preface to Amabilis he says:

“Up to this point you have repeatedly requested by letter that I explain to you in a historical exposition the ten visions which are the most obscure passages in Isaiah . . . and you often reminded me as I put off, from time to time, this most tiresome kind of explanation. But this year you sent our son Heraclius the deacon, who summoned me to court hand-to-hand and demanded the fulfillment of my promise at every moment.”

Near the end he says:

“If I attempt to explain the matter at greater length, many books will be required, and the journey of my exacting petitioner will be deferred to another year. Therefore, as you wish, I shall attach brief statements to each testimony, so that I may not so much explain what I think as leave you, in a few words, what should be understood. I dictate these things; I do not write them. As the hand of the notaries runs, the speech runs on.”

As for the chronological indication, there seems to be no room for doubt that this work should be assigned to the year 397, in which Heraclius first returned from Palestine to Pannonia.

For when he traveled again from that region to the East, he carried with him a letter from the priest Vitalis to Jerome. In his reply, Jerome mentions Isaiah’s prophecy and says that he had *recently* interpreted it among the ten visions.

At that time, however, the year was 398, as we shall shortly show in its proper place with certain arguments [Col. 0111]. This is particularly clear from another letter of the same year to Lucinius, in which the holy Father uses the same chronological indication, “recently,” and says that he had explained the very obscure visions of Isaiah in a historical exposition.

He therefore expounded them in the immediately preceding year, just as he also wrote the letter to Castrucius mentioned shortly before.

## CHAPTER XXIX

I. As Rufinus prepares to return to the West, he is reconciled with Jerome in the church of the Anastasis after their enmity.  
II. The year in which this occurred is established by new arguments.  
III. Whether at this time, chiefly through the efforts of Rufinus and Melania, the schism in Jerusalem was completely extinguished and peace restored between John and the remaining monks as well.  
IV. Arguments on behalf of those who assert this are answered, and others are offered that deny it.  
V. Some incidental remarks about Palladius.  
VI. Meanwhile, the holy Father falls into ill health and suffers from fever for three months.  
VII. Nevertheless, he writes several works, which are reviewed.  
VIII. Among them, commentaries on Matthew.  
IX. Also, works against John, addressed to Pammachius and to Theophilus.  
X. The date of these writings is established and defended.  
XI. Finally, after peace has been restored among all parties, he writes to Fabiola concerning the priestly vestment.

### I

After spending so many years in the East, Rufinus resolved to return to the West and to his native home. He may have grown weary of the disturbances that were troubling the Church of Jerusalem; or, what is closer to the truth, he may have wished to accommodate Melania, who was planning a journey to Rome for other reasons, and to accompany her at her side.

Before setting out, however, he considered it his duty to seek to incline Jerome’s mind toward peace and reconciliation, so that he would not heap a new injury upon a man who was offended and uncertain about his faith, and leave behind in Palestine a private enemy whom he had much reason to fear.

Accordingly, in the customary manner, in the Anastasis, after the sacrifice of the Mass, he joined his right hand with Jerome’s. With both minds disposed toward peace, he returned from enmity to friendship.

Some think that, in this peace, the errors of Origen were silently condemned. Others say that Rufinus was found guilty of no error. He himself boasts grandly in Book II of his *Invectives*:

“I have never followed one who was in error, or anyone else, unless I follow the Catholic Church. Can you produce any of my writings in which you can prove that I went astray, even in my youth?”

Jerome speaks sincerely and in good faith:

“In the Anastasis, after the Lamb had been sacrificed, we joined right hands.”

A little earlier he says:

“We gave peace; we did not receive heresy. We joined right hands and accompanied one another when we departed.”

This indicates that at that time they had recovered their spirits from nothing more than a private quarrel.

When Jerome calls the place where they were reconciled the Anastasis, he means the Temple of the Lord’s Resurrection, built long ago by Constantine the Great and dedicated to the memory of the risen Christ.

That great emperor built two temples or basilicas at Jerusalem. One was at the place of the Passion and was called both the Cross and the Martyrium; the other was at the place of the Resurrection and had the proper name *Anastasis* [Col. 0112], from the Greek term.

The Benedictine editor therefore committed a sufficiently careless error when he read *Anastasii* for *Anastasi* in the cited text of Jerome. We have restored the correct word.

Elsewhere, in his book *Against John*, the holy Father says: “Did you not, when proceeding from the Anastasis to the Cross, and so forth?” Some manuscripts also preserve the Greek letters Ἀναστάσει.

But enough of this.

## II.

Among scholars there is no real disagreement that the year in which these events occurred, or in which Rufinus sailed to the West, was 397—the point to which we have at last arrived in our account of Jerome’s affairs. The recent biographer of Rufinus, Fontaninus, likewise takes this as certain and gathers many testimonies from antiquity in support of it, especially from Paulinus of Nola; indeed, relying on this preconceived opinion, he even ventures to reconstruct the order and chronology of Paulinus’s Letters and Natalicia.

With due respect to learned men, however, I must say that they seem to us to be mistaken, partly because they have not considered accurately enough at what point in the year Rufinus actually set out, and partly because they neglected to compare this matter with other testimonies from Jerome. For many important points both in Jerome’s life and in the history of those times—and especially in the Origenist controversy—depend upon a correctly established date for Rufinus’s departure. This is why we should dwell on the matter for a while.

First, from Palladius, who describes Melania’s journey with Rufinus in the *Historia Lausiaca*, it is certain that they were transported from the East to Italy at great speed. “She boarded a ship,” he says in chapter 118, “and, sailing from Caesarea, reached Rome in twenty days.”

It is also known from Paulinus, when they came to Nola in Campania by land on their way to Rome, what season of the year it was: the beginning of spring. For in Letter 29 to Sulpicius Severus he says that Victor, Severus’s monk and courier, arrived at Nola in those days in which Melania too had arrived from Palestine; in an earlier letter to the same man he writes that he had received Victor at Nola “as winter was already coming to an end.” Thus, toward the end of winter—words that indicate rather the end of February than the beginning of March—both Victor, whom Paulinus mentions in this connection, and Melania with her Rufinus turned aside to Nola to visit the relatives of her household.

It is worth hearing Paulinus again:

> “I shall pass over the rest of her affairs and the dates of them, and I shall cross over by the same route by which she sailed on her return, so as to imitate her course and bring my account more quickly to its conclusion by describing her arrival—a matter in which I was a spectator of God’s great grace. She was brought to Naples, a city separated by a short distance from the Nolans’ city where we live. There, welcomed by the meeting with her sons and grandsons, she soon hastened to Nola, to the lodging of our humility.”

If, then, they came to Nola as winter was ending (Letter 29), and had boarded the ship in the harbor of Caesarea twenty days earlier, it is reasonable to believe that, when they had previously departed from Jerusalem by land—or indeed before they departed, when they obtained peace from Jerome—the year had scarcely begun.

[Col. 0113]

Unless I am mistaken in making these calculations, I think it impossible that this could have been 397, as they maintain, when only its first month, January, was still in progress. For many writings and actions of Jerome are assigned, without dissent, not merely to the beginning of that year but to a point when it was already well advanced; yet it is absolutely certain that they preceded the peace with Rufinus. Such are the matters which we listed in the immediately preceding chapter, and especially that Letter of the holy Father to Theophilus in which he says that the saints were displeased because Theophilus showed great patience toward a wicked heresy (Letter 63). Nor can the sequence of Jerome’s affairs—from the Commentary on Jonah, which we could scarcely place before the close of the immediately preceding year, down to this period—be compressed into the very few months that intervene.

But let us now refute that opinion by its own arguments and show that those who support it are not consistent with themselves. They maintain that the holy Father’s book to Pammachius against John of Jerusalem was written in this year, 397. Indeed, they pursue this with great effort and, to speak plainly, force him into it against the evidence and against his will, although he reveals that it was written almost two years later.

Let it nevertheless have been written in that year, as they wish, since they themselves think that it cannot possibly be assigned to an earlier date and do not need an older epoch in order to serve their hypothesis. I assert and openly demonstrate that Rufinus had not yet crossed from the East into Italy in that year. For if he arrived as winter was declining, the book was certainly written around autumn; and even if both his arrival and the composition of the book occurred in the same year, 397, the latter nevertheless followed the former by almost half a year—namely, the interval between the end of winter and the end of summer, or the beginning of autumn.

I shall produce the holy Father himself as witness. Near the end of the book he indicates that he is writing it a few months after Pentecost, around August or September:

> “A few months ago, around the days of Pentecost, when the sun was darkened and the whole world feared that the Judge was already about to come, we presented forty persons of different ages and sexes to your presbyters to be baptized.”

But in their hypothesis Rufinus’s departure must have preceded this; indeed, this is the chief point of their argument. They say that when he returned to the West the Jerusalem schism had already been entirely removed and peace had been restored among all parties. Therefore Rufinus arrived after that book—which plainly could not have been written before the year 397—and he arrived at the beginning of the following year, 398.

These, then, are the consequences of their mutually conflicting arguments. Moreover, many other testimonies from antiquity readily persuade us that it was only in this second year that Melania and Rufinus with her sailed to the West.

Palladius, in chapter 118, states that Melania returned to her homeland twenty-seven years after she had withdrawn from Rome to Egypt. This period, reckoned inclusively, as they say, from the year 372, when she crossed over there, ends in 398. [Col. 0114] For it is certain from Palladius that he counts the year inclusively, even though it had only begun—especially since it is highly probable that he included in that number the month or two spent on the first voyage, which began in the winter of the preceding year, 371, perhaps in November.

Since Paulinus, using a round number, said that Melania returned after five lustra, it is clear from his method of calculation that he spoke less precisely than he usually does in such matters. His statement must therefore be understood and explained in accordance with Palladius’s total. Fontaninus, however, with misguided zeal, forces Palladius to conform to Paulinus’s calculations. Everyone can see that he is mistaken—and makes Palladius serve his mistake—in order to support his preconceived opinion.

For Paulinus himself elsewhere indicates that Rufinus arrived in this very year, 398, not in the preceding year, as they interpret him. At the end of the Letter just cited he says that he read aloud to Melania, then his guest, the *Life of Saint Martin*, formerly composed by Sulpicius Severus, just as he had previously read it to the venerable bishop and most learned Nicetas, who had come from Dacia to the admiration of the Romans (Letter 29).

Nicetas had arrived in winter; he was present on 14 January, the feast of Saint Felix, on which Paulinus annually sang the *Natalicium* poem. As it has been learnedly observed by Baronius and gathered from the holy author himself, this was the fifth *Natalicium* at which Nicetas was present. It therefore belonged to the year 398, being the fifth after the first, since Chiffletus and Pagius establish by certain arguments that these poems began to be composed in 394.

Thus, at the beginning of this year, after Nicetas, Melania and her Rufinus arrived at Nola. This is the more accurate date for their return from the East to their ancestral homes. You will understand from what follows why we have pursued this matter at such length, although at first sight it seemed irrelevant.

## III.

It is commonly believed among scholars that, once Jerome and Rufinus had reconciled their dispositions, had exchanged greetings, and had mutually offered and received assurances of peace, the Jerusalem schism was thereby removed and extinguished, and peace was restored among all parties—that is, among the other monks and John.

They produce a particularly clear testimony for this from Palladius’s *Historia Lausiaca*, in the ancient version of Heraclides, chapter 118, where, speaking of Rufinus and Melania, he says that peace among all had been restored through their efforts:

> “They also restored to the holy Church those four hundred monks who, because of Paulinianus, were separating themselves from the Church.”

There is no doubt that *Paulini* should be read there as *Pauliniānī*, as Vastelius once observed: namely, Jerome’s brother, whose ordination by Epiphanius John used as a pretext for breaking communion.

The number of monks also agrees. That they were indeed very numerous while they remained in schism is indicated by the holy Father in his book against John, in these words:

> “So great a multitude of brothers and choirs of monks who do not communicate with you in Palestine.”

On the other hand, it is reasonable to believe that just as they had Jerome as their leader when they separated from John, [Col. 0115] so they immediately followed his example if he himself had first returned to concord.

Thus, they say, after a period of three years the Jerusalem schism was finally removed, although it had seemed capable of being removed only by heaven.

## IV.

The sequence of Jerome’s writings and actions persuades us otherwise. We believe that the holy Doctor—and with him the monks of Bethlehem—abstained from communion with John not only until Rufinus’s departure from Palestine (which occurred in 398, not in the preceding year, as they think), but for some further period of time, perhaps nearly a year.

This was not because Our Father was insufficiently concerned to establish peace, but because orthodox faith seemed likely to suffer if he communicated readily with those burdened by suspicion of heresy.

In the end, complete concord was restored not through Rufinus or Melania but, as it also appeared to Baronius, through the agency of Theophilus, who intervened with renewed zeal and, by his own merit and favor, finally achieved what previously could not be achieved because of Isidore’s fault.

The truth of this opinion will shortly be established by an almost conclusive argument, when we show that in the following year, 399—or certainly in the year with which we are now concerned, as it was approaching its end—the holy Doctor wrote certain works against John in a sharper style and with a more offended spirit than elsewhere. No one can persuade himself that these could have been written after peace had already been established.

I mean the Letter to Theophilus, number 82 in our recension, and specifically the book entitled *To Pammachius against John of Jerusalem*. Once we have proved that these were published after Rufinus’s departure, it will also be entirely clear that John did not return to concord and favor with Jerome and his companions at the same time as Rufinus.

This part of the discussion must therefore be referred to that point, or the arguments which we construct concerning the date of those writings must be brought back here.

## V.

Nevertheless, from what has already been said, it is possible to reach a suitable judgment on this matter. For neither Rufinus nor Jerome, when they mention or reproach one another concerning that mutual peace, says anything more than that an end was put to their private hostility.

Indeed, the holy Father says plainly and in express terms:

> “We offered peace; we did not accept heresy. We joined right hands; we escorted you on your departure, so that you might be Catholics, not so that we might become heretics.”

These words are so far from indicating that peace had been restored among all parties that they scarcely signify anything more than the restoration of the Christian duties of courtesy between two men and of a friendship that had long existed.

As for Palladius’s testimony, I do not know what weight it has in this matter. The most learned men, led by Baronius, did not hesitate to diminish his authority, since he was extremely friendly to Rufinus and Melania, with whom he had lived for some time, and was wholly devoted to their cause.

We also know that they were mistaken in confusing this author of the *Historia Lausiaca*—first, as they say, bishop of Helenopolis in Bithynia and later bishop of Aspona in first Galatia, a man of established reputation—with another Palladius, surnamed the Galatian. Jerome calls the latter [Col. 0116] a man of servile wickedness (*Prologue to the Dialogue against the Pelagians*) and a restorer of the Pelagian heresy; Epiphanius says that he needed the mercy of God because he preached and taught the heresy of Origen (Letter 51 among Jerome’s letters).

Even if this provides no reason for detracting from the former man’s credibility, it remains true that he reveals himself as excessively devoted to Rufinus and Melania and is entirely occupied with praising her. He also testifies that, while staying at her house in Rome, he was loaded with every kind of kindness and received the most generous assistance when he departed from it.

By contrast, he was unfair to Jerome. While staying at Bethlehem throughout the year 388, he lent an ear to the solitary Possidonius when he spoke against the holy Doctor (chapter 21), and assigned every possible distinction to Possidonius above Jerome—although he himself does not deny this in chapters 77 and 122 of his history.

Perhaps I should also pass over the possibility that his words may be explained in such a way that, although he uses the example of Melania and Rufinus, he does not intend to attribute the monks’ reconciliation, which followed later, to their present activity.

## VI.

Jerome and his companions at Bethlehem therefore still abstained from communion with John and were struggling under the harsher circumstances described above when, in this same year 398, a new accumulation of troubles arose and the holy Father himself was attacked by ill health.

A fever seized him either from the end of the immediately preceding December or certainly in the first days of this year, and continued for three months. At first it was bearable, but then it grew steadily worse, forcing his slight and labor-worn body to bed and wasting him miserably.

At last he improved, and during the days of Lent he began to rise from his illness and recover.

> “I,” he says in Letter 71 to Lucinius, “held by a long illness, scarcely began to breathe again during the days of Lent, when the notaries were departing.”

And in the Prologue to the *Commentaries on Matthew*, addressed to Eusebius:

> “With Easter now approaching, you force me to dictate, although you know that I have been so ill for three months that only now am I beginning to walk.”

Then, in Letter 73 to Evangelus:

> “After a long illness, I could scarcely free myself from fever during the days of Lent. As I was preparing myself for another work, I spent the few remaining days on the exposition of Matthew, and I resumed my interrupted studies with such eagerness that what benefited the exercise of my tongue harmed the health of my body.”

He immediately relapsed into fever and the weakness from which he had not yet properly recovered, and he continued to suffer from a persistent illness almost until the end of the year.

At that time, replying to Rufinus the Roman presbyter—clearly a different man from Rufinus of Aquileia—he counts that very month, or those few days of Lent during which he had begun to breathe somewhat more freely, among the period during which he had continuously struggled against ill health. In Letter 74 he writes:

> “We, lying here in our little bed and exhausted by a long illness, scarcely dictated even these words to be written quickly by the notary.”

A little later he says:

> “Pray to the Lord for our health, so that after twelve months during which I have been worn down by continual weakness, I may be able to write something worthy of your wishes; and forgive me if my abundant speech flows in an unusual course.”

[Col. 0117]

Nevertheless, do not suppose that he entirely refrained from writing. Whenever the intervals between his fevers allowed, he either wrote something himself or dictated it to his notaries, and he never failed to do so.

Indeed, in this very year, during which he was almost continually ill and confined to his bed, we possess from him as many writings as perhaps one of us today who devotes himself to letters might scarcely compose with full strength and good health.

Among these letters, our recension preserves numbers 73 through 75. Each contains not merely the ordinary duties of friendship but treatises on matters of the greatest importance.

The first replies to a certain Magnus, a Roman rhetorician whom Sidonius also seems to remember, who asked why the holy Father used testimonies from secular literature in his short works (Book 5, Letter 10). Jerome explains why he had done this, to what extent it was permissible, and whose example he followed.

He knew well enough whose insinuations had prompted Magnus to raise the question: Rufinus, of course, whom Jerome calls there, in order to spare his real name, “Calpurnius Lunarius,” because of his love of the histories of Sallust.

In Book 1 against the same man he says:

> “This, of course, is the Calpurnius Sallustianus who, through the orator Magnus, had raised no small question for us.”

Rufinus had therefore already arrived at Rome and was attempting to create hostility toward Jerome’s name.

The second letter is addressed to Lucinius of Baetica. Jerome urges him, with the consent of his wife Theodora, to persevere in his resolve regarding chastity and to sail quickly to Jerusalem, as he had proposed. He also discusses fasting, the reception of the Eucharist, and ecclesiastical traditions.

His mention of the illness from which he had only then begun to recover somewhat leaves no doubt that the letter belongs to the year to which we assign it. There is also a more notable indication of its date: he says that he had recently discussed, in a historical explanation, the ten extremely obscure visions of Isaiah which he sends as a gift to Lucinius.

We have explained above what “recently” means in this context.

The same chronological indication appears in the following letter to Vitalis the presbyter, concerning Solomon and Ahaz. Jerome teaches there that it must be held as certain that Solomon and Ahaz fathered sons in the eleventh year of their lives, although he does not deny that the Scripture which asserts this can be explained in another way.

He again mentions his poor health in the following letter to Evangelus concerning Melchizedek. In it he refutes a book by an anonymous author who denied that Melchizedek belonged to the human race and claimed instead that he was the Holy Spirit or an angel.

Jerome demonstrates not only, chiefly from the opinions of the ancient Christians, that Melchizedek was a human being, but also that he was of Canaanite stock; and, if the Jews are to be trusted on this matter, that he was Shem himself, Noah’s first son.

Finally, Letter 74 to Rufinus, whom we have identified as the Roman, was also written toward the end of the year. Jerome says that he dictated it to his notary not so much while lying in bed as while exhausted by a long illness and twelve months of continual weakness.

In it he discusses with great learning the judgment of Solomon and the quarrel of the two prostitutes, which he interprets allegorically as the Church gathered from the Gentiles and the synagogue of the Jews.

We have touched briefly on the subjects of these letters so that it may seem remarkable that a man confined to bed should have discussed such important matters.

## VII.

[Col. 0118]

But—and this is the principal point—at the same time he also expounded the Scriptures in splendid works. I mean the *Commentaries on Matthew*, which he poured forth in four complete books in scarcely fifteen days, at the approach of Easter, having only just recovered from the fever of the preceding three months.

This occurred when Eusebius of Cremona, suddenly preparing to sail from the East to Rome, had asked that this work be supplied to him as a kind of traveling provision.

The holy Father himself notes the circumstances of the work in the letters cited above, such as that to Lucinius:

> “Held by a long illness, I scarcely began to breathe again during the days of Lent.”

And in another letter to Evangelus:

> “After a long illness, I could scarcely be free from fever during the days of Lent. As I was preparing for another work, I spent the few remaining days on the exposition of Matthew, and I resumed my interrupted studies with such eagerness that what benefited the exercise of my tongue harmed the health of my body.”

Most clearly of all, he says in the Prologue to these same *Commentaries*:

> “I am sufficiently astonished, dearest Eusebius, that, as you were suddenly preparing to sail to Rome, you wished this to be given you by me as a kind of traveling provision, so that I might briefly expound Matthew, etc. … If you remembered my reply, you would never have asked for the work of years within a few days.”

A little later:

> “But you force me to dictate in two weeks, with Easter already approaching and the winds blowing, without considering when the notaries will take down the words, when the sheets will be written, when they will be corrected, and in what time they will be arranged in a finished form—especially since you know that I have been ill for three months, so that only now am I beginning to walk, and cannot compensate for the magnitude of the labor by the brevity of the time.”

That year Easter fell on 18 April. It is therefore entirely plausible that the holy Father began dictating this work toward the end of the preceding March, while Eusebius, on the other hand, did not entrust himself to the voyage until after the Easter days had passed—that is, at the beginning of May.

It was important to observe this chronological indication carefully, since it creates a difficulty which we shall explain later: the holy Doctor seems to say that Eusebius crossed to the West a year after Rufinus’s departure.

## VIII.

When Jerome says that he had previously been preparing for another work before writing on Matthew, the passage invites speculation about what that work finally was.

Nothing seems to us closer to the truth, or at least to probability, than that he was referring to the book addressed to Pammachius against John of Jerusalem. Its *Apology*, circulated in every direction, had already drawn the minds of many people into opposing camps, and the holy Father could no longer tolerate the true and genuine cause of the dispute being rejected while a false cause of his anger was alleged against him.

But this work was full of danger: it sharpened his style against his own bishop. For this reason the holy Father deliberately concealed the subject of the writing.

Moreover, it does not seem that the author had yet put the finishing hand to it. This too supports our position. First, he was interrupted by the composition of the *Commentaries on Matthew*; then, overcome by a relapse of fever, he was forced by illness to suppress the book while, meanwhile, peace among all parties was finally restored through Theophilus’s zeal.

Finally, this treatise [Col. 0119] remained hidden from Rufinus, against whom he certainly would not have failed to direct the full force of his anger in his books of invective. Rufinus was not in Palestine when Jerome composed it, but in Rome; nor could the work have reached his hands, since it had been completed neither by its author nor published by him for the public.

All these considerations strengthen our position and increase the credibility of the opinion that the work was composed not in another year but in the year we have identified—398—into which all the circumstances fit with great appropriateness.

The Letter of the holy Doctor to Theophilus, number 82, also belongs to that same year, as everyone now agrees. Whether one prefers to place it before the book or after it makes no difference to us, provided that one does not separate the two by a long interval extending beyond the limits of that year.

The date of the book must therefore be confirmed by new arguments, from which the history of Jerome’s affairs and the definite end of the Jerusalem schism, as noted above, become known.

## IX.

At the very beginning of the book the holy Father says that, so that he may not be accused either of impatience or rashness, he has finally spoken against John only after three years.

He says the same below, in section 14, concerning Epiphanius, whom John had offended in many ways:

> “He, throughout the entire three years thereafter, swallowed his injuries, disregarding private hostility, and sought only the correction of the faith.”

By these words Jerome himself indicates where he begins to count those three years: from the year 395, after Paulinianus’s consecration and after Epiphanius’s letters to John had been sent.

From that time, the bishop of Jerusalem, considering himself openly provoked by Epiphanius, never ceased to hurl curses at him, pouring abuse upon him both orally and in writing. Epiphanius, concerned only with the correction of the faith, silently swallowed those injuries.

I know that scholars commonly begin those three years with the immediately preceding year, 394, in which Paulinianus was ordained, and thus bring them to an end at the beginning of 397.

But by the same reasoning they could have begun them in the preceding year, 393, since the disagreement between John and Epiphanius first began then, and from that time John was subjected to such abuse.

Since they do not do this—because all their calculations would be overturned by that date—it is clear that they make their calculations in such a way as to serve their hypothesis.

The holy Father, however, clearly indicates the period that he ought to indicate: the time when John broke out into open hostility, after Epiphanius had sent him letters that were most courteous and *parainetic*—παραινετικαί, that is, exhortatory—but which John nevertheless tore apart with insults and venomous attacks.

After John had long awaited the satisfaction concerning the faith, and since he could never be induced to provide it, he came under the gravest suspicion of heresy. This gave Jerome and the monks under him cause to separate themselves from John’s communion.

In a word, Jerome counts the three years from the time when the Jerusalem schism was formed, which the preceding history shows to have occurred in 395.

Apart from this, those who begin the three years in 394 and conclude them at the beginning of 397 are also plainly mistaken, and are forced by their hypothesis to do so, even though it is clear that the book was written near the end of the year, or a few months after Pentecost. [Col. 0120]

A second argument of no less weight is drawn from what the holy Father says in section 17: that he had composed the *Commentaries on Ecclesiastes* approximately ten years earlier.

We have proved in its proper place, by decisive arguments which it would take too long to repeat here, that those *Commentaries* belong to the end of the year 388. If ten intervening years are added to that date, one arrives precisely at the year to which we maintain that this book must be assigned.

Finally, there is an especially decisive point in our favor, one that creates a serious difficulty for those who think otherwise. In section 41, when John accuses the holy Father of arrogating primacy to himself, Jerome replies:

> “If you are speaking of me and the presbyter Vincentius, you have slept for a very long time, since, now awakened after thirteen years, you say these things. For that reason I left Antioch, and he Constantinople, those most famous cities—not so that we might praise you preaching before the crowds, but so that, grieving over the sins of our youth in the fields and solitude, we might turn Christ’s mercy toward us.”

In the chronology of the book which we have constructed, it is easy to show from what point those thirteen years must be counted, so that both the sequence of events and the calculation of time agree perfectly.

By contrast, those who assign the book to the beginning of the preceding year torment themselves miserably. They cannot reconcile the statements with one another and are finally driven either to accuse Jerome of carelessness in reckoning the years or rashly to alter his text, wishing to replace thirteen with sixteen.

Yet the holy Father calculated with the utmost precision. He intended the thirteen years to be counted from 386, the one year in which he could most truly say of himself that he had preferred the fields and solitude to the honors of the Church of Antioch.

When he was ordained, he did not withdraw from the dignity and service of that Church in order to lead a solitary life, but in order to travel freely, especially for the sake of study.

When, however, in that year after the death of Damasus, he returned to Antioch together with Vincentius in order to withdraw into the desert, he abandoned the Church to which he also belonged by the right of his ordination and in which, had he wished, he could have enjoyed the rank of presbyter with considerable distinction. He could easily also have been persuaded by the encouragement of Bishop Paulinus and his friends to exercise that office.

He therefore counts the thirteen years from that year, reckoning both endpoints together, as is required by the most precise method of calculation. He makes it plain and marks it, as it were, with his finger: the year in which he wrote these words was 398.

## X.

These are the arguments which, unless we are greatly mistaken, should compel assent even from those unwilling to give it.

Nevertheless, we must admit that certain objections can be raised which may appear troublesome. Chief among them is what the holy Father says in this same book and in the section cited above concerning his brother Paulinianus:

> “You see that he is subject to his own bishop and is living in Cyprus. He sometimes comes to visit us, not as your man but as another’s—that is, as the man of the one by whom he was ordained.”

If Jerome was writing in 398, as we have established, [Col. 0121] this seems scarcely reconcilable with another statement of his in Book 3 against Rufinus. There, replying to his slanderous rival, who accused him of sending his accusers to Rome, he says:

> “Paulinianus and Eusebius departed a year after your voyage.”

It has already been established that Eusebius sailed to Rome around the middle of this very year, 398, carrying the *Commentaries on Matthew*. It is therefore difficult to maintain what we have argued throughout this discussion: that Rufinus arrived in the city at the beginning of this same year—especially if, as the holy Father seems to say, Paulinianus sailed together with Eusebius.

We have so far proceeded on the assumption that Jerome wrote this book toward the end of the year, in which he says that his brother was living in Cyprus and sometimes came to visit him. Paulinianus, then, would already have had to leave for the West several months earlier.

This is the kind of obstacle against which the ingenuity of critics has stumbled. Yet they could have avoided it easily if they had examined the matter more closely.

It must above all be carefully observed that Eusebius and Paulinianus sailed at different times, and that Eusebius sailed much earlier; we learn that Paulinianus did not return to the West until the following year, 399.

Once this distinction is observed, the matter is clear. The statement that he departed for Rome a year after Rufinus’s voyage properly refers to Paulinianus, even though another man—Eusebius—arrived there only a few months later.

There are similar examples of expression in Jerome, in which the truth of the matter applies perfectly to one or another of several things that he joins together.

I shall give one example from Book 1 against the same Rufinus, section 2:

> “I praised Eusebius in his ecclesiastical history, in his arrangement of chronological periods, and in his description of the Holy Land; and, translating these very little works into Latin, I gave them to men of my language.”

Yet it is established that Jerome never translated Eusebius’s *Ecclesiastical History* into Latin, but only the other two works which we have discussed in their proper places: the *Chronicon* or *Chronological Canon*, and the book *On the Places of Scripture*.

The passage must therefore be understood conveniently: Jerome says that he translated these works into Latin, but that he merely praised the other work, the *Ecclesiastical History*.

The situation in the matter before us is no different. In truth, Paulinianus departed a year after Rufinus, and the chronological expression properly concerns him.

Indeed, the statement is even more accurate in this case. Although Eusebius of Cremona, whom the holy Father joins with Paulinianus, did not sail a full intervening year after Rufinus but only a few months later, he nevertheless sailed after Rufinus *aplōs*—ἁπλῶς, simply or absolutely—which is sufficient for the truth of the statement to stand.

It is also possible that “after a year” should be understood in the same way as “in the following year.” If this is accepted, Jerome may easily have been referring elsewhere to the beginning of Rufinus’s departure, which occurred at the end of the preceding year, perhaps in December; and the same statement concerning Eusebius will then be clear.

However the matter may stand, these objections are certainly not of such weight that they should disturb us or conflict with the other arguments by which the position has thus far been established.

Let us return to Jerome.

[Col. 0122] **XII.** Once satisfaction had been rendered in good faith—sincerely and wholeheartedly, as is fitting, on John’s part—the ancient hostility between him and Jerome was entirely effaced, and peace was established among the adherents of both sides. Thus they returned to friendly relations with one another, so that thereafter they treated each other as members of their own households. Immediately the Holy Father regained possession of the church situated at the place of the Lord’s Nativity, from whose entrance he had long been barred; and he never ceased to venerate it more and more because of the holiness of the place and to hold it dear. This is easily understood as what Postumianus intended to say to Sulpicius in the *Dialogue*, where he said that Jerome governed that church of the place—Bethlehem—the parish of the bishop who holds Jerusalem (*Dialog.* 1). For we have already shown above, in chapter XVIII, that he neither exercised pastoral care over souls nor ever wished to perform the sacrifices due to his title, that is, to discharge the office of a presbyter.

Moreover, Jerome did not neglect to inform his friends how well things were going for him, taking the opportunity to do so. Indeed, at the very end of this year, or at the beginning of the following year, 399, he wrote to Fabiola the letter *On the Priestly Garment*. In it, rejoicing over the peace that had now been achieved and over the favorable fortune he was enjoying, he makes her long for that life, as the saying goes:

> You, indeed, enjoy your desired leisure, and perhaps sigh for the Bethlehem fields beside Babylon—that is, Rome. We, in Ephrata, now that peace has at last been restored, hear the Infant wailing from the manger, and we desire his complaints and little cries to reach your ears.

Indeed, these very words gave us reason to postpone the letter until the present point, although elsewhere—and in the chronological notes attached to it—we ourselves assigned it to the preceding year, following the commonly accepted view. We now regard it as certain that the peace he mentions is none other than the peace he entered into with Bishop John. For the view held by some—that the reference is to the peace which followed the incursions of the Huns, discussed shortly before—is plainly contrary to the mind of the holy Doctor, as is shown by what he immediately adds about the manger and the Infant wailing there. In these words he seems to congratulate himself that, through the reconciliation of the friendships, he had recovered the church of that place, whose entrance he had previously been forbidden.

He had indeed been prohibited from entering it up to the time when he was writing his book against John. There he laments this, saying:

> Up to the present day we see only the cave of the Lord; and, placed far away, we sigh while heretics enter.

The letter to Fabiola, therefore, must be considered to have been written a few months after that book; it cannot in any case be postponed to a later time.

# CHAPTER XXX

I. A new dispute arises with Rufinus over his translation of Origen’s book *Periarchon*, and over Jerome’s praise in the Preface.  
II. Pammachius and Oceanus provoke Jerome to answer Rufinus.  
III. Jerome writes back to him in a friendly spirit, complaining about this matter.  
IV. In a splendid letter addressed to them, he clears himself and sends them his faithful translation of the book *Periarchon*.  
V. He also writes various letters on various subjects, which are listed.  
VI. Meanwhile Theophilus condemns Origen and his followers, and writes about the matter to Jerome and to Pope Anastasius.  
VII. Anastasius likewise condemns the blasphemies excerpted from Origen’s book and writes on the matter to Simplicianus, Bishop of Milan.  
VIII. He also summons Rufinus to Rome to give an account of himself.  
IX. Rufinus refuses to go and sends an *Apology* on his behalf.  
X. At the same time he writes an *Apology* against Jerome, or books of *Invectives*.

[Col. 0123]

**I.** Scarcely had peace been established in the East when a new storm of discord arose in the West, for that same Origenist reason. Macarius, a monk of some renown at Pineto, on the Roman estate near the sea, had begun, through Rufinus—who at that time was living in that same monastery—to acquire some taste for the works of Origen. He repeatedly begged Rufinus to translate for him into Latin the books *Περὶ Ἀρχῶν*, that is, *On Principles*, or *On Powers*—as the title is said to be translatable in the Prologue.

Rufinus complied with his request and translated the first two books together with the preface, intending to test the opinion of the public. Then, at the subsequent urging of other friends, he translated the remaining two as well. But did he translate them? Rather, he interpolated them. As he himself admits in the earlier Preface—for he supplied two Prefaces—when he encountered certain serious obstacles in the Greek, he smoothed everything away in translation and purged it, so that the Latin reader would find nothing in the books contrary to our faith. In the other Preface he says:

> I must necessarily point out that, just as we did in the earlier books, so also in these we observed the rule that we should not translate those things which appeared contrary to the rest of his opinions and to our faith; rather, as though they had been inserted and falsified by others, we passed them over.

But there was a far greater evil: having no confidence in his own conscience, and not doubting that the novelty of the doctrine concealed beneath his deceptive translation would disturb many, he dared to seek protection for himself from Jerome’s authority. He used Jerome’s example as a pretext for his own cause and pursued his praises throughout that entire Preface. Hence came the greatest stain upon the affair and the origin of discords that afterward had no end.

Once the book was published, it certainly deceived the simplicity of many priests, monks, and ordinary Christians (*Epist.* CXXV). Yet it so alarmed most people that Jerome reports that, after Rufinus’s translation, the whole world burst into hatred of Origen and shuddered at the translated work.

He likewise states (*Book I against Rufinus*) that Marcella, a young Roman woman, was the first to detect the error. She had long restrained herself lest she seem to be acting out of rivalry; but once she perceived that the faith praised by the apostolic voice was being violated in many places (*Epist.* CXXVII), she also took courage to suppress it.

Rufinus, meanwhile, realizing that he was already being pointed out almost as a heretic, decided to leave. He obtained ecclesiastical letters from Siricius, Bishop of the City, who, as Jerome says, judged others by his own character, so that he might boast of communion with the Church (*ibid.* and *Against Rufinus*, Book III). Armed with these, he returned to Aquileia by way of Milan, which at that time was generally the more convenient route from Rome. The year was already 398, beyond its midpoint, when he completed that translation; when he left Rome, the year was hastening toward its end.

[Col. 0124]
