**II.** Pammachius and Oceanus, Roman nobles distinguished above all by their friendship with Jerome, secretly sent him copies of Rufinus’s translation—which had not yet been published and had been handed to them furtively—together with that deceptive Preface. Rufinus, for his part, maintained that the copies had been crusted over in places with false statements. They complained about certain passages that seemed to them less than Catholic, as well as about other passages suppressed by the translator that could reveal the author’s manifest impiety (*Book II against Jerome* and elsewhere).

They concealed Rufinus’s name, since Rufinus himself had not dared to attach it to his work. They strongly urged the holy Doctor to answer him, and asked him to translate the same books with greater fidelity, expose what had been interpolated, and refute what had been wrongly explained (*Epist.* LXXXIII). Above all, they urged him to clear himself of the suspicions cast upon him: he should realize that, through that Preface’s oblique praises, he had been placed among the Origenists, and that heresy was seeking protection from the reputation of his name.

**III.** Jerome had already received these copies when Rufinus’s own letter to him was delivered. Although the letter itself has perished, we can gather something of its contents from the holy Father’s reply. Rufinus evidently said that he had remained in Rome longer than he wished because, after receiving news of his mother’s death, grief had prevented him from returning to his homeland: he could not bear, while present in his mother’s house, the pain that he had scarcely been able to suppress in his mind while absent.

Nevertheless, he said that he had been recalled there by the longing of his spiritual parents, Chromatius and Eusebius. But he had immediately been attacked by his rivals, especially by Jerome’s close associates, so that he appeared to complain that, at Jerome’s instigation—or at least with his knowledge—he had incurred their hatred. Rufinus claimed that he was faithfully preserving the peace that had been restored between himself and Jerome and desired that Jerome should observe it with equal devotion.

Jerome replied in Letter LXXXI of our recension that he had meanwhile neglected no duty toward him:

> The Lord is witness to our conscience that, after our friendships had been reconciled, no resentment intervened by which we might injure anyone. Indeed, we took every precaution lest even an accident should be turned into malevolence. But what can we do if everyone thinks that he is acting justly in what he does, and seems to himself to be biting rather than being bitten?

He then complains, in a friendly and gentle manner, that the Preface had indirectly—or rather openly—made such a request, and warns Rufinus not to praise him in a similar way in the future.

This letter might have brought their somewhat offended spirits back together. But those who had received it for delivery, and were to send the restored harmony from Rome, Jerome’s friends—namely Pammachius and Oceanus—suppressed it, whether from better judgment I do not know, but certainly without a favorable result.

> I wrote to you immediately, a brief letter complaining about your praises. But because you were not in Rome, my friends refused to send it to you, saying that you were boasting among your companions, under an unworthy Christian name, about my way of life. I have appended a copy of it to this volume, so that you may know how great a grief I restrained with how much moderation for the sake of our relationship.

And in Book III:

> You also think that I invented a new lie, composing a letter to you in my own name as though it had been written long ago, so that I might appear good and modest—a letter that you never received at all. This matter can very easily be proved. Many people in Rome possess copies of it from approximately three years ago, but they did not wish to send it to you, knowing what you were boasting about me, how unworthy of a Christian, and how unspeakable were the fabrications you were making. I wrote, not knowing, as though to a friend; they did not deliver it to one whom they knew to be an enemy, sparing both my mistake and your conscience.

**IV.** Those distinguished friends of Jerome had also received from the same bearer of letters, Rufinus, another Syrian—whom the holy Father had sent through Rome to Milan for a certain purpose and whom it is important to distinguish from his Aquileian namesake—a newly prepared translation of the books *Περὶ Ἀρχῶν*, together with a splendid letter specifically addressed to them. In that letter Jerome defended his own faith before them and cleared himself of every suspicion.

He admits that he had praised Origen’s intellect and learning, but categorically denies that he held—or holds—his doctrines:

> I praised the translator, not the dogmatist; the intellect, not the faith; the philosopher, not the apostle.

And he continues:

> If they wish to know my judgment concerning Origen, let them read my Commentaries on Ecclesiastes, let them examine the three volumes on the Epistle to the Ephesians, and they will understand that I have always opposed his doctrines. If you believe me, I was never an Origenist; if you do not believe me, I have now ceased to be one.

And in the following chapter:

> Suppose that I erred in my youth, that I had been instructed in the studies of philosophers—that is, of the pagans—and that, at the beginning of my faith, I did not know Christian doctrines and thought that I found in the Apostle what I had read in Pythagoras, Plato, and Empedocles. Why do you follow the error of one who was a little child and an infant in Christ? Why do you learn impiety from one who did not yet know piety? After shipwreck, the second plank is to confess one’s fault frankly. You imitated one who was in error; imitate one who has been corrected.

He then makes many accusations against the man—he continually withheld Rufinus’s name—who had dared to pour Origen’s doctrinal poisons into Roman ears:

> Whoever you are, advocate of new doctrines, I beg you to spare Roman ears; spare the faith that was praised by the voice of the Apostle. Why do you try, after four hundred years, to teach us what we previously did not know? Why do you bring into the open what Peter and Paul did not choose to publish?

Finally, he attacks the man who had assumed the role of patron of Origen’s cause through disguised praises:

> I would rather endanger my reputation than my faith.

He adds:

> My friends—Rufinus, certainly—have brought me to this position: if I remain silent, I am judged guilty; if I answer, I am judged an enemy. Both conditions are harsh, but of the two I shall choose the lighter. Hostility can be restored to friendship; blasphemy does not deserve pardon.

**V.** As for the translation of the books *Περὶ Ἀρχῶν* that Jerome joined to the letter, he says that he endured much labor in preparing it, since to alter anything in the Greek is not to translate but to overthrow (*Book I against Rufinus*). Elsewhere he testifies that he prepared it for this purpose: not so that the reader would believe what he translated, but so that he would not believe what another had translated earlier.

I consider this the sole reason why learned men have occasionally wondered why this translation by the holy Doctor perished—one that was faithfully matched to the Greek text and carefully prepared by a translator thoroughly skilled in both languages—while Rufinus’s translation survives, although it lacked those praises and, from the moment of its first publication, was almost destroyed by the abuse of good men and devoted to every curse.

The reason is that Jerome’s translation reproduced Origen’s blasphemies just as they had been uttered by the author himself, in the same arguments and almost the same words. At first contact, such impious writings would naturally repel and horrify Christian minds. Rufinus’s translation, however, omitted the more destructive passages and commended the remaining doctrine—of very doubtful reliability—by covering it with a verbal gloss. It therefore did not deter readers from reading or copying it.

Furthermore, the Roman nobles circulated Jerome’s translation, and especially that letter, while suppressing the letter to Rufinus. They pressed it upon everyone, proclaimed it publicly, and produced it as a witness to Jerome’s orthodoxy. Some add—and not implausibly—that they supplied and exaggerated, by something resembling an oral commentary, what was missing from the letter according to their wishes. For they would have preferred the rival to be attacked by Jerome in explicit terms.

In reality, Jerome exercised considerable restraint and did not attack Rufinus by name or by any distinctive mark:

> In a public letter—I mean the one to Pammachius and Oceanus—I carefully took precautions lest you think that anything had been said about you.

But they attributed everything to Rufinus that the holy Father had said broadly and deliberately against heretics. They also claimed that the conflict between his translation and Rufinus’s perfidy sharpened Rufinus’s resentment to such an extent that he now thought Jerome had violated the rights of friendship and was exercising his former hatred against him. He therefore undertook to resist Jerome as an enemy who was bringing weapons against him.

Thus, through error rather than through the fault of either party, their friendship was broken once again, and thereafter it was never restored. Consequently Rufinus suffered damage to his reputation even after his death, although in other respects he was greatly esteemed among the most learned and holy Fathers produced by that age.

We shall return later to Jerome’s translation of the book *Περὶ Ἀρχῶν*, when we review the letter to Avitus, written approximately ten years afterward. While these events were taking place, the year of Christ 400 was drawing toward its close.

**VI.** Meanwhile Jerome also wrote many letters to various people, which are listed in our edition beginning with Letter LXXV. In the first of these he consoles Theodora, the widow of Lucinius, to whom, as we showed in its proper place, he had written the preceding year, over the death of her husband. He says that he had not deserved to see the face of that man, whom he had hoped would shortly come to him at Bethlehem.

From this we infer that this letter is separated by approximately one year from the letter addressed to Lucinius and that it cannot easily be postponed to a later date. Since only once—indeed, just in the immediately preceding year—had correspondence passed between Lucinius and Jerome, we must surely believe that it was in that letter that Lucinius gave the holy Doctor hope of going to Jerusalem. Nor, when Jerome says here that he would shortly have embraced him in the Holy Places, does he indicate a period longer than the one we have established.

Immediately afterward that holy widow Theodora entered upon the path of perfection. The holy Father refers to her in a letter to Abigaus near the end:

> I commend to you in my own words my holy daughter Theodora, sister of blessed Lucinius, who has been entrusted to me, so that she may not grow weary on the journey she has begun.

These words unmistakably point to this same year.

The same author himself reports that two other letters were written at the same time, or toward the end of that year. In the first he follows Fabiola, already dead, with a kind of funeral eulogy. She was certainly a most holy woman, as the deeds we have recounted above in various places demonstrate. He himself calls her “the praise of Christians, the wonder of pagans, the mourning of the poor, and the consolation of monks.” After her conversion to Christ, she truly lived as a Christian and deserved a glorious end to her life.

He testifies that he was writing this letter when the circle of the fourth summer had already elapsed from the time when, in writing Nepotian’s *Epitaph*, he had expended whatever strength he had possessed in that earlier grief. Therefore, if that work was correctly dated to the beginning of 396—which we certainly think we have established by decisive arguments—there is no doubt that the fourth summer afterward was the summer of this very year whose history we are pursuing.

The other letter, addressed to Fabiola herself and concerning the forty-two stations in the desert, had indeed been begun by Jerome much earlier, when she was living at Bethlehem. Yet its publication, to use Jerome’s preferred expression, belongs to this period. It was not delivered to her while she was alive, but to her memory.

It is best to hear the matter from him himself. In the letter just mentioned he says:

> One day, when we were holding the Book of Numbers in our hands, she—Fabiola—modestly asked me what such a great accumulation of names meant, why, and so forth . . . I answered as best I could, and I seemed to have satisfied her question. But as she turned through the book, she reached the place where the catalogue is given of all the stations through which the people, departing from Egypt, reached the streams of the Jordan. As she sought the causes and explanations of each one, I hesitated over some, ran forward without stumbling over others, and in most cases simply confessed my ignorance. Then she began to press me more strongly, as though I were not permitted not to know what I did not know, and complained that she was unworthy of such mysteries. What more can I say? The shame of refusing forced me to promise her a work of this sort, a little treatise in discussion. This work, delayed until the present time—as I now understand, by the will of the Lord—will be delivered to her memory, so that, clothed in the priestly garments of the earlier volume addressed to her, she may rejoice that she has at last come through the solitude of this world to the Promised Land.

We have also assigned to this period the letter that the holy Father wrote to Salvina, a widow of the noblest family. He consoles her over the death of her husband Nebridius and then instructs her how she ought to raise the children who survived him and what manner of life she herself ought to lead.

The principal reason for assigning it here was the statement that Salvina’s mother was then with her at Constantinople:

> Certainly, since your holy mother is with you . . .

She must be believed to have gone to Constantinople only after the death of her husband Gildo, in 398. We have explained the remaining reasons in the chronological notes attached to the letter, showing why it should not be postponed to a later time.

Finally, in this same year—or, at the latest, at the beginning of the following year—Jerome replied to the questions Paulinus had put to him. Almost the whole structure of the letter indicates this. Most decisive is the passage in which the holy Father excuses the delay in his reply:

> Recently, at the command of our Pammachius, I translated the books *Περὶ Ἀρχῶν* . . . Detained by this work, I could not fulfill what I had promised you, and I postponed our Daniel once again. Although Pammachius is a man most devoted to me and of outstanding character, I would have postponed the will of this one man to another time, unless nearly the whole brotherhood of that same City had made the request, asserting that many were in danger and yielding to perverse doctrines. Thus necessity compelled me to translate books in which there is more evil than good, and to observe this measure: neither to add anything nor to take anything away, but to preserve the Greek faith with Latin integrity. You can borrow copies of these from the brother mentioned above, and so forth.

**VII.** Let us return to the history of the disputes between Jerome and Rufinus, to which the passage just quoted draws our attention. When, as usually happens, Roman opinion divided into two parties, some favoring Rufinus and others Jerome, a certain Apronianus—by far the noblest of the Romans, formerly brought from the worship of idols to faith in Christ through the efforts of Rufinus and Melania, and most devoted to his spiritual father in Christ—sent Rufinus a copy of Jerome’s translation and letter at Aquileia and, as we may reasonably believe, urged him to reply.

The chief cause of these disagreements must indeed be attributed to the partisans of both names. Although they were excellent Catholics, acting with good judgment and good will, they feared for themselves the stumbling-blocks involved and were carried away by devotion to the party whose name they had adopted. In this way they stirred up such flames of dissension.

> We could not remain silent, Rufinus says, without violating our conscience, since some were treating our silence as almost a betrayal of their own faith.

Having received Jerome’s writings, which he believed had been composed as an insult to himself, Rufinus immediately applied his mind to answering them, considering that they could not be neglected.

Before I speak of his reply, however, the events that preceded it in the East, and that bear especially upon this matter, must be explained.

As soon as Theophilus, Bishop of Alexandria, had reconciled peace between John and Jerome, he suddenly changed his attitude toward Origen, whom he had previously favored with great enthusiasm, and turned his forces against him. After making a few particularly bitter attacks or statements against those who approved Origen’s views, he anathematized the Origenist doctrine and all its adherents with a terrible anathema, either as the year 399 was hastening to its close or, if one prefers, at the beginning of the following year.

Although Pagius and others contend that no synod was then held against the Origenists, Prosper seems to have remembered this synod in his *Imperial Chronicle*, where he says:

> A dispute arising from the teaching of Origen compelled a synod to assemble at Alexandria. Its decision was that anyone who approved the works of the aforesaid man should be outside the Church.

Soon afterward Theophilus sent a letter to Pope Anastasius, who had succeeded Siricius in the Roman see. He informed him that he had declared Origen a heretic to the peoples entrusted to him, and urged Anastasius likewise to condemn him in the Western Church and prohibit the reading of his works.

He also sent Jerome a letter of the same kind, announcing that wicked and deranged men, seeking to establish Origen’s heresy in the monasteries of Nitria, had been cut down by the prophetic sickle. He urged Jerome to correct, with suitable words from Scripture, any others who had been deceived.

The holy Father translated this letter into Latin; it is numbered LXXXVII in our recension. In the reply he made to it, after praising Theophilus’s zeal in the highest terms, he adds:

> Indeed, concerning this matter—the Origenist cause—even before you wrote, I had sent letters to the West, revealing to those who speak my language the tricks of the heretics—namely, the letter to Pammachius and Oceanus. I think it happened by God’s providence that, at the same time, you too wrote to Pope Anastasius and, without knowing my judgment, strengthened it. Now, however, having been warned by you, we shall apply ourselves more earnestly so that here and far away we may call the simple-minded back from error.

Near the end he adds:

> The presbyter Vincentius came from the City two days before I sent this letter. He respectfully greets you and repeatedly celebrates you in conversation, saying that Rome and almost all Italy have been liberated, after Christ, by your letters.

A considerable time had therefore elapsed since the Alexandrian pontiff had sent his letter to the Roman one. Since this reply of Jerome’s must nevertheless be included within the limits of the same year, 400, the former was written in winter, while the latter was composed at least by the approaching summer. Let us now see what Anastasius did in the meantime.

**VIII.** After receiving Theophilus’s letter, Anastasius was also presented by Eusebius of Cremona, that old friend of Jerome, with certain chapters of blasphemy which Eusebius had excerpted from Rufinus’s translation of the books *Περὶ Ἀρχῶν*, in order to intensify still further the hatred of Origen’s doctrine.

Anastasius then understood that it was his responsibility immediately to strike the dangerous head and silence the hissing mouths of the hydra. A synod was therefore convened at Rome—as we may reasonably believe. For, as the holy Leo the Great testifies, it was customary, following the prescriptions of the ancient Fathers, to hold assemblies of bishops twice each year, in spring and autumn (*Epist.* IV, chapter 7). After carefully weighing the matter on both sides, Anastasius branded Origen’s errors with the mark of heresy.

Testimonies to the condemnation pronounced against Origen, and indeed by synodal authority, occur frequently among the ancients, especially in Jerome. In Letter XCVII to Pammachius and Marcella he says:

> It has been widely proclaimed in public speech that the blessed Pope Anastasius, burning with the same zeal because he possesses the same Spirit, persecuted the heretics who were hiding in their dens, and that his letters show that what was condemned in the East was also condemned in the West.

And in Book II against Rufinus:

> The blessed bishops Anastasius, Theophilus, Venerius, and Chromatius, together with the entire Catholic synod of both East and West, denounce him—Origen—as a heretic to the peoples, with one and the same judgment because they possess one and the same Spirit.

Then, in Book III against the same man:

> Do you see that the lie does not hold together? And that what served you at a critical moment, enabling you to evade the judgment of the bishops, has now been exposed and examined?

Finally, Theophilus says in a letter to certain monks, a fragment of which Justinian quotes in his letter to Menas, and which reads in Latin as follows:

> Therefore, pronouncing anathema against Origen and the other heretics, as was done by us and by Anastasius, bishop of the holy Roman Church . . . whom the entire assembly of the blessed bishops of the West follows, accepting the judgment pronounced by the Church of Alexandria against the impious man.

Nothing is equally clear, however, as the evidence that fortune has allowed us to bring to light from an ancient manuscript of the Ambrosian Library. It contains the holy Pontiff’s own letter on this matter.

Anastasius immediately sent a letter to Simplicianus, Bishop of Milan, praising Theophilus’s zeal at length and reporting that he had been summoned by Theophilus’s letter. He begins by pronouncing anathema against the Origenist heresy:

> To the lord brother Simplicianus, Anastasius.
>
> A shepherd is shown to have great concern and vigilance over his flock . . . In the same spirit, the holy and honorable man Theophilus, our brother and fellow bishop, does not cease to watch over the interests of salvation, lest the people of God, by reading Origen throughout the various churches, fall into great blasphemies. Having been summoned by the letter mentioned, I address Your Holiness: just as we, established in the City of Rome—which the glorious Peter, prince of the Apostles, founded and confirmed by his faith—have condemned these things we have mentioned and have earnestly requested that no one read them contrary to the command, and so that the ordinances of the Gospels . . .  
>
> Therefore, adhering to this command, we have declared that whatever was written by Origen in opposition to our faith is alien to us and has been punished. We have written this to Your Holiness through the presbyter Eusebius, who, carrying the warmth of faith and possessing love toward the Lord, presented certain chapters of blasphemy which we not only abhorred and judged, but which also led us to declare that, if any other things have been set forth by Origen, you should know that we have condemned them together with their author.

The date of this letter to Simplicianus can be inferred from its very address. Certain records establish that Simplicianus had already died by May or June of this year, 400, at the latest. Writing near the end of June, Paulinus of Nola reveals in Letter XX that Venerius had already succeeded him in the Milanese see:

> The new bishop of Milan also, your son until now and now your brother, Venerius, had already written to us after his ordination, and so forth.

The mention of Eusebius of Cremona, the presbyter whom Anastasius identifies as the bearer of the letters, also fits the circumstances. The sequence of events that we have touched upon indicates that Eusebius came to Milan at this very time, having still been staying in Rome.

It also appears that the event mentioned by Rufinus in Book I against Jerome occurred there: namely, that Eusebius adulterated copies of Rufinus’s translation with some impious statement. Rufinus says:

> When he was reciting such a statement at Milan, and I told him that what he was demanding was false, he was asked where he had received the copies and replied that a certain matron had given them to him.

Finally, thinking that he had made little progress, Anastasius turned against Rufinus himself, the author of the disturbance, and summoned him to Rome to give an account of himself.

Jerome indicates that Rufinus was not summoned alone, but that all the others throughout Italy who favored Origen were repeatedly called to clear themselves of suspicion of heresy. He attributes particular praise to Marcella because she had devoted all her strength to this task:

> This was the beginning of the condemnation of the heretics: when she brought forward witnesses who had first been instructed by them and afterward corrected from their heretical error; when she showed the multitude of the deceived; when she produced the impious volumes *Περὶ Ἀρχῶν*, which were shown to have been corrected by the hand of the scorpion—Rufinus; when the heretics, summoned by repeated letters to come and defend themselves, did not dare to come; and when the force of conscience was so great that they preferred to be condemned in their absence rather than be convicted in person.

**IX.** Rufinus was struggling with this harsher fortune when he decided to protect his reputation with pen and writings. First he undertook to answer Jerome’s letter to Pammachius, from which he sensed that the greater part of the harm against him had arisen.

The distinguished scholars Huetius, Cave, and others still maintain that this response has perished. They consider the books commonly entitled *Invectives* to be a work different from that response and believe that they were written to refute Jerome’s *Apology*, not his letter.

But Rufinus opposed them to the letter itself, as is clear from the entire context of his writing; even if no other arguments existed for the matter, this would be evident. He says that he was justly compelled, at least in part, to answer, since, unless he removed the mark of heresy that had already been fastened upon him, his reputation among many people would be endangered.

In the first book—for he divided this *Apology*, or *Invectives*, as they are usually called under their offensive title, into two books—he is occupied almost entirely with refuting accusations concerning his faith. He demonstrates that his doctrine concerning the Trinity, the Incarnation, the Resurrection, the Second Coming, and the future Judgment of the Savior—matters in which he was particularly accused of Origenist prejudices—is plainly one and the same as the doctrine of the Catholic Church.

He then says that he has no concern about Origen:

> Whether he stands with God or has fallen, he himself must see to it.

Nevertheless, he defends the translation of Origen’s books *Περὶ Ἀρχῶν* that he had prepared, using arguments and reasons that are certainly not contemptible. He complains bitterly about those who had dared, with malicious intent, to publish his uncorrected copies, obtained by theft, and who had attempted to disgrace him not only through distorted interpretation but also through the adulteration of his words.

In the second book he attacks Jerome chiefly and exercises a merciless criticism of all his actions and statements, especially of his Commentaries on Paul’s Epistles. We do not have time to pursue these matters.

Sixtus of Siena carefully excerpted each of Rufinus’s accusations in Book VI of his *Bibliotheca*—in the notes numbered 287 and following—and compared them with Jerome’s replies. It will be worthwhile to consult him.

### X.

Rufinus wrote this Apology not with the intention either of sending it to Jerome himself or of making it publicly available, but in order to share it with his Roman friends, especially Apronianus, to whom he had dedicated it, and thereby clear himself of the suspicion of heresy in their eyes—for it was of the greatest importance to him to have a good reputation among them. It also happened according to the author’s wish that it was by no means circulated among the general public, but, as Jerome says, was read only in corners and among those belonging to Rufinus’s own circle.

Jerome, however, interprets this as having been done with malicious deceit, so that they might deceive the credulity of simple people and deprive him of the opportunity to answer on his own behalf. Rufinus’s intention, on the other hand—as is gathered from the holy Father’s third book against him—was that it should be sent only to those who had been offended by Jerome’s words, and not to a wider audience. Indeed, it remained concealed from others for a long time, kept in the chests of friends, so that Pammachius and Marcella were later able to hear only certain principal points of it and send them, here and there, in abridged form to Jerome.

This explains why, when the complete work finally came into his hands after nearly three years, Our author said that Rufinus had labored for three years in composing it (Book III, Against Rufinus). That passage formerly misled, and still misleads, highly learned men who assert that Rufinus really spent three years working on the composition, whereas the sequence of events that we have set out makes it clear that it was begun and completed within a few days of the year 400, when that year was already drawing to a close.

But although the Aquileian presbyter had made himself highly acceptable to his Roman friends through that writing of his, he still had to satisfy Pope Anastasius, by whom, as we have just seen, he had been summoned to Rome to give an account of his case. At the same time, therefore, he sent him another, shorter Apology in defense of his faith, declining to make the journey by using these excuses:

> “Since,” he says, “I was restored to my parents after nearly thirty years, it would have been harsh and inhuman if I had abandoned so quickly those whom I had revisited only after so long a time. At the same time, the hardship of so long a journey has made me less capable of undertaking further exertions.”

He openly declares, however, that he is writing this chiefly in order to dispel the envy that his rivals had stirred up against him before Anastasius—not, as he says, “to wipe away a stain of suspicion from your holy mind, which, like a shrine of God, admits nothing unjust.”

He then clears himself by setting out his faith concerning the doctrines that were charged as heretical against Origen as author and against himself as translator: the Trinity of the Word, the Incarnation, the resurrection of the flesh, the Last Judgment, the eternal condemnation of the Devil, and finally the origin of souls.

Then, in defense of his translation of the books *On First Principles* (*Περὶ Ἀρχῶν*), which was virtually the central issue, he says:

> “I am neither Origen’s defender, nor his advocate, nor his first translator. Others performed this same work before me; I did it last, when asked by the brethren. If an order is given that something must not be done, the order is normally observed [Col. 0133] (or: ought to be observed) thereafter. If those who acted before the order are blamed, let the blame begin with the first. For, apart from this faith which I have set out above—that is, the faith held by the Roman Church, the Alexandrian Church, and our own Aquileian Church, and preached at Jerusalem—I have never had, nor do I have, nor shall I have any other faith in the name of Christ.”

This is, in a certain sense, the third book of his Apology. Jerome certainly counted it, together with two other writings against himself, when, at the beginning of his first book against Rufinus, he testified that Rufinus had composed “three books against me in Attic elegance,” and elsewhere referred to three volumes.

In reality, the holy Father understood this Apology addressed to Anastasius also to have been written against him, and he answered it point by point. Nevertheless, since only two books properly attack him—the books of the *Invectives*—the most learned men, in explaining this difficulty, have departed too far from the truth; nor, in the Preface to the second volume, did we previously succeed in determining the matter as it actually stood.

## CHAPTER XXXI

I. Theophilus declaims against the Origenists in his Paschal Letter. II. He then expels them from the monasteries of Nitria after convening a synod there. III. He also writes a synodical, or general, letter against them. IV. Other writings by him and by others on the same matter. V. Jerome translates all of them into Latin. VI. Beginning with the Paschal Letter. VII and VIII. From it the chronological order of his other translations is restored. IX. The authenticity of Jerome’s work in these matters is established.

### I.

For approximately the two-year period that followed the disturbances of the Western Church described above, the Origenist faction harassed the East with disorders and actions of the most savage kind. We shall touch briefly only on those matters most closely connected with the sequence of Jerome’s life, although almost the entire history of the affair is contained either in Jerome’s original writings or in those of others that he rendered into Latin.

As soon as Theophilus received the letters of Anastasius that have just been mentioned as lost—letters in which, as the holy Father appears to have noted, Anastasius stated that what had been condemned in the West had been condemned in the East (Epistle XCVII)—Theophilus took courage and became bolder. He declared a new and much more vigorous war against the Origenists.

It had long been customary in the Alexandrian Church, whose throne he occupied, for the bishops to announce each year at the beginning of the coming Easter, through circular letters to all the bishops of Egypt, the date on which it would fall. These letters were called *Paschal Letters* for that reason. On the occasion of Easter they exhorted the bishops to guard carefully the deposit of the true faith and to lead their lives in holiness, according as the circumstances of the Church required.

This year therefore occupies the first place in our recension among the three letters that Jerome translated into Latin—by which I mean that it occupies that place contrary to all the editions that preceded ours, in which the order is wholly inverted and confused. But more on this later.

In this letter Theophilus heaped together everything that might create hatred for Origenist opinions and devote the author himself to dire curses, mixing insults into every third word. Here he calls Origen guilty of the most shameless boldness; elsewhere, of manifest error, madness, ignorance, arrogance, impiety, delirium, stupidity, and whatever other terms might sharpen the malevolence of the readers. [Col. 0134]

Finally, he calls him one who acted under a demonic spirit, a patron of demons, perpetually blasphemous, and the most wicked author of blasphemies. Nor does he attack the adherents of Origen’s teaching in much milder terms. He orders them to depart, calls them “the most foolish of mortals,” and tells them to descend into Hell so that they may see with their own eyes that their teacher of impiety is there.

A little earlier he says:

> “Let those, therefore, be silent at last who, dreaming of the end of Christ’s kingdom, desire to be parasites upon Origen’s verbosity, and who, not walking with the faithful, pretend to possess a faith which they do not have,” and so forth.

Near the end he says:

> “Captivated by the sound of Origen’s eloquence, they do not look upon the truth of his doctrines. They are ashamed to confess their former error, and, blinded by the swelling of arrogance, they refuse to be disciples, lest, once corrected, they should appear to have previously been in error.”

By these words he attacks especially the monks of Nitria, who were deeply devoted to Origen and had by no means acquiesced in his condemnation at the preceding year’s synod. Yet they had not simply obeyed later either. They did indeed condemn those errors of their own accord, but they maintained that the errors were not Origen’s; rather, they belonged to heretics who had corrupted his works and inserted their own material into them.

### II.

Theophilus’s anger was provoked by the monks’ obstinacy. He was, by his own nature, a man unable to control his rage, but for the moment he decided that it was better to suppress his hatred, so that he might slaughter them at a suitable opportunity for revenge.

For a long time, if we may believe Palladius, the author of the *Life of Saint John Chrysostom*—who is certainly not the author of the *Historia Lausiaca*—as well as Socrates and Sozomen, he had been disguising private animosities under the pretext of the Church’s cause. He certainly hated his close and well-known kinsmen, the brothers commonly called “the Long Ones” because of their height, as well as the Isidore mentioned so often above. The ancient sources report various reasons for this hatred, though none of them can excuse Theophilus’s excessive severity toward Isidore.

Let us hear from Palladius, chapter VI near the end, how far his anger proceeded, whether under the pretext of Origenism or in order to pursue private injuries:

> “Theophilus sent letters to the neighboring bishops [of Nitria] and ordered certain leading men to be expelled from the mountain and from the inner desert—distinguished monks, without adding any reason. When these monks came down to Alexandria with the elders, they asked Theophilus to state the reason for which they had been condemned and expelled.
>
> “But he, fixing his bloodshot eyes like a dragon and looking grimly in the manner of a bull, was at one moment livid, at another pale, and at another bitterly smiling. Carried away by immoderate anger, he himself put an omophorion around the neck of Ammonius, a very old man, after striking his cheeks and bloodying his nose with his fists, crying out: ‘Heretic, anathematize Origen!’ Nothing concerning Origen had been proposed except Isidore’s request for a hearing.
>
> “For such anger, like a dog, gives birth blindly to both words and deeds.” [Col. 0135]

Thus, covered with blood and having received no answer, the monks returned to their monasteries and continued their established way of life, sharpening their minds through knowledge of the Scriptures, through which salvation is acquired. They cared all the less about his madness because they were conscious of no wrongdoing.

Theophilus was not satisfied with this. He sent to the neighboring bishops and convened a council against the monks, without summoning the monks themselves to defend themselves or granting them the opportunity to speak. He excommunicated three of the leading men, fearing at the same time to pronounce a sentence against the multitude, and made the perversity of their doctrines his pretext.

Those whom he had honored more highly than bishops as teachers, because of their life, doctrine, and age, he was not ashamed to call impostors, merely because they were favorably disposed toward Isidore.

Palladius then relates how Theophilus suborned five men from the monastery of Nitria itself to submit written accusations against the three elders, and himself composed the words of the false charge. He entered the office of the prefect and requested that these men be expelled from all Egypt by military force.

> “After receiving,” he continues, “a force apparently for this purpose, together with the order, he gathered a crowd of criminals who linger around positions of power and are ready for anything. He suddenly invaded the monasteries by night, after first stuffing with wine the boys who were with him.”

A little later, concerning Dioscorus, he says:

> “Then he plunders the mountain, assigning the little possessions of the monks as booty to the younger men. After the cells had been stripped, he searched for the three men whom they had lowered into a well, after placing a door over the mouth of the well. When he did not find them, he set fire to their cells with brushwood, burning all their books along with them,” and so forth.

When his uncontrolled anger had cooled somewhat, Theophilus returned to Alexandria, giving those holy men an opportunity to flee. Taking their cloaks immediately, they departed for Palestine and reached Aelia. Three hundred of the best monks of that mountain left with them, besides presbyters and deacons; the others dispersed to different places.

It was worthwhile to set these events out at somewhat greater length, even though the source from which they come is not entirely trustworthy in these matters. For when one compares them with what Theophilus relates in his Synodical, or General, Letter about the Origenists driven from the mountain of Nitria, one sees that all these events belong here. It is not another story or a narrative from another period, although Theophilus arranged the sequence of events to his own advantage.

### III.

Theophilus therefore immediately wrote the letter that Our author calls the Synodical, or encyclical, general, and uniform Letter to the bishops of Palestine and Cyprus, who had gathered at Aelia for the Encaenia.

In it he announced that, after assembling the bishops from the surrounding region—who, perhaps properly (*probe*) or perhaps nearly (*prope*), filled out the number required for a synod—he had proceeded to Nitria. There, in the presence of many Fathers who had hurried together from almost the whole of Egypt, the books of Origen were read, books in which he had labored with impious toil, and which were condemned by the agreement of all.

He then identified the principal errors, which he also said had previously been struck down by his own anathema. He stated that, because some of the monks of Nitria could not bear to see the author of so great an evil condemned together with his error, they had formed a mob and rushed to Alexandria, intending to kill him:

> “They joined their company certain poor men and slaves, enticed by the hope of food, and, forming a wedge, attempted to use force against us as we sat in Alexandria [Col. 0136].”

He adds:

> “I pass over how they attempted to inflict death upon us and by what ambushes they contrived it,” and so forth.

Then, representing them as deserters—though not as men expelled by himself from the monasteries—he adds:

> “They have been condemned and expelled from the Church. But, with stupidity joined to arrogance, they oppose the judgments of the bishops, striving by sedition to defend their fellow-heretic. Wandering through foreign provinces, they have the condemned man as their leader and take pride in this work.
>
> “I therefore beseech you, dearest brothers, that if they come there, you provoke them to tears by the commands of the Gospel . . . . . But, as I hear, imitating Satan, they run here and there and seek those whom they may devour by means of their impieties . . . . .
>
> “If, therefore, anywhere they attempt to disturb the brothers and the people entrusted to you, guard the Lord’s flock and restrain their mad assaults.”

### IV.

These are the very words that Jerome rendered into Latin from Theophilus’s Greek text, as he also rendered those passages that we extracted above from the first Paschal Letter.

The holy Father, though he detested Origenism with extraordinary hatred and was eager to contribute his labor to its eradication, both because he was often asked to do so and because he wished to do so voluntarily, found nothing more suitable for that purpose than to publish at greater length the judgments and writings of those who had attacked the Origenists by their authority, and to make them available in the language of his own people.

For this service he deserves the greatest gratitude. Even if human weakness and private hatreds may have entered into the conduct of the affair, the monuments by which the heretical faction was overthrown—and which the holy Father translated—are nevertheless free from that stain.

Moreover, since the Greek copies of those writings had long ago been lost, almost all the material available for the history of Origenism and for the defense of the Catholic faith as it was then asserted in the authentic acts must be drawn from these translations.

Jerome translated not only that Paschal Letter and the Synodical Letter, but also many other writings relating to the same affair, both by Theophilus and by others: the reply of the Synod of Jerusalem, and the writings of Dionysius, bishop of Lydda, of Epiphanius, and of others. In all likelihood, he translated everything that was composed against the Origenists during this year.

We have now brought the greater part of these writings to light and, since they were either wholly unknown before or had long been believed lost, have added them to Jerome’s other works as unquestionably genuine offspring of his intellect.

They are arranged there in a different order from the one that would now perhaps be more pleasing, and it seems not unreasonable to demand that they be arranged here according to that order. Yet, to state frankly what I think, that order is not sufficiently established either, and I do not see how anyone can be certain of the sequence amid such a great diversity of mutually conflicting testimonies—a diversity that no one who has not handled these documents would readily believe.

### V.

The holy Father therefore began with the translation of the Paschal Letter. It stands first in our edition and, in accordance with the most reliable rules of the Paschal cycle, announces the Easter of this very year 401, which is assigned to the nineteenth day of the month Pharmuthi, that is, April 14 [Col. 0137].

He probably rendered it into Latin at the beginning of spring. Thus, from that time until the summer of the following year, when he composed the third book against Rufinus, he could truthfully say that nearly two years had intervened. We shall cite the passage below.

Here it is appropriate to mention that the holy Translator himself notes the first part of that year when, in Epistle XCVII to Pammachius and Marcella, sending another Paschal Letter, he says:

> “Again I enrich you with Eastern wares, and I send Alexandrian treasures to Rome at the beginning of spring.”

Thus the phrase “at the beginning of spring” should refer to both Paschal Letters—the one for this year and the one for the following year—because of the adverb “again,” which affects both parts of the sentence.

The order of events therefore requires us to arrange the chronology in this way, so that some principle may subsequently become evident.

### VI.

Yet he himself names the Synodical Letter before the Paschal Letter, as appears from the remarkable testimony in Book III against Rufinus, where he says that he translated Theophilus’s writings:

> “For nearly two years I have translated his two letters—the Synodical and the Paschal, against Origen and his disciples, and others against Apollinaris and the same Origen—and I have given them to the people of our language to be read for the edification of the Church.”

Evidence for the same conclusion may also be drawn from the place occupied by the Synodical Letter in a manuscript of the Ambrosian Library, a codex whose gold is to be valued no less than its gems. It contains almost all the documents concerning the Origenist controversy and condemnation that Jerome translated into Latin, and there the Synodical Letter immediately precedes the Paschal Letter of this year.

It precedes it not through the whim or chance of a careless ancient copyist, but deliberately, as may be gathered from what follows. Otherwise the order and subject matter of the events would have required the reply of the Synod of Jerusalem to follow it, rather than that Paschal Letter, which is inserted between the two. On the evidence of a very ancient exemplar, and one easily attributable to Jerome’s own period, the arrangement indicates that it was once placed there.

We repeat these points because they still concern us in practice and because we wish them to be weighed by more learned readers. We also do so lest we should appear, when we formerly published the Synodical Letter itself, to have drawn too hastily from this order the conclusion that it had priority among the translations.

But if we say that the Synodical Letter was rendered into Latin first, it could not have become known to Jerome before September. For approximately the middle of that month it was sent, still written in Greek by its author, to the Palestinian bishops gathered at Aelia for the Encaenia.

The chronology of nearly two years noted by the holy Translator will therefore not stand unless we suppose that the letter was written in the preceding year, 400. That was once our view. But the subsequent sequence of events later appeared to oppose it, especially the fact that the Paschal Letter says nothing about the monks who had fled or about the many disturbances mentioned by the Synodical Letter. These belong to a later period, when those events occurred.

The letter may therefore be considered to have been written approximately nine months after the Paschal Letter, and Jerome translated it not long afterward, either toward the end of the same year, 401, or at the beginning of the following year.

### VII.

[Col. 0138]

As regards the translation itself, two other letters, unless we are very much mistaken, preceded it. One was Theophilus’s letter to Jerome, and the other was Jerome’s reply to him. In our edition they are designated respectively by the numbers LXXXIX and LXXXVI.

Theophilus writes through the monk Theodore, who was sailing to Rome. Since Theodore was glad to carry Anastasius the news of the defeat of the Origenists, he did not wish to depart before embracing and visiting Jerome and the holy brothers who were with him in the monastery, as though they were his own inmost being.

Theophilus adds:

> “When you have received him, rejoice for the peace of the Church. He has seen all the monasteries of Nitria and can report the self-restraint and gentleness of the monks: how, after the followers of Origen had been destroyed and driven away, peace was restored to the Church and the Lord’s discipline preserved. Would that those who are said secretly to be undermining the truth would also lay aside their hypocrisy among you.”

These appear to be Theophilus’s first letters to Our author in which he announced the expulsion of the Origenist monks from the mountain of Nitria.

Some time had already passed since the event. The monks who had remained at Nitria had already settled down after the uprising, and Theophilus had sent envoys to Palestine to pursue those who had fled, namely Priscus and Eubulus. Jerome politely complained that they had given him no letter to deliver to Theophilus:

> “Although, through the holy brothers Priscus and Eubulus, your message to us has ceased,” he says, “nevertheless, because . . .”

This letter of the holy Doctor—the second, I mean, among those under discussion—is, as many think, and not implausibly, a reply to that letter of Theophilus. It certainly gives a much clearer indication of its date.

> “Recently,” he says, “I received a letter from Your Blessedness, correcting the former silence and calling me back to my customary duty.”

Those writings, as I understand it, were none other than the frequently mentioned Synodical Letter. On receiving it, the holy Father says that he was recalled to his customary duty—namely, to translate it into Latin.

The former silence that the letter corrected, however, was not chiefly silence toward Jerome himself, but silence concerning the Origenist affair, as the following context makes clear:

> “You have shown that the silence until now was a dispensation, not an agreement. I speak freely to Your Reverence. We grieved that you were too patient, and, ignorant of the master's governance, we eagerly desired the destruction of the lost. But, as I see, you extended your hand for a long time and suspended the blow, so that you might strike more forcefully.”

The reference of the silence, and of the entire context, is clear. After composing the first Paschal Letter—that is, from the beginning of this year until then—Theophilus had kept silent and had conducted himself with considerable patience toward that contentious and combative class of monks who had never obeyed the repeated synods and admonitions of the bishops.

But in this year, around September, recognizing that he had now kept silent long enough and that action was necessary, he extended his hand and began to punish them. Palladius, Socrates, and Sozomen exaggerate these events somewhat because of their less favorable attitude toward Theophilus, but the affair was nevertheless no different from what the Synodical Letter itself indicates. [Col. 0139]

The recent writer who thinks that Jerome’s words just quoted refer to another period rather than to the time when the Origenists were expelled from the monasteries of Nitria and the Synodical Letter against them was composed has therefore departed entirely from what is probable.

### VIII.

It is also possible that two other letters were translated into Latin by Jerome before the Synodical Letter. One was written by Theophilus to Epiphanius, and the other by Epiphanius to Our author.

It matters little, however, to investigate too scrupulously which translation came first, since all of them were given Roman dress within a few months and before the following year.

In the first letter Theophilus tells Epiphanius that the serpents of Origen, emerging from their caves, had been cut down by the sword of the Gospel, and that the second group of monks of Nitria had been freed from the infectious disease.

He then says:

> “I was able to include in the General Letter—that is, the Synodical Letter—which I sent collectively to everyone, a few of the events that took place, as the shortness of time permitted.”

He asks Epiphanius, who had often fought such battles before them, to console those engaged in the struggle, assemble all the bishops of the island, and send Synodical Letters both to Theophilus and to the bishop of Constantinople—for Theophilus had understood that the monks who fled had sailed there—and to any others whom Epiphanius might think appropriate, so that by the agreement of all, Origen himself by name and the wicked heresy might be condemned.

The other letter, sent shortly afterward, records Epiphanius’s joy at the proscription of the Origenists. He sends Jerome Theophilus’s General Letter, evidently so that Jerome might easily translate it into Latin and publish it more widely.

Finally, he advises him to publish the books he had written against that heresy.

These indications show both that Jerome had not yet rendered the Synodical, or General, Letter into Latin and that this letter to him was written only a short time afterward.

We shall say shortly what evidence establishes that these translations too are genuinely Jerome’s.

### IX.

Afterward, then, he translated the Synodical Letter that has been praised a hundred times and for whose sake all this discussion has been undertaken. Unless the probable sequence of events deceives us, he did so in October or November. The chronology compels this conclusion, since we have determined that the autograph sent by the Alexandrian bishop collectively to the bishops was dispatched at the beginning of September.

At the same time, and in the same undertaking, he translated the reply of the Synod of Jerusalem to that letter—namely, another Synodical Letter from the bishops gathered at Aelia for the Encaenia, addressed to Theophilus.

It begins:

> “To the Lord and most honorable Bishop Theophilus, Eulogius, John, and the other bishops who were found at Jerusalem on the holy day of the Encaenia.”

The substance of the letter is that almost all Palestine, through the grace of Christ, was free from the scandal of heretics, except for a few who accepted the errors of Apollinaris.

The bishops nevertheless declare that they abhor those whom Theophilus had denounced in his letters, and that they will not receive those whom he had separated from communion either because of the perversity of their doctrines or for other reasons, until Theophilus himself grants pardon for their repentance, provided that they wish to condemn their errors. [Col. 0140]

At the same time Our author translated into Latin another reply to Theophilus, written by Dionysius, bishop of Lydda. Dionysius congratulates him on the expulsion (the manuscript reads “election”) of the most wicked blasphemers, the disciples of Origen (perhaps read “blasphemous”), and urges him not to cease persecuting them.

We have rescued these two letters, precious among all the monuments of ecclesiastical learning, from obscurity and almost complete destruction. They fill, in a most distinguished manner, a part of Jerome’s works that had previously been lacking.

That all these letters were given Latin form by Jerome is established, without considering the many other arguments, by the testimony of the holy Translator himself.

Nothing is clearer than the testimony already quoted above from his third book against Rufinus:

> “For nearly two years I have translated his [Theophilus’s] two letters, the Synodical and the Paschal, against Origen and his disciples, and others against Apollinaris and the same Origen, and I have given them to the people of our language to be read for the edification of the Church.”

As for the remaining letters, nothing is more explicit than what he says in Book I of the *Apology* against the same Rufinus, section 12:

> “If you think that whatever is said against Origen and his followers is said against you, then the letters of Pope Theophilus, and of Epiphanius and the other bishops, which I recently translated at their command, attack you and tear you to pieces.”

No other bishops besides those named above can reasonably be meant as having written letters against Origen and his followers that Jerome translated into Latin at that time—unless, above all, the Fathers of the Synod of Jerusalem and this Dionysius of Lydda are excluded, whose letters are here produced.

The circumstances themselves also required that when Jerome translated Theophilus’s Synodical Letter to them, he should translate their replies to him as well, since those replies greatly advanced the Church’s cause against the Origenists.

In Dionysius’s case, there was an additional reason for translating his letter: Jerome had long been joined to him by friendship. When Jerome had separated himself from communion with John of Jerusalem, he had sent him the catechumens whom he had in his monastery for baptism.

> “We sent them,” he says, “to Diospolis to be baptized by Dionysius, the confessing bishop.”

Everyone knows that Diospolis and Lydda are one city under different names.

With these works, then, the sequence of Jerome’s translations for this year comes to an end. It will be useful to place them before the eyes of readers as a kind of index:

- Theophilus’s First Paschal Letter.
- His letter to Jerome, beginning *Didici*.
- Jerome’s letter to Theophilus, beginning *Nuper*.
- Theophilus’s letter to Epiphanius.
- Epiphanius’s letter to Jerome.
- Theophilus’s Synodical Letter to the bishops of Palestine and Cyprus.
- The Synodical Letter of the Council of Jerusalem to Theophilus.
- Dionysius, bishop of Lydda, to the same.

## CHAPTER XXXII

[Col. 0141]

I. He translates Theophilus’s second Paschal Letter. II. He then replies to Rufinus’s synopsis of the books against him. III. The time at which he builds a hospice beside the monastery. IV. Rufinus sends him a complete copy of his *Invectives*. V. Together with a now-lost letter in which he attacks him and his books most bitterly. VI. Our author composes the third book of his *Apology* against him. VII. Although Saint Chromatius, bishop of Aquileia, asked him to refrain from writing against Rufinus. VIII. Concerning a spurious letter to the Africans published under his name. IX. He writes letters to various persons, which are listed.

### I.

The following year, scarcely begun, saw the publication of Theophilus’s second Paschal Letter against Apollinaris and Origen. It begins, “The first day of the solemn festival,” and it has been established that, contrary to all the editions that preceded ours, it must be assigned to this year according to the Paschal cycle.

Jerome immediately rendered it into Latin and, as soon as the sea became open to navigation, sent it to Rome together with the Greek exemplar, to establish the fidelity of his translation against his detractors. He sent it to Pammachius and Marcella.

He also sent them a letter, number XCVII in our recension, to which he attached the Paschal Letter and gave this opening:

> “Again I enrich you with Eastern wares, and at the beginning of spring I send Alexandrian treasures to Rome.”

This must have been at the beginning of March. The words themselves readily suggest “at the beginning of spring,” and I would have this date carefully noted for the purpose that I shall immediately explain.

A little later he says:

> “You lights of the Christian Senate, receive both the Greek and the Latin Letter this year as well, lest the heretics again claim that we have added or altered many things. In translating it I confess that I labored to preserve the elegance of the words with an equal gracefulness of interpretation.”

Earlier in the letter he had said much against the Origenists and against his rivals, who stitched together scraps of abuse from here and there. He then proceeds to speak especially against Rufinus, whom he repeatedly attacks sharply without naming him.

Yet he never mentions, even in a single word, the *Apology* that he had composed against Rufinus.

He necessarily should have mentioned it if it had already been completed at that time. First, he would have composed it only a few days before translating the Paschal Letter—for it is absolutely certain, as we shall soon show in its proper place, that it could not have been written earlier in this very year. Second, he addressed and sent this letter to the same Pammachius and Marcella, whom he was speaking to here in Rome. He could not have failed to mention to them the most recent work that he had sent them so recently that they could not yet have received it.

He therefore composed the *Apology* afterward.

But what need is there to say more? All the circumstances make it clear that the holy Doctor began this year by writing to Rome, and that he had sent none of his writings there during the preceding winter—that is, during approximately the two months that had just passed.

## II

Immediately, therefore, after these letters, and at the very beginning of this spring, the Holy Father set his hand to writing the *Apologies* [Col. 0142] against Rufinus. Those who think that this work was undertaken earlier, and that the books were written in the preceding year but published and sent to Rome only now, have escaped the notice of learned men because of the rest of their reasoning. For although they themselves freely admit that they could not have been sent to Rome before the spring of the following year—namely, this year—since, with winter already closing in and the sea moreover stormy, as they knew, a season suitable for navigation had to be awaited, they immediately destroy their first assumption by this second argument.

Indeed, they were not sent on the same occasion as the translation of the Paschal Letter, as is clear from all the circumstances of the case. Nor could they have been sent earlier, since that translation was ordered to hurry to Rome as soon as the sea opened, and the Letter to Marcella that accompanied it, concerning those books, as we showed some time ago, is entirely silent about them. The matter therefore proceeded in this order and manner.

When Pammachius and Marcella had been unable, without making any special effort, to obtain a complete copy of Rufinus’s work, they hastily extracted from it the principal points of the objections and sent them to Jerome. They added a letter in which they urged him more sharply to reply. They easily entrusted these things for delivery to his brother Paulinianus, who at this very time was returning from the West to Jerusalem and could report from personal testimony how abusively Jerome was being attacked by Rufinus’s friends.

We shall speak shortly of his departure and return, which preserve a memorable example of Jerome’s piety, lest we interrupt the thread of the history we have begun.

When Jerome had received these books, he immediately seized his pen to blunt his rival’s calumnies and wrote a twofold *Apology* against him. He dedicated it to those same Roman nobles who had sent him the synopsis of Rufinus’s work—namely, Pammachius and Marcella, not Marcellinus, as was once incorrectly read.

He began as follows:

> “From letters both yours and those of many others I have learned that I am being reproached in the school of Tyrannus—‘the tongue of my dogs among my enemies,’ as he himself has it—for translating the books *Περὶ Ἀρχῶν* [*On First Principles*] into Latin.”

We too noticed that Rufinus’s first name was Tyrannius, but only in a second investigation after Fontanini, whereas previously the word had seemed to us to derive from the name of a place. Jerome therefore calls him Tyrannus, or calls his school Tyrannian, twisting the name for purposes of ridicule; or else he is alluding to Acts 19:9, where it says that Paul was disputing in the school of Tyrannus.

In the first book he replies to each of his rival’s accusations. He also intersperses much concerning Pamphilus’s *Apology for Origen*, which he denies was the work of that martyr, and concerning Didymus, Eusebius of Caesarea, and other writers devoted to Origen; and he shows with what disposition and caution he himself had treated them.

In the second he specifically refutes Rufinus’s *Apology to Pope Anastasius*, in which he thought that a calumny was being contrived against him. He repeatedly quotes its individual passages word for word—as one may infer from this, that he had the whole work before his eyes—and engages with it as with an enemy. When he has accused its arguments of unsoundness or falsehood, he pursues the very wording and attacks the barbarism [Col. 0143] of its language with laughter and abuse.

At the end, after having pleaded in favor of his own translation of the Scriptures from Hebrew, he says that he is awaiting three volumes from his friend and is entirely absorbed in considering the mass of his accusations; except, he adds, that “it is less burdensome to beware of an avowed enemy than to endure a hidden foe under the name of a friend.”

It will become clear from what must shortly be said how great an effort this work cost the Holy Doctor. It appears to have been prepared with such haste that perhaps it was completed in one or two late-night sessions; certainly it was sent to Rome during this very month of March.

## III

Let us now mention briefly what we have learned about Paulinianus.

The reason why Jerome sent him to Stridon about two years and some months earlier, approximately in the middle of 399, he explains to Pammachius in these words, near the end of Letter 66:

> “In this province, after building a monastery and constructing beside it a hospice, lest perhaps Joseph with Mary, coming even now to Bethlehem, should find no lodging, we are overwhelmed by such crowds of monks pouring in from the whole world that we are able neither to abandon the work we have begun nor to carry a burden beyond our strength. Since what is said in the Gospel has almost happened to us—that we did not first calculate the expense of the tower that was to be built—we have been compelled to send our brother Paulinianus to our homeland, so that he might sell the half-ruined little estates that escaped the hands of the barbarians, as well as the property of our common parents, lest, by abandoning the ministry we have begun for the saints, we should provide laughter for slanderers and rivals.”

We formerly said that this Letter had been written nearly two years earlier, using other arguments. We now understand, however, from these remarks about Paulinianus—whose departure from the East we assign to this very year—that it must at least be placed in the middle of the year 399; and we are further convinced that it should be assigned to that date.

What we learn from these passages—and this is the main point—is an exceptionally striking example of Jerome’s piety, worthy of a principal place among the recollections of his life. For when he had already built a monastery, with Paula’s resources and efforts, to receive almost innumerable companies of monks, he also took to heart the guests who converged there from the whole world, drawn both by the sanctity of the place and by the fame of his name, and he could not fail in his duties toward them.

Since he had nothing else available for building a hospice, he did not spare even the patrimony of his family: he sold his parents’ property and little estates to pay for the construction, and so that he might generously provide whatever was necessary for daily life to those who came to him or passed through.

It is more astonishing still that he could devote such care to these matters, when his manner of life—and especially at this time, when he was troubled by disputes with heretics—kept him occupied with entirely different labors and studies. For several years earlier, when writing to Lucinius (Letter 71), he complained that, because of the continual presence and crowds of visitors, he had been unable to reread what he had written.

At this particular time, however, when his brother Paulinianus brought the proceeds from the estates, Jerome devoted himself wholly both to this work and to his writings. He himself indicates this clearly enough when, writing shortly afterward the third book against Rufinus, he says:

> “In the monastery hospitality is close [Col. 0144] to our heart, and we welcome all who come to us with a cheerful face of kindness. For we fear that Mary with Joseph may find no place in the hospice, and that Jesus may say to us, when excluded: ‘I was a guest, and you did not receive me.’”

Let us pursue the history.

## IV

The Holy Father had scarcely completed those books of the *Apology* when a copy of them was sent from the East to Rufinus at Aquileia by some merchant whose identity I do not know. It is uncertain whether Jerome himself entrusted them to the messenger, or someone else did so, as often happens, with the intention of sharpening the controversy still further.

The merchant, otherwise an unknown man, delivered those papers to the Aquileian presbyter and declared that, circumstances being as they were, he would immediately make the crossing back to the place from which he had come. He therefore granted only two days for a reply.

“Two days before the bearer of these things was to depart,” Rufinus says in the third *Apology* preserved by Jerome, “they came into my hands—the things you had declaimed against me.”

The Holy Father himself repeats this in the work just mentioned:

> “You testify that two days before you wrote your Letter to us my little books came into your hands, and for that reason you had no leisure to reply at ease. Otherwise, if you had spoken against us after reflection and preparation, you would have seemed to be hurling thunderbolts, not accusations.”

Jerome gave no credence to this. Indeed, he insisted that Rufinus could not even have read his writings in two days. But this belongs elsewhere.

Pressed by the narrow limit of two days—or perhaps a few more—Rufinus was unable to answer his adversary point by point. He therefore gave the very books that Jerome had refuted, but which Rufinus had not yet received, to the same merchant returning to the East, to deliver to Jerome, using the expedient we mentioned shortly before. He added a Letter filled with every kind of insult and threat, as we shall soon see.

“Do not,” he says, “buy off my secretary with much gold, as your friend Eusebius of Cremona did with regard to my drafts of the *Periarchon*, which had not yet been properly arranged, so that they might more easily falsify them—something no one, or scarcely anyone, would otherwise possess. Receive from me free of charge the codex that you would have wished to acquire at great expense.”

Jerome too speaks of these matters in Letter 102 to Augustine:

> “Calpurnius, surnamed the Wool-worker, sent me, with his customary recklessness, his slanders, which I have learned reached Africa as well through his efforts,” and so forth.

The Aquileian presbyter evidently thought that these books afforded him sufficient vengeance, so that he sent them everywhere and thought he had nothing to fear from his rivals.

## V

It is worthwhile to know the Letter he appended and specifically opposed to the books of Jerome that he had recently received. Although the Letter disappeared long ago, so that Gennadius does not even list it in his *Catalogue*, it is sufficiently known from the passages that the Holy Father repeatedly quotes from it.

At the beginning Rufinus rebukes Jerome and warns him not to continue this quarrel, lest his dispute become an offense to Christians and, by wrangling with one another, they bring spiritual death upon others.

“You write a Letter to me,” Jerome says, “to admonish me and to have me corrected, lest I become a scandal to the rest, and lest, while some rage, others be slaughtered.”

Gradually, however, Rufinus, driven on by the goads of anger [Col. 0145], attempts to frighten Jerome away from writing. He threatens him with death and demands punishment for what he has done through insults and disgraceful abuse, which he hurls at the Holy Doctor with the greatest severity.

Take a specimen from these passages; we are ashamed to recount them all. After ironically calling him a philosopher, rhetorician, grammarian, dialectician, Hebrew, Greek, Latin, and “trilingual” scholar, Rufinus continues:

> “You, who keep watch with the eyes of so many disciplines—how can you be forgiven if you have erred, rather than being covered by perpetual silence of shame?”

Again:

> “I wished to imitate you; but since he who was returning to you was hastening, I preferred to write a few words to you rather than write more widely to others about your slanders. My rebuke in a few particulars was superfluous, since what you openly profess is held against you in everything.”

And shortly afterward:

> “There, I tell you: who, I ask, permitted you to write in your commentaries some things about Origen, some about Apollinarius, and some about yourself, rather than writing everything either about Origen or from yourself or from another?”

Finally:

> “Do you have anything further with which to stretch the sinews of your loquacity?”

And:

> “You are indignant if I accuse you of speaking obscenely, although you, an ecclesiastical writer, take up the indecencies of comedies and the amusements of prostitutes and their lovers.”

As for the threats, they are attested not by Rufinus’s own words directly, but by Jerome, who repeatedly reproaches him for them.

“In the final part of the Letter,” he says, “you terrify me by announcing death, so that I dare not reply.”

And again:

> “You threaten me with death … you threaten destruction unless I remain silent.”

Finally:

> “You terrify me with your swords and threaten not an ecclesiastical judgment now, but the tribunals … If you believe otherwise, why do you wish to kill? Is anyone who disagrees with you to be killed?”

There are many other passages of this kind, but it would be tedious to recount them.

## VI

Jerome, however, was so far from being frightened by the words of his threatening rival that they rather increased his courage to publish Christian doctrine. Scarcely had he received Rufinus’s Letter when he sharpened his pen against it—if ever he had sharpened it more spiritedly against any other—and composed his own work, which is entitled the third book of his *Apology*.

The principal accusations that he had already refuted in the earlier books he again dismantles here, turning them back upon his adversary in such a way as to leave him no refuge.

He takes that Letter itself as the particular object of his refutation. After quoting its passages gradually and in order, he appends his own reply—entirely truthful, indeed, but steeped in sharp vinegar.

As for the point Rufinus raised—only one, since it bears most directly on the history we have undertaken to recount—concerning the narrow two-day period granted him for replying, Jerome answers:

> “Who will believe you, a most truthful man, that the merchant of Eastern goods—who had to sell what he had brought from here and purchase there what he would bring back here—was at Aquileia for only two days, so that you were forced to dictate a Letter against us hurriedly and extemporaneously? Are your books, which you polished for three years, more eloquent?”

And after a short interval:

> “The lie about the length of time is so obvious that I will not say you could not answer my writings in two days; you could not even read them in that time. From this it appears that you wrote that Letter over several days, or, if it was a hasty dictation, that you are excessively careless—since, though you are such an extemporaneous writer, you were worse when you had time to reflect.”

The whole remaining texture [Col. 0146] of the book is woven in the same spirit and style of eloquence. It is certainly no shorter than the two preceding books and is no less polished.

That it was nevertheless prepared in haste, perhaps in one or two late-night sessions, as was Jerome’s custom, is persuaded by the very sequence of events. For the first two books do not seem to have been capable of being delivered to Rufinus before April of this very year—unless we are mistaken in subtracting the periods that must be reckoned from their composition. Indeed, it is reasonable to believe that they were not delivered until about the middle of that month.

Rufinus then dispatched that thunderbolt of a Letter immediately after the two-day period—or, as Jerome insists, and as is more plausible, after several days. It certainly required nearly another month for the Letter to be returned to Jerome, given the maritime distance between Aquileia and Bethlehem.
