We have therefore reached approximately the end of May, the latest point to which the Holy Father’s reply can be deferred. For Jerome still thought that Anastasius was alive, since he had not yet received news of his recent death.

“Suppose,” he says in section 21, “that I fabricated the Letter of the preceding year. Who sent the recent writings to the East—in particular, Pope Anastasius’s Letter to John concerning Rufinus—in which Pope Anastasius adorns you with such flowers that, when you read it, you will begin to wish more to defend yourself than to accuse us? And do you produce the Letter of Siricius, who now sleeps in the Lord, while you disregard the words of Anastasius, who is alive?”

Anastasius died, however, not in December of the preceding year, as Pagius, Papebrochius, Constantius, and we ourselves once believed on the basis of other arguments, but in this very year, on the fifth day before the Kalends of May—that is, 27 April—the date on which his memory is recorded in most ecclesiastical calendars.

Baronius once calculated the matter in this way as well, and Tillemont later confirmed it with further arguments. Finally, the sequence of Jerome’s writings establishes the point.

Jerome could have remained unaware of his death for approximately one month, at most. No one should persuade himself that it remained unknown to him any longer.

The Holy Father therefore composed his book against Rufinus late in this month of May, having received only a very few days earlier the Letter of his adversary, which he was about to refute.

## VII

It appears that, on this same occasion—or certainly before Jerome began writing—he had been asked by the Aquileian bishop Saint Chromatius, with whom Rufinus was staying, to put an end to this great controversy, which had already begun to offend the minds of Christians.

Jerome wished to comply with this eminent man, to whom he was bound by an especially longstanding friendship and who was distinguished by the praises of piety and learning; he testified under oath that he had intended to do so.

But when he realized that, by being deterred from replying through threats, he would seem to confess the charge by abandoning his defense, he could not bring himself to endanger his reputation. He regretted being forced against his will to write.

“At the beginning of this very book,” he says:

> “I call Jesus, the judge of my conscience, as witness—he who will judge both this Letter and yours—that at the admonition of Saint Pope Chromatius I wished to remain silent, to put an end [Col. 0147] to our quarrels, and to overcome evil with good. But because you threaten me with destruction unless I remain silent, I am compelled to reply, lest by remaining silent I seem to acknowledge the crime, and lest you interpret my gentleness as the crime of a bad conscience.”

Moreover, the slanders that Rufinus’s messengers—whom Jerome calls Cereales and Anabasii—were spreading against him among the people, both at Rome and throughout Italy and the islands of Dalmatia, were numerous and serious. They were scattered like flying arrows of falsehood throughout the whole world. Jerome therefore had not merely the right but the necessity to receive them upon the shield of truth.

## VIII

Among these was a fabricated Letter circulated publicly under the name of the Holy Doctor. In it Jerome was made to declare that he deeply regretted having allowed himself, in his youth, to be deceived by the Hebrews and to render their volumes—which contained no truth at all—into Latin.

Eusebius of Cremona had first indicated that he had found this Letter among African bishops who had come to the imperial court on ecclesiastical business. They may easily have been the envoys sent by the Council of Carthage held on 13 September of the preceding year to the Emperor, to request from him the authority to manumit slaves in the Church. Augustine tells us that this permission was granted.

Fontanini, however, thinks that *comitatus* means the papal court, and believes that the envoys were sent to Anastasius on behalf of Venerius of Milan and Honorius Augustus, who had brought that Letter with them from Africa.

Whatever the facts may have been, the Holy Father was astonished when he heard this. He was even more amazed when the writings of many brothers from Rome informed him of the same matter. They asked whether the report was true and by whom the Letter had been circulated, and they communicated the news with tears.

It was not difficult for Jerome to demonstrate from the style and form of the language that the Letter had been falsely attributed to him, nor to conjecture that Rufinus was its author. Having removed the calumny of the writing, however, he spared the name of the forger.

But when Rufinus, realizing that he was being accused, repeatedly protested that he had never perpetrated anything of the kind, the Holy Father seems to have turned this very excuse into a charge against him: Rufinus had wrongly thought that something had been said against him which had not been attributed specifically to anyone.

Jerome nevertheless did not release him from responsibility for the crime.

“To what point,” he says in this third book, “will such unrestrained audacity not break forth? He attributed another’s crime to himself, so that we might appear to have invented it. What was said without a name he takes as said against himself; and while clearing himself of external sins, he is concerned only about the security of his own innocence.

“He swears that he did not write to the Africans under my name a Letter in which I confess that I was induced by Jews to translate lies; and he sends books containing precisely the things that he swears he did not know.

“I marvel how his prudence could have agreed with another’s wickedness, so that what another lied about in Africa this man would harmoniously affirm as true, and some ignorant person could imitate the elegance of his style.”

If, then, Rufinus himself fabricated that Letter—or if someone from his school did so, though not without his knowledge—Jerome was not unjust in treating him as guilty in either case.

## IX

It appears that for this reason in particular the Holy Father took care that this book of his should be brought to Africa as quickly as possible [Col. 0148]: namely, so that he might remove the calumny especially among those in whose midst it was said to have been fabricated.

Accordingly, in this very year he wrote to Augustine in Letter 102 and appended a copy of this very little book of his.

“Calpurnius, surnamed the Wool-worker,” he says, “sent me, with his customary recklessness, his slanders, which I have learned reached Africa as well through his efforts. I replied briefly and in part, and I sent you copies of his little book. I shall send the larger work—the first two books of my *Apology*—at the earliest opportunity, when circumstances permit. In it I took care not to injure Christian reputation, but only to refute the delirium, ignorance, and madness of a liar.”

There are also other Letters to Augustine, and Letters from Augustine to Jerome, written in this same year. We shall review them in the following chapter, where they properly belong within the sequence.

There is, moreover, another Letter that appears to have been written at this time, or in the immediately following year, on the basis of an argument drawn from the history of this controversy. Since it lacks more certain chronological markers, it may nevertheless appropriately be placed here, as the sequence of events permits.

It is an outstanding Letter among all Jerome’s exegetical writings on Holy Scripture, addressed to Sunnia and Fretella—men of Getic origin, as some maintain, and exceedingly eager for sacred learning. In it Jerome answers each of the questions they had put to him from the Psalms and teaches which readings among the Greek and Latin variants should be preferred to the others and which approach more closely to the Hebrew source.

In the chronological notes to that Letter we observed that it does not seem to have been composed before the books of the *Apology* against Rufinus. For when his rival accused him of despising the Seventy Interpreters and of preparing a new translation from the Hebrew in order to disparage them, the Holy Father would surely have opposed to him this very work of his, in which those Interpreters are consistently praised. It would have been unreasonable to overlook this splendid testimony in his own favor and instead to gather examples here and there from other works of his zeal toward them.

We added that the Letter did not seem to have been written much later, since it may be mentioned in the subsequent Letter to Laeta, where it is said that the Huns are learning the Psalter. That Letter seemed to have to be assigned either to this very year or to the beginning of the following year, 403.

Setting aside that conjecture for the present, we argue from another consideration that the Letter was written recently after Rufinus had been defeated. In commenting on Psalm 88, Jerome ironically calls Rufinus “the most eloquent interpreter of this age,” because he translated the Greek word *ἐξουδὲνωσας*—“you have annihilated,” or “you have nullified,” or “you have reduced to nothing”—and whatever other verbal monstrosities may be found among the unlearned.

All these arguments, however, are proposed as far as conjecture allows us to reach; we do not press them as certainties.

As for the Letter to Laeta, I would now prefer to assign it to the preceding year, 401, rather than defer it to the following year, 403, which had scarcely begun—although in our recension of the Letters I attached it to the latter year.

Laeta had married Toxotius, the son of Saint Paula, and by him had a daughter who was named Paula the Younger after her grandmother. The Holy Father teaches by what practices [Col. 0149] this child ought to be trained in Christian piety from the very beginning of her life.

Since her grandfather Albinus still persisted in paganism, Jerome, among the matters he magnificently praises as adornments and advances of the Christian cause, mentions something from which the date of the writing becomes sufficiently clear:

> “Marnas,” he says, “is mourning shut up in Gaza and continually fears the destruction of his temple.”

From the *Life of Saint Porphyry*, bishop of that city, it is known that in the year 398 a deacon was sent to the Emperor Arcadius to arrange for the suppression of the temple’s profane rites. A law was issued for this purpose in that same year, and not long afterward, by its authority, the doors of the temple itself were closed and Marnas was shut up.

Three years later, through a new embassy of Porphyry, permission was obtained for its complete destruction, and in fact the temple was consumed by fire.

When the Holy Father says, therefore, that Marnas continually fears the destruction of his temple, that calamity was already threatening the idol. This is more properly a sign of the year 401, which was hastening toward its end, than of the immediately following year.

The same period is also indicated clearly by the words that follow:

> “The red-haired and blond army of the Getae carries its tents around the churches, and for that reason perhaps they fight against us in an even battle, because they trust with equal religious conviction.”

For beginning in the year 400, the Goths invaded Italy and subsequently spread into other provinces. They fought vigorously—and not unsuccessfully—against the Roman army, as the histories of those times relate.

# Chapter XXXIII

I. A dispute arises between Jerome and Augustine.  
II. Letters are sent back and forth concerning this matter.  
III. A commentary on Obadiah is assigned to this period.  
IV. Saint Paula dies, and the Holy Father celebrates her praises in a Letter to Eustochium.  
V. At this time he translates Theophilus’s Paschal Letter into Latin.  
VI. Likewise, the Rule of Saint Pachomius, together with his Letters and those of Theodore, and their mystical sayings.  
VII. He disputes again against Augustine.  
VIII. Their Letters concerning this matter.  
IX. Certain other writings of the Holy Father belonging to this period.

## I

Long ago, when Augustine was reading Jerome’s commentaries on the Letter to the Galatians, he was somewhat offended at the passage where the Apostle recalls Peter from a pernicious dissimulation.

Jerome, for his part, did not think that Paul had truly opposed the Apostle Peter. Rather, he held that the event had occurred by a dispensation of both: Paul, a new soldier employing the old art of warfare, corrected Peter’s dispensation—by which Peter wished the Jews to be saved—with a new dispensation of contradiction. He opposed Peter to his face, not by criticizing his intention, but by seeming to contradict him publicly, so that, from the fact that Paul resisted him by reproving him, those who had believed from the Gentiles might be saved.

This interpretation troubled the bishop of Hippo. He thought that it undertook the defense of a lie through that dissimulation and that it was exceedingly destructive to believe that a lie could be found in the sacred books—that is, that the men through whom that Scripture was supplied and written for us had lied in their writings.

Augustine wished to resolve the difficulty in another way: namely, that Paul, observing the Law at that time in a manner [Col. 0150] that was not necessary, had not erred at all, but had rightly rebuked Peter, who by his example was compelling Gentiles to observe it.

This was the entire, or at least the principal, substance of the dispute. It had arisen much earlier, but only at this time began to be debated between them.

## II

The unhappy, so to speak, fate of the Letters sent back and forth was the reason why Jerome sometimes replied with an expression of irritation as well.

Augustine had first written about this matter as early as the year 394, but that Letter was never delivered to Jerome. Then, nearly three years later, he sent another to the same man. It wandered for a long time through Rome and Italy, and because it both urged Jerome to sing a *παλινῳδίαν*—a recantation—concerning his interpretation of the passage and was fairly lengthy, it gave rise to the rumor that the holy bishop had composed a book against Jerome and sent it to Rome.

Augustine himself, unaware of where this popular report had originated, wrote a third Letter to Jerome in the immediately preceding year, 402. He affirmed that he had done nothing of the kind that was being reported and that he in no way wished to incur the displeasure of one whom he respected and loved from the heart.

These Letters were finally delivered to Jerome in that same year, when Asterius the subdeacon was on the very point of departing from Palestine for Africa.

On this occasion Jerome replied:

> “It is indeed well that you satisfy me by saying that you did not send a book to Rome against my insignificance.”

But he adds:

> “Copies of a certain Letter, supposedly written to me by our brother the deacon Sysinnius, have reached us. In it you urge me to sing a *παλινῳδίαν* concerning a certain passage of the Apostle.”

For this reason, somewhat irritated, he continues:

> “I frankly confess to your Dignity that, although your style and *ἐπιχειρήματα*—your arguments—seemed to me to be yours, I did not think that copies of Letters should be trusted rashly, lest, if I replied, you might justly complain that I had been offended because I should first have proved that the words were yours, and only then written back.”

This Letter of the Holy Father, entrusted to Asterius, was nevertheless carried to Africa much later than it should have been.

Meanwhile Jerome wrote another very brief Letter to Augustine, in which he commended Praesidius to him and sent greetings to Alypius (Letter 103). The rest of it is filled with expressions of respect and affection. We have discussed it at length in the chronological notes, and we recommend that it be consulted there.

In the meantime Augustine, still unaware of Jerome’s reply, sent him two further Letters. The first is said to have been lost through the ravages of time. The other begins, “From the time when I began to write to you.” To it Augustine appended copies of his earlier Letters, since he did not know whether Jerome had received them.

In this Letter he opened the way to a new controversy by freely declaring that he did not approve of Jerome’s activity in translating the Scriptures from Hebrew, whose novel vocabulary often disturbed those accustomed to the old translation from the Greek.

He therefore reports that an uproar had arisen in Africa, in the Church of Oea, over the word “ivy,” which Jerome had used in a passage of Jonah instead of “gourd,” as the old Version [Col. 0151] read.

Jerome replies to the first of these Letters—to the one that has been lost—in Letter 105 of our recension. He protests against the injury he considered himself to have suffered from the bishop of Hippo much more sharply than before and complains that he had been provoked to reply by a Letter circulated publicly without a straightforward intention.

“If you criticize what I say face to face, demand an account of my writings, compel me to correct what I have written, and challenge me to a *παλινῳδίαν*, restoring my eyes to me, then friendship is injured and the rights of our relationship are violated.”

He nevertheless intersperses expressions of goodwill. So that one may understand that he wished to attribute the blame for the controversy chiefly to those who had delivered the entrusted Letters either too late or not at all, he concludes with these words:

> “Observe this request of mine: whatever you write to me, arrange that it reach me first.”

He does not mention his translation from Hebrew at all. This is clear evidence that, in the year 403, when he wrote this Letter—as we established in the chronological notes—he had not yet received Augustine’s other Letter on that subject, the one we mentioned earlier.

This was the end of their controversy for that year. It was renewed toward the end of the following year, 404, with somewhat greater intensity of feeling, but their love remained intact despite the dispute.

## III

We are convinced that during this period the Holy Father composed his commentaries on Obadiah, contrary to the opinion of almost all learned men, who maintain that he explained that prophet five years earlier, at the same time as Jonah.

The Holy Author himself says in the Preface to Book III on Amos:

> “Third, after a long silence, I have expounded Obadiah and Jonah for you, Pammachius, at your command.”

We have shown in the Preface placed before Volume VI, insofar as conjecture has allowed, how this passage should be understood and interpreted so that it may agree both with itself and with the other testimonies concerning this matter.

We derive the principal argument for assigning that work to this period from the Holy Father’s own words in the Prologue to the prophet, so that he himself may seem to assemble the chronology for us.

He says that from the time when, in his youth, he had attempted a sample of this commentary, he had already labored and sweated in the work of God for thirty years.

Then he explains what period this had been:

> “When, my Pammachius, we left the school of the rhetoricians and were carried along by different pursuits; when Heliodorus, my dearest companion, and I were striving together to inhabit the solitude of Chalcis.”

These words clearly mark the year 373 or the following year, as is known from the entire course of Jerome’s life and from the history prescribed in Chapter IX.

Nor could he more conveniently have attempted that exercise than during the time he spent at Antioch, immediately before withdrawing to the solitude of Chalcis, when, having recently heard the ecclesiastical teachers—especially Apollinarius—he tested the powers of his intellect.

If, therefore, you add thirty years to the year 373, the interval that elapsed, as he himself says, between that youthful trial of his talent and this work of mature old age, you arrive at 403 [Col. 0152]. We readily believe that the commentary was composed in that year.

The Holy Father’s account of that earlier exercise is well known:

> “I hoped that what I had written lay hidden in little chests, and I had consigned the first rashness of my small talent to the flames, when suddenly, after as many years as had elapsed since I had once written it, a copy was brought from Italy by a certain young man, praising my little work. I confess that I was astonished: however badly someone may have written, he finds a reader like himself. He praised it; I was ashamed. He raised its supposed mystical meanings to heaven; with bowed head I was constrained to confess my shame.”

So it happened, in accordance with the Author’s wish, that when this new commentary, complete in every respect, was published, that earlier specimen gradually disappeared and had already long since fallen into oblivion.

## IV

At the beginning of the following year, Saint Paula, Jerome’s supreme support and distinction, died. Then indeed his circumstances were shattered, and that entire gathering of saints—and especially of the virgins—was deprived, so to speak, of its light. She had been a woman of admirable holiness: as second to none in nobility of birth and wealth, so in the praises of Christian virtues she was by far the noblest, beyond what words can encompass. After her husband Toxotius, to whom she had borne five children, died, she devoted herself wholly to God and lived for a long time in Rome in her holy vocation. Then, after distributing among the poor nearly all the wealth of her extremely rich household, mindful neither of children, household, possessions, nor anything else belonging to this world, she sailed to the East and the holy places, despising her love for her children through a greater love for God, and finding contentment only in her daughter Eustochium, who was both her companion in her vocation and on her voyage. After carefully visiting the sacred places of Judaea and the monasteries of Egypt as far as Alexandria, together with Jerome, she settled at Bethlehem beside the Lord’s manger. There, after building a monastery for virgins, it is scarcely possible to say by what disciplines she fashioned herself after the pattern of the angelic life, or by what further examples and precepts she governed others.

Among her extraordinarily abundant virtues, humility, the first virtue of Christians, somehow stood out above all; then an almost unparalleled patience; a contempt for the world beyond admiration; and toward the poor and the sick, a charity and generosity that exceeded all measure. To these was added continual meditation on the Scriptures, together with knowledge of the Greek and Hebrew languages, by which she sustained the life of her soul, as though with heavenly nourishment, and advanced daily further in devotion and in knowledge of divine things. Though frequently afflicted by illnesses, and though her aged and weakened little body was broken, she practiced such great abstinence that even when she was at the point of death she refused to use wine for the restoration of her body, and allowed herself to be persuaded to do so neither by the physicians, nor by Jerome, nor finally by the man then present, a person of the highest piety and dignity, Blessed Pope Epiphanius.

Finally, laden with praises of virtues that almost surpass belief, the holy and blessed Paula fell asleep on the seventh day before the Kalends of February, on the third day of the Sabbath after sunset. She was buried on the fifth day before those same Kalends, during the consulship of Honorius Augustus for the sixth time and Aristenaetus. She lived in her holy vocation in Rome for five years, and in Bethlehem for twenty. The whole span of her life amounted to fifty-six years, eight months, and twenty-one days.

Jerome, who had been the constant admirer of all her virtues, was struck by such grief of heart that, although he wished to pursue her praises and had undertaken this task for her daughter Eustochium, he was for some time unable to do so because of his sorrow. For, he says:

> Whenever I tried to set my pen to work and to compose the promised work, my fingers stiffened, my hand fell, and my mind grew faint.

Nevertheless, he continued, and not long afterward did so with sufficient magnificence, dictating, in two nocturnal sittings, a book or Letter to which, as was customary, he gave the title *Epitaphium*, and which he addressed to that same virgin Eustochium. It now occupies place 108 in our recension; from it, too, most of the passages were taken from which we have just sampled the praises of the holy matron.

## V

We likewise assigned to that work the first place among the writings of this year. Since that holy woman flew away to heaven in January, scarcely after half the month had passed, it seemed least of all likely that Jerome, once he had recovered from that misfortune and had been able to turn his mind to writing, would have begun with any other composition than this one—which was especially dear to his heart and was owed to her memory, as an expression of gratitude. After fulfilling this duty, therefore, he proceeded to commit other matters to writing.

First, he translated into Latin Theophilus’s Paschal Letter—namely, the Paschal Letter of this year, 404, as is established by its announcement of Easter on the twenty-second day of the month Pharmuthi, that is, 18 April. It occupies number 100 in our recension; we have added the reasons for this in the Chronological Notes. This is the third of the Paschal Letters which the holy Father explained in Latin. Those who call it the fourth, and who argue with Baronius that the Paschal Letter of the immediately preceding year was also rendered into Latin by Jerome—although it has not survived—are completely mistaken.

It is preferable, however, to hear the holy Translator himself speaking about the matter in Letter 99, in which he excuses himself to Theophilus for translating it late, delayed partly by Paula’s death and partly by his own illness:

> From the time when I received the letters of Your Blessedness, together with the Paschal book, until the present day, I have been so harassed both by the sorrow of mourning and by anxiety, and by various rumors circulating here and there concerning the condition of the Church, that I could scarcely translate your volume into Latin. For you know very well, according to the ancient saying, “Eloquence cannot be sorrowful”—especially when bodily illness has been added to the sickness of the soul. And I dictated this very Letter while burning with fever and already confined to my bed for the fifth day, in excessive haste, briefly indicating to Your Blessedness that I had endured great labor in translating it, so as to transfer all its sentences with equal elegance, and so forth.

A little later he adds:

> Therefore I beg you to forgive my tardiness as well. For I have been so overcome by the death of the holy and venerable Paula that, apart from the translation of this book, I have written no other work of God down to the present day. For, as you know, we have suddenly lost the consolation which—God is witness to the conscience of us all—we do not count among our own necessities, but among the refreshment of the saints, for whom she carefully labored.

## VI

Some time afterward, still in this same year, and while the wound inflicted by Paula’s death had not yet closed, he prepared another translation from the Greek.

The circumstances were as follows. Since many Latins were living in the monasteries of the Thebaid and in the Monastery of Metenoea who did not know the Egyptian or Greek language in which the precepts of Pachomius, Theodore, and Orsiesius had been written, a certain man of God, the presbyter Silvanus, sent Jerome the books containing those precepts. They had already been translated from Egyptian into Greek. Silvanus repeatedly begged him to render them from Greek into Latin. For this purpose he also sent the presbyter Leontius and the other brothers with him, so that they might press the work forward and demand it almost moment by moment.

Our author therefore accepted the task and, pouring that Greek version into Latin, dictated it after summoning a secretary, so that he might obey men who, as he says, commanded rather than merely requested. When the work was complete, he prefixed to it a Preface of his own, in which he explains both the matters already touched upon and many other circumstances connected with the undertaking; these also provide information about its date.

At the beginning he indicates that it had long been since he had exercised his pen. He compares it to a sharp and polished sword which, if kept for a long time in its sheath, grows dull with rust and loses the brilliance of its former beauty. Hence, he continues:

> I, mourning over the falling asleep of the holy and venerable Paula … because I sighed for the comforts of many cut off by her death, received [this task], and so forth.

Among the other reasons for preparing this translation, he adds the following: that he might, as they say, break a long silence under a favorable omen, return to his former studies, and refresh the soul of the holy woman Paula, who had always burned with love for monasteries. He adds also that the venerable virgin, her daughter Eustochium, might have something to assign to the Sisters for their practice, and that our brothers might follow the examples of the Egyptians—that is, of the Tabennesian monks.

He proceeds to mention certain principal features, as they appear to be, of their way of life. After briefly setting these out, he speaks of the mystical Alphabet and the Letters of Cornelius and Syrus, who was then said to have lived beyond the age of one hundred and ten years. He declares that he had set down the elements as he found them, while in the rest he had imitated the simplicity of the Egyptian language, lest rhetorical speech should alter apostolic men who were wholly filled with spiritual grace. Finally, he says that he had deliberately omitted other matters contained in their treatises, because they seemed to be things that should be learned from their authors and sought out again from the sources themselves.

We were the first to add this Rule to the collection of Jerome’s works.

## VII

As this year was drawing to a close, the dispute with Augustine was renewed. Asterius the subdeacon, to whom our author had entrusted letters to be delivered to Augustine, together with another *Apology* against Rufinus, finally reached Africa. By then the Bishop of Hippo, unaware of Jerome’s response, had sent him the two other letters mentioned above. When Augustine received these, he understood that the holy Father’s mind was irritated and offended with him.

He therefore acted diligently to recover his good will. At the first opportunity offered by friends traveling to Palestine, he wrote him a Letter, numbered 110 in our recension, in which he addresses him with every expression of respect and strives to soothe him as humbly and submissively as possible. He also adds certain remarks about Jerome’s *Apology* against Rufinus, which he says he had received. Although he does not wish to pass judgment in either direction, he nevertheless grieves deeply and laments the miserable vicissitudes of human affairs, since they could make such great men, once the closest of friends, hateful to one another through so bitter a discord.

He attached another letter to this one, addressed to Praesidius—the very man whom Jerome had once commended to him and whom he knew to be joined to him by an old friendship. He earnestly asks Praesidius to ensure that the letter is delivered to Jerome and to reconcile him to Augustine by adding letters of his own. For this purpose he also appends copies of Jerome’s letters and of his own reply, so that Praesidius might understand more closely how to write to Jerome. At the same time he begs him to inform him as soon as possible, so that he might correct it, if anything he had written to the holy old man seemed unacceptable to him.

## VIII

Meanwhile, while these events were taking place—and certainly before he had received these latest letters from Augustine—our author replied in a single Letter to all the questions Augustine had raised with him in the earlier correspondence. This letter occupies place 112 in our recension. Although he says that, because the brother who was about to cross to Africa was in haste and almost already on the point of departure, he was replying in an improvised style and in a tumultuous manner—not with the deliberation of a writer, but with the rashness of one dictating—he nevertheless does not fail either himself or his arguments.

First, he satisfies Augustine concerning the title of the book in which he had enumerated both Greek and Latin ecclesiastical writers. He explains that the work is either *On Illustrious Men* or, more precisely, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, and not an *Epitaph*, as a certain brother had incorrectly reported to Augustine.

Second, he attempts to defend his opinion concerning Peter, whom Paul rebuked, against the charge of an officious lie. He vigorously supports it, as far as he can, both by the authority of the ancient commentators and by examples from Scripture and the context of sacred history, and finally by the force of the arguments which he develops and presses on both sides.

Indeed, he often sharply mocks Augustine’s opposing interpretation:

> Who, he says, could patiently hear this from Christians, which is contained in your Letter: “Paul was a Jew, but after becoming a Christian he had not abandoned the Jewish sacraments … and therefore undertook to celebrate them when he was already an Apostle of Christ, in order to teach that they were not harmful to those who wished to preserve them as they had received them from their parents through the Law.”

He then explains what it means that, in his earlier translation from the Septuagint, he had placed asterisks and obeli. He defends the other translation, derived from the Hebrew source, with great erudition, and proves that his labor in preparing it was not only well spent but also necessary for conquering the perfidy of the Jews and would be especially useful to the Churches.

Finally, he blows away the story about the ivy in place of the gourd in Jonah. He does not concern himself either with the ignorance of the populace, which had raised a riot for that reason, or with the malice of the Jews of that city, who had declared that their books contained what was found in the Greek and Latin versions. For he clearly demonstrates that the Hebrew word *qiqayon* can be translated more correctly as nothing other than “ivy.”

At the end of the Letter he asks that, through Augustine, he might be permitted to remain in peace as an old man who had completed his labors.

We have pursued these matters at somewhat greater length because it seemed useful to know what the causes of Jerome’s controversy and irritation had been. There is no doubt, however, that he recovered his composure as soon as he received the Letter of Augustine mentioned above, which was filled with so many expressions of submission and respect.

He received it only a few days later. Although he did not reply on that occasion, he nevertheless indicated not long afterward that he considered the matter settled, when Firmus, the necessary companion of the holy Bishop, was returning from Palestine to Africa and Jerome wrote him Letter 115. It displayed every sign of love and goodwill. Jerome also excused himself for having replied too freely and asked Augustine that, setting aside questions of this kind in the future, he converse amicably with him in the field of the sacred Scriptures.

This gave Augustine confidence to reopen the question of Peter rebuked by Paul, now secure from any offense on Jerome’s part, and to reply to him more carefully in an extended Letter, number 116 in our recension, affirming that Peter had been rebuked truthfully and deservedly.

In all other respects it is remarkable how humbly he conducts himself toward Jerome: he asks forgiveness if he has offended him anywhere through more careless expressions, and excuses himself because the earlier Letter had circulated through many hands, through no fault of his own, before reaching Jerome.

This was the end of that celebrated dispute between Jerome and Augustine, between whom thereafter there existed the closest grace and friendship. The year was drawing on when the controversy was brought to an end: it was 405, as is established by the Chronological Notes attached to the Augustine Letter just mentioned.

## IX

There is no doubt that during this period Jerome committed certain other works to writing.

In the immediately preceding year, the presbyter Riparius of Tarragona had informed him that Vigilantius taught that the ashes of the martyrs should not be honored and condemned the customary vigils of the faithful at their tombs. Jerome wrote him a Letter, number 109 in our recension, in which he attacks the impious heresy and, as though preparing for battle, offers himself ready to refute the man if the holy presbyter would send him Vigilantius’s pamphlets.

In the following section we shall show that the holy Father’s treatise against Vigilantius was composed in the year 406. In it Jerome himself testifies in the clearest words: “Concerning vigils and overnight services, often celebrated in the basilicas of the martyrs, I replied briefly in the Letter which I wrote nearly two years earlier to the holy presbyter Riparius.” There is therefore no room for doubt, after the dates are reckoned, that this Letter must be assigned to the year 404.

In the following year, 405, he wrote another Letter, or Letter 117, in the form of a little book to a mother and daughter living in Gaul. Its principal insistence and teaching was that widows and virgins ought to avoid domestic association with those from whom danger to either chastity or reputation might arise.

A certain brother from Gaul had reported to him that he had a virgin sister and a widowed mother who lived in separate cells in the same city. Whether because of the loneliness of their lodging or to guard their small possessions, they had taken certain clerics as their protectors, so that they were joined to strangers with greater disgrace than they had previously been separated from one another. The brother therefore asked the holy Father to correct them by letter and restore them to harmony.

When Jerome undertook this task and his Letter had been published for public circulation, some people claimed that he had invented the subject so that he could declaim with rhetorical exaggeration. He himself reports that this objection was made in the book against Vigilantius mentioned earlier, which we said was composed in 406:

> Lest the malicious interpreter should again say that I invented a subject to which I responded with rhetorical declamation—as I did with the subject of the mother and daughter in Gaul who were at odds with one another.

By this he clearly indicates that the work had recently been prepared by him. This is even more likely if, as scholars generally believe, that malicious interpreter was none other than Rufinus. Since Rufinus made no such accusation in his books of invective, he must be thought to have later babbled it orally. The work should therefore be assigned to this period, whether to the year 404 or to the following year.

# CHAPTER XXXIV

I. He translates from Greek Theophilus’s book against Saint John Chrysostom.  
II. He composes Commentaries on the Prophets Zechariah and Malachi, and also on Hosea, Joel, and Amos.  
III. He writes a book against Vigilantius.  
IV. Then, to Minervius and Alexander, concerning the Apostle’s words, “We shall all indeed sleep,” and so forth.  
V. And a Commentary on Daniel.  
VI. On this occasion he undergoes a very serious accusation.  
VII. His Letters to various persons.  
VIII. Finally, a Commentary on Isaiah.

## I

The Letter which bears number 113 in our recension was formerly joined with the following Letter as one continuous composition. This caused difficulty for the editors of Jerome’s works and led the writers of his Life astray. We have separated the text of the two and assigned them to two different authors: we have shown that one, although mutilated through the greater part of its length, has Jerome as its translator, while the other, which appeared to be complete, has him as its author.

The former, therefore, is Theophilus’s Letter, which he had prefixed to his book against John Chrysostom, or which he had sent together with the book to Jerome, asking him to translate it into Latin. Indeed, the whole structure of the dictation, although brief, bears the stamp of a translator rather than an author; this is all the more evident from the work’s purpose, since it mocks the sufferings of the most holy Father Chrysostom, who had again been driven from the See of Constantinople and sent into exile, and imputes monstrous crimes and offenses to him.

Even if Jerome was ultimately persuaded by Theophilus to pour those curses into Latin, it is wholly unbelievable that he ever cast such words against the holy Bishop from his own resources, however badly Chrysostom may have been spoken of in his presence. We have treated these matters at greater length in the Notes to that Letter.

Attached to it was the actual Book of Invectives, which our author likewise explained in Latin. Facundus of Hermiane, Book VI, chapter 5, calls it “an unshapely book, excessively horrible in its insults and curses.” But it has long since perished, as it deserved, meeting the fortune it had earned. For even at the time when it prevailed, it was received, as they say, with sidelong eyes, so that Facundus excuses himself, on the grounds of sheer necessity, for recalling certain passages from it.

We, having prefaced the same request for pardon, collected the fragments which Facundus quotes from Jerome’s version, as he himself testifies. We do not greatly regret the loss of the rest of that work of the holy Father. Would that he had never undertaken that translation, although we do not charge him with any fault for what he composed.

The other Letter, number 114, is Jerome’s own Letter to Theophilus, in which he returns to him his book translated into Latin and gives numerous reasons why he translated it late.

> Many obstacles intervened, he says, which delayed my returning your book, translated into Latin, to Your Blessedness: the sudden incursion of the Isaurians, the devastation of Phoenicia and Galilee, and the terror throughout Palestine, especially Jerusalem. In addition, there was the severity of winter and intolerable famine, particularly for us, who have been burdened with responsibility for many brothers. Amid these difficulties, the translation grew through profitable and, so to speak, stolen work by night. It was already being kept in drafts when, during the days of holy Lent, I needed only to make a clean copy after collating it. Then I was seized by a very serious illness and, as I entered the threshold of death, was preserved by the mercy of the Lord and by your prayers.

These circumstances once seemed to us to designate the year 406, since both the incursion of the Isaurians and the devastation of Palestine occurred in that year, followed by intolerable famine. The winter of that year also seemed to be indicated, for it is described as harsher than usual in several letters of Chrysostom, who had already been deposed.

But when the holy Father adds that during the days of Lent he was seized by a very serious illness and almost entered the threshold of death, if—as seems likely—he is referring to the same grave illness which he mentions in the third Preface to Amos, then just as this illness certainly occurred in 406, so the translation and the Letter must be assigned to that same period.

## II

Whatever the precise circumstances may have been, this much is certain: in this year Jerome illuminated with Commentaries five of the Minor Prophets who still remained to be explained—namely, Zechariah and Malachi—and, after some interval, three others: Hosea, Joel, and Amos.

He himself bears witness to this in the clearest words in the third Preface to Amos, mentioned earlier:

> In the present year, which entered the calendar under the consulship of Arcadius Augustus for the sixth time and of Anitius Probus—I mean 406, as the consular lists and other ancient records demonstrate—I have interpreted Zechariah for Exsuperius, Bishop of the Church of Toulouse, and the Prophet Malachi for Minervius and Alexander, monks of that same city. Immediately returning to the beginning of the volume, I could not refuse you, Pammachius, Hosea, Joel, and Amos.

And after his most serious bodily illness, he displayed his rashness by the speed of his dictation, so that he committed to chance—whose effects always follow those who dictate—what others do not dare to write after repeatedly revising their style. Thus he risked his ability and learning, since, as he often testified, he was unable to endure the labor of writing with his own hand.

## III

This work was interrupted by another brief book against Vigilantius, which the holy Father composed immediately after explaining Malachi and before returning to Hosea.

We indicated earlier what heresy that man had sown and in what places. He was in Gaul, for he was of that nation, as Gennadius reports; more precisely, he was from Calagurris, or from a village called Calagurris near the city of Convenae, in lower Aquitaine at the foot of the Pyrenees. There, as Gennadius likewise reports, he held a church in the capacity of parish priest. Since it bordered the parishes of the holy presbyters Riparius and Desiderius, those men greatly feared his proximity.

The Bishop under whose authority he lived also seemed to indulge his frenzy, either neglecting to correct his insane agitation or lacking the courage to do so.

These were the main points of his heresy: first, that there were no martyrs, that their relics should not be venerated, that vigils should not be held at their tombs in churches, and that no honors should be offered to them. Then, that we are not helped by the prayers of the saints, whose concern does not touch our needs and whose signs benefit only unbelievers. Third, that certain ceremonies of the Church, especially the lighting of candles during the day, bore the odor of pagan superstition, and that the Alleluia should be sung only at Easter.

He also taught that renunciation of worldly possessions was not a matter for praise; rather, the poverty and solitude of monks appeared to be idleness and a shameful flight. He condemned alms that were customarily sent to Jerusalem for the support of the saints. Finally, he maintained that clerics ought not at all to be celibate, that no one’s chastity should be trusted, and that no celibates could be ordained.

This was the babbling of a man who had once practiced the trade of innkeeping as his way of life. He also committed these teachings to writing so that the poison might spread more widely.

Jerome had long been awaiting these writings. As soon as he received them, at the request of the holy presbyters Riparius and Desiderius, he refuted them point by point, just as he had undertaken to do for them two years earlier. He carried this out in a little book which he dictated in a single night’s work, since he could not afford to miss the opportunity provided by the extreme haste of the brother Sisinnius, who was traveling from Jerusalem to Egypt and then returning from there to Gaul.

That same Sisinnius was the man to whom the holy Father entrusted the Commentaries on Zechariah to be delivered to Exsuperius, Bishop of Toulouse. Jerome likewise cites his haste as the reason for the work’s completion in the Preface.

Since Jerome himself says that he composed these Commentaries, as we showed earlier, in the year 406—and indeed at its beginning, as we infer from the same Preface through other chronological considerations—it follows that this Book against Vigilantius must also be assigned to approximately the same part of that year.

The point mentioned earlier in our recension of the Letter to Riparius also reveals this same date. The holy Author himself testifies that from the time when he wrote that Letter concerning vigils and overnight services in the basilicas of the martyrs, nearly two years passed before he composed this little book. That Letter is undoubtedly assigned to the year 404.

## IV

At the same time, certainly taking advantage of Sisinnius’s departure, the holy Father replied to the questions put to him by the monks Minervius and Alexander.

He did not then answer all of them, but dealt specifically with the question concerning the Apostle’s words, “We shall all indeed sleep,” and so forth (1 Corinthians 15:51). This question seemed more difficult than all the others and had been proposed with greater urgency. He explains that he did not satisfy the remaining questions because of the narrowness of the time and the excessive pressure of other writings and letters which were being demanded from him simultaneously.

It is better to hear the matter in his own carefully formulated words, from which the date of this Letter itself also becomes clear:

> At the very moment of the departure of our holy brother Sisinnius, who had brought me your writings, I am compelled to dictate this reply, whatever it may be. Nor can I conceal the matter from your prudence; but I beg you not to refer this statement to glory, but rather to complete necessity, since I speak to you as though I were speaking to myself. He brought me many questions from holy brothers and sisters in your province, and I thought that I would have ample time to answer them, up to the day of Epiphany. While I was dictating answers to most of them in stolen hours of nighttime work, and, after completing the others, was reserving yours as though it were the most difficult, he suddenly arrived, declaring that he would depart at once. When I asked him to postpone his journey, he began to plead the famine in Libya, the needs of the monasteries of Egypt, the low level of the Nile’s waters, and the hunger of many people, so that I was almost guilty of offending God by wishing to retain him any longer. Accordingly, the under-thread and warp, the heddles and the web which I had prepared for your tunic, I have sent to you unfinished, so that whatever is lacking in me may be woven by your eloquence.

You may refer the remaining matters here yourself.

## V

The holy Father had now completed all his Commentaries on the Minor Prophets when he turned his attention to illuminating Daniel by the same labor.

In the Preface he says:

> Let us weave together the words of the Prophet himself, not according to our usual practice, setting everything forth and discussing everything, as we did in the Twelve Prophets, but explaining briefly and at intervals only those passages which are obscure.

The year 406 had therefore already passed, and the final explanation among the Twelve Prophets—the one on Amos—belongs, from the sequence of events and from the date given as the sixth consulship of Arcadius Augustus and the consulship of Anitius Probus, approximately to its latter part.

On the other hand, the year 408 had not yet begun, as will be clear from what we shall soon say about Stilicho’s death. This Commentary, then, was composed in the intervening year, 407. In its Preface the holy Author explains the entire *οἰκονομία*—the arrangement or providential plan—and the reasons for undertaking the work.

He then refutes the slanders of Porphyry, who had written a book specifically against Daniel, the twelfth in his series. He continually demonstrates that none of the Prophets spoke so openly about Christ:

> For he does not merely write that He is going to come, which He shares with the others; he also teaches when He will come. He arranges the kings in order, counts the years, and foretells the clearest signs.

He dedicates the work to Pammachius and Marcella, whom he addresses there in the most honorable terms:

> I beg you, Pammachius, most eager for learning (*φιλομαθέστατε*), and Marcella, the unique exemplar of Roman holiness, joined by faith and blood, to support my efforts with your prayers.

## VI

It then happened, through the wickedness of certain men who envied Jerome’s studies and the fame of his name, that a passage in one of his Commentaries was twisted into a very serious accusation, as though it had insulted Stilicho, then the leading man, who had risen from service among foreign peoples to command of the Roman army.

In explaining the great statue which Nebuchadnezzar had seen in an imagined vision, the holy Father said, according to Daniel, that the mystery of the fourth kingdom properly concerned the Romans, and that the statue’s feet and toes, partly iron and partly clay, were being most clearly demonstrated in his own time:

> For just as at the beginning nothing was stronger or harder than the Roman Empire, so at the end of the world nothing will be weaker, since in civil wars and against various nations we need the assistance of other barbarian peoples.

That these words were aimed at the barbarian commander was almost self-evident, so that his rivals would not have had to work very hard to fabricate an accusation against the holy Doctor. On the contrary, all the care of his supporters had to be devoted to referring the meaning elsewhere through a favorable interpretation of the passage and removing the not insignificant suspicion of injured majesty.

The matter turned out especially well for him because Stilicho was killed before evidence of the alleged crime could be brought forward. Jerome himself recounts the matter in the Preface to Book 11 of his Commentary on Isaiah, which he composed nearly three years later:

> One must not flatter rulers in such a way that the truth of the Sacred Scriptures is neglected. Nor is a general discussion an injury to one person, Stilicho; and when the benevolent care of my supporters was guarding against this, it was suddenly removed by God’s judgment.

The year was 408, and it was the month of August, when Stilicho was removed by violent hands. It is reasonable to suppose that six or seven months earlier, before that event, the holy Father’s Commentary had already reached the hands of the public, so that the accusation against him could be prepared, pressed by his rivals, and cautiously prevented and interpreted favorably by his supporters.

It is therefore established, as we were saying, that the year 408 had not yet dawned when he wrote on Daniel; rather, the immediately preceding year, 407, was clearly approaching its end.

## VII

The nearly two years that followed were spent writing letters to various persons, letters which, by their length and the character of their composition, had the appearance of books and treatises. One or two of these may be regarded as having been written in the preceding year; nevertheless, we have postponed reviewing them here lest we interrupt the historical sequence already begun.

The first place among them belongs to the letter to Julian, numbered CXVIII in our edition, in which the holy Father consoles a man formerly very wealthy because, within a few days, he had lost two daughters and his wife, as well as a considerable portion of his property through the incursions of the barbarians. He urges him toward the perfect life, following the example of Pammachius and Paulinus. Since he still calls Paulinus a presbyter, he clearly indicates that he wrote this before the year 409, in which Paulinus was made bishop. On the other hand, the year 407, more or less, is indicated when, among Julian’s afflictions, he recalls the devastation of the whole province by an enemy barbarian, and, amid the general depopulation, the destruction of Julian’s private property, the driving away of his herds of cattle, the binding and killing of his slaves, and similar calamities. These disasters occurred under Radagaisus in Tuscany and Italy, from which region Julian appears to have come, as the *Chronicle of Prosper* and other histories of those times show.

Soon afterward the holy Doctor received from the farthest regions of Gaul twelve Questions addressed to him by Hedibia, and eleven others from Algasia—women distinguished in many respects by piety and innocence, but especially eminent for their devotion to the study of the sacred Scriptures. Answering them individually and treating each set of questions with considerable accuracy, indeed in lengthy letters resembling commentaries (Letters CXX and CXXI), he nowhere mentions the devastation inflicted upon Gaul by the invasion of the Vandals and Alans. He would scarcely have passed over that disaster in silence had he written immediately after it. That event appears to have taken place, if we calculate the chronology correctly from the historical records of the period, on the day before the Kalends of January in the year 408.

It is highly probable, moreover, that the same Apodemius who had brought Algasia’s Questions—Prosper mentions him in the *Chronicle*—also carried from the same regions of Gaul those which Hedibia had sent. It is equally reasonable to believe that the answers to both women were sent at the same time, on the occasion of Apodemius’ return to his homeland. For since, in answer to Algasia’s tenth Question, the holy Father says that he had discussed Rempham in the prophet Amos more fully, and since that commentary belongs approximately to the end of the year 406, those letters must certainly be assigned to the following year, 407, or to 408.

The Letter CXXII to Rusticus, which follows these, likewise belongs to this period. Because Rusticus had broken the continence promised together with his wife Artemia, Jerome urges him to do penance and to visit the holy places, following his wife’s example. He also says that Rusticus was being summoned by the adverse fortunes of Gaul and by the miserable devastation of his province, which he places before his eyes:

> “But if the remnants of your property hold you back—so that you may see the deaths of your friends and fellow citizens, and the ruins of cities and villages—at least amid the evils of captivity, the fierce faces of the enemy, and the endless shipwrecks of your province, hold fast to the tablet of repentance.”

He magnifies such miseries in the following year, 409, when writing to Ageruchia to dissuade her from a second marriage:

> “Spain, already on the point of perishing, and Rome herself, fighting in her own lap not for glory but for survival—or rather, not even fighting, but purchasing her life with gold and all her possessions” (Letter CXXIII).

This was after the year 408, when, after its middle had passed, Rome was besieged by Alaric and, in order to purchase its survival, paid an enormous quantity of gold to the barbarian leader; this occurred through the crime of the half-barbarian traitor Stilico.

Finally, in this same year or in the immediately following one, he also wrote to Avitus, as the opening words of that letter themselves indicate:

> “About ten years ago the holy man Pammachius sent me certain notes by a man named Rufinus, containing translated volumes of Origen’s *Περὶ Ἀρχῶν* (*On First Principles*), or rather corrupted volumes, earnestly requesting that the translation preserve the Greek truth in Latin” (Letter CXXIV).

Indeed, around the year 399 Pammachius sent those notes to Jerome, as was demonstrated above in Chapter XXX. Nor should we omit the history which Jerome himself appends concerning that book of Origen, translated by him into Latin. He says:

> “He did as he wished, and I sent him the books. When he had read them, he was horrified and locked them away in a chest, lest, if they were brought before the public, they should wound the minds of many. A certain brother, who possessed zeal for God but not according to knowledge, asked that they be handed over for reading, promising to return them immediately. Because of the shortness of the time, he was unable to suspect the deception. The man who had received them for reading, having summoned scribes, copied the entire work, and returned the book much sooner than he had promised. With the same recklessness—or, to put it more mildly, stupidity—he entrusted to others what he had stolen badly, and they handled it worse. Since large books discussing mystical matters can scarcely retain the abbreviations of notes, especially when they are dictated secretly and rapidly, everything in them became confused, so that in most places they lack both order and meaning.”

For this reason, when Avitus earnestly requested it, Jerome sent him a copy of his translation, and throughout the letter noted what impious statements had been made by Origen and what precautions ought diligently to be taken against them.

## VIII

By this time the holy Father was writing his Commentary on Isaiah, a much greater work than any he had previously undertaken, in eighteen books. Of these, however, he had published the fifth—treating ten Visions in historical exposition—long before he undertook to explain the entire Prophet, having earnestly complied with the request of Bishop Amabilis, to whose name he dedicated it. We discussed this book above in Chapter XXVIII, as well as in the chronological notes to Letter LXVIII, where we showed that it belongs to the year 397.

Yet he appears not to have begun and completed the Commentary on the entire Prophet within a single year. It was a lengthy work; he complains in the prefaces that he was then occupied with other concerns, suffered from a shortage of scribes, and was nearly exhausted by old age and bodily weakness. He began it toward the end of 408, as he himself indicates in the passage mentioned earlier from the preface to Book XI, where he recounts that Stilico was suddenly removed by God’s judgment. He completed it after the middle of the following year, 409, as we infer from the preface to the first book of his Commentary on Ezekiel, and shall soon demonstrate more clearly from the continuous sequence of events.

Certainly he had completed the whole work before he received the news that Rome, once mistress of the world, had been captured and plundered by Alaric. The passage that seems to conflict with this chronology occurs at the beginning of Book III:

> “About thirty years ago, when I was in Constantinople and was being instructed in the study of the holy Scriptures by the most eloquent man Gregory of Nazianzus, then bishop of that city, I know that I dictated a brief and spontaneous treatise on this Vision, so as to test my little talent.”

This passage, which once caused difficulty for us as well, requires a considerate reader. For since, as we demonstrated above in its proper place, the year 381 was in progress when the holy Father was in Constantinople with Gregory of Nazianzus, and since Gregory in fact held the see of the imperial city only from May until July of that year, it would follow that the beginning of this Commentary had to be postponed by a full two years, that is, to the year 411 or at least 410. But Jerome himself, by using a round number, as it is called, together with the adverb “about,” leaves room for a more precise calculation, so that even if only thirty-two years had intervened, his statement remains consistent with both himself and his chronology.

# CHAPTER XXXV

I. Stunned by the news of Rome’s capture and Marcella’s death, he loses heart.  
II. Nevertheless, he later resumes his Commentary on Ezekiel.  
III. In a reply to Marcellinus, he complains of an invasion by the Saracens, from which he barely escaped alive.  
IV. He then writes Marcella’s epitaph to Principia.  
V. He also writes letters to Rusticus and Gaudentius.  
VI. He completes his Commentary on Ezekiel.  
VII. He writes to Demetrias and Dardanus.  
VIII. Some other writings and events in his life.

After Alaric had exacted an enormous quantity of gold from the Romans and made an agreement with them concerning the freedom of the city, he violated the treaty in the following year, 409. Returning with a powerful army of barbarians, he plundered Rome miserably on August 24 and throughout the following two days, devastating it with sword and fire.

Olympiodorus, quoted by Photius in *Codex* LXXX, Rufinus in the preface to Origen’s *Homilies on Numbers* as cited by Valesius, and Palladius in *The Lausiac History*, chapter CXVIII, report the most terrible slaughter. Following their chronology, we have assigned the fall of the city to this year, together with the most learned of chronologists, Pagi. We know, however, that the opinion of others is commonly accepted, according to which the event is transferred to the following year, 410; indeed, we ourselves once embraced that view.

Many Roman nobles suffered in this great disaster, including several of those who were connected with Jerome by friendship. Among them were Pammachius, whom the holy Father praises by name, and Marcella, whose epitaph he later composed, as we shall soon relate. When he received news of these calamities, he was so overwhelmed that he himself testifies that he was almost struck dumb. For a long time—indeed, for a full year and more—he was overcome by grief and remained silent, and he allowed the Commentary on Ezekiel, which he had scarcely begun, to fall from his hands.

## II

It is best to understand this from Jerome himself, when he finally returned to the work. He says in the first Prologue to Ezekiel:

> “After completing eighteen volumes of exposition on Isaiah, I wished to pass to Ezekiel, as I had often promised you and your mother of holy memory, Paula, O virgin of Christ Eustochium, and to lay, as they say, the final hand upon the prophetic work. And behold, suddenly the death of Pammachius and Marcella, the siege of Rome, and the death of many brothers and sisters were announced to me. I was so stunned and overwhelmed that for days and nights I thought of nothing except the salvation of all. I considered myself captive among the captivity of the saints, and I could not open my mouth until I learned something more certain, while I anxiously hung between hope and despair and tortured myself with the misfortunes of others. But after the brightest light of all the world had been extinguished—or rather, after the head of the Roman Empire had been cut off; or, to speak more truly, after the whole world had perished in one city—I became silent and was humbled, etc.

> “But because you persistently urge this upon me, and because a scar is gradually forming over the great wound; because the scorpion Rufinus is being pressed beneath the soil of Sicily between Enceladus and Porphyrion, and the many-headed hydra has at last ceased to hiss against us; and because a time has been granted when we ought not to answer the plots of heretics but to devote ourselves to the exposition of the Scriptures, I shall undertake the Prophet Ezekiel, whose difficulty is attested by the tradition of the Hebrews, etc.”

Rufinus, therefore, had already died; Jerome says that he was now pressed beneath the soil of Sicily. More precisely, this was at Messina, the last city of Italy, where Rufinus had taken refuge from the barbarian storm together with the two Melanias and others, amid the Sicilian mountains which, according to the fables of the poets, were superimposed upon the giants Enceladus and Porphyrion. “Porphyrio,” read incorrectly before our time, should be “Porphyrion.”

Rufinus died after the devastation of Rome, Latium, and subsequently Magna Graecia in the following year, 410, probably near its middle, if we give credence to the Martyrology repeatedly cited by the associates of the Bollandists under the name of the *Florarium Sanctorum*, in which his memory is recorded on June 14.

Jerome had at last obtained enough leisure to be free from the plots of the heretics and to devote himself calmly to the exposition of Scripture. All these circumstances clearly indicate that he had reached the beginning of the year 411.

## III

The same holy Father continued the account of his circumstances and life in Letter CXXVI, which he wrote in this same year, after several other letters that have been lost, to Marcellinus and Anapsychia. After explaining at length that he had once wished to expound the book of Ezekiel but, when calamities descended, had almost lost heart and remained silent for a long time because it was a time for tears, he adds:

> “But this year, after I had explained three books, a sudden attack of the barbarians … swept across the frontier of Egypt, Palestine, Phoenicia, and Syria like a torrent, carrying everything away with it, so that by Christ’s mercy we were scarcely able to escape their hands. I have sent two books to my holy daughter Fabiola”—the younger Fabiola, who withdrew from the devastation of the city and her homeland and took refuge in Africa—“and if you wish to have copies of them, you can borrow them from her. Because of the shortness of time I could not have others copied.”

The reason he could not have even the third book copied was easily that he was overwhelmed by the incredible crowds of people fleeing to him from the whole world and was occupied in performing the duties of hospitality toward everyone. He himself complains of this in the preface to the same book:

> “Every day holy Bethlehem receives as beggars men and women once distinguished and overflowing with every kind of wealth. Because we cannot help them, we grieve with them and join tears to tears. Burdened by the weight of our sacred task, and unable to bear seeing the crowds who stream to us without groaning, we have abandoned the exposition of Ezekiel and almost every other study; we desire to turn the words of Scripture into deeds, and not merely to speak holy things but to do them.”

## IV

During this period the holy Father was often and urgently asked by the virgin Principia to entrust the memory of the holy Marcella to writing. Until then, although two years had passed since Marcella’s death, he had remained silent under an extraordinary burden of grief, since he thought that he could produce nothing worthy of her praises. At length, finding a suitable opportunity, he addressed Letter CXXVII to Principia in our recension, by which, in a single composition, he discharged the duty owed to Marcella’s virtues.

He praises her magnificently as second to none both in the distinction of her family and in her devotion to God. Widowed in the seventh month after her marriage, she rejected the consul Cerealis when he sought to marry her and was the first woman of noble birth in Rome to profess the monastic life. By her example she drew many others to the same way of life.

He also elaborates at length upon the fact that, inflamed by devotion to the study of the sacred Scriptures, she had learned the divine writings with the utmost diligence from him while he was then living at Rome. To impress them more deeply upon her mind, she often wrote to him when he was absent, requesting explanations of difficult passages.

He further recounts what was accomplished through her efforts and her love of undefiled religion: the faction of the Origenists, which had begun to grow powerful at Rome, was exposed and destroyed. Finally, during the sack of Rome and her own captivity, he praises her especially because she maintained such steadfastness of mind that, when beaten with clubs and scourges, she seemed not to feel the tortures; amid bloodstained swords she found a place for piety; and after several days she fell asleep in the Lord with her body sound, whole, and vigorous.

## V

The holy Father should also be thought to have written around this time two other letters, one to the monk Rusticus and the other to Gaudentius. The first teaches in detail how a life worthy of a monk ought to be ordered. When he urges that poverty above all be embraced, he says:

> “Moreover, in accordance with the miseries of the present age and the swords raging everywhere, he is sufficiently rich who has no need of bread.”

A little earlier he reveals that he is referring to no other calamities than those just described—not, as some others maintain, to events that occurred five years earlier—when he indicates that Rufinus had already died, mocking his slowness under the name of Grunnius:

> “Grunnius advanced toward speech with a tortoise-like gait and, at certain intervals, barely snatched a few words, so that you would have thought him to be hiccupping rather than speaking. Yet whenever the table had been set and he had displayed a pile of books, with raised eyebrow, contracted nostrils, and wrinkled brow, he would snap his two fingers, etc.”

From these details you must admit that he intended to attack none other than Rufinus, who had died not long before.

The other letter, in which he instructed a little girl approximately two years old, named Pacatula, in the precepts that she would later read, so as to form her in Christian piety, gives the same indications of its date. Among the other calamities of the age that he laments, he says:

> “The world is collapsing … The renowned city, the head of the Roman Empire, has been swallowed up in a single conflagration; there is no region that does not contain Roman exiles.”

A little later:

> “Our Pacatula was born in these times. Amid such childish toys she passed through the first stage of life, destined to know tears before laughter.”

She must then have scarcely entered her third year. For he says that meanwhile she babbled with a talkative voice in her mother’s lap; and if she had by then learned the elements of letters, she could have done no more than join syllables.

## VI

The holy Father immediately returned to his Ezekiel. As his grief gradually subsided, he continued the work from Book IV through Book IX, toward the end of the year 412 and the beginning of the following year. The labor cost him so much that he could scarcely devote to the work the productive—or rather stolen—hours of the night. He says in the preface to Book VII:

> “I confess that I promised the expositions on Ezekiel long ago, but, occupied by people coming here from the whole world, I cannot fulfill my promise. There is no hour and no moment in which we do not encounter crowds of brothers, to such an extent that we must either close our door or abandon the study of the Scriptures, through which doors are to be opened. Therefore, during the productive—or rather stolen—hours of the night, which have begun to grow longer as winter approaches, we try to dictate by the little lamp whatever this work may be, and to relieve the weariness of our burning mind through interpretation.”

A little later he adds:

> “To this difficulty of dictating is added the fact that, because our eyes are dimmed by old age, we are wholly unable to reread the volumes of the Hebrews by the light of night. Even in the brightness of the sun and day, the smallness of the letters blinds us. We know the commentaries of the Greeks only through the voice of the brothers.”

Hindered by these difficulties, and by new ones continually arising, whenever he had obtained a little respite from his occupations and his delays, he dictated the remaining books at intervals. Thus he spent not only the remainder of the year 413 on this exposition, but also a large part of the following year.

Indeed, toward the end of that year he indicates that he had prepared Book IX, where he reports that Heraclianus, the count of Africa, a man more impious than the barbarians themselves, had *recently* paid the penalty for his treachery. This occurred in the year 413, when Lucianus was his colleague in the consulship, after the year had already passed its midpoint, or in the month of August. Prosper says that Heraclianus, guilty of revolt in Africa, lost both his office and his life.

The adverb “recently” must therefore refer to a period of time no longer than this—indeed, almost to the final days of that same year. The remaining books can consequently easily be assigned to the following year, 414. This is plainly established for the final two books, which explain the Vision of the Temple. When Jerome reached that part of the sanctuary in which the Holy of Holies and the altar of incense are described, he testifies that he preferred to interrupt the work for a while in order to write to the virgin Demetrias. As he himself says, he would “pass from altar to altar.”

## VII

Shortly before bringing that Commentary to an end, he therefore wrote this letter to the distinguished virgin, the daughter of Juliana and granddaughter of Proba. Having rejected an illustrious marriage and dedicated herself to Christ, she is urged to persevere in her holy purpose, and he teaches her by what duties and studies she may accomplish this.

That the year then in progress was 414 he makes sufficiently clear in several passages, especially where he says that thirty years earlier he had composed for Eustochium a book with a similar title, *On Preserving Virginity*. We have pursued the remaining details fully enough in the chronological notes.

In the same year, as it was drawing toward its end, he also wrote Letter CXXIX in our recension to Dardanus, concerning the Promised Land, apparently after completing his Commentary on Ezekiel. Dardanus is said already to have completed two terms of the prefecture, namely the prefecture of the Gauls. He had held the first in 409 and the second in 413, as is clear from the *Chronicle* of Prosper of Aquitaine, who records that Jovinus the usurper was overthrown chiefly through Dardanus’ efforts, after King Athaulf had withdrawn from Jovinus’ alliance.

That the letter should not be placed later is prevented by another testimony of the holy Father in Book I of his Commentaries on Jeremiah. He certainly composed that work in the immediately following year, and in Chapter III he refers to a law recently published by him (Gothofred, *Codex Theodosianus*, Book XII, title I, “Concerning Centurions,” Law 171).

## VIII

After this, ecclesiastical writers began to debate the origin of the soul, and the decision in this controversy was referred to Jerome. Paul Orosius, observing that the stain of Origenism was gradually infecting Spain, crossed over to Augustine in Africa. Among the many matters he raised with him was this question, since it was regarded as deriving from the sources of Adamantius—that is, Origen.

The Bishop of Hippo, however, did not dare to pronounce a judgment and advised Orosius to sail to Palestine to Jerome, as though to seek an oracle. Augustine also gave him two letters to deliver to Jerome on this matter, numbered CXXXI and the following in our recension.

The first reviews various opinions concerning the origin of the soul and asks to be taught which should chiefly be maintained, and how the position which Augustine had suggested in his letter to Marcellinus and Anapsychia—that new souls are created for those who are born—could be defended against the doctrine of the Pelagians. The second asks about the passage in the Letter of James: “Whoever offends in one point has become guilty of all.”

Orosius arrived around the springtime and remained there for some time.
