For, as we shall soon relate, he was present in that same year, 415, still in July, when he entered the lists against Pelagius at Jerusalem. Jerome lacked the leisure to answer Augustine’s letters, being occupied with so many controversies against the heretics from every direction. We shall relate this in due course, and Jerome himself gives this as the reason in Letter CXXXIV, which he wrote to Augustine in the following year.

# CHAPTER XXXVI

I. Pelagius brings his heresy into Palestine.  
II. Jerome attacks him while writing his Commentary on Jeremiah.  
III. He soon attacks him in a letter addressed to Ctesiphon.  
IV. He does the same in the second and third prefaces to Jeremiah.  
V. Then in his own work, namely the three books of the *Dialogues*.  
VI. He returns once more to his Commentaries, but leaves the work unfinished.  
VII. The Pelagians maltreat him and attack his monastery with fire and slaughter.  
VIII. Pope Innocent sends him consolatory letters concerning this.  
IX. He changes his residence but does not cease to oppose the heresy.  
X. Eustochium dies.  
XI. The holy Father himself dies.

## I

The Pelagian plague had by now intruded into Palestine from Africa and had infected several leading men of the Jerusalem Church. Everyone knows that this heresy received its name from Pelagius, its author. A few facts about him should be noted.

He was born in humble circumstances in Scotland. Hence Jerome calls him oppressed by Scottish porridge (Prologues I and II on Jeremiah), “a white dog, and corpulent,” from *Albin* or *Albion*, the name by which the Scots called their native island. Others call him “the British serpent” and “the Briton” (Prosper, *On the Origin of Augustine’s Error*, Book I, Letter 186).

Having adopted the discipline of the monastic life, he lived for a long time at Rome, not without some reputation for holiness, secretly scattering the seeds of his error while greatly fearing public exposure. He later came to Africa once and again, where he established Caelestius as the foremost of his disciples in error. Caelestius, having obtained the dignity of the presbyterate at Carthage, sounded the trumpet against the grace of Christ even more loudly than his master.

Pelagius himself went to Palestine and lived at Jerusalem, where he is said to have formed a friendship with Jerome while the latter did not yet know him well. The holy Father later testified that he had acted patiently toward that heresy lest he appear to injure an old relationship (Prologue IV on Jeremiah).

Nevertheless, he soon recognized that poisons of the heart lay hidden beneath the honey of Pelagius’ words. Already in the preceding year, 413, while composing Book VI of his Commentary on Ezekiel, he complained in the Prologue that the Hydra’s young shoots were reviving; that although the heretics had been struck down by God’s hand, the heresy itself had not died; and that it had left behind hereditary offspring of its hatred who, while pretending to be ours, did not abandon the poisons of their ancient mother.

Writing also to Demetrias—whom Pelagius himself had addressed in a letter ostensibly intended to instruct that most noble virgin, but steeped in the poison of his heresy—Jerome warned her to beware of the impious and criminal doctrine, namely the Pelagian doctrine, which he suspected had arisen from Origenism:

> “It once existed in Egypt and the eastern regions, and now, concealed as though in vipers’ dens, it exists among many people and pollutes the purity of those regions,” etc.

## II

In the following year Jerome undertook to write his Commentaries on Jeremiah. If his heretical opponents and rivals had allowed it, he wished to lay the final hand upon the prophetic work. This very heresy, however, prevented him from completing what he desired. From time to time he was compelled to turn his words and style against it; he interrupted the work he had begun, and as old age advanced, together with the other ailments that shortly preceded his death, he gradually abandoned it.

Nevertheless, he did not restrain himself in this very form of writing from attacking the impious doctrine and assailing its author, even though he spared his name. In the Prologue to the first book he calls him an unlearned slanderer, “snoring in excessive madness”; the most foolish follower of Grunnius and even of Jovinianus, who blasphemed through the words of others and was so ignorant that he did not even possess curses of his own.

## III

After completing this book, a certain Ctesiphon—Urbicus, or Urbicius, as he is called in some manuscripts—from the council of a holy and illustrious household, which appears to have supplied Pelagius and his associates with resources for sustaining life, consulted Jerome about this doctrine, which was already disturbing many people.

Jerome immediately answered him in Letter CXXXIII, arranged in the form of a treatise. He feared none of the threats of the heretics; rather, those threats gave him courage, since the heretics threatened him with the thunderbolts of their writings.

First, he rejects as fabrications of diabolical pride the *apatheia* (ἀπάθεια) and *amartēsia* (ἀμαρτησία)—the immunity from passions and the sinlessness—with which that excessively proud heresy propped itself up as though with a double support. He shows that these notions had been derived from the polluted springs of the philosophers, especially the Pythagoreans, who make man equal to God, and that they are carried over to the destruction of the Christian faith.

He then so firmly establishes the grace of God, by whose help we strive and are governed in every work, that he leaves no room for the verbal deceptions with which the heretics, under the pretext of free will, mocked the simpler-minded.

He challenges them to answer, to speak openly what they believe, and to deny nothing they have once written. Finally, he begs and warns Ctesiphon not to allow that holy and illustrious household to shelter, through one man—or at most three insignificant men—the filth of such enormous heresies; not to allow the disgrace of diabolical presumption and the most sordid association to exist where virtue and holiness had once been praised. Those who provide resources for such men should know that they are gathering a multitude of heretics, making enemies of Christ, and nourishing His adversaries.

That this was written in the year we have assigned, 415, is confirmed by the previously cited Orosius, *Apology*, chapter IV. Speaking of the Jerusalem assembly, which certainly took place toward the end of July of that year, and of Pelagius’ error—that a man can keep God’s commandments by his own powers—Orosius says:

> “The blessed Jerome condemned this in his letter which he recently published to Ctesiphon.”

## IV

The holy Father immediately returned to his Commentaries on Jeremiah. In the Prologue to the second book he says that he turned his ears aside for a while, lest he hear the judgment of blood and mourn the souls of those slain—those who, under the reputation of virtue, daily fall into pride and consider themselves like God.

He adds:

> “We have answered their madness as we were able, and, if the Lord grants life, we shall answer more fully.”

Meanwhile he published the third book, complaining in its Prologue that the Devil—a name by which he designates Pelagius’ sect—would not allow him to enjoy the desired peace and devote himself to the exposition of the sacred Scriptures. Instead, it worked day and night, openly and by ambush, mixing falsehoods with truths, or rather coating all its lies with a deceptive honey, so that the person who hears the sweetness of its words does not fear the poisons in its breast.

After other remarks of this kind, he says:

> “He barks through Albinus, the great and corpulent white dog”—Pelagius—“who can rage more with his heels than with his teeth. He has the offspring of the Scottish race, from the neighborhood of the Britons; for, according to the fables of the poets, he must be struck with a spiritual club so that, with his master Pluto, he may fall silent in eternal silence. But this belongs elsewhere,” etc.

## V

After completing this book, Jerome was in fact compelled once more to withdraw his hand from the prophetic exposition and undertake the work of his own which he had promised to produce against the heretics.

He composed it in the form of dialogues, under the names of Atticus the Catholic and Cretobulus the heretic, explaining in order the entire controversy concerning divine grace and free will, and answering each heretical proposition word for word.

The date at which he undertook it is worth noting. At the end of July of the present year, when the Jerusalem presbyters were striving against the enemy of the ancient faith, John the bishop, who favored the heretic, summoned a synod of the entire clergy. Orosius was also called to it and ordered to explain what he had brought from Africa against the Pelagian doctrine.

Pelagius was then introduced as well. Since he had a judge favorable to his party and interpreters drawn from his faction, who rendered Orosius’ Latin words into Greek, he avoided judgment by the synod and even turned the charge of heresy against his accuser.

Some days later John accused Orosius of blasphemy, a charge which Orosius was soon compelled to remove by publishing an *Apology*. In that work, while sometimes praising the faith defended by Jerome’s testimony, Orosius also reports that Jerome was at that time laboring over books of Dialogues against the heretical doctrine:

> “The blessed Jerome refutes this in the book which he is now writing, setting out the dispute in the form of a dialogue.”

The year was therefore already approaching its end when the books were completed and published, for the month of September was already underway when the Spanish presbyter wrote that Apology.

## VI

Somewhat later the holy Father returned for a third time to the Commentaries on Jeremiah. Distracted by various occupations, he prepared three more books, bringing the work as far as Book VI and the thirty-second chapter of the Prophet.

Yet he could not forget his battle against the heretics and was always alert for an opportunity to attack the enemies of the faith. In the Prologue to the fourth book he calls the patriarchs of their wicked sect Pythagoras, Zeno, Origen, Grunnius, Evagrius Ponticus, and Jovinianus. Introducing his own writings, he says:

> “Having long kept silence in answer to him, devouring my grief in silence, I have been compelled by the repeated complaints of the brothers; yet I have not hitherto gone so far as to set down the names of the authors”—especially Pelagius and Caelestius—“preferring that they be corrected rather than disgraced,” etc.

In the Prologue to the fifth book he says that in Jeremiah the bitterness of the heretics’ treachery is demonstrated by the “calathus,” and that they are identified with the persons of Hananiah, Shemaiah, and the priest Zephaniah, who conspired to bring about the Prophet’s death.

Finally, toward the end of the sixth book he gathers many testimonies from Scripture to blunt the impudence of those who think that man can fulfill everything he has promised to do.

The holy Father composed no further books of Commentaries on the remaining portion of the Prophet, as we appear to have proved in its proper place and in the general preface by certain arguments. Or, if he later added two or three books to complete the work—not, certainly, another fourteen, as was wrongly believed until now—those books must already have perished while the holy author was still alive, before they were published, in the plundering of his monastery which the Pelagian followers soon carried out. We shall relate that event shortly.

### VII

The history of that most wicked crime is as follows. Pelagius, having escaped from the assembly at Jerusalem through the intervention of John, as we have said, was summoned, after about five months, to Diospolis—the city called Lydda in Scripture—for a council at which approximately fourteen bishops from Palestine were present. The articles of error brought against him, as Pope Innocent puts it, he partly evaded and suppressed, partly confused in utter obscurity by turning many words back upon himself; some he cleared, as it might appear for the time being, by arguments that were rather false than sound; some he denied, and others he distorted through a false interpretation.

For the Greek bishops, being unable adequately to examine the heretical opinions written in Latin, and with no opponent present to press the case—for Erotes and Lazarus, who had come to Palestine from Gaul for this purpose, were unable to attend the synod because of the grave illness of one of them [Augustine, *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*]—he again deceived the judges. He left the Council of Diospolis as though acquitted, although his doctrine had plainly been condemned. Then the heretic celebrated a triumph, and, having circulated a letter of carnal vanity and arrogance [the same author, ibid.], he began to exalt himself and grow insolent, as though he had broken the attack of the Gauls, and to encourage both himself and his followers against the defenders of the true faith.

But against Jerome, who was then present and hostile to him, and against the holy brothers of his monastery, violence was inflicted not by writings or words but by fire and slaughter. At that time—the words are Augustine’s, near the end of his *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, where he recounts the impious deed with execration and tears—it is said that a great many evils were perpetrated with incredible audacity by some band of desperate men, who were reported to support Pelagius with great perversity: the servants and handmaids of God attached to the care of Saint Jerome were subjected to a most criminal massacre; a deacon was killed; the monastery buildings were burned; and scarcely could a more strongly fortified tower, by God’s mercy, protect Jerome himself from this assault and attack by the impious.

### VIII

There were many indications that John, the bishop who favored Pelagius, was not unaware of so great a crime. Jerome himself, as well as Eustochium and the younger Paula, immediately wrote letters on this matter to Innocent at Rome—none of which, however, survived to our time. They complained at length to the Pontiff about the impious and savage crime of those desperate men, imploring him to bring some aid to those suffering in their extremity, while saying that they still feared more than they complained of what they had endured. Yet, in keeping with their Christian modesty, they concealed both the man’s name and the cause.

The holy Pontiff replied in three letters, which are listed among Jerome’s letters as numbers 135 and following in the next two sections. The first, addressed to Aurelius and consisting of only a few lines, asks him to ensure that another letter be delivered as quickly as possible to Jerome. In that letter he consoles the holy Father in the gentlest terms and orders him to be of good courage, since, having suffered for the truth, he should await blessedness—the reward for labors undertaken in Christ—which he himself continually proclaimed to others. “Then,” he says, “if you have brought an open and manifest accusation against certain men, I shall either appoint competent judges, or, if anything more urgent and diligent can be done by us, I shall not delay.” Meanwhile, he explains what he thought should be done for the time being and what he subsequently did.

He addressed the third letter to John himself, the bishop whom, by the authority of the Apostolic See, he rebuked with sufficient severity. He charged him with guilt because he ought to have seen to it that the crime was not committed: “For,” he says, “the gravity of a priest is utterly condemned by the fact that so great a crime was completed in the Church.” Unless John thereafter corrected or checked the matter, ecclesiastical law would compel him to answer for the case of those who had been injured, since he had not defended them.

In the chronological notes attached to these letters, we have shown that they were written at the beginning of the year 417, several months after the crime committed against Jerome. From that point, recover the chronological sequence of the arguments. Innocent died shortly afterward, on the twelfth day of March, and was succeeded by Zosimus. Ancient records also indicate that not long afterward John of Jerusalem died and was succeeded by Praylus.

### IX

There are, however, other matters that continue the chronology of the period and the account of the holy Father’s writings. Letter 138, addressed to Riparius, indicates that Pelagian doctrines were finally rejected and that Catiline was expelled not only from the city but also from the territory of Palestine. It is not plausible that Jerome intended by that name to designate anyone other than Pelagius. He grieves greatly that many associates in the conspiracy remained, lingering at Joppa.

“But it seemed better to us,” he adds, “to change our location than to lose the truth of the faith and the pleasantness of the buildings and residences, or to be polluted by communion with those with whom, for the present, we would either have to yield or certainly fight every day, not with the tongue but with swords. You have, I think, learned everything through widespread report concerning what we have suffered and how the exalted hand of Christ has raged on our behalf against the enemy.”

Likewise, in the subsequent letter to Apronius, he announces that the heretics in the East had already been routed. “Here,” he says, “everything is quiet. Although they have not lost the poisons of their hearts, they nevertheless do not dare to open the mouth of impiety, but are like deaf adders that stop their ears” [Col. 0174]. “Our household, although utterly overthrown in its material possessions by the persecutions of the heretics, is, through Christ’s favor, full of spiritual riches.”

He reports more or less the same in Letter 141, addressed to Augustine, and in the letter that follows it. In the former, rejoicing in Augustine’s vigor against the Pelagians, he turns it to the glory of that same truth that all the heretics detest him. “They persecute me also,” he says, “with equal hatred, so that those whom they cannot kill with swords they may kill by their desire.” The latter letter indicates that many still remained who, even with their necks broken, did not bow, retaining their attachment to their former error, although they no longer possessed the freedom to preach it. There was also at least one powerful person who secretly favored them. “Jerusalem,” he says, “is captured and held by Nebuchadnezzar, nor does it wish to heed the counsels of Jeremiah,” and so forth.

All these matters, together with the remaining part of the year 417 and either all or at least the greater part of the following year, are clearly indicated by the additions to the history of Pelagius and by the various conditions of affairs.

### X

The following year, 419, brought Jerome, who was now hastening toward the end of his life, an accumulation of labors and sorrows. Eustochium died. Ever since the foundation of the Bethlehem monastery, after her mother Paula, she had been his one remaining light. She was a virgin, the holiest ornament of the Christian religion and of monastic life. I could not, in words, encompass her praises or the examples of virtue displayed by her over nearly twenty-five years.

Born into a leading Roman family—her father was Toxotius, of the Julian clan, from which she herself was also called Julia, and her mother, as we have said, was Saint Paula, descended from the line of the Scipios and the Pauluses—she considered all human things worthless amid the crowds and splendor of an exceedingly wealthy household and city. Despite the strongest efforts of her grandfather Hymetius and his wife Praetextata, she devoted her chastity to God.

She then followed her holy mother to Palestine. After the monastery of virgins had been built at Bethlehem, she strove with her mother in the same holy vocation toward the summit of evangelical perfection. After her mother had been called to heaven nearly fifteen years earlier, she alone administered the monastery, which Palladius reports consisted of fifty virgins. The fact that she lived through the extremely difficult times described above makes this clear.

More learned authorities assert that she died in this year, 419 [*Laus*, chapter 26]. The Roman Martyrology records the day on which she is commemorated as September 28, the day immediately preceding the memorial of her teacher Jerome.

Jerome was so overwhelmed with grief at her death that he almost lost heart. He himself testifies to this in Letter 143, written shortly afterward, though still within that same year, to Alypius and Augustine. With all his affairs already afflicted, he says that he no longer cared to reply to his enemies or those of the Church:

“As for what you ask—whether I have written against the books of Anianus, the false deacon of Celedae, who is abundantly fed so that he may supply the frivolous words of another’s blasphemy—you should know that I received the books themselves, sent on sheets, from our holy brother Eusebius, the presbyter [of Cremona], not long ago. From that time, either because illnesses were coming upon me or because of the death of your holy and venerable daughter Eustochium, I was so distressed that I almost thought them unworthy of consideration,” and so forth.

[Col. 0175]

### XI

No other writing of Jerome survives after this letter, nor is there any later mention of his deeds. It is easy to believe that God called the holy old man, worn out by age, labors, and illnesses, and dragging out rather than actively living his life, to the heavenly homeland and the deserved crown of glory in this year, 420.

Certainly, in that same year, Augustine wrote to Optatus of Milevis a letter numbered 144 in our recension. This letter, which was discovered and first published not long ago at Vienna, testifies that he had received no letter from Jerome concerning the question of the origin of the soul—a question that Jerome had undertaken to explain if life had permitted him to do so.

In the *Enchiridion*, however, which is said to have been written in the immediately following year, 421 [question 2, number 10, and question 1, number 4], Augustine mentions Jerome as having long since died and honors him with the title “of holy memory.”

Prosper agrees with this, and he deserves credence in this chronological matter, although we have shown that he is not sufficiently consistent with himself in assigning the date of Jerome’s birth. He says that Jerome ceased to live in the year 420, during the consulship of Theodosius IX and Constantius III, on the day before the Kalends of October. The calendars of the Church record that day as his memorial.

Unless we are mistaken, therefore, if we begin from approximately the year 346 when we trace the date of his birth—for we believe that we established this with many and by no means weak arguments in chapter I of this history—when the holy Father died he was in his seventy-fourth year.

We are not deterred by the fact that he calls himself almost decrepit in one place [Letter 142] and worn out by old age, descriptions that may not seem appropriate for a man who had only slightly passed seventy. Nor are we deterred by the fact that he calls Augustine, who was born scarcely eight years after him, his father in rank but his son in age [Letter 134]. As we showed long ago in the cited chapter I, such expressions are drawn from that ancient method of reckoning human age by periods of twenty years; they often designate the weakness of the body rather than age itself.

Yet these matters became the reason why later writers, whose testimonies we shall presently quote, extended the life of the holy Father for many more years, even to ninety-seven and beyond. Some even write that he passed his hundredth year. They also relate that his strength failed so completely that he could not rise from bed unless he grasped with his hands a rope hanging from a beam for that purpose. Then, they say, he fell into a slight fever, which dissolved him, already dead in the flesh.

They report that monks, virgins dedicated to Christ, and others from all around the holy places were present beside him, and that he looked upon them with a lively and joyful face; along with other similar details. Although these accounts are not without probability, they are asserted by no certain authority.

I pass over the fables of the pseudo-Eusebius addressed to Damasus of Porto, whose credibility I would not have considered at all. Jerome was buried at Bethlehem, where he had spent the greater part of his life. Later transferred to Rome, he is venerated with the greatest devotion by the throngs of the people in the church of Saint Mary Major above the Esquiline, and has been honored with the title of the greatest among the Doctors of the Church.

These are the matters concerning Jerome’s life that I have had to commit to writing, Most Eminent Cardinal RIVERA, and which I wished to inscribe to your most illustrious name, so that it may be evident to all that, if I have achieved anything in preparing an edition of his works, I owe it to your protection and encouragement.

[Col. 0175]

## HERE BEGINS [Note: [Col. 0175]]

The illustrious Mabillon was the first to publish this life from ancient manuscripts and attributed it to Gennadius of Marseille; several others from the scholarly circle followed him. Martianaeus himself also did so—a man thoroughly experienced in the revision, not merely the reading, of Jerome’s works—who declared that the attribution seemed plausible to him, both because of the style and because of the silence concerning the case of Rufinus of Aquileia, whom Gennadius strongly favored.

Yet both the subject itself and the entire structure of the work persuade us otherwise. Gennadius favored Rufinus against Jerome so strongly that, in his *Catalogue*, he calls the former a detractor driven by rivalry and the latter no small figure among the Doctors of the Church. It is utterly incredible that he would ever have wished to adorn with praise the deeds of one whose name and virtues he treated so unfairly.

Moreover, this life contains nothing that the true Gennadius could, or indeed should, have reported. Whoever its author was, he was content to describe Jerome and has almost nothing that he did not transfer from Jerome’s own writings. Almost everything he added from himself is false and gives off the odor of tales from later times.

Finally, the somewhat less polished style than that of Gennadius, and the whole appearance of the composition, point to a writer of the eighth or ninth century rather than the fifth.

## LIFE OF SAINT JEROME, PRESBYTER [Note: [Col. 0176]]

We compared this little book with three ancient and sufficiently corrected manuscript codices and established its text according to their testimony. The first is designated Vaticanus, number 641. The other two are also from the same library, but they are among those that once belonged to Queen Christina of Sweden; hence we refer to them by that name. One is designated number 488, the other number 523.

Finally, we also consulted the Variant Readings that Martianaeus published separately and referred to the end of this very Life, and we have transferred them here. They were excerpted from five manuscript codices, which he calls “most ancient”: one from Corbie, another from the Church of Narbonne, a third from the Monastery of the Great Forest near Bordeaux, a fourth from Luxeuil, and a fifth from Saint Gall.

Here, in the very first words, the other Regina manuscript has *Blessed* in place of *Saint*. The Vatican manuscript adds *and Confessor* after *Presbyter*. Three of those cited by Martianaeus read *Orthodox Presbyter*. The Narbonne manuscript diverges farther and offers another title: *On the Nativity of Saint Jerome the Presbyter*.

### HIERONYMUS, PRESBYTER. (C, S)*

[Col. 0175]

Our Jerome was born to his father Eusebius in the town of Stridon, which, now destroyed by the Goths, was once situated on the border of Dalmatia and Pannonia. He assumed the garment of Christ at Rome and was educated there from childhood in Greek and Latin letters. In grammar he had Donatus as his teacher, and in rhetoric the orator Victorinus.

After he had acquired the entire literature of worldly studies [Note: [Col. 0177] These manuscripts unanimously read: “the whole study of worldly literature.” One Narbonne manuscript has: “the whole literary learning of worldly studies.” The Corbie manuscript has: “all knowledge through the studies of worldly literature,” and so forth], he also imitated the clothing and manner of life of the most approved monks [Note: [Col. 0177] I do not think Gennadius would have used the word *factum* to denote the customs and institutions of monks]. By continually and sincerely trampling down the soul’s desire and perpetually breaking the body’s pleasure through fasting, he taught many good and religious men to become better by his own discipline.

One day, therefore, while Jerome, as was his custom, opened the divine books for reading [Note: [Col. 0177] One Vatican manuscript has *acumina* (“acumen”), which I would not reject. Soon afterward the other Regina manuscript reads: “whenever he turned over such books,” and so forth], he recalled Tullius, the mortal author of his library. Immediately he was chastised from heaven with a saving blow, so that he would not henceforth read such books.

For he himself writes about himself to the virgin Eustochium:

“When many years ago I had, for the sake of the kingdom of heaven, cut myself off from house, parents, sister, relatives, and—what was more difficult than these—from the habit of more luxurious food, and was traveling to Jerusalem as a soldier, I could not bear to be without the library that I had assembled at Rome with the greatest care and labor.

“Thus, wretched man that I was, I fasted in order to read Tullius. After frequent vigils through the night, after tears that the recollection of my past sins drew from the depths of my entrails, Plautus was taken up; Plato was taken up in my hands. Whenever, returning to myself, I began to read the Prophets, their speech seemed uncultivated; and because I did not see the light with blind eyes, I blamed not my eyes but the sun.

“While the ancient serpent was thus deceiving me, around the middle of Lent a fever, infused into my marrow, invaded my exhausted body. Without any respite—and what is almost incredible to say—it consumed my unhappy limbs so thoroughly that scarcely anything remained attached to the bones [Note: [Col. 0177] The other Regina manuscript has: “I scarcely clung to the bones”].

“In the meantime my funeral was being prepared, and the warmth of my living spirit, while my whole body was already growing cold, throbbed only in my still-warm little breast. Suddenly I was carried away in spirit and dragged before the tribunal of the Judge. There was such a great light there, and such a radiance from the brightness of those standing around, that, thrown upon the ground, I did not dare to look upward.

“When asked about my condition, I answered that I was a Christian. But the one presiding said: ‘You lie; you are a Ciceronian, not a Christian. Where your treasure is, there your heart is also.’

“Immediately I fell silent. Amid the blows—for he had ordered me to be beaten—I was tortured more by the fire of conscience, repeating to myself that verse: ‘But in the underworld, who will confess to you?’ Yet I began to cry out and say, wailing: ‘Have mercy on me, Lord; have mercy on me.’ This cry resounded amid the lashes.

“At last those who were standing nearby fell upon the knees of the one presiding [Note: [Col. 0177] All our codices read: “those who had been present”] and begged him to pardon my youth and grant a place for repentance to my error, while imposing subsequent punishment if I ever read pagan literature again.

“I, bound by so great a crisis and wishing even then to promise greater things, began to swear. Calling upon his name, I said: ‘Lord, if I ever possess secular books, if I ever read them, I have denied you.’ With these words of oath I was dismissed and returned to the world above. To the amazement of all, I opened my eyes, drenched in such a flood of tears that even unbelievers would have been convinced by the pain.

“Nor was that sleep an empty one, like the vain dreams by which we are often deceived [Note: [Col. 0178] The Narbonne and Bordeaux manuscripts read: “or vain dreams.” One Corbie manuscript has: “The tribunal is witness. The judgment is witness, which I feared.” Shortly afterward nearly all the manuscripts read *liventes* (“bruised”), while one Regina manuscript has *lividas* (“livid”). The same manuscript has *after the dream*, more correctly than *through the dream*. At the end it reads *I read*, in place of *I had read*]. The tribunal before which I lay is witness; the judgment that I feared is witness. May it never happen to me to face such an examination again. I confess that I had bruised shoulders and felt the blows in the dream; and thereafter I read the divine books with as much zeal as previously I had read mortal works.”

Meanwhile, Jerome, presbyter of the Roman Church, the mouth of the priest Damasus, investigator of the sacred library, and interpreter of the divine books, was honored as dear and welcome to the people for three continuous years. By everyone’s judgment he was deemed worthy of the highest priesthood [Note: [Col. 0178] These words are absent from the other Regina manuscript: “for three continuous years.” The Vatican manuscript also omits the following words: “and by everyone’s judgment he was deemed worthy of the highest priesthood”].

Certain men from the orders of clerics and monks, wandering about in wantonness and gluttony, plotted to drive Jerome from the city, because he had detected and exposed the vices of both groups in writing [Note: [Col. 0178] The Vatican manuscript reads: “writing about each of them, he had detected their vice.” One Regina manuscript continues: “For which reason, whether this man…” The Bordeaux manuscript has: “For truly, whether this man…” and so forth].

But I would call the outcome of this flight fortunate, arranged by Christ’s judgment, since it corrected the matter. I believe that he was prepared by the persecutions of wicked men [Note: [Col. 0178] Some books have *pacatum* (“pacified”) in place of *paratum* (“prepared”). The Vatican manuscript omits the words “having been taught the truth,” and shortly afterward, together with both Regina manuscripts, adds: “with Jerome’s spiritual zeal.” Compare the entire passage, which is seriously obstructed here through the fault of the copyists, with the passage found in the following Life, column 253, near the middle] so that the Roman Church, established under the governance of Peter and instructed in the truth of all the books of the Old Testament, might, with Christ God’s will and Jerome’s special labor, also possess the Hebrew truth; and so that the frivolity of certain Greeks, which used to boast that the Romans had received all the divinely inspired Scriptures from them, might recognize that they possessed what it did not.

Accordingly, Jerome left Rome and traveled toward the East, proceeding to Gregory Nazianzen, bishop of Constantinople. There he devoted himself so earnestly to progress [Note: [Col. 0178] All our manuscripts read: “he devoted himself to progress, so that he might be instructed in the study of the holy Scriptures,” omitting the intervening words. One Bordeaux manuscript reads: “he devoted himself and progressed, so that he might be endowed with marvelous knowledge; and so that he might be instructed in the study of the holy Scriptures,” and so forth] that he was endowed with marvelous knowledge.

In order to be fully instructed in the study of the holy Scriptures, he approached this teacher as a humble and teachable disciple and attended upon him in Constantinople. After completing this discipleship, Jerome went to Syria. While staying at the estate of the presbyter Evagrius, he encountered Malchus the monk, who had at one time been a captive. After questioning him, he learned the entire story of his captivity and later published it in writing and sent it to the Roman faithful. In the preface to that history he inserted the following:

“I have decided to write, if God grants me life and if my detractors cease pursuing me, even when I am fleeing and shut away.” [Note: [Col. 0179] The same Bordeaux manuscript adds: “from the Advent of the Savior up to our own age,” words that follow in the Preface cited here. Shortly afterward it reads *from there* in place of *then*. The Vatican manuscript later has *wishing* in place of *had wished*, and, with three others in Martianaeus, *to have traveled* in place of *to have returned*]

Then he approached the deserted places to which he had once wished to hurry in order to do penance, so happily and eagerly equipped that you would have thought he had flown there rather than returned.

“How, however, he did penance continuously for four years with the help of Christ, and what he willingly endured [variant: suffered], Jerome himself indicated in these words, showing that God’s grace was present:

“‘Whenever I was established in the desert, in that vast solitude which, scorched by the heat of the sun, provides the monks with a terrible dwelling, I thought that I was present amid the delights of Rome. I sat alone because I was filled with bitterness. My limbs, deformed by the sackcloth, bristled; my grimy skin had assumed the appearance of Ethiopian flesh. Every day there were tears, every day groans; and whenever impending sleep overcame me in spite of myself, I struck the bare ground with my bones, which scarcely clung together.

“‘Of food and drink I say nothing, since even those weakened there use cold water, and to have received anything cooked is considered luxury. Thus I, who had condemned myself to such a prison out of fear of Gehenna, the companion only of scorpions and wild beasts, often found myself amid choruses of girls.

“‘My face grew pale with fasting, and my mind burned with desires. In a cold body, and before my own self—already dead in the flesh—only the fires of lust were springing up. Therefore, deprived of every aid, I lay at the feet of Jesus, watered them with tears, dried them with my hair, and subdued my rebellious flesh through weeks of hunger. I am not ashamed of my misery; rather, I mourn that I am not what I once was.

“‘I remember that I often joined day to night while crying out, and that I did not cease beating my breast until tranquility returned at the Lord’s command [Note: [Col. 0179] The Bordeaux manuscript, together with the Vatican, has *rebuking* in place of *commanding*].

“‘I even feared my own cell, as though it were conscious of my thoughts. Angry and severe with myself, I alone penetrated the desert. Wherever I saw hollow valleys, rugged mountains, or steep crags, there I placed myself in prayer, in the prison of my most wretched flesh. And—as the Lord is my witness—after many tears, after fixing my eyes upon heaven, I sometimes seemed to myself to be present among the ranks of angels; and, joyful and rejoicing, I sang: “We run after you, drawn by the fragrance of your perfumes.”’”

When the four years of devoted penance [variant: completed penance] had ended [Col. 0180], Jerome returned to the town of Bethlehem, where, like a prudent animal, he offered himself to remain at the Lord’s manger.

He shut up the library that he had established for himself with the greatest care, and, rereading all the books whose contents he almost retained by heart, he spent the day fasting until evening. Many religious men who had learned of his way of life immediately gathered around him; and good disciples kept watch over the good Teacher, who still lived in a small hut [Note: [Col. 0180] The Bordeaux manuscript has “beneath a little hut.” Shortly afterward two other manuscripts, preserved by Martianaeus, add: “which faces west”].

Not long afterward, because of the number of his disciples and the frequent arrival of visitors, he built for himself a small dwelling near the Bethlehem gate, which faces west and appears to those going out toward the north.

Meanwhile Jerome traversed and contemplated the humble subterranean dwellings of eminent hermits and monks; he questioned them about their lives in a reverent voice; he explained the truth in writing; and, composing many other works and letters in his monastery, he set them forth.

Then the blessed Damasus, the most eloquent Pontiff of the Church of the city of Rome, urged him in the following words not to cease, through constant labor, writing and sending books to the Church of the city of Rome [Note: [Col. 0180] More correctly, in the Vatican manuscript the word *city* is omitted. It then has *negligent*; afterward it reads *because of being remiss* in place of *because of you being remiss*]:

“Damasus to his dearest son Jerome.

“I have decided to rouse you, since you have been sleeping and for a long time have preferred reading to writing, by sending you little questions—not because you ought not to read, for by this, as by daily food, eloquence is nourished and grows rich, but because the fruit of reading is this: that you write.

“Therefore, since you said, when I sent a courier to you, that you now had no letters except those that you had once dictated in the desert, which I read and copied with complete eagerness, and since you voluntarily promised that, if I wished, you could dictate some others through the stolen labor of the nights [Note: [Col. 0180] The Narbonne and Bordeaux manuscripts read: “And you further promised that, through the stolen labor of the nights, you could dictate some if you wished.” The Vatican manuscript has *you* in place of *as*, and *if you wish, you can*], I gladly accept from one who offers what I had intended to request, even if you had refused.

“For I do not think there could be any more worthy conversation for our discussion than that we should converse with one another about the Scriptures: that is, that I should ask and you should answer. I think that nothing in this life is more delightful than such a life, and that all honey is surpassed by such nourishment for the soul. ‘How sweet are your words to my throat,’ says the Prophet, ‘sweeter than honey to my mouth.’

“Since, as the eminent Orator says, human beings differ from beasts because we can speak, how worthy of praise is the person who surpasses others in the very thing by which human beings excel beasts?

“Therefore gird yourself and explain to me what follows, preserving moderation in both directions, so that neither the questions require a solution [Note: [Col. 0180] The other Regina manuscript has: “so that they require no answers,” and the other: “nor the solutions brevity.” One Bordeaux manuscript reads: “because his letters, without the article τῶ, are very numerous.” We omit obvious errors] nor the letter brevity.

“I confess to you that I do not willingly read the books you gave me concerning the faith of Lactantius, because many of his letters extend to the length of a thousand lines, and he rarely discusses our doctrine. The result is that their length produces weariness in the reader, while whatever is brief in them is more suitable for schoolmen than for us. He discusses meters, the location of regions, and philosophers.

“What does the statement in Genesis mean: ‘Anyone who kills Cain shall pay sevenfold vengeance’? Yet if God made everything very good, why does he command Noah concerning clean and unclean animals, when nothing unclean can be good?

“And in the New Testament, after the vision shown to Peter, when he said, ‘By no means, Lord, because nothing common and unclean has ever entered my mouth,’ a voice from heaven replied: ‘What the Lord God has cleansed [Note: [Col. 0181] All our manuscripts read: “Do not call common what you…”]. Do not then call common.’

“Why does God say to Abraham that in the fourth generation the children of Israel would return from Egypt, and afterward Moses wrote: ‘But in the fifth generation, or progeny, the children of Israel went out from the land of Egypt’? Unless this is explained, the statements appear contradictory.

“Why did Abraham receive the sign of circumcision? Why did Isaac, righteous and dear to God, bless not the one he wished but the one he did not wish, deceived by error?”

Now it remains to append how, with what daring and with how many labors, Jerome alone among all the Romans learned the Hebrew language and letters, indeed even the Chaldean language, as he himself bears witness. He says:

“When I was young, and the deserts of solitude hemmed me in, I could not bear the incitements of vice and the ardor of nature [alternatively: ‘which’]. Although I broke this by frequent fasts, my mind nevertheless seethed with thoughts. To tame it, I placed myself under the instruction of a certain brother who had believed among the Hebrews, so that, after the refinements of Quintilian, the eloquence and weight of Cicero, the gravity of Fronto, and the gentleness of Pliny, I might learn the alphabet and practice uttering harsh, panting words. What labor I expended there, what difficulty I endured, how often I despaired and how often I stopped, my conscience is witness—both to what I suffered and to what those who lived with me suffered. And I give thanks to God that from the bitter seed of letters I am gathering sweet fruits.”

[Note: The Vatican manuscript reads “with what labors”; then, when two other Regina manuscripts are joined to it, it says that he learned the Hebrew language and letters, indeed the Chaldean language, omitting the intervening words. The phrase “ardor of nature” is absent from the Vatican manuscript and certain others. The Vatican then has: “To correct it, I gave myself into instruction under a certain brother …” The Corbie manuscript reads “I undertook”; after “I stopped,” the Vatican adds: “and began again through the effort of learning,” followed by: “My conscience is witness to what I suffered, as is that of those who lived with me; I know what I endured.” Other manuscripts read “both my conscience and that of …” We have replaced “Daniel” with the Book of Job from another Regina manuscript.]

Moreover, when Jerome translated the Book of Job into Latin, although it was written in Hebrew letters but in the Chaldean language, he had as his teacher the man whom he names below:

“I remember that, for the understanding of this volume, I purchased at no small price a certain Liddeus, who was considered foremost among the Hebrews. Whether I made any progress through his teaching, I do not know; this one thing I do know: I could not interpret anything except what I had previously understood.”

[Note: One manuscript more correctly omits the second little word; then, together with the Vatican manuscript, it reads “he was considered learned” where the others read “first.” Finally, one Bordeaux manuscript reads: “I could not interpret except what I had understood.”]

As for the labor and sweat by which he learned the Chaldean language, Jerome himself says and affirms the following:

“As a young man, after reading Quintilian and Tully and the flowers of rhetoric, when I had shut myself up in the mill of this language, and after much sweat and much time had scarcely begun to sound out its panting and harsh words, and, as though walking through a crypt, was looking upon a scant light from above, I finally stumbled upon Daniel. I was affected by such weariness that, in sudden despair, I wished to abandon all my former labor. But when a Hebrew encouraged me and repeatedly impressed upon me in his own language the words, ‘Hard labor conquers all things,’ I, who had seemed to myself somewhat learned among them, began once more to be a Chaldean student. And, to speak more truthfully, to the present day I am better able to read and understand Chaldean speech than to pronounce it.”

[Note: The Bordeaux manuscript reads: “But when a Hebrew encouraged me, and he impressed that saying upon me …”; then: “I began again to be a Chaldean student.” One Regina manuscript omits “student,” and the same manuscript shortly afterward omits “and understand.”]

Thus, having attained faith through the grace of Christ, and learned in Greek, Latin, and Hebrew letters, Jerome translated into Latin, in an authentic edition, all the books of the Hebrews contained in the Old Testament, and composed commentaries on them all. He also set down in Roman style Daniel, who spoke in the Chaldean language. The Psalter, which Jerome, at Sophronius’s request, rendered word for word from the Hebrew Canon so that it might be sung in Latin melody, he briefly expounded and called an *Enchiridion*.

[Note: The same manuscript reads “which are contained canonically”; and shortly afterward, together with another Regina manuscript, it calls the Psalter an *Enchiridion*. Here it entirely omits the following words, “He explained two books of Solomon”; the other manuscript reads “explaining.” Two Regina manuscripts read “from the book of Didymus the Seer.” Shortly afterward, the Vatican manuscript, together with the Bordeaux manuscript, reads: “For he discussed the sixteen prophets …” and, with several others subsequently found, “four and seventy”; some others omit the two words “four and.”]

He explained two books of Solomon. He translated the Song of Songs from Origen’s interpretation, just as he translated into Latin the book of Didymus the Seer on the Holy Spirit. He also made Matthew’s Gospel Roman from the Hebrew, and interpreted it for diligent readers in an explanation more concise than tedious. He discussed the sixteen books, or prophecies, of the Prophets, which no Roman had previously been found either to remember or to begin writing about, and composed commentaries on them in seventy-four books. In addition, he discussed most of Paul’s Epistles and the Revelation of John.

Amid the numerous pages of his work, all marked beforehand by their respective prefaces, he arranged in order one hundred and thirty-five illustrious ecclesiastical writers, from the Passion of Christ to the fourteenth year of the Emperor Theodosius, and briefly set forth everyone who had transmitted anything memorable concerning the Holy Scriptures.

He also labored with great intellectual effort against Celsus, Porphyry, and Julian Augustus—rabid dogs against Christ—and against the persecutors of the Church, as well as against those who thought that the Church had possessed no philosophical or eloquent teachers, so that they might know what sort of men, and how great, had founded, built, and adorned it, and might cease accusing our faith of rustic simplicity and instead recognize their own ignorance.

[Note: The Vatican manuscript reads “recognize.” Martianaeus had omitted the entire following passage, beginning “Moreover, in innumerable books of the Apostles …” and continuing to “I alone am gnawed by the glory of all.” We considered it our duty to supply it, with all the manuscripts we consulted bearing witness. We do not deny, however, that it had been badly handled by scribes and that its sense limps in places—something that could easily have been restored, had we wished. The learned Tillemont says that he has no idea what “constructions” means; it seems to us that the word should be understood in a grammatical sense.]

Moreover, in innumerable books [on] the grammatical constructions of the Apostles and Prophets; and shortly afterward: “Even now the mystery of iniquity is at work.” Everyone chatters whatever he thinks; I alone am the one gnawed by the glory of all.

Finally, he was worn out by such great exhaustion that, even while lying on his bed, he had himself raised by a cord suspended from a beam, grasping it with his hands held upward, so that he might perform the duties of the monastery as best he could. For many days he continued, his body emaciated and his voice faint.

Then Jerome, supported by the abundance of his books, and having dedicated his words to the Holy Spirit [alternative: “Spirit”], issued, as an immovable tower of the Catholic Church against the darts of the faithless, against Helvidius, Pelagius, and Jovinianus, volumes of the clearest kind, fortified by Catholic correction and written with great acumen.

[Note: Two of our manuscripts, as well as certain others, read “also to the jurists,” as though a book written to them, which never existed, were being mentioned. Immediately afterward, one Regina manuscript reads “the lives of most hermits and fathers”; the Bordeaux manuscript reads “he wove into a history, in very truthful eloquence, the lives of most hermits and fathers distinguished by their way of life.”]

He also composed a singular and thunderous book for the jurists. He wove into historical narrative, in very truthful eloquence, the lives of most distinguished hermit fathers. He wrote one book on the Stations of the Israelite people. He also elegantly expounded the Gospel history concerning the thrifty and the prodigal son, and explained it in conciliatory discussions [preferably: *conciliatoriis*, close to Cotelerius’s emendation of *conciliatoris*], so that he considered it to be a single account.

[Note: He is referring especially to the Commentaries on Matthew, in which he repeatedly attempts to remove the appearance of ἀφονιῶν [*aphoniōn*] in the Gospels. Likewise, in his Letter to Hedibia he reconciles the Evangelists’ passages concerning the Resurrection.]

“For I reply briefly to the many who say that I write this work inflamed by the torches of envy: I have never spared the heretics, but have acted with every effort so that the enemies of the Church might also become my enemies.”

Thus the Catholic elders repeatedly continued to visit and console Jerome while he was engaged in his labor.

To the blessed Bishop Augustine, who in spirit was working with him in the Catholic Church but in body was writing in Africa, he wrote the following concerning the rest of his work:

“We have had our time; we have run as far as we could. Now that you are running and traversing long distances, leisure is owed to us.”

[Note: The Bordeaux manuscript reads “this life, now indeed perfect in body, he offered to him”; another Regina manuscript also omits “old.” In place of “chaste, pleasing,” the praised manuscript and most others read “cautious, pleasing.”]

Thus Jerome offered to Christ God the life which, as a young man, he had vowed to him, now perfect in bodily old age: chaste, pleasing, and devoted to a single penitential life in the wilderness of Bethlehem.

[Note: The same manuscript reads: “after his books had been irreproachably completed at Bethlehem by spiritual labor, he filled the whole world.”]

Moreover, after completing his books over fifty-six years without any leisure among the Bethlehemites, and irreproachably filling the whole world with spiritual labor, he rested in the Lord in the eighty-eighth year of his age.

Bethlehem, the nourishing mother, holds him, to be offered again when the Lord comes.

The blessed Jerome died in the twelfth year of the reign of the younger Theodosius.

[Note: One Regina manuscript adds: “with our Lord Jesus Christ working.”]

His years of life are reckoned as follows. He was ordained a presbyter at Rome at the age of twenty-nine.

[Note: The older Regina manuscript omits the words “for three years”; shortly afterward it reads “fifty-six years and six months.” The subsequent total of Jerome’s life varies more widely among the manuscripts. The Bordeaux manuscript calculates eighty-seven years; the Vatican, eighty-nine. The remainder, beginning “He died …,” is absent from that Vatican manuscript and from another Regina manuscript.]

He lived three years at Bethlehem and fifty years and six months in his chosen way of life. He completed the whole period of his life in eighty-eight years and six months. He died in the Lord on the day before the Kalends of October.

[Col. 0183]

## The Life of Saint Eusebius Hieronymus, the Incomparable Teacher of the Church of Christ and a Man of Outstanding Holiness, Collected Especially from His Own Writings and Also from the Treatises of the Holy Fathers Augustine, Damasus, Gregory, Gelasius, and Several Others

[Note: We collated two manuscripts of especially good reputation from the Ambrosian Library at Milan, one marked with the letter F and number 18, the other with I and 53. It is entitled there: “Here begins the Life of Saint Jerome, collected from his Treatises and from those of the saints Augustine, Damasus, Gregory, Gelasius, and other holy fathers.”]

When I had read the life of the blessed Jerome published by various authors, I discovered that they had inserted certain matters that contributed little to his praise. Conversely, they had omitted many things that were useful, especially those which had been handed down by Jerome himself in his Treatises and seemed appropriate to be read on his feast day.

Moved by his example—for in the divine books he had cut away what earlier translators had needlessly included, while restoring to their proper places what had been omitted—I too attempted, although as far inferior to him in merit as in style, to extract from the writings of the aforesaid author and from the sacred statements of other saints whatever seemed relevant, and to arrange it in a suitable order. Thus, by forming something like a single body from many parts, I might in some measure lighten the labor of those who wished to possess without weariness the material concerning the life and virtues of the holy man, which had been distributed through various volumes.

If rashness is censured in this undertaking, let the devotion owed to him—not without reason—be considered: he saved my mother from the danger of death while she was carrying me in her womb.

The aforesaid teacher was born, as he himself asserts in his Book on Illustrious Men, in the twenty-sixth year of the reign of the great Constantine, in the town of Stridon, which, destroyed by the Goths, once lay on the border of Dalmatia and Pannonia.

[Note: Both manuscripts omit the word “superfluously.” Then one of them adds: “But what had been omitted he supplied. I too attempted …,” without the words “to their proper places.”]

When he came to Rome in childhood with Christian parents, where he received the garment of Christ, he is said to have been entrusted for instruction to distinguished men. In grammar he had Donatus as his teacher, and in rhetoric Victorinus.

[Note: Both manuscripts read: “When he excelled in the liberal arts …” One of them, the older manuscript marked I, reads: “He flourished in the liberal arts, both Greek and Latin, and, receiving the garment of Christ in the aforementioned city, imitated [the conduct] of suitable ecclesiastical men,” which is much closer to the truth. The material concerning the conduct of the monks comes from the Pseudo-Gennadius. The same manuscript shortly afterward reads: “At the age of twenty-nine—an entire decade less—he was ordained presbyter by Liberius, bishop of the Apostolic See,” omitting the later and much more legendary material concerning the Roman church of the title of Saint Anastasia.]

Since he also excelled in the liberal arts, in both Greek and Latin, he imitated the dress and conduct of the most approved monks. He then ascended through the appropriate ecclesiastical ranks to the dignity of cardinal.

For when he was thirty-nine years old, he was ordained presbyter of the Roman church of the title of Saint Anastasia by Liberius, bishop of the Apostolic See.

But when, after almost four years, that same Apostolic bishop turned into an apostate and consented to the Arian doctrine, while many concealed themselves through fear of the persecution stirred up by Constantius—

[Note: In this passage and shortly below, where Constantius Augustus is written, our manuscripts prefer “Constantine.”]

—Jerome, in accordance with the prophetic word, set himself as a wall for the house of Israel, so that he might stand in battle on the day of the Lord. Although he was subjected to insults and struck with terrors, he never yielded to the heretics. Rather, shooting forth the arrows of his eloquence according to the wisdom given him, he scattered them; multiplying the flashes of divine judgments, he threw them into confusion.

At that time Catholics were also prevented from freely using their own property, while both Constantius Augustus and the Pontiff Liberius persecuted them.

Then a certain matron named Paula, noble by birth but nobler in holiness, seeing the blessed Jerome laboring with great manliness in defense of the faith, began to offer him assistance and to provide for him from her resources. The most prudent man, observing her devotion and merit, frequently commemorates her and her daughter Eustochium in his Treatises. He also took care to instruct them in knowledge of the divine Scriptures.

He consoled Paula in affectionate writings when she was distressed by the recent deaths of her daughters, Blesilla and Paulina. For this reason certain pseudo-clerics and monks, whose life he had exposed in writing, seized the opportunity to slander him, and the most wretched men attempted to brand him with infamy. Since they themselves were subject to carnal vices, they imposed the same charge upon Jerome, “to make excuses for sins.”

[Note: The entire passage beginning “Finally, they placed a woman’s garment near his bed, which he would put on when he rose for matins,” a memory belonging to a ridiculous—indeed, to say no more, absurd—story, is entirely absent from the other Ambrosian manuscript. It plainly seems that it should be deleted as untrustworthy.]

Finally, they placed a woman’s garment near his bed, which he was to put on when he rose for matins.

When Jerome therefore saw that he was being attacked no less by false brothers than by heretics, he recalled the Gospel saying, “If they persecute you in this city, flee to another.” He resolved to yield to their malice and to migrate to the eastern regions in order to serve the Lord.

Jacob is likewise said to have done this in the case of his brother Esau, and David in the case of his father-in-law Saul: one withdrew to the Syrians, the other to the Philistines, preferring to be subject to enemies rather than to envious men.

Jerome himself, writing to Rufinus, recounts the course of his departure from the City as follows:

“In the month of August, with the west winds blowing, I safely boarded a ship in the Roman harbor with the presbyter Saint Vincentius, my adolescent brother, and other monks who now reside in Jerusalem. A very great crowd of saints accompanied me. I came to Rhegium and stayed for a short time on the Scyllean shore, where I learned the ancient tales: the headlong course of deceitful Ulysses, the songs of the Sirens, and the insatiable whirlpool of Charybdis.

When the inhabitants of that place told me many things and advised me to sail not to the Pillars of Proteus but to the port of Dione [Juno?]—the former being the course of fugitives and troubled men, the latter that of a secure man—I preferred to proceed through Malea and the Cyclades to Cyprus. There I was received by the venerable Bishop Epiphanius, whose praise you proclaim in your testimony.

Afterward I came to Antioch, where I enjoyed the communion of the bishop and confessor Paulinus. Led by him in midwinter, in the most severe cold, I entered Jerusalem. I saw many miracles and confirmed by the judgment of my eyes what rumor had previously brought to me.

From there I went up to Egypt and toured the monasteries of Nitria. Amid the choirs of the saints, I observed asps lying concealed.”

[Note: The same manuscript teaches that the inept gloss “in the most severe cold” should be deleted; likewise, shortly afterward, one should read “I proceeded to Egypt” rather than “I went up to Egypt.”]

Who would not call the outcome of this flight blessed, and arranged by Christ’s providence, so that the Roman Church, established under Peter’s governance, might have, through Jerome’s labor, the Hebrew and Greek certainty of all the books of both the Old and the New Testament?

[Note: The older Ambrosian manuscript reads: “that it might possess the Hebrew truth and the certainty of certain Greek books.”]

And because the levity of certain Greeks—who boasted that the Romans had received all the Scriptures divinely inspired from them—caused them to desist from their mockery, Jerome, after visiting the venerable places mentioned above, proceeded to Constantinople to hear the venerable man Gregory Nazianzen, his teacher and then bishop of that city, so that he might be instructed in the study of the Holy Scriptures.

[Note: The same manuscript reads: “Gregory Nazianzen, as he himself recalls in the third book of his Explanations of Isaiah, where the Prophet testifies that he saw God, saying: ‘Concerning this vision, when I was in Constantinople and with the most eloquent man Gregory Nazianzen, my teacher …’” These words may easily have been omitted because of the recurrence of the same name, Gregory Nazianzen, a frequent scribal error. The same passage continues in Jerome’s own words: “Then, while I was being instructed in the studies of the Holy Scriptures by the bishop of that city, I know that I dictated a brief and sudden treatise. But what …”]

What more excellent statement—nothing else [delete *aliud*, “other”]—can be made concerning this man’s indefatigable study and elegant diligence, which he displayed in learning Greek, Latin, Hebrew, Syriac, and Chaldean, than the words he himself professes in what he sent to Pammachius and Oceanus?

[Note: The same manuscript reads: “and Chaldean, which he devoted himself to learning.”]

[Note: From the same manuscript we restore *decebat* (“it was fitting”) in place of the erroneous *docebat* (“was teaching”). The same manuscript shortly afterward has *Baraniam* for *Barrabanum*; the holy father himself calls him *Baraninam*.]

“When I was young, I burned with an extraordinary love of learning; nor, contrary to the presumption of some, did I teach myself. I frequently heard Apollinaris at Antioch and honored him. My head was already being sprinkled with gray hairs, and it was more fitting for me to be a teacher than a student. Nevertheless, I proceeded to Alexandria and heard Didymus. I thank him for many things, because I learned what I did not know; and what I knew, I did not lose under his instruction.

People thought that I had reached the end of my learning. I came again to Jerusalem and Bethlehem. At what labor and at what price did I have Barrabanus as my teacher by night? For he feared the Jews, and he presented himself to me as another Nicodemus.”

Likewise, in his letter to the monk Rusticus:

“When I was young, and the deserts of solitude hemmed me in, I could not bear the incitements of vice and the ardor of nature. Although I broke this by frequent fasts, my mind nevertheless seethed with thoughts. To tame it, I placed myself under the instruction of a certain brother who had believed among the Hebrews, so that, after the refinements of Quintilian, the eloquence of Cicero, the gravity of Fronto, and the gentleness of Pliny, I might learn the alphabet and practice harsh, panting words.

What labor I expended there, what difficulty I endured, how often I despaired and how often I stopped, and how, through the effort of learning, I began again, my conscience is witness—both mine, since I suffered it, and that of those who lived with me. And I give thanks to the Lord that from the bitter seed of letters I reap sweet fruits.”

[Note: The same manuscript further reads: “I could scarcely practice the words”; it then adds, after the words here omitted, “how often I stopped,” “I began again.”]

And in the prologue to the Book of Job, which, translated and expounded in Latin through his efforts, earned him this distinction, he says:

“I remember that, for the understanding of this volume, I purchased at no small price a certain Liddeus as my teacher, who was considered learned among the Jews.”

[Note: Here, from the same manuscript, we restore “Liddeus” for “Judaeus,” which was the erroneous reading. Shortly afterward, that manuscript reads “Hebrews” for “Jews.” It also omits the two words “I was a young man.”]

[Note: Here, from the same manuscript, we correct *rarum* (“a scant [light]”) for the corrupt reading *earum*.]

As for the labor by which he attained knowledge of the Chaldean language, Jerome himself explains it concerning himself in the prologue to Daniel:

“As a young man, after reading Quintilian and Tully and the flowers of rhetoric, when I had shut myself up in the mill of this language, and after much sweat and much time had scarcely begun to sound out its panting and harsh words, and, as though walking through a crypt, was looking upon a scant light from above, I finally stumbled upon Daniel. I was affected by such weariness that, having fallen into despair, I wished to abandon all my former labor.

But when a Hebrew encouraged me and repeatedly impressed upon me in his own language the words, ‘Hard labor conquers all things,’ I, who had seemed to myself somewhat learned among the Hebrews, began once more to be a Chaldean student. And, to speak more truthfully, to the present day I am better able to read and understand Chaldean speech than to pronounce it.”

[Note: The manuscript marked with the letter I omits the two words “and understand.” It then transfers here a rather long passage, filling nearly both columns of page 263, beginning with the words “Therefore, the fullness of wisdom and holiness” [alternatively: “of knowledge”] and continuing to “he clearly indicates it to be probable.” The place for discussing these matters will return below.]

Meanwhile he proceeds to Syria, and while staying at the estate of the presbyter Evagrius, he encounters the monk Malchus, who had at some time been a captive. After questioning him, he learned the whole sequence of his captivity and wrote its history. And as he contemplated the holy monks and hermits while visiting their humble dwellings, devoting himself without interruption to prayer and restraining the pleasure of the flesh by daily labor and fasting, he taught by his own example that many of them were superior in goodness.

[Note: [Col. 0188] The same manuscript adds: “He himself also imitated their dress and conduct, for he persisted in prayer without interruption, etc.” We discussed the monks’ conduct in the preceding writing of the Pseudo-Gennadius, from which these details seem to have been taken.]

Since, therefore, he devoted himself so intensely to these good works that he even interrupted his study of writing, Damasus, bishop of the City, being concerned for the benefit of the Church, urged him in writing not to desist from his constant work of composition, as follows:

“To his dearest son Jerome, Damasus.

“I have decided to rouse you, since you have been sleeping and for a long time now have been reading rather than writing, by sending you some little questions. Not that you ought not also to read—for speech is nourished and grows fat upon this as upon daily food—but because the fruit of reading consists in this, that you write. Therefore, since you promised that, if I wished, you could dictate something during your stolen nocturnal labors, I gladly accept from the one offering what I might have been able to request, had you refused.

“Nor do I think that any more worthy subject for our conversation could be found than that we speak together about the Scriptures: that is, that I ask and you answer. In this life I think nothing more pleasant in this light, and all honey is surpassed by this food of the soul. ‘How sweet,’ says the Prophet, ‘are your utterances to my palate, sweeter than honey to my mouth.’

“‘The foremost orator,’ he says, ‘declares: Since human beings differ from beasts in this, that we are able to speak, what praise is due to one who surpasses others in that very respect in which human beings surpass beasts?’ Gird yourself, therefore, and explain to me what follows.

“What is meant by what is written in Genesis: ‘Everyone who kills Cain shall pay sevenfold vengeance’? If God made everything very good, why did Noah give instructions about clean and unclean creatures, when nothing unclean can be good? Why does God tell Abraham that the children of Israel would return from Egypt in the fourth generation, while Moses afterward writes: ‘But in the fifth generation the children of Israel went out from the land of Egypt’? Why did Abraham receive the sign of his faith through circumcision? Why did Isaac, a just man, bless one whom he did not wish to bless?”

The blessed Jerome gave a completely satisfactory answer to all these questions, and he wrote the works listed below at various times to Pope Damasus: Homilies on the Song of Songs.

[Note: [Col. 0189] The same manuscript again adds two, correctly. Then, concerning Osianna, it gives one book, preferring the form “Osanna,” commonly used without an intervening *h*, which has the appearance of an interpolator’s gloss.]

One book on Osianna, commonly called Osanna; one book on the death of Uzziah, the Seraphim, and the burning coal; one book on the prodigal son; and one book on the Holy Spirit. He carefully corrected the text of the four Gospels, which had been corrupted through the negligence of scribes. He also translated the Psalter from Greek into Latin according to the recension of the Seventy Interpreters, and revised it at the request of Paula and Eustochium. Finally, at the request of Sophronius, he rendered it from Hebrew and briefly explained the book, calling it the *Enchiridion*.

During the same period he wrote the life of Paul the monk and the life of the blessed Hilarion; a letter of exhortation to Heliodorus on contempt for the world; and a letter to Nepotianus on the life of the clergy. He also wrote a *Chronicle* of universal history and many other letters to various persons.

Moreover, the enemy of the human race, who had persecuted him at Rome through his agents, raised up the Arians against him even in the solitude. Writing to the blessed Damasus about them, he complains as follows:

“I who received Christ’s garment in the city of Rome am now confined within the barbarous frontier of Syria. Yet, as the pagan poet says, ‘The man who hastens across the sea changes his sky, not his mind.’ Thus the enemy has pursued me incessantly from behind, so that I now suffer greater wars in the solitude. Here the Arian madness, supported by the world’s defenses, roars. Here the Church, split into three parties, hastens to drag people over to itself. Here the ancient authority of the monks living in the vicinity rises against me.

“Meanwhile I cry out: If anyone is joined to the Chair of Peter, he is with me. Meletius, Vitalis, and Paulinus say that they cling to you. I could believe this if one person asserted it; but now either two are lying, or all of them.”

[Note: [Col. 0189] From the same manuscript we restored *here* in place of the corrupt reading *certainly*, and *I cry out* in place of *I shall cry out*. For *is with me*, the same manuscript has *is mine*.]

Concerning these persecutions also he speaks in a certain letter to Malchus, the reverend man of Chalcis:

“If it pleases my persecutors, let them condemn me as a heretic with the West, as a heretic with Egypt—that is, with Damasus and Peter. If a stream flows thinly, the fault lies not with the channel but with the spring. I have taken nothing away from anyone; I receive nothing while idle. Every day we seek our food by our hands and our own sweat, knowing that the Apostle wrote: ‘If anyone will not work, neither let him eat.’

“They wish me to leave here; I am already leaving. For they have torn away from me the dearest brothers, a part of my soul. Look, they wish to depart—indeed, they are departing, judging it better to dwell among wild beasts than with such Christians.”

He then withdrew to the deserted places so gladly and eagerly that one would have thought he had flown there rather than walked.

[Note: [Col. 0190] The same manuscript more correctly reads *withdrew* here. It did not know, however, the material that follows concerning how he merited the visitation of the Lord; nor, a little later, the passage beginning the letter: “Hear, daughter, and see,” in which he says, among other things:]

How he afflicted himself and thereby extinguished even harmful thoughts within himself, and how he also merited the visitation of the Lord, so that he often seemed to take part in angelic choirs, is attested by Jerome’s own writings to Eustochium. The letter begins: “Hear, daughter, and see.” In it he says, among other things:

“Because it is impossible,” he says, “for an impulse not to rush into the human mind, and for the heat of the marrow not to be stirred, yet that person is praised and proclaimed blessed who, as soon as he begins to think, kills his thoughts and dashes them against the rock; and the rock is Christ.

“How often, while I was living in the desert, in that vast solitude which, scorched by the sun’s heat, provides the monks with a dreadful dwelling, did I imagine myself present amid the pleasures of Rome. I sat alone, because I was full of bitterness; my misshapen limbs bristled beneath sackcloth, and my squalid skin was covered with the dirt of an Ethiopian body. Every day there were tears, every day groans; and whenever approaching sleep overcame me despite my resistance, I struck my bones, scarcely clinging to me, against the bare ground.

“As for food and drink, I say nothing, since even sick monks use cold water as food, and regard having received anything cooked as a luxury.

[Note: [Col. 0190] The manuscript reads *to have eaten*. Shortly afterward it has *and my mind was burning, without desires*; and later, more correctly, *already in its own flesh* instead of *already in dry flesh*, and finally *I do not blush to confess the misery of my unhappiness* instead of *I grow pale with shame at the misery of my unhappiness*.]

“I, then, who because of fear of Gehenna had condemned myself to such a prison, the companion only of scorpions and wild beasts, often found myself among choirs of girls. My face grew pale from fasting, my mind burned with desires in my cold body, and in flesh already almost dead before the human eye the fires of lust alone boiled.

“Thus deprived of every aid, I would throw myself at Jesus’ feet, water them with tears, and dry them with my hair. I subdued my rebellious flesh through weeks of hunger. I do not blush at the misery of my unhappiness; rather, I lament that I am not what I once was.

“I remember that I often joined day to night in crying out, and that I did not cease beating my breast until, by the Lord’s command, tranquility returned. I even feared my little cell, as though it were conscious of my thoughts. Angry and severe with myself, I alone penetrated the desert. Wherever I saw hollow valleys, rugged mountains, or precipitous cliffs, there was the place of my prayer; there I would establish the prison of my most wretched flesh.”
