[Note: [Col. 0190] The manuscript lacks the word *I would establish*, and also omits the words that shortly follow, “in that vast solitude mentioned above.”]

“And, as God himself is my witness, after many tears and after my eyes had remained fixed upon heaven, I sometimes seemed to myself to be among the ranks of angels; and, joyful and rejoicing, I sang: ‘After you we run, drawn by the fragrance of your ointments.’”

After spending four years in this vast solitude, the blessed Jerome, sensing that every pleasure of the flesh had been burned out within him and that nothing remained there to resist the spirit, returned to Jerusalem, in order to pour out his springs abroad and divide the waters of his knowledge in the streets, so that many might drink wines from the stream of his tongue—many who could scarcely have found him in the desert, on the trackless and waterless road.

Accordingly, he approached the bishop of that city, named Cyril, and asked him to grant him a place to live at Bethlehem, situated six miles from Jerusalem toward the south. He desired, like a prudent animal, to cling continually to the manger of his Lord. What he devoutly requested was immediately and fittingly granted.

Thereupon, with the Lord’s favor, he built a monastery, as he himself says in his letter to Pammachius, near the end of his account of the death of Paulina, in these words:

“So we too, after building a monastery in this province and constructing a lodging beside it, lest Joseph, even now coming with Mary to Bethlehem, should find no lodging, are overwhelmed by such crowds of monks flowing together from the whole world that we can neither abandon the work we have begun nor bear the burden beyond our strength. Since therefore almost the words of the Gospel have come true for us—that we did not first calculate the expense of the tower that was to be built—we have been compelled to send our brother Paulinianus to our homeland, so that he might sell the half-ruined little estates that escaped the hands of the barbarians, along with the property of our common parents. Otherwise, by abandoning the ministry we have begun for the saints, we should provide laughter for the slanderers and our rivals.”

In this monastery, living according to the rule established by the Apostles, he began, as he had greatly desired, to dwell with the distinguished man Eusebius of Cremona and with other holy brothers. From these men, who continually labored in divine service, the morning office now observed especially in the western regions was first established by canonical institution.

Cassian also testifies to this, saying:

“The office of the morning solemnity was first established, while it was still new, in the Bethlehem monastery, where our Lord Jesus Christ deigned to be born of a virgin for the redemption of the human race. From that time the custom of celebrating this morning service spread throughout the whole world.”

At that time the blessed Pope Damasus, with the blessed Jerome arranging this office,

[Note: [Col. 0191] The same manuscript reads “with the blessed Jerome suggesting it,” instead of “with the blessed Jerome arranging this office.”]

ordained that psalms should be sung day and night in all the churches, and that the following hymn should be added at the end of each one:

“Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit; as it was in the beginning, is now, and ever shall be, world without end. Amen.”

Many religious people who had learned of his reputation for life and knowledge therefore flocked to him. Good disciples frequented the good teacher and marveled at the effectiveness of his instruction.

For he was so abundant in giving explanations that, whatever he was asked, he had a ready and appropriate answer without delay. At one moment he gently encouraged the humble; at another he broke the necks of the proud; at another he repaid his detractors with necessary sharpness; at another he praised virginity; at another he defended chaste marriages; at another he warmly commended the glorious contests of virtue; at another he vehemently denounced lapses among clergy or monks.

While he was still governing his titular cardinal-priesthood at the Church of Saint Anastasia in Rome, he also permanently excluded three clerics from his presence and table for no other reason than that they walked in a disorderly and undisciplined manner.

[Note: [Col. 0192] The same manuscript entirely lacks the words “of the cardinal-priesthood in the Church of Saint Anastasia,” which appear to have been inserted into the text by a later hand.]

For an undisciplined gait is an evident sign that the condition of the inner person is badly ordered. Thus he says in the life of Saint Paula:

“Through the outward person,” he says, “the life of the inner person is also revealed.”

Moreover, he was endowed with such mastery of languages that, whenever he took into his hands books in one language, he transcribed them into another without hesitation.

[Note: [Col. 0192] The manuscript reads *he would run through*. We have corrected it to *he would pour back* in place of *he would pour forth*. Shortly afterward the same manuscript reads *he completed*. This brief work was poured forth with such speed by lamplight that it would certainly have been better to restore the passage.]

You would have thought that they had been written in that language, so smoothly did his unimpeded speed render them. Accordingly, in disparagement of his rivals, he concluded a certain letter as follows:

“Nor was this little nocturnal work so suffused with brilliance by lamplight that the tongue could outrun the hands of the scribes.”

During the same period he sent a remarkable letter to Paulinus, a former senator and presbyter, in which he briefly and summarily touched upon the mystery of each book of both the Old and the New Testament.

For what could escape Jerome’s keen intelligence, not only in divine writings but also in secular literature? From these secular writings he was sometimes compelled to insert something into his treatises, in order to prove that what the holy Prophets had foretold before the ages was contained in the writings of Greeks, Latins, and other nations as well.

We must not believe that he did this because the books of the Gentiles delighted his mind so greatly, since earlier he had been recalled to the heavenly tribunal and had paid the penalty for such reading after being chastised by a divine and salutary scourging.

How this happened is read in the aforementioned letter to Eustochium, where Jerome himself reports, among other things:

“Although many years earlier I had, for the sake of the kingdom of heaven, cut myself off from home, parents, relatives, and—what is more difficult than these—from the habit of richer food, and although I was traveling to Jerusalem as a soldier, I could not do without the library that I had assembled for myself at Rome with the greatest care and labor.

“Thus, miserable man that I was, while intending to read Cicero, I fasted. After frequent vigils during the night, after tears that flowed from the deepest recesses of my heart in remembrance of my former sins, Plato was taken up in my hands. Whenever, returning to myself, I began to read the Prophets, their unpolished style horrified me. And because I did not see the light with my blind eyes, I thought the fault lay not in my eyes but in the sun.

“While the ancient serpent was thus mocking me, in the middle of Lent a fever penetrated my marrow and invaded my exhausted body. Without any respite—and what I am about to say is incredible—it consumed my unhappy limbs so thoroughly that, while preparations were already being made for my burial, and the warmth of my vital spirit had grown cold throughout my body, my chest alone suddenly continued to palpitate.

“Then, suddenly caught up in spirit, I was dragged before the tribunal of the Judge. There was so much light from the radiance and brilliance of those standing around that, thrown upon the ground, I did not dare to look upward. Asked about my condition, I answered that I was a Christian. But the one presiding said: ‘You are lying. You are a Ciceronian, not a Christian. Where your treasure is, there your heart is also.’

“Immediately I fell silent, and amid the blows—for he had ordered me to be beaten—I was tortured more by the fire of conscience, repeating to myself that verse: ‘But in hell, who will confess you?’ Then I began to cry out and, wailing, to say: ‘Have mercy on me, Lord; have mercy on me.’ This voice resounded repeatedly amid the lashes.

“At last those who stood by fell upon the knees of the one presiding and begged him to pardon my youth and grant a period for repentance, while threatening that he would exact the punishment if I ever again read books of pagan literature. I, bound as I was by so great a crisis, and willing even to promise more, began to swear and, invoking his name, say: ‘Lord, if I ever possess secular books, or if I read them, I have denied you.’

“Amid these words of my oath I was released and returned from the world above. To the amazement of everyone, I opened my eyes, drenched in such a flood of tears that even unbelievers would have been convinced by my grief.

“Nor had that been sleep or the empty dreams by which we are often deceived. The tribunal before which I lay is my witness; the judgment that I feared is my witness. May I never again fall into such an examination. For I confess that I had shoulders full of wounds, that I felt the blows even after the dream, and that thereafter I read divine books with as much zeal as I had previously read mortal ones.”

After this, one day, while he was explaining the sacred Scriptures to the brothers according to custom, a huge lion entered the monastery precincts, limping on three feet and holding up the fourth. When the frightened brothers took flight, the man of God presented himself to it as though to an arriving guest. Understanding that its paw had been wounded by thorns, he ordered the brothers, once they had laid aside their fear, to care for it.

When this was done attentively, the lion abandoned all its ferocity and became so tame that, at the command of the blessed Jerome, the brothers entrusted it with a certain donkey, which it was to guard in the pastures when the animal returned from its work.

Meanwhile, one day, while the lion was asleep, some merchants traveling to Egypt saw the donkey wandering alone. Overcome by greed, they joined it to their caravan. When the lion awoke and failed to find the animal entrusted to it, it returned in confusion to the monastery. As though conscious of its guilt, it did not dare to enter the common dwelling alone.

The brothers, together with the blessed Jerome, considered the matter and assumed that the absent donkey had been devoured by the lion. Nevertheless, not wishing to provoke it, they assigned it the work of the missing animal: namely, to bear the loads that the donkey had previously carried.

Nor should the brothers have been surprised that, while living innocently, the lion rendered such service, since we read, as a testimony to the first creation, that lions and birds served holy men humbly ministering to God, that the blows of wild beasts ceased, and that the venom of serpents did no harm.

Thus, while the lion continually performed the task assigned to it, one day it looked out from an elevated place and saw the travelers mentioned above approaching in the distance, together with their camels and its own companion. Immediately, as though hostile forces had been detected, it gave a terrible roar and leapt violently against them, scattering the men in different directions. Then, driving the laden camels along with the donkey, it brought them to the monastery gate.

When the brothers had reported this to the blessed Jerome in amazement, he ordered the loads to be removed, the camels’ feet to be washed, fodder to be placed before them, and a meal to be prepared for the arriving guests.

And behold, they came immediately, prostrated themselves at the feet of the holy Father, and asked pardon for the theft they had committed. He received them kindly and led them with great cheerfulness to the guests’ cell. Seeing such clemency in the servant of God, they offered the monastery half the oil they had brought from Egypt. They also solemnly promised that each year both they and their heirs would provide a full jar of oil to the same monastery.

The blessed Jerome refreshed them with a kindly admonition, strengthened them with a spiritual blessing, and dismissed them in peace.

Meanwhile, the venerable Paula, whom we mentioned above, admired the religious life of the revered bishops Paulinus of Antioch and Epiphanius of Salamis.

[Note: [Col. 0194] The manuscripts we use add “of Cyprus”; shortly afterward they omit “and of Jerome.” Finally, they read “returning to their own sees” instead of “receiving them.”]

The Apostolic See was detaining these bishops on account of certain ecclesiastical affairs. Inflamed by their virtues and those of Jerome, Paula was considering leaving the city of Rome—or rather Babylon.

When they had returned to their own sees, she abandoned her children, Toxotius and Rufina, and her possessions, and, accompanied only by Eustochium, sailed after them with all her desire. Finally, after many dangers and immense labors, she entered Jerusalem. Having diligently visited the holy places, she returned to Bethlehem and built cells and monasteries for various pilgrims. Of these monasteries, under the direction of the blessed Jerome, she entrusted one to the governance of men.

She divided the virgins whom she gathered from various places into three groups and monasteries. Among them she humbled herself with such humility that anyone who heard her would have thought her the lowest of maidservants.

[Note: [Col. 0194] The same books read *I saw* instead of *I heard*. A little later they have “whom he himself, in response to the pious petition,” etc. They entirely omit the following sentence, beginning “Concerning whose holy life” and ending “of Paula.”]

When she saw her sisters devoted with such fervor to the worship of the holy Mother and Virgin of God, she and her daughter begged the blessed Jerome to compose a sermon on her Assumption containing a marvelous panegyric of that Virgin. He, equally devoted, accepted their pious request and fulfilled what they asked with the greatest care.

Jerome treats and explains at length her holy life, her departure from Rome, her journey along the road, her arrival at Jerusalem, and all the matters mentioned above in the treatise he wrote on the death and passing of Saint Paula.

[Col. 0195]

Among the countless treatises that he sent to various people, he wrote a letter to a certain virgin named Asella. In it he thanks her for the service she had shown him and, declaring himself innocent of a charge long laid against him, rebukes the envy of his rivals. He had learned that these men had also whispered against him at the departure of Saint Paula.

The text of the letter is as follows:

[Note: [Col. 0195] The older manuscript, without mentioning the name of the letter, prefixes this ridiculous heading: “The noble Dalmatian Jerome sends greetings to the virgin Asella.”]

“If I thought I could offer you thanks, I should have no understanding. God is powerful enough to restore to your soul what it deserves. For I, unworthy as I am, could never have judged myself capable of, or desired, so great an affection from you in Christ.

“And although some think me wicked, overwhelmed by crimes—and, for my sins, even these charges are small—you do well to regard even the wicked as good, according to your own mind. It is dangerous to judge another’s servant, and it is not easy to obtain pardon for speaking wrongly about those who are upright.

“That day will come, it will come, and you will grieve with me amid no small burning. I am infamous, I am deceitful and slippery, I am a liar and one who deceives by the art of Satan. Who would have wished either to believe or even to suspect such artifices concerning the innocent—or even concerning the guilty?

“Some kissed my hands and, with viperous mouths, disparaged me. They grieved with their lips and rejoiced in their hearts. The Lord saw them and mocked them, and reserved miserable me, his servant, for judgment with them in the future.

“One man slandered my gait and my laughter; another attacked my appearance; another suspected something else in my simplicity. I lived with them for almost three years. A great crowd of virgins often surrounded me, and I explained the divine books to some of them as I was able. Reading had produced assiduity; assiduity, familiarity; familiarity, confidence.

“Let them say whether they ever perceived anything in me other than what was fitting for a Christian. Let them say whether I accepted anyone’s money, or whether I failed to reject gifts, small or great. Did any person’s money ever sound in my hand?

[Note: [Col. 0195] The manuscripts read *sounded*. They also omit “except when Paula was setting out for Jerusalem,” along with Melania, who does not belong to this period and had sailed with Rufinus long before.]

“Nothing is brought against me except my sex; and this is never brought against me except when Paula and Melania set out for Jerusalem. They believed one who was lying; why do they not believe one who denies it? The man himself is the same as he was before. The one who shortly before proclaimed him guilty now confesses him innocent.

“And certainly tortures express the truth more clearly than laughter—unless it is easier to believe something that is not fabricated, or something that is not driven to be fabricated.

“Before I knew the household of Saint Paula, the judgments of the City were in agreement about me. By almost everyone’s verdict I was judged worthy of the highest priesthood. Damasus of blessed memory was the subject of my discourse. I was called holy; I was called humble and discreet.

“I never entered the house of any lascivious woman. I was never seized by silken garments, glittering jewels, painted faces, or the ambition for gold. There was never a matron in Rome who could tame my mind, except Paula, mourning and fasting, filthy with squalor and almost blinded by tears, whom the sun often found praying for the Lord’s mercy throughout the nights.

“Her song was the psalms; her speech, the Gospel; her pleasures, continence; her life, fasting.

[Col. 0196]

“Nothing could ever delight me except her, whom I never saw eating. But after I began to venerate, honor, and receive her because of the merit of her chastity, all the virtues immediately deserted me. O envy, which first bites at yourself! O cunning of Satan, always persecuting what is holy!

“Yet I give thanks to my God that I am worthy to be hated by the world.

[Note: [Col. 0196] From the same manuscripts we restored *a sorcerer* in place of the two-word reading *a bad man*.]

“Some chatter that I am a sorcerer; I recognize the title as belonging to a servant of the faith. The Jews too call their Lord a magician, and the Apostle has been called a deceiver. Temptation has not seized me except in a human manner. What portion of afflictions have I suffered, who serve the cross?

“They brought upon me the disgrace of a false accusation; but I know that one reaches the kingdom of heaven through good repute and bad repute alike.

“Having therefore attained the fullness of wisdom and knowledge,

[Note: [Col. 0196] The manuscripts prefer *holiness* instead of *knowledge*. With their help we also supplied shortly afterward the word *edition*, which was missing.]

he caused the abyss to give forth its voice, and the bitter waters of Hebrew were sweetened at his word; hidden things concealed from ages and generations were revealed.

“For he translated all the books of the Old Testament into Latin, first from Greek and afterward, in a more accurate edition, from Hebrew. And, with almost the same Spirit revealing everything by whose instruction they had been produced, he carefully explained them.

“He wrote one book on Genesis, apart from the questions addressed to Damasus; and he translated all the Homilies of Origen on the Pentateuch from Greek into Latin. He prudently explained in two books the questions on Kings, or Chronicles, which are called *Hebrew Questions*, apart from the three exceedingly obscure questions that he had explained at greater length in writing.

“The first of these is: Why did David voluntarily go with Achish to attack Saul? The second: Why, when David was dying, did he command his son to kill Joab, the commander of the army? The third concerns Shimei, who hurled insulting curses at David as he fled.

“He also explained another question proposed concerning the same books: namely, how Solomon and Achaz fathered sons within twelve years.

“Furthermore, he wrote a commentary on Isaiah in eighteen books; on Jeremiah in twenty books; on Ezekiel in fourteen books; on Daniel in three books; and on the Twelve Prophets in twenty books. In these works, so that nothing might remain obscure, he also beautifully revealed the meanings their names ought to bear through their proper etymologies.

“He published brilliant treatises on certain psalms, commentaries on Ecclesiastes, and two homilies on the Song of Songs addressed to Damasus.

“He also restored the New Testament to the Greek standard. From it he explained Matthew and Mark to diligent readers in a concise rather than tedious exposition. He also translated into Latin twenty-nine homilies on Luke published by Origen, and explained most of the Apostle’s Epistles and the Apocalypse of John.

“Finally, taking precautions for the future in case anything should at some time be corrupted in either the New or the Old Testament, he indicates in writing to Lucinus by what care it ought to be restored. ‘The reliability of the ancient books,’ he says, ‘must be tested against the Hebrew volumes; likewise, the standard of the Greek language is required for the new books.’”

[Col. 0197]

Finally, I too, following his admonitions, when I was wavering among conflicting Latin copies of the Old Testament, returned to the Hebrew truth, from whose source I had tasted. By its testimony I distinguished corrupt from uncorrupt readings and formed my judgment.

When I discovered that shoots of weeds had sprung up among the wheat of the divine books, I endeavored to uproot them all from the root. I also marked throughout the books passages especially liable to corruption and explained in a brief work the circumstances on account of which copies are most commonly corrupted.

The Roman Church, whose judgment governs everything, was not unaware of the skill of this most learned man. Seeing that his translation was more truthful than the others, it accepted it both for reading in the churches and for exposition.

Concerning this, the blessed Gregory says in his book of *Morals*: “I am explaining a new translation.” And, explaining in Ezekiel the statement concerning the living creatures, “Each covered his body with two wings,” after adding, “and likewise another was covered,” he immediately continued:

“After carefully examining the translation of the Seventy Interpreters, Aquila, Theodotion, and Symmachus, we find nothing of this kind in these words. But, rereading the writings of the blessed Jerome, we learned that he had found this meaning set down in the Hebrew truth—not indeed according to the word, but according to the sense. For the skilled translator, so as to omit absolutely nothing, sometimes rendered word for word, while sometimes, when the barbarism of the language resisted him, he expressed only the meaning of the words.”

Jerome himself clearly indicates that this method of translation is acceptable in the book he published on the best kind of interpretation.

He also wrote against Jovinianus.

[Note: [Col. 0197] The manuscripts add “two books.”]

He wrote one book against Helvidius on the perpetual virginity of blessed Mary. In the former work he proves Jovinianus, who asserted that there would be no difference among merits in the future and who continually served the pleasures of the flesh, to be a heretic and an Epicurean among Christians. Helvidius, who attempted to demonstrate from the Scriptures that the untouched Mother of God had other children, he rebuked as a simpleton and one utterly ignorant of the Scriptures.

Moreover, he confounded another heretic—not by writing, but by engaging him in conversation. This man, holding opinions about the resurrection of the flesh contrary to the Catholic faith, proposed questions of the following kind:

“At what age will we rise? If at the same age at which we die, then after the resurrection nurses will also be needed. If at another age, there will be not a resurrection of the dead but a transformation into others.

“Will there also be a difference of sex between male and female, or will there not? If there will be, then marriages, intercourse, and procreation will follow. If there will not be, then, with the difference of sex removed, the same bodies will not rise, but bodies that are tenuous and spiritual.”

He attempted to prove these points by introducing the Apostle’s statement: “The natural body is sown; the spiritual body will rise.”

To this the blessed Jerome replied:

“When I had heard this, and necessity had been laid upon me, I answered the most wicked viper and met him with questioning alone. ‘Do you believe,’ I said, ‘in the resurrection of the dead, or not?’

“When he answered that he believed, I continued: ‘Will the same bodies rise, or different ones?’

“When he said, ‘The same,’ I asked: ‘In the same sex, or in another?’

“When he remained silent in response to the questions and, like a serpent, shifted his head from one side to another so as not to be struck, I said: ‘Because you are silent, I will answer for you and draw the conclusion.

“‘If neither woman nor man will rise, there will be no resurrection of the dead, because, since sex has limbs, the limbs constitute the whole body. But if there are neither sex nor limbs, where will the resurrection of the dead be?’

[Note: [Col. 0198] The manuscripts give the passage somewhat differently: “There will be no resurrection of bodies, because without sex it does not consist in limbs. But if there is no resurrection of bodies, there will certainly be no resurrection of the dead.” Compare Letter CVIII to Eustochium, §22, in our recension, from which this passage is cited.]

[Col. 0198]

“‘As for your objection concerning marriages: if the same limbs exist, and marriages therefore follow, the Savior dissolves the objection with these words: “They err because they do not know the Scriptures or the power of God. For in the resurrection they will neither marry nor be given in marriage, but will be like the angels.”

“‘Where it says, “They will neither marry nor be given in marriage,” the difference of the sexes is shown. No one says of a stone or a piece of wood, “They will neither marry nor be given in marriage,” because they do not possess the nature of marrying; rather, this is said of those who could marry but, through the grace and power of Christ, will not marry.

“‘If you then object, “How shall we be like the angels, since among the angels there is neither male nor female?” listen briefly: what is promised is not the angels’ substance but their preservation and blessedness. Likeness is promised; nature is not changed.’”

[Note: [Col. 0198] We restored *is not changed* from the same manuscripts and from the text of the letter itself, in place of *is not nourished*.]

“But if you ask at what age we shall rise, according to the traditions of the churches and the Apostle Paul, this must be answered: We shall rise as a perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ. The Jews maintain that Adam was created at this age, and the Savior—”

We read that the Lord rose again. “And I have brought forward,” he says, “many other passages from both Testaments to stifle the heretic.” But did he cleanse the Church of only these heresies? No heresy ever arose in his time that he did not cut down with the sickle of his eloquence. For he never spared heretics, as he himself asserts; rather, he acted with every effort so that the enemies of the Church might also become his own enemies [Note: [Col. 0198] With the aid of the same books we have restored *fierent* (“might become”) here in place of *fuerint*.].

This is also why he is said to have incurred the enmity of Rufinus, a most learned man and his colleague, with whom he had been accustomed to taste the honey of the Holy Scriptures: because he vigorously corrected him for holding a wrong view concerning free choice. The Roman Church approves his zeal for the rectitude of the faith, so that the blessed Pope Gelasius, a most discerning investigator of the Scriptures, appears to reject the books of that same Rufinus, although they were composed in distinguished language, issuing this order in his decrees:

> Rufinus, a religious man, published many books of ecclesiastical composition; he also interpreted certain Scriptures. But since the most blessed Jerome censured him on some points concerning free choice, we hold those opinions which we know the aforesaid man to have held.

And not only concerning Rufinus, but also concerning all those whom the man so often mentioned reproved out of zeal for God and devotion to the faith, he spoke likewise. We receive for reading certain works of Origen, which [Col. 0199] the blessed Jerome does not reject; but all the rest, together with their author [Note: The same manuscripts read “together with their author,” namely Origen.], we declare to be rejected.

Among the distinguished works of his studies, he wrote a book *On Illustrious Men*, following the example of Tranquillus and the Greek Apollonius, from the holy Apostles down to his own age. After listing many others, he placed himself at the end of the volume as though an abortive and the least of all Christians. There it was necessary for him to record briefly, up to the fifteenth year of the emperor Theodosius, whatever he had written [Note: More correctly, following Jerome himself, our manuscripts count “the fourteenth year of Theodosius.”].

Among other things, which have been noted above in various places, he recalls that he had written: one book, *The Dispute between the Luciferian and the Orthodox*; one book *On Places*; one book *On the Essence of God*; one book *On Hebrew Names*; one book of letters to various persons; and one book of letters to Marcella. “To Paula,” he says, “and Eustochium, since they are written daily, I am uncertain.”

Who among us can read as much as this blessed man Jerome wrote? Who would not marvel at this spirit, burning in the Scriptures and fervent in the service of God? Who would not call him an angel rather than a man, since nothing fits him better than that prophetic saying:

> The lips of the priest guard knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts.

Certainly, if, while remaining in the flesh, he had walked according to human nature, he would never have reached such a summit of knowledge. Nor would he have desired to be dissolved with Paul [Note: The manuscripts read: “with Paul, unless he were with Christ,” and so forth.], nor would he have been confident that he would reign among the angels with Christ.

But because he had triumphed over the world, and was already secure, as it were, in the reward for his labor, he said to Heliodorus:

> Believe me, I seem to see some greater light. I long, once the burden of the body has been cast aside, to fly forth into the pure radiance of the ether.

At last he was so exhausted by weariness that, even while lying on his bed, he would raise himself upright by grasping with his hands a cord that he had hung from a beam. In this way he performed, as best he could, the duties of the monastery. Yet his soundness of understanding remained no less vigorous for giving an answer, whenever and from whatever quarter he was questioned.

For he also fully satisfied the blessed Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, when Augustine challenged him with his questions—or, more truly, when “abyss called to abyss.” Judging himself as though a veteran [Note: The same manuscripts read “indicating that he was a veteran.”], he deterred him from further challenging him in these words:

> We have had our time and have run as far as we could. Now that you are running and crossing long distances, let us be granted some rest. And, if I may say so with your pardon and honor, do not appear to have been the only one to set something from the poets before me. Remember Dares and Entellus, and the common proverb: “The weary ox plants his foot firmly.”

To this the blessed Augustine humbly replied:

> Why, then, do I strive against a contracted stream, rather than piously beg pardon? I beg you: if I have offended you, forgive me. And if you are an ox, as you seem to think yourself, weary perhaps from old age in body, though not in vigor of mind, nevertheless sweating with fruitful labor in the Lord’s threshing floor—here I am: if I have said anything wrongly, plant your foot more firmly. The burden of your age ought not to trouble me, provided the chaff of my fault is crushed.

Moreover, in the book that Augustine himself wrote against the error of the Pelagian Julian [Note: In one Ambrosian manuscript, *Manichaei* is incorrectly read instead of *Pelagiani*. It continues there with a different meaning: “He wanted marriage to be condemned; but what was born from it was free from every obligation of sin.”], who held that marriage was condemnable because nothing born from it was free from every obligation of sin, after introducing many Catholic witnesses against his pernicious doctrine, he introduced the same Jerome with these words:

> Do not think that the holy presbyter Jerome is to be despised. Learned in Greek and Latin, and moreover in the Hebrew language, he passed from the Western Church to the Eastern and lived in the holy places and in sacred letters almost to decrepit old age. His eloquence shone for us from East to West like the sun. In short, everyone who before him read anything concerning the doctrine of the Church from either side of the world [*ex utraque parte orbis*; an alternative reading is *ex utraque parte urbis*, “from either side of the city”] neither held nor advanced, on any other matter, an opinion other than the one I have stated.

Thus, after the blessed Jerome had erected, through the overflowing abundance of his writings, an impregnable tower of the Church of Christ against the darts of the heretics [Col. 0200], he departed to the Lord in his ninetieth year, and in the twelfth year of the reign of Theodosius, in a good old age—namely, on the last day of September, at the final hour of that same day, when the sun was setting [Note: The same manuscript further exaggerates this as “in the ninety-sixth year of his age,” and then reads “in the twelfth year of the younger Theodosius.” Finally, it omits the following: “namely, on the last day of September, and at the final hour of that same day, when the sun was setting.”].

The holy and venerable women Paula and Eustochium—who, following his example and admonition, had despised the world and carried the cross of Christ—had emigrated before his death when the Bridegroom called them. While the blessed Jerome was still alive, he had made himself a tomb by cutting the stone at the entrance of the cave of the Lord’s manger, not far from the tomb of the holy women mentioned above. There, after the perversity of the world had been overcome, he was buried on the day before the Kalends of October.

Perhaps the Reader will wonder that such holy persons could have had envious enemies. But this is not to be wondered at: envy always persecutes virtue, and lightning strikes the highest mountains. Nor should it seem surprising that such things happen to the good [Note: [Col. 0200] The same manuscript reads, “that these things happen to men.”], since the Lord himself was crucified because of the zeal of the Pharisees, and all the saints have had rivals.

Esau persecuted Jacob. Saul sought David’s life, and the Lord himself raised up Hadad the Idumean against Solomon. Jezebel also compelled the priests to flee, and the Jewish people persecuted all the Prophets. The Apostle Paul complains of false brothers and is lowered over a wall so that he may not be captured by his enemies. And, while recounting dangers of many kinds, he speaks of himself and those like him:

> We have become a spectacle to this world, and to angels and to human beings.

And:

> We are fools for Christ’s sake.

And:

> What is foolish in God is wiser than human beings.

For this reason the Savior also says to the Father:

> You know my foolishness.

In the Gospel, his relatives regarded him as though he were out of his mind, while his adversaries slandered him, saying:

> He has a demon [Col. 0201].

And:

> He is a Samaritan.

And:

> By Beelzebub, the prince of demons, he casts out demons.

But blessed is the one who can say with the Apostle:

> This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience, that we have conducted ourselves in the world in holiness and sincerity and the glory of God [Note: [Col. 0201] Both Ambrosian codices read “and the grace of God” instead of “and the glory of God,” and so forth.].

Accordingly, he hears the Lord saying:

> Therefore the world hates you, because you are not of the world. For if you were of the world, the world would love what was its own.

It is dangerous to speak evil of the good. For just as this leads those approved to a crown, so it contributes to the heap of condemnation [formerly, “tomb”] for those who reproach them [Col. 0202]. The blessed Augustine also attests to this, saying:

> Let no one tear apart the servants of God, because it is not advantageous to those who tear them apart. False accusations increase the reward of God’s servants, but punishment also increases for those who make the accusations.

For it was not said without reason:

> When people hate you and reproach you, falsely, rejoice and exult, because your reward is abundant in the heavens.

Therefore, let us console one another with these words, blessing the Lord in all his ways.

He lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0201]

**The Life of Saint Jerome, by an Unknown Author (C, S)**

[Note: [Col. 0201] We append this third Life of Saint Jerome, likewise composed by an incompetent compiler, so that nothing might be lacking from such ancient monuments as others before us have printed. Indeed, we endured so much of this laborious undertaking that we examined manuscript codices from beginning to end, especially one belonging to the Queen of Sweden, now numbered 439 in the Vatican Library. Erasmus formerly stated with good reason that this history scarcely corresponds to the merits of so great a man, and that he certainly would not have published such trifles—more truly called nonsense than books—unless he had already resolved to omit nothing that either a learned reader might desire or an unlearned reader might need.]

I do not doubt that most people know where illustrious men were born, under which teachers and in what branches of learning they were educated, and in what place holy Jerome now rests. Nevertheless, those who have no leisure, or are unable to read much, can learn this if they wish, in a brief and concise work.

Blessed Jerome, then, was born of noble stock. His father was named Eusebius, and his birthplace was the town of Stridon, which was destroyed by the Goths and had once stood on the boundary of Dalmatia and Pannonia. Appropriately, he was begotten by a father named Eusebius. For *Eusebius* in Greek is rendered in Latin as “pious.” Likewise *Hieronymus* in Aeolic, and entirely in Latin, means “sacred law.” Jerome, therefore—that is, “sacred law”—was rightly born of a pious father, so that through his devoted labor the nourishing Law might be revealed from the writings of the Hebrews without [Note: [Col. 0201] The Queen’s manuscript has *absque omni scrupulositate* (“without any scruple”) and then *fieret lex* (“the Law might become”) instead of *pateret* (“might be revealed”). We omit the errors that occur among the variant readings.] scruple: a Law that, once its austerity had been removed, would announce to the human race that a pious, sacred, and merciful Father was to come.

When he was passing through the intervening years between boyhood and adolescence, touched by a heavenly impulse, he abandoned all his relatives and his father’s estate so that he might become a perfect imitator of the Gospel. He boarded a ship, with a favorable breeze blowing, and by the dispensation of divine mercy hastened to the threshold of the exalted Apostles Peter and Paul and reached the city of Rome. [Note: [Col. 0201] The same manuscript inserts here, “hastening.”] There he was thoroughly and diligently educated in Greek and Latin letters, [Col. 0202] and, having assumed the garment of Christ, was also ordained there as a cardinal presbyter.

For, in order that the Lord might raise up for His Church an unconquerable wall against faithless and senseless heretics, many *καθηγηταί* (*kathegetai*), that is, teachers, instructed this man in literary studies. Donatus the grammarian, instructing him in Roman letters and sufficiently filling him with the flavor of the liberal arts, became his teacher, as Jerome himself records in his *Chronicle*, saying: “Victorinus the rhetorician and Donatus the grammarian, my teachers and instructors, were renowned in Rome.” [Note: [Col. 0202] The lesser manuscript, and the more correct reading, has “my teacher and instructor”; it also reads *habentur* (“are held”) instead of *habebantur* (“were held”).]

He likewise testifies that Gregory of Nazianzus was his *didascalus*, that is, his teacher—as he reports in the third book of his explanations of Isaiah. When he came in that Prophet to the passage where he had to explain something concerning the Seraphim, he introduced it as follows:

“About this vision, approximately thirty years ago, when I was in Constantinople and was being instructed in the study of the sacred Scriptures by the most eloquent man Gregory of Nazianzus, my teacher, then bishop of that same city, I know that I dictated a brief and impromptu treatise, both to test my little talent and to obey the requests of my friends.”

What more distinguished testimony can be given concerning this man’s refined industry in learning the elements of Latin, Greek, Hebrew, Arabic, and Chaldean than the words he himself sent to Pammachius and Oceanus, where he says:

“When I was young,” he says, “I was carried along by an extraordinary eagerness to learn; nor, contrary to the presumption of certain people, did I teach myself. I frequently listened to Apollinarius at Antioch and honored him. Even then, when he was instructing me in the sacred Scriptures, his head was covered with white hair; and it was more fitting for him to be a teacher than a pupil. Nevertheless, I went on to Alexandria and listened to Didymus. I give him thanks for many things. What I did not know, I learned; what I knew, I did not lose under his instruction. People thought that I had reached the end of my studies. I returned again to Jerusalem and Bethlehem. At what price and with what labor did I have Barabbas the Hebrew as a nocturnal teacher?” [Note: [Col. 0203] The same manuscript prefers “Baraninas.”] “For he feared the Jews and presented himself to me as another Nicodemus.”

I have set these things down so that those who wish to know may learn, as I said, where so great a man was born and under what teachers he was formed.

While Jerome was staying in Rome, preserving the virginity of mind and body and repentance for sins, he preached to the faithful and corrected many books, together with the volumes of the Septuagint and the Psalter, while Liberius presided as pontiff over the Apostolic See. At that time, without doubt, Arian heresy was staining the Roman people under the Emperor Constantius.

Therefore, having obtained the opportunity he had always desired, as has been said above, the aforementioned man left his home, parents, sister, relatives, and the celebrated and most glorious city of Peter, [Note: [Col. 0203] The manuscript reads: “the most religious city of Peter, bearing only his body and whatever things were useful for the journey, together with …”; then: “he had completed at Rome, bringing it together to Jerusalem, having come as a young man to serve for the sake of the heavenly kingdom. And when, after spending several days there, he had learned that he could not live without danger to his soul, he prudently wished to be near the Lord’s manger, like a sensible animal, which is six miles from Jerusalem,” etc. These words continue in the following page, or column 273. The entire intervening history, almost two hundred lines, is wholly absent. It can hardly be thought that it was cut out by accident or mutilated by a later hand from an ancient exemplar, since the context of the discourse itself suggests the contrary: namely, that it never existed there, but had been inserted and stitched in from the preceding Lives, as had many other passages, especially those excerpted from Jerome’s own letters.] and, carrying only his body and whatever things could be useful on the journey, together with the library he had assembled with the utmost care in that city, he came to Jerusalem as a young man prepared to serve for the sake of the heavenly kingdom.

After he had acquired the whole range of secular learning, he also imitated the life and conduct of the most approved monks. Trampling down the desires of the soul with constant sincerity and continually breaking the pleasure of the body through fasting, he taught by his own example that many of the good and religious would become better.

On one occasion, while Jerome, as was his custom, was opening the divine books for reading and remembering Tullius, the immortal author of his library, he was soon chastised from heaven with a saving scourge, so that he might never again turn over such books. He himself makes this assertion about himself in a letter to Eustochium:

“When many years ago I had cut myself off from my home, parents, sister, relatives, and—from what is more difficult than all these—the habit of richer food, for the sake of the kingdom of heaven, and was setting out to serve as a soldier at Jerusalem, I could not bear to be without the library that I had prepared for myself at Rome with the utmost care and labor. Thus, wretched man that I was, I would fast in order to read Tullius. After frequent vigils at night, after the tears that remembrance of my past sins drew from the depths of my heart, Plautus would be taken up in my hands. If, [Col. 0204] when I had come back to myself, I began to read the Prophets, their speech seemed uncultivated. And because I could not see the light with blinded eyes, I thought the fault lay not in my eyes but in the sun.

“While the ancient serpent was thus mocking me, around the middle of Lent a fever, poured into my marrow, seized my exhausted body; and without any respite—what is almost incredible to relate—it consumed my unhappy limbs so completely that scarcely any flesh clung to the bones. Meanwhile my funeral rites were being prepared, and, while the warmth of my living soul was already growing cold throughout my body, it fluttered only in my little breast, which alone remained warm.

“Suddenly, snatched away in spirit, I was dragged before the tribunal of the Judge. There was so much light there, and such brilliance from the radiance of those standing around, that, thrown upon the ground, I did not dare to look upward. Asked about my condition, I replied that I was a Christian. But he who presided said: ‘You lie. You are a Ciceronian, not a Christian. For where your treasure is, there your heart is also.’

“Immediately I fell silent. Yet amid the blows—for he had ordered me to be beaten—I was tortured more by the fire of conscience, recalling that verse: ‘But in hell, who will confess to you?’ I began to cry out and to say, lamenting: ‘Have mercy on me, Lord; have mercy on me.’ This cry resounded among the lashes.

“At last those who stood by fell upon the knees of the presiding judge and begged him to pardon my youth and grant my error a place for repentance, while declaring that he would exact punishment from me thereafter if I ever read books of pagan literature. I, constrained in that great crisis and willing even to promise more, began to swear and, invoking his name, to say: ‘Lord, if I ever possess secular books, if I ever read them, I have denied you.’

“After these words of the oath I was released and returned to the world above. To the amazement of everyone, I opened my eyes, drenched in such a flood of tears that even unbelievers would have been convinced by my grief. Nor had that been a sleep or an empty dream, by which we are often deceived. That tribunal before which I lay is my witness; that terrible judgment, which I feared, is my witness.

“May I never again fall into such an examination. I said that my shoulders had been full of bruises and that I had felt the wounds in my dream; thereafter I read the divine books with as much zeal as I had previously read mortal literature.”

The same Jerome, as we had omitted to mention, while he was still in the city of Rome—the mouth of Pope Damasus, the investigator of the sacred library, and the interpreter of the divine books—was honored for three continuous years, dear and welcome to the people. By everyone’s judgment he was deemed worthy of the pontificate, and, as was written above, had been ordained cardinal presbyter by the aforementioned Pope.

Certain men from the ranks of the clergy and monks, roaming about in insolence and gluttony, laid plots to drive this same Jerome from the city, because he had written about and reproved the vices of both groups.

But I would call this man fortunate. I believe that the outcome of this flight was arranged rather by the judgment of Christ, who corrects, than prepared by the persecutions of wicked men—namely, so that the Roman Church, established under the rule of Peter, might, if Christ God willed it and Jerome labored with spiritual zeal, possess the Hebrew truth of all the books of the Old Testament, and so that the frivolity of certain Greeks, who boasted that they had received all the Scriptures as divinely inspired from God, might recognize that they possessed what it did not possess.

Thus Jerome, as has already been said, left Rome and turned toward the East, proceeding to Gregory of Nazianzus, bishop of the city of Constantinople. There he strove to advance so that he might be instructed in the study of the sacred Scriptures. As a suppliant and teachable disciple, he approached his teacher and remained under his instruction in Constantinople.

After completing this discipleship, Jerome went to Syria. While staying on the estate of the presbyter Evagrius, he happened to find Malchus the monk, who had once been a captive. After questioning him, Jerome learned the whole story of his captivity, which he later published in writing and sent to the faithful at Rome. In the prologue to that history he inserted these words:

“I have resolved to write,” he says, “if God grants me life, and if my detractors at least cease pursuing me while I flee and remain shut away.”

He then approached the deserted places to which he had formerly desired to hasten in order to perform penance there. He came so joyfully and eagerly prepared that you would think he had flown rather than walked. How, during four continuous years, he performed penance by the help of Christ, and how he himself acknowledged that divine grace had been present in what he voluntarily endured, Jerome indicated in these words:

“How often, when I was established in the desert, in that vast solitude which, scorched by the sun’s heat, offered the monks a dreadful dwelling, I thought,” he says, “that I was in the midst of the luxuries of Rome. I sat alone, because I was filled with bitterness. My deformed limbs bristled beneath sackcloth, and my squalid skin was covered with the filth of an Ethiopian body. Every day there were tears; every day groans. And whenever impending sleep overcame me despite my resistance, I would dash my bones, scarcely clinging to me, against the naked earth.

“As for food and drink, I say nothing, since even the ailing monks use cold water, and to have received anything cooked is considered luxury. Yet I, who had condemned myself to be without such things through fear of Gehenna, had only scorpions and wild beasts as companions, yet often joined choirs of girls in imagination. My face was pale from fasting, but my mind burned with desire. In a cold body, and with my flesh already half-dead before its own master, only the fires of lust were boiling.

“Thus deprived of every aid, I would lie at the feet of Jesus; I would water them with tears; I would wipe them with my hair; and I would subdue my rebellious flesh by a week’s starvation. I am not ashamed of my misery; rather, I mourn that I am not what I once was. I remember that I often joined day to night with my cries, and did not cease beating my breast until, when the Lord rebuked me, tranquility returned.

“I feared even my little cell, as though it were conscious of my thoughts. Angry and stern with myself, I would penetrate the desert alone. Wherever I saw hollow valleys, rugged mountains, or precipitous cliffs, there was the place of my prayer, there the prison of my wretched flesh. And—as the Lord himself is my witness—after many tears, after my eyes had clung to heaven, I sometimes seemed to myself to be present among the ranks of angels; and, joyful and rejoicing, I sang: ‘After you we shall run in the fragrance of your perfumes.’”

[Col. 0206]

When the four years devoted to penance had been completed, the same Jerome returned to the town of Bethlehem. There, like a prudent animal, he betook himself to the Lord’s manger, which lies six miles from Jerusalem, toward the south. He approached the bishop of that city, named Cyril, and asked him to grant him a place to live in the parish situated at Bethlehem. [Note: [Col. 0206] The Queen’s codex reads: “which he devoutly requested”; then: “since he lived there worthily, permission to inhabit Bethlehem was granted, with the neighboring villages approaching,” etc.]

He immediately granted what Jerome had devoutly requested. Indeed, with the assistance of the neighboring Catholic villages, he built a monastery worthy of the place. There, living according to the rule established by the Apostles, he began to do what he had long desired: to live with brothers. He also lived with Eusebius of Cremona, a nobleman, at whose request he translated a certain letter from Greek into Latin.

It must truly be known that the morning psalmody now observed, especially in the western regions, was first established in the monastery as a canonical office, where the aforementioned man certainly cannot be thought to have been idle. Through his translation of the divine Scripture he rendered such service to us that we scarcely need to approach the Hebrew source, since he is recognized to have satisfied us with the great abundance of his eloquence. Through many books and copious letters, which by the Lord’s favor he deigned to write, he made us blessed.

Among the other works of his studies, beginning with blessed Peter and continuing down to himself, he wrote *On Illustrious Men*, imitating Tranquillus and the Greek Apollonius. There he says of himself:

“After the catalogue of many men, I placed myself also at the end of the volume, as an abortive and the least of all Christians. It was therefore necessary for me briefly to record what I had written up to the fourteenth year of the reign of Theodosius.”

Moreover, by publishing innumerable books constructed from the writings of the Apostles and Prophets, he completed the immovable tower of the Catholic Church against the darts of the faithless. He translated all the books of the Old Testament from Hebrew codices into Latin. He also rendered the prophet Daniel, who spoke in the Chaldean style, and righteous Job, who spoke in Arabic, into the Roman language, giving both authors a complete translation. [Note: [Col. 0206] The same manuscript has “he displayed” instead of “he translated.” After several lines it reads: “he wonderfully demonstrated, wonderfully indicated, clearly,” etc.]

He likewise made Matthew Roman from the Hebrew. He sent a remarkable letter to Paulinus, formerly a senator and now a presbyter, teaching him how to read the divine Scriptures carefully. In it he briefly and wonderfully indicated the power of each book of the Old and New Testaments: wonderfully clear, honorably learned, and sweet, with a ready abundance of words, he turned his talent toward every subject, so that whatever question was put to him, he had a ready and fitting answer without any delay.

At one moment he gently flatters the humble; at another he breaks the necks of the proud; [Col. 0207] at another he returns the necessary retaliation to his detractors with biting force; at another he praises virginity; at another he defends chaste marriages; [Note: [Col. 0207] Our manuscripts lack the word “chaste.”] at another he warmly commends the glorious contests of virtue; at another he accuses the fallen among the clergy and the monks of depravity.

Yet wherever the occasion arose, he mingled examples from pagan authors with a most pleasing truth. This was not, however, his own preference but—as I might say—a grave necessity: to prove that the things foretold by the holy prophets before the ages were contained in the writings of Greeks, Latins, and other peoples. He explained everything, adorned everything, and proceeded through various kinds of disputation, always eloquent and even-tempered. [Note: [Col. 0207] The same manuscripts read “expositions” instead of “disputation.”]

He possessed such mastery of both languages that, whenever he took up any Greek books, he moved through them in Latin without difficulty; and again he reread Latin works in Attic speech, so that you would think that what his mouth poured forth with unhindered speed had been written in that language.

I would truly say that this man’s Catholic prudence [Note: [Col. 0207] Here our manuscripts have “knowledge” instead of “prudence,” and shortly afterward “Paula” instead of “Eustochium.”] and sound doctrine remained firm in the strength of faith wherever he lived. Those who, sick with the disease of ignorance and envy, imagine that he deviated from the faith of the Catholic Church—that is, from the faith of blessed Peter—or that he was a heretic, are certainly deluded. They base this judgment on his having written to Eustochium:

“Take care, I beg you, lest God ever say of you: ‘The virgin of Israel has fallen; there is no one to raise her up.’”

In order to terrify the careless and incautious, since God is a just judge, the teacher added these words:

“I speak boldly: although God can do all things, he cannot raise up a virgin after her fall. He can indeed free her from punishment, but he cannot restore her.” [Note: [Col. 0207] Again, the manuscripts have “crown” instead of “restore,” and shortly afterward “this man” instead of “that woman”; they also read “he wrote to Paula” instead of “he wrote to Eustochium.”]

By saying this, without doubt he did not take omnipotence away from God; rather, by revealing Him as a just judge, he asserted the point. For, unless I am mistaken, we read words of admonition addressed to Domitilla, the niece of the Emperor Domitian, similar to those that holy Jerome addressed to Eustochium.

I think it pleasant to hear why those words were spoken to her. This virgin had as chamberlains the eunuchs Nereus and Achilleus, whom the most blessed Apostle Peter had won for Christ. When they saw their mistress adorned with jewels, clothed in purple garments and in garments woven with gold, they said to her:

“With what care you adorn your body in order to take as your husband Aurelian, the mortal son of a consul! If you adorned your soul with equal care, you could gain as your bridegroom the immortal King, the Son of God. He would also make you eternal and would never allow an end or limit to come to you, your adornments, or your joys.” [Note: [Col. 0207] The same manuscripts have: “or allow it to come to an end”; then: “so that both the dignity of your family and the memory of your name would not perish.”]

Domitilla replied [Col. 0208] and said:

“What love can be better than to have a husband and bear children through whom the most delightful posterity may be propagated, and through whom both the dignity of one’s family and the memory of one’s name may not be destroyed?”

Nereus answered her:

“Virginity is better. When you came forth from your mother’s womb, it was born with you, nursed with you, and has always remained with you, untouched by the corruption of the flesh. It is beloved by God and dear to His angels. If any virgin loses it, she can indeed escape the guilt of that loss through repentance, but she can in no way regain the integrity itself.

“For every kind of holiness, whenever it has been violated or lost through some pleasure or necessity, and every virtue that has been lost, can be recovered and restored to its former state, integrity, or glory through the tears of repentance. Virginity alone, if once it has perished, cannot in any way return to the stability of its former integrity.”

While Nereus and Achilleus were discoursing on these matters, praising virginity and offering many other arguments by which eternal life might be merited through deeds, the most prudent virgin Domitilla said:

“If only that sentence of God had once reached me, and I had never taken the name of bride, nor accepted the marriage proposal of a mortal man!” [Note: [Col. 0208] Our manuscripts read: “nor would I have accepted the name of the bride of a mortal man. But now …” Shortly afterward they have “Euphronisa” instead of “Eufrosina,” and “marriage contracts” instead of “bridegrooms.”]

“But now, because God has opened your mouths to win my soul, whatever you want me to do, hasten to do as quickly as possible.”

Why say more? Consecrated by Saint Clement the Pope, and rejecting Aurelian as her bridegroom, she was exiled for this reason to the island of Pontiana. From there she was brought to Tarracina. When she refused to sacrifice to idols, she and Eufrosina and Theodora—the brides of Sulpitius and Servilianus—were burned by Luxurius, Aurelian’s brother, and received the palm of martyrdom. Saint Caesarius the deacon, who was himself later martyred by the aforementioned Luxurius, placed them together in a new sarcophagus and buried them.

Although these matters were not necessary to discuss here, we have added them because almost exactly what Nereus had said to the most prudent virgin Domitilla was this: a virginity that had been lost could obtain forgiveness for its guilt through repentance, but could never become virgin again as it had been before.

Saint Jerome took care to commend this same teaching to Eustochium as an exhortation to better things:

“Although God can do all things, he cannot raise up a virgin after her fall.”

For what else does “cannot” mean here but “does not will”? This could have been expressed in other words. For a certain wise man is said to have addressed God:

“But you, ruler of strength, judge with tranquility and arrange all things with great reverence. For power is subject to you whenever you will; therefore, where God’s will is absent, power is lacking.”

For just as God is unchangeable in nature, so He is unchangeable in will. Since He is truthful and just, neither falsehood nor injustice suits Him. For just as He cannot lie, being truth, so He cannot be unjust—that is, He does not will to do anything unjust. For, as the Prophet bears witness, “Whatever the Lord willed, He did in heaven and on earth,” and all His judgments are just.

While we were therefore striving to show what can be done when God wills it and what cannot be done when He does not will it—and so that no empty talker might presume to attack that truthful and outstanding Teacher, with whom, while he lived, no one dared to compare himself in any branch of knowledge—we have digressed farther from the order with which we began.

Nevertheless, anyone who wishes can learn more fully what kind and how great a man Jerome was from the testimony of Saint Augustine alone. [Note: [Col. 0209] Previously the text had *Nam* (“for”), whereas it should read *Num* (“whether”). The same manuscript also has “he said” instead of “he taught.” Recall what we noted concerning this passage in the immediately preceding Life.]

For when Augustine, in the first book he had written against the error of Julian the Manichaean—who unquestionably said that marriage was condemned, but that what was born from marriage was entirely free from the obligation of sin—had introduced many Catholic witnesses against this poisonous dogma, he continued as follows:

“Nor should you think that Saint Jerome, who was a presbyter, is to be despised. He was learned in Greek and Latin and, in addition, in Hebrew eloquence. Passing from the Western Church to the Eastern, he lived in the holy places and in the sacred writings almost to an advanced old age. His eloquence shone for us from East to West like the light of the sun. In short, he read all, or nearly all, who before him had written anything concerning ecclesiastical doctrine in either part of the world, and he held and expressed no other judgment on this matter than the one I have stated. When he was explaining the Prophet Jonah, he said most clearly that even infants were held liable to the sin of Adam’s offense.” [Note: [Col. 0209] From the words “Augustine says these things” through the entire following section up to “they would become enemies,” a passage of more than twenty lines is missing from our manuscript. We discussed the contents of that passage in another Life at this point.]

These are Augustine’s words in the book mentioned above.

The same Jerome also labored with great intellectual power against Celsus, Porphyry, and Julian Augustus, rabid dogs hostile to Christ, and against the persecutors of the Church, or those who thought that the Church had possessed no philosophers or eloquent teachers. He did so so that they might learn what sort and how great the men were who founded, built, and adorned it, and cease accusing our faith of rustic simplicity, recognizing instead their own ignorance. He did this, moreover, in innumerable books constructed from the writings of the Apostles and Prophets.

A little later he says:

“Now the mystery of iniquity is at work, and each person chatters whatever he thinks. I alone am the one whose glory is attacked by everyone.”

He says also:

“To the many who say that I write this work inflamed by the torches of envy, I shall answer briefly: I have never spared heretics, but have acted with every effort so that the enemies of the Church might also become my enemies.”

It is altogether impossible, and would take too long, to recount everything about this man, his disciplined life, and his character. I shall therefore attach to this concise account a certain ancient-like miracle of this monastery, whose memory has not yet been erased through the reports of successive generations and which was brought here by religious men who had come to Bethlehem out of love for their heavenly homeland.

One day, as evening was falling, blessed Jerome had sat with the brothers, as is the custom of monks, to hear the sacred reading and was explaining the divine commandments. Suddenly a huge lion entered the monastery precincts, limping on three feet and holding the fourth raised. When some of the brothers saw this, they were terrified and, as human frailty naturally does under fear, turned to flight.

But Saint Jerome went out to meet it as it approached. When the two had come near one another, and since the lion could not speak, as is natural to its kind, it presented to the father, as best it could, the sole of the injured foot. Jerome then called the brothers and ordered them carefully to wash the wounded foot and investigate why the lion was limping.

When they had carefully examined it, they found the sole of the lion’s foot wounded by thorns. After proper care and nourishment had been applied to the injury, it immediately recovered.

Having laid aside all the rage of beastly ferocity, it began to live among them, going back and forth like a domestic and peaceful animal. When blessed Jerome learned this, he said to the brothers:

“Come, brothers, I earnestly ask you to consider together what suitable work we can assign this lion for our benefit, so that it may be lightly and effectively performed by him. For I certainly believe that God did not send him here merely for the health of his foot—for God could have healed him without us—but rather that by the sign of his visitation He might show us that He wishes, through this creature, wonderfully to provide assistance for our needs.”

Then the brothers gave their father this answer together and humbly:

“You know well, Father, that the ass accustomed to carry wood from the woodland for our use requires careful supervision, and we are very much afraid that it may be devoured by some vicious beast. Therefore, if it pleases you and seems right, let the care of our little ass be entrusted to this lion, so that it may follow him, lead him to pasture, and bring him home again on his return.”

And so it was done. The care of the ass was assigned to the lion, which proceeded like a diligent shepherd. Going to pasture, it was his constant companion on the journey; in the fields, while the ass grazed, it was everywhere his protector and was entirely trustworthy. [Note: [Col. 0210] Our manuscript reads “so that he might rest”; shortly afterward it has “the pasture of the place.” Another manuscript reads “they might go on to Egypt.” It omits “who took him.” We are already ashamed to linger over such trifles.]

Nevertheless, in order to feed itself and allow the ass to perform its customary work, it always returned home with the ass at the appointed hours.

Meanwhile, as these things continued over a period of time, one day, when the ass had been led out to pasture, the lion was overcome by an unusually heavy sleep and fell asleep. While the lion was thus soundly sleeping, it happened that merchants passing along the same road were traveling to Egypt to buy oil. They often saw the ass grazing, and, when they noticed that no guardian was present, an unjust desire crept over them; they seized the ass and led it away with them.

When the lion awoke, not knowing what loss had befallen him, he nevertheless began to go in search of the grazing animal entrusted to him. When the ass did not appear in its usual place of pasture, the lion, troubled by the danger and anxious with grief, went about roaring for part of the day, searching here and there for the companion he had lost.

But when every hope of finding the ass had disappeared, he came and stood at the monastery gate. Conscious of his guilt, he did not dare enter, as he had formerly done with the little ass. Blessed Jerome and the brothers saw him lingering at the door of the cell without the ass. Since he had not returned at the usual hour, and since hunger compelled him, they thought that he had killed his animal. Unwilling to give him his customary ration, they said:

“Go and eat whatever remains of the ass that is left to you, and fill your belly.”

Although they said these things to him, they were uncertain whether or not he had committed this evil.

Therefore the brothers went out to the pasture of the place, where the lion had been accustomed to lead the aforementioned animal. They searched far and wide so that they might find some indication of its death. When they found no sign that it had been killed, they returned and took care to report this to blessed Jerome.

When he heard it, he said to the brothers:

“I beg you, brothers: although you have suffered the loss of the ass, do not anger this creature or cast the lion away. Rather, govern him and provide him with food as before, and feed him. Cut wood in the forest and bind it moderately, so that, carrying and bringing it here in place of the ass, he may be able to perform this service for us.”

And so it was done. When he had repeatedly carried the bundle that had been tied for him, and the time came for the merchants to return, he completed one day’s work and, although a brute animal, divinely prompted, as I think, went out toward the fields. He ran about here and there, circling around, eager to learn more fully what had happened to his companion.

After becoming extremely tired, he eventually reached a high point beside the public road. There, anxious, he looked around as best he could and saw men approaching from a distance with camels laden with burdens. The ass was walking in front of them. But because they were still very far away, he could not recognize it. Nevertheless, he slowly went forward to meet them.

For, they say, it is the custom of that region that whenever people travel a considerable distance with camels, the camels follow an ass going ahead of them, with a rope hanging from the ass’s neck and connected to the camels.

When the travelers—that is, the merchants—had approached the lion, he recognized the ass, roared fiercely, and rushed upon them with an enormous uproar, harming no one. They immediately abandoned everything and, becoming crazed—as was fitting—turned to flight.

As they fled, the lion roared terribly and struck the ground violently with his tail. He forced the terrified camels, laden as they were, to go before him toward the cell.

Therefore, when the brothers saw this extraordinary thing—that the donkey which had gone ahead, with the baggage in the midst of the camels, and the lion following, were all coming together—they immediately went out modestly and took care to report it to blessed Jerome. When he heard this, he went outside and kindly ordered the monastery gates to be opened; he commanded complete silence, saying:

[Note: The same manuscript reads “and at the same time he commanded” instead of “and he commanded complete silence,” etc.; then another reads, “removing the loads, lighten their burdens.”]

“Lift the burdens from our guests—that is, the camels and the donkey—and relieve them; wash their feet, provide them with food, and wait to see what the Lord wishes to show his servants through this event.”

When everything that had been ordered concerning the camels had been carried out, the lion began, as before, to go joyfully here and there through the cloisters of the monastery, lying down at the feet of each of the brothers and, as though jesting over a fault he had not committed, wagging his tail and asking forgiveness.

When the brothers saw this, they repented of having charged him with cruelty and said:

“Behold our shepherd, whom shortly before we were cruelly condemning as a devourer! With what a miraculous proclamation, in order to remove this accusation from him, the Lord has deigned to send him to us.”

Blessed Jerome, who knew what was to come, then said to the brothers:

“Be ready with those things necessary for refreshment, so that those who are to be our guests may be received without inconvenience, as is fitting.”

Immediately they followed his instructions, and everything required was completed with ready obedience.

When the orders had likewise been carried out, and the brothers were conversing with blessed Jerome, a messenger suddenly arrived and announced that guests were standing before the monastery gates and wished to see the father of the community. When the often-mentioned father heard this, he ordered the doors of his cell to be opened and commanded them to enter to him.

Although they had been summoned, they nevertheless entered shamefacedly; and when they saw blessed Jerome, they prostrated themselves at his feet and asked forgiveness for their fault. He kindly raised them up and admonished them to use their own possessions with thanksgiving and not presume to touch what belonged to others; and thereafter to live always with caution in the presence of God.

When this exhortation had been completed, he ordered them to be refreshed and, after taking back their camels, to depart.

Then they all said with one voice:

“We beg you, father, to order that, for the lamps of the church and the needs of the brothers, half the quantity of oil that the camels have brought be accepted; for we know and are certain that we went to Egypt to conduct this business more for your benefit than for our own.”

Blessed Jerome replied:

“Undoubtedly you are not asking rightly. Indeed, it seems very harsh that we, who ought to sympathize with others and relieve their needs by giving, should burden you by taking away what is yours and what we do not need.”

Then they said:

“Neither food here nor anything that belongs to us will we accept unless you first order that what we have requested be done. Therefore, as we said, accept now half the quantity of oil that the camels have brought; and henceforth we promise that we and our heirs will give you and your successors every year a measure of oil, a *hin*. ”

[Note: From both manuscripts the editor has substituted *hin*, the name of a measure, for *hic*, the adverb previously printed.]

Thus blessed Jerome, constrained and compelled by their forceful entreaties, ordered that their request be fulfilled. After they had eaten and had received a blessing together with their camels, they returned home rejoicing and giving thanks.

These events are said to have taken place at Bethlehem, and the inhabitants of that place have maintained that they occurred in this way down to the present.

Bethlehem was a splendid place, the city of David in the tribe of Judah. There, once, in order that prophecy might be fulfilled—“Truth has sprung up from the earth”—the Lord and Savior deigned to be born of the Virgin in a manger within a cave, and as a little child he wailed.

That manger, adorned with gold and silver—as Saint Anthony relates—has lamps burning in it continually,

[Note: One manuscript reads “Antoninus” for “Antonius.”] and is surrounded on every side by the dwellings of many servants of God. The mouth of the cave is altogether narrow for entering. At its entrance, therefore—that is, at the very entrance to the manger—blessed Jerome, carving the rock, ordered a monument to be made for himself.

[Note: Everything that follows from here almost to the end of this composition, or down to the words “under that ruler,” etc., is absent from both our manuscripts. In its place they continue as follows: “where, by the Lord’s help, the perversity of the ground having been overcome, he was laid to rest on 30 September, having completed the ninety-first year of his life. But in the twelfth year of the reign of Honorius [Col. 0214], under that ruler whose years neither begin nor end. Who lives,” etc.]
