The same man was so worn out by bodily exhaustion that even while lying on his bed he had to be raised by a rope suspended from a beam, which he grasped with his hands stretched upward, so that he might perform the duties of the monastery as best he could. Thus many days passed while his body wasted away and his voice grew weak.

After this, the blessed man, supported by an abundance of books, completed, through his writings dedicated to the Holy Spirit, the immovable tower of the Catholic Church against the arrows of the faithless.

Catholics likewise went to visit and console Jerome while he was laboring; one who was cooperating with the Catholic Church in spirit, though writing in Africa in body, wrote among other things:

“We have had our day, and we have run as far as we could. Now, while you are running and traversing long distances, leisure is owed to us.”

Thus that most blessed man, having irreproachably completed the days of his life in spiritual labor, rested in the Lord in the ninety-eighth year of his age. Kindly Bethlehem holds him, to offer him again when the Lord comes.

Blessed Jerome died in the twelfth year of the reign of the younger Theodosius—under that ruler whose years will never end—who lives and reigns throughout immortal ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0213]

## Selected Testimonies of the Ancients concerning Jerome and His Writings

### Saint Augustine, *The City of God*, Book XVIII, chapter XLII

Although in our own time there was the presbyter Jerome, a most learned man and skilled in all three languages, who translated these same Scriptures not from Greek but from Hebrew into Latin eloquence.

### The Same, *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, Book III, chapter VI

This much I know, however: Saint Jerome, who even today is renowned in ecclesiastical letters for his outstanding learning and labor, employs this most certain proof, without any dispute, in order to resolve certain questions in his books.

### The Same, *Against Julian*, Book I

Nor should you think Saint Jerome contemptible because he was a presbyter. Learned in Greek, Latin, and Hebrew eloquence, he passed from the Western to the Eastern Church and lived to an advanced old age in the Holy Places and in the sacred Scriptures.

### The Same, Letter 261, to Oceanus

But why say more about this, since I and the aforementioned venerable brother Jerome have dealt sufficiently in writing with this question, and in his most recent work, which he has just published under the name of Critobulus against Pelagius, he maintained concerning this matter the same judgment, based on the Apostolic statements, which we too followed from the most blessed Cyprian?

Rather, concerning the origin of souls—not because of adulterous births, but because of the condemnation, God forbid, of the innocent—which, I think, is not foolishly asked, if you have learned from such a great and eminent man anything that can properly be answered to those who are uncertain, I ask you not to refuse to share it with us.

You have appeared to me so learned and agreeable in your letters that it is worthwhile to converse with you in writing. I now ask you not to delay sending us the book of that same man of God which the presbyter Orosius brought and gave to your affection to be copied, and in which he is praised for having argued splendidly concerning the resurrection of the flesh.

We pass over here many other testimonies of Augustine concerning Jerome, since they are already found in the letters that he wrote to him and that we have included among the Jeromean letters.

For the same reason we also omit the testimonies of Damasus, as well as those of others, whose reciprocal letters (*ἀμοιβαῖαι*, mutual letters) appear there.

### Sulpicius Severus, *Dialogues*, Book I, chapter VII

This greatly encouraged me: although Jerome, a thoroughly Catholic man and most learned in sacred law, was initially thought to have followed Origen, he would now condemn especially either Origen himself or all his writings.

### The Same, chapter VIII

After departing from there, I set out for the town of Bethlehem, which is six miles from Jerusalem and sixteen stages from Alexandria. The presbyter Jerome governs the church of that place, for it is a parish of the bishop who holds Jerusalem.

I had already become acquainted with Jerome during my earlier pilgrimage, and he had easily persuaded me that no one else should more rightly be sought out by me. For, besides the merit of his faith and the endowment of his virtues, he was so trained not only in Latin and Greek but also in Hebrew letters that no one would dare compare himself with him in any branch of knowledge.

I am surprised if you have not also come to know him through the many works he has written, since he is read throughout the whole world.

### The Same, chapter IX

“I,” said Postumianus, “spent six months with Jerome. His continual battle and unceasing struggle against wicked men have stirred up against him the hatred of the lost.

“The heretics hate him because he never ceases to attack them; the clergy hate him because he pursues their way of life and their crimes. But all good people plainly admire and love him, for those who think him a heretic are insane.

“I would truly say that the man’s Catholic learning is sound doctrine. He is always wholly engaged in reading, wholly in books; he does not rest by day or night. He is always either reading something or writing.

“Had I not fixed in my mind and promised, with God as my witness, that I would go to the desert I had chosen, I would not have wished to depart from such a man even for the briefest moment.”

### Orosius, *Apology concerning Free Will against Pelagius*, p. 621

I was therefore hiding in Bethlehem, sent by Father Augustine so that I might learn the fear of the Lord, sitting at the feet of Jerome.

### The Same, again, p. 623

This too has been said by blessed Jerome, whose eloquence the whole West awaits like dew upon a fleece. For many heretics have already been crushed, together with their doctrines, when he attacked them, and he condemned them in his letter that he recently published to Ctesiphon.

Likewise, in the book that he is now writing, he refutes them through a disputation conducted in the manner of a dialogue. For this is to hold the dragon in the Antichrist’s slippery grasp, so that he cannot escape.

### Idacius, *Chronicle*

Jerome, mentioned above, preeminent in everything and also most skilled in the Hebrew elements, continually meditating day and night on the law of the Lord, as it is written, left countless works of his labor.

Finally, he crushed the sect of the Pelagians, together with its founder, with the adamantine hammer of truth. Against these and other heretics his most proven monuments remain.

### Caelius Sedulius, Preface to *The Paschal Work*

Do not be ashamed to imitate the example of Jerome, interpreter of the divine Law and cultivator of the heavenly library; nor to send the proofs of your own discussion to noble women also, women supported by the glory of an excellent nature, in whose minds the earnest study of sacred reading has established a sober dwelling of wisdom.

### Cassian, Book VII, *On the Incarnation*

Jerome, teacher of Catholics, whose writings shine throughout the whole world like divine lamps, in his book to Eustochium, and so forth. For Jerome was a man of the greatest learning and of thoroughly approved and pure doctrine, and so forth.

### Prosper, *Poem against the Ungrateful*, chapter II

Then also the illustrious guest of Bethlehem,

graceful in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin eloquence,

an example of character and teacher of the world,

Jerome, in books of outstanding excellence,

cut down the enemy, and made known

with what whirlwind the arisen darknesses

wished to obscure the true light.

### Prosper, *Chronicle*, Olympiad 291, 386 years, under Arcadius and Bauto

At this time the presbyter Jerome, already famous throughout the whole world, lived in Bethlehem, endowed with exceptional talent and serving the universal Church through his devotion.

### Sidonius Apollinaris, Book IV, Letter III

He instructs like Jerome, destroys like Lactantius, builds up like Augustine, and so forth.

### The Same, Book IX, Letter II

For when Jerome the interpreter, Augustine the dialectician, and Origen the allegorist bring forth for you ears of Scripture pregnant with the harvest of salutary teaching, surely the dry straw of my fasting tongue will not rattle before you in place of my contribution?

### Claudianus Mamertus, *On the State of the Soul*, Book II, chapter IX

And since he proves by great reasonings and irrefutable argument that this is so, and in addition asks Jerome’s opinion, he recovers from Jerome’s writings only material for his praise.

Indeed, Jerome undoubtedly says that nothing truer can be thought about the soul and that nothing more perfect can be argued. Behold two most distinguished men, far surpassing others in the preeminence of their virtues and learning, agreeing with us about the state of the soul . . .

Hence I am greatly surprised that Jerome was cited to you as a witness, since he, the foremost of interpreters, was scarcely able to argue both for the soul and against the soul.

### The Same, Book II, chapter X

Jerome, the foremost of interpreters.

### Pope Gelasius, Canon *Sancta Romana*, distinction 15

Likewise, Ruffinus, a religious man, published many books of ecclesiastical work and also interpreted some Scriptures. But because blessed Jerome censured him in certain matters concerning free will, we hold those opinions which we know the aforementioned blessed Jerome held; and this applies not only to Ruffinus but also to all those whom the often-mentioned man rebuked out of zeal for God and devotion to the faith.

Likewise, we accept for reading certain small works of Origen that blessed Jerome does not reject. All the rest, however, we declare must be rejected together with their author.

### The Same, Letter V, to the Bishops throughout Picenum

A still greater crime was added: under the sight and in the presence of priests, he dared to tear apart Jerome and Augustine of blessed memory, lights of ecclesiastical teachers, like a dying fly, as it is written, destroying the oil of sweetness.

### Ennodius of Ticinum, *Diction* VIII

Our Jerome, unless he called Gregory his teacher, would be considered better than him. But the good qualities must be attributed to the one named, from whom they seem to have taken their origin. In short, as I said, the teacher’s reputation strikes heaven through the perfection of the disciple.

### Marcellinus Comes, *Chronicle*

Down to this fourteenth year of the reign of Theodosius, blessed Jerome, beginning with the Apostle Peter after the ascension of our Lord Jesus Christ and ending with himself, described the ecclesiastical works of 135 illustrious men.

He lived at the town of Bethlehem, where he also founded a monastery and wrote many other works, having likewise been instructed in Hebrew letters. He ended his life at a very advanced age and was buried there: for Catholics, an unassailable tower of the Church; for all heretics, an indefatigable opponent, fighting both through the manner of life he had chosen and through the assertions of the books he had published.

### Facundus of Hermiane, Book IV, chapter II

Our Jerome too, a very learned man, who had read so extensively that he read all, or almost all, the interpreters of the divine Scriptures, whether in Greek or Latin eloquence, wrote a book entitled *On Illustrious Men*. In it he mentioned not only Catholics but also heretics who had written something concerning the Holy Scriptures in either language.

He did not remain silent about who had been founders of heresies, who their defenders, or even those whom some accused of being heretics while others defended them, and so forth.

### The Same, *Against Mutianus*

If even the concern and caution of the holy and most learned orthodox man Jerome are displeasing, and so forth.

### Cassiodorus, *Divine Readings*, chapter XXI

Blessed Jerome too, the outstanding expander of the Latin language, gave us so much in his translation of the divine Scripture that we scarcely need approach the Hebrew source, since he is known to have satisfied us with the great abundance of his eloquence.

Through the many books and copious letters that, by the Lord’s favor, he deigned to write, he made us blessed. Clear, learned, sweet, and equipped with a ready abundance of speech, he turns his talent toward every subject.

At one moment he gently flatters the humble; at another he breaks the necks of the proud; at another he repays his detractors with the necessary sharpness; at another he praises virginity; at another he defends chaste marriages; at another he highly commends the glorious contests of virtue; at another he censures the falls and corrupt practices of clerics and monks.

Yet wherever the occasion presented itself, he interwove examples from the Gentiles with the sweetest variety, explaining everything, adorning everything, and proceeding always eloquently and evenly through the various kinds of disputation.

For although he offers other books with great abundance, the sweetness of his expressions always makes him pleasing. I do not think that he lived idly at Bethlehem, except so that in that land of miracles his eloquence too might shine for us from the East like the sun.

He sent a wonderful letter to Paulinus, Senator, and Presbyter, teaching how the divine Scriptures should be read with caution. In it he briefly and marvelously indicated the force of each book of the Old and New Testament.

Had I found it earlier, yielding to his eloquence, I might perhaps have been content to say nothing about that subject. But since he wrote one thing and I something different in a work already completed, by the Lord’s gift, I believe that the diligent reader will not occupy himself uselessly with this little work as well.

He wrote to a new reader of the divine Law who was nevertheless educated in secular letters, so much so that he prudently and elegantly composed a book about the Emperor Theodosius. Nor, as may be understood, did that age possess so many writers on its own side to urge him to read them in order, since at that time the soldiers of Christ were still laboring with salutary sweat in the gymnasium of the divine law, concerning whom he himself later wrote much.

### The Same, *Chronicle*

In the consulship of Arcadius and Bauto, the presbyter Jerome, established at Bethlehem, was regarded as marvelous throughout the whole world.

### Isidore of Seville, *Etymologies*, Book VI

The presbyter Jerome, also skilled in three languages, translated these same Scriptures from Hebrew into Latin eloquence and rendered them eloquently. His translation is rightly preferred to the others, for it is both more faithful to the words and clearer in the transparency of its meaning.

### Bede, *On the Calculation of Time*

Jerome, interpreter of the divine History.

### An Anonymous Author, in Canisius, Volume VI, *Ancient Readings*

Jerome, most learned interpreter in many languages,

Bethlehem celebrates you; the whole world resounds with your name.

Our library too proclaims you through your books.

### Einhard, Letter to Lupus

There were at hand distinguished teachers, not merely not to be despised but in every respect to be heard and followed: namely, the glorious martyr Cyprian and the most illustrious interpreters of the sacred divine writings, Augustine and Jerome.

Encouraged by their opinions and most salutary counsels, I tried to lift my heart upward, though it had been weighed down by deep sorrow.

[Col. 0219]

### Theodulf of Orléans, Poem IV to Gisela, Book III

For I commanded this Psalter to be written for you,

which you see shining with silver and gold.

In it the earlier Hebrew page agrees with the truth,

and the later edition follows from it as the ancient one.

How well Jerome transfers this one and corrects that one!

Believe me, both shine for distinguished old men.

[Note: F. reads *sensibus* (“meanings”) instead of *senibus* (“old men”).]

### Saint Columbanus, Letter to Pope Gregory

I openly confess to you that anyone who comes against the authority of Saint Jerome will be rejected by the churches of the West as a heretic. For they place unquestioning faith in him in every matter concerning the divine Scriptures.

### Nicholas I, Letter LI to Lothair

Hear what Jerome, the cultivator of the heavenly library, says: “A heavy burden of vices,” and so forth. From chapter IX of the *Commentary on Matthew*.

### Ratramnus of Corbie, *On the Nativity of Christ*, chapter X, from D’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, Volume I, p. 339

Jerome, interpreter of the sacred Law, most learned in every discipline, an unshaken tower of faith, most splendid in the lamp of Wisdom, most eloquent in speech, and most learned in the Latin, Greek, and Hebrew languages.

### Servatus Lupus, *On Three Questions*

Our authors, easily superior in wisdom because they obey divine eloquence, which they reveal when they wish and conceal when they wish—I mean Cyprian, Augustine, Jerome, Ambrose, and certain others—both examined the mind of the divine utterances in depth and expressed it for us beneficially . . .

Jerome, preeminent in divine and secular learning, and, as it were, a parent together with Augustine of that ecclesiastical philosophy which neither greatly seeks human learning nor despises it in every respect, vigorously defeated the recently arisen Pelagian heresy, saying: “If only in this,” and so forth.

### Agobard, *Book against the Objections of Fredegisus*, chapter IX

The edition of our interpreter, the presbyter Jerome, is also faithful: he magnificently translated it from Hebrew into Latin.

### Haymo of Halberstadt, Book X, chapter VIII

At that time the presbyter Jerome was regarded as famous at Bethlehem—or rather throughout the whole world.

I cannot help wondering with great admiration why Ruffinus omitted him from this historical narrative, especially since he honored in eloquence the other illustrious men and his contemporaries, who were either inferior to him in knowledge or, if his equals or superiors, certainly less useful to the churches in every respect.

Perhaps Ruffinus did this deliberately, lest he seem to do an injustice to the little book that blessed Jerome himself wrote *On Illustrious Men*, where he also mentions himself at the end.

It is also said that they at one time had quarrels; and, if it is permissible to say this of such holy and prudent men, they looked at each other with sidelong glances and marked each other in their words. Hence perhaps Ruffinus distorted this historical account because of blessed Jerome.

Whether he omitted him for this reason or for that, I do not know. God knows.

### Rabanus, *Martyrology*, September 30

At Bethlehem of Judah, the burial of the presbyter Jerome, whose life and teaching stand everywhere praised in the churches of Christ: he translated the divine books from the Hebrew language into Latin and expounded the prophetic books in an allegorical sense.

When he had completed eighty-eight years of life, he left the present life and departed to eternal rest.

### Prudentius of Troyes, *On Predestination against John Scotus Eriugena*, chapter I

### Hincmar of Reims, Volume I of His Works

And Saint Jerome, most skilled in the Hebrew, Greek, and Latin languages, who, as it is said, breaking the nut beside the kernel, deserved, by investigating the marrow and very entrails of Holy Scripture, to penetrate them under the inspiration of the Lord, says thus in his exposition of the prophet Ezekiel, and so forth.

[Greek text: “Jerome too, the renowned presbyter, wrote to Ctesiphon against those who assert *apatheia*, or against Pelagius; and this Pelagius was a monk who had acquired Caelestius as a disciple.”]

### Sigebert, *Chronography*, under A.D. 421

After completing his books over fifty-six years, Jerome died at Bethlehem in the ninety-eighth year of his age, his chest so weakened by labor that he could not rise from bed unless he grasped with his hands the rope hanging for this purpose from a beam.

### Honorius of Autun, *On the Lights of the Church*, chapter CXXXVI

Jerome, born to Eusebius at the town of Stridon on the borders of Pannonia, wrote under Theodosius:

- the life of Paul the Monk;
- one book of letters to various persons;
- an exhortatory letter to Heliodorus;
- the disputation of a Luciferian and an orthodox Christian;
- a *Chronicle* of universal history;
- he translated twenty-six homilies of Origen on Jeremiah and Ezekiel;
- three homilies on the Seraphim, on “Hosanna,” and on the thrifty and the prodigal son;
- two homilies on the Song of Songs;
- one letter against Helvidius concerning Saint Mary;
- one letter to Eustochium concerning the preservation of virginity;
- one book of letters to Marcella;
- four books of commentaries on Paul’s Letter to the Galatians;
- three books on the Letter to the Ephesians;
- one book on the Letter to Titus;
- one book on the Letter to Philemon;
- commentaries on Ecclesiastes;
- one book of Hebrew Questions on Genesis;
- one book *On Places*;
- one book *On the Holy Spirit*;
- thirty-eight homilies on Luke;
- seven treatises on the Psalms from the tenth through the sixteenth;
- a work on the captive monk;
- the life of blessed Hilarion;
- the life of Paula.

He translated the New Testament from Greek and the Old Testament from Hebrew into Latin. He expounded the twelve prophets, composed countless letters, and produced innumerable other works.

### Chronicle of Tours, in Martène, Volume V, p. 928

In the eleventh year of Honorius, Jerome died at Bethlehem in the eighty-eighth year of his age, remaining in virginity, always either reading or writing, learned in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin letters, a wall of the Church, most devoted to poverty, the rule of monks, and a mirror of holiness.

Finally, after completing books over fifty-six years, his body had become so weakened by labor that he could not rise from bed unless he grasped with his hands the rope that hung from a beam for this purpose.

### Bernard, *Parable concerning Christ and the Church*

But immediately the outstanding soldiers of the Christian court, seeing that the enemy’s crafty malice was prevailing, recovered their spirit and seized the weapons of faith.

Bravely removing the evil from their midst, Alexander struck Arius with many others; Augustine struck down the Manichaean and many others; Jerome struck down Epicurean Jovinianus; and the rest, attacking the remaining plagues of heresies and schisms, either courageously slaughtered them or prudently drove them from the camp, restoring peace and joy to the Church.

### Ado of Vienne, *Martyrology*, September 30

Likewise, at Bethlehem of Judah, the burial of Saint Jerome the presbyter.

He was born in the town of Stridon, formerly on the border of Dalmatia and Pannonia, to his father Eusebius. As a boy he took up the garment of Christ at Rome, where from his earliest years he was educated in Greek and Latin letters.

After he had acquired every branch of secular literary study, he also imitated the habit and conduct of the most approved monks. Later he was ordained presbyter of the Roman Church.

For three continuous years he was cherished and honored by the people, and by everyone’s judgment was deemed worthy of the highest priesthood. Certain men from the orders of the clergy and monks, however, roaming about in licentiousness and gluttony, plotted to drive Jerome from the city, because in writing he had detected and exposed both of their vices.

But he himself, for the sake of the kingdom of heaven, left Rome and abandoned his home, parents, sister, and relatives. Going to Jerusalem to serve God as a soldier, he first approached Gregory of Nazianzus, then bishop of Constantinople, as a humble and teachable disciple, so that he might be instructed in the study of the Holy Scriptures.

From there he went to Syria and stayed for a while on the estate of the presbyter Evagrius. Then he approached the deserted places so joyfully and eagerly equipped that you would have thought he had flown there rather than traveled.

He spent four years in that vast solitude, which, scorched by the heat of the sun, provides the monks with a dreadful dwelling. From there he returned to the town of Bethlehem, where, like a prudent animal, he presented himself at the Lord’s manger to remain there.

He spent the day fasting until evening, rereading his library, which he himself had established with the greatest care, and the prayers of all the books, which he retained almost by heart.

Many religious men, once they had learned of the fame of his life, immediately flocked to him, and good disciples watched over the good teacher, who still lived beneath a small shelter.

Not long afterward, because of the abundance of his disciples and the frequent arrival of visitors at the Bethlehem gate—which faces west and is seen by those going out toward the north—he built a small dwelling there.

With what efforts and labors he learned the Hebrew language, the Chaldean language, and the Hebrew letters, I shall state in his own words: “When I was,” and so forth.

### Gerard of Auvergne, to Ivo, Abbot of Cluny

It is read in the *Conferences of the Holy Fathers*, which Jerome translated, that John the Evangelist, a disciple of Christ, handled a partridge in his hands, wearied by his divine studies.

### Notker, *Martyrology*, September 30

On the same day, at Bethlehem of Judah, the burial of Saint Jerome the presbyter.

He was born in the town of Stridon, formerly on the border of Dalmatia and Pannonia, to his father Eusebius. As a boy he took up the garment of Christ at Rome, where from his earliest years he was educated in Greek and Latin letters. He also imitated the habit and conduct of the most approved monks.

Ordained presbyter of the Roman Church, he was judged by everyone to be most worthy of the highest priesthood. But after he was driven from Rome by the envy of his rivals, he visited Gregory of Nazianzus, bishop of Constantinople, for the sake of learning.

From there he went to Syria and, entering the deserted places, spent four years in a dreadful solitude. Then, approaching the town of Bethlehem, he withdrew like a prudent animal to the Lord’s manger, intending to remain there.

How many vigils and fasts he undertook there, and with what persistence he inserted the libraries of the Hebrews into the ears of the Latins, is known by the one to whom he offered his labors.

Finally, after completing a way of life pleasing to God, he rested in peace at Bethlehem in the ninety-eighth year of his age, on the second day before the Kalends of October, in the twelfth year of the Emperor Honorius.

[Col. 0223] He completed his books over fifty-six years.

### Laurentius Justinianus, *Works*, p. 680, Sermon on the Solemnity of Blessed Jerome, Doctor and Confessor
In the Spiritual Tabernacle, glorious Jerome obtained the highest place. For the Church rightly honors him who guarded, protected, and nourished her with the bulwark of knowledge. He was truly a silver column, upright, shining, and solid. Like a column founded upon golden bases, his mind was raised toward heaven and pierced the heights of heaven, so that it might behold the light of truth in the Light. Yet he could never have brought forth from himself a rain of doctrine unless he himself had also been imbued with heavenly things. For the fountain of wisdom, the Word of God, is on high, and his commandments are eternal. Drawing near to him through love, he received the streams of wisdom. For God grants wisdom according to his gift and good pleasure to those who love him.

The wisdom of which we speak is not such as can be claimed by human ingenuity: it is obtained through prayers, received with purity of heart, and preserved through humility. Wisdom will not enter a malevolent soul, nor dwell in a body subjected to sins. Let him empty himself of pride, wash away the torches of his crimes, and entreat the Lord with groans—whoever desires to know the truth of divine wisdom. With how many exhortations, I ask, did this holy man cleanse the lodging of his mind; with what floods of tears, with what labors of vigils, with what power of humility, so that he might be deemed worthy of wisdom’s companionship? Indeed, he desired, sought, found, and held her, and possessed her in her most chaste embrace. Hence, as to one who was his closest friend, she disclosed to him innumerable mysteries, hidden and obscure, of the sacred utterances.

Through constant meditation on the Scriptures he had plainly become the temple of God, the seat of wisdom, the minister of the Paraclete, a clean vessel, the revealer of eternal light, a master of knowledge, and an imitator of the angels. His body was held on earth, but in truth his mind dwelt in heaven. He had built for himself a Spiritual Ladder, whose summit touched the heavens, and by which he frequently ascended and descended. He ascended by contemplating heavenly things and meditating on divine matters; he descended when necessity required him to indulge himself or his neighbor.

Accustomed to such pursuits, he shone among men with singular holiness, like a lamp kindled and translucent, illuminating the whole house of the Church. Everywhere he was renowned, his goodness radiating its splendor. Who in the bosom of the Church was not instructed by Jerome’s knowledge? Who was not edified by the example of his life? Who was not strengthened by his intercessions? He became the common father, the light of the world, the herald of the kingdom, the intercessor for the age, the mirror of holiness, the model of virtues, and the stoutest champion of the faithful.

Indeed, without shedding blood he obtained the glorious triumph of martyrdom. What he did not endure by the executioner’s sword, he accomplished within himself through love of chastity. “O how often,” he says, “when I was established in the desert, in that vast solitude which provides a dreadful dwelling for monks, did I imagine myself to be present amid Roman luxuries! I sat alone, for I was full of bitterness. My deformed limbs bristled beneath the sackcloth, and my squalid skin was covered with the foulness of Ethiopian flesh. Every day, tears; every day, groans. And whenever impending sleep overcame me while I resisted it, I would scarcely strike my bones, clinging to the bare earth. I, then—the man who, out of fear of Gehenna, had condemned myself to such a prison, the companion only of scorpions and wild beasts—found myself among choirs of girls.”

Do you see with what firmness of spirit he fought manfully against himself? He spared himself not at all, in order to spare himself. For when he became cruel and rigid toward himself, he became his own outstanding victor. This is the singular trophy: to subject the flesh to the spirit, and the spirit to the Creator. No one can ever be subject to God who has been unable to command his own mind.

Hence the lover of God must first be a lover of virtue. The love of God is proved by devotion to virtue. Remove virtue from the heart, and the structure of charity will collapse. “Charity,” says the Apostle, “is patient, is kind; it does not act wrongly; it is not ambitious, is not puffed up, does not think evil, does not rejoice over iniquity, rejoices with the truth, can do all things, believes all things, endures all things. Charity never fails.”

Let us therefore emulate, beloved, the charity which this Saint whom we are discussing emulated. Through it he was higher than the world, wiser than the Devil, stronger than himself, and more powerful than death. Adorned especially by this grace, he did not yield to temptations, was not provoked by insults, was not broken by rivalries, was not overthrown by the allurements of the flesh, was not made foolish by honors, was not exalted by praises, nor wearied by labors. Rather, he remained pure of heart, exalted in humility, distinguished by purity, renowned for chastity, unconquerable in courage, increased in authority, devoted in mind, and clothed in the radiance of every virtue.

The whole course of his life is plainly a mirror of the Christian religion. From the beginning of his youth he bore the Lord’s yoke. He pursued the study of sacred letters, so that he was regarded as incomparable in knowledge. He trod upon the arid world, leaving home, fatherland, and parents in their flower, and departing from Rome he entered the deserts of the wilderness.

No one was more useful than he in explaining the divine utterances; no one was more severe than he against his own body. Who was bolder than he in correcting crimes? He utterly refused to flatter men, and did not know how to conceal vices by silence, being inflamed by an excessive zeal for divine love. He was truly as fierce a persecutor of his own faults as of those of others. For he so washed away even the smallest offenses by watering them with tears that, if one did not know him, one would have to admit that Jerome was the greatest of sinners.

Finally, he so faithfully completed the whole span of life granted to him as though he were to die every day. He fought bravely, lived temperately, conducted himself justly, and persevered with the greatest prudence. He fought the good fight of holy religion; he completed the course of his pilgrimage by living commendably; he preserved the true faith for the Lord Christ through perseverance; and thus, in a good old age, full of days, rich in merits, and most renowned for holiness, he fell asleep in the Lord, was gathered to his fathers, joined to the angels, and crowned by Christ, the Bridegroom of the Church, who is God, blessed above all, forever and ever. Amen.

JO. BAPT. PLATINA, in *Innocent I*

At the same time Jerome, a priest dwelling in Bethlehem, wonderfully increased the faith of Christ by his talent and eloquence, as his writings also make clear.

FRANC. PHILELPHUS, Book VI, final letter, to Aloysius Crottus

I have conveniently sent you the letters of Jerome and Augustine that you requested. Therefore, when you have read them repeatedly at your pleasure, take care that they return to me. As for what you ask—what I think of each of them, both regarding doctrine and eloquence—hear it briefly.

First of all, it is not for me to judge concerning divine matters, but for one possessing ecclesiastical dignity and authority. Nevertheless, I think that both possessed the knowledge of all divine subjects in the most excellent manner. But in all the remaining branches of philosophy, Augustine alone was by far the more acute, more learned, and more subtle. Augustine was an outstanding dialectician, and likewise a physicist and mathematician.

Jerome surpassed him greatly in elegance of expression rather than in learning; this can be observed from the discourse of each. Jerome was thoroughly skilled in Greek literature; Augustine less perfectly. Jerome is also regarded as learned in Hebrew, whereas Augustine was entirely ignorant of that language. Jerome was harsh in his manner of life, while Augustine was gentle. If one man could have been made from those two, nature would have produced nothing more complete.

On this judgment of Philelphus, read the discussions of Echius and Erasmus, Book II, Letters XXV and XXVI.

RAPHAEL VOLATERRANUS, *Urban Commentaries*, Book XVI

To recount the life of Jerome, chief of the Doctors, might perhaps be a digression, since it has been entrusted to the records of so many illustrious men. Nevertheless, I shall bring forward certain passages from his books in which he speaks of himself, especially those pertaining to his writings.

First, in his book *On Illustrious Men*, he confesses that he was born in the town of Stridon, of his father Eusebius. He came to Rome as a fairly young man and there devoted himself to the liberal arts. Concerning these matters he himself writes as follows in his *Apology to Pammachius*, and so forth.

JACOB. PHILIPPUS BERGOMENSIS, in the *Chronicle*, under the year of Christ 429

Jerome, a very intimate man and a most celebrated Doctor, a cardinal priest of the holy Roman Church, an Italian by nation, was from the town of Stridon, situated in the province of Histria; this town had indeed been destroyed by the Goths. It had once been on the boundary of Pannonia and Dalmatia. Born of his father Eusebius, he departed to the Lord this year at Bethlehem, a city of Judea, on the day before the Kalends of October, in the ninety-first year of his life. He was a supremely eloquent man who possessed skill in many different kinds of literature and knowledge of languages, eloquence of speech, correct interpretations of fables, a rich memory of histories, knowledge of natural things, moral discourse, and also understanding of sacred Scripture and true theology.

Thus, since he was sound in faith and most pure in life, after he had completed the first years of his youth, he invented and composed for the Dalmatians, his neighboring people, [Note: [Col. 0226] This is an old error, which we refute elsewhere.] certain letters, especially different from the Latin and Greek ones, which were later called Sclavonic because he gave them to certain Sclavonic peoples of Germany. He not only composed those letters, but also translated and adapted the Office that we use from Greek into that same language. In recent times Pope Eugene IV, the supreme pontiff, also confirmed this for them.

His most holy life could indeed be explained at length, but since that is not my purpose, we shall pass it over and discuss his writings more fully. Since he was a most eloquent and articulate man, he published for the benefit of humanity not only the little works set out below, but many others that could by no means be found, and so forth.

TRITHEMIUS, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*

Jerome, a priest and monk, born of his father Eusebius in the town of Stridon, was a man highly learned in secular literature and, among all the Doctors, the most learned in the divine Scriptures. Distinguished by his knowledge of many languages, he was an interpreter of the sacred law, a hammer of heretics, and their most powerful conqueror.

He is the true evangelical steward, faithful and prudent, bringing forth from his treasury new things and old, and giving his fellow servants the measure of spiritual wheat in due season. He stripped the proud Hebrews and enriched the humble Latins.

He is the eminent Doctor of the Church of Christ who, together with the pious mother Rebecca—that is, the grace of God—brought forth the garments of Esau, wandering through the byways of error and lying uselessly stored at home, and clothed the gentle Jacob, faithful and serving Christ.

This is Jerome, the sincere lover of Jesus Christ, who allowed no time to pass uselessly. Day and night he meditated on the law of the Lord and, scarcely granting his body the sleep necessary for it, always wrote, read, taught, or prayed by day and night, as is attested by the almost innumerable books that he published.

He is the defender of truth, the cultivator of virtue, and the fiercest enemy of vices. When he was a priest of the Roman Church and steadfastly rebuked the crimes of clerics, he withdrew from the city because of their envy. Coming to Judea, he visited the glorious tomb of the Lord, and establishing his dwelling beside the Bethlehem manger, he became known and celebrated throughout the world. Divine providence clearly arranged that the light of the world should rest there where the true Sun of Justice had made himself known to humanity by being born.

He was a holy and fitting inhabitant of that most holy place: firm in faith, inflamed with charity, mature in conduct. Prosperity could not seduce him, nor could any adversity ever cast him down from his holy purpose.

But why should I, a sordid praiser of a man, touch his holy crown with impure lips? It would have been more fitting for me to remain humbly silent than to speak inadequately of so holy a man. Let us therefore now set down in order what we have found concerning his writings and little works. These are as follows, and so forth.

DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM, Book II, Letter 1, to Leo X, Supreme Pontiff

The divine Jerome is so much the chief of theologians among the Latins that we possess almost only him as a theologian worthy of the name. This is not because I condemn the others, but because men otherwise illustrious, when compared with him, are so obscured by his eminence that they seem almost invisible.

In short, he was endowed with so many outstanding gifts that learned Greece itself scarcely possesses anyone whom it could set beside this man. How great in him was Roman eloquence! How great his knowledge of languages! How great his acquaintance with all antiquity and all histories! How faithful his memory! How fortunate his combination of every subject! How complete his knowledge of mystical writings! Above all, what ardor was his, what an admirable inspiration of the divine breast! Thus by one quality he greatly delights, by another he teaches through learning, and by his holiness he carries the reader away, and so forth.

THE SAME, Book V, Letter XXVI, to John Eck

I think of Augustine as one ought to think of a holy man endowed with outstanding gifts. I do not, as you write, cast shadows upon his glory; but I do not permit Jerome’s glory to be obscured. Jerome would plainly suffer an injustice if he were placed behind one whom he far surpassed.

THE SAME, Book V, Letter XIX, to Greverard

For a long time now my mind has burned with incredible ardor to illuminate Jerome’s letters with a commentary. I do not know what god has kindled my breast and drives me to dare conceive in my mind so great a work, one that no one has yet attempted.

I am moved by the piety of a heavenly man who, beyond dispute, was by far the most learned and eloquent of all Christians; yet, although his writings deserve to be read and memorized everywhere by everyone, scarcely a few read them, fewer admire them, and very few understand them.

Immortal God! Scotus, Albert, and authors still rougher than these will resound through every school, while that one champion, illuminator, and light of our religion—Jerome, who deserved to be celebrated as the one man above all others—will alone remain silent? But I see an outrageously unworthy situation: Jerome is neglected because of the very qualities by which he deserved not to be neglected. His eloquence, which benefited religion, harms its author. His more abstruse learning, by which he ought especially to have been commended, alienates many. Thus few admire the man whom very few understand.

If such an author were illuminated by a worthy commentary, I foresee that Jerome’s glory, as though it had received a new light, would shine as widely as possible, so that he would everywhere be read and memorized in schools, lecture halls, churches, at home, publicly and privately.

Nor am I so deceived about the bold undertaking I have presumed in my mind. First, consider how difficult it will be to eradicate the errors that have been deeply rooted for so many centuries. Then consider how much antiquity, how much Greek literature, and how much history there is in him; and also what phrasing and what art of expression—an art by which he seems to have left not only all Christians far behind him, but even to contend with Cicero himself.

For my part, unless my love for the most holy man deceives me, when I compare Jerome’s discourse with Cicero’s, I seem to myself to miss something in Cicero himself, the prince of eloquence. So great is the variety in our Jerome, so great the weight of his thoughts, so great the fluidity of his enthymemes.

To indicate this art in writing on eloquence is as difficult as it is exceedingly useful. I trust that I shall complete the task—provided that he himself is favorable—so that those who have hitherto admired Jerome’s eloquence will confess that they had not known him to be eloquent.

Whatever can be accomplished for Jerome by vigils, constant study, moderate learning, and my very poor talent shall be diligently offered to him.

Other eulogies of Jerome by Erasmus may be found elsewhere in his prefaces and letters.

POLYDORUS VERGILIUS, *On the Inventors of Things*, Book VII, chapter III

Jerome, son of Eusebius, was born at Stridon, a town that once belonged to Pannonia and Dalmatia but was plundered and destroyed by the Goths. He was excellently educated at Rome in Greek and Latin literature. For the sake of a holier life he went to Judea, where he also learned the Hebrew language.

Thus learned in three languages, he undertook the burden of writing about divine matters, in which he exerted every power of his age, diligence, and learning. His writings were received as sacred by the Fathers soon afterward, and, once received, were approved.

Although I know that there are some who falsely attribute this action to Pope Damasus, even though Damasus had died a long time before Jerome.

Finally, he built a dwelling for himself near Bethlehem, where he spent the rest of his life according to the apostolic manner. From this it came about that many later imitators of Jerome’s own institution arose, and a new kind of family came into being. They were called Hieronymians after Jerome, whom they made in some fashion the founder of their institution, although their way of life differed greatly from his.

They wear their natural-colored habit and a cloak gathered over the tunic. The upper part of the cloak is split from top to bottom, and they gird the tunic with a leather belt and protect their feet with wooden clogs.

FROM A VATICAN MANUSCRIPT, formerly belonging to Queen Christina, no. 571

Augustine to Jerome:

Bethlehem celebrates you; the whole world resounds with you;

Our library, too, proclaims you through your books.

FROM ANOTHER MANUSCRIPT, in my possession

Behold, I shall unfold the praises of the splendid Priest,

While mention of the Saint strikes the innermost chambers of my heart,

Whose fame, four-square, grows throughout the world,

And whose wisdom shines to the furthest boundaries:

He who was Interpreter and guardian of virgin modesty,

Turning the Hebrew oracles into Roman words.

For he opened the abyss of the ancient and obscure law,

Unlocking the seventy-two books of the page,

Which sacred writing now records on consecrated sheets.

Moreover, he drew forth treatises truly wondrous,

And by sure commentaries unraveled the hidden sayings

Of the prophets, revealing the mysteries of things.

This renowned master endures through age after age.

Now what is rightly written throughout the world is four-square,

And although a distinguished company of readers is spread throughout the world,

He was born of Eusebius, as he himself has related,

Enumerating the published volumes of the ancient Fathers,

From the time when the Savior took upon himself

The cradle of our flesh on earth, cleansing the sins of the age;

When he mounted the gibbet of the Cross with his sacred body,

And, having endured wounds, cleansed the human race,

Polluted by the fraud of the Evil One, with red blood.

Who ever strives with such zeal to study the two tablets of the Law,

Or to search them with such diligence?

Thus the same teacher of sacred things had meditated,

As the Psalmist sings, day and night on the little books, and so forth . . .

CAELIUS CALCAGNINUS, on an image of Saint Jerome carved in a walnut shell

Who fixed you breathing within a narrow border,

Father—your bent knee, your uncombed hair,

Your body filthy and foul with much uncleanness,

Your gray beard, your face pale with hunger,

Your limbs bristling with much wasting,

Protruding from sackcloth and girded with a spotted fawnskin,

And so often beating your breast against the hard rock?

That breast so fertile in blessings, which poured forth for us

In abundant streams the hidden volumes of Moses,

And the divine treasures, the oracles of the ancient seers—

From which salvation, and the beginning of a better life,

Is revealed to all peoples by a decree given in due season.

Yet although no boundary of such great genius

Can be set, nor any boundary contain the power of your tongue,

Now you stand wholly within the thin shell of a walnut.

And the walnut’s broad space remains empty, since only one

Part of its divided mass was subjected to the sharp iron;

The other still remains rigid and deprived of its companion’s praise.

But you, learned old man, are wholly in it, not alone:

For with you rises an inaccessible rocky crag,

Rough, lifting its monstrous summit toward heaven.

See also the shady grove, wearied by the heavy wind,

And the barren sands rolling this way and that,

While twisting serpents are mingled with the sands themselves.

On the other side hangs, in the customary fashion of a sacred trophy,

A purple-colored crest, which a double-knotted band

Binds, and which bears witness to honors renounced.

From here you see how far it extends, lying prone upon its belly,

While that lofty lion protects the master’s vast recesses

And occupies them—that terror of the Libyan coast.

Now he lies there and gathers within his treasures his claws,

Those claws once dripping with frequent slaughter.

Do you see how, now that he has laid down his neck, he reclines,

And with outstretched tongue licks the old man’s feet?

But you, holy Father, are distracted neither by rocks nor dreadful crags,

Nor by wild beasts nor by the uproar of the grove:

Your whole mind gazes toward Olympus; your whole breast sighs for Jesus.

Him you conceive in your mind, him with your eyes, him with your whole utterance;

Him alone you behold hanging from the lofty wood,

His hands pierced through, his breast pierced,

And—alas, alas!—his whole head cruelly torn and displayed:

Enduring these things so that he might wash away our offenses with blood,

And add the wretched to the heavenly spirits.

Therefore the marvels of such great things now move you,

Now the piety, now the supreme mercy of the Father,

And the gifts and promised honors pass before your mind.

Surely it is glorious to ascend the heavenly seats

And at last increase the number of the great gods.

Thus it is well: your hoary faith and your illustrious virtue

Delight my holy mind, trained by holy deeds.

Yet I grieve that you, yourself innocent and free from every crime,

Alas, drive yourself with examples so cruel.

Are you so pious toward everyone, and impious toward yourself alone?

What did your harshly punished back, what did your bruised neck deserve?

What did these cheeks, rigid with lashes and tears,

Do to commit so great an offense against the powers above?

What did these sides, cruelly covered with Cilician bristles

And entangled with thorns, do?

What such wickedness did this inspired breast commit?

What did the mind, filled with heavenly fires

And destined one day to become a great part of heaven, commit?

What did it dare, even now breathing nothing but heaven,

In a foul prison? What expiations were worthy of such punishments?

With tears and anxious sobs, continually,

By night and day you torment yourself.

Look: scarcely does dry skin cling to your limbs,

And your ribs adhere in an abraded framework.

You are no longer the man who, once born beside the cold Ister,

Sought the fields scorched by the Palestinian Crab.

Now only a slender shadow of him can scarcely be recognized.

Why were you permitted so much against yourself?

Would a savage enemy dare this? Would monsters wandering through those woods?

Are you more cruel toward yourself than toward monsters and a savage enemy?

Spare yourself, Father, spare yourself, Father!

These words, these lashes, befit us—

Those whom a mad impulse carries away in a thousand ways

While we repeatedly provoke heaven and the gods above of our own accord.

From one side ambition calls us; from another, insane desire drags us.

Anger drives its goads from here; fear restrains us from there.

From another side pleasure presses upon us,

Ever returning in the mind.

Let us therefore chastise the spirited horse that leaps

And drags us in different directions,

So that, confined within unjust bounds,

It may acquire good habits and submit to its master's laws.

But since, without the protection and divinity of the gods,

We strive in vain, and human strength gives way,

Come, then, with a compassionate mind, to our arduous labors.

Come here, Father, and look more closely upon our affairs,

And may your wounds and your lashes benefit us.

JULIUS CAESAR SCALIGER, on Saint Jerome

You who could impose laws upon great nature,

And turn upon yourself the ordinances of your native heaven—

Come down graciously! You see the frenzied hearts

Of the crowd and kingdoms divided by wavering faith.

All things rush headlong, scattered in unhappy turmoil,

And the end of affairs will be nothing but destruction.

Now it is considered worthwhile to feel wrongly and turn away from truth,

And they now wish neither to do nor to become what is good.

But if the laws of earth are forbidden to you,

So that your mind may be less able to be present before us,

Implore the propitious thunderbolts of the avenging right hand.

The earth—a sewer—deserves a worse death.

JOSEPHUS SCALIGER, *Prolegomena to Eusebius’s Chronicle*

What we have said concerning Eusebius we may rightly believe also concerning the great Jerome: that among Latin writers there is no one to whom ecclesiastical literature owes more, both in matters pertaining to sacred origins and in those concerning the interpretation of the divine books.

Nor could our age have found a more suitable interpreter of Eusebius than the man who was most devoted to Eusebius and most skilled in the subjects Eusebius treated. Would that, amid his occupations, he had had leisure not to dictate these things to a secretary, but to write them himself!

For since he was compelled to answer many people, whether invited or provoked, and since he was given no rest from his labor, while he could neither endure nor wish to lose even the smallest amount of time, it is evident that, when he dictated his interpretation of this *Chronicle*, he was at the same time occupied with writing other matters and dictating to the same secretary.

It was therefore inevitable that certain things, which could not be avoided, should slip from so great a man in the ordinary course of human affairs. Yet today these matters are received by petty teachers and little critics not with pardon, but with abuse and insults—not as errors, but as crimes.

SIXTUS OF SIENA, Book IV, *Sacred Library*

Jerome of Stridon, whom Severus Sulpicius calls the rector of the Bethlehem parish, while all the Greeks call him the Jerusalemite priest, was the son of Eusebius and came from the town of Stridon. Stridon had been destroyed by the Goths and had once stood on the boundary of Dalmatia and Pannonia.

He was a man completely accomplished in every kind of learning. By the brilliance of his language and the power of his eloquence—skills in which he advanced under the grammarian Donatus and the rhetorician Victorinus, men of the highest distinction—he left all the writers of the Latin Church far behind him.

He also possessed such knowledge of languages that he knew Greek, Hebrew, Chaldaean, and Latin equally well, as well as Dalmatian, his mother tongue. Nor did he leave untouched anything in the schools of the philosophers concerning Aristotle, Plato, or Zeno—that is, concerning the Peripatetics, Academics, and Stoics.

Equipped with these resources, he turned to the study of the sacred writings, using as his teachers Apollinarius of Laodicea, Didymus of Alexandria, and Gregory of Nazianzus. Under them he acquired such learning and such a reputation for learning in divine matters that, whenever difficulties arose in obscure passages of the sacred volumes, Pope Damasus, the most learned Augustine, Paulinus, Chromatius, Heliodorus, and many other highly learned bishops throughout Italy, Gaul, Spain, Africa, Palestine, and Greece had recourse to this one man, as to someone who, assisted by the manifold variety of his languages, had read all the interpreters of sacred Scripture, Greek, Hebrew, and Latin.

Augustine openly demonstrates this in these words in Book I *Against Julian*: “The holy presbyter Jerome, learned in Greek, Latin, and Hebrew speech, passing from the Western Church to the Eastern, lived to old age in the holy places and in the sacred writings. He read all, or almost all, who before him had written on ecclesiastical doctrine in either part of the world.”

ANTONIUS POSSEVINUS, Volume I, *Apparatus*

Saint Jerome was so perceptive regarding the divine Codex, or its versions, that Pope Gelasius, together with seventy bishops, testified that he had approved those books which Jerome himself had approved, and that in all things he had chosen to follow Jerome’s judgment, while rejecting what Jerome had rejected.

Jerome also obtained from the Church the title of Greatest Doctor in the sacred writings, and Pope Damasus, the supreme pontiff, appointed him almost as a kind of arbiter of the divine Scriptures.

Moreover, since Saint Augustine regularly consulted him by letters and through Orosius, whom he sent to Jerome, on difficult questions, and called Jerome’s books against Jovinian “most lucid, most delightful, and most brilliant,” we understand how highly the treasures contained in Jerome’s writings must be valued.

RICHARD SIMON, in the *Critical History*

After Origen, Jerome is regarded as the most learned man; one might rightly call him the Origen of the Latins. He wished to do for his own Church what Origen had earlier done for his. Yet he was superior to Origen in this respect: he was much more skilled than Origen in Hebrew matters and made greater use of the Jews, although in subtlety and acuity he was inferior to him.

Consequently, he does not so often play with allegories as Origen does. Moreover, most of Jerome’s allegories, etymologies, and allusions depend upon words. He should be selected and studied before other interpreters, both because he knew Hebrew, Syriac, Greek, and Latin, and because he had read the translations of all the others and consulted Jews every day.

Furthermore, he was exceedingly learned in profane subjects. Yet he was not exact everywhere, because he did not meditate sufficiently long on what he dictated. Rather, as he himself admits, he was content to dictate what he had read among others or received from Jews.

For this reason, not everything found in his Commentaries should be attributed to him. Sometimes he dictated the opinions of Jews, and sometimes those of heretics. To enable the reader to distinguish these from his own, he laid down rules. In this way he dispelled the charge of inconsistency that had been fastened upon him.

His best Commentaries of all are those on the Prophets, and so forth.

[Col. 0231]

PETRUS PAULUS VERGERIUS OF JUSTINOPOLIS, *Oration on the Divine Jerome*

[Col. 0231] I wish to praise correctly the most holy Doctor of our faith, Jerome, whose solemn feast has arrived, in such a way that, while praising him, I do not seek my own praise. Rather, as my speech is dedicated to him, so may my mind also be dedicated to him with sincere intention.

Although I do not see what hope of praise there can be for one who speaks here, where the greatness of the subject overwhelms every force of eloquence and every speech is unequal to the excellence of his merits. Least of all is it fitting for me to entertain such hope. If any such thought enters my mind, I foolishly take pleasure in it.

For although I usually perform this duty of praise each year, yet whenever I have begun, I have afterward been affected throughout the following years in such a way that I feel my desire increasing while my ability diminishes.

This perhaps happens either because I have not yet sufficiently weighed the powers of my own talent, since I do not fear undertaking the burden of so great a task—although I understood its magnitude somewhat long ago and perceive it more clearly day by day—or because the merits of this Saint, insufficiently observed by many but considered by me with the greatest zeal, attract the affection of my mind more strongly as they shine forth more brightly, and increasingly discourage the keenness of my talent from hoping to attain them.

Or perhaps it happens because, in proportion to my desire and devotion to him, my talent seems to me to be held back, while the eagerness of my will runs ahead.

Although I do not deny that both of the first explanations may be involved, I earnestly desire the last to be present. For he himself, or anyone else, has no need of my service or that of another in returning praises to him. I think he takes pleasure in them only for the sake of our own improvement and progress, since in himself he enjoys infinite and personal blessedness in that happy and eternal life.

But as regards devotion, worship, religion, piety, and faith—both toward him and toward the other heavenly saints—we ourselves need these for our own sake. I above all, who have clearly discovered by experience that, through the merits of this glorious Saint, I have often obtained many great benefits from the immortal God and, in the most difficult circumstances, have been freed from grave dangers through his aid and intercession.

If previously I owed him any devotion, I must now certainly offer much more, so that here I may represent the place of my father who most recently died—he was deeply devoted to you, holy Father Jerome—and whose prayers on my behalf I have often experienced to have had great force with you.

Thus, just as I was the disciple of his living devotion to this illustrious institution and familiar devotion, so may I also be his heir after his death; and whatever patronage I had through him may now be wholly present in me.

Yet I trust that, through your merits and prayers, and also because he was a righteous man who feared God, he has been led, as he departed from this light, to those places where, through you and from you, he can obtain anything much more easily.

What concerns me, therefore, is this: just as devotion of the soul must be preserved and increased, so this annual offering of returning praises must in no way be neglected. In it, whatever the quality of the speech may be, so long as the mind is sincere and wholly devoted to him, I do not think eloquence should be highly valued; rather, I wish to be more grateful toward him than eloquent. Nor am I unaware that anyone who approaches to praise some illustrious person—and especially when the matter concerns divine things—ought himself also to be worthy of praise and free from every blemish, lest the speech rebuke the life of the speaker, and sordid morals deprive beautiful words of credibility. Even if this is not found in me, nevertheless it is usually a sign of a good and pious disposition to praise virtue earnestly and to show exceptional reverence toward sacred matters.

If someone should ask me what I consider the first and foremost praise of this glorious Saint, I shall answer without hesitation: that, in my judgment, he cannot be worthily praised by human speech. In addition, in every category of praise that belongs to a learned, upright, and wholly religious Christian, individual points may be excellently praised in him. But if, in praising him, I should begin by mentioning his mastery of letters, his knowledge of various languages, his eloquence, his sound interpretations of narratives, his extensive memory of history, his knowledge of natural things and of moral discourse, and then his understanding of Holy Scripture and true theology, I might perhaps not seem to be saying anything remarkable, since these things can also come to bad men. For such things do not make men good, but learned.

Or if, in addition, I should recall among his praises temperance, courage, prudence, constancy, gentleness, patience, and kindness, even then perhaps I would not be judged to have adorned him greatly, since many of the Gentiles also possessed these virtues. These praises are indeed owed to a good man, but they are not uniquely proper to a Christian. Finally, if I should demonstrate his steadfast faith, sure hope, ardent charity, and every form of holiness, together with his observance of ceremonies and zeal for religion, even then perhaps the praise would not be extraordinary, since every upright and faithful Christian ought to display these very things in himself.

But if I should testify that all these qualities, and whatever is contained under these names or under the name of virtue generally, were present in him in their entirety—and that they were present not moderately, nor in some ordinary and superficial fashion, but most excellently and incomparably—must not something divine necessarily be seen in a human being? Indeed, when I mention these familiar words—learning, eloquence, courage, prudence, faith, charity, and the rest of this kind—I seem to myself to be saying things such as are commonly found in human life, and not those supreme virtues that are known to have existed in the most excellent men, few though they have been in every age. [Col. 0234]

For this reason I am accustomed to grieve and to resent the Latin language, because it is not permitted to express the most exquisite praises with proper and carefully chosen names—praises that differ from ordinary virtues almost as much as virtue differs from vice. Yet I pray that what speech lacks may be supplied by the understanding of the listener, and that he may receive not merely what I say, but what I wish to say.

This may also be understood from the following consideration: a few of these qualities, or even one or another of them, when present in someone at an intense degree, are accustomed to make a great man; and a person who has attained several of them is regarded as possessing admirable excellence. What, then, ought to be thought of one who had gathered within himself the sum of all virtues and all the good arts, not superficially but to the highest degree—whose life was an example of complete holiness, whose eloquence was astounding, and whose learning was a marvel?

Thus he possessed not merely a holy name—which is itself signified by the name Jerome—but holiness itself. For when sacred religion was founded in the beginning upon two things, namely, the preaching of the Apostles and the blood of the martyrs—when the Apostles taught by speech what the martyrs established through prisons and tortures and, finally, death itself—the holy doctors succeeded to the place of both, each in his proper order. They explained more fully what the Apostles had taught concisely, and what the martyrs had attested with their blood they confirmed by the holiness of their lives. They stood firm for the faith and justice against every heresy and every stain of vice, serving at once as soldiers and as commanders.

Jerome endured many and various wars in this life, like a brave soldier. He waged war against the world and conquered it when, already a priest and considered worthy of the highest priesthood, he withdrew from Rome and renounced the pomp of the age and every ambition for worldly honors. He fought against the flesh and against demons in that vast desert across the sea which, as he himself says, scorched by the sun’s heat, provided the monks with a harsh dwelling-place: there he subdued the flesh by fasts and drove away spiritual enemies by prayers. He fought against wicked men and rivals, against whom he often inveighed in writing, sometimes through prefaces and sometimes through letters. He fought against heretics, whom he repeatedly convicted of various errors by writing books and treatises, and defeated by the force of argument in debate.

He bore, therefore, the name of Doctor, and he diligently fulfilled the office attached to it while alive: instructing those present by voice and example, and those absent by his writings. He aided the learning of living teachers, both of his own age and of posterity, through volumes in different languages and through varied translations. He delighted the less learned with history, and instructed the more perceptive by explaining the hidden meanings of Scripture.

I would certainly now attempt to praise his eloquence, which, flowing gently like a most limpid stream, delights both the eye and the ear, if he himself did not recommend it to readers far better than I can through his own elegance. To praise it worthily would require his own eloquence. Nor does the fact that Jerome was once condemned in connection with this study deter me. He was carried away in an ecstatic vision to the tribunal of the eternal Judge and, when asked what he was, heard the name “Ciceronian” brought against him instead of the name “Christian,” which he professed amid fear and trembling. For it was perhaps not the thing itself that was condemned, but his excessive devotion to it; without eloquence, sacred writings would scarcely be read at all, and certainly not with such pleasure.

These gifts, then, together with the other qualities I have briefly mentioned, procured for him many bitter and hostile rivals. In order to yield to their wickedness, he left Rome; and he who had been regarded as a teacher renowned throughout the world placed himself under the discipline of Gregory of Nazianzus. After his studies, when he had withdrawn from the most crowded city, he moved into the desert. He who in the most urban of cities had endured bestial human beings experienced human beasts in the most deserted wilderness. There a lion, savage by nature, submitted to his authority, while this man, gentle by nature, was savage toward himself.

Jerome therefore exchanged Rome for Bethlehem. He was not so much driven out of the wealthy city as he voluntarily withdrew from it, choosing to live in poverty where the poor Christ had been born, and to seek salvation from the place where the author of salvation himself had arisen. For what could anywhere be safe from malignity, when such great virtue was not without a persecutor? If anything similar should happen to us, we ought to console ourselves from his example. Meanwhile, with his help, may we overcome slanderers by doing good and conquer their hatred toward us through the virtue of patience and gentleness—he who lives and reigns forever and ever.

[Col. 0235]

FROM AN ANCIENT CODEX OF THE AMBROSIAN LIBRARY AT MILAN, NO. 173. THE LIFE OF SAINT JEROME, EDITED BY EUSEBIUS OF CREMONA, BEGINS. (S)*

[Col. 0235] Jerome, son of the most noble man Eusebius, was born in the town of Stridon, which lies on the borders of Dalmatia and Pannonia. While still a boy he went to Rome and was thoroughly educated in Greek, Latin, and Hebrew letters. In grammar he had Donatus as his teacher, and in rhetoric the orator Victorinus. In the divine Scriptures he exercised himself day and night, and eagerly drew from them what he later poured forth abundantly. At a certain time, as he himself relates in his Letter to Eustochium, while he eagerly read Tully by day and Plato by night, because the unpolished style of the prophetic books displeased him, around the middle of Lent he was suddenly seized by such a severe and burning fever that, although his entire body was already growing cold, vital heat throbbed only in his breast [MS: “colour”].

While preparations were therefore being made for his funeral, he was suddenly dragged before the tribunal of the Judge. Asked what condition he belonged to, he freely professed himself to be a Christian. The Judge said to him: “You are lying; you are a Ciceronian, not a Christian. For where your treasure is, there also is your heart.” Then Jerome fell silent, and immediately the Judge ordered him to be beaten most severely. He cried out and said: “Have mercy on me, Lord.” Those standing by then pleaded that he grant pardon to the young man. But Jerome began to swear by God and say: “Lord, if I ever possess secular books, if I ever read them, I shall deny you.”

Upon this oath he was released and immediately revived. Then he found himself completely drenched in tears, and he discovered that his shoulders were terribly bruised from the blows he had received before the tribunal. From that time onward he read the divine books with as much zeal as he had ever read the books of the Gentiles.

When he was thirty-nine years old, he was ordained in the Roman Church as a Cardinal Priest. After Pope Liberius died, everyone acclaimed Jerome as worthy of the highest priesthood. But when he rebuked the wantonness of certain clerics and monks, they became exceedingly indignant and plotted against him. They even shamefully mocked him by means of a woman’s clothing, as John Beleth says. For when Jerome rose at the customary hour for Matins, he found a woman’s garment, which his rivals had placed beside his bed; believing it to be his own, he put it on and proceeded to church dressed in it. His rivals did this so that he would be believed to have a woman in his bedroom.

When he saw this, he gave way to such madness and went to Gregory, Bishop of Constantinople. After learning the sacred writings from him, he hastened into the desert, where he himself relates to Eustochium what he endured for Christ, saying: “How often, established in the desert, in that vast solitude,” and so forth, “until sharing the ranks of the angels.” After carrying out his penance in this manner for four years, he returned to the town of Bethlehem, where, like a prudent animal, he offered himself to remain at the Lord’s manger.

He kept his library, which he had assembled and closed with the greatest care, and, rereading his other books, passed the day fasting until evening. Gathering many disciples, he labored in holy purpose and in translating the Scriptures for fifty years and six months, and remained a virgin until the end. Although it is said here that he was always a virgin, he himself writes of this matter as follows: “I prefer virginity in heaven, not because I possess it, but because I desire more strongly what I do not possess.”

He was so wearied by exhaustion that, lying on his bed with a cord suspended from a beam, he would raise himself onto his back by his hands. One evening, as Jerome was sitting with his brothers to hear the sacred reading, a certain lame lion entered the monastery; what follows is given above in the same words in column 309 and following.

When formerly everyone in the Church sang whatever he wished, the Emperor Theodosius, as John Beleth says, asked Pope Damasus to entrust the ordering of the ecclesiastical office to some learned man. Knowing that Jerome was perfect in Latin, Greek, and Hebrew and supreme in all wisdom, Damasus therefore entrusted this office to him.

Jerome accordingly divided the Psalter according to the weekdays, assigned a proper Nocturn to each weekday, and established that the Gloria Patri should be said at the end of every psalm. Then he rationally arranged the Epistles and Gospels to be sung throughout the yearly cycle, together with the other things pertaining to the office, apart from the singing. He sent this arrangement to the Supreme Pontiff, and it was highly approved by him and by the Cardinals and authenticated in perpetuity.

Afterward he built himself a monastery at the mouth of the cave in which the Lord came and lay. There, after completing ninety-eight years and six months, he was buried.

How greatly Augustine revered him is clear from the letters he sent him. In one of them he writes to him as follows:

“To the most beloved Lord Jerome, worthy to be honored and embraced with the observance of the sincerest charity, Augustine.”

Elsewhere he writes of him in this manner:

“Saint Jerome the priest, learned in Greek, Latin, and Hebrew eloquence, lived to extreme old age in the holy places and in sacred letters. His eloquence shone for us from East to West like the lamp of the sun.”

Blessed Prosper, in his Chronicles, says:

“Jerome the priest, already famous throughout the world, lives at Bethlehem, serving the universal Church with outstanding talent and zeal.”

In the Dialogue of Severus, a disciple of Saint Martin who lived in Jerome’s time, the following is also written about him:

“Jerome the priest was so instructed in Latin, Greek, and Hebrew letters, through the merit of his faith and the endowment of his virtues, that no one would dare compare himself with him in any branch of knowledge. He was continually engaged in battle and perpetual conflict against the wicked. Heretics hated him because he never ceased attacking them. Wicked clerics hated him because he pursued their way of life and their crimes; but all good men both admire and love him. Those who think him a heretic are plainly insane.

“He is always wholly devoted to reading and wholly devoted to books; he rests neither by day nor by night. He is always either reading something or writing.”

This is what Severus says. As these words show, and as Jerome himself often attests, he endured many persecutors and many detractors. How willingly he bore these persecutions is evident from what he says in his Letter to Asella:

“I give thanks to God because I have been judged worthy to be hated by the world. They mutter that I am a sorcerer, but I know that one reaches the kingdom through ill repute and good repute.”

Again:

“Would that, for the sake of the name and justice of my Lord, the entire multitude of the unbelieving should persecute me. Would that this world should rise up more solidly against my disgrace—provided only that I may deserve to be praised by Christ and hope for the reward of his promise. Temptation whose reward is obtained from Christ is therefore welcome and desirable; nor is that curse grievous which imitates divine praise.”

The aforementioned Lord Jerome died around the year 398 of Our Lord Jesus Christ. The end.

[Col. 0237]

FROM ANOTHER AMBROSIAN CODEX, I. LIII. THE TRANSLATION OF THE BODY OF SAINT JEROME. HOW THE BODY OF THE LORD JEROME WAS BROUGHT TO ROME AND MOST DEVOUTLY PLACED IN THE BASILICA OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN MARY BEFORE THE LORD’S MANGER. (S)

[Col. 0237] Among the praiseworthy privileges that divine clemency has abundantly bestowed upon the nourishing City with reverence, it joyfully granted her the bodies of the principal Apostles—Peter and Paul, Philip and James, Bartholomew and Matthias, Simon and Jude—as well as those of precious martyrs, confessors, and virgins, so that she might possess them for firm protection and perpetual glory. Through their most powerful intercessions she might shine, magnificently exalted in temporal matters, and might perpetually gleam in the heavens, glorified by eternal joy.

Among these, blessed Jerome, the outstanding Doctor, deserved to obtain a magnificent place in the aforesaid Basilica of the perpetual Virgin Mary, which is situated at the Manger. Thus he might rest more fittingly in her royal house, whom during his life he had diligently and faithfully commended with magnificent and most devout praises.

How, then, the body of this wonderful Doctor was brought from Bethlehem, where it had been buried, to the aforesaid court of the glorious Virgin, we shall relate in a brief account, for the pleasure of our readers, just as we received it in truthful testimony from holy and honorable bishops, from ancient Fathers, and from priests who feared God.
