After that holy city of Jerusalem, because of the sins of mortals, remained deprived of its most holy—indeed, of all—relics, with only the body of the venerable Doctor remaining [lacuna] … his most holy body was brought back to the magnificent city from which he had earlier withdrawn as a cardinal, and reverently placed in the aforementioned house of the Mother of the Most High.

He appeared to a certain most holy monk living in the regions beyond the sea and said to him in a calm and gentle oracle:

“Beloved brother, destined to dwell with me in heavenly glory, know that, with the help of the Queen of Heaven, I have obtained from God that you should exhume my body at your own labor and expense, and as quickly as possible carry it whole and devoutly to Rome. Take care to place it in a humble tomb at the entrance of that most blessed crypt called the Manger of the Lord, so that my body may remain attached to that holy Basilica of the sweetest Queen whom, while alive, I loved from my childhood, sought in my youth, and proclaimed with all my strength, though insufficient, in old age; and whom I praised until my end with pious and holy testimonies from the Scriptures.”

When that holy man heard these things from blessed Jerome in the visitation, he rose quickly and went to the place. Carefully accompanied by two companions, he lifted the most blessed body, while an abundance of wondrous fragrance spread there. He returned secretly to his own country, lest scandal arise in those regions, and kept the matter concealed until he came to the City, as the Saint had requested, with due devotion.

Since the monk, a most faithful servant of Christ, had understood from Saint Jerome that in such acts of service he should avoid popular acclaim, lest the Curia diminish his relics in any way, he came secretly by night with those two companions to the aforesaid Basilica. Only the Canons of that court were present, offering most devout praises to God and to the Blessed Virgin in subdued voices, with both heart and mind. With complete vigilance of mind, he buried the body among the columns of the Basilica and near the entrance to the Manger.

In this burial service, the Canons named above, together with the monk and his two companions, sensed an indescribable sweetness of fragrance and saw with blessed eyes an immense brightness such as they had never before seen in that Basilica. Present at the burial of her most learned praiser and most devoted Jerome was the Virgin Mary, brighter than the shining moon and more splendid than the sun, sweeter than every adornment, surrounded by mystical roses and precious lilies of the valleys. The most splendid Virgin provided all these things in honor of her most faithful servant and so that he might possess the ineffable eternal glory he had deserved. She herself bears sweet testimony concerning herself through Solomon: “Whoever makes me shine forth shall possess eternal life.”

Rejoice, therefore, blessed Doctor; rejoice and exult, friend of Jesus Christ, founded upon true charity. For that sweetest Queen of heaven and earth, whom during your earthly life you illuminated with immense praises and precious preaching, wondrously honored you at your arrival, magnified you with equanimity before that heavenly Judge of ours, crowned you perpetually in the heavenly palace with the angels and archangels, and finally prepared for you an appropriate place honorably in this royal and precious court of hers.

We also ask you, venerable priest of the most blessed Virgin: although unworthy, we are constant and most devoted praisers of so great and glorious a Virgin and of your holiness. Just as we magnify your most sacred body on earth with continual praises, so by your prayers commend us sinners effectively to our Savior in heaven. May he grant this, who is God blessed above all forever and ever. Amen.

[ON THE DEATH OF SAINT JEROME.]

[Col. 0239]

NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING LITTLE WORK.

[Col. 0239] Oudinus argues in a special dissertation on his life and works that this work, and the two little works that follow it, have Damasus of Porto as their author; he was made Roman Pontiff toward the end of the ninth century and called himself Formosus. His arguments, however, did not seem sufficiently sound and weighty to persuade us of the matter. The fact that Damasus pursued Saint Jerome with singular devotion and wished to be regarded as his disciple in learning shows that he also employed absurd inventions to obtain what he sought. Erasmus and the sons of the Critics, before whose censor’s mark these writings have come, warn that there is nothing here in which anyone should spend even an hour.

[Col. 0239]

EUSEBIUS, ON THE DEATH OF JEROME, TO DAMASUS. (S)*

To the most reverend Father Damasus, Bishop of Porto, and to the most Christian Theodosius, Senator of the Romans: Eusebius, once the disciple of the most holy Jerome, now deprived of that same light, sends pious grief and most sweet joy.

### CHAPTER I

In many ways and by many means God formerly spoke to all of us through his beloved son, Saint Jerome, concerning the holy Scriptures, through the many virtues and wonders that the Lord himself performed through him in our midst, as you know. We too are witnesses, for we saw him and observed his holiness with our own eyes, and our hands touched the word of his knowledge and teaching, through which life was manifested. What we have seen and heard, therefore, we announce to you.

For we were like wandering sheep, astray amid erroneous and superstitious fables, not hearing sound doctrine but heaping up for ourselves false prophets who, rising among the people as lying teachers, introduced sects of varied destruction. Then this day dawned, shining like the sun, and for fifty years and six months, amid many labors and hardships, in readings and vigils, he shone forth in the temple of God. He labored to break for us the bread of doctrine, dispelling the darkness of errors and freeing all from destruction.

Beginning in the East and extending to the West, he removed the wars of the heretics, shattered their bow, and burned their weapons and shields with fire. For in him God placed wonders upon the earth, so that his name might become manifest among the nations.

### CHAPTER II

Then, passing as far as the ends of the earth, he healed those oppressed by the arrows of heretics, enlightened human minds, unlocked the riddles of Scripture, untied knots, clarified obscure matters, explained doubtful ones, refuted and corrected falsehoods, and gathered the truest things from very many languages into one, so that he might make known to us the ways of life and fill us with joy, gladness, and exultation.

He strengthened the temple of the Lord and made its entrance known to all posterity more excellently than all others, like a lamp set not under a bushel but upon a lampstand in the Lord’s court, abundantly made fruitful by the Lord’s life-giving dew, through the singular elegance of his words: so that they might go to the city of habitation and find the place of glory, and might not become like their predecessors, a most bitter race, whom he guided and freed from the destruction of errors.

### CHAPTER III

Since I am like stubble before the face of the wind, and like the stammering mud of the streets, unable to speak or fully form words, what praise of him shall I offer you, dearest fathers and lords? Indeed, according to the Apostle’s saying: “If I were to speak in the tongues of men and of angels,” I would still not attain the proper manner of praising him.

Therefore I shall not trust in my bow, nor shall my sword save me; rather, the Lord shall be my illumination. He taught and will teach my hand to write, and he directs my tongue to speak, as once he did the tongue of Balaam’s she-ass. For his is the kingdom and the dominion, and he rules from sea to sea and from the river to the ends of the earth. All things are placed under his authority; before him kings shall fall, and no one can resist his will.

For whatever he wished, he did in heaven, on earth, in the sea, and in the abysses. Thus my tongue shall meditate upon the praise of such a man and shall announce his name to all.

### CHAPTER IV

He was truly an Israelite in whom there was no deceit, chosen according to the heart of the Lord to speak to all nations and kingdoms everything that the Lord had commanded him, and given as a teacher among the nations: to tear up the thorns, destroy, annihilate, and scatter them, and to sow, build, and plant true wisdom.

He is a lover of the brethren. He is the one who transferred for the Christian people so many volumes of books from the Hebrew and Greek languages into Latin, at no small cost. He was the first to order the office of the Church, and he made all the rough places of sacred Scripture smooth.

Certainly, in his light we see light; nourished by the bread of his saving doctrine, we walk onward to the mountain of God, Horeb. He is the river of living water, splendid like crystal, proceeding from the throne of God in the midst of the Church. On either side of it is the tree of life, bearing its fruit in due season; the leaves of that tree are for the healing of the nations.

This man appeared most gentle among his people, beloved by God and by human beings. He now prays for the holy Church. Truly he is a wondrous vessel, adorned with every precious stone, the work of the Most High.

### CHAPTER V

Yet what more shall I say about him, whose glory the heavens declare and whose written works the firmament proclaims? There are neither utterances nor speeches whose words of teaching are not heard, since his sound has gone out into all the earth.

O ineffable mercy of the Savior, who gathered together in Jerome such a multitude of graces that scarcely anyone among human beings, except in some particular respect, is permitted to aspire to what he alone possesses.

He is certainly the leader of our faith, drawing those who run to him into the citadel of heaven. The nations marveled at him, adorned above all others with the most excellent insignia of dignity, in songs and proverbs, works and interpretations. His virtue became known among the peoples, for he was filled with wisdom like a river.

But, to speak truly, in accordance with the words of the Queen of Sheba: “Greater is his wisdom and his works than the report that you heard.” How good he is, certainly, to those who are upright in heart, since he always hated wickedness. For he performed wonders in our land. “We sat under his shadow, and his fruit was sweet to our throat.” Yet how shall we announce all that we have heard and learned about him?

### CHAPTER VI

Who am I to recount his praise, his virtues, and the wonders he performed? But since I have not been eloquent from yesterday or the day before, to put it briefly—if you are willing to accept it—he is John the Baptist himself: both were virgins, both hermits.

Of John it is said: “John was clothed in camel’s hair in the desert.” Of himself Jerome says: “My deformed limbs bristled beneath a sackcloth, and a squalid covering had formed over my Ethiopian flesh.”

Again of John: “He ate locusts and wild honey.” Of himself Jerome again says: “I say nothing of food and drink, since even sick monks use cold water, and to have received anything cooked is considered luxury.”

What more is there to say? John was a martyr for the sake of justice. Jerome, although material iron did not take away his spirit, was nevertheless not deprived of the reward of martyrdom. For martyrdom is twofold: one form is to succumb to the swords of the wicked; the other is to preserve patience of soul amid infirmities and adversities.

### CHAPTER VII

Certainly he is a martyr who, for the sake of justice and gentleness and the saving words of his teaching, bravely endured a strong contest against the company of evil men in the sea of tears that is this world, knowing that wisdom is stronger than all.

He did not act impiously in the sight of God, but in all his tribulations called upon the Lord and did not sin with his lips; nor did he speak anything foolish against God.

Let me say nothing of how many tribulations, labors, afflictions, torments, struggles, scourges, hunger, thirst, bitterness, storms, temptations, abstinences, vigils, journeys, mortifications of the flesh, nakedness, fasts, and hardships—and not only these but heavier and innumerable sufferings—he endured in his most glorious body for the name of Jesus Christ, as he himself says:

“I was living in the desert, established in that vast solitude which, scorched by the sun’s heat, provides the monks with a harsh dwelling-place, imagining that I possessed the pleasures of Rome; every day there were groans, every day tears. And whenever sleep, pressing upon me, overcame me as I resisted, I would scarcely strike my bones, clinging to the bare earth.

“My deformed limbs bristled beneath a sackcloth. In my weakness I used cold water, and to have received anything cooked was luxury. Because of discomforts my skin was squalid, and a covering had formed over my Ethiopian flesh. Yet, although I was a companion of scorpions and wild beasts, I often found myself among choirs of girls; and in my cold body, in a man already almost dead, the fires of lust alone seethed.

“God is my witness: I remember that I often joined day to night and did not cease beating my breast until, at the Lord’s command, tranquility returned to me. I wept continually and subdued my rebellious flesh by weeks of fasting.

“I dreaded my little cell as though it were conscious of my thoughts; angry with myself and severe, I alone penetrated the desert. Whenever I saw hollow valleys and precipitous mountains, that was the prison of my most wretched flesh; there was the place of my prayer.”

### CHAPTER VIII

Who, then, was infirm, if not he? Who was scandalized, if not he? But if the Saints are to be praised for infirmities and labors, certainly he too must be praised.

I shall now come to the insults and persecutions that he endured from wicked and false brothers in this valley of misery. What else was his life in this world always but a kind of continual battle and unceasing conflict against the wicked ranks of all heretics and evil men?

The heretics roared over him like lions, because he rebuked them and caused their souls to waste away like [Note: [Col. 0243] Incorrectly read: “like sands.”] spiders’ webs; he destroyed their fruits from the earth and their seed from among the children of men.

Clerics devoted to wantonness opened their mouths against him, despised him, spoke with deceitful lips, and hated him with unjust hatred, because he pursued their wicked way of life and their crimes.

Many dogs surrounded him, and fat bulls besieged him. Unjust witnesses rose up against him, sharpening their tongues like serpents, with the venom of asps beneath their lips. They devised wickedness in their hearts, appointed battles all day long, and sought to trip his steps. They stretched ropes into snares for his feet, to erase his memory from the earth and drive him out from among the nations, so that he might become a reproach to his neighbors.

### CHAPTER IX

His magnificence was over the Roman people, his virtue was wondrous in words, and he was holy in all his works: raising up the fallen, loosening the bound, enlightening the blind, and directing the just; giving strength and power to the people of God; and, like a loud-sounding trumpet, announcing their crimes to all the wicked.

He shattered the gates of sinners and their iron bars with the sword of his teaching. When the wicked heard these things, they were cut to the heart; gnashing their teeth at him, they plotted and spoke wickedness. They bent their bow, prepared it, and prepared in it instruments of death.

But he was filled with the Holy Spirit, persevering in prayers and good works, mortifying vices and bringing good things to life, raising the needy from the dust and lifting the poor from the dungheap. For he took pleasure neither in the strength of a horse nor in the tents of a man, and he did not hope in riches. Strengthened by the Lord’s power, he did not fear his adversaries, but thundered against them through corrections and holy teachings, giving power to his king and exalting the horn of his Christ.

He taught others through his labor, like a good soldier of Christ, knowing that no one who competes in the contest will be crowned unless he has competed lawfully.

When the wicked men saw these things, they became angry, and anguish seized them, because they were a crooked and perverse generation, children in whom there was no faith. They provoked him in their counsels and stirred him to anger by their abominations.

Having lost counsel and discipline, they mocked him in a woman’s garment, as though he were a wanton and wicked man, and with one accord attacked him and drove him outside the city of Rome. But he, benign, patient, humble, and gentle, gave way to their madness, casting all their sins behind his back.

## CHAPTER X

Departing from there, he traveled to Constantinople, to the most holy bishop Gregory of Nazianzus.

O ineffable man, O wondrous vessel of virtues, O splendor of patience, O radiant lamp, O diadem of honor and glory, most steadfast cornerstone, model of innocence, golden pillar, and foundation of the whole Church! The more you are thundered against, the less you are confounded. Innocent lamb, what are you saying, pressed at the neck by so many yokes?

“I give thanks to my God, because I have been considered worthy for the world to hate me. For I know that I shall reach heavenly glory through disgrace and good repute.”

His patience opened the heavens, because there the power of his glory was always confirmed; he placed his firm strength in God, and his heart never withdrew from the Lord. The bow of the strong was overcome; he himself was girded with strength and prevailed in his weakness. He became strong in battle, and his right hand was glorified in power. His right hand crushed his enemies, for the Lord became his helper and protector unto salvation.

Therefore let us sing to the Lord, for he has done magnificently. Let us proclaim this throughout the whole earth. Let us draw water with joy from the fountains of the Savior.

The wicked vanished in their thoughts, because their foolish heart was darkened; and although they believed themselves wise in their wickedness, they became fools, because they exchanged the truth for a lie. Yet truth has sprung from the earth, and righteousness has looked forth from heaven. Indeed, fools fell into the pit which they had opened and into the ditch which they had dug. But the righteous man was never disturbed, because the Lord strengthened his hand.

## CHAPTER XI

Therefore, most holy Fathers and lords, consider this man: how faithful and just he was always in the house of the Lord, teaching us, illuminating the hidden things of darkness, and driving away the wickedness of sins.

Concerning him our discourse would be great and impossible to express; but I have become exceedingly weak, because trembling has entered my bones and the ground beneath me has been shaken, lest I ascend too high. For the gate is narrow and the way constricted, and this solid food belongs to the wise and perfected, who have their senses trained for discernment.

Therefore, leaving aside no small matters, I wish to disclose very briefly certain things about the ineffable end of so great a man—whose praise fills the earth, whose splendor is like the moon [variant: “light”], and whose horns are in his hands.

For almighty God, whose mercy goes before his face, who is just and whose judgment is righteous, rendering the reward of the labors of his saints; the true and good shepherd, ordering all things in mercy and gathering [Col. 0245] his sheep into his bosom—after these sheep had at last, in these days, happily completed the intolerable and burdensome course of a most grievous contest, in which the flesh desires against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh—now that the long-desired harbor had been reached, he called his beloved son Jerome from the voyage of this stormy sea, in which there are innumerable creeping creatures and hostile armies wrestling to deceive and slaughter those upright in heart.

He called him forth stripped of the robe of mortality and of this wretched flesh’s corruption, adorned with the everlasting crown of immortality, and summoned him to the heavenly court, so that what he had seen here in a riddle he might there see face to face.

## CHAPTER XII

When, at his final hour, death was pressing him to depart from his body—he had already completed ninety-six years and was burning with a severe fever—he wished his sons, whom he had established from his youth like tender plantings, to be gathered together around him.

[Note: [Col. 0245] But you will learn what is nearer to the truth from the life of the holy Doctor.]

Seeing their faces weighed down with grief, he, as a pious and merciful man, was briefly moved by their tears; he groaned in spirit and wept. Then, raising his eyes slightly, he said in a calm voice:

“Son Eusebius, why are you shedding these useless tears? Is it not futile to shed tears over one who has died? Who among the living will not see the dissolution of this body? What God has once spoken, and you have heard, do you dare contradict? And you know that no one can resist his will.

“Now, my son, I ask you: do not walk according to the flesh; cease weeping. Certainly, the weapons of our warfare are not carnal.”

Then, with a cheerful and joyful face, addressing the other sons in a lively voice, he exclaimed:

“Let mourning cease; let grief depart; let there be one voice of rejoicing among all. For behold, this is the acceptable time; behold, this is the day of jubilation and joy, above all the days of my life. In it the faithful Lord in his words and holy in all his works has opened his hand, so that he may recall my exiled soul from this prison of death, where it has remained on account of the guilt of my forefather Adam, to the heavenly homeland, recovered through the precious blood of his Son.

“Do not, dearest sons, whom I have always held in the depths of charity, hinder my joy. Do not prevent me from returning to the earth what belongs to it. Strip my body at once and give it to the earth from which it was made, so that it may return to where it came from.”

When he had finished speaking, all the brothers, drenched in tears, stripped his most sacred body. It was so emaciated and disfigured by abstinence that it was terrifying to behold; indeed, it was so wasted that his bones could have been counted joint by joint. It was so bloodied by scourging that it seemed rather to be the body of a leper. They immediately laid it upon the bare ground and covered it with a linen sackcloth.

## CHAPTER XIII

But when the man of God felt the roughness of the earth, he was exceedingly glad. Turning toward the brothers, who were pouring forth floods of tears from grief and anguish, he said:

“I urge you, my dearest and most beloved sons, whom I have begotten in the depths of Jesus Christ, by the love and charity with which I have loved you: be reconciled now and have peace.

“For you ought, as is fitting for ministers, household members, and friends of God, to aspire to spiritual things, so that you may be an example to others. You who are spiritual [Col. 0246], why are you shedding so many fruitless tears?

“Let the remembrance of sins always bring tears to you. Be as ready for tears as you were for guilt. If anyone dies in sin, weep. For if an evil person rises from death through repentance, the angels rejoice in heaven; certainly, if a good person dies through sin, the angels grieve.

“But do not mourn me as one who is dying; rejoice with me as one who is reaching the harbor of salvation.

“What is weaker than the misery of this life, in which we are surrounded by so many armies of sorrows and sufferings that scarcely an hour passes in which any living person is free from pain?

“If he is rich, he is troubled on every side by fear lest he lose what he possesses. If he is poor, he never rests while seeking to find a livelihood. If he is good, on one side he fears the devil’s danger; on the other, he is greatly afraid lest the ship of his mortal body be wrecked upon the sea of this world.

“Therefore no sex, age, or condition passes through this life without suffering, so long as it remains in this misery. If you know that there is anything in me hindering my journey, grieve.

“Alas, how many people, sailing across this great and spacious sea in which I am, with so many different kinds of enemies wrestling according to the measure of each person’s strength, after much successful sailing and many victories, now believing that they were about to reach their eagerly desired end, have through some diabolical suggestion and their own lack of discernment fallen at this hour into the snare of perdition!

“Alas, how many are commended here both for their life and their reputation, yet over whom dreadful death and ruin hang because of a single assent to sin!

“Therefore, brothers, fear while you live. The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord. Our life is warfare upon the earth; whoever conquers here will be crowned elsewhere. While we are covered with this skin, no certain victory belongs to us. If our forefather had feared, he would never have fallen.

“The beginning of all evils is presumption about oneself. Whoever does not fear presumes upon himself. How can anyone burdened with gold walk securely among robbers?

“What else does the Savior teach us except to fear? ‘Watch,’ he says, ‘because you do not know at what hour the thief will come.’ For if the master of the house knew at what hour the thief would come, he would certainly watch and would not allow his house to be broken into.

“That supreme keeper of the keys, Peter, says: ‘Be sober, brothers, and watch, because your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking someone to devour.’”

## CHAPTER XIV

No one lives securely among serpents. The holier and wiser a person is, the more he must always fear. For whoever falls from a greater height suffers greater falls.

The devil’s bait is chosen: he does not concern himself with the wicked, because they are his own. The wise Solomon fell; and his father David also fell, he who was chosen according to God’s heart.

Fear, brothers; again I ask you, fear on every side, because blessed is the man who fears the Lord. Even if armies encamp against him, his heart will not fear. If battle rises against him, even then he will hope.

Perfect fear of God casts out empty fear. Love has no empty fear. Love and the fear of God are one.

Considering these things, the Prophet cried out, saying: “Fix my flesh with your fear.”

Whoever among you desires to see good days, let him come here and be enlightened, and his face will not be put to shame. Whoever [Col. 0247] fears God will do good, and his soul will dwell in good things, and his descendants will possess the earth as an inheritance. For the Lord is a stronghold to those who fear him, and his covenant is that it may be manifested to them.

If you do anything good, fear it with great caution.

[Note: Gregory, *Homily XII on Matthew*: “Hold fast with great caution to the good things you do”; the final word appears here also to have been intended to be restored as “fear.”]

Many do good deeds whose fruit is stolen by the appetite for human praise. There were ten virgins, yet half of them were excluded from the door of heaven.

Alas, how many today have been reborn through holy baptism and bear the Christian name, though it would have been better for them not to have existed! For the punishment of the pagans in Gehenna is infinitely less than that of wicked Christians. Would that such people did not constitute the greater part.

A ship sound on every side is sunk by a single hole. People have gone astray in this broad wilderness: some submitting their necks to the yoke of greed, others disfigured by the foulness of lust like the most shameful swine, others occupied in plundering useless things. Thus, having cast aside the use of reason, they became collaborators, like senseless beasts of burden—and would that they had merely been like them—and they did not find the road to the city of the new Jerusalem.

No reprobate enters the kingdom of heaven. Its way is a hundred times narrower than it is believed to be, although it is broad enough for those who truly fear.

To the centurion who feared, Christ promises to come to him; to the presumptuous ruler, he refuses to go with him.

## CHAPTER XV

In truth, not everyone today obeys the Gospel. “The time will come,” the Apostle said, “when people will not endure sound teaching.”

Many preach, but not all preach the truth; they bind the hearts of the simple in sins. They bind heavy burdens over minor sins, while they pass over grave ones with a winking eye.

A false teacher is a double-edged sword: on one side he cuts by his conduct and example; on the other he strikes and kills with deceitful and wicked words.

How can fire give coldness, or water warmth? How can a stone climb upward? And how will a lustful man preach chastity? Even if he preaches it, what benefit will come from it to those who hear? What can the hearer say except: “Why do you preach with your voice what you deny by your conduct?”

The one who speaks well with his mouth but lives badly in his deeds condemns himself.

The Psalmist shows how acceptable such preaching is to God: “God said to the sinner: Why do you recount my righteousnesses and take up my covenant in your mouth? Yet you have hated discipline and cast my words behind you.”

Many read lofty things, learn difficult matters, dispute subtly, and speak elegantly so that they may receive honors from the people and be called teachers among the congregations—and they do nothing.

If one should trust an experienced person, trust me: the holiness of life moves human hearts far more than polished speech. Do, and afterward preach.

Jesus began by doing and afterward by preaching. Doing without preaching is effective; preaching without doing is not.

God did not say, “Whoever preaches the will of my Father,” but “whoever does it.” I do not condemn preaching, except when those who preach do not do what they preach.

A teacher of subtle words only, and not of works, is a kind of light inflation of the ears and a smoke of truth, quickly passing away without fruit [Col. 0248].

Understand, brothers; understand what I say: he who does and preaches deserves far more than he who does and remains silent. If I alone do good, I benefit only myself; but if I do good while preaching, I benefit both myself and others.

Therefore those who instruct many in righteousness will be like stars for everlasting ages. Holy preachers are light for illumination, because through their teaching hearts darkened and blinded by the cloud of sin are enlightened by Christ, the true light who shines in darkness.

They are also salt for seasoning the word of God, which is food for the soul through good works.

Every person who possesses knowledge is charged with the duty of preaching, provided that he acts; indeed, to say more: whoever knows and merely acts, but does not teach others, will be held by the Lord to account.

For according to the Apostle John, “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer”; and, “Whoever possesses the substance of this world and sees his brother suffering need, yet closes his heart against him—how does the love of God remain in him?” How much more, then, is the person who sees his brother wandering and oppressed by deadly sins, yet does not minister to him the word of teaching? That learned person is a murderer and without charity.

## CHAPTER XVI

Fear, O teachers and rulers, to whom the Lord entrusts the duties of preaching, so that you may minister the word of the Lord to his people. For as many die in sins either through your example or through your negligence, so many will the Lord require from your hand.

The higher your rank, the greater the torments with which you will be tortured. You are not lords, but shepherds. There is one Lord and one chief shepherd, who knows his sheep and will demand them from your hands.

Alas, how many today in the Church are not shepherds but hirelings, to whom nothing concerning the sheep of Jesus Christ belongs! Indeed, to speak the truth—and they themselves know it—they are ravenous wolves, who both seize and scatter the sheep.

Certainly nothing is worse or more abominable than when the person who ought to guard the flock destroys it.

Alas, that today among certain men in the Church—who are not shepherds but destroyers, and they are not the smaller portion—it has come to pass that they swallow the possessions and labors of human beings insatiably, like hell.

They not only fail to correct people from their sins, but themselves draw them into unlawful things, either through their own negligence, through their worst ministers, or through their wicked deeds [Col. 0249].

I shall indeed say this: if God were to leave such men unpunished, God would no longer be God.

Therefore, as has often been said, dearest sons, while you live, serve the Lord in fear and rejoice in him with trembling. Take hold of his discipline, lest you perish from the right way.

Taste, my dearest sons—I say again, taste and see that the Lord is sweet.

The rich became needy and hungry, and while sleeping here amid their riches and pleasures, they found nothing in their hands. But those who seek the Lord will lack no good thing.

“I was young and now I am old, and I have never seen the righteous abandoned at the end, nor his descendants begging bread.”

## CHAPTER XVII

Be imitators of poverty, so that you may follow the footsteps of him who, though he existed in the form of God and carried all things by the word of his power, and in whose house are riches [Col. 0249] and glory, emptied himself, taking the form of a servant. He was born poor and needy.

Poor and pious—how destitute he was as long as he lived! He died and was buried in utter poverty.

Therefore, as that same one says: “Foxes have dens and the birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to rest his head.”

He also commands the Apostles not to carry a purse or a bag. And he advised the young man to sell what he possessed and distribute it to the poor.

If you believe Christ to be God, believe that he cannot be deceived [variant: “cannot deceive”]; otherwise he would not be God. And if you believe that he cannot be deceived, follow him.

It is impossible to abound in riches and follow Christ. Nature forbids contrary things from being mixed. Either I am mistaken, or the rich will be deceived at the end. Those who do not believe me will believe when their riches have passed into poverty.

The rich man feasted splendidly every day, dressed in purple and fine linen; but when he died, because he had refused to believe Moses and the Prophets, he found himself in torment.

“No one serving God entangles himself in secular affairs.”

“A king is not saved by his great strength, nor is a rich man saved by his riches.” For the horse is a deceptive thing for salvation.

Is pride not joined to riches? And where pride is, there is something worse. Do not all evils arise from pride as from a single root?

When a man becomes rich, and the glory of his house has increased, does he not become proud? And when he has become proud, are not his ways polluted at all times?

Then, sitting in ambush among the rich in secret, he devises how to kill the innocent. His eyes look upon the poor, and he lies in wait secretly, so that he may seize him like a lion in its den, saying in his heart: “God has forgotten; he has turned away his face so that he may not see to the end.”

For the Lord is sometimes sleeping, as though drunk with wine. Yet the longer God delays in his patience before inflicting judgments, the more he is inflamed with anger. Therefore he must be feared a hundred times more when he tolerates evils with long-suffering than when he punishes them hastily.

For a time God permits the good to be tormented by the wicked and proud, so that sinners may build upon the backs of the good and prolong iniquity for themselves.

And therefore, although God may for a little while seem to forget, he will not finally forget to have mercy on the poor. For he himself is the helper of the orphan, the poor man is entrusted to him, and God resists the proud while giving grace to the humble.

He breaks the arm of the sinner and the wicked, hearing the desire of the poor and judging in favor of the orphan and the humble, so that the proud man may no longer continue to exalt himself upon the earth.

## CHAPTER XVIII

Therefore, my dearest sons, if you are poor, humble yourselves beneath the powerful hand of God, lest—God forbid—you lose the things you do.

Poverty is not pleasing to God without humility. God preferred to become incarnate from blessed Mary on account of humility rather than on account of any other virtue. For just as all evils arise from the single root of pride, so all good things are generated from the single root of humility.

Learn from the Savior, because he is gentle and humble of heart. He humbled himself for us, becoming obedient unto death—even death on a cross.

Therefore I say to you: if you wish to be humble, be obedient also to every human [Col. 0250] creature for God’s sake.

Consider, dearest sons, by what name you are called: “monk,” that is, “one.” It is not fitting for a monk to wish to have and not to have, except in the matter of not sinning. Thus, in all good things and in lawful matters, let your willing and not willing be one through obedience.

Do not require several commands before you act. He is not obedient but negligent who waits for a second order.

The voice of a single command teaches you that Peter and Andrew, leaving their nets and everything they had, followed the footsteps of the Lord.

True obedience always desires this: never to obey one’s own will, but reverently to obey another’s.

Christ left this example at the Last Supper when, washing the feet of his disciples, he said to Peter that unless he became obedient, he would have no share with him.

Therefore, dearest sons, just as you have one name, “monk,” so let there be one will and one refusal. For it is good and pleasant for brothers to dwell together in unity.

Let there be no greater or lesser among you; rather, let the predecessor become like the junior, lest, after the manner of the kings of the nations, the one who is greater among you dominate the other brothers and rejoice in being lifted up by their empty praises.

Instead, after the example of King Jesus Christ, let the greater become, through humility, like the lesser among those whom he governs.

Let your superior, through humility, be a companion to the lesser when he acts well; but when he sins, let him stand firmly against vice through zeal for justice.

Let there never be a pact with vices. Let a person be loved in such a way that his vice is hated.

It is a great sign of love to rebuke a person even in the smallest matters. Often excessive humility causes great harm. It is not true humility to permit vices by remaining silent.

“Cry out,” Isaiah says, “do not cease; lift up your voice like a trumpet; declare to my people their crimes.”

Would that every creature cried out against vices! For even if a sinner does not fear God, he nevertheless respects human beings.

The Apostle teaches us this when he says: “Be angry and do not sin. Let not the sun go down upon your anger.”

The Lord is just and has loved justice; his face has seen equity. If he is just, then you also be just.

The negligence and empty humility of a shepherd make it possible for wolves to dare attack the lambs. Do not look to the face of the powerful; there is no partiality with God.

## CHAPTER XIX

Practice what is just everywhere. True justice wishes to render to each person what belongs to him.

It is necessary to obey God rather than human beings. If you remain silent about the truth through fear of the powerful, do you not judge among yourselves and become judges of your own thoughts on their behalf? Does your righteousness not then exceed that of the scribes and Pharisees?

Do not honor the rich more than the poor unless he is better. Indeed, to speak more truly, honor the poor much more.

For the image of Jesus Christ shines forth in the poor; in the rich, the image of the world. We have all been born from one root of flesh; we are all members of one another in one body, whose head is Jesus Christ.

What greater honor, then, has the rich and powerful man deserved than the poor man? Perhaps because he is rich and powerful? But if so, why do we detest riches in this world? Why do we preach that the glory of the world must be despised?

Certainly, I do not think anyone should be honored [Col. 0251] for the practice of evil. If you honor the rich for his riches more than the poor, you place the world before God. And if you love anything in the world more than God, you are not worthy of God.

Please render to God the things that are God’s, and to the world the things that are the world’s. Let goodness be honored everywhere; let wickedness be utterly disfigured.

But since my discourse now concerns those who glory in their perishable riches, and who take pride in the nobility, power, and dignity of a certain foul flesh that will shortly return to ashes—being exalted by the empty and light puffing-up of certain foolish names, while they depress others by despising them, and therefore believe that they have attained the glory which the merciful Lord has prepared only for the humble and for those who despise the world—what should I say about them as is fitting?

Woe, woe to you who hasten toward the kingdom of heaven by the road of riches! For it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven.

These are not my words, but Christ’s. If this sentence can be revoked, Christ is not God at all. “Heaven and earth,” he likewise says, “will pass away, but my words will not pass away.”

Wail, you wretched ones, over the name of unstable fortune—you nobles and powerful people who confuse others and trample them down as though they were ignoble. Blinded by the smoke of this world’s honors and false dignities, when the thread of your exceedingly brief life is cut by death, as by a weaver—perhaps this very night—you will be tortured in hell, more than others, in an endless end, dying continually.

## CHAPTER XX

Living upon the labors of others, you do not belong to the world; rather, although you do not merely fail to bear the labors with other people, you do not permit those who labor to live. Therefore you will be scourged not with human beings but with devils.

The greater your glory and joy were in the world, the greater the punishment prepared for you in hell.

But what shall I say? We confess that Christ chose twelve Apostles.

[Note: [Col. 0251] These are matters of uncertain tradition, invented by each person from his own imagination. We know that Matthew was a tax collector, and that Peter and Andrew, with James and John, the two sons of Zebedee, were fishermen; of the rest, we do not know either the nobility of their birth or by what trade they supported themselves. Indeed, the author of the Greek index published by Cotelerius at the end of the second book of the *Apostolic Constitutions* makes Bartholomew “the son of Sosthenes and Urinia, a keeper of pasture, or a planter of vegetables.” Add that it is plainly contrary to Jerome’s view that Bartholomew alone was of noble birth, since in the *Epitaph of Marcella* he attributes such great nobility to John: “Jesus,” he says, “loved John the Evangelist greatly, who, because of the nobility of his family, was known to the High Priest and did not fear the plots of the Jews, so much so that he brought Peter into the courtyard,” etc. Yet it is altogether uncertain whether the person said in the Gospel to be known to the High Priest was John the Apostle. Certainly, the Evangelists call him, his brother, and his father fishermen, or ναύτας [sailors], as Origen calls them in *Against Celsus*, book 1.]

Of all of them, Bartholomew alone was noble by origin of flesh, while Matthew was occupied with riches before he accepted the apostolate. The others were exceedingly poor fishermen.

Listen to why I have mentioned this. If Christ is truthful, and if everything I heard from his mouth is not false, scarcely one such person out of a thousand is found fit for the kingdom of God. Those who do not believe me will shortly understand this when placed in torments.

But perhaps someone already blinded by the light of truth will wonder. If he were to question me about this, I would answer him: Do we not believe [Col. 0252] that a person is condemned by a single mortal sin? But if this is so, he will say, how will a hundred thousand be saved?

What else is a rich man, nourished on the fleeting breath of mortal fame, than a kind of rotting vessel of all sins? Where are pride, greed, and lust? Are they not among the rich, noble, and powerful?

Are they not robbers who violently plunder the wages of the poor, oppress them, and kill them? They take from the abundance of the Lord’s household what they received so that they might distribute it to the poor, and they use it for wicked purposes.

Certainly, they add excessive clothing to excessive abundance, caring nothing for the poor who are dying from cold and nakedness. They build palaces and great structures to be gazed upon by human eyes, while the poor die of hardship in the streets.

They frequently prepare banquets for other rich people, so that they may fill the gluttony of their bellies with the most delicate dishes, while the poor perish from hunger. What else is their life than sins?

If the belly is filled with such an abundance of food, is lust not waiting at its doors? And what more can I say, when the tongue of all mortals would fail to tell of the thousands of sins they commit?

They do not know God except as in a dream, and, I think, they do not believe that they will die. For a person who thinks that he will die does not easily fall into sins, and he knows that God will be his judge.

Truly, the one who has no memory of these things is exceedingly weak and wretched if he does not easily despise all diabolical temptations.

Therefore I shall speak truly: if they recognized God as their judge and believed that they would die, they would at least not sin so securely.

Why do these most wretched men hurry to the churches to attend the divine mysteries? Is it so that they may gaze upon the faces of women? This is their meditation, their preaching, and their knowledge of God.

Thus they inquire into the divine law: they travel across land and sea, with repeated vigils and meditations, gathering money for themselves and their sons; they continually change their clothing in society with astonishing variety of workmanship; indeed, they provide their companions in turn with games, jousts, dances, revelries, drunkenness, great banquets, and delicate dishes, and they keep enough women to satisfy their pleasure.

## CHAPTER XXI

But woe to you, wretched people! You do not recognize what you are doing. You destroy the body before its time and kill the soul.

From where do such illnesses and such premature death come, if not from an excessive quantity of food and frequent intercourse with women?

Do you think you can deceive God? Certainly, you deceive yourselves. For the sake of the body you forget the soul, and behold, you destroy the body together with the soul before its time.

Therefore rejoice, delight yourselves, and be glad in this very brief span of time that you possess, so that afterward you may mourn without end, for all time, with the devils.

Do not delay what you are doing. Change your clothes as frequently as possible, lest your nobility perish and no one surpass you, so that in hell you may receive shame and confusion.

Where are the banquets? Where are the delicate dishes? Where are the expensive wines mixed with honey and prepared with spices?

Feast and become drunk, for after death you will do so no longer. Instead, with the rich man who feasted splendidly every day, you will long for the smallest drop of water [Col. 0253] in the torments of Gehenna, and you will not be able to have it.

Enjoy your amusements; satisfy your pleasures in luxury. Sow in corruption, so that from corruption you may reap the divine sentence which that just judge will pronounce on the great day of judgment:

“Go, accursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.”

Alas, stony heart! If, when you consider that such a sentence threatens you on account of the wicked pleasures of this world, you do not fear, what will move you?

If you await that day so terrible and cruel, on which you will have to render an account to the Lord not only for luxuries, clothing, drunkenness, feasting, and all the time you lost while you lived, but also for every vain thought, why are you not corrected?

Why do you delay, wretched man, turning to the Lord from day to day? Why have you not yet repented of your evils?

Behold, death hastens to crush you, running day and night. Behold, the devil is already hastening to receive you. Behold, your riches will fail you. Behold, the worms await the body which you nourish with such care, so that they may gnaw it until, reunited with the soul, it suffers endless punishments together with it.

Why do you wander through the trackless places of this age seeking comforts in vanities? You will not find here riches, joys, glory, and the other things pleasing to you, because they are not here.

## CHAPTER XXII

But if you seek true joys, hasten toward that heavenly glory for which you were made. There are certainly the true joys which eye has not seen, ear has not heard, and which have not entered into the human heart.

Please abandon perishable and momentary things and seek to possess things everlasting.

But what shall I say about those who cease neither from sins through fear of God, love of God, nor fear of death and the torments that follow, but grieve if they cannot do evil as they wish?

Woe, woe to you wretched ones who laugh here, because you will weep. Woe to you when you desire these temporal joys, because against your will you will endure the torments of hell.

Behold, little time remains for you. Fill up the measure of your wickedness, so that all divine indignation may come upon you.

Enjoy this brief time in amusements, drunkenness, fights and quarrels, dances, and revelries; do not let any time pass unused.

Why do you delay while you live? Gather honors, riches, and power for your sons; increase your nobility and reputation, so that your sons may also be able to complete what you have done, and so that together with them you may suffer greater torments in hell.

## CHAPTER XXIII

But perhaps someone will say: “The Lord is kind and merciful; he receives every sinner who returns to him and forgives him.”

I confess that this is indeed true. The Lord is kinder than he is believed to be, and he spares each person who returns to him as is fitting.

Is the Lord not most kind, since he tolerates such great injuries from sinners, giving them time to reform?

But know this: just as he is kind in tolerating, so he is just in punishing.

But perhaps someone will say again: “A man who did evil throughout the whole time he lived will obtain forgiveness from God if he accepts penance at the point of death.”

Alas, how empty a suspicion and false a supposition! Scarcely one person out of a hundred thousand whose life has always been evil deserves to receive [Col. 0254] indulgence from God.

A man entirely born and raised in sins, who has neither seen nor recognized God, nor wished to hear about him, who does not know that he has sinned, and who knows what repentance is only, perhaps, in sleep; a man still completely bound by secular affairs, pressed by anxiety over the sons he is leaving behind, crushed by illness, shaken by grief over riches and temporal goods when he sees that he can no longer enjoy them—how can he receive as acceptable to God a repentance that he would not accept if he believed that he could still be healed?

Certainly I shall conclude truly: whoever, while healthy and young, does not fear offending God will not deserve to obtain divine forgiveness at death.

What kind of repentance is it, dearest sons, when someone accepts it only because he sees that he can no longer continue living—someone who, if he recovered from his illness, would become worse than before?

I know not a few wealthy men who, after accepting repentance at the point of death, recovered bodily but became worse in their way of life.

This I hold; this I consider true; this I have learned through manifold experience: the end is not good for the person whose life has always been evil, who did not fear sinning but always lived in the vanities of the world.

“The death of his saints,” says the Prophet, “is precious in the sight of the Lord”; and, “The death of sinners is very evil.”

## Chapter XXIV

And therefore, my most beloved sons, gird yourselves with strength; be strong sons, and do not fear the feeble power of these wretched rich and powerful men—whose weakness and misery we have already shown to be so great that no human tongue could express it—when you practice righteousness. For he who suffers persecution for righteousness is blessed, and it will go well with him; and if he dies, he is more blessed still. For “precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints.”

If you desire to possess life in Christ, do not fear death for Christ. For you cannot endure for Christ what is proportionate to the future glory that will be revealed, when our glory, which is above and not upon the earth, appears. Let no one who does not labor expect a reward. The name “Christian” alone is not enough. You are a Christian: imitate Christ. In vain does that man bear the name Christian who follows the devil. Indeed, he is not a Christian at all, but an Antichrist, according to the saying of blessed John the Evangelist: “You have heard that Antichrist is coming; now there are many Antichrists.”

Do you therefore wish to reign with Christ? Suffer with Christ. If it was necessary for Christ the Lord and King, whose name is above every name, to suffer in order thus to enter into his glory, what confidence do you have that you will enter without labor? O how foolish and slow of heart we are to believe! We want to rejoice here with the world and afterward reign with Christ. Will the Lord enter naked, while the servant enters weighed down with an excess of garments, gold, and gems? He fasting, and this one full of gluttony and luxury? He dying on the cross for him, and this one sleeping delicately in bed? Will the servant do what the Lord does not do? The Lord promises his kingdom to the sons of Zebedee if they can drink the cup that he was to drink.

Thus foolish are the sons of men, judging wrongly and recognizing neither what is true nor what is right, calling evil good and good evil. [Col. 0255] Return to your hearts; come and hear me, and I will tell you what I have heard and learned, and what our fathers have told me; let it not be hidden from the sons of men. It is good to cling to God, and to walk as he walked. Just as Christ laid down his life for us, so we too, if necessary, ought to lay down our lives for the truth, which is God himself.

“He who loves his life in this world will lose it.” Christ suffered for us, leaving us an example so that we might follow in his footsteps. Let no one consider himself a Christian who has not found himself prepared to die for Christ. He who serves Christ must follow him.

You may say, O man who are a Christian only in name and word: “I have and proclaim the faith of Christ.” That is good—but where are the works? Faith without works is dead. I will certainly say this: he who praises Christ only with his mouth and not in his deeds denies him. For if you believed what he says, you would at least fear him and be ashamed of your sins. And if you believe and do evil, are you not to be punished a hundredfold more? Is not a sin committed with deliberate malice infinitely worse than a sin committed through ignorance? An angel sinned, and a human being sinned: one could find forgiveness, the other could not. Why? The former sinned from his own malice; the human being through the devil’s suggestion.

## Chapter XXV

And perhaps you will say: “I too sin through the devil’s suggestion.” To which I reply: “What reward do you, wretch, deserve if you have no struggle?” Does not an earthly soldier expose himself to every danger in order to please his king? Certainly you can have no excuse if you say that you sin through the devil’s suggestion, as he did, because you do not have the circumstance that he had. He had only one commandment: not to eat from the tree. He did not yet know what the devil’s suggestion was, nor did he know how greatly sin displeases God. But you, as you say, know it, and believe it well, and yet commit so many thousands of sins.

And what shall I conclude? Such Christians “love him with their mouth, and with their tongue they lie to him. But their heart is not steadfast with him, nor are they faithful to his covenant.” If anyone loves Christ, if anyone is a true Christian—and especially a priest or monk, in whom perfection shines as in a mirror—he must not only renounce all that he possesses, but also deny himself, so that he may be wholly dead to the world. For unless the grain of wheat that falls into the ground dies, it remains alone.

He who lives amid the affairs of the world is dead to God. A person who wishes to attain and retain perfection must be so dead to the world that, like a dead man, he feels nothing concerning secular affairs, so that he may say with the Apostle: “Our citizenship is in heaven.” And again: “I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me.”

Therefore, he who is truly righteous must not fear losing this life, which is death, so that he may be able to find the life that is Christ. Let him not fear those who kill the body, because they cannot kill the soul. Here let him endure tribulations that quickly pass away, so that he may possess joys that remain without end. This alone is the way by which one goes to the homeland of heaven. Certainly, if it were possible to go there by another path, God would be entirely a liar.

For I did not receive the words I speak to you from a human being, nor did I learn them through a human being, but through his Gospel. Therefore we must acquire the kingdom of God through many tribulations. He goes astray on the road who hastens to travel through riches and pleasures. It is a sign of manifest condemnation to attain one’s desires in this world and to be loved by the world. Those whom God loves, he often reproves and chastises.

## Chapter XXVI

If one must glory in the world, glory willingly in your tribulations and adversities. For Christ promised these things to his disciples, whom he loved to the end, as a sign of his special love, when at the Last Supper he said: “Amen, I say to you: you will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice.”

Rejoice, my most beloved sons, when the world hates you. Desire to suffer insults and reproaches from human beings, because “you will be blessed when people curse you, persecute you, and speak every evil against you falsely for the sake of the Son of Man. Rejoice then and exult, for your reward is abundant in heaven.”

Would that this entire world rose up against you! Know that you are not of the world, because if you were of the world, the world would love what was its own. Consider all your joy to consist in having many reproaches and adversities in this age, knowing that strength and patience arise from them. Patience, however, accomplishes a perfect work.

Virtues are tested in a human being through patience, just as gold is tested by fire. Whoever possesses the other virtues without patience carries gold in vessels of clay. “By your patience,” the Savior said, “you will possess your souls.” Strength is joined to patience. A patient man is strong in spirit. Whoever is patient and strong can confidently hope for the good things of the life to come.

Keep patience in your hearts, and while there is time, exercise it in action. Patience is a sail by which our ship, amid the storms of this world, sails safely wherever the wind blows, fearing no danger. Let none of you be stirred to vengeance or hatred of your neighbor by insulting words.

## Chapter XXVII

Be merciful, just as your merciful Father is merciful, who sends rain upon the just and the unjust and makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil. “Judgment without mercy will be shown to the one who has not acted mercifully.” Mercy triumphs over judgment.

If you do not forgive from your heart those who offend you, neither will your Father forgive you. In vain does he ask for mercy who denies mercy to others. “You endure it,” says the Apostle, “if someone enslaves you, if someone strikes you in the face.” Here your virtue is established: this is the whole reward and recompense—that we love our friends in God and our enemies for God’s sake.

That wicked servant, after receiving mercy, denied mercy to his fellow servant, and therefore deserved to encounter the severity of justice. Justice without mercy is cruelty; therefore mercy must be mingled with justice. Our entire law consists in mercy. Because of sin, God could also have condemned us by justice, whom he saved by his mercy.

Therefore, whoever lacks mercy is not a Christian. It is impossible to be merciful and pious without appeasing divine anger. “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.”

[Col. 0257] A priest or monk without mercy is like a ship in the middle of the sea, pierced through on every side. Religion that lacks mercy is vain. It profits little to be distinguished from secular people in clothing while being like them in life. A person is not a priest or monk merely by clothing and rank, but by life.

Alas, what shall I say? Often, out of great abundance of sorrow, a person says many things. Behold, the world everywhere serves monks and priests; and yet priests and monks are already exceedingly rare, so that scarcely one in a hundred is found to be good.

Certainly there is no beast in the world so cruel as a bad priest or monk. He cannot bear correction, nor can he ever hear the truth; and, to put it briefly, he surpasses all others in wickedness. Such priests and monks are so only in habit and name, and their religion is vain.

“Pure and undefiled religion before God the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their tribulation and to keep oneself unstained from this age.”

Alas, how greatly greed has grown in certain spiritual persons in habit and name—or, to speak more truly, how avarice is the cause of this supposed spirituality. Such men are certainly ravenous wolves in sheep’s clothing. Wherever a priest or monk is greedy and without mercy, flee from him more than from a serpent.

## Chapter XXVIII

There are also some who consider their entire profit to consist in building churches and monasteries in marvelous fashion and workmanship from the earnings of the poor. In them greed is so powerful that they think the earth and everything else insufficient for themselves. Their heart, their mind, and their constant thought are fixed on how they may strip the purses of others.

The Savior rebuked such men, saying: “Woe to you who build the tombs of the prophets.” Behold, those who build monasteries and furnish churches with marvelous craftsmanship seem to be doing a good work. But if they show mercy to the poor, it is good. Do you want your work to please God? Make the poor rejoice because of it.

What temple is dearer to God than a human being? “You are the temple of God,” says the Apostle. When you extend your hand to a poor person, when you help someone in his needs, when you bring an erring person back to the right path—O what an admirable and pleasing temple to God you have built!

“Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the poor and homeless into your house.” Let no one excuse himself by saying: “I have nothing to give to my poor brother.” If you possess clothing or anything beyond your most basic need and do not help a poor person in need, you are a thief and a robber.

We, my most beloved sons, are merely stewards of temporal goods, not possessors. If we possess something superfluous while a brother is in need of it, we are stealing—indeed, worse than one who steals something out of poverty and necessity. This person retains beyond his need that by which a hundred people who are perishing from hunger could live. The other commits theft against one person; this person against as many as he does not relieve in their need.

Perhaps you will say, miserable man: “It is mine; my parents left it to me.” How could they leave you what was not theirs? “But if it was theirs,” you will say. Where did they get it? Who gave it to them? What did they bring with them when they came into the world? What will they carry away when they depart?

Certainly the things belonging to the poor that we possess will cry out for vengeance on the day of judgment before the eyes of divine justice. Let him who has ears to hear, hear. Whoever does not wish to believe me—alas, how severely he will feel it when his riches have passed into poverty!

## Chapter XXIX

The natural law commands this: that what we desire from others, we should do to others. What else does the old law proclaim? And if one examines the teaching of the Gospel in every direction, what else does it suggest? Truly, these things will be witnesses before God the Judge.

What, then, shall I say about those who merely gather stones and raise walls high, whose heart and thought are fixed on making their work appear impressive to human eyes? The building is praised, and do they consider their entire righteousness to consist in this?

There are also some who offer God gifts and sacrifices taken from robbery and from the sweat of the poor. Such offerings are by no means acceptable before divine mercy; rather, they are abominable. Who is so foolish as not to understand that such buildings contribute not to the glory of God but to the pomp of the world?

But if someone should say: “What are you saying? Is it not good to build monasteries from which God may be honored?” I reply: It is good, provided that the poor have not suffered violence and do not cry out to God against those responsible.

How can I build a house pleasing to God or to his saints from money over which the poor weep? What sort of justice can it be to honor the dead while stripping the living, and to offer to God what has been taken from the poverty of the poor? Certainly, if such justice pleased God, he would be an accomplice to violence. And if he wanted such an offering from us, he would become an accomplice in sin. But if it displeases God, it cannot please the saints.

Therefore, my beloved sons, putting aside all malice, all deceit, hypocrisy, envy, and every form of slander, desire the rational, guileless milk, like newborn infants, so that by it you may grow toward salvation—if indeed you have tasted that the Lord is sweet.

## Chapter XXX

Truly, unless you become like little children, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven. A little child, seeing a beautiful woman, does not take pleasure in her. Looking at an expensive garment, he does not desire it. He does not persist in anger; when injured, he does not remember it or hate. He follows his father and does not leave his mother.

Therefore, let no one imagine that he can attain the kingdom of heaven unless he strives to imitate this innocence and simplicity of a child—that is, to possess chastity, despise the world, love his brother, maintain patience, follow Christ the Father, and always rest in the lap of Mother Church.

And put off the old person, my beloved, and put on the armor of God, so that you may be able to stand against the snares of the devil. The devil possesses nothing in the world. Therefore, stripped of worldly things, which are momentary and quickly pass away like shadows, fight against the world.

He who wrestles with the devil while weighed down by garments is more quickly thrown to the ground, because he gives the devil something by which to seize him. Do you wish to fight firmly with the devil? Throw off your garments, lest you succumb. All earthly things are like garments of the body. Whoever possesses nothing will conquer more quickly.

Let chastity, patience, humility, and charity be your weapons as you go into battle. These are the weapons against the devil’s cunning. If you are armed with them, you will gird your loins with strength and strengthen your arm. Strength and dignity will be your clothing, and when you are in battle, you will laugh. You will not fear the cold of snow, and your house will truly be founded upon the firm rock, which is Christ.

## Chapter XXXI

The devil’s sword is lust. Alas, how many people that blade kills! There is no sin by which the devil so often proves victorious. Flee lust. For just as virginity makes a human being equal to the angels—or rather, makes him more than an angel—so lust makes a human being more like a beast, and, so to speak, makes him far worse than a beast.

Of no other sin is it written that God said he regretted having made the human being. Lust produces these effects: it weakens the body and almost continually destroys it along with life; it blackens one’s reputation; empties one’s purse; encourages theft; causes murder; dulls the memory; takes away the heart; blinds the eyes of both persons; and, beyond other sins, provokes God’s anger.

It arises from the root of gluttony. For no other offense did God exercise such manifest justice without mercy as for this one. Because of this sin, Scripture says that God brought the flood upon the world, burned Sodom and Gomorrah, and killed many other people.

This is the devil’s net: whoever is caught in it is not quickly released. Yet in this severe battle no one can conquer unless he flees, and no one can endure firmly unless he subdues the flesh. Whoever uses wine carries fire in his bosom. “Do not,” says the Apostle, “become drunk with wine, in which there is lust.” This battle cannot be endured except through abstinence and fasting.

Wine does harm, but the appearance of women does a hundred times more. A woman is the devil’s arrow, by which a man is quickly drawn into lust. Let no one living place confidence in himself here. If you are holy, you are nevertheless not secure. A woman steals the precious soul of a man.

“Can a man hide fire in his bosom and his garments not be burned? Or can he walk upon burning coals and his feet not be scorched?” Man and woman are fire and straw. The devil never ceases to blow upon them so that they may be kindled. No one will ever become victor in this battle except by fleeing.

Let there never be prolonged conversations between a man and a woman. Let necessity alone cause them to speak together. Let a man reject every gift and flattering word from a woman if he does not wish to be caught in the snares of lust. There should be such little familiarity between man and woman that neither knows the other’s name.

Many very holy people have already fallen through this vice because of excessive confidence. Fear, my sons, if there is reason to fear in other sins; in this one, fear much more. But I will say it plainly: today, under the name of spirituality, many are creating a new kind of fornication.

Alas, what shall I say? Today people are not ashamed; indeed, they boast when they have done evil. Some modesty exists among women, though little; but among men this wickedness has grown so great that the person is considered foolish who is not skilled in such things.

What more can I say? This is their festival; this is their whole preaching. For this reason they frequent churches: to see women and converse with them, so that the appetite for lust may thereby increase further.

But why, miserable man, do you glory in this wickedness? Perhaps because you are powerful in iniquity? You sin a hundred times more than the woman. The woman is weak, while you consider yourself strong. She sits at home, while you, wandering about, ensnare her in a thousand ways and sometimes compel her to act by force.

When you do these things, because God is silent, you imagine that he is like you. But the time will come when he will rebuke you and set your deeds before your face.

Therefore, sons, be prudent as serpents and innocent as doves, and fight manfully with the ancient serpent. Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning in your hands. Then act courageously, and let your heart be strengthened, because those who used to wage war against you will be afraid; you will act valiantly in God, and he himself will bring to nothing those who afflict you.

## Chapter XXXII

My beloved, love one another. For I did not receive this from a human being, but from the Savior. “This is my commandment,” he says, “that you love one another.”

In love alone the good of all virtues consists. Just as many branches grow from one root, so all virtues are born from charity. “If I spoke,” says the Apostle, “with the tongues of human beings and of angels, if I possessed all prophecy and knew all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I had all faith so as to move mountains, but did not have charity, I am nothing.”

Whoever possesses true charity is kind and patient. He possesses true charity who loves not only his neighbors through the affection of kinship and flesh, as the Gentiles and tax collectors do, but loves an enemy as a friend. By this one thing a person can know whether he remains in charity: whether he is loved by the one who opposes him.

This must certainly be considered with the greatest care. There are very many who love, but wrongly. They love someone so greatly that they lose the love of God. Those who love anything above God are not worthy of God.

Temperance is required in all virtues. Virtue always seeks the mean. To love too much is evil; to love too little is evil; but to love as justice requires is good. Every love that causes harm must be avoided.

Because of excessive love some have fallen into lust; because of insufficient love some have fallen into envy; many have abandoned prayers and service to God. Excessive love does this: it makes a person always want to see the one whom he loves.

Such love is excessive and foolish. It is ignorant of justice and truth, lacks reason, knows no measure, and can think of nothing except the object of its love. This love finds no consolation in impossibility and no remedy in difficulty. It is impossible for a person who has such love to offer prayers acceptable to God or to please him. This love is not charity but foolishness.

We ought to love all our brothers as ourselves, yet in such a way that vices are not loved. To punish evil is charity; to love the better person more is just. People must be loved in such a way that goodness is exalted and vice disgraced.

True charity requires us to love God with all our heart, with all our mind, and with all our strength, and to love nothing else together with God in the same way; and to love our neighbor as ourselves. On these two commandments hang the whole Law and the Prophets.

Whatever is without charity is without God, because God is charity and charity is God. Whoever remains in charity has already begun to dwell in heaven. Charity was born in heaven among all the blessed.

[Col. 0261] Where true charity exists, there is no envy, no ambition, no murmuring, no slander, and no mockery; rather, there is one and the same will among all. Know this, brothers: if you do not possess perfect charity, you are under the devil’s power, and God no longer dwells with you. Whoever is without God is in hell.

## Chapter XXXIII

Therefore, my most beloved sons, I exhort you, while you have time, not to receive the grace of God in vain. The grace of God has been given to all through the death of his Son. While we live during this very brief time, let us sow what we shall afterward reap in its proper season.

The days of a human being are short. Your life is cut short like thread from a weaver’s loom; death comes like a thief. When a person dies, the glory of his house does not descend with him. The rich, even in the smallest possessions, spend their days, and in an instant descend to hell. Everyone’s works follow him.

It is exceedingly rare that the death of a person whose life was always evil is good. Whether evil or good, whatever we do during this time, we shall find the same thing after death’s end. Do not wait, for this is the acceptable time. While you have the light, do not walk in darkness. Whoever walks in darkness does not know where he is going.

Your light is Christ, who shines in the darkness and enlightens every person coming into this world. Therefore, so that you may be children of light and darkness may not seize you, draw near to the living stone, rejected indeed by human beings but chosen and glorified by God. And you yourselves, like living stones, will be built upon it.

In everything present yourselves as ministers of God: in great patience, in tribulations, in necessities, in distress, in beatings, in prisons, in disturbances, in labors, in vigils, in fastings, in chastity, in knowledge, in forbearance, in gentleness, in the Holy Spirit, in genuine love, in the word of truth, and in the power of God.

Let there be no lie among you. Every liar is hateful to God. For God is truth, and falsehood opposes truth. Flee every idle word, for we shall give an account to God for every idle and empty word. Love silence. Where there is much speaking, there is often falsehood; where there is falsehood, there is sin.

Speech reveals what kind of person someone is. Let there never be a word in the mouth of a priest or monk in which the name of Christ does not resound; let him always meditate upon the divine law.

For he who meditates on the law of the Lord day and night, who does not walk in the assembly of the wicked or stand in the path of sinners, will be like a tree planted beside channels of water. Its leaves will not fall, but it will yield its fruit in its season, and everything he does will prosper.

Certainly nothing harms a person so much as bad companionship. A person becomes like those whose companionship he enjoys. A wolf never dwells with a lamb. A chaste man certainly flees the company of the lustful.

I consider it more than impossible for a man to remain long in good works if he keeps constant company with the wicked. With the Psalmist he cries: “With the holy man you will be holy; with the innocent man you will be innocent; with the chosen man you will be chosen; and with the perverse man you will become perverse.”

For just as bad companionship harms, so good companionship benefits. Nothing can be compared with this treasure. Whoever finds good companionship finds life and abounds in riches. Truly, I say: a person very rarely becomes either good or bad except because of companionship.
