A child’s heart is said to be like a tablet on which nothing has been painted. Whatever it receives from companionship, it retains into old age, whether good or evil. A young person rarely dwells with another young person. For when fire is brought near fire, it does not extinguish the heat but nourishes it.

A man who delights in wisdom should always make himself the companion of someone older in age and wisdom. Otherwise, if he associates with someone like himself, through constant companionship he will slide from foolishness into foolishness.

## Chapter XXXIV

Above all, my sons, do not swear at all—not by heaven, nor by earth, nor by anything else under oath. Let your speech be “Yes, yes,” and “No, no.” When an oath frequently resounds in someone’s mouth, there is little knowledge and love of God in that person.

If what I swear is not true, I deny God. For God’s commandment forbids it, saying: “You shall not take the name of God in vain.”

Persist in continual prayers. Frequent and devout prayer has great power. Prayer lifts a person from the earth, carries him to heavenly things, and enables him to speak with God. It obtains graces from him, provided that it is devout and mingled with tears.

Frequent prayer sprinkled with tears has great power in winning divine mercy and obtaining the benefit of being heard. Hezekiah immediately obtained grace from the Lord through his tears and prayers, so that God changed the sentence he had pronounced against him. The Lord delivered Susanna from a judgment of cruel death because of prayer and tears. Through Elijah’s prayers, heaven gave rain after it had been closed for three years and six months.

If you lack anything, ask the Lord for it in prayers and tears, doubting nothing in faith. For whoever has faith like a grain of mustard seed will immediately receive whatever he asks. The same Lord is rich in all things, he who was then and is now.

Let God always be your hope, your joy, your thought, and your every desire. For from him, in him, and through him are all things; in him we live, through him we move, and without him we are absolutely nothing.

## Chapter XXXV

Now, my sons, I will not speak much with you, for the hour has come for which I was born. I came here under this condition: that I should depart. I would never have been born if I had not been destined to die.

The Lord did not spare his own Son, but made him die for us all upon the wood of the cross; through his death, our death was put to death. None of us lives for himself or dies for himself. Whether we live, we live for the Lord; whether we die, we die for the Lord. Therefore, whether we live or die, we belong to the Lord.

For this reason Christ is called Lord of the living and of the dead. If Christ died—for certainly the servant is not greater than his master—then we too shall die. But if he rose, we have the firmest hope that we too shall rise.

And if Christ rose in such a way that he would die no more, then certainly after our resurrection we too shall never die, but shall stand forever with him in glory. [Col. 0263] For when Christ died, our old self died together with him, so that the body of sin might be destroyed and we might become one body with him.

Therefore, if Christ rose, we too shall rise with him, because we are his members. And if Christ will die no more, neither shall we.

Accordingly, my most beloved sons, if I am now dying, I believe that my Redeemer lives, and that on the last day I shall rise from the earth. Again I shall be clothed with this skin, and in this very flesh of mine I shall see that Savior himself—the one whom I myself, who now speak, shall see; the one whom you now see dying here, and certainly not another in my place. These very eyes of mine, with which I see you, shall behold him.

Therefore, my most beloved sons, see how carefully you walk—not as foolish people but as wise. Do not walk according to the flesh, because if you walk according to the flesh, you will die. But walking by the Spirit and putting to death the deeds of the flesh, rejoice with me now, sing, and chant psalms.

Cast off the garments of mourning and sorrow. Scatter the ashes from your head. Rejoice in God; sing a psalm to his name; give glory to his praise, because until now I have passed through fire and water, and behold, now he is bringing me into refreshment.

“I will enter the house of the Lord, and day by day I will fulfill my vows.”

## Chapter XXXVI

O what a gain it is for me to die, since henceforth to live will be Christ. Behold, the earthly house of this dwelling is dissolved, so that another may succeed it: an eternal dwelling in heaven, not made by human hands.

Behold, I am stripping off the garment of mortality so that I may put on the eternal one. Until now I have been a pilgrim; now I return to my homeland. Behold, I receive the prize for which I ran in the contest. Behold, I reach the harbor for which I longed with such great desire.

Behold, I am carried from darkness into light, from dangers into safety, from poverty into riches, from battle into victory, from sadness into joy, from temporal life into everlasting life, from stench into the sweetest fragrance.

Here I am blind, and I am given sight; wounded everywhere, and I am healed. Here I have always been sorrowful, and behold, now I am made joyful. Truly, while living here I was dead, and now I am truly made alive.

The life of the world is not life but death: a deceptive life, a life burdened with sorrows, weak and shadow-like, a lying life. Now you flower, and immediately you wither; a life depriving of life the one in whom you dwell; a fragile, momentary, and falling life. The more you grow, the more you decline. The farther you advance, the nearer you come to death.

O life full of snares, how many people in the world you ensnare; how many through you now endure infernal torments! How blessed is the person who recognizes your deceptions; how much more blessed the one who does not care for your empty flatteries; how supremely blessed the one who has rightly been deprived of you!

The commerce of death is better than silver and gold; its first fruits are purest. O sweet and delightful death! Certainly you are no death, for you bestow true life; you drive away fevers and wounds, extinguish hunger and thirst.

O death most just and kind to the good, harsh to the wicked! You humble the proud, the rich, and the powerful, and exalt the humble. Through you the poor are satisfied when you cast down the greedy. You give punishment to the wicked and eternal reward to the just.

Come, my sister, my bride, my friend, my beloved; tell me whom my soul loves. Show me where my Lord pastures his flock, where my Christ lies down. Do not leave me wandering any longer through the pathless places of my exile.

Arise, my glory. Extend your hand to me; draw me after you. My heart is open, so that I may arise and run after you in the fragrance of your ointments, until you bring me into the chambers of the house of my Lord, so that I may exult and rejoice when I appear before his face.

Then I shall sing and chant a psalm to the Lord. Behold, you are beautiful, my friend; do not delay any longer. Behold, all my days have failed, and my years have passed like a shadow.

Turn toward me for a little while, because I rejoiced to find you and delighted in you throughout all the days of my life. Receive me, for when you received my Lord, you saved me and gave me life.

Now look upon me, save me, and deliver me from many waters and from the hand of foreign sons. Bring my soul out of prison and lead it back through the grace that you accomplished by receiving my Lord—from the place of which I was exiled through the guilt committed by my ancestor Adam.

Through you I shall come into the garden of my beloved, so that I may eat the fruit of his trees.

### CHAPTER XXXVII

“My days have passed away like smoke, and my flesh has already withered like grass. Behold, now the time has come for you to pity me; do not delay, hasten to rescue me, for I languish with love. Through you, O good death, we receive the fruit of the good things we do; we come to know the rewards for which we hope. Before you come, we know God in part; when you come, we shall see him perfectly as he is.

“You are black, but beautiful; you are fair and comely, with honeycomb dripping from your lips. You are terrifying—and who can resist you? You are indeed terrifying to the kings of the earth: you take away the breath of princes, you make your power known to the humble, you break the horns of sinners, and you exalt the horns of the righteous. Your flashes have illuminated the world; the earth saw them and was shaken.

“Open for me, sweet sister and my friend, the gates of life which you promised to open for me when you were with my Lord, so that my place may now be in peace and my dwelling in Zion. Strip from me this mortal garment which I wear, so that I may clothe myself in garments of joy. My soul has melted, so that I may find my beloved, whom I sought in the world and did not find. The watchmen who go about the city found me in this wilderness; they struck me and wounded me, and the watchmen of the walls took away my cloak.

“I have been struck and humbled by the voice of evils and sorrows. All day long my enemies reproached me: speaking against me with a deceitful tongue, surrounding me with words of hatred, and attacking me without cause; they repaid me evil for good and hatred for my love.

“Therefore now, O good death, hasten; break the bow, the horn, the shield, the sword, and the warfare. If you delay, my spirit will soon fail because of the multitude of my sorrows; now let your consolations gladden my soul. Today, when you hear my voice, do not harden your heart. When shall I come and appear before the face of God, that I may dwell in his house for length of days?

“[Col. 0265] In the misery of this life, my tears have been my bread by day and by night: labors, insults, afflictions, hardships, hunger, thirst, fasts, vigils, temptations, and pestilences. Hear the groans of the bound; loose my bonds. Receive here this son, hungry in a foreign land, and return him to his father; receive him full of sores and place him in the bosom of Abraham the Patriarch.

“Make me enter the vineyard of the Lord of hosts, so that I may not stand here idle. Receive me from the hand of iniquity and lead me into eternal life. Bring me out of darkness and the shadow of death. Break the bonds, release the fettered, give light to the blind, raise up the fallen, protect the stranger and the orphan. To him who sits in darkness and dwells in the land of the shadow of death, show your light; enlighten me now, so that I may never again fall asleep in death.”

### CHAPTER XXXVIII

As the most holy man continued with these and similar words, the grief and sorrow of all who stood by increased. None of us could restrain himself from tears, but there was one voice among all who mourned: “What shall we do without you, father? Where shall we go? You brought this vineyard out of Egypt and planted it; why do you turn your face away from it? We walked in the light of your countenance; you were the glory of our strength. Alas, what shall we do without you any longer?

“You are father, teacher, and refuge; you are the model of innocence. Would that we might be permitted to die with you! We shall now come to nothing; we shall be like sheep without a shepherd. We shall come to nothing like running water; there will be no one to comfort us. Your children will become orphans and will suffer hunger like dogs; wandering everywhere, they will not find you. Alas, how great a fire has fallen upon us!

“We shall no longer see you, our sun. What will the congregation of the faithful do without you? You were the disperser of the heretics, their slaughterer by the sword of your mouth; you were their hammer and axe, crushing their teeth in their mouths, breaking the grinders of lions, and leading them into the pit of destruction. Now they will rejoice and exult; they will humble your people and harass your inheritance. They will lie in wait for the life of the righteous and condemn innocent blood. They will set fire to the sanctuary of God and tear apart the truth of the faith.”

### CHAPTER XXXIX

Then, moved by these words, he wept a little, for he was always overflowing with the inward mercies of the Lord. Turning to them, he answered them as they wept:

“Come now, good soldiers of Christ; trust in the Lord and in the might of his strength. Do not be afraid; you will obtain mercy from the Lord if you hope in him. For he is kind and merciful, and abandons no one who hopes in him. Who has trusted in the Lord and been forsaken? But if I now abandon you, will not the Lord receive you? He himself will establish his law for you in his way; he will direct you onto the straight path and will not hand you over to the souls of those who persecute you.

“Act bravely, therefore; let your heart be strengthened, and wait for the Lord. For there is a merciful and compassionate God in heaven, who knows how to help his servants in a thousand ways. Let your heart not be troubled or afraid. Hope in the Lord and pour out your hearts before him, for he will be your helper.

“[Col. 0266] For if I depart now, you will see me again, and we shall rejoice together. For not many days after I go, you also will be able to come; and where I shall be, there you will be also, in a joy which no one will take from you.

“Remember, dearest sons, how after the death of Moses God chose Joshua as leader and protector of his people; and when he raised Elijah into heaven in a whirlwind and a fiery chariot, he made Elisha a prophet among the people, and the spirit of Elijah rested upon him doubly. Has the hand of the Lord now been weakened? Has God forgotten to show mercy, or will he restrain his mercy in anger? The Lord will be the portion of your inheritance and your cup, and he himself will restore your inheritance to you.”

### CHAPTER XL

“For he will raise up from among you another shepherd, to whom he will give the word of evangelizing; and he will enter without blemish and practice righteousness. And I ask my God, who led me out and brought me back according to his will, that if there was in me any spirit for obeying his commands, it may be doubled in this one whom he will send you as comforter and shepherd.

“Behold, you will have with you Eusebius, my most beloved son, and you will listen to him as to me. For he will be a father to you, and you will obey him as sons, in charity, with all humility and gentleness, and with all patience. If you have any need, refer it to him.

“I beg you to be diligent in preserving the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. Be one body and one spirit, just as you were called in the one hope of your calling. One is God and Father of all, Jesus Christ; may you desire to please him alone, living together in one brotherhood.

“Therefore be imitators of him, as beloved sons, and walk in love, just as he loved you and gave himself for you, to redeem you and make you acceptable to himself as followers of good works. May he give each of you grace according to the measure of his gift. May he give you abundantly of the dew of the Holy Spirit, so that you may have a heart for worshiping him. May he open your heart to his law and his commands, so that you may know him and do his will, and may he never abandon you.”

### CHAPTER XLI

“But you, my son Eusebius, arise; put on strength. Always be subject to the Lord, and do not envy him, so as to act wickedly. God will be your salvation forever, and your righteousness shall not fail. Be humbler than all. Lift your eyes to heaven; let the law of God always be in your heart.

“Do not fear the reproach of men, and do not dread their blasphemies. If you hope in the Lord, you will take strength; wings like an eagle’s will come to you, and you will fly and not grow weary. You will speak all the law of the Lord confidently to everyone.

“Do not fear the face of men, because the Lord is always with those with whom truth is. He descends with them into the pit and does not abandon them in their bonds, but protects them from deceivers and is their helper and protector in the time of tribulation.

“Certainly, one who sees himself acting well does not easily fear this death—or rather, to say more, he hates this life. Behold, I set you over this society, to uproot, destroy, scatter, and annihilate, to rebuild and to plant. [Col. 0267] For you must be blameless. One who corrects others cannot do so well if the one whom he corrects can say to him, ‘You do the same.’

“From now on your labor will be greater, but so will your reward. Be sober, prudent, chaste, hospitable, and a teacher. Do violence to no one, but love all equally—and the more so, the better you are. Do not be a persecutor, but moderate; neither quarrelsome nor greedy.

“But you, preach the word of God in season. Every Scripture inspired by God is useful for teaching. Acquire through prayers the words you are to preach. Such preaching and teaching is effective for enlightening and reproving, for correcting and instructing in righteousness, so that the hearer may be perfect and equipped for every good work.

“For Christ Jesus sits in heaven at the right hand of the power of God, revealing mysteries and teaching all knowledge. In all things, dearest son, present yourself as an example of good works, in all holiness and goodness. For when the head suffers, the whole body is weakened. Therefore, to teach you briefly: you will do all things well if you fear God.”

### CHAPTER XLII

“When you write to my most reverend father, Damasus, Bishop of Porto, remember me, so that he may have me in his prayers and not allow the works which I have woven with such great labor to be corrupted by wicked and deceitful men, by whom I have often been attacked from my youth.

“Let him prudently guard the Church, knowing that evil men will rise up, ensnaring the souls of the simple, whom I have tried to lead into the right way—men who speak with their mouths and have a sword upon their lips. For I have become mute and silent regarding good things, and have been cast into the tomb, sleeping.

“For I hope in the Lord, who is kind, and he will not abandon his faithful. I have great joy and consolation, relying upon the Lord’s mercy, because after me I leave the remarkable man Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, a man of great knowledge and goodness. Because of him I have great confidence in Christ Jesus that your faith will be sustained.

“When writing to him about me, ask him this very thing: that, like a faithful soldier, he fight so that evils may not come—God forbid—upon our people. Commend me to Senator Theodosius and to all the brothers in Christ.”

### CHAPTER XLIII

When these words had ended, the most holy man turned to the brothers and said in a joyful voice:

“Come here, so that I may touch you, my sons, before I depart from you.”

As they approached him, he embraced each one with his arms as best he could and gave each the kiss of peace. Then, raising his voice moderately, with a calm and joyful face, his hands extended toward heaven and his eyes turned toward the Lord, while tears of joy poured forth, he said:

“Merciful Jesus, my strength, my refreshment, my receiver and my liberator, my praise—you in whom I have hoped, whom I have believed in and loved; supreme sweetness, tower of strength, and my hope from my youth: call me, guide of my life, and I will answer you.

“To the work of your hands, which you, Creator of all, formed from the clay of the earth; which you joined together from bones and sinews; to which, when dying, you gave life and mercy—extend the right hand of your clemency.

“Command, Lord; [Col. 0268] do not delay, for it is time for dust to return to dust and for the spirit to return to you, the Savior who sent it here. Open to it the gates of life. For when you hung upon the wood of the cross like a thief in my place, you promised me that you would receive it.

“Come, my beloved; let me hold you, and I will not let you go. Bring me into your house. You are my receiver, my glory, and the one who lifts up my head; my salvation and my blessing. Receive me, merciful God, according to the multitude of your mercies. For when dying upon the cross, you received the thief running to you.

“May I possess you, eternal blessedness. Give light with the radiance of your eternal vision to the blind man crying beside the road, ‘Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me.’ O invisible light, deprived of which Tobias cried, ‘What joy is there for me, when I sit in darkness and do not see the light of heaven?’

“O light without which there is no truth, no discernment, no wisdom, and no goodness: enlighten my eyes, lest I ever sleep in death, lest my enemy should say, ‘I have prevailed against him.’

“My soul is weary of my life; I will speak in the bitterness of my soul. I am sick. My life has been weakened in poverty, and my bones have been roasted as in a frying pan. Therefore I run to you, Lord, as physician. Heal me, Lord, and I shall be healed; save me, and I shall be saved. And because I trust in you, I shall not be ashamed.

“But who am I, most merciful God, that I should speak so boldly to you? I am a sinner, born, begotten, and raised entirely in sins; a rotting corpse, a foul vessel, food for worms.”

### CHAPTER XLIV

“Alas for me, Lord; spare me. What victory would it be if, by fighting against me, you conquered me, who am less than straw before the face of the wind? Forgive all my sins and raise the poor man from the dung.

“Indeed, Lord, if it pleases you, I shall say this: you ought not to drive away me, who am running to you, for you are my God. Your flesh is from my flesh, and your bones from my bones. For this reason, without leaving the right hand of the Father, you clung to my humanity, becoming God and man, while remaining what you previously were in one and the same person.

“And why did you accomplish this so arduous and unexpected thing, unless so that I might run to you confidently as to a brother, and so that you might mercifully grant me your divinity? Therefore arise and help me, Lord; arise, and do not reject me forever.

“As the deer longs for springs of water, so my thirsty soul seeks you, the living fountain, that it may draw water with joy from the springs of the Savior and thirst no more. When shall it come and appear before your face? My Lord, when, looking upon me, will you restore my soul from their evildoings and from the lions my only one?

“Would that my sins, by which I deserved anger, and the calamity which I suffer, were weighed in a balance; this would appear heavier than the sand of the sea. Hence, if you wait longer, I shall find tribulation and sorrow.

“Come, joy of my spirit, that I may delight in you. Reveal your mercy to me, joy of my heart; let me find you, my desire. As a servant awaits the end of his work, so I await you. Let my petition enter into your presence, Lord, and let your hand be ready to save me.

“[Col. 0269] Behold, I am a man who, going down from Jericho, was seized by robbers and wounded; I have been left half-dead. You, merciful Samaritan, receive me.

“I have sinned greatly in my life and done evil before you. I did not know you; I was ungrateful for so many of your benefits; I did not praise you as I ought. Perhaps many times I kept silent about the truth. When you knocked at the door of my heart, I was sluggish in receiving you reverently.

“I loved this putrid body, which bends like a shadow, with excessive affection. I defiled my mouth with empty words. My mind was not always in the testament of your law. I did not turn my eyes away so that I might not at some time see vanity. At times I defiled my ears with useless words. Many times I did not extend my hands to the need of my neighbor. I ran with my feet toward iniquity.

“What more shall I say? From the sole of my foot to the crown of my head there is no health in me. Indeed, unless you had helped me by dying upon the wood of the cross, my soul deserved to dwell in hell.

“I, merciful Jesus, am part of so great a price; for me you poured out your precious blood. Do not reject me. I am the sheep that has wandered; seek it, good shepherd, and place it in your fold, so that you may be justified in your words. For you promised me that whenever a sinner groans, he will be saved.

“I have become sorrowful; I acknowledge my iniquities, and my offenses are before me. Truly I am not worthy to be called your son, because I have sinned against heaven and before you. You will give joy and gladness to my hearing. Turn your face away from my sins. Blot out my iniquities according to your great mercy. Do not cast me away from your face. Do not deal with me according to my sins, nor repay me according to my iniquities.

“But help me, God my Savior, and for the honor of your name deliver me. Deal kindly with me according to your good will, so that I may dwell in your house all the days of my life, and praise you forever and ever with those who dwell there.

“Rise, hasten, most beloved bridegroom of my soul, and do not consider that she is dark and black with sins. Show her your face. Let your voice sound in her ears—your voice, sweet, and your face, beautiful. Do not turn her away from me, and do not withdraw at this hour from your servant.

“Do not hand me over to the souls of those who persecute me. I await you, Lord. I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living. Come, therefore, my beloved; let us go out into the field; let us see whether the vineyard has blossomed. Turn my mourning into joy for me. Incline your ear to me; hasten to rescue me from this valley of tears and miseries.”

### CHAPTER XLV

When the most holy man had spoken these words amid uninterrupted tears, with his hands raised toward heaven, he was silent for a little while. Then he looked at the brothers and said:

“I command you, my dearest sons, by the power and name of the Lord Jesus, that when my body has been dissolved, you bury it naked in the earth beside the manger of our Lord, so that, returning, it may carry with it what it brought when it came. Naked I came forth from there; naked I shall return there. Let earth be joined to earth; earth may not be joined to stones. For naturally everything desires its like.

“Again I ask you to bring [Col. 0270] the body of my Lord, so that in his light I may see light, and, fixing his eyes upon me, he may give me understanding and instruct me in the way in which I walk.”

Then a certain brother approached and offered the most sacred body of Jesus Christ. When the man of the Lord was able to see it, with our assistance he prostrated himself face downward upon the ground and cried out as loudly as he could, in voice and tears:

“Lord, who am I, that I should be worthy for you to enter under my roof? Has a sinful man deserved this? Indeed, Lord, I am not worthy. Am I better than all my fathers? You did not wish to show yourself to Moses with a single glance of the eye. Why do you now humble yourself so greatly as to endure descending to a publican and a sinner? And not only do you wish to eat with him, but you command that you yourself be eaten by him.”

### CHAPTER XLVI

When the priest was near him, the glorious man rose, kneeling, while all supported him. With great tears and sighs, striking his breast repeatedly, he said:

“You are my God and my Lord, who suffered for me—or perhaps another? Indeed, you are the one who, although you were God alone before all ages and were begotten without beginning by God the Father in an eternal and unsearchable generation, and although with the Father and the Holy Spirit you are one God, remaining the same as you were and are, enclosed yourself within the little body of a single girl, becoming man as I am.

“Truly you are both God and man. For you assumed humanity in the virginal womb in such a way that you are neither God without man nor man without God—although humanity is not divinity, nor divinity humanity. The natures are not confused, although there is one and the same person in you.

“Are you not flesh and my brother? Truly you are. You were hungry, thirsty, and wept; you had my weaknesses as I do. Yet in you there was no weakness or defect of sin as in me, for you could not sin as I can.

“In you, bodily, there was and is the whole fullness of grace; for grace was not given to you by measure. For your soul, as soon as it was inseparably united to divinity, immediately knew and could perfectly do all that divinity itself knows and can do.

“As regards the divine nature which is in you, you are equal to God the eternal Father. But because of the humanity which you assumed for our redemption, you are lesser; yet you incur no reproach on that account.

“You are indeed the one over whom, when John baptized you in the stream of the Jordan, the paternal voice suddenly thundered from heaven, saying: ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him.’ And the Holy Spirit, descending upon you in the form of a dove, declared that you are one with the Father and of the same substance with him.

“You, good Jesus, endured for me the great punishment of the cross in this very body which I now see present, so that you might destroy the death which I had incurred by my crimes; recover the souls of the ancients, whom the devil’s power had long held in misery in infernal dwellings; and restore the whole human nature, which had fallen into perpetual death, to unending life, reconciling the Father with it by your precious blood, which you poured out for it.

“Rising on the third day, you firmly confirmed the certainty of that life from the abyss in which you had lain dead. [Col. 0271] By this our faith was made firm and our hope increased, so that, just as you rose incorruptible, impassible, and immortal, so likewise we may rise.

“You, good and merciful Lord, after your wondrous and singular resurrection, when forty days had been completed—during which the clear evidence of many signs declared that you had risen alive from the dead, and so that no shadow of doubt might arise—you ascended into heaven by your own power while all the disciples looked on. Opening the gates of paradise for me, you sat at the right hand of God the almighty Father, where you sit without end.”

### CHAPTER XLVII

“Moreover, good Jesus, appointed by God as judge of the living and the dead, just as you ascended on that day, so you will descend on the awesome and terrible day of universal judgment, to repay each according to the works they have done.

“Then kings will certainly fall before you; all dominion will be prostrate. Then all who now despise you will fear you. What will the wretched say to you then, who now glory when they have done evil—those who will see you as knowing all things, when no remedy of mercy will remain for them?

“What will the miserable do in the presence of the mighty one who sees all things and judges only what is just—those who have squandered all their time in the vanities and crimes of the world, pursuing deceptive riches rather than you; loving sons and daughters and the fleeting glory of the world rather than you?

“What will they do then when they see your face angry against them, when they await so severe a sentence, when their own conscience, the host of demons, and every creature whom they offended by offending you, God, accuse them even of the least thought?

“When they see that, as soon as the sentence has been proclaimed, they will obtain torments in which body and soul together will be tortured with the demons forever, expecting no refreshment from them in perpetuity?

“Woe, woe to the wretched who, drunk with the most worthless temporal goods in this very brief time—goods which not only do not remove poverty from their possessors but themselves create their need—are reduced through neglect to the condition of beasts.

“Woe, woe to those who, even under so great a fear, do not cease sinning and provoking your anger, if they will not do so for love of you, as they ought.

“But how, merciful Jesus, you whose magnificence is so great that no creature can express it; whom the heavens, the sea, and all that is contained within their compass cannot contain; who are wholly present everywhere, neither enclosed within nor excluded outside; who are likewise in heaven at the Father’s right hand, the blessedness and glory of all the citizens above who contemplate the appearance of your majesty; who are likewise on earth, containing and enclosing it in your fist; who are likewise in the sea and in the abysses, ruling and preserving all things at your command; who are likewise powerfully ruling in hell—how are you contained under such a smallness of bread, not partially but wholly, perfectly, and inseparably?”

### CHAPTER XLVIII

“O ineffable wonder, O novelty of all novelties! The eyes see whiteness in you; the taste senses flavor; the sense of smell, fragrance; and touch discovers subtlety. But hearing represents to the heart that in you [Col. 0272] these are not accidents.

“Here, certainly, accidents exist by themselves without a subject; for you are not bread, as you appear to human senses, but the whole Jesus Christ, just as you sit in heaven at the Father’s right hand, God and man.

“Hail, bread of life, who descended from heaven, giving life to those who worthily receive you—not like the manna which rained upon our fathers in the desert, of which all who ate died. Certainly, whoever worthily receives you, although the soul is separated from the body by bodily death, will not die forever; for that separation is not death but a passage from death to life.

“Therefore whoever worthily eats you in this world begins, at death, to live eternally with you. O how precious is that death, before which human beings were dead and after which they begin to live!

“You are the bread of angels; by your vision you refresh and glorify the angels. You are food for the soul, not the body; fattening the mind, not the belly. Whoever is not enriched by you in virtues lies exceedingly sick in vices.

“You transform the one who eats you, as is fitting, into yourself, so that through participation in you he may become God; yet you are not transformed into him, as other bodily food does. But woe to those who receive you unworthily. Indeed, to their own punishment and guilt they crucify you again—not because that eating judges you, since you are wholly impassible and immortal.”

### CHAPTER XLIX

“Alas, my Lord, what shall I say? Today priests eat you on the altar like the flesh of cattle and birds—or worse. At night they engage in the most shameful intercourse with women, and in the morning they chew and eat you. Where are you hiding, Lord? Are you asleep, or are you awake? Is this sacrifice acceptable to you? Is this the offering which you choose? Do you hear their prayers from heaven, from the seat of your majesty?

“Truly, Lord, if you desired this sacrifice and libation, you would become a liar and a partner in sins. Indeed, Lord, if what you spoke through the mouths of the prophets is true—if you are present only to righteous supplications, and if equity pleases you—such a sacrifice must be prevented from taking place, although in itself and by its nature the sacrifice is good and cannot be violated by wicked priests; for wickedness does not judge the sacrifice.

“Therefore such a sacrifice becomes a cause of prejudice and condemnation for the priest, nor does it benefit those for whom it is offered. Indeed, to speak most truthfully, whoever recognizes the priest’s life and has him celebrate for himself becomes a participant in his sin and also a sharer in his punishment.

[Note: [Col. 0272] This is abhorrent not only to Jerome, whose supremely Catholic judgment on this matter we have set out elsewhere and in the Dialogue against the Luciferians, but also to the Christian faith itself—unless someone considers it capable of a more lenient interpretation.]

“O great and inscrutable mystery! The accidents of bread are broken into parts, yet in every particle you remain whole and entire, Christ, just as you were before. O deception of human senses! Those things which appear in you to human senses as accidents are broken, yet you are neither broken nor corrupted. Your teeth appear to chew you as material bread, yet you are never chewed.

“O noble banquet, in which, under the appearance of bread and wine, the whole Christ, God and man, is received—whole in the appearance of bread and in each of its particles, and in the appearance of wine with every drop, just as in the combined appearance of the whole bread and [Col. 0273] wine.

“For the whole, perfect, and complete Christ is contained under the appearance of bread and under every particle, however small; and that same whole Christ remains under the appearance of wine and in every drop.

“O most sacred food, by truly eating which a person becomes God, according to the saying: ‘I have said, You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High.’ He is freed from evils, filled with good things, and made undoubtedly immortal.

“O sacred provision for our pilgrimage, by which one passes from this wicked age into fellowship with the heavenly Jerusalem. Our fathers in the desert ate manna but did not reach the promised land. Whoever eats you will walk in your strength as far as the mountain of God, Horeb.

“O most delicate food, in which there is the sweetness of every flavor and fragrance, every delight, every medicine, every support, and every rest from labor, as well as everything that can be desired.

“You are indeed the life by which every creature lives and without which it dies. You are living, sweet, lovable, and joyful life. The sweetness of your fragrance revives the sick and weak, whom your flavor makes healthy and very strong. You are that incomprehensible light which enlightens every person coming into this world.”

### CHAPTER L

“Yours, my Lord, is all power; yours is the whole kingdom. Every knee will bend before you. Whatever you will, you do in heaven, on earth, in the sea, and in the abysses. Nothing can resist your will.

“Come, therefore, faithful soul; rejoice and feast. Do not delay to be nourished by these delights; do not hesitate to enjoy this banquet, in which not the flesh of goats or bulls, as once under the law, but the body of your Savior is set forth to be received.

“O sign of unforeseeable love, that the giver should be the same as what is given, and the donor the same as the gift itself.

[Note: [Col. 0273] Read, with the old Lyons edition, *datum* (‘given’), not *datur* (‘is given’).]

“How great is your sweetness, Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you and perfected for those who hope in you! O most excellent dish, to be venerated, worshiped, adored, glorified, and embraced; to be exalted with every praise, raised up with every proclamation, firmly retained in the depths of the heart, and bound to the soul for all time.

“Man fell through the food of the forbidden tree into misery; through you he is raised to eternal glory. You certainly dwell in upright and instructed thoughts. You detest the most wretched, arrogant, and proud rich man; you send him away empty and vacant, hungry for you. The just, devout, and humble poor man you satisfy with every wealth, filling him with the abundance of your house.

“In you and through you are right judgment and equity; with you are prudence, strength, and every victory. Through you the saints reign in heaven. Through you teachers preach. Through you the righteous man fights bravely against enemies. You cast down the proud powerful man from his seat, exalting the humble.

“With you are all riches and glory. You love those who love you. Those who watch for you with a pure heart find you, because you walk with the simple and upright of heart.

“[Col. 0274] You alone existed before every beginning, the end and the beginning of all things. You alone were eternally begotten without time by God the Father.

“How blessed are those who love you, who desire nothing other than you, who think constantly about you, who worthily eat you, and who, remaining with you, keep all your ways at all times. Indeed, those who find you find life, for they also draw up unending life.

“O wondrous and astonishing food, delightful and joyful, safest and most desirable above all! In you so many signs have been renewed and wonders changed. In you every delight is possessed, and through you we advance toward the increase of every grace.

“How singular and unheard-of is your generosity! How superabundant and lavish your bounty, since you exclude no one from you unless he scorns to come to you.

“If anyone is little, let him come confidently to you; eating you, let him become great, and abandoning the paths of childhood, let him walk by the ways of prudence. If anyone is weak, let him turn to you, and immediately he will become strong. If anyone is sick, he will be healed. If anyone is dead, if he wishes to hear you, he will seize unending life.

“But let the one who is great and strong not abandon you either; for in you he will find more than enough by which to be nourished. Certainly no one can live even for a moment without you.”

### CHAPTER LI

“You alone give life to all creatures. Therefore my heart and my flesh have failed: God of my heart, and God my portion forever. In you alone my heart delights; in you my soul exults. My mind desires to cling to you alone, because those who distance themselves from you will perish.

“But you, Lord, do not take your help far from me; incline to me your merciful ear. Let the poor and needy eat you and be satisfied; then, living, the heart will praise you.

“O invisible, unquenchable light, truly enlightening all things, have mercy on me, this blind man sitting beside the road. Son of David, hear me crying out; grant me sight, I beg you, so that I may see you.

“Be favorable, I beg you, Lord, to this sinner, so that you may be my help and place of refuge, and save me. Then, even if I walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I shall fear no evil, because you are with me.

“Behold, I lie dead, merciful Jesus; arise and raise me from the dead, and I shall confess you. I am sick and infirm, and there is no longer any health in my flesh; you are the physician—heal me.

“I am naked and afflicted by cold; you are rich—clothe me. I am perishing from hunger in this wilderness; you are food—satisfy me. I thirst; you are a health-giving drink—inebriate me.

“I am stuck in deep mire, and there is no firm ground. I have come into the depths of the sea, and the storm has overwhelmed me. I have grown weary crying out; my throat has become hoarse. The waters have already entered even into my soul.

“Lead me out of this snare, my protector, my governor, my support, my refuge, my guide, my king, and my God. Into whose hands I commend my spirit, which you redeemed upon the wood of the cross and to which you gave life and mercy.

“Look upon my humiliation, Lord, and do not shut me up in the hands of the enemy. Today I shall enter with you into the place of the wondrous tabernacle, so that I may dwell in your house for length of days, forever and ever.”

## CHAPTER LII

When these things had been finished, the man of God, receiving the glorious sacred Body of the Lord, returned supine to the ground. [Col. 0275] Then, holding his hands in the form of a cross upon his breast, he chanted the prophecy of the Prophet Simeon. When it was finished, suddenly, before the eyes of all who were present, so great a divine light shone forth in the place where he lay that, like the rays of the sun, its brilliance struck the eyes of everyone, so that they could not in any way look upon the glorious dying man.

While this light remained for a time, those standing around saw an angelic host there, moving about in every direction, just as sparks customarily dart through a bed of reeds. Some, however, did not see the angels, but heard a voice descending from heaven saying:

“Come, my beloved; for it is time for you to receive the reward for the labors which, for my sake, you bravely endured.”

Others neither saw the angels nor heard this voice; but, together with the others, after that voice had ended, they heard these words from blessed Jerome:

“Behold, I come to you, merciful Jesus; receive the soul which you redeemed with your blood.”

Then suddenly that light disappeared, and that most holy soul, shining like a star with every virtue, freed from the mire of the flesh, entered gloriously into the realms of heaven. There it now certainly shines like a conspicuous luminary, both with the splendor of blessedness and with the flashing forth of many wonders. For a city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden.

Nor did God will that the holiness of him whose life had been the cause of holiness and of the salvation of the whole Church militant should remain concealed in his death. Finally, after that most holy soul had departed, such a fragrance continued for many days that perhaps no age, however old, will remember its like. Yet it was certainly fitting that his merits should be made manifest especially by the evidence of fragrance, since by the odor of his words he had summoned his foul members to the unity of undefiled faith.

For the hour, dearest Fathers and Lords, was the last hour of the glorious day of his passing. On that day, in order to display the glory of his athlete and to bring forth a clear light for all who dwell in the house of the Church, the Lord himself revealed the passing of the glorious Jerome to Bishop Cyril in the following manner.

## CHAPTER LIII

When that hour had already been announced, Bishop Cyril was devoted to prayers in his cell. Suddenly, carried upward in spirit and as if transported into ecstasy, he saw a marvelous and most beautiful road extending from the monastery from which the most holy man had departed all the way to heaven. Its beauty and magnificence were so great that—as we later learned from his own testimony—he was stupefied and, as though out of his mind, gazed about in wonder and for a little while believed that he had forgotten himself.

While he was thus placed in the anguish of his mind, he raised his eyes. And behold, a great company of angels was coming from the monastery, singing in alternation with melodious voices and honey-sweet songs. Heaven and earth, and everything contained within their compass, seemed to resound everywhere with their voices.

Each of the angels also carried in his hands a lighted candle, whose brightness drove back the light of the sun. But what greater wonder could be added to wonder? Turning his eyes toward heaven, Cyril saw no smaller number of angels, coming in a similar manner to meet the others. Anxiously awaiting the outcome of this event, he would indeed have asked what it meant; but astonishment had so overwhelmed him that he did not know what to say.

As he waited there for some time, he saw the glorious soul of Jerome, adorned with marvelous beauty and coming before all the angels who went ahead and followed. At its right hand was the Savior, coming together with it.

When the soul reached the place where Cyril lived, it set down its step and stood before him, speaking to him in this way:

“Do you recognize me?”

He replied:

“Not at all. Who are you, then, who surpass the others by so great an honor?”

But it said:

“Have you ever had any acquaintance with Jerome?”

He answered:

“Certainly. I love with singular affection of charity the one whom you name. But, I ask, are you he?”

And it said:

“I am his soul, and I now possess the glory which I had hoped for. Go to my sons and announce what you have seen, so that they may cease from mourning and rejoice with me in the state which I have chosen.”

When all these things had been completed, that entire blessed vision vanished from his eyes. Cyril immediately returned to himself, overflowing with ineffable joy; nevertheless, throughout that whole night he could not restrain his tears because of the joy in his mind.

## CHAPTER LIV

How marvelous, then, is the Lord in his saints: marvelous in majesty, performing wonders. “The right hand of the Lord has shown strength; the right hand of the Lord has exalted him,” making his power known among the peoples.

O immensity of divine love, abundance of divine generosity! What honor and grace could he have bestowed upon this son of his that he did not bestow, when his munificence toward him was so abundant both in life and in death?

For the Lord gave him eternal glory and made him inherit an eternal name; he made him heir of the joys above, in which he will remain forever. What singular honor and wondrous glory, surpassing almost the glory and honor of the other saints! For not only do all the heavenly hosts accompany that most holy soul, but the Savior himself does so.

Nor does that blessed soul alone shine in heaven with its distinguished dignity; even its body does not cease to radiate miracles on earth. It is fitting to return to the account of these.

When the most holy man had died, as has been said, at the hour of Compline, we kept watch around him throughout that sleepless night. His body was fragrant with such perfumes. We spent the night in great weeping because of the loss that had befallen everyone, and in joy because of the glory he had already obtained.

When morning came, after the divine mysteries had been performed, as was fitting, and the due services had been completed with proper honor, we buried that most sacred body, covered with a linen cloth over sackcloth, in the earth at Bethlehem, beside the manger in which Christ, for our sake, had been born there of the undefiled Virgin and had wailed as an infant, just as he had ordered.

How many glorious miracles the Lord performed through his holy son Jerome on that very day, and continues to perform even now, no tongue of flesh would certainly be sufficient to relate. Nevertheless, I shall report some of the many, so that our discourse may not be prolonged excessively.

## CHAPTER LV

A man blind from birth obtained the gift of sight on the very day of the burial by touching the holy body. A young man who was deaf and mute also kissed the most holy body; when the bonds of his ear and tongue had been loosed, he was granted the ability both to speak and to hear.

And it was certainly fitting that he who had illuminated with his most holy teachings and examples those blinded by the darkness of blindness to the true light, which is Christ, and who had exercised true healing for the deaf and mute in divine works—so that they might understand the teachings of God and confess the principles of the Catholic faith which they had spurned—should, on the day of his glorious death, grant bodily light to the blind and health to the deaf and mute.

Very many people, as those who saw them assert, had been overshadowed by wicked spirits. At the place where the holy body rests, while the demons cried out in dreadful voices, “Saint Jerome, why do you persecute us so severely? You were always our scourge, both while alive and now that you are dead,” they were wonderfully freed through him.

A certain heretic, while blaspheming the blessed Jerome mentioned above and saying that his body deserved to be burned, was changed into the form of a piece of wood by divine vengeance, as a terror to the other heretics. Suddenly, before the eyes of all who were present, fire from heaven seized him and burned him in such a way that he was completely turned into ashes.

At this, a great multitude of heretics, recognizing such an experience of his holiness and being called back to the truth of the sacred faith by so many and such clear signs—as though by heralds crying aloud—returned to the light of that most sacred and undefiled faith.

## CHAPTER LVI

What more shall I say? Certainly, from generation to generation, I could scarcely proclaim all that God wished to reveal through him, in order to magnify him and present him as worthy of veneration to everyone.

How great indeed is this man, performing so many wonders, one who certainly has no equal according to his works! Great marvels concerning him resound throughout the whole world. The fame of his glorious triumph leaps forth into every land, and his shining signs gleam to the farthest reaches of the earth. The undefiled faith is now strengthened by the multitude of so many miracles.

To relate that he granted the sick the complete and much-desired restoration of health would extend without limit. Time, life, and every human faculty would fail if one wished to investigate everything he has accomplished in our days—things that we have heard with our ears and that have not been hidden from the children of men.

Therefore let the entire assembly of the faithful rejoice, and let them loudly resound to God a song of joy and exultation, because from their midst has sprung a shining star whose rays of radiant light guide them toward entering the heavenly homeland.

His most sacred life is a rule for everyone. His conduct is the instruction of all the faithful. Today, let holy Mother Church offer pious tears for the departure of so great a son, and immeasurable joy for his great glory.

Let her therefore be permitted, like a pious mother, to offer him pious lamentations, since she sees herself deprived of so great a son, widowed of her husband, bereft of her champion and captain, and with her vine, which she planted and cultivated in the field of faith, cut off from its shoot.

Please do not charge me, a son deprived of so great a father, with saying things unbecoming because of grief at so immeasurable a loss. For often, from an excessive abundance of the heart, a person says more than he would wish.

What, alas, shall I now report to you, dearest Fathers and Lords? I look all around and go about, as though perhaps I might find my father Jerome, whom dreadful death has taken away; but I do not find the one whom my soul loves, for whose love I languish.

## CHAPTER LVII

“My soul is weary of my life,” because my life has been taken from me. I have been shaken like a locust, my strength has dried up, and the light of my eyes has been extinguished.

What joy can there be for me any longer in the world, since I cannot see my light? My sun has indeed been darkened, and the moon does not remain in its order.

What can a sheep do among wolves when deprived of the protection of its shepherd? How can a tree flourish when its root has been cut away?

What, alas, have you done, dreadful death? Why, while receiving the father, did you leave behind a son so poor and exiled from every good? O cruel death—not to him, but to me and nearly to the whole Church—for you have stolen away the champion!

Why did you not delay receiving him? Why did you not turn your face away from him for a little while? Do you know what you have done? Did you not consider whom you so quickly snatched away from us—one who has no equal in the world in teaching and holiness?

Here was indeed a prince of peace, a leader of justice, a teacher of truth and equity, a standard-bearer of undefiled faith, a strong warrior against heretics, whose arrow never turned backward, whose shield never gave way in battle, and whose spear was never turned aside.

Renowned Christian people, weep, for your leader has fallen. Let a voice sound in Ramah. Let the Church piously mourn the departure of so great a son.

Now many dogs will surround her, and a council of evildoers will besiege her, because her helper has gone far from her. He no longer looks to her defense. Tribulation is now near, and there is no one to help.

Her accustomed protector now lies in the tomb; certainly he will not rise up against those who act wickedly against her.

Therefore cry out in sackcloth and mourning, pious mother; put on the garment of widowhood, widowed of so great a son.

Alas, false prophets will prophesy, and they will announce lying visions, deceitful divinations, and the deceptions of their own hearts among us; and certainly there will be no one to resist them. For the fountain of life has dried up, and the vein of living waters has vanished.

## CHAPTER LVIII

But what will you say, dearest father Damasus? Where is Jerome, whom you loved more than yourself? Where is the guide of your journey, your counselor, teacher, and rector? Where has he gone?

When, I ask, will you write to him:

“I am without your counsel, dearest Jerome, like a member severed from the body. Write, write, I beg you; do not delay. If, because of the distance between our places, I am deprived of your much-desired presence, at least let your memory be frequently present to me through your constant and gracious letters.”

With God as my witness, I have fixed the anchor of my hope in no living person as I have in you. Weep, then, weep; let your eyes pour out tears by day and by night, because the anchor of your hope has failed.

The hand of the writer has dried up like hay’s flower. You will no longer have his memory with you. His sweet and pleasant voice, which was the sweetest honey in the ears of the faithful, has fallen silent.

Alas, what a counselor and helper you have lost! Certainly, you have now failed amid the multitude of your counselors. There will be no one to break for you the bread of life.

The lamp shining in the midst of the Church has been extinguished, so that it may shine not for us but for him, not for the world but for heaven.

What, then, shall I say? To whom shall I complain? From where will help come to me in this matter, so that I may be consoled?

Certainly, as I see it, this has been done by the Lord, and therefore I shall say to him:

“Why, good Jesus, have you so quickly taken away from your bride—whom you betrothed when dying on the cross—so great a son, her protector and warrior against her enemies? Perhaps you wanted him to be with you. Certainly, Lord, you did not need him as she did. You have indeed helped him well, but you have left us orphans.

“I do not complain that you have done anything other than what is just and right, since he already deserved to bring the labors of this life to an end and to be with you. But I grieve that the Church has suffered so great a loss by his departure.

“If only you would return him, so that he might govern, strengthen, and defend your Church as before. What, good Lord, will his sons do from now on, lying down hungry, wandering about the city famished like dogs, with no one to break bread for them? They are wandering sheep without a shepherd, disciples without a teacher, blind people without a guide.”

## CHAPTER LIX

Alas, pious father Jerome, where are you, the staff of our support? What will your chariot do without you, gentle charioteer? Where do you lie? Tell us.

Why are you now a companion of the earth, you who wished nothing earthly to exist in you, whose flesh certainly gave off no earthly or carnal scent?

Bethlehem, Bethlehem, city of Judah, which retains no lesser one among the princes of the Church—what have you done? Return to us the father whom you retain.

And you, earth, why do you dare to retain a man who does not belong to you, who did nothing earthly, whose flesh certainly bore no carnal odor?

And you, most merciful Theodosius, hang up your instruments upon the willows. Let pious weeping not cease whenever you remember your beloved Jerome, whom you have lost. Let the affection of your grief be as great as your love was; let your lamentation be as great as the loss.

But what mortal tongue could explain how great was the benefit he brought to the whole Church while he lived, how great the salvation he brought to individual Christians, how great his struggle, and how great the destruction and dispersal he inflicted upon heretics?

He was certainly beloved by all Christians and honorable in his life; therefore each person may weep at his departure, and no one can hide or excuse himself.

So that our discourse may not be prolonged excessively, let me briefly conclude what concerns our grief over our loss. Just as the usefulness and joy that came to everyone through him cannot be adequately expressed, so neither can the lamentation of grief.

Let grief therefore cease and sadness depart—although we cannot reach the things we would wish, which not only provide no remedy for grief but increase it.

If we love our father, let us rejoice in his joy. The person who loves only his own advantage does not truly love.

Therefore, even if we grieve over the loss that has befallen us, let us rejoice with him over the joys he has received. Let there therefore be for us today a cause of great joy.

Let each of us sing a new song to the Lord. Let Mother Church rejoice with resounding voices. Let the Catholic people clap their hands today in hymns and confessions. Let the Christian assembly rejoice everywhere.

[Col. 0280]

## CHAPTER LX

Today Jerome has certainly obtained what he desired so ardently. Today, after conquering his enemies, he has obtained a secure triumph. Certainly, after all his labors have been completed, he possesses rest without end.

Now he will no longer hunger or thirst, nor will the sun fall upon him, nor any heat. Every tear has been removed from his eyes, for mourning has departed. Now, certainly, he will have no further sorrow; he has received the reward for which he labored throughout his entire life.

Let us therefore take comfort and give magnificence to our God, because the works of God are perfect and all his ways are judgments.

Let us confess to the Lord and praise our God and Savior, because he did not abandon his saint without help amid the tribulations which surrounded him in the struggle of this most wretched life. Rather, becoming his helper and protector, he freed his body from destruction, from the snare of an iniquitous tongue, and from the lips of those who practice falsehood; and he placed him sublimely within the dwellings of the Father, where there is every joy, every delight, and everything that can be desired.

There is the glorious and blessed refreshment of souls after labors and hardships; there is the sweet solemnity of the angels; there is one fellowship and charity of all the citizens above.

There, certainly, no fear or sorrow shakes anyone. There, no anguish, tribulation, or adversity is known at all. No infirmity is named there. For no one is deprived of his desire.

Death is far away there. There is absolutely no diminution of the glory now present, but rather an increase, namely, when the universal resurrection of all the dead takes place. Then the body of each of the blessed, together with the soul, will possess with interminable duration the glory which the soul now possesses alone.

## CHAPTER LXI

What angel or human being would be sufficient to explain how great even the smallest portion of the joys and glory that are there is? What understanding would be capable of comprehending things that “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have entered into the human heart”?

Certainly, if the greatness of these joys were considered, all earthly things would appear more worthless than any dung. If this temporal life were compared with that one, every human being would burn with desire to extinguish this life as quickly as possible, so as to become capable of possessing that one.

This fleeting and momentary life, in comparison with that one, ought rather to be called death than life. All the world’s deceptive and empty joy is a most bitter burden and a heavy load.

Laying down this burden, most sacred Jerome chose that best portion which will never be taken away from him.

I ask you: rejoice and exult, sing and chant psalms, because our glorious father has already brought a ship full of heavenly riches and eternal merchandise into the long-desired harbor and has securely fastened the tranquil anchor of hope in its station.

*(From the second Homily of Saint Maximus on Saint Eusebius.)*

He now possesses the prize for which he ran in the contest of this age, abstaining from everything illicit. Now, victorious over his enemies, he has triumphed over them, fighting bravely against them while armed with the shield of the Lord’s love.

Now he has received the denarius for which he labored with such effort in the vineyard of holy Church. Now he has returned the talent doubled to the Lord, for whose reward he deserved to enter into the joy of the Lord.

Because of these things, I shall rejoice with joy and sing a new song to my beloved father, so that his praise may be in the Church of the saints.

Behold my beloved father, white, most beautiful, chosen from among thousands, in whom there is no stain; he feeds among the lilies in the vineyard of the Lord of hosts.

Behold the flower of the field and the rose exuding an exceedingly strong fragrance, recently transplanted from the garden of the Church into the Lord’s garden.

Behold the cypress, lifting itself to the height of heaven. Let his name be proclaimed to distant islands, so that his memory may remain forever in blessing.

## CHAPTER LXII

Rejoice, therefore, dearest Fathers and Lords; be glad and praise, because it is fitting to praise the Lord, who declares himself marvelous in his saints.

Let the whole world rejoice. Let deceitful heretics be ashamed and now recognize that they have come to nothing.

Certainly he is not dead, as his enemies suppose, but he reigns victorious in the land of the living. Certainly his glory now shines through the eternal palaces. Having laid aside his old and fragile weapons, he has now put on new and everlasting ones.

Today, let joy arise everywhere among the Christian people. Let holy Mother Church especially rejoice, for today her glorious son, cultivator, lover, and chief defender, after all heretical doctrines with their deceitful authors have been uprooted from the field of the Catholic faith, shines like the sun among the ranks of the blessed, with his most sacred teachings and resplendent signs and wonders.

Farewell, therefore, glorious Jerome. Always remember us before God, so that through your most holy intercession we may be protected from all harmful things in the present and may attain in the future the joys which you now possess.

# LETTERS CONCERNING SAINT JEROME

[Col. 0281]

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING TWO LETTERS

[Col. 0281] They are also regarded as spurious, both the letter attributed to Cyril and the one attributed to Augustine, before which the following judgment of the Louvain theologians is placed:

“Whoever forged the following letters concerning the death of Jerome under the names of Saint Augustine to Cyril, Bishop of Jerusalem, and of Saint Cyril to Augustine was an unlearned impostor. For it is established that Cyril died before Jerome.

“Accordingly, Jerome writes in his book *On Illustrious Men*: ‘Cyril, Bishop of Jerusalem, was often expelled from the Church and restored; finally, under the emperor Theodosius, he held the episcopate undisturbed for eight years.’

“Moreover, this false Cyril, in his reply, chapter 4, calls Sabinianus a pestilential heresiarch because he asserted two wills in Christ; and he adds that Jerome published a letter concerning the destruction of this error.

“It follows from this that this author was a heretic and an impostor.

“These few points, among many, but the most important ones, are sufficient against these letters.”

[Col. 0281]

## OF AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, TO CYRIL, BISHOP OF JERUSALEM, ON THE GREAT DEEDS OF BLESSED JEROME (C,S)*
Most glorious champion of the Christian faith, cornerstone of holy Mother Church, upon whom she stands most firmly established; now a shining star in heavenly glory—do you think, venerable Father Cyril, that the praises of Jerome, once a presbyter, should be left unspoken? Or do you suppose that I, a stammering child, a man unclean of lips, shall speak? “The heavens declare the glory of God,” and all that the Lord has made praises Him in His saints. Should rational creation remain silent in praise of God while irrational creation does not? Shall I be silent, or shall I speak, when, if I remain silent, I am commanded to cry out even through stones? Certainly I shall speak; I shall not cease with all my strength to praise the outstanding Jerome.

Although I am unworthy and inadequate as a praiser—for “praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner”—[Col. 0282] nevertheless I shall by no means desist from his praises. Let our hand, then, be strengthened, and let our tongue not cling to our palate, for this most holy man is certainly great, wondrous, and fearsome above all who are around us. He is certainly great in the holiness of his most excellent life; great in the unfathomable depth of his wisdom; great in the magnitude of the greater glory he now possesses. Wondrous in his unfamiliar miracles; fearsome because of the power entrusted to him by the Lord.

How great this most glorious Jerome was in the holiness of his most excellent life—how could my tongue make that known, when the tongues of all mortals together would scarcely suffice to explain his excellence? Let it therefore be said: he was another Elijah, another Samuel, another John the Baptist, in the holiness of his most excellent life.

Elijah and John the Hermit mortified the flesh through great austerities of food and clothing. The most glorious hermit Jerome was no less austere: for four years he remained in the desert, with wild beasts alone for companions. For fifty years—as the letter of the venerable Eusebius, which I received the day before yesterday, more fully attested, and as you yourself, who know the matter more certainly, also know—he did not taste wine or any intoxicating drink in the slightest degree. He abstained so completely from eating meat, and even fish, that he scarcely wished to name them. He ate cooked food only twice, and then during his final illness. He mortified his flesh with a haircloth sack like an Ethiopian, and covered himself above with the vilest cloth. He knew no bed other than the earth.

Once a day only he was nourished by fruits, or by the leaves or roots of plants. After Vespers he gave himself to prayer and thereafter kept vigil every day until the second hour of the night. Then, wearied with sleep, he slept on the ground and rested until midnight. Rising immediately at that hour, he devoted himself to readings and the sacred Scriptures—by which the whole Church shines like a display of precious stones—and continued until the hour of eating. [Col. 0283]

He wept over the lightest sins as though someone might have thought that he had killed a man. Three times every day he continuously scourged his flesh with dreadful blows, so that streams of blood flowed from his body. He fled from every idle word as from the greatest plague. He had no leisure for himself: he was always occupied either with sacred reading, writing, or teaching everyone.

Why should I say more? If I searched through the lives of each of the saints, I do not think I would find anyone greater than he. But since above we named Samuel, let us show that he was this Samuel. Certainly he was that Samuel who was summoned away from vain literary studies by blows and assigned to the ministry of sacred Scripture. Upon whose face, as divine grace poured forth its light, we saw the radiance of both Testaments; and by the strength of whose arm the greater part of the heretics was scattered.

He was the one who, transferring both Testaments from the language of the Hebrews into Greek and likewise into Latin, and arranging them for posterity forever, explaining riddles and obscure, doubtful, and difficult matters, preparing the order of offices for all the ministers of the Church, built almost the whole Church. Hence he plainly appears great in the unfathomable depth of wisdom.

He knew the liberal arts so perfectly that, by everyone’s testimony, no one comparable to him has yet appeared. As for the sacred Scriptures, I learned from the experience of many of his letters which he sent to me that we have never known anyone equal to him. He knew the languages and scripts of the Hebrews, Greeks, Chaldeans, Persians, Medes, Arabs, and nearly all nations as though he had been born and raised among them.

What more shall I say? Whatever Jerome did not know in human nature, no human being ever knew. Do not think, venerable Father, that I say these things because I imagine that you know Jerome’s life and virtues less well than I do, since you were his companion for a long time. But I call God to witness that, because of the holiness of so ineffable a man, if I had wished to remain silent, I could not have done so.

The heavens themselves, in which he dwells forever—great, and greater than many of the saints in the magnitude of his glory—testify to his wonders and holiness. No one, therefore, doubts that within the Father’s dwelling places he occupies one of the greater and loftier seats. For since a person is rewarded according to his works, and since he was possessed of an almost perfect life, it is plainly evident that he will be one of the greater and loftier citizens of the heavenly Jerusalem.

So that this may be believed by us more fully and certainly while we remain in this world, he appears exceedingly wondrous, through unfamiliar prodigies and countless miracles, above all whom our age remembers. The venerable Eusebius has related some of these to me in writing. As for the other prodigies that occur wondrously every day, I continually learn of them through the reports of many and eagerly desire to hear more. I therefore beg you yourself, dearest Father, not to refuse, as soon as opportunity permits, to send me in a small volume whatever true and useful miracles you can collect, out of devotion to that same most holy Jerome.

But so that the many merits of the most holy Jerome may not remain hidden, I shall relate what happened to me, by the favor of divine mercy, on the very day of his death. On that same day and hour when the most holy Jerome, having removed the garment of the corruption and uncleanness of the flesh, put on the clothing of perpetual immortality, immeasurable joy, and glory, I was resting in my cell at Hippo and eagerly considering the magnitude of the glory and joys present to the souls of the blessed who rejoice with Christ. Wishing to compose a brief treatise on this subject, and urged by the prayers of our Severus, formerly a venerable disciple of Martin, Bishop of Tours, I took paper, pen, and writing tablet in my hands and wished to write a brief letter to be sent to the most holy Jerome, so that he might respond with whatever he thought about the matter. For I knew that in so difficult a question no one among the living could teach me more clearly.

As I was already writing the opening of the salutation to Jerome, suddenly an ineffable light, unseen in our times and impossible to express in our languages, entered the cell in which I was standing at the hour of Compline, together with an ineffable and unheard-of fragrance of every kind of scent. When I saw it, I was overcome with astonishment and wonder and suddenly lost the powers of my mind and limbs.

For at that time I did not know that the wondrous right hand of God had exalted His servant, making His powers known among the peoples. I did not know that the God of ancient mercy had released His faithful servant from the uncleanness of the flesh and prepared for him so lofty a seat in heaven. I certainly did not know the unsearchable ways of the Lord. I did not know the treasures of God’s infinite wisdom and knowledge. I did not recognize God’s secret and hidden judgments, because He brings those whom He wills to the knowledge of Himself through His ineffable wisdom. Those whom He predestines, He calls, justifies, and glorifies, as He discerns to be fitting.

Thus, because my eyes had never before seen such a light and my sense of smell had never perceived such a fragrance, I was stunned by wonders so new and unheard of. Meanwhile, as my thoughts clamored within me, asking what this might be, a voice broke forth from the light and said:

“Augustine, what are you seeking? Do you think you can pour the entire sea into a small vessel, enclose the whole earth in a small fist, or make the heavens stand firm so that they no longer perform their customary motions? What no human eye has been able to see—will your eye see it? What no ear has taken in through sound—will yours hear it? What the human heart has in no way understood or even conceived—do you think you can understand it? What will be the end of an infinite matter? By what measure will you measure what is immeasurable?

“Rather, the whole sea might be enclosed in the narrowest vessel; rather, a tiny fist might hold the globe of the earth; rather, the heavens might cease from their continual motion, than you understand even the smallest portion of the joys and glory which the souls of the blessed possess without end—unless, as I was, you are taught by experience. Continue through the brief span of time still remaining. Do not attempt the impossible until the course of your life has been completed. Do not seek here what can be found nowhere except where I am hastening so happily.

“Here strive to perform such works that afterward, there, you may possess completely and eternally what you wish here to understand in some small measure. Those who enter there never leave.”

At this I stood trembling with fear and nearly deranged with astonishment at something so unseen, almost deprived of all strength. Taking some courage, I said in a trembling voice:

“If only it were permitted me not to doubt, O you who are so blessed and glorious, proceeding honorably toward those joys, who pour such sweet words into my throat!”

He replied: “Are you asking my name? I am the soul of that presbyter Jerome to whom, as you began writing, you intended to send a letter. At this hour, in Bethlehem of Judah, I laid down the burden of the flesh and, accompanied by Christ and the entire heavenly host, adorned with every beauty, illumined with every splendor, clothed in that gilded garment of immortality, surrounded by every variety of good and joy, triumphant over all earthly things, crowned with every diadem, and enclosed by every blessedness and happiness, I proceed in glory and ineffably toward the kingdoms of heaven, where I shall remain without end.

“For henceforth I expect no decline in glory, but only increase, when I shall again be joined to a glorified body that will not die, and shall possess with it the glory that I now possess alone—namely, on the day of the universal judgment.”

Then, gathering greater strength of spirit within me, and unable to stop weeping for joy, I answered:

“If only I might deserve to become your attendant, O outstanding man! But I beg you to remember your little servant, however worthless, whom you loved in the world with such great affection of charity, so that through your intercessions I may be cleansed from sins; under your guidance I may proceed by the straight path with an unhindered step; through your continual defenses I may be protected from enemies who constantly lie in wait for me; and under your holy leadership I may reach the harbor of salvation. Would that you might be willing to answer some question I have.”

She replied: “Say what you wish, knowing that I shall answer your every desire.”

“I should like to understand,” I said, “whether the souls of the blessed can desire something which they are unable to obtain.”
