She replied: “Know this one thing, Augustine: the souls of the saints are so solidified and established in God in that eternal glory that they have no other will than God’s. They can desire nothing except what God wills; therefore they can obtain whatever they desire. For whatever they desire, God both wills and fulfills.

“None of us is cheated of his desires, because none of us desires anything apart from God. Since we always possess God as we wish, our desires are always fulfilled most completely.”

A lengthy succession of words would be required, dearest Father Cyril, if I were to write in this brief letter everything that the glorious soul disclosed to me when I questioned her. I hope that, after not many cycles of years, I shall come to Bethlehem to visit such relics, and that there I shall see clearly what I heard and committed to writing.

For many hours that most glorious soul remained there with me and disclosed to my eager mind the Unity of the most holy Trinity and the Trinity of the Unity; the generation of the Son from the Father; the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son; the angelic hierarchies and orders; the mysteries of those blessed spirits; the happiness of the blessed souls; and other matters useful and weighty for human understanding. If I spoke with the tongues of all men, I could not express how subtly, clearly, and wondrously she revealed these things to me. [Col. 0286]

Then that light vanished from my eyes, but for many days afterward the ineffable sweetness of the fragrances remained.

How wondrous, then, is this man, performing so many miracles and so many great prodigies unfamiliar to human beings? Let us therefore cry out to him with our mouths and rejoice; let us give glory to his praise, for he is certainly worthy of all praise, and we are not sufficient to praise him.

He entered the house of the Lord white and most beautiful, where without doubt he occupies one of the loftier and more illustrious seats of glory. To make the light of truth shine forth again more clearly, I decided to add the testimony of more than one witness to the above: namely, that our aforesaid Severus, a man distinguished for learning and wisdom, saw in the city of Tours, on the very day and hour of Jerome’s death, together with three other men, what I saw. Only he himself, coming to me the day before yesterday, was my witness concerning this.

Since God wished the lofty glory of Jerome not to remain hidden from the world—just as his lofty holiness, almost the greatest among all the living, was not hidden—lest those who delighted in following the footsteps of that holiness, ignorant that he would receive a reward, should at some time depart from the path of holiness; and so that others, seeing that so many and such great rewards had been granted to him, might cling to the footsteps of that holiness and virtue—for the hope of rewards lightens the burden of labor—God declared in the following manner to Severus and the three others standing with him the glory that He was to grant to the glorious Jerome on the day and hour when he happily departed this life.

At the hour of Compline on that day, Severus was in his house with three Catholic men, two of whom had formerly been monks of the venerable Martin’s monastery. As he was reading the divine Scriptures, he suddenly heard in heaven, in the air, and upon the earth countless voices singing melodies of extraordinary sweetness—unheard, ineffable, and incredible—as well as the sounds of organs, drums, psalteries, and the entire harmony of instruments, by which heaven, earth, and everything, as it seemed to him, resounded on every side. Their sweetness almost caused their souls to leave their bodies.

Immediately, astonished, they all raised their eyes and saw the whole sky, the air, and everything contained within their circumference shining with a light seven times brighter than the splendor of the sun. From it every kind of fragrant spice poured forth.

Seeing these things so wondrous, they entreated God in prayer that He would not conceal from them why such things were happening. A voice coming from heaven said to them:

“Let no astonishment disturb you. Let nothing appear wondrous to you if you both see and hear such things. For today the King of kings and Lord of lords, Christ the Lord, comes entirely in festal procession to meet the soul of the most glorious presbyter Jerome, who dwelt in Bethlehem of Judah, as it departs from this wicked age. He comes to introduce it into His kingdoms with honor, excellence, and sublimity proportionate to the greater height and holiness of its life compared with others.

“Today all the orders of angels rejoice and, singing responsively with such voices, accompany their Lord. Today the assembly of all the patriarchs and prophets; today the choir of the apostles and disciples; today all the holy martyrs; today the confessors; today the glorious Mother of God, accompanied by all the holy virgins; today the joyful and festal souls of all the blessed come to meet their fellow countryman and fellow citizen.”

After these words the voice fell silent. Nevertheless, the light, singing, and fragrance continued for another hour and then ceased.

Thus it is plainly evident that he is one of the loftier and greater citizens, since he is great, wondrous, and fearsome above almost all the saints because of the power entrusted to him. No one should doubt that he is able to obtain whatever he wishes, more than others, just as his will is more closely united to the divine will than theirs.

Let no one think me so audacious as to assert that he surpasses in glory John the Baptist—of whom the Savior Himself testified that no one greater had arisen—or Peter and Paul and the other twelve apostles, who were chosen and sanctified by Christ Himself. Yet even if reason forbids anyone to obtain greater glory than they in the kingdom of heaven, I see no reason why it should be forbidden to say that Jerome will be their equal in glory, provided that he was not unlike them in holiness of life. For God is not a respecter of persons, but determines the merits of each and renders to everyone what he has deserved.

If anyone thinks that Jerome will possess less glory than John and the apostles, let him think that he possesses only slightly less, since, when he clearly sees the merits of his holiness, the heavy burdens of his labor, and the fruits of his writing, of his most truthful translation of both Testaments, and of his ordering of ecclesiastical offices—not only for the present but also for the future—he will, I think, as God is my witness, judge that Jerome differs from them in glory by scarcely anything.

Moreover, lest I appear to set a snare for ridicule by confessing that the most holy Jerome is equal to John and the apostles in holiness and glory, I shall relate one thing which I saw in a vision less than four days after the events just mentioned, so that the truth may not remain hidden and so that no one may think that I am repeating these praises either out of carnal affection—which most of all causes a person to depart from knowledge of the truth—or through the ignorance of a deranged mind, or for any other reason.

Let no one think that I learned this from a human being. It came through a revelation granted by almighty God, who exalts His saints and magnifies them through their exaltation.

On the fourth night afterward, while I was eagerly considering what praise or due reverence I might briefly set forth for Jerome, God showed me the following. While, as I have said, I was preparing to write this letter to you and thinking of finding suitable material for praise, sleep overcame me when midnight arrived. And behold, a very great multitude of angels appeared before me. Among them were two men shining more brightly than the sun, so similar and alike that no difference could be seen by which one might be distinguished from the other, except that one wore three wreaths upon his head, made of gold and precious stones, while the other wore two.

They were dressed in the whitest tunics, woven throughout with gold and jewels, and were of such beauty that no one could imagine it. Both approached me and stood silently for a little while. Then the one who wore three wreaths addressed me in these words:

“Are you considering, Augustine, what praise concerning Jerome you ought to speak truthfully? Indeed, although you have thought for a long time, you do not yet know. But we have both come here to disclose his glory to you. This companion of mine whom you see is Jerome himself. Just as he was my equal in holiness of life, so in every respect he is my equal in glory. Whatever I can do, he can also do; whatever I will, he also wills; just as I see God, so he sees Him, knows Him, and understands Him, in whom consists the blessedness of our glory and of the glory of all the saints.

“One saint possesses greater or lesser glory than another only insofar as he contemplates or knows the divine appearance more or less fully. The third wreath which I bear in addition to him is the aureole of martyrdom, by which I completed my bodily life. Although, because of his labors, penances, hardships, afflictions, beatings, insults, and the reproaches and mockery of men, together with all the other very grievous things which he endured so peacefully and joyfully for God that he rejoiced in his weaknesses, he was a true martyr and did not lose the rewards of martyrdom, nevertheless, because he did not end his life by the sword, he does not possess the aureole which is given as a sign of martyrdom.

“The other two wreaths which we possess are aureoles given only to virgins and teachers, so that they may be distinguished from others.”

To this, as it seemed to me, I replied: “Who are you, my lord?”

He answered: “I am John the Baptist. I have descended here to you to announce Jerome’s glory, so that you may announce it to the nations.

“Know this: the honor and reverence shown to each of the saints are shown to all the others. Do not think that there is any envy in heaven as there is in the world. For just as in the world every human being would prefer to rule over others rather than be subject to them, so in heaven, because of the ineffable charity with which the blessed souls love one another, each saint rejoices in another’s glory as in his own.

“Indeed, each would wish to be greater so that each lesser one might be his equal and almost greater, because the other’s glory would be his own. Thus the lesser rejoices in the greater’s glory as though he possessed it himself; nor would he wish to possess it if the other did not possess it. Rather, if it were permitted, he would share his own glory with the other.

“Therefore the glory of each is the glory of all, and the glory of all is the glory of each.”

After these words, the entire company departed. When I awoke from sleep, I suddenly felt within me such ardors of charity as I had never before experienced. From then until now there has never been in me any desire or thought of envy, pride, or arrogance.

God, who knows all things before they happen, is my witness that such a fervor of charity arose in me from that moment that I rejoice more in another’s good than in my own, and I desire more to be subject to everyone than to rule over anyone.

I have said these things not to acquire a reputation for praise, but so that no one may think these were empty dreams by which our minds are often deceived. For God often discloses hidden and very great things through dreams.

Let us therefore magnify His works, for they are perfect and there is no injustice in them. For God’s sake, let us magnify the holy Jerome, with whom He reigns securely, because in his life he acted magnificently and in his death he received magnificent things.

Therefore he is great among us, holy and exalted in the holiness of his most excellent life; great, holy, and exalted in the unfathomable depth of his wisdom; great, holy, and exceedingly exalted in the magnitude of his greater glory now; wondrous, praiseworthy, and glorious in prodigies unseen, unheard, and unfamiliar; fearsome, to be honored and venerated because of the power, honor, and everlasting glory entrusted to him by the Lord.

Let us therefore, I beg you, magnify him and not remain silent, for he is greater than all praise. Let us make the praises of his glory known among the peoples. Let no one wonder if we praise and honor the one whom God has magnified and honored. Let no one be reluctant to venerate and honor the one whom God has honored and venerated.

Let no one think that by equating Jerome with John and the apostles in glory and holiness we do injury to John and the apostles, for if they could, they would wish him to surpass them both in glory and in holiness. His glory and blessedness are their glory, and their glory and blessedness are his.

The honor, praise, and reverence which we offer to Jerome are offered to each of them; and what is offered individually to them is offered to Jerome. If, therefore, you wish to venerate John the Baptist and the apostles, venerate him together with them, for he is equal to them in every respect.

With a secure mind, then, having driven away all fear, let us confess with complete devotion and reverence that John the Baptist is equal to Jerome, not greater—for “no one greater has arisen.” If we make Jerome lesser, we diminish John’s glory and inflict injury rather than offer praise.

Although this work of my unskilled speech has been completed by us inadequately, most humbly, and as though it were nothing, I nevertheless send it to you, venerable Father, with a pure heart and great devotion. I beg you to read with due charity and equanimity the little words of my small talent which, from the poverty of my ignorance, I have offered in praise of the outstanding Jerome, rather than ridiculing them.

Whatever I have said less appropriately in praise of so great a man, attribute to my ignorance, to the brevity of the letter, and to the immeasurable majesty of his praises. For certainly, even if the tongues of all mortals alone uttered his praises, it would still be less than sufficient.

Remember me, a sinner, venerable Father, so that when you stand in that place where the sacred body of the outstanding Jerome rests, you may commend me through his intercessions, for there is no doubt that Jerome can immediately obtain whatever he desires. For he is in no way cheated of his desire.

[Col. 0289]

## CYRIL, BISHOP OF JERUSALEM, ON THE MIRACLES OF JEROME, TO SAINT AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO (C,S)*

To the venerable man, outstanding among bishops, Augustine, bishop of Hippo, Cyril, pontiff of Jerusalem and the least of all priests.

### CHAPTER I

To follow the footsteps of him whose holiness on earth never ceases to radiate—namely, the glorious Jerome, whose memory will be blessed forever and ever—you likewise know very well how great he is, having especially enjoyed his conversation and instruction. That I should wish to speak about him, when I am wholly reprobate and unworthy, seems to me almost audacious.

Nevertheless, because your affection compels me to write to you about other prodigies unfamiliar to human beings which the Lord performed through him in our days, so as to make him celebrated throughout the world and glorious to all people, I shall undertake the work trusting in your prayers, as your devotion demands, and shall touch briefly upon a few matters from among many.

I do not doubt that you know of his glorious death, my vision, and the wondrous things that occurred at that time. For the venerable man Eusebius, a noble citizen of Cremona and his disciple—in whom the holiness and learning of his master shone forth, and whose wisdom, probity, and excellence you do not fail to know—was taken from the misery of our mortality two years afterward and followed his most beloved master Jerome into the heavenly homeland. His frequent miracles indicate this, and I shall also discuss some of them below.

At that time he informed the revered Father Damasus, Bishop of Porto; Theodosius, Roman senator; his brother Severus, a most upright man; Eustochium, a most holy woman; you; and many others whose names need not be listed individually, through letters describing the whole sequence of Jerome’s death.

It would therefore be superfluous to repeat at greater length what you already know, and it would impede what must be said. Omitting these matters, then, let our pen turn to the miracles of the same man, which continually continue to shine forth, as your devotion requires. Let it begin first with Eusebius, the most holy man and disciple of that same most holy Jerome.

### CHAPTER II

After the glorious Jerome’s death, a certain heresy—or sect—arose among the Greeks and spread even to the Latins. It attempted by its wicked arguments to prove that the souls of the blessed would be deprived until the day of the universal judgment, when they were to be reunited with their bodies, of the divine vision and knowledge in which the whole blessedness of the saints consists. It likewise maintained that the souls of the condemned would suffer no punishments until that day.

Their argument was as follows: just as the soul earned merit or sinned together with the body, so it receives rewards or punishments together with the body. The most wicked members of that sect also asserted that there would be no place of purgation in which souls that had not yet completed full repentance for their sins in this world could be purified.

As that pestilential sect increased, such grief fell upon us that we became weary even of living. Therefore, after summoning all my suffragan bishops and other Catholic men, I prescribed fasts and prayers for them, so that divine goodness might not permit the faith entrusted to us to be shaken in this way.

A wondrous event, and perhaps one never before seen like it: after three full days of fasting and prayer, on the following night the glorious Jerome appeared plainly to his most beloved son Eusebius, who was engaged in prayer. Comforting him with a kindly address, he told him that there was no need to fear this pestilential sect, since its end was already at hand.

Eusebius looked upon him shining with such brilliance that the human eye could not bear to gaze at him. As though awakening from a deep sleep, he poured forth sweet tears through his eyes and, scarcely able to form his voice, began to cry out as loudly as he could:

“Are you my father Jerome? Why do you reject my companionship? I shall certainly hold you and not let you go; nor will you proceed without your son, whom you loved.”

The glorious Jerome answered him: “I shall not abandon you, dearest son. Take courage, for on the twentieth day you will follow me, and together we shall remain in joy without end. But tell Cyril and all the brothers that tomorrow they must all assemble together beside the Lord’s manger, where my body rests, both the Catholics and the men of that sect.

“You shall also have the unburied corpses of three men who died in this city during the night carried to the place where my body has been buried. Place upon them the sack which I used, and they will immediately be restored to their former life and will eradicate this heresy from its roots.”

After bidding him farewell, the glorious Jerome disappeared.

When morning came, the venerable Eusebius came to me, who was then in Bethlehem, and related everything he had seen. Giving immense thanks to the Creator, and with everyone gathered at the place mentioned above, where the Savior was born for us from the undefiled Virgin and where the most sacred body of Jerome had also been buried, I had the corpses of the deceased brought there.

O wondrous mercy and providence of God toward human beings! In how many ways He knows how to help those who hope in Him! With how many and how great honors He exalts His saints!

Meanwhile, the followers of that sect mocked us, believing that the hand of the Lord had been emptied of power. Let the whole assembly of the faithful therefore rejoice, and let them sing psalms to God with a voice of exultation when we receive mercy in the midst of His temple.

The venerable Eusebius approached each corpse, knelt, raised his hands toward heaven, and prayed in the hearing of everyone:

“God, for whom nothing is impossible and nothing is difficult, whose invincible strength and power perform great wonders alone, and who despises none of those who hope in You: now hear the prayers of Your faithful. So that the faith which You have given may remain pure and inviolate throughout the ages, and so that the error of these men may be revealed, through the merits and intercessions of Your glorious beloved Jerome, introduce into these corpses the souls which You willed to depart from them.”

When this prayer was finished, he touched each corpse with the sack which the glorious Jerome had used upon his flesh, and immediately introduced the spirit of life into them. Their eyes opened, all the signs of life appeared, and they were perfectly restored to life.

They began, in a clear voice, to make known to everyone the glory of the blessed souls and the punishments of sinners, both in Purgatory and in Hell. For, as they later told me when I questioned them, blessed Jerome had led them with him through Paradise, Purgatory, and Hell, so that they might reveal to everyone what was occurring there.

He had told them that they must return to their bodies and there do penance for the sins they had committed, because on the day and hour when the venerable Eusebius was going to die, they too would die; and that, if they performed their penance well, they would attain glory with him. This also happened, as I shall explain below.

When these things had been accomplished, a very great multitude of people—both the faithful and the defenders of that sect—who had gathered for the great spectacle, seeing so certain an indication and proof of the truth, as well as the outstanding merits of the blessed Jerome, gave immense thanks in loud voices to the Creator, who does not abandon those who hope in Him.

And so, dearest Augustine, the merciful Lord permits the little boat of His most sacred faith to be tossed upon the sea of this world by the waves spewed up by evil men, but He does not permit it to be shipwrecked.

Therefore, I beg you, be strong in spirit; act manfully; do not fear to fight courageously against the persecutors of the faith beneath the shadow of the wings of so merciful a father. He does not allow the prayers of his faithful to be ineffectual, provided that they are offered with complete hope and a pure heart. For our prayers cannot fail to be heard unless our hope does not rest perfectly in God, or because we ask for what ought not to be asked.

When we are afflicted, let us cry out to the Lord not only with our mouths but with our whole hearts. He who rules by His power and looks upon us daily with the eye of mercy will not permit us to be tempted beyond what we can bear.

But so that I may not now stray too far from my purpose, let me return to what I began. I shall first complete the account of the death of the venerable Eusebius and then write likewise of the departure of those three men whom you know to have been restored to life. Since they were removed from this world and from the valley of misery at the same hour and on the same day as Eusebius, I shall introduce some of Jerome’s miracles from among the many.

### CHAPTER III

When the day arrived on which the venerable Eusebius had learned from blessed Jerome, in the vision of which I spoke above, that he would depart—on the third day, as it approached—he was violently shaken by the weakness of fever. Remembering his master, he had himself carried naked upon the ground by the brothers, and he strengthened each brother with kindly consolation, exhorting them to remain steadfast in their holy resolve.

Then he had the sackcloth in which the glorious Jerome had been clothed brought to him, ordered it placed over him, and arranged that he himself, naked, should be buried in the likeness of his glorious master, outside the church in which the holy body of Jerome lay. After this, having fortified himself with communion of the most sacred body of Jesus Christ, he commended himself to the Lord and to blessed Jerome. Thus, deprived of speech and bodily sight for three days, he lay there while the brothers around him read continually, taking turns, the Psalter, the Passion of the Lord, and other sacred texts.

What I am relating is hard and frightening to all who live rightly in this world. On the day on which he was to die, two hours before the departure of his blessed soul, the venerable Eusebius began to perform such terrifying actions that the monks standing around him, struck with fear, lay on the ground like madmen. For at times, with his eyes turned sideways, his hands clasped, his face terrible, and his voice dreadful, he cried out as though raging:

> “I will not do it, I will not do it! You lie, you lie!”

After this, returning to the ground, he pressed his face against it as firmly as he could, crying:

> “Help me, brothers, lest I perish!”

When the monks saw this, they asked him through tears and trembling:

> “What is wrong, father?”

He replied:

> “Do you not see the hosts of demons who desire to overpower me?”

And they said:

> “What did they want you to do when you said, ‘I will not do it’?”

He answered:

> “They are trying to make me appear a blasphemer of the divine Name; therefore I was crying out that I would not do this.”

And they asked:

> “Why, father, were you hiding your face against the ground?”

He replied:

> “[Col. 0293] So that I would not see the face of the one who is so vile and terrible that, in comparison with him, almost all the fears that exist in the world are nothing.”

Amid these words, repeating his earlier actions, he continued all the way to the final hour. The brothers who stood by, terrified by fear and grief, stood like dead men, not knowing what to do.

Glorious is God in his saints, wondrous in his majesty, kind and merciful to those who love him; he does not abandon his saints in the time of need. For, as the final hour of the venerable Eusebius approached, the glorious Jerome appeared, comforting him kindly. At his arrival, that entire, almost countless crowd of demons, terrified by fear of him, vanished from his presence like smoke. Many monks testify to this—those who say that, by divine dispensation, they saw it with their own eyes.

The matter is confirmed still more strongly by this: all those standing around heard Eusebius say:

> “Where are you coming from, father? Why have you delayed so long?”

Immediately, with everyone listening, another voice answered him:

> “Wait, my son; do not be afraid, for I will not abandon you, whom I love so greatly.”

When this voice had been heard, after a short interval had passed, the venerable Eusebius breathed his last.

At that very hour, the three men who had been restored to life also departed; and, as I think, they reached eternal joys together with Eusebius. For during all those twenty days after they had been restored to life, as you know, they devoted themselves to such great penitence that without doubt they now possess and receive the reward of eternal blessedness.

I do not think that I should pass over in silence what I learned from those same three men during the days in which they lived. Throughout this entire period, I spent alternate days with one or another of them until evening, desiring to investigate the secrets of that life which we await after this brief and momentary existence. Although I learned many things from them, I shall nevertheless relate only a few for the present, for the sake of brevity; the rest I shall omit, intending to tell them on another occasion.

Once it happened that I went to one of them. I found him weeping bitterly and admitting no consolation from my words, so I began to ask him the reason for such weeping. I questioned him about this several times, but he did not answer what I asked. At last, compelled by my persistence, he replied:

> “If you knew what I experienced yesterday, you would always have cause to weep.”

I said to him:

> “Please explain what you saw.”

Then, remaining silent for a little while, he said:

> “What punishments and torments do you think are prepared not only for the condemned, but also for those who are in Purgatory?”

I replied:

> “What true judgment can be offered about things that are uncertain? For, as I think, they cannot be compared with the punishments by which we are afflicted here.”

He answered:

> “If all the punishments, torments, and afflictions that can be imagined in the world were compared with the lesser punishment and torment that exist there, they would be consolations. Indeed, any living person—if he knew those punishments by experience—would prefer to be tortured without remedy until the end of the world by all the punishments together that all human beings from Adam until now have individually endured, rather than to be tormented for one day in Hell or in Purgatory by the lesser punishment that exists there.

> “And therefore, if you ask the cause of my weeping, it is fear of the punishments that are [Col. 0294] justly imposed upon sinners. For I know that I have sinned against my God, and I do not doubt that he is just. Therefore do not be surprised that I weep; rather, if I did not weep, you ought to be greatly amazed. Instead, marvel at why people who do not doubt that they will die—at least on the evidence of others—live here with such security and do not think how they may escape such punishments.”

Struck inwardly by grief, so that I could scarcely form words, I said:

> “Alas, what am I hearing? But please tell me: in what way do the torments of Hell differ from those that are in Purgatory?”

He replied:

> “They differ in nothing, because the punishments of Purgatory and of Hell are equal in magnitude. But there is one respect in which they can differ: the punishments of Hell do not await an end, but an increase—namely, on the day of the universal judgment, when the bodies there will be tortured together with the souls. The punishments of Purgatory, however, have an end. For after the penance has been completed, those who are released from there will enjoy the greatest joys.”

I asked:

> “Are the torments equal for everyone who is in Purgatory, or are they different?”

He answered:

> “They are different: greater for some and lighter for others, according to the magnitude of their sins. For in the homeland of the blessed, all the glorious souls contemplate the divine appearance; in this consists all their glory. Although each of them has as much joy as it can desire or conceive, they are nevertheless not equal in their joys: one possesses greater joys, another lesser, according to the works they performed.

> “If this should give rise to wonder in you—how there can be a diversity of joys among the saints, whose cause is God alone, in whom there can never have been any diversity—the solution is quite clear. Since divine contemplation and knowledge, or understanding, are the whole reward and glory, they can be lesser in one saint and greater in another. Therefore, although all souls together see and know God as he is, one sees and understands less, and thus possesses lesser glory; another sees more clearly and understands more subtly, and thus possesses greater glory.

> “The same can be said of the punishments of those wretched condemned souls. Although all the souls of the condemned are in one place of punishment, they are nevertheless tormented by different punishments according to the kinds of their vices.

> “There is such a difference between the punishments of the Christians who are tortured there and those of the pagans that the torments of the pagans, in comparison with what false Christian sinners endure, are almost nothing—although they are unspeakable and cannot be conceived by the living. And rightly so. For those false Christians received the grace of God in vain, and while they lived they did not wish to be corrected from their sins, despite the sacred Scriptures crying out continually, which they considered worthless.”

Then I said:

> “What you say is horrible; would that it were deeply impressed upon the minds of mortals, so that, if they would not cease from evil out of love for glory, at least they might cease from it through fear of such punishments. But please tell me briefly what happened to you yesterday when your soul departed.”

He replied:

> “When the hour of my death arrived, such a multitude of wicked spirits was present in the place where I lay about to depart that, because of their number, they could not possibly be counted. [Col. 0295] Their appearance was such that nothing more loathsome or more horrible can be imagined. Indeed, any human being would prefer to expose himself to burning flames rather than to behold those forms with the glance of his eyes.

> “When they came to me, they recalled to my memory all the deeds I had committed against God, persuading me not to hope any longer for the divine mercy whom I had offended so gravely. And know this for certain: unless divine compassion had helped me, I would not have been able to resist them. For, when I was deprived of all strength of spirit and began to assent somewhat to their words, the glorious Jerome appeared, surrounded by a great host of angels, his appearance brighter than the sun, and comforted me.

> “When he saw those unclean spirits harshly tormenting me, he was greatly angered against them and said to them in a terrible voice:

> “‘Why have you come to this man, spirits of wickedness and every curse? Did you not know that he was to be cherished by my aid? At once leave him and go away; keep your wickedness far from him, as far as the rising of the sun is from its setting.’

> “Terrified by this, that company of accursed spirits crossed the threshold of the place where I lay, with dreadful howls and cries. Then the glorious Jerome ordered certain angels not to leave me but to wait until he returned, and he departed hastily with the other angels.

> “After he had gone, the angels who had remained to guard me began to comfort me, promising me gentle and sweet things if I persevered with a courageous spirit. While these consoling conversations were taking place, and about an hour had passed, blessed Jerome came for the second time. Standing at the threshold, he said:

> “‘Come quickly.’

> “Then suddenly the soul left the body, with such severity and anguish that the human mind could not comprehend how great the pressure and distress had been, unless it had learned them by experience, as I did. For if all human understanding were to estimate whatever anguish and pain it wished, it would count them as nothing in comparison with the soul’s dissolution from the body.”

While he was speaking these and other matters no less difficult and greatly frightening to mortals, the day began to close with the setting of the sun. Since it was necessary for me to leave unfinished what had happened to him after death, and because I was especially eager to hear the rest, on the following day I returned to the sequence of his account, having summoned the other two men together with him. I wanted to hear it from those other two also, so that I might be instructed more firmly by the testimony of all three.

When they began to dictate, I replied:

> “Although these matters are useful, and I would not be weary of repeating them often even in vain, nevertheless, setting aside what I have already heard, please reveal to my eager mind what happened to you after the dissolution of the body.”

The one who had narrated to me the events you heard the previous day replied:

> “What you ask, Cyrille, cannot be fully expressed, because spiritual things are not at all comprehended by our senses. You know that you will not be without a soul, and yet you do not recognize what or what kind of thing the soul is. Certainly you know that God is the beginning and end of all things, from whom all things begin and toward whom they tend; yet, while you carry the exceedingly heavy [Col. 0296] and corruptible burden of this flesh, you do not understand what God is or what he is like except through a mirror and in an enigma. The same is evident concerning angels and the other incorporeal beings.

> “Since we cannot understand, through the deficiency of our small intelligence, many things that are very well known in nature, how shall we understand heavenly and spiritual things, utterly foreign to natural knowledge?”

“As you say,” I replied, “so it is. But please speak as you are able.”

He answered:

> “I shall describe indirectly what you desire, and I shall say almost what I cannot say. Those who experienced with me what I related yesterday will bear witness, if this is so.

> “Yesterday my soul, after being dissolved from the body by so many pressures and pains—as I said above—was suddenly, in the twinkling of an eye, carried ineffably before the presence of God the judge. But by whom and how, I do not know. Nor is this surprising: for now I am weighed down by the mass of the flesh, but then the soul will be without flesh.

> “The souls of these men were also there, fearing with unimaginable terror what the judge would do. Alas, why do mortals not know what will happen to us then! Certainly, if there were no ignorance of that, they would not sin so often.

> “Nothing of the sins we had committed throughout the whole course of our lives could be hidden from the judge. Indeed, everything we had done was clear to all who stood present, as though it were happening before their eyes, so that even the least of our thoughts appeared exactly as it had been.

> “Consider, then, by what and by how many terrors we were agitated. On one side stood a multitude of demons, bearing witness to the evils we had committed and declaring the place, manner, and times. On the other, we ourselves were entirely unable to contradict the things brought against us, both because we knew that the judge knew everything and because each of us recognized him as perfectly just.

> “Alas, what shall I say? We awaited the sentence, and at its remembrance I now tremble. From every side, evils everywhere cried out for vengeance to the judge, and scarcely any good appeared from which we might hope for mercy. From every side all who were present cried out that we were worthy of punishment.

> “When nothing remained except that the sentence deserved by sinners should be publicly pronounced, behold, the glorious Jerome, brighter than all the stars, accompanied by blessed John the Baptist, the supreme prince of the Apostles Peter, and a great multitude of angels, came to the throne of the presiding judge. He obtained that our sentence be suspended for a short time and that we be given to him, both out of reverence and devotion for what we had offered him, and because of the need to destroy error, as he wished.

> “Then, taking us with him and surrounded by that entire blessed company, he explained to us what was being done there, so that we might give testimony concerning it, in the place where the souls of the faithful enjoy immeasurable glory forever.

> “After this, leading us to Purgatory and Hell, he not only showed us what was there but also wished us to undergo the experience of the punishments.

> “When all these things had thus been accomplished, at the hour when the venerable Eusebius touched our corpses with the sackcloth once used by blessed Jerome, that same glorious Jerome ordered us to return to our bodies. He commanded us to testify concerning what we had seen, and promised us that on the twentieth day, if we practiced the [Col. 0297] penance due for the sins we had committed, we would attain, together with blessed Eusebius, who was then about to depart from this world, glory without end. Thus our souls were joined again to our bodies.”

I plainly learned many other things, dearest Augustine, that are frightening and, if impressed upon the minds of mortals, would, I think, utterly eradicate from them the love of all passing earthly things and the vigilant care through which so many people go astray. If I were to set them down in these pages, the work would require more thought, and I would not be able to fulfill what I have already promised to write.

Therefore, since I expect you shortly to visit the relics of the glorious Jerome, I shall explain to you what the letters I received yesterday attest, and whatever else I am then able to recall. I shall close all this by touching upon the burial of the venerable Eusebius, so that I may return to narrating the miracles which I promised above to recount.

I have inserted into the preceding account, as briefly as I could, the sequence of the death of the venerable Eusebius and of the three men mentioned above, adding, as I think, certain remarks out of affection. The account of their burial is as follows.

After the death of the venerable Eusebius, many miracles were seen by all, bearing witness to the holiness of his preceding life. For the present I shall mention only two. A monk of a certain monastery had lost the physical light of his eyes through tears and vigils; as soon as he touched the venerable body of Eusebius with his face, he regained the grace of his former sight. A certain demoniac, while we were carrying the sacred body to the church, met it and was immediately delivered.

Near the church in which the most holy body of the glorious Jerome had been buried, we buried the venerable body of Eusebius naked, with the honor due to him, in the likeness of his master. In the cemetery of that church, the bodies of those three men who had died at the same hour were also laid in the tomb.

With this said, let all matters concerning the venerable Eusebius fall silent, so that the great and unspeakable miracles of the outstanding blessed Jerome, already promised, may now take their place.

### CHAPTER IV

I have been placed, as it were, in the pleasant and most joyful meadow of the miraculous deeds of the most holy Jerome. Like one making a garland, I shall gather, as far as I am able, the outstanding and beautiful flowers of his miracles, for the adornment of this little work and for the benefit of our salvation and that of those who come after us.

First I shall relate what happened yesterday concerning the pestilential heresiarch Sabinianus, whom you know. Sabinianus was a heresiarch and supporter of heretics, asserting that there were two wills in Christ, and, what is worse, that they were at times discordant with each other. To prove this utterly unexpected falsehood, he introduced what Christ said in the Gospel:

> “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me,”

drawing from it extremely grave and almost insoluble arguments. He claimed that Christ wished to flee from the Passion by one will, while by another he was compelled to undergo that same Passion. From this he argued that Christ willed many things which he could not obtain. He inflicted such pain upon us that we cannot explain its magnitude.

That pestilential serpent, that ravening wolf who clothed himself in sheep’s clothing, was perverting the flock entrusted to us. [Col. 0298] To exercise the savagery of his wicked heart more effectively, he had compiled a certain little work, proving by false arguments that this was so. To make us believe him, he had entitled the work with the name of the glorious Jerome, the mirror of all truth.

When I learned of this falsehood—knowing that the glorious Jerome had not long before his death issued a letter concerning the destruction of this error—I invited the aforesaid heresiarch, together with his disciples and the ministers of his wickedness, to the Jerusalem church on a certain Sunday, to debate and establish his most wicked error.

On that day, when all my suffragan bishops and many other orthodox men, as well as the heresiarch himself with his impious disciples, had assembled in the aforementioned church, the debate began at the ninth hour and continued until evening.

When the heresiarch cited against us a little work falsely composed by himself and entitled with the name of the glorious Jerome, the archbishop Sylvanus of the holy church of Nazareth—of blessed memory—could not endure these great insults against blessed Jerome. He honored blessed Jerome with such affection of heart and devotion that, whenever he did anything, he would place the divine Name and that of blessed Jerome first; hence he was called “Jerome” by almost everyone.

Sylvanus immediately rose against the heresiarch, harshly reproving him for having committed so many and such great wickednesses. When a long dispute arose between them, and each hurled insults at the other as best he could, in the end they jointly agreed on this: if, by the ninth hour of the following day, blessed Jerome clearly showed that this work had been falsely composed, the heresiarch would be put to death; otherwise, the archbishop would be.

When this had been settled, each returned to his own place. Throughout the night, each of us devoted himself to prayer, so that help might come to us in our need from the Lord, who has never despised anyone who hopes in him.

Great is the Lord and worthy of very great praise; his wisdom is without number.

On the appointed day and hour, the heresiarch came joyfully into the church with the sons of his wickedness. Running here and there, he sought the servant of God like a roaring lion prepared to devour him, as though God were ignorant and did not hear the prayers of his servants.

Yet, when the fool thought that he was standing more firmly, he fell more disastrously. The entire assembly of the faithful stood in the church, each one crying out the name of Saint Jerome. The glorious Jerome had closed his ears, pretending to sleep and refusing to attend to the prayer of those who pleaded, so that he might appear more wondrous.

But I, drenched entirely in tears, astonished and amazed, waited to see what would happen next and wondered why Jerome was absent in this way.

At last, when no miracle appeared, the heresiarch began to rage with canine fury, so that Sylvanus might now fulfill what he had promised. The most holy Sylvanus came gladly and fearlessly to the place where he was to be beheaded, as though he were going to a wedding. He comforted the weeping bishops and all the other Catholics who had gathered for this purpose with these words:

> “Rejoice with me, dearest ones; [Col. 0299] be glad and do not grieve, because God does not abandon those who hope in him. If I am not heard, I have deserved this through the sins I have already committed.”

After this he bent his knees and said:

> “Holy Jerome, if it pleases you, stand by me. Although I am worthy of a greater punishment, nevertheless, lest falsehood prevail, come to the aid of truth. But if it is not permitted that I be helped, be merciful to me at the hour of death, so that I may not be deprived of glory without end.”

Having said this, he offered his neck to the executioner and asked him to strike. The executioner raised his sword, desiring to cut off the head of the venerable bishop with a single blow.

Suddenly the glorious Jerome appeared before all who were watching, holding the sword with an outstretched hand, and ordered Sylvanus to rise. Then he rebuked the heresiarch, indicated that the writings had been falsely composed, threatened him, and disappeared from everyone’s sight.

May the same thing happen to this man and those like him! As soon as the glorious Jerome vanished, the heresiarch’s head fell to the ground, severed from his body, as though the executioner’s hand had cut it off with a single stroke of the sword.

### CHAPTER V

All who were present and saw this astonishing event were immediately amazed and gave thanks to God and to the glorious Jerome, and the heresiarch’s disciples returned to the path of truth.

Behold how effective the venerable bishop’s confidence in the Lord and in blessed Jerome was: he did not fear at all to die for the truth. The venerable bishop certainly became an example to the other Christians. For that person is not a Christian who fears to die for the truth.

If Christ laid down his soul for us in order to redeem us from every form of servitude, then let us also not fear to lay down our souls for him while there is still time, because no one can obtain the crown of glory unless he contends lawfully.

But since you know that something has been said about Sylvanus, I shall relate another event concerning him that was no less wonderful, as I think. It had so many witnesses that the cities of Nazareth and Bethlehem still contain people who saw it with their own eyes.

That ancient serpent, the devil, cast down into the depths of Hell because of his pride, envying the excessive holiness of the venerable bishop Sylvanus, was violently enraged against him and plotted against him with the cunning that surpasses that of all living creatures. He wished to make the man of God infamous, so that those who were being lifted up toward the paths of right conduct by the example of his holiness might fall through his supposed disgrace into worse things.

One night, taking the form of the holy man, he appeared to a most noble woman who was already resting in bed. Pretending that he wished to approach her illicitly, he sought her consent to sexual intercourse.

The woman was terrified. Not recognizing the man’s appearance, she saw herself alone in the bedchamber with a man and did not know what to do. She began to utter dreadful cries, so that by her continual shouting all the sleepers were awakened—not only those in that house but also the neighbors.

They all ran to the woman’s bedchamber and asked her in fear what had happened. Meanwhile, the cunning serpent hid beneath the bed. Those who had arrived, hearing what had happened, began to search everywhere for the man.

After they had investigated for a long time, they finally came to the place [Col. 0300] where the pestilential serpent was hiding and found a man concealed under another’s appearance. When they looked at him by the light of candles, they believed him to be Sylvanus, the archbishop.

All who were present were astonished and became like madmen, as though they did not know what to do or say, since they knew the reputation of his holiness. Seeing this detestable and unforeseen deed, they asked him why he had committed such wickednesses.

He replied:

> “What evil have I done, if this woman invited me to such an affair?”

When the woman heard this, she tearfully replied that he was lying.

Then, in order to incite those men to still greater hatred against the man of God, so that they might defame him more quickly, he began to utter such words, and words so abhorrent, that no one could bear to listen because of the turmoil.

Therefore, enraging him with insults and reproaches, they forcibly drove him outside the house. When morning came, they recounted what had happened and cried out that Sylvanus the archbishop was a hypocrite, worthy of being burned.

Because of this, almost all Nazareth was stirred up against the archbishop, so that whoever heard his name blasphemed him.

What marvelous patience in this man, and what a great sign of holiness! The report of such a danger flew to the ears of the innocent bishop, yet his mouth did not move against the insults. Amid so many adversities, his heart remained unmoved and did not turn toward any impatience. He always gave thanks to the divine Name and confessed that he had deserved this through his own fault.

Alas, what shall I say, Augustine? Not only do I flee insults and reproaches as best I can, but I am also broken by the slightest words; I desire rewards and do not care about hardships, although I know that no one reaches the kingdom of heaven except by the path of labor and affliction. What else should I judge, when I find myself discordant from the saints in conduct and life, except that I shall also be found discordant from them in death and reward?

Mournful and grievous things confront me when I recall the life of the saints and my own. People such as I am turn over the deeds of the saints with amazement, and yet they themselves wish to accomplish nothing.

Moreover, what I shall say exposes my folly. I know that I have often heard from the mouth of that same Sylvanus that he had never been so happy as when he saw himself despised and trampled upon by people.

His infamy grew so greatly that his reputation was carried as far as Alexandria, Cyprus, and almost all the neighboring cities by the mouths of nearly everyone. Yet no one dared touch the threshold of the innocent bishop’s house.

The Lord, remaining above and watching over all things, allows his saints to fall into the hardships of tribulations, so that patience may then make them faithful; but when necessity demands it, he does not abandon them amid their distresses.

When a year had passed since the devil’s cunning had perpetrated such things against the man of God, the man of God secretly left the city of Nazareth, in order somehow to lessen the scandal among those peoples. He came to the church where the body of the glorious Jerome lay buried and resting, as to a harbor of refuge, and placed himself at the place of burial to pray.

While he remained there for the space of two hours, a certain man inflamed by the spirit of wickedness entered the aforementioned [Col. 0301] church. Finding the holy man engaged in prayer upon the tomb, he ran at him like a dragon and reproached him for continually inciting women’s minds and their lustful desires.

The innocent lamb Sylvanus, rejoicing to be despised, invited him with his customary humility and gentle conversation to say such things to him as often as he wished.

When that worst of robbers heard this, he drew with his shameless right hand the sword hanging at his side from its sheath and raised it in order to plunge it into the throat of the bishop Sylvanus.

But when the venerable bishop opposed him with the words, “Help, glorious Jerome,” the man’s right hand was thrown backward, and the raised sword was plunged into his own throat.

Thus, as was fitting, the utterly wicked man killed himself, so that he fell into the pit which he had dug.

This was marvelous, but what remains is no less wonderful. Another utterly wicked man happened to come along. When he saw what had been done by divine vengeance, he immediately seized the sword, supposing that the man had been killed by the man of God, and attempted to kill Sylvanus.

To avoid excessive detail, what had happened to the first man happened to this one also. Before this second man had yet fallen to the ground, two other men entered the church. Seeing what had happened, but ignorant of the divine judgment, they supposed only that a crime had been committed by the man of God.

One of them, taking the matter more seriously than the other, was inflamed everywhere by the fury of madness. That robber began to cry out as loudly as he could:

> “How long will your wickedness continue? You force women into your lustful pleasures and secretly kill men. Surely today will be the end of your wickedness!”

Suddenly he ran as fast as he could to destroy him, brandishing and drawing his naked sword.

But when Sylvanus, as was his custom, cried out, “Help, glorious Jerome,” that man, like the first two, killed himself with his own hand and sword.

The other man who had come with him, seeing this, trembled at the sight and ran to the church doors. Thinking that it had been done by magic, he began to shout as loudly as he could:

> “Run here, everyone! Behold the magician Sylvanus, the archbishop! He not only disgraces a woman, but by his enchantments he also kills men with all his power!”

When they heard this, an immense crowd of men and women gathered. Their voices beat the air with harsh cries, proclaiming that Sylvanus the archbishop was a most wicked man worthy of burning.

These things reached my ears. Sad and weeping, I went toward so great a monstrosity. The lamb stood among the most savage wolves, raging like famished dogs with no small fury, while he remained mild and joyful, as though he were enjoying prosperity, saying nothing except:

> “I suffer justly, because I have sinned grievously against my God.”

The innocent man was beaten and seized by everyone, so that he might be led to punishment all the more joyfully the heavier the punishment was.

While I tried with my hand to silence the crowd, wishing to calm its excessive fury, I explained the matter; but the more I did so, the more the people were inflamed with anger and rage.

When Sylvanus had been seized and was already being led outside the church, suddenly the glorious Jerome appeared—as it seemed—rising from the place where he lay. He was surrounded by such a great light that rays flashed back from the eyes of those who looked at him. He appeared before everyone in order to give aid to his most devoted bishop. Taking the right hand of the [Col. 0302] venerable Sylvanus in his own right hand, he ordered those who were holding the captured bishop to release him, with a terrible voice.

This apparition was of such power that, before the voice had finished, such great fear suddenly seized everyone that, deprived of all bodily strength, they fell to the ground like dead men.

Meanwhile, a woman overshadowed by an unclean spirit, bound with chains and shackled with iron fetters and handcuffs, was carried to the church by the hands of several men in order to obtain deliverance.

As soon as the woman’s foot touched the threshold, the devil began to utter howls and terrible cries:

> “Have mercy on me, glorious Jerome, for through you I am tormented before the appointed time!”

The glorious Jerome said to him:

> “Accursed spirit, come out of this handmaid of God, and reveal the deceits that you practiced against Sylvanus, showing yourself to all in Sylvanus’s form.”

Then, as the glorious Jerome had commanded, the devil appeared in the form of Sylvanus, so that everyone thought he was Sylvanus the archbishop, and he recounted what he had done in order to defame the servant of God.

When he had said these things, the accursed spirit vanished from the temple with dreadful cries and howls.

When this astonishing matter had been accomplished, the glorious Jerome did not release the bishop’s right hand. In a gentle voice he said:

> “What do you desire, dearest Sylvanus? What would you have me do for you?”

He replied:

> “My lord, do not leave me here any longer.”

The glorious Jerome answered him:

> “Let what you ask be done. Follow me quickly.”

Having said this, he withdrew himself from the sight of all.

After an interval of one hour, Sylvanus the archbishop breathed his last.

Because of this, all were struck by unheard-of amazement and wonder. From every direction a crowd of women and men, as well as children, gathered. The earth was wet with the outpouring of tears, and voices, lamentations, howls, groans, and sighs resounded in Rama. Everyone cried out, asking forgiveness because he considered himself guilty of what he had committed against Sylvanus.

Throughout the following night, the multitude of the peoples did not leave the church. When morning came, and the clergy had prepared for the bishop’s funeral, his body was carried to the church of Nazareth, accompanied by a multitude of people from both that city and the other city, namely Bethlehem.

In that church at Nazareth, we buried the venerable body as was fitting.

There are certainly still many lengthy words and marvelous miracles that fully deserve to be told concerning the merits of Sylvanus, the venerable bishop. But since the field of what remains to be said is exceedingly large, I shall bring the deeds of that venerable bishop to an end, intending to narrate certain other matters no less great in a brief outline of words.

## CHAPTER VI

I think I should relate something sufficiently remarkable, which I learned partly from the report of truthful witnesses and partly by seeing it with my own eyes.

Two very noble men, wealthy in transitory goods, although ignorant of the truth of the Catholic faith, were nevertheless, as men born into pagan observance, sufficiently good. Hearing of the wonders of the glorious Jerome, they set out from the city of Alexandria, having gathered together many possessions and fervently devoted to him, in order to visit the relics of that same glorious Jerome.

When, after beginning their journey, they had entered a certain woodland away from the road, where no traces of human beings or horses could be seen, [Col. 0303] they invoked the name of blessed Jerome and entrusted themselves to his protection. In that same woodland there lived a chieftain of brigands who had under him more than five hundred robbers. He was assigning these men and those to various routes, so that they might kill travelers and bring their spoils back to him and the others.

When this chieftain saw the travelers passing, he summoned three brigands and ordered them to approach and kill them. Eager to fulfill their chieftain’s commands, they took up their weapons and hastened at a rapid pace toward the place where the Alexandrians were walking.

Great indeed were the merits of the glorious Jerome, and great were his miracles—perhaps, I think, such things had never before been seen even by the lesser saints. The brigands hurried forward to slaughter the travelers; but when they drew near, the two whom they had previously seen alone now appeared to be almost innumerable. Among them walked a man surrounded by such great light that it was in no way permissible to look directly at him.

Fear, astonishment, and wonder seized the brigands. They did not know what else to do except return to the other robbers. But when, already at a distance, they were heading back, they again saw only the two men, as before. The brigands were exceedingly amazed; thinking themselves deceived, they began to turn back toward the travelers.

When they had come near, they saw them just as they had seen them before. More and more astonished, and realizing that they had returned to nothing, the brigands turned their backs and quickly came to their chieftain, who was awaiting an account of what they had done.

The chieftain rebuked them, asking why they had taken so long. But when he heard what had happened, he considered them foolish and witless. He summoned twelve other brigands and set out with them toward the travelers.

Again, from a distance, they saw two men; but when they came near, they saw them just as the first brigands had seen them. At once their knees trembled, their hearts faltered, and they became like madmen, deprived of all strength of spirit. Finally recovering themselves, they followed the travelers secretly, eager to learn what would happen next.

The travelers, however, unaware of this, became frightened when they saw the men and anxiously asked one another who they might be. At last, as the day was declining toward sunset and they did not know what they should do during the night, they decided to turn aside toward the twelve brigands, whom they took to be travelers, in order to consult them.

But when they began to make their way toward the brigands, the brigands themselves saw only two men. Taking courage from this, they immediately went to meet the travelers. When all had come together, they greeted one another.

Meanwhile the brigands asked who they were, where they had come from, and where they were going. They replied:

“We are from Alexandria, and we have come from there; we are going to Bethlehem to visit the relics of the glorious Jerome.”

At this the chieftain of the brigands said:

“Who were the men who until now were traveling with you?”

The travelers were astonished that he should speak in this way. They said that, after entering the woodland, they had seen and heard no one except themselves and three other men.

Then the chieftain related to them what had happened, begging them to tell him, if they knew, for what reason this had occurred. [Col. 0304] They replied that they did not know of any other reason except that they had entrusted themselves to the protection of the glorious Jerome.

At this, the Holy Spirit—who breathes where he wills—suddenly inspiring the brigands, they cast aside all the ferocity they had previously possessed. Falling prostrate at the travelers’ feet, they asked pardon for the crimes they had devised and led them to the other brigands.

What I am saying is no less evident to behold. At the first hour of the night they reached the brigands who were waiting for them, explained what had happened, and humbly begged them to go with them to visit the glorious corpse of Jerome, now that their accustomed crimes had been abandoned.

The other brigands mocked these words. They promised their chieftain and the others that they would suffer the harshest death if they dared to speak such things again.

When the travelers did not cease repeating their earlier words, many of the brigands, raging like dogs in their madness, immediately rose against them with drawn swords. They were indeed able to raise their blades; but when the travelers called upon the aid of the glorious Jerome, they were utterly unable to lower their swords, until those who were about to be killed called upon Jerome.

O ineffable clemency of the Savior! In how many ways does he bring those whom he wills to the knowledge of his name?

Suddenly, when that whole gathering of brigands saw this extraordinary event, they offered due praises to God and to the glorious Jerome in loud voices, vowing to visit his relics.

When morning came, more than three hundred men who were then there and who had been committing such deeds left the woodland with the Alexandrians and came to the tomb of the glorious Jerome, recounting to everyone the extraordinary miracles.

The pagan Alexandrians were then baptized; and, trampling underfoot all the vanities of the world, they led a religious life in a certain monastery. Those brigands likewise reached, through divine grace and the merits of the glorious Jerome, the light of truth and a holy and praiseworthy life.

## CHAPTER VII

As I learned from letters specially sent to me from Constantinople concerning this matter, after no long interval of days, almost a similar miracle to the one I have just related occurred to two young Romans who were coming from the city of Rome to Bethlehem to visit the body of the glorious Jerome. I shall relate it as briefly as I can.

When those two young men were approaching a certain estate situated perhaps twelve miles from Constantinople, and before they entered the estate from a distance of two miles, it happened at almost that same hour that two men were killed. When the report of their deaths resounded through the estate, the men of the place gathered from all around and began earnestly to inquire who had killed them.

As they searched diligently everywhere, they saw that no one was present except the aforementioned young men, who had already drawn near. Finding them, they immediately seized them, believing that the men had been killed by them.

The young men, ignorant of what had happened, were astonished and swore with all their strength that they knew nothing of it. But the others counted their words as worthless and hurried to lead them, now captive, to the estate.

Afterward, since jurisdiction over those men did not belong to the inhabitants of the estate, the captured youths were sent with accusations to the authority of Constantinople.

To avoid prolonging the account with words: [Col. 0305] although they had not committed the deed, the young men were made to confess through the severity of torture, and, as was customary, the sentence of beheading was added.

Alas, what heart, hearing so many lamentations of innocent men—whom the greatest beauty of youth, physical loveliness, and noble birth adorned—could restrain itself from tears?

Thus the young men wept, wetting their pale faces with heavy tears, and did not cease uttering cries, groans, and sighs:

“Glorious Jerome,” they said, “is this the sort of reward you grant to those who obey you? Is this what we have earned through the labor of our journey? Alas, Rome, aware of our birth, we did not believe you would be ignorant of the end awaiting us.”

The innocent youths were led to the place of such punishment, where a very great crowd of the local inhabitants was waiting.

O ineffable mercy of our God, with which heaven and earth overflow, who forgets to show mercy to no one who runs to him!

Kneeling at the place where they were to be punished, both youths raised their hands to heaven and said in a loud voice:

“Glorious Jerome, harbor of our salvation and aid, most healthful and life-giving anchor of our hope, incline your compassionate ears at this hour to our unworthy prayers. If we have not committed the crime for which we are being punished, may we experience, according to your accustomed compassion, the resources of your deliverance. But if we have committed it, let us be condemned as justice requires.”

When they had said this, they extended their necks to the executioners, saying nothing except: “Help, help, glorious Jerome!”

What wonder is it if Jerome, compassionate helper of all who run to him, could not refrain from showing mercy amid so many tears, when he moved the hearts of all who stood by, even those of the executioners, to compassion?

The executioners raised their swords and struck the youths’ necks. Their necks received the marks of the blows as though they were porphyry stones.

The executioners were astonished, believing that they had missed their blows. Again they raised their swords as high as they could and struck; but then, as before, the youths’ necks remained insensible.

Again and again they struck, but the swords never injured the youths, as though they were mere wisps of straw.

Amazement arose among those standing by, and the greatest astonishment seized them all. Crowds gathered from every side to witness so extraordinary a sight.

The one who had pronounced the sentence heard of it and ran there. He ordered the executioners to strike again in his presence; yet the youths’ necks remained entirely unharmed.

The judge became increasingly astonished. Knowing nothing of such a miracle, he could think of no explanation except to suppose that magic was involved.

He therefore ordered his servants, without any delay, to hand the naked youths over to the flames of a pyre, where they were to be burned.

A great fire was immediately kindled around them. Oil and pitch were poured onto the wood so that their lives might be destroyed more quickly.

What wonder is it if the glorious Jerome, who had proved able to protect his own from swords, could also rescue from the flames the youths who called upon him persistently?

The flames of the fire rose enormously upward. But the youths, standing beneath the wings of the glorious Jerome, remained safe, as though they were resting in a pleasant and delightful garden.

After this, the judge, wishing to determine more certainly whether the event should be attributed to miracles or to magic, decided that if the youths lived while hanging for eight days, they should then be released and allowed to go wherever they wished.

[Col. 0306] They were therefore hanged at once. The presence of the glorious Jerome was by no means absent: holding the soles of their feet in his hands, he mercifully preserved them unharmed and alive for the appointed days.

On the eighth day men from the entire city and from the neighboring villages ran there; the judge also came. They clearly witnessed the glorious miracle, while those appointed to guard the youths revealed what they had seen.

Everyone was astonished and, in loud voices, offered praises to the Creator and to the glorious Jerome.

The innocent youths were immediately taken down from the gallows and honored by the entire people with the greatest marks of respect.

They had entered the city of Constantinople as captives and in the deepest sorrow; they left as free men, honorably and with indescribable joy.

At last, with God’s approval, accompanied by many people from Constantinople, they reached Bethlehem and visited the relics of the glorious Jerome with the honor due to them.

Immediately abandoning every worldly concern, they entered the monastery in which the glorious Jerome had lived. Devoting themselves day and night to penance and prayers, they still remain in that monastery, living a renowned life of evident holiness.

## CHAPTER VIII

The preceding miracle of the youths was a cause of great wonder, joy, and devotion; but the following event is a cause of great fear, especially for those established in sacred orders.

In the upper Thebaid, it is said that two years ago there was an outstanding and wealthy monastery of women, adorned with every beauty and excellence. Nearly two hundred women lived there, honorable in life, continuously enclosed in religious observance, and distinguished by virtuous conduct.

Let those who possess these things fix their ears upon them, lest what one ear has heard the other pour out. However sound and intact a ship may be, it is of little or no use if, wishing to cross the deep sea, it leaves a small hole in its bottom through which it cannot avoid dreadful shipwreck.

Why I have said this, the story of the present narrative will disclose.

The aforementioned monastery, powerful in many virtues, retained one very evil fault by which it fell: the sin of simony. For, at the devil’s instigation, this abuse was observed among those women: if they wished to receive someone as a nun, they accepted her not so much with regard to charity, mercy, and the goodness of the woman to be received as with regard to money.

No one could enter the monastery to remain there unless a fixed amount of money accompanied her.

In that monastery there was a certain religious woman, an elderly lady, who from her infancy had lived for God, detached from all earthly filth through fasts and prayers. She greatly abhorred that vice.

One night, while she was engaged in prayer as usual, the glorious Jerome appeared to her, illuminating that place with immense light. He commanded her to go in the morning to the abbess and the other nuns of that monastery, announcing that unless they withdrew their hand from the sin that had now grown old among them, they should expect divine vengeance at once.

Having said this, he disappeared.

Terrified by the extraordinary vision, the religious woman spent the entire night sleepless, eagerly turning over in her mind who he might have been who had commanded such things to be announced.

[Col. 0307] At daybreak she gathered all the nuns in the chapter house, after ringing the little bell.

While they wondered why they had been summoned to the chapter house with such urgency, the religious woman rose among them and disclosed to all what she had seen and heard.

The nuns immediately mocked her. They called her a fool and chattered amid many derisive jokes that perhaps she had dreamed this because of excessive drunkenness.

She, however, accepting the insult and arming herself with the shield of patience, grieved deeply over their obstinacy but rejoiced in her own humiliation. She returned to her customary prayers, continually begging that what she had heard might not befall her fellow nuns.

After ten days had passed, the same glorious Jerome appeared again to the religious woman in the middle of the night while she was engaged in devout prayer concerning this matter. In a kindly address he commanded her once more to announce fearlessly to the nuns what she had previously announced.

She said to him:

“Who are you, Lord, who command me to say such things?”

He replied:

“I am Jerome.”

And he vanished from her sight.

Knowing their hardness, she did not know what she should do or say. Nevertheless, preferring to be considered insane and drunk by the nuns rather than to oppose divine commands, she gathered the nuns again and wished to tell them what she had seen and heard.

But when the wicked nuns saw her rise, ignorant as they were of the divine judgment that was soon to come upon them, they left the chapter house with loud laughter before she could begin to speak.

Moreover, after three further days had passed, the glorious Jerome appeared in the middle of the night to the religious woman while she slept, surrounded by an ineffable company of angels. He awakened her and immediately ordered her to leave that monastery and not await the judgment that was soon to come.

When she begged him with many tears not to let this happen, the glorious Jerome said:

“Go to the abbess and the others without delay and announce to them that unless they repent, they will feel divine vengeance this very night. But if they remain in their obstinacy, leave at once and do not remain any longer in the monastery.”

Having finished, he departed.

When the religious woman heard this, anxious and filled with sorrow, she went to the chapter house and began to ring the bell violently so that the nuns might come there.

The abbess awoke from sleep and, realizing that the bell had been rung by this woman, hurried angrily to the chapter house. When she saw her, she rebuked her with dreadful threats, refused to hear a single word, and promised that unless she stopped doing this, she would not remain with her any longer in the monastery.

The religious woman said to her:

“Please do not delay in doing what you promise. Know for certain that I shall not remain in this place any longer. The glorious Jerome appeared to me and revealed only that judgment was immediately to come upon this monastery.”

When the abbess heard this, she began to mock her, thinking that she was speaking with a deranged mind. Calling the doorkeeper, she ordered her to drive the woman out of the monastery at once. She instructed her that, after leaving her outside for some time, she should later allow her to reenter, so that she might cease from the works she had begun.

The religious woman was glad about this. As quickly as she could, she left the monastery, [Col. 0308] drenched in tears and filled with sorrow over what she knew would happen to it.

For God is terrible, strong, and mighty. Who can resist him?

Alas, why do people not fear him, knowing that they cannot in any way escape from his hands, so that his great and indescribable judgment may not overtake them? Let such wretched examples at least terrify them.

Let those who trust in their riches, and who provoke the Most High Lord to anger through the dryness of their greed, hear what judgment was hurled from heaven against this monastery, because God had turned his face away from it on account of its money.

The religious woman had almost crossed the threshold of the door when suddenly the entire monastery collapsed, crushing all the nuns, so that not one of them remained alive.

The religious woman, however, still lives with exceptional holiness in a certain venerable monastery of women in the lower Thebaid.

## CHAPTER IX
