I considered it fitting to join to the miracles already related certain other manifestations of God’s evident judgment against sinners, so that perhaps, under the pressure of so many indications, the stubborn hearts of sinners—harder than stone—might be changed into hearts of flesh, and, when they saw themselves becoming beasts on account of their sins, might strive through reason and self-knowledge to become human beings.

For when human beings cast aside the reason by which they are human, they are reduced below brute animals.

One day a certain Greek heretic was publicly disputing with a priest in the Jerusalem church. When the priest, defending his side, cited an authority of the glorious Jerome in order to refute the Greek’s arguments, the wicked Greek, with reckless and poisonous speech, did not blush to say aloud that Jerome, the light of all truth, had been a liar.

But because he had perpetrated such wickedness with his voice, from then on he formed no voice whatsoever.

## CHAPTER X

Furthermore, another wicked heretic of the Arians, during a disputation, replied with reckless insolence to a man who brought forward the authority of the glorious Jerome against him:

“He lies.”

Immediately he was struck by divine vengeance. For before he had even finished the word aloud, he did not cease crying out throughout the entire day without interruption:

“Have mercy on me, glorious Jerome, for I am tormented by you with the harshest punishments!”

Crying this out throughout the whole day with as loud a voice as he could, he died miserably at the hour of compline, in the sight of all who had gathered to witness it.

## CHAPTER XI

May the merciful Lord bring an end, before my death, to another heretic of the poisonous Arian heresy.

When he saw an image of the glorious Jerome in the church of Zion, he said:

“If only I had held you in my hands while you were alive, for I would have slaughtered you with my sword.”

As soon as he had said this, he drew his sword and drove it with all his strength into the throat of the image.

How great was this Jerome, who performed so many miracles, and to whom no one appears comparable according to his deeds! The heretic was indeed able to drive the sword with his right hand into the feeble throat of the image; but he was utterly unable to pull either the sword from the image or his hand from the sword until the matter became known.

Immediately a stream of blood flowed from the place struck, as though from the body of a living man, and it has never ceased to flow down to the present, [Col. 0309] for the miracle to be proclaimed.

At the very hour when this had happened, the same glorious Jerome appeared to the judge, who was standing in the atrium, with the sword fixed in his throat. He demanded that vengeance be exacted for such an offense and explained what had been done to him. Having said this, he departed.

The judge, astonished, hurried to the church with the others who were present. There he found the heretic holding the sword with his hand, fixed in the throat of the image. As soon as they saw him, the heretic was able to remove his hand from the sword.

The heretic remained obstinate. He babbled that he was sorry for nothing except that he had not held Jerome alive. The crowd then slaughtered him with stones, sticks, swords, and spears.

## CHAPTER XII

My nephew John, whom you know, resplendent in every beauty, whom I adopted in place of a son—I think I told you yesterday what happened to him. Nevertheless, so that the matter may be more firmly committed to memory, I shall not pass over it in silence.

Two years ago the same John was captured by the Persians and sold to the ministers of the Persian king. Because of his outstanding beauty, he was assigned to perform services for the king.

After he had remained for a year at the royal court with no little sorrow and distress, on the same day of the year’s cycle, while serving the king at dinner, he could not restrain himself from tears because of his grief.

When the king saw this, he eagerly asked him the reason for his tears. After learning it, he ordered certain soldiers to guard him in a particular fortress.

The following night, while he was in that fortress, drenched on every side with bitter tears, the glorious Jerome came to him in a dream. Taking his hand, as it seemed to him, he led him with him to the city of Jerusalem.

When he awoke in the morning, he thought that he was still being held by soldiers in the house in the fortress; but he found himself in the place where I live.

Struck with astonishment and almost out of his mind, he could not discern whether he was in the fortress or in my dwelling. Finally recovering himself, he raised his voice and awakened the household that was sleeping.

The servants then ran to me, announcing with indescribable joy that John was present. I hurried there in disbelief and saw before me the man whom I had thought was bound among the Persians.

When he related what had happened to him, the greatest praises were offered to God and to the glorious Jerome.

## CHAPTER XIII

A certain religious woman, almost the most beautiful of all women, young in age but very mature in the wisdom of her spirit, most devoted to blessed Jerome, still lives, as I believe, in a monastery of women of great holiness. It is said that the event you are about to hear happened to her.

Let this woman be an example to others who never cease running here and there through streets and alleyways, ensnaring the souls of foolish men by their appearance. The devil catches souls in no net as numerous as those he catches in the most evil snare of women.

This religious woman, as the testimony of all the women confirms, never set foot outside her cell unless the greatest necessity compelled her. [Col. 0310] She performed no other activity except to devote herself to prayers, occupy herself with reading and meditation, restore her body through sleep, or work with her hands at some task, while always meditating upon sacred Scripture.

The ancient, hardened serpent, the devil, envying these works and wishing to draw her away from her holy purpose, inflamed the mind of a certain very noble young man with such desire for that religious woman that he could think of nothing else, day or night, except how he might reach her.

Blinded around the monastery of the true light, he continued to go there and could find no other remedy. He was so darkened by the cloud of his ignorance that, often seeing himself disturbed by his destructive passions, he wished to cast himself into the water and drown.

The foolish young man was bound day by day by the chain of his foolish love. He did not dare to let this reach the religious woman’s ears, because of her chastity.

Having been deprived of every other means of achieving this, he found a certain magician who practiced demonic sorcery and wicked incantations by his arts. He approached him and promised a large sum of money if he experienced what he desired.

The sorcerer then summoned a demon by his spells and, for the purpose of deception, sent it swiftly in the middle of the night to the holy nun.

When the demon approached the cell, it was unable, because of great fear, to cross the threshold beyond the image of Jerome painted inside the cell.

A remarkable thing, Augustine: as numerous examples make clear, such fear of the glorious Jerome exists in the devil that he does not dare appear even before his painted image. For if a precious image is shown to a possessed body, the devil is immediately driven away from it.

Thus, despairing of completing the wicked task assigned to it, the evil spirit returned to the one who had sent it and explained that access to the nun had been denied because of the image of the glorious Jerome painted in the cell. The magician mocked it and dismissed it.

Then he summoned another demon and sent it as quickly as possible to complete such a task. The same thing happened a second time as had happened at first.

The second demon remained there perhaps for an hour. Then, compelled, it began to cry out in a loud voice:

“Jerome, if you allow me to depart from here, I shall not return here again.”

The woman, astonished, had been engaged in prayer in her cell. She asked with great fear who was uttering these cries.

The devil did not cease shouting in this way. The nuns of that monastery were awakened, struck with fear, and trembling greatly, ran to her cell, with the Lord’s cross going before them.

When they learned that it was an evil spirit, they adjured it to tell them for what reason it had come.

The devil related the whole matter and, revealing itself through groans and howls, declared that Jerome was holding it bound with fiery chains. It begged them to obtain permission for it to depart through their prayers.

When the nuns heard this, they returned praises to God and to the glorious Jerome, humbly asking that he drive the demon from the monastery so that it would never return.

Hardly had they finished the words of their prayer when the devil withdrew from that place with great shrieks and went to the magician. Seizing him, it flogged him with such severe blows and torments that for many hours scarcely any sign of life appeared. It cried out terribly:

“You were the cause of my torment, sending me to that nun. Certainly I shall exact vengeance upon you through these same beatings.”

Amid such dreadful blows, when the magician saw himself almost near destruction, and realized that his own arts could provide him no help, he turned, now shipwrecked, to the harbor of every refuge, the glorious Jerome: [Col. 0311]

“Glorious Jerome,” he said, “come to the aid of this wretched man who runs to your mercy, and do not deny him the great gifts of your customary compassion. For I promise that if, aided by your help at this hour, I do not succumb to such terrible destruction, I shall henceforth, stripped of every deceit, never depart from your service.”

When he had finished, the evil spirit vanished from him like smoke.

For a year the magician lay there, so powerless in his body because of the beatings that he could move only with another’s assistance.

Afterward, having received a penance, and before rising from his bed, he burned all the books with which he had practiced those most wicked arts. He sold everything he possessed and distributed the proceeds to the poor. When the year had been completed, he shut himself away in a certain cave in the desert to perform his penance. In that cave the glorious Jerome had once lived for four years. There he flourishes in great holiness of life and in the austerity of penance.

Let all young men run here, I beg, and learn from the example of the mad young man, lest they later regret that what happened to him has happened to them.

The mad young man, bound by so many snares of lust, saw himself completely deprived of the object of his most wretched and abominable desire. One night he hanged himself with a noose, and thus the unhappy man deprived himself both of temporal life and of eternal life.

Behold how clearly the most shameful vice of lust is the cause of so many evils. I consider no crime so ready to bring ruin upon soul and body alike as this most wicked offense. From it arise murders, drunkenness, quarrels, and almost every evil, as is evident from the countless examples of the Old and New Testaments and is also demonstrated by constant and manifest experience.

Moreover, so that young men may be given greater prudence for guarding themselves—for no condition is more dangerous than that of foolish youth—I have decided, though with great sorrow, to add another example concerning my nephew Rufus, perhaps eighteen years of age.

## CHAPTER XIV

There is no doubt that what I am beginning to relate is recalled to my memory amid great tribulations. Nevertheless, as has been said, because it may serve as an example to everyone, and especially to young men, I cannot pass it over in silence.

A certain nephew of mine, named Rufus, deprived of both parents when he was one year old, came into my hands. If only he had never emerged from his mother’s womb, so that what he suffered might not have happened to him.

I raised him with such care, to his own misfortune, that many thought he had been begotten by me. As the unhappy boy grew older, he increased in age but not in wisdom. He possessed immense bodily beauty but not beauty of soul; although adorned, in vain, with dignity, honorable and good conduct, and the elegance of much wisdom, he was cherished by everyone with excessive affection.

In the eighteenth year of his age, weak and most wretched, he died.

On his account such mourning resounded from everyone that it could scarcely come to an end for a month. But mourning was certainly insufficient for what had happened.

Because I was devoted to him with excessive affection, I repeatedly begged the glorious Jerome to reveal to me what had happened to my nephew. The glorious Jerome therefore assented to my prayers, and I obtained what I desired.

One day, while I was praying [Col. 0312] at the ninth hour, such a stench arose that I could not endure it in my nostrils. As I silently considered this with myself and wondered where such a great stench could be coming from, I raised my eyes above my head and saw my unhappy nephew in a terrifying vision, so dreadful that I did not dare fix my gaze upon him.

For bound with fiery chains, he burst forth with the most foul flames like a furnace.

At this vision such violent fear suddenly seized me that, although I repeatedly wished to speak, I was utterly unable to form my voice.

Finally recovering myself somewhat, I began to ask in a trembling voice whether he was my nephew.

He replied amid howls and sighs:

“Would that I had not been, so that I might not have been assigned to such dreadful torments. For know that I shall remain forever in the dwellings of Tartarus.”

Alas, what shall I say? After he had spoken these words, such grief came upon me that I have often wondered how I did not immediately depart from this life.

After our long conversation had ended, I asked him why he had been so deprived of divine mercy, since in the world he had abounded in so many virtues.

“Know,” he said, “that I was condemned for no other reason except that I took the greatest delight in games. But because, at death, I foolishly postponed receiving and confessing penance as I ought, I did not deserve to obtain divine pardon.”

Having said this, he vanished from my sight.

After he departed, such a stench remained that no one has dared to enter that place down to the present.

Behold how greatly the eyes of the divine Majesty abhor the most shameful crime of games.

Let us therefore fear lest such a sudden death seize us bereft of good works, lest we fail to repent of our vices while time remains; for afterward repentance would be useless.

Therefore, so that the wickedness of gaming may flee far from Christians, lest it bring so great a ruin—or rather, so that it may be erased from the memory of all—I shall add several other examples as briefly as I can.

## CHAPTER XV

In Samaria, before fifteen days had passed, a certain wretched man, while playing and having apparently consumed everything he could possess, began to blaspheme the name of the glorious Jerome with reckless insolence.

He had scarcely finished the wicked words of blasphemy when, before the eyes of everyone, who stood astonished, lightning came immediately from heaven and killed him.

## CHAPTER XVI

The following happened to three other men who were playing in Tyre, as I shall relate.

When they wished to begin their game, they said, according to those who claim to have heard this from them and to have seen the entire sequence of events themselves:

“Exert whatever force you can, Jerome, for against your will we shall cheerfully finish this game.”

After saying these things, they began their game. When it had scarcely begun, almost in the space of a single instant, the earth opened beneath them and swallowed them alone, so that nothing more was ever seen of them.

### Chapter XVII

What is known by sight is confirmed by the most trustworthy testimony. Therefore, although what I say could be confirmed by very many witnesses, I shall nevertheless confirm it through myself as witness, since I learned these things by personal vision.

Near my dwelling in Jerusalem there lived a certain most noble soldier, exceedingly wealthy in passing possessions. He had one son, and, struck blind by the blindness of a most foolish love for him, he not only failed to correct him from his wicked ways but even tried himself to instruct him in them. Foolish parents and those like them, please direct the eyes of your minds here, so that they may not remain ignorant of what the end will be. For many people have fallen into great ruin of soul and body through the foolishness of wicked parents.

As the soldier’s son grew, deprived of every good moral habit, losing all his time from day to day in perjury, games, blasphemies, and every impurity, at his father’s instigation, he reached the age of twelve. One evening, while engaged in his customary games with his father, and while the game was not proceeding as it increased in intensity, he suddenly burst into these words:

“If that Jerome can do anything—he who forbids games to be played—let him do it now; for, against his will, I shall not rise from here except as victor.”

While he was pursuing these words, an exceedingly evil spirit, in the form of a terrifying man, approached the place where he was playing at a swift pace, in the sight of everyone, and snatched away the unhappy boy. But where he carried him no human being has yet discovered. In my opinion, however, he carried him to Hell.

At that very hour I happened to have placed myself at a window of my house, situated opposite the place where the father and son were staying at play. Thus it was necessary for me to see, with perfectly clear certainty, the whole sequence of that dreadful event.

Let young men therefore learn, during the time of youth—which is superior to all other periods—to support themselves with desirable moral habits, lest a youthful spirit formed by vile and fleeting customs be unable to change its condition in old age. What is written on a new tablet is not easily erased.

Let foolish parents also learn to educate their children by correction and blows. Let them not allow the briars of vice to put down roots that cannot easily be torn out, lest the outcome bring them cause for weeping both here and in the future.

For, unless I am mistaken, there exists an exceedingly narrow road—known certainly to very few and without any ambiguity—by which one arrives at the homeland of eternal joys. The way to perdition, however, is broad and filled with many, indeed almost innumerable, boundaries. Every mortal person builds for himself a pathway toward destruction through his sins.

It is clear that there are many who persist in manifold crimes—not only pagans, but also those washed by the water of holy Baptism. For concerning pagans there is no question that they are condemned. Among these people scarcely any correction is ever observed.

Indeed, I say this comparatively: when good and evil people alike are considered, there is no one who does good, not even one; all follow their own wicked and most depraved pleasures. Consequently, it must be concluded that only the rarest people proceed to the joys of eternal blessedness.

Countless—indeed, almost all—the authorities of Sacred Scripture testify to this, and we could clearly observe countless examples sufficient to demonstrate this truth more fully. This single conclusion must be drawn from all of them, and it cannot be otherwise: no one can reach eternal joys in any way unless, having eradicated not merely some but all vices, he hastens along the path of virtue.

Having now brought this to an end, and as I draw near to the conclusion of this work, I shall briefly introduce certain examples and miracles. I shall first relate two especially marvelous events that I learned from the venerable Nicholas, Archbishop of the Island of Crete, who reported them.

### Chapter XVIII

The same venerable Archbishop, coming to Bethlehem on the day before the feast of the glorious Jerome with immense devotion, in order to visit his relics, which ought to be honored by all honors, did not wish to return, though wholly burning with charity, until he had filled me with extraordinary joy through his most welcome visit.

As though he were bestowing the foremost of gifts, and wished according to his custom to give me the most welcome presents in overflowing abundance, he was not content merely to visit me but deigned to remain with me for several days—and he still remains. May this last a long time. In Christ, my dearest Augustine, the same venerable bishop greets you.

Thus, many times, the same venerable bishop recounted to me, who was eager for his words, that the following event had occurred in the city of Candia.

A certain priest, the custodian of his principal church, an immodest man devoted to lust and drunkenness, departed from this world before a year had been completed. His body was buried in the courtyard of the other priests, so that his punishment might become known to all as an example.

On the following night such a great uproar arose in the church and its cemetery that the inhabitants of that city, awakened by the tremendous noise and seized by immense fear, ran to the church like madmen. They all stood around the church, hearing violent disturbances and the ringing of bells. Some implored divine mercy, asking that it reveal why these things were happening, but they perceived no help in being heard.

When this ceased at dawn, they found everything that had been in the church overturned and apparently damaged everywhere by flames of fire.

Thereupon the bishop mentioned above ordered prayers to be offered by the people and commanded them to await what would happen on the following night. To avoid dwelling too long on the details, the next night a disturbance twice as great and a distress of terror followed.

The people, filled with bitterness and sorrow, seeing that no help came to them from the Lord, remained as though wounded men thrown down to sleep in tombs.

When day began to dawn and everyone had gathered in the church for prayers, the glorious Jerome suddenly entered the church, brighter than the sun by sevenfold radiance. He descended from the altar and, in the sight and amazement of all, remained silently for perhaps an hour.

Then he announced to the astonished people that this had occurred because the corpse of that most wretched priest had been improperly buried in the holy places, as a terror to sinners. He ordered them to disinter the miserable corpse, which after the resurrection of all was destined for the dwellings of Tartarus, and immediately hand it over to the flames to be burned; otherwise, he said, the pestilence that had begun would not depart.

With this, he vanished from the eyes of those watching.

As he had ordered, the rejoicing people immediately carried it out, offering outstanding praise to God and blessed Jerome. Thus the plague ceased. From that time onward they all unanimously began to honor the most blessed Jerome with the greatest devotion.

### Chapter XIX

In the same city there was also a very handsome young man named Titus, upright in morals, brilliant in intellect, born of no ignoble family, extremely wealthy, and placing almost all his devotion and confidence in blessed Jerome.

This young man, shining with the whiteness of virginity, persevered in the purpose of holy virginity with honorable conduct until his twentieth year. At that time, urged on by the wicked counsel of his brother, he despised the most noble jewels of virginity, trampled upon the precious metal of gold, and turned violently toward the filth, mud, and stench of lust. He joined himself in marriage to a certain girl radiant in every bodily beauty.

He became so entangled in the nets of her love that he could scarcely think of anything besides her, and from day to day began to forget the worship of God. But because the wretched man abandoned justice and forgot God, who sustained him, the Lord forgot to show him mercy.

When a year had been completed during which the foolish young man had lived with the girl—not joined to her in marriage but for the fulfillment of lust—his brother, prompted by diabolical cunning and ensnared by love of the girl, having long eagerly sought to enjoy her embraces, at last obtained what he desired.

Young men, come here and learn prudence from this young man’s example.

What had happened became known to the young man, who was the girl’s husband. He kept silent and eagerly considered how he might discover the certainty of the matter. For several days he waited, pretending not to know it.

Then one day he arranged to leave the city and set out abroad. Hiding in the city during the day, he came home in the middle of the night. After the servant girl opened the locks, he proceeded secretly, as they had previously arranged, with her as far as the bedroom where his brother and wife were in bed, and asked that it be opened to him.

They were astonished and, terrified by intense fear, neglected to open the door for the one who knocked. At last, after the bedroom locks had been broken, the young man, inflamed everywhere with anger and overwhelming fury like a burning furnace, first drew his sword and killed his wife. Then, finding his own brother hiding beneath the bed, he killed him.

After these deeds, he left the city and wandered for a long time throughout the world. With certain others he began to rob travelers on the road and even to murder them.

After Titus had been involved in such activities for ten years, the most glorious Jerome appeared to him one day as the light was already declining, in the form of a merchant, as a saving and life-giving refuge. He did this so that Titus might not be deprived of the rewards of the devotion he had once possessed.

For although Titus continually practiced so many detestable and immense vices, he nevertheless retained some devotion to blessed Jerome. He commended himself to him every day and never failed to do something daily in his honor.

When Titus saw the merchant, he summoned his wicked companions to their customary acts of evil and hurried with them toward him. Brandishing their spears, they went to meet Jerome in the guise of a merchant.

Titus immediately attacked him and ordered his companions to hold him until a sword could be thrust into his side. Then he raised the hand holding the sword in order to complete so great a crime.

At this, the glorious Jerome said:

“For the love of Jerome, whom you love, let me be granted a brief permission to speak. Afterwards, if you wish, do what you desire.”

Titus replied:

“For the love of the one whom you have named, permission to speak and to live is granted to you, as you request. Only now set down the merchandise you carry.”

The glorious Jerome said:

“I myself am Jerome, who have come here for your liberation, so that the service you have rendered me might not pass away in vain. Repent now of all the sins you have committed; return to yourself and do not be afraid. Know that until now I have stood before God on behalf of your salvation, both of body and of soul, and have pleaded against the divine justice that was angry with you, so that it might not exercise upon you the punishments you deserve.

“Go, therefore, as quickly as possible along the road of repentance, and now lay aside the works of sin. Otherwise you will no longer have me as your guardian and advocate.”

After saying this, the glorious Jerome disappeared from their sight.

At this Titus, and those who were with him, were so astonished and overcome by fear and wonder that they fell to the ground and could not rise for an hour.

Then suddenly the grace of the Holy Spirit was poured out upon Titus and those who were with him, and heavenly light illuminated them. Immediately transformed into other men, they rejected all the filth of vice and returned to the path of repentance.

Afterward they hurried to remote and unknown caves of the desert and devoted themselves to great bodily austerities and a most holy life.

### Chapter XX

I have learned from the most trustworthy testimony of reliable witnesses that another miracle was performed in the upper regions of Egypt. I consider it appropriate to add it to the preceding miracle as an example for people, and especially for young men, however chaste they may be, so that they may avoid the danger of women.

A certain young monk, handsome, outstanding in uprightness, mature in character, and, as though an old man, a guardian of virginal chastity, was a mirror of holiness to all the monks of that monastery and a most devoted lover of the glorious Jerome.

He had lived in the monastery for twelve years, continually devoting himself to prayers and to the study of the Scriptures. Because he feared for the sake of chastity that his heart might in any way be violated, he detested the sight of women beyond expression, so that he even feared their memory.

The ancient serpent, the devil and enemy of humankind, envying this purpose, stirred up against him, from his long-practiced wickedness, manifold deceits and devices. The worst tempter continually afflicted the young man with the goads of thought and did not cease tempting him day or night for two months.

But the prudent young man, commending himself to the protection of the Lord and of blessed Jerome, for whose love he burned, triumphed with victorious strength. He fortified himself with fasts and prayers and overcame the devil’s assaults.

Young men and old, please gather here and learn especially from this example how great a danger lies in the deceptive beauty of women.

When the treacherous devil, the asp, saw himself overcome by the young man, like a roaring lion he began to seek subtler arts of harming him. Thus a fierce battle arose between them.

On one side the worst enemy built his camp against the young man by his customary cunning; on the other, the young man’s prayers and Jerome’s protection laid the defenses of their camp and despised the enemy’s forces in a noble triumph.

Meanwhile, when his father became dangerously ill and death approached, the young man was compelled to come from the monastery into the city, to his paternal home, for a visit. His father repeatedly proclaimed with loud cries that he would die in the greatest sorrow if he were deprived of seeing his son.

The monk was distressed by this. Fearing that the sight of women might violate his pure heart, radiant with virgin whiteness, he would rather have exercised cruelty toward his father for the Lord’s sake than leave the monastery and show compassion to the sick man—unless he had been persuaded by the pleas of his fellow brothers.

For he knew that nothing was so harmful, detestable, and deadly to a monk as moving through villages and cities and among crowds of people. No peace of mind remains in a person entangled in the words and empty talk of many. What water does for fish, silence does especially for monks.

The monk remained in his father’s house for three days and was afflicted by such intense weariness that he seemed to himself to have been confined in gloomy prisons.

When the third day was completed, as he happened, because of his father’s illness, to be rubbing his father’s legs together with his sister, who was of extraordinary beauty, the sister’s right hand accidentally touched his right hand. Suddenly, at the devil’s instigation, his heart was wounded by such dreadful darts of lust and foolish, abominable desire for that very sister that he almost invited her to unlawful acts, wholly abhorrent to human beings, had the fear of shame not intervened.

Alas, what shall I say? What observance of chastity will remain in those monks who continually feast their eyes upon women while conversing with them?

A man remains chaste while constantly looking at the faces of women just as straw remains standing in fire. Certainly the beauty of a woman is a deceptive fall, close to the greatest ruin, and an unavoidable danger.

The fear that the monk had feared came upon him. What he had dreaded for so long happened to him, and not without a great warning for others.

It was not commanded that parents be obeyed when danger to the soul is feared.

The monk unwillingly left the monastery, but when the heat of such abominable lust inflamed his heart, thinking of nothing except seeing the face of his unsuspecting sister with the wicked gaze of his eyes, he scarcely remembered ever having been in the monastery.

Meanwhile his father recovered. But the monk, inventing excuses, delayed his return to the monastery from day to day.

When he remained in his father’s house for three months, he caused the monks on one side and his father on the other, and the entire household, the greatest astonishment: why had such a violent and unheard-of change and alteration crept over him?

They did not know the cause of the matter and therefore could not understand its effect.

At last he returned to the monastery with two monks sent from it to fetch him, reporting on his return the same weariness that he had brought with him when he departed.

Thus the monk’s body began to live in the monastery, but his heart did not in any way withdraw from his sister. His study of the Scriptures became a means of reaching the worst thing he desired; his contemplation of divine matters became a means of finding how to accomplish his sins.

Alienated from himself and having strayed from knowledge of the truth, he was continually struck by the devil—with new arrows of lust—under whose oppressive yoke he had bowed his feeble neck.

His days faded like smoke; his bones were broken as though in a frying pan; his life was weakened by pains; and he became like an irrational animal.

He entirely forgot to implore divine mercy, thinking all day about what suitable opportunity might appear for him to taste the cup of death.

Alas, how needy and wretched they are, exiled from and lacking every good, who distance themselves from the Lord!

A human being in sin becomes worse than brute animals, from whom God is farther removed in soul than the distance between heaven and earth or between east and west—whereas, when supported by divine grace, he surpasses those same animals.

At last, while the monk was thinking—I do not know by what light of truth—how to find a way to obtain the most abominable pleasure, horrible even to hear of, the devil, sower of evil counsel, secretly insinuated this plan into the empty thoughts of his heart:

In the middle of the dead of night, while everyone was sleeping, he should remove his monastic clothing, put on secular dress, leave the monastery, and secretly approach his father’s dwelling. He should enter the house stealthily at nightfall and hide beneath his sister’s bed until she was asleep; then he should approach her and satisfy his lustful desires.

The counsel pleased his insane and ignorant mind, and he studied with all his strength to put it into effect as quickly as possible.

Accordingly, in the middle of the following night, he hurried silently toward the monastery gates, holding the keys in his hands. But when he reached the doors, he ran about there all night and could not find where they had been placed.

Terrified by astonishment and wonder, and not knowing why this had happened, he was compelled to return to his cell when the hour of morning approached, at which the monks kept vigil for the due praises of the Lord.

He remained in his cell throughout that day in amazement and resolved to do on the following night what he had not done.

A feeble hand dares what it cannot accomplish; a foolish beast hopes to win the glory of triumph while fighting against a lion.

Why do you think foolishly? Do you suppose that a worthless beast can do what the strongest lion, Jerome, opposes?

Cease to bend your knees before the image of the glorious Jerome; cease to salute him any longer, and you will immediately be granted the power to fall into the pit you are digging, so that you may now suffer dreadful shipwreck.

Services rendered to the glorious Jerome cannot, however they are performed, be emptied of their rewards.

That misguided and wandering monk, enslaved to diabolical power, kept in his cell an image of the glorious Jerome marked upon a panel. Each day, according to his ancient custom, he bent his knees before it and commended himself to him several times.

Therefore, so that his wondrous mercy might become known to all, Jerome held him back on that day, preventing him from doing the evil he wished.

The monk, however, did not know this and on the following night again went toward the monastery gates. But what he had done on the preceding night, he did again on this one.

So as not to linger over the details, this happened continually every night for approximately a month.

When, as I think, the month had been completed, blessed Jerome appeared in a dream to a certain most holy monk of that monastery, who was resting in his bed at night. He revealed to him what this monk was doing and commanded him to explain to the erring monk how Jerome had protected him, because of the reverence shown to him, so that he could not see the doors and carry out the crime he had conceived.

He also commanded him to say that unless the monk quickly amended his undertaking, Jerome would withdraw his protection from him. Then he immediately departed from him.

When morning came, the monk told another monk what he had seen. But the other, protesting with several solemn oaths that he did not understand what this meant, began to say that these dreams had arisen from emptiness of the brain.

The monk remained silent and withdrew.

The other rejoiced and resolved that on the following night, showing Jerome no further customary reverence, he would open the monastery gates at his own pleasure and carry out the wicked deed he had desired for so long.

To speak briefly: the wretched man had long contemplated evil with an eager mind. Once deprived of his customary honor toward Jerome, and with the opportunity handed over to him, he carried it out as he wished. Yet even at the end the mercy of the glorious Jerome did not fail.

He left the monastery at night, concealed by another’s clothing, and came to his father’s house. He spent that day wandering around it.

When he had entered the house at nightfall, he secretly approached the bed where his virgin sister was accustomed to sleep. He hid beneath it for as long as he thought he could suppose that she was asleep.

Then he came out, removed his clothing, and lay down beside his sister’s right side.

The sister, sleeping lightly, awoke. Feeling a man beside her with her hand, she was exceedingly terrified and, uttering dreadful cries, summoned everyone to her.

Everyone ran with lights to the girl’s bedroom, and at last they found him lying in the bed.

The parents were astonished and stunned. All who had run there saw the matter and grieved.

The father asked his son the cause of such a grave danger. The son confessed his guilt in silence.

As I have said, the glorious Jerome wished him to experience his own folly, so that afterward he might become humbler and more prudent in taking precautions and defending himself in battle, and so that no one might henceforth trust or rely on holiness because of his example.

For the greater a person’s holiness, while he sails in the stormy sea of this world, filled with enemy forces, in the little ship of weak flesh, the greater must be his fear and prudence in defending himself.

That worst tempter, the devil, possesses innumerable arts of harming. Whoever proceeds carelessly is captured with the greatest ease. Whoever fears in all things is feared by all demons.

Certainly nothing does more harm than walking according to one’s own will after despising the counsel of others. Whoever trusts only his own will will find a hateful end in everything he does.

This example, now completed, clearly demonstrates to us all a great fear concerning our extreme frailty and the devil’s cunning and craft; it also declares the hope of forgiveness for sinners.

When the monk saw himself thus disfigured, deceived, and held captive by the devil in such misery, he immediately recognized, through the aid of the most glorious Jerome—to whom he had always been devoted—his own misery and most grievous guilt. He returned to himself, left his father’s house, abandoned every delay, and hastened, mourning and grieving, to the fountain of repentance.

Afterward, in his monastery, he afflicted himself for two years with such severe abstinence that the human heart would be incapable of imagining it. When the two-year period had been completed, he departed happily from this world only a few days later.

### Chapter XXI

From letters received the day before from the venerable Damasus, Bishop of Porto, I learned with an eager heart certain things written in them, which, out of reverence for him, I shall not omit.

In Rome there was a certain Cardinal named Caelestine, a rival and detractor of the glorious Jerome. One day, while he was in the customary assembly of the Cardinals, he uttered insulting words against Jerome with bold and reckless speech. Suddenly, driven by pain in his entrails, he hurried to the place for the discharge of nature, and all his entrails immediately poured out; before he could leave that place, he expired.

### Chapter XXII

There was also another Cardinal priest, named Andrew—not like the former, but a most devoted worshiper of the glorious Jerome—who died recently in the same city of Rome, with many people standing around him.

His funeral rites, such as are customarily performed for the burial of the bodies of the faithful, had already been prepared in the church. The supreme Pontiff was present with almost the entire clergy and Roman people, who had gathered to honor Andrew.

Amid wailings and repeated groans from the bier, while everyone was astonished and had become almost like madmen, he marvelously rose, as though awakening from the sleep of death.

When the Roman Pontiff had removed the whole people from the great church of blessed Peter the Apostle, closed the doors, and questioned him, he spoke these words:

“While I stood awaiting judgment before the divine tribunal, I was already being condemned to the torments of Tartarus because of the excessive superfluity of clothing and food that I had used until then. Suddenly there came someone brighter than the sun and whiter than snow. Those standing there told one another that this was the glorious Jerome. Bending his knees before the presiding judge, he obtained through his prayers that my soul be joined to my body.”

When he had finished these words, his soul immediately departed from that place and, as you see, was joined to his body.

At this the supreme Pontiff and the others who heard him were amazed. The matter became known to the people waiting outside the church. They immediately broke open the church doors and entered, all praising God and the glorious Jerome with loud voices.

### Chapter XXIII

Great anguish of mind moves and grieves us when we understand that very many bishops deny God and the Lord Jesus Christ, whose place they occupy. Clinging to earthly things, whose god is their belly, they fill the gluttony of their stomachs from the stipends of the poor and the blood of Jesus Christ, consuming the most delicate dishes with actors and other wealthy people, to incite the foulness of lust.

Day by day they abuse themselves with extravagance in clothing, caring nothing for the poor who are dying of hunger and cold, while they devour with the hand of robbery the wages they have snatched from them.

These are certainly not bishops but devils. A bishop is either most holy or a devil.

The episcopal office is certainly a state of great merit, but also of infinite danger. The lightest sin, when charged against others, is charged against a bishop as the gravest. For the vice of a bishop spreads among his subjects by example. The greater the gifts he receives, the greater his account increases.

For however many sheep of Christ stray into sins through the negligence or example of a bishop, for that many he must render an account to the Lord.

Alas, my dearest Augustine, what shall I say? A heavy burden and a heavy load lie upon us. But with my weak shoulders, what shall I carry? Certainly anguishes surround me everywhere and torment me.

When I continually observe the grave dangers ready for me, I am afflicted and grieved by ever-increasing fear.

It is safer to flee the episcopal state than to seek it. I praise the episcopate as the vicariate of our Lord Jesus Christ, but I do not praise those who live in it as soldiers of earthly things, seeking the glory and pomp of the world. Rather, I advise them to flee as far as they can.

It would certainly have been better for them to live among earthly people as earthly people than, while doing these things at the summit of the pontificate, to fall into the lowest and deepest regions of Hell, to be tormented more than others in proportion as they have received more gifts than others.

We understand that very many bishops bear the name rather than the reality: that they are ravenous wolves rather than shepherds of Christ’s sheep; that they are destroyers of Christ’s Church rather than rulers. They plunder the alms of Christians and devour and consume the wages of the poor with wolfish jaws in the excesses of food and clothing.

This is absurd, abominable, and to be lamented.

I have said these things so that such an abomination may become known to all peoples, in order that, if they do not fear God, they may at least fear human beings and be restrained to some degree from their abominations.

Let such bishops, I ask, hear what we propose to narrate, and at least be terrified by the calamities of others.

### Chapter XXIV

In the upper regions of Egypt, in a certain desert uninhabitable to human beings because of the hardships of life, there lived a very old monk named Elias, radiant with great holiness of life. During the life of the most blessed Jerome he had been exceedingly close to him. The same most blessed Jerome repeatedly said that Elias possessed the spirit of prophecy.

One day, as several monks of venerable life and trustworthy faith testified to me—men who said that they had heard these things many times from the mouth of that holy man—Elias was engaged in his customary prayers when sudden sleep came upon him and he dozed for a little while.

And behold, in a vision—by which means Almighty God often discloses great and hidden mysteries to his faithful—he found himself, as it seemed to him, in a palace of marvelous and ineffable beauty, such as mortals had never seen.

As he walked about that palace for an hour, admiring its extraordinary beauty, he saw a tribunal being prepared by certain youths of excessive beauty. Carpets were spread out, and the walls all around were enclosed with fabrics decorated with gold, gems, and great variety of workmanship.

Afterward a certain great and handsome king arrived, accompanied by an assembly of men brighter than the sun. His appearance possessed such sweetness that no one would wish to have anything else. He took his seat to exercise judgment.

Meanwhile the soul of a certain man—whom Elias later understood from some people standing there to have been a bishop of Ancona—was brought before the royal majesty by wicked spirits. It was bound with chains and fiery bonds and emitted sulphurous flames like a furnace.

Before he was questioned about anything, he began to proclaim in dreadful voices that he was entirely worthy of the dwellings of Hell. Among other reasons, he assigned this above all: that, intent upon the empty pomp of the world, he delighted in banquets, clothing, and such follies.

When he had finished, the judge pronounced sentence that he should be handed over to infernal punishments until, once joined to his body, he should suffer double punishments forever. Immediately the entire crowd of wicked spirits carried him away with them and departed from that place amid dreadful cries.

Then the soul of another man—whom Elias likewise understood to have been Theodosius the senator, brother of the aforementioned venerable Damasus, Bishop of Porto—was brought before the royal majesty. Many wicked spirits stood around him, accusing him most severely.

While the devils prolonged their accusation, and no one answered anything on the opposite side, a man seven times brighter than the sun and, as it seemed to Elias, almost more eminent than all the others standing there, who was seated at the king’s right hand, rose to his feet.

When he rose, the king himself ordered silence from everyone with his hand.

Then the one who had stood up, opposing all the accusers, declared that Theodosius had been his most faithful and devoted servant and had continually shown him special reverence. He immediately deprived them of the boldness to speak and marked them with silence.

Afterward he bent his knees before the king and, through his customary piety, infinite mercy, and clemency, obtained for his most faithful servant forgiveness and eternal rest—provided, however, that because of the crimes committed in the world he should be purified in Purgatory—as he wished.

Then the entire multitude of wicked spirits, groaning and howling, immediately withdrew from that place.

After an interval of one hour, a very handsome young man came swiftly through the palace and approached the one who had risen so prominently and gloriously to aid the senator Theodosius. He said that he had been sent by Peter, patrician of the Romans and Jerome’s most devoted servant, so that, hearing his prayers, Jerome might deign to obtain for him a son from the Lord.

At this the king said:

“What Peter asks of my son Jerome shall certainly be done.”

When all these things had been completed, the monk Elias immediately awoke from that sleep, giving immense thanks to God and to the glorious Jerome.

He marked down the day on which he had seen such wonders. Later, on that same day, he learned that the Bishop of Ancona and the senator Theodosius had departed from this world.

From this it is plainly evident that these were not empty dreams.

## CHAPTER XXV

You thought, dearest Augustine, that you would arouse great admiration in some people, as though you were proposing something new and unheard-of, when in your earlier letters, which I received, you demonstrated by arguments undoubtedly effective and by marvelous visions that the most holy Jerome was equal in holiness and glory to John the Baptist and the other Apostles. Certainly there is no real ambiguity: this is entirely true and worthy of every faith and devotion. Nor do I think that anyone who is not ignorant of his most holy life and of his many prodigies, so unfamiliar to human beings, could fail to feel some admiration.

But since your arguments for declaring this truth were such that it would not be fitting for me now to set my very slight and inexperienced efforts alongside them, I shall omit everything else and briefly introduce the remarkable vision which the venerable Cyril, Bishop of Alexandria, affirmed in letters sent to me some days ago that he had seen.

After the glorious death of blessed Jerome, when a year had been completed, on the day of the nativity of the most glorious John, the Lord’s forerunner, after the morning praises had been completed, the aforesaid bishop, as was his custom, being alone in the church before the altar of that glorious forerunner of the Lord, while contemplating his glory and excellence on bended knees with great sweetness of spirit, suddenly fell asleep there for a little while.

And behold, as it appeared most clearly to him, an exceedingly great crowd of extraordinarily beautiful men came into the church in pairs, singing the sweetest alternating chants in wondrous order, beyond human estimation. Then, proceeding in pairs to the altar and bending their knees there, they each took their places to sit. When the church had become very full of these men, after all the others two men more distinguished than the rest, entirely alike and equal, brighter than the sun in its infinite radiance, entered the church together. They were clothed in garments of dazzling whiteness, flashing indescribably everywhere with gold and jewels.

At their entrance, all those sitting in the church immediately bent their knees and paid them the highest reverence. Then, after those two men had received this reverence before the altar, they both sat down together in two golden chairs, adorned with wondrous variety and beauty of precious stones, which certain very handsome young men had prepared for them. They remained silent in this way for a little while.

Meanwhile, after silence had arisen between them, one of the two began urging the other to speak. When a long dispute had arisen between them over who should begin preaching first, they began each to acclaim in loud voices the praises and magnificence of the other—Jerome, those of John, whose solemnity it was that day.

One of them then immediately began his speech. He wove together praises of the blessed forerunner of the Lord with such sweetness of speech, such adornment of words, and such weight of meaning that it would not be lawful for a human tongue to express it.

When that speech had ended, the other, whom all who were present [Col. 0324] called John the Baptist, giving many thanks to him, spoke these words to the bystanders in his honor and glory:

> “This dearest companion of mine, Jerome, equal to me in glory and also equal in holiness, has thus far continued the sequence of my praises. Therefore it is fitting that I should now dwell upon his praises.
>
> “He truly is the light of the Church, dispelling the darkness of errors and illuminating all people who are blind with the radiance of truth.
>
> “He is the fountain of saving wisdom’s water, to which the thirsty approach and are most abundantly satisfied.
>
> “He is a very lofty tree, whose crown rises to heaven. Beneath the foliage of his teaching, from the sweet fruit of his mouth, the birds of heaven—that is, people of great understanding—and the beasts of the earth—that is, people of little understanding—are most abundantly nourished.
>
> “This man was a hermit with me in the world; certainly he mortified his flesh with abstinences no less than I did.
>
> “This man was a shining and pure virgin with me.
>
> “This man was enlightened with me by the prophetic spirit.
>
> “This man was a teacher of truth with me.
>
> “I abandoned bodily life for the sake of justice and truth. Although he did not lose bodily life for the sake of the truth of his justice and exceptionally clear teaching, he nevertheless spent all his time in the world in martyrdom, afflictions, and pain.
>
> “I went before as the messenger of the Christian faith and inviter of the nations; he came afterward and became its supporter and defender against the heretics who were tearing it apart.
>
> “Once, in baptism, I touched Christ the Lord with my own hands in the Jordan. He not only held him many times with his own hands upon the altar, but also ate him with his own mouth.
>
> “He was in every respect equal to me in holiness; now we both rejoice together in an equal reward of eternal life.”

As blessed John continued with these and many other things, which the same blessed Cyril was unable to commit entirely to memory, the first hour of the day had already arrived. The church’s custodian entered and, seeing the bishop asleep, awakened him with his hands.

The bishop awoke, filled with the utmost astonishment, admiration, and joy, and recounted through tears to the custodian what he had seen. Then, celebrating Mass with great solemnity that day, he declared the remarkable vision to the whole people.

## CHAPTER XXVI

There are infinitely more true and useful miracles that could be related than those inscribed in this brief little work. But, lest the length of the work cause any tedium for readers, this work will be brought to completion with a single miracle that took place at Bethlehem less than a month ago.

When the Sunday after the octave of Pentecost had passed, and all my suffragan bishops together with a very great multitude of men and women had assembled in the church in which the most holy body of Jerome rests, with due honor and equally due and devout reverence, I myself, first putting on the sacred vestments, approached the place of the pit in which the venerable body lay. I began to dig out the earth of the burial, so that, after that most sacred body had been removed, it might afterward be placed in a marble tomb, decorated on every side with wondrous beauty, which had been constructed for this purpose.

When the pit was already empty, [Col. 0325] the whole assembly looking on, the most blessed body remained whole in the middle of the pit, as though suspended in the air and touching the earth nowhere; it had not been violated by any corruption. We lifted it from there and, amid such an exceedingly powerful and sweet fragrance as human smell had never experienced, placed it on the altar, so that the people might see the most holy relics.

But I would in no way be capable of explaining how many glorious miracles were performed that day, while I and all who were present stood there. Sixteen blind people, touching those relics with their faces, immediately received their sight. Three especially possessed men, bound in chains and carried into that church by the hands of many people, were immediately freed.

A poor widow’s little boy, her only son, was suffocated in the church by the press of the crowd. When his mother found him, grieving and lamenting, she immediately carried the boy’s corpse in her arms to the pit in which the body of glorious Jerome had been buried. She threw him into the pit, saying these words:

> “Glorious Saint Jerome, I shall not leave this place until you restore to me my only son whom I have lost.”

Truly wondrous is God in his saints, performing unfamiliar prodigies. As soon as the earth touched the body of the dead boy, his soul was joined to it.

A certain man took the body of one of his sons from the grave in which it had lain for three days, brought it immediately to that pit, and threw it into the pit in this way. The young man was at once restored to his former life.

There were almost innumerable [Col. 0326] miracles performed from morning until evening, during which time the glorious body of Jerome, disinterred, remained placed upon the altar. Nevertheless, I shall not proceed farther with miracles of this kind; I shall not be silent about one that occurred on the following night.

## CHAPTER XXVII

In the evening, then, we placed that most sacred body in the monument that we had prepared. But in the morning the monument was found empty, and we found the most holy body restored to its former pit.

While I was greatly astonished by this, blessed Jerome appeared to me in a vision during the following night, while I was asleep, and revealed many great things to me. Among other words, he said this to me:

> “Know, Cyril, that my body will not in any way be removed from the pit in which it lies until the city of Jerusalem has been captured by unbelievers. At that time it will be carried to Rome, where it will rest for a long period.”

Having awoken at this, I recounted to all the bishops and to the other Catholic men what I had seen. I do not otherwise know what these things mean or when they will occur.

If I have said anything useful or good in this letter, let it be attributed not to my merits but to those of the most glorious Jerome. But if anything is excessive, useless, or bad, let everyone judge that this happened solely because of my foolishness and negligence.

Remember me, dearest Augustine, in your prayers.

[Col. 0325]

# THE LETTERS OF SAINT EUSEBIUS HIERONYMUS, PRESBYTER OF STRIDON, ARRANGED ACCORDING TO THE ORDER OF TIME WITH THE GREATEST ACCURACY AND DIVIDED INTO FOUR CLASSES (C, S)

## FIRST CLASS

Containing chiefly the letters written from the wilderness of Chalcis, from the year of Christ 370 to 380.

## LETTER I

[Note: Also numbered 49. Written around the year 370.]

### TO INNOCENTIUS

[Note: Older printed books incorrectly have “to Pope Innocentius.” For this is a different Innocentius, who joined Jerome as his companion in Syria and died there two years later. See Letter 3, note a, to Rufinus.]

### ON THE WOMAN STRUCK SEVEN TIMES

[Col. 0325]

Jerome relates to Innocentius, at his request, the history of a certain miracle that occurred at Vercellae in Liguria during his own lifetime. A certain woman, falsely accused by her husband of adultery, and a young man denounced together with her, are tortured to extract the [Col. 0326] truth. Unable to bear it, the young man confesses what he had not done; she steadfastly denies it and cannot be brought by any force to confess a crime she had not committed. Both are led to execution. The young man is killed, but the woman, though struck repeatedly, cannot die. At last, when she appeared to have succumbed to death, the body that had been removed comes back to life; and when she is again demanded for execution, Evagrius obtains her pardon from the Emperor through his prayers.

### 1

You often asked me, dearest Innocentius, not to remain silent about the [Col. 0327] miracle of that event which occurred in our own age. When I modestly and truthfully—so I now discover—denied that I could do this, and distrusted my ability to accomplish it, whether because every human speech is inferior to heavenly praise, or because leisure, like a kind of rust upon the mind, had dried up even the small power of my former eloquence, you, on the contrary, maintained that in divine matters one ought to look not at ability but at intention; and that words cannot fail the person who has believed in the Word.

[Note: Alternatively, “in the things of God”; shortly afterward the Veronese manuscript reads “to lack a word.”]

### 2

What, then, shall I do? I do not dare deny what I cannot fulfill. I am placed as an inexperienced passenger upon a cargo ship. And I, a man who has not yet steered a small boat (*scalmus*) on a lake, am entrusted to the breakers of the Euxine Sea.

[Note: For *scalmum*, some codices read *clavum* (“rudder”), others *scapham* (“boat”). It is clear that *scalmum*, a smaller skiff, is elegantly contrasted with the larger cargo vessel.]

Now, as the lands vanish from sight, there is heaven on every side and sea on every side:

> “Now sea and sky on every side”  
> (*Aeneid* V).

Now the wave bristles beneath the darkness, and in the blind night of storms the foaming waves grow white.

You urge me to hang up the swollen sails, loosen the ropes, and guide the helm. I already obey your command; and because love can do everything, I shall trust the Holy Spirit to continue the voyage, expecting consolation in either outcome. If the storm drives me into the harbors I desire, I shall be thought an inadequate helmsman; if my unpolished speech stops amid the rough turns of the argument, you may perhaps seek ability, but you certainly cannot demand willingness.

[Note: Latinius prefers *humida* (“moist”) to be read.]

[Note: Martianus has *attulerit* (“has brought”); Victorius, who is weaker, does not have the following word. The passage will be more complete if that word is referred either to the following clause by changing the punctuation, or if, with a negative particle prefixed, it is read as: “I shall not be thought an inadequate helmsman.” But all manuscripts and printed editions have the reading we have published.]

### 3. Vercellae, a City of the Ligurians

Vercellae, a city of the Ligurians situated not far from the roots of the Alps, once powerful, is now half-ruined and sparsely inhabited. When the governor visited it according to custom, he confined a certain little woman who had been brought before him together with her alleged adulterer—for her husband had brought this charge against her—in the horror of a penal prison.

Not long afterward, when the bloodstained claw was striking livid flesh and pain was seeking the truth through furrowed sides, the most wretched young man, wishing to avoid long tortures by taking the shortcut of death, lied against his own blood and accused the other person. Miserable beyond all others, he seemed rightly to be struck because he had left the innocent woman nothing by which she could deny the charge.

But the woman, weaker in sex and stronger in courage, when the rack stretched out her body and filthy hands, reeking of the prison, were restrained behind her back by bonds, raised her eyes—which alone the torturer could not bind—to heaven. As tears flowed over her cheeks, she said:

> “You are my witness, Lord Jesus, to whom nothing is hidden, who searches the kidneys and the heart. I do not wish to deny this because I fear perishing, but I do not wish to lie because I fear sinning.”

[Col. 0328]

> “But you But you, most wretched man, if you hasten to die, why are you killing two innocent people? I too desire to die; I desire to cast off this hated body, but not as an adulteress. I offer my throat; I receive the flashing blade without fear, yet I shall carry my innocence with me. No one dies who is killed in such a way as to live.”

[Note: Victorius likewise has “I do not wish to deny God,” but this is corrupt. We do not record certain other matters of lesser importance.]

[Note: We have altered the passage on the unanimous authority of all the manuscripts, including those examined by the Benedictine editor. Previously it read *jussus est* (“he was ordered”) and *qui* instead of *quia* (“who” instead of “because”). Shortly afterward Victorius read *sexu fortior suo* (“stronger in his own sex”) instead of *sexu infirmior, virtute fortior* (“weaker in sex, stronger in courage”), which is found in the manuscripts and in other printed editions.]

### 4

Then the governor, his eyes glutted with blood like a wild beast that, once it has tasted blood, always thirsts for it, orders the tortures to be doubled. Gnashing his teeth savagely, he threatened a punishment like that of the executioner unless the weaker sex confessed what masculine strength had been unable to conceal.

### 5

Help, Lord Jesus! For one of your people how many punishments have been devised. Her hair is tied to a stake; with her whole body bound more tightly to the rack, fire is placed close to her feet; the executioner pierces both sides, and no respite is granted even to her breasts.

The woman remains unmoved and, overcome in spirit by bodily pain while enjoying the goodness of her conscience, forbids the tortures to rage around her. The cruel judge is lifted up as though defeated; she entreats God. Her limbs are loosened from their joints; she raises her eyes to heaven. As though another were confessing a common crime, she denies on behalf of the confessor; while herself in danger, she vindicates another who is in danger.

[Note: The old reading incorrectly had *separato* (“separated”). Barthius, in his *Adversaria*, not idly argues that the little word ought to be transposed and the passage read *et dolore corporis a spiritu superato* (“and with bodily pain overcome by the spirit”), so that the meaning is that bodily pain was overcome by the spirit, not the reverse. But the manuscripts do not support this.]

### 6

There is meanwhile one cry:

> “Kill, burn, tear me apart—I did not do it. If faith is removed from words, the day will come that will carefully distinguish this crime. I have my judge.”

[Note: I would prefer to read *judicem Deum* (“God as my judge”), as in the letter to the deacon Julian: “I shall not fear human judgment, having God as my judge.”]

Now the exhausted torturer was sighing into a groan, and there was no place left for a new wound. Now his savagery defeated, he shuddered at the body he had mangled.

At once the governor, stirred to anger, said:

> “Why are you astonished, bystanders, if the woman prefers to be tortured rather than die? Adultery certainly cannot be committed without two people, and I consider it more credible that a guilty woman denies the crime than that an innocent young man confesses.”

### 7

A sentence having therefore been pronounced equally against both, the executioner drags away the condemned. The entire populace pours out to the spectacle, so that the city seemed virtually to be migrating; the crowd surges through the packed gates and grows dense.

The sword immediately cuts off the wretched young man’s head at the first blow, and the headless corpse rolls in its own blood.

But when they came to the woman, and, with her knees bent to the ground, the flashing sword was raised above her trembling neck, the executioner drove his extended right hand with all his strength. At the first touch of the body, the deadly blade stopped and, merely grazing the skin, sprinkled a little blood from the scratch.

[Col. 0329]

[Note: From an ancient copy Gravius has: “With a slight scratch he sprinkled the powerless hand with blood. The striker was terrified.”]

The executioner was terrified by the powerless hand. Amazed at his defeated right hand and the sword growing dull, he turned it for a second attack.

[Note: Veronese manuscripts and others have *iratus* (“angry”); for the words which some add before it, *sine bello* (“without a fight”), are a glossator’s error.]

Again the languid blade slipped down toward the woman, and, as though the iron feared to touch her, it became harmlessly numb around her neck.

Thus the lictor, raging and panting, with his cloak twisted back around his neck, while expending [or: releasing and applying] all his strength, shook to the ground the clasp that fastened the edges of his military cloak, and, unaware of what had happened, balanced his sword over the wound.

The woman said:

> “Look, gold is falling from your shoulder. Pick up what was acquired with much labor, lest it be lost.”

### 8

Good God, what security is this? She does not fear the death hanging over her; she rejoices when struck. The executioner grows pale. Eyes that do not see the sword see only the clasp. And, as though it were not enough that she did not fear death, she provides a benefit to the man who is raging against her.

The third blow had now also frustrated the sacrament of the Trinity.

[Note: Older printed editions incorrectly have: “The third blow had frustrated the sacrament of the Trinity.” The reading restored by Martianus is confirmed by our manuscripts. Yet he had read *speculator* (“watcher”) incorrectly instead of *spiculator* (“executioner”). Gravius decided that the passage should read: “Now the third blow had frustrated the sacrament of the Trinity.”]

The executioner, terrified and no longer trusting the iron, fitted the blade to her throat, so that what could not cut might at least, under the pressure of his hand, be buried in her body. O event unheard-of throughout all the ages! The sword bends back toward its hilt and, as though defeated while looking upon its master, confessed that it could not strike.

### 9

Bring me here, here, the examples of the three boys who, amid the cold globes of flame, uttered hymns instead of tears (Dan. 3). Around their *saraballa*—that is, their head-coverings—and their holy hair, the harmless fire played.

[Note: In several printed editions and manuscripts the word is written with *r*, *sarabara*, as are the Septuagint form *σαράβαρα* in the neuter gender, and Julius Pollux, Hesychius, Photius, and several of the older Latin writers, including Tertullian, write it more than once. Our Jerome disapproves of that spelling in Daniel 3:21 and maintains, on the basis of other evidence, that it should be read *saraballa*, as we have printed it. Others, including Saint Augustine, prefer *saraballas* in the feminine gender. Since the interpretation of this word is so varied—and we shall have more to say about it in its proper place in the commentaries on Daniel—it seems that Jerome here preferred the meaning “coverings of the head,” which Isidore also reports to have been approved by other authorities, I.19.23. Shortly afterward we read *innoxium* (“harmless”) from the Veronese manuscript; previously it was *innoxiam*, but not in the sense intended by Jerome, who also says below, *innoxium lusit incendium* (“the harmless fire played”).]

Let the history of blessed Daniel be recalled here, beside whom the mouths of the lions, wagging their fawning tails, feared their prey. Now let noble Susanna, strong in faith, enter everyone’s thoughts; condemned by an unjust judgment, she was saved when the Holy Spirit filled a boy.

[Note: One Veronese manuscript has *Major Susannae nobis fidem mentes subeat*; all other manuscripts and printed editions retain *mentes*, or *mentibus*.]

Behold, the Lord’s mercy is not unlike in either case. One was freed by a judge so that she would not go to the sword; the other, condemned by a judge, was acquitted through the sword.

### 10

At last, therefore, the populace arms itself to avenge the woman. Every age and every sex drives away the executioner, and, as the gathering forms a circle, shouts out. Almost everyone refuses to believe what he sees.

[Note: The principal printed edition does not have the word *exclamat* (“shouts”). The verse below is somewhat different in Virgil:

> “Disfiguring the gray hair, covered with filthy dust.”]

The nearby city is thrown into confusion by such a [Col. 0330] report, and the entire troop of lictors gathers together. From among them the man in the middle, to whom the care of the condemned had been entrusted, burst forth:

> “Why do you seek my head, citizens? Why do you offer me as his substitute? If you are merciful, if you are compassionate, if you wish to save the condemned woman, surely I ought not to die innocent.”

The crowd’s spirit was shaken by this lament, and a gloomy stupor spread through everyone. Their will was wondrously changed: what they had defended before had been an act of compassion; now it seemed an act of compassion to allow him to be killed.

### 11

A new sword and a new executioner are therefore brought forward. The victim stands, strengthened only by Christ’s favor. Struck once, she is shaken; struck again, she is battered; wounded a third time, she is thrown down.

O majesty of divine power, worthy of being exalted! She who had previously been struck four times without being injured was therefore seen shortly afterward to die, lest an innocent man perish on her behalf.

### 12. The Duty of the Clergy in Burying Corpses

[Note: These clergy, whose duty this was, were called *fossarii* (“grave-diggers”). Pseudo-Jerome says in the letter on the seven grades of the Church, which we shall give in the final volume: “The first order among the clergy, therefore, is that of the grave-diggers,” etc. Thus one should not agree with Victorius that their only duty was to accompany a funeral with prayers.]

The clergy whose duty this was wrapped the bloodstained corpse in linen and, constructing a grave of earth and stones, prepared a tomb according to custom.

The sun hastened toward setting in its rapid course, and, by the mercy of the Lord, night came with a swifter course than nature’s usual one.

[Note: Gravius, supported by an ancient book, has: “Night, moving at a more rapid pace, came early.” In the *Life of Malchus*: “By now night had come, darker than usual and too early for me.”]

Suddenly the woman’s breast began to beat, and, while her eyes sought the light, her body was restored to life. She breathes, she sees, she is raised up, and she speaks. She can now burst into these words:

> “The Lord is my helper; I shall not fear what man can do to me” (Ps. 117).

### 13

Meanwhile, a certain old woman, who was supported by the resources of the church, gave back the spirit owed to heaven; and, as though by deliberate arrangement in the orderly course of events, a substitute body was covered in the tomb.

In the uncertain light, the devil met the lictor, asked for the corpse of the slain woman, and demanded that the tomb be shown to him. He thought her alive, since he was astonished that she could have died.

The freshly laid turf was shown by the clergy, and the earth recently heaped over it was thrown in his face, together with these words to the man who demanded it:

> “Dig up, of course, the bones that have already been buried. Bring a new war upon the tomb; and, if that is not enough, tear apart the limbs so that birds and wild beasts may rend them. Struck seven times, she must endure something beyond death.”

### 14

Thus, while the executioner was confounded by such envy, the woman was secretly restored at home. And, lest the frequent visits of a physician to the church perhaps open a path to suspicion, she was sent away with certain virgins to a more secluded estate, her hair having been cut.

There, little by little, after changing her clothing to a man’s dress, the wound was covered with a scar.

And, O truly supreme justice, supreme wickedness! After so many miracles, the laws still rage.

### 15

See how the order of events has carried me along. For now we have [Col. 0331] reached the name of our Evagrius.

If I think that I can speak of his labor for Christ, I shall show poor judgment; if I wish to remain completely silent, I shall be unable, since my voice bursts forth into joy. For who could sing in worthy praise how Auxentius, entrenched at Milan, was almost buried by Evagrius’s vigilance before he was dead?

[Note: Previously Martianus had *Mediolanis* (“at Milan”), a reading which he praises. Auxentius, an Arian and highly factious man, Bishop of Milan, was condemned and deposed by a Roman synod in the year 369. Evagrius may have devoted his efforts to this matter; Jerome soon afterward praises him also because he defended Damasus’s party against Ursicinus.]

Who could sing of the Roman Bishop Damasus, already almost entangled in the snares of faction, both overcoming his adversaries and not harming those he had defeated?

[Note: These were evidently the followers of Ursinus, or Ursicinus, who on 15 November 367 was exiled to Gaul by an imperial decree, “so that no further impious contention might shatter the peoples,” as is clear from the preface of Marcellinus and Faustinus.]

But I myself, shut out by narrow limits, shall pass over these matters and leave them for others to remember after me:

> “But I, shut out by adverse limits,  
> pass over them and leave them for others to recount after me”  
> (*Georgics* IV).

I am content only with the conclusion of the present matter. He approaches the Emperor Valentinian deliberately, wears him down with prayers, appeases him by his merit, and wins him by his concern, so that he might restore to freedom the woman who had been restored to life.

## LETTER II

[Note: Also numbered 38. Written in the year 374.]

### TO THEODOSIUS AND THE OTHER ANCHORITES

[Note: The old codex of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem adds *de Urbe intrinsecus commorantes* (“living within the city”). This Theodosius is believed to be that same man whose history Theodoret wrote in *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 10. He had established a monastery at Rhossus in Cilicia, on the seacoast.]
