He asks Theodosius and the other anchorites under his direction to obtain from God by their prayers that, having completely renounced the world, he may wish and be able to live in the desert.

How I wish I could now be present at your assembly and embrace with complete joy that admirable fellowship, although these eyes do not deserve to behold it. I would see the desert more beautiful than every city. I would see places deserted by their inhabitants, as though transformed into a kind of paradise, surrounded by gatherings of saints.

But because my sins have brought this about—that a head besieged by every crime should not be inserted into the fellowship of the blessed—I therefore beg you, since I do not doubt that you can obtain this, to free me from the darkness of this world through your prayer.

[Note: Victorius had removed the little word *ut* (“that”).]

As I said before when present, and as I now continue to declare my desire through letters, my mind is being swept toward this pursuit by every form of longing. Now it is your task that fulfillment should follow the will. It is mine to wish; it is the task of your entreaties that I should both wish and be able.

[Note: The same editor has, less satisfactorily, *ut quod velim* (“that I may obtain what I wish”).]

I am like a diseased sheep wandering away from the whole flock. Unless the good Shepherd carries me back upon his shoulders to his sheepfolds (Luke 15), my steps will falter, and in the very attempt the footprints of one rising will collapse.

I am that prodigal son who, having squandered every portion that his father had entrusted to me, have not yet bowed my knees to my parent; I have not yet begun to drive away from myself the allurements of my former dissipation.

And because I have not so much ceased from vices as merely begun to wish to cease, the devil now binds me with new nets; now, setting new obstacles before me, he surrounds me with seas on every side and sea on every side:

> “Now the sea on every side, and the sky on every side”  
> (*Aeneid* V).

Now, positioned amid the element, I neither wish to go back nor am able to go forward.

It remains that, through your prayer, the breeze of the Holy Spirit may carry me onward and accompany me to the harbor of the shore I desire.

## LETTER III

[Note: Also numbered 41. Written at Antioch in the middle of summer, 374.]

### TO RUFINUS THE MONK

[Note: In the Veronese manuscript the title reads: “To Rufinus concerning Bonosus the monk.”]

He fervently desires to see and address Rufinus of Aquileia, whom he had heard had gone to Egypt, and informs him of his own condition and of that of Bonosus, his dearest companion, who had withdrawn to a certain island in order to complete his penance. Finally, he begs him to persevere in their mutual love.

### 1

Although I had already learned from the mystery of the sacred books that God often grants more than one asks and frequently gives what “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man” (1 Cor. 2), I have now proved it in my own case, dearest Rufinus.

[Note: Earlier editions incorrectly read *ministerio* (“service”). Jerome himself calls by the same Pauline word *mysterium* what is said through Isaiah: “what eye has not seen, nor ear heard,” etc.]

For I, who thought that I had sufficiently dared to hope if, through an exchange of letters, we could deceive ourselves with an image of one another’s presence, hear that you are penetrating the hidden places of Egypt, visiting the choirs of monks, and traveling around the heavenly household on earth.

[Note: Older common editions, Erasmus, and Victorius read “I thought that I could be made sufficiently bold by desire.” All our manuscripts confirm the reading printed.]

Oh, if the Lord Jesus Christ would suddenly grant me either Philip’s translation to the eunuch (Acts 2), or Habakkuk’s to Daniel (Dan. 14), how I would now clasp your neck in close embraces, and how I would press with my lips that mouth which once either wandered or was wise together with me!

But since I do not deserve that you should come to me in this way, nor that I should go to you in this way—and since frequent illnesses have often broken my feeble little body, even when it is healthy—I send these substitutes for me, which, bound to you by the bond of love, may bring you all the way to me.

[Note: Two manuscripts have: “With what embraces I would now clasp your neck.”]

[Note: *Invalidum* here means Jerome’s “frail little body.”]

### 2

The first report of unexpected joy and happiness was brought to me by the brother Heliodorus. I did not believe what I wished to be certain, especially since he said that he had heard it from someone else and the novelty of the matter removed credibility from the report.

Again, a certain Alexandrian monk, who had been sent to the Egyptian Confessors—men already martyrs in their will—through the pious service of the people, and who was himself a manifestly trustworthy source for believing the report, had stirred up my suspended hopes and wavering mind [Col. 0333].

[Note: We follow the old handwritten copies, whose sense is more polished. Previously the reading was *suspensam voto nutante mentem* (“the mind suspended by wavering hope”). In the older Veronese manuscript, instead of *monachus* (“monk”) there is *Dei famulus* (“servant of God”), and in what follows it has *jamdudum ignorat* (“has long been ignorant”). The Egyptian Confessors whom Jerome mentions here are, whatever the Benedictine interpreter may think, none other than those whom the Emperor Valens ordered into exile around the year 372 because they confessed the divinity of Christ.]

I confess that my judgment faltered in this matter too. For although he did not know your homeland or your name, he nevertheless seemed to offer more weight because he asserted the same things that another had already reported.

At last the full weight of truth burst forth: a large number of travelers reported that Rufinus was in Nitria and had gone to blessed Macarius. Then I loosened all the restraints of belief, and only then did I truly regret being ill.

And if the strength of my weakened body had not hindered me with a kind of fetter, neither the heat of midsummer nor the sea, always uncertain for sailors, would have been able to resist me as I hurried forward in pious haste.

Believe me, brother: the sailor tossed by a storm does not look toward harbor in this way; thirsty fields do not long for rain in this way; nor does an anxious mother sitting upon the curved shore await her son in this way.

### 3

After a sudden storm tore me away from your side; after an impious rupture wrenched me away from the bond of love to which I clung:

> “Then the blue rain-cloud stood above my head;  
> then the sea on every side, and the sky on every side”  
> (*Aeneid* III).

At last, wandering uncertainly through my exile, after Thrace, Pontus, Bithynia, the whole journey through Galatia and Cappadocia, and the land of Cilicia had exhausted me with its burning heat, Syria appeared to me like a most faithful harbor to a shipwrecked man.

There I experienced whatever illnesses there could be. From my two eyes I lost one, for a sudden fever seized Innocentius, the part of my soul.

[Note: The sudden death of Innocentius. This is the same Innocentius to whom Jerome dedicated the letter on the woman struck seven times, Letter 1 here, although some have imagined otherwise.]

Now I enjoy our Evagrius as my one and complete light, to whom I, always weak for labor, came as an additional burden.

[Note: Some editions older than Erasmus have *toto mihi carissimo lumine* (“my wholly dearest light”), and afterward *infirmus quidem ad laborem* (“indeed weak for labor”).]

Hylas, the servant of holy Melania, was also with us. By the purity of his conduct he had washed away the stain of servitude; and he too reopened a scar not yet healed.

[Note: The Benedictine editor has *Sanctae Melaniae* (“of Saint Melania”), but *Melanii* (“of Melanius”) is more correctly read, as we have printed it; nor should *Sancti* (“of Saint”) be retained, as the older printed editions incorrectly have. Thus in Saint Paulinus, Letter 31, we find *Sancta Melanius*, and in Letter 29, *Sanctae feminae Melanii*. Evidently feminine names ending in *-ius* were expressed in diminutive form. Thus one finds *Eubulium* for *Eubole*, and *Gregorius* for *Gregoria*, beautifully formed in the interlocutors of Methodius’s *Symposium*. I omit Glycerium, Philarium, Erotium, Adelphasium, Philocomasium, Philomathium, and others given such names by a kind of verbal endearment.]

But because the Apostle’s word forbids us to grieve over those who sleep, and because the excessive force of grief has been tempered by the arrival of a joyful report, we tell you these things so that, if you do not know them, you may learn them; and, if you already knew them, we may rejoice together.

### 4. If you praise Bonosus, and his solitude

Your Bonosus—or, more truly speaking, ours, my foretold ladder—has already begun to climb, like Jacob in his dream. He carries his cross and gives no thought to tomorrow; he does not look back. He sows in tears, that he may reap in joy. In accordance with the mystery of Moses, he has hung up the serpent in the wilderness (Num. 21:9). Let the false miracles fabricated by both Greek and Roman literary style yield to this truth.

Behold a boy trained with us in the respectable arts of the world, [Col. 0334] who possessed abundant wealth and enjoyed outstanding distinction among his peers—[Note: The Veronese manuscript reads: “distinction first.”]—has despised his mother, his sisters, and his own dearly loved brother, and settled like a new cultivator of paradise on a shipwrecked island surrounded by the sea, where rugged cliffs, bare rocks, and solitude inspire terror. No farmer, no monk—not even the little Onesimus, whom you know and with whom he enjoyed the intimacy of a brother’s embrace—is at his side as a companion amid so great a desolation. He is alone there—or rather, now that Christ accompanies him, he is not alone. He sees the glory of God, which even the Apostles had not seen except in the wilderness. He does not, indeed, behold cities with their towers; but he has enrolled his name in the register of the new city. His limbs bristle beneath a disfiguring sackcloth; but thus he will more readily be snatched up in the clouds to meet Christ. He enjoys none of the pleasantness of gardens; but he drinks the water of life from the Lord’s side.

[Note: Formerly the reading was “Let this be set before you,” or “Set this before yourself.” Later, our manuscripts do not recognize that very sweet epithet.]

Set these things before your eyes, my dearest friend, and turn your whole mind and spirit toward the reality of them. Then you will be able to praise the victory, once you have recognized the labor of the combatant. All around the island the mad sea roars, and the water, dashed against the winding mountain-cliffs, resounds. No earth grows green with grass; no flowering field is thick with little shades. Broken crags enclose him as a kind of prison of horror. He, secure and fearless, wholly armed with the Apostle’s armor (Eph. 6:16), now listens to God while rereading divine writings; now he speaks with God when he prays to the Lord. Perhaps, following the example of John (Rev. 1:9), he sees something while dwelling on the island.

### 5

What snares do you suppose the devil is now weaving? What ambushes do you imagine he is preparing? Perhaps, remembering his ancient deception, he will try to persuade him to hunger. But he has already received the answer: “Man lives not by bread alone” (Matt. 4). Perhaps he will set wealth and glory before him. But he will be told: “Those who desire to become rich fall into a trap and into temptations” (1 Tim. 6); and, “For me all boasting is in Christ” (Gal. 6).

He will shake his limbs, wearied by fasting and weighed down by illness; but he will be beaten back by the Apostle’s words: “For when I am weak, then I am stronger” (2 Cor. 12); and, “Power is perfected in weakness” (ibid.). He will threaten death; but he will hear: “I desire to depart and to be with Christ” (Phil. 1). He will hurl fiery darts, but they will be received by the shield of faith. And, not to repeat many things (Eph. 6): Satan will attack, but Christ will protect.

Thanks be to you, Lord Jesus, that on your day I have one who can pray to you on my behalf. You yourself know—for the breasts of each person lie open to you, and you search out the secrets of the heart; you see the Prophet enclosed in the belly of so great a beast in the depths—how he and I alike grew from tender infancy to flourishing manhood; how the same nurses’ breasts and the same embraces of our attendants cherished us; and how, after our Roman studies, when we enjoyed the same food and equal hospitality beside the half-barbarous banks of the Rhine, I was the first to begin wishing to honor you.

I ask you to consider for a moment that this warrior of yours was once a recruit with me. I have your promise of majesty: “Whoever teaches and does not practice will be called least in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5).

[Note: Older printed editions add another saying from Matthew, more appropriate to the subject: “But whoever teaches and practices will be called great in the kingdom of heaven.” Martianaeus removed it without informing the reader; since we did not find it in the manuscripts, we have not dared to add it.]

May he enjoy the crown of virtue and, clothed in a robe because of his daily martyrdoms, follow the Lamb (Rev. 14): “For there are many dwelling places with the Father” (John 14). “And star differs from star in glory” (1 Cor. 15). Grant me—[Note: From Tertullian, *On the Apparel of Women*, as Gravius notes: “And would that on that day of Christian rejoicing I, most wretched, might raise my head even among your heels.”—]that I may lift my head among the heels of the saints; so that, when I have wished it, he may have accomplished it. Forgive me because I could not fulfill it, and grant him the reward he deserves.

Perhaps I have prolonged this at greater length than the brevity of a letter allowed; but this always happens to me whenever something must be said in praise of our Bonosus.

### 6

But, to return to the point from which I departed, I beg you not to let the mind lose, along with the eyes, a friend who is long sought, scarcely found, and difficult to preserve.

[Note: The Benedictine editor changes the passage as follows: “Let anyone shine with gold, glitter with sumptuous vessels, and let metals gleam from his baggage.” We restore from the manuscripts the older reading, which is more genuine and much more elegant. The salutation at the end, “Farewell in Christ,” is likewise absent from them.]

Let anyone shine with gold, and let metals glitter from sumptuous vessels and gleam from baggage. Love cannot be compared with anything. Affection has no price. A friendship that can cease was never true. Farewell in Christ.

## LETTER IV

[Note: Formerly Letter 5. Written at the same time as the preceding letter and attached to it.]

### TO FLORENTIUS

[Note: In the Chronicle under the year 381 he is called Florentinus and described as a distinguished monk, “so compassionate toward the needy that he was commonly called the father of the poor.” But Ruffinus himself reads *Florentium* when he quotes this passage in Book 2 *Against Jerome*.]

He joins the preceding letter, which was to be delivered to Ruffinus, to this one addressed to Florentius. He praises Florentius at length for living in Jerusalem and assisting the needs of many poor people; then he also adds praise of Ruffinus.

### 1

You can estimate how great a report of Your Blessedness has filled the mouths of different peoples from this: I begin to love you before I know you. For, as the Apostle says, “The sins of some people are manifest, going before them to judgment” (1 Tim. 5); so, conversely, the fame of your love is spreading, so that the person who loves you is not so much to be praised as the person who does not love you is thought to be committing a crime.

I pass over the countless people in whom you have supported, fed, clothed, and visited Christ. The need of our brother Heliodorus, assisted by you, could loosen even the tongues of the mute: with what thanks, with what praise, he reported that the hardships of his journey had been relieved by you! Thus I—[Note: The old edition of 1496, supported also by certain manuscripts, reads in the opposite sense: “so that I, that ardent man whom intolerable illness afflicted”—]so sluggish, worn down by an intolerable illness, have greeted you, as they say, on winged feet, with the gesture and wish of affection, and have even embraced you.

I therefore congratulate you and pray that the Lord may deign to unite our budding friendship.

### 2. Ruffinus and Melania

And since our brother Ruffinus, who is said to have come from Egypt to Jerusalem with Saint Melania, is joined to me by an inseparable affection of brotherhood, I ask you not to find it burdensome to deliver to him the letter of mine attached to this letter of yours.

Do not measure us by his virtues. In him you will behold the clear marks of holiness; [Note: Victorius preferred “traces” instead. Shortly afterward, however, the Benedictine editor had wrongly read one word for *et iam*, as we have corrected it.] while I, ashes and the vilest part of clay, already turning into dust—[Cluniac manuscript: “while I am still flourishing”—]am sufficiently content if the weakness of my eyes can endure the radiance of his character.

He has just washed himself and is clean, whitened like snow; I, stained with every filth of sin, wait day and night in trembling to repay the last farthing. Yet because the Lord releases those bound in chains (Ps. 45; Isa. 66) and his words rest upon the humble and trembling person, perhaps even to me, lying in the tomb of crimes, he may say: “Jerome, come outside.”

The holy Presbyter Evagrius sends you many greetings. We also jointly salute our brother Martinianus, whom I long to see but to whom I am bound by the chain of illness. Farewell in Christ.

## LETTER V

[Note: Formerly Letter 6. Written several months after the preceding letter, in 374.]

### TO FLORENTIUS

He replies to Florentius and informs him that he has already taken up residence in the solitude adjoining Syria and the Saracens. He then asks him for certain books and offers him others that he possessed in abundance.

### 1

While I was living in that part of the desert which adjoins Syria and the Saracens, a letter expressing your affection was brought to me. When I read it, my desire to travel to Jerusalem was rekindled so strongly that what benefited affection almost harmed my purpose.

Now, therefore, since I cannot come in person, I present myself to you through a letter. Although absent in body, I come in love and spirit. I ask you earnestly not to let our budding friendship, joined by Christ’s bond, be torn apart by the vastness of time or place; rather, let us bind it more firmly through letters sent in both directions. Let them run between us, let them meet one another, let them speak with us. Affection will not lose much if it converses with itself in such a manner.

### 2

As you write, our brother Ruffinus has not yet come; and even if he comes, he will not greatly benefit my longing, since I shall no longer see him. He too is separated from me by so great a distance that he cannot make his way here; [Col. 0337] and I am confined within the boundaries of the solitude I have undertaken, so that I have now begun to be unable to do what I wished.

For this reason I ask you—and I earnestly beg you to ask him—to prevail upon the blessed Rheticius, Bishop of Autun, to lend you his *Commentaries* for copying. In them he expounded the Song of Songs with sublime eloquence.

A certain elderly Paul, from the homeland of the aforesaid brother Ruffinus, also wrote to me that his copy of Tertullian is with him, and that he urgently requests its return. Therefore I ask you to have those books which the attached brief list will inform you that I do not possess copied by a scribe on paper.

I also ask you to send me David’s interpretation of the Psalms and the very extensive book of Saint Hilary on the Councils, which I myself copied for him at Trier. You know that this is food for the Christian soul, if one meditates on the law of the Lord day and night (Ps. 1).

You welcome others as guests, comfort them with consolation, and assist them at your own expense. If you grant what I ask, you will have given me everything. And since, through the Lord’s generosity, we possess many copies of the sacred Library—[Note: “Sacred Library” means the Bible]—command me in return to send you whatever you wish. Do not think it burdensome for me if you give the order.

I have pupils—[Note: Older printed editions, supported by some manuscripts, read: “pupils who teach me the ancient art,” which I do not doubt is erroneous. The *antiquarian art* is plainly the art practiced in copying the works of the ancients.]—who serve the antiquarian art. Nor do I promise a favor in return for what I request.

Brother Heliodorus told me that you are searching for many things in the Scriptures and are not finding them; or, if you possess everything, affection begins to claim more for itself and to ask for more.

### 3

As for the tutor of your boy, about whom you were kind enough to write—there is no doubt that he is the boy’s kidnapper—Presbyter Evagrius often rebuked him in my presence while I was still at Antioch.

He replied to him: “I fear nothing. He says that he was dismissed by his master; and if that pleases you, here he is—send him wherever you wish.” I think I would not be committing a sin if I did not allow a wandering man to flee farther.

Therefore, since I am established in this solitude and cannot do what you ordered, I asked my dearest Evagrius to pursue the matter earnestly both for your sake and for mine. I wish you health in Christ.

## LETTER VI

[Note: Formerly Letter 73. Written in the year 374.]

### TO JULIAN, DEACON OF AQUILEIA

[Note: All the manuscripts agree in making this Julian a deacon of Aquileia. No one doubts that he is the same Julian whose advice Jerome says in the following letter to Chromatius brought about the conversion of Julian’s sister; from this it may be inferred that he was not far from the holy Doctor’s homeland. It is therefore most probable that he was at Aquileia, despite the hesitation I once felt on that account, since Aquileia seemed to lie farther from Jerome’s homeland; for that reason I formerly omitted “at Aquileia,” although all the manuscripts add the name. I respected the authority of P. de Rubeis, who says in *Monumenta Ecclesiae Aquileiensis*, p. 78, that this reading, found in all the manuscripts, may perhaps be corrupt. The idea that Aquileia lay so far from Jerome’s homeland was so deeply fixed in his mind that Julian could not easily have undertaken the conversion of Jerome’s sister. We have shown, on the contrary, that this was convenient for him because of the proximity of the place. See the Life of the Holy Doctor that we wrote.]

He excuses himself to Julian for his silence in correspondence. When Julian first reported that his sister was persisting in what she had begun, Jerome asks him to make him happier by frequent letters about her resolve. He adds that meanwhile he despises his detractor.

An ancient saying is—[Note: Aristotle, cited by Diogenes Laertius]—that liars bring it about that no one believes even those who speak the truth. I see that this has happened to me with you, since you have rebuked me for my silence in correspondence.

Shall I say, “I often wrote, but it was the negligence of the carriers”? You will answer: “That is the old excuse of everyone who does not write.”

Shall I say, “I found no one to carry the letters”? You will say: “Many people went from here to there.”

I shall insist that I entrusted letters to them too. But since they did not deliver them, they will deny it; and between absent persons knowledge will remain uncertain.

What, then, shall I do? I shall ask pardon without guilt, judging it more fitting to seek peace by withdrawing than to stir up conflicts on equal terms. Yet both bodily illness and sickness of soul have so continually consumed me that, with death approaching, I scarcely remembered even myself.

To prevent you from thinking this false—[Note: This whole passage, added rhetorically after the arguments as witnesses are called, is absent from the Veronensis manuscript]—I shall call witnesses after the arguments, in the manner of an advocate.

The holy brother Heliodorus was here. He had wished to live in the desert with me, but, driven away by my crimes, he departed. Yet my present flood of words will excuse all blame.

For, as Flaccus says in the satire, “All singers have this fault among their friends: when asked never to sing, unbidden they never cease” (Horace, Book 1, *Satires*, Sat. 3). So from now on I shall bury you beneath such a mass of letters that, conversely, you will begin to ask me not to write.

I rejoice, since you were the first to report it, that my sister, your daughter in Christ, is persisting in what she had begun. Here, where I now am, I do not know not only what is happening in my homeland but even whether my homeland still exists.

And although a hostile Iberian monster may tear me apart with its mouth—[Note: Manuscripts and older printed editions read “with the mouth or manner of the Iberian serpent.” By the name “Iberian serpent” he mocks a very wicked man, whether he was Bishop Lupicinus or someone else. It is neither necessary nor probable to invent a Spanish man merely because he calls him Iberian. Shortly afterward, we have preferred *God* to *myself*, as the more elegant sense and as supported by the manuscripts]—I shall not fear human judgment, since I shall have God as judge, in accordance with the saying:

“Though the world, shattered, should fall upon him, the ruins will strike an unafraid man” (Horace, Book 3, *Odes*, Ode 3).

Therefore I ask you, remembering the Apostle’s command that our work must endure (1 Cor. 3), both to secure for yourself from the Lord a reward through her salvation and to make me happier by frequent reports of our shared glory in Christ.

## LETTER VII

[Note: Formerly Letter 43. Written in the same year as the preceding letter.]

### TO CHROMATIUS, JOVINUS, AND EUSEBIUS

He returns greetings to the brothers Chromatius and Eusebius, together with his friend Jovinus and also their mother and virgin sisters, all living holily in the same household. He praises their common life at length. He then adds and approves the praises of Bonosus, about whom they had written. Finally, he commends to them his sister, who had no good teachers of life in her homeland.

### 1

Paper ought not to divide those whom mutual love has joined; nor should the duties of my discourse be divided among individuals, since you love one another so much—[Note: Chromatius and Eusebius]—that affection joins three no less than nature joined two. Indeed, if the circumstances permitted, I would enclose your undivided names under a single letter’s heading, since your letters to me provoke me to think of three as one and of one as three.

For after the letters were brought to me by Saint Evagrius in that part of the desert which stretches as a vast frontier between the Syrians and the Saracens, I rejoiced as though I had won the day of Roman good fortune on which, after the battle at Cannae, Marcellus first cut down Hannibal’s forces at Nola.

Although the brother mentioned above often visits me and cherishes me as his own inward parts in Christ, yet, separated from me by a long distance, he left me no less longing when he departed than he had brought joy when he came.

### 2

Now I converse with your letters. I embrace them; they speak with me; here they alone know Latin. Here one must either learn a barbarous half-language—[Note: The Veronensis reads, “a barbarous old man’s speech must be learned.” This is certainly corrupt, since Jerome could not at that time have called himself an old man]—or remain silent.

Whenever familiar hands bring back the impressions of faces most dear to me, either I am no longer here or you are here. Believe love when it speaks the truth: as I wrote this, I was seeing you.

My first complaint against you is this: why, with so many stretches of sea and land intervening, did you send such a short letter? Unless I deserved it because, as you write, I had not written to you previously.

I do not think that paper was lacking, since Egypt supplies the trade. And even if some Ptolemy had closed the seas—[Note: The more elegant reading is “even if some Ptolemy had done so.” Compare Pliny, Book 13, chapter 11, where he says that, through rivalry between the royal libraries of Ptolemy and Eumenes, Ptolemy suppressed the supply of paper, and Varro reports that parchment was discovered at Pergamum]—King Attalus had nevertheless sent parchment from Pergamum, so that the scarcity of paper might be compensated by skins. Hence the name “Pergamene” has been preserved to this day, handed down by succeeding generations.

What, then? Should I suppose that the carrier hurried? Yet one night is sufficient for a long letter. Or were you detained by some occupation? No necessity is greater than love.

Two possibilities remain: either you were reluctant, or I did not deserve a letter. Of these, I prefer to accuse you of delay rather than condemn myself as undeserving. Negligence can more easily be corrected than love can be born.

### 3. The praises of Bonosus

Bonosus, as you write, like a son of the fish—[Note: The Veronensis manuscript omits the interpretation of the Greek word. Jerome’s statement is extremely learned and elegant: Bonosus, like a son of the fish, *ichthys* (ἰχθύος), seeks the watery places. From the earliest times of the Church, believers devised five letters so that, by concealing their faith from pagans, they could form the word *ichthys*, that is, “fish.” Each letter also contained its own name and meaning: the first signified Ἰησοῦν, Jesus; the second, Χριστόν, Christ; the third, Θεοῦ, of God; the fourth, υἱόν, Son; and the last, σωτῆρα, Savior. Symbols of this kind belonging to the ancient Christians still survive to this day. Among them is an especially fine gem in our household museum, representing the Lord Christ under the figure of a fisherman, with the letters ΙΧΘΥΣ marked upon it. From this the holy Fathers drew several mysteries: Augustine, *City of God*, Book 18, chapter 23; Prosper, *On Predestination*, chapter 19; Paulinus, Letter 33; Optatus, *Against Parmenianus*, Book 3; and especially Tertullian, *On Baptism*, chapter 1, who likewise interprets water and the watery realm as the Church. Jerome, however, hints that his Bonosus established his hermitage on an island of Dalmatia.]

—seeks the watery realm. We, stained by our former corruption, pursue whatever is dry like little serpents and scorpions. He already treads upon the serpent’s head; we are still food for the serpent that, according to the divine sentence, eats earth.

He can already climb the highest Psalm of the Steps; while we, still weeping—or flowing—[al. “flowing”] on the first ascent, do not know whether we shall ever be able to say: “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from where my help will come” (Ps. 120:1).

He, seated safely amid the threatening waves of the world in the lap of the island—that is, of the Church—perhaps already devours the book after the example of John (Rev. 10). I, lying in the tomb of my crimes (John 11) and bound by the chains of sins, await the Lord’s cry from the Gospel: “Jerome, come outside.”

Bonosus, I say—[Note: I would prefer to transpose the word *because* approximately as follows: “Bonosus, I say, because, according to the Prophet, all the devil’s strength is in his loins …” Otherwise the Prophet’s name is less suitably referred to Job, since it belongs to Jeremiah]—because, according to the Prophet, all the devil’s strength is in his loins (Jer. 13), carried his loincloth across the Euphrates and hid it there in a cleft of the rock (Job 40:11). Later, finding it torn, he sang: “Lord, you have possessed my reins” (Ps. 138); “You have broken my bonds; to you I shall sacrifice a sacrifice of praise” (Ps. 105).

But Nebuchadnezzar led me, bound, to Babylon—that is, to the confusion of my mind. There he placed upon me the yoke of captivity; there, fastening an iron ring to my nostrils, he ordered me to sing the songs of Zion (Ps. 136). I said to him: “The Lord releases those bound in chains; the Lord gives light to the blind” (Ps. 145).

To bring this contrast, once begun, to a brief conclusion: I beg for forgiveness; he awaits a crown.

### 4

My sister is the fruit of Saint Julian in Christ. He planted; you water; the Lord will give the increase (1 Cor. 6). Jesus gave her to me in place of the wound the devil had inflicted, restoring a living person in place of one who was dead.

Toward her, as the Gentile poet says—[Virgil, Book 4 of the *Aeneid*]—I fear everything, even what is safe. You yourselves know the slippery path of youth, on which I too stumbled and across which you pass, not without fear.

Now that she is entering it most fully, she must be supported by every instruction, sustained by every consolation—in other words, strengthened by frequent letters from your holiness. And since love bears all things, I ask you to obtain letters from Pope Valerianus as well—[Note: Valerianus, Bishop of Aquileia]—to encourage her.

You know that young minds are often strengthened by such things when they understand that they are objects of concern to their elders.

### 5

In my homeland’s rustic vernacular—[al. “rusticity”—]the belly is god, and people live for the day; the richer a man is, the holier he is thought to be.

A fitting lid was added to this pot, according to the familiar proverb of the people: the priest Lupicinus, who is like the Crassus of whom Lucilius said that he laughed only once in his life. [Note: Marcus Tullius reports this in *On Ends*, Book 5: “Lucilius said that Marcus Crassus laughed only once in his life; yet it did not follow that for this reason he was called less *agelastos*—‘without laughter’—as the same author says.”]

“The lips have a lettuce like their own”: an ass eats thistles. In other words, a weak pilot guides a pierced ship, and a blind man leads the blind into a pit. Let the ruler be such as those who are ruled.

### 6

We salute our common mother—with the honor you know—who is united with you in holiness and surpasses you in this respect, that she gave birth to such children; her womb may truly be called golden.

We also salute all the sisters who must be welcomed with her—[al. “all the sisters must be welcomed”—]women who have conquered both their sex and the world, who, with abundant oil prepared for their lamps, await the Bridegroom’s arrival (Matt. 25).

O blessed household, in which dwell the widow Anna, the virgin prophetesses, and the twin Samuel, nurtured in the temple! O happy roofs, beneath which we see a martyr mother surrounded by the crowns of the Maccabean martyrs!

Although you confess Christ daily by keeping his commandments, this public and open confession has also been added to your private glory: through you, the poison of the Arian doctrine was once driven out of your city. [Note: The doctrine of Arius was expelled from Aquileia through Chromatius and others.]

Perhaps you wonder that at the very end of the letter I have begun again. What can I do? I cannot deny my voice to my heart. The brevity of the letter compels me to be silent; longing for you forces me to speak. My speech is hasty; my discourse is confused and disordered; love knows no sequence.

## LETTER VIII

[Note: Formerly Letter 42. Written shortly after the preceding letter.]

### TO NICEAS, SUBDEACON OF AQUILEIA

He urges Niceas, an old companion and fellow traveler who has now returned to his homeland, to write to him at last, following the example of the brothers Chromatius and Eusebius.

The comic poet Turpilius, treating the reciprocity of letters, says: “It is the one thing that makes absent people present.” Nor did he give a false judgment, although he expressed it concerning something unreal—[Note: Jerome’s commentators, Victorius and Martianaeus, understand “something unreal” to mean comedy, because Turpilius uttered the saying in one of his comedies, a fictional work. It seems much more probable to us that Jerome meant the same as if he had said “something not physically real,” since the presence produced by letters is neither actual nor proper presence]—for what is so present, so to speak, among absent people as both speaking through letters to those we love and hearing them?

Even those unrefined men of Italy—[Note: Ennius, from a fragment of Book 1 of the *Annals*:

> Those men whom once the land of Laurentum received,  
> whom first the peoples of the Casci, the Latins, held.

Cicero says of them in Book 1 of the *Tusculan Disputations*: “That one characteristic was implanted in those ancient men whom Ennius calls Casci,” and so forth. Livy, Book 1, calls them the ancient Latins; Virgil says in Book 5, “and taught the ancient Latins to celebrate.” Festus interprets *cascus* as “ancient,” and Varro, Book 4 *On the Latin Language*, reports that the word has Sabine origins.]—whom Ennius calls Casci, and who, as Cicero says in the *Rhetorica*, sought their livelihood in a bestial manner, before the use of paper and parchment, used either wooden tablets smoothed for writing or tree bark to send one another the conversations of letters.

Hence they called the carriers of such letters *tabellarii*, and their writers *librarii*, from the books of trees. How much more, then, ought we, in a world already refined by the arts, not to neglect what they provided for themselves, when they possessed a raw rusticity and were in a sense ignorant of civilization?

Behold, blessed Chromatius, with holy Eusebius, united to him not more by equality of nature than of character—[Note: Gravius reads “equal to him as a brother”—]has challenged me to the service of writing.

You, however, now departing from us, sever a recent friendship rather than loosen it, which Laelius wisely forbids in Cicero’s dialogue *Laelius*. [Note: See Cicero’s work entitled *Laelius*.]

Unless perhaps the East is so hateful to you that you fear even your letters coming here. Wake up, wake up! Rise from sleep! Give affection one sheet of paper.

At some point sigh amid the delights of your homeland and the journeys we shared. If you love me, write to my entreaty; if you are angry, write even in anger. I shall have great consolation for my longing if I receive a letter from my friend, even if he is indignant.

## LETTER IX

[Note: Formerly Letter 44. Written at the same time as the preceding letter.]

### TO CHRYSOGONUS, MONK OF AQUILEIA

He reproaches Chrysogonus, a monk of Aquileia and a recent friend, because he has written nothing to him.

What my feelings toward you are, our dear Heliodorus could faithfully report; he loves you no less than I love you. Your name is always on my lips; at every conversation I recall the companionship so delightful to me; I admire your humility, exalt your virtue, and proclaim your love.

But you possess by nature what lynxes are said to possess—[Note: From an old manuscript of Gravius: “so that, when they look behind them, they do not remember what came before”—]so that, when looking behind them, they do not remember what came before and the mind loses what the eyes have ceased to see; thus you have so completely forgotten our relationship that you have erased—not with a light stroke, but, as they say, down to the deepest wax—the letter that the Apostle says is written in the hearts of Christians (1 Cor. 3:2).

Those wild beasts we mentioned, lurking beneath a leafy branch and seizing fleeing does or timid deer, catch their prey; and while they tear apart the quarry running uselessly away from them with their savage mouths from above, they remember hunting only as long as an empty belly irritates their dry throat with hunger.

But when their ferocity, fed on blood, has filled their distended entrails, satiety is followed by forgetfulness. They no longer know what they are capturing until hunger recalls their memory.

You are not yet satisfied with us; why, then, do you join the conclusion to the beginning? Why do you lose something before you possess it? Unless perhaps, always accompanied by the excuse of negligence, you claim that you had nothing to write, when you ought to have written precisely this: that you had nothing to write.

## LETTER X

[Note: Formerly Letter 21. Written at approximately the same time as the preceding letter.]

### TO PAUL, AN ELDER OF CONCORDIA

[Note: He is also mentioned in the Catalogue under Tertullian. Concordia was not, as Victorius writes in the Life of Saint Jerome, a town near Mirandola, but one of Italy’s best-known cities, situated between Aquileia and Altinum. It must not be confused with another city of the same name in Spain, as some have done.]

He praises Paul of Concordia, who was approaching his hundredth year yet retained a sound and vigorous body. Meanwhile, he sends him the Life of Paul the Hermit, which he had recently composed, and asks him for several books.

### 1

The brevity of human life is the condemnation of sins. Often, at the very beginning of the light, death has followed the one being born, and the ages that daily slide into vice proclaim this.

For when the serpent had led the first inhabitant of paradise, entangled in its viperous coils, down to earth, eternity, changed into mortality, had postponed the sentence of the accursed man—[Note: You will find this word used with the same meaning by other Latin authors. Our Zeno, in his sermon on the martyrdom of Isaiah, says: “When Isaiah was preaching Christ, or announcing to the people of Israel the proclamation of their future condemnation …”—]for nine hundred years and more, granting him, in a sense, a second immortality.

Thereafter, as sin gradually grew more savage, the impiety of the Giants brought about the shipwreck of the whole world. After that baptism of the world, cleansed, so to speak, the life of human beings was contracted into a brief span.

We have nearly squandered even this period, since our crimes continually struggle against divine commands. For how few either pass beyond the age of one hundred, or reach it without regretting that they have done so, in accordance with what Scripture testifies in the Book of Psalms:

“The days of our life are seventy years; and if by reason of strength, eighty. Whatever remains is labor and sorrow” (Ps. 89:10).

24

### 2

“Why,” you say, “have these matters been traced back from so lofty a beginning, and begun so far back that someone might rightly mock us with Horace’s jest:

> ‘And he begins the Trojan War from the twin egg’  
> (*Ars Poetica*)?

Obviously, so that we may praise your old age, and your head made white in the likeness of Christ (Rev. 1:14), in fitting words. Behold, the hundredth circuit of your life is already turning, and you, always keeping the Lord’s commandments, [Note: A Veronese manuscript reads: “you meditate upon the outstanding examples of future blessedness.”] meditate, through present examples, upon the blessedness of the life to come.

Your eyes are vigorous with pure light; your feet plant firm footsteps; your hearing is penetrating; your teeth are white; your voice melodious (another reading: “sonorous”); your body solid and full of vigor; your gray hairs contrast with your ruddy complexion; your strength disagrees with your age. Older age has not dissolved the tenacity of your memory, as we see in many people. Cold blood has not blunted the sharpness of your warm intelligence. Nor does a brow ploughed with wrinkles make rough a face uncontracted by wrinkles. Finally, a trembling hand does not guide a stylus wandering along the curved paths of wax.

In you the Lord has shown us the vigor [Manuscript: “strength”] of the resurrection to come, so that we may know that it is the fault of sin when others, though still alive, die before their time in the flesh; and that it is the work of righteousness when you, in an alien age, simulate youth. And although we see this bodily health occur even among many sinners, nevertheless the devil supplies it to them so that they may sin; the Lord grants it to you so that you may rejoice.

### 3

The most learned Greeks—of whom Cicero, speaking in defense of Flaccus, says eloquently, “inborn frivolity and learned vanity”—used to proclaim the praises of their kings or rulers in return for payment. Since I am doing this now, I ask a price for my praises. And lest you think what I request is insignificant, you are being asked for a pearl from the Gospel.

> “The sayings of the Lord are pure sayings, silver tested by fire, tried in the earth, purified sevenfold” (Ps. 11:7);

namely, the commentaries of Fortunatianus, and, for information about the persecutors, the history of Aurelius Victor, together with the letters of Novatian, so that, while we learn to recognize the poisons of a schismatic man, we may drink more eagerly the antidote of the holy martyr Cyprian.

[Note: We have emended a previously corrupt passage with the help of a Veronese manuscript and two Roman manuscripts. Formerly, *persecutionum* stood where *persecutorum* belongs, making Jerome appear to say that he wished to possess a “History of the Persecutions” written by Aurelius Victor. The sense is instead that he wished to acquire knowledge of the persecutors—that is, of those rulers who persecuted the Church of God—from the history of that same Victor, in which the lives of the emperors down to Julian are discussed. Marianus Victorius is therefore mistaken when he writes that a work of Aurelius Victor on the persecutions of the Church down to Diocletian existed in the Vatican Library in his day. Andreas Schottus rightly argued that this Victor, being by no means a Christian, could not have written such a history; but he consequently invented several other Victors, including one Christian Victor whom Jerome supposedly mentioned here.]

Meanwhile, we have sent you yourself to yourself—that is, the elder Paul [Note: He refers to the Life of Paul the First Hermit, written by himself] to the elder—Paul in whom we have labored greatly to make the style accessible to simpler readers. But somehow, even if the vessel is full of water, it still preserves the same scent with which it was steeped when it was new. If this little gift pleases you, we also have other things stored away, which, together with many eastern commodities, will sail to you if the Holy Spirit breathes favorably.

## LETTER XI [Note: Elsewhere numbered 39. Written at the same time as the preceding letter.]

### TO THE AEMONIAN VIRGINS

[Note: All printed editions, except the old edition of 1496, read *Hemonenses*; many manuscripts likewise incorrectly read *Hermonenses*. Two especially good Veronese manuscripts, with whose help we have corrected the text, read *Aemonenses*. The error arose from ignorance of the city of Aemona, leading people to suppose that these virgins lived on Mount Hermon in Palestine. Yet the context of the letter itself shows that they lived in a city where Jerome had spent a considerable time; he had not yet reached Palestine. See note d to the following letter to Antonius, who was a monk of the same place and may have been responsible for these virgins’ failure to answer Jerome.]

He complains that the virgins living at Aemona, within the borders of Italy, although often addressed by him in letters, have never replied; and he shows that his detractors are not to be believed.

The smallness of the paper indicates solitude; and therefore I have compressed a long discourse into a narrow space, because I wanted to speak with you at greater length, while the limited size of the sheet forced me to remain silent. Now, then, poverty has been defeated by ingenuity. The letters are small, but the conversation is long. And yet, in this crisis of necessity, observe my affection, since even the scarcity of writing materials could not prevent me from writing.

But forgive me, I beg you, in my grief; for I speak as one wounded, I speak as one weeping [Note: Most manuscripts also contain the words “and angry,” which Victorius rejects]: and I speak as one angry. You have not granted even a single jot to one who has so often performed a service for you.

I know that there is no communion between light and darkness, no fellowship between a sinner and the maidservants of God. Yet even a prostitute washed the Lord’s feet with her tears (Luke 7), and dogs eat the crumbs from their masters’ table (Matt. 15). The Savior himself came not to call the righteous but sinners. For the healthy do not need a physician (ibid. 5:31). He desires the sinner’s repentance more than his death. He carries the wandering little sheep back upon his shoulders. And the joyful father welcomes the returning prodigal son (Luke 15).

Indeed, the Apostle says:

> “Do not judge before the appointed time” (1 Cor. 4:5).

For who are you to judge another’s servant? He stands or falls before his own master (Rom. 14:4). And let the one who stands take care lest he fall. “Bear one another’s burdens” (Gal. 6:2).

Otherwise, dearest sisters, human spite judges one way, Christ another. The sentence of his tribunal is not the same as that of whisperers in a corner. There are ways that seem right to human beings (Prov. 14:12), but afterward they are found to be crooked. And treasure is often stored in earthen vessels.

Peter’s bitter tears restored him to his proper place after his threefold denial (Matt. 26). The one to whom more is forgiven loves more (Luke 7:47). The whole flock is passed over in silence, while the angels rejoice in heaven over the salvation of one sick sheep. [Note: Some copies read “the soul of one animal.”]

And if this seems unworthy to anyone, let that person hear the Lord:

> “Friend, if I am good, why is your eye evil?” (Matt. 20:15).

## LETTER XII [Note: Elsewhere numbered 45. Written at the same time as the preceding letter.]

### TO ANTONIUS THE MONK

[Note: A few manuscripts address the letter “to Ammonius”; two address it “to Chrysochomas, deacon of Aquileia”; the great majority, as we have printed it, give the present title. Some add “on modesty”; the Nonantulanus manuscript more correctly reads “he urges him to write.” I prefer those manuscripts that identify this Antonius as a monk of Aemona. Among these are two very ancient manuscripts examined by Martianaeus, although he incorrectly wishes the name *Hemona* to be changed to *Hermona*, so as to agree with the other old corruption by which the virgins of this monastery were wrongly called *Hermonenses* of Palestine instead of *Aemonenses*. Aemona, or Ἠμωνα (*Emona*, as it is more correctly written in Greek), was a colony of Pannonia, as is stated by Pliny, book 3, chapter 25. Herodian, however, assigns it to Italy and calls it “the first,” or “border,” city of Italy, πρὼτην Ἰταλίας πόλιν. Ptolemy, most accurately, and others call it a city bordering on Italy, μεταξὺ Ἰταλίας ὑπὸ τὸ Νορικόν Παννονίας, “between Italy, beneath Noricum, and Pannonia.” Jerome stayed here for some time, and it was not far from his native city of Stridon.]

Jerome reproaches Antonius, a monk of Aemona, because, although repeatedly asked, he has never replied; and he again urges him to love one who loves him and to answer the one who writes to him.

Our Lord, the teacher of humility, when the disciples were disputing about rank, took one of the little children and said:

> “Whoever among you has not been converted and become like a child cannot enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 18).

And lest he should seem merely to teach this without doing it, he fulfilled it by example: when he washes the disciples’ feet (John 13); when he receives the betrayer with a kiss (Luke 22); when he speaks with the Samaritan woman (John 4); when, with Mary sitting at his feet, he discusses the kingdom of heaven (Luke 7); when, after rising from the dead, he first appears to women (Mark 16).

But Satan fell from the height of an archangel for no other reason than the pride opposed to humility. And the Jewish people, claiming for themselves the first seats and greetings in the marketplace, were destroyed when the Gentile people succeeded them—those Jews who had previously been assigned to the drop of a bucket (Isa. 40).

Against the sophists and wise men of this world, fishermen—Peter and James—are sent. Scripture gives the reason:

> “God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble” (1 Pet. 5:5).

See, brother, how great an evil it is to have God as one’s adversary. For this reason, in the Gospel the arrogant Pharisee is rejected, while the humble tax collector is heard.

If I am not mistaken, I have already sent you ten letters full of both courtesy and prayers, [Note: These ten letters of Jerome have been lost. Some manuscripts retain the words “if I am not mistaken.” For the following interjection *mu*, see Varro, book 6. Lucilius writes: “Never to praise a man, nor even to make a *mu*”—that is, not to utter even the smallest syllable. The common proverb is οὐδὲ γρῦ, “not even a grunt.”] while you do not deign to make even a *mu*; and although the Lord speaks with his servants, you do not speak, brother, with your brother.

“You speak far too insultingly,” you will say. Believe me, if the modesty of the pen did not restrain me, though so deeply injured I would heap upon you such words that you would begin to answer me, even if in anger. But since anger is human, while not committing an injury is Christian, I return to my former custom and ask again: love one who loves you, and let a fellow servant grant speech to his fellow servant.

[Note: This greeting is absent from the Veronese and Nonantulanus copies.]

Farewell in the Lord.

## LETTER XIII [Note: Elsewhere numbered 36. Written at approximately the same time as the preceding letter.]

### TO CASTORINA, HIS MATERNAL AUNT

He exhorts his maternal aunt Castorina, with whom he had had some disagreement, to peace and reconciliation, as he had also done in earlier letters.

The same John, Apostle and Evangelist, says in his letter:

> “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3:15);

and rightly so. Since murder often arises from hatred, whoever hates is a murderer in intention, even if he has not yet struck with a sword.

“Why,” you ask, “such a beginning?” Obviously, so that, after laying aside our old resentment, we may prepare our hearts as a pure dwelling place for God.

David says:

> “Be angry, and do not sin” (Ps. 4:5).

The Apostle interprets more fully what this means:

> “Let not the sun go down upon your anger” (Eph. 4:26).

What will we do on the day of judgment, over whose anger the sun has set—not for one day, but as witness to so many years?

The Lord says in the Gospel:

> “If you are offering your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar and go; first be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift” (Matt. 5:23).

[Note: The words “leave your gift there before the altar” are absent from our manuscripts.]

Woe to me in my misery—not to say also to you—who for so long have either not offered a gift at the altar or, while anger remained [Note: This refers to the clause “without cause,” which in certain manuscripts was added to the Lord’s words in Matt. 5:22, “Everyone who is angry with his brother.” Jerome himself later insisted in his Commentary on Matthew and in book 3 of his letter to the Ephesians that these words should be deleted. Many ancient Latin and Greek Fathers nevertheless read them, and we will cite them in their proper place. Even today our oldest Veronese manuscript, which is commonly believed to contain the Old Latin version, includes them. Again, Jerome writes in book 2 Against the Pelagians, composed near the end of his life: “In the same Gospel we read: ‘Whoever is angry with his brother without cause will be liable to judgment,’ although in most ancient manuscripts ‘without cause’ is not added, so that we should understand that we must not become angry even with cause.”], have offered it without cause.

How could we ever have said in our daily prayer:

> “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6:12),

while our heart disagreed with our words and our prayer contradicted our actions?

I therefore beg what I had also asked in an earlier letter a year ago [Note: We have lost this earlier letter]: let us possess the peace that the Lord left to us (John 14); and may Christ look upon both my desire and your mind. Before his tribunal, in a brief moment, reconciliation—or a torn-apart concord—will recover either its reward or its punishment.

But if you, which may it be far from you to do, refuse, I shall be free. This letter of mine, once it has been read, will acquit me.

## LETTER XIV [Note: Elsewhere numbered 1. Written at the same time, or in the year 373.]

### TO HELIODORUS, A MONK

[Note: This is the genuine title, not the one found in other manuscripts, “to Heliodorus the presbyter” or “bishop,” nor the title preferred by Martianaeus, “to the monk, later bishop.” The old edition reads, “to Heliodorus, not yet bishop.” Since Heliodorus had been ordered from being a monk of Aquileia to become bishop of Altinum and had conducted himself with great distinction in that office, scribes substituted the more illustrious title “bishop” for the title “monk,” which Jerome had written at that time.]

Jerome invites Heliodorus, his companion on his journey, whom he had unsuccessfully tried to keep with him in the desert as a partner in his way of life, to come to him, as he had promised when Heliodorus departed; and he praises the blessedness of the eremitical life.

### 1

The heart conscious of our mutual affection acknowledges with what love and eagerness I strove for us to live together in the desert. These letters too are witnesses to the lamentation, grief, and groaning with which I followed you as you departed; you see them stained with tears.

But you, like a pampered child, fostered by your caresses your contempt for one who entreated you, and I, unprepared, did not know what to do at the time. Should I remain silent? But I could not moderately conceal what I ardently desired. Should I plead more earnestly? But you did not want to listen, because you did not love in the same way.

Affection, despised, did the one thing it could. What it could not retain when present, it now seeks when absent. Since you yourself, as you departed, had asked me to send you an invitation after I had moved to the deserts, and I had promised to do so, [Note: One manuscript cited by Gravius reads “I send” instead of “I invite.” This may be more correct. Shortly afterward, *necessitudinum* should perhaps be read for *necessitatum*.]

I invite you: hurry now. I do not want you to remember your former necessities.

> **THE DESERT LOVES THE NAKED.**

I do not want the difficulty of your earlier wandering to frighten you. You believe in Christ; believe also his words:

> “Seek first the kingdom of God, and all these things will be added to you” (Matt. 6:33).

You need take neither purse nor staff. He is abundantly rich who is poor with Christ.

### 2

But what am I doing? Am I again pleading imprudently? Let prayers depart; let entreaties withdraw. Injured love ought to become angry. Perhaps you will listen to one rebuking you, though you despised one who pleaded.

What are you doing, delicate soldier, in your father’s house? Where is the rampart? Where is the trench? Where is the winter spent beneath hides?

Behold, the trumpet sounds from heaven. Behold, the armed commander goes forth with the clouds to wage war against the world. Behold, the two-edged sword proceeding from the king’s mouth (Rev. 1:16) cuts down everything in its path. And you, from your bedroom to the battle line; you, from the shade, go out into the sun?

[Note: Gravius notes that this is taken from Tertullian’s *To the Martyrs*: “No soldier comes to war with luxuries, nor does he proceed from a bedroom to the battle line, but from stripped-down and tightened tents, where every hardship…” Shortly afterward: “From shade into the sun, from the sun into the sky, from tunic into cuirass, etc.”]

A body accustomed to a tunic cannot bear the burden of armor. A head covered with linen refuses a helmet. A hand softened by idleness is roughened by the hard hilt.

Hear the decree [Note: Some manuscripts read, “the decree of your Lord”] of your king:

> “Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters” (Luke 11:23; Matt. 12:30).

Remember the day of your enlistment, when, buried with Christ in baptism, you swore in the words of the sacrament that for his name’s sake you would spare neither mother nor father.

Behold, the adversary is trying to kill Christ within your breast. Behold, the enemy camp longs for the military bonus that you received when you enlisted.

Even if a little nephew hangs upon your neck [Note: Nepotianus, to whom Jerome addressed another letter]; even if your mother, with disheveled hair and torn clothing, displays the breasts that nursed you; even if your father lies on the threshold, go forward over your trampled father, and fly with dry eyes to the banner of the cross.

> **In this matter, cruelty alone is a kind of devotion.**

### 3

#### The prayer of the saints in heaven for travelers

A day will come—yes, it will come—when you return victorious to your homeland; when, as a brave man crowned, you walk through the heavenly Jerusalem. Then you will receive citizenship with Paul. Then you will claim for your parents the right of that same city. Then you will pray for me, who urged you to conquer.

Nor am I unaware of the fetter by which you say you are now hindered. We do not possess an iron breast or hardened entrails. Hyrcanian tigresses did not nurse us, born as we were from flint.

We too passed through these things. Now a widowed sister clings to you with tender arms. Now the household servants with whom you grew up say:

> “To whom are you leaving us to serve?”

Now the former nurse, already an old woman, and the foster-father, a second father after natural affection, cries out: [Note: The old edition of 1496 inserts more material: “They cry out, ‘To whom are you leaving us when we are about to die? Wait a little and bury us, who perhaps will die tomorrow. Perhaps also, with loosened…’ *Mammae* is the customary lullaby of nurses. Cornutus, commenting on Persius, Satire 3: “Or why do you cry when ordered by your nurse to sleep? For nurses often say *lalla, lalla* to infants so that they will sleep.” Gravius found in other manuscripts: “The father cries out, dying: Wait a little, and you will bury me.”]

> “Wait a little for those who are about to die, and bury us.”

Perhaps your mother too, with breasts hanging loose, her forehead furrowed with wrinkles, repeating the ancient lullaby of the breast, will echo the cry.

Let the grammarians say, if they wish:

> “On you the whole household leans and reclines” (*Aeneid* 12).

The love of God and fear of Gehenna easily break these bonds.

Scripture, on the other hand, commands obedience to parents; but whoever loves them above Christ loses his soul. The enemy holds a sword in order to kill me, and I am to think about my mother’s tears? Shall I abandon Christ’s service for my father, to whom I do not owe burial for Christ’s sake, although for Christ’s sake I owe burial to everyone?

Peter, timidly advising the Lord who was about to suffer, became a stumbling block (Matt. 16). Paul answered his brothers who were trying to prevent him from going to Jerusalem:

> “What are you doing, weeping and troubling my heart? For I am ready not only to be bound but also to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus Christ” (Acts 21:13).

This battering ram of filial devotion, by which faith is shaken, must be blunted against the wall of the Gospel:

> “My mother and my brothers are those who do the will of my Father who is in heaven” (Luke 8:21; Matt. 12:30).

If they believe in Christ, let them favor me as I fight for his name. If they do not believe, let the dead bury their own dead (Matt. 8:22).

“But this,” you say, “applies to martyrdom.”

### 4

You are mistaken, brother, mistaken, if you think that a Christian ever does not suffer persecution. **You are opposed most of all when you do not know that you are being opposed.**

Our adversary, like a roaring lion seeking [another reading: “desiring”] someone to devour, prowls about (1 Pet. 5:8), and you think you are at peace?

He sits in ambush with the rich, and in secret he kills the innocent. His eyes look upon the poor. He lies in wait secretly, like a lion in its den; he lies in wait to seize the poor (Ps. 9:30). And you, sheltered beneath the shade of a leafy tree, future prey, are enjoying soft sleep?

From there luxury persecutes me. From there avarice tries to break in. From there my belly wants to be my god instead of Christ. Lust compels me to drive away the Holy Spirit dwelling in me, to violate his temple.

The enemy with a thousand names persecutes me—

> “A thousand arts of harming”  
> (*Aeneid* 7);

and shall I, miserable man, consider myself victorious while I am being captured?

### 5

I do not want you, dearest brother, after weighing the gravity of sins, to consider the things we have mentioned less serious than the crime of idolatry [another reading: “the crimes”]. Rather, learn the Apostle’s judgment:

> “For this you know and understand: that every fornicator, or unclean person, or covetous person, or swindler—which is the service of idols—has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God” (Eph. 5:5).

[Note: For these two terms, “covetous person” and “swindler,” the Greek has one word, πλεονέκτης (*pleonektēs*), “one who is greedy or grasping.” The Latin copies likewise do not all contain both terms together: some, like the present text, have the first; others, including older copies, have only the second. Jerome seems to have joined both here to express the two possible interpretations of the Greek word, and perhaps also to allude to 1 Thessalonians 4:6: “that no one transgress against or defraud his brother in business.” Jerome himself explains this passage, following the ancient Fathers, in his Commentaries on Ephesians as referring to lustful and impure men who by deceit and flattery entice other men’s wives into the filth of immorality. He also attests there that avarice itself is used in place of adultery.]

And although whatever belongs to the devil is generally directed against God, and whatever belongs to the devil is idolatry, to which all idols are enslaved, nevertheless in another place he specifies and names the matter directly, saying:

> “Put to death your members that are upon the earth, putting away fornication, uncleanness, evil desire, and greed, which are the service of idols; because of these the wrath of God is coming” (Col. 3:5–6).

#### Idolatrous service in vices and sins

Idolatrous service does not consist only in someone throwing incense upon the burning altar with two fingers [Note: Elsewhere the reading is “pressed incense into the tomb,” as some manuscripts also read. This may perhaps be used to correct Lactantius, book 5, chapter 19, who, speaking from the pagan perspective, writes: “For to prefer being tortured and killed rather than throw incense, held between three fingers”—read “pressed”—“into the fire seems so foolish,” etc.], or pouring unmixed wine from a cup into a bowl.

Let the person who can call avarice anything other than idolatry deny that it is idolatry—the person who can call it justice that the Lord was sold for thirty pieces of silver.

Let the person deny that there is sacrilege in lust—the person who has violated, by unholy defilement, the members of Christ and the living sacrifice pleasing to God [Note: The passage is explicitly taken from Tertullian’s *On the Apparel of Women*: “What less do those most wretched victims of public lust possess?” Gravius notes the source] together with the victims of public depravity.

Let the person deny that fraud is idolatry—the person who resembles those who, in the Acts of the Apostles, kept back part of the price of their property and perished by immediate punishment (Acts 5).

Understand, brother, that you are not permitted [another reading: “it is not permitted”] to retain anything from your possessions. The Lord says:

> “Everyone who does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14:33).

Why are you a Christian with a timid heart?

### 6

Look at the net left by Peter [another reading: “Look with Peter at the net left behind”]. Look at the tax collector rising from the toll booth and immediately becoming an Apostle.

> “The Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head”;

and you measure spacious colonnades and immense expanses of buildings?

[Note: Some manuscripts have a reading that seems more characteristic of Jerome: “Are you awaiting the inheritance of the world, a fellow-heir of Christ? Interpret…”]

> **WHILE AWAITING THE INHERITANCE OF THE WORLD, YOU CANNOT BE A FELLOW-HEIR OF CHRIST.**

Interpret the word *monk*; that is your name. What are you doing in the crowd, when you are alone?

And I say this—not as one whose vessel or cargo is intact, nor as a sailor ignorant of the waves [Note: Gravius preferred “and as an unlearned sailor,” which is quite correct; but the manuscripts do not support it] who gives instruction—but as one recently cast onto the shore by shipwreck, warning those about to sail in a trembling voice.

In that swell, the Charybdis of luxury swallows salvation. There, with a virgin’s face, lust flatters, smiling like Scylla [Note: Victorius and Martianaeus read “Scylla, as though smiling,” which is neither sufficiently elegant nor correct. We immediately thought that the one word *Scyllacaeum* might be read, a term which Maro also used for shipwreck. Nevertheless, we have preferred to follow the older printed editions and the large body of manuscripts. Two manuscripts, though apparently in a glossator’s hand, read: “In that heat of the sea there is a certain whirlpool and precipice among the waves, the Charybdis of luxury,” and so forth. The story of Charybdis and Scylla is very well known, as are the poets’ myths about them.], in order to bring about shipwrecks against chastity.

Here is a barbarous shore; here is the pirate devil, carrying chains with his companions for those who are to be captured.

Do not believe; do not be secure. Even if the sea, spread out like a pond, smiles; even if scarcely a breath ruffles the surface of the motionless element, this broad plain contains great mountains. Danger is enclosed within; the enemy is within.

Make the ropes ready; hoist the sails. [Note: The Cistercian manuscript, several others, and printed editions read “Let the cross of the yardarm be fixed.” Ancient writers were accustomed to compare the ship’s yardarm to the Cross. Hence the Pseudo-Jerome, in a sermon on the Nativity: “The yardarms of ships and the horns of sails fly beneath the figure of our Cross.” Similar passages are found frequently in Minucius Felix, Maximus of Turin, and others.]

Let the yardarm of the Cross be fixed upon your foreheads. This calm is a storm.

But perhaps you will say: “What then? Are those who live in the city not Christians?” Your situation is not the same as that of the others. Listen to the Lord saying:

> “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have and give to the poor, and come, follow me” (Matt. 19:21).

You, however, have professed yourself perfect. For when, having abandoned military service [another reading: “having abandoned your household, military service”], you castrated yourself for the sake of the kingdom of heaven, what other life did you pursue than the perfect life?

> **BUT THE PERFECT SERVANT OF CHRIST HAS NOTHING EXCEPT CHRIST.**

Or, if he has anything besides Christ, he is not perfect. And if he is not perfect, although he promised God that he would be perfect, he lied beforehand.

> “The mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wis. 1:11).

Therefore, to conclude: if you are perfect, why do you desire your father’s possessions? If you are not perfect, you have deceived the Lord.

The Gospel thunders with divine voices:

> “You cannot serve two masters” (Luke 16:13);

and does anyone dare to make Christ a liar by serving both Mammon and the Lord?

He often cries out:

> “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (ibid. 9:23).

And am I, weighed down with gold, to think that I am following Christ?

> “Whoever says that he believes in Christ ought to walk as he walked” (1 John 2:6).

### 7

But if you have nothing—as I know you will answer—why, being so well prepared for war, do you not serve as a soldier? Unless perhaps you think you are doing this in your homeland, although the Lord did not perform his signs in his own.

And why is that? Take the explanation from authority:

> “No prophet has honor in his own country” (Luke 4).

“I am not seeking honor,” you will say. “My conscience is enough for me.”

Nor was the Lord seeking it, since, to prevent the crowds from making him king, he fled. But where there is no honor, there is contempt. Where there is contempt, there is frequent insult. Where there is insult, there is indignation. Where there is indignation, there is no rest. Where there is no rest, the mind is often led away from its purpose.

And when something is taken away from devotion by unrest, the devotion becomes less than it was before; and where there is less, it cannot be called perfect.

From this calculation arises the final conclusion: a monk cannot be perfect in his homeland. But to refuse to be perfect is to sin.

### 8

#### The rank of the clergy

But having been driven from this rank, you will appeal to the clergy. Dare I say anything about them, who certainly remain in their own cities? Far be it from me to speak anything unfavorable about them, because, succeeding to the apostolic rank, they prepare the **body of Christ** with their sacred mouth; through them we too are Christians.

They possess the keys of the kingdom of heaven and, in a certain sense, judge before the day of judgment. They preserve the Lord’s bride in sober chastity.

But, as I have briefly indicated earlier, the situation of monks is one thing, that of clergy another. The clergy feed the sheep; I am fed. They live from the altar; for me, as for a barren tree, an axe is laid at the root if I do not bring a gift to the altar.

Nor can I plead poverty, since in the Gospel the Lord praised the poor widow who put into the treasury the two coins that were all she had left (Luke 21:24).

I am not permitted to sit before a presbyter; but if I sin, he is permitted to hand me over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved (1 Cor. 5:5).

Under the old Law, whoever did not obey the priests was either placed outside the camp and stoned by the people, or, with his neck subjected to the sword, expiated his contempt with blood (Deut. 17:12). Now the disobedient person is cut down by a spiritual sword, or, expelled from the Church, is torn apart by the ravenous mouths of demons.

But if the pious entreaties of the brothers also urge you toward this same order, I shall rejoice at your ascent but fear your fall.

> “Whoever desires the office of bishop desires a good work.”

We know this. But join to it what follows:

> “It is necessary, however, that such a person be irreproachable, the husband of one wife, sober, chaste, prudent, well ordered, hospitable, able to teach, not addicted to wine, not violent, but moderate” (1 Tim. 3).

After setting out the other qualifications that follow concerning him, he showed no less care in the third rank. [Note: Since he calls the deacon the third rank, observe how plainly he here acknowledges the preeminence of bishops over presbyters, contrary to what heterodox writers repeatedly prattle that he believed.] He says:

> “Deacons likewise must be chaste, not double-tongued, not addicted to much wine, not greedy for disgraceful gain [another reading: “not desirous of shameful profit”], holding the mystery of the faith in a pure conscience.”

[Note: Gravius corrects *ministerium* to *mysterium* from the Greek ἔχοντας τὸ μυστήριον τῆς πίστεως, “holding the mystery of the faith.”]

> “And let these also first be tested; then let them serve, being free from accusation.”

Woe to the person who enters the banquet without a wedding garment. Nothing remains except that he immediately hear:

> “Friend, how did you come in here?”

And when he is silent, let the attendants be told:

> “Bind him hand and foot, take him away, and throw him into the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. 22:12–13).

Woe to the one who, tying up the talent he received in a cloth, while the others were making profits, preserved only what he had received. Immediately he will be struck by the cry of the indignant Lord:

> “Wicked servant, why did you not put my money on the table, so that when I came I might have collected it with interest?” (Matt. 25:16–17).

That is: you should have deposited it at the altar, since you were unable to carry it. For while you, a lazy merchant, hold on to the coin, you have occupied the place of another who could have doubled the money.

Therefore, just as the one who serves well acquires for himself a good rank, so the one who approaches the Lord’s cup unworthily will be guilty of the Lord’s body and blood (1 Cor. 11).

### 9. Not All Bishops Are Bishops

You look to Peter; but consider Judas as well. You admire Stephen; but look also at Nicolas, whom the Lord condemns in his Apocalypse—one who devised such shameful and abominable things that the heresy of the Nicolaitans [Note: Some manuscripts, especially the Cistercian formerly Nonantulanus, read *Neophytes* instead of *Nicolaitans*. Others more correctly add “or Ophites”; I believe this derived from Jerome’s pen, for, as we shall show more fully elsewhere, Saint Epiphanius, the author of the catalogue of heresies falsely attributed to Jerome, Saint Augustine, and others derive the Ophites from the Nicolaitans. See the Letter to Sabinian.] sprang from that root.

Let each person test himself, and then let him approach. Ecclesiastical rank does not make a Christian. Cornelius the Centurion, while still a Gentile, is cleansed by the gift of the Holy Spirit (Acts 10). The boy Daniel judges the elders (Dan. 13). Amos, while stripping mulberries, suddenly became a prophet. David, the youngest, is chosen as king (1 Kings 16). Jesus loves the youngest disciple most dearly.

Take the lower place at table, so that when someone of lesser rank arrives you may be ordered to go up higher (Luke 14). Upon whom does the Lord rest, if not upon the humble and quiet person who trembles at his words (Isa. 66:2)? To whom more has been entrusted, from him more is required. “The mighty will suffer mighty torments” (Wis. 6:6).
