Let no one applaud himself merely for the bodily purity of his chastity [Note: Elsewhere, Grav. notes, “only for chastity”], since people will have to give an account on the day of judgment for every idle word they speak (Matt. 12:36), and since even an insult against a brother incurs the guilt of homicide.

It is not easy to stand in Paul’s place or to hold Peter’s rank, now that they reign with Christ—lest an angel come and tear apart the veil of your temple and remove your lampstand from its place (Rev. 2:5). If you are going to build a tower, calculate the cost of the work beforehand (Luke 14:28). Salt that has lost its savor is useful for nothing except to be thrown outside and trampled by pigs.

If a monk falls, a priest will pray for him. Who will pray for the priest’s fall?

### 10.

But since [Note: From Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations*, Book 4, and elsewhere.] our discourse has sailed away from rocky places, and its fragile skiff has advanced into the deep among hollow cliffs and foaming waves, the sails must now be spread to the winds. Once the reefs of the questions have been crossed, the epilogue must be sung like the song of rejoicing sailors. [Note: A *celeuma* is properly the sailors’ shout, which they raise most loudly when they are near the harbor. It is also called a *keleusma*, and examples are found everywhere among ancient writers. Sidonius, Book 6, Letter 10: “With the banks responding, alleluia, he raises the river’s *keleusma* to Christ.” Paulinus, *On the Return of Nicetas*: “The joyful sailors will sing the customary *celeuma*, changing their melodies into hymns.” Our Jerome also transfers the term to those who tread the winepress, in Jeremiah, chapter 25.]

O desert, blooming with the flowers of Christ! O solitude, in which those stones are born from which the city of the great King is built (Rev. 21:18)! O wilderness, rejoicing in greater intimacy with God!

What are you doing in the world, brother, when you are greater than the world? How long will the shadows of buildings weigh upon you? How long will the prison of smoky cities confine you? Believe me, I seem to see something more of the light. [Note: Grav. appears to have taken this from the conclusion of Pythagoras’ *Golden Verses*: “And when, having left the body, you come into the free ether,” etc.]

I long, casting aside the burden of the body, to fly upward into the pure radiance of the ether.

Are you afraid of poverty? But Christ calls the poor blessed. Are you terrified by labor? No athlete is crowned without sweat. Are you thinking about food? Faith does not fear hunger. [Note: Grav. observes that what follows is taken from Cyprian’s Letter to the Martyrs: “Do your exhausted entrails lie upon the ground from labors? Yet it is not punishment to lie with Christ. Does the half-shorn hair of your head bristle? But since Christ is the head of the man, whatever that head may be must be fitting when it is distinguished for the Lord’s name. Do your limbs, without baths, bristle with neglect and become disfigured by filth? Yet what is dirtied carnally on the outside is washed spiritually within.”]

Do you fear striking your limbs, worn away by fasting, against the bare ground? But the Lord lies with you. Does the unkempt hair of your dirty head horrify you? But Christ is your head. Does the boundless vastness of the desert terrify you? Walk through paradise in your mind. Whenever you climb there in thought, you will not be in the desert.

Does your skin become rough because there are no baths? But whoever has once been washed in Christ does not need to wash again (John 13). And, to put it briefly, listen to the Apostle’s answer concerning everything: “The sufferings of this present age are not worthy to be compared with the glory that is to come, which will be revealed in us” (Rom. 8:18).

You are delicate, brother, if you wish both to rejoice here with the world and afterward to reign with Christ.

### 11.

That day will come—yes, it will come—when this corruptible and mortal nature puts on incorruption and immortality. Then blessed is the servant whom the Lord finds watching (Luke 12:43). Then, at the sound of the trumpet, the earth will tremble with its peoples, while you rejoice.

When the Lord comes to judge, the world will groan mournfully, and tribe after tribe will beat its breast. Once most powerful kings will tremble with their sides exposed. Venus will be displayed with her offspring. [Note: Understand “with her son Cupid.” Victorius, supposing that a numerous offspring was implied by these words, changed the text in accordance with certain manuscripts to: “Then truly fiery Jupiter will be displayed with his offspring; he will also be brought with his own,” etc. He interprets “fiery” as condemned to the eternal punishment of fire.]

Then fiery Jupiter will be brought forward, and foolish Plato with his disciples. Aristotle’s arguments will be of no help. Then you, rustic and poor, will rejoice and laugh and say: “Here is my crucified one; here is the judge who, wrapped in swaddling clothes, cried in a manger. This is the son of a workman and of a prostitute.” [Note: I do not see why Latinius prefers *quaestuariae* (“of a prostitute”), especially since the manuscripts strongly resist it. The passage is taken from Tertullian, *On the Spectacles*, near the end: “This is he—I shall say it—who is the son of a carpenter and of a prostitute, the destroyer of the Sabbath, the Samaritan,” as Grav. notes.]

This is he who, carried in his mother’s arms, fled into Egypt before a man, though he was God (Matt. 2). This is he dressed in scarlet; this is he crowned with thorns; this is he accused of being a magician, demon-possessed, and a Samaritan.

Look at the hands, Jew, which you pierced. Look at the side, Roman, which you opened. Look at the body: is it the same body which you used to say the disciples had secretly carried away at night?

Your love compelled me, brother, to say these things to you, so that you might happen to be present at those events for which the labor is now hard for you. [Note: We have judged this the better and more authentic sense, as it is given by the Cistercian book and supported also by the oldest edition: namely, that you—whose labor is hard now—may be present at the things he has described above on the day of judgment. Martianaeus instead reads: “And so that those for whom the labor is now hard may happen to be present at these things, undertake it.” Other early editors have: “so that they may then be present, for whom the labor is now hard.”]

## LETTER XV [Note: Elsewhere numbered 57. Written near the end of the year 376.]

### To Pope Damasus

He asks him to indicate whether the three Hypostases in God ought to be spoken of or avoided, and with whom he ought to communicate at Antioch.

### 1. The Chair of Peter Must Be Consulted. How Different Are the Conditions of East and West

Since the ancient East, riven by the mutual fury of its peoples, tears into fragments the undivided and seamless garment of the Lord, and foxes are destroying Christ’s vineyard, so that among broken cisterns that hold no water (Jer. 2:13) it is difficult to discern where the sealed fountain and that enclosed garden may be (Song 4:12), I have therefore judged that the chair of Peter and the faith praised by the apostolic mouth must be consulted. From there I now request food for my soul, from the place where I once received Christ’s garments.

Nor could the vast expanse of the flowing element and the intervening distance of lands prevent me from seeking the precious pearl. “Wherever the body is, there the eagles will be gathered” (Matt. 24:28).

After the inheritance was squandered by an evil offspring, among you alone the heritage of the fathers is preserved intact. [Note: Some manuscripts read “the authority is preserved.” Then the very old Ambrosian manuscript S. 33 reads: “where, in turf,” etc.] There, in fruitful soil, the purity of the Lord’s seed returns a hundredfold fruit. Here, grain buried in the furrows degenerates into darnel and wild oats.

Now in the West the sun of righteousness rises; in the East, that Lucifer who had fallen has set his throne above the stars. You are the light of the world; you are the salt of the earth (Matt. 5:14, 13). You are vessels of gold and silver; here there are vessels of clay or wood (2 Tim. 2:20), awaiting an iron rod and an everlasting fire.

### 2. Outside the Church There Is No Salvation

Although your greatness frightens me, your kindness nevertheless invites me. From the priest I ask the salvation of the victim; from the shepherd I ask protection for the sheep. [Note: The same manuscripts read “the saving victim”; other printed editions, “the victim of salvation.”] Let envy depart; let the ambition of the Roman summit withdraw. I speak with the successor of the Fisherman and the disciple of the cross. [Note: Four manuscripts read, “I speak with the disciple of Christ.” Compare what follows with Cyprian’s *On the Unity of the Church*, from which Jerome seems to have drawn this passage.]

Following no one first except Christ, I associate myself in communion with Your Beatitude—that is, with the chair of Peter. I know that the Church is built upon that rock. Whoever eats the Lamb outside this house is profane. If anyone was not in Noah’s ark, he will perish when the flood reigns.

And because my sins have brought me to that solitude [Note: Called Calcidis.] which marks the boundary of Syria beside the frontier of Arabia [Note: The Ambrosian copy reads “which separates Syria”; elsewhere it reads “divides.” Moreover, “the Holy of the Lord” commonly meant the sacred Eucharist, which formerly pastors sent to one another as a sign of their common faith.] and I cannot always seek the Holy of the Lord from Your Holiness across so many intervening distances, I therefore follow here your Egyptian confessors, your colleagues. [Note: By this designation I do not understand, as others—especially the distinguished P. Constantius—interpret it, Peter of Alexandria alone and those attached to him. Rather, I understand those Egyptian confessors themselves whom Jerome praises in Letter 3 to Rufinus: namely, those Egyptian bishops who, having previously been exiled by Valens to Diocaesarea in Palestine, remained in exile. Jerome would not correctly say that he followed them if at that time they had already been restored to their churches, as was later ordered by the law of Gratian in the year 378. See the Chronological Notes.]

I hide beneath cargo ships in a little boat. I do not know Vitalis; I reject Meletius; I do not recognize Paulinus. Whoever does not gather with you scatters; that is, whoever is not Christ’s is Antichrist’s.

### 3. Violence Used against Jerome to Make Him Confess Three Hypostases in God

Now, alas, after the faith of Nicaea, after the decree of Alexandria together with the West, [Note: The Council of Alexandria in 362, at which the defenders of both one and three Hypostases were questioned and were found to hold one and the same position against both Arius and Sabellius. The Fathers therefore decreed that the faith promulgated by the Fathers at Nicaea was superior and more exact in its terminology, that its words ought to suffice, and that they should be used.]

after the three Hypostases were demanded of me by the offspring of the Arians, the Campenses, [Note: We have preferred the reading of the Ambrosian and other manuscripts, since until now the text had been understood as “the Campenses, as though they were of a different faction from the Arian bishop,” whereas the Campenses are followers of the Arian bishop. The phrase “offspring of the Arians, the Campenses” refers either to Meletians, since their father Meletius was transferred by the Arians Acacius and George from Sebastia to Antioch, as Jerome himself reports in his *Chronicle*, or to those called Campenses because they were forced to hold their assemblies in the fields or in the church called Palaea outside the city. In this sense Jerome calls the Donatists *Campates* in the *Dialogue against the Luciferians*. The Ambrosian manuscript’s reading, “the Campenses, offspring of the Arians,” is preferable; see the Chronological Notes. We understand these Campenses to be different from those whom the holy Father mentions in the *Dialogue against the Luciferians*.]

a new term is being demanded from me, a Roman.

Who, I ask, handed this down from the Apostles? What new teacher of the nations, Paul, taught this? We ask what they think three Hypostases can mean. They say, “Three subsistent persons.” We reply that we believe this. It is not enough: they demand the word itself, because I do not know what poison lies hidden in the syllables.

We cry out: “If anyone does not confess three Hypostases as three *enhypostata*—that is, three subsistent persons—let him be anathema.” And because we do not learn the terminology, we are judged heretics.

But if someone, understanding Hypostasis as *ousia*—substance—does not say that there is one Hypostasis in three persons, he is alien from Christ. Under this confession we are branded together with you with the branding iron of Unionism. [Note: This means that they were said to profess one single person. In the following Letter to Marcus Jerome says, “I am accused of Sabellian impiety.” Since Sabellius professed only one *prosopon enhypostaton*—one subsistent person—his heresy was simply called the Heresy of Union, as learned men have rightly noted, especially Saint Hilary, *On the Synods*, 26. Prudentius wrote his poem against the Unionists—that is, against the Sabellian heretics—in the *Apotheosis*.]

### 4. Why It Is Not Permitted to Say “Three Hypostases”

Decide, I beg you, if it pleases you, and I will not fear saying “three Hypostases.” If you order it, let a new creed be composed after Nicaea, and let us confess orthodoxy in the same words as the Arians.

The entire school of secular literature knows no meaning for Hypostasis except *ousia*, substance. [Note: In those times and earlier, among the Greeks and Latins the word Hypostasis signified *ousia*, substance. Thus *ousia* and *hypostasis* are often found among the ancients used for the same thing. But when the Greeks who asserted three Hypostases openly explained what they meant by the term—which could suitably be understood as subsistence—the Latins substituted the word “person.” On this subject see especially Saint Gregory Nazianzen, Oration 32, and Basil, Letter 349 to Terentius. Soon afterward, some manuscripts read: “but it is its own, that which is.”]

And who, I ask, will proclaim three substances with sacrilegious lips? There is one and only one nature of God, which truly is. For that which subsists does not derive its being from elsewhere but possesses it as its own. The other things that have been created, even though they appear to be, are not, because once they did not exist; and what once did not exist can again cease to exist.

God alone, who is eternal—that is, who has no beginning—truly bears the name of essence. Therefore he says to Moses from the bush: “I am who I am”; and again: “He who is has sent me” (Exod. 3:14).

Angels, heaven, earth, and seas certainly existed at that time; so how does God properly claim for himself the common name of essence? But because that nature alone is perfect, and the one Godhead subsists [variant: persists] in three persons, which truly is and is one nature, [Note: The reading of the Ambrosian copy appears more correct: “God claims it as his own, because that alone is an uncreated nature and subsists in three persons, since it is truly one nature.” Nevertheless, the printed reading can also defend its place, and therefore we have not altered it.]

whoever says that there are three—that is, three Hypostases, or *ousiai*—tries, under the name of piety, to assert three natures.

And if that is so, why do we separate ourselves from Arius’s [variant: the Arians’] walls, joined to him by our faithlessness? Let Ursinus be joined to Your Beatitude; let Auxentius be associated with Ambrose. [Note: Later writers call this man Ursicinus. As is well known, he was Damasus’s rival for the pontificate and suspected of Arian heresy. Auxentius was a fierce Arian, against whom Saint Ambrose composed his sermon *On Not Handing Over the Basilicas*.]

Let this be far from the Roman faith. Let religious hearts among the peoples not swallow such sacrilege. Let it suffice for us to say: one substance, three subsistent persons, perfect, equal, and coeternal. Let “three Hypostases” be silent, if you wish, and let “one” be retained. It is not a good sign when words disagree although the meaning is the same.

Let the faith already mentioned suffice for us. Or, if you think that we ought to say “three Hypostases” together with their interpretations, we do not refuse. But believe me: poison lies beneath honey. “Satan’s angel disguises himself as an angel of light” (2 Cor. 11:14). They interpret Hypostasis well; yet when I say that I hold what they explain, I am judged a heretic.

Why do they cling so anxiously to one word? Why do they hide beneath ambiguous speech? If they believe as they interpret, I do not condemn what they retain. If I believe as they pretend to understand, let them permit me also to express their meaning in my own words. [Note: The Ambrosian manuscript reads: “If they believe as they interpret, let them interpret.”]

### 5.

Therefore I adjure Your Beatitude by the crucified salvation of the world and by the Trinity of one *homoousion*, [Note: We restore the reading found in numerous older manuscripts and more elegantly phrased: “by the salvation of the world through the Crucified One, and by the Trinity of one substance,” whereas the previously printed text had “by the crucified salvation of the world.”] to grant me authority in your letters either to refrain from speaking of the Hypostases or to speak of them.

And lest the obscurity of the place in which I live deceive the bearers of the letters, deign to send your written reply to the presbyter Evagrius, whom you know very well.

At the same time, indicate with whom I ought to communicate at Antioch, because the Campenses, joined to the heretical Tharsenses, [Note: We have explained above who the Campenses are. The Tharsenses were heretics, followers of the bishop of Tarsus—that is, certain Semi-Arians or Macedonians—who, after sending Silvanus of Tarsus to Liberius in the year 366, were received into communion and shortly afterward also at the Council of Tyana, after pretending to withdraw from heresy. Others understand them as followers of Diodore, whom Meletius, on returning from exile, appointed bishop of Tarsus; but they misunderstand Jerome’s meaning and the chronology.] seek nothing else than, supported by the authority of your communion, to preach three Hypostases in the old sense.

## LETTER XVI [Note: Elsewhere numbered 58. Written several months after the preceding letter.]

### To Pope Damasus

He again adjures him to indicate with which of the three parties dividing the Church of Antioch he ought to communicate.

### 1.

The importunate woman in the Gospel at last deserved to be heard (Matt. 15:28), and when the door had been shut with the servants inside, even at midnight a friend received bread from his friend (Luke 11:8). God himself, whom no forces can overcome, is conquered by the prayers of a tax collector. The city of Nineveh, which had perished through sin, stood firm through tears (Jonah 3:10).

Why have I repeated this lengthy introduction? Clearly, so that you may look upon the small person as great; so that you, a wealthy shepherd, may not despise a sick sheep.

Christ brought the thief from the cross into paradise (Luke 23:43); and, lest anyone should think that a late conversion was hopeless, he made the punishment for homicide a martyrdom. [Note: Several manuscripts read, “made martyrdom the punishment for homicide,” a reading that is not entirely unsuitable. Victorius preferred *poenam* (“punishment”) in place of *poena* (“penalty”).]

Christ, I say, joyfully embraces the returning prodigal son (Luke 15:20), and leaving the ninety-nine sheep, he carries the one little sheep that remained upon the shoulders of the good Shepherd (Luke 15:5). Paul becomes a preacher from being a persecutor. He is blinded in his bodily eyes so that he may see more with his mind; and he who led Christ’s imprisoned servants to the council of the Jews later boasts even of Christ’s bonds (Acts 9).

### 2.

As I have already written, I received Christ’s garment in the city of Rome, but now I am held at Syria’s barbarian frontier. And lest you think that someone else passed judgment on me, I myself decided what I deserved.

But, as the Gentile poet says, “He who crosses the sea changes the sky, not his mind” (Horace, Book 1 of the *Epistles*), so the unceasing enemy followed me from behind, and now I suffer greater battles in solitude.

From here, supported by the forces of the world, Arian madness roars. [Note: This refers to Meletius, who, by the law of Gratian and through the judgment of the military commander Sapor, obtained the Arian churches under dispute and, relying on his protection, insistently demanded from Jerome a profession of three Hypostases.]

From here the Church, split into three parts, hastens to drag me to itself. The ancient authority of the monks who live nearby rises against me. [Note: The older edition and some manuscripts read “of the monks who remain with me.” These monks are attacked at greater length in the following Letter to Marcus, section 2.]

Meanwhile I cry out: “If anyone is joined to the chair of Peter, he is mine.” Meletius, Vitalis, and Paulinus all say that they adhere to you. I could believe it if only one asserted this. Now either two are lying, or all of them.

Therefore I adjure Your Beatitude by the cross of the Lord, by the necessary glory of our faith, and by the passion of Christ: since you follow the Apostles in honor, follow them also in merit; so may you sit upon the throne with the twelve when you judge; so may another gird you in your old age with Peter; [Note: The words clearly allude to Christ’s prediction of Peter’s martyrdom: “When you grow old, another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish to go.” For this reason we do not approve the reading of some manuscripts, *jungat* (“join”) instead of *cingat* (“gird”).] so may you obtain citizenship in heaven with Paul—indicate to me in your letter with whom I ought to communicate in Syria. [Note: Two reliable manuscripts read, “with whom I ought to communicate in Syria.”]

Do not despise the soul for which Christ died.

## LETTER XVII [Note: Elsewhere numbered 77. Written at the beginning of the year 379.]

### To Marcus the Presbyter

[Note: The older editions make this Marcus the presbyter of Celeda. Most manuscripts, however, call him a presbyter or bishop of Chalcis. It is very likely that the reading should be “of Teleda,” as other manuscripts have it; for Teledan was a large town in the region of Chalcis, and from Theodoret’s *Life of the Fathers*, chapter 4, we learn that the monastery of Saint Eusebius was not far from it. Thus its presbyter could acknowledge the faith of the people of Chalcis.]

He sets out for Marcus his profession of faith concerning the Trinity, agreeing with the Roman and Alexandrian Churches. He greatly laments that his friends have been forced by the Arian faction to leave the desert, while he himself is daily pressed to abandon those places.

### 1.

I had indeed decided to use the Psalmist’s words: “When the sinner stood against me, I was silent and humbled myself, and kept silent from good things” (Ps. 38:2). And again: “I was like a deaf man and did not hear, and like a mute who does not open his mouth; I became like a man who does not hear” (Ps. 37:14–15).

But because love conquers everything and affection overcomes resolve, I am not so much returning injury to those who inflict it as answering you, who have asked me to do so. Among Christians, as someone has said, it is not the one who suffers but the one who inflicts insult who is wretched. [Note: Saint Cyprian, Letter 55, to Cornelius: “For it is not the one who suffers but the one who commits the insult who is wretched.” Cicero likewise says in Book 5 of the *Tusculan Disputations*: “It is better to receive an injury than to inflict one.”]

### 2. He Complains that His Faith Is Offended, Although It Is the Same as That of Damasus and Peter of Alexandria

Before I speak with you about my faith, which you know very well, I am compelled to cry out against the barbarism of this place in the familiar verse:

> What race of men is this? What country permits  
> Such barbarous customs? We are forbidden the hospitality of the shore.  
> They wage war, and forbid us to stand upon the first land.  
> And so forth. (*Aeneid*, Book 1)

We have taken these words from a Gentile poet so that one who does not preserve Christ’s peace may at least learn peace from a pagan.

I am called a heretic because I preach the Trinity of one *homoousion*. I am accused of Sabellian impiety because I proclaim, with tireless voice, three subsistent, true, complete, and perfect persons. If I am accused by Arians, they are right according to their principles. But if I am accused by the orthodox, then those who accuse such a faith have ceased to be orthodox—or, if it pleases them, let them condemn me as a heretic together with the West, as a heretic together with Egypt—that is, together with Damasus and Peter.

Why do they accuse one man apart from his companions? If a stream flows narrowly, the fault is not the riverbed but the spring. I am ashamed to say it: from the caves of our cells we pass judgment upon the world. Rolling about in sackcloth and ashes, we pronounce judgment upon bishops.

What does a royal spirit do beneath a penitent’s tunic? Chains, filth, and uncut hair are not signs of a diadem but of weeping. Let them permit me, I beg, to say nothing. Why do they tear apart one who does not deserve their envy?

I am a heretic—what is that to you? Be quiet; it has already been said. Clearly you fear that an eloquent man may travel through the churches in the Syrian or Greek language, seduce the peoples, and create a schism. I have taken nothing from anyone; I accept nothing while idle. Each day we seek food by our hands and our own sweat, knowing that it is written by the Apostle: “If anyone will not work, neither let him eat” (2 Thess. 3:10).

### 3.

Jesus is witness with what groaning and what sorrow I have written these things, venerable and holy Father. “I have been silent; shall I always be silent?” says the Lord (Ps. 49:21; Isa. 42:14).

I am not granted even one corner of the desert. Every day my faith is demanded, as though I had been born again without faith. I confess as they wish, but they are not satisfied. I subscribe, but they do not believe. The only thing that pleases them is that I leave this place.

Now, now I yield. They have torn from me part of my soul, my dearest brothers. Look: they want to depart—indeed, they are departing—saying that it is better to live among wild beasts than with such Christians. And I myself, if bodily weakness and the severity of winter did not hold me back, would have fled already.

Nevertheless, until spring arrives, I beg that the hospitality of the desert be granted me for a few months. Or, if even this seems too long, I will leave. “The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness” (Ps. 23:1). Let them alone ascend to heaven; let Christ have died for them alone; let them possess and glory in him.

But as for me, far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me and I to the world (Gal. 6:14).

### 4.

Concerning the faith which you were kind enough to write, I gave a written profession to the holy Cyril. [Note: It is not easy to determine from Jerome’s words who this Cyril was. Some think that he was the famous Cyril of Jerusalem, who, having been driven from his episcopal see, was at that time wandering through the deserts of Syria. This conjecture rests on exceedingly weak arguments, especially since Jerome is known to have been almost hostile to Cyril’s name. Whatever the case, this passage gave an impostor the opportunity to forge a work entitled *Explanation of the Faith to Cyril* under the name of the holy Doctor; it will be presented in the final volume of the works.]

Whoever does not believe in this way is alien from Christ.

For the rest, I have as witnesses to my faith your ears and those of the blessed brother Zenobius, whom all of us who are here greet most warmly together with you.

## LETTER XVIII [Note: Elsewhere divided into two letters under numbers 142 and 143; written around the middle of the year 381. The Vatican manuscript 215, formerly Reginae, begins: “A brief and sudden treatise of Blessed Jerome on the Seraphim mentioned in Isaiah’s vision.” Jerome composed it while still a pupil of the most eloquent Gregory Nazianzen at Constantinople, testing his own understanding and responding to the request of his friends; he entitled it *On the Seraphim*. Jerome himself testifies at the beginning of his commentary on Isaiah 6 that he dictated this little book suddenly, both to test his modest talent and to obey his friends. Since this treatise nowhere bears the character or style of a letter, Sixtus of Siena argues that it was falsely addressed to Damasus. Since, however, the title “Letter to Damasus” has remained in printed books to this day—whether through the judgment of ancient scribes or because Jerome gave the explanation to Damasus to read when he was in Rome and later dedicated it to him—we have not been permitted to alter it, especially since Jerome himself joins it in his catalogue of works with another letter to Damasus, concerning Hosanna.]

### To Pope Damasus: On the Seraphim and the Coal

He explains the vision in the sixth chapter of the prophet Isaiah and, after some discussion of the history and death of King Uzziah, treats in his customary learned manner of the Seraphim and the Trisagion.

And it came to pass in the year in which King Uzziah died: I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and exalted, etc. (Isa. 6:2). Before speaking about the Vision, it seems necessary to examine who Uzziah was, how many years he reigned, and who his contemporaries were among the other nations. As for his person, as we read in the Books of Kings and Chronicles (4 Kings 15; 2 Chron. 26:18), he was a just man and did what was right in the sight of the Lord: he built the Temple, constructed a water conduit, offered vessels, and, on account of this merit, overcame his adversaries. The greatest indication of his piety was that he had many prophets in his kingdom.

As long as Zechariah the priest, surnamed “the Understanding,” lived, Uzziah pleased God and entered His sanctuary with every mark of reverence. But after Zechariah died, wishing to offer gifts himself, he invaded the priestly office, not so much piously as audaciously. When the Levites and the other priests protested, “Are you not King Uzziah, and not a priest?” he refused to listen, and immediately leprosy covered his forehead. [Note: Many manuscripts read “was struck.”] This accords with the Prophet’s saying: “Fill their faces, Lord, with disgrace” (Ps. 82:17).

The forehead was the part of the body protected by the priest with a golden plate, which the Lord commands in Ezekiel to be marked with the impression of the letter *tau* (Ezek. 9). Concerning it David exults, saying: “The light of your countenance has been marked upon us” (Ps. 4:7), O Lord. It was also on this part of the body that the insolent foreigner, struck by a slingstone, perished. [Note: Previously the corrupt reading was “struck by the blow of a slingstone”; we have corrected it from the manuscripts.]

Uzziah reigned for fifty-two years (2 Kings 17). During this period Amulius ruled among the Latins, and Agamestor, the eleventh king, among the Athenians. After Uzziah’s death, the Prophet Isaiah saw this Vision, which we are now attempting to explain—that is, in the year in which Romulus, the founder of the Roman empire, was born. This will be clear to those who wish to read the *Book of Times*, which we translated into Latin from the Greek language. [Note: We have deleted the word “It follows,” which printed editions incorrectly place before this verse.]

“And it came to pass in the year in which King Uzziah died: I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and exalted” (Isa. 6). After the historical account, the spiritual understanding follows; for this reason the history itself has been repeated. [Note: In the Cistercian manuscript we find “is to be repeated”; the reading, although itself somewhat incongruous, is not entirely impossible.]

While the leprous king lived and, as far as lay in his power, destroyed the priesthood, Isaiah could not see the Vision. As long as he held the kingdom in Judah, the Prophet did not raise his eyes toward heaven (Isa. 6): the heavenly things were not opened to him, the Lord Sabaoth did not appear, nor was the name “Holy” heard three times in the mystery of faith. But when Uzziah died, everything that the following passage will display revealed itself in open light. [Note: An old edition adds “as far as can be understood,” and shortly afterward, in agreement with certain manuscripts, reads “Holy” three times instead of “of the Holy.”]

Something similar is written in Exodus (chap. 2). While Pharaoh lived, the people of Israel, oppressed by work with clay, bricks, and straw, did not sigh toward the Lord; while he reigned, no one sought the God of their fathers, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. But when he died, the children of Israel sighed, as Scripture says: “And their cry went up to the Lord” (Exod. 2:23). Yet according to the historical account they ought rather to have rejoiced at that time and sighed earlier, while he was alive. [Note: Martianay awkwardly repeats the name “Pharaoh” here, although neither the printed editions nor the other manuscripts contain it.]

Likewise, while Ezekiel was prophesying, Phaltias son of Benaiah died. After the death of the worst leader, Ezekiel says: “I fell upon my face, and cried with a loud voice, and said: Alas, alas, Lord Adonai, you are bringing the remnant of Israel to an end” (Ezek. 11:13). If, then, you understand Uzziah, Pharaoh, Phaltias, and the other figures of this kind as hostile powers, you will see how, while they are alive, none of us sees, sighs, or falls into repentance.

“Let not sin reign,” says the Apostle, “in your mortal body” (Rom. 6). While sin reigns, we build cities for the Egyptians; we live amid ashes and filth; instead of grain we pursue straw, and instead of solid rock we pursue works of clay.

### 3. The Lord Seen upon a High and Exalted Throne

It follows: “I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and exalted” (Dan. 7). Daniel also saw the Lord sitting, but not upon a throne high and exalted. Elsewhere the divine voice promises, saying: “I will come, and I will sit, and I will judge the people in the valley of Jehoshaphat,” which is interpreted as “the judgment of the Lord” (Joel 3:12).

The sinner, who is like me, sees the Lord sitting in the valley of Jehoshaphat—not on a hill, not on a mountain, but in a valley, and in the valley of judgment. But the one who is righteous and like Isaiah sees Him sitting upon a throne high and exalted.

To add another point: when I consider intellectually how He reigns among Thrones, Dominions, Angels, and the other Powers, I see His throne as exalted. But when I consider how He governs the human race and is often said to descend to earth for our salvation, I see His throne as humble and close to the earth.

### 4. The Seraphim

It follows: “I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and exalted; and the house was full of his majesty, and Seraphim stood around him” (according to the Septuagint). Some before me, both Greeks [Note: Origen was among them, as Jerome himself says in his Letter to Pammachius and Oceanus: “In the interpretation of Isaiah, where two Seraphim are described as crying out, and he interprets them as the Son and the Holy Spirit, did I not change a detestable interpretation into the two Testaments? The book is in circulation; it was published twenty years ago, etc.”] and Latins, in explaining this passage, interpreted the Lord seated upon the throne as God the Father, and the two Seraphim, said to stand on either side, as our Lord Jesus Christ and the Holy Spirit.

Although they are extremely learned, I do not agree with their authority. For it is much better to speak the truth plainly than to present falsehood eloquently—especially since John the Evangelist writes that, in this same Vision, not God the Father but Christ was seen.

When he spoke of the unbelief of the Jews, he immediately explained the causes of their unbelief, saying: “And therefore they could not believe in him, because Isaiah said: You shall hear with your ears and shall not understand; and seeing, you shall look and shall not see. He said these things when he saw the glory of the Only-Begotten, and testified about him” (Isa. 6:9–10; John 12:40–41).

Thus, in the present book of Isaiah, the one seated upon the throne commands him to say: “You shall hear with your ears and shall not understand.” According to the Evangelist, the one who gives this command is Christ. Therefore it follows that the Seraphim cannot be understood as Christ, since Christ Himself is the one seated upon the throne.

And although in the Acts of the Apostles, speaking against Jews who were disputing among themselves, Paul says:

> “The Holy Spirit spoke rightly through Isaiah the Prophet to our fathers, saying: Go to this people and say: You shall hear with your ears and shall not understand; and seeing, you shall see and shall not perceive. For the heart of this people has grown dull, and they have heard heavily with their ears, and they have closed their eyes, lest they should ever see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, and turn to me, and I should heal them” (Acts 28:25ff.).

[Note: Some manuscripts read “and turn themselves, and I shall heal them.” The Greek in both places is καὶ ἐπιστρέψωσι καὶ ἰάσωμαι, “and they should turn, and I should heal.”]

Nevertheless, the difference of persons does not create a problem for me, since I know that Christ and the Holy Spirit are of one substance; that the words of the Spirit are no different from those of the Son; and that the Son commanded nothing different from the Spirit.

### 5. The House Filled with Majesty

It follows: “And the house was full of his majesty.” The house of God that is above is seen to be full of glory. As for this house below, I do not know whether it is full of glory, unless perhaps in accordance with the Psalmist’s meaning: “The earth is the Lord’s, and its fullness” (Ps. 23:1).

Let us too say that those on earth are full of glory who can say: “We have all received from his fullness” (John 1:16). Wise women build this house, while foolish women destroy it with their hands (Prov. 14).

Isaiah also speaks of this house: “And it shall come to pass in the last days: the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the highest mountains, and it shall be exalted above the hills” (Isa. 2:2). [Note: The Royal manuscript has “the manifest mountain of the Lord, and the house of God upon the highest mountains,” etc. The Septuagint reads exactly: ἐμφανὲς τὸ ὄρος κυρίου καὶ ὁ οἶκος τοῦ θεοῦ, etc. For at that time Jerome was not reciting the Scriptures according to the Hebrew truth.]

This is the house of which the aforementioned Paul also bears witness in sacred language: “And Moses indeed was faithful in all his house as a servant, for a testimony of those things that were to be spoken. But Christ, as a Son over his house, whose house we are—if only we hold firm to the beginning of his substance unto the end” (Heb. 3:5–6).

He also speaks of this to Timothy: “I am writing these things so that you may know how it is necessary for you to conduct yourself in the house of God, which is the Church” (1 Tim. 3:14–15).

### 6. The Six Wings of the Seraphim

It follows: “And Seraphim stood around him; six wings for one, and six wings for the other; with two they covered their face, with two they covered their feet, and with two they flew; and they cried out, one to the other, and said: Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord God Sabaoth; the whole earth is full of his glory.”

We wish to know what the Seraphim are who stand around God; what the six wings of each are, which together make twelve; how they cover their face with two, their feet with two, and fly with two, when they are said above to stand around God; or how they stand around Him when there are two of them, while elsewhere they fly; what it means that they cry out, one to the other; why they repeat the name “Holy” three times; and how the house was earlier said to be full of glory, while now the earth is said to be so.

### Prayer Before Interpreting Scripture

Since these questions raise no small cloud of dust and immediately present the difficulty of interpretation, let us together entreat the Lord that a coal may also be sent to me from the altar, so that, cleansed of every stain of sin, I may first be able to behold the mysteries of God and then relate what I have seen.

As we find in the interpretation of Hebrew names, *Seraphim* means “burning,” “conflagration,” or “the beginning of their mouth.” We ask what this burning is. The Savior says: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what I desire is that it burn” (Luke 12:49). [Note: A large number of manuscripts read this way; previously they read “to the two disciples.” Immediately afterward the same manuscripts read: “Was not our heart burning within us on the way, when he opened,” etc.]

The two disciples to whom the Lord had opened the Scriptures on the way, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, after their eyes were opened and they recognized Him, said to one another: “Was not our heart burning within us while he spoke to us on the way and opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke 24:32).

In Deuteronomy (chap. 4), God Himself is written to be a consuming fire. In Ezekiel (chap. 8), He likewise appears fiery from the loins to the feet. “The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tested by fire, tried upon the earth, purified sevenfold” (Ps. 17). There are many other passages; if I wished to repeat them from all the Scriptures, the task would be too long.

Let us therefore ask where this saving fire is. There can be no doubt that it is in the sacred books, through whose reading all human vices are cleansed. But concerning what follows—“the beginning of their mouth”—and how it can be referred to the Scriptures, I fear that, if we begin to speak, we may seem less to interpret than to do violence to the Scriptures.

### The Hebrew Language as the First and Common Language

The beginning of the mouth, the beginning of common speech, and everything that we speak: all antiquity has handed down the Hebrew language, in which the Old Testament was written, as the first language. But afterward, when the diversity of languages was assigned in the construction of the tower because of God’s displeasure, the variety of speech was dispersed among all nations.

Thus both the burning and the beginning of the mouth are perceived in the two Testaments. It is not surprising that they stand around God, since through them the Lord Himself is learned.

“Six wings for one, and six wings for the other.” Our Victorinus interpreted these as the twelve Apostles. We can also understand them as the twelve stones of the altar, untouched by iron, and the twelve gems from which the priest’s insignia was constructed (Exod. 28). [Note: Up to this point all printed editions read “a distinguished diadem was constructed.” Since one of the ancient copyists did not sufficiently understand the word “insignia,” he added “diadem” to make the phrase clearer. This was certainly erroneous, but the word was afterward incorporated into the text and continued to mislead editors, so that they failed to notice that the twelve gems were not used to construct a diadem, or *cidaris*, but the insignia of the High Priest, namely the garment called the *rationale*. We have corrected the passage on the authority of the Royal exemplar.]

Ezekiel also mentions these gems (chap. 28), and the Apocalypse does not omit them (chap. 21). God will determine which interpretation is true; which is probable, we shall explain in what follows.

### 7. The Wings Covering Face and Feet

It follows: “With two they covered their face, with two they covered their feet, and with two they flew.”

They covered not their own face but God’s. For who can know His beginning—what He was in the eternity of things before He created this world; when He created the Thrones, Dominions, Powers, Angels, and the entire heavenly ministry? [Note: We have followed the testimony of all the manuscripts and of the oldest edition. Other printed editions read “meanwhile.” Compare the Letter to Titus, chap. 1, where Jerome, either expressing his own opinion or reporting that of others, says that the angels existed many ages before the creation of the world: “Six thousand years of our world have not yet been completed; and how many eternities before it, how many ages, how many beginnings of ages must we suppose there were, during which Angels, Thrones, Dominions, and the other Powers served God and, at His command, subsisted without the changes and measures of time.” See what we shall note there.]

It follows: “And with two they covered their feet”—not their own, but God’s. For who can know His end? What will happen after the consummation of the age, what life will follow after the human race has been judged? Will another earth perhaps exist again, and after its passing other elements, or another world and sun have to be created?

“Declare to me the former things, and the last things that are to come, and I shall say that you are gods,” says Isaiah (chap. 41:23), signifying that no one can explain what existed before the world and what will happen after the world.

“And with two they flew.” We know only what lies in the middle, what is disclosed to us through the reading of the Scriptures: when the world was made; when the human being was formed; when the Flood occurred; when the Law was given; how the whole expanse of the earth was filled from one man; and how, at the end of time, the Son of God took flesh for our salvation.

But the other matters we have mentioned were covered by these two Seraphim with their face and feet.

“And they cried out, one to the other.” The phrase “one to the other” is beautifully placed.

### Nothing Discordant in the Old and New Testaments

Whatever we read in the Old Testament, we find in the Gospel as well; and whatever has been read in the Gospel is derived from the authority of the Old Testament. There is nothing discordant or different between them.

“And they said: Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord God Sabaoth.” The Trinity is proclaimed in both Testaments.

That our Savior is also called *Sabaoth*, receive an example from Psalm 23. The Powers that ministered to the Lord called out to other heavenly Powers to open the gate for the Lord returning:

> “Lift up your gates, O princes,”

or, as Aquila interprets it, “Lift up your heads, O gates,” and the King of glory will enter.

Again, those Powers, amazed by the new mystery at seeing Him clothed in flesh, ask: “Who is this King of glory?” (Ps. 23:9). They receive the answer: “The Lord of powers—He is the King of glory,” which in Hebrew is written, “The Lord Sabaoth.”

It should be understood that wherever the Septuagint translators have rendered “Lord of powers” or “Lord Almighty,” the Hebrew has *Lord Sabaoth*, which Aquila translates as “Lord of armies.”

The Lord Himself is also here represented by four letters, a form properly used of God: JOD HE, JOD HE—that is, two *ja*s—which, doubled, produce that ineffable and glorious name of God. [Note: The printed editions corrupt this important passage, especially because they read “with two” instead of “with two and two”; others read “thus” for “two.” Jerome himself also deserves correction for saying that the ineffable name of God is composed of two Jod-He letters, since everyone knows that it consists of Jod-He-Vau-He, or *Jahveh*. Martianay thinks that Jerome was referring to the famous Greek IIIIII, by which the Greeks wrote the Hebrew letters composing the divine name, so that *jaja* could have been read in Hebrew fashion. But perhaps Jerome more likely had in mind the opinion of certain Jews who thought that the divine name was written as two *ja*s, although one of them had changed into *Vau*, a letter differing from *Jod* scarcely except in size. It should meanwhile not be overlooked that the Cistercian manuscript reads “Jod-He-Vau-He,” that is, “two and two,” which, when doubled, etc. This is indeed the more correct sense and reading, and is not exposed to the difficulty mentioned above. Yet I fear that it may have come from the pen of some critic, since it bears the mark of critical ingenuity.]

“The whole earth is full of his glory.” This too is said by the Seraphim concerning the coming of the Lord and Savior: how His preaching extends throughout the whole earth and the sound of the Apostles penetrates to the boundaries of the world.

### 8. The Raised Lintel and the Smoke-Filled House

It follows: “And the lintel was raised by the voice with which they cried out.”

We read in the Old Testament that the Lord always spoke to Moses and Aaron at the door of the Tabernacle (Lev. 1 and 4; Num. 10), as though before the Gospel He had not yet brought them into the Holy of Holies. But afterward the Church of God was brought in, saying: “The king brought me into his chamber” (Song 1:3).

When, therefore, our Lord descended to earth, that lintel—that is, a kind of obstacle to those wishing to enter—was lifted away, and this whole world was filled with smoke, that is, with the glory of God.

Where in Latin we read *elevatum*, “raised,” the Greek has ἐπήρθη, “was lifted away.” But because the ambiguity of the verb can be interpreted in either way, our translators rendered it as “raised” instead of “removed.”

“And the house was filled with smoke.” As we said above, God is fire. When He descended upon Mount Sinai to Moses, lamps appeared to move about at His coming, and the whole mountain was full of smoke. Hence it is said in the Psalms: “He touches the mountains, and they smoke” (Ps. 103:32).

From fire, therefore, since we cannot contain its entire substance, a lighter and—so to speak—more diffuse nature of smoke is dispersed throughout the world. Receiving this, let us say: “We know in part and we prophesy in part” (1 Cor. 13:9); and: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma” (ibid. 13:12).

### 9. The Seraphim and the Destruction of Jerusalem

“And Seraphim stood around him: six wings for one, and six wings for the other.”

A certain Greek who was exceptionally learned in the Scriptures [Note: Perhaps Gregory of Nazianzus.] explained the Seraphim as certain powers in heaven who stand before God’s tribunal, praising Him and being sent on various ministries, especially to those who need purification and deserve to be cleansed in part by punishments because of their former sins. [Note: The two words “who deserve to be purified” are absent from the Royal manuscript, though the sense remains complete. Elsewhere, in Ezekiel chap. 30, Jerome seems to reject this opinion, saying: “For it is not good but evil angels who have been appointed over torments.” We shall discuss this matter more fully in its place, in the commentary on Daniel chap. 7. Shortly below, the same manuscript also lacks the words “which we now see destroyed,” as does the Cistercian manuscript. That manuscript reads here “and the burning of ruined Jerusalem” instead of “the burning of all [Jerusalem],” etc.]

He said that the lintel being lifted and the house being filled with smoke signified the destruction of the Jewish Temple and the burning of all Jerusalem, which we now see destroyed.

Others agree with him in the earlier points but differ in the final part. They say that the lintel was lifted at the time when the veil of the Temple was torn and the whole house of Israel was confounded by a cloud of error (Matt. 27; Mark 15; Luke 23). At that time, Josephus reports, the priests heard a voice from the inner sanctuaries of the Temple, saying: “Let us pass from these dwellings.” [Note: Jerome mentions this miracle from Josephus also in his Letter to Hedibia, question 8, in the letter of Paula and Eustochium to Marcella, and frequently elsewhere. Josephus himself, in Book VI of *The Jewish War*, chapter 5, does not relate it to Christ’s death, when the Temple veil was torn, but to five years before the destruction of that same Temple and approximately thirty-two years after Christ’s passion, among the portents that preceded the city’s destruction. It appears that Eusebius in his *Chronicle* misled Jerome—either because he encountered corrupt manuscripts of Josephus or because he drew from another author; certainly he did not find this in Josephus. We shall give the words of both elsewhere, where we shall discuss the matter at greater length. Meanwhile, we note that Jerome himself correctly applies that saying in his commentary on Isaiah chap. 66 to the time of Jerusalem’s destruction.]

### 10. Another Interpretation of the Twelve Wings

There is a certain man from whom I rejoice that I have learned many things, and who has polished the language of the Hebrews so thoroughly that he is considered a Chaldean among their scribes. He approached the matter by a very different path.

He says that no prophet except Isaiah saw Seraphim standing around God, and that the Seraphim themselves are not read of elsewhere. He then says that the Vision was given beforehand as a sign of the consummation and captivity of Jerusalem, which occurred under Nebuchadnezzar.

From Uzziah, under whom Isaiah began to prophesy, to Zedekiah, who was the last king and was led blind into Babylon, there were eleven kings, and a twelfth, Gedaliah, whom the king of Babylon had appointed over the land. Ishmael son of Nethaniah killed him amid a banquet, a parricide of the remnants of his homeland (2 Kings 25; 2 Chron. 36; Jer. 41). These, he says, are the twelve wings: four of them cover their faces, four fly, and four cover their feet, as is found in certain copies.

Of these twelve kings, only four were righteous: Uzziah, Jotham, Hezekiah, and Josiah. Through the successive captivities they dared, in exalted fashion, to glorify God: “Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord God Sabaoth.” The others, because of their sins, covered their faces; and those who were led into captivity covered the traces of their feet.

He explained the lintel being lifted and the house being filled with smoke, as we said above, as the overthrow of Jerusalem and the burning of the Temple.

### 11. Isaiah’s Purified Lips

Since I have begun to report his opinion, let us also touch upon matters that I have not yet addressed. He asserted that the tongs by which the altar-coal was grasped and the lips purified referred to Isaiah’s own suffering, namely the way in which he was killed under King Manasseh. At that time, with his lips truly purified, he said to the Lord: “Here am I; send me,” and: “Alas for me, for I am pierced” (according to the Septuagint).

As long as Uzziah lives, Isaiah, you do not understand that you are wretched; you are not pierced, you are not moved. But when Uzziah dies, then you perceive that you do not have clean lips; then you recognize yourself as unworthy of the Vision of God.

Would that I too might be pierced, and after being pierced become worthy of the Vision of God, since I am a human being, have unclean lips, and dwell among a people also having unclean lips. [Note: The Cistercian manuscripts read “may I become worthy of God”; the old edition reads “worthy by God’s preaching.” Shortly afterward they read “since I am a human being,” or, as one manuscript has it, “who, since I am,” etc.]

As a righteous man, Isaiah had sinned only in speech. Therefore he had unclean lips alone, not an unclean conscience. But I, because I look with my eyes in order to lust, am a cause of scandal with my hand and my foot, and sin with every part of my body, have everything unclean. And because, having once been baptized in the Spirit, I have again stained my garment, I need the cleansing of a second baptism—that is, of fire (Matt. 3:11).

### 12. Words in Scripture Are Not Simple

As some suppose, the words in Scripture are not simple; much is hidden within them. The letter signifies one thing, the mystical sense another.

Behold, in the Gospel the Lord girds Himself with a linen cloth, prepares a basin to wash the disciples’ feet, and performs the service of a slave (John 13). Let it be so: let Him be teaching humility, let Him be teaching us to minister to one another. I do not deny or reject this.

But what does He mean when He says to Peter, who refuses: “Unless I wash your feet, you will have no part with me”? And Peter replies: “Lord, not only my feet, but also my hands and my head” (ibid. 13:8–9).

Since the Lord was about to ascend to heaven—and since the Apostles, as human beings standing upon the earth, still had feet soiled by the filth of sins—He wished to free them entirely from their offenses, so that the prophetic saying might apply to them: “How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim peace” (Isa. 52:7). Thus they could imitate the words of the Church: “I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?” (Song 5:3).

And if, after the Resurrection, dust later clung to them, they were to shake it off against the impious city as a testimony to their labor, because they had struggled for the salvation of all, becoming as Jews to the Jews and as Gentiles to the Gentiles, and had even defiled their own footprints to some degree.

To return, then, to our subject: just as the Apostles needed the purification of their feet, so Isaiah, who had sinned only in speech, had unclean lips. And, as far as I judge, because he had not rebuked Uzziah when he rushed into the Temple, nor openly identified the impious man as Elijah had done, he had unclean lips.

“I dwell among a people having unclean lips.” Isaiah, who is pierced and declares himself wretched, is made worthy of purification. But the people, not only failing to repent but not even knowing that they had unclean lips, do not deserve the remedy of purification.

Under this example, therefore, we must take care not only to be righteous ourselves but also not to remain among sinners, because the Prophet counts this too as part of sin and misery.

### 13. How God Is Seen

It follows: “And I saw the King, the Lord Sabaoth.” The Jews say that Isaiah was killed by his ancestors for this reason: Moses saw the back parts of God, whereas Isaiah writes that he saw the Lord Sabaoth with bodily eyes, despite God’s saying: “No one shall see my face and live” (Exod. 33:20).

If we ask them how God says in the Law that He appeared to other prophets in visions and dreams, while He spoke with Moses face to face; and how the statement “No one shall see my face and live” stands when Scripture admits that He spoke with Moses face to face, they will surely reply that God was seen according to human capacity—not as He is, but as He wished to be seen.

To this we too say that Isaiah saw Him in the same way, with the essential issue remaining whether Moses saw God or did not see Him. If he saw Him, then Isaiah also saw Him, and you impiously killed him when he said that he had seen Him, because God can be seen. If he did not see Him, then kill Moses along with Isaiah, because he is guilty of the same falsehood, saying that he saw the one who cannot be seen.

Whatever understanding they have in explaining that passage concerning Moses, we shall apply the same to Isaiah’s Vision.

### 14. The Coal from the Altar

It follows: “And one of the Seraphim was sent to me, and in his hand he had a coal, which he had taken with tongs from the altar; and he touched my mouth and said: Behold, this has touched your lips, and it shall take away your iniquities and cleanse your sins.”

According to all the editions that we have explained above—whether you wish to understand the two Testaments, or certain ministering powers in heaven, or a kind of shadow prefigured as a sign of a future captivity and of the future truth—now understand the Seraphim.

Since we follow the first interpretation, we assert that the Gospel Testament was sent to the Prophet. Containing within itself both commandments—its own and those of the Old Testament—it grasped the fiery word of God with the twofold edge of the commandments. When it touched the lips, whatever ignorance there had been—for we interpret the unclean lips in this way—it drove away by the truth of its purification.

Jacob sees these tongs in the ladder (Gen. 28). This is the two-edged sword. These are the two small coins that the widow puts into the offerings of God (Mark 12). This is the coin worth two denarii, found in the fish’s mouth and paid for the Lord and Peter (Matt. 17).

By these two tongs, held together by the power of unity, the coal is grasped and sent to the Prophet. We know that this was granted to the Prophet in Psalm 119, when he prayed to God:

> “Lord, deliver my soul from lying lips and from a deceitful tongue.”

And after the Holy Spirit’s question:

> “What shall be given to you, or what shall be added to you, against a deceitful tongue?”

the answer is given:

> “The sharp arrows of the mighty one, with desolating coals” (Ps. 119:2ff.).

Truly, the desolating coal that makes the tongue pure from sin is the divine word. Of it Isaiah also says:

> “You have coals of fire; you shall sit upon them, and they shall be your help” (Isa. 47:14 according to the Septuagint).

### 15.

It follows: “And I heard the voice of the Lord saying, ‘Whom shall I send, and who will go to this people?’ And I said, ‘Here am I; send me.’ And he said, ‘Go, and say to this people: You shall hear with the ear, and shall not understand. And seeing, you shall look, and shall not see,’” and the rest which the text of the prophecy contains.

These are the words of the Lord asking, not commanding, whom he should send and who would go to the people; and the Prophet readily answers, “Here am I; send me.” After this offer, he is commanded to say: “Go, and say to this people: You shall hear with the ear, and shall not understand; and seeing, you shall look, and shall not see,” and so forth.

Here I heard my Hebrew teacher engage in no small discussion, of which I shall set down a little, so that you may perceive the man’s meaning. He said: “Let us inquire who acted better, Moses or Isaiah. Was it Moses, who, when he was sent by God to the people, said, ‘I beg you, Lord, I am not worthy,’ and again, ‘Provide another whom you may send’ (Exod. 4:13)? Or Isaiah, who, although he had not been chosen, offered himself voluntarily, saying, ‘Here am I; send me’?

“I do not fail to recognize,” he continued, “that it is dangerous to dispute the merits of the saints, or to wish to say either less or more about one whom the Lord has crowned. But since he himself said, ‘Seek, and you shall find; knock, and it shall be opened to you’ (Matt. 7; Luke 11), we too— not in order to diminish anyone, but so that, knowing the meaning of Scripture, we may direct ourselves toward its examples—ought to investigate a matter that can give rise to a question.

“One who defends Moses,” he said, “praises his humility and gentleness: judging himself unworthy of God’s ministry, he thereby became greater. Isaiah, however, who offered himself voluntarily and began to prophesy, began with curses: ‘You shall hear with the ear, and shall not understand,’ and ‘Seeing, you shall look, and shall not see.’

[Note: [Col. 0371] Thus we have supplied from the manuscripts the remainder of the verse, for which the printed editions had only “etc.” We also emend here and there below some other matters of lesser importance; it is tiresome to pause repeatedly to note them.]

As a result, after suffering many evils and being regarded by the whole people as insane, when the divine voice again said to him, ‘Cry out,’ remembering what he had endured because he had offered himself too readily at the earlier opportunity, he did not say, ‘Here am I; send me.’ Instead, he asked what it was that he ought to cry out, and said, ‘What shall I cry?’”

A similar case occurs in Jeremiah: “Take from my hand this cup of unmixed wine, and you shall give it to drink to all the nations to which I send you; and they shall drink, vomit, and become mad, and fall before the sword which I shall send among them” (Jer. 25:15–16). When the Prophet heard this, he did not refuse; he did not follow Moses’ example and say, “I beg you, Lord, I am not worthy; provide another whom you may send” (Exod. 4:13). Rather, as a lover of his people, and thinking that the hostile nations would be killed and fall through drinking the cup, he gladly accepted the cup of unmixed wine, understanding that Jerusalem too was included among all the nations.

Thus, among the other nations, he says: “And I took the cup from the hand of the Lord, and gave all the nations to drink to which the Lord sent me: Jerusalem, and the cities of Judah, and its kings and its rulers, to make them a desolation, a wilderness, and a hissing” (Jer. 25:17–18).

Although in most books the order of this prophecy is confused, listen to what he says elsewhere: “You deceived me, Lord, and I was deceived; you laid hold of me and overcame me. I have become a laughingstock; I have spent the whole day in mockery” (Jer. 20:7).

[Note: We have restored the true reading of this verse from a very carefully corrected Royal manuscript. Until now an ancient error had become established, so that it was read, “I have become a laughingstock all day long; I went out into derision,” instead of “I spent the whole day in mockery,” as the Greek text has: πᾶσαν ἡμέραν διετέλεσα μυκτηριζόμενος. Perhaps the copyist originally wrote exegi in the customary manner; then some clever fellow altered it to exivi, and transferred “all day long” to the preceding clause.]

“On the other hand, the defender of Isaiah,” he said, “will bring forward the following arguments. Isaiah, trusting not so much in his own merit as in the mercy of God, after he had heard from the Seraphim, ‘Behold, this has touched your lips, and it shall take away your iniquities and cleanse your sins,’ did not wish to languish in idleness. Rather, as though freed from sins, he offered himself voluntarily for God’s service, moved by zeal for faith.

“Moses, however, because he had been educated in secular disciplines, and because his conscience had been stained to some extent by the killing of an Egyptian (Exod. 2), was addressed from the bush by a voice saying, ‘Do not come nearer. Remove the sandals from your feet, for the place on which you stand is holy ground.’ And because he knew that a struggle awaited him against the magicians and against Pharaoh, that worst of kings, he excused himself, saying, ‘I beg you, Lord, I am not worthy.’ In Hebrew it reads, ‘I have uncircumcised lips’; the Seventy rendered the sense rather than the word, expressing the meaning rather than the wording.

“From this it can plainly be understood that Isaiah, after his lips had been circumcised, rightly offered himself for God’s service, whereas Moses, with his lips still uncircumcised, refused so great a ministry.”

[Note: We have repaired the text from manuscripts. Previously it read rather “the sense than the word,” and formerly “rather what I said than the word,” and so forth.]

### 16.

“You shall hear with the ear, and shall not understand; and seeing, you shall look, and shall not see.”

This entire passage, as the Savior says in the Gospel, refers to the time when he deigned to descend to earth and performed signs among the Jews, who did not understand them.

Since a lengthy and varied exposition follows to the end of the chapter, and we have already exhausted the wax tablets of the scribe taking this down [manuscripts: “completed”], let it be sufficient to have dictated this much. For a discourse that is not polished by the stylus of the author’s own hand is, when rough in itself, much more wearisome if, through its length, it doubles the tedium it causes—so that, tortured by the pain of our eyes, we devote ourselves only to our ears and tongue.

### 17.

[Note: Almost all manuscript copies conclude the letter at this point with the words, “Here ends Jerome’s work on the Seraphim,” and do not append what follows in this interpretation. The older printed editions likewise begin another letter here, with a different number. Martianaeus joined the two portions together on the authority of a certain manuscript; we do not disapprove of his decision, provided only that the larger division be retained, since they seem to have been dictated at the same time, though not in the same spirit, and since this later portion is nothing other than a fuller explanation of what was explained at the end of the preceding portion. Jerome himself, therefore, cites this treatise under the title of a single little book at the beginning of his Commentary on Isaiah 6: “Where,” he says, “about thirty years ago, when I was at Constantinople and was being instructed in the study of the Holy Scriptures under the most eloquent man Gregory of Nazianzus, then bishop of that city, I know that I dictated a brief and impromptu treatise, etc. To that little book, therefore, I send the reader, etc.”]

The Seventy: “And one of the Seraphim was sent to me.”

Aquila and Theodotion: “And one of the Seraphim flew to me.”

[Note: In not only the printed editions of Erasmus and Victorius, but also in several manuscripts, the name and reading of Symmachus are missing.]

Symmachus: “And one of the Seraphim flew to me.”

Every day a Seraph is sent to us; every day the lips of those who groan and say, “Wretched man that I am, for I am pierced,” are cleansed. Once they have been freed from sins, they prepare themselves for God’s service.

As for the fact that the other translators said “flew” instead of “was sent,” understand this as indicating the swift arrival of the divine word upon those judged worthy of sharing in it.

There is also a difference of gender. The Seventy, Aquila, and Theodotion translated Seraphim in the neuter gender; Symmachus used the masculine. We must not suppose that there is sex among God’s Powers, since even the Holy Spirit itself is expressed in the feminine gender according to the properties of the Hebrew language—RUHA; in Greek, neuter, τὸ πνεῦμα; in Latin, masculine, Spiritus. From this it must be understood that, when masculine or feminine forms are used in discussions of higher matters, they signify not so much sex as the idiom of the language.

[Col. 0373] Indeed, the invisible and incorruptible God is expressed in the masculine gender in almost every language, although sex does not apply to him.

The error of those persons is also pious, but nevertheless must be corrected, who dare to say in their prayers and offerings, “He who sits upon the Cherubim and Seraphim.” It is written that God sits upon the Cherubim, as in the passage, “You who sit upon the Cherubim, show yourself” (Ps. 79:2). But no Scripture mentions God sitting upon the Seraphim; nor, except in the present passage, do we find the Seraphim themselves—who stand around God—mentioned anywhere in all the Holy Scriptures.

### 18.

The Seventy: “And in his hand he held a coal, which he had taken with the tongs from the altar, and he touched my mouth.”

Aquila and Theodotion: “And in his hand was a stone in the tongs, which he had taken from the altar, and he touched my mouth.”

Symmachus: “And in his hand was a stone in the tongs, which he had taken from the altar, and he brought it to my mouth.”

As far as the historical sense is concerned, God appears to be sitting in the Temple of Jerusalem, and a coal is brought from the altar before him to Isaiah, according to the Seventy—whether from the altar of incense or from the altar of burnt offerings.

As far as mystical meanings are concerned, the fire that is sent to him is the fire which Jeremiah could not bear. When it has penetrated the secrets of our soul, it dissolves us and cooks us away from the old man into the new, so that we can burst forth into the words: “Yet I live—not I, but the grace of God that is in me” (Gal. 2:20).

Although, according to the other translators, the tongs were always part of the priestly equipment, we ought to understand them as various graces through which God formerly spoke to our fathers in the Prophets in many portions and in many ways.

Since the Hebrew has stone rather than coal, and the other translators agree on this point, it seems to me that the divine word is signified by the designation “stone.” For just as a stone is a kind of very hard and round rock, and perfectly smooth in its purity, so the word of God, which cannot yield to the contradictions of heretics or of any adversaries, is called a stone.

By this stone Zipporah circumcised her son; Jesus cleanses the people from their vices; and in the Apocalypse the Lord promises the victors that they will receive a stone, and that a new name will be written upon it.

[Note: The printed editions up to this point, through the carelessness of the printers, incorrectly read levissimi without the diphthong, although it is clear that the meaning must be “smooth” and “clear.” Greek λεῖος means “level” or “polished.”]

It seems to me, moreover, that the Seventy, by translating ἄνθραξ, “coal,” understood the same thing as the others. For ἄνθραξ, which we translate as “carbuncle,” is a kind of shining and glittering stone, such as we also find among the twelve stones.

Whether, therefore, we understand it as a stone or as a carbuncle, in the stone the truth and severity of the divine word are shown; in the carbuncle, its shining and manifest teaching.

“For the words of the Lord are pure words, silver tested by fire, purified seven times” (Ps. 11:7). And elsewhere: “The commandment of the Lord is clear, enlightening the eyes” (Ps. 18:9).

When he says, “He held a coal in his hand,” let us understand “hand” as action, as in the passage, “In the hand of the tongue are death and life” (Prov. 18:21), and in the Psalm, “They shall fall into the hand of the sword” (Ps. 62:11).

Or else a real hand appeared, so that, through the likeness of human form, when the hand of the one extending it was seen, the Prophet would not be afraid. In the same way, we have seen both God himself and the angels assume human forms, so that fear might be removed from those who saw them.

### 19.

The Seventy: “And he said, ‘Behold, this has touched your lips, and it shall take away your iniquities, and it shall cleanse your sins.’”

[Note: The Cistercian manuscript and an old edition read here aufert, “takes away,” and purgat, “cleanses,” in the present tense. We have observed above that others read the forms in the past tense.]

Aquila: “Behold, this has touched your lips, and your iniquity shall depart, and your sin shall be forgiven.”

The other translators agree with Aquila’s wording.

First, it is necessary that our lips be touched. Then, once they have been touched, iniquity must be driven away. When iniquity has been driven away, the Lord is propitiated, because with him is propitiation, and, according to the Apostle, “He himself is the propitiation for our sins.”

Once our sins have been cleansed, we shall hear the voice of the Lord saying, “Whom shall I send?” And we shall answer, “Here am I; send me.”

### 20.

The Seventy: “And I heard the voice of the Lord saying, ‘Whom shall I send, and who will go to this people?’”

Aquila, Theodotion, and Symmachus: “And I heard the voice of the Lord saying, ‘Whom shall I send? And who will go for us?’”

We discussed elsewhere the comparison between Isaiah and Moses—how one refused the ministry, while the other, offering himself voluntarily, suffered harsh things.

[Note: In the preceding exposition.]

[Note: Martianaeus interprets this passage as referring simultaneously to the preceding exposition, and at the same time reads disputabimus, “we shall discuss,” with the earlier printed editions. Unless he believed that this second portion, which he also presented in second place, had been written before the portion he placed first—a supposition which no reasoning permits—we must clearly read disputavimus, “we discussed,” as we have corrected it from three manuscripts and an old edition. Immediately afterward the Cistercian manuscript reads: “having omitted something of what the Jews call deuteron, or deutrosis.”]

But lest we seem to have omitted something from those traditions which the Jews call δευτερώσεις (deuterōseis), and in which they place the whole of their knowledge, we shall now briefly touch upon the question why the Hebrew has “who will go for us?”

For just as in Genesis it is said, “Let us make man according to our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:26), so here also, I think, it says, “Who will go for us?”

But who else should “us” be understood to mean except the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, for whom goes whoever obeys their will? In the fact that the person of one speaker is presented, the unity of the divinity is indicated. In the fact that “for us” is said, the diversity of the Persons is signified.

We read in the Song of Songs the voice of the Bridegroom speaking to the bride: “Arise, come, my nearest one, my beautiful one [or: my bride], my dove; for behold, winter has passed, and the rain has gone away” (Song 5:2).

When the soul experiences tranquillity in its thoughts, when it is founded upon the rock and its faith is fixed with a deep root, all the waves of temptation pass over it; they do not pass over the one who is being tempted.

But notice how, in response to what the Lord had said, “Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?” the Prophet answered only in part: “Here am I; send me,” and remained silent about the second question. He understood that no human being was worthy to go for God and to make his whole journey belong to the one who sent him.

The Lord noticed this humility—namely, that he considered himself unworthy of what followed—and commanded the next words, saying, “Go.”

[Note: The old edition reads, “because he thought himself unworthy of following,” and so forth.]

### 21.

The Seventy: “And he said, ‘Behold, I am; send me.’”

Aquila and Theodotion: “Behold, I am here; send me.”

Symmachus: “Behold, send me.”

God calls into existence things that do not exist as though they did exist. He said, “I am who I am,” and elsewhere, “He who is has sent me” (Exod. 3:14). Whoever he calls, he immediately causes to subsist.

This is sufficiently clear from the examples of Matthew the Evangelist, who was alive, and Lazarus, who had already been dead four days: as soon as they were called by the Lord, the former left behind the tomb of greed, and the latter the tomb of his death (Mark 2; Luke 5; John 11).

**FOR ALL THINGS** that are apart from him do not exist.
