Thus the Prophet, cleansed from vices, dared to say, “Behold, I am,” although in the Latin books, because of the variety of the translators, sum, “I am,” has not been added.

Some think it should be observed to which Prophets the expression “of the one sending” or “of the one sent” is applied—a term which in Greek is Ἀπόστολος, “Apostle.” They wish this to be the distinction: that all who are sent are both Prophets and Apostles, whereas those to whom the expression “of the one sending” is not applied are Prophets only. I consider this superfluous.

Since we have once come to discuss this term, it should be known that Silas, Paul’s companion, is called “Apostle” in the Hebrew language; he writes several letters together with Paul. It is erroneous to read “Silvanus” instead of “Sila,” since we do not read of Silvanus in the Acts of the Apostles.

## SECOND CLASS, CONTAINING THE LETTERS WHICH JEROME WROTE AT ROME OVER ALMOST THREE YEARS, FROM THE END OF THE YEAR OF CHRIST 382 TO BEYOND THE MIDDLE OF 385

### LETTER XIX

[Note: Alternatively 124. Written around the beginning of the year 383.]

**POPE DAMASUS TO JEROME**

He asks for a clear explanation of what **OSANNA** means among the Hebrews.

To his most beloved son Jerome, Damasus, Bishop, sends greetings in the Lord.

When I was reading commentaries written formerly and recently by our own people—that is, by orthodox men—in Greek and Latin concerning the interpretation of the Gospels, on the passage that reads, “Hosanna to the Son of David” (Matt. 21:9), they offered not merely different but even mutually contradictory explanations.

[Note: The most ancient Vatican manuscript, no. 355, reads: “By that ardent talent of your vigorous mind”—perhaps the single barbarous word studiositatis should be read here, although in this place it is preferable to strenuitatis, “vigour.” Others have: “Therefore we ask the devotion of your affection that …” or “For this reason we ask the affection of your goodwill that …”]

It belongs to your affection, with that ardent energy of your vigorous intellect, to cut away opinions and dispel ambiguities, and to write, with living understanding, what the word means among the Hebrews, so that in this matter also, as in many others, they may give thanks to your care in Christ Jesus.

## LETTER XX

### OR JEROME’S REPLY TO DAMASUS

He explains what the word **OSANNA** means according to the Hebrew source, and why this Hebrew word has been left as it stands among the Hebrews in all languages.

### 1. The interpretations of various writers

Many have fabricated different explanations concerning this word. Among them our own Hilary, in his Commentary on Matthew (ch. 21, no. 3), wrote as follows: “In the Hebrew language, Osanna signifies ‘the redemption of the house of David.’”

[Note: It is obvious that the single word Osanna cannot signify all three things at once—“redemption of the house of David.” Hence Jerome does not approve Hilary’s interpretation. It is also readily apparent that Hilary wished to render the entire acclamation in Latin, not merely the first word: “Osanna to the house of David,” or “Osanna to the son of David.” His greater error lies in taking Beth, “house,” for Ben, “son,” rather than in inventing etymologies that did not exist. Ambrose also, in his Commentary on Luke, book 9, no. 15, interprets “Osanna to the son of David” as “the redeemer of the house of David.”]

First, “redemption” is rendered in Hebrew by PHEDUTH. Next, “house” is BETH. Moreover, it is obvious to everyone that David is not an inserted name in this passage.

Others have thought that Osanna means “glory.” But “glory” is called CHABOD. Some have taken it to mean “grace,” although “grace” is called THODA or ANNA.

### 2. We must return to the Hebrew source

It remains, then, that, setting aside the streams of opinion, we return to the very fountain from which the Evangelists took the expression. For just as we cannot find in Greek or Latin books the words, “so that what was spoken through the Prophets might be fulfilled: ‘He shall be called a Nazarene’” (Matt. 2:23), nor the words, “Out of Egypt I called my son” (ibid., v. 15), so now too the truth must be drawn from the Hebrew books. From them the crowd—and especially the mutually harmonious throng of children—burst forth with this cry.

Matthew says: “But the crowds that went before and that followed cried out, saying, ‘Hosanna to the son of David; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord; hosanna in the highest’” (Matt. 21:2).

Mark has it this way: “They cried out, saying, ‘Hosanna; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord; blessed is the kingdom that comes in the name of the Lord, our father David; hosanna in the highest’” (Mark 11:9).

John agrees in the same words: “And they cried out, ‘Hosanna; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the king of Israel’” (John 12:14).

Luke alone did not include the word Hosanna, although he agrees in the remainder of the interpretation: “Blessed is the king who comes in the name of the Lord; peace in heaven, and glory in the highest” (Luke 19:38).

Therefore, as we have said, the Hebrew words themselves must be set down, and the opinion of all the translators arranged, so that the reader may more easily discover for himself, from a reconsideration of the whole, what ought to be thought about this matter.

[Note: The Cistercian manuscript reads ex tractatione, “from the discussion”; most printed editions have lector quid sequatur inveniat, “so that the reader may discover what follows.”]

### 3. The translators’ view of the Hebrew text

In Psalm 117, where we read, “O Lord, save me; O Lord, grant prosperity; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord,” the Hebrew reads:

**ANNA ADONAI, OSIANNA, ANNA ADONAI ASLIANNA; BARUCH ABBA BASEM ADONAI.**

Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion, and the Fifth Edition, so that we should not seem to alter anything in the Latin, render it as follows:

**ὦ δὴ Κύριε σῶσον δή, ὦ δὴ Κύριε εὐόδωσον δή, εὐλογημένος ὁ ἐρχόμενος ἐν ὀνόματι Κυρίου.**

[Note: Previously the phrase was in Latin. Shortly afterward one manuscript has σῶσον με, “save me,” instead of δή.]

Only the Sixth Edition agrees with the Seventy, in that where the others wrote ὦ δή, it wrote merely ὦ.

Since **OSIANNA**, which through ignorance we corrupt into **OSANNA**, is rendered “save,” or “save me,” by all the translators, our present concern is to determine what the word **ANNA** alone signifies, without the addition of the verb “to save.”

It should be known that in this passage **ANNA** occurs three times. The first and second are written with the same letters—ALEPH, NUN, HE—but the third is HE, NUN, HE.

Symmachus, therefore, who in Psalm 117 had agreed with all the translators, provides a clearer understanding in Psalm 114, where it says, “O Lord, deliver my soul.” He translates: “I beg you, Lord, deliver my soul.”

Where the Seventy translated ὦ and Symmachus translated “I beg,” Aquila and the other editions, translating ὦ δή, have **ANNA** in Hebrew—but written with ALEPH at the beginning, not HE.

From this we observe that, if **ANNA** is written with ALEPH, it means “I beg”; but if it is written with HE, it is a conjunction or interjection corresponding to the Greek δή, as in σῶσον δή, whose force Latin does not express.

[Note: These words, without the addition of the verb “to save,” seem to have been spoken by Jerome in such a sense as to exclude and set aside the syllable anna which is added to the verb meaning “to save,” that is, osia. In that case only three instances remain: the first and second with initial aleph before Adonai, and the third in the word aslia, with its final vowel marked at the beginning by dagesh. The same is in fact found in the verb osia, but Jerome says that he deliberately sets it aside. The Benedictine editor, failing to notice Jerome’s meaning, unjustly accused him of carelessness because, writing to Damasus while still young, he said that anna occurs only three times in this Psalm, although it is evidently found a fourth time. Victorius, on the other hand, devised the excuse that the Hebrew copies formerly had anna only three times.]

### 4.

But since these minutiae and the secret details of this kind of discussion, because of the barbarism both of the language and of the letters, weary the reader, I shall come to a concise explanation.

Psalm 117 plainly prophesies about Christ, and was read very frequently in the synagogues of the Jews, and was therefore more familiar to the people.

[Note: Alternatively, “with the greatest frequency.” Two of our manuscripts have legitur, “is read,” instead of legebatur, “was read.”]

From that Psalm these verses were taken: the one who had been promised from the line of David had come to save Israel. David says:

“The stone which the builders rejected has become the cornerstone. From the Lord this has come to pass. This is wonderful in our eyes. This is the day which the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it. O Lord, save me; O Lord, prosper me; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord. We have blessed you from the house of the Lord. God is the Lord, and he has shone upon us” (Ps. 117:22ff.).

[Note: Victorius has “This stone has become,” and “it is wonderful,” and so some ancient handwritten Psalters read; Cyprian also has this form in book 2 of his Testimonies. Augustine, however, has “it has become to him,” and so forth.]

Hence the Evangelists’ writing also records that the Pharisees and scribes were angered because they saw the people understand the prophecy of the Psalm as fulfilled in Christ. The children cried out, “Hosanna to the son of David,” and they said to him, “Do you hear what these are saying?” Jesus answered them: “Have you never read, ‘Out of the mouth of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise’?” (Matt. 21; Luke 19; John 12), confirming Psalm 117 by the testimony of Psalm 8.

As for the words that could easily be translated, “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord,” the writings of all the Evangelists agree. But because they could not transfer the word **OSIANNA** into Greek, they placed the Hebrew word itself, just as we see done with **ALLELUIA**, **AMEN**, and many other expressions, saying **OSIANNA**.

Luke, therefore, who was the most learned in Greek among all the Evangelists—being a physician and having written his Gospel in Greek—saw that he could not translate the peculiarity of the expression. He therefore judged it better to remain silent than to include something that would create a question for the reader.

### 5.

In short, just as in the Latin language we have certain interjections—for example, when insulting we say “vah,” when expressing amazement “papae,” and when grieving “heu”; and when we wish to impose silence, we restrain our breath with clenched teeth and produce only a hissing sound, saying “sith”—so the Hebrews, among the other peculiarities of their language, have an interjection used when they wish to beseech the Lord. They use a word expressing the feeling of one who asks, and say, “ANNA, Lord,” which the Seventy translated, “O Lord.”

Therefore **OSI** means “save”; **ANNA** is the interjection of one who beseeches.

If you wish to make a single word from these two, you will say **OSIANNA**, or, as we pronounce it, **OSANNA**, with the middle vowel elided, as we commonly do in Virgil’s verses when, instead of *mene incepto desistere victam*, we scan *men incepto*.

[Note: The same manuscripts, together with the Cistercian manuscript, read “in the verses,” as in the line of Virgil.]

The first letter of the following word, ALEPH, excludes the final letter of the preceding word, AIN, when the two are brought together.

[Note: This makes it entirely clear that Jerome read in his copy Osi anna, not as the manuscripts now commonly display it. Since the final letter of the first word, ain, has the same sound as yod, he assigns the Masoretic form aleph to the following word na and joins them. The same is also found in the verb osia, but he says that he is setting it aside.]

Therefore, to return to the origin of the question, where we read in Latin:

“O Lord, save me; O Lord, be pleased to prosper me; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord,”

we may read, according to the Hebrew sense:

“I beg you, Lord, save; I beg you, Lord, prosper, I beg you; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.”

“Save” is said with the people of Israel—or, in general, the world—understood.

Finally, Matthew, who composed his Gospel in the Hebrew language, wrote:

**OSANNA BARRAMA**, that is, “Hosanna in the highest.”

[Note: Understand this to mean the special copy of the Nazarenes, which Jerome elsewhere says was written in Hebrew letters but in the Chaldean-Syrian language, especially in his Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers, chapter 2. We have gathered more material on this subject there. In this way you can readily reconcile Jerome’s view with that of those who maintain that Matthew’s Gospel was written in Greek rather than Hebrew. In Hebrew it is written as follows.]

When the Savior was born, salvation reached as far as heaven—that is, even to the heights—peace having been made not only on earth but also in heaven, so that the saying might at last cease: “My sword has become drunk in heaven” (Isa. 34:5).

### 6.

For the present I have dictated these remarks briefly and concisely, according to the limited measure of my understanding.

But let Your Beatitude know that in discussions of this kind the reader ought not to become irritated by the difficulty. We too could easily have fabricated something that would resolve the question through a single word, just as we have shown that others did. It is more fitting, however, to labor for a little while on behalf of the truth and to lend one’s ear to an unfamiliar expression than to report a fabricated meaning from another language.

[Note: Martianay reads “to bear,” which is less suitable for the person being instructed. Some manuscripts have “false” instead of “fabricated”; others, followed by the old Vulgate editions, retain both readings: “fabricated and false.”]

## LETTER XXI

[Note: Also numbered 140. Written around the end of the year 383.]

### TO DAMASUS, ON THE TWO SONS

At Damasus’s request, Jerome interprets in the manner of a commentary the Gospel parable found in Luke concerning the prodigal son and the dutiful son.

### 1.

Your Beatitude’s question was itself a discussion; and by asking in this way you provided a path toward the answers. Wisdom is rightly attributed to one who asks wisely.

You say:

“Who is this father in the Gospel who divides his substance between two sons (Luke 15)? Who are the two sons? Which is the elder, and which the younger? How does the younger squander the substance he received with prostitutes? After famine has arisen, how is he placed in charge of pigs by the ruler of the region, and how does he eat their pods? How does he return to his father, receive a ring and a robe, and have the fattened calf slaughtered for him? Who is the elder brother, and how, returning from the field, does he begrudge the reception given to his brother?”—and the other matters which are explained more fully in the Gospel.

You add:

“I know that many people have given different interpretations of this reading, and have considered the elder brother to be the Jewish people and the younger the Gentile people. But I ask how the following words can be applied to the Jewish people: ‘Behold, for so many years I have served you, and I have never transgressed your commandment, and you have never given me a kid, so that I might feast with my friends.’ And also: ‘Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours.’

[Note: A little book on this subject, falsely attributed to Jerome, does indeed interpret the passage as referring to the righteous person and the sinner; we present it in the final volume of the Works. In the other respects, however, the two works proceed in almost the same order and with the same arguments. Victorius has “But if you wish,” without the particle ut.]

“If, as you say, we wish the parable to concern the righteous person and the sinner, it cannot suit the righteous person to grieve over another’s salvation, especially that of his brother. For if through the envy of the devil death entered the world, and those who belong to his party imitate him, can such monstrous envy be fitted to the character of the righteous person—so that he would stand outside, stubbornly oppose the most merciful father, and, tormented by jealousy alone, refuse to take part in the joy of the household?”

## 2

Thus, just as with the other parables whose reason for being spoken by the Savior is not explained, we are accustomed to inquire why they were spoken, so we must do likewise here: why the Lord burst forth in words of this kind, and in response to what question the comparison was offered. The scribes and Pharisees were muttering, saying:

[Note: Victorius: “Because here, and shortly afterward, ‘all the tax collectors’ [omnes publicani], according to the Greek text, πάντες οἱ τελῶναι.”]

“Why does this man receive sinners and eat with them?” (Luke 15:2). For the preceding passage had stated: “Tax collectors and sinners were drawing near to him, wishing to hear him.” Thus all the envy arose from this: why did the Lord not avoid the conversation and table fellowship of those whom the precepts of the Law condemned?

This is what Luke says. Matthew, however, speaks as follows: “When he was reclining at table in the house, behold, many sinners and tax collectors came and were reclining with Jesus and his disciples” (Matthew 9:10). When the Pharisees saw this, they said to his disciples: “Why does your teacher eat with sinners and tax collectors?” When he heard this, he said: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. Go and learn what this means: ‘I desire mercy, and not sacrifice’; for I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners.” Mark likewise agrees in the same wording.

Thus, as we have said, the whole question arose from the Law. For the Law, tenacious of justice, had no clemency; rather, whoever was held guilty of adultery, murder, fraud, or, to speak briefly, a capital crime, was released from his offense by no pardon granted through repentance. They were ordered to exact eye for eye, tooth for tooth, life for life (Exodus 21). Therefore all had turned aside; together they had become worthless. “There was none who did good, not even one” (Psalm 13). “But where sin abounded, grace abounded even more” (Romans 3:20).

And God “sent his Son, made of a woman” (Galatians 4:4),

[Note: In place of “made of a woman,” two manuscripts of Cistercian provenance, omitting that phrase, substitute the following: “made under the Law.”]

who, having destroyed the dividing wall, made the two one (Ephesians 2:2), and tempered the austerity of the Law with the grace of the Gospel. Hence Paul, writing to the churches, says: “Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ” (Romans 1)—grace which was not repaid on the basis of merit but granted by the giver.

Peace, moreover, is that by which we have been reconciled to God, having as our propitiator the Lord Jesus Christ, who forgave us our sins and erased the bond of death that stood against us, fastening it to the cross; and he made a spectacle of principalities and powers, triumphing over them on the tree.

What greater clemency could there be than that the Son of God should be born the Son of man?

[Note: For “was born,” two manuscript copies read “was thought to be born.” Agobard quotes this passage from Jerome and presses it against Felix in chapter 10, but in his text “madness” appears instead of “clemency.”]

That he should endure the distastefulness of ten months? Await the arrival of birth? Be wrapped in swaddling clothes? Be subjected to his parents? Grow through each successive age? And after insults, blows, and scourging, should also become a curse on the cross for us, so that he might free us from the curse of the Law, becoming obedient to the Father unto death; and should accomplish in deed what earlier, speaking in the person of the mediator, he had entreated, saying: “Father, I will that just as you and I are one [or: the same], so they also may be one in us” (John 17:22).

Therefore, because he had come for this purpose—to overcome by ineffable mercy what was impossible through the Law, since no one was justified by it—he summoned tax collectors and sinners to repentance, also seeking their company at table, so that they might be instructed at the meal. This will be clear to anyone who reads the Gospels with attentive mind: how his food and drink, his walking about, and everything he did in the body served to procure the salvation of human beings.

Seeing this, the scribes and Pharisees said that he acted against the Law: “Behold, a glutton and a wine-drinker, a friend of tax collectors and sinners” (Matthew 11:19). Earlier they had also reproached him for healing on the Sabbaths.

Therefore, to overcome their accusation by a merciful argument, the Lord proposed three parables. One concerns the ninety-nine sheep left in the mountains and the one that was lost, which was carried back on the shepherd’s shoulders. Another concerns the drachma that a woman searched for after lighting a lamp; when she found it, she summoned her neighbors to rejoice, saying: “Rejoice with me, because I have found the drachma that I had lost” (Luke 15:9). The third concerns the two sons, about which you ordered me to say a few things.

## 3

Although the sheep and the drachma belong to one and the same interpretation, discussion of them does not belong to the present occasion. It is enough to say that these parables were proposed so that, just as there is joy among the angels and the neighboring beings who remain there when the animal and the drachma are found, so there ought to be joy at the repentance of tax collectors and sinners among all those who have no need of repentance.

Hence I am greatly astonished that Tertullian, in the book he wrote against repentance, *On Modesty*, and in which he dissolves the ancient opinion by a novel view, wished to maintain that the tax collectors and sinners who ate with the Lord were Gentiles. He appeals to Scripture:

[Note: Tertullian’s passage in *On Modesty*, chapter 9, is as follows: “Or if anyone doubts that the tax collectors were Gentiles in Judea, which had long since been usurped by the hand of Pompey and Lucullus, let him read Deuteronomy: ‘There shall be no tribute-paying person from the sons of Israel.’” However, in this passage of Deuteronomy the Hieronymian manuscripts do not read the words “from the sons of Israel,” although Victorius has added them.]

“There shall be no tribute-paying person from Israel” (Deuteronomy 23:18, according to the Septuagint)—as though Matthew too had not been a tax collector from the Circumcision; and as though the man who prayed with the Pharisee in the Temple, not daring to raise his eyes toward heaven, had not been a tax collector from Israel; or as though Luke did not record: “And all the people who heard, and the tax collectors, justified God, having been baptized with the baptism of John” (Luke 7:29); or as though it could seem credible that a Gentile had entered the Temple, or that the Lord had shared a meal with Gentiles, when he was especially careful not to appear to abolish the Law.

He first came to the lost sheep of the house of Israel. To the Canaanite woman who pleaded for her daughter’s healing he replied: “It is not right to take the children’s bread and give it to dogs.” And elsewhere he instructed his disciples: “Do not go into the way of the Gentiles, and do not enter the cities of the Samaritans” (Matthew 10:5).

From all this we learn that in the tax collectors we may understand not so much the Gentiles as, in general, all sinners—that is, those who were both from the Gentiles and from the Jews. But the man who, in company with his mad and blasphemous women, defended that doctrine by which he refused to receive Christians who repented argued in vain that tax collectors were not Jews, so that in their person only the Gentile people might be understood.

Therefore, not to prolong matters, I shall set out the very words of the Gospel and append, in commentary fashion, what seems to me to be meant by each one.

## 4

**“A certain man had two sons” (Luke 15:11).**

That a man is called God is confirmed by many testimonies, as in the passage: “The testimony of two men is true. I bear witness concerning myself, and the Father who sent me bears witness” (John 10:17–18).

In one parable he is called a shepherd, in another a householder; in one he leases out a vineyard, in another he invites people to a wedding. Through different comparisons he signifies the same matter, in order to reject the pride of the Jews and approve the repentance common to all sinners, whether Gentiles or Israelites.

But when he says “two sons,” nearly all Scripture is filled with mysteries concerning the calling of two peoples.

## 5

**“And the younger said to him: Father, give me the portion of the substance that falls to me.”**

The substance of God is everything by which we live, understand, think, and burst forth into speech. God has bestowed these things equally and in common upon all, as the Evangelist says: “This was the true light, which enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1:9).

This is the right eye that must be guarded against scandals; this is the lamp of the body; this is the talent that must not be wrapped in a cloth—that is, handled delicately and idly—nor buried in the earth, namely, obscured by earthly thoughts.

## 6

**“Who divided the substance among them.”**

The Greek reads more significantly: **διεῖλεν αὐτοῖς τὸν βίον**, that is, “he gave them free choice”; he gave them freedom of their own mind, so that each person might live not by God’s command but by his own obedience—not from necessity but from willing choice. Thus virtue would have a place, and we would differ from the other living creatures, since, in the likeness of God, we were permitted to do what we wished.

Accordingly, just judgment would be rendered against sinners and a just reward bestowed upon the holy and righteous.

## 7. How We Are with God or Depart from Him

**“And not many days afterward, when he had gathered everything together, the younger son departed into a distant country.”**

If God holds heaven in the span of his hand and the earth in his fist; if Jeremiah says, “I am God who is near, and not God from afar” (Jeremiah 23); and if David likewise proclaims that no place exists without him, how does the son depart into a foreign land and leave his father?

We must therefore understand that it is not by distances of place but by affection that we are either with God or depart from him. For just as he says to the disciples, “Behold, I am with you all days, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28:20), so to those who put forward their own self-display and do not deserve to be with the Lord he says: “Depart from me; I do not know you, you who work iniquity” (ibid. 7:23).

## 8

The younger son therefore departed from his father with all his substance and went into a foreign land. Cain too went out from the presence of the Lord and lived in the land of Naid, which is interpreted as “wandering.”

Whoever departs from God is immediately shaken by the world’s waves, and his feet are set in motion. For after human beings were moved from the east and withdrew from the true light, then they built a tower against God in the impiety of their rebellion; then they devised the prides of doctrines, wishing through illicit curiosity to penetrate the heights of heaven itself. That place was called Babel, that is, “confusion.”

## 9

**“And there he dissipated his substance, living extravagantly.”**

Extravagance, hostile to God and hostile to the virtues, destroys the whole substance of the father. By flattering a person with present pleasure, it prevents him from considering future poverty.

## 10

**“And when he had consumed everything, a severe famine arose in that region.”**

He had received resources from his father so that through visible things he might recognize the invisible attributes of the father, and from the beauty of created things might consequently understand the Creator. But by suppressing the truth in unrighteousness and worshiping idols instead of God, he consumed all the goods of nature. When everything had been consumed, he began to lack the virtues, having abandoned the fountain of virtues.

“A severe famine arose in that region.” Every place in which we dwell while the father is absent is a place of famine, want, and poverty.

[Note: All the editors up to this point have corrupted this passage in various ways, especially the Greek words. The older editors read **λίμου ἰσχύρου**, that is, “a severe famine,” borrowing the words from the Gospel. Erasmus attempted to correct this reading from manuscripts and substituted **fames autem μετὰ ἐκστάσεως ἰσχυρὸς**. This is the reading which Victorius approves only insofar as he wishes **ἔκτασις** to be read instead of **ἔκστασις**, since **ἔκτασις** signifies production or extension, and the famine would therefore be called “severe with extension.” But both are censured by a Benedictine editor, who congratulates himself on having restored the passage with the aid of ten manuscript copies as follows: **Famis autem μεταφορικῶς valide haec est regio**, “But metaphorically, the famine is severe; this is the region,” and so on. We deny that the Greek letters have been properly read in the manuscripts, although our older copies either do not contain them at all or contain them in a thoroughly corrupt form. We read **μετὰ ἐμφάσεως valide**, “with emphasis, severely”—a minimal alteration, as you see, from the readings of others, **μετὰ ἐκστάσεως** or **ἐκτάσεως**, and **μεταφορικῶς**. Yet the alteration is necessary for the sense to stand and the author’s intention to be clear. Jerome wishes the word “severely” to carry a more significant and weightier sense, one that is figurative and emphatic, or **μετὰ ἐμφάσεως**.]

This, then, is the region of which the prophet says: “You who dwell in the region of the shadow of death, light will shine upon you” (Isaiah 9:2).

By contrast, there is another region which we shall possess when we live with a pure and clean heart, the region desired by holy David, who says: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Psalm 26:13).

## 11

**“And he himself began to be in want; and he went and joined himself to one of the rulers of that region.”**

Having abandoned the one who had generously given him everything at his first request, he joined himself to the ruler of this world, that is, to the devil, the governor of darkness.

[Note: Victorius adds “of these.” Shortly afterward, the Cistercian book omits the name “Behemoth.”]

Scripture calls him by many names: sometimes the enemy, sometimes the unjust judge, sometimes the dragon, sometimes Satan, sometimes the hammer, sometimes the partridge, sometimes Belial, sometimes the roaring lion, sometimes Leviathan, sometimes *Thaninim*, sometimes Behemoth, and by many other titles.

When it says “to one of the rulers,” this must be understood to mean that there are many who fly through this air and, through the deceit of various vices, subject the human race to their slavery.

## 12

**“Who sent him into his field to feed swine.”**

The pig is an unclean animal that delights in mud and filth. Such is the multitude of demons, which, through handmade idols,

[Note: It is Origen’s view that demons are nourished by odors and blood, since they supposedly require food. Tertullian holds similar views in *Against the Nations*, chapters 22 and 23, and in *On Idolatry*, chapter 7, as well as elsewhere. Athenagoras also expresses them in his *Plea for the Christians*, and so do Gregory of Nazianzus in Oration 18, Arnobius in Books 3 and 5 *Against the Nations*, and other ancient ecclesiastical writers. These pagan opinions are not entirely rejected by them. See below, *Synodical Letter*, no. 3, and our notes there. Jerome, however, should readily be understood to have spoken allegorically here about the demons’ food, since he frequently reproaches Origen for believing that demons were corporeal, whereas Jerome himself held them to be entirely incorporeal.]

on the blood of cattle and sacrificial victims; and finally, when fattened by a particular kind of offering, it is filled by the death of the human being himself. Thus he sent him into his own possession—that is, made him his servant—to feed swine, sacrificing his own soul to him.

## 13

**“And he desired to fill his belly with the pods of the pigs, and no one gave him any.”**

This is expressed with rebuke to Jerusalem in Ezekiel:

“And what was done in you was more perverse than with women,

[Note: Although we have not altered the text, we consider the reading of the Cistercian manuscript more accurate: “more than women in your fornication; and after you they have not committed fornication.” This is the form of Ezekiel’s text in all books, unless one excepts the absence of the negative particle in the Septuagint, and that only in the Vatican copy.]

who committed fornication before your fornication and after you, in that you gave payment, but payment was not given to you” (Ezekiel 16:34).

We see this fulfilled in the younger son. He lost his substance in the region of the ruler; and after losing his resources, he was sent to the pigs and wasted away from poverty.

**THE FOOD OF DEMONS** is drunkenness, extravagance, fornication, and every vice. These things are flattering and wanton; they soothe the senses with pleasure, and as soon as they appear, they summon people to use them.

The extravagant youth could not be filled with them because pleasure always produces hunger for itself: what has passed does not satisfy. And when Satan has deceived someone by his craft and laid his own yoke upon him, he no longer provides an abundance of vices, knowing that the person is already dead—just as we see many idolaters exhausted by the misery and poverty of bread.

These are the people in whom the prophetic word is fulfilled:

“Payment is given to all prostitutes; but you gave payments to all your lovers, and you did not receive payments” (Ezekiel 16:33).

We may also interpret the pods in another way. The food of demons is the poetry of poets, secular wisdom, and the pomp of rhetorical language. All these things delight by their own sweetness; and while they captivate the ears with verses flowing in a sweet rhythm, they also penetrate the soul and bind the inner parts of the heart.

But when they have been read with the greatest zeal and labor, they give their readers nothing except an empty sound and the clamor of words: **NO SATIETY OF TRUTH** is found there, and no refreshment of righteousness. Their students remain hungry for truth and in poverty of virtues.

A type of this wisdom is also described in Deuteronomy under the figure of a captive woman. The divine voice commands that if an Israelite wishes to take her as his wife, he should shave her head, cut her nails, and remove her hair; and when she has been made clean, then she may pass into the embrace of her conqueror.

If we understand these things literally, are they not ridiculous? Therefore we too act in this way when we read philosophers, when books of secular wisdom come into our hands: if we find anything useful in them, we convert it to our doctrine; but whatever is superfluous—concerning idols, love, and the care of worldly affairs—

[Note: Two manuscripts read: “if something concerning idols appears superfluous.”]

we scrape away, shave it, as it were, and cut it off with the sharpest iron in the manner of fingernails.

Hence the Apostle also forbids anyone to recline in an idol’s temple, saying:

“See to it, however, that this freedom of yours does not become a stumbling block to the weak. For if someone sees one who has knowledge reclining in an idol’s temple, will not his conscience, being weak, be built up to eat food sacrificed to idols? And will the weak brother perish through your knowledge, the brother for whom Christ died?” (1 Corinthians 8:9).

Does he not seem to say in other words that you should not read philosophers, orators, and poets, nor rest in reading them? Nor should we flatter ourselves if we do not believe what is written in them, since another person’s conscience may be wounded and we may appear to approve what, while reading it, we do not reject.

Otherwise, what would it mean to suppose that the Apostle approved the conscience of the one who ate in an idol’s temple and called perfect the one whom he knew to eat food sacrificed to idols?

Far be it that these words should sound from a Christian mouth: “Almighty Jupiter,” “by Hercules,” “by Castor,” and the other expressions that are more monsters than divinities.

Yet even now we see priests of God, abandoning the Gospels and the Prophets, reading comedies, singing the amorous words of bucolic verses, and keeping Virgil in their hands; and they make into a crime of pleasure what **in boys** is a necessity.

[Note: Another reading is “of will,” and shortly afterward “lest she be captive” instead of “if we wish to have a captive woman.”]

Therefore, if we wish to take a captive woman as a wife, we must beware of reclining in an idol’s temple; or, if indeed we have been deceived by love for her, we must cleanse her and purify her from every defilement of error, lest a brother, for whom Christ died, be scandalized when he hears songs composed in praise of idols resounding from a Christian’s mouth.

## 14. Who the Mercenaries Are

**“But coming to himself, he said: How many hired servants abound in my father’s house with bread, while I am perishing here from hunger.”**

According to another interpretation, we understand the hired servants as those from the Jews who keep the precepts of the Law solely for the sake of present goods.

[Note: Martianaeus gives a different interpretation.]

They are righteous and merciful, not for the sake of righteousness itself or of the good of mercy itself, but so that they may obtain from God the reward of earthly happiness and long life.

Anyone who desires these things is rightly compelled to obey the commandments, lest by transgressing what has been commanded he be deprived of the things he desires. But where there is fear, there is no love. Perfect love casts out fear. For the one who loves does not keep what has been commanded because he is compelled either by fear of punishment or by eagerness for a reward, but because the very thing commanded by God is good.

The meaning, then, is this: How many among the Jews do not depart from the service of God merely because of present goods, while I am being consumed by poverty?

## 15

**“I will arise and go to my father.”**

He says beautifully, “I will arise,” for while his father was absent he had not been standing. It belongs to sinners to lie down; it belongs to the righteous to stand.

Moses is told: “But you, stand here with me” (Deuteronomy 5:31). And in the hundred and thirty-third Psalm: “Behold, now bless the Lord, all servants of the Lord, who stand in the house of the Lord.” The Prophet urges those who stand in the house of the Lord to bless the Lord.

## 16

**“And I will say to him: Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you; I am no longer worthy to be called your son.”**

He had sinned against heaven because he had abandoned heavenly Jerusalem, his mother. He had sinned before the father because, after abandoning the Creator, he had worshiped wood. He was not worthy to be called a son of God because he had preferred to be a servant of idols.

“For everyone who commits sin is born from the devil as father” (1 John 3:7).

[Note: Older printed editions insert the words “is a slave of sin,” and so forth. But these have been borrowed from another passage of Scripture.]

## 17

**“Make me like one of your hired servants.”**

“Make me,” he says, “like one of the Jews who venerate you merely because of the promises of present things.” Receive the repentant son, whom you have so often spared when he sinned as one of your hired servants.

## 18

**“And he came to his father.”**

We come to the father when we withdraw from feeding pigs, according to the saying: “As soon as you have turned and groaned, you shall be saved” (Ezekiel 18).

## 19

**“And while he was still far away, his father saw him and was moved with compassion.”**

Before he returned to his former father through worthy deeds and true repentance, God—before whom all future things already exist as accomplished and who knows all things in advance—hastened toward his coming. Through his Word, which took flesh from the Virgin, he anticipated the return of his younger son.

## 20

**“And running ahead, he fell upon his neck.”**

He came to the earth before the son entered the house of confession. He fell upon his neck—that is, he assumed a human body.

And just as John reclined upon the breast of Jesus (John 13), becoming a participant in his secrets, so he also placed his easy yoke—that is, the easy commandments of his precepts—upon the younger son, more by grace than by merit.

## 21

**“And he kissed him.”**

This accords with what the Church asks concerning the bridegroom’s coming in the Song of Songs:

“Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song of Songs 1:1).

“I do not want him,” she says, “to speak to me through Moses; I do not want him to speak through the Prophets. Let him himself assume my body; let him himself kiss me in the flesh.”

Thus we may also apply to this interpretation what is written in Isaiah:

“If you seek, seek; and dwell with me in the forest” (Isaiah 21:12, according to the Septuagint).

There too the weeping Church is commanded to cry out from Seir, because *Seir* is interpreted as “hairy” and “bristling.” It signifies the ancient horror of the Gentiles, to which the Church responds in a corresponding likeness:

“I am black but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem” (Song of Songs 1:4).

[Note: We restore this reading from the oldest edition we use frequently, since other printed editions and manuscripts had the error “less fittingly,” contrary to Jerome’s intention. Jerome compares the horror of the Gentiles with Seir, which is interpreted as hairy and bristling.]

## 22

**“But the son said to him: Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you; I am no longer worthy to be called your son.”**

He says that he is not worthy to be called a son, yet, from the voice of nature and from that substance which the father had once bestowed upon him, he tremulously breaks forth into the name of truth: “Father,” he says, “I have sinned against heaven.”

Therefore some argue in vain that the name “father” applies only to the saints, since here even the man who confesses himself unworthy of the name “son” calls God “father”—unless perhaps he dares to call him father for this reason: because he has turned back with a complete mind.

## 23

**“But the father said to his servants: Bring out quickly the former robe and put it on him.”**

The robe which Adam lost through sin; the robe which in another parable is called the wedding garment (Matthew 22), that is, the garment of the Holy Spirit. Whoever does not have it cannot participate in the king’s banquet.

## 24

**“And put a ring on his hand.”**

The seal of the likeness of Christ, according to the saying:

“In him, when you believed, you were sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise” (Ephesians 1:13).

And to the prince of Tyre, who had lost the likeness of the Creator, it is said:

“You are the seal of likeness and the crown of beauty; you were born in the delights of the paradise of God” (Ezekiel 28:12–13).

Isaiah also speaks of this seal: “Then those who are sealed will be revealed.”

This seal is given on the hand when Scripture signifies works of righteousness, as in the passage: “The word of the Lord came to the hand of Haggai the prophet” (Haggai 1 and 2), who says to Jerusalem: “I adorned you with an ornament, and I put bracelets around your hands” (Ezekiel 16:11).

Again, another passage displays the place of the seal on the one who is clothed in a long robe:

“Pass through the midst of Jerusalem, and put a seal on the foreheads of the men who groan and grieve over all the iniquities that are committed in their midst” (ibid. 9:4).

Why? So that afterward they may be able to say:

“The light of your countenance, Lord, has been marked upon us” (Psalm 4:7).

[Note: Victorius reads: “to that man who …”]

## 25

**“And shoes on his feet.”**

For he had lost the dignity of a bridegroom and could not celebrate Passover with bare feet. These are the shoes of which the Lord says:

“And I shod you with hyacinth. And shoes on his feet” (Ezekiel 16:10).

Nor would the lurking serpent seize the sole of the one who entered; rather, he would walk more securely over scorpions and serpents, so that he might be prepared for the Gospel of peace—no longer walking according to the flesh but according to the spirit—and so that the prophetic saying might apply to him:

“How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim peace, who proclaim good things” (Isaiah 52:7).

## 26

**“And bring the fattened calf, and kill it, and let us eat and feast, because this son of mine was dead and has come to life; he was lost and has been found.”**

The fattened calf that is sacrificed for the salvation of the penitent is the Savior himself, whose flesh we feed upon daily and whose blood we drink.

Faithful reader, you understand with what fatness we are filled, so that we burst forth into his praise, saying:

“My heart has poured forth a good word; I speak my works to the king” (Psalm 44:1).

Some, however, considering the text of the Psalm less carefully than they should, superstitiously rather than truthfully think that this is understood as spoken in the person of the Father.

[Note: Erasmus, followed by Martianaeus, reads “of repentance” instead of “for the penitent,” namely, the son; shortly afterward he reads “because of the fatness” instead of “because of his fatness.” Two manuscripts more correctly read “because of the fatness proceeding from him.” This passage, and the one that follows, should be noted as referring to the sacrament of the Eucharist.]

But when he says, “Let us feast, because this son of mine was dead and has come to life; he was lost and has been found,” this belongs to the same meaning as the preceding parable, in which it is said:

“So I tell you, there will be joy before the angels of God over one sinner who repents.”

## 27

**“And they began to feast.”**

This banquet is celebrated every day; every day the father receives the son. Christ is sacrificed for believers continually.

## 28

**“But his older son was in the field.”**

Up to this point the discussion has concerned the person of the younger son, whom, according to the present parable, we must understand as the tax collectors and sinners whom the Lord summoned to repentance. According to the mystical interpretations, however, the future calling of the Gentiles is also prophesied.

Now the discourse turns to the older son, whom many refer simply to the person of all the saints, while many refer him specifically to the Jews.

The interpretation concerning the saints is not difficult in the statement, “I have never transgressed your commandment,” although the fact that he envies his brother’s return seems to stand in the way.

With regard to the Jews, envy does fit their attitude toward their brother’s salvation, but this conflicts with their saying that they have never transgressed his commandment. What seems to us to be the case concerning them we shall attempt to explain in its proper places.

**“His older son was in the field,”** sweating with labor in earthly works, far from the grace of the Holy Spirit and estranged from his father’s counsel.

He is the one who says:

“I bought a field, and I must go out and see it; I ask you to excuse me” (Luke 14:18).

He is the one who bought five yokes of oxen and, weighed down by the burden of the Law, enjoys the pleasure of earthly sensations. He is the one who, having taken a wife, cannot go to the wedding; having become flesh, he cannot become one with the spirit.

In his person the laborers of that other parable also find their place: at the first, third, sixth, and ninth hours—that is, through various callings—they are sent into the vineyard, and they are indignant that the laborers of the eleventh hour are made equal to them.

## 29

**“And when he came and drew near to the house, he heard music and dancing.”**

What is written as a superscription in one of the Psalms, **MELETH**, corresponds to this interpretation. For *Meleth* is said to mean a chorus singing together in unity.

Some Latins incorrectly think that *symphonia* is a type of instrument, whereas this word signifies harmonious concert in the praises of God. For **συμφωνία** is expressed in Latin by *consonantia*, “consonance.”

[Note: From this passage Saint Isidore, in the *Etymologies*, took the statement—certainly derived from older sources—that “symphony” is commonly called a hollow piece of wood stretched with leather on both sides, which musicians strike here and there with rods.]

## 30

**“And he called one of the servants and asked what these things might be.”**

Even now he asks Israel why God rejoices at the acceptance of the Gentiles. Tormented by jealousy, he cannot know the father’s will.

## 31

**“He said to him: Your brother has come, and your father has killed the fattened calf, because he has received him back safe and sound.”**

The cause of the joy is that throughout the whole world there is a common song in praise of God: it is the salvation of the Gentiles; it is the salvation of sinners. The angels rejoice; all creation joins in the joy. But concerning Israel alone it is said:

## 32

**“But he became angry and would not enter.”**

He is angry that his brother has been received while he is absent; he is angry that the one whom he thought dead is alive. And now Israel stands outside; even now his mother and brothers stand outside while the disciples listen to the Gospels in the Church, seeking him (Matthew 12).

## 33

**“But his father went out and began to plead with him.”**

How kind and merciful the father is! He pleads with his son to become a participant in the joy of the house. The father pleads through the Apostles; he pleads through the preachers of the Gospel.

Among them Paul says:

“We beseech you on behalf of Christ: be reconciled to God” (2 Corinthians 5:20).

And elsewhere:

“It was necessary that the word of God should first be announced to you; but because you rejected it and judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13:46).

34. “But he answered and said to his father, ‘Behold, for so many years I have served you.’” The father humbly pleads for reconciliation; but he, following the righteousness that is in the Law, does not submit to the righteousness of God. What righteousness of God, moreover, is greater than to forgive those who repent [Note: Some manuscripts read: “to forgive those who offend,” etc.] and to receive a returning son?

“Behold, for so many years I have served you, and I have never transgressed your command.” As though this very thing were not to transgress the command: to begrudge another’s salvation and to boast of one’s righteousness before God, although no one is clean in his sight. For who will boast of having a pure heart, even if it has been so for only one day? David confesses: “I was conceived in iniquities, and my mother conceived me in sins” (Ps. 50:7). And elsewhere: “If you observe iniquities, Lord, who will endure?” (Ps. 129:3). Yet this man says that he has never transgressed the command, though he was so often handed over to captivity because of idolatry.

“Behold, for so many years I have served you, and I have never transgressed your command.” This is what the Apostle Paul says: “What shall we say, then? That the Gentiles, who did not pursue righteousness, have attained righteousness, but the righteousness that comes from faith. Israel, however, by pursuing the law of righteousness, did not attain to the law of righteousness” (Rom. 9:30–31). [Note: Martianay, following Erasmus, had deleted the two words “but righteousness,” although they are found in the manuscripts of this letter attributed to Jerome that we use and in all the other Greek and Latin codices of the sacred text.] Why? “Because it was not from faith, but as though from works of the Law.” Therefore this may also be said in the person of the one who, according to the same Apostle, lived blamelessly in the righteousness that is from the Law. Yet it seems to me that the Jew is boasting rather than speaking the truth, after the example of that Pharisee who said: “God, I thank you that I am not like the rest of men, extortioners, unjust, adulterers, or even like this tax collector” (Luke 18:11).

I ask you: does it not seem to you that what he said about the tax collector, this man says about his brother? “This is the one who consumed all his substance, living with prostitutes.” But with regard to what he says, “I have never transgressed your command,” the father’s words do not agree with him. For he did not confirm that what the son had said was true; rather, he restrained the angry man by another argument: “Son, you are always with me.” Does he mean: “You speak well and have done everything I commanded”? No. [Note: At this point the Cistercian manuscript prefixes a negative particle; from the same manuscript, a little below, we read “far country,” whereas all the earlier printed editions had “long country.”] “You are always with me,” he says. You are with me under the discipline by which you are bound; you are with me while you are being instructed even through captivities; you are with me, not because you have fulfilled my commands, but because I have not allowed you to depart into a far country; you are with me to the end, according to what I spoke to David:

“If his sons forsake my law and do not walk in my judgments; if they profane my ordinances and do not keep my commandments, I will visit their iniquities with a rod and their injustices with scourges; but I will not remove my mercy from them [variant: my justifications]” (Ps. 88:31 ff.).

By this testimony [Col. 0391] it is also shown that what the elder son boasts of is false, since he does not walk in God’s judgments and does not do his commands. And how is he said to have been always with the father when he does not do these things? He is with him when, as a sinner, he is visited with the rod, and when mercy is not denied him after he has been visited.

Nor is it surprising that he dared to lie to his father, since he was able to envy his brother—especially when, on the day of judgment, some will lie even more brazenly, saying: “Did we not eat and drink in your name, perform many miracles, and cast out demons?” (Matt. 7:22). What, then, is meant by “all that is mine is yours” will be explained more appropriately in its proper place.

35. “And you never gave me a young goat, so that I might feast with my friends.” “So much Israelite blood,” he says, “has been poured out; so many thousands of men have been slain, and none of them became the redeemer of our salvation. Even Josiah, who pleased you in your sight (4 Kings 23), and recently the Maccabees, who fought for your inheritance, were unlawfully slain by the swords of their enemies, and none of their blood restored our freedom. Behold, we are still subject to Roman rule. No prophet, no priest, no righteous man has been sacrificed for us. But for the profligate son—that is, for the Gentiles, for sinners—the glorious blood of all creation has been poured out. Although you gave less to those who deserved it, you granted greater things to those who did not deserve them.

“‘You never gave me a young goat, so that I might feast with my friends.’ You are mistaken, Israel. Say rather, ‘so that I might feast with you.’ Or can there be any enjoyment for you unless the father celebrates the banquet with you? At least let the present example teach you. When the younger son returned, both the father and the servants rejoiced. ‘Let us eat and feast,’ he says—not, ‘Eat and feast.’ But you, with the same mind with which you envy your brother, with which you withdraw from the father’s presence, and with which you are always in the field, now also wish to begin a banquet while he is absent.

“‘You never gave me a young goat.’ A father never gives inferior gifts. You have the slaughtered calf; enter and eat with your brother. Why do you ask for a young goat when a lamb has been sent? And lest you pretend not to know that he has been sent, John pointed him out to you in the wilderness: ‘Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world’ (John 1:29).

“And the father, as though merciful and granting repentance, urges you toward the calf; he does not sacrifice the young goat, whom he knows to stand on the left. But at the end of the age you yourself will sacrifice the young goat for yourself—the Antichrist—and with your friends, the unclean spirits, you will be filled with his flesh, when the prophecy has been fulfilled: ‘You crushed the head of the great dragon; you gave him as food to the people of Ethiopia’ (Ps. 73:14).”

36. “But when this son of yours came, who devoured all his substance while living with prostitutes, you killed for him the fattened calf.” Israel now also confesses that the calf which was killed was fattened. They understand that Christ has come, but they are tormented by envy and do not wish to be saved while their brother does not perish.

37. “But he said to him, ‘Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours.’” He calls him “son,” although he refuses to enter. But how are all God’s things the Jews’ things? Are the angels, Thrones, Dominations, [Col. 0392] and the other Powers theirs? Let us therefore understand these words as referring to the Law, the Prophets, and the divine utterances. He gave these to them so that they might meditate on his law day and night, according to the rule of Scripture that we have often explained: “all” is not always to be referred to the whole, but to the greater part, as in: “All have turned aside; together they have become useless” (Ps. 13). And elsewhere: “All who came before me were thieves and robbers” (John 10:8). And Paul says to the Corinthians: “I have become all things to all, so that I might win all” (1 Cor. 9:22). And to the Philippians: “For all seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ” (Phil. 2:21).

Although we should not suppose that he ever denied anything to the one whom he urges to eat the calf [Note: The Cistercian manuscript and the old edition cited above likewise urge him to eat his own calf.]

38. “It was necessary for us to feast and rejoice, because this brother of yours was dead and has come to life; he was lost and has been found.” Let us therefore trust that we too can come to life through repentance, although we had been dead through sins. Here the son himself returns; in the earlier parables, however—that of the sheep and that of the drachma—the thing that had gone astray is brought back, and what had been lost is found. The three parables are closed with a similar conclusion, since in this one it is said, “he was lost and has been found,” so that we may understand that different likenesses signify the same reception of sinners. Let this be said concerning the person of the Gentile and of the Jew.

39. Let us now see how this parable may be understood generally of the holy person and the sinner. There is no doubt that it also applies to the righteous in other respects. The difficulty that troubles the reader is why the righteous should envy the sinner’s salvation and be so filled with anger that he is overcome neither by his brother’s mercy, nor by his father’s pleas, nor by the joy of the entire household.

We shall answer briefly: all the righteousness of this world is not righteousness when compared with God. For just as Sodom is justified by the sins of Jerusalem—not because Sodom itself is righteous, but because greater sins make lesser sins [Note: Some manuscripts read “appear” instead of “become,” with the same meaning; similarly, a little later they read “height” instead of “depth.”]—so the whole righteousness of all human beings is no righteousness when compared with God’s righteousness.

Finally, Paul, who had said, “As many as are perfect, let us think this way” (Phil. 3:15), confesses and cries out elsewhere: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways!” (Rom. 11:33). And elsewhere: “We know in part, and we prophesy in part”; and, “Now we see through a mirror in a riddle” (1 Cor. 13:9, 12). And to the Romans: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the body of this death?” (Rom. 7:24).

From all these passages we learn that perfect righteousness belongs to God alone. He makes his sun rise upon the just and the unjust; he gives the late and the early rain alike to those who deserve it and those who do not; he invites people from the alleys, corners, and streets to the wedding, and [Note: This entire clause, “and he casts out from within some who were already secure,” was removed by Bishop of Rieti, following certain Brixian and Florentine codices, as foreign to the subject and apparently disruptive of the sense. Since our copies and all the other printed editions contain it, we have not dared to remove it, but have merely changed its position.] from within he casts out some who were already secure [Col. 0393]. He seeks and finds the sheep which, as an example of the penitent son, could not—or would not—return by itself, and, having found it, carries it back on his shoulders (Luke 15). For it had grown weary through much wandering.

40. To show that envy can also affect the saints, and that pure clemency belongs to God alone, let us consider the example of the sons of Zebedee. When their mother, moved by maternal affection, had asked for excessively great things on their behalf, the other ten disciples became indignant. Jesus summoned them and said:

“You know that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and those who are greater exercise authority over them. It shall not be so among you. Whoever wishes to be greater among you must be your servant; and whoever wishes to be first among you must be your slave; for the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Matt. 20:25 ff.). [Note: The same editor of Rieti, omitting the preceding word “your,” reads “how” instead of “for,” in accordance with the Greek and the Vulgate.

Let no one think it dangerous or blasphemous that we have said that the evil of envy could also creep into the Apostles, since we think that the same has been said even of the angels: “The stars are not pure in his sight, and against his angels he perceived something perverse” (Job 15:15; 4:18). And in the Psalms it is said: “No living person will be justified in your sight.” He does not say, “No human being will be justified,” but “no living person”—that is, neither an evangelist, nor an apostle, nor a prophet.

I ascend to greater things: neither angels, nor Thrones, nor Dominations, nor Powers, nor the other Virtues. God alone is the one in whom sin does not occur. Since all other beings possess free will—for man too was made in the image and likeness of God—they can turn their will in either direction.

If this statement does not persuade you, at least let the authority of that parable move you in which laborers are sent into the vineyard throughout the whole day (Matt. 20). At the first hour Adam, Abel, and Seth are called; at the third, Noah; at the sixth, Abraham; at the ninth, Moses; and at the eleventh, the people of the Gentiles, to whom it is said: “Why do you stand here idle all day?” They answered: “No one has hired us.”

That the final hour signifies the coming of our Savior is attested by the Apostle John, who says: “Brothers, it is the last hour. For just as you have heard that the Antichrist is coming, so now many Antichrists have appeared; therefore we know that it is the last hour” (1 John 2:18).

If this interpretation displeases you, I will follow wherever you lead, provided that you acknowledge that those who were called first are righteous. Once I have obtained this, I shall add: how did the righteous murmur against the householder, saying:

“These last have worked for one hour, and you have made them equal to us, who have borne the burden of the day and the heat”?

They seem to speak justly: the one who sweated from the first hour until night ought to have a reward equal to that of the one who labored for a single hour. But this justice contains envy, since it begrudges another’s happiness. Therefore the Lord also rebukes their envious eye, saying [Note: Here too Victorius deleted the word “Friend,” because it does not occur in his manuscript copies. The whole passage should be compared with Tertullian’s *On Modesty*, chapters 8 and 9, so that one may see both through whom the holy Doctor made progress and with what discrimination he introduces into the Catholic [text, word uncertain] the same statements which Tertullian perversely twists in order to deny repentance to the fallen]: “Friend, is your eye evil because I am good?”

Hence the Apostle says that God alone is just and immortal—not because the angels are unjust and mortal, but because he himself is immortal and just, in comparison with whom all righteousness is found to be iniquity.

41. To understand the injustice of the hired workers in this same parable, which we have now proposed, pay attention for a little while. The one hired at the first hour deserves more than the one sent into the vineyard at the third hour. Again, the worker of the third hour precedes the worker of the sixth hour, and the worker of the sixth hour surpasses the worker of the ninth hour.

How, then, do all envy the last worker, while they do not demand the same justice among themselves? You who were hired at the ninth hour, why do you envy the one who was sent into the vineyard at the eleventh hour? Whatever you answer—even if you assert that the labor was different, so that you deserve a greater reward for the different labor—you will be subject to the same judgment in the case of the sixth hour.

And you who were hired at the sixth hour envy the last worker because he receives with you the denarius—that is, an equal salvation. Although the glory of salvation may be different according to the labor, the worker of the third hour can say the same about you, and the worker of the first hour in turn about the third.

Yet among themselves, because of unequal labor and different intervals of calling, they gladly accept an equal reward. Only in the case of the last worker—that is, in the salvation of the Gentiles—do they disagree; they insult the Lord and are convicted of envy throughout all the parables.

42. I do not doubt that our speech seems to you unpolished, but I have often pleaded that discourse cannot be refined unless it has been polished by the author’s own hand. Therefore forgive eyes that are suffering—that is, forgive one who dictates—especially since in ecclesiastical matters words are not sought, but meaning: life must be sustained by bread, not by husks.

## LETTER XXII [Note: Elsewhere numbered 22; written in A.D. 384.]  
### TO EUSTOCHIUM, THE DAUGHTER OF PAULA [88]

#### On the Custody of Virginity

He teaches Eustochium, a virgin and the daughter of Paula, the most noble Roman matron, how she ought to guard the virginity which she had professed. He also sharply attacks those who, under the appearance of chastity, serve their belly and their greed.

1. “Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear; forget your people and your father’s house, and the king will desire your beauty” (Ps. 44:11).

In the forty-fourth Psalm, God speaks to the human soul, commanding it, after the example of Abraham, to leave its land and its kindred and to abandon the Chaldeans—who are interpreted as demons—and to dwell in the land of the living. Elsewhere the Prophet longs for this, saying: “I believe that I shall see the goodness of the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. 26:13).

Yet it is not enough for you to leave your land unless you forget your people and your father’s house, so that, despising the flesh, you may be joined to the embraces of the bridegroom. “Do not look back,” he says, “nor remain anywhere in the surrounding region; save yourself on the mountain, lest you be seized” (Gen. 19:17). Having laid hold of the plow, it is not fitting to look behind; nor should one return home from the field, or descend from the roof to take another garment after having put on Christ’s tunic (Matt. 24).

A great miracle: the Father urges his daughter not to remember her father. “You are of your father the devil, and you wish to do the desires of your father,” it is said to the Jews (John 8:44). And elsewhere: “Whoever commits sin is of the devil” (1 John 3:8).

Born first from such a parent, we are black; and after repentance, although we have not yet climbed to the summit of virtue, we say: “I am black, but beautiful, O daughters of Jerusalem” (Song 1:4). I have gone out from the house of my childhood; I have forgotten my father; I am reborn in Christ.

What reward do I receive for this? The passage continues: “And the king will desire your beauty.” This, then, is the great sacrament. “For this reason a man will leave his father and his mother and cling to his wife, and the two will be one”—not, as there, “in one flesh” (Gen. 2:24), but “in one spirit.”

Your bridegroom is not arrogant or proud. He took an Ethiopian woman as his wife. As soon as you wish to hear the wisdom of the true Solomon and come to him, he will confess to you all that he knows. The king will bring you into his chamber, and, wonderfully changed in color, that saying will suit you: “Who is this who ascends, made white?” (Song 3:6; 8:5).

2. **Virgins should be addressed as ladies.**—For this reason, my Lady Eustochium, I write these things to you—for I ought to call you “Lady,” since you are the bride of my Lord—so that from the very beginning of your reading you may understand that I am not now going to praise virginity, which you have proved to be best and have attained; nor am I going to enumerate the troubles of marriage: how the womb swells, the infant cries, a rival wife torments, household cares cause anxiety, and death finally cuts short all the things that are thought good.

Married women too have their proper order, honorable marriage, and an undefiled bed (Heb. 13). But I want you to understand that, as you leave Sodom, you must fear the example of Lot’s wife (Gen. 19). There is no flattery in this little book. For a flattering friend is an enemy. There will be no rhetorical parade of speech that places you even among the angels and, after setting forth the blessedness of virginity, subjects the world to your feet.

3. I do not want pride to come to you from your calling, but fear. You walk burdened with gold; you must avoid the robber. This life is a racecourse for mortals; here we contend so that elsewhere we may be crowned. No one walks securely among serpents and scorpions.

“The sword of the Lord,” he says, “is drunk in heaven” (Isa. 34), and you imagine that there is peace on earth, which produces thorns and briars and which the serpent devours? “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of this world’s darkness, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. 6:12). [Note: A very carefully prepared separate edition of this letter, published at Rome by Paulus Manutius in 1562, adds here, “the Apostle says.” Soon afterward, the name “rulers,” absent from the Benedictine editor, has been supplied from all the printed editions and manuscripts.]

We are surrounded by great armies of enemies; everything is full of foes. **FRAGILE FLESH**, which will shortly become ashes, fights alone against many. But when it has been dissolved, and the prince of this world comes and finds no sin in it [Note: Victorius reads “finds nothing in it apart from sin.”], then you will securely hear through the Prophet:

“You will not fear the terror of the night, nor the arrow that flies by day, nor the business that walks in darkness, nor the assault and the demon of noonday. A thousand will fall at your side and ten thousand at your right hand, but they will not come near you” (Ps. 90:5–6).

If their multitude troubles you, and you begin to burn at each incitement to vice, and your thought says to you, “What shall we do?”, Elisha will answer you: “Do not fear, for there are more with us than with them.” He will pray and say: “Lord, open the eyes of your servant-girl, that she may see” (2 Kings 6:16). With your eyes opened, you will see the fiery chariot which lifts you, after the example of Elijah, into the stars (Ps. 123:7). Then, joyful, you will sing:

“Our soul has been rescued like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters; the snare has been broken, and we have been set free” (ibid. 2).

4. **In this life there is no certain victory.**—As long as we are confined in this fragile body, as long as we have this treasure in earthen vessels (2 Cor. 4), and the spirit desires against the flesh and the flesh against the spirit (Gal. 5), there is no certain victory.

Our adversary, the devil, goes about like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour (1 Pet. 5). [Note: Many manuscripts read *Zabulus*. Since this word occurs frequently elsewhere, not only in Jerome but also in other Latin writers, it should be noted once here that it is pronounced according to the Aeolic Greek dialect: “for the Aeolians,” grammarians say, “call *dia* *za*, and *diaplouton* *zaplouton*.” Hence also *Zaconus* for *Diaconus*. Latin writers use *Zaconus*; Jerome’s manuscripts also prefer *Azabenicus* for *Adiabenicus* in the *Chronicle* at year 201, and Isidore reads *Zanium* for *Dianium*, a town in Spain, along with many similar examples.] “You appointed darkness,” David says, “and it became night. In it all the beasts of the forest pass through. The young lions roar as they seize their prey and seek their food from God” (Ps. 103:20).

The devil does not seek unbelieving people, nor those who are outside, whose flesh the king of Assyria burns in the pot. He hastens to snatch them from the Church of Christ. According to Habakkuk, his chosen foods are the elect. He desires to overthrow Job, and, after devouring Judas, he seeks power to sift the Apostles.

The Savior did not come to bring peace upon the earth, but a sword. Lucifer fell, he who rose at dawn; and he who was nourished in the paradise of delights deserved to hear: “Though you exalt yourself like an eagle, from there I will bring you down, says the Lord” (Obad. 4). For he had said in his heart: “I will set my throne above the stars of heaven, and I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14:13).

Therefore God speaks daily to those who descend by the ladder of Jacob in a dream: “I said, ‘You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High.’ But you shall die like men, and fall like one of the princes” (Ps. 81:6–7).

The first devil fell. And when God stands in the assembly of gods and judges among the gods, the Apostle writes to those who cease to be gods: “When there are divisions and jealousies among you, are you not human, and do you not walk according to the human way?” (1 Cor. 3:3).

5. If the Apostle, a chosen vessel and set apart for the Gospel of Christ, restrains his body and subjects it to slavery because of the sting of the flesh and the incitements of vice, lest, after preaching to others, he himself should be found rejected; and if nevertheless he sees another law in his members warring against the law of his mind and leading him captive into the law of sin; if, after nakedness, fasts, hunger, prison, scourges, and punishments, when he returns to himself he cries out: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the body of this death?” (Rom. 7:24)—do you think that you ought to be secure?

Take care, I beg you, lest God one day say of you: “The virgin of Israel has fallen, and there is no one to raise her up” (Amos 5:2). I shall speak boldly: although God can do everything, he cannot raise up a virgin after her fall. He can indeed deliver her from punishment, but he does not wish to crown one who has been corrupted.

Let us fear that prophecy, lest it also be fulfilled in us: “The good virgins will fail” (Amos 8:13). Observe what he says: “the good virgins will fail,” because there are also bad virgins. “Whoever looks upon a woman in order to desire her,” he says, “has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. 5:28).

Virginity therefore perishes even in the mind. These are the bad virgins: virgins in the flesh, not in the spirit; foolish virgins who, having no oil, are shut out by the bridegroom.

6. But if even those who are virgins are not saved by their bodily virginity because of other faults, what will happen to those who have prostituted Christ’s members and changed the temple of the Holy Spirit into a brothel? Immediately they will hear:

“Come down and sit on the ground, virgin daughter of Babylon. Sit on the ground; there is no throne for the daughter of the Chaldeans. You shall no longer be called tender and delicate. Take the millstone and grind flour; uncover your veil, bare your legs, cross the rivers; your shame will be revealed, your disgrace will be seen” (Isa. 47).

And this after the bridal chambers of the Son of God, after the kisses of the cousin and bridegroom; she of whom prophetic speech once sang: “The queen stood at your right hand, clothed in gold, surrounded by variety” (Ps. 44:10)—she will be stripped. Her buttocks will be placed before her face; she will sit beside the waters of the desert; setting down her vessel [Note: Other books, as Gravius notes, read “she will carry vessels”], she will spread her legs to every passerby and be polluted to the crown of her head.

**IT WOULD HAVE BEEN BETTER** for a person to submit to marriage, to walk on level ground, than, striving toward higher things, to fall into the depths of hell [Col. 0398].

May the faithful city of Zion not become a prostitute, I beg you; may it not be that, after housing the Trinity, demons dance there and sirens and hedgehogs build their nests. Let not the breast-band be loosened. Rather, as soon as lust has tickled the senses, or the gentle fire of pleasure has spread through us with sweet warmth, let us burst forth in the words: “The Lord is my helper; I will not fear what flesh can do to me” (Ps. 117:9). [Note: Victorius reads, “and when shortly afterward.”]

When the inner person has begun for a little while to waver between vices and virtues, say: “Why are you sorrowful, my soul, and why do you trouble me? Hope in the Lord [variant: God], for I shall confess to him, the salvation of my countenance and my God” (Ps. 41:12).
