I do not want you to allow thoughts to grow. Let nothing Babylonian, nothing belonging to confusion, mature within you. While the enemy is small, kill him; lest wickedness grow like weeds, let it be crushed in the seed.

Hear the Psalmist saying: “Miserable daughter of Babylon, blessed is the one who repays you with the recompense with which you repaid us. Blessed is the one who will seize and dash your little ones against the Rock” (Ps. 136:8). [Note: This clause of the Psalm, “with which you repaid us,” had been omitted from the earlier printed editions; we have supplied it from two manuscripts and from the reading of this letter found in the Aquisgranian Council cited above.]

For since it is impossible that the innate warmth of the marrow should not rush into a person’s mind, that one is praised and called blessed who, as soon as he begins to think filthy thoughts, immediately kills them and dashes them against the rock. The rock is Christ (1 Cor. 10:4).

7. **Jerome’s temptations in the desert.**—How often, when I was living in the desert, in that vast solitude which, scorched by the sun’s heat, provides the monks with a dreadful dwelling, I thought that I was present amid the pleasures of Rome. I sat alone because I was filled with bitterness. My deformed limbs bristled beneath sackcloth, and my grimy skin had assumed the complexion of Ethiopian flesh.

Every day there were tears; every day, groans. And whenever approaching sleep overcame my resistance, I would strike my barely clinging bones against the naked ground. I say nothing of food and drink, since even the sickly monks use cold water, and it is considered luxury to have received anything cooked. [Note: We restore the word “monks” from most printed editions and manuscripts.]

And yet I—the man who, from fear of Gehenna, had condemned myself to such a prison, the companion of scorpions and wild beasts—often imagined myself among choruses of girls. My face was pale from fasting, and my mind burned with desire in my chilled body; and before a human being, already dead in the flesh, the fires of lust alone boiled.

Thus, deprived of every aid, I would throw myself at Jesus’ feet, water them with tears, and dry them with my hair; and I would subdue my resisting flesh with weeks of fasting. I am not ashamed to confess the misery of my unhappiness [Note: Some manuscripts and printed books add the words “to confess” and “the misery”; all printed books except Erasmus and the Benedictine editor omit them], but rather I lament that I am not what I once was.

I remember that I often joined day to night with my cries, and did not cease beating my breast until, when the Lord rebuked it, tranquility returned. I feared even my own cell, as though it were aware of my thoughts. Angry and severe with myself, I alone penetrated the desert.

Wherever I saw hollow valleys, rugged mountains, or steep crags, there was the place of my prayer; there was the prison of my most wretched flesh. And—as the Lord himself is my witness—after many tears, after eyes fixed upon heaven, I sometimes seemed to myself to be present among the ranks of angels, and, joyful and rejoicing, I sang: “We shall run after you in the fragrance of your perfumes” (Song 1:3).

8. But if this is endured by those whose bodies are wasted and who are attacked only by thoughts [Note: The edition of Manutius cited above reads differently: “But if those who, with their bodies consumed, endure these temptations of lust,” etc.], what does a girl suffer who enjoys luxuries? Surely the saying of the Apostle: “She who lives in pleasure is dead” (1 Tim. 5:6).

If there can be any advice in me, if one with experience may be believed, this is my first warning and exhortation: let the bride of Christ flee wine as poison. These are the first weapons of demons against youth. Avarice does not shake us so much, pride does not inflate us so much, ambition does not delight us so much. We easily do without other vices; this enemy is shut up within us. Wherever we go, we carry our enemy with us.

**WINE AND YOUTH** are a double fire of pleasure. Why add oil to the flame? Why supply fuel to a burning little body? Paul says to Timothy: “No longer drink water, but use a little wine, for the sake of your stomach and your frequent illnesses” (1 Tim. 5:23).

See for what reasons the drinking of wine is permitted: so that by it stomach pain and frequent illness may be cured. And lest we perhaps flatter ourselves concerning our illnesses, he commanded that only a little be taken, more according to a physician’s advice than an Apostle’s—although the Apostle is also a spiritual physician—and lest Timothy, overcome by weakness, be unable to complete his ministry of preaching the Gospel.

Otherwise, he remembered that he had said: “Wine, in which there is excess” (Eph. 5:18), and, “It is good for a person not to drink wine and not to eat meat” (Rom. 14:21).

Noah drank wine and became drunk (Gen. 9:21). After the Flood, when the world was still primitive and the vineyard had then been planted for the first time, he perhaps did not know how wine intoxicates. And so that you may understand the sacramental meaning of Scripture in every detail—for the word of God is a pearl that can be pierced from every side—after drunkenness the uncovering of the thighs followed, and lust was joined to excess. First the belly is distended, and then the other members are stirred.

“For the people ate and drank, and they rose up to play” (Exod. 32:6).

Lot, the friend of God, saved on the mountain (Gen. 19), and found to be the only righteous man among so many thousands of people, is made drunk by his daughters. Although they thought that the human race had perished and did this more from a desire for children than from lust, they nevertheless knew that a righteous man would not do such a thing unless he were drunk. Finally, he did not know what he had done. And although the will itself is not blameworthy, the error is nevertheless culpable.

From this the Moabites and Ammonites were born, enemies of Israel, who, even to the fourth and tenth generation and forever, do not enter the Church of God.

9. When Elijah was fleeing from Jezebel and, exhausted, was lying under an oak in the wilderness, an Angel came to him, roused him, and said: “Arise and eat.” He looked, and behold, at his head was a round loaf of bread and a vessel of water (4 Kings 19:5–6).

[Note: [Col. 0399] The above-mentioned edition of Manutius reads otherwise: “But if he withstands these temptations of lust, he who, when worn away, etc.”]

[Note: [Col. 0400] The words “in the wilderness” and, a little later, “could he not?” are absent from the Victoriana edition.]

Indeed, could God not have sent him prepared unmixed wine, choice foods, and meats softened by pounding? Elisha invites the sons of the prophets to dinner; while feeding them on wild herbs, he hears the diners crying out together: “Death is in the pot” (4 Kings 4:40). The man of God was not angry with the cooks—for he had no habit of a more luxurious table—but, having thrown flour on top, he sweetened the bitterness, by the same power of the Spirit by which Moses had changed Marah into sweetness.

And listen also to what sort of banquet he ordered for those who had come to seize him, whom he had led into Samaria, blinded alike in eyes and mind, without their knowing it: “Set bread and water before them,” he said; “let them eat and drink, and let them return to their master” (4 Kings 6:22).

Food from the royal dishes might also have been brought to Daniel, a richer table; but Habakkuk brought him the meal of harvesters, rustic, I suppose. Therefore he was also called “a man of desires,” because he did not eat the bread of desire and did not drink the wine of lust.

10. There are innumerable divine testimonies from the Scriptures that condemn gluttony and approve [or: provide] simple foods. But since it is not now my purpose to discuss fasting and to pursue everything—for that would belong both to another heading and to another volume—let these few things, drawn from many, suffice.

Otherwise, following these examples, you can gather for yourself how the first man was cast from paradise into this valley of tears because he obeyed his belly more than God. And how Satan tempted the Lord Himself with hunger in the desert. And how the Apostle cries out: “Food is for the belly, and the belly for food; but God will destroy both it and them” (1 Corinthians 6:13). And concerning the luxurious, “whose god is their belly” (Philippians 3). For each person worships what he loves. Hence one must carefully ensure that hunger restore those whom satiety expelled from paradise.

11. God is not pleased by our starvation.—But if you wish to reply that, since you were born of noble stock and have always lived amid delicacies, always on feather beds, you cannot abstain from wine and richer foods, nor live under such strict laws, I will answer: Then live by your own law, since you cannot live by God’s.

It is not that God, Creator and Lord of the universe, takes pleasure in the rumbling of our intestines, the emptiness of our belly, or the burning of our lungs; rather, chastity cannot otherwise be kept safe. Job, dear to God and, by God’s own testimony, blameless and upright—hear what he suspects concerning the devil: “His strength is in his loins, and his power in his navel” (Job 40:16).

The sexual organs of man and woman have been decently called by altered names. Thus it is promised that one from David’s loins will sit upon his throne. And seventy-five souls entered Egypt who came forth from Jacob’s thigh. But after the breadth of his thigh withered when the Lord wrestled with him, he ceased from the work of begetting children. And the one who is to celebrate Passover is commanded to do so with his loins girded and mortified. And God says to Job: “Gird your loins like a man” (ibid. 38:3). John is girded with a leather belt [Note: [Col. 0401] Victorius adds: “around his loins.”], and the Apostles are commanded, with their loins girded, to hold the lamps of the Gospel.

But concerning Jerusalem, which, sprinkled with blood, is found in the field of error, it is said in Ezekiel: “Your navel was not cut” (Ezekiel 16:4). Therefore all the devil’s power against men is in the loins; all his strength against women is in the navel.

[Note: Thus the old Latin translator sometimes prefers to speak, even if with a less Latin word, as is evident from other passages of Scripture, where *collyrida* and *collyridam* occur. For this reason we do not approve Victorius’s emendation, by which he substitutes *collyra* on the basis of examples from Plautus and others—not because it is correct, but because he wished to read it more elegantly. A little later, where it says “Indeed, could he not?”, he orders the negative particle to be removed.]

12. Do you wish to know that matters are as we say? Take examples. Samson, stronger than a lion and harder than rock, who, alone and unarmed, pursued a thousand armed men, became weak in Delilah’s embraces. David, chosen according to the heart of the Lord, who had often sung with his mouth of the holy Christ who was to come, after he had been captivated by Bathsheba’s nakedness while walking on the roof of his house, joined adultery to murder.

Here, and pay brief attention to this, no sight is safe, even within one’s own house. Therefore, repenting, he says to the Lord: “Against you alone have I sinned, and I have done evil before you” (Psalm 50:5). For he was king and feared no other man.

Solomon, through whom Wisdom itself sang, who discoursed from the cedar of Lebanon even to the hyssop that grows out through the wall, departed from the Lord because he was a lover of women. And lest anyone trust in closeness of blood, Amnon, the brother of his sister Tamar, burned with an illicit passion.

13. I am ashamed [or: distressed] to say how many virgins [Note: [Col. 0401] The Roman edition and others frequently add: “consecrated to God.”] fall every day, how many the Church loses from her own womb, over whom the proud enemy sets his throne among the stars; how many rocks he hollows out, and the serpent dwells in their cavities.

You may see many women pretending to be widows before they have been married, covering an unhappy conscience with a merely deceptive garment. Unless the swelling of the womb and the cries of infants betray them [Note: [Col. 0401] After *vagitus* (“cries”), the Council of Aachen and Victorius add: “they glory that they are holy and chaste.” Although these words suit the context, they seem to have been brought here from another passage of this letter.], they walk with uplifted necks and dancing feet.

Others drink potions to procure sterility and commit murder of a human being not yet born.

[Note: [Col. 0401] This is the reading of the old manuscripts inspected both by us and by the bishop of Rieti; only the Cistercian copies differ, reading “they drink and have enough men.” The Benedictine editor used a thoroughly corrupt manuscript: he read *praebent* for *praebibunt* and *nati hominis* for *sati*, although it is plain that Jerome is here attacking women who drink some drug beforehand so as not to conceive through their crime. Other praised manuscript codices read “they pretend sterility”; but *nati* (“born”) in place of *sati* is the evident reading.] Some, when they realize that they have conceived through sin, devise poisons for abortion; and often, having themselves died along with the child, they are brought to the underworld guilty of three crimes: murderers of themselves, adulterers against Christ, and parricides of their unborn child.

These are the women accustomed to say: “All things are clean to the clean” (Romans 14:20). “My conscience is sufficient for me. God desires a clean heart. Why should I abstain from foods that God created for use?”

And whenever they wish to seem witty and festive, after they have gorged themselves on unmixed wine, joining sacrilege to drunkenness, they say: “Far be it from me to abstain from Christ’s Blood.”

And any woman whom they see pale and sorrowful they call wretched and a Manichaean; for fasting undertaken with such an intention is heresy.

[Note: [Col. 0402] Martianay reads “a wretched nun and Manichaean.” But the word “nun” occurs neither in the manuscripts nor in other printed books; plainly the similarity of the names *Monacha* and *Manichaea* is being turned into an insult. Moreover, the Manichaeans, whom Jerome shortly calls heretics, did not eat meat and abstained from wine because of their heretical commitment to fasting, calling it the gall of the Prince of Darkness. By contrast, the false virgins called the wine with which they gorged themselves Christ’s Blood.] These are the women who conspicuously walk about in public and, by furtive glances from their eyes, draw behind them crowds of young men. They constantly hear through the Prophet: “You have the face of a prostitute; you have no shame” (Jeremiah 3).

[Note: Hilary’s passage in the letter to Abram’s daughter illustrates this. Because of custom, let the purple be very narrow in the garment, but let the purple itself not spread through the clothing; this distinguishes it from the broader purple mentioned by Tertullian in *On the Pallium*, section 4. Hence also the broad stripe (*latus clavus*) mentioned by the same author in section 13 of *On the Crown*.]

Only a thin strip of purple on the garment, the head loosely bound so that the hair falls down, a cheaper slipper, and over the shoulders a hyacinth-colored cloak (*laena hyacinthina*) flying about; narrow sleeves clinging to the arms, and a manner of walking with the knees unrestrained. This is their entire virginity.

[Note: The Benedictine editor deleted the words *hyacinthina laena* because he had not found them in his manuscripts. But our manuscripts, as well as other printed copies, contain them, and there is no doubt that the holy Doctor drew them from Persius, *Satires* 1.32: “Someone whose hyacinth-colored cloak hangs around his shoulders.” The nature of a *laena*—a cloak—is well known. As for *maforte*, *Mavors*, *maphorium*, or finally *mafors*, in which the letter V is used for digamma F and conversely, as is customary, one may learn from Isidore, Book 19, chapter 25; Cassian, Book 1 on the habit of the monk; and others. It is commonly believed to have been half of a *stola*; when thrown back over the shoulders, it was called a *ricinium* and, according to Servius and Nonius, a *mavorte*.]

Let them have such admirers, so that under the name of virginity they may perish all the more profitably.

[Note: [Col. 0402] Earlier printed editions had the corrupt reading *ista huiusmodi* (“these such”), in two words. The Cistercian copy reads *lucris suis* (“by their profits”) where the text adds “all the more profitably”; other copies have “more safely,” but most, “more quickly.” We follow the latter reading, which Victorius does not approve, though it is truer and more consonant with another passage in the Letter to Demetrias: “That they may perish more saleably under the name of virginity.”]

We gladly do not please such people.

98. 14. I am ashamed to say it—shameful indeed; it is sad, but true: whence has the plague of the Agapetae entered the churches?

Whence this other name for wives without marriage? Rather, whence this new kind of concubines? I will go further: whence women who are prostitutes yet have one husband? They live in the same house, in one bedroom, often in one little bed, and they call us suspicious if we suppose anything.

A brother abandons his virgin sister; a virgin spurns her celibate brother, seeks an outsider as her brother, and, while pretending that they share the same purpose, seeks spiritual comfort from strangers so that they may have carnal intercourse at home.

Solomon condemns such people in Proverbs, saying: “Can anyone carry fire in his bosom and his garments not be burned? Or can he walk upon burning coals and his feet not be scorched?” (Proverbs 6:27–28).

[Note: At this point the old handwritten copies vary, but most add: “The brother who is spiritual.” Sulpicius, however, does not acknowledge the words; in his *Dialogue* he quotes this period from Jerome as an example of biting style.]

15. Therefore, having driven out and expelled those women who do not wish to be virgins but merely to appear so, let all my speech now be directed to you. The more you began as a noble virgin of the city of Rome, the more you must labor, lest you lose both present and future blessings.

You learned the troubles of marriage and the uncertainties of married life from a domestic example, when your sister Blesilla, older in age but inferior in purpose, was widowed in the seventh month after taking a husband. O unhappy human condition, ignorant of the future! She lost both the crown of virginity and the pleasure of marriage.

Although widowhood holds the second rank of chastity, imagine what crosses she must endure every moment as she looks daily upon her sister: she has lost what the other possesses, and, having experienced pleasure with greater difficulty and then lost it, has a lesser reward for continence.

[Note: Older printed editions read: “Let her know that she possesses continence,” and so forth. The following reference to the hundredfold and sixtyfold fruit alludes to Matthew 13:8: “Others fell on good soil and yielded fruit, one a hundredfold, another sixtyfold, another thirtyfold.” The last of these, when compared with marriage, should be compared with Saint Cyprian, *On the Habit of Virgins*, p. 73, where he arranges these proportions differently.]

Yet let her be secure and joyful. The hundredfold and the sixtyfold fruit come from one seed of chastity.

16. A virgin must avoid the company of married women; the vices of widows and clergy.—I do not want you to associate with married women; I do not want you to visit noble households; I do not want you frequently to see what you despised when you wished to be a virgin.

Little women are accustomed to applaud themselves over husbands who are judges or who hold some position of rank. If a crowd of people seeking greetings rushes to the emperor’s wife, why do you insult your husband? Why do you, the bride of God, hasten to the wife of a man? Learn a holy pride in this matter; know that you are better than they.

Nor do I want you to avoid only those whose pride comes from their husbands’ honors, whom crowds of eunuchs surround, and whose garments are woven with metals drawn out into threads of gold. Flee also those whom necessity, not their will, made widows—not because they ought to have wished for their husbands’ death, but because they did not willingly accept the opportunity for chastity.

[Note: We prefer the reading of the Cistercian manuscript as more truthful and more consonant with Jerome’s meaning. Previously the text had, with a different sense, “because they had wished for it.”]

Now, although the garment alone has been changed, their former ambition has not.

[Note: [Col. 0404] It is worth hearing Chrysostom, rebuking in nearly the same words the arrogance of women, *Homily 20 on Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians* 5: “The woman wears gold and is carried about in a pair of white mules; everywhere she has herds of servants and a swarm of eunuchs.” A *basterna* was a kind of litter, much like ours, as an old epigram teaches:

“An ivory *basterna* encloses chaste matrons,
its shining broad side open on either hand.”

Augustine, Letter 9 to Nebridius: “May a vehicle most suitable for you be sent to you? For our Lucinianus assures us that you can ride harmlessly in a *basterna*.” Isidore’s glossary explains the word as a covered hand-borne conveyance, that is, a carrying-chair borne by servants’ hands. But, from the same author’s *Etymologies*, 20.12, since such a litter was customarily placed on the back of beasts of burden, others interpret it differently.]

A procession of covered litters precedes them, with a troop of half-men; their skin is stretched over reddening cheeks, stuffed and distended, so that you would think they had not lost their husbands but were seeking them. Their house is full of flatterers, full of banquets.

The clergy themselves—whom it was fitting to be teachers of learning and fear alike—kiss the heads of married women and, with an extended hand, so that if you did not know better you would think they wished to bless them, receive fees for giving greetings.

Meanwhile, those women who see that priests require their protection are lifted into arrogance; and because they have experienced the domination of husbands, they prefer the freedom of widowhood. They are called chaste and *Nonnæ*; and after a doubtful dinner, they dream of the Apostles.

[Note: *Nonnæ* does not mean, as some have thought, “old women,” but women so called because they were virgins devoted to God and lived chastely. Fulbertus writes in his *Penitentials for Laymen*: “If anyone corrupts a Nonna, let him do penance for seven years.” For the dinner called “doubtful,” see the commentators on Terence’s *Phormio*, at “A doubtful dinner is served.”]

17. Let your companions be women whom fasting has made thin, whose faces are pale, whom both age and life have tested, and who daily sing in their hearts: “Where do you pasture? Where do you lie down at noon?” (Song of Songs 1:6).

Let them say from the heart: “I desire to depart and be with Christ” (Philippians 1:23). Be subject to your parents; imitate your bridegroom. Let your appearances in public be rare. Let martyrs be sought in your chamber. You will never lack a reason for going out if you go out whenever it is necessary.

Let your food be moderate, and never let your belly be full. For many women, although sober with regard to wine, are drunk with the abundance of food. When you rise at night for prayer, let it be not indigestion that causes you to belch, but emptiness.

Read frequently; learn as much as possible. Let sleep steal upon you while you hold the book, and let the holy page receive your falling face. Let fasting be daily for you, and let your nourishment flee satiety.

[Note: [Col. 0404] For “flee satiety,” the Roman edition of this letter printed separately reads: “satiety at evening.”]

IT IS OF NO BENEFIT TO CARRY AN EMPTY BELLY after passing two or three days without food, if it is then overwhelmed in the same way, if fasting is balanced by satiety. At once the mind, filled, grows dull, and watered soil produces thorns of lust.

Whenever you sense the outer person sighing for the flower of youth, and, after taking food, when the sweet procession of lust has shaken you as you lie arranged in bed, seize the shield of faith, by which the flaming arrows of the devil are extinguished.

“Their hearts are like an oven, all of them adulterers” (Hosea 7:4). But, accompanied by the footsteps of Christ and attentive to his words, say: “Was not our heart burning within us on the way, when he opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke 24:32). And this: “Your word is exceedingly refined by fire, and your servant has loved it” (Psalm 118).

It is difficult for the human soul not to love something, and it is necessary that our mind be drawn toward some object of affection. The love of the flesh is overcome by love of the spirit. Desire is extinguished by desire. Whatever diminishes from the one grows from the other.

Rather, repeat constantly and say upon your bed: “By night I sought him whom my soul loves” (Song of Songs 3:1). “Therefore,” says the Apostle, “put to death your members that are upon the earth” (Colossians 3:5).

Hence afterward he himself confidently said: “I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20). Whoever puts his members to death and walks in the image does not fear saying: “I have become like a wineskin in the frost” (Psalm 118:83). Whatever moisture of lust was in me has been boiled away.

And: “My knees have grown weak through fasting.” And: “I have forgotten to eat my bread. Because of the sound of my groaning, my bone has clung to my flesh” (Psalm 101:6).

[Note: Some printed copies, in agreement with the reading of the Council of Aachen, have: “It is necessary that our mind be drawn toward some object of affection, and that the love of the flesh be overcome by love of the spirit.”]

[Note: Perhaps other copies more correctly repeat: “Upon my bed, by night,” from which the verse of the Song itself begins. A little farther on we correct a few minor matters.]

18. Be a cricket of the nights. Wash your bed each night; water your couch with your tears. Keep watch and be like a sparrow in the wilderness.

Sing psalms with the spirit; sing psalms also with understanding: “Bless the Lord, my soul, and do not forget all his rewards: he forgives all your iniquities; he heals all your diseases and redeems your life from corruption” (Psalm 101:1ff.).

And who among us can say from the heart: “For I ate ashes like bread and mingled my drink with weeping” (Psalm 101:10)?

Should one not weep, should one not groan, when the serpent again invites me to unlawful foods? When he wishes to clothe those expelled from the paradise of virginity in leather tunics, which Elijah, returning to paradise, cast upon the ground?

What have I to do with pleasure, which soon perishes? What have I to do with this sweet and deadly song of the Sirens? I do not want you to be subject to the sentence by which condemnation was imposed upon humanity: “In pains and anxieties you shall give birth” (Genesis 3:16).

That is the law of a woman, not mine: “And your turning shall be toward your husband.” Let the turning of the woman who does not have Christ as her husband be toward her husband. And finally: “You shall die by death.” That is the end of marriage; my purpose is without sexual distinction.

Let married women have their own time and title. For me, virginity is consecrated in Mary and in Christ.

19. Someone may say: “Do you dare to disparage marriage, which has been blessed by God?”

It is not disparaging marriage when virginity is preferred to it. No one compares an evil with a good. Let married women also glory, since they are second to virgins.

“Be fruitful,” he says, “and multiply, and fill the earth” (Genesis 1:28). Let him be fruitful and multiply who is to fill the earth. Your troop is in heaven.

“Be fruitful and multiply”—this command is fulfilled after paradise and nakedness, and after the fig leaves that inaugurated the itching of marriage. Let him marry, and let him be given in marriage, who eats his bread in the sweat of his face, whose earth produces thorns and thistles, and whose grass is choked by brambles.

My seed is made fertile with a hundredfold harvest. “Not all receive the word of God, but those to whom it has been given” (Matthew 19:11). Let necessity make one person a eunuch; let my will do so for me.

“There is a time for embracing and a time for abstaining from embraces; a time for throwing stones and a time for gathering them” (Ecclesiastes 3:5). After the sons of Abraham were begotten from the hardness of the nations, “holy stones began to roll upon the earth” (Zechariah 9:16).

For they pass through the storms of this world and, in God’s chariot, are rolled along with the speed of wheels. Let those sew tunics who have lost the seamless tunic from above, those who delight in the cries of infants and, at the very beginning of the light, mourn in weeping that they have been born.

Eve was a virgin in paradise; after the leather tunics, marriage began. Your realm is paradise. Preserve what you were born as, and say: “Return, my soul, to your rest” (Psalm 124:7).

And so that you may know that virginity belongs to nature and marriage came after sin: flesh is born a virgin from marriage, and in its fruit gives back what it had lost in its root.

“A shoot shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root” (Isaiah 11:1). The shoot is the Mother of the Lord, simple, pure, sincere, with no external branch attached to it, and fruitful in unity.

[Note: Understand this as singularity, corresponding to the Greek *monas* (μονάς). Jerome frequently uses the word *unio* in this sense elsewhere, as in the end of his commentary on Hosea 13: “A simple and most pure shoot, fruitful in unity,” and in his commentary on Ezekiel 40, at the words “and their columns . . . one on this side and another on that”: “He did not say two . . . but one, which is the perfect number and, by its unity, imitates God,” and so forth.

It therefore appears that he intended here also to say that, just as God the Father begets the Word alone, without a mother, so Mary the Virgin alone, without a man, bore Christ. Other Fathers likewise used this word in that sense, especially Saint Hilary in his books on the Trinity. Meanwhile, the Cistercian manuscript and certain others read *unitate* (“unity”), a synonym of *unio*, as it is found in Tertullian against Praxeas; although, according to the usage of the holy Fathers, *unitas* properly refers to nature and *unio* to person.]

The flower of the shoot is Christ, who says: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (Song of Songs 2:1). In another place he is proclaimed as “the stone cut from the mountain without hands” (Daniel 2), the Prophet signifying that a virgin would be born from a Virgin.

“Hands” are understood as the work of marriage, as in: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me” (Song of Songs 2:6).

In keeping with this meaning is also the fact that the animals brought into Noah’s ark in pairs are unclean: for the odd number is clean. Moses and Jesus son of Nun are commanded to walk barefoot into the holy land. The disciples, without the burden of sandals and the bindings of leather, are sent to preach the new Gospel. And the soldiers, having divided Jesus’ garments by lot, had no sandals to take away [or: had no shoes that they could remove]. For the Lord could not have what he had forbidden to his servants.

20. I praise marriage; I praise wedlock—but because they produce virgins for me. I gather a rose from thorns, gold from earth, a pearl from a shell. Will the plowman plow all day? Will he not also rejoice in the harvest of his labor?

[Note: The Cistercian copy, together with the separate Roman edition of this little work, reads: “But perhaps your mother will say, ‘Married women are honored more,’” and so forth. We do not dare to insert these few words into the text, since the passage retains its complete meaning without them; nevertheless, we do not reject them, since they fit the whole context very well, especially the words “Why do you envy your daughter, mother?”]

Marriage is honored more when what is born from it is loved more. Why do you envy your daughter, mother? She was nourished by your milk, raised from your womb, and grew in your lap. You carefully preserved her as a virgin. Are you indignant that she did not wish to be the wife of a soldier but of a king? She has bestowed a great benefit upon you. You have begun to be the mother-in-law of God.

[Note: Ruffinus sharply criticizes this statement of the holy Doctor in Book 2 of his *Invectives*: “You said that God has a mother-in-law; and what is so impious or profane that any of the pagan poets could even have said it?” He says other things as well, which will be found in the proper place.

But since ecclesiastical authority permits us to call the virgins brides of Christ—as Sulpicius Severus says in Letter 2, “virgins,” meaning those who vowed virginity for religious reasons, “are said to marry Christ”—Ruffinus ought not to have twisted into an evil sense the statement that the mother of a nun who is a virgin is called the mother-in-law of God. This is relevant because the virgins themselves are frequently called “ladies” in ancient writings: “I must call him Lord,” Jerome says, “whose bride is my Lord’s.”]

The Apostle says: “Concerning virgins, I have no command of the Lord” (1 Corinthians 7:25). Why? Because even he, in choosing to be a virgin, was not under compulsion but acted by his own will.

Nor should we listen to those who invent that he had a wife, since, discussing continence and urging perpetual chastity, he says: “I wish that all were as I myself am” (1 Corinthians 7:8). And afterward: “I say to the unmarried and to widows: It is good for them if they remain as I do.” And elsewhere: “Do we not have authority to lead about women, as do the other Apostles?” (ibid. 9:5).

Why, then, does he not give a command of the Lord concerning virginity? Because what is not compelled but offered has the greater reward. For if virginity had been commanded, marriage would have seemed to be taken away; and it would have been exceedingly harsh to compel people against nature, to extort from human beings the life of angels, and in a certain sense to condemn what had been created.

[Note: Victorius reports that in certain manuscripts the words *per suam imitationem* (“through his own imitation”) are inserted here, and he rightly approves them. Those who attributed a wife to Paul in antiquity are exceedingly rare; I do not know whether Jerome had here before his eyes only Clement of Alexandria, whose view concerning the Apostle’s marriage he condemns in Book 3 of the *Stromata*.]

21. There was another kind of blessedness under the Old Law. There it is said: “Blessed is he who has seed in Zion and household members in Jerusalem.”

[Note: [Col. 0407] On this passage of Scripture, see Sabatier’s edition of the Old Italian Version. The present Vulgate reads: “The Lord has spoken, whose fire is in Zion and whose furnace is in Jerusalem.” The Greek of Isaiah 31, final verse, reads: “Blessed is he who has offspring in Zion and members of his household in Jerusalem.” See also Montfaucon, *Hexapla*, vol. 2, p. 144. This passage is praised again below, Letter 57, no. 11.]

And: “Cursed is the barren woman who did not give birth” (Isaiah 10). And: “Your children are like olive shoots around your table” (Psalm 127). There is also the promise of riches. And: “There shall be no weak person in your tribes” (Isaiah 56).

[Note: [Col. 0407] The same Victorius reads: “Now it is said to eunuchs.”]

Now it is said: Do not consider yourself a dry tree. You have, in place of sons and daughters, an everlasting place in the heavenly realms. Now the poor are blessed, and Lazarus is preferred to the rich man in purple.

[Note: As Gravina more correctly observes, some copies read “to the man clothed in purple,” as Jerome says elsewhere.]

Now the weak person is stronger. The world was empty; and, not to speak of the symbolic figures, the blessing of children alone was present. Therefore Abraham, already an old man, is joined to Keturah; Jacob is bought with mandrakes; and Rachel, beautiful yet with a closed womb, complains as a figure of the Church.

But as the harvest gradually increased, a reaper was sent in. Elijah was a virgin, Elisha was a virgin, and many of the sons of the prophets were virgins.

Jeremiah is told: “And you shall not take a wife” (Jeremiah 16:2). Sanctified in the womb and with captivity near at hand, he is forbidden to take a wife.

The Apostle says the same thing in other words: “I consider this good because of the present necessity, that it is good for a person to be so” (1 Corinthians 7:26). What is this necessity that removes the joys of marriage? “The time has been shortened. It remains that those who have wives should be as though they did not have them” (ibid. 29).

Nebuchadnezzar is close at hand. The lion has advanced from his lair. Why should marriages serve that most proud king? Why should there be little children, over whom the Prophet laments, saying: “The tongue of the suckling child has clung to his palate in thirst. The little children asked for bread, and there was no one to break it for them” (Lamentations 4:4)?

Thus, as we have said, this good of continence was found among men alone, and Eve continually gave birth in pains. But after the Virgin conceived in her womb and bore for us a child, “whose dominion is upon his shoulders” (Isaiah 9:6), God, the Mighty One, the Father of the age to come, the curse was loosed.

Death through Eve; life through Mary. Therefore the gift of virginity flowed more abundantly among women, because it began from a woman.

As soon as the Son of God entered upon the earth, he established a new household for himself, SO THAT HE WHO WAS WORSHIPPED BY ANGELS IN HEAVEN might have angels also on earth.

Then Judith, practicing continence, cut off the head of Holofernes (Judith 13). Then Haman, whose name is interpreted as “iniquity,” was burned in his own fire (Esther 15). Then James and John, leaving their father, net, and boat, followed the Savior, abandoning together the affection of blood, the bonds of the world, and the care of their household.

Then it was first heard: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me.” No soldier goes to battle with his wife.

A disciple who wished to go and bury his father was not permitted to do so (Matthew 8). “Foxes have dens and the birds of heaven nests where they may rest; but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Luke 9:58).

Do not perhaps become sad if you remain in straitened circumstances. “The unmarried man is concerned with the things of the Lord, how he may please the Lord. But the married man is concerned with the things of the world, how he may please his wife. The woman is divided, and so is the virgin. The unmarried woman considers the things of the Lord, so that she may be holy in body and spirit” (1 Corinthians 7:31ff.).

[Note: Paul’s passage is quoted here from the old Latin translator, as also by Tertullian in *On the Veiling of Virgins*. Other editors are therefore wrong to print “and the virgin who is not married,” which, according to the sense of that translator, who sets the woman against the virgin, must be corrected by a different punctuation: “The woman is divided, and the virgin. She who is not married considers…” The Greek reads: μεμέρισται ἡ γυνὴ καὶ ἡ παρθένος, “the woman and the virgin are divided.”

This is the sense that the holy Doctor elsewhere presses against Helvidius on the basis of the Latin copies. But in the first book *Against Jovinian* he rejects the older reading: “I briefly point out that in the Latin manuscripts this passage is read as follows: ‘The virgin and the woman are divided.’ Although this has its own meaning, and I too have explained it in this way according to the character of the passage, it is nevertheless not the truth of the Apostle, since the Apostle wrote: ‘He is concerned with the things of the world, how he may please his wife, and he is divided.’ Once this statement has been completed, he passes to virgins and the continent, and says: ‘The unmarried woman and the virgin consider the things of the Lord.’” This is the Vulgate reading. See Augustine, *On Holy Virginity*, chapter 22, and *On the Good of Widowhood*, chapter 2, where he explains this reading.]

For the woman who is married considers the things of the world, how she may please her husband.

## 22

How many troubles marriage entails, and by how many anxieties it is beset, I think I expressed briefly in the book that we published against Helvidius, *On the Perpetual Virginity of Blessed Mary*. To repeat the same things now would take too long; and if anyone wishes, he can draw from that little fountain. Yet, lest I seem entirely to have omitted the matter, I shall now say this: since the Apostle commands us to pray without interruption, while the man who fulfills his marital obligation cannot pray, either we pray always and are virgins, or we cease praying in order to serve marriage. “And if a virgin marries,” he says, “she does not sin; nevertheless such persons will have tribulation in the flesh” (1 Cor. 7:28).

At the beginning of the little book I stated in advance that I would say either nothing at all or only a little about the anxieties of marriage. I now give the same warning: if you wish to know by how many troubles a virgin is free and by how many a wife is bound, read Tertullian’s *To His Friend the Philosopher*,

> **[Note: [Col. 0409]** We do not accept what Victorius adds, namely “writing”; for the title of the book seems to have been *To His Friend the Philosopher*, which he cites elsewhere against Jovinian, but which disappeared long ago. Shortly afterward: “the Cistercian manuscript, which he recently wrote as a little work to his sister.” There are, however, three books of Ambrose addressed to his sister Marcellina, which he composed around the year 347.]

and his other little books *On Virginity*, as well as the splendid volume of blessed Cyprian, and the works of Pope Damasus on this subject, composed both in verse and in prose; also the little works of our Ambrose which he recently wrote to his sister. In them he poured himself out with such eloquence that he searched out, expressed, and arranged everything pertinent to the praises of virgins.

## 23

We must proceed by a different route. We not only exalt virginity, but preserve it. It is not enough to know that something is good unless what has been chosen is guarded with the greatest care: the former belongs to judgment, the latter to labor; the former is shared with many, the latter with few.

> “The one who perseveres,” he says, “to the end will be saved” (Matt. 24:13).

And:

> “Many are called, but few are chosen” (ibid. 20:16 and 22:14).

Therefore I adjure you before God and Christ Jesus and his chosen angels,

> **[Note: [Col. 0409]** We have added “that you may keep what you have begun” from the Cistercian manuscript and the Roman edition of this little book, since these words connect so naturally with what precedes that they seemed necessary.]

that you keep what you have begun, lest you bring out too readily into public view the vessels of the Lord’s temple, which it has been granted to priests alone to see; lest some profane person gaze upon God’s sanctuary. Uzzah, touching the Ark which he was not permitted to touch, was struck down by sudden death. For the golden and silver vessel was not so dear to God as the temple of a virginal body. The shadow went before; now the reality is here.

You speak, indeed, simply, and do not despise any stranger who addresses you gently,

> **[Note: [Col. 0409]** Gravius adds *voce*, “with a voice,” meaning with a flattering voice.]

but unchaste eyes see otherwise. They do not know how to contemplate the beauty of the soul, but only that of bodies. Hezekiah displays God’s treasure to the Assyrians; but the Assyrians ought not to have seen what they desired. Finally, when Judea was shaken by continual wars, the Lord’s vessels were the first things captured and carried away. Amid banquets and troops of concubines—for it is the height of vice to pollute what is honorable—Belshazzar drinks from the sacred vessels.

## 24

Do not incline your ear to words of wickedness. For those who speak something indecent often test the judgment of your mind: whether you willingly listen, virgin, to what is said; whether you allow yourself to be carried away by every joke. Whatever you say, they praise; whatever you deny, they deny:

> **[Note: [Col. 0410]** Instead of *facetam*, some manuscripts read *castam*, others *innocentem*.]

They call you witty and holy, a woman in whom there is no deceit:

> “Behold, truly a handmaid of Christ,”

they say; “behold, complete simplicity.” Not like that grim, ugly, rustic, terrifying woman, who perhaps had no husband for the very reason that she could not find one.

We are led by a natural evil. We gladly favor our flatterers, and although we answer that we are unworthy, and a warm blush floods our faces, nevertheless the soul within rejoices at its own praise.

The bride of Christ is the Ark of the Testament, gilded within and without, guardian of the Lord’s law. As there was nothing in that Ark except the tablets of the Testament, so in you also let there be no outward thought. Upon this mercy seat, as upon the cherubim, the Lord wishes to sit. He sends his disciples so that he may sit in you as upon the foal of an ass; so that, freed from worldly cares,

> **[Note: [Col. 0410]** Gravius reads *solvant*, “may free,” so that the word refers to the disciples.]

you may leave behind the straw and bricks of Egypt, follow Moses in the wilderness, and enter the promised land.

Let no one prevent this—not your mother, not your sister, not your kinswoman, not your brother. The Lord has need of you. If they wish to hinder you, let them fear the scourges of Pharaoh, who, when unwilling to release God’s people to worship him, suffered the things that are written.

Jesus entered the Temple and cast out what did not belong to the Temple. For God is jealous, and he does not wish his Father’s house to become a den of thieves. Otherwise, where coins are counted, where cages of doves are kept, and simplicity is slaughtered; where the care of worldly business seethes in a virgin breast—the Temple veil is immediately torn, the bridegroom rises in anger, and says:

> “Your house will be left to you desolate” (Matt. 15:38).

Read the Gospel and see how Mary, sitting at the Lord’s feet, is preferred to Martha’s activity. Certainly,

> **[Note: [Col. 0410]** The name *Martha*, which was lacking here, has been supplied from other printed editions and manuscripts; from the same sources we have supplied two further words, “to whom Jesus.” A little farther on, where the text reads “but few things are necessary, as one,” although the current Greek and Latin sacred manuscripts read otherwise, most manuscripts have *aut unum*, “or one,” as does the author of the *Moralia* attributed to Basil the Great, rule 38, and Olympiodorus on Ecclesiastes 1, who read: ὀλίγων δέ ἐστι χρεία καὶ ἑνός, “but few things are necessary, and one.” We did not wish to alter the text in a doubtful matter.]

Martha was diligently preparing a meal for the Lord and his disciples as an act of hospitality. Jesus said to her:

> “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things; but few things are necessary—or one. Mary has chosen the good portion, which will not be taken away from her” (Luke 10:41–42).

Be Mary yourself: prefer instruction to food. Let your sisters run about and seek how they may receive Christ as a guest. Once you have cast off the burden

> **[al. honor]** of the world, sit at the Lord’s feet and say:

> “I found him whom my soul sought; I will hold him and will not let him go” (Song 3:4).

And let him answer:

> “My dove, my perfect one, is one; she is the only one of her mother, the chosen one of her who bore her” (ibid. 6:8),

that is, of the heavenly Jerusalem.

## 25

### In prayer we speak to God, etc.

Let the privacy of your chamber always guard you; let the bridegroom always play with you inwardly. You pray: you speak to the Bridegroom. You read: he speaks to you. And when sleep has overcome you, he will come behind the wall, put his hand through the opening, and touch your belly. Awakening, you will rise and say:

> “I am wounded with love.”

And again you will hear from him:

> “A garden enclosed is my sister, my bride; a garden enclosed, a sealed fountain” (Song 4:12).

Take care not to leave the house and wish to see the daughters of a foreign land, even though you have patriarchs as brothers and rejoice in Israel as your ancestry: Dinah went out and was corrupted.

I do not want you to seek the Bridegroom through the streets. I do not want you to go around the corners of the city, even if you may say:

> “I will rise and go around the city; in the marketplace and in the streets I will seek him whom my soul has loved” (ibid. 3:2).

And if you ask:

> “Have you seen him whom my soul has loved?” (ibid. 3),

no one will deign to answer you. The Bridegroom cannot be found in the streets.

> “Narrow and difficult is the way that leads to life” (Matt. 7:14).

Finally, what follows is:

> “I sought him and did not find him; I called him and he did not answer me” (Song 5:6).

And would that not finding him were enough! You will be wounded, stripped, and will tell the story with groans:

> “The watchmen who go around the city found me; they struck me and wounded me; they took away my cloak” (ibid. v. 7).

But if this happens to the woman who goes out, although she had said:

> “I sleep, but my heart is awake” (Song 5:2),

and:

> “My beloved is a bundle of myrrh to me; he will lie between my breasts”—

what will become of us, who are still young girls; who, when the bride enters with the bridegroom, remain outside?

Jesus is jealous; he does not want your face to be seen by others. You may make excuses and complain that you covered your face with a drawn veil, and say:

> “Tell me, you whom my soul has loved: where do you pasture, where do you lie at midday, lest I become like one who is veiled among the flocks of your companions?” (Song 1:6, according to the Septuagint).

He will be indignant, swell with anger, and say:

> “If you do not know yourself, O beautiful among women, go out in the footsteps of the flocks and pasture your young goats beside the shepherds’ tents.”

Even if you are beautiful, and your appearance is loved by the Bridegroom above that of all women, unless you know yourself and guard your heart with every care; unless you flee the eyes of young men, you will leave my bridal chamber and pasture the young goats that are to be placed on the left.

## 26

Therefore, my daughter Eustochium—daughter, lady, ward, sister (for one name belongs to age, another to merit, another to religious commitment, and this one to affection)—hear Isaiah speaking:

> “My people, enter your chambers. Shut your doors; hide yourself for a little while, until the Lord’s anger has passed” (Isa. 26).

Let foolish virgins wander outside; remain within with the Bridegroom. For if you shut the door and, according to the Gospel command,

> **[Col. 0412]**

pray to your Father in secret, he will come, knock, and say:

> “Behold, I stand before the door and knock. If anyone opens to me, I will enter and dine with him, and he with me” (Rev. 3:20).

Immediately, anxious, you will answer:

> “The voice of my beloved knocking [some add: ‘and saying’]: Open to me, my sister, my neighbor, my dove, my perfect one” (Song 5:2).

> **[Note: [Col. 0412]** The words “my dove” were absent from Erasmus’s and the Benedictine edition. Then, instead of “There is no need,” Victorius reads “It is necessary,” contrary to Jerome’s meaning and the course of the argument.]

Nor should you say:

> “I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I soil them?”

Rise at once and open, lest, while you delay, he pass by, and afterward you complain and say:

> “I opened to my beloved, but my beloved had passed by.”

Why should the doors of your heart be closed to the Bridegroom? Let them be open to Christ and closed to the devil, according to the saying:

> “If the spirit of one who has power rises against you, do not abandon your place” (Eccl. 10:4).

Daniel remained in his upper chamber,

> **[Note: [Col. 0412]** Victorius, having deleted the words “remained in the upper chamber,” had read “in a lofty upper room,” a reading he greatly preferred. We thought it better not to depart from the authority of the manuscript copies.]

for he could not remain in a low place. He had windows open toward Jerusalem. You too should have open windows—but windows through which light may enter, through which you may see the city of the Lord. Do not open those windows of which it is said:

> “Death entered through your windows” [some read “our windows”] (Jer. 9:21).

## 27

### Empty glory must be avoided

You must also take care to avoid being seized by the burning desire for empty glory.

> “How can you believe,” Jesus says, “when you receive glory from human beings?” (John 5).

See what kind of evil this is: whoever possesses it cannot believe.

Let us instead say:

> “For you are my glory” (Ps. 3:4).

And:

> “Let the one who glories, glory in the Lord” (2 Cor. 10:17).

And:

> “If I were still pleasing human beings, I would not be Christ’s servant” (Gal. 1:10).

And:

> “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.”

And:

> “In you we shall praise all day long; in the Lord my soul shall be praised” (Ps. 33).

When you give alms, let God alone see it. When you fast, let your face be cheerful. Let your clothing be neither very clean nor dirty, and not remarkable for any peculiarity, lest the crowd of passersby stop to meet you and you be pointed out with a finger.

> **[Note: [Col. 0412]** Eustochium’s only brother was Toxotius, who was not yet alive at that time, and lived long afterward; her sister Blesilla was still living as a widow. Jerome therefore cannot be understood as speaking of them, nor of others of his family, as a recent writer wrongly interprets the passage concerning a relative and Blesilla. From what follows—“Take care lest, while you do these things repeatedly, you yourself die”—it is clear that the holy Doctor is speaking generically, indicating that men and women devoted to piety had forfeited the merit of good works through the fault of vainglory. Thus, in his letter to Furia, he says: “Oh, if you could see your sister Eustochium”—although Eustochium was not Furia’s sister except spiritually. Sophronius, whom he attacks below after his death, may perhaps be understood here under the name “brother.” It is worth noting in this connection that formerly people commonly used filthy black garments as a pretext for mourning the death of relatives. Hence, in what follows, those who professed the monastic life, as it existed in those times, apparently lacked the distinctive clothing of their profession, whether black or otherwise appropriate, and would pretend to be wearing such dirty clothing on account of the funerals of fellow monks or sisters.]

“Your brother has died; your sister’s little body must be carried out. Take care lest, while you do these things repeatedly, you yourself die.”

Do not wish to appear sufficiently religious, nor more humble than necessary, lest in fleeing glory you seek glory. For many who avoid observers of poverty, mercy, and fasting

> **[Note: [Col. 0413]** The Cistercian manuscript reads otherwise: “avoiding the glory of poverty, misery, and fasting,” as I think.]

wish to please precisely by this very fact, that they despise pleasing; and, strangely, praise is sought while it is being avoided.

Of the other disturbances in which the human mind rejoices, grieves, hopes, and fears, I find many people free. Of this vice scarcely anyone is free; and the best person is the one who, like a beautiful body, is sprinkled with only a rare stain.

I am not warning you not to glory in riches, not to boast of the nobility of your family, or not to set yourself above others. I know your humility; I know that you say from the heart:

> “Lord, my heart is not exalted, nor are my eyes lifted up” (Ps. 130:1).

I know that with you and your mother there is no place at all for the pride by which the devil fell. Therefore it would be superfluous to write to you about this. It is exceedingly foolish to teach someone what the person being taught already knows.

But take care lest even this produce boasting in you: that you have despised the world’s boasting. Let not a secret thought creep in, so that, since you have ceased to please in gilded clothing, you try to please in filthy clothing. And if at any time you come into an assembly of brothers or sisters,

> **[Note: [Col. 0413]** I do not reject the reading found in some manuscripts, “sit on the ground”; nevertheless, most manuscripts have “sit more humbly,” leaving aside corrupt copies. A little later some printed editions likewise omit the negative particle, though the sense remains the same if *tenues* is connected with the preceding *ne*.]

sit humbly, and pretend that you are unworthy of a footstool. Do not intentionally weaken your voice as though exhausted by fasts, nor, imitating the gait of one who is faint, lean upon another’s shoulders.

There are some women who disfigure their faces so that they may appear to people to be fasting. As soon as they see someone, they groan, lower their eyebrows, and, with their face covered, scarcely free one eye [manuscripts read “balance”] for looking. Their clothing is black, their belt is of sackcloth, their hands and feet are dirty, but their stomach alone, because it cannot be seen, burns with food.

To such women that Psalm is sung every day:

> “The Lord will scatter the bones of those who please themselves” [the Gallican Psalter and the Vulgate read “of those who please human beings”] (Ps. 52:6).

Others, adopting masculine dress and changing their clothing, are ashamed to be women, though they were born women. They cut off their hair and shamelessly raise eunuch-like faces. Some dress in hair shirts and imitate owls and horned owls with cleverly made hoods, so as to return to infancy.

## 28

But lest I seem to argue only about women, avoid men also when you see them chained, with feminine hair contrary to the Apostle, goats’ beards, black cloaks, and bare feet enduring the cold. All these are signs of the devil.

Rome once lamented such an Antimus,

> **[Note: [Col. 0413]** Some read *Antonius* instead of *Antimus*, but they certainly wrongly identify that monk, to whom Jerome’s Letter 12 is extant.]

and recently such a Sophronius. After they have entered the houses of nobles and deceived little women burdened with sins, always learning and never arriving at knowledge of the truth, they feign sadness and, as though enduring long fasts, prolong themselves through stolen meals at night.

I am ashamed to say what follows, lest I seem to attack rather than admonish. There are others—men of my own order, I mean—who seek the priesthood and diaconate for the purpose of seeing women more freely. Their whole concern is with their clothing: whether it smells good, whether their foot does not swell beneath loose skin. Their hair is curled by the marks of the curling iron; their fingers shine with rings; and, lest the damp road soil their soles, they scarcely set down the tips of their feet.

When you see such men, consider them bridegrooms rather than clerics.

Some have devoted all their effort and life to learning the names, houses, and habits of married women. I shall briefly and summarily describe one of them, the leader of this art, so that once you know the master, you may recognize his disciples more easily.

He rises hurriedly with the sun. An order of calls is arranged for him; shortcuts through the streets are sought; and the intrusive old man enters almost as far as the bedrooms of those who are sleeping. If he sees a cushion, an elegant towel, or anything of household furniture, he praises it, admires it, and handles it. Complaining that he needs these things, he does not so much obtain them as extort them, because each woman fears offending the city’s postman.

Chastity is his enemy; fasting is his enemy. He judges a meal by its aromas:

> **[Note: [Col. 0414]** Since this is an extremely difficult passage of Jerome, and the manuscripts present it corruptly and variously, the interpreters have attempted to restore and explain it by conjecture. Erasmus thought that one should read either *geranopeta*, from the cooking of cranes, or *geranokopta*, from some flour-producing instrument. Victorius, however, read *et altili* and *geron ho pepōn*, by which he argued that an effeminate, soft, and luxurious old man was meant; since he approved of the flesh of fattened birds, he said that he was commonly called *pipizo*. Caelius Rhodiginus, *Ancient Readings* 3.11, prefers *geranopipas*: “an intoxicated old man,” he says, “whom we conjecture was called *pipizo* in popular speech, since *pipizein* means ‘to suck.’” Aldrovandi strongly rejects Caelius’s emendation in *Ornithology* 20.5 and maintains that the reading should be *geranoupipos*, “the crane’s cock,” or *vipio*. Martianay took another path; see him at the end of the book.

“To explain our opinion in the briefest possible terms, we come closer to Aldrovandi and think that the reading should be *et altili geranopipē*, which is commonly called *pipizo*. For the earliest manuscripts largely agree on something like *geranopepa*, especially in the ending *pepa* or *pepan*. This could easily have been pronounced in popular speech as *pippa*, from *pippus*, ‘young creature,’ with the Latin word *pepa* likewise slightly corrupted according to ordinary popular pronunciation. It seems most probable to me that the young crane, or more precisely a smaller crane, was once designated by this word. For, as Pliny says in Book 10, chapter 49, ‘vipiones [or *pipiones*] were held in honor at tables; they call the smaller cranes by this name’; Cornelius Nepos says they were highly valued; and Varro, in *On Foods*, and Plutarch, *Oration* 11, also report the method of fattening them, to omit other authorities.

“The fact that it is commonly called *pipizo* does not move us to suppose that it was derived from the faulty speech of the people in place of *pipio*, for *pipizōn* is formed from the verb *pipezō*; Ducange also notes the use of this word in later Latin.

“We therefore think that the passage should now be written and read as follows: ‘He approves a meal by its aromas, and calls it the sacred banquet’ (*hieran agapēn*). We reject the other words inserted between these, which the scholiasts added on their own. Not knowing what *hieran agapēn*, or ‘sacred banquet,’ meant, they first wrote their conjecture in the margin, thinking that it referred to a fattened bird, and later thrust it into the text.

“In Jerome’s time, and indeed long before it, there were certain overly indulgent Christians who, when they sought out and prepared luxurious dishes, dared to call this banquet an *agapē*, or sacred banquet—properly, *hieran agapēn*. Clement of Alexandria strongly rebukes this in the *Paedagogue*, Book II, chapter [the passage is supplied here only in Latin, since the Greek was not at hand]:

‘The carnal life which some dare to call an *agapē*, using unrestrained language: certain banquets smelling of rich dishes and sauces, they call a beautiful and salutary work of the Word; they dishonor the sacred *agapē* with pots of who knows what, clear sauces and drink, and pursue that Name with the curse of luxury and smoke. They are deceived by their expectation, as though they hoped to purchase God’s promise with little meals.’”]

and a fattened *geranopepa*, commonly called *pipizo*.

His mouth is barbarous and shameless, always armed for abuse. Wherever you turn, he is first to appear. Whatever new sound is heard, he is either its author or the one who magnifies the rumor. His horses are changed every hour; they are so sleek and spirited that you might think him the own brother of the Thracian king.

> **[Note: [Col. 0415]** Namely, of Diomedes, whose horses Lucretius mentions in Book 5:

> “And the horses of Diomedes, breathing fire from their nostrils.”]

## 29

The cunning enemy fights with varied ambushes. The serpent was wiser than all the beasts that the Lord had created upon the earth. Hence the Apostle says:

> “We are not ignorant of his schemes.”

Neither affected dirtiness nor elaborate cleanliness suits a Christian. If you do not know something, if you are uncertain about something in the Scriptures, ask the person whose life commends him, whose age excuses him, whose reputation does not discredit him—someone who can say:

> “For I betrothed you to one husband, to present a pure virgin to Christ” (2 Cor. 11:2).

Or, if there is no one who can explain it, it is better to remain safely ignorant of something than to learn it at the risk of danger.

Remember that you walk in the midst of snares. Many aged virgins of unquestioned chastity have, at the very threshold of death, lost the crown from their hands.

If there are little servant girls who share your way of life, do not rise up against them; do not puff yourself up as their mistress. You have begun to have one Bridegroom; you sing psalms together; you receive Christ’s body together. Why should your mind be different?

> **[Note: [Col. 0415]** Some manuscripts in Victorius read “why should the mind be hostile?”; others read “why should the mind be different?”]

Let the others also be encouraged. Let the honor shown to virgins be an invitation to the rest. If you sense that one is weaker in faith, take her in, console her, speak gently to her, and make her chastity your gain.

If one is pretending, fleeing servitude, read the Apostle openly to her:

> “It is better to marry than to burn” (1 Cor. 7:9).

But virgins and widows who, being idle and inquisitive, go around the houses of married women, who with worn-down foreheads

> **[Note: [Col. 0415]** Formerly the text read *abstrito*. We changed it according to the Cistercian manuscript, which also has *parasiti diversantes in modum*, almost as the first two editions do, instead of “they surpass the parasites of the mimes.”]

surpass the parasites of the mimes—cast them away as plagues. “Evil conversations corrupt good morals” (1 Cor. 15:33).

They have no concern except for the belly and what is near the belly. Such women customarily urge others, saying:

> “My little darling, enjoy your possessions and live while you live; are you really saving them for your children?”

> **[Note: [Col. 0415]** Perhaps *vinulae*, “little wines,” is more correct, as elsewhere.]

Wine-drinking and wanton, they insinuate every kind of evil and soften even iron minds toward delights.

> “When they have grown wanton against Christ, they wish to marry, incurring condemnation because they have rejected their first faith” (1 Tim. 5:11–12).

Do not wish to appear very eloquent, nor to play in meter with festive lyric poems.

Do not pursue the delicate saliva of languid married women, who now with clenched teeth, now with loosened lips, control a stammering tongue in half-formed words, thinking everything rustic that is natural.

> **[Note: [Col. 0415]** Victorius changes the text to *noscitur*, “is recognized,” but the earlier reading *nascitur*, “is born,” should be retained. It is found in all the ancient copies and means “whatever is native or natural.” The following passage should certainly be added from our Zeno, *Sermon on the Gospel according to Luke*, concerning the two kinds of temptation: “An unjust mind, thinking little of what is born,” etc. See also Minucius Felix, *Octavius*, chapter 38, Cambridge edition, p. 182 and following: “Whatever is born, as an inviolable gift of God, is corrupted by no workmanship,” etc. In place of *adeo*, which we have restored, some printed editions read *inde*, “from there.”]

Thus even adultery of the tongue pleases them:

> “For what fellowship is there between light and darkness? What agreement does Christ have with Belial?” (2 Cor. 6:14).

What does Horace have to do with the Psalter? What does Maro have to do with the Gospels? What does Cicero have to do with the Apostle? Is not a brother scandalized if he sees you reclining in an idol’s temple?

Although all things are clean to the clean, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving, nevertheless we ought not to drink at the same time from the cup of Christ and the cup of demons.

I shall relate to you the story of my own misfortune.

## 30

Many years ago, when for the sake of the kingdom of heaven I had made myself a eunuch, leaving home, parents, sister, and relatives, and—what was more difficult than all these—from the habit of richer food, and when I was traveling toward Jerusalem to serve as a soldier,

> **[Note: [Col. 0416]** Tillemont preferred to read “Antioch” instead of “Jerusalem,” since, when Jerome wrote this, he apparently had not yet been to Jerusalem. But since the manuscripts and printed books resist the change, the passage can very conveniently be understood as indicating that he intended to go there, even though, after changing his plan, he stopped first at Antioch and then in the wilderness.]

I could not entirely do without the library that I had prepared for myself at Rome with the greatest care and labor. And so, wretched man that I was, while preparing to read Tully, I fasted. After frequent vigils through the nights, after tears which the remembrance of my past sins drew from the depths of my entrails, Plautus was taken into my hands [some copies read “into my hands,” plural].

Whenever, recovering myself, I began to read the Prophets, their unpolished speech repelled me; and because my blind eyes did not see the light, I thought the fault lay not in my eyes but in the sun.

While the ancient serpent was thus mocking me,

> **[al. the ancient enemy]**

in the middle of Lent, a fever that penetrated to the marrow attacked my exhausted body. Without any respite—which is incredible even to relate—it consumed my miserable limbs so completely

> **[Note: [Col. 0416]** The Cistercian manuscript reads, “so that bone scarcely clung to bone.”]

that I scarcely remained attached to my bones.

Meanwhile my funeral was being prepared. The warmth of my living soul, while the whole body was already growing cold, trembled only in the one small area of my still-warm breast. Suddenly, seized in spirit, I was dragged before the tribunal of the Judge. There was so much light there, and such a brilliance from the radiance of those standing around, that, thrown upon the ground, I did not dare to look upward.

When asked about my condition, I answered that I was a Christian. But the one presiding said:

> “You lie. You are a Ciceronian, not a Christian. For where your treasure is, there your heart is also” (Matt. 6:21).

Immediately I fell silent. Amid the blows—for he had ordered me to be beaten—I was tortured more severely by the fire of conscience, recalling this verse:

> “But in hell, who will confess you?” (Ps. 6:6).

Nevertheless I began to cry out and, lamenting, to say:

> “Have mercy on me, Lord; have mercy on me.”

This voice resounded amid the lashes. At last those who were standing there fell at the knees of the presiding one and begged him to forgive my youth and grant my error a period for repentance, imposing punishment afterward if I should ever read books of pagan literature.

I, who in so great a crisis wished to promise even more, began to swear an oath and, calling upon his name, say:

> “Lord, if I should ever possess secular books, if I should ever read them, I have denied you.”

> **[Col. 0417]** We follow the testimony of the Bishop of Rieti, who supplied the word *fateor*, “I confess,” apparently from the manuscripts, although none of ours contains it, nor do the other printed editions.]

After I had been released upon these words of the oath, I returned to the world above. To everyone’s amazement, I opened my eyes flooded with such a torrent of tears that even unbelievers were persuaded by my grief.

Nor had that been sleep or empty dreams, by which we are often deceived. That tribunal before which I lay bears witness; that grim judgment which I feared bears witness. May it never happen to me again to fall into such an inquiry.

I confess that my shoulders were bruised and that I felt the blows after waking. From that point onward I read divine books with as much zeal as I had previously read mortal ones.

## 31

You too must avoid the evil of greed—not so that you do not desire what belongs to others, for public laws also punish that, but so that you do not preserve as your own what belongs to you and is therefore alien to you.

> “If you have not been faithful in what belongs to another,” he says, “who will give you what is yours?” (Luke 16:12).

The weights of gold and silver are alien to us; our possession is spiritual. Of this it is said elsewhere:

> “The redemption of a man is his own riches” (Prov. 13).

No one can serve two masters. For either he will hate one and love the other, or he will endure one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and Mammon (Matt. 6:24), that is, “riches.” For in the pagan language of the Syrians, *Mammon* is the name for riches.

The thought of sustenance is a thorn to faith. The root of greed is the care of the Gentiles.

But you say: “I am a delicate girl, unable to work with my hands. If I reach old age, if I begin to be ill, who will have pity on me?”

Hear Jesus speaking to the Apostles:

> “Do not think in your heart about what you will eat, nor about what you will put on your body. Is not the soul more than food, and the body more than clothing? Look at the birds of the sky, for they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and your heavenly Father feeds them” (Matt. 5:25–26).

If clothing is lacking, let the lilies be set before you. If you hunger, hear the blessing of the poor and hungry. If some pain afflicts you, read:

> “For this reason I am pleased with my weaknesses.”

And:

> “A thorn in my flesh was given to me, an angel of Satan, to buffet me” (2 Cor. 12:7).

> **[Note: [Col. 0417]** The Cistercian manuscript reads: “Do not exalt yourself; rejoice,” etc.]

Rejoice in all the judgments of God.

> “For the daughters of Judah rejoiced in all your judgments, O Lord.”

Let this voice always resound in your mouth:

> “Naked I came from my mother’s womb, and naked shall I return” (Job 1:21).

And:

> “We brought nothing into this world, nor can we take anything away.”

## 32

But now you may see most women filling wardrobes with clothing, changing tunics every day, and yet unable to overcome the moths. The more religious woman wears out one garment and drags clothes from full chests.

The fabrics are dyed purple. Gold is melted into letters; books are clothed with jewels; and Christ, naked, dies before their doors.

When they extend their hand to the needy, they sound trumpets. When they invite someone to a banquet, a herald is hired.

Recently I saw—I will not name her, lest you think this a satire—the most noble of Roman women in the Basilica of Blessed Peter, with half-men preceding her, distributing individual coins to the poor with her own hand so that she might be thought more religious.

Meanwhile,

> **[Note: [Col. 0418]** The same old manuscript reads *ut usui nostro perfacile est*, “as is very easy for our use”; then it has *pannis obsita*, “covered with rags,” without the word *annis*, “years.”]

a certain old woman, covered with years and rags, ran ahead to receive another coin. When she came to her in due order, a fist was extended instead of a denarius, and blood was shed for so great an offence.

Greed is the root of all evils, and therefore it is called by the Apostle the service of idols. Seek first the kingdom of God, and all these things will be added to you. The Lord will not let a righteous soul die of hunger.

> “I was young, and now I am old, and I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his offspring seeking bread” (Ps. 36:25).

Elijah is fed by ravens serving him. The widow of Zarephath, herself and her children about to die that night, feeds the hungry Prophet; and, wonderfully, once the container has been filled, she who had come to be fed feeds him.

The Apostle Peter says:

> “Silver and gold I have none; but what I have, this I give you. In the name of the Lord Jesus, rise and walk” (Acts 3:6).

But now many, although they remain silent in words, speak through their actions:

> “Faith and mercy I do not have; but what I have, silver and gold, this I do not give you.”

> “Having food and clothing, with these we shall be content” (1 Tim. 6:8).

Hear what Jacob asks for in his prayer:

> “If the Lord is with me and guards me on this journey that I am making, and gives me bread to eat and clothing to wear” (Gen. 28:20).

He asked only for what was necessary. After twenty years, he returned to the land of Canaan as a rich master and an even richer father.

Countless examples are available from the Scriptures teaching that greed must be avoided.

### 33

But since something is now said about it in part (and, if Christ permits, the rest is reserved for another volume), we shall report what happened at Nitria not many years ago [Note: [Col. 0418] Only one old copy, and that according to Victorius, dating from many years earlier.].

One of the brothers, more frugal than greedy, and unaware that the Lord had been sold for thirty pieces of silver, died leaving behind one hundred solidi, which he had earned by weaving linen. A council was convened among the monks—for about five thousand lived in that place, in separate cells—to decide what ought to be done. Some said that the money should be distributed to the poor; others, that it should be given to the Church; several, that it should be sent back to his parents.

But Macarius, Pambo, Isidore, and the others whom they call the Fathers, with the Holy Spirit speaking through them, decreed that the money should be buried with its owner [Note: [Col. 0418] Earlier the text read *with the same*: “which we have published as ‘with its master’; we have drawn this from the manuscripts.”], saying: “May your money be with you unto perdition” (Acts 8:10 [Col. 0419]). No one should think that this was done cruelly: such terror seized everyone throughout Egypt that leaving even one solidus behind was considered a crime.

### 34

And since we have mentioned monks, and I know that you willingly listen to what is holy, lend your ear for a little while. There are three kinds of monks in Egypt.
