The first are the Coenobites, whom they call *Sauses* in their native language; we may call them those who live in common. The second are the Anchorites, who live alone in the deserts and are so called because they have withdrawn far from human beings. The third kind is that which they call *Remoboth*, the worst [another reading: most dreadful] and most neglected, and which in our province is either the only kind or the first [Note: [Col. 0419] The manuscripts read *Auses*, others *Sauches*. For the word occurring below, *Remoboth*, others have *Renuoth* and *Remnoth*. Cassian, *Conferences* 18.7, and Benedict, Humbert, Ivo, and others describe their way of life more fully under the name *Sarabaites*. See also, if desired, Peter Crinitus, *De honesta disciplina* III.15, and others. As for Jerome’s statement that this kind exists “in our province,” learned men commonly misunderstand him as meaning Palestine, whereas Pannonia or Italy is more likely intended. For who could persuade himself that in Palestine—where monastic institutions flourished exceedingly—this most disgraceful kind was either the only one or the first? The Sarabaites seem to have been so called from [a word omitted in the source], which denotes a stubborn and refractory person. Those who prefer to derive *Remoboth* from the Greek ῥεμβός (*rhμβos*), meaning a wandering and errant person, can easily believe that the word was distorted from it. Those who prefer *Rehoboth* derive it from [a word omitted in the source], an Arabic word denoting a monk. Isidore, *On Ecclesiastical Offices* II.15, says: “In the language of the Egyptians the Sarabaites, or Renuites, are so called”; this plainly has the same meaning as *Renuit*. Yet the second etymology of the name is not Latin, although Odo of Cluny also treated it as Latin, *Collation* 3: “We wretched men are not monks, as we are falsely called, but Sarabaites, that is, Renuites, because we reject the yoke of regular discipline.” The reading *Renuoth*, formerly found in the text, is confirmed by this, whence *Renuites*; although others wish to write *Rehoboth* as *Rehivites*, by an easy alteration in Latin, making it clearer that both names derive from the Egyptian language.].

These men live in groups of two or three, or not many more, according to their own will and authority. Whatever they have worked for, they contribute in shares to a common fund, so that they may have common food. They live mostly in cities and fortified towns; and, as though their craft were holy rather than their life, whatever they sell commands a higher price.

Quarrels often arise among them, because, living on their own food, they do not allow themselves to be subject to anyone. They habitually compete in fasting and make a secret matter into a victory. Everything among them is affected: loose sleeves, bulging leggings, coarser clothing [the manuscripts read *grosser*], frequent sighs, visits to virgins, slander of clerics; and whenever a feast day arrives, they gorge themselves to the point of vomiting.

### 35. The Coenobites

Having thus driven out these kinds of pest, let us come to those who are more numerous and live in common—that is, those whom we have said are called Coenobites.

Their first rule of association is to obey their superiors and to do whatever they command. They are divided into groups of ten and one hundred, so that one man presides over nine. Again, the hundredth has ten superiors under him. They remain apart in separate cells [Note: [Col. 0419] Someone may prefer Victorius’s reading, *with joined cells* rather than *with separated cells*; but a little earlier he also said *in divided cells*.].

Until the ninth hour, as the rule prescribes, no one goes to another, except the deans whom we have mentioned, so that if someone happens to be troubled by his thoughts, the dean may console him by speaking with him. After the ninth hour they all come together; psalms resound, and the Scriptures are recited as usual. When the prayers have been completed and everyone has taken his seat, the one whom they call the Father begins to give an exhortation.

While he speaks, such silence prevails that no one dares look at another or even clear his throat. The praise of the speaker is expressed in the tears of his hearers. Tears silently roll down their faces, and their grief does not even break into sobs. But when he begins to proclaim the coming kingdom of Christ, future blessedness, and glory, you may see everyone, with restrained sighs and eyes lifted toward heaven, saying within himself: “Who will give me wings like a dove, and I shall fly away and be at rest?” (Ps. 54:7).

After this the assembly is dismissed, and each group of ten goes with its superior to the tables, where they take turns serving each week. There is no noise during the meal; no one speaks while eating. They live on bread, legumes, and vegetables seasoned only with salt [Note: [Col. 0420] Most manuscripts read: “seasoned with salt and oil.” Immediately afterward, the manuscripts and the Roman edition read “with the little ones,” in place of the earlier reading “and with the little ones.”].

Only the old men receive wine. They often eat with the children, so that the weariness of the older may be supported and the beginnings of the younger may not be broken. Then they rise together, and after singing a hymn return to their cells. There each man speaks with his companions until evening, saying: “Did you see this man and that one? How much grace is in him! How great his silence! How restrained his walk!”

If they see someone ill, they console him; if someone is fervent in the love of God, they encourage him to pursue his devotion. And because each man keeps vigil at night in his own cell, apart from the public prayers, they go around to the individual cells and, putting their ears to them, carefully investigate what the occupants are doing. If they discover someone slower than the rest, they do not rebuke him. Concealing what they know, they visit him more frequently; beginning the practice themselves, they invite him to pray more rather than compel him.

The work of the day is fixed. Once it has been handed over to the dean, it is taken to the steward, who himself renders an account each month to the Father of all, with great trembling. When the food has been prepared, he tastes it first. And since no one is permitted to say, “I do not have a tunic, a cloak, or a mat woven from rushes,” he regulates everything in such a way [Note: [Col. 0420] All editions before Martianaeus are faulty in reading: “no one has what he requests,” or “no one does not have what he requests”; the latter reading is also more common in the manuscripts. The word *dehabere*, though barbarous, was formerly used to mean “to have less,” as numerous examples show.], that no one lacks what he requests and no one has too little.

If someone begins to fall ill, he is transferred to a larger chamber and cared for so attentively by the old men that he neither longs for the luxuries of cities nor seeks a mother’s affection. On Sundays they devote themselves only to prayer and readings; and they do the same at all times after their daily tasks have been completed. Every day something is learned from the Scriptures.

The fast of the entire year is uniform, except during Lent, when a stricter way of life alone is permitted [Note: [Col. 0420] The Reatinus translator reads, “From Easter to Pentecost”; several manuscripts support this reading.]. From Pentecost onward, suppers are changed into midday meals, both to satisfy ecclesiastical tradition [Col. 0421] and to prevent the stomach from being burdened with a doubled quantity of food.

Philo, an imitator of Platonic speech, and Josephus, the Greek Livy, report such men among the Essenes in the second history of the Jewish captivity [Note: [Col. 0421] Some manuscripts and older editions corruptly read, “he reports that we ought to be,” as Abelard also formerly read it, *Theologia Christiana* II. Philo wrote about the Essenes in his book *That Every Good Man Is Free* (ὅτι πᾶς σπουδαῖος ἐλεύθερος). The passage of Josephus to which Jerome alludes is *The Jewish War* II.8.].

### 36

But since, while writing now about virgins, I have discussed monks at almost unnecessary length, I shall come to the third kind, whom they call Anchorites. When they leave the coenobia, they take nothing more into the deserts except bread and salt.

Paul was the founder of this way of life, Antony its embellisher; and, going back to earlier times, its chief was John the Baptist. The prophet Jeremiah likewise describes such a man, saying:

> “It is good for a man when he has borne the yoke from his youth. He will sit alone and remain silent, because he has taken the yoke upon himself; he will offer his cheek to the one who strikes him; he will be filled with reproaches, because the Lord will not reject him forever” (Lam. 27 and following).

At another time, if you wish, I shall explain their labor and their way of life in the flesh but not according to the flesh. Now let me return to my subject, since in discussing greed I had come to the monks. Setting their examples before you, I do not mean gold and silver and other riches, but that, despising earth itself and heaven and joined to Christ, you will sing: “The Lord is my portion.”

### 37

Although the Apostle commands us to pray always, and for the saints even sleep itself is prayer, we should nevertheless have fixed hours for prayer, so that if we happen to be detained by some task, the appointed time itself may remind us of our duty.

There is no one who does not know the third, sixth, and ninth hours, as well as dawn and evening. No food should be taken without prayer preceding it; no one should rise from the table without giving thanks to the Creator. At night we must rise two or three times and turn over in our minds what we have memorized from the Scriptures.

When we leave our lodging, prayer should arm us; when we return from the street, prayer should meet us before we sit down. The little body should not rest before the soul has been nourished. In every action and every movement, let the hand draw the cross of the Lord.

Do not slander anyone, and do not place a stumbling block before the son of your mother. Who are you to judge another’s servant? “He stands or falls before his own master. And he will stand, for the Lord is able to make him stand” (Rom. 14:4).

Nor, if you have fasted for two or three days, should you think yourself better than those who do not fast. You fast and become angry; he eats and puts on a cheerful face. You digest the distress of your mind and the hunger of your stomach by quarreling [another reading: “you expose them”]; he is nourished more moderately and gives thanks to God.

Hence Isaiah cries out daily: “I have not chosen such a fast, says the Lord” (Isa. 58:5). And again:

> “On your fasting days your own desires are found, and you goad all those who are under your power. You fast amid lawsuits and disputes, and strike the humble with your fists” (ibid. v. 3).

Why do you fast for me? What sort of fast can that be whose anger is occupied not merely through the night, but lasts through the entire moon?  Considering yourself, do not glory in another’s ruin, but in your own work.

### 38. Examples of the wicked; the examples of the better are to be followed

Do not set before yourself the example of those women who, while caring for the flesh, calculate the income from their possessions and the daily expenses of their households. The eleven Apostles were not shattered by Judas’s betrayal; nor, when Phygelus and Alexander suffered shipwreck, did the others cease from the course of faith [Note: [Col. 0422] Victorius preferred *Philetus*. But since both Phygelus and Philetus are said in the second Epistle to Timothy to have fallen away from the faith, I did not wish to alter the reading that had long prevailed and is supported by the manuscripts.].

Nor say: “This woman or that enjoys her property; she is honored by human beings; brothers and sisters gather around her.” Did she therefore cease to be a virgin? First, it is doubtful whether such a woman is a virgin at all. “For God does not see as a human being sees. A human being looks at the face, but God looks at the heart” (1 Kings 16). Moreover, even if she is a virgin in body, I do not know whether she is a virgin in spirit. The Apostle defined a virgin in this way: “That she may be holy in body and spirit” (1 Cor. 7:34).

At the end of the matter, let her have her own glory. Let her overcome Paul’s judgment, enjoy her pleasures, and live. Let us follow the examples of those who are better.

Set before yourself blessed Mary, who possessed such purity that she was found worthy to be the Mother of the Lord. When the angel Gabriel descended to her in the form of a man and said, “Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you” (Luke 1:28), she was terrified and overwhelmed and could not answer. For she had never been greeted by a man. Finally she learned the message and spoke. She who had feared a human being conversed fearlessly with an angel.

You too can be the Mother of the Lord. Take for yourself a great, new scroll and write on it with the stylus of a human being: “Quickly seize the spoil.” After you have approached the prophetess, conceived in your womb, and given birth to a son, say [Note: [Col. 0422] Many manuscripts add: “in your heart.” A little farther below, for the reading which we have emended from the manuscripts after Victorius, Martianaeus and Erasmus had *that one* instead of *the one whom*, and so forth.]:

> “Because of your fear, O Lord, we conceived, and we were in labor, and we gave birth to the spirit of your salvation, which we brought forth upon the earth” (Isa. 26).

Then your son too will answer you and say: “Behold my mother and my brothers” (Mark 3:34).

And, wonderfully, the one whom you had shortly before described in the breadth of your breast, whom you had inscribed with the stylus in the newness of your heart, after he has recovered the spoil from his enemies, after he has stripped the principalities and powers and nailed them to the cross, grows from conception and, having become greater, begins to have you as his bride rather than as his mother.

A GREAT LABOR—but a great reward—to be what the martyrs are, what the Apostles are, what Christ is.

All these things are beneficial when they are done within the Church: when we celebrate Easter in one house; when we enter the Ark with Noah; when, as Jericho perishes, Rahab the prostitute, herself justified, shelters us.

But virgins such as are said to exist among various heresies, and among the most impure Manichaean, are to be considered prostitutes, not virgins. For if the devil is the creator of their bodies, how can they honor the work formed by their enemy? [Col. 0423] But because they know that the name “virgin” is glorious, they conceal wolves under sheep’s skins. Antichrist pretends to be Christ, and they dress the shamefulness of their life in the false honor of a name.

Rejoice, sister; rejoice, daughter; rejoice, my virgin; because what other women merely pretend to be, you have truly begun to be.

### 39

All these things that we have set forth will seem harsh to the woman who does not love Christ. But she who has regarded all the pomp of the world as refuse, and has considered everything under the sun vain in order to gain Christ; she who has died with her Lord, risen with him, and crucified the flesh with its vices and desires, will freely proclaim:

> “Who will separate us from the love of God [another reading: of Christ]? Shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword?”

And again:

> “I am certain that neither death nor life, neither angels nor principalities nor powers, neither things present nor things to come, neither strength nor height nor depth nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Rom. 8:35 and following).

The Son of God became the Son of man for our salvation [Note: [Col. 0423] The Benedictine editor reads “ten”; all other Vulgate editions and our manuscript codices, as we have published them, read “nine.” Nevertheless, elsewhere we know that not only Jerome but also other ancient writers count ten months as the period during which infants are carried in the womb. Baluzius cites more than twenty authors in support of this view in his notes on Cyprian’s Epistle to Fortunatus; we could produce many more who count only nine.]. He waits nine months in the womb to be born, endures nausea, comes forth bloodied, is wrapped in swaddling clothes, and is soothed by caresses [another reading: mocked]; and he who holds the world in the hollow of his hand is confined within the narrowness of a manger.

I say nothing of the fact that until he was thirty years old he remained obscure, content with the poverty of his parents. He is beaten and remains silent; he is crucified and prays for those crucifying him.

> “What, then, shall I repay the Lord for all that he has repaid me? I will take the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord. Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Ps. 115:4–6).

This is the only WORTHY REPAYMENT: when blood is compensated with blood, and we who have been redeemed by the blood of Christ willingly die for our Redeemer.

Which saint has been crowned without a struggle? Righteous Abel is killed; Abraham is placed in danger of losing his wife. And lest I extend this into an immeasurable volume, seek and you will find that each one endured adversity.

Solomon alone lived in pleasures, and perhaps for that reason he fell. “For whom the Lord loves, he reproves [another reading: scourges]; and he chastises every son whom he accepts” (Prov. 3:12).

Is it not better to fight for a short time, carry the rampart, take up arms, grow weary beneath the cuirass, and afterward rejoice as the victor, than through the impatience of a single hour to serve forever? [Note: [Col. 0423] The Cistercian copy has *to fight, to strike, to surround the rampart with arms, to challenge*, and so forth.]

### 40

Nothing is hard for those who love; no labor is difficult for one who desires. Consider how much Jacob endured for Rachel, the wife he had been promised.

> “And Jacob served,” says Scripture, “for Rachel seven years. And they seemed to him like a few days, because he loved her” (Gen. 29:20 [Col. 0424]).

Hence he himself later recalls: “By day I was burned by heat, and by night by frost” (Gen. 31:40) [Note: [Col. 0424] The same manuscript reads, “later he recalls.” After the words “By day …,” and a little farther below, after Paul’s words “but hope does not disappoint,” it adds, “because the love of God has been poured into our hearts”; this is also found in the older editions.].

Let us also love Christ and continually seek his embraces. Then every difficulty will seem easy; we shall regard everything that is long as brief; and wounded by his arrow, we shall say at every moment:

> “Woe is me, for my sojourning has been prolonged” (Ps. 119:2).

“For the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Rom. 8:18), “because tribulation produces endurance, endurance produces testing, and testing produces hope; but hope does not disappoint” (ibid. 5:3–4).

When what you endure seems burdensome, read Paul’s Second Epistle to the Corinthians:

> “In labors exceedingly; in prisons more abundantly; in blows beyond measure; in deaths often. From the Jews I received five times forty less one. Three times I was beaten with rods; once I was stoned; three times I suffered shipwreck; I spent a night and a day in the depths of the sea. In journeys often, in dangers from rivers, dangers from robbers, dangers from my own people, dangers from the Gentiles, dangers in the city, dangers in the wilderness, dangers at sea, dangers among false brothers; in labor, in hardship, in many vigils, in hunger and thirst, in very frequent fasts, in cold and nakedness” (2 Cor. 11).

Which of us can claim even the smallest portion of these virtues for himself? Because of them he later said confidently:

> “I have completed the course; I have kept the faith. There remains for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the just judge, will repay me on that day” (2 Tim. 4:7–8).

If the food is rather tasteless, we grieve; and when we drink wine diluted with more water, we think we are offering God some benefit [Note: [Col. 0424] The Cistercian copy again reads, “when we drink water.”]. The cup is broken, the table overturned; blows resound, and slightly warmer water is avenged with blood.

> “The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matt. 11:12).

Unless you do violence to yourself, you will not seize the kingdom of heaven. Unless you knock persistently, you will not receive the bread of the Sacrament.

Does it not seem to you violence when the flesh desires to become what God is, and ascends to the place from which the angels fell, intending to judge angels?

### 41. The reward of virgins and chastity

Come out, I beg you, for a little while from your prison, and paint before your eyes the reward of your present labor—what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and what has not entered the human heart.

What will that day be like, when Mary, the Mother of the Lord, accompanied by choirs of virgins, comes to meet you? When, after the Red Sea, Pharaoh and his army having been drowned, Mary the sister of Aaron, holding a tambourine in her hand [Note: [Col. 0424] These words are absent from the Victorian edition: “Mary the sister of Aaron in her hand,” so that this clause too may be referred to the Mother of the Lord.], leads the response:

> “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously exalted; horse and rider he has thrown into the sea” (Exod. 15:1).

Then Thecla will fly joyfully into your embrace. Then the bridegroom himself will come to meet you and say:

> “Arise, come, my near one, my beautiful one, my dove, for behold, winter has passed, the rain has gone away” (Song 1:10–11).

Then the angels too will marvel and say:

> “Who is this who looks forth [another reading: goes forth] like the dawn, beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun?” (ibid. 6:9).

Daughters will see you and praise you; queens and concubines will proclaim you.

From there another choir of chastity will come to meet you: Sarah will come with the married women; Anna, the daughter of Phanuel, with the widows. Your mothers will be present in different groups of flesh and spirit. The one will rejoice that she gave birth to you; the other will exult that she taught you.

Then truly the Lord will mount the donkey and enter the heavenly Jerusalem. Then the little children of whom the Savior speaks through Isaiah—“Behold, I and the children whom God has given me” (Isa. 8:18)—will raise the palms of victory and sing with one voice:

> “Hosanna in the highest! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord; hosanna in the highest!” (John 12:13).

Then the one hundred forty-four thousand will stand before the throne and the elders, holding harps, and they will sing a new song. No one will be able to sing that song except the appointed number.

> “These are they who have not defiled themselves with women, for they remained virgins. These are they who follow the Lamb wherever he goes” (Rev. 14:4).

Whenever the empty ambition of the world delights you, whenever you see something glorious in the world, pass over in your mind to paradise. Begin to be what you are going to be, and you will hear your bridegroom say to you [Note: [Col. 0425] The Roman edition of this epistle reads *signaculum* (“seal”) instead of *umbraculum* (“shade”), and so do both the Vulgate and the Septuagint.]:

> “Place me as a shade over your heart, as a seal upon your arm” (Song 8:6).

Then, protected in body and mind alike, you will cry out and say:

> “Many waters could not extinguish love, and rivers will not cover it” (ibid. v. 7).

## Epistle XXIII [Note: [Col. 0425] Elsewhere numbered 24. Written in the same year as the preceding letter.]

### To Marcella: On the death of Lea

He compares the death of the most devout woman Lea with the death of the consul designate who had died at about the same time, showing what a difference there is between the deaths of saints and of pagans.

### 1

When, at about the third hour of the present day, we had begun reading Psalm 72—that is, the beginning of the third book—and were compelled to explain that part of its title belonged to the end of the second book and part to the beginning of the third, namely, that “The hymns of David, son of Jesse, have come to an end” was the conclusion of the earlier book, while “A psalm of Asaph” was the beginning of the next; and when we had reached the passage where the righteous man says, “If I said, I will speak thus, behold, I would betray the generation of your children” (Ps. 72:15)—which is not expressed in this way in our Latin manuscripts—suddenly we were told that the most holy Lea had departed from the body.

There I saw you turn so pale that truly there is scarcely any soul, or perhaps none, which, when it bursts from its clay vessel, does not emerge in grief. You were not grieving because you were uncertain about her future, but because you had not paid the sad tribute owed at her funeral. Finally, in the midst of our conversation [*colloquies*], we learned again that her remains had already been carried to Ostia.

### 2

You may ask what this repetition has to do with the matter. I shall answer you in the words of the Apostle: “Very much in every way.” First, because she ought to be accompanied by the joy of all, since, having trampled upon the devil, she has already received the crown of security. Second, so that her life may be briefly explained. Third, so that we may show that the consul designate, taking off his own slippers [another reading: ages], is in Tartarus [Note: [Col. 0426] This was Vettius Agorius Praetextatus, as an old inscription teaches. He was urban prefect under the consuls Valentinian II and Valens II, as Marcellinus writes; then, as praetorian prefect under Theodosius, he died after being designated consul for the following year.].

Who could praise the way of life of our Lea with worthy eloquence? She was so wholly converted to the Lord that she became head of a monastery and mother of virgins; after the softness of fine clothing, she wore her limbs down in sackcloth; she passed sleepless nights in prayer; and she taught her companions more by example than by words.

She possessed such great and submissive humility that she, who had once been mistress of many, was thought to be the servant of all [another reading: of one man]—except that she was all the more Christ’s servant precisely because she was not thought to be mistress of human beings. Her clothing was unadorned, her food poor, her head neglected; yet in everything she did she avoided display, lest she receive her reward in the present age.

### 3

Now, therefore, she enjoys eternal blessedness in return for a brief labor. She is welcomed by choirs of angels, cherished in Abraham’s bosom, and, together with the once-poor Lazarus, sees the rich man in purple—and not a consul clothed in palms, but one clothed in black—seeking a drop from the tip of a little finger.

What a great change in circumstances! The man whom, only a few days earlier, the summits of every dignity preceded; who, as though he were celebrating a triumph over conquered enemies, ascended the citadel of the Capitol; whom the Roman people received with applause and rejoicing; at whose death the entire city was shaken—now lies desolate and naked, confined not in the milky palace of heaven, as his unhappy wife claims [Note: [Col. 0426] Praetextatus’s wife was Paullina, chief priestess of Ceres, as appears from an ancient inscription reported by Smetius. She falsely claimed that her husband’s soul dwelt in the milky palace of heaven, since pagans placed the abode of those enrolled among the gods in the Milky Way, or road of immortality, and assigned them palaces there.], but in filthy darkness.

But she whom the solitude of a single room enclosed, who seemed poor and insignificant, whose life was thought madness, follows Christ and says: “Whatever we have heard, we have also seen in the city of our God” (Ps. 47:9), and the rest.

### 4

Therefore I warn you, and, weeping and lamenting, solemnly urge you: while we run the course of this world, let us not be clothed in two tunics—that is, in a double faith. Let us not be weighed down by the skins of shoes, namely, by dead works. Let not the purse of riches press us down to the earth. Let us not seek the help of the rod—that is, of secular power. Let us not wish to possess both Christ and the world at the same time. Instead, let eternal things replace what is brief and passing; and although each day we are already dying beforehand (I speak according to the body), let us not regard ourselves as permanent in other matters, so that we may be eternal.

## Epistle XXIV [Note: [Col. 0427] Elsewhere numbered 15. Written two days after the preceding letter.]

### To the same Marcella: On the praises of Asella

He praises to Marcella the virgin Asella, who lived in Rome with the utmost holiness, leading a solitary life as though in the desert; Marcella had heard of her sanctity.

### 1

Let no one criticize the fact that in letters we sometimes praise people and sometimes censure them, since reproving evils is a correction for others, while praising the best rouses the good to pursue virtue.

The day before yesterday we had said something about Lea of blessed memory. Immediately it pricked my conscience, and I remembered that we ought not to remain silent about a virgin when we have spoken of the second rank of chastity.

Accordingly, the life of our Asella must be briefly explained. I beg you not to read this letter to her, for she is burdened by her own praises. Rather, deign to read it to young women, so that, modeling themselves on her example, they may regard her way of life as a standard of perfection.

### 2

I pass over the fact that she was blessed in her mother’s womb before she was born; and that, in a flask of shining glass, purer than any mirror, she was delivered as a virgin to her father in a dream. I pass over the fact that, still wrapped in the swaddling clothes of infancy and scarcely past her tenth year [Note: [Col. 0427] Understand this as a private consecration, not a solemn one; there are other such examples among the ancients. For the third Council of Carthage, canon 4, prohibited the consecration of virgins before the age of twenty-five. Later Pope Leo I extended this period, in the ancient Pontifical, up to the age of forty.], she was consecrated in honor of the blessedness that awaited her.

Let everything that preceded her labor be attributed to grace—although God, foreknowing the future, sanctified Jeremiah in the womb, made John leap in his mother’s womb, and separated Paul for the Gospel of his Son before the foundation of the world.

### 3

I come to those things which, after her twelfth year, she chose, seized, held, began, and completed by her own sweat. Confined within the narrowness of a single cell, she enjoyed the breadth of paradise. The same ground served both as the place of her prayer and as the place of her rest.

She regarded fasting as a game and hunger as refreshment. And when not desire for eating but human weakness drew her to food, bread, salt, and cold water aroused her hunger more than they extinguished it.

And because I have almost forgotten what I ought to have said at the beginning: when she first undertook this way of life, she sold, without her parents’ knowledge, the gold chain around her neck, which the common people call a *murenula* [Note: [Col. 0427] Some manuscripts more correctly omit *indeed*. A *murenula* was so called because, with the metal spread into rods, a chain of a winding pattern was woven, resembling the fish called the *murena*. Anastasius, in his account of Gregory IV, mentions a *murena* on which thirteen hyacinth-colored gems hung, as well as “prasinian necklaces” and a three-stranded *murena*, and so forth.]. She then put on a dark tunic which she could not obtain from her mother, and, with this pious act of commerce as her auspicious beginning, suddenly consecrated herself to the Lord, so that all her relatives might understand that nothing else could be extorted from one who had already condemned the world in her clothing.

### 4

But, as we had begun to say, she always conducted herself with such moderation and guarded herself within the privacy of her chamber that she never set foot in public and never knew the conversation of a man. And what is even more remarkable, she loved her virgin sister rather than seeing her.

She worked with her own hands, knowing that it is written: “If anyone does not work, neither should he eat” (2 Thess. 3:10). She spoke with her Bridegroom either in prayer or in psalmody. She hastened almost unseen to the thresholds of the martyrs.

Although she rejoiced in her chosen way of life, she rejoiced more intensely in the fact that no one knew her. And although throughout the entire year she nourished herself by constant fasting, remaining in this state for two or three days at a time, during Lent she spread the sails of her vessel and joined almost all the weeks together with a cheerful face.

What may perhaps be impossible for human beings to believe, but is possible through God’s help, is that she reached the age of fifty without suffering stomach pain, without injury to her entrails, without the dry ground breaking her prostrate limbs, and without her skin, roughened by sackcloth, contracting any foul odor or dirt. Sound in body and sounder in soul, she considered solitude a delight and found a monks’ desert in the tumultuous city.

### 5

You know these things better, since we learned a few of them from you, and since your eyes saw the hard calluses on her knees, like those of camels, in that holy little body from frequent prayer.

We explain what we are able to know. Nothing was more delightful than her severity; nothing more severe than her delight; nothing sadder than her sweetness; nothing sweeter than her sadness.

Her face was so pale that, although it indicated self-restraint, it did not give off the odor of display. Her speech was silent, and her silence spoke. Her walk was neither hurried nor slow. Her manner was always the same. Her cleanliness was neglected, and her clothing unadorned [Note: [Col. 0428] Formerly the reading was “unadorned clothing”; Martianaeus also incorrectly used two words, “in unadorned clothing.” It is tedious to dwell on such matters, which we often correct without troubling the reader.], yet her very dress was a form of adornment without adornment.

By the simple consistency of her life she earned this: in a city of pomp, licentiousness, and pleasures—where humility is regarded as misery—the good praised her, and the wicked did not dare slander her. Let widows imitate her, virgins honor her, married women respect her, the guilty fear her, and priests admire her.

## Epistle XXV [Note: [Col. 0428] Elsewhere numbered 136. Written in the same year, 384.]

### To the same Marcella: On the ten Names of God

He explains to Marcella, who had requested it of him, the ten names by which God is called among the Hebrews.

Reading the ninetieth Psalm, at the passage where [Col. 0429] it is written, “[The one] who dwells in the help of the Most High will abide under the protection of the God of heaven” [Ps. 90:1], I had said that among the Hebrews, instead of “God of heaven,” *SADDAI* was written, which Aquila interprets as ἱκανὸν (*hikanon*), “sufficient,” which we may understand as “strong and sufficient for accomplishing everything.” This is one of the ten Names by which God is called among the Hebrews.

[Note: The old copy belonging to the Queen has: “Aquila interprets IKANON AMANOY,” which we would read as ἱκανὸν οὐρανοῦ, “sufficient of heaven”; for I suspect that this is Aquila’s complete reading. Formerly, in Victor and Erasmus, it was incorrectly printed as ἅλκιμον, “mighty,” and Erasmus too was unjustly of the opinion that this letter was a fragment from some commentary on the Psalms.]

At once you most earnestly requested that I set out for you all the Names together with their interpretations. I shall do what you asked.

The first Name of God is **EL**, which the Seventy translate as “God,” while Aquila, expressing its etymology, interprets it as ἰσχυρόν (*ischyron*), that is, “strong.”

Next are **ELOIM** and **ELOE**, which likewise are called “God.”

[Note: The older printed editions of Erasmus and Victor incorrectly read these in Hebrew letters; Drusius rightly corrects them.]

The fourth is **SABAOTH**, which the Seventy translated as “of powers,” and Aquila as “of armies.”

The fifth is **ELION**, which we call “Most High.”

The sixth is **ESER IEJE**, which is read in Exodus: “He who is, sent me” [Exod. 3:14].

[Note: I think our manuscripts more correctly read, with the aspiration, HIEIE, by which the characteristic of the future tense of the letter aleph is indicated. The Royal parchment omits the word *Eser*.]

The seventh is **ADONAI**, which we generally call “Lord.”

The eighth is **IA**, which is used only of God; its final syllable is also heard in **ALLELUIA**.

The ninth is **τετράγραμμον** (*tetragrammon*), “four-lettered,” which they thought to be ἀνεκφώνητον (*anekphonēton*), that is, “unutterable.” It is written with these letters: JOD, HE, VAV, HE. Some, not understanding this and misled by the similarity of the characters, customarily read **ΠΙΠΙ** when they encountered it in Greek books.

[Note: In the Greek fragment of the Anonymous writer on the Ten Names of God that we have just mentioned, the name ΠΙΠΙ is also discussed. In this passage John Nicolai writes in his book *On Abbreviations*, p. 283: “We think that this must be explained either because the name of God was represented among the Samaritans by two Jods, which seemed very close in shape to the Greek ΠΠ; or because words were used by the Greeks in backward reading and writing, from which ΠΙΠΙ could easily have arisen; or because the Copts and Egyptians designated God by an article. Since ΠΙ is an Egyptian article, it could have happened that ΠΙΠΙ represented something like ὁ ὁ, just as among the Hebrews it is frequently represented by *per* [reading uncertain].”

“The word ΠΙΠΙ in this Fragment is a clear indication that it is of venerable antiquity. For that word occurs only in Origen, Jerome, and in that excellent Paris manuscript in which the Prophets are contained according to the version of the Seventy. In the margin of that manuscript Stephen Le Moyne found the word ΠΙΠΙ, with great satisfaction, in his *Dissertation on Jeremiah* 23:5; see there for more details. [Col. 0430] The error found in the editions of Erasmus and Victor is that they interpret the passage contrary to the text of Ezekiel 10:5: φωνὴ θεοῦ Σαδδαὶ, “the voice of God Saddai.” On this passage consult the commentaries of our Jerome.”]

The tenth is **SADDAI**, mentioned above; in Ezekiel it is left untranslated.

[Note: Some manuscripts have “uninterpreted,” from which the reading arose easily.]

We must also know that **ELOIM** is a common-number form: both one God and several gods are called by it. In the same way heaven is called both “heaven” and “heavens,” that is, **SANAIM**.

[Col. 0430] Hence translators too often vary. We have an example of this in our own language: Athens, Thebes, Salona.

## LETTER XXVI

[Note: Elsewhere numbered 102. Written shortly after the preceding letter.]

### TO THE SAME MARCELLA: On Certain Names

He explains why certain Hebrew names have remained without interpretation in translations of Scripture and what they mean.

1. Recently, when we were together, you did not ask me by letter, as you had formerly been accustomed to do, but in person you yourself asked what those words, which we have not rendered from Hebrew into Latin, mean in their own language, and why they have been placed without interpretation—for example, **Alleluia, Amen, Maran atha, Ephod**, and the other expressions scattered throughout Scripture that you mentioned.

2. To this I reply briefly, since the constraints of dictation press upon me. Whether the Seventy Translators or the Apostles took care to preserve these words, the reason was that the first Church had been gathered from the Jews, and they wished to introduce nothing that might scandalize believers: they transmitted them just as they had received them from the beginning.

[Note: The same manuscript omits the words “so that they might hand on what they had absorbed from the beginning.” A little later it reads *delatus* rather than *dilatatus*, and this is not incorrect.]

Afterward, when the preaching of the Gospel had spread among all nations, what had once been accepted could no longer be changed. Origen also maintains in his books, which he calls ἐξηγητικοί (*exēgētikoi*), “exegetical,” that because of the vernacular idiom of each language, such words cannot sound among other peoples as they did among their own people; and that it is much better to leave them untranslated than to weaken their force through interpretation.

3. Accordingly, **ALLELUIA** is rendered “Praise the Lord.” For **JA** is one of the ten Names of God among the Hebrews. In the Psalm where we read, “Praise the Lord, for the Psalm is good” [Ps. 146:1], the Hebrew reads: **ALLELUIA CHI TOB ZAMMER**.

[Note: The same manuscript has *zamer* with a single *m*. Perhaps this was found in Jerome’s exemplar; certainly we have found no manuscript containing an *m* in which *zimra* or *zamera* is read, as in the Hebrew text of today. Yet the same orthographic analogy by which *Sel* is written for *Sela* above and elsewhere is found in all the manuscripts. Eusebius’s Commentary on Psalm 104 should be consulted, especially these words: τὸ μὲν ἀλληλοῦ, αἶνος νοεῖται, ὅς εἰς θεὸν τὴν ἀναφορὰν ἔχει, τὸ δὲ ἴα ἕν τῶν ἑρμηνευτικῶν τῆς θείας ἐστὶν ὄνομα: “The one part, *allelu*, is understood as praise, which has reference to God; the other, *Ia*, is one of the interpretive names of the divine nature.” The word *allelu* means “praise,” which is directed toward God; *Ia* itself is one of the Names by which the divine nature is signified.]

**AMEN**, however, Aquila renders as πεπιστωμένως (*pepistōmenōs*), which we may say means “faithfully.”

[Note: We have restored this reading from most printed editions and manuscripts; Martianus has *dictum*. Immediately afterward, the Royal manuscript has *amuna* instead of *Amen*. Since this word means “faith,” a better sense can be obtained by changing the punctuation and deriving the adverb from the noun for faith, namely *amuna*, which is how it is said in Hebrew. In any event, I do not approve of repeating the word *Amen* here. As for the division of the Psalter into five books according to the Hebrews, recall the note above on Letter 23 to Marcella.]

4. The Septuagint renders it γένοιτο (*genoito*), that is, “may it be.” Hence at the end of the books—for among the Hebrews the Psalter is divided into five volumes—they translated **Amen Amen** as “may it be, may it be”: for in Hebrew **AMEN AMEN** is written, by which what has been said above is confirmed as true. Hence Paul too asserts that no one can respond “Amen,” that is, confirm what has been preached, unless he has understood the preaching.

**MARANATHA** is more Syriac than Hebrew, although, because the two languages are adjacent, it also has something Hebrew about its sound. It is interpreted, “Our Lord has come,” so that the sense is: “If anyone does not love the Lord Jesus Christ, let him be accursed” [1 Cor. 16:22]; and, once this has been completed, the words “Our Lord has come” are added afterward. It would be pointless to persist in hatred against one whose coming is already established.

5. I should also like to write something to you about the **Diapsalm**, which is written among the Hebrews as **SELA**; and about the **Ephod**, and about the phrase found in the title of a certain Psalm, **PRO AIELETH**, and other matters of this kind—unless I exceeded the proper limits of a letter and thereby gave you greater reason to ask questions by delaying the answers.

[Note: We prefer the reading of the Royal manuscript, *deberem facere quaestionis*, “I should give you cause for inquiry”; but we have not altered the text.]

For the proverb is familiar: “Goods offered freely become worthless.” Therefore we deliberately keep silent about what ought to be said, so that you may be more eager to hear what has been left unsaid.

## LETTER XXVII

[Note: Elsewhere numbered 120. Written shortly after the preceding letter.]

### TO THE SAME MARCELLA

He responds to those who reproached him for changing certain readings already established from the New Testament and for criticizing the association of virgins with men.

1. All the words of Scripture are divinely inspired. The corruption of the Latin manuscripts must be traced back to the Greek source.—After the preceding letter, in which I had touched briefly upon Hebrew words, it was suddenly reported to me that certain little men were eagerly slandering me because, contrary to the authority of the ancients and the opinion of the whole world, I had attempted to correct certain passages in the Gospels.

Although I could rightly disregard them—for a lyre sings uselessly to an ass—nevertheless, lest they accuse us of arrogance, as they are accustomed to do, let them have this answer: I was not so dull of heart, nor so rustic in ignorance—for they regard that alone as holiness, asserting that they are disciples of fishermen, as though they were holy for knowing nothing—as to think that anything in the Lord’s words should be corrected or was not divinely inspired. Rather, I wished to restore the corruption of the Latin manuscripts, which is demonstrated by the diversity of all the books, to the Greek source from which they themselves do not deny that they were translated.

If they dislike the water of the purest spring, let them drink muddy streams; and let them discard, when reading Scripture, the diligence with which they know the forests of birds and the whirlpools of shellfish. In this matter let them be so simple as to regard Christ’s words as rustic, although for so many centuries the minds of so many people have labored over them, so that they have guessed at the force of each word more than they have expressed it. Let them accuse the Apostle of ignorance, since he is said to have gone mad because of his many writings.

2. I know that when you read this you will wrinkle your brow and fear once again that my freedom may become a seedbed of quarrels; and, if possible, you will want to restrain my mouth with your finger, lest I dare to say what others are not ashamed to do.

I ask: What have we said so freely? Have I described idols engraved upon plates? Have I ever, amid Christian banquets, entangled virginal eyes in the embraces of Bacchants and Satyrs? Has my speech ever assailed anyone with excessive bitterness? Have we ever grieved that beggars became rich? Have I ever criticized hereditary tombs?

I, poor man, said only that virgins ought more often to be with women than with men, and I offended the eyes of the entire city; everyone points the finger at me. “Those who hate me without cause are more numerous than the hairs of my head, and I have become a byword to them” [Ps. 119]. And you think I am going to say anything further?

3. But, lest Flaccus laugh at us—“The amphora began to be formed; why does the jar emerge while the wheel is turning?” [Horace, *Art of Poetry*]—let us return to our two-legged little asses and sound a trumpet in their ears rather than a lyre.

[Note: Most manuscripts read *divertamur*, “let us turn aside,” and shortly afterward *concrepemus*, “let us rattle or clang.”]

Let them read, “rejoicing in hope, serving the season” [Rom. 12:12 and 11]; let us read, “rejoicing in hope, serving the Lord.” Let them think that an accusation against a presbyter ought by no means to be received; let us read, “Do not receive an accusation against a presbyter except on the evidence of two or three witnesses; those who sin, rebuke before all” [1 Tim. 5:19].

[Note: Hilary the Deacon, who is also called Ambrosiaster, does not know this condition concerning two or three witnesses; nor does Jerome himself read it elsewhere, nor Primasius, Oecumenius, or Cyprian. Some think that these words were falsely inserted into Paul’s text; others think that they were erased from ancient books as superfluous. As for the other reading, “serving the season,” it is known to many of the Fathers, although the reading “serving the Lord” is rejected and preferred. The variation arose from the Greek manuscripts: in some, because of the similarity of the letters, there was τῷ καιρῷ, “the season,” while in others there was τῷ κυρίῳ, “the Lord”; and several of the oldest Latin manuscripts likewise vary.]

Let them approve, “A human saying, and worthy of all acceptance”; let us, with the Greeks—that is, with the Apostle, who spoke Greek—make our mistake: “A faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptance.”

Finally, let them rejoice in Gallic **cantherii**.

[Note: A *cantherius* is a gelded horse. Varro and Cato derive the etymology from the removal of its seed. Plautus also mentions Gallic *cantherii* in the *Aulularia*; there is also an epigram of Claudian on Gallic mules, and another by Ennodius against Claudian on the same subject. This does not, however, adequately establish that Jerome intended by these words to identify his detractor’s homeland, as some have thought. Martianus reports that certain manuscripts prefer the gloss, “for he was a Gaul who had criticized the translation.” Nor is any follower of Montanus necessarily indicated by these words, as the Benedictine editor thinks; rather, he refers to certain ignorant men who, because they ignorantly slandered him, he calls “great asses.” For κανθήλιος (*kanthēlios*) means “a very large ass,” and hence some would prefer *cantheliis* to *cantheriis*. Certainly, in Jonah 4 he writes: “A certain Cantherius”—or *Canthellius*—“of the very ancient family of the Cornelii, or, as he himself boasts, descended from Asinius Pollio, is said to have accused me at Rome some time ago of sacrilege because I translated ‘ivy’ instead of ‘gourd.’ We shall have more to say about this in its proper place.”]

Let us be pleased by that little ass of Zechariah, freed from bonds and prepared for the service of the Savior, who, after offering his back to the Lord, began to echo Isaiah’s prophecy: “Blessed is the one who sows beside every water, where the ox and the ass tread” [Isa. 32 according to the Seventy].

## LETTER XXVIII

[Note: Elsewhere numbered 138. Written at the same time as the preceding letter.]

### TO THE SAME MARCELLA: On the Word “Diapsalm”

He explains what *Sela*, or *Diapsalm*, is; then he reproduces Origen’s letter word for word in Latin, so that Marcella may learn more fully what Origen thought about the question under discussion.

1. What you have received must be returned with interest, and a strong delay produces usury. You had asked for my opinion concerning the Diapsalm. We excused ourselves on the grounds of the letter’s brevity and pretended that the matter could not be explained in writing.

[Note: We have followed the reading of the Benedictine editor, based on the Cluniac and Saint-Cyran manuscripts, with the support of two of our own. The word signifies one who exacts a work, and Jerome uses it elsewhere. Formerly, but incorrectly, the text read: “What benefit is there in keeping silent with my greater …”]

But what good does it do to my taskmaster, ἐργοδιώκτης (*ergodiōktēs*)? Your desire is stirred up more by silence. Therefore, so that I do not delay you longer, accept a few things in place of many.

2. Some have said that the Diapsalm is a change of meter; others, a pause for breath; still others, the beginning of another sense. There are those who think it is a division of rhythm; and because at that time the Psalms were sung in connected vocal performance to the accompaniment of an instrument, they suppose that it indicates a certain musical variation or silence.

[Note: These two words, “they suppose silence,” are absent from the Royal manuscript. It reads *varietates* rather than *varietatis*, “variations” rather than “variation”; the sense is complete, though not better.]

None of this seems correct to us, since Aquila, who is the most careful interpreter of the Hebrew words, always translated **SELA**, that is, *Diapsalm*, written with Samekh, Lamed, and He, and since we find *Diapsalm* placed even at the end of Psalms.

Thus in the third Psalm: “You have broken the teeth of sinners; salvation belongs to the Lord, and your blessing is upon your people, *sela*,” that is, “always.”

And in the twenty-third Psalm: “Who is this King of glory? The Lord of powers—he is the King of glory, always.”

On the other hand, it is entirely absent from Psalms containing many verses, namely the thirty-sixth, the seventy-seventh, and the one hundred eighteenth.

Again, the ninth Psalm is divided by the Song of the Diapsalm, although, if the Diapsalm is, as some think, the beginning of silence, a Song of Silence cannot exist.

[Note: We have restored this passage from the manuscripts, especially the Royal manuscript. It had hitherto been corrupt and defective in all printed editions, which read with an incomplete sense: “although, as some think, the Diapsalm cannot be an indication of silence.” In fact, since the same word for “silence” would occur twice, the ancient copyist was mistaken. He also errs elsewhere, writing *sicut* for *si ut*, and *indicium* for *initium*.]

3. From this we observe that the word connects what comes before with what follows, or at least teaches that what has been said is everlasting.

Thus in the third Psalm: “Many say to my soul, ‘There is no salvation for him in his God,’ always.”

And again: “With my voice I cried to the Lord, and he heard me from his holy mountain, always.”

And in the fourth: “Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood? always.”

[Note: All the editions print this incorrectly and elsewhere, since this is a verse of the same Psalm, with one verse intervening after the preceding one.]

And again: “What you say in your hearts, and in your beds you are pierced, always.”

And in Habakkuk: “God will come from the south, and the Holy One from Mount Paran, always.”

And below: “The oaths to the tribes which you spoke, always” [Hab. 3].

4. We must know that among the Hebrews, at the end of books, one of three words is customarily appended: either **AMEN**, or **SELA**, or **SALOM**, which means “peace.” Hence Solomon is called “peaceful.”

Just as we customarily place *Explicit*, or *Feliciter*, or something of that kind between completed works, to mark the transition to another work, so the Hebrews too customarily add such words to confirm what has been written. They say **AMEN**, or “forever,” or, to indicate what is to be written, they place **SELA**; or they declare that the work has ended successfully, writing “peace” at the end.

[Note: This sentence was badly corrupted in all earlier editions, partly through punctuation and partly through scribal error. We have repaired it in a way that, to speak frankly, depends more on our own judgment than on the manuscripts. In the manuscripts the words *aut*, *ut*, and *et*, on which the entire force of the meaning depends, have been confused through the negligence of ancient copyists. The subject itself, however, requires the reading as we have printed it. Formerly the passage read: “They customarily do this, so that they may say ‘Amen,’ or ‘forever’; or they mention what is to be written, so that they may place *Sela*, or …” The Royal book has: “and they mention what has been written and what is to be written.”]

5. We have tasted these things from the innermost fountain of the Hebrews, not following the trickling streams of opinions, nor frightened by the variety of errors with which the whole world is filled, but desiring both to know and to teach what is true.

If it is not burdensome to you, I shall interpret word for word what Origen thought about the Diapsalm, so that, since you despise new wine, you may at least be guided by the authority of old wine.

6. [Note: We thought it appropriate to append here this letter of Origen, which Montfaucon first published in the *Hexapla*, since Jerome professes to interpret it word for word. The Royal book mentioned above reads: “Often inquiring …”]

“Having often inquired into the reasons why the Diapsalm is inserted in certain Psalms, I observed the matter most carefully in the Hebrew and compared it with the Greek. I discovered that wherever the Hebrew language has **SELA**, while the Greek has *always* or something of that kind, there the Seventy, Theodotion, and Symmachus translated *Diapsalm*.

Nor is it difficult to confirm what we say by examples. In the seventy-fourth Psalm, whose beginning is, ‘We will give thanks to you, O God, we will give thanks and call upon your name,’ after the words, ‘I confirmed its pillars,’ the Seventy, Theodotion, and Symmachus have *Diapsalm*.

[Note: Some manuscripts add a second occurrence of *tibi*, “to you,” in accordance with Origen’s reading.]

[Col. 0435] Aquila has instead, ‘I weighed its pillars, always.’

[Note: The printed editions add *et*, “and,” but the sense and the Greek text reject it.]

“In the Fifth Edition: ‘I am the one who prepared its pillars, always.’ In the Sixth: ‘I made its pillars firm continually.’

[Note: Some manuscripts have *constitui*, “I established,” instead. The Greek had corruptly printed ἐσταθμίσαμεν, which we corrected to ἐσταθμισάμην. Again, before the verb ἠτοίμασα, “I prepared,” the article ὁ may perhaps have dropped out; thus the phrase would mean, “the one who prepared.” In the Latin Royal manuscripts the reading is: “I am the one who confirmed.”]

“In Hebrew, after **AMUDA**, which means ‘its pillars,’ there is **SELA**.

“Again, in the seventy-fifth Psalm, whose beginning is, ‘God is known in Judea,’ we find in the Seventy and Theodotion, after ‘shield and sword and war,’ *Diapsalm*. In Symmachus, after ‘shield and sword and war,’ likewise *Diapsalm*.

[Note: Erasmus has “instead of which, Aquila.”]

“In Aquila: after ‘shield and sword and war,’ ‘always.’ In the Fifth Edition: after ‘shield and sword and war,’ ‘always.’ In the Sixth: after ‘shield and sword and war,’ ‘to the end.’

“In Hebrew, after **UMALAMA**, which means ‘and war,’ there was **SELA**.

[Note: Here too the old editions corruptly read *Umilhama*. They also read the following Hebrew word as *Aneve erez*, according to the modern Masoretic text, whereas the Hebrew word following it is *Anie ares*, and Origen, and evidently Jerome after him, seem to have read it so. The two expressions are often confused in the sacred text: one means “in a condition of humility,” the other “humble in spirit and meek.” Finally, for *Ares* Origen has ἄρς (*ars*), which I do not reject, just as I do not reject *Sel* for *Sela*, a form that, in accordance with the Greek σέλ, most of the better manuscripts consistently have above and below.]

“And in the same Psalm, after the passage, ‘that he may save the meek of the earth,’ there is *Diapsalm*. Symmachus likewise has *Diapsalm*, and Aquila has *always*, as does the Fifth Edition. In the Sixth, however, it has ‘to the end.’ In Hebrew, after **ANIE ARES**, which means ‘the meek of the earth,’ there was **SELA**.

“And so, when we had discovered the view of each Edition, we recorded these things. Whether those who interpreted *Diapsalm* understood it as a change in a certain musical song or of rhythm, or whether they understood something else, I leave to your judgment.”

[Note: The Royal manuscripts read, “whether they sensed something else, or what they understood.” Below, the old editions wrongly prefer *peritiam*, “skill,” to *imperitiam*, “lack of skill”; Erasmus nevertheless preferred *prudentem imperitiam*, “wise ignorance.”]

7. Thus far Origen. In this discussion alone, we preferred to follow his lack of knowledge rather than possess the foolish knowledge of those who do not know.

## LETTER XXIX

[Note: Elsewhere numbered 130. Written at the same time as the preceding letter.]

### TO THE SAME MARCELLA: On the Ephod and the Theraphim

In response to Marcella’s request that he explain what **Ephod Bad** means in the First Book of Kings, he also adds what **Theraphim** signifies in the Book of Judges.

1. It is the duty of a letter to write something about household affairs or daily conversation, and in a certain sense to make absent people present to one another, while they mutually report what they want or what has happened; although sometimes this banquet of conversation is seasoned with the salt of instruction as well.

But you, while wholly occupied with treatises, write nothing to me except what torments me and compels me to read Scripture. Indeed, yesterday, after proposing a highly celebrated question, you asked me to write back immediately with my opinion. As though I held the chair of the Pharisees, so that whenever there is a dispute about Hebrew words I must be summoned as judge and arbitrator of the litigation.

[Note: Victor and Martianus, relying on corrupt manuscripts, have “letters are not pleasant when they do not please and smell of …” The sense, as anyone who pays attention will see, is either nonexistent or expressed in sheer empty babbling. We have restored to the text, on the authority of a single Veronese manuscript, the genuine reading that Erasmus had conjectured from traces of ancient copies and that Victor approves. That manuscript reads not *Epulae*, “banquets,” as the other printed books do, but *Epistolae*, “letters,” which gives a more coherent sense: he is saying that letters dealing with Hebrew words are unpleasant, not with cakes, the seasonings of Apicius, and the “masters” of his time whom he properly attacks in these words. Hence Erasmus does not seem to have conjectured very successfully that *magirorum*, “cooks,” should perhaps be read instead of *magistrorum*, “masters.” Nevertheless, *epulae* is not unacceptable, since it was almost an axiom of gluttonous people that banquets were more agreeable when prepared like pastries. See the London edition of the *Observationes in Laertium*, p. 144.]

“Letters are not pleasant when they do not smell of cake, when Apicius does not season them, and when nothing in them smokes of the culinary arts of the masters of our time.”

But because the carrier and messenger of our conversation is hurrying back, I shall state a great matter more quickly than I possess it: **although, in disputing about the holy Scriptures, words are not so necessary as meaning**.

If you seek eloquence, read Demosthenes or Cicero; if divine mysteries, examine our manuscripts, which do not sound correctly when translated from Hebrew into Latin.

2. At the beginning of your letter you had written: “What does it mean that in the First Book of Kings it is written: ‘And the boy Samuel served before the presence of the Lord, girded with an Ephod bad, and he had a little robe, which his mother had made for him; and she brought it to him from days to days when she went up with her husband to sacrifice the sacrifice of the days’” [1 Reg. 2:8–9].

Thus you ask what **EPHOD BAD** is, with which the future Prophet is girded: whether it is a belt, or, as some think, a censer, or some kind of garment. And if it is a garment, how is he girded with it? And after *Ephod*, why is *bad* added to it?

You also write that you have read the following: “A man of God came to Eli and said to him: ‘Thus says the Lord: I plainly revealed myself to the house of your father, from all the tribes of Israel, when they were in the land of Egypt serving in the house of Pharaoh. And I chose the house of your father from all the tribes of Israel for myself as a priesthood, so that they might go up to my altar, burn incense, and carry the Ephod’” [1 Reg. 2:27–28].

Proceeding through the whole order of the book, you also took an example from the passage in which Doeg the Edomite killed the priests at the king’s command: “And Doeg the Syrian turned and himself slew the priests of the Lord; and he killed on that day three hundred and five men” [1 Reg. 22:18–19]—or, as it is read in Hebrew, eighty-five—“all who carried the Ephod. And he struck Nob, the city of the priests, with the edge of the sword, from man to woman, from child to nursing infant, and ox and ass and sheep, with the edge of the sword. And one son of Ahimelech son of Ahitub escaped; his name was Abiathar, and he fled after David.”

[Note: Just as the Greek copies of the Seventy vary among themselves and from the Hebrew, so do Jerome’s manuscripts. Some, through an old error, have *Abimelech*; others have *Ahimelech* or *Achimelech*, following the Hebrew.]

3. I cannot refrain from anticipating the order of the problem with my answer, concerning the passage where we now read, “And all who carried the Ephod” [1 Reg. 22].

[Note: The Greek text, and consequently the Latin translation, read only *Ephod* and ἐφούδ, not *bad* as the Hebrew does. Jerome indicates that the main argument of his answer is drawn from this comparison of the texts. It is therefore clear with what careless error, and at the cost of the meaning, the Benedictine edition omitted the words “in Hebrew it has: carrying the Ephod, to which *bad* is joined.” We have restored them from other manuscripts and editions.]

In Hebrew it has “carrying the Ephod bad.” Why I have said this you will learn in what follows.

You also added what follows: “And it happened, when Abiathar son of Abimelech fled to David, that he himself went down with David to Keilah, having the Ephod in his hand; and it was reported to Saul that David had come to Keilah” [1 Reg. 23:6 and following]. When the king’s arrival and the siege of the city were feared, David said to Abiathar: “Bring the Lord’s Ephod.”

These are the passages you excerpted from the Book of Kings. Then you moved to the Book of Judges, where Micah of Mount Ephraim is said to have returned to his mother the eleven hundred shekels of silver that she had vowed; and she made from it a carved image and a molten image.

You add that shortly afterward these are called **Ephod** and **Teraphim**, although, if the Ephod is a belt or a kind of garment, it cannot be a carved or molten image.

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “If it is a belt, it cannot be a garment or a kind of garment,” omitting the intervening words.]

I recognize the error of nearly all the Latins, who thought that the Ephod and Teraphim mentioned afterward had been cast from the silver that Micah had given his mother. Scripture reports the matter as follows:

“And his mother”—clearly Micah’s mother—“took the silver and gave it to the founder, and he made it into a carved image and a molten image. And it was in the house of Micah; and the man Micah had a house of God. And he made an Ephod and Teraphim, and filled the hand of one of his sons, and he became his priest” [Judg. 17:4–5].

[Note: The sense is that Micah consecrated himself and his household to that carved idol. Victor, however, preferred to read, on the basis of the Roman copy of the Seventy, “which was in the house of Micah,” and “the house of Micah was the house of his god.” On this matter the Benedictine editor rebukes him sufficiently.]

If you think that what was previously called a carved and molten image is afterward called Ephod and Teraphim, learn that they are not the same things.

For after his mother’s idol, which is called a carved and molten image, Micah made an Ephod and Teraphim, as is demonstrated by what follows:

“And the five men who had gone to inspect the land answered and said to their brothers: ‘Do you know that in these houses there are an Ephod and Teraphim and a carved and molten image?’” [Judg. 18:14 and following].

And after many things that you omitted in between:

[Note: Ducaeus insists that a certain manuscript at Agen has a more suitable reading: “We omit these things,” so that it appears that Jerome, not Marcella, is the one doing the omitting.]

“And the five men went up, and they burst in there, and took the carved and molten image, the Ephod, and the Teraphim. And the six hundred men who were girded with weapons of war entered the house of Micah and took the carved and molten image, the Ephod, and the Teraphim” [Judg. 18:17–18].

[Note: Victor; from this passage the opinions of the others are refuted. Among the editors there is a major dispute over whether the reading should be *indissolubilem*, “indissoluble,” with Erasmus, or, in the contrary sense, *dissolubilem*, “soluble,” as Victor preferred. There are plausible arguments on both sides; nevertheless, more manuscripts support *dissolubilem*. But whichever way one reads it, and whatever reasoning those who interpreted the Ephod as a silver vessel used—whether to resolve the question or to make it indissoluble—it makes no difference to the discussion.]

Thus he refutes the opinion of those who, in order to make the question indissoluble, thought the Ephod was made of silver.

Notice briefly that it is never mentioned except in connection with the priesthood. Samuel, who is reported to have been girded with it, was a Levite, and the priests of Nob also wore it as the insignia of their dignity.

[Note: Erasmus had read: “and the priests of Nob wore *bad*, that is, the insignia of their dignity.” Victor and Martianus correct him.]

And—something that is not found in the Latin manuscripts—when David, fleeing from Saul, came to Ahimelech and asked for a sword, saying, “See whether you have at hand a spear or a sword, for I did not take my sword or my equipment in my hand,” the priest answered: “Behold, the sword of Goliath the Philistine, whom you struck in the Valley of the Terebinth; here it is, wrapped in a garment behind the Ephod in the sanctuary” [1 Reg. 21:8–9].

Thus the Ephod was kept in storage.

This too, which we have now quoted, where a carved and molten image is mentioned, although it is an idol, nevertheless, because religion was mistakenly thought to reside in it, an Ephod and Teraphim were made for its veneration, just as for the service—or, according to another reading, the mystery—of God.

### 4. What the Theraphim Is

If there is enough time for dictation, we shall discuss what the Theraphim is. For the moment, however, we must explain the Ephod, as we began to do. In Exodus, where Moses is commanded to order the making of the priestly garments, we read after the other items:

> “And these are the garments which they shall make: the breastpiece, and the shoulder-piece, and tunics [*kosymbōtas*], and the turban, and the sash” (Exod. 28:4).

[Note: The same manuscript has: “and the shoulder-piece and the robe, and tunics.” Thus Exod. 28:31 in the Septuagint: *hypodytēn podērē*, “the ankle-length robe.”]

[Note: This signifies a fringed garment; the Vulgate has “a linen garment tightly drawn.”]

Where we have placed *superhumerale* (“shoulder-piece”), the Greek translators rendered it *epōmis* (ἐπωμίς), evidently because this kind of garment comes over the shoulders. Then it is added:

> “And they shall take gold, violet, scarlet, purple, and fine linen, and make the shoulder-piece of twisted fine linen, a work of varied weaving.”

Why say more? The whole book of Exodus is filled with descriptions of this kind of clothing. For at the end of the same book it is written:

> “And every skillful worker among those engaged in the work made the garments of the sanctuary, which belong to Aaron the priest, as the Lord commanded Moses. And they made the shoulder-piece of gold, violet, purple, scarlet, and twisted fine linen” (Exod. 39:1–2).

But since Exodus merely commands that this kind of garment be made, and afterward reports that it was made, without yet stating that Aaron wore it, Leviticus explains how he was clothed in the priestly garments:

> “And Moses brought Aaron and his sons near, and washed them with water, and clothed him in a tunic, and girded him with a belt, and clothed him in an under-tunic”—

[Note: Martianaeus, following the Alexandrian copy of the Septuagint and certain Hieronymian manuscripts, reads *ependytēn* (ἐπενδύτην); the other manuscripts and printed books, which we follow, read *hypodytēn* (ὑποδύτην), which may properly be translated “undergarment,” or “under-tunic.” The older printed editions have *hypendytēn* (ὑπενδύτην), with no difference in meaning.]

which we may translate as “the under-tunic,” or “the tunic with which he was clothed underneath.”

> “And he placed the shoulder-piece upon him,” it says, “and girded him according to the workmanship of the shoulder-piece, and fastened it upon him” (Lev. 8:6–7).

You therefore see that Aaron was girded with this shoulder-piece, just as Samuel was girded with that Ephod *bad*, whatever it was. But, lest I delay you too long, hold to this conclusion: wherever in the Septuagint translators—that is, in our manuscripts—*epōmis* (ἐπωμίς), that is, “shoulder-piece,” is read, the Hebrew has *Ephod*. Why they wished to translate it in some places and leave it untranslated in others is not for me to judge, since they did the same in many instances: after expressing the same things in different ways in different places, finally, wearied by the variety of translation, they set down the very Hebrew words.

[Note: Alternatively, “left untranslated.” I think Hieronymus says this concerning *ephod* in Judges 8:27 and 17:5, as well as *ephod bad* in 1 Kings 21, or, as it appears through an old textual corruption, *ephod bar*. When he adds that the Septuagint translated it differently in different places, he means *epōmis*, *stolē*, and once *hierateia* in Hosea 3.]

[Note: This passage, which incompetent copyists of old—and especially critics—had disfigured with various interpolations, was restored by Martianaeus from fifteen manuscripts, including our two. Consult his note at the end of the book.]

Aquila, however, called what they called *hypodytēn* and *epōmida* (ὑποδύτην and ἐπωμίδα) *enduma* and *ependuma* (ἔνδυμα and ἐπένδυμα), that is, “garment” and “outer garment.” For the *enduma*, which in Hebrew is called *mail*, signifies the lower tunic, whereas the *ependuma*, that is, the *epōmis*, which in Hebrew is called *Ephod*, signifies the upper cloak with which the entire priestly array is covered.

### 5. The Meaning of *Bad*

Perhaps you will ask: if the Ephod is a priestly cloak, why is *bar* added in certain passages? When I hear *bar*, I cannot keep from laughing. For since the Hebrew says *bad*, it is clear that the Septuagint translators themselves translated it in that way. The reading *bar* in place of *bad* arose through error.

[Note: This is an old error, found widely among other ancient writers; even Aquila’s rigid precision did not avoid it, for he translated it *ependuma exaireton* (ἐπένδυμα ἐξαίρετον), “a special outer garment.”]

In the Hebrew language, *bad* means “linen,” although linen is expressed more precisely by *phestha*. Finally, where we read:

> “And make for them linen undergarments, to cover the shame of their nakedness, from their loins to their thighs” (Exod. 28:42),

the Hebrew has *bad* for “linen.”

The man who is shown to Daniel was dressed in this material:

> “I lifted up my eyes and saw, and behold, one man clothed in *baddim*” (Dan. 10:5),

by which plural form linen garments are designated.

Samuel and the eighty-five priestly men are therefore said to have worn a linen Ephod because only the high priest had permission to wear an Ephod that was not linen, but—as Scripture records—woven with gold, violet, purple, scarlet, and fine linen. The others had an Ephod not distinguished by that variety, nor adorned with the twelve stones that rested upon each shoulder, but linen, simple, and perfectly white in its entire brightness.

### 6. The Meaning of the Theraphim

But since I had promised above that, if there were enough time for dictation, I would also discuss the Theraphim briefly—and since no interrupter has appeared in the meantime—know that Aquila translates *Theraphim* as *morphōmata* (μορφώματα), which we may call “figures” or “representations.”

In that passage where Saul sent messengers to seize David, and they reported that he was seriously ill, he sent them again, saying:

> “Bring him to me in the bed, so that I may kill him.”

The messengers came, and behold, there were cenotaphs in the bed (1 Sam. 19:15). In place of *cenotaphia*, the Hebrew has *Theraphim*, that is, *morphōmata*.

[Note: The Benedictine editor rejected the true reading to the margin of the book and inserted into the text the false reading “a goat’s liver,” which had also appeared in other printed editions. Yet it is certain that the Septuagint translated *ēpar tōn aigōn* (ἧπαρ τῶν αἰγῶν), “a goat’s liver,” and that this is the error of the Latin manuscripts which Hieronymus notes. In our view this happened because, through a very common error, they repeatedly took *daleth* for *resh*, and because they thought that what means “liver” was written where the word for a cushion or mattress of goats’ wool should have stood.]

It was not, therefore, “a goat’s liver,” as our manuscripts have it, but a little cushion sewn from goatskin, whose unshorn hair, wrapped around it as a head, would make it pretend to be a person lying in a bed.

To explain the truth of both languages equally, in Hosea God threatens that he will remove every favor from the adulterous people, saying:

> “For many days the children of Israel shall sit without a king and without a prince, without sacrifice, without altar, without priesthood, and without manifestations” (Hos. 3:4).

[Note: The Benedictine edition again errs, substituting “without the Law” for “without a king.”]

For “priesthood and manifestations,” the Hebrew has “without Ephod and without Theraphim,” as Theodotion and Symmachus translated it. From this we understand that *Ephod*, according also to the Septuagint, who translated the sense rather than the words, is to be interpreted as “priesthood”; whereas in *Theraphim*, that is, “representations” or “figures,” we are to understand the various works that are called Theraphim.

[Note: Ducaeus wishes *varia opera* to be understood from two manuscripts, deleting “which are called Theraphim” and restoring “which are called.” This is certainly more coherent.]

For in Exodus and elsewhere, where garments woven by the embroiderer’s art are described, the work is said to have been made as *opus Cherubim*, that is, varied and depicted work. Yet the word *Cherubim* does not contain the letter *vau*, because wherever it is written with that letter it signifies animals more than works.

[Note: See the passage in Ezekiel where the name *Cherub* denotes an ox or calf, chapter 10, verse 1. There, exactly as we read it, *vau* is present: “the face of a Cherub,” although today copies as accurate in other respects as Hieronymus observed are no longer extant. See also what we shall note in the letter to Paulinus on the study of Scripture.
