You will scarcely, if at all, find among lexicographers the meaning by which *Cherubim* is interpreted as “varied and depicted.” Yet in my judgment this is its primary meaning, from which all the others—and *Cherubim* itself as *morphōmata*—are derived: these were figures composed of several forms, a man, an eagle, a lion, and an ox, with the last of these nevertheless predominating.]

Accordingly, in this sense Micah too is shown to have made Theraphim, together with a priestly garment and the other things belonging to priestly adornment.

### 7. The Priesthood and Its Garments

How I wish I could now explain to you the entire priestly attire and, through each kind of garment, disclose the divine mysteries. But since in this very matter we have exceeded the brevity appropriate to a letter, and since Josephus and Philo, the most learned men among the Jews, as well as many of our own writers, have treated the subject at great length—

[Note: Josephus pursued this subject in *Antiquities* 3.7, and Philo in *The Life of Moses*. The writings of the Latin Fathers, which he says belonged to many authors, have not survived. Hieronymus later fulfilled this wish in his letter to Fabiola.]

[Note: “You will hear me pursuing the matter in person, as they say, with living voice, and thereafter, if you wish, in person,” and so forth, from the Agen manuscript; we do not approve this reading.]

—you will hear from me in person whatever else you wish to ask, as a present questioner, so that, if by chance we do not know something, it may die in a trusted ear without witness or judge.

[Note: The following words, “If our common mother is well, I rejoice, and I pray the Lord that she may be well”—understand Albina—are absent from several manuscripts and printed books.]

If our common mother is well, I rejoice, and I pray the Lord that she may be well. As you know, we have been detained by the reading of the Hebrews, and have allowed rust to gather over our Latin tongue, to such an extent that even when we speak, a certain non-Latin screech intrudes. Therefore forgive my dryness. “And if I am unskilled in speech,” says the Apostle, “yet not in knowledge.” He possessed both, and humbly disclaimed one. We lack both, because we have lost even what, as boys, we possessed for applause, nor have we attained the knowledge we desired—like the dog in Aesop’s fable, who, while pursuing greater things, lost even the smaller ones.

## LETTER XXX

[Note: Alternatively numbered 155. Written in the same year as the preceding letters.]

### TO PAULA  
### On the Hebrew Alphabet of Psalm 118

He teaches the holy Paula the etymologies and interpretations of the Hebrew letters, and briefly explains how great the divine mysteries are contained in the combination of these same elements.

### 1

The day before yesterday, when I was attempting to introduce you to Psalm 118 and saying that the entire moral subject was contained in it, and that, just as philosophers customarily divide their discussions into Physics, Ethics, and Logic, so the divine utterances either discuss nature—as in Genesis and Ecclesiastes—or morals—as in Proverbs and throughout the books in scattered form—or Logic, for which our writers claim the *Theoricen*, as in the Song of Songs and the Gospels (although the Apostle often proposes, assumes, confirms, and concludes matters that properly belong to the dialectical art)—you earnestly sought to know what the Hebrew letters meant that seemed to be inserted into the Psalm we were reading.

[Note: We learned from Origen himself, in the homilies on the Song of Songs that we have assigned to volume 10, how this passage should be read. There the translator says: “There are three general disciplines by which one arrives at knowledge of things, which the Greeks called Ethics, Physics, and *Theorice*; we may call them Moral, Natural, and Contemplative. Some among the Greeks also placed Logic, which we may call Rational, as a fourth.” Martianaeus therefore acted without sufficient judgment when he substituted “Theology” for *Theorice*, the genuine ancient reading that was current and which we restore. This is the error of a superficial corrector, although it has crept into most manuscripts. In this matter Henricus Valesius also errs, claiming that Hieronymus’s books read the Greek *theologia*. No one is unaware that *Theorice*, or the contemplative faculty, consists solely in contemplation and inspection. Origen says more clearly that it is the contemplative faculty by which, having risen above visible things, we contemplate something divine and heavenly and behold it with the mind alone. See this same correction in the Letter to Algasius, Question 10, and in the Commentary on Ecclesiastes, and elsewhere.]

### 2

I replied that it was composed according to the order of the letters: namely, eight verses began with the first letter, which among them is called *Aleph*. Again, the same number of verses began with the following letter, *Beth*; afterward the same number was completed with *Gemel*; and so on, all the way to *Thau*, which is their final letter. Thus the Psalm was written, and from each individual element what follows must be understood according to their interpretations.

Again and again you demanded that I tell you the interpretations of each letter. I did so, I confess; but because, on account of the barbarism of the language, memory loses everything we have said, you desire a little commentary to be made, so that, if you should stumble in anything, reading may console your forgetfulness.

### 3. The Four Alphabetical Psalms

Before I discuss each one individually, you should know that four Psalms begin according to the order of the Hebrew letters: Psalm 110, Psalm 111, the one about which we are now writing—Psalm 118—and Psalm 144.

[Note: The Ambrosian manuscript places Psalm 36 here, as does an old edition of 1496. It is rightly absent from the other editions and manuscripts, since it exceeds the defined number of four. Hieronymus himself, both elsewhere and especially in the *Galeatian Prologue*, also counts a fifth: “The Psalms, too—Psalm 36, Psalm 110, Psalm 111, Psalm 118, and Psalm 144—although written in different meters, are woven according to the same alphabet. More must be said about this in order to reconcile the holy Doctor’s statements with one another, as will also be the place for discussing the Hebrew verses, which he compares with Latin and Greek meter.”]

You should know, however, that in the earlier Psalms individual verses, consisting of iambic trimeter, are attached to each letter.

[Note: The Regius manuscript has “verses, which are known to be attached in iambic meter, as is the Song of Deuteronomy,” and so forth.]

The later Psalms, on the other hand, consist of iambic tetrameter, just as the Song of Deuteronomy was written. In Psalm 118, eight verses follow each letter. In Psalm 144, two verses are assigned to each letter.

[Note: We restore the word “two,” which the sense and the subject themselves require, from the Ambrosian manuscript and an old edition. To understand that this has been done correctly, compare Psalm 144 with the preceding Psalms 110 and 111 in the Hebrew text.]

Some think that other Psalms also begin in this order, but their opinion is false.

In the Lamentations of Jeremiah you also have four alphabets. The first two are written almost in Sapphic meter, because a heroic colon concludes the three connected verses that begin with one and the same letter. The third alphabet is written in trimeter, and three verses begin with the same letter. The fourth alphabet resembles the first and second.

The Proverbs of Solomon also close with an alphabet, counted in iambic tetrameter, beginning at the passage where it says:

> “Who can find a strong woman?” (Prov. 31:10).

### 4

Just as with our own letters no one can proceed to read words and weave them together unless he has first begun with the elements, so in the divine Scriptures we cannot know the greater things unless we have made a beginning with Ethics, according to what the Prophet says:

> “From your commandments I gained understanding” (Ps. 118:104),

that is, he began to possess knowledge of hidden things after his works.

But now what you requested must be completed, so that an interpretation appended to each element may convey its meaning.

### 5. The Meanings of the Hebrew Letters

*Aleph* means “teaching.”  
*Beth*, “house.”  
*Gemel*, “fullness.”  
*Deleth*, “tablets.”

[Note: The printed editions have *Daleth*, as they do *Gimel* and several others, following the ingenuity of the Masoretes. We conscientiously follow the testimony of the ancient interpreters and the agreement of our manuscripts. Lexicographers know neither this interpretation of “tablets”—or, as Hieronymus himself explains below, of “books”—nor any meaning of the letter *Deleth* other than “door.” Certain learned men, in order to explain that etymology, bring in the custom of the Hebrews, who tropologically call the first page of a book a “door.” But I think it is clearer than daylight that the Greek name *deltos* (δέλτος), “book” or “tablet,” reveals what force and meaning that word once had in Hebrew as well. Josephus, an ancient Christian author, therefore most correctly interprets *Deleth* as *deltōs* in his *Hypomnesticon*. The rest are as follows: *He*, “this”; *Vau*, “and”; *Zai*, “lives”; *Heth*, “living”; *Caph*, however; *Lamed*, “learn,” and so forth. See Drusius, *On the Hebrew Alphabet*, and John Morin, *Biblical Exercises*, p. 504.]

*He*, “this.”  
*Vau*, “and.”  
*Zai*, “these.”  
*Heth*, “life.”  
*Tet*, “good.”  
*Iod*, “beginning.”  
*Caph*, “hand.”  
*Lamed*, “discipline,” or “heart.”  
*Mem*, “from them.”  
*Nun*, “everlasting.”  
*Samech*, “help.”  
*Ain*, “fountain,” or “eye.”  
*Phe*, “mouth”—understand “from the mouth,” not “from the bone,” so that you are not misled by the ambiguity of the letters.  
*Sade*, “justice.”  
*Coph*, “calling.”  
*Res*, “head.”  
*Sen*, “of teeth.”  
*Thau*, “signs.”

[Note: The Ambrosian manuscript has *Fe*, as do certain ancient witnesses. Hieronymus says in Isaiah, “The Hebrew language does not have the letter P, but uses the Greek PHI in its place.” See also Daniel 11.]

### 6

After the interpretation of the elements, the order of their meaning must be explained.

The first combination is *Aleph*, *Beth*, *Gemel*, *Deleth*: “teaching, house, fullness, tablets”—that is, the teaching of the Church, which is the house of God, is found in the fullness of the divine books.

### 7

The second combination is *He*, *Vau*, *Zai*, *Heth*: “this, and this, life.”

> For what other life can there be without knowledge of the Scriptures, through which Christ himself is also recognized, he who is the life of believers?

### 8

The third combination contains *Tet*, *Iod*: “good beginning.” For although we now know all that has been written, we know only in part and prophesy only in part; and now we see through a mirror, in an enigma. But when we have been deemed worthy to be with Christ and have become like the angels, then the teaching of books will cease, and we shall see face to face the good beginning as it is.

[Note: The words from here to the end of the sentence are absent from most manuscripts.]

### 9

The fourth combination is *Caph*, *Lamed*: “hand, discipline,” or “heart.” Hands are understood in action; heart and discipline are understood in meaning. For we can do nothing unless we first know what must be done.

### 10

The fifth combination is *Mem*, *Nun*, *Samech*: “from them, everlasting, help.” This needs no explanation; it is clearer than any light that eternal aids are supplied from the Scriptures.

### 11

The sixth combination contains *Ain*, *Phe*, *Sade*: “fountain or eye, of the mouth, of justice,” according to what we explained in the third section.

[Note: All the manuscripts have this reading, and there is no doubt that it refers to the third combination; thus the placement under the fourth number in earlier editions is erroneous.]

### 12

The seventh and final combination is—since the number seven itself also contains a mystical meaning—*Coph*, *Res*, *Sen*, *Thau*: “calling, of the head, of teeth, signs.”

Through the teeth articulated speech is produced, and through these signs one reaches the head of all, who is Christ, through whom one comes to the everlasting kingdom.

[Note: Compare the frequently cited *Hypomnesticon* of Josephus, the Christian author, chapter 26, where he sometimes interprets these letters differently and forms somewhat different combinations. See also Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel* 10.5 and 11.6.]

### 13

I ask you: what is more sacred than this sacrament? What pleasure is more delightful than this? What foods, what honeycombs are sweeter than knowing the wisdom of God, entering into his hidden things, contemplating the mind of the Creator, and learning with spiritual wisdom the words of the Lord your God, which are mocked by the wise men of this world?

Let others, if they wish, possess their riches, drink from gems, shine in silk, and delight in the applause of the people; and through various pleasures let them be unable to surpass their wealth. Let our riches be to meditate on the law of the Lord day and night, to knock at the door that is not open, to receive the breads of the Trinity, and, with the Lord going before us, to tread upon the waves of the world.

### 14

Greet Blaesilla and Eustochium, our little novices. Greet Feliciana, truly blessed in the virginity of flesh and spirit.

[Note: Martianaeus has “Felicity,” without consulting the reader.]

Greet the rest of the choir of chastity, and your household Church, for whose safety I fear everything, even what is secure, lest while the master of the house sleeps, the enemy sow weeds over it. Although they may even dare to say:

> “I am a fortified city, a city that is not attacked” (Isa. 27:3, according to the Septuagint).

No one is secure when a hostile army is blockading him. No one is, as blessed Cyprian says, “safe enough while near danger.”

[Note: Saint Cyprian, Letter 4 to Pomponius on virgins: “No one is safe for long who is close to danger.”]

Give our most industrious Marcella the copy of the letter, if she wishes to receive it.

[Note: *Philoponotatē* (φιλοπονοτάτη), that is, “most devoted to labor.”]

And remember me, entreating that our Lord Jesus Christ may soon crush Satan beneath our feet.

## LETTER XXXI

[Note: Alternatively numbered 19. Written in the same year, 384.]

### TO EUSTOCHIUM  
### On Little Gifts

He gives a mystical interpretation, directing toward the formation of character, to certain little gifts that Eustochium sent him on the feast of Saint Peter.

### 1

I have received gifts small in appearance but great in love from the Virgin: bracelets, a letter, and doves. Since honey is not offered in God’s sacrifices, excessive sweetness has been altered by art and seasoned, so to speak, with the austerity of pepper. For nothing pleasurable, nothing merely sweet, pleases God unless it contains within itself something of biting truth. Christ’s Passover is eaten with bitter herbs.

### 2. How the Feast of Blessed Peter Should Be Celebrated

It is a feast day, and the birthday of blessed Peter; it must be made more festive than usual, yet in such a way that playful speech does not depart from the central principle of Scripture, nor do we wander too far from the prescribed arena of our contest.

Jerusalem is adorned with bracelets in Ezekiel.

[Note: Martianaeus, following Erasmus, incorrectly has “armed.”]

Baruch receives letters from Jeremiah. The Holy Spirit comes in the form of a dove (John 1).

Therefore, so that something may bite you—something of pepper—and so that you may remember even now my earlier little book, take care not to abandon the ornaments of your works, which are the true bracelets of the arms; do not tear the letter of your heart, which the profane king cut with a knife after it had been delivered by Baruch; do not, after the likeness of Ephraim, hear through Hosea:

> “You have become foolish, like a dove” (Hos. 7:11).

“You are being excessively harsh,” you will reply, “and this is not suitable for a feast day.” You provoked such gifts by your own gifts: while bitter things are joined with sweet, you will receive from us things of the same kind, and praise will be accompanied by bitterness.

### 3

But lest I seem to have diminished your gifts, we also received a basket filled with cherries, so red and so modestly virginal that I might think they had been brought here by Lucullus.

[Note: Florus relates this in book 3, chapter 5; Plutarch in the *Life of Lucullus*; Pliny in book 15, chapter 25; and others. Tertullian, *Apology Against the Gentiles*: “Lucullus was badly treated, since he was the first to bring cherries from Pontus into Italy.”]

After Pontus and Armenia had been conquered, he was the first to bring this kind of fruit from Cerasus to Rome (Pliny, book 15, chapter 25). The tree therefore took its name from its homeland.

[Note: Some manuscripts have “taken from Cerasus,” which is not an unsuitable reading. That city is properly called Cerasus, or *Kerasous* (κερασοῦς), although, just as Sipus gives Sipuntum and Hydrus gives Hidruntum, it could also be called Cerasuntum.]

Since in Scripture we read of a basket full of figs but do not find cherries, in what has been brought we praise what has not been brought; and we wish you to become one of those fruits that are set against the Temple of God, concerning which God says:

> “Because they are good, very good.”

For the Savior loves nothing intermediate. And just as he does not shrink from the cold but delights in what is hot, so in the Apocalypse he says that he will vomit out the lukewarm (Rev. 3).

We must therefore take the greatest care to celebrate the solemn day not so much with an abundance of food as with spiritual exultation.

> For it is exceedingly absurd to wish to honor with excessive satiety a martyr whom you know pleased God by fasts.

You should always eat in such a way that prayer and reading follow the meal. If this displeases some, sing the Apostle’s words:

> “If I were still trying to please human beings, I would not be Christ’s servant.”

## LETTER XXXII

[Note: Alternatively numbered 74. Written a few days after the two preceding letters.]

### TO MARCELLA

He excuses himself for writing briefly, since he is occupied with comparing Hebrew volumes with Aquila’s translation. He compensates for the brevity of this letter with the two preceding letters sent to Paula and Eustochium, which he sends to Marcella to read.

### 1

There were two reasons why I wrote such a short letter: the letter-carrier was in a hurry, and I, being occupied with another task, did not wish to devote myself to this as though it were a side matter (*parergō*).

You ask what such a great and necessary task could be that it excluded the duty of epistolary conversation. For a long time now I have been comparing Aquila’s edition with the volumes of the Hebrews, lest perhaps the synagogue has altered something out of hatred for Christ. And, to confess the truth to a friend, I find more that tends to strengthen our faith.

Now that I have carefully reviewed the Prophets, Solomon, the Psalter, and the books of the Kingdoms, I am holding Exodus, which they call *Elle Smoth*, and am about to proceed to Leviticus. You see, then, that no duty ought to be placed before this work.

Nevertheless, lest our Currentius perhaps have run in vain, I have appended to this little discourse the two letters that I sent to your sister Paula and to her child Eustochium—

[Note: Namely, the two preceding letters, one addressed to Paula concerning the Hebrew alphabet, the other to Eustochium concerning little gifts.]

—so that, when you read them and find in them something both instructive and graceful, you may think that what was written to them was also written to you.

### 2

I wish our common mother Albina to be well. I speak of her bodily health, for I know that she is well in spirit. I beg you to greet her on my behalf and to refresh her with the double duty of affection, since in one and the same Christian woman both mother and beloved are cherished.

## LETTER XXXIII

[Note: Written around the year 384.]

### TO PAULA  
### A Partial Section

[Note: This letter has been taken here from book 2 of Rufinus’s *Invectives*. Hieronymus himself mentions it in *On Illustrious Men*, under Origen, where he says: “I placed an index of his works, in the volumes of the letters that we wrote to Paula, while comparing it with Varro’s works, in a certain letter against Varro’s works.” The letter itself appears to have been lost for the most part. Saint Isidore also mentions and copies it in *Etymologies* 6.7.]

While comparing an index of Origen’s works with Varro’s works, he shows that the Church of Christ possessed a writer who surpassed all Greeks and Latins even in the multitude of books he published.

### 1. Varro and Chalcenterus, Most Prolific Writers

Antiquity admires Marcus Terentius Varro because among the Latins he wrote an uncountable number of books. The Greeks extol Chalcenterus with marvelous praise because he composed so many books that no one among us could copy them all by hand, even if he were copying the works of others.

[Note: This means Didymus the Alexandrian grammarian, who, because of his indefatigable passion for writing and his constant occupation with books, acquired the name Chalcenterus, “bronze-gutted” or “brazen-breasted.” He is said to have written four thousand books, not one of which has survived to the present day.]

Since it would now be tedious to compile an index of Greek volumes for Latin readers, I shall mention a few things about one who wrote in Latin, so that we may understand that we are sleeping the sleep of Epimenides, and that the zeal they devoted to the education provided by secular writings we devote to accumulating wealth.

### 2

Varro therefore wrote forty-five books of *Antiquities*; four on the life of the Roman people . . . .

### 3. Origen

“Why,” you ask, “has mention been made of Varro and Chalcenterus?” Clearly, so that we may come to Adamantius, our own Chalcenterus, who labored with such zeal in the work of the sacred Scriptures that he rightly received the name Adamantius.

Do you wish to know how many monuments of his genius he left behind? The following title makes it clear.

He wrote thirteen books on Genesis; two books of mystical homilies; excerpts on Exodus; excerpts on Leviticus . . . . . . Also *Monobiblia*; four books *On First Principles* (*Peri Archōn*, Περὶ Ἀρχῶν); two books *On the Resurrection*; and two other dialogues *On the Resurrection* . . . .

[Note: He also enumerates the same number in the following Letter 36 to Damasus, at the end of the first question. Eusebius, however, mentions only twelve books in 6.24, and Suidas, under “Origen,” and Nicephorus in 15.5 follow him. Since we cannot suspect an error in our Hieronymus, who in the passage cited in the letter to Damasus explicitly says that Origen dictated “the twelfth and thirteenth books on Genesis” concerning Cain’s punishment, it may be supposed that in the copy he had before him the twelfth book had been divided into two, one of which was marked as the thirteenth. Apart from the book *On First Principles*, and that indeed in Rufinus’s translation, the other works mentioned here have perished.]

### 4

Do you see that both Greeks and Latins alike have been surpassed by the labor of one man? For who could ever read as much as he himself wrote?

And what payment did he receive for this labor? He was condemned by Demetrius the bishop, except by the priests of Palestine, Arabia, Phoenicia, and Achaia. The city of Rome agreed in his condemnation; it itself convened the senate against him—not because of any novelty in his doctrines, nor because of heresy, as rabid dogs now pretend against him, but because they could not endure the glory of his eloquence and knowledge, and while he spoke everyone else seemed mute.

### 5

You can understand why I have written these things, and dictated them rapidly, though not cautiously, by the little flame of a poor lamp, if you think of the Epicureans and Aristippuses.

[Note: These names are applied satirically to the Roman presbyters who attacked Hieronymus immediately after the death of Damasus.]

## LETTER XXXIV

[Note: Alternatively numbered 141. Written in the same year, 384.]

### TO MARCELLA  
### On Several Passages of Psalm 126

[Note: Consult the later chronological notes to this letter in the Preface.]

He elegantly explains what the “bread of sorrows” is and what the “sons of the cast out” are in Psalm 126, while excusing the holy Hilary because, deceived by the presbyter Heliodorus, he did not properly understand the word “banished.”

1. The blessed martyr Pamphilus, whose life Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, set forth in nearly three volumes [Note: [Col. 0448] That is, complete volumes; for *ferme* here is almost equivalent to “easily,” and we do not approve the opinion of those who infer from the fact that, in the *Catalogue*, Jerome simply says “three books” that the volume was something more than a book in Jerome’s time.]—when he wished to rival Demetrius of Phalerum and Pisistratus in their devotion to the sacred library and to search throughout the whole world for images of intellect, which are true and everlasting monuments—then pursued Origen’s books with especially great diligence and dedicated them to the Caesarean Church. Acacius and Euzoius, priests of that same Church, later attempted to restore part of it, which had been corrupted, on parchment.

Although Pamphilus found much and left us a catalogue of his discoveries, he confessed by not entitling it that he had not found Origen’s commentary on Psalm 126 and his treatise on the letter *Phe* [Note: [Col. 0448] Martianaeus thinks that treatises published by Origen on the letters of the Hebrew alphabet are intended; to us it seems much more likely that the reference is to that portion of the preceding Psalm 118 which is set under *Phe*. For among the ancients each letter was given its own separate treatise, as may be seen in Hilary, Augustine, and others, so that there were, as it were, as many distinct psalms as there are verses beginning with a single letter.]. This was not because such a great man—we mean Adamantius—had passed over anything, but because the negligence of later generations had failed to preserve it down to our own memory.

I have said this so that, since you asked me about the same psalm—what the “bread of sorrows” might be in the words, “It is vain for you to rise before daylight; rise after you have sat down, you who eat the bread of sorrows”—I might show that I have no opinion of Origen’s commentaries on this matter.

2. Accordingly, turning back to the Hebrew, I found that in place of “bread of sorrows” it has written *LEEM AASABIM*, which Aquila translated as ἄρτον τῶν διαπονημάτων, that is, “bread of labors” [Note: [Col. 0448] The old edition has, less correctly, διαπονούντων; and some think that κακοπαθουμένων, “of those suffering hardship,” should be read for Symmachus, though this is not sufficiently accurate.]. Symmachus has ἄρτον κακοπαθούμενον, which means “distressful bread” or “bread of misery.” The Fifth Edition and Theodotion, who elsewhere agrees with the Septuagint translators, have “bread of idols.” The Sixth has πλάνης, that is, “of error.”

Nor is it surprising that Aquila should use *διαπονήματα* for “idols,” since idols are the works of human hands, and the people are prophetically reproved for rising uselessly at dawn to go to the temple and hastening to the sanctuary after resting, while they worship idols with the honor due to God. Thus Ezekiel wrote that the priests sacrificed to idols in the very temple [Col. 0449].

To convince you more fully that “idols” has been placed in the Hebrew where we have “sorrow,” this same word—namely, *ASABIM*—is also written in Psalm 113, and the Septuagint likewise translated it as “idols” [156]. For where we read, “The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of human hands,” the Hebrew has *ASAREEM*, which Aquila interprets as “their labors.” Since the truth is therefore as I have explained, some do not without reason understand the “bread of sorrow” as the mysteries of heretics; others interpret it as the labor of this miserable and wretched life, in which we eat our bread in the sweat of our face, and in which the nourishment of our brief existence grows among thorns and thistles.

3. You also deigned to ask about the same psalm: Who are “the sons of the shaken-out”? I am surprised that you did not read in Hilary’s commentaries that he interprets “the sons of the shaken-out” as peoples of believers. He evidently thought that the Apostles were called by this name, since in the Gospels they were commanded that, if they entered any city and were not received, they should shake the dust from their feet as a testimony concerning those who did not believe (Matt. 10; Mark 6).

You cleverly anticipated the objection that the Apostles cannot be understood under the name “shaken-out,” since “those shaking out” and “those shaken out” are different: those shaking out are the ones who shake something out, while those shaken out are the ones shaken out by others. It would be inappropriate, therefore, to call the Apostles “shaken-out,” since they ought rather to be called “those who shake out.”

What, then, shall I do? I do not dare to criticize so great a man, and one so eloquent in his own time [Note: [Col. 0449] Jerome modestly rejects Hilary’s opinion, or rather assigns the entire fault, if there is any, to Heliodorus. Otherwise, the very learned Benedictine editor of St. Hilary maintains that Hilary was not understood by Jerome because Hilary took “shaken-out” actively from *excussor*, not passively from *excussus*. This is entirely false, as becomes clear to anyone who attends to Hilary’s passage.], who, by the merit of his confession, the rigor of his life, and the brilliance of his eloquence, is celebrated wherever the Roman name is found. The fault should not, however, be attributed to him, for he was ignorant of Hebrew and had only begun to acquire some acquaintance with Greek literature. Rather, it should be attributed to the presbyter Heliodorus, with whom he was closely associated and whom he asked how Origen had expressed matters that he himself could not understand.

Since Heliodorus could not find Origen’s commentary on this psalm, he preferred to suggest his own opinion rather than confess his ignorance. Hilary, having adopted it, explained it in polished language and expounded another’s error with greater eloquence [Note: [Col. 0449] Two of our reliable manuscripts, and others in Martianus, read *et alieno errore disertius excusatus est*, “and he was more eloquently excused for another’s error.”].

157 4. It remains, therefore, that we should return once more to the source of the Hebrew language and see how it is written. Where we have “as the sons of the shaken-out,” it reads *CHEN BNE ANNAURIM*, which Aquila translated, “as the sons of puberty.” Symmachus and Theodotion have, “as the sons of youth.” The Sixth has ἡκόνεος νοῦ, which we may render, “of sharpened understanding” [Note: [Col. 0449] If the reading is more correct and more faithful to the manuscripts, and certainly more harmonious in meaning, Victorius and Drusius read ἠκονηθέντος. Martianaeus made ἀκόνεος from the manuscripts; others again prefer ἐκόνεως. In either form, however, the word signifies not “sharpened” or “made sharp,” as Jerome intends, but “sharpness” itself; and thus “sons of sharpness” would not quite correctly mean “sons of the sharpened.” We have judged that the reading ἠκόνεος ought to be restored, and have extracted it from the manuscripts by a new attempt. Although ΕΚΟΝΕΟΣ is usually pronounced there with the initial letter Ε, that letter has the same sound as Η and is not very different in form; in any event, Α is much closer. Moreover, the Greek word has a far more convenient derivation: the author of this Sixth Version could easily have derived the adjective ἠκονής from the verb ἀκονέω, “to sharpen,” since νεοκονής, “newly sharpened,” is known to have been used by Sophocles and other authors of better Greek.].

From this it is clear that peoples of adolescence are understood as Christians, according to the example in which God is said to stretch out his saints in the manner of a bow and arrows. Thus in the prophet Zechariah: “For I have stretched you out for myself, Judah, like a bow” (Zech. 9:13). And the Savior says of himself: “I have made myself like a chosen arrow; and in his quiver he hid me” (Isa. 49:2).

Finally, in the following verse, except for the Septuagint, who translated it differently, I find the same wording in the Hebrew and in all the editions: “Blessed is the man who has filled his quiver from them,” so that, since he had once taken up a metaphor from arrows, the translation might also preserve it in the reference to the quiver.

Ordinary human speech calls the “shaken-out” vigorous, strong, and ready for action. The Septuagint interpreters themselves, in the book of Ezra, translated the word by “young men.” It is written there: “And it came to pass from that day onward that half of the shaken-out were doing the work, while half of them held spears, shields, bows, and breastplates; and the leaders were behind the whole house of Judah, those building on the wall” (Neh. 4:16).

From this we observe that in the present passage too “shaken-out” has been put for “adolescents” and “young men,” not—as he supposed—for the Apostles, who are said to have been shaken out because of the shaking out of dust from their feet.

I have also read a certain man’s book and found in it an elegant interpretation: that the Jews are called “shaken-out” from the temple, from the law, and from the grace of the Lord, in the sense that they are rejected; and that their sons are the Apostles, born from their stock and held in the hand of the Lord in the likeness of arrows.

5. In the following psalm, Heliodorus also erred more than our Hilary. Concerning the passage in which it is written, “You shall eat the labors of your fruits,” he formed various opinions and asserted that the sense would stand better if one wrote [Note: [Col. 0450] Jerome is therefore not mocking Hilary because he preferred “the labors of fruits” to “the labors of hands,” as the Benedictine editor of Hilary persuades himself. Rather, he is criticizing the fact that either Hilary himself, or more likely Heliodorus, without consulting the Greek text, approved “fruits of labors” instead of “labors of fruits,” and declared that interpretation more coherent. See the *Treatise on Psalm 127*, nos. 4 and 5.]: “someone eats the fruits of labors,” rather than “the labors of fruits.” Hence, he said, a spiritual interpretation ought to be sought.

On this occasion he entered into a lengthy discussion and used as much labor to persuade people of what he wanted them to understand as falsehood always needs in order to appear true. In this passage, however, it was not the Septuagint translators but the Latins, deceived by the ambiguity of the Greek word, who translated καρπούς as “fruits” rather than “hands,” since καρποί can also mean “hands.” The Hebrew has *CHAPHACH* [Col. 0451]. Symmachus and the Fifth Edition translated it, “of your hands,” so as to avoid the ambiguity of the earlier language.

6. While, as they say, the swift hand of a secretary was setting down these words by my dictation in a little nocturnal work stolen from sleep, and while I was thinking of saying more, almost the fourth hour of the night had passed. Suddenly I was roused by certain pangs of an aching stomach and burst into prayer, so that, at least during the remaining hours, if sleep crept upon me, my illness might be frustrated.

## EPISTLE XXXV [Note: [Col. 0451] Elsewhere numbered 124. Written in the year 384.]  
### FROM POPE DAMASUS TO JEROME

Damasus earnestly asks Jerome, whose writings he professes to read with great eagerness, to answer the five questions set forth below from the Old Testament.

**Damasus to his dearest son Jerome.**

1. “I have decided to rouse you, who have been sleeping and for a long time have been reading rather than writing, by sending you these little questions [Note: [Col. 0451] Some manuscripts read *debui*, “I ought.”]. This is not because you ought not to read as well: for speech is nourished and grows fat on this as on daily food. Rather, the fruit of reading lies in writing.

Therefore, since yesterday, when the letter-carrier was sent back to me, you said that you had no letters left except those which you had once dictated in the desert [Note: [Col. 0451] Formerly the reading was “Etherius the letter-carrier,” though we have found it in not a single manuscript. But the Bishop of Rieti, having convinced himself from Baronius’s preconceived opinion for the year 378 that this letter had been sent from Jerusalem by Jerome, strove zealously to defend the fabricated reading.], and which I read and copied with the greatest eagerness [Note: [Col. 0451] The Vatican manuscript reads, “and because you promised”; it also has “of stolen nightly work,” whereas most manuscripts read “in stolen nighttime hours” or “by stolen nighttime labors.”], and since you voluntarily promised that you could dictate some more by stolen nighttime labor if I wished, I gladly accept from one who offers what I had intended to request, even if you had refused [Note: [Col. 0451] The manuscripts of Victorius omit *etiam*, “even.”].

Nor do I think that any conversation for our discussion could be more worthy than for us to speak with one another about the Scriptures: that is, for me to ask and for you to answer. I think that nothing in this life is more delightful than such an exchange, by whose nourishment for the soul all honey is surpassed.”

“How sweet,” says the prophet, “are your words to my throat, sweeter than honey to my mouth” (Ps. 118:103) [Note: [Col. 0451] Other manuscripts, with the order slightly reversed, read: “Your words, O Lord, are sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth.”].

“For since, as the distinguished orator says, human beings differ from beasts in that we can speak, how worthy of praise is the person who surpasses others in that very faculty in which human beings surpass beasts?”

2. “Gird yourself, therefore, and explain to me what follows, preserving moderation in both respects: let neither the questions require a solution that is too brief, nor the letter lack brevity [Note: [Col. 0451] The Vatican reads *utrobique*, “in both respects,” and shortly afterward *Epistolae*, as do other manuscripts, rather than *Epistola*.].

I confess to you that I do not read with pleasure the books of Lactantius that you formerly gave me, because many of his letters extend to the length of a thousand lines, and they rarely discuss our doctrine. Consequently, their length creates weariness in the reader; and if any passages are brief, they are more suitable for schoolmen than for us, since they discuss meters, the situation of regions, and philosophers [Note: [Col. 0452] Quite a few manuscripts read *disputandis*, “to be discussed,” and others *disputantibus*, “for those discussing,” which can be referred to the preceding word, “schoolmen.” Elsewhere too the old parchments vary considerably: instead of *metris*, some have *muniis*, others *meritis*.].

1. “What does the statement written in Genesis mean: ‘Everyone who kills Cain shall pay sevenfold vengeance’?” (Gen. 4:15.)

2. “If God made all things very good, why did Noah receive a command concerning clean and unclean animals, since nothing unclean can be good? And in the New Testament, after the vision shown to Peter, when he said, ‘By no means, Lord, for nothing common or unclean has ever entered my mouth,’ a voice from heaven answered: ‘What God has cleansed, you must not call common’” (Acts 10:14–15) [Note: [Col. 0452] The Vatican reads *fecit*, “made,” and shortly afterward in this same question *introivit*, “entered,” instead of *introibit*, “will enter.”].

3. “Why does God say to Abraham that in the fourth generation the children of Israel would return from Egypt, and afterward Moses writes: ‘But in the fifth generation the children of Israel went up from the land of Egypt’ (Exod. 13:18, according to the Septuagint) [Note: [Col. 0452] The Cistercian manuscript, formerly Nonantulanus, reads *exituri*, “would go out.”]? Unless this is explained, it certainly appears contradictory.”

4. “Why did Abraham receive the sign of his faith in circumcision?”

5. “Why did Isaac, a just man and dear to God, bless not the one he wished, but the one he did not wish, deceived by his mistake?”

## EPISTLE XXXVI [Note: [Col. 0452] Elsewhere numbered 125. Written on the day after the preceding letter.]  
### OR JEROME’S REPLY TO DAMASUS

After offering an apology for his delays and omitting only two of the little questions—the second and the fourth, which had been discussed by Tertullian, Novatian, and Origen—Jerome answers the remaining three at length.

**Jerome to the most blessed Pope Damasus.**

1. After I received the letter of Your Holiness, I immediately summoned a secretary and ordered him to take it down. Once he had prepared himself for the task, I first sketched mentally what I was about to dictate aloud. Meanwhile, both he and I were already moving—he his writing instrument and I my tongue—when suddenly a Hebrew appeared [Note: [Col. 0452] The same Cistercian manuscript reads, “a certain Hebrew appeared.”], bringing quite a few volumes which he had received from the synagogue, supposedly to read.

“Here,” he said at once, “you have what you requested.” His sudden arrival so frightened me, uncertain as I was what to do, that I abandoned everything and flew to writing. Indeed, I am still doing so.

But because you said that yesterday, when you sent a deacon to me [Note: [Col. 0452] The same Cistercian manuscript reads “yesterday from a deacon”; Vatican 395, “yesterday from an archdeacon.” Victorius, following the preconceived opinion rejected in connection with the preceding letter, reads “from Etherius the deacon.”], you were awaiting what you consider a letter and what I regard as a commentary, and because you desired a brief response to matters that individually require the length of great volumes [Col. 0453] [Note: [Col. 0453] The Vatican manuscript lacks the word *prolixitate*, “length.” The Greek words, which the manuscripts often corrupt, mean in Latin: “I have sketched these matters for you extemporaneously.”], I have sketched these matters for you, *ταῦτά σοι ἐσχεδίασα*, omitting only two of the little questions. This was not because I could not answer them, but because they have already been published in Latin by very eloquent men, namely Tertullian, our Latin author [Note: [Col. 0453] In the Vatican manuscript and other older copies *nostro* is absent. In Jerome’s sense and idiom, the word signifies nothing other than a Latin author.], and Novatian; and if we wish to introduce new material, the discussion would have to be much longer.

Certainly I await your decision: whether you wish the answers arranged for you in the brevity of a letter, or whether separate books should be composed. Origen, too, discussed circumcision magnificently in the fourth volume of his *Expositions* on Paul’s Letter to the Romans [Note: [Col. 0453] Two reliable manuscripts entirely omit the Greek word ἐξηγήσεων, which in Latin means “expositions” or “commentaries”; others read ἐξηγητικῶν.]. He also discussed clean and unclean animals at length in Leviticus. Thus, even if I could find nothing myself, I could nevertheless borrow from his sources.

And, to speak more accurately, I have in my hands Didymus’s book *On the Holy Spirit*, which I wish to dedicate to you in translation, so that you will not think that I merely sleep, since you regard reading without a stylus as sleep.

Accordingly, having set before me the problems that you had appended to your letter, I added what seemed to me appropriate, asking pardon alike for my haste and for my delays: for my haste, because I wished to dictate in one little night-work a task belonging to many days [Note: [Col. 0453] The Vatican reads: “I wished to dictate a work of many days.”]; and for my slowness, because, being occupied with another work, I did not immediately reply to your questions.

2. What does the statement written in Genesis mean: “Everyone who kills Cain shall pay sevenfold vengeance”?

Before discussing the question, it seems right to set out the editions of the individual translators alongside the Hebrew itself [Note: [Col. 0453] The two words *conferentes sermone* can conveniently be deleted without loss of sense; no manuscript, or only some later manuscript, recognizes them. The Vatican also lacks *etiam Scripturae sensus*, and shortly afterward reads *Sobothai* for *Sobathaim*. The very ancient Ambrosian manuscript P. 60 has *lachem* and *Saphataim*. See the *Questions on Genesis*.], so that the meaning of Scripture may more easily be understood.

*VAIOMER LO ADONAI LOCHEN CHOL OREC CAIN SOBATHAIM JOCCAMO.*

Aquila: “And the Lord said to him: Therefore everyone who kills Cain shall be avenged sevenfold.”

Symmachus: “And the Lord said to him: Not so, but everyone who kills Cain shall be avenged by a hebdomad, or by the seventh” [Note: [Col. 0453] Almost all manuscripts have *hebdomadas*, whence Erasmus read *hebdomada*. I would prefer *hebdomatos*, from the Greek ἑβδομάτος, which in Latin is *seventh*. Martianaeus conjectures that *hebdomos*, or ἕβδομος, may perhaps be read. Although the sense is the same, it is farther from the manuscript reading. *Hebdomas*, a word invented by Victorius, was adopted by all the others, but it lacks the authority of the ancient manuscripts and is especially inappropriate: it signifies not “seventh,” but a group of seven and a period of seven days. Meanwhile, the Ambrosian manuscript gives Symmachus’s entire interpretation as follows: “Symmachus: And the Lord said to him: Therefore everyone who kills Cain shall be avenged by hebdomads, or seven times.”].

The Septuagint and Theodotion: “And the Lord said to him: ‘Not so, but everyone who kills Cain shall pay sevenfold vengeance.’”

After Cain had killed his brother, the Lord questioned him: “Where is Abel your brother?” He replied insultingly, “I do not know. Am I my brother’s keeper?” Therefore, condemned by a curse to live groaning and trembling upon the earth, he did not wish to beg forgiveness. Rather, adding sins to sins, he considered the crime so great that the Lord could not forgive it.

Finally, he replied to the Lord: “My guilt is greater than that I should be forgiven,” that is, “I have sinned more than I deserve to be acquitted.” “Behold, you drive me out today from the face of the earth, and I shall be hidden from your face, and I shall be groaning and trembling upon the earth; and everyone who finds me will kill me.”

“I am driven,” he says, “from your sight, and, unable to bear the light itself because of the consciousness of my crime [Note: [Col. 0454] Printed editions add here *tremebundus*, “trembling,” which most manuscripts do not have; it does not affect Jerome’s interpretation.], I shall hide myself so that I may lie concealed. ‘And everyone who finds me will kill me’: for from the trembling of my body [Note: [Col. 0454] Other manuscripts read: “while he understands that he is agitated by a deranged mind”; shortly afterward, “of a shortened death.” The Ambrosian has: “while, through the extreme agitation of his body and his deranged mind, he understands him,” and so forth.] and the agitation of my deranged mind he will understand that I am one who deserves to be killed.”

But God, unwilling to bring his torments to an end by a short death, and unwilling to hand him over to the punishment by which he had condemned himself, said: “Not so”—that is, “You will not die as you suppose, nor will you receive death as a remedy. Rather, you will live until the seventh generation and will be tormented by the fire of your conscience, so that whoever kills you will, according to a twofold interpretation, either free you in the seventh generation or free you from the seventh torment.

This does not mean that the person who kills Cain is himself to be subjected to seven punishments. Rather, the killer pays the seven acts of vengeance that continued against Cain for so long, by killing the one who had been left alive for punishment.

3. To make what we are saying clearer, let us give an example from ordinary life. Let a slave say to his master amid blows: “Because I burned down your house and squandered all your property, kill me.” Let the master reply: “You will not die as you wish and end your punishments by death. Rather, you will be guarded for a long time in order to remain alive, and you will live so unhappily in this world that whoever kills you will do a kindness to the man killed, since he will free you from so many torments.”

According to the edition of the Septuagint, this seems to be the sense intended here.

163 4. As for Aquila’s translation, “sevenfold,” and Symmachus’s, “a hebdomad or the seventh shall avenge,” this is the opinion of our predecessors: they think that Cain was killed by Lamech in the seventh generation.

Adam begot Cain; Cain begot Enoch; Enoch begot Irad; Irad begot Maviael; Maviael begot Mathusala; Mathusala begot Lamech, who, being seventh from Adam, killed Cain unintentionally—as is written in a certain Hebrew volume [Note: [Col. 0454] The Cistercian manuscript, together with the Vatican and others, reads: “Enoch begot Cainam” (others have Gaidad); “Cainan begot Mahalaleel; Mahalaleel begot Methuselah,” and so forth.].

He later confesses this himself: “For I have killed a man by my wound, and a young man by my bruise; for Cain shall be avenged seven times, but Lamech seventy-seven times” (Gen. 4:23–24).

As for Cain, then, that he was killed by Lamech in the seventh generation and, according to another edition, paid the penalty for his crime; that he lived upon the earth groaning and trembling for so many generations [Note: [Col. 0455] In very many manuscripts *a Lamech* is absent, and shortly afterward the entire passage—“that he lived upon the earth groaning and trembling for so many generations”—is also absent.], I think that nothing obscure remains.

5. **The seventy-seven acts of vengeance to be exacted upon Lamech.**—Now, while we are discussing another matter, something you did not ask about has slipped in: what are the seventy-seven acts of vengeance to be paid in Lamech?

They say that from Adam to Christ there are seventy-seven generations. Read the Evangelist Luke and you will find that it is so, as we say.

Therefore, just as Cain’s sin was undone in the seventh generation—for God does not exact punishment twice for the same matter, and the one who has once received evils in his life will not suffer in death the same torments that he suffered in life—so too Lamech’s sin, that is, the sin of the whole world and of the blood that was shed, would be dissolved by Christ’s coming [Note: [Col. 0455] Earlier printed editions have *solvetur*, “will be dissolved.” Shortly afterward the Cistercian manuscript reads: “who takes away the sins of the world.”].

He took away the sins of the world; he washed his garment in the blood of the grape and trod the winepress alone. As he ascended from Edom to heaven, red with blood (Isa. 63:1, 3), he offered the angels a marvel, while they cried: “Lift up your gates, O princes, and the King of glory shall enter” (Ps. 23:7), and so forth.

A certain Hebrew told me that in apocryphal books seventy-seven souls from Lamech’s descendants are said to have been found, and that they were destroyed by the flood. In this number, he said, vengeance was exacted from Lamech, because his line endured up to the cataclysm.

6. **Cain’s seven sins.**—Others form various conjectures about Cain’s seven acts of vengeance. They assert that his first sin was that he did not divide correctly. The second was that he envied his brother. The third was that he acted deceitfully when he said, “Let us go out into the field” (Gen. 4:8). The fourth was that he killed him. The fifth was that he brazenly denied it, saying, “I do not know; am I my brother’s keeper?” (v. 9). The sixth was that he condemned himself, saying, “My guilt is greater than that I should be forgiven” (v. 13). The seventh was that, although condemned, he did not repent as did the people of Nineveh and King Hezekiah of Judah, who removed the impending death by their tears [Note: [Col. 0455] These words seem to me to bear the character of a gloss: “so that those who had been condemned would not perish, but by repenting might obtain God’s mercy.” They are absent from the oldest Vatican manuscript and from manuscripts of the best quality, nor does Jerome’s intention and context require them; indeed, they make the sense looser. They are also expressed differently and corruptly in the Ambrosian manuscript. Perhaps some diligent reader had written them in the margin of a book, after which they slipped into the text.].

For they say that the most merciful God postponed his punishment until the seventh generation so that, compelled at least by his very miseries and by the length of his life in sorrow, he might repent and deserve to be acquitted [Note: [Col. 0456] Several manuscripts have “by the sorrow of a long life,” without any difference in meaning.].

7. Some interpret the number seven as complete and perfect, gathering testimonies from many passages of Scripture. They say that this is the meaning we touched on above: whoever killed Cain would free him from the immense affliction [Note: [Col. 0456] Two manuscripts read “whoever should kill,” and shortly afterward “would free.” The Vatican, while otherwise preserving the full sense, omits the word “affliction.” The Ambrosian then has “passing over to all punishments,” which it refers to Cain.] and all the punishments that had come upon him.

8. There are also those who repeat Peter’s question from the Gospel: “Lord, how often will my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? Up to seven times?” Jesus says to him: “I do not say to you up to seven times, but up to seventy times seven” (Matt. 18:21–22).

They think that death and sin rested in the seventh generation, when Enoch was taken away: “and he was not found, because God transferred him” (Gen. 5:24). As for the seventy-seven, they follow the interpretation that at Christ’s coming the sting of death and sin was broken.

9. I shall also set forth another opinion, so that I may not seem to have passed over anything. Some interpret the seventh year of remission, the fiftieth year of the Jubilee, and the four hundred and ninetieth year—which they wish to be understood as seventy times seven—in many ways. They assert that for this reason the number fifty, and the number five hundred, were regarded as sacred [Note: [Col. 0456] The Vatican, Ambrosian, and ten other manuscripts read *sacrate*, “sacredly,” meaning “mystically,” although the Latin is less correct and perhaps the meaning more accurate.], and that the debtor was placed in the Gospel; and they interpret the fiftieth Psalm as a psalm of repentance, since it is completed in seven weeks and bursts forth into the beginning of the octave.

But, so that the discussion may not proceed too far, let it suffice to have spoken this much on the subject. From what we have scattered here, you yourself will be able to construct an immense forest of discussion, knowing that Origen dictated the twelfth and thirteenth books of his work on Genesis solely on this question [Note: [Col. 0456] Eusebius, Nicephorus, Suidas, and the others whom we cited above in Epistle 33 to Paula enumerate no more than twelve books of Origen on Genesis. There we also explain how it happened that Jerome knew of a thirteenth.].

10. Why does God say to Abraham that in the fourth generation the children of Israel would return from Egypt, while Moses afterward writes: “But in the fifth generation the children of Israel went up from the land of Egypt”? Unless this is explained, it certainly appears contradictory.

When I read this problem, I began silently to wrestle with it. Immediately running through Genesis and Exodus, I found the passages in which the statements that seem to create the question are written.

At first, comparing spiritual things with spiritual things, I thought them insoluble, as many other matters are. It is written that Methuselah lived fourteen years after the flood, yet he did not enter the ark with Noah. And although God himself said to Abraham, “Know assuredly that your offspring will be a stranger in a land that is not theirs, and they will enslave and oppress them, and humble them for four hundred years” (Gen. 15:13), Moses afterward writes in Exodus: “And it came to pass after four hundred and thirty years that all the power of the Lord went out from the land of Egypt” (Exod. 12:41) [Note: [Col. 0457] The Benedictine edition reads, “all the people of the Lord went out.” But the Greek, with which the Hebrew also agrees, has πᾶσα ἡ δύναμις, “all the power,” and this is what we have also rendered, following fifteen of Jerome’s manuscripts. Shortly afterward, instead of “about eighteen,” quite a few manuscripts have “about sixteen”; Victorius has “seventeen.”].

Hagar also carries Ishmael on her shoulders as though he were an infant and tender, although he is found to have been about eighteen years old or more; and it would be ridiculous for so large a young man to sit on his mother’s neck. Rehoboam, moreover, the son of Solomon, began his reign in the forty-first year of his age and reigned sixteen years, although his father, who began to reign in his twelfth year, reigned forty years and could not have fathered his son in his eleventh year.

11. While I was anxiously turning these and many similar matters over in my mind, he who holds the key of David opened the door for me and led me into his chamber; he set me in the cleft of the rock. After the raging spirit, after the earthquake of my land, after the fire of ignorance in which I was burning, a voice of gentler breeze came to me, so that I could say: “I have found the one whom my soul sought; I will hold him and will not let him go” (Song 3:4).

For although Scripture may appear to contradict itself, both statements are true, though they are different.

The children of Israel went out from the land of Egypt in the fourth generation. Review the genealogy of Levi: Levi begot Kohath; Kohath begot Amram; Amram begot Aaron; Aaron begot Eleazar; Eleazar begot Phinehas. Kohath entered Egypt with his father Levi. Again, Eleazar went out of Egypt with his father Aaron.

From Kohath to Eleazar four generations are counted, although some wish to begin with Amram and reach Phinehas, just as we have proceeded to Eleazar [Note: [Col. 0457] We supplied the passage from our manuscripts; previously Martianaeus had *ab Amram usque ad Finees*, “from Amram to Phinehas.”].

If, however, you wish to demonstrate a different number—how, according to Exodus, the children of Israel went out from the land of Egypt in the fifth generation—let the tribe of Judah and its order be counted for you. Judah begot Perez; Perez begot Hezron; Hezron begot Aram; Aram begot Amminadab; Amminadab begot Nahshon; Nahshon begot Salmon.

Perez entered Egypt with his father Judah. Nahshon is described as the leader of the tribe of Judah in the wilderness, and his son Salmon entered the promised land.

Count from Perez to Nahshon: you will find five generations, although some—as we showed in the tribe of Levi—begin with Hezron and proceed as far as Salmon.

### 12

I think the problem has been resolved; but if this is unsatisfactory, I shall come to the point and say that the Hebrew does not differ. Aquila, who interprets word for word—not, as some think, contentiously, but painstakingly—translated the passage where the Septuagint reads, “And in the fifth generation the children of Israel went up from the land of Egypt” (Exod. 13:18), as follows: **Καὶ ἐνοπλισάμενοι ἀνέβησαν οἱ υἱοὶ Ἰσραήλ ἀπὸ τῆς γῆς Αἰγύπτου**, that is, “And armed, the children of Israel went up from the land of Egypt.”

[Note: The Vatican manuscript reads **ἐνωπλισμένοι**, which I think is the more correct reading than **ἐνοπλισάμενος**; for Diodorus, too, when quoting this passage of Aquila in the *Catenae*, reads **ἐνωπλισμένοι**. Nor should it be overlooked that the same Vatican manuscript has **τῆς ἀπὸ γῆς**, which is perhaps the more accurate reading—an especially exacting translator’s rendering, intended to reproduce the Hebrew more closely.]

Although, instead of what we have rendered “armed,” one may understand “equipped” or “provided,” in accordance with the ambiguity of the Greek expression, because of the possessions with which they despoiled the Egyptians.

### 13

When I thought that my curiosity had come to an end, a greater eagerness to inquire arose; and, like Jeremiah, I am undone on every side and cannot endure it (Jer. 20). Why, then, did the Septuagint translate “in the fifth generation,” while Aquila translated “armed”? I reopen the Hebrew scroll—which Paul, according to some, calls **φενόλην**—and, attentively examining the very letters, I find it written:

**VAMUSIM ALU BNE ISRAEL MEAREZ MESRAIM.**

[Note: The manuscripts we collated have *penolen*, or *phenolen*, or *penolam*; nor are the older printed editions sufficiently reliable when they give **φαιλόνην** or **φελώνην**. The following passage is written in Hebrew letters as follows: [Hebrew text is not present in the supplied source.]]

In the rest, the translations do not disagree; the entire dispute concerns the word **AMUSIM**, written with these letters: **HETH, MEM, SIN, JOD, MEM**—whether it means “five” or “armed.”

[Note: In attempting, as far as possible, to measure the ancient translations against the Hebrew text, Jerome seems, in the haste of writing, to have paid too little attention to the grammatical rules of the Hebrew language when he allows that the word can mean “five,” whereas it actually means “fifty.”]

We certainly cannot deny that “five” is expressed in this language. Yet it is “five” in the plural, not “fifth,” as they translated it in the singular. Nor is the word “generation” joined to it; in Hebrew, that word is **DOR**. Thus, if it meant “fifth generation,” their language would read **AMESA DOR**.

[Note: Critics sharply ridicule this passage because he joined the feminine adjective *amesa* to the masculine noun *Dor*. But I fear that they themselves have been misled by a faulty reading. For several manuscript codices—including the exceedingly well-corrected Cistercian manuscript—have *amese*, which could easily have been read from the masculine form. We have not altered the printed reading, since it is not sufficiently certain what the author actually wrote.]

But now only **AMUSIM**, that is, “five”—or rather “fifth”—is written, so that the sense is almost: “And in the fifth the children of Israel went up from the land of Egypt.” Because this seemed less intelligible, the word “generation” was added.

All Judea loudly proclaims that Aquila translated this passage correctly, as he did others and especially this one; and all the benches of the synagogues resound with the same agreement: namely, that the same word, written with the same letters, has among them different pronunciations and meanings. To make this clear, let us give one example. “Shepherds” and “lovers” are written with the same letters: **RES, AIN, JOD, MEM**; but “shepherds” is read **ROIM**, while “lovers” is read **REIM**. Hence, when Jerusalem is accused in the Prophets of the crime of fornication with her lovers, our manuscripts have substituted the name “shepherds” for “lovers.”

### 14

I know that these matters are tedious for the reader. But one who is discussing Hebrew letters ought not to assemble Aristotle’s arguments, nor should a little stream be drawn from the river of Cicero’s eloquence. The ears should not be soothed with Quintilian’s flowers and schoolroom declamation. What is needed is plain, everyday speech, resembling ordinary language and smelling of no late-night study: speech that explains the matter, unfolds the meaning, and makes obscure things clear—not speech that grows leafy through the arrangement of words. Let others be eloquent and be praised as they wish; let them weigh words foaming from their inflated cheeks. For me it is enough to speak so that I may be understood; in discussing the Scriptures, I wish to imitate the simplicity of the Scriptures.

### 15

Why did Isaac, a just man beloved by God, in the deception of error bless not the one he wished to bless, but the one he did not wish to bless? (Gen. 27.)

I shall postpone for a little while the figures and pass over what our predecessors have explained concerning this passage—not because I do not accept their opinion, but because you ask only this: why a just man should have been ignorant of something and should have acted against his own will.

The answer is categorical: **NO HUMAN BEING**, except the one who deigned to assume flesh for our salvation, possessed complete knowledge and absolutely certain truth. Paul, after all, knows in part and prophesies in part (1 Cor. 13:9); now he sees through a mirror, in an enigma; and he says that we do not know how to pray as we ought (Rom. 8:26), because, “when that which is perfect has come, then that which is in part will be destroyed” (1 Cor. 13:10).

The prophet Samuel, counted alongside Moses in the Psalter, was sent to anoint a king. When he saw Eliab, the eldest of Jesse’s sons, he said, “Surely the Lord’s anointed is before him” (1 Sam. 16:6).

[Note: Up to this point the Vulgate had read *in the priesthood of God*, a reading we did not hesitate to change on the authority of more than thirty manuscripts, which we or other editors consulted. The reference is to Psalm 98:6: “Moses and Aaron among his priests, and Samuel among those who call upon his name.” The Vatican manuscript soon omits the name Eliab.]

And the Lord said to Samuel: “Do not look upon his face, nor upon the height of his stature, because I have rejected him; for God does not see as man sees. Man looks at the face, but God looks into the heart” (ibid., v. 7). As he proceeds through them one by one, he is described as continually ignorant, up to David.

[Note: Most printed editions have *always* instead of *seven*; and immediately afterward a large number of manuscripts read *nescit* (“he does not know”) rather than *nescisse* (“to have been ignorant”), which is the shorter reading.]

Elisha also, who was glorified by a double portion of the Spirit, whose bones restored life to a dead body (2 Kings 1 and 13), was visited by the Shunammite woman on the mountain. When she came and fell sorrowfully at his feet, and Gehazi tried to stop her, he said: “Let her alone, for her soul is in bitterness, and the Lord has hidden it from me and has not told me” (2 Kings 4:27).

There are more examples than we need to prove that holy men, beloved by God, knew only what had been revealed to them by the Lord, and were ignorant of what had not been revealed to them. Thus, at each vision, Zechariah and Daniel question the angel and humbly beg him to explain to them what the things they see mean.

It is therefore not surprising that Isaac, especially for his own benefit, did not know what he was doing. At that time he was all the more in error because he wished to exalt the son devoted to bloodthirsty pleasure, the one who could later kill his brother, while passing over the one who lived innocently at home; and he wished to do his own will rather than God’s.

I think it was part of the divine dispensation that his eyes should be blinded. Although he said, “The voice is the voice of Jacob, but the hands are the hands of Esau” (Gen. 27:22), he nevertheless did not understand that the younger son who had come forward to seize his brother’s blessing was standing before him.

### 16. The Mystical Interpretation of the Martyr Hippolytus

Since we promised to add what this event signified figuratively, let us set down the words of the martyr Hippolytus, from whom our Victorinus does not differ greatly—not because he has explained everything more fully, but because he may provide the reader with an occasion for broader understanding.

[Note: These few passages have been preserved and translated into Latin from the book of Saint Hippolytus *On What Follows the Six Days*, as Eusebius calls it, though Jerome appears to regard it as a commentary on Genesis. That work, however, has perished.]

“Isaac bears the image of God the Father; Rebecca, of the Holy Spirit; Esau, of the earlier people and of the devil; Jacob, of the Church or of Christ.

“Isaac’s growing old indicates the consummation of the world; his eyes becoming dim signifies that faith has perished from the world and that the light of religion has been neglected before him.

[Note: Some manuscripts read *meditatur et loquitur* (“he meditates and speaks”).]

“That the elder son is named signifies the Jews’ reception of the Law. That the father loves his food and his catch signifies human beings saved from error, whom every righteous person hunts through instruction.

“The word of God is the promise of blessing and the hope of the future kingdom, in which the saints will reign with Christ and celebrate the true Sabbath.

“Rebecca, full of the Holy Spirit, knowing what she had heard before she gave birth—that ‘the elder shall serve the younger’ (Gen. 25:23)—but being more truly a figure of the Holy Spirit, who knew beforehand what was to come in Christ, first meditates upon it in Jacob.

“She says to the younger son: ‘Go to the flock and bring me from there two young goats’ (Gen. 27:9), prefiguring the bodily coming of the Savior, in which he would especially deliver those held under the bondage of sins; for throughout the Scriptures goats are understood as sinners.

“That he is commanded to bring two signifies the taking up of two peoples. That they are young signifies souls that are good, teachable, and innocent.

[Note: One must supply “is signified”; for I do not approve the reading found in the older printed editions: “it signifies souls that are teachable and innocent.” In the next phrase we have restored *vestimentum* (“garment”) on the authority of the same editions, the Vatican manuscript, and several others.]

“Esau’s robe, or garment, is the faith and Scriptures of the Hebrews, with which the people of the Gentiles have been clothed.

“The skins wrapped around his arms are the sins of both peoples, which Christ, in the extension of his hands, fastened together with himself to the cross.

“That Isaac asks Jacob why he has come so quickly signifies his wonder at the swift faith of believers.

[Note: Two manuscripts read *admiratur* (“he wonders”), as the sentence requires: “he wonders at the swiftness of believers,” whereas previously the reading was *admirabatur* (“he admired”).]

“That desirable foods are offered signifies the sacrifice pleasing to God, the salvation of sinners. After eating, the blessing follows, and he enjoys its fragrance, openly proclaiming the power of the resurrection and of the kingdom: namely, that his brothers will worship him and serve him, those from Israel who believe.

“Because iniquity is the enemy of righteousness, Esau is stirred to hostility and deceitfully devises murder, saying in his heart: ‘Let the days of my father’s passion draw near, and I will kill my brother Jacob’” (Gen. 27:41).

[Note: Victorius altered *Appropinquent* (“let them draw near”) against the authority of the manuscripts. Then two old copies have *dies mortis* (“the days of death”), although they do not preserve that reading in the passage below.]

“The devil, who had previously premeditated the fratricidal Jews in Cain, confesses it most clearly in Esau, also indicating the time of the killing: ‘Let the days of my father’s passion draw near,’ he says, ‘so that I may kill my brother.’

“Therefore Rebecca—that is, patience—announced the brother’s plot to her husband. He summoned Jacob and commanded him to go to Mesopotamia and take a wife from the family of Laban the Syrian, his mother’s brother.

“Just as Jacob, fleeing his brother’s schemes, went toward Mesopotamia (Gen. 28), so Christ, compelled by the unbelief of the Jews, goes to Galilee, intending to take the Church as his bride from among the Gentiles.”

Thus far the man mentioned above.

### 17

We, however, say that the Lord came only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel; that he did not wish to take the children’s bread and give it to dogs; and that he first brought the blessing to the Jewish people, to whom the oracles of God were entrusted (Rom. 3:2), together with the promise, the giving of the Law, and the making of the Covenant (Rom. 9:4).

[Note: Other manuscripts read “the confession of the covenant.”]

But because they did not wish to believe, the blessing was transferred to Jacob, the younger people. Yet the elder son was not entirely rejected, because, when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel will be saved (Rom. 11:25–26).

## LETTER XXXVII  
### TO MARCELLA

[Note: Otherwise numbered 133. Written in the same year, 384.]

[Note: In the oldest manuscripts of Queen Christina’s collection it is otherwise entitled *Concerning Eadin and Tharsis*.]

### Concerning the Commentaries of Rheticius on the Song of Songs

He reproves Saint Rheticius, bishop of the Aedui, because in his commentaries on the Song of Songs he absurdly understood Tharsis as Tarsus of Cilicia, and the gold of Ophaz as Peter, the chief of the Apostles.

### 1

Recently, when I had read through the commentaries of Rheticius, bishop of Augustodunum, who had once been sent to Rome by the Emperor Constantine under Bishop Sylvester on account of the Montenses,

[Note: Compare what Jerome says about this same Rheticius in the *Catalogue*. Victorius is mistaken in thinking that the Montenses were named after Montanus the heretic. Jerome writes in his *Chronicle*, under the year 356: “Some followers of Donatus are also called Montenses, because they first began to have a church at Rome on a hill.” In the *Dialogue against the Luciferians* he calls them Montenses or Campates. See Optatus, book 2, and Augustine, Letter 52 and *On Heresies*, chapter 69.]

I was greatly astonished that an eloquent man, beyond the absurdities of his other interpretations, should have thought that the city of Tharsis was Tarsus, where the apostle Paul was born, and that the gold of Ophaz signified Peter because Cephas in the Gospel is the name by which Peter is also called.

[Note: In both the Vulgate and Jerome’s own version, Ezekiel and Daniel have *chrysolithus* for Tharsis. Jerome himself, in his commentary on Daniel 10, explains that the name Tharsis means “sea”: “According to what we read in the Psalm, ‘In the violent wind you will crush the ships of Tharsis,’ that is, of the sea.”]

Surely he had encountered the same word in Ezekiel, where the four living creatures are described: “And the appearance of the wheels was like the appearance of Tharsis” (Ezek. 10:9); and in Daniel concerning the Lord: “And his body was like Tharsis” (Dan. 10:6).

Aquila translates it as “chrysolith,” and Symmachus as “hyacinth.” And in the Psalm: “In a violent wind you will crush the ships of Tharsis” (Ps. 47:8). Among the stones set into the priestly vestments and engraved with the names of the tribes, the name of the same stone is also inserted; and almost the whole of Scripture is filled with this word.

What shall I say about Ophaz, when the prophet Daniel himself, in the third year of Cyrus, king of the Persians, after three weeks of fasting and mourning, says: “I lifted up my eyes and saw, and behold, one man clothed in linen, whose loins were girded with gold of Ophaz” (Dan. 10:5)?

[Note: The Vulgate reads *obrizo*, “refined gold.”]

There are, in fact, many kinds of gold among the Hebrews. Therefore, to distinguish it, **OPHAZ** is used here, lest anyone think it is **ZAAB**, which in Genesis is mentioned together with the carbuncle stone (Gen. 2:12).

### 2

You ask: If Tharsis is the stone chrysolith or hyacinth, as the different translators maintain, after the likeness of whose color the appearance of God is described, why is the prophet Jonah said to have wished to go to Tharsis (Jonah 1), and why did Solomon and Jehoshaphat possess ships in the books of Kings that used to conduct commerce with Tharsis (1 Kings 10)?

[Note: The Queen Christina manuscript reads *solitae sint afferre* (“were accustomed to bring”), or *exercere*, and so on. The Greek expression below, **ὁμώνυμον**, is rendered in Latin by an equivocal term.]

The answer is easy: the word is **ὁμώνυμον**, “a homonym.” That is, the name is applied both to a region of India and to the sea itself, because the sea is blue and, often struck by the rays of the sun, takes on the color of the stones mentioned above; from that color it received its name.

[Note: Josephus says that Tharsus—the second son of Javan—gave his name to the Tarsians, the ancient peoples of Cilicia, as evidence that the city most famous among them, and also called their metropolis, was named Tarsus, without aspiration, since they changed theta to tau in pronouncing the name: **τὸ ταῦ πρὸς τὴν κλῆσιν, ἀντὶ τοῦ θῆτα μεταβαλλόντων**. Hence Erasmus perhaps read in Jerome: “Josephus, with the letter tau substituted for theta.” Victorinus retained this reading, at least in the Aldine edition before me, although Martianaeus assigns him another reading. We venture nothing beyond the authority of the manuscripts. See the Byzantine Geographer, Zonaras, Nicephorus Callistus, and others.]

Although Josephus, with the letter **TAU** substituted, thinks that the Greeks called it Tarsus instead of Tharsis.

### 3

There are innumerable things in his commentaries that seemed to me to be worthless. His language is indeed polished and flows in the Gallican buskin,

[Note: Understand “in an ornate and elevated style,” as Jerome himself explains in Letter 5.2 to Florentius. Sidonius likewise speaks of “the buskin of Latin eloquence” in book 2, letter 9. Pliny too says of the painter Nicophanes: “He had buskin and gravity of art.” Soon afterward some manuscripts read: “not how he himself may appear eloquent, but how he may make the reader understand him,” and so forth.]

but what does that matter in an interpreter, whose profession is not to appear eloquent himself, but to make the person who will read understand in the same way as the author understood who wrote it?

Did he not have Origen’s ten volumes? Did he not have the other interpreters? Surely he had at least some of the necessary Hebrew scholars, whom he could either question or read, to learn what the things he did not understand meant.

But he seems to have thought so poorly of posterity

[Note: We have corrected this from royal parchment manuscripts and others, including the Cluniac manuscript, in which both readings are given. Martianaeus rejected the better reading and followed the printed editions, reading *de ceteris* and *possit* instead of *posset*.
