A little farther on, two of our manuscripts read *cum mihi in illis multa displiceant*: “since many things in them displease me.”]

that no one would be able to judge his errors.

### 4

You therefore ask for the commentaries of this same man from me in vain, since far more things displease me in them than please me. If you object that I have given them to others, you will hear that not everyone ought to eat the same foods.

In the desert Jesus feeds many people with barley loaves, but fewer with wheat loaves. The Corinthians, among whom fornication was heard of such a kind as had not even been heard of among the Gentiles, are fed with milk, because they were not yet able to receive solid food. The Ephesians, however, against whom no crime is charged, are fed by the Lord himself with heavenly bread and recognize the mystery hidden for ages.

Nor should you be guided by the authority or age of those to whom I have given copies, since Daniel as a boy judges elders, and Amos, a shepherd of goats, attacks the leaders of the priests.

## LETTER XXXVIII  
### TO MARCELLA

[Note: Otherwise numbered 23, written at the same time as the preceding letter.]

[Note: One Veronese manuscript and several others have the title *On the Conversion of Blaesilla*, which is also not inappropriate. In the letter itself, immediately after the passage about Hezekiah, another Veronese manuscript has *spatio protelatur ad vitam* (“her life is prolonged for a space”).]

### Concerning the Illness of Blaesilla

He praises Blaesilla, the daughter of Paula, who, after her husband’s death and after being struck by a severe fever, had turned herself wholly toward Christ and begun to profess herself a nun; and he responds to those who criticized her decision.

### 1

Abraham is tested in his son and is found more faithful. Joseph is sold into Egypt so that he may feed his father and his brothers. Hezekiah is terrified by approaching death, so that, after pouring himself out in tears, fifteen years are added to his life. The apostle Peter is shaken by the Lord’s Passion, so that, weeping bitterly, he hears: “Feed my sheep” (John 21:17).

Paul—the ravening wolf and the younger Benjamin—in ecstasy (Gen. 49; Ps. 67:28) is blinded so that he may see; and, surrounded by the sudden horror of darkness, he calls upon the Lord whom he had long persecuted as a man.

[Note: Jerome alludes here to two passages at once, since Saint Paul was from the tribe of Benjamin: Genesis 49:27, “Benjamin is a ravening wolf,” and Psalm 67:28, “There is Benjamin, the younger one, in an ecstasy.”]

### 2

So now, too, my Marcella, we saw our Blaesilla burning continually with the heat of fever for nearly thirty days, so that she might learn that the delights of the body must be rejected, since shortly afterward it will be dug through by worms.

The Lord Jesus also came to her, touched her hand, and behold, she rose and ministered to him. Something of negligence clung to her, and, bound in the wrappings of wealth, she lay in the tomb of the world. But Jesus groaned and, troubled in spirit, cried out, saying: “Blaesilla, come outside” (John 11:43, concerning Lazarus).

She was called, rose, and, having come out, eats with the Lord. Let the Jews threaten [or: marvel] and swell with rage; let them seek to kill the woman who has been raised. Let the Apostles alone rejoice. She knows that she owes her life to the one who restored it. She knows that she embraces the feet of the one whose judgment she had shortly before feared.

Her body lay almost lifeless, and approaching death shook her breathless limbs. Where then were the assistance of her relatives? Where were words more empty than smoke? You owe nothing to the ungrateful ties of kinship, for you have perished to the world and come back to life for Christ. Let the Christian rejoice; whoever is angry shows that he is not a Christian.

### 3

A widow who has been released from the bond of marriage has nothing to do except persevere. Yet someone is scandalized by a darker garment. Let him be scandalized by John, than whom no one born of women was greater; who was called an angel and baptized the Lord himself; who was clothed in a covering of camel hair and girded with a leather belt.

Are humbler foods displeasing? Nothing is humbler than locusts. Let those women rather scandalize Christian eyes who paint their faces and eyes with rouge and various cosmetics; whose plaster-white faces, disfigured by excessive pallor, imitate idols; and if a drop of tears should happen to escape them unawares, it runs down in a furrow.

They cannot be taught by the number of their years that they are old women. They build up the crowns of their heads with someone else’s hair and polish their former youth upon the wrinkles of old age. Finally, they arrange themselves trembling before a flock of grandchildren like little girls.

[Note: Martianaeus preferred to read *interjecta ut vocula, trementes, ut virgunculae*—“with the inserted little word, ‘trembling like little girls’”—and altered the passage according to his own understanding, since Jerome repeats it in chapter 2 of his letter to Titus. But besides the fact that the manuscripts contain this little word in neither passage, he failed to understand its ironic force, on which the entire elegance of the meaning depends.]

Let a Christian woman be ashamed if she forces nature’s beauty, if she takes care of the flesh for lust; for, according to the Apostle, those who live in such things cannot please Christ.

### 4

Our widow formerly adorned herself rather laboriously and spent the whole day examining herself in the mirror to see what she lacked.

[Note: Two Veronese manuscripts and an old edition read: “She was formerly adorned with necklaces.”]

Now she speaks confidently: “But we all, with unveiled face beholding the glory of the Lord, are transformed into the same image, from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord.”

Then servant girls arranged her hair, and the innocent crown of her head was confined with curling bands. Now her neglected head knows that what is veiled is sufficient for it.

At that time even the hardness of feathers seemed soft, and she could scarcely lie upon piled-up couches. Now she rises eagerly for prayer and, with a tinkling voice [or: a little hymn-like voice], beginning before the others and taking the “Alleluia” from them, is the first to praise her Lord.

Her knees bend upon the bare ground, and her face, previously soiled with white cosmetic, is cleansed by frequent tears. After prayer, the Psalms resound; her weary neck, trembling knees, and eyes sinking toward sleep scarcely obtain permission to rest from the excessive ardor of her mind.

A dark tunic is less soiled when she lies upon the ground. Her humbler slipper gives the needy the price of gilded shoes. Her belt is not decorated with gold and gems, but is woolen and wholly pure in its simplicity—and able to hold her garments together rather than tear them.

If the scorpion envies this purpose and, with flattering speech, persuades her to eat again from the forbidden tree, let an anathema strike him as a sandal, and let it be said to him as he dies in his own dust: “Get behind me, Satan” (Mark 8:33), which is interpreted as “adversary.” For he is truly the adversary of Christ, and the Antichrist, since he dislikes Christ’s commands.

### 5

Tell me, I beg you, what have we ever done like the Apostles, so that people are rightly scandalized?

They leave behind an aged father with his little boat and his net. The tax collector rises from the customs booth and follows the Savior. A disciple who wishes to return home and first bid farewell to his family is forbidden by the master’s voice. Burial is not granted to his father—and **to be impious for the Lord is a kind of piety**.

Because we do not wear silk clothing, we are judged to be monks. Because we are not drunk and do not contort our faces with laughter, we are called self-controlled and gloomy. If our tunic is not white, immediately comes the street-corner insult:

[Note: In his Letter to Furia he says in Greek: **Γραικός ὁ ἐπιθέτης**—“‘Greek’ is the epithet.”]

“Impostor! Greek!”

Let them mock as cleverly as they please, and let them carry themselves about, stuffed with a fat belly,

[Note: That is, let them behave arrogantly. Jerome often compares such men with pompous banquets; they walk slowly, not without contempt for others.]

our Blaesilla will laugh and will not disdain to hear the insults of chattering frogs, since her Lord was himself called Beelzebub.

## LETTER XXXIX  
### TO PAULA, ON THE DEATH OF HER DAUGHTER BLAESILLA

[Note: Otherwise numbered 25. Written about three months after the preceding letter.]

Blaesilla, who died shortly after her husband’s death and her own conversion, is the subject of Jerome’s consolation to her mother Paula. He rebukes Paula’s excessive grief and interweaves an account of Blaesilla’s virtues and life.

### 1

“Who will give water to my head and to my eyes a fountain of tears, and I shall weep” (Jer. 9:1)—not, as Jeremiah says, “the wounded of my people,” nor, as Jesus did, the misery of Jerusalem, but I shall weep over holiness, mercy, innocence, and chastity; I shall weep because all these virtues have perished together in the death of one person.

Not because she who has departed should be mourned, but because we grieve too impatiently that we have ceased to see such a person.

Who could recall with dry eyes a young woman of twenty years who raised the banner of the cross with such ardent faith that she grieved more over the loss of her virginity than over her husband’s death?

Who could pass without sobs over her persistence in prayer, the purity of her speech, the strength of her memory, and the sharpness of her intellect?

If you had heard her speaking Greek, you would have thought that she did not know Latin; if she turned her tongue to the Roman sound, her speech showed no foreign trace at all.

And then—something that the whole of Greece admires even in Origen—within not merely a few months but a few days she had mastered the difficulties of the Hebrew language so completely that, in learning and singing the Psalms, she competed with her mother.

[Note: The sense appears more elegant in the old edition: “something that I admire in Origen also, and which all Greece admires in him,” and so forth.]

The humility of her clothing did not, as it usually does in many people, reveal a swelling spirit; rather, when she had humbled herself inwardly, there was no middle ground between her and the dress of the servant girls, except that she was more easily distinguished because she walked more carelessly.

Her steps faltered from illness; her pale and trembling face was scarcely supported by her slender neck; and yet she always held either a prophet or the Gospel in her hands.

Her face was filled with tears, sobbing seized her voice, and her agitated entrails would not release her tongue when it stuck.

When the heat of fever consumed her holy little body and a circle of relatives surrounded her half-dead bed, she sent them these final words:

“Pray to the Lord Jesus that he may forgive me, because I could not fulfill what I wished.”

“Be confident, my Blaesilla,

[Note: Martianaeus inserted this passage of two verses, from “sensing” through “we are confident,” from the Cluniac manuscript. We reproduce it at length on the authority of the Cistercian manuscript and others of the highest quality.]

“knowing that your garments are white at all times. The whiteness of your garments is the purity of perpetual virginity. We are confident that we shall prove true what we say: **CONVERSION IS NEVER TOO LATE**.

“This saying was first dedicated in the case of the thief: ‘Truly I say to you, today you will be with me in Paradise’” (Luke 23:43).

After she had cast off the burden of the flesh, her soul flew back to its author and, after a long pilgrimage, ascended to its ancient possession. The funeral rites were prepared according to custom, and, with a procession of nobles going before, a golden covering was spread over the bier.

At that moment it seemed to me that she cried out from heaven:

[Note: Gravius calls this the sharper reading: “I do not recognize these garments; this covering is not mine.”]

“I do not recognize these garments. This covering is not mine. This adornment belongs to another.”

2. But what are we doing? While trying to restrain the mother’s tears, we ourselves are weeping. I confess my feelings: this entire book is written with tears. Jesus too wept for Lazarus, because he loved him (John 11). He is not the best comforter whose own groans overcome him, whose softened heart forces broken words out through tears. I call Jesus to witness, my Paula—Jesus whom Blaesilla now follows; I call the holy angels to witness, in whose company she rejoices—that I endure the same torments of grief that you do: that I am a father in spirit, a nurse in affection, and that I sometimes say, “May that day perish on which I was born” (Jer. 20:14). And: “Woe is me, my mother, why did you give birth to me, a man [Note: [Col. 0466] Our predecessor, the Bishop of Reate, testified that many variations of the manuscripts are found at this point; nevertheless, he displayed none of them and wished to change nothing. The copies we use, however, generally agree in reading: “who should be judged and discerned for all the earth,” which agrees especially well with the Greek interpretation, ἄνδρα δικαζόμενον καὶ διακρινόμενον—“a man being judged and discerned.”] who should be called a point of contention throughout all the earth” (ibid. 15:10). And this: “You are righteous, O Lord; nevertheless I shall speak to you concerning your judgments. Why is it that the ways of sinners prosper?” And: “My feet were almost moved, [Col. 0467] my steps nearly slipped. [Note: [Col. 0467] The words “My feet were almost poured out, because I was jealous of sinners” are absent from most manuscript codices. Nor do a few manuscripts have *I rejected* a little later, instead of *I transgressed*.] For I was jealous of sinners, seeing the peace of sinners. And I said: How has God known, and is there knowledge in the Most High? Behold, these are sinners, and they abound in the world; they have obtained riches.”

But again this occurs to me: “If I should speak thus, behold, I would have betrayed the generation of your children.” Is this same wave not often dashed against my own mind? Why do impious old men enjoy the riches of the world? Why is inexperienced youth and sinless childhood cut down in its untimely bloom? Why is it that infants of two or three years, and sucklings at their mother’s breast, are often seized by a demon, filled with leprosy, or devoured by jaundice, while, on the other hand, the impious, adulterers, murderers, and sacrilegious men, vigorous and secure in their health, blaspheme God? Especially since the father’s injustice does not overflow onto the son, and “the soul that sins, it shall die.” Or, if that ancient sentence remains—that the sins of the fathers must be repaid upon the children (Exod. 34)—it is unjust to charge innocent infancy with the countless offenses of a long-lived father.

“And I said: Therefore I have cleansed my heart without cause, and washed my hands among the innocent; and I have been scourged all day long” (Ps. 72:13–14). But while I was thinking these things, I immediately learned with the Prophet: “And I undertook to understand; this is labor in my sight, until I enter the sanctuary of God and understand their final destiny” (ibid., v. 16). “For the judgments of the Lord are a great abyss.” And: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How inscrutable are his judgments, and [Note: [Col. 0467] It should be corrected to *unsearchable*, as, apart from the Greek text, Jerome himself reads above in Epistle 21 to Damasus, no. 39: ἀνεξιχνίαστοι αἱ ὁδοί—“his ways are untraceable.”] unsearchable his ways!” (Rom. 11:33.)

God is good, and everything that the good God does must be good. I have suffered the bereavement of a husband; I grieve over what has happened. But because this pleases the Lord, I shall endure it with an even spirit. An only son has been taken away: it is hard, certainly, but tolerable, because he who had given him has taken him away. If I become blind, the reading of my friends will console me. If deaf ears also deny me hearing, I shall be free from vices: I shall think of nothing else but the Lord. In addition to these things, severe poverty, cold, sickness, and nakedness may threaten me; I shall await the final death, and I shall consider the evil brief because a better end will follow.

Let us consider what that ethical Psalm says: “You are righteous, O Lord, and your judgment is right” (Ps. 118). No one can say this except one who magnifies the Lord in everything he suffers and, attributing it to his own merit, glories in the Lord’s mercy amid adversity. “For the daughters of Judah rejoiced in all the judgments of the Lord.” If *Judah* is interpreted as “confession,” and every believing soul is confessing, then whoever says that he believes in Christ must rejoice in all Christ’s judgments.

I am healthy: I give thanks to the Creator. I am weak: in this also I praise the Lord’s will. “For when I am weak, then I am strong [or: stronger]” (2 Cor. 12), and the strength of the spirit is perfected in the weakness of the flesh. The Apostle too suffers something he does not wish to suffer, and for this he entreats the Lord three times. But he is told: “My grace is sufficient for you, because strength is perfected in weakness” (2 Cor. 12:9). And, to humble the pride produced by revelations, a reminder of human weakness is added, after the manner of triumphal processions, in which an attendant riding behind the triumphator in the chariot repeated, with each acclamation of the citizens: “Remember that you are a human being.” [Note: [Col. 0468] Gravius observes this from Tertullian, *Apologeticus*: “The emperor, even while triumphing in that most exalted chariot, is reminded that he is a human being; for behind him someone says: ‘Look behind you; remember that you are human.’”]

3. But why should what must sometimes be endured be hard? And why do we grieve for anyone who has died? [Note: [Col. 0468] Martianaeus, together with certain printed editions, reads this without the negative particle, though under an interrogative mark. We prefer the authority of the manuscripts, which Victor also preferred.] We were not born for this purpose, that we should remain forever. Abraham, Moses, Isaiah, Peter, James, John, Paul—the chosen vessel—and, above all, the Son of God, die. Yet we are indignant that someone leaves the body who perhaps was taken away for this reason: “lest wickedness should alter his understanding; for his soul was pleasing to God. Therefore he hastened to bring him out from the midst of iniquity” (Wis. 4), lest, through the long journey of life [or: “lest, on the long journey of life”], he wander through crooked paths.

Let the dead be mourned—but the one whom Gehenna receives, whom Tartarus devours, for whose punishment eternal fire burns. We, whose departure is accompanied by a throng of angels, toward whom Christ comes to meet us, should be more troubled if we linger too long in this tabernacle of death. For as long as we remain here, we are away from the Lord (1 Cor. 5). Let that desire possess us, that desire which says: “Woe is me, for my sojourning has been prolonged; I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Cedar; my soul has been a long-time sojourner” (Ps. 119).

If Cedar means “darkness,” and this world is darkness—for “the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it” (John 1:5)—let us favor our Blaesilla, who has migrated from darkness to light and, amid the fervor of beginning faith, received the crown of perfected work.

Indeed, if death had snatched her away prematurely while she was thinking of worldly desire and—God avert it from his people—the pleasures of this life, she would have deserved to be mourned and lamented with every fountain of tears. But now, since, with Christ’s favor, nearly four months earlier she had, in a certain second baptism, washed herself in accordance with her purpose, and thereafter lived in such a way that, having trampled upon the world, she was always thinking of the monastery, are you not afraid that the Savior will say to you: “Are you angry, Paula, because your daughter has become my daughter? Are you indignant at my judgment, and by rebellious tears do you envy the one who possesses her?” You know what I think of you and of your other children. You deny yourself food—not out of devotion to fasting, but from grief. I do not approve this frugality. These fasts are hostile to me. I receive no soul that is separated from the body against my will.

Let foolish philosophy have such martyrs; let it have Zeno, Cleombrotus, or Cato. [Note: [Col. 0468] These three killed themselves; their stories are well known.] My spirit rests upon no one except “the humble and quiet and the one who trembles at my words” (Isa. 66, according to the Septuagint).

Is this the monastery that you promised me? Did you merely appear more religious because, by clothing yourself differently from other matrons, you seemed more devout? The mind that mourns belongs to silk garments. You are intercepted and dying, and, as though you would not come into my hands, you flee a merciless judge. Once the spirited Prophet Jonah also fled, but in the depths of the sea he was mine.

If you believed your daughter alive, you would never mourn that she had migrated to better things. This is what I had commanded through my Apostle: that you should not grieve for those who sleep, like the Gentiles. You should be ashamed: [181] you are surpassed by the compassion of a pagan woman. She, though a servant of the devil, imagines that her unbelieving husband has been transferred to heaven; you either do not believe, or do not wish to believe, that your daughter is dwelling with me.

3. But you say: How do you forbid me to mourn, when Jacob also wept for Joseph in sackcloth, and, after gathering all his relatives to himself, refused consolation, saying: “I shall descend to my son mourning into the underworld” (Gen. 37:35)? And David lamented Absalom with his head covered, repeating: “My son Absalom, Absalom, my son! Who will grant that I die for you, my son, Absalom?” (2 Sam. 18:33.) And was not solemn mourning also displayed for Moses, Aaron, and the other saints?

The answer to these questions is very easy. Jacob mourned the son whom he thought had been killed, and to whom he himself would descend into the underworld, saying: “I shall descend to my son mourning into the underworld” (Gen. 37), because Christ had not yet broken open the gates of Paradise, nor had his blood extinguished that flaming sword and the revolving movement of the Cherubim stationed there. [Note: [Col. 0469] Compare the author’s commentaries on Ecclesiastes, chapters 3 and 9, and Origen’s homily on the Ventriloquist Woman, where these matters concerning the flaming sword guarding the entrance to Paradise are explained more fully.] Hence Abraham, although he was in a place of refreshment, is nevertheless said to have been in the underworld with Lazarus (Luke 16).

And David rightly wept for his parricidal son, while he did not weep for the other little child after he had been unable to obtain his life, because he knew that the child had not sinned (2 Sam. 12). As for Moses and Aaron, that mourning was displayed for them according to ancient custom is not surprising, since, even in the Acts of the Apostles, when the Gospel was already shining forth, the brothers in Jerusalem made great mourning for Stephen (Acts 8). Certainly, “great mourning” should be understood not as the swooning or death of the mourners, as you suppose, but as the pomp of the funeral and the multitude accompanying the rites.

Finally, Scripture speaks of Jacob in this way: “Joseph went up to bury his father, and with him went all the servants of Pharaoh, and the elders of his household, and all the elders of the land of Egypt, and the whole household of Joseph and his brothers.” A little later: “With him went up chariots and horsemen, and the camp was exceedingly great.” Then: “They mourned for him with a great and very intense mourning” (Gen. 50:7 and following). This solemn mourning does not impose long tears upon the Egyptians; it displays the adornment of the funeral. In the same manner, it is clear that Aaron and Moses were also mourned.

I cannot sufficiently praise the mysteries of Scripture or admire the divine meaning contained in words that are simple enough. What does it mean that Moses is mourned, while Jesus son of Nun, a holy man, is reported as having been buried, yet no mourning is recorded? Surely it means that in Moses—that is, in the ancient Law—all were held under the condemnation of Adam’s sin, and, when they descended to the underworld, tears consequently followed them, according to the Apostle, who says: “Death reigned from Adam until Moses, even over those who had not sinned” (Rom. 5:14).

But in Jesus—that is, in the Gospel—through whom Paradise has been opened, joys accompany death. To this day the Jews weep, roll about in ashes with bare feet, and lie in sackcloth. And, so that nothing may be lacking to their superstition, following the most empty custom of the Pharisees, they take lentils as their first food, evidently showing by what dish they lost their birthright. They deserve this, because, not believing in the Lord’s resurrection, they are being prepared for the coming of Antichrist.

But we, who have put on Christ and have become, according to the Apostle, a royal and priestly race (1 Pet. 2), ought not to grieve over the dead. “And Moses said,” it says, “to Aaron and Eleazar and Ithamar, his sons who were left: You shall not uncover your heads, and you shall not tear your garments, lest you die and wrath come upon the whole congregation” (Lev. 10:6). “Do not tear your garments,” he says, “and display Gentile mourning, lest you die.” Our death is sin.

And, although it may seem cruel to some, it is necessary to faith: in the same Leviticus it is written that the high priest is forbidden to approach a dead father, mother, brothers, or children, lest the soul devoted to God’s sacrifices and wholly occupied with his mysteries be hindered by any affection.

Is not the same thing commanded in other words in the Gospel—that the disciple should not [Note: [Col. 0470] Martianaeus omits the negative particle, so that the sense becomes “that he should bid farewell,” contrary to Matthew 8:21 and to Jerome above in Epistle 23, no. 5: “The disciple wishing to return home and first bid farewell to his family is forbidden by the voice of the Master.”] bid farewell to his household, and that he should not provide burial for his dead father? “And he shall not go out from the sanctuary,” it says, “and he shall not profane the sanctification of his God, because the holy oil of his anointing from God is upon him” (Lev. 21).

Certainly, after we have believed in Christ and received the oil of his anointing, carrying him within us, we must not go out from the temple—that is, from the Christian purpose. We must not go outside, mingling with the unbelief of the Gentiles, but remain always within, that is, minister to the Lord’s will.

4. We say these things so that ignorance of Scripture might not provide you with authority for mourning and so that you might not appear to err rationally. Until now I have spoken as though I had encountered an ordinary Christian woman among the crowds. But now, since I know that you have renounced the whole world, and that, having rejected and trampled upon the pleasures of the age, you devote yourself daily to prayer, fasting, and reading; since, following Abraham’s example, you desire to leave your land and your kindred, so that, abandoning both the Chaldeans and Mesopotamia, you may enter the promised land; since you have either distributed all your small property generously to the poor or, before death, given it to your children who were already dead to the world [Note: [Col. 0471] Some read “to your daughter” and “to the deceased,” but the reading is certainly corrupt.]—I am astonished that you are doing things which, if other women did them, would seem worthy of reproach.

You recall her conversation, her endearments, her speech, her companionship, and you cannot bear to be without these things. We pardon a mother’s tears, but we seek moderation in grief. If I think of you as a parent, I do not reproach you for weeping; but if I think of you as a Christian and a nun, the mother is excluded by these names. The wound is fresh, and this touch with which I caress you heals less than it irritates. Nevertheless, what time must soften, why is it not overcome by reason?

Naomi, fleeing famine in the land of Moab, lost both her husband and her sons. When she was deprived of the support of her own people, Ruth, a foreigner, did not leave her side (Ruth 1). See how great a merit it is to have offered comfort to one who was abandoned: Christ arose from her seed.

Look at Job, how much he endured, and you will see that you are excessively delicate, while he, with his eyes raised toward heaven, amid the ruins of his house, the pains of his sores, countless bereavements, and finally his wife’s treachery, maintained unconquered patience.

I know what you will answer: that these things happened to him, as a righteous man, for the sake of testing. Then choose whichever of the two you wish: either you are holy and are being tested, or you are a sinner and complain unjustly, enduring less than you deserve.

Why should I repeat ancient examples? Follow those of the present. [Note: [Col. 0471] Recall our note on Epistle 3 to Rufinus, and especially these words from Jerome’s *Chronicle* under the year of Christ 377: “Melania, the noblest of Roman women and formerly the daughter of the consul Marcellinus, leaving behind her only son, then city praetor [thus we correct *Praetore*], sailed to Jerusalem, where she was such a marvel of virtues, especially humility, that she received the name of Thecla.” Recall also what we remarked above concerning the name Melania in Epistle 3, addressed to Rufinus, and below in Epistle 143, addressed to Alypius and Augustine.]

The holy Melania, the true nobility of the Christians of our time—may the Lord grant you and me a share with her on his day—while her husband’s body was still warm and had not yet been buried, lost two sons at once. I shall tell something incredible, but, with Christ as my witness, not false. Who would not then have expected her to behave in the manner of one distraught, with hair scattered, clothing torn, and assailing her torn breast? Not a tear fell. She stood motionless and, throwing herself at Christ’s feet as though she held him, smiled.

“I shall serve you more readily, Lord,” she said, “because you have freed me from so great a burden.”

But perhaps she was overcome in other matters. On the contrary, she proved how she despised them by what she later did with her only son: after assigning him all the property she possessed, she sailed to Jerusalem when winter was already approaching.

5. Spare yourself, I beg you; spare your daughter who now reigns with Christ; spare at least your Eustochium, whose still tender age and almost childish infancy are being guided by you as her teacher [or: “under your instruction”]. The devil rages now, and because he sees one of your children triumphing, he grieves that he has been crushed and seeks in the one who remains the victory he has already lost in the one who went before.

Great affection toward one’s own is impiety toward God. Abraham gladly kills his only son, while you complain that one of several daughters has been crowned?

I cannot utter without a groan what I am about to say. When they were carrying you, lifeless, from the middle of the funeral procession, the crowd muttered among themselves: “Is this not what we often used to say? She grieves that her daughter was killed by fasting because she did not at least preserve grandchildren for herself from a second marriage. How long will that detestable race of monks not be driven from the city? Why are they not crushed with stones? Why are they not thrown headlong into the waves? They seduced this pitiable matron; and the fact that she did not wish to be a nun is proved by this: no pagan woman ever mourned her children so much.”

What grief do you suppose Christ felt at such words? How Satan rejoiced—Satan who now hastens to snatch away your soul and, presenting you with the allurements of supposedly dutiful grief, keeps the image of your daughter continually before your eyes. He wishes at once to kill the mother of the victorious daughter and to invade the solitude of the sister who remains.

I do not speak in order to frighten you, but, as the Lord is my witness, I address these words to you as though standing before his tribunal. These tears are detestable, full of sacrilege and utterly full of unbelief; they have no measure and come close to the border of death. You howl and cry out, and, as though kindled by torches, insofar as it lies with you, you are always your own murderer. [Note: [Col. 0472] The Cistercian manuscript reads: “But to you that merciful one enters,” and so forth.]

But to such a woman the merciful Jesus enters and says: “Why are you weeping? The girl is not dead but sleeping” (Mark 5:39; Luke 8:52). Let those standing around laugh: this is the unbelief of the Jews.

If you too wish to roll about at your daughter’s tomb, the angel will rebuke you: “Why do you seek the living among the dead?” (Luke 24:5). Because Mary Magdalene had done this, after she recognized the voice of the Lord calling to her, she threw herself at his feet and heard: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father” (John 20:17)—that is, you do not deserve to touch the risen one whom you suppose to be dead in the tomb.

6. What crosses do you now imagine our Blaesilla is suffering? What torments does she endure when she sees Christ angered against you? She now cries out to you in your mourning:

“If you ever loved me, mother; if I suckled at your breasts; if I was instructed by your teachings, do not envy my glory, and do not act in such a way that we are separated from one another forever. Do you think I am alone? I have Mary, the Mother of the Lord, with me. I see here many whom I did not know before. Oh, how much better is this company! I have Anna, who once prophesied in the Gospel; and, so that you may rejoice still more, I have attained in three months the labors of so many years. We have received one palm of chastity.

“Do you pity me because I have left the world? But I grieve over your lot, you whom the prison of the world still encloses; you who fight daily in the battle line and are dragged to ruin now by anger, now by greed, now by lust, now by the incitements of various vices.

“If you wish to be my mother, take care to please Christ. I do not recognize as my mother one who displeases my Lord.”

She says many other things, which I pass over, and she prays the Lord for you. And, as I am confident [or: “as I am secure”] concerning her mind, she obtains pardon for my sins: because I admonished her, encouraged her, and endured the envy of her relatives so that she might be saved. [Note: [Col. 0472] Several printed editions and manuscripts read: “Why do you not wish to please Christ?”]

7. Therefore, as long as the spirit governs these limbs, as long as we enjoy the passage of this life, I promise, pledge, and affirm that she will resound through my tongue; my labors will be dedicated to her, and my intellect will sweat for her. No page will exist that does not sound with Blaesilla’s name. Wherever the memorials of my speech reach, she will travel abroad with my little works. Virgins, widows, monks, and priests will read of her fixed in my mind. The brief span of life will be compensated by eternal memory.

She who lives with Christ in heaven will also live in human speech. The present age will pass away, and future ages will follow, which will judge without love or envy. Her name will be placed between the names of Paula and Eustochium. She will never die in my books. I shall always hear her speaking with her sister and with her mother.

## EPISTLE XL [Note: [Col. 0473] Elsewhere numbered 100. Written at approximately the same time.]

### TO MARCELLA, CONCERNING ONASUS

He ridicules a certain detractor, Onasus, who thought that what Jerome had written in his books against vices was directed as an insult against him.

1. Physicians whom they call surgeons are thought cruel, and they are wretched. Is it not wretchedness not to grieve over the wounds of others and to cut dead flesh with an unmerciful blade? Not to shudder at what the sufferer himself shudders at, and to be regarded as an enemy? Nature is so constituted that truth is bitter, while vices are considered pleasant.

Isaiah, as an example of the captivity that was to come, walks naked without shame (Isa. 20). Jeremiah is sent from the midst of Jerusalem to the Euphrates River in Mesopotamia (Jer. 13), so that among hostile nations—where the Assyrian is and the camps of the Chaldeans are—he may place a *perizoma* (περίζωμα), a waistband [Note: [Col. 0473] Some manuscripts add the interpretation of the Greek word: “that is, a loincloth.”], destined to be ruined.

Ezekiel is ordered first to eat bread made with every kind of grain, mixed with human dung and then with cow dung (Ezek. 4:12–15), and he sees the death of his wife with dry eyes. Amos is driven out of Samaria (Amos 7). Why, I ask? Clearly, he is driven out because spiritual surgeons, cutting away the sins of sinners, exhort them to repentance. The Apostle Paul says: “I have become your enemy by telling you the truth” (Gal. 4:16). And because the Savior’s words seemed hard, many of his disciples went back.

[Col. 0474] 2. Therefore it is not surprising if we too offend many people by attacking vices. I have decided to cut off a stinking nose; let the scrofulous man beware. I want to criticize the chattering little crow; let the hoarse [or: “rancid”] crow understand that she is meant.

Is there only one person in the city of Rome who has “a mutilated nose from a dishonorable wound”? (Aeneid 6.) Is Onasus of Segesta the only one who weighs hollow words, swollen like bladders, on puffed-out cheeks? [Note: [Col. 0474] Victor, following a preconceived opinion, reads “Onasus of Segesta.” Since one Segesta was a city of Pannonia and another of Liguria, it is not easy to determine which is meant here. More probably, however, Segestum in Pannonia is intended.]

I say that certain men have attained some sort of dignity through crime, perjury, and falsehood. What is that to you, if you know yourself to be innocent? I laugh at the advocate who needs a patron. I mock with my nose an eloquence worth a farthing [Note: [Col. 0474] Another reading is “unworthy,” that is, “not worth even a farthing.”]; what is that to you, if you are eloquent?

I want to attack priests who deal in money. You who are rich—why are you angry? [Note: [Col. 0474] The Bishop of Reate reads with the negative particle: “you who are not rich”; the sense is better, but neither the manuscripts nor the other printed books support it.]

I want Vulcan, enclosed within his own fires, to burn. Are you his guest or neighbor, that you try to remove the blaze from the idol’s shrine? I enjoy laughing at ghosts, at the owl, at the horned owl, and at the monsters of the Nile. Whatever is said, you think it is said against you. Whatever vice the point of my stylus turns against, you loudly proclaim that you are being singled out.

You join battle and summon me before the court, and foolishly accuse a satirical writer of writing prose. [Note: [Col. 0474] Satire is properly composed only in verse; therefore it is foolish to call someone writing in prose a satirical writer, as though someone were to say in Italian, “a writer of sonnets in prose.” What is added—“you are called by a fortunate name”—is explained by Martianaeus as meaning that Onasus is the same as Onesimus, whom Jerome interprets in his *Book of Names* as “beautiful.” I think it more likely that the name derives from the Greek root ὁνάω, meaning “to help” or “to benefit,” so that Onasus could be rendered in Latin as *Profuturus*, “one who will benefit,” and thus be called by a fortunate name.]

Do you therefore seem handsome to yourself because you are called by a fortunate name? As though a grove (*lucus*) were not so called because it shines least of all; as though the Fates (*Parcae*) were not so called because they spare no one; as though the Eumenides were not Furies because they are not benevolent; and as though Ethiopians were not commonly called “silver men.”

But if you are always angered by descriptions of ugly things, I shall now sing to you, with Persius:

> May king and queen desire you as a son-in-law, and girls  
> > Carry you off: whatever you tread upon, may it become a rose.  
> > (Satire 2.)  
> [Note: [Col. 0474] Older printed editions and several manuscripts read: “May they desire you as a handsome son-in-law,” and so forth.]

3. Nevertheless, I shall give you advice by which, if you conceal certain things, you may appear more handsome. Let your nose not be visible on your face; let your speech not be heard when you speak. In this way you may appear both handsome and eloquent.

## EPISTLE XLI [Note: [Col. 0474] Elsewhere numbered 54. Written in the same year, 384.]

### TO MARCELLA [Note: [Col. 0474] Older printed editions and several manuscripts add: “against Montanus.”]

He refutes the doctrines of the heretic Montanus and shows the difference between his errors and the teaching of the Church.

1. You have been confronted with testimonies gathered from the Gospel of John by a certain follower of Montanus, in which our Savior promises that he will go to the Father and send the Paraclete. The Acts of the Apostles testify to the time for which these promises were made and the time at which they were fulfilled.

It states that on the tenth day after the Lord’s ascension—that is, on the fiftieth day after the resurrection—the Holy Spirit descended and the tongues of believers were divided, so that each person spoke in the language of all the nations. At that time some who still had little faith asserted that they were drunk with new wine. Peter, standing in the midst of the Apostles and of the entire assembly, said:

> “Men of Judea, and all who dwell in Jerusalem, let this be known to you, and listen to my words. For these men are not drunk, as you suppose, since it is the third hour of the day. But this is what was spoken through the Prophet Joel: ‘In the last days, says the Lord, I shall pour out from my Spirit upon all flesh; and their sons and their daughters shall prophesy; and their young men shall see visions, and their elders shall dream dreams. Indeed, upon my male servants and female servants I shall pour out from my Spirit.’”  
> (Acts 2:14 and following.)

2. The Church founded upon Peter.—If, therefore, the Apostle Peter, upon whom the Lord founded the Church, declared that both the prophecy and the Lord’s promise had been fulfilled at that time, how can we claim another time for ourselves?

And if they wish to reply that the four daughters of Philip subsequently prophesied, that the Prophet Agabus is found, that in the distribution of the Spirit among the Apostles and teachers prophets too were formed, according to the Apostle’s writing, and that the Apostle Paul himself prophesied many things concerning future heresies and the end of the age, let them know that we do not so much reject prophecy—which has been marked out by the Lord’s passion—as refuse to accept those who do not agree with the authority of both the Old and the New Scripture.

3. First, we disagree in the rule of faith. [Note: [Col. 0475] Others deny this, among them St. Epiphanius, *Against Heresies* 2.48, concerning the Cataphrygians or Montanists. He explicitly states that they “hold the same doctrine concerning the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit as the Catholic Church.” But there were two Montanist sects, one called according to Proclus and the other according to Aeschines. Jerome must be understood as referring to the latter, which, as we learn from Tertullian, *On the Prescription Against Heretics*, chapter 52, blasphemously asserted that Jesus Christ was both Father and Son.]

We place the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, each in his own person, although we unite them in substance. They, following the doctrine of Sabellius, compress the Trinity into the narrow limits of a single person.

We do not so much desire second marriages as permit them, since Paul commands that young widows should marry. They consider repeated marriages so criminal that whoever does this is regarded as an adulterer.

We fast one Lent, in accordance with the tradition of the Apostles and in harmony with the whole world. [Note: [Col. 0475] Martianaeus suspects that Erasmus read “throughout the whole year,” a reading also found in other earlier printed editions and in several manuscripts. I do not know which reading is more accurate. Meanwhile, it is especially noteworthy that Jerome says that the fasts established by the Apostles—and observed from necessity, not from personal choice—are those prescribed for Lent. Caesarius of Arles expresses this very clearly: “On other days, to fast is either a remedy or a reward; in Lent, not to fast is a sin,” and so forth.]

They make three Lents in the year, as though three Saviors had suffered. This is not to say that it is impermissible to fast throughout the entire year, except during Pentecost; [Col. 0476] rather, offering a gift from necessity is one thing, and offering it voluntarily is another.

Among us, bishops hold the place of the Apostles; among them, a bishop is third. They have as their first rank the Patriarchs of Pepuza in Phrygia [Note: [Col. 0476] Pepuza was an obscure town in Phrygia, completely ruined in Jerome’s own time, where the Cataphrygians, also called Pepuzians after it, assembled. Epiphanius likewise mentions it in *Against Heresies* 48.14 and calls it “a certain deserted place in Phrygia, once called the city of Pepuza,” and so forth.]; second, those whom they call Cenonas [Note: [Col. 0476] Some manuscripts read *Zenonos* instead of *Cenonas*; one manuscript of the Bononian monastery of St. Savior reads *Cenonos*; others, including the manuscripts cited by Victor, read *Iconomos*. It should therefore be considered whether the word ought to be read as οἰκονόμοι, from the Greek, meaning “stewards,” so that priests of the second order were called administrators, just as the first were patriarchs and the third bishops. We are entirely ignorant of what *Cenones* might be as a word or what it might mean.]; and thus bishops are relegated to the third—that is, almost the lowest—place, as though their religion became more ambitious if what is first among us is last among them.

They almost entirely shut the doors of the Church against every offense. We, however, read daily: “I desire the repentance of the sinner rather than his death” (Ezek. 18:23). And: “Shall not the one who falls rise again? says the Lord” (Jer. 8:4). And: “Turn back to me, rebellious children, and I will heal your rebellions” (Jer. 3:22, according to the Septuagint).

They are rigid—not because they themselves do not commit worse sins, but because this is the difference between us and them: they are ashamed to confess their sins, as though they were righteous; while we, when we practice repentance, more readily obtain pardon.

4. I pass over the wicked rites that are said to concern a suckling child, [Note: Earlier, as though the discussion concerned two separate persons or rites, the preposition *de* (“concerning”) was repeated. See also St. Augustine, *On Heresies*, on the Cataphrygians; the author of the *Praedestinatus*, Heresy 26; and others. Nevertheless, to put it in a word, some authors either deny that these and other wicked rites—concerning an infant pierced through with tiny punctures, who would have been regarded as a high priest had he lived, and as a martyr had he died—along with certain other doctrines reported above by Jerome, are truly to be attributed to the Montanists, or deliberately pass over them as uncertain.] and said to be compounded with a martyr who was to live. I would rather, I say, not believe it: let everything involving blood be false.

The manifest blasphemy of those who say that God first wished to save the world in the Old Testament through Moses and the Prophets, but because he was unable to accomplish this, took a body from a Virgin and, preaching in Christ under the appearance of the Son, suffered death for us, must be exposed. And because he could not save the world through two stages, they say that finally he descended through the Holy Spirit upon Montanus, Prisca, and Maximilla, insane women, declaring the fullness that Paul did not possess when he said: “We know in part, and we prophesy in part” (1 Cor. 13:9), and, “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma” (1 Cor. 13:12)—and that Montanus was cut off and half a man.

These are matters that require no refutation: to expose their faithlessness is already to overcome it. Nor is it necessary for the shorter discourse of a letter to overturn each of the ravings they put forward, since you yourself, possessing the Scriptures thoroughly, have been moved not so much by their questions as by your desire to learn from me what I think.

## LETTER XLII

[Note: Also numbered 149; written around the same year, 384.]

### TO MARCELLA

Against the Novatian heretics.

[Col. 0477]

In reply to Marcella’s question about what it means to speak against the Holy Spirit, he answers, showing that Novatian’s interpretation is false.

1. The question you sent is brief, and the answer is clear. If, then, concerning what is written in the Gospel—“Whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven; but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come” (Matt. 12:32; Mark 3:29)—Novatian maintains that no one can sin against the Holy Spirit except one who is a Christian and later denies it, it is evident that the Jews who were blaspheming at that time were not held guilty of the sin of blasphemy. For they were impious tenants who, after killing the Prophets, were plotting the Lord’s death, and were so lost that the Son of God declared that he had come in order to save them.

Therefore, from the entire sequence of Scripture he must be convicted that the blasphemy called unforgivable was not spoken of those who, compelled by tortures and torn apart by various sufferings, denied the Lord, but of those who, while seeing the works of God in his miracles, slandered them and loudly declared that the power belonged to a demon, and that all the signs performed belonged not to divine majesty but to the devil (Matt. 12; Mark 3; Luke 11).

Thus our Savior’s entire argument is directed toward teaching that Satan cannot be cast out by Satan, and that his kingdom is not divided against itself. Since the devil’s purpose is to injure God’s creature, how could it be his will to heal the sick and drive himself from possessed bodies? Let Novatian therefore prove that one of those who were compelled to sacrifice before a judge’s tribunal declared that everything written in the Gospel had been accomplished not by the Son of God but by Beelzebub, the prince of demons. Then he will be able to establish that blasphemy against the Holy Spirit is unforgivable.

2. But let us ask something more pointedly: let him explain what it means to speak against the Son of Man and to blaspheme against the Holy Spirit. For, following his interpretation, I maintain that those who denied Christ during the persecution spoke against the Son of Man and did not blaspheme against the Holy Spirit.

When someone is asked whether he is a Christian and answers that he is not, by denying Christ—that is, the Son of Man—he certainly does not insult the Holy Spirit. But if, by denying Christ, he also denied the Spirit, let the heretic explain how one who denied the Son of Man does not sin against the Spirit. Or if he thinks that “the Holy Spirit” in this passage should be understood as the Father, the denier made no mention of the Father when he denied him.

When the Apostle Peter, terrified at the servant girl’s questioning, denied the Lord, did he sin against the Son of Man or against the Holy Spirit? If he wishes absurdly to interpret Peter’s words, “I do not know the man,” as meaning that he did not deny Christ but merely “the man,” he will make the Savior a liar, since the Savior had foretold that he—that is, the Son of God—would be denied (Matt. 26; John 13).

But if Peter denied the Son of God, why did he weep bitterly, and why did he erase his threefold denial by a threefold confession afterward? It is clear that sin against the Holy Spirit cannot be forgiven because it contains blasphemy: when one sees God in the works of power, one slanders those deeds as belonging to Beelzebub.

Let him therefore show us a denier who called Christ Beelzebub, and I will go further and affirm that a denier cannot obtain forgiveness after his fall. It is one thing to yield to tortures and deny oneself to be a Christian; it is another thing to call Christ the devil, as Scripture itself and its context, read more attentively, will be able to demonstrate. [Alternative reading: “were able to demonstrate.”]

3. The discussion ought indeed to have been longer; but since we cannot refuse our presence to the friends who have gathered at our little lodging, and since it seemed exceedingly arrogant not to answer you immediately, we have compressed an extensive argument into a brief discourse, so that what we dictated would be not so much a Letter as a little commentary.

## LETTER XLIII

[Note: Also numbered 18; written around 385.]  
[Note: Consult the later chronological notes in the Preface to Letter XXXIV.]

### TO MARCELLA

He urges Marcella, after leaving Rome, to withdraw to the countryside, showing by contrast both how many troubles Rome contains and how many advantages solitude offers.

1. Ambrose—who supplied the paper, expenses, and secretaries—reports in a certain Letter that our Adamantius, our man of bronze, explained so many countless books. [Note: Here Ambrose is called “first a Marcionite, then corrected by Origen, a deacon of the Church, and distinguished by the glory of confessing the Lord” in the *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 56. Since “through his industry, expense, and infinite persistence Origen dictated volumes,” he was called Origen’s *ergodióktēs*—that is, the one who drove him to his labors. Jerome, however, seems to err through a lapse of memory when he attributes this Letter to Ambrose concerning Origen’s arduous labor, since a fragment of the adamantine Origen’s Letter to someone about Ambrose survives, reporting the contrary. Yet I fear that the attribution may itself be false.]

Ambrose says that he never took food in Origen’s presence without reading, and never went to sleep unless one of the brothers was reciting the sacred writings. He did this by day and by night, so that reading might give way to prayer and prayer to reading.

2. What have we, creatures of the belly, ever done like that? If he finds us reading even at the second hour, we yawn; rubbing our faces with our hands, we hold back our stomachs; and, as though after great labor, we again occupy ourselves with worldly business. I pass over the banquets by which the burdened mind is weighed down.

I am ashamed to mention the stream of greetings: either we ourselves go every day to visit others, or we wait for the others who come to us. Then conversation begins; time is worn away in talk; those who are absent are torn apart; other people’s lives are described; and by biting one another, we consume one another. Such is the food that occupies and dismisses us.

When our friends have departed, we calculate accounts. Now anger puts the appearance of a lion upon us [alternative: “imposes it upon us”]; now needless anxiety plans for many years to come. We do not remember the Gospel, which says: “Fool, this night your soul will be required of you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?” (Luke 12:20).

Clothes are sought not merely for use but for luxury. Wherever there is profit, the foot is quicker, speech more rapid, and the ear more attentive. If a loss has been reported—as often happens in household affairs—the face is weighed down with grief. We rejoice over a coin and grieve over a small piece of money. [Note: Victorius and other older editions read “we grieve after losing a small coin,” but the manuscripts do not support the former wording.]

Since, then, in one person the appearance of the mind is so varied, the Prophet begs the Lord, saying: “Lord, destroy their image in your city” (Ps. 72:20). For although we were created in the image and likeness of God, through our fault we put many masks upon ourselves.

Just as on the theatrical stage one and the same actor, now robust, displays Hercules, now softens into Venus, now trembles as Cybele, so we—who, if we were not of the world, would be hated by the world—have as many likenesses of masks as we have sins. [Note: Martinaeus reads, with no equivalent or with a sense contrary to Jerome’s, “we have as many likenesses of sins,” etc. We have restored *masks* from other editions and manuscripts.]

3. Therefore, since we have already passed through many stretches of life by drifting, and our ship has been shaken now by the whirlwind of storms, now pierced by the deceitfulness of reefs [alternative: “disturbed”], let us enter, as soon as possible, some kind of harbor in the seclusion of the countryside.

There, bread for food, vegetables watered by our own hands, and milk—the luxuries of the country—will provide humble but innocent nourishment [alternative: “may provide”]. Living in this way, neither sleep will call us away from prayer nor fullness from reading.

If it is summer, the shade of a secluded tree will provide shelter. If autumn, the very mildness of the air and the leaves spread beneath us will offer a place of rest. In spring the field is painted with flowers, and amid the complaining birds the Psalms will be sung more sweetly. If there is cold and winter snow, I shall not buy firewood, and I shall keep vigil—or sleep—more warmly. At least, so far as I know, I shall not be cold more cheaply.

Let Rome keep its own disturbances; let the arena rage, the circus go mad, the theaters luxuriate, and—since we must speak of our own people—let the senate of married women be visited every day.

“For us it is good to cling to the Lord and to place our hope in the Lord God” (Ps. 72), so that when the kingdoms of heaven exchange this poverty for something else, we may cry out: “For what have I in heaven, and besides you what have I desired upon earth?” Then, when we find such great things in heaven, we shall grieve that we sought small and perishable things on earth. [Note: In the old editions there is here an encomium of Bethel, beginning “But, to return to the little villa of Christ.” The comparison between the villa and Rome continues to this point, including, as it is commonly called, love songs. The same words occur in the Letter of Paula and Eustochium to Marcella, which we shall place shortly below as Letter 46; there is no doubt that they were transferred from there because of the similarity of subject.]

Farewell.

## LETTER XLIV

[Note: Also numbered 20; written around the same time as the preceding Letter.]

### TO MARCELLA

On gifts.

He interprets allegorically and jokingly the little gifts sent by Marcella to himself, Paula, and her daughter Eustochium.

To console the absence of our bodies by the companionship of the Spirit, each of us does what he can. You send gifts; we send back Letters of thanks. Yet, since the gifts belong to veiled virgins, we shall show that certain mysteries are contained in the gifts themselves.

The sackcloth is a sign of prayer and fasting. The chairs are so that the virgin may not move her feet outside. The candles are so that, with the light kindled, the bridegroom’s arrival may be awaited. The cups signify the mortification of the flesh and a soul always prepared for martyrdom. “For the cup of the Lord, how splendid it is, making one drunk” (Ps. 22:5).

But the little fly-swatters that you also offer to the married women, for driving away small animals, are an elegant indication that luxury must quickly be extinguished, since flies destined to die destroy the oil they have contaminated. [Note: The same Veronese manuscript reads “we offer equal things to small animals to be fanned away” [perhaps *ventilabra*]. From this one may infer that both the printed and manuscript readings contain several errors, although we do not sufficiently understand how the passage should be restored. See the chronological notes.]

This is the type for virgins; this is the figure for married women. As for us, although in an inverted sense, your gifts suit us: sitting is appropriate for the idle, lying in a sack for penitents, and possessing cups for drinkers. And, because of nighttime fears and souls always apprehensive because of a bad conscience, it is also pleasant to have lit candles.

## LETTER XLV

[Note: Also numbered 99; written in August 385.]

### TO ASELLA

As he is about to leave Rome by ship, he clears himself of the slanders of his detractors, among whom he had incurred great hatred because he had drawn Paula and Eustochium, prominent women, to the monastic way of life.

1. If I think that I can give you thanks, I am not wise. God is able, in regard to my person, to restore to your holy soul what it deserves. For I, unworthy as I am, could never estimate or desire that you should grant me so great an affection in Christ.

And although some consider me wicked, buried beneath every disgrace, and think that even these small faults are insignificant compared with my sins, you do well to regard even the wicked as good according to your own mind. It is dangerous to judge another’s servant (Rom. 14:4), and forgiveness is not easily obtained for speaking evil of what is good. That day will come—yes, it will come—when you will grieve with me that not a few are burning.

2. I am disgraceful, deceitful, and slippery; I am a liar, deceiving through Satan’s art. What is safer: to have believed these things about the innocent, or invented them, or even to have refused to believe them about the guilty?

Some kissed my hands and slandered me with a viper’s mouth; they grieved with their lips but rejoiced in their hearts. The Lord saw and mocked them, and reserved me, his wretched servant, for judgment with them in the future. One slandered my gait and my laughter; another disparaged my face; another suspected something else in my simplicity.

For almost three years, certainly, I lived among them. A great crowd of virgins frequently surrounded me. I often explained the divine Books to some of them as I was able. Reading had created constancy, constancy familiarity, and familiarity confidence.

Let them say what they ever perceived in me that was not fitting for a Christian. Did I accept anyone’s money? Did I refuse gifts, small or great? Did anyone’s bronze coin ring in my hand? Was there crooked speech or a wanton glance? Nothing is alleged against me except my sex, and this is never alleged except when Paula departs for Jerusalem. [Note: Victorius errs when he adds “and Melania,” who had departed long before Paula, as we noted above in Letter 39, concerning the death of Blesilla.]

Granted that they believed a liar: why do they not believe one who denies it? The man himself is the same as before. He now declares innocent the man whom he was recently describing as guilty; and certainly tortures express the truth more clearly than laughter—unless it is simply that what is invented is more readily believed when it is gladly heard, or that what is not invented is driven toward being treated as invention.

3. Before I knew the house of the holy Paula, the enthusiasm of the entire city was united in my favor. By almost everyone’s judgment I was considered worthy of the highest priesthood. Damasus of blessed memory was the theme of my conversation. I was called holy; I was called humble and eloquent.

Did I ever enter the house of some more wanton woman? Did silk garments, shining jewels, painted faces, or the allure of gold ever captivate me? There was no other matron in Rome who could subdue my mind except one who mourned and fasted, rough with filth, almost blinded by tears, whom the sun repeatedly found during the nights imploring the Lord’s mercy.

Her song was the Psalm; her speech, the Gospel; her delight, self-restraint; her life, fasting. No other woman could delight me except one whom I never saw eating. But after I began to venerate, honor, and admire her because of the merit of her chastity, all my virtues immediately abandoned me.

4. O envy, the first to gnaw at yourself! O cunning of Satan, always persecuting holy people! No others furnished Rome with a subject for gossip except Paula and Melania, who, despising their possessions and abandoning their children, raised the cross of the Lord like a banner of devotion.

If they had sought baths, chosen perfumes, possessed riches and widowhood as material for luxury and freedom, they would be called ladies—and holy women. [Note: Jerome frequently counts visiting baths among the enticements of softness and particularly forbids them to women. The Benedictine editor read *Baiae* here instead of *baths*, a reading that I do not reject despite the resistance of the manuscripts. For the ancients called other places of pleasure and estates *Baiae*, from the name of the most pleasant and famous town in Campania; Cicero likewise says in his speech *For Caelius*: “Into whose gardens, house, and Baiae the lusts of all would rightly make their way.” A few manuscripts somewhat later read “the material of luxurious freedom” instead of “of luxury and freedom.”]

Now they wish to appear beautiful in sackcloth and ashes, and to descend into the fire of Gehenna with fasts and filth—as though they were not permitted to perish amid crowds while the people applauded.

If Gentiles attacked this way of life, if Jews did so, there would be consolation in displeasing those who displease Christ. But now—shameful to say!—Christian men, neglecting the beam in their own eye, seek a speck in another’s eye. They tear apart a holy purpose and consider it a remedy for their own punishment if no one is holy; if everyone is slandered; if there is a crowd of the perishing; if there is a multitude of sinners.

5. You take pleasure in washing every day; another regards these cleansings as filth. You belch up a partridge and boast of having eaten sturgeon; [Note: Apicius praises the partridge in book 6, chapter 3. Pliny mentions the sturgeon in book 9, chapter 17. Athenaeus, *Deipnosophistae*, book 7, says: “Archestratus, who lived the life of Sardanapalus, when speaking of the Rhodian shark, thinks it is the fish that the Romans call sturgeon [Greek: *akkipēsion*], and which they carry around at banquets with flutes and crowns, even crowning those who carry it. But the sturgeon is smaller and has a longer snout,” and so forth.] I fill my stomach with beans. [Note: Gravius reports that elsewhere *itiba* is read, for which he would prefer *stoecha*, concerning which see Pliny, book 21, chapters 15 and 22.]

You delight in flocks of laughing people; I delight in Paula and Melania mourning. [Note: Formerly the text read “Melanius”; see the preceding note on Letter 3 and the note on Letter 143 to Alypius and Augustine.] You desire what belongs to others; they despise what belongs to themselves. Wines smeared with honey delight you; they drink cold water, finding it sweeter.

You think yourself ruined by whatever you have not possessed, eaten, or devoured in the present; they desire future things and believe that what is written is true. Granted, they are foolish and empty-headed because they have been persuaded of the resurrection of bodies—what is that to you?

Conversely, we dislike your life. May you be fat for your own good; I take pleasure in thinness and pallor. You consider such people wretched; we consider you more wretched. Like answers like, and we each seem insane to the other.

6. My lady Asella, I wrote these things hastily, weeping and grieving, when I was already boarding the ship. I give thanks to my God that I am worthy to be hated by the world.

Pray, however, that I may return from Babylon to Jerusalem, so that Nebuchadnezzar may not rule over me, but Jesus the son of Josedec. May Ezra come—his name means “helper”—[Note: The words “who is interpreted as helper,” which greatly support Jerome’s purpose, were lacking in Erasmus and Martianaeus. We have restored them from manuscript codices and an older edition, together with Victorius.] and lead me back to my homeland.

I was foolish to wish to sing the Song of the Lord in a foreign land and, after abandoning Mount Sinai, to seek the help of Egypt (Jer. 42). I did not remember the Gospel, which says that the one who leaves Jerusalem immediately falls among thieves; he is stripped, wounded, and killed.

But although the priest and the Levite despise him, that merciful Samaritan is present (Luke 10). When he was told, “You are a Samaritan and have a demon” (John 8), he rejected the demon but did not deny that he was a Samaritan, because the one whom we call a guardian the Hebrews call a Samaritan.

Some babble that I am a sorcerer; as a servant I acknowledge the title of faith. They call him a magician, and the Jews call my Lord one. He was called both deceiver and Apostle. “Let no temptation seize me except what is human” (1 Cor. 10).

What part of my troubles have I suffered, I who serve the cross? They charged me with the disgrace of a false accusation; but I know that through good and bad repute one reaches the kingdoms of heaven.

[Col. 0484] 7. Greet Paula and Eustochium, whether the world wishes it or not, my own in Christ. Greet their mother Albina, their sister Marcella, also Marcellina and holy Felicitas, and tell them: “Before the tribunal of Christ we shall stand together; there it will appear with what intention each person has lived.”

Remember me, example of modesty and distinction of virginity, and calm the waves of the sea by your prayers.

## THIRD CLASS

Containing the Letters written from the monastery at Bethlehem from the year 386 until the end of the fourth century, and Origen, condemned at the Alexandrian Synod in the year 400.

[Col. 0483]

## LETTER XLVI

[Note: Also numbered 17; written around 386.]

### PAULA AND EUSTOCHIUM TO MARCELLA

On the holy places.

[Col. 0483]

Paula and her daughter Eustochium, after arriving at the holy places, urge Marcella to leave Rome and migrate to them at Bethlehem, where she will enjoy all the memorials of Christ in the places where most of the mysteries of our religion were accomplished.

1. Love has no measure, impatience knows no limit, and desire cannot endure. Therefore, forgetting our own strength and thinking only of what we want, we desire to teach our teacher as pupils—and, as the common proverb says, “the sow Minerva,” that is, the sow teaching the goddess of wisdom.

You who first applied a spark to our tinder, who encouraged us to this pursuit both by speech and by example, and who gathered us like a hen gathering her chicks under her wings (Matt. 23)—will you now allow us to fly freely without our mother, to fear the hawk, and to tremble at every shadow cast by birds flying overhead?

Therefore, the only thing we can do while absent, we pour forth plaintive prayers; and we testify to our desire not so much with tears as with wailing, asking you to restore our Marcella to us. Do not allow that gentle, sweet woman, sweeter than every honey and sweetness, to be harsh and wrinkle her brow in sadness among those whom, by her graciousness, she provoked to pursue a similar life.

2. Certainly, if the things we request are better, our desire is not shameless. If all the voices of Scripture agree with our judgment, we are not acting boldly when we urge you toward those things to which you so often urged us.

The first word of God to Abraham was: “Go out,” he said, “from your land and from your kindred, and go into the land that I will show you” (Gen. 12:1). The Patriarch, to whom the first promise concerning Christ was made, is commanded to leave the Chaldeans, to leave the city of confusion and Rehoboth—that is, its expanses. [Note: Some manuscripts more correctly read the plural *expanses* instead of the singular *breadth*, as in earlier editions.]

He is commanded to leave the plain of Shinar, where a tower raised in pride reaches toward heaven; and, after the storms of this age, after the rivers beside which the saints sat and wept when they remembered Zion, after the mighty whirlpool of Chebar, from which Ezekiel was lifted by the hair of his head and carried all the way to Jerusalem, to inhabit the promised land.

That land is not watered from below like Egypt, but from above. It does not produce vegetables as food for the feeble, but awaits from heaven the early and the latter rain. This land is mountainous and set on high; to the extent that it is free from the delights of the world, it possesses greater delights of the spirit.

Indeed, Mary the mother of the Lord, after the angel’s promise had been made to her and she understood that her womb was to be the house of the Son of God, left the lowlands and went to the hill country.

From this city, after the foreign enemy had once been overcome and the audacity of the devil’s forehead struck, after he fell headlong upon his face, a crowd of exultant souls proceeded; and a choir singing in the tens of thousands proclaimed the victory of our David.

In this place the angel, holding a sword and laying waste the entire city of impiety, marked out the Lord’s temple on the threshing floor of Ornan, king of the Jebusites. Even then he signified that the Church of Christ would arise not in Israel but among the nations.

Return to Genesis, and you will find Melchizedek, king of Salem, prince of this city. [Note: Jerome maintains that this was not the Salem later called Jerusalem, but another town of that name near Scythopolis, of which Melchizedek was king, in the Letter to Evangelus discussed below. Paula and Eustochium state here the more common opinion, and elsewhere too they differ from the views of St. Jerome.] Even then, as a type of Christ, he offered bread and wine and consecrated the Christian mystery in the blood and body of the Savior.

3. Perhaps silently you will criticize us for not following the order of Scripture, but for proceeding randomly, as though a turbulent discourse were touching upon whatever happens to come before it. At the beginning we testified that love has no order and impatience knows no measure. Hence in the Song of Songs the difficult command is given: “Set love in order within me” (Song 2:4). We now say the same thing: we have wandered not through ignorance but through affection. [Col. 0485]

Therefore, since we are about to present something much more disordered, we must return to earlier matters. In this city—or rather, in this very place at that time—Adam is said both to have lived and to have died.

Hence the place where our Lord was crucified is called Golgotha, because there the skull of the ancient man was buried, so that the second Adam—that is, the blood of Christ dripping from the cross—might wash away the sins of the first Adam, the prostrate first-formed man. [Note: The reference is to the interpretation of the name Adam found in Greek fragments concerning Hebrew names: “Adam, blood,” with the preference for the nominative “blood,” the initial letter *a* being excluded and only the remaining *dam* being explained. Hence earlier editions are not entirely correct when they read *of the second* instead of *the second*, and *and* instead of *that is.*]

Then the Apostle’s saying would be fulfilled: “Awake, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you” (Eph. 5:14).

It would take too long to enumerate how many Prophets and how many holy men this city produced. The whole mystery of our faith is native to this province and city. It demonstrates faith in the three names of the Trinity. It is called Jebus, Salem, and Jerusalem: the first name means “trodden down,” the second “peace,” and the third “vision of peace.”

Little by little we reach the end, and after being trampled down we are raised to the vision of peace. From that peace Solomon—that is, “peaceful”—was born there, and “his place was made in peace” (Ps. 75). In a figure of Christ, under the etymology of the city’s name, the Lord of lords and King of kings received his name.

What shall we say about David and his entire lineage, which reigned in this city? As Judea surpasses the other provinces, so this city surpasses all of Judea. And, to speak more briefly, the glory of the whole province is claimed by its capital; whatever praise belongs to the limbs is all referred to the head.

4. The very tips of the letters sense that you have long been wishing to break into speech, and the page understands the question approaching. You will answer and say that this was once the case, when “the Lord loved the gates of Zion above all the dwellings of Jacob” (Ps. 86), and its foundations were in the holy mountains—although these things too can be interpreted more profoundly.

But after that voice of the rising Lord thundered: “Your house will be left to you desolate” (Matt. 23:38), and he prophetically lamented its ruin, saying: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, which kills the Prophets and stones those who are sent to you! How often I wanted to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were unwilling. Behold, your house will be left to you desolate” (Luke 13:34–35);

and after the veil of the Temple was torn, Jerusalem was surrounded by an army, and polluted with the Lord’s blood, then even the protection of the angels and the grace of Christ departed from it.

Indeed, Josephus, who is a native Jewish writer, [Note: It is tiresome to point out again this error, which we noted in the Letter to Damasus concerning the Seraphim and elsewhere, where we showed that Jerome had attributed Eusebius to Josephus.] asserts that at the time when the Lord was crucified, voices burst forth from the inner sanctuaries of the Temple of the heavenly Powers, saying: “Let us depart from these dwellings” (Josephus, *The Jewish War*, book 6, chapter 5).

From these and other facts it is clear that where grace abounded, sin abounded even more. After the Apostles heard, “Go and teach all nations” (Matt. 28:19), the Apostles themselves said: “It was necessary that the word of God be announced to you first; but since you were unwilling, behold, we are turning to the nations” (Acts 13:46). At that point, through the Apostles, the entire mystery of Judea and its ancient intimacy with God was transferred to the nations.
