5. The question is indeed a serious one, and one capable of shaking even those who have touched something of the Scriptures; but it is very easily resolved. The Lord would never have wept over Jerusalem as it was falling unless he loved it. He also wept over Lazarus because he loved him.

But understand this at the outset: the sin belonged not to the place but to the people. Yet because the killing of the people is the captivity of the city, the city was destroyed so that the people might be punished; and the Temple was overthrown so that the typological sacrifices might be removed.

As for the place itself, however, through the progress of the ages it is now far more glorious [alternative: “far narrower”] than it was before. Formerly the Jews venerated the Holy of Holies because the Cherubim, the mercy seat, the Ark of the covenant, the manna, Aaron’s staff, and the golden altar were there.

Does the Lord’s tomb not seem more venerable to you? Whenever we enter it, we see the Savior lying in the shroud; and after remaining there a little while, we again see the angel sitting at his feet and the folded cloth at his head.

We know that the glory of this tomb, long before it was hewn out by Joseph, was prophesied in Isaiah’s prediction: “And his resting place will be honor” (Isa. 11, according to the Septuagint)—that is, the place of the Lord’s burial would be honored by all.

### 6

“But,” you will say, “how do we read in the Apocalypse of John: ‘And the beast that rises from the abyss will kill them’”—there can be no doubt that these are the Prophets—“and their bodies will lie in the streets of the great city, which is spiritually called Sodom and Egypt, where their Lord was also crucified” (Rev. 11:7–8, 13 and following)?

[Note: Incorrectly, following Erasmus, the Benedictine editor reads, “For thus you say.” All manuscripts and most printed editions have the reading we have given. Gravius orders that it be read more seriously: “For if, as he says, it is a city,” etc.]

“If,” you say, “the great city in which the Lord was crucified is none other than Jerusalem; but where the Lord was crucified, it is spiritually called Sodom and Egypt; therefore Jerusalem is Sodom and Egypt, in which the Lord was crucified.”

First, we want you to know that all Holy Scripture cannot contradict itself, and especially that one book cannot disagree with itself; and, to say even more, that one passage of the same book cannot disagree with itself.

[Note: Gravius reads and punctuates this differently: “the passage in the Apocalypse about which you are now speaking,” etc.]

For in the Apocalypse, from which you have just produced this testimony, approximately ten verses earlier it is written: “Rise and measure the temple of God, and the altar, and those who worship in it. But cast out the court that is outside the temple and do not measure it, because it has been given to the nations, and they will trample upon the holy city for forty-two months” (Rev. 11:1–2).

If the Apocalypse was written by John long after the Lord’s Passion, and in it Jerusalem is called the holy city, how can it again be called spiritually Sodom and Egypt? Nor can you immediately say that the holy Jerusalem mentioned here is the heavenly Jerusalem that is to come, while the Sodom that fell is the city being named; for the passage speaks of the future beast that will rise from the abyss, wage war against the two prophets, overcome and kill them, and leave their bodies lying in the street of the great city.

Concerning this city, at the end of the same book it is written: “And the city is set foursquare, and its length and breadth are as great as its height. And he measured the city with a golden reed”—[Note: The word “golden” is absent from the Cistercian manuscript and from several others; nor is it found in the Greek copies]—“twelve thousand stadia. Its length and breadth and height are equal. And he measured its wall, one hundred and forty-four cubits, the measure of a man, which is that of an angel. And the structure of its wall was of jasper. The city itself was of pure gold,” and so forth.

Where there is a square, neither length nor breadth can properly be distinguished. And what kind of measurement is this, in which its length and breadth are as great as its height, its walls are of jasper, the whole city is of pure gold, its foundations and streets are of precious stones, and its twelve gates gleam with pearls?

### 7

Since these things cannot be understood literally—for it is absurd to proclaim that a city twelve thousand stadia long and broad is also twelve thousand stadia high—each detail must be understood spiritually. The great city, which Cain first built and named after his son, is to be understood as this world. The devil, the accuser of his brothers and the fratricide destined to perish, built it with vices, founded it upon crimes, and filled it with iniquity. It is spiritually called Sodom and Egypt.

[Note: Paula and Eustochium, I think, had written “which she saw (namely, Saint John’s) earlier,” etc.; the two words *saw* and *and* were evidently easily changed into one. Certainly the manuscripts read *saw*; I would prefer their reading if they also added the conjunction *and*. Victorius preferred *first* in place of *earlier*.]

Concerning that Sodom it is written: “Sodom will be restored to its former state”—that is, the world will be restored to what it was before. For we cannot believe that Sodom and the others—Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboiim—will be built again; rather, they are to be left in perpetual ashes.

We never read of Egypt as referring to Jerusalem, but always as referring to this world. And because it would take too long to gather countless examples from Scripture, let us offer one testimony in which this world is most clearly called Egypt.

[Note: We read from the Cistercian manuscript, “in the Catholic Epistle.” Only much later, and in Cassiodorus’s age, were those seven epistles called by that name. Jerome certainly never said “Canonical,” but always “Catholic,” as we do not doubt that these disciples of his did as well.]

In the Catholic Epistle, Jude the Apostle, brother of James, writes: “But I wish to remind you, though you know all things once for all, that Jesus, having saved the people from the land of Egypt, afterward destroyed those who did not believe” (Jude 5).

And lest you think that this refers to Jesus the son of Nun, he immediately continues: “And the angels who did not keep their own principality, but abandoned their dwelling, he has kept in eternal bonds under darkness for the judgment of the great day.”

And so that you may understand that wherever Egypt, Sodom, and Gomorrah are mentioned together, it is not places but this world that is being interpreted, he immediately adds an example: “Just as Sodom and Gomorrah and the neighboring cities, having fornicated in like manner and gone after other flesh, have been set forth as an example, undergoing the punishment of eternal fire.”

And why is it necessary to seek further evidence, when the Evangelist Matthew records, after the Passion and Resurrection of the Lord: “And the rocks were split, and the tombs were opened, and many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep arose; and coming out of the tombs after his resurrection, they entered the holy city and appeared to many” (Matt. 27:51 and following)?

[Note: Nevertheless, Jerome himself, their teacher, holds this opinion, both elsewhere and especially in Letter 60 to Heliodorus, §3. In connection with that passage we shall also cite other Fathers—Origen, Hilary, Rufinus, and others—who taught that the bodies of those who had fallen asleep were seen not in the earthly but in “the heavenly Jerusalem.”]

Nor is the heavenly Jerusalem to be understood here, as most absurdly suppose, since there could have been no sign among human beings of the Lord’s resurrection if the bodies of the saints were seen in the heavenly Jerusalem.

Since, then, both the Evangelists and all the Scriptures call Jerusalem the holy city, and the Psalmist commands us to worship in the place where his feet stood (Ps. 131), do not allow it to be called Sodom and Egypt—the city by which the Lord forbids us to swear, because it is the city of the great King.

[Note: The same manuscript, from which we have just supplied the words “in the place,” reads: “do not allow her to be called,” etc.]

### 8

They call the land accursed because it drank in the Lord’s blood. And how do they regard as blessed the places in which Peter and Paul, commanders of the Christian army, shed their blood for Christ? If the confession of servants and human beings is glorious, why should the confession of the Lord and God not be glorious?

Everywhere we venerate the tombs of the martyrs, and, placing the holy ash before our eyes, if permitted, we even touch it with our mouths; yet some consider the monument in which the Lord was buried deserving of neglect?

[Note: Saint Gaudentius, Sermon on the Day of the Dedication of the Basilica of the Forty Martyrs: “We have taken a portion of the relics, and are confident that we possess no less, while in their ashes we honor and embrace the whole forty.” Pliny explains the term in Book 19, chapter 1, concerning what he calls “living linen”: “The funeral tunics of kings,” he says, “separate the body’s ashes from the remaining ash.”]

If we do not believe us, let us at least believe the devil and his angels. Whenever they are driven out of possessed bodies before that monument, they tremble and roar as though standing in the presence of Christ’s tribunal, and too late regret having crucified the one whom they fear.

If, after the Lord’s Passion—as that wicked voice cries out—this place is detestable, what did Paul intend by hastening to Jerusalem to keep Pentecost there? When those who resisted him tried to dissuade him, he said: “What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart? For I am ready not only to be bound but also to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus” (Acts 21:13).

What of all the other holy and distinguished men whose vows and offerings, after Christ had been preached, were carried to the brothers who were in Jerusalem?

### 9

It would take too long now to pass through each generation from the Lord’s Ascension to the present day, recounting which bishops, which martyrs, and which men eloquent in ecclesiastical teaching have come to Jerusalem, thinking that they possessed less religion and less knowledge, and had not, so to speak, received the finishing touch of virtue, unless they had worshiped Christ in those places from which the Gospel first flashed forth from the gallows.

Certainly, if even the celebrated Orator thinks someone deserving of criticism because he learned Greek literature not at Athens but at Lilybaeum, and Latin not at Rome but in Sicily—

[Note: Cicero criticizes Quintus Caecilius, who wanted to conduct the prosecution of the Sicilians against Verres, in these words: “If you had learned Greek literature at Athens, not at Lilybaeum, and Latin at Rome, not in Sicily,” etc.]

—for each province evidently possesses something distinctive that another cannot possess equally, why do we suppose that anyone has reached the heights of learning without our own Athens?

### 10

Nor do we say this because we deny that the kingdom of God is within us, or that holy men exist in other regions as well; rather, we assert especially that those who are foremost throughout the world gather here together.

We have come to these places not as to the first but as to the last, in order to see in them those who are first among all nations.

[Note: The Cistercian manuscript omits the words “not as to the first but as to the last.” Erasmus, and Martianus following him, read “the first and the last.”]

Certainly, a kind of flower and most precious stone among the ornaments of the Church is the choir of monks and virgins. Whoever is foremost in Gaul hastens here. The Briton, separated from our world, if he has advanced in religion, leaves the setting sun behind and seeks a place known to him only by reputation and by reports in the Scriptures.

Why mention the Armenians, the Persians, the peoples of India and Ethiopia, Egypt itself, fertile in monks, Pontus and Cappadocia, Coele-Syria and Mesopotamia, and all the swarms of the East? They come in accordance with the Savior’s saying: “Wherever the body is, there the eagles will gather” (Matt. 24:28).

They converge upon these places and display to us examples of different virtues. Their speech is diverse, but their religion is one. There are almost as many choirs of those singing psalms as there are varieties of nations.

Amid all this—one of the chief virtues among Christians—there is nothing arrogant, nothing of haughty self-restraint.

[Note: Victorius reads, “They arrogate nothing to themselves from the pride of their continence.” Others read, “nothing of arrogance, nothing,” etc. One of our manuscripts has “nothing of boastful pride,” etc.]

There is a contest in humility among them all. Whoever is the last is considered first. There is no distinction in clothing, no admiration. However one chooses to walk, it is neither a cause of slander nor of praise. Fasting, too, raises no one up; no honor is given to starvation, and moderate fullness is not condemned. Each person stands or falls for his own Lord. No one judges another, lest he be judged by the Lord.

And what is customary in many provinces—that they tear one another with a gnashing tooth—is entirely absent here. Luxury is far away; pleasure is far away.

[Note: These words do not seem to us to connect sufficiently with what precedes. The dislocated passage is also suggested by the following encomium of Bethel and its comparison with Rome under sections 10 and 11. These words were once repeated at the end of Letter 43 to Marcella; we have removed them, since this indicates that the passage had long ago been moved from its original position and no longer fits its present setting very well.]

There are so many places of prayer in the city itself that a single day would not suffice to visit them all.

### 10

But, to come to the little village of Christ and the lodging of Mary—for each person praises most what he possesses—by what language, with what voice, can we describe to you the Savior’s cave? And that manger in which the tiny child whimpered is to be honored more by silence than by feeble speech.

Where are the broad porticoes? Where are the gilded ceilings? Where are the houses clothed in the sufferings of the poor and the labor of the condemned? Where are the basilicas built like palaces from the wealth of private individuals, so that the frail body of a human being may walk more expensively, and, as though anything could be more splendid than the world, may wish to gaze upon straight lines rather than upon heaven?

Behold: in this small hole in the earth the Creator of the heavens was born. Here he was wrapped in rags; here he was seen by shepherds; here he was pointed out by a star; here he was worshiped by the Magi.

And I think this place is holier than the Tarpeian Rock, which, struck by lightning from heaven so often, showed what displeased the Lord.

### 11

Read the Apocalypse of John, and observe what is sung about the woman clothed in purple, the blasphemy written upon her forehead, the seven hills, the many waters, and the downfall of Babylon.

“Come out of her,” the Lord says, “my people, so that you may not share in her sins and receive none of her plagues” (Rev. 18:4).

[Note: In Victorius, the words from “Returning also to Jeremiah” through “observe” are missing.]

Returning also to Jeremiah, observe what is written: “Flee from the midst of Babylon, and let each one save his own life. For Babylon the great has fallen, has fallen, and has become a dwelling place of demons and a prison of every unclean spirit” (Jer. 51:8).

Certainly the holy Church is there; there are the trophies of the Apostles and martyrs; there is the true confession of Christ; there is the faith preached by the Apostle; and the Christian name, once trampled by paganism, rises daily to prominence.

But the ambition, power, and greatness of the city itself—being seen and seeing, being greeted and greeting, praising and slandering, hearing or speaking, and even unwillingly seeing such a great crowd of people—are alien to the purpose and tranquility of monks.

For either we see those who come to us and lose our silence, or we do not see them and are accused of arrogance. Sometimes, in order to return the visit of those who have visited us, we go to proud doors and, amid the tongues of servants who bite with gossip, enter gilded doorposts.

But in Christ’s village, as we said above, everything is rustic, and outside the Psalms there is silence. Wherever you turn, the plowman guiding the plow-handle sings “Alleluia.” The sweating reaper diverts himself with psalms, and the vine-dresser, pruning the vine with his curved sickle, sings something Davidic.

These are the songs of this province; these are, as the common saying has it, its love songs. Here is the shepherds’ whistle; these are the weapons of cultivation.

### 12

But what are we doing? We do not consider what is fitting; we see only what we desire. O when will that day come when a breathless traveler brings the news that our Marcella has landed on the shores of Palestine, and all the choirs of monks and all the companies of virgins resound?

We already long to run out to meet her, and, without waiting for a vehicle, to carry our eager bodies on foot. We shall hold her hands and look upon her face, and we shall scarcely be torn away from the embrace we have desired.

Will that day, then, never come when we may enter the Savior’s cave? Weep in the Lord’s tomb with a sister, weep with a mother?

[Note: “Sister” means Mary, the wife of Alphaeus—or, according to John, of Clopas—the mother of James the Younger and therefore a sister of the Virgin Mary.]

Then kiss the wood of the Cross, and on the Mount of Olives be lifted up in desire and spirit with the ascending Lord? See Lazarus come forth bound in grave cloths, and the streams of the Jordan purer for the Lord’s washing?

From there proceed to the shepherds’ folds; pray at David’s mausoleum.

[Note: Many, following Baronius, infer from this that Jerome selected an oratory for himself in David’s tomb. It is quite plausible that this tomb, after having previously been plundered of enormous treasures by Hyrcanus, was later ruined and collapsed in Hadrian’s time, and that Jerome selected a place for prayer among its ruins. The royal tombs were at the edge of Mount Zion, or near the walls, in the garden of the royal palace, which is mentioned in 1 Kings 25:4 and 2 Chronicles 26:23, where King Uzziah is said to have been buried “in the field of the royal tombs,” not in the royal tombs themselves. Compare, if desired, Benjamin of Tudela, Itinerary, etc.]

Even now see the Prophet Amos sounding his pastoral horn upon his own rock.

[Variant: “looking out” instead of “seeing.”]

Hasten either to the tents or memorials of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and also of the three distinguished women.

[Note: By the three distinguished women understand Sarah, Rebekah, and Leah—not Rachel, as Victorius supposes. See Gen. 49:31.]

See the spring in which the eunuch was baptized by Philip. Go to Samaria and venerate together the ashes of John the Baptist, Elisha, and Obadiah. Enter the caves in which, during the time of persecution and famine, the companies of the Prophets were nourished.

We shall go to Nazareth and, in accordance with the interpretation of its name, see the flower of Galilee. Not far from there Cana will be seen, where water was changed into wine.

We shall proceed to Itabyrium, Mount Tabor, and see the Savior’s tents—not as Peter once wished, with Moses and Elijah, but with the Father and the Holy Spirit.

From there we shall come to the Sea of Gennesaret and see five thousand and four thousand men satisfied in the wilderness with five and seven loaves.

[Note: These are two different miracles of Jesus Christ. The first, in Matthew 14:21, involved five thousand men being fed with five loaves and two fish; the second, in Matthew 15:38, involved four thousand men being fed with seven loaves and some fish.]

The town of Nain will appear, at whose gate the widow’s son was raised. Hermonim will also be seen, as well as the torrent of Endor, at which Sisera was defeated.

Capernaum, familiar with the Lord’s signs, and all Galilee likewise will be seen. And then, with Christ accompanying us, when we have returned to our cave by way of Shiloh, Bethel, and the other places in which churches have been erected like banners of the Lord’s victories, we shall sing continually, we shall weep frequently, we shall pray without ceasing, and, wounded together by the Savior’s dart, say:

“I have found him whom my soul sought; I shall hold him, and I shall not let him go” (Song 3:4).

## EPISTLE XLVII

[Note: Otherwise 154. Written around the year 393.]

### TO DESIDERIUS

He commends Desiderius and his sister Serenilla, from whom he had received a letter, beginning with an etymological interpretation of their names; he urges them to come to the holy places and fulfill their purpose, and explains why in the meantime he is sending them none of his works.

### 1

Having read the address of Your Dignity, which your goodwill bestowed upon me when I was not expecting it, I rejoiced indeed at the testimony of an honorable and eloquent man; but, returning to myself, I was sufficiently distressed that I was being overwhelmed rather than lifted up by praises and commendation so great.

For you know our doctrine: we hold aloft the banner of humility and, walking through the lowest places, climb toward the highest. Who, then, and how great am I, that I should deserve the testimony of an educated voice, or that the palm of eloquence should be awarded to me by one who, writing most eloquently, deterred me from writing?

Nevertheless, one must dare, so that charity—which seeks not what is its own but what belongs to one’s neighbor—may perform the duties of greeting, since it cannot fill the place of a teacher.

[Note: The Veronese manuscript reads: “Nevertheless, this must be heard; and charity,” etc., which gives an appropriate sense.]

### 2

I congratulate you and your holy and venerable sister Serenilla, who, having trampled the waves of the world, has reached the calm of Christ as one whose name is fulfilled in her.

[Note: We have taken the Greek word and letters from a Veronese manuscript. In Greek, φερωνύμος means “bearing one’s name appropriately,” or “name-fitting”; the term suits her especially well. Thus Serenilla, because she dwells in tranquility, says that she has acted φερωνύμως, “in a manner befitting her name.” Compare the beginning of the commentary on Obadiah: “Obadiah, he says, feeds the churches of Christ, and φερωνύμως, just as Stephen was crowned with martyrdom in the Acts of the Apostles, so this man too was called the servant of the Lord.”]

Although this destiny of her name was also predestined in you.

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “although this gift and prophecy was also destined for you,” which is not pleasing. The word supplied by us from the Veronese manuscript, and formerly proposed for insertion by Gravius, perfectly restores the passage and reveals Jerome’s meaning.]

For we read that the holy Daniel too was called a man of desires (Dan. 9), and a friend of God, because he desired to know his mysteries.

Therefore, what the venerable Paula asked me to do, I do willingly; and I urge and entreat you, through the love of the Lord, to grant us the sight of you and, by taking advantage of the opportunity to visit the holy places, enrich us with so great a gift.

Certainly, even if our companionship should displease you, worshiping where the Lord’s feet stood is a portion of faith, as though one had seen the traces of his birth, Cross, and Passion while they were still fresh.

### 3

I have sent none of my little works, since many of them have flown from their nest and been published with the rash distinction of an edition; I was afraid that I might perhaps send the same things you already possessed.

But if you wish to borrow copies, you can obtain them either from the holy Marcella, who lives on the Aventine, or from the Lot of our age, Domnio, a most holy man.

[Note: Learned men have been led by this passage to suppose that this Desiderius was someone other than the Aquitanian presbyter at whose urging Jerome later wrote against Vigilantius, and that he was a Roman. But from the fact that Marcella’s house on the Aventine is pointed out to him, he is shown to have come to Rome as a visitor and to be unfamiliar with that city and its places. Therefore he does not seem to us to be distinguishable from the Aquitanian, whom we also identify with the Desiderius for whom Jerome translated the Pentateuch from Hebrew, to whom Saint Paulinus’s Letter 43 survives, and to whom Sulpicius dedicated the Life of Saint Martin.]

I, however, while awaiting your arrival, shall either give you everything when you come, or, if some difficulties prevent this, I shall gladly send whatever you order.

I have written a book On Illustrious Men, from the Apostles down to our own age, imitating Tranquillus and the Greek Apollonius. After a catalogue of many people, I placed myself also at the end of the volume, like an abortive and the least of all Christians. There I was obliged briefly to record what I had written up to the fourteenth year of the Emperor Theodosius.

[Variant: “of Theodosius the Emperor and Prince.”]

When you have received this book from the persons mentioned above, if you find anything lacking from the index, I shall gradually have it written out for you, if you wish.

## EPISTLE XLVIII

[Note: Otherwise 50. Written around the end of the year 393.]

### OR, AN APOLOGETIC BOOK, TO PAMMACHIUS, ON BEHALF OF THE BOOKS AGAINST JOVINIAN

He defends his books against Jovinian, which Pammachius had received, because his detractors maliciously represented them as excessively praising virginity and, conversely, as unfair to marriage.

### 1

The reason I have not written to you until now was your silence. For I was afraid that, if I wrote to one who was silent, you might think me troublesome rather than dutiful.

Now, however, summoned by your sweetest letter—such a letter as would summon me to the philosophy of our doctrine—I receive my former fellow student, companion, and friend with open arms, as they say, and prepare a defense of my little works.

[Variant, perhaps: “the defense” of my little works.]

I shall do so, however, only if I first find you a reconciled judge; indeed, if I equip my advocate to answer all the charges brought against me. This is also what your Cicero says; and before him, in a brief and solitary volume, Antonius wrote: “The first cause of victory is to learn carefully the case for which you are going to plead.”

[Note: Cicero, in *On the Orator*, says: “Marcus Antonius,” he writes, “to whom the age of our fathers awarded the first place in eloquence, a man naturally very acute and prudent, in the one book that he left,” etc. Cicero mentions the same book elsewhere, and Quintilian frequently calls it unfinished. From the manuscripts we read, “the chief cause of victory,” rather than the less correct printed reading, “the first victory is the cause.”]

### 2

Some criticize me because, in the books I wrote against Jovinian, I was excessive either in praising virgins or in reproaching married women—or marriages.

[Variant: “marriages” instead of “married women.”]

They say that I have in some way condemned marriage, praising chastity so highly that no comparison seems to remain between a wife and a virgin.

If I remember the question correctly, the dispute between Jovinian and us is this: he makes marriage equal to virginity, while we subordinate it; he says that the difference is little or nothing, while we say that it is great.

In the end, it was precisely for this reason that he was condemned, with you acting under the Lord: he dared to compare marriage with perpetual chastity.

[Variant: “virginity” instead of “perpetual chastity.”]

Or, if the virgin and the married woman are thought to be the same, why could Rome not hear this statement without treating it as a crime?

[Note: We do not understand why all editions before Martianus, and indeed many manuscripts, read: “Victorinus could not be heard at Rome.” Nevertheless, we have thought it appropriate to alert the reader, since nothing has been altered by us after the Benedictine edition.]

A virgin is generated from a man, not a man from a virgin. There can be no middle position: either my opinion must be followed or Jovinian’s.

If I am criticized because I subordinate marriage to virginity, let the man who compares them be praised. But if he was condemned because he considered them equal, let his condemnation bear witness to my work.

If worldly people resent being placed on a lower level than virgins, I am surprised that clergy, monks, and the continent do not praise what they themselves do. They castrate themselves from their wives in order to imitate the chastity of virgins; yet do they want married people to be what virgins are?

Let them therefore join themselves to the wives whom they had renounced; or, if they abstain, even while silent they will confess that what they preferred to the work of marriage is better.

Was I unskilled in the Scriptures, then, and reading the sacred books for the first time, that I could not preserve a distinction—or, so to speak, a delicate thread of argument—between virginity and marriage?

Evidently I did not know the saying: “Do not be excessively righteous” (Eccl. 7:17). And while defending one side, I was wounded on the other; or, to speak more plainly, while fighting Jovinian with measured steps, I was stabbed in the back by Manichaeism.

“Did I not, I ask, state these things at the very beginning of my work? For we do not, by following the doctrines of Marcion and Manichaeus, disparage marriage. Nor, deceived by the error of Tatian, the leader of the Encratites, do we consider all sexual intercourse impure; for he condemns and rejects not only marriage but also the foods that God created for use.

We know that in a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver but also vessels of wood and clay. And upon the foundation of Christ, which Paul the architect laid, some build gold, silver, and precious stones; while others, on the contrary, build hay, wood, and straw.

[Note: Formerly the text read: “another builds upon it.”]

We do not deny that marriage is honorable and the marriage bed undefiled. We read God’s first command: ‘Increase and multiply, and fill the earth’ (Gen. 1:28).

But we accept marriage in such a way that we prefer virginity, which is born from marriage. Will silver cease to be silver if gold is more precious than silver? Or is a tree and a crop dishonored if apples and fruits are preferred to root and leaves, stalk and ears?

As apples come from a tree and grain from straw, so virginity comes from marriage.

The hundredfold, sixtyfold, and thirtyfold fruit, although it grows from one earth and comes from one seed, nevertheless differs greatly in number.

The thirtyfold refers to marriage, because the joining of the fingers, embracing and binding itself as though with a gentle kiss, depicts husband and wife.

The sixtyfold refers to widows, because they are placed in hardship and tribulation. Hence they are represented by the finger above the ring finger: for the greater the difficulty of abstaining from the allurements of pleasures once experienced, the greater the reward.

The hundredfold number, however—please, attentive reader, consider this carefully—is transferred from the left hand to the right, using the same fingers but not the same hand. By forming a circle, it signifies the crown of virginity, just as on the left hand the same fingers signify married women and widows.”

### 3

I ask you: does the man who says these things condemn marriage?

We called virginity gold and marriage silver. We explained that the hundredfold, sixtyfold, and thirtyfold fruit arise from one earth and from one seed, although they differ greatly in number.

Will any reader be so unjust as to judge me not by what I have said but by his own opinion?

And certainly we have been far more lenient toward marriage than almost all Latin and Greek interpreters, who refer the hundredfold number to martyrs, the sixtyfold to virgins, and the thirtyfold to widows. According to their opinion, husbands are excluded from the good earth and from the householder’s seed.

[Note: Saint Cyprian uses the same interpretation near the end of On the Dress of Virgins: “The first hundredfold is the fruit of the martyrs; the second, sixtyfold, is yours.” Prudentius does likewise in his poem on Saint Agnes and in Book 2 against Symmachus, concerning a virgin. Origen is also cited from Homily 1 on Joshua: “Here fruits sixtyfold—ten times six—are gathered into the barns.”]

But lest I was cautious at the beginning and perhaps careless in the rest, did I not, after dividing the work, when I came to the questions, immediately say: “I ask you, virgins and continent persons of both sexes, married people and those married twice, to assist my efforts with your prayers”?

Jovinian is the enemy of all of them alike. I need the prayers of those whom I beg to assist my work; can I condemn those whose help I ask as being in the error of Manichaeus?

### 4

Let us move on to what remains. For the brevity of a letter does not permit us to linger longer over individual points.

In interpreting the Apostle’s testimony—“The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband; likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife” (1 Cor. 7)—we added the following (Book 1, chapter 4):

[Note: The two words “or a woman” do not occur in the treatise *Against Jovinian*, and the Greek itself has only γυναικός, “a woman.” The following words concerning the Egyptian woman are also presented there somewhat differently and in another sequence of expression.]

“Every aspect of this question concerns those who are married: whether they may dismiss their wives, which the Lord also forbade in the Gospel. Hence the Apostle says: ‘It is good for a man not to touch a woman’ (Matt. 5)—as though there were danger in touching her, as though the one who touched her could not escape.

Hence Joseph, because an Egyptian woman wanted to touch him, fled from her hands and abandoned his cloak.

But because a man who has once taken a wife cannot abstain without her consent, and cannot divorce a wife who has committed no offense, let him render the debt owed to his spouse, since he willingly bound himself so that he might be compelled to render it.”

Can the man who says it is the Lord’s command that wives must not be dismissed, and who says, without mutual consent, “What God has joined, let no human being separate” (Matt. 19:6)—can he be said to condemn marriage?

Again, later on: “‘Each person,’ he says, ‘has his own gift from God: one in this way, another in that’” (1 Cor. 7:7).

In explaining this statement, we added the following (Book 1, chapter 8):

“‘What I want,’ he says, ‘is clear. But since there are different gifts in the Church, I grant that marriage too is a gift, lest I seem to condemn nature. At the same time, consider that the gift of virginity is one thing and the gift of marriage another.

For if the reward of married women and virgins were the same, he would certainly not have said, after the command concerning continence: “But each person has his own gift from God: one in this way, another in that.”

Where there is individual distinction, there is difference on the other side as well.

I grant that marriage is a gift of God, but there is a great difference between gift and gift.

Finally, the Apostle also says of a certain person who repented after incest: “On the contrary, you should forgive him and comfort him; and if you have forgiven anyone anything, I have forgiven it also” (2 Cor. 2:7).

And lest we think that a human being’s gift should be despised, he added: “For whatever I have forgiven, if I have forgiven anything, it was for your sake in the presence of Christ”—or, according to another reading, “in the person of Christ.”

The gifts of Christ are different. Hence Joseph, as a type of Christ, had a variegated tunic.

And in the forty-fourth Psalm we read: “The queen stood at your right hand in a garment of gold, clothed in variety.”

And the Apostle Peter says: “As co-heirs of the manifold grace of God” (1 Pet. 3:7).

The Greek word expresses this more significantly: ποικίλης, that is, ‘varied.’”

[Note: Victorius altered the reading by conjecture to “as stewards.” We have demonstrated the authenticity of our reading in the book Against Jovinian.]

5. I ask: what is this contentiousness, to close one’s eyes and refuse to look upon the clearest light? We said that there are different gifts in the Church, one gift of virginity and another of marriage. And shortly afterward: “I concede that marriage too is a gift of God. But there is a great difference between gift and gift.” And although we proclaim in the clearest terms that it is a gift of God, we are said to condemn it?

Furthermore, if Joseph is understood as a type of the Lord, his varied and differentiated tunic is found in virgins, widows, continent women, and married women. And can one who speaks of Christ’s tunic appear, as it were, an outsider, when we have also said that the queen herself—that is, the Church of the Savior—is clothed in a golden garment and surrounded by the same variety?

“But also, in what follows, when discussing marriage, we followed the same meaning. This passage [Note: 1 Corinthians 7:10; Jovinianus abused this passage above all in the present controversy.] does not pertain to the present controversy. For, in accordance with the Lord’s judgment, it teaches that a wife is not to be divorced except on account of fornication, and that a divorced woman is not to marry another while her husband is alive, or certainly that she ought to be reconciled to her husband. And likewise in another passage: ‘A wife is bound for as long as her husband lives. But if her husband should fall asleep, she is released from the law of her husband: let her marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord’ (1 Cor. 7:39), that is, a Christian.” [Note: They do indeed add, with Victorius, that the reading is *to the law*, apparently following the Vulgate; for in Greek copies τῷ νόμῳ is often absent. Moreover, neither the Vulgate, nor the Greek, nor Jerome himself in *Against Jovinianus* recognizes the following words, “of the law of the husband.” All earlier printed editions also wrongly punctuated the following sentence as a question, giving it another sense.] Thus he who permits second and third marriages “in the Lord” prohibits a first marriage with a pagan.

6. Let my detractors, I beg, open their ears and see that I have permitted second and third marriages in the Lord. Since I did not condemn second and third marriages, could I have condemned a first marriage?

Even in that passage where we interpret the Apostle’s chapter, “Was anyone called while circumcised? Let him not draw over the foreskin. Was anyone called in the foreskin? Let him not be circumcised” (ibid., v. 18)—although certain very learned interpreters of Scripture insist that this was said about circumcision and servitude to the Law—do we not preserve the marriage covenant most plainly? For we said (Book 1, ch. 6):

“If anyone was called in the foreskin, let him not be circumcised. You had a wife, he says, when you believed: do not think that the faith of Christ is the cause of separation, since God called us in peace. Circumcision is nothing, and the foreskin is nothing, but the observance of God’s commandments (1 Cor. 7:19; Gal. 5:6). For neither celibacy nor marriage is of any benefit without works; since even faith, which properly belongs to Christians, is said to be dead if it has no works. By this rule, even the virgins of Vesta and the *univirae* of Juno—women of one husband—could be counted among the saints.”

And shortly afterward:

“You have been called as a slave; do not let it trouble you. But if you can become free, make use of it rather (1 Cor. 7:21). Even if you have a wife, he says, and are bound to her, and pay the debt, and have no authority over your own body—and, to speak more plainly, are your wife’s slave—do not on this account be sad, nor sigh over your lost virginity. But even if you can find some grounds for separation, so that you may enjoy the freedom of chastity, do not seek your salvation through another’s ruin.”

Keep your wife for a little while, and do not run ahead of one who is delayed; wait until she follows. If you act patiently, your wife will be changed into a sister.

7. In that passage too, where we discussed why Paul had said, “Concerning virgins I have no commandment of the Lord, but I give advice, as one who has obtained mercy from the Lord to be faithful,” we so exalted [variant: preferred] virginity that we nevertheless preserved the order of marriage.

“If the Lord had commanded virginity, he would seem to condemn marriage and to remove the seedbed of the human race, from which virginity itself is born. If he had cut off the root, how would he seek fruits? If he had not first laid foundations, how would he construct the building and set a roof over everything above?”

If we have called marriage the root and virginity the fruit; if marriage is the foundation and perpetual chastity the building or roof—who could be so envious, or so blind a detractor of mine, as to see the building or roof in the same house while failing to recognize the foundation that supports the building and roof?

Moreover, in another passage, when we set forth the Apostle’s testimony in which he says, “Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek release. Are you released from a wife? Do not seek a wife” (1 Cor. 7:27), we immediately added this (Book 1, ch. 7):

“Each of us has his own boundaries. Return to me what is mine, and you hold on to what is yours. If you are bound to your wife, do not divorce her. If I am released from a wife, I shall not seek a wife. Just as I do not dissolve marriages once they have been bound, so you should not bind what has been released.”

But another testimony also makes perfectly clear what we thought about virginity and marriage (Book 1, ch. 7):

“The Apostle does not place a snare upon us, nor force us to be what we do not wish to be; rather, he urges what is honorable and seemly, and makes us serve the Lord attentively, always to be solicitous and to await the Lord’s will as something ready to hand [Note: Some older editions read *paratum* here and in the work *Against Jovinianus*; this is less correct.], so that, whenever he commands something, we may immediately fulfill what has been commanded like a vigorous and armed soldier, and do so without any delay—that delay which, according to Ecclesiastes, has been granted to the people of this world so that they may be occupied with it.”

At the end of our comparison between married women and virgins, we concluded our discussion in these words (Book 1, ch. 7):

“Where there is a good and a better, the reward of the good and the better is not one and the same; and where the reward is not one, there are certainly different gifts. Thus the difference between marriage and virginity is as great as that between not sinning and doing good—or, to put it more mildly, as great as that between the good and the better.”

8. Furthermore, in what follows, when we say (Book 1, ch. 8):

“Having finished our discussion of marriages and virginity, so that, with careful moderation of instruction, he might turn neither to the left nor to the right, but walk along the royal road and fulfill the saying, ‘Do not be excessively righteous’” (Eccl. 7:17),

we again compare monogamy with digamy; and just as we had subordinated marriage to virginity, so we subordinate digamy to marriage. [Note: That is, first marriage; this word has perhaps fallen out here, for it occurs in that treatise.] Did we not thereby show plainly what in the holy Scriptures is left and what is right, and what is meant by “Do not be excessively righteous”?

The left, plainly, is to follow the lust of Jews and Gentiles and to burn continually with desire for intercourse; the right is to follow the error of the Manichaeans and, under the appearance of chastity, to become entangled in the nets of impurity. The royal road, however, is to desire virginity in such a way that marriage is not condemned.

Moreover, what judge of my little works could be so unjust as to say that I condemn first marriages, when he has also read what I said about second marriages?

“The Apostle permits second marriages—but to those who wish them, to those who cannot contain themselves—lest, having grown wanton against Christ, they desire to marry, bearing condemnation because they have nullified their first faith; and he permits this because many have turned back after Satan (1 Tim. 5). Otherwise they will be more blessed if they remain as they are. Immediately he adds apostolic authority: ‘According to my advice.’ And lest the Apostle’s authority seem weaker as that of a mere human being, he added: ‘But I think that I too have the Spirit of God.’ Where he urges continence, he used the counsel not of a human being but of the Spirit of God [Note: Another reading is: “The counsel is the Spirit of God.”]. But where he grants permission to marry, he does not name the Spirit of God; rather, he balances his advice according to prudence, granting relaxation to individuals in such a way that each can bear it.”

After setting forth the testimonies in which the Apostle permits second marriages, we immediately added:

“Just as, on account of the danger of fornication, he permits marriages to virgins and makes excusable what is not desired for its own sake, so, on account of the same fornication [Note: In that book, “to be avoided” is added. Manuscripts vary here: some read “the danger of fornication,” and shortly afterward read “that same fornication” in the nominative.], he permits widows a second marriage. ‘For it is better, even if it be a second or third marriage, to know one man than many’; that is, it is more tolerable to be prostituted to one man than to many.”

Let the slander cease. Here we discussed a second, a third, and, if one wishes, a fourth marriage—not a first marriage. But lest anyone refer what we said, “It is more tolerable to be prostituted to one man than to many,” to the first husband [variant: first marriage], since our entire discussion concerned digamy and trigamy, we concluded our discussion of digamy and trigamy with these words:

“‘All things are lawful, but not all things are expedient’” (1 Cor. 6).

“I do not condemn those married twice, nor indeed those married three times, or, if it can be said, eight times. I shall go further: I also receive a fornicator who repents. Whatever is permitted equally should be weighed in an equal balance.”

9. Let my slanderer blush, who says that I condemn first marriages, when he reads: “I do not condemn those married twice, nor those married three times, or, if it can be said, eight times.”

It is one thing not to condemn, another to praise; one thing to grant pardon, another to praise virtue. But if I seem harsh because I said, “Whatever is permitted equally should be weighed in an equal balance,” I think he will not judge me cruel and rigid if he reads the other passages that I prepared for virginity and marriage, and others for those married three or eight times and for penitents.

Christ was a virgin in the flesh and monogamous in the spirit, because he had one Church, as our remaining discussion has testified; and we are believed to condemn marriage!

Am I said to condemn marriage? Whose words are these? (Book 1, ch. 13.)

“No one doubts that the priests descended from the line of Aaron, Eleazar, and Phinehas—who themselves also had wives—would rightly be brought forward against us if, led astray by the error of the Encratites [Note: We have added the word *ducti* from some manuscripts, in accordance with the reading found in his treatises.], we were to contend that marriages ought to be rejected.”

Did we criticize Tatian, the leader of the Encratites, who rejects marriages, and ourselves condemn marriage?

Again, when I compare virgins and widows, what I thought about marriage, and how I established three degrees—virginity, widowhood or continence, and marriage—the written words themselves make clear:

“I do not deny that widows who have remained so after baptism are blessed; nor do I detract from the merit of those who persevere in chastity with their husbands. But just as these women have a greater reward before God than married women who fulfill their marital duty, so let them also bear with an even temper the fact that virginity is preferred to them.”

[Note: Jovinianus had objected: “If a virgin and widows have been baptized and have remained so, there is scarcely any difference between them.” Jerome refutes this objection at great length in chapter 18.]

10. When we also set forth the Apostle’s testimony to the Galatians, “By works of the law no flesh shall be justified” (Gal. 2:16), we introduced this sort of interpretation (Book 1, ch. 23):

“Works of the law include marriage. Hence women who have no children are cursed in it. Although these things are also permitted in the Gospel, it is one thing to grant indulgence to weakness and another to promise rewards to virtues.”

There you have it: we plainly said that marriage is permitted in the Gospel, but nevertheless that marriage, remaining within its proper function, cannot receive the rewards of chastity.

If husbands take this indignantly, let them not be angry with me but with the holy Scriptures—or rather with bishops, presbyters, deacons, and the entire priestly and Levitical choir, who know that they cannot offer sacrifices if they devote themselves to marital intercourse.

But in that passage too where we introduced a testimony from the Apocalypse (Book 1, ch. 25), is it not clear what we thought about virgins, widows, and married women?

“These are the ones who sing the new song, which no one can sing except one who is a virgin. These are the firstfruits of God and of the Lamb, and they are without blemish” (Rev. 14:5). If virgins are the firstfruits of God, then widows and continent married women will come after the firstfruits—that is, in the second and third degree. We place widows and married women in the second and third degree, and yet in heretical fury we are said to condemn marriage?

11. There are many things that we said throughout the whole book, with careful moderation, about virginity, widows, and marriage. But, for the sake of brevity, I shall add one more testimony, which I do not think anyone will contradict unless he wishes either to prove himself my enemy or to show himself senseless.

For when I had stated that the Lord had gone to the wedding at Cana of Galilee, I added, among other things, this (Book 1, ch. 25):

“He who went once to a wedding taught once that one ought to marry, and marriage could be detrimental to virginity only if we did not place marriage after virginity and the chastity of widowhood, in the third degree. But since it is characteristic of heretics to condemn marriage and to despise God’s creation, whatever he may say in praise of marriage we gladly hear. For the Church does not condemn marriages but subordinates them; it does not reject them but administers them, knowing—as we said above—that in a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and earthenware, and that some are for honor and others for dishonor (1 Tim. 2:21). And that whoever cleanses himself will become a vessel for honor, useful and prepared for every good work.”

Whatever he may say [variant: they may say] in praise of marriage, I said, we gladly hear. We gladly hear marriage praised, and yet we condemn marriage?

The Church does not condemn marriage but subordinates it. Whether you wish it or not, the husband is subordinate to virginity and widowhood. The Church subordinates marriage—marriage remaining within its proper function; it does not condemn or reject it but administers it. It lies within your power, if you wish, to ascend according to the degree of chastity. Why are you indignant if, standing in the third, you do not wish to hasten to what is higher?

12. Therefore, since I have so often and repeatedly warned the reader, and have walked like a cautious traveler through nearly every thousand paces of my discussions, receiving marriage in such a way that I preferred continent women, widows, and virgins to it, a prudent and kindly reader ought to have judged even those things that seem harsh in light of the rest, and not accused me, in one and the same book, of having expressed contradictory opinions.

For who is so dull [Note: Martianaeus nevertheless retained *hebes* (“dull”). When we correct such minor matters, we often do not notify the reader.] and so unskilled in writing that he praises and condemns the same thing? That he destroys what he has built and builds what he has destroyed? That, having overcome his opponent, he is finally struck by his own sword?

If rustic people, ignorant of either rhetorical or dialectical art, had attacked me, I would have granted their ignorance forgiveness and would not have censured their accusation, since I would have seen not intention but lack of knowledge at fault. But now, since eloquent men, educated in the liberal arts, prefer to injure rather than to understand, let them receive this brief answer from me: they ought to correct faults, not criticize them.

The field is open, the battle line stands opposite, and the opponent’s doctrine is clear. And, to introduce something Virgilian, “Look at him opposite, who calls” (Aeneid 2). Let them answer the opponent. Otherwise, let them hold the manner of disputing [Note: Despite the manuscripts’ opposition, Erasmus insisted that *nodum*, “knot,” should be read instead of *modum*, “manner”: “For,” he says, “the embraces of athletes and wrestlers are called knots, and one who argues holds his opponent in this way, concealing the knot in order to entangle him.” There is no opportunity here to refute this unfortunate conjecture at length. Nevertheless, below Jerome says: “He is strong, knotty, and tenacious in disputing”; and I do not know what reference to the “rod” in teaching ought, conversely, to answer to this.] in one way and the rod in teaching in another; and let them show me in their books what I have either omitted or added.

I do not listen to censors; I follow teachers. It is a delicate doctrine to dictate blows from behind a wall to one who is fighting, and, while you yourself are smeared with ointments, to accuse the bloodied soldier of cowardice. Nor, in saying this, am I immediately guilty of boasting because I alone fought while the others slept. I say only that those can fight more cautiously who have seen me wounded.

Do not enter upon a contest in which you merely shield yourself and, while your right hand is numb, wave your shield with the left. You must either strike or fall. I cannot judge you a victor unless I see the opponent slain [variant: unless I shall see him slain].

13. We learned, most learned men, in the schools together, and at the same time we learned those Aristotelian teachings—or those flowing from the fountains of Gorgias—that there are, plainly, several kinds of speaking. Among other distinctions, it is one thing to write *gymnastikōs* (γυμνατικῶς), “in a mode of exercise or contest,” and another to write *dogmatikōs* (δογματικῶς), “in a dogmatic or declarative mode.”

In the former, the discussion is wandering: one responds to an opponent by proposing now this, now that. One argues as one pleases; one thing is said and another done; as the proverb has it, one points out bread while holding a stone.

In the latter, however, an open face and, so to speak, candor are necessary. It is one thing to inquire and another to define. In one case one must fight; in the other one must teach.

Let a diligent teacher instruct me while I stand in battle and risk my life. Do not inflict a wound obliquely, from a direction no one expects. Strike with a straight sword. It is shameful for you to wound an enemy by deceit rather than by strength. As though it were not also the highest art of combatants to threaten in one place and strike in another.

Read, I beg you, Demosthenes; read Cicero. And lest perhaps you dislike rhetoricians—whose art is to say what is plausible rather than what is true—read Plato, Theophrastus, Xenophon, Aristotle, and the others who, flowing from Socrates’ fountain, ran in different streams. What in them is open, what straightforward? What words do not carry meanings? What meanings do not carry victory?

Origen, Methodius, Eusebius, and Apollinaris [variant: Apollinarius] write many thousands of verses against Celsus and Porphyry. Consider by what arguments, and with what slippery [Note: Some manuscripts read *problemata*, “problems,” a reading also favored by Gravius. The Benedictine editor, as he admits, makes the following context worse by reading *dicunt adversus eos qui dicuntur esse gentiles*, “they speak against those who are said to be Gentiles.” Nor is the printed reading entirely satisfactory; it may be more complete if, following the older edition in part and slightly altering the punctuation, one reads: “to speak what they do not think, but what necessity requires, they say against those things which the Gentiles say,” etc.] problems woven by the spirit of the devil they overthrow them; and because at times they are compelled to speak not what they think but what necessity requires, they speak against the things that the Gentiles say.

I say nothing of the Latin writers—Tertullian, Cyprian, Minucius, Victorinus, Lactantius, Hilary—lest I seem to have defended myself less than I have accused others. I shall bring forward the Apostle Paul, whom, whenever I read him, I seem to hear not words but thunder.

Read his Epistles, especially those to the Romans, Galatians, and Ephesians, in which he is wholly engaged in combat; and you will see, in the testimonies he takes from the Old Testament, how skillful, how prudent, how artfully concealing he becomes in what he is doing.

His words appear simple, almost those of an innocent and rustic man, one who knows neither how to lay nor to avoid ambushes. But wherever you look, there are thunderbolts. He clings to his case and seizes everything he touches; he turns his back in order to conquer; he pretends to flee in order to kill.

Let us therefore slander him and say: “The testimonies that you used against the Jews or against the other heresies sound one way in their original passages and another way in your Epistles. We see examples taken captive and serving you for victory, though they do not fight in their own books.”

Does he not speak to us, together with the Savior, in one way outside and another way at home? The crowds hear parables; the disciples hear the truth (Matt. 13). The Lord proposes questions to the Pharisees and does not explain them. It is one thing to teach a disciple and another to overcome an adversary.

“My mystery is for me, my mystery is for me and mine,” he says (Isa. 24:16).

14. You are indignant with me because I did not teach Jovinianus but defeated him. Rather, those are indignant with me who grieve that he was anathematized; and while they praise what they are, they accuse what they pretend to be.

As though he ought to have been asked to yield to me, rather than being led, unwilling and resisting, into the bonds of truth.

I would say this if, in my desire to conquer, I had said anything contrary to the rule of Scripture, and, as strong men customarily do in controversies, had redeemed a fault with a reward. But since I was more an interpreter of the Apostle than a dogmatist, and performed the office of a commentator, whatever seems harsh should be attributed more to the one whom we explained than to us, who explained him.

Unless perhaps he said something else and we distorted the simplicity of his words through malicious interpretation. Let the one who makes this accusation prove it from the Scriptures themselves.

“We said: ‘If it is good not to touch a woman, then it is bad to touch one, for nothing is contrary to the good except the bad. But if it is bad and is forgiven, it is permitted so that something worse than the bad may not occur.’”

And so on, up to the proposition of the next chapter. We added this because the Apostle had said: “It is good for a man not to touch a woman; but because of fornication, let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband” (1 Cor. 7:2).

In what do my words differ from the Apostle’s meaning? Unless perhaps in this: he makes a declaration, whereas I express a doubt; he defines, whereas I inquire; he says openly, “It is good for a man not to touch a woman,” whereas I cautiously [variant: daily] ask whether it is good not to touch a woman. The one is the language of doubt, not of confirmation.

He says, “It is good not to touch.” I add what could be contrary to the good. And immediately afterward:

“Observe the Apostle’s prudence. He did not say, ‘It is good for a man not to have a wife,’ but, ‘It is good for a man not to touch a woman’—as though there were danger even in touching her, as though one who touched her could not escape.”

You see, therefore, that we are not explaining husbands and wives but discussing intercourse in general: in comparison with chastity, virginity, and angelic likeness, it is good for a man not to touch a woman.

“Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity,” says Ecclesiastes (Eccl. 1:2). If all creatures are good because they were created by the good Creator, how is everything vanity? If the earth is vanity, are the heavens, the angels, thrones, dominions, powers, and the other virtues vanity as well?

But things that are good in themselves, because they were created by a good Creator, are called vanity in comparison with better things. For example, a candle is nothing in comparison with a lamp; a lamp does not shine in comparison with a star; compare a star with the moon, and it is blind; join the moon to the sun, and it does not glow; compare the sun with Christ, and it is darkness.

“I am who I am,” he says (Exod. 3:14). If, therefore, you compare every creature with God, it does not stand.

“Do not hand over your inheritance,” Esther says, “to those who are not” (Esth. 14:11)—that is, to idols and demons. Certainly idols and demons existed, and she prayed that they not receive the inheritance. In Job too we read that Bildad [variant: Baldach] said of the wicked:

“His confidence shall be removed from his tent, and the king of destruction shall trample upon him. Let his companions, who are not, dwell in his tent.”

There is no doubt that this refers to the devil: he has companions, and he would not have them unless he existed; yet because he has perished with respect to God, he is said not to be.

Therefore, in this comparative sense, “we called it bad to touch a woman”—although no mention was made of a wife—“because it is good not to touch.”

And we added:

“Calling virginity wheat, marriage barley, and fornication cow dung.”

Certainly wheat and barley are creatures of God. Yet in the Gospel the greater crowd is fed with barley loaves and the smaller with wheat loaves (Mark 6:44): “You will save humans and beasts, O Lord” (Ps. 33:7).

We said the same thing in other words when we called virginity gold and marriage silver; and when we spoke of the 144,000 virgins who had not been defiled with women. By this we wished to show that all who have not remained virgins are, in comparison with the purest and angelic chastity and with our Lord Jesus Christ himself, defiled.

If this seems harsh and worthy of censure to anyone, because we have made so great a difference between virginity and marriage as there is between wheat and barley, let him read St. Ambrose’s book *On Widows*. Among the other things he discussed about virginity and marriage, he will find that he also said this:

“The Apostle did not so prefer marriage that he would extinguish the pursuit of virginity [Ambrose: integrity]. Beginning with persuasion toward continence [variant: perfection], he descended to remedies for incontinence. And although he had shown the prize of the heavenly calling to the strong, he nevertheless allowed no one to fail on the way, applauding those who went first without despising those who followed. For he himself had learned that the Lord Jesus showed barley bread to some, so that they would not fail on the way (John 6:5 ff.), and his own body to others, so that they might strive toward the kingdom (Matt. 26).”

And afterward:

“Marriage intercourse is therefore not to be avoided as though it were a fault, but as though it were a burden of necessity. For the Law binds a wife so that she may bear children amid labor and sorrow: ‘Her turning shall be toward her husband, and he shall rule over her’ (Gen. 3:16). Therefore the married woman, not the widow, is subjected to labor and pain in the bearing of children; and the one joined in marriage, not the virgin, is subjected to the husband’s rule.

“And in another place: ‘You were bought for a price; do not become slaves of human beings’ (1 Cor. 7:23). You see how clearly marriage is defined as slavery.”

And shortly afterward:

“If, therefore, a good marriage is slavery, what is an evil one, when husband and wife cannot sanctify one another but destroy one another?”

[Note: This reading has been adopted into the text by us; Victorius had restored it, and a large number of Jerome’s and Ambrose’s manuscripts prefer it. The Benedictine editors of this work repeat the word *conjugii*, evidently reading, “What is an evil marriage?” But Martianaeus, following Erasmus, is entirely wrong: “If, therefore, a good marriage is slavery, what is an evil one, when,” etc.]

Everything that we set forth at length in three books about virginity and marriage, he compressed into a brief summary, embracing much in little. He praises virginity as persuasion toward continence and marriage as a remedy for incontinence. Significantly descending from greater things to lesser, he shows virgins the prize of the heavenly calling and comforts married women lest they fail on the way. He praises some without despising others. He compares marriage to barley and virginity to the body of Christ. And I think the distance between wheat and barley is far less than that between barley and the body of Christ.

Finally, he says that marriage is to be avoided as a burden of necessity and defines it as the clearest form of slavery. And he says many other things that he treated at great length in three books about virgins.

15. From all these things it is perfectly clear that I have said nothing new about virgins and married women, but have followed in every respect the judgment of the ancients—both of this writer and of the others who have discussed ecclesiastical doctrines:

“WHOSE NEGLIGENCE I DESIRE TO EMULATE” more than the obscure diligence of others.

Let husbands swell up against me because I said:

“I ask you, what sort of good is that which forbids prayer, which does not permit one to receive the body of Christ? When I fulfill the duty of a husband, I do not fulfill that of one who practices continence.”

The same Apostle commands elsewhere that we pray always (1 Thess. 5).

“If one must always pray, then one must never serve marriage. For whenever I render the debt to my wife, I cannot pray.”

Why I said this is clear, because I was interpreting the Apostle’s statement:

“Do not defraud one another, unless perhaps by mutual consent for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer” (1 Cor. 7:5).

The Apostle Paul says that when we have intercourse with our wives we cannot pray. If through intercourse the lesser thing is hindered—that is, prayer—how much more is the greater thing, receiving the body of Christ, prohibited?

Peter urges continence: “So that our prayers may not be hindered” (1 Pet. 3:7).

What, I ask, is my sin here? What have I deserved? What have I done wrong? If muddy and turbid waters flow, the fault is not in the channel but in the spring.

Or am I accused because I dared to add from myself:

“What sort of good is that which does not permit one to receive the body of Christ?”

I shall answer this briefly: What is greater, to pray or to receive the body of Christ?

Certainly, to receive the body of Christ. If the lesser is hindered through intercourse, much more is the greater.

We said in the same volume (Book 1, ch. 10) that David and his companions could not eat the bread of the Presence from the Law unless they had answered that they had kept themselves pure from women for three days (1 Sam. 21). This plainly does not refer to prostitutes, which the Law condemned, but to wives, with whom they were lawfully joined.

We also said that when the people were about to receive the Law on Mount Sinai, they were ordered to abstain from their wives for three days (Exod. 19).

I know that it is the custom in Rome for the faithful always to receive Christ’s body. [Note: From this it appears that the custom still prevailed at this time for the faithful to keep the sacrament of the Eucharist at home for their own reception.] I neither censure nor approve this, for “each person abounds in his own understanding” (Rom. 14).

But I confront the consciences of those who communicate on the same day after intercourse and, in Persius’ words, “purify the night with a river” (*Satire* 2). Why do they not dare go to the martyrs? Why do they not enter the churches? Is Christ one in public and another at home?

What is not permitted in church is not permitted at home. Nothing is closed to God, and even darkness shines before God.

Let each person examine himself and then approach the body of Christ—not because one day or two days of delayed communion makes a Christian holier, as though what I did not deserve today I might deserve tomorrow or the day after, but because, while I grieve that I have not communicated in the body of Christ, I abstain for a little while from my wife’s embrace, so that I may prefer love of Christ to love of my wife.

It is harsh, and cannot be endured. Who among worldly people can bear it? Whoever can bear it, let him bear it; whoever cannot, let him see to it himself.

Our concern is not to say what each person can or wishes to do, but what the Scriptures command.

16. This too is criticized in my little commentaries on the same Apostle, in which I said (Book 1, ch. 4):

“But lest anyone think, from what follows—‘so that you may devote yourselves to prayer, and return again to the same thing’ (1 Cor. 7:5)—that the Apostle wants this, and does not grant it on account of the danger of a greater fall, he immediately adds: ‘so that Satan may not tempt you because of your lack of self-control.’

“A beautiful indulgence indeed: ‘and return again to the same thing’ [Note: Older editions place before this: “He grants the return. Which …”]. What he is ashamed to call by its proper name, what he attributes to the temptation of Satan, what has incontinence as its cause—we labor to explain as though it were obscure, although the writer himself has explained it.

“But this I say,” he says, “according to indulgence, not according to command.”

And yet we continue to mutter that he does not call marriage an indulgence but a command—as though second and third marriages were not granted in the same way, and so on.

What have I said here that the Apostle did not say? Surely this: “What he is ashamed to call by its proper name.”

I think that when he says “return again to the same thing” and leaves the matter itself unspoken, he does not openly name intercourse but indicates it modestly.

Or is it because of what follows: “What he attributes to temptation by Satan, what has incontinence as its cause”? Is this not the same thing expressed in another order of words as “so that Satan may not tempt you because of your lack of self-control”?

Or is it because I said: “And yet we continue to mutter that he does not call marriage an indulgence but a command”? If this is harsh, let it be charged to the Apostle, who says, “But this I say according to indulgence, not according to command”—not to me, who, apart from the reversed order, have changed neither the meaning nor the words.

### 17

Let us pass on to the rest, for the argument hastens onward with epistolary brevity:

> “I say,” the Apostle says, “to the unmarried and to widows: it is good for them if they remain as I am. But if they cannot contain themselves, let them marry; for it is better to marry than to burn” (1 Cor. 7:8–9).

We interpreted this passage in the following way:

> “After he had granted to married people the use of marriage and had shown what he himself wished and what he permitted, he turns to the unmarried and widows, and sets forth his own example, calling them blessed if they remain as they are. But if they cannot contain themselves, let them marry—saying the same thing as above: ‘Because of fornication,’ and, ‘Lest Satan tempt you because of your lack of self-control.’ He also gives the reason why he said, ‘If they cannot contain themselves, let them marry’: ‘For it is better to marry than to burn.’ It is therefore better to marry because it is worse to burn. Take away the heat of lust, and he will not say that it is better to marry. ‘Better’ always looks toward comparison with something worse, not toward the simple and incomparable goodness of something good in itself. It is as if he were to say: ‘It is better to have one eye than none.’ And shortly afterward, when I had addressed an apostrophe to the Apostle, I added: ‘If marriage is good in itself, do not compare it with fire; simply say, “It is good to marry.” I mistrust the goodness of a thing which the magnitude of another evil compels to be considered the lesser evil.’ But I want not a lesser evil, but a simple good in itself. The Apostle wishes the unmarried and widows to remain without intercourse, and summons them to follow his example, calling them happier if they remain so. But if they cannot contain themselves, and wish to extinguish the heat of lust not so much through continence as through fornication, it is better to marry than to burn.

“Accordingly, we added: ‘It is better to marry because it is worse to burn’—not putting forward our own opinion, but interpreting the Apostle’s statement, ‘It is better to marry than to burn,’ that is, ‘It is better to take a husband than to fornicate.’ If you teach that burning or fornication is good, then a better thing will be preferred to a good thing. [Note: The old edition reads: ‘But if burning is an evil, and what is preferred to an evil …’] But if marriage is better because it is preferred to an evil, it is not of genuine and pure integrity, nor of that blessedness which is compared with the angels.

“If I say, ‘It is better to be a virgin than to be married,’ I have preferred a better thing to a good thing. But if I proceed to the second comparison—‘It is better to marry than to fornicate’—then I have not preferred a better thing to a good thing, but a good thing to an evil. There is a great difference between the ‘better’ which is placed before marriage and that which is placed before fornication.

“I ask you: what have I done wrong in this exposition? My purpose was not to drag the Scriptures toward my own will, but to say what I understood the Scriptures to wish. It is the commentator’s task to explain not what he himself wants, but what the person whom he interprets means. Otherwise, if he says the opposite, he will be not so much an interpreter as an adversary of the one whom he attempts to explain.

“Certainly, wherever I am not interpreting Scripture but speak freely from my own judgment, let anyone accuse me of having said something harsh against marriage. But if he finds no such passage, let him attribute whatever seems austere or harsh to the authority of the Writer, not to the interpreter’s office.” [Note: The same edition reads: “let him attribute it to the authority of the Writer, not to the interpreter’s office.”]

### 18

Who could endure this reproach directed against me? In explaining the Apostle’s passage in which he wrote concerning married people, “Such persons will have tribulation in the flesh” (1 Cor. 7:28), I said:

> “We, ignorant of the matter, thought that marriage at least possessed the joy of the flesh. But if there is tribulation even in the flesh for those who marry—the flesh in which alone they seemed to possess delights—what remains for which they should marry, when there is tribulation in spirit, soul, and the flesh itself?”

What condemnation of marriage is there in saying that the cries of infants, the deaths of children, miscarriages [another reading: divorces], the losses of the household, and other things of this kind are the tribulations of marriage?

While Damasus, of holy memory, was still alive, I wrote a book against Helvidius, *On the Perpetual Virginity of Blessed Mary*. In it, in order to proclaim the blessedness of virginity, it was necessary for me to say much about the troubles of marriage. Did that distinguished man, learned in the Scriptures and a virgin, the teacher of the Church’s virgin, find anything to criticize in that discourse? In the book addressed to Eustochium, too, we said much harsher things about marriage, and no one was offended on that account. [Note: Yet not long afterward he complains to Nepotianus about insults directed against that book, Epistle 52 at the end: “After the little book on virginity had been stoned …”]

For a lover of chastity eagerly receives praise of purity with an attentive ear. Read Tertullian, read Cyprian, read Ambrose; with them either accuse me or acquit me.

There have appeared Plautine families [another reading: Plautine fables] and mere little pedants intent only on disparagement, who wish to display their learning by tearing apart everyone’s statements. In one and the same case they criticize both sides—that is, both me and my opponent—and, although one of the two must necessarily prevail, they insist that both have been defeated.

When, moreover, in discussing those married twice and three times, we said, “Even if one has known a second and a third husband, it is better to know one husband than many”—that is, “It is more tolerable to be prostituted to one man than to many”—did we not immediately add why we had said this? For the Samaritan woman in the Gospel, who said that she had had a sixth husband, is rebuked by the Lord because he was not her husband (John 4).

Even now I proclaim with a free voice that digamy is not condemned in the Church, indeed not even trigamy; and that it is permitted to marry a fifth, a sixth, or more times, just as it is permitted to marry a second husband. But just as these marriages are not condemned, so neither are they praised. They are consolations for misery, not praises of continence.

Thus, in another place I said:
