> “When one husband has been exceeded, it makes no difference whether the second or the third has been taken, because the person ceases to be monogamous. All things are permitted, but not all things are expedient. I do not condemn those married twice, nor even those married three times, or, if one may say so, eight times. Let her have an eighth husband, whoever she wishes, and cease to be a prostitute.”

### 19

I shall come also to the passage in which I am accused because I said (Book 1, chapter 9) that, according to the Hebrew Truth alone, on the second day there was not added, as on the first, third, and remaining days, “God saw that it was good” (Gen. 1). I immediately added:

> “We are left to understand that the number two is not good, because it divides what is united and prefigures the covenants of marriage. Hence, in Noah’s ark, all the animals that enter two by two are unclean. An odd number is clean.”

In this matter, concerning the second day, I do not know what is being criticized. Is it because it is written and we said that it was not written? Or because, even if it is written, we understood it differently from what the simplicity of Scripture permits?

That “God saw that it was good” is not written concerning the second day—let them accept not my testimony, but that of all the Hebrews and of the other translators, namely Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion.

But if it is not written, although it is written concerning the other days, then let them either provide another more plausible reason why it was not written, or, if they cannot find one, let them accept unwillingly what we have said.

Furthermore, if all the animals which enter Noah’s ark two by two are unclean, and an odd number is clean—and no one doubts that this is written—let them explain why it was written. If they do not explain it, then, whether they wish to or not, they will accept what I have explained. Either bring forth better food and use me as your guest, or be content with our little dinner, whatever its quality.

Surely I must now enumerate which ecclesiastical writers have discussed the odd number: Clement, Hippolytus, Origen, Dionysius, Eusebius, Didymus; and among our own writers, Tertullian, Cyprian, Victorinus, Lactantius, and Hilary. [Note: In nearly all the old printed editions before Martianaeus, “Hilary” was read instead of “Cyprian,” although all manuscript copies reject this. Victorinus’ homonym Fortunatus, who wrote the life of Hilary’s daughter, caused the error. He was thought to be the same Hilary to whom the book on the number seven was addressed, and therefore that book was attributed to Hilary. This is a hallucination of Victorinus, full of anachronism and other errors.]

Cyprian’s book addressed to Fortunatus is evidence of what and how much he said when discussing the number seven, that is, the odd number.

Or should I bring forward Pythagoras, Archytas of Tarentum, and Publius Scipio in the sixth book of *The Republic*, discussing the odd number? [Note: The Verona manuscript has in Greek, *tēs politeias*, “in the sixth book of *The Republic*,” “concerning the odd number,” and so forth. But this can be no other work than the Latin book, or books, which Cicero wrote *On the Republic*, in the sixth book of which Publius Scipio is introduced discussing the odd number. Of that work, only a few fragments now survive in Seneca, Nonius, Aulus Gellius, Lactantius, and Augustine.]

And if my critics refuse to listen to these men, I shall make the schools of the grammarians shout to them:

> “The god rejoices in the odd number” (Virgil, *Eclogue* 8).

### 20

What a great sacrilege! The churches have been overthrown! The world cannot bear to hear that we have said virginity is purer than marriage, that we have placed the even number beneath the odd, and shown that the types of the Old Testament have advanced toward evangelical truth.

I consider the remaining points criticized in my book either less important or pertaining to the same subject. Therefore I did not wish to answer them, lest I exceed the proper size of this little book and seem to distrust your judgment, since I had already chosen you as the patron of my case before I asked you to be so.

Therefore, with this final declaration, I protest that I have neither condemned nor do I condemn marriage; that I answered my adversary and did not fear the snares of my own people.

I exalt virginity to heaven, not because I possess it, but because I admire all the more what I do not possess. It is an honest and modest confession to praise in others what one lacks oneself.

Surely, because I am attached to the earth by a heavy body, I do not admire the flight of birds, nor praise the dove because it

> “Skims the liquid path and does not move its swift wings”  
> (*Aeneid* 5).

Let no one deceive himself; let no one hurl himself headlong through flattering praise. The first virginity is from birth [Note: Victorinus reads: “from the first birth.”]; the second virginity is from the second birth.

This is not my saying; it is an ancient maxim:

> “No one can serve two masters” (Matt. 6:24),

the flesh and the spirit.

> “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh; for these oppose one another, so that we do not do the things we wish” (Gal. 5:17).

When anything in our little work seems harsh to you, do not look to my words, but to the Scripture from which my words have been drawn.

### 21

Christ is a virgin; the Mother of our Virgin is a perpetual virgin, both mother and virgin.

Jesus entered through closed doors, and in his tomb, which had been newly hewn in the hardest rock, no one had previously been placed, nor was anyone placed afterward.

> “A garden enclosed, a sealed fountain” (Song 4:12),

from which, according to Joel (3:18), that river flows which waters the torrent—or the “valley of ropes,” as the Hebrew text has it, or “the valley of thorns,” as the Septuagint translators have it. [Note: The first expression belongs to the Hebrew text; the second to the Septuagint translators, *choinōn*.]

The ropes are the sins by which they were formerly bound [another reading: by which we were formerly bound]; the thorns are those which choked the seed of the master of the household.

This is the eastern gate, as Ezekiel says, always closed and shining, enclosing within itself—or bringing forth from itself—the Holy of Holies. Through it the Sun of righteousness and our High Priest according to the order of Melchizedek enters and departs.

Let them answer me how Jesus entered through closed doors, when he showed hands to be touched, and his side to be examined, and displayed bones and flesh, lest the reality of his body be thought a phantom; and I shall answer how holy Mary is both mother and virgin: a virgin after giving birth, a mother before she was married.

Therefore, as we had begun to say, Christ the virgin and Mary the virgin consecrated the beginnings of virginity for both sexes. [Note: Formerly, with Victorinus: “They dedicated the virginity of both sexes. The Apostles …”]

The Apostles were either virgins or continent after marriage.

[Note: This passage of Epiphanius, *Against the Heresies* 59, which concerns the Cataphrygians, section 4, is especially relevant here: “Moreover, he says, even the man who still lives in marriage and begets children, although he is the husband of one wife, is nevertheless by no means admitted to the order of deacon, presbyter, bishop, or subdeacon, but only one who has abstained from intercourse with one wife, or has been deprived of her. This is observed especially in those places where ecclesiastical canons are especially maintained.” The final words, concerning ecclesiastical discipline, deserve particular consideration.]

Bishops, presbyters, and deacons are chosen either from virgins, from widowers, or at least from those who, after priestly ordination, remain chaste forever.

Why do we deceive ourselves and become angry when, though our desires continually rush toward intercourse, the rewards of chastity are denied us? We want to eat lavishly, cling to the embraces of our wives, and reign with Christ among the virgins and widows.

Will hunger, then, receive the same reward as gluttony; filth the same as cleanliness; sackcloth the same as silk?

Lazarus received evil things during his life, while that rich man, clad in purple, fat and sleek, enjoyed the goods of the flesh while he lived; but after death they occupy different places (Luke 16). Miseries are exchanged for delights, and delights for miseries.

It lies within our choice either to follow Lazarus or the rich man.

## EPISTLE XLIX [Note: Also numbered 32. Written at the same time and joined to the preceding letter.]

### TO PAMMACHIUS

He sends Pammachius the preceding apologetic letter and congratulates him because everyone considered him worthy of the priesthood; finally, he invites him to read his translations from the Hebrew and his other little works.

### 1

It is sometimes a matter of Christian modesty to remain silent even among friends, and to console one’s humility more through silence than, by revisiting old friendships, to incur the charge of ambition.

As long as you remained silent, I remained silent, nor did I ever wish to complain about this matter, lest I seem to be seeking not a friend but someone more powerful.

But now, summoned by the duty of correspondence, I shall always try to take the first place—not so much to reply as to write—so that it may be recognized both that I have until now remained silent modestly and that I have now begun to speak more modestly still.

### 2

I know very well how wisely and affectionately you acted concerning my little books against Jovinianus, by withholding copies. But that diligence achieved nothing, since some who came from the City would read back to me the very things they reported having received at Rome.

The books had already been circulated in this province as well; and, as you yourself have read,

> “A word once sent forth does not know how to return”  
> (Horace, *Art of Poetry*).

I am not as fortunate as many writers of this age, who are able to correct their trifles whenever they wish. As soon as I have written something, either my admirers or my envious critics—though differing in purpose, yet competing with equal zeal—scatter our writings among the public. They are excessive either in praise or in blame, following their own stomach rather than the merit of the style.

Accordingly, the only thing I could do was to dedicate to you an *apology*—*apologetikón*—for the work itself, which I addressed to you—*prosephōnēsa*. [Note: Erasmus and Victorinus read: “I sent you the apology, which I addressed to you, and published it at your request.” The phrase *prosephōnēsa* was misunderstood by an inexperienced glossator, who did not recognize that the verb *prosphōnein* means “to name” or “to address” in this passage.]

When you have read it, you yourself will satisfy everyone else on our behalf—or, if you too wrinkle your nose, you will be compelled to expound differently that *pericope*—*perikopē*, “passage”—of the Apostle in which he discusses virginity and marriage.

### 3

I do not say this to provoke you to write, for in the sacred Scriptures I place your diligence before my own, but so that you may compel those who tear us apart to do so.

They know letters and imagine themselves learned. They can either refrain from criticizing me or teach me. If they write anything, my interpretation will be disregarded all the more by comparison with their work.

Read, I beg you, and examine the Apostle’s words carefully. Then you will see that, in order to avoid slander, I have been much more lenient toward husbands than he wished.

Origen, Dionysius, Pierius, Eusebius of Caesarea, Didymus, and Apollinaris have interpreted this Epistle at great length. When Pierius was examining and explaining the Apostle’s meaning, and had proposed to expound the words,

> “But I wish that all were as I myself am” (1 Cor. 7:7),

he added:

> “By saying this, Paul openly preaches celibacy” (*tauta legōn ho Paulos antikrýs agāmian kēryssei*).

What, I ask, was my fault here? What harshness? Everything I wrote is extremely mild [another reading: extremely slight] by comparison with this statement.

Read through the commentaries of all those whom I have mentioned above, and enjoy the libraries of the churches; then you will reach your desired and intended goal more swiftly.

### 4

I hear that the interest of the entire City has been stirred in your favor. I hear that the will of the pontiff and of the people is united in agreement.

> “It is less to hold the priesthood than to deserve it.”

If you read the sixteen books of the Prophets which I translated into Latin from the Hebrew language, and I learn that you take pleasure in this work, you will urge us not to keep the other works, which are locked away in our cabinet, hidden any longer.

Recently I translated Job into our language. You can borrow a copy from your cousin, the holy Marcella. Read the Greek and Latin versions together, and compare the old edition with our translation; you will clearly see how great the difference is between truth and falsehood.

I sent some of my *commentaries*—*hypomnēmata*—on the twelve Prophets to the holy father Domnio, together with Samuel and Malachim, that is, the four books of Kings. [Note: A Benedictine annotator says: “These commentaries on the twelve Prophets do not exist,” evidently supposing that this passage refers to commentaries on each of the twelve minor Prophets—works which would certainly have to be considered different from those that survive, since the first three and final two were not commented on until more than a decade later. But Jerome said only that he had sent some of his *hypomnēmata*, or commentaries, not all of them; and not commentaries on each individual minor Prophet, but on the book simply entitled *The Twelve Prophets*. It is therefore easy to suppose that he sent Domnio the interpretations he had completed from Micah through Haggai since the preceding year, 392, and that there is no need to invent other lost works.]

If you wish to read them, you will recognize how difficult it is to understand divine Scripture, especially the Prophets, and how what flows among its own people in the purest stream of speech, through the fault of translators, runs among us filled with defects.

As for the eloquence which, for Christ’s sake, you despise in Cicero, do not seek it in little children. Ecclesiastical interpretation, even if it possesses elegance of expression, ought to conceal and avoid it, so that it may speak not to the leisure schools of philosophers and a few pupils, but to the whole human race.

## EPISTLE L [Note: Also numbered 51. Written shortly after the preceding letter.]

### TO DOMNIO

Having been informed by Saint Domnio of the abuse with which many people at Rome attacked the books against Jovinianus—especially a certain young monk, a rumor-monger—he vigorously attacks this man and rebukes his ignorance, challenging him to write.

### 1

Your letter sounds equally of love and complaint: of your love, by which, in carefully warning me, you fear even what is safe in us; and of the complaint against those who do not love, who seek occasions in our sins, chatter against their brother, and place a stumbling-block against the son of their mother (Ps. 39:20).

For you write that they—or rather, I do not know whom from the alleys, crossroads, and streets: a market-place monk, a rumor-monger, a pettifogger and cunning only for slander—are preaching against me and gnawing, tearing, and rending with a dog’s tooth the books I wrote against Jovinianus.

This dialectician of your city, this pillar of the Plautine family, has not read Aristotle’s *Categories*—*katēgorias*—nor *On Interpretation*—*peri hermēneias*—nor the *Analytica*—*analytika*, “Analytics”—nor even Cicero’s *Topics*—*topous*. Yet, moving through the circles of the ignorant and the drinking parties—*symposia*—of little women, he weaves *asyllogistic* syllogisms—*syllogismous asyllogistous*—and dissolves our arguments by clever reasoning, as though they were sophisms.

How foolish I was to think that I could not know these things without philosophers; I who read the better part of style as that which erased rather than that which wrote.

In vain, therefore, did I work through the commentaries of Alexander [Note: Learned men commonly understand this as referring to commentaries by Alexander of Aphrodisias translated into Latin by Jerome, and they count this translation among his lost works. But the holy Doctor did not say that he translated them into Latin or another language; he merely said that he “turned them over,” which here means that he studied and repeatedly worked through them, as numerous examples show in the Preface.]—in vain did a learned master introduce me to Logic through Porphyry’s *Isagoge*—*eisagōgē*—and, to speak of human learning, did Gregory of Nazianzus and Didymus serve as my instructors in the sacred Scriptures.

The learning of the Hebrews was of no benefit to me, nor the daily meditation, from adolescence to this age, upon the Law, the Prophets, the Gospels, and the Apostles.

### 2

A man has been found who is perfect without a teacher, inspired—*pneumatophoros*—and self-taught—*kai autodidaktos*—who surpasses Cicero in eloquence, Aristotle in argument, Plato in prudence, Aristarchus in learning, Chalcenterus in the multitude of his books, Didymus in knowledge of the Scriptures, and all the writers of his own age.

Finally, he is said to demand a subject and, offering something from Carneades [Note: Another reading has “Carneadean.” Concerning Carneades of Cyrene, see Diogenes Laertius, Book 4; Plutarch, *Cato the Elder*; and others], to argue on both sides—that is, both for justice and against justice.

The world has been delivered from danger, and hereditary or centumviral cases have been dragged out of the abyss, because this man, neglecting the forum, transferred himself to the Church. Who would have been innocent if he had not wished it? [The edition notes: read “if he had wished it.”] What criminal would this man’s speech not have saved, once he began dividing the case on his fingers and stretching out the nets of his syllogisms?

For if he had stamped his foot, fixed his eyes, wrinkled his brow, waved his hand, and twisted his beard [Note: We prefer the reading preserved in the Cistercian manuscript. Formerly the text had *verba tornasset* or *tonasset*, a reading that is not merely unsuitable but false. Jerome is here mocking his opponent by saying that his gestures alone, before he uttered a word, could have cast a spell over the judges. The custom of twisting or turning the beard in a circle, and the gesture made when preparing to speak, are also noted by others among Eastern peoples], he would immediately have spread darkness before the eyes of the judges [another reading: “poured darkness”].

Nor is it surprising that this most Latin and eloquent man should overcome me, who have long been absent and have had no practice in the Latin language, being half-Greek and barbarous. He even overwhelmed the present Jovinianus—good Jesus, what sort and what great man! No one could understand his writings, though he sang only to himself and the Muses—beneath the weight of his eloquence.

### 3

I ask you, therefore, dearest father, to warn him not to speak against his own profession; not to promise chastity by his dress and destroy it by his words; not to compare married women [another reading: husbands] with virgins; and not to have fought so long and uselessly against a man of such eloquence.

I also hear that he gladly goes around the cells of virgins and widows and, with raised eyebrow, philosophizes among them about the sacred Scriptures.

What does he teach these little women in private, in the bedroom? That virgins are the same as married women? That they should not neglect the flower of their age, but eat and drink, visit the baths, pursue cleanliness, and not reject perfumes? Or rather, that they should practice modesty, fasting, and bodily filth?

Surely he teaches the things that are full of virtue. Let him confess publicly what he says at home. Or, if at home he teaches the same things as in public, he must be kept away from the company of girls.

I am amazed that a young man and monk who, as he thinks, is eloquent—whose mouth pours forth charms, and whose speech is so elegant that it is sprinkled with comic wit and humor—does not blush to visit the houses of the nobility, cling to the greetings of married women, turn our religion into a contest [Note: Erasmus and Victorinus make “our religion” pagan. Martianaeus reads “turn our religion into a battle.” We have followed the manuscripts and the older edition, understanding the expression to mean that he turns religion into a contest, since the monk presents one thing in dress and religious profession and another in words and conduct—or rather, that he turns the doctrines of religion into material for disputation and controversy], and torture the faith of Christ through verbal contention, while slandering his brother.

If he thought that I was mistaken—for we all offend in many things, and “if anyone does not offend in word, he is a perfect man” (James 3:2)—he ought either to have rebuked me or to have asked me by letter. That is what the learned and noble Pammachius did; to him I gave an apology—*apelogisamēn*—as best I could and explained in a longer Epistle (the preceding Epistle XLVIII) what I meant in each passage.

At least he should have imitated your modesty. You extracted and arranged in order those passages which seemed to cause scandal to some people, asking me either to correct or explain them. He should not have thought me so insane as to write for marriage and against marriage in one and the same book.

### 4

Let him spare himself, spare me, and spare the Christian name. Let him learn that a monk is known not by talking and running about, but by silence and sitting.

Let him read Jeremiah, who says:

> “It is good for a man when he has borne the yoke from his youth. He shall sit alone and be silent, because he has taken the yoke upon himself” (Lam. 3:27–28).

Or if he has truly taken up the censor’s rod against all writers, and therefore considers himself learned because he alone understands Jovinianus—for there is a proverb, “A stammerer understands a stammerer’s words best”—let us all be called *not writers*—*pantes ou syngrapheis*—by the judgment of Attilius. [Note: We have not altered the reading of the Benedictine edition, since our old manuscripts do not provide sufficient assistance. Other printed editions, with a more plausible—or at least more harmonious—meaning, read *pantas syngrapheis pellomen*, “we expel all writers.” We would in fact prefer this reading, especially because Jerome elsewhere speaks of men who arrogated so much to themselves that they expelled other writers from the honor and rank of authors. Thus, in the Epistle to Rusticus the Monk, speaking of Rufinus: “To mark as censor whoever he wished and exclude him from the Senate of the learned.” Again, in the Epistle against Vigilantius to Riparius: “You alone, with your most learned skull, are permitted to pass judgment on all Greek and Latin writers, and, as with a censor’s rod, to eject some from the libraries and admit others,” and so forth.

It is commonly believed that M. Attilius Regulus is meant here, who held the office of censor with great severity, as Valerius Maximus records in Book 2, chapter 9; but that has little relevance here. We think this Attilius is rather the man mentioned by the younger Pliny in Book 1, Letter 9, whom he calls both extremely learned and extremely witty. Or, more correctly, M. Atilius—or Acilius—Palicanus, who is mentioned in the fragments of Sallust, Book 6, as a Picenian of low birth, more talkative than eloquent. These words are quoted from Sallust by Quintilian, 1.4.2, and Gellius, and by Jerome himself in *Against Helvidius. The words that follow appear to be spoken by Jovinianus.]

Jovinianus himself, an unlettered author—*syngrapheus agrammatos*—will rightly proclaim to him:

> “What the bishops condemn in me is not reason, but conspiracy.”

I do not want this or that man to answer me—men whose authority can crush me but cannot teach me. Let a man write against me whose language I can understand. When I have defeated him, I shall have defeated all men at once.

For I know well—believe one who has experienced it—

> “How high he rises against the shield, with what whirling force he hurls the spear”  
> (*Aeneid* 10).

He is strong, knotty, and tenacious in disputation, and fights with an oblique and arched head [Note: Formerly the text read “with a pointed head,” a reading defended by Victorinus and others, but one that is unsuitable. Elsewhere, against Vigilantius, Jerome speaks of an “arched wound” and elsewhere of an “arched attack.”]

Often he shouted against us in the streets from night until evening. He has the flanks and strength of an athlete, and is agreeably corpulent.

He seems to me secretly to be a follower of my doctrine. Moreover, he is never ashamed and does not consider what he says, but how much. He has reached such an opinion of his eloquence that his sayings are commonly said to be “dictations of Ciriatus.”

How often has this man made me rage in the circles and driven me to anger? [Note: Concerning this ancient insult of spitting, Petronius writes: “He summons all the ragwomen and the filthiest part of the household, and orders me to be spat upon.” See Seneca, *On the Injuries of the Wise Man*, chapter 1.] How often has he spat, only to depart after being spat upon?

But these are common insults, and any of my followers could inflict them. I appeal to books, to a memory that may be transmitted to posterity. Let us speak through our writings, so that the silent reader may judge us; and just as I lead a flock of disciples, so may his followers be called Gnathonics or Phormionics after his name.

### 5

It is no great feat, my Domnio, to chatter in alleyways and doctors’ shops and pass judgment on the world: “This man spoke well, that one badly; this one knows the Scriptures, that one raves; this man is talkative, that one utterly speechless.”

What claim to such judgment has one who has earned no authority by it?

To make a commotion against anyone at random in the crossroads and heap up abuse rather than accusations is the work of buffoons and of those always prepared for quarrels.

Let him move his hand, fix his pen, exert himself, and show in writing whatever he can. Let him give us an opportunity to answer his eloquence. I can bite back [another reading: “answer”] if I wish; if wounded, I can sink in my canine tooth.

We too have learned our letters:

> “We too have often withdrawn our hand from the rod”  
> (Juvenal, *Satire* 1).

It may also be said of us:

> “He has hay on his horn; flee far away”  
> (Horace, *Satires* 1.4).

But we would rather be disciples of him who said:

> “I gave my back to the scourging, and I did not turn my face away from the shame of spitting”  
> (Isa. 50:6, according to the Septuagint).

> “When he was reviled, he did not revile in return”  
> (1 Pet. 2:23).

And after slaps, the cross, scourging, and blasphemies, he finally prayed for those who crucified him, saying:

> “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing”  
> (Luke 23:34).

I too forgive my brother’s error. I understand that he has been deceived by the devil’s art.

Among little women he seemed to himself learned and eloquent. After my little works reached Rome, he recoiled from me as from a rival and sought glory from attacking me as well, so that no one on earth would displease his eloquence except those whose power he does not spare but yields to—in other words, those whom he does not honor but fears.

This most learned man wished, like a veteran soldier, to strike both of us with a single sweep of his sword and show the people that whatever he himself wished was what Scripture meant.

Let him therefore deign to send us his discourse and correct our loquacity not by criticism but by teaching. Then he will understand that the forum has one kind of force and the dining room another, and that one does not debate the doctrines of divine law in the same manner among spinning distaffs and girls’ baskets as among learned men.

Now he freely and shamelessly boasts before the public and shouts that he condemns marriage [Note: That is, Jerome, against whom this charge is directed. Some manuscripts instead read “he condemned.”]. Among swollen wombs, the cries of infants, and the beds of married people, he keeps silent about what the Apostle said, in order to make me alone hateful.

But when he comes to books, sets foot against foot, and either proposes something from the Scriptures or hears someone else propose it, then he will sweat, then he will stick fast. Away with Epicurus; far away with Aristippus. Swineherds will not be present, nor will the sow grunt.

> “And we, father, scatter missiles and no feeble iron from our right hand;  
> and blood follows from the wound we have made.”  
> (*Aeneid* 12).

Moreover, if he does not wish to write and thinks that the matter should be handled only with curses, let him hear, across all the intervening lands, seas, and peoples, [Note: In place of *echo*, the reading previously had *et hoc* incorrectly; we did not hesitate to emend it even without manuscript support.] at least the echo of my cry: I do not condemn marriage; I do not condemn wedlock. And so that he may hold my opinion more certainly, I want all those who perhaps cannot sleep alone because of nighttime fears to take wives.

# LETTER LI [Note: Elsewhere numbered 60. Written and translated into Latin around the same year, 394.]

## SAINT EPIPHANIUS TO JOHN, BISHOP OF JERUSALEM

Translated into Latin by Jerome.

[Col. 0517]

Epiphanius, Bishop of Salamis in Cyprus, excuses himself to John, Bishop of Jerusalem, for having ordained the presbyter Paulinian without consulting him. He then admonishes him to abstain from the errors of Origen.

**To the most beloved Lord and Brother, John the Bishop: Epiphanius.**

### 1.

We ought, most beloved, not to abuse the honor of the clergy for the sake of pride, but to make our conduct—through the keeping of God’s commandments and the most diligent observance of them—correspond to what we are called. For if Holy Scripture says, “Their clergy shall not profit them” (Jeremiah 12, according to the Septuagint), what advantage can clerical arrogance bring us, when we sin not only in thought and feeling but also in speech? [Note: See below, Letter 57, *On the Best Kind of Translating*, in which Jerome defends himself against Rufinus, who quibbles over these earlier words of Epiphanius, which are in Greek, ἔδει γὰρ ἡμᾶς, αγαπητὲ, μὴ τῇ ὀιήσει τῶν κλήρων φέρεσθαι—“For we ought, beloved, not to be carried away by the conceit of clerical offices”—but which the holy Doctor rendered badly into Latin.]

For I have heard that you are swelling up against us, that you are angry, and that you threaten to write to the ends of the earth, so as not to name the places and provinces. And where is the fear of God, which ought to shake us with that trembling expressed by the Lord: “If anyone is angry with his brother without cause, he shall be liable to judgment”? (Matthew 3:23.) Not that I care very much if you write whatever pleases you. For letters were written, even “papyrus letters,” according to Isaiah, and were sent upon the waters, which quickly pass away with the world. [Note: In the Hebrew text of Isaiah the expression means “in vessels of papyrus”; but the Septuagint, reading another letter—letters that are very easily confused—translated it as ἐπιστολὰς βιβλίνας, taking *biblos* to mean either papyrus or a letter, since letters were written on papyrus. See Pliny, Book XIII, chapter 11, and Cassiodorus, Book XI, Letter 38. Hence Aldhelm, concerning the nightingale: “I am written in Roman books, but with a Greek voice.” And Ennodius: “Not suffering poems to lie idle in Nile-born books, I ploughed,” and so forth. But more must be said elsewhere about the deeper interpretation and use of this passage, in Book 2 against the Pelagians. For the present we have restored the preceding little word to you from the manuscripts.]

We have done you no harm, committed no injury against you, and forcibly extorted nothing. In the monastery of the brothers, and of the foreign brothers, [Note: Two older Vatican manuscripts have “who owed nothing to your province.” Paulinianus was Jerome’s brother, whom Epiphanius ordained first deacon and soon afterward presbyter in the monastery of the foreign brothers, which did not belong to John’s diocese. The Cistercian manuscript, however, reads: “lest they should seem, through a certain harshness and through the consciousness of the ancient faith which we shared, to be separated from the Church.” The Ambrosian manuscript reads: “They had only recently begun to have fellowship, and lest they should seem, through a certain harshness,” and so forth.] who owed nothing to your province, and because of our lowliness and the letters that we frequently sent them, they also began to have a disagreement with your communion, lest they should seem, through some harshness and through consciousness of our ancient faith, to be separated from the Church. We ordained him deacon; and after he had served, again as presbyter. For this you ought to have rejoiced, understanding that we were compelled to do it through fear of God—especially since there is no difference in the priesthood of God, and since the welfare of the Church was being provided for.

For although the individual bishops of the churches have churches under them, over which they seem to exercise care, and although no one extends himself over another’s jurisdiction, nevertheless the love of Christ is set above everything, and in it there is no pretense. Nor should one consider merely what was done, but when, how, among whom, and why it was done.

When I saw that a multitude of holy brothers was living in the monastery, and that the holy presbyters Jerome and Vincent, out of modesty and humility, were unwilling to perform the sacrifices due to their office or to undertake this part of the ministry, which is the chief salvation of Christians; and since you could not find and apprehend the servant of God, who often fled from you because he did not wish to accept the heavy burden of the priesthood, [Note: The Ambrosian manuscript may read more correctly, omitting the word *you*.] nor could any other bishop easily find him—for this reason I was greatly astonished at how, by God’s dispensation, he came to us with the monastery’s deacons and the other brothers, so that he might satisfy me, because I was troubled by some matter against them.

When the assembly was being celebrated in the church of a village near our monastery, we ordered that he be seized by many deacons, although he knew nothing of it and had not the slightest suspicion, and that his mouth be held, lest, wishing to free himself, he should adjure us by the name of Christ. First we ordained him deacon, presenting to him the fear of God and compelling him to serve. He resisted very strongly, crying out that he was unworthy and protesting that the burden was beyond his strength. [Note: The words “crying out and protesting that the burden was beyond his strength,” which were absent from all earlier editions, have been supplied from the Ambrosian manuscript.]

At last we compelled him and persuaded him by the testimonies of Scripture and by setting forth God’s commandments. After he had served in the holy sacrifices—or, according to another reading, while he was serving—we again ordained him presbyter, with great difficulty, his mouth being held, and by the same words with which we had previously persuaded him we urged him to sit in the order of the presbytery.

After this we wrote to the holy presbyters of the monastery and to the other brothers, and reproved them for not having written to us about him, although a year earlier I had heard many of them complain that they did not have someone to celebrate the Lord’s sacraments for them, and although all of them requested him on the strength of their testimony and attested the great common benefit to the monastery. Why, then, when the opportunity had been found, had they not written to us or requested anything concerning his ordination?

### 2.

These things were done as I have said, in the love of Christ, which I believed you possessed toward our lowliness, although I ordained him in a monastery and not in a parish subject to you.

O truly blessed gentleness and goodness of the bishops of Cyprus—and our rusticity, worthy, according to your judgment and decision, of the mercy of God! For many bishops of our communion ordained presbyters in our province whom we could not apprehend, and sent us deacons and subdeacons, whom we received with gratitude.

I myself also exhorted the bishop of blessed memory, Philo, and the holy Theoprepus, [Note: We have emended this from the oldest Vatican and Ambrosian manuscripts. Earlier editions had *Theoprobos*, partly in Latin and partly in Greek form. The old edition also lacks the word “deacons” a little earlier.] to ordain presbyters in the churches of Cyprus that were near them but seemed to belong to my parish, since the province was large and extensive, and to provide for the Church of Christ.

I have never ordained deaconesses and sent them to foreign provinces, nor have I done anything to divide the Church. Why, then, did it seem right to you to swell up so violently and boast against us over an act of God that was done for the building up, not the destruction, of the brothers?

I was also exceedingly astonished that you spoke to my clerics, claiming that through the holy presbyter and abbot of the monks, Gregory, you had ordered me not to ordain anyone, and that I had promised to do so, saying, “Am I a young man, or do I not know the canons?”

Hear, then, the truth in the word of God: I neither heard nor knew this, and I have absolutely no recollection of such a conversation. I suspected, however, that perhaps, amid many matters, I had forgotten it like a human being. For this reason I questioned the holy Gregory and the presbyter Zeno, who is with him. Abbot Gregory replied that he knew nothing whatever of it. Zeno, however, said that when the presbyter Rufinus was speaking briefly with him about some other matters, he had also said: “Do you think that the holy bishop is going to ordain anyone?”—and that the conversation had gone no further.

I, Epiphanius, neither heard anything nor replied. Therefore, most beloved, do not let fury precede you, nor indignation seize you, nor let yourself be needlessly agitated and, grieving over one matter, turn to others, so that you may seem to have found an occasion for sinning. The Prophet, avoiding this, prays to the Lord, saying: “Do not incline my heart to words of malice, to make excuses for sins” (Psalm 140:4).

### 3.

I was also astonished when I heard that certain people—those who habitually carry rumors back and forth and always add something to what they have heard, so as to stir up sadness and quarrels among brothers—had troubled you as well, saying that in prayer, when we offer sacrifices to God, we customarily say for you: “Lord, grant that John may believe rightly.”

Do not think us so rustic that we could have said this so openly. Although I always pray for this in my heart, yet, to speak plainly, I have never uttered it in another’s hearing, lest I seem to think little of you, most beloved.

When, however, we complete the prayer according to the rite of the mysteries, and say for everyone, and also for you, “Guard him who preaches the truth”—or, at any rate, “You, Lord, grant and guard that he may preach the word of truth”—we speak according as the occasion for the wording presents itself and the prayer’s sequence requires.

Therefore I beg you, most beloved, and, lying prostrate at your feet, I pray you: grant both to me and to yourself that you may be saved, as it is written, “from a crooked generation”; and withdraw from the heresy of Origen and from all heresies, most beloved.

For I see that all your [another reading: our] indignation has been stirred up for this reason: because I said to you that you ought not to praise Arius’s father, the root and parent of other heresies. [Note: The printed editions insert here the words “namely, Origen,” after “Arius’s father,” but no manuscript recognizes them. On the authority of the manuscripts we have removed them as though they came from the hand of a glossator.]

When I begged you not to err in this way and admonished you, you contradicted me and brought me to sadness and tears. Not only me, but also many other Catholics who were present. This, as I understand it, is the source of all your indignation and this fury.

And therefore you threaten to send letters against me, so that your speech may run here and there; and, stirring up hatred against me in defense of heresy, you break the love that we have had for you—to such an extent that you have made us repent of having communicated with you, since you defend the errors and doctrines of Origen. [Note: The phrase “defending them” can conveniently be referred to us; the Ambrosian manuscript, however, reads “to those defending,” referring it to you.]

### 4.

I speak plainly—or, according to another reading, “I shall speak plainly”: in accordance with what is written, we do not spare even our eye, so as not to tear it out if it causes us to stumble; nor our hand or foot, if it causes us to stumble. Therefore, whether you are our eyes, our hands, or our feet, you too will suffer the same treatment.

For what Catholic could endure calmly—and what person who adorns his faith with good works could endure hearing the doctrine and counsel of Origen, or believing his splendid proclamation: “The Son cannot see the Father, nor can the Holy Spirit see the Son”? These things are written in the books *On First Principles* (*περὶ Ἀρχῶν*); we read them in these words, and this is how Origen spoke:

“For just as it is incongruous to say that the Son can see the Father, so it is inconsistent to suppose that the Holy Spirit can see the Son.”

Who could also endure Origen saying that souls were angels in heaven, and that after they sinned in the heights they were cast down into this world and, as into tombs and sepulchers, confined in these bodies to pay the penalties for their former sins? Or that the bodies of believers are not temples of Christ but prisons of the condemned?

From that point, corrupting the truth of history by allegory and falsehood, he multiplies endless words. Undermining the simple with various forms of persuasion, he now asserts that souls are called *ψυχαί* (*psychai*)—“souls”—according to the Greek etymology, ἀπὸ τοῦ ψύχεσθαι, “from becoming cold,” because, coming from heavenly places to lower regions, they have lost their former warmth. [Note: Older editions read ἀπὸ τοῦ ψυχρίζεσθαι, “from becoming cold,” and therefore continue, “because …” Another reading has “from becoming angelic”; *algescending*—“growing cold”—should perhaps be read. The Vatican manuscript is faulty in the phrase “according to the Greek etymology,” where it says, “because you call bodies prisons,” and so forth. It is well known that Origen took this notion from Pythagoras through Plato.]

At another time he says that this body is called *δέμας* among the Greeks, that is, “bond,” or, according to another usage, “corpse,” because souls have fallen from heaven. [Note: I would prefer that the Greek term itself be inserted, reading, “according to another usage, πτῶμα, that is, corpse.” In Greek, an inanimate body is called *πτῶμα* from *πίπτειν*, “to fall,” just as Latin *cadaver* is derived from *cadere*, “to fall.” Since Origen twists the Greek etymology itself to serve his heresy, it would have been better to include it here, as above and below. The Vatican and Ambrosian manuscripts, however, omit *σῶμα* and “that is,” and read continuously: “According to the varied resources of the Greek language, they interpret body as *σῆμα*, that is, memorial—or monument.” Plato, from whose teaching Origen spoke, said in the *Cratylus* and the *Gorgias* that bodies serve souls as sepulchers, and that *σῶμα*—body—was so called as if it were *σῆμα*—tomb. Plato writes: Καὶ γὰρ σῆμά τινες φάσιν αὐτὸ εἶναι τῆς ψυχῆς ὡς τεθαμμένης ἐν τῷ νῦν παρόντι, followed by other words that are better heard in Latin: “For some say that *σῶμα* is the *σῆμα* of the soul, as though the soul were buried in the present body, or that it is rightly called *σῆμα* because the soul uses the body’s service to signify and explain the things it has sealed within itself.” And in the *Gorgias*: Καὶ ἡμεῖς τῷ ὄντι ἴσως τέθναμεν, ὅπερ ἤδη που ἔγωγε καὶ ἤκουσα τῶν σοφῶν, ὡς νῦν ἡμεῖς τέθναμεν καὶ τὸ μὲν σῶμα ἐστὶν ἡμῶν σῆμα. “And perhaps we really are dead. I have heard this from the wise: that we are now dead, and that our body, *σῶμα*, is a *σῆμα*, a tomb.”]

The majority, however, interpret *σῶμα*—“body”—as *σῆμα*—“monument”—according to the varied resources of the Greek language, because it holds the soul enclosed within it just as tombs and burial mounds hold the corpses of the dead.

And if this is true, where is our faith? Where is the proclamation of the resurrection? Where is the apostolic teaching that has endured in the churches of Christ to this day? Where is that blessing given to Adam and his offspring, to Noah and his sons: “Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth” (Genesis 1:28 and 9:7)?

For according to Origen there will now be not a blessing but a curse, since he turns angels into souls and makes them descend from the lofty height of their dignity to lower regions—as though God could not give souls to the human race by blessing unless angels had sinned, and as though there were as many falls in heaven as births on earth.

We must therefore abandon the teaching of the Apostles, the Prophets, the Law, and the Lord and Savior himself, who thunders in the Gospel. In contrast, Origen commands and lays down a law—indeed, I might say he compels his disciples—not to pray to ascend into heaven, lest they sin again more grievously than they had sinned previously on earth and be cast down into the world.

He commonly asserts such nonsense and delirium by a perverted interpretation of Scripture, making it signify something other than what is true. Thus he says: “Before I was humbled by wickedness, I transgressed” (Psalm 118:67); and: “Return, my soul, to your rest” (Psalm 114:7); and also: “Bring my soul out of prison” (Psalm 141:8); and elsewhere: “I will confess to the Lord in the land of the living” (Psalm 114:8)—although the divine Scripture clearly has another meaning than the one to which he maliciously twists it in the service of his heresy.

The Manichaeans, Gnostics, Ebionites, the followers of Marcion, and eighty other heresies do the same. [Note: The Ambrosian manuscript counts thirty; other manuscripts count forty. But, as Victor also correctly observed before us, Epiphanius names eighty because he wrote against that many heresies, which had proliferated up to his own time.] They take testimonies from the purest source of Scripture but do not interpret them as they are written; instead they want the simplicity of ecclesiastical speech to signify what they themselves think.

### 5.

I do not know whether I should grieve or laugh at the further claim he attempts to make. The outstanding teacher dares to teach that the devil will again become what he once was, return to the same dignity, and ascend to the kingdoms of heaven. What impiety! Who could be so witless and foolish as to accept that Saint John the Baptist, Peter, John the Apostle and Evangelist, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and the other Prophets should become the devil’s co-heirs in the kingdom of heaven?

I pass over his frivolous exposition concerning the garments of skins, and the effort and arguments by which he tries to make us believe that the garments of skins were human bodies. Among many other things he says:

“Was God a leatherworker or a dealer in hides, so that he would prepare the skins of animals and sew from them garments of skin for Adam and Eve? It is therefore clear,” he says, “that he is speaking about our bodies.”

And if this is so, how do we read that Adam, before the garments of skin, before disobedience, and before his fall from paradise, spoke not allegorically but truly: “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh” (Genesis 2:23)?

Or whence comes that which the divine word attests: “And God cast a deep sleep upon Adam, and he slept; and he took one of his ribs, and filled up flesh in its place, and built the rib that he had taken from him into a woman” (Genesis 2:21)?

Or what bodies did Adam and Eve cover with fig leaves after they had eaten from the forbidden tree?

Who, moreover, could patiently endure Origen’s denial, through slippery arguments, of the resurrection of this flesh, as he most clearly declares in his volume of explanations of the first psalm and in many other places?

Or who could listen to Origen assigning paradise to us in the third heaven, transferring there the paradise that Scripture mentions as being on earth, and understanding all the trees written of in Genesis allegorically—as though the trees were angelic Powers—when truth does not allow this?

For divine Scripture did not say, “God placed Adam and Eve on the earth,” but, “He cast them out of paradise and made them dwell opposite paradise.” [Note: The Vatican manuscript and the old edition read, “He made them dwell opposite paradise,” and do not add “beneath paradise.”] It does not say “beneath paradise.” “And he placed the flaming sword and the Cherubim to guard the entrance to the tree of life” (Genesis 3). It did not say “the ascent.”

“And a river went out from Eden”; it did not say, “descended from Eden.” This river is divided into four sources: “The name of the one is Pishon, and the name of the second is Gihon” (Genesis 2:10). I have seen the waters of Gihon, waters that I observed with these fleshly eyes. This is the Gihon that Jeremiah points out, saying: “What have you to do with the way of Egypt, to drink the water of Gihon, turbid water?” (Jeremiah 2:18.)

I drank also from the great river Euphrates—ordinary water, which you can touch with your hand and drink with your mouth, not spiritual waters. [Note: Martianay and others formerly had “from this great river.” The two earlier editions and two manuscripts read: “They are rivers and the waters are drunk and seen,” which is entirely correct.]

Where there are rivers that can both be seen and drunk, it follows that there are also figs and other trees, concerning which God says: “You shall eat from every tree that is in paradise” (Genesis 2:16). [Note: These two lines—“They are like other trees,” and so forth—were removed by Victor because he had not found them in his manuscripts and thought that they disturbed the sense. Since, on the contrary, they seemed to us to follow the sense quite well, we have restored them from three very ancient manuscripts and from all the printed editions.]

They are like other trees and plants, just as rivers are like rivers and waters. But if the water that is seen is truly water, it is necessary that the fig too be real, and the other trees; and that Adam, like Eve, was formed bodily from the beginning and not in an apparition, and that after the fall he did not, as Origen wishes, receive a body later on account of sin.

But you say: “We read that Saint Paul was caught up to the third heaven and into paradise” (2 Corinthians 12). You speak well. When he says “the third heaven” and afterward adds “and into paradise,” he shows that heaven is in one place and paradise in another.

Who would not immediately reject and despise those tricks, when Origen says that the waters above the firmament are not waters but certain Powers of angelic authority, and again that the waters above the earth—that is, below the firmament—are opposing Virtues, namely demons?

And how do we read that in the Flood the windows of heaven were opened and the waters of the deluge poured forth? How were the fountains of the abyss opened, and the whole world covered with waters? (Genesis 7.)

### 6.

O the madness of human beings joined to folly! They abandoned what is said in Proverbs: “Hear, my son, the instruction of your father, and do not reject the law of your mother” (Proverbs 6:20), and turned to error. They say to the fool, “Let him be his own master,” and do not despise the foolish things spoken by a fool, as Scripture testifies: “The fool speaks foolish things, and his heart understands vanity” (Isaiah 32:6).

Therefore I beg you, most beloved, and, sparing you as one of my own members, I entreat you in writing and prayer, because of the love I have for you, to fulfill what is said: “Do I not hate those who hate you, O Lord, and did I not waste away because of your enemies?” (Psalm 138:21.)

The words of Origen are hostile, worthy of hatred, and opposed to God and to his saints—not only those I have mentioned, but countless others as well. For it is not my present purpose to dispute against all the doctrines of Origen.

Origen has taken nothing from me, nor was he part of my generation; I have not undertaken hatred and struggles against him because of any worldly possessions or inheritance. But, to speak plainly, I grieve—and grieve exceedingly—when I see many of the brothers, especially those who have made a substantial profession and have risen to the highest rank of the priesthood, deceived by his persuasions and made, through his most perverse teaching, into food for the devil.

In them is fulfilled what is said: “He laughs at every stronghold, and his food is choice, and he gathers captivity like sand” (Habakkuk 1).

May God deliver you, brother, and the holy people of Christ entrusted to you, and all the brothers who are with you, and especially the presbyter Rufinus, from the heresy of Origen, from the other heresies, and from their destruction.

For if, because of one or two words contrary to the faith, many heresies have been cast out of the Church, how much more will this man be counted among the heretics, since he invented so many perverse and such evil doctrines against the faith and became an enemy of God and the Church?

Among his many evils he even dared to say that Adam had lost the image of God, although Scripture nowhere at all indicates this. For if it were so, everything in the world would never serve Adam’s offspring, that is, the whole human race, just as the Apostle James says: “Everything is tamed and subjected to human nature” (James 3:7).

All things would never have been subjected to human beings if human beings did not possess, in accordance with the authority by which they rule over all things, the image of God.

The divine Scripture, joining and associating the grace of the blessing given to Adam with the generations descended from him, lest anyone should perhaps dare, by a malicious interpretation, to say that God’s grace was given to one man alone and that he alone was made in the image of God—because he had been formed from the earth, and his wife had been created from the man’s rib, while those conceived in the womb and not born like Adam did not possess the image of God—immediately links the matters in sequence and says:

“And Adam lived two hundred and thirty years, and knew Eve his wife, and she bore him a son according to his likeness and according to his image, and he called his name Seth” (Genesis 5:3).

Again, in the tenth generation, after two thousand two hundred and forty-two years, [Note: From the creation of the world to the people destroyed by the Flood, Eusebius, Jerome, Bede, and others, following the Septuagint, calculate two thousand two hundred and forty-two years. Others, likewise with Augustine in *The City of God*, Book 15, count 2,262. Since Epiphanius’s intention was not clear, and the earlier printed books, followed also by Martianay, read “sixty-two,” Victor, on the evidence of the manuscript copies, preferred “forty-two.” Two of our manuscripts also support this reading, and we follow them. The Ambrosian manuscript most correctly presents both readings: “after two thousand two hundred seventy-two years, or, as it is found in other copies, two thousand two hundred forty-two years.” From this the easy mistake of other scribes is apparent, owing to the near identity of the words.] God, vindicating his image and showing that the grace he had given to human beings remained in them, says:

“You shall not eat flesh with its blood; for I shall avenge your blood upon every person who sheds it, because I made human beings in the image of God” (Genesis 9:4–6).

Again, after another ten generations up to Abraham, and from Abraham to David fourteen more generations, making twenty-four generations altogether and two thousand one hundred seventeen years, the Holy Spirit, in the thirty-eighth psalm, when lamenting all human beings because they walk in vanity and are subject to sins, says:

“Nevertheless every human being walks about in an image” (Psalm 38:7).

And after David, under Solomon his son, we read something of this kind concerning the image of God. For in the book of Wisdom, which bears Solomon’s name, it says:

“God created human beings incorruptible, and gave them the image of his own nature” (Wisdom 2:23).

And again, after approximately one thousand one hundred and eleven years, more or less, we read in the New Testament that human beings had not lost the image of God. For the Apostle James, the brother of the Lord, whom we mentioned above as well, instructs us not to be caught by Origen’s snares, teaching that the human being possesses the image and likeness of God.

After speaking at length about the human tongue, he adds:

“It is an unstable evil; with it we bless God the Father, and with it we curse human beings, who have been made according to the likeness of God” (James 3:8–9).

Paul too, the vessel of election, who completed the evangelical teaching through his preaching, teaches us that human beings were created in the image and likeness of God, saying:

“A man ought not to nourish long hair, since he is the glory and image of God” (1 Corinthians 11:7). He simply calls it “image” by its proper name, while he signifies “likeness” by the term “glory.”

### 7.

In place of the three testimonies that you said would suffice for you if I found them in Holy Scripture, behold, we have given seven testimonies. Who, then, could endure the absurdities of Origen? I will not speak of anything more serious, lest I become like him or like his disciples, who dare, at the peril of their souls, to assert whatever comes into their mouths, and presume rather to command God than to pray to him or learn truth from him.

Some of them say that the image of God, which Adam first received, perished when he sinned. Others suppose that the body which the Son of God was to have from Mary is itself the image of the Creator. Some say that the soul is the image; others, the understanding; others, virtue; some, baptism; others, that human beings rule over everything because they are made in the image of God. Like drunkards, they belch out one opinion or another.

They ought simply to have fled from the danger and not denied what God says, but to have believed plainly and to have allowed God the certain and true knowledge of his gift—namely, in what part he created human beings in his image and likeness. [Note: In all earlier editions there was the disgraceful error *certamen*, “contest,” instead of *certam*, “certain,” together with two words; we have corrected it from the manuscripts.]

Abandoning these matters, they entangled themselves in many questions and through them sank into the mire of sins. We, however, most beloved, believe what the Lord has spoken and know that the image of God remains in all human beings. We allow God himself to know in what part the human being was created in the image of God.

Nor should anyone be deceived by what some, reading the Letter of John, do not understand, where he says:

“Now we are children of God, and we do not know what we shall be. But we know that when he is revealed, we shall be like him, for we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2). [Note: Earlier editions had, in agreement with the Vulgate and Greek text, “and it has not yet appeared what we shall be.” The Ambrosian, Vatican, and Cistercian manuscripts, together with the old edition, read as we have printed it. Epiphanius frequently uses passages of Scripture in this letter whose wording does not sufficiently agree with current copies.]

This was said on account of the glory that will be revealed there to his saints, just as we read elsewhere: “from glory to glory” (2 Corinthians 3:18). The saints have already received a pledge and a portion of this glory in the present age.

The first of them was Moses, whose face shone exceedingly and radiated like brightness and the sun. The second was Elijah, carried into heaven in a fiery chariot and feeling no harm from the fire. Stephen was being stoned, and his face had the appearance of an angel, visible to everyone.

What we have said here about a few must be understood of all, so that what is written may be fulfilled: “Everyone who sanctifies himself will be numbered among the blessed. Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8).

### 8.

Since these things are so, most beloved, guard your soul and cease murmuring against us—or, according to another reading, “around us.” For divine Scripture says:

“Do not murmur against one another, as some murmured and perished by serpents” (1 Corinthians 10:9–10).

Rather, yield to the truth, and love us who love you and the truth. May the God of peace, according to his mercy, grant that Satan be crushed beneath the feet of Christians, that every perverse occasion be cast away, and that the bond of love and peace and the proclamation of right faith not be torn apart among us.

## 9. A Little Story Worth Noting

[Col. 0526]

[Note: Martianaeus, together with certain other printed editions, has the faulty reading *Praeterea quod audivi* (“Furthermore, what I heard”); unless perhaps *Praeterea* alone should be read here.]

Furthermore, I heard some people murmuring against me because, when we were traveling together to the holy place called Bethel, so that I might celebrate the *Collecta* with you there according to ecclesiastical custom, and when I had come to the village called Anablatha and, passing by, had seen a burning lamp there, and had asked what place it was and learned that it was a church, and had entered to pray, I found there a curtain hanging in the doorway of that same church, dyed and painted, bearing an image as though of Christ or of some saint—for I do not sufficiently remember whose image it was.

[Note: The words *et detestatus essem* (“and had detested it”), which had previously been missing, have been supplied from manuscripts of good authority.]

When, therefore, I had seen this and had detested the fact that an image of a human being was hanging in the church of Christ contrary to the authority of the Scriptures, I tore it apart and gave the custodians of that place the further advice that they should use it to wrap and carry out a poor dead man.

“And they, murmuring against this, said: ‘If he wanted to tear it, it was only just that he should give another curtain and replace it.’” When I heard this, I promised that I would provide one and send it immediately. There was, however, a brief delay while I looked for a good curtain to send in its place; for I thought that one would have to be sent to me from Cyprus.

Now I have sent what I was able to find, and I ask that you order the presbyter of that place to receive from the [Col. 0527] reader the curtain sent by us, and thereafter instruct that curtains of this kind, which are contrary to our religion, not be hung in the church of Christ.

[Note: Most manuscripts and printed editions have the plural *presbyteros* (“presbyters”), and shortly afterward *a latore* (“from the bearer”) instead of *a Lectore* (“from the reader”). The reading of the manuscript copies seemed to us more probable and more genuine.]

For it befits your honesty to show greater concern, so that it may remove the scruple that is unworthy of the church of Christ and of the peoples entrusted to you.

[Note: The Vatican manuscript, together with the old edition, reads: “so that, once the scruple has been removed, he may consider what is worthy of the Church of Christ and of the peoples entrusted to you”—or something similar; *digna* should grammatically be *digna sunt*, and *intumetur* should be *intueatur*. The Ambrosian manuscript, however, has the most correct reading: “to have the concern and scrupulous care worthy of the Church of Christ and of the peoples,” etc. Yet, amid such great variation among the copies, it was not thought best to alter the printed reading.]

Beware also of Palladius the Galatian, who was once dear to us and now needs the mercy of God, because he preaches and teaches the heresy of Origen, lest he perhaps lead some of the people entrusted to you into the perversity of his error.

[Note: Most manuscripts and older printed books do not contain this salutation. Others have *valeas* (“may you fare well”) instead of *valeatis* (“may you fare well,” plural.]

I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.

# LETTER LII

[Note: Elsewhere numbered 2. Written in the year 394.]

## To Nepotianus

### On the Life of Clerics and Monks

To Nepotianus, nephew through his sister of Heliodorus, he prescribes a form of life which clerics and monks ought to follow, expounding paraenetically, virtue by virtue, the most salutary precepts pertaining to their life.

### 1

[Note: Manuscripts and other books, I do not know whether more accurately, omit the kind of heading found here—“The presbyter Jerome to the presbyter Nepotianus, greeting”—which Martianaeus, following Erasmus, places first.]

You ask me, dearest Nepotianus, in letters sent across the sea—and you ask repeatedly—that I arrange for you in a brief volume the precepts of conduct, and explain by what path one who has abandoned the warfare of the world and begun to be either a monk or a cleric may keep to the straight way of Christ, lest he be dragged toward the various byways of vices.

[Note: This passage is discussed and explained in the Life of the holy Doctor which we have recently prepared.]

When I was an adolescent, indeed almost still a boy, and was restraining the first impulses of a wanton age by the harshness of the desert, I wrote an exhortatory letter to your uncle, the holy Heliodorus, full of tears and laments, and displaying the affection of a companion in the wilderness. But in that work, given my age, I played; and, with my rhetorical studies and training still hot, I painted certain things with scholastic ornament.

Now, with my head already gray, my forehead furrowed with wrinkles, and wattles hanging from my chin like those of oxen,

> Cold blood stands stiff around the heart.  
> *(Virgil, Georgics, Book 2.)*

And elsewhere the same Poet sings:

> Age carries everything away, even the mind.

And shortly afterward:

> Now so many songs have slipped from me,  
> and my voice itself has fled from Moeris.  
> *(Bucolics, Eclogue 8.)*

### 2

And lest I seem to produce examples only from pagan literature, learn the mysteries of the divine books. David, seventy years old, once a warlike [Col. 0528] man, could not be warmed when old age was growing cold. Therefore a girl is sought from all the boundaries of Israel: Abishag the Shunammite, who was to sleep with the king and warm his aged body (1 Kings 1).

[Note: Older printed editions and the Vatican copy incorrectly read *de universis filiabus* or *filiis* (“from all the daughters” or “sons”).]

If you follow the letter that kills, does this not seem to you either a scene from a mime or an Atellan farce?

[Note: This is the well-known kind of comedy named after Atella, a town of the Oscans near Aversa in Campania. See Livy, Book 7, chapter 2.]

The cold old man is wrapped in clothing and does not grow warm unless he embraces the young girl. Bathsheba was still alive; Abigail remained, as did his other wives and concubines, whom Scripture mentions. All are rejected as though cold, and the aged man grows warm only in the embraces of one young girl.

Abraham was much older than David, yet while Sarah was alive he did not seek another wife. Isaac had twice David’s years, and, although Rebecca was already an old woman, he never grew cold. I say nothing of the men before the Flood, who, after nine hundred years, with joints not merely aged but almost decayed, nevertheless did not seek the embraces of girls. Certainly Moses, leader of the Israelite people, was one hundred and twenty years old, and did not change Zipporah.

[Note: Formerly, “did not change his wife.”]

### 3

What, then, is this Shunammite, at once wife and virgin, so ardent that she warmed the cold, yet so holy that she did not provoke the warm man to lust? Let the most wise Solomon explain the delights of his father and recount the embraces of the peaceful warrior:

> “Acquire wisdom, acquire understanding. Do not forget, and do not turn away from the words of my mouth.  
> Do not abandon her, and she will take hold of you; love her, and she will preserve you. The beginning of wisdom is: acquire wisdom; and with all your possessions acquire understanding. Surround her, and she will exalt you; honor her, and she will embrace you, so that she may give your head a crown of graces. May a crown of delights also protect you.”  
> *(Proverbs 4:5 ff.)*

Nearly all the virtues of the body change in old men, and, while wisdom alone increases, the rest decline: fasting, vigils and almsgiving, sleeping on the ground, journeys here and there, receiving travelers, defending the poor, assiduity in prayer, perseverance, visiting the sick, the labor of the hands by which alms may be provided—and, not to prolong my speech, all the activities performed through the body become less when the body is broken.

[Note: Martianaeus, following Erasmus, wrongly reads *caeterae virtutes* (“the other virtues”), against all our manuscripts, the Victorine manuscripts, and other printed editions. The Cistercian copy reads “frequent fasts”; the Vatican manuscript and old edition omit “almsgiving.” *Chameunia*, Greek χαμευνία, means sleeping on the ground.]

[Note: The Cistercian copy likewise reads that these things “necessarily become less.”]

I do not mean that wisdom grows cold in young people and those still of more vigorous age—at least not in those who have attained knowledge through labor, the most ardent zeal, holiness of life, and frequent prayer to the Lord Jesus—while in most old men it withers with age. Rather, I mean that youth endures many battles of the body; amid the kindling of vices and the [Col. 0529] titillations of the flesh, wisdom is stifled like a fire in green wood and cannot unfold its brightness.

But the old age of those who have trained their youth in honorable disciplines and meditated on the law of the Lord day and night becomes more learned with age, more polished through experience, wiser with the passage of time, and gathers the sweetest fruits of its former studies.

(Compare the Preface to Book 2 of the Commentary on Amos.)

Thus that wise man of Greece, Themistocles, is said to have declared, when he had completed one hundred and seven years and saw that he was dying, that he was sorry to be leaving life just when he had begun to become wise.

[Note: All the editions and manuscripts we have examined have *Themistocles*. But it is not possible to understand here the famous Athenian general Themistocles, while the two other Themistocles, Stoics—one mentioned by Longinus and the other introduced as a speaker by Plutarch in Book 1 of the *Symposium*—cannot conveniently be referred to here. It is therefore most probable that *Themistocles* should be read as *Theophrastus*, the celebrated philosopher of Greece, who, as is clear from Diogenes Laertius, although he had lived a very long time, still did not think that he had lived long enough. Laertius gives his years as eighty-five, but the number is corrupt there and should be 105, or, more correctly, as Jerome calculates, 107; for Theophrastus himself states in the Preface that he was ninety-nine when he wrote the *Characters*.]

Plato died while writing in his eighty-first year. Isocrates completed ninety-nine years in the labor of teaching and writing.

[Note: Some manuscripts and older printed editions wrongly insert Socrates instead of Isocrates. Lucian, in the *Macrobii*, gives Isocrates’s age as the same, so that one may see that Victorius is mistaken in calculating 101 years from the same source. All this is taken from Cicero’s *Dialogue on Old Age*: “For there is a calm and gentle old age belonging to a life spent quietly, purely, and elegantly—the old age we have heard belonged to Plato, who died while writing in his eighty-first year; and to Isocrates, who is said to have written the book entitled the *Panathenaicus* in his ninety-fourth year and lived five years afterward … Sophocles composed tragedies in extreme old age. Because, through his devotion to study, he seemed to neglect his household affairs, his sons brought him to court, seeking to have the judges remove him from the management of his property as though he were a spendthrift, just as, by our custom, fathers who manage their estates badly are sometimes interdicted from their goods. Then, it is said, the old man recited before the judges the play he had in hand and had most recently written, *Oedipus at Colonus*, and asked whether that poem appeared to be the work of a madman. After he had recited it, he was acquitted by the judges’ verdict. Did old age, then, force this man, or Hesiod, or Simonides, or Stesichorus, or those I mentioned earlier—Isocrates, Gorgias, Homer—or the leading philosophers Pythagoras, Democritus, Plato, Socrates, or later Zeno, Cleanthes, or the man whom you also saw at Rome, Diogenes the Stoic, to fall silent in their studies? Was not the activity of study equal throughout the lives of all these men?” Jerome heightens these final words by saying that, near death, they sang something swanlike and sweeter than usual—though, except for the unique example of Sophocles, I do not know whether this can truly be said of the others.]

I say nothing of the other philosophers—Pythagoras, Democritus, Xenocrates, Zeno, and Cleanthes—who flourished in the pursuits of wisdom even in advanced old age.

I come to the poets: Homer, Hesiod, Simonides, and Stesichorus, who, advanced in years, sang something—I scarcely know what—swanlike and sweeter than usual, as death drew near.

When Sophocles was accused by his sons of madness because of his extreme old age and neglect of his household affairs, he recited before the judges the play *Oedipus*, which he had recently written. He displayed so much wisdom in an already weakened old age that he turned the severity of the tribunal into the applause of the theater.

Nor is this surprising, since even Cato the Censor, the most eloquent of the Roman people, already an old man, neither blushed nor despaired of learning Greek literature.

Certainly Homer relates that the speech of Nestor, already very old and almost decrepit, flowed sweeter than honey from his tongue.

But the mystery [Col. 0530] of Abishag’s very name also indicates the greater wisdom of the old. It is interpreted as “my father is superfluous” or “the roar of my father.” The word “superfluous” is ambiguous; in the present passage it signifies virtue, because it is more abundant in old men, overflowing and rich in wisdom. Elsewhere, however, “superfluous” is used in the sense of unnecessary.

Abishag—that is, “roar”—is properly so called when the waves of the sea resound and, so to speak, a roar coming from the deep is heard. From this it is shown that an exceedingly abundant thunder, beyond the human voice, of divine speech dwells in old men.

Moreover, in our language *Shunammite* means “scarlet,” signifying that wisdom is warm and burns with divine reading. Although this indicates the mystery of the Lord’s blood, it also displays the fervor of wisdom.

Therefore the midwife in Genesis (chapter 38) ties a scarlet thread on the hand of Pharez, who, because he had divided the wall separating two peoples before him, received the name “divider,” that is, Pharez.

And Rahab the prostitute, as a type of the Church, hangs out a cord containing the mystery of blood so that her house may be saved when Jericho perishes.

[Note: Another reading has “it was added in the window.”]

Hence, in another passage, Scripture says of holy men: “These are they who came from the heat of the house of the father of Rechab” (1 Chronicles 2:55).

And our Lord says in the Gospel: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and how I wish that it were already burning!” (Luke 12:49).

This fire, kindled in the hearts of the disciples, compelled them to say:

> “Was not our heart burning within us while he spoke to us on the way and opened the Scriptures to us?”  
> *(Luke 24:32.)*

### 4

Why have I repeated these things at such length as an introduction? Do not ask me for childish declamations, little flowers of aphorisms, verbal adornments, or certain sharp and briefly rounded conclusions at the end of each chapter, designed to provoke the applause and shouting of the audience.

Let wisdom embrace me now, and let our Abishag, who never grows old, rest in my bosom. For she is undefiled and of perpetual virginity; like Mary, she remains incorrupt although she gives birth and is always in labor.

Hence I think that the Apostle also said, “Be fervent in spirit” (Romans 12:11). And in the Gospel I believe the Lord foretold that at the end of the world, when, according to the prophet Zechariah, the foolish shepherd begins to be, [Col. 0531] the love of many will grow cold (Matthew 24; Zechariah 11).

Listen, therefore, as blessed Cyprian says: “not eloquent, but forceful.”

[Note: Saint Cyprian, Letter 1 to Donatus: “Finally, receive words not eloquent but forceful, not adorned with cultivated speech and disguised to entice popular audiences, but simple in their unpolished truth for proclaiming divine mercy.” Shortly afterward, when Jerome calls Heliodorus “the pontiff of Christ,” understand that he was bishop of Altinum, a dignity in which he took part in the Council of Aquileia in 381 under Damasus.]

Listen to a brother in office and a father in age, who may lead you from the cradle of faith to mature age, establishing precepts of conduct at every stage and teaching the others through you.

I know, of course, that from your uncle, the blessed Heliodorus, who is now a pontiff of Christ, you have both learned what is holy and learn it daily, and that you have his way of life as an example of virtues. But receive our offerings, whatever they may be, and join this little book to his little book, so that, while he has trained you as a monk, this one may teach you to be a perfected cleric.

### 5
