Therefore the cleric who serves the Church of Christ must first interpret his own title and, having stated the definition of his name, strive to be what he is called.

For if *klēros* (κλῆρος) is called *sors* in Latin, “lot,” clerics are so called either because they belong to the Lord’s lot or because the Lord himself is the lot—that is, the portion—of clerics.

But whoever is himself the Lord’s portion, or has the Lord as his portion, ought to present himself in such a way that he both possesses the Lord and is possessed by the Lord.

Whoever possesses the Lord and says with the Prophet, “The Lord is my portion” (Psalm 15:5; 72:26), can have nothing outside the Lord. But if he has anything else besides the Lord, the Lord will not be his portion.

For example, if he has gold, silver, estates, or varied furnishings, the Lord will not deign to become his portion along with these other portions.

But if I am the Lord’s portion and the cord of his inheritance, and I receive no portion among the other tribes, but live like a Levite and priest from tithes, and, serving the altar, am sustained by the altar’s offering, possessing food and clothing and content with these, I shall follow the naked cross naked.

I therefore beg you, and repeating the warning I shall admonish you again and again: do not think that the office of cleric is a form of the ancient military service—that is, do not seek worldly profits in the warfare of Christ. Do not possess more than you did when you began to be a cleric, lest it be said to you, “Their portion shall not profit them” (Jeremiah 12:13, according to the Septuagint).

[Note: Older printed editions add a gloss of this sort: “For some monks are richer than they had been as laymen, and clerics”—the word “clerics” is absent from the older copies—“who possess wealth under the poor Christ which they had not possessed under the rich and deceitful devil, so that the Church might receive as rich those whom the world had previously held as beggars.” This has been transferred here improperly from the *Epitaph of Nepotianus* and is found in no manuscript copy. As for what Jerome adds here concerning the hospitality and commercial activity of clerics, the constitution of Constantius from the year 343 should be compared. In it he exempted clerics from the burden of receiving guests and granted immunity to those who wished to engage in commerce for the sake of livelihood. Jerome disapproves of both practices here, wishing clerics to receive the poor and travelers as guests, even though they might appear excused by that law, and maintaining that such commercial gains, already regarded as undignified, are impermissible—gains that many other authors and Fathers likewise condemn.]

Let the poor and travelers, and Christ with them as their guest, know your table.

Flee a cleric who is a merchant, a man who has become rich from poverty and honored from obscurity, as though he were a kind of plague.

“Bad conversations corrupt good morals” (1 Corinthians 15:33).

You despise gold; another loves it. You trample wealth; he pursues it. You value silence, gentleness, and privacy; he values loquacity, a hardened face, markets and public squares, and the shops of physicians.

In such disagreement of character, what concord can there be?

[Note: Gravius, supported by a very old copy, directs that *ostiolum* (“little door”) be read.]

Let your little lodging be traversed by women’s feet either rarely or never.

Ignore all the girls and virgins of Christ equally, or love them equally. Do not remain under the same roof with them, and do not trust in past chastity.

You cannot be holier than David or wiser than [Col. 0532] Solomon.

[Note: Victorius, together with certain other printed copies, adds “nor stronger than Samson”; other books, especially the manuscripts, omit this, and it seemed best to follow them.]

Always remember that a woman drove the inhabitant of paradise from his possession (Genesis 3).

When you are sick, let any holy brother, and your sister or mother, or any woman of proven reputation among all, attend you.

But if persons of this kind, related to you and chaste, are not available, the Church supports many old women who can provide the service and receive a benefit by ministering, so that your illness too may bear the fruit of almsgiving.

I know that some have recovered in body and begun to sicken in spirit.

The person whose face you frequently watch serves you at your peril.

If, because of the clerical office, you visit either a widow or a virgin, never enter the house alone.

Choose as companions people whose association will not bring you disgrace. If a reader, acolyte, or psalmist follows you, let them be adorned not with clothing but with character; let them not curl their hair with the curling iron, but promise chastity by their dress.

Do not sit alone with a woman alone, in private and without an observer or witness.

If something more intimate must be said, she has an older female attendant of the household—a virgin, widow, or married woman. She is not so inhuman as to have no one besides you to whom she would dare entrust herself.

Avoid every suspicion, and beforehand avoid whatever could plausibly be fabricated, so that it may not be fabricated.

Frequent little gifts, small towels, ribbons, garments applied to the face, foods offered and tasted, and soft, sweet little letters have no place in holy love.

“My honey, my desire, all the delights and charms,” and the witty pleasantries worthy of laughter, along with the other absurdities of lovers, make us blush in comedies and disgust us in worldly people—how much more in monks and clerics, whose priesthood is adorned by their profession and whose profession is adorned by their priesthood?

I do not say this because I suspect such things either in you or in holy men, but because in every profession, every rank, and every sex there are both good and evil people: and the condemnation of the evil should be the praise of the good.

### 6

I am ashamed to say it: priests of idols, actors, charioteers, and prostitutes receive inheritances. This is forbidden to clerics and monks alone by law, and it is forbidden not by persecutors but by Christian rulers.

[Note: This refers especially to the constitution of the Emperor Valentinian addressed to Pope Damasus: “Ecclesiastics, or those descended from ecclesiastics, or those who wish to be called by the name of the continent, should not enter the houses of widows and orphans,” etc. Saint Ambrose also speaks of this in Letter 18.13 to the younger Valentinian: “The profits of private succession are denied to us by recent laws, and no one complains,” etc. That law was later repealed by the Novel of the Emperor Marcian, preserved in the Theodosian Code, Book 16, title 3. Meanwhile, may both Jerome’s and Ambrose’s passages serve as an example that clerics and monks ought not seek temporal profits; their only concern should be the gain of souls, not coveting wealth under the pretext of piety.]

I do not complain about the law; I grieve that we deserved such a law. The cauterizing iron is good, but why should I have a wound requiring cautery? The law’s provision is prudent and severe, yet even so avarice is not restrained.

[Note: The constitution of Valentinian mentioned above provided that clerics and monks could not receive anything either by donation or by testament through an intermediary person. Jerome asks how, astonishingly, the law is still circumvented through trusts.]

We evade the laws through trusts; and, as though the decrees [Col. 0533] of emperors were greater than those of Christ, we fear the laws and despise the Gospels.

Let the Church be heir—the mother of the children, that is, of her flock—which gave them birth, nourished them, and fed them. Why do we insert ourselves between mother and children?

The glory of a bishop is to provide for the poverty of the poor. The disgrace of all priests is to devote themselves to their own riches.

Born in a poor household and a rustic cottage, when I could scarcely satisfy my growling stomach with millet and coarse bread, I now disdain fine flour and honey.

I know the kinds and names of fish; I am skilled in identifying on what shore a shellfish was gathered.

[Note: The Cistercian and two other manuscripts have the faulty reading “on what shore they were gathered.” Petronius, *Civil-War Fragment*: “They sell shellfish dragged from the Lucrine shores for feasts, so that through their losses they may renew their hunger,” etc.]

I distinguish the provinces by the flavors of birds; the rarity of expensive foods, and finally the very losses they cause, delight me.

I also hear of the shameful servitude of certain men toward old men and old women without children. They themselves place the chamber pot, besiege the bed, and receive with their own hands the stomach’s discharge and the lungs’ phlegm.

They tremble at the doctor’s entrance and, with trembling lips, ask whether the patient is more comfortable. If the old man is a little more vigorous, they are in danger: beneath their feigned joy, the avaricious mind is tortured within.

For they fear losing their service and compare the lively old man with the years of Methuselah.

O what a great reward before God they would have if they expected no payment in the present! With what toil is a worthless inheritance sought! The pearl of Christ could have been bought with less labor.

### 7

Read the divine Scriptures frequently—indeed, let sacred reading never leave your hands.

Learn what you are to teach. Hold fast the faithful word that accords with sound doctrine, so that you may be able to exhort in sound teaching and refute those who contradict it.

Remain in what you have learned and what has been entrusted to you, knowing from whom you learned it, always ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you for a reason concerning the hope and faith that are in you.

Let your deeds not bring shame upon your speech, lest, when you speak in the Church, someone silently answer: “Why, then, do you yourself not do what you say?”

A delicate teacher is one who discusses fasting with a full stomach.

Even a robber can accuse greed.

Let the mouth, mind, and hands of Christ’s priest agree.

Be subject to your pontiff and receive him as the parent of your soul. It belongs to sons to love and to servants to fear.

“If I am a father,” he says, “where is my honor? If I am a lord, where is my fear?” (Malachi 1:2.)

You must observe several names in the same man: monk, pontiff, your uncle, who has already taught you everything holy.

I also say this: bishops must know that they are priests, not lords.

[Note: Elsewhere: “that they are fathers, not lords.”]

Let them honor clerics as clerics, so that clerics in turn may honor them as bishops.

The saying of the orator Domitius is well known: “Why should I regard you as a [Col. 0534] prince, when you do not regard me as a senator?”

[Note: This is Lucius Licinius Crassus, who was the colleague of Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus in the censorship, as Victorius notes from the third book of Cicero’s *On the Orator*. But he thinks the manuscripts corrupt and blames the copyists, wishing *Crassi* to be read instead of *Domitii*. We think a lapse of memory in our author more probable, since both men were colleagues.]

Let us understand that what Aaron and his sons were, the bishop and presbyters are: one Lord, one temple, and one ministry also.

Let us always remember what the Apostle Peter commands priests:

> “Tend the flock of the Lord that is among you, overseeing it not under compulsion but willingly according to God; not for shameful gain but eagerly; not as domineering over the clergy but becoming examples of the flock from the heart; so that, when the chief shepherd appears, you may receive the unfading crown of glory.”  
> *(1 Peter 5:2 ff.)*

It is a very bad custom in certain churches to silence presbyters and prevent them from speaking in the presence of bishops, as though the bishops either begrudged them the opportunity or did not deem them worthy of hearing.

[Note: Canon 33 of the fourth Council of Carthage had granted presbyters permission to speak in the Church, with the sole restriction that they should not preach in the presence of bishops. The holy Doctor condemns this very bad custom, although it long prevailed in certain churches; the Pseudo-Jerome who wrote the Letter on the Seven Orders of the Church imitated him. See also the Letter of Augustine and Alypius to Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, and other authors in various places.]

“If something is revealed to another while he is seated,” the Apostle Paul says, “let the first be silent. For you can all prophesy one by one, so that all may learn and all be comforted; and the spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets. For God is not a God of discord but of peace” (1 Corinthians 14:30 ff.).

“A wise son is the glory of his father” (Proverbs 10:1).

Let the bishop rejoice in his own judgment when he has chosen such priests for Christ.

### 8. Preaching in the Church

When you teach in the Church, let not the shouting of the people but their groaning be aroused. Let the tears of your hearers be your praises.

The presbyter’s speech should be seasoned with the reading of the Scriptures.

I do not want you to be a declaimer, a brawler, or a babbler without reason, but an expert in the mysteries and most learned in the sacraments of your God.

To roll out words and, through rapid speech, to make oneself admired by an ignorant crowd is characteristic of uneducated people.

A hardened face often interprets what it does not know; and once it has persuaded others, it arrogates knowledge to itself as well.

My former teacher, Gregory of Nazianzus, when I asked him to explain what the phrase in Luke, *deuterōprōton sabbaton* (δευτερόπρωτον), that is, “second-first,” meant (Luke 6:1), made an elegant joke: “I shall teach you about this in the Church,” he said, “where, with the entire people applauding me, you will be forced, unwillingly, to know what you do not know. Or certainly, if you alone remain silent, you alone will be condemned by everyone as a fool.”

Nothing is easier than deceiving a worthless and uneducated crowd by the fluency of one’s tongue. Whatever it does not understand, it admires all the more.

M. Tullius—of whom there is that most beautiful compliment, “Demosthenes robbed you of being the first orator; you robbed him of being the only one”—in his speech for Quintus Gallio, [Col. 0535] observe what he says about the favor of the crowd and ignorant preachers, lest you be deceived by such tricks.

[Note: This is the only mention in Jerome of this Ciceronian speech, which has long since perished, and it is consequently uncertain whether *Gallio* or *Gallo* should be read; both readings are supported by manuscripts and printed editions. The older editions formerly had *pro Q. Ligario Gallo* (“for Quintus Ligarius Gallus”). Shortly afterward, the Cistercian copy reads *convivia* (“banquets”) instead of *colloquia* (“conversations”), perhaps more correctly, since dialogues of this kind used to be called *symposia* (συμπόσια), drinking parties.]

I am speaking of what I myself recently experienced. A certain poet of repute, a highly learned man, whose works include conversations among poets and philosophers, when he makes Euripides and Menander debate with one another, and elsewhere Socrates and Epicurus discuss matters—although we know that their lifetimes were separated not by years but by centuries—how much applause and shouting does he arouse?

For he has many fellow students in the theater, who likewise have not learned literature.

### 9. What His Dress Should Be. The Different Members in the Church

Avoid dark garments just as much as white ones.

[Note: Peter of Cluny most correctly explains this passage as merely warning Nepotianus to avoid pride in the use of black and white, not, as others—especially Baronius—interpret it, as proving that clerics in antiquity wore neither black nor white but a color intermediate between the two.]

Adornment should be avoided in the same way as filth, because one suggests luxury and the other vainglory.

It is praiseworthy not to go about without a linen cloak, but not to possess the price of linen garments.

Otherwise it is ridiculous and disgraceful to boast, with a full purse, that you have neither a sweat-cloth nor a neck-cloth.

There are people who give a little to the poor so that they may receive more, and under the pretext of almsgiving seek riches. This should be called hunting rather than a form of almsgiving.

In this way beasts are caught, birds are caught, and fish are caught. A little bait is placed on the hook so that the purses of married women may be dragged out by it.

Let the bishop to whom the Church has been entrusted know whom he should appoint to administer and care for the poor.

It is better to have nothing to give than shamelessly to request what I will store away.

But it is also a kind of arrogance to want to appear more merciful than Christ’s pontiff.

We cannot all do everything. In the Church one person is an eye, another a tongue, another a hand, another a foot, an ear, a stomach, and so forth.

Read Paul’s Letter to the Corinthians: how different members form one body (1 Corinthians 12).

Yet let neither the rustic and simple brother think himself holy merely because he knows nothing, nor the learned and eloquent person judge holiness by his tongue.

It is much better, among two imperfect people, to have holy rusticity than sinful eloquence.

### 10. The Adornment of Churches

Many build walls and lay foundations for church columns: the marble gleams, the ceilings glitter with gold, the altar is embellished with gems, and there is no selection of Christ’s ministers. Let no one object to me that, in Judaea, the Temple, the table, the lamps, the censers, the bowls, the cups, the mortars, and other objects were skillfully fashioned from gold (3 Kings 5–6). These things were approved by the Lord then, when priests were sacrificing victims and the blood of animals was the redemption of sins. Although all these things preceded us in figure—for “they were written for us, upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Cor. 10:11)—now, when the poor Lord has consecrated the poverty of his house, let us consider his cross, and we shall regard riches as filth.

Why are we surprised that Christ calls mammon unrighteous? (Luke 16.) Why do we admire and love what Peter gloriously declares that he does not possess? (Acts 3.) Otherwise, if we follow only the letter, and a simple reading delights us in gold and riches, then along with the gold let us observe the other things as well. Let Christ’s high priests take virgin wives; let one who has a scar, though sound of mind, and is disfigured, be deprived of the priesthood; let bodily leprosy be preferred to defects of the soul. Let us increase and multiply and fill the earth; let us neither sacrifice a lamb nor celebrate the mystical Passover, because the Law forbids these things to be done without the Temple.

[Note: The enactment is found in Deuteronomy 16:6, where it was forbidden to slaughter the Passover anywhere one pleased. Augustine especially has this passage in view, *Retractions* 1.10, concerning the Jews: “They could not sacrifice among the nations, just as we now see them left without sacrifices—unless, perhaps, what they sacrifice at Passover, a sheep, is to be counted as a sacrifice.” Add our Zeno, Sermon 7 on Exodus and Sermon 13 on the same subject. In the former: “I do not see how the Pharisee can celebrate the legitimate Passover, since that eminent and famous Temple of his lies buried beneath its own dust, leveled with the ground by pitiable devastation. In the other: ‘Receive briefly, Christian, that the Jews cannot celebrate the legitimate Passover. Since Solomon’s Temple lies buried, overwhelmed by hostile destruction together with its ruins, where do they sacrifice?’”]

Let us pitch a tabernacle in the seventh month and sound the trumpet for the solemn fast. But if, comparing spiritual things with spiritual and knowing with Paul that “the law is spiritual” (Rom. 7:14), we understand these matters as our Lord also understood and interpreted the Sabbath, then either let us reject gold along with the other superstitions of the Jews, or, if gold pleases us, let the Jews please us as well; and together with the gold we must either approve them or condemn them.

### 11. Banquets to Be Avoided

You must avoid the banquets of worldly people, especially those swollen with honors. It is disgraceful that before the doors of a crucified and poor priest of Christ—one who even ate food belonging to others—lictors of consuls and soldiers should keep watch, and that the provincial governor should dine better at your house than in the palace.

If you claim that you do these things so that you may plead for the wretched and the subject, the worldly judge will show more respect to a temperate cleric than to a rich one, and will reverence your holiness more than your wealth. Or if he is the sort of man who will not listen to clerics pleading for those in distress unless he is among goblets,

[Note: “Among cups and bowls” in another reading.]

I shall gladly forgo such a favor and shall ask Christ on behalf of the judge, who can help more and more quickly than the judge: “It is better to trust in the Lord than to trust in man. It is better to hope in the Lord than to hope in princes” (Ps. 117:8–9).

Never smell of wine, lest you hear the philosopher’s saying: “This is not offering a kiss, but pouring wine.” The Apostle condemns wine-drinking priests, and the ancient Law forbids it (Lev. 10): those who serve at the altar must not drink wine or strong drink. In Hebrew, *sicera* denotes every drink that can intoxicate—whether one made from grain; or from the juice of fruits; or one in which fruits are boiled with honey into a sweet and barbarous drink; or one in which the fruit of palms is pressed into liquid; or one in which, after grains have been cooked, the thicker water is colored.

[Note: We think *colatur* should be read instead of *coloratur*, which all the books have. As for his calling it a “barbarous drink,” this should be understood as a drink of barbarian peoples, especially those of the north. Others think *amara* (“bitter”) ought to have been written, but incorrectly.]

Flee everything that intoxicates and overturns the settled state of the mind just as you flee wine. I do not say this because God’s creation is to be condemned—for the Lord himself was called a drinker of wine (Matt. 11), and a small drink of wine was prescribed to Timothy when his stomach was troubled (1 Tim. 5)—but we require moderation in drinking according to age, health, and bodily constitution.

If, without wine, I burn with youthful vigor, am inflamed by the heat of my blood, and have a vigorous, well-nourished body, I shall gladly do without a cup in which I suspect poison. There is a fine saying among the Greeks, and I do not know whether it sounds equally well among us: “A fat belly does not produce a subtle mind.”

[Note: Another reading has “mind”; and the Greek hexameter runs: παχεῖα γαστήρ λεπτὸν οὐ τίκτει νόον—“A fat belly does not produce a subtle mind.”]

### 12. Moderation in Fasting

Impose upon yourself only as much fasting as you can bear. Let your fasts be pure, chaste, simple, moderate, and free from superstition. What does it accomplish to abstain from oil while seeking out all sorts of troublesome and difficult foods—figs, pepper, nuts, dates, fine flour, honey, pistachios? The entire cultivation of gardens is harassed so that we may not eat ordinary bread,

[Note: The words “and while we pursue delicacies we are withdrawn from the kingdom of heaven” are absent from two manuscripts. A little later, Victorius substituted *berries* (*baccarum*) for the invented word *beets* (*betarum*).]

and while we pursue delicacies we are withdrawn from the kingdom of heaven.

I hear, moreover, that some people, contrary to the nature of things and of human beings, do not drink water and do not eat bread, but consume delicate little broths and crushed vegetables; they drink beet juice not from a cup but from a shell. Shame on us! We are not embarrassed by such absurdities, nor are we weary of superstition. We even seek a reputation for abstinence amid delicacies. The strongest fast is water and bread. But because it brings no glory, and because we all live on bread and water, it is not considered a public and common fast.

### 13. Glory to Be Avoided; Superstitious Adornment

Take care not to hunt after the whispers of men or exchange God’s displeasure for the praise of the people. “If I were still pleasing men,” says the Apostle, “I would not be a servant of Christ” (Gal. 1:10). He ceased to please men and became Christ’s servant.

Through good reputation and bad, on the right and on the left, the soldier of Christ advances. He is not lifted up by praise or broken by blame; he does not swell with riches or shrink through poverty; he despises both joy and sorrow. “By day the sun shall not burn you, nor the moon by night” (Ps. 120:6).

I do not want you to pray in the corners of the streets, lest popular applause break the straight path of your prayers. I do not want you to enlarge your fringes, display phylacteries, and, while your conscience resists, surround yourself with Pharisaic ambition.

[Note: This entire passage, nearly ten verses—from here as far as “Do you wish to know”—either does not belong to Jerome or has been greatly corrupted and rearranged by copyists. Certainly, if it is deleted, the context flows extremely well; if it is retained, everything is tangled and the sense abrupt. Moreover, the printed editions and the manuscripts differ very greatly both in wording and arrangement, and the manuscripts also differ among themselves, which is another indication that the passage is a gloss. The words “From this the Gospel depends, from this the Law and the Prophets. Faithful reader, you understand with me what I am silent about and what I say by my silence. As many rules as there are kinds of glory” are presented in this order in the manuscripts, immediately followed by “How much better it would be,” and so forth. Although this order has seemed inverted to other editors, it is nevertheless older and more coherent. We do not follow it completely only because the entire passage seems better corrected by a single deletion. It is also riddled with interpolations, such as the words “or sacred and Apostolic doctrine,” and the phrases “before the rules” and “may run through vanities,” whose meaning I cannot understand at all.]

How much better it would have been to carry these things not on the body but in the heart, and to have God as your supporter rather than the eyes of men! From this the Gospel depends, from this the Law and the Prophets—or rather, sacred and Apostolic doctrine. “It is better to carry all these things in the mind than on the body.” Faithful reader, you understand with me what I am silent about and what I say even more through silence.

Let as many rules as there are kinds of glory pass before you. Do you wish to know what adornments the Lord seeks? Possess prudence, justice, temperance, and fortitude. Enclose yourself within these four regions of heaven; let this four-horse chariot carry you swiftly to the goal like a charioteer of Christ.

[One reading adds “upward”; another has “carry.”]

Nothing is more precious than this necklace; nothing is more richly adorned with variety of gems. You are adorned, girded, and protected on every side; these gems are your ornament and your defense, and they are transformed into shields.

### 14. Slander to Be Avoided

Take care also not to have either an itching tongue or itching ears—that is, neither to slander others yourself nor to listen to those who slander. “You sat and spoke against your brother, and you placed a stumbling-block against the son of your mother. You did these things, and I was silent. You thought wickedly that I would be like you; I shall rebuke you and set you before your own face” (Ps. 49:20–21).

[Note: The Cistercian reads the following complete clause very differently, in God’s person: “I shall overhear your words and everything you have said about others, so that you may be judged by your own sentence and be caught in the very things you accused others of.” The remaining manuscripts, which we follow, differ from the printed editions in only this word: *sentence* rather than *conscience*.]

Refrain from a slanderous tongue; guard your speech; and know that through everything you say about others you are judged by your own sentence, and that you yourself will be caught in the things you accused others of. Nor is this a valid excuse: “I cannot wrong someone by reporting what others have said.” No one willingly reports to an unwilling listener. An arrow never lodges in a stone; sometimes, rebounding, it strikes the one who directed it.

Let the slanderer learn, when he sees that you do not listen willingly, not to slander easily: “Do not associate with slanderers,” says Solomon, “for their destruction will come suddenly, and who knows the ruin of them both?” (Prov. 24:21–22)—namely, both of the one who slanders and of the one who lends an ear to the slanderer.

### 15. Silence and Secrecy

It is your duty to visit the sick, to know the households of married women and their children, and to guard the secrets of noble men. It should be your duty not only to keep your eyes chaste but also your tongue. Never discuss the appearance of women, nor let one household learn through you what is being done in another household.

[Note: Gravius has the fuller reading: “nor what is being done in anyone’s household.”]

Hippocrates binds his disciples by oath before teaching them and compels them to swear by his words. By an oath he extorts silence, and he prescribes their speech, walk, dress, and character. How much more must we, to whom the medicine—or care—of souls has been entrusted, love the households of all Christians as our own? Let them know us as comforters in their sorrows rather than as dinner companions in their prosperity.

A cleric who, when frequently invited to dinner, does not refuse to go is easily despised.

### 16. Receiving Rarely; A Cleric Does Not Arrange Marriages; Defrauding the Church Is Sacrilege

Never accept when you ask; rarely accept when you are asked. For “it is more blessed to give than to receive” (Acts 20). Somehow even the person who entreats you to accept, when you have accepted, judges you inferior; and, remarkably, if you have rejected him when he was asking, he later reverences you more.

A preacher of continence must not arrange marriages.

[Note: This is noteworthy as it concerns the marriage ceremonies customary in the earliest centuries of the Church. Jerome disapproves of them on sound grounds, whereas Tertullian formerly praised them. Two passages of Tertullian particularly illuminate our Doctor’s judgment: one in *To His Wife* 2, at the very end, where he praises the happiness of a marriage arranged by the Church; the other in *On Monogamy* 11, where he says: “You ask for a marriage from those from whom you ask it, though it is not permitted to have one—from a monogamous bishop, from presbyters and deacons of the same sacrament,” and so forth.]

Whoever reads the Apostle saying, “Those who have wives should live as though they had none” (1 Cor. 7:29), why does he compel a virgin to marry? If he is a priest committed to monogamy, why does he urge a widow to become a digamist—to marry a second time?

How can clerics be stewards and administrators of other people’s houses and estates when they are commanded to despise their own possessions?

[Note: This was always forbidden in the Church: “Clerics becoming administrators of worldly affairs while despising divine stewardship,” as Cyprian laments in *On the Lapsed*. On this subject compare canon 16 of the Council of Carthage held under Pope Honorius XII and Theodosius VIII; then Sulpicius Severus, *History* 1; Gregory, Book 8, Letter 11, against Basil, Bishop of Capua; and many other passages of the same kind.]

To steal something from a friend is theft; to defraud the Church is sacrilege. To have received what should be distributed to the poor, and, while so many are hungry, either to wish to keep it in reserve or to be timid—or, what is the most flagrant crime, to remove anything from it—surpasses the cruelty of every bandit.

I am tortured by hunger, and you decide how much is enough for my stomach? Either distribute immediately what you have received, or, if you are a timid steward, leave the donor to distribute it himself.

[Another reading, in Gravius: “so that he himself may distribute it of his own accord.”]

I do not want your purse to be full on my account. No one can preserve what belongs to me better than I can. The best steward is the one who keeps nothing back for himself.

### 17

Dearest Nepotianus, you have compelled me, after the little book on virginity—which I had written at Rome for the holy Eustochium—had already been stoned,

[*Letter 22, On the Preservation of Virginity.*]

to open my mouth again at Bethlehem after ten years and expose myself to be pierced by the tongues of everyone. Either nothing should have been written, so that we would not have to face the judgment of men—a course you forbade me to take—or, once we write, we must know that the weapons of every slanderer are turned against us.

I beg them to be quiet and cease their abuse. We wrote not against enemies but for friends; nor did we attack those who sin, but warned them not to sin. We were not severe judges only toward them, but toward ourselves as well: wishing to remove the speck from another’s eye, we first cast out our own beam.

I injured no one; not even one person’s name was marked by any description.

[Another reading: “by my writing.”]

My speech struck no one in particular. This is a general discussion of vices.

[Note: Compare Cicero, *For the Manilian Law*: “I name no one. Therefore no one will be able to become angry with me unless he first wishes to confess that the matter concerns himself.” See a similar statement in the First *Apology against Rufinus*.]

Whoever wishes to become angry with me will first confess of himself that he is such a person.

## EPISTLE LIII [Note: Otherwise 103. Written about A.D. 394.] TO PAULINUS. On the Study of the Scriptures [Note: That is, Paulinus of Nola, whatever Baronius may have thought at the year 394, and other learned men. Their principal argument was drawn from the contradiction which seemed to exist between this letter and another to Paulinus, here no. 58, beginning “A good man.” Anyone who compares the contexts of both more carefully will establish that no contradiction exists. Martianay further adds “the presbyter,” though all the other printed books and manuscripts are silent about this rank.]

By examples of all the wise, he urges the study of sacred literature and shows how much difficulty it contains. Then, in order to kindle the reader more strongly toward its study, he briefly commends the individual books, authors, and subjects with certain encomia. Finally, he exhorts him to free himself wholly from worldly concerns.

### 1. True Kinship; the Travels of Wise Men

Brother Ambrose, bringing me your little gifts, also delivered your most delightful letter. From the beginning of our friendship it displayed the faith of a faith already proved and of an old friendship. [Note: An old edition of the Bible, without indication of place, date, or printer, inserts here the word “new.”] For that is true kinship, joined by the cement of Christ, which is brought about not by advantage in household affairs, not merely by bodily presence, not by cunning and fawning flattery, but by the fear of God and the study of the divine Scriptures.

We read in ancient histories that certain persons travelled through provinces, visited unfamiliar peoples, and crossed seas, so that they might also see in person those whom they had known from books. Thus Pythagoras sought the seers of Memphis; thus Plato most laboriously travelled through Egypt, to Archytas of Tarentum, and through that coast of Italy which was once called Greater Greece, so that he who was a powerful teacher at Athens, and whose teaching rang through the gymnasia of the Academy, became a traveller and a pupil, preferring modestly to learn what belonged to others rather than shamelessly to thrust forward his own learning. Finally, while he pursued literature as it fled, as it were, throughout the whole world, he was captured by pirates and sold; he even submitted to the most cruel tyrant, Dionysius of Sicily, as a captive, bound, and enslaved man. Yet because he was a philosopher, he was greater than the man who bought him.

We read that certain nobles came from the remotest borders of Spain, from Gades, and of Gaul, to Titus Livy, who flowed with the milky fountain of eloquence; and those whom Rome had not drawn by the sight of itself were brought there by the fame of one man. That age possessed a miracle unheard of in all ages and worthy of celebration: men entered so great a city in order to seek something outside the city.

Apollonius—whether the Magician, as the common people call him, or the Philosopher, as the Pythagoreans relate—entered Persia, crossed the Caucasus, the Albanians, Scythians, and Massagetae, penetrated the exceedingly rich kingdoms of India, and finally, having crossed the very broad river Physon, the Ganges, came to the Brahmans. There, among a few disciples, he heard Iarchas teaching while seated on a golden throne and drinking from the fountain of Tantalus, concerning nature, motions, and the courses of the stars. [Note: Understand the statue representing Tantalus which stood in Iarchas’s school. In its hand was a cup full of water, from which the philosophers drank before retiring. Jerome calls it a fountain because, however much was drawn from it, the same amount was immediately supplied. Philostratus relates the story, book 3, chapter 7. We do not delay over the preceding matters, which you may learn at length from Laertius, Pliny, Herodotus, and others. Meanwhile Martianay read *de moribus* (“concerning customs”) for *de motibus* (“concerning motions”); Victorius, however, read “concerning the customs of the stars and the course of the days.” The old edition of the Bible mentioned above likewise reads in this letter: “concerning nature, customs, and the course of days and stars.”]

Returning thence through the Elamites, Babylonians, Chaldaeans, Medes, Assyrians, Parthians, Syrians, Phoenicians, Arabs, and Palestinians to Alexandria, he proceeded to Ethiopia, that he might see the Gymnosophists and the most celebrated table of the Sun in the sand. That man found everywhere something to learn; and, always making progress, he always became better. Philostratus wrote a most full account of this in eight books.

### 2

Why should I speak of worldly men, when the Apostle Paul, the chosen vessel and teacher of the nations, who spoke from awareness of so great a guest dwelling within him—“Do you seek proof of Christ who speaks in me?” (2 Cor. 13:3)—after travelling through Damascus and Arabia, went up to Jerusalem to see Peter and remained with him fifteen days? For by this mystery of the week and the eighth day, the future preacher to the Gentiles had to be instructed. Again, after fourteen years, taking Barnabas and Titus with him, he set before the Apostles the Gospel, lest perhaps he might be running, or have run, in vain.

The living voice possesses some hidden power, and, when it is conveyed from the author’s mouth into a disciple’s ears, it sounds more strongly. Thus Aeschines, when he was an exile at Rhodes and Demosthenes’ speech against him was being read, while everyone marvelled and praised it, sighed and said: “What if you had heard the beast himself making his own words resound?” [Note: Cicero, who translated both speeches, says in book 3 of *On the Orator*: “How much more would you have marvelled if you had heard him himself!”]

### 3

I say these things not because there is anything in me that you either can or wish to learn, but because your ardour and zeal for learning should be proved even without us, of itself. A teachable natural ability is praiseworthy even without a teacher. We consider not what you find, but what you seek. Soft wax, easy to shape, even if the hands of the craftsman and modeller are idle, nevertheless contains potentially, *tē dynamei*, everything that it can become. [Note: Another reading: “yet it is all by virtue,” etc. Shortly afterward, “of the Lord” stood in place of “of Moses.” We correct lighter matters below.]

The Apostle Paul glories that he learned the Law of Moses and the Prophets at the feet of Gamaliel, so that, armed with spiritual weapons, he could later say confidently: “The weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God for the destruction of fortifications, destroying counsels and every height raised against the knowledge of God, and taking every understanding captive unto obedience to Christ, and being ready to subject all disobedience” (4 Cor. 10:4–5).

He writes to Timothy that he had been instructed in sacred letters from infancy, and urges him to devote himself to reading and not neglect the grace given him through the laying on of the hands of the presbytery. He directs Titus, among the other virtues of the bishop whom he depicts in brief compass, to choose—or, in another reading, understand—knowledge of the Scriptures also: “Holding fast,” he says, “the faithful word which is according to doctrine, so that he may be able to exhort in sound doctrine and refute those who contradict” (Tim. 1:9). For holy rusticity benefits itself alone; and insofar as it builds up the Church of Christ by the merit of its life, it harms it if it does not resist those who destroy it. [Note: We follow the correction of the interpreter of Rieti. Previously Erasmus and Martianay had “Malachi” in both places instead of Haggai, a reading introduced indeed by some smatterer who thought that this alluded to Malachi 2:7: “The lips of the priest shall keep knowledge, and they shall seek the law from his mouth”; whereas these words are really in Haggai 2: “Thus says the Lord of hosts: Ask the priests concerning the law, saying,” etc.] Haggai the prophet—or rather the Lord through Haggai—says: “Ask the priests concerning the Law” (Hag. 2).

### The Priest’s Office; Why Paul Is Called the Chosen Vessel

To such an extent is it the priest’s duty to answer questions about the Law. And in Deuteronomy we read: “Ask your father, and he will tell you; your elders, and they will speak to you” (Deut. 32:7). Likewise, in the one hundred and eighteenth Psalm: “Your statutes were songs to me in the place of my pilgrimage” (v. 54). And in the description of the righteous man, when David compared him to the tree of life which is in paradise, he included this also among his other virtues: “His will is in the Law of the Lord, and in his Law he will meditate day and night” (Ps. 1:2).

At the end of his most sacred vision Daniel says that the righteous shine like stars, and that the understanding, that is, the learned, shine like the firmament. You see how far apart righteous rusticity and learned righteousness are: some are compared with stars, others with heaven. Yet according to the Hebrew truth both may be understood of the learned; for this is how they read it: “But those who have been learned shall shine like the splendour of the firmament; and those who instruct many unto righteousness, like stars for everlasting eternities” (Dan. 12:3).

Why is the Apostle Paul called the chosen vessel? Surely because he is the repository of the Law and of the holy Scriptures. [Note: Victorius’s “vessel of the Law” is vain, since it is clear that in this place *vas* means a repository. Likewise, *theodidaktoi*, which is more correctly expressed by one word than by the two words “taught by God,” follows the Apostle’s passage to the Thessalonians: *hymeis theodidaktoi este*—“you are taught by God”—to which Jerome alludes.] The Pharisees are astonished at the Lord’s teaching, and marvel how Peter and John know the Law although they have not learned letters. For whatever practice and daily meditation on the Law usually bestow on others, the Holy Spirit suggested to them; and they were, as it is written, *theodidaktoi*, “taught by God.” The Saviour had completed twelve years, and in the Temple, by wisely questioning the elders about questions of the Law, he taught the more.

### 4

Unless perhaps we call Peter rustic, and John rustic, though either could say: “Though unskilled in speech, yet not in knowledge” (2 Cor. 11:6). John rustic, a fisherman, unlearned? Then whence, I ask, came that utterance: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1)? For *logos* in Greek has many meanings: it means word, reason, reckoning, and the cause of each thing by which all subsisting things exist. We rightly understand all these meanings in Christ. Plato the learned did not know this; Demosthenes the eloquent did not know it. “I will destroy,” he says, “the wisdom of the wise, and reject the prudence of the prudent” (1 Cor. 1:19).

True wisdom will destroy false wisdom. And although in the Cross there is the foolishness of preaching, Paul nevertheless “speaks wisdom among the perfect; yet wisdom not of this age, nor of the rulers of this age, who are being destroyed, [Note: Martianay, after Erasmus, reads “which is being destroyed,” against the Vulgate, Greek text, and most Jerome manuscripts.] but he speaks God’s wisdom in a hidden mystery, which God predestined before the ages” (1 Cor. 2:7). God’s wisdom is Christ: “For Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God” (ibid., v. 24).

This wisdom is hidden in a mystery, and the title of the ninth Psalm is prefaced “for the hidden things of the Son.” In him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge; and he who was hidden in a mystery was predestined before the ages. He was predestined and prefigured in the Law and the Prophets. Hence the prophets were also called Seers, because they saw him whom others did not see. “Abraham saw his day and rejoiced” (John 8:56). The heavens were opened to Ezekiel, though they were shut to the sinful people. “Unveil,” says David, “my eyes, and I shall behold wondrous things from your Law” (Ps. 118:18). For the Law is spiritual, and revelation is needed in order that it may be understood and that, with unveiled face, we may behold the glory of God.

### 5

In the Apocalypse a book sealed with seven seals is shown (Rev. 5). If you give it to a man who knows letters, that he may read it, he will answer: “I cannot, for it is sealed.” How many today think that they know letters and hold the sealed book, yet cannot open it unless he opens it “who has the key of David, who opens and no one shuts, shuts and no one opens” (ibid. 3:7).

In the Acts of the Apostles the holy eunuch—or rather a man, for Scripture so calls him—was reading Isaiah. Asked by Philip, “Do you think you understand what you are reading?”, he answered: “How can I, unless someone teaches me?” (Acts 8). To speak meanwhile of myself, I am neither holier nor more diligent than this eunuch. He came from Ethiopia, that is, from the ends of the world, to the Temple; he left the royal court; and he was so great a lover of the Law and divine knowledge that even in his carriage he read the sacred letters. Yet though he held the book, conceived the Lord’s words in thought, rolled them on his tongue, and sounded them with his lips, he did not know him whom, unknowingly, he revered in the book. Philip came and showed him Jesus, who lay hidden, shut up in the letter. O wonderful power of a teacher! In that same hour the eunuch believes, is baptized, and becomes faithful and holy; from a disciple he becomes a teacher. At the fountain in the desert he found more of the Church than in the gilded Temple of the synagogue.

### 6

I have touched on these matters briefly—for the limits of a letter did not allow a more extended digression—so that you might understand that you cannot enter upon the holy Scriptures without one to precede and show you the path. I say nothing of grammarians, rhetoricians, philosophers, geometers, dialecticians, musicians, astronomers, astrologers, and physicians, whose knowledge is most useful to mortals and is divided into three parts: *to dogma, tēn methodon, tēn empeirian*—doctrine, method, and experience. [Note: As usual, the older printed editions and certain manuscripts add this interpretation of the Greek words: that is, into doctrine, theory, and practice. They also, shortly afterward, read “tongue” instead of *logos*, along with most others.]

I shall come to the lesser arts, which are administered not so much by reason, *logō*, as by hand. Farmers, masons, craftsmen, cutters of metal or wood, wool-workers and fullers, and all others who make varied household goods and cheap little articles, cannot become what they desire without a teacher:

> “Physicians promise what belongs to physicians; craftsmen practise crafts.”
>
> —Horace, *Epistles* 1.1

### 7

The art of the Scriptures alone is one which everyone everywhere claims for himself.

> “The unlearned and the learned alike write poems everywhere.”
>
> —Ibid.

The talkative old woman, the deranged old man, the verbose sophist, and everyone else presume upon it, tear it apart, and teach it before they learn it. Some, with knitted brow and weighing grand words, philosophize about the sacred letters among little women. Others—shame!—learn from women what they are to teach men; and, lest this be too little, with a certain fluency of words, or rather audacity, they expound to others what they themselves do not understand.

I say nothing of men like myself, who perhaps, after secular literature, come to the holy Scriptures and, having charmed the ears of the people with polished speech, think that whatever they say is God’s Law. Nor do they deem it worthwhile to know what the Prophets and Apostles meant; instead, they fit incongruous testimonies to their own meaning, as though it were a great thing, and not the most vicious kind of teaching, to corrupt meanings and drag Scripture, resisting them, to their own will. As though we had not read Homeric and Virgilian centos, and could not in this way call Virgil himself a Christian without Christ, because he wrote:

> “Now the Virgin returns; the Saturnian kingdoms return;
>
> now a new progeny is sent down from high heaven.”
>
> —Virgil, *Eclogue* 4

And, with the father speaking to the son:

> “Son, you alone are my strength, my great power.”

And, after the words of the Saviour on the cross:

> “Such things he continued to recall, and remained fixed.”

These are childish things, like the play of mountebanks: teaching what you do not know; indeed, to speak with indignation, not even knowing that you do not know it.

## 8.

Genesis is obviously the clearest book. In it are written the nature of the world, the origin of the human race, the division of the earth, the confusion of languages, and the descent of the Hebrew people as far as Egypt.

[Note: Following Erasmus’s inclination, the Benedictine editor prints “and of the Hebrews from the confusion of languages and nations up to their departure.” Yet, as Victorius observed, the departure of the Hebrews from Egypt is not described immediately after Genesis, but many chapters after the beginning of Exodus. We have restored the true reading from editions printed before 1500, following Victorius and the manuscripts.]

Exodus is evident, with its ten plagues, its Decalogue, and its mystical and divine commandments. The book of Leviticus is at hand, in which each sacrifice—indeed, almost every syllable—the garments of Aaron, and the entire Levitical order breathe heavenly mysteries. And does not Numbers contain the mysteries of the whole science of arithmetic, of Balaam’s prophecy, and of the forty-two encampments through the wilderness? Deuteronomy also, the second law and a foreshadowing of the evangelical law, does it not set forth the former things in such a way that everything is nevertheless new, proceeding from the old?

[Note: Most printed editions read: “Up to this point Moses, up to this point the Pentateuch.” Jerome is alluding to the Apostle’s passage noted above, where he says, “In the church I would rather speak five words with my understanding.” Jerome mystically interprets these words according to the sense of the ancient Fathers, referring Paul’s five words to the five books of the Pentateuch.]

“Up to this point the Pentateuch”—with these five words (1 Cor. 14:19), the Apostle boasts that he wishes to speak in the church.

[Note: The fact that he places Job’s history immediately after the books of Moses—although, according to the consistent canon of all the ancients and Jerome himself, Job is listed after the Prophets among the Hagiographa—has a very plausible explanation, unless the passage has been dislocated through the carelessness of copyists: namely, that he considered it to be a book by the same author, or written by Moses himself. This opinion is held by more than a few of the ancients and is not far from the truth. But if the reading noted above in certain manuscripts is accepted as genuine—“Up to this point Moses”—then he must be understood to have had in mind the sequence of the ages and Job’s extremely remote antiquity.]

Is not Job the model of patience, whose discourse encompasses mysteries? It begins in prose, proceeds in verse, and ends in prose; and it establishes all the laws of dialectic—proposition, assumption, confirmation, and conclusion. Every word in it is full of meaning. And, to say nothing of the rest, he prophesies the resurrection of bodies in such a way that no one has written of it either more plainly or more cautiously:

“I know,” he says, “that my Redeemer lives, and on the last day I shall rise from the earth; and again I shall be clothed in my skin, and in my flesh I shall see God. Whom I myself shall see, and my eyes shall behold, and not another. This hope of mine is laid up in my bosom” (Job 19:25–26).

I shall come to Jesus son of Nun, who, as a type of the Lord not only in his deeds but also in his name, crossed the Jordan, overthrew the kingdoms of the enemy, and divided the land among the victorious people. Through its individual cities, villages, mountains, rivers, streams, and borders, he describes the spiritual kingdoms of the Church and of the heavenly Jerusalem.

In the Book of Judges, as many leaders of the people as there are, so many figures are there. Ruth the Moabite fulfills Isaiah’s prophecy:

“Send forth, O Lord, the lamb, the ruler of the earth, from the rock of the desert to the mountain of the daughter of Zion” (Isa. 16:1).

Samuel, in the death of Eli and in Saul slain [variant: “the slaying of Saul”], shows the old law abolished. In Zadok and David, moreover, he bears witness to the mysteries of the new priesthood and the new empire.

Malachim—that is, the Third and Fourth Books of Kings—describes the kingdom of Judah and the kingdom of Israel, from Solomon to Jeconiah, and from Jeroboam son of Nebat to Hoshea, who was led away into Assyria. If you consider the history, the words are simple; if you look into the hidden meaning within the letters, they tell of the Church’s smallness and the wars of heretics against the Church.

The Twelve Prophets, compressed into the narrow limits of a single volume, foreshadow much more than their literal wording conveys. Hosea frequently names Ephraim, Samaria, Joseph, Jezreel, the harlot wife and the children of fornication, and the adulterous woman shut up in her husband’s chamber, sitting widowed for a long time beneath mourning garments and awaiting her husband’s return.

Joel son of Pethuel describes the land of the twelve tribes, ravaged and corrupted by the caterpillar, the locust, the grasshopper, and the mildew. After the overthrow of the former people, the Holy Spirit is to be poured out upon the servants and handmaids of God—that is, upon the hundred and twenty names of believers upon whom he was to be poured out in the upper room of Zion. These hundred and twenty, rising gradually and by increments from one to fifteen, form the number of the fifteen steps mystically contained in the Psalter.

Amos, a shepherd and rustic, “plucking brambleberries,” cannot be explained in a few words. Who could adequately express the three or four crimes of Damascus, Gaza, Tyre, Idumea, the children of Ammon, Moab, and, at the seventh and eighth stages, Judah and Israel? He speaks to the fat cows on the mountain of Samaria and declares that the greater and the lesser house will fall. He himself sees the maker of the locust, and the Lord standing above a plastered or adamantine wall, and a hook for fruit, drawing punishments upon sinners, and famine upon the land—not a famine of bread or a thirst for water, but of hearing the word of God.

Obadiah, whose name means “servant of God” [variant: “servant of the Lord”], thunders against bloody Edom, the earthly man. With a spiritual spear he also strikes the perpetual rival of his brother Jacob.

Jonah, “dove,” most beautiful, foreshadowing the Lord’s Passion through his own shipwreck, calls the world back to repentance; and under the name of Nineveh he announces salvation to the nations.

Micah of Moresheth, “co-heir” of Christ, announces the devastation of the daughter of the robber and sets a siege against her, because she struck the cheek of the judge of Israel.

Nahum, “consoler” of the world, rebukes the city of bloodshed, and after its overthrow says:

“Behold, upon the mountains are the feet of the evangelizer and of him who announces peace” (Nah. 1:15).

Habakkuk, a strong and resolute “wrestler,” stands at his watch and plants his foot upon the fortification, so that he may contemplate Christ upon the cross and say:

“His glory covered the heavens, and the earth is full of his praise. His brightness shall be like the light; horns are in his hands, and there his strength is hidden” (Hab. 3).

Zephaniah, “watchman” and knower of the Lord’s secrets, hears a cry from the Fish Gate, a wailing from the Second Gate, and a crushing from the hills. He also announces a howl to the inhabitants of the mortar, because all the people of Canaan have fallen silent; all who were wrapped in silver have perished.

Haggai, “festive” and joyful, who sowed in tears in order to reap in gladness, rebuilds the destroyed Temple and introduces the Lord and Father speaking:

“Yet a little while, and I will shake heaven and earth, the sea and the dry land, and I will shake all the nations; and the Desired One of all nations shall come” (Hag. 2:7–8).

Zechariah, “mindful of his Lord,” manifold in prophecy,

[Note: Understand Joshua son of Jehozadak the high priest.]

sees Jesus clothed in filthy garments, and the stone with seven eyes, and the golden lampstand with as many lamps as eyes, and two olive trees, one on the left and one on the right of the lamp.

[Note: We follow the reading restored by Victorius from the Brixian manuscripts, since it is most likely that Jerome is referring to the first chapter of Zechariah, not the sixth, as Martianay seems to have thought after Erasmus when he read “variegated, red, and white horses, and scattered chariots,” and so forth.]

After prophesying and proclaiming the red, black, white, and variegated horses, the scattered chariots from Ephraim, and the horse from Jerusalem, he foretells the poor king seated upon a colt, the foal of a submissive donkey.

Malachi, plainly, and at the end of all the Prophets, speaks of Israel’s rejection and the calling of the nations:

“I have no desire for you, says the Lord of hosts, and I will not accept an offering from your hand. For from the rising of the sun even to its setting, my name is great among the nations; and in every place sacrifice is made, and a pure offering is presented to my name” (Mal. 1:10).

Who could either understand or explain Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Daniel? The first of these seems to me to weave not a prophecy but a Gospel. The second joins together the almond rod [Vulgate: “the watchful rod”], the boiling pot from the face of the north, the leopard stripped of its colors, and a fourfold alphabet in different meters—the Lamentations.

The third has its beginnings and its end wrapped in such great obscurities that among the Hebrews these sections, together with the beginning of Genesis, have not been read for thirty years.

The fourth, who is also the last among the four Prophets, conscious of the ages and a lover of history and learning, clearly declares the stone cut from the mountain without hands, overthrowing all kingdoms.

[Note: Most manuscripts read *Philostoricus*; Erasmus and Martianay have the wholly corrupt *Philostoros*. We have written *φιλοΐστωρ*, “eager for learning,” following the better received editions.]

David, our Simonides, our Pindar and Alcaeus, and also our Horace, Catullus, and Serenus, makes Christ resound upon the lyre and raises him, risen from the underworld, upon the ten-stringed psalter.

Solomon, the peaceful and beloved of the Lord, corrects morals, teaches nature, joins the Church to Christ, and sweetly sings the epithalamium of the holy marriage.

Esther, in the figure of the Church, delivers the people from danger; and after Haman—whose name means “iniquity”—has been killed, she sends the portions of the feast and the festive day down to posterity.

The book of Chronicles—that is, the epitome (*ἐπιτομή*, “abridgment”) of the Old Instrument—is so great and so important that anyone who wishes to claim knowledge of the Scriptures without it mocks himself. For throughout its individual names and verbal connections, the histories passed over in the Books of Kings are touched upon, and innumerable questions of the Gospel are explained.

Ezra and Nehemiah—“helper” and “consoler from the Lord”—are compressed into a single volume. They restore the Temple and build the city walls. And that whole crowd of people returning to their homeland, together with the list of the priests, Levites, Israelites, and proselytes, and the division by individual families of the work on the walls and towers, presents one thing on the surface and retains another in the marrow.

## 8.

You see that, carried away by love of the Scriptures, I have exceeded the proper length of a letter, and yet have not fulfilled what I wished. We have heard only what we ought to know and what we ought to desire, so that we too may be able to say:

“My soul has desired to long for your justifications at all times” (Ps. 118:20).

But that Socratic saying is fulfilled in us: “This only I know, that I know nothing.”

I shall also touch briefly upon the New Testament. Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John, the Lord’s chariot and the true Cherubim—which is interpreted as “a multitude of knowledge”—are full of eyes throughout their whole body; sparks flash forth, lightning bolts dart about, their feet are straight and stretch upward, and their backs are winged and flying everywhere.

[Note: Jerome presses this interpretation elsewhere and explains it in his Lexicon, though it does not seem consonant with the truth to most; others labor hard to defend it. Yet that the older Hebrews used this word to denote a multitude of knowledge is shown by Philo’s testimony concerning the figures on the Ark: *χερουβίμ . . . ἐπίγνωσις καὶ ἐπιστήμη πολλή* (“Cherubim . . . abundant knowledge and understanding”); and by Clement of Alexandria: *ἔθελεν δὲ τὸ ὄνομα τῶν χερουβὶμ δηλοῦν ἐπίγνωσιν πολλήν* (“he intended the name Cherubim to signify abundant knowledge”). Isabar Ali, in his Lexicon, adds: “Another interpretation of this is a multitude of knowledge.” Finally John, Metropolitan of Dara: “And what is the name Cherubim? A multitude of knowledge, or an outpouring of wisdom, or abundance and wealth of wisdom.” The etymology appears to be derived, by transposition of letters, from the cognate Arabic *Kabir*, denoting one who is learned, prudent, and knowledgeable.]

They hold one another, are entwined with one another, and roll like a wheel within a wheel; they go wherever the breath of the Holy Spirit leads them.

The Apostle Paul writes to seven churches

[Note: See the book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 5, concerning Paul.]

—for the eighth, the one addressed to the Hebrews, is excluded from the number by many. He instructs Timothy and Titus and pleads with Philemon on behalf of the runaway slave Onesimus. On this subject I think it better to remain silent than to write only a few words.

The Acts of the Apostles seem, indeed, to recount bare history and to set forth the infancy of the nascent Church. But if we know that their author is Luke the physician, whose “praise is in the Gospel,” we shall likewise perceive that all his words are medicine for the sick soul.

James, Peter, John, and Jude the Apostles published seven Epistles, as mystical as they are concise, both short and long: short in words, long in meaning, so that few are those who do not stumble [variant: “are shaken”] in reading them.

The Apocalypse of John contains as many mysteries as words.

I have said too little for the worth of the book. All praise falls short: in each individual word multiple meanings lie hidden.

## 9.

I beg you, dearest brother, is it not already, here on earth, a dwelling-place of the heavenly kingdom to live amid these things, to meditate upon them, to know nothing else, and to seek nothing else?

Do not be offended in the Holy Scriptures by the simplicity, or apparent lowliness, of their words. Whether because of the fault of translators or by deliberate design, they were expressed in such a way as to instruct a rustic congregation [variant: “disputation”] more easily, and so that in one and the same statement the educated listener would hear one thing and the uneducated another.

I am not so presumptuous or foolish as to claim that I know these things and can grasp on earth the fruits whose roots are fixed in heaven.

[Note: Victorius restored *in terra* (“on earth”) from the Brixian manuscripts; in a manuscript of St Paul outside the Walls he says that he found *sedenti me praefero* (“I put myself forward as sitting”).]

But I confess that I desire to do so. I put myself forward as one sitting at your feet; refusing to be a master, I promise to be a companion. To the one who asks, it is given; to the one who knocks, it is opened; the one who seeks finds. Let us learn on earth what will remain our knowledge in heaven.

## 10.

I shall receive you with open arms, and, to babble something foolish about the bombast of Hermagoras,

[Note: Formerly, but incorrectly, “timidity”; then Martianay too read *effundam* for *effutiam*. Jerome alludes to a passage of Cicero, *De Inventione* 1: “Hermagoras seems neither to attend to what he says nor to understand what he promises.” A little later Cicero says: “Relying on his own knowledge, Hermagoras seems to have explained not what the art could do, but what he himself could do.”]

whatever you ask, I shall try to learn together with you.

Here you have Eusebius, your most devoted brother, who has doubled my gratitude for your letters by reporting your upright character, your contempt for the world, your fidelity in friendship, and your love of Christ. For prudence and elegance of expression, even without his testimony, the letter itself displayed them.

Hasten, I beg you, and cut rather than loosen the rope of the little boat that is clinging to the shoal. No one who is about to renounce the world can sell well what he despised in order to sell. Whatever you take from your possessions for expenses, count as profit.

[Note: Some attribute this to Seneca, but John of Salisbury, in the poem prefixed to his *Policraticus*, had already attributed it to Ennius and Cato: “The miser lacks what he has as much as what he does not have.” See Theophilus Paschal, III, no. 15.]

It is an ancient saying:

“The miser lacks what he has as much as what he does not have.”

[Note: Jerome frequently cites this saying, as do other Fathers—often Augustine, Cassian in *Conferences* 24.26, and Bernard in the *Life of Saint Malachy*. Among the Greeks it is found in Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* 2, and elsewhere. In the Septuagint it appears in Proverbs 17, after verse 6: “For the faithful, the whole world of possessions; but for the faithless, not even an obol.”]

“To the believer the whole world is wealth; but the unbeliever needs even an obol.”

Let us live as though possessing nothing, yet possessing everything. Food and clothing are the riches of Christians. If you have control over your property, sell it; if you do not, throw it away. To the one who takes your tunic, your cloak must also be left. Surely, unless you, always putting things off and dragging one day after another, sell your little possessions cautiously and step by step, Christ has nothing with which to feed his poor.

He gave everything to God who offered himself. The Apostles left behind only their boat and nets. The widow put two small coins into the treasury and is preferred to the riches of Croesus. It is easy for the one who always thinks that he is going to die to despise everything.

# LETTER LIV

[Note: Elsewhere numbered 10. Written about A.D. 394.]

## To Furia: On Maintaining Widowhood

## 1.

You entreat me by letter, and humbly beg me to write—or rather to write back to you—how you ought to live and preserve the crown of widowhood with your chastity unharmed.

[Note: Some printed editions and manuscripts read “that I write again,” or rather “that I write,” and also omit the words “so that she might obtain” a little farther below.]

My spirit rejoices, my inmost being exults, my affection leaps for joy that, after your husband’s death, you desire to be what your mother Titiana, of holy memory, was for a long time while married. Her prayers and supplications have been heard. She obtained in her only daughter what she herself possessed while alive.

You also possess the great privilege of your family: from the time of Camillus (Lucius Furius Camillus), it is recorded that either none or very few women of your family entered into a second marriage. Thus you should be not so much praised if you persevere as a widow as condemned if, as a Christian, you do not preserve what pagan women guarded for so many centuries.

## 2.

I say nothing of Paula and Eustochium, the flowers of your family, lest on the occasion of exhorting you I seem to be praising them. I pass over Blaesilla, who, following her husband—your brother—completed, within the brief span of her life, many years’ worth of virtues.

[Note: Many manuscripts and the old edition incorrectly add “after her husband,” and then read “having obtained” instead of “having followed.” Blaesilla was joined to one husband, your brother; she followed him shortly after his death.]

And would that men imitated the praises bestowed upon women, and that wrinkled old age rendered what youth freely offers!

Knowingly and deliberately I thrust my hand into the flame: eyebrows will be raised, arms will be extended, and angry Chremes will rage with puffed-up mouth.

[Note: Two handwritten copies read, “And angry Terentian Chremes,” according to which reading see Terence, *Heautontimorumenos*, Act 5, Scene 5, and elsewhere. The wording is actually a verse of Horace in the *Art of Poetry*, where the reading is *delitigat*, not *desaeviet*.]

The leading men will rise up against my letter; the patrician crowd will thunder me down [variant: “denounce me”], shouting that I am a magician and a seducer and should be deported to the ends of the earth. If they wish, let them add “Samaritan,” so that I may recognize the title of my Lord.

Certainly I do not separate a daughter from her parent, nor do I say that Gospel saying: “Let the dead bury their own dead” (Matt. 8:22; Luke 9:60). For the one who believes in Christ is alive. And whoever believes in him must surely walk as he walked (1 John 2:6).

## 3. When Parents Are to Be Honored

Let envy be gone—that envy which the native malice of slanderers always fastens upon the Christian name—so that, while people fear insults, they are not provoked to virtue.

[Note: Against many manuscripts and the old edition, which read “they may not be provoked,” the reading is “they may be provoked.” Some add *sermo* or *livor* after *genuinus*: “speech” or “malice.” Someone who did not recognize that *genuinus* means “of the teeth,” and that the expression is borrowed from Persius, added this gloss from his own conjecture.]

Except in letters, we know nothing of one another. And the sole basis for filial devotion exists where there is no knowledge of the flesh. Honor your father—but only if he does not separate you from the true Father. Know the bond of blood only so long as he knows his Creator. Otherwise David will immediately sing to you:

“Listen, daughter, and see, and incline your ear; forget your people and your father’s house. And the king will desire your beauty, for he is your Lord” (Ps. 44:11).

What a great reward for forgetting your parent [Cistercian manuscript: “for abandoning or forgetting a parent”]: “The king will desire your beauty.”

Because you listened, because you saw, because you inclined your ear, and because you forgot your people and your father’s house, therefore the king will desire your beauty and will say to you:

“You are altogether beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you” (Song 4:7).

What is more beautiful than a soul called the daughter of God, which seeks no adornments from outside [manuscripts: “embraces”]? She believes in Christ and, enriched by this ambition, proceeds to the Bridegroom, having the same one as Lord whom she has as husband.

## 4. The Hardships of Marriage

You learned at the wedding itself what hardships marriage entails, and, as though you had been filled to nausea with quail meat (Num. 11), your throat experienced the bitterest bile. You expelled sour and unhealthy foods; you relieved your overheated stomach. Why do you wish to put back into yourself what harmed you?

“A dog returns to its vomit, and a washed sow to the mire” (2 Pet. 2:22).

Even brute animals and wandering birds do not fall into the same snares and nets twice. Or do you fear that the line of Furius will fail, and that your father will not have from you a little boy to crawl upon his breast and smear his neck with filth?

[Note: The older editions read *quippe ni*, or *quippe ne hi*, expressions which some others more correctly omit; the words must be read ironically.]

All those who have married have children, and those to whom children were born have answered to their own lineage. Did Cicero’s son display his father’s eloquence? Did your Cornelia, an example of both chastity and fertility, rejoice that she had given birth to her Gracchi?

[Note: Furia was related to Paula, whom Jerome calls “the offspring of the Gracchi” in her epitaph, as is clear from this very letter. Cornelia, the wife of Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus, had Tiberius and Gaius as sons; they were killed because they defended the people’s cause against the Senate. We mention the name “Gracchi” here because the opportunity arises: Terentius Scaurus, following Varro, teaches that it should be written without the mark of aspiration.]

It is ridiculous to hope for something as certain when you see that many both lack children and, when they have had them, have lost them.

To whom will you leave such great wealth? To Christ, who cannot die. Whom will you have as heir? The one whom you also have as Lord. Your father will grieve, but Christ will rejoice; your family will mourn, but the angels will give thanks.

Let your father do what he wishes with his property. You do not belong to the one to whom you were born, but to the one to whom you were reborn—and to the one who redeemed you at a great price, with his blood.

## 5. Nurses and Slaves to Be Avoided

Beware of nurses, foster-mothers, and such poisonous creatures, who wish to fill their bellies from your hide.

[Note: Several manuscripts read “rumor-mongering creatures” and “wine-loving animals.” I would prefer *vinnula*, meaning soft, enticing, and sweetly deceiving; Plautus, *Asinaria* 1.3, has “addressing her tenderly, kissing her, with a soft and charming manner of speech.” In that sense I greatly prefer the manuscript reading.]

They do not advise what benefits you, but what benefits themselves. And they often mutter that line:

“Are you alone to waste your youth in perpetual mourning?

[Col. 0552]

And know neither sweet children nor the rewards of Venus?” (*Aeneid* 4)

Where there is the sanctity of chastity, there is frugality. Where there is frugality, there are losses for the little servants. Whatever they have not carried off [variant: “brought in,”] they think has been taken from them; they do not consider how much they receive, but only how much they might receive.

Whenever they see a Christian, they immediately repeat the street-corner saying:

“The Greek, the impostor” (*ὁ γραικός, ὁ ἐπιθέτης*).

They spread the most disgraceful rumors. What has come from their own mouths, they pretend to have heard from others, being both the authors and the amplifiers. A reputation arises from a lie [Cistercian manuscript: “from infamy”]; when it reaches married women and has been circulated by their tongues, it penetrates the provinces.

You may see many raging with savage mouths, their faces stained, their eyes encircled like vipers, and their teeth filed smooth, gnawing at Christians.

Here one woman—

“[lacuna] whose shoulders are covered by a hyacinth-colored cloak;

She mutters something rancid, speaking thickly through her nose.

She makes a great din and trips the words upon her tender palate.”

(*Persius, First Satire*)

The whole chorus joins in, and every bench howls. Members of our own order join them—men who are both gnawed at and gnaw at others. Against us they are loquacious, though mute in their own defense, as though they themselves were anything other than monks, and as though whatever is said against monks did not rebound upon the clergy, who are the fathers of monks.

The injury of the flock is the shepherds’ disgrace. Conversely, the monk’s life is worthy of praise when he venerates Christ’s priests and does not disparage the rank through which he became a Christian.

## 6.

I have said these things to you, daughter in Christ, not doubting your resolve—for you would never have asked for letters of exhortation if you were uncertain about the goodness of monogamy—but so that you might understand the wickedness of the little servants who carry you about as merchandise, the snares of your relatives, and your parent’s pious error.

As for granting him love toward you, I do not grant him knowledge of love, saying something with the Apostle:

“I bear them witness that they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge” (Rom. 10:1).

Rather imitate—indeed, I shall repeat this often—your holy mother. Whenever I remember her, there comes to mind her ardor for Christ, her pallor from fasting, her almsgiving to the poor, her service to the servants of God, the humility of her clothing and heart, and her measured speech in all things.
