May your father, whom I name out of respect—not because he is of consular rank and a patrician, but because he is a Christian—fulfill his name. Let him rejoice that he fathered a daughter for Christ, not for the world. Rather, let him grieve that you have both lost your virginity in vain and forfeited the fruits of marriage.

Where is the husband whom he gave you? Even if he had been lovable, even if he had been good, death would have undone everything and destroyed the bond of the flesh.

Seize the opportunity, I beg you, and make a virtue of necessity. Among Christians it is not beginnings but endings that are sought. Paul began badly, but ended well. The beginnings of Judas are praised, but his end is condemned by his betrayal.

Read Ezekiel:

“The righteousness of the righteous man will not save him on whatever day he sins; and the wickedness of the wicked man will not harm him on whatever day he turns from his wickedness” (Ezek. 33).

This is Jacob’s ladder, by which the angels ascend and descend.

[Note: The latest Benedictine edition, following other older editions, reads only “ascend,” and reads “weary” in place of “fallen”; Victorius had already corrected this in the Erasmian edition. We have restored “fallen,” lest the passage commit the fault of tautology, since it immediately calls those ascending the steps “weary.”]

The Lord leans upon it, stretching out his hand to those who have fallen and supporting, through contemplation of himself, those who are weary as they climb its steps.

But just as he does not desire the death of the sinner, only that he may turn and live, so he hates the lukewarm, and they quickly make him sick.

To whom more is forgiven, he loves more.

## 7. The Care of Clothing

That woman of the Gospel, a prostitute baptized by her tears and saved when she wiped the Lord’s feet with the hair by which she had previously deceived many, had no curling headdresses, no creaking little shoes, and no eyes darkened with cosmetic.

The uglier she was, the more beautiful she became.

What place do rouge and white lead have upon a Christian woman’s face? One falsely imitates the redness of cheeks and lips; the other, the whiteness of the face and neck. They are the fire of young men, fuel for lust, and signs of an immodest mind.

How can she weep for her sins when she strips the skin with tears and draws furrows across her face? That adornment is not the Lord’s; that veil belongs to Antichrist.

With what confidence does she raise toward heaven a face which the Creator does not recognize?

[Note: We have corrected this from the manuscripts; previously the reading was “does not acknowledge us.” Compare Letter 22 to Eustochium, section 13.]

Youth is vainly offered as an excuse, and girlhood is invoked in defense. A widow who has ceased to please her husband, and who according to the Apostle is truly a widow, needs nothing except perseverance.

She remembers her former pleasure; she knows what she has lost and in what she delighted. The burning arrows of the devil must be quenched by the rigor [variant: “chill”] of fasts and vigils.

Either we must speak as we dress, or dress as we speak. Why do we promise one thing and display another? The tongue proclaims chastity, while the whole body presents immodesty.

## 8.

This concerns habit and adornment. But the widow who lives in luxury—these are not my words but the Apostle’s—is dead while she lives.

What does he mean by saying, “She is dead while she lives”? (1 Tim. 5:6.) To the ignorant she seems to live and not to be dead through sin, but she is dead to Christ, whom hidden things do not deceive.

“The soul that sins shall die” (Ezek. 18).

“The sins of some people are manifest, going before them to judgment; but in the case of others they follow afterward. Likewise, good works are manifest; and those that are otherwise cannot be hidden” (1 Tim. 5:24–25).

His meaning is this: some people sin so freely and openly that, once you have seen them, you immediately understand that they are sinners. But others, who cleverly conceal their vices, we recognize from their subsequent conduct. Likewise, in some people good works are displayed openly; in others we learn of them through long acquaintance.

Why, then, do we need to boast of chastity when, without its companions and appendages—self-restraint and frugality—it cannot prove itself genuine?

The Apostle disciplines his body and subjects it to the authority of the soul, lest he himself fail to observe what he commands to others. And is a young woman, with her body heated by rich foods, secure in her chastity?

## 9.

In saying these things I do not condemn the foods that God created to be used with thanksgiving. But from young men and girls I remove the incentives to pleasure.

[Note: Nearly all manuscripts and the older editions read, “I assert that they are incentives to pleasure,” as does the Council of Aachen in A.D. 816, from which much of this letter is copied in Book 2.]

The fires of Etna, the land of Vulcan, Vesuvius, and Olympus do not burn with such heat as the marrow of young people filled with wine and inflamed by rich dishes.

Avarice is trampled by many and laid aside together with the purse. An imposed silence corrects a slanderous tongue. Bodily grooming and the style of one’s clothing can be changed within a single hour. All other sins are external, and what is external can easily be cast off.

Only lust, implanted by God for the procreation of children, if it exceeds its proper bounds, overflows into vice and, by a kind of law of nature, eagerly bursts forth into intercourse.

It is therefore a great virtue and a matter of watchful diligence to overcome what you were born to be: to live in the flesh but not according to the flesh; to fight with yourself every day; and to watch the enemy shut inside you with the hundred eyes of Argus, as the story tells.

This is what the Apostle expressed in other words:

“Every sin that a person commits is outside the body; but the one who commits fornication sins against his own body” (1 Cor. 6:18).

Physicians, and those who have written about the nature of human bodies—especially Galen in the books entitled *Περὶ Ὑγιεινῶν* (*On Maintaining Health*)—

[Note: Up to this point the works commonly circulated incorrectly read *περὶ ὑγιειῶν*, except for the old edition often used here. From that edition, and especially from the manuscripts, we have restored *ὑγιεινῶν*. This is also the title of Galen’s book; moreover, the plural *ὑγίειας* is not used in Greek, any more than the Latin plural *valetudines* is used.]

say that the bodies of children and young people, and of men and women in the prime of life, boil with innate heat, and that foods which increase heat are harmful to these ages; they say that it is beneficial to take everything cold in food and drink.

Conversely, for the elderly, who suffer from phlegm and cold, warm foods and old wines are beneficial. Hence also the Savior says:

“Take heed to yourselves, lest your hearts be weighed down with overeating and drunkenness and the cares of this life” (Luke 21:34).

And the Apostle says:

“Do not become drunk with wine, in which is debauchery” (Eph. 5:18).

Nor is it surprising that the Potter understood this about the vessel he himself fashioned, since even the Comic poet, whose purpose is to know and describe human behavior, said:

“Without Ceres and Liber, Venus grows cold.” (Terence, *Eunuchus*)

[Col. 0555] **10. What young men should avoid in their food.**—First, then, if the strength of your stomach permits it, until you pass beyond the years of girlhood drink water, which by nature is extremely cold. Or, if weakness prevents this, hear what was said to Timothy: “Use a little wine for the sake of your stomach and your frequent infirmities” (1 Tim. 5:23). Next, avoid all hot foods themselves. I am not speaking only of meats, concerning which the chosen vessel pronounces: “It is good neither to drink wine nor to eat meat”; but even among vegetables all that cause bloating and heaviness [variant: “pregnancy”] must be avoided. Know that nothing is so beneficial to Christian adolescents as eating vegetables. Hence, in another place: “Let the one who is weak eat vegetables” (Rom. 14:2); and the heat of the body must be moderated with cooler foods. Thus the three boys and Daniel lived on vegetables. They were boys, and had not yet come to the frying pan in which the Babylonian king fried the elderly judges. [Note: [Col. 0555] Victorius most correctly interprets “frying pan” here as the burning and boiling flesh of lust. Hebrew tradition says that the old men were the judges Ahab and Zedekiah—the very men who attempted Susanna’s chastity—whom Jeremiah says were condemned by fire, while Daniel says they were stoned. See Jerome’s Commentaries on both passages.]

We seek in them not bodily refinement, which—apart from the privilege of God’s grace—had arisen from such foods, but strength of soul, which becomes stronger through the weakness of the flesh. Hence it is that some of those who desire a chaste life fall in the middle of the course, because they think only of abstaining from meat and load their stomachs with vegetables, which, when eaten moderately and sparingly, are harmless. And, to speak what I think, nothing so inflames the body and titillates the sexual organs as undigested food and violent belching. I would rather, my daughter, that you be briefly embarrassed than that the cause itself be put in jeopardy. Consider whatever is a seedbed of pleasure to be poison. Sparing food and a belly always hungry are preferable to three-day fasts; and it is much better to take a little every day than enough only rarely. The best rain is that which descends upon the earth little by little. A sudden and excessive downpour overturns the fields headlong.

**11.** When you eat, consider that you must immediately pray and at once read. Fix for yourself a prescribed number of verses from the Holy Scriptures; render this allotted task to your Lord. Do not give your limbs rest until you have filled the basket of your breast with this woven covering. After the Holy Scriptures, read the treatises of learned men—only those whose faith is known. You do not need to search for gold in mud; buy one pearl with many pearls. Stand, according to Jeremiah, at the crossroads (Jer. 6:16), so that you may reach that road which leads to the Father [variant: “homeland”]. Transfer your love of necklaces, gems, and silk garments to knowledge of the Scriptures. Enter the promised land, flowing with milk and honey (Exod. 2). Eat fine flour and oil; clothe yourself with Joseph in garments of many colors (Gen. 37); let your ears be pierced with the word of God, as Jerusalem’s were, so that grains of new harvest may hang from them as precious ornaments. You have Saint Exsuperius, a man of proven age and faith, who may frequently instruct you by his admonitions. [Note: [Col. 0556] This is Exsuperius, Bishop of Toulouse, to whom Jerome also dedicated his Commentaries on Zechariah, and whose praises he develops more fully in his Letter to Rufinus.]

**12.** Make friends for yourself from unrighteous mammon, who may receive you into eternal dwellings (Luke 16). Give your wealth to those who eat not Phasian birds but the bread that sustains life—the bread that drives away hunger, not that which increases luxury. “Understand concerning the poor and needy” (Ps. 40). Give to everyone who asks you, but especially to those of the household of faith; clothe the naked, feed the hungry, visit the sick (Luke 6). Whenever you extend your hand, think of Christ. Beware lest, while the Lord your God is begging, you increase another’s wealth.

**13. Conversations with young men must be avoided. Confidence in conversation among widows. Holy love has no impatience. Praise of the virgin Eustochium.**—Flee the company of young men. Let the roofs of your house not see long-haired, carefully groomed, and wanton youths. Let the singer be driven out as harmful. Drive from your house female musicians, harpists, and that sort of choir of the devil, as though they were deadly songs of sirens [variant: “avoid and drive out”]. Do not keep going out into public and, with an army of eunuchs preceding you, be carried about with the freedom of widows. It is a very bad custom when a fragile sex and a feeble age abuse their own judgment and think that whatever they wish is permitted: “All things are lawful, but not all things are beneficial” (1 Cor. 6:12).

Let neither a curled steward, nor a handsome foster-brother, nor a fair [variant: “fair-skinned”] and ruddy attendant cling to your side. Sometimes the character of mistresses is judged from the appearance of their maidservants. Seek the companionship of holy virgins and widows. And if necessity requires you to converse with men, do not choose wealthy witnesses; let your confidence in conversation be such that when another enters you neither fear nor blush. The face is the mirror of the mind, and silent eyes confess the secrets of the heart.

Recently we saw a certain disgraceful man flying throughout the whole East as a rumor. [Note: [Col. 0556] There is no doubt that the word “rumor” contains an error. For how can a rumor be visibly described by human appearance, manners, and dress? Yet the manuscripts and printed editions we have consulted unanimously preserve it, and we do not dare depart from their authority. Since the earlier editors neither emend nor attempt the passage, we would prefer one of two alternatives: either, as in the older edition, to delete the word entirely, which can conveniently be done without loss of meaning; or to transfer it to the following clause by changing the punctuation and read: “Rumor and age, etc.,” which perhaps would be more correct and more in keeping with the holy Doctor’s meaning.]

Age, dress, appearance, gait, indiscriminate companionship, elaborate banquets, and royal display proclaimed the weddings of Nero and Sardanapalus. Let another’s wound be our warning. “When the pestilent man is scourged, the fool will become wiser.” (Prov. 19). [Note: [Col. 0556] Hebrew, Greek, and Latin manuscripts of Proverbs, as well as most of Jerome’s copies, support this reading, although Erasmus and Martianay prefer: “The wise man will become wiser,” etc.]

Holy love has no impatience. False rumor is quickly crushed, and later life judges the earlier. Indeed, no one can pass through the course of this life without being bitten by human beings; and it is the consolation of the wicked to attack the good, since they think that the multitude of sinners diminishes the guilt of sin. Yet the fire of straw quickly subsides, and the overflowing flame, when its fuel fails, gradually dies out. If rumor lied last year, or if it certainly told the truth, let the vice cease, and rumor too will cease.

I say this not because I fear anything sinister concerning you, but because, out of an affection of piety, I fear even what is safe. O, if you could see your sister [Note: [Col. 0557] Eustochium seems to be intended. She was indeed a relative of Furia, but not her sister—unless she is to be called a sister in the spiritual sense, as we have also noted above in Letter 22, no. 27.] and hear that eloquence of her sacred mouth in your presence, you would perceive great courage in a small body. You would hear the whole wealth of the Old and New Testament seething from her heart. She treats fasting as a game and prayer as a delight. She holds the tambourine after the example of Miriam and, with Pharaoh drowned, leads the choir of virgins in song:

> “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously magnified;  
> horse and rider he has cast into the sea” (Exod. 15:1).

She teaches these harpists for Christ and trains these lyre-players for the Savior. Thus the day, thus the night, is spent; and with oil prepared for the lamps, she awaits the Bridegroom’s coming. Imitate, then, your kinswoman as well. Let Rome possess what Bethlehem, more exalted than the city of Rome, possesses. [Note: [Col. 0557] Most printed editions and manuscripts read “narrower,” but this is erroneous and contrary to the holy Doctor’s meaning, as is clear from other similar passages.]

**14.** You possess wealth; it is easy for you to provide the needy with the means of sustenance. Let what was prepared for luxury be consumed by virtue; let no woman who intends to despise marriage fear poverty. Redeem virgins whom you may lead into the king’s bedchamber. Receive widows whom you may mingle among the lilies of virgins and the roses of martyrs, like violets; compose such garlands instead of the crown of thorns in which Christ bore the sins of the world.

Let your most noble father rejoice and be helped; let him learn from his daughter what he had learned from his wife. His head has already grown white, his knees tremble, his teeth fall out; his forehead is furrowed with the wrinkles of old age, death stands near the doors, and the funeral pyre is being prepared nearby. Whether we wish it or not, we grow old. Let him prepare provisions for himself, necessary for a long journey. Let him carry with him what he will unwillingly leave behind; indeed, let him send to heaven what, if he refuses it, the earth will take.

**15.** Young widows, some of whom have turned back after Satan when they have grown wanton in Christ, commonly say when they marry [Note: [Col. 0557] The final Benedictine edition reads “panting,” an unsuitable reading here. The other printed editions and manuscripts read as we have published it. Gravius nevertheless supports the other reading from ancient manuscripts.]:

“My little patrimony is perishing day by day; the inheritance of my ancestors is being dissipated; a slave has spoken insolently; a maidservant has disregarded my authority. Who will go out in public? Who will answer for the taxes on the estates? Who will educate my little children, and who will raise the young household slaves?”

And, shamefully, they put forward as a reason for marriage what by itself ought to have prevented marriage. She brings into the household for her children not a nurse but an enemy, not a parent but a tyrant. Inflamed by lust, she forgets her own womb; and amid little children who do not know her misery, she who had recently mourned now prepares herself as a new bride.

What do you plead—your patrimony? What do you plead—the arrogance of your little slaves? Confess your disgrace. No woman takes a husband for the purpose of not sleeping with her husband. Or, if lust truly does not drive her, what madness is it to prostitute chastity after the manner of harlots so that wealth may increase, and for a worthless and perishable possession to defile modesty, which is both precious and eternal? If you have children, why do you seek marriage? If you do not have them, why do you not fear a sterility already experienced, and prefer an uncertain matter to certain modesty?

**Marriage contracts. The miseries of second marriages.**—Marriage contracts are now being written for you, so that shortly afterward you may be compelled to make a will. [Note: [Col. 0558] Compare Ammianus Marcellinus, book 28, where he condemns at length that fraud by which spouses compel one another to make wills: “On the other side, the wife compels her husband to make a will, and the husband presses the wife insistently to do the same. Legal experts are brought in from both sides,” etc. Our Zeno likewise says in Sermon 2, On Avarice: “Hence it is that spouses, resisting the most sacred yoke of marriage and each striving for himself, seek to seize one another’s inheritance through excessive affection.”]

Your husband’s illness will be feigned; what he will want to make you do as though you were dying, he will do as one who expects to live. Or, if it happens that you have children by a second husband, domestic conflict and civil war arise. You will not be permitted to love your children or look upon those whom you bore with impartial eyes. You will secretly offer them food, and he will resent the dead man; and unless you hate the children, you will still appear to love their father.

But if, having children by a former wife, he brings you into his house, then, even if you are most gentle, all comic writers, mime-writers, and the commonplaces of rhetoricians will declaim against you as the fiercest stepmother. If your stepson falls ill and complains of a headache, you will be branded a poisoner. If you do not give him food, you will be called cruel; if you do give it, a sorceress. I ask you, what great good do second marriages possess that it can compensate for such evils?

**16.** Do we wish to know what widows ought to be like? Let us read the Gospel according to Luke: “And there was,” it says, “Anna the prophetess, daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher” (Luke 2:36). Anna is interpreted as “grace.” Phanuel, in our language, sounds like “the face of God.” Asher is rendered either “blessedness” or “riches.” Since, then, she had borne the burden of widowhood from her youth until eighty-four years of age and did not depart from the temple of God, serving with fastings and prayers day and night, she deserved spiritual [variant: “special”] grace and to be called the daughter of the face of God; and she is reckoned among the ancient forefathers for blessedness and riches. [Note: [Col. 0558] Victorius reads “to be reckoned among the forefathers in blessedness and riches.”]

Let us remember the widow of Zarephath, who preferred the hunger of Elijah to the salvation of herself and her children, so that, although she was to die that very night with her son, she might leave her guest alive, choosing to lose her life rather than her almsgiving. From a handful of flour she prepared for herself the seed of the Lord’s harvest. Flour is sown, and an oil-cruse springs forth. In Judea there is a scarcity of grain. For the grain of wheat there had died there (John 12), and in the widow of the nations streams of oil flowed.

We read in Judith—if anyone is willing to accept the book—of a widow exhausted by fastings and made filthy in mournful dress, who was not mourning her dead husband but, through the squalor of her body, seeking the Bridegroom’s coming. I see an armed hand and a bloody right hand. I recognize the head of Holofernes carried back from the midst of the enemy (Judith 8 and following). A woman conquers men, and chastity cuts down lust. Having suddenly changed her dress, she returns to her victorious squalor, purer than all the adornments of the world. [Note: [Col. 0559] I consider it unnecessary to list the earlier authorities who praise this book: Clement, in his Letter to the Corinthians; those who falsely attribute it to the Apostolic Constitutions; Origen in several places; Africanus; another Clement of Alexandria, Stromata 4; Tertullian, On Monogamy, chapter 17; Ambrose, On Duties 3 and On Widows; not to mention Augustine, Christian Instruction, book 2, chapter 8, and the Third Council of Carthage, canon 47, together with countless other testimonies that can be produced from later periods. It would be preferable to consult Jerome’s entire Preface to this book, which he translated from Chaldean; we cite it here to explain the meaning of this passage, while you otherwise understand well that its authenticity cannot today be called into question.]

**17.** Some incompetently count Deborah also among the widows and suppose the commander Barak to have been Deborah’s son, although Scripture records otherwise. [Note: [Col. 0559] He seems especially to be criticizing Saint Ambrose, On Widows, chapter 8. Ambrose understands Barak to be the son of Deborah, which most others deny, including those who count Deborah among the widows. Scripture calls her the wife of Lapidoth; from this some rightly wish her to be called a widow, either because her husband was already dead or because Lapidoth is not a man’s name but the name of a craft, so that the phrase should be translated “the woman who makes lamps.”]

For us she will be mentioned because she was a prophetess and is counted among the Judges. And because she could say, “How sweet are your words to my throat, more than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth” (Ps. 118:103), she received the name “bee,” nourished on the flowers of Scripture, steeped in the fragrance of the Holy Spirit, and composing sweet ambrosial juices with her prophetic mouth.

Naomi—whose name among us sounds like παρακεκλημένη, “comforted,” as we may translate it—after her husband and children had died abroad, brought her chastity back to her homeland. Sustained by this provision for her journey, she kept the Moabite daughter-in-law [Note: [Col. 0559] Namely Ruth, who married Boaz and bore Obed, from whom came Jesse and David, through whom came Jesus Christ.] so that Isaiah’s prophecy might be fulfilled:

> “Send forth the lamb, O Lord, the ruler of the earth,  
> from the rock of the desert to the mountain of the daughter of Zion” (Isa. 16:1).

I come to the widow in the Gospel, the poor widow (Luke 21), richer than the entire Israelite people. Taking a mustard seed and putting leaven into three measures of flour, she tempered the confession of the Father and the Son with the grace of the Holy Spirit, and she put two small coins into the treasury. Whatever she could possess in material goods, and all her riches, she offered in the two Testaments of her faith. These are the two seraphim glorifying the Trinity three times and stored in the treasuries of the Church. Hence, by the tongs of both Testaments, the burning coal is seized and cleanses the sinner’s lips.

**18.** Why should I repeat ancient examples and bring forth the virtues of women from books, when you can place before your eyes many whom you ought to imitate in the city where you live? And lest I seem to run through them one by one in flattery, Saint Marcella is sufficient for you; responding to her son-in-law, she has related something from the Gospel.

Anna had lived seven years with her husband after her virginity; Marcella, seven months. Anna awaited Christ’s coming; Marcella possesses the one whom Anna had received. Anna sang of him as an infant [variant: “saw him as an infant”]; Marcella proclaims him triumphant. Anna spoke of him to all who awaited the redemption of Israel [variant: “Jerusalem”]; Marcella, with the redeemed nations, cries out: “A brother does not redeem; a man will redeem” (Ps. 48:8). And from another Psalm: “A man was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her” (Ps. 86:5).

I know that nearly two years ago I published books against Jovinianus in which, by the authority of Scripture, I crushed the objections raised from the opposite side, where the Apostle permits second marriages. It is not necessary to write the same things out in full again, since you can borrow from what has already been written. I wish only to warn you of this, lest I exceed the limits of a letter: **Consider every day that you are going to die, and you will never think of a second marriage.**

[295] **LETTER LV** [Note: [Col. 0560] Elsewhere numbered 147. Written around the same year, 394.] **TO AMANDUS.**

Jerome responds point by point to Amandus the Presbyter, who had proposed three questions to him in writing and had also sought his advice concerning the situation of a certain sister.

To his truly holy and worthy brother, Amandus the Presbyter, Jerome.

**1.** A short letter cannot explain long questions, nor, by compressing many things into a narrow space, can it adequately express in words what has been expanded in meaning. You ask what that saying in the Gospel according to Matthew means: “Do not be anxious about tomorrow, for tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Sufficient for the day is its own evil” (Matt. 6:34).

“Tomorrow” in the Holy Scriptures signifies future time, just as Jacob says in Genesis: “Tomorrow my righteousness will answer for me” (Gen. 30:33). And when an altar is built by the two tribes of Reuben and Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh, an embassy is sent to them by all Israel; they replied to Phinehas the priest that they had built the altar so that tomorrow their children would not be denied the possession of worshipping God (Josh. 22:24). You will find many examples of this kind in the Old Testament.

He, therefore, who forbade us to think about the future granted us permission to think about the present, because of the frailty of human life. As for what he adds, “Sufficient for the day is its own evil” (Matt. 6:34), understand it in this way: It is enough for us to think about the present troubles of this age. Why should we extend our understanding to uncertain and future things, which we either cannot attain or perhaps, once quickly found, will lose?

The word κακία, which the Latin translator rendered as *malitia*, “evil,” has two meanings among the Greeks: “malice” and “affliction,” which the Greeks call κακώσις; here it ought more appropriately to have been translated as “affliction.” [Note: [Col. 0561] Thus read the old printed editions and manuscripts. Martianay, however, reads the Latin as “the older things.” The Vatican manuscript 355 has the form which the Latin translator renders; read: “is translated.”]

But if someone argues obstinately, unwilling that κακία should mean affliction and distress rather than malice, it must be explained in the sense in which the world is said to lie in the evil one—that is, in evil—and in which we say in the Lord’s Prayer, “Deliver us from evil” (Matt. 6:13): so that it is enough for us to have a present struggle against the malice of this age.

**2.** In the second place you asked about the first Letter of the blessed Apostle Paul to the Corinthians, where he says: “Every sin that a person commits is outside the body; but the one who commits fornication sins against his own body” (1 Cor. 6:18). Let us read a little higher up and come thus to these words, lest we wish to know the whole meaning from the final parts—or, so to speak, the tail—of the chapter.

“The body,” he says, “is not for fornication but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body. God, who raised up the Lord, will also raise us up by his power. Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ? Shall I therefore take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute? Certainly not. Or do you not know that whoever joins himself to a prostitute is one body with her? For, he says, the two will become one flesh” (ibid. 13 and following). “But whoever joins himself to the Lord is one spirit. Flee fornication. Every sin that a person commits is outside the body; but the one who commits fornication sins against his own body” (Gen. 2:24; Mark 10:8), and the rest.

The holy Apostle, arguing against luxury and having said above, “Food is for the stomach and the stomach for food, and God will destroy both one and the other” (1 Cor. 6:13), proceeds accordingly to fornication. For luxury is the mother of lust; and when the belly has been distended with food and irrigated with wine, sexual pleasure follows. As it is said elsewhere, the order of vices follows the order of the members.

Every other sin—for example theft, murder, robbery, perjury, and the rest of the same kind—has repentance after the deed; and although profit invites it, conscience nevertheless bites. Pleasure and lust alone, even at the very time of repentance, continue to suffer the former goads, the tickling of the flesh, and the incentives to sin, so that through thinking about those things which we wish to correct, there may again be material for transgression.

Alternatively: other sins are external. Whatever we do, we do against others; fornication alone not only stains the fornicator’s conscience but also the body. According to the Lord’s saying, “For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two will become one flesh” (Mark 10:7–8), the fornicator himself becomes one body with the prostitute and sins against his own body, making the body that is Christ’s temple into the body of a prostitute.

Let us explain it in another way as well, so that we do not seem to pass over any Greek interpretation. It is one thing to sin *through* the body and another to sin *in* the body. Theft, murder, and other sins apart from fornication are carried out externally by the hand; fornication alone is practiced inwardly in our own body, not through the body against others. The preposition *through* indicates agency, whereas *in* indicates that the action is suffered in oneself.

[Note: [Col. 0562] According to the reading of the same Vatican manuscript; those who argue in this way say “that, according to Scripture, the wife is the body of the husband, and whoever commits fornication sins against his own body, that is, against his wife, by polluting her through his fornication and making her, though she has not sinned, sin through his intercourse.”]

There are those who explain it in this way: according to Scripture, the wife is the husband’s body, and whoever commits fornication sins against his own body—that is, against his wife—when he pollutes her by his fornication and makes her, though she has not sinned, sin through his intercourse.

[Note: [Col. 0562] All books printed before Martianay introduce a third question here and append at the end, without changing the sequence, what follows below concerning the woman who took another husband. That order may indeed seem more harmonious, but since it relies on the authority of no manuscript exemplar that we have seen or know of, we may not depart from their testimony. Perhaps Jerome himself joined these sections because they bear some unknown relation to the question he has just explained. Meanwhile the Vatican manuscript reads “indicated” rather than “inserted.”]

**3.** I found attached to your letter and brief memorandum [variant: “commentary”] a short sheet containing almost the following question:

“Ask him—that is, me—whether a woman who has left a husband who is an adulterer and a sodomite, and has been taken by another through force, may communicate with the Church without repentance while the man whom she previously left is still alive.”

When I read this, I remembered the verse: “To make excuses for excuses in sins” (Ps. 140). For all human beings favor their own vices, and what we do by our own will we attribute to necessity of nature. Thus a young man may say: “I suffer bodily force; passion drives me to lust; the very organs of my sexual members and the structure of my body seek women’s embraces.” And again the murderer may say: “I was in poverty; I needed food; I had no covering for my body. Therefore I shed another’s blood, lest I myself die of hunger and cold.”

Answer, then, the sister who asks us about her situation not with our judgment but with the Apostle’s. “Or are you ignorant, brothers—for I speak to those who know the Law—that the law is binding on a person only as long as he lives? For a married woman is bound by law to her husband while he lives; but if her husband dies, she is released from the law concerning her husband. Accordingly, while her husband lives, she will be called an adulteress if she marries another man” (Rom. 7:1 and following). And in another place: “A wife is bound as long as her husband lives. But if her husband sleeps, she is free; let her marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord” (1 Cor. 7:39).

Thus, cutting off every excuse, the Apostle defined most plainly that while her husband lives a woman is an adulteress if she marries another. Do not bring before me the violence of the ravisher, the persuasion of the mother, the authority of the father, the crowd of relatives, the plots of servants, or the contempt and losses of the household. As long as her husband lives—even if he is an adulterer, even if he is a sodomite, even if he is covered with every disgrace, and even if she has left him because of these crimes—he is still reckoned her husband, and she may not take another.

Nor does the Apostle decree this on his own authority; he followed the words of Christ, speaking through him, who says in the Gospel: “Whoever dismisses his wife, except on account of fornication, makes her commit adultery; and whoever marries a dismissed woman commits adultery” (Matt. 5:32). Notice what he says: “Whoever marries a dismissed woman commits adultery.” Whether she herself dismissed her husband or was dismissed by her husband, the man who takes her commits adultery.

Therefore, understanding the heavy burden of marriage, the Apostles said: “If such is the case, it is not expedient to marry.” The Lord answered them: “The one who is able to receive this, let him receive it” (Matt. 19:10, 12). Immediately afterward, under the example of the three kinds of eunuchs, he introduces the blessedness of virginity, which is bound by no law of the flesh.

**4.** Nor could I sufficiently understand what she intended by saying that she had been taken by another man through force. What does “taken by force” mean? A crowd was gathered, and he carried her off against her will. [Note: [Col. 0563] The same Vatican manuscript adds: “and afterward the woman who had been carried off dismissed the man who had carried her off.” Read on, etc.] Why, then, did the woman who had been carried off not afterward dismiss the ravisher?

Let her read the books of Moses, and she will find that if a betrothed woman is violated in the city and does not cry out, she is punished as an adulteress (Deut. 22). But if she is violated in the countryside, she is innocent of the crime, and the violent man is subject to the laws.

Therefore this sister also, who says that she suffered violence in order to be joined to another, if she wishes to receive the body of Christ and not be considered an adulteress, must do penance—provided only that from the time of her repentance she is not joined to the second man, who is not called a husband but an adulterer.

If this seems harsh to her, and she cannot abandon the man whom she once loved or place the Lord before pleasure, let her hear the Apostle crying aloud: “You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons. You cannot share in the table of the Lord and the table of demons” (1 Cor. 10:20). And in another place: “What partnership has light with darkness? What agreement has Christ with Belial?” (2 Cor. 6:14–15).

I am speaking of something new—or rather not new, but old, confirmed by the authority of the Old Testament. If she leaves the second man and wishes to be reconciled to the first, she cannot. For it is written in Deuteronomy:

> “If a man takes a wife and possesses her, and she does not find favor in his sight because he has found some indecency in her, he shall write a bill of divorce, give it into her hand, and send her away from his house. When she has gone out and married another husband, and he too hates her, gives her a bill of divorce, and sends her away from his house—or when he dies—the former husband may not take her again as his wife, because she has been defiled and become abominable before the Lord. Do not cause the land that the Lord your God has given you to possess to sin” (Deut. 24:1 and following). [Note: [Col. 0563] Some manuscripts read, “and he shall give it to her and send her away,” but I think this is erroneous.]

Therefore, I beg you, console her—or rather, urge her toward salvation. Rotten flesh requires the sword and the cautery. The fault lies not with the medicine but with the wound, when the physician does not spare with merciful harshness: he is severe in order to spare, he acts harshly in order to show mercy.

**5.** [Note: [Col. 0564] Here the old manuscripts begin another letter, prefaced by this rubric in red ink: “Epistolary discourse to the person mentioned above; or, the epistolary response of the same person mentioned above. The question concerned the same Apostle,” etc. Or: “Your question was.”]

Your third—that is, final—question concerned the same Letter of the Apostle, where, discussing the resurrection, he comes to the passage in which it is written:

> “For he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet. The last enemy to be destroyed is death. For he has put all things under his feet” (1 Cor. 15:25–26).

Since he has said that all things have been subjected to him, there is no doubt that the one who subjected all things to him is excepted. But when all things have been subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subjected to the one who subjected all things to him, “so that God may be all in all.”

I am amazed that you wished to ask me about this, since Saint Hilary, Bishop of Poitiers, completed his eleventh book Against the Arians with this question and its solution. Nevertheless, let us say at least a few things.

The whole scandal in this passage concerns why the Son is said to be subject to the Father. What is more shameful or inferior: to be subjected to the Father—which is often an act of piety, as it is written in the Psalm, “Will not my soul be subject to God?” (Ps. 61:1)—or to be crucified and become the curse of the cross? “Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree” (Deut. 21:23).

He, therefore, who became a curse for us in order to free us from the curse—do you wonder if he is subjected for our sake, so that he may make us subject to the Father, saying in the Gospel: “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14:6), and, “When I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things to myself” (John 12:32)?

Christ is subject to the Father in those who are faithful, because all believers—or rather, the whole human race—are reckoned members of his body. But in those who are unbelieving, that is, Jews, Gentiles, and heretics, he is said to be unsubdued, because part of his members is not subject to faith.

At the end of the world, however, when all the members have seen Christ reigning—that is, his body—they too will be subjected to Christ, that is, to his body, so that the whole body of Christ may be subjected to God and the Father, “so that God may be all in all.”

He does not say, “so that the Father may be all in all,” but “so that God may be all in all.” This is the proper name of the Trinity and can be referred equally to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, so that humanity may be subjected to divinity.

By “humanity” here we mean not gentleness and clemency, which the Greeks call φιλανθρωπία, “love of humanity,” but the entire human race.

Furthermore, when he says, “so that God may be all in all,” this must be understood in the following sense: our Lord and Savior is not now all things in everyone, but is present in part in each person. For example, in Solomon there is wisdom; in David, goodness; in Job, patience; in Daniel, knowledge of the future; in Peter, faith; in Phinehas and Paul, zeal; in John, virginity; and in others, other virtues.

But when the end of all things arrives, then he will be all things in all, so that each of the saints will possess every virtue, and Christ will be wholly present in all.

**LETTER LVI** [Note: [Col. 0565] Elsewhere numbered 86. Written around the year 394, but not delivered.] **AUGUSTINE TO JEROME.**

Augustine to Jerome, complaining about the new translation of the Old Testament after the Septuagint, and about Peter’s being rebuked by Paul in Galatians 2, while reproaching him for undertaking here the defense of an officious lie.

[Note: [Col. 0565] The Cistercian manuscript, according to the Benedictine editors of Augustine, reads: “observing and following, and embracing more fully, etc. greetings in the Lord.” One Corbie manuscript, held by Martianay, has at the end: “Augustine the Presbyter”; on this matter see the Chronological Notes.]

To the most beloved lord and brother Jerome, whom I serve and embrace with the sincerest devotion of charity, his fellow presbyter AUGUSTINE.

### 1.

“No one has ever become so readily known to anyone else as the quiet joy and truly liberal exercise of your studies in the Lord have become known to me. Although, therefore, I greatly desire to know you completely, I lack a small part of you—namely, your bodily presence.

[Note: Victorius reads *munus* (“gift”), and explains the reading by taking the bodily presence, perceived only through another’s report, as the “small gift” meant here.]

Even this, after the most blessed brother Alypius—now a bishop, but then already worthy of the episcopate—had seen you and, on his return, had appeared before me, I cannot deny was impressed upon me in large part through his report: when he saw you there, and I saw you too, but through his eyes. For who would say that he and I were two in mind, rather than in body, except that we were united by the firmest harmony and intimacy, not by merits, in which he excels?

[Note: Alypius was made bishop of Tagaste in 394, the very year in which Augustine is thought to have written this letter.]

Since, therefore, you first love me through the communion of the spirit by which we are joined into one,

[Note: Martianay, following the Erasmian manuscripts, reads *in unum nitimur* (“we strive toward unity”), which Victorius corrects, since, as he says, the phrase should correspond more closely to the word *communionis*.]

and since you now love me through his words, I commend to your brotherly affection, without the least embarrassment, as though he were unknown to you, our brother Profuturus,

[Note: When this Profuturus was setting out for Palestine, he was appointed bishop of Cirta and died shortly afterward. Hence this letter was not delivered to Saint Jerome at that time, as is clear from Augustine’s Letter 65, cited below. Profuturus is also mentioned by Paulinus in Letter 32 and by Evodius in Letter 158; this was noted before us by the Benedictine editors.]

whom we hope will truly profit from our efforts and, thereafter, from your assistance—unless, perhaps, he is such that through him I myself may become more commendable to you than he through me.

I might perhaps have written only this much, had I wished to be content with the customary brevity of formal letters. But my heart overflows with conversations to share with you about our studies, which we pursue in Christ Jesus our Lord, who deigns, also through your charity, to provide us with many benefits and certain provisions for the journey He has shown us.

[Alternative reading: “has shown us the journey, and already….”]

### 2.

“We therefore ask—and with us asks the whole devoted fellowship of the African churches—that you not hesitate to devote care and labor to interpreting the works of those who have treated our Scriptures most excellently in Greek. For you can make it possible for us too to possess such men, especially one whom you mention most willingly in your writings, namely Origen.

“As for translating the canonical holy Scriptures into Latin, I would not want you to undertake the labor except in the manner in which you translated Job: namely, with signs added so that the difference between your translation and that of the Septuagint, whose authority is exceedingly weighty, may be apparent.

“I cannot sufficiently marvel if something is still found in the Hebrew writings and manuscripts that escaped so many interpreters who were most skilled in that language. I say nothing of the Septuagint, concerning either their unity of purpose or their greater harmony of spirit—as though they had been one person—for I do not dare to adopt a definite position on that question, except that I believe their pre-eminent authority in this work must be granted without controversy.

“I am more troubled by those who, translating later and clinging stubbornly—as is reported—to the path and rules of Hebrew words and expressions, not only failed to agree among themselves but also left many things remaining to be dug out and published long afterward. For if these matters are obscure, it is believed that you too could have been mistaken in them; but if they are clear,

[Note: Martianay errs again, following Erasmus, in reading: “But if they are clear, it is superfluous that you should have wished to explain what could not have escaped them.” As Victorius notes, these words belong to Jerome, from the letter beginning “Tres simul,” which was wrongly inserted here in place of the reading restored from all the manuscripts and from most printed editions: “it is not believed that they could have been mistaken in them.” The quotation is also confirmed by Jerome’s testimony, when he repeats Augustine’s words: “If they are obscure, it must be believed that you too could have been mistaken in them. But if they are clear, it is evident that they could not have been mistaken in them.”]

it is not believed that they could have been mistaken in them. Therefore, after you have set out the reasons for this matter in accordance with your charity, I beg you to make me certain of your judgment.”

### 3. The defense of a lie

“I have also read certain writings said to be yours concerning the Epistles of the Apostle Paul. When, in wishing to explain one of them, the Epistle to the Galatians, you came upon that passage where the Apostle recalls Peter from a pernicious simulation, I confess that I am deeply grieved that a defense of falsehood was undertaken there—whether by you, such a man, or by someone else, if you did not write it—until the arguments that trouble me have been refuted, if indeed they can be refuted.

“For it seems to me exceedingly destructive to believe that a lie exists in the holy books: that is, that the men through whom that Scripture was delivered and composed for us should have lied in their writings.

“One question is whether good men may ever lie; another is whether the writer of the holy Scriptures ought to have lied—or rather, this is not another question, but no question at all. For once any sort of officious lie has been admitted to so great a height of authority, no part of those books will remain which, whenever it seems difficult for conduct or incredible for faith, could not by the same most destructive rule be referred to the intention and duty of the lying author.

“For if the Apostle Paul was lying when, rebuking the Apostle Peter, he said:

> ‘If you, though you are a Jew, live as a Gentile and not as a Jew, how do you compel the Gentiles to Judaize?’

and if Peter seemed to him to have acted rightly, although Paul both said and wrote that he had not acted rightly (Galatians 2:14), ‘in order, as it were, to soothe the spirits of those who were in an uproar’—what shall we answer when perverse men arise, forbidding marriage, whom Paul himself foretold would come, and say that everything the same Apostle said to establish the rights of marriage was a lie told for the sake of people who might become agitated through love of their spouses: that he did not really think this, but said it to calm their opposition?

“There is no need to recall many examples. Even officious lies about the praises of God might appear permissible, so that love of Him might be kindled in more sluggish people; and thus the authority of chaste truth would nowhere remain certain in the holy Scriptures.

“Do we not observe that the same Apostle, with immense care to commend the truth, says:

> ‘But if Christ has not been raised, our preaching is empty, and your faith is empty. We are also found to be false witnesses of God, because we have testified against God that He raised Christ, whom He did not raise’ (1 Corinthians 15:14–15)?

“If someone said to him: ‘Why do you shrink from this lie, since you have said what, even if false, contributes most greatly to the praise of God?’—would he not, abhorring such madness, expose the inner chambers of his heart to the light with whatever words and indications he could, crying out that it is no lesser—or perhaps even a greater—crime to praise falsehood in God than to blame the truth?

“Therefore, a person should approach the knowledge of the divine Scriptures who thinks so holily and truthfully about the holy books that he would not wish any part of them to delight him through officious lies, but would rather pass over what he does not understand than prefer his own heart to that truth. For when such a person says this, he seeks to be believed, and acts so that we will not believe the authority of the divine Scriptures.”

### 4.

“And I, with whatever strength the Lord supplies, would show that all those testimonies which have been brought forward to support the usefulness of lying ought to be understood otherwise, so that their firm truth might everywhere be taught. For just as testimonies ought not to be lies, so they ought not to favor lying. But I leave this to your intelligence. Once you have applied more careful consideration to the reading, you may perhaps see it much more easily than I do.

“Piety will compel you to undertake this consideration, because you recognize that the authority of the divine Scriptures is made to waver if everyone believes in them whatever he wishes and refuses to believe whatever he does not wish—once it has been persuaded that the men through whom these things were delivered to us could, in their Scriptures, have lied officiously.

“Unless, perhaps, you are going to lay down certain rules by which we may know where it is appropriate to lie and where it is not. But if this can be done, I beg you not to explain it by any means through lying and doubtful arguments.

“And do not judge me burdensome or shameless, by the most truthful humanity of our Lord. For, not to say that my error is entirely free of blame, certainly my error is not a great one, if it favors the truth. If truth can rightly favor falsehood in you, then so may my error.”

[Col. 0568]

### 5.

“I would like to speak many other things with your most sincere heart and to converse about Christian learning, but no letter is sufficient for this desire of mine. I can discuss the same matters more fully through our brother Profuturus, whom I rejoice to have sent to you so that he might be mingled with and nourished by your sweet and useful conversations.

“And yet how much I wish that even he himself—if I may say so with his permission—could contain it all, although I would in no way place myself above him.

[Note: We have inserted *in*, following Victorius.]

“For I confess that I am more capable of receiving you; but I see him becoming fuller, by which he unquestionably surpasses me. After he has returned, if his journey prospers with the Lord’s help, when I have shared in the fullness of his heart with which you have enriched him, he will not fill what in me is still empty and eager for your thoughts. Thus it will come about that I too will then be more needy, while he will be more abundant.

“Certainly that same brother is carrying with him some of our writings. If you deign to read them, I beg you to apply to them sincere and brotherly severity. For I understand the following passage in no other way:

> ‘Let the righteous man correct me in mercy and rebuke me; but let not the oil of the sinner fatten my head’ (Psalm 140:5);

unless it means that the rebuking physician who heals is loved more than the flatterer who anoints the head.

“BUT I find it extremely difficult to be a good judge of what I have written, whether I am more timid than is right or more eager than is right. I sometimes see my own faults as well, but I prefer to hear of them from better men, lest, when I perhaps rightly rebuke myself, I should again flatter myself and appear to have passed upon myself a sentence that was fearful rather than just.”

[Note: Four manuscripts held by the Benedictine editors read *a senioribus* (“from elders”); one reads *a Majoribus* (“from greater men”).]

## LETTER LVII

[Note: Formerly Letter 101. Written around the middle of 395.]

### To Pammachius

On the best method of translation

When Rufinus criticized Jerome for having translated incorrectly the preceding Letter 51 of Epiphanius to John, Bishop of Jerusalem, Jerome, after complaining that someone had, without his knowledge, stolen the letter from his chests before it had been fully corrected, demonstrates, by the testimonies of all the ancient learned men as well as of the holy Scriptures, what the best method of translation is. He shows that it is the method he himself used in translating that letter: namely, translating sense from sense, not word from word.

### 1.

The Apostle Paul, standing before King Agrippa and preparing to answer the charges against him, congratulates himself at the very beginning, confident of victory in his case and mindful of what his hearer would be able to understand, saying:

> “Concerning all the things of which I am accused by the Jews, King Agrippa, I consider myself blessed that I am to defend myself before you today, since you especially know all the customs and controversies that exist among the Jews” (Acts 26:13).

For he had read the words of Jesus:

> “Blessed is the one who speaks into the ears of a hearer” (Ecclesiasticus 25:12, according to the Septuagint),

[Note: Some printed editions and manuscripts incorrectly attribute this saying to Isaiah. It is from Jesus son of Sirach, commonly called Ecclesiasticus.]

and he knew that the words of an orator advance only as far as the judge’s understanding perceives them.

Therefore, I too consider myself blessed in this matter alone: that I am about to answer before learned ears with an unskilled tongue—ears that accuse me either of ignorance or of falsehood, if I either did not know how to translate another’s writings accurately or did not wish to do so. The first is an error; the second, a crime.

And lest my accuser should perhaps, through the ease with which he speaks about everything and the impunity with which he thinks everything permitted to him, also accuse me before you, just as he accused Pope Epiphanius, I have sent this letter so that it may make the sequence of events known to you and, through you, to others who deign to love us.

### 2. Epiphanius’ letter to Bishop John. Eusebius of Cremona, ignorant of Greek. What the false monk did.

Nearly two years earlier, the aforementioned Pope Epiphanius had sent a letter to Bishop John, reproving him concerning certain doctrines and afterward gently calling him to repentance. Copies of it were eagerly snatched up throughout Palestine, either because of the merit of its author or because of the elegance of its composition.

There was in our monastery a man of no little standing among his own people, Eusebius of Cremona. When this letter was flying from mouth to mouth and both learned and unlearned admired it for its learning and purity of language, he began urgently to ask me to translate it for him into Latin and to explain it more openly for ease of understanding. For he was entirely ignorant of Greek eloquence.

I did what he wanted. Calling in a secretary, I dictated the translation hastily and quickly, briefly noting in the margin of the page,

[Note: That is, from the little tablet called in Greek *ἡ πλίνθος* (*hē plinthos*). See the Commentary on Ezekiel, chapter 4, verse 1: “Take a brick for yourself.”]

what sense each section contained within it. Indeed, he had insistently requested that I do this for him alone. I also asked him in return to keep a copy at home and not readily publish it among the people.

The matter continued for a year and six months, until the aforementioned translation migrated from his chests to Jerusalem through a new piece of trickery. For a certain false monk, either after receiving payment—as is clearly indicated—or through gratuitous malice, as the corrupter vainly tries to persuade us, having rifled through his papers at his expense, became a Judas and a betrayer, and gave my adversaries an opportunity to bark against me. Thus they could proclaim among the ignorant that I was a falsifier, that I had not rendered word for word, that I had translated “dearest” for “honorable,” and that through a malicious translation—shameful even to say—I had refused to translate *αἰδεσιμώτατον Πάππαν* (*aidĕsimōtaton Pappan*, “the most revered Pope”).

These and similar trifles are the crimes laid against me.

### 3.

Before I answer concerning the translation, I wish first to ask those who call malice prudence: Where did you get a copy of the letter? Who gave it to you? With what face do you produce what you bought through crime? What will be safe among human beings if we cannot conceal our secrets even within walls and chests?

If I brought this charge against you before the tribunals of judges, I would subject you to the laws, which, even for the sake of the interests of the treasury, impose penalties on harmful informers—or, according to another reading, “various informers”—and, though they admit denunciation, condemn the betrayer. Profit, apparently, is pleasing; intention is displeasing.

[Note: Some think that this Hesychius—not “Esychius,” as the printed editions incorrectly give it—should be changed, since he is not found among the consuls, to Eutychianus, who appears in Cassiodorus’ Fasti as consul under Arcadius and Honorius in 398. But since Jerome says that this man was condemned “long ago,” that is, recently, by Theodosius, while the man who pronounced the death sentence against him died at the beginning of 395, it is clear that Eutychianus cannot be intended. It seems to us much more likely that Hesychius, proconsul of Achaia, is meant. To him is addressed Theodosius’ law in the Theodosian Code, the final book, concerning the chiefs of the *agentes in rebus*; and a very brief letter of Saint Nilus is also preserved, not to mention other evidence.]

Not long ago Theodosius, the emperor, condemned to death Hesychius, a man of consular rank, against whom the patriarch Gamaliel had exercised the gravest hostility, because he had induced a secretary and seized that man’s papers.

We read in the ancient histories that the schoolmaster who had betrayed the children of the Faliscans was bound and handed over to the boys, then sent back to those whom he had betrayed; and that the Roman people did not accept a victory obtained through crime (Livy, First Decade, book 5).

When Pyrrhus, king of Epirus, was being treated in his camp for a wound, Fabricius considered it wrong to have him killed through the treachery of his physician. Rather, he bound the physician and sent him back to his master, so that crime might not be approved even against an enemy (Florus, book 1).

What public laws protect, what enemies protect, what is held sacred amid wars and swords—this was not protected for us among monks and priests of Christ.

And one of them dares, with raised eyebrows and snapping fingers, to belch out and say: “What of it, if he bought it, if he induced him? He did what benefited him.”

A MARVELOUS DEFENSE OF CRIME—as though robbers, thieves, and pirates do not also do what benefits them. Certainly Annas and Caiaphas, when they led the wretched Judas astray, did what they thought useful to themselves.

### 4.

I want to write whatever nonsense I please in my little papers: to comment on the Scriptures, to bite back at those who injure me, to digest my anger, to exercise myself in commonplaces, and to store up arrows sharpened for battle—or, as some read, “for assault.”

As long as I do not publish my thoughts, even if they are abusive, they are not crimes—indeed, not even abuse, since public ears have not heard them.

You corrupt servants, bribe clients, and, as we read in the stories, penetrate to Danaë through gold (Metamorphoses, book 4). Then, concealing what you have done, you call me a falsifier, although in accusing me you confess against yourself a much worse crime than the one you charge against me.

One person accuses you of heresy, another charges you with perverting doctrine. You yourself remain silent; you do not dare to answer. You tear apart the translator, quibble over syllables, and think your entire defense is secured if you slander one who is silent.

Suppose that in translating I either made a mistake or omitted something. This is the whole hinge of your case—or, as some read, “of your entire ingenuity.” This is your defense. Does it follow that you are not a heretic if I am a bad translator?

I do not say this because I know you to be a heretic; let the man who accused you know that, and let the man who wrote it know it. I say only that it is the height of folly for one person who has been accused by another to accuse someone else, and, when his own body is wounded everywhere, to seek comfort in the wound of a sleeping man.

### 5.

Until now I have spoken as though I had altered something in the letter, and as though a simple translation could contain an error but not a crime. But now the letter itself demonstrates that nothing has been changed in meaning, that no matters have been added, and that no doctrine has been fabricated.

> “They make themselves understood, indeed, so as to understand nothing” (Terence, *Andria*, Prologue).

While they wish to convict another’s ignorance, they reveal their own.

For I not only admit but openly profess that in translating Greek authors—apart from the holy Scriptures, where even the order of the words is a mystery—I do not render word for word but sense from sense.

I have Tully as my teacher in this matter. He translated Plato’s *Protagoras*, Xenophon’s *Oeconomicus*, and two magnificent speeches of Aeschines and Demosthenes directed against each other. It is not the present occasion to say how much he omitted, added, and changed in them so that he might express the peculiarities of the other language through the peculiarities of his own.

For me the authority of the translator himself, Cicero, is sufficient. In the preface to those same speeches he writes:

> “I thought that I should undertake a labor useful to students, though not necessary for myself. I translated from Attic the celebrated speeches of the two most eloquent men, Aeschines and Demosthenes, opposed to one another; and I did not translate as an interpreter but as an orator, preserving the same thoughts and their forms, with figures as well as words adapted to our usage. In these I did not consider it necessary to render word for word; rather, I preserved the entire character and force of the words. For I did not think that I ought to count them out to the reader, as it were, but to weigh them.”

Again, at the end of the discourse he says:

> “If, as I hope, I have expressed their speeches by employing all their virtues—that is, their thoughts, their figures, and the order of their matters—and by following their words only insofar as they do not conflict with our own manner of expression, then, even if everything has not been translated from Greek, we have worked to make it belong to the same kind.”

[Note: The Benedictine editor incorrectly reads *sicut* for *si, ut*, along with other similar errors, especially in punctuation, which there is not space to indicate throughout.]

Horace too, an acute and learned man, gives the same instruction to the educated translator in the *Art of Poetry*:

> “Nor will you take care to render word for word, as a faithful interpreter.”

Terence translated Menander, and Plautus and Caecilius translated the ancient comic poets. Do they cling to the words, rather than preserve beauty and elegance more fully in translation?

What you call fidelity of translation, learned people now call *κακοξηλία* (*kakoxēlia*, “bad affectation” or “affected literalism”).

Thus, instructed by such men approximately—

[Note: No one doubts that Jerome wrote “fifteen,” not “twenty,” since otherwise the chronology would not fit: the interval from the translation of the *Chronicle* in 380 to this letter, written around the middle of 395, is too short. Ancient copyists easily mistook the Roman numeral XV for XX when writing quickly, and the error spread through all the printed books and manuscripts we have seen. See the chronological arguments concerning this letter, where the point is demonstrated clearly. Nevertheless, although the error is certain to us, we have scrupled to alter the text without manuscript support.]

twenty years ago, and myself then deceived by a similar error, certainly without knowing that you would one day bring this charge against me, I used, among other things, the following preface when translating Eusebius of Caesarea’s *Chronicle* into Latin:

> “It is difficult, when following another’s lines, not to stumble somewhere; and it is arduous for what has been well expressed in one language to preserve the same elegance in translation. Something has been signified through the particular force of a single word, but I do not possess an equivalent with which to express it. While I seek to complete the thought through a lengthy circumlocution, I scarcely complete the brief spans of life—or, according to another reading, ‘the brief spaces.’ There are also the winding paths of hyperbaton, differences in case, varieties of figures, and finally the language’s own character, its native manner of expression, so to speak. If I translate word for word, the result sounds absurd; but if necessity leads me to alter something in the order or wording, I will seem to have abandoned the translator’s duty.”

And after much else, which it would now be tedious to repeat, I added this:

> “If anyone does not think that the grace of a language is changed in translation, let him render Homer word for word into Latin. I will say something more: let him interpret the same poet in his own language through the words of prose. You will see a ridiculous order and the most eloquent of poets scarcely speaking.”

### 6.

But lest the authority of my writings be small—although I have wished to prove only this, that from my youth I have always translated not words but meanings—learn from the text itself what sort of preface there is concerning this method in the book in which the life of blessed Antony is described, namely, in Evagrius’ preface to Innocent:

> “A word-for-word translation expressed from one language into another conceals the sense and, like luxuriant grass, chokes the crops. For while speech serves cases and figures, what could have been indicated briefly it scarcely explains after being led around through a lengthy circuit.”

Avoiding this, therefore, I rendered the life of blessed Antony at your request in such a way that nothing is lacking in meaning, even though something is lacking in words. Let others hunt syllables and letters—or, according to another reading, “occupy themselves with syllables and letters”; you seek the thoughts.

My day would end before I could repeat the testimonies of all who have translated according to meaning. For the present it is enough to name Hilary the Confessor, who translated into Latin from Greek many homilies on Job and numerous treatises on the Psalms. He did not sit clinging to a sluggish letter or twist himself through the stale translation of rustic people; rather, like captives, he transferred the meanings into his own language by the right of a conqueror.

### 7.

Nor is this surprising in other men of the world or of the Church, since the Septuagint translators, the Evangelists, and the Apostles did the same thing in the sacred books.

We read in Mark that the Lord said:

> “TALITHA CUMI,”

and immediately it is added:

> “which is translated, ‘Girl, I say to you, arise’” (Mark 5:41).

Let the Evangelist be accused of falsehood: why did he add “I say to you,” when the Hebrew has only “Girl, arise”? He added it to make the expression more emphatic—*ἐμφατικώτερον* (*emphatikōteron*)—and to express the sense of one calling and commanding.

Again, in Matthew, after the traitor Judas had returned the thirty pieces of silver and a potter’s field had been bought with them, we read:

> “Then was fulfilled what was spoken through Jeremiah the Prophet, saying: ‘And they took the thirty pieces of silver, the price of the one whose price had been set by the children of Israel, and they gave them for the potter’s field, as the Lord appointed me’” (Matthew 27:9).

This is found nowhere at all in Jeremiah, but in Zechariah, with entirely different words and a wholly different order. For the commonly used edition reads:

> “And I said to them: ‘If it is good in your eyes, give me my wages; or refuse.’ And they weighed out my wages, thirty pieces of silver. And the Lord said to me: ‘Cast them into the smelting furnace, and see whether it is tested, as I have been tested by them.’ And I took the thirty pieces of silver and cast them into the house of the Lord, into the smelting furnace” (Zechariah 11:12–13).

[Note: When the name “Vulgate” is used here, it should be understood as referring to the old Latin translation made from the Septuagint edition, which was then in use.]

It is obvious how far the Septuagint translation differs from the Evangelist’s testimony. But in the Hebrew, although the sense is the same, the words are arranged differently and are almost entirely unlike it:

> “And I said to them,” he says, “‘If it is good in your eyes, bring my wages; and if not, cease.’ And they weighed out my wages, thirty pieces of silver. And the Lord said to me: ‘Throw it to the statuary—the handsome price at which I was valued by them.’ And I took the thirty pieces of silver and threw them into the house of the Lord, to the statuary.”

[Note: Some manuscripts read “the price at which he was valued,” which Victorius argues should be read in place of “the price at which I was valued.”]

Let them accuse the Apostle of falsehood because he agrees neither with the Hebrew text nor with the Septuagint translators—and, what is more, because he errs in the name, putting Jeremiah in place of Zechariah.

But far be it from us to say this of Christ’s attendant, whose concern was not to hunt words and syllables but to set forth the meanings of doctrines.

Let us turn to another testimony from the same Zechariah, which the Evangelist John adopts according to the Hebrew Truth:

> “They will look upon him whom they pierced” (Zechariah 12:10; John 19:37).

For this, in the Septuagint, we read:

> “καὶ ἐπιβλέψονται πρός με, ἀνθ’ ὧν ἐνωρχήσαντο,”

which the Latins translated:

> “And they will look upon me because of the things with which they mocked,” or “insulted.”

The Evangelist’s translation, that of the Septuagint interpreters, and ours differ; yet the variety of expressions agrees through the unity of the Spirit.

In Matthew too we read that the Lord foretold to the Apostles their flight and confirmed it with this testimony from Zechariah:

> “It is written,” He says, “‘I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered’” (Zechariah 13:7; Matthew 26:31).

But in the Septuagint and in the Hebrew it is very different. It is not spoken in the person of God, as the Evangelist presents it, but in the person of the Prophet, who is asking God the Father:

> “Strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered.”

According to the judgment of certain clever people, the Evangelist is guilty of sacrilege in this passage because he dared to refer the Prophet’s words to the person of God.

The same Evangelist writes that, at the angel’s warning, Joseph took the child and his mother, entered Egypt, and remained there until Herod’s death, “so that what was spoken by the Lord through the Prophet might be fulfilled”:

> “Out of Egypt I called my son.”

Our copies do not contain this wording. But in Hosea, according to the Hebrew Truth, it is written:

> “Because Israel is a child, and I loved him; and out of Egypt I called my son” (Hosea 11:2).

For this, in the same place, the Septuagint translated:

> “Because Israel is a child, and I loved him; and out of Egypt I called his sons.”

Are they therefore to be entirely rejected because they translated differently this passage, which pertains above all to the mystery of Christ? Or should pardon rather be granted them as human beings, according to the saying of James:

> “We all offend in many things; and if anyone does not offend in word, that person is a perfect man and is able to bridle the whole body” (James 3).

[Note: Victorius again reads *potens* (“able”) in place of *et potest* (“and is able”), following the Greek *δυνατός* and the manuscripts he consulted. Our manuscripts, as well as all the printed editions, have the latter reading.]

But what is written in the same Evangelist is even more striking:

> “And coming, he lived in a city called Nazareth, so that what was spoken through the prophets might be fulfilled: ‘He will be called a Nazaraean’” (Matthew 2:23).

Let the *λογοδαίδαλοι* (*logodaidaloi*, “word-artificers”) and fastidious critics of all interpreters answer where they have read this; and let them learn that it is placed in Isaiah.

[Note: In his Commentaries on this passage of Matthew, Jerome prefers the plural “through the prophets” because this particular statement is not found in any one definite prophet but occurs throughout the prophets whenever they call Christ holy. Thus they interpret “Nazaraean” from such passages as Genesis 49 and Deuteronomy 33, under the figure of Joseph, and Judges 13, under the figure of Samson; both of these men were called by the name “Nazaraean.”]

For in the place where we read and have translated:

> “A branch will go forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower will rise from his root” (Isaiah 11:1),

the Hebrew, according to the *ἰδίωμα* (*idiōma*, “idiom”) of that language, reads:

> “A branch will go forth from the root of Jesse, and a Nazaraean will grow from his root.”

Why did the Septuagint omit this, if it is not permitted to translate word for word? It is sacrilege either to conceal the mystery or to have failed to understand it.

## 8.

Let us pass on to the rest; for the brevity of a letter does not permit us to dwell longer on individual points. Matthew himself says:

> “Now all this took place so that what had been spoken by the Lord through the Prophet might be fulfilled, saying: Behold, a virgin shall have [a child] in her womb and bear a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel” (Matt. 1:22–23; and Isa. 7:14).

The Septuagint translated this:

> “Behold, a virgin shall receive in her womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Emmanuel.”

If they criticize the words [or: if we criticize the words], certainly “she shall have” and “she shall receive” are not the same, nor are “they shall call” and “you shall call.” But in Hebrew we read it written as follows:

> “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and she shall call his name Emmanuel.”

It is not Ahaz, who was being accused of unbelief, nor the Jews, who were about to deny the Lord, who shall call him; rather, he says, she herself who conceives, that very virgin who bears him, shall call him.

In the same Evangelist we read that Herod was disturbed at the arrival of the Magi. After summoning the scribes and priests, he asked them where Christ was to be born; and they answered:

> “In Bethlehem of Judea. For thus it is written in the Prophet: ‘And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah; for from you shall come forth a ruler who will govern my people Israel.’”

In the Vulgate Edition this passage reads:

> “And you, Bethlehem, house of Ephratha, you are small, so as to be among the thousands of Judah; from you there shall come forth for me one who will be ruler in Israel.”

[Note: The words “so as to be” are found neither in our manuscripts nor in the older Vulgate copies. We shall explain and reconcile this passage of Matthew in the Commentaries.]
