You will be still more astonished at the extent of the disagreement between Matthew and the Septuagint in their wording and order if you consult the Hebrew, where it is written:

> “And you, Bethlehem Ephratha, you are little among the thousands of Judah; from you there shall come forth for me one who is to rule in Israel.”

Consider step by step what the Evangelist has written: “And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah.” In place of “land of Judah,” the Hebrew has “Ephratha”; the Septuagint has “house of Ephratha.” In place of “you are by no means least among the rulers of Judah,” the Septuagint reads, “you are small, so as to be among the thousands of Judah”; in Hebrew, “you are little among the thousands of Judah.” The sense is contrary, although in this particular passage the Septuagint agrees with the Hebrew.

For the Evangelist said that it is not little among the rulers of Judah, whereas the opposite is stated: “You are indeed little and small; nevertheless, from you, little and small as you are, a ruler shall go forth for me in Israel,” according to the Apostle’s statement:

> “God chose the weak things of the world in order to confound the strong” (1 Cor. 1).

Moreover, it is clear that what follows—“who will govern,” or “who will shepherd, my people Israel”—is expressed differently in the Prophet.

## 9.

I repeat these things not to accuse the Evangelists of falsehood—for that is the work of the impious, Celsus, Porphyry, and Julian—but to accuse my critics of ignorance, and to obtain from them the concession that, in a simple letter, they grant me what, whether they wish it or not, they will have to grant to the Apostles in the Holy Scriptures.

Mark, the disciple of Peter, begins his Gospel in this way:

> “The beginning of the Gospel of Jesus Christ, as it is written in Isaiah the Prophet: ‘Behold, I send my Angel before your face, who will prepare your way before you. A voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight.’”

This passage is composed from two Prophets, namely Malachi and Isaiah. For the first statement—

> “Behold, I send my Angel before your face, who will prepare your way before you” (Mal. 3:1)

—is written at the end of Malachi. But the following words—

> “A voice of one crying in the wilderness,”

and what follows, we read in Isaiah. How, then, did Mark, immediately at the beginning of his work, write:

> “As it is written in Isaiah the Prophet: ‘Behold, I send my Angel’” (Isa. 40:3),

when, as we have said, this is not written in Isaiah, but at the end of Malachi, the last of the Twelve Prophets? Let ignorant presumption solve this little problem, and I shall ask pardon for my error.

The same Mark introduces the Savior speaking to the Pharisees:

> “Have you never read what David did when he was in need and was hungry, he himself and those who were with him: how he entered the house of God under Abiathar the high priest and ate the loaves of the Presence, which it was not lawful for anyone to eat except the priests alone?” (Mark 2:25–26; and Luke 6:3–4).

Let us read Samuel—or, as the common title has it, the Books of Kings—and there we shall find that it is not Abiathar but Abimelech the high priest who is named. Later he was struck down by Doeg [or Doec], together with the other priests, at Saul’s command.

Let us proceed to the Apostle Paul. He writes to the Corinthians:

> “For if they had known the Lord of glory, they would not have crucified him. But, as it is written: ‘What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart, the things God has prepared for those who love him.’”

[Note: He is attacking especially the Gnostics and the disciples of Basilides, as appears at great length from the letter to Desiderius prefixed to the Pentateuch and from chapter 64 of the Commentary on Isaiah. Origen, too, does not escape censure; in Treatise 35 on Matthew 27 he taught the same thing and said that this testimony is found in no single book except in the hidden writings of the Prophet Elijah. For this reason Hegesippus is also accused by Stephen Gobarus, in Photius, of rejecting this testimony as false. See what we note elsewhere on Isaiah 64 and in the cited letter to Desiderius. Some copies corruptly read “of the Apocalypse of the Church.”]

At this passage certain people habitually pursue the ravings of apocryphal writings and say that the testimony was taken from the Apocalypse of Elijah. Yet in Isaiah, according to the Hebrew, it reads:

> “From of old they have not heard, nor perceived with their ears. No eye has seen, O God, besides you, the things you have prepared for those who wait for you” (Isa. 64:4).

The Septuagint translated this quite differently:

> “From of old we have not heard; nor have our eyes seen a God besides you; your works are true, and you will show mercy to those who wait for you.”

[Note: The Greek text has καὶ τὰ ἔργα σου ἃ ποιήσεις τοῖς ὑπομένουσιν ἔλεον. It therefore seems that Jerome read in his copy, instead of the single relative pronoun ἅ, ἀληθῆ καὶ—“true, and you will do,” and so forth—although no trace of such a variant exists in the surviving Greek copies. Rather, learned men conjecture that Jerome was mistaken here, having read ἀληθεῖ in one word instead of the two words ἃ λήθει, a sense more suitable to the context; but the Hebrew text has only this: “apart from you,” that is, “he will do for those who await him.” I think, however, that the Septuagint cited by Jerome is not the Greek text but an old Latin translation. [Col. 0577] “[He] who was Shechem” [context uncertain]; and thus Jerome may, with still greater correctness, have counted this too among the divergences from Genesis.]

We understand, then, where the testimony was taken from; yet the Apostle did not reproduce it word for word, but expressed the same sense in other language, by way of paraphrase (παραφραστικῶς).

In the Epistle to the Romans the same Apostle Paul, taking an example from Isaiah, says:

> “Behold, I place in Zion a stone of stumbling and a rock of scandal” (Isa. 8:14).

He differs from the old translation, yet agrees with the Hebrew truth. For in the Septuagint the sense is contrary:

> “Not that you might encounter a stone of stumbling, nor a rock of ruin.”

The Apostle Peter, too, agreeing with Paul and with the Hebrews, wrote:

> “But to the unbelieving, a stone of stumbling and a rock of scandal” (Rom. 9:33; 1 Pet. 2).

From all these examples it is clear that the Apostles and Evangelists, when interpreting the ancient Scriptures, sought the sense, not the words; nor did they take great care over the order or phrasing, so long as the meaning of the matter was clear.

## 10.

Luke, an Apostolic man and Evangelist, writes that Stephen, the first martyr of Christ, declared in a Jewish assembly:

> “In seventy-five souls Jacob went down into Egypt; and he himself died, and our fathers were transferred to Shechem and placed in the tomb which Abraham bought for a price of silver from the sons of Emmor, the father of Shechem” (Acts 7:15–16; and Gen. 23).

[Note: Cistercian: “in a Jewish controversy.”]

[Note: The same person, Emmor, son of Shechem. I do not object if you wish to say that “father” is a false reading; nevertheless, this could be an old error of the ancient Vulgate version, and it would have arisen easily. For the Greek author has παρὰ τῶν υἱῶν Ἑμμὸρ τοῦ Συχίμ, “from the sons of Emmor.”]

This passage is found very differently in Genesis. Abraham, namely, bought from Ephron the Hittite, son of Seor, near Hebron, for four hundred drachmas of silver, the double cave and the field around it, and buried Sarah his wife there. In the same book we read that Jacob later returned from Mesopotamia with his wives and sons, pitched his tent before Salem, a city of the Shechemites in the land of Canaan, lived there, and bought the portion of the field where he had pitched his tents from Emmor, the father of Shechem, for one hundred lambs. There he established an altar and invoked the God of Israel (ibid. 33).

Abraham did not buy the cave from Emmor, the father of Shechem, but from Ephron, son of Seor; nor was he buried at Shechem, but at Hebron, which is corruptly called Arboch. The twelve Patriarchs, however, were not buried at Arboch but at Shechem, whose field was not bought by Abraham but by Jacob (Josh. 24:32).

I postpone the solution of this little problem as well, so that my detractors may investigate and understand that in the Scriptures one must consider not the words but the meanings.

The beginning of the twenty-first Psalm according to the Hebrews is the very same utterance that the Lord spoke upon the cross:

> “ELI, ELI, LAMA AZABTHANI,”

which means:

> “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”

[Note: In Syriac, as it appears in Matthew 27:46 and Mark 15:34, the word is sebactani; and since Christ uttered it from the cross in the vernacular language of the Syrians, many Hieronymian manuscripts also read it here.]

Let them explain why the Septuagint translators inserted:

> “Look upon me” [or: “look in me”].

For they translated it:

> “God, my God, look upon me; why have you forsaken me?”

They will certainly answer that the meaning suffers no harm if two words have been added. Let them hear from me also that the condition of the Churches is not endangered if, through the speed of dictation, I have omitted some words.

## 11.

It would take too long now to review how much the Septuagint added from its own resources and how much it omitted—things marked in the Church copies by obelisks and asterisks. [Note: See above, Epistle XIII, chapter 2.]

For example, what we read in Isaiah—

> “Blessed is the one who has offspring in Zion and household members in Jerusalem” (Isa. 31 according to the Septuagint)

—the Hebrews habitually mock when they hear it. Likewise in Amos, after the description of luxury:

> “They considered these things standing and not fleeing” (Amos 6 according to the Septuagint).

Truly, this is rhetorical sense and Ciceronian declamation. But what are we to do with the authentic books, in which these words are not found written [Note: Many manuscripts read: “were not written”], along with many similar passages? If we attempted to produce them all, innumerable books would be required.

As for how much they omitted, either the witnesses of the asterisks, as I have said, testify to it, or our translation does, if a careful reader compares it with the old translation. Yet [Note: Martianay: he rebukes Victorius, who preferred *vires* (“forces”) to *jure* (“rightly”).] the Septuagint Edition rightly prevailed in the Churches, either because it was the first and was made before Christ’s coming, or because it was used by the Apostles, among whom it nevertheless does not differ from the Hebrew.

Aquila, however, a proselyte and contentious translator, who tried to transfer not only the words but also the etymologies of words, is rightly rejected by us. For who could either read or understand, in place of “grain, wine, and oil”:

> χεῦμα, ὀπωρισμόν, στιλπνότητα,

which we may render “a pouring, a fruiting, and a brilliance”?

[Note: This passage of Aquila, χεῦμα ὀπωρισμόν, which Jerome criticizes, is from Deuteronomy 7:13. The other example is from Genesis 1:1. The Greek words are especially corrupted in older editions: στιλβότητα occurs for στιλπνότητα, the word πρόαρθρα is omitted, and σείει is read for σύν. Aquila used this word for the Hebrew article. Martianay restored it after Gravius, and the reading is also supported by the authority of our manuscripts. Consult, if you wish, the annotation of the same Benedictine editor.]

Or because the Hebrews have not only ἄρθρα, “articles,” but also πρόαρθρα, “pre-articles,” Aquila perversely interprets syllables and even letters, saying:

> σὺν τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ σὺν τὴν γῆν,

“with the heaven and with the earth,”

something that Greek and Latin speech utterly rejects. We can take an example of this from our own language. How many things are well said among the Greeks which, if translated word for word, do not sound in Latin; and conversely, things that please us, if translated according to their order, will displease them.

## 12.

But, to pass over innumerable matters and to show you, most Christian of all noblemen and noblest of Christians, the kind of falsehood with which they reproach me in the translation of a letter, I shall set down the beginning of that letter together with the Greek wording, so that from one charge the rest may be understood:

> Ἓ δει ἡμᾶς ἀγαπητέ μὴ τῇ οἰήσει τῶν κλήρων φὲρεθαι

which I remember translating as follows:

> “We ought, dearest, not to abuse the honor of the clerical office into arrogance.”

“Look,” they say, “at how many lies there are in a single little sentence. First, ἀγαπητός means ‘beloved,’ not ‘most beloved.’ Next, οἴησις means ‘estimation,’ not ‘arrogance’; for he did not say οἰήματι [or οἰδήματι], but οἰήσει. The former signifies swelling, the latter judgment. And the whole expression that follows—‘not to abuse the honor of the clerical office into arrogance’—is your own.”

What do you say, O pillar of literature and Aristarchus of our age, who pass judgment on all writers?

> “Then we have studied in vain for so long,
> and have often withdrawn our hand from the rod.”
> (Juvenal, Sat. 1)

On leaving the harbor, we immediately struck something. Since it is human to err, and prudent to confess an error, whoever you are who criticize me, I beg you: correct me as a teacher and express the words word for word.

“You ought,” he says, “to have said: ‘We ought, beloved, not to be carried away by the estimation of the clergy.’”

This is Plautine eloquence; this is Attic charm, worthy, as they say, to be compared with the language of the Muses.

The common proverb is fulfilled in my case:

> “He loses his oil and his expense who sends an ox to the ceroma.”

[Note: Ceroma does not mean merely, as Martianay thinks, the ointment with which athletes were anointed; it also means the place itself in which they exercised. Thus the ancients used the word. Pliny, Book 35, chapter 2: “He adorns the palaestras of athletes with images and their ceromata.” Indeed, Jerome here indicates the place itself.]

This is not the fault of the man who performs a tragedy under another’s name, but of his teachers, Rufinus and Melania [Note: Two manuscript copies omit the names Rufinus and Melanius, as well as the following sentence concerning them.], who taught him, at great expense, to know nothing.

Nor do I criticize lack of eloquence in any Christian. Would that we possessed that Socratic saying:

> “I know that I do not know,”

and the saying of another wise man, believed to be Chilon:

> “Understand yourself.”

I have always revered not wordy rusticity but holy simplicity. Whoever says that he imitates the Apostle in speech should first imitate the virtues in the lives of those whose simplicity of speech was excused by the greatness of their holiness [Note: Older editions read: “In speaking, he will excuse simplicity, and presently refute it,” with a more rhetorical and forceful sense.]; and the syllogisms of Aristotle and the twisted subtleties of Chrysippus were refuted by a dead man rising again.

But it is ridiculous if one of us, living amid the wealth of Croesus and the pleasures of Sardanapalus, boasts only of rusticity—as though all robbers and those guilty of various crimes were eloquent, and hid their bloody swords beneath the volumes of philosophers rather than in the trunks of trees.

## 13.

I have exceeded the measure of the letter, but I have not exceeded the measure of my grief. For although I am called a forger and torn apart among the distaffs of little women and in weaving rooms, I am content to deny the charge, not to return it.

Therefore I leave everything to your judgment, so that you may read the letter itself, both Greek and Latin; and you will immediately understand the trifles and shameful complaints of my accusers. For me it is enough to have instructed my dearest friend and, hiding in my little cell, to await only the day of judgment.

I wish, if it can be done and if my adversaries permit it, to write for you commentaries on the Scriptures rather than the Philippics of Demosthenes and Cicero.

# LETTER LVIII

[Note: Also numbered 13. Written in the year 395, or thereabouts.]

## TO PAULINUS

[Note: In most manuscripts it is entitled “To Paulinus the Presbyter, on the Formation of Clerics”; in others there is added, “and of Monks, and on Various Expositions of Divine History.”]

Because of Christian humility, he declines Paulinus’s praises, returning praises for praises on account of his eloquence and upright character; he urges him to pursue the study of the divine Scriptures and sets before him a rule for living a holy and chaste life.

## 1.

> “The good man brings forth good things from the good treasure of his heart” (Matt. 12),  
> “and a tree is known by its fruits” (Luke 6:44).

You measure us by your own virtues and, though great yourself, exalt the small. You take the last place at the banquet so that you may be advanced by the judgment of the master of the house. For what, or how little, is there in us that we should deserve the praise of a learned voice? That we should be praised by the mouth by which the most religious Prince is defended?

[Note: He alludes to Paulinus’s panegyric in praise of the Emperor Theodosius after his victory over the tyrants, as Gennadius says in chapter 48. Jerome praises it greatly below in this same letter, but it has long since perished.]

Therefore, dearest brother, do not measure us by the number of our years, nor reckon wisdom by gray hairs; rather, reckon gray hairs by wisdom, as Solomon bears witness:

> “The gray hair of a human being is his understanding” (Wis. 4:8).

Moses, too, is commanded to choose seventy elders (Num. 11), whom he himself knew to be elders—certainly to be judged not by age but by wisdom. Daniel, though still a boy, judges the aged, and wanton age condemns the shameless elders.

Do not, I say, weigh faith by time; nor think me better because I began to serve in Christ’s army earlier. The Apostle Paul, the chosen vessel, transformed from persecutor, last in rank but first in merits, is last in sequence yet labored more than all.

Judas, who had once heard:

> “But you, a man who took sweet food with me, my leader and my acquaintance; we walked in the house of God with the assembly” (Ps. 54:14–15),

is condemned by the Savior’s voice as the betrayer of his friend and teacher:

> “And he ties the knot of shapeless death to a high beam.”
> (Aeneid, Book XII)

Conversely, the thief exchanges the cross for paradise and makes the punishment of murder into martyrdom.

How many people today, by living too long, carry their own funerals, and, like whitewashed tombs, are full of the bones of the dead?

[Note: Cyprian, On the Lapsed: “You have begun, while still walking, to carry your own funeral”; and in Optatus, Book 2: “They carry away the funerals of the dignity they have recovered.”]

Sudden heat overcomes prolonged lukewarmness.

## 2.

Finally, when you heard the Savior’s saying:

> “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you possess, give it to the poor, and come, follow me” (Matt. 19:21),

you turn words into deeds; and, naked, following the naked cross, you climb Jacob’s ladder more freely and lightly. You change your tunic together with your spirit, and, without a full purse, you seek glorious rags. With clean hands and a pure heart, you glory in being poor both in spirit and in deeds.

For it is no great thing, with a sad and sallow face, either to pretend to fast or to display one’s fasts; to abound in the revenues of possessions and boast of a shabby little cloak.

Crates of Thebes, once a very wealthy man, when he was going to Athens to study philosophy, threw away a great weight of gold; he did not think he could possess both virtues and riches at the same time.

We, stuffed with gold, follow poor Christ; and, under the pretext of almsgiving, clinging to our former wealth, how can we distribute another’s property faithfully when we guard our own anxiously? A full belly easily discusses fasting.

[Note: From Cicero, Pro Murena. A little later, the words “which are praised” are absent from several books.]

It is not being in Jerusalem that deserves praise, but having lived well in Jerusalem. The city to be sought and praised is not the one that killed the Prophets and shed Christ’s blood, but the city made glad by the river’s stream (Ps. 45:4; Luke 11), which, set upon a mountain, cannot be hidden; which the Apostle proclaims the mother of the saints; in which he rejoices to possess citizenship with the righteous.

[Note: Erasmus could not determine with certainty where Jerome had taken this sentence. Victorius points to the Epistle to the Hebrews and another to the Galatians, and Martianay follows him. It is now clear that it was taken from Philippians 3:20: “Our citizenship is in heaven,” where the Greek text has ἡμῶν γὰρ πολίτευμα, literally “our civic community.” Tertullian also quotes it in Against Marcion, Book 3, chapter 21, and On the Resurrection of the Flesh, chapter 47.]

## 3.

In saying this I do not accuse myself of inconsistency or condemn what I am doing, so that I may seem to have left my own people and country in vain as an example of Abraham. But I do not dare to confine the omnipotence of God within narrow limits or restrict to a small part of the earth the one whom heaven cannot contain.

Each believer is weighed not by differences of place but by the merit of faith. True worshipers worship the Father neither in Jerusalem nor on Mount Gerizim, because God is Spirit, and his worshipers must worship in spirit and truth.

> “The Spirit breathes where he wills. The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness” (John 3:8; Ps. 23:1).

After the fleece of Judea had been dried out and the whole world had been drenched with heavenly dew, and many came from east and west and reclined in Abraham’s bosom, God ceased to be known only in Judea and his great name only in Israel. The Apostles’ sound went forth into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world (Ps. 75; and 18).

The Savior, speaking to his disciples while he was in the temple, said:

> “Rise; let us go from here” (John 14:31),

and to the Jews:

> “Your house shall be left to you desolate” (Matt. 23:38).

[Note: In fact, the first statement was spoken to the disciples in the upper room, while the second was spoken to the Jews in the temple. Jerome nevertheless referred these two very different sayings of Christ to one time and place. Thus in his Commentary on Isaiah 1: “The Lord left his temple, and, rising in anger, said: ‘Rise, let us go from here,’ and ‘Your house shall be left to you desolate.’” Perhaps he drew this not, as we note in the margin, from John and Luke, but from Matthew’s Gospel according to the Hebrews, which he frequently mentions and cites. Certainly one must suppose a special copy that joined these statements and presented them as spoken in the same place.]

If heaven and earth will pass away, then certainly everything earthly will pass away. Therefore the places of the Cross and Resurrection benefit those who carry their cross and rise daily with Christ—those who show themselves worthy of so great a dwelling place.

But those who say, “The temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord” (Jer. 7), should hear the Apostle:

> “You are the temple of the Lord, and the Holy Spirit dwells in you” (2 Cor. 6:16).

The heavenly court is equally open from Jerusalem and from Britain:

> “For the kingdom of God is within you.”

Antony, and the swarms of monks throughout Egypt, Mesopotamia, Pontus, Cappadocia, and Armenia, did not see Jerusalem; yet the gate of paradise is open to them without this city.

Blessed Hilarion, although he was a Palestinian and lived in Palestine, saw Jerusalem only once, so that he would neither despise the holy places because of their proximity nor, on the other hand, seem to confine the Lord to a place.

From the time of Hadrian until the reign of Constantine, for approximately one hundred and eighty years, a statue of Jupiter stood at the place of the Resurrection; and on the rock of the Cross, a marble statue of Venus was worshiped by the pagans.

[Note: Compare Eusebius, Book 3 of The Life of Constantine; Socrates, Theodoret, and Sozomen in their histories; and George Hamartolus in his Chronicle. Hence Mount Calvary also seems to have been called “the Venus shrine” in a sermon of Ambrose on Psalm 47: “According to the course of heaven, the Lord suffered in the Venus shrine, which was on the northern side.”]

The instigators of the persecution believed that they would destroy our faith in the Resurrection and the Cross if they polluted the holy places with idols.

A grove of Thamuz, that is, Adonis, overshadowed our Bethlehem, now the most august place in the world, of which the Psalmist sings:

> “Truth has arisen from the earth” (Ps. 84:12).

[Note: The present tense “overshadows” is incorrect; the name is Thamus, elsewhere printed Thamnus, more accurately Thamuz, from the Hebrew and Greek θάμμουζ. A king of Egypt by this name is mentioned by Plato in the Phaedrus and by Philostratus 6.5. The Vulgate renders this word in Ezekiel 8:14 as “Adonis,” and Jerome comments there: “The one whom we have translated as Adonis is called Thamuz in Hebrew and Syriac.” The story of this lover of Venus is very widely known.]

And in the cave where Christ once wailed as an infant, the lover of Venus was mourned.

## 4.

“But why,” you will say, “have these matters been repeated at such length at the beginning?”

Clearly, so that you may not think anything lacking in your faith because you have not seen Jerusalem, nor consider us better because we enjoy dwelling in this place. Rather, whether here or elsewhere, you should receive equal reward from our Lord according to your works.

To speak frankly of the movement of my mind: when I consider both your purpose and the ardor with which you renounced the world, I think there is a distinction between places if, after abandoning cities and the crowds of cities, you live in a little field, seek Christ in solitude, pray alone on the mountain with Jesus, and enjoy only the proximity of holy places—that is, if you are free of the city without abandoning the purpose of a monk.

What I am saying concerns neither bishops, priests, nor clerics, whose office is different, but a monk—and a monk formerly noble in the world—who therefore laid the price of his possessions at the Apostles’ feet, teaching that money must be trampled underfoot, so that, living humbly and quietly, he may always despise what he once despised.

If the places of the Cross and Resurrection were not in this most famous city, in which there are a senate-house, a soldiers’ court [Note: I nearly read “a wing of soldiers”; but since no manuscript supports it, it would be irreverent to alter anything by conjecture.], prostitutes, actors, buffoons, and everything found in other cities; or if it were frequented only by crowds of monks, then such a dwelling would truly be desirable for all monks.

But now it is the height of folly to renounce the world, abandon one’s country, leave the cities, profess oneself a monk, and live among vast populations in exactly the same way as one would have lived in one’s homeland.

[Note: The Cistercian manuscript, as also the Erasmian copies and other older editions, reads: “to proceed among vast populations, to live better than you would have lived in your homeland,” and so forth. Victorius changed this to the better sense: “to live more dangerously among vast populations than you would have lived.” Martianay reads “to live abroad,” claiming to have drawn the reading from all the manuscripts; but the defective and alien sense shows that it is corrupt and contrary to Jerome’s meaning. From “abroad” we have conjecturally formed “equally,” that is, “in the same way,” using a single word, rare but Latin, to clarify and complete the sense. Cicero, in Brutus: “There are altogether three kinds of speaking, in each of which certain men have flourished; but very few have flourished equally in all.”]

People come here from the entire world. The city is full of every kind of human being, and the crowding of both sexes is so great that what you formerly fled in part elsewhere, here you are compelled to endure in its entirety.

## 5.

Since you ask fraternally by what path you should proceed, I shall speak to you openly. If you wish to exercise the office of a presbyter, if the work or honor of the episcopate perhaps attracts you, live in cities and fortresses; make the salvation of others the gain of your own soul.

[Note: He aptly speaks of the office of a presbyter. For when Paulinus had already been unwillingly ordained to the presbyterate, he nevertheless allowed himself to be consecrated on the condition that he would not be required to exercise the office of presbyter anywhere, but would devote himself to the service of whichever church he wished; or, as he says of himself in Epistle 1, he was dedicated only to the priesthood of the Lord, not also to a place in a church. Jerome himself underwent an ordination of much the same kind.]

But if you wish to be what you are called—a monk, that is, a solitary—what are you doing in cities, which are certainly not dwellings for the solitary but for the many? Every way of life has its own leaders.

Let Roman commanders imitate Camillus, Fabricius, Regulus, and Scipio. Let philosophers set before themselves Pythagoras, Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle. Let poets emulate Homer, Virgil, Menander, and Terence. Let historians emulate Thucydides, Sallust, Herodotus, and Livy. Let orators emulate Lysias, the Gracchi, Demosthenes, and Cicero.

And, to come to our own concerns, let bishops and presbyters have the Apostles and apostolic men as examples; possessing their honor, let them strive also to possess their merit.

But let us have as the leaders of our way of life Pauls and Antonys, Julians, Hilarions, and Macarii.

[Note: Namely, the Julian who, together with his wife Basilissa, preserved his flesh as a virgin for Christ by a most holy vow, so that he became the father of ten thousand monks, as recorded in his Passion.]

And, to return to the authority of Scripture, our leader is Elijah, our leader is Elisha; our commanders are the sons of the Prophets, who lived in fields and solitudes and made themselves huts beside the streams of the Jordan.

Among these are also the sons of Rechab, who did not drink wine or strong drink, who lived in tents, whom the voice of God through Jeremiah praises (chapter 35), and to whom it is promised that a man from their line will never cease to stand before the Lord.

I think this is also signified by the title of the seventieth Psalm:

> “Of the sons of Jonadab and of those who were first led into captivity.”

[Note: The Hebrew text does not have this title, but the edition of the Septuagint does.]

This is Jonadab, son of Rechab, who in the Book of Kings is said to have mounted the chariot with Jehu. His sons are those who, always living in tents, were finally compelled to enter Jerusalem because of the invasion of the Chaldean army, and are said to have endured the first captivity. After the freedom of solitude, they were shut up in the city as though in a prison.

## 6.

I beg you, then, since you are bound by the bond of your holy sister, your wife Therasia, and proceed with a step not entirely free, whether here or there, to flee crowds of people, official duties, greetings, and banquets as though they were chains of pleasure.

Let your food be cheap and eaten in the evening: vegetables and legumes; and sometimes count little fish among your greatest delicacies. Whoever desires Christ and feeds on that bread does not greatly concern himself with how precious the food may be from which he makes dung. Whatever is not perceived after the belly has eaten it, let that be the same for you as bread and vegetables.

You have my books Against Jovinianus, which discuss more fully contempt for the belly and the throat.

Let sacred reading always be in your hand. Pray frequently, and, with the body bent, raise the mind to the Lord. Keep frequent vigils, and sleep more often with an empty stomach.

Flee rumors, little boasts, and flatterers who pat you on the back as though they were enemies. Distribute refreshments to the poor and to the brothers from your own hand and at your own expense.

Faithfulness is rare among human beings. Do you not believe what I say? Think of Judas’s money-box.

Do not seek humility of dress with a puffed-up spirit. Avoid the society of worldly people, especially the powerful. Why do you need to see frequently those whom you began to be a monk by despising?

Your sister above all should avoid the conversations [or company] of married women; and, among women surrounded by silk garments and jewels, she should neither defile herself nor grieve nor marvel.

[Note: The first is repentance for one’s way of life; the second is a seedbed of boastfulness.]

Beware lest, as the formerly trusted and famous steward of your family, you accept another’s money to distribute. You understand what I am saying; for the Lord has given you understanding in all things.

Have the simplicity of a dove, so that you plot no deceit against anyone; and the cleverness of a serpent, so that you are not overthrown by the snares of others.

It is not very different in guilt whether a Christian is able to deceive or is deceived.

If you find someone speaking to you always, or frequently, about money, except in the case of almsgiving, which is open equally to all, regard him as a shopkeeper rather than as a monk.

Apart from food, clothing, and obvious necessities, give nothing to anyone, lest dogs eat the bread of the children.

7. But the true temple of Christ is the soul of the believer: adorn it, clothe it, offer gifts to it, receive Christ within it. **What use is it for walls to glitter with jewels while Christ is endangered by hunger in the poor?** [Note: “More gravely: *now they are not*, restored from an old manuscript.”] What you possess is no longer yours; it is an administration entrusted to you. Remember Ananias and Sapphira. They timidly kept what was theirs; you must take care lest you thoughtlessly squander Christ’s substance—that is, lest by immoderate judgment you give the property of the poor to those who are not poor—and, according to the saying of the wisest man, lest generosity perish through generosity (Cicero, *On Duties* 2).

Do not

> Look to the trappings and empty names of Catos.  
> (Persius, *Satires* 3)

> I know you within and on the skin.  
> (Lucan, *Pharsalia* 10)

It is a great thing to **be** a Christian, not merely to appear one. And somehow those who displease Christ please the world more. I say this not as they say, “the pig teaching Minerva,” but as a friend warning a friend who is entering the sea: I preferred that you should ask for my judgment rather than my favor, so that where I had gone astray, you might proceed with a firm step.

### 8. Paulinus’s Book on Behalf of Theodosius

I gladly read your book, which you sent me, composed prudently and elegantly on behalf of the emperor Theodosius; and I especially liked its division into sections. Although you surpass others in the opening parts, in the penultimate ones you surpass yourself. Its style is also compressed and polished; while it shines with Ciceronian purity, it is rich in sententiae. For, as someone says, an oration in which only the words are praised lies inert. [Note: Quintilian, *Institutio oratoria* 8, preface near the end: “I do not understand an oration to be inert in which the words are praised.”]

Moreover, there is a great coherence among its subjects, and one point depends upon another. Whatever you take up is either the conclusion of what precedes or the beginning of what follows. Happy Theodosius, who is defended by such an orator of Christ! You have illuminated his purple robes and consecrated the usefulness of his laws to future ages. Well done in virtue: if these are your beginnings, what kind of seasoned soldier will you be?

Oh, if only I were permitted to lead such talent not through the Aonian mountains and the peaks of Helicon, as the poets sing, but through Zion, Itabyrium [Thabor], and lofty Sinai! If I could teach what I have learned and, as though hand to hand, transmit the mysteries of the Prophets [or: the Scriptures], something might arise among us that learned Greece did not possess.

### 9.

Listen, then, my fellow servant, friend, brother; listen for a little while, so that you may learn by what path you should walk through the holy Scriptures. Everything that we read in the divine Books shines and glitters even on the surface, but it is sweeter in the marrow. Whoever wishes to eat the kernel must break the nut (from Plautus).

> “Open my eyes,” David says, “and I shall contemplate the wonders of your law” (Psalm 118:18).

If so great a Prophet confesses the darkness of ignorance, how do you suppose that we, little ones and almost infants, are surrounded by the night of ignorance? This veil has been placed not only over the face of Moses, but also over the Evangelists and Apostles. The Savior spoke to the crowds in parables, and, declaring that what was said was mystical, he added:

> “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Luke 8:8).

Unless all that was written is opened by him who holds the key of David—who opens and no one shuts, and shuts and no one opens—it will not be disclosed by anyone else. If you possessed this foundation—or rather, if the finishing touch were, so to speak, applied to your work—nothing more beautiful, learned, sweet, or truly Latin than your volumes would exist for us. [Note: Some manuscripts read, “would be applied to your work.” Shortly afterward, between the two readings, “nothing more learned, nothing sweeter,” one seems to have been substituted for the other, with the latter reading perhaps being an expansion.]

### 10.

Tertullian is rich in sententiae but difficult in expression. Blessed Cyprian proceeds like a most pure spring, sweet and tranquil; and although he is wholly occupied with exhorting to virtue, being pressed by the hardships of persecution, he did not discourse at all on the divine Scriptures. The renowned Victorinus, crowned by martyrdom, cannot express what he understands. Lactantius is like a river of Ciceronian eloquence—if only he had been able to assert our truths as easily as he demolished those of others. Arnobius is uneven and excessive, confused by the lack of divisions in his work. Saint Hilary is raised upon a Gallic cothurnus; and although adorned with the flowers of Greece, he is sometimes entangled in long periods and is far removed from the reading level of simpler brothers. I say nothing of the others, whether dead or still living; concerning them others after us will judge in both directions.

### 11.

Let me come to you yourself, my fellow initiate, my companion and friend—my friend, I say, before you were known—and let me ask you not to suspect flattery in our relationship. Rather, consider me either mistaken or led astray by affection than suppose that I would deceive a friend through praise.

You have great talent and an infinite store of language; you speak easily and purely, and that ease and purity are joined with prudence. For when the head is sound, all the faculties are vigorous. If to this prudence and eloquence there were added either diligence or understanding of the Scriptures, I would soon see you holding the citadel of our people and, ascending with Joab to the roof of Zion (1 Chronicles 11), singing on the housetops what you had learned in your chambers. [Note: After Erasmus, Victorius and other editors incorrectly print *curam Jacob* after *ascendentem*. The allusion is to 1 Chronicles 11:6: “Then Joab son of Zeruiah went up first,” and so forth.]

Gird yourself, I beg you—gird yourself. “Life has granted mortals nothing without great labor” (Horace, *Satires* 1.9). Let the Church possess you as a nobleman, just as the Senate once did. Prepare for yourself riches that you may distribute each day; let them never fail while your age remains vigorous, while your head has not yet been sprinkled with gray hair—before “diseases, and gloomy old age, and toil, and the harsh cruelty of death” overtake you. [Note: The Benedictine edition altered the text to the opposite meaning: “while gray hair is still being scattered over your head,” as several manuscripts in fact read. But in those manuscripts the error arose because older copies read *adhuc non* (“not yet”) differently, and the final negative particle easily dropped out through the carelessness of later copyists; one inept corrector also changed *viget* (“is vigorous”) to *urget* (“presses”). In any event, either *nondum* or its equivalent *adhuc non* is plainly required by the whole context and by the age of Saint Paulinus himself, who had scarcely reached forty-three, an age to which gray hair cannot be attributed.]

I am not content that there be anything mediocre in you: I desire everything supreme, everything perfect.

[Note: This Vigilantius seems to have been different from the man against whom Jerome wrote, according to Gravius and other learned men, who do not think he could have been called a saint. At that time, however, he had not yet broken out into heresy; and when he was traveling from Aquitania—the region from which Saint Paulinus also came—to Palestine out of devotion, he was commended to Jerome by Paulinus’s letters. Jerome himself testifies to this in his letter to Riparius and in another letter here numbered 61, addressed to the same Vigilantius, especially in these words: “I trusted the letters of the holy Presbyter Paulinus, and, because of his judgment concerning you, I did not think that he was mistaken.”]

It is better for you to learn from his own words than from mine with what eagerness I welcomed the holy Presbyter Vigilantius. I cannot say why he departed from us and left us so quickly, lest I seem to injure anyone. Yet, as he passed by and hurried on, I detained him briefly and gave him a taste of our friendship, so that through him you may learn what you should desire in us. I wish, through you, to greet your holy fellow servant, who serves alongside you in the Lord.

# LETTER LIX

[Note: Also numbered 148. Written in the year 395 or the following year.]

## To Marcella

### On Certain Questions of the New Testament

He answers the five questions that Marcella posed to him, one by one.

### 1.

You challenge us with weighty questions; and while you question me, my intellect, grown sluggish through idleness, is instructed. Your first inquiry was about those things “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor entered into the heart of man, which God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Corinthians 2:9), and how the same Apostle could then add, “But God has revealed them to us through his Spirit” (ibid., verse 10). If they were revealed to the Apostle, we ought to understand how he revealed them to others.

The brief answer is that we should not ask what that thing is which eye has not seen, ear has not heard, or heart has not conceived. For if it is unknown, how can it be known? What is promised for the future is not perceived in the present.

> “For hope that is seen is not hope” (Romans 8:24),

but already a certain possession. It would be like someone saying: “Show me what is invisible; speak what cannot be heard; explain what human thought cannot comprehend.”

Therefore, the Apostle must be understood to have spoken in this sense: spiritual things cannot be comprehended by bodily eyes, a bodily ear, or mortal thought.

> “Even if we once knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him in that way” (2 Corinthians 5:16).

And in John’s Epistle it is written:

> “Beloved, now we are children of God, and it has not yet been revealed what we shall be. We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2).

The fact that he testifies that it was revealed to him and to the saints through the Spirit does not immediately imply that he himself revealed it to others. Otherwise, in Paradise he heard unspeakable words that he could not recount to others (2 Corinthians 12); or, if he did recount them, they would not be unspeakable.

### 2.

Your second question concerned your saying that you had read in passing in my little works that the sheep standing on the right and the goats standing on the left (Matthew 25) are Christians and gentiles, rather than good and wicked people. I do not remember ever saying this; and if I had said it, I would not persist obstinately in error.

As far as I can recall from what came to mind while dictating, I know that I discussed this passage in the second book against Jovinianus—not only this passage, but also the related question of the separation of bad fish from good fish (Matthew 13). What was fully said there therefore seems best omitted here.

### 3.

Third, you asked about what the Apostle says concerning the coming of the Lord and Savior: that some who are alive will be caught up in the clouds to meet him, so that they will not be preceded by those who have fallen asleep in Christ (1 Thessalonians 4). You wish to know whether they will meet him in their bodies and therefore not die beforehand, since our Lord also died, and Enoch and Elijah are said, according to John’s Apocalypse, to be destined to die (Revelation 11)—so that no one, apparently, would fail to taste death (Psalm 88).

This can be known from the content of the passage itself: the saints who are found in the body at the Savior’s coming will meet him in those same bodies, yet in such a way that what is dishonored, corruptible, and mortal will be changed into glory, incorruption, and immortality (1 Corinthians 15), so that the bodies of the living may likewise be transformed into such a condition as the bodies of the dead will have when they rise.

Hence the Apostle says elsewhere:

> “For this reason we do not wish to be unclothed but clothed over, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life” (1 Corinthians 5:4),

so that the body may not be deserted by the soul; rather, while the soul dwells in the body, what was formerly inglorious may become glorious.

As for Enoch and Elijah, whom the Apocalypse reports as coming and as destined to die (Revelation 11), that is not a question for the present time, since the whole book must either be understood spiritually, as we believe, or, if we follow a literal interpretation, we must accept Jewish fables: that Jerusalem will be rebuilt and sacrifices offered in the Temple, and that, with spiritual worship diminished, bodily ceremonies will prevail.

### 4.

The fourth question you asked was how, in John’s Gospel, after the resurrection, Mary Magdalene is told:

> “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father” (John 20:17),

while Matthew records that the women fell at the Savior’s feet (Matthew 28). Obviously, touching his feet after the resurrection and not touching them are not the same thing.

Mary Magdalene was the woman from whom he had cast out seven demons (Mark 16), so that where sin had abounded, grace might abound all the more (Romans 5). Because she thought the Lord was the gardener, spoke with him as with a human being, and sought the living among the dead, she rightly heard:

> “Do not touch me” (John 20:17).

The sense is: “You do not deserve to cling to my footsteps, or to worship me as Lord, or to hold the feet of one whom you do not believe to have risen. For I have not yet ascended to my Father for you.”

The other women, however, who touch his feet confess him as Lord and deserve to cling to the footsteps of him whom they trust to have ascended to the Father.

Even if the same woman is reported in different Gospels both to have held his feet and not to have held them, the solution is easy: she could first have been corrected as an unbeliever and afterward not rejected, as one who had changed her error through confession. The same may be understood concerning the thieves, since one Evangelist reports that both blasphemed, while another says that one confessed (Matthew 27; Mark 15).

### 5.

The final note asked whether, after the resurrection, the Lord remained with his disciples for forty days (Luke 24), and was nowhere else; or whether he secretly ascended to heaven and descended again, while nevertheless not denying the Apostles his presence.

If you consider that he is the Son of God about whom we are speaking, and that he is the one who says:

> “Do I not fill heaven and earth? says the Lord” (Jeremiah 23:24),

and of whom another Prophet testifies:

> “Heaven is my throne, and the earth is the footstool of my feet” (Isaiah 66:1),

and again elsewhere:

> “He holds heaven in his palm and the earth in his fist” (ibid. 40:12),

of whom David sings:

> “Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your presence? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into the underworld, you are present. And if I dwell at the ends of the sea, even there your hand will lead me, and your right hand will hold me” (Psalm 138:7 and following),

you will certainly not doubt that, even before the resurrection, God the Word dwelt in the Lord’s body in such a way that he was both in the Father and enclosed the circuit of heaven, and was infused and diffused through all things [or: all people]—that is, that he penetrated all things within and contained all things without. [Note: Two manuscripts read “penetrated, entered, and contained.”]

It is foolish, therefore, to restrict the power of him whom heaven cannot contain to the smallness of a single body. Yet he who was everywhere was also wholly present in the Son of Man. For the divine nature and the word of God cannot be divided into parts or separated by places; but, since he is everywhere, he is wholly everywhere.

Thus at one and the same time he was with the Apostles for forty days, with the angels, in the Father, and at the ends of the sea; he was present in every place: with Thomas in India, with Peter in Rome, with Paul in Illyricum, with Titus in Crete, with Andrew in Achaea, and with each Apostle and apostolic man in each and every region.

When it is said that he abandons or does not abandon certain people, this does not establish a limit to his nature; rather, it describes the merits of those among whom he deigns—or, according to another reading, disdains—to be present.

# LETTER LX

[Note: Also numbered 3. Written at the beginning of the year 396.]

## To Heliodorus

### Epitaph for Nepotianus

He consoles Heliodorus, Bishop of Altinum and Nepotianus’s uncle, over the death of the Presbyter Nepotianus. He shows that death should not be feared, since Christ has conquered it; then, after presenting many examples from the ancient pagans, he explains Nepotianus’s praises and finally urges contempt for life in view of the calamities of those times.

### 1.

Small talents cannot sustain great subjects [or: endure them]; and when they dare beyond their strength in the very attempt, they collapse. The greater the matter that must be said, the more completely the person who cannot express its magnitude in words is overwhelmed.

My Nepotianus—yours, ours, or rather Christ’s, and because Christ’s all the more ours—has left old men wounded by the dart of longing and exhausted by unbearable grief [alternative reading: “has exhausted”]. We thought we were to have him as heir; we now hold his funeral. For whom will my talent now sweat? For whom will my little letters eagerly strive to please? Where is our *ergodiōktēs* [Greek: ἐργοδιώκτης, “pursuer or promoter of work,” perhaps “taskmaster”], whose voice was sweeter than the song of a swan? [Note: Most printed editions have *ergodiōktēs*, that is, “shopkeeper” or “promoter of work”; but manuscripts, which often corrupt Greek words in reading, here retain *epōdiōtēs* or *epōdiōtēs*, and one older manuscript, according to Victorius, has *epōdos*, meaning “enchanter” or “one who attracts minds by songs.” One of these readings would seem preferable if it rested either on sufficiently correct writing or on the authority of several copies, in view of what follows, “and a voice sweeter than a swan’s song.” We do not approve the printed reading, but leave it nearly unchanged so as not to indulge our conjectures excessively. On examining the traces of the letters in the Verona manuscript more carefully, however, it occurred to us that this desperate passage could be restored quite well. It is written there as ΟΚΟΚΖΗΚΝΣ; if the letters are slightly corrected and their strokes returned to the form of the proper spelling, ΟΚΟΚΠΙΖΗΚ, an elegant meaning and, as we think, a very true reading immediately emerge. It is *osoasizēs* [Greek: ὀσοασίζης], the chaffinch, or more precisely the brambling, Italian *fringuello*, a well-known bird named from the sound it makes in song. Aristotle discusses it in *History of Animals* 8.3, and Martial in *Epigrams* 6.55:

> “Now he hears the needy starlings and the complaints of chaffinches,”

and so forth. Jerome has compared Nepotianus very elegantly to that bird, or called him an *osoasizēs*, perhaps because, while alive, he often whispered to Jerome, asking him for some task; yet Jerome says that his voice was sweeter to him than a swan’s song. Certainly, the final words prove that he intended to designate a bird.]

My mind is stunned, my hand trembles, my eyes grow dim, my tongue stammers. Whatever I say seems mute because he does not hear it. The stylus itself, as though sharing my feeling [or: resisting me], and the wax, somewhat darkened either by rust or by neglect, are covered over. Whenever I strive to burst into words and scatter the flowers of this epitaph over his tomb, my eyes are filled with tears, and, as grief is renewed, I am wholly at the funeral.

Once it was customary for children to pronounce before the public assembly the praises of the deceased over their bodies, and, like mournful songs, to stir the hearts of the listeners to tears and groans. Behold, the order of things among us has been changed, and nature has lost its rights through our misfortune. What a young man ought to offer to the old, we old men offer to a young man. [Note: Victorius reads “over the corpses of deceased parents,” a reading supported by what follows, “the children would speak praises.” But our copies do not contain the word *parents*, nor does Victorius indicate where he took it.]

### 2.

What, then, shall I do? Shall I join my tears to yours? But the Apostle forbids this, calling the dead of Christians “those who sleep” (1 Thessalonians 4). And the Lord says in the Gospel:

> “The girl is not dead, but sleeping” (Mark 5:39 and Luke 8:52).

Lazarus too was raised because he had slept (John 11).

Shall I rejoice and be glad because “he was taken away, lest wickedness should change his understanding,” and because “his soul was pleasing to God” (Wisdom 4)? Yet against my will and resistance, tears flow down my cheeks; and amid the commands of virtue and the hope of resurrection, the emotion of longing breaks my trusting mind.

O death, which divides brothers and cruelly and harshly separates those joined by love! The Lord brought a scorching wind ascending from the desert; it dried up your veins and laid waste your spring (Hosea 13:15). You devoured Jonah, but he was alive in your belly. You carried him as though dead, so that the storm of the world might be stilled and our Nineveh might be saved by his preaching.

He—he conquered you; he slaughtered you: the fugitive Prophet who left his home, abandoned his inheritance, and placed his beloved life in the hands of those who sought him [or: her]. Through Hosea he once threatened you sternly:

> “I shall be your death, O death; I shall be your sting, O underworld” (Hosea 13:14).

By his death, you died; by his death, we live. You devoured, and you were devoured. While you were enticed by the bait of the assumed body and thought the prey yours with greedy jaws, your innermost parts were pierced by the hooked tooth.

### 3.

We give you thanks, Christ our Savior, we your creatures, because by killing our powerful adversary you killed him. [Note: This is the reading of the Verona copy; previously either the little word *te* was absent or the text read something much worse.]

Who was more miserable than man before you? Struck down by the terror of eternal death, he had received the sense of living for this one purpose: to perish.

> “Death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who had not sinned in the likeness of Adam’s transgression” (Romans 5:14).

If Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob were in the underworld, who could be in the kingdom of heaven? If your friends were under punishment because of Adam’s offense, and those who had not sinned were held liable for the sins of others, what must be believed about those who said in their hearts, “There is no God”? Those who “were corrupt and became abominable in their desires,” who “turned aside and together became worthless; there is no one who does good, not even one” (Psalm 13:1)?

If Lazarus appears to be in Abraham’s bosom and in a place of refreshment, what likeness is there between the underworld and the kingdoms of heaven?

**Before Christ, Abraham was among the dead; after Christ, the thief was in Paradise.**

Therefore, at his resurrection, many bodies of the sleeping rose and appeared in the heavenly Jerusalem. [Note: The ancients did not hold one uniform opinion on this matter. Some attributed an eternal resurrection to those who rose with Christ, others a temporary one. According to the former, the bodies of the saints appeared in the heavenly Jerusalem; according to the latter, in the earthly Jerusalem. The former view, toward which Jerome leans here, is supported by Origen on Matthew 27, Eusebius in *Demonstration of the Gospel* 4, Saint Hilary in his *Treatise on Psalm 2*, Rufinus in his exposition of the Creed, and others. Most others defend the second view, among them Augustine, *Letter 99 to Evodius*, Chrysostom on the Epistle to the Hebrews, and Theodoret in the same place. Especially relevant is Paula and Eustochium’s letter to Marcella, Letter 46.7, where they say: “Nor is the heavenly Jerusalem immediately understood in this passage, as most absurdly suppose, since there could have been no sign among human beings of the Lord’s resurrection if the bodies of the saints had been seen in the heavenly Jerusalem.”]

Then that saying was fulfilled:

> “Rise, you who sleep, and arise, and Christ will illuminate you” (Ephesians 5:14).

John the Baptist cries out in the wilderness:

> “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near. From the days of John the Baptist the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matthew 3:2; 11:12).

That flaming sword, the guardian of Paradise, and the cherubim presiding at its gates have been extinguished and unlocked by Christ’s blood.

Nor should it surprise us that this is promised to us in the resurrection, since all who live in the flesh but not according to the flesh possess citizenship in heaven; and, while we are still placed here on earth, it is said:

> “The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke 17:21).

### 4.

Add that before Christ’s resurrection,

> “God was known only in Judah; his name was great in Israel” (Psalm 75).

Yet even those who knew him were dragged down to the underworld. Where then were the people of the whole world, from India to Britain, from the frozen region of the north to the heat of the Atlantic Ocean—so many innumerable peoples and multitudes of nations?

> “How varied in tongues, in dress, and in weapons,”  
> (Virgil, *Aeneid* 8)

they were. In the manner of fish and locusts, and like flies and gnats, they were crushed; for without knowledge of their Creator, every human being is cattle.

Now, however, the passion of Christ and his resurrection resound in the voices and letters of all nations. I say nothing of the Hebrews, Greeks, and Latins, nations which the Lord dedicated to his faith in the title of the Cross. The immortal soul, surviving after the dissolution of the body—which Pythagoras dreamed of, Democritus did not believe, and Socrates discussed in prison as a consolation for his condemnation—is now philosophized about by the Indian, Persian, Goth, and Egyptian.

The savagery of the Bessi and the crowd of fur-clad peoples, who once sacrificed human beings at the funeral rites of the dead, have broken their shrill cries into the sweet melody of the Cross, and the whole world has one voice: Christ. [Note: On the Bessi, see Strabo, Book 7, who notes that they occupied most of Mount Haemus, were called robbers because of their banditry, and lived a hard and rugged life. See also Herodotus, Solinus, Ovid, Pliny, and many others. By “fur-clad” he means especially peoples descended from the Getae or Dacians, who covered themselves with animal skins. Saint Paulinus praises the conversion of both groups most elegantly in Poem 17:

> “And the Bessi, harder than their own snow,  
> have now become sheep.”

A little later:

> “And the Getae run, and both Dacians,  
> one who dwells in the middle of the land,  
> and the other, wearing the cap of the wealthy ox,  
> who inhabits the bank.”]

### 5.

What shall we do, O soul? Where shall we turn? What shall we take up first? What shall we leave unsaid? Have the precepts of the rhetoricians slipped from your memory? Overcome by grief, oppressed by tears, impeded by sobs, do you no longer preserve the order of speech?

Where is that devotion to letters cultivated from childhood, and the ever-praised saying of Anaxagoras and Telamon:

> “I knew that I had begotten a mortal”?

We have read Crantor, whose book Cicero followed in soothing his own grief (*On Consolation*, now lost). We have gone through the little works of Plato, Diogenes, Clitomachus, Carneades, and Posidonius for calming mourning; at different times they attempted to lessen the grief of different people through books or letters, so that even if our own talent were parched, it might be watered from their springs. [Note: See Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* 3, from which Jerome drew nearly all these examples of illustrious men. Some also appear in Valerius Maximus, especially Book 5, and in Aelian, Book 3, chapter 2.]

They bring forward countless men, especially Pericles and the Socratic Xenophon. One of them, after losing two sons, spoke in the assembly while wearing a crown; the other, when he heard during a sacrifice that his son had been killed in battle, is said to have removed the crown from his head and replaced it after learning that his son had fallen while fighting bravely in the line. [Note: Two words have been supplied from manuscripts and Victorius’s edition. See Aelian, Book 3, chapter 3, concerning Xenophon.]

Why should I mention the Roman commanders, whose virtues make Latin history glitter like so many stars? Pulvillus, while dedicating the Capitol, ordered that his son, reported dead, be buried immediately in his absence. Lucius Paulus entered the city in triumph after spending seven days among the funerals of his two sons.

I pass over the Maximi, Catos [Note: Some copies read *Caios* instead of *Gallos*, which I do not reject, since Gaius was Gallus’s praenomen. For *Marios*, however, Victorius reports that some prefer *Martios*, implying Quintus Marcius Rex, who, after losing in his consulship his only son, a young man of great promise, bore his death with such equanimity that he immediately summoned the Senate from the funeral pyre to the curia, as Valerius Maximus relates.], Galli, Pisones, Bruti, Scaevolas, Metelli, Scauri, Marios, Crassi, Marcelli, and Aufidii, whose courage in mourning was no less than in war, and whose bereavements Tully explained in his *Book of Consolation*, lest I seem to have sought examples from others rather than from our own people. [Note: Cicero’s separate book *On Consolation*, which he composed after the death of his daughter, has been lost; he attests to it in the fifth book of the *Tusculan Disputations*.]

Although these things have also been said briefly to rebuke our grief, if faith does not surpass what unbelief has displayed.

### 6.

Let us therefore come to our own examples. I shall not mourn with Jacob and David for sons dying under the Law; rather, with Christ I shall receive them rising in the Gospel.

**The mourning of the Jews is the joy of Christians.**

> “In the evening grief will linger, but in the morning there will be joy” (Psalm 29:6).  
> “The night has passed, and the day has drawn near” (Romans 13:12).

Thus Moses is mourned when he dies (Deuteronomy 34), while Jesus is buried on the mountain without funeral or tears. Whatever can be said from Scripture concerning lamentation, we explained briefly in the book in which we consoled Paula at Rome. Now we must reach the same place by another path, lest we seem to tread upon traces once passed over and erased.

### 7.

We know indeed that our Nepotianus is with Christ, mingled with the choirs of the saints, and that what here on earth he examined from afar with us and sought by conjecture, he now sees face to face and says:

> “As we have heard, so also we have seen, in the city of the Lord of hosts, in the city of our God” (Psalm 47:9).

Yet we cannot bear the longing caused by his absence, grieving not for his sake but for our own. The happier he is, the greater our sorrow, because we lack so great a good.

The sisters also wept for Lazarus (John 11), although they knew he would rise again. And, to express the genuine emotion of a human being, the Savior himself wept for the one he was about to resurrect (ibid.).

The Apostle too, who said,

> “I desire to depart and to be with Christ” (Philippians 1:23),

and elsewhere,

> “For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (ibid., verse 21),

gives thanks that Epaphras [or: Epaphroditus] was restored to him from the brink of death, so that he would not have sorrow upon sorrow (Philippians 2)—not because of fear born of unbelief, but because of the longing of love.

How much more do you, both uncle and Bishop—that is, father both in the flesh and in the spirit—grieve at the absence of your own heart and sigh as though your entrails had been torn from you? But I beg you to impose a limit upon your grief, remembering the saying, “Nothing in excess.” Bind the wound for a little while, and listen to the praises of one whose virtue always brought you joy. Do not grieve that you lost such a man; rejoice that you possessed such a man.

And just as those who paint the locations of lands on a small tablet provide a sketch rather than a full representation, so in this little volume see the outlines, not the complete forms, of his virtues; and accept from us not power, but goodwill.

### 8. The Precepts of the Rhetoricians

These are the precepts of the rhetoricians: the ancestors of the person being praised, and their deeds, should be traced back from the beginning, and the discourse should reach the person himself by degrees. Thus he becomes more illustrious through his ancestral and paternal virtues, and he appears either not to have degenerated from good forebears or to have adorned even mediocre ones himself.

I shall not seek the good qualities of the flesh—which he himself always despised—in the praises of the soul. Nor will I boast of lineage, that is, of the good qualities of others [alternative reading: “foreign-born persons,” a reading also preferred by Gravius], since Abraham and Isaac, holy men, fathered Ishmael and Esau, who were sinners (Genesis 16 and 25). Conversely, Jephthah, who is counted by the Apostle among the catalogue of the righteous, was born of a prostitute (Hebrews 11; Judges 11).

> “The soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezekiel 18:4);

therefore the soul that has not sinned shall itself live. Neither the virtues nor the vices of parents are charged to their children. We are reckoned from the time when we are reborn in Christ.

Paul, the persecutor of the Church, who in the morning was a ravening wolf, Benjamin (Genesis 49), “in the evening gave food,” submitting his head to Ananias like a sheep (Acts 9). [Note: As manuscripts vary here in the Greek text, some preferring *didōse* [δίδωσε, “gave”], others *diadōsei* [διαδώσει, “will give”], so the printed and manuscript books of our author also vary: some read *dedit* (“gave”), while others—most of them—read *dividit* (“divides”); and, with the Verona manuscript, they read *spolia* (“spoils”) instead of *escam* (“food”).]

Thus our Nepotianus too, like a little infant babbling and an inexperienced child, is suddenly born for us, as though from the Jordan.

9. Another might perhaps write that for his salvation you abandoned the East and the desert, and enticed me, your dearest companion, with the hope of returning, so that first, if it could be done, you might preserve your widowed sister with her little child; then, if she rejected the proposal, at least your sweetest nephew. For this is the one of whom I once prophesied to you: even though your little nephew hangs upon your neck. Another, I say, might report that, while serving in the palace guard,[^c0070-1] his body was worn down by a hair shirt beneath his military cloak and gleaming linen; that, standing before the powers of this age, he bore a sallow face from fasting; that, while still wearing another man’s garments, he served another; and that he had accepted the belt so that he might assist widows, orphans,[^c0070-2] the oppressed, and the wretched. I do not approve of these delays in an incomplete service of God. When I read that the centurion Cornelius was righteous, I immediately hear that he was baptized (Acts 10).

10. Nevertheless, let us approve these as a kind of cradle of the faith that was coming to birth, so that the devoted soldier who served beneath another’s standards may be worthy to receive the laurel after he has begun to serve his own king. Having laid aside his belt and changed his clothing, he distributed among the poor whatever military property he possessed. For he had read: “If anyone wishes to be perfect, let him sell everything he has, give it to the poor, and follow me” (Matthew 19). And again: “You cannot serve two masters, God and Mammon” (Matthew 6:14). Except for a cheap tunic and a corresponding covering, with which he could cover only his body and keep out the cold, he reserved nothing further for himself. His clothing itself, following the custom of the province, was conspicuous neither for elegance nor for squalor.

Although he burned daily with the desire either to go to the monasteries of Egypt, to visit the communities of Mesopotamia, or at least to occupy the solitudes of the Dalmatian islands, which are separated from Altinum only by a strait, he did not dare to abandon his uncle the Bishop, seeing in him so many examples of virtue and having at home a teacher from whom he could learn. In one and the same man he imitated the monk and revered the bishop. Familiarity did not produce contempt in him, as usually happens to many; rather, he honored him as a parent and admired him as though he saw him every day for the first time.

What more need I say? He became a cleric and, through the customary grades, was ordained a presbyter. Good Jesus, what groans, what lamentations, what refusal of food, what avoidance of everyone’s eyes! Then, for the first and only time, he became angry with his uncle. He complained that he could not endure it and pleaded that his youthful age was unsuitable for the priesthood. But the more strongly he resisted, the more he stirred everyone’s esteem for him; by refusing what he did not wish to be, he DESERVED it, and was all the more worthy the more he proclaimed himself unworthy. We saw the Timothy of our own age,[^c0070-3] gray-haired in wisdom, and a presbyter chosen by Moses, whom he himself knew to be a presbyter.

Thus, understanding the clerical office not as an honor but as a burden, his first concern was to overcome envy through humility, and then to give no scandalous tale of indecency about himself: so that those who criticized his age might be astonished at his continence. He assisted the poor, visited the sick, invited people into his hospitality, soothed them with kind words, rejoiced with those who rejoiced, and wept with those who wept. He was a staff for the blind, food for the hungry, hope for the wretched, and consolation for the grieving. In each individual virtue he stood out as though he possessed no others.

Among the presbyters and his peers, he was first in work and last in rank. Whatever good he had done, he attributed to his uncle. If something had turned out differently from what he expected, he said that his uncle had not known of it and that he himself had erred. In public he recognized him as bishop, at home as father; he tempered the gravity of his conduct with cheerfulness of countenance. In his smile one would perceive joy, not loud laughter. He honored Christ’s virgins and widows as mothers and exhorted them as sisters, with complete chastity.

But once he had withdrawn home and, leaving the cleric outside, had surrendered himself to the austerity of the monks, he was constant in prayers and watchful in supplication, offering his tears to God, not to men. He moderated his fasts, like a charioteer, according to his weariness and bodily strength. He attended his uncle’s table and tasted each dish that was served in such a way that he avoided superstition while preserving continence.

Throughout the meal, his conversation consisted in proposing something from Scripture, listening willingly, answering modestly, accepting what was sound, and refuting what was wrong without harshness. When someone argued against him, he sought rather to teach than to conquer. With the ingenuous modesty that adorned his age, he would simply acknowledge whose work was being cited: “That is Tertullian’s; this is Cyprian’s; this belongs to Lactantius; that to Hilary.” Thus Minucius Felix spoke; thus Victorinus; in this way Arnobius expressed himself. Since he loved me also because of his affection for his uncle, he sometimes brought me forward as well. Through constant reading and prolonged meditation, he had made his breast a library of Christ.

[^c0070-1]: He belonged, evidently, to those whom the ancient writers call *agentes in rebus*, the imperial couriers or agents; they attribute to such men the military cloak and linen garment, or, as Libanius says in his *Oration Against Florentius*, “cloaks and trousers,” together with the belt. See the letter to Salvina, where Nepotianus is discussed. Fortunatus the Presbyter, *Life of Saint Martin* 1.1: “A soldier’s white cloak is more than a king’s purple.” Hence other writers commonly speak of “candidates,” that is, white-clad soldiers. Corippus the African, *On the Praises of Justin* 3: “And, standing with the Palatine tribunes, a white-clad throng,” etc. Claudian, *Panegyric on the Fourth Consulship of Honorius*, calls them “snow-white cohorts”; Trebellius Pollio, in *Gallienus*, calls them “whitened soldiers.”

[^c0070-2]: Victorius adds “orphans.”

[^c0070-3]: This evidently refers to Timothy, who was made a bishop while still young; Jerome compares Nepotianus with him. See 1 Timothy 4:12.

[Column 0596] 11. How often did he plead with me through letters from overseas that I should write something to him? How often did he set before me the midnight petitioner of the Gospel and the widow who importuned the harsh judge? (Luke 15:5.) When I refused him more by silence than by letters, and by the shame of my silence covered the shame of the petitioner, he set his uncle before me as an advocate—one who could ask more freely on behalf of another and, out of reverence for the priesthood, obtain his request more easily.

I therefore did what he wished, and in a short booklet consecrated our friendship to everlasting memory. Once he had received it, he boasted that he had surpassed the wealth of Croesus and the riches of Darius. He held it before his eyes, in his hands, against his breast, and upon his lips. When he frequently unfolded it in bed, the sweet page would often fall upon the breast of the sleeping man. If some traveler or friend arrived, he rejoiced in our testimony about him. Whatever was lacking in the little work, he made up for through measured emphasis and variety of delivery, so that, in reciting it, he himself might seem each day either to please or to displease.[^c0070-4]

From where came this fervor, unless from the love of God? From where this tireless meditation on Christ’s law, unless from desire for him who gave the law? Let others add coin to coin and, suffocating beneath their moneybags, hunt down the wealth of married women through acts of service. Let monks be richer than they had been as laymen; let them possess under poor Christ the wealth that they had not possessed under the wealthy devil; let the Church sigh for those as rich whom the world previously held as beggars. Our Nepotianus tramples gold underfoot and pursues little papers. But just as he despises himself in the flesh and walks more nobly in poverty, so he investigates the entire adornment of the Church.[^c0070-5]

[^c0070-4]: I prefer *sibi* (“for himself”) to *ipse* (“himself”), since *sibi* is absent from the Veronese manuscript.

[^c0070-5]: Older printed editions, Erasmus and Victorius, with the support also of some manuscripts, read “the adornment of the soul” instead of “the adornment of the Church.” But the reading printed here, found in the Veronese manuscript and most other codices, as well as in what follows in Jerome’s text, strongly supports “of the Church.”

12. Compared with what we have said above, what we are about to say is indeed modest; yet the same spirit is displayed even in small matters. Just as we do not admire the Creator only in heaven, earth, the sun, the ocean, elephants, camels, horses, oxen, leopards, bears, and lions, but also in the smallest animals—ants, gnats, flies, worms, and creatures of that kind, whose bodies we know better than their names—and venerate the same ingenuity in all of them, so a mind devoted to Christ is equally attentive to great and small things, knowing that an account must be rendered even for an idle word.

He was therefore careful whether the altar was shining, whether the walls were free of soot, whether the floors were swept, whether the doorkeeper was regularly at the entrance, whether curtains were always hung in the doorways, whether the sanctuary was clean, whether the vessels were gleaming [another reading: “shining”]. He neglected no duty, whether lesser or greater, and arranged every ceremony with pious diligence.

Wherever you sought him in the church, you would find him. Antiquity admires the noble Quintus Fabius,[^c0070-6] who was also a writer of Roman history, though he gained his reputation more from painting than from letters. Scripture testifies that our Bezalel was filled with wisdom and the Spirit of God. It likewise speaks of Hiram, the son of a Tyrian woman, because one fashioned the furnishings of the tabernacle and the other those of the Temple (Exodus 31; 1 Kings 5).
