For just as fruitful crops and fertile fields sometimes luxuriate in stalks and ears (see Virgil, *Georgics* 1), SO EXCELLENT talents and a mind full of virtues overflow into the elegance of various arts. Hence the Greeks praise that philosopher who boasted that everything he used, down to his cloak and ring, had been made by his own hand.[^c0070-7]

We can say the same of Nepotianus, who shaded the basilicas of the Church and the chapels of the martyrs[^c0070-8] with varied flowers, leafy trees, and vine branches, so that whatever pleased the eye in the church testified, both by its arrangement and its appearance, to the labor and zeal of the presbyter.

[^c0070-6]: Jerome seems, through a lapse of memory, to confuse Gaius Fabius with Quintus Fabius and make one person out of two. The first excelled in the art of painting and painted the Temple of Salus in the year 450 from the foundation of the City, as Pliny testifies (*Natural History* 35.4); hence he received the surname “Pictor,” or “Painter.” The other was his descendant and was called Quintus Fabius Pictor. He wrote a history of the Second Punic War. Appian says of him: “The Senate sent Quintus Fabius, who himself had also written a history of the Hannibalic war, to Delphi to consult the oracle.” Livy likewise testifies in book 22, chapter 7, that he regarded Fabius, who was of the same period as that war, as his principal source.

[^c0070-7]: Hippias of Elis, whom Cicero praises after Plato in the *Lesser Hippias*, and whom Lucian and others also mention.

[^c0070-8]: Chapels dedicated to martyrs, also called *martyria* and “gathering places of the martyrs.” Hence ancient writers speak of sermons delivered at the dedication of a martyrs’ shrine; in the Roman Martyrology one likewise finds *concilia martyrum* in this sense.

13. Well done in virtue! What will the end be, when the beginnings are such? O wretched human condition—and without Christ, all that we live is vanity! Why do you withdraw? Why do you evade me, speech? As though we could delay his death and lengthen his life, we fear reaching the end.

“All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass” (Isaiah 40:6). Where now is that beautiful face? Where is the dignity of his whole body, with which the beauty of his soul was clothed as with a lovely garment? Alas, the lily withered when the south wind blew, and the violet’s purple gradually passed into pallor. As he burned with fever and heat drained the springs of his veins, he consoled his saddened uncle with weary breathing.

His face was cheerful, and while everyone around him wept, he alone smiled. He threw off his cloak, extended his hands, saw what others did not see, and, rising as though to meet someone, greeted those who were coming. You would understand that he was not dying but departing, changing friends rather than leaving them.

Tears roll down my face, and despite my resolute spirit I cannot conceal the grief I suffer. Who would believe that at such a time he would remember our relationship and, while his soul struggled, know the sweetness of our studies? Taking his uncle’s hand, he said:

“Send this tunic, which I wore in the ministry of Christ, to the one most dear to me, my father in age and my brother in fellowship; and transfer to him whatever affection was owed by you to your nephew, whom you loved equally with me.”

With such words his speech failed him, as he touched his uncle’s hand in remembrance of me.[^c0070-9]

[^c0070-9]: From this one may certainly infer that priests had used a special garment from those times onward when they performed sacred rites—whether it differed from everyday clothing only in cleanliness, or also in form.

14. I know that you did not wish to prove in this way the love of your fellow citizens for you, nor to seek the affection of your native land more in prosperity. But such a duty is more pleasing in good times and more welcome in adversity.

The whole city mourned him; all Italy mourned him. The earth received his body; his soul was given back to Christ. You were seeking a nephew; the Church was seeking a priest. Your successor preceded you. What you were, he deserved, in everyone’s judgment, to be after you. Thus the dignity of a double episcopate went forth from a single household: in one case there is rejoicing that he held it; in the other, grief that he was taken away before he could hold it.

Plato’s opinion, expressed in the *Phaedo*, is that the whole life of wise men is a meditation on death. Philosophers praise this and exalt it to heaven. But the Apostle speaks much more powerfully: “I die every day, by your glory” (1 Corinthians 15:31). For it is one thing to attempt and another to accomplish; one thing to live as one who will die, another to die as one who will live. The former is going to die because of glory; the latter dies continually for glory.

We too must therefore anticipate in our minds what we shall one day be; and whether we wish it or not, that day cannot be far away. For even if we surpassed nine hundred years of life, as the human race lived before the Flood, and the years of Methuselah were granted to us, the length that had passed and ceased to exist would still be nothing. Indeed, between the one who lived ten years and the one who lived a thousand, once the same end of life has arrived and the unavoidable necessity of death has come, all that has passed is equal—except that the old man departs more heavily burdened by the weight of sins.

> Every best day of life first flees from wretched mortals;  
> then illnesses approach, and old age, with its worn-out limbs,  
> and toil, and the harsh violence of pitiless death, carry them away.  
> (Virgil, *Georgics* 3)

The poet Naevius says: “A mortal must endure many evils.” Hence antiquity imagined Niobe, because she had wept so much, transformed into stone and various wild beasts.[^c0070-10] And Hesiod, lamenting the births of human beings, rejoices at the funeral; while Ennius wisely says:[^c0070-11]

> “The common people,” he says, “have a place of precedence in this matter before the King:  
> It is permitted for a commoner to weep; for a king it is not honorable.”

As with a king, so with a bishop—or rather, less is permitted to a bishop than to a king.[^c0070-12] The king rules over unwilling subjects, the bishop over willing ones; the king subjugates by fear, the bishop rules through service; the king guards bodies unto death, the bishop preserves souls unto life.

All eyes are directed toward you. Your household and your conduct, set as though upon a watchtower, are teachers of public discipline. Whatever you do, everyone thinks he ought to do the same. Take care not to do something that those who wish to criticize may seem justified in tearing apart, or that those who wish to imitate may be compelled to do wrong.[^c0070-13]

Conquer, as far as you can—or rather, even more than you can—the softness of your spirit, and restrain the tears that flow abundantly, lest your great affection for your nephew be interpreted by unbelieving minds as despair of God. You should long for him as one absent, not as one dead, so that you may seem to await him rather than to have lost him.

[^c0070-10]: Antiquity indeed represented Niobe as changed into stone, but, so far as I know, not into various animals as well. Jerome himself says in his letter to Oceanus: “You would think her Niobe, who was turned into stone by excessive weeping.” Something therefore seems to be missing here and ought perhaps to be supplied: “and others transformed into various animals,” etc.; or the words “and various animals” should be deleted.

[^c0070-11]: We restore these two lines of Ennius to the ancient reading. Note that *plebes* is used for *plebs* according to ancient usage, just as *trabes* is used for *trabs* in the singular.

[^c0070-12]: The Veronese manuscript lacks the words “or rather, less is permitted to a bishop than to a king.” Martianaeus reads them in the opposite sense: “rather, less is permitted to a king than to a bishop,” and sharply accuses the printed reading of being false. The entire context makes clear that he is mistaken: Jerome’s meaning is that a bishop is less permitted to grieve than a king.

[^c0070-13]: One might prefer *conantur* (“who endeavor”), with the punctuation changed: “or those who endeavor to imitate may be compelled to do wrong.”

15. But what am I doing? I am treating a grief that I already believe has been calmed by both time and reason. Why do I not instead set before you the neighboring misfortunes of kings and the calamities of our own age, so that he who has been deprived of this light should be less mourned than the one who has escaped from such great evils?

Constantius, a supporter of the Arian heresy, while preparing against an enemy and rushing impetuously into battle, died at the village of Mopsus,[^c0070-14] leaving the empire to his enemy with great sorrow. Julian, the traitor to his own soul and butcher of the Christian army, encountered Christ in Media, whom he had first denied in Gaul; and, while wishing to extend the Roman borders, he lost what had already been extended.

Jovianus [another reading: Jovinianus], having tasted royal power only briefly, died suffocated by the stench of burning coals, showing everyone what human power is.[^c0070-15] Valentinian, after his native land had been devastated, leaving his country unavenged, was extinguished by a vomiting of blood. His brother Valens, defeated in the Gothic war in Thrace, had the same place for his death and his tomb. Gratian, betrayed by his own army and not received by the cities he encountered, became a mockery to his enemy; and your walls, Lyons, bear witness to the traces of his bloodstained hand.

The young Valentinian, almost still a boy, after flight, exile, and the recovery of an empire at the cost of much blood, was killed not far from the city that knew his brother’s death; and his lifeless corpse was dishonored by being suspended. What shall I say of Procopius, Maximus, and Eugenius, who, while they held power, were terror to the nations? All were captured and stood before the faces of their conquerors; and—what is most wretched for those once so powerful—they were first subjected to the disgrace of slavery before being struck down by the enemy’s sword.

[^c0070-14]: Learned writers generally understand this as the village of Mopsus, Mopsuestia in inland Cilicia. I would rather understand Mopsucrena, a city situated at the foot of the Taurus, where Constantius died, as Ammianus Marcellinus, book 31, chapter 15, the *Alexandrian Chronicle*, and others testify. The enemy mentioned is Julian, who, having been acclaimed emperor in Gaul, was advancing toward Constantinople in order to seize the empire.

[^c0070-15]: Compare the letter to Praesidius on the Paschal Candle, which is attributed to our Jerome and certainly taken from him: “Recently,” he says, “when the emperor Valentinian was raging more violently in council against the Sarmatians and Quadi because of the devastation of Illyricum, and sternly threatening the destruction of the entire nation, he burst a blood vessel and died. What shall I say of his brother, whom fire in Thrace consumed in opposition to the height of royal power? Not yet has a full year passed since the emperor Gratian, betrayed by his own army, was first overwhelmed by shameful captivity and then by a more pitiable death.” See also Ammianus Marcellinus 30.6, together with Socrates 4.26 and, following him, Sozomen 6.36. Victor, in the *Epitome*, reports Valentinian’s death somewhat differently; Zosimus, book 4, and an ancient author cited by Suidas under *leias* agree with him.

16. Someone may say: Such is the condition of kings, and “lightning strikes the highest mountains” (Horace, *Odes* 2.10). Let me come to private dignities, and let me not speak of those who last more than two years. To pass over the others, it is enough for us to record the different fates of three men who had recently been consuls.

Abundantius, impoverished, is in exile at Pityus.[^c0070-16] The head of Rufinus was carried on a pike to Constantinople, and his severed right hand, as a disgrace to his insatiable greed, went from door to door begging alms. Timasius, suddenly hurled down from the highest rank of dignity, considers himself to have escaped because he lives without honor at Oasis.

I am not recounting the calamities of wretched men, but the fragile condition of human life. My spirit shudders to trace the ruins of our times. For twenty years and more, Roman blood has been shed daily between Constantinople and the Julian Alps. The Goth, Sarmatian, Quadi, Alan, Hun, Vandal, and Marcomannian ravage, drag away, and plunder Scythia, Thrace, Macedonia, Dardania, Dacia, Thessaly, Achaea, Epirus, Dalmatia, and all the Pannonias.[^c0070-17] How many married women, how many virgins of God, how many freeborn and noble bodies have been the playthings of these beasts? Bishops have been captured, presbyters killed, and the offices of clerics of every kind overthrown. Churches have been overthrown, horses stabled at Christ’s altars, and the relics of martyrs dug up. Everywhere mourning, everywhere groaning, and “the likeness of death in its fullest form” (from Virgil, *Aeneid* 2).

The Roman world is collapsing, yet our neck remains erect and does not bend. What do you think the Corinthians, Athenians, Lacedaemonians, Arcadians, and all Greece now feel, when Barbarians rule them? And I have named only a few cities, in which once there were considerable kingdoms.

The East seemed free from these evils and was shaken only by reports. But look: last year, wolves sent against us from the furthest crags of the Caucasus—not of Arabia now, but of the North—traversed such great provinces in a short time.[^c0070-18] How many monasteries were captured? How many rivers were turned into human blood? Antioch was besieged, as were the other cities past which the Halys, Cydnus, Orontes, and Euphrates flow. Flocks of captives were dragged away; Arabia, Phoenicia, Palestine, and Egypt were held captive by fear.

> Not even if I had a hundred tongues and a hundred mouths,  
> a voice of iron, [lacuna]  
> could I run through all the names of punishments.  
> (Virgil, *Aeneid* 6)

For I have not undertaken to write history, but briefly to lament our own miseries. Otherwise, to explain these matters properly, both Thucydides and Sallust would be struck dumb [another reading: “would be silent”].

[^c0070-16]: Some report that Abundantius was exiled not at Pityus but at Sidon in Phoenicia, and Timasius at Oasis in Egypt. The accounts can be reconciled from Asterius of Amasea’s homily for the Kalends of the year 398: Abundantius’s place of exile appears to have been changed, since Asterius says that he was then exiled in Colchis, whereas previously he had been at Sidon.

[^c0070-17]: The printed editions err up to this point by inserting Thessalonica instead of Thessaly. Thessalonica is a city of Macedonia, whereas Jerome here is merely listing provinces. The reading has been corrected with the help of the Veronese manuscript, which also omits the name Achaea.

[^c0070-18]: Understand the Huns, whom Rufinus sent into the imperial provinces to assist his revolt. He is also alluding to Habakkuk 1:8, where, according to the Septuagint, it is said of the Chaldeans: “They are swifter than the wolves of Arabia.”

17. Happy Nepotianus, who does not see these things; happy he who does not hear them. We are wretched, who either suffer them ourselves or see our brothers suffering such things—and yet we wish to live, and regard those who are free from these evils as worthy rather of weeping than of happiness.

We perceive that God has long been offended, yet we do not appease him. Because of our sins the Barbarians are strong. Because of our vices the Roman army is overcome; and, as though these disasters were not enough, civil wars have consumed almost more people than the enemy’s sword.

Wretched Israelites, in comparison with whom Nebuchadnezzar is called a servant of God [another reading: “is said to be a servant of God”] (Jeremiah 25:9). Unhappy are we, who displease God so greatly that, through the rage of the Barbarians, his anger rages against us.

Hezekiah repented, and one angel destroyed 185,000 Assyrians in a single night (2 Kings 19:25). Jehoshaphat sang the praises of the Lord, and the Lord conquered on behalf of the one who praised him (2 Chronicles 20:21). Moses fought against Amalek not with a sword but with prayer (Exodus 17:11). If we wish to be lifted up, let us prostrate ourselves.

Shame upon us, and upon a mind foolish even to the point of unbelief! The Roman army, victor and master of the world, is defeated by these people, fears them, and is terrified at the sight of them, though they cannot walk properly and, if they touch the ground, think themselves dead.[^c0070-19] Yet we do not understand the words of the prophets: “A thousand shall flee at the rebuke of one” (Isaiah 30:17). Nor do we cut away the causes of the disease, so that the disease itself may likewise be removed; then we would immediately see arrows yield to javelins, tiaras to helmets, and nags to warhorses.

[^c0070-19]: Here again he is referring to the Huns, whom Ammianus Marcellinus 31.2 describes as wearing shoes “fitted by no shape or pattern, which prevent them from walking with free steps.” Hence an ancient writer cited by Suidas calls them “footless” and “unsteady,” and says: “Without horses a Hun would not easily tread the earth.” Jerome therefore rightly says that they are unable to walk properly and, if they touched the ground, would think themselves finished, since on foot they could not escape an enemy pursuing them. The other point, concerning their terrifying appearance, is attested by Jordanes, *On the Gothic Peoples*: “Though perhaps they were not at all superior in war, by the terror of their faces they inflicted such fear that they put their enemies to flight.”

18. We have exceeded the proper measure of consolation, and, while forbidding the mourning of one man’s death, we have mourned the dead of the entire world. That most powerful king Xerxes, who overturned mountains and spread roads across the seas, is said to have wept when, from an elevated place, he saw an immeasurable multitude of people and an innumerable army, because after a hundred years none of those whom he then saw would still be alive.

If only we could ascend such a watchtower that we might see the whole earth beneath our feet! I would show you the ruins of the entire world: nations colliding with nations, kingdoms with kingdoms; some tortured, others killed, others swallowed up [another reading: buried] by the waves, others dragged into slavery; here weddings, there mourning; some being born, others dying; some abounding in wealth [another reading: sins], others begging; and not merely the army of Xerxes, but all the people of the world who now live, soon to be gone.

Speech is defeated by the magnitude of its subject, and everything we say is too little.

19. Let us therefore return to ourselves and, as though descending from heaven, look for a little while upon our own condition. Do you know, I ask you, when you became an infant, when a boy, when a young man, when a man in full strength, when an old man? Every day we die; every day we change; yet we believe ourselves eternal.

This very thing that I say, that is written, that I reread, that I correct, is taken away from my life. As many marks as the copyist makes, so many are the losses of my time. We write and rewrite; letters cross the sea; and as the keel cleaves its furrow [another reading: the open sea], the moments of our life diminish with every wave.

The only profit we possess is that we are joined to one another by the love of Christ.

> Love is patient and kind; love does not envy, does not act improperly, is not puffed up; it bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. Love never fails.

This always lives in the breast. Because of it our Nepotianus, though absent, is present; and, though separated by such vast distances of land, he embraces us with both hands. We possess one another as pledges of mutual love. Let us be joined in spirit and bound together in affection, and let us imitate in a son the strength of mind that the blessed Pope Chromatius displayed at the death of his brother Eusebius.[^c0070-20]

Let our little page celebrate him; let all letters resound with him [another reading: “let our letters resound with him”]. Since we cannot hold him in body, let us hold him in memory. And with one to whom we cannot speak, let us never cease speaking about him.

[^c0070-20]: The reference is to the death of his brother Eusebius.

# LETTER 61[^c0070-21] TO VIGILANTIUS

[In the Veronese manuscript it is entitled “To Vigilantius, on Origen,” and begins at once: “It would indeed have been useful,” in place of “It would indeed have been right,” etc.]

Jerome rebukes Vigilantius, who, after returning to the West, was defaming Jerome’s name and his friends. He urges him to come to his senses at last and stop slandering him, sharply refuting his blasphemies at the end.

[^c0070-21]: Elsewhere numbered 75. Written in the same year, 396.

1. It would indeed have been right not to answer you at all by letter, since you did not believe your own ears; for you cannot be satisfied by a written page when you did not trust spoken words. But because Christ gave us in himself an example of perfect humility, giving a kiss to his betrayer and accepting the repentance of the thief upon the cross, I tell you in your absence what I also said when you were present: I have read, and do read, Origen in the same way as Apollinarius [another reading: Apollinaris] or the other commentators whose books, in certain respects, the Church does not accept.

I do not mean that everything contained in their volumes must be condemned, but I acknowledge that certain things must be censured. Yet since it is my work and study to read many authors, so that I may pluck different flowers from many sources—not so much to approve everything as to select what is good—I take many books into my hands so that I may learn many things from many people, according to what is written: “Reading all things; holding fast what is good” (1 Thessalonians 5:21).

I am therefore sufficiently astonished that you wished to charge me with the doctrines of Origen, whose error in most matters you have remained entirely ignorant of up to this day. Am I a heretic? And why, I ask you, do heretics not love me? Are you orthodox? You who, even against your own opinion and the position proclaimed by your tongue, either signed unwillingly and are a renegade, or signed willingly and are a heretic.[^c0070-22]

You left Egypt,[^c0070-23] and abandoned all the provinces in which many openly defend your sect, and you chose me as the object of your attack—I who criticize and condemn aloud every doctrine opposed to the Church.

[^c0070-22]: The same manuscript adds: “against your conscience,” etc.

[^c0070-23]: Older editions, with the support of the Bononiensis manuscript, less appropriately read “your own provinces”; other manuscripts read “your sect” instead of “your own.” This passage seems to concern Vigilantius’s faith, which Rufinus had in mind when he said that Vigilantius had contracted heresy at Alexandria. Jerome answered him in *Apology* 3.6: “I do not know what you dream under the name of Vigilantius. Where have I written that he was defiled by heretical communion at Alexandria? Produce the book; bring forward the letter; nowhere at all will you find it.” Victorius is again mistaken in making this Vigilantius different from the man who is called a heretic and against whom Jerome wrote a book.

2. The errors of Origen.—Origen is a heretic: what of that, coming from me, who do not deny that he is a heretic in many respects? He erred concerning the resurrection of the body [another reading: bodies]; he erred concerning the state of souls and the repentance of the devil; and, more serious than these matters, he declared in his *Commentaries on Isaiah* that the Son of God and the Holy Spirit are Seraphim.[^c0070-24]

If I did not say that he had erred, and if I did not anathematize these doctrines every day, I would be a partner in his error. We must not accept his good teachings in such a way that we are also compelled to embrace his bad ones.[^c0070-25]

Yet he interpreted many passages of Scripture well, explained obscure passages of the prophets, and revealed the greatest mysteries of both the New and Old Testaments. If, therefore, I have transmitted what is good, while cutting out, correcting, or passing over what is bad, am I to be accused because through me Latin readers possess his good teachings and remain ignorant of his bad ones?

If this is a crime, let Confessor Hilary also be accused, because he translated the interpretation of the Psalms and the homilies on Job from Origen’s books—that is, from Greek into Latin. Let Eusebius of Vercelli, likewise a confessor, share the blame, because he translated into our language the commentaries on all the Psalms by a heretical man, Eusebius of Caesarea, even though he omitted the heretical material and translated only the best parts.

I say nothing of Victorinus of Pettau,[^c0070-26] and the others who merely followed and reproduced Origen in his explanations of Scripture, lest I seem less to be defending myself than seeking partners in guilt.

Let me come to you yourself: why do you possess his treatises on Job, in which, while arguing against the devil and discussing the stars and the heavens, he said certain things that the Church does not accept? Is it permitted only to you, with your “most learned skull” (τῷ σοφωτάτῳ κρανίῳ),[^c0070-27] to pass judgment on all Greek and Latin commentators—to expel some from libraries with a censor’s stroke and admit others, and, whenever it pleases you, pronounce me either Catholic or heretic? Are we not permitted to reject what is perverse and condemn what we have often condemned?

Read my books *To the Ephesians*; read my other little works, especially my *Commentaries on Ecclesiastes*. You will see clearly that from my youth I have never been deterred by anyone’s authority from refusing to assent to heretical perversity.

[^c0070-24]: The Bononiensis manuscript omits “of God,” and shortly afterward omits “him.”

[^c0070-25]: The Veronese manuscript reads: “For he also interpreted the Scriptures well.”

[^c0070-26]: Older editions falsely read “of Poitiers,” contrary to the manuscripts. He was not a bishop in Aquitaine II but in Upper Pannonia, as has previously been noted by others.

[^c0070-27]: The Veronese and a few other manuscripts add a translation of the Greek expression: “that is, with your most learned brain.”

### 3.

It is no small matter to know what you do not know: it is the mark of a prudent man to recognize his own measure, and not, driven on by the devil’s jealousy, make the whole world a witness to his ignorance. [Note: Col. 0604. Alternatively, with the Bologna manuscript: “Clearly you wish to boast, so that in your homeland you may proclaim that I, etc.”] Clearly, you also wish to boast, and in your homeland you proclaim that I was unable to answer your eloquence and feared the acuity of Chrysippus in you. Christian modesty restrains me, and I do not wish to expose the hiding places of my little cell with biting speech. Otherwise I would bring forward [Note: Among the many variant readings of manuscripts and printed copies, we follow the reading that has long prevailed. For it is not easy to affirm which is genuine, since some—including two Verona manuscripts—offer *pasan ten narstran*, or *πᾶσαν τὴν ἀριστερίαν*, or *πᾶν τὸ ἃτλος*, and shortly afterward most have *τροπαίφορον*, while others read *τροπέοφον*, or *τροπαίων νεωτέρων ὠμώφορον*, along with other monstrosities of this kind. In the Latin interpretation appended to the passage, almost all vary in the first part: some, like the Verona manuscripts, read “all your weakness”; others, “all your battles”; and still others, “all your strength.” They agree more nearly in the second part, “also sung by the voices of little ones,” or “sung with the voice of little ones,” even those manuscripts in which a gap occurs in the Greek letters, such as the Bologna manuscript. Martianaeus nevertheless appended this Greek phrase, failing to notice that it must belong to the Latin interpretation, and thus included words that did not come from Jerome’s pen—a fault that the older editors wisely avoid. If this corrupt passage requires surgical treatment, we think the Greek should be restored from the Latin words. If we follow the Verona manuscripts, which have “weakness,” then, for *ἀριστείαν*, with a very slight alteration one should read *ἀῤῥωστίαν* (“weakness”); and since there is nothing in the Greek corresponding to the Latin *parvulorum voce cantatum* (“sung by the voice of little ones”), one might read, in place of *τροπαιόφορον*, as most manuscripts have it, *τὸ παιδόφωνον* (“the voice of children”). We make few conjectures; let the reader follow whichever reading he prefers.] “all your valour and triumph-bearing.” But I leave these matters to others, either to discuss or to ridicule.

I, speaking as a Christian to a Christian, beg you, brother, not to wish to be wiser than you are; not to parade in writing either your innocence, your simplicity, or at least those things which I leave unspoken and which others understand though you do not, thereby giving everyone cause to laugh at your absurdities. You learned something else from childhood; you were accustomed to other disciplines. It is not the same man who approves both golden coins and the Scriptures, who tastes wines and understands the Prophets or Apostles.

You wound me; you call the holy brother Oceanus into the guilt of heresy; and the judgment of the presbyters Vincentius and Paulinianus and of the brother Eusebius displeases you. [Note: The Bologna manuscript has “and Paulinus,” though corruptly. Perhaps one should read “of the brother Paulinianus and Eusebius.”] You alone are the Cato of the Roman race, most eloquent, wishing us to believe your testimony and wisdom. Recall, I beg you, that day when, as I was preaching about the Resurrection and the truth of the body, you leapt up beside me, clapped your hands, stamped your foot, and shouted that I was orthodox. [Note: The same reading has *subsultabas, et applaudebas pede*, omitting *et plaudebas manu* (“you leapt up and applauded with your foot,” omitting “and clapped with your hand”); it then reads *et orthodoxum clamabas* (“and you shouted ‘orthodox’”), an inept glossator’s error.]

After you began to sail, and the rot of the bilge reached the innermost part of your brain, then you remembered that we were heretics. What am I to do with you? I trusted the letters of the holy presbyter Paulinus, and I did not think that his judgment concerning your character could be mistaken. Although, as soon as I received your letter, I understood your speech to be *ἀσυμάρτητον* [Note: The Verona and Bologna manuscripts and an old edition add “that is, unformed,” which Erasmus approves. Properly, however, *ἀσυνάρτητος* means “incongruous” or “not at all fitting.”], I nevertheless thought you showed rusticity and simplicity rather than stupidity.

Nor do I blame the holy man: he preferred to conceal from me what he knew rather than accuse a poor client and letter-carrier in his own correspondence. But I blame myself, who yielded to another’s judgment rather than my own; and, while my eyes saw one thing, believed the writing before me to say something else.

### 4. He wittily attacks the ignorance of Vigilantius

Therefore stop provoking me and overwhelming me with your volumes. At least spare your money, with which you hire notaries and scribes, using them both as writers and as supporters; perhaps they praise you for that very reason, so that they may make a profit by writing [variant: “by the writings”] for you.

If you wish to exercise your intellect, devote yourself to grammarians and rhetoricians; learn dialectic; equip yourself with the schools of the philosophers. Then, when you have learned everything, at least begin to keep silent. Yet I would act foolishly by seeking teachers for the teacher of all and imposing a limit [variant: “setting a place”] upon one who does not know how to speak and cannot keep silent. The Greek proverb is true: “a lyre for an ass” (*ὄνῳ λύρα*). [Note: Formerly the reading was *ὄνος πρὸς λύραν*, with the same meaning; Martianaeus had no reason to accuse that reading of falsity.]

I think that your name too was given to you *κατ’ ἀντίφρασιν*, “by contraries.” For in your whole mind you are asleep, and you snore not so much in the deepest sleep as in a lethargy.

Among the other blasphemies that you uttered with your sacrilegious mouth, you dared to say that the mountain [Note: Gennadius, indeed, in chapter 35 reports that Vigilantius, with perverse ingenuity, expounded Daniel’s second vision; here, however, the first is indicated, the vision set out in Daniel chapter 2—unless he took the second chapter for the second vision.] from which the stone was cut without hands in Daniel (Daniel 2) is the devil, and that the stone is Christ, who, because he assumed a body from Adam—who had previously been joined to the devil through his vices—was born of a Virgin, so that he might separate the human being from the mountain, that is, from the devil. O tongue that ought to be cut off and torn apart limb by limb and fragment by fragment!

Would any Christian interpret God the omnipotent Father in the person of the devil and stain the ears of the whole world with so great a sacrilege? If anyone—let me not say a Catholic, but even a heretic or pagan—has ever accepted your interpretation, then what you have said may be pious. But if the Church of Christ has never heard such wickedness, and if he himself, through your mouth for the first time, interpreted himself as the mountain—the one who had said, “I will be like the Most High”—then do penance: wrap yourself in sackcloth and ashes, and wash away so great a crime with continual tears, if indeed this impiety can be forgiven you. According to Origen’s error, you will then obtain pardon when the devil too obtains it—the devil, who is never discovered to have blasphemed more greatly than through your mouth.

I bore my own injury patiently; I could not endure impiety against God. Therefore I seemed to write more sharply at the end of the letter than I had promised. [Note: The Verona manuscripts read, “and I dared to write more biting words at the end of the letter,” which seems the smoother reading.] [Note: The Verona manuscripts read, “and I dared to write more biting words at the end of the letter,” which seems the smoother reading.] Since I had already committed the former offense for which you asked my pardon, it would be most foolish to commit it again and thus have to do penance once more. May Christ grant you that you may hear and be silent, understand and then speak.

## EPISTLE LXII

[Note: Otherwise numbered 7. Written in 396 or the following year. Cassiodorus, *Institutions*, chapter 1, calls him Tranquillus.]

### TO TRANQUILLINUS

Jerome teaches his friend Tranquillinus to what extent Origen should be embraced and read.

### 1.

If we once doubted that the bonds of the spirit are stronger than those of the body, we have now proved it: your holiness remains fixed in my mind, and I am joined to you by the love of Christ. For I speak openly and simply to your most candid heart; this very letter and these mute marks of writing breathe into us the affection of your mind.

### 2. Oceanus opposed the Origenists

You say that many have been deceived by Origen’s error, that my holy son Oceanus resists their madness, and I both grieve and rejoice: I grieve because simple people have been overthrown, and rejoice because erring people are being aided by an educated man.

Since you seek the judgment of my littleness—whether, following brother Faustinus, Origen should be entirely rejected, or, as some think, read in part—I believe that, because of his learning, Origen should sometimes be read in the same way as Tertullian, Novatus, Arnobius, Apollinarius, and certain other ecclesiastical writers, Greek as well as Latin: so that we may choose what is good in them and avoid what is contrary, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying, “Test everything; hold fast what is good” (1 Thessalonians 5). [Note: Older editions read “hold fast what is good,” rejected by the manuscripts and the sacred text. Two Verona codices read: “Certainly, those who are led either by excessive love for him or by a perverse disposition of mind into moderate zeal, etc.” All printed editions and manuscripts unanimously print *Novatus*; we therefore did not choose to alter it. Yet we would prefer *Novatianus* to be read in place of *Novatus*: for Novatian was the presbyter of the Roman Church, whose learning Jerome somewhat admired; Jerome lists his works in the *Catalogue*, chapter 70, and in Epistle 10 to Paulinus, section 3, asks that Novatian’s letters be sent to him, so that, knowing the poisons of the schismatic, they might drink more gladly the antidotes of the holy martyr Cyprian. Novatus, however, was the Carthaginian presbyter who advocated refusing reconciliation to the lapsed and to bigamists; Novatian joined him in defending that doctrine, but Novatus’s writings are not produced.]

But those who are driven either by excessive love for him or by the perversity of their own resentment seem to me to fall under the prophetic curse: “Woe to those who call evil good and good evil, who make bitter sweet and sweet bitter” (Isaiah 5). For neither should corrupt doctrines be accepted because of his teaching, nor should he be entirely rejected because of the corruption of his doctrines, if he has published useful commentaries on the holy Scriptures.

If his admirers and detractors pull against one another in contentious rivalry, so that they seek no middle course and preserve no measure, but approve or disapprove everything alike, I would more willingly choose pious simplicity than learned blasphemy.

The holy brother Tatianus the deacon [Note: The Verona parchment manuscripts omit his rank as deacon; they likewise read *salutat* instead of *resalutat*.] sends you his warmest greetings.

## EPISTLE LXIII

[Note: Otherwise numbered 68. Written around 397.]

### TO THEOPHILUS

[Col. 0607]

He declares, in reply to Theophilus, that nothing is more important to him than preserving the rights of Christ; he gives thanks meanwhile for the admonition concerning the ecclesiastical canons, but does not approve Theophilus’s leniency in the case of the Origenists.

### HIERONYMUS TO THE MOST BLESSED POPE THEOPHILUS

#### 1.

Your Blessedness remembers that, at the time when you were silent together with us, my speech never ceased from its duties, nor did I consider what you were then doing in accordance with your stewardship, but what it was fitting for me to do. [Note: The Verona manuscript reads, in place of “what you were then doing in accordance with your stewardship,” “what you had not done, but, etc.” In other printed editions *nobiscum* (“with us”) is lacking. With that word removed, the manuscripts vary in place of *tacebas* (“you were silent”): some read *monebas* (“you were admonishing”), others *manebas* (“you were remaining”), though the latter readings are not very suitable. Some learned men think that one reading may refer to the time when Theophilus admonished Jerome to conceal his quarrels with John of Jerusalem, and the other to the time when Theophilus was staying with the holy Doctor himself, having come to Palestine around 396 to settle those same disputes. But the one genuine sense is established by the printed reading *tacebas*, especially by the sequence of the discourse and the words “now that I have received the letters of Your Dignity.”]

And now, having received the letters of Your Dignity, I see that I have begun to derive some fruit from the reading of the Gospel. For if the persistent petition of a woman softened the sentence of a harsh judge (Luke 18:15), how much more are a father’s bowels softened by earnest supplication?

#### 2.

We thank you for your admonition concerning the ecclesiastical canons: “For whom the Lord loves, he disciplines, and chastises every son whom he receives” (Hebrews 12:6). Yet know that nothing is more important to us than preserving the rights of Christ, not crossing [variant: “transgressing”] the boundaries of the Fathers, and always remembering the Roman faith, praised by the apostolic mouth, of which the Church of Alexandria boasts that it shares.

#### 3.

That you show great patience [Note: In Erasmus and Martianaeus the reading was, less well, “that you act with great patience.” The more correct reading is that of the very carefully corrected Milan manuscript H. 59, which we follow; it reads shortly afterward “by the strength of the Church” rather than “by the bowels of the Church.”] toward the unspeakable heresy of the Origenists, and think that those who lie upon the vitals of the Church can be corrected by your gentleness, displeases many saints: lest, while you await the repentance of a few, you nourish the boldness of the lost, and the faction grow stronger.

Farewell in Christ.

## EPISTLE LXIV

[Note: Otherwise numbered 128. Written in 397 or earlier.]

### TO FABIOLA

[Note: In Queen Christina’s manuscript 215 it is entitled, “The little book of Saint Jerome to Fabiola concerning priestly foods and the pontifical garment.” To be candid, I think this title more accurate; for, to omit other considerations, below, in section 8, Jerome says: “You compelled me, Fabiola, by your letters to write to you about Aaron’s priesthood and garments. I offered more, so that I might compose a preface concerning the foods and firstfruits of the priests and the observance of the Pontiff.”]

### On the Priestly Garment

He explains to Fabiola—who had gone to Bethlehem to live there with Paula and Eustochium, but, when the barbarians invaded, had suddenly been compelled to return to Rome—the mystery contained in the clothing of priests and Levites. He adds, as a kind of supplement, material concerning the rite and ceremonies of sacred things and the vessels of the Temple. He also modestly invites her, since the region around Bethlehem was now peaceful, to return to her former companionship.

#### 1.

To this day, in the reading of the Old Testament, a veil is placed over the face of Moses. He speaks with a glorified face, and the people cannot bear the glory of the one speaking (Exodus 34). But when we have turned to the Lord, the veil will be removed [variant: “is removed”]: the letter that kills dies, and the spirit that gives life rises again. For the Lord is spirit, and the law is spiritual.

Therefore David also prayed in the psalm, “Open my eyes, and I shall contemplate the wonders of your law” (Psalm 118:18). “Does God care for oxen?” (1 Corinthians 9:10.) Certainly not. Still less does he care for the liver of an ox, a ram, or goats, or for the right shoulder, the breast, and the belly where excrement is digested. [Note: Alternatively, “the little breast.” Philo says *ἀπὸ δὲ τοῦ στήθους ὄσον πῖον*, “the fat of the breast.” Yet the reading of the Royal manuscript mentioned above, and of two others cited by Martianaeus, is not to be despised: “the shoulder of the right foot and the belly.” Compare Philo’s book *On the Rewards and Honours of Priests*, from which Jerome seems to have drawn the following mystical exposition. Philo calls the belly *ἤνυστρον*, “omentum.”] Of these, the priests receive two for food; Phinehas merits the third as a reward.

Of the peace offerings, the fat that surrounds the breast and the lobe of the liver are offered upon the altar; but the breast itself and the right arm are given to Aaron and his sons as a perpetual due from the children of Israel (Leviticus 7).

The meaning lies in the heart, whose dwelling place is the breast. The question is where the ruling faculty of the soul is located. [Note: The ancients called this ruling faculty of the soul the *hegemonikon* (Greek *ἡγεμονικόν*). Tertullian discusses, from the opinions of philosophers, whether it exists and where it exists in *On the Soul* and *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, chapter 15; citing Scriptural testimonies, he proves that the ruling faculty of the soul is established in the heart. Our author agrees with this view here and especially in his commentary on Matthew chapter 15: the ruling faculty of the soul is not in the brain according to Plato, but in the heart according to Christ.] Plato places it in the brain; Christ shows that it is in the heart: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God”; “From the heart proceed evil thoughts”; and “Why do you think evil in your hearts?” (Matthew 5:8; 15:18; 9:4).

Pleasure and desire, according to those who discuss natural philosophy, reside in the liver. Its lobe, flying in different directions and bursting outward through the windows of the eyes, the priests offer to God, so that after they have said to God through their deeds, “May your sacrifice be made fat” (Psalm 19), and have burned up desire, the seedbed of lust, in the fire of the Spirit, they may deserve to receive the reward: the breast and the arm.

In the breast are pure thoughts, knowledge of the law, and the truth of doctrines; in the arm are good works and the struggle against the devil, the armed hand, so that what they have conceived in the mind they may prove by example. For Jesus “began to do and to teach” (Acts 1).

The breast itself is also called *epithema* (*ἐπίθεμα*), that is, “addition,” or “the principal and distinguished part.” [Note: Martianaeus, following Erasmus, had read the word in the genitive, from Leviticus 7, *ἐπιθέματος*, but, unlike Erasmus, did not append the interpretation “of an addition.” We preferred the reading of Victorius, who has the word in the nominative, taken from Leviticus 8, although our manuscript copies do not support it.] For *thenupha* (*THENUPHA*) has more nearly this meaning. From this we understand, according to Malachi—“The lips of the priest guard knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth” (Malachi 1:7)—that priests must possess an exceptional knowledge of the law and of doctrine. Through the addition of spiritual grace such a man must be formed that he can resist those who contradict him (Titus 1), and have no sinister work in himself that could lead him to Tartarus, but possess a right and separated arm, so that the works of a priest, in comparison with his virtues, may be separated from those of all other human beings.

This is what concerns the victims and the things offered upon the altar and given by the Lord to the priests.

#### 2.

Besides the first portions of sacrifices, three other parts are assigned to priests, whether from private animals or from the public market, where there is no religious observance but only the necessity of food: the arm, the jaw, and the belly.

We have already spoken of the arm. [Note: In his commentary on Malachi chapter 2 Jerome also adds the tongue, as the Babylonian Jews do. Below, some printed editions and manuscripts used by the older editors read *confixus* (“pierced through”), others *defossus* (“stabbed”), in place of *confossus* (“pierced”).] The jaw signifies eloquence and learning, so that what we conceive in the breast we may bring forth with the mouth. The belly, the receptacle of food, pierced by the priestly dagger in the Midianite harlot (Numbers 25), condemns all human labors and the momentary pleasures of the throat to the end of excrement; it shows consecrated minds that everything for which we care—everything we consume—is cast into the privy. [Note: Again agreeing with Erasmus, the Benedictine editor adds here “what we busy ourselves about.” As Victorius once did, we have deleted these two words on the authority of several manuscripts. Yet we do not think the integrity of the passage sufficiently secured by this: some have printed *currimus* (“we run”) where we have *curamus* (“we care for”), and we suspect both readings to be false unless *curamus* refers to human labours mentioned just above. Perhaps the text was *gluttimus* (“we gulp down”), or something similar; but we do not venture beyond manuscript authority.]

Therefore the Apostle says: “Food is for the belly and the belly for food, but God will destroy both it and them” (1 Corinthians 6:13). Conversely, concerning the pleasure-seekers: “Their god is their belly, and their glory is in their shame” (Philippians 3:19).

The people drank the dust of the calf that Israel had worshiped, as a contempt for superstition, so that they might learn to despise what they had seen cast into the privy.

Priests are commanded not to drink wine or strong drink when they are about to minister in the Temple, lest their hearts be weighed down by drunkenness, gluttony, and the cares of this life; nor may they have any portion in the land except God alone (Leviticus 10), so that they bear no bodily defect. [Note: The Benedictine edition, wrongly following Erasmus, has *segnes* (“sluggish”) here instead of *insignes* (“marked,” “distinguished”). We have restored the latter from other printed editions and nearly all manuscripts.]

They must not be marked by mutilated ears, a damaged eye, flattened nostrils, a lame foot, or altered skin color—all of which refer to vices of the soul. For it is the will in a human being, not nature, that is condemned.

If one of the priests suffers a seminal discharge, he is forbidden to approach the priestly table. Conversely, a widow whose womanhood has ceased with Sarah is admitted into her father’s household because of her continence and chastity, and is fed from the treasury of the Temple. If she has children, she is restored to her offspring, so that, according to the Apostle, she may be provided for as one “who is truly a widow” (1 Timothy 5:3), and so that she who is sustained by priestly food may not be bound by love for anyone else.

A neighbor and a hired servant are excluded from the priests’ banquet; slaves are allowed the leftovers of the food.

Even then Phygelus and Hermogenes were rejected, while Onesiphorus was received. [Note: Ducaeus, with the agreement of the manuscripts and the first Mainz edition of 1470, insists that *Onesimus* be retained. Moreover, Onesimus was the slave of Philemon, according to Paul’s letter to him, verse 15 and following; Onesiphorus was not a slave but a free man and a host of the Apostle.]

The firstfruits of foods, and of all grain and fruit, are offered to the overseer, so that, possessing food and clothing, he may serve the Lord securely, freely, and without any impediment. The priests receive the firstborn of clean animals; for unclean animals, their price. The firstborn of human beings are also redeemed, and because the condition of birth is the same for all, the price is offered equally—moderate and light, [Note: Some printed editions and manuscripts wrongly read, “because the human condition of birth is common, all offer the price equally.”] so that neither does the rich swell with pride nor is the poor burdened.

The attendants and doorkeepers receive tithes, and in turn offer a tithe of tithes to the priests (Numbers 18 and 35): they are as much lower than the priests as the priests themselves are higher than the people.

Forty-eight cities are set apart for the Levites and priests to inhabit. Six cities of refuge are chosen, across the Jordan and within the Jordan; and the end of exile is the death of the Pontiff.

All that my hurried speech has touched upon, and whose mysteries I have merely knocked upon without opening them, concerns all priests. But how many privileges belong to the Pontiff, I shall briefly explain.

#### 3.

“He shall not uncover his head” (Leviticus 21). He wears a turban and bears the name of God upon his forehead. He is adorned with a royal diadem; he has come to the perfect age of Christ and must always be protected by his glory. He shall not tear his garments, because they are white, undefiled, and follow the Lamb, being made from the wool of a shorn sheep.

Thamar, having lost her chastity, tore her garment (Genesis 38). Caiaphas, having lost the priesthood, publicly tore his garments (Matthew 26). “He shall not enter in over any soul who has died” (Leviticus 21:11). [Note: This is the old translator’s rendering of the Greek *ἐπὶ πᾶση ψυχῇ τετελευτηκυίᾳ*, and therefore, in place of the earlier *in instanti*, we have printed *ingredietur* (“he shall enter”). Such words here and elsewhere are not Jerome’s words but those of Scripture.]

Wherever there is sin, and death in sin, the Pontiff does not approach. “The soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezekiel 18). Even if the person is rich, powerful, and offers a multitude of victims, if he is dead, he is not touched or regarded by the Pontiff. [Note: The Queen’s copy reads, “he is not touched by the priest or Pontiff; he is not seen.” Shortly afterward it has *reviviscit* (“he comes to life again”) instead of *resurgit* (“he rises again”).]

But if he rises again, comes out of the tomb at the voice of the Savior, and walks freed from the bindings of his sins (John 11 and 12), the Pontiff will enter to him; there he will make his dwelling, and he will dine with the one who has risen.

#### 4.

“Over his father and his mother he shall not be defiled” (Leviticus 21:11).

Affection compels us to do many things; and while we regard bodily kinship, we offend the Creator of both body and soul. Whoever loves father or mother more than Christ is not worthy of him (Luke 9). A disciple who desired to go to bury his father is forbidden to do so by the command of the Savior.

How many monks, while pitying their father and mother, have lost their souls! We may not be defiled over father and mother—how much less over brother, sisters, cousins, household members, and servants! We are a royal and priestly race.

Let us attend to that Father who never dies, or who dies for us: who was dead while living for this reason, that he might give life to us who were dead.

If we have anything from Egypt that the prince of this world could recognize as his own, let us leave it with the Egyptian woman who held on to the cloak (Genesis 39). The young man covered with a linen cloth followed the bound Lord (Mark 14); he would have fallen into snares unless, unencumbered and naked, he had avoided the attack of his pursuers.

Let us give parents what belongs to parents—if indeed they are alive, and if, as servants of the Lord, they glory in having their children preferred to themselves.

#### 5.

“And he shall not go out from the sanctuary, nor profane the sanctification of his God” (Leviticus 21:12).

We shall have to give an account even for an idle word, and everything that does not build up those who hear turns into danger for those who speak. If I do or say something deserving of criticism, I go out from the sanctuary and profane the name of Christ in which I take pride.

How much more, then, must this be true of a Pontiff and bishop, who ought to be without blame (Titus 1), and possess such virtues that he always dwells among holy things, ready to offer sacrifices for the people, a mediator [Note: The same statement occurs in the commentary on Malachi, chapter 2; Origen, in Homily 2 on Leviticus; Basil, *Monastic Constitutions*, chapter 22; and other ancient writers agree with it. Augustine, however, in *Against Parmenianus* 2.8, rebukes this Donatist for saying that the bishop is a mediator between human beings and God, since Christ Jesus is the one mediator. Jerome’s statement must therefore be understood in the sense that he wishes the bishop to be a mediator only in ministry and intercession.] between human beings and God, and one who prepares the flesh of the Lamb with his sacred mouth: “Because the holy oil of Christ, his God, is upon him.” [Note: From the Greek *ὅτι τὸ ἅγιον ἔλαιον τὸ Χριστοῦ τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐπ’ αὐτοῦ*. The name “Christ” is absent from the older Jerome editions but appears in the manuscripts. It may easily be a corruption for *chrisma* (“anointing oil”), or, more correctly, “Christ” should be read in its place.]

He shall not go out from the sanctuary, lest he profane the garment with which he is clothed. For as many as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ (Galatians 3). Let us preserve the tunic we have received; let us guard the holy garment in the holy place.

That mountain-dwelling man who was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho was not wounded until he had been stripped. Oil—a gentle medicine tempered with mercy—is poured into his wounds; and because he ought to feel the pain of his negligence, he is bitten by the harshness of wine (Luke 10), so that through the oil he may be summoned to repentance and through the wine feel the severity of the judge.

#### 6.

“He shall take a virgin as his wife, but he shall not take a widow, a divorced woman, or a prostitute; he shall take a virgin from his own people, and he shall not profane his offspring among his people. I am the Lord who sanctifies him” (Leviticus 21:14).

I know that many understand the Pontiff to whom these commandments are now given as Christ, and that the statement “He shall not be defiled over father and mother” is explained of the Virgin Mary’s birth. The interpretation concerning the Lord is much easier, since we read in the Psalm: “You are a priest forever, according to the order of Melchizedek” [Psalm 109:4]. And in Zechariah: “Hear, Jesus, great priest” (Zechariah 3:8). It is he whose filthy garments—our sins—are removed, so that they may receive the glory that he had with the Father before the world existed.

#### 7.

But lest anyone think that I am forcing Scripture and love Christ so much that I deprive history of its truth, I shall interpret it in the members as referring to the head; [Note: Two Royal codices wrongly read “the body” in place of “the head.” We have also corrected some minor matters below.] I shall understand it of the servants as being fulfilled in the Lord. Although the Lord’s glory is also the glory of his servants.

Whenever the opportunity of the passage allows, I shall speak of the true light in such a way that it is extended to those to whom Christ granted that they should be lights.

This Pontiff, whom the Mosaic text describes, does not marry a divorced woman, a prostitute, or a widow. A widow is one whose husband has died. A divorced woman is one who is cast off by a living husband. A prostitute is one who is open to the lust of many.

But, he says, he shall take a virgin as his wife, from his own people, not a foreigner, lest the grain of noble seed degenerate in bad soil. Not a prostitute, who is exposed to many lovers. Not a divorced woman, who was unworthy even of her first marriage. Not a widow, lest she remember former pleasures. Rather, he shall take that soul which has neither spot nor wrinkle, which, reborn with Christ, is renewed from day to day, and of which the Apostle says: “For I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (1 Corinthians 11:2).

I do not want the Pontiff’s disciple and wife to retain anything of the old person. If we have risen with Christ, let us set our minds on the things above, forgetting what lies behind and eager for what is to come.

Unhappy Simon! Because after baptism he was thinking about his former marriage and had not attained virginal purity, he was unworthy of Peter’s company.

#### 8.

You compelled me, Fabiola, by your letters to write to you about Aaron’s priesthood and garments. I offered more, so that I might compose a preface concerning the foods and firstfruits of the priests and the observance of the Pontiff. [Note: In agreement with the old edition of 1496, another Royal manuscript reads, “so that I might write to you about Aaron’s garments,” without any mention of the priesthood. It may be more correct to omit that phrase, since Jerome does not explain the mysteries of that dignity.]

Having gone out from Sodom and hastening toward the mountains, you do not wish to dwell in the little city of Zoar. Passing beyond proselytes, you pass beyond Israelites; leaving behind the Levitical rank and flying over the priests on swift wings, you come to the Pontiff.

But while you carefully inquire into his garments and the breastpiece, our company has displeased you. You enjoy the leisure you desired, and perhaps, beside Babylon, you sigh for the fields of Bethlehem.

We in Ephrathah, now that peace has at last been restored, hear the infant crying from the manger; and we wish his complaints and little cries to reach your ears.

#### 9.

We read in Exodus about the tabernacle, the table, the lampstand, the altar, the columns, the curtains, scarlet, fine linen, hyacinth, and purple; about vessels of gold, silver, and bronze; the tabernacle divided into three parts; twelve loaves placed upon the table each week; seven lamps on the lampstand; the altar set out for sacrifices and burnt offerings; bowls, cups, censers, basins, mortars, pegs, red skins, goats’ hair, and imperishable wood (Exodus 35 and following).

Such great and varied things are offered in the tabernacle of God that no one should despair of salvation. One offers the gold of the senses, another the silver of eloquence, another the voice of bronze.

The whole world is described in the mystery of the tabernacle. The first and second vestibules are open to everyone, for water and earth have been given to all mortals. But into the Holy of Holies, as though toward the ether and heaven, only a few have entrance and flight.

The twelve loaves signify the cycle of the twelve months. The seven lamps signify the seven wandering stars.

And, so that I do not make this long—for it is not my purpose now to write about the tabernacle—I shall come to the priestly garments. Before I investigate their mystical meaning, I shall, in the Jewish manner, explain simply what has been written, so that once you have seen the priest dressed and all his adornment has been revealed to your eyes, [Note: Martianaeus reads *ornamentum* (“ornament”), retaining *omnis*, which is scarcely Latin.] we may then examine together the reasons for each part.

### 10.

Let us first learn about the common garments of the priests and those of the high priests. With linen undergarments reaching to the knees and the hamstrings, the private parts are concealed, while the upper portion is tightly fastened below the navel, so that, whenever they slaughter victims unencumbered, drag bulls and rams, carry burdens, or are engaged in ministering—even if they should fall and expose their thighs—what has been covered may not be exposed. For this reason steps are also forbidden to be made for the altar, lest the lower people see the private parts of those ascending. In the Hebrew language this kind of garment is called MACHNASE; in Greek, περισκελῆ (*periskelē*), and among us *feminalia*, or breeches reaching to the knees.

Josephus reports—for the Temple still stood in his day, and Vespasian and Titus had not yet overthrown Jerusalem, while he himself was of priestly descent, and what is seen with the eyes is understood far more clearly than what is received through the ears—that these undergarments were customarily woven from twisted byssus for strength and, after being cut, sewn together with a needle. For such a thing cannot be made on a loom.

**Note [Col. 0613].** In most manuscripts the reading is *Machinasen*; in two of the Regina manuscripts, *Maschense*; Erasmus had read *Michense*, Frobenius *Michnese*, and other printed copies have *Maschinase* and *Machinase*. In Greek: μαχανσήν or μαχανασύν, and in Josephus, corruptly, μεχανασίν and μαναχασήν. In place of περισκελῆ, Erasmus formerly had περισκελὴς, while the manuscripts have περισκελές. The Chaldeans say *micnesin*, or, in the dual number, *micnesain* and *macnesin*—that is, συνακτῆρες, “constricting garments,” from a verb that properly means “to bind.” In the sacred text, however, the material is immediately added, as in the two [unreadable expressions]. See our notes on Daniel 3.

### 11.

The second garment is the linen tunic, ποδήρης (*podērēs*), that is, ankle-length, made of a double linen cloth, which Josephus also calls *byssina*. It is called CHOTONATH, that is, χετὼν (*chetōn*), a word which in Hebrew is rendered “linen.” This garment clings to the body and is so close-fitting, with tight sleeves, that there is no wrinkle at all in the whole garment; it descends as far as the legs.

For the convenience of the reader, I shall use the common term. Soldiers customarily wear linen garments, which they call *camisiae*, fitted so closely to their limbs and bodies that they are unimpeded whether for running or for battle, for directing a javelin, holding a shield, wielding a sword, or for whatever necessity may summon them. Therefore priests also, prepared for the service of God, wear this tunic, so that, possessing the beauty of garments, they may move with the speed of those who are naked.

**Note [Col. 0613].** It is better to hear Josephus’s own words: “And over this he wears a linen garment of a double cloth; woven of byssus, it is called … .” “This signifies linen; for what we call linen, we call χεθόν.” No one should therefore rashly suspect that here too Hieronymus should be read as having χεθὸν or χεθὼν instead of χιτὼν. The word is derived from *Cettan* among the Chaldeans and Arabs, which in Latin is *linum*, “linen”; hence *linea* is a linen garment, contrary to Martianaeus’s spelling without *vau*. From this derive the Greek χετὼν and the Latin *tunica*: there is no doubt about the word’s origin.

**Note [Col. 0614].** See Macrobius, *Saturnalia* 7.13. Dionysius likewise speaks of the linen or shirts of soldiers in these verses:

> “And he adorned his snow-white body with a linen robe,  
> Such as warriors always wear beneath their breastplate.”

Later Greeks, according to Eustathius on the *Iliad* 22, called it ἐπικαμισα. There he argues that χαιτῶνα (*chaitōna*) is not simply an under-tunic.

### 12.

The third kind of garment is what they call ABANET; we may call it a girdle, belt, or sash. The Babylonians call it HEMIAN, using a new term. We give several names so that no one may be confused by the terminology.

This belt is woven in the likeness of a serpent’s skin, with which it casts off its old age. It is woven round, so that one might think it a long purse. It is made with a scarlet, purple, and hyacinth-colored weft and a byssine warp, both for beauty and for strength. It is worked in such a variegated fashion that one might think the various flowers and gems had not been woven by the craftsman but added afterward by his hand.

They fasten with this belt the linen tunic of which we spoke above, between the navel and the chest. The belt is four fingers wide and hangs down on one side to the legs; when speed and readiness are required for sacrifice, it is thrown over the left shoulder.

**Note [Col. 0614].** It is now called in Persian *hemia*, a word signifying a belt; the Persians easily learned it from the Babylonians.

**Note [Col. 0614].** The Regina manuscript reads: “with which it sheds itself in summer.”

**Note [Col. 0614].** The same [manuscript reads] “descending for the most part … .”

### 13.

The fourth kind of garment is a rounded cap, such as we see painted on Ulysses, as though a hemisphere had been divided and one half placed upon his head. The Greeks and our people call it τιάρα (*tiara*); some call it a cap. The Hebrews call it MISNEPHETH.

It has no point at the top and does not cover the entire head down to the hair. Rather, it leaves one-third of the forehead uncovered; then it is fastened at the back of the head with a band, so that it does not easily slip from the head. It is made of byssus and so skillfully fashioned from fine linen that no trace of the needle appears on the outside.

**Note [Col. 0614].** Formerly the text read *in Ulysse* or *in Ulyxeo*, a word which Victorius interprets as the portico in which deeds of Ulysses could be seen painted. Formerly it was written *in Ulyxi*, and good authorities support both spellings. It is well known from Pliny and others that in the painting of the wandering Ulysses, by the painter Nicomachus, a sailor’s cap was placed upon the head of the extremely crafty hero. The learned write the name *Ulyxes*: the ancient Latins did not say *Ulysses*, and in nearly all ancient Latin copies *Ulyxes* is written; printed books, however, improperly prefer the other spelling. See Plutarch, *Marcellus*: “but those things belonging to Ulysses, that is, Odysseus.” Consult Homer, *Iliad* 22, concerning Ulysses’ cap, and Eustathius again on that passage. Ducaeus nevertheless prefers *Ulixeo*, because the Latins pronounce Greek names ending in -ευς with the syllable -eus, as in *Achilleus*, *Theseus*, and so forth.

**Note [Col. 0614].** In Josephus the form is μασναεμφθὴς, or, closer to the Chaldean, μεσναέφθης, *Masnaephtes*. Formerly Hieronymus was read as having *Manephet* or *Masnephet*, with *A* substituted for *I* according to the Syriac usage in words of this form beginning with Mem and Hiriq. Neither Hebrew form, *Misnephes*, is found in the Regina manuscripts. What the holy Doctor adds—that it does not have a point at the top—is contradicted by the error of modern interpreters, who say that its upper part extended to a point. Shortly afterward, where the text has “appear outwardly,” the manuscripts read “appear”; formerly it read “appear externally.”

### 14.

Priests and high priests alike use these four garments: the undergarments, the linen tunic, the belt woven of purple, scarlet, byssus, and hyacinth, and the cap of which we have just spoken.

The remaining four belong properly to the high priests. The first of these is called MAIL, that is, an ankle-length tunic, entirely hyacinth-colored. It has sleeves of the same color sewn to its sides, and at the upper part, where it is put over the neck, it is open in the place commonly called the neck-opening. Its edges are woven with the greatest firmness so that they do not easily tear.

At the lower edge, that is, at the feet, are seventy-two bells and as many pomegranates, woven in the same colors as the belt above. Between two bells there is one pomegranate, and between two pomegranates one bell, so that each alternates with the other and stands between its companions. The reason is given: bells were attached to the garment so that, when the high priest entered the Holy of Holies, he might proceed wholly vocal; otherwise he would immediately die.

**Note [Col. 0615].** Josephus says, “It is called *Meïr* in our language.” Hieronymus derives the term from [the Hebrew words] which the Septuagint variously rendered, sometimes as ὑποδύτης χιτὼν, “the tunic beneath the ephod,” that is, an undertunic, as in Letter 29 to Marcella, 2; sometimes as ἐπενδύτης, “the garment worn over the tunic.” The word *superula*, or ἐπενδύτης, properly signifies a garment worn over another from its origin.

**Note [Col. 0615].** Victorius argues that the reading should be *rumpatur*, “the ankle-length tunic may be torn.”

### 15.

The sixth garment is called in Hebrew EPHOD. The Septuagint call it ἐπωμίς (*epōmis*), that is, a shoulder-garment. Aquila calls it ἐπένδυμα (*ependuma*), “an outer garment.” We retain EPHOD as its proper name. Wherever “shoulder-garment” is read in Exodus or Leviticus, we should know that among the Hebrews it is called *Ephod*.

I remember having written that this is the garment of the high priest in a certain letter, and all Scripture bears witness that it is something sacred and suited only to high priests. We should not immediately object that Samuel, who was a Levite, is said in the First Book of Kings to have possessed, while still a little child, an *ephod bad*, that is, a linen shoulder-garment; for David too is reported to have worn the same before the ark of the Lord. One thing is to have a garment woven from the four colors mentioned above—hyacinth, byssus, scarlet, and purple—and from gold; another is to have a simple linen garment resembling those of ordinary priests.

Plates of gold, that is, thin leaves, are stretched with extraordinary delicacy. From them, when they have been cut into strips, threads are twisted, together with a weft of three colors—hyacinth, scarlet, and purple—and a byssine warp. The result is a little mantle of extraordinary beauty, flashing before the eyes like *caracallae*, but without hoods. Nothing is woven over the chest, and a place is left for the future Rationale.

On each shoulder it has one stone enclosed and fastened in gold. In Hebrew these are called SOOM. Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion translate them as onyx stones; the Septuagint translate them as emeralds; Josephus calls them sardonyxes, agreeing with the Hebrew and with Aquila either in indicating the color of the stones or their place of origin.

On each stone are engraved six names of the patriarchs, by whom the Israelite people are divided.

**Note [Col. 0616].** The old edition reads “twice six,” incorrectly. The elder sons of Jacob are written on the right shoulder and the younger on the left, so that, when the high priest enters the Holy of Holies, he may carry upon his shoulders the names of the people on whose behalf he is going to entreat the Lord.

**Note [Col. 0615].** Two manuscripts read: “They are made with great thinness; after they have been cut, seven threads are twisted from them.” In others we find “are cast.” Compare Exodus 36:3 and Philo, *Life of Moses*.

**Note [Col. 0615].** The Regina manuscript reads: “a little mantle of variegated beauty”; below, Josephus calls them “Sardians” instead of sardonyxes.

**Note [Col. 0616].** All Hieronymian manuscripts ascribe the same version to Symmachus and Theodotion; hence Drusius incorrectly thought that these two names had been inserted and that the reading should be attributed solely to Aquila.

**Note [Col. 0616].** As far as the Hebrew is concerned, I believe Hieronymus is alluding to the name translated “sardonyx,” for we know no other name by which it is written in the Hebrew text—in Exodus, Isaiah, and Ezekiel. The interpretation of the name also fits, since it refers, as he himself suggests, to the stone’s color: it is called “red,” and hence is commonly known as a ruby. When he adds that Josephus agrees with Aquila, I think he means another edition of Aquila, since he had just said that Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion call them onyx stones. Finally, in wishing the name to indicate the stone’s homeland, he agrees with Pliny, who says that the sard gem shares its name with the sardonyx, and in the final book testifies that the *sarda* was first found at Sardis—that is, among the Lydians—but is most highly valued around Babylon. Saint Epiphanius likewise, in this very letter, more than once speaks of the gems when quoted by Hieronymus: “The first stone of the breastpiece is a sard; it is fiery in appearance and blood-colored. It is found in Babylon toward Assyria. The stone is transparent,” and so forth. These words require no interpretation.

### 16.

The seventh garment is small in size but holier than all those mentioned above. Pay attention, I ask, so that you may understand what is being said. In Hebrew it is called HOSEN, in Greek λόγιον (*logion*), and we may call it the Rationale, so that from the name itself you may immediately know that what is being described is mystical.

It is a short cloth woven of gold and the same four colors as the shoulder-garment. It is a span square and double, so that it may not easily tear. Woven into it are twelve stones of extraordinary size and value, arranged in four rows, with three stones in each row.

In the first row are sardius, topaz, and emerald. Symmachus differs concerning the emerald, translating it as ceraunium, “thunderstone,” because the substance glitters like a spark. In the second row are carbuncle, sapphire, and jasper. In the third are ligure, agate, and amethyst. In the fourth are chrysolite, onyx, and beryl.

I am sufficiently astonished that the most precious hyacinth is not included among these stones, unless perhaps it is the same stone under another name, the ligure. Searching the writers who have discussed the nature of stones and gems, I have not been able to find the ligure.

On each stone are engraved the names of the twelve tribes, according to their generations. We read of these stones in the diadem of the prince of Tyre and in the Apocalypse of John, from which the heavenly Jerusalem is built (Ezek. 28; Rev. 21). Under their names and appearance, either the order or the diversity of the virtues is indicated.

At the four corners of the Rationale are four golden rings, corresponding to four others on the shoulder-garment. Thus, when the λόγιον has been placed in the space which we said had been left open in the Ephod, ring meets ring, and they are joined to one another by hyacinth-colored bands.

Moreover, lest the size and weight of the stones should tear the woven threads, they were bound and enclosed in gold. Even this was not sufficient for strength unless chains of gold were also made; for the sake of beauty these were covered with golden tubes. The Rationale had two larger rings above, which were attached by hooks to the golden rings of the shoulder-garment, and two others below. For behind, on the shoulder-garment opposite the chest and stomach, there were golden rings on both sides; these were joined by chains to the lower rings of the Rationale. Thus the Rationale was fastened to the shoulder-garment and the shoulder-garment to the Rationale, so that to observers they appeared to be a single woven garment.

**Note [Col. 0616].** The Greek is κεραύνιον, because this substance glitters like a spark. Below, from the old edition, we restore *ligure* or *lygure* in place of *lyncure*, as will be explained shortly.

**Note [Col. 0616].** The text has been printed in this form since Erasmus, but *ligure* should be read according to the ancient manuscripts, as others before us have noticed. *Lyncure* is something else, more probably amber than a kind of hyacinth or another gem which Pliny could have seen in his own time. Hence Hesychius has λυγκούριον, ἤλεκτρον, “lyncure, amber,” although Theophrastus and other ancient writers improperly confused amber, λιγύριον, or λιγγύριον, with the more valuable ligure. Hieronymus copied this from Epiphanius, who likewise confesses that he does not know the nature of the gem; Psellus also lists it among unknown gems.

### 18.

The eighth is a golden plate, that is, SIS ZAAB, on which the name of God is written in four Hebrew letters: JOD, HE, VAV, HE. Among them this name is called ineffable. It is added to the linen cap common to all priests, and in the case of the high priest it is fastened above the cap by a hyacinth-colored band at the forehead, so that the name of God may crown and protect the high priest’s entire beauty.

### 19.

We have learned which garments are common to priests and which are particular to the high priest. If there was so much difficulty in earthen vessels, how great must be the majesty of the treasure hidden within?
