Let us therefore first say what we have received from the Hebrews; afterward, according to our custom, let us open the veils of spiritual understanding.

The four colors correspond to the four elements from which the whole universe subsists. Byssus is assigned to the earth, because it is produced from the earth. Purple belongs to the sea, because it is dyed from its shellfish. Hyacinth belongs to the air, because of its resemblance in color. Scarlet belongs to fire and to the ether, which is called SANI in Hebrew. Aquila translated this as διάφορον, Symmachus as δίβαφον. Instead of *coccus*, “scarlet,” Hebrew has THOLATH, that is, “worm.”

They say that it was right for the high priest, adorned with all created things, to pray not only for Israel but also for the whole world, since this world consists of earth, water, air, and fire, and these are the elements of everything.

Thus the first, linen garment signifies the earth. The second, hyacinth-colored garment represents the air in its color, because we are gradually lifted from earthly things to lofty ones. The same hyacinth garment, extending from the head to the ankles, indicates that the air is poured out from heaven as far as the earth.

The pomegranates and bells placed below signify flashes of lightning and peals of thunder, or earth and water and the harmony of all the elements with one another. Everything is so interwoven with everything else that all things are found in each individual element.

The fact that the colors mentioned above are woven with gold is understood to signify that vital heat and the providence of divine understanding penetrate everything.

The shoulder-garment and the two stones, whether emeralds or onyxes, which are placed above and cover both shoulders, are interpreted as the two hemispheres, one above the earth and the other beneath it; or as the sun and moon, which shine above.

The belt by which the priest’s chest is tightened, and by which the linen tunic—that is, the earth—is constricted, is interpreted as the ocean.

The Rationale, placed in the middle, they explain as the earth. Although it is like a point and contains everything within itself, it is nevertheless surrounded by all the elements.

The twelve stones are interpreted either as the zodiacal circle or as the twelve months. They assign one season to each row and allot three months to each.

Let no one think this interpretation pagan. For if pagans have defamed heavenly things and the disposition of God by applying the names of idols to them, God’s providence—which proceeds and is carried along according to a fixed law and governs all things—is not therefore to be denied. In Job too we read of Arcturus, Orion, MAZUROTH—that is, the zodiacal circle—and the other names of the stars (Job 9 and 39). This is not because the Hebrews use the same vocabulary, but because we cannot understand what is said except through familiar expressions.

It is beautifully named the Rationale, because all things are full of reason, and earthly things cling to heavenly things. Indeed, the ordering of earthly things and of times, heat and cold, and the twofold balance between them descends from the course and order of heaven. For this reason the Rationale is fastened more firmly to the Ephod.

As for the statement that within the Rationale there are δήλωσις and ἀλήθεια—that is, “manifestation” and “doctrine,” or “truth”—this signifies that there is never falsehood in the reason of God. Truth itself is displayed to human beings through many signs and proofs and comes down even to mortals.

Thus we came to know the ordering of the sun, moon, year, months, seasons, hours, weather, clear skies, winds, and all things, receiving wisdom implanted by God, while he himself, as indweller and teacher, reveals to us knowledge of his dwelling and its construction.

Above everything, the diadem and the hyacinth-colored band signify heaven. The golden plate on the high priest’s forehead, bearing the name of God, shows that everything beneath is governed by God’s will.

I think the same thing is represented under other names in the Cherubim and the four living creatures. They are so intermingled and joined to one another that the others are found in each one, and they move continually forward before them without turning back. For times slip away, leaving the past behind and hastening toward the future.

Their perpetual motion signifies what philosophers too conjecture: that the world runs in its ordered course and turns without ceasing like a wheel on its axle. Thus there is a wheel within a wheel—that is, time within time—and the year revolves back upon itself. The wheels themselves are lifted toward heaven; above the crystal is a throne of sapphire, and above the throne the likeness of one seated. His lower parts are fiery, his upper parts like electrum, to show that the lower regions need fire and purification, while those above remain in the purity of their creation.

Just as here the golden plate is placed above the priest’s vestments, so in Ezekiel electrum is placed upon the chest and crown (Ezek. 1 and 8).

It was therefore right—as we said partly above—for the high priest of God, bearing in his garments the type of all created things, to indicate that all things need the mercy of God. When he sacrificed to God, the universal creation was purified, so that he might pray not for children, parents, and relatives alone, but for the whole creation, both in voice and in dress.

**Note [Col. 0617].** Most manuscripts read “and to the air.” But Josephus, Book 3, chapter 7, from whom Hieronymus translated this material, and Philo make no comparison either of scarlet with air or with ether. Origen, too, repeats the following as though it were universally known: “Hyacinth, then, is referred to the air, for the color itself indicates this; just as scarlet is referred to fire, purple represents water, since it receives its dye from water, and byssus represents earth, because it arises from earth.” For διάφορον below, Drusius read διάφανον, as does the Roman edition of the Septuagint under Aquila, and almost all editions based on the printed Hieronymian manuscripts; and instead of Symmachus’s δίβαφον, most manuscripts incorrectly have *diafor* in Latin letters.

**Note [Col. 0617].** One Regina manuscript reads: “so that the high priest, adorned with all created things, not only … .” This seems to us to preserve Hieronymus’s own text rather than a glossator’s invention. Below, in the same sense: “It was right, therefore, as we said above in part, that the high priest of God, bearing in his garments the type of all created things, should indicate that everything needs the mercy of God.”

**Note [Col. 0618].** Victorius reads *sustollitur*, “is lifted up,” referring to the air, and supports this reading from what follows, accusing the printed text of falsity. We follow our manuscripts.

**Note [Col. 0618].** The Cluniac manuscript reads *lecrio* in Martianaeus. Since it constricts the earth, this agrees more closely with Josephus’s Greek text: “The belt encircling the ocean signifies [the ocean], for it too encompasses all things,” which Hieronymus has translated almost literally.

**Note [Col. 0618].** Not through a printer’s error, as Martianaeus thinks, but from the Hebrew text of 2 Kings 23, Erasmus and Victorius had read *Mazoloth*, although in Job 39:32, the passage noted by Hieronymus, the Septuagint have *Mazuroth* or *Mazaroth*, as Hieronymus himself reads elsewhere in his book on names at 2 Kings. Theodoret writes concerning that passage: “I think *Mazuroth* is the name of a star, and I conjecture that the morning star is so called.” *Muzuroth*, I think, is the name of a star, and I conjecture that Lucifer is so named.

**Note [Col. 0619].** The Regina manuscripts, which we chiefly use, read: “those things which are upon the earth.”

### 20.

We have touched upon the Hebrew interpretation, and, reserving the boundless forest of meanings for another time, have laid certain foundations for the house that is to come.

Concerning the linen undergarments they are accustomed to say that the principle of seed and generation, pertaining to the flesh, is assigned through it to the earth. Hence God says to Adam: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. 3:19). The reasons for this—that from a tiny seed and the most shameful beginnings so much beauty should arise, whether of human beings or of different things—are hidden and do not lie open to human eyes.

We read in Leviticus (Lev. 8) that, according to God’s command, Moses washed Aaron and his sons. Even then the sacraments of Baptism signified the cleansing of the world and the holiness of all things. They do not receive the garments until their filth has first been washed away, nor are they adorned for sacred duties unless they are reborn as new people in Christ. For new wine is put into new wineskins.

The fact that Moses washes them is an indication of the Law. “They have Moses and the Prophets; let them listen to them.” And: “All sinned, from Adam to Moses.”

We must be washed by the commands of God. When, prepared for the clothing of Christ, we have put off the tunics of skins, then we shall be clothed in a linen garment containing no trace of death, but wholly bright. Rising from Baptism, we shall gird our loins in truth, and all the shamefulness of our former sins shall be concealed. Hence David says: “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered” (Ps. 31:1).

**Note [Col. 0619].** Understand “the flesh,” through which it is assigned to the earth. Martianaeus read *proxima*; Erasmus and Victorius, *per ea*. We have preferred to follow the Cluniac manuscript, which the Benedictine editor rejected, together with the authority of another Regina manuscript and of the oldest edition; through these the most truthful and clear sense emerges.

### 21.

After the undergarments and linen tunic, we put on the hyacinth-colored garment and begin to ascend from earthly things to lofty ones.

This hyacinth-colored tunic is called by the Septuagint ὑποδύτης (*hypodutēs*), that is, an undertunic, and properly belongs to the high priest. It signifies that the understanding of heavenly things is not open to everyone, but to the greater and more perfect.

Moses and Aaron and the Prophets possessed it, and all those to whom it is said: “Ascend upon the high mountain, you who evangelize Zion” (Isa. 40:9).

The earlier washing away of sins, the grace of Baptism, and more secret instruction are not enough for us unless we also possess works. Hence the Ephod, that is, the shoulder-garment, is joined to it and attached to the Rationale, so that it may not be loose or slack, but that they may cling to one another and assist one another.

Reason needs works, and works need reason, so that what we grasp in the mind we may carry out in deed.

The two stones on the shoulder-garment signify either Christ and the Church, containing the names of the twelve Apostles who were sent to preach, or the letter and the spirit, in which all the mysteries of the Law are contained. On the right is the spirit; on the left, the letter. Through letters we descend to words; through words we arrive at meaning.

What a beautiful order, demonstrating the mysteries through the garment itself! On the shoulders are works; on the chest is reason. Hence the priests eat the breast [of the sacrifice].

This Rationale is twofold: open and hidden, simple and mystical. It contains twelve stones and four rows, which I think are the four virtues—Prudence, Fortitude, Justice, and Temperance—which cling to one another; and, when they are mutually intermingled, produce the number twelve.

Or they may be the four Gospels, which are described in the Apocalypse as full of eyes (Rev. 14:6) and, radiant with the light of the Lord, illuminate the world: four in one and one in each of the four.

Therefore δήλωσις and ἀλήθεια—that is, doctrine and truth—are on the priest’s chest. When someone has been clothed in a many-colored garment, it follows that he should bring forth in speech the truth which he holds in his heart. For this reason there is truth in the Rationale—that is, knowledge, so that he may know what ought to be taught—and manifestation and doctrine, so that he may instruct others in what he has conceived in his mind.

Where are those who say that innocence can be sufficient for a priest? The Old Law agrees with the New: Moses says the same as the Apostle. The former adorns the priest’s knowledge in garments; the latter instructs Timothy and Titus in disciplines.

But the order of the garments itself is also of the greatest importance. Let us read Leviticus. It was not first the Rationale and then the shoulder-garment, but first the shoulder-garment and afterward the Rationale (Lev. 8).

“I have gained understanding from your commandments,” he says (Ps. 118:104). Let us first act, and then teach, lest the authority of teaching be destroyed by empty works.

This is what we read in the Prophet: “Sow for yourselves in righteousness, and reap the fruit of life; enlighten yourselves with the light of knowledge” (Hos. 10:12). First sow in righteousness and reap the fruit of eternal life; afterward claim knowledge for yourselves.

Nor is perfection immediately complete if someone possesses the shoulder-garment and the Rationale, unless these are strengthened by a firm bond between them and joined together, so that action clings to reason and reason to action. When these have preceded, doctrine and truth should follow.

**Note [Col. 0620].** Erasmus and Victorius read “animals,” a word which we believe they inserted into the Hieronymian text. All the manuscripts examined by us and by the Benedictine editor, as well as the old editions, retain “Gospels.” Hieronymus could quite elegantly have applied, metaphorically, to the Gospels themselves what in the Apocalypse is attributed to the symbols of the Gospels; all the more because the words “one in four, and four in one” are properly spoken of the Gospels. Unless perhaps the holy Doctor wrote both “the four Gospels” and “the four living creatures,” with one of the two expressions later lost because of the repetition. Shortly afterward, instead of “radiant with the Lord’s light,” some manuscripts read “burning lamps of the Lord.”

**Note [Col. 0620].** All printed editions except Martianaeus add “manifestation,” or something similar; I do not know whether that reading is more correct.

### 22.

If I had the time to discuss the four elements of which we spoke above, the two stones—whether onyxes or emeralds—and the twelve gems set in the Rationale, I would explain to you the nature and significance of each, what each one represents, and how each corresponds to the individual virtues, after a fuller investigation.

It is enough to say that the holy Pope Epiphanius also published an excellent volume on this subject. If you wish to read it, you will attain the fullest knowledge. I already understand that I am exceeding the proper measure of a letter, and I see that the wax tablets of the one receiving it are full. Therefore I pass on to what remains, so that the discourse may finally come to an end.

The golden plate gleams on the forehead, for all learning is of no benefit to us unless we are crowned with the knowledge of God.

We put on the linen garments, are adorned with the hyacinth-colored garments, are girded with the sacred belt, are given works, and have the Rationale placed upon our chest. We receive truth, and speech brings forth doctrine. All these things are incomplete unless a worthy charioteer is sought for so beautiful a chariot, and unless the Creator, standing above his creatures, himself governs what he has made.

What was once displayed on the plate is now shown in the sign of the Cross. The blood of the Gospel is more precious than the gold of the Law.

Formerly, according to Ezekiel’s word, the sign was set upon the foreheads of those who groaned (Ezek. 9:4). Now, bearing the Cross, we say: “The light of your countenance has been marked upon us, O Lord” (Ps. 4:7).

Twice in Exodus (Exod. 28 and 29) we read that, at the Lord’s command and with Moses carrying out the orders, there were eight kinds of garments for the high priest. In Leviticus it is written concerning seven [lacuna] (Lev. 8), and it is related how Moses clothed his brother Aaron in them.

Nothing is said about the undergarments, for this reason, as I think: the Law does not lay its hand upon our genitals and private parts, but we ourselves must cover and veil what is more secret and worthy of shame, reserving the conscience of the purity of our thighs for God the Judge.

As for the other virtues—for example, wisdom, fortitude, justice, temperance, humility, gentleness, and generosity—others may judge them. Chastity is known by conscience alone, and human eyes cannot be reliable judges of it, except for those who are everywhere given over to lust in the manner of brute animals.

Hence the Apostle says: “Concerning virgins I have no command of the Lord” (1 Cor. 7:25), as though Moses were speaking: “I do not clothe anyone with undergarments, nor impose necessity upon anyone. Whoever wishes to be a priest must clothe himself.”

Oh, how many virgins, and the hoped-for chastity of how many people, will be disgraced on the day of judgment; and how many whose chastity has been defamed will be crowned by God the Judge!

Let us therefore ourselves take up the undergarments; let us ourselves cover our private parts; let us not seek the eyes of others. Let the genitals be covered so that they are exposed to no one’s eyes, lest, whenever we enter the Holy of Holies, if any shamefulness should appear, we die.

23. The discourse is now coming to an end, and I am drawn back to what I said above. Such must be the knowledge and learning of God’s High Priest that his very steps, movements, and all his utterances may be expressive. Let him conceive the truth in his mind and make it resound through his entire bearing and attire, so that whatever he does and whatever he says may be the instruction of the peoples. For without the bells, and the various colors, gems, and flowers of the virtues, he can neither enter the Holy Places nor possess the name of Bishop. These remarks I dictated in haste for a single little night’s work, when the cable was already being cast off from the shore and the sailors were calling out more frequently—everything I could retain in memory and everything I had gathered through long reading of the breastplate (*rationale*) of my heart. I understood well enough that I was flowing more from the impulse to speak than from the judgment proper to a writer, and that, like a torrent, I was bringing forth turbid speech. It is reported in the catalogue of Septimius Tertullian that there is a book on Aaron’s vestments.

[Note: This book of Tertullian has long since perished; indeed, we learn that it was composed by him almost solely from this one testimony of Jerome.]

If it should be found among you because of the renown of the City, I ask you not to compare my little trickle with that river. I should not be judged by the talents of great men, but by my own abilities.

373

## LETTER LXV

### TO THE VIRGIN PRINCIPIA, OR, AN EXPOSITION OF PSALM XLIV

[Note: [Col. 0622] Alternatively no. 140. Written about the middle of the year 397.]

He interprets the Forty-Fourth Psalm, which begins, “My heart has poured forth a good word,” in which the wedding song of Christ the Bridegroom and the Church his Bride is sung, for the Roman virgin Principia, after defending himself against slanders and defending the female sex, which in the exposition of Scripture he sometimes preferred to men.

### 1

I know, Principia, daughter in Christ, that I am criticized by many because I sometimes write to women and prefer the weaker sex to men. Therefore I must first answer my detractors, and then proceed to the brief discussion you requested.

If men were asking questions about the Scriptures, I would not speak to women. If Barak had been willing to go to battle, Deborah would not have triumphed over the defeated enemies (Judg. 5). Jeremiah is shut up in prison (Jer. 36), and because Israel, destined to perish, had not accepted a man who prophesied, a woman, Huldah, is raised up for them (2 Kings 22). The priests and Pharisees crucify the Son of God (Matt. 27), while Mary Magdalene weeps at the cross, prepares spices, seeks him in the tomb (Mark 16), questions the gardener, recognizes the Lord (John 20), goes to the Apostles, and announces that he has been found. They doubt; she believes.

Truly she is a πυργίτης (*pyrgitis*), truly a tower of whiteness and of Lebanon, who looks toward the face of Damascus (Song 7), that is, toward the blood of the Savior calling it to repentance in sackcloth.

[Note: That is, “tower-like,” from *turris*, “tower,” just as *montanus*, “mountainous,” comes from *mons*, “mountain,” as Jerome himself prefers in his book of Names. He again plays elegantly on the name Damascus, which signifies “sack of blood.”]

Sarah’s womanly functions had failed, and therefore Abraham is subjected to her, and it is said to him: “Whatever Sarah tells you, listen to her voice” (Gen. 18). Her womanly functions had failed; you have never possessed womanly functions. Your sex is devoured by virginity; you carry Christ in your body. You already possess what you are destined to become.

Rebecca goes to inquire of God and hears an oracle worthy of her answer: “Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples shall be divided from your belly” (Gen. 25:23). She gives birth to two who are divided; you conceive, bear, and give birth to one every day—fruitful in unity, manifold in majesty, harmonious in the Trinity.

374

[Note: The meaning is that he is fruitful through his unity or singularity. Jerome uses the word “unity” in this sense both elsewhere and especially in Letter 22, no. 19, to Eustochium on virginity, where the matter is explained at greater length.]

Mary, the sister of Moses, sings the Lord’s victories (Exod. 15), while Rachel marks our Bethlehem and Ephrath through the lineage of her name for generations to come (Gen. 35). The daughters of Zelophehad deserve to receive an inheritance among their brothers (Num. 27). Ruth, Esther, and Judith possess such glory that they have given their names to sacred books.

The prophetess Anna gives birth to a Levite, prophet, and judge, venerable for his sacred hair, and offers him in the tabernacle of God (1 Sam. 1–2). The woman of Tekoa traps King David with a question, teaches him by a riddle, and softens him by God’s example (2 Sam. 14). We also read of another wise woman who, when a city was under siege and the army commander Joab was battering its walls with a battering ram because of one rebel, spoke to the people in her wisdom and, by a woman’s authority, calmed the danger threatening so great a multitude (2 Sam. 20).

[Note: Understand this to refer to Sheba son of Bichri, whose well-known story is found in the Second Book of Samuel.]

What shall I say of the queen of Sheba (ibid.), who came from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon’s wisdom and, by the testimony of the Lord, will condemn all the men of Jerusalem? Elizabeth prophesies both in her womb and with her voice (Matt. 2). Anna, the daughter of Phanuel, becomes a temple of God in the Temple, and through daily fasting finds the heavenly bread (Luke 1). Women follow the Savior and minister to him from their own means (ibid. 2).

The one who fed five thousand people from five loaves, apart from women and children, does not refuse to receive the food of holy women. He speaks with the Samaritan woman at the well and, satisfied by the conversion of the believer, neglects the food that had been purchased.

[Note: Others have not noticed where this example was taken from. Yet it is genuinely a spurious passage attributed to Jerome, in his letter on Romans, chapter 16. “In the ministry,” he says, “we find women privately teaching, such as Priscilla, whose husband was named Aquila.”]

Apollo, an apostolic man and most learned in the Law, is instructed and taught by Aquila and Priscilla concerning the way of the Lord (Acts 18:25). If it was not shameful for Apollos to be taught by a woman, why should it be shameful for me, after teaching men, to teach women also?

### 2

I have touched briefly on these and similar matters, most revered daughter (*semnotatē*), so that you would neither regret your sex nor allow men to lift up their name—since, to their condemnation, the life of women is praised in the Holy Scriptures.

I rejoice, and my spirit is carried away as if in a kind of triumphal dance, when Daniel, Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael are found in Babylon. O how many elders and judges of Israel there are whom the Babylonian king fries in his own frying pan!

375

[Note: In the same sense he said in Letter 54, no. 10, to Furia, that the three boys had not yet come to the frying pan in which the Babylonian king fried the elderly judges. The elderly judges who lusted after Susanna—judges named Ahab and Zedekiah, according to the Hebrews—are said by Jeremiah to have been fried in a frying pan by the king of Babylon, although Daniel says that they were stoned.]

How many Susannas—her name means “lily”—arrange garlands for the bridegroom in the whiteness of chastity and transform the crown of thorns into the glory of the triumphant one.

There you have Marcella and Asella in their devotion to Scripture and in the holiness of mind and body. May the one lead you through green meadows and the varied flowers of the divine Books to him who says in the Song: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (Song 2:1); may the other, herself the Lord’s flower, deserve to hear with you: “As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among the daughters” (ibid. 2).

And since we have begun to speak of flowers and lilies, and virginity is always compared with flowers, it seems appropriate to me, writing to Christ’s flower, to discuss many flowers.

### 3

When reading the Forty-Fourth Psalm, I found this in the title: “For the end, for those who shall be changed, of the sons of Korah, for understanding, a song for the beloved.” In Hebrew it is written:

**LAMANASSE AL SOSANNIM LABNE CORE MESCHIL SIR IDIDOTH**

We translate this into Latin as: “For the Victor, concerning the lilies of the sons of Korah, a song of understanding, of the most beloved.”

[Note: Some manuscripts prefer *intelligentia in recto*, “understanding in the straightforward sense”; but the older reading seemed preferable, especially since other ancient Latin versions read *ad intellectum*, “for understanding.” The Hebrew letters which the older editors, following the ingenuity of the Masoretes, read are as follows; the Benedictine editor, perhaps through the carelessness of the printers, has corrupted them in more than one place.]

Symmachus, in his usual manner, translated it more plainly as “a triumphal song concerning the flowers.”

Thus *SOSANNIM* is translated either as “for those who shall be changed” or as “lilies” and “flowers.” *MESCHIL* likewise means “understanding” and “most learned.” *SIR* means “song.” *IDIDIA* is an ancient name of Solomon, who in another sense is called “the peaceful one.”

Four Psalms, although they differ in the latter part of their titles, are prefaced by this same opening: the Forty-Fourth, Fifty-Ninth, Sixty-Eighth, and Seventy-Ninth. Of these, the two middle ones are inscribed “of David,” while the first and last are “of the sons of Korah” and “of Asaph.” It is not the time to speak of all of them; let us explain the one we have begun.

### 4

Rightly are those who are to be changed at the end of the ages referred to the end, of whom the Apostle speaks: “We shall all sleep, but we shall not all be changed” (1 Cor. 15:51). This very mystery prepares the reader for spiritual understanding. For where the meaning is simple and open, what need is there to forewarn the hearer of understanding and say to him, “Let the one who has ears to hear, hear” (Matt. 13)?

A song is also sung for the one who is most dear and beloved, because for his sake the change promised to the saints will come. This can indeed be understood in the present life, when we put off the old person and put on the new, who is renewed in knowledge according to the image of the Creator; and, contemplating the glory of the Lord, we are transformed into the same image, as from glory to glory.

There is no time in which the saint is not changed, forgetting what lies behind and reaching forward to what is ahead, while our inner person is renewed day by day. The unchanging God, who speaks through the prophet, “I am God, and I do not change” (Mal. 3:6), has for our sake changed his appearance and taken the form of a servant. Migrating from Judea to the Philistines—who are interpreted as “those falling into the cup,” for they had been drunk from Babylon’s golden cup—he was first mocked because of the folly of the cross and then received because of the glory of his triumphs.

That beloved one is he of whom Isaiah sings: “I will sing a song for my beloved, the song of my vineyard” (Isa. 5:1); and the Gospel says: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him” (Matt. 17:5). It is not one prophet but the entire chorus of the sons of Korah who now sings his praises.

Who the sons of Korah are—that is, the sons of the Skull—is discussed more suitably in the Forty-First Psalm.

[Note: Be careful not to understand this as an argument made by Jerome himself; it is more appropriately said of the sons of Korah in that Psalm.]

And so that we may know that the text of the song agrees with its title, it speaks of a change from one thing to another, so that the daughter who is commanded to forget her ancient parent may prepare herself for the embraces of the king.

He is the Victor who says, “Take courage; I have conquered the world” (John 16:33). And he to whom belongs the prayer of the young man, “From you come victory, wisdom, and glory, and I am your servant” (3 Esd. 4:59), surely understands that, when the Lord conquers, he has overcome, shares in his triumphs, and has woven for the Savior an unfading crown of glory from the whiteness of good works and the variety of virtues.

[Note: It is strange that Jerome should bring forward testimony from the apocryphal book of Esdras, since he especially detested such writings. Elsewhere, writing against Vigilantius, he says: “You propose to me an apocryphal book which you and your associates read under the name of Esdras,” and shortly afterward: “Why is it necessary to take into our hands what the Church does not receive?”]

### 5

“ My heart has poured forth a good word.”

For this Symmachus translated:

[Note: In Greek, in the Hexapla: ἐκινήθη ἡ καρδία μου λόγῳ ἀγαθῷ, “My heart was moved by a good word.”]

“My heart was moved by a good word.”

He indicates that the heart of the speaker was moved by the speech of another, and that, with the Holy Spirit revealing beforehand the mysteries of Christ, this speaker too broke forth into eloquence, so that just as the others had spoken about his coming, he also might speak.

A belch properly means the digestion of food and the exhalation of digested nourishment into wind. For just as, according to the quality of the food, a belch bursts forth from the stomach and indicates a breath of good or bad odor, so the thoughts of the inner person produce words, and “the mouth speaks from the abundance of the heart” (Matt. 12:34).

The righteous person, while eating, fills his soul; and once he has been satisfied with sacred teachings, he brings forth from the treasury of a good heart the things that are good, and says with the Apostle: “Do you seek proof of the one who speaks in me—Christ?” (2 Cor. 13:3)

[Note: Origen had rejected their opinion long before for this reason: Εἰ γὰρ τῷ υἱῷ ὁ πατὴρ ἀπήγγειλεν, εὑρεθήσεται ἀγνοῶν ὁ υἱὸς καὶ τῶν ἔργων μεταγενέστερος—“For if the Father announced these things to the Son, the Son would be found ignorant of them and later than the works.”]

Some wish this to be understood as spoken in the person of the Father, who from the innermost vital organs and secrets of the heart brought forth his Word, which had always been in him, according to the prophecy of another Psalm: “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you” (Ps. 109:3).

Just as “womb” does not signify a womb—for God is not divided into bodily members—but demonstrates the same substance of the Father and the Son, so the heart and the word brought forth from the heart may indicate the Father and the Son.

They apply to this interpretation what follows: “I speak my works to the king” (Ps. 32:9), together with: “He himself spoke, and they were made; he himself commanded, and they were created” (John 14). In other words, when the Father spoke, the Son acted. For whatever the Father does, the Son also does in the same way, and the Father, remaining in him, works all things through the Son.

### 6

“ I speak my works to the king.”

The prophetic chorus, about to speak the mysteries of Christ and the Church, lest it appear unworthy of song and lest, because of consciousness of sin, it be addressed with the words, “Why do you recount my righteous deeds and take my covenant upon your mouth?” (Ps. 49:16), confesses its works to the king whom it is about to praise, so that, if they are good, he may accept them, or, if they are bad, cleanse them.

It does what it has been commanded: “Declare your iniquities, so that you may be justified” (Isa. 43:26). And, “The righteous person is his own accuser at the beginning of his speech” (Prov. 18:17).

It is an idiom not only of Hebrew but also of Latin to use *opuscula* (“little works”) for compositions and writings. Therefore this one too, who is about to sing praises to the Lord, consecrates his song and little work to him, and instead of the Muses of the Gentiles invokes at the beginning the very one whom he is about to praise.

### 7

“ My tongue is the pen of a swift-writing scribe.”

For this we translated:

“My tongue is the stylus of a swift scribe.”

This is the final part of the prologue. Join what follows to what came before: “My heart has poured forth a good word in praise of God, and I have consecrated to him above all my little works with which I am about to proclaim him.”

I must therefore prepare my tongue as a stylus and pen, so that through it the Holy Spirit may write upon the hearts and ears of those who hear. It is my task to offer my tongue as an instrument; it is his task to sound through the instrument what belongs to him.

A stylus writes on wax; a pen writes on paper or parchment, or on any material suitable for writing. My tongue, in the likeness of a swift scribe—which we may understand as a shorthand writer—has written upon the tablets of the fleshly heart, by a kind of abbreviated system of signs, the concise and compressed language of the Gospel.

For if the Law was written by the hand of the Mediator with the finger of God, and what was destroyed was glorified, how much more will the Gospel, which is to remain, be written by the Holy Spirit through my tongue, so that the praises of him to whom Isaiah says, “Quickly strip the spoils; swiftly plunder” (Isa. 8:1), may be inscribed by a swift word upon the hearts of believers.

### 8

“ You are more beautiful in form than the sons of men.”

In Hebrew: “You are more beautiful in appearance than the sons of men.”

[Note: He translated this from Eusebius, who testifies in his Commentaries that the older translators ended the preceding prologue in this way, so that the exposition begins ἀπὸ ἑτέρας ἀρχῆς, “from another beginning.” He adds his own example and says that, correspondingly, we too have taken “You are more beautiful in form than the sons of men” from a different beginning.]

With the prologue finished, this is the beginning of the narrative. An apostrophe is now addressed to the most beloved and dear one, the king, to whom the speaker’s works have been consecrated.

The question arises how he can be more beautiful than all the sons of men, when we read in Isaiah: “We saw him, and he had neither appearance nor beauty, but his appearance was dishonored and lacking in comparison with the sons of men. A man placed in affliction and knowing how to bear weakness, because he turned his face away” (Isa. 53:2–3).

Nor should Scripture immediately seem discordant, because there the lowliness of his body is being recalled on account of the scourges, spittle, blows, nails, and injuries of the cross; here, the beauty of virtues in the sacred and venerable body.

[Note: Previously the reading was *videtur*, “it seems”; but such small textual alterations, which it is not worth troubling the reader to mention, we often silently correct.]

This does not mean that Christ’s divinity is more beautiful in comparison with human beings, for divinity admits no comparison; rather, apart from the sufferings of the cross, he is more beautiful than all.

A virgin from a virgin, born not by the will of a man but from God. For unless there had been something star-like in his face and eyes, the Apostles would never have followed him immediately, nor would those who came to seize him have fallen backward (John 18).

Finally, in the present testimony also, where it says, “A man placed in affliction and knowing how to bear weakness,” it gives the reasons why he suffered these things: “Because he turned his face away,” that is, having for a little while withdrawn his divinity, he abandoned his body to injury.

Some join this verse to what precedes, so that “more beautiful in form than the sons of men” refers not to Christ but to the pen.

[Note: Editions before Martianay read *non formosior*, “not more beautiful,” in which the negative particle does not change the meaning, but rather makes it clearer—whatever the Benedictine editor may think, since he was the first to remove it with the support of certain manuscripts. For this passage concerning Christ’s superior appearance, compare Jerome’s discussion in chapter 9 of Matthew. From it one may infer that Jerome did not think the radiance and star-like beauty of Christ’s body was permanent, but that it appeared only for a time, when he wished to attract people to himself, terrify them, or draw them into admiration of God, as happened in the mystery of the Transfiguration and elsewhere.]

### 9

“ Grace has been poured out upon your lips; therefore God has blessed you forever.”

In the Vulgate edition we read “anointed you” instead of “blessed you.” But it must be understood that the error of scribes should not be attributed to the translators of the Septuagint, who agree here with the Hebrew truth.

When we read, “Jesus advanced in age and wisdom and grace with God and human beings” (Luke 2:52), and elsewhere, “They marveled at the words of grace that came forth from his mouth” (Luke 4:22), and that “he had authority in his speech” (Mark 1:22), we can understand in what sense it was said: “Grace has been poured out upon your lips.”

Noah found grace before the Lord in his generation, as did Moses and the other prophets. But the whole abundance of grace was poured out upon the lips of the Savior, and in a short time filled the entire world.

He himself came forth like a bridegroom from his bridal chamber. “His going forth is from the highest heaven, and his course reaches to its summit” (Ps. 18:7).

Holy Mary too, because she had conceived him in whom the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily, is greeted as “full of grace” (Luke 1:28).

The Apostle, knowing that by his preaching—not through worldly eloquence but through the power of God—he had surpassed all the teachings of the world, says: “My speech and my preaching were not in persuasive words of human wisdom, but in the demonstration of the Spirit and of power, so that our faith might not rest in human wisdom but in the power of God” (1 Cor. 2:4–5).

And correcting himself because he had said, “I labored more than all,” he immediately added: “Yet not I, but the grace of God that is with me.” And again: “His grace toward me was not empty” (1 Cor. 15:10).

The word “pouring” is especially applied to the Savior to signify the generosity of grace, according to: “I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh” (Joel 2:28); and, “The love of God has been poured out in our hearts” (Rom. 5:5).

Note also that he refers the meaning of everything being said to the person who was assumed from Mary: he is said to be blessed forever because of the grace of his lips. The Apostle proclaims something similar: “He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross. Therefore God also exalted him and gave him a name above every name” (Phil. 2:8–9).

For just as there the form of a servant signifies the injury of the Passion, while the exaltation and bestowal of the name return to the Father, so here the pouring out of grace and the eternal blessing must be referred to him who can be humbled and can grow.

### 10

“ Gird your sword upon your thigh, O most powerful one; in your appearance and your beauty.”

In Hebrew: “Gird your sword upon your thigh, O mighty one. Your glory and your beauty.”

[Note: The word “your” is absent here both from the Hebrew text and from Jerome’s own version.]

I think you understand this passage very well: girded with the sword of Christ, you wage war. To show you that virginity always possesses the sword of chastity, by which it cuts off the works of the flesh and overcomes pleasures, even pagan error imagined virgin goddesses armed.

Peter also girded his loins and held a burning lamp in his hands.

You will be taught by these brief examples that the thigh signifies the works of marriage. Abraham, sending the chief servant of his household to seek a wife for his son Isaac, says to him: “Place your hand beneath my thigh, and I will make you swear by the Lord, the God of heaven” (Gen. 24:2)—plainly by the one who was to be born from his seed.

After Jacob wrestled with the man who had appeared to him at the torrent of Jabbok, and, leaving Mesopotamia, entered the Promised Land, he did not receive the name Israel until the sinew of his thigh had withered.

And to his son he says: “A ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his thighs” (Gen. 49:10). Again, as he is dying, he makes Joseph swear by his thigh that he will not bury him in Egypt.

In the Book of Judges we also read: “Gideon had seventy sons, who came forth from his thighs” (Judg. 8:30).

In the Song of Songs it is said: “Behold, Solomon’s bed, sixty mighty men around it, from the mighty men of Israel, all holding swords, trained for war, a man and his sword upon his thigh” (Song 3:7–8).

Therefore, through his glory and beauty—that is, through the appearance and beauty of his divinity—he mortified the works of the flesh; and, born from a virgin, he became the prince of virginity for future virgins.

### 11

“ And prosper, go forth, and reign, because of truth, meekness, and righteousness; and your right hand shall lead you wondrously.”

In Hebrew: “In your beauty, prosper and ascend; because of truth and the meekness of righteousness, and your right hand shall lead you wondrously.”

[Note: Jerome himself translated, “and will teach you terrible things,” which corresponds especially well to the Hebrew, unlike the printed text here, “and your right hand shall lead you wondrously,” which I readily believe entered from the Greek or from the old Latin translation.]

The Hebrew text repeats “in your beauty,” so that no one may think it was repeated through the fault of copyists. This is the figure which rhetoricians call repetition.

In the manner of a panegyric, in which speakers address those whom they exalt with praises, the prophet exhorts the armed one to battle, so that he may not abandon the war once undertaken, but, advancing victoriously over the slaughter of his enemies, may prepare a kingdom for himself among those whom, rescuing from the power of the devil, he has joined to his own rule.

He says: “But I have been appointed king by him over Zion, his holy mountain” (Ps. 2:6).

No one doubts that Christ is called truth, meekness, and righteousness, for he says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6); “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11:29); and, “He was made for us by God our righteousness, redemption, and sanctification” (1 Cor. 1:30).

All these things are said in the body so that they may be required in its members. The Lord’s victory is the triumph of his servants. The teacher’s learning is the progress of his disciples.

What follows—“Your right hand shall lead you wondrously”—must be understood either of the signs he performed in the Gospel or, figuratively (*tropikōs*), of the slaughter he inflicted upon his enemies.

“The heart of the wise is at his right hand, and the heart of the fool is at his left.” Christ is entirely on the right; Antichrist is on the left.

The Hebrew interpretation differs in words, but not in meaning.

### 12

“ Your sharp arrows, O most powerful one, the peoples shall fall beneath you into the hearts of the king’s enemies.”

[Note: Some read and interpret “O most powerful one.” The Greek, however, has δυνατέ, “O mighty one.” In any case, that “O most powerful one” was intruded here from the preceding verse, “Gird yourself,” is shown in the Letter to Sunnia and Fretella. Shortly afterward, I would prefer *in corde*, “in the heart,” to *in corda*, “into the hearts,” since the Greek has ἐν καρδίᾳ, “in the heart,” as does the Hebrew reading that agrees with Jerome’s testimony.]

In Hebrew, without “O most powerful one,” the rest is similar.

This verse is especially suited to you, who, wounded by the Lord’s dart, sing with the bride in the Song: “I am wounded by love” (Song 2:5).

Nor is it surprising if your bridegroom has many arrows, of which it is said in the One Hundred Nineteenth Psalm: “The sharp arrows of the mighty one, with coals of desolation.” For he himself is the Father’s dart and says through Isaiah: “He made me like a chosen arrow; in his quiver he hid me” (Isa. 49:2).

With these arrows Cleopas, wounded on the road with his companion, said: “Was not our heart burning within us while he spoke to us on the way and opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke 24:32).

And elsewhere we read: “As arrows in the hand of the mighty one, so are the sons of those who have been cast out” (Ps. 126:4).

The whole world was wounded and captured by these arrows.

[Note: Here he imitates Origen, who interprets rational arrows as those “who sufficiently preach on behalf of the truth and powerfully refute falsehood” (τοῦ ἱκανῶς πρεσβεύοντος ὑπὲρ ἀληθείας καὶ δυνατῶς τὸ ψεῦδος καταιροῦντος).]

Paul was the Lord’s arrow. After being sent from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum on the Lord’s bow, he flew here and there and hurried to go to Spain, so that, like a swift arrow beneath the feet of his Lord, he might overthrow east and west.

And because there are many enemies of the most powerful king, who had been wounded by the devil’s fiery arrows and, like a stag struck by a dart in the liver, so the Lord’s arrows are sent forth, burning with coals of desolation, so that whatever vice may be in the heart of the king’s enemies they may burn out, driving away the destructive fire with a saving fire.

### 13

“ Your throne, O God, is forever and ever; the scepter of uprightness is the scepter of your kingdom. You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions.”

In Hebrew:

“Your throne, O God, is forever and for eternity; the scepter of equity is the scepter of your kingdom. You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of exultation above your companions.”

[Note: Jerome reports that Aquila did this by writing the name of God in the vocative, Θεέ, rather than Θεός, and immediately admits that he himself did the same, writing *Dee* for the sake of understanding. Therefore, although we read *Deus*, “God,” here in agreement with all the books, it would be more correct according to Jerome’s intention to read *Dee*, even if that form is less Latin. Yet without manuscript support we may not alter it, especially since Jerome himself seems to have said that he wrote *Dee* with the mark of the vocative, O God.]

[Note: Earlier the reading was *in saeculum saeculi*, “forever and ever,” despite the resistance of many manuscripts, both of this letter and of the Psalter from the Hebrew. There, as we have restored it, the text reads “forever and for eternity,” from the Hebrew words which Jerome also interprets in the same way at the end of this Psalm, near the end of the letter.]

Understand two persons here: the one who is anointed by God and the one who anoints.

Therefore Aquila interprets the Hebrew word *ELOIM* not in the nominative but in the vocative, saying Θεέ, “O God.” For the sake of clarity, we have also written *Dee*, which Latin does not accept, lest anyone perversely think that the God of the beloved, dear, and king is twice called the Father.

Although the Father is in the Son, the Son in the Father, and each is both dwelling-place and throne for the other, here the speech is directed to the king who is God. It is said to him that his rule—and by “throne” I understand his rule, according to what is written, “From the fruit of your womb I will place upon your throne” (Ps. 131:11)—will have no end.

The angel also announced this to Mary: “The Lord God will give him the throne of David his father, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end” (Luke 1:32–33).

Nor should we think this contrary to what the Apostle says when writing to the Corinthians: that the Son will hand over the kingdom to God and be subjected to the one who subjected all things to him, so that God may be all in all (1 Cor. 15:24–28).

For he did not say, “He will hand it over to the Father,” as though he wished to separate the Son, but, “He will hand it over to God,” that is, to God dwelling in the assumed body, so that God may be all in all, and Christ—who previously existed individually in each person through a few virtues—may dwell in all through all virtues.

The scepter and rod signify the insignia of a ruler; the prophet himself indicates this when he says: “The scepter of equity, the scepter of your kingdom” (Isa. 11:1).

Some, bringing forward Isaiah’s testimony, “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root,” understand the human being who was assumed, to whom authority is given, who is said to reign because he loved righteousness and hated iniquity, and to be anointed with the oil of exultation above his companions—as though he were to receive an anointing as the reward for loving righteousness and hating iniquity.

We are taught that in both respects—the love and the hatred—we possess the seeds of these things, since he himself, who lifted the firstfruits of our bodies to heaven, loved righteousness and hated iniquity.

Hence David says: “Do I not hate those who hate you, O Lord, and waste away because of your enemies? I hate them with perfect hatred” (Ps. 138:21–22).

What follows—“God, your God, has anointed you”—must be understood with the first name of God in the vocative and the second in the nominative. I am very surprised that Aquila, having begun by interpreting the first verse in the vocative, did not do so here also, but used the nominative, thereby naming the God who anointed the aforesaid God.

[Note: Some manuscripts, to which the oldest edition agrees, read: “I am surprised that he calls the sole God of God into accusation, as though Arius would claim the words ‘Your seat, or throne, O God, is forever and ever’ and draw them into his heresy.”]

In this passage Photinus is overthrown, but Arius raises his head, bringing forward the testimony from the Gospel: “I am ascending to my Father and your Father, my God and your God” (John 20:17).

But when he hears that the beloved one is girded with a sword upon his thigh, reigns because of truth and meekness, is anointed because he loved righteousness and hated iniquity, and is anointed above his companions, of whom it is written, “We have become companions of Christ, if indeed we hold the beginning of his substance firm unto the end” (Heb. 3:14), I am amazed that he calls only the God of God into accusation, as though everything that has been said applied to the divinity of the Word and not to the humility of the human being.

Let him hear the Acts of the Apostles: “Jesus of Nazareth, whom God anointed with the Holy Spirit” (Acts 10:38). Let him hear the Gospel: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35).

Let him hear the Lord himself thunder: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me” (Isa. 61:1).

By “companions” he signifies the Apostles and believers, to whom he grants the title of his anointing, so that from the Anointed One they may be called the anointed—that is, from Christ, Christians.

14. “Myrrh and a drop and cassia perfume your garments, from ivory houses, by which the daughters of kings have delighted you in your honor.” In the Hebrew: “Myrrh and stacte and cassia are in all your garments, from ivory houses, by which the daughters of kings have gladdened you in your honor.”

The preface itself taught you why I wished to explain this Psalm: because, writing to a virgin, I found a title referring to lilies and flowers. Accordingly, I shall apply these verses also to you, for whom this volume is written.

You have mortified your members upon the earth, and every day offer myrrh to Christ. You are the good fragrance of Christ, and therefore you offer stacte—that is, a drop or distillation—to the Lord. Those who know the properties of aromatics also say that stacte is the flower of myrrh. What follows, cassia, is what others call *σῦριγξ* (*syrinx*), that is, a reed or pipe—vocal in the praises of God, and by its heat consuming all the phlegms and discharges of pleasures.

Where our manuscripts read “drop,” or “stacte,” the Hebrew has *MALOTH*. Hence Nicodemus also prepared one hundred pounds of myrrh and aloes for the burial of the Lord. And the bridegroom says to the bride: “Myrrh and aloe with all the finest perfumes” (Song 4). And she replies: “My hands dripped with myrrh; my fingers were full of myrrh” (ibid. 5:5).

You too, cast away the works of death. Buried with Christ in baptism, die to this world, and, thinking of nothing except heavenly things, say to your bridegroom: “My hands have dripped with myrrh; my fingers are full of myrrh.”

We also read of the priestly anointing, which David mentions: “Like oil upon the head, running down upon the beard, the beard of Aaron, running down upon the hem of his garment” (Ps. 132:2). In this anointing stacte is mixed with the other spices. The Magi also offer myrrh.

In the present passage, the beginning of Christ’s garments is to receive his death and display it in one’s own flesh. Prepare these garments for your bridegroom; let him walk forth adorned in these garments supplied by you. And when you have woven such garments for him, you will yourself become the temple of God, and you will gladden him “from ivory houses”—or, as it is better written in Hebrew, “from the temple of teeth.” You will sing praises to the Lord, and, wholly dead to the world, imitate the choirs of angels.

The very nature of the words testifies that ivory and teeth are emblems of death and of the voice. And consequently it is added: “By which the daughters of kings have delighted you in your honor.”

Your bridegroom is the King of kings and Lord of lords.

[Note: Origen likewise explains the kings as holy disciples who have obtained the kingdom of heaven, and the daughters of kings as *τὰς ὑπ’ αὐτῶν γεννωμένας κατ’ ἀρετὴν ψυχάς*, “souls begotten by them according to virtue,” that is, souls formed or generated by them according to the norm of virtue. Adamantius likewise interprets the queen herself in gilded dress as the Catholic Church.]

These kings, who are petty kings under so great a king, are your fathers, who begot you through evangelical teaching. Their daughter, you honor him in all garments, with good fragrances and with an ivory temple—him of whom it was said above: “Grace is poured upon your lips”; and: “Gird your sword upon your thigh, O most mighty”; and: “Your arrows are sharp”; and: “Your throne, O God, is forever and ever.”

[Note: In place of our rendering “ivory houses,” because the Greek has *ἀπὸ βαρέων ἐλεφαντίνων*, certain Latin translators, on account of the ambiguity of the word, rendered it “from heavy things,” although *βάρις* is a local or vernacular word of Palestine, as it is called by Jerome. Earlier interpreters do not seem to have understood its meaning, for they all write *βαρύς* with upsilon, meaning “heavy,” and shortly afterward, in the same sense, the plural *βαρεῖς*. Jerome, however, wants *βάρις* and *βάρεις* to be written not to signify something heavy, but to signify large houses. The Greek scholia in Drusius say: “*βάρεις* are locally called among the Syrians large houses.” *Baris*, or, according to the language of the place, the Syrians’ term for large houses. In the singular Josephus likewise reports in *The Jewish War*, book 1, chapter 6, that a tower was called *βάρις*, later named Antonia: “a fortress . . . formerly called *baris*”; for houses built in the manner of towers were properly called *βάρεις*. In Hebrew the word is *Birah*: first in 1 Chronicles 29:1, where it means a magnificent building, or temple; then in the plural in 2 Chronicles 17:12, which the Vulgate translates “houses like towers.” More truly, however, it is a Chaldean name, which in 2 Esdras 1:1, Daniel 8:2, Esther 1:2, and elsewhere is added to the name Susa: “Susa-Birah,” that is, “Susa the Citadel,” or “the Royal Palace.” See Jerome on Amos, chapter 1:12, and at the end of his commentary on Isaiah.]

For what we have translated “ivory houses,” since the Greek reads *ἀπὸ βαρέων ἐλεφαντίνων*, certain Latins, because of the ambiguity of the word, interpreted it as “from heavy things,” although *βάρις* is a local word of Palestine; and even to this day houses enclosed on every side and built in the form of towers and public fortifications are called *βάρεις*.

15. “The queen stood at your right hand in a garment of gold”; and what follows, “surrounded by variety,” no interpreter except the Vulgate Edition has translated. In the Hebrew: “The consort stood at your right hand in a golden diadem.” Where we translate “consort,” the Hebrews read *SEGAL*. For this Aquila has *σύγκοιτον*, that is, “concubine”; Symmachus and the Fifth Edition, *παλλακήν*, that is, “concubine”; while the Septuagint, Theodotion, and the Sixth Edition translated it “queen.”

[Note: Victorius reads *σύγκοιτιν*, as Agellius had formerly read.]

Then, where I rendered “in a golden diadem,” Symmachus translated “in first-rate gold”; Aquila, the Fifth, and the Sixth Edition, “in dye,” or “in the gold of Ophir.”

Those who are daughters of kings and are prepared for the embraces of the bridegroom delight him through myrrh, stacte, cassia, and ivory houses—the one whose throne is forever and ever.

The Catholic Church, already established upon Christ the rock with a firm root, is one dove, perfect and close at hand, standing at his right hand, and possessing nothing left-handed or sinister in itself. She stands in garments of gold, passing from the words of Scripture to their meaning, and full of every virtue; or, as we translated it, “in a golden diadem.” She is a queen and reigns with the king. Her daughters may be understood both as the souls of all believers collectively and, more particularly, as the choirs of virgins.

[Note: Martianaeus enumerates the individual terms from Drusius; consult him, if desired, at the end of the book. We shall explain them more accurately elsewhere.]

*Ophir* is a kind of gold, named either from a place in India or from its color. There are, in fact, seven words for gold among the Hebrews. Let us also understand “wife” and “concubine” from Solomon’s Song, where she cannot sleep without her bridegroom or husband.

16. “Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear, and forget your people and your father’s house, and the king will desire your beauty; for he is the Lord your God, and they will worship him.”

In the Hebrew: “Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear, and forget your people and your father’s house, and the king will desire your beauty; because he is your Lord, and worship him.”

Up to this point the Holy Spirit speaks through the prophet’s tongue, which he compares to the pen of a writer writing swiftly, addressing the king himself, the warrior, and God, and also the bridegroom. From this point the person of the Father is introduced, speaking to the bride of his Son and exhorting her, once she has rejected the error of her former paganism and idolatry, first to attend to what is being said. For this reason she is called the daughter of a foreign people. Then she is to see either the things themselves that are spoken or the whole order of creation, understanding invisible things from visible things and perceiving the Creator from created things. She must carefully incline her ear so that she may retain in memory what is said.

When she has heard, seen, inclined her ear, wholly surrendered herself to the teaching and to the understanding of what is said, she must first forget her former people, and, like Abraham departing from Chaldea, leave the land of her birth and her kindred.

No one doubts that our father, before we were adopted by God, was the devil; hence the Savior says: “You are born from your father the devil” (John 8:44).

[Note: Contrary to the testimony of the earlier manuscripts and editions, and also of Saint Cyprian in his treatise *On the Lord’s Prayer*, which likewise asserts this reading in John, Victorius ought not to have altered it and removed the word “born” in accordance with the Vulgate text.]

“When,” he says, “you have forgotten your ancient father and have shown yourself such—having laid aside your former filth, so that, whitened, you may ascend upon your kinsman—and such as my Son can love, then the king will desire your beauty. And lest you think that the one from whom you are to be loved is merely one of the crowd: he himself is your King and your Lord.”

Since those who are sometimes called kings and lords are indeed kings and lords by power, yet are of the same nature as those over whom they rule and reign, I tell you that he is also your God, and that you must worship him.

The Seventy Translators did not say, “and you will worship him,” but “they will worship him,” so that the sense is: “He who will love you, who will desire your beauty, is God, and is to be worshiped by all.”

What we have expounded concerning the Church gathered from the nations, let each person apply to himself: let him understand the believing soul, which, having abandoned its former vices, is adopted as a daughter; let it incline its ear and forget its former way of life. Let it, with the Apostle, leave the dead father to bury his own dead, and show itself worthy to be loved by the king.

[Note: Jerome seems to understand that the disciple to whom Jesus said, “Follow me, and let the dead bury their dead” (Matt. 8:22), was one of those who were later called Apostles.]

For he is its Lord, before whom it must bend the knee and, laying aside pride, take up the yoke of humility.

17. Let us ask the Jews who this daughter is to whom God speaks. I do not doubt that they will answer: the Synagogue. And how is it said to the Synagogue and to the Israelite people: “Leave your people and your father’s house”? Will it abandon the Hebrew nation and Abraham, its ancient father?

If they say that Abraham’s calling is meant—Abraham who left the Chaldeans—who is this king who will desire Abraham’s beauty? Certainly the one who speaks is different from the one of whom it is said: “Hear, daughter,” and: “The king will desire your beauty.” The other is not only king, but also Lord and God, and he is to be worshiped.

18. “The daughter of Tyre will entreat your face with gifts; the rich among the people.”

In the Hebrew: “O daughter of the mighty one, the rich among the people will entreat your face with gifts.”

The Hebrew word *SOR*, which in Ezekiel, according to the Septuagint, may be interpreted as “Tyre,” “tribulation,” “mighty one” or “mighty woman,” and “flint,” that is, a very hard stone, gave rise to the error in the present passage.

[Note: Contrary to the Hexapla prepared by Montfaucon, Aquila and the Fifth Edition are credited with leaving the word *Sor*, or *Σόρ*, untranslated. In the following interpretation of Symmachus, since our manuscripts often read corruptly, we do not depart from Martianaeus’s edition. Formerly the reading was *κρατίστην*, “mightiest,” as is clear from the fact that the other interpreters translated it.]

For Aquila, the Septuagint, Theodotion, and the Fifth Edition translated it “Tyre.” The Sixth Edition retained the Hebrew word *Sor*. Symmachus has *κραταιὰν*, that is, “mighty.”

We referred the same word to God, so that she to whom he had said above, “Hear, daughter, and see,” might now be called “daughter of the Mighty One.” Or certainly she herself is mighty because she has imitated the strong Father, whose face the rich among the people will entreat with various gifts.

They are rich in all good works and in knowledge; or they are those considered rich in this world, the wise of this age, educated in the disciplines of the philosophers. Or, what is better, they are those who formerly were rich, possessing the utterances of God, the Testaments, and the Prophets—that is, those from the people of Israel.

For before the Savior’s coming, those who were from Tyre—that is, from the people of the nations—and wished to become proselytes, entreated the rich people of Israel and were introduced by them into the Temple. Likewise, after the Lord’s coming, whoever among Israel wishes to believe—formerly rich in familiarity and protection with God—will come to the daughter of Tyre and, offering various gifts of virtue and confession of Christ, will entreat her, so that they may find among the nations the salvation they lost in Judea.

19. “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within; she is clothed round about with varieties, with golden borders.”

In the Hebrew: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within; she is clothed with golden bands.”

Where the Septuagint has *ἔσωθεν*, which we also translated as “within,” some copies have *ESEBON*, which means “thoughts.”

[Note: The Benedictine editor’s reading is confirmed by the ancient books we consulted: formerly the Greek reading was *ἐξ ἐννοιῶν*, while others have something closer to *ἐχερὼν*. The Septuagint has *ἐσεβὼν*, which the Ethiopian Psalter is also said to read as *Hesbon*.]

From this it is shown that all the glory of the Church—to which it was said above, “Hear, daughter, and see,” and “O daughter of Tyre,” and which is now called the king’s daughter—is inward, in thoughts, that is, in the inner person, and in circumcision not made by hands but by the Spirit. She possesses confidence of conscience before God, and her entire beauty is placed more in the meaning of the senses than in the bloom of words.

Just as the under-thread is woven into the warp from which the borders hang, and the entire strength of the garment lies in the warp, so in the varied meanings of Scripture, in which the whole garment of the Church is woven, elements from nature and from morals are intermingled.

[Note: The first edition, and indeed quite a few manuscripts, read “golden” rather than “varied.”] This is also signified by Aaron’s vestment, woven of gold, purple, scarlet, fine linen, and hyacinth (Exod. 28:39), which the women made, to whom God gave wisdom for weaving.

And so that we may understand that all the adornment of the king’s daughter is inward, she herself speaks in the Song: “The king brought me into his chamber” (Song 1:4; Matt. 6). In that chamber, with the door of the lips shut, we are commanded to pray to God the Father.

In the ninth Psalm also the title is written: “For the hidden things of the Son.” Joseph too had a variegated tunic (Gen. 37), which Mother Church wove for him. From these borders the Savior’s *αἱμορροοῦσα*—the woman suffering from a flow of blood—touched one, and was healed (Matt. 9; Mark 6; Luke 8).

As for what is written in the Hebrew, “She is clothed with golden bands,” this signifies the same as what was said above: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within.” The inner members of the Church are wrapped in bands of divine meanings, and the whole expanse of the womb is covered.

[Note: Thus, where Victorius formerly had *inferiora* in Erasmus, we correct it in Martianaeus to *interiora*, on the authority of the manuscripts and the ancient edition; this is also required by the sense of the context.]

The bride cannot forget these bands, according to Jeremiah (chapter 2), which bind the breasts and protect the chest, in which thoughts reside.

20. “Virgins will be brought to the king after her; her companions will be brought to you. They will be brought with joy and exultation; they will be brought into the temple of the king.”

According to the Septuagint, the first verse still sings of the adornment of the daughter; the next is directed to the bridegroom himself and the king.

According to the Hebrew, however, the whole passage is addressed to the bride up to the place where it says: “You will appoint them princes throughout all the earth.” It reads:

“In embroidered garments she will be led to the king; virgins will follow her; her companions will be led there. They will be led in joys and exultation; they will enter the king’s bridal chamber.”

[Note: In the books printed up to the present, *ducentur* was incorrectly read here. Certain manuscripts then continue with *laetitia* rather than *laetitiis*. Consult, if desired, Jerome’s own version from the Hebrew.]

The great diversity among souls who believe in Christ is demonstrated by the Song of Songs, in which it is written: “There are sixty queens, and eighty concubines, and maidens without number. One is my dove, my perfect one, my close companion”; of her it is said: “The daughters saw her, and called her blessed; the queens and concubines saw her and praised her” (Song 6:7 and following).

Therefore she who is perfect and holy in body and spirit deserves to be called both dove and close companion. This is the daughter of whom it was said above: “The queen stood at your right hand in a garment of gold.”

Those who have surpassed the six days of the world and long for the kingdoms to come are called queens.

[Note: One Cistercian manuscript, very carefully corrected, has *munda*, referring the word to the kingdoms. Jerome, however, compares the number of sixty queens and eighty concubines with the six days in which the world was created and with the eighth day of legal circumcision, and interprets it mystically of the soul.]

But if someone possesses the circumcision of the eighth day and has not yet come to the marriage, she is called a concubine. The diverse multitude of believers, who are not yet able to be joined to the embraces of the bridegroom or to bear children by him, is called the maiden.

I think that among these virgins who follow the Church and are placed in the first rank, you too are included, as are all who persevere in virginity of body and soul.

[Note: A Cistercian manuscript omits both “you too” and the second “and.”]

The close companions and friends are widows and those who practice continence within marriage. All these are led with joy and exultation to the temple and into the bridal chamber of the king: into the temple as priests of God, into the bridal chamber as brides of the king and bridegroom.

John also saw this temple in the Apocalypse (Rev. 21), and the Prophet longs for it: “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I shall seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life” (Ps. 26:4). And again: “Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house and the place where your glory dwells” (Ps. 25:8). And elsewhere: “For I shall pass into the place of the wondrous tabernacle, even to the house of God, amid the voice of joy and praise, the sound of those celebrating a feast” (Ps. 41:5).

The embroidered garments with which the queen is adorned for her bridegroom are the same things that we read in the Septuagint as “surrounded by variety.”

21. “In place of your fathers, sons have been born to you; you will appoint them princes over all the earth.”

In the Hebrew: “In place of your fathers, sons will be born to you; you will appoint them princes throughout all the earth.”

The speech may be understood as proceeding from the person of the Father—not concerning the daughter, but again addressed to the daughter—and also from the person of the Holy Spirit and of the sons of Korah.

If the speech is directed to the daughter and bride, and the bride has been gathered from the nations, to whom it was said above, “Forget your people and your father’s house,” we must know the bride’s fathers in order afterward to know her sons.

“In place of your fathers”—those about whom you spoke in Jeremiah: “Our fathers possessed false idols, and there is none among them who sends rain” (Jer. 14:22; 16:19). In place of Plato and the other teachers of various doctrines and errors, sons have been born to you, whom you appointed as your princes and made teachers among the peoples.

Or certainly in another way: O Church, your sons whom you have begotten for yourself will become your fathers when you make teachers of them from disciples and place them, with the testimony of all, in the priestly rank.

[Note: Adamantius actually interprets the passage in this way: “In place of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and the other men who pleased him in the Old Testament, disciples were born, and we who through them believed and became heirs of their faith and knowledge.” See the Greek in the Catena of Barbarus.]

But if we understand the fathers of the Church to be Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and the remaining patriarchs, let us understand the sons, who have been born to her in the honor of fathers, to be the Apostles, who were sent by the Lord to preach to the ends of the earth and to baptize believers in the name of the Trinity.

But it is asked how the Church from the nations can have Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as fathers, when it was said to her above: “Forget your people and your father’s house.”

Let us read the Gospel: “Do not say, ‘We have Abraham as our father’; for God is able from these stones”—that is, from the hard hearts of the nations—“to raise up children for Abraham” (Matt. 3:9). And elsewhere: “If you were Abraham’s children, you would do the works of Abraham” (John 8:39). And in Genesis God speaks to Abraham himself: “In your seed all the nations will be blessed” (Gen. 12:3).

For just as he was justified by faith while still uncircumcised, so we too will be justified in the same faith, if we have the faith and works of our father Abraham.

This may also be said of the Savior, either by the Father, or by the prophetic choir and the Holy Spirit. “In place of your fathers”—that is, the stock of the Jews, who abandoned and denied you—“sons have been born to you”: the Apostles and believers from the nations, whom you appointed princes throughout all the earth.

22. “I will remember your name in every generation and generation. Therefore the peoples will confess you forever and unto ages of ages.”

In the Hebrew: “I will remember your name in every generation and generation. Therefore the peoples will confess you forever and eternally.”

What we translated as “they will confess to you,” Symmachus rendered “they will praise you.”

[Note: Clearly, *ὑμνήσουσί σε*, in which wording Aquila and Theodotion also agree.]

The queen who had stood at the king’s right hand in a garment of gold, and who had been commanded to forget her people and her father’s house, and to whom it had again been said, “In place of your fathers sons have been born to you; you will appoint them princes over all the earth”—understanding how greatly she must be adorned with glory and with what rewards she must be raised up—turns her voice to the bridegroom and promises that she will always remember the bridegroom’s name, in every generation and generation.

We see the fulfillment of what she promised. She herself imposed upon all of us Christians the Christian name: the new name in which “all the families of the nations will be blessed” [or: “are blessed”].

She remembers not in one generation only, but in all: either signifying all nations, or the two generations, Jews and Gentiles.

And because it is not enough for the Lord’s name to be remembered in two generations, therefore the peoples who will have been in the Church will confess and praise the Lord forever and unto ages of ages.

When you too, O daughter Principia, mingled with the choir of the saints, are led among the virgins to the king, and delight the bridegroom in your honor from the ivory houses, then remember me also, who, with the Lord’s revelation, have given you the understanding of this Psalm, and say: “I will remember your name.”

Then, if life accompanies you, you who have understood part of the song may understand the whole Song of Songs.

[Note: Hence the reference to Eusebius, in the preface to his Commentary on Matthew: “I ask you, when you come to Rome, to give a copy to the virgin of Christ, Principia, who asked me to write on the Song of Songs. Illness of long duration excluded me from that work, and I postponed my hope for the future.” But we do not know that he was afterward able to complete it.]

# LETTER LXVI [Note: Elsewhere numbered 26. Written toward the end of the year 397.] TO PAMMACHIUS

He praises Paulina, the daughter of Paula, who had married Pammachius, a young man especially learned and noble, after her death. He also exhorts Pammachius, who immediately after her death had undertaken the monastic way of life and distributed his wealth for the support of the poor, to persevere in his holy undertaking.

1. When a wound has healed and the skin has grown over into a scar, if medicine tries to restore its color, while seeking the beauty of the body it renews the painful wound. So I too, a late comforter, who kept silent inopportunely for two years, fear that I may now speak even more inopportunely

[Note: Martianaeus, as do other editors, reads corruptly *ego servus consolator* (“I, a slave, a comforter”) for *serus* (“late”), which we correct as the context itself requires.] and, touching the wound of your heart, which time and reason have healed, reopen it by recalling her.

For what ears are so hard, what hearts carved from flint and nourished on the milk of Hyrcanian tigresses, that they could hear the name of your Paulina without tears?

Who could see a rose in childbirth and a clustered, nipple-like flower—before the circle is poured into the basket and the whole expanse of reddening petals is opened—cut down before its time and with impartial eyes watch it wither?
