[Note: From an ancient epigram “On Roses”: “First the spike, extending a nipple-like corymb, etc.”]

The most precious pearl has been broken. The green gem of the emerald has been crushed. Illness shows how good health is. We felt more deeply what we possessed after we ceased to possess it.

1. In the field of good soil we read of three fruits: a hundredfold, sixtyfold, and thirtyfold (Matt. 13). In three women joined by blood and virtue, I recognize the three rewards of Christ.

Eustochium harvests the flowers of virginity; Paula treads the laborious threshing floor of widowhood; Paulina preserves the chaste marriage bed. Supported by such a company of daughters, their mother claims for herself on earth all that Christ promised in heaven.

And so that one household might send forth a four-horse chariot of holiness, and men might correspond to the virtues of the women, Pammachius is added as their companion—the true Cherub of Ezekiel, kinsman, son-in-law, husband, or rather most loving brother, because holy unions of the spirit do not retain the names of marriage.

[Note: Namely, a relative of Eustochium, Paula’s son-in-law, and Paulina’s husband.]

Jesus presides over this four-horse chariot. Of these horses Habakkuk also sings: “You will ascend upon your horses, and your riding is salvation” (Hab. 3:8).

[Note: Gravius wishes *ascendes* to be read from the Greek, rather than *ascende*. Shortly afterward, where *unum aurigae jugum* occurs, he directs that *quadrigae* be restored in place of *aurigae*. Jerome himself truly recalls the chariot of Pammachius, Paula, Eustochium, and Paulina at the end of the letter.]

By unequal courses but with equal spirit they strive toward the palm. The horses are of different colors but united in will; they draw one yoke of the chariot, not waiting for the blows of the whip but burning at the encouragement of the voice.

3. Four mutually connected virtues.—Let us say something also about the philosophers. The Stoics describe four virtues so interconnected and mutually joined that whoever lacks one lacks them all: prudence, justice, courage, and temperance.

You each possess all of these in such a way that each of you excels in one. Prudence is praised in you, justice in your mother, courage in the virgin, temperance in the married woman.

For who is wiser than he who, despising the folly of the world, followed Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God?

Who is more just than the mother who, distributing her wealth among her children, taught them by despising riches what they ought to love?

Who is braver than Eustochium, who broke the gates of nobility and the arrogance of consular lineage through her virginal purpose, and in the foremost city subjected the foremost rank to chastity?

Who is more temperate than Paulina, who, reading the Apostle’s words, “Marriage is honorable and the marriage bed undefiled” (Heb. 13:4), dared aspire neither to her sister’s happiness nor to her mother’s continence, but preferred to proceed safely on lower ground rather than waver on the heights with an unstable step?

Although, once she had entered marriage, she thought of nothing day and night except that, after bearing the fruit of marriage, she might attain the second degree of chastity and, as a woman who had undertaken so great a deed (Aeneid 1), might join her husband to her purpose—not abandoning a companion of salvation, but waiting for him.

While, through repeated miscarriages and tested fertility in conception, she did not despair of children, and preferred her mother-in-law’s eagerness and her husband’s sorrow to her own weakness, she endured something like Rachel’s experience; and, instead of the son of sorrow and of the right hand (Gen. 35:18), bore an heir for the husband of her desire.

I have learned from reliable authorities that she did not wish to serve either the first command of God—“Be fruitful and multiply, and fill the earth” (Gen. 1:28)—or the duty of marriage, but desired children for this purpose: that she might bear virgins for Christ.

4. We also read that the wife of Phinehas the priest, upon hearing of the capture of the Ark of the Lord, was suddenly seized by the pains of childbirth and gave birth to a son, Ichabod (1 Sam. 4:19), and between the hands and services of the women breathed out her soul together with her child.

From the first woman came Benjamin—that is, “son of virtue” and “of the right hand”; from the second, the illustrious priest of God, whose name derived from the Ark, was born.

[Note: The name Ichabod means in Latin, “Where is the glory?” with an interrogative sign; for *kabod* means “glory,” and *i* means “where?” He is said to have been named Ichabod from the name of the Ark, since the glory and riches of the Israelites were frequently called *Kabod*, “the Ark of the Lord.”]

After Paulina’s sleep and repose, the Church bore Pammachius, a monk, as a posthumous child—patrician through the nobility of his father and wife, rich through almsgiving, exalted through humility.

The Apostle writes to the Corinthians: “See your calling, brothers, that not many are wise, not many noble” (1 Cor. 1:26).

[Note: Gravius adds: “according to the flesh.”]

These were the demands of the beginnings of the newborn Church, so that the mustard seed might gradually grow into a tree (Luke 13:19), and so that the leaven of the Gospel might gradually raise the whole mass of the Church to a greater height.

In our times Rome possesses what the world previously did not know. Then Christians were few among the wise, the powerful, and the noble; now there are many monks who are wise, powerful, and noble.

Among all these, my Pammachius is wiser, more powerful, and nobler: great among the great, first among the first, *ἀρχιστράτηγος*, commander-in-chief of the monks.

Such children Paulina gave us by her death, whom while alive she had desired to possess.

“Rejoice, barren woman who do not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not travail” (Isa. 54:1), for as many poor as there are in Rome, so many children you have suddenly borne.

5. Blazing gems, which previously adorned the necks and faces of women, now fill the stomachs of the needy. Silk garments and gold stretched into threads have been changed into soft woolen clothing with which the cold may be driven away, not clothing by which vanity may be exposed.

The furnishings once devoted to luxury are consumed by virtue.

That blind man who stretches out his hand and often cries out where no one is, is Paulina’s heir and Pammachius’s co-heir.

That man whose feet are crippled and who drags himself along with his whole body is supported by the hand of a tender girl.

The doors that formerly spewed forth crowds of greeting visitors are now besieged by the wretched.

One man, with his belly swollen by water, gives birth to death; another, speechless and mute, possessing not even the means to ask, asks all the more because he cannot ask.

This man, weakened from childhood, does not beg alms for himself.

[Note: Valesius insists that *a lepra* should be corrected, but this does not please us, especially since all the ancient books unanimously prefer the printed reading, and since it can easily be understood to mean someone weakened from his earliest years, or from childhood, who cannot beg alms for himself. Add that writers of that age generally treat leprosy and the royal disease, which is mentioned immediately afterward, as one and the same illness. Jerome himself, in the Life of Saint Hilarion, says of Hadrian: “After some time he wasted away from the royal disease,” although elsewhere he seems to distinguish them.]

That man, putrefied by the royal disease, outlives his own corpse.

“Even if I had a hundred tongues and a hundred mouths,

I could not run through all the names of punishments.” (Aeneid 6)

Accompanied by this army, he goes forward; in these people he cherishes Christ, and by their filth he is made white. The **Muncrarius** [or *Munerarius*] of the poor and the candidate of the needy thus hastens toward heaven.

[Note: Formerly, if we conceal nothing, we thought that *Numerarius* ought to be read instead of *Munerarius*. For just as those who contributed public money to the treasury were called *Numerarii*—as Isidore of Seville reports (*Etymologies* 9.4)—so the poor man’s *Numerarius*, who contributed his wealth for their support, seemed more properly so called. But we must by no means abandon the widely transmitted reading. In these two words, *Munerarius* and *Candidatus*, a double allusion is made to kinds of public entertainments that ancient pagan sponsors of spectacles gave to mimes, actors, charioteers, and others. It is certainly in this sense that Saint Cyprian calls those who distribute alms *Munerarii*, in his book *On Works and Almsgiving*, near the middle:

> “What kind of gift is it,” he says, “whose presentation is celebrated while God looks on? If, in the entertainment of the pagans, it seems great and glorious to have proconsuls or emperors present, and if the equipment and expense are greater for the sponsors of the games so that they may please their superiors, how much more illustrious is the entertainment, and how much greater its glory, when God and Christ are the spectators?”

Saint Ambrose alludes no less elegantly to the other kind in a sermon formerly numbered 81: “Let us prepare new and most splendid gifts. Let us present the first *Candida*, in the clothing of the naked,” and so forth. An entertainment was called *Candida* when it was provided by magistrates at their own expense or from the public treasury. Thus, in Herwart’s Calendar, *Munus Arca* and *Munus Candida* are set in opposition. In the account of the martyrdom of Saint Boniface, it is written of Aglaë, a Roman matron, that she had presented a *Candida* three times in the city of Rome. But there is no need for further examples, which are supplied by Sismondo and Baluze.]

Other husbands scatter violets, roses, lilies, and purple flowers over the tombs of their wives, and console the grief of their hearts by these services. Our Pammachius waters the holy ashes and venerable bones with the balsams of almsgiving. With these perfumes and fragrances he cherishes the resting ashes, knowing that it is written: “As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin” (Ecclesiasticus 3:33). Saint Cyprian, too, discusses at length the power that mercy possesses and the rewards with which it ought to be repaid; he approves Daniel’s counsel, who knew that the most impious king would have been saved by supporting the poor, had he been willing to listen.

[Note: In his book *On Works and Almsgiving*, immediately after the beginning, speaking of Nebuchadnezzar’s dream and the adversities that followed, he says: “He could have escaped and avoided them if he had redeemed his sins by almsgiving.”]

The mother of this sort of daughter rejoices in her heir. She does not grieve that wealth has passed to another, since she sees it being distributed to the same people to whom she herself had wished it distributed. Rather, she gives thanks that, without her labor, her wishes are being fulfilled. For it is not a diminution of the estate, but a change of its steward.

### 6

Who could have believed that the great-grandson of consuls, the glory of the Furian family, would walk among the purple-clad senators in a dark, mourning tunic, and would not be ashamed to meet the eyes of his companions—so that, by laughing at them as they mocked him, he would himself mock them?

“There is a shame that leads to death, and there is a shame that leads to life” (Ecclesiasticus 4).

The first virtue of a monk is to despise human judgments and always to remember the Apostle, who says: “If I were still pleasing human beings, I would not be Christ’s servant” (Galatians 1:10).

The Lord likewise says something similar to the prophets: that he had made their faces like a bronze city, a diamond-like stone, and an iron pillar (Jeremiah 1), so that they would not fear the insults of the people, but would crush the insolence of their mockers by the firmness of their brow (Ezekiel 3).

Minds liberally educated are more easily overcome by shame than by fear. Those whom tortures do not conquer are sometimes conquered by embarrassment. It is no small thing for a nobleman, an eloquent man, a wealthy man, to avoid the company of the powerful in the streets, mingle with crowds, associate with the poor, join himself to peasants, and become, from a prince, one of the common people. But the humbler he is, the more exalted he is.

### 7

A pearl shines amid filth, and the radiance of the purest gem gleams even in mud. This is what the Lord promised: “Those who glorify me, I will glorify” (1 Samuel 2:30). Let others understand this of the future, when sorrow will be turned into joy and, when the world has passed away, the crown of the saints will not pass away. I see the promises made to the saints being fulfilled even in the present.

Before he served Christ with his whole mind, he was known in the Senate, but [Note: In other books and in Gravius: “but also many others.” Shortly afterward, *islands* is probably a typographical error for *insignia*; Martianus reads *infulas*.] many others held proconsular insignia. The whole world is full of honors of this kind. He was first, but only among the first. He preceded others in rank, but he also followed others.

**HOWEVER DISTINGUISHED**, an honor becomes worthless in a crowd; and among good men the dignity itself becomes less honorable when many unworthy people possess it. Hence Cicero speaks excellently of Caesar: when, he says, Caesar wished to honor certain men, he did not ennoble them, but disturbed the honors themselves.

But now all the churches of Christ speak of Pammachius. The world is amazed at the poor man whom, until now, it had known as wealthy.

What is more illustrious than the consulship? It is an annual honor, and once another has succeeded, the former comes to an end. Laurels lie hidden in the multitude, and triumphs are sometimes stained by the filth of those who triumph. What was formerly handed down through patrician hands, and possessed by nobility alone—so that Marius, consul, victor over Numidia, the Teutons, and the Cimbri, was considered unworthy because of the obscurity [or novelty] of his family; what Scipio earned beyond the ordinary term through his virtue—now belongs to military service alone, and [Note: At that time barbarians generally held the highest positions; hence barbarian names frequently appear marked by the ordinary consulship. The phrase “a shining palm surrounds” signifies a palm-embroidered consular garment, of the sort seen on several consular diptychs.] a shining palm surrounds bodies that not long ago were rustic.

We have therefore received more than we gave. **WE HAVE GIVEN UP LITTLE**, and we possess great things. Christ’s promises are returned with interest multiplied a hundredfold. In such a field Isaac once sowed, he who, prepared for death, bore the evangelical cross before the Gospel.

### 8

“If you wish to be perfect,” he says, “go, sell everything you possess, give it to the poor, and come, follow me” (Matthew 19:21).

“If you wish to be perfect.” Great things are always placed within the will of those who hear. For this reason the Apostle does not command virginity, because the Lord, speaking of eunuchs who had made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven, concluded: “Let the one who can accept it accept it” (ibid. 12). “For it depends neither on the one who wills nor on the one who runs, but on God who shows mercy” (Romans 9:16).

“If you wish to be perfect.” No necessity is imposed upon you, so that the reward may belong to the will. If, then, you wish to be perfect, and desire to become what the prophets, the apostles, and Christ are, sell—not part of your estate, lest fear of poverty become an occasion for unbelief and you perish with Ananias and Sapphira—but everything you possess.

And when you have sold it, give to the poor, not to the wealthy and not to the proud. Give where necessity will be sustained, not where wealth will be increased. When you read the Apostle’s words, “You shall not muzzle the ox while it is treading out the grain,” and, “The laborer is worthy of his wages” (1 Corinthians 9:9; 1 Timothy 5:18), and, “Those who serve at the altar share in what comes from the altar” (1 Corinthians 9:13), remember also this statement: “Having food and clothing, with these we shall be content” (1 Timothy 6:8).

When you see serving dishes smoking, and Phasian birds being cooked in slow vapors; when you see quantities of silver, and [Note: Older printed editions and some manuscripts read *ferventes Burichos mannos*, “boiling Burichi foals,” so that it might be clear what *manni* were, namely small horses; someone added the more familiar word *Burichus* in the margin, and it later entered the text. *Burichus* is not a type of garment, nor is the name derived from the city of Bourris in Achaea, as some have written in their notes on this passage. Rather, as the ancient commentators on Horace explain in Ode 27 of Book 1, and in Epode 4 and elsewhere, it means a small horse, which they called *burdus*, *buridus*, *burdo*, and *burichus*. Hence an old Glossary interprets *manni* as βουρίχους (*bouríchous*, “small horses”). See Saint Isidore, Book 12, chapter 1.] hot little horses, long-haired boys, costly garments, and embroidered carpets—there the wealthier person is the one to whom gifts ought to be given.

It is part of sacrilege to give the property of the poor to people who are not poor. Yet it is not enough for a perfect and complete man to despise wealth, squander money, and throw away what can be lost and found again in a moment. Crates of Thebes did this; Antisthenes did it; very many did it, whom we read to have been most vicious. A disciple of Christ must surpass the philosopher of the world, that creature of glory and saleable slave of popular favor and rumor.

It is not enough for you to despise wealth unless you follow Christ. **CHRIST**, however, is followed by the one who puts away sins and is the companion of virtues. We know Christ as wisdom. This treasure is born in the field of the Scriptures; this gem is purchased with many pearls.

But if you have fallen in love with a captive woman—that is, with worldly wisdom—and have been captivated by her beauty, shave her head, and cut away the allurements of her hair and the ornaments of her words together with her dead fingernails. Wash her with the prophetic natron, and then, resting with her, say: “His left hand is beneath my head, and his right hand will embrace me” (Song of Songs 2:6). The captive woman will give you many offspring and will be transformed from a Moabite into an Israelite.

Christ is sanctification, without which no one will see the face of God. Christ is redemption, both the redeemer and the price. Christ is everything, so that the one who has abandoned everything for Christ may find one thing in place of everything and may freely proclaim: “The Lord is my portion” (Psalm 72:26).

### 9

I perceive that you burn with divine teachings, and that you do not, with the rashness of certain people, teach what you do not know, but first learn what you are going to teach. Your simple letters smell of the prophets and taste of the apostles. You do not strive after a high-flown eloquence, nor, like boys, do you construct clever little maxims at the ends of your sentences.

**QUICKLY SWELLING**, foam dissipates; and however great the swelling, it is contrary to health. That saying of Cato’s is also well known: “Soon enough, if well enough.”

[Note: Gravius prefers *dira* (“dire”) to *dura* (“harsh”); Jerome calls necessity “dire” in the *Epitaph of Paula* and in his commentaries on Hosea 13 and Habakkuk 3.]

“I remember that when we were young men, we laughed when it was spoken by a perfect orator in a brief preface.” I think you remember our mutual mistake, when the whole Athenaeum resounded with the voices of the students: “Soon enough, if well enough.”

“Happy,” says Fabius [Note: This is a saying of Fabius Pictor preserved by Quintilian.], “would the arts be if only craftsmen judged them.” A poet cannot be known except by one who can construct a verse. No one understands philosophers except one who knows the variety of their doctrines. Works made by hand and tolerated by the eyes prove craftsmen all the more.

You can perceive how harsh our necessity is from this: one must stand by the judgment of the common people, and the person whom, when you see him alone, you would despise must be feared when he is in a crowd. I have touched on this in passing so that, content with the ears of the educated, you may not greatly care what little rumors the unlearned spread about your talent. Instead, drink daily the marrow of the prophets, as Christ’s initiate and the intimate companion of the patriarchs.

### 10

Whether you read or write, keep watch or sleep, let **Amos** [or *love*] always sound like a trumpet in your ears. Let this clarion awaken your soul. Maddened by this love, seek on your bed the one whom your soul desires (Song of Songs 3:1), and speak boldly: “I sleep, but my heart is awake” (ibid. 3:2).

When you have found him and taken hold of him, do not let him go. And if he slips from your hands while you are sleeping, do not immediately despair. Go out into the streets and adjure the daughters of Jerusalem (ibid. 3:2). You will find him lying at midday, weary, drunk, his face wet with the night, among flocks of companions, amid a variety of spices, among the fruits of paradise.

There, give him your breasts, that he may suck from your learned bosom (ibid. 7:12); let him rest among the midst of the lots (*cleros*), “the wings of a silvered dove, and her inner feathers shining like gold” (Psalm 67:14). This little one and child, who is fed on butter and honey (Isaiah 7:15), who was nourished among mountains rich in cheese, quickly grows into a young man; swiftly, in you, he strips your enemies, promptly plunders Damascus, and conquers the Assyrian king.

### 11. Xenodochium Built by Pammachius

I hear that you have built a hospice in the Roman harbor and planted Abraham’s branch from a tree on the Ausonian shore.

[Note: That tree represents the hospice under which Abraham received three angels as guests in the vale of Mamre; and he most elegantly calls the hospice that Pammachius built on the Ausonian shore “a branch from that tree,” after Abraham’s example.] As though you were laying out a new camp like Aeneas, and, above the waters of the Tiber—where once, compelled by poverty, he did not spare the destined crusts and broad, flat loaves—you are building our little village, that is, the house of bread, Bethlehem; and you are compensating prolonged hunger with sudden fullness.

“Bravo! You surpass our beginnings; you occupy the highest position: from the root you reach the summit. First among monks, in the first city, you follow the first patriarch.”

[Note: Martianus reads *Euge: noster hinc transgrederis*, which makes no sense. Older printed editions and some manuscripts read *Euge noster initia transgrederis*, which can conveniently be explained as “Bravo, our Abraham,” or “the Aeneas of our age.” But we have chosen to restore *nostra initia*, a much more harmonious reading, as the context that follows also shows. See below, section 14, concerning the monastery he had begun to build at Bethlehem.]

Let Lot, whose name means “one who turns aside,” choose the plains and, in accordance with Pythagoras’ letter [Note: That is, the letter Y, of which we shall speak below in the Letter to Laeta.], pursue what is easier and leftward. But in the steep and rocky places, prepare a tomb for yourself with Sarah (Genesis 23). Let a city of letters lie nearby; when the giants, the sons of Anak [or Anakim], have been destroyed, let your inheritance receive joy and laughter.

Abraham was rich in gold, silver, livestock, property, and clothing (Genesis 24). He had such a large household that, at sudden summons, he could arm an army with chosen young men and, having pursued at Dan the four kings whom the five kings had put to flight, kill them. Yet, after so many acts of hospitality, because he did not refuse to receive human beings, he deserved to receive God.

He did not order servants and maidservants to minister to his guests, thereby diminishing through others the good work he was performing. Rather, as though he had found a prize, he alone devoted himself to hospitality with his Sarah. He himself washed their feet; he himself carried the fattened calf from the herd upon his shoulders. He stood as a servant while the foreigners dined, and, intending to fast himself, placed before them food cooked by Sarah’s hands.

### 12

I say these things, dearest brother, out of the devotion with which I love you, so that you may offer to Christ not only your money but yourself: a living, holy, pleasing sacrifice to God, your rational service (Romans 12:1). I want you to imitate the Son of Man, who did not come to be served but to serve (Matthew 20:28).

What the patriarch offered to strangers, the Master and Lord offered to disciples and servants. “Skin for skin, and everything that a person possesses he will give for his life. But stretch out your hand,” says the devil, “and touch his flesh; surely he will curse you to your face” (Job 2:4–5).

The ancient enemy knows that the struggle over self-restraint is greater than the struggle over money. **WHAT CLINGS TO THE OUTSIDE IS EASILY CAST OFF**; the inward war is more dangerous. We tear apart things joined together; we sunder what is united [or sew apart what is joined].

Zacchaeus was rich; the apostles were poor. Zacchaeus returned fourfold what he had stolen, divided half of his remaining property among the poor, and received Christ as his guest; salvation came to his house (Luke 19). Yet because he was small and could not stretch himself to apostolic stature, he was not numbered among the twelve apostles.

The apostles, though they had nothing in regard to wealth, left the whole world together in regard to their will. If we offer Christ our possessions together with our soul, he will gladly receive them. But if we give to God what is outside us and to the devil what is within us, the division is not just, and it is said to us: “If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, have you not sinned?” (Genesis 4:7, according to the Septuagint).

### 13

Since you, who are of patrician stock, first among the first, have begun to be a monk, let this not be an occasion for pride but for humility, knowing that the Son of God became the Son of Man.

[Note: Pammachius was first among the first because of his patrician family, as was stated above in section 6 in the same words. The reading that has prevailed until now in printed books is therefore most unsatisfactory: it referred the words “first among the first” to the monks, with faulty punctuation, which we have corrected, and it restored *monachus* in place of *monachos*.]

**HOWEVER MUCH** you humble yourself, you will not be humbler than Christ. Suppose that you walk barefoot, wear a dark tunic, make yourself equal to the poor, and graciously enter the cells of the needy; suppose that you become the eyes of the blind, the hands of the weak, and the feet of the lame; that you carry water yourself, cut wood, and build the fire. Where are the chains? Where are the blows? Where are the spittings? Where are the scourges? Where is the cross? Where is death?

And when you have done everything I have mentioned, you will be surpassed by your Eustochium and Paula—not in deeds, perhaps, but certainly in sex.

I was not in Rome, for the desert held me then—and would that it had continued to hold me—when, while your father-in-law Toxotius was alive [Note: Toxotius the elder was the husband of Saint Paula and the father of Paulina, who married Pammachius.], they were serving the world. Yet I hear that those who could not bear the filth of the streets, who were carried in the hands of eunuchs, and who found uneven ground most troublesome to cross; those for whom silk garments were a burden and the heat of the sun a conflagration—now, soiled and mourning, yet strong in comparison with themselves, they either trim or light lamps, build fires, sweep floors, clean vegetables, throw bundles of greens into a boiling pot, set tables, hand around cups, distribute food, and hurry back and forth.

And certainly a great chorus of virgins lives with them. Could they not have ordered others to perform such services? **BUT THEY DO NOT WISH** to be surpassed in bodily labor by those whom they themselves surpass in strength of spirit.

I say this not because I doubt anything about the ardor of your mind, but so that I may urge one who is already running, and increase the fervor of one who is fighting fiercely by fervor. [Note: Older printed editions have *fervorem favore augeam*, “may I increase fervor by favor,” an equally sound reading; some manuscripts also read *fervorem fervore augeam*, “may I increase fervor by fervor.”]

### 14. Monastery Built by Jerome

After building a monastery in this province and constructing a hospice beside it, lest perhaps Joseph, coming now with Mary to Bethlehem, should also fail to find lodging (Luke 2), we are overwhelmed by such crowds of monks pouring in from the whole world that we can neither abandon the work we have begun nor bear the burden beyond our strength.

Because almost what is said in the Gospel happened to us—that we had not first calculated the expense of the tower we were going to build (Luke 14)—we were compelled to send our brother Paulinianus to his homeland, so that he might sell the half-ruined little estates that had escaped the hands of the barbarians [Note: Victorius thought the following reading of certain copies attractive and very elegant: “and the estates of our common parents, which contain their ashes, he should sell,” and so forth. We find it in the older printed editions, but not in the manuscripts; without their support we venture nothing.], together with the property of our common parents, lest, by abandoning the ministry we had begun for the saints, we should provide laughter for slanderers and rivals.

### 15

At the end of the letter I remembered your four-horse team, and that, for your purpose, the fifth—Blaesilla—was missing. I almost forgot to speak of her, the first of you to go before the Lord. Truly, we now see the five divided into three and two: she, together with her sister Paulina, enjoys sweet sleep; while you, standing between the two, will fly more lightly to Christ.

## LETTER LXVII

[Note: Otherwise numbered 87. Written around the year 397.]

### Augustine to Jerome

Augustine asks Jerome about the title of the book on ecclesiastical writers that Jerome had published; then about Peter, whom Paul had reproved—not deceitfully—a matter he had also asked about in the preceding Letter 56. Finally, he asks him to indicate what errors Origen and other heretics had held.

To the most beloved lord, brother Jerome, worthy of honor and embrace with the most sincere devotion of charity, and fellow presbyter, Augustine.

### 1

“I give thanks that you returned to me a full letter in response to the salutation written below, but one much shorter than I would wish to receive from you, a man from whom no speech is too long, however much time may occupy you.

Although, therefore, we are surrounded by immense concerns over the affairs of others—and secular affairs at that—I would not easily forgive the brevity of your letter unless I considered how much shorter a reply it would receive from me.

Therefore, I beg you, begin this literary conversation with us, lest bodily absence have too much power to separate us, although we are joined in the unity of the spirit in the Lord, even when we cease writing and remain silent.

The books that you composed from the Lord’s granary display almost your whole self to us.

[Note: This letter of Jerome’s has not survived, or at least had not yet come to light.] For if we do not know you because we have not seen your bodily face, then by this method you do not know yourself either, since you do not see it yourself. But if you are known to yourself for no other reason than that you know your own mind, then we too know it, and not to a small degree, in your writings. In them we bless the Lord because he has given you such a character—to you, to us, and to all the brothers who read you.”

### 2

“Not long ago one of your books came into our hands among the rest. We still do not know its title. The codex itself did not display it, as is customary, on its opening page. The brother in whose possession it was found said that it was called an *Epitaphium*, and we would believe that you had wished this name to be given to it if we had read there only the lives or writings of people who had already died.

But since the little works of many people who were alive both when it was written and even now are mentioned there, we wonder why you either gave it this title or were thought to have given it. Nevertheless [or “Indeed”], we very much approve the fact that you wrote the book usefully.”

[Note: Martianay, following Erasmus, deleted the word *ibi* (“there”), which Victorius had supplied from the manuscripts and which all the books retain.]

### 3

“In your exposition of the Apostle Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, we also found something that greatly troubles us.

[Note: Victorius removed *illud* (“that”) as superfluous.] For if ‘dutiful lies’ are admitted into the sacred Scriptures, what authority will remain in them? What judgment will finally be pronounced concerning those Scriptures, by whose weight the wickedness of contentious falsehood may be overthrown?

As soon as you produce a statement, if the person who opposes you understands it differently, he will say that the writer made a lie out of some honorable duty. For where will he be unable to do this, if it was possible in the narrative that the Apostle began by saying: ‘As for what I am writing to you, behold, before God, I am not lying’ (Galatians 1:20)—if he can be believed and asserted to have lied at the point where he said concerning Peter and Barnabas, ‘When I saw that they were not walking correctly according to the truth of the Gospel’ (Galatians 2:14)?

If they were walking correctly, he lied. But if he lied there, where did he tell the truth? Or will he seem to have told the truth wherever he says what the reader thinks? Yet whenever something contrary to the reader’s understanding appears, will it be attributed to a dutiful lie?

There will never be a shortage of reasons for thinking that a person not only could have lied but ought to have lied, if this principle is admitted. There is no need to pursue this matter at length, especially with you, to whom a word spoken with wisdom and foresight is sufficient.

I would certainly not presume to enrich with my pennies your intellect, golden through divine gift; nor is anyone more capable than you of correcting that work.”

### 4

“You do not need me to teach you how to understand what the same Apostle says: ‘I became as a Jew to the Jews, in order to win the Jews’ (1 Corinthians 9:20), and the other statements made there, through **COMPASSION** (*compassione*) and mercy, not through deceitful pretense.

A person becomes like a sick man who ministers to the sick—not by pretending to have fevers, but by considering with a compassionate mind how he would wish to be served if he himself were sick. For, of course, he was a Jew. Having become a Christian, he had not abandoned the Jewish sacraments that this people had received appropriately and at the lawful time.

[Note: The Benedictine editors differ slightly: “Therefore he undertook them,” and shortly afterward, “but in order to teach.”]

Rather, he had undertaken to celebrate them as one who was already Christ’s apostle, so that he might teach that they were not harmful to those who wished to preserve them as they had received them from their parents through the Law, even after they had believed in Christ—provided that they no longer placed their hope of salvation in them, since through the Lord Jesus the salvation signified by those sacraments had arrived.

For this reason, he judged that they should in no way be imposed upon the Gentiles, since, being unaccustomed to them, they would recall them from the faith through a heavy and unnecessary burden.”

[Note: Again Victorius, from the Brescia codices, reads “heavy and unnecessary burdens.”]

### 5

“Therefore Peter did not correct him because he observed the traditions of his ancestors. If Peter wished to do this, he would neither be acting deceitfully nor incongruously. Although those traditions were already superfluous, customary practices would not be harmful.

Rather, Paul corrected him because Peter was compelling the Gentiles to Judaize (Galatians 2:14). He could not have done this unless he acted as though those practices were still necessary for salvation even after the Lord’s coming—a view that the truth proclaimed through Paul’s apostleship vigorously rejected.

The Apostle Peter did not fail to know this. But he acted out of fear of those who were of the circumcision. Thus he himself was truly corrected, and Paul truly narrated what happened, lest the holy Scripture, which was given for the faith of later generations, totter and waver entirely once the authority of lying had been admitted.

It is impossible—and it is unnecessary—to explain in writing how many and how inexplicable evils would follow if we conceded this. The point could be demonstrated appropriately and with less danger if we were speaking together face to face.”

### 6

“Paul had abandoned from Judaism what was evil; above all, this: that, being ignorant of God’s righteousness and wishing to establish their own righteousness, they were not subject to the righteousness of God (Romans 10:3).

Next, he rejected the belief that, after Christ’s passion and resurrection and after the sacrament of grace had been given and revealed according to the order of Melchizedek, the ancient sacraments still had to be celebrated not merely from customary solemnity but from necessity for salvation. Yet if they had never been necessary, the Maccabean martyrs would have suffered death for them fruitlessly and in vain (2 Maccabees 7:1).

Finally, he rejected the fact that the Jews persecuted the Christian preachers of grace as enemies of the Law.

These errors and vices, and others of the same kind, he says he considered ‘loss and refuse’ in order to gain Christ (Philippians 3:8):

[Note: Most printed editions read: “he says that he condemns them and has considered, or considers them, loss and refuse.”] not the observances of the Law if they were celebrated according to ancestral custom, as he himself celebrated them without any necessity for salvation; [Note: The negative particle is absent from some printed editions and from most manuscripts in the Benedictine edition.] **not** as the Jews thought they ought to be celebrated, nor through the deceitful pretense that he had reproved in Peter.

For if he celebrated those sacraments because he pretended to be a Jew in order to win them, why did he not also sacrifice with the Gentiles, since he became as one without the Law to those who were without the Law, in order to win them also (1 Corinthians 9)? The only explanation is that he did the former as a Jew by nature, and that he said all this not so that he might deceitfully pretend to be what he was not, but so that, with mercy, he might judge that he ought to help them as though he himself were struggling with the same error.

**NOT, CLEARLY, THROUGH THE CUNNING OF ONE WHO LIES**, but through the affection of one who suffers with another. In that very passage he made the general statement: ‘I became weak to the weak, in order to win the weak’ (ibid. v. 22). Thus the following conclusion—‘I have become all things to all people, so that I might win all’—must be understood as referring to his appearing, through compassion, to experience each person’s weakness as though it were his own.

For when he said, ‘Who is weak, and I am not weak?’ (2 Corinthians 11:29), he did not mean that he pretended to another’s weakness rather than suffering with it.”

### 7

“Therefore, I beg you, take up a candid and truly Christian severity joined with charity, to correct and amend that work, and sing a *palinōdia* (παλινωδίαν), as it is called—a recantation or retraction.

The truth of Christians is incomparably more beautiful than the Helen of the Greeks. **FOR THIS TRUTH**, our martyrs fought more courageously against this Sodom than those men fought for Helen against Troy.

I do not say this so that you may recover the eyes of your heart—far be it from me to suggest that you have lost them—but so that you may notice what you have turned away from through some dissimulation, though your eyes are sound and vigilant: namely, the consequences that follow if it is once believed that the writer of divine books can honestly and piously lie in some part of his work.

[Note: Victorius formerly observed that *scriptorem*, “the writer,” could honorably and piously be understood in this way.]

### 8

“I had once already written a letter to you, but it was not delivered because the man to whom I had entrusted it did not proceed on his journey. From that letter this thought was suggested to me as I dictated the present one, and I ought not to omit it here: if your opinion is different, and your opinion is the better one, may you willingly forgive my fear.

For if you think differently, and what you think is true—for unless it is true, it cannot be better—then, not to say that my error is entirely without fault, certainly my error favors the truth, if in any matter truth can properly favor a lie.”

### 9

“As for Origen, regarding whom you were kind enough to write back, I already knew that in ecclesiastical writings, and indeed in all writings, you approve and praise whatever we find that is right and true, while disapproving and criticizing what is false and corrupt.

But I was, and still am, missing this from your prudence and learning: that you make known to us the very errors by which that great man is proved to have departed from the faith of the truth.

In the book in which you recalled all the ecclesiastical writers whom you could remember, together with their writings, I also think it would have been more useful if, after naming those whom you know to have been heresiarchs [or *heresiotes*, “heretics”], you had added the points on which they should be avoided—especially since you omitted some others as well, and I would like to know for what reason this was done.

Or, if you did not wish to burden that volume, and therefore did not wish to add, after mentioning the heretics, the matters on which Catholic authority condemned them, I beg you not to consider it burdensome to your literary labors—through which, by the grace of our Lord God, you have greatly kindled and assisted the studies of the saints in the Latin language—to do what fraternal charity, through my humility, requests of you.

If your occupations allow it, publish, in a single brief book, a concise arrangement of the perverse doctrines of all the heretics who, up to this time, have tried through ignorance, incompetence, or obstinacy to corrupt the integrity of the Christian faith. Let this be made known to those who either have no leisure, because of other business, or are unable, because of their unfamiliarity with another language, to read and learn so much.

[Note: Augustine believed that Jerome had composed such a booklet *On Heresies* some years later, and says that he learned this from others’ reports in one of his later works, namely his commentary on Jeremiah, chapter 88. But the book now extant under that title, to be printed by us in the final volume, falsely claims Jerome as its author.]

I would ask you at length, were it not that doing so is ordinarily a sign of someone who has less confidence in another’s charity. Meanwhile, I strongly commend to your kindness our brother Paul in Christ, whose good reputation in our regions we attest before God.”

## LETTER LXVIII

[Note: Also numbered 33. Written in this year, 397.]

### To Castrutius

To Castrutius of Pannonia, who had decided to sail in order to visit Jerome, Jerome gives thanks and consoles him concerning the blindness of his eyes, teaching that such blindness is sometimes sent by a merciful God.

## 1.

My holy son Heraclius the deacon reported to me that, out of desire for us, you had come as far as Cissa [Note: The Verona manuscript, which is addressed “to Castricianus concerning blindness of the eyes,” and the Cistercian manuscript, which is addressed simply “to Castrianus,” here prefer the reading “as far as Edessa,” though this is less probable. For Edessa is a city of Macedonia, and for Castrutius to reach it he would not have had to face the dangers of the Aegean Sea; whereas, if he came to Cissa, a city of Thrace on the Hellespont, he would have had to do so. Ferrarius, however, following Pliny, places this Cissa at the mouth of the Timavus on the Adriatic Sea. This opinion persuaded us to understand these dangers of the seas not as those which Castrutius had already escaped, but as those which he would gladly and resolutely have undertaken.] And you, a Pannonian— that is, an earthly creature—were not afraid to face the waves [another reading: the sandbanks] of the Adriatic Sea and the dangers of the Aegean and Ionian seas. And unless pious affection for the brethren had held you back, you would have carried your intention into action. I therefore give you thanks and count it as received. For among friends it is not the deed that is sought, but the willingness; the one is often supplied even by enemies, while the other is bestowed by love alone.

At the same time I beg you not to suppose that the weakness of body which you suffer has come upon you because of sin. The Apostles, indeed, suspecting this concerning the man who had been born blind, and asking the Lord and Savior, “Did this man sin, or his parents, that he should be born blind?” hear the answer: “Neither did this man sin, nor his parents; but that the works of God might be manifested in him” (John 9:2–3). [Note: The Benedictine editor, following Erasmus, had deleted two words in the text itself.]

How many Gentiles and Jews, heretics and men of various doctrines, do we see wallowing in the filth of lust, drenched in blood, surpassing wolves in savagery and hawks in rapacity, while nevertheless the scourge does not approach their tents (Ps. 90), nor are they beaten together with other human beings; and for that reason they grow proud against God, and their mouths pass even to heaven. By contrast, we know holy men to be tortured by illnesses, miseries, and poverty, who perhaps say, “Therefore I have sanctified my soul in vain, and washed my hands among the innocent” (Ps. 72:13). [Note: The same manuscripts incorrectly read “I” for “Therefore.”] And immediately correcting themselves, they say: “If I should speak thus, behold, I would have rejected the nation [another reading: generation] of your children” (ibid. 13, 15).

If you think blindness is caused by sin, and that what physicians frequently remedy brings down God’s anger, you will also accuse Isaac, who was so deprived of this world’s light that, deceived by error, he blessed even the one whom he did not wish to bless (Gen. 27). You will charge Jacob with guilt, whose sight had grown dim, so that although with his inward eyes and prophetic spirit he saw far ahead what was to come, and perceived that Christ would arise from the royal line, he could not see Ephraim and Manasseh (Gen. 48–49). [Note: Two older manuscripts read: “and proclaimed Christ as destined to come from the royal tribe, and shortly afterward, pierced, slain in his place.”]

Who was holier among kings than Josiah? Yet he was killed by an Egyptian sword (2 Kings 23). What was loftier than Peter, what than Paul? They reddened Nero’s sword with their blood. And—not to speak of human beings—the Son of God endured the shame of the cross. Do you think, then, that those are blessed who enjoy the prosperity and delights of this age?

Great indeed is God’s anger when he is not angry with sinners. Thus also in Ezekiel he says to Jerusalem: “Now I will no longer be angry with you; my jealousy has withdrawn from you” (Ezek. 16:42). “For whom the Lord loves, he disciplines” (Prov. 3:12), and “he chastises every son whom he receives” (Heb. 12). A father does not educate anyone except the child whom he loves. A teacher does not rebuke a pupil except one whom he sees to possess a more ardent intelligence. If a physician ceases to treat, he has given up hope.

[Note: Thus all the printed books and manuscripts read; but there is evidently an error in these words. “For if you should answer” produces a broken and abrupt sense contrary to the holy Doctor’s meaning. I would read, “Therefore you will answer,” or something similar. Unless one prefers, with slightly altered punctuation and with the little word “for” removed from the saying of Nahum, to connect that saying directly with what precedes, as though it were the answer to the preceding objection. The Verona manuscript meanwhile reads “you answer,” and “he will have received.”]

But if you should answer, “How, then, did Lazarus receive evil things in his lifetime?” (Luke 16), I shall gladly endure torments now, so that glory may be reserved for me hereafter; for “the Lord will not avenge the same thing twice” (Nahum 1). Why holy, blameless, and just Job suffered so much in his generation is contained in his own book.

## 2.

And lest, by repeating ancient histories, I make this too long and exceed the measure of a letter, I shall relate to you a brief story [little narrative] that occurred in the days of my childhood.

When blessed Antony had been summoned to the city of Alexandria by Saint Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, for the refutation of the heretics [Arians], and the very learned man Didymus, who was blind, had gone to him, they held various conversations about the holy Scriptures. Antony admired his intelligence and praised the sharpness of his mind; then he asked him: “Are you sad because you lack the eyes of the flesh?”

When Didymus remained silent out of embarrassment, Antony asked him a second and a third time, and at last drew from him a frank confession of his sorrow. Antony said to him: “I am astonished that a prudent man should grieve over the loss of something possessed by ants, flies, and gnats, and should not rejoice in possessing what only the saints and Apostles have deserved.”

From this you can see that it is far better to see with the spirit than with the flesh, and to possess those eyes into which the splinter of sin cannot fall (Luke 6).

Although you have not come this year, we nevertheless do not despair of your arrival. If the holy deacon who carries this letter is once again entangled in your embraces, and you come here in his company, I shall gladly accept the delay in your charge being doubled by the magnitude of its interest [Note: We have restored the reading “again” from the very carefully corrected Verona and Cistercian manuscripts; from this it may be understood that Heraclius was Castrutius’s traveling companion from the beginning. At the end, some manuscripts read “doubled,” others “enlarged.” Gravius prefers “of the doubled”—that is, “of the interest doubled.”]

# Letter LXIX [Note: Elsewhere numbered 83. Written around A.D. 397.] To Oceanus

He defends the ordination of Carterius, a Spanish bishop who had taken one wife before baptism and another after baptism, the first having died, so that Carterius should not be considered a bigamist, contrary to Oceanus’s opinion. Taking this as his occasion, he discusses the Apostle’s words, “the husband of one wife,” and the virtues required above all in a bishop.

## 1.

I never thought, my son Oceanus, that the indulgence of a prince would have to endure the slander of accused men, or that those coming out of prison, after the filth and marks of chains, would grieve that others had been released. In the Gospel, the envious man hears the rebuke of one else’s salvation: “Friend, if I am good, why is your eye evil?” (Matt. 20:15).

“God has shut all things up under sin, that he might have mercy on all” (Rom. 11:32). “Where sin abounded, grace abounded even more” (ibid. 5:20). The firstborn of Egypt were struck down (Exod. 12), yet not even an Israelite animal was left behind in Egypt.

And behold, the Cainite heresy [Note: Everyone knows that the Cainite heresy was so called in the second century because it paid particular honor to Cain. Here, however, the holy Doctor makes a new allusion to the name: just as Cain declared his guilt greater than could be forgiven by God, so those against whom he writes would say that there were sins which Christ could not cleanse with his blood or forgive in baptism.] rises up against me, an ancient viper that had long been dead lifting its crushed head; and it now overthrows not merely part, as it had formerly been accustomed to do, but the whole sacrament of Christ.

[Note: Gravius prefers “for, by saying,” and shortly afterward “what else does it do?” so that the sentence forms one period with what follows.]

For it says that there are certain sins which Christ cannot cleanse with his blood, and that scars of former crimes adhere so deeply to bodies and souls that his medicine cannot diminish them. What else does it do but make Christ’s death useless? His death was useless if he cannot give life to some. John the Baptist lies when, pointing Christ out with finger and voice, he says, “Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1:29), if there still exist in the world people whose sins Christ has not taken away.

Either it must be shown that those whom Christ’s mercy does not know are not of the world; or, if they are of the world, one of two alternatives must be chosen. Those freed from sins demonstrate Christ’s power; those not freed, still standing accused, demonstrate his weakness. But far be it from us to believe of the Almighty that he is powerless in any respect. “Whatever the Father does, the Son also does in like manner” (ibid. 5:19). The Son’s weakness would redound to the Father. All the limbs of the little sheep have been carried; all the Apostle’s Letters resound with the grace of Christ.

And lest the simple naming of grace seem insufficient: “Grace,” he says, “and peace be multiplied to you” (1 Pet. 1:2). Multiplication is promised, while we assert scarcity.

## 2.

Why do I say this? [Note: Other manuscripts read, “What are these problems that you know?” or, “Why do you know these problems?”] You know your question. Carterius, bishop of Spain, a man advanced both in age and in priestly office, took one wife before he was baptized and another after the washing, the first having died; and you suppose that he acted against the Apostle’s judgment, who commanded that a bishop be ordained as “the husband of one wife” in the catalogue of virtues.

I am surprised that you have brought forward one man, when the whole world is full of such ordinations. I do not speak of presbyters, nor of the lower rank; I come to bishops. If I wished to name them one by one, so great a number would be gathered that the multitude of the Council of Ariminum would be surpassed. [Note: About three hundred bishops attended. Severus Sulpicius increases the number to more than four hundred, but he is mistaken. Jerome himself, in his Apology, book 1 against Rufinus, moderates the force of such ordinations, no longer saying that the world is full of them, but only that there are some priests of this sort in the Church.]

But it is improper to defend one in such a way that you seem to accuse many, and to defend by association with sinners one whom you cannot defend by reason.

At Rome I endured from a very eloquent man a “horned,” as they say, syllogism, so that whichever way I turned, I was held fast. “Is it a sin,” he said, “to take a wife, or is it not?” I, being simple and unable to avoid his traps, replied that it was not a sin.

He then proposed another question: “In baptism are good works forgiven, or evil ones?” With the same simplicity I answered that sins are forgiven.

When I thought myself secure, horns began to grow on me from every side, and the edges previously hidden began to widen. “If taking a wife is not a sin,” he said, “but baptism forgives sins, whatever is not forgiven remains.”

Immediately, as though I had been struck by a powerful boxer, darkness began to cloud my eyes. I at once remembered Chrysippus’s [another reading: Chrysippean] sophism: “If you lie, and you say that you lie truthfully, you are lying.” Recovering myself, I turned the trick of the proposition against my opponent.

“Please answer me,” I said. “Does baptism make a person new, or not?”

He scarcely granted that it makes him new. I proceeded step by step: “Does it make him wholly new, or only partly?”

He answered, “Wholly.”

Then I asked: “Therefore, is nothing of the old person retained in baptism?”

He nodded.

I immediately began to weave the argument: “If baptism makes a new person, and creates him wholly new, and nothing of the old person is retained in him, what once belonged to the old person cannot be charged against the new.”

Our little “Spinosulus” [Note: Cicero reproaches Piso, who was a stammerer but could not keep silent, for the hesitation of his speech, saying that he could neither be silent nor speak. We therefore conjecture that “Spinosulus” should read “Pisonulus,” that is, “little or young Piso,” a name which copyists may easily have corrupted because of its unusual form, substituting another word resembling it. Jerome, however, seems to have written the more elegant word from his own ingenuity, especially since he added our pronoun.] first fell silent; afterward, with Piso’s defect, he could not speak, yet could not keep silent. His forehead nevertheless began to sweat, his cheeks to grow pale, his lips to tremble, his tongue to stick, his saliva to dry, and his body to contract more from fear than from age.

At last he burst out: “Have you not read in the Apostle that the husband of one wife is to be admitted to the priesthood, and that the text does not define the time?”

Since he had challenged me with syllogisms, and I saw that he was moving toward tortuous little questions, I hurled his own weapons back at him.

“Did the Apostle choose baptized men for the episcopate,” I asked, “or catechumens?”

He did not want to answer. I nevertheless pressed the same question, asking it a second and a third time. You would have thought him Niobe, who was turned into stone through excessive weeping.

I turned to the audience: “Good judges, it makes no difference whether I bind an alert or a sleeping opponent, except that it is easier to fasten bonds on someone at rest than on one who resists.

“If the Apostle did not bring catechumens into the clergy but believers, and the person ordained bishop is a believer, the vices of the catechumen cannot be charged against the believer.”

I kept hurling such darts and directing flashing spears at the lethargic man. At last he yawned, and, as though belching and vomiting through mental intoxication, he disgorged: “The Apostle Paul taught these things.”

## 3.

The Apostle’s Letters are therefore produced, one to Timothy and the other to Titus.

In the first it was written:

> “If anyone desires the office of bishop, he desires a good work. Therefore the bishop must be irreproachable, the husband of one wife, sober, prudent, well ordered, hospitable, able to teach, not given to wine, not violent, but moderate, not quarrelsome, not greedy, ruling his own household well, having his children submissive with all chastity. But if anyone does not know how to rule his own household, how will he care for the Church of God? He must not be a recent convert, lest, being lifted up with pride, he fall into the judgment of the devil. Moreover, he must have a good testimony from those outside, so that he does not fall into reproach and the devil’s snare” (1 Tim. 5:1 and following).

At the very beginning of the Letter to Titus these commands are likewise given:

> “For this reason I left you in Crete, so that you might correct what was lacking and appoint presbyters in every city, as I directed you. If anyone is blameless, the husband of one wife, having believing children, not accused of debauchery or disobedience. For the bishop must be blameless, as God’s steward, not arrogant, not irritable, not given to wine, not violent, not greedy for shameful gain, but hospitable, kind, prudent, just, holy, self-controlled, holding firmly to the faithful word that accords with the teaching, so that he may be able both to exhort in sound doctrine and to refute those who contradict it” (Titus 1:5 and following).

In both Letters, whether concerning bishops or presbyters—for among the ancients bishops and presbyters were the same, since one name denotes rank and the other age—they are commanded to be chosen for the clergy as monogamous.

Certainly no one doubts that the Apostle is speaking of baptized people. If, therefore, all the qualities sought in the ordination of a bishop do not prejudice the candidate, even though he did not possess them before baptism—for what is asked is what he is, not what he was—why should the name of a wife alone impede him, when that alone was not a sin?

You say: because it was not a sin, it was not forgiven in baptism. I hear something new: because it was not a sin, it will be counted as a sin. All prostitutes and the filth of public corruption, impiety toward God, parricide, incest against parents, and nature transformed toward the extraordinary pleasures of both sexes are cleansed in Christ’s fountain; but the stains of a wife will remain, and brothels will be preferred to marriage chambers?

I do not charge you with armies of prostitutes, herds of catamites, bloodshed, and rolling like a pig in every mire of lust; yet you drag out for me from the grave a little wife who died long ago, whom I took precisely so as not to do what you did.

Let the Gentiles hear—those harvests of the Church with which our granaries are filled each day. Let the catechumens hear, those candidates for the faith: let them not take wives before baptism, let them not enter honorable marriages; [Note: In book 2 Against Jovinianus he says: “The nation of the Scots does not have its own wives … no woman among them is a wife of her own, but they indulge promiscuously, like animals, with whomever they please.” Thus, shortly afterward, when he describes the shameful customs of the barbarous Atticoti or Attacoti, he himself confirms the reading printed here, in place of which Erasmus substituted “of prostitutes and Azoti,” and Victorius “of Asoli,” from Greek ἄσωτος, “dissolute.”] rather, following the custom of the Scots and Atticoti, and in the manner of Plato’s Republic, let them have promiscuous wives and common children. Indeed, let them beware of any name whatever for a wife, lest, after they have believed in Christ, it become known that they once had not concubines or prostitutes, but wives.

## 4.

Let each person recall his own conscience and mourn the wounds of his entire life. When he has shown himself to be the true judge of his former offenses, let him hear Jesus rebuking him:

> “Hypocrite, cast the beam out of your own eye, and then you will see to cast the splinter out of your brother’s eye” (Matt. 7:5; Luke 6:42).

Truly, like the scribes and Pharisees, straining out a gnat and swallowing a camel, we tithe mint and dill while neglecting God’s judgment (Matt. 23).

What resemblance is there between a wife and a prostitute? Is the misfortune of a dead wife charged against a man, while a prostitute’s lust is crowned? If his first wife were alive, he would not have another wife; but you, who joined yourself to marriages indiscriminately like a dog, what excuse can you offer?

Perhaps you will say that you feared that, if you entered into marriage, you might one day be unable to be ordained a cleric. He desired children from his wife; you lost offspring through a prostitute. While he served nature and the Lord’s blessing—“Increase and multiply, and fill the earth” (Gen. 1:28)—the privacy of bedchambers covered him; the public face of society condemned you as you burned for intercourse.

He concealed what was permitted with modest shame; you thrust before everyone’s eyes what was not permitted, shamelessly. Of him it is written: “Marriage is honorable, and the bed undefiled” (Heb. 13:4); of you it is read: “God will judge [another reading: destroy] fornicators and adulterers” (ibid.), and “Whoever corrupts the temple of God, God will corrupt him” (1 Cor. 6:17).

“You say that all our crimes were forgiven in baptism, and that after pardon the severity of the judge is no longer to be feared,” quoting the Apostle:

> “And such were some of you; but you were washed, but you were sanctified, but you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God” (ibid. 3:17).

“All sins were forgiven”—well and faithfully said. But I ask how your filth was washed away while my purity was defiled.

“I do not say that your purity was defiled,” you reply, “but that it remained in the condition in which it had been; for if it had been filth, it would certainly have been washed as mine was.”

What sort of evasion is this, and what kind of wit, blunter than any pestle? Because it is not a sin, it is a sin; because it is not filthy, it is filthy? The Lord did not forgive it because there was nothing he could forgive; and because he did not forgive it, that which was not forgiven remains.

## 5.

How great is the power of baptism, and what grace the water sanctified in Christ possesses, I shall teach a little later. For the moment, according to the common proverb, “For a bad knot in a tree, a bad wedge must be sought.”

The phrase “the husband of one wife” can also be explained in another way. The Apostle was a Jew, and the first Church of Christ was gathered from the remnant of Israel. He knew that the Law permitted, and that the example of the patriarchs and of Moses made familiar to the people, the begetting of children from many wives. Even the priests themselves possessed this liberty.

He therefore commanded that the priests of the Church should not claim the same liberty, and should not take two or three marriages at once, but should have one wife at a time.

Lest you cry out that what we have said is contentious, accept another explanation as well—unless you wish to join not the will to the Law, but the Law to your own will.

Some construe the “wives” as Churches and the “husbands” as bishops. They say that this too was decreed by the fathers at the Council of Nicaea: that a bishop should not be transferred from one Church to another, and should not despise the companionship of a poor virgin in order to seek the embrace of a richer adulteress. [Note: Learned men commonly understand this as canon 15 of Nicaea, but it seems more likely to us that the first canon of Sardica is intended; it is well known that the canons of that council were formerly taken as Nicene. Certainly the following phrase—“lest, despising the companionship of a poor virgin, he seek the embrace of a richer adulteress”—corresponds especially well with Hosius’s words at the same Sardican council: “Since no bishop has been found in this matter who would pass from a greater city to a smaller one.” Moreover, the practice of calling bishops’ Churches their “wives” was already long established in the Church, and examples occur frequently.]

Thus, just as the fault and vice of children are understood in the λογισμοί—that is, in the thoughts—and the administration of a household is referred to soul and body, so also the wives of bishops are said to be Churches.

Concerning these it is written in Isaiah: “Women who are coming from the spectacle, come; for it is not a people possessing understanding” (Isa. 27:11, according to the Septuagint). And again: “Rich women, rise up and hear my voice” (ibid. 32:9). And in Proverbs: “Who will find a strong woman?” (Prov. 31:10, according to the Septuagint.) “She is more precious than precious stones.” “The heart of her husband trusts in her.” And in the same book: “Wise women built a house, but the foolish woman destroyed it with her hands” (ibid. 14:1).

Nor, they say, should this seem unworthy of bishops, since it is also written concerning God: “As a wife despises her husband, so the house of Israel despised me” (Jer. 3). And the Apostle says: “I betrothed you to one man, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Cor. 11:2).

In all these testimonies, understand “woman”—γυνή [Note: Thus also Saint Ambrose, although in his book On the Institution of a Virgin, chapter 5, he argues that “woman” is the name not of corruption but of sex, while admitting that the word commonly has another meaning. In the writings of the ancients it is more often found as a term for a married woman than for one who has never known a man; indeed, a virgin is contrasted with a woman. The holy Doctor establishes this interpretation for the purpose which he notes shortly afterward: namely, that the Apostle’s phrase “the husband of one wife” may be understood as “the husband of one woman,” referring more to sexual intercourse than to marriage contracts.]—rather as “wife.”

“You will say that this interpretation is forced and quite harsh.” Then restore the simplicity of Scripture, lest we fight you with laws you have made against yourself.

I shall ask this also: if someone had a concubine before baptism, and, after she died, was baptized and took a wife, should he become a cleric or not?

You will answer that he may, because he had a concubine, not a wife. Therefore it is marriage contracts and dowry rights, not sexual intercourse, that the Apostle condemns.

We see many people, because of extreme poverty, avoiding the burden of wives and keeping their slave women as wives, raising the children born from them as their own. If such men should happen to be enriched by the emperor, and should obtain the stola for those women, they will immediately submit their necks to the Apostle and be forced, against their will, to receive them as wives. [Note: It is remarkable how much trouble trifling matters sometimes cause learned men. Since all the books we have seen read “they will have deserved his stola,” we understood that the sense had been corrupted through the carelessness of copyists and needed correction. For who could ever have deserved the emperor’s stola? And even if someone had deserved it, how would that relate to marriage, so that a man who had previously kept a concubine would be forced, even unwillingly, to take her as a wife because he had deserved it? Accordingly, a very learned man whom we consulted thought that *stolus*, not *stolam*, should be read, referring to a share of public grain which some people obtained through the emperor’s gift. Thus the Codex Theodosianus mentions *Stolus Alexandrinus* more than once, and others ought to have been supplied on that model. But this does not fit the passage or the context, as Jerome’s whole argument readily shows even without our intervention. Nor should the passage be tampered with in that part: *stolam* should be retained, but not understood as referring to the emperor; rather, *illis* should refer to the slave women who were concubines. For the *stola* was not only properly a woman’s garment but the garment of an honorable woman and head of a household, as Ulpian and others teach. A slave woman, and a woman of servile status, could not wear it, as numerous ancient testimonies establish—least of all a concubine or prostitute, whom the law excluded from matronly adornments, as Tertullian clearly states in his work On the Dress of Women. Furthermore, if someone obtained the stola from the emperor for his slave concubine, he would then treat her, under Roman law, not as a slave and concubine but as a legitimate wife and honorable matron; and therefore, according to those interpreters of the Apostle whom Jerome says he follows, since marriage contracts and dowry rights rather than intercourse are condemned, he would submit his neck, even unwillingly, to the Apostle’s teaching about the husband of one wife. If, however, because of poverty he could not obtain the imperial rescript, the Church’s regulations would be altered in accordance with Roman law, so that he might continue to keep his concubine. This may also explain a passage of Isidore, which in turn sheds light on ours: in *Origins*, book 9, chapter 7, he says that marriage is a lawful agreement of nobles—either because it belonged only to Roman citizens, or because marriages were conducted with auspices, whereas the plebeians had no ancient auspices, as is known from Livy.]

But if his poverty should prevent him from obtaining the imperial rescript, the regulations of the Church will be altered in accordance with the Roman laws. See whether the phrase “the husband of one wife” can be understood as “the husband of one woman,” referring more to sexual intercourse than to marriage contracts.

We set all this forth not to resist the true and simple interpretation, but to teach you to understand the holy Scriptures as they are written, and not to empty the Savior’s baptism of its power or make the whole sacrament of the cross ineffectual.

### 6

Let us fulfill what we promised shortly before, and, leaving the school of the rhetoricians, let us praise the waters and proclaim baptism. [Note: A more serious reading, from an old manuscript: “The raw world, and presently the multitude—or magnitude—of the abysses and the shapeless darknesses oppressed it.”] The raw world, before the sun shone red, before the moon grew pale, and before the stars glittered, oppressed the unformed and invisible matter with the vastness of the abysses and the shapelessness of darkness. The Spirit of God alone was borne over the waters in the manner of a charioteer (Gen. 1:2), and was bringing forth the nascent world in the figure of baptism.

Between heaven and earth the firmament is erected as an intermediate realm; and, according to the etymology of the Hebrew language, heaven—that is, *SAMAIM*—derives its name from the waters. The waters that are above the heavens are separated for the praises of God. Hence, in the prophet Ezekiel, crystal is seen stretched out above the cherubim (Ezek. 1), that is, waters compacted and made denser.

First, from the waters, that which lives emerges, and it lifts the winged faithful from earth to heaven. Man is fashioned from clay (Gen. 2:7), and the mysteries of the waters are handled between the hands of God. Paradise is planted in Eden (ibid., v. 8), and one spring is divided into four headwaters. Later, flowing out from the temple and going toward the rising of the sun (Ezek. 47:1), it gives life to bitter and dead waters.

The world sins, and it is not cleansed without the Flood of waters (Gen. 7:17). Immediately the dove of the Holy Spirit, after the most loathsome bird had been driven away, flies down to Noah as to Christ in the Jordan, and with a branch of refreshment and light announces peace to the world (ibid. 8:11).

Pharaoh, unwilling to let the people of God depart from Egypt, is drowned as a type of baptism (Exod. 14:13). In the Psalms, concerning his destruction, it is written: “You established the sea by your strength; you crushed the heads of the dragons in the waters; you broke the heads of the great dragon” (Ps. 73:13). [Note: Formerly, “to permit the people of God to depart.” Furthermore, the use of Pharaoh as a type of the demon or sin drowned in the waters of baptism was widespread among the Fathers.]

Hence basilisks and scorpions also pursue whatever is dry; and, once they have come to water, they make people hydrophobic—ὑδροφόβους (“water-fearing”)—and frenzied.

The sea is transformed by the mystery of the cross, and the seventy palms of the Apostles are watered by the sweetened streams of the Law. Abraham and Isaac dig wells, while the foreigners oppose them. Beersheba, the city of the oath (Gen. 21), and the kingdom of Solomon take their names from springs (1 Kings 1). Rebecca is found at a well (Gen. 24). Rachel, because of the waters, is greeted by the kiss of the supplanter (ibid. 29). Moses, at an open well, rescues the daughters of the priest of Midian from injury.

The Lord’s Forerunner prepares the people for Christ in the waters of the springs beside Salim, which is interpreted as “peace” or “perfection” (Matt. 4:27). The Savior himself, after baptism and after the waters of the Jordan had been sanctified by his washing, begins to preach the kingdom of heaven.

He performs his first sign from water (John 2:9). The Samaritan woman is summoned to the well, and the thirsty person is invited to drink. To Nicodemus he says secretly: “Unless someone has been born again of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of heaven” (John 3). [Note: Victorius adds “Holy” from Brixian manuscripts, although he rejected the Greek exemplar.]

Because he had begun with waters, he ended in waters. Christ’s side is pierced by a lance, and the mysteries of baptism and martyrdom are poured forth together.

After the resurrection he sends the Apostles to the Gentiles and commands them to baptize them in the mystery of the Trinity. The Jewish people repent of their deed, and immediately Peter sends them to baptism. Before she travails, Zion gives birth, and a nation is born at once (Isa. 66:7–8).

Paul, the persecutor of the Church and the ravenous wolf of Benjamin, submits his head to the sheep Ananias; nor does he recover his sight before he cures his blindness through baptism (Acts 9:18).

The eunuch of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, is prepared for Christ’s baptism by the prophetic reading. The Ethiopian changes his skin contrary to nature, and the leopard its spots (Jer. 13:23).

Those who had received John’s baptism are baptized again because they did not know the Holy Spirit, so that no one might suppose that, for Gentiles and Jews alike, waters without the Holy Spirit could suffice for salvation. [Note: An old edition reads, “so that no one might suppose from among the Gentiles,” and therefore the conjunction *and* that immediately follows should be deleted, with a mark of punctuation placed before it. The sense would then be that some from among the Gentiles might have supposed that, for Jews, water without the Holy Spirit could suffice.]

“The voice of the Lord is over the waters; the Lord is over many waters; the Lord makes the Flood dwell” (Ps. 28:3).

“His teeth are like a flock of shorn sheep that have come up from the washing, all bearing twins, and none among them is barren” (Song 4:2). If none is barren or sterile, all have breasts dripping with milk, and with the Apostle they can say: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Gal. 4:19); and, “I gave you milk to drink, not solid food” (1 Cor. 3:2).

Micah prophesies the grace of baptism: “He will turn again and have mercy on us; he will plunge our iniquities, and cast all our sins into the depths of the sea” (Mic. 7:19).

### 7
