How, then, are all sins submerged in the washing, if one wife floats upon the surface? “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven, and whose sins are covered. Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not imputed sin” (Ps. 31:1–2). I think that we too can add something to this song: “Blessed is the man to whom the Lord will not impute a wife.”

Let us also hear Ezekiel, the son of man, declaring the power of him who is to be the Son of Man: “I will take you from the nations, and I will sprinkle clean water upon you, and you shall be cleansed from all your impurities; and I will give you a new heart and a spirit.” “From all your filth,” he says, “I will cleanse you” (Ezek. 36:25–26). Nothing is omitted in the word “all.” If filth is cleansed away, how much more are things clean not defiled?

“I will give you a new heart and a new spirit.” For “in Christ Jesus neither circumcision has any power, nor uncircumcision, but a new nature” (Gal. 5:6). [Note: In Greek it is καινὴ κτίσις, “a new creation,” as the Vulgate translator also rendered it, and Victorius followed that exemplar.]

Hence we sing a new song, and, having put off the old person, we do not walk in the oldness of the letter but in the newness of the spirit (Rom. 7:6). This is the new pebble, upon which a new name is written, which no one knows how to read except the one who receives it (Rev. 2:17).

“For as many of us as were baptized in Christ Jesus were baptized into his death. For we were buried with him through baptism into death [variant: in death], so that, just as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life” (Rom. 6:3).

So often we read of newness, and yet the stained name of a wife cannot be erased by any newness? We were buried with Christ in baptism, and we rose through faith in the working of God, who raised him from the dead. And when we were dead in transgressions and in the uncircumcision of our flesh, he made us alive together with him, forgiving all transgressions; he erased the bond of the decree that stood against us and was contrary to us, and he removed it from our midst, fastening it to the cross (Col. 2).

All our things died with Christ; all the sins of the old bond were erased. Does only the name of a wife remain alive? My days would fail me if I wished to set out from the Holy Scriptures everything pertaining to the power of baptism and to establish the mysteries of the second birth—or rather, of the first birth in Christ.

### 8

Before I bring my dictation to an end—for I already realize that I am exceeding the measure of the letter—I wish to explain briefly the preceding chapters, in which the life of a future bishop is described, so that we may receive the Apostle not merely in his commendation of one wife, but in everything he commands, as the Teacher of the Gentiles.

At the same time I beg that no one should think that I have written what I have written as an attack upon the priests of the present age, but for the benefit of the Church. For just as orators and philosophers, when they describe the kind of person they wish a perfect orator or philosopher to be, do not insult Demosthenes and Plato but define the matters themselves apart from particular persons, so in the description of a bishop and in the exposition of what has been written, a mirror of the priesthood is set before us. It is now in the power and conscience of each individual to see what sort of person he appears there, so that he may either grieve at his deformity or rejoice at his beauty.

“If anyone desires the episcopate, he desires a good work” (1 Tim. 3:1). [Note: Compare the discussion in the Letter to Titus, chapter 1, where he comments with the same understanding and nearly the same arguments.] A work, not a dignity; labor, not pleasures; a WORK by which he may diminish through humility, not swell through elevation.

Therefore a bishop must be blameless (ibid. 2). The same is said to Titus: “If anyone is without accusation” (Tit. 1:6). He encompasses all virtues in a single statement and almost demands something contrary to nature. For if every sin, even in an idle word, deserves blame, who is there who lives in this world without sin, that is, without blame? Yet the future shepherd of the Church is chosen as one in comparison with whom the others may rightly be called a flock.

The rhetoricians define an orator as a good man skilled in speaking. First his life is sought, and then a blameless tongue, so that he may rightly be held in esteem. For he loses the authority to teach when his speech is destroyed by his conduct.

“A husband of one wife”: we have discussed this above. Now we merely point out that if a husband of one wife is sought even before baptism, then let us also seek, before baptism, the other things that have been commanded. For it is not appropriate to understand everything as applying after baptism and this one commandment as applying before baptism.

“Sober,” or “watchful”—νηφάλιος signifies both. Prudent, decorous, hospitable, a teacher (Lev. 10). Priests who minister in God’s temple are forbidden to drink wine and strong drink, lest their hearts be weighed down by gluttony and drunkenness, and so that the faculty of understanding, performing its service, may always remain vigorous and clear.

The word “prudent,” moreover, excludes those who excuse the stupidity of priests under the name of simplicity. For unless the brain is sound, all the limbs will be diseased.

“Decorous” also, ἐπίτασις, is an intensification [Note: Older editions add this interpretation of the Greek word, namely “increase” or “intensification.”] of the preceding word, that is, “blameless.” One who has no vices is called blameless; one who abounds in virtues is decorous.

We can understand something else from this word as well, in accordance with Cicero’s statement: “The chief principle of art is to make what you do appropriate.” For there are some who do not know their own measure and are so foolish and senseless that, in movement, gait, dress, and ordinary speech, they provoke laughter in those who watch them. And, as though they understood what decorum is, they adorn themselves with clothing and bodily refinements and prepare the feasts of a more luxurious table, although all such adornment and cultivation are fouler than filth.

That teaching is required of priests is commanded both in the precepts of the old Law and is written more fully to Titus. For an innocent life without speech benefits as much by example as it harms by silence. The rage of wolves must be driven away by the barking of dogs and the shepherd’s staff.

“Not addicted to wine, not violent” (Tit. 1:7). He set vices against virtues.

### 9

We have learned what we ought to be; let us learn what priests ought not to be.

Drunkenness belongs to buffoons and revelers; and a belly seething with wine quickly foams over into lusts. In wine there is debauchery, in debauchery pleasure, and in pleasure immodesty. He who lives in debauchery is dead while alive; therefore he who becomes drunk is both dead and buried.

Noah uncovers his thighs for the drunkenness of a single hour (Gen. 9:21), although he had covered them through six hundred years of sobriety. Through drunkenness Lot, unknowingly, mingles incest with lust; and wine conquered the man whom Sodom had not conquered.

The one who condemns a violent bishop is he who offered his back to scourging and, though cursed, did not curse in return (Isa. 50; Mark 15).

“But temperate” (1 Tim. 3). He set one virtue against two vices, so that drunkenness and anger might be restrained by temperance.

“Not quarrelsome, not greedy.” Nothing is more shameless than the arrogance of rustic people who consider loquacity authority and are always ready for disputes, thundering with swollen speeches over the flock subject to them.

Samuel also teaches that greed must be avoided in a priest, proving before the people that he had taken nothing from anyone (1 Sam. 12). So too does the poverty of the Apostles, who accepted the necessities of expenditure from the brethren and boasted that they neither possessed nor desired anything beyond food and clothing. In the letter to Timothy he calls it greed; to Titus he plainly calls it the desire for shameful profit (Tit. 1).

“Managing his own household well.” Not so that he may increase his wealth, prepare royal banquets, pile up engraved dishes, or cook Phasian birds over a slow fire that reaches the bones without dissolving the surface of the flesh through its skillful regulation, but so that what he is about to command the people he may first require of his household.

“Having children who are submissive, with all chastity,” lest they imitate the sons of Eli, who slept with women in the vestibule of the Temple; and, considering religion a means of plunder, they turned whatever was best among the sacrificial offerings into their own pleasures (1 Sam. 2). [Note: That is, plundering under the pretext of religion. Thus, in Letter 50 to Domnio, no. 3, he reproaches a certain rumor-spreading monk for making religion into a battle, as we have read there from the manuscripts; this passage further confirms the point. Shortly afterward, *opimum* occurs for *optimum*. Jerome had written it, although there is no reason to reject the printed reading.]

“Not a recent convert, lest, being lifted up in pride, he fall into the judgment of the devil” (1 Tim. 3; Tit. 1).

I cannot sufficiently marvel at the great blindness of human beings: they dispute about wives before baptism, and drag into accusation something that died in baptism—or rather, was made alive with Christ—while no one observes such an open and evident commandment.

Yesterday a catechumen, today a bishop; yesterday in the amphitheater, today in the Church; in the evening in the circus, in the morning at the altar; recently a patron of actors, now a consecrator of virgins.

Did the Apostle not know our evasions, or was he ignorant of the foolishness of our arguments? The same man who said, “the husband of one wife” (ibid.) also commanded that he be blameless, sober, prudent, decorous, hospitable, a teacher, temperate; not addicted to wine, not violent, not quarrelsome, not greedy, not a recent convert. We close our eyes to all these requirements and see only wives.

But when he says, “lest, being lifted up in pride, he fall into the judgment of the devil,” who would not prove the truth of this by experience? A suddenly appointed priest does not know humility or the gentleness of country people; he does not know Christian kindness; he does not know how to despise himself. He is transferred from one dignity to another: he has not fasted, wept, often reproved his own habits, or corrected them through constant reflection; he has not distributed his possessions to the poor.

He is led, so to speak, from one chair to another—from pride to pride. The judgment and downfall of the devil are, without doubt, arrogance. Those who in a moment of time are not yet disciples but already teachers fall into it. [Note: The reference is to one who is appointed priest suddenly, not gradually and by stages. For the word *momentaneus*, you will find it either nowhere among approved authors or, in later Latin, with another meaning. Tertullian, *Against Marcion* 3.17, uses it of Christ: “who did not extinguish the burning flax, that is, the momentary ardor of the nations.”]

“He must also have a good testimony from those who are outside.” The beginning is like the conclusion. One who is blameless is praised with a harmonious voice not only by his household but also by outsiders. Those outside and beyond the Church are Jews, heretics, and Gentiles. Let Christ’s bishop therefore be such that those who attack the religion do not dare attack his life.

But now we see many either buy the favor of the people, like charioteers, at a price, or live in such hatred among all people that they cannot extort money as the mimes obtain it by their gestures.

### 10

Examine these matters, son Oceanus, with anxious care [variant: examine them]; these are what the teachers of the Church must guard; these are the canons they must observe when choosing priests. They must not interpret Christ’s law according to their own hatreds and private quarrels, nor according to envy, which is always attacking its own author.

Consider how great a testimony this is concerning the husband whom they accuse, against whom his rivals can bring no charge except the marital bond—and that bond existed before baptism.

“He who commands, ‘You shall not commit adultery,’ also said, ‘You shall not kill’” (James 2:11). If we do not commit adultery but kill, we are transgressors of the law. “Whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles in one point becomes guilty of all” (ibid. 10).

Therefore, when they oppose us with a wife before baptism, let us require from them everything that was commanded after baptism. They pass over what is forbidden and object to what is permitted.

## LETTER LXX [Note: Otherwise 84. Written at approximately the same time as the preceding letter.] TO MAGNUS, THE ORATOR OF THE CITY OF ROME

To a certain Roman rhetorician, Magnus, whom Rufinus had suborned to ask Jerome why he inserted examples from secular literature in his little works, Jerome gives an explanation, showing to what extent this is permissible and whose example he follows in doing so.

### 1

We learned that our Sebesius has advanced through your admonitions, not so much from your letter as from his own repentance. And, remarkably, he pleased us more when corrected than he had offended us when he was in error.

The indulgence of the father and the devotion of the son competed with each other: the one does not remember past matters, while the other promises duties even for the future. Hence both he and we must rejoice with you, because we have received back a son, while you have approved a disciple.

[Note: In some manuscripts we find *Severus*; in others Martianaeus notes that *Sebastius* is read.]

### 2

As for what you ask at the end of your letter—why we sometimes insert examples from secular writings in our little works and pollute the purity of the Church with the filth of the pagans—accept a brief answer.

You would never ask this unless Cicero possessed you entirely. If you read the Holy Scriptures, if, setting aside Volcatius, you unfolded the works of their interpreters— [Note: We think that the reference is not to Volcatius Sedigitus the poet, of whom only a few verses survive, but to another Volcatius of the same name, Volcatius the Noble, who taught civil law to Caecilius, as Pliny testifies in book 8, chapter 40. Some manuscripts, however, read *supercilio* instead of *Volcatio*.]

For who does not know that in Moses and in the books of the Prophets certain things were taken from the books of the Gentiles, and that Solomon both proposed certain matters to the philosophers of Tyre and answered some of them? [Note: Josephus mentions these questions between Solomon and the philosophers of Tyre in *Antiquities* 8.2, and also in *Against Apion* 1; so does Saint Theophilus of Antioch in *To Autolycus* 3. As testimony to this, both cite Menander of Ephesus, who wrote a history of Tyre. Shortly afterward, some printed editions read “subtle parables of words.”]

Hence, at the beginning of Proverbs, he urges us to understand “the words of prudence, the subtleties of sayings, parables, and obscure speech, the sayings of the wise, and riddles” (Prov. 1), which properly belong to dialecticians and philosophers.

The Apostle Paul also made use of a verse by the poet Epimenides when writing to Titus: “Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy bellies” (Tit. 1:12). [Note: Erasmus and Victorius add the Greek verse of Epimenides, Κρῆτες ἀεί ψεῦσται, κακὰ θηρία, γαστέρες ἀργαί, “Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy bellies,” although the manuscripts omit it.] Callimachus later used its heroic half-line. Nor is it surprising that a translation expressed word for word does not preserve the meter in Latin, since even in Homer the same verse in the same language scarcely holds together when turned into prose.

In another letter he introduces a senarius of Menander: “Evil conversations corrupt good morals.” [Note: Here too the same printed editions place Menander’s Greek words first: φθείρουσιν ἤθη χρησθ᾽ ὁμιλίαι κακαί, “evil conversations corrupt morals,” which the manuscripts omit. Yet Socrates (*History* 3.14) and Nicephorus 10.26 seem to be mistaken in attributing the senarius to Euripides, since it is from Menander’s *Thais*, as Jerome notes. See the Letter to Demetrias. Thus some manuscripts of the sacred text note Menander in the margin.]

And when disputing among the Athenians in the court of the Areopagus, he calls Aratus as a witness: “For we are indeed his offspring,” which in Greek is τοῦ γάρ καὶ γένος ἐσμέν, and is the close of a heroic verse.

And, as if this were not enough, the leader of the Christian army and unconquered orator pleading Christ’s cause even twists a chance inscription by art into an argument for the faith. For he had learned from the true David to wrench the sword from the hands of his enemies and cut off the head of the most arrogant Goliath with his own blade.

He had read in Deuteronomy the Lord’s command that the head, eyebrows, all the hair, and the nails of a captive woman be shaved or cut away, and that she then be taken in marriage (Deut. 21). What wonder, then, if I too wish to make secular wisdom, because of the beauty of its eloquence and the loveliness of its limbs, an Israelite from a maidservant and captive? And if I cut away or shave whatever in it is dead—idolatry, pleasure, error, and lust—and, myself joined to its most pure body, beget from it native-born children for the Lord Sabaoth? [Note: Up to this point earlier editions incorrectly read *mixtos*, referring it to the native-born children, whereas it clearly refers to the person speaking. Abaelardus also asserts the reading we have restored; in book 1 of his *Theologia Christiana* he transcribes most of this letter. Gravius prefers *nixus*, “leaning upon.” Shortly afterward, Gravius supplied from manuscripts *Gomer daughter of Diblaim*, that is, “of sweetnesses”; the final two words are absent from other copies. Perhaps *dulcedinum*, “of sweetnesses,” should be read.]

My labor benefits the household of Christ; intercourse with a foreign woman increases the number of fellow servants.

Hosea took as his wife Gomer, daughter of Diblaim, a prostitute, and a son was born to him from the harlot, Jezreel, whose name means “seed of God” (Hos. 1). Isaiah shaves the beard and legs of sinners with a sharp razor (Isa. 7), and Ezekiel, as a type of Jerusalem’s prostitution, shears her hair, so that whatever in her is without sense and life may be removed.

### 3

Cyprian, a man distinguished in eloquence and martyrdom, is criticized—according to Firmianus’ account—because, when writing against Demetrianus, he used testimonies from the Prophets and Apostles, which Demetrianus called fabricated and invented, rather than testimonies from philosophers and poets, whose authority he, as a pagan, could not oppose. [Note: Some manuscripts read *Formianus* or *Formanus*. There is no doubt, however, that Lactantius Firmianus is intended; in *Institutes* 5.4 he accuses Cyprian on this matter.]

Celsus and Porphyry wrote against us. Origenes answered the former, and Methodius, Eusebius, and Apollinaris answered the latter with the greatest force. Origenes wrote eight books against him; Methodius extends to ten thousand verses; Eusebius and Apollinaris composed twenty-five and thirty volumes respectively. Read them, and you will find us most unlearned by comparison with them; after so long a period of leisure, we scarcely remember, as though in a dream, what we learned as boys.

The emperor Julian vomited out seven books against Christ during the Parthian expedition, and, in accordance with the fables of the poets, wounded himself with his own sword. If I attempt to write against him, I suppose you will forbid me to strike the rabid dog with the teachings of philosophers and Stoics—that is, with the club of Hercules [variant: to strike him back]. Yet he immediately felt our Nazarene—or, as he himself used to say, our Galilean—in battle, and received the reward of his foul tongue when a spear pierced his groin. [Note: Victorius reads *conto in iliis*, “with a spear in the groin”; earlier editions had *contumeliis* or *contumelia*, both incorrectly.]

Josephus, in establishing the antiquity of the Jewish people, wrote two books against Apion of Alexandria, the grammarian. He produces so many testimonies from secular writers that I am astonished how a Hebrew man, educated from infancy in the sacred Scriptures, could have examined the entire library of the Greeks.

What should I say about Philo, whom critics pronounce either “another Plato” or “the Jewish Plato”? [Note: The earlier text had incorrectly read “either the second or another Jewish Plato.” We have removed the two superfluous words, *vel secundum*, which seemed to have slipped into Jerome’s text from some gloss, on the authority of the manuscripts.]

### 4 — Ecclesiastical writers educated in secular literature

I shall pass through them one by one.

Quadratus, a disciple of the Apostles and an Athenian bishop of the Church: did he not present a book on behalf of our religion to the emperor Hadrian when Hadrian was visiting the sacred rites of Eleusis? And his outstanding intelligence so amazed everyone that it brought the most severe persecution to an end.

The philosopher Aristides, a man of the greatest eloquence, presented the same emperor with an *Apology* for the Christians, composed from the sayings of philosophers. Later Justin, himself also a philosopher, imitated him and presented to Antoninus Pius, his sons, and the Senate a book against the Gentiles, defending the disgrace of the cross and proclaiming the resurrection of Christ with complete freedom.

What shall I say of Melito, bishop of Sardis? What of Apollinarius, priest of the Church of Hierapolis; of Dionysius, bishop of the Corinthians; of Tatian; of Bardesanes; and of Irenaeus, successor to the martyr Photinus? In many volumes they explained the origins of the various heresies and the philosophical sources from which they flowed.

Pantaenus, a philosopher of the Stoic school, was sent to India by Demetrius, bishop of Alexandria, because of the renown of his exceptional learning, to preach Christ among the Brahmans and the philosophers of that nation.

Clement, presbyter of the Church of Alexandria, in my judgment the most learned of all, wrote eight books of *Stromata*, an equal number of *Hypotyposes* (ὑποτυπώσεων), another work against the Gentiles, and three volumes of the *Paedagogue*. What is unlearned in these works? Indeed, what is not drawn from the heart of philosophy?

Following him, Origenes wrote ten *Stromata*, comparing the opinions of Christians and philosophers with one another and confirming all the doctrines of our religion from Plato, Aristotle, Numenius, and Cornutus.

Miltiades also wrote an excellent volume against the Gentiles. Hippolytus and Apollonius, a senator of the city of Rome, likewise composed works of their own. [Note: Following Erasmus, the Benedictine editor incorrectly read “senators,” although the reference is evidently only to Apollonius, as the *Catalogue* makes clear. Indeed, some doubt whether Apollonius himself was ever a senator, or whether Jerome exaggerated the matter from his own imagination. We shall discuss this in its place in the *Catalogue*.]

There are also the books of Julius Africanus, who wrote histories of the times; of Theodorus, who was later called Gregory—Saint Gregory Thaumaturgus—a man of apostolic signs and virtues; and of Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria; of Anatolius, priest of the Church of Laodicea; and of the presbyters Pamphilus, Pierius, Lucian, and Malchion; of Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea; Eustathius of Antioch; Athanasius of Alexandria; Eusebius of Emesa; Tryphilius of Cyprus; Asterius of Scythopolis; Serapion the Confessor; Titus, bishop of Bostra; and the Cappadocians Basil, Gregory, and Amphilochius.

All of them so thoroughly patch their books with the teachings and opinions of the philosophers that you do not know what you ought first to admire in them: the learning of the secular world or their knowledge of the Scriptures.

### 5

I shall come to the Latins.

What was more learned than Tertullian, or what sharper? His *Apology* and his books against the Gentiles contain [variant: possess] the entire discipline of the secular world.

Minucius Felix, an advocate of the Roman forum, in the book entitled *Octavius*, and in another against the mathematicians—if the title does not falsely identify the author—what part of the writings of the Gentiles did he leave untouched?

Arnobius published seven books against the Gentiles, and his disciple Lactantius an equal number. Lactantius also composed two volumes, one on anger and one on the workmanship of God. If you wish to read them, you will find in them an epitome (ἐπιτομή) of Cicero’s dialogues.

In the books of the martyr Victorinus, although learning is lacking, the desire for learning is not lacking. Cyprian, in *That Idols Are Not Gods*—with what brevity, what knowledge of all history, and what splendor of words and ideas has he treated the matter?

Hilary, the confessor and bishop of my own times, imitated Quintilian’s twelve books both in style and in number. In the short book he wrote against Dioscorus the physician, he showed what he was capable of in literature.

The presbyter Juvencus, under Constantine, set forth the history of the Lord and Savior in verse, and was not afraid to subject the majesty of the Gospel to the laws of meter.

Of the others, whether dead or living, I say nothing; their strength and their intention are both evident in their writings.

### 6

Do not immediately be misled by a false opinion into thinking that this is permissible against the Gentiles but must be concealed in other discussions, since almost all books by almost all authors—except those who, together with Epicurus, never learned letters—are filled with learning and instruction.

Although I think rather that what came to my mind as I dictated this is that you do not fail to know what learned men have always practiced, but that through you a question is being put to me by another person who perhaps, because of his love of the histories of Sallust, is Calpurnius by the surname Lanarius. [Note: Martianaeus, following Erasmus, again incorrectly reads *Calphurnius*. The Calpurnius whom Sallust mentions, Calpurnius by surname Bestia, was consul of Numidia; Sallust says that he betrayed the Republic because of infamous greed in the Jugurthine War. Calpurnius Lanarius, however, is mentioned not by Sallust but by Plutarch in the life of Sertorius, who says that Lanarius killed Julius Salinator by treachery. What Valerius Maximus, book 8, chapter 2, and Cicero, *On Duties* 3, report about Calpurnius Lanarius has no relevance here. Perhaps Jerome deliberately combined these two Calpurnii, Bestia and Lanarius, as his words also seem to indicate, in order to mock the various bad methods and vices of his opponent Rufinus. It is clear that he had Rufinus entirely before his eyes in *Apology against Rufinus* 1, where he says: “Surely this is that Calpurnius Sallustianus who, through Magnus the Orator, had raised no small question for us.”]

I beg you to persuade him, toothless though he is, not to envy the teeth of those who eat, nor, being a mole, to despise the eyes of goats.

As you see, the material for discussion is abundant; but the narrow confines of a letter must now be brought to an end.

## LETTER LXXI [Note: Otherwise 28. Written in the year 398.] [Note: This letter is denied to Jerome in the Verona manuscript and is said to be by Blessed Lucidius to Lucianus Baeticus; we discuss this in the Preface. Other codices call this Lucinius “Lucianus” or “Licinius,” while Cassiodorus calls him “Lucius.” Some older printed editions add *Baeticus*—that is, from Baetica in Spain—to the heading; the manuscripts are silent.] TO LUCINIUS

Lucinius, a Baetican by birth, who lived a chaste life with his wife Theodora and had resolved to sail to Jerusalem, is encouraged to persist in his purpose and make the voyage. Meanwhile Jerome sends him several works that he had requested, together with four small hair-shirts and a codex of Isaiah; he then discusses fasts, the reception of the Eucharist, and ecclesiastical traditions.

1. While I was not expecting it, your letter was suddenly delivered to me. The more unforeseen it was, the more filled with joy, and it revived my resting soul, so that at once I embraced in affection one whom I did not know by sight; and silently I murmured to myself: “Who will give me wings like a dove, and I shall fly away and rest” (Ps. 54:7), so that I may find the one whom my soul loves. Truly, the Lord’s word has now been fulfilled in you: “Many shall come from the East and from the West, and shall recline in the bosom of Abraham.” Cornelius, the centurion of the Italian cohort, already prefigured the faith of my Lucinius. The Apostle Paul, writing to the Romans, said: “When I begin to set out for Spain, I hope that, as I pass through, I shall see you, and be escorted there by you” (Rom. 15:24); by such great fruits [variant: “waves”] he demonstrated what he was seeking from that province. Having laid the foundations of the Gospel in a short time from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum, he entered Rome in chains, so that he might set free those bound by the errors of superstition. He remained for two years in a rented lodging, in order to provide us with an enduring home for both Testaments.

[Note: Two manuscripts read “my wasting-away soul.” Shortly afterward, Martianay deleted the verse from Psalm 54 and the following words, “Truly, the Lord’s word has now been fulfilled in you,” because he did not find them in his manuscripts; we have restored them to their former, as it were, possession from all the other manuscripts and printed books that we collated.]

The Fisher of men, having cast the apostolic net, has also drawn you, like a most beautiful sea-bream among innumerable kinds of fish, to the shore. You have abandoned the bitter waves, the salt whirlpools, the [reading uncertain: *scissuras monitum*, “the clefts, a warning”], and Leviathan reigning in the waters; and, seeking the wilderness with Jesus, you have despised them, so that you may sing that prophetic verse: “In a desert land, in an impassable and waterless place, so I appeared before you in the sanctuary” (Ps. 62:3). And again: “Behold, fleeing far away, I remained in solitude. I was waiting for him who saved me from faintheartedness of spirit and from the storm” (Ps. 54:8–9).

I beg and admonish you with a father’s affection: since you have abandoned Sodom and are hastening toward the mountains, do not look back. Do not let go of the plough-handle, nor of the Savior’s fringe, nor of his locks, wet with the dew of night, which you once began to hold. Do not descend from the roof of your former virtues in search of clothing; do not return from the field to the house; do not love the plains with Lot and the pleasant gardens, which are not watered from heaven, like the holy land, but from the muddy stream of the Jordan, after it has changed its sweet waters by mingling with the Dead Sea.

2. Many begin, but few reach the summit. Those who run in the stadium all run, but one receives the crown (1 Cor. 9:24–25). Yet it is said to us: “Run in such a way that you may obtain it.” Our contest-judge is not envious, nor does he prepare the palm for one and disgrace for another [variant: “nor does he prepare the palm for one and disgrace for another”]. He desires all his athletes to be crowned.

My soul rejoices, and in the greatness of my joy I endure a kind of sorrow. Ruth bursts into words amid tears. Zacchaeus, for the conversion of a single hour, was deemed worthy to have the Savior as his guest. Martha and Mary received the Lord after preparing a banquet. The sinful woman washes his feet with tears and consecrates the burial of the Lord’s body with ointments of good works. Simon the leper invites the teacher with his disciples, and is not rejected.

Abraham is told: “Go out from your land, from your kindred, and from your father’s house, and go into the land that I shall show you” (Gen. 12:1). He leaves Chaldaea; he leaves Mesopotamia. He seeks what he does not know, lest he lose the one whom he had found [variant: “lest he lose what he had found”]. For he did not suppose that he could possess both his homeland and the Lord at once; rather, he was already then fulfilling in deed that saying of the prophet David: “I am a sojourner with you and a pilgrim, like all my fathers” (Ps. 38:13).

Hebrew means *περάτης* (*peratēs*), “one who crosses over” or “transient” [other manuscripts read *περώτης*; others replace the Greek term with “guest”]. Since he is not content with present virtue, but forgets what lies behind and stretches forward to what is ahead, and knows the saying, “They shall go from strength to strength” (Ps. 83:8), he has received a mystical name and opened the way for you: you should seek not what belongs to you, but what belongs to another; and you should regard as parents, brothers, relations, and kindred those who have been joined to you in Christ. “My mother and my brothers,” he says, “are these who do the will of my Father” (Matt. 12:48).

3. You have with you one who was formerly your companion in the flesh and now is your companion in the spirit; from being a wife she has become a sister, from being a woman a man, from being subject an equal. Under the same yoke she hastens together with you toward the heavenly kingdom.

Careful management of household affairs, returning to the accounts [the Verona manuscript reads “returning to the folds”], is not quickly laid aside. Joseph could not escape without his Egyptian tunic. That young man who, covered only with a linen cloth, followed Jesus, when he was seized by the attendants, abandoned his earthly covering and escaped naked. Elijah, carried up to heaven in a fiery chariot, left his mantle on earth. Elisha turned his oxen and the yokes of his former work into offerings.

The wisest man says: “Whoever touches pitch will be defiled by it” (Ecclus. 1:13). As long as we are occupied with worldly affairs and our soul is bound by the management of possessions and revenues, we cannot think freely about God. “For what partnership has righteousness with iniquity? Or what fellowship has light with darkness? What agreement has Christ with Belial? Or what portion has a believer with an unbeliever?” (2 Cor. 6:14ff.). The Lord says: “You cannot serve God and Mammon” (Matt. 6:24).

Laying down gold belongs to beginners, not to the perfect. Crates of Thebes did this; Antisthenes did it. To offer oneself to God belongs properly to Christians and to the Apostles. These two, casting into the treasury the coins of their poverty together with the widow, gave the Lord the whole sum they possessed, and deserve to hear: “You shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19:28).

4. You yourself understand how I should repeat these things, and that, under different words, I am inviting you to make your dwelling in the holy places. Your abundance has supported the poverty of many, so that their riches might in turn overflow into your need. You have made friends for yourself from unrighteous Mammon, who may receive you into eternal dwellings (Luke 16).

This is a praiseworthy deed, to be compared with the virtues of apostolic times, when believers, after selling their possessions, brought the money and poured it out at the Apostles’ feet, demonstrating that avarice must be trampled underfoot. But the Lord seeks the souls of believers more than their wealth. We read: “The ransom of a man’s soul is his own riches” (Prov. 13:8, according to the Septuagint). We may indeed understand “one’s own riches” as wealth that does not come from another’s property or from plunder, in accordance with the saying: “Honor God from your just labors” (ibid. 3:9). But the better interpretation is that we should understand “one’s own riches” as hidden treasures, which neither a thief can dig out nor a violent robber seize (Luke 12).

5. My little works, which you say you desire not because of their own merit but because of your goodness, I gave to your men to copy, and I saw them copied in parchment manuscripts. I repeatedly warned them to compare them more carefully and correct them. For, because of the constant stream of visitors and crowds of pilgrims, I could not reread such extensive volumes; and, as those present themselves testified, having been held back by a long illness, I scarcely began to recover during the days of Lent, when they were departing.

Therefore, if you find slips of the pen, or if some passages have been copied incompletely in a way that obstructs the reader’s understanding, you should not blame me, but your own people and the incompetence of the notaries and the carelessness of the scribes, who write not what they find but what they understand; and while attempting to correct the errors of others, they display their own.

Moreover, a false report has reached you that I translated the books of Josephus and the volumes of the holy Papias and Polycarp. For it is beyond both my leisure and my strength to render such great works with equal elegance into another language [Cassiodorus, *Divine Institutes*, ch. 17: “Josephus, almost a second Livy, extensively unfolded in the books of the Jewish Antiquities, whom Father Jerome, writing to Lucinius of Baetica, declares that because of the length of the extensive work he was unable to translate,” etc.].

I translated a few works of Origen and Didymus, wishing in part to show our people what Greek learning contained [all the common editions add the title “Saint” to Didymus, but Jerome nowhere applies it to him elsewhere, and it is scarcely credible that he would have done so at that time; therefore, following the authority of the manuscripts, especially the Verona manuscript, we have omitted it].

I gave my copy of the Hebrew Canon of Truth, except for the Octateuch, which I now have in hand, to your boys and notaries to be copied [formerly the reading was “the Heptateuch,” that is, seven books rather than the first eight books of Scripture; but two manuscripts read “the Pentateuch,” so that it cannot be understood with sufficient certainty from this passage which books Jerome had translated at that time]. I do not doubt that you also possess the edition of the Septuagint; and many years ago I gave a very carefully corrected copy to men devoted to study.

I rendered the New Testament according to the authority of the Greek. For just as the reliability of the ancient books must be examined against the Hebrew volumes, so the new books require the standard of the Greek language.

6. Fasting on Saturday and daily reception of the Eucharist

Regarding the Sabbath, which you ask about—whether one ought to fast—and regarding the Eucharist, whether it should be received daily, which the Roman Church [variant: “the Church of Rome”] and the churches of Spain are said to observe, the most eloquent man Hippolytus did indeed write, and various writers have published excerpts from different authorities. But I think I should briefly admonish you that ecclesiastical traditions—especially those that do not harm the faith—should be observed as they have been handed down by our ancestors, and that one custom should not be overturned by another’s contrary practice.

Would that we could fast at all times, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles that the Apostle Paul and the believers with him did during the days of Pentecost and on the Lord’s Day (Acts 13:2–3). Yet they should not on that account be accused of the Manichaean heresy, since bodily food ought not to be preferred to spiritual food.

Let us also always receive the Eucharist without condemnation of ourselves and without a pricking conscience, and hear the Psalmist say: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. 39:9), and sing with him: “My heart has poured forth a good word” (Ps. 44:1).

I do not say this because I think that one ought to fast on feast days, or because I would abolish the festival period extending over fifty days [a corrupt edition omitted “ought to fast,” without which the entire sense is lost; we have restored it from the manuscripts and other printed editions, which nevertheless read “on Sundays” rather than “on feast days”]. Rather, let each province abound in its own understanding, and let it regard the precepts of its ancestors as apostolic laws.

7. Two cloaks and an amphimallum

I have received from your possessions two little cloaks and an *amphimallum*, either for my own use or to give to the saints [Pliny, book 8, chapter 48, says that a shaggy garment was formerly called *amphimaelē*, and Pollux mentions an *ἀμφίμαλλος χιτών*, “a tunic rough with shag.” Ecclesiastical writers, however, more often write *amphibalum*, which in its ordinary sense is a kind of loose garment enveloping the body on every side. Severus Sulpicius, *Dialogues*, book 2, *Life of St. Martin*, chapter 1: “The saint, without the poor man seeing, secretly draws a tunic for himself from within his amphibalum.”].

I have sent you and your sister the insignia of poverty and daily symbols of repentance: four little haircloth garments suited to your purpose and needs; and a book—that is, ten very obscure visions of Isaiah, which I recently discussed in a historical explanation [we supplied “ten” from the Verona manuscript, for Jerome had interpreted the visions from the third chapter through the twenty-fourth chapter of Isaiah and had dedicated them to Bishop Amabilis. Of these commentaries, this is the fifth book on Isaiah as a whole]—so that whenever you see my little works, you may remember your dearest friend, and prepare for the voyage that you had postponed for a short time.

And because “a man’s way is not in himself, and the steps of a man are directed by the Lord” (Jer. 10:23), if perhaps—God forbid—some impediment should arise, I ask that those whom love joins together should not be separated by the distance between lands; and that, although our Lucinius is absent, we may always feel him present through the exchange of letters.

# Letter LXXII [Note: Formerly numbered 132. Written in this year, 398]

## To Vitalis the Presbyter

[Note: In the Verona manuscript and others: “To Vitalis the Presbyter: how Solomon and Ahaz are said to have begotten sons at eleven years of age.”]

### On Solomon and Ahaz

In reply to another letter from Vitalis, Jerome teaches that it must be accepted as true that Solomon and Ahaz fathered sons in their eleventh year. Scripture, however, which appears to assert this, may be explained in another way. He discourages anxious investigation of questions of this sort.

1. Zenon the shipmaster, through whom you tell me that the letters of your holiness were sent, delivered only one short letter from the blessed Pope Amabilis, containing the customary little gifts [the older editors Erasmus and Victorius, thinking that Amabilis was not the bishop’s proper name and that the title “Pope” especially suited the Roman bishop, inserted the name Damasus here, falsely and incongruously reading “of the blessed Pope Damasus Amabilis.” But Damasus had died long before, and the entire context of the letter and the manuscripts contradict that reading. Amabilis is the same man for whom Jerome had recently interpreted the ten visions of Isaiah, and whom he praises greatly in the preface to that work].

I am sufficiently astonished at what reason there could have been for him, although he had faithfully carried both your blessings and those of the other man, to be found negligent in delivering the letter [for “to be delivered,” Martianay retains “to be kept,” while other editions read “kept.” Jerome calls blessings what others also have noted: little gifts and alms, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying, “He who sows in blessings shall also reap from blessings.” See Fortunatus, book 2, poems 12ff., and Albaspinaeus, *On Eulogies*, book 1, observation 8].

For I do not think that you, a disciple of truth, were deceived—unless perhaps the Latin language wandered among the papers of a Greek. Accordingly, I am replying to a second letter, which my holy son Heraclius the Deacon returned to me [the most ancient Verona manuscript reads simply “Heraclius returned,” without the addition “the Deacon”]. In it, among other things, you beg me to explain to you why Solomon and Ahaz are said to have fathered sons at eleven years of age.

If Solomon received the kingdom over Israel in his twelfth year and reigned forty years in Jerusalem, and his son Rehoboam succeeded him in the kingdom when he was forty-one years old [our manuscripts and several others consulted by Martianay count only forty years; but at 3 Kings 14:21 we read: “Rehoboam was forty-one years old when he began to reign,” etc.], it is clear that Solomon was eleven years old—or ten, because the mother claims ten months from conception to birth—when he fathered him.

Again, Ahaz, the son of Jotham, was twenty years old when he was appointed king over the two tribes, Judah and Benjamin (4 Kings 16), and reigned sixteen years (2 Chronicles 28). When he died, Hezekiah, at the age of twenty-five, succeeded his father in the kingdom (4 Kings 18). From this it is understood that Ahaz likewise fathered Hezekiah in his eleventh—or tenth—year [Victorius and other older authorities read “twelfth”].

2. If the Septuagint interpreters had it one way in their histories and the Hebrew Truth another, we could take refuge in our customary defenses and hold fast to the native language [that is, the language proper to Scripture, or the Hebrew text, which Jerome later calls authoritative]. But now the authentic text itself and the other interpreters agree with equal authority; the difficulty lies not in Scripture but in its meaning.

For who among mortals would believe that an eleven-year-old boy could father a son? Many other things are also said in Scripture that appear unbelievable, yet are true. Nature cannot prevail against the Lord of nature; nor can the vessel say to the potter, “Why have you made me this way or that?” Although what occurs as a miracle, sign, or portent cannot make a law for nature [the earlier reading had *natura* in the nominative. This portent is also reported at Lydda by Augustine, *City of God*, book 16, chapter 8, and in the *Enchiridion on Faith, Hope, and Charity*, where he recalls and praises this passage from Jerome’s letter: “that two-bodied one,” he says, “who was recently born in the East, about whom very faithful brothers reported that they had seen him, and which the presbyter Jerome left in writing.” Anastasius Bibliothecarius’s history says that it occurred around A.D. 374 *in Palestine*, at Emmaus; Theophanes likewise says *in Palestine, in the village of Emmaus*, although he places it four years later. It is scarcely credible, however, that two such monsters, at Lydda and Emmaus, neighboring places, occurred at the same time].

Does the fact that in our own age a twofold human being was born at Lydda—a man with two heads, four hands, one belly, and two feet—mean that all human beings must be born in that way? Let us read the ancient histories, especially the Greek and Latin ones, and we shall find that, according to the error of the ancients, monstrous offspring, both among human beings and among herds and cattle, were expiated by means of lustral sacrifices [some manuscripts read “historians,” both Greek and Latin. Many examples of such explanations can be found in Livy. Ammianus Marcellinus, book 19, chapter 12, is particularly appropriate to our subject: “Such portents,” he says, “are often born … but since they are not expiated publicly, as among the ancients, they pass unheard of and unknown.”].

I heard this, and—God is my witness—I am not lying. A certain little woman was raising an exposed infant, feeding him drop by drop, acting as his nurse, and sleeping with the child, who had already reached his tenth year. It happened that she drank more wine than modesty allows; and, inflamed by lust, she led the infant to intercourse through obscene movements. The first drunkenness made a habit of the following night and of the nights thereafter. Before two months had passed, behold, the woman’s womb swelled. What more need be said? By God’s providence it happened that she who, against nature, was abusing the child’s simplicity to the contempt of God was exposed by the Lord of nature, fulfilling the saying: “Nothing is hidden that shall not be revealed” (Matt. 10:26).

3. Let us also consider that Scripture secretly accuses both Solomon and Ahaz of pleasure and impiety. Both, although they were of David’s stock, departed from the Lord. One pursued lust to such an extent that he had seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines, as well as young women and promiscuous prostitutes, whose number was beyond counting [understand “wandering,” “unrestrained,” and, if you prefer, even “low and common.” Tertullian used “the promiscuous license of concubines” in this sense, that is, license practiced openly. The reading *passim* formerly stood here, but is contradicted by the manuscripts]. Neglecting the God of his fathers, he built idols for very many nations, and was no longer, as before, *Jedidiah*, that is, “beloved of the Lord,” but “a lover of women” (3 Kings 11).

The other sent to the king of Assyria to request assistance; and, in the time of his distress, increased his contempt for the Lord. He sacrificed victims to the gods of Damascus, his attackers, and in all the cities of Judah [variant: “of Judaea,” which Ducaeus does not reject] built altars for burning incense; and he provoked the Lord, the God of his fathers, to anger (2 Chronicles 28). To such an extent did he go that, after plundering and breaking the vessels of the Lord’s house, he closed the doors of the Temple of God; made altars for himself in every corner of Jerusalem; walked in the ways of the kings of Israel; cast images of the Baals; burned incense in the valley of the sons of Hinnom; and passed his sons through fire according to the rites of the nations whom the Lord had destroyed at the coming of the children of Israel.

From this it is clear that people devoted to lust from an early age are shown by their premature offspring to have begun sinning at the time when nature does not permit it.

4. In summary, it may be said that, when Solomon was twelve years old, he obtained his father’s throne during David’s reign. Afterwards, since Scripture leaves it uncertain, David may have lived for some years while his son was already reigning—years that should be reckoned to David and not to Solomon. After his father’s death, the son may then have reigned for forty years, during which he reigned without his parent. Thus both the beginning of Solomon’s reign and the period during which he alone ruled are demonstrated by the historical account. Yet it does not follow that all the years of his life were confined to a total of only fifty-two years.

If you doubt that, when sons reign while their fathers are still living, the period of rule is reckoned not to the sons but to the parents, read the book of Kings itself. You will find that King Uzziah of Judah, after being struck with leprosy, lived in a separate house, while his son Jotham governed the kingdom and judged the people of the land until the day of his father’s death (4 Kings 5). Yet after his father’s death he is said to have reigned for sixteen years when he was twenty-five years old—years during which he alone reigned.

What we have understood about Solomon must likewise be understood about Ahaz, who was the son of Jotham and the father of Hezekiah (2 Chronicles 27–28). I heard a Hebrew tell a story of this kind in connection with Isaiah’s prophecy, which I recently interpreted among the ten visions [these now constitute the fifth book of the Commentaries on Isaiah, which, as we said above, are dedicated to Bishop Amabilis].

When Ahaz died, Philistia rejoiced, and afterward Scripture threatens and says:

> “Do not rejoice, all Philistia,  
> because the rod of your smiter has been shattered.  
> For from the root of the serpent shall come forth a basilisk,  
> and its offspring shall devour the flying creature” (Isa. 14).

That is, Hezekiah shall be established as king in place of Ahaz. From this he wished it to be understood that the son was not immediately installed in power after his father’s death, but that his reign was delayed either by popular rebellions, or by certain interregnums [this passage had previously been corrupted by several interpolations; Victorius restored it, and our manuscripts, together with many others, support his text. Another reading was “between the kingdoms.” Ducaeus reads *internis* in his manuscripts, a reading he approves on the grounds that there could have been not many interregnums but one between Ahaz and Hezekiah. He would reconstruct the passage conjecturally as follows: “either by popular rebellions, by certain internal disturbances, or by external evils pressing upon him,” etc.], or at least by pressing troubles and wars arising on various sides.

5. In obscure matters we set forth different opinions, so that you may seem not so much to be reading what I write as hearing me speak to you face to face. But when the Apostle forbids endless genealogies and Jewish fables, he seems to me to be prohibiting questions of this kind. For what benefit is there in clinging to the letter and attacking either a copyist’s error or the sequence of years, when it is written most plainly: “The letter kills, but the spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3:6)?

Read again all the books of both the Old and the New Testament, and you will find such disagreement in the years, and such confusion in the number between Judah and Israel—that is, between the two kingdoms—that to cling to questions of this sort appears to be characteristic not so much of a diligent person as of one with nothing to do.

I gladly received the little gifts you sent, and I earnestly pray that you may persevere to the end in the love with which you have begun to seek us. For it is not beginning but persevering that belongs to virtue. Receive, in turn, what has been sent through Desiderius [presumably the presbyter from Aquitaine].

# Letter LXXIII [Note: Alternatively numbered 126. Written around the middle of 398]

## To Evangelus the Presbyter

[Note: Most manuscript codices have no name in the superscription, but only “Here begins the Letter concerning Melchizedek.” Others variously read *Evangelium* and *Evagrium*; the printed editions preferred the former. Yet, if the Benedictine editor is to be believed, all the manuscripts he inspected read *Evangelium* or *Evangelum*. He unwisely preferred the former, since *Evangelius* is the correct form according to Greek analogy. In Macrobius’s *Saturnalia* (7.5), an Evangelius speaks. Procopius, *Secret History*, p. 133: “Among the rhetoricians at Caesarea there was an Evangelius, a man of no small distinction, who, enjoying a favorable breeze of fortune, became master of other wealth and much land; later he also purchased a coastal village named Porphyrion for three gold centenaria.”]

An anonymous author’s book, which maintained that Melchizedek the priest was not a man but the Holy Spirit, he refutes on the basis of the opinions of the ancient Christians. He demonstrates that Melchizedek really was a human being of Canaanite origin—or, if the Jews are to be believed, Shem, the first son of the patriarch Noah.

1. An anonymous book without an author

You sent me an anonymous and masterless volume, *ἀνώνυμον ἀδέσποτον* [the older printed editions more elegantly insert the conjunction *καί*, although it is absent from our manuscripts and from Martianay’s manuscript]. I do not know whether you removed the name from the title, or whether the writer, wishing to avoid the danger of debate, refused to acknowledge his authorship.

When I had read it, I understood that the notorious question concerning the priest Melchizedek had been developed there through many arguments, to the point that the author attempted to teach that the one who blessed so great a patriarch [one manuscript of Santa Croce in Rome adds “that is, Abraham”] must have been of a more divine nature and should not be considered among human beings.

Finally, he dared to say that the Holy Spirit appeared to Abraham and was himself the one who was seen in human form. But how the Holy Spirit brought forth bread and wine and received the tithes of the spoils that Abraham had carried off after defeating the four kings, he did not wish to address at all. You ask me to reply with my opinion both of the writer and of the question.

I confess that I wanted to conceal my judgment and not involve myself in a dangerous and *φιλεγκλήμων* discussion [Erasmus preferred *φιλεγκέμων*. *Φιλεγκλήμων* means “fond of accusing,” or one readily exposed to accusation, even to slander]. Whatever I might have said, I would have had critics. But when I read the letter again and found at the end of the page that I had been adjured by extraordinary entreaties not to despise the petitioner, I reviewed the books of the ancients, so that I might see what each one said and answer you, as though on the advice of many.

2. At once, at the beginning of Genesis, I found the first of Origen’s Homilies written on Melchizedek [the older editors, Erasmus and Victorius, and also some manuscripts, both ours and Benedict’s, report this as written in the first of Origen’s Homilies]. In it, after arguing at length in many ways, he arrived at the point of calling Melchizedek an angel. He spoke of the heavenly powers in almost the same arguments with which your writer spoke of the Holy Spirit.

I passed on to Didymus, his follower, and saw that he had followed his teacher’s opinion step by step. I turned to Hippolytus, Irenaeus, Eusebius of Caesarea, and Eusebius of Emesa; also to Apollinaris and our Eustathius, who, as the first bishop of the Church of Antioch, sounded the trumpet of war against Arius with the clearest voice [our manuscripts variously present “Apollinaris” and “Apollinarius.” Only two add *noster* here, together with the editions of Erasmus and Victorius, reading “our Apollinarius also, and Eustathius, who …” Martianay rejects this reading on several grounds].

I discovered that all their opinions, by different arguments and side paths, arrived at one crossroads: they said that Melchizedek was a Canaanite human being, king of the city of Jerusalem, which was first called Salem, afterward Jebus, and finally Jerusalem.

There is nothing strange in describing him as a priest of God Most High without circumcision, the legal ceremonies, or descent from Aaron. Abel, Enoch, and Noah also pleased God and offered sacrifices; and in the book of Job we read that Job himself was both an offerer of gifts and a priest, and daily sacrificed victims for his sons (Job 1). They also say that Job himself was not of the tribe of Levi but descended from Esau, although the Hebrews assert otherwise [namely, “by contrast, the Hebrews maintain that he was descended from the line of Nahor,” as Jerome himself says in his *Questions on Genesis*, chapter 36. He confirms that opinion with his own judgment in chapter 22: “Some therefore wrongly think that Job was of Esau’s race,” and what follows; nevertheless, neither arguments nor the authority of the writers seem to establish anything certain or proven. The common opinion of the ancient Fathers does, however, assign to Job the honor of the priesthood].

3. When Noah became drunk in his house and was stripped and mocked by his middle son [two of our manuscripts and two manuscripts of the Benedictine editor read “by his eldest son,” while another reads “by his youngest.” We have found “middle” nowhere; indeed, since most older copies have only “by his son,” we would not object if someone deleted it. None of the manuscripts examined by Martianay contained the name Ham, which is added here; we found it in one manuscript of Santa Croce in Jerusalem, no. 59. A little below, some manuscripts read “about to die” rather than “dead,” which is preferable] (Gen. 9), he presented a type of the Savior, and Canaan a type of the Jewish people; Samson likewise, lover of the harlot, poor Delilah, killed far more enemies in his death than during his life (Judg. 16), thereby expressing the passion of Christ.

Nearly all the saints, patriarchs, and prophets expressed the figure of the Savior in some respect. Thus Melchizedek too, because he was a Canaanite and not of Jewish descent, went before as a type of the priesthood of the Son of God, of whom it is said in the hundred and ninth Psalm: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.”

They interpret his “order” in many ways: he alone was both king and priest; he exercised the priesthood before circumcision; and thus the Jews received the priesthood from the nations, not the nations from the Jews. He was not anointed with priestly oil, as the precepts of Moses prescribe (Lev. 8:1), but with the oil of gladness and the purity of faith. He did not offer victims of flesh and blood, nor receive the entrails of brute animals [the printed editions err up to this point, reading “and received with his right hand the blood of brute animals”; Victorius persuaded himself that he had corrected the previously corrupted passage even more badly, and Martianay follows him. We have restored the true reading on the authority and unanimous agreement of all our manuscripts, remarkably enough, supported by the old edition of 1496. The gloss retained after the word “entrails”—“that is, whatever is above the food”—was probably the cause of the entire error, as will be clear to anyone who considers the matter carefully]. Rather, through bread and wine, by a simple and pure sacrifice, he consecrated the sacrament of Christ—and many other things that the brevity of a letter cannot accommodate.

### 4.

Moreover (perhaps: “I pass over”) this has been treated more fully in the Epistle to the Hebrews (chapter 7), which all the Greeks accept, and some Latins as well: namely, that this Melchizedek—that is, “king of righteousness”—was king of Salem, that is, “king of peace,” without father, without mother, [Note: [Col. 0678] Some manuscripts insert here an interpretation of the following word, ἀγενεαλόγητος, which perhaps they transferred from the margin into the text; they read: “without father, without mother, without genealogy,” etc.] and that the meaning of this can be explained immediately in the single word ἀγενεαλόγητος, “without genealogy”: not that he existed without father and mother, since Christ also, according to both natures, had both father and mother, but because he is suddenly introduced in Genesis as appearing to Abraham when he was returning from the slaughter of his enemies, and because his name is recorded neither before nor afterward.

The Apostle affirms that the priesthood of Aaron—that is, of the Jewish people—had both a beginning and an end; whereas that of Melchizedek—that is, of Christ and the Church—is eternal, both in the past and in the future, and had no author; and that, when the priesthood is transferred, there is also a change of the law: so that the word of the Lord and the law of God proceed no longer from Hagar the slave-woman and Mount Sinai, but from Sarah the free woman and the citadel of Zion, from Jerusalem.

He first emphasizes the difficulty of the matter, saying: “Concerning which we have much to say, and it is difficult to explain” (Hebrews 5:11). [Note: [Col. 0678] Earlier editions read *prooemio*, “in the preface,” incorrectly; for this passage occurs nearly in the middle of the epistle. We have substituted the word *primo* from the Regina manuscript, 215, although both manuscripts omit much of the passage and contain other readings worthy of consideration. After *ininterpretabilis*, for which the Vulgate and a few manuscripts cited by Martianaeus have *interpretabilis*, everything that follows up to “If the chosen vessel” is absent from the Regina manuscripts.] This is not because the Apostle could not interpret it, but because it was not yet appropriate to that time. For he was persuading Hebrews—that is, Jews—not those who were already believers, to whom he might openly disclose the mystery.

Nevertheless, if the chosen vessel is astonished at the mystery, and confesses that what he discusses is ineffable, how much more ought we little worms and fleas to confess that our only knowledge is our ignorance, and to display a very spacious house through a small opening, so to speak? Let us say, then, that two priesthoods are compared with one another by the Apostle: that of the former people and that of the later people.

He pursues this throughout his discussion: that before Levi and Aaron there was a priest from the Gentiles, Melchizedek, whose merit so far preceded that of the future Jewish priests that Abraham blessed him in his loins. [Note: [Col. 0679] Most manuscripts, and the old edition mentioned so frequently, read this way. Previously the text had *praedicat*, “proclaims.”]

Everything that follows in praise of Melchizedek is to be referred to the type of Christ, whose advance is the mysteries of the Church.

### 5.

I have read these things in the volumes of the Greeks, and, as though displaying the broadest regions of the earth on a small tablet, I wished to set them forth—not extending the spaces of the meanings and discussions, but signifying boundless matters through certain points and brief summaries—so that, in a short Epistle, you might learn the opinions of many at once.

But since you ask affectionately, and since everything I have learned must be poured into your trusting ears, I shall also set down the opinion of the Hebrews; and, so that nothing may be lacking to your curiosity, I shall append the Hebrew words themselves [probably *subnectam*, “I shall append”]:

> **UMELCHISEDEC MELEC SALEM MOSI LEHEM VAJAIN, UHU CHOEN LEEL ELION: VAIBAR CHEU VAIOMER BARUCH ABRAM LEEL ELION CONE SAMAIM VA ARES: UBARUCII EL ELION ESER MAGGEN SARACH BIADACH VAJETHEN LO MAASER MECCHOL** (Genesis 14:18).

This is interpreted into Latin as follows:

> “And Melchizedek, king of Salem, brought forth bread and wine; and he was priest of the Most High God. And he blessed him and said: ‘Blessed be Abram by the Most High God, who created heaven and earth; and blessed be the Most High God, who delivered your enemies into your hand.’ And he gave him tithes of everything.”

They also report that this man was Shem, Noah’s first son, and that, at the time when Abram was born, he was 390 years old; the calculation is made as follows.

In the second year after the Flood, when he was one hundred years old, Shem fathered Arphaxad. After his birth he lived another five hundred years, making six hundred years in all. Arphaxad, at the age of thirty-five, fathered Shelah; Shelah, himself thirty years old, fathered Eber, whom we read fathered Peleg at the age of thirty-four. Again, Peleg, after completing thirty years, fathered Reu; and Reu, after reaching the thirty-second year of his life, brought forth Serug. When Serug had reached thirty years, Nahor was born from him; and Nahor, at the age of twenty-nine, fathered Terah. We read that Terah, when he was seventy, fathered Abram, Nahor, and Haran.

Add up the number of years in each generation, and you will find 390 years from the birth of Shem to the generation of Abram. Abraham died in the 175th year of his age. By this calculation it is found that Shem outlived Abraham, his tenth-degree descendant, by thirty-five years. [Note: [Col. 0680] The older parchment manuscripts do not repeat Abraham’s name here; in the printed editions the sense is consequently even more obscure, and it was also marred by faulty punctuation.]

### 6.

They likewise report that, until the priesthood of Aaron, all the firstborn descendants of Noah—whose succession and order are described—were priests and offered sacrifices to God. These are the birthrights that Esau sold to his brother Jacob (Genesis 27).

Nor is it surprising if Melchizedek went out to meet the victorious Abram and brought bread and wine for the refreshment both of him and of his warriors, and blessed him, since by this right he owed it to his great-grandson; and if he received from him tithes of the spoil and victory—or, according to the ambiguous reading, if he himself gave him [Note: [Col. 0680] Some manuscripts have *primitiae*, “firstfruits,” instead of *substantiae*, “possessions,” and *abavi*, “of a great-grandfather,” instead of *avitam*, “ancestral.”] tithes of his possessions, displaying ancestral generosity toward his descendant.

Both interpretations are possible, according to the Hebrew and according to the Septuagint translators: that he himself received tithes of the spoils and gave Abraham tithes of his possessions. Nevertheless, the Apostle in his Epistle to the Hebrews (chapter 7) defines the matter most clearly: Abraham did not receive tithes of Melchizedek’s riches, but the priest received a portion from the spoils of the enemies.

### 7.

Salem, however, is not, as Josephus and all our people think, Jerusalem—a name composed from Greek and Hebrew, which its mixture of foreign languages shows to be absurd—but a town near Scythopolis, which to this day is called Salem. There the palace of Melchizedek is pointed out, its size of ruins revealing the magnificence of the ancient structure.

Concerning this place it is also written in the latter part of Genesis: “Jacob came to Succoth,” that is, “to tents,” “and built houses and shelters for himself there, and crossed over to Salem, a city of the region of Shechem, which is in the land of Canaan” (Genesis 33:17–18).

### 8.

It must also be considered that, when Abraham was returning from the slaughter of the enemies whom he pursued as far as Dan (Genesis 14)—which is today called Paneas (or Pameas)—Salem was not Jerusalem, lying off the road, but the town of the metropolitan region of Shechem, and was situated along the route. [Note: [Col. 0680] The editions published before ours distort, indeed remove, the meaning by reading “not Jerusalem off the road” as two words, followed by “but the town of the metropolis,” etc. We have corrected the text with the help of three very old manuscripts, as the text and sequence require.]

We also read in the Gospel: “John was baptizing in Aenon near Salim, because there were many waters there” (John 3:23). It makes no difference whether it is called Salem or Salim, since the Hebrews very rarely use vowel letters in the middle of words, and, according to the preference of readers and local variation, the same words are pronounced with different sounds and accents.

### 9.

We learned these things from the most learned men of that people. They reject so completely the idea that Melchizedek was the Holy Spirit or an angel that they even assign him the definite name of a human being.

And truly it is foolish, concerning what is said in the type—that the priesthood of Christ has no end, and that he himself, both king and priest, has given us both offices, so that we may be a royal and priestly race (1 Peter 2:9), and, as the cornerstone, has joined the two walls together (Isaiah), and has made one flock from two herds (Ephesians 2:16)—for some to refer everything to ἀναγωγή, “higher interpretation,” in such a way as to remove the truth of the history and say that he was not a king, but that an angel was represented under the image of a man.

The Hebrews, on the contrary, strive so earnestly to demonstrate that Melchizedek, king of Salem, was Shem, Noah’s son, that they arrange the preceding text as follows:

> “And the king of Sodom went out to meet him”—there can be no doubt that “him” means Abraham—“after he had returned from the slaughter of Chedorlaomer and the kings who were with him, in the Valley of Save; this is the King’s Valley.” Immediately afterward it continues: “And Melchizedek, king of Salem, brought forth bread and wine” (Genesis 14), and the rest.

If, therefore, this is the king’s city and the king’s valley—or, as the Septuagint translated it, the plain, which the Palestinians today call Aulon—it is clear that he was a man who ruled in an earthly valley and city (or: “who had ruled”).

### 10.

You have what I heard and what I read about Melchizedek. My task was to cite (or: recite) the witnesses; yours must be to judge the credibility of the witnesses.

But if you reject them all, you will certainly not accept that spiritual interpreter of yours who, though unskilled in speech and knowledge, pronounced Melchizedek to be the Holy Spirit with such arrogance and authority that he proved true the saying sung among the Greeks:

> ἀμαθὶα μὲν θράσος, λογισμὸς δὲ ὄκνον φέρει.

“Ignorance produces confidence, but reflection produces hesitation.” [Note: [Col. 0681] Victorius had noted that this saying was attributed to Thucydides. *Ignorance produces confidence, but deliberation produces hesitation.*]

After a long illness I was scarcely able to become free from fever during the days of Lent, and, while preparing myself for another work, I spent the few remaining days on the exposition of Matthew. I resumed my interrupted studies with such eagerness that what benefited the exercise of my tongue harmed the health of my body.

---

## EPISTLE LXXIV [Note: [Col. 0682] Otherwise numbered 131. Written toward the end of the year 398.]

### TO RUFFINUS THE PRESBYTER

[Note: [Col. 0682] An older Veronese manuscript, with which several other handwritten copies agree, has: “To Ruffinus, Roman presbyter, on Solomon’s judgment”; some add, “in the division of the child.” This Ruffinus, moreover, is different from, and quite unlike, the Aquileian. If the very inscription of the letter, which calls him Roman, does not establish this, the words at the end of §6 certainly do: “We dictated these things to be written quickly, lest at the beginning of our friendship we seem to deny anything to one making a request.” Yet for this reason the view of Martianaeus and scholars generally, who identify this Ruffinus with the one whom the holy Doctor mentions below in Epistle 81 to his namesake at Aquileia—“We sent the holy presbyter Ruffinus to Rome and Milan for a certain reason,” etc.—does not please us. For here, as is clear from the words just cited and from all that follows, he addresses a man unknown to him by sight and entirely ignorant of his affairs, and either a Roman or at least residing in Rome in this very year, 398. These descriptions cannot in any way apply to that Ruffinus who was sent to Milan, since he was sent from the East and must have been known by sight to Jerome. In addition, the chronology, which shows that he was sent in the same year in which this letter was given, altogether prevents his being regarded as the person to whom this letter is now written.]

On the quarrel of two prostitutes and the judgment of Solomon.

[Col. 0682]

After briefly referring to the duties arising from his recent friendship with Ruffinus, he interprets allegorically the quarrel of the two prostitutes as concerning the Church gathered from the Gentiles and the Jewish Synagogue.

### 1.

Fame frequently lies in both directions, and by false rumor celebrates evil things about the good as well as good things about the evil. [Note: [Col. 0682] The older printed editions, together with certain manuscripts, incorrectly join the words as *falsorum ora concelebrant*, or *ore concelebrat*.]

Therefore I do rejoice at the testimony of your holiness toward me and at the affection of the holy presbyter Eusebius. [Note: [Col. 0682] This is Eusebius of Cremona, for whom Jerome, as he was departing from the monastery at Bethlehem for Rome, composed his commentaries on Matthew as though they were a traveling provision. Once he was in Rome, he was readily ordered to become a presbyter.]

Nor do I doubt that you praise me publicly, but I fear the silent judgment of your prudence. I therefore beg you to remember me more fully and to make me worthy of your praise.

That you were the first to prompt this duty, and that I was assigned the second place in replying (or: writing), did not arise from carelessness toward friends, but from ignorance; for if I had known, I would have anticipated your message.

### 2.

The interpretation of Solomon’s judgment concerning the quarrel of the two prostitute women (1 Kings 3), insofar as it concerns the simple historical sense, is clear: a boy of twelve judged, contrary to the measure of his age, the deepest affection of human nature. Hence all Israel both admired and feared him, since manifest matters did not escape him who had so wisely detected what was hidden.

As for the typological meanings, since the Apostle says, “All these things happened to them in figure, but they were written for us, upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Corinthians 10:11), some of the Greeks think that the passage should be understood of the Synagogue and the Church, and that everything should be referred to the time when, after the cross and resurrection, the true Solomon—that is, the peaceful one—began to reign both over Israel and over the people of the Gentiles.

There is no doubt that in Scripture the Synagogue and the Church are called adulterous women and prostitutes.

### 3.

At first sight this also appears blasphemous. But if we turn to the prophets—to Hosea, who took a prostitute as his wife and fathered children of prostitution (Hosea 1), and afterward an adulterous woman; and to Ezekiel, who reproves Jerusalem as a prostitute because she followed her lovers, spread her legs to every passer-by, and built a brothel in a public place (Ezekiel 16)—we shall understand that Christ came for this reason: to give prostitutes in marriage and to make one fold from two flocks. After destroying the dividing wall (Ephesians 2), he gathered into the same sheepfold sheep that had previously been diseased.

These are the two rods joined together in Ezekiel (chapter 37), concerning which the Lord says through Zechariah: “I took for myself two rods; I called one Beauty, and I called the other Cord, and I tended the flock” (Zechariah 11:8).

That prostitute woman in the Gospel who washes Jesus’ feet with her tears, dries them with her hair, and whose sins are all forgiven plainly represents the Church gathered from the Gentiles (Luke 7).

I have repeated this at the outset so that no one may find it incongruous if the Synagogue and the Church are called prostitutes, one of whom was granted possession of the son by Solomon’s judgment.

A prudent listener may ask how the Church can be a prostitute when she has neither spot nor wrinkle (Ephesians 5). We do not say that the Church remained a prostitute, but that she once was one. It is also written that the Savior entered a banquet in the house of Simon the leper (Matthew 26)—not because he was a leper at the time when he had the Savior as his guest, but because he had previously been a leper.
