Matthew likewise is called a tax collector in the catalogue of the Apostles—not because he remained a tax collector after his apostolic dignity, but because he had previously been a tax collector—so that “where sin abounded, grace might abound all the more.”

### 4.

At the same time, consider what the Church says against the calumniating Synagogue: “I and this woman lived in one house” (1 Kings 3:17).

After the resurrection of the Lord and Savior, one Church was gathered from both peoples. And how beautifully she says: “I gave birth in her chamber.” For the Church from the Gentiles, which previously did not possess the Law and the Prophets, gave birth in the house of the Synagogue; she did not leave the chamber, but entered it.

Hence she says in the Song of Songs: “The king brought me into his chamber” (Song of Songs 1:3). And again: “Indeed, I shall not reject you. Taking you, I shall bring you into the house of my mother and into the chamber of her who conceived me” (Song of Songs 3:4). [Note: [Col. 0683] In accordance with the Greek, τῆς συλλαβούσης με, “of her who conceived me.” The Veronese manuscript and others, together with the earlier editions, read “of her who gave birth to me.”]

“On the third day, after I had given birth, she too gave birth.”

If you consider Pilate washing his hands and saying, “I am innocent of the blood of this righteous man” (Matthew 27:24); the centurion confessing before the cross, “Truly this was the Son of God” (Mark 15:39); and those who, before the Passion, desired to see the Lord through Philip, you will not doubt that the Church gave birth first and that afterward the Jewish people were born, for whom the Lord prayed: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

On one day three thousand believed, and on another day five thousand (Acts 2 and 4). “And we were together”—for “the heart and soul of the multitude of believers were one” [Note: [Col. 0684] Victorius reads, “one new heart.” The Veronese manuscript reads, “there was one heart and soul.”]—and no one else was in the house with us, except the two of us: neither blaspheming Jews nor Gentiles serving idols.

But the son of this woman died during the night. For, while she followed the observance of the Law and joined the yoke of the Gospel’s grace to Mosaic doctrine, she was covered by the error of darkness. Her mother, sleeping, crushed him; she could not say, “I sleep, but my heart is awake” (Song of Songs 5:2).

Rising in the middle of the night, she took the child from the side of the sleeping Church and placed him in her own lap. [Note: [Col. 0684] Again, this follows the Greek, καὶ ἀνέστη μέσης τῆς νυκτός, “and she rose in the middle of the night.” In its place the Vulgate translator has: “And rising in the silence of the dead of night.”]

Read through the whole Epistle of the Apostle to the Galatians, and you will notice how the Synagogue hastens to make the children of the Church her own, and how the Apostle says: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Galatians 4:19).

She took the living child, not in order to possess him, but to kill him. She did not do this out of love for the child, but from hatred of her rival; and she placed her own dead child, through the ceremonies of the Law, in the lap of the Church.

### 5.

It would take a long time if I wished to go through each point. [Note: [Col. 0684] Another manuscript reads: “if I wished to review each individual matter.” But we frequently pass over many things of this kind.]

Through the Apostle Paul and ecclesiastical men, the Church understood that the one held under the Law was not her son; and in the light she recognized the one whom she had not seen in the darkness.

From this the quarrel arose in the presence of the king, one saying: “Your son is dead, but mine is alive”; the other replying: “You are lying, for my son is alive and your son is dead.” In this way they contended before the king.

Then King Solomon—who is plainly understood as the Savior, according to the Seventy-First Psalm, which bears Solomon’s title, where there is no doubt that everything said applies not to the dead Solomon but to the majesty of Christ—pretends ignorance and, in accordance with the dispensation of the flesh, pretends human emotions, just as in another passage he says: “Where have you laid Lazarus?” (John 11:34), and to the woman with the issue of blood: “Who touched me?” (Matthew 9).

He asks for the sword of which he had said: “Do not think that I have come to bring peace upon the earth. I have not come to bring peace, but a sword. For I have come to divide a man against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; and a man’s enemies will be those of his own household” (Matthew 10).

The Lord tests nature against nature, and according to the will of both women wishes to divide the living son between the Law and Grace—not because he approves this, but because, in order to expose the Synagogue’s calumny, he says that this is what he wishes.

The woman who did not want the Church’s son to live in grace or to be freed through baptism gladly consents to the child being divided—not in order to possess him, but to kill him.

The Church, who knows that he is her own, gladly yields him to her rival, provided that he may at least live with the adversary, lest, divided between the Law and Grace, he be struck by the Savior’s sword.

Hence the Apostle says: “Behold, I, Paul, tell you that if you observe the Law, Christ will be of no benefit to you” (Galatians 5:2).

### 6.

Let these things have been said under the cloud of allegory. Your prudence knows very well that the rules in the shadows of tropological interpretation are not the same as those in the truth of history.

If anywhere we have stumbled, and what we have written seems frivolous to a wise reader, let him lay the blame upon the author. For even these things we dictated rapidly to a secretary while lying in bed, exhausted by a long illness—not to fill out the subject, but lest, when you asked something of me at the beginning of our friendship, I should seem to refuse you.

Pray to the Lord for our health, so that after twelve months during which I have been worn down by continual illness, I may be able to write something worthy of your wishes. And forgive me if my overflowing speech does not flow in its customary course. [Note: [Col. 0685] Victorius reads: “does not flow in its usual course.” The words that follow are taken from Horace, *Satires* 1.10: “Often you should turn your stylus, to write again what deserves to be read,” etc. No one is unaware of the source.]

For we do not dictate with the same elegance with which we write: when writing, we often turn the stylus so that we may write again what is worthy of being read; when dictating, whatever comes to our lips we pour forth in rapid speech.

I was pleased to see Caninius, who will be able to tell you how difficult and dangerous a wound in my right hand I endured up to the present day, on which I dictated these words.

## EPISTLE LXXV [Note: [Col. 0685] Otherwise numbered 29. Written around the year 399.]

### TO THE WIDOW THEODORA

Jerome consoles Theodora, Lucinius’s widow, concerning her husband’s death, praising his virtues, especially his chastity.

### 1.

Overcome by the mournful report of the holy and venerable Lucinius’s falling asleep, I could scarcely dictate a brief Epistle. It is not that I grieve for his condition, since I know that he has passed to better things, as Moses says: “As I pass by, I shall see this great vision” (Exodus 3:3); rather, I am tormented by the longing that I was not worthy to see the face of that man whom I believed would come here shortly.

That prophetic oracle concerning the necessity of death is true, the necessity that separates brothers (Hosea 13) and cruelly and harshly sunders names most dear to one another.

But we have consolation, because it is slain by the word of the Lord, and the word is spoken to it: “I shall be your death, O death; I shall be your sting, O hell.” And in what follows: “The Lord will bring a burning wind from the desert, rising up; it will dry up all its veins and lay waste its spring” (ibid.). [Note: [Col. 0685] Victorius again mangles the Lord’s words, through whom it is said to her, etc.]

For “a shoot has gone forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower has blossomed from the virgin shrub” (Isaiah 11:1), who speaks in the Song of Songs: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (Song of Songs 2:1).

Our flower is the destruction of death; therefore he also died so that death might die through his death.

As for the statement that he would be brought from the desert, the virgin womb is indicated: without intercourse or the seed of a man, it poured forth God as an infant for us. By the heat of the Holy Spirit he dried up the springs of lust, and he sang in the Psalm: “In a desert land, pathless and waterless, so I appeared before you in the sanctuary” (Psalm 62:3).

Against the harshness of death and this most cruel necessity, we are therefore raised up by this consolation: that shortly we shall see those whom we grieve to be absent.

For it is called not death, but falling asleep and sleep. Hence the blessed Apostle forbids us to grieve over those who sleep (1 Thessalonians 4), so that, knowing that they sleep, we may believe that they can be raised; and, after their sleep has been digested, that they will keep watch with the saints and say with the angels: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14).

In heaven, where there is no sin, there is glory, perpetual praise, and unwearied proclamation. On earth, however, where there are sedition, wars, and discord, peace must be prayed for—and not peace among all, but among those who are of good will and hear the apostolic greeting: “Grace to you and peace from God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ be multiplied” (Romans 1:7).

Thus “in peace is his place, and his dwelling is in Zion” (Psalm 75:2)—that is, in the watchtower, in the sublimity of doctrines and virtues, in the soul of the believer, whose angel daily sees the face of God (Matthew 18:10) and, with unveiled face, contemplates the glory of God.

### 2.

Therefore I beg you—and, as they say, I urge you while you are already running—to desire your Lucinius as a brother, but to rejoice that he reigns with Christ: “Because he was taken away, lest wickedness should change his understanding. For his soul was pleasing to God, and in a short time he fulfilled many years” (Wisdom 4:11, 13–14).

It is we who should grieve, for every day we stand in the battle of sins, are stained by vices, receive wounds, and will have to give an account for every idle word.

He is already secure and victorious; from on high he looks upon you and favors you in your labor. He prepares a place for you beside him, with the same love and charity with which, even on earth, having forgotten the duties of a husband, he had begun to regard you as a sister—indeed, as a brother, because a chaste union has no nuptial distinction of sex.

[Note: [Col. 0686] Martianaeus reads *quia*, “because”; we have corrected many other passages of this kind.]

And if, while we are still placed in the flesh and reborn in Christ, we are not Greek and barbarian, slave and free, male and female, but all are one in him, how much more, when this corruptible has put on incorruption and this mortal has put on immortality (Galatians 3:28), will they neither marry nor be given in marriage, but will be like the angels in heaven? (Matthew 22; Luke 20.)

When he says, “They will neither marry nor be given in marriage, but will be like the angels in heaven,” the nature and substance of bodies are not removed; rather, the greatness of their glory is shown. For it is not written, “They will be angels,” but “like the angels,” where likeness is promised and identity denied.

“They will be,” he says, “like the angels,” that is, similar to angels; therefore they will not cease to be human beings. They will be illustrious and adorned with angelic splendor, but nevertheless human: so that the Apostle will remain an apostle, and Mary will remain Mary.

And the heresy will be confounded which makes uncertain and grand promises for the very purpose of taking away what is certain and moderate. [Note: [Col. 0687] The reference is evidently to the Origenists, whose teaching was gaining strength at that time and whom Jerome frequently attacks below and, at length, in the middle of the *Epitaph for Paula*. The same things, however, were also promised by the Pelagians, as is known from Hilary’s Epistle to Augustine. Several manuscripts likewise read: “let the heresies be confounded, which promise,” etc.]

### 3.

And since we have once mentioned heresy, by what worthy trumpet of eloquence can our Lucinius be proclaimed? While the utterly filthy heresy of Basilides was raging throughout the Spains and, like a pestilence and disease, devastating all the provinces between the Pyrenees and the Ocean, he preserved the purity of the Church’s faith. He did not accept Armagil, Barbelon, Abraxas, Balsamum, or the ridiculous Leusibora, nor the other things that are more portents than names, which they draw as though from Hebrew sources in order to excite the minds of the ignorant and of little women, terrifying the simple with their barbarous sound, so that what they do not understand they may admire all the more.

[Note: [Col. 0687] These portentous names appear to be drawn as though from Hebrew sources, especially Armagil, Ealsamon, and Leusiboram; they are scarcely, or not at all, found among other writers, and certainly are not explained by Irenaeus. Two, however, are well known: Barbelon and Abraxas. The former signifies “son of God,” or “son of Bel,” from an expression contracted to *Bel*; Greek βῆλος is a familiar name of an idol. The latter is a fabricated name derived from the number 365, the number of the positions of the local heavens, as Irenaeus says.

We think, however, that Armagil is the same as the name written Harmogenes, Harmoge, Harmogen, and Armazenon, and in most manuscripts Armazel. However one reads it, suppose that Oromazus is meant—or, as others prefer, Oromagdam—the god of the ancient Persians according to Zoroaster. Plutarch, in his *Alexander*, seems to indicate the Hebrew etymology of the name by reference to the excellence and magnitude of light.

Balsamum is the name of the sun, which the Phoenicians also worshiped, calling it in their native language Beelsamen, as Sanchuniathon testifies in Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel* 1.10. In the same work, chapter 7, Philo, speaking of the Phoenician worship of the sun, says: “They thought that this god was the sole ruler of heaven, calling him Beelsama, which in the Phoenician language signifies ‘of men,’ but in Greek ‘Zeus.’” From this arose the Punic Baalsamen, mentioned by Augustine, *Book of Expressions* 7.1. You will also find Balsamen instead of Baalsamen in Plautus, *Poenulus*, act 5, scene 2.

Just as Belenus comes from Belen, and Belus from Bel, so the Latins may have said Balsamum for Balsamen, signifying, from the Hebrew root, “God” or “Lord of heaven.” Hence in an inscription cited by Selden, Minerva is called Belisama.

Finally, Leusibora, which may be interpreted as “the innermost part of light,” seems to us to be the same as what Irenaeus, according to the heretics’ view, calls “the Great Light,” anointed by the Father so that it might become perfect, and from this called Christ. On this subject it will be useful to consult the passage of Saint Irenaeus, book 1, chapter 29.]

Irenaeus, a man of apostolic times, a disciple of Papias, the hearer of the Evangelist John, and bishop of the Church of Lyons, reports that a certain Marcus, descended from the family of Basilides the Gnostic, first came to Gaul and polluted by his teaching the regions through which the Rhône and Garonne flow. He especially seduced noble women by promising them certain secret mysteries and by this error, winning their love through magical arts and secret sensual pleasure.

[Note: [Col. 0688] Here and much later, in Epistle to Hedibia, question 10, and in the Commentary on Isaiah, chapter 64, Jerome perhaps relying on memory attributes to Irenaeus Marcus the Egyptian’s journey into Spain, conflating two heretics of that name into one. The first was the magician whom Saint Irenaeus refutes and who infected Gaul with his corruption—or, as Irenaeus himself says in chapter 9, seduced many women in the Rhone regions. The other, a younger Egyptian or Memphite, invaded Spain nearly two hundred years later, where, as Sulpicius Severus relates, he had Agape, Helpidius, and Priscillian as his followers; they were condemned at the Council of Zaragoza in the year 380. For a clearer account of the truth, compare Sulpicius with Isidore of Seville in his discussion of Hydatius, and compare both with Irenaeus.]

From there he crossed the Pyrenees and occupied Spain. He made it his special aim to pursue the houses of the wealthy, especially the women in them, who are driven by various desires, always learning but never arriving at knowledge of the truth.

He wrote this approximately three hundred years ago. [Note: [Col. 0688] I would prefer “two hundred” instead of “three hundred,” since Irenaeus wrote *Against Heresies* around the year 180 and seems to assume that Marcus, whom he attacks, was still alive.]

And he wrote these things in the books that he composed against all heresies in the most learned and eloquent language.

### 4

From this your prudence may judge how worthy of praise our Lucinius is, who closed his ears so as not to hear a bloody judgment; and he scattered all his possessions and gave them to the poor, “so that his righteousness might endure forever” (Ps. 111). Nor was he content with generosity toward his own country: he sent to the Churches of Jerusalem and Alexandria as much gold as could relieve the needs of many. While many admire and proclaim this, I shall praise in him still more his fervor and devotion to the Scriptures. With what longing did he demand our little works, and, having sent six copyists—for in this province there is a shortage of writers in the Latin language [Note: Earlier editions and writers read *scriptorumque* less correctly than *scriptorum*. We have corrected several other minor points above.]—have everything that we had dictated from our youth up to the present time copied out for himself? He did not honor us, who are small and least among all Christians and, because of the consciousness of our sins, inhabit the rocks of the Bethlehem countryside; rather, he honored Christ, who is honored in his servants and promises the Apostles, saying: “Whoever receives you receives me; and whoever receives me receives him who sent me” (Matt. 10).

### 5

Therefore, dearest daughter, consider this letter of my affection for him an epitaph; and whatever you know that I can do in spiritual work, command me boldly, so that future ages may know that he who says in Isaiah, “He made me like a chosen arrow; in his quiver he hid me” (Isa. 49), wounded two men separated from one another by such vast distances of sea and land with his keen point, so that, although they do not know one another in the flesh, they might be joined by the love of the spirit.

### Subscription

May that Samaritan preserve you holy in body and spirit—that is, the Savior and guardian, of whom it is written in the Psalm: “He shall neither slumber nor sleep who guards Israel” (Ps. 120). May Hir, whose name means “watchful,” who descended to Daniel [Col. 0689], come also to you, so that you may be able to say: “I sleep, but my heart is awake” (Song 5).

## LETTER LXXVI [Note: Elsewhere 32. Written shortly after the preceding letter.] TO ABIGAUS

Jerome excuses himself to the presbyter Abigaus for not having written to him, and consoles him, telling him not to be distressed by bodily blindness, since he sees with his mind. Finally, he praises his integrity and commends to him Theodora, the widow of Lucinius.

### 1

Although I am conscious of many sins and every day, kneeling in prayer, say, “Do not remember the sins of my youth and my ignorances” (Ps. 24:7), nevertheless, knowing that the Apostle said, “Lest, being puffed up with pride, he fall into the judgment of the devil” (1 Tim. 3:6), and that it is written elsewhere, “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (Jas. 4:6), from childhood I have tried to avoid nothing so much as a swollen spirit and an erect neck, provoking God’s hatred against itself.

For I know that my Master, Lord, and God, in the humility of the flesh, said, “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart” (Matt. 11:29), and that earlier, through the mouth of David, he had sung, “Remember, Lord, David and all his meekness” (Ps. 131:1). We also read elsewhere: “Before glory a man’s heart is humbled, and before ruin it is lifted up” (Prov. 18:12).

Therefore I beg you not to think that I had remained silent before receiving your letters, or to attribute to me the infidelity or negligence of others. What reason could I have had to remain silent when summoned by your courtesy, and by my silence to repel your friendship, when I customarily seek the companionship of good men of my own accord and offer myself to their affection? “For two are better than one; and if one falls, he will be supported by the other. A threefold cord is not easily broken, and a brother helping his brother will be exalted” (Eccl. 4:9).

Write, therefore, boldly, and overcome the absence of our bodies by frequent conversation. [Note: We have retained the printed reading, since most manuscripts agree with it; some editions, however, perhaps more correctly, have *junge* (“join”) instead of *vince* (“overcome”). For the arguments that follow concerning the need to endure bodily blindness courageously, compare what is written to Castrutius in Letter 68.]

### 2

Nor should you grieve if you do not possess what ants, flies, and serpents possess—that is, eyes of flesh. Rather, rejoice that you possess that eye of which it is said in the Song of Songs: “You have wounded me, my sister, my bride, with one of your eyes” (Song 4:9), the eye by which God is seen; concerning which Moses says, “As I pass by, I shall see this great vision” (Exod. 3:3).

[Note: Democritus and Metrodorus, whom Cicero, in the *Tusculan Disputations* and Book V of *On Ends*, reports to have put out their own eyes so that they might investigate the secrets of nature more subtly.]

Finally, we read that certain philosophers of the world even put out their eyes so that they might compel their whole thought toward purity of mind. And the Prophet says, “Death has entered through your windows” (Jer. 9:21). The Apostles also hear: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. 5).

[Note: The manuscripts have this form according to the Septuagint. Some printed editions, however, have *nostras* (“our [windows]”) with the Vulgate translator. Shortly afterward, in place of *jam moechatus est eam in corde suo* (“has already committed adultery with her in his heart”), which had stood there, we have restored the remaining words from two manuscripts and an old edition.]

Hence they are commanded to lift up their eyes and see the fields white and ready for harvest (Luke 21; and John 4).

### 3

As for your request that, through our admonitions, Nebuchadnezzar, the Rabsaces, Nabuzardan, and Holofernes might be slain within you: you would never have sought our assistance if they were alive in you. But because they are dead, and because with Zerubbabel, and with Jesus son of Josedec the high priest (1 Esd. 3), and also with Ezra and Nehemiah, you have begun to rebuild the ruins of Jerusalem; and because you do not put your wages into a pierced purse, but prepare treasures for yourself in heaven, therefore you seek our friendship, judging us to be servants of Christ.

I commend to you my holy daughter Theodora, the sister of blessed memory Lucinius, who is already commended by her own character, so that she may not grow weary on the journey she has begun; so that she may reach the Holy Land through the wilderness with great labor; so that she may not think that virtue is complete merely because one has departed from Egypt, but may arrive through innumerable ambushes at Mount Nebo and the Jordan River (Num. 33); so that she may receive a second circumcision at Gilgal; so that Jericho may fall for her, overturned by the blasts of the priestly trumpets; so that Adonizedek may be slain; and so that Ai and Hazor, once most beautiful cities, may fall (Josh. 3, 5, 6, 10, 11).

[Note: Victor reads *muri Jericho* (“the walls of Jericho”). Martianaeus has *turbarum*, which is perhaps a typographical error. Finally, instead of *Adonisedec*, older editions and several manuscripts have *Adonibezech*. But the latter is a different man, whose fingers and toes alone were cut off after the death of Joshua. Adonizedek was slaughtered together with five other kings. See Joshua in the passages cited.]

The brothers who are with us in the monastery greet you. Through you we offer an especially warm greeting to the saints who deign [variant: endeavor] to love us.

## LETTER LXXVII [Note: Elsewhere 30. Written in the year 399.] TO OCEANUS

### On the death of Fabiola

Jerome praises the noblewoman Fabiola because, after her fall, she turned to Christ, led a truly holy and Christian life, and deserved a glorious end to her life. He then joins to this letter another letter on the Forty-two Stations and dedicates it to her memory.

### 1

Several years have passed since, concerning the death of Blaesilla, I consoled Paula, a venerable woman, while the wound was still fresh (Letter 39, *On the Death of Blaesilla*). The circle of the fourth summer is now turning since, when writing to Bishop Heliodorus the epitaph of Nepotianus, I expended whatever strength I possessed in that grief. Almost two years ago I gave my Pammachius a brief letter concerning Paulina’s sudden departure, being embarrassed to say more to so eloquent a man and to press upon him what was his own, lest I should seem less to console a friend than to teach him with foolish ostentation how to be perfect.

Now, my son Oceanus, you impose upon me, willingly and eagerly, a duty that is owed, so that, in view of the novelty of her virtues, I may make old material new. In those earlier cases, the affection of a parent, the grief of an uncle, or the longing of a husband had to be restrained; and, according to the difference of the persons, different remedies had to be applied from the Scriptures.

### 2. Praise of Fabiola

At present you place before me Fabiola—the praise of Christians, the wonder of pagans, the mourning of the poor, and the consolation of monks. Whatever I take up first becomes insignificant by comparison with what follows.

Shall I praise her fasting? Her almsgiving is stronger. Shall I praise her humility? The ardor of her faith is greater. Shall I say that she sought filthy garments, and, in condemnation of silk clothing, chose the dress of the common people and the garments of servants? More is involved in laying aside one’s spirit than in laying aside one’s adornment. It is more difficult to lack arrogance than to lack gold and jewels. For after these have been rejected, we sometimes swell with pride over glorious rags and offer a marketable poverty to popular applause.

Hidden virtue, nourished in the secrecy of conscience, looks to God alone as its judge. Therefore she must be celebrated with new praises, and, leaving aside the order of the rhetoricians, we must begin entirely from the cradle of her conversion and repentance [variants: confession and conduct].

Someone else, perhaps mindful of the schoolroom, might bring forward Quintus Fabius Maximus:

> The one who, by delaying, restored the state to us  
> (Aeneid 6),

and might set the whole race of the Fabii before us; he might tell of battles, describe wars, and boast that Fabiola had come through the stages of such great nobility, so that what could not be shown in the branch might be demonstrated in the roots. But I, a lover of the Bethlehem lodging and the Lord’s manger, in which the virgin mother poured forth God as an infant, shall present Christ’s handmaid not from the nobility of ancient history, but from the humility of the Church.

### 3

And because at the very beginning, like some reef and storm, the accusation of her detractors is set against me—that, having contracted a second marriage, she had left the first—I shall not praise the convert unless I first absolve the accused.

Her first husband is said to have had such great vices that not even a prostitute or a worthless slave could have endured them. If I wished to describe these things, I would diminish the virtue of the woman who preferred to incur the blame of separation rather than defame a part of her own body and expose its stains. I shall bring forward only what is sufficient for a modest matron and a Christian woman.

The Lord commanded that a wife should not be dismissed except on account of fornication, and that, if she were dismissed, she should remain unmarried (Matt. 5 and 19). Whatever is commanded to men consequently applies also to women. For an adulterous wife is not to be dismissed while an adulterous husband is retained. “Whoever is joined to a prostitute becomes one body” (1 Cor. 6:16); therefore a woman who is joined to a fornicator and an impure man also becomes one body with him.

The laws of the Caesars are one thing, those of Christ another; Papinianus commands one thing, our Paul another. Among the former, the reins of sexual misconduct are loosened for men: once only fornication and adultery have been condemned, lust is permitted everywhere in brothels and with slave-girls, as though dignity, rather than intention, made the fault.

[Note: Augustine, *City of God* 14.17: “In the use of prostitutes, which the earthly city has made a permitted disgrace, although what is done is something that no law of that city prosecutes,” and so forth. See also the *Digest*, Book 48, and the *Code*, Book 9, title *Ad legem Juliam de adulteriis*, laws 1, 22, and 25.]

[Note: Gravius doubts whether Jerome wrote the passive form *passiva* instead of *passim*, as has elsewhere been noted from Tertullian.]

Among us, what is not permitted to women is equally not permitted to men; and the same servitude is imposed under an equal condition.

Therefore, they say, she dismissed a vicious man; she dismissed one guilty of this and that crime; she dismissed—I almost said—one whom, while the neighborhood cried out, his wife alone did not expose.

But if she is accused of why, after repudiating her husband, she did not remain unmarried, I shall readily acknowledge the fault, provided that I also state the necessity. “It is better,” says the Apostle, “to marry than to burn” (1 Cor. 7:9). She was a young woman and could not preserve her widowhood. She saw another law in her members warring against the law of her mind (Rom. 7:23), and saw herself dragged, bound and captive, toward intercourse.

She thought it better openly to confess her weakness and undergo a kind of pitiable marriage under cover than, beneath the glory of a one-husband marriage, to practice the deeds of prostitutes. The same Apostle wishes young widows to marry, bear children, and give the adversary no opportunity for reproach (1 Tim. 5). He immediately explains why he wishes this: “For some have already turned back after Satan.” Thus Fabiola, because she had persuaded herself and believed that she had rightly dismissed her husband, and did not know the force of the Gospel, in which every pretext for marrying is removed from women while their husbands live, avoided many wounds of the devil but, through carelessness, received one wound.

### 4. Fabiola’s public repentance

But why do I linger over matters abolished and ancient, seeking to excuse a fault whose repentance she herself confessed? Who would have believed that, after the death of her second husband, she would come to herself at the very time when negligent widows usually, having shaken off the yoke of servitude, live more freely, visit the baths, flit through the streets, and display prostitutes’ faces?

Would she put on sackcloth to confess her error publicly, and, with the whole city of Rome watching, stand among the penitents before Easter in the Basilica of the Lateran, once belonging to Plautius Lateranus, who was beheaded by the imperial sword, while the bishop, presbyters, and all the people wept with her; and would she bow her disheveled hair, pale face, filthy hands, and dirty neck?

[Note: Plautius Lateranus, who, as Tacitus relates in *Annals* 15.60, was discovered to have conspired against Nero and was slaughtered in complete silence. Constantine later occupied his palace on the Caelian Hill and then gave it as a gift to Pope Silvester; it was converted by him into the Basilica of Saint John, which to this day is called the Lateran from his name.]

What sins would such weeping not cleanse? What long-standing stains would such lamentation not wash away?

Peter wiped out his three denials by a threefold confession (John 21). Aaron’s sacrilege and the calf’s head cast from gold were corrected by his brother’s prayers (Exod. 32).

[Note: Another reading is *ob conflatum* (“because of the molten image”), and some manuscripts, preserved by Victor, have *ex conflato ex auro vituli capite* (“because of the calf’s head cast from gold”).]

David, that holy and most gentle man, expiated both murder and adultery by seven days of fasting (2 Sam. 11–12). He lay on the ground, rolled in ashes, and, forgetting his royal power, sought light in darkness. Looking only to the one whom he had offended, he said in a tearful voice, “Against you alone I have sinned, and I have done evil before you” (Ps. 50:6). And: “Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and strengthen me with a governing spirit” (ibid. 14).

Thus it happened that the man who had first taught me by his virtues how not to fall while standing taught me through repentance how to rise after falling.

What so impious a man among kings do we read of as Ahab, concerning whom Scripture says: “There was no one like Ahab, who sold himself to do evil in the sight of the Lord” (1 Kings 21)? When Elijah reproved him because of Naboth’s blood, and he heard the Lord’s anger through the Prophet—“You have killed and also taken possession; and behold, I shall bring evil upon you and cut off your descendants,” and the rest—he tore his garments, covered his flesh with sackcloth, fasted in sackcloth, and walked with his head bowed.

Then the word of God came to Elijah the Tishbite, saying: “Have you not seen Ahab humbled before me? Because he has humbled himself for my sake, I shall not bring the evil in his days.”

O blessed repentance, which drew God’s eyes toward itself and, when error was confessed, changed God’s raging sentence!

We read that Manasseh did the same in Chronicles (2 Chron. 33; supply the book reference), and Nineveh in the Prophet (Jonah 3–4), and the tax collector in the Gospel (Luke 16). Of these, the first deserved to receive not only pardon but also his kingdom; the second broke the impending wrath of God; the third, beating his breast with his fists, did not lift his eyes toward heaven; and the tax collector departed much more justified by his humble confession of sins than the Pharisee by his proud display of virtues.

It is not the place here for me to praise repentance and, writing against Montanus and Novatian, to say that it is an offering pleasing to the Lord (Ps. 26), and, “The sacrifice to God is a contrite spirit” (Ps. 50:19), and, “I desire the repentance of the sinner rather than his death” (Ezek. 18:23), and, “Arise, arise, Jerusalem” (Isa. 60:1; and Baruch 5:5), and many other things that the trumpets of the prophets proclaim.

[Note: These two heretics denied repentance to those who had fallen.]

### 5

I shall say only what will be useful to readers and appropriate to the present case. She was not ashamed of the Lord on earth, and he will not be ashamed of her in heaven (Luke 9). She opened her wound to everyone, and Rome, weeping, saw the discoloration [variant: disgrace] of the scar on her body.

She had her sides uncovered, her head bare, and her mouth closed. She did not enter the Lord’s Church, but sat outside the camp, separated like Miriam, Moses’ sister (Num. 12:15), so that the one whom the priest had expelled might be recalled by him.

She came down from her throne of delights, took up the millstone, made flour, and crossed streams of tears with bare feet. She sat upon burning coals.

[Note: Erasmus wrongly interprets this as “David’s desolating coals,” or the coal by which Isaiah’s lips were cleansed; Victor rebukes him and shows that these are the coals referred to near the end of Isaiah 47, where Isaiah exhorts Babylon to repentance: “You have coals of fire; you shall sit upon them; they will be your help.”]

These became her aid. She struck the face that had pleased her second husband; she hated jewels, could not bear to see fine linens, and fled ornaments. She grieved as though she had committed adultery and, at great expense in remedies, sought to heal a single wound.

### 6

We have lingered long over her repentance, in which we have, as it were, sat down in shallow places, so that the greater field of her praises might open before us without any obstacle.

After she had been restored to communion in the sight of the whole Church, what did she do? Certainly, “in the good day she did not forget the bad” (Eccl. 11). After her shipwreck, she did not wish to test the dangers of sailing again. Rather, she squandered and sold all the property she could possess—it was very considerable and befitting her family—and converted it into money, which she prepared for the use of the poor.

She was the first to establish a *nosokomeion* (νοσοκομεῖον), a hospital, in which she gathered the sick from the streets and warmed the limbs of the wretched, exhausted by illness and hunger.

[Note: Erasmus again interprets *nosokomeion* as *νοσουντοκώμιον*, “the bond of the sick.” He may have been led to this because in some older printed editions the Greek word *νοσοκομεῖον* was accompanied by this interpretation, “the dwelling of the sick.”]

Shall I now describe the various calamities of human beings—mutilated noses, gouged-out eyes, half-burned feet, livid hands, swollen bellies, wasted thighs, distended legs, and little worms boiling out from flesh that had been eaten away and had rotted?

How often did she herself carry on her shoulders people wasted by jaundice and filth? How often did she wash the purulent discharge of wounds that another could not bear to look at? She offered food with her own hand and moistened a breathing corpse with little sips.

I know that many rich and devout people perform this kind of mercy through the services of others because of the weakness of their stomachs, and are compassionate with their money, not with their hands. I do not condemn them, nor do I interpret tenderness of stomach as unbelief. But just as I grant pardon to weakness of the stomach, so I praise the ardor of a perfect mind to heaven.

Great faith despises such things. I know [variant: He knows] what the purple-clad rich man once failed to do for Lazarus, and by what punishment his proud mind was condemned (Luke 16). The man whom we despise, whom we cannot look upon, at whose sight we vomit, is like us; he was formed from the same clay with us and composed of the same elements. Whatever he suffers, we too can suffer. Let us regard his wounds as our own; and every hardness of spirit toward another will be broken by compassionate reflection upon ourselves.

> If I had a hundred tongues and a hundred mouths,  
> an iron voice,  
> I could not run through all the names of diseases  
>   
> (from Aeneid 6),

all of which Fabiola transformed into such great relief for the wretched that many poor people, restored to health, envied those who remained sick.

Although she showed similar generosity toward clergy, monks, and virgins, what monastery was not supported by her resources? Whose nakedness and sickness were not clothed by Fabiola’s garments? Into whose need did her headlong and swift generosity not pour itself?

Rome was too narrow for her mercy. Therefore she traveled through the islands, across the whole Etruscan Sea and the province of the Volscians, and through the hidden bays of winding shores, where choirs of monks dwell, visiting them either in person or through generosity sent by holy and faithful men.

### 7

Therefore, suddenly and contrary to everyone’s expectation, she sailed to Jerusalem, where she was received amid the arrival of many and stayed for a short time in our lodging. When I remember that companionship, I seem still to see the woman I saw.

Good Jesus, with what fervor and zeal was she intent upon the divine books! As though desiring to satisfy a kind of hunger, she ran through the Prophets, the Gospels, and the Psalms, both proposing questions and storing their answers in the little chest of her heart.

Nor was she satisfied with the desire to hear; as she added knowledge, she added sorrow (Eccl. 3), and, as though adding oil to a flame [variant: after adding oil], she took nourishment for a still greater ardor.

One day, when we had the Book of Numbers in our hands, she modestly asked me what such a great accumulation of names meant; why the individual tribes were joined in different ways in different places; and how Balaam the diviner prophesied the mysteries of Christ so clearly (Num. 20) that scarcely any of the Prophets had foretold him so openly.

I answered as best I could and seemed to satisfy her question. Turning the book, she came to the place where the catalogue of all the Stations is given—the places through which the people, departing from Egypt, reached the waters of the Jordan (Num. 33).

When she began to ask for the causes and explanations of each one, I hesitated over some, proceeded without stumbling through others, and frankly confessed my ignorance in most cases. Then she began to press me more forcefully, as though I had no right not to know what I did not know, and said that she was unworthy of such great mysteries.

What more is there to say? The shame of refusing compelled me to promise that I would compose for her a work of this kind, a little discussion which, as I now understand, has been delayed until the present time by the Lord’s will and will be delivered to her memory. Thus, clothed in the priestly garments of the earlier volume addressed to her, she may rejoice that through the wilderness of this world she has at last reached the promised land.

### 8

But let us continue what we began. While we were seeking a dwelling worthy of so great a woman, and while she desired solitude so much that she did not wish to be deprived of Mary’s lodging, suddenly, as messengers hurried about, the whole East trembled [variant: resounded].

From the farthest Maeotis, between the frozen Tanais and the monstrous peoples of the Massagetae, where the gates of Alexander restrain savage nations among the rocks of the Caucasus, swarms of Huns had burst forth. Flying here and there on swift horses, they filled everything alike with slaughter and terror.

[Note: The narrow passes of Mount Taurus are what Pliny, Book 6, calls the Caucasian Gates and describes quite accurately; most other authors call them the Caspian Gates.]

The Roman army was then absent and was held in Italy by civil wars.

[Note: Argobastes had stirred up a civil war. After killing the younger Valentinian, he established Eugenius as emperor. When Theodosius marched against him in 394, he took with him the Roman legions that were still in Italy, while the Huns were ravaging the lands of the empire in 395.]

Herodotus reports that this people, under Darius, king of the Medes, held the East captive for twenty years and exacted an annual tribute from the Egyptians and Ethiopians.

[Note: Herodotus recounts this in Book 1, chapter 106, under the name of the Scythians. But Herodotus’s manuscripts today give twenty-eight years, which is why Jerome is criticized by Scaliger for calculating only twenty. Others have observed that this number in Herodotus presents great difficulty. I have no doubt that there is an error, and therefore think that Herodotus should be corrected from Jerome—not, as Scaliger wrongly holds, Jerome from Herodotus—since Jerome appears to have read it in this way. I am the more willing to do so because Josephus and Eusebius also support the shorter calculation.]

May Jesus keep such beasts away from the Roman world forever.

They appeared everywhere unexpectedly, and, outrunning rumor with their speed, spared neither religion, rank, nor age; they did not pity even infancy’s wailing. Those who had not yet begun to live were forced to die, and, ignorant of their own misery, they laughed amid the hands and weapons of their enemies.

A common rumor spread that they were making for Jerusalem and rushing toward that city because of their excessive desire for gold.

[Note: Two manuscripts and an old edition omit *muri* (“walls”). Shortly afterward they read, with a meaning that is easily better, “Neglect of peace was repairing the neglected walls. Antioch was under siege. Tyre, wishing to tear itself away from the mainland, sought the ancient island,” and so forth. By the ancient island understand Old Tyre; see also Pliny, Book 5, chapter 19, and the ancient geographers.]

Neglected walls were being repaired through neglect of peace. Antioch was under siege. Tyre, wishing to tear itself away from the mainland, sought the ancient island.

Then we too were compelled to prepare ships, remain on the shore, and guard against the arrival of the enemy. In the raging winds we feared the barbarians more than shipwreck, looking not so much to our own safety as to the chastity of the virgins.

At that time there was a certain disagreement among us.

[Note: This is evidently the famous dispute with John of Jerusalem and Ruffinus concerning the Origenists. Shortly afterward some manuscripts and older editions read, “The faith, already fixed, held firm.”]

Domestic wars surpassed the battle with the barbarians. Our established homes and our long-standing longing for the holy places held us in the East.

She, who was wholly occupied with packing and a stranger in every city, returned to her homeland, so that she might live as a poor woman where she had been rich; remaining among strangers, though she had previously hosted many strangers; and, not to prolong the account, she distributed before the eyes of the Roman city to the poor what, as she herself testified, she had sold.

### 9

This alone we mourn: that we have lost the most precious jewel of the holy places. Rome received what it had lost, and the bold and malicious tongue of the pagans was refuted by the evidence of their own eyes.

Let others praise her mercy, humility, and faith; I shall praise her ardor of spirit still more. She knew by heart the book with which, when I was still a young man, I had urged Heliodorus toward the wilderness (Letter 14). When she saw the walls of Rome, she lamented that she was shut in.

Forgetful of her sex, mindful neither of weakness nor of anything but solitude, she was wherever she dwelt in spirit. She could not be restrained by the counsels of her friends; she longed to burst out of the city as though from chains.

She called the administration and cautious distribution of money a kind of unbelief. She did not wish to entrust the distribution of alms to others; rather, after scattering everything herself, she wished to receive alms for Christ.

She hurried and was so impatient of delay that you would have thought she was about to depart. Thus, while she was always preparing, death could not find her unprepared.

### 10

Amid the praises of the woman, my Pammachius suddenly rises before me. Paulina sleeps so that he may keep watch. She goes before her husband, so that she may leave him as a servant of Christ.

Here the husband is the heir of his wife, and others are possessors of the inheritance. Husband and wife competed to see who would pitch a tent in the Port of Abraham, and this was their contest: which of the two would surpass the other in kindness.

Each conquered, and each was conquered. Both confess themselves defeated and victorious, since each accomplished what the other desired. They join their resources and unite their wills, so that what rivalry would have scattered might grow through concord.

The word had scarcely been spoken, and it was already done. A lodging is purchased, and a crowd gathers at the lodging. “There is no toil in Jacob, nor pain in Israel” (Num. 23:21, according to the Septuagint).

They bring from the seas those whom the land may receive in its bosom. Let Rome send those who are hastening [variant: sailing], so that the gentle shore may shelter those who will sail.

What Publius once did on the island of Melite for one Apostle—and, lest there be room for contradiction, in one ship—these people do frequently and for many. They not only support the needs of the poor, but their generosity, flowing toward everyone, provides something even for those who possess means.

[Note: Previously, when he was at Mytilene, Gravius, on the basis of manuscript copies, read “Miletus.”]

The whole world has heard of the hospital situated in the Roman Port. In a single summer Britain learned what Egypt and Parthia already knew:

[Note: Gravius was not sufficiently satisfied with the reading and, from one old manuscript, preferred to rewrite it in another sense: “What Egypt and Parthia had acknowledged: truly what was written,” and so forth.]

truly.

### 11

What is written—“For those who fear God, all things work together for good” (Rom. 8:28)—we saw confirmed in the death of so great a woman.

With some foreknowledge of the future, she had written to many monks, asking them to come and release her from the heavy burden with which she struggled, so that she might make friends for herself from unrighteous mammon who would receive her into eternal dwellings (Luke 16:9). They came and became her friends. She slept as she wished, and, at last laying down her burden, flew lighter toward heaven.

How great a wonder Rome had found in the living Fabiola, she demonstrated in the dead woman. She had not yet breathed out her spirit, had not yet returned her soul owed to Christ,

> and already flying Rumor, herald of such great grief  
> (Aeneid 1),

was gathering the people of the whole city for the funeral rites.

The Psalms rang out, and the gilded roofs of the temples, echoing, shook the *Alleluia* upward.

[Note: In Erasmus and Martianus, *tecta* (“roofs”) was missing; without that word the sense limps. We have supplied it from other printed editions and manuscripts. The ancient Christian custom of rejoicing at the funerals of the devout, which many other writers approve, is rightly called by our Jerome in the *Life of Paul the Hermit* a Christian tradition.]

> Here a chorus of young men, there of old men,  
> who in song might celebrate her praises  
> and her deeds as a woman.  
> (ibid., Book 8)

Not so did Furius triumph over the Gauls, Papirius over the Samnites, Scipio over Numantia, or Pompey over the peoples of Pontus. They conquered bodies; she subdued spiritual wickedness.

I hear the ranks of those who went before and the multitude flocking in companies to her funeral. Neither the streets, nor the porticoes, nor the roofs rising above them could contain the spectators.

Then Rome saw its peoples united as one. All rejoiced in the glory of the penitent. Nor is it surprising that human beings exulted over her salvation, since the angels in heaven rejoiced over her conversion.

### 12

To you, Fabiola [variant: my Fabiola], I have offered this old man’s gift of my talent; I have dedicated to you these funeral offerings of duty.

We have often praised virgins, widows, and married women, whose garments were always white, women “who follow the Lamb wherever he goes” (Rev. 14:4). Blessed is the praise that is stained by no impurity of a whole life.

Away with ill will; let envy depart. If the master of the household is good, why is our eye evil?

She who had fallen among robbers was carried back on Christ’s shoulders (Luke 10). “There are many dwelling places with the Father” (John 14). “Where sin abounded, grace abounded still more” (Rom. 5). “The one to whom more is forgiven loves more” (Luke 7).

## LETTER LXXVIII [Note: Elsewhere 127. Published at the same time as the preceding letter.] OR AN EXEGETICAL BOOK TO FABIOLA

### On the Forty-two Stations of the Israelites in the Wilderness

After teaching that the departure of the Hebrews from Egypt and the history of their long journey are to be understood spiritually, Jerome proceeds through the order of the Stations, explaining each one according to tropology; and he thus delivers to Fabiola’s memory the work that he had promised her while she was alive.

1. In the seventy-seventh Psalm, which we believe was spoken, according to the Evangelist Matthew (chap. 13:35), in the person of the Lord, the history of the ten plagues in Egypt and of Israel’s departure into the wilderness is recounted. Although no one doubts that the events written down actually happened, the letter seems to say one thing while the spirit holds another concealed:

> “I will open my mouth in a parable; I will utter sayings from the beginning. All that we have heard and seen, our fathers have told us” (Ps. 77:2–3).

Hence the Apostle too, in the same words and therefore by the same Spirit, says:

> “All these things happened to them as a figure; but they were written for our admonition, upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Cor. 10:11).

[Note: At this passage, where above, in Letter 74 to Ruffinus, no. 2, we rendered “for our admonition,” or “for our correction,” from the manuscripts as “of us,” the manuscript authority here does not agree. Tertullian indeed reads “to admonish us,” and the Greek itself has πρὸς νουθεσίαν ἡμῶν (“for our admonition”), which supports the printed reading.]

And again:

> “I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that all our fathers were under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea; and all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them; but the rock was Christ” (ibid. 1 ff.).

If, then, part of the account of the journey from Egypt is understood spiritually, it will be shown that the other matters which the Apostle omitted because of the constraints of time possess the same meaning. For the same Prophet who elsewhere had said:

> “I dwelt with those who dwell in Cedar; my soul was for a long time an exile” (Ps. 119:5),

unable to endure his absence from the Holy Land, laments tearfully and says:

> “These things I remembered, and I poured out my soul within me, until I pass into the place of the wonderful tabernacle, to the house of God, amid the voice of exultation and confession, the sound of one feasting” (Ps. 41:5).

And in another Psalm:

> “Open my eyes, and I shall contemplate the wonders of your law” (Ps. 118:18).

Paul likewise says:

> “The law is spiritual” (Rom. 7:14).

And the Lord himself:

> “If you believed Moses, you would also believe me; for he wrote about me” (John 5:47).

And the Gospel according to Luke:

> “Beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things that had been spoken about himself” (Luke 24:27).

Let the Jews, therefore, who are little children and cannot swallow solid food but are still nourished with the milk of infancy (1 Cor. 3), read of a fleshly Pharaoh, the Red Sea by which one sails to India, manna resembling coriander, and hear bodily of everything that has been written: the leprosy of houses, the leprosy of skin and of cloth; the bull guilty of homicide and the beast accused of adultery; and the Hebrew who, wishing to serve because of his wife and children, has his ear pierced with an awl.

[Note: Older printed editions, together with some manuscripts, read: “wishing to serve, let them whistle through a pierced ear.” Capernaum, however, is very suitably interpreted here as “a most beautiful field,” although in another reading in the Book of Names it is “field of consolation.”]

But let us leave Capernaum, once “a most beautiful field,” and go out with Jesus into the wilderness, where we may feed on his loaves (Matt. 14; Mark 6): if we are foolish and like beasts, on barley loaves; but if we are rational creatures, on wheat loaves made from ground grain—the grain which, falling into the earth and dying, produced much fruit.

Egypt was struck by nine plagues, and Pharaoh was broken so that he would release God’s people. Finally, he lost his firstborn, so that Israel’s firstborn might be consecrated to the Lord. Those who had previously wished to hold them now drive them out insistently. The Destroyer passes through, yet does not dare touch the pastoral land of Goshen, watered by the rains; for their doorposts were marked with the blood of a lamb, and their deeds spoke:

> “The light of your countenance, Lord, has been marked upon us” (Ps. 4:7).

Hence the feast itself is called *Phase*—Passover—which we may call “passing over,” because, as we proceed from worse things to better, we leave dark Egypt behind. But now it is time, as we fulfill what was promised, to continue the order of Israel’s Stations.

2. It is written in the final part of the Book of Numbers (chap. 33), which among the Hebrews is called *VAJEDABBER*:

> “These are the encampments of the children of Israel, who went out from the land of Egypt by their companies, under the hand of Moses and Aaron.”

The Greeks call these *aparseis* (ἀπάρσεις).

[Note: This is what the Septuagint calls them: *aparseis*, that is, departures and removals, from the Greek root *airō* (αἴρω). For when the camp is moved, the tents and the army’s other baggage are lifted up. Rabanus, however, who is known to have worked most diligently at transferring into his writings enormous pieces taken from our Author, when copying this passage did not read *aparseis*, but [lacuna]αμον[lacuna], or “Stations and encampments.”]

We, because of the distinctiveness of our language, more significantly call them “Stations,” or, since the term concerns an army, “encampments,” and have translated it accordingly. A catalogue of the Stations is made from the first to the last, and forty-two are counted altogether. Matthew speaks of these when he says:

> “From Abraham to David there were fourteen generations; from David to the deportation to Babylon, fourteen generations; and from the deportation to Babylon to Christ, fourteen generations”—that is, forty-two generations altogether (Matt. 1:17).

Through these Stations runs the true Hebrew, who hastens to pass from earth into heaven; and, leaving behind the Egypt of this world, enters the promised land.

[Note: The Hebrew derives his name from “passing over” and is also called in Greek περάτης, “one who passes over,” as Jerome noted above in Letter 71, no. 2, and below at Station 31.]

Nor is it surprising that, through that sacred number, we arrive at the kingdoms of heaven: under that number the Lord and Savior proceeded from the first Patriarch to the Virgin, as to the Jordan, which flowed with a full current and overflowed with the graces of the Holy Spirit.

[Note: That is, forty-two generations intervene between Abraham and Christ; and under the same number of forty-two Stations we too may arrive at the true land of promise, which is Christ, and at the glory of the blessed.]

As for the statement that they went out “under the hand of Moses and Aaron,” understand this as the law and the priesthood, works and the worship of God, each of which requires the other. For it is of no benefit to practice virtues unless you know the Creator; nor does reverence for God advance one toward salvation unless you fulfill the commands of the Creator.

With these two hands, as with two Seraphim, we burst forth into confession of the Holy Trinity, saying:

> “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts.”

## First Station

> “They moved camp from Rameses in the first month, on the fifteenth day of the first month. On the day after Passover the children of Israel went out under a high hand, in the sight of all the Egyptians; and the Egyptians were burying those whom the Lord had struck among them, every firstborn in the land of Egypt. And the Lord executed judgments upon their gods” (Num. 33:2 ff.).

Some interpret *RAMESSES* as “turbulent agitation” or “bitterness and the agitation of the moth”; but we consider “thunder of joy” to be expressed more accurately.

[Note: The words of Jerome that follow, in which he explains the proposed etymologies of *Ramesses* one by one, persuade us easily that an error entered this passage from the word “moth,” which had previously consumed itself, and that “eating” should be read instead of “agitation.” In the Book of Names, *Ramesses* is indeed translated as “food of the moth,” while in Origen’s lexicon Ραμεσὴ ποιμασία ἐκ σητὸς means “Ramesse, pasture or eating from the moth” (*sētos*, not *sitou*, is the required correction). Jerome should not be thought to have omitted, among the many interpretations of this name, the one that perhaps had wider currency. His preference for interpreting it as “thunder of joy” results from his having read a double *sin* rather than *samekh* at the end; these letters are very easily confused with one another. In that case, since they signify “thunder” and “joy,” there is no room for doubt. We shall discuss the rest more fully in the Book of Names.]

To this city, which lay at the very borders, the people gathered, wishing to go out into the wilderness: for, abandoning the tumult of the world, they were moved away from their former vices and from the sins that had previously consumed them like a moth. Thus, turning all bitterness into sweetness, they would hear the voice of God thundering from above on Mount Sinai.

That divine words and the utterances of Scripture are called thunder amid the wheel of this age and world, the Psalmist declares:

> “The voice of your thunder is in the wheel” (Ps. 76:12).

Those who heard the voice of God the Father at the Savior’s baptism thought it was thunder.

[Note: In some manuscripts *Salvatoris* (“of the Savior”) is absent. Since they thought that thunder had occurred not at the baptism but when Jesus asked the Father to glorify his name, as John 12:29 testifies, Jerome is rightly believed to have taken this from an apocryphal book, perhaps the Gospel of the Nazarenes, which he had explained in Latin and subsequently cited.]

When we have been moved by the evangelical trumpet and awakened by the thunder of joy, we go out in the first month, when “winter has passed and gone away” (Song 2), when spring begins, when the earth gives birth, when all things are renewed. We go out on the fifteenth day of the first month (Exod. 12), on the day after Passover, in the full light of the month, after eating the spotless lamb, with our feet shod according to the Apostle (Eph. 6), our loins girded with chastity, and staffs prepared in our hands.

Although in Egypt we celebrated Passover on the fourteenth day of the month and ate the lamb, the full light is completed for us when, under a high hand, we leave Rameses behind. It is called “high,” either because it struck Egypt or because it protected Israel, in the sight of the Egyptians, who marvel that we are leaving the world, are tormented by envy, and later, when they wish to hold us back, are suffocated in persecutions.

Then the Egyptians bury their firstborn, and fathers dead to earthly works bury their dead sons. The firstborn of the Egyptians seem to me to signify the doctrines of the philosophers, by which they held deceived and ensnared human beings. When Israel has escaped from them alive, they surround their own dead, lest they imitate the example of those who are departing.

As for what follows—“In their gods he executed judgments” (Num. 33:9), or, as the Septuagint translated it, “vengeances”—the Hebrews maintain that on the night when the people went out, all the temples in Egypt were destroyed, either by an earthquake or by strokes of lightning. Spiritually, however, we learn that when we go out from Egypt, the idols of error fall and every worship of perverse doctrines is shaken.

## II. Station

> “The children of Israel set out from Rameses and encamped at Succoth” (Num. 33:5).

The Second Station. Here they bake unleavened bread and first pitch their tents; hence the place received its name from what occurs there. *SOCCOTH*, in our language, means “tabernacles” or “tents.” For this reason, in the seventh month, on the fifteenth day of the month, there is the feast of Tabernacles (Lev. 23).

When, therefore, we have gone out from Egypt, we first pitch our tents, knowing that we must proceed farther. Then we do not eat the leaven of Egypt, the leaven of malice and wickedness, but eat the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth (1 Cor. 5), bringing the Lord’s commands to completion in our works:

> “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees” (Matt. 16:11).

In this Station we are commanded always to remember our departure from Egypt; to celebrate the passing-over, that is, the Lord’s Passover; and, in place of Egypt’s slain firstborn, to consecrate to the Lord the firstborn of our womb and of all our virtues.

## III. Station

> “They set out from Succoth and encamped at Etham, which is at the edge of the wilderness” (Num. 33:6).

The Third Station is offered after the tents. In it the Lord is first seen by night in a pillar of fire and by day in a pillar of cloud, so that he may precede the people and become their guide on the journey.

*ETHAM* signifies for us “strength” and “perfection,” concerning which David also sings:

> “You broke open the rivers of Etham” (Ps. 73:15),

that is, “of the strong.”

[Note: Other editions read “sounds to us” or “agrees with us.”]

[Note: The Hebrew forms cited in this note are not legible in the supplied source. Victorius maintains that the form in the original text has been corrupted into one of two cited alternatives, on the basis both of the similar reading in Exodus 13:20 and Numbers 33 and especially of Jerome’s rendering “perfection”: in his view it could not signify perfection unless the word ended with the relevant letter. But Victorius failed to notice the Chaldean ending, which the Psalmist likes to use, and that the cited forms, like several other cited pairs, have the same meaning. It is therefore rightly concluded that *Etham* is first associated in Exodus or Numbers with “perfection,” and that the *Ethan* of the Psalm is the same word, differing in spelling only through the final letter characteristic of Chaldean.]

It is a great strength to leave Egypt behind and dwell at the edge of the wilderness. From this we understand that Succoth was still near the regions of Egypt. For when it says that Etham is “at the furthest borders of the wilderness,” it shows that it lies between the boundaries of the desert and Egypt.

Let us prepare strength for ourselves and assume perfect vigor, so that amid the darkness of errors and the confusion of night the light of the knowledge of Christ may appear. Let our day also have a protecting cloud, so that under these guides we may be able to reach the Holy Land.

[Note: Some older printed editions add “and the night fire”; Victorius had long ago deleted these words as wrongly inserted, but the Benedictine editor restored them to the text.]

## IV. Station

> “They set out from Etham, turned back toward Pi-hahiroth, which is opposite Baal-zephon, and encamped before Migdol” (Num. 33:7).

The Fourth Station is *PHIAHIROTH*, which means “mouth of nobles” and is written with the letter *Heth*. Some incorrectly think that *hiroth* means “villages”; their error is evident because they read the letter *AI* in place of the element mentioned above.

*BEEL-SEPHON* is translated into our language as “lord of the north,” or “watchtower of ascent,” or “one who possesses secrets.” *MAGDOL* means “greatness” or “tower.”

Having therefore assumed strength, we are ennobled in the Lord. We reject the secrets of the idol Baal-zephon and turn away from its magnificence and tower-like pride. For he does not come from the south, whence the Lord comes, nor from the south where the bridegroom reclines among the flowers; rather, he is the possessor of the north wind, the coldest of winds, from which evils burn upon the earth. Although it is the coldest, he is called “right,” falsely assuming the name of virtue and the right hand, when he is wholly on the left.

## V. Station

> “They set out from Pi-hahiroth, passed through the midst of the sea into the wilderness, traveled a three-days’ journey in the wilderness of Etham, and encamped at Marah” (Num. 33:8).

The Fifth Station is at *MARA*, which means “bitterness.” They could not have reached the waters of the Red Sea and seen Pharaoh perish with his army unless they had first had “nobility” in their mouth—that is, virtues in the confession of the Lord—when they believed God and Moses his servant, and heard him say:

> “The Lord will fight for you, and you will be silent” (Exod. 14:14).

Then, as conquerors, with Miriam leading the song, they began to resound on tambourines and in dances the songs of triumph:

> “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously honored; horse and rider he has cast into the sea” (Exod. 15:1).

After the preaching of the Gospel, after the tents of those who migrate, after strength has been assumed, after the nobility of confession, Egyptians and Pharaoh appear again.

[Note: The manuscripts we consulted read: “after the nobility of confession, dangers again arise.”]

From this we learn always to beware of snares and to invoke God’s mercy, so that we may escape the pursuing Pharaoh and he may be drowned for us in spiritual baptism.

After they had gone out from the Red Sea, the wilderness of Shur confronted them, which is also called the wilderness of Etham. Entering it for three days, they had no water, and they came to Marah, which received its name from bitterness. The spring had water but no sweetness. The people murmur when they see the water and cannot bear to drink it.

Understand Marah as the waters of the dying letter. If the confession of the cross is thrown into them and the mysteries of the Lord’s Passion are joined to them, everything that seemed undrinkable, sad, and harsh is turned into sweetness. Hence it is written:

> “God established for the people a law and judgments, and tested them” (Exod. 15:25).

For where the greatness of grace is, there the greatness of testing is also. Do not be frightened if, after victory, you come to bitterness: for those who truly celebrate Passover eat unleavened bread with bitter herbs, and temptation produces proof, proof produces hope, and hope produces salvation (Rom. 5).

Among physicians too there is an antidote, called by a word meaning “bitterness,” which moderates harmful humors. It is made sweet and restores health.

[Note: This is *pikra* (πικρά), a kind of medicine compounded from aloe. It is also called by the two-word expression *hiera pikra* (ἱερὰ πικρά), but in isolation, even in Galen’s time, it was called *pikra* because of its remarkable bitterness, as is clear from books 2 and 8 of *On Places*. See the Preface to the Letter to Algasi[a].]

So, conversely, pleasure and luxury end in bitterness, as Scripture says:

> “What for a time makes your throat fat, at the end you will find more bitter than gall” (Prov. 5:3, according to the Septuagint).

## VI. Station

> “They set out from Marah and came to Elim, where there were twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees; and there they encamped” (Num. 33:9).

The Sixth Station is translated as “strong rams.” What a beautiful order of virtues: after victory, testing; after testing, refreshment.

From bitterness we come to rams, and to the strong leaders of the flock, whom the Lord says through Ezekiel (Ezek. 34) he will judge because some trampled the waters and oppressed the sheep, while others were gentle and peaceable.

The twenty-eighth Psalm also speaks of them:

> “Bring to the Lord, sons of God; bring to the Lord the sons of rams.”

We are staying at the Sixth Station. Purest springs never appeared before, except where the teaching of teachers burst forth. There is no doubt that the reference is to the twelve Apostles, from whose springs the waters derived irrigate the dryness of the whole world.

Beside these waters seventy palm trees grew. We understand these also as teachers of a secondary order, as the Evangelist Luke testifies that there were twelve Apostles and seventy disciples of a lower rank, whom the Lord also sent ahead of him in pairs (Luke 6 and 10).

Paul likewise reports concerning them (1 Cor. 15:5–7) that the Lord appeared first to the eleven and then to all the Apostles.

[Note: One manuscript has “the twelve,” a reading that should not be dismissed, since he intends to distinguish the Apostles of the first order from the other seventy. Moreover, the Greek text of Paul is more frequently found in the better books with *dōdeka* (δώδεκα, “twelve”) than with *hendeka* (ἔνδεκα, “eleven”).]

Let us drink from springs of this kind, and, devouring the sweet fruits of victory, prepare ourselves for the remaining Stations.

## VII. Station

> “They set out from Elim and encamped beside the Red Sea” (Num. 33:10).

[Note: The editions of this work confuse the words of Scripture with Jerome’s interpretation, twisting and corrupting the meaning. Since the same words—“the Red Sea”—conclude the sacred text and begin Jerome’s exposition, they omit them in one place, following corrupt manuscripts in which, through the customary error of ancient scribes, those words had dropped out. We have restored and corrected the passage from Rabanus, who copied it before the text was corrupted.]

The Red Sea, which in Hebrew is called *JAM SUPH*, is the Seventh Station. It is asked how, after crossing the Red Sea and reaching the spring of Marah and Elim, they came again to the Red Sea—unless perhaps, as they proceeded on their journey, some inlet of the sea appeared, beside which they encamped. For it is one thing to cross the sea and another to pitch tents nearby.

From this we are warned that even after evangelical discipline and the sweetest foods of triumph, the sea sometimes appears before us and past dangers are set before our eyes. Yet there is a great difference between crossing the sea and seeing the sea from afar.

The expression *JAM SUPH* is composed among the Hebrews of “sea” and “red.” *SUPH*, however, is called both “red” and “rush.”

[Note: Learned men have long observed that among the Hebrews *suph* nowhere means “red,” but rather “seaweed” or “rush.” Thus the Old Testament never really speaks of the Red Sea, but of a sea of seaweed. By that name some understand the Arabian Gulf, others the Persian Gulf, which is commonly called the Erythraean or Red Sea. Jerome’s words can therefore easily be explained as meaning that, by a catachrestic usage, he understands the Erythraean Sea to be signified by the word *Suph*.]

We may therefore suspect that they came to some marsh or lake filled with reeds and rushes. There can be no doubt that Holy Scripture calls every gathering of waters “the sea.”

This Station does not occur in Exodus. Instead, it is written that from the Red Sea they came to the wilderness of Sin, which lies between Elim and Sinai, on the fifteenth day of the second month after their departure from Egypt (Exod. 16:1), that is, the thirty-first day after they left Rameses.

## VIII. Station

> “They set out from the Red Sea and encamped in the wilderness of Sin” (Num. 33:11).

The Eighth Station, although according to the order of Exodus it is the seventh. It should be understood that all the wilderness as far as Mount Sinai is called “Sin,” and that a place within the whole region also received the name of one Station, just as Moab is the name both of a city and of a province.

There are five Stations in this wilderness: Jam Suph, about which we spoke above; the wilderness of Sin; Dephca; Alus; and Raphidim, concerning which we shall speak in what follows.

*SIN* means “bush” or “hatred.” Both meanings suit the mystical interpretations: after we have come to the place from which the Lord will speak to us, may we deserve the great hatred of the enemy. Then we shall see the bush burning without being consumed: the Church inflamed by persecutions yet not perishing, because the Lord speaks within it.

Notice also that in the Eighth Station, where our winepresses are, and from which the Eighth Psalm is given its title, we take possession of the wilderness of the bush, because “the children of the desolate woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband” (Isa. 54).

## IX. Station

> “They set out from the wilderness of Sin and encamped at Dephca” (Num. 33:12).

[Note: Perhaps the name *Dephca* should be supplied again, and the passage should be read as follows: “Dephca is the Ninth Station. This name …”]

The Ninth Station. Among the Hebrews this name is called *krouma* (κρούμα), that is, “a knocking,” in accordance with what the Lord says:

> “Knock, and it will be opened to you” (Matt. 7).

In the Book of Hebrew Names, however, we translated it as “adhesion” or “release,” which should not trouble the reader.

[Note: Older editions have “adhesion and retention,” perhaps with a better meaning and wording, since the term sounds more like “glue.” But the manuscripts of both this letter and the Book of Hebrew Names contradict that reading. One of the latter, a particularly well-corrected manuscript in our library, which we acquired not long ago, will often be cited hereafter.]

Nor should anyone think that we write contradictory things. There we published the reading according to what is commonly found.

[Note: That is, if *Dephca* is written *Debca*, as the author of the Book of Hebrew Names appears to have read it.]

Here, however, I found it written in the Hebrew volume with *Phe*, a letter that expresses “knocking” more than “glue.” The meaning is clear: after the Lord’s answers, after the eighth number of the resurrection, we begin to knock at the mysteries of Christ.

I ask the prudent and diligent reader to understand that I translate the names according to the Hebrew Truth. Otherwise, in Greek and Latin books we find almost everything corrupted, apart from a few items. I marvel that certain learned and ecclesiastical men wished to translate things that are not found in Hebrew and to seek fabricated explanations for badly interpreted readings.

Thus, in the present passage, instead of *Dephca* they read *Rephca*.

[Note: He attacks the reading of the Septuagint, which has *Rhaphaka* (Ῥαφακὰ or Ῥαφακαὺ), replacing *Daleth* with *Res*, an obvious error. The letters differ by only a small stroke, and they interpret the word as “healing,” from which they then pursue a similar allegory.]
