## X. Station

> “They set out from Dephca and encamped at Alus” (Num. 33:13).

The Tenth Station is not found in Exodus and is believed to be included within the wilderness of Sin, as that book itself relates. “The whole multitude of the children of Israel set out from the wilderness of Sin by their Stations, according to the command of the Lord, and came to Raphidim.” From this it is clear that several Stations are designated by the name of one region.

*ALUS* means “leaven,” which a woman took and mixed into three measures of flour until the whole was leavened (Matt. 13:33). In this wilderness the people murmur because of hunger, turn their eyes toward the cloud, and behold from afar the glory of God. In the evening they receive quail, and in the morning of the following day manna (Num. 11).

And notice that in the Tenth Station leaven is introduced, while after the eating of meat manna is given, fulfilling the Scripture:

> “Man ate the bread of angels” (Ps. 77:35).

## XI. Station

> “They set out from Alus and encamped at Raphidim; and there was no water for the people” (Num. 33:14).

The Eleventh Station is one which I found violently interpreted in the Book of Hebrew Names as “a sufficient mouth for them,” or “the vision of the mouth of the strong.” It is better translated as “the dissolution of the strong,” or “the healing of the strong,” or, according to the character of the Syriac language, “the remission of hands.”

This Station is also read about in Exodus (chap. 17:1), after the departure from the wilderness of Sin. There the people complain because of the heat of thirst. A spring bursts forth and flows from the rock of Horeb. Because they tested God, the place received the name *Raphidim*, and also the name of testing, that is, *MESSE* or *Masa*.

Moses ascends the mountain; Jesus wages war against Amalek. At the sign of the cross the enemy is overcome. When the hands of the one praying are lowered, the enemy pursues as victor.

Moses sits upon the stone mentioned by Zechariah (chap. 2:5), which had seven eyes. In the Book of Samuel it is called *ABEN EZER*, that is, “stone of help” (1 Sam. 4:1). Aaron and Ur—that is, “mountainous” and “luminous”—support both his hands.

After the adversary has been defeated, Jethro arrives, brings Zipporah and both sons, and gives the counsel of the seventy elders. As a type of the Church gathered from the Gentiles, the “remission” of the Law is completed through the Gospel.

[Note: Victorius, relying on manuscript authority, reads “diminution” and supports his reading from the sequence of the context: namely, that the Law signified by Moses was weak and diminished, since the Law brought nothing to perfection, and its deficiency is supplied by the riches of the Gospel. Jerome himself teaches that the council of the seventy elders pertains to the Gospel. Nevertheless, it was not necessary to alter the text, for “remission” is understood in the better sense as freedom from a burden and release from office—the condition enjoyed at that time by Moses, who is understood under the name of the Law, when the seventy elders were appointed to govern the people.]

It is beautifully called “the dissolution” and “the healing of the strong,” *RAPHIDIM*, either because Amalek was dispersed or because Israel was healed.

But if, according to the Syrians, *RAPHIDIM* means “remission of hands,” we shall say that this name was imposed upon the place because of the people’s offense, since they murmured against the Lord.

[Note: To mention at last the proper etymology of the name, it should be derived from the lesser number and receives the force of its name from a Hebrew word not legible in the supplied source, meaning “spread out,” hence “spread-out places” or “encampments.” But the Talmud passage in *Bechoroth* agrees especially well with Jerome’s appended interpretation: “Why was this place called Raphidim? Because there they let their hands grow slack from the words of the Law.”]

We touch upon these matters rather than explain them, content to indicate briefly that after the leaven of Alus and the Messa of the Church, manifold temptations of demons customarily rise up against us.

## XII. Station

> “They set out from Raphidim and encamped in the wilderness of Sinai” (Num. 33:15).

The Twelfth Station. Let the number of the Apostles immediately come to mind. It is one among many, but greater than all, not separated in rank and surpassing them in merit.

[Note: Earlier editions wrongly read “greater than all of them.” In this sense an old author of a similar treatise in the Appendix to the Works of St Ambrose—who sometimes copies Jerome—also calls this Station the most celebrated of all.]

They arrive at this place on the forty-seventh day, as Scripture says:

> “In the third month after the children of Israel had gone out from Egypt, on this day they entered the wilderness of Sinai. They set out from Raphidim and came to the wilderness of Sinai, and encamped in the wilderness. Israel sat there opposite the mountain, and Moses went up to God. And the Lord called him from the mountain, saying …” (Exod. 19:1 ff.).

And again:

> “Go,” he said, “to the people and sanctify them today and tomorrow. Let them wash their garments and be ready for the third day, because on the third day the Lord will descend upon Mount Sinai in the sight of all the people” (ibid. 10).

And so it happened. They washed their garments, abstained from intercourse with their wives, and on the third day the Lord descended upon the mountain. As it smoked, and flashes of light, thunder, darkness, sound, and trumpet terrified mortal hearts, Moses spoke and the Lord answered him.

Let us calculate the number, and we shall find that on the fiftieth day after Israel’s departure from Egypt the Law was given on the summit of Mount Sinai. Hence the feast of Pentecost is celebrated, and afterward the mystery of the Gospel is completed by the descent of the Holy Spirit.

Thus, just as the Law was given to the earlier people on the fiftieth day—the true Jubilee, the true year of remission, and the true fifty and five hundred denarii forgiven to debtors—

[Note: Another reading has “to the Apostles,” followed shortly by “one hundred and twenty.”]

so also the Holy Spirit descended upon the Apostles and those who were with them, numbering one hundred and twenty according to the number associated with the Mosaic age; and, with the tongues of believers divided, the whole world was filled with evangelical preaching.

It would be a lengthy task to review everything commanded in the Law: how the tabernacle was constructed; the variety of sacrifices; the diversity of vessels; the garments of the High Priest, the priests, and the Levites; what ceremonies they performed; how the people were numbered. I shall say only that half of Exodus, the entire Book of Leviticus, a considerable portion of the precepts of Numbers, the distribution among the individual tribes of the people, and the offerings of the princes are described in this Station. The discussion of many volumes could scarcely suffice for this place.

*SINAI* means “bushes”: not one, as above in the wilderness of Sin, but many. Thus in that place there is a beginning, here perfection; there a solitary number, here multiplicity. For it is one thing to possess one grace, and another to possess all graces.

## XIII. Station

> “They set out from the wilderness of Sinai and encamped at the Graves of Lust” (Num. 33:16).

### Thirteenth Station

The thirteenth Station, whose name [Note: The printed editions are incorrect in giving the interpretation; they are corrected from the manuscripts.] is supplied from its interpretation, is called among the Hebrews **CABATORH ATTHAVA** [Note: Several manuscripts, together with the older printed editions, read *Atava*; but after Erasmus, Victorius mistakenly introduced the form *Cibaroth Ataave* from elsewhere. Since in reading Hebrew words they follow the Masoretic method, there is no time—or inclination—to correct them at every other word.]. Its meaning is that passage from the Gospel in which Jesus, after being baptized, was immediately led by the Spirit into the desert and tempted [another reading: “was being tempted”] by the devil.

Thus Israel also, after familiar conversation with the Lord, and after dwelling beside Mount Sinai for one year and four days, went forth from the encampment, arranged in a marvelous order, into the wilderness of **PHARAN**, which is interpreted as “wild ass” or “wildness.” There it succumbed to the evil beast, disdaining the bread of heaven and desiring the flesh-pots of Egypt [Note: Martianus had wrongly written [a term absent from the supplied text] for [a term absent from the supplied text], unless he invented that name in order to indicate more precisely the source from which the interpretation of the name was drawn; for the name [term absent] is derived from [term absent], “wild ass.” But it is established that Jerome sometimes attended to the sound, rather than the letters, when interpreting Hebrew names.]; when many of them had been suddenly devoured by fire, and Moses interceded (Num. 11:1–2), the devouring flame consumed the ground. Then they received quail and devoured them to the point of nausea and vomiting.

Seventy elders were chosen. They went to the door of the tabernacle; two remained behind, Eldad and Medad—not neglecting authority, but submitting in humility, considering themselves unworthy of the honor. Hence, though absent, they prophesied. When the people had been filled, while the food was still in their mouths, the wrath of God rose against them and killed their stoutest ones, and struck down the chosen men of Israel (Ps. 77:5), lest they should hasten too quickly toward evil. Hence the place was called “the graves of craving,” or, as we read in the Septuagint, “the memorial of desire.”

[Note: The author cited above, in the Appendix to the Works of St. Ambrose, writes: “From these things we learn that those who have abandoned the conduct of the world should not, shortly afterward, desire the poisonous things of the Egyptians, which are ‘great meats’; elsewhere some read ‘purulent substances,’ and others ‘brothy substances.’” Jerome, however, elsewhere—and not in only one place, as Martianus observed—says that “the Egyptians” are “great meats.”]

From all these things we all learn—those who have abandoned secular wisdom and despised the Egyptian pots—not to murmur against the heavenly bread of the Scriptures, nor to seek the poisonous things of the Egyptians, which are “great meats,” but to seek the simple food of manna. Otherwise, if we desire them again, we shall devour them until nausea overtakes us; and immediately we shall be tormented by the Lord’s fire [Note: The same ancient author reads “the wrath of the Lord.”], and our desire will be turned into tombs, so that we become whitewashed tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful to people, but inwardly are full of the bones of the dead and every kind of uncleanness.

### XIV. STATION

“And they departed from the graves of craving and encamped at Aseroth” (Num. 33:17).

The fourteenth Station is in the wilderness of Pharan, which is translated as “courts” [Note: More closely in Hebrew, “suburbs” or “villages,” which are, as it were, the vestibules of cities]. Here Aaron and Miriam murmur against Moses because of the Ethiopian woman, and, as a type of zeal against the Church gathered from the Gentiles, the Jewish people are covered with the defilement of leprosy. Nor does it return to the tabernacle [Note: Rabanus adds: “so that she may receive her former health”] and regain its former health until the appointed time of the fullness of the Gentiles is fulfilled [another reading: “until it is fulfilled”].

And the discerning reader should note this: after virtue had been completed in the number twelve, Israel became proud and desired Egyptian flesh in the graves of craving; it therefore lays another foundation and enters the courts—that is, the vestibule of virtue—showing us that those who stand can fall, and that those who have fallen can rise again. For Jesus has been appointed for the falling and rising of many (Luke 2), and he himself speaks through the Prophet: “Shall one who falls not rise again?” (Jer. 8:4).

### XV. STATION

“And they departed from Aseroth and encamped at Rethma” (Num. 33:18); whereas above, in this same book, we read: “After the people departed from Aseroth, they encamped in the wilderness of Pharan.”

This is the fifteenth Station. It should be noted that the remaining eighteen Stations, whose catalogue is now briefly described, from Rethma to Asion-gaber—that is, to the thirty-second Station—are included under the name of the wilderness of Pharan. We understand all the events recorded in them to have occurred at different times. Since they are not distributed among the individual Stations, we shall discuss them together, so that afterward we may return to the rest.

**RETHMA** is translated as “sound” or “juniper,” although many maintain that the Greek word **ἄρκευθος** denotes another kind of tree. “Juniper” is also found in the first of the Psalms of Degrees, according to the Hebrew Truth [Col. 0710], where it says: “What shall be given to you, or what shall be added to you, for a deceitful tongue?” (Ps. 119:3–4). The Prophet answers: “The sharp arrows of the mighty, with coals of juniper”; where our text reads “desolating coals.” They say that this wood preserves fire for a very long time, so that if embers are covered with its ashes, they last until the following year.

From this we learn that after the graves of craving and the vestibules, we pass to wood that retains heat for a long time, so that we may be fervent in spirit and proclaim the Lord’s Gospel with a clear and loudly exalted voice.

From this Station, then, to the thirty-second, such events are included. Twelve scouts are sent to the Holy Land; a cluster of grapes is brought back on a piece of wood [Note: Some of the Fathers commonly take the cluster, which the scouts carried on a transverse piece of wood because of its size, as a type of the Savior hanging from the wood of the Cross.], and Christ’s Passion is briefly indicated. The Jewish people murmur, fearing the attack of giants. They fight against Amalek and the Canaanite contrary to God’s will, and, when defeated, understand what sacrifices they ought to offer in the Holy Land.

Dathan and Abiram and the sons of Korah rise up against Moses and Aaron and are swallowed by a chasm in the earth. Between the dead and the living the High Priest enters, armed with a censer, and the wrath of God, running [another reading: “raging,”] is halted by the priest’s voice. Aaron’s staff produces both blossom and leaves, and its greenness, though dried, is consecrated as an eternal memorial (Num. 17) [Note: Victorius argues that *consecratur* should be read *conservatur*, citing, besides the testimony of certain manuscripts, this passage from Num. 17: “Bring Aaron’s staff before the testimony, so that it may be preserved there as a sign for the rebellious,” etc. Other manuscripts shortly afterward read: “They had not yet served the temple, being assisted,” or “they had not yet,” etc.].

There was not yet a temple, yet there were already temple-servants; there were not yet priests, yet the Levites offered sacrifices, and mystical discourse describes their portions. A red heifer is burned as a whole burnt offering, and its ashes are a sacrificial purification by sprinkling (Num. 19). The figures of all these things demand books of their own, and I think it better to remain silent than to say too little.

### XVI. STATION

“And they departed from Rethma and encamped at Remmon-phares” (Num. 33:19).

The sixteenth Station is interpreted in Greek as **ῥοιᾶς ἀποκοπή**, in Latin “the division of a pomegranate,” which some call “a granate apple” [Note: The same source, relying on Brixian manuscripts, has **εἰναίρεσις** instead of **ἀποκοπή**; the latter means rather “cutting off” or “section,” and Erasmus is said to have introduced it only by conjecture. But the traces of the Greek letters found in the manuscripts do not at all approach Victorius’s reading. For another reason, however, the word **ἀποκοπή** itself is attractive, or perhaps **διακοπή**, which more properly denotes division and interruption.].

The fruit of this tree is understood in Scripture in two ways: either as the Church’s embrace, which covers the whole multitude of believers with its rind; or as the variety and harmony of virtues, according to what is written: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul” (Acts 4:32). Thus the individual ranks are divided [another reading: “different”], yet all are held together by the same structure.

### XVII. STATION

[Col. 0711]

“And they departed from Remmon-phares and encamped at Lobna” (Num. 33:20).

The seventeenth Station may be translated as “brick,” although some, translating **Lebbonah**, have incorrectly interpreted it as “whiteness” [Note: There is indeed **[uncertain Hebrew term]**, or libnah, Greek **πλίνθος**, “brick,” or “bricklet.” Yet the opinion of those who derive it from whiteness should not be rejected; the Septuagint sometimes does this. Properly, *libnah* is a white poplar, and it seems likely that this Israelite station received its name from the abundance of that tree.].

We read of the Egyptian bricks in Exodus, which the people made and for which they groaned (Exod. 1:14). We read in Malachi (1:4) of bricks in place of which Edom, after its destruction, attempts to restore hewn stones [Note: This is found in this manner in all the books and in Rabanus. Martianus, however, attributes it either to a lapse of memory on Jerome’s part, to a difference in ancient manuscripts of Malachi, or finally to the carelessness of scribes who substituted Malachi for Isaiah. He insists that the words intended are those of Isaiah 9:10: “The bricks have fallen, but we shall build with hewn stones,” although he admits that these words are spoken by the people of Ephraim and the inhabitants of Samaria, not by the Idumeans. Apparently he failed to notice, or entirely overlooked with the other editors, the passage from Malachi cited above: “If Judah says, ‘We have been destroyed, but we shall return and rebuild what has been destroyed,’” etc., which Jerome clearly indicates.].

And we read of a brick in Ezekiel (14:1), on which a representation of besieged Jerusalem is depicted. From these things we learn that, on the journey of this life, and in passing from one state to another [Note: The Benedictine edition again errs by reading *transitum* instead of *transitu*], **NOW WE GROW**, now we diminish, and after the ecclesiastical order we often move on to the work of bricks.

### XVIII. STATION

“And they departed from Lobna and encamped at Ressa” (Num. 33:21).

The eighteenth Station is translated as “bridles” [Note: Presumably in the Book of Names, from **[uncertain Hebrew term]**, meaning “rein” or “bridle”; but perhaps it is more correctly derived from **[uncertain Hebrew term]**, meaning “breach” or “dripping.” There are other examples of this form.].

If, after making progress, we descend again to the work of clay, we must be bridled, and our wandering and headlong course must be directed by the restraints of Scripture. As far as memory serves, I do not know of having found this word elsewhere in the Holy Scriptures among the Hebrews, except in the apocryphal book called by the Greeks **λεπτὴ γένεσις**, that is, “Little Genesis” [Note: Older printed editions and several manuscripts have **μικρογένεσις**, as Rabanus also reads; hence Erasmus and Victorius did not invent the word, contrary to the opinion of the Benedictine editor. But the Greeks more often call it **λεπτὴ γένεσις**, as in Epiphanius, *Against Heresies* 39, Zonaras, Book I of the *Annals*, Syncellus in the *Chronography*, and others. We have therefore retained the printed reading. It appears from Jerome that this apocryphal book was written in Hebrew, not Greek, as some think.].

There, in the building of the tower, it is used for the racecourse in which boxers and athletes train and the speed of runners is tested. The Psalmist also says: “Restrain their jaws with bit and bridle, who do not draw near to you” (Ps. 31:9). And the Apostle: “Do you not know that those who run in the stadium all run, but one receives the prize? So run that you may obtain it” (1 Cor. 9:24).

### XIX. STATION

[Col. 0712]

“And they departed from Ressa and encamped at Caaltha” (Num. 33:22).

The nineteenth Station is interpreted as “Church.” The wandering steps of those who run are drawn back by bridles to the Church, and they hasten to enter again through the doors they had previously left.

### XX. STATION

“And they departed from Caaltha and encamped at Mount Sapher” (Num. 33:23).

The twentieth Station is interpreted as “beauty,” and is situated on the mountain of splendor. Of it the beginning of the fourteenth Psalm also speaks: “Lord, who shall dwell in your tabernacle, or who shall rest upon your holy mountain?” See what benefit the bridles provide. They draw us back from vices, lead us into the choirs of virtues, and make us dwell in Christ, the most beautiful mountain.

According to Daniel, this is the stone cut from the mountain without hands, which grew into a great mountain and filled the whole earth (Dan. 2:34). According to Ezekiel, this is the one who wounded the prince of Tyre (Ezek. 27) [Note: Consult the *Commentaries on Ezekiel*, chapter 28]. To this mountain the peoples stream together in Isaiah and Micah, saying: “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob; and he will teach us his ways, and we shall walk in his paths” (Isa. 2:2; Mic. 4:1).

### XXI. STATION

“And they departed from Mount Sapher and encamped at Arada” (Num. 33:24).

The twenty-first Station is translated as “miracle.” What a beautiful order of progress, what an excellent fabric of believers! After the work of brick we are bridled; after the bridles we are brought into the Church; after dwelling in the Church we ascend to Christ, the mountain, where we stand in astonishment and wonder, so that our speech in praising him is surpassed, as we find in him things “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor entered into the heart of man” (1 Cor. 2).

### XXII. STATION

“And they departed from Arada and encamped at Maceloth” (Num. 33:25).

The twenty-second Station is translated as “assemblies.” For in this place the multitude of believers is gathered: the Church of the firstborn, the harmony of all virtues. Then we can truly say: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity” (Ps. 132:1). And: “The Lord makes those of one disposition dwell in a house” (Ps. 67:7).

### XXIII. STATION

“And they departed from Maceloth and encamped at Thaath” (Num. 33:26).

The twenty-third Station may be understood as “beneath,” but we shall interpret it better as “terror” [Note: This was expressed very learnedly by a transposition of letters from **[uncertain Hebrew term]**, which means “consternation” or “terror.”].

You have come to the Church; you have ascended the most beautiful mountain; through astonishment and wonder you confess the greatness of Christ; you see there many companions in virtue. Do not be high-minded, but fear. For “the Lord resists the proud but gives grace to the humble” (Jas. 4). And “let the one who stands take heed lest he fall” (1 Cor. 10). “The mighty shall suffer mighty torments” (Wis. 6:7).

**FEAR IS THE GUARDIAN OF VIRTUES; SECURITY EASILY LEADS TO A FALL.** Hence in a certain Psalm, after the Prophet had said: “The Lord shepherds me, and I shall lack nothing; in a place of pasture he has settled me” (Ps. 22:2), he joins fear, which guards blessedness, and continues: “Your rod and your staff, they have comforted me” (ibid. 4). The meaning is: while I fear punishment, I have preserved the grace I received.

### XXIV. STATION

“And they departed from Thaath and encamped at Thare” (Num. 33:27).

The twenty-fourth Station is translated by some as “wickedness” or “pasture.” They would not be wrong if it were written with the letter **Ay**, but since there is a double aspiration in the final syllable, the source of the error is obvious. I find the patriarch Abraham written with this same word and the same letters. In the aforementioned apocryphal volume of Genesis, after driving away the crows that ravaged human grain, he received the name “driver away” or “repeller” [Note: In *Little Genesis*, or **λεπτὴ γένεσις**. Compare the Book of Names under this word from Numbers.].

Let us therefore imitate Terah, and diligently prevent the birds of heaven—which hasten to devour the wheat sown beside the road—from doing so. For the patriarch Abraham also, as a type of Israel, divided the limbs of the sacrificial victims and did not allow the birds to devour them (Gen. 15:11) [Note: In all earlier printed editions, *hostiarum* had been corrupted to *hostium*, so that Abraham was absurdly said to be a type of enemies, as well as of Israel. The rest was also less coherent. We have restored the authentic reading from Rabanus, who transcribed this passage before it was corrupted by incompetent scribes.].

And the crows from the ravines tear out the eye that scorns its father and despises the birth of its mother [Note: This alludes to Prov. 30:17: “The eye that mocks its father and despises the birth of its mother—the ravens of the torrent shall dig it out.” The Septuagint has **ἐκ τῶν φαράγγων**, “from the valleys.”]. The true Moses leads an Ethiopian woman, and Elijah is fed by crows.

If you have fear, you will be watchful; if you are watchful, the lion will not be able to enter the folds of your sheep. Apply this either to the leaders of the Churches or to the guardianship of your soul, into which the lion—the devil—tries to enter through the various openings of vices (1 Pet. 5).

### XXV. STATION

“And they departed from Thare and encamped at Methca” (Num. 33:28).

The twenty-fifth Station is translated as “sweetness.” You have ascended to the heights, admired the choirs of virtues, feared a fall, and driven away ambushers; immediately the sweet fruit of your labor follows you. In the manner of the letters, the sweetness of fruits will compensate for the bitterness of their roots, and you will say: “How sweet are your sayings to my throat, sweeter than honey to my mouth” (Ps. 111:103).

And you will hear the Bridegroom singing to you: “Your lips drip honey, my sister, my bride” (Song 4:11) [Col. 0714]. For what is sweeter than discipline? What is better than instruction? What is sweeter than the Lord? “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. 33:9).

Hence Samson, who had driven birds away from his fruits, tied up the foxes that destroy vineyards, and killed the roaring lion, found a honeycomb in the mouth of the dead lion (Judg. 14).

### XXVI. STATION

“And they departed from Methca and encamped at Asmona” (Num. 33:29).

The twenty-sixth Station in our language signifies “hastening,” according to what is written in the Psalm: “Ambassadors will come from Egypt” (Ps. 67:32). In Hebrew, instead of “ambassadors,” we read “those who hasten.” Thus, after we have harvested the sweet fruits of labor, we must not be content with rest and leisure; rather, hastening toward what lies farther ahead, we should forget what is behind and stretch ourselves toward what is to come.

### XXVII. STATION

“And they departed from Asmona and encamped at Moseroth” (Num. 33:30) [Note: Rabanus has: “which Samson broke,” etc.].

The twenty-seventh Station signifies “bonds” or “disciplines,” so that with rapid step we may proceed to teachers, wear down their thresholds, and regard the precepts of virtues and the mysteries of Scripture as eternal bonds, according to what is said in Isaiah: “The Sabeans, men of stature, shall pass over to you and shall be yours; they shall walk behind you, bound with bracelets” (Isa. 45:14). And: “Paul, the prisoner of Jesus Christ” (Eph. 3:4).

There are two kinds of bonds in Scripture [Note: In most manuscripts the word “miserable” is absent]; as long as Samson broke them, he conquered his enemies. Of the harlot we read: “Bonds are in her hands” (Eccl. 7:27). And in the person of the Lord it is said: “Let us break their bonds and cast their yoke from us” (Ps. 2:3). And elsewhere: “The snare is broken, and we have been freed” (Ps. 123:7).

But the bonds of Christ are voluntary and are turned into embraces. Whoever is bound by them will say: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand will embrace me” (Song 2:6).

### XXVIII. STATION

“And they departed from Moseroth and encamped at Banejacan” (Num. 33:31).

The twenty-eighth Station is translated as “sons of necessity” or “of gnashing.” If one begins with the number one and gradually adds until reaching seven, the result is twenty-eight. Who these sons of necessity are, the Psalm itself teaches us: “Ascribe to the Lord, sons of God; ascribe to the Lord the sons of rams” (Ps. 28:1).

What is this great necessity imposed upon the unwilling? When you have been instructed in the divine Scriptures and have learned that their laws and testimonies are the bonds of truth, you will contend with adversaries, bind them, and lead them captive in chains. From enemies who were once miserable and captive [Note: In most manuscripts the word “miserable” is absent] you will make children of God, so that suddenly you may say with Zion: “I was barren and did not give birth, exiled and captive—and who raised these? I was abandoned and alone—and where were these?” (Isa. 49:21).

Do you marvel at Isaiah? Learn the mysteries of the same Psalm: “The voice of the Lord in strength, the voice of the Lord in majesty, the voice of the Lord breaking the cedars” (Ps. 28:4). After he has broken the adversaries and shaken the peoples of the nations who were previously desolate, let stags be prepared in the mountains, and let the Beloved be like the son of unicorns, while all say glory in his temple.

As for what we have translated “sons of gnashing,” refer it to this meaning: through fear of punishment and of that place where there is “weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Luke 13), the multitude of believers abandons the devil’s bonds and submits its neck to Christ the Lord.

### XXIX. STATION

“And they departed from Banejacan and encamped at Mount Gadgad” (Num. 33:32).

The twenty-ninth Station is interpreted as “messenger,” or “expedition,” and “girding,” or, as we think more accurately, **κατακοπή**, that is, “cutting to pieces.”

We cannot otherwise make them sons of necessity, as teachers of disciples and believers, unless we have killed their instructors. Let us be cruel in their slaughter; let our hand spare nothing—not even a shoulder or the tip of an ear from the lion’s mouth. “Cursed is the one who does the work of the Lord negligently, and who withholds his sword from blood” (Jer. 48:10). Hence David also says: “In the morning I was killing all the sinners of the land” (Ps. 100:8).

Of “messenger” and “girding” we can briefly say that we should offer the sons of necessity powerful incentives toward virtue when we announce to them the rewards of the future and teach those who are girded to enter battle. Whatever a teacher does in these three respects, he stands upon the mountain.

### XXX. STATION

“And they departed from Mount Gadgad and encamped at Jetabatha” (Num. 33:33).

The thirtieth Station is interpreted as “goodness.” When we have reached the perfect man, the priestly degree, and the measure of the fullness of Christ (Eph. 4)—the state in which Ezekiel also was beside the river Chebar (Ezek. 1:1)—we shall be able to sing with David in the thirtieth Psalm: “In you, Lord, I have hoped; I shall not be confounded forever.” For “the good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep” (John 10).

### XXXI. STATION

“And they departed from Jetabatha and encamped at Hebrona” (Num. 33:34).

The thirty-first Station is interpreted as **παρέλευσις**, that is, “passing” or “transit” [Note: The Bishop of Reate argues in many places that **περαίωσις**, “passing over” or “crossing,” should be read instead of **παρέλευσις**, since the latter conflicts with Jerome’s interpretation that follows and by its nature seems to signify arrival, or passage beyond, rather than transit. We perceive nearly the same difficulty in the formation of both words, which is unknown to Greek writers; nevertheless, we have retained the printed reading because it is found in most manuscripts. Someone may perhaps prefer **παράβασις**, a word and meaning more nearly suited to the passage.].

To this place comes the true Hebrew—that is, **περάτης**, or “one who passes over”—who can say: “As I passed by, I saw this great vision” (Exod. 3:3). Of this the Psalmist also sings: “Nor did those who passed by say, ‘The blessing of the Lord be upon you’” (Ps. 128:8).

For the form of this world is passing away (1 Cor. 7), and therefore the saints desire to pass over to better things; not content with their present condition, they groan daily: “When I remembered these things, I poured out my soul within me, for I shall pass into the place of the wondrous tabernacle, even to the house of God” (Ps. 41:5).

It would be too much if I wished to collect examples concerning the word “passing” from all the Scriptures.

### XXXII. STATION

“And they departed from Hebrona and encamped at Asion-gaber” (Num. 33:35).

The thirty-second Station is translated as “wood of a man” or “hewing of a man” [Note: Formerly the editions had *dedolationes*; Victorius later incorrectly printed **ξυλακισμοφόρος** instead of **ξυλοκισμοὶ ἀνδρός**, which our manuscripts also confirm. The place received the name “woodcutting of a man” from the man who gathered wood on the Sabbath and was punished with death (Num. 15:32). Many examples show that ancient interpreters often used **Ay** for **Gimel**; hence someone has suggested that this letter once had two pronunciations, one of them being pronounced approximately like *gain*.], which in Greek is more significantly called **ξυλοκισμοὶ ἀνδρός**. It is written with the letter **Ay**, not, as the Greeks and Latins mistakenly suppose, with **Gimel**.

What else could the multitude of wood be in the wilderness except the discipline of a diligent and careful teacher, cutting unformed wood, hewing it, and making various vessels that are necessary in a great house? (2 Tim. 2). “The woodcuttings of a man” may signify the kinds of woodland and all varieties of trees, and therefore the multitude of believers, as David says: “We found it in the fields of the forest” (Ps. 131).

Up to this point the wilderness of Pharan contains eighteen Stations. Although they are described in the catalogue, they are not included in the earlier itinerary.

### XXXIII. STATION

“And they departed from Asion-gaber and encamped in the wilderness of Sin; this is Cades” (Num. 33:36).

It is asked why the eighth Station is now called the thirty-third. It should be understood that the former is written with the letter **Samekh** and interpreted as “thornbush” or “hatred”; this one, however, is written with **Tsade** and translated as “command” [Note: Suppose this is derived from *commanded*, or from *commandment*. The interpretation is nevertheless quite forced.].

The word joined to it, **Kadesh**, does not mean “holy,” as many think, but “changed” or “transferred.” We read in Genesis (28:21), according to the Hebrew Truth, where Judah, thinking Tamar to be a prostitute, sent gifts, and the intermediary of the gifts asks, “Where is the *kadesha*?” that is, “the prostitute,” whose dress had been changed from that of other women. We find the same usage in many places.

But if it is interpreted as “holy,” it must be understood **κατὰ ἀντίφρασιν**, by antiphrasis: just as the Fates are called by a name derived from sparing, although they spare no one; and war is called by a word suggesting peace, although it is by no means peaceful; and a grove is called by a word connected with light, although it gives no light.

In this Station Miriam dies and is buried. Because of the waters of contradiction, Moses and Aaron offend the Lord and are forbidden to cross the Jordan. Messengers are sent to Edom and request passage, but their request is denied.

Who would have feared, after so many advances, the murmuring of the people, the offense of the leaders, and the denial of passage along the road? It seems to me that in Miriam, Prophecy died; in Moses and Aaron, an end was imposed upon the Law and the Jewish priesthood. Neither could cross over into the promised land, nor lead the believing people out of the wilderness of this world.

Note that after the death of Prophecy and the waters of contradiction, they cannot cross Idumea, carnal and earthly [another reading: “the Idumean woman”]. Although they seek the road with many prayers and great effort, they do not obtain it; instead Edom goes out against them with a numerous people and a strong hand.

The interpretation of the name also suits death, offense, and denied passage: where there is a commandment, there is sin; where there is sin, there is offense; where there is offense, there is death. This is the Station of which the Psalmist sings: “The Lord will shake the wilderness of Kadesh” (Ps. 28:8).

### XXXIV. STATION

“And they departed from Cades and encamped at Mount Or, at the edge of the land of Edom. And Aaron the priest ascended Mount Hor according to the Lord’s command, and died there in the fortieth year after the departure of the children of Israel from the land of Egypt, in the fifth month, on the first day of the month. Aaron was one hundred and twenty-three years old when he died on Mount Or. And the king of Arad, the Canaanite who lived in the south in the land of Canaan, heard that the children of Israel had come” (Num. 33:17 and following).

The thirty-fourth Station is interpreted by most as “light” [Note: We have supplied the Hebrew names here and often elsewhere. It should not be omitted, however, that although Moses and the whole narrative state that Aaron the priest died on Mount Hor, Deuteronomy 10:6 says: “The children of Israel departed from Beeroth of the children of Jaakan to Moserah, where Aaron died and was buried, and Eleazar his son served as priest in his place,” etc. Some attribute this contradiction to the confused and inverted order of Stations XXVII, XXVIII, and XXV; others offer more plausible explanations. Consult the commentators on that passage if desired.]. They would not be wrong if it were written with the letter **Aleph**. Others translate it as “skin,” and they too would be correct if the letter were **Ay**. Some interpret it as “hole,” which could be accepted if it contained the letter **Heth**. But since it is read with **He**, “mountain” is the more likely meaning. It may be read: “Aaron the priest ascended into the mountain of the mountain,” that is, to its summit.

From this we observe that the High Priest did not die simply on a mountain, but on the mountain of the mountain, so that a place worthy of his merits might be shown. He died in the year in which the new people were about to enter the land of promise, at the outermost boundaries of the land of the Idumeans.

Although on the mountain he handed the priesthood over to his son Eleazar, and although the Law, for those who fulfill it, leads them to the summit, that very elevation is not beyond the waters of the Jordan, but at the extreme boundaries of earthly works. The people mourned him for thirty days [Note: Compare Letter 39 to Paula, section 3, where he gives a particularly elegant explanation of this matter.].

Aaron is mourned; Jesus is not mourned. **IN THE LAW THERE IS A DESCENT INTO THE UNDERWORLD; IN THE GOSPEL, A PASSAGE INTO PARADISE.**

The Canaanite also heard that Israel had come and, at the place of the scouts where he had once known that the people had offended [Note: Previously the plural *noverant* was less correctly printed; read *ineunt praelium*, “they enter battle,” and shortly afterward *ducunt*, “they lead away.”], he engaged them in battle and took Israel captive. Battle was fought again in the same place. The victor, bound by a vow, was defeated; the defeated prevailed; and the place was called **Horma**, that is, “anathema.”

I am not reluctant to repeat these things; they are necessary for readers. The human condition is always tossed about on the road of this age: one dies in a valley, another in the plains, another on a mountain—not simply on a mountain, but on the mountain of the mountain, that is, on its lofty summit.

When, deprived of God’s help, the enemy attacks us and leads us captive, let us not despair of salvation, but arm ourselves for battle again. It may happen that we conquer where we were defeated and triumph in the very place where we had previously been captives.

### XXXV AND XXXVI. STATIONS

“And they departed from Mount Or and encamped at Selmona. And they departed from Selmona and came to Phinon” (Num. 33:41–42).

These two Stations, the thirty-fifth and thirty-sixth, are not found in the sequence of the narrative; instead, this is written in their place: “They departed from Mount Or by the way of the Red Sea and went around the land of Edom” (Num. 21:4).

This shows that they were situated at the boundaries and around the land of Edom. Nor is it written according to the usual formula: “They departed from Mount Or and encamped at Selmona,” or “at Phinon.” Rather, after going around the land of Idumea, the account reaches its conclusion and says: “The children of Israel departed and encamped at Oboth” (Num. 33:43).

It does not say, “They departed from” one place or another [Note: Rabanus has: “from that place to that place”], because it had silently passed over two Stations, which, although omitted in the reckoning, it restores in the total.

The first Station, **Selmona**, is interpreted as “a little image.” The second, **Phinon**, means diminutively “mouth”—understand it as derived from *mouth*, not from *bone*.

In these places Aaron dies; they murmur against God and Moses; they grow weary of manna; they are wounded by serpents; and, as a type of the Savior, who triumphed over the ancient and true serpent on the gallows of the Cross, the poisons of the devil are overcome.

Thus the little image of the true and expressed image of the Son of God is preserved as it gazes upon his Passion. What it believes in its heart, it professes with its mouth, reading the Apostle’s words: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10:10).

At the same time, note that both Stations are called diminutively, **ὑποκοριστικῶς** [Note: That is, in diminutive form—“little image” and “little mouth,” or “small mouth”], because “we see in part and prophesy in part,” and “now we see through a mirror in an enigma” (1 Cor. 13:12).

### XXXVII. STATION

[Col. 0719]

“And they departed from Phinon and encamped at Oboth” (Num. 33:43).

The thirty-seventh Station is translated as “magicians,” or “python-spirits”; or, according to the words of Elihu, “large wineskins which, when they have been filled with new wine, burst immediately for lack of air.” The magicians fought against Moses and Aaron (Exod. 7 and following chapters); and the woman who was at Endor, who according to the Septuagint had a “python-spirit,” and according to the Hebrews was a “magician,” mocks the king of Israel (1 Sam. 28). There are many deceptions and innumerable snares by which human souls are caught; but let us say, trusting in the Lord, “The snare has been broken, and we have been set free” (Ps. 123:7). And: “Though I walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me” (Ps. 22:4). “A thousand shall fall at your side, and ten thousand at your right hand” (Ps. 90:7). We shall not fear the attack, nor the demon of noonday; but we shall stop our ears, so as not to hear the voices of sorcerers, and shall disregard the songs of the Sirens. After the image of God, which is displayed in the reasoning of the heart, and the confession of faith, which is uttered by the mouth, serpents arise, and magical arts provoke us to battle.

[Note: Recall Numbers 21:6–7. Since the Israelites came to Oboth after the fiery serpents on their first departure, it seems that they gave that place its name from the serpents. Certainly the Hebrew Oboth is very close to the Egyptian term Οὐβαῖον, which Horus Apollo, speaking of the Egyptians, testifies is rendered in Greek as “golden serpent,” that is, in Greek, Βασίλικον χρυσοῦν, etc.]

### XXXVIII. STATION

“And they departed from Oboth and encamped at Jeabarim, at the borders of Moab” (Num. 33:44).

The thirty-eighth Station means “crossing heaps of stones.” There are holy stones that roll over the earth—smooth, polished, and, by their roundness, resembling the courses of wheels. There are also others which the Prophet commands to be removed from the road, lest the feet of those walking stumble over them. Who are these walkers? Clearly, travelers and passers-by who hasten through this age toward other Stations.

As for what is said, “at the borders of Moab,” while it was written above, “in the wilderness that faces Moab toward the sunrise,” this shows, according to the literal sense, that up to this point they had been within the borders of the land of the Edomites, and now they come to the boundaries of Moab, passing from one province to another.

[Note: Rabanus adds this, as was already said above.]

For one must not always devote one’s effort to a single virtue. Rather, as it is written, “They shall go from strength to strength” (Ps. 81:8): one must pass from one virtue to another, because they cling to one another and are so closely joined that whoever lacks one lacks them all. Yet to pass from one to another belongs especially to those who contemplate the rising of the Sun of Justice.

### XXXIX. STATION

“And they departed from Jeabarim—or, as you find it in the second place among the Hebrews, Iim—and encamped at Dibon-Gad” (Num. 33:45).

The thirty-ninth Station is interpreted as “a temptation firmly understood.” In the sequence of the historical account I have found it written differently. For after they had encamped at Jeabarim, at the borders of Moab, opposite the rising of the sun, we read:

“From there they departed and turned toward the torrent of Zared. And departing from that place, they encamped beyond Arnon, which is in the wilderness of the borders of the Amorites, because Arnon lies on the boundary between the Moabites and the Amorites” (Num. 21:12–13).

After this they came to the well, where Israel sang this song:

“Rise up, well, which the princes dug, and which the leaders of the peoples opened, with the giver of laws and with his staff; and from the wilderness to Mattana [variant: Marthana]; and from Mattana to the torrents of God; and from the torrents of God to the heights; and from the heights to the valley which is in the territory of Moab, at the summit of Pisgah, which looks toward the wilderness” (ibid. 17 ff.).

Some interpreters, taking these places to be in the territory of the Amorites, think that they are not Stations but crossings, and that an unusual interpretation should not prejudice the catalogue of the Stations. Others, comparing spiritual things with spiritual, do not wish regions to be signified, but rather, through the names of the places, progress in the virtues. Thus, after the magicians and the gathering of stones, we frequently come to the torrents of “Zared,” which is interpreted as “alien descent”:

[Note: In the book of names, Zared is explained through two etymologies as “alien” or “descent.” Properly, however, Zared is a branch; hence “in the valley of branches,” as the Targum of Jonathan explains the Hebrew words: “in the valley that produces many willows and mandrakes.” We shall consider the rest in its proper place in the Book of Names.]

Being placed in descent, we pass to “Arnon,” which means “curse,” and which is situated within the borders of the “Amorites,” who are either “bitter” enemies or boastful men who “speak many words.”

But if we cross the borders of Moab, who was begotten through incest and withdrew from his true father, a well immediately meets us—a well dug by none of the common people, no obscure person, but by princes and leaders who give laws to the peoples. Singing a song over the water of the well and giving thanks for God’s gifts, they prophesy where they are going to pass and what places they will reach: namely, that from the wilderness they come to “Mattana,” which means “gift”; from Mattana to “Naḥaliel,” which is called “the torrents of God”; from Naḥaliel to “Bamoth,” which is interpreted as “heights,” or “approaching death,” when we are conformed to the death of Christ.

From Bamoth the valley of humility meets us. Yet this valley is situated at the summit of Mount “Pisgah,” which is interpreted as “hewn,” because it has nothing misshapen or crude in it, but is polished by the hand of the craftsman. This mountain looks toward the wilderness, which in Hebrew is called *Yeshimon*. For when we have been established at the summit of the virtues, then we look upon the ruins of the whole world and the devastation of all sins.

We almost forgot, as our discourse proceeded, to say why “Dibon-Gad” is interpreted as “a temptation firmly understood.” After Dibon-Gad, war is waged against Sihon, king of the Amorites, and Og, king of Bashan. We learn that, when we have reached the summit and drunk from the fountain of princes and kings, ascending Mount Pisgah, we must not be lifted up into pride; rather, we must recognize the wilderness set before us in the opposite direction. For before destruction the heart of a man is lifted up, and before glory it is humbled.

### XL. STATION

“And they departed from Dibon-Gad and encamped at Almon-Diblathaim” (Num. 33:46).

The fortieth Station is translated as “contempt of cakes,” or “of reproaches.”

[Note: We have removed from this passage an enormous error by conjecture. All the manuscripts, as well as the printed editions, are equally corrupt, so that no earlier interpreter seems to have suspected any error. All read *Diblathaim* as “contempt of wounds,” although no meaning of this sort can in any way be extracted from the name. Moreover, Jerome’s interpretation that follows—explaining the contempt of all sweet things and the allurements of pleasures—is enormously distant from such an etymology. We have therefore supplied “cakes” in place of “wounds.” For *palatha*, from the Greek πάλαθη, is, as Jerome himself testifies in the Book of Names, “a mass that is usually compacted from fresh figs; the Hebrews call it *debelath*, the Greeks *palatha*.” More fully, in Hosea 1 he says of *palatha*: “It is a mass of fat figs, which they shape like bricks and press together so that they may remain uninjured for a long time.” Thus *Diblathaim* will be the plural of *palatha*, “cakes.” The author whom we cited shortly before, in the Book of the Forty-Two Stations appended to the works of St. Ambrose, says: “This term, Almon-Diblathaim, just as it is twofold, also indicates two things, namely contempt of figs—that is, contempt of earthly sweetness, for figs signify sweetness,” etc., just as Jerome also interprets it. You should therefore have no doubt about our correction and reading.]

Through this we learn that all sweet things and the allurements of pleasures in the world are to be despised, and that we must not become drunk with wine, in which there is debauchery (Eph. 5). Honey is not offered in God’s sacrifices (Lev. 2), and wax, which contains sweetness, does not shine in the Tabernacle; rather, it is the purest oil, drawn from the bitterness of the olive, that gives light (Exod. 25). For honey drips from the lips of the prostitute (Prov. 5). I think that Jonathan, according to mystical interpretations, tasted of this honey, and, when he was discovered, was scarcely rescued by the prayers of the people (1 Sam. 14). As for the fact that reproaches are to be despised—and that, when falsely inflicted, they produce blessedness—the Savior teaches most fully.

### XLI. STATION

“And they departed from Almon-Diblathaim and encamped in the mountains of Abarim, opposite Nebo” (Num. 33:47).

The forty-first Station is translated as “the mountains of those who cross,” and it is opposite Mount Nebo, where Moses dies and is buried, having seen the promised land beforehand (Deut. 34). Nebo is interpreted as “conclusion,” in which the Law comes to an end and its memory is no longer found. But the grace of the Gospel extends without any end. “Its sound has gone out through all the earth, and its words to the ends of the world” (Ps. 18).

At the same time, consider that the dwelling-place of those who cross is situated in the mountains and still requires further progress. For after many mountains we descend to the plains of Moab and the streams of the Jordan, which is interpreted as “descent.”

[Note: Thus, at least, the Syrians call the Jordan from *descent*. In Syriac pronunciation it is [the Syriac form is omitted in the supplied text], which the Hebrews would express in the dual form [the Hebrew form is omitted in the supplied text]. The Greeks, however, prefer to call it Ἰορδάνης from another etymology, as though it derived from two Hebrew words, namely “the river of Dan.” Jerome approves this opinion both often elsewhere and especially in his Questions on Genesis, chapter 14, where he says: “Dan is one of the sources of the Jordan, for the other is called Jor, which means ῥεῖθρον, that is, a stream.”]

For, as we have often said, nothing is so dangerous as the desire for glory, boasting, and a spirit swollen with the consciousness of its virtues.

### XLII. STATION

“And they departed from the mountains of Abarim and encamped in the plains of Moab, beyond the Jordan near Jericho; and there they pitched their tents, from Beth-Jeshimoth as far as Abel-Shittim, in the plains of Moab” (Num. 33:48–49).

In the forty-second and final Station, let us briefly recount what happened there. While the people were dwelling in it, Balaam, the divine seer whom Balak son of Zippor had hired, blessed them at God’s command, and the curse was changed into praises. He heard the Lord’s voice resounding from a profane mouth:

“A star shall rise out of Jacob, and a man shall arise from Israel; and he shall strike the princes of Moab and devastate all the sons of Seth, and Edom shall be his inheritance” (Num. 24:17–18).

The people fornicate with the daughters of Midian; and Phinehas, son of Eleazar, zealous with the zeal of the Lord, pierces Zimri and the Midianite prostitute with a dagger. For this he received a reward in everlasting remembrance: the shoulder of the victim.

The people are counted again (Num. 26),

[Note: Rabanus and other printed books, together with some manuscripts, add: “and the Levites are counted.”]

so that, after the worst have been killed, a new people may be reckoned as God’s people. The five daughters of Zelophehad bring their case forward and, by the Lord’s judgment, receive an inheritance among their brothers (Num. 28:6); thus the female sex is not excluded from possession of God’s inheritance.

Joshua succeeds Moses on the mountain and learns from the Law what he ought spiritually to offer in the Church: first what is to be offered each day; then what on the Sabbath; what at the New Moons; what at Passover; what at Pentecost; what at the New Moon of the seventh month; what at the fast of that same month, on the tenth day; and what at the Feast of Tabernacles, when the tents are erected, on the fifteenth day of the aforesaid month.

The vows of wives and daughters are declared void without the authority of fathers and husbands. There is war against the Midianites, the death of the divine Balaam, the division of the spoils, and an offering from them in the Tabernacle of God.

The first tribes—Reuben and Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh—receive their possession beyond the Jordan in the wilderness. For they had very many animals and had not yet reached the point where they could dwell with the Temple.

The people are instructed to destroy the idols in the Holy Land, and no one from the former inhabitants is to be spared. The province once desired is described, and the inheritance of the two and a half tribes is separated. The leaders of the tribes who are to enter the Holy Land are counted (Num. 34).

The Levites receive forty-two cities with their suburbs, extending a thousand paces all around—exactly as many cities as there are Stations. Six further cities of refuge are added, three on this side of the Jordan and three beyond the Jordan, so that there are forty-eight altogether (Num. 35). It is explained which fugitives are to be received, which must be killed, and which are to be kept until the death of the high priest.

Deuteronomy follows, the “second Law,” a meditation on the Gospel.

[Note: Jerome uses this word in the same sense in his second book Against Jovinianus: “Our throat becomes a place of meditation, a latrine.” See what we have noted there. Some manuscripts and Rabanus read *meditatorium* instead; that reading is also not without a sound interpretation.]

There we briefly learn what Moses said to the people between Pharan, Tophel, Laban, and Hazeroth, and the golden places, after the removal of the most wretched Judas, on the eleven-day journey from Horeb by way of Mount Seir to Kadesh-Barnea. He sings his final Song (Deut. 32), in which the Synagogue is very plainly rejected and the Church joined to the Lord:

“He grew fat and thick and broad, and the beloved kicked back and forgot God his Savior.”

And again:

“A most wicked generation, unlearned children: they provoked me to jealousy with what was not God. They angered me with their carved images, and I will make them jealous with a nation; against a foolish people I will provoke them” (Jer. 5).

The children of Israel are blessed. And again the pitiable Judas is excluded in Simeon.

Moses ascends Mount Nebo, to the summit of Pisgah, which is opposite Jericho. The Lord shows him all the land of Gilead as far as Dan, and Naphtali, and Ephraim, and Manasseh, and the whole land of Judah as far as the Great Sea toward the south, and the plain of Jericho, the city of palms, as far as Zoar (Deut. 34).

Who can know such great mysteries?

[Note: Victorius reads this under an affirmative mark, that is: “He will understand who is established at the boundaries of the Law and of this life.”]

Who, established at the boundaries of the Law and of this life, understands that he must always be fighting, and that full victory is granted if he is in the plains; if, in Abel-Shittim—interpreted as “mourning of thorns”—he has mourned his former sins and the thorns that choked the seed of God’s word (Luke 8), of which the Prophet says, “I was afflicted while the thorn was fixed in me” (Ps. 31:4); and if, thus prepared, when the manna has failed, he crosses the Jordan under the leadership of Joshua (Josh. 5); and, circumcised by the knife of the Gospel, first eats of the heavenly bread; and if the commander of God’s army meets him, so that he may eat the true Passover not in Egypt but in the borders of the Holy Land.

O depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How inscrutable are his judgments, and how unsearchable his ways.

[Note: It is surprising that Jerome, through an old error, inserted this reading for “unsearchable” without consulting the reader, especially since elsewhere he read the correct form. But we may go no further than the evidence of the manuscripts permits.]

Who is wise and will understand these things? Who is discerning and will know them? For the ways of the Lord are straight, and the righteous will walk in them; but transgressors will fall in them.

## LETTER LXXIX

[Note: Elsewhere numbered 9. Written around A.D. 400.]

### TO SALVINA

Jerome consoles Salvina, a most noble woman, over the death of her husband Nebridius. After praising her dead husband, he teaches how she ought to raise the children he left behind and what kind of life she ought herself to lead, and he dissuades her from a second marriage.

### 1

I fear that my duty may be thought ambition, and that, by doing what he did who said, “Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matt. 11:29), we may be accused of seeking glory; that I am not addressing a widow in distress but insinuating myself into the royal court, and, under the pretext of a letter, seeking the friendship of powerful people.

No one who knows that this commandment exists will clearly think so: “You shall not show partiality to the poor in judgment” (Lev. 19:15), lest under the pretext of mercy we judge what is unjust. For each person must be judged not by the weight of human beings but by the weight of things.

[Note: All printed books and manuscripts of men indeed read this way; nevertheless, someone may prefer *nominum* (“of names”), since “name” and “thing” are rightly set against one another, and it is easy to see how the occurrence of the same letter *n* may have misled the copyist. Some manuscripts also read *unumquodque* (“each thing”) and *judicandum*. In the following Letter 83, to Pammachius and Oceanus, concerning the errors of Origen, he says: “Each thing must be judged not by the persons but by the weight of the matters.”]

Nor do riches harm the rich person if he uses them well; nor does poverty make the poor person more commendable if, amid rags and want, he does not avoid sins. Abraham the patriarch and daily examples furnish testimony to both propositions: one of them was a friend of God amid the greatest riches, while others, caught every day in crimes, pay the penalties imposed by the laws.

We therefore address a poor rich woman, so that she may not know what she possesses.

[Note: Some read differently: “a rich woman who does not know that she herself is poor,” etc.]

For we are not examining her purse but the purity of her soul. We speak to one whose face we do not know but whose virtues we know; whom reputation commends to us; whose youth makes her chastity all the more venerable. She mourned the death of her young husband in such a way as to give an example of marriage; she bore it in such a way as to believe that he had departed rather than been lost. The magnitude of her bereavement became an occasion of religious devotion. She seeks her Nebridius as absent in such a way that she knows him to be present in Christ.

Why, then, do we write to one whom we do not know? There are surely three reasons. First, because in fulfillment of our priestly duty we love all Christians as children, and their progress is our glory. Second, because the father of the deceased was joined to me by an intimate relationship. Finally—and this is the strongest reason—because I could refuse nothing to my son Avitus when he asked it. By frequent letters he overcame the importunate widow who troubled the unjust judge (Luke 18), and by setting before me examples of many to whom I had previously written on this same subject, he so covered me with the shame of refusal that I considered more what he desired than what it was fitting for me to do.

### 2

Someone else might perhaps praise Nebridius because, born from the sister of the Empress and brought up in his aunt’s embrace,

[Note: Here receive, once and for all and in brief, the whole prosopography. Nebridius the elder, to whom Jerome says he was joined by an intimate relationship, seems to be the Nebridius of whom Ammianus Marcellinus sometimes speaks and whom he says was Praetorian Prefect in the East in the year 365. His son, the younger Nebridius, was the husband of our Salvina; he was born from the sister of the Empress, namely Aelia Flacilla, wife of Theodosius the Great. Salvina was the daughter of Gildo, who was brother of Firmus, king of Mauretania. After Firmus’s death in 373, Gildo held the kingdom under Roman protection. For more on these matters, see Ammianus Marcellinus, book 29, chapter 5 and following.]

he was so dear to the unconquered Prince that the Prince sought for him a most noble wife and, through him as a kind of hostage, made Africa, torn by civil wars, loyal to himself.

From the very beginning, however, I must proclaim this about him: as though aware that death was near, amid the splendor of the palace and the heights of honors that surpassed his age, he lived as one who believed that he was going to depart to Christ.

Sacred history tells us that Cornelius, a centurion of the Italian cohort, was so acceptable to God that he sent an angel to him and showed that the whole mystery by which Peter was transferred from the narrowness of circumcision to the breadth of the uncircumcised belonged to Cornelius’s merits. He was the first baptized by the Apostle and dedicated the salvation of the Gentiles. It is written of him:

“There was a certain man in Caesarea named Cornelius, a centurion of the cohort called Italica, devout and fearing God with all his household, giving many alms to the people and always praying to God” (Acts 10:1–2).

Whatever is said about Cornelius, I claim for my Nebridius, with the name changed. He was so devout and a lover of chastity that, though a virgin, he received a wife. He feared God with all his household in such a way that, forgetting his rank, he maintained every association with monks and clergy. He gave such abundant alms to the people that swarms of poor and infirm persons crowded his doors. Certainly he was always praying to God, so that whatever was best for him might happen.

He was taken away so that wickedness might not change his mind, because his soul was pleasing to God (Wis. 4:11). Thus I too can truly apply to him the Apostle’s words:

“Truly I understand that God is not a respecter of persons, but in every nation whoever fears him and works righteousness is acceptable to him” (Acts 10:34–35).

His military cloak, belt, and the crowds of attendants did him no harm, because beneath one form of service he served another. Conversely, a shabby little cloak, a dark tunic, bodily filth, and feigned poverty benefit others nothing if by their deeds they destroy the dignity of their name.

We also read in the Gospel the Lord’s testimony concerning another centurion: “I have not found such faith in Israel” (Matt. 8:10).

And, to return to what came before, Joseph, who displayed examples of virtue both in poverty and in riches, who as both slave and master taught the freedom of the soul—was he not, after Pharaoh, adorned with royal insignia, so dear to God that he became the father of two tribes above all the patriarchs?

Daniel and the three young men presided over the wealth of Babylonia,

[Note: It should read *operibus* (“works”), as some manuscripts retain, with Victorius as witness; this is plainly established by Daniel 2:49: “Nebuchadnezzar appointed Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego over the works of the province of Babylon.” Nevertheless, all the printed editions and most manuscripts read *opibus* (“wealth”), perhaps because a copyist wrote it through an abbreviation of the letters.]

and were so placed among the leaders of the city that, though clothed according to Nebuchadnezzar’s rank, they served God in their minds. Mordecai and Esther, amid purple, silk, and jewels, overcame pride through humility; and they were of such merit that, though captives, they ruled over their conquerors.

### 3

The purpose of this discourse is to show that my young man’s connection with royal blood, his abundance of riches, and the insignia of power became material for virtue, as Ecclesiastes says: “As wisdom protects, so money protects” (Eccl. 7:12).

Nor should we immediately think this opposed to that testimony: “Truly I say to you, it is difficult for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 19:23–24). And again: “I say to you, it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven” (Mark 10:24–25).

Otherwise Zacchaeus the tax collector, whom Scripture records as exceedingly rich, would seem to have been saved contrary to this statement. But how what is impossible with human beings becomes possible with God, the Apostle’s advice teaches when he writes to Timothy:

“Command the rich of this age not to be high-minded, nor to place their hope in the uncertainty of their riches, but in the living God, who gives us all things abundantly for enjoyment. Let them do good, be rich in good works, give readily, share, and store up for themselves a good foundation for the future, so that they may grasp the true life” (1 Tim. 6:17–19).

We have learned how a camel can enter through the eye of a needle: how a crooked animal, laying aside the weight of its burdens, may take for itself the wings of a dove (Ps. 54) and rest in the branches of the tree that grew from the mustard seed (Matt. 13).

We read in Isaiah of camels from Midian, Ephah, and Sheba bringing gold and frankincense to the city of the Lord (Isa. 60). In the type of these camels, Ishmaelite merchants carry storax, frankincense, and resin, which grows in Gilead and covers wounds (Jer. 8), to the Egyptians. They are so fortunate that they buy and sell Joseph (Gen. 37), and their merchandise becomes the salvation of the world.

The fable of Aesop also teaches that a belly full of mice cannot emerge through a narrow opening.

### 4

Thus my Nebridius turned over daily the words:

“Those who desire to become rich fall into temptation and the devil’s snare, and into many desires” (1 Tim. 6:9).

Whatever the Emperor’s generosity and the island of honor had bestowed, he devoted to the needs of the poor. For he knew that the Lord had commanded:

“If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have, give to the poor, and come, follow me” (Matt. 19:21).

And because he could not fulfill this saying—having a wife, young children, and a large household—he made friends for himself from unrighteous mammon, so that they might receive him into eternal dwellings (Luke 16:9). He did not cast off his burden all at once, as the Apostles did when they left their father, their nets, and their boat (Luke 5); instead, by equality of distribution, he shared his abundance with the poverty of others, so that afterward their riches might sustain his need (2 Cor. 8:14).

The woman to whom this little book is written knows that I am recounting not what I have seen but what I have heard, and that, like the Greek writers, I am not repaying a favor with words. Let such suspicion be far from Christians:

“Having food and clothing, with these we shall be content” (1 Tim. 6:8).

Where there is a little cheap vegetable, household bread, and moderate food and drink, there are superfluous riches and no flattery, which especially looks toward profit. From this it follows that the testimony is faithful because it has no reason to lie.

### 5

And lest anyone think that I praise only Nebridius’s almsgiving—although it is a great thing to have practiced it, since it is said, “As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin” (Sir. 3:30)—I shall proceed to his other virtues, each of which we find in only a few people.

Who entered the furnace of the king of Babylon without being burned? (Dan. 3.) Which young man’s cloak did the Egyptian mistress not seize? (Gen. 39.) What wife of a eunuch bears no children after having spent her life in pleasure?

[Note: Some explain the somewhat difficult sentence in this way: “What wife of a eunuch, content with pleasure alone, does not associate with other men in order to produce children?” The name “eunuch” is understood here in its ordinary sense, not in the sense in which it signifies a particularly noble office in the king’s court—the sense actually preferred by the story of Potiphar, to which Jerome alludes.]

Who is not terrified by that disputation of the human mind:

“I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin which is in my members” (Rom. 7:23)?

It is astonishing to say: raised in the palace, a companion and fellow student of the Augusti [Arcadius and Honorius], whose tables the world serves and for whom lands and seas labor, amid the abundance of all things, in the very flower of youth he possessed such modesty that he surpassed even virginal chastity and gave no opportunity for the slightest tale of indecent rumor about himself.

Moreover, a relative, companion, and cousin of the imperial purple, educated in the same studies as both emperors—something that wins even the minds of outsiders—he was not inflated with pride and did not look down upon other people with an haughty face. Rather, he was lovable to everyone. He loved the princes as brothers, revered them as masters, and acknowledged that his own safety was placed in theirs.

He had so joined their attendants and the entire order of the palace, where royal ambition is continually surrounded by crowds, to himself through affection that those who were rightly inferior considered themselves his equals in service.

It is difficult to surpass glory through virtue, and to be loved by those whom one surpasses. What widow was not supported by his assistance? What orphan did not find a father in him? The bishops of the whole East brought to him the petitions of the wretched and the desires of those in distress. Whatever he requested from the Emperor became alms for the poor, a ransom for captives, and mercy for the afflicted. Thus the princes themselves willingly supplied what they knew would be granted not to one person but to many.

### 6

Why do we delay any longer?

“All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass” (Isa. 40:6).

The earth has returned to its own earth. He slept in the Lord and was gathered to his fathers, full of days and light, nourished in a good old age. For a man’s gray hairs are his wisdom (Wis. 4:9). In a brief lifetime he completed many ages.

We retain his sweetest children in his place. His wife, the heir of his chastity, is its reward.

[Note: More correctly, as it seems, with the word *pretium* (“price”) omitted, the Cistercian manuscript reads: “His wife is the heir of chastity.”]

The little Nebridius presents himself to those who seek his father:

“Thus he bore his eyes, thus his hands, thus his face” (Aeneid 3).

A spark of his father’s vigor shines in the son, and the likeness of his character bursts forth through the mirror of the flesh.

“He turns great spirits within a narrow breast” (Georgics 4).

His sister is joined to him, a basket of roses and lilies, a mingling of ivory and purple. She reproduces her father in her face, though inclined toward greater beauty. She depicts her mother through a mingled likeness, so that in one body you recognize both parents. She is so sweet and honeyed that she is an honor to all her relatives.

The Emperor does not disdain to hold her; the Empress rejoices to cherish her in her lap.

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “The Empress rejoices in her royal embrace.”]

Everyone eagerly snatches her to themselves. She hangs from their necks and clings to each person’s arms. Babbling and lisping, she becomes sweeter through the stumbling of her tongue.

### 7

You have, then, Salvina, those whom you may nourish, in whom you may believe that you possess an absent husband. “Behold, the inheritance of the Lord: sons are his reward, the fruit of the womb” (Ps. 126:3). In place of one man you have received two sons; the number of your affections has increased. Whatever you owed your husband, repay to your sons. Temper your longing for the absent one by love for those who are present. It is no small merit before God to raise children well. Hear the Apostle’s admonition:

> “Let a widow be enrolled who is not less than sixty years old, who has been the wife of one husband, bearing witness in good works: if she has raised children, if she has been hospitable, if she has washed the feet of the saints, if she has generously supplied the afflicted, if she has pursued every good work” (1 Tim. 5:9–10).

You have learned the catalogue of your virtues: what you owe your name, and by what merits you possess the rank of chastity. Nor should it trouble you that a widow of sixty is to be enrolled, so that you might think that the Apostle rejects young women. Believe that you too are chosen by him who had said to his disciple, “Let no one despise your youth” (ibid. 4:12)—not continence, but age. Otherwise, all women widowed before sixty would take husbands under this law. But because he was instructing Christ’s inexperienced Church and providing for every class, especially the poor, whose care had been entrusted to him together with Barnabas, he wishes those women to be supported from the Church’s resources who cannot work with their own hands, who are truly widows, whom both age and life commend.

The priest Eli offended God because of his children’s vices. Therefore, conversely, God is appeased by their virtues, “if they remain in faith and love and holiness with chastity” (1 Tim. 2:15).

> “O Timothy, keep yourself chaste” (1 Tim. 5:22).

[Note: The Vulgate has “with sobriety,” a reading our Jerome by no means approves in Book 1, chapter 14, Against Jovinianus. The words that follow, “O Timothy, keep yourself chaste,” we have interpreted in accordance with the sacred text, although no printed or handwritten book supported us. But the passage is complete in Paul’s First Letter to Timothy, chapter 5, verse 22, which the earlier editors do not seem to have noticed. Moreover, this sense was also incongruous and disjointed: “O Timothy. Keep yourself chaste,” etc., especially since the preceding name referred to the Apostle, while the remaining words, with the punctuation marked here, were referred to Jerome’s text. After writing this, we noticed that the old edition of 1496 also read it in the manner in which we correct it here.]

Far be it from me to suspect anything sinister concerning you; but to warn a vulnerable age out of an abundance of caution is an act of piety. Understand what I am about to say as spoken not to you, but to the years of girlhood.

> “The widow who lives in luxury is dead while she lives” (1 Tim. 5:6).

This is spoken by the chosen vessel; it comes from that treasury from which he confidently said:

> “Do you seek proof of Christ speaking in me?” (2 Cor. 13:3).

He declares this who freely acknowledged, in his own person, the frailty of the human body:

> “For I do not do the good that I wish, but the evil that I do not wish” (Rom. 7:19).

And therefore:

> “I discipline and bring my body into subjection, lest, after preaching to others, I myself should be found disqualified” (1 Cor. 9).

If he is afraid, who among us can be secure? If David, the Lord’s friend, and Solomon, his beloved, were overcome like men, so that their falls might offer us examples for caution and their repentance examples for salvation, who would not fear falling on a slippery road?

Keep far from your banquets the Phasian birds, fat turtledoves, the Ionian partridge, and all birds by which the most ample estates fly away. Nor should you therefore think that you may not eat meat if you reject the delicacies of wild boar, hares, deer, and four-footed animals. For these things are judged not by the number of their feet but by the pleasure of their taste.
