[Note: There were formerly such gourmands who wished to be considered religious because they abstained from the flesh of quadrupeds while eating birds and fowl. Saint Prosper of Aquitaine, Book 2, chapter 23, *On the Contemplative Life*: “But if, abstaining from quadrupeds, they enjoy fat pheasants or other costly birds or fish, they do not seem to me to cut off the pleasures of their body, but to change them; nor, out of abstinence, but as though from some unknown impurity—or rather, what is truer, from the fastidiousness of a nauseated stomach—they reject those common and cheap delicacies in order that they may satisfy their pleasures with other flesh, not only flesh, but also more delicate and costly flesh.” See Prudentius, in the hymn *After Food*; and the Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 39.]

We know that the Apostle said:

> “Every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving” (1 Tim. 3:4).

But he also says:

> “It is good not to drink wine and not to eat meat” (Rom. 14:21).

And elsewhere:

> “Do not become drunk with wine, in which there is debauchery” (Eph. 5:18).

“Every creature of God is good.” Let women who are anxious about how to please their husbands hear this. Let them eat meat—those who serve the flesh, whose heat foams over into intercourse, who, bound to their husbands, devote themselves to generation and children. Let the entrails of those whose wombs bear fetuses also be filled with meat.

But you, who buried all pleasures together in your husband’s tomb; who washed with tears, upon his bier, the face that had been painted with rouge and white lead; who exchanged the black tunic and dark shoes for the laying aside of white clothing and gilded slippers—you have no other need than to persevere in fasting.

[Note: The very carefully corrected Cistercian manuscript reads, “but to persevere in fasting. Pallor and filth,” etc. This seems the more correct reading if the punctuation marked here is observed.]

Let pallor and dirt be your jewels; let the softness of feathers not warm youthful limbs. Let the heat of the baths not inflame a young woman’s fresh blood. Hear what the pagan poet sings, speaking in the person of the continent widow Dido:

> He who first joined me to himself took away my loves;  
> Let him keep them with him and preserve them in the tomb.  
> (Aeneid, Book 4)

If the cheapest glass is worth so much, how much is the most precious pearl worth? If a Gentile widow condemns all pleasures by the common law of nature, what ought to be expected from a Christian widow, who owes her chastity not only to him who has died, but also to him with whom she is to reign?

### 8

I ask you not to let general admonitions, and language appropriate to a girl’s age, arouse in you the suspicion of injury, or make you think that I write in the spirit of one reproving rather than one afraid—for my wish is that you should not know what I fear. Among women, the reputation of chastity is a delicate matter; like a most beautiful flower, it quickly withers at a light breeze and is corrupted by the slightest breath, especially when age itself inclines toward vice and the authority of a husband is absent, whose shadow is a wife’s protection.

What is a widow to do amid a multitude of household members, amid companies of servants? I do not wish her to despise them as servants, but to blush before them as men. Certainly, if an ambitious household demands these services, let it place over them an elderly man of honorable character, whose dignity may be an honor to his mistress.

I know that many women, though they have closed their doors to the public, have not escaped the disgrace brought by household slaves whom either excessive grooming, the sheen of a corpulent body, an age suited to lust, or the swollen confidence born from awareness of a hidden love made suspect. Even when carefully concealed, this frequently breaks out into public view, and the woman despises her fellow servants as though they were slaves.

Let this have been said out of an abundance of caution, so that you may guard your heart with every diligence and beware of anything that can be invented about you.

### 9

Let there not walk beside you a curled Procurator, an actor whose manner has been broken into that of a woman, the poisoned sweetness of a demonic singer, or a young man smooth-shaven and elegant.

[Note: Earlier editions read *cultus*, “groomed,” not only in the printed books but also in most manuscripts. We have rejected that reading and restored the other, *volsus*, on the authority of the Veronese manuscript, especially since it is easy to suppose that unlearned men, offended by the unfamiliarity of a rarer ancient word, substituted something that came closest to its appearance. The ancients used *volsus* most elegantly of smooth-skinned men devoted to luxury, and of bodies from which the hair had been plucked and which had been cosmetically adorned in a feminine fashion. See Propertius, Book 4, Elegy 8; more examples are unnecessary.]

Let nothing from the theatrical arts, nothing soft, be associated with you in your service. Keep with you choirs of widows and virgins; keep the consolations of your own sex. Mistresses are judged also by the character of their maidservants.

Certainly, since a holy mother is with you and a perpetual virgin, your aunt, clings to your side, you ought not dangerously to seek the company of outsiders when you are secure in the fellowship of your own people.

Let sacred reading always be in your hands, and let your prayers be so frequent that by such a shield all the arrows of thought with which youth is customarily wounded may be driven back.

It is difficult—indeed, rather impossible—for anyone to be free from the beginnings of disturbances, which the Greeks more expressively call *propatheiai* (προπάθειαι).

[Note: Some manuscripts and the old edition read *propáthē* (προπάθη) or *propátē* (προπάτη), incorrectly.] We can render the word literally as “pre-passions,” because the incitements of all vices tickle the mind, and, as it were, our judgment lies midway between them, either to cast away the thoughts or to receive them.

Thus the Lord of nature spoke in the Gospel:

> “From the heart come evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false testimonies, blasphemies” (Matt. 15:19).

From this it is clear, in accordance with the testimony of another book, that the human heart is more inclined to evil from childhood (Gen. 8); and that between the works of flesh and spirit, which the Apostle enumerates (Gal. 5), the soul fluctuates in the middle, desiring now one thing, now another.

> No one is born without vices; the best man is he  
> Whom the least of them oppress.  
> (Horace, Book 1, Satire 3)

Or as though you were reproving

> Moles sprinkled over an excellent body.  
> (Ibid., Satire 6)

This is what the Prophet signifies in other words:

> “I was troubled and did not speak” (Ps. 76:5).

And in the same volume:

> “Be angry, and do not sin” (Ps. 4:5).

And that saying of Archytas of Tarentum to a negligent steward:

> “I would already have beaten you to death, had I not been angry.”

“For the anger of man does not accomplish the justice of God” (Jas. 1:20).

What has been said of one disturbance may be applied to the others.

[Note: Here one may compare what Saint Augustine distinguishes elsewhere between committing evil and completing evil. In his view, to commit evil is to be tempted; to complete evil is to succumb to temptation. Further below, in the letter to Demetrias, our Jerome says nearly the same thing: “To become angry is human; to put an end to anger is Christian.”]

Just as it is human to become angry, but Christian not to carry anger through to completion, so all flesh indeed lusts for the things of the flesh and draws the soul, by various enticements, toward deadly pleasures. But it is ours to restrain the heat of pleasure by a greater love of Christ and to bring the wanton beast under the bridle of fasting, so that it may seek and desire not lust but food, and may carry the Holy Spirit, its rider, with a measured and disciplined gait.

### 10

Why say these things? So that you may know yourself to be human and, unless you take care, subject to human passions. We have all been made from the same clay, fashioned from the same beginnings. In silk and in rags the same lust holds sway. It fears neither royal purple nor despises the squalor of beggars.

It is much better for your stomach to hurt than your mind; to command your body than to serve it; to stagger in your step than in your chastity. Nor should the remedies of repentance immediately flatter us, since they are the remedies of the wretched. We must beware of a wound that is healed through pain.

It is one thing to enter the harbor of salvation with the ship intact and the cargo safe; another to cling naked to a plank and be dashed repeatedly by the returning waves against the harshest rocks.

Let a widow not know the indulgence of digamy, nor recognize the Apostle’s saying:

> “It is better to marry than to burn” (1 Cor. 7:9).

Remove what is worse—burning—and marrying will not in itself be good. Far from us be the calumnies of heretics.

[Note: This likely refers to the Novatians, Montanists, and Cataphrygians, who condemned second marriages; unless he understands and mocks his own opponents, who so vehemently accused the holy Doctor of twisting and wrongly explaining Paul’s passage into an adverse meaning. Compare Letter 48 and the books Against Jovinianus throughout.]

We know that marriage is honorable and the marriage bed undefiled (Heb. 13:4). Even Adam, expelled from Paradise, had one wife. Lamech, the first accursed and bloodstained man, descended from Cain’s line, divided one rib between two women; and the planting of digamy was immediately overthrown by the punishment of the Flood.

[Note: That is, he was the first to have two wives.]

Hence the Apostle’s statement, which he was compelled to permit out of fear of fornication, when writing to Timothy:

> “I wish younger women to marry, bear children, manage households, and give the adversary no occasion for reproach” (1 Tim. 5:14).

And he immediately added why he permitted it:

> “For some have already turned aside after Satan.”

From this we understand that he extends a hand not to those standing, but to those lying fallen. See what second marriages are like when they are preferred to brothels, “because some have turned aside after Satan.”

Therefore, a young widow who cannot—or will not—remain continent should take a husband rather than the devil.

### 11

A beautiful and desirable thing indeed, which is undertaken in comparison with Satan! Jerusalem once fornicated and spread her legs before every passerby (Ezek. 16:2). In Egypt she was first deflowered, and there her breasts were broken. When she came to the wilderness and, impatient with the delays of Moses her leader, said, raging as though stung by the goad of lust,

> “These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt” (Exod. 32:4),

she received “ordinances that were not good” and “judgments by which she should not live but be punished.”

What wonder, then, if to wanton widows—of whom the Apostle had said elsewhere,

> “When they have grown wanton against Christ, they wish to marry, incurring condemnation because they have nullified their first faith” (1 Tim. 5:11),

he granted the ordinances of digamy that were not good and the worst judgments, permitting a second husband, and then a third, and, if she wished, even a twentieth—so that they might know that what had been given them was not so much husbands as the removal of adulterers?

These things, dearest daughter in Christ, I impress upon you and repeat frequently, so that, forgetting what lies behind, you may reach forward to what lies ahead. You have women of your own order to follow: Judith from Hebrew history, and Anna, the daughter of Phanuel, from the Gospel’s radiant light, who spent their days and nights in the Temple and preserved the treasure of chastity through prayers and fasts.

Thus one of them, as a type of the Church, cut off the devil’s head; the other was the first to receive the Savior of the world, being acquainted with the future mysteries.

At the conclusion of this discourse, I ask you to judge that the brevity of the little book has arisen not from poverty of eloquence or sterility of subject matter, but from the greatness of modesty: I fear imposing myself for too long upon unfamiliar ears and dread the hidden judgment of my readers.

## LETTER LXXX

[Note: In the ancient editions, Letter 63. It is lacking in the Benedictine edition.]

### Or Rufinus’s Preface to Origen’s Books *ΠΕΡΙ ΑΡΧΩΝ* (*On First Principles*)

[Col. 0733]

Rufinus, wishing to thrust Origen upon everyone as though cleansed of the errors attributed to him, praises Jerome as an ally of his own position and falsely represents him as a supporter of Origenist opinions. This produced the greatest disagreement between the two men.

#### 1

“I know that very many of the brethren, stirred by their desire for knowledge of the Scriptures, have asked several learned men, skilled in Greek letters, to make Origen Roman and present him to Latin ears. Among them, when our brother and colleague had been entreated by Bishop Damasus, after translating two Homilies on the Song of Songs from Greek into Latin, he introduced that work so elegantly and magnificently that he aroused in anyone a desire to read Origen and seek him out most eagerly, saying that the following words suited Origen’s soul:

> ‘The king brought me into his chamber’ (Song 1:3),

and asserting that, although he surpasses everyone in his other books, in the Song of Songs he had surpassed even himself.

[Note: In six manuscripts belonging to Father de la Rue, the reading is *dictum est quia introduxit*, “it was said because he brought in,” followed shortly by *cum editis*, “asserting him,” with the printed editions.]

[Note: From the same edition we have removed the little word *cum*, or *eum*, as other printed editions have it. We have restored it below in several places.]

[Note: Jerome by no means promises this there. But Rufinus confuses Jerome’s preface to Damasus on the Homilies on the Song of Songs with another preface addressed to Eusebius, concerning the fourteen Homilies on Ezekiel.]

He certainly promises in that very Preface that he will present to Roman ears both those books of Origen on the Song of Songs and many others. But he, as I see, delighting in his own style, pursues the greater glory, wishing to be the father of the word rather than its interpreter.

We therefore follow a work begun and approved by him; but we cannot adorn the sayings of so great a man with equal powers of eloquence. Hence I fear that, through my fault, that man whom he rightly approved—or approves—as the second teacher of the Church after the Apostles in knowledge and wisdom may appear far inferior because of the poverty of our language.”

#### 2

“Considering this often, I kept silent and did not yield to the brethren who frequently entreated me to undertake this work. But your insistence, most faithful brother Macarius, is so great that not even incompetence can resist it. Therefore, so that I might no longer endure you as so demanding a petitioner, I yielded, even against my intention, but on this condition and according to this arrangement: that, insofar as possible, I should follow in translation the rule of my predecessors, and especially that of the man whom we mentioned above, Jerome.

Although he translated into Latin more than seventy of Origen’s books, which he called Homiletical, he also translated several of the *Tomoi* written on the Apostle. Although some stumbling blocks are found in the Greek, he so polished and purified everything in translation that the Latin reader finds nothing in them that disagrees with our faith.

We too, therefore, follow him—not, indeed, in eloquence, but insofar as we can, in the rules of discipline—taking care not to bring forth those things found in Origen’s books that contradict or differ from himself. I have explained the cause of this diversity more fully for you in the *Apology* that Pamphilus wrote on behalf of Origen’s books, which we published with a very brief supplementary book. In it, as I believe, we showed by evident proofs that his books had been corrupted in very many places by heretics and malicious persons.

This applies especially to the books you now demand that I translate, namely *περὶ ἀρχῶν* (*On First Principles*, or *On Principalities* [alternatively, *Powers*]), which are in fact elsewhere both exceedingly obscure and extremely difficult. For there he discusses matters about which philosophers, after spending their entire lives, could discover nothing.

Here, however, our author did all he could to turn toward piety the faith in the Creator and the account of created things [alternatively, the nature of creatures], which they had drawn toward impiety. Therefore, whenever in his books we found something contrary to what he had elsewhere faithfully defined concerning the Trinity [alternatively, concerning piety], we either omitted it as adulterated and foreign, or presented it according to the rule that we frequently found affirmed by him.

If, while speaking as though to experts already acquainted with the subject, he expressed something obscurely because he wished to pass over it briefly, we added, to make the passage clearer, what we had read more plainly concerning the same matter in his other books, devoting ourselves to explanation. Yet we said nothing of our own; although in other places, we restored to him his own statements [alternatively, restored his statements to himself].

I have mentioned this in the Preface so that perhaps slanderers might not think they had found material for making accusations against us again.

[Note: *Iterum*, “again,” must certainly be read in place of *inde*, as Rufinus himself, a reliable witness concerning his own writings, testifies against Jerome in Book 1 of his *Invectives*: ‘The reason I said “again” is that they had already accused the letter of the holy Bishop John, written concerning faith to the holy Theophilus, when they were inventing that the human body was something other than flesh; for that reason I used “again.”’]

But let them look to themselves and see what perverse and contentious men do.”

#### 3

“In the meantime, this great labor has been undertaken—if God, in answer to your prayers, has granted it—not so that we might close the mouths of slanderers, which cannot be done, although perhaps God will do even this, but so that we might provide material for those who wish to advance in knowledge.

I solemnly charge and adjure before God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit everyone who will either copy or read these books: by the faith of the kingdom to come, by the mystery of the resurrection from the dead, and by that eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels—may he not possess as an eternal inheritance that place where there is weeping and gnashing of teeth (Matt. 8:12), and where their fire will not be extinguished and their worm will not die (Mark 9:43)—if he adds anything to this writing, removes anything, inserts anything, or alters anything.

Rather, let him compare it with the copies from which he transcribed it, correct it letter by letter, and punctuate it; and let him not retain a manuscript that has not been corrected or punctuated, lest the difficulty of the meanings, if the manuscript is not punctuated, generate still greater obscurities for readers.”

## LETTER LXXXI

[Note: Elsewhere, Letter 66. Written in the year 399.]

[Note: This letter was not returned to Rufinus, as is clear from the first book of Jerome’s *Apology* and from Rufinus’s own second book of *Invectives*.]

### To Rufinus

Since Rufinus’s oblique praises were bringing suspicion of the Origenist heresy upon him, and friends were also urging him, Jerome replies to the preceding letter and warns him not to praise him in a similar manner thereafter.

#### 1

Your own manner of speech showed that you had remained for a long time in Rome. Nor do I doubt that you were recalled to your homeland by longing for your spiritual parents, while grief for your mother prevented your departure, lest you should grieve more bitterly in her presence over what, in her absence, you could scarcely endure.

[Note: He indicates that Rufinus delayed returning to his homeland because, while staying at Rome, he learned of his mother’s death, lest he grieve more deeply in her presence over a misfortune that, while absent, he had scarcely been able to bear.]

Your complaint that everyone serves his own inclination and does not submit to our judgment is a witness to our conscience: after our friendship had been restored, no resentment remained by which we might injure anyone. Rather, we took every precaution lest even an accident should be turned into ill will.

But what can we do if everyone thinks that he acts justly in what he does, and seems to himself to be biting back rather than biting?

True friendship ought not to conceal what it feels. A little preface to the books *περὶ ἀρχῶν* (*On First Principles*) was sent to me. From its style I understood it to be yours. In it I am attacked obliquely—or rather openly. You must judge with what intention it was written; how it is to be understood is clear even to fools.

I too, who have very often declaimed on figurative controversies, could have revived something from my old art and praised you in your own manner. But far be it from me to imitate in you what I criticize. Rather, I moderated my judgment so that I might escape the charge brought against me and, insofar as I could, though injured, avoid injuring a friend.

But I ask you, if henceforth you wish to follow anyone, be content with your own judgment alone. Either the things we desire are good or they are evil. If they are good, they do not need another’s support; if they are evil, a multitude of sinners does not provide a defense for error.

I preferred to bring these matters before you as a friend rather than, provoked publicly, rage openly, so that you might observe that I cultivate restored friendship purely and do not, in accordance with the saying of Plautus, hold a stone in one hand while offering bread with the other.

#### 2

My brother Paulinianus has not yet returned from his homeland, and I think you saw him at Aquileia with the holy Pope Chromatius. We also sent the holy Presbyter Rufinus to Milan through Rome for a certain reason and asked him to visit you as a sign of our affection and goodwill.

[Note: We conjecture that this was Rufinus the Syrian, from whom Caelestius said he had heard, while Rufinus was staying at Rome with Pammachius, that sin is not transmitted.]

We conveyed the same message to our other friends, so that, “biting one another,” you might not “be consumed by one another.”

[Note: All the manuscripts read this way; the printed editions, however, read “that we might be consumed.”]

Now it is a matter for your moderation and that of your companions not to give any occasion to the impatient, lest you fail to find everyone like me, able to take pleasure in figurative praise.

## LETTER LXXXII

[Note: Elsewhere, Letter 62. Written toward the end of the year 399.]

[Note: See the later chronological notes to this and the following letter in the Preface.]

### To Theophilus: Against John of Jerusalem

When Theophilus, Bishop of Alexandria, sent letters to Jerome and to the monks who lived with him, in order to reconcile peace between them and John, Bishop of Jerusalem, Jerome replies that he desires nothing more than that the disagreement be settled and the peace of Christ restored between them. He then defends his Latin translations of Origen and the ordination of his brother Paulinianus against John’s complaints.

#### 1

Your letter, declaring you to be the possessor of the Lord’s inheritance, testified that you had become a participant in that blessedness in which the one departing to the Father said to the Apostles:

> “I give you my peace; I leave you my peace” (John 14:20).

You flatter like a father, teach like a master, and instruct like a pontiff. You came to us not with the severity of a rod but in a spirit of kindness, gentleness, and meekness, so that from your very first discourse you might echo the humility of Christ, who saved the human race not by flashing lightning and thunder but by wailing in a manger and remaining silent upon the cross.

For you had read, in the type that preceded him:

> “Remember, Lord, David and all his meekness” (Ps. 31:1),

and afterward, in the one who was presented as its fulfillment:

> “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11:19).

Thus, touching briefly on many passages from the sacred books in praise of peace, and flying like bees over the various fields of Scripture, you gathered with skillful eloquence whatever was sweet and suited to concord. We were therefore stirred to hasten toward peace. The sails were spread for our voyage, and the more frequent breeze of your exhortation filled them, so that we might drink the sweet streams of peace not reluctantly or disdainfully, but eagerly and with full mouths.

#### 2

But what are we to do when the will for peace is in our power, but not its fulfillment? Although the will itself receives from God the reward of its intention, nevertheless an unfinished work grieves even those who desire it. The Apostle knew this, and understood that perfect peace consists in the will of both parties:

> “So far as it depends on you, live at peace with all people” (Rom. 12:18).

And the Prophet says:

> “Peace, peace.”  
> And where is peace? (Jer. 4:10, according to the Septuagint)

For it is no great achievement to proclaim peace in words and destroy it in deeds. One thing is to strive; another is to display. To sound concord with words, but to demand servitude in reality.

We too desire peace, and not only desire it: we ask for it. But we desire the peace of Christ, true peace, peace without enmity, peace in which no war is concealed; peace that does not subdue adversaries but joins friends.

Why do we call domination peace and refuse to give each thing its proper name? Where there is hatred, let it be called enmity; where there is love, let it alone be called peace.

We neither divide the Church nor separate ourselves from the fellowship of the fathers; rather, from our very cradles, so to speak, we have been nourished on Catholic milk. For no one is more ecclesiastical than one who has never been a heretic. But without love we do not recognize peace, nor communion without peace.

We also read in the Gospel:

> “If you offer your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar and go first to be reconciled to your brother; then come and offer your gift” (Matt. 5:23–24).

If we cannot offer our gifts without peace, how much more cannot we receive the body of Christ?

With what conscience shall I approach the Eucharist of Christ and answer “Amen,” while I doubt the love of the one who offers it?

[Note: The Veronese manuscript, the only one available for comparison with this letter—for Martianaeus found no manuscript, and Victorius mentions none—does not recognize the two words *accedam* and *respondebo*, “I shall approach” and “I shall answer,” and seems more correct in this respect, for it expresses only one idea. Jerome says that it is difficult to answer “Amen” to one offering the Eucharist when one doubts his love. In ancient times, during the sacred Eucharistic rite, the minister offering it said, “The body of Christ,” and the recipient answered, “Amen.” The same word was then added by the recipient when the minister handed him the chalice, saying, “The blood of Christ; the cup of life.” Hence Augustine, Sermon 272 in the modern edition: “You hear, ‘The body of Christ,’ and you answer, ‘Amen.’” And in Book 12, chapter 10, Against Faustus: “The blood of Christ has a great voice on earth, when, having received it, all answer, ‘Amen.’” See also Clement, Constitutions, Book 8, chapter 10; Cyril, *Catechetical Lecture* 5; Ambrose, *On the Sacraments*, Book 4. Recall also the notable passage in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book 6, chapter 43.]

#### 3

I ask you to hear me patiently and not to consider truth flattery. Does anyone communicate with you unwillingly? Does anyone turn away his face with an outstretched hand and offer Judas’s kiss amid the sacred feasts?

At your arrival, as I think, the crowd of monks does not tremble but rejoices, since they come out eagerly to meet you and, leaving the hiding places of the desert, wish to surpass you in humility.

Who compels them to come out? Is it not their love for you? Who gathers those separated throughout the desert into one body? Is it not your affection?

A parent ought to love. A parent and bishop ought to be loved, not feared. There is an ancient saying:

> “Whom someone fears, he hates; whom he hates, he longs to see perish.”  
> (Cicero, Book 2, *On Duties*)

[Note: The saying is Ennius’s, quoted by Cicero in the cited passage: “Whom they fear, they hate; whom each person hates, he desires to perish.”]

Hence, in our own writings, although the beginnings of little children consist in fear, perfect love casts out fear (1 John 4:18).

You do not seek to have the monks subject to you; therefore you have them all the more subject. You offer a kiss, and they submit their necks. You display a soldier and obtain a commander, as though you were one among many so that you might be one of many.

Freedom quickly becomes indignant if it is oppressed. No one gains more from a free person than one who does not compel him to serve.

We know the Church’s canons. We are not ignorant of the orders of individuals. Through reading and daily examples, we have learned and experienced much even to this age. He who strikes with scorpions and thinks that he has fingers thicker than his father’s loins quickly destroys the kingdom of gentle David (3 Kings 12).

Certainly, the Roman people tolerated arrogance in no king. That leader of the Israelite army, who had afflicted Egypt with ten plagues and at whose command heaven, earth, and seas obeyed, is proclaimed the meekest of all the human beings whom the earth then produced. For forty years he held the leadership because he tempered the arrogance of power with gentleness and meekness.

The people stoned him, and he prayed for those who stoned him; indeed, he wished to be blotted out of God’s book lest the flock entrusted to him perish. For he desired to imitate the Shepherd whom he knew would carry even wandering sheep upon his shoulders.

> “The good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep” (John 10:11).

The disciple of the good shepherd longs to become an anathema for his brothers and relatives, who are Israelites according to the flesh (Rom. 9:3–4). And if he desires to perish so that the perishing may not perish, how much more must good parents take care not to provoke their children to anger and, by excessive harshness, compel even the gentlest to become harsh?

## 4.

The letter compels me to speak briefly; grief makes me speak at greater length. In those letters of his—peaceful, as he wishes, but, as I see it, most biting—he writes that he has never been injured by me, nor called a heretic. How, then, does he himself injure me by proclaiming that I am sick with the worst disease and rebellious against the Church? When provoked by others, does he rush to spare his adversaries while harming one who has not harmed him?

Before my brother Paulinianus was ordained, he never said that there had been any dispute between himself and the holy Pope Epiphanius concerning doctrines. And when reason compelled him—as he finally writes himself [Note: The Veronese book reads, “on the day when he was disputing among the people.” From this, “to dispute for a long time among the people” is the more serious reading.]—why did he then dispute among the people, when no one was asking about the matter? Your prudence knows that questions of this kind are dangerous, and that nothing is safer than silence—unless, perhaps, it is necessary to speak about matters of great importance.

Certainly, what an extraordinary talent and torrent [alternate reading: thunderbolt] of eloquence he must possess, if in a single treatise of the Church he claims to have embraced everything about which we know that the most learned men have written countless thousands of verses on each individual subject! But what has this to do with me? Let him who heard him know; let the man who wrote it know; and let him himself release me from the charge against him. I was neither present nor did I hear it. I am one of the people—or rather, not even one, since, while many were shouting, I was silent. Let us compare the persons of the accuser and the accused, and let us place our confidence more readily in the one whose merit, life, or learning has preceded the other.

## 5.

Do you see how, as they say, with closed eyes I touch upon the highest matters only superficially: not expressing as eloquently what I have conceived in my mind, but indicating what I am withholding? [Note: An older edition reads, “I understood you,” and shortly afterward, “because you were consulting the peace of the Church.”]

I understood and approved your policy [alternate reading: discussion], since, consulting the peace of the Church, you pass by with your ears stopped, as though against the songs of the Sirens. Otherwise, because you have been educated in the sacred Scriptures from childhood, you know in what sense each statement is made: how, in ambiguous sentences, your measured speech neither condemns what belongs to others nor denies what belongs to us.

But pure faith and an open confession do not seek verbal evasions or arguments. What is believed simply must be confessed simply. I could indeed have cried out freely, and even amid Babylonian swords and fires have said: Why is something other than what is asked being answered? Why is the confession neither simple nor open? He fears everything, moderates everything, leaves everything ambiguous, and walks as though upon sharp ears of grain. Yet, out of zeal and expectation for peace, although his stomach is burning, he answers not as the words are being demanded.

[Note: Together with the older edition, our manuscript reads: “Those who freely injure, whom he himself, though injured, does not dare to injure.”]

Others injure freely, whom he himself, though injured, does not dare to injure. For the moment I remain silent: now I shall pretend that my own policy is either ignorance or fear. What will he do to me when I accuse him, if—as he himself testifies—he takes away praise from those who deserve it?

## 6.

His entire letter is filled not so much with exposition as with insults against me [alternate reading: against us]. My name is repeatedly introduced, picked apart, and tossed about without any of those courtesies with which people usually flatter one another, as though I had been erased from the book of the living: as though his letters had branded me. [Note: I do not know whether our manuscript more correctly omits the second *quasi* and reads continuously: “as though I had been erased from the book of the living, his letters had branded me.”] Or as though I had ever sought such nonsense, when from adolescence I have been shut up in the cells of a monastery and have preferred to be something rather than to seem something.

He addresses some of us with honor in such a way as to tear us apart, as though we too could not say what no one keeps silent about. He reproaches one who was made a cleric from a slave, although he himself has some clerics of that kind; and he has read that Onesimus, reborn amid Paul’s bonds, began as a deacon from a slave (Philem. 1).

He proclaims that I am a sycophant, and, so that he will not be forced to prove it, says that he has heard so. If only I too were willing to say what many loudly proclaim, and to rest content with the insults of others! Then he would understand that we know what everyone knows, and that I too hear what no one is ignorant of.

He says that recompense has been returned to him as though it were a reward for slander. Who would not shudder at so sharp and crafty an intellect? Who could answer such a thunderbolt [alternate reading: torrent] of eloquence? What is more difficult: to endure slander or to commit it? To accuse someone whom you later love, or to grant forgiveness to one who has sinned? What is less tolerable: for a sycophant to become an aedile [Note: Here he compares a simple presbyter to an aedile and a bishop to a consul, reproaching John of Jerusalem for having become a bishop from a sycophant.] or a consul?

He knows himself what I keep silent about, what I say, and what I too have heard; he knows what, perhaps out of fear of Christ, I do not believe.

## 7. Hilary translated Origen.

He accuses me of translating Origen into Latin. I was not the only one to do this; the confessor Hilary did it as well. Yet both of us, cutting away whatever was harmful, translated what was useful.

Let him read it himself [Note: Augustine, Letter 179, addressed to this same John of Jerusalem, says that John heard his letters through an interpreter—that is, in Latin. Orosius too, in his Apology, suggests that he was unskilled in the Latin language.], if he knows it—for I think that, through continual conversation and daily association with Latins, he is not unfamiliar with Roman speech. Or, if he has not thoroughly absorbed it, let those who ordinarily do so interpret it for him; then he will know that I deserve praise precisely in the matter for which he attacks me.

For just as I have always attributed the interpretation and idioms [Note: The Veronese manuscript has ὑπομνήματα, “commentaries”; another manuscript, cited by Gravius, has ἑρμηνεύματα, “interpretations,” in place of “idioms.” The older edition shortly afterward reads: “I have always passed over the things attributed to him; thus I removed the impiety of his doctrines.”] of the Scriptures to Origen, so I have most steadfastly removed the truth of his doctrines. Am I associating Origen with the other commentators? [Note: Earlier editions read, though not without a solecism, “I know that I regard the Apostles differently.” The manuscript reads, “Do I associate myself with the other commentators? regard the Apostles differently,” etc.; the broken sense is easily restored by inserting *I know*: “Do I associate myself with the other commentators? I know that I regard the Apostles differently,” etc. We judged the word *me* better deleted. The term *tractator* (“commentator”) should also be noted: it is properly distinguished from the authoritative writers, Prophets and Apostles. Vincent of Lérins writes in the *Commonitorium*: “The teachers who are now called commentators, whom this same Apostle sometimes also calls prophets, because through them the mysteries of the Prophets are opened to the peoples.”]

I know that the Apostles are different, and that the other commentators are different. The Apostles always speak truth; the others, as human beings, err in certain matters. This is a new kind of defense: not to deny Origen’s faults, yet to accuse the rest along with him. Since you do not dare to defend him openly, you protect him by appealing to the similar error of many.

[Note: John and Rufinus accused Saint Epiphanius because he had said that he had read so many books of Origen. Jerome, Against Rufinus, Book 2 of the Apology: “Do not send me to the six thousand books of Origen, which you accuse the blessed Pope Epiphanius of having read.”]

No one could have read the six thousand volumes of Origen, which he did not write. I more readily believe that the witness to this statement, rather than its author, was lying.

## 8.

He says that my brother Paulinianus is the cause of the disagreement: a man who rests in a monastic cell and regards the clerical office not as an honor but as a burden. Although he has deceived us up to the present day by a pretended show of peace, he has stirred up the ears of the Western priests by saying that Paulinianus, a young man and almost a boy, was appointed presbyter in his own parish of Bethlehem.

If this is true, none of the bishops of Palestine is unaware of it. The monastery called “the Old Monastery” in the name of the holy Pope Epiphanius [Note: Erasmus reads “old” with the preceding word; the manuscript reads “old was brought,” both corrupt, as everyone agrees.], in which my brother was ordained presbyter, is situated in the territory of Eleutheropolis, not in the territory of Aelia.

His age is known to Your Blessedness as well; and since he has already reached approximately thirty years, I think his age cannot be faulted on this account, since, according to the mystery of the assumed humanity in Christ, it is complete. Let him recall the ancient law, and he will see that after twenty-five years a man was to be chosen from the tribe of Levi for the priesthood (Num. 8).

Or, if in this testimony alone he follows the Hebrew Truth, let him know that a man becomes a priest at thirty years of age. And lest he perhaps say, “The old things have passed away, and everything has become new” (2 Cor. 5:17), let him hear Timothy: “Let no one despise your youth” (1 Tim. 4:12).

Certainly, when he himself was ordained bishop, he was not much older than my brother now is. Or, if this is permitted in the case of bishops but not in that of presbyters—lest, by antiphrasis, they appear to contradict their own title [Note: Since “presbyter” in Greek means “elder”]—why did he himself appoint as presbyter either a man of his own age or one younger, and, what is more, a minister of another Church?

If he cannot be at peace with a brother except with a subordinate, and only when the bishop of his ordination resigns [Note: The Vulgate reads, “with the bishop resigning.” The manuscript and older edition, in the same sense, read: “and not being content with another’s quiet and leisure, provided that he retains intact what he threatens,” etc.], he shows that he does not so much desire peace as seek revenge under the pretext of peace. Nor is he content with the leisure of rest and peace unless he retains intact what he threatens.

Even if he himself had ordained him, and, as a lover of solitude, wished him to remain at rest, he should have required him to do nothing. If he were to divide the Church, he would owe him nothing except the honor owed to all priests.

## 9.

Thus far his apology—or rather, his indictment—and his tattered speech against us have been extended. I answered him briefly and in passing in my letter, so that from what I said he might understand what I had left unsaid; and so that he might know that we are rational animals and that his prudence is capable of understanding us—not so dull of heart that, like brute animals, we hear only the sound of words and not their meaning.

Now I ask you to grant indulgence to my grief; and if it was arrogant to answer, it was far more arrogant to accuse. Yet I answered in such a way that I indicated my silence more than I made a speech.

Why do they seek peace from afar and wish it to be imposed upon us by others? Let them be peaceful, and peace will immediately follow. Why do they abuse the name of Your Holiness against us as a means of terror, when your letter sounds of peace and gentleness while their words threaten harshness?

Finally, we prove how peaceful and directed toward concord were the letters you sent us through the presbyter Isidore by this fact: those who falsely boast of peace refused to deliver them [Note: Victorius incorrectly reads “which” instead of “who”; the manuscript has “to wish,” a false reading.].

Let them choose what they want: either we are good or we are evil. If we are good, let them allow us to remain at rest; if we are evil, why do they seek the companionship of the wicked?

He has learned by experience how powerful humility is. The man who now tears apart what he once joined together by his own counsel—things that had previously been separated—shows that he now rends apart what was then united according to another’s will.

## 10. Jerome’s exile obtained by John.

Recently he requested and obtained exile for us. Would that he had been able to carry it out, so that, just as the will is counted to him as the deed, we too might receive the crown of exile not only by our willingness but by its accomplishment.

The Church of Christ was founded by the shedding of blood and by suffering rather than by inflicting insults. It grew through persecutions and was crowned through martyrdoms.

Or, if only these people among whom we live love severity and do not know how to endure persecution but only how to inflict it, there are Jews here as well; there are heretics of various doctrines, especially the utterly impure Manichaeans. Why do they not dare to injure any one of them even with a word? Do they wish to expel only us? Are we alone, because we communicate with the Church, said to be dividing the Church?

I beg you, is this not a fair request: either let them expel those people together with us, or let them keep us together with them? Except that by doing so they honor those whom they at least separate from heretics through exile.

A monk—alas!—threatens monks with exile and obtains it [alternate reading: brings it about]; and this is a monk who boasts that he occupies the Apostolic See. This nation does not know how to yield to terror; when a sword threatens, it offers its necks more readily than its hands.

“For what monk exiled from his homeland is not exiled from the world?” What need is there for public authority, the expense of an official rescript, and journeys throughout the whole world? Let him merely touch us with his little finger, and we shall depart of our own accord. “The earth is the Lord’s, and its fullness” (Ps. 23:1). Christ is not confined to a place.

## 11.

Moreover, when he writes that we communicate through you and the Roman Church with the one from whom we appear to be separated in communion [Note: We follow the Veronese manuscript and, in part, the older edition. Other printed books falsely and incongruously read: “that we go with you to Rome and communicate with the Church,” etc. The older edition reads, not badly, “from whom we are commanded to be separated in communion.” Jerome now clearly says that he does not need to bring forward communion with Theophilus and the Roman Church, lest he appear separated from the Jerusalem Church, since in this way, in Palestine itself and through the presbyters of that same Jerusalem Church, he remains joined to it in communion and is not separated from it.], there is no need to go so far: here in Palestine we are joined to him in the same way.

And lest this distance be a hindrance, in the little village of Bethlehem, as far as lies within our power, we share communion with his presbyters. From this it is clear that a private grievance must not be considered the cause of the Church, nor the anger of one man—or rather, of others through him—be given the general name of the Church.

Therefore, what I said at the beginning of the letter I repeat now: we desire the peace of Christ and long for concord; and we ask you to admonish him [alternate reading: them] that peace is not to be extorted but desired. Let him be content with the pain of the insults we suffered in the past. Let him at least erase old wounds through new charity. Let him be what he was before, when he loved us according to his own judgment. Let words not flow from him out of another man’s anger. Let him do what he wishes, not what he is compelled to wish.

Either, as a pontiff, let him command all equally; or, as an imitator of the Apostle, let him serve the salvation of all impartially. If he presents himself in this way, we shall gladly offer our hands and extend our arms. Let him have us as friends and relatives, and let him perceive that in Christ we are subject to him just as we are to all the saints.

“Charity is patient, charity is kind, charity does not envy, it is not puffed up; it endures all things, it believes all things” (1 Cor. 13). Charity is the mother of all virtues; and, like a threefold cord [Note: The cord referred to is the one mentioned in Ecclesiastes 4.], it is strengthened by the Apostle’s saying: faith, hope, charity. We believe and hope, and thus through faith and hope we are joined by the bond of love.

For this reason we too left our homelands: so that we might live in quiet, without any quarrels, in the countryside and in solitude; so that we might revere Christ’s bishops—provided that they preach the true faith—not through fear of masters but with the honor due to fathers; so that we might honor bishops as bishops and not be compelled, under the name of one person, to serve others whom we do not wish to serve.

We are not so puffed up in heart that we do not know what is owed to Christ’s priests. For whoever receives them receives not so much them as the one whose bishops they are. But let them be content with their honor. Let them know that they are fathers, not masters—especially among those who, having rejected worldly ambitions, prefer nothing to quiet and leisure.

May Christ, Almighty God, grant through your prayers that we may be joined not by peace falsely named, but by true and faithful love, lest, biting one another, we be consumed by one another (Gal. 5).

# LETTER LXXXIII

[Note: Also numbered 64. Written in the year 399 or the following year.]

Pammachius and Oceanus urge Jerome to translate the book *Περὶ Ἀρχῶν* (*On First Principles*) accurately into Latin, to clear himself of the accusations of Rufinus and the suspicions of men, and to demonstrate that he is alien to the error of the Origenists.

## Pammachius and Oceanus to the presbyter Jerome, greetings.

A certain holy brother brought us some sheets containing a translation into Latin of Origen’s work entitled *Περὶ Ἀρχῶν* (*On First Principles*). Since these sheets contain many things that trouble the weakness of our intellect, and which we consider to have been stated in a manner insufficiently consonant with Catholic teaching [Note: Two manuscripts omit the words “which we consider to have been stated in a manner insufficiently Catholic,” etc.], we suspect that, in order to excuse the author, much has been removed from his books that could have displayed his evident impiety.

We therefore ask Your Eminence to undertake a work that will be especially useful not so much to us as to all who live in the City: reveal the aforesaid book of Origen in your language according to the authentic text, exactly as it was issued by the author himself; and expose whatever has been interpolated by his defender.

Also refute and convict whatever, in the sheets we have sent to Your Holiness, has been published either contrary to the Catholic rule or through incompetence.

Indeed, in the preface to his work he subtly made mention—without naming Your Holiness—that he himself had completed the work promised by you [Note: The word “mention” was absent in Victorius. We have restored several other readings from the manuscripts.], implying indirectly that you held the same opinion. Clear away, therefore, the suspicions of men and convict the accuser, lest, if you remain silent, you appear to consent.

# LETTER LXXXIV

[Note: Also numbered 65. Apparently written in the year 400.]

In reply to the preceding letter, Jerome explains with what disposition he read and praised Origen, whom he wishes everyone to read if this can be done without danger to piety. He refutes the accusations of his rivals and dispels the suspicions of men. Forced to do so, he exposes Origen’s errors, which those who were trying to defend their own heresy under Origen’s pretext were vainly attempting to defend.

## Jerome to his brothers Pammachius and Oceanus, greetings.

### 1.

The sheets you sent inflicted upon me an honorable insult, praising my intellect in such a way as to remove the truth of my faith. Since good men in Alexandria and Rome [Note: The editors have removed, on manuscript authority, the word “I had heard,” which all the printed books had inserted here, falsely and contrary to the holy Doctor’s meaning.], and in almost the whole world have been accustomed to boast about my name in this same way, and love me so much that heretics cannot exist without me, I shall pass over persons and respond only to facts and charges.

For it does not help a case to return insults to those who insult, or to bite one’s adversaries in retaliation, when we are commanded not to return evil for evil but to overcome evil with good (Rom. 12; 1 Thess. 5): to be filled with reproaches and to offer the other cheek to the one who strikes (Matt. 5).

### 2. Why he praised Origen.

They object to my having praised Origen at some time. Unless I am mistaken, there are two passages in which I praised him [Note: The Veronese manuscript and the Vatican manuscript formerly numbered Regina 490 omit this passage, “in which I praised him.”]: the short preface addressed to Damasus for the *Homilies on the Song of Songs*, and the prologue to the book of *Hebrew Names*.

What is said there about the doctrines of the Church? What about the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit? What about the resurrection of the flesh? What about the condition and substance of the soul? A simple interpretation and teaching is praised in simple words. Nothing there concerns faith; nothing there contains doctrines. Only a moral passage is treated, and the cloudiness of allegory is dispersed by a clear exposition.

I praised the interpreter, not the doctrinal theologian; the intellect, not the faith; the philosopher, not the apostle.

If they wish to know my judgment concerning Origen, let them read my commentaries on Ecclesiastes; let them examine the three volumes on the Epistle to the Ephesians; and they will understand that I have always opposed his doctrines. What folly is it to praise someone’s teaching in such a way that one also follows his blasphemy?

The blessed Cyprian, too, uses Tertullian as a teacher, as his writings prove; and although he delights in the intellect of that learned and ardent man [Note: The Veronese manuscript reads *eristici*, perhaps more correctly: a term derived from Greek ἐριστικός, “contentious and clamorous,” which is not ill suited to Tertullian’s disposition.], he does not follow Montanus, Maximilla, or Tertullian with him. Apollinarius writes very powerful books against Porphyry; Eusebius composed a beautiful ecclesiastical history; yet one of them introduced a half-complete *οἰκονομία*—a “dispensation” or economy—of Christ [Note: Most manuscripts have the Greek οἰκονομία. The ancients used this term for the mystery of the Incarnation. It is well known that Apollinaris, or Apollinarius—for both forms are used indiscriminately—taught that Christ assumed a half-humanity. Jerome calls this a half-complete *oeconomia*. See the note below.], while the other was an open defender of Arius’s impiety.

“Woe to those,” says Isaiah, “who call good evil and evil good, who make bitter sweet and sweet bitter” (Isa. 5:20). Nor should one detract from the good qualities of adversaries, if they possess anything honorable; nor should the faults of friends be praised. Each thing must be judged not by the standing of the persons but by the weight of the matter.

Lucilius too is criticized because he proceeds with an irregular foot; yet his wit and charm are praised.

[Note: From Horace, *Satires* 1.4, where he says of Lucilius that he was “of discerning nose, but rough in composing verses.”]

### 3.

When I was young, I was carried along by an extraordinary eagerness to learn, and, contrary to the presumption of certain people, I did not teach myself. I frequently heard Apollinarius of Laodicea at Antioch and honored him. Although he instructed me in the sacred Scriptures, I never adopted his contentious doctrine concerning the mind [Note: Some manuscripts and the older edition omit “concerning the mind.” The reading found in most others is entirely correct and should be understood as though he had said “concerning the intellect” or “about the intellect.” As Nemesius observes in chapter 1 of *On the Nature of Man*, Apollinarius, following Platonic principles, held that νοῦς (*nous*, mind) or πνεῦμα (*pneuma*, spirit) was a substance separable from the soul. Since he thought that one thing could not be composed of two perfect and complete things, he mutilated the human being assumed by the Lord in the rational part and transferred its functions to the Word, so that Christ might be called one according to his own understanding.].

My head was already becoming gray, and it was more fitting for me to be a teacher than a student. Nevertheless, I went on to Alexandria and heard Didymus. In many matters I give him thanks. What I did not know, I learned; what I knew, I did not lose when he taught me.

People thought that I had finished learning. I returned again to Jerusalem and Bethlehem. With what labor and at what price I had Baraninas as a nighttime teacher! For he feared the Jews and presented himself to me as another Nicodemus (John 3:1).

I frequently mention all these men in my little works. Certainly the doctrines of Apollinarius and Didymus contradict one another. Let both groups therefore tear me apart from opposite sides, since I confess both as teachers.

If it is useful to hate people and detest an entire nation, I oppose the circumcised with extraordinary hatred [Note: Gravius, supported by an older book, prefers the shorter reading; it is not convincing.]. To this day they persecute our Lord Jesus Christ in the synagogues of Satan.

Someone may object: Why did I have a Jew as a teacher? And a certain person dares to produce my letter to Didymus as though it were addressed to a teacher! What a great crime for a student to have called an educated and elderly man “teacher.” Yet I wish to examine the letter itself, which has been preserved for so long for the purpose of slander. It contains nothing except a salutation and an expression of honor.

These charges are foolish and trivial. Accuse me instead of where I defended heresy, where I praised Origen’s perverse doctrine. In the reading of Isaiah—chapter 6—in which two Seraphim are described as crying out, when he interpreted them as the Son and the Holy Spirit, did I not change that detestable interpretation into an interpretation of the two Testaments? The book is available; it was published twenty years ago.

My many little works, and especially my commentaries, tear apart the pagan sect whenever the occasion of the passage permits.

As for their objection that I gathered Origen’s books more than all other men: would that I possessed the volumes of all the commentators, so that I might compensate for the slowness of my intellect by diligence in reading! I did gather his books, I admit; and for that very reason I do not follow his errors, because I know everything he wrote.

Believe one who has experience: I speak as a Christian to Christians. His doctrines are poisoned, alien to the sacred Scriptures, and doing violence to the Scriptures. I read Origen—I say, I read him—and if there is guilt in reading, I confess it. Our purse was emptied by Alexandrian paper.

If you believe me, I was never an Origenist; if you do not believe me, I have now ceased to be one. But if even this does not lead you to believe, you force me to defend myself by writing against your beloved, so that, if you do not believe one who denies it, you may at least believe one who accuses him.

Yet you more willingly believe me when I am in error than when I have been corrected. Nor is this surprising: they think that I am their fellow initiate—συμμύστης (*symmystēs*)—and that I do not wish to confess the doctrines openly because of animal-like and clay-bound people.

Their decree, they say, is that pearls should not readily be cast before swine, nor what is holy given to dogs (Matt. 7), and, with David, “I have hidden your words in my heart, so that I may not sin against you” (Ps. 118:11). And in another passage, concerning the righteous: “He speaks truth,” he says, “with his neighbor” (Ps. 14:3; 23:4)—that is, with those who are members of the household of faith.

From this they wish it to be understood [Note: Jerome appears to speak here from the perspective of Origen’s defenders. Earlier he had said that they considered him Origen’s συμμύστης, or fellow initiate, who, because of rustic and clay-bound people—whom he later calls “Pelusians”—would not want to confess the doctrines openly and would make timely use of a lie.], that we who have not yet been initiated ought to hear a lie, lest, being little ones and infants, we be choked by the eating of more solid food.

That they bind themselves together in orgies of perjury and falsehood is clearly shown by the sixth book of the *Stromata*—in which he compares our doctrine with Plato’s opinions [Note: This is the reading of the older editions and most manuscripts; earlier editions had “according to Plato’s opinion.” Origen’s ten books of *Stromata* have long since perished.].

### 4.

What, then, shall I do? Shall I deny that I hold the same doctrine as he? They will not believe me. Shall I swear? They will laugh and say, “Such things arise among us at home.”

I shall do the one thing they most fear: I shall bring their sacred rites and mysteries into public view, so that all their prudence, by which they deceive us simple people, will be exposed; and those who do not believe a denying voice will at least believe an accusing pen.

They fear this above all: that their writings might at some time be held against their own author. They easily say under oath what they later dissolve through another perjury. They evade signing and seek evasions [Note: The Royal manuscript and the older edition read *suffragia*, perhaps more correctly: “votes” or “support.”].

One says, “I cannot condemn what no one has condemned.” Another says, “Nothing has been decreed by the Fathers concerning this,” so that, while the authority of the whole world is challenged, the necessity of signing may be postponed.

Someone else says more boldly: “How shall we condemn those whom the Council of Nicaea did not touch? For the Council which condemned Arius would certainly also have condemned Origen, if it had rejected Origen’s doctrines.”

Obviously, they ought to have cured all diseases at once with a single medicine [Note: Earlier editions incorrectly read *debere*; we have corrected it from the manuscripts.]. And therefore the majesty of the Holy Spirit must be denied because that Council was silent about his substance.

The question then concerned Arius, not Origen; the Son, not the Holy Spirit. They confessed what was being denied; they were silent about what no one was asking.

Yet, indirectly, they struck at Origen as the source of Arius. For by condemning those who deny that the Son is of the substance of the Father, they condemned him and Arius alike.

Otherwise, by this argument neither Valentinus, nor Marcion, nor the Cataphrygians, nor Manichaeus ought to be condemned, because the Council of Nicaea does not name them—although there is no doubt that they existed before the Council.

But whenever they begin to be pressed, and either must sign or leave the Church, you will see remarkable evasions. They adjust their words, alter their order, and construct every ambiguity so that they may retain both our confession and that of their adversaries, hearing one thing as heretics and another as Catholics.

It is as though Apollo Delphicus, Apollo Loxias, had not uttered oracles to Croesus and Pyrrhus at different times while deceiving both through the same trick [Note: Compare Cicero, *On Divination* 2, and Herodotus, Book 1, where he recounts what the Delphic Apollo answered Croesus. Some wish to derive the name Loxias, Λοξίας, from his oblique answers; others from the oblique course of the zodiac, attributing the same name to Apollo. It was used proverbially. Thus Marius Mercator, *Commonitorium*, p. 14: “I ask whether you too, like Loxias addressing Croesus and Pyrrhus, speak under the spirit of error simply and not in a divided manner,” etc.].

I shall offer a few examples.

### 5.

“We believe,” they say, “that there will be a future resurrection of bodies.” If this is said properly, it is a pure confession. But because there are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies, and because this air and the thin atmosphere are called bodies according to their nature, they say “body,” not “flesh,” so that the orthodox person, hearing “body,” may understand “flesh,” while the heretic recognizes “spirit.”

This is their first snare. If it is detected, they construct other traps [Manuscript reading: “build other traps”], pretend innocence, call us malicious, and say, as though they were simple believers: “We believe in the resurrection of the flesh.”

When they have said this, the uneducated crowd thinks it sufficient, especially because the same thing is believed in the Creed. If you ask further, the noise of the circle is stirred up, and their supporters shout: “You heard the resurrection of the flesh; what more are you asking?” Once their sympathies have been perversely reversed, we are called sycophants and they are called simple.

But if you harden your face and begin to press the question, holding the flesh between your fingers, asking whether they mean that the flesh that is seen, touched, walks, and speaks will rise again, at first they laugh, then they nod.

When we ask whether the resurrection will restore hair and teeth, chest and belly, hands and feet, and the other limbs in their entirety, then they truly cannot contain their laughter. Opening their mouths in a guffaw, they throw barbers, pastries, doctors, and shoemakers at us [Manuscript reading: “good men”].

They even ask whether we believe that the sexual organs of both sexes will rise again; whether our cheeks will be hairy and those of women smooth; and whether the bodily form will differ according to the distinction between male and female.

If we grant this, they immediately demand the vulva and sexual intercourse, and the other things that are in and beneath the belly.

They deny each individual limb, yet say that the body, which consists of limbs, will rise again. [Note: The Veronese manuscript corrects the printed reading *non resurgere* (“does not rise again”), which is false and contrary to Jerome’s meaning; the correctness of the present reading is clear from the context.]

6. It is not the time to brandish rhetorical language against a perverse doctrine. Let Cicero’s rich eloquence not suffice me, nor Demosthenes’ impassioned oratory be able to fill the ardor of my spirit, if I wish to expose the fraudulence of the heretics, who confess the resurrection in words but deny it in their minds. For their women commonly hold their breasts, pat their bellies, touch their loins, genitals, and [Note: [Col. 0748] Others: thighs. Most manuscripts, however, read “pure cheeks,” which they touch.] decaying armpits, and say: “What benefit is the resurrection to us, if a fragile body will rise again?” And “in the future we shall be like angels and possess their nature.” [Note: [Col. 0748] We again restore the word “angels,” which Ruffinus had also read, from the Verona manuscript and others. Formerly the text read: “and at the time of the future resurrection we shall have the nature of angels.”] They evidently disdain rising again with flesh and bones, although Christ rose with them.

But suppose 528 that I was mistaken in my youth, and, educated in the studies of philosophers—that is, of the Gentiles—was ignorant of Christian doctrines at the beginning of my faith, and thought the same of the Apostles as I had read in Pythagoras, Plato, and Empedocles: “Why do you follow the error of children in Christ and of those still nursing? Why do you learn impiety from one who did not yet know piety?” After shipwreck, the second plank is to confess one’s fault plainly. You imitated one who was erring; imitate also one who has corrected himself. We erred in youth; let us amend in old age. Let us join our sighs and unite our tears; let us mourn and turn to the Lord, who made us (Psalm 94). Let us not await the devil’s repentance. That presumption is vain and drags one into the depths of Gehenna: here one either seeks life or loses it. If I never followed Origen, you seek in vain to defame me [Ms. “desire”]; if I was his disciple, imitate one who repents. You believed me when I confessed; believe me also when I deny it.

7. “If,” he says, “you knew these things, as you claim, why did you praise him in your little works?”

“I would praise him today as well, unless you were praising his errors; his talent would not displease me, unless some of you took pleasure in his impiety. The Apostle also commands: ‘Reading everything, retain what is good’ (1 Thessalonians 5). Lactantius, in his books, and especially in his letters to Demetrianus, altogether denies that the Holy Spirit has substance, and, in the manner of Jewish error, says that he must either be referred to the Father or to the Son, and that the sanctification of both persons is signified under his name. Who can forbid me to read his books of the *Institutes*, in which he wrote most vigorously against the Gentiles, simply because the preceding opinion is detestable? Apollinarius wrote excellent volumes against Porphyry. I approve the man’s labor, although I despise his foolish doctrine in many matters.

“Confess that Origen too was mistaken in certain matters, and [Note: [Col. 0749] See Letter 12 to Antonius, Note c.] I shall do no more [the reading is uncertain: *me ultra non faciam* may be intended]. Say that he thought wrongly about the Son, worse about the Holy Spirit; that he impiously brought forward the souls’ descent from heaven; that he confessed the resurrection of the flesh only in words but destroyed it in his assertion; and that, after many ages and one restoration of all things, Gabriel himself would be what the devil is, Paul what 529 Caiaphas is, and virgins what prostitutes are. Once you have rejected these things and separated them from the faith of the Church, as though with a censor’s mark, I shall safely read the rest; and I shall no longer fear the poisons once I have drunk the antidote.

“It will not harm me if I say: ‘Although Origen surpassed everyone in his other books, in the *Song of Songs* he surpassed himself’; nor shall I fear the judgment by which, when I was still a young man, I once called him ‘a teacher of the churches.’ [Note: [Col. 0749] In the Preface to Origen’s Homilies on Ezekiel.] Unless, perhaps, I ought to have accused the man at whose request I was translating his little works, and said in the preface: ‘This man whose books I am translating is a heretic; beware, reader, lest you read them; flee the viper. Or, if you wish to read them, know that what I have translated was corrupted by wicked men and heretics—although you ought not to be afraid, for I have corrected everything that had been corrupted.’ This would be to say in other words: ‘I, who am translating him, am a Catholic; this man whom I am translating is a heretic.’

“Finally, you yourselves, quite simply, candidly, and without malice—clearly placing little value on rhetorical precepts and the tricks of orators—while confessing his books *On First Principles* (*περὶ Ἀρχῶν*) to be heretical and attempting to shift the charge onto others, implanted a doubt in your readers, so that they examined the author’s entire life and formed an opinion about the present question from his other books. I, the clever man who corrected him, kept silent about what I wished and concealed his crimes, and therefore did not bring odium upon the criminal.

“Physicians too say that great illnesses should not be treated, but left to nature, lest the remedy aggravate the weakness. Nearly one hundred and fifty years have passed since Origen died at Tyre. Which Latin has ever dared to translate his books *On the Resurrection*, *On First Principles* (*περὶ Ἀρχῶν*), the *Stromata* (*στρωματέας*), and the *Treatises* (*τόμους*)? [Note: [Col. 0749] The words ‘and the *Treatises*’ (*καὶ τόμους*) are absent from the Verona and Regius copies.] Who would wish to disgrace himself through an infamous work? We are neither more eloquent than Hilary nor more faithful than Victorinus, who translated his treatises not as interpreters but as authors of their own work. Recently Saint Ambrose compiled his *Hexaemeron* from Origen in such a way that he followed the opinions of Hippolytus and Basil more closely.

“I myself—whose imitators you claim to be, while, like moles toward others, you possess the eyes of goats against me—if I had been ill-disposed toward Origen, would have translated the very books I mentioned above, so that his errors might also become known to the Latins. But I never did so, and I refused to yield to the many who asked. For I am not accustomed to mock the errors of those whose talents I admire. Origen himself, if he were still alive, would be angry with you, his supporters, and would say with Jacob: ‘You have made me hateful in the world’ (Genesis 34).”

8. Does someone wish to praise Origen? Let him praise him as I do: a great man from childhood, and truly the son of a martyr [Col. 0750] [Leonides the Martyr]. He directed the ecclesiastical school at Alexandria, succeeding the highly learned presbyter Clement. He fled pleasures to such an extent that, out of zeal for God—but not according to knowledge [Note: [Col. 0750] Nicephorus, book 5, chapter 8, reports that he did not cut them off with a knife but dried them up with medication; this view has been accepted by others. Epiphanius, however, leaves the matter uncertain.]—he cut off his genitals with a knife. He trampled avarice underfoot. He knew the Scriptures by heart and labored at their exposition by day and by night. He delivered more than a thousand discourses in the Church. [Note: [Col. 0750] Victorius omits the word “which”; some manuscripts, conversely, read: “more than a thousand treatises which he delivered in the Church.”] In addition, he published countless commentaries, which he himself calls *tomes* (*τόμοι*); I now pass them over, lest I seem to compose a catalogue of his works. Who among us can read as much as he wrote? Who would not marvel at his burning zeal for the Scriptures?

“But if some Judas the Zealot should set his errors before us, let him hear freely:

> At times even great Homer nods.
>
> Yet in a long work it is permissible for sleep to creep in.  
> *(Horace, *Art of Poetry*)*

“Let us not imitate the vices of one whose virtues we cannot follow. Others, both Greeks and Latins, have erred in the faith; it is unnecessary to name them, lest we appear to defend him not on his own merits but because of the errors of others.

“‘This,’ you will say, ‘is not to excuse Origen but to accuse the others.’

“Quite so—if I were not saying that he erred, or if, at least in the perversity of the faith, I believed that the Apostle Paul or an angel from heaven ought to be heard (Galatians 1). But now, since I plainly confess his error, I shall read him as I read the others, because he erred as the others did.

“But you may say: ‘If the error is common to many, why do you persecute him alone?’

“Because you alone praise him as an apostle. Remove the excess of love (*ὑπερβολὴν*), and we shall remove the magnitude of hatred. You extract the vices of others from their books only to defend his error; you exalt Origen to heaven by saying that he never erred. Whoever you are, advocate of new doctrines, I beg you to spare Roman ears; spare the faith that was praised by the voice of the Apostle. Why, after four hundred 531 years, do you attempt to teach us what we did not previously know? Why bring forward what Peter and Paul did not choose to publish? Until this day the Christian world existed without this doctrine.

“I shall hold in old age the faith in which I was reborn as a child. [Note: [Col. 0750] Some earlier editions and manuscripts less correctly read ‘born’ instead of ‘reborn,’ since it is clear that he is speaking here of baptism. The name ‘Pelusiotes’ is derived from the Greek word *πηλός*, meaning mud, whence *luteos* means ‘muddy,’ not, as Baronius thinks, from the Latin word *pilus*, ‘hair’; we correct this elsewhere.] They call us Pelusiotes, and muddy, animal, and fleshly, because we do not accept the things that are of the Spirit—those, of course, being the Jerusalemites whose mother is in heaven.

“I do not despise the flesh in which Christ was born and rose again. I do not disdain the mud which, baked into the purest pottery, reigns in heaven. Yet I wonder why those who disparage the flesh live carnally, and cherish and delicately nourish their enemy, unless perhaps they wish to fulfill the Scripture that says: ‘Love your enemies; do good to those who persecute you’ (Luke [Col. 0751] 6; Matthew 5).

“I love chaste flesh, virgin flesh, fasting flesh. I love not the works of the flesh but its substance. I love flesh that knows it must be judged. I love flesh that, for Christ, is beaten, mangled, and burned in martyrdom.

10. Whether Origen’s books were corrupted. — As for their claim that his books were tampered with by certain heretics and malicious men, its absurdity can be demonstrated as follows. Who could be found more prudent, learned, or eloquent than Eusebius and Didymus, the defenders of Origen? One of them, in six books of his *Apology* (*τῆς ἀπολογίας*), confirms that Origen held the same opinions as he himself did; the other attempts to excuse his errors in such a way that he nevertheless admits they were Origen’s, not denying what was written but explaining the writer’s meaning.

“It is one thing if certain passages were added by heretics; it is another if someone defends them as though they were well said. [Note: [Col. 0751] Someone once wrote the name of Didymus in the margin, as can still be seen today in the very ancient Regius copy, to identify the person who explained how one might defend Origen’s doctrines as well expressed. From this it happened that, when the name was introduced into the text, the words ‘it is another if someone’ were wrongly deleted in all the other manuscripts and printed books known to us, except the Regius. In these the sense is broken and incomplete: ‘It is another if anything was added by heretics, Didymus defending it as though it were well said. He alone…’ You owe the true reading we have restored to the Regius codex.] Origen alone was found to be the man whose writings were falsified throughout the entire world, so that, as though in accordance with Mithridates’ letters, all truth might be erased from his volumes on a single day. [Note: [Col. 0751] Mithridates’ letter, or edict, was reportedly to the effect that all persons of Roman origin throughout Asia should be killed simultaneously and alike. The authors are Appian, Plutarch, Florus, and others, though Jerome seems to have taken it from Cicero’s *Pro Lege Manilia*.
