The reading is more elegant in a manuscript of his which reads *pariter falsarentur*—‘might alike be falsified’—instead of *pariter raderetur*.] If one book was tampered with, could all his works, published in different places and at different times, have been corrupted at once?

“Origen himself, in the letter he wrote to Fabianus, bishop of the city of Rome, repents of having written such things and attributes the causes of his rashness to Ambrose, because Ambrose had brought into public circulation what was privately published. [Note: [Col. 0751] This genuine letter to Fabianus has disappeared. Ruffinus also cites it at the end of *Invective* 1, using this very passage of Jerome. The lament that survives, and that falsely presents itself as Jerome’s translation, is a later production. See Eusebius 6.36 and the catalogue of Gelasius.] Why do they still make excuses (*ἐυρεσιλογοῦσιν*)—that is, why do they argue with trivial and elaborate words? [Note: [Col. 0751] Earlier editions read *αἰτιολογοῦσιν*, that is, ‘they make excuses,’ a reading which Martianaeus refutes at length. Moreover, *ἐυρεσιλογεῖν* means to speak or argue with trivial and recherché words.]

11. Whether Pamphilus was a praiser of Origen. — As for their producing Pamphilus as his praiser, I thank them in my own name for considering me worthy to be slandered together with a martyr. For if you say that Origen’s books were corrupted by his enemies so that he would be disgraced, why may I not say that a volume was composed by his friends and followers under Pamphilus’ name, in order to vindicate him from disgrace by the testimony of a martyr?

“Look: you make corrections in Origen’s books concerning what he did not write, and you are surprised if someone publishes a book that he did not publish. You can be refuted in a work that has been published; he, who published nothing else, is more easily exposed to slander. Produce any other work of Pamphilus: nowhere will you find one. This is the only one. How, then, do I know that it belongs to Pamphilus? Surely its style and saliva will be able to teach me.

“I shall never believe that a learned man devoted the first fruits of his talent to controversy and disgrace; and the very name of the apology reveals an accusation: one defends only what is under accusation.

“I shall now bring forward one point to which only a fool or an impudent person could object. From the beginning of Eusebius’ sixth book in defense of Origen to approximately a thousand lines, this book called Pamphilus’ contains the material. In the remainder, the author of the same work produces testimonies by which he attempts to prove that Origen was a Catholic.

“Eusebius and Pamphilus were so perfectly united that you would think them men of one soul, and that one received his name from the other. How, then, could they disagree, so that Eusebius, throughout his entire work, proves Origen to hold Arian doctrine, while Pamphilus makes him a defender of the Council of Nicaea, which occurred later? This shows that the little work belongs either to Didymus or to someone else who, cutting off the beginning of the sixth book, joined the remaining limbs together. 533

“But let us grant, for the sake of argument, that it belongs to Pamphilus—but not yet to the martyr; for he wrote it before he suffered martyrdom.

“‘And how,’ you will say, ‘was he worthy of martyrdom?’

“Clearly, so that by martyrdom he might erase his error, and cleanse one fault by the shedding of his blood. How many martyrs throughout the world were subject to various sins before they were put to death? Let us therefore defend sins, since those who later became martyrs were previously sinners.”

12. These things, dearest brothers, I dictated in haste in response to your letter, overcoming my intention to write against one whose talent I had previously praised, preferring to endanger my reputation rather than my faith. My friends have placed me in this position: if I am silent, I am judged guilty; if I answer, I am judged an enemy. Both conditions are harsh; but of the two I shall choose the lighter. Estrangement can be restored; blasphemy deserves no pardon.

“But what labor I endured in translating the books *On First Principles* (*περὶ Ἀρχῶν*), I leave to your judgment. To alter anything in Greek is not to translate but to destroy; yet to render everything word for word is not at all the work of one who wishes to preserve the beauty of expression.”

# LETTER LXXXV [Note: [Col. 0752] Elsewhere numbered 153. Written shortly after the preceding letter.]  
## TO PAULINUS

He briefly answers the second of the two questions proposed to him by Paulinus. He omits the first because it is explained in the books *On First Principles* (*περὶ Ἀρχῶν*) that he recently translated into Latin. He then explains with what attitude he read Origen.

1. Your voice summons me to write; your eloquence frightens me; and in epistolary style you nearly reproduce Tully. You complain that I send you little and unadorned letters. This does not arise from negligence but from fear of you, lest by speaking to you at greater length I send more things deserving criticism. And, to confess frankly to your holy mind, during a single season of sailing to the West so many letters are demanded from me at once that, if I wished to reply to each person on every matter, I could not keep pace. Hence it happens that, setting aside arrangement of words and the concern of writers, I dictate whatever comes to my lips, and regard you as a friend of my sayings alone, not as their judge. [Note: [Col. 0752] These shorter letters seem to have been lost.]

2. Your letter presented two little questions. The first was: Why was Pharaoh’s heart hardened by God (Exodus 4, 7, 10, 14), and why did the Apostle say, “It is not of him who wills or of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Romans 9:16), along with the other passages that seem to abolish free will? [Note: [Col. 0753] The passage at 1 Corinthians 7:13 gives rise to this second question: “For the unbelieving husband is sanctified through the believing wife, and conversely; otherwise our children would be unclean, but now they are holy.”] The second was: How are those who are born of believers—that is, of the baptized—holy, since they cannot be saved without the gift of grace later received and preserved?

3. The books *On First Principles* translated into Latin. — Origen answers the first question with great force in the books *On First Principles* (*περὶ Ἀρχῶν*) which I recently translated at the command of our Pammachius. Detained by this work, I could not fulfill what I had promised you, and I again postponed our Daniel. Indeed, although Pammachius is a man most devoted to me and most excellent, I would have deferred the will of one man to another time, unless nearly the entire brotherhood in the City had made the same request, asserting that many were in danger and yielding to perverse doctrines.

“Thus necessity compelled me to translate books in which there is more evil than good, and to maintain this measure: neither to add anything nor to subtract anything, but to preserve the Greek faithfully in Latin integrity. You can borrow their copies from the brother mentioned above. Greek may be sufficient for you, and you ought not to seek the turbid streams of my little mind when you drink from the very fountains.”

4. With what attitude Origen should be read. — Moreover, since I am speaking to a learned man, educated both in the divine Scriptures and in the literature of the world, I wish to remind Your Dignity not to suppose that, like the rustic buffoon Balatro, I reject everything Origen wrote. This is what his [Note: [Col. 0753] The factious men whom Jerome, suppressing their name, calls *ἀκαιροσπουδασταί*, that is, “untimely zealots.” Formerly, because he did not understand the Greek word, someone thought this referred to Ruffinus and his disciples and substituted “Calpurnius the fuller and his disciples,” a reading that entered the printed books. Martianaeus later restored the true reading from the traces of the Greek letters, and our manuscripts also confirm it.] *ἀκαιροσπουδασταί* accuse me of, as though they were charging me, like the philosopher Dionysius, with suddenly changing my opinion. [Note: [Col. 0753] Dionysius of Heraclea, who, because he repeatedly changed teachers and defected from the Stoics to the Cyrenaics, was also called *μεταστρέμενος*, “the deserter.”]

“But I reject only perverse doctrines. For I know that those who call good evil and those who judge evil good are subject to equal reproach—those who make bitter sweet and sweet bitter (Isaiah 5). Or what persistence is so great as to praise someone’s teaching in such a way that you follow his blasphemy?”

5. Concerning your second problem, Tertullian discussed it in his books *On Monogamy*, asserting that the children of believers are called holy because they are, as it were, candidates for the faith and are not polluted by the filth of idolatry. At the same time, consider that we also read of the sacred vessels in the tabernacle, [Col. 0754] and of the other things pertaining to the rite of ceremonies, although they certainly cannot be holy unless they perceive and venerate God. It is therefore an idiom of the Scriptures to call things “holy” at times when they are clean, purified, and expiated. Thus Bathsheba too is written to have been sanctified from her uncleanness, and the Temple itself is called a sanctuary.

6. I beg you not to accuse me, in the silent judgment of your mind, either of vanity or of falsehood. God is witness to my conscience that, from the very beginning of the campaign and [Note: [Col. 0754] He calls it an “interpretation,” not the Chaldaic version itself, which he had completed six years earlier and sent to Rome, as can be gathered from Letter 31 to Pammachius, but his commentaries on Daniel, which he had promised to Paulinus and completed several years later, dedicating them to Pammachius and Marcella.] outset of the translation, the necessity mentioned above drew me back; and you know that what is done with an occupied mind is not done well.

“I gladly accepted the little woven cap, short in its fabric but broad in affection, to warm my aged head, rejoicing both in the gift and in its giver.”

# LETTER LXXXVI [Note: [Col. 0754] See the later chronological notes concerning these six letters, LXXXV–XCI, in the Preface.] [Note: [Col. 0754] Elsewhere numbered 70. Written in the year 401.]  
## TO THEOPHILUS

He praises Theophilus’ prudence, through whose efforts the faction of the Origenists was defeated.

## TO THE MOST BLESSED POPE THEOPHILUS, FROM JEROME

1. Recently I received writings from Your Blessedness that ended your former silence and summoned me to my customary duty. Therefore, although your communication to us had ceased through the holy brothers Priscus and Eubulus, because we saw them stirred by zeal for the faith, hastily traversing the regions of Palestine and pursuing the scattered rulers—the Basilisks—even into their hiding places, we write briefly that the whole world may rejoice and glory in your victories [Note: [Col. 0754] Two manuscripts of good authority read: “and let the raised standard of the Alexandrian cross, and the shining trophies against heresy, be seen by the rejoicing crowd of peoples.” More probably, the Mediolanensis omits the word “cross,” agreeing with Epiphanius’ letter to Jerome, which follows shortly: “that he might place the standard against Origen upon the altar of the Church of Alexandria.”]: and that the rejoicing crowd of peoples may behold the standard of the cross raised at Alexandria and the shining trophies against heresy.

“Well done for your courage, well done for your zeal for the faith! You have shown that your silence until now was a matter of prudence, not consent. I speak freely to Your Reverence. We were grieved that you were too patient, and, ignorant of the helmsmanship of your teacher, we longed for the destruction of the lost. [Note: [Col. 0754] The Mediolanensis likewise reads: “But because you have raised your hand…”] But, as I see, you raised your hand for a long time and held back the blow, so that you might strike more forcefully.

“You ought not to grieve against the bishop of this city concerning the reception of a certain man. [Note: [Col. 0754] Some think that John of Jerusalem is not being indicated, but Chrysostom. Jerome, however, says “a certain man who was received”; Chrysostom received fifty at once. The words “of this city” readily indicate Jerusalem, which was not far from the place where Jerome was writing.] For you gave no command about him in your letters, and it was rash to pass judgment on someone concerning what he did not know. Nevertheless, I think that he neither dares nor wishes to injure you in any way.”

# LETTER LXXXVII [Note: [Col. 0755] Elsewhere numbered 69. Written in the year 400.]  
## FROM THEOPHILUS TO JEROME

He announces that the Origenists have been expelled from the monasteries of Nitria and urges Jerome to correct any others who have been deceived.

## THEOPHILUS, BISHOP, TO HIS DEAREST AND MOST BELOVED BROTHER, THE PRESBYTER JEROME

“Bishop Agatho, together with the beloved deacon Athanasius, has been sent on an ecclesiastical matter. When you learn of it, I have no doubt that you will approve our undertaking and rejoice in the Church’s victory. For certain wicked and mad men, wishing to sow and establish [or: pour out] the heresy of Origen in the monasteries of Nitria, have been cut down by the prophetic sickle. For we remembered the Apostle’s admonition: ‘Rebuke them severely’ (Titus 2:15).

“Hasten, therefore, that you too may receive a share in this reward, and correct all who have been deceived with appropriate words from the Scriptures. We hope, if it can be accomplished in our days, to preserve the Catholic faith and the rules of the Church among the peoples subject to us, and to silence all novel doctrines.” [Note: [Col. 0755] From the Vatican, formerly Regius, manuscript 242, we have supplied words fitting the Scriptures that were absent from the printed editions. Other manuscripts, including those of good authority, read “those whomsoever” instead of “all who.”]

# LETTER LXXXVIII [Note: [Col. 0755] Elsewhere numbered 71. Written shortly after the preceding letter.]  
## TO THEOPHILUS

He responds to the preceding letter and praises Theophilus, through whom not only Egypt and Syria but all Italy has been freed from heresy.

## TO THE MOST BLESSED POPE THEOPHILUS, FROM JEROME

Your Blessedness’ letter bestowed a double favor upon me: it was carried by the holy and venerable Bishop Agatho and the deacon Athanasius, and it demonstrated zeal for the faith against the most wicked heresy. Your Blessedness’ voice resounded throughout the entire world, [Note: [Col. 0755] The Ambrosian manuscript fittingly reads: “And in all the Churches of Christ the poisons of the hidden Devil were silenced.”] and, while all the Churches of Christ rejoiced, the devil’s poisons fell silent. The ancient serpent no longer hisses; rather, twisted and disemboweled, hiding in the darkness of caves, it cannot endure the clear sunlight.

“Indeed, concerning this matter, even before you wrote, I had sent letters to the West, revealing to men of my own tongue the tricks of the heretics. I think it happened by God’s providence that, at the same time, you too wrote to Pope Anastasius and, without knowing it, strengthened our judgment. [Note: [Col. 0755] We present at the end of this collection the previously unpublished letter of this Roman pontiff to Simplicianus, together with the Synodical letter of Theophilus mentioned here by Jerome. Most manuscripts incorrectly call him Athanasius.] Now, instructed by you, we shall devote ourselves more diligently to calling the simple back from error, both here and far away.

“Nor should we fear incurring the hatred of certain people; for we must not please human beings but God—although they defend the heresy more ardently than we attack it. At the same time, I beg you: if you have any synodical letters, send them to me, so that, strengthened by the authority of so great a bishop, I may open my mouth for Christ more freely and confidently.

“Presbyter Vincent came from the City two days before I sent this letter, and he reverently greets you. He repeatedly celebrates the fact that Rome and almost all Italy have been freed by your letters, after Christ. [Note: [Col. 0756] Most other printed editions omit the adverb “almost.” The Ambrosian manuscript shortly afterward reads: “Most blessed Pope,” and again, “write to the Western fellow-presbyters.”]

“Therefore, strive, most beloved and most blessed Pope, and write on every occasion to the Western bishops, so that they may not cease to cut down with the sharp sickle the evil shoots—as you yourself indicate.”

# LETTER LXXXIX [Note: [Col. 0756] Elsewhere numbered 72. Written in the year 400.]  
## FROM THEOPHILUS TO JEROME

He urges Jerome to pursue any Origenists who may be hiding in Palestine, after those who had been exposed were expelled.

## THEOPHILUS, BISHOP, TO HIS DEAR AND MOST BELOVED BROTHER, THE PRESBYTER JEROME

“I have learned that Your Holiness also knows the monk Theodore, and I have approved his zeal, because, when he was setting out from us to sail to Rome, he refused to depart before embracing and visiting you and the holy brothers who are with you in the monastery, as though they were his own inmost being. When you receive him, rejoice for the peace of the Church.

“For he saw all the monasteries of Nitria and can report the continence and gentleness of the monks: how, after the followers of Origen had been extinguished and driven away, peace was restored to the Church and the Lord’s discipline preserved. Would that those who are said secretly to undermine the truth would also lay aside their hypocrisy among you! Brothers who do not think well of them in those regions [Note: [Col. 0756] He alludes to the synodical letters he received from the Palestinian bishops, which we make public shortly below.] have prompted me to write these things.

“Therefore beware of and flee such men, according to what is written: ‘If anyone does not bring the Church’s faith to you, do not even greet him’ (2 John 2). Although it is superfluous for me to write this to you, [Note: [Col. 0756] The Ambrosian manuscript reads: “you who can recall others from error.”] since you are able to recall those who are in error from their error, nevertheless it does no harm for prudent and learned men to be admonished out of concern for the faith.

“I wish all the brothers who are with you to be greeted in my name.”

# LETTER XC [Note: [Col. 0756] Elsewhere numbered 67. Written after the middle of the year 400.]  
## FROM THEOPHILUS TO EPIPHANIUS

He urges Epiphanius to do everything possible so that, once a synod has been convened, the heresy of the Origenists may be condemned by public authority. At the same time, he sends him the Synodical letter he himself wrote.

[Note: [Col. 0756] We have taken the heading, which is absent from more recent printed editions, from an older source.]

## THEOPHILUS TO HIS DEAR BROTHER AND FELLOW BISHOP EPIPHANIUS

“The Lord who said to the Prophet, ‘Behold, today I have appointed you over nations and kingdoms, to uproot and to tear down, to destroy and to overthrow, and again to build and to plant’ (Jeremiah 1:10), grants the same grace to his Church in each age: that the body may be preserved intact and that the poisons of no heretical doctrine may prevail in any respect.

“We now see this accomplished. For the Church of Christ, ‘which has neither spot nor wrinkle nor anything of the kind’ (Ephesians 5), has cut down with the evangelical sword the serpents of Origen as they emerged from their caves, and 539 has freed the army of the monks of Nitria from their pestilential contagion. [Note: [Col. 0757] The printed editions and manuscripts alike read “the second”; no one doubts, however, that *fecundum*—‘fruitful’—should be read.]

“I have therefore included in the General Letter, which I sent to everyone collectively, a few of the events that occurred, as the pressure of time allowed. [Note: [Col. 0757] Most manuscripts read poorly, “in such a letter,” whereas he clearly refers to the General or Synodical Letter, which we shall shortly append, translated into Latin by Jerome and previously unpublished.]

“It is the duty of Your Dignity, which has often fought before us in such battles, to encourage those stationed in the battle line, to gather the bishops of the entire island, and to send synodical letters both to us and to the bishop of Constantinople, and to anyone else you deem appropriate, [Note: [Col. 0757] Again the Ambrosian manuscript reads: “to the holy bishop of the city of Constantinople,” who at that time was John Chrysostom, whom Theophilus persecuted fiercely.] so that by the agreement of all, both Origen by name and the abominable heresy may be condemned.

“For I have learned [or: You say] that the slanderers of the true faith, Ammonius, Eusebius, and Euthymius, raging with a novel madness on behalf of heresy, have sailed to Constantinople, both to deceive any new converts they can and to join themselves to the old companions of their impiety. [Note: [Col. 0757] The printed editions formerly read “Eutinius” corruptly. Jerome mocks these three Origenists by name in Letter to Ctesiphon, chapter 2.]

“Let it therefore be your concern to make the course of events known to all the bishops throughout Isauria and Pamphylia and the neighboring provinces, and, if you deem it worthy, to append our letter, so that all, gathered with one spirit, may, by the power of our Lord Jesus Christ, hand them over to Satan for the destruction of the impiety that possesses them.

“And so that what we have written may reach Constantinople more quickly, send an able man, one of your clergy, just as we have sent from the monasteries of Nitria fathers of the monks together with other holy and most continent men, who can explain in person to everyone what has happened.

“Above all, we ask you to pour out fervent prayers to the Lord, so that we may also obtain victory in this contest. For no small joy has spread through the hearts of the people both in Alexandria and throughout Egypt since a few men were expelled, so that the body of the Church might remain pure.

“I greet the brothers who are with you. The people who are with us greet you in the Lord.”

# LETTER XCI [Note: [Col. 0757] Elsewhere numbered 73. Written toward the end of the year 400.]  
## FROM EPIPHANIUS TO JEROME

He announces that, through Theophilus’ efforts, the faction of the Origenists has been condemned; and, sending him a copy of the Synodical Letter, he urges him to publish for the general public the books he had written against that heresy.

## EPIPHANIUS GREETS IN THE LORD HIS DEAREST SON AND BROTHER, THE PRESBYTER JEROME.

540 [Note: [Col. 0758] Theophilus’s Synodical letter, which Jerome rendered into Latin, we append from an Ambrosian manuscript.] “The General Letter, written to all Catholics, concerns you especially, since you possess zeal for the faith against all heresies and particularly oppose the disciples of Origen and Apollinarius [Note: [Col. 0758] More aptly, in the Milanese manuscript: “you oppose the disciples,” and immediately afterward, “the Almighty brought [them] into the open.”]. Their poisonous roots and deeply fixed impiety almighty God has brought into the open, so that, exposed in Alexandria, they might wither throughout the whole world. Know, dearest son, that Amalek has been destroyed down to its stock, and that the trophy of the cross has been erected on Mount Rephidim. For just as, when Moses’ hands were stretched upward, Israel prevailed (Exod. 17), so the Lord strengthened his servant Theophilus to set up a standard against Origen on the altar of the Alexandrian Church; and what is said was fulfilled in him: ‘Write this as a memorial, for I will utterly blot out the heresy of Origen from the face of the earth, together with Amalek.’

“And lest I seem to repeat the same things again and weave a more extended letter, I have sent you the very letter that was written to you [Note: [Col. 0758] Previously, *ipsam ad vos scriptam* was referred to the letter itself, rather obscurely and inelegantly; we correct this from the Milanese manuscript.], so that you may know what he wrote to us, and how great a benefit the Lord has granted to my final years, so that what I have always cried out might be confirmed by the testimony of so great a pontiff. I now think that you too have published some work and, in accordance with my earlier letter [Note: [Col. 0758] This letter is not extant today.], by which I urged you concerning this matter, have polished a book for people of your language to read. For I hear that the shipwrecks of certain men have reached the West as well: men who, not content with their own destruction, wish to have more people share their death; ‘as though the multitude’ of sinners diminished the crime, and as though the flame of Gehenna did not grow greater through the abundance of fuel. We salute most warmly, in the Lord, the holy brothers who serve the Lord with you in the monastery, both with you and through you.”

[Note: [Col. 0758] Previously unpublished. Written in September of the year 400.] EPISTLE XCII [Note: [Col. 0758] It now emerges for the first time from the very ancient Milanese manuscript of the Ambrosian Library, formerly belonging to Saint Columbanus of Bobbio, marked with the letter H and number 59. It contains almost all the records of the Origenist controversy and condemnation written by Theophilus, Epiphanius, Jerome, and others. This Synodical letter itself follows another letter of the same Theophilus to Epiphanius, which here occupies place XC in the order of Jerome’s letters. That letter was joined to this Synodical letter and was sent at the same time to the bishop of Salamis; hence from Theophilus’s own mouth we obtain the following clear testimony concerning it: “I have included in the GENERAL LETTER, which I sent collectively to everyone, a few matters from what took place, as the shortness of time allowed.” Another Synodical letter, however, belonging to another year—probably the preceding year, 399—was written in the name of the bishops of Egypt and Alexandria against Origen’s teaching; from it Justinian quotes certain Greek fragments in his letter to Menas. It must therefore not be confused with this one, although this error has prevailed among scholars until now.] OR, THE SYNODICAL LETTER OF THEOPHILUS TO THE PALESTINIAN AND CYPRIOT BISHOPS.

[Col. 0759] On the condemnation of the Origenist heresy [Note: [Col. 0759] Apart from the arguments collected in our Preface, Jerome himself, the guarantor of his own faith, proves this. First, in the preceding Letter 88, where he says to Theophilus: “I beg you, if you have any Synodical letters, send them to me, so that, strengthened by the authority of so great a pontiff, I may open my mouth for Christ more freely and confidently.” More clearly still, in *Apology against Rufinus* I.3, he says: “For nearly two years I have translated his [Theophilus’s] two letters, the Synodical and the Paschal, against Origen and his disciples, and have given them to people of our language to read for the edification of the Church.”] Rendered into Latin by Saint Jerome.

541 He announces that bishops have been summoned in a synod at Alexandria against certain monks of Nitria who were raging impiously on behalf of Origen’s heresy. Enumerating its principal errors one by one, he declares that they were unanimously condemned by the Fathers. Then he laments that factious men used force against him in order to rescue Isidore the presbyter, the leader of heretical impiety and guilty of other crimes, from the judgment of the bishops. Finally, again cursing Origen’s teaching, he authoritatively commands all the Churches, under the mark of anathema, not to receive it or its adherents.

[Note: [Col. 0759] This is how it is inscribed in the archetype, which we reproduce with the utmost fidelity. Theophilus had evidently arranged for Epiphanius to assemble a synod of bishops in Cyprus, so that Origen might be condemned. Socrates, Book VI, chapter 10, in Valesius’s translation, says: “He also arranged that a synod of bishops should be held in Cyprus by the same man [Epiphanius], at which Origen’s books might be condemned. Epiphanius, endowed with exceptional piety and the utmost simplicity of character, was easily persuaded by Theophilus’s letters; and after gathering a council of all the bishops of the island, he prohibited the reading of Origen’s books.” To show that this was held by Epiphanius after the synod at Constantia and that the Alexandrian synod was then celebrated by Theophilus, he adds: “When Theophilus had therefore drawn Epiphanius, renowned above all for his piety, over to his opinion, and saw that the matter was succeeding according to his wishes, he took greater confidence and summoned more bishops; and he struck the books of Origen, who had died two hundred years earlier, with the same sentence of condemnation as Epiphanius.” Sozomen follows Socrates, but Valesius rightly censures both for reversing the chronological order; this letter will make the matter clearer. Valesius himself is also mistaken in assigning the Synodical letter to the year 399.] This letter was sent in identical form to the bishops of PALESTINE and CYPRUS. We have reproduced the beginnings of both.

542 TO THE PALESTINIANS.

To the most beloved lords, brothers, and fellow bishops Eulogius [Note: [Col. 0759] Bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, and from the time of the Council of Nicaea metropolitan of all Palestine, and therefore superior even to John of Jerusalem down to this period; later writers report the matter differently. See the fragment of the Diospolitan Synod in Augustine, Book I, chapter 5, *Against Julian*. This is the same Eulogius who summoned Pelagius to judgment.], John [Note: [Col. 0759] The bishop of Jerusalem, very well known in this very Origenist controversy, especially from Jerome’s writings against him.], Zebianus [Note: [Col. 0759] Also written Zebinnus and Zebenus; in Saint Augustine’s cited book *Against Julian*, chapter 5, section 19, Zoboenus; and in the Vatican manuscripts of that work, Zoboemius. He was bishop of Eleutheropolis, to whom, Sozomen reports, the venerable relics of the holy prophets Habakkuk and Micah were divinely revealed.], Auxentius, Dionysius, Gennadius, Zeno, Theodosius, Dicterius [Note: [Col. 0759] From the mutilated manuscript letters we have represented the name as it appears; yet it is not unreasonable to suspect that Eleutherius should be substituted for this Dicterius, or Decterius, a name which a Latin copyist could easily have corrupted. Eleutherius was then bishop of Jericho; he is mentioned in the letter of the presbyter Lucian concerning the revelation of Saint Stephen the martyr.], Porphyrius [Note: [Col. 0760] Apparently the celebrated bishop of Gaza, who, to use Jerome’s words, forced the temple of Marna to mourn in confinement. Augustine, in the cited book *Against Julian*, nevertheless mentions two bishops named Porphyrius who took part together in the Palestinian synod; it is therefore not sufficiently clear which of the two this man was.], Saturninus, Alanus [Note: [Col. 0760] We have reproduced the reading of the archetype, but perhaps ALANUS, or another similar episcopal name, should be written.], Paul, Ammonius [Note: [Col. 0760] Perhaps the same man who is called Ammonianus by Saint Augustine in his book against Julian; the Vatican manuscripts of that work also call him Ammonius.], Helianus, another Paul, Eusebius, and all the Catholic bishops gathered at the Encaenia of Aelia [Note: [Col. 0760] The first day of the Encaenia, or Dedication, of the Jerusalem temple was 14 September, as Nicephorus reports in Book VIII of his *History*, chapter 10.]—Theophilus sends greeting in the Lord.

He speaks to the CYPRIOTS.

To the most beloved lords, brothers, and fellow bishops Epiphanius [Note: [Col. 0760] The bishop of Salamis in Cyprus, known to everyone for his holiness and writings, including those against Origen’s errors. The remaining names have occasionally merely been restored to their proper spelling; it was not equally easy to determine which Churches they held.], Marcianus, Agapetus, Boethius, Helpidius, Eutasius, Norbanus, Macedonius, Aristo, Zeno, Asiaticus, Heraclides, another Zeno, Cyriacus, Aphroditus—Theophilus sends greeting in the Lord.

543 1. I suppose that, even before our letter, swift rumor has brought you news that certain men in the monasteries of Nitria [Note: [Col. 0760] An antiquarian wrote in the margin of the book, “Origen’s books, or writings.” Since the copy had earlier read *in haeresim* with a preposition, which was a scribal error, he tried to explain it as though it meant “for establishing the heresy.” It is well known from Nicetas, *Treasury of the Orthodox Faith* I.4, Heresy 31, that the monks who inhabited Mount Nitria, and those who came from the small region of Scetis and were therefore called Scetians, were the first to be infected with the poison of Origenism. The chief among them were Dioscorus, Ammonius, Eusebius, and Euthymius, brothers by blood, whom Theophilus undoubtedly indicates here under the name of certain men.] were sowing the heresy of Origen and serving a turbid drink to the purest company of monks. For this reason, fearing the prayers of the saints, and especially of the fathers and presbyters who preside over the monasteries, we were compelled to go to the very places [Note: [Col. 0760] An old marginal note again adds “to cross over” or “to proceed.” But perhaps *compulimus* should be read instead of *compulsi sumus*; or certainly the phrase *pertimescentes* should be moved from its present position and placed after *monasteriis*, so that the sense may be clear.], lest, while we delayed going, those who flatter itching ears should corrupt the hearts of the simple.

[Note: [Col. 0760] Jerome himself says something similar near the end of *Against Helvidius*: “You have become famous in crime.” And in *Apology against Rufinus*, Book I, chapter 1: “Previously unknown, you have become famous through your recklessness.”] Their renown lies in crime, and their fury is so rabid toward every deed suggested by ignorance and pride that they rush headlong and do not understand their own measure, but, wise in their own eyes—which is the source of error—they deem themselves greatest though they are not [Note: [Col. 0760] I would prefer “thinking that they are.” Such transpositions, which unquestionably entered through scribal error, we reproduce faithfully wherever they occur; the reader can easily correct them for himself.].

Finally, they rushed into such madness [Col. 0761] [the manuscripts read “such madness”] that they turned their hands against themselves and cut off their own limbs with iron, imagining, by the judgment of foolish thought, that they would thereby prove themselves religious and humble if they went about with mutilated foreheads and severed ears. One doctor even amputated part of his tongue [Note: [Col. 0761] Read *mordicus*, “with his teeth he cut off.” Here he is specifically attacking Ammonius, who mutilated his own ear so that he would not become a bishop; and when he was nevertheless unwillingly proposed for the episcopate, he threatened that he would cut out his own tongue with his teeth.], so that he might show even to the ignorant how fearfully he kept the laws of God’s word [the manuscripts read “how fearfully they kept and displayed”] and how violently his heart seethed with fury.

544 Because I found them with certain foreigners who had spent a short time in Egypt, having migrated to your province [Note: [Col. 0761] They were making for Constantinople, and Palladius numbers the foreign companions whom they had with them at fifty. In the preceding letter to Epiphanius, which is joined to this same Synodical letter, he likewise says: “I have learned that the slanderers of the true faith, Ammonius, Eusebius, and Euthymius, raging with a new fury for the sake of heresy, have sailed to Constantinople, both to deceive any new people they can and to join themselves to the old companions of their impiety.” Palladius and Sozomen report that the Origenists went there after receiving the envoys sent by Theophilus; Baronius denies this under the year 400, chapter 61, relying on Chrysostom’s integrity, since he would never have received them into foreign communion if Theophilus’s envoys had previously brought him these letters of the Alexandrian synod. Nothing seems able to be established with certainty here, unless one prefers to give Baronius’s opinion greater weight than the ancient authorities. Certainly, when Theophilus wrote this, he did not know where the heretics were heading. Soon after, *habitaverant* should easily be written instead of *habitant*.], and that, having enticed poor men by favor and money—men who ought to seek their livelihood by hand and labor, so that what is written might be fulfilled in them, “The wicked will walk about” (Ps. 11. 19) [Note: [Col. 0761] The copy corruptly read *ambulabant*, which we have not hesitated to correct from the Greek *περιπατήσουσι*, the rendering of the ancient translators; Chrysostom notes it, and Jerome himself translated it into Latin. We also deleted a second *et*, which obscured the sense.]—they wished to imitate the Jews by being consumed first by fire rather than seeing Origen’s writings condemned; proclaiming in a manner: “We have made falsehood our hope, and we shall be sheltered by falsehood” (Isa. 28:19, according to the Septuagint), lest perhaps in those regions too they disturb the minds of people [Ms. *plebs*] and monks, and, though they ought to have been rebuked for their crime and to do penance, might strive against us [Note: [Col. 0761] The manuscript read *utantur*, by a common error, for *nitantur*.] and undermine the truth by the tunnels of lies. I judged it most just to write to your Holiness and briefly announce that, with the neighboring bishops gathered—bishops who nearly filled the number of a synod [Note: [Col. 0761] From the manuscript’s abbreviations it is not easily determined whether the reading should properly be *ne*, or *prope*. In any case, the text indicates that this synod was fuller than the preceding ones and that it properly constituted the number of bishops. For Sulpicius Severus says in *Dialogues* I.3: “At Alexandria shameful contests were carried on between bishops and monks, because priests had often gathered together and seemed, in frequent synods, to have decreed that no one should read or possess Origen’s books.” By contrast, Prosper in his *Imperial Chronicle*, under the seventh year of Honorius’s reign after Theodosius the Great, mentions this one as a proper synod: “A dispute arising from Origen’s teaching stirred up a synod at Alexandria, whose decision was that anyone who approved the works of the aforesaid man should be outside the Church.” Shortly afterward we preferred *perrexerim* in the text, rather than what appears in the manuscript as *perrexerint*.]—I proceeded to Nitria [Col. 0762]. In the presence of many fathers who had flocked together from almost all Egypt, Origen’s books were read, in which he had labored with impious effort, and they were condemned with the agreement of all.

2. The errors of Origen. For when the volume entitled *περὶ Ἀρχῶν*—which we may call *On First Principles*—was read, in which it is written that [Note: [Col. 0762] This principal blasphemy of the Origenist heresy is most corruptly read in the Ambrosian archetype as follows: “that the Son, compared with us, is truth; compared with the Father, suffering, falsehood.” We have corrected it from Jerome’s letter to Avitus, chapter 1, where he attacks the statement made by Origen: “The Son, in relation to the Father, is not truth; in relation to us, he is imaginary truth.” Most plainly, Augustine says in *On Heresies to Quodvultdeus*, Heresy 43: “Origen further says that, compared with holy men, the Son of God is truth, but, compared with the Father, falsehood.” The Palestinian bishops’ subsequent letter gives the same statement—which, as we indicated above, must especially be noted—and Guido Perpinianus copies it in his *Summary of Heresies* against the Origenists: “That, compared with us, the Son is truth, but, compared with the Father, falsehood; and that what Peter and Paul are in comparison with the Savior, the Only-Begotten Son and God the Word are in comparison with the Father.” Origen apparently said this in Book I, chapter 2, of *On First Principles*, which Rufinus concealed through an artful interpretation as follows: “Our Savior is therefore the image of the invisible God the Father; in relation to the Father himself, he is truth, but in relation to us, to whom he reveals the Father, he is the image through which we know the Father.” It is useful for us to examine the doctrines of Origen noted here from Theophilus, Jerome, and other writers in this controversy, so that they may be elucidated more clearly and the authenticity of this document may be established with complete certainty by comparing the passages. Meanwhile, it should not be omitted that the archetype’s blank page contains the heading: “In these statements or teachings the heresy of Origen is condemned.”] “The Son, compared with us, is truth, but compared with the Father, falsehood.” And again: “As much as Paul and Peter differ from the Savior, so much less is the Savior than the Father.” And again: “Christ’s kingdom will at some time come to an end, and the Devil, freed from all the filth of sins, will be honored equally and will be subjected together with Christ.” [Note: [Col. 0762] The manuscript had the abbreviated reading *abls*, from which *Diabolus* must unquestionably be printed. Jerome, Theophilus, and Epiphanius frequently charge Origen with this error concerning the Devil’s repentance; it is unnecessary to explain it by adducing testimonies. The same Fathers, Augustine against the Priscillianists, and Justinian’s letter to the Fifth Synod, reported by Cedrenus, among others, also accuse him of holding that Christ’s kingdom is to end after the restoration (*ἀποκατάστασις*) of all things. For, as the most learned Huet observes, in Origen’s books now extant no passage occurs from which credence could be given to so dreadful an accusation.] And in another book, entitled *On Prayer* [Note: [Col. 0762] The archetype had the corrupt one-word reading *decoratione*, followed by *scribitur*. The book *On Prayer* by Adamantius, addressed to Ambrose and Tatiana, is well known. The accusation that the Son should not be prayed to, nor the Father with the Son, is pressed elsewhere by Theophilus in Paschal Letter 1, and from him by Jerome and Augustine in *On Heresies to Quodvultdeus*, Heresy 43.]: “We must not pray to the Son, but only to the Father, nor to the Father with the Son.” We stopped our ears [Note: [Col. 0762] It was an ancient custom among Christians, whenever they heard something impious and alien to the Catholic faith, immediately to cover their ears. A clear example occurs in Book II of Clement’s *Recognitions*. Especially relevant here is Jerome, *Against Rufinus*: “Having recently read Pope Theophilus’s letters, in which he sets forth Origen’s errors, he is said to have stopped his ears and condemned the author of such great evil in a loud voice before everyone.” There is no doubt that these words refer to this very passage of the Synodical letter.], and with one voice condemned both Origen and his disciples, lest a little leaven corrupt the whole lump (1 Cor. 5:6; Gal. 5:9).

What shall I say of the resurrection of the dead, concerning which he blasphemes openly and says that [Note: [Col. 0763] Jerome likewise reports in his letter to Avitus, chapter 1, that Origen declared: “Bodily substances will utterly dissolve, or at the end of all things the bodies will become what the ether, the sky, and whatever other body can be understood as more refined and purer now are.” He adds: “Since this is so, what he thinks about the resurrection is obvious.” Theophilus says similarly in Paschal Letter 1: “Among other things, he so corrupts and violates the resurrection from the dead, which is the hope of our salvation, that he dares to say that our bodies, once again subject to corruption and death, will be raised”; and later: “He says that the bodies which rise, after many ages, will dissolve into nothing, and that they will become something only when souls have fallen from their heavenly dwellings to lower places and need us—read, ‘new ones’—to be made again, with the former bodies entirely destroyed.” Then below: “If, as Origen falsely supposes, not only a corruptible but also a mortal body is to be raised, then corruption and incorruption are one and the same.”] after many cycles of the ages our bodies will gradually be reduced to nothing and dissolved into a thin vapor. And, as though this were not enough, he added: “The body, when it rises, will be not only corruptible but mortal.” Thus the Lord and Savior has destroyed the Devil, who held the power of death, in vain, if even after the resurrection corruption and mortality rule over human beings once their bodies have been dissolved into nothing.

[Note: [Col. 0763] In the Preface to *On First Principles* he had established these doctrines concerning the angels, although they are softened in places by Rufinus’s translation. Leontius of Byzantium plainly reveals Origen’s teaching in his *Scholia on Acts* 10, where he says that, at the Devil’s fall, “all the other powers fell away with him; those who had sinned most became demons, those who had sinned less became angels, and those who had sinned still less became archangels; and so, in succession, each received his position according to his particular sin.”] He also concocted certain rash doctrines about the angels, saying that all the ministries in heaven that serve God were not created in heaven, but that, through various falls and collapses, they received different names of offices; and that earlier causes preceded them, through which they had increased or diminished. Amid all this, as though unable to endure his grief, while the people cried, “The Jerusalem above is free,” he contends that there is nothing pure in it, nothing free from faults, and nothing secure through perpetual virtue.

Nor did this profane discussion of the angels stop there; rather, advancing in wickedness [Note: [Col. 0763] In Book III *Against Celsus*, where he says that “demons continually roll about among sacrifices and blood and the fumes and stench arising from blood”; and in Book VII, that they are “nourished by the smoke of incense and the odor of blood and holocausts,” and again in Book VIII, as well as more extensively in the *Protrepticus to Martyrdom*. We do not know that he taught the same about good angels, unless he said so in the book *On First Principles*, where Rufinus artfully concealed it. See what we noted on Letter 21 to Damasus, section 2.], he says: “Just as demons were fed by the fragrance of sacrifices while sitting beside the altars of the Gentiles, so angels, delighted by the blood of victims that Israel sacrifices as a type of spiritual realities, lingered near the altars and were nourished by such foods.” Who would not think that he could find nothing further into which his deranged mind might fall?

He also attributes foreknowledge of the future, which belongs to the Lord alone [Col. 0764] [Note: [Col. 0764] See Augustine, *City of God* V.1, where he refutes this doctrine of Origen; and Eusebius, who presents a fragment of that same Adamantius’s *Commentary on Genesis* in *Preparation for the Gospel* VI. There he asserts that the stars contain signs of future events. This accusation against Origen had long been current: that he had said astronomy brings about the events that are to occur, as is clear from the anonymous author of his *Apology* preserved by Photius, codex 117.], to the movements of the stars, so that demons may learn future things from their courses and the variety of their configurations, and either perform certain actions themselves or assign them to be performed by others. From this it is clear that he approves idolatry, astrology, and the various tricks of the fraudulent divination of the Gentiles.

3. Certain men who held and taught these and similar doctrines under the name of monks were living in the monasteries. When they could not bear to see the author of so great an evil condemned together with his error, they induced certain poor men and slaves, enticed by the hope of food, to join their company [Note: [Col. 0764] Theophilus was often subjected to violence, but it is not easy to determine from his history exactly what he is lamenting here. The best-known incident is the one Cassian relates in *Conferences* 10.2: namely, that Egyptian monks, offended by Theophilus’s opinion in a Paschal letter, in which he proved by firm arguments that God is incorporeal, came to Alexandria with weapons in hand to kill him. He restrained them with the ambiguous statement: “I saw you as though I were seeing the face of God.” More probably, however, he is now complaining of what George of Alexandria in the *Life of Chrysostom* and Symeon Metaphrastes in his life report: monks driven from Egypt by the many and great persecutions of Theophilus went to Alexandria and so moved the populace by their miserable appearance that the people demanded the hidden bishop’s death, and could scarcely be calmed at last by the governor’s exhortations.], and, forming a wedge, attempted to use force against the man seated in Alexandria 548, wishing to bring the case of Isidore [Note: [Col. 0764] He was an Alexandrian presbyter and monk, formerly beloved by Theophilus, but later treated with extraordinary hatred for certain reasons that we shall examine below. As commonly happens in factional disputes, some, including Palladius in the *Lausiac History*, praise him lavishly, while others attack and reproach him. Jerome, *Against John of Jerusalem*, to Pammachius: “This Isidore, whom your praises raise to heaven, is accused in Alexandria of the very thing for which you praise him in Jerusalem; from this it appears that he came not as an envoy but as an accomplice.” The anonymous author of Chrysostom’s life and Symeon Metaphrastes are mistaken in confusing him with Isidore of Pelusium, unless perhaps he too came from Pelusium, although he is commonly called an Alexandrian. Isidore of Pelusium severely reproaches Theophilus in Letter 132 for persecuting John Chrysostom unjustly: “When,” he says, “he found in his own perversity an occasion for hostility and hatred against the man who shared my name.”] forward. Out of shame and concern for ecclesiastical discipline, we had reserved him for presentation before the judgment of the bishops, rather than exposing things shameful to say to pagan ears and stirring up sedition and disturbances against the Church; but God frustrated their plans, as he did those of Ahithophel (2 Sam. 15).

Their entire effort was directed toward defending the heresy under Isidore’s name. He had been separated from communion with the saints for various reasons by many bishops [Note: [Col. 0764] The reasons for which Isidore was expelled from the Church and Theophilus became hostile to him are reported as uncertain and trivial even by writers of that period. Sozomen says that many reported that, after a woman infected with Manichaeism had been admitted by Peter, archpresbyter of the Alexandrian Church, to communion in the mysteries for the sake of profit, before she had renounced the heresy Isidore confirmed her by his testimony, saying that Peter had done this according to Theophilus’s decision; Theophilus therefore expelled both of them from the Church. But Sozomen says that he learned a different account from a man accustomed to associate with the Nitrian monks. Theophilus, he says, had two reasons for attacking Isidore: one shared by Isidore and Peter, namely, that they had refused to testify that Theophilus’s sister had been named as his heir; the other peculiar to Isidore, namely, that although he cared for the poor, he refused to give Theophilus the funds distributed for their use, because Theophilus wished to spend them on constructing churches. Palladius gives a similar account in the *Life of Chrysostom*. But what the Alexandrian bishop introduces here about the woman and the adolescent boy, about written accusations against Isidore, and about the wound inflicted, presents a very different picture. Palladius actually says in his *Dialogue* that Theophilus brought against Isidore an accusation of the utmost gravity, so serious that the accuser himself did not dare to express in words the enormous crimes he alleged Isidore had committed.]. Meanwhile, a woman and her adolescent son are brought forward by these men and placed in a famous location in the city, which, if I am not mistaken, they call Genium [Note: [Col. 0765] This sounds more like an interpreter than the author; Theophilus could not have spoken hesitantly about the name of a place. It appears to be *Ξένιον*, Xenion, a place where guests would assemble.]. They shout whatever they thought would bring us into disrepute, inciting the pagan populace against us with things that unbelieving ears would gladly hear. Among these matters, also, [there was talk] of the destruction [Note: [Col. 0765] The most famous temple in the entire pagan world was the Serapeum at Alexandria, which Dionysius calls the temple of Zeus of Sinope and describes magnificently.] ...

> Where stands the great house of Sinopean Zeus,  
> Adorned with precious gold; no other temple  
> More divine than that could you behold among mankind.  
> —See Eustathius on this passage.

But here, in our author, the sense is disturbed by the words *who put to flight*; in their place one might readily write *who raged against us*, or *who drove us away*, or *and at their flight*—namely, that of the idols—or finally, *and putting us to flight*.

They raise a cry over Serapis and the other idols, “urging [them] to flight” (the transmitted sense is confused).

[Note: [Col. 0765] “Idol-shrines” (*Idoliorum*) should unquestionably be read instead of “idols” (*Idolorum*), for Theophilus was the fiercest enemy of pagan superstition and everywhere overthrew its shrines or temples, especially that of Serapis at Alexandria. Eunapius, in the *Life of Aedesius*, records that Evagrius, the prefect of Egypt, and Romanus, the commander of the military forces, rendered distinguished assistance to that bishop in destroying it: “The sacred places around Canopus suffered the same fate, while Theodosius was then emperor, Theophilus was in command, Evagrius was governing the civil administration, and Romanus had charge of the soldiers in Egypt.” It may be gathered that the temple of Serapis was destroyed around the year 391, from Theodosius’ law to Evagrius under the title *Concerning Pagans*, or, as Valesius observes, from the *Chronicle* of Marcellinus under the year 389, when Timasius and Promotus were consuls; and from Zosimus, book 1, where he reports that Theodosius, when Cynegius was sent to Egypt, ordered him—he was prefect of the praetorium—to destroy the pagan shrines. Cynegius died during his consulship in the year 388. See also Idatius in the *Fasti*. Compare Pagi, [Col. 0766] who, under the year 389, no. 13, attacks Valesius on this matter.]

They did not act in this way with regard to the rights of the temples in the monasteries of Nitria. They did all these things, however, thinking that in this way crowds of unbelievers would be assembled, and that Isidore would be snatched from the judgment of the bishops; so that, when he was heard together with his mother and the boy, they might bring hatred upon us, who wished him to be heard patiently in the church, in the presence of the clergy and the faithful people, and wished the ecclesiastical rule to be observed in his case with all fear of God and gentleness.

For we are not his enemies, nor have we harmed him in anything, any more than we harmed the few servants and fugitives who are partners in his affair. Rather, we preferred the fear of God and the standard of evangelical strictness to our former familiarity and association.

[Note: [Col. 0765] The Alexandrian bishop had previously loved Isidore greatly and bound him to himself by benefits, so much so that even after Nectarius’ death he had made every effort to raise him to the see of Constantinople.]

When he was summoned to answer before the bishops and the entire clergy, and was repeatedly called to the proceedings, he began to evade them and postpone the day from one day to the next—apparently in the hope, as many people reported, that he might gradually purchase the woman’s silence. By doing this he wounded the hearts of the holy brothers.

For who doubts that confidence belongs to a good conscience, whereas flight and evasion, to speak more cautiously—or, to state openly what I think—are judged by most people to be a kind of confession? Especially since the woman, having submitted written accusations, charged him with a serious crime, and this was being proclaimed among the people: namely, that he was making every effort to bring the matter to an end by any means rather than through the judgment of the bishops.

Without my knowledge, this woman was enrolled, through the efforts of his friends, in the register of widows, so that the pain of her wound might be soothed by the relief provided by charitable alms.

After I learned this from a certain deacon, who fearlessly reported that the woman had been entered among the widows so that she would keep silent about what she had alleged, I immediately disclosed the matter to Isidore through many people and warned him to prepare himself for the judgment of the bishops, while the woman alone was separated from the company of the others until we could see the outcome of the case.

For it was not lawful that she should be supported by the resources of the Church if she had either rashly made such a serious accusation or had kept silent about it.

This is the standard-bearer of the heretical faction. They use him as their leader and chief resource—those whom we described at the beginning of the letter—because he can provide them with food and support the hardships of their journey. Where frenzy and slaughter are required, they need the aid of no one else; where expenses and various expenditures are involved, nothing is more accommodating than a benefactor.

### 4

They are angry with me and rage because I have not allowed the solitudes and dwellings of the monks, in which a holy way of life is practiced, to be polluted by the impious doctrines of Origen.

To pass over the rest, among the books *On the Resurrection* which he wrote to Ambrose, imitating the dialectical method of disputation, in which there is a question and an answer, this advocate of magic says:

[Note: [Col. 0766] Understand this as referring to the two dialogues *On the Resurrection*, mentioned by Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* 6.24, and carefully distinguished by Jerome in a fragment of the letter now numbered 33 to Paula from two other books on the same subject. It is fortunate that we learn from this that they had been dedicated by Origen to Ambrose, his celebrated pursuer (*ergodiōktēs*), for they have long since perished. The archetype soon afterward had *suscitatus* instead of *sciscitatio*; compelled by the sense of the passage, we corrected it conjecturally.]

“Magic does not seem to me to be the name of anything possessing substantial existence; but even if it exists, it is in no way an evil work, nor something that can rightly be held in contempt.”

[Note: [Col. 0766] Theophilus, or his translator Jerome, uses the same words in *Paschal Letter* 1.1: “Origen, also granting protection to magical arts, spoke these words in his treatises: ‘Magic does not seem to me to be the name of anything possessing substantial existence; but even if it exists, it is not an evil work, lest anyone be able to hold it in contempt.’” The anonymous writer cited above by Photius, among his accusations against Origen, also records this charge: that he said, “Magic is not evil.” Eustathius of Antioch, who appears somewhat more hostile to the same Origen, makes the same accusation in his book *On the Ventriloquist*.]

In saying this, he plainly contradicts the Lord, who speaks through the prophet:

“Stand now with your enchantments and with your many sorceries, which you have learned from your youth, if they can perhaps profit you. You have wearied yourself with your counsels. Let the astrologers of heaven stand and save you, those who contemplate the stars; let them announce to you what is going to happen to you” (Isaiah 47:12–13, according to the Septuagint).

Moreover, in the books *On First Principles* (*περὶ ἀρχῶν*) he tries to persuade us of this also: that the living Word of God did not assume a human body.

[Note: [Col. 0767] From the Greek *logos* (*λόγος*), which means “Word.” Theophilus again vehemently condemns this doctrine concerning Christ’s soul in *Paschal Letter* 1: namely, that Origen referred Paul’s words, “He did not regard it as robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:7), to Christ’s soul, believing it equal to God, and holding that it was not the Word himself but only his soul that came down to earthly things. See Justinian’s letter to Menas near the end, where he attacks this madness from the books *On First Principles*; for in Rufinus’ translation it is concealed.]

Going against the Apostle’s teaching, he wrote that the one who was in the form of God and equal to God was not the Word of God, but a soul descending from the heavenly region, which emptied itself of the form of eternal majesty and assumed a human body.

In saying this, he most openly contradicts John, who writes, “And the Word became flesh” (John 1:14). Nor can it be believed that the Savior’s soul, rather than God the Word, possessed both the form and the equality of the Father’s majesty.

In his frenzy he exults in other impieties as well, wishing that our Lord Jesus Christ, who at the consummation of the ages suffered once for all for the destruction of sin, would at some time also suffer crucifixion for demons and spiritual wickednesses.

[Note: [Col. 0767] These claims are again anathematized in *Paschal Letter* 1, where it is said that Origen taught that Christ must be crucified above for demons and spiritual wickednesses. Jerome likewise says in *Apology Against Rufinus*, book 1, chapter 5: “Your Origen is permitted to say that Christ suffered often and will suffer more often, so that what once profited may always profit when assumed.” In his letter to Avitus, chapter 4, Jerome elaborates this and shows that it would follow—even if Origen did not say it—that just as a man became man for human beings in order to redeem human beings, so for the salvation of demons God would become what those beings are whom he is going to redeem. Compare, to avoid producing more testimonies, Orosius’ *Memorandum*, and Sulpicius Severus’ *Dialogues*, book 1, chapter 1, as well as Justinian’s frequently cited letter to Menas.]

Nor does he remember Paul’s words:

“It is impossible for those who have once been enlightened, who have tasted the heavenly gift, who have become sharers in the Holy Spirit, who have tasted the good Word of God and the powers of the age to come, and who have fallen away, to be renewed again to repentance, since they crucify the Son of God again for themselves and hold him up to contempt” (Hebrews 6:6).

If he had wished to know this—or rather, if he had not despised what he knows—he would never, while contradicting the Apostle, have said that Christ would suffer even for demons and would have exposed him to contempt.

Passing over what we read with closed ears, “Christ, having risen from the dead, dies no more; death shall no longer rule over him. For the death that he died, he died to sin once for all; but the life that he lives, he lives to God” (Romans 6:9–10): the word “once” admits neither a second nor a third occurrence. Therefore, knowing that Christ was crucified once, the Apostle declares with complete confidence in the Letter to the Hebrews: “For this he did once for all, offering himself” (Hebrews 7:27).

### 5

For these and many other reasons, which the form of a letter does not permit me to set down, they were condemned and expelled from the Church. But, with folly joined to pride, they contradict the judgments of the bishops, striving through sedition to defend their fellow heretic; and, wandering through foreign provinces, they have the condemned as their leader and take pride in this undertaking.

I therefore beseech you, dearest brothers, that if they come there, you may move them to tears by the commandments of the Gospel. It is our desire to correct both them and their other errors through repentance, so that, behaving in a manner worthy of their name, those who are called monks—if indeed they wish to be what they are called—may love silence and the Catholic faith, to which nothing whatsoever is to be preferred.

[Note: [Col. 0768] Supply *esse*, or, more correctly, read *conversari*; see *Paschal Letter* 2.22 toward the end, where the same statement is made about monks.]

But, as I hear, imitating the Devil, they run here and there and seek whom they may devour through their impieties (1 Peter 5:8). For they consider madness to be faith, boldness to be courage, and recklessness to be strength; and so, puffed up with pride, they prefer Origen’s teaching—which is mingled with idolatry—to the Church’s preaching.

Therefore, if anywhere they attempt to disturb the brothers and the people entrusted to you, guard the Lord’s flock and restrain their mad assaults. We have harmed them in nothing; we have inflicted no injury upon them. Our only cause of their hatred is that we are prepared to defend the faith even unto death.

[Note: [Col. 0768] We direct that the lacuna be supplied and read “we inflicted no injury upon them.” Theophilus himself confirms our conjecture in *Paschal Letter* 2.23: “We inflicted no injury upon them, we harmed them in nothing,” and so forth.]

### 6

I pass over the rest: how they tried to bring death upon us, and by what plots they contrived it, when, after they had been condemned, they seized the church situated in the monastery of Nitria, so that both we and the many bishops with us, as well as the fathers of the monks—venerable in life and age—might be prevented from entering it by hired freedmen and slaves, who, for the sake of their appetite and belly, are armed for every crime.

And when they held the more vulnerable places of the church as though under siege in a city, they concealed clubs and staffs beneath palm branches, so that under the insignia of peace they might conceal their minds prepared for slaughter.

[Note: [Col. 0768] We correct the passage conjecturally and establish that *quasi* should be read for *qui*, and *tenerent* for *tenerentur*. These were two scribal errors in the archetype that destroyed the sense. Jerome has a very similar passage above concerning staffs concealed beneath the leaves of trees to disguise the slaughter, although it did not come to mind here.]

To make the faction stronger and the band more ready for bold action, they distributed money to many freeborn men. These men accepted it not to consent to the crime, but to provide us with information about their plans and disclose their prepared ambushes, so that we might take precautions.

[Note: [Col. 0768] I would prefer *proderent*—“so that they might betray or reveal [their plans]”—because it gives a smoother sense.]

When the innumerable crowd of monks saw this, they all began to shout, frightening the rage of the few with a united outcry, so that at least they would permit the Collection to be held and the rights of the church to be preserved.

And unless God’s grace had restrained the force of the multitude, something would have happened of the sort that usually occurs in riots. For these wicked men had burst into such recklessness—or rather, madness—that even the monks of holy conduct, who had always been most gentle, could no longer endure their fury.

[Col. 0769]

We bore all these things patiently and humbly before God’s ears, taking thought for the salvation of those who were fighting against us with hostility; but only on the condition that we would not surrender ecclesiastical rules and the true faith to anyone’s friendships. May the Lord, who is powerful, grant this jointly to us and to all his servants: that we may prefer the unity of the faith to human relationships.

[Note: [Col. 0769] Jerome easily wrote “to deaf ears,” as we direct it should be read instead of “to God’s ears,” which is an antiquarian’s error; nevertheless, we do not alter the text.]

We also ask you that each of you, together with the peoples entrusted to you, pray more earnestly and implore God for mercy, so that, resisting the plots of the heretics, we may have peace with those who have always fought for the truth, and that all together we may await the crown of righteousness.

The brothers who are with you, and the people who are with me, greet you in the Lord.

[Note: [Col. 0769] The assembly of the bishops had by now been dissolved; the letter was sent some time afterward.]

[Col. 0769]

[Note: [Col. 0769] Otherwise unpublished. Written a few days after the preceding letter.]

## LETTER XCIII

OR, THE RESPONSE OF THE JERUSALEM SYNOD TO THE FOREGOING LETTER OF THEOPHILUS

[Note: [Col. 0769] This now first appears from the same Ambrosian manuscript, in which it follows the second Paschal letter of Theophilus.]

As it seems, translated by Saint Jerome.

[Note: [Col. 0769] We think that this has been established by sufficiently probable evidence from Jerome’s own words in book 1 of his *Apology Against Rufinus*, near the beginning, where he says: “If you think that whatever is said against Origen and his followers is said against you, then the letters of Pope Theophilus, and of Epiphanius, and of the other bishops—which I recently translated at their command—attack you and tear you apart.” Who, then, can those other bishops be understood to be who wrote letters against Origen and his followers, which Jerome translated into Latin at that time, unless they are above all the fathers of this Jerusalem synod, whose letters are here produced? This is further supported by the character of the Ambrosian manuscript, which contains almost exclusively works associated with Jerome, although some are his own compositions and others are Latin translations from Greek.]

The fathers of the synod reply that Palestine is free from the Origenian heresy, which they repeatedly execrate; nevertheless, they declare that they condemn the doctrines and persons whom Theophilus condemned in his preceding synodical letter.

To the lord and most honorable Bishop Theophilus: Eulogius, John, and the other bishops who were found at Jerusalem on the day of the Encaenia in the Holy City.

[Note: [Col. 0769] We have already noted above, on the testimony of Nicephorus, *History* 8.10, that the first day of the Encaenia of the Jerusalem temple was September 14.]

1. “You know, Lord, that everything is laudably carried out, and even before our letter, that almost all Palestine, through the grace of Christ, is free from the scandal of heretics, except for a few who, assenting to the errors of Apollinaris, meditate upon the harmful writings of their teacher.

And would that, through the prayers of the saints, the Jewish serpents, the incredible folly of the Samaritans, and the manifest impieties of the pagans did not disturb us—those whose very great multitude, completely stopping their ears to the preaching of truth and surrounding Christ’s flock like wolves, impose no small watchfulness and labor upon us while we seek to guard the Lord’s sheep, lest they be torn apart by them.

[Note: [Col. 0769] Jerome himself notes this in Letter 82.10: “Here there are Jews, heretics of various doctrines, and especially the utterly impure Manichaeans,” and so forth. Concerning the Samaritans’ incredible folly, as the fathers of the synod call it, see the notable evidence in Epiphanius, *Heresy* 9; Philaster; Leontius of Byzantium, *On Sects*, act 11; and Gregory the Great in several passages. Add Baronius, [Col. 0770] *Annals* 35.]

And because Your Holiness wrote to us that certain people had been found in Egypt who wished to introduce certain deadly teachings from the doctrines of Origen into the churches and deceive the hearts of the simple, we therefore thought it necessary to inform Your Holiness that such preaching is foreign to our ears.

For we have never heard anyone teach that Christ’s kingdom will ever come to an end. Let this be far from the ears of the faithful, since the angel Gabriel spoke to Mary concerning the Christ who was to be born and said, ‘He will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end’ (Luke 1:33).

Nor have we heard that the Devil, once freed from all the vices of sinners, will obtain the dignity that he possessed before his fall, so that both he and Christ might be brought under the one rule of God the Father. Those who believe this are going into the darkness prepared for the Devil and his angels.

But if there are any who have handed down in their treatises that, compared with us, the Son is truth, but, compared with the Father, falsehood; and that, as they say, what Peter and Paul are in comparison with the Savior—that is, the Only-Begotten Son and the Word of God—in comparison with the Father, so is the Son—

[Note: [Col. 0770] The Ambrosian manuscript read corruptly, “that the Son is compared with us as truth.” We corrected it as in the preceding synodical letter, section 3, from Augustine’s *On Heresies to Quodvultdeus*: “Origen further said that, compared with holy men, the Son of God is truth, but, compared with the Father, falsehood.” More precisely, Guido Perpinianus, a Carmelite, in his *Summary of Heresies*, where he transcribes this very passage among the Origenian doctrines, used a more accurate copy and read: “that the Son, compared with us, is truth,” and so forth. This testimony of a good writer deserves particular weight because he calls this decretal of the Palestinian bishops by name and knew it more than four hundred years ago.]

and, to state our position briefly—for there is no need to discuss the same matters again—whoever proclaims this, and those things which Your Beatitude indicates must be condemned, and all those teachings that disagree with the faith which our fathers wrote down in pious judgment at Nicaea, let both the persons and their doctrines be anathema to the Church, together with Apollinaris, who, going against the holy Scriptures, says that an imperfect human being was assumed by our Lord Jesus Christ, and that full salvation was not given through the assumption of both his soul and his body.

[Note: [Col. 0770] For the sense to be sound and clear, delete the *m* at the end of the words *plenam assumptionem*, since it means “full assumption”; those who have consulted ancient manuscripts know how often this letter was wrongly added to the sixth case by the defective pronunciation of old scribes. A literate stone from our domestic museum supplies another example: it bears a pagan inscription on one side and a Christian one on the other, and in the older pagan inscription one reads, “SINE ALTERITRUM. ANIMI. LESIONEM” (“without injury to either soul”).]

For we, following the footsteps of the fathers and instructed by the words of Scripture, teach and proclaim in the churches, and confess, that the uncreated and eternal Trinity is one in three subsistences and, in one Godhead, of one substance.

[Note: [Col. 0771] Read, if you please, and at my own risk, *substantiae*—“of one substance”—instead of the reading preserved in the manuscripts, *adorantes*—“worshiping.” The similarity of the letters composing the two words will be easier to see if they are written in capital characters; perhaps the worn initial letters in the archetype also completely deceived the inexperienced scribe. The sense, which cannot stand otherwise, the word *unius*, which would otherwise have no substantive noun to which it could refer, and finally the word *adorantes* itself, which is certainly erroneous in this place, not only support but compel our correction. Compare this exceptionally clear confession of the most holy Trinity with Jerome’s Letters 15 and 16 to Damasus, and recall our notes on them, if they are worth the effort.]

But if anyone whom Your Reverence separates from communion, whether because of the perversity of his doctrines or for other reasons, as you have deigned to inform us, know that such a person is not to be received in our churches until you have granted him forgiveness through repentance, provided that he is willing to condemn his perversities.

Greet all the priests who are with you.”

[Col. 0771]

[Note: [Col. 0771] Otherwise unpublished. Written at the same time as the preceding letter.]

## LETTER XCIV

OF DIONYSIUS TO THEOPHILUS

[Note: [Col. 0771] It follows immediately upon the preceding letter of the Palestinian bishops in the Ambrosian manuscript, from which it is now first published.]

As it seems, translated into Latin by Saint Jerome.

He praises Theophilus throughout because the Origenian heresy had been condemned through his efforts, and earnestly urges him not to cease pursuing it to the end.

To the most blessed lord Theophilus, Dionysius, Bishop of Lydda.

[Note: [Col. 0771] Also called Diospolis. Lucian, *On the Revelation of the Body of Saint Stephen*: “I reported to the bishop, when he was in Lydda, which is Diospolis, what had happened.” See our holy father’s book *Against John of Jerusalem*, near the end, where he speaks about this Dionysius.]

“Our good God, who is glorified in the assemblies of the saints (Psalm 88:2) and prepares friends and prophets for himself in every age—if you consider the succession of our generations—has raised you, most blessed lord and brother, as a champion of the true faith, so that with apostolic rigor you might crush the heretical superstition flowing from the fountain of the pagans, and lead back to its Shepherd the human race, dragged through many errors, and Christ’s scattered flock.

For at the time of his Passion he gave his life for all precisely so that we believers might now say, ‘Truly, God is among us’ (1 Corinthians 14:25).

For who is so foolish or impious that he would not confess that you have bestowed the greatest gift upon the world by expelling the most wicked blasphemers, the disciples of Origen, lest Christ’s Church be polluted by those whose cancer and incurable leprosy have so infected the hearts of many that even those who pretend to repent join heresy to perjury, while they do not cease to hate us, whom they compel to remain silent?

### 2
