Be strong, therefore, and act manfully (1 Chronicles 22:13), servant of God, and pursue the fabrications of Origen to the very end, lest the minds of the simple be captured beneath the shadow of his wisdom by seductive enticements, and division become a schism in the body of Christ.

For all who set their minds on the things above eagerly proclaim you as the Father, hope, and crown of the faith, because with the sword of the Gospel you have struck down the teacher of Arius and his disciples.

[Note: [Col. 0772] Jerome also commonly calls Origen the teacher of Arius and explains very accurately the reasons for doing so. But there is no basis for calling him simultaneously a disciple; here one must unquestionably read *discipulos*, in the plural, indicating the Origenist heretics.]

The brothers of my cell greet you warmly, as do the brothers who are with you.”

## LETTER XCV

[Note: [Col. 0772] Elsewhere unpublished. Apparently written at the beginning of the year 400.]

OF POPE ANASTASIUS TO SIMPLICIAN

[Note: [Col. 0772] It appears from the same Ambrosian manuscript as the preceding three letters. There it occupies the place between Epiphanius’ letter to John of Jerusalem—which in our recension is Letter 51—and another letter, now numbered 90, of Theophilus to Epiphanius.]

He praises Theophilus’ zeal and vigilance. Having been informed by his letter, Anastasius reports to Simplician, Bishop of Milan, that he too has pronounced an anathema against the Origenian heresy.

[Note: [Col. 0772] There is no doubt that this is the bishop of the Milanese Church. Yet, to conceal nothing, this address to Simplician at one time made us suspicious of the letter’s authenticity. The synodical letter of Theophilus, as has been established elsewhere by reliable arguments, belongs to the year 400; and since it is addressed to the bishops assembled with the Palestinians at the Encaenia of Aelia, while the Encaenia of that temple falls on September 14, it must be assigned to that month and approximately those days. Consequently, Anastasius could not have received the letters of that Alexandrian bishop, by which he was summoned and informed of Origen’s condemnation, as quickly as one might suppose—before the end of that same September—and then, after some interval, have taken the opportunity presented by Eusebius to write to Simplician. Yet Simplician had died nearly two months earlier, since the most reliable records of the Milanese Church place his death on August 15 of that very year. It is hardly credible that his death remained unknown to the Roman pontiff for so long that he would write to him as though he were still alive, especially since the same ecclesiastical records show that Venerius succeeded him immediately, or at the beginning of September. Moreover, Anastasius’ letters concerning the condemnation of Origen are said by various authorities, including Anastasius himself, to have been sent to Venerius. In his reply to John of Jerusalem, he notes that he is sending him a letter written to Venerius, in which he had expressed his judgment concerning Origen and the destructive interpretation of Origen’s book with greater care. But no letters from the Roman pontiff to Simplician have ever been mentioned by any writer dealing with his case—not by Theophilus, not by Epiphanius, and, what matters more, not by Jerome. Jerome certainly never read or knew any letters addressed otherwise than to Venerius, and he frequently brings them forward against his opponents. He would unquestionably have done the same, and even more forcefully, had he known of letters to Simplician of this kind, in which Origen’s doctrine is explicitly condemned and the express command is given that “whatever is contrary to our faith, once written by Origen, must be alien to us and punished.” [Col. 0773] These, then, were the two principal arguments that led us to doubt the matter, and it is by no means useless to explain them to diligent readers.

But when we considered the matter more carefully, we understood that, when Anastasius says he was summoned by Theophilus’ letters in order to condemn Origen, he is not referring to the encyclical letters addressed to the Palestinian and Cypriot bishops, which unquestionably belong to September of the year 400, but to earlier letters, whether private or, if you prefer, issued from some assembly of the Egyptian fathers—for example, those praised by Justinian in his letter to Menas, which seem to belong to the preceding year. Such, certainly, are the letters which Jerome mentions in Letter 88 to the Alexandrian bishop: “I think that by God’s providence it happened that, at the same time, you too wrote to Pope Anastasius and, without knowing it, strengthened our judgment.” Jerome wrote this before translating the synodical letter which we publish here, as both the chronology of the letter and the continuation of the context below prove.

A second argument comes from this very letter of Anastasius. He notes that he received the chapters of blasphemy—which he condemns together with their author—from Eusebius, namely Eusebius of Cremona, the bearer of this letter; he does not derive them from Theophilus’ letters. Yet they would necessarily have been derived from those letters if they had not been different from the synodical letters we have published. I believe that in those letters Origen’s blasphemies are examined more carefully and refuted with greater authority than in Eusebius’ catalogue, which may have been compiled from a single book of Origen, perhaps *On First Principles*, from Rufinus’ translation, in order to create greater hostility toward the translator.

In any case, we willingly grant that Jerome was not acquainted with this letter of Anastasius to Simplician, but was well acquainted with the one to Venerius. Innumerable reasons for this ignorance could be proposed, which the reader can easily devise and construct for himself, so that we may not be too lengthy, from examples found throughout ecclesiastical history.

Yet I do not know whether Jerome himself does not indicate the matter clearly enough in his letter to Demetrias:

“When you were still a little girl, and Anastasius, of holy and blessed memory, governed the Roman Church, a savage storm of heretics from the eastern regions tried to pollute and undermine the simplicity of the faith praised by the Apostle’s voice. But that man of richest poverty and apostolic vigilance immediately struck down the harmful head and silenced the hissing mouths of the hydra.”

Moreover, Theophilus himself, in a sermon to certain monks, testifies that Origen had been condemned by both himself and Anastasius:

“Anathematizing Origen and the other heretics, following the example of ourselves and Anastasius, Bishop of the Holy Roman Church, who, renowned for his ancient struggles, was appointed leader of that most noble people, and whom the entire synod of the Western bishops follows—the synod which received and approved the judgment pronounced by the Church of Alexandria against the impious.”

Justinian quotes these words of Theophilus in his letter to Menas.

To the lord brother Simplician: Anastasius.

### 1

“It is acknowledged that a shepherd must maintain great concern and watchfulness over his flock. Likewise, from a high tower, a careful sentry watches over the safety of the city day and night.

[Col. 0773]

[Note: [Col. 0773] The archetype had *exultare*, which made no sense. We did not hesitate to correct it conjecturally to these three words, *from a high tower*, which are required both by the sequence of the sentence and by the clarity of the sense. It would have been easy for an old scribe who did not understand the abbreviations in his exemplar to copy one word in place of the three.]

A prudent master of a ship, in a time of storm and danger, suffers great agitation of mind, lest the ship be dashed against the rocks by gales and the harshest waves.

[Note: [Col. 0773] It is astonishing how many errors the old copyist committed in this very short passage. The manuscript read: “A master thus far of a ship, at the hour of storm, of the liver and danger, the great…” We ventured to alter the text solely on the basis of conjecture, since there was no loss of sense, so that the reader would not be offended by such monstrosities. We entirely removed *ecoris*, which is not a word.]

With a similar spirit the holy and honorable man Theophilus, our brother and fellow bishop, does not cease to watch over the interests of salvation, lest God’s people, by reading Origen in the various churches, fall into great blasphemies.”

## 2

“Concerning the assembly mentioned in the letter, I address Your Holiness, so that, [Note: [Col. 0774] Here *sicuti*, an adverb, is used for *similiter*, ‘similarly,’ or ‘in the same manner’; examples of this usage are found among the older Latin writers. If, however, one reads *ut si*, the sense will also become perfectly clear: for the whole passage is nearly everywhere fragmentary through the fault of the copyists.] just as we, established in the city of Rome—which the glorious Peter, prince of the apostles, founded and confirmed by his faith—have condemned these things we have mentioned, so that no one may read them contrary to the command, and have earnestly requested that the ordinances of the Gospels, which the judgment of God and Christ taught from His own mouth, [Note: [Col. 0774] Some words are missing here, having fallen out through the carelessness of the ancient copyists—for example, ‘may be preserved,’ and ‘we decreed,’ or something similar. Nevertheless, despite the many corruptions that obstruct the sentence, the holy pontiff’s meaning is not obscure.] should not be abandoned in any respect, but that what the venerable apostle Paul foretold and admonished should be recalled to mind: ‘If anyone preaches to you a gospel contrary to what was preached to you, let him be accursed’ (Galatians 1:8). Therefore, holding fast to this command, we have declared that whatever was once written by Origen contrary to our faith is alien to us and condemned by us.”

## 3

“We have written these things to Your Holiness through the presbyter Eusebius, who, bearing the fervor of faith and possessing love for the Lord, [Note: [Col. 0774] This was evidently Eusebius of Cremona, who, while he was at Rome from the year 398 onward, was the first publicly to denounce Origen’s books *On First Principles* (*περὶ Ἀρχῶν*), after Rufinus had rendered them into Latin; he then extracted from them the chapters of blasphemy. While he was at Milan, during the very period in which he delivered this letter of Anastasius to Simplicianus, he recited, in Rufinus’ presence, a passage from Rufinus’ translation containing an opinion of Origen’s. Rufinus himself records that he refuted it in Book 1 of his *Invectives*.] brought forward certain chapters of blasphemy, which we not only shuddered at and condemned, but concerning any other things expounded by Origen also, know that we have condemned them, together with their author. May the Lord preserve you unharmed, Lord brother, deservedly honored.”

# FOURTH CLASS, CONTAINING THE LETTERS FROM THE BEGINNING OF THE YEAR 401 TO 420, THAT IS, TO THE END OF JEROME’S LIFE

[Col. 0773]

# LETTER XCVI

[Note: [Col. 0773] In other editions it has no number. Written at the beginning of the year 401.]

## OR THE PASCHAL LETTER FOR THE YEAR 401 OF THEOPHILUS, BISHOP OF ALEXANDRIA

[Note: [Col. 0773] In Martianaeus’s edition it is incorrectly entitled the second Paschal Book, [Col. 0774] and is also placed second, although the chronological note found at the end shows that it belongs to the year 401 and precedes the others.]

## TO THE BISHOPS OF ALL EGYPT, TRANSLATED INTO LATIN BY SAINT JEROME

Christ’s divinity is chiefly asserted against Apollinaris; most of Origen’s errors are then set out individually [Col. 0774] and refuted; finally, love toward one’s neighbors, especially in celebrating the Lord’s Pascha as is fitting, is praised as the chief virtue.

## 1

Let us once again praise Christ Jesus, Lord of glory, dearest brothers, with harmonious voice; let us adore Him joyfully and fulfill the words of the prophet [Col. 0775] who says: “Sing to the Lord a new song” (Psalm 149). All of us who share in the faith that leads to the kingdoms of heaven, let us welcome the coming of the holy solemnity and celebrate with the festivity of the whole world the feasts that are at hand. [Note: [Col. 0775] The often-cited Ambrosian manuscript H. 59 reads: “that we may celebrate the approaching feast days with the festivity of the whole world,” etc.; for the earlier published editions wrongly had “of the city.”] One of the wise cries out:

“Come, eat your bread with gladness,
and drink your wine with a good heart,
for your works have pleased God” (Ecclesiastes 9:7).

For those who practice good works, abandoning the milk of infancy and receiving the nourishment of more solid food, contemplate divine truths more deeply; and, filled with spiritual nourishment, they have God as the praiser and witness of their life. To such banqueters Ecclesiastes says: “Let your garments be white at all times, and let oil never fail from your head” (Ecclesiastes 9). Thus, clothed in the garment of virtues, let us imitate the brightness of the sun; and by daily reading of the holy Scriptures, let each person pour oil into his understanding and prepare the lamp of his mind, so that, according to the command of the Gospel, it may shine for all who are in the house (Matthew 5).

## 2

Therefore, imitating such banqueters and those who thus celebrate together the feasts of the Lord’s Passion, let us say with the holy man: “I will praise the Lord during my life; I will sing psalms to my God as long as I exist” (Psalm 103). Let us hasten to the metropolis of the angels, which is free and stained by no defilement of wickedness, where there are neither dissensions nor falls, nor transmigration from one to another. Trampling every pleasure underfoot and restraining the waves of lust that rise up so frequently against us, let us mingle with the heavenly choirs, so that, already transferred there in mind and beholding more august places, we may be what we shall be.

The Jews made themselves unworthy of this blessedness. Abandoning the riches of holy Scripture [Note: [Col. 0775] Again we repair this passage from the Ambrosian manuscript. In earlier editions it read: ‘and, acquiescing rather in poverty of understanding, even to this day,’ and so forth. By ‘poverty of understanding’ the Western text is evidently meant; this is well known.] and acquiescing in teachers of impoverished understanding, they hear today: “They always err in heart” (Psalm 94). Yet, with Christ present, they refuse to say: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Psalm 117).

Especially since His works, clearer than any voice, testify that He is God; and He does not say, “Thus says the Lord,” but, “I say to you.” By this He shows Himself to be the bearer of the laws, the true Lord and God, and not merely one of the prophets.

## 3

Nor could the assumption of a servant’s form obscure His divinity, which is confined by no limits of place; nor could the narrowness of a human body restrict His ineffable [Note: [Col. 0775] The little word *ejus* was missing; we have restored it here from the edition of the Paschal Letters found in the *Bibliotheca Patrum*. Whenever we later use the testimony of that edition, we shall indicate it by the letters B. P. Although it teems with innumerable errors, it nevertheless preserves many excellent traces of a more accurate reading and has provided us great assistance in correcting several passages. Shortly afterward, we read *comprobat*, ‘proved,’ rather than the previously printed *comprobabat*, ‘was proving’; this we have taken from the Ambrosian manuscripts.] power of His majesty—Him whom the greatness of His works proved to be the Son of God.

When He had restored to sudden calm the towering billows of the raging sea, swelling like mountains, [Col. 0776] [Note: [Col. 0776] This passage might easily appear dislocated. It can be restored to its original condition by reading it, without changing the order, as follows: ‘and the depths of the waters had felt the authority of the Lord present, after the boat of the apostles had been delivered from shipwreck; and when …’] after the boat of the apostles had been delivered from shipwreck, and the depths of the waters had felt the authority of the Lord present, and when, while the winds struggled and waves were raised on every side, such great dangers had ceased at the Savior’s command, those who were sailing together, as though inspired by the divine Spirit, said: “Truly, you are the Son of God” (Matthew 14). They had no doubt concerning His divinity, whose greatness the works proclaimed.

For the prophetic oracle concerning Him is: “You rule the power of the sea; you still the movement of its waves” (Psalm 88). And the prophet himself marks [variant: signifies] the song, [Note: [Col. 0776] These words occur in Greek in a treatise of Saint Cyril of Alexandria addressed to the Council of Ephesus, entitled *To the Most Religious Queens*. Compare them with Jerome’s translation:

“so that He might be believed to be not only God in word but also in power, the true God who appeared, the greatness of the deeds revealing the certainty concerning Him. Although He was fully God, He became man of His own will and left nothing outside Himself of human likeness except sinful wickedness alone. For even when He became an infant, He was acknowledged as Emmanuel, while the Magi came to Him and cried out, by worshiping Him, that the One who had appeared was also God. For even when He was crucified in the flesh, He caused the rays of the sun to contract; and by the strange miracle He made His own divinity clear, neither scattering Himself anywhere nor dividing Himself into two saviors. He also said to the disciples: ‘Do not call anyone teacher on earth, for one is your teacher, Christ.’ When He gave this command to the apostles, He did not distinguish His own divinity from the body that appeared; nor, when He testified that He Himself was Christ, did He distinguish soul from flesh. Thus He was both God and man: seen as a servant and recognized as Lord. He concealed the loftiness of His divinity beneath the lowliness of His incarnation, while He raised up the lowliness of the visible body by the surpassing activity of His divinity.”]

so that He might be believed to be not only God in word but also in power, the true God who appeared, the excellence of His works revealing what was hidden.

Being perfect God, of His own will assuming whatever belonged to human nature and condition—except sin alone and wickedness, which possesses no substance—He is born as an infant and worshiped as EMMANUEL. Magi come from the East and, kneeling, confess the Son of God as God. At the time of His Passion, hanging upon the cross, He darkens the rays of the sun, expressing the greatness of His divinity by a new and unheard-of miracle.

He is undivided and inseparable, not divided, according to the error of certain people, into two saviors. Hence He also said to the disciples: “Do not call anyone teacher on earth, for one is your teacher, Christ” (Matthew 23:8). When He said this to the apostles, He was not separating the excellence of His divinity from the body visible to the eyes. Nor, when He testified that He was one Christ, the Son of God, was He dividing soul from flesh. He was not one and another, but one and the same, subsisting as both God and man: seen as a servant and adored as Lord. For in the lowliness of the human body He concealed the ineffable God, and again surpassed the frailty of the flesh by divine works. [Note: [Col. 0776] The conjunction *et*, which is unnecessary in Latin and slightly disturbs the sense, is supported by the character of the Greek language. The Ambrosian manuscript nevertheless lacks it and reads in the opposite sense, ‘so that He might be believed to be just anyone.’]

He was not to be believed to be merely one of the saints, as many have thought. Rather, He is the One whom Paul, wishing to show this, writes of in these words: “One God, one mediator also between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus.” And again: “A mediator belongs not to one party, but God is one” (1 Timothy 2). He is the one Son of the Father and our mediator; He neither lost His equality with the Father nor was separated from our fellowship: invisible God and visible man. He was concealed in the form of a servant, and the Lord of glory is confirmed by the confession of believers.

## 4

The Father did not deprive Him of the name of His nature after He became man and poor for our sake. Nor, when He was baptized in the Jordan, did He call Him by another name, but by that of the only-begotten Son: “You are my beloved Son, [Note: [Col. 0777] The Ambrosian manuscript adds: ‘in you I am well pleased.’ The words that follow in the Greek text are preserved by Theodoret in *Dialogue* 2:

‘Neither is our likeness, with which He shared, changed into the nature of divinity, nor is His divinity transformed into our likeness. For He remains what He was from the beginning, God; and He remains also the One who prepares our existence.’] in whom I am well pleased” (Luke 2).

Our likeness was not changed into the nature of divinity, nor was divinity transformed into the likeness of our nature. Rather, while remaining what He was from the beginning, God the Word, He glorifies us in Himself. He did not come, according to Jeremiah, to say:

“Alas for me, mother, why did you bear me,
a man who am judged and disputed by the whole earth?
I have benefited no one, nor has anyone benefited me” (Jeremiah 15:10).

He came to bestow freedom. Nor, according to Isaiah, did He cry out:

“Woe is me, for I am a man, and have unclean lips;
I dwell among a people having unclean lips,
and I have seen with my eyes the King, the Lord of hosts” (Isaiah 6:6).

[Note: [Col. 0777] The Ambrosian manuscript reads: ‘for I am a man of unclean lips,’ in agreement with the sacred text and especially with the Greek, which reject the reading found here.]

For He Himself was the King of glory, as it is written in the twenty-third Psalm: victorious upon the cross and restraining hostile wars, so that He might make the human being formed from the earth an inhabitant of heaven and grant him a share in His triumph.

## 5

Therefore, although those who think that He was changed into another being do not wish this to be so, “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever” (Hebrews 13:8). He will never have an end to His kingdom, contrary to Origen’s wicked error, lest, when the kingdom ceases, He also be deprived of eternity. He spoke openly before all: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 11:34).

Wishing to teach us that the Father in the Son and the Son in the Father rule over all creatures, He reinforced this by adding: “I and the Father are one” (John 14:11). Thus no one, on account of human flesh, might divide His kingdom from that of the Father.

But if, according to Origen’s madness, Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, is someday to lose His kingdom, how could He Himself say to the apostles, “I and the Father are one,” if He was not to possess one dominion forever? He would then have the glory that He was later to lay aside. And where would there be the truth that the Son is always in the Father and the Father in the Son, if the Son’s kingdom were not [Note: [Col. 0777] The context more correctly suggests *not coeternal*, as the Ambrosian manuscript has; the point is asserted more clearly below: ‘Let us believe Christ’s kingdom to be eternal.’ For the present we have restored this little word.] certain?

But let those who insist that this is so perish, unless they repent; and let Moses, moved by zeal for faith and piety, speak to them: “Cursed shall you be in the city, and cursed shall you be in the field” (Deuteronomy 28). The Psalmist likewise rebukes them: “Let sinners perish from the earth, and the wicked, so that they may exist no longer” (Psalm 103).

## 6

I cannot understand with what presumption Origen, fabricating such things and following not the authority of the Scriptures but his own error, dared to bring forth before everyone doctrines harmful to all. He evidently thought that no one would ever arise to contradict his assertions, if he mixed the subtleties of philosophers into his own treatises and, proceeding from an evil beginning into certain fables and ravings, made Christian doctrine a game and a joke.

He used not the truth of divine teaching [variant: striving toward it], but the judgment of the human mind; and, swelling into such pride under his own instruction, he did not imitate the humility of Paul. Paul, full of the Holy Spirit, conferred the Gospel with the earlier apostles, “lest somehow he should be running or should have run in vain” (Galatians 2:2). [Note: [Col. 0778] The editors printed *sed ignorans*, ‘but being ignorant,’ an adversative particle that disturbs the sense; with the help of the manuscripts we have removed it. Shortly afterward, on manuscript authority, we have corrected *putaret* to *putare*, since the former was faulty.]

Origen did not understand that it was the prompting of a demonic spirit to follow the sophistries of human minds and to consider anything divine that lay outside the authority of Scripture. Let those, therefore, who dream of an end to Christ’s kingdom and desire to be parasites upon Origen’s verbosity, cease at last. Let them not walk with the faithful while pretending to possess a faith they do not have.

Rather, let them learn [Note: [Col. 0778] We have followed the Ambrosian manuscript; the commonly printed text is faulty, reading that every fraud displays one thing and another. We correct several minor matters below.] that every deceit and fraud is one thing while displaying another, attempting to conceal vices beneath the appearance of virtue.

For when Christ did not cease to be Lord of glory in the disgrace of the cross that He endured for us, according to the blessed Apostle, the Jews cried out against Him: “You who destroy the temple and rebuild it in three days, save yourself. If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross” (Matthew 27). Yet while suffering in the flesh and hanging upon the cross, He displayed the strength of His own majesty, causing the sun to halt in its course and drawing from the thief, by the greatness of His signs, a confession full of faith: “Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom” (Luke 23).

He will never lose His kingdom after the glory of the resurrection, though Origen hurls countless stones of blasphemy against Him. For what consistency would there be in promising the disciples an everlasting kingdom and saying, “Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 25), while He Himself lacked the kingdom He gave to others?

Or how, when Paul writes to the Corinthians, “You reign without us—and would that you did reign, so that we might reign with you” (1 Corinthians 4), could it be understood that Christ’s kingdom would end after many ages? This is especially impossible since John cries out: “He who comes from above is above all” (John 3:31), and the Apostle writes: “Their fathers are theirs, and from them, according to the flesh, is Christ, who is God over all, blessed forever” (Romans 9:5).

## 7

Thus no one can doubt that He who remains God forever possesses the kingdom at the same time and is called the everlasting King even over those to whom He has granted possession of the kingdom. His dominion is appropriate to His divinity; nothing in Him is crude or new except the assumption of human frailty.

For if, according to Origen’s madness, Christ’s kingdom is to end after many cycles of ages, it follows from his impiety that he must also say that God Himself will someday cease to be. Whoever sets limits to the kingdom is compelled to hold the same concerning divinity, which naturally possesses everlasting dominion.

But if the Word of God (*Λόγος Θεοῦ*, “Word of God”) reigns, He is certainly God. From this it follows that whoever attempts to impose an end upon His kingdom is driven to the point of having to believe that Christ will also cease to be God.

Let the unlearned teacher babble such things [Note: [Col. 0779] Again we have adopted the reading of the Ambrosian manuscript, since the faulty printed editions have *peccatoribus*, ‘for sinners.’ Theophilus’ meaning is not to condemn sinners in general, but the impious followers of an unlearned teacher.] with his impious followers. We believe Christ’s kingdom to be eternal, and on the solemn day we sing with the angel and say: “His kingdom shall have no end” (Luke 1:33).

For if He is one with the Father, He will never cease to be one with what is one; and the union of the Father and the Son will never be divided into parts, so that what is said—“they are one”—might at some time cease to mean that they are one. [Note: [Col. 0779] The common editions read *nec quod dicitur*, and shortly afterward *desistent*, both of which are inferior.]

## 8

Let the most foolish of mortals depart; indeed, let them descend alive into hell (Psalm 54:16), as the Psalmist testifies. There, seeing the teacher of their impiety, let them cry out: [Note: [Col. 0779] Martianaeus noted that this passage is repeated from Ezekiel, although it is not found in precisely this form in our copies. Since Theophilus was reciting the passage from memory, it is credible that he repeated the same ideas in different words.]

“You also are captured as we are;
you have been counted among us;
your glory has descended into hell,”

and the rest.

Such a shepherd of a diseased flock everywhere assails Christ with insults and exalts the devil in honor, asserting that the devil, once cleansed of vices and sins, will someday recover his former glory, while Christ will cease to reign and, together with the devil, be placed under the Father’s rule.

Thus the astonished prophet might cry out more at Origen’s blasphemies than at the outcry of the Jews: [Note: [Col. 0779] Martianaeus noted that these words are taken from the Greek: “Heaven was amazed at this, and trembled exceedingly,” and so forth. The Vulgate differs: “Be astonished, heavens, at this, and be desolate at its gates exceedingly,” and so forth.]

“Heaven was astonished at this,
and was greatly horrified, says the Lord,
because it has committed two evils” (Jeremiah 2:12).

Origen, asserting that Christ will cease to reign and that the devil will climb again to the summit from which he had fallen, digs for himself such a deep pit of wickedness that it cannot hold water. As far as lies within him, he makes the Son of God equal to the devil, stripping Him of the glory of everlasting kingship and subjecting Him, together with the demons, to the Father’s authority. [Note: [Col. 0779] The earlier text read: “he made the devil equal to the Son of God.”]

But let this impious utterance be trampled down, so that we may know Christ’s kingdom to be perpetual. He Himself says to His disciples: “You have remained with me in my temptations, and I establish for you an eternal covenant, so that you may always eat and drink at my table in my kingdom” (Luke 22:28–29). How can the word “always” be fulfilled unless the kingdom is perpetual and closed by no end?

The Magi also understood this. Converted to repentance, they diligently asked: “Where is he who has been born King of the Jews? For we saw his star in the East and came to worship him” (Matthew 2:22). The Magi confess Christ to be King, while Origen denies it, saying that He will not reign forever; and he does not notice that he resembles the blasphemies of the Jews.

## 9

We read in the Gospel that, when the Lord and Savior was ascending the cross and displaying an exemplary sign of His strength and patience, Pilate wrote a title and placed it above His head. It was written: “Jesus the Nazarene, King of the Jews” (John 19:19).

Many of the Jews read this title, which was written in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin. The chief priests and the Jews therefore said to Pilate: “Do not write, ‘King of the Jews,’ but that he said, ‘I am King of the Jews.’” Pilate answered: “What I have written, I have written” (ibid., 29).

Since Pilate could be induced neither by sedition nor by entreaties to remove Christ’s kingdom from the title, let Origen know that he does without any necessity what the Jews did when he supposes that Christ’s kingdom must end.

They denied a King who had been placed upon earth; Origen, for his part, attempts as far as he can to detract from Him who reigns in heaven, so that Pilate may stand as the accuser of his crime—the Pilate who answered the Jews: “What I have written, I have written.”

Let the prophetic word also come forward and proclaim Christ’s kingdom with complete freedom:

“Rejoice, daughter of Zion;
proclaim it, daughter of Jerusalem;
be glad and exult with all your heart,
daughter of Jerusalem” [variant: Israel].
“The Lord has taken away your iniquities;
he has redeemed you from the hand of your enemies.
The King of Israel is in your midst;
you shall no longer see evils” (Zephaniah 3:14, from the Greek).

For He will not cast down from heaven a second time those whom He once saved, abandoning them, according to Origen’s ravings and fables, so that they might again fall from the heights.

The statement “You shall no longer see evils” [variant: “you shall no longer see”] is an indication of eternal security. Those who have once been delivered and have enjoyed possession of the kingdom of heaven will never be dragged down to earth by vices, nor deprived of God’s help. According to the prophetic utterance, He will place a wall and a surrounding rampart around them, enclosing them by His own power.

Hence the Psalmist sings: “He who dwells in Jerusalem shall not be moved forever” (Psalm 124). And the Lord declares: “I will not abandon you, nor forsake you.”

It is useless to dream that souls ascend into heaven and descend again, now advancing and now falling to lower regions, so that they may die repeatedly through innumerable falls and Christ’s Passion may be rendered fruitless.

For He who once died for us has given us the eternal joy of His victory, which no mass of vices can diminish [variant: restrain]. No human being will die repeatedly, as Origen dared to write—a most impious doctrine of the Stoics, which he desires to support by the authority of the divine Scriptures.

[Col. 0781]

## 10. CHRIST WILL SUFFER FOR THE DEMONS

But why do we recall these things, when he has fallen into such great [Note: [Col. 0781] The editions printed up to this point read *in tantam eruperit victoriam*, “has broken forth into such a great victory,” through an obvious error. We correct it here from the often-mentioned manuscript. We had long conjectured that *vecordiam*, “insanity,” must once have been read from a similar passage in the *Letter to Evangelus*, where Jerome says that he marvels that someone who equated deacons with presbyters had fallen into such great insanity.] insanity—indeed, madness—that he adds another crime against the Savior, saying that He is also to be crucified in the heavens for demons and spiritual wickednesses?

He does not understand into what deep abyss of impiety he is falling. For if Christ suffered for human beings and became man, as the utterances of Scripture testify, Origen will consequently have to say that, since He is to suffer for demons, He will become a demon. Necessity will force him to infer this, lest he appear to depart from what he has begun, imitating the blasphemies of the Jews [Note: [Col. 0781] From the same manuscript we have received a more complete and also more accurate sentence. The older copyists shortened it because of the occurrence of similar words, *imitetur* and *imitatur*. Previously the sense was incomplete: “he appears to differ, an imitator of the Jews. For they likewise spoke similarly of Christ …”; or, much more corruptly in other editions: “he imitates, and they likewise …”], whom he always imitates.

For they too spoke similarly of Christ: “You have a demon”; and, “By Beelzebul, the prince of demons, he casts out demons” (Luke 11:15).

But far be it from us to believe that Christ will suffer for demons, lest He Himself become a demon. Those who believe this crucify Him again and hold the Son of God up to contempt (Hebrews 6:6). He will not, just as He took hold of Abraham’s seed, also take up the demons [variant: a demon], so as to be crucified for them as well.

Nor, seeing God suffering for them, will demons cry out with the prophet: “He bore our sins and suffers for us.” Nor will they say with Isaiah: “By his bruise we were healed” (Isaiah 53:4). Christ will not be led like a sheep to sacrifice for demons, as He was for the human race; nor will it be said for their salvation: “He did not spare his own Son” (Jeremiah 11).

For demons will not cry out: “He was delivered up for our sins and rose for our justification” (1 Corinthians 11). Paul indeed writes: “For I delivered to you as of first importance what I also received: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures” (1 Corinthians 15). He calls the Scriptures as witnesses and wishes to establish through their authority what might be doubted. Origen, however, attempts to do violence to the truth without any testimony from the divine voice, seeking to find it after extinguishing the lamp.

## 11

A supporter of demons rather than of human beings, he attacks the Son of God with repeated calumnies and crucifies Him again, not understanding into what deep and dreadful gulf of impiety he is being dragged.

For it follows that whoever accepts the earlier propositions must also accept what follows. Whoever says that Christ is crucified for demons must also accept that it must be said to them: “Take and eat: this is my body. And: Take and drink: this is my blood” (Matthew 26:26). If He is crucified for demons, as the advocate of these new doctrines asserts, what privilege or what reason would there be for human beings alone to share in His body and blood [Col. 0782] and not the demons as well, for whom He poured out His blood in His Passion?

But demons will not hear: “Take and eat,” or, “Take and drink.” Nor will the Lord abolish His own commands, for He says to the disciples: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor throw your pearls before swine, lest they perhaps trample them under their feet and, turning, tear you apart” (Matthew 7).

And the Apostle, writing, “I do not want you to become participants with demons. You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons; you cannot share in the table of the Lord and the table of demons” (1 Corinthians 10), demonstrates by these words that it is impossible for demons to drink from the Lord’s cup or to share at His table.

The devil’s food is those who deny God, as Habakkuk says: “His chosen foods” (Habakkuk 1). But the food of all the impious is the devil himself, as the prophet’s oracle resounds: “You gave him as food to the peoples of Ethiopia” (Psalm 73:14).

All these things prove that Christ cannot be crucified for demons, lest demons become participants in His body and blood.

## 12

Since the Apostle also declares concerning the Savior, “He did this once, offering himself” (Hebrews 7:27), while Origen contradicts that statement with such confidence, it is time to bring forward the words: “Earth, earth, hear the word of the Lord; write down this man as rejected” (Jeremiah 22).

What hell can receive such evils? What Tartarus can even conceive of such things? What madness of giants has proved so rebellious and built such a tower of impiety? What wanton lust, wasting away in love of demons, has spread open the legs of its mind to every passing doctrine [Note: [Col. 0782] Martianaeus and other printed editions incorrectly read *dogmatis*, “of doctrine.” The manuscripts are corrected to *dogmati*, “against doctrine,” as is also clear from the immediately following phrase, *toto corde*, “with all his heart”; the Benedictine edition has *toto orbe*, “throughout the whole world.”]?

Who has drunk so deeply from the Sodomitic vine that, intoxicated by its wine of fury, he has fallen with all his heart? Who has been so watered by the streams of Babylon that he abandoned the living fountains of Israel? Who, leaving Jerusalem and imitating Jeroboam son of Nebat, built so many altars of error and kindled profane incense upon the altars (1 Kings 12)? [Note: [Col. 0782] The Benedictine edition again reads incorrectly *ararum profanatura*. The correct two words are *profana thura*, “profane incense,” a reading also found in the more carefully corrected editions of the printed text.]

Why do Dathan and Abiram, who committed lesser sins, not come before Christ’s tribunal and condemn him by comparison with themselves—him who, outside the Savior’s Church, filled censers of varied doctrines with diabolical fire?

The Lord who speaks through the prophet, “I multiplied visions, and I was represented in the hands of the prophets” (Hosea 12:10, according to the Septuagint), did not teach him to produce adulterous doctrines. Nor did those who saw and served Him from the beginning, nor the chorus of prophets, who were once called “seers,” instruct him in these things.

Rather, relying on the judgment of his own mind, serving the fury of demons, and deceived by the seductive error of his thoughts, he poured a flock—or, so to speak, a swarm—of perverse doctrines throughout the whole world into the minds of the unlearned.

He is the one who opened his mouth to the Assyrian and Babylonian rivers, who attempted to cover with waves the ship of the Church, full of the good merchandise of saving doctrine [Note: [Col. 0782] The Ambrosian manuscript reads: “to cover with the salty waves of doctrine the ship full of good merchandise” [Col. 0783] and so forth. Perhaps *salsis* was formerly written *falsis* or *falsae*. For the present, the incongruous reading is itself not impossible.], while he is lifted up by the praise of the unlearned [Note: [Col. 0783] The editions printed up to this point incorrectly read *Imperatorum laude*, “by the praise of emperors,” instead of *imperitorum laude*, “by the praise of the unlearned.” Martianaeus even invents in the margin of the book a reference to Mammæa, the mother of the emperor Alexander, who had summoned Origen. We do not deny that Origen enjoyed great favor and commendation among the emperors themselves, nor do we question the letters he sent to Philip and his wife. We assert only that these matters have nothing to do with the present passage and that the false reading is to be corrected from the Ambrosian manuscript, as the context itself makes clear.] and, expounding the meaning of the Scriptures otherwise than truth requires, glories in his own confusion.

Who has written such innumerable books, so loquacious and full of verbosity and ignorance, and joined days to nights in tireless labor, that, leaving behind monuments of error, he deserved to hear: “You have been deceived by your many journeys”?

For he used a most evil guide, popular applause, and many volumes written out with false knowledge. Fighting against God with a rebellious mind, he mixed a kind of pus and the stench of his own foulness into the ointment of heavenly teachings, so that it might again be said to his soul: “Unclean and infamous, and excessive in iniquities.”

He did not wish to hear the prophet’s warning: “Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?” (Psalm 4:3). He is the one who affixes Christ to the cross for demons, so that He may become mediator not only of God and human beings but also of demons.

But far be it from us to believe such monstrous wickedness concerning the Savior: that He will lose the temple of His body, which He deigned to raise up for us, and affix to Himself another temple of demonic condition, so that, having assumed their likeness also, He might undergo the cross for them.

## 13

I beseech you, dearest brothers, to forgive my grief as I resist impious doctrines. In attempting to strike back at the shamelessness of his followers, I have brought into the open the structure of his armor and the deceits of his poisoned breast, so that this saying might also be fulfilled in him: “I will reveal your shame and display it to your lovers” (Ezekiel 16:36).

Among other things, he also corrupts and violates the resurrection from the dead, which is the hope of our salvation, daring to say that our bodies will indeed be raised, but in such a way that they will again be subject to corruption and death.

Answer me, head of impiety: how, according to the Apostle Paul, did Christ conquer the one who held the power of death—that is, the devil—if corruptible and mortal bodies are to rise again? What benefit did Christ’s Passion bring us if death and corruption are again to possess our bodies?

Or what does the Apostle mean when he writes, “For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive” (1 Corinthians 15), if savage death is to rule over those who rise? Or how can those who believe these things sincerely say, “Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24), when they wish death to be stronger than He—death which will destroy bodies raised by Him, so that He will not be shown to have conquered it in every respect?

But our Lord Christ, against Origen who resists so impiously, conquered both death and the devil, who held the power of death, and destroyed him by His own power [Col. 0784], preparing for us in heaven the triumph of His victories.

He will not raise bodies so that they may perish again; rather, for their perpetual incorruption, He has abolished death and corruption.

14. Therefore, freed from all evils, let us celebrate the feasts of the Lord’s Passion and, in accordance with the Gospel parable (Matt. 22), seeing that Wisdom sacrifices bulls and fattened animals, let us feed on stronger fare, rich in sinew, and on the fattier foods of doctrine, so that, abandoning the milk of infancy, we may receive more solid nourishment and flee the cause of all evils: ignorance. This, after binding the feet of many with various heresies, especially enjoys its lover Origen, who among other things dared to say that it is permissible not to pray to the Son, nor to the Father together with the Son. Thus, after many ages, he revived Pharaoh’s blasphemy, who said: “Who is he, that I should obey his voice? I do not know the Lord, and I will not release Israel” (Exod. 5:2).

To say “I do not know the Lord” is nothing other than what Origen says: “The Son is not to be prayed to”—although we certainly confess him as Lord [Note: [Col. 0784] Ambrose likewise confesses this, but in another sense. In the following text from Isaiah, the words “and in you they will pray” derive from the Greek καὶ ἐν σοὶ προσεύξονται, whereas the Vulgate rejects the preposition *in*.]. And although he has burst forth into such open blasphemy, nevertheless he to whom the Prophet bears witness must be prayed to, when he says: “And they will worship you, and in you they will pray, because God is in you, and there is no God besides you” (Isa. 45:14). And again: “Everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved” (Rom. 10:13). Paul, too, arguing the point, says: “How will they call upon him in whom they have not believed?” (ibid., v. 14). One must first believe that he is the Son of God, so that his invocation may be right and fitting. And just as he who is not God is not to be prayed to, so conversely he who is established to be God must be worshiped and prayed to.

Thus Stephen also, kneeling and imploring on behalf of those who were stoning him, said to the Son: “Lord, do not hold this sin against them” (Acts 7). Likewise, “at the name of Jesus every knee shall bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth.” The statement “every knee shall bow” is an indication of earnest and most humble prayer. Therefore Origen does not believe the Son of God to be God, since he does not think him [Note: [Col. 0784] The account that Origen taught, in his work entitled *On Prayer*, that one should not pray to the Son of God but only to the Father, and not to the Father together with the Son, is transmitted elsewhere by Theophilus, especially in the Synodical Letter which we have published. Origen did allow prayer to the Son, but only insofar as he was invoked as Mediator and with a lower form of prayer than that offered to the Father—an utterly insane position. The Alexandrian bishop therefore argues from this that Origen did not believe the Son of God to be God, since he did not think him worthy of prayer. Hence it is clear that the earlier editions read corruptly, “whom he does not think worthy of worship”; for Origen had not held that view. Rather, from his position concerning invocation of Christ, this could be deduced only as a consequence of his error. The Ambrosian manuscript informed us of the genuine reading.] worthy of prayer, and he assails him with insults. Although he flatters himself on his memory of the Scriptures and thinks that he understands them, he does not hear Moses speaking against him: “The man who curses God shall bear his sin, and he who names the name of the Lord shall die the death; the whole congregation shall stone him” (Lev. 24:16).

But who heaps such great insults upon Christ as does this man, who dared to say, “He ought not to be prayed to,” granting him only an empty and void name of divinity?

15. But why is it necessary to linger over such impious matters? Let us pass to another of his errors. He says that the bodies which rise will, after many ages, be dissolved into nothingness, and that there will be future bodies only when souls, having fallen from the heavenly dwelling places to the lower regions, require new bodies, which will again be made, while the former bodies are entirely destroyed [Note: [Col. 0785] Both printed editions and manuscripts are mistaken when they impose on us the reading “new,” namely, bodies which souls fallen to the lower regions would require, the former bodies having been dissolved into nothingness. We did not hesitate to correct this obvious and frequently occurring error by conjecture.].

Who, hearing this, would not tremble both in mind and body? For if bodies are reduced to nothingness after the resurrection, the second death will be stronger than the first, since it will be able completely to destroy bodily substance. Why does Paul write: “Death will no longer have dominion over him; for the death he died to sin, he died once for all” (Rom. 6:10), if bodies are to be utterly destroyed? Or how will the word “once” remain firm, when the flesh, separated from the companionship of the soul, is to be reduced to nothingness?

For what reason did he add again: “It is sown in corruption, it will rise in incorruption; it is sown in weakness, it will rise in power; it is sown in dishonor, it will rise in glory; it is sown an animal body, it will rise a spiritual body” (1 Cor. 15)? If incorruption reduces bodies to nothingness, it would have been consistent to say that they are reserved forever for corruption, and corruption would be stronger than incorruption [Note: [Col. 0785] The manuscripts read: “For if corruption reduces bodies to nothingness, corruption would be stronger than incorruption.” This latter reading is preferable; others, following the printed editions, have “incorruption stronger than corruption.”].

But far be it from Paul to write things contrary to himself, or for incorruption and corruption to have the same nature. If, as Origen falsely thinks, not merely a corruptible but also a mortal body is to be raised, then corruption and incorruption, death and life, will be called one and the same thing; they will exercise the same power over the bodies that have been raised; and corruption and incorruption, death and life, will be distinguished not in reality but only in name.

But if a corruptible and mortal body is to rise, it would have been more consistent for the Apostle to say: “It is sown in corruption, it will rise in corruption; it is sown in weakness, it will rise in weakness; it is sown in dishonor, it will rise in dishonor; it is sown an animal body, it will rise an animal body.”

If, however, he removes corruption, weakness, and dishonor from the bodies that have been raised, and says, on the contrary, that bodies are to be clothed in incorruption, strength, and glory, and that in place of an animal body a spiritual body is to be given, then death will be dissolved, and in the bodies that have been raised immortality and incorruption will reign in place of death and corruption. For the body itself will rise immortal and incorruptible, so that it may remain coeternal with the soul.

Therefore the Savior also, giving our bodies the pledge of salvation in the resurrection of his own body, cannot be believed to die again, since the Apostle agrees with this judgment: “Christ, having risen from the dead, dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him” (Rom. 6:9). If death did not have dominion over him, neither will it have dominion over us.

16. Magic is not an evil. — Let Origen be confounded, since, among the other kinds of wickedness that he fabricates, he also offers protection to magical arts. For in his treatises he spoke these words:

“Magic does not seem to me to be the name of any existing thing; but even if it is, it is not an evil work” [Note: [Col. 0786] In Martianay’s edition, *quam* was printed corruptly in place of *nam*; other editions have *quod*. The Ambrosian manuscript supplied the correction. By the treatises he mentions, understand the two dialogues *On the Resurrection*, as we noted in the Synodical Letter, no. 5.].

—“so that no one may hold it in contempt” [Note: [Col. 0786] The Benedictine edition likewise reads “so that no one may hold it in contempt”; other printed editions have “so that it cannot be held in contempt,” or “so that no one may regard it as contemptible,” and similar forms. Terence, *Phormio*: “So that a citizen might not admit anything shameful against himself.” In the meantime, the reading we have preferred is more consistent with the manuscripts and with the Synodical Letter, where this opinion of Origen is quoted in precisely the same words from the books *On the Resurrection* which he wrote to Ambrose.].

In saying this, he clearly shows himself to be a supporter of Elymas the magician, who opposed the Apostles, and of Jannes and Jambres, who resisted Moses by magical arts. But Origen’s defense will have no force, because Christ destroyed the tricks of magicians by his coming.

Let the advocate of this new impiety answer—or rather, let him hear plainly: if magic is not evil, idolatry also will not be evil, since it relies upon the powers of magic. But if idolatry is evil, magic too will be evil, since idolatry derives its existence from it. And since idolatry has been destroyed by the majesty of Christ, this shows that its parent, magic, has likewise been dissolved along with it, as the Prophet clearly proclaims: “Stand now in your enchantments and in your many sorceries, which you learned from your youth, if they can profit you” (Isa. 47:12).

Since the writings of the Prophets testify to this, and no one has ever dared to hand down to memory that the arts of magicians should be counted among the best things, while public laws also punish magicians and sorcerers, I cannot understand what moved Origen—who boasts that he is a Christian—to imitate the false prophet Zedekiah and make iron horns for himself, with which he might go armed against the doctrines of truth, while understanding nothing of the heavenly Jerusalem and imitating neither Moses, nor Daniel, nor Peter, nor the other saints who, standing as if in battle array against magicians and enchanters, fought with unwearied struggle.

With these saints let us lead the dances of the festal day, because, passing through the dangers of Babylon, we have avoided Origen’s poisons [al. “we avoid them”] and obeyed the words of the Prophet who commands: “Go out from Babylon, you who flee from the land of the Chaldeans” (Jer. 50:8), so that we might enter Jerusalem, where the preaching of truth is found.

17. Although, while resisting falsehood, we have suffered something like the three young men who overcame the nature of the flames in the furnace of blazing fire, nevertheless the Babylonian fire did not prevail against us, nor were our hairs burned (Dan. 3:94)—that is, the extreme doctrines of ecclesiastical truth. Nor were our garments changed, which the wisdom of Holy Scripture has woven for us as a protection for our souls [Note: [Col. 0787] The same manuscript reads: “Nor is Origen’s flame of perverse knowledge running through us.” The printed reading is certainly incomplete, since the sense requires something further; one should perhaps read “with the flame of perverse doctrine running through us,” or insert a negative particle: “nor is the flame of perverse doctrine…” Compare below the letter of St. Epiphanius to John of Jerusalem, in our recension, 51, no. 4.].

Nor is there in us the smell of fire, the flame of perverse knowledge spreading through us. For we have not assented to the doctrine of the man who, because of the fall of rational creatures, supposes that bodies came into being. Following the etymology of the Greek word, he says that souls are so called because they lost the warmth of the mind and their most fervent love for God, and that they received their name from their coldness—lest we should also think that the soul of the Savior was subject to the same absurdities.

Nor do we maintain that the courses of the sun, moon, and stars, and the whole world’s most beautiful harmony in diversity, came about through preceding causes, various sins, and the vices of souls. Nor do we say that God’s goodness waited for a long time, so that he would not make visible creatures until invisible creatures had sinned.

Nor do we call bodily substance vanity, as he supposes, thereby falling, in other words, into the doctrines of Manichaeus [*concedens*, “conceding,” in one manuscript], lest the body of Christ also be subject to vanity. Of that body we are nourished, and every day we chew again the words of him who says: “Unless someone eats my flesh and drinks my blood, he will not have a share with me” (John 13).

For if corporeal nature is vain and futile, according to Origen’s error, why did Christ rise from the dead? Why will he raise our bodies? What does Paul mean when he writes: “If the dead do not rise, neither has Christ risen; but if Christ has not risen, our faith is vain” (1 Cor. 13)?

18. From this it is evident that it is not the nature of bodies that is vain, but those who do not think that it will rise and remain forever believe in vanity [Note: [Col. 0787] The same manuscript reads: “but those who think that it will rise and not remain forever believe in vanity.”].

Let him also despise honorable marriage, denying that bodies exist unless souls first sinned in heaven, so that, cast down from there, they might be bound as though in certain prisons of the body. Let him think as he wishes and speak as he dares [Note: [Col. 0787] The printed reading is scarcely satisfactory, and the manuscripts do not help. The Ambrosian manuscript reads: “Let him think as he speaks, so that he does not fear.” Nothing suitable can be extracted from these readings unless *non timet* is retained, in the sense that Origen, being a eunuch, did not fear that souls should descend from heaven on his account.]. Let him hear us, crying out with Paul into his own ears: “Marriage is honorable, and the bed undefiled” (Heb. 13:4).

And how is it undefiled if a soul stained by vices is surrounded by flesh? Will Anna, the wife of Elkanah, also be subject to guilt because she asked for male offspring, so that, on account of a woman’s desire, souls in heaven might be endangered and one of them might fall to earth through sin [Note: [Col. 0787] The printed editions read “through a grave sin.” The following words of our Theophilus, which we once copied from a very ancient catena on Genesis in Vatican manuscript 747, are especially relevant here and in the passages below concerning the descent of souls into bodies after they had sinned:

Ὅτι οὐ δι’ ἁμαρτίας αἱ ψυχαὶ, ὡς Ὠριγένει ἔδοξε, καταβεβλημέναι σώματι συνεπλάκησαν, ἐχρησάμεθα τῷ Μωσέως ῥήματι λέγοντι (perhaps λέγοντος) τοῖς υἱοῖς Ἰσραήλ· Κύριος ὁ Θεὸς ὑμῶν προσθείη ὑμῖν σήμερον ὡς ἔστι χιλιοπλασίως, καὶ εὐλογήσαι ὑμᾶς καθότι ἐλάλησεν ὑμῖν· οὐ γὰρ εὐλογία κατὰ Ὠριγένην ἐστὶν ἡ τῶν σωμάτων ποίησις· ἀλλὰ κατάρα πλανωμέναις ψυχαῖς.

“That it may be established that souls were not cast down and joined to bodies because of sin, as seemed to Origen, let us use the words of Moses, who says to the children of Israel: ‘May the Lord your God increase you today a thousandfold as you are, and bless you as he spoke to you.’ For, according to Origen, the production of bodies is not a blessing but a curse for wandering souls.”].

and abandon its former blessedness?

Nor was Moses, when he prayed and said, “May the Lord, the God of your fathers, multiply you, and behold, you are today as numerous as the stars of heaven. May the Lord, the God of your fathers, add to you a thousandfold as you are, and bless you as he has spoken” (Deut. 1:10–11), asking that the heavenly multitudes of souls, after sinning, should establish the nation of Israel.

The contradiction is perfectly clear. The man who had prayed on behalf of the people’s sin, “If you forgive this sin of the people, forgive it; but if not, blot me out of the book which you have written” (Exod. 32:32, according to the Greek), would not, if he knew that the children of Israel were increasing through the ruin of souls, pray instead for their multiplication, lest, because of the vices of the better substance, the inferior nature should be created [Note: [Col. 0788] We have somewhat repaired this passage by adding *si* from a manuscript.].

Why does David pray in the Psalm: “May the Lord bless you from Zion, and may you see the good things of Jerusalem all the days of your life, and may you see your children’s children” (Ps. 128:5), if the race of a righteous man is increased through the expulsion and destruction of souls [Note: [Col. 0788] The Ambrosian manuscript has the shorter reading: “if the race of a righteous man is increased through the sin of souls?”]?

And he dares to say: “Behold, thus shall the man be blessed who fears the Lord” (ibid., v. 4), although he knows that sinful souls are bound in the chains of bodies and, in such a prison, suffer the punishment of their sins by God’s judgment?

How does God speak through the Prophet: “If you had listened to my commandments, your peace would have been like a river, and your righteousness like the waves of the sea, and your offspring like the sand, and the issue of your womb like the dust of the earth” (Isa. 48:18–19, from the Greek)? Those who preserve God’s commandments ought not to receive as a reward the ruin of souls from heaven, souls which, bound to bodies, would multiply the growth of their offspring.

But if they wish to learn what the origins of the human race are, let them hear Moses say: “God took from the earth and formed the human being, and breathed into his face the breath of life, and the human being became a living soul” (Gen. 2:7)—that is, an immortal soul. And God, blessing Adam and Eve, said: “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth” (Gen. 9:1, 7).

19. If souls are sent into the lands after sin, to be born in bodies, it was unreasonable to bless Adam and Eve, since the cause of sin would rather have deserved a curse. Indeed, after he had formed them, he followed with words of blessing those whom he later struck with a curse when they sinned by their own will.

From this it follows that the nature of bodies did not come into being because of the sins of souls [Note: [Col. 0788] The printed reading, “to have undergone,” gives a less fitting sense. This passage proves that the production of bodies, and the nature of bodies in general, did not arise because of the sins of souls. We restore the reading from the Ambrosian manuscript.].

Let them hear him say again: “I made the earth, and the human being upon it” (Jer. 27:5 [LXX]; 32:17 in the Hebrew tradition) [Note: [Col. 0788] According to the Septuagint this is 31:5, but it is not found in this form in Jeremiah. It departs even from the Greek exemplars; Jerome evidently recited it from memory in this manner.]. And David says: “The heaven of heavens belongs to the Lord, but the earth he gave to the children of human beings” (Ps. 113).

Let them cease henceforth to follow the errors of their own thoughts and be guided instead by the authority of Scripture. For just as those who have been weakened by pleasures, and whose breast is ruled by lust, when contemplating the beauty of bodies do not seek the beauty of character but that of limbs—and their understanding, weighed down by earthly filth, sees nothing higher—so those who are led by the elaborate arrangement of words, and captivated by the sound of eloquence, do not look upon the truth of doctrines. They are ashamed to confess their former error and, blinded by the swelling of arrogance, refuse to become disciples, lest, after being corrected, they should appear to have previously gone astray.

20. Therefore, having cast aside Origen’s evils and passed over the snares of the Scriptures called apocryphal [al. “apocryphal and hidden”], that is, hidden—“For I have not spoken in secret,” says the Lord (John 18:20)—I again and again beseech you, dearest brothers: let us celebrate the feasts of the Lord’s Passion, adorning faith by our conduct [Note: [Col. 0789] The same manuscript reads: “showing mercy to the poor, let us imitate God.” Shortly afterward, in the same manuscript, we read “in all people,” where the printed editions have “toward all people.”].

Let us imitate God in mercy toward the poor, for no form of bodily nature is like him. Let us bear the image of his goodness in all things. Let us correct our errors through repentance. Let us pray for our enemies and entreat God for our detractors, imitating Moses, who by prayer wiped away the guilt of his sister when she spoke against him.

With the oil of almsgiving let us wash away the filth of sins. Let us regard the bonds of captives as binding us, and let us implore God’s favor upon them. Let daily humaneness sustain those confined in prison. Let us serve with solicitous care those whose bodies are seized by the royal disease and whose limbs are dissolved by continual wasting, for the sake of the reward stored up in heaven.

Whenever the power of judgment has been given to us and the case of disputing brothers has been brought before us, let there be no consideration of persons but of facts. When people are falling and placed in tribulation, let us also fall with them in sympathy. Let the laws uphold the norm of truth. Let charity be inclined toward mercy, not insulting those who sin but grieving with them; for the fall into vices is easy, and the weakness of human condition ought to fear in itself whatever it sees in another.

When someone has been corrected for an error, let his amendment be our warning. And above all, as the summit and crown of the virtues, let devotion toward God be preserved with fear from the whole heart. While execrating the plurality of gods, let us confess the one and undivided substance of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, in whom we have also received eternal life through baptism.

And if God’s mercy grants it, we shall be worthy to celebrate the Lord’s Pascha with the angels, beginning Lent on the eighth day of the month called Phamenoth according to the Egyptians [Note: [Col. 0789] The manuscript reads *Phamenoth*. The reference indicates that Lent began on March 4, Holy Week on April 8, and Easter Sunday was celebrated on the fourteenth day of that month—namely, in the year 401—as can be clearly inferred from these indications of the Roman months.].

With him supplying strength, let us fast more attentively, laying the foundations of Holy Week, that is, of venerable Easter, on the thirteenth day of the month Pharmuthi. Let us finish our fasts, in accordance with the evangelical traditions, at the dead of night on the eighteenth day of the aforementioned month Pharmuthi. On the following day, which is the symbol of the Lord’s resurrection—that is, on the nineteenth day of the same month—let us celebrate the true Pascha.

Let us add to these the remaining seven weeks, in which the feast of Pentecost is woven, and let us make ourselves worthy of communion in the Body and Blood of Christ. Thus we shall deserve to receive the kingdoms of heaven in Christ Jesus our Lord, through whom and with whom glory and dominion belong to God the Father, with the Holy Spirit, now and always and throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

581 21 [Note: [Col. 0790] The Ambrosian manuscript does not contain what follows.]

“Greet one another with a holy kiss. The brothers who are with me greet you.”

## LETTER XCVII [Note: [Col. 0790] Elsewhere numbered 78. Written in the year 402.]

### TO PAMMACHIUS AND MARCELLA

He sends another Paschal letter of Theophilus against Origen, which he has rendered into Latin; and because the Origenists had falsely accused him of altering the previous letter, he now joins the Greek exemplar to his translation, and briefly attacks the heretics.

1. [Note: [Col. 0790] He had also easily dedicated the Latin translation of the previous Paschal letter to the same Pammachius and Marcella.]

Again I enrich you with merchandise from the East, and for the first time send Alexandrian wealth to Rome. “God will come from the South, and the Holy One from Mount Pharan, from dense shade” (Hab. 3:3) [Note: [Col. 0790] From the Greek ἐξ ὄρους Φαρὰν κατασκαίου δασέος; for in the last words the Vulgate begins a new verse with a different sense.].

Hence the bride also rejoices in the *Song of Songs*, saying: “In his shadow I desired and sat, and his fruit was sweet in my throat” (Song 2:3).

Now Isaiah’s prophecy is truly fulfilled: “On that day there will be an altar of the Lord in the midst of the land of Egypt” (Isa. 19:19). “Where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more” (Rom. 5:20).

Those who had cherished the little Christ now defend the adult Christ with the warmth of faith, so that he who had escaped Herod’s hands through them may escape the blaspheming heretic. Demetrius drove him from the city of Alexandria [Note: [Col. 0790] It is well known that Origen, returning from Achaia and already having attained the rank of presbyter, was compelled to leave Alexandria by Demetrius, bishop of Alexandria, who was hostile to him for many reasons.]; Theophilus, to whom Luke wrote the Acts of the Apostles and who received his name from the love of God, drives him throughout the whole world.

Where now is the twisting serpent? Where is the most venomous viper?

“The first face of a man, committed to the womb of wolves” (*Aeneid* 3) [Note: [Col. 0790] He immediately takes a swipe at Rufinus, who, in the preface to the books *On First Principles* (*περὶ Ἀρχῶν*), had falsely alleged that Jerome agreed with him in Origenist doctrines—an accusation that the holy Doctor refutes in the first book of his *Apology* and elsewhere.].

Where is the heresy that hissed throughout the world, boasting that both I and Pope Theophilus shared its error, and falsely claiming our agreement through the barking of the most shameless dogs in order to deceive the simple? It has been crushed by his authority and eloquence, and, like demonic spirits, it speaks from the earth. For it does not know the one who, coming from above, speaks of the things that are above.

2. If only the serpentine generation would either simply acknowledge us as its own or consistently defend its own position, so that we might know whom to love and whom to avoid. But now there is a new kind of repentance: they hate us as enemies, although they dare not publicly deny our faith.

I ask: what is this grief that is cured neither by time nor by reason? Amid flashing swords, fallen bodies, and streams of flowing blood, hostile hands are often joined, and sudden peace changes the fury of war. These alone are followers of this heresy who cannot enter into an alliance with ecclesiastical people, because what they are forced to say with their mouths they condemn in their minds.

And whenever open blasphemy has been revealed to the ears of the public, and they see the crowd of listeners roaring against them, then, pretending simplicity, they say that they have only now heard what they had previously not known their teacher to say. While their writings are held in their hands, they deny with their voices what they confess in writing.

Why is it necessary to besiege the Propontis, to change places, to travel through different regions, and to tear apart with rabid mouths the most illustrious bishop of Christ and his disciples? [Note: [Col. 0791] The reference is evidently to Constantinople, where the Origenists had defected to St. John Chrysostom. Theophilus also laments this in the following Paschal Letter, no. 22, because they were tearing apart the mother church in the great cities.]

If you speak the truth, exchange the former ardor of error for the ardor of faith. Why do you sew together scraps of slander here and there and attack the lives of those whose faith you cannot resist? Are you therefore not heretics if some have believed, on the basis of your assertion, that we are sinners [al. “on the basis of our assertion”]? Will your mouth, defiled by impiety, not be impious if you can point out a scar in our ear?

What does your faithlessness accomplish, or what benefit do you derive from Ethiopian skin and a leopard’s variegated coat, if a blemish should appear on our body? Behold, Pope Theophilus openly charges Origen with being a heretic. His followers do not defend his statements but pretend that they were altered by heretics, and they say that the books of many others were similarly corrupted, so that they may defend him not by his own faith but by the errors of others.

Let this suffice against the heretics who, raging against us with unjust hatred, acknowledge their secret in their minds [al. “with their minds”] and testify through incurable pain to the poisons of their hearts.

3. You lights of the Christian senate, receive both the Greek and the Latin Letter this year as well, lest the heretics again lie that much has been added or changed by us. I confess that I labored in it to preserve the elegance of the words with an equal beauty of interpretation, and, running within the prescribed limits without exceeding them at any point, not to lose the flow of his eloquence, but to transfer the same matters in the same style.

Whether I have achieved this or not, I leave to your judgment. Know that it has been divided into four parts. In the first, he exhorts believers to celebrate the Lord’s Pascha; in the second and third, he strikes down Apollinarius and Origen; in the fourth, that is, the final part, he urges the heretics to repentance.

If anything has been said here less fully against Origen, it is contained in the Letter of the preceding year. This letter, striving for brevity, ought not to say more than it does. Against Apollinarius, however, a concise and pure confession of faith is not lacking in dialectical subtlety; it pierces its adversary after wrenching the dagger from his hands.

4. Therefore pray to the Lord that what is pleasing in Greek may not displease in Latin, and that what the entire East admires and proclaims Rome may receive with an open heart. May the see of the Apostle Peter also confirm by its preaching the preaching of the see of Mark the Evangelist.

Although it has been widely reported in public discourse that the blessed Pope Anastasius, moved by the same fervor because he possesses the same Spirit, pursued the heretics hiding in their holes, and although his letters teach that what was condemned in the East was condemned in the West [Note: [Col. 0792] Recall what we said above concerning Anastasius’s own Letter on this subject. We nevertheless admit that these words do not make it sufficiently clear whether he means the letter addressed to Simplicianus or another later letter addressed to Venerius.], we pray for many years for him, so that, through his zeal, the revived shoots of heresy, dried up for a long time, may die [Note: [Col. 0792] Jerome was not yet aware of Anastasius’s death. Even according to those who place it later, it is recorded on April 27 of this year, 402. More accurately, however, on the evidence of Socrates, book 7, chapter 9, and the ancient catalogues of the Roman pontiffs, it should be assigned to the middle of December of the preceding year.].

## LETTER XCVIII [Note: [Col. 0792] In some copies it has no number. Written in the year 402.]

### OR THE SECOND PASCHAL LETTER OF THEOPHILUS OF ALEXANDRIA FOR THE YEAR 402, TO ALL THE BISHOPS OF EGYPT, WITH ST. JEROME AS TRANSLATOR

First he exhorts believers to celebrate the Lord’s Pascha; then, in the second place, he attacks and destroys the errors of Apollinarius; in the third, those of Origen; finally, he urges the heretics to repentance.

1. First, the divine word of the august solemnity, flashing from the regions of heaven and surpassing the sun’s radiance with its splendor, pours the clearest light into the souls that long for it. When, with the full gaze of their hearts, they have been able to endure its rays, it draws them into the very inner chambers of the heavenly Jerusalem and, so to speak, into the Holy of Holies.

Therefore, if we wish to share in salvation, to cling zealously to the virtues, to cleanse the vices of our souls, and to wash away whatever filth is in us through continual meditation on the Scriptures, let us contemplate the open knowledge of doctrine beneath the clear sky, hasten to celebrate the feasts of heavenly joy, and join ourselves to the choirs of angels, where crowns and rewards, certain victory, and the desired palm are set before the triumphant.

Let us not delay, freed from the swelling waves of the flesh amid the various shipwrecks of pleasures on every side, in taking hold of the helm of the virtues and, after the great dangers of the sea, entering the safest harbor of heaven.

2. Therefore, awakening those whom the empty cares of this life trouble, and whom the depths of disturbances surround with a noise like roaring whirlpools, as though from a deep sleep, let us summon them to the riches of wisdom. Let us show them the true wealth of divine meanings and the inspired joys of the holy celebration.

Let all our present labor be directed toward preparing both those who are somewhat negligent and ourselves for eternal glory. Hence Wisdom, inviting those who lack understanding to her banquet in Proverbs, cries out: “Come, eat of my bread, and drink the wine that I have mixed for you” (Prov. 9:5).

For the heaven that we behold is not illuminated by choirs of stars, nor do the sun and moon—those two brightest eyes of the world, so to speak, by whose course the year unfolds and by whose alternation the seasons change—pour such a clear light upon the earth as our solemnity shines and radiates with its choir of virtues.
