Those who seek its treasures and riches [al. “those who are seeking”] sing with David’s harmonious voice: “Who will give me wings like a dove? And I will fly and rest” (Ps. 55:7).

Exulting and rejoicing in a kind of festive dance, and, as it is written, their hearts filled with inexpressible joy, they cry out again: “We have no lasting city here, but we seek the one that is to come” (Heb. 13:14), whose designer and builder is God [Note: [Col. 0793] We have corrected this by conjecture, since the sense of the passage itself requires it. The former reading, “as in all the books,” not only disturbed the meaning but completely overturned it.].

For they know that this hope has been stored up for all their labors, in which they struggle and run in this world, and that these rewards have been established for the future. Fearing no dangers for their sake, they direct the course of their lives daily, avoiding above all the impiety and snares of heretics, by which the blind lead the blind into a pit and, as though by some aged and most filthy decay, stain the hearts of those who have been deceived.

Nor content with this decay [Note: [Col. 0793] It seems highly probable to us that the word *carie* should here be repeated in place of *calce*, but we have not altered the text.], they drink in the innermost marrow of the Scriptures, condemning the truth of doctrines by a falsely named knowledge.

### 3

Understanding this, the patriarch Jacob sees in a dream a ladder whose top reached to heaven, by which one ascends to the heights through the various degrees of the virtues, and people are summoned, leaving behind the lowly things of earth, to celebrate with the Church of the first Christians the festivals of the Lord’s passion. “Surely,” he says, “this is nothing other than the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven” (Gen. 28). David, observing it with keener insight and seeking it with the whole desire of his mind, examining in thought the principles of this journey and, as though grinding and crushing precious spices with greater force so that they might spread the fragrance of their most sweet scent far and wide, summons those hastening to the solemnity, saying: “Open to me the gates of righteousness, and entering through them I will confess to the Lord: this is the gate of the Lord; the righteous will enter through it” (Ps. 117 [118]). There is therefore no solemnity belonging to heretics—none at all; nor can those who have been deceived by error rejoice in communion with it. For it is written: “If a beast touches the mountain, it shall be stoned” (Heb. 12:20). Nor can those who contradict the Church’s divine doctrines receive the sacraments of heavenly words.

Let us therefore cleanse our souls with all our strength from every contamination and prepare them worthy of the celebration that is at hand, so that we may be able to sing with the saints: “The Lord is God, and he has shone upon us” (Ps. 117 [118]). Another Prophet, likewise aware of future things, bears witness to this in a mystical utterance: “The Lord will appear among them, and he will destroy all the gods of the nations” (Zeph. 2:11).

[Note: The Greek reads Ἐπιφανὴσεται κύριος ἐπ’ αὐτούς, καὶ ἐξολοθρεύσει πάντας τοὺς θεοὺς τῶν ἐθνῶν (“The Lord will appear upon them, and he will destroy all the gods of the nations”), whereas the Vulgate has: “The Lord will be terrifying over them, and he will weaken all the gods of the earth.”]

When words have been changed into deeds and the truth of things is displayed before doubting eyes, so that through the accomplishment of what was foretold the truth of the words might be confirmed, God makes us sharers in his victory, so that we may both share with the saints in the solemnity and continually proclaim the heralding praises of his glorious coming.

For the whole earth had been corrupted by various enticements, reckoning vices as virtues and, conversely, virtues as vices. As time advanced, it considered custom to be the law of nature; the wicked had gone before with tyrannical arrogance and had strengthened falsehood by the passage of time, and they were regarded as fathers and teachers of truth. Thus it had come about that human error increased, and people, ignorant of what was useful in the manner of brute animals, despised the true shepherd, the Lord. Carried away by fury, they worshiped tyrants and rulers as gods, consecrating their own weakness in men of the same nature. In this way it happened that they escaped the immediate danger of death and won the favor of those whose clemency was more savage than cruelty.

### 4

Therefore, when all had been led astray by error, the living Word of God came to our aid upon the earth, to lands that did not know the worship of God and were enduring the desolation of truth. The witness to this is the one who says: “All have sinned; together they have become useless” (Rom. 3). And the Prophets, imploring the help of Christ, say: “Lord, bow your heavens and descend” (Ps. 143 [144]).

Not that he changed his place—he in whom all things exist—but that, for the sake of our salvation, he assumed the flesh of human weakness, as Paul sings the same truth: “Though he was rich, for our sake he became poor, so that we might become rich through his poverty” (1 Cor. 8). He came upon the earth, and, having become man and come forth from the virginal womb that he sanctified, he confirmed by his dispensation the meaning of his name, EMMANUEL—that is, “God with us.” In a wondrous manner he began to be what we are, and did not cease to be what he had been, assuming human nature in such a way that he did not lose what he himself was.

[Note: Previously the text had *interpretationem sui*, without *nominis* (“the interpretation of himself,” instead of “the meaning of his name”); we supplied *nominis* from B. P.]

Although John writes, “The Word became flesh” (John 1), that is, in other words, “man,” yet he was not changed into flesh, because he never ceased to be God. To him David also speaks: “But you are the same” (Ps. 101 [102]). And the Father bears witness from heaven and says: “You are my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Luke 2). Thus, even though he became man, our confession declares that he remains what he was before he became man, while Paul proclaims the same truth with us: “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever” (Heb. 13).

For by saying “the same,” he shows that Christ did not change his former nature, nor diminish the riches of his divinity. Though he became poor for our sake, he had assumed the complete likeness of our condition. From the same kind and quality as those from which all of us were created, he assumed man—without sin, certainly—not in part, but whole: “the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Tim. 2:5). He lacked nothing that belongs to our likeness except sin alone,

[Note: The printed editions had a most corrupt reading: “which does not have an inanimate substance without a soul” (*quod substantiam non habet inanimam sine anima*). For one cannot say that he had an inanimate flesh without a soul, and so forth. We have removed from the text the words *inanimam sine anima* (“inanimate, without a soul”), which had hitherto prevailed, without doubting that they were a gloss on the immediately following word *inanimam*. Someone diligent had written it in the margin of the book to explain what that word was intended to mean—whether *inanimam* meant the same as *sine anima*, “without a soul.” Later, through the careless ignorance of copyists, these words entered the text. To understand clearly that they mean nothing and do not belong to the sequence of the argument, recall the following passage from *Paschal Sermon* 3, whose words are almost identical with those here: “Perfect God, assuming by his own will whatever belonged to human nature and condition, except sin alone and wickedness, which has no substance, is born an infant,” and so forth. Likewise, this passage from *Paschal Sermon* 3: “The living Word of God, leaving nothing of our likeness except sin alone, which has no substance, graciously deigned in a new manner to come to us.” Here he says that sin—which is nothing other than transgression of the Law—has no substance, and consequently that it was not assumed along with human nature by the Word, as everyone can readily understand.]

which has no substance. For he did not have an inanimate flesh, with God the Word himself in it in place of a rational soul, as the disciples of Apollinaris, sunk in sleep, suppose.

Nor, when he says in the Gospel, “Now my soul is troubled” (Matt. 26:38), does he testify—or, according to another reading, “testify”—that his divinity was subject to agitation, as those are inevitably driven to say who maintain that divinity was present in his body in place of a soul. Nor, again, by joining only a soul to himself, did he complete the man whom he had assumed, lest, because of the likeness of the flesh and the dissimilarity of the soul, he be thought to have fulfilled a partial assumption. He would then be like us in flesh, but in soul like irrational animals—if, according to them, the Savior’s soul is irrational and without mind and understanding. This is impious to believe and far removed from the faith of the Church, lest he immediately be struck by the judgment with which the Prophet rebukes the sinner, saying: “Ephraim is like a senseless dove that has no heart” (Hos. 7:11).

And, as though he were irrational, let him hear: “He has been compared to foolish beasts and has become like them” (Ps. 48 [49]). For no one doubts that an irrational soul, without understanding or mind, is compared with irrational beasts. Hence Moses also writes: “You shall not muzzle an ox when it is treading out the grain” (Deut. 25). And Paul, explaining the written text, says: “Does God care about oxen? Or does he surely say this for our sake?” (1 Cor. 9:10).

### 5

The Savior therefore became man for our sake, not for the sake of brute and irrational animals, so that he might assume the likeness of the souls of beasts, without understanding and reason.

[Note: The previous reading was: “But lest the sinners of that same heresy quibble over this.” We have corrected it to: “Nor does the Church accept that which the followers of that same heresy quibble and chatter.”]

Nor does the Church accept what the followers of that same heresy quibble and chatter: that the Savior’s soul should be thought to be “the mind of the flesh,” when the Apostle plainly calls the mind of the flesh hostile to God and death (Rom. 8:7). It is impious to say this of the Lord, so that his soul would be believed to be death and hostile to God.

For if he commands us, “Do not fear those who can kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matt. 10:28), they will be forced by their foolish argument to accept that our souls are better than the Savior’s soul, since that soul is asserted to be the mind of the flesh, which is death and hostile to God, whereas ours cannot die.

But this must by no means be understood in such a way, dearest brothers. Even the mind of the soul cannot be called the soul, and the two differ greatly from each other. Although the mind belongs to the soul whose mind it is, one thing is the possessor and another the thing possessed: the first is the soul, while the second exists in the soul. If the mind of the soul is not the soul, how much more cannot the mind of the flesh be called a soul?

Let them stretch the nets of their syllogisms as far as they wish; setting out the snares of their sophistries, let them entangle themselves in traps, not even knowing what they boast of knowing in their vain knowledge. Let them learn from us—whom they gratuitously compel to undertake this sort of argument—that one thing is what is wise, another is wisdom, and another is what is apprehended.

These things differ from one another not only in words but also in meaning. That which is wise is the rational soul. That which proceeds from it and belongs to it, but is not itself that which is wise, is called wisdom. What is apprehended, however, is the thing toward which it looks; it is generated by the wise person through wisdom,

[Note: In several printed editions the words “and not the one who understands himself, nor understanding itself” are absent.]

and is neither the one who understands himself nor understanding itself.

Let them finally cease to twist the simple decrees of the Church’s faith by the turns of dialectical art, calling the Savior’s soul the mind of the flesh, which the Apostle declares to be death and hostile to God.

### 6

We must also argue against them in this way. It is written concerning the Word of God: “All things were made through him” (John 1:3). Is it believable that the mind or understanding of the flesh—which they understand to be the Savior’s soul—was created by the Word of God, so that he himself might become the author of death and hostility against God, and join these things to himself—a thought that it is impious even to utter?

If it is impious to believe this, and the Savior’s soul possesses every virtue, then the mind of the flesh will not be his soul, lest he be believed to have joined death and hostility against God to himself.

[Note: The text had one word, *subjunxisse* (“to have joined”), for which Martianaeus had noted in the margin *subornasse* (“to have added”); we have used two words, *sibi junxisse* (“to have joined to himself”). The reader may judge from the context how correct this is.]

Let the disciples of Apollinaris cease defending what he said contrary to the Church’s rules on account of his other writings. Although he wrote against the Arians and Eunomians and overthrew Origen and other heretics in his arguments, nevertheless anyone who remembers the command, “You shall not show partiality in judgment” (Lev. 19:15; Deut. 1:17), must always love the truth, not persons. He must know that, in the dispensation of the man whom the only-begotten Son of God graciously assumed for our salvation, the one who perversely understood and wrote about his soul is not free from guilt.

For just as the Apostle says, “If I spend all my possessions, and if I hand over my body so that I may burn, but do not have love, it will profit me nothing” (1 Cor. 13), so whether it is this man of whom we are now speaking, or Origen, or other heretics, even though they have written some things that do not conflict with the Church’s faith, they will nevertheless not be without guilt when, in matters that are primary and pertain to the salvation of believers, they conflict with the Church’s faith.

For our Lord and Savior did not, as he himself and his followers strive to prove, assume a soul without understanding or mind, or only a middle part of it—two parts out of three, or a third part—in order to save man imperfectly.

[Note: This point had already been observed from Nemesius above, in Letter 84, no. 3. Apollinaris learned from Platonic doctrines that *nous*, or mind and understanding, was a certain substance separable from the soul; hence he deprived the Savior of understanding and made divinity perform its function. Compare the notes there.]

For neither the middle part nor the remaining parts will receive the name “perfect.” And just as what is perfect is free from the defect of imperfection, so what is imperfect cannot be called perfect.

And if he had assumed our likeness imperfectly, or only in part, how could he have spoken in the Gospel: “No one takes my soul from me; I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again” (John 10:18)? That which is taken and laid down cannot be called irrational or without mind and understanding; on the contrary, it is rational and capable of understanding, possessing a mind and sensation.

### 7

Thus the very order of the argument proves that the Lord assumed nothing imperfect, but assumed man fully and saved him completely and perfectly. For no one doubts that the souls of irrational animals are not laid down and taken up again, but perish with their bodies and dissolve into dust.

[Note: Theodoretus quotes this passage from the Greek text of Theophilus in the third dialogue of the *Eranistes*. It will be useful to compare it with Jerome’s translation:

“Since the souls of irrational creatures are neither taken away nor laid down again, but perish together with their bodies and dissolve into dust, the Savior, having taken his own soul from its proper body at the time of the cross, placed it again in the body when he raised it from the dead. Confirming this for us, he foretold it through the Psalmist, crying out: ‘You will not abandon my soul to Hades, nor will you allow your holy one to see corruption.’”]

But the Savior, taking his soul and separating it from his body at the time of his passion, received it again in the resurrection. And long before he did this, he spoke in the Psalm: “You will not abandon my soul to Hades, nor will you allow your holy one to see corruption” (Ps. 15 [16]).

It is not believable that his flesh descended to the underworld, or that the mind of the flesh—which had been called a soul—appeared there. Rather, his body was placed in the tomb, and he did not say, concerning either his body and the wisdom of the flesh or his divinity, “You will not abandon my soul to Hades.” He spoke truly of the soul of our nature, to show that a perfect, rational, intelligible, and perceptive soul had descended to the underworld.

We exhort those who hold such opinions,

[Note: B. P. has a different reading: “that, abandoning heretical errors, they may…”]

to abandon the errors of heretics and yield to the truth of the Church. Let them not make the solemnity of the Lord’s passion imperfect by denying in the Savior the principal and greater part of man, asserting that his body was without a soul and mind.

For if this were so, what did he intend to be understood by saying: “The good shepherd lays down his soul for the sheep” (John 10)? And if he had assumed only the flesh of man, why did he say during his passion: “The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matt. 26)?

### 8

From this we must understand that, presenting the mystery of human condition in every respect in a balanced manner, he assumed the perfect likeness of our condition—not flesh alone, nor an irrational and senseless soul, but joining to himself the whole body and the whole soul. In himself he demonstrated the perfect man, so that through himself he might bestow perfect salvation on all human beings.

Sharing in our condition—for we were formed from the earth—he did not bring flesh down from heaven, nor did he join to his body a soul that had previously existed and had been created before his flesh, as the disciples of Origen strive to teach.

For if the Savior’s soul, before he assumed a human body, dwelt in the regions of heaven, and was not yet his soul,

[Note: We have left this as it appears in the printed books, since it cannot be restored without manuscript support; we did not wish to alter it merely by conjecture. Theophilus clearly perceives that, according to the teachings of the Origenists, it necessarily followed that they would be forced to say that the same soul both was and was not the Lord’s, since he joined to his body a soul that had previously existed and had been created before his flesh. That is what Adamantius devised: that Christ’s soul had been joined to the Word before it was joined to the body, a doctrine he explains at length in book 2, chapter 6, of *On First Principles*. Here, however, the words by which that meaning was to be expressed are so fragmentary, defective, and confused—both in this sentence and in the following one, apparently through the fault of copyists—that anyone attempting to supply and correct them by conjecture would seem to be wasting his labor. I nevertheless think that a little farther below, instead of “It is one thing,” we should read “We must dare,” or something similar.]

it is utterly impious to say that she was the Lord’s before the body, active and vigorous in some way, and was afterward changed into his soul.

Let them state, if they can prove it from the Scriptures, that before he was born from Mary God the Word possessed this soul, and that before the assumption of the flesh it was called his soul. But if both the authority of Scripture and reason itself compel them to accept that Christ did not have a soul before he was born from Mary—for in the assumption of man his soul too was assumed—they are plainly convicted of having to say that the same soul both was his and was not his.

[Note: The word order was faulty: “And if by the authority…” We have corrected it.]

But let them, mad with impiety toward novel doctrines, cease. Following the rule of the Scriptures, let us proclaim with complete courage of heart that neither his flesh nor his soul existed before he was born from Mary. Nor did his soul dwell previously in heaven, to be joined to him later. For the Lord brought down with him nothing of our condition from heaven.

Therefore, cutting down with the evangelical sickle whatever is contrary to the truth, he says: “Every planting that my heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted” (Matt. 15:13). By the deed he brings the threat to completion, and by the fulfillment of events proves the power of his words, so that the truth of what was done might exhibit whatever the Word had promised.

### 9. Origen Attacked

Let those who follow Origen—the hydra of all heresies, to borrow an image from the fables of the poets—and who boast that they have in him a teacher and leader of error, know that they are strangers to this solemnity and cannot celebrate the Lord’s passion with us.

For although he composed countless books and left the world an inheritance of his loquacity, like a ruinous possession, we nevertheless know that the Law commands: “You shall not set over yourself a foreign man, because he is not your brother” (Deut. 17:15).

Since he wandered by a different path from the rules of the Apostles, like one unworthy and profane of Christ’s choir and of participation in his mysteries, he is expelled from Christ’s solemnity and driven far away by the fathers and elders who founded the Church of the Savior. He strives to sew the torn and ancient rags of philosophers onto the Church’s new and most durable garment, joining falsehoods to truths so that, by their proximity, weakness may appear stronger and the beauty of the Church may be violated.

### 10. Origen’s Principal Heresies

What reasoning, what sequence of arguments led him to remove the truth from the Scriptures through the shadows of allegory and empty images? Which Prophet taught him to think that, because souls had fallen and lapsed from heaven, God had been compelled to fashion bodies?

Who, in accordance with blessed Luke (chap. 1, v. 2), handed down to him for instruction that God, provoked by the negligence, movement, and decline from higher things of rational creatures, created the diversity of this world? Moses, explaining its creation, said—

[Note: The scriptural passage has undoubtedly dropped out. It may have been: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth.” This would fit the present argument extremely well.]

—nor did he indicate, or according to another reading, “judge,” that for some preceding causes sensible things came from rational things, visible things from invisible things, and worse things from better things, which is what Origen openly proclaims.

For he says that the world began because of the sins of intelligible creatures. He is unwilling to celebrate Easter with the saints or to say with Paul: “The invisible things of God are understood and seen from the creation of the world through the things that have been made” (Rom. 1). Nor is he willing to cry out with the Prophet: “I considered your works and was astonished.”

For the beauty of the world could not otherwise have endured unless its varied adornment had filled it with creatures. In the beginning, therefore, the sun and moon—the two great lights—and the remaining stars, before becoming what the function of their daily courses shows that they were created to be, were not without bodies. Nor, as he dreams, did they abandon their original simplicity for some reason and become enclosed in bodies, thereby constructing doctrines contrary to the faith.

Nor did souls sin in the regions of heaven and therefore get banished into bodies. For if this were so, the Savior ought not himself to have assumed a body, and he should have liberated souls from bodies at the time when, in baptism, he forgives sins—immediately releasing the baptized person from the bonds of the body, which he says were made in condemnation because of sins.

Moreover, he promises the resurrection of bodies in vain if it is better for souls to fly lightly upward to heaven without the burden of bodies. He himself, when rising again, ought not to have raised his flesh, but only to have joined his soul to divinity, if it is better to live without bodies than with bodies.

### 11. On Bodies

What does he mean by repeatedly proclaiming that souls are both bound to bodies and separated from them, and by bringing many deaths upon us? He does not understand that Christ came not to release souls from bodies after the resurrection, or to clothe liberated souls again in other bodies, descending from the regions of heaven and clothing them in blood and flesh, but to grant once and for all to resurrected bodies incorruption and eternity.

[Note: Previously the text incorrectly read *Si ut* as two words. We have joined them as *Sicut* (“Just as”), so that the meaning is clear. In B. P. the reading is: “Christ died once.”]

For just as Christ, having died, does not die again, and death will no longer rule over him, so resurrected bodies neither perish a second time nor repeatedly after the resurrection; death will no longer rule over them, nor will they be dissolved into nothingness, because the coming of Christ will save the whole man.

[Variant: *salvavit*, “saved,” instead of *salvabit*, “will save.”]

### 12. On Angels

Origen is also made a stranger to Christ’s solemnity by asserting that Principalities, Powers, Virtues, Thrones, and Dominions were not created as such from the beginning, but were made worthy of some honor after their creation, when others like them had fallen to lower places through negligence; and that these were therefore called by illustrious names.

Thus, according to his error, God did not create them as Principalities and Powers and the rest; rather, the sins of others supplied them with the material for their glories.

[Note: In the Benedictine edition the text incorrectly read *dignas fecisse* (“to have made them worthy”); formerly we thought *dignas fuisse* (“to have been worthy”) should be read, but now we have preferred the reading of B. P.]

And how could the Apostle Paul write:

> “All things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, were created in Christ, whether Thrones or Dominions or Principalities or Powers; all things were created through him and in him, and he is before all things” (Col. 1),

if he understood the force of the word “through whom,” when he says that all things were created through Christ? He would surely have known that these beings were created in this way from the beginning, and that it was not the negligence of others, nor their fall to lower places, that gave God the occasion to name them Principalities, Powers, Virtues, and the rest—especially since the beauty of creation consists in an order of dignities.

[Note: The word *per quem* (“through whom”) seems more appropriately referred to Christ, since Theophilus presses the Apostle’s phrase, “all things were created through him and in him.” But if it is referred, according to the wording, to the evil one, to whom it is immediately joined, examples of such a construction may nevertheless be found among ancient grammarians, especially the older ones. A similar case is noted below, at the beginning of the Letter to Riparius concerning Vigilantius, in the words: “You ask about things which it is sacrilegious either to utter or to hear.”]

For just as it is written concerning the sun, moon, and stars: “God made two great lights: the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night, and the stars; and he placed them in the firmament of heaven to shine upon the earth” (Gen. 1)—and they did not receive the reward of good works by shining in the firmament of heaven after their creation and succeeding one another in days and nights—so we understand that the Principalities and Powers created in the regions of heaven did not advance to these positions after good works, but were created in this way from the beginning.

For we do not imitate the error of Origen and his disciples, who think that, in imitation of the demons and the devil—who by their own will obtained such names and offices—the Principalities, Powers, Virtues, Thrones, and Dominions accomplished some good after their creation, so that, when others had fallen to lower places, these might ascend to higher ones and be marked by these names, subsequently possessing what they had not possessed before.

In saying this they do not understand that they contradict Paul’s statement that the Principalities, Powers, Thrones, and Dominions were created in Christ. When he says “created,” there is no doubt that they were created in this manner from the beginning, and did not later receive such dignities.

### 13. On the Holy Spirit

But it is enough to have established these points briefly. Let us turn to another of his impieties, which he pours forth as though from the deepest darkness and has left to the world as a most evil memorial of his blasphemies.

For he says that the Holy Spirit does not operate upon things that are inanimate, nor reach irrational beings.

[Note: Through a gross error that nevertheless spread through all the books, the text read *in anima* (“in the soul”) as two words—not only here but also below, and not just once, so that one might not suppose it a typographical error. The sense clearly demands the reading we have adopted, *inanima* (“inanimate”). Compare the second volume of Origen’s commentary on John, near the end, where he taught that “all rational beings participate in Christ” (*Χριστοῦ μὲν πάντα μετέχειν τὰ λογικά*), while other things do not; and the preceding volume, where he establishes three classes of rational beings: angels, human beings, and the infernal beings, that is, demons.]

In asserting this he does not consider that the mystical waters of baptism are consecrated by the coming of the Holy Spirit; that the Lord’s bread, by which the Savior’s Body is shown and which we break for our sanctification, and the sacred cup—which are placed on the Church’s table and are certainly inanimate—are sanctified through the invocation and coming of the Holy Spirit.

If the power of the Holy Spirit does not reach irrational beings and things without a soul, why does David sing: “Where shall I go from your Spirit?” (Ps. 138 [139]:8)? By saying this he shows that all things are contained by the Holy Spirit and surrounded by his majesty. If he is “all in all,” then irrational and inanimate things are included as well.

And elsewhere we read: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the world” (Wis. 1:7).

Scripture would never have mentioned this if all irrational and inanimate things were not filled by his divine power.

But he is not content with this end of his blasphemy. Like lunatics who display their madness by gnashing their teeth and spitting foaming saliva, he again spews forth his words and says that the Son of God—that is, reason (*τὸν Λόγον*, “the Word”)—and his word and power reach only those things that are rational.

When I hear this, I wonder where he got it, or how he can fail to know that he read: “All things were made through him” (John 1). From this it is proved that the power of the Word of God reaches all things.

Perhaps he has forgotten that event when Lazarus was raised by Christ’s power. At the time when his body was rising from death to life, it was without reason no less than it was without the soul.

He has also forgotten that five thousand men, besides women and children, were satisfied with five loaves, and that twelve baskets of fragments remained (Matt. 14). Christ’s power certainly accomplished this.

I think he has not remembered that other miracle either, when Christ, treading upon the irrational waves of the sea with his divine foot, restored tranquility to those sailing. It was Christ’s power, and not the command of another, that performed this.

How, then, does he not shudder with all his heart, mind, and body when he says that the power of the Word of God cannot reach irrational creatures?

And let him who boasts of his knowledge of the Scriptures and thinks he has read as much as no human being has read know that it is written that the sick were carried on their beds and placed in the streets and squares so that Peter’s shadow might touch them and heal them (Acts 5). The sacred Acts of the Apostles testify to this, refuting Origen’s folly, by which it is proved that the shadow of the Apostle accomplished what he asserts that the Son of God, the Word of God, could not accomplish.

[Note: The text incorrectly had *per quam* (“through which”), making it refer to Origen’s folly, whereas the words should refer to the Acts of the Apostles. We have corrected it from B. P.]

### 14. On the Providence of God

Deceived by a similar error and not knowing what he is saying,

[Note: For the sense to be intelligible in any way, something has dropped out here, perhaps *factus est sectator* (“he became a follower”), or *dux* (“leader”), or something similar; it was entirely omitted through the carelessness of copyists.]

he became a follower—or perhaps a leader—of those who do not want God’s providence to descend to all creatures and to the lower regions of the world, but wish it to remain only in the regions of heaven, so that, evidently, Peter’s shadow accomplished what the Savior’s power could not accomplish.

But let us come also to this point. Since the Apostle clearly proclaims concerning the firstborn Son of God:

> “Let each person understand this in us which is also in Christ Jesus, who, though he was in the form of God, did not consider equality with God robbery, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. 2),

he dared to say that the Savior’s soul emptied itself and took the form of a servant, so that John might be believed to have lied when he said, “The Word became flesh” (John 1), presenting the Savior as like us in condition.

For it is not he himself who emptied himself and took the form of a servant, but his soul.

[Note: The text previously had *animam* in the accusative, with an opposite meaning, whereas the author’s intention plainly requires the nominative *anima*, “the soul.”]

And by his impiety he dissolves the faith established by the confession of all.

For if it is the Savior’s soul that was “in the form of God” and “equal to God,” according to Origen’s madness—and the Son of God is equal to God, while whatever is equal to God is proved to be of the same substance—then the very order of the argument leads us to believe that the soul and God are of one nature.

When he says this, it follows that he must also claim that our souls are not of a nature different from God—and that our souls and the Savior’s soul are of one substance—

[Note: It may be that *concedat* (“he should concede”) ought to be restored here. For Jerome notes, near the end of his Letter to Avitus, from book 4 of *On First Principles*, that this madness is not explicitly proposed by Origen but follows from his preceding teaching: namely, that all rational natures—the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; angels, Powers, Dominions, and the remaining Virtues; and human beings themselves according to the dignity of the soul—are of one substance.]

so that creator and creature would now be of one nature.

And how could all things have been created in Christ if human souls are of the same substance as the Creator?

But it is not so, brothers. It was not the Savior’s soul, but the Son of God himself, who, being in the form of God and equal to God, emptied himself and took the form of a servant.

Origen, however, sunk into the mire of profound impiety, does not understand that he shares in the error of the Gentiles. They worshiped idols as God, “claiming to be wise, they became fools, and they exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of the image of corruptible man” (Rom. 1).

He too, falling into this error, has been deceived by a similar mistake. By affirming that the Savior’s soul was in the form and equality of God, as the preceding discussion has shown, he is equal to the impiety of the pagans.

For just as they exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of the image of corruptible man, saying that those who were not gods were gods, so he has exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God by asserting that the Savior’s soul, which was created, was in God’s form and equality; and that this soul emptied itself, while the Word of God did not come to earthly things, as the authority of the Apostle affirms.

15. Nor is he ashamed, forgetful of himself amid his loquacity, and unwilling to call the human soul by that name from the beginning of its creation, but only because what previously was mind and perception had taken on the chill of negligence and unbelief. This etymology is more appropriate to the Greek language than to the Latin. But if he asserts that the Savior’s soul was equal to God and constituted in his form, then it too has received its name from the chill of love and has lost the dignity of its former name. For his general argument is that human souls are called *souls* because they have lost the heat of their former fervor. Therefore, if all souls, having acquired this chill, received their name from it, and he confesses that the Savior possessed a soul, it follows that he must also say that the Savior’s soul passed over from mind and perception into such a designation. Although he does not say this explicitly, and although the manifest impiety of the claim restrains his madness, necessity itself compels him to say it, since what follows is linked in order to what he said earlier. Either he must deny that the Savior possessed a soul, and thus openly contradict the authority of the Gospels; or, if he cannot speak against himself, he must also confess that this soul was named from the chill of love, having passed over from mind and perception. For he judges that all souls which have withdrawn from God and lost the warmth of divine love are called *souls* from their chill. Who could believe that he would be satisfied with this limit of sacrilege?

[Note: [Col. 0803] In all the printed editions previously, this passage had an incorrect and incoherent meaning, although the wording does not say *tace* (“is silent”) for a single word but rather *sermone* (“in speech”), as we have emended it on the basis of conjecture; for he says that this is again to follow from, not to be asserted by, his doctrine.]

[Note: [Col. 0804] It is preferable to reproduce this entire chapter from Theophilus’ own Greek text, which is found in Theodoret, *Dialogues* 2.4:

“But although he does not keep silent, he again blasphemes by slandering the Son of God and saying in these very words: ‘Just as the Son and the Father are one, so also the soul which the Son assumed and the Son himself are one.’ He does not understand that the Son and the Father are one because they possess one substance and the same divinity, whereas the soul and the Son are distinct from one another in substance and nature. For if, just as the Father and the Son are one, so also the Son’s soul and the Son himself are one, then the Father and the soul will also be one, and the soul will one day say, ‘Whoever has seen me has seen the Father.’ But this is not so—God forbid! For the Son and the Father are one because they do not differ in qualities; whereas the soul and the Son are different both in nature and in substance, since the soul too was made through him and is consubstantial with you. For if, in the same way that the Father and the Son are one, the soul and the Son are also one according to Origen, then the soul too will be, like the Son, ‘the radiance of God’s glory and the imprint of his substance.’ But this is impossible; therefore it is also impossible for the Son and his soul to be one in the same way as he and the Father are one. And what will he do when he again falls into contradiction with himself? For he writes as follows: ‘Surely the soul that was troubled and exceedingly sorrowful was not the Only-begotten and Firstborn of all creation; for the Word of God, being superior to the soul, himself—the Son—says, “I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it again.”’ If, then, the Son is superior to his own soul, as he is admittedly superior, how can his soul be equal to God and in his form? By saying that it was itself the one who emptied himself and took the form of a servant, he has made himself more notorious than the other heretics by the enormity of his impieties, as we have noted. For if the Word exists in the form of God and is equal to God, and he thinks that the Savior’s soul exists in the form of God and in his equality, daring to write thus, how can one equal be greater than another? For things that are lower in nature testify, by their being subordinate, to the superiority of those above them.”]

16. Again he attaches another slander to the Son of God and speaks in these words. [Note: [Col. 0804] The common editions have the faulty reading *Si sicut* (“If just as”), which we correct from the Greek; from that Greek, however, the passage would appear to require a change of punctuation and should be read as follows: “Just as,” etc. In Theophilus’ own text, however, *blasphemei* (“he blasphemes”), with Origen as its subject, should be read instead of *blasphemeis* (“you blaspheme”).]

“Just as the Father and the Son are one, so also the soul which the Son assumed and the Son himself are one.” Yet he does not understand that the Father and the Son are one because they share one substance and the same divinity, whereas the Son of God and his soul are of different and mutually very distant natures. For if, just as the Father and the Son are one, so also the Son’s soul and the Son himself are one, then the Father and the Savior’s soul will be one, and the soul itself will be able to say: “Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John 14:9). But this is not so; let this be far from the faith of the Church. The Son and the Father are one because there is no different nature between them; but the soul and the Son of God differ from one another both in nature and in substance, since the soul itself was created by the Son and belongs to our condition and nature. If, then, just as the Father and the Son are one, so also the soul of the Son of God and the Son himself are one, then, as we have already said, the soul and God the Father will be one; and the Savior’s soul will be believed to be the radiance of his glory and the form of his substance. But it is impious and blasphemous to say this. Therefore it is an impiety of the same kind to say that the Son and his soul are one, and to deny that the Father and the Son are one.

Again forgetful of himself, he speaks contrary to his own position. For he says: “The soul that was troubled and became sorrowful” (Mark 14:34) was not itself the Only-begotten and Firstborn of all creation, nor the Word of God, who, being superior to the condition of the soul, and truly the Son of God, was speaking in the Gospel: “I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it again” (John 10:18). Therefore, if the Son of God is better and more powerful than his soul—as no one doubts—how could his soul be in the form of God and equal to God, when he says that this soul emptied itself and took the form of a servant? [Note: [Col. 0805] In the Benedictine and other editions, this sentence was burdened with several defects. We have restored it partly from B. P. and partly by conjecture to its former purity and meaning. It previously read approximately: “when he says that he emptied himself and took the form of a servant? He surpasses all heretics,” etc.]

By the magnitude of his blasphemy he surpasses all the heretics. For if the Word of God is in the form of God and equal to God, while the Savior’s soul is in the form of God and in his equality, how can one equal be greater and another less? For things belonging to an inferior nature testify, by their own abasement, to the superiority of the higher nature and substance.

17. This blasphemy is not enough for him. Rather, directing the chariot of his folly across the rivers of Ethiopia, [Note: [Col. 0805] In B. P., the margin notes *cursum* (“course”) instead of *currum* (“chariot”).] he again raves and exults, saying that God created as many rational creatures by his will as he was able to govern, so that he compares God’s power with human weakness and with the other things that have been created. For in the human body, his strength sustains and governs as many limbs as it can vivify when infused into them; and he grants us the degree of balance that he is able to govern by his presence, sustaining by his power only as much as human limbs are able to bear.

But God is greater than the things he himself fashioned. When he assigned them at creation the measure that the order of things required—and no more than they could sustain—he is able to do more than the things that have been made can contain. Yet that pillar of truth asserts that God’s strength is limited and inferior to human arts. Builders and those skilled in the art of constructing houses can build larger structures than they have built, provided they are able to support the foundations on which the superstructure is to be raised; nor is the full extent of their skill exhausted by what they have constructed. And when they have completed works as large as necessity required, while possessing a measure beyond which any further construction would be judged indecent and useless, the art itself contains more in the mind than it has displayed in the work. Nor is the end of knowledge imposed by the limit of things, provided—as I have said—that whatever the mind has conceived, and whatever the imagination has expanded in contemplating the magnitude of its works, can be sustained by what lies beneath it.

How, then, is it not impious to place no limit upon human art, or to equate the skill of craftsmen with their works, but to say that God made as many rational creatures as he was able to make? Let the impious man hear and learn: God’s power is not only as great as the rational creatures he is said to have made; rather, having imposed a measure upon his works beyond which they could not exist, and having enclosed the number of things within the art of his ordering, he himself is not bound by measure or number.

From this it plainly appears that he did not make as many things as he could, but that his power made as many as the necessity of things required. Let us offer an example, so that what we are saying may become clearer. If a wealthy head of a household wished to invite guests to dinner and to serve such dishes as could satisfy the appetite of those dining, it would not immediately follow that the rich master possessed only as much food as they ate or as much as had been prepared for them. Rather, he provided as much as the dignity of the banquet demanded. So also almighty God, surpassing the example by which we compare him, did not make as many creatures as he could, but as many as ought to have been made.

But that man weaves and repeats the seedbed of loquacity and says: [Note: [Col. 0806] Martianay distinguishes and annotates the passage in such a way that Origen himself is called “that seedbed of loquacity” (*the seed of loquacity*). This interpretation is by no means satisfactory.]

[Note: [Col. 0806] It is remarkable that in the preceding Synodical Letter this doctrine—or rather madness—concerning God’s limited power is not attributed to Origen, although all his other doctrines are examined so carefully. We indeed think that Origen’s intention was not what his opponents attribute to him. Nevertheless, our Theophilus is echoed by Justinian in his letter to Menas, where he produces a fragment from the lost first book of *On First Principles* as evidence for this opinion; Methodius does likewise in Photius, codex 235. Most explicit of all is that Syrian, Rufinus, whose little book *On the Faith* Sirmond published. “Origen impiously and wickedly declared,” he says, “when he said: ‘God did not make everything he wished, but only those things which he was able to contain and comprehend.’ By saying this, he deprived the Lord of the power over all things, as though he had been granted only half the power of making. For if, as he supposes, he does not possess the ability to contain and subject to himself the things he makes, then he will evidently not even possess the power to create. For whoever possesses the power to create will likewise possess the power to subject created things to himself.’ We pass over Origen’s remaining doctrines, which are subsequently attacked in these writings, since they are examined in the preceding Synodical Letter.]

“God made as many things as he was able to comprehend and keep subject to himself and govern by his providence.” Nor does he heed the Prophet who says: “If all the nations are like a drop from a bucket, and are reckoned as the moment on a balance, and shall be counted as spittle, etc.; to whom have you likened God?” (Isaiah 40:15, 18). And again: “Who has measured the waters in his hand, and the heavens with a span, and all the earth with a handful?” (ibid. 12). If, in comparison with God’s strength, water is measured by the hand, the heavens by a span, and all the earth by a handful—and these expressions are metaphorical, so that the insignificance of created things may be demonstrated by the majesty of their maker, for God is not composed of limbs of different kinds—how can he be said to have made as many things as he was able to comprehend by his power?

18. Let us press on with what we have begun and explain our meaning more fully. “If all the nations are like a drop from a bucket, and like the moment on a balance they shall be reckoned, and like spittle they shall be counted”: by these words the insignificance and small substance of all creatures are demonstrated, so that God’s incomparable sublimity may become apparent. Therefore his strength too would be reckoned like a drop from a bucket, like the moment on a balance, and like human spittle, if, according to Origen, he fashioned as many things as he was able to comprehend by his power. And God’s strength must be equated with the number and measure of his works if he could not make anything greater than what he made.

But I do not think that anyone—not merely a human being, but not even a demon—would dare to fabricate such things about God as he both conceived and wrote: that God made as much material as he was able to adorn and divide into forms of things. [Col. 0807] Holding this view, let him once again learn from us that God was able to make more than he made; rather, God fashioned as much as the order of things required, possessing art and strength far greater than the number and measure of the things that were made.

Let him know also that this is confirmed by the testimonies of the Prophets. One of them says: “His power covered the heavens”; another cries out: “But he made the earth as nothing,” so that they might proclaim [or: *proclaim he might*] that God’s power is greater than the things that have been made. Moreover, when he said, “He made the earth as nothing,” the Apostle interprets this concerning all creatures and says: “He calls those things which are not as though they were” (Romans 4:17). By these words too we learn that God’s strength is greater than the things made by him.

And he is not ashamed, arguing against God’s strength, to say that God can do only as much as the material supplied him for his work! He does not understand that the nature of things made is one thing, and the nature of God, their maker, another; nor that the material from which something is made can be as powerful as the one who fashions something from it. For substances of different kinds have different powers and conditions.

19. Therefore, if those who prefer Origen’s ravings to the authority of the Scriptures wish to celebrate the Lord’s Pascha with the Church, let them hear God crying out: “And I did not show them to you so that you might walk after them.” And let them hear the Prophet’s tearful warning: “Ho, ho! Flee from the land of the north, says the Lord, for I shall gather you from the four winds. Save yourselves in Zion, you who dwell with the daughter of Babylon” (Zechariah 2).

Leaving behind the darkness of error and the chill of ignorance, let them turn toward the rising of the sun of righteousness, joining the zeal of the Magi. Dwelling in the sunniest region of heaven—which is perceived in the fervor of the Scriptures—let them, having spurned Origen’s madness, question the shepherds of the Church and say: “Where is he who has been born king of the Jews?” (Matthew 2:2). When they have found him lying in a manger—that is, in the humble language of the Scriptures—let them offer him gold, frankincense, and myrrh; that is, a tested faith shining with every splendor of truth, the fragrance of a kindly way of life, and continence that dries up luxury and the flowing provocations of the flesh.

For those who, after repeated warnings, contradict the faith of the Church are held by a double sickness: wickedness and ignorance. Turned wholly toward earthly things like snakes, and clinging to the ground, they prefer evil to good; they do not know the difference between vices and virtues; and they reject from the holy Scriptures the medicines intended for their correction and healing. Like pregnant women, they suffer an aversion to the truth: they reject their customary foods and pursue whatever is harmful. They are unable to direct the clear light of the soul against the rays of truth. Despising ecclesiastical discipline, they roll about in the mud like pigs and scorn perfumes.

Yet it is right that at least through the examples we bring forward they should receive healing. For just as inflammation harms the eye, fever ravages the whole body, and rust gradually consumes bronze and iron, so the destructive contagion of perverse doctrines violates the beauty of negligent souls and covers them with the disfiguring pallor of lies. I beg you, brothers, to forgive my grief as I bring criminal doctrines into the open.

Although we have crossed the rivers of Babylon in order to persuade the captives dwelling there to journey to the festival of Jerusalem, we nevertheless did not ourselves experience captivity, by spreading the sails of Scripture to favorable winds through God’s mercy. Nor did the swelling floods of heretical doctrines overwhelm us; the storm of lies did not terrify us; nor did the torrents of iniquity drag us through the midst of that sea where, as the Psalmist sings, “there are creeping things without number” (Psalm 103:25), and where the dragon—the devil—dwells, that most poisonous creature, exposed to the sport of the saints.

Nor, to sum everything up briefly, were the gusts of wind rising from every side able to overturn the ship of the Church or bury the rowing of our studies beneath a savage whirlwind. Sailing with the Lord our Savior, like his disciples, we crossed over and, entering the harbor of peace, embraced the fairest shore of the divine books. Plucking various flowers of knowledge and pressing kisses upon the snow-white limbs of wisdom, [Note: [Col. 0808] The text reads *oculis* (“with the eyes”), while the blank of the page had *osculis* (“with kisses”). We did not hesitate to accept the latter, after removing the earlier reading, which is certainly an error. Immediately afterward the text had *in eis*, which we changed to the more harmonious and correct reading found in B. P., *in ejus* (“in her”).] we cling to her embrace; and, if the Lord grants it, living with her and persevering in her love, we shall sing: “I became a lover of her beauty” (Wisdom 8:2). For all who read the holy Scriptures with greater diligence and run through the painted meadows of heavenly speech enjoy [or: *will enjoy*] this blessedness.

But those who abandon the greenness of the Lord’s solemn festival and cross over into deserts endure the hostile assaults of demons, like cities without walls.

20. Therefore, as we celebrate the approaching festivals, let us understand both ourselves and all that belongs to us; and let us embrace with every effort knowledge and our rational soul as a mother, possessing the root of speech and the understanding of rational knowledge, while speech is, so to speak, the vestibule of action. Let the work of speech and knowledge be completed roofs, and let a very firm roof be placed upon the house. [Note: [Col. 0808] The editor of B. P. indicates that *perficit* (“he completes”) should be corrected to *perfecta* (“completed”), and *imponit* (“he places”) to *impositum* (“placed”).]

For speech, reason, knowledge, and faith without action are empty and unstable. And, to appear to take something from that doctrine for the sake of those trained in dialectical arts: just as, when we join a verb to a noun, a complete sense is produced, whereas a verb by itself, or a noun without a verb, is entirely meaningless, so knowledge without action and action without faith are weak and fleeting. Conversely, knowledge joined to action is an indication of perfect virtue. [Col. 0809]

The silent thought of the mind is its secret speech, [Note: [Col. 0809] In the Benedictine edition: “namely, the thought.”] which, sounding outwardly through the tongue, expresses the mind’s judgment. And when speech has been completed by action, an end is placed upon our knowledge and thought. Yet we shall give an account in judgment of our thought, speech, and action, when our thoughts accuse or defend one another, on the day when God will judge the hidden things of human beings through Jesus Christ, as the Apostle Paul writes.

21. Since this is so, as the Lord’s festival approaches, let us say to those whom Origen’s error has entangled and his deceit holds captive: “Flee from the midst of Babylon, and let each one save his own soul” (Jeremiah 51). Although, according to the prophet’s oracle, Babylon is said to be a golden cup, and through the arrangement and charm of its words to display the beauty of truth and transform itself into an angel of light, nevertheless it must be understood that all who drink of its wine are shaken and fall, and are worthy of lamentation in their ruin.

But let us resist deadly disturbances, fortify the valley of the soul with continence, and protect its freedom by daily exercise in virtue. For just as slaves who have been sold are called the servants and slaves of those who paid the price for them, so those who have sold their souls to various desires are called the servants of whatever desires they have surrendered themselves to, and obey them as cruel masters.

And when they scorn the correctors of their error with an unyielding face, defending their folly through recklessness, they do not understand that audacity is nothing other than, as I see it, a judgment without perception or reflection, driving the governor—the mind—far from itself amid disturbances. When the soul has been stripped of such protection, it is carried headlong into the depths of impiety and, like some exceedingly bitter discharge, darkens the light of the mind and surrounds its eye, according to the language of Scripture, with an intractable night of darkness.

22. Therefore, let those who delight in Origen’s errors not expect the proclamation of the Lord’s festival. Let them not seek perfumes, gold, and pearls in the mud, nor tear apart in the great cities their mother Church, which gave birth to them and nourished them. [Note: [Col. 0809] “The great cities” probably means Constantinople, to which city the Origenists had fled, as was noted above in section 3 and elsewhere. In B. P. the following is read: “who once, because of him and his disciples, etc.”]

They surpass the hatred of the Gentiles toward us, and in their love for them heap curses upon us; they besiege the doors of the rich and are not afraid to hear, together with the Jews: “I have begotten and exalted children, but they have rejected me” (Isaiah 1:2).

They seem to me to be ignorant of every word of truth, which has no foundation. Even if it has enticed a hearer for a time, making him think that what is not true is true, it is gradually dissolved and reduced to nothing; and the whole argument, [Col. 0810] which pours forth like a torrent from an evil mind, overwhelms its author. It leaves behind the letters and syllables from which it had been woven, stripped of sense, sound, and every image, and, like a most venomous serpent, strikes its utterer, immediately draws back its head, and, as though in a cave of the mind, wastes away and is consumed. For the end of lies is destruction.

Those who once boasted that they were lovers of solitude should at least build a small cell for concealing their curses above the lips of their fury—not from the holy stones of Jerusalem, but from the shapeless rocks of Babylon, which, unhewn and uneven, might support the walls of a house destined to collapse.

Although with their effeminate [read: *savage*] ears they commend themselves to the hatred of the Gentiles by maligning us, attacking ecclesiastical discipline, and using our patience as a kind of fuel for their recklessness, let them nevertheless at some point be silent and keep quiet, and hear the Prophet saying: “Keep your tongue from evil, and your lips from speaking deceit” (Psalm 33).

Let them desire to know those things that are worthy of a holy life, and let them not grieve God by distressing the ruler and [Note: [Col. 0810] The reading in B. P., where *solitary life* is used instead of *holy life*, may easily seem preferable, since he is reproaching the Origenist monks, his detractors, who wander here and there. In the Synodical Letter 5: “It is our wish that both these men and the others correct their errors through repentance and live in a manner worthy of their name, so that those who are called monks—if indeed they wish to be what they are called—may love silence and the Catholic faith.” Immediately afterward, instead of *magistrum* (“teacher”), which appeared incorrectly in most other editions, we did not hesitate to substitute *magistratum* (“ruler”), first on conjectural grounds and then with the support of B. P.]

23. But I beseech you, brothers, let us pray together for them and say in the prophetic voice: “Who will give water to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes? And I shall weep day and night for the wounded of the daughter of my people” (Jeremiah 9). Let us implore God’s mercy to free them from the error by which they are bound and to change into love the hatred with which they rage against us in vain.

Therefore, forgetting their injuries, we desire to receive them into our most indulgent embrace, and we count their healing and conversion to God as our own healing and glory. And if they cannot be healed in any other way than through our humility, let us willingly make amends to them: we have inflicted no injury upon them and have harmed them in nothing. [Note: [Col. 0810] This is Theophilus’ customary disclaimer, which he repeats in the same words in Synodical Letter 5. “We have harmed them in nothing; we have inflicted no injury [upon them]”—the words whose restoration we indicate. B. P. has here: “We have inflicted nothing upon them; we have harmed them in nothing.” It is therefore remarkable that the same error should occur in different places and books, and by different hands.]

Yet they are indignant and rage against the Church’s medicines, by which healing is restored to the wounded. We speak what we know and proclaim what we have learned, praying that those who despise ecclesiastical rules may receive the norm of truth and may not, because of human shame—which ordinarily makes it difficult to correct the erring—lose the benefit of repentance.

Now we say, and we said before, and we repeat frequently: we do not want them to wander or err through foreign provinces. Rather, to the exiles and the frenzied we cry out with the Prophet and say: “Save yourselves from the land, and return, and do not stand still; remember the Lord from far away, and let Jerusalem rise into your hearts” (Jeremiah 51:50). [Note: [Col. 0811] The common version has: “You who have fled from the sword, come, do not stand still; remember the Lord from afar,” etc.]

24. Perhaps, on hearing these words, love for the ecclesiastical congregation will enter them, and they will remember the shared joy of the brethren and the hymns with which, together with the others, they sang to the Lord. Perhaps they will exchange the chill of hatred for the warmth of love and understand that we are physicians, not enemies; most indulgent fathers, not men swollen with hostile pride.

For it cannot be that we should wish those whom we want to save to perish, and not want the ecclesiastical rod to be turned into a staff for them—provided that, abandoning error, they wish to follow the truth and to lay aside the recklessness of wanton children.

But if they reject this, despise ecclesiastical discipline, raise their horn against its rules, and cast salutary counsels behind them, let them hear the Lord threatening: “The man who acts presumptuously and refuses to listen to the priest who stands to minister in the name of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0811] The text had *tui* (“of your”), although the sacred text does not support it. The rest must be checked against the Greek exemplar, since it differs from the Vulgate.] your God, or to the judge, whoever he may be in those days—that man shall die; and you shall remove the evil from Israel. And all the people, hearing, shall fear and shall no longer act impiously” (Deuteronomy 17:12).

But lest, occupied with healing the wounded, we become forgetful of ourselves and neglect our own concerns, and lest, according to what is written, “while preaching to others, we ourselves should be found rejected” (1 Corinthians 9:27), let us warn those who stand to beware, lest, while they extend a hand to those lying prostrate, they themselves fall; and, while maintaining ecclesiastical discipline, let them fear the judgment to come.

25. Therefore, as we celebrate the Lord’s Pascha, let us be purified by the holy words of Scripture; and, looking toward the Savior’s trophies, let us remove from our midst every obstacle by which the course of our life is delayed.

Avoiding avarice as the worst moneylender, let us strangle the desire for empty glory as an insatiable beast, and let us avoid with watchful mind the seductive and slippery serpent of fornication. Whenever a more favorable breeze of circumstances comes to us, let us temper the swelling of the spirit with humility and gentleness. If adverse winds blow, let us raise up the spirit when it has been crushed and lies prostrate through courage; and let us be accusers of our own sin, so that, knowing ourselves, we may correct ourselves and, through constant meditation, restore to the soul—oppressed by vices—the freedom of virtue.

Therefore, placed amid the contest, sweat, and toil of the present, and preparing for ourselves the future glory of the heavenly solemnity, let us correct past sins through repentance before we stand before Christ’s tribunal. Let us redeem future joys through present weeping, and, like bees, drive away the harmful drones of sins with the sting of conscience, preserving our hives full of wax and honey.

Let us care for the various wounds of vice, and let us restrain through repeated warnings the plundering of the rich, by which this class of people is especially ensnared. In this way we shall be able to undertake the journey of the approaching fasts.

The days of Lent will begin [Note: [Col. 0811] B. P. reads: “Beginning Lent on the thirtieth,” etc. [Col. 0812] The words *we shall celebrate*, which occur below, are omitted. The thirtieth day of Mechir corresponds to February 24; the fifth day of Pharmuthi to March 1; and the eleventh to April 6. From these dates it has been established that the passage refers to Easter in the year 402.] on the thirtieth day of the month Mechir. We shall celebrate the week of the saving Pascha on the fifth day of the month Pharmuthi, ending the fasts according to the Gospel traditions on the evening of the tenth day of Pharmuthi, which is Saturday; and immediately at dawn on Sunday we shall celebrate the festivals on the eleventh day of the same month, [Col. 0812] joining to these the remaining seven weeks of holy Pentecost. Thus, together with those who confess the one divinity of the Trinity, we may receive rewards in heaven, through Christ Jesus our Lord, through whom and with whom glory and dominion belong to God the Father, with the Holy Spirit, for ages of ages. Amen.

26. Greet one another with a holy kiss. All the brothers who are with me greet you. We also write this necessarily, so that you may know that, in place of the holy and blessed bishops who have fallen asleep in the Lord, the following have been ordained: in Lemnado, in place of Heron, Naseas; in Erythrus, in place of Sabbatius, Paul; in Omboe, in place of Silvanus, Verres. Therefore write to these men and receive from them letters of peace, according to ecclesiastical custom.

[Note: [Col. 0812] Charles of Saint Paul reads *Lemnado* and places that city in the province of Libya Pentapolis. This is based, however, on this single testimony of Theophilus’ letter, since it is not mentioned by any other ancient geographers or in the ancient lists of bishoprics, although it may easily be inferred that it is the same place Antoninus calls Limniades on the route from Ptolemais to Alexandria. The Erythra mentioned next is likewise assigned to the province of Libya Pentapolis in the list of the Alexandrian Patriarchate. Elsewhere it is called Erythrus and Erythron by Ptolemy and in the Acts of the Council of Chalcedon, Act 1, where it is written ἐρυθρός. Finally, for *Omboe*, the Greek lists and Greek writers generally use ὄμβροι, *Ombroe*, and most correctly assign it to the second Thebaid.]

## LETTER XCIX

[Note: [Col. 0812] Elsewhere numbered 31. Written in the year 404.]

TO THEOPHILUS.

Jerome excuses himself to Theophilus for having translated the accompanying Paschal Letter late, being delayed partly by Paula’s death and partly by his own illness.

### TO THE MOST BLESSED POPE THEOPHILUS, JEROME

1. Jerome’s illness. From the time when I received the letters of Your Blessedness, together with the Paschal book, until the present day, I have been so shaken both by the grief of mourning and by anxiety, and by various rumors circulating here and there concerning the condition of the Church, that I could scarcely translate your volume into Latin. For you know very well the ancient saying: “There is no eloquence in sadness,” especially when bodily illness is added to distress of mind.

I dictated this very letter while burning with fever and already confined to my bed for the fifth day, in excessive haste, briefly informing Your Blessedness that I had endured great labor in translating it, so that I might render all its statements with equal elegance and make Latin eloquence answer, at least to some extent, to the eloquence of Greek.

2. At the beginning you philosophize; and while instructing everyone in general, you strike down one man in particular. In the rest—and this is especially difficult—you join philosophers to rhetorical eloquence, and associate Demosthenes and Plato with us. What great things are said against luxury! With what praises continence is exalted! And from the innermost disciplines of wisdom you describe the day and night, the course of the moon, the order of the sun, and the nature of this world. You refer this entire discussion to the authority of Scripture, lest in your Paschal book you seem to have borrowed anything from secular sources.

What more can I say? In praising you in these matters I fear incurring the charge of flattery. It is an excellent book, both philosophical and concerned with its chosen subject, without envy toward particular persons.

Therefore I beg you to forgive even my tardiness. For I have been so overcome by the death of the holy and venerable Paula that, apart from translating this book, I have written nothing else in divine service up to the present. We have suddenly lost, as you yourself know, the consolation which—as the Lord is witness to our conscience—we do not count as serving our own needs but the refreshment of the saints, for whom she carefully labored.

Your holy and venerable daughter Eustochium, who receives no consolation for her mother’s absence, and the whole Brotherhood [Note: [Col. 0813] The Brotherhood here plainly means the company of brothers who lived a solitary life with Jerome. Among ecclesiastical writers, however, the use and meaning of this word vary; it is not uncommon for it to mean the Church, and often one finds much mystery and religious significance invested in it. See Optatus of Milevis, beginning of book 1, *On the Schism of the Donatists*, and the notes of learned men upon it.] earnestly greet you.

Send us the books which you announced some time ago that you had written, either for us to read or to translate. Farewell in Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0813] We think that no other books are meant here than those *Invectives against Saint John Chrysostom*, which Jerome did indeed render into Latin, but which have not survived either in the Greek original or in the Latin translation, except for very short fragments preserved by Facundus of Hermiane. Consult Letter 114 below and our notes there.]

## LETTER C

[Note: [Col. 0813] In some copies it is unnumbered; written and translated into Latin in the year 404.]

OR, THE PASCHAL LETTER OF THEOPHILUS, BISHOP OF ALEXANDRIA, TO ALL THE BISHOPS OF EGYPT, FOR THE YEAR 404, TRANSLATED BY THE BLESSED JEROME

[Note: [Col. 0813] Jerome did not translate the Paschal Letter for the preceding year, 403, into Latin. Those who think that it has been lost are therefore seriously mistaken, as are especially those who, in order to fill a gap, assign the earlier letter of 401 to the year 403, following Baronius.]

Ceasing from sins, by adopting a habitual practice of virtues through which the mind may be prepared to celebrate Easter. The holy observance of the Lenten fasts and right faith in God are set forth. Origen’s errors, which ought to be detested before the Lord’s Easter. Greed must likewise be trampled down, and love of God joined to love of one’s neighbors.

### 1

Now also the living Wisdom of God summons us to celebrate the holy Easter, desiring all to share in it. Therefore, hastening toward it with swift steps, and fighting against the activity of the opposing virtues through fasts, abstinence, and every affliction of the body, let us reduce pleasures to nothing, supported by the Savior’s help. Let us confess our sins simply to God, who is able to heal, and let us fear the true judgment of conscience, so that, crying out with David and saying, “Do not remember the sins of my youth and my ignorance” [Note: The Greek has ἀγνοίας, in the singular genitive and the plural accusative. Thus, together with the printed reading, Augustine, two Roman Psalters, one from Germanus, and another from Chartres have it.] “according to your mercy remember me” (Ps. 27:7), we may consume our growing vices with the terror of eternal fire [al. “let us consume”]. Their end is to do nothing further of the same kind, and the beginning of salvation is forgetfulness of what has passed.

For just as the beginning of a good way [f. “of life”] is to do what is right, so the beginning of ceasing from sins is to restrain their impulses, whether they are curbed by reason or prevented by fear from rushing headlong. When remembrance of the Law enters the mind, they immediately flee; and, ceasing to advance any farther, they yield to the camp of the triumphant virtues [Note: This amounts to saying that they are led captive by the virtues and are triumphed over. Martianay, however, inserts the negative particle, giving the opposite sense: “they do not enter the camp of the triumphant virtues.”]. Gradually, by repentance, drawing back their step, and avoiding the judgment of the wise, they dissolve into nothing like smoke.

Evils that are not crushed as soon as they begin to grow are difficult to heal. Their eradication is easy when those who previously sinned are converted through repentance to prudence and find the benefit of repentance in bringing sinning to an end. For we cannot crush the incitements of vices unless we begin to practice virtues; nor will old things cease before they are excluded by the works of new ones. Just as past sins are erased when we resist pleasures that arise later with a steadfast mind, so, if forgetfulness of what has passed endures, future offenses will no longer be able to increase.

Those who do evil, as though reducing to their own control those who could prevent them but do not, rage with complete madness toward sinning. Turning silence into assent, they strive to carry out in action whatever lust has suggested to the mind. Freedom for present vices generates future vices; and if you neglect what came first, it is the fountain and seedbed of what will follow.

### 2. Sins must be prohibited

Since this is so, those who can prevent sinners but, through avoidance of labor and inert silence, conceal the matter and allow evils to grow will rightly be judged partners of those who are the authors of crimes, and they will pay the penalties of negligence, because they preferred irrational idleness to the sweat of those who punish evil, choosing culpable ease rather than severity that cuts down vices.

For if we withdraw from vices, they will utterly perish and their deceptive sweetness will dry up; every impulse toward pleasure will, so to speak, grow torpid through a kind of languor, when our mind has become the dwelling place of virtue. Remembrance of the Law does not permit sins to be generated, nor does it allow them to grow. When they have considered the future tribunal and the terrifying day of judgment [Note: I would prefer “when it has considered,” referring to the mind. But afterward one must certainly read “the beginning, the middle, and the end,” or simply “the beginning,” if one prefers. What the editors of the printed editions put forward as “the day of the beginning,” although we do not alter it, is certainly corrupt.], it will prohibit the beginning, middle, and end of sin, and will dry up its bitter waves and swelling whirlpools all the way to the very spring and channels. Virtue, accompanied by the Law, will crush the seeds of vice and raise the mind from lowly things to lofty ones.

By contrast, vices, unless restrained, grow proud and drive those who obey them down to the underworld.
