Once they have taken possession of souls, they overwhelm them with the enticements of pleasures and do not permit them to look upward, upright and elevated, according to the condition of the human body; rather, like cattle, they bend them toward earthly things. Concerning such people the Psalmist testifies, saying, “They called their names in their lands” (Ps. 48).

### 3. Vices must be stripped off

Someone may say: If vices possess such strength, and overthrow so many through persuasion so alluring, what should those do who recognize that they are sinning and desire to exchange sins for virtues, rejecting worse things through love of what is better?

Let such people hear Moses speaking: “You have sinned? Cease,” overturning what came before by ending sin and correcting vices with the most effective medicine—the cessation of vices. Avoid the sweet enticements of an evil life and the flattering pleasures of the body as though they were harmful poisons. Do not enter by the slippery and soft path of delights, because the solemnity of fasting and abstinence is attained only with effort, and only with difficulty, through labor and sweat, can we exchange evil things for good and overcome pleasures that resist us.

[Note: Since this passage is found nowhere in the Pentateuch, we think from its character that it is of the sort Chrysostom discusses in Homily 7 on First Corinthians: passages are said to be written when they are expressed not in words but in substance, “as in histories, or when the same thought is written, although not in the same words.” Yet that it existed in its proper place in the manuscripts of the older version called the Itala is indicated by this same holy Father near the end of his Letter to Sabinianus, Genesis 4:13: “What was said to Cain, consider said to you: You have sinned; cease.”]

Few are those who, having trampled down vices, keep to the path of truth, while wickedness employs innumerable arts of harming and cannot be conquered unless we are supported from above by the help of wisdom, which cries out to us: “Do not fear, for I am with you” (Gen. 26:24).

The destruction of evil is to do evil no longer; the root of vices is to disregard what the Law commands. Just as negligence causes sins to sprout, so vigilance produces virtues. The Law, when observed, drives away disgrace; when neglected, it gives birth to punishments. And just as, when despised, it imitates the savagery of a severe judge [Note: Again, without the aid of manuscript codices, I would prefer “threatens” in place of “imitates.” The latter neither answers well to the following isocolon nor, as far as we can see, gives a suitable sense.], so, when kept, it displays the gentleness of a most merciful father.

Therefore, the cessation of sin is the beginning of virtue. The medicine for past, present, and future vices is the tireless meditation of the Law [Col. 0816]. When it has secured its possessor, it is free from every disturbance. Wisdom works good in us after we have provided it with a pure heart as a dwelling and have turned our thoughts into deeds.

There is no doubt that we possess free power in either direction, whether to do or not to do good, and that, once evil things have been suppressed, right things arise. Then the choir of virtues sings in harmony with itself, when there is solitude from vices in the souls.

For just as abstinence, when it holds the chief place in our bodies, prevents illnesses from arising; neither weakens nor destroys those who love it; restores past disorders to their former health; and, expelling what is contrary to nature, recalls what accords with nature, so that the order of this life may be preserved in an even balance—so the soul, preserving the commands of the Laws, is separated from the contagion of evils to the extent that human nature can receive it. Watchful in every respect and looking around itself, it permits nothing to enter that is contrary to noble thoughts.

Indeed, transformed into the temple of God, it continually enjoys a heavenly solemnity, possessing the riches of observance of the Law. The Law raises up those who lie prostrate; by punishing the wicked, it corrects others; and, always crying out, “Will the one who has fallen not rise again? Or will the one who has turned away not return?” (Jer. 8), it grants hope of salvation to the repentant. It admonishes so that its admonition may benefit; it rebukes so that the person may amend; and, instilling shame for former sins, it makes people pursue better things. No one can desire these unless he has first condemned the wounds of his conscience.

### 4

But because the Law hastens to recall those who neglect it and are sunk in error to better things through its excellent counsels, as though it were a standard for evil deeds, and does not permit those who obey it to remain without reward or to be oppressed by eternal distress, let all of us who celebrate the holy Easter make the Lawgiver our friend through abstinence and fasts. The Prophet promises this to those who celebrate Easter: “You shall be a crown of beauty in the hand of the Lord, and a diadem of kingship in the hand of your God” (Isa. 62:3).

Let us seek the rich banquet of virtues, adorning ourselves with knowledge of the Scriptures as with ceremonial garments. Let us prepare holy kisses, while the Angels rejoice with us in heaven, driving away every negligence and breaking through delay, so that with eager steps we may go to the Savior with the disciples and say to him, “Where do you wish us to prepare the Passover for you?” (Matt. 26).

[Note: These words bring to mind a passage of our Theophilus which, while we were staying in Rome, we copied from a certain Catena in the most ancient Vatican Codex 699. It is said to have been taken “from the tenth Easter discourse.” We append it here all the more gladly because it has not yet been published. It runs as follows:

“Ἵνα πάλιν τὸ παραπέτασμα καὶ κάλυμμα τῆς λέξεως ἀναστείλαντες ἀνακεκαλυμμένῳ προσώπω τὴν διαβατήριον τοῦ θείου πάσχα πανήγυριν κατοπτρίζωνται βοῶντες τῷ Ἰησοῦ· ποῦ θέλεις ἐτοιμάσωμεν σοι τὸ πάσχα; ὅτι καὶ μαθόντες παρ’ αὐτοῦ ἐν ἀναγαίῳ δεῖν ἐπιτελεῖν τοῦτο, ἄνω τῶν γεωδεστέρων πραγμάτων ἐγίνοντο εἰς τὰ ἅγια τῶν ἁγίων δρομαῖοι τῇ γνώμῃ βαδίζοντες. Ἐνθα ὁ Χριστὸς αὐτὸς ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν εἰσῆλθεν, τοῦ κατὰ τὸν τύπον ἀρχιερέως πέπαυκε τὴν χρείαν, ἡμῖν αἰωνίαν λύτρωσιν εὑράμενος· καὶ ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν ἐμφανισθεὶς τῷ προσώπῳ τοῦ θεοῦ· τότε μὲν γὰρ ἅπαξ τοῦ ἐνιαυτοῦ μόνος ὁ ἀρχιερεὺς εἰσήρχετο εἰς τὰ ἅγια τῶν ἁγίων, ἔξω τοῦ λαοῦ μένοντος διὰ τὸ μικρὸν τῆς δυνάμεως, ὁ δὲ σωτὴρ ἐπιβὰς ἀδείαν τοῖς βουλομένοις εἰσελθεῖν δέδωκεν.”

“The remaining words that follow there do not seem to have Theophilus as their author, even though they are attributed to him. We translate the earlier passage as follows:

‘In order that, once again, having drawn aside the veil and covering of the letter, they may, with unveiled face, contemplate the solemnity of the Lord’s Passover—the passage-sacrifice—crying aloud to Jesus: “Where do you wish us to prepare the Passover for you?” For, learning from him that this must be accomplished in the upper room, which is above earthly affairs, they hasten upward in mind and proceed in thought to the Holy of Holies. Christ himself entered that place for us and brought the service and function of the Levitical High Priest to an end, finding eternal redemption for us and appearing for us before the face of God. Formerly, once a year, the high priest alone entered the Holy of Holies, while the people remained outside because they did not possess sufficient access. But the Savior, entering, granted authority to all who wished to enter.’”]

And, established in the upper room of heaven [al. “and” / “so that”], celebrating the mystical Passover, may we be able to sing, “How beloved are your tabernacles, Lord of hosts!” (Ps. 83).

There we shall find choirs of Angels; and, celebrating the feast with them, we shall have them as companions in the mysteries of God. We shall rejoice with unspeakable exultation, learning with them the sacraments of wisdom. There is no deception of fraud there; there the one who does not possess a wedding garment is forbidden to enter the banquet, even if in the present age he boasts that he is righteous.

Everything there is filled with the prudence of age and maturity; and, according to the Prophet, no one of immature wisdom will be found there: “For,” he says, “the youth shall be a hundred years old” (Isa. 65:20) [Note: From the Greek ἔσται γὰρ ὁ νέος ἑκατὸν ἐτῶν. The Vulgate has a different sense: “for the child of a hundred years shall die.”] The greatness of the number indicates the perfection of instruction.

Therefore, brothers, participants in a holy and heavenly calling, let us hear the Savior crying out through the Prophet: “I shall come to gather all nations, and they shall come and see my glory, and I shall set upon them the sign of the world” (Isa. 66).

### 5

Let us therefore hasten to the solemnity and say, “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of Christ” (Gal. 6). He will indeed—yes, I say, he will—give joy to those who labor; and, blessing those who fast, he will say: “They shall be to the house of Judah for joy and gladness and for good solemnities, and you shall rejoice; love truth and peace” (Zech. 8:16). For the solemnity does not belong to everyone, but to the house of Judah, that is, to the Church of Christ.

Since, according to the Psalmist, “It is time to act for the Lord” (Ps. 118:126), and Paul writes, “The night has passed, but the day has drawn near,” let us therefore cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light. Let us walk honorably as in the day, not in reveling and drunkenness, not in beds and indecencies, not in quarrels and rivalry; but “put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh in its desires” (Rom. 13:12).

It is right that all who have been purified by the fear of the Lord should perform a solemnity worthy of it, redeem chastity also through abstinence and fasts, and awaken the sleeping mind with vigilant faith. Let us imitate the most wise Daniel, of whom it is written: “There is a man in your kingdom in whom is the spirit of God, and in the days of your father vigilance and wisdom were found in him” (Dan. 5:11).

Those who care for themselves so as to progress toward better things, having the Law as a most powerful leader, obey its commands and overthrow the sins that come against them. They illuminate the festival of Easter by the splendor of their works, and, disregarding the darts of disturbance through the security of conscience, anticipate victory by hope.

Those who imitate them seize the palm of triumph through their desire for virtue before they enter battle, and, as victors, possess in the heavens the crown of victory over slippery pleasure. With unveiled face, contemplating in mind, they will cry out and say: “The Lord God is my strength, and he will make my feet” [Note: From the Greek εἰς συντέλειαν, “to completion.” The Vulgate, from the Hebrew, has something like “the feet of hinds,” and shortly afterward τοῦ νικῆσαι, “that I may conquer,” which the Vulgate renders in another sense, “victorious.”] “for completion, setting me upon the heights, so that I may conquer in his song.”

### 6

Nor should we think, dearly beloved brothers, that the contest is everlasting, so that we become weary on that account. Rather, let us know that the end of this contest is the crown of righteousness, which no age of the world corrupts. The effort of this life and contest is temporary; but those who run with an unobstructed step and reach the goal of their rewards will find new dwelling places, displaying their victory in songs.

Since the grace of the Lord promises us triumphs over the most wicked demons, let us duly observe the fasts, so that we may also duly share in the solemnity. During the days of Lent, let us by no means, as luxurious rich men are accustomed to do, sigh for a cup of wine, nor, when we are on the front line and in battle, where labor and sweat are necessary, delight in eating meat.

[Note: For some time this passage seemed to us excessively harsh, especially since shortly afterward, and in section 8, Theophilus expressly and consistently commands abstinence from wine during the time of fasting, as from meat. For if one were to understand the passage simply, concluding that the faithful were formerly forbidden to drink wine during the Lenten fasts, many considerations would come to mind that could be brought against it. Those who describe the various customs of the Churches—Socrates, Book 5, chapter 22, and Sozomen, Book 7, chapter 19—do not report that this was observed at all, much less that it was sanctioned by the Church. If some Christians abstained from wine so completely, this should rather be attributed to their devotion than to an ecclesiastical rule, whatever others may think.

Finally, a passage of Tertullian conveniently provides very clear evidence for the same point. “Some,” he says in On the Cultivation of Women, chapter 9, “forbid themselves God’s own creation, abstaining from wine and banishing animal foods, whose produce is subject to no danger or anxiety; but they offer to God the humility of their soul also in the restraint of their diet.”]

For gluttony and drunkenness, and the other enticements of this life, drain the richest treasure of souls and suffocate the most abundant seed of knowledge and teaching by their admixture. Therefore the Lord and Savior, urging his disciples toward the rigor of abstinence, said: “Take heed to yourselves, lest perhaps your hearts be weighed down with gluttony and drunkenness and the cares of this life, and that day come upon you suddenly; for like a snare it will come upon all who sit upon the face of the whole earth” (Luke 21:34–35).

[Note: The passage would be somewhat restored if “for” were placed before it, since the negligence of copyists has certainly affected the text.]

“Rise; let us go from here” (John 14:31)—those who, because of neglect of themselves, will immediately be overtaken by punishment.

Those who keep the precepts of the Laws, however, do not know wine during fasts, reject the eating of meat, and restrain insatiable greed through fear of God. Therefore Scripture cries out daily to those who practice abstinence: “They shall not drink wine or strong drink” (Judg. 13:4, 7, 14).

By contrast, the Jews hear this because of their guilt:

[Note: The gap in this passage is indicated by the suspended and incomplete sentence of Scripture. To fill it, the old edition of the Benedictine Fathers supplied us with some assistance, although that edition itself is often highly unreliable and here too is defective. It reads: “You gave the holy men and the Prophets wine to drink, and you commanded them, saying, ‘They cannot,’ etc.” We therefore conjecture that the text should be supplemented as follows: “and you commanded the Prophets, saying, ‘Do not prophesy.’” These words are from Amos 2:12: “You gave the Nazirites wine to drink, and you commanded the Prophets, saying, ‘Do not prophesy.’” It is wholly incredible that Theophilus would quote the latter part mutilated and with its sense reversed. But the similarity between the words “to the Prophets” and “do not prophesy” easily misled the copyists; and the words “Do not” and “They cannot” likewise deceived the copyists of the source from which the Benedictine edition was taken, causing them to omit the intervening words. We have already observed several times above, and the examples scattered throughout ancient books make clear, that scribes most often err where the same words are immediately repeated or doubled. Moreover, from the Greek ἡγιασμένους, he interprets the word here as “holy,” whereas the Vulgate translator, from the Hebrew, renders it “Nazirites.”]

“You gave the holy men wine to drink, and the prophets” (Amos 2:12).

Those who are captured by the delight of luxury cannot accept correction, nor restrain the greed of the belly by reason and counsel. Through love of fasting, they should do so, but instead, by laziness and a pleasure that quickly perishes, they disgrace the pursuit of virtue. They are not ashamed secretly to drink wine, avoiding witnesses with greedy throats, and in their bedrooms to drink honeyed wine, exchanging through luxury and drunkenness the hunger and fasts that they ought voluntarily to seek during the time of fasting.

They do not know that, even if they evade human awareness, and behind closed walls eat meat and fattened birds during the days of Lent, and, as Easter approaches, tear them apart with unclean hands, promising fasting outside with a gloomy face, the Lord rebukes such people and says: “These commit great iniquities, so that they may depart from my holy ones.”

It is not fitting for those who are fasting during a time of struggle and battle to eat meat, as Scripture admonishes: “You shall afflict your souls” (Lev. 16:29). Nor should they seek out pheasants with anxious effort and stuff their fatty flesh, or that of chattering birds, into an open throat. Nor should they search for highly paid cooks who will soothe the belly’s madness with elaborate sauces, transformed meats, and varied flavors, while steaming dishes and their fragrance flatter the fury of the throat, and wines of various taste and color are sought in insult [al. “with insult”] to abstinence.

### 7

The history of holy Daniel and the virtue of the three young men teaches us to desire and honor consonant fasts. To state a long account briefly, when freedom had been exchanged for servitude, although as captives they ought to have longed for delicacies, they despised the Babylonian dishes and preferred simple food to the royal table.

King Nebuchadnezzar had commanded the chief of the eunuchs to bring from the children of Israel in captivity, and from the royal stock, young men without any blemish, beautiful in body, and capable of learning wisdom thoroughly. They were to be brought into the palace, to serve in the king’s court, to learn the literature and language of the Chaldeans, and to live on what remained from his table and drink the wine supplied from it (Dan. 1:4–5).

Thus, from the tribe of Judah, Daniel, Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael were chosen, alike in lineage and faith, whose noble birth servitude had not altered [Note: The three young men had just been said to have exchanged freedom for servitude, but their noble birth had not likewise been changed. The Benedictine edition wrongly indicates the opposite, reading without the negative particle: “servitude had changed their nobility.” We correct it from the Benedictine Fathers’ edition, in which the phrase “for whom Daniel” is likewise found without the preposition.].

Of these, Daniel, as Scripture testifies, “resolved in his heart not to defile himself with the king’s table” (ibid. 1:8).

The three young men, joined not less by religion than by kinship, accept the counsel of the man and approve his wisdom. Together they entreat the chief of the eunuchs, and, with God’s merciful assistance, obtain what they desire. Thus they preserve the nobility of their lineage in the land of captivity.

For they soften the official’s fear that the brighter appearance of the other young men might condemn him to capital punishment by reason and counsel, speaking these words: “Test your servants for ten days, and let us be given seeds, and we shall eat, and we shall drink water. Then let our faces and the faces of the young men who eat from the king’s table be seen in your presence; and according to what you see, so deal with your servants” (Dan. 1:12).

[Note: The plural number is found here, and the Benedictine Fathers’ edition reads somewhat differently: “For they saw that the desire for virtue, sustained by God’s mercy, preserved beautiful and strong bodies,” and so forth.]

For he saw that the desire for virtue, sustained by God’s mercy, preserved beautiful and strong bodies; that abstinence maintained their appearance; that faith overcame every deformity; and that no emaciation altered the radiance of their beauty.

### 8

We have repeated these things, dearly beloved brothers, so that, knowing the words of the Apostle Paul, who proclaims the virtues of the saints and says, “Considering the outcome of their way of life, imitate their faith” (Heb. 13:7) [Note: The Benedictine edition wrongly had “we persuade.” Its punctuation was also defective, and—what we regret more—passages cited from Scripture were almost nowhere marked or distinguished from the continuous text. Neglect of this distinction has cast an almost indescribable darkness over many passages and caused us much labor and weariness.], we may urge those who delight in eating meat during the time of fasting to imitate the abstinence of the saints.

They could not be overcome by any force so as to abandon the rigor of virtue. They did not fear the authority of the Babylonians and thereby reveal that pleasure had taken them captive. Rather, they remained free, overcame the desires of the belly by reason, and conquered the luxury that tickles the throat. They left us examples of their courage, dwelling bodily in Babylon but, in understanding and faith, living with the Angels in the heavenly Jerusalem.

Thus they taught every succeeding age that, during the time of fasting, one must abstain from wine and meat, take seeds from the earth, and drink water—companions with which chastity associates.

### 9

Why should I recall the distinguished victories of the Maccabees (2 Macc. 7)? To avoid eating forbidden meat and touching common foods, they offered their bodies to torture. They are proclaimed throughout all the churches of the world in praise of Christ [Note: It is true that in the most ancient martyrologies the feast of the Maccabean Brothers occurs, and that it is recorded on the Kalends of August from the earliest times. Nevertheless, these words of Theophilus do not correspond to the twenty-second Oration of St. Gregory Nazianzen: “What of the Maccabees? For the present festival belongs to them. They are honored by many, although their contest did not occur after Christ; yet they deserve to be honored by all, because they endured for the institutions of their fathers.” “What of the Maccabees? For this present solemnity belongs to them. They are indeed honored by not many, since their contest was not after Christ; nevertheless, they deserve to be honored by all, because they endured for the institutions of their fathers.” Theophilus, by contrast, testifies that they are already celebrated in the praises of Christ throughout the churches of the whole world.] They were stronger than their punishments and more ardent than the fires in which they were burned.

Every device of cruelty was defeated in them; whatever the persecutor’s anger had found, the strength of those who endured overcame. Amid punishments they remembered their father’s Law more than their sufferings. Their entrails were torn; their limbs dissolved in corruption and gore; yet their resolve remained immovable. Their mind was free and despised present evils in hope of future things [al. “their minds despised”].

The torturers grew weary, but faith did not grow weary. Bones were broken, and on the revolving wheel the entire structure of nerves and limbs was loosened. Fires breathing death rose to immense heights. Frying pans full of boiling oil resounded with an incredible terror as the bodies of the saints were fried. Yet, amid all these things, walking through paradise in their minds, they did not feel what they were suffering but what they desired to see.

A mind fortified by the fear of God surpasses flames and scorns the various pains of torments. Once it has surrendered itself to virtue, it tramples down and despises whatever adversity may occur. Such was Paul when he wrote, “In all these things we conquer through him who loved us” (Rom. 8:37). What the frailty of the flesh cannot endure, overcome by natural weakness, the mind conquers by speaking with God through faith.

### 10

Therefore, those who imitate fasting—that is, the angelic way of life—on earth [Note: Previously the common reading was “they remember”], should remember the saying, “The kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness, joy, peace, and gladness” (Rom. 14).

Through abstinence these people, with brief and small labor, secure for themselves great and eternal rewards. They receive much more than they offer, and they mitigate present hardships through the glory of the future, because for those who fight for virtue in this arena the contest will one day come to an end.

Those who enter battle against vices, dedicate their souls to the disciplines of wisdom, and, insofar as human condition permits, seek knowledge of future things—beholding the kingdoms of heaven through a mirror and image, by understanding and faith—will obtain eternal rewards, enclosed by no limit of time.

Day and night succeed one another in fixed intervals of hours. Gradually diminishing, they recover what they lose and give what they recover. Twice each year they meet at the same measure; they do not remain in the same condition but distinguish the moments by the shortness and length of the hours, so that they may make the diversity of times useful to the world.

For day, by its order and circuit [Note: Perhaps “day borrows and completes its order and circuit” should be restored], borrows from the periods of night, and night again receives what it has given. While they in turn give and receive, and while, in a certain circle, they gradually recover what they had slowly lost as they diminished, they interpret the wisdom of God the Creator.

From this alternation of intervals there arises either the moon’s monthly course, or the year of the sun returning along its own tracks is completed. They increase and diminish; through the passing of former things, future things succeed; the same times are continually changed into other times.

Thus the moon, created by God’s most prudent art, changing the variety of its forms, moves toward fullness and hastens toward decrease, so that whatever it had acquired while increasing, it may lose and abandon while diminishing. It does not remain in the same state, but ascending and descending by certain degrees, proceeds from poverty to riches and returns from riches to poverty. By the very diversity of its forms it shows that it is changeable and created.

Who could express in worthy speech the course of the sun and the circuit of the year, which corresponds to the order of the month [Note: The word “lunar,” or “of the moon,” is absent from the Benedictine Fathers’ edition]? As it revolves through the four seasons and always returns to itself, ascending and descending by the same measure and moving in an eternal order, the interval that the moon completes in thirty days and nights is restored by the sun’s course in the spaces of the revolving year.

When the sun reaches equality between day and night and stands for a short time at the balance of its just course, it hastens toward inequality, abandoning the point it had reached. I think Ecclesiastes says this in his book, so that we need not draw from foreign sources: “The spirit goes, going around, and the spirit returns to its circuits” (Eccl. 1), signifying the annual course of the sun.

The same wheel of time returns upon itself, coming back to the point from which it had departed.

### 11

The holy and heavenly solemnity, sending us the rays of its splendor, is bounded by no intervals. When the contests of the saints and the labor of the present age have come to an end, everlasting joy and eternal festivity will follow.

Therefore, perfect men, separating their souls from every darkness of error, already now sing the festival: “Let us enter his gates with confession, his courts with hymns” (Ps. 94), proclaiming the Savior’s coming with joyful voices.

When wickedness reigned throughout the whole world and demons had poured darkness over human eyes, and no one could help them, according to what is written, “I looked, and there was no one to help; I considered, and there was no one to support” (Ps. 99), so that impiety might finally have an end and the deceit of idolatry be destroyed, the living Word of God, leaving out nothing of our likeness except sin—which has no substance—deigned to come to us in a new manner, so that he might become the Son of Man and remain the Son of God.

Born, in fact, from a Virgin, he was thought by foolish minds to be only what the eyes demonstrated. But through his works and the greatness of his signs, the invisible God was perceived by the wise. The one whom his face showed to be a man, his mighty works revealed to be God, concealed beneath the lowliness of a servant’s form.

Although the Jews handed him over and loudly demanded with impious voices that he be crucified, blaspheming the Lord through the killing of his body—indeed, through the slaying of the Lord’s flesh becoming servants of impiety—nevertheless, approaching death fearlessly to provide us an example of virtue, the Lord of glory was shown in his very passion. He remained impassible in the majesty of his divinity, while in the flesh he was found capable of suffering, according to the proclamation of blessed Peter.

Therefore, suffering for us, he did not flee death, lest through fear of his death we should lose the victory while fighting for his particularity [Note: We think that the word “particularity,” if the passage is sound, has been used in place of “singularity,” corresponding to the Greek κατ’ ἰδίαν, though we have no authority for this. If conjecture is permitted, one might suspect that it should be read as two words, “for piety,” in which sense he says again below, “Which of his disciples would willingly have fought for religion?” Whoever offers a better reading will earn our great gratitude.].

For if he had feared the cross and acted contrary to what he had taught, which of his disciples would willingly have fought for religion? He is therefore mocked by the foolish and unbelieving—the one who subjected the whole world to his faith and granted the saints the dignity of the Christian name.

Although the greatness of his virtues shines before everyone [al. “is clear”], they do not cease to blaspheme. But the God who is mocked has been demonstrated by his works, so that he might overthrow the temples of demons and expose the slippery impiety of the Origenists. Their author, Origen, so deceived the ears of the simple and the light-minded by his persuasion as waves coming from the deep are wont to dash upon the shore and break themselves into foaming masses.

### 12.

Let us therefore, stirred by zeal for the faith, address the one who has dared to write that bodies are the ruin of rational creatures:

“If such impiety pleases you, how does the Apostle Paul write: ‘I desire that young women marry and bear children’ (1 Tim. 5)? Did he therefore command marriage so that the bodies born from women, when the angels fell from heaven and, according to you, were changed into souls, might prepare prisons for them [or: might prepare a prison]? Or did he command it so that, in the marital union, serving God’s decree, the human race might be preserved? For if he desires young women to marry and bear children, through whom human bodies are born, while souls that have gone astray are joined to bodies because of punishments and torments, there can be no doubt that marriage bonds are assigned to young women because of the punishment of souls, and not for the order of generation.

“But far be it from us to believe that this is so, or to believe that the bonds of husband and wife were joined not for blessing but because of sin. Nor, when God fashioned Adam and Eve, did he unite them in the blessing, saying, ‘Increase and multiply, and fill the earth’ (Gen. 1:28), on account of souls falling from heaven and the fall of rational creatures [B. P. reads: *Benedictione vocabit*, “he will call by a blessing,” in place of *sociavit*, “he united”]. For if souls were sent down to earth because of sins previously committed in heaven, in order to be bound to bodies, Paul lies when he writes: ‘Marriage is honorable, and the bed undefiled’ (Heb. 13:4). But he certainly does not lie.

“Therefore bodies are not fashioned because of the fall of souls, but so that the world may make good, through the succession of those being born, the losses caused by those who die, and may overcome the brevity of human life through perpetual succession. For if souls that have fallen and been joined to bodies are blessed by God, they will be in a better condition after they have received bodies [or: after they shall have received them]. But if they are said to be blessed for this reason—that they receive bodies as punishment for their sins—how are they blessed in the bodies into which they came because of their sins? [This is the reading of the Benedictine edition and of B. P., though it is wholly corrupt, if we know how to distinguish a faulty text from a sound one. We formerly conjectured that *benedicuntur*, “they are blessed,” should be read; this is now rejected, and, in accordance with Theophilus’s meaning, we judge that *labuntur*, “they fall,” must be restored.] For one of two things must be true: either they were in a state of blessing before the fall, or, after the fall and their union with bodies, they cannot be blessed at all. If blessing follows that former life, it abandons this one; if it is transferred to this one, it is proved not to have existed in the former.

“And if, before they fell and before they were clothed with human bodies, they were in a state of blessing, and, when falling and possessing bodies, were blessed again, then, according to the condition of blessing, the former life and the later life will be alike. But this does not follow at all, because it is the sinners who deserve punishments, not those who do not sin, who deserve blessing.

“Whatever they answer is true of the two alternatives, it will be subject to error, since they refuse to preserve the rule of ecclesiastical teaching. For if souls fell from heaven because of sins and were fastened to bodies as to a prison and chains, let them answer how Adam and Eve, male and female, living in bodies, were blessed. For, according to their delirious notions, it is not naked souls that are called man and woman, but bodies that distinguish the two sexes.

“But if they dwelt in heavenly places before receiving bodies, and their life there without bodies was then blessed and worthy of blessing, by what reasoning were they blessed either before they fell, or after they fell and, as punishment for their fall, were joined to gross bodies, and then received blessing again? For blessing and punishment are not the same thing; they are far removed from one another both in name and in operation, nor can things so sharply opposed be joined together in any way.

“And how is a multitude of children also promised to the righteous as a blessing, when the Prophet says: ‘The one who is least shall become a thousand, and the one who is last, a great nation’?”

### 13.

Therefore those who wish to celebrate the Lord’s festivals should also despise the images of Origen and overcome the shamefulness of his doctrines by reason. For just as the most impious of the pagans place error and custom before truth, fashioning idols in the likeness of human beings and blaspheming the invisible God by pretending that they possess form, limbs, and sexual organs—confessing them now male, now female—“and exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of the image of corruptible man” (Rom. 1:23), with its various forms [B. P. reads *in eo esse*, “to exist in it,” and, a little below, omits the word *zelo*, “zeal”]:

“So Origen, relying on the credulity and impiety of believers, has lowered, as it were, shrines of idols through the monuments of his treatises. We overthrow these by the authority of the Scriptures and by zeal for the faith, making use of the following comparison:

“For just as masons, wishing to build a square house, measure walls equal on every side, directing them by rule and plumb line, and construct in their work what they have designed in their minds; and join four sides of equal dimensions at right angles above and below, preserving the equality with which they began and its gradual growth, so that the beauty of the work may unite the diversity of the material and the craftsman’s structure may maintain the angular lines:

“So the teachers of the Church, possessing the testimonies of the Scriptures, make the foundations of their doctrine firm and remain fearless, offering their works to Christ and saying: ‘Establish me in your words’ (Ps. 119:28). For he of whom it is written, ‘The stone which the builders rejected, this has become the cornerstone’ (Matt. 21:42), joins us and those who are above in one solemn celebration [the common reading was: ‘joining us,’ which gives an incomplete sense]. Toward this celebration, as we hasten with swift course, we need not fear the madness of the waves of heretics, which will quickly be broken apart.”

### 14.

For just as the captains of great ships, when they see an immense swell coming from the open sea, receive the foaming waves like hunters receiving a most savage beast, and support them by presenting the ship’s prow against them, turning the rudders in different directions and, as the blasts of the winds and necessity require, tightening or loosening the ropes; and when the wave has subsided, release the strained fastenings of the nails on both sides of the ship, so that, resting for a little while, they may be prepared for the swell that is coming:

“When it has come again, they tighten the heads of the nails and spread the oars, so that, with the winds torn and divided this way and that, the labor on both sides may be equal, and what could not be endured all at once may become more tolerable when divided:

“Those who care for themselves imitate this example and, using the divine words as a rudder, confront the storm of the heretics and, retaining God’s law as their skill, strive to raise up those who had fallen [or: had been corrupted], so that those who stand may persevere in a firm course and all may be preserved together through the help of doctrine.

“For what the nail is to the helmsman, the law of God is to the mind. In observing the Lord’s Pascha, let us prefer nothing in the world to the love of God and neighbor. Let us not change our judgment according to the variations of human circumstances, which turn this way and that, so that, if the winds should perhaps blow again and poverty should be changed into wealth, humility into exaltation, and disgrace into glory, we should suddenly turn against those whom we formerly served with shameful flattery because of their power, resisting openly those whom we formerly deemed worthy of reverence, weighing the bond between us by circumstances rather than by faith [B. P. adds: “if perhaps we serve”].

“Indeed, displaying hidden enmities in a time of need and coming forth from our dens like serpents, we may be not merely utterly ungrateful toward those by whose benefits we were sustained, rejoicing if we have borne the title of their clients, but may pursue them as public enemies even to bloodshed; trampling upon the fallen and prostrate—those whom, because of their wealth, we formerly looked up to [or: welcomed]—and proclaiming them the worst of all once their riches have been exchanged for poverty; praising power and slandering misfortune; honoring or despising someone not according to the nature of things but according to changes of circumstance; calling those whom we formerly called masters and patrons by the names of brigands and most worthless slaves.

“Thus our wickedness becomes apparent in every respect, when either we praise those unworthy of praise or pursue with slander those worthy of praise [in the same edition: “while we pursue with praise or slander those undeserving of it”], imitating what they said reproachfully to blessed Job: ‘You have been scourged for the few things in which you sinned’ (Job 11:6).”

### 15.

Therefore let us love not uncertain riches, but the most steadfast virtue. Let not the harshness of poverty humble us, nor riches exalt us, since they habitually depress and raise up the most foolish of human beings. Rather, let us regulate both according to the honorable nature of things, enduring sorrowful and joyful circumstances with equal spirit.

The concern for riches interrupts the sweetest sleep, contrives accusations against the innocent, and, when it has amassed boundless wealth, prepares material for eternal fires. Once insatiable frenzy has settled upon the wealth it has acquired, avarice is not satisfied: it despises laws, looks down upon the flames of Gehenna, and considers the future tribunal of judgment nothing.

Nor do adversaries fight against their enemies as fiercely as riches fight against virtues, unless they are tempered by reason and mercy toward one’s neighbors. In cities riches are preferred to nobility; they give new men an ancient family. The desire for riches can never be satisfied by any riches.

The miser is always in want. He does not know the measure [Martianaeus incorrectly has: “your mind does not know…”; we think the reading *mensuram*, “measure,” which we once supplied conjecturally, was also found in the old Benedictine edition, though that book is presently unavailable. Shortly below the sense is: “he has one measure: always to seek beyond measure.” See Epistle 53 to Paulinus, no. 10]—for what he possesses falls as far short as what he does not possess.

The underworld is not filled by the dead; the more it receives, the more it desires. Avarice imitates it and cannot be satisfied: whatever it has, it demands more. It considers everything it possesses less than what it desires; it is always immense, always immoderate, never extinguishing the sinner’s ardor through the magnitude of his wealth.

At banquets it devours not food but injustice; in the courts it mixes quarrels [or: quarrels are mixed], and conflicts; it gives birth to envy, through which one arrives at murder. It is not in possession of its mind, but, like a drunken person, it sways, having one measure: always to seek beyond measure.

The sea is enclosed by shores, and the waves coming from the open sea, together with the fury of raging swells, are kept back by harbors either built by human hands or made exceptionally secure by nature. But the desire for riches, unless restrained by reason, is controlled neither by counsel nor moderated by law, nor satisfied by any abundance.

It is not ashamed and does not fear the future judgment [Martianaeus again incorrectly has: “does not fear the judgment of the future”]. Rather, from the desire to possess more, just as the voluptuous, devoted to pleasures, leap eagerly into embraces and rage toward lust, so avarice fills cities, villages, and country estates with accusations and dissensions.

Avarice possesses islands, seas, lands, shores, roads, crossings, and enterprises [we have adopted the singular *possidet avaritia*, “avarice possesses,” instead of the common printed reading *possident avaritiae*, “avarices possess.” Martianaeus errs still more by inserting the word *se*, “itself,” in “while it is driven by the desire…”; we removed it on the authority of the old Benedictine edition].

While driven by the desire to possess more, it moves merchandise here and there through trade and lays the inexhaustible foundations of riches through frauds and perjuries.

### 16.

Therefore, despising such madness, let us seek the riches of the worship of God and the most secure possessions of chastity and holiness [the Benedictine edition has “the holiness of chastity,” but the printed reading does not fit well; perhaps the text should read simply “the worship of God,” so that nothing need be said about the faulty punctuation].

Let us adore the one divinity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, believing that the resurrection of the dead is incorruptible and enduring forever. For death cannot overcome that which has been strengthened by Christ’s passion, raising up the incorruptible and everlasting temple of his body.

Let us pray for the most devout Emperors, and let us adorn the precepts of fasting through observance of God’s law. For virtue, without any compulsion, guards its followers and raises the mind, wavering amid various thoughts, from earthly things to the heights. It contemplates not the beauty of bodies but the order of conduct and morals [we read this from the old Benedictine edition; the Benedictine text had “the manner of life”], showing the mind the choirs of the rejoicing angels in heaven and teaching it the flashes of resplendent disciplines, so that in the present age, like a most courageous athlete, it may endure the blows inflicted upon it and await the glory that will come in return.

Let it be subject to no vices, but raise the inner person to eternal things through desire for itself [we supplied *sui*, “of itself,” which was absent from the Benedictine edition]. Let it restrain every impulse of pleasure by reason and consider what it is destined to become. As far as human frailty can endure, let it withdraw from concern for bodily things, preferring spiritual things to carnal, so that, despising the body itself and persuading it to enter upon a life harsher but better than the pleasures of the present [either *voluptatum*, “of pleasures,” should be read as *voluptatem*, “pleasure,” or some word such as *illecebras*, “enticements,” must be supplied to complete the sense], the one who once served lust may serve chastity in a good freedom and, drawn back from precipices, may accept the gentle reins of fasting.

For if the weak nature of the body is without a driver and teacher, and refuses to obey the commanding mind, it brings countless shipwrecks upon itself and its ruler [the earlier printing carelessly had “itself and its ruler” in a corrupt form], drags the mind toward the most shameful lusts and the abyss of pleasures, so that it considers nothing honorable, but, fleeing what is good, remains in filth and squalor.

But when virtue has governed the mind as a charioteer [or: in the manner of a charioteer] and, standing as if in a chariot, has brought its impulses and various desires under control with the reins of teaching [perhaps: “restrained them”], it lifts the mind from lowly things to the heights. It displays invisible and eternal things in place of visible things, prepares a dwelling in heaven, and makes as friends for it those who, serving in the ministry of God, enjoy spiritual delights.

Thus what the mind saw here in an image, there it may perceive in reality, and may see a brightness greater than the rays of the sun—a brightness that has descended to us here only in part, so that we may advance from lesser things to greater, and, as though through letters and syllables, make progress toward reading. For those things require these, and these require those [the common editions had the erroneous reading “needing”].

When we have been joined there to the fellowship of the blessed, we shall hear: “Well done, good and faithful servant, because you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things. Enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. 25:21, 23).

### 17.

The fasts of holy Lent begin [or: “as we begin the fasts of holy Lent”] on the eleventh day of the month Phamenoth, and the sixteenth day of the month Pharmuthi is the Sunday of the Passion week. We shall end the fasts on the evening of Saturday, the twenty-first day of that same month Pharmuthi, and on the following Sunday we shall celebrate Pascha [or: “let us celebrate Pascha”], on the twenty-second day of the same month.

After this we shall join the seven weeks of holy Pentecost [or: “let us join…”], remembering the poor, loving God and neighbor, praying for enemies, showing kindness to persecutors, and raising up the fallen among the sick through consolation and mercy. Let the tongue always resound with the praises of God. Let the just judgments of the Church never be destroyed by irrational clemency, nor human decisions be preferred to the law of God.

If we desire his friendship [or: “if we have desired his friendship”], we shall attain heavenly glory in Christ Jesus our Lord, through whom and with whom, to God the Father, be glory and dominion with the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

[The eleventh of Phamenoth corresponds to March 7; the sixteenth and twenty-first of Pharmuthi correspond to April 11 and April 17. These dates identify the Pascha of the year 404. The total is one day more than forty days, from which it follows that the Alexandrian Lent began on the Monday of the sixth week before Pascha, not on the preceding Sunday, as some have incorrectly supposed. Socrates, Book V, chapter 22, says: “Those in Alexandria fast the fast before Pascha for six weeks, calling it Lent.” The Milanese Church preserves this custom to the present day.]

### 18.

Greet one another with a holy kiss. The brothers who are with us greet you. You should also know this:

The following have been appointed in the respective places of the deceased bishops: in the city of Nichium, Theodosius in place of Theopemptus; in Terenuthis, Arsintius; in the town of Geras, in place of Eudemon, Pirozus; among the Achaeans, in place of Apollo, Musaeus; in Athribis, in place of Isidore, Athanasius; in Cleopatris, Offellus; in the town of Laton, in place of Timothy, Apelles.

Write to these men, therefore, and, according to custom, receive ecclesiastical letters from them.

[The earlier text incorrectly had *constitutis*, “appointed”; read *Nicium* instead of *Nichium.” Stephanus, in another context, mentions the inhabitants of this city as “the Nicians of Nicium” (*οἱ τῆς Νικίου Νικιῶται*) and attests that it is a city of Egypt. In the *Notice* of the Alexandrian Patriarchate, by Charles, Paul of Saint-Paul, and Schelestratius, it is listed first in Egypt.

Instead of *Theopemptus* the text had *Heopemptus*, a name found nowhere. Terenuthis, an Egyptian city, is also mentioned by Stephanus in Hermothis; in the *Notice* it is assigned to the Second Thebaid.

The same source mentions the Gerrhaean peoples in Chatramotis from Strabo; therefore, here too *Gerrhas* should apparently be restored in place of *Geras*. The ancient *Notices* place them in First Augustamnica.

In place of *Achaeans*, *Acchenians* is easily corrected, since the Achaeans outside Greece, whom Pliny mentions in Book 6, chapter 11, are wholly irrelevant here. Stephanus places the peoples called Acchenians, Greek *Ἀκχενούς*, “at the narrows of the Red Sea” (*ἐπὶ τῶ αὐχέσι ἐρυθρᾶς θαλάσσης*); Ptolemy, in his description of Arabia, calls them Achitae, and Pliny, Book 6, chapter 28, calls them Achenas in my copy.

Nor does it seem to us that the Antaeans of First Thebaid can be intended here. In the following name, *Athrividi* is also corrupt and should be corrected to *Athlibis*—Greek *Ἄθλιβις*—in Strabo, Herodotus, and Stephanus, or *Athribis*. Stephanus reports that the name was formerly written with an *r* by Nicanor, and the *Notices* regularly read it in Second Augustamnica.

Cleopatris, which follows, was more frequently called Arsinoe by the ancients, and Ptolemy also uses this name in Book 4, chapter 5. Strabo says: “the city Arsinoe, which some call Cleopatris” (*πόλιν Ἀρσιόνην, ἣν ἔνιοι Κλεοπατρίδα καλοῦσι*), although shortly afterward he makes two different cities of them, as it were; it is not the place to examine the reasons for this. We learn from the *Notices* that it was situated in First Egypt.

Finally, for *Laton*, Martianaeus had noted in the margin of the book that in the manuscript of St. Thierry it was written *Jabon*. This reading too is not entirely unsuitable, if Jambon is assigned in the *Notices* to Second Thebaid, which Charles of Saint-Paul takes for Ombos—though I fear incorrectly, since Theophilus calls Ombos by its proper name in the preceding Paschal letter, p. 603, and reports that Verres, not Timothy, was appointed to that city in place of Sylvanus.

We insist, however, that *Laton* be retained. Strabo mentions this town in Book 17 in connection with the animals worshiped by the Egyptians, from which they also derived the names of cities; he says that from *Lato*, a kind of fish in the Nile, the inhabitants were called *Latopolitae*. The town is assigned to Second Thebaid in the *Notice* and is called Leto by Schelestratius, although there may have been another town with nearly the same name, located in First Egypt. See, in so few lines, how many errors there are, and how many things have also been omitted that required explanation.]

## Epistle 101 [Note: Elsewhere numbered 90. Written around the year 402.]

### Augustine to Jerome

He denies having written a book against Jerome, being mistaken in this only because someone had called a lengthy letter a book.

To his most beloved, most desired [the Benedictine editors of Augustine’s works here prefer “most desirable”; at the conclusion of the letter they prefer “most desired”], and honored brother and fellow presbyter in Christ, Jerome: Augustine sends greetings in the Lord.

1. “I have heard that my letters have reached your hands; but because I have not yet deserved a reply, I would by no means attribute this to any lack of affection on your part. Doubtless some obstacle intervened. From this I recognize that I ought rather to beseech the Lord to grant your will the opportunity to send what you will have written in reply. For he has already granted you the ability to reply, since, whenever you wish, you can do so very easily.

2. “I also hesitated whether to believe what was certainly reported to me [the same editors read: “Even this, indeed reported to me—whether indeed …”], but for this reason too I ought not to have hesitated about writing something to you [Martianaeus reads: “But this brief message was reported …”]. I was told that this had been suggested to your affection by certain brothers: that I had written a book against you and sent it to Rome. Know that this is false. I call our God to witness that I did not do this.

“But if perhaps something is found in some of my writings in which I appear to have thought differently from you, you should recognize—or, if it cannot be recognized, believe—that it was not written against you, but that I wrote what seemed right to me. I say this in such a way that I am not only entirely ready, if anything in my writings has disturbed you, to receive fraternally what you think to the contrary, rejoicing either in my correction or in your own goodwill, but I also ask and earnestly request this from you.

3. “O if only it had been permitted me to enjoy you in the Lord for frequent and sweet conversation—not as one living under the same roof, at least as a neighbor! But since this has not been granted, I ask you to strive to preserve, increase, and perfect this very thing: that in the Lord we are together as far as possible, and not to despise replies, however rare [Erasmus, followed through great carelessness by Martianaeus, read: “that we may be together as far as possible”; Victorius had formerly corrected both words].

“Greet the holy brother Paulinianus with my respectful devotion, and all the brothers who, with you and because of you [the Benedictines read “who rejoice in the Lord,” in place of “who glory in the Lord”], glory in the Lord. May you be remembered before the Lord in every holy desire of yours, my most beloved, most desired, and honored brother in Christ.”

## Epistle 102 [Note: Elsewhere numbered 91. Written shortly after the preceding letter.]

### Jerome to Augustine

Having received Augustine’s letters, which contain a question concerning a useful lie, he still doubts whether they are Augustine’s and says that he will not reply until their authorship is certain. He also recalls Rufinus under an assumed name.

To the truly holy and most blessed Pope Augustine: Jerome sends greetings in the Lord.

1. At the very moment of the departure of our holy son Asterius, my deacon and close associate, your letters reached me. In them you satisfy me that you did not send a book to Rome against my insignificance. I had not heard that this had been done either, but copies of a certain letter, supposedly written to me through our brother the Deacon Sisinnius, reached this place. In it you urge me to sing a *palinode* (*παλινῳδίαν*) concerning a certain passage of the Apostle and to imitate Stesichorus, who wavered between blaming and praising Helen, so that, having lost his sight by speaking against her, he might recover it by praising her.

“I plainly confess to your graciousness that, although your style and arguments [the Greeks call arguments *ἐπιχειρήματα*, as Cicero testifies in *Ad Herennium*] seemed to me to be yours, nevertheless I did not think that copies of letters should be trusted rashly. Otherwise, if I replied, you might justly complain in offense that I ought first to have proved that the words were yours and only then replied.

“To this delay was added the long illness of the holy and venerable Paula. For while we sat beside her in her weakness for a long time [or: “while we sit beside her in her weakness”], we almost forgot your letter—or that of whoever had written under your name—remembering the verse: ‘Music in mourning is an untimely tale’ (Sirach 22:6).

“Therefore, if the letter is yours, write openly, or send more reliable copies, so that, without any bitterness or resentment, we may engage in discussion of the Scriptures and either correct our own error or show that we have rebuked another person in vain.

2. “Far be it from me to dare to touch anything in the books of your blessedness. It is enough for me to prove what is mine and not criticize what belongs to another. Your prudence knows very well that each person should abound in his own judgment, and that it is the mark of childish boasting—something young men once customarily did—to seek fame for their own name by accusing illustrious men.

“I am not so foolish as to think myself harmed by the diversity of your explanations, any more than you are harmed if we have thought differently. But true criticism among friends is this: that, not seeing our own bag, we examine, in Persius’ phrase, the bag of others [the former text had a corrupt reading, which our work corrected; Erasmus also adopted the correction. The Benedictines further note that this alludes to Aesop’s fable in which each mortal is given a bag, carrying behind him the part filled with his own vices while the part containing the vices of others hangs in front for him to see. The reference is also to Persius’ *Satires*:

‘Thus no one tries to descend into himself, no one,
but looks at the bag hanging from the back before him.’].

“It remains that you should love one who is diligent toward you, and that, in the field of the Scriptures, you should not challenge an old man, young though you are. We have had our time and have run as far as we could. Now that you are running and traversing long distances, leisure is owed to us.

“And, if I may say so with honor and your permission, do not seem to me to be the only one who has proposed something from the poets. Remember Dares and Entellus (Virgil, *Aeneid* 5), and the common proverb: ‘The tired ox plants its foot more firmly.’ We dictated these things sadly. Would that we might deserve your embraces and, through mutual conversation, either teach or learn something.

3. “With his customary rashness, Calpurnius, surnamed the Wool-Merchant, sent me his curses; through his efforts I have learned that they have reached even Africa [it is clear that Rufinus is being ridiculed under this name, and that his books of invectives are meant by these “curses”]. I have replied to them briefly and in part, and I sent you copies of his little book. When the proper time comes, I shall first send the fuller work. In it I took care not to injure Christian reputation in any respect, but only to refute the falsehood and folly of a delirious and ignorant man.

“Remember me, holy and venerable Pope. See how much I love you: although provoked, I have not wished to reply, nor shall I believe that what I might perhaps criticize in another belongs to you.”

Our common brother respectfully greets you.

## Epistle 103 [Note: Elsewhere numbered 98. Written in the year 403.]

### To Augustine

He commends Praesidius to Augustine and sends greetings to Alypius.

To the truly holy and most blessed Pope Augustine: Jerome sends greetings in Christ.

1. Last year, through our brother Asterius the Subdeacon, I sent a letter to your graciousness, offering the ready service of a greeting. I suppose that it was delivered to you.

“Now also, through my holy brother Praesidius the Deacon, I ask first that you remember me. Then I ask you to hold the bearer of the letter in your favor and know that he is most closely connected with me, and, whenever necessity requires, cherish and support him—not because, by Christ’s gift, he lacks anything, but because he most eagerly seeks the friendship of good men and considers himself to have received the greatest benefit when he is joined to them.

“You will be able to learn from him himself why he has sailed to the West.

2. “We who are established in the monastery are shaken by various waves from every side and endure the hardships of our pilgrimage. But we trust in him who said: ‘Take courage; I have overcome the world’ (John 16:33), believing that, with him granting it and presiding over us, we shall gain victory over the enemy, the devil.

“I ask you to greet our holy and venerable brother, Pope Alypius, on my behalf. The holy brothers who hasten to serve the Lord with us in the monastery greet you warmly.

“May Christ our Lord and Almighty preserve you unharmed and mindful of me, truly holy and worthy of acceptance Pope.”

## Epistle 104 [Note: Elsewhere numbered 88. Written in the year 403.]

### Augustine to Jerome

He dissuades Jerome from translating the books of the Old Testament from Hebrew; rather, he advises him to restore to its true form the Septuagint version, which has been gravely corrupted and made variable. He approves Jerome’s correction of the New Testament.

To the venerable and desirable holy brother and fellow presbyter Jerome: Augustine sends greetings in the Lord.

1. Ever since I began writing to you and desiring your writings, no better opportunity has arisen for me than that my letter should be brought to you by a servant of God, a most faithful minister, and one very dear to me—our son the Deacon Cyprian.

“Through him I confidently hope for your letters, so that I cannot hope for anything more certain in this kind of matter. For our aforesaid son will lack neither zeal in requesting replies, nor favor in obtaining them, nor diligence in preserving them, nor eagerness in carrying them, nor faithfulness in delivering them.

“Only, if in some way I may deserve it, may the Lord help me and be present to your heart and my desire, so that no greater desire may impede our brotherly willingness.

2. “Since I have already sent two letters but have received none from you afterward, I wished to send those same letters again, believing [Victorius, from Brescian manuscripts, adds ‘to you’] that they had not reached you.

“Even if they did reach you, and perhaps yours were unable to reach me, send again the very writings you already sent, if they have perhaps been preserved. If not, write again what I may read, provided that you do not disdain to answer them [or: “do not refuse to answer,” which I have been awaiting for a long time].

“I also wished to send now the first letters that, while still a presbyter, I had prepared to send to you through a certain brother of ours, Profuturus, who afterward became our colleague and has already departed this life. At that time he himself could not carry them, because, just as he was preparing to depart, he was detained by the burden of the episcopate and then died shortly afterward.

“I send them now so that you may know how long I have been burning for conversation with you, and how much I suffer because the bodily senses of you, my sweetest brother and honored among the members of the Lord, are so far from me. Through those senses my mind might approach your mind.”

3. “In this letter I add what we learned afterward: that you translated Job from Hebrew, when we already possessed a translation of that same Prophet made from the Greek into Latin. In the latter, however, you marked with asterisks what exists in Hebrew but is absent from the Greek, and with obeli what is found in the Greek but not in Hebrew—with such remarkable diligence that in certain places we see individual stars placed beside individual words, indicating that those same words exist in Hebrew but not in Greek.

“In this later translation, which was made from Hebrew, the same faithfulness in the wording does not appear. It greatly disturbs one who reflects upon the matter: either why, in that first translation, asterisks were affixed with such care that they indicated even the smallest particles of speech missing from the Greek manuscripts but present in the Hebrew; or why, in this second translation, which is from Hebrew, the matter was handled more negligently, so that the same particles were not found in their proper places [the Benedictine editors of Augustine’s works omit the negative particle, though without changing the sense: ‘so that the same particles would be found…’].

“I wanted to give an example of this, but for the moment I lacked the Hebrew codex. Nevertheless, because you surpass others in understanding, you understand, I think, not only what I have said but also what I wished to say. I trust that, once you have explained the matter, you will clarify the reason for what troubles me.”

## 4

I would certainly prefer you to interpret for us the Greek canonical Scriptures that are said to possess the authority of the Septuagint translators.[^c0095-1] For it will be exceedingly difficult if your translation begins to be read more widely throughout the churches, because the Latin churches will then differ from the Greek churches—especially since an objector can easily be refuted by producing a Greek book, that is, in the best-known language. But whoever is disturbed by something unusual in what has been translated from Hebrew, and brings an accusation of falsity, will reach the Hebrew witnesses by which the objection may be defended either only with difficulty or not at all. And even if he does reach them, who could endure the condemnation of so many Latin and Greek authorities? Moreover, consulted Hebrews may give a different answer, so that you alone may appear necessary, since you could even refute them themselves; yet it would be remarkable if you could find a judge by whose decision that could be done.

[^c0095-1]: The Benedictines read: “which is said to be that of the Septuagint translators, without authority.”

## 3

For our brother the Bishop, when he had begun having your translation read in the church over which he presides, encountered something expressed quite differently by you in the Prophet Jonah (chapter 4, verse 6) from what had become fixed in everyone’s understanding and memory and had been sung through successive generations. Such a great uproar arose among the people—especially when the Greeks accused it and inflamed the charge of falsity—that the Bishop was compelled to demand the testimony of the Jews (for it was indeed a city in which many Jews lived).[^c0095-2]

*[From Erasmus and the Louvain recension we restore* inflammantibus *("inflaming"); in more recent editions,* inclamantibus *("crying out") had hitherto prevailed, neither suitably nor correctly. For all the manuscripts carefully consulted by Martianaeus read with us; Cicero too, in* Against Verres, *said that to “inflame hatred” is to increase it.]* Whether they replied through ignorance or malice that the Hebrew codices contained what the Greeks and Latins had, I do not know.[^c0095-3] What more is there to say? The man was forced, as it were, to correct an error, unwilling after so great a danger to remain without his congregation. Hence it seems to us that you too may occasionally have been mistaken in some matters. And consider how serious this is in writings that cannot be corrected by comparing the testimony of the customary languages.

[^c0095-2]: Martianaeus attacks Pezronius more than sufficiently, and unjustly, for thinking that one should read *Oea quippe erat civitas* (“for it was the city of Oea”), and so forth, instead of *ea quippe* (“for it”). Isaac Vossius had earlier wished to substitute the proper name Oea for that word in a letter to Schotanus, and had supported his conjecture with arguments by no means contemptible. Indeed, he thought he could gather with sufficient certainty that Marinianus was Bishop of that city at the time. We do not wish to alter the text without the support of manuscript codices; nevertheless, we think it obvious to everyone that it could very easily have happened that ancient copyists, offended by the unusual word Oea, substituted from their own ingenuity a word that most closely resembled it. For the context of the received reading does not seem to us, as it does to Martianaeus, to be more correct. On the contrary, if emendation is permitted, the sense could easily be that the testimony of the Jews was sought in Oea, a city in which many of them lived—not that the city itself was a Jewish one, as he falsely presents it. Nor should one adopt the punctuation used by the Benedictine editors of Augustine’s works, according to which *ea*, that is, “such,” refers to the city’s character, so that *Judaeorum* belongs with *testimonium* rather than with *civitas*. In either form the sentence is either false or obscure and impeded. Nor does what Martianaeus presses most strongly persuade us: that a town, or small town, is called Oea by Jerome below, in Letter 112, section 21, while Oea—now called Tripoli—is said to have been and still to be a large city. For Augustine too calls it a city here, and the fact that it was a bishop’s seat confirms this; moreover, everyone knows that all towns are cities, but not every city is a town. See Pliny, Solinus, Mela, and the *Acts of the Council of Carthage*.

[^c0095-3]: The Benedictines add: “and they said.”

## 6

Accordingly, we give no small thanks to God for your work, by which you translated the Gospel from Greek, because there is almost nowhere any offense when we compare it with the Greek Scripture. Thus, if anyone stubbornly favors an old error, once the codices have been produced and compared, he is either very easily instructed or refuted. And if some exceedingly rare points reasonably cause concern, who is so hard-hearted that he would not readily forgive work so useful, for which a sufficient return of praise cannot be made?

But I should like you to deign to explain why, in many places, the authority of the Hebrew codices differs from that of the Greek codices, which is called the Septuagint. For that authority is not of little weight: it has earned such renown, and not only does the matter itself show that the Apostles used it, but I also remember that you have borne witness to this. Therefore you will be of the greatest benefit if you restore to Latin truth that Greek Scripture which the Septuagint produced. It varies so greatly in different codices that it can scarcely be tolerated, and it is so suspect that one hesitates to bring forward or establish anything from it lest something different be found in the Greek.

I had thought this letter would be brief; but somehow it has become so sweet for me to proceed in it as though I were speaking with you. But I beg you by the Lord: do not be troubled to answer everything and to grant me your presence as far as you are able.

# Letter 105

*[Previously numbered 92. Written around the year 403.]*

## To Augustine

He complains about Augustine’s letter, circulated throughout Italy, in which a passage was criticized as having been incorrectly expounded by him in his Letter to the Galatians.

To the truly holy and most blessed lord Pope Augustine, Jerome sends greetings in the Lord.

### 1

You send me frequent letters and often urge me to reply to one of your letters. As I have already written, copies of it reached me through our brother the Deacon Sysinnius without your subscription; and you say that you sent it to me first through our brother Profuturus and later through someone else. Meanwhile Profuturus was recalled from his journey, made a bishop, and taken away by a swift death; while the man whose name you conceal was afraid of the dangers of the sea and changed his plan of sailing.

Since this is so, I cannot sufficiently marvel that this same letter is said to be possessed by many people in Rome and throughout Italy, yet has not reached me alone, although I alone was its intended recipient—especially since the same brother Sysinnius said that, among your other treatises, he had found it not in Africa and not with you, but on the island of Adria, nearly five years ago.

### 2

All suspicion must be removed from friendship, and one must speak with a friend as one ought to speak with another. Some of my close associates, vessels of Christ—of whom there is a very large number in Jerusalem and the holy places—suggested that you had acted not with a straightforward mind, but in pursuit of praise, popular rumor, and a little public glory: that you might grow at our expense; that many might learn that you challenged me while I feared you; that you wrote as the learned man while I kept silent as the ignorant one; and that at last you had found someone who could impose a limit and silence upon my loquacity.[^c0095-4]

To speak frankly to your esteem, I first did not wish to reply because I did not believe the letter was genuinely yours. Nor did I want—as the popular proverb has it concerning certain matters—to mistake a sword smeared with honey for something harmless. Secondly, I was afraid that I might seem insolently to answer a bishop of my communion and to criticize something in a letter that criticized me, especially since I judged certain things in it to be heretical.

[^c0095-4]: Martianaeus reads *requirentem* (“seeking”), a reading formerly condemned by Victorius in the Erasmian manuscripts.

### 3

Finally, I did not want you justly to complain and say: “What? You had seen my letter and recognized the marks of the familiar hand in the subscription, yet you could so easily injure a friend and turn another’s malice into an insult against me?”

Therefore, as I have already written, either send that same letter signed in your own hand, or stop attacking an old man hiding in his little cell. But if you wish either to exercise or display your learning,[^c0095-5] seek young, eloquent, and noble men—of whom Rome is said to have very many—who can and dare to engage with you and, in disputation over the holy Scriptures, bear the yoke with a bishop.

I was once a soldier; now I am a veteran. I ought to praise both your victories and those of others, not once again to fight with an exhausted body. Otherwise, if you frequently drive me to write in reply, I may recall that history in which Quintus Fabius Maximus broke the youthful exuberance of Hannibal by his patience.[^c0095-6]

> Age takes everything away, even the mind:
>
> Often I remember, as a boy, burying long days in song.
>
> Now so many songs are forgotten by me; even my voice itself
>
> has already fled from Moeris.  
> *(Virgil, Eclogue 9.51)*

And, to speak more especially of the holy Scriptures, that Barzillai the Gileadite, leaving to his youthful son all the benefits and pleasures of King David (2 Samuel 19), showed that old age ought neither to desire such things nor accept them when offered.

[^c0095-5]: Martianaeus, following Erasmus, reads *ostendere* (“to display”).

[^c0095-6]: This is found in Livy, Third Decade, book 2; Virgil refers to Fabius Maximus in the words: “The one man who, by delaying, restored our fortunes.”

### 4

You swear that you neither wrote nor sent to Rome a book against me—a book that you say you did not write; but if anything should be found in your writings that differs from my view, you say that I have not been injured by you, but that you wrote what seemed right to you. Please listen to me patiently.

You did not write the book—then how were writings criticizing me by you brought to me through others? Why does Italy possess what you did not write? Why do you demand that I reply to what you deny having written?

I am not so dull that, if you held a different opinion, I would think myself injured by you. But if you criticize my statements face to face, demand an account of my writings, compel me to correct what I have written, and challenge me to a *palinode* (*παλινῳδία*, a recantation), then friendship is injured and the rights of our relationship violated.

So that we may not seem to quarrel childishly or provide material for our supporters and detractors to contend over against one another, I write these things because I wish to love you sincerely and in a Christian manner, retaining nothing in my mind that differs from my lips.

For it is not fitting that I, who from youth to this age have labored in a little monastery with holy brothers, should dare to write anything against the bishop of my communion—and a bishop whom I began to love before I knew him; who first invited me into friendship; and whose growth, after my own, in the learning of the divine Scriptures I rejoiced to see.[^c0095-7]

Therefore either deny that the book is yours, if it is not yours, and stop demanding a reply to what you did not write; or, if it is yours, acknowledge it frankly. Then, if I write anything in my own defense, the fault will lie with you, who provoked me, not with me, who was compelled to answer.

[^c0095-7]: Some manuscripts omit “of the divine Scriptures.”

### 5

You further add that, if anything in your writings should trouble me and I wished to correct it, you would receive this fraternally, and would not merely rejoice in my goodwill toward you; indeed, you entreat me to do precisely this.[^c0095-8]

Again I say what I think: you provoke an old man, spur on one who is silent, and seem to display your learning. Yet at my age I ought not to be thought hostile toward one to whom I owe rather favor.

If perverse people find in the Gospels and the Prophets something on which they can base criticism, are you surprised if, in your books—and especially in an exposition of the Scriptures, which are often exceedingly obscure—some things appear to depart from the straight line?

I say this not because I already judge that there are things in your works deserving criticism. I have never devoted myself to reading them, nor are copies of them plentiful among us, except for your books of the *Soliloquies* and certain commentaries on the Psalms. If I wished to examine these, I would show them to differ—not from me, who am nothing, but from the interpretations of the ancient Greeks.

Farewell, my dearest friend, my son in age and my parent in rank. And observe this request of mine: whatever you write to me, make sure that it reaches me first.
