[^c0095-8]: Victorius substituted *de* (“about”) for the transmitted preposition. Augustine writes above, in Letter 101, section 2: “I shall rejoice in your goodwill toward me,” and so forth.

# Letter 106

*[Previously numbered 135. Written around the year 403.]*

*[Martianaeus had earlier published this letter separately in his* Prodromus of Jerome*, with much greater care and labor than the others, in order to offer a specimen of the new edition he had undertaken. He then reprinted it in two facing columns, so that the falsity of the older editions might appear at a glance in one column and the truth, as he himself calls it, which he had composed in the other. Many errors had crept in, especially in the Hebrew words, in Erasmus and Victorius; Martianaeus corrected them throughout. Even if he had accomplished nothing else, Jerome’s admirers would still have had reason to acknowledge their great debt to him. Yet no one has ever approved that arrangement, which was designed to create envy against men of great name, because of the reader’s weariness and the waste of paper. We append the variants in the customary manner and have also used four manuscripts, all extremely ancient and of the highest quality: one Veronese and three Roman manuscripts, namely Vatican 15, the second Regina Svecorum 286, and Palatine 39. How much further we have advanced by means of them will be for the reader to judge.]*

## To Sunnia and Fretela

After congratulating Sunnia and Fretela—men of Getic origin, it is true, but outstanding in their study of the divine Scriptures—Jerome answers the questions they had submitted from the Psalms and resolves all their difficulties. He shows which readings among the Greek and Latin variants are to be preferred and which approach the Hebrew source more closely.

To the most beloved brothers Sunnia and Fretela, and to all the others who serve the Lord with you, Jerome sends greetings.

*[It has long been established that Sunnia and Fretela were not women but men, as the Benedictine editor and others had previously demonstrated at length; there is no need to add to their arguments. It should nevertheless be considered that a recent author of* Sacred Moravia *has proposed that Fretela—whom he thinks was also called Frederick—was bishop of Juliomontium, or Olomouc, and Sunnia bishop of Nitravia. As evidence he cites a letter of Eugenius II, dated 828, addressed to the bishops of Moravia and Pannonia, as well as Aventinus, in book 2 of his* Annals of the Bavarians*. Although he seems to have supported the rest with sound conjectures, he certainly errs in saying that those men had been appointed bishops from the year 397. He should have said after the year 404, since the context clearly shows that when Jerome wrote this letter to them they held no ecclesiastical dignity.]*

### 1

The apostolic and prophetic saying has truly been fulfilled in you:

> “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Psalm 18:5; Romans 10:18).

Who would have believed that the barbarian tongue of the Getae would seek the Hebrew Truth, and that Germany itself would search out the words of the Holy Spirit while the Greeks were drowsing—or rather, contending? In truth I have learned that God is not a respecter of persons, but that in every nation whoever fears God and practices righteousness is acceptable to him (Acts 10:34–35).

Hands once hardened by holding a sword-hilt, and fingers better suited to handling arrows, are becoming supple for the stylus and pen; and warlike breasts are being transformed into Christian gentleness.

Now we also see Isaiah’s prophecy fulfilled in deed:

> “They will beat their swords into plowshares and their spears into pruning-hooks; nation will not take up sword against nation, nor will they learn war anymore” (Isaiah 2:4).

And again in the same prophet:

> “The wolf will feed with the lamb; the leopard will rest with the kid; the calf, the lion, and the bull will feed together; and a little child will lead them. The ox and the bear will pasture together; their young will rest side by side; and the lion and the ox will eat straw” (Isaiah 11:6–7 and following).

This does not mean that simplicity passes into wildness, but that wildness learns simplicity.

*[Some older editions read “despising,” which may perhaps be more accurate. Shortly afterward, where Martianaeus incorrectly read* operatus *through a typographical error, some manuscripts add “of God.”]*

### 2

You ask of me a task of great labor and even greater unpopularity, in which not the writer’s talent but his learning will be tested, so that while I myself wish to judge others, I offer myself to everyone for judgment. In the work of the Psalter, according to the arrangement of your memorandum, you ask me to indicate, wherever there is disagreement between the Latins and Greeks, what agrees best with the Hebrews.[^c0095-9]

I briefly warn you of this, so that you may know that there is one edition which Origen, Eusebius of Caesarea, and all the Greek commentators call the *Common* (*Κοινή*), or *Vulgate*, and which most people now call the Lucianic (*Λουκιανός*); and another, that of the Septuagint translators, which is found in the *Hexapla* (*Ἑξαπλοῖς*) codices, has been faithfully translated by us into Latin, and is sung in Jerusalem and the churches of the East.

My holy son Avitus had often inquired about this matter. And since the opportunity was provided by our brother Firmus the Presbyter, who delivered your letter to me, I reply to you both together in a single answer. Thus I bind myself by a great, freely given debt of friendship—but the more we pay, the more we owe.

Just as, in the New Testament, whenever a question arises among the Latins and there is a difference among the copies, we return to the source of the Greek language in which the New Instrument was written, so in the Old Testament, whenever there is a difference between the Greeks and Latins, we flee—or, in another reading, return—to the Hebrew truth, seeking in the streams whatever proceeds from the source.

This *Common* edition, then, is itself the edition that is also called the Septuagint. But the difference between them is that the *Common* edition, because of places, times, and the will of copyists, is an old and corrupted edition. The edition contained in the *Hexapla*, however, and the one that we have translated, is preserved in the books of the learned as the uncorrupted and undefiled translation of the Septuagint translators.[^c0095-10]

Whatever therefore differs from this edition undoubtedly also differs from the authority of the Hebrews.

[^c0095-9]: Erasmus and Victorius read *distinctionem* (“arrangement”) instead of *digestionem*. For the Greek word *Κοινή*, four of our manuscripts and several examined by Martianaeus read *ΚΟΙΝΑ*. For *Λουκιανός*, some manuscripts read *Λουκιάνειος* or *Λουκιάνιος*, which seems to mean the same as *τοῦ Λουκιανοῦ*, “of Lucian,” as other manuscripts give it, using only Latin.

[^c0095-10]: Some think Jerome mistaken here, since the *Common* or *Vulgate* edition sometimes agrees with the Hebrew more closely than the purer Hexaplaric edition. Jerome himself cites certain passages from the Psalms that establish this by example. Accordingly, Husserius preferred to read *ab eorum* (“from their authority”) instead of *ab Hebraeorum* (“from the authority of the Hebrews”), so that the sense would be that no one could doubt that the Common edition disagrees with the authority of the Septuagint translators wherever it differs from the Hexaplaric edition, which is the uncorrupted and undefiled translation of those same translators. But neither the printed nor manuscript copies support this conjecture, and Jerome’s meaning can be understood without difficulty: Origen had adjusted that Hexaplaric edition to the Hebrew exemplar from the other versions, using obeli and asterisks, so that it contained neither more nor less than the Hebrew text. Above, for *vetus* (“old”), Erasmus and Victorius read *veterum* (“of the old versions”).

### 3

The first question concerned the fifth Psalm:

> “Nor will the wicked dwell beside you” (Psalm 5:6).

The Greek has:

> *οὔτε παροικήσει σοι πονηρὸς*  
> or *πονηρευόμενος*,

as the Vulgate edition contains it.

You are surprised that the Latin translator did not render *παροικία*—that is, “sojourning” or “dwelling as a resident alien”—but put *habitation*, which in Greek is called *κατοικία*. Indeed, he is shown to have done this elsewhere:

> “Woe is me, for my sojourning has been prolonged” (Psalm 119:5).

And again, in the fourteenth Psalm, he put “habitation” for “sojourning”:

> “Lord, who will dwell in your tabernacle?” (Psalm 14:1).

It should be understood that if we wished to say, “Lord, who will sojourn in your tabernacle?” or, in the fifth Psalm, “Nor will the wicked sojourn beside you,” we would lose *euphony* (*εὐφωνία*, pleasing sound). In following the pedantic literalism of a translation (*κακοζηλία*), we would lose all the beauty of the rendering.

This is the rule of a good translator: to express the idioms (*ἰδιώματα*) of another language through the characteristic usage of his own language. We can demonstrate that Cicero did this in Plato’s *Protagoras*, in Xenophon’s *Oeconomicus* (*Οἰκονομικός*), and in Demosthenes’ speech *Against Aeschines*; and that Plautus, Terence, and Caecilius, highly educated men, did it in translating Greek comedies.

Nor should anyone think the Latin language extremely narrow because it cannot translate word for word. The Greeks too render many of our expressions by circumlocution; and they seek to express Hebrew words not through the faithfulness of verbal translation, but through the characteristic resources of their own language.

*[The name is* Protagoras*, as we affirm from two Vatican manuscripts; nearly all the other manuscripts examined by Martianaeus corrupt it into* Pythagoras*.]*

### 4

Concerning the same Psalm:

> “Make my way straight before me” (Psalm 5:9).

The Greek has:

> *κατεύθυνον ἐνώπιόν σου τὴν ὁδόν μου*,

that is:

> “Make my way straight before you.”

The Septuagint does not have this, nor Aquila, Symmachus, or Theodotion, but only the *Common* edition.

Finally, I found it written in Hebrew:

> **OSER LAPHANAI DARCHACH**

All translated it in substantially the same words:

> “Make my way straight before me.”

This accords with what is said in the Lord’s Prayer:

> “Our Father, who are in heaven, hallowed be your name” (Matthew 6:10).

This does not mean that what is holy in itself is made holy by our prayers; rather, we ask that what is holy by its own nature may be hallowed in us.

So here too the Prophet asks that the Lord’s way, which is straight in itself, may also be made straight for him.

*[Erasmus and Victorius print* hajesar laphanai darchecha*. The first word, *hajesar*, follows the Masoretic *qere*. The remaining forms, as may be said once for all, follow the grammatical pointing, which is later than Jerome’s time. For* starchah*, our manuscripts, as well as most of Martianaeus’s, read* darchachi*, through an easy scribal error.]*

### 5

Concerning the sixth Psalm:

> “Let all my enemies be put to shame and greatly troubled” (Psalm 6:1).

You say that the Greek does not contain “greatly.” I know—but that is true of the Vulgate edition. In Hebrew, however, it has **MOD**, that is, “greatly,” and all the translators rendered it similarly with *σφόδρα*, “very greatly.”

*[Erasmus and Victorius likewise print* Meod*, but all the manuscripts read* Mod*. Although the masters of Hebrew letters teach that a *shewa* must always be read at the beginning of a word, the ancients never read it. The same editors err more seriously in the Hebrew word that follows, where they invent* zidekatheca *instead of* Sedechah*. There is no need to reproduce the remaining Hebrew readings as they appear in those editions unless they teach something beyond the Masoretic manner of reading, which still obtains today.]*

### 6

Concerning the seventh Psalm:

> “Judge me, Lord, according to my righteousness” (Psalm 7:9).

The Greek has:

> *κατὰ τὴν δικαιοσύνην σου*,

that is:

> “according to your righteousness.”

But this too is wrong. For the Hebrew has **SEDECI**, which means “my righteousness,” not **SEDECACH**, which means “your righteousness.” All the translators likewise rendered it “my righteousness.”

No one should think it presumptuous that he asks to be judged according to his righteousness, since the following verse also means precisely this:

> “And according to my innocence upon me” (Psalm 7:9).

The sixteenth Psalm begins:

> “Hear, Lord, my righteousness” (Psalm 16:1).

The seventeenth also says:

> “The Lord will repay me according to my righteousness, and according to the purity of my hands he will recompense me” (Psalm 17:25).

The twenty-fifth Psalm says:

> “Test me, Lord, and try me; burn my kidneys and my heart” (Psalm 25:2).

And the fourth says:

> “When I called, the God of my righteousness heard me” (Psalm 4:1).

The eighty-fifth says:

> “Guard my soul, for I am holy” (Psalm 85:2).

Jacob also speaks in Genesis:

> “Tomorrow my righteousness will answer for me” (Genesis 30:33).

### 7

Concerning the eighth Psalm:

> “For I shall see your heavens” (Psalm 8:4).

You say that the Greek does not contain “your.” That is true; but in Hebrew it reads **SAMACHA**, which means “your heavens.” It was added from Theodotion’s edition in the Septuagint under an asterisk. I shall briefly explain the meaning of this to you.

Where something is lacking in the Greek compared with the Hebrew Truth, Origen added it from Theodotion’s translation and placed the sign of an asterisk—that is, a star—which illuminates what previously seemed hidden and brings it into the open.

Where, however, something not present in Hebrew is found in the Greek codices, he placed before it an obelus, that is, a lying or horizontal stroke, which we can call in Latin a *veru*, “spit.” This shows that the material not found in the authentic books ought to be struck through and pierced.

These signs are also found in the poems of the Greeks and Latins.

### 8

In the sixteenth Psalm:

> “Let your eyes see uprightness” (Psalm 16:2).

You say that you read in the Greek:

> *οἱ ὀφθαλμοί μου*,

that is, “my eyes.” But “your eyes” is more correct, because above he had said:

> “From your face let my judgment come forth” (Psalm 16:2).

And the eyes of God in the Prophet see what is right, not what is wrong.

In the same Psalm:

> “Guard me as the apple of the eye” (Psalm 16:8).

You say that the Greek reads:

> “Guard me, Lord.”

But this is found neither in the Hebrew nor in any translator.

Again in the same Psalm:

> “Rise up, Lord; go before him and trip him up” (Psalm 16:13).

The Greek has:

> *πρόφθασον αὐτούς*,

that is:

> “Go before them and trip them up.”

But it is better read in the singular, since the statement concerns the wicked man, about whom it immediately continues:

> “Go before him and trip him up; rescue my soul from the wicked.”

There is no doubt that the devil is signified.

*[The Vatican manuscript does not contain the Greek word* πρόφθασον *here, but only* αὐτούς*, which is sufficient for Jerome’s meaning. The older printed editions, on the other hand, give the entire verse: *ἀνάστηθι, κύριε, πρόφθασον αὐτούς, καὶ ἀποσκέλισον αὐτούς*, with its translation, “Rise up, Lord, go before them and trip them up,” and so forth. They follow the same practice shortly before in the preceding verse, which they corrupt, and immediately below: instead of being content with the words that present the difficulty and that Jerome alone adduces, they complete the whole verse from Scripture and add its translation. It is enough to have noted this once and again, so that we need not mark it at every individual passage.]*

*[Against the evidence of the manuscripts, Erasmus and Victorius add* ἰδέτωσαν εὐθύτητας*, “let them see uprightness,” together with its translation, “let them see uprightness.” The Palatine manuscript, like those manuscripts, later has “the eyes of the Lord,” and correctly reads “working uprightly” instead of “for the upright,” the latter word being absent from the Vatican manuscript.]*

### 9

In the seventeenth Psalm:

> “Hail and coals of fire” (Psalm 17:13).

You ask why the Greek does not contain this verse a second time, with two verses inserted between. It should be understood that it was added from the Hebrew and from Theodotion’s edition in the Septuagint under an asterisk.

*[This shows how much shorter the divisions of verses were among the ancients. The present fourteenth verse was formerly divided into three, as follows; the same division is still found in the oldest Veronese manuscript, written in uncial letters, which contains both the Greek and Latin versions of the Psalter:*

> “And the Lord thundered from heaven,
>
> and the Most High gave his voice;
>
> hail and coals of fire.”]*

In the same Psalm:

> “He made my feet like those of deer” (Psalm 17:34).

You write that the Greek has:

> *ὡσεὶ ἐλάφου*,

that is, “like a deer,” using the singular instead of the plural. But the Hebrew uses the plural, **CHAJALOTH**, and all the translators rendered it in the plural.

*[Some manuscripts read* ὡς *instead of* ὡσεὶ*. We have restored the word* positus*, rejected by Martianaeus, from all the printed editions and from all the manuscripts we examined.]*

Again in the same Psalm:

> “And you gave me the protection of your salvation” (Psalm 17:36).

You say that you read in the Greek:

> *τῆς σωτηρίας μου*,

that is, “of my salvation.” But the Hebrew **JESACHA** means “your salvation,” not “my salvation,” and all the translators rendered it accordingly.

Again:

> “You have tripped up those rising against me beneath me” (Psalm 17:40).

You say that you found more in the Greek:

> “All those rising against me.”

But “all” has been added.

Again:

> “The Lord lives, and blessed is my God” (Psalm 17:47).

You say that the Greek does not contain “my.” This was translated not under an asterisk but by the Septuagint themselves from the Hebrew Truth, and all the translators agree in this respect.

Again:

> “My deliverer from the nations enraged” (Psalm 17:48).

You say that you found in the Greek:

> “From my strong,” or “powerful,” “enemies.”

Since we are devoted to the truth, if something has been corrupted either through the haste of the translator or through the fault of copyists, we ought simply to acknowledge and correct it.[^c0095-11]

The Hebrew has nothing other than this:

> “My deliverer from my enemies.”

The Septuagint added “enraged.” And where the Hebrew and all the translators have “enemies,” “nations” has been put in its place. I am astonished that “nations” was substituted for “enemies.”

[^c0095-11]: The older printed editions had: *ὁ ῥύστης μου ἐξ ἐχθρῶν μου ὀργίλων*, that is, “my deliverer from my enraged enemies.” In Hebrew there is nothing else.

*[The reading of the outstanding Regina manuscript 286 is not negligible: it omits the word “my.” In Hebrew the attached pronoun in this word, which Jerome recognizes here and in his translation, is not read by others according to a different assignment of the vowel points. Nor do the Septuagint themselves show it in the Vatican manuscript, nor does the ancient translator who translated from them: “from the nations enraged.”]*

### 10

In the eighteenth Psalm:

> “He rejoiced like a giant to run his course” (Psalm 18:7).

You say that the Greek does not contain “his.” But we found this added under an obelus, and it is clear that it is absent from the Hebrew.

### 11

In the nineteenth Psalm:

> “May he grant you according to your heart” (Psalm 19:5).

You say that in this verse you found the name “Lord” added in the Greek. This is superfluous, because from what precedes,

> *ἐπακοῦσαι σου Κύριος*,

“May the Lord hear you,” is understood. The Psalm likewise began:

> “May the Lord hear you in the day of tribulation” (Psalm 19:2),

so that here too it says, with the same meaning:

> “May he grant you according to your heart,”

that is, the Lord himself, who was mentioned above.

In the same Psalm:

> “And hear us on the day when we call upon you” (Psalm 19:10).

You say that you read instead:

> “on whatever day.”

But the former agrees with the Hebrew Truth, where **BIOM** is written, meaning “on the day.”

*[Up to this point all the printed books, together with Martianaeus, and also nearly all the manuscripts, give for the Greek words* ἐπακοῦσαι σου Κύριος *the reading* ἀπὸ Κοινοῦ*. This can easily be understood as a corruption produced by the ingenuity of critics or copyists after the word* Κύριος *had been erased from* ἐπακούσαι σου*, or, as seems most likely to us, because the words had once been contracted by shorthand writers, or had been copied from a torn and worn exemplar. But* ἀπὸ Κοινοῦ *made no sense: the Lord is not supplied from the Common edition, for a word is not understood from one book in another, but from the preceding context of the same book. Nor did Jerome set out to emend something in the Hexaplaric edition from the Common; on the contrary, he required the Common to conform to the Hexaplaric. In short, the appeal to the Common edition would be pointless, since not only it, but also the Hexaplaric edition, the Hebrew text, and every other version necessarily have the name “Lord” above, in the first verse, from which Jerome wishes it to be understood here. The Palatine manuscript 159 alerted us to the true reading. We have followed its authority especially, although it reads* ἐπακούσει *instead of* ἐπακοῦσαι*.]*
### 12. Twenty-first

“But you, O Lord, do not remove your help far from me” (Ps. 21:20). You say that you found *meum* (“my”), which is both correct and should be restored.

[Note: [Col. 0842] The Vatican and Palatine manuscripts, and the old edition of 1496, which is often of good quality. What you say you found is not *meum*. Instead of *Brevi enim*, Erasmus, Victor, and others, both printed and manuscript, have *Neque enim*; and in place of *credimus* we should read *debemus*, though the sense is not different.]

For, if anything has been altered through the error of scribes, it is foolish to defend it by obstinate argument.

In the same psalm: “All the seed of Jacob, magnify him” (ibid. 24). In Greek, you say, it is written δοξάσατε αὐτόν, that is, “glorify him.” But it should be understood that wherever “glorify” is written in Greek, the Latin translator rendered it *magnify*, in accordance with the passage in Exodus: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously magnified” (Exod. 15:1). In Greek, instead of this, “he has been glorified” is written.

[Note: [Col. 0843] The older printed editions put δεδόξασται here; this is also found in the very ancient Regina manuscript no. 11, and—what is more surprising—with an asterisk prefixed.]

But if it is transferred into Latin, the rendering is inelegant. When we formerly corrected the Psalter, therefore, wherever the sense was the same, we did not wish to alter the custom of the older translators, lest excessive novelty frighten the reader away from study.

### 13. Twenty-second

“My cup, making me drunk, how excellent it is” (Ps. 22:5). Instead of this, you say that you read in Greek, “your cup.” But this has prevailed as an error in the κοινή (*Koinē*).

[Note: [Col. 0843] All the printed editions are in error; the reading is less satisfactory.]

The Septuagint, the Hebrew, and all the translators, however, have “my cup,” which in Hebrew is written CHOSI. Otherwise, if it were “your cup,” it would be written CHOSACH.

### 14. Twenty-fourth

“Let all who act wickedly be put to shame” (Ps. 24:4). You say that the word “all” is absent from the Greek, and rightly so; for it is also absent from the Hebrew, but has been added in the Septuagint under an obelus.

In the same psalm: “The innocent and upright have adhered to me, because I have waited for you” (ibid. 21). You say that you found “Lord” in the Greek; this is superfluous.

### 15. Twenty-sixth

[Note: [Col. 0843] One Palatine manuscript appears to have been tampered with by a glossator: “And now he has exalted my head above my enemies.” Instead of this, you said that you found in the Greek: “And now I have exalted—behold—my heart.” But “behold” is superfluous.]

“And now, behold, he has exalted my head” (Ps. 26:5). But “behold” is superfluous.

In the same psalm: “My face has sought” (ibid. 8). Instead of this, the Greek is said to read: “My face has sought you.” But the former is better.

### 16. Twenty-seventh

“Hear the voice of my supplication” (Ps. 27:2). Instead of this, you said that you found: “Hear, O Lord.” But this too has been added.

### 17. Twenty-eighth

“And in his temple everyone will say, ‘Glory’” (Ps. 28:9). Instead of this, the Greek has πᾶς τίς. If we wished to render this word for word as “everyone who,” we would fall into *κακοζηλία*—an affected imitation—in translation, and the result would be absurd.

In the same psalm: “The Lord makes the flood dwell” (ibid. 10). Instead of this, you say that you read: “The Lord dwells in the flood.” The former pertains to grace in believers; the latter, to the dwelling-place of him in whom they believe.

[Note: [Col. 0843] Some manuscripts, together with other commonly circulated copies, have *pertinet credentium*, or *credentibus*, without the preposition *in*. The difference in the Greek edition is that some copies have κατοικεῖ, while others give κατοικιεῖ, as Saint Athanasius also read.]

But since the Hebrew verb JASAB is ambiguous and can signify both things—for it means both “sitting” and “dwelling”—and since in the psalm itself, concerning the grace of baptism, it was said: “The voice of the Lord is over the waters; the Lord is over many waters”; and: “The voice of him who prepares the deer, and he will reveal the dense places, and in his temple everyone will say, ‘Glory’” (ibid. 3 ff.), we wish to understand this of those who glorify the Lord. Accordingly, we translated: “The Lord makes the flood dwell” (Ps. 30:5).

[Note: [Col. 0843] The Vatican manuscript, together with Erasmus and Victor, reads: “Then, ‘The voice of the Lord is over many waters,’ and ‘The voice of the Lord preparing,’ etc.”]

### 18. Thirtieth

“For you are my protector.” Here again the name of the Lord has been added. Since I should not repeat the same point constantly, you ought to observe that the name of the Lord and of God has very often been added, and that you should follow what we corrected from the Hebrew and from the Septuagint translators.

In the same psalm: “But I said in the excess of my mind” (Ps. 30:23). Instead of this, the Latin manuscripts read “in my fear,” and we translated according to the Greek, ἐν τῇ ἐκστάσει μου, that is, “in the excess of my mind.” Latin speech cannot otherwise express ἔκστασις except by “excess of mind.” I know that I read it differently in the Hebrew: “in my amazement and wonder.”

### 19. Thirty-first

“And there is no deceit in his spirit” (Ps. 31:2). Instead of this, you say that you read in the Greek, ἐν τῷ στόματι αὐτοῦ, that is, “in his mouth.” Only Symmachus has this reading.

[Note: [Col. 0844] The Greek word δόλος and the Latin *dolus* (“deceit”), which all the printed editions add at this point, are absent from the better manuscript copies; we deleted them because they were redundant.]

The Septuagint translators, Theodotion, the Fifth and Sixth Editions, Aquila, and the Hebrew itself all have “in his spirit,” which in Hebrew is written BRUCHO. If it were “in his mouth,” it would be written BAFFIO.

In the same psalm: “I turned in my affliction” (ibid. 4). You suggest that the Greek lacks “my.” This has been added from the Hebrew and from Theodotion’s translation under an asterisk, and in Hebrew it is written LASADDI.

[Note: [Col. 0844] The Hebrew word LASADDI, which is properly rendered “my moisture,” is repeated twice by our three better manuscripts; we do not understand why.]

### 20. Thirty-fourth

“All my bones will say, ‘Lord’” (Ps. 34:10). Instead of this, you say that you found “Lord” twice in the Greek. But it should be understood that among the Hebrews there are many copies that do not have “Lord” even once.

[Note: [Col. 0844] Modern copies have it only once, and Jerome himself translated it only once from the Hebrew. The Vatican manuscript has *sint*.]

### 21. Thirty-sixth

“And he will desire his way” (Ps. 36:23). You say that in the Greek you read “he will desire exceedingly.”

[Note: [Col. 0844] The Alexandrian, Aldine, and Complutensian copies have θελήσει σφόδρα.]

This has been added and is found in none of the translators.

[Note: [Col. 0844] It seems that the Septuagint wished by σφόδρα, that is, “exceedingly,” to explain the force of the verb. Fretela, however, had before him the Greek that was a Septuagint manuscript. The old edition mentioned above, and the Florentine Royal manuscript in Martianaeus, falsely read ἐπίβλεπε instead of πρόσεχε.]

### 22. Thirty-eighth

“Nevertheless every person is troubled in vain” (Ps. 38:6). You say that you did not find “is troubled” in the Greek. But this too has been added in the Septuagint under an obelus.

From this an error arises among you and among many others: through scribal negligence, the whole distinction is confused when critical strokes and asterisks are omitted.

### 23. Thirty-ninth

“And your law is in the midst of my heart” (Ps. 39:9). Instead of this, you say that you found “in the midst of my belly” in the Greek, and this is also written in the Hebrew: BATTHOCH MEAI. But for euphony in Latin it was translated “in my heart.” Nevertheless, we should not remove what is true.

In the same psalm: “Lord, look to my help” (ibid. 14). Instead of this, you say that you found in the Greek σπεῦσον, that is, “hasten.” But in the Septuagint it is written πρόσεχε, that is, “look.”

[Note: [Col. 0844] By that time σπεῦσον had already become established in some Greek copies of the Septuagint in place of πρόσεχε; this can still be seen today in the Alexandrian manuscript. For Sunnia and Fretela were not referring to Aquila’s version, to which this rendering, σπεῦσον, is commonly attributed, but to the Greek text they had before them.]

### 24. Fortieth

“And if he entered in order to see” (Ps. 40:7). You say that “if” is not present in the Greek.

[Note: [Col. 0845] We supplied the missing particle *si* from other manuscripts.]

Yet it is most plainly written both in the Hebrew and in all the translators, and the Septuagint translated it, καὶ εἰσεπορεύετο τοῦ ἰδεῖν, “and if he entered in order to see.”

[Note: [Col. 0845] All manuscripts and printed books are defective here, having only καὶ εἰσεπορεύετο. This error also entered the Alexandrian manuscript, plainly through a scribal lapse caused by the repeated occurrence of εἰ. Jerome undoubtedly guarded against this; accordingly, we corrected the text from the Vatican manuscript by adding εἰ: καὶ εἰ εἰσεπορεύετο, “and if he entered,” as the Septuagint actually has it. The Hebrew likewise has “and if he comes,” etc.

Nevertheless, to conceal nothing, although we left this entire passage untouched, we are persuaded that it is disfigured by a serious error and that its sense has been reversed by the falsity and obscurity of the statement. Sunnia and Fretela seem to say that the clause “and if he entered in order to see” is altogether missing in the Greek, to which Jerome replies that it is plainly present in the Hebrew and in all the translators. But the first claim is either false or at least exceedingly difficult to believe, since it cannot be demonstrated from any book or ancient testimony that this sentence was absent from their Greek copy, whatever edition it represented. Moreover, Jerome’s reply would be almost pointless; if we know his method, he would have attributed the omission to scribal error, rather than arguing from the Hebrew, all the translators, and again the testimony of the Septuagint.

What was truly missing in the κοινή edition—the edition represented by the Alexandrian manuscript and which they simply call “the Greek”—was the little word εἰ. It had “and he entered” instead of “and if he entered,” that is, καὶ εἰσεπορεύετο instead of καὶ εἰ εἰσεπορεύετο. This could easily have prompted Sunnia and Fretela to ask about the reason for that variation or omission, but not to say that the entire clause was missing from the Greek.

To make this entirely clear from their own statement, the corrupt wording of our manuscripts should be corrected by the very slight addition of one little word, and we should read: “You say that *if* is not present in the Greek.” Those who have labored over the work of copying will readily concede that this little word could easily have dropped out before the following occurrence of *sit*. We also have some support for restoring it in the old edition that we frequently cite, where the passage reads: “And you say that *if* is not present in the Greek.”]

### 25. Forty-first

“Salvation of my face, my God” (Ps. 41:7). Instead of this, you say that you found “and my God.” But it should be understood that this occurs twice in the psalm: the first time it is written, “salvation of my face, my God”; the second time, at the end of the psalm, “salvation of my face, and my God.” This is so only in the sense that the conjunction “and” has been added from the Hebrew and Theodotion under an asterisk.

In the same psalm: “Those who afflict me reproached me” (ibid. 11). Instead of this, you said that you found οἱ ἐχθροί μου, that is, “my enemies.”

[Note: [Col. 0845] The Greek ὠνείδισόν με and its interpretation, *exprobraverunt mihi* (“they reproached me”), are wholly absent and have entered Jerome’s text from another hand, even in Martianaeus’s edition. The Royal and Palatine parchment manuscripts, the best of all, do not recognize them; they have only “you said that you found οἱ ἐχθροί μου,” that is, “my enemies.” We have published the text according to their authority.]

But the Septuagint has οἱ θλίβοντές με, and the Hebrews have SORARAI, that is, “my enemies.”

[Note: [Col. 0845] The sense of this passage requires that the noun “enemy” be given a meaning not only different from “adversary,” but also different from the meanings noted by grammarians, so that it corresponds to the Hebrew *sorarai*, which properly signifies “those who afflict and persecute,” just as the Greek θλίβοντες does. Consider the sense of “assailant,” which we have observed to occur in some older Latin writers.]

In the same psalm: “Hope in God, for I will still confess him” (ibid. 12). You say that “still” is not found in the Greek. It has been added under an asterisk. For in the Hebrew we likewise find CHI OD, represented by ὅτι ἔτι and rendered in Latin *quoniam adhuc*, “for still.”

[Note: [Col. 0846] Erasmus and Victor have εἴσετι instead of ἔτι. On Jerome’s authority we wish this word to be supplied in the Hexapla prepared by the distinguished Montfaucon.]

The same point should also be understood in the forty-second psalm.

### 26. Forty-third

“And you will not go forth with our powers” (Ps. 43:10). Instead of this, you say that you found in the Greek: “And you will not go forth, O God” (ibid. 15); but this is superfluous.

In the same psalm: “You have made us like the nations” (ibid. 15).

[Note: [Col. 0846] We supplied the entire clause—“Instead of this, in the Greek it is written ἐν τοῖς ἔθνεσιν”—from the Palatine and Regina manuscripts. Until the present day all editors have printed Jerome’s incomplete text without it. Another Regina manuscript has ἐν ἔθνεσιν, without τοῖς.]

Instead of this, the Greek has ἐν τοῖς ἔθνεσιν. But if it had been rendered in Latin as “in the likeness among the nations,” it would have been harsh-sounding; therefore, without loss of meaning, the elegance of the translation was preserved.

Otherwise, I found it written this way in the Hebrew: “You have made us a proverb among the nations.”

[Note: [Col. 0846] Erasmus and Victor impose the Hebrew words *Thesimenu mosel bagoim* here. There is neither trace nor indication of them in the manuscripts, except for the Florentine Royal manuscript cited by Martianaeus, in which there is a blank erased space, as there is also in the old edition of 1496, which we frequently cite.]

In the same psalm: “Rise up, help us” (ibid. 26). As usual, the name of the Lord has been added in the Greek.

### 27. Forty-fourth

“Your arrows are sharp” (Ps. 44:6). Instead of this, you say that you read in the Greek: “Sharp, most powerful.”

[Note: [Col. 0846] The same printed editions wrongly say that this was added from the preceding third verse. In Jerome’s time it could not have been counted as the third verse, but at least as the sixth according to the ancient division mentioned above. Another Regina manuscript does not have the two words *male et* (“wrongly, and”). Compare Epistle 65 to Principia, no. 12, and note b.]

But this has been wrongly added from the preceding verse, in which we read: “Gird your sword upon your thigh, O most powerful one” (ibid. 4).

### 28. Forty-seventh

“For behold, the kings are gathered together” (Ps. 47:5). Instead of this, you say that you read in Greek: “For behold, its kings are gathered together.” That this is superfluous is shown by the text of the reading itself. In the older Latin codices it was written “kings of the earth,” which we removed [perhaps: “deleted”], because it is found neither in the Hebrew nor in the Septuagint.

[Note: [Col. 0846] The Vatican manuscript erroneously adds *terrae*, “of the earth,” a word that Jerome says below he removed from the Latin manuscripts. Understand this as referring to the correction of the Psalter, commonly called the Gallican Psalter. Nor does it seem characteristic of Jerome to repeat the same verse immediately from the Greek, when the two words “its kings” would have been sufficient. In the old edition, *quoniam* is absent; but without manuscript support we change nothing.]

“Have we heard, so have we seen” (ibid. 9). Instead of this, you say that you found in the Greek: “so also have we seen,” which is superfluous. For in the Hebrew it reads CHEN RAINU, translated by οὕτως εἴδομεν, that is, “so have we seen.”

In the same psalm: “We have received your mercy, O God, in the midst of your temple” (ibid. 10). Instead of what we translated from the Hebrew and the Septuagint translators, “your temple,” you say that you read in the Greek, “your people,” which is superfluous.

[Note: [Col. 0846] He should have said that this is false. It is not redundant, but λαοῦ, “of the people,” is being read in place of ναοῦ, “of the temple.” This reading is found in Greek and Latin Fathers and in several ancient translations. The words τοῦ ναοῦ σου, “of your temple,” are absent from the other Regina manuscript.]

In Hebrew it is written ECHALACH, that is, τοῦ ναοῦ σου, “of your temple,” and not AMMACH, which means “your people.”

### 29. Forty-eighth

“A man, when he was in honor” (Ps. 48:14). Instead of this, you say that you found in the Greek: “And a man, when he was in honor.” But it should be understood that this verse occurs twice in the psalm: the first occurrence has the conjunction “and” added, while the final occurrence does not.

In the same psalm: “And the righteous will rule over them” (ibid. 15). Instead of “the righteous,” you say that you read in the Greek εὐθεῖς, that is, “the upright.” But it was rendered this way in Latin for the sake of euphony.

Otherwise, in the passage where we read “in the book of τοῦ εὐθοῦς,” we understand “the book of the righteous” (Josh. 10:13), and we ought not to reproduce the word mechanically, so that by following syllables we lose the meaning.

[Note: [Col. 0847] There was no reason to allow the certain scribal error εὐθεῖς for εὐθοῦς to remain longer in Jerome’s text. The Septuagint in the Aldine and Oxford copies reads: οὐχὶ τοῦτο γεγραμμένον ἐπὶ βιβλίου τοῦ εὐθοῦς, “Is this not written in the book of the Upright?” This is the sort of passage Jerome is citing.]

In the same psalm: “From the hand of the underworld, when he has delivered me” (Ps. 49:20). Instead of this, you say that you read in the Greek: “when he has received me.” We too translated it this way from the Septuagint, and I am surprised by whom it was corrupted in your manuscript.

[Note: [Col. 0847] Some read here in Jerome’s text: “From the hand of the underworld he delivered me,” so that the difference between the translations lies not only in *liberavit* (“he delivered”) instead of *accipiendi* (“receiving”), but also in the form of the verb and in the omission of the conjunction *cum*.]

### 30. Forty-ninth

“Sitting, you spoke against your brother” (ibid. 16). Instead of this, you say that you found in the Greek κατὰ τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ σου κατελάλεις, and you think it was not well translated because we said, “you spoke against your brother,” whereas we should have said, “you slandered your brother.”

That this is faulty and does not work in our language is obvious even to fools. We are not unaware that καταλαλιά means “slander.” But if we wished to use that word, we could not say, “you slandered against your brother”; we would have to say, “you slandered your brother.” If we did that, a contentious faultfinder of words would again ask why we had not rendered κατὰ τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ σου literally, that is, “against your brother.”

These are needless objections. We should not torment ourselves with an inelegant translation of words when there is no loss of meaning, since every language, as I have already said, speaks according to its own idiom.

In the same psalm: “Lest he seize, and there be no one to rescue” (ibid. 22). You say that in the Greek you found: “And there be no one to rescue.” This is also how we translated it, and this is how it stands in our manuscripts. I am surprised that you attribute the fault of a drowsy copyist to the translator—unless perhaps the text was: “Lest he seize, and there be no one to rescue,” and the scribe wrote *et* (“and”) instead of *nec* (“nor”).

[Note: [Col. 0847] The words “Lest he seize” are more correctly absent from the other Regina manuscript. Likewise, shortly below, the Florentine Royal manuscript—which, according to Martianaeus, is otherwise extremely corrupt—retains only the first three Greek words, Πάτερ, δόξασόν με, “Father, glorify me.” The old edition agrees with it. Erasmus and Victor copied the entire reading from the commonly circulated Greek text of the Gospel, from which the text we have printed from the manuscripts differs in several places.]

In the same psalm: “The sacrifice of praise will honor me.” In Greek it is written δοξάσει με, that is, “will glorify me,” concerning which we also spoke above.

In the Gospel, where we read in Greek Πάτερ δόξασόν με τῇ δόξῃ ᾗ εἶχον παρὰ σοι πρὸ τοῦ τὸν κόσμον γενέσθαι, “Father, glorify me with the glory that I had with you before the world existed,” the Latin reads: “Father, glorify me” (John 17:5). We therefore did not wish to alter what was read by the ancients, since the sense was the same.

### 31. Fifty-fourth

“I was waiting for him who saved me” (Ps. 54:9). You say that you found in the Greek: “I was waiting for God.” This has been added.

In the same psalm: “Because of faintness of spirit” (ibid.). You say that you found in the Greek ἀπὸ ὀλιγοψυχίας, which properly means “because of faintness of spirit.” But it should be understood that Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion, and the Fifth Edition translated ὀλιγοψυχία as ἀπὸ πνεύματος, that is, “from the spirit.”

In Hebrew it is written MERUA.

[Note: [Col. 0848] Our manuscripts and those of Martianaeus have *Merucha* and *Meruha*. But the ancients, and Jerome himself, read the letter at the end of the word without aspiration. Thus the Greeks have λαρουή for the Hebrew word used in Genesis 3:8 for “spirit” or “breeze.”]

The entire sense is read among them as follows: “I will hasten, that I may be saved from the spirit of the storm and the whirlwind” (Ps. 55:9 according to the Hebrew).

In the same psalm: “For if an enemy had cursed” (ibid. 13).

[Note: [Col. 0848] The Palatine manuscript has “had cursed me,” as do the older printed editions. With them, in Greek, ὠνείδισέ με, that is, etc.]

In Greek, ὠνείδισεν, that is, “had reproached,” is written. But it is clear that there is no difference in sense between curses and reproaches.

### 32. Fifty-fifth

“For many are fighting against me; from the height of day I will fear” (Ps. 55:3–4). You say that you found in the Greek “I will not fear.” This has been added.

The order is: “Since many fight against me, therefore I will fear from the height of day”; that is, I fear not those who fight against me, but your exalted light.

In the same psalm: “In anger you will bring down the peoples” (ibid. 8).

[Note: [Col. 0848] We left the passage untouched so that, since it must be reconstructed in its entirety, we would not appear to have rashly tampered with it. Nevertheless, we have determined that it should be read as follows.

Instead of the Greek κατάξεις, that is, “you will lead down” or “you will cast down,” the Latin has wrongly come to read κατεάξεις, that is, “you will shatter.” For in the Hebrew as well there is a corresponding form, etc.

Since Jerome’s whole purpose in this letter is to investigate and judge wherever there is disagreement between the Latin and Greek Psalter texts, if both the Latin and Greek read “you will shatter,” what disagreement or difficulty remains? But we would be less troubled by this if the entire period were not disfigured by more than seven errors in scarcely seven lines.

Where we have applied a corrective hand, we have emended one thing by plausible conjecture and the rest with the aid of manuscripts. First, delete the words ἐν ὀργῇ λαούς, “in anger the peoples,” which are found neither in the better manuscripts nor in the frequently cited old edition, and which have no place here. Then, instead of “you will shatter,” we read “you will lead down.” We assert this on our own initiative, since no manuscripts support it. But there are at least two considerations that, in our view, establish our correction.

First, the Greek κατάξεις has never meant, nor properly does it mean, “you will shatter,” but certainly means “you will lead down.” Second, “you will lead down” is itself the old Latin translation from the Greek that prevailed before Jerome; Hilary and Augustine read and explain it in their Psalters, to say nothing of the exceedingly ancient Verona Psalter manuscript and many other arguments that support our conjecture.

Below, in place of καταβαλεῖς, which is Theodotion’s translation and not that of the Septuagint, restore κατάξεις from the principal manuscripts we use, two Regina manuscripts and the Palatine. Consequently, in place of κατάξεις, on the authority of those same manuscripts, read and correct κατεάξεις, from the verb κατάγνυμι or καταγνύω, which means “to shatter.” Thus Matthew 12:20 has Κάλαμον συντετριμμένον οὐ κατεάξει, “he will not shatter a bruised reed.” We need not burden the discussion with examples from Lucian, Aristophanes, and others, which you can seek in the lexicons, for ignorance of this verb has generated so many perplexities both formerly and to the present day.

Next, the words “in anger the peoples,” which we have never found in any manuscript, must be entirely removed. Finally, let us prefer to Symmachus’s κατασεῖσαι, which rests on either no testimony or insufficient testimony, the certain reading κατάγαγε, found in the Regina manuscript and confirmed by Eusebius and by the two Royal manuscripts cited by Montfaucon in the Hexapla. These corrections are based on manuscripts; if conjecture were permitted, the passage might perhaps be restored more elegantly.]

Instead of this, the Greek reads ἐν ὀργῇ λαοὺς κατάξεις, that is, “in anger you will shatter the peoples.” Among the Latins, however, in place of “you will cast down,” that is, καταβαλεῖς, the erroneous reading κατάξεις, “you will shatter,” has prevailed, producing “in anger you will shatter the peoples.”

For in the Hebrew it has HORED, that is, καταβίβασον, which we can render “put down”; and Symmachus translated it κατασεῖσαι.

### 33. Fifty-eighth

“For God is my protector” (Ps. 58:10). Instead of this, the Greek has: “You are my protector.” But it should be understood that neither “are” nor “you” is written in the Hebrew; both are found only in the Septuagint.

In the same psalm: “My God, his will will go before me” (ibid. 10). Instead of this, the Greek has τὸ ἔλεος αὐτοῦ, that is, “his mercy,” which is also more accurate. But the Hebrew reads: “My mercy will go before me.”

[Note: [Col. 0849] The Palatine manuscript incorrectly has “his mercy.” The Hebrew text does indeed have this, but the *Qere* in the margin records the older reading, which was also found in Jerome’s copy.]

In the same psalm: “God will show me among my enemies” (ibid. 10). Instead of this, the Greek has “my God”; but “my” has been added.

In the same psalm: “Do not kill them, lest they forget your people” (ibid. 11). Instead of this, the Greek has “your law.” But in the Septuagint and in the Hebrew it does not have “your people,” but “my people,” and this is how we translated it.

[Note: [Col. 0849] The surviving manuscripts of the Septuagint today have not “people,” but “law,” νόμον rather than λαόν. Among the ancient translators Symmachus supports this, ingeniously joining both readings: μὴ πότε ἐπιλάθωνται ὁ λαός σου τοῦ νόμου μου, “lest your people forget my law.” This almost persuades us that both readings once existed in the Hebrew text, and that the diversity of translations arose because one had dropped out of some copies.]

In the same psalm: “And they will know that God will rule Jacob, the ends of the earth” (ibid. 14).

[Note: [Col. 0849] Here and below the Regina manuscript has *dominatur*, “rules.”]

Instead of this, the Greek has: “And the ends of the earth.” But the conjunction “and” has been added. The order is: “They will know that the God of Jacob will rule the ends of the earth.”

### 34. Fifty-ninth

“Who will lead me as far as Idumea?” (Ps. 59:11). Instead of this, the Greek has “or who will lead me?” But “or” is superfluous.

[Note: [Col. 0849] That is, “or” is superfluous; in the Vatican and other better Greek manuscripts the word ἤ is not found.]

### 35. Sixtieth

“For you, my God, have heard my prayer” (Ps. 60:6). Instead of this, the Greek reads: “For you, God, have heard me.” “My” is absent from the Hebrew and from the Septuagint translators and has been added in the Latin.

[Note: [Col. 0849] The Greek, in all copies and among all translators, has not “me,” but “my prayer.” The Hebrew likewise has “my vows.” This has been noted so that you may understand that the addition Jerome is criticizing is not this one, but the word “my” attached to “God.”]

In the same psalm: “I will sing to your name for ever and ever” (ibid. 9). Instead of this, the Greek has “for ever.” The Hebrew has LAED once, meaning “for eternity,” not LOLAM, meaning “for an age.”

### 36. Sixty-first

“For God is our helper forever” (Ps. 61:9). In Greek it is: “God is our helper.” Therefore “forever” is marked with an obelus.

### 37. Sixty-second

“My soul thirsted for you” (Ps. 62:2). Instead of this, the Greek has: “My soul thirsted in you.”

[Note: [Col. 0850] Perhaps the preposition “in” should be absent here, and we should read “it thirsted for you,” since the Greek has ἐδίψησέ σε without the preposition “in.”]

But the Hebrew does not have ATTHA, which means “you,” but LACH, which means “for you”; and all the translators rendered it accordingly. Therefore it has been translated into Latin according to the idiom of the language.

### 39. Sixty-third

“The arrows of the little ones have become their wounds” (Ps. 63:8). Instead of this, the Greek has “the arrow of the little ones.” But if we say this in Latin—“the arrow of the little ones have become their wounds”—it does not sound right.

[Note: [Col. 0850] Martianaeus restored the following passage, which Erasmus and Victor omitted. All our manuscripts have it, as does the old edition.]

The Hebrew has a better rendering: “God will strike them with a sudden arrow, and their wounds will be inflicted.”

### 39. Sixty-fourth

“You who trouble the depths of the sea, the sound of its waves” (Ps. 64:8). You say that the Greek adds: “Who will endure?” This is superfluous, for the sense is understood: “You who trouble the depths of the sea and trouble the sound of its waves.”

In the same psalm: “You have prepared their food, for so is its preparation” (ibid. 10). You say that the Greek does not have “its.” But in the Hebrew THECHINA plainly means “its preparation.” “Its” refers to the earth, of which he had said above: “You visited the earth and drenched it” (ibid.).

### 40. Sixty-fifth

“I will offer you sacrifices rich in marrow, with the incense of rams” (Ps. 65:15). Instead of this, you say that you found: “with incense and rams.”

[Note: [Col. 0850] Two Regina manuscripts have “with incense, with rams,” without the conjunction “and,” although the Greek copies of the Septuagint have it. One of them also aspirates the word HELIM. Unless all the ancient parchments deceive us, Jerome reads the plural form *Catoroth*, whereas the Masoretes have the singular. Either this was how Jerome’s copy read, or firm rules concerning the ancient reading cannot yet be established. Moreover, in the other Regina manuscript the Greek μετὰ θυμιάματος κριῶν and its Latin equivalent are absent.]

But in the Hebrew it is written EM CATOROTH ELIM, which is translated μετὰ θυμιάματος κριῶν, that is, “with the incense of rams.”

In the same psalm: “Therefore God heard” (ibid. 19). Instead of this, you say that you found in the Greek: “God heard me.” But “me” is superfluous.

[Note: [Col. 0850] The old edition has “which is superfluous”; and the conjunction “and” is lacking.]

### 41. [pp. 657–658; cols. 0850–0851] Psalm sixty-seventh

“Rejoice in his presence” (Ps. 67:6). You say that you found in the Greek, “And rejoice in his presence.” This is how we translated it, but I cannot know by whom it was corrupted in your copy.

In the same psalm: “For indeed they do not believe that the Lord will dwell” (v. 19). You say that you read in the Greek, *καὶ γὰρ ἀπειθοῦντες τοῦ κατασκηνῶσαι*—“for indeed, disbelieving that he would dwell”—but both readings are wrong. We translated: “For indeed, not believing that the Lord God would dwell.” The sense should depend upon what precedes:

“You ascended on high, you led captivity captive, you received gifts among human beings, and those who did not believe that the Lord could dwell among mortals.”

[Note: Not “for indeed,” but “moreover” (*insuper*) is what he himself translated, much more elegantly. Furthermore, Martianaeus adds the word “God,” which, although it is present in the Hebrew and in Jerome’s own version, is found in none of the handwritten copies—or even in the printed books. But when Jerome said that both the Latin and the Greek were wrong, understand him to mean the word *ἀπειθοῦντες*, for which *ἀπειθοῦντας* should be read, in the accusative case. We have thought it necessary to mention this because no trace of this correction or reading appears anywhere among the Septuagint, nor in the Hexapla, and because it greatly contributes to the clarity of this passage.]

In the same psalm: “God, blessed is the Lord day by day” (Ps. 67:20). You say that you found in the Greek: “The Lord, blessed God; blessed is the Lord day by day.” But the former reading is better and more accurate.

In the same psalm: “They saw your entrances, O God” (v. 25), whereas the Greek is written: “Your entrances, O God, were seen.” In Hebrew it reads [Note: Our copies agree remarkably in reading *Rachu alichatach*. The Palatine manuscript, omitting “Aquila,” adds after the name of Theodotion, “the Fifth and Sixth Editions”; the printed editions and the Hexapla agree with this. We think the more accurate reading is *οἱ λοιποὶ ἐθεώρησαν τὰς πορείας* and so forth, as in the Coislinian manuscript cited by Montfaucon.]: *RAU ALICHOTHACH*, which Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion translated: “They saw your journeys, O God,” followed by: “The journeys of my God and King who is in the sanctuary.”

Therefore it should be read by us as follows: “They saw your steps, O God”; and the copyist’s error should be left standing, since he put the nominative for the accusative. Yet I have also found in both the Septuagint and the *Hexapla*: [Note: We think it is clear that Jerome indicates that the passage should be read actively, differently from the form he established: “They saw your steps,” and so forth. In the Septuagint, including the Hexaplaric copies, it is found in the passive voice. This is in fact confirmed. The editors have therefore hitherto read this passage falsely and contrary to the holy Doctor’s intention as *ἔθεώρησαν*—or, more ineptly, as Victorius printed it, *ἐθεωρήθησαν*—*τὰς πορείας*. We have learned shortly before that this was the translation of Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion, whereas all the books testify that the Septuagint read *ἐθεωρήθησαν αἱ πορεῖαί σου*, “your journeys were seen,” and we have restored this reading, as required by the sense and, moreover, by the authority of the Regina manuscript, the oldest of all.]

*ἐθεώρησαν αἱ πορεῖαί σου, ὁ θεός*—“They saw your journeys, O God.” Instead of *ἐθεώρησαν*, that is, “they saw,” many copies have *ἐθεωρήθησαν*, “they were seen”; and this latter reading has become customary.

In the same psalm: “The entrance of my God, my King, who is in the sanctuary” (v. 25). The phrase “they saw” is understood: “They saw the entrance of my God and my King.”

But your claim that “my” is not attached to “King” in the Greek is an utterly blatant falsehood. It occurs a second time: “both my God and my King,” as an expression of affectionate devotion, so that he who is God and King of all may become specially “my God” and, by reason of service, “my King.” Finally, the Hebrew reads *HELI MELCHI*, which means “my God and my King.”

[Note: In the Regina manuscript, “in” appears instead of “of”; in the Greek, the old edition more explicitly has “in the Greek,” with “my” not appended in the second position. In fact, the Septuagint does not have it.]

In the same psalm: “Kingdoms of the earth, sing to God; sing psalms to the Lord” (v. 33). [Note: In the old edition and several manuscripts, this sentence is badly disfigured by a large lacuna in the Greek and by other corruptions. For understanding the passage, it is preferable to compare the Hebrew text: “Kingdoms of the earth, sing to God; sing psalms to the Lord. Selah. To him who rides upon the heaven of heavens toward the east.”]

You say that “Sing psalms to the Lord” is not written in this verse, because “Sing psalms to God, who ascended above the heaven of heavens toward the east” immediately follows, with *Diapsalma*. But according to the Hebrew Truth this verse ought rather to read: “Sing to God; sing psalms to the Lord.” The following words at the beginning of the next verse—“Sing psalms to God”—are not found in the authentic books, but are marked beforehand with an obelus.

Therefore you should read what is true, lest, by accepting an addition, you abandon what was written by the Prophet.

### 42. [pp. 658–659; col. 0852] Psalm sixty-eighth

“I will praise the name of God with a song” (Ps. 68:31). You say that in the Greek you found “of my God.” But “my” is superfluous.

### 43. Psalm seventieth

“God, do not withdraw from me” (Ps. 70:12). You say that “my God” is found in the Greek. “My” is superfluous.

In the same psalm: “God, you have taught me from my youth” (v. 17). Here also, you say that you found “my God” among the Greeks. “My” is superfluous.

In the same psalm: “Until I proclaim your arm” (v. 18). You say that in the Greek you found “your wonders,” which belongs to the preceding verse, and “until now I will proclaim your miracles.” [Note: All the printed editions, and most of the manuscripts, read “your pitiable things.”] “Arm” is therefore correctly placed here.

### 43. Psalm seventy-first

“And all kings shall worship him” (Ps. 71:11). The phrase that you say you found in the Greek, “the kings of the earth,” is superfluous.

In the same psalm: “Blessed is the Lord God, the God of Israel” (v. 18). You say that the Greek does not have “God” twice, although it is present in the Hebrew and among the Septuagint; and the very clear threefold naming of the Lord and God signifies the mystery of the Trinity.

In the same psalm: “And blessed be the name of his majesty forever.” Therefore, the words that you say you found in the Greek—“forever and unto the age of the age”—should be recognized as an unnecessary addition by the Greeks, since neither the Hebrew nor the Seventy translators has them.

[Note: The two older manuscripts read “He will come forth,” then “they will come forth”; and instead of *ἐξηλεύσατο* they again have *ἐξελεύσεται*. This is certainly erroneous, but the reading *ἐξηλεύσατο* is nowhere found in the Septuagint copies. Moreover, the words added afterward, *ἡ ἀδικία αὐτῶν*, have nothing to do with the difficulty under discussion. It is surprising if Jerome himself added them, since he concealed in the Hebrew that “eye” was read instead of “iniquity,” and that the Septuagint read it as “their iniquity.”]

### 45. Psalm seventy-second

“It came forth as from fat” (Ps. 72:7). You say that you found among the Greeks *ἐξελεύσεται*, that is, “will come forth.” This is false. For among the Septuagint translators it is written:

*ἐξηλεύσατο ὡς ἐκ στέατος ἡ ἀδικία αὐτῶν*—

“Their iniquity came forth as from fat.”

In the same psalm: “How does God know?” (v. 11). You say that “God” is absent from the Greek, although it is written among the Septuagint: *Πῶς ἔγνω ὁ θεός*, “How did God know?” All the translators likewise rendered it from the Hebrew.

In the same psalm: “I will understand in their latter days” (v. 17). You say that in the Greek you read “and I will understand.” Here “and,” the conjunction, is superfluous.

In the same psalm: “My flesh and my heart failed” (v. 26). Some perversely preserve the wrong order: “My heart and my flesh failed.”

In the same psalm: “That I may proclaim all your proclamations” (v. 28). You said that you read in the Greek *τὰς αἰνέσεις σου*, that is, “your praises.” It should be known that the Hebrew reads *MALOCHOTHACII*. [Note: We would prefer to defer to the authority of the ancient copies—not only those we consulted, but also those consulted by Martianaeus—which, with remarkable agreement, read *Malochochah*, a word barbarous to Latin ears. It is quite possible that the Hebrew exemplar used by Jerome read not the form found today but the form found in Nahum 2: last verse, with the same meaning. The Regina manuscript, which is also the oldest of all, would then be entirely correct in reading *Malochochah*.] Aquila translated it *ἀγγελίας σου*, “your messages”; the Septuagint, *τὰς ἐπαγγελίας σου*, “your proclamations” or “your promises.” [Note: The old printed editions have “Aquila: your angels,” and shortly afterward “the Septuagint: your promises,” contrary to the evidence of the manuscripts. No copies other than Hexaplaric ones should be introduced as belonging to the Septuagint.] Yet both “praise” and “proclamation” convey the same meaning.

### 46. [pp. 660–661; cols. 0853–0854] Psalm seventy-third

“Why, O God, have you rejected us forever?” (Ps. 75:1). Among the Greeks the order is wrongly altered to: “Why have you rejected us, O God?”

In the same psalm: “How greatly the enemy has acted wickedly in the sanctuary” (v. 3). I am astonished that someone, correcting your copy, distorted it by replacing “in the sanctuary” with “in the sanctuaries,” since “in the sanctuary” is also found in our copy.

In the same psalm: “Let us burn all the feast-days of God from the earth” (v. 8). The Greek has *καταπαύσωμεν*, and we translated it accordingly: “Let us cause all the feast-days of God to cease from the earth.”

I am astonished that some reckless person thought that a note written in the margin should be copied into the text. We wrote it for the instruction of the reader in this form: “It does not have *καταπαύσωμεν*, as some think, but *κατακαύσωμεν*, that is, ‘let us burn.’” Since the holy presbyter Firmus, who supervised this work, reported to me that much discussion had arisen on this point, it seems necessary to discuss it more fully.

The Hebrew reads *SARPHU CHOL MOEDAU EL BAARES*. [Note: Martianaeus suspects that Jerome’s Hebrew exemplar read a form different from the present one. The Palatine manuscript, with aspiration, has *MOEDAHU HEL*. Erasmus and Victorius then read *ἐνέπρησαν* instead of *ἐνεπύρισαν*, and “feasts” instead of “assemblies”; for they were not acquainted with the Hexapla.]

Aquila and Symmachus translated it:

*ἐνεπύρισαν πάσας τὰς συναγωγὰς τοῦ Θεοῦ*—

“They burned all the assemblies of God.”

The Fifth Edition has *κατεκάυσαν*, “they burned up”; the Sixth, *κατακαύσωμεν*, “let us burn up.” It is clear that the Septuagint also translated it according to the truth of the Hexapla. Theodotion likewise rendered it *ἐμπυρίσωμεν*, “let us set fire to.” [Note: Three of our copies have *ἐνεπυρίσαμεν*, another *ἐνεπύρισαν*; the same reading is attributed to Theodotion in the Hexapla. But all have “let us set fire to,” which leads us to think that *ἐμπυρίσωμεν* should be read.]

It is therefore clear that the psalm should be sung as we translated it; nevertheless, one must know what the Hebrew Truth contains. What the Septuagint translated should be sung in the churches because of its antiquity; the other reading should be known by the learned for knowledge of the Scriptures.

Therefore, if anything has been added in the margin for the sake of instruction, it should not be placed in the text, lest the earlier translation be disturbed at the will of copyists.

In the same psalm: “You crushed the heads of the dragons in the waters; you shattered the head of the dragon” (vv. 13–14). The order of the reading is such that the first verse does not have “you,” but the second does. “Waters” should be written in the plural, not the singular, just as Aquila translated the Hebrew word *AMMAIM*: *τῶν ὑδάτων*, “of the waters.” [Note: Two manuscripts have *Ammichim*.]

In the same psalm: “Do not forget the voices of your enemies” (v. 23). You say that the Greek has *τῶν ἱκετῶν σου*, “of those who beseech you.” But the Hebrew reads *SORARACH*. Aquila translated it “of your enemies”; Symmachus, “of those fighting against you”; the Septuagint and the Sixth Edition, “of your enemies.”

The sense depends upon what precedes: “Remember your reproaches, those uttered all day long by the fool; the voices of your enemies”—that is, “Do not forget the voices that blaspheme you and speak against you among your people.” Hence it follows: “The pride of those who hate you rises continually” (v. 23)—that is, while you delay their punishment, they advance in their blasphemies.

### 47. Psalm seventy-fourth

“We shall recount your wonders” (Ps. 74:3). The Greek wrongly reads: “I shall recount all your wonders.”

### 48. Psalm seventy-fifth

“All men of wealth, with their own hands” (Ps. 75:6). Not “in their hands,” as you read in a copy corrupted—I do not know by whom.

In the same psalm: “Terrible, and to him who takes away the breath of princes” (v. 13). You say that “to him” is not written in the Greek. That is true; but unless we add “to him,” the Latin sentence does not sound right. We cannot properly say: “Terrible, and who takes away the breath of princes.”

### 49. [col. 0854] Psalm seventy-sixth

“And I meditated at night with my heart, and I exercised myself, and I swept my spirit” (Ps. 76:7). In the Hebrew we read: “I remembered my psalms at night; I spoke with my heart, and I swept my spirit.” [Note: The old printed editions, and the Florentine Royal manuscript cited by Martianaeus, wrongly have “your.” The punctuation in his edition is also faulty: “At night I spoke with my heart,” where the conjunction “and” is missing, an error no less serious. Finally, for the word *ἀδολεσχίαν* that follows, the Regina manuscript substitutes in the margin *ἠδολέσχουν*, the proper verb of the Septuagint translators.]

For “exercise,” the Septuagint translated *ἀδολεσχίαν*, that is, a kind of recitation and meditation. For our “I swept,” they put *ἕσκαλλον*, which Symmachus translated *ἀνηρεύνων*, “I searched out” or “I investigated”; the Fifth Edition does likewise.

Properly, *σκαλισμός* is used in agriculture for hoeing or cultivating. Just as weeds are sought out with a hoe so that they may be cut away, so this person figuratively represented the reconsideration [or: review] of his thoughts by means of a hoe. It should be understood that *ἕσκαλλον* does not signify this only once, but frequently.

In the same psalm: “From generation to generation” (v. 9). The words that you say you found next in the Greek—“He completed the word”—are rightly absent from the Latin, since they occur in none of the translators. [Note: Other printed editions, following the Greek, have “which,” and shortly afterward omit it from the Latin. As for the matter itself, both Breitinger’s Greek edition and the Zurich copy cited by him contain the words: *Συνετέλεσε ῥῆμα ἀπὸ γενεᾶς εἰς γενεάν*, “He completed the word from generation to generation.” In the former they are marked with an asterisk; in the latter they stand without qualification.]

### 50. [pp. 662–663; cols. 0855–0856] Psalm seventy-seventh

“And they shall recount it to their children” (Ps. 77:6). The Greek has *ἀπαγγελοῦσιν*, which means “they shall announce.” But it should be known that the Hebrew reads *IASAPHPHERU*, which Aquila and Symmachus translated “they shall recount.”

In the same psalm: “And he killed their fat ones” (v. 31). The Hebrew has the same, namely *BAMASMNEHEM*. Aquila translated it *ἐν λιπαροῖς αὐτῶν*, “among their fat ones”; Symmachus, *τοὺς λιπαρωτέρους αὐτῶν*, “their fattest ones”; the Septuagint, Theodotion, and the Fifth Edition, *ἐν τοῖς πίοσιν αὐτῶν*, “among their fat ones.” Some, not understanding this, supposed that *πλείoσιν* was written instead of *πίοσιν*.

In the same psalm: “They loved him with their mouth, and with their tongue they lied to him” (v. 36). The Hebrew likewise reads *ICHAZBULO*, and all translated it in similar terms: *ἐψεύσαντο αὐτῷ*, “they lied to him.” Whoever wished to put “him” in the accusative instead of “to him,” and thereby corrupt the copies, is not my responsibility.

In the same psalm: “And he became merciful toward their sins, and did not destroy them” (v. 38). You say that the Greek does not have “them.” That is true; but we completed the Latin sentence according to its own character, so that the meaning would not hang unfinished.

If anyone thinks that *διαφθερεῖ* does not mean “destruction” but “corruption,” let him recall the title in which it is written: *εἰς τὸ τέλος μὴ διαφθείρῃς*—“For the end: do not destroy”—and not, as many zealously but incorrectly interpret it, “do not corrupt.”

In the same psalm: “And he led them to the mountain of his sanctification, the mountain that his right hand acquired” (v. 54). The Septuagint reads:

*ὄρος τοῦτο ἐκτήσατο ἡ δεξιὰ αὐτοῦ*—

“This mountain his right hand acquired.”

[Note: Erasmus and Victorius, together with some manuscripts, have “not as you place it.” Then, along with the old edition and the Florentine manuscript, they have *ἡ ἐκτήσατο* instead of *ὃ ἐκτήσατο*. The printed reading requires an Oedipus—that is, a clever interpreter—to discover what the author means. The words, left unchanged by us, seem to reject the relative pronoun “which” in favor of the demonstrative “this,” or at least to say that the two should not be combined. Yet Jerome himself translated from the Hebrew, “this mountain, which he possessed.” We would therefore prefer to derive the difficulty from the similarity between the words *ἐκτήσατο* and *ἐκτίσατο*: the former means “acquired” or “possessed,” the latter “founded” or “created.” The latter may have stood in Sunnia’s copy, without the copyists and critics noticing it. The text would then have to be supplied and rewritten: not as you read it, *ὃ ἐκτίσατο*, “which he created,” but *ὃ ἐκτήσατο*, “which his right hand acquired,” and so forth.]

It is therefore better, according to the Hebrew idiom, that Symmachus translated it: “the mountain that his right hand acquired.”

In the same psalm: “And they turned aside and did not keep the covenant, like their fathers” (v. 57). I know that “covenant” is not present in the Hebrew. But since all translated it with the same word, *ἠσυνθέτησαν*, and since among the Greeks *συνθήκη* means “covenant,” the single verb expresses the meaning: “they did not keep the covenant,” although the Septuagint put *ἠθέτησαν*, “they rejected.”

In the same psalm: “In the land which he founded forever” (v. 68). You say that you found written: “In the land he founded him forever.” The Hebrew is written as Symmachus translated it: [Note: All the printed editions contain a serious error, which Martianaeus also failed to avoid: they corrupt Symmachus’s reading as *εἰς τὴν γῆν* instead of *ὡς τὴν γῆν*, as it is correctly written in Eusebius and Theodoret, and as we have restored it, with the support of a single manuscript. The sense itself required this. The Hebrew text has *Caares*, “like the earth,” or as Jerome himself translated it, “as the earth,” not *Baares*, “in the land.” The Septuagint may have read this through a common error and translated *ἐν τῇ γῇ*, but it could not have translated *εἰς τὴν γῆν*.]

*ὡς τὴν γῆν ἣν ἐθεμελίωσεν εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα*—

“Like the earth which he founded forever.”

But if the statement is not about the earth being founded, but about some other thing that appears to have been founded on the earth, let them demonstrate from what precedes and follows what sense there can be in making something unmentioned appear to have been founded on the earth. If they think that the sanctuary was founded on the earth, it should have been written: “In the earth he founded it forever.”

In the same psalm: “And he led them by the understandings of his hands” (v. 72). It does not have, as you write, *ἐν τῇ συνέσει*, in the singular, but *ἐν ταῖς συνέσεσιν*, which means “by understandings,” just as the Hebrew has *BATHABUNOTH*, “in understandings.”

### 51. Psalm seventy-eighth

“They made Jerusalem a guardhouse for orchards” (Ps. 78:1). In Greek it is called *εἰς ὀπωροφυλάκιον*, [Note: Martianaeus had read *ὡς* instead of *εἰς*, which he later corrected, just as below he corrected *λιθαόριον* to *λιθόριον*. The manuscripts also contain *λιθύριον*, which Drusius likewise read. Some ancient parchment copies have *Lichin* instead of the Hebrew word *Liin*. Such towers, generally built in the middle of fields, are described in 2 Chronicles 26:10: “He also built towers in the wilderness and dug many cisterns, for he had much livestock both in the lowlands and in the wilderness,” and so forth. The Gospel also refers to them in Luke 14:28: “Which of you, wishing to build a tower,” and so forth. Greek commentators call them *περιωπή*, or a lookout.] and it cannot be translated otherwise than as we have translated it.

It means a lookout tower of the kind that keepers of sown fields [or: fields] and orchards commonly have, so that from a very large city scarcely a little hut remained.

This is according to the Greeks. In the Hebrew, however, it reads *LIIN*, which Aquila translated *λιθόριον*, that is, “a heap and a pile [or: mound]” of stones, with which vineyards and fields are usually cleared.

### 52. Psalm seventy-ninth

“And you planted its roots here” (Ps. 79:10). You say that “here” is absent from the Greek; and rightly so, for it is absent from our copies as well. I am astonished that some ignorant person falsified your books.

### 53. Psalm eighty-second

“Let us possess the sanctuary of God as an inheritance” (Ps. 82:12). You say that the Greek reads *κληρονομήσωμεν ἑαυτοῖς*, that is, “Let us possess for ourselves.” [Note: We have restored the Greek words *κληρονομήσωμεν ἑαυτοῖς*, which Martianaeus had deleted, on the basis of all our manuscripts and the printed books.]

This is a superfluous question. Whenever “let us possess” is said, “for ourselves” is understood.

### 54. [p. 664; cols. 0856–0857] Psalm eighty-third

“My heart and my flesh rejoiced in the living God” (Ps. 83:3). You say that the Greek reads “rejoiced,” in the plural. There is no disagreement here. If we read “rejoiced,” the meaning is that both my heart and my flesh rejoiced. If, however, we read “they rejoiced,” then two things rejoiced together: heart and flesh.

I ask you to avoid such absurd and superfluous disputes where there is no alteration of meaning.

In the same psalm: “Blessed is the man whose help is from you.” You say that you found in the Greek: “whose help is his from you.” [Note: Here too Martianaeus appears to have erred by removing the word “his,” without which both the truth of the reading and the entire force of Jerome’s text collapse. We have restored it from the printed editions and manuscripts, although in them “to him,” as also in the old edition, is consistently found below instead of “his.” The meaning is not different, since the Greek likewise varies: some books prefer *αὐτῷ*, others *αὐτοῦ*.]

Since we avoid this in the Latin translation, you say that we are censured. Who could fail to see that, if we wished to say “whose help is his,” it would be an obvious error? When “whose” has preceded, “his” should not follow—unless we are accused of error because we avoided an error.

In the same psalm: “In the valley of tears” (v. 7). You say that the Greek reads *κλαυθμῶνος*, “of weeping.” But whether we say “weeping,” “lamentation,” “crying,” or “tears,” the meaning is one and the same. We follow the rule that, where there is no change of meaning, the elegance of the Latin language should be preserved.

### 55. Psalm eighty-fourth

“You blessed your land, O Lord” (Ps. 84:1). For “you blessed,” you say that the Greek has *εὐδόκησας*, and you ask how this verb should be expressed in Latin.

If we examine the words and syllables contentiously, we can say: “Your land pleased well, O Lord.” But while following the words, we lose the order of the meaning. Or something must be added to preserve the order of the expression, and we could say: “Your land pleased you, O Lord.” If we do this, we will again be asked [or: it will be asked] why we added “you,” since it is found neither in the Greek nor in the Hebrew.

We must therefore follow the same rule of translation that we have often stated: wherever the language into which we translate suffers no loss of meaning, its euphony and idiomatic character should be preserved.

In the same psalm: “Mercy and truth met one another” (v. 11). You say that the Greek does not have “one another.” Neither does the Hebrew; among the Septuagint it is marked beforehand with an obelus. When such signs are carelessly left by most copyists as though they were superfluous, great error arises in reading.

If “one another” is not added, people will think that mercy and truth met not each other but someone else, and that righteousness and peace did not kiss each other but another person.

### 56. [p. 665; col. 0857] Psalm eighty-fifth
