“And they did not set you before their eyes” (Ps. 85:14). You say that “you” is absent from your copy. Add “you,” and by correcting your copyist’s error you will also correct your own error. [Note: The Palatine manuscript reads, “you will correct your copyist’s error. In the same psalm,” and so forth, omitting the remaining words that are inserted.]

In the same psalm: “But you, Lord God, compassionate and merciful” (v. 15). You say that you found in the Greek: “And you, Lord, my God.” This is superfluous. “My” is found neither in the Hebrew nor among the Septuagint. [Note: In the Aldine and Complutensian copies, *θεὸς μου οἰκτίρμων*, “my compassionate God,” remains.]

### 57. Psalm eighty-eighth

“Great and terrible” (Ps. 88:8). You say that you found in the Greek *φοβερός*, which means “terrible,” “to be feared,” or “frightening.” I think that “terrible” (*horrendus*) means the same thing—not what the common people think, namely, “despicable” and “squalid,” as in the following:

“Cold horror shakes my limbs.”

And:

“Everywhere horror in my mind; even the silences themselves terrify.” (Virgil, *Aeneid* 3)

And:

“A huge, fearsome monster.” (Virgil, *Aeneid* 2.20)

And many similar passages.

In the same psalm: “Then he spoke in a vision to his holy ones.” You say that the Greek has “to your sons.” But it should be known that the Hebrew reads *LAASIDACH*, which all translated as *τοῖς ὁσίοις σου*, “to your holy ones.” [Note: The Hexapla and the old printed editions have *ἁγίοις* rather than *ὁσίοις*, which seems more accurate. The phrase *τοῖς υἱοῖς σου*, “to your sons,” is said to belong to all the Greek copies.] Only the Sixth Edition translated it “to your prophets,” expressing the sense rather than the word. In the *Koine* I found “sons” only in place of “holy ones.”

In the same psalm: “But you rejected and regarded with favor” (v. 39). You say that you found in the Greek *ἐξουδένωσας*. The change of a single letter has caused you a great error. We did not translate it “you regarded with favor,” but “you despised,” “you counted as nothing.” [Note: On the authority and reliability of our copies, we have corrected what the Benedictine and other editors, failing to grasp the sense, corrupt here through gross error: “you despised.”]

Unless you perhaps think that *ἐξουδένωσας* should not be translated “you despised,” but, according to the eloquent interpreter of that period, “you annihilated,” “you annulled,” or “you nullified,” together with whatever other monstrosities of language may be found among the ignorant.

### 58. [p. 666; col. 0858] Psalm eighty-ninth

“From age to age, you are God” (Ps. 89:2). You say that “God” is absent from the Greek. It is plainly present among them. The Hebrew has it, as do all the other translators, and the Septuagint likewise translated:

*ἀπὸ τοῦ αἰῶνος καὶ ἕως τοῦ αἰῶνος σὺ εἶ ὁ Θεός*—

“From age to age, you are God.”

In Hebrew this is *MEOLAM AD-OLAM ATH EL*. [Note: It is now impossible to find the added *ὁ θεός* in any Greek manuscript. Nor do the better printed editions have it. Breitinger supplies it in smaller type, and Montfaucon admits that in the Hexapla he takes it from this very passage of Jerome’s letter.]

In the same psalm: “For gentleness has come upon us, and we shall be chastened” (v. 10). You say that the Greek reads: “Gentleness is upon us.” But this too is superfluous. [Note: All the Greek books in fact have *ἐφ’ ἡμᾶς*, “upon us.”]

### 59. Psalm ninetieth

“He will say to the Lord, ‘You are my protector’” (Ps. 90:2). You say that the Greek does not have “you are.” I will tell you more: among the Hebrews it has neither “you are” nor “you”; but among the Septuagint and the Latins these words were placed for euphony and for the continuity of the sentence.

### 60. Psalm ninety-third

“Blessed is the man whom you instruct, O Lord” (Ps. 93:12). You say that “you” is absent from the Greek; and that is true. But it was placed among the Latins for euphony. If we say, “Blessed is the man whom you instruct, O Lord,” the elegance of the composition is lacking. And [or: But] when “O Lord” is spoken and the address is made to the Lord, it does no harm to the meaning if “you” is also included.

In the same psalm: “And in their wickedness he will destroy them” (v. 23). You say that the Greek does not have the preposition “in,” but reads: “He will destroy their wickedness.” It should be known, however, that both the Hebrew and all the translators have “In their wickedness he will destroy them.”

If we wish to read “He will destroy their wickedness,” the word “them,” which follows at the end of the verse in the Septuagint, will be both superfluous and defective.

### 61. Psalm ninety-seventh

“He remembered his mercy” (Ps. 97:3). You say that in the Greek you found: “His mercy toward Jacob.” But “Jacob” is a superfluous name here. [Note: This is because Jacob is absent from the Hebrew, although all the Greek books have it, and many Latin copies do as well. Perhaps “Jacob” was written in the following verse instead of the name “Israel,” as we find in many copies of Jerome’s Hebrew version. It may also have stood in some Hebrew original, with “Israel” subsequently substituted at the margin of the book, after which the Septuagint themselves assigned the earlier name to the earlier verse.]

### 62. Psalm one hundredth

“My eyes are upon the faithful of the earth, so that they may sit with me” (Ps. 100:6). You say that in the Greek you found:

*τοῦ συγκαθῆσθαι αὐτοὺς μετ’ ἐμοῦ*—

“so that they themselves might sit with me.”

Who would not reject such a translation, which renders word for word and says: “so that they themselves might sit with me”?

### 63. Psalm 101

“**I kept vigil and became like a solitary sparrow on the roof**” (Psalm 101:8). You say that in the Greek you found *ἐπὶ δώματι*, which the ancient Latin codices translated as “in a building.” In the eastern provinces, *δῶμα* means the same as “roof” among us.[^c0098-1] For in Palestine and Egypt, where the divine Books were either written or translated, roofs do not have pitched coverings, but *δώματα*, which at Rome are called either roof-terraces or *maeniana*—that is, flat roofs supported by transverse beams.[^c0098-2]

Peter too, in the Acts of the Apostles (10:9), when he went up onto a *dōma*, must be understood to have gone up onto the roof of a building. And when we are commanded to make a crown around our *dōma*, the command is that on the roof we make projections all around it, lest someone easily fall headlong (Deuteronomy 22:8). In the Gospel: “What you hear in the ear, you shall proclaim upon the rooftops” (Matthew 10:27)—that is, upon the roofs. And in Isaiah: “What is the matter with you, that you have all gone up upon the rooftops?”—or, according to another reading, “the new rooftops” (Isaiah 22:1, according to the Septuagint)—and many similar passages.

In the same Psalm: “I became like a *νυκτικόραξ* in a dwelling” (Psalm 101:7). The same reading is found in Greek; and you ask what *νυκτικόραξ* means in Latin. In Hebrew, instead of *nycticorax*, we have a word written which Aquila, the Septuagint, Theodotion, and the Fifth Edition translated as “night-heron”; Symmachus rendered it *upupa* [hoopoe], while the Sixth Edition rendered it “owl,” which we too follow more readily.[^c0098-3] Thus, where our Latin versions and the Greek read, “I became like a night-heron in a dwelling,” the Hebrews have, “I became like an owl among ruins.” Most people obstinately think that a horned owl is meant.

In the same Psalm: “Because of the face of your anger and indignation.” You say that in the Greek you found, “Because of the face of your anger,” although it is clear that among the Hebrews and the Septuagint translators the text reads: *ἀπὸ προσώπου τῆς ὀργῆς καὶ τοῦ θυμοῦ σου*—“from the face of your anger and your wrath.”[^c0098-4]

In the same Psalm: “For your servants have taken pleasure in its stones, and they will pity its dust” (Psalm 101:15). [A lacuna of several verses is suspected here, since it is hardly believable either that the difficulty at the beginning of this verse was proposed by the German brothers without purpose, or that Jerome omitted it. It is quite easy, and usual, for a period to have begun with the little word “For,” and for a copyist, having reached the final occurrence of the word, to have thought that he had read the first and omitted what lay between. Consider, therefore, whether the passage might suitably be supplied approximately as follows: “For which you say you read in the Greek, ‘your servants,’ in the nominative: *ὅτι εὐδόκησαν οἱ δοῦλοί σου*—that is, ‘For your servants have been well pleased,’ or, ‘your servants have thought well.’ But it was translated into Latin for the sake of euphony, as we have shown above [on Psalm 84]. As for ‘the earth,’ and so forth …” If this does not satisfy the reader, an educated reader will repair the corrupt passage according to his own judgment. Consult the ancient Latin Psalters translated from the Greek.]

For “dust,” the Hebrew has **AFAR**, which all translated as *χοῦν* [dust, earth]. It may be rendered either “dust” or “soil,” that is, “earth.”[^c0098-5]

### 64. Psalm 102

“He will not be angry forever” (Psalm 102:9). You say that in the Greek you found, “He will not be angry to the end.” But the Hebrew word **NESE** can, according to the character of the passage, mean “forever,” “end,” or “victory.”

### 65. Psalm 103

“You make your angels spirits” (Psalm 103:4). You say that in the Greek you found: *ὁ ποιῶν τοὺς ἀγγέλους αὐτοῦ*—that is, “who makes his angels.”[^c0098-6] Ask them briefly how, when the speech is addressed to God, the Prophet suddenly changes as though speaking about another person—especially since he begins:

“Lord, my God, you have been greatly magnified; you have clothed yourself with confession and beauty. You cover his upper chambers with waters”—that is, the heavens. “You make the cloud your ascent,” or “you walk upon the wings of the winds.” Immediately there follows: “You make your angels spirits, and your ministers a burning fire. You founded the earth upon its stability.” A little later: “At your rebuke they will flee; at the voice of your thunder they will be afraid.” And: “In the place that you founded for them.” “You send forth springs in the valleys.” And: “That you may bring bread out of the earth.”

If, therefore, everything is addressed to the second person, that is, to God, how is a third person suddenly introduced in a single verse and out of order? In the same Psalm: “At the voice of your thunder they will be afraid” (Psalm 103:7). The Hebrew too has “your thunder,” and I wonder how, through scribal error among the Latins, it was omitted.

In the same Psalm: “This sea is great and spacious with hands” (Psalm 103:25). You say that “with hands” is not found in the Greek, and I know that it is not. But it was added to the Septuagint from the Hebrew and from Theodotion’s edition under an asterisk. In Hebrew it is written: **ZE HAIAM GADOL VARAB IDAIM**, which Aquila translated: *αὐλὴ καὶ πλατεῖα χερσίν*; and all the interpreters: *αὕτη ἡ θάλασσα ἡ μεγάλη καὶ εὐρύχωρος χερσίν*. This is said metaphorically, according to the Hebrew idiom: it is as though the sea had great, outstretched hands and received everything into itself.[^c0098-7]

In the same Psalm: “That you may bring bread out of the earth” (Psalm 103:15). You say that you found “that he may bring bread out” instead. But one thing cannot be said of him and another about him. Either the Prophet spoke throughout as though addressing God, or he referred everything throughout to another as being about God. Since most of the passage is directed to God himself, the ambiguous expressions must also be directed to his person.

In the same Psalm: “The house of the heron is their leader” (Psalm 103:18). Instead of “heron,” the Hebrew has **ASIDA**. Symmachus translated it as *ἰκτίνα* [or *ἰκτίνον*], that is, “kite.” Thus we too translated it into Latin: “There the birds will nest; the kite’s house is the fir tree”—because kites are accustomed always to make their nests in lofty and steep trees. Hence the Sixth Edition translated it more clearly: “For the kite to nest in the cypress.” Instead of “fir trees” and “cypresses,” however, the Hebrew has **BARUSIM**, which signifies fir trees more than cypresses.[^c0098-8]

In the same Psalm: “The rock is a refuge for the *herinacius*.” The Hebrew has **SPHANNIM**, and all translated the word similarly as *χοίρογρυλλίοις*, except the Septuagint, who translated it “hares.” It should be known, however, that this is an animal no larger than a hedgehog, resembling both a mouse and a bear. Hence in Palestine it is called *ἀρκτόμυς* [bear-mouse]. These animals are extremely abundant in those regions, and they are accustomed always to live in cavities of rocks and holes in the earth.

### 66. Psalm 104

“Their land brought forth frogs” (Psalm 104:30). You say that in the Greek you read *ἐξῆρψεν*. This can be translated: “Their land boiled forth frogs.” But here too there is no change of meaning, and, following the ancient translation, we did not wish to alter what did no harm.

In the same Psalm: “And he crushed the wood of their boundaries” (Psalm 104:33). You say that in the Greek you found “every tree.” But this too is an addition and is superfluous.

In the same Psalm: “For he remembered his holy word, which he had with Abraham his servant” (Psalm 104:42). You say that in the Greek you read *ὃν διέθετο*, that is, “which he arranged” or “appointed.” Thus it is found both in Hebrew and among the Septuagint translators: *ἐμνήσθη τοῦ λόγου τοῦ ἁγίου αὐτοῦ, τοῦ πρὸς Ἀβραὰμ τὸν δοῦλον αὐτοῦ*—“He remembered his holy word, which he spoke to Abraham his servant.” Therefore what is said in the Greek, *ὃν διέθετο*, is superfluous here and should be deleted.[^c0098-9]

### 67. Psalm 105

“Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good” (Psalm 105:1). You say that in the Greek you read, “for he is *χρηστός*,” that is, “pleasant” or “kind.” But it should be understood that *χρηστός* may be translated both as “good” and as “pleasant.” In Hebrew it is written **CHI TOB**, which all translated with the same expression: “for he is good.” It is therefore clear that *χρηστός* is understood as “good.”

In the same Psalm: “They did not remember the multitude of your mercies.” You say that in the Greek you found, “And they did not remember.” The conjunction “and” is superfluous.

In the same Psalm: “And they provoked him as they went up into the Red Sea.” You say that in the Greek you found *παρεπίκραναν*, and you think the word should be translated word for word as “they made bitter.” But this interpretation is akin to “annulment” or “annihilation.” Read Ezekiel, and you will find *παραπικρασμός* consistently expressed as “provocation” and “exasperation,” where it says *οἶκος παραπικραίνων*, that is, “an exasperating house” (Ezekiel 7:5–6 and following).

In the same Psalm: “And he saw when they were afflicted, and he heard their prayer” (Psalm 105:44). Whatever else you say that you found in the Greek beyond this is superfluous.[^c0098-10]

### 68. Psalm 106

“And he turned its storm into a breeze, and its waves were silent” (Psalm 106:29). Therefore what you say that you found in the Greek in addition to this—*καὶ ἐπετίμησεν τῇ καταιγίδι αὐτῆς, καὶ ἔστη*—is superfluous.[^c0098-11]

In the same Psalm: “And he led them into the harbor of their desire” (Psalm 106:30). You say that you found instead, “into the harbor of his desire.” But the Hebrew does not have **EPHSAU**, which means “of his desire”; it has **EPHSAM**, which means “of their desire.”[^c0098-12]

### 69. Psalm 107

“Awake, my glory” (Psalm 107:3). You say that this is absent from the Latin. It is rightly absent from this Psalm, because it is found neither among the Hebrews nor in any of the interpreters. It does occur in Psalm 56 (Psalm 56:11), and it seems to me to have been transferred by someone from that place into this one.

In the same Psalm: “Foreigners became my friends” (Psalm 107:10). You say that in the Greek you found *ὑπετάγησαν*, that is, “they were subjected.” But this is written in Psalm 59. In the present passage we find in all the translators: *ἐμοὶ ἀλλόφυλοι ἐφιλίασαν*—that is, “foreigners became my friends.” In Hebrew this is **ETHROE**.[^c0098-13]

### 70. Psalm 109

“The Lord will send the rod of your power from Zion” (Psalm 109:2). You say that in the Greek codices you did not read “of your power.” This is plainly found both in Hebrew and among the Septuagint translators.[^c0098-14]

In the same Psalm: “Rule in the midst of your enemies” (Psalm 109:2). You say that the Greek reads, “And rule.” But this is found neither in Hebrew nor among the Septuagint, and it is superfluous.

### 71. Psalm 110

“I will confess to you, Lord, with my whole heart” (Psalm 110:1). You say that in the Greek you found, “with my whole heart.” But “my” is superfluous.

### 72. Psalm 113

“But our God is in heaven” (Psalm 113:13). You say that in the Greek you read, “in heaven and on earth.” But this too is superfluous.[^c0098-15]

### 73. Psalm 114

“And in my days I will call upon you” (Psalm 114:2–3). You say that “you” is absent from the Greek; and rightly so: it should also be deleted from your codices.

In the same Psalm: “I will please the Lord in the land of the living” (Psalm 114:9). You say that in the Greek you read, “I will please in the sight of the Lord.” But this is superfluous.

### 74. Psalm 117

“And in the name of the Lord, because I have avenged myself upon them” (Psalm 117:10). You say that “because” is not found in the Greek codices; but in the Latin it should be read under an asterisk.[^c0098-16]

### 75. Psalm 118

“And I meditated on your commandments, which I loved” (Psalm 118:47). You say that in the Greek you read the addition “exceedingly.” But this is superfluous.

In the same Psalm: “I lifted up my hands to the commandments, which I loved” (Psalm 118:48). You say that in the Greek you read, “to your commandments.” But this too is superfluous.[^c0098-17]

In the same Psalm: “I considered my ways” (Psalm 118:59). You say that in the Greek you read, “your ways.” But this is superfluous, and “my ways” is the more correct reading.[^c0098-18]

In the same Psalm: “And I turned my feet toward your testimonies” (Psalm 118:59). You say that in the Greek you read, “and you turned.” But this too is superfluous.[^c0098-19]

In the same Psalm: “But I will search out your commandments with my whole heart” (Psalm 118:69). You say that in the Greek you read, “with my whole heart.” But here “my” is superfluous.

In the same Psalm: “My soul is always in my hands, and I have not forgotten your law” (Psalm 118:109). You say that in the Greek you read, “My soul is always in your hands.” But it should be known that among the Hebrews, the Septuagint, and all the other interpreters, it is written “in my hands,” not “in your hands.” In Hebrew this is **BACHAFFI**. All the Greek ecclesiastical interpreters explain the passage in this way, and its brief sense is: “Every day I am in danger, and I carry my blood, as it were, in my own hands; yet I do not forget your law.”[^c0098-20]

In the same Psalm: “Streams of waters flowed from my eyes, because they did not keep your law” (Psalm 118:136). You say that in the Greek you read, “because I did not keep your law.” But this is superfluous, since the Hebrew also reads, “Streams of waters flowed from my eyes, because they did not keep your law.”[^c0098-21]

In the same Psalm: “My tongue shall declare your utterance” (Psalm 118:172). You said that in the Greek you read *φθέγξεται* instead of “shall declare.” Whether one says “shall declare,” “shall utter,” or “shall speak,” the word has the same meaning. Thus we too translated it from the Hebrew: “My tongue shall speak your word.”[^c0098-22]

### 76. Psalm 119

“Lord, deliver my soul from lying lips and from a deceitful tongue” (Psalm 119:1). You say that in the Greek you read “and from a deceitful tongue.” But the conjunction “and” is superfluous.

### 77. Psalm 126

“Blessed is the man who shall fulfill his desire from them” (Psalm 126:5). You say that “man” is absent from the Greek. Yet it is plainly contained both in the Hebrew and among the Septuagint translators.

### 78. Psalm 129

“Because of your law I have waited for you, Lord” (Psalm 129:4). You say that in the Greek you found, “Because of your name.” We admit that many copies read this way. But because we are devoted to truth, we must simply state what is found in Hebrew.

Instead of “name” or “law,” the Hebrews have **THIRA**, which Aquila translated *φόβον*, “fear”; Symmachus and Theodotion translated it *νόμον*, “law,” thinking that the word was **THORA**, because of the resemblance of the letters *jod* and *vau*, which differ only in size. The Fifth Edition translated it “terror,” and the Sixth, “word.”[^c0098-23]

### 79. Psalm 131

“As he swore to the Lord, he vowed a vow to the God of Jacob” (Psalm 131:2). Instead of what we translated as “he vowed a vow,” you say that in the Greek you read *ἤυξατο*, and you think it ought to have been translated “he prayed.” But this is incorrect, for *εὐχή*, depending on the context, means both “prayer” and “vow,” as in: “Pay your vows to the Lord” (Psalm 49:14), that is, *τὰς εὐχάς σου*—“your vows.”[^c0098-24]

### 80. Psalm 135

“Who made the great lights” (Psalm 135:7). You say that in the Greek you found “great alone.” But this belongs to the preceding verse, where we read: “Who alone made great wonders” (Psalm 135:4). It should therefore be read there and, as superfluous here, should not be written.[^c0098-25]

### 81. Psalm 137

“For you have magnified your holy word above every name” (Psalm 137:2). You say that in the Greek you found “above all names.” But in the Septuagint it reads: *ὅτι ἐμεγάλυνας ἐπὶ πᾶν τὸ ὄνομα τὸ ἅγιόν σου*, just as we translated it into Latin.

Know, moreover, that among the Hebrews it is: “For you have magnified above every name your word.” According to the Latin edition, the sense is: “For you have magnified above every name”—that is, above everything in heaven and on earth that can be called holy—“your Son.”[^c0098-26]

### 82. Psalm 138

“Because there is no word in my tongue” (Psalm 138:4). You say that in the Greek you read, “Because there is no deceit in my tongue,” which only the Sixth Edition translated in that way. But among the Septuagint, all the other interpreters, and the Hebrew itself, it is written either *λαλιά* or *λόγος*—that is, “utterance” or “word.” In Hebrew it is called **MALA**.

### 83. Psalm 139

“They stretched out ropes as a snare” (Psalm 139:6). You say that in the Greek you found: “They stretched out ropes as a snare for my feet.” But this is superfluous here.

In the same Psalm, instead of “The upright shall dwell in your presence” (Psalm 139:14), you say that in the Greek you found, “And the upright shall dwell.” But here too the conjunction “and” is superfluous.

### 84. Psalm 140

“Our bones were scattered beside the underworld” (Psalm 140:8). You say that in the Greek you read, “their bones.” But this too is superfluous.

### 85. Psalm 146

“Nor will the legs of a man be pleasing to him” (Psalm 146:10). You say that instead of “to him,” you read “to the Lord.” But this is not found.[^c0098-27]

### 86. Explanation of Certain Greek Words

Because you too ask this at the end of your memorandum, and my holy son Avitus frequently requests it, I have briefly noted how the Greek words should be interpreted.

*Neomenia* is the beginning of a month, which, according to the usage of the Latin language, we may call the Kalends. But since among the Hebrews the month is reckoned according to the course of the moon, and among the Greeks *μήνη* means “moon,” *neomenia* is called “new moon.”

*Ἔρημος* means “desert” or “solitude.”

*Θρόνος* means “seat” or “throne.”

*Νυκτικόραξ*, as we have said, means “owl.”

*Κυνόμυια* is not, as the Latins translated it, “dog-fly,” written with the Greek letter upsilon. According to the Hebrew interpretation it should be written with the diphthong *oi*, so that it is *κοινόμυια*, that is, “every kind of fly.” Aquila translated it *πάμμικτον*, “a fly of every kind.”

*Λαξευτήριον*, which the Latin translator rendered “axe,” we interpret as a kind of iron tool with which stones are dressed. Thus, translating from the Hebrew, we said: “And now they have together scraped away its carvings with axe and stone-cutting tools” (Psalm 73:6). *Λαξευτήριον* may therefore be rendered “a stone-dressing tool.”[^c0098-28]

[^c0098-1]: The printed note reads: “The editions and some manuscripts have ‘roof’ among the Latins.”

[^c0098-2]: The note corrects a printed form *Mediana* to *Maeniana*. Jerome, in his commentary on Ezekiel 41, says that the Greeks call *ἐξώστρας* what Romans call *solaria*: structures projecting from the walls of upper rooms. They were called *maeniana* after their first inventor, Maenius. When Maenius sold his house so that the Basilica Porcia might be built there, he reserved the right to one column, over which he could project a roof from projecting boards, so that gladiatorial games could be watched. The note cites Asconius and Isidore, *Etymologies* 15.3, and adds Isidore’s quotation from an ancient grammarian: “Some built *maeniana* in porticoes, some of stone and others of masonry, so called from their first inventor; and they added them to doorways and houses.”

[^c0098-3]: The Hebrew does not have **BOS** but **COS**, a word meaning “owl.” Since the exchange of letters is very easy—but not the exchange of *B* and *C* in Latin—some prefer to accuse Jerome of haste. It seems more likely that a Latin scribe changed the less familiar **COS** into the well-known **BOS**. The name of Aquila is absent from the Palatine manuscript.

[^c0098-4]: The present Hebrew text has “your” in both places: “your anger” and “your indignation.” Jerome himself must also have had this reading when preparing his translation, since he translated “your indignation and your anger.” Nothing is asserted here about the Septuagint interpreters, since someone might object that the Hexaplaric edition, which has perished, is being cited. The note argues that the Greek should retain *σου* after *ὀργῆς*—“your anger”—which later critics rashly removed from Jerome’s text.

[^c0098-5]: All the manuscripts consulted by the editor read *Afar*, not *Aphar*. The Hebrew form is **Alphara** with its suffix. Jerome often uses *F* rather than *P* to represent a Hebrew letter in Latin. Yet in his commentary on Isaiah he says that Hebrew has no *P* and uses Greek *Phi* in its place.

[^c0098-6]: For the solution of the question proposed, one may prefer to consult the similar passage at Ephesians 2:16, which the holy Doctor explains very learnedly from the ambiguity of the Greek pronoun. Grammarians teach that *αὐτόν* is sometimes used in the sense of *ἐμαυτόν*, *σεαυτόν*, or *ἑαυτόν*; Laertius confirms this in his account of Hipparchia: *ἀλλὰ μὴ κακῶς σοι δοκῶ βεβουλεῦσθαι περὶ αὐτῆς*, for *ἐμαυτῆς*—“But do I not seem to you to have taken good counsel concerning myself?” If you take *ὁ ποιῶν τοὺς ἀγγέλους αὐτοῦ* (or *ἁυτοῦ*, with aspiration) in that sense here also—“making his own angels”—no difficulty will remain.

[^c0098-7]: The editions before Martianaeus corrupted Aquila’s interpretation by mixing it with the other versions. Martianaeus himself attributed to Aquila the reading belonging to Symmachus, Theodotion, and the others. The note restores what it considers Aquila’s genuine words: *αὐλὴ καὶ πλατεῖα χερσίν*. The word *αὐλή* is used by good Greek writers not for a palace or court but for a broad, spacious place. The editor also judged that the clause “and this is said metaphorically according to the Hebrew idiom,” found in the older manuscripts and editions, should be restored.

[^c0098-8]: Martianaeus printed “of the kite” (*milvi*), and “is” stands for “its”; but in the translation from Hebrew, as here, the text reads: “There the sparrows will nest: the heron’s house is theirs, or is regarded as theirs.” The note also observes that *ἡγεῖται* among the Septuagint is not best understood as “is leader” or “provides leadership,” as the Latin versions have it, but rather as “is considered,” “is regarded,” or simply “is.”

[^c0098-9]: The word is not found today, so far as the editor knows, in any Greek manuscript, although all the Latin versions have “which he appointed,” “which he had,” or “which he spoke.” Hebrew.

[^c0098-10]: The Greek phrase presumably includes the name *Κύριος*: *Καὶ εἶδε Κύριος ἐν τῷ θλίβεσθαι αὐτοὺς ἐν τῷ αὐτὸν εἰσακοῦσαι τῆς δεήσεως αὐτῶν*—“And the Lord saw when they were afflicted, when he heard their prayer.” The remaining words serve chiefly euphony and correspond more closely to the Hebrew.

[^c0098-11]: The note suspects that the short passage has been corrupted by interpolation. It proposes reading approximately: “And he turned the storm into a breeze. Therefore what you say that you found in the Greek beyond this—*αὐτοῦ* and *καὶ ἔστη*—is superfluous.” The old manuscripts vary considerably here. The words *καὶ ἐπετίμησεν τῇ καταιγίδι*, “and he rebuked the storm,” may have been added by inexperienced critics. Some manuscripts have *ἐπέταξεν*, “he commanded,” instead of *ἐπετίμησεν*.

[^c0098-12]: Erasmus and Victorius read *bephzi*, with the first-person suffix, but Martianaeus corrects them. The two manuscripts consulted by the editor support the reading discussed in the text.

[^c0098-13]: The surviving fragments of Aquila and the Fifth Edition read differently. In a reading attributed by Drusius to all the interpreters, *ἐφιλίασαν* is changed to *ἐφιλιώθησαν*. The Palatine manuscript pronounces the Hebrew word with aspiration: *ethbroeeh*.

[^c0098-14]: The note clarifies that the issue concerns only the word “your,” not “power.” “Power” is absent from no biblical manuscript; “your” alone is absent from the common Septuagint editions. The note therefore recommends reading “he will send it to you” (*ἐξαποστελεῖ σοι*), with *δύναμεως*—“of power”—but without *σου*—“your.”

[^c0098-15]: The Greek reads *ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ καὶ ἐν τῇ γῇ*, “in heaven and on earth,” while most ancient Latin translations add “above in heaven, in heaven, and on earth.”

[^c0098-16]: Some manuscripts read “because I have avenged myself upon them,” without the preposition *in*.

[^c0098-17]: The note argues that “your commandments” is not superfluous: it appears in the Septuagint, all the other books, and the Hebrew original. The actual superfluous word in some Greek and Latin copies is “exceedingly” (*σφόδρα*): “the commandments which I loved exceedingly.” The note therefore proposes that Jerome’s sentence be reconstructed as: “You say that in the Greek you read ‘the commandments which I loved exceedingly,’ not ‘your commandments’; but this too is superfluous.”

[^c0098-18]: The editor suspects that Jerome’s text originally read: “In the Greek you say that you read, ‘because I considered your ways,’ but this is superfluous; and more correctly, ‘my ways,’ is read.” The superfluous word would then be “because,” not “my.”

[^c0098-19]: Three manuscripts reverse the readings, placing “you turned” first and “I turned” second. Another omits the whole passage. The ancient edition reads “And I turned my feet,” while some Greek-based Latin copies have “and I turned away my feet.” Augustine confirms the reading “And I turned away my feet,” while noting that some copies have “because I considered, and you turned my feet.”

[^c0098-20]: Bachaffi was read in the singular by one editor, who translated it “in my palm,” rather than **Bachaffai** in the plural. The whole question concerned whether “my” or “your” should be read. Augustine observes that some manuscripts have “in my hands,” but more have “in your hands,” and says that he does not know how “my soul is in my hands” should be understood, since the words belong to the righteous rather than the wicked. Some Greek manuscripts likewise read *χερσίν σου*, “in your hands,” instead of *μου*, “in my hands.”

[^c0098-21]: The note suspects that Jerome’s explanation is partly mutilated, since the earlier difficulty proposed by the German brothers—whether the Greek underlying “flowed down” was *κατέβησαν*, “they descended,” or *διέβησαν*, “they passed over”—is passed over. Greek manuscripts vary between *κατέβησαν*, “they descended,” and *διέβησαν*, “they passed over.” Augustine notes that some copies read “they passed over,” as though the speaker were exaggerating by saying that streams of water had passed from his eyes through weeping. Some copies also read “because I did not keep your law,” and the Greek has *ἐπεί οὐκ ἐφύλαξα*, “because I did not keep.”

[^c0098-22]: Martianaeus incorrectly thought that “in the Hebrew” referred to Jerome’s Latin translation of the Psalms. Other minor errors in that edition are corrected above.

[^c0098-23]: The present Hebrew text has **THORA**, “law,” written with *aleph*, not **THIRA**. The note explains that the confusion may have arisen from the similar sound of the final letters, not merely from their graphic similarity. Theodoret says that Theodotion too translated *ἕνεκεν τοῦ φόβου*, “because of the fear,” like Aquila.

[^c0098-24]: Some manuscripts and the ancient edition add *τῷ θεῷ*, “to God.”

[^c0098-25]: Augustine devised an argument to show that the reading is neither inappropriate nor inelegant.

[^c0098-26]: Jerome may have read “name” with an emphatic Chaldean-style *aleph*, rather than the Hebrew form “your name.” Two manuscripts add “your” in Latin. In the Greek manuscripts that read *τὸ ὄνομά σου τὸ ἅγιον*, “your holy name,” the note suspects that *λόγιον*, “word,” has been corrupted into *ἅγιον*, “holy,” since the Hebrew has no word meaning “holy” here but has “your word.”

[^c0098-27]: Several printed books add a few words in Greek.

[^c0098-28]: Hesychius likewise explains *λαξευτήριον* as *λιθοτόμον σιδήριον*, “an iron instrument for cutting stones.” The old Latin translator, who used *ascia*, employed an ambiguous word more appropriate to a carpenter’s tool than to a stonecutter’s. This passage should be noted by those who still debate the old formula *sub ascia dedicavit*.

# LETTER 107

[Note: Also numbered 7. Written in the same year, 403.]

## To Laeta

[Note: Some manuscripts—including the excellent Regina manuscript 68—consistently read *Aleta* here and below; others read *Aletha*.]

### On the Education of Her Daughter

Jerome urges Laeta to train her daughter in Christian piety from the very beginning, and gives highly salutary instructions concerning dress, food, the proper education of adolescence, devotion to Scripture, and avoidance of apocryphal books.

### 1

The Apostle Paul, writing to the Corinthians and instructing the inexperienced Church of Christ in sacred disciplines, included among his other commands the following:

“If any woman has an unbelieving husband, and he consents to live with her, let her not dismiss her husband. For the unbelieving husband has been sanctified through the believing wife, and the unbelieving wife has been sanctified through the believing husband. Otherwise your children would be unclean, but now they are holy” (1 Corinthians 7:13–14).

[Note: The Greek uses the preposition ἐν (*en*) in both places: ἐν τῇ γυναικί, ἐν τῷ ἀνδρί, “in the wife,” “in the husband.” The Vulgate has “through the woman” and “through the man” in both places. The authority of all our manuscripts compels us to read the first phrase with the Vulgate, but the second according to the Greek.]

If anyone has hitherto thought that the restraints of discipline were relaxed too much, and that the teacher’s indulgence was rash, let him consider the household of your father—a man indeed of great distinction and learning, but still walking in darkness—and he will understand that the Apostle’s counsel succeeded in this way: the sweetness of the fruits compensated for the bitterness of the root, and lowly twigs exuded precious balsam.

You were born from an unequal marriage; from you and my Toxotius Paula was born. Who would have believed that the granddaughter of the Pontiff Albinus would be born through her mother’s promise [al. “martyrdom”]; that, with her grandfather present and rejoicing, her still-tiny tongue would lisp forth Christ’s **ALLELUIA**, and that an old man would nurture a virgin of God in his own lap?

[Note: The Regina manuscript reads: “lisping *Alleluia* and ‘Virgin of Christ,’ etc.”]

And we have awaited this well and happily. A holy and faithful household sanctifies the unbeliever. He is already a candidate for the faith, surrounded by the believing crowd of his children and grandchildren. I think that even he, had he possessed such a family while still a young man, could have believed in Christ.

[Note: Interpreters have struggled with this passage, and it continues to trouble them. They hesitate over the word *juvenem* (“as a young man”), which Erasmus, Victorius, Martianaeus, and those who followed them changed, against the testimony of all the manuscripts, into *Jovem* (“Jove”). They explain this as an extravagant expression, intended to heighten the example of that holy family: if Jupiter himself had possessed such a family, he too would have believed in Christ. But neither does the context permit that name, nor could anyone properly say that Jupiter might have believed in Christ. The manuscript reading is also highly elegant in sense. Albinus was a pagan Pontiff, Laeta’s father from an unequal marriage; although he still refused to believe, he could be called a candidate for the faith on account of the faithful crowd of his children and grandchildren. Had he possessed the same family when he himself was young, he could easily have believed in Christ—for examples kindle the minds of the young more powerfully than those of the old. His conversion is nevertheless still to be hoped for from this association. Thus, in Book 1, chapter 5, *Against Jovinian*, while explaining Paul’s statement in 1 Corinthians 7:10, Jerome indicates the reasons and adds that an unbeliever is a candidate for the faith if he is unwilling to leave a believing spouse.]

Let him spit upon my letter and mock it, if he wishes, and proclaim me either foolish or insane; his son-in-law did the same before he believed. Christians are made, not born.

The gilded Capitol is falling into squalor. All the temples of Rome are covered with soot and spiders’ webs. The city is shaken from its foundations, and the surging population runs before half-ruined shrines to the tombs of the martyrs. If prudence does not extort faith, let shame at least do so.

### 2

Let this be said to you, Laeta, most devout daughter in Christ, so that you may not despair of your father’s salvation, and so that by the same faith through which you deserved to receive a daughter, you may also receive your father and enjoy the blessedness of the whole household, knowing what the Lord has promised:

“What is impossible with human beings is possible with God” (Luke 18:27).

Conversion is never too late [manuscript: “confession is never too late”]. The thief passed from the cross into paradise. Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, after being driven into savagery of body and mind and condemned to live among beasts in the wilderness, recovered a human understanding.

And, to leave aside ancient examples, lest they seem too fabulous to unbelievers, in recent years your kinsman Gracchus—

[Column 0869]

a man whose name proclaimed patrician nobility—while he was serving as Urban Prefect,

[Note: Baronius, in order to assign the destruction of Mithras to the year 383, applies this passage to Gracchus’s urban prefecture, although he prefers the title “Praetorian Prefect.” Gothofredus, on the other hand, followed by Pagius, changes the inscription of two laws in the *Theodosian Code* addressed to Gracchus, reading P.V., “Prefect of the City,” instead of P.P., “Praetorian Prefect,” and assigns them to 376 and the following year. More recently, Philippus a Turre, in the final chapter of his work on Mithras, has established by argument that Gracchus did not begin his urban prefecture before 378, when, at his command, all Mithraic superstition was overthrown. Prudentius, Book 1 *Against Symmachus*:

> Now why should I run through in song the people-loving Gracchi,  
> Supported by the authority of office and foremost in the Senate’s citadel,  
> Who ordered the images of the gods to be torn down,  
> And together with their lictors consecrated themselves,  
> Humbly, to almighty Christ for the governance of the state?]

did he not overthrow, shatter, and cast out the cave of Mithras and all its monstrous images, through which Corax, Nymphus,

[Note: These monstrous images in the cave of Mithras, and the names symbolizing stars and planets, represented the following. Omitting passages from Porphyry in which he says that these were animals and that they belonged to the circle of the Zodiac, Origen gives the matter plainly in Book 6 *Against Celsus*: “In the rites of Mithras, a double circuit of stars is displayed, that of the fixed stars and that of the wandering stars. Of these constellations—not all are listed here—some are within and some outside the Zodiac.”

*Corax*, from the Greek κόραξ (*korax*), “raven,” is a star outside the Zodiac in the southern region, situated opposite Libra.

*Nymphus* is Νύμφη (*Nymphē*), “Virgin,” a sign of the Zodiac. Some signs had both masculine and feminine images and names; Porphyry reports that all the initiates were called males, “lions,” and females, “hyenas” (*On Abstinence*, Book 4). Julius Firmicus likewise mentions male and female images of the Mithraic Jupiter.

*Miles*, “Soldier,” is the northern sign better known under the name Hercules.

*Leo*, “Lion,” is itself in the Zodiac.

*Perseus* faces Taurus from the north.

Of the remaining three—Helios, Dromo, and Pater—we shall speak shortly.

Furthermore, the devotees of Mithras assumed names from such signs when they were initiated. Images or little figures were painted in the cave or carved there with a tool, to serve the mysteries. Among these are the images which Jerome ridicules here; when they were found in the Mithraeum at Alexandria, Sozomen reports that they were extremely ridiculous and foreign-looking.

The initiates were also divided into definite classes according to the name and dignity of the image they assumed. Fixed ceremonies and festivals accompanied the same idols. The *Coracica* are mentioned by the author of the Commentary on Paul’s Epistles attributed to Ambrose, and an ancient inscription has *Hierocoracica*; hence Porphyry also teaches that the Mithraic ministers were called “Ravens.”

The same applies to *Leontica*, from which we have noted that the priests were called “Lions.” *Persica* may be found in other writers and in several inscriptions collected by Gruterus.

Tertullian, in *On the Crown*, Gregory of Nazianzus in Oration 3, and other ancient writers describe the initiation of the Soldier in the cave at length; later writers who have labored to explain these names have generally wasted their effort.]

Soldier, Lion, Persian—

[Note: Although Martianaeus, along with most manuscripts, reads *Heliodromus pariter initiantur* (“Heliodromus is likewise initiated”), this is corrupt. The adverb *pariter* has no place here and should be replaced by *Pater*, which was the chief dignity in the Mithraic rites. Eunapius has Πατὴρ τῆς Μιθριακῆς τελετῆς, “Father of the Mithraic rite.” Porphyry says that *Patres* in the Mithraic rites were given the names of the eagle and hawk. An ancient stone collected by Gruterus records a certain Ulpius Egnatius as *Pater* and *Hierocorax* of Mithras; *Patrica* ceremonies likewise occur in other Mithraic inscriptions.

As for *Heliodromus*, this too is clearly an error. The subject here is human beings who received the rites and names of Mithras under those images. *Heliodromus*, meaning “the course of the sun,” is neither an animal nor a person; it cannot bestow its name or image, and no one has ever said that the sun’s course was initiated into the rites.

The passage must therefore be read with two words, the first being *Elios*, which signifies the sun and is one of Mithras’s own names—for what, ultimately, is Mithras but the sun? Ancient monuments attest both the Mithraic idol and the people consecrated to these mysteries, and the term *Eliaca* is also found in this ritual in Gruterus.

What remains is *Dromus*, for which the early editors printed *Bromius*, or rather *Bromius Pater* as a single phrase. Even now distinguished scholars defend that reading, the only one that could be forced out of the manuscripts, and labor to connect it with the religion of Mithras on the basis of a passage in Xenophon’s *Cyropaedia*: “The kings of the Persians were permitted to become drunk on only one day, the day on which they conducted the rites of Mithras.”

But if the matter is examined, they are mistaken. Bacchus nowhere belonged to the Mithraic rites.

We restore the corrupt passage as follows, retaining the old writing wherever possible: *Dromo*. Dromo is Cancer, from the Greek Δρόμων, which is why Pliny also calls crabs *Dromones* in Book 32, at the end.

Cancer is again a heavenly sign, located in the Zodiac; and in Mithraic rites it was especially auspicious. It frequently appears in the reliefs of the cave together with a dog, serpent, raven, and other figures whose mysteries we have explained above.]

Helios, Dromo, and Pater were initiated,

[al. “were supported”]

and so, having first set these images before him as hostages, he obtained the baptism of Christ.

Paganism suffers desolation even in the City. The gods once worshiped by the nations have remained on solitary rooftops with owls and night-owls.

[Note: Compare Justin Martyr, *Apology* 2; Eusebius, Book 2, *Life of Constantine*. Prudentius expresses the matter most elegantly in Book 2 *Against Symmachus*:

> Christ, clothed in purple and woven into jeweled gold,  
> Marked the Labarum, etc.]

The military standards are now insignia of the cross. The purple robes of kings and the blazing jewels of their diadems are adorned by the image of the saving gallows.

[Note: This refers to the temple of Serapis in Egypt, demolished at Alexandria by order of Theodosius in 389, with another temple dedicated there to God, in which Theophilus deposited the relics of Saint John the Baptist. See Theophilus’s Synodical Letter 3. We shall discuss the idol Marnas of Gaza more fully in the *Life of Saint Hilarion*.]

The Egyptian Serapis has now become a Christian. Marnas of Gaza mourns, shut up within his temple, continually fearing its destruction [al. “trembling at its destruction”].

Every day we receive crowds of monks from India, Persia, and Ethiopia. The Armenian has laid down his quiver.

[Note: By “Sunnias and Fretela,” to whom the preceding Letter 106 is addressed and which deals entirely with the reading of the Psalms, we understand the Huns. See the chronological notes.]

The Huns are learning the Psalter. The cold of Scythia burns with the warmth of faith. The red-haired and blond army of the Goths carries the tents of the churches about with it; and perhaps for that reason they fight against us on equal terms, because they trust in the same religion.

### 3

I have almost slipped into another subject, and while the wheel was turning, as I thought of making a jug, my hand fashioned a jar.

My intention had been, at the invitation of Saint Marcella and at your prayers, to address a discourse to the mother—that is, to you—and to teach you how you ought to train our Paula, who was consecrated to Christ before she was born,

[Note: It was the discipline of that age that parents were permitted to dedicate their sons and daughters to God from infancy, as Salvian says in Book 2 *Against Avarice*, indeed even before they were born, and to devote them to the Church and perpetual virginity. Jerome says below, section 6: “Whether you should offer your daughter or not was within your power,” etc. The Fourth Council of Toledo, canon 48, says: “A monk is made either by paternal devotion or by his own profession. Whichever of these has occurred will bind him,” etc. Gregory III, in Letter 4 to Boniface, declared it unlawful for children offered to God by their parents in infancy to leave monasteries and marry after completing puberty. Baluzius has collected notable examples and records on this matter in his notes to the cited passage of Salvian. But in Celestine III, whose decree is cited under *Cum simus* concerning religious orders, this parental right over children was entirely removed; nor were there lacking people in earlier centuries who openly condemned that authority. Among them was Saint Gaudentius of Brescia, Sermon 8, near the beginning.]

than she was born, whom you vowed before you conceived her.

In our own times we have seen something from the prophetic books:

[Note: According to the division of the Hebrew canon, the Books of Kings are counted among the Prophets.]

Hannah changed the barrenness of her womb into fruitfulness (1 Samuel 1). You have exchanged mournful fruitfulness for children destined for life. I speak confidently: you will receive children, since you first gave your offspring back to the Lord.

These are the firstborn who are offered under the Law (Exodus 13:2). Thus Samuel was born; thus Samson arose (Judges 13); thus John the Baptist leaped and played at Mary’s arrival (Luke 1).

For he heard the words of the Lord thunder through the Virgin’s mouth and longed to burst forth from his mother’s womb to meet him.

Therefore, she who was born through a promise should receive from her parents an upbringing worthy of her birth. Samuel is nourished in the Temple; John is prepared in the wilderness. The former is venerable in his sacred hair and drinks neither wine nor strong drink; while still a child, he speaks with the Lord. The latter flees the cities, girds himself with a leather belt, feeds on locusts and wild honey, and, as a type of the repentance he is to proclaim, clothes himself in the skins of the most crooked animal—the camel.

### 4

Thus must the soul be educated which is to become the temple of God. Let her learn to hear and speak nothing except what pertains to the fear of God. Let her not understand obscene words, nor know the songs of the world; while her tongue is still tender, let it be steeped in the sweet Psalms.

Let the wanton age of boys remain far away. Let the girls and nursemaids themselves be kept from worldly associations, lest they teach worse what they have learned badly.

[Note: Nearly the whole of this section is expressed from Quintilian, *Institutio Oratoria* 1.2: “I do not exclude,” he says, “what is well known: that, to encourage infancy to learn, even ivory forms of letters may be offered as toys.” A little later: “When the child has begun to follow drawn lines, it will not be useless for the letters to be carved as carefully as possible on a tablet, so that the stylus may be led along them as through grooves; for he will not go astray, as he would on wax—for the grooves will be enclosed by borders—nor will he be able to go beyond the prescribed path; and by following the fixed tracks more quickly and more frequently he will strengthen [al. form] his fingers, nor will he need the help of someone guiding his hand by laying another hand over it,” etc.]

Let her have letters made of boxwood or ivory, and let them be called by their proper names. Let her play with them, so that her play itself may be instruction. Let her not only retain the order of the letters and turn the memory of their names into song; let the order itself frequently be disturbed, with the last letters mixed among the first and the middle letters among the others, so that she may recognize them not merely by sound but also by sight.

When she begins to guide the stylus over the wax with a trembling hand, either let another hand be placed over hers to guide her fingers, or let the letters be carved on a tablet, so that the traces may be drawn through the same grooves enclosed by borders and cannot wander outside.

[Note: The word *inclusa* (“enclosed”) has been supplied from Victorius.]

Let her join syllables as a reward, and invite her with little gifts of the kind that delight or charm that age [al. “soften” it]. Let her have companions in learning, whom she may envy and whose praise may sting her into effort. She should not be scolded if she is slower, but her intelligence should be aroused by praise, so that she may rejoice when she wins and grieve when she is defeated.

[Note: Again Quintilian: “Nor am I so ignorant of the differences of age as to think that tender minds should immediately be pressed harshly or required to give their full effort. Above all, care must be taken lest a child who cannot yet love studies should hate them, and lest the bitterness once tasted should make him dread them even beyond his early years,” etc.]

Above all, care must be taken that she does not hate her studies, and that the bitterness of their instruction in infancy does not extend beyond her early years.

[Note: Martianaeus reads *percepta*, “once perceived,” and shortly afterward *consuevit*, “became accustomed.”]

The very names by which she gradually learns to join words should not be accidental, but fixed and deliberately gathered—namely, the names of the Prophets and Apostles, and the whole succession of Patriarchs from Adam. Let her descend from Matthew and Luke, so that, while she is doing something else, she may be prepared for the memory of the future.

A teacher of sound age, life, and learning must be chosen. I do not think that a learned man will be ashamed to do for a near relative or noble virgin what Aristotle did for the son of Philip, namely, to impart the rudiments of letters for the sake of the usefulness of books.

[Note: Older printed editions, together with one Veronese manuscript, read *librariorum vilitate*, “through the lowliness of scribes,” which may perhaps be the more correct reading; nevertheless, it is preferable to follow most of the others. Some of these, however, corruptly read *in Philippo* instead of *Philippi filio*, “in Philip” instead of “for Philip’s son”; and the Regina manuscript reads *monstraret* instead of *traderet*. Quintilian, in the passage cited, says: “Would Philip, king of the Macedonians, have wished the first elements of letters to be taught to his son Alexander by Aristotle, the greatest philosopher of his age, or would Aristotle have undertaken this duty, if he had not believed that it was of the highest importance for the beginnings of study to be handled by the most accomplished person?” etc.]

Small things must not be despised, without which great things cannot stand.

[Note: The Regina manuscript reads: “the order of the elements and the teacher’s small instruction,” and otherwise.]

Even the sound of the elements and the first instruction of teachers comes differently from an educated mouth than from a rustic one.

Therefore you must take care that your daughter does not become accustomed, through the foolish endearments of women, to speak half-formed words and play in gold and purple. The one harms her speech, the other her character. Let her not learn in childhood what she will afterward have to unlearn.

[Note: Some manuscripts corruptly read *Graecorum* (“of the Greeks”). Quintilian, Book 1, chapter 2, says: “We are told that Cornelia, the mother of the Gracchi, contributed greatly to their eloquence from infancy; her highly learned speech was handed down to posterity in her letters.” A little later the manuscripts read *praebiberunt*, “drank in beforehand,” whereas the printed editions have the less satisfactory *perbiberunt*.]

It is recorded that the speech of their mother contributed greatly from infancy to the eloquence of the Gracchi. The oratory of Hortensius grew strong in his father’s embrace [al. “between his father’s arms”]. What inexperienced minds have drunk in is difficult to eradicate. Who can restore the purple dye of wool to its former color [al. “brightness”]? A new jar retains for a long time both the taste and the smell with which it was first filled.

Greek history tells how Alexander, the most powerful king and conqueror of the world, could not escape, either in his character or in his manner of walking, the faults of his tutor Leonidas, with which he had been infected as a child.

[Note: Again Quintilian, in the passage cited: “Leonidas, Alexander’s tutor, as Diogenes of Babylon reports, infected him with certain faults which followed that powerful and mighty king even from his childhood education.”]

The imitation of evil is easy; those whose virtues you cannot attain, you quickly imitate in their vices.

The nurse herself must not be a drunkard, wanton, or chatterbox. Let her have a modest nursemaid and a serious male attendant. When the child sees her grandfather, let her leap onto his breast and hang from his neck; let her sing her **ALLELUIA** to him even when he does not wish it.

Let her grandmother snatch her up; let her recognize her father by his laughter; let her be loved by everyone; let the whole family rejoice in the rose that has sprung from it.

Let her immediately learn that she has another grandmother and an aunt. Let her know for which commander and army the little recruit is being raised. Let her long for them and threaten you that she will go to them.

[Note: The Regina manuscript reads: “Let her imitate those women for you by leaving,” which appears to have been altered by scribal ingenuity from a damaged and worn manuscript. The sentence concerning clothing that follows is absent there; instead it immediately reads, “Take care that her ears…” A little later Martianaeus reads *capillum irradas*, “scratch her hair,” instead of *irrufes*, “redden her hair.”]

### 5

Her very bearing and clothing should teach her to whom she has been promised. Take care not to pierce her ears. Do not paint the face consecrated to Christ with white lead and rouge. Do not press her neck with gold and pearls, burden her head with jewels, or redden her hair, thereby giving her something from the fires of Gehenna as her first offering.

Let her have other pearls, which she may later sell in order to purchase the pearl of greatest price.

A very noble woman, once clothed in the purple-bordered garment, changed her dress and adornment at the command of her husband Hymetius, who was the uncle of the virgin Eustochium. She arranged her neglected hair in worldly fashion, seeking to overcome both the virgin’s resolve and her mother’s desire.

[Note: Elsewhere Jerome uses *pexuit*, “combed.” Victorius adds *sibi*, “for himself,” that is, “desiring to conquer for himself”; shortly afterward Martianaeus reads “Behold, for himself” instead of “for you.”]

And behold, that same night she dreamed that an angel with a terrifying face [al. “voice”] had come and threatened her with punishment, breaking forth in these words:

“Did you dare to place a man’s command above Christ? Did you dare to touch with your sacrilegious hands the head of a virgin of God—hands which will now wither, so that, tortured, you may feel what you have done—and, after the completion of the fifth month, be led down to the realms below? But if you persist in your crime, you will be deprived both of your husband and of your children.”

Everything was fulfilled in due order, and a swift death marked the unhappy woman’s tardy repentance.

Thus Christ avenges those who violate his temple; thus he defends jewels and the most precious ornaments.

[Note: Again the Regina manuscript reads “against those who violate,” and shortly afterward “so that I may warn you.”]

I have related this not because I wish to insult the misfortunes of the unhappy, but to warn you with how much fear and caution you must preserve what you have promised to God.

### 6

Eli the priest offended God on account of the vices of his children (1 Samuel 1 and 4). A man who has dissolute and disobedient children cannot become a bishop (1 Timothy 3). Conversely, it is written of a woman that she “will be saved through the bearing of children,” if they remain in faith, love, and holiness, with modesty (1 Timothy 2:15).

If mature age and the exercise of one’s own will are charged to parents, how much more the nursing child, still weak and fragile, who, according to the Lord’s saying, does not know the right hand from the left—that is, the difference between good and evil?

If you carefully guard your daughter lest she be struck by a viper, why do you not take equal care lest she be struck by the hammer of the whole earth (Jeremiah 50:23); lest she drink from Babylon’s golden cup; lest she go out with Dinah and wish to see the daughters of a foreign land (Genesis 34:1); lest she dance with her feet or trail her garments?

Poisons are given only when smeared with honey, and vices deceive only when they appear under the form and shadow of virtues.

“But how,” you will say, “are the sins of fathers not repaid to their children, nor those of children to their parents, but ‘the soul that sins shall itself die’ (Ezekiel 18:20)?”

This is said of those who are able to understand, of whom it is written in the Gospel: “He is of age; let him speak for himself” (John 9:21).

But while a child is little and understands as a child, until she reaches the years of understanding and the letter Y of Pythagoras leads her to the crossroads, both her good and her evil are charged to her parents.

[Note: The letter of Pythagoras is Y, which the ancients celebrated as a symbol of human life: one of its branches represents the way of virtue, the other the way of vice. Persius, *Satire* 3:

> And the letter that divided the Samian branches for you  
> Showed the rising path along the right-hand way.

Ausonius, *Idyll* 16:

> The fork of Pythagoras opens into two branches, the ambiguous Y.]

Unless you suppose that, if Christian children do not receive baptism, they alone are guilty of sin and the crime does not also fall upon those who refused to give it—especially at a time when those who were to receive it could not object—just as, conversely, the salvation of infants is the gain of their elders.

Whether or not to offer your daughter was within your power—although your situation is different, since you vowed her before you conceived her. But once she has been offered, whether you neglect her belongs to the danger you incur.

[Note: Some manuscripts omit the negative particle and read: “But that you neglect the one offered…” Recall what we noted above in section 3.]

Whoever offers as a sacrifice a lame, mutilated, or in any way defiled victim is guilty of sacrilege (Deuteronomy 15). How much more will one be punished who, having prepared a part of her own body and the purity of an unblemished soul for the embraces of the King, proves negligent?

### 7

When she begins to grow larger and, in the likeness of her bridegroom, increases in wisdom, age, and favor with God and human beings, let her go with her parents to the temple of the true Father; but let her not leave the temple with them.

Let them seek her on the road of the world, amid crowds and the company of relatives, and let them find her nowhere else (Luke 2) except in the inner sanctuary of Scripture,

[Note: The Regina manuscript reads: “in the hearing of Scripture.”]

questioning the Prophets and Apostles about spiritual marriages.

Let her imitate Mary, whom Gabriel found alone in her chamber; and perhaps she was terrified at the sight because she saw a man where she was not accustomed to see one.

Let her emulate the woman of whom it is said: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within” (Psalm 44:14). Let her also speak to her beloved, wounded by the dart of love: “The king brought me into his chamber” (Song of Songs 1:3).

Let her never go outside, lest those who go about the city find her, strike and wound her, take away her mantle of chastity, and leave her naked and covered in blood. Rather, whenever someone knocks at her door, let her say:

“I am a wall, and my breasts are towers. I have washed my feet; I cannot soil them” (Song of Songs 8:10; 5:3).

### 8

Let her not eat in public—that is, at her parents’ table—lest she see foods for which she will desire. Although some think that greater virtue consists in despising pleasure when it is present, I consider it the safer form of self-control not to know what one might seek.

I once read as a boy in the schools: “You can scarcely condemn what you allow to become a habit.”

Let her now also say that she does not drink wine, in which there is excess. Before the years of robust maturity, abstinence is dangerous and burdensome for the young. Until that time, if necessity demands it, let her visit the baths, use a little wine for the sake of her stomach, and sustain herself with meat, lest her feet fail before she has begun to run.

I say this by way of indulgence, not command: I fear weakness; I do not teach luxury.

Otherwise, what Jewish superstition practices in part by rejecting certain animals and foods, and what the Brahmans of India and the Gymnosophists of Egypt observe by living solely on porridge, rice, and fruit—why should a virgin of Christ not practice entirely?

If glass is so highly valued, why should the pearl not be more valuable? She who was born through a promise should live as those who were born through a promise lived. Let her have an equal grace and an equal labor.

Let her be deaf to musical instruments. Let her not know why the flute, lyre, and cithara were made.

### 9

Every day let her render you a portion gathered from the flowers of Scripture.

[Note: The Regina manuscript likewise reads: “Every day a portion from the flowers of Scripture.”]

Let her learn the meter of Greek verse.

[Column 0875]

Let Latin education immediately follow. If Latin does not shape the tender mouth from the beginning, the tongue is corrupted into a foreign sound and the native language is soiled by alien faults.

[Note: These passages too are taken from Quintilian, *Institutio Oratoria* 1.2: “I prefer a boy to begin with Greek speech, because Latin, which is more widely used, presents itself to us even against our will; and also because he must first be trained in Greek disciplines, from which our own have flowed. Yet I would not have this done so superstitiously that he should speak Greek alone for a long time or learn it in the manner customary among many. For this produces many faults of pronunciation, corrupted into a foreign sound; and when Greek constructions have clung to the language through constant habit, they persist obstinately in other forms of speech as well.”]

Let her have you as her teacher; let her infancy imitate you.

[Note: Victorius reads: “Let you, the unformed infancy, admire.”]

Let her see nothing in you or in her father that she would sin by imitating. Remember that you are the parents of a virgin, and that she can be taught more effectively by examples than by words.

Flowers quickly fade; violets, lilies, and crocus are quickly spoiled by a pestilential breeze. Let her never go out in public without you. Let her not visit the basilicas of the martyrs or the churches without her mother.

Let no young man, no curled-haired fop, smile at her.

Let our little virgin celebrate vigils and solemn overnight services in such a way that she does not depart from her mother even by the breadth of a fingernail.

I do not want her to love one of her maidservants more than the others, so that she whispers frequently in her ear. Whatever she says to one, let all know.

Let her companion be pleasing not because she is adorned, beautiful, and wanton, or because she modulates a sweet song with a clear throat,

[Note: Again Victorius reads: “not adorned, beautiful, or wanton, who…”]

but because she is serious, pale, dirty, and somewhat sad.

Let a virgin of proven faith, conduct, and chastity be appointed over her—a mature woman who can teach her and accustom her by example to rise at night for prayers and Psalms; to sing hymns in the morning; at the third, sixth, and ninth hours to stand in formation like a soldier of Christ; and, after lighting a small lamp, to offer the evening sacrifice.

Let the day pass in this way; let the night find her at work. Let reading follow prayer, and prayer follow reading. The time occupied by such varied works will seem short.

[Note: Martianaeus corruptly reads “by such varied sequences of days”; we have restored *operum*, “of works,” from Victorius.]

### 10

Let her also learn to make woolen thread, hold the distaff, place the basket in her lap, turn the spindle, and draw out the threads with her thumb.

Let her despise silkworm fabrics, the fleeces of Seres, and gold stiffening upon a girl’s body. Let her prepare clothing that drives away the cold, not clothing in which covered bodies are stripped bare.

Let her food be vegetables and meal, and only rarely little fish. And, not to prolong my instructions about appetite—for I have spoken more fully elsewhere—

[Note: Namely, in Book 2 *Against Jovinian*, where he discusses at greater length and according to his purpose contempt for the belly and throat.]

let her eat in such a way that she is always hungry, so that immediately after eating she can read and sing Psalms.

[Note: Victorius reads: “read, pray, and sing Psalms.”]

I dislike, especially in tender ages, long and excessive fasts in which whole weeks are joined together and oil is forbidden in food, as are fruits.

Experience has taught me that a donkey on the road, when it becomes tired, seeks side paths. Let the worshipers of Isis and Cybele do this—

[Note: In the rites of both Isis and Cybele, their worshipers abstained from bread and ate meat instead. Arnobius, Book 5: “Why do you abstain from bread as food, giving this practice the name *Castus*?” Thus they called those foods—or this abstinence from bread—*Castus*. Jerome likewise says in Book 2 *Against Jovinian*, chapter 34: “They boast of abstinence from foods, as though the Gentile superstition did not also observe the *Castus* of the Mother of the Gods and of Isis.” This should be restored as *Castus*, and is repeated below in chapter 41, where we explain it more fully.]

who, in their gluttonous abstinence, devour Phasis birds and smoking turtle-doves, lest they contaminate the gifts of grain.

[Column 0876]

Let this be the perpetual fast prescribed: that strength may endure for a long journey, lest we fall in the middle after running at the first announcement.

[Note: Martianaeus reads *supparentur*, “be supplied,” as Gravius had restored it.]

But, as I wrote earlier, in Lent the sails of self-restraint must be spread wide, and all the reins of the charioteer must be loosened for the horses rushing forward.

Although the condition of worldly people is one thing, and that of virgins and monks another: the worldly person, during Lent, boils down the excess of his belly and, living like a snail on its own juice, prepares his little stomach for future feasts and fattening. A virgin and a monk should release their horses during Lent in such a way that they remember they must always be running.

A labor that ends is greater; one that is without end is more moderate. In the first case we take breath; in the second we move forward continually.

### 11

Whenever you go out to the suburbs, do not leave your daughter at home; let her neither know how to be without you nor be able to live without you, and when she is alone, let her be afraid. Let her have no conversations with secular people, nor the companionship of bad girls. Let her not attend the weddings of servants, nor mingle with the noisy bustle of a household. I know that some have instructed that a virgin of Christ should not bathe with eunuchs, nor with married women: for the former do not lay aside [variant: lay aside] the minds of men, while the latter, with swelling wombs, display [variant: display] their ugliness. I have an absolute dislike of baths for a grown virgin, who ought to blush at herself and be unable to look upon herself naked. For if she scourges her body with vigils and fasts and brings it into subjection; if she wishes to extinguish the flame of lust and the incentives of a fervent age by the coldness of continence; if she hastens to defile [variant: disturb] her natural beauty with desired dirtiness—why does she, conversely, rekindle dormant fires by the warm applications of baths?

### 12

In place of gems and silk, let her love the divine books, in which there is no Babylonian hide with gold and vermilion decoration [Note: These are thought to be the same as those elsewhere called Persian skins. But the phrase ἐκ βαβυλῶνος δέρματα, “Babylonian skins,” is also praised by Zonaras in his account of Constantius, where he speaks of Hormisdas; he reports that these skins were highly valued and elegantly painted in various colors. An old glossary defines βαβυλωνικὸν δέρματος εἷδος as “a kind of Babylonian skin.” Elsewhere Jerome condemns similar luxury in the binding of books.] but an exact and learned distinction that pleases by its fidelity. Let her first learn the Psalter; let these songs draw her away from other things, and let her be instructed for life in Solomon’s Proverbs. In Ecclesiastes let her become accustomed to trampling underfoot the things of the world. In Job let her follow examples of virtue and patience. Let her proceed to the Gospels, never laying them down from her hands. Let her absorb the Acts of the Apostles and the Epistles with the whole devotion of her heart. And when she has enriched the storeroom of her breast with these treasures, let her commit to memory the Prophets, the Heptateuch [variant: Pentateuch], the books of Kings and Chronicles, and also the volumes of Ezra and Esther.

Finally, let her learn the Song of Songs without danger; for if she reads it at the beginning, not understanding beneath its carnal words the epithalamium of spiritual marriages, she may be wounded. Let her beware of all apocryphal writings. And if at any time she wishes to read them, not for the truth of their doctrines but out of reverence for their signs, let her know that they are not by the authors whose names are written in their titles; and that much corrupt matter has been mixed into them, and that it is a mark of great prudence to seek gold in mud. Let her always keep the little works of Cyprian in her hand. Let her run through the Letters of Athanasius and the books of Hilary with an unhindered step. Let her take delight in the treatises and intellects of those whose books do not make the piety of their faith waver. Let her read the others in such a way that she judges them rather than follows them.

### 13

You will answer: “How shall I, a secular woman, be able to guard all these things at Rome, amid such a throng of people?” Do not, then, undertake a burden that you cannot bear. But after you have weaned her with Isaac and clothed her with Samuel, send her to her grandmother and aunt. Return the most precious jewel to Mary’s chamber, and place her in the cradle of the infant Jesus as he cries. Let her be raised in a monastery; let her be among choirs of virgins; let her not learn to swear, let her consider lying sacrilege, let her know nothing of the world, let her live like an angel, let her be in the flesh without the flesh, and let her regard every human being as like herself.

And, to say nothing of the rest, at least let her free you from the difficulty of guarding her and the danger of custody. It is better for you to long for one who is absent than to tremble at every detail: what she may say, with whom she may speak, to whom she may nod, whom she may willingly look upon. Entrust the little girl to Eustochium, whose very crying is now a prayer for you: a companion in holiness and a future heiress. Let her see her, love her, and admire her from her earliest years (Aeneid VIII), since her speech, her walk, and her dress are instruction in the virtues.

Let her be in the lap of her grandmother, who may repeat in her granddaughter whatever she formerly passed on in her daughter; who through long experience has learned to raise, preserve, and teach virgins; in whose crown the chastity of the hundredfold number is woven daily [Note: Compare what we note in the first book Against Jovinianus, chapter 1, especially this passage: “The number one hundred, made with the same fingers but not with the same hand by which married women and widows are signified on the left, forms a circle and represents the crown of virginity.”]

Happy virgin, happy Paula, daughter of Toxotius, who through the virtues of her grandmother and aunt is nobler in holiness than in birth. O, if only it were granted you to see your mother-in-law and your kinswoman, and to behold immense spirits in little bodies! Because of the modesty innate in you, I would not doubt that you would surpass your daughter and change the first sentence of God by the second law of the Gospel. Surely you would think little of the longing of others for children and offer yourself more completely to God.

But because there is a time for embracing and a time for being far from embraces; because a wife does not have authority over her own body (1 Cor. 7:4); because each person must remain in the calling in which he was called, in the Lord; and because one who is under the yoke must run in such a way that he does not leave his companion behind in the mud—return wholly in your offspring what you have meanwhile deferred in yourself.

Anna, after she had offered in the Tabernacle the son whom she had vowed to God (1 Reg. 1), never took him back. She considered it improper that a future prophet should grow up in her house, although she still desired to have other children. Finally, after she conceived and gave birth, she did not dare approach the Temple and appear before the Lord empty-handed until she had first returned what she owed. After offering that sacrifice, she returned home and bore five children for herself, because she had borne her firstborn for God.

Do you marvel at the blessed woman’s good fortune? Imitate her faith. If you send Paula, I promise that I will be both her teacher and her nurse. I shall carry her on my shoulders; as an old man I shall shape her stammering words [Note: The manuscripts of Regia read: “I shall strengthen the old man’s stammering words.”], much more gloriously than the philosopher of the world: for I shall educate not a Macedonian king destined to perish by Babylonian poison, but a handmaid and bride of Christ, destined to be offered to the heavenly kingdoms.

## LETTER 108 [Note: Otherwise Letter 27, written in the year 404.] [Note: In the Regia manuscript 497 it is entitled *Life of Saint Paula the Widow, written by the blessed Jerome, priest*.]

### TO EUSTOCHIUM, A VIRGIN

### The Epitaph of Paula, Her Mother

He recounts the life of Paula, whom he praises first for the nobility of her lineage, but above all for the virtue of her character: after the death of her husband Toxotius, she devoted herself wholly to God and lived for a long time at Rome in her holy vocation. He then describes in the greatest detail her journey, during which, after traversing the holy places of Judaea and Egypt as far as Alexandria, she settled at Bethlehem. He explains what monasteries for virgins she built and by what examples and instructions she governed them.
