He praises abundantly her humility, patience, contempt for the world, charity toward the poor and sick, knowledge of the divine Scriptures, purity of faith, and the many other virtues displayed throughout her life. Finally, he describes at length her death and funeral.

### 1

If all the members of my body were changed into tongues, and all my limbs resounded with human speech, I still could say nothing worthy of the virtues of holy and venerable Paula. Noble by birth, but much nobler in holiness; once powerful in riches, but now more distinguished by the poverty of Christ; a Greek by descent, offspring of the Scipios, heiress of Paulus, whose name she bears, true and legitimate descendant of Marcia Papyria, the mother of Africanus [Note: Two ancient manuscripts of Regia, 407 and 500, read Metia, a reading supported by another manuscript of Saint Maximus cited by Bollandus. It is also known that Papyria Marcia, daughter of Marcus Papyrus Mason, was the wife of Lucius Aemilius Paulus and the mother of Fabius and the younger Africanus.], she preferred Bethlehem to Rome and exchanged roofs glittering with gold for the mean ugliness of mud.

We do not mourn that we have lost such a woman; rather, we give thanks that we had her—or rather, that we still have her. For all things live to God; and whatever returns to the Lord is counted among the members of his household. Although her loss is habitation in a heavenly home—for as long as she was in the body, she was away from the Lord (2 Cor. 5)—and she always complained in a plaintive voice, saying: “Woe is me, for my sojourning has been prolonged; I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Kedar, my soul has been a long-time sojourner” (Ps. 19:5) [Note: Other manuscripts, following the Vulgate, read: “I was a long-time sojourner,” and so forth.]

Nor is it surprising that she lamented her dwelling in darkness—for this is what Kedar means—since the world lies in the evil one; and just as its darkness is, so also is its light (Ps. 138:12), while the light shines in the darkness (John 1:5), and the darkness did not comprehend it. Hence she also frequently repeated: “I am a stranger and a sojourner, like all my fathers” (Ps. 38:13). And again: “I desire to depart and be with Christ” (Phil. 1:23).

Whenever she was afflicted by the weakness of her little body—what incredible abstinence and doubled fasts she endured!—she kept turning these words over in her mouth: “I discipline my body and bring it into subjection, lest, after preaching to others, I myself should be found disqualified” (1 Cor. 9:27). And: “It is good neither to drink wine nor to eat meat” (Rom. 14:21). And: “I humbled my soul with fasting” (Ps. 34:13). And: “You have turned all my bed in my sickness” (Ps. 40). And: “I have been afflicted in misery while a thorn is fixed in me” (Ps. 31) [Note: The older manuscript of Regia reads: “And amid the other pains which she endured with marvelous…”].

And amid the stings of pain that she bore with marvelous patience, as though she saw the heavens opened above her, she would say: “Who will give me wings like a dove’s, and I shall fly away and rest?” (Ps. 54:7).

### 2

I call Jesus and his saints to witness, and the very Angel who was the guardian and extraordinary companion of this admirable woman, that I shall say nothing to curry favor and nothing in the manner of flatterers. Whatever I am about to say, I shall say as testimony; indeed, it is less than her merits, which the whole world proclaims: priests marvel, choirs of virgins long for her, and crowds of monks and poor lament her.

Do you wish, reader, to know her virtues briefly? She dismissed all her poor people as poorer than herself. Nor is it surprising to say this of her relatives and little household, whom, from servants and maidservants of both sexes, she had changed into brothers and sisters, when she left the virgin Eustochium, the devoted daughter of Christ, for whose consolation this little book is fashioned, rich not in noble birth but in faith and grace [Note: We have supplied the word “Angels” from the edition of the Lives of the Holy Fathers and from Bollandus, who likewise shortly afterward reads “to say nothing in the manner of flatterers,” instead of “to say nothing in the manner of praisers.”]

### 3

Let us therefore take up the order of our narrative. Let others go further back and, beginning with her cradle and, so to speak, her very rattles, bring forward her mother Blaesilla and her father Rogatus: the one was descended from the Scipios and the Gracchi; the other is said, through nearly all the Greek lands down to the present day, to derive his blood from Agamemnon, who destroyed Troy by a ten-year siege, and to possess genealogies, riches, and nobility.

We shall praise nothing except what is proper to her and flows from the purest fountain of her holy mind. Although the Lord and Savior teaches in the Gospel, when the Apostles ask what they will receive in return for having left everything for his name, that they will receive a hundredfold in the present age and eternal life in the future (Mark 10), we understand from this that it is not praise-worthy to possess riches, but to despise them for Christ; not to swell with honors, but to think little of them for the faith of God.

Truly, what the Savior promised his male and female servants, he returned in the present life. For she who despised the glory of one city is celebrated by the reputation of the whole world. While she lived at Rome, no one outside Rome knew her; now, hidden at Bethlehem, both barbarian and Roman lands admire her. For what people do not come to the holy places? And who, in the holy places, has found anything more worthy of admiration among human beings than Paula?

As the most precious jewel shines among many gems, and the radiance of the sun overwhelms and obscures the little sparks of the stars, so by her humility she surpassed the virtues and powers of all. She was the least among everyone, so that she might be greater than everyone. And the more she humbled herself, the more she was lifted up by Christ. She was hidden, and yet she was not hidden. By fleeing glory, she deserved glory—the glory that follows virtue like a shadow and, abandoning those who seek it, seeks those who despise it.

But what am I doing? I am abandoning the order of the narrative, lingering over each detail instead of observing the rules of composition.

### 4

Born, then, from such a stock, she was joined to Toxotius, who traced the loftiest blood of Aeneas and the Julians. Hence his daughter, the virgin of Christ Eustochium, is also called Julia:

“Julius, a name descended from great Iulus.”  
(AENEID 1)

We say these things not because they are great in those who possess them, but because they are marvelous in those who despise them. The people of the world welcome those who are endowed with such privileges. We praise those who have spurned them for the Savior; and, in a remarkable reversal, those whom we think little of when they possess them, we proclaim when they do not wish to possess them [Note: Martianaeus adds “despising,” a word supported neither by the better manuscripts nor by the older printed editions. In a manuscript of Saint Maximus cited by Bollandus, the reading is: “Thus adorned by such ancestors, born, I say, for such…”].

Born, I say, from such ancestors, and proved by fertility and chastity—first to her husband, then to her relatives, and to the testimony of the whole city—she bore five children: Blaesilla, whose death I consoled her for at Rome; Paulina, who left as heir the holy and admirable man Pammachius, devoted both to his vocation and to his possessions, to whom we published a little book on her death; Eustochium, who is now in the holy places a precious jewel of virginity and the Church; Ruffina, whose premature death overwhelmed the pious heart of her mother; and Toxotius, after whose birth she ceased bearing children, so that you might understand that she did not wish to serve the marital duty for long, but obeyed her husband’s desire, since he wished for male children [Note: The oldest manuscript of Regia, 500, corrects the reading found previously in all printed editions and most manuscripts, which was “he who wished for a male, to have borne children.” That reading is less suitable, for children cannot be born in accordance with a husband’s desire, and although Paula is said to have given birth, she would not have fulfilled his wishes as long as she bore females. The reading restored here is also confirmed by the manuscript of Saint Maximus.].

### 5

After her husband died, she mourned him so deeply that she herself nearly died; then she turned so entirely to the service of the Lord that she seemed to have wished for his death. Why should I recount how all the wealth of a once extensive, noble, and exceedingly rich household was distributed among the poor? Why describe her most merciful spirit, whose goodness extended even to those whom she had never seen? What poor man died without being wrapped in her garments? What sick person was not supported by her resources [Note: Two manuscripts read “clergy” instead of “sick people,” an erroneous reading.]? Searching for them throughout the entire city with the greatest care, she considered it a loss if any sick or hungry person were sustained by someone else.

She stripped her children of their inheritance and, while her relatives reproached her, declared that she was leaving them a greater inheritance: the mercy of Christ.

### 6

Nor could she long endure the visits and crowds of those who came because of her exalted standing in the world and her most noble family [Note: Another manuscript of Regia reads: “the crowds whom she grieved…”]. She was distressed by her own honor and hastened to avoid and flee the faces of those who praised her.

When imperial letters had brought the bishops of East and West to Rome because of certain disputes among the churches [Note: This probably refers to the Roman Synod of the year 382, convened under Pope Damasus by the commands of Gratian, Valentinian the Younger, and Theodosius, to suppress the disturbances and factions of the bishops who simultaneously claimed the church of Antioch: Paulinus and Flavian. Compare Letter 127 to Principia, section 10: “When ecclesiastical necessity had also drawn me to Rome with the holy bishops Paulinus and Epiphanius…”], she saw two admirable men and bishops of Christ: Paulinus, bishop of Antioch, and Epiphanius of Salamis in Cyprus, now called Constantia. She received Epiphanius as her guest; Paulinus, who was staying in another’s house, she treated with such kindness as though he were her own.

Kindled by their virtues, she began thinking at every moment of abandoning her homeland. Forgetful of her house, her children, her household, her possessions, and everything belonging to the world—alone, if that can be said, and without companions—she longed to go to the desert of Antony and Paul. At last, when winter had passed, the sea was opened, and the bishops were returning to their churches; she too sailed with them, impelled by her vow and desire.

What more need I say? She went down to the port, accompanied by her brother, relatives, kinsmen, and—more important than these—her children, who wished to overcome their most merciful mother by their devotion. The sails were already being stretched, and by the pull of the oars the ship was being drawn out to sea. Little Toxotius stretched out supplicating hands from the shore. Ruffina, now of marriageable age and silently pleading with tears that she should wait for her wedding, remained there. Yet Paula kept her eyes raised dryly toward heaven, overcoming her affection for her children with her affection for God.

She did not know herself to be a mother, so that she might prove herself a handmaid of Christ. Her vitals were torn, and she struggled with her pain as though she were being pulled away from her own limbs [manuscript: “they were being pulled away”]. She was all the more admirable because she conquered a great love. Amid the hands of enemies and the harsh necessity of captivity, nothing is more cruel than for parents to be separated from their children. Faith contrary to the laws of nature endured this—or rather, a joyful spirit desired it. Despising the love of her children through a greater love for God, she found consolation only in Eustochium, who was both the companion of her vocation and of her voyage.

Meanwhile the ship cut through the sea. While all who traveled with her looked back toward the shore, she kept her eyes turned away, lest she see those whom she could not see without torment [Note: The manuscripts of Regia read: “she went down to the port, accompanied by her relatives, kinsmen, and…” without mentioning her brother.]. I confess that no mother ever loved her children so much—before departing, she had given them everything—as she did: disinheriting herself on earth in order to find an inheritance in heaven.

### 7

Brought to the island of Pontia [Note: A number of manuscripts of Regia read “to the Pontian islands.” Eusebius, or Jerome in his Chronicle under the year 16 of Domitian, should be recalled here: “Bruttius writes that very many Christians suffered martyrdom under Domitian, among them Flavia Domitilla, niece through her sister of Flavius Clemens the consul, who was banished to the island of Pontia because she confessed herself to be a Christian.”], which the exile of Flavia Domitilla, once the most illustrious of women, had made famous under the emperor Domitian because of her confession of the Christian name, she saw the little rooms in which Domitilla had endured a long martyrdom. Taking wings of faith, Paula desired to see Jerusalem and the holy places.

The winds were slow, and every speed was sluggish. Believing herself committed to the Adriatic sea between Scylla and Charybdis, she came, as though across a pond, to Methone. There, after briefly refreshing her little body,

“Laying her sea-worn limbs upon the shore,

through Malea and Cythera, and the Cyclades scattered across the sea,

…and straits stirred by frequent lands,”  
(AENEID 1)

she passed Rhodes and Lycia and at last saw Cyprus. There she threw herself at the feet of the holy and venerable Epiphanius and was detained by him for ten days—not, as he supposed, for rest, but for the work of God, as the event proved. For, inspecting all the monasteries of that region, she left whatever relief from expenses she could provide for the brothers whom the love of the holy man had brought there from the whole world.

From there she crossed in a short journey to Seleucia. From Seleucia she went up to Antioch, where she was detained for a short time by affection for the holy confessor Paulinus. In midwinter, though the air was warm with the fervor of faith, this noble woman, who had previously been carried by the hands of eunuchs, set out riding on a donkey.

### 8

I omit the journey through Coele-Syria and Phoenicia—for I have not undertaken to write her itinerary. I shall name only those places that are contained in the sacred books.

Leaving Berytus, a Roman colony, and the ancient city of Sidon, she entered the little tower of Elijah on the shore of Sarepta (1 Kings 17) [Note: Phocas, published by Allatius, follows precisely the same route; it will sometimes be useful to compare him: Μετὰ τὴν Σιδῶνα, τὸ Σαραφθὰ κάστρον περὶ τὸ κλύσμα τῆς θαλάσσης τεθεμελίωται, καὶ ναὸς προφήτου Ἡλιοῦ ἐπὶ τῇ οἰκίᾳ τῆς ξενισάσης αὐτὸν χήρας, μέσον τοῦ πολίσματος ἵδρυται. “After Sidon, the fortress of Sarepta is founded upon the very alluvial shore of the sea, and a temple of the prophet Elijah rises in the house of the widow who had received him as a guest, in the middle of the town.” Jerome calls it a little tower.]

After worshiping the Lord and Savior there, she passed through the sands of Tyre, where Paul bent his knees, and arrived at Acco [Note: All our manuscript codices read Acho; in its place there was formerly “ad Coth,” and Martianaeus emended it to Acco, apparently by conjecture, since he cites no manuscript witnesses. The reading is also supported by the previously mentioned Phocas: ἐκεῖθεν ἐστὶν ἡ Ητολεμαις, ἤτοι τὸ Ἀκκε, “From there is Ptolemais, that is, Acco.” This city is also mentioned in Judges 1:31.], now called Ptolemais (Acts 21:5).

Passing through the fields of Megiddo, witnesses to the death of Josiah, she entered the land of the Philistines. She marveled at the ruins of Dor, once a very powerful city; and, conversely, at Strato’s Tower, called Caesarea by King Herod—whether the Herod of Ascalon or the Great—in honor of Caesar Augustus. There she saw the house of Cornelius, now a church of Christ, and the little buildings of Philip, and the four rooms of the four virgin prophetesses [Note: Two manuscripts of Regia have the singular “room” and “four,” and so forth. Isidore also read this way; he copied nearly everything from here in the fifteenth book of the Origins, chapter 1.].

Next came Antipatris, a half-ruined little town that Herod had named after his father; and Lydda, changed into Diospolis, famous for the resurrection of Dorcas and the restoration of Aeneas to health (Acts 9) [Note: This does not seem to agree with Saint Luke. In the Acts of the Apostles he says that Peter raised Dorcas, or Tabitha, at Joppa, while at Lydda Aeneas, who was paralyzed, was restored to health.].

Not far from there was Arimathea, the village of Joseph who buried the Lord; and Nob, once a city of priests, now a mound of the slain [Note: He refers to the story in 1 Samuel 22, where Saul, enraged that Abimelech had received David at Nob, ordered Doeg to slaughter eighty-five men wearing the ephod, and put the other inhabitants of Nob, a priestly city, to the sword.].

She also visited Joppa, the port of the fleeing Jonah (Jon. 1:2), and—to touch briefly upon the tales of the poets—viewed Andromeda fastened to the rock [Note: It formerly read “Andromades.” The following passage belongs here: In his Commentary on Jonah 1, speaking of Joppa, Jerome says: “This is the place where, even to the present day, rocks are shown on the shore to which Andromeda was fastened and from which she was once freed by the aid of Perseus.” Mela, Josephus, and Pliny agree. The first reports that a clear trace of Andromeda, saved by Perseus, is shown there: the huge bones of the sea monster. The second says in Book 3 of The Jewish War: ἔνθα, he says, καὶ τῶν Ἀνδρομέδης δεσμῶν ἔτι δεικνύμενοι τύποι πιστοῦνται τὴν ἀρχαιότητα τοῦ μύθου, “There the remains of Andromeda’s chains, still displayed, confirm the antiquity of the story.”].

Retracing her route, she came to Nicopolis, formerly called Emmaus, near which the Lord was recognized in the breaking of bread (Luke 24:38). There she dedicated the house of Cleophas as a church. From there she set out and climbed Lower and Upper Beth-horon, cities founded by Solomon but later destroyed by the changing storms of war.

Looking to the right, she saw Ajalon and Gibeon, where Jesus son of Nun, fighting against five kings, commanded the sun and the moon; and where, because of their deceit and the stratagem by which they obtained a treaty, he condemned the Gibeonites to be water-carriers and woodcutters (Josh. 9 and 10).

At the city of Gibeah, destroyed to its foundations, she paused briefly, recalling its sin, the concubine divided into pieces, and the three hundred men of the tribe of Benjamin [Note: Gravius reads “six hundred,” following Judges 20], preserved on account of the Apostle.

### 9

Why delay at length? On the left, after leaving Helena’s mausoleum [Note: Josephus, Antiquities XX.4, relates that the bones of Helena, queen of Adiabene, and of her son Izates were buried ἐν ταῖς πυραμίσιν, ἃς ἡ μήτηρ κατεσκευὰκει, τρεῖς τὸν ἀριθμὸν, τρία στάδια τῆς τῶν Ἰεροσολυμιτῶν πόλεως ἀπεχούσας, “in the pyramids which their mother had built, three in number and three stadia distant from the city of Jerusalem.” Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History I.2.12, calls them στήλαι, “pillars,” located ἐν τοῖς προαστείοις τῆς Αἰλίας, “in the suburbs of Aelia.” For the rest concerning the three names of Jerusalem, see Josephus, Antiquities VII.5 and The Jewish War VI.4, although he errs more than once in the etymology of the city, deriving the origin of the word partly from Hebrew and partly from Greek.], she entered Jerusalem, the city with three names—Jebus, Salem, and Jerusalem—which later, from its ruins and ashes, was raised by Aelius Hadrian into Aelia.

When the proconsul of Palestine, who knew her family very well, had sent attendants ahead and ordered a residence to be prepared, she chose a humble cell. She visited every place with such fervor and enthusiasm that, unless she hurried on to the remaining sites, she could not be drawn away from the first.

Prostrate before the Cross, she worshiped as though she saw the Lord hanging upon it. Entering the tomb of the Resurrection, she kissed the stone that the angel had moved from the entrance of the tomb [Note: Cyril of Jerusalem is a supporting witness, Catechesis 13, where he says of that stone: ὁ μέχρι σήμερον παρὰ τῷ μνημείῳ κείμενος, “which lies beside the tomb even to this day.” Jerome places it near the sarcophagus, directly opposite the cave of the tomb. Soon afterward, for fideli, “faithful,” the older manuscripts read fidei, “of faith.”].

With faithful lips she licked the very place where the Lord had lain, as though she were thirsty for the desired waters. All Jerusalem bears witness to how many tears, how many groans, and how much grief she poured out there; the Lord himself bears witness, the Lord whom she entreated.

Leaving there, she climbed Zion, whose name means citadel or watchtower. David once captured and rebuilt this city. Of the captured city it is written: “Woe to you, city Ariel”—that is, “lion of God”—“and once most mighty, which David captured” (Isa. 29:1). Of the city that was built it was said: “Its foundations are in the holy mountains; the Lord loves the gates of Zion above all the tents of Jacob” (Ps. 86:1).

These are not the gates that we see today dissolved into ash and dust, but the gates against which hell does not prevail, through which the multitude of believers enters to Christ.

A column supporting a portico of the church was shown to her, stained with the blood of the Lord; to this column, it is said, he was bound and scourged [Note: Victorius, on the basis of certain Vatican manuscripts, preferred “he is said to have been bound and scourged.” Our manuscripts read as printed, with only the Cistercian manuscript having “there” instead of “to her.” Bede, On the Holy Places, says: “A marble column stands in the middle of the church, to which the Lord was fastened and scourged.” The author of the gloss on Luke 23 says: “The column itself testifies to the place to which the Lord was bound; even to this day it displays to those who see it unmistakable signs of the Lord’s blood.”]

The place was shown where the Holy Spirit had descended upon the souls of more than one hundred and twenty believers, so that the prophecy of Joel might be fulfilled.

### 10

Then, distributing money among the poor and fellow servants according to her modest means, she went on to Bethlehem. On the right side of the road she stopped at Rachel’s tomb, where Benjamin was born—not as his mother, dying, had called him, Benoni, that is, “son of my sorrow” (Gen. 35:18), but, as his father prophetically declared in the Spirit, “son of the right hand.” From there she entered Bethlehem [variant: “into Bethlehem”] and, going into the Savior’s cave, saw the holy lodging of the Virgin and the stable in which she recognized “the ox knows his owner, and the donkey the manger of his master” (Isa. 1:3).

Thus was fulfilled what is written in the same Prophet: “Blessed is he who sows beside all waters, where the ox and the donkey tread” (Isa. 32:20, according to the Septuagint) [Note: Gravius prefers “above all waters.”].

While I was listening, she swore that she saw with the eyes of faith the infant Lord wrapped in swaddling clothes and crying in the manger; the Magi worshiping; the star shining above; the Virgin Mother (Matt. 2); the attentive foster father; the shepherds coming at night to see “the word that had been made” (Luke 2:16); and that already then they were dedicating the beginning of the Evangelist John: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word became flesh” (John 3) [Note: One book of Regia reads “to see the new thing that had happened,” but the Greek has ῥῆμα, “word,” and the following context rules out that reading.].

She saw the children slain, Herod raging, Joseph and Mary fleeing into Egypt. With joy mixed with tears, she spoke:

“Hail, Bethlehem, house of bread, in which was born that bread which descended from heaven. Hail, Ephrathah, most fertile region and καρποφόρε [variant: καρποφόρα], ‘fruit-bearing,’ whose fruitfulness is God.

Of you Micah once prophesied:

‘And you, Bethlehem, house of Ephrathah, are not the least among the thousands of Judah. From you shall come forth for me one who will be ruler in Israel; his going forth is from the beginning, from the days of eternity. Therefore he will give them up until the time when she who is in labor gives birth. She will give birth, and the remnant of his brothers will return to the children of Israel’” (Mic. 5:2–3) [Note: The same source reads “Are you not the least?” Compare Letter 37 to Pammachius, section 8. Shortly afterward some read “he will give” instead of “you will give”; the Greek also varies between δώσει, “he will give,” and δώσεις, “you will give.” See the Commentaries on Micah.].

For in you was born the ruler who was begotten before Lucifer (Ps. 109), whose birth from the Father surpasses every age. And the origin of David’s line remained in you until the Virgin gave birth, and the remnant of the people believing in Christ returned to the children of Israel and openly proclaimed: “It was necessary that the word of God should first be spoken to you; but since you rejected it and judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13:46).

For God [variant: the Lord] had said: “I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. 15:24). And at that time the words of Jacob concerning him were fulfilled: “The ruler shall not depart from Judah, nor the leader from his loins, until he comes to whom it has been reserved; and he will be the expectation of the nations” (Gen. 49:10, according to the Septuagint).

David rightly swore and rightly made vows, saying: “If I enter the tent of my house, if I climb upon the bed of my couch; if I give sleep to my eyes and slumber to my eyelids, and rest to my temples, until I find a place for the Lord, a dwelling for the God of Jacob” (Ps. 131:3ff.). Immediately he explained what he desired, and with prophetic eyes he saw him whom we now believe has come, while David saw that he would come: “Behold, we heard of him in Ephrathah; we found him in the fields of the forest” (ibid. 6).

ZO [Note: Our manuscripts have Zob or Zoli; others, in Martianaeus, have Zop or Zod. The last reading would not be displeasing, since the Hebrew could have expressed it in the neuter gender. The Benedictine discusses the printed reading at length; consult him at the end of the book, if desired. We establish only this from that discussion: in Jerome’s Hebrew exemplar it was once written with one of several forms meaning “this” or “that.” Likewise, after the verb, although the Septuagint read otherwise, the Hebrew manuscripts still have forms with a feminine suffix, “we heard of her and found her.” Shortly afterward, instead of “with you teaching,” that is, Jerome in another manuscript of Regia has “as though from one teaching.”]

For, as I learned from your instruction, the Hebrew word does not signify Mary, the mother of the Lord—that is, αὐτήν, “her”—but him, that is, αὐτόν, “him.” Hence he speaks confidently: “We shall enter his tabernacle; we shall worship in the place where his feet stood.”

And am I, wretched and sinful, considered worthy to kiss the manger in which the little Lord cried? To pray in the cave in which the Virgin, having given birth, brought forth the infant Lord? This is my rest, because it is the homeland of my Lord. Here I shall dwell, because the Savior chose her. I prepared a lamp for my Christ (Ps. 137:37). My soul shall live for him, and my offspring shall serve him (Ps. 21:31).

Not far from there she descended to the tower of Ader, that is, “of the flock” (Gen. 35:21), near which Jacob pastured his flocks; and the shepherds keeping watch at night were worthy to hear: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14) [Note: In some manuscripts, “he watered his flock.”].

While they were guarding the sheep, they found the Lamb of God with a pure and spotless fleece, which in the dryness of the whole earth had been drenched with heavenly dew (Judg. 6:37); and whose blood took away the sins of the world and, when smeared on the doorposts, drove away the destroyer of Egypt (Exod. 12).

### 11.

Immediately, with hurried steps, she began to travel along the old road that leads to Gaza, “to the stronghold” or “to the riches of God.” She silently revolved in her mind how the Ethiopian eunuch, prefiguring the peoples of the nations, had changed his skin, and, while reading the ancient Instrument, had found the fountain of the Gospel. From there she turned to the right.

[Note: Gravius prefers, by changing one word, *transita Bethsur* for *transit a Bethsur*: “Bethzur having been passed, she comes,” etc.]

From Bethzur she came to Eshcol, which means “a cluster” (Num. 13:24–25). As a testimony to the fertility of the land and as a type of Him who says, “I have trodden the winepress alone, and of the nations there was no man with me” (Isa. 63:3), the spies carried back a cluster of extraordinary size (Num. 13).

[Note: Two Regina manuscripts read “there was no man with me,” with even the Greek disagreeing: οὐκ ἔστιν, “there is not.”]

After no great distance she entered Sarah’s little chambers, seeing Isaac’s cradle and the remains of Abraham’s oak, beneath which he saw Christ’s day and rejoiced. Then, rising from there, she climbed Hebron, which is Kiriath-arba, that is, “the city of the four men”: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Adam the great, whom the Hebrews believe was buried there, according to the book of Joshua son of Nun.

[Note: This is a Hebrew tradition to which Joshua’s words (14:15) gave occasion. They say that the greatest Adam lies there among the Anakim. Yet these words do not designate Adam the first father, but simply a very large and renowned man (for “adam” in Hebrew means “man”), who, since his name was Arbe—meaning “four”—gave the city its surname, and was himself buried there after his death. See what we note under the word “Arbe” in the book *On Places*. Those who regard Caleb as the fourth argue from the fact that Joshua assigned the city of Hebron to him.]

Nevertheless, most regard Caleb as the fourth, and his memorial is shown at the side.

After inspecting these places, she did not wish to proceed to Kiriath-sepher, that is, “the bond of letters,” because, despising the letter that kills, she had found the life-giving Spirit. She was even more astonished by the upper and lower waters that Othniel son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite had received in exchange for the southern, arid territory (Judg. 1), and by whose channels he made the dry fields of the former Instrument irrigated, so that she might find the redemption of ancient sins in the waters of baptism.

[Note: Erasmus and Martianay incorrectly print “and by the watercourse,” instead of “by whose,” as Victorius himself had corrected before us.]

The next day, when the sun had already risen, she stood on the brow of Caphar Barucha, that is, “the village of blessing.”

[Note: Saint Epiphanius also mentions Caphar Baricha, as he calls it, a place three thousand paces from Hebron. It also seems to be the place called “the Valley of Blessing” in 2 Chronicles 20:26.]

To this place Abraham accompanied the Lord. From there, looking down upon the broad wilderness and upon the land once belonging to Sodom and Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboiim, she contemplated the balsam vineyards at Engedi, and the heifer “terrifying” (Isa. 15), which had previously been called Bela and which, in Syriac, was rendered Zoar, that is, “little.”

[Note: See the Commentary on Isaiah, chapter 15. In some places one finds the corrupt reading *consternantem* or *consternatam*; *conternans* means “terrifying,” that is, producing the number three.]

She remembered Lot’s cave and, bursting into tears, warned the accompanying virgins that they must beware of wine, in which there is wantonness, whose offspring are the Moabites and Ammonites (Gen. 19).

### 12.

I linger for a long time in the south, where the bride found the bridegroom lying down, and Joseph became intoxicated with his brothers (Song 1:6; Gen. 43:16).

[Note: It is by no means unusual for those who pursue allegorical interpretations to employ equivocal meanings. Here our author draws and adapts to the southern region what was enacted at midday, or in the middle of the day, by the bride of the Song and by Joseph.]

“I shall return to Jerusalem, and by way of Tekoa and Amos I shall look upon the Cross shining on the Mount of Olives,” from which the Savior ascended to the Father.

[Note: Victorius reads “light” instead of “Cross,” and argues that the text must be corrected in this way, since Christ was not crucified on the Mount of Olives but ascended from it to the Father. Although a temple was built there, he says, it could never have been covered with a roof, so that the open path of Christ’s ascent might remain visible. He evidently did not know of the sign of the Cross erected on the summit of the Mount of Olives, which Jerome attests in more than one place, especially in his Commentary on Zephaniah, chapter 1, where he says that the Jews, forbidden to enter Jerusalem, mourned the ruins of their temple from the Mount of Olives beneath the shining banner of the Cross. Compare Letter 46, to Paula and Eustochium, §12. Moreover, for *I shall return*, which occurs shortly before, and *I shall look upon*, which follows, the Reatine translator changed the forms to “she was returning” and “she was looking,” apparently on his own initiative, in order to present Jerome, rather than Paula, as the speaker.]

On this mountain, every year, the red heifer was burned as a holocaust to the Lord, and its ashes purified the people of Israel (Num. 19).

[Note: The Rabbis are mistaken when they say that only one heifer was sacrificed from Moses to Ezra, and six—or at most nine—from Ezra until the destruction of the Temple.]

On this mountain, according to Ezekiel, the Cherubim, migrating from the Temple, founded the Lord’s Church.

Afterward she entered the tomb of Lazarus and saw the lodging of Mary and Martha; and Bethphage, “the village of priestly jaws,”

[Note: He himself does not sufficiently approve this interpretation in the book *On Names*. “Some,” he says, “think it is called the house of jaws.” Yet at the beginning of chapter 21 of Matthew he again calls Bethphage “the house of jaws,” which was a village of priests. From this you may understand why he has added “priestly,” unless you prefer to argue from the fact that the jaw was a special portion belonging to priests under the Law. Theophylact combines both explanations in his Commentary on Luke 19, copying Origen word for word: *bēthphagē, oikos siagónōn hieratikos ōn topos*—“Bethphage, the house of jaws, a place belonging to priests; for jaws were given to priests, as it is written in the Law.”]

and the place where the colt, the unruly creature of the nations, received God’s bridle and, covered with the Apostles’ garments, offered its gentle back for riding.

By the direct road she descended to Jericho, recalling the man wounded in the Gospel and the mercy of the Samaritan—that is, the guardian—while the priests and Levites passed by in the savagery of their minds. The Samaritan placed the half-dead [or: half-alive] man upon his own beast and carried him to the inn of the Church (Luke 10).

She also recalled the place Adummim, which is interpreted as “of blood,” because much blood was poured out there through the frequent attacks of robbers; and the sycamore tree of Zacchaeus, that is, the good works of repentance by which he trampled sins once bloodstained and harmful through his robberies. She beheld the exalted Lord from the height of the virtues.

She also saw, beside the road, the places of the blind (Matt. 20:30), who, having received their sight, had already proclaimed the mysteries of both peoples believing in the Lord.

Entering Jericho, she saw the city founded by Hiel in Abiram, his firstborn, and whose gates he set in Segub, his youngest son (Josh. 5:5; 4 Kings 8:4).

[Note: Consult Joshua 6:26 and 1 Kings 16:34 again for the interpretation of this passage. One of the Regina manuscripts reads “she saw the tower” instead of “the city,” and “which Hiel founded”; another has “Achiel,” from the Greek Ἀχιήλ.]

She looked upon the camp of Gilgal, the heap of foreskins, and the mystery of the second circumcision; and the twelve stones which, transferred there from the bed of the Jordan, had established the foundations of the twelve Apostles.

She also saw the once exceedingly bitter and barren spring of the Law, which the true Elisha seasoned with his wisdom and changed into sweetness and abundance (2 Kings 2:22).

Hardly had the night passed when, in the fiercest heat, she came to the Jordan. She stood on the riverbank, and, when the sun had risen, remembered the Sun of righteousness: how, in the middle of the riverbed, the priests had planted dry feet (Josh. 3:5), and how, at the command of Elijah and Elisha, the waters stood on either side and the wave provided a passage (2 Kings 2). The Lord, by His baptism, had cleansed the waters polluted by the Flood and stained by the destruction of the whole human race.

### 13.

It would take too long if I wished to speak of the Valley of Achor, that is, “of tumult and disturbances,” in which theft and avarice were condemned (Josh. 7:25); and of Bethel, the House of God, where naked and poor Jacob slept upon the bare ground. Having placed beneath his head the stone described in Zechariah as possessing seven eyes (Zech. 3:9), and called in Isaiah the cornerstone (Isa. 28:16), he saw a ladder extending to heaven, upon which the Lord leaned above (Gen. 28), stretching out His hand to those ascending and hurling down from the heights those who were negligent.

She also reverently visited the tombs on Mount Ephraim: those of Joshua son of Nun and Eleazar son of Aaron the priest, facing one another. One was buried at Timnath-serah [or: Thamnitsare], on the northern side of Mount Gaash (Josh. 24:30); the other at Gibeah [manuscripts: Gaab] of his son Phinehas. She was sufficiently astonished that the distributor of inheritances had chosen for himself a mountainous and rugged region.

What should I say of Shiloh, where the ruined altar is still shown today, and which preceded Romulus’s abduction of the Sabine women by the tribe of Benjamin?

She passed through Shechem—not, as many mistaken readers write, Sychar, which is now called Neapolis—and entered the Church built beside Jacob’s well, at the foot of Mount Gerizim.

[Note: Previously, in Martianay, the text incorrectly read “at the side of.”]

The Lord sat there, thirsty and hungry, and was satisfied by the Samaritan woman’s faith (John 4:6). Having abandoned the error of Dositheus, she found the true Messiah and the true Savior, after her five husbands—the five books of Moses—and the sixth, whom she claimed to possess.

[Note: He compares the Samaritan woman’s five husbands with the five books of Moses, since the Samaritans accepted only those books as part of divine Scripture. A second error was added to their error through the new heresy of Dositheus. Eusebius records in *Preparation for the Gospel*, books XI and XII, that Dositheus defected to the Samaritans because he had been unable to obtain the leading place among the Jews, who are called *Deuterōtai*. See the *Dialogue against the Luciferians*.]

Turning aside from there, she saw the tombs of the twelve Patriarchs, and Sebaste, that is, Samaria, which Herod named Augusta in the Greek language in honor of Augustus. There lie Elisha and the prophet Obadiah, and John the Baptist—“than whom no greater has arisen among those born of women.”

There she trembled, overwhelmed by many marvelous sights. She saw demons roaring under various torments, and human beings howling before the tombs of the saints like wolves, barking with the voices of dogs, roaring like lions, hissing like serpents, and bellowing like bulls. Some spun their heads around and touched the ground with the crown of their heads; and, with their feet suspended, women did not let their garments fall over their faces.

[Note: Through a notable error, most printed books and manuscripts lacked the negative particle and read: “their garments fell over their faces.” The Cistercian manuscript alerted us to the problem, and the context itself persuaded us that the marvel’s reality required the negative. Hilary also supports this reading in book 1 of *Against Constantius*, §8, a passage Jerome has almost copied here: “The venerable bones of the martyrs bear witness every day, when demons roar among them, illnesses are driven away, and wondrous works are seen: bodies lifted without ropes, and women suspended by the feet, yet their garments do not fall over their faces,” and so forth. See also, if desired, Sulpicius Severus, *Dialogues on Saint Martin* 3: “You could see wretched people tormented in various ways: some with their feet raised into the air, yet their garments did not fall over their faces, lest the exposed part of their bodies cause shame,” and Saint Paulinus, *Natale* 7 of Saint Felix. To these may be added Benedict Paulinus of Petrocorius, *Life of Saint Martin*, book V:

> Amid the emptiness, one guilty man hung suspended, while his tormentor was in the air,
>
> His feet stretched upward, his garments drawn tight and thrown back,
>
> Covering his limbs, the cloth clinging to his hidden body,
>
> Lest, bent backward in its own curve or slipping behind,
>
> It expose the shameful limbs of the hanging man.]

She pitied them all and, shedding tears for each one, prayed for Christ’s mercy.

Although she was weak, she climbed the mountain on foot. In its two caves, during a time of persecution and famine, the prophet Obadiah fed one hundred prophets with bread and water (1 Kings 18:4).

From there she quickly traversed Nazareth, the Lord’s nurse; Cana [manuscripts: Chanaam] and Capernaum, familiar with His signs; the Sea of Tiberias, sanctified when the Lord sailed upon it; and the wilderness in which many thousands of people were fed with a few loaves, and twelve baskets were filled with the leftovers of those who had eaten—the twelve tribes of Israel.

She climbed Mount Tabor, on which the Lord was transfigured. From a distance she looked upon Mount Hermon and Hermoniim, and the broadest plains of Galilee, where Sisera and all his army were struck down when Barak conquered, and the torrent of Kishon, which divided the middle of the plain (Judg. 4). The town beside Nain was also pointed out, where the widow’s son was raised.

The day would end before my account if I wished to recount everything that the venerable Paula traversed with her incredible faith.

### 14.

I shall pass on to Egypt. I shall pause briefly at Succoth and at the spring of Samson, which he drew forth from the tooth of a millstone-like jawbone (Judg. 15:19), and wash my parched mouth there, so that, refreshed, I may see Moresheth, once the tomb of the prophet Micah and now a church.

[Note: Victorius prefers: “and between Succoth and Samson’s spring, etc.” In the meantime, retain the description of the journey begun here from the Bethlehem monastery.]

From the side I shall leave the Horites, the Gittites, Mareshah, Idumea, and Lachish. Then, crossing the exceedingly soft sands that erase the footprints of travelers, and the broad waste of the desert, I shall come to the Egyptian river Sihor, whose name means “muddy.”

I shall pass through the five cities of Egypt that speak the language of Canaan (Isa. 19:18), the land of Goshen, and the fields of Tanis, in which God performed wonders. I shall also see the city of No, later changed into Alexandria, and the town of the Lord, Nitria, where the stains of many people are daily washed in the purest nitre of the virtues.

When she saw this place, and encountered the holy and venerable Bishop Isidore the Confessor,

[Note: Saint Isidore of Pelusium, or bishop of Pelusium, also called of Damietta.]

as well as innumerable throngs of monks, many of whom were raised to priestly and Levitical rank, she rejoiced at the Lord’s glory but confessed herself unworthy of such honor.

What, then, should I say of the Macarii, the Arsenii, the Serapions, and the other names of Christ’s columns?

[Note: Bollandus reads *Arsatas*, but would prefer *Arsisius*, concerning whom he cites Palladius’s testimony in the *Lausiac History*, chapter 7: Palladius says that for a whole year he lived on Mount Nitria among the holy fathers—the great Arsisius, Putaphastus, Hagio, Cronius, and Serapion. In truth, if *Arsenius* is retained, no one else seems intended but the celebrated former tutor of Arcadius; yet chronology opposes this, since he began to become famous when the Macarii and Serapion had passed away. Nevertheless, Socrates, book 4, chapter 27, calls the monk Arsenius by name, in Greek Ἀρσήνιον, and lists him after Ammon and Didymus together with Isidore, Pambo, and the Macarii, so that there is no doubt that he belonged to these times. But I fear that Ἀρσῆνος has there been corruptly written for Ἀρσίσις, and that Orsiesius—or, as the Greeks prefer to say, Arsesius—must certainly be understood. For Sozomen, book 6, chapter 30, after Didymus and Cronion, places the great Arsisius, or Orsiesius, with Putabastus, Serapion, and others.]

Whose cell did she not enter? At whose feet did she not fall? In every saint she believed that she saw Christ, and whatever she bestowed upon them, she rejoiced that she had bestowed upon the Lord.

A marvelous zeal, and a courage scarcely credible in a woman! Forgetful of her sex and bodily weakness, she wished to live among the many thousands of monks with her young companions. Perhaps, if all had welcomed her, she would have obtained this, had not a greater desire for the holy places drawn her back.

Because of the fierce heat, she traveled by ship from Pelusium to Maiuma and returned with such speed that one would have thought her a bird.

Not long afterward, intending to remain forever in holy Bethlehem, she stayed for three years in a narrow lodging, until she built little cells and monasteries and established beside the road lodging places for various pilgrims, where Mary and Joseph had found no lodging.

[Note: Gravina understands this in the sense that Mary and Joseph would find lodging.]

Thus far let her journey be described—the journey she made, accompanied by many virgins and by her daughter.

### 15.

Now let her virtue be described more fully, the virtue that was uniquely hers. In setting it forth, with God as judge and witness, I declare that I add nothing and exaggerate nothing, as eulogists do; rather, lest I go beyond the truth of the matter [or: the limit], I shall omit much, lest among detractors—who constantly gnaw at me with their genuine tooth—I be thought to invent and to adorn Aesop’s crow with borrowed colors.

[Note: Some manuscripts apud Bollandus read “whose genuine character is always to gnaw the innocent with a proud tooth,” evidently through the invention of an unlearned glossator.]

The first virtue of Christians is humility. She humbled herself so deeply that anyone who had not seen her, but wished to see her because of the fame of her name, would not have believed that she was Paula, but rather the lowest of servant girls.

Although she was surrounded by frequent choirs of virgins, in dress, voice, bearing, and gait she was the least of all.

Never after her husband’s death, until the day of her falling asleep, did she eat with any man, even though she knew him to be holy and established at the height of episcopal dignity.

She did not go to the baths unless she was in danger. Even during the most severe fever she had no soft bedding on her bed, but rested upon the hardest ground, spread with little haircloths—if that can be called rest which she joined day and night to almost unbroken prayers—fulfilling the words of the Psalter: “Every night I will wash my bed; with my tears I will water my couch” (Ps. 6:7).

[Note: Victorius found in two manuscripts: “In which fountain of tears, etc.”]

You would have thought that she had fountains of tears: she wept so much over slight sins that you might have thought her guilty of the gravest crimes.

When we repeatedly urged her to spare her eyes and preserve them for reading the Gospel, she would say:

“My face must be disfigured, the face that I often painted against God’s command with rouge, white lead, and kohl. The body that had indulged in many luxuries must be afflicted. Long laughter must be repaid with continual weeping. Soft linen and the most precious silks must be exchanged for the roughness of haircloth. I pleased my husband and the world; now I desire to please Christ.”

If I wished to praise chastity in her, I might seem superfluous, since even when she was still a woman of the world she was an example to all the matrons of Rome. She conducted herself in such a way that even slanderous rumor never dared fabricate anything against her.

Nothing was gentler than her spirit, and nothing more gracious toward the humble. She did not court the powerful; yet neither did she disdainfully despise the proud and those seeking petty glory.

If she saw a poor person, she supported him; if a rich person, she urged him to do good. Her generosity alone exceeded all measure.

By providing interest-bearing loans, she also frequently took on debts herself, so that she might deny no alms to anyone who asked.

[Note: Two Regina manuscripts incorrectly offer *usuram iterum*—“interest again”—instead of *versuram*. See Donatus on Terence’s *Phormio* 5.2 at the end.]

I confess my error: because she was excessively lavish in giving, I reproved her, citing the Apostle:

“Not that there should be relief for others and distress for you, but that, by equality at the present time, your abundance should supply their need, and their abundance your need” (2 Cor. 8:13).

I also cited this saying from the Savior’s Gospel: “Let the one who has two tunics give one to the person who has none” (Luke 3:11).

I told her that she must take care lest she should always be unable to do what she gladly did, and I advanced many arguments of this sort. With remarkable modesty and very few words she disposed of them all, calling God as witness that she did everything for His name. Her one desire, she said, was to die a beggar; not to leave a single coin to her daughter; and to be wrapped at her funeral in someone else’s shroud.

Finally she added:

“If I ask, I shall find many who will give to me. But if this beggar does not receive from me what I can give him even from another’s property, and he dies, from whom will his soul be required?”

[Note: One Regina manuscript reads: “and if he should die.” Shortly afterward, some manuscripts read “but she, with more ardent faith.”]

I wished to be more cautious with household resources, but she, with more ardent faith, was joined to the Savior with her whole heart. She followed the poor Lord, poor in spirit, returning to Him what she had received and becoming poor for His sake.

In the end she obtained what she desired and left her daughter deeply in debt. To this day she trusts that the debt will be repaid, not by her own strength, but by Christ’s mercy.

### 16.

Most matrons are accustomed to give gifts to their trumpeters and, after lavishing their generosity upon a few, to withdraw their hand from the rest.

[Note: One Regina manuscript reads: “Most Roman women customarily give gifts to their trumpeters.”]

Paula was entirely free of this fault. She distributed her money to each person according to what each required—not for luxury, but for necessity.

[Note: The sentence “No poor person ever returned from her empty-handed,” absent from the older Regina manuscript, is not found there. Perhaps it has also been misplaced through a faulty transposition.]

No poor person ever returned from her empty-handed. She achieved this not through the magnitude of her wealth but through prudent distribution, always repeating:

“Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. 5:7).

And:

“As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin” (Ecclus. 16:9).

And:

“Make friends for yourselves from the unrighteous mammon, so that they may receive you into the eternal dwellings” (Luke 16:9).

And:

“Give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you” (Luke 11:41).

She also repeated Daniel’s words, by which he admonished King Nebuchadnezzar to redeem his sins through almsgiving (Dan. 4).

She did not wish to pour money upon these stones, which pass away with earth and the world, but upon living stones that roll upon the earth (Zech. 9:36 according to the Septuagint), from which, as John’s Apocalypse says (chapters 16 and 22), the city of the great King is built. Scripture records that these stones are to be transformed into sapphire, emerald, jasper, and the other precious gems.

### 17.

Yet these things can be shared with the few, and the devil knows that they are not placed at the highest summit of virtue.

Therefore he speaks to the Lord, after Job’s possessions had been lost, his house overthrown, and his children killed:

“Skin for skin; and all that a man possesses he will give for his life. But stretch out your hand and touch his bones and his flesh, unless he blesses you to your face” (Job 2:4).

We know that many have given alms but have given nothing from their own bodies; that they have extended a hand to the needy but, overcome by the pleasure of the flesh, have whitened what was outside while inwardly being full of dead men’s bones.

But Paula was not such a person. She possessed such great self-restraint that she nearly exceeded the proper measure and brought bodily weakness upon herself through excessive fasting and labor.

Except on feast days, she scarcely took oil in her food. From this one fact one may judge what she thought of wine, sauces, fish,

[Note: The words “and milk,” retained by nearly all manuscripts and printed books, had also been omitted by Martianay after Erasmus.]

milk, honey, eggs, and the other things pleasant to the taste. Some people think themselves extremely abstinent in these matters; and if they have stuffed their bellies with such foods, they imagine their chastity secure.

### 18.

Virtue is always followed by envy, and “lightning strikes the highest mountains” (from Horace).

It is not surprising that I say this of human beings, since even our Lord was crucified through the zeal of the Pharisees, and all the saints have had rivals. Even in paradise there was a serpent, through whose envy death entered the world (Wis. 2:24).

The Lord had raised up against her Hadad the Idumean, to buffet her lest she should exalt herself (1 Kings 11:14), and, as though by a thorn in the flesh, He frequently admonished her (2 Cor. 12:7),

lest the greatness of her virtues should carry her too high and, because of the vices of other women, she should think herself established in the heights.

[Note: Most manuscripts and printed copies read: “lest, through the greatness of her virtues, she should think more highly.” The reading we have retained agrees better with Paul’s meaning.]

I used to say that one must yield to envy and make room for madness, as Jacob had done with his brother Esau and David with his most obstinate enemy Saul: the one fled to Mesopotamia; the other surrendered himself to the Philistines, preferring to be subject to enemies rather than to the envious.

But she replied:

“You would rightly say this if the devil did not fight everywhere against God’s servants and handmaids, and did not go ahead of those who flee to every place; if I were not held here by love of the holy places, and if I could find my Bethlehem elsewhere in the world.

Why should I not overcome envy by patience? Why should I not break pride by humility and, when struck on one cheek, offer the other? Does not the Apostle Paul say, ‘Overcome evil with good’ (Rom. 12:21)?

Did the Apostles not rejoice when they suffered insult for the Lord? Did not the Savior Himself humble Himself, taking the form of a servant, and become obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross (Phil. 2:7), so that He might save us through His passion?

If Job had not fought and conquered in battle, he would not have received the crown of righteousness, nor would he have heard the Lord say, ‘Do you think that I have spoken to you in any other way than that you might appear righteous?’ (Job 4:2 according to the Septuagint).

In the Gospel those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake are called blessed (Matt. 5:10). A secure conscience knows [perhaps: “is secure”] that we suffer not because of sins, and that affliction in this world is the material of rewards.

When the enemy became more insolent and even rushed into quarrelsome words, she sang this from the Psalter:

‘When the sinner stood against me, I became silent and was quiet from good things’ (Ps. 38:2).

And again:

‘I, like a deaf man, did not hear, and like a mute who does not open his mouth.’

And:

‘I became like a man who does not hear and has no reproofs in his mouth’ (Ps. 37:14).

In temptations she revolved in her mind the words of Deuteronomy:

‘The Lord your God tests you, to know whether you love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul’ (Deut. 13:3).

In tribulations and distress she repeated Isaiah’s words:

‘You who are weaned from milk, you who are drawn away from the breast, expect tribulation upon tribulation, hope upon hope; yet a little while, because of the evil of lips, because of an alien tongue’ (Isa. 28:9ff. according to the Septuagint).

[Note: Two manuscripts apud Bollandus read “because of an alien tongue,” more closely corresponding to the Greek διὰ γλώσσης ἑτέρας.]

She explained the testimony of Scripture for her consolation: those who have been weaned—that is, those who have reached mature age—must endure tribulation upon tribulation in order to deserve to receive hope upon hope.

‘Knowing that tribulation produces endurance, endurance testing, and testing hope; and hope does not disappoint’ (Rom. 5:3–4).

And:

‘Although our outward man is corrupted, the inward man is renewed.’

And:

‘For this momentary lightness of our tribulation works in us an eternal weight of glory, since we do not look at the things that are seen but at those that are not seen. For the things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are not seen are eternal’ (2 Cor. 4:16ff.).

She would say that the time would not be long, even if it seemed slow to human impatience, before God’s help followed, since He says:

‘At an acceptable time I heard you, and on the day of salvation I helped you’ (Isa. 49:8).

Nor were deceitful lips and the tongues of the wicked to be feared, when we rejoice with the Lord as helper and ought to hear Him warning us through the Prophet:

‘Do not fear the reproaches of men, and do not dread their blasphemies. For as a garment, so the worm will consume them; and as wool, so the moth will devour them’ (Isa. 51:7–8).

And:

‘By your patience you will possess your souls’ (Luke 21:19).

And:

‘The sufferings of this present time are not worthy of comparison with the future glory that will be revealed in us’ (Rom. 8:18).

And elsewhere:

‘To endure tribulation upon tribulation’ (Eph. 3).

Thus we must act patiently in everything that happens to us.

‘The patient man is very wise; but the fainthearted is exceedingly foolish’ (Prov. 14:29).

[Note: One Regina manuscript more correctly reads, it seems, “the man who is abundant in prudence,” from the Greek πολύς ἐν φρονήσει.]

## 18

In illnesses and frequent weakness she would say: “When I am weak, then I am strong” (2 Cor. 12:10). “We have this treasure in earthen vessels” (ibid. 4:7), until “this mortal puts on immortality, and this corruptible is clothed with incorruption” (1 Cor. 15:53). And again: “As the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so through Christ our consolation also abounds” (2 Cor. 1:5). And thereafter: “As you are partners in the sufferings, so shall you be in the consolation” (ibid. v. 7).

In sorrow she sang: “Why are you sad, my soul, and why do you trouble me? Hope in God, for I shall yet confess him, the salvation of my countenance and my God” (Ps. 41:12). In dangers she would say: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Luke 9:23). And again: “Whoever wishes to save his soul will lose it.” And: “Whoever loses his soul for my sake will save it” (ibid. 24).

When she was informed of the loss of her household property and the ruin of her entire patrimony, she would say: “For what does it profit a person if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul? Or what exchange shall a person give for his soul?” (Matt. 16:25). And: “Naked I came from my mother’s womb, and naked shall I return. As it pleased the Lord, so it has happened. Blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1:21). And this: “Do not love the world, or the things that are in the world. For everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of this life; it is not from the Father, but from the world. And the world passes away, and its desire” (1 John 2:15–17).

I know that severe illnesses of her children, and especially of her Toxotius, whom she loved most dearly, had been reported to her. When she had fulfilled that saying by her courage—“I was troubled, and I did not speak” (Ps. 76)—she burst out with these words: “Whoever loves son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me” (Matt. 10:37). And while praying to the Lord she said: “Take possession, Lord, of the children of those who have been put to death” (Ps. 78:11), those who daily put their bodies to death for you.

A certain slanderer—an especially pernicious kind of person—pretended to be well disposed and reported that, because of the excessive fervor of her virtues, some people thought her insane and said that her brain ought to be soothed. To him she replied: “We have become a spectacle to the world, to angels, and to human beings” (1 Cor. 4:9). And: “We are fools for Christ’s sake, but what is foolishness in God is wiser than human beings” (ibid. 1:25). Hence the Savior also says to the Father: “You know my foolishness” (Ps. 68:6). And again: “I have become as a portent to many, but you are my strong helper” (Ps. 70:7). “I have become like a beast before you, and I am always with you.”

In the Gospel, his relatives, as though he were not in possession of his mind, wished to bind him (John 10), while his opponents mocked him, saying: “He has a demon, and he is a Samaritan” (ibid. 8:48). And: “By Beelzebul, the prince of demons, he casts out demons” (Matt. 12:24).

But let us hear the Apostle exhorting us: “This is our glory, the testimony of our conscience, that we have conducted ourselves in the world in holiness and sincerity and in the grace of God” (1 Cor. 1:12). And let us hear the Lord saying to the Apostles: “Therefore the world hates you, because you are not of the world. For if you were of the world, the world would love what was its own” (John 15:19).

And she turned these words toward the Lord himself: “You know the hidden things of the heart.” And: “All these things have come upon us, yet we have not forgotten you, nor have we acted wickedly against your covenant, nor has our heart turned back” (Ps. 43:18–19). And: “For your sake we are put to death all day long; we are counted as sheep for slaughter” (Rom. 8:36). “But the Lord is my helper; I shall not fear what a human being can do to me” (Ps. 117:6).

[Note: Previously the reading was *legi*, “I have read,” less suitably. Shortly afterward, *extra eum* should be understood instead of *extra Dominum*, “outside the Lord.” This is a more serious matter.]

For she had read: “My son, honor the Lord, and you shall be strengthened, and fear no one outside the Lord” (Prov. 7:1, according to the Septuagint).

With these and similar testimonies, as with the armor of God, she armed herself against every vice, but especially against raging envy. By enduring insults, she calmed the fury of a savage heart. Finally, right up to the day of her death, both her patience and the zeal of others were evident to all: that envy gnaws at its own author, and while it tries to injure a rival, rages in its own fury against itself.

## 19

I shall also speak of the organization of the monastery, and how she turned the continence of holy women to her own gain. She sowed carnal things in order to reap spiritual ones (1 Cor. 9); she gave earthly things in order to receive heavenly ones; she granted what was brief in exchange for what was eternal.

After the monastery of the men, which she had entrusted to men to govern, she gathered from various provinces many virgins—both of noble, middle, and lowly birth—and divided them into three companies and monasteries.

[Note: The older Regina manuscript does not recognize the word “three”; and, instead of *monasteriaque*, one manuscript of Saint Maximinus, according to Bollandus, reads *per monasteria*, “through the monasteries.” He himself would have preferred *monasterium* in the singular; for Jerome had just announced that he would speak of the order of one monastery, not of monasteries. The number “three companies” is very likely an invention of others based on the classification found here—noble, middle, and lowly in birth. Paula could easily have assigned those virgins to fewer or more companies, not according to rank of birth, but with regard to age, studies, disposition, virtues, and other such considerations. As for the monastery, we are less concerned whether one or several should be mentioned, since it is certain that all were enclosed within the same precinct and assembled several times a day, especially for the chanting of the canonical hours. Quaresmius, in *Pilgrimage* 2.14, thinks that he discovered it from ancient ruins and from Paula’s name, by which it was marked, and describes it.]

She arranged matters so that they were separated in work and food but joined in psalmody and prayers. After the *Alleluia* had been sung—which served as the signal that they were to assemble—no one was permitted to remain seated.

[Note: See Letter 38 to Marcella, §4, concerning Blaesilla: “Now she quickly rises to pray, and with her ringing voice, taking the *Alleluia* from the others, she is the first to begin praising her Lord.”]

The first to arrive, or one of the first, awaited the arrival of the others, urging them to work by modesty and example, not by fear. In the morning, at the Third, Sixth, and Ninth Hours, at Vespers, and at midnight, they sang the Psalter in order.

[Note: This was the custom in many places, especially in the churches and communities of monks in Egypt: the Psalms were not sung, as today, by everyone together in alternating verses, but individually, one Psalm being sung by each person in turn. This is what Jerome here and elsewhere, and other writers of his and later ages, call “singing the Psalter in order.” Cassian offers a notable passage in Book 2, chapter 5: “When those who wish to celebrate the daily offices of prayer rise to do so, one person rises in the midst to sing the Psalms, while all sit—as is still the custom in parts of Egypt—and fix their whole attention upon the words of the one singing. And in chapter 20: ‘Such silence is maintained by all that, although so numerous a multitude of brothers has gathered together, apart from the one who rises and sings the Psalm in the midst, no human being at all seems to be present.’ See below, §39, and Letter 125 to Rusticus.”]

No sister was permitted to be ignorant of the Psalms or to fail to learn something daily from the holy Scriptures. Only on Sunday did they go out to church, which stood beside the place where they lived.

[Note: This was the cave of the Nativity of Christ, which Constantine and Helena had built.]

Each group followed its own mother-superior. Returning together from there, they applied themselves to their assigned work and made garments either for themselves or for the others.

If one was noble, she was not permitted to have a companion from her own household, lest, remembering former practices, she revive the old error of a frivolous childhood and renew it through frequent conversation. Their clothing was the same for all. They used linen only for wiping their hands.

Their separation from men was so strict that she kept them apart even from eunuchs, lest she provide any opportunity for malicious speech, which is accustomed to attack holy people as a consolation for wrongdoing.

If any woman came late to the Psalms or was slow at her work, she dealt with her in various ways. If she was irascible, she used gentleness; if patient, correction, imitating the Apostle’s words: “What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod, or with love and a spirit of gentleness?”

Except for food and clothing, she allowed them to possess nothing, according to Paul: “Having food and clothing, with these we shall be content” (1 Tim. 6:8).

[Note: Elsewhere the reading is *consuetudo* in the nominative. Sallust, *Catiline* 11, whom Jerome copies, says: “Avarice is always boundless and insatiable; neither abundance nor want diminishes it.” See Theophilus, *Paschal* III, no. 15, and Letter 53 to Paulinus, no. 10.]

She did not want the habit of possessing more to provide an opening for avarice, which is satisfied by no resources: the more it has, the more it seeks, and neither abundance nor poverty diminishes it.

When they quarreled with one another, she reconciled them with the gentlest speech. She broke the wanton flesh of the young women by frequent and repeated fasts, preferring that their stomachs should suffer rather than their minds.

If she saw someone more elaborately dressed, she reproved her error by furrowing her brow and making her face stern, saying that bodily cleanliness and elegance of dress were uncleanness of the soul. She also said that an indecent or wanton word should never be uttered by a virgin’s mouth, since such signs reveal a lustful mind and the vices of the inner person through the outward person.

If she noticed that a woman was talkative, chattering, shameless, and fond of quarrels, and that, although often admonished, she refused to change, she made her pray among the last and outside the company of the sisters, at the entrance to the dining room, and eat separately. Thus shame corrected the one whom rebuke had not corrected.

She detested theft as sacrilege. What among worldly people is considered trivial or nothing at all, she said was a very serious offense in monasteries.

What should I say about her kindness and diligence toward the sick, whom she comforted with extraordinary attentions and services? Although she provided everything generously to other sick women, even giving them meat to eat, whenever she herself was ill she showed herself no indulgence. In this she seemed unequal, changing kindness toward others into harshness toward herself.

## 20

No young woman, though possessing a sound and vigorous body, had devoted herself to such continence as she did with her broken, aged, and weakened little body. I admit that in this matter she was excessively stubborn: she spared herself nothing and yielded to no one who admonished her.

I shall relate what I myself experienced. In the month of July, during the fiercest heat, she was seized by a burning fever. After she had been given up for dead and then, by God’s mercy, began to recover, the physicians insisted that, for the restoration of her body, she needed a little and weak wine, lest by drinking water she develop dropsy. I secretly asked blessed Pope Epiphanius to admonish her—indeed, to compel her—to drink wine.

She, being prudent and quick-witted, immediately perceived the plot. With a smile, she indicated that what he would say was my doing. What more is there to say? When the blessed Pontiff had gone outside after many exhortations, I asked him what he had accomplished. He replied: “I achieved only this: she nearly persuaded an old man not to drink wine.”

I report this not because I approve of burdens undertaken thoughtlessly and beyond one’s strength—the Scripture warns, “Do not take a burden upon yourself”—but because I wish to show by this perseverance also the ardor of her mind and the desire of her faithful soul, as she sang: “My soul thirsted for you; how greatly my flesh also thirsted for you” (Ps. 62:2).

It is difficult to keep the proper measure in all things. Indeed, according to the philosophers’ saying, **μεσότης ἡ ἀρετή, ὑπερβολὴ κακία**—“virtue is the mean, excess is vice.”

[Note: Older printed editions add the verb *πέλεται* and an interpretation of the whole sentence, namely, “moderation is virtue, and excess is reckoned vice.” The manuscripts have neither, nor did these words proceed from Jerome’s pen. The word *κακία* is correctly read in the nominative; in the Benedictine edition it was wrongly printed as *κακίαν*. This saying is attributed to Aristotle, who explains it at greater length in his letter to Demetrias.]

We can express the same thing in one brief saying: “Nothing in excess” (Terence, *Andria*, Act 1).

She had such stubbornness in abstaining from food; yet in mourning she was gentle and was shaken by the deaths of her loved ones, especially her children. For at the deaths of both her son and her daughters she was always in danger.

When she marked her mouth and stomach with the sign of the cross, trying to ease her motherly grief by that impression, emotion overcame her. Her trusting mind and a parent’s inward feelings threw her into turmoil; though she conquered in spirit, she was conquered by the frailty of the body. Once illness seized her, it possessed her for a long time, bringing anxiety to us and danger to herself.

In this condition she rejoiced, repeatedly saying: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7:24).

Let the discerning reader say that I am writing blame instead of praise. I call to witness Jesus, whom she served and whom I desire to serve, that I am inventing nothing on either side, but, as a Christian writing about a Christian, am presenting what is true: that is, I am writing history, not a panegyric, and what were her vices were the virtues of others.

I call them vices according to my own judgment and that of all the sisters and brothers who love her and seek her in her absence.

## 21

For the rest, she completed her course and kept the faith, and now enjoys the crown of righteousness (2 Tim. 4:7). She follows the Lamb wherever he goes (Rev. 14). She is satisfied, because she hungered, and joyfully sings: “As we have heard, so also have we seen, in the city of the Lord of hosts, in the city of our God” (Ps. 47:9).

O blessed exchange of things! She wept so that she might always laugh. She rejected broken cisterns so that she might find the Lord, the fountain. She was clothed in sackcloth so that she might now wear white garments and say: “You have torn my sackcloth and clothed me with gladness” (Ps. 29:12).

She ate ashes like bread and mixed her drink with weeping (Ps. 101:10), saying: “My tears have been my bread day and night” (Ps. 41:4), so that she might feed forever on the bread of angels and sing: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. 33:9). And: “My heart has uttered a good word; I speak of my works to the King” (Ps. 44:1).

She saw fulfilled in herself the words of Isaiah—or rather, of the Lord through Isaiah: “Behold, those who serve me shall eat, but you shall hunger. Behold, those who serve me shall drink, but you shall thirst. Behold, those who serve me shall rejoice, but you shall be put to shame. Behold, those who serve me shall exult in joy” [the manuscripts supply “in joy,” as does the Septuagint, ἐν εὐφροσύνῃ; the Hebrew is not different in sense], “but you shall cry out because of the pain of your heart, and because of the anguish of spirit you shall howl” (Isa. 65:13–14).

I had said that she had always fled broken cisterns in order to find the Lord, the fountain, so that she might joyfully sing: “As the deer longs for springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God. When shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Ps. 41:1).

## 22

Let me therefore touch briefly on how she avoided the muddy pools of heretics and regarded them as pagans.

[Note: Baronius thinks this man was Palladius, since, as is learned from the *Lausiac History*, ch. 77, he lived for one year at Bethlehem and was especially devoted to Origenist errors. One manuscript reads *sanctiolus*, a new and rather barbarous word, instead of *sciolus*. Gravius reads *veterator et callidus*.]

A clever and crafty deceiver, who seemed to himself learned and somewhat educated, began, without my knowledge, to put questions to her and say: “What sin did an infant commit that it should be seized by a demon? At what age shall we rise again? If at the same age at which we die, then nurses will be needed after the resurrection.”

[Note: Some printed editions prefer: “If at another age.” But even earlier, instead of *morimur*, “we die,” one might perhaps read *nascimur*, “we are born,” so that nurses would be needed. Augustine reports that such quibbles were commonly used by pagans to attack and ridicule the resurrection, *City of God* 22.12. Origen himself did not depart very far from them. It is worthwhile to append here the following passage from his commentary on Psalm 1:5, as translated by Petavius:

“Therefore, if we ask what sort of thing the resurrection will be, they answer that it will be of the bodies that surround us. When we press them to say whether the whole substance of those bodies will return, before they have carefully considered the matter they declare that the whole will return. If, adapting ourselves to their simplicity and saying nothing about the fluid and changeable nature of bodies, we ask again whether all the blood that has at various times flowed from a cut vein will rise again, and likewise all the hairs that have ever grown, or only those that appeared near the time of our death, they sometimes stumble over the question and say that the matter must be left to God, so that he may determine whatever he wishes. At other times, as though agreeing with us, they assert that only those hairs which we had near the end of life will rise with us.
