But those among them who are more energetic, lest they be forced by their argument to gather together all the blood that has usually been discharged from our bodies, and likewise all the flesh that through illnesses has passed into sweat or some similar substance, declare that our bodies will rise as they were at the time of death.”]

“If it is otherwise, there will certainly not be a resurrection of the dead, but a transformation into others. Will there also be a difference of sex, male and female, or will there not? If there is, marriages and intercourse will follow, and also generation. If there is not, then, once the difference of sex has been removed, the same bodies will not rise. For ‘the earthly dwelling weighs down the mind that thinks of many things’ (Wis. 9:15). But they will be subtle and spiritual, as the Apostle says: ‘It is sown an animal body; it will rise a spiritual body’ (1 Cor. 15:44).”

By all this he wanted to prove that rational creatures had fallen into bodies because of certain vices and ancient sins, and that, according to the variety and deserts of their sins, they were born in one condition or another: either enjoying bodily health and the wealth and nobility of their parents, or entering diseased bodies and the homes of the poor, paying the penalty for their former sins and being shut up in the present age and in bodies as in a prison.

When she heard this and reported it to me, pointing out the man, I was forced to resist the most wicked viper and deadly beast of which the Psalmist speaks: “Do not hand over the souls of those who confess you to beasts” (Ps. 73:19). And: “Rebuke the beasts of the reed” (Ps. 67:31), those who write iniquity, speak falsehood against the Lord, and lift their mouths on high.

I confronted the man and, by a brief question, refuted his arguments, directed at the woman whom he was trying to deceive. I asked him whether he believed that there would be a resurrection of the dead or not.

[Note: Victorius reads *conclusi dicens, utrum*, etc. We should prefer *quaerens*, “asking,” or something similar; but neither reading is found in the manuscripts.] When he answered that he did believe, I continued: “Will the same bodies rise, or different ones?” When he said, “The same,” I asked: “In the same sex, or in another?”

When he remained silent in response to the questions and, like a serpent, moved his head this way and that so as not to be struck, I said: “Because you are silent, I shall answer for you and draw the necessary conclusions. If a woman will not rise as a woman, nor a man as a man, there will be no resurrection of the dead, because sex has limbs, and limbs make up the whole body. But if there will be neither sex nor limbs, where will be the resurrection of bodies, which do not exist without sex and limbs? And if there is no resurrection of bodies, there will certainly be no resurrection of the dead.”

As for your objection concerning marriage—that if the same limbs remain, marriage must follow—the Savior dispels it when he says: “You are in error, not knowing the Scriptures or the power of God. For in the resurrection of the dead they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like the angels” (Matt. 22:29–30).

When he says “they neither marry nor are given in marriage,” he demonstrates the persistence of the distinction between the sexes. No one says of a stone or a piece of wood, “They neither marry nor are given in marriage,” since such things do not possess the nature of marrying. Rather, he speaks of those who could marry but, through the grace and power of Christ, do not marry.

If you object, “How then shall we be like the angels, when among angels there is neither male nor female?” listen briefly: the Lord promises us not the substance of angels, but their manner of life and blessedness. Thus John the Baptist was called an angel before he was beheaded (Luke 7:27), and all the saints and virgins of God, even in this age, express the life of angels in themselves. When it is said, “You shall be like the angels,” likeness is promised; nature is not changed.

## 23

Answer this as well: how do you interpret the fact that Thomas touched the hands of the risen Lord and saw his side pierced by the spear (John 20)?

[Note: Martianaeus had printed *tetigerit*, “had touched.” All our manuscripts and Victorius, as we have restored the text, read *palpaverit*, which agrees with the Gospel text and with what Jerome immediately adds: “whose hands were touched,” and so forth.]

Peter saw the Lord standing on the shore and eating a piece of broiled fish and a honeycomb (Luke 24). Whoever stood certainly had feet. Whoever showed his wounded side certainly had a belly and a chest, without which there are no sides joined to the belly and chest. Whoever spoke spoke with a tongue, palate, and teeth. For just as a plectrum strikes the strings, so the tongue strikes against the teeth and produces articulate sound. The one whose hands were touched consequently also had arms.

Since he is said to have had all his limbs, he necessarily had a whole body, which is composed of limbs—not a female body, but a male one, that is, of the same sex in which he died.

If you object, “Then shall we also eat after the resurrection?” and ask how he entered through closed doors, contrary to the nature of solid and substantial bodies, you will hear the answer: Do not drag the faith of the resurrection into ridicule on account of food. For he also commanded food to be given to the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue after she had been raised (Mark 5:43). And Lazarus, who had been dead four days, is written to have dined with him (John 12:2), so that their resurrection would not be thought a phantom.

But if he entered through closed doors, and for that reason you try to prove that he had a spiritual and airy body, then, before he suffered, because he walked upon the sea contrary to the nature of heavy bodies, he also had a spiritual body. And the Apostle Peter, who likewise walked upon the waters with an unsteady step, must be believed to have had a spiritual body, since God’s power and might are displayed all the more when something occurs contrary to nature.

And so that you may know that in the greatness of miracles the omnipotence of God, not a change of nature, is demonstrated: he who was walking by faith began to sink through unbelief, unless the Lord’s hand had lifted him up, saying: “You of little faith, why did you doubt?” (Matt. 14:31).

But I am amazed that you harden your forehead when the Lord says: “Put your finger here and touch my hands; and extend your hand and place it in my side; and do not be unbelieving, but believing” (John 20:27).

And elsewhere: “See my hands and my feet, because it is I myself. Touch me and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me have.” And when he had said this, he showed them his hands and feet (Luke 24:34, 40).

You hear of bones, flesh, feet, and hands, yet you invent for me Stoic globes and certain airy ravings.

[Note: Some manuscripts read “hands and side” instead of “feet,” as does the Greek καὶ τοὺς πόδας, “and the feet.” Compare the discussion of the Stoics’ spheres, which he mentions immediately afterward, in Letter 133 to Ctesiphon, §3, where he ridicules Plato’s ἀψῖδες, “arches.” Tertullian, *On the Soul*: “Our sleep is in the ether with Plato, or around the moon with the Stoics’ Endymions.” See also Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* 1.]

## 24

Furthermore, if you ask why an infant is seized by a demon when it has committed no sins, or at what age we shall rise, since we die at different ages, you will reluctantly have to accept the words: “The judgments of God are a great deep” (Ps. 35:7). And: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How inscrutable are his judgments and searchable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?” (Rom. 11:33–34).

[Note: Some manuscripts read *O profundum*, “O depth,” instead of *altitudo*, “height”; the former reading is more common in Jerome. Concerning the following word, *investigabiles*, “searchable,” instead of *ininvestigabiles*, “unsearchable,” see the end of Letter 78 to Fabiola.]

The difference of ages does not change the reality of bodies. Since our bodies daily flow away and either grow or diminish, are we then as many different human beings as we undergo daily changes? Was I one person when I was ten years old, another when I was thirty, another when I was fifty, and another now that my head is entirely gray?

Therefore, according to the traditions of the churches and the Apostle Paul, we must answer that we shall rise “to a perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ” (Eph. 4), in which state the Jews suppose Adam was created.

[Note: See *Midrash Tehillim* on Psalm 92, and the *Book of Kuzari*, Part I, chapter 95, as well as others—although, as usual, they teem with exceedingly foolish fables about Adam’s condition. Augustine’s *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter 13 and following, should also be consulted. Different writers explain Paul’s testimony differently; Ambrose, for example, says: “By ‘perfect man’ he does not signify temporal age and measure.”]

And we read that the Lord the Savior rose; and I have brought forward many other things from both Testaments to choke the heretic.

## 25

From that day onward she began to detest the man and all who held the same doctrine, so that she publicly proclaimed them enemies of the Lord.

I have said this not in order briefly to refute a heresy to which many volumes would have to be devoted, but to display the faith of so great a woman, **who preferred** to endure the perpetual hostility of human beings rather than provoke the offense of God by harmful friendships.

## 26

Let me therefore continue as I began: nothing was more teachable than her intellect. She was slow to speak and quick to hear (James 1:19), mindful of that command: “Hear, O Israel, and be silent” (Deut. 27:9, according to the Septuagint).

She knew the holy Scriptures by heart. Although she loved the historical sense and called it the foundation of truth, she nevertheless followed the spiritual understanding more closely, and by this summit protected the soul’s edification.

Finally, she compelled me to read through the Old and New Testaments with her daughter while I explained them. I refused out of modesty, but because of her persistence and repeated requests I complied, teaching what I had learned—not from myself, that is, from presumption, the worst teacher, but from distinguished men of the Church.

Whenever I hesitated and openly confessed that I did not know, she would not at all be satisfied with my answer. Instead, by continual questioning she compelled me, from the many and varied opinions, to indicate which seemed to me the more probable.

I shall say something else that may seem incredible to her detractors. She wished to learn Hebrew, which I had partly learned from adolescence through much labor and sweat, and which I do not abandon through tireless study, lest it abandon me. And she did learn it, so that she sang the Psalms in Hebrew and pronounced the language without any trace of Latin pronunciation.

[Note: Some manuscripts, including those cited by Bollandus, perhaps more correctly read: “and the Greek language as well.” Concerning Hebrew, he had testified to the same thing much earlier in Letter 39 to this same Paula, where, speaking of Blaesilla, he says: “She had overcome the difficulty of the Hebrew language so completely that, in learning and singing the Psalms, she competed with her mother Paula.”]

We see this to the present day in her holy daughter Eustochium, who always clung to her mother and obeyed her commands, so that she never slept without her, never went out without her, and never took food without her. She did not possess even a single coin under her own control, but rejoiced that her mother distributed both her paternal and maternal little inheritance among the poor, and regarded piety toward her parent as the greatest inheritance and wealth.

I must not pass over in silence how greatly she rejoiced when she heard that her granddaughter Paula, born of Laeta and Toxotius—or rather conceived through a vow and the promise of future virginity—was already babbling the *Alleluia* in her cradle and among her rattles, and breaking off the names of her grandmother and aunt into half-formed words.

[Note: Recall the preceding letter, §1, especially the passage: “With her grandfather present and rejoicing, little Paula’s still-babbling tongue resounded with Christ’s *Alleluia*”; and §3, where it says that she was born from a promise, consecrated to Christ before she was born, and conceived by her mother in the womb only after she had first been conceived through vows.]

In this alone she felt a longing for her homeland: that she might know that her son, daughter-in-law, and granddaughter had renounced the world and served Christ. And she obtained this in part. Her granddaughter is reserved for Christ’s bridal veil; her daughter-in-law, surrendering herself to eternal chastity, follows her mother-in-law in works, faith, and almsgiving, and strives at Rome to reproduce what the other accomplished at Jerusalem.

## 27

What are we doing, my soul? Why are you afraid to come to her death? For a long time now this book has been growing excessively long, while we fear reaching the end, as though her death could be delayed if we remained silent and occupied ourselves with her praises.

Thus far we have sailed with favorable winds, and the keel has furrowed the rippling surface of the sea.

[Note: One manuscript of Saint Maximinus reads “gliding over the sea’s back”; *tambens*, “rising and swelling,” may perhaps be better. Immediately afterward, instead of *montibus*, “mountains,” Victorius and others read *motibus*, “movements.” Finally, our manuscripts and others cited by Bollandus read *utriusque monasterii*, “of both monasteries,” instead of *utrique nostrum*, “for both of us.”]

Now our speech has run upon the rocks, and amid the swelling mountain-waves shipwreck threatens both of us. We are forced to say: “Teacher, save us; we are perishing!” (Mark 4:38; Luke 8:24). And this: “Awake! Why do you sleep, O Lord?” (Ps. 43:23).

For who could narrate Paula’s death with dry eyes? She fell into a very serious illness—or rather, she found what she desired: to leave us and be joined more fully to the Lord.

During this illness, the always-tested devotion of her daughter Eustochium toward her mother was demonstrated even more clearly before all. Eustochium herself sat beside the little bed, held the fan, supported her mother’s head, placed a cushion beneath her, rubbed her feet, warmed her stomach with her hand, arranged the soft bedding, tempered the warm water, placed the cloth—or, according to another reading, the chamber pot—within reach, anticipated the duties of all the maidservants, and considered anything another person might have done to have been taken away from her own reward.

With what prayers, lamentations, and groans she moved back and forth between her reclining mother and the Lord’s cave, lest she be deprived of such companionship, lest she live in her mother’s absence, lest she be carried on the same bier!

But, O fragile and fleeting nature of mortals—and unless Christ’s faith lifts us to heaven and promises the soul immortality—the condition of bodies is the same as that of beasts and cattle. The same death comes to the just and the unjust, the good and the bad, the pure and the impure, the one who sacrifices and the one who does not sacrifice. As is the good person, so is the sinner; as is the one who swears, so is the one who fears an oath. Human beings and animals alike dissolve into ash and dust.

28. [Note: [Col. 0904] In all our manuscripts, in other words: “Why do I delay so long and, lingering over other matters, make my grief longer?”] Why do I delay so long and, by postponing my grief, make it longer? The wisest of women sensed that death was near; and while one part of her body and limbs was growing cold, only the warmth of her soul still throbbed in her sacred breast. Nevertheless, as though she were going to her own people and leaving strangers behind, she whispered these verses:

“Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house and the place where your glory dwells” (Psalm 25:8). And: “How beloved are your tents, Lord of hosts! My soul longs and languishes for the courts of the Lord” (Psalm 83:1). And: “I have chosen to be rejected in the house of my God rather than to dwell in the tents of sinners” (ibid. 11).

When I asked her why she was silent, why she did not wish to answer when I called out to her whether anything pained her [Note: [Col. 0904] We have added, on their authority, the word *inclāmantī* (“calling out”), which all the older manuscripts we use contain.], she replied in Greek that she had no trouble at all [Note: [Col. 0904] Οὐδέν ἐμοί γέγονε χεῖρον: “Nothing worse has happened to me.” See Aelian, book 2, concerning Gorgias.], but saw everything as quiet and peaceful. After this she fell silent; and, with her eyes closed, as though she were already looking down upon mortal things, she repeated the same verses until her soul departed, so that we could scarcely hear what she was saying [Note: [Col. 0904] Two copies of Regina’s text read: “she repeated the verses, scarcely so that we could hear by bringing our ear close—or rather, scarcely so that we could hear what she was saying.” The Cistercian version is shorter: “scarcely so that I could hear what she was saying.”]. Holding her finger to her lips, she traced the sign of the cross upon them. Her spirit was failing, and she was gasping toward death; and her soul, eager to break free, turned even the rasping sound by which mortal life comes to an end into praises of the Lord.

The bishops of Jerusalem [Joannes] and of the other cities were present, together with priests of the lower rank [or: lower-ranking priests] and an innumerable multitude of Levites. The entire monastery was filled with choirs of virgins and monks. As soon as she heard the Bridegroom calling, “Arise, come, my nearest one, my beautiful one, my dove; for look, winter has passed and gone, the rain has departed” (Song of Songs 2:10–11), she answered joyfully: “Flowers have appeared on the earth; the time of pruning has come” (ibid. 12). And: “I believe that I shall see the goodness of the Lord in the land of the living” (Psalm 26:13).

29. From then on there was no howling or mourning, as usually occurs among worldly people; instead, swarms of voices resounded with psalms in different languages [Ms.: “from the heart”]. When she had been carried by the hands of the bishops, who placed their necks beneath the bier, while some prelates carried lamps and wax candles before it and others led choirs of psalm-singers, she was laid in the middle of the Church of the Savior’s cave.

The whole multitude of the cities of Palestine gathered for her funeral. What monk hidden in the desert remained in his cell? What secluded chambers of virgins concealed them [Note: [Col. 0904] Here too all the manuscripts agree. Victorius instead read: “they considered it sacrilegious”]? He considered it sacrilege not to have rendered the final service to such a woman.

Widows and the poor displayed the garments she had supplied to them, after the example of Dorcas (Acts 9:39). The entire multitude of the needy cried out that they had lost their mother and their nurse [Mss.: “little nurse”]. And—what is remarkable—no pallor had altered her face; rather, a certain dignity and gravity had filled her features, so that you would have thought her not dead but asleep.

[Note: [Col. 0905] We have deleted the word *Hebraeo* (“in Hebrew”), which earlier editions prefixed here and which Martianaeus asserted on the basis of a single, marginal note in the Cluniac manuscript. It was absent from the other manuscripts, and we have never found it in any of them. Moreover, as Bollandus also observed, Syriac was the vernacular language there, and there were surely few at that time who knew Hebrew so well. A little later the Regina manuscript reads: “not only for three days, and until,” etc.]

Psalms sounded in sequence in Greek, Latin, and Syriac [Note: [Col. 0905] See above, p. 705, note c], not only for the three days, until she was buried beneath the church and beside the cave of the Lord, but throughout the entire week, for all who had come and who believed that the funeral was their own and the tears their own.

Her venerable daughter, the virgin Eustochium, like a child weaned upon her mother, could not be torn away from her parent: she kissed her eyes, clung to her face, embraced her whole body, and wished to be buried with her mother.

30. Jesus is my witness that she left her daughter not even a single coin; rather, as I have already said, she left a great burden of debt. And, more difficult still, she left an immense multitude of brothers and sisters, whom it is hard to support and impious to abandon.

What is more remarkable than this virtue: that a woman of the noblest family, once possessed of great wealth, distributed everything with such faith that she came almost to the extremity of poverty? Let others boast of their money, of the bronze cast into God’s treasury, and of gifts hung from golden chains. No one gave more to the poor than she who kept nothing for herself.

Now she enjoys riches and those blessings “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have entered the human heart” (2 Corinthians 2:9). We mourn our own condition, and if we wished to weep longer over her reign, we would seem rather to envy her glory.

31. Be at peace, Eustochium: you have been enriched with a great inheritance. The Lord is your portion; and, so that you may rejoice more, your mother has been crowned by a long martyrdom. For not only the shedding of blood in confession is reckoned as martyrdom; the unblemished service of a devoted mind is also a daily martyrdom.

One crown is woven from roses and violets [Ms. S. Max.: “is woven”], the other from lilies. Hence it is written in the Song of Songs: “My beloved is white and ruddy” (Song of Songs 5:10), granting the same rewards to those who conquer in peace and in war.

Your mother, I say, heard with Abraham: “Go out from your land and from your kindred, and come into the land that I will show you” (Genesis 12:1). And through Jeremiah she heard the Lord commanding: “Flee from the midst of Babylon and save your lives” (Jeremiah 48:6) [Note: [Col. 0905] The Bishop of Reate adds: “And she went out from her land”; there is no trace of this in our copies. A little later, manuscripts commonly have jurulentias for virulentias, and Rosweidus read jurulentias; in support of this reading is Celsus, book 11, chapter 27: “Every flesh is jurulent”—that is, full of broth or gravy.].

Until the day of her death she did not return to Chaldaea; nor did she long for the pots of Egypt and the poisonous foods of meat [virulentias] (Exodus 16:3). Rather, accompanied by choirs of virgins, she became a citizen of the Savior; and, ascending from little Bethlehem to the heavenly kingdoms, she says to the true Naomi: “Your people shall be my people, and your God my God” (Ruth 1).

32. I dictated this book for you during two little night-watchings, under the same grief that you bear. For whenever I tried to set pen to paper and write the work I had promised, my fingers stiffened, my hand fell, and my mind grew faint. Thus the uncultivated style bears witness to the writer’s purpose without any elegance or charm of language.

33. Farewell, Paula, and aid the final old age of your servant by your prayers. Your faith and works unite you to Christ; now that you are present, you will more readily obtain what you ask.

“I have completed a monument more lasting than bronze” (Horace, Odes, final ode of book 3), which no old age can destroy. I engraved an inscription for your tomb and placed it beneath this volume, so that wherever our discourse may reach, the reader may recognize that you have been praised and buried in Bethlehem.

[Note: [Col. 0906] Here the manuscripts substitute: “The title of Paula the widow’s tomb follows.”]

The inscription of the tomb follows.

Whom Scipio begot and Paul’s parents brought forth,

A descendant of the Greeks, illustrious offspring of Agamemnon,

Lies here in this tomb; the elders called her Paula,

Mother of Eustochium, first of the Roman Senate:

She followed Christ’s poverty and the fields of Bethlehem.

[Note: [Col. 0906] Ms. S. Maximus, according to Bollandus: “And on the front of the tomb you find the following,” etc.]

On the front of the cave:

Do you see the narrow tomb cut into the sheer rock?

It is Paula’s lodging, while she possesses the heavenly kingdoms.

Leaving behind brother, kindred, Rome, and her fatherland,

Her riches and offspring, she is buried in the cave of Bethlehem.

Here is your manger, Christ, and here the Magi,

Bearing their mystical gifts, gave them to the human being and to God.

34. The holy and blessed Paula fell asleep on the seventh day before the Kalends of February, on the third day of the week after sunset. She was buried on the fifth day before those same Kalends [Note: [Col. 0906] The year 404 is indicated by the consular fasti], when Honorius Augustus was consul for the sixth time and Aristaenetus was consul. She lived according to her holy purpose for five years in Rome and twenty years in Bethlehem. She completed the whole span of her life in fifty-six years, eight months, and twenty-one days.

## LETTER 109 [Note: [Col. 0906] Elsewhere numbered 53. Written in the year 404.]

### TO THE PRESBYTER RIPARIUS

Having been informed by a letter from the presbyter Riparius that Vigilantius taught that the ashes of the martyrs should not be venerated and condemned the solemn vigils of Christians at their tombs, Jerome uses this letter as a skirmish and prelude to battle, showing that he is ready to refute the man’s error if Riparius will send him his books.

### 1.

When I first received your letter, not to reply would be arrogance; to reply would be rashness. For you ask about matters which it is sacrilege either to bring forward or to hear [Note: [Col. 0907] All our manuscripts, with complete agreement, and Victorius likewise read “which”; Martianaeus substituted “that.” If this change occurs in the manuscripts, it must be attributed to the rashness of critics, for it often happens even among the best writers of good Latin that *res quod* and *rerum quae* are joined in the neuter. Cicero, Letters 16.4.5: “do not spare expense in anything that is needed for health.” Sallust, *Jugurtha* 41: “an abundance of those things which mortals consider first.” Livy 32.29: “when the other divine and human matters which had to be carried out by them had been completed.” Finally Aulus Gellius, to omit others, 1.3: “after the many great things which he had done well and kindly for the Samnites after peace had been restored.”].

You say that Vigilantius—who is called by this name by way of antithesis, for “Dormitantius” would be more accurate—has again opened his foul mouth and uttered the most polluted stench against the relics of the holy martyrs; and that he calls us, who receive them [or: look upon them], “cinerary-men” and idolaters because we venerate the bones of dead men.

O unhappy man, deserving to be lamented with every expression of grief, who in saying these things does not understand that he is a Samaritan and a Jew, who regard the bodies of the dead as unclean and even suspect that vessels in the same house are polluted—following the dead letter and not the life-giving spirit.

But we do not worship and adore the relics of the martyrs—indeed, not even the sun and moon, nor angels, archangels, cherubim, seraphim, or every name that is named both in the present age and in the age to come (Ephesians 1:21)—lest we serve the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever.

We honor the relics of the martyrs so that we may worship the one whose martyrs they are. We honor the servants so that the honor shown to the servants may redound to the Lord, who says: “Whoever receives you receives me” (Matthew 10:40).

Are the relics of Peter and Paul, then, unclean? Will the little body of Moses be unclean—that body which, according to the Hebrew Truth, was buried by the Lord himself (Deuteronomy 34:6) [Note: [Col. 0907] See Saint Epiphanius, *Heresies* 60 and 64, where he explains this tradition of the Hebrews and Christians as well]?

And whenever we enter the basilicas of the apostles and prophets, and of all the martyrs, do we then venerate temples of idols? Are the candles kindled before their tombs insignia of idolatry?

I shall say something more, which may rebound upon the author’s own head and either heal his mad brain at last or destroy it, lest the souls of the simple be overthrown by such great sacrileges.

Was the body of the Lord, then, unclean when it was placed in the tomb? And did the angels, who wore white garments, keep watch over a dead and polluted corpse, so that after many centuries Dormitantius might dream—or rather belch forth—the foulest drunkenness, and, together with the persecutor Julian, destroy the basilicas of the saints or convert them into temples?

### 2.

I am astonished that the holy bishop, in whose parish he is said to be a presbyter, submits to his madness, rather than breaking the useless vessel with the apostolic rod and the iron rod and handing him over to the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved (1 Corinthians 5:5).

Let him remember that saying: “When you saw a thief, you ran with him, and you placed your portion with adulterers” (Psalm 49:18). And in another place: “In the morning I killed all the sinners of the earth, to destroy from the city of the Lord all who work iniquity” (ibid. 100:8). And again: “Do I not hate those who hate you, Lord, and do I not waste away over your enemies? With perfect hatred I hate them” (ibid. 138:21–22).

If the relics of the martyrs are not to be honored, how do we read: “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (ibid. 115:6)?

If their bones pollute those who touch them, how did the dead Elisha raise a dead man and give him life—the body which, according to Vigilantius, lay unclean? (2 Kings 13) [Note: [Col. 0908] In Erasmus and the older editions, *corpori* stood for *corpus*; Martianaeus omitted both words. We restore the one from the manuscripts and the Victorian edition as necessary, and prefer *corpori*, which, as Victorius also notes, better suits the question: the dead body is said to have given life to the corpse, rather than Elisha.].

Were all the camps of the Israelite army and people of God therefore unclean, because they carried the bodies of Joseph and the patriarchs through the wilderness? And did they bring unclean ashes into the Holy Land?

Was Joseph also, who went before as a type of the Lord the Savior, a criminal because with such ceremony he carried Jacob’s bones to Hebron, so that he might join the unclean father to the unclean grandfather and great-grandfather, and unite the dead with the dead [Note: [Col. 0908] A manuscript of the monastery of Saint Savior at Bologna reads: “that such pomp of funeral ceremony should precede, and should cause Jacob’s bones to be carried to Hebron.” We read the final verb really only conjecturally, so that the sense may in some way stand]?

His tongue ought to be cut out by physicians—or rather, his insane head should be cured—so that one who does not know how to speak may eventually learn to keep silent.

I once saw this portent and tried to bind the madman with the testimonies of Scripture, as with the bonds of Hippocrates. But he went away, escaped, got loose, broke out, and, while declaiming against us, shouted across the waves of the Adriatic and the Alps of King Cottius. For whatever a lover says must be called shouting and clamoring.

### 3.

Perhaps you silently reproach me in your thoughts for attacking one who is absent. I shall confess my grief to you: I cannot patiently listen to so great a sacrilege.

For I have read of the *seiromastes* of Phinehas (Numbers 25) [Note: [Col. 0908] This is what the Septuagint calls the spear with which Phinehas pierced the Midianite prostitute], the severity of Elijah (1 Kings 18), the zeal of Simon the Cananaean [Note: [Col. 0908] The apostle Simon Zelotes, whom he called Cananaean from the Hebrew etymology; it means the same as “Zelotes” among the Greeks, perhaps to avoid the cacophony of saying “the zeal of Simon Zelotes.”], the severity of Peter, who struck Ananias and Sapphira dead (Acts 5:5), and the steadfastness of Paul, who condemned Elymas the magician, resisting the ways of the Lord, to eternal blindness (Deuteronomy 13 and 11).

It is not cruelty when it is piety for God’s sake. Hence it is also said in the Law: “If your brother, your friend, or your wife who lies in your bosom wishes to turn you away from the truth, let your hand be upon them, and you shall shed their blood and remove the evil from the midst of Israel” (ibid. 13 and 28).

I say again: are the relics of the martyrs unclean? And what had the apostles suffered, that they should ceremoniously precede the unclean body of Stephen and make great lamentation for him, so that their mourning might be turned into our joy?

As for your claim that he condemns vigils, he also acts contrary to his own name, wishing Vigilantius to sleep and refusing to hear the Savior say: “Could you not watch with me for one hour? Watch and pray, so that you do not enter into temptation. The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matthew 26:40 and Mark 14:37).

And in another place the Prophet sings: “At midnight I rose to confess you, because of the judgments of your righteousness” (Psalm 118:62).

We also read in the Gospel that the Lord spent the night in prayer, and that the apostles, shut up in prison, kept watch throughout the night, so that while they were singing psalms the earth was shaken [Note: [Col. 0909] Again the Bologna manuscript reads: “the whole earth was shaken”], the jailer might believe, and the magistrates and the city might be terrified.

Paul says: “Devote yourselves to prayer, keeping watch in it” (Colossians 4:2). And in another place: “Frequently in vigils” (2 Corinthians 11:27).

Let Vigilantius therefore sleep, and while sleeping with the Egyptians let him be suffocated by the destroyer of Egypt. Let us say with David: “He will neither slumber nor sleep who guards Israel” (Psalm 120:4), so that the holy one may come to us, and *air*, which means “watchful” (Daniel 4:10).

And if on account of our sins he should ever sleep, let us say to him: “Arise; why do you sleep, Lord?” (Matthew 8:25). Let us awaken him; and, while the little boat is tossed by the waves, let us cry: “Teacher, save us; we are perishing.”

### 4.

I had intended to dictate more, if the brevity proper to a letter did not impose upon us the shame of remaining silent; and if you had wished to send us the songs of his books, so that we might know to what we ought to reply [or: what we ought to answer].

But now we have beaten the air and have disclosed not so much his unbelief, which is evident to everyone, as our own faith.

However, if you wish us to write a longer book against him, send me his dirges and absurdities, so that he may hear John the Baptist preaching: “Already the axe has been laid at the roots of the trees. Every tree that does not produce good fruit [Note: [Col. 0909] We supplied *good* from Victorius; the Vulgate prefers this word, as does the Greek *karpon kalon*] will be cut down and thrown into the fire” (ibid. 3:10).

## LETTER 110 [Note: [Col. 0909] Elsewhere numbered 93. Written in this year, 404.]

### AUGUSTINE TO JEROME

Augustine endeavors to soothe Jerome, who had been somewhat offended by his letters. He testifies that he has received Jerome’s defense against Rufinus, lamenting that such bitter discord had arisen between men once bound by the closest friendship.

To the revered and most desired lord, his brother and fellow presbyter, JEROME, AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

### 1.

Although I think that before you received this, my letter had already come into your hands—the one I sent through God’s servant, our son the deacon Cyprian—in which you would certainly recognize that the letter was mine, since you mentioned that copies of it had reached you [or: had arrived there], I therefore suppose that by now I have been struck by your replies, as though by the heavy and sharp boxing-gloves of Entellus (Aeneid 5), as though audacious Dares had begun to be beaten and battered.

[Note: [Col. 0909] The Benedictines, following the older editions, read *glandibus* (“with missiles”), a reading which they could in some measure support because certain leaden balls were set in boxing-gloves, as in those of Entellus, which were stiff with sewn-in lead and iron. See the illustrations of boxing-gloves from sculptures on tombs and ancient engraved gems in Mercurialis, *De gymnastica*, book 2. Martianaeus, however, reads *grandibus* (“great”), and in the errata directs: “Do not read *glandibus* here.” Even if that correction was sound, Entellus’ gloves could hardly have been called great, since Virgil states in book 5 that Entellus laid aside the larger gloves with which fierce Eryx had been accustomed to fight, because Dares refused to contend with them: “Then Anchises’ son brought forth equal gloves, / and bound both men’s hands in equal arms.” Nor did we ever think there was an allusion to: “How many hailstorms rattle upon roofs; / so with thick blows the hero strikes and turns Dares / again and again with either hand.” Accordingly, writing *grandinibus* (“with hailstorms”) instead of *glandibus* or *grandibus* would be unacceptable. We now judge that *gravibus* (“heavy”) must unquestionably be read, from the Virgilian allusion, where the heavy gloves or blows of Entellus are described; he himself is called “strong in memory and bulk,” and: “Heavy Entellus stands, unmoved in his exertion”; then: “He himself, heavy, fell heavily to the ground with vast weight.”]

Nevertheless, I shall now answer those very letters of yours, which you were kind enough to send me through our holy son Asterius. In them I found many indications of your most affectionate goodwill toward me, and again certain signs of some displeasure on your part toward me [Note: [Col. 0910] Victorius rejects this reading and, from other copies, produced: “again, some displeasure of your soul.” But the present reading is defended by the Benedictines, together with the editions of Badius and Erasmus, and by sixteen manuscripts].

Thus, where I was soothed while reading, there I was immediately wounded—especially astonished by this: you say that, because you did not rashly believe the copies of my letters, lest, if you replied, I should justly protest that you ought first to have proved the words to be mine and then written back; yet afterward you command me, if the letter is mine, to write openly or to send more reliable copies, so that without any bitterness of stomach we may engage in discussion of the Scriptures.

For how can we engage in this discussion without bitterness if you prepare to wound me? Or, if you do not prepare to wound me, how could I, without your wounding me, justly protest against you for having failed first to prove that the words were mine and then writing back in this manner—that is, in such a way as to wound me [Note: [Col. 0910] Martianaeus reads “and then write,” though Victorius himself formerly corrected this]? Unless you had wounded me by writing back, I could not justly have protested.

Therefore, when you write back in such a way as to wound, what room is left to us for engaging in the discussion of Scripture without any bitterness?

For my part, God forbid that I should be wounded if you are willing and able, by a sound argument, to demonstrate that you have understood some passage from the Apostle’s letter—or anything else in the holy Scriptures—more truly than I have.

Indeed, God forbid that I should fail to reckon it among my gains, with thanksgiving, if I am instructed by you as my teacher or corrected by you as one who sets me right.

### 2.

Yet, dearest brother, if you did not think yourself wounded by my writings, you would not think that I could be wounded by your replies. For I could in no way have thought of you what you do not suppose yourself to have suffered—namely, that, although you wrote back in such a way as to wound me, you yourself were wounded [Note: [Col. 0910] Again, Martianaeus, following the Erasmus manuscripts without sufficient reason: “not thinking that you were wounded, if nevertheless you write back,” etc.].

Or, if I was thought capable of being wounded because of my excessive foolishness, even though you did not write back in such a way, then you certainly wounded me by having such an opinion of me.

But you would in no way rashly believe that I—whom you had never found to be such—was such a person, when you refused to believe rashly in copies of my letters even though you knew my style.

For if you rightly judged that I would justly protest if you rashly believed letters to be mine which were not mine [Note: [Col. 0911] Victorius wishes *vidisti* to be replaced by *judicasti*], how much more justly would I protest if I myself had rashly been thought to be the kind of person which the one making that judgment had not found me to be?

You would therefore by no means have fallen so far as to think that, even if you did not write back in a way that wounded me, I—nevertheless excessively foolish—could have been wounded by such a reply from you.

### 3.

It remains, then, that you intended to wound me by writing back, if you knew with certain evidence that those letters were mine.

And since I do not believe that you would unjustly think I ought to be wounded, it remains for me to acknowledge my fault: I wounded you first by those letters, which I cannot deny to be mine.

Why then do I struggle against the current of the river instead of asking pardon? I beg you, therefore, by the gentleness of Christ, that if I wounded you, you forgive me, and do not repay evil for evil by wounding me in turn.

You will wound me, however, if you keep silent about my error, should you find one in my writings or words [Note: [Col. 0911] In the Benedictine edition, *in factis*, “in deeds,” instead of *in scriptis*, “in writings”].

For if you reproach me for things that ought not to be reproached, you wound yourself rather than me [or: wound yourself more than me]. Far be it from your character and holy purpose to do this out of a desire to wound, censuring in me with a malicious tooth something which you know, with a truthful mind, ought not to be censured.

Accordingly, either rebuke with a benevolent heart even one who lacks the fault for which you think he should be rebuked, or soothe with paternal affection one whom you cannot cast away [Note: [Col. 0911] Martianaeus, with Erasmus and a few other editions, adds “whom you cannot add”—a reading that cannot be sustained].

For it can happen that something seems to you different from what the truth contains, provided that what you do is not different from what charity requires.

I shall gladly accept your most friendly correction, even if the matter did not deserve correction and can rightly be defended. Or I shall acknowledge at once both your goodwill and my fault; and, insofar as the Lord grants it, I shall be found grateful in one respect and corrected in the other.

### 4.

What then? Perhaps I shall fear your harsh but certainly wholesome words like the boxing-gloves of Entellus. He was beaten, not treated; and therefore he was conquered, not healed.

But if I calmly receive your medicinal correction, I shall not be distressed. If, however, a weakness—whether human or my own—is truthfully reproved, it cannot fail to be saddened to some degree [or: can only be saddened to some degree]. Better for the swelling of the head to hurt while it is being treated than while it is being spared—and not healed [Note: [Col. 0911] In the Benedictine edition, *absque* is omitted, so that the phrase reads “while it is spared, it is not healed.”].

This is what the man clearly saw who said that enemies who rebuke are generally more useful than friends who fear to rebuke. For while those enemies quarrel, they sometimes speak truths which we may correct; but the friends display less freedom in the cause of justice than they ought, fearing to embitter the sweetness of friendship.

Therefore, even if you are, as you seem to yourself, an ox weary from bodily old age but still laboring fruitfully in the Lord’s threshing floor with undiminished spirit, here I am: if I have said anything wrongly, press your foot down more firmly [Note: [Col. 0912] The Benedictines perhaps place the adverb after the words: “although you are an ox, weary from old age and perhaps from bodily weakness.” Shortly afterward Victorius wishes *desudas* to be read instead of *desudans*].

The burden of your age ought not to trouble me, provided that the chaff of my fault is crushed.

### 5.

Accordingly, what you placed at the end of your letter I read and reread with a sigh of great longing:

“Would that we might deserve your embraces,” you say, “and in mutual conversation either teach or learn something.”

I say in return: Would that we lived at least in neighboring regions, so that, if our conversations could not mingle, our letters might at least be more frequent [Note: [Col. 0912] Likewise: “so that at least letters might be possible,” etc.].

But now we are so far removed from one another by distance of place that, concerning those words of the Apostle to the Galatians, I remember having written to your holiness when I was a young man; and now, behold, I am an old man and have not yet deserved a reply [Note: [Col. 0912] About ten years had passed since he wrote that letter to Jerome, numbered 56 in our recension. Among the ancients, youth was reckoned the fourth stage of life, ending around the fiftieth year; it was followed immediately by old age, the sixth stage, extending to about seventy].

The copies of my letter reached you more easily—through some intervening circumstance—than the letter itself reached you by my efforts. For the man who had then received it neither delivered it to you nor reported back to me [or: neither delivered it nor reported back].

Yet such great things appear in the letters of yours that have been able to reach our hands that, if I could, I would prefer nothing in my studies to clinging to your side.

Since I cannot do this, I am considering sending one of our sons in the Lord to you for instruction, if I also deserve a reply from you about this matter. For I neither possess, nor can now possess, as much knowledge of the divine Scriptures as I see to be present in you.

And whatever ability I may have in this matter, I expend it, as best I can, for the people of God. But because of ecclesiastical responsibilities I absolutely cannot devote myself to study more diligently than is necessary for instructing the people who listen.

### 6.

I do not know what slanderous writings concerning you have reached Africa [Note: [Col. 0912] We would prefer to read “may have reached,” since Jerome complains in Letter 102 that Rufinus had caused his slanders to reach even Africa, and replies that nothing of the sort had arrived there. From this the reading found in many printed books—“we have heard that they reached”—is shown to be false; the Benedictines also note this].

Nevertheless, we received what you were kind enough to send in reply to those slanders. After reading it, I confess that I grieved greatly that, between persons so dear and familiar, bound by a bond of friendship known to almost all the churches, so great an evil of discord had arisen.

How much you restrain yourself, and how you hold back the barbs of your indignation lest you return slander for slander, is sufficiently evident in your letters.

Yet when I read them, I wasted away with grief and stiffened with fear. What would those things which he wrote against you have done to me, if they had perhaps come into my hands?

“Woe to the world because of scandals” (Matthew 18:7). Behold, it happens; behold, precisely what the Truth says is fulfilled: “Because iniquity has abounded, the love of many will grow cold” (Matthew 24:12).

To whose trustworthy hearts can people now safely pour themselves out? Into whose bosom can secure affection wholly throw itself [Note: [Col. 0913] Victorius, using three copies, printed *pectora toto ore fundantur*, “hearts may pour themselves out with their whole mouth,” and insists that this must be restored. But he does not seem to have sufficiently grasped the sense of the passage. Shortly afterward, most printed editions have *sensus* instead of *sinum*; the latter, however, is found in fifteen manuscripts among the Benedictines and seemed preferable to us].

Finally, what friend would not be feared as a future enemy, if what we lament could arise between Jerome and Rufinus?

O miserable and pitiable condition! O unreliable knowledge of what is present in the wills of friends, where there is no foreknowledge of what is to come!

But why should I consider this something to be lamented by one person about another, when a human being is not even known to himself with regard to the future? He knows, scarcely and perhaps only vaguely, what he is now; but what he will be later, he does not know.

### 7.

Moreover, if this knowledge of what each person is, and also foreknowledge of what each will be, exists among the holy and blessed angels, I do not at all see how the devil could once have been blessed while he was still a good angel, if he knew his future wickedness and eternal punishment.

Concerning this matter, if indeed it is necessary for us to know it, I should like to hear from you what you think.

See what the lands and seas do that separate us bodily. If I were this letter of mine that you are reading, you would already be telling me what I asked. But now, when will you reply? When will you send the reply? When will it arrive? When will I receive it?

And yet, would that what we desire so greatly might at some time happen, even though we endure with as much patience as we can the fact that it cannot happen as quickly as we wish.

Therefore I return to those sweetest words of your letter, filled with your holy longing, and make them mine in turn:

“Would that we might deserve your embraces, and in mutual conversation either teach or learn something”—if only it could in some way happen that I might teach you anything.

### 8

“In these words, which are no longer yours alone but also mine, I find delight and refreshment; and even in the very fact that the desire of us both hangs suspended and is not fulfilled, I am consoled to no small degree. Yet there I am again pierced by the sharpest goads of grief, when I consider that among you—whom God had granted this very thing that both of us desired, abundantly and generously, so that, as the closest and most intimate of friends, you might lick together the honey of the sacred Scriptures—such a ruin of bitterness has intruded: when would it not be to be feared, where would it not be, and for what person would it not be feared?

**[Note: Col. 0913]** Again Victorius prefers *formidandum* (“to be feared”).

“This occurred when, having already cast aside the burdens of worldly affairs and being now unencumbered, you were following the Lord; and when, in that land where you saw together the Lord walking with human feet and saying, ‘My peace I give you, my peace I leave you’ (John 14:27), this could happen to men mature in age and dwelling in the word of the Lord.

“Truly, human life upon earth is a trial” (Job 7:1). Alas for me, who cannot find you both together somewhere! Perhaps, moved as I am, grieving and afraid, I would fall at your feet, weep as much as I could, and plead as much as I loved. Now I plead with each of you on his own behalf, with both of you for one another, and for the others—especially the weak, for whom Christ died—who watch you, as though in the theater of this life, at great peril to themselves.

Beware lest, by writing and disseminating things about one another which you will not be able to erase when at some time you are reconciled—though you now refuse to be reconciled—or things which, when reconciled, you would fear to read lest you quarrel again.

**[Note: Col. 0914]** The Benedictines note that ten manuscripts read: “which, since you will not be able to erase them when reconciled, you refuse to be reconciled”; and one Cistercian manuscript: “which, whenever you will not be able to erase them when reconciled, you refuse to be reconciled.” Victorius preferred: “which, whenever you are reconciled, etc.”

### 9

“I tell your charity the truth: nothing has made me tremble more than this example, when I read in your letter certain indications of your indignation—not those concerning Entellus and the weary ox, where you seemed to me rather to be joking cheerfully than threatening angrily, but that which plainly appears to have been written by you in earnest, and from which I spoke above, perhaps at greater length than I ought, but not at greater length than I feared: where you said, ‘Lest, having been justly injured, you should protest.’

“I beg you, if it can be done, let us seek and discuss among ourselves something by which our hearts may be nourished without the bitterness of disagreement. But if I cannot say what seems to me in need of correction in your writings, nor you in mine, except with the suspicion of envy or injury to friendship, let us refrain from these matters and spare our life and well-being. Let that which inflates attain less, provided that which edifies is not offended.

“I feel myself to be far from that perfection of which it is written: ‘If anyone does not stumble in word, he is a perfect man’ (James 3:2). Yet, plainly, I think that by God’s mercy I may easily ask forgiveness from you if I have offended in something which you ought to disclose to me; so that, when I have heard you, ‘you may gain your brother’ (Matthew 18:15).

“For you ought not, merely because the distance between our lands prevents you from doing this between me and you, to allow me to go astray. Insofar as concerns the very matters which we wish to know, if I know, believe, or suppose that I hold some truth on which you think otherwise, I shall try, insofar as the Lord grants and without injury to you, to defend it. But insofar as concerns your offense, whenever I sense that you are angry, I shall do nothing other than beg your pardon.”

### 10

“I shall certainly suppose that you could have been angry only if either I said what I ought not to have said, or said it in a manner in which I ought not to have said it. For I am not surprised that we know one another less than we are known by our closest and most intimate friends. Into the affection of such friends I readily cast myself whole, I confess, especially when wearied by the scandals of the world; and in it I rest without any anxiety. For while I perceive that the one into whom I securely cast myself, and in whom I securely rest, is there, I rest without anxiety.

“Nor, in this security of mine, do I fear altogether that uncertainty of human frailty concerning tomorrow, over which I groaned above. For when I feel that a man is aflame with Christian love, and that by this love he has become a faithful friend to me, whatever counsels and thoughts of mine I entrust to him, I do not entrust them to a man, but to the one who dwells in him, making him such a man. ‘God is love, and whoever remains in love remains in God, and God in him’ (1 John 4:6). If he should abandon that love, he must cause as much grief as, while remaining in it, he had caused joy.

“Yet if an intimate friend becomes an enemy, let the clever man seek for himself something to fabricate; let him not, in anger, find something to betray. This each person easily achieves, not by concealing what he has done, but by not doing what he would wish to have concealed.

“If God’s mercy grants good and godly people that they may associate freely and securely among friends, however they may prove in the future, let them not disclose the sins of others entrusted to them, which they fear might be disclosed, and let them themselves commit nothing.

“For when something false is fabricated by a slanderer, it is either not believed at all, or at least only his reputation is troubled, while his integrity remains unharmed. But when an evil deed is actually committed, the intimate friend is an enemy, even if the talkativeness or quarrel of no intimate friend spreads the matter abroad.

“Therefore, which prudent person would not see how tolerably even you endure the incredible hostility of one who was once your closest and most intimate friend, with your conscience consoling you; and how you count either what he boasts about or what perhaps some people believe as weapons in the left hand—arms with which one fights against the devil no less than with those in the right hand?

“Nevertheless, I would prefer him somehow milder than to have you armed in this fashion. It is a great and sad miracle that from friendships such as these you have come to hostilities such as these. It will be a joyful and far greater one if from hostilities such as these you return to your former harmony.”

**[Note: Col. 0915]** Victorius reads *consolante te conscientia* (“with your conscience consoling you”).

**[Note: Col. 0915]** An alternative reading has *atque* (“and”) for *eaque* (“and by it”).

**[Note: Col. 0915]** The Benedictine edition omits the preposition *si* (“if”); shortly afterwards, from six manuscripts, they substituted *amicos* (“friends”), where the printed editions had previously read *inimicos* (“enemies”).

**[Note: Col. 0915]** In the editions of the Benedictines, Martianaeus, and other earlier editors, the text read: “But when an evil deed is committed, he is an enemy,” and so forth. We have restored the more elegant reading from Victorius, which is also confirmed by fourteen manuscripts among those used by the same Benedictines.

**[Note: Col. 0915]** Paul’s statement in 2 Corinthians 6:7 is very learnedly added: “by the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left, by glory and dishonor, by ill repute and good repute.” The Apostle assigns a good reputation to the weapons on the right and a bad reputation to those on the left.

---

## Letter 111

**[Note: Col. 0915]** Alternatively, 95. Written with the preceding letter.

### Augustine to Praesidius

Augustine asks Praesidius to arrange for the preceding letter to be delivered to Jerome, and also to make Jerome favorably disposed toward him by a letter of his own.

To his most blessed lord, deservedly venerable brother and fellow priest, Praesidius, Augustine sends greetings in the Lord.

### 1

“As I asked your sincerity in person, so now also I remind you: do not hesitate to send my letter to our holy brother and fellow presbyter Jerome. So that your charity may know how you ought also to write to him on my behalf, I have sent copies both of my letters to him and of his to me. When you have read them, your holy prudence will readily discern both the manner which I thought should be observed and the emotion which I did not fear without reason.

“Or, if I have written something that I ought not to have written, or in a manner in which I ought not to have written it, do not send him a speech about me, but rather send me one about myself, in fraternal love. Thus corrected, I shall ask him to forgive me, if I myself recognize my fault.”

**[Note: Col. 0916]** Alternatively, *videbis* (“you will see”).

---

## Letter 112

**[Note: Col. 0916]** Alternatively, 89. Written around the end of the year 404.

### Jerome to Augustine

Jerome at last responds to Augustine’s questions raised in Letters 56, 67, and 104: concerning the title of his book recounting ecclesiastical writers; concerning Peter’s being rebuked by Paul in the Epistle to the Galatians; concerning the translation of the Old Testament; and concerning the word “ivy” in Jonah. He vigorously defends his writings and interpretations against Augustine.

To the truly holy and most blessed Pope Augustine, Jerome sends greetings in Christ.

### 1

“Through the deacon Cyprian I received three letters at once—or rather, brief treatises—from your Dignity. They contain, as you call them, various questions; as I understand them, criticisms of my little works. If I wished to answer them, a book of considerable size would be required. Nevertheless, I shall try, as far as I can, not to exceed the limits of a lengthy letter and not to delay the brother who is in haste. Three days before he was due to depart, he demanded letters from me, so that I was compelled to pour out these things, whatever they are, almost under marching orders, and to reply in a hurried discourse—not with the maturity of a writer, but with the rashness of one dictating. Such haste usually turns not into learning but into chance, just as sudden wars throw even the bravest soldiers into confusion, forcing them to flee before they can seize their weapons.

### 2

**[Note: Col. 0916]** Martianaeus has *compelleret* (“might compel”); Victorius, from six Florentine and several Brescian manuscripts, reads *compellar* (“I might be compelled”).

“Nevertheless, Christ is our armor, and the instruction of the Apostle Paul, who writes to the Ephesians: ‘Take up the armor of God, so that you may be able to resist on the evil day’ (Ephesians 6:13). And again: ‘Stand therefore, having girded your loins with truth, and having put on the breastplate of righteousness, and having shod your feet in readiness for the gospel of peace; above all, taking up the shield of faith, with which you may extinguish all the flaming darts of the evil one; and receive the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God’ (ibid. 14ff.).

“With these weapons King David once armed himself and went forth to battle. Taking five smooth stones from the stream, he showed that amid the storms of this age there was in his understanding nothing rough or filthy, drinking from the stream on the way. Therefore he lifted up his head and cut off the exceedingly proud Goliath with his own sword, striking the blasphemer in the forehead (1 Samuel 17); he wounded him in that part of the body in which Uzziah, presuming upon the priesthood, was also struck with leprosy (2 Chronicles 26), and in which the holy man glories in the Lord, saying: ‘The light of your countenance has been marked upon us, O Lord’ (Psalm 4:6).

**[Note: Col. 0916]** We have restored from Victorius and older books the reading which most plainly alludes to the final verse of Psalm 109 [110]: “He shall drink from the brook in the way; therefore shall he lift up his head.” The Benedictines read: “and therefore, having lifted up the exceedingly proud head of Goliath”; or, in Martianaeus, “of Golias.” At the least, a comma should have been placed after *caput* (“head”).

“Let us therefore say also: ‘My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready; I will sing and make melody in my glory. Awake, psaltery and lyre; I will awake at dawn’ (Psalms 57:8–9; 108:1–2), so that this may be fulfilled in us: ‘Open your mouth, and I will fill it’ (Psalm 81:10); and: ‘The Lord will give the word to those who proclaim the gospel with great power’ (Psalm 68:12).

“I do not doubt that you also pray for this very thing: that, while we contend with one another, truth may prevail between us. For you are not seeking your own glory but Christ’s. When you win, I too shall win, if I understand my error; and conversely, when I defeat you, you prevail, because children do not store up treasures for their parents, but parents for their children. We also read in the Book of Chronicles that the children of Israel went forth to battle with peaceful minds: amid the swords, bloodshed, and corpses of the fallen, they were thinking not of their own victory but of the victory of peace.

“Let us therefore answer everything and, if Christ commands it, resolve these many questions in a brief discourse. I pass over the duties of greeting, with which you caress my head; I am silent about the flatteries with which you try to console me for your criticism. I shall come to the matters themselves.”

### 3

“You say that you received my book from a certain brother, without a title, in which I had listed Ecclesiastical Writers, both Greek and Latin. When you asked him—using your own words—why the opening page had not been inscribed, or under what title it should be classified, he replied that it was called *Epitaphium* (“Epitaph”). You argue that it would rightly be so called if you had read there only the lives or writings of those who were already dead. But since the little works of many who were alive both when it was written and still are today are mentioned there, you wonder why I gave it this title.

“I think your prudence can understand that you could have grasped the title from the work itself. You have read both Greek and Latin authors who wrote the lives of famous men, and you know that they never gave such works the title *Epitaphium*, but rather ‘On Illustrious Men’—for example, generals, philosophers, orators, historians, epic, tragic, and comic poets. An *epitaph* properly belongs to the dead; I know that I once composed one upon the repose of the holy memory of the presbyter Nepotianus.

“Therefore this book ought to be called ‘On Illustrious Men,’ or more precisely ‘On Ecclesiastical Writers,’ although many ignorant correctors have caused it to be entitled ‘On Authors.’”

**[Note: Col. 0917]** The same editors say: “They would never have written *Epitaphium* as the title of this work, but …”

### 4

“In the second place, you ask why I said in my Commentaries on the Epistle to the Galatians that Paul could not have reproved Peter for something he himself had done, nor accused another of hypocrisy when he himself was guilty of it. You assert that the apostolic rebuke was not a matter of prudent dispensation but a genuine rebuke, and that I ought not to teach falsehood, but that everything written should sound exactly as it is written.

“To this I answer first that your prudence ought to have remembered the preface to my Commentaries, which speaks in my person:

“‘What, then? Am I foolish or rash to promise what he could not do? Certainly not. Rather, in this respect I seem to myself more cautious and timid, since, recognizing the weakness of my powers, I followed Origen’s Commentaries. For that man wrote five proper volumes on Paul’s Epistle to the Galatians and filled the tenth book of his *Stromata* with a concise exposition of it. He also composed various treatises and excerpts which, even by themselves, could have been sufficient. I pass over my teacher Didymus the Seer, the Laodicean, recently departed from the Church, and Alexander, the ancient heretic, as well as Eusebius of Emesa and Theodore of Heraclea, who likewise left behind various brief commentaries on this subject. If I were to extract even a little from these authors, something would result that would not be wholly despised.

“‘To speak frankly, I read all these works, gathering a great deal into my mind, and then, summoning a secretary, dictated either my own words or those of others, remembering neither the order, nor the wording, and sometimes not even the sense. It is now a matter of the Lord’s mercy that, through our ignorance, things well said by others should not perish and that things which please among one’s own people should not fail to please among strangers.’”

“If, then, you thought something in my exposition deserved criticism, it was your duty, as a learned man, to ask whether what we had written could be found among the Greeks, so that, if they had not said it, you might then condemn it as my own opinion. This is especially so since I freely confessed in the preface that I had followed Origen’s Commentaries and had dictated either my own words or those of others. At the end of the very chapter you criticize, I wrote:

“‘If anyone does not approve this interpretation, by which neither Peter is shown to have sinned nor Paul to have reproved his superior insolently, he must explain by what logical sequence Paul reproved in another what he himself had committed.’

“By this I showed that I was not deliberately defending as my own a position I had read in the Greek authors. I expressed what I had read, leaving it to the reader’s judgment whether it should be approved or rejected.”

**[Note: Col. 0918]** The Benedictines read: “and rash, who promises what he …”; here Marius Victorinus is meant.

**[Note: Col. 0918]** Martianaeus and other earlier editors omitted the word *ut*. The Palatine manuscript 340 reads: “Rather, as I seem to myself, more cautious and timid, recognizing the weakness …”

**[Note: Col. 0918]** The reading was corrupt in Jerome’s editors: *propria* or *propia*.

**[Note: Col. 0918]** In the actual preface: “retaining in memory.” Then: “This is wholly a matter of the Lord’s mercy.”

**[Note: Col. 0918]** Martianaeus, following Erasmus, unwisely inserted the name Apollinaris into the text. Victorius and other learned men testified long ago that this name is absent from most of the more accurate manuscripts. The matter is clear from the preface itself to the Commentaries on the Epistle to the Galatians, and especially from Augustine’s response in the following Letter 116, section 3. Here the name should be omitted: “For the Laodicean,” he says, “whose name you suppress, you say has recently departed from the Church …”

### 5

“You, then, rather than doing what I had asked, discovered a new argument and asserted that Gentiles who had believed in Christ were free from the burden of the Law, whereas those who believed from among the Jews were subject to the Law. Thus, by the persons of both groups, Paul could rightly rebuke those who observed the Law, as the teacher of the Gentiles, while Peter could rightly be rebuked because, as the leader of the circumcision, he had imposed upon Gentiles what only those who were Jews ought to observe.

“If this pleases you—or rather, since it does please you, since you hold that all who believe from among the Jews are debtors bound to perform the Law—you, as a bishop renowned throughout the whole world, ought to promulgate this opinion and draw all your fellow bishops into agreement with you. I, in a small hut with monks—that is, with my fellow sinners—do not dare to decide matters of such importance, except to confess frankly that I read the writings of the ancients and, in my Commentaries, place various explanations according to the custom of everyone, so that each person may choose from among them whatever he wishes. I think you have read and approved this practice both in secular literature and in the divine books.”

### 6

“This explanation, which Origen first introduced in the tenth book of his *Stromata*, where he interprets Paul’s Epistle to the Galatians, and which the other interpreters subsequently followed, was introduced above all for the purpose of answering Porphyry, the blasphemer. He accuses Paul of insolence because he dared to rebuke Peter, the chief of the Apostles, and to challenge him to his face, constraining him by argument for having acted wrongly—that is, for having fallen into the very error in which he himself stood when he accused another of wrongdoing.

“What shall I say of John, who until recently governed the Church of Constantinople in the episcopal rank and wrote a very extensive book specifically on this chapter, in which he followed the opinion of Origen and the ancients? If, then, you criticize me for erring, allow me, I beg you, to err along with such men. And when you see that I have many companions in my error, you ought at least to produce one supporter of your truth. This is what I say concerning the interpretation of one chapter of the Epistle to the Galatians.

“But lest I seem to resist your reasoning by relying upon the number of witnesses and to evade the truth under cover of illustrious men, or to shrink from joining battle, I shall briefly offer examples from the Scriptures.

“In the Acts of the Apostles a voice came to Peter, saying: ‘Rise, Peter; kill and eat’ (Acts 10:13)—that is, all four-footed animals, reptiles of the earth, and birds of the air. By this saying it is shown that no human being is unclean by nature, but that all alike are called to the grace of Christ.

“Peter replied: ‘By no means, for I have never eaten anything common or unclean.’ And a voice came to him a second time from heaven: ‘What God has cleansed, you must not call common.’ He therefore went to Caesarea, and entering the house of Cornelius, he opened his mouth and said: ‘In truth I have discovered that God is not a respecter of persons, but in every nation whoever fears him and practices righteousness is acceptable to him.’

“Finally, the Holy Spirit fell upon them, and the faithful of the circumcision who had come with Peter were astonished that the grace of the Holy Spirit had also been poured out upon the Gentiles. Then Peter answered: ‘Can anyone forbid water, so that these should not be baptized who have received the Holy Spirit just as we have?’ And he ordered them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ.

“The Apostles and the brothers who were in Judea heard that the Gentiles too had received the word of God. When Peter went up to Jerusalem, those who were of the circumcision disputed with him, saying: ‘Why did you enter men who were uncircumcised and eat with them?’ (Acts 11:1–3). Having explained everything fully, he finally concluded his speech with these words: ‘If, therefore, God gave them the same gift as he gave us who believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I that I could hinder God?’ When they heard this, they fell silent and glorified God, saying: ‘Then to the Gentiles also God has granted repentance unto life.’

“Again, much later, when Paul and Barnabas had come to Antioch and, after the Church had been assembled, had reported how much God had done with them and how God had opened the door of faith to the Gentiles (Acts 14:26–27), certain men who had come down from Judea were teaching the brothers and saying: ‘Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved’ (Acts 15:1).

“When a considerable disturbance had arisen against Paul and Barnabas, it was decided that both those who were accused and those who accused them should go up to Jerusalem to the Apostles and presbyters concerning this question. When they had reached Jerusalem, some believers from the sect of the Pharisees rose up and said: ‘They must be circumcised, and they must be commanded to keep the Law of Moses.’

“When a great dispute arose over this statement, Peter, with his customary freedom, said: ‘Men, brothers, you know that from ancient days God chose among us that through my mouth the Gentiles should hear the word of the gospel and believe. And God, who knows hearts, bore witness to them, giving them the Holy Spirit just as he did to us, and making no distinction between us and them, cleansing their hearts by faith. Now, therefore, why are you testing God by placing upon the necks of the disciples a yoke which neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear? But we believe that we are saved through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, just as they are.’ The whole multitude fell silent, and the Apostle James and all the presbyters joined in his decision.”

**[Note: Col. 0919]** Saint John Chrysostom, who only a few months before these words were written had been driven from the Church of Constantinople on the very day of the Great Sabbath and sent into exile; he had also first been deposed in the preceding year, 403. See the following letter, or fragment, of Theophilus to Jerome.

**[Note: Col. 0919]** The Veronese manuscript, along with some printed editions, reads: “called to the gospel of Christ.”

**[Note: Col. 0920]** After Erasmus, the word *Deum* (“God”) was missing in Martianaeus’s edition; all other books preserve it, as does the Greek text: *νῦν οὖν τί πειράζετε τὸν θεόν*, “Now therefore why are you testing God?” The Veronese manuscript reads *Dominum* (“the Lord”).

### 8

“These things ought not to be burdensome to the reader, but useful both to me and to him, so that we may show that, before the Apostle Paul, Peter was not ignorant—indeed, was the principal author—of the decree that the Law was not to be observed after the Gospel.

“Peter was of such great authority that Paul wrote in his letter: ‘Then after three years I went up to Jerusalem to see Peter, and I stayed with him fifteen days’ (Galatians 1:18). Again, later in the same letter: ‘Then after fourteen years I went up again to Jerusalem with Barnabas, taking Titus also. I went up according to a revelation, and I set before them the gospel which I preach among the Gentiles’ (Galatians 2:1), showing that he had not had confidence to preach the gospel unless the judgment of Peter and of the other Apostles who were with him had confirmed him.

“Immediately he continues: ‘Privately, however, before those who seemed to be something, lest perhaps I should be running, or should have run, in vain.’ Why privately, and not publicly? So that no stumbling block might arise for the faithful who were of Jewish stock and thought that the Law had to be observed, and that belief in the Lord and Savior had to be joined to it.

“Therefore, at that time also, when Peter came to Antioch—although the Acts of the Apostles do not record this, we must believe Paul when he asserts it—Paul writes that he resisted Peter to his face, because he was blameworthy. Before certain men came from James, Peter ate with the Gentiles; but when they came, he withdrew and separated himself, fearing those who were of the circumcision. The other Jews also joined him in this hypocrisy, so that even Barnabas was led into that hypocrisy by them.

“But when I saw,” Paul says, “that they were not walking uprightly according to the truth of the gospel, I said to Peter before them all: ‘If you, although a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew, how do you compel the Gentiles to judaize?’” And so forth.

“No one, therefore, can doubt that the Apostle Peter was the first author of this very judgment of which he is now accused as a transgressor. The cause of his transgression, however, was fear of the Jews. Scripture says that he had first eaten with the Gentiles, but when certain men came from James, he withdrew and separated himself, fearing those who were of the circumcision. He feared the Jews over whom he was an Apostle, lest through the occasion of the Gentiles they should withdraw from the faith of Christ; and, as an imitator of the good shepherd, he feared losing the flock entrusted to him.”

**[Note: Col. 0921]** The Benedictines note that one Vatican manuscript has *observantiae ejus* (“of its observance”), a Cistercian manuscript *observationis* (“of its observance”), and the Veronese book *observandae ejus sententiae* (“of the observance of his judgment”).

**[Note: Col. 0921]** The same editors read: “and the other Jews also joined him …”
