**[Note: Col. 0921]** The Benedictines and the Veronese manuscript read: “and I set before them the gospel which I preach among the Gentiles.” In them the reading is *roboratum* (“confirmed”), rather than *roboratus* (“confirmed,” masculine).

### 9

**[Note: Col. 0921–0922]** For *viduae* (“widow”), one should apparently read *Judaeae* (“Jewish woman”); this is an easy error of old copyists, not of Jerome. The Vulgate and, more importantly, the Greek read: *γυναικός τινος Ἰουδαίας πιστῆς*, “of a certain faithful Jewish woman,” although a few books do have *χήρας*, “widow.” The Veronese manuscript omits *fidelis* (“faithful”).

“Therefore, as we have shown that Peter thought correctly concerning the abolition of the Mosaic Law, but was compelled by fear to pretend to observe it, let us see whether Paul himself, who rebuked another, did something of this kind.

“We read in the same book: ‘Paul went through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches’ (Acts 15:41). He came to Derbe and Lystra, and behold, there was a certain disciple named Timothy, the son of a faithful widow and a Gentile father. The brothers who were in Lystra and Iconium gave good testimony concerning him. Paul wanted him to set out with him; and he took him and circumcised him because of the Jews who were in those places. For they all knew that his father was a Gentile’ (Acts 16:1–3).

“O blessed Apostle Paul, who had rebuked hypocrisy in Peter because he had withdrawn from the Gentiles out of fear of the Jews who had come from James: why did you shave your head? Why did you compel Timothy to be circumcised against your own judgment? He was the son of a Gentile—and therefore himself a Gentile, for he was not a Jew, since he had not been circumcised. You will answer me: ‘Because of the Jews who were in those places.’ If, then, you forgive yourself for the circumcision of a disciple who came from the Gentiles, forgive also Peter, your predecessor, for having done something out of fear of believing Jews.

“Again it is written: ‘After Paul had stayed many days, he said farewell to the brothers and sailed for Syria, and with him Priscilla and Aquila; he had his head shaved at Cenchreae, for he had a vow’ (Acts 18:18). Grant that there he was compelled by fear of the Jews to do what he did not wish to do. Why did he grow his hair under a vow and afterward cut it at Cenchreae according to the Law, as the Nazirites who had dedicated themselves to God customarily did in accordance with the command of Moses (Numbers 6:18)?”

**[Note: Col. 0922]** Gravius suggests restoring *qui se devoverunt* (“who dedicated themselves”), in place of *pro Deo voverint* (“had vowed for God”).

**[Note: Col. 0922]** The Benedictine edition reads: “by which he withdrew himself,” and shortly afterward asks why the word *cur* (“why”) is absent. Finally, it asks: “why are you compelled to circumcise at the end of the sentence?”

### 10

“But these things are small in comparison with what follows. Luke, the sacred historian, reports: ‘When we had arrived in Jerusalem, the brothers received us gladly’ (Acts 21:17). On the following day James and all the elders who were with him, having approved his gospel, said to him:

“‘You see, brother, how many thousands there are among the Jews who have believed, and they are all zealous for the Law. They have heard about you that you teach the Jews who live among the Gentiles to depart from Moses, saying that they ought not to circumcise their children or walk according to the customs. What, then, is to be done? The crowd will certainly assemble, for they will hear that you have arrived. Therefore do what we tell you. There are four men with us who have a vow upon themselves. Take them, purify yourself with them, and pay their expenses so that they may shave their heads. Then everyone will know that the things they have heard about you are false, but that you yourself walk in observance of the Law.’

“Then Paul took the men, and on the following day, having purified himself, he entered the temple with them, announcing the completion of the days of purification, until the offering should be presented for each one of them.

“O Paul, here again I question you: why did you shave your head? Why did you undergo the barefoot observances of the Jewish ceremonies? Why did you offer sacrifices, and why were victims sacrificed according to the Law on your behalf? Surely you will answer: ‘So that those who among the Jews had believed might not be scandalized.’

“You therefore pretended to be a Jew in order to win the Jews; and James and the other presbyters taught you this very pretense. Yet you could not escape. For when a riot arose and you were about to be killed, you were seized by the tribune and sent by him to Caesarea under careful military guard (Acts 23:23), lest the Jews kill you as one who pretended to observe and then destroyed the Law.

“From there you reached Rome and, in the lodging you had rented, preached Christ both to Jews and to Gentiles (Acts 28:14, 30), and your judgment was confirmed by Nero’s sword.”

**[Note: Col. 0922]** Alternatively: “Grant that there he was compelled by fear of the Jews to do what he did not wish to do.”

### 11

“We have learned that, because of fear of the Jews, both Peter and Paul equally pretended to observe the precepts of the Law. With what face, then, and with what audacity does Paul rebuke in another what he himself committed?

“I—or rather, others before me—have explained the cause as they thought it should be explained. They were not defending an officious lie, as you write, but were showing an honorable dispensation, both to demonstrate the prudence of the Apostles and to restrain the insolence of the blasphemer Porphyry. He says that Paul and Peter fought with one another in a childish contest; indeed, that Paul burned with jealousy of Peter’s virtues and boastfully wrote things which he either had not done or, if he had done them, had done insolently, rebuking in another what he himself had committed.

“They interpreted the passage as best they could. How will you explain it? Surely you will say something better, since you rejected the opinion of the ancients.”

**[Note: Col. 0923]** Gravius reads instead: “that Paul burned with envy.”

### 12

“You write to me in your letter (Letter 67):

“‘You do not need to be taught by me how to understand the statement in which he says: “I became as a Jew in order to win the Jews” (1 Corinthians 9:20), and the rest of what is said there—through compassionate mercy, not through deceptive pretense. For he becomes like a sick man who ministers to the sick, not by pretending that he has a fever, but by considering with a compassionate mind how he would wish to be served if he himself were sick.

“‘For of course he was a Jew; but having become a Christian, he had not abandoned the Jewish sacraments, which that people had received appropriately and at the proper, appointed time. Therefore he undertook to celebrate them even when he was already an Apostle of Christ, in order to teach that they were not harmful to those who wished to preserve them, as they had received them from their parents through the Law, even after they had believed in Christ. They were not, however, to place their hope of salvation in them any longer, since through the Lord Jesus the salvation itself had arrived which those sacraments signified.’”

**[Note: Col. 0923]** We have supplied from the Veronese manuscripts and the Benedictine edition: “in order to win the Jews,” which is absent from the other printed editions.

**[Note: Col. 0923]** Eight manuscripts, according to the Benedictines, and one Veronese manuscript read: “through compassionate mercy, not through deceptive pretense.”

“The whole meaning of your discourse, which you have extended at great length in argument, is this: Peter did not err in thinking that the Law had to be observed by those who had believed from among the Jews; rather, he departed from the straight path in compelling Gentiles to judaize. And he compelled them not by the authority of a teacher, but by the example of his conduct. Paul, likewise, did not say anything contrary to what he himself had done; rather, the question is why Peter compelled those who were Gentiles to judaize.”

### 13

This, then, is the whole substance of the question—or rather, of your opinion: that after the Gospel of Christ believing Jews do well if they keep the commandments of the Law; that is, if they offer sacrifices, as Paul offered them, if they circumcise their sons, and if they observe the Sabbath, as Paul did in Timothy and as all Jews observed it. If this is true, we fall into the heresy of Cerinthus and Ebion, who were anathematized by the Fathers for no other reason than that they mixed the ceremonies of the Law with the Gospel of Christ, and thus professed the new while not abandoning the old.

What shall I say about the Ebionites, who pretend to be Christians? To this day throughout the synagogues of the East there is a heresy among the Jews called that of the Minaeans.^1 The Pharisees still condemn them; in common usage they are called Nazarenes. They believe in Christ the Son of God, born of the Virgin Mary, and say that he is the one who suffered under Pontius Pilate and rose again—the one in whom we also believe. But while they wish to be both Jews and Christians, they are neither Jews nor Christians.

I beg you, then: you think that our little wound needs treatment because it has been pierced—or rather, as the expression goes, pricked with a needle. Treat the wound in this opinion of yours, which has been struck by a spear, or, so to speak, by the bulk of a *phalarica*.^2 For it is not the same crime to set out different opinions of our predecessors in explaining the Scriptures and to introduce once more into the Church a most wicked heresy. But if we are compelled to receive Jews together with their lawful observances, and if they are permitted to practise in the Churches of Christ what they practised in the synagogues of Satan, I shall say what I think: they will not become Christians; rather, they will make us Jews.

### 14

For what Christian could patiently hear what your letter contains?

> Paul was a Jew; but after becoming a Christian he had not abandoned the Jewish sacraments, which that people had received appropriately and at the proper time, when it was required. Therefore, when he was already an Apostle of Christ, he undertook to celebrate them, in order to teach that they were not harmful to those who wished to keep them as they had received them from their parents through the Law.

Again I beg you: hear my grief with indulgence. Paul observed the ceremonies of the Jews when he was already an Apostle of Christ; and you say that they are not harmful to those who wish to keep them as they received them from their parents?

I shall speak in opposition, and, while the world protests, I shall declare in an open voice: the ceremonies of the Jews are both harmful and deadly to Christians; and whoever observes them, whether he is from the Jews or from the nations, has been hurled into the abyss of the devil.

“For Christ is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Romans 10:4)—that is, to Jew and Gentile alike. For it will not be the end of the Law “for everyone who believes” if the Jew is excepted.

We read in the Gospel: “The Law and the Prophets were until John the Baptist” (Matthew 11:12). And elsewhere:

> Therefore the Jews sought all the more to kill him, because he not only broke the Sabbath, but also called God his own Father, making himself equal with God (John 5:18).

And again:

> From his fullness we have all received, grace for grace; because the Law was given through Moses, but grace and truth came through Jesus Christ (John 1:15).

In place of the grace of the Law, which has passed away, we have received the enduring grace of the Gospel; and in place of the shadows and images of the Old Testament, truth has come through Jesus Christ.

Jeremiah too prophesies in the person of God:

> Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will complete a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah—not according to the covenant that I established with their fathers, on the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt (Jeremiah 31:31).

Notice what he says: he promises the new covenant of the Gospel not to the Gentile people, who had previously received no covenant, but to the Jewish people, to whom he had given the Law through Moses. Thus they should no longer live in the oldness of the letter but in the newness of the Spirit.

Paul, however, over whose name the present dispute is being argued, repeatedly expresses such opinions. For the sake of brevity I shall append a few of them:

> Behold, I, Paul, say to you that if you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing (Galatians 5:2).^3

And again:

> You have been severed from Christ, you who are justified in the Law; you have fallen away from grace.

And below:

> If you are led by the Spirit, you are no longer under the Law.

From this it is clear that the person who is under the Law does not possess the Holy Spirit—not “dispensationally,” as our predecessors wished, but truly, as you understand it.

Let us learn from the Lord’s teaching what sort of things the legal precepts are:

> I gave them precepts that were not good, and ordinances by which they should not live (Ezekiel 20:25).

We say this not in order to destroy the Law, as Manichaeus and Marcion did—for, in accordance with the Apostle, we know it to be holy and spiritual—but because, after faith and the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son,

> made from a woman, made under the Law,

so that he might redeem those who were under the Law, so that we might receive adoption as sons, and so that we might live no longer under a pedagogue but as adults and as heirs under the Lord.

### 15

Your letter continues:

> Peter was not corrected because he observed the traditions of his fathers; and if he wished to do so, he would act neither deceitfully nor improperly.

I say again: since you are a bishop and teacher of the Churches of Christ, in order to prove the truth of what you assert, receive some Jew who has become a Christian. Let him circumcise a son born to him; let him observe the Sabbath; let him abstain from the foods that God created to be used with thanksgiving; let him slaughter a lamb at evening on the fourteenth day of the first month. When you have done this—or rather, when you have not done it—for I know that you are a Christian and will not commit such a sacrilege—whether you wish it or not, you will reject your own opinion. Then you will learn by experience that it is more difficult to establish one’s own position than to criticize another’s.

And lest perhaps we should not believe you—or rather, should not understand what you were saying—for speech drawn out at length often lacks intelligibility, and when it is not understood it is less criticized—you insist and repeat:

> Paul had abandoned that which the Jews possessed as evil.

What was the evil of the Jews that Paul had abandoned? Clearly, what follows:

> For, being ignorant of God’s righteousness and seeking to establish their own, they did not submit to the righteousness of God (Romans 10:3).

Then, after the passion and resurrection of Christ, when the sacrament of grace according to the order of Melchizedek had been given and revealed, they still thought that the old sacraments had to be celebrated—not from the custom of a solemn observance but from the necessity of salvation. Yet, if they had never been necessary, the Maccabean martyrs would have suffered for them uselessly and in vain.

Finally, they persecuted Jewish Christians who preached grace as though they were enemies of the Law.

> He says that he condemned these and similar errors and vices and regarded them as refuse, in order to gain Christ (Philippians 3:8).

### 16

Through you we have learned what evils of the Jews the Apostle Paul abandoned. Let us now, again under your instruction, learn what good things of theirs he retained. “The observances of the Law,” you will say, “which they celebrate according to ancestral custom, just as Paul himself celebrated them, without any necessity for salvation.”

I do not sufficiently understand what you mean by “without any necessity for salvation.” If they do not bring salvation, why are they observed? But if they ought to be observed, then certainly they bring salvation—especially those whose observance makes martyrs. They would not be observed unless they brought salvation.

For they are not indifferent things between good and evil, as the philosophers argue. Continence is good; luxury is evil. Between the two are indifferent actions: walking, evacuating the bowels, expelling nasal discharges from the head, and casting out phlegm by spitting. These are neither good nor evil. Whether you do them or do not do them, you will possess neither righteousness nor unrighteousness.

But observing the ceremonies of the Law cannot be indifferent: it is either good or evil. You say it is good; I assert that it is evil—not only for those who come from the Gentiles, but also for those who have believed from the Jewish people.

Here, if I am not mistaken, while avoiding one danger you fall into another. While fearing Porphyry the blasphemer, you run into the snares of Ebion, deciding that those who believe from the Jews must observe the Law. And because you understand that what you are saying is dangerous, you again try to moderate it with superfluous words: “without any necessity for salvation”—not as the Jews think it should be celebrated, nor through the deceptive pretence that Paul rebuked in Peter.

### 17. Deceptive Pretence

Peter, then, pretended to observe the Law. This critic of Peter, however, boldly observed the lawful rites.

For your letter continues:

> If he celebrated those sacraments because he pretended to be a Jew in order to win them, why did he not also sacrifice with the Gentiles? For he became as one without the Law to those who were without the Law, in order to win them also (1 Corinthians 9:21). Unless it was because he did the former as a Jew by nature, and said all this not so that Paul might pretend to be what he was not, but so that he might compassionately judge that he ought to assist them as though he himself were struggling in that error—not by the craft of one who lies, but by the affection of one who sympathizes.

You defend Paul well: he did not pretend to share the error of the Jews, but was truly in error. Nor did he wish to imitate the lying Peter, who concealed what he was because of fear of the Jews; rather, he declared with complete freedom that he was a Jew.

What new clemency in an Apostle! Wishing to make Jews Christians, he himself became a Jew. He could not lead the luxurious back to frugality unless he had proved himself luxurious, nor, as you say, compassionately assist the wretched unless he himself felt wretched.

Truly pitiable and deserving of compassionate lament are those who, by their contention and their love for an abolished Law, made the Apostle of Christ a Jew.

There is not much difference between your opinion and mine. I say that both Peter and Paul, because of the fear of Jewish believers, practised—or rather pretended to practise—the commandments of the Law. You assert that they did this compassionately, not through the craft of one who lies but through the affection of one who sympathizes. Let this at least remain certain: whether from fear or from compassion, they pretended to be what they were not.

The argument you use against us—that Paul ought to have become a Gentile to the Gentiles if he became a Jew to the Jews—actually supports our position. For just as he was not truly a Jew, so he was not truly a Gentile; and just as he was not truly a Gentile, so he was not truly a Jew.

He imitates the Gentiles in this respect: he receives the uncircumcision in the faith of Christ and permits people indiscriminately to eat foods condemned by the Jews—not, as you think, the worship of idols. For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything, but the keeping of God’s commandments (Galatians 5:6 and 6:15).

### 18

I beg you, therefore, and again and again entreat you to forgive my little disputation; and whatever has gone beyond my proper measure, charge to you, since you compelled me to write back and, with Stesichorus, deprived me of my eyes.

Do not think me a teacher of falsehood, since I follow Christ, who says:

> I am the way, the truth, and the life (John 14:6).

It cannot be that a worshipper of truth should submit his neck to falsehood.

Nor should you stir up against me the uneducated crowd who venerate you as a bishop and, when you declaim in church, esteem you for the dignity of your priesthood, while they despise me, an old man at the end of life and almost decrepit, devoted to the seclusion of a monastery and the countryside. Seek people for yourself whom you may teach or rebuke.

For, separated from you by such great distances of sea and land, we scarcely receive the sound of your voice. And if perhaps you write letters, Italy and Rome will receive them before they are delivered to me, the person to whom they are sent.

### 19

As to what you ask in other letters—why my earlier translation in the canonical books has asterisks and obeli marked before it, while I later published another translation without these signs—allow me, with your permission, to say that you seem not to understand what you asked.

That translation is the work of the Seventy Translators. Wherever there are obeli, that is, little strokes, it signifies that the Seventy said more than is found in the Hebrew. Wherever there are asterisks, that is, shining little stars, material from Theodotion’s edition was added by Origen.

There we translated the Greek; here we expressed what we understood from the Hebrew itself, sometimes preserving the truth of the sense rather than the order of the words.

I am astonished that you read the books of the Seventy Translators not in their purity, as they were issued by them, but corrected by Origen—or corrupted by obeli and asterisks—and yet do not follow the little translation of a Christian, especially since he translated what was added from the edition of a Jewish and blasphemous man after Christ’s passion.

Do you wish to be a true lover of the Seventy Translators? Do not read what is under the asterisks; indeed, scrape it from the volumes, so that you may prove yourself a supporter of antiquity. But if you do this, you will be compelled to condemn all the libraries of the Churches. Scarcely one or two books will be found that do not contain these additions.

### 20

Moreover, when you say that I ought not to have interpreted after the ancient translators, you employ a new syllogism:

> Either the things interpreted by the Seventy were obscure or they were clear. If obscure, it must be believed that you too could have been mistaken in them. If clear, it is evident that they could not have been mistaken in them.

I answer you in your own manner. All the ancient interpreters who preceded us in the Lord and who interpreted the holy Scriptures interpreted either obscure things or clear ones.

If obscure, how did you dare to discuss them after those who could not explain them? If clear, it was superfluous for you to wish to discuss what could not have escaped them—especially in explaining the Psalms, which among the Greeks were interpreted in many volumes: first by Origen, second by Eusebius of Caesarea, third by Theodore of Heraclea, fourth by Asterius of Scythopolis, fifth by Apollinaris of Laodicea, and sixth by Didymus of Alexandria. Treatises by various authors on a few Psalms are also circulated. But now we are speaking of the Psalter as a whole.

Among the Latins, Hilary of Poitiers and Eusebius, bishop of Vercelli, translated Origen and Eusebius; our Ambrose too followed the former in certain passages.

Let your wisdom answer me: why, after so many and such interpreters, did you think differently in your explanation of the Psalms? If the Psalms are obscure, it must be believed that you too could have been mistaken in them. If they are clear, it is not believed that those men could have been mistaken in them. Therefore, in either case, your interpretation will be superfluous. On this principle, no one will dare to speak after those who came before, and once another person has occupied a subject, no one else will have permission to write about it.

Rather, it is a mark of your humanity that, in the matter where you grant pardon to yourself, you should extend indulgence to others also.

For I did not so much attempt to abolish the old translations—having corrected them for speakers of my language and translated them from Greek into Latin—as to bring forward those testimonies that had been omitted or corrupted by the Jews, so that our people might know what the Hebrew Truth contained.

If anyone does not wish to read them, no one compels him against his will. Let him drink the old wine with pleasure and despise our new wine, which has been published in the explanation of earlier works, so that wherever those earlier works are not understood, our versions may make them clearer.

As for the method of interpretation that should be followed in the holy Scriptures, the book I wrote *On the Best Kind of Interpretation*, together with all the prefaces to the divine books that we placed before our edition, explains it. I think the prudent reader should be referred to those works.

And if, as you say, you accept me in the correction of the New Testament and explain that you accept me because many people possessing knowledge of Greek can judge my work, you ought to have trusted the same integrity in the Old Testament as well. We did not fabricate it ourselves; we translated the divine words as we found them among the Hebrews. If you doubt anything, ask the Hebrews.

### 21

But perhaps you will say: What if the Hebrews are unwilling to answer, or wish to lie? Will the entire multitude of Jews remain silent about my translation? Will no one be found who has knowledge—or understanding—of the Hebrew language? Or will all imitate those Jews whom you say were found in a little town of Africa and conspired to slander me?

For in your letter you weave the following story:

> A certain brother of ours, a bishop, had begun having your translation read in the church over which he presides. In the prophet Jonah he encountered something rendered very differently by you from what had become fixed in everyone’s understanding and memory and had been sung through the succession of so many generations. Such a great tumult arose among the people—especially when the Greeks accused him and loudly proclaimed the charge of falsehood—that the bishop was compelled to demand the testimony of the Jews—for it was the city of Oea. Whether from ignorance or malice, they replied that the Hebrew books contained what the Greek and Latin books contained and what they asserted. What more is there to say? Wishing, after so great a danger, not to be left without his people, the man was compelled to correct it as though it were a falsehood. Hence it also seems to us that you too may sometimes have been mistaken.

### 22

You say that I translated something incorrectly in the prophet Jonah and that, while the people shouted in revolt because of the discrepancy of a single word, a bishop almost lost his priesthood. Yet you withhold what it was that I supposedly translated incorrectly, taking away the opportunity for my defence, so that whatever you say may be impossible for me to resolve by answering—unless perhaps, as happened many years ago, the gourd was brought into the matter, when that Cornelius and Asinius Pollio of the period asserted that I had translated “ivy” instead of “gourd.”^5

We have answered this matter more fully in the Commentary on the Prophet Jonah. For now let it be enough to say that where the Seventy Translators rendered the word as “gourd,” and Aquila, together with the others, rendered it as “ivy”—that is, *kissos* (κισσός)—the Hebrew volume has written *CICEION* [or: contains *CICEION*], which the Syrians commonly call *CICEIA*.^6

It is a kind of shrub with broad leaves, shaped like vine leaves. Once planted, it quickly rises into a little tree without any supports of reeds or stakes, on which gourds and ivy depend; it supports itself by its own trunk.

If, explaining the word word for word, I had wished to translate *CICEION*, no one would have understood it. If I had translated it “gourd,” I would have said something that is not found in Hebrew. I chose “ivy” in order to agree with the other translators.

But if your Jews, as you assert, said through malice or ignorance that the Hebrew books contained what appears in the Greek and Latin copies, it is clear either that they do not know the Hebrew letters or that they wished to lie in order to mock the advocates of the gourd.

At the end of my letter I ask you not to force a resting old man, long a veteran, back into military service and again expose him to danger. You are young and occupy the summit of the episcopate: teach the peoples and enrich the Roman roofs with Africa’s new fruits. For me it is enough to whisper with a poor listener and reader in a corner of the monastery.

## Letter 113

### To Jerome from Theophilus

[This letter was previously unpublished among the letters. It was written in the year 405.]

### A Certain Part or Beginning

He testifies that he had always wished well to John Chrysostom and had not rashly believed his accusers, until, when the judgment of the Council broke forth, John was expelled from his Constantinopolitan see and driven into exile.

> To the dearest and most beloved brother Jerome, Theophilus sends greetings in the Lord.

---

^1 Previously the reading was *Mineorum*. The Minaeans are, as it is worth noting, named from the Hebrew term [Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text], which has the same meaning as “heretics” (*αἱρετικούς*, *haereticos*), just as the ancients also called their doctrine—“heresy” (*αἵρεσιν*, *haeresim*)—by a related designation. What Jerome notes here is confirmed by Jewish records, in which it is reported that in the time of Gamaliel the Elder the Minaeans had become so numerous that a special formula of imprecation against them had to be devised. These people readily referred to Christians, whom the Jews still call *Minim* in their commentaries.

^2 A very large kind of weapon.

^3 Victorius replaced *proderit* (“will profit”) with the reading found in the Vulgate and the Greek text, *ὠφελήσει* (“will benefit”).

^5 Compare the following passage from the Commentary on Jonah, chapter 4:

> At this point a certain Canthelius, of the very ancient family of the Cornelii—or, as he himself boasts, descended from the line of Asinius Pollio—is said long ago to have accused me at Rome of sacrilege because I translated “ivy” instead of “gourd.” He was evidently afraid that, if ivy grew instead of gourds, he would have no vessel from which to drink secretly and in darkness. Indeed, on the very gourds of vessels that are commonly called *saucomaria*, they are accustomed to shade images of the Apostles, from whom that man too took a name that was not his own. If names are changed so easily that, in place of the seditious tribunes called Cornelii, the consuls of the Aemilian family are named, I do not see why I should not be permitted to translate “ivy” for “gourd.”

Victorius therefore advises that the conjunction be removed here and that the reading should be “Cornelius Asinius Pollio,” since the man who boasted that he descended from two families should have both names joined together. Erasmus, on the other hand, decided that two more famous critics and censors of literary men were indicated in a single person; that Asinius Pollio had been Cicero’s rival is known from Seneca. Certainly Jerome uses the name in this sense in Book 1 of the *Apology against Rufinus*: “I speak against the envious, and the edge of my style wounds Luscius Lanuvinus, or Asinius Pollio of the Cornelian family.” Most manuscripts and almost all printed editions retain this reading.

^6 The Barberini manuscript of the Hexapla contradicts this, stating that Aquila and Theodotion translated the term as *κυκεών* (*kykeōn*), that is, expressed the Hebrew word itself in Greek letters, perhaps because they did not know what it meant. Jerome consistently says in his Commentary on this passage: “We followed the ancient translators, who themselves also translated it as ivy, which in Greek is called *κισσός* (*kissos*); for they had no other word to use.” In the Verona manuscript the reading here is *ΚΙΚΗΟΝ*, so that one might suspect that Jerome originally wrote *Aquila and Theodotion, κυκεῶνα*, while the others translated it “ivy,” that is, *κισσόν*, and that the accidental similarity of the Greek words caused the intervening words—which we supply—to be omitted by the customary error of scribes.

^7 Martianaeus reads *Ciceja*. Martinius, in the preface to the *Pugio Fidei*, follows manuscripts in reading *quiquayan*, and above *quiquayon*. Thus the Hebrew word can be found written in Hebrew letters. In the Verona manuscript, however, the forms are *ΚΟΥΚΑΙΟΝ* and *ΚΗΚΗΑΝ*. From this it is clear that the older editions could both be mistaken and cause error: in them *Elkeroa*, an Arabic name, was substituted by conjecture for *Ciceja*. All the manuscripts oppose this, and in any case the Syriac language is known not to differ from Hebrew in this matter. Indeed, the Hebrew *Cicajon* is *Cicajan* in Syriac, with the customary change of *o* to *a*. The teachers of that language say that it entirely lacks the vowel *o*.

^8 See the Commentary on Jonah at the cited passage. It shows that many people are mistaken, especially the rabbis Kimchi, in his *Book of Roots*, and Jarchi, following Maimonides, who classify *Ciceion* among herbs. Herodotus also refers to this plant in Book 2, chapter 94, saying: “The Egyptians call it *KIKI*.” Pliny, in Book 15, chapter 7, calls it a tree abundant in Egypt; some call it *croton*, others *phili*, and others wild sesame. Others more correctly identify it as castor, commonly called the palm of Christ, because the shape of its leaves somewhat resembles a palm with its fingers spread.

^9 Elsewhere we found *certis* (“certain”) instead of *ceteris* (“the other”). Since the Hebrew *Cicejon* corresponds satisfactorily neither to the gourd of the Seventy and the old Latin translator nor to ivy, Jerome nevertheless preferred the latter in order to agree with several good interpreters.

^10 The earlier arrangement was the reverse: “To the most beloved and most loving Pope Theophilus, Bishop, Jerome,” and so forth. The editors had assigned this letter to Jerome on the preconceived assumption that he had received it from Theophilus and merely translated it into Latin. Jerome’s own testimony makes the matter clear:

> I translated your letter into Latin and placed it at the beginning of this volume so that all who read it might know that I undertook this burden beyond my strength not through rashness or boastfulness, but at the command of Your Blessedness.

Theophilus, who had long been hostile to Chrysostom because Chrysostom had received Origenists, not only arranged for him to be expelled from the see of Constantinople into exile but also wrote against him a monstrous book, excessively full of insults and curses, as Facundus calls it in Book 6, chapter 5. Jerome translated it so that Latin ears might hear it, at Theophilus’s request. This is the very letter in which Theophilus sent the volume to be translated and asked that it be translated.

Whether through laziness or through the misguided care of later editors, the final words in which he made this request have been lost together with the complete volume; nevertheless, the abbreviated surviving text indicates the matter clearly. Theophilus says that he had once been unwilling to believe the causes of Chrysostom’s ruin, but now, after Chrysostom’s condemnation, he is bringing those causes and offences into the open. Knowing the Saviour’s command, “Judge with righteous judgment,” he wishes no one to think him unjust toward Chrysostom; therefore, in the complete book, he sets those sins before the public and asks that they become known through a Latin translation even among the Churches of the West, with which John, although deposed, continued to communicate.

Jerome, wishing to avoid the odium of the matter, spoke with sufficient restraint about Chrysostom when he returned the book in Latin. In a letter to Theophilus, which we append below, and so that he would not appear to have done this through rashness or boastfulness, he prefixed to the same volume the very letter by which he had been commanded to translate it.

The letter, therefore, was written by Theophilus to Jerome, not by Jerome to Theophilus, as the context itself proves. It continually bears the imprint of Greek phrasing; its style is less polished, does not flow in its usual course, and does not reflect Jerome’s talent when he is not constrained by the bonds of rendering a translation. Its opinions also scarcely suit Jerome but suit Theophilus very well.

Moreover, the title itself exposed the falsification and caused us to dare to alter it in the opposite direction. It had read: “To the most beloved and most loving Pope Theophilus, Bishop,” and so forth. But Jerome never called Theophilus “the most beloved and most loving Pope”; out of reverence for his episcopate he called him “Most Blessed.” Conversely, Theophilus repeatedly addresses Jerome as “the most beloved and most loving brother.” See the letters exchanged between them, numbers 86, 87, and those that follow.

In addition, the phrase “Pope, Bishop” was entirely novel and ridiculous. But it is tiresome to dwell longer on these points.

^11 The editorial note breaks off after the words “indeed,” and continues beyond the supplied fragment.

Additional textual and editorial notes omitted from the draft:

[Col. 0925, on Jeremiah 31:31.] The Benedictine editors read *quando* (“when”) in place of *qua* (“on which”). Eleven of their manuscripts, together with the Verona manuscript, read *fuerat* (“had made”) rather than *fecerat* (“had made”); Martianay notes that the Verona manuscript had previously read *non fecerat Testamentum* (“had not made a covenant”).

[Col. 0925, on “under the Law.”] Martianay, following Erasmus, reads *dispensatione* (“by dispensation”), a reading rejected by the manuscripts.

[Col. 0925, on Galatians 4:4.] From the Greek *γενόμενος ἐκ γυναικός* (*genomenos ek gynaikos*, “made from a woman”): the manuscripts read *factum* (“made”), not *natum* (“born”), as most printed texts do, although *γενόμενον* also occurs in some Greek books.

[Col. 0926, before the quotation beginning “Paul had abandoned.”] The Benedictine edition reads “*An ne*, etc.”; this is perhaps a printer’s error.

[Col. 0926, on the preceding sentence.] The same editors read: “when it is not understood, it is less criticized; you insist,” etc., followed by “Paul had abandoned this evil of the Jews,” etc. The Verona manuscript agrees, except that it reads *reprehenditur* (“is criticized”) more correctly for *reprehendit* (“criticizes”).

[Col. 0926, on Philippians 3:8.] Martianay, with most other editions and the Verona manuscript, reads: “he says that he condemns them and regards them as dung.” See Letter 67, section 6, note e.

[Col. 0926, on indifferent acts.] Victorius preferred *egerere* (“to evacuate”); the Verona manuscript adds *vestiri* (“to clothe oneself”) and agrees with the printed reading in the remaining words.

[Col. 0927, on Peter’s dissimulation.] Two Vatican manuscripts in the Benedictine edition read: “so that, through fear of the Jews, he might pretend to be what he was not.” The Verona manuscript reads: “he might pretend the fear of the Jews.”

[Col. 0928, on Origen’s recension of the Septuagint.] The printed reading is confirmed by the Verona manuscript, and its sense better weakens the degree of trust which Augustine placed in Septuagint copies. Victorius notes that six Brescian manuscripts read *correctos* (“corrected”), as some printed editions do; this is unacceptable, since *emendare* and *corrigere* have the same meaning. He thinks *correptos* (“rebuked”) should rather be read, a reading which six Florentine manuscripts are said to preserve; but it comes back to the same sense as *correctos*.

[Col. 0930, on the African city in the Jonah story.] The explanation given above identifies *ea civitas* as the city of Oea, rather than taking *ea* as a pronoun. The Verona manuscript reads *eorum* (“of them”) for *ea*. Martianay reports that a Cluniac manuscript, corrected by the same hand, reads: “Whether they did this through ignorance or malice, I do not know. But that this is, etc.” This appears to us a pointless gloss: nothing is missing from the text, and, as Victorius had already observed against Erasmus, the verb *fecerint* (“they did”) is understood. More seriously, the question whether they answered through ignorance or malice that the Hebrew codices contained what the Greek and Latin had is preferable to the pretended authentic reading.

[Col. 0931, before Letter 113.] In the books hitherto printed—and, I suppose, in the manuscripts as well, for none has come under our view—this short fragment of Theophilus’s letter to Jerome is joined in one continuous text to Jerome’s reply to Theophilus. Even Valesius, who rightly suspected that these were two distinct works, the former, mutilated of part of itself, to be assigned to the Alexandrian bishop, and the latter to the priest of Bethlehem, did not correctly determine where the first fragment ended and the following letter began. He wished the first part to extend as far as the Saviour’s saying, “Do not judge according to appearance, but judge righteous judgment”; from that point he begins Jerome’s entire letter with the words, “Lest I should too slowly, to Your Blessedness, etc.” Yet we cannot see what sense can be forced from that reading, since there is no sense at all—or rather, a contrary one. Jerome alleged obstacles because he had rendered Theophilus’s book into Latin too slowly, not because he had done so too quickly, as the words “lest I should too slowly” would imply.

We correct this error below and show how the text must be divided. For Valesius again errs in his notes on Socrates, Book 6, chapter 14, where he supposes that Jerome prefixed this letter to Theophilus’s Paschal letters. He should have said that Jerome translated into Latin, in compliance with Theophilus, the book of invectives against St John Chrysostom which Theophilus had written in Greek, as we shall show in the following note. Whatever Valesius’s twofold error may be, Martianay, with Valesius showing him the light, could easily have taken the right road, or at least, by following him in error, could have gone less seriously astray. Instead, following the error of the old editors and of a manuscript which we have often found corrupt, he chose again to weld these two works into one continuous discourse and to pass them off as a single letter of Jerome to Theophilus. This is wholly intolerable. At the end of the book, see how idly he excuses Jerome for attacking John Chrysostom, how carelessly he departs from Valesius, and how miserably he tortures himself to extract some meaning from that combined text—especially from the words “therefore, knowing that the Saviour said” and “lest I should too slowly,” by which he joins the two works; indeed, “he joins a horse’s neck to a human head.”

[Col. 0932, on the address of Letter 113.] The former arrangement was the reverse: “To the most beloved and most loving Pope Theophilus, Bishop, Jerome,” and so forth. On the preconceived assumption that Jerome had written this letter, editors until now ascribed it to him, although he had received it from Theophilus and merely translated it into Latin. This will be fully clear from Jerome’s own testimony, mentioned in the preceding note, in the following letter: “I translated your letter into Latin and placed it at the beginning of this volume so that all who read it might know that I undertook a burden beyond my strength, not through rashness or boastfulness, but at the command of Your Blessedness.”

Theophilus, long hostile to Chrysostom because he had received the Origenists, not only brought it about that he was driven from the see of Constantinople into exile, but also wrote against him an enormous book, appallingly full of insults and curses, as Facundus calls it in Book 6, chapter 5. As noted above, Theophilus asked Jerome to render this book into Latin as well, for Latin ears. This is the very letter in which he sent the volume for translation and requested that Jerome translate it. Whether through negligence or the misplaced care of others, the final words in which he made that request have been lost with the complete volume; yet the shortened and mutilated context indicates it clearly enough. Theophilus says that he had formerly refused to believe the grounds for Chrysostom’s ruin, but that now, after his condemnation, he is publishing those charges and offences. Knowing the Saviour’s saying, “Judge righteous judgment,” and wishing no one to think him unfair toward Chrysostom, he brings those very sins forward in the complete book and asks that they be made known, by a Latin translation, even in the Western Churches, with which the deposed John continued to communicate.

Jerome, in order to avoid the odium of the case, sent back the book in Latin and wrote to Theophilus, in the letter appended below, with sufficient restraint about Chrysostom. So that he might not seem to have acted through rashness or boastfulness, he prefixed to the volume this very letter commanding him to translate it. The letter was therefore written by Theophilus to Jerome, not the reverse. The context itself proves this: it continually has the flavour of Greek phrasing; its style is less polished, does not flow in its usual course, and does not reflect Jerome’s talent when he is not restricted by the bonds of translating. Its opinions do not at all suit Jerome, but do suit Theophilus. The false address itself also convicted the error and led us to change it in the opposite sense. Jerome never called Theophilus “most beloved and most loving Pope,” but, out of reverence for his episcopate, “Most Blessed”; conversely, Theophilus continually calls Jerome “most beloved and most loving brother.” See Letters 86, 87, and those following. Moreover, the addition of “Pope” to “Bishop” was entirely novel and ridiculous. But it is tiresome to dwell longer on these matters.

### 1.

At the outset, it is pleasing to set forth the judgment of truth briefly. But when the Lord says through the Prophet, “And my judgment goes forth like a light” (Isaiah 51:4)—those who are surrounded by the horror of darkness and do not discern the nature of things with a clear mind are covered with everlasting shame, and at the very end recognize that their efforts have been fruitless. Hence we too always hoped that John, who formerly governed the Church of Constantinople, would please God, and we were entirely unwilling to believe the causes of his ruin toward which he was being heedlessly carried. But he—passing over his other crimes—[Note: Recall the history in Socrates, Book VI, chapters 9, 10, and following.] by admitting Origenists into his intimacy and promoting very many of them to the priesthood, and for this crime causing no small grief to Epiphanius of blessed memory, that man of God who shone among the bishops as a brilliant star throughout the world, deserved to hear: “Babylon has fallen, has fallen” (Isaiah 21:9).

[Note on Isaiah 51:4: We supposed that the passage cited was Isaiah 51:4, where, however, the Greek has a different sense: νόμος παρ’ ἐμοῦ ἐξελεύσεται, καὶ ἡ κρίσις μου εἰς φῶς ἐθνῶν, “The law shall go forth from me, and my judgment as a light for the nations,” and the Latin: “The law shall go forth from me, and my judgment into the light of the peoples.” But elsewhere too we have observed that Theophilus was not altogether precise in quoting the words of Scripture.]

### 2.

Knowing, therefore, that the Savior said, “Do not judge according to appearances, but judge with righteous judgment” (John 7:24), lest, in some way—[Note: The remainder is missing. We have attempted, in the preceding note, to supply the sense as best we could.] [lacuna]

## Letter 114

[Note: In another edition, joined to the preceding letter. Written in the same year, 405.]

### Jerome to Theophilus

He gives several reasons why he translated only later the book written by Theophilus against John Chrysostom. He then praises the doctrine and arguments of that book and asks pardon if at any point he has not rendered the Greek meanings adequately in Latin.

### To the Most Blessed Pope Theophilus, Jerome sends greetings.

#### 1.

That I was slower to return to Your Beatitude your book translated into Latin was due to many obstacles.

[Note: We said that Valesius began the letter with the words “Lest I be delayed any longer,” joining the two words with which the preceding letter ends; but, retaining *quod* from an old error, that reading has either no sense at all or one certainly contrary to Jerome’s meaning.]

[Note: This is plainly the work which Theophilus composed in Greek against St John Chrysostom and which Jerome rendered in Latin. We have thought it useful to append here the small surviving fragments of that translation preserved in Facundus of Hermiane, Book VI, final chapter—though, with Facundus himself, we can be excused for even mentioning them only by necessity. Theophilus says: “Brothers, John persecutes [us] with the unclean spirit by which Saul was suffocated”; and again, “He has killed the ministers of the saints.” He calls him “defiled, impious in the Church of the Firstborn, a pestilential madman, raging with the insanity of a tyrannical mind and glorying in his madness,” and says that “he surrendered his soul to the devil to be defiled.” We have set down all these things exactly as they stand in Theophilus’s own book. He also calls him “the enemy of humanity, one who by his crime surpassed the audacity of robbers, the leader of sacrilegious men, practicing an impious priesthood and offering sacrilegious oblations, a petitioner and a man of the hardest brow.” He further adds that “John is held fast not by snares which might someday be loosed, but by those through which, as his crime deserved, he would hear God threatening and saying: ‘Judge between me and John; I waited for him to do judgment, but he did iniquity—not justice, but a cry.’” He also says that “as Satan transformed himself into an angel of light, so John was not what he appeared”; and he calls him not merely like Satan, but “an unclean demon, dragging along, like a torrent, the filth of words,” declaring that he had proved “impious toward Christ” and “the companion of Judas the traitor.” He adds that John is accused “of having stretched out impious hands against God,” and that what the Apostle James said of certain people greedy for worldly things—“You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly”—the blessed Theophilus asserts that the blessed John said of Christ: “He dared,” he says, “to declare in church that Christ prayed and was not heard because he did not pray well.” “What heretic,” Theophilus reports John to have blasphemed, “has blasphemed more wickedly?” He asserts that John “gave himself over to participation in Jewish impiety, and with his customary rashness offers what the Jews offered, deceiving himself and the people, and emulating Dathan and Abiram. Let him hear with the Jews: ‘Your iniquity has been greatly increased.’” He adds: “Arians and Eunomians delight in John’s blasphemies against Christ; in comparison with you, Jews and idolatrous Gentiles have been justified.” Again he says: “John is not only not a Christian, but is worse than the king of Babylon, far more criminal than Belshazzar; John is more criminal than idolaters and pagans. Present disgrace and eternal punishment in ages to come will be rendered to you.” The same blessed Theophilus also seems to have said: “The Savior cried out and said, ‘Take John away and cast him into the outer darkness,’” and again, “Before God’s tribunal he supplied most abundant fuel for his own fire.” Nor did all this suffice for his anger and fury, unless he also said of the aforesaid most holy man John “that another punishment must be sought for him, because the greatness of his crime surpasses the multitude of torments.”]

There was the sudden incursion of the Isaurians; the devastation of Phoenice and Galilee; the terror throughout Palestine, especially in Jerusalem; and the building not of books but of walls. In addition came the severity of winter, intolerable famine, especially for us, who have been charged with the care of many brothers. Amid these difficulties the translation grew through work done in spare—or, so to speak, stolen—hours of the night, and it was already being kept in draft form. When, during the days of Holy Lent, I needed only to make a fair copy by comparing the text, I was suddenly seized by a most serious illness and entered the threshold of death; but by the Lord’s mercy and your prayers I was preserved.

Perhaps I was preserved so that I might fulfill your command and render, with the same grace with which you composed it, that most eloquent volume which you wove together from the flowers of Scripture. Yet bodily weakness and sorrow of mind have blunted the keenness of my intellect and delayed words that otherwise would have flowed easily, as though impeded by certain obstacles.

[Note: Perhaps “I needed to copy it out again” should be read.]

#### 2.

We have marveled at the usefulness of your work for all the Churches, so that those who are ignorant may learn, instructed by testimonies from Scripture, with what reverence they ought to receive holy things and to serve at the altar of Christ; and that they may understand that the sacred chalices, holy veils, and everything else belonging to the worship of the Lord’s Passion are not empty objects, devoid of sense and holiness, but, through their association with the Body and Blood of the Lord, are to be venerated with the same majesty as His Body and Blood.

[Note: These words seem to designate a work other than the one we have identified. Tillemont therefore also notes that Jerome’s Life, chapter 70, appears to refer not to a book against Chrysostom but to the Paschal Letter of the year 405. We, however, are not persuaded by this: Jerome did not translate the Paschal Letter of that year, nor has any ancient writer reported that he did. On the contrary, all the remaining passages of both this and the preceding letter point to the book against Chrysostom; and Facundus says that it was translated by the presbyter Jerome, from which he quotes not only its arguments but its very words. Moreover, if Jerome especially notes the usefulness of such a book for the Churches, so that those who are ignorant may learn with what reverence they should receive holy things, while passing over its curses and insults, he surely does so wisely, in order to avoid the odium attached to the name of Chrysostom. Finally, from the fragments quoted above we learn that Theophilus habitually accused Chrysostom of being “the leader of sacrilegious men, practicing an impious priesthood and offering sacrilegious oblations,” and of “offering, with his customary rashness, what the Jews offered, deceiving himself and the people and rivaling Dathan and Abiram.” Theophilus could therefore easily have abused this opportunity for detraction and wandered beyond the subject while explaining matters relating to divine worship—which is precisely what Jerome chiefly praises.]

#### 3.

Receive, then, your book—or rather, my book, and, to speak more truly, ours. When you favor me, you will be favoring your own cause. For my talent has labored for you, and I wished to balance Greek eloquence against the poverty of the Latin language. I did not, as skilled translators do, render word for word; nor did I count out the money you had given me in separate portions, but weighed it as a whole, so that nothing might be lacking in meaning even if something were lacking in words.

[Note: We demonstrated above, in Letter 113, note c, that the preceding letter clearly shows this.]

I translated your letter into Latin and placed it at the beginning of this volume so that all who read it might know that I undertook a burden beyond my strength not through rashness or boastfulness, but at the command of Your Beatitude. Whether I have succeeded, I leave to your judgment. Certainly, if you criticize my weakness, you will grant pardon to my good intention.

## Letter 115

[Note: In another edition, Letter 96. Probably written in 405.]

### To Augustine

He returns Augustine’s greetings, apologizing for having replied with excessive freedom. He again mentions the gourd and asks that, setting aside contentious questions, they henceforth confer with one another as friends and converse peacefully in the field of Sacred Scripture.

### To the Truly Holy and Most Blessed Lord Pope Augustine, Jerome sends greetings in Christ.

[Note: In eight Vatican manuscripts and six others used by the Benedictines, the name Firmus is absent; in the opening of the following letter it occurs in nearly all manuscripts.]

#### 1.

When I was anxiously asking our holy brother Firmus how you were, I was glad to hear that you were well. Again, when I was not merely hoping for your letter but demanding it—without your knowledge—he said that he had set out from Africa. I therefore return greetings to you through one who embraces you with unique affection, and I also beg you to forgive my embarrassment, since I could not refuse the one who commanded me to write back, even though I delayed for a long time.

Nor did I answer you, but rather the cause answered the cause. And if it is a fault to have replied, I ask you to listen patiently: it is a much greater fault to have provoked the reply. But let such complaints be dismissed. Let there be pure brotherhood between us; and henceforth let us send one another letters not of controversy but of charity.

The holy brothers who serve the Lord with us salute you abundantly. I ask you to greet on my behalf the holy men who with you bear Christ’s easy yoke, especially the holy and venerable Pope Alypius. May Christ our God, almighty Lord, truly holy and most blessed Pope, protect you safe and mindful of me.

If you have read the book of my explanations of Jonah, I think you will not accept the ridiculous question about the gourd. But if the friend who first attacked me with a sword has been repelled by the pen, it belongs to your humanity and justice to rebuke the accuser, not the respondent. If you please, let us play with one another in the field of Scripture, without causing each other pain.

## Letter 116

[Note: In another edition, Letter 97. Written shortly after the preceding letter.]

### Augustine to Jerome

[Col. 0936]

He replies more fully to Jerome’s letters 105, 112, and 115 concerning the interpretation of the passage in the Letter to the Galatians, affirming that Peter was rightly and truthfully rebuked by Paul. He also asks pardon if, through some incautious expressions, he has offended Jerome’s feelings, explaining that through no fault of his own the letter passed through many hands before reaching the person to whom it had been written.

### To his most beloved lord, honored in the heart of Christ, the holy brother and fellow presbyter Jerome, Augustine sends greetings in the Lord.

#### 1.

“Some time ago I sent your Charity a lengthy letter in reply to yours, which you recall having sent through your holy son Asterius, now not only my brother but also my colleague. I still do not know whether it deserved to reach your hands, except that you write through the most sincere brother Firmus: ‘If the man who first attacked you with a sword has been repelled by the pen, it belongs to my humanity and justice to rebuke the accuser, not the respondent.’ From this very slight indication I can somehow infer that you read that letter of mine.

In it I lamented that such disagreement had arisen between you, whose great friendship had been celebrated everywhere by rumor and had rejoiced the brotherly affection of others. I did not do this by finding any fault with your brotherhood—for I have not dared to say that I recognized any fault of yours in the matter—but by grieving over human misery, since in preserving friendships through mutual affection, however great that affection may be, permanence remains uncertain.

Yet I had preferred to learn from your reply whether you had granted me the pardon I had requested. I wish this to be made clearer to me, although a certain cheerfulness in the expression of your letter seems to indicate that I have obtained it—provided that the letter was sent after you read mine, which is by no means apparent from it.”

[Note: Martianay reads, “If he is the one who first attacked me,” as Jerome had written. But when Augustine repeats the words, Victorius argues that the persons have been changed. The Benedictines read “you,” but their reading depends on taking it for “if” and is not convincing, unless it is a printer’s error.]

#### 2.

“You ask—or rather, in the confidence of charity you command me—to play with one another in the field of Scripture without causing each other pain. For my part, I would prefer us to treat this matter seriously rather than as a game. If you chose to use this word because of its ease, I confess that I ask something greater from the kindness of your strength and from your wisdom: wisdom learned, unoccupied, mature, diligent, and ingenious—wisdom which the Holy Spirit not only grants but also dictates to you—so that in great and laborious questions you may help me, not as someone playing in the field of Scripture, but as one panting while climbing the mountains.

If, however, you thought that ‘let us play’ should be said because of the cheerfulness that ought to exist between dearest friends in discussion, then whether the place from which we converse is open and level or steep and difficult, teach me, I beg you, how we may attain this: whenever something perhaps troubles us which, if we attend less carefully—or, rather, understand more slowly—we do not find convincing, and we try to assert what seems to us contrary, let us speak with somewhat freer confidence without falling under suspicion of childish boasting, as though we were seeking fame for our own names by accusing illustrious men.

But if something harsh is drawn out by the necessity of refutation, let us surround it with gentler language so that it may become tolerable, lest we seem to unsheathe a sword smeared with honey [or: be judged to do so].”

[Note: Nineteen manuscripts among the Benedictines lack the particle “lest.”]

“Unless, perhaps, the way for us to avoid both these faults—or the suspicion of fault—is to dispute with a more learned friend in such a manner that whatever he says must be approved, and that we are not allowed to resist even slightly, at least for the sake of inquiry.”

#### 3.

“Then indeed one plays without any fear of giving offense; but it would be remarkable if we were not being mocked. For I confess to your Charity that I have learned to grant fear and reverence only to those books of Scripture that are now called canonical, so firmly that I believe none of their authors made an error in writing.

If I should encounter in them something in writing that seems contrary to truth, I will have no doubt that either the manuscript is corrupt, or the interpreter has not grasped what was said, or I myself have not understood it. But I read other authors in such a way that, however greatly they may excel in holiness and learning, I do not consider something true because they themselves thought so; rather, I accept it because through those canonical authors, or by a probable argument, they have been able to persuade me that it does not depart from the truth.

Nor do I think, my brother, that you hold a different view. I certainly do not think that you wish your books to be read as though they were the books of the Prophets or Apostles, whose writings it would be sacrilegious to doubt are free from every error. May this be far from your pious humility and truthful judgment concerning yourself; for unless you possessed these qualities, you would surely not say, ‘Would that we might deserve your embrace and, by mutual conversation, either teach or learn something.’”

[Note: The Benedictines read, “I do not think that you hold anything else.”]

[Note: Victorius adds “your” from a certain Medicean manuscript and others.]

#### 4.

“And if I believe that you said this about yourself after considering your life and conduct, not in pretence or deceit, how much more reasonable is it for me to believe that the Apostle Paul meant nothing other than what he wrote when he said of Peter and Barnabas: ‘When I saw that they were not walking rightly toward the truth of the Gospel [variants: “were walking,” “walk”], I said to Peter before everyone: If you, although a Jew, live both as a Gentile and as a Jew, how do you compel the Gentiles to Judaize?’ (Galatians 2:14).

For what can I be certain of—that he will not deceive me by writing or speaking—if the Apostle was deceiving his children, whom he was again bringing forth in labor until Christ, that is, the truth, was formed in them? After prefacing his words by saying, ‘Now concerning what I write to you, behold, before God, I do not lie’ (Galatians 1:20), he was nevertheless not writing truthfully but deceiving them by some dispensational pretense, saying that he had seen Peter and Barnabas not walking rightly toward the truth of the Gospel and that he had opposed Peter to his face, solely because he was compelling the Gentiles to Judaize.”

#### 5.

[Note: Martianay reads, “that the Apostle Paul did not write something truthfully.”]

“But surely it is better to believe that the Apostle Paul wrote something untruthfully than that the Apostle Peter did something wrong. If this is so, let us say—which God forbid—that it is better to believe that the Gospel lies than that Peter denied Christ; and that the Book of Kings lies than that so great a prophet, so exceptionally chosen by the Lord God, committed adultery by desiring and taking another man’s wife and committed so terrible a murder by killing her husband.

Rather, I shall read Holy Scripture, placed at the highest and heavenly summit of authority, certain and secure in its truth. In it I shall learn truthfully that human beings have either been approved, corrected, or condemned, rather than allowing the divine utterances themselves to become everywhere suspect because I am afraid to believe that in certain persons of outstanding excellence there may occasionally be human actions deserving of reproach.”

[Note: The Benedictines note that the Louvain edition reads, “rather than human deeds, not merely in certain…”; other editions and manuscripts read differently.]

[Note: Victorius removes the conjunction “and,” believing that it disrupts the sense.]

#### 6.

“The Manichaeans assert that many passages of the divine Scriptures are false because, when the clear transparency of their meaning exposes their abominable error, they cannot twist them into another sense. Yet they do not attribute this falsehood to the Apostles who wrote them, but to certain corruptors of the manuscripts.

Because they have never been able to prove this either from a greater number of manuscripts or from more ancient copies, or by the authority of the earlier language from which the Latin books were translated, they are overcome and depart in confusion, defeated by a truth known to everyone.

Does your holy prudence not understand how great an opportunity for their wickedness would be opened if we were to say that the apostolic writings had not been falsified by others, but that the Apostles themselves had written falsehoods?”

#### 7.

“‘It is not believable,’ you say, ‘that Paul accused Peter of doing what Paul himself had done.’ I am not now asking what he did; I am asking what he wrote. This bears most directly on the question I have undertaken, so that the truth of the divine Scriptures, entrusted to memory for the building up of our faith—not by just anyone, but by the Apostles themselves, and therefore received into the supreme authority of the canonical books—may remain true and beyond doubt in every respect.

For if Peter did what he ought to have done, Paul lied when he said that he saw him not walking rightly toward the truth of the Gospel. Whoever does what he ought to do certainly acts rightly; therefore the person who says that he did not act rightly speaks falsely about someone whom he knows ought to have done it.

But if Paul wrote the truth, then it is true that Peter was not at that time walking rightly toward the truth of the Gospel. He was therefore doing what he ought not to have done. And if Paul himself had already done something of that kind, I shall believe rather that he too was corrected and could not disregard the correction of his fellow Apostle than that he inserted a lie in his letter.

And if this was not in just any letter, how much more must it be true of the letter in which he had first said: ‘Now concerning what I write to you, behold, before God, I do not lie’?”

[Note: The same editors read, “and in any letter whatever; how much more…”]

#### 8.

“I believe that Peter acted in such a way as to compel the Gentiles to Judaize. For this is what I read Paul wrote, and I do not believe that Paul lied (Galatians 1:20); therefore Peter was not acting rightly in this matter.

For it was contrary to the truth of the Gospel that those who believed in Christ should think they could not be saved without those ancient sacraments. Those who had believed from the circumcision party were maintaining this at Antioch, and Paul fought against them persistently and fiercely.

Paul himself, however, did not act for this purpose when he circumcised Timothy (Acts 16:1), or fulfilled a vow at Cenchreae (Acts 18:18), or, having been admonished by James at Jerusalem, undertook with those who had made vows to perform the prescribed rites (Acts 21:24), as though it might appear that Christian salvation was also granted through those sacraments. Rather, he acted so that he would not be thought to condemn as idolatry those things which God had commanded to be done in earlier times, appropriately for those times, in the shadows of things to come.

This is what James said had been heard about him: that he taught apostasy from Moses (Acts 21:21). It is surely impious that believers in Christ should be severed from the Prophet of Christ as though they detested and condemned his teaching. Of Moses Christ Himself says: ‘If you believed Moses, you would believe me also, for he wrote about me’ (John 5:46).”

[Note: Martianay, following Erasmus, reads “from the Prophets,” in the plural. Victorius formerly corrected this, since only Moses is being discussed.]

[Note: The Benedictines read “who knew,” unless this is a printer’s error. See Acts 21:23: “There are four men among us who have a vow upon themselves.”]

#### 9.

“Consider, I beg you, James’s very words: ‘You see, brother, how many thousands there are in Judea who have believed in Christ, and they are all zealous for the Law. They have heard about you that you teach apostasy from Moses among the Jews who live among the Gentiles, saying that they ought not to circumcise their children or walk according to the custom.

‘What, then, is to be done? The multitude must certainly come together, for they will hear that you have arrived. Therefore do what we tell you. We have four men who have a vow upon themselves. Take them with you, sanctify yourself with them, and pay their expenses so that they may shave their heads. Then everyone will know that the things they have heard about you are false, but that you yourself also walk in observance of the Law.

‘As for the Gentiles who have believed, we have written our judgment that they should observe none of these things, except that they should keep themselves from what has been sacrificed to idols, from blood, and from fornication’ (Acts 21:20 and following).

[Note: The omitted “what is strangled” is readily explained by “blood”; indeed, *and what is strangled* is absent from some Greek manuscripts.]

It is not, I think, obscure that James gave this instruction so that those who had heard these things about Paul—Jews who had believed in Christ but were still zealous for the Law—might know that they were false, and might not think that the things delivered through Moses to the fathers were being condemned as sacrilegious by the teaching of Christ, as though God had not commanded them.

This was not being spread about Paul by those who understood the spirit in which these practices should then be observed by Jewish believers: namely, to commend the divine authority and the prophetic holiness of those sacraments, not to obtain the salvation that was already being revealed in Christ and administered through the sacrament of baptism. Rather, it was spread by those who wanted the practices observed as though believers could not have salvation in the Gospel without them.

They had recognized Paul as a most vigorous preacher of grace and as strongly opposed to their intention, teaching that a person is justified not through those things but through the grace of Jesus Christ, on whose coming those shadows in the Law had been commanded. Therefore, by stirring up hatred and persecution against him, they accused him of being an enemy of the Law and of the divine commandments.

He could not more appropriately avoid the odium of this false accusation than by performing the very rites which he was thought to condemn as sacrilegious. In this way he would show that Jews at that time were not to be prohibited from them as impious, nor Gentiles compelled to them as necessary.”

[Note: Martianay, again following Erasmus, reads “through that,” although Victorius had long before indicated that the legal observances mentioned above had signified this.]

#### 10.

“For if he truly rejected these practices in the way that had been reported about him, and therefore undertook them in order to conceal his real opinion by a feigned action, James would not have said to him, ‘Everyone will know’; rather, he would have said, ‘Everyone thought that the things they heard about you were false’ (Acts 21:24).

This is especially so because, in Jerusalem itself, the Apostles had already decreed that no one should compel the Gentiles to Judaize; they had not decreed that no one should then prevent Jews from Judaizing, although Christian teaching no longer compelled even the Jews to do so.

Therefore, if after this apostolic decree Peter maintained at Antioch that pretense by which he compelled the Gentiles to Judaize—something to which he himself was no longer compelled, although he was not prohibited from it for the sake of commending the divine utterances entrusted to the Jews—why should it be surprising that Paul freely compelled him to affirm what he remembered having decreed with the other Apostles at Jerusalem?”

#### 11.

“But if Peter did this—as I consider more likely—before the council at Jerusalem, it is still not surprising that Paul wished not timidly to conceal but confidently to assert what he already knew Peter shared as his conviction, whether because he had discussed the Gospel with him, or because in the calling of Cornelius the centurion he had received him as divinely instructed about this matter, or because he had seen him eat with Gentiles before those whom Peter feared arrived at Antioch.

For we do not deny that Peter was already of the opinion in which Paul also stood. Paul was therefore not then teaching him what was true in the matter; rather, he was reproving his pretense by which the Gentiles were being compelled to Judaize. He did so for no other reason than that all those actions were being performed as though what those people said were true—namely, that believers could not be saved without circumcision of the foreskin and the other observances that were shadows of things to come.”

#### 12.

“Thus he circumcised Timothy so that the Jews, especially his mother’s relatives, would not think that those who had believed in Christ from among the Gentiles detested circumcision, as idolatry is to be detested: God had commanded the one, whereas Satan had persuaded people to practice the other.

But he did not circumcise Titus so that he would not provide an opportunity for those who said that believers could not be saved without any circumcision to claim, for the deception of the Gentiles, that Paul too held this view.

He himself makes this sufficiently clear when he says: ‘But not even Titus, who was with me, although he was a Greek, was compelled to be circumcised. But because of the false brothers who had slipped in, who had entered in to spy out our freedom, which we have in Christ Jesus, so that they might bring us into slavery, we did not yield in submission to them even for an hour, so that the truth of the Gospel might remain among you’ (Galatians 2:3–5).

From this it is apparent what he understood them to be seeking. For that reason he did not do what he had done in the case of Timothy, although he could have done it in the freedom by which he had shown that those sacraments were neither to be sought as necessary nor condemned as sacrilegious.”

[Note: The Benedictines read “without that circumcision”; two Vatican manuscripts read “not to be able,” and this is what the Teacher of the Gentiles is said to have meant.]

[Note: Some manuscripts among the Benedictines read “by which he might show.”]

#### 13.

“But evidently we must take care in this discussion lest, like the philosophers, we call certain human actions intermediate between right action and sin—actions that are counted neither among right actions nor among sins—and thus be pressed by the claim that observance of the ceremonies of the Law cannot be indifferent but must be either good or evil.

For if we call them good, we will be compelled to observe them ourselves; but if evil, we will have to believe that the Apostles observed them not truthfully but in pretense.

For my part, I fear for the Apostles not so much the example of the philosophers—who do say some true things in their discussions—as that of courtroom advocates, who lie when pleading another person’s case.

If such a comparison was thought appropriate in the very exposition of the Letter to the Galatians in order to confirm the pretense of Peter and Paul, why should I be concerned before you about the name of philosophers? They are not vain because they say everything falsely, but because they trust in many false things and, when they encounter truths, remain alien to the grace of Christ, who is truth itself.”

#### 14.
