“Why should I not say that those ancient sacramental commandments were neither good, because people are not justified by them—for they are shadows announcing the grace by which we are justified—nor evil, because they were divinely commanded and suited to their times and persons?

A prophetic passage also assists me, in which God says that He gave that people commandments that were not good (Ezekiel 20:23). Perhaps for this reason He did not say ‘evil,’ but merely ‘not good’: that is, not such as would make people good, or without which people could not become good.

I should like your kindly sincerity to teach me whether some holy Easterner, when he comes to Rome, fasts on the Sabbath—except on the day of the Paschal vigil—merely in pretense. If we say that this is evil, we shall condemn not only the Roman Church but also many churches nearby and somewhat farther away, where the same custom is observed and remains.

But if we think that not fasting on the Sabbath is evil, with what recklessness shall we accuse so many Churches of the East, and a much greater part of the Christian world?

Would you be willing for us to say that it is something intermediate, yet acceptable to the person who practices it not in pretense but in appropriate fellowship and observance?

And yet we do not read in the canonical books that anything of this kind was commanded to Christians. How much less dare I call evil that which I cannot deny, on the basis of the Christian faith itself, that God commanded—since I have learned that I am not justified by it, but by the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord?”

[Note: Victorius reads “many churches neighboring it,” and somewhat more distant, and criticizes the printed reading because the discussion concerns Churches.]

[Note: The alternative reading is “because I have learned that I am not justified by it, but by the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord.”]

### 15

“I say, then, that circumcision of the foreskin and other practices of this kind were divinely given to the former people through the Testament called ‘old,’ as signs of future things that had to be fulfilled through Christ. When those things had arrived, these practices remained for Christians to read only for the understanding of the prophecy previously announced, but not as things necessary to perform—as though the revelation of faith, which these signs indicated would come, were still to be awaited.

“Although, therefore, these practices were not to be imposed upon the Gentiles, they ought not for that reason to have been removed from the custom of the Jews as though they were detestable and condemnable. Thus, gradually and little by little, as the sound preaching of Christ’s grace grew ardent—the grace by which alone believers would know that they were justified and saved, not by those shadows of things formerly future but now coming and present—the whole practice of the shadows was to be brought to an end in the calling of those Jews whom the bodily presence of the Lord and the apostolic times had found in that condition. For them it was enough, by way of commendation, that the practices should not be avoided as detestable and like idolatry; beyond that, they were not to advance, lest they be thought necessary—as though salvation came from them or could not exist without them.

“This was the opinion held by the heretics who, while wishing to be both Jews and Christians, were able to be neither Jews nor Christians. You kindly deigned to warn me most benevolently that I must avoid their position, although I had never belonged to it. Peter fell into the simulation, not the agreement, of that position through fear, so that Paul very truthfully wrote of him that, when he saw him ‘not walking rightly according to the truth of the Gospel,’ he said to him—most truthfully—that he ‘was compelling the Gentiles to Judaize’ (Gal. 2:14).”

[Note: Five manuscripts read *consummaretur* (“should be brought to completion”).]

[Note: Victorius changes *volunt* (“they wish”) to *voluerunt* (“they wished”).]

[Note: The Benedictines read *quod eum vidisset* (“when he had seen him”).]

“Paul certainly did not compel anyone to do this. For that reason he truthfully observed those ancient practices wherever necessary, in order to show that they were not to be condemned; yet he persistently preached that believers are saved not by those practices but by the revealed grace of faith, so that he might not compel anyone to undertake them as necessary.

“This, I believe, is how the Apostle Paul truthfully carried out all those practices. Yet now I neither compel nor permit anyone who has become a Christian from the Jews to celebrate such things truthfully—just as you, who think that Paul merely simulated them, neither compel nor permit this person to simulate such things.”

### 16

[Note: The earlier editions, as Victorius notes, read *bene faciant* (“do well”).]

“Do you want me also to say that this is the substance of the question, indeed of your position: that, after the Gospel of Christ, Jewish believers do well if they offer the sacrifices that Paul offered, if they circumcise their sons, and if they observe the Sabbath, as Paul did in the case of Timothy (Acts 16:3), and as all Jews observed, provided that they perform these practices deceitfully and falsely?

“If this is so, we are now falling not into the heresy of Ebion, or of those commonly called Nazarenes, or into any other ancient heresy, but—I do not know into what new one—which is more pernicious because it proceeds not from error but from deliberate and deceitful intention.

“But if, to clear yourself of this position, you reply that the Apostles laudably simulated these practices so that the weak would not be scandalized—the many who had believed from among the Jews and did not yet understand that these things should be rejected—whereas now, since the doctrine of Christian grace has been confirmed among so many nations, and since the reading of the Law and the Prophets has likewise been confirmed throughout all the Churches of Christ, these passages are to be recited for understanding, not observed: then whoever wishes to practice them by simulation would appear insane. Why may I not say that the Apostle Paul and other Christians of upright faith ought at that time to have commended those ancient sacraments by observing them truthfully for a little while, lest people think that the observances expressing those prophetic signs, which the most devout fathers had kept, were to be detested by their descendants as diabolical sacrileges?

“For when faith had come—the faith previously announced by those observances and revealed after the Lord’s death and resurrection—they had lost, as it were, the life of their function.

“Nevertheless, just as dead bodies had to be escorted, in a certain sense, to burial with the rites proper to them, not deceitfully but reverently, so they were not to be immediately abandoned or thrown away to be torn by the bites of enemies’ slander, like the bodies of dogs.

“Therefore, now whoever among Christians, even if he is of Jewish origin, wishes similarly to celebrate these practices is not a pious escort or bearer of a body, but an impious violator of a burial.”

[Note: The Benedictines read: “whoever wishes to practice these things by simulation is insane. Why …”]

[Note: Martianaeus, following Erasmus, had wrongly read *detestata* (“detested”) here.]

[Note: Twenty-two manuscripts omit the word *officii* (“function” or “office”).]

### 17

“I freely acknowledge that in what my letter contains I said too little concerning the fact that Paul had undertaken to celebrate the Jewish sacraments when he was already Christ’s Apostle, in order to teach that it was not harmful for those who wished to preserve them as they had received them from their ancestors through the Law—at least only during that period when the grace of faith was first revealed. For at that time this was not harmful.

[Note: Some printed editions read: “But as time progressed, it became harmful unless those observances were abandoned by all Christians; so that, if they were then performed, it would not be recognized that what God commanded his people through Moses differed from what the unclean spirit instituted in the temples of demons.” The Benedictines note that the words “it became harmful unless” are absent from twenty manuscripts. They further note that *fieret* (“should be done”) has the same meaning as *ne si primo illo tempore desererentur* (“lest they be abandoned at that first time”).]

“Rather, my negligence should be blamed, because I did not add this, than your rebuke. Yet long before I received your letters, when writing against Faustus the Manichaean, I explained the same passage, though briefly, and did not omit this point there. If your kindness does not disdain to read it, and if you wish, our beloved friends through whom I have now sent this writing will assure you that I dictated this before. Believe me concerning my own mind: speaking before God, and invoking the obligation of charity, I insist that it never seemed to me that Christians who had come from the Jews ought, with any feeling or intention whatsoever, to celebrate those ancient sacraments, or that it was in any way permitted to them to honor them. I have always understood Paul in this way, ever since his letters became known to me—just as you too think that no one at the present time should simulate these practices, although you believe that the Apostles did so.”

[Note: Martianaeus, following the older editions, reads: “to celebrate them with any feeling or intention whatsoever, or that they ought to be honored by them in any way, since I have always understood Paul in this way,” and so forth.]

### 18

“Accordingly, just as you speak in the opposite way, and, as you write, proclaim with a free voice, even though the world protests, that Jewish ceremonies are both harmful and deadly to Christians, and that whoever observes them—whether from the Jews or from the Gentiles—has been plunged into the abyss of the devil, so I entirely affirm this statement of yours, and add: Whoever observes them—whether from the Jews or from the Gentiles—not only truthfully but also by simulation, has been plunged into the abyss of the devil.

“What more do you seek? But just as you distinguish the Apostles’ simulation from the circumstances of the present time, so I distinguish the Apostle Paul’s truthful conduct in all these matters at that time from the present observance of Jewish ceremonies, even if that observance is entirely without simulation: for then it was to be approved, now it is to be detested.

“Thus, although we read, ‘The Law and the Prophets were until John the Baptist’ (Luke 16:16); and because the Jews sought to kill Christ for this reason, that he not only broke the Sabbath but also called God his own Father, making himself equal with God (John 5:18); and because ‘we have received grace in place of grace’ (John 1:16); and because ‘the Law was given through Moses, but grace and truth came through Jesus Christ’ (ibid. 17); and because through Jeremiah it was promised that God would give a new Testament to the house of Judah, not according to the Testament that he established with their fathers (Jer. 31:31–32)—I nevertheless do not think that the Lord himself was deceitfully circumcised by his parents.

“Or, if his age prevented that from being prohibited, I do not think that he deceitfully said to the leper—for it was not that observance commanded through Moses but he himself who had given the command—‘Go and offer for yourself the sacrifice that Moses commanded, as a testimony to them’ (Mark 1:44).

“Nor did he go up deceitfully to the feast. He went so far without doing so for the sake of display before men that he did not go up openly, but secretly” (John 7:10).

### 19

“But, someone says, the same Apostle said: ‘Behold, I Paul tell you that if you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing’ (Gal. 5:2). Did he therefore deceive Timothy and make Christ profit him nothing? Or, because this was done deceitfully, did it therefore do no harm?

“Yet Paul did not qualify his statement in this way. He did not say, ‘If you are circumcised truthfully,’ just as he did not say ‘deceitfully’; rather, without any exception, he said: ‘If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing.’

“Therefore, just as you wish to make room here for your position by wanting it to be understood as ‘unless deceitfully,’ so I not shamelessly demand that you also allow us to understand that the words ‘if you are circumcised’ were addressed to those who wanted to be circumcised because they thought that otherwise they could not be saved in Christ.

“Whoever was circumcised at that time with this mind, this will, and this intention received absolutely no benefit from Christ, just as he says plainly elsewhere: ‘For if righteousness is through the Law, then Christ died for nothing’ (Gal. 2:21).

“This is what he declares in the passage you yourself mentioned: ‘You have been severed from Christ, you who are justified in the Law; you have fallen away from grace’ (Gal. 5:4). He therefore rebukes those who believed that they were justified in the Law, not those who observed those legitimate practices in honor of the one who had commanded them, understanding both the manner in which they had been commanded as announcements of the truth and the point up to which they were to endure.

“Hence his statement: ‘If you are led by the Spirit, you are no longer under the Law’ (ibid. 18). Hence, as you infer, it appears that the person who is under the Law is not under it dispensatively, as you think our ancestors intended, but truly, as I understand it, because he does not possess the Holy Spirit.”

[Note: The same edition reads *imprudenter* (“imprudently”).]

[Note: Most printed editions read *velut colligis apparet* (“as you infer, it appears”); two Vatican manuscripts more elegantly read *apparet* (“it appears”), as the Benedictines note.]

### 20

“It seems to me a major question what it means to be under the Law in the manner condemned by the Apostle. For I do not think that he says this on account of circumcision, or of those sacrifices that were once offered by the fathers but are not now offered by Christians, or of other practices of this kind, but also on account of the very command that the Law gives: ‘You shall not covet’ (Exod. 20:17), which we certainly confess that Christians ought to observe and which is especially proclaimed in the light of the Gospel.

“He says that the Law is holy, and that the commandment is holy, just, and good (Rom. 7:12). Then he adds: ‘Has what is good, therefore, become death to me? By no means! Rather, sin, so that it might appear to be sin, through what is good worked death in me, so that through the commandment sin—or the sinner—might become exceedingly sinful’ (ibid. 13).

[Note: Victorius orders the passage to be emended from the Vulgate as follows: “so that sin might become sinful beyond measure,” which he says agrees with the Greek text, *ἁμαρτωλὸς ἡ ἁμαρτία* (“sin is sinful”), and with two manuscripts from Florence. He does not wish Augustine to have taken *ἤ* as “or.”]

“What he says here, that sin becomes exceedingly sinful through the commandment, he says elsewhere in this way: ‘The Law entered in so that the trespass might increase. But where the trespass increased, grace abounded all the more’ (Rom. 5:20).

“And elsewhere, when he had spoken above about the dispensation of grace, which justifies, he asks, as it were: ‘What, then, is the Law?’ And he immediately answers this question: ‘It was added because of transgressions, until the offspring should come to whom the promise had been made’ (Gal. 3:19).

“Those, then, he says are damnably under the Law whom the Law makes guilty: they do not fulfill the Law because, failing to understand the benefit of grace for carrying out God’s commandments, they presumptuously rely on their own strength with proud self-confidence.

“For ‘the fullness of the Law is love’ (Rom. 13:10). And the love of God has been poured into our hearts not through ourselves, but through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (Rom. 5:5). But explaining this matter as fully as is sufficient would perhaps require a longer discussion and a work of its own.

“If, then, the command of the Law, ‘You shall not covet’ (Rom. 13:9), holds a person guilty under itself and condemns the transgressor rather than freeing the sinner, unless human weakness has been aided by God’s grace, how much less could those practices commanded for the sake of signification—circumcision and the rest—which had to be abolished as the revelation of grace became more widely known, justify anyone?

“Nevertheless, for that reason they were not to be shunned as the diabolical sacrileges of the Gentiles, even when the grace that had been announced through such shadows had already begun to be revealed. They were to be permitted for a little while, especially to those who had come from the people to whom they had been given. Afterwards, however, once they had been buried with honor, they were to be abandoned irreversibly by all Christians.”

[Note: The Benedictines read: “what the Law says.”]

### 21

“But what does this mean, I ask you, when you say ‘not dispensatively, as our ancestors intended’? Either this is what I call an officious lie, so that this dispensation is a service consisting in lying honorably; or I altogether fail to see what else it can mean—unless, perhaps, by adding the name ‘dispensation,’ a lie becomes not a lie. But if that is absurd, why do you not openly say that an officious lie must be defended?

“Perhaps the name troubles you, because the term ‘office’ is not so customary in ecclesiastical books. Our Ambrose was not afraid of it: he wished to call some of his books, full of useful instructions, *On Duties* (*De Officiis*).

“Or is someone to be blamed if he lies officiously, but approved if he lies dispensatively? I ask you: let the person who thinks this lie wherever he chooses. For this too is a major question: whether a good man—or rather, a Christian man—may ever lie, when such men have been told, ‘Let your yes be yes, and your no, no, so that you do not fall under judgment’ (Jas. 5:12; Matt. 5:37), and when they hear in faith, ‘You will destroy all who speak falsehood’ (Ps. 5:7).”

### 22

“But this, as I have said, is itself a major question, as are other matters. Let the person who holds this view choose where he will lie, provided that he firmly believe and entirely defend that falsehood is absent from the writings of the authors of the sacred Scriptures, and especially of the canonical Scriptures.

“Otherwise the stewards of Christ, of whom it is said, ‘What is required of stewards is that each one be found faithful’ (1 Cor. 4:2), might appear to think that they had faithfully learned something great: to lie in place of dispensing the truth. Yet in Latin the word *fides* (‘faith’ or ‘fidelity’) is said to derive its name from the fact that what is said (*dicitur*) is done (*fit*). Where what is said is done, there is certainly no place for lying.

“The Apostle Paul therefore undoubtedly displays faithfulness to us in writing, for he was a steward of truth, not of falsehood. Accordingly, he wrote truthfully that he had seen Peter not walking rightly according to the truth of the Gospel and had opposed him to his face because he was compelling the Gentiles to Judaize (Gal. 2:14).

“Peter, for his part, received what Paul had done usefully through the freedom of charity with the holy and kindly piety of humility. Thus he offered later generations a rarer and more sacred example, so that they would not disdain to be corrected even by those who came after them if they had perhaps abandoned the straight path. Paul offered the example by which even those of lesser rank might confidently resist their superiors in defense of evangelical truth, while preserving brotherly charity.

“For although it is better never to deviate from the path than to deviate from it at any point, it is nevertheless much more remarkable and praiseworthy willingly to accept correction than boldly to correct one who is straying. Thus there is the praise of just freedom in Paul and of holy humility in Peter.

“As far as I can judge, this ought rather to have been defended against the slanderer Porphyry than to have given him a greater opportunity for attack, enabling him to accuse Christians much more bitterly of deceitfully either writing their own letters or handling the sacraments of their God.”

[Note: The Benedictines read *sacramenta portare* (“to carry the sacraments”).]

### 23

“You demand that I show at least one person whose opinion I have followed in this matter, since you have mentioned by name so many who preceded you in asserting what you maintain. You ask me to allow you to err with such men in the matter for which I criticize you.

“I confess that I have read none of them. Yet of those six or seven, you yourself weaken the authority of four. You say that the Laodicean—whose name you do not mention—has recently left the Church; Alexander was an ancient heretic; and I read in your more recent questions that you criticize Origen and Didymus, although earlier you praised Origen wonderfully.

“I therefore think that you err with these men, since you yourself would not endure it—although this is said as though they had not erred in this opinion. For who would wish to err with just anyone?

“Three, then, remain: Eusebius of Emesa, Theodore of Heraclea, and the John whom you mention a little later, who long ago governed the Church of Constantinople in the rank of bishop.”

### 24

“Moreover, if you ask or recall what our Ambrose thought about this matter, and likewise what our Cyprian thought, you may perhaps discover that we too were not without predecessors whom we could follow in what we assert.

[Note: It is difficult to find, in the surviving writings of Ambrose, anything resembling Augustine’s position. Nevertheless, in the commentaries on Paul’s letters printed in the appendix to the second volume, one finds: “Because of an occasion of negligence or error, the Apostles appear to disagree with one another. And: ‘Certainly he was open to rebuke from the truth of the Gospel, to which this action was opposed.’” These passages may perhaps have been excerpted from genuine works of Ambrose by a recent interpolator.

“As for Cyprian’s testimony, it is, we think, the passage suggested in Letter 71 to Quintus: ‘Nor did Peter, when Paul later disputed with him concerning circumcision, arrogantly claim anything for himself or presumptuously assume anything, saying that he held the primacy and that newcomers and those who came after ought rather to obey him. Nor did he despise Paul because he had previously persecuted the Church; rather, he accepted the counsel of truth and readily agreed with the legitimate reasoning that Paul defended.’ Augustine himself certainly cites this passage at the beginning of Book 2 of *On Baptism, against the Donatists*, to support this position of his.]

“Nevertheless, as I said shortly before, I owe this frank servitude only to the canonical Scriptures: I follow them alone in such a way that I have no doubt that their writers made no error at all in them and inserted nothing deceitfully.

“Therefore, when I seek a third person, so that I too may set three against three, I could easily find one, I think, if I had read many works. Yet in place of all these—or rather above them all—the Apostle Paul himself comes to mind. I take refuge in him. Against all interpreters of Scripture who think otherwise, I appeal to him; I question and interrogate him concerning what he wrote to the Galatians: that he had seen Peter not walking rightly according to the truth of the Gospel and had therefore opposed him to his face because, through that simulation, he was compelling the Gentiles to Judaize (Gal. 2:14). I ask whether he wrote the truth, or whether perhaps he lied through some dispensative falsehood.

“And I hear him crying out to me a little earlier, at the beginning of that same account, in a devout voice: ‘Now concerning the things I write to you, behold, before God, I do not lie’” (Gal. 1:20).

### 25

“Let anyone who thinks otherwise pardon me. I place greater faith in so great an Apostle swearing in his own letters than in any learned man disputing about the writings of another.

“Nor am I afraid that it may be said that I defend Paul in this way: that he did not simulate the error of the Jews, but was truly in error. For the one who, with apostolic freedom and in a manner suited to that time, commended those ancient sacraments by practicing them where necessary was not simulating error. Those sacraments had been established not only so that Satan’s cunning might deceive human beings, but also by God’s providence as prophetic announcements of future realities.

“Nor was he truly in the error of the Jews, since he not only knew but also insistently and forcefully preached that those who thought these practices had to be imposed upon the Gentiles or were necessary for the justification of any believers were in error.”

### 26

“When I said that he became as a Jew to the Jews and as a Gentile to the Gentiles, I do not think you paid sufficient attention to what I meant. Indeed, perhaps I did not explain it adequately.

“For I did not say this because he mercifully simulated those things, but because he did not simulate the things in which he acted like the Jews—just as he did not simulate the things in which he acted like the Gentiles, which you too mentioned. In this respect, I acknowledge that you helped me, and not ungratefully.

“When I asked you in my letter how he could be thought to have become as a Jew to the Jews because he deceitfully undertook the Jewish sacraments, since he also became as a Gentile to the Gentiles without deceitfully undertaking the sacrifices of the Gentiles, you replied that he became as a Gentile to the Gentiles in that he restored the foreskin and indiscriminately permitted himself to eat foods that the Jews condemn.

“Here I ask: did he do this by simulation as well? If that is utterly absurd and false, then so too, in those matters in which he prudently accommodated himself to Jewish custom through freedom, not through servile necessity—or, more disgracefully, through a deceitful rather than faithful dispensation—he acted truthfully.”

### 27

“For, as he himself testifies, to the faithful and to those who know the truth, ‘every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving’ (1 Tim. 4:4)—unless perhaps he is lying here too.

[Note: The Louvain edition reads *vero* (“indeed”); other editions and manuscripts, as the Benedictines note, read *viro* (“man”).]

“Therefore, for Paul himself—not merely as a man but especially as a most faithful steward, not merely as one who knew but also as a teacher of the truth—every creature of God in the matter of foods was truly good, not merely by simulation.

“Why, then, although he took up nothing deceitfully from the sacred rites and ceremonies of the Gentiles, but held and taught a true view concerning foods and the foreskin, did he become as a Gentile to the Gentiles, while he could become as a Jew to the Jews only by deceitfully undertaking the Jewish sacraments?

“Why, when the wild olive was grafted in, did he preserve the faithful truth of the dispensation, while upon the natural branches, established not outside but within the tree, he spread some veil of dispensational simulation?

“Why, when he became as a Gentile to the Gentiles, did he teach what he thought and think what he said, whereas, when he became as a Jew to the Jews, did he conceal one thing in his heart and express another in his words, actions, and writings?

[Note: Fourteen manuscripts, as the Benedictines note, read *quod agit sentit* (“what he does, he thinks”) for *quod ait, sentit* (“what he says, he thinks”).]

“May it be far from us to think this. For he owed to both groups love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith. Accordingly, he became all things to all people, so that he might win all—not through the cunning of one who lies, but through the compassion of one who suffers with others: that is, not by deceitfully doing all the evils of human beings, but by providing the careful attention of merciful medicine for all the evils of all others, as though they were his own.”

### 28

“Therefore, when he did not refuse to perform even those sacraments of the Old Testament himself, he was not deceiving out of compassion. Rather, without deceiving at all, he commended the fact that these practices had been commanded by the Lord God to last until the dispensation of a definite time, and he distinguished them from the sacrilegious rites of the Gentiles.

“At that time he became as a Jew to the Jews, not through the cunning of one who lies but through the compassion of one who suffers with others, when he wished to free them from the error by which they either refused to believe in Christ or thought that through their ancient priesthoods and observance of the ceremonies they could be cleansed from sins and made safe.

“He wished to free them as though he himself were held by that error, loving his neighbor as himself and doing for others what he would want others to do for him if he had needed it. When the Lord had given this instruction, he added: ‘For this is the Law and the Prophets’” (Matt. 22:40).

[Note: Victorius preferred *sacrificia* (“sacrifices”) and criticizes the printed reading; nevertheless, only two manuscripts among those cited by the Benedictines support him.]

### 29

“In the same Letter to the Galatians he commands this compassionate attitude, saying: ‘If a person is overtaken in any transgression, you who are spiritual should instruct such a one in a spirit of gentleness, watching yourself, lest you also be tempted’ (Gal. 6:1).

[Note: The same editor removed the word *si* (“if”), saying that it was redundant and found in no manuscripts. The Benedictines then note that Augustine uses *fiere* in the imperative elsewhere in manuscripts, while one Vatican manuscript reads *fias*.]

“See whether he did not say, ‘Become as that person,’ so that you might win him. Certainly not so that he might deceitfully act as though he were what he was not, or pretend to possess such a condition; rather, so that in another’s offense he might consider what could also happen to himself, and thus mercifully assist the other as he would wish to be assisted by another. That is, not through the cunning of one who lies, but with the compassion of one who suffers with another.

“Thus Paul became as a Jew to the Jew, as a Gentile to the Gentile, and as any other person in error or established in some sin—not by pretending to be what he was not, but by compassionately considering what he might have been, as one who recognized that he was human—so that he might win all.”

### 30

“If you please, I beg you to look for a little while at yourself—at yourself, I say, in relation to me. Recall, or, if you have it written down, reread your words in that shorter letter which you sent me through our brother, now my fellow bishop, Cyprian. After you had gravely complained that I had committed certain offenses against you, you added these words with how truthful, genuine, and complete an affection of charity:

“‘In this friendship is injured; in this the rights of our relationship are violated: lest we seem to contend childishly and furnish our respective supporters or detractors material for contention.’

“I feel that these words of yours were spoken not only from your heart but also with a kindly intention to advise me.

[Variant: *Denique* (“Finally”) for *Deinde* (“Then”).]

Then you add what would have been evident even if you had not added it, saying:

“‘I write this because I wish to love you purely and as a Christian, and to retain in my mind nothing that differs from my lips.’

“O holy man, loved by me with a truthful heart—as God sees my soul—the very thing that you set down in your letter, by which I have no doubt that you exposed yourself to me, I believe the Apostle Paul also displayed entirely in his letters, not to one individual, but to the Jews, Greeks, and all the Gentiles who were his children, whom he had begotten in the Gospel and for whom he was in labor; and then to so many thousands of faithful Christians in later generations, for whose sake that letter was committed to writing, so that he might retain in his mind nothing that differed from his lips.”

[Variant: *commendabatur* (“was commended”) for *mandabatur* (“was committed”).]

### 31

“Certainly you too became as I am—not through the cunning of one who lies, but through the compassion of one who suffers with another—when you considered that I should no more be abandoned in the fault into which you thought I had fallen than you would wish to be abandoned if you had fallen into it yourself.

“Therefore, while thanking your benevolent attitude toward me, I also ask you not to be angry with me because, when certain things in your little works troubled me, I made my disturbance known to you. I wish everyone to observe toward me what I myself wish to be observed toward you: that, whatever they think ought to be censured in my writings, they neither conceal it in a deceitful heart nor criticize it before others while keeping silent before me.

[Variant: Fourteen manuscripts read *nec claudant subdolo pectore* (“nor conceal it in a deceitful heart”); the Benedictines suggest Augustine may allude to Jerome’s words, “nor retain anything in my mind,” etc.]

“For I think that friendship is injured and the rights of relationship violated precisely in this way. I do not know whether those should be considered Christian friendships in which the common proverb, ‘Compliance wins friends; truth breeds hatred,’ carries more weight than the ecclesiastical saying, ‘The wounds of a friend are more faithful than the voluntary kisses of an enemy.’”

### 32

“Therefore, with all the earnestness we can muster, let us teach our dearest friends who sincerely favor our labors this lesson: that among beloved friends it is possible for one to contradict the other in speech without charity itself being diminished and without truth, which is owed to friendship, producing hatred—whether what is contradicted is true or whether, with a truthful heart, whatever it may be is said without retaining in the mind anything that differs from the lips.

“Let our brothers, your associates, to whom you bear witness that they are vessels of Christ, believe that it happened against my will, and that my heart contains no small grief over this matter: that my letters reached the hands of many before they were able to reach you, to whom they had been written.

“How this happened would take too long to recount—or, if I am not mistaken, it would be unnecessary. It is enough, if I am believed in this matter, that it did not happen with the intention that is supposed, and that it was not at all my will, arrangement, consent, or even, at least, thought that it should happen.

[Note: Martianaeus, with the older editions, reads *cognitionis* (“knowledge”) here.]

“If they do not believe this, although I speak with God as witness, I have nothing more that I can do. Yet far be it from me to think that they maliciously suggested these things to your holiness in order to stir up hostility between us—may the mercy of our Lord God avert such hostility from us. Rather, I readily suppose human faults in a human being without any intention of doing harm.

“For this is the fair thing for me to believe about them, if they are vessels of Christ, made not for dishonor but for honor, and placed by God in a great house for every good work.”

[Note: The Benedictines read “for a good work.”]

“If, after this testimony of mine comes to their attention, they wish to act in that way, you too see how wrong their action would be.”

### 33

“What I had written—that I had sent no book against you to Rome—I wrote for this reason: I distinguished the title of the book from the letter itself. Accordingly, I had supposed that you had heard something else altogether. I had sent to Rome not the letter itself, but had sent it to you; and I did not think that what I had done in the sincerity of friendship—whether as something requiring admonition or as something by which you or I might be corrected by the other—was directed against you.

“Setting aside your associates, I beg you, by the grace through which we have been redeemed, not to think that whatever good qualities of yours, granted to you by the goodness of the Lord, I have mentioned in my letters were inserted by me through insidious flattery. But if I have sinned against you in any way, forgive me.

“Nor should you take more seriously than I said the incident concerning some poet, which I perhaps recalled less aptly than elegantly in writing. I immediately added that I had not said this so that you might recover the eyes of your heart—far be it from me ever to think that you had lost them—but so that you might take notice of the fact that you possessed them sound and vigilant.

“Therefore, I thought that this point should be taken up solely because of the *παλινῳδία* (*palinode*, or recantation), which should be imitated if we write something that we later have to destroy in a subsequent writing—not because of Stesichorus’ blindness, which I neither attributed to nor feared in your heart. I ask you again and again to correct me confidently wherever you see that this is necessary.

“For although, according to the titles of honor that ecclesiastical custom has now established, the episcopate is higher than the presbyterate, nevertheless in many matters Augustine is lesser than Jerome—although correction ought not to be avoided or disdained even when it comes from anyone at all junior.”

[Note: Learned men argue that Jerome later conceded the more accurate position to Augustine from the passage in *Dialogue 1 against the Pelagians*, chapter 8. There, saying that no bishop—or only very few—is irreproachable, Jerome adds: “Who will be indignant that what the Prince of the Apostles did not possess is denied to him?” The position that Jerome had drawn from the writings of the Greek Fathers was also embraced by Cassian, *Conferences* 17; Augustine’s position, however, was adopted by many others, especially those called the Scholastics.]

[Note: Martianus, following the older editions, reads *prospexeris* (“you have foreseen” or “you have perceived”).]

### 34

“Concerning your translation, you have now persuaded me of the purpose for which you wish to translate the Scriptures from the Hebrew: namely, to bring into public view those things that have been omitted or corrupted by the Jews.

“But please deign to explain to me from which Jews these readings come: whether from those very Jews who translated the Scriptures before the Lord’s coming; and, if so, from which translators or from which one of them; or whether from those later Jews who might be thought to have either removed certain things from the Greek manuscripts or corrupted them in those manuscripts so that they would not be convicted by those testimonies concerning the Christian faith.

“As for the earlier translators, I cannot discover why they would have done this.

“Then, I beg you, send us your translation of the Septuagint, which I did not know you had published. I also wish to read your book, which you mentioned, *On the Best Kind of Translation*, and to learn how the translator’s mastery of languages is to be brought into comparison with the conjectures of those who explain and interpret the Scriptures. Even when such interpreters are orthodox and of one faith, they must produce differing opinions concerning many obscure passages; yet this diversity in no way conflicts with the unity of the same faith.

“Indeed, even one interpreter, while adhering to the same faith, can explain the same passage in different ways, because its obscurity permits this.”

35. “I desire your translation of the Septuagint for this reason also: so that, as far as we are able, we may be free from the incompetence of so many Latin translators—whatever sort of men they were—who have dared to undertake this work; and so that those who think that I begrudge your useful labors may finally understand, if possible, that I do not want your translation from the Hebrew to be read in the churches because we would greatly disturb the Christian peoples by seeming to introduce something new against the authority of the Septuagint. Their ears and hearts have grown accustomed to hearing that translation, which was also approved by the Apostles.

“Thus, concerning that plant in Jonah (Jonah 4:6), if in Hebrew it is neither ivy nor gourd, but I know not what other thing, which, resting on its trunk, rises without needing any supporting props, I would now prefer that ‘gourd’ be read in all the Latin copies. For I do not think that the Septuagint placed this word there without reason, unless they knew that this plant too was similar to it.”

[Col. 0953] 36. “I believe that I have answered your three letters—indeed, perhaps more than sufficiently—in which two reached me through Cyprian and one through Firmus. Write back whatever you think will be useful for instructing us or others. I shall take greater care, as far as the Lord assists me, that the letters I write to you reach you before they reach anyone through whom they might be more widely circulated. For I admit that I do not want what has happened to my letters to you to happen to your letters to me, which you very properly complain of.

“Nevertheless, let us mutually approve not only affection but also the freedom of friendship. Neither you withhold from me, nor I from you, whatever in our letters moves us in turn—provided that we do so with that disposition which, in the sight of God and within brotherly love, is not displeasing. But if you think this cannot be done between us without a harmful offense against love itself, let it not be done. For the love I would have with you is certainly greater; but this lesser love is better than none.”

[Note: Older printed editions and Martianaeus read *melior* (“better”).]

## LETTER CXVII

[Note: Otherwise numbered 47. Written in the year 405.]

### TO A MOTHER AND DAUGHTER

[Note: Formerly the title stood simply as *On Avoiding Suspicious Co-habitation*. We follow the manuscripts, which add the words “residing in Gaul.” Jerome himself says in *Against Vigilantius*, section 3: “Let the malicious interpreter say that I invented the subject to which I respond in rhetorical declamation, just as I did with the one I wrote to Gaul, concerning a mother and daughter at odds with one another.” Erasmus likewise suspected that Jerome had taken up and treated the subject in the manner of a rhetorical exercise.]

**To those residing in Gaul.**

He teaches widows and virgins that they must avoid domestic companionship with persons from whom there is danger either to chastity or to reputation. He explains the subject of the letter more fully in the Preface.

### PREFACE

1. A certain brother from Gaul reported to me that he had a virgin sister and a widowed mother who lived in separate rooms in the same city. Either because of the loneliness of their lodging or in order to guard their modest possessions, they had taken certain clerics as protectors for themselves; and so they were joined to strangers with greater disgrace than they had been separated from one another.

When I groaned and conveyed by my silence much more than by my speech, he said: “I ask you to rebuke them in a letter of yours and restore them to harmony, so that the mother may acknowledge her daughter and the daughter her mother.”

I replied: “You are assigning me an excellent task: that I, an outsider, should reconcile women whom neither son nor brother has been able to reconcile. As though I held an episcopal chair, rather than being shut up in a little cell and removed far from the crowds, either lamenting past faults or striving to avoid present ones. Besides, it is incongruous to hide bodily while one’s tongue roams throughout the whole world.”

He answered: “You are excessively fearful. Where is that former firmness with which, scouring the world with much wit, you produced something Lucillian? [Note: Martianaeus reads *detulisti* (“you brought forth”), a word found in the manuscripts, though they corruptly read some “Lucilian.” Horace, *Satires* 1.10, calls Lucilius the man who “scoured the City with much salt,” and so forth.]”

“That,” I said, “is precisely what frightens me and prevents me from parting my lips. For after I became a criminal by censuring crimes, and, according to the proverb commonly repeated by the people—‘With everyone quarreling and denying’ [Note: Two manuscripts read *jurantibus* (“swearing”) and *negantibus* (“denying”).]—I believe that I have neither ears nor sense of touch. The very walls resounded with curses against me, and those who drank sang against me [Psalm 68]. Forced by evil, I learned to keep silent. I judged it more proper to set a guard over my mouth and a fortified door upon my lips [Psalm 38] than to incline my heart toward words of malice and, while cutting away faults, to fall into the fault of detraction.”

When I had said this, he replied: “It is not detraction to speak the truth, and private correction does not constitute general teaching, since scarcely anyone—or no one—falls under the guilt of this offense. So I ask you not to let me, wearied by so long a journey, have come in vain. The Lord knows that, after my visit to the holy places, this was my chief reason for coming: that with your letter I might heal both sister and mother.”

“All right,” I said. “I shall do what you want. The letters are to cross the sea, and a written discourse specially directed to particular persons can rarely find anyone whom it wounds. But I ask you to keep this discourse secret. When you have carried it with you as traveling provisions, if it is heard, let us rejoice together; but if it is despised—as I rather expect—I shall have lost my words, and you the length of your journey.”

**The Preface ends.**

2. First I want you to know, sister and daughter [Note: This is how all the manuscripts and printed editions read, except Victorius, who, failing to notice that Jerome is addressing an older woman by the name “sister in Christ,” supplied *mater* (“mother”) from his own conjecture; Martianaeus censures him for this.], that I am not writing because I suspect anything sinister about you, but lest others suspect that I am urging your reconciliation [Note: We have restored the true reading from Ambrosian manuscript 66, Erasmus, and the older edition that we frequently follow. Victorius and Martianaeus printed, with faulty meaning, “that your harmony is in error,” although the whole context makes clear that Jerome is pleading for harmony between women who were at odds with each other, living separately, and thereby giving others cause for suspicion.].

Otherwise—God forbid—if I thought you had been joined by the glue of sin, I would never write, and I would know that I was telling a tale to the deaf. Next I ask this of you: if I write anything somewhat biting, do not attribute it so much to my severity [another reading: *authority*] as to the disease. Rotten flesh is treated with the sword and cautery; poisons are driven out by a serpentine antidote. What hurts severely is driven out by a greater pain.

Finally, I say this: even if your conscience has no wound of crime, your reputation nevertheless bears disgrace. Mother and daughter: names of piety, terms of duty, bonds of nature, a union second only to God. It is no praise if you love one another; it is a crime that you hate one another.

The Lord Jesus was subject to his parents [Luke 2]. He revered his mother, whose father he himself was. He honored his foster-father, whom he had himself nourished. He remembered that he had been carried in one person’s womb and in another’s arms. Therefore, even as he hung upon the cross, he entrusted his mother to his disciple [John 19], though he had never before the cross sent her away.

[Col. 0955] 3. But you, daughter—for now I shall cease addressing the mother, whom perhaps age, weakness, and solitude make excusable—you, I say, daughter, judge the house of one whose womb was not too narrow for you. You lived enclosed in her womb for ten months, yet you cannot endure one day with your mother in one room?

Can you not bear her eyes? And you, who flee a witness within the household, cannot tolerate the woman who, as the one who gave birth to you, nourished you, and brought you to this age, more readily understands all your movements? If you are a virgin, why do you fear careful supervision? If you are corrupted, why do you not marry openly? It is a second plank after shipwreck to moderate what you have begun badly by this remedy at least.

I do not say this because, after sin, I would remove repentance, so that what began badly should continue badly [another reading: “so that you should begin and persist badly”]; rather, I despair of separation in a relationship of this kind. Otherwise, if after your fall you move to your mother, you will more easily be able to mourn with her what you lost through her absence. But if you are still undefiled and have lost nothing, take care not to lose it. Why do you need to remain in a house where each day you must either perish or conquer?

Does any mortal sleep securely beside a viper? Even if it does not strike, it certainly causes anxiety. It is safer to be unable to perish than not to have perished while beside danger. In the one case there is tranquility; in the other, management. There we rejoice; here we escape.

4. But perhaps you will answer: “My mother is not well behaved. She desires worldly things, loves wealth, knows nothing of fasting, smears her eyes with cosmetics, wants to appear elegantly dressed, and harms my purpose. I cannot live with such a woman.”

First, even if she is as you claim, you will have a greater reward if you do not abandon her. She carried you for a long time in her womb, nourished you for a long time, and with tender devotion endured the more difficult habits of infancy. She washed the filth from your clothing and was often soiled by unclean excrement. She sat beside you when you were sick; and she who endured her own disgusts for your sake also endured yours. She brought you to this age and taught you to love Christ.

Do not be displeased by the way of life of the woman who consecrated you as a virgin to your bridegroom. But if you cannot bear her and flee her pleasures—and, as the common expression has it, your mother is worldly—you have other virgins; you have a holy choir of chastity. Why, in abandoning your mother, do you choose [another reading: “love”] a man who perhaps has abandoned his own sister and mother?

She is difficult, but he is easy. She is quarrelsome; therefore he is conciliatory. I ask whether you followed this man or found him afterward. If you followed him, it is evident that you abandoned your mother. If you found him afterward, you show what you were unable to find in your mother’s hospitality.

The pain is harsh, and it wounds me with my own sword. “The one who walks simply walks confidently,” Scripture says [Proverbs 10]. I would be silent if my conscience did not reproach me, if I did not censure my own crime in others, and if through the beam in my own eye I did not see another’s splinter. [Note: The third negative particle has been deleted so that the passage may make sense in this form: “I would be silent if my conscience did not reproach me, if I did not censure my own crime in others, and if through the beam in my own eye I did not see another’s splinter.” Since the old manuscripts provide no support for our emendation, we refrain from laying a hand upon the wound.]

But now, while I live far from the brothers, enjoy their companionship honorably under witnesses, see them rarely, and am rarely seen by them, it is the height of shamelessness for you not to follow the modesty of one whose example you claim to follow.

If you say, “My conscience is sufficient for me; I have God as judge, who is witness to my life; I do not care what people say,” listen to the Apostle writing: “Providing what is good not only before God but also before all people” [Romans 12].

If someone censures you because you are a Christian, because you are a virgin, do not be concerned. If you have therefore left your mother so that you might live among virgins in a monastery, such detraction is your praise. Where there is no lust in the girl of God but only harshness being censured, this cruelty is piety. For you prefer to her the one whom you are commanded to prefer even to your own soul. If she herself also prefers him, she will recognize you both as daughter and as sister.

5. What then? Is it a crime for a holy man to have a female companion? You drag me by the neck before the court, so that I must either approve what I do not want to approve or incur the hatred of many.

A holy man never separates a daughter from her mother. He receives and reveres both. However holy the daughter may be, a widowed mother is evidence of chastity. If this man is your contemporary, let him honor your mother as his own; if he is older, let him love you as a daughter and submit you to the discipline of a parent.

It is not good for the reputation of either of you that you love him more than your mother, lest he appear to choose affection in you rather than age. And I would say this if you did not have a monk for a brother and lacked domestic protection. But now, alas, between a mother and her brother—between a widowed mother and a monastic brother—why does a stranger insert himself?

It is a good thing for you to know yourself both daughter and sister. But if you cannot be both, and your mother is rejected as though she were harsh, at least let your brother please you. If your brother is more severe, let the woman who gave birth to you be more gentle.

Why do you turn pale? Why do you burn with agitation? Why do you flood your face with blushes and, with trembling lips, bear witness to the impatience of your heart? Nothing surpasses the love of a mother and brother except the affection of a husband alone.

6. I also hear that you visit suburban estates and the pleasant grounds of villas with relatives and relations, and with people of that sort. I do not doubt that either a female cousin or a sister is present, as a companion of a new kind, to whose consolation you are led.

For heaven forbid that, although these men are very close to you and related, I should suspect you of seeking the company of men. I ask you, therefore, virgin, to answer me: Do you travel alone in the company of your relatives, or with your lover?

However shameless you may be, you will not dare to present him to the eyes of secular people. For if you do this, the whole household will sing about both you and him. Everyone’s finger will point at you. Even the sister, relation, or kinswoman who, to flatter you, calls the holy man a “Nonnius” [Note: Older printed editions sometimes read “holy man before you,” and Victorius approves this reading, while relegating the reading we defend to the variants. Elsewhere we have explained that *Nonnii* were formerly called pious men, particularly those who had vowed virginity to God.] will laugh at your monstrous husband when she has turned away for a little while.

But if you go alone—as I rather think you do—you will walk among adolescent servants, married women and women about to marry, wanton girls, and young men with carefully dressed hair and cosmetics [Note: Printed editions have *linteatos*, *lineatos*, or *limatos*. The reading is corrected from the manuscripts to mean men made up or painted with cosmetics; elsewhere Jerome calls such men *calamistrati*, “curled with the curling iron.”], wearing a dark garment.

Any little bearded fellow will offer you his hand and support you when tired; and with fingers pressed tightly together, either he will be tempted or he will tempt you. You will dine among men and married women; you will watch others kiss and eat food that has been tasted beforehand. Without bringing scandal upon yourself, you will admire in others their silk garments and gilded ornaments.

At the very banquet you will be compelled, as though unwilling, to eat meat. If you drink wine, God’s creature will be praised. If you wash in the baths, filth will be removed. And whenever you reluctantly do any of the things they urge, they will all proclaim you pure, simple, a lady, and truly freeborn.

Meanwhile some singer will sound at the table, and amid the psalms flowing in sweet melody—because he will not dare to address another man’s wife—he will look repeatedly at you, who have no guardian. He will speak with gestures and communicate through expressions whatever he fears to say.

Amid these and so many enticements of pleasure, lust conquers even minds of iron. In virgins it suffers a greater hunger, since it considers everything it does not know to be sweeter. The stories of the pagans tell that sailors were driven headlong upon the rocks by the songs of the Sirens, and that at Orpheus’ lyre trees, beasts, and the hardness of stones were softened.

Chastity is difficult to preserve amid banquets. A shining complexion reveals a filthy mind.

7. As boys we read about these things in school, and we have seen the bronze instruments breathing in the streets. We have seen someone scarcely held together by his bones who burned with illicit loves and lost his life before he was freed from that plague.

What will you do, a girl of sound body, delicate, plump, flushed, and burning amid meats, wines, and baths, beside married men [another reading: married women], beside young men [another reading: young women]? Even if you do not do what you are asked, yet, if you are asked, you may take it as testimony to your beauty. [Note: It seems far most likely to us that Jerome wrote *de forma putes testimonium* (“you will provide testimony concerning your appearance”), that is, you may infer from the question that you are considered beautiful, rather than the single word *deforme* (“ugly”), found in Erasmus and Martianaeus, which makes no sense and contradicts the author’s intention. Victorius’s reading, *formae*, pointed us toward this solution.]

A lustful mind pursues what is shameful with greater ardor, and imagines what is forbidden to be sweeter. The garment itself, cheap and dark, is an indication of a silent mind—if it has no wrinkle; if it is dragged along the ground so that you may appear taller [Note: Incorrectly printed, and rejected by the manuscripts. Victorius includes the negative particle, “is not dragged.”]; if the tunic has been deliberately ripped so that something beneath may appear, covering what is ugly and revealing what is beautiful. [Note: The old manuscripts add: “All these things will arm young men more eagerly for your violation,” as Gravius attests.]

The little black shoe of the woman walking, shining and creaking, also calls young men to itself. The breasts are compressed with bands, and the chest is tightened more narrowly by a crimped girdle. The hair falls either over the forehead or over the ears.

[Col. 0958] Sometimes the little cloak slips down to expose the white shoulders, and, as though she did not wish to be seen, she hurriedly covers what she had deliberately uncovered. And when in public she covers her face as though out of modesty, with the art of a brothel she displays only that which, once displayed, can please more.

8. You will answer: “How do you know me? How, placed so far away, do you cast your eyes upon me?”

The tears of your brother have told me this, and his intolerable sobs at every moment. Would that he had lied, and had said this more from fear than accusation. But believe me: no one weeps while lying.

He grieves that you have preferred a young man—not indeed one with carefully dressed hair or silk clothing [Note: The Ambrosian manuscript reads *trosulum*; other manuscripts and older printed editions read *rosulum*, with the same meaning. Some, wishing to preserve the balanced structure throughout, propose reading *non vestitu sericatum* instead of *non vestium sericarum*; this is overly elaborate.]—but one soft and pampered amid filth, who himself bears the mark of the world, keeps a workshop, distributes the allotted tasks, manages the household, and buys whatever is needed from the marketplace.

He is steward and master, anticipating the duties of the servants, whom all the domestics gnaw at with their complaints. Whatever the mistress has not given, they loudly claim that he has stolen. Servants are a complaining race, and however much you give them, it is always too little. They do not consider how much there was, but how much is given; and they console their own distress by whatever slanders they can devise.

One calls him a parasite, another an impostor, another a legacy-hunter, and another by any new name that happens to occur. They boast that he sits beside her little bed, summons midwives when she is weak, carries the chamber pot, warms the linens, and folds the bands.

People more readily believe evil, and whatever is fabricated at home becomes public rumor. Nor should you be surprised if the slave girls and household servants invent such things about you, since your mother also complains of the very same thing, as does your brother.

9. Do what I advise and beg you to do: first be reconciled with your mother, and then, if that cannot be done, at least with your brother. Or, if you abhor dividing, as enemies, names so dear to you, separate from the man whom you are said to have preferred to your own family.

But if you cannot do even this—though you will return to your family if you can leave him—then at least use your companion more honorably. Let your houses be separated and your meals divided, lest malicious people accuse you, because you live under one little roof, of also sharing one bed.

You can have the companionship you desire for your needs and still, in some measure, escape public disgrace. Yet the stain must be avoided which, according to Jeremiah, can be washed away by no soap and no fuller’s herb [another reading: “diluted”].

When you want him to see you and visit you, bring in witnesses: friends, freedmen [another reading: freeborn persons], and servants. A good conscience flees no one’s eyes. Let him enter without fear and leave secure. Silent eyes, speechless conversation, and the posture of the whole body sometimes speak either fear or security.

Open your ears, I beg you, and hear the clamor of the entire city. You have already lost your proper names and taken titles from one another: you are called his, and he yours. Your mother and brother hear this. They are ready and beg you to divide yourselves from each other and to turn the private disgrace of your union into a common praise. You remain with your mother; let him remain with your brother.

You will love your brother’s companion more boldly; your mother will love her son’s friend more honorably than her daughter’s. But if you refuse, if you contemptuously reject my advice with a wrinkled brow, this letter will proclaim to you in a free voice:

“Why do you hold hostage another’s servant? Why do you make Christ’s minister your own servant? Look at the people; observe the faces of each one. He reads in the church, and everyone looks at you—unless it is that you almost boast of your disgrace with the license of a wife. You can no longer be satisfied with secret dishonor. You call shamelessness freedom. Your face has become the face of a prostitute; you do not know how to blush” [Jeremiah 3].

10. Again you cry out that I am malicious, again suspicious, again a spreader of rumors. Am I suspicious? Am I malevolent? I who, as I stated in the preface to this letter, wrote precisely because I was not suspicious?

Or are you negligent, careless, and contemptuous? At twenty-five years of age [Note: The Veronese parchment manuscripts read “thirty-one years of age”], have you enclosed a young man who is not yet properly bearded within your arms as though within nets?

A truly excellent tutor he is, to admonish you and frighten you with the severity of his brow. And although lust is safe at no age, even a gray head at least protects one from open disgrace.

The time will come—it will come, for the day approaches while you do not know it—when this handsome youth of yours, since women grow old quickly, especially those who are beside men, will either find someone richer or someone younger. Then you will regret your decision and grow weary of your stubbornness, when you have lost both your property and your reputation, when what was badly joined will be properly divided. Unless perhaps you are confident that, with affection strengthened by so long a period, you need not fear separation.

11. You also, mother, who on account of your age do not fear curses, do not defend yourself in such a way that you sin. Let your daughter learn from you to separate herself, rather than you to be separated from her.

You have a son, a daughter, and a son-in-law—or rather, your daughter’s companion. Why do you seek the consolations of another and rekindle fires that have already been put out? It is more honorable for you at least to bear your daughter’s fault than to seek an occasion for your own.

Let your monastic son be with you, the protection of your piety and widowhood. Why do you seek a strange man, especially in a house that could not contain son and daughter? You are now of an age at which you could have grandchildren through your daughter.

Invite both of them to your home. Let the woman who went out alone return with a man. I said “man,” not “husband.” Let no one accuse me of slander. I meant to indicate sex, not marriage.

Or if she is ashamed, hesitates, and considers the house in which she was born too narrow, go to her little lodging. Although it is cramped, it can more easily contain a mother and brother than a strange man with whom she certainly could not remain chastely in one house, in one room. [Note: Two manuscripts of good authority read more briefly: “with whom she could not remain chastely in one room.” To change the printed reading as little as possible, we nevertheless judged that what had been printed—“without a room,” or “in no room,” or “in another’s room”—had to be corrected, since it made no sense. Gravius reads *sine* (“without”).]

Let there be two women and two men in one house. But if that third man, your [Greek: γηροβόσκος] *gērobóskos* [Col. 0960], does not want to live there and stirs up seditions and disturbances, let there be a pair, let there be a trio: let your brother be her son, and let him provide that man with a sister and a mother. [Note: Formerly the text read [Greek: τριτοβόσκος], which could be translated “a third nourisher” or “a shepherd.” Most manuscripts preserve only traces of the Greek letters, [Greek: ΤΗΡΟϹΚΟϹ]. But the printed editions correctly have [Greek: γηροβόσκος], “nourisher of the aged,” referring to the mother’s support. Yet from the sequence of the discourse and the preceding words—“Let there be two women and two men in one house”—it is clear that the same earlier printed editions were mistaken in reading “he does not want to leave” instead of “he does not want to live there”; we have substituted and corrected the reading from the Veronese copy. Gravius prefers [Greek: πρόσοικος], “neighbor” or “one dwelling nearby.”]

Let others call him stepfather and son-in-law; let him call him foster-father and brother. [Note: The printed editions incorrectly read *exhibebis* (“you will present”); the manuscripts correct this, as they do many other matters that it is not worth pointing out to the reader each time.]

12. I dictated these words as a brief nocturnal composition and in hurried speech, wishing to satisfy the request of the one who asked and, as though practicing a school exercise, to train myself in a scholastic theme.

For the very same person who was to depart was knocking at my door that morning. [Note: The Veronese manuscript reads *qui*; the printed editions read *qua*.] At the same time I wanted to show my detractors that I too can say whatever comes to my mouth. Therefore I touched only briefly upon the Scriptures, and I did not weave my discourse, as I am accustomed to do in my other books, with their flowers.

It is an extemporaneous dictation, poured forth with such ease by lamplight that the hands of the scribes ran ahead of my tongue, and the rapidity of the speech overwhelmed the marks and turns of the words.

I have said this so that whoever does not forgive my talent may at least forgive the lack of time.

## LETTER CXVIII

[Note: Otherwise numbered 34. Written in the year 406.]

### TO JULIAN

He consoles a certain very wealthy Julian, who within a few days had lost two daughters and his wife and, when the barbarians invaded, a considerable part of his property. By comparison with Job and by the example of Pammachius and Paulinus, he exhorts him to the perfect life—that is, to a complete contempt for the world—since fortune itself seems to summon him to this.

1. My son, your brother Ausonius, at the very moment of his departure, after having given me only a late opportunity to see him and having quickly taken it away, after saying “Hail” and “Farewell” almost in the same instant, thought that he would return empty-handed unless he carried you some little trifle of mine in a hurried discourse.

Already, after the public horse had been saddled upon the surrender of the official travel token [Note: This should certainly be retained as *synthemate*, not altered, as many others have done—and as Martianaeus himself noted in the margin—to *schemate*. It was [Greek: σύνθεμα] or [Greek: σύνθημα], for the old Glossary edited by Labbaeus gives both forms: a conveyance, or a sign, seal, token, or tessera; ultimately, a diploma without which one could not use the public transport system. Julian Augustus, in a letter to the quaestor Libanius, explicitly said that a [Greek: σύνθημα] was necessary for using a public horse or vehicle: “How useful the travel token would be to us when we are delayed; for instead of trembling and fearing while being carried in a public carriage …” Nor should we heed the otherwise eminent scholars who, following Salmasius in his notes on Lampridius, take *synthema* to mean a garment; hence the recent French translator of Jerome’s letters rendered it “country dress.” Victorius likewise thought it a kind of garment suited to noblemen and business, based on the jurist Scaevola’s words: “I ask whether, from the entire wardrobe—that is, from the *synthesis*—he may choose individual tunics and little Sempronian cloaks.” Also from a certain epigram: “While the knight and lord of the senate delights in *syntheses*”; and, “For one *synthesis* makes great protection against the cold.” But Jerome said *demisso*, or *dimisso synthemate* (“after the travel token had been lowered or surrendered”), not *demissa synthesi* (“after the garment had been lowered”), to say nothing of how awkwardly they invent a *synthesis* here.] a public horse was being readied, and a noble young man dressed in a purple tunic was encircled by a belt. Yet, having set a notary beside me, he compelled me to speak, so that the swift hand might follow what was quickly uttered and capture the speed of my tongue in written signs.

Thus, not through the diligence of the writer but through the recklessness of the speaker, I break the long silence toward you, offering you the bare willingness to serve you. This is an extemporaneous letter, without orderly thought, without embellishment or composition of words, so that you will find in it a friend in his entirety, but nothing of an orator.

You may think it poured out on the march, and that provisions were thrust upon one eager to depart. Divine Scripture says: “Music in mourning is an untimely tale” [Ecclesiasticus 22:6]. Therefore, scorning the tricks of rhetorical art and the elegance of childish and applause-seeking eloquence, we flee for refuge to the gravity of the Holy Scriptures, where there is true medicine for wounds and certain remedies for grief:

There the mother receives her only son upon a bier; there the crowd standing around is told, “The girl is not dead, but sleeping” [Mark 5:39]; there the four-day-old dead man comes forth bound at the voice of the Lord who cries out [John 11].

2. I hear that in a short time you carried out almost simultaneous funerals for your two young daughters and that your most chaste and faithful wife, Faustina—indeed, your sister in the warmth of faith, in whom alone you found consolation after losing your children—was taken from you by a sudden sleep.

It was as though, after surviving shipwreck on the shore, you encountered robbers, and, according to the words of the Prophets, while fleeing from a bear fell upon a lion; and, stretching your hand toward a wall, were bitten by a snake.

Then came the losses to your household, the devastation of the entire province by the barbarian enemy, and, amid the general depopulation, the ruin of your private estates; the herds of cattle and flocks of sheep driven away; the household servants bound and killed; and, in your only daughter—whom so many bereavements had made more precious to you—a most noble son-in-law whom you had chosen, from whom, to pass over everything else, you received more grief than joy.

This is the catalogue of your trials; this is the battle of the ancient enemy with Julian, a young recruit of Christ. If you look only at yourself, these things are great; if you look at the most courageous warrior, they are a game and a shadow of battle.

For blessed Job, after the succession of his calamities, had his worst possible wife preserved for him so that through her he might learn to blaspheme. Your excellent wife was taken away from you, so that you might lose the consolation of your sufferings.

It is one thing to endure what you do not want; it is another to long for what you love. In the midst of the deaths of all his children, Job had the ruin of his house as one grave. Tearing his garments to show a parent’s affection, he fell to the ground in worship and said:

“Naked I came from my mother’s womb, and naked shall I return. The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has happened. Blessed be the name of the Lord” [Job 1:21].

You, to put it as mildly as possible, amid the duties of many relatives and consoling friends, followed the funeral rites of your loved ones.

He lost all his wealth at once, and, as messengers of calamity succeeded one another, he was struck by each blow without moving, fulfilling in himself the praise proclaimed by the Wise Man:

“If the world should break and fall, its ruins would strike the fearless man” [Horace, *Odes* 3.2].

For you, the greater part of your substance has been left, so that you are tested only as much as you are able to bear. For you have not yet reached the stage at which the whole army is deployed against you in battle.

### 3

A man who was once rich, and a father richer still, is suddenly childless and naked. And although in all that had happened to him he had not sinned before the Lord, nor spoken anything foolish, the Lord, rejoicing in the victory of his servant and counting Job’s endurance his own triumph, said to the devil:

“Have you considered my servant Job? For there is no one like him on the earth: an innocent man, a true [or: truthful] worshiper of God, abstaining from every evil, and still persevering in his innocence” (Job 2:3).

He fittingly added, “and still persevering in his innocence,” because it is difficult for innocence pressed down by misfortunes not to grieve, and not to have one’s faith endangered by seeing oneself unjustly enduring what one suffers.

To this the devil replied to the Lord:

“Skin for skin, and all that a man has he will give for his life. But stretch out your hand and touch his bones and his flesh; surely he will bless you to your face [that is, curse you]” (Job 2:4–5).

The most cunning adversary, long practiced in evil days, knows that some things are external [Note: [Col. 0962] We have supplied this from the manuscripts, which the printed editions generally support, except Erasmus and Martianay, who read *nominentur* and omit the conjunction *-que*.]—and are also called by the philosophers of the world *adiaphora* (ἀδιάφορα), that is, “indifferent things”—and that perfect virtue is not demonstrated in their loss and contempt; while other things are inward and desired, so that their loss compels the loser to grieve.

Therefore he boldly rejects God’s testimony and says that one should by no means praise a man who has given nothing of himself, but everything outside himself; who has offered the skins of his children in exchange for his own skin, and laid aside his purse in order to enjoy bodily health.

Hence your prudence may understand that your trials have reached this point: that you have given skin for skin, skin for skin, and are prepared to give everything you possess [Note: [Col. 0962] The Veronese manuscripts correct *parum* to *paratum*, since the former was far from Jerome’s meaning and the sequence of the context.] for your life. But God’s hand has not yet been stretched out against you; your flesh has not yet been touched, nor your bones broken—sufferings whose pain it is difficult not to lament, and in the face of which to bless God, rather than curse him.

Thus Naboth too is said in the Books of Kings to have blessed God and the king, and for that reason he was stoned by the people (1 Kings 21).

But because the Lord knew that his athlete—indeed, a most courageous man—could not be overcome even in this final and perfect contest, he said: “Behold, I deliver him to you; only preserve his life” (Job 2:6).

**THE FLESH OF THE HOLY MAN** is given into the devil’s power, while the health of his soul is preserved; for if the devil had struck what contains the perception and judgment of the mind, the fault would not have been that of the sinner, but of the one who had overthrown his mental state.

### 4

Let others praise you and celebrate your victories over the devil in panegyrics: that you bore the deaths of your daughters with a cheerful face; that on the fortieth day after their falling asleep you changed your mourning garment; that the dedication of the Martyr’s bones restored white clothing to you, so that you did not feel the grief of your bereavement, which the whole city felt, but rejoiced in the Martyr’s triumph; and that you escorted your most holy wife not as a dead woman but as one departing.

I will not deceive you with flattery, nor trip you up with slippery praise. Rather, I shall say what it is useful for you to hear:

“My son, when you come to serve God, prepare your soul for temptation” (Sirach 2:1); and, “When you have done everything, say, ‘I am an unworthy servant; I have done what I was obliged to do’” (Luke 17:10).

You have taken back the children whom you yourself had given. You have received back the handmaid whom you had lent me for a brief consolation. I do not grieve that you have received back what was yours; rather, I give thanks that you gave it.
