Once, a rich young man boasted that he had fulfilled everything commanded in the Law. To him the Lord said in the Gospel: “One thing is lacking to you. If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you possess and give it to the poor; then come, follow me” (Matthew 19:21).

The man who said he had done everything cannot overcome riches in the first contest. Hence the rich enter the kingdom of heaven with difficulty: it desires inhabitants unencumbered and lifted up by the lightness of wings.

“Go,” he says, “and sell”—not part of your substance, but everything you possess—and give it to the poor: not to friends, not to relatives, not to kinsmen, not to your wife, not to your children. I shall add something further: reserving nothing for yourself out of fear of poverty, lest you be condemned with Ananias and Sapphira (Acts 5), give everything to the poor and make friends for yourself from the mammon of iniquity, so that they may receive you into the eternal dwellings [Luke 16:9] [Note: Some manuscripts, without changing the sense, insert the negative particle, so that the passage reads: “that you may follow me, the Lord; that you may not possess the world’s property,” and so forth.].

Do this so that you may follow me, the Lord of the world, and possess your inheritance; so that you may sing with the Prophet, “The Lord is my portion” (Psalm 15:5; 72:26), and, as a true Levite, possess nothing of an earthly inheritance.

This is what I urge: if you wish to be perfect; if you desire the summit of apostolic dignity; if you wish, after taking up the cross, to follow Christ; if, having grasped the plow, you do not look back; if, placed upon a lofty roof, you despise your former garments; and if, in order to escape the Egyptian mistress, you abandon the cloak of the world (Genesis 39).

For this reason Elijah, hastening to the kingdoms of heaven, cannot go with his cloak, but leaves behind the garments of the world in the world (2 Kings 2).

But you say that this is proper to apostolic dignity and to one who wishes to be perfect. Why, then, do you not wish to be perfect? Why should you, who are first in the world, not be first in Christ’s household?

Is it because you have had a wife? Peter had one too, and yet he left her, together with his nets and boat. The all-wise Lord, desiring the salvation of all and preferring the sinner’s repentance to his death, has taken away this excuse from you, so that she may not draw you back to earth, but that you may follow her as she draws you onward [or: strives toward] the kingdoms of paradise.

Provide good things for your children, who went before you to the Lord, so that their portions may not increase their sister’s riches, but may contribute to the redemption of your soul and to the sustenance of the poor.

These necklaces of your daughters ask them of you; with these jewels they wish their heads to be adorned. **WHAT WAS DESTINED TO PERISH** in silk should be preserved in the cheap tunics of the poor.

They demand their portions from you; united with the Bridegroom, they do not wish to appear poor and lowly, but desire their own ornaments.

### 5

Nor is there any reason for you to plead noble birth or the weight of your riches. Look to the holy man Pammachius and to Paulinus the presbyter, whose faith was most fervent. They offered not only their riches but themselves to the Lord. In opposition to the devil’s evasive claim, “skin for skin,” they consecrated to the Lord not merely skin for skin, but their flesh, bones, and souls.

By example and by speech—that is, by deed and by word—they can lead you to greater things.

You are noble, and so are they, but they are nobler in Christ. You are rich and honored, and so are they—or rather, from being rich and honored they became poor and without glory; and for that very reason they are richer and more renowned, because they are poor and dishonored for Christ.

You do well, certainly, in being said to minister to the needs of the saints, to support monks, and to offer very many things to the churches. But these are the beginnings of your military service.

You despise gold; the philosophers of the world despised it too. One of them, to say nothing of the others, threw the value of many estates into the sea, saying: “Away into the depths with you, evil desires; I shall drown you, lest you drown me.” [Note: [Col. 0964] Jerome calls this philosopher Crates of Thebes by name in Book 2 *Against Jovinianus*. Gregory of Nazianzus, however, says in his oration in praise of Saint Basil that, when he cast his wealth into the sea, he applauded himself with another saying: “Crates of Thebes grants Crates freedom.”]

A philosopher—a creature of glory and a wretched slave of popular applause—laid down the whole burden at once [or: all at once]. And do you think yourself established at the summit of virtue if you offer only a part of the whole?

The Lord wants you yourself as a living sacrifice, pleasing to God: you, I say, not your possessions.

Therefore he admonishes you through various trials, because Israel is instructed through many blows and sufferings. “The Lord chastises the one whom he loves, and scourges every son whom he accepts” (Proverbs 8:13).

A poor widow put two tiny coins into the treasury. Because she offered everything she had, she is said to have surpassed all the wealthy in the offerings made to God (Mark 12; Luke 21). These offerings are weighed not by their monetary weight, but by the will of those who offer them.

Even if you have distributed your wealth to many, and some rejoice in your generosity, there are nevertheless far more to whom you have given nothing. For neither the wealth of Darius nor the riches of Croesus can satisfy the poor of the world.

But if you give yourself to the Lord, and, perfected in apostolic virtue, begin to follow the Savior, then you will understand where you have been and what the lowest place you have occupied in Christ’s army.

You did not mourn your dead daughters, and the father’s tears were dried upon his cheeks by fear of Christ. How much greater was Abraham, who by his will slaughtered his only son (Genesis 22), and, although he had heard that he would be the heir of the world, did not despair that he would live even after death.

Jephthah offered his virgin daughter (Judges 11), and for that reason he is placed by the Apostle among the saints.

I do not want you to offer to the Lord only those things which a thief can steal, an enemy invade, or a proscription confiscate; things which can increase and diminish, and which, like waves and breakers, are seized by successive owners; in a word, things which, whether you wish it or not, you will leave behind at death.

Offer that which no enemy can take from you and no tyrant seize; that which will go with you to the underworld—or rather, to the kingdoms of heaven and the delights of paradise.

You build monasteries, and a large number of saints throughout the islands of Dalmatia is supported by you. But you would do better if you yourself lived as a saint among saints.

“Be holy, because I am holy,” says the Lord (Leviticus 19:2; 20:7).

The Apostles glory in having left everything and followed the Savior (Matthew 19). Certainly, we do not read that they left anything except their nets and boat; nevertheless, they are crowned by the testimony of the future Judge.

**BECAUSE, BY OFFERING THEMSELVES,** they had left everything they possessed.

### 6

I say this not to disparage your works, nor to diminish your generosity and almsgiving, but because I do not want you to be a monk among secular people and a secular man among monks. I ask everything of you, since I hear that your mind is devoted to divine worship.

If a friend, follower, or relative resists this counsel of ours and recalls you to the pleasures of a shining table, understand that he is thinking not of your soul but of his own belly, and that all wealth and sumptuous banquets come to an end in sudden death.

In the space of twenty days, at the age of sixty-eight years, you lost two daughters; and do you imagine that an old man can live for long?

To one who wishes his years to be prolonged, David says: “The days of our life are seventy years; and if they are more, eighty; and what exceeds this is labor and sorrow” (Psalm 89:10).

Blessed and worthy of every happiness is the one whom old age finds serving Christ, whom his final day finds serving as a soldier for the Savior, who will not be ashamed when he speaks with his enemies in the gate (Psalm 126:5), and to whom, at the entrance to paradise, it will be said: “You received evil things during your life, but now rejoice here” (Luke 16:25).

For the Lord will not exact punishment twice for the same matter.

The rich man clothed in purple was received by the flame of Gehenna. Lazarus, poor and covered with sores, whose rotting flesh the dogs licked, and who scarcely sustained his pitiful life with crumbs from the wealthy man’s table, is received into Abraham’s bosom and rejoices in that great patriarch as his father.

It is difficult—indeed, impossible—for anyone to enjoy both present and future goods: to fill his belly here and his mind there; to pass from one luxury to another; to be first in both worlds; and to appear glorious both in heaven and on earth.

### 7

If a silent thought should trouble you and ask, “Why is the admonisher himself not such as he wants you to be?”—and if you see some people collapse halfway along the road—I shall answer briefly: what I say is not mine, but belongs to the Lord and Savior.

I am not instructing you in what I myself can do, but in what the one who is to be Christ’s servant ought to desire [or: ought to do] [Note: The two words *vel facere*, which Victor had once restored from ten manuscript codices, were later removed by the Benedictine editor, who followed the printed Froben editions; we have restored them from other ancient copies.].

Athletes too are stronger than their own encouragers [Note: [Col. 0966] The Veronese manuscript’s reading *suis unctoribus* (“their own anointers”) may seem truer; nevertheless, we have retained the printed reading, since it is not itself incongruous.]; nevertheless, the weaker man urges the stronger one to fight.

Do not look at Judas denying, but look at Paul confessing.

Jacob, the son of a very rich father, proceeds alone and naked toward Mesopotamia with only his staff. Exhausted on the journey, he uses a stone for a pillow, although his mother Rebekah had raised him in the greatest luxury.

He saw a ladder stretching from earth to heaven, with angels ascending and descending upon it and the Lord leaning above it (Genesis 28), so that he might extend his hand to those who had fallen and encourage those ascending to labor by his own appearance.

Hence the place itself is called Bethel, that is, “House of God,” in which one ascends and descends every day.

For even saints fall if they are negligent, and sinners recover their former rank if they wash away their filth with tears [Note: Martianaeus mistakenly printed *lassis*; long before him the Bishop of Reate had pointed out the error to Erasmus from the following Hieronymian context, namely, “for even saints fall if they are negligent.”].

I have said this so that those descending may not frighten you, but those ascending may inspire you.

One never takes an example from the wicked. Even in worldly matters, I always draw incentives to virtue from the better side.

Forgetting my purpose and the brevity appropriate to a letter, I wanted to dictate more. In view of the dignity of the subject and the worthiness of your person, everything that is said is too little.

But look: our Ausonius has begun demanding his tablets, pressing the scribes, and, with the neighing of an eager horse, hastening to expose the slowness of my little mind.

Remember us, therefore, and take care that you may be strong in Christ.

And, to say nothing of the rest, follow the domestic examples of the holy Vera [Note: She is believed to have been the sister of Juliana.], who truly followed Christ, endures the hardships of pilgrimage, and may be for you such a guide to so great a deed as a woman was [“and let such a woman be your guide to so great an undertaking,” adapting *Aeneid* 1].

## LETTER CXIX

**TO MINERVIUS AND ALEXANDER** [Note: Alternatively numbered 152. Written around the end of the year 406.]

**MONKS** [Note: In the Veronese manuscript it is entitled, “To Minervius and Alexander, concerning a very difficult question of the Apostle Paul.” Older editions call him “Minerius.” Moreover, Jerome dedicated to these same brothers—or monks—of Toulouse his Commentaries on Zechariah and Malachi, and in the Preface calls them united in blood and religion.]

Jerome replies to Minervius and Alexander, who had asked him through the monk Sisinnius, son of Saint Exuperius, bishop of Toulouse, about the Apostle’s words, “We shall all sleep,” and so forth, postponing to another time other questions of the same kind that had been proposed together.

### 1

At the very moment of the departure of our holy brother Sisinnius, who had brought me your letter, I am compelled to dictate these words, whatever they may be. I cannot conceal the matter from your prudence, but I beg you not to interpret this statement as self-praise; rather, understand it as arising from sheer necessity, since I speak to you as though I were speaking to myself.

He brought me many questions from holy brothers and sisters in your province, and I thought that I would answer them by Epiphany, which allowed ample time. While I was composing answers to most of them during the stolen little vigils of the night, and, having completed the others, was reserving yours as though it were the most difficult, he suddenly arrived and declared that he was about to depart immediately.

When I asked him to postpone his journey, he began pleading to me the famine of Libya, the needs of the monasteries of Egypt, the Nile’s insufficient waters, and the hunger of many people [Note: [Col. 0967] Earlier printed editions had the adverb *libere* in place of “of Libya,” which makes no sense here. Sisinnius was adducing the famine in Libya and the needs of the Egyptian monasteries, which he was hastening to assist with his alms.]—so that it would almost have been an offense against the Lord to wish to hold him back any longer.

Accordingly, beneath the covering, the warp, the heddles, and the webs that I had prepared for your tunic, I have sent you unfinished material, so that whatever is lacking in me may be woven together by your eloquence.

You are prudent and learned, and from what Appius calls “dog-like eloquence” you have migrated to the eloquence of Christ [Note: Probably “forensic eloquence.” Prudentius, *Hamartigenia* 400: “From there canine eloquence barks in the forum,” and similarly elsewhere in Jerome. Two fragments of Sallust also survive in which this saying of Appius is quoted.].

I need no great labor with you; the stories tell of a philosopher who had to deal with a rustic in the art of persuasion. “I had scarcely said half of it,” he said, “when the man already understood.”

Thus, pressed for time, I have set before you the opinions of each of those who left short commentaries on Holy Scripture, and I have translated most of them word for word. In this way I may free myself from the question, and send you the authority of the earlier interpreters, so that, as you read and assess each one, you may rest not on my judgment but on your own.

### 2

You ask in what sense the statement was made, and how it should be read in the Apostle Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians:

“We shall all indeed sleep, but we shall not all be changed” (1 Corinthians 15:51).

Or should it be read according to certain copies:

“We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed”?

Both readings are found in Greek manuscripts. [Note: [Col. 0967] Some Greek manuscripts read Πάντες μὲν οὖν κοιμηθησόμεθα, ἀλλ’ οὐ πάντες ἀλλαγησόμεθα (“We shall all indeed sleep, but we shall not all be changed”); some Latin books also preferred this reading, as Augustine reports in *City of God* 20.20, although he observes elsewhere (*Epistle* 205) that it was properly the reading of Greek codices. Yet nearly all Greek writers and very many interpreters in that language read the contrary sense: Πάντες μὲν οὐ κοιμηθησόμεθα, πάντες δὲ ἀλλαγησόμεθα (“We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed”).]

On this subject Theodore of Heraclea, a city formerly called Perinthus, spoke as follows in his brief commentary on the Apostle:

“We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed.

“Enoch and Elijah, having overcome the necessity of death, were transferred from earthly existence to the heavenly kingdoms in the bodies in which they were (Genesis 5:24; 2 Kings 2). Therefore the saints who are to be found in their bodies at the consummation and judgment will be caught up in the clouds to meet Christ in the air together with the other saints who will rise from the dead, and they will not taste death. They will always be with the Lord, having trampled underfoot the most grievous necessity of death.

“Hence the Apostle says: ‘We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed.’ Those who rise from the dead, and those who are caught up alive in the clouds, will pass into incorruption and will be changed from mortality into immortality [Note: [Col. 0967] Again, the Veronese manuscript reads, “and they changed mortality into immortality.”]; not over a period of time, nor even in a brief interval, but in an atom and a point of time, in the moment in which the eyelid of the eye can move, at the last trumpet.

“For the resurrection of the dead will occur with such speed that the living whom the time of the consummation finds in their bodies will not be able to precede the dead rising from the underworld.

“Paul clearly explains this when he says: ‘For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed. For this corruptible thing must put on incorruption, and this mortal thing must put on immortality’ (1 Corinthians 15:52–53), so that it may remain perpetually in either condition, whether in punishments or in the kingdom of heaven.”

### 3

Diodorus, bishop of Tarsus, briefly noted the following in what comes next, after passing over this chapter:

“With regard to what is written, ‘The dead will rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed’: if the dead will rise incorruptible, there is no doubt that they too will be changed for the better. Why, then, was it necessary to say, ‘and we shall be changed’?

“Did he intend it to mean that incorruption is common to everyone, but change belongs properly to the righteous, since they receive not only incorruption and immortality but also glory?”

### 4

Apollinarius, although using different words, asserted the same thing as Theodore: that some will not die but will be snatched from the present life into the future one, so that, with their bodies changed and glorified, they may be with Christ. This is what we now believe concerning Enoch and Elijah.

### 5

Didymus, passing over not in his steps but in his words to Origen’s opinion, proceeds by the opposite route:

“I speak to you of a mystery: we shall all indeed sleep, but we shall not all be changed.”

He explained it as follows:

“If the resurrection did not need an interpreter, and if its meaning contained no obscurity, Paul would never, after saying many things about the resurrection, have added: ‘Behold, I tell you a mystery: we shall all indeed sleep’—that is, we shall die—‘but not all will be changed; only the saints will be changed.’

“I know that in some manuscripts it is written: ‘We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed.’ But we must consider whether what follows can agree with the statement already made, ‘we shall all be changed’: ‘The dead will rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed.’ If everyone will be changed, and this is common to the others as well, it was superfluous to say, ‘we shall be changed.’

“Therefore it should be read: ‘We shall all indeed sleep, but we shall not all be changed.’

“For if all die in Adam, and there is sleep in death, then we shall all sleep, or die. According to the idiom of Scripture, the one who has died sleeps in hope of the future resurrection. Everyone who sleeps certainly awakens—provided that a sudden force of death has not overwhelmed him and death has not been joined to sleep.

“When all have thus slept according to the law of nature, only the saints will be changed in body and soul for the better, so that incorruption belongs to all who rise, but glory and change belong properly to the saints.”

With regard to what follows according to the Greek text, *en atomō, en rhopē* or *en ripē ophthalmou*—“in an atom, in a movement” or “in a flicker of the eye” (both readings are found)—and which our translators rendered “in a moment and in the blink [or movement] of an eye,” the same Didymus [Note: [Col. 0969] In manuscripts of better quality, the words “the same Didymus” are absent; the text then proceeds directly, “The present discourse signifies the resurrection of all together,” omitting the intervening words, “they will be caught up to meet Christ,” and so forth.] explained it as follows:

“With the resurrection of all occurring together, they will be caught up to meet Christ—but here the text refers to those whom death has dissolved.

“For when he says that the resurrection of all will occur in a point of time, in the movement of an eye, and in a moment, he excludes the fable of a first and a second resurrection, according to which some would be believed to rise first and others last.

“An atom is a point of time which cannot be cut or divided. Hence Epicurus constructs and fashions the world from his atoms.

“The blink or movement of the eye, which in Greek is called *rhopē* (ῥοπὴ), passes with such speed that it almost escapes the perception of the one who sees.

“But since in many manuscripts *ripē* (ῥιπή), that is, ‘a blow’ or ‘a movement,’ is read instead of *rhopē*, we should understand it in this way: just as a light feather, or a straw, or a thin, dry leaf is carried away by the wind and breath and transferred from earth to a higher place, so, at the blink of an eye [Note: Two manuscripts read “or at the movement of God,” evidently rendering the Greek word *rhopē* here as well. At the same time, it should not be overlooked that the two words *ripē* and *rhopē*—the one transferred from the stroke of an arrow, the other from the movement of a balance or scales—had long before been confused by Hesychius. Thus it is by no means necessary to follow those who thought that *in ictu*, “in a blow,” should be read *in nictu*, “in a blink.”], and at God’s command, all the bodies of the dead will be moved, ready for the Judge’s arrival.

“What he then joins to this and says—‘at the last trumpet: for the trumpet will sound, and the dead will rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed. For this corruptible thing must put on incorruption, and this mortal thing must put on immortality’—has a twofold meaning.

“The sound of the trumpet may indicate the greatness of the voice, according to what is written: ‘Like a trumpet, raise your voice’ (Isaiah 58:1); or it may indicate the open resurrection of all, according to what we read in the Gospel: ‘When you give alms, do not sound a trumpet before you’ (Matthew 6:2)—that is, perform mercy secretly and in private, lest you appear to glory in another’s misery.

“But we ask why he wrote that the dead would rise at the last trumpet. For when it is called the last, other trumpets must have preceded it.

“In the Apocalypse of John, seven angels are described with trumpets. As each one sounds—the first, second, third, fourth, fifth, and sixth—the events accomplished by each are indicated (Revelation 8–9).

“But when the last, that is, the seventh, resounds with the clear sound of the trumpet, the dead are raised, receiving incorruptible the bodies that they previously had as corruptible.

“Therefore, after the last trumpet, the Apostle explains what follows: ‘For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will rise incorruptible, but we shall be changed.’

“When he says ‘we,’ he indicates that he and those who are with him are distinct from the dead.

“To understand this, some say that the dead who rise incorruptible are the bodies of the dead, while those who are said to be changed should be understood as souls, when they have been transformed into greater glory and have attained the perfect man, ‘to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ’ (Ephesians 4:13).

“Others, however, assert that the dead should be understood as sinners, who will rise incorruptible so that they may endure eternal punishments, while those who are changed are the saints, who are transferred from virtue to virtue and from glory to glory.

“Accordingly, after speaking of the incorruption of the dead, he added: ‘For this corruptible thing must put on incorruption.’ But to what he had said, ‘we shall be changed,’ he added: ‘and this mortal thing will put on immortality.’

“For immortality is one thing and incorruption another, just as mortality is one thing and corruptibility another.

“Whatever is mortal is also corruptible; but what is corruptible is not necessarily mortal at once. Bodies that lack a soul are corruptible, and yet they are not mortal, because they never possessed life, which properly belongs to living creatures.

“Therefore the Apostle deliberately joined incorruption to corruptibility and immortality to mortality at the future time of the resurrection.”

### 6

Acacius, bishop of Caesarea—which was formerly called Strato’s Tower—after Eusebius Pamphilus, proposed this same question in the fourth book of his *Miscellaneous Questions* (συμμίκτων ζητημάτων) [Note: [Col. 0970] Earlier editions altered the title to συλλεκτῶν ζητημάτων, “Collected Questions,” in place of συμμίκτων, “Miscellaneous” or “Mixed.” The alteration likely arose from manuscript confusion between doubled lambda and doubled mu, but is certainly erroneous. The Veronese manuscript restores συμμίκτων, and Jerome himself confirms it in *Catalogue* 98, where he lists Acacius’s six books of συμμίκτων ζητημάτων.] and discussed it at greater length. Accepting both readings, although they appear contradictory to one another, he spoke as follows after the beginning, which we have omitted:

“Let us first speak about what is found in the majority of manuscripts:

‘Behold, I tell you a mystery: we shall all indeed sleep, but we shall not all be changed.’

“He said ‘mystery’ in order to make his hearers attentive, since he was about to discuss the resurrection more fully.

“Sleep signifies the death that is common to all. Hence he most correctly stated that we shall all sleep—that is, die—as he said above: ‘As all die in Adam, so also all will be made alive in Christ.’

“Since, then, all are going to die, hear the mysteries that I proclaim: we shall all die [or: sleep], but we shall not all be changed.

“For the trumpet will sound, undoubtedly the seventh angel’s trumpet, and the dead will rise incorruptible.

“But if the dead will be incorruptible, how will they not be changed, since incorruption itself is a change?

“Here, however, the change by which Paul and the saints are to be changed is understood as glorification. Incorruption is common to everyone for this reason: sinners will be more miserable in it, since they will be perpetual for the sake of eternal torments and will not be dissolved in a mortal and corruptible body.

“We read in the same letter, where the Apostle discusses the sacred diversity of the resurrection, that the difference lies not in the nature of bodies but in the variety of glory: some rise to everlasting punishments, others to eternal glory.

“‘There is one flesh of birds, another of fish, another of animals; there are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies. So also,’ he says, ‘is the resurrection of the dead’ (1 Corinthians 15:39–42).

“In this opinion the Church more readily acquiesces: that we all die a common death, but that we are not all changed into glory, according to what Daniel writes: ‘Many of those sleeping in the dust of the earth will rise, some to everlasting glory, others to everlasting shame and contempt’ (Daniel 12:2).

“Those who rise to everlasting shame and contempt will not rise to eternal glory, into which Paul and those who are with him will be changed.

“Since these things are so and are understood by us in this way, we should accept change only for those who will rise to glory. As for sinners and unbelievers, who are called dead and will rise incorruptible, we must say that they will not be changed, but will undergo eternal punishments.”

### 7.

Let us pass to the second reading, which is found in most manuscripts: “We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed.” From this some maintain that many will be found alive in their bodies; and if all do not sleep, not all will die; but if all do not die, not all will rise again. For properly speaking, the person rises who previously fell by dying.

Hence they also wish Paul to have written in the First Epistle to the Thessalonians: “We who are alive, who will remain [or: who remain] at the coming of the Lord, shall not precede those who have slept [Note: Thus most manuscripts, the Vulgate translator, and the Greek text, τοὺς κοιμηθέντας, ‘those who have fallen asleep.’ Martianay, however, with Erasmus, reads ‘those who sleep’]: for the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God; and the dead in Christ will rise first [or: as the first]; then we who are alive, who remain, will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet Christ in the air; and thus we shall always be with the Lord” (1 Thess. 4:14 ff.).

From these words they try to prove that the Apostle Paul, and those who wrote the Epistle with him, thought that they would not die but would be found bodily present on the day of consummation. If this is true, Paul was mistaken and was deceived by human conjecture, thinking that he would be found in the body; but the outcome of events proved this false.

The Thessalonians themselves had understood the matter in this way, not knowing the mysteries of mystical speech, and they were wavering amid various conjectures. They said: “If Paul is to be found in the body, the day of judgment is near.” Therefore, when writing the Second Epistle, he corrects them:

“We ask you, brothers, by the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and by our gathering to him, not to be quickly shaken in mind or alarmed, either by spirit, or by word, or by a letter supposedly sent by us, as though the day of the Lord were at hand. Let no one deceive you in any way; for unless the rebellion comes first and the man of sin is revealed, the son of perdition, who opposes and exalts himself above everything called God or worshiped, so that he sits in the temple of God, displaying himself as though he were God. Do you not remember that, when I was still with you, I told you these things?” (2 Thess. 2:1 ff.).

By these words he acts to recall them from their error, so that they would not think that the day of judgment was approaching, and so that they would not understand what he had written—“We who are alive, who remain at the coming of the Lord, shall not precede those who have slept”—in a way different from that intended by the writer himself.

For it cannot be that the man who had written to Timothy, “For I am already being poured out, and the time of my departure is at hand” (2 Tim. 4:6), thought that he would remain perpetually in the flesh and would never die, and would pass immediately from earthly life to the heavenly kingdoms [Note: The Benedictine editor, following Erasmus, wrongly and against the testimony of all the older manuscripts, read ‘everlasting life’ in place of ‘earthly life’; Victorius had long before restored the latter reading from eight codices]—especially since, writing to the Romans, he had said the same thing: “Who will deliver me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7:24). And to the Corinthians: “While we dwell in the body, we are away from the Lord. But we would rather depart from the body and be with the Lord” (2 Cor. 5:8).

[Note: The old edition reads “and to be present with the Lord,” as do nearly all versions of the Vulgate and Tertullian, *On the Resurrection of the Flesh* and *Against Marcion*, book five, “to dwell with,” or “to be present with, the Lord.” The Greek reads καὶ ἐνδημῆσαι πρὸς τὸν Κύριον, “and to be at home with the Lord.”]

The man who said these things certainly knew that he would die.

It is therefore better to understand spiritually what is written: in the present passage, “sleep” should be understood not as death, by which the soul is separated from the body, but as sin after faith and offense against God, and as sleep after baptism. About this he also spoke to the Corinthians: “For this reason many among you are weak and sick, and a great number sleep” (1 Cor. 11:30). And in another passage: “Then those also who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished” (ibid. 15:18). Although they have died, they will not perish with everlasting death, because they are not held in a mortal crime, but in a light and minor sin.

Another holy man, wishing to avoid this, said: “Lest I sleep in death” (Ps. 12:4). There is a sleep of sin that leads to death, and there is another sleep of transgression that is not bound by death.

Whoever therefore has lived by that life which says, “I am life” (John 14:6)—for “our life is hidden with Christ in God” (Col. 3:3)—and has never been separated from it, nor sinned unto death, is said to belong to the living, and to those who live forever. Concerning them the Savior also bears witness in the Gospel of John in mystical language: “Whoever believes in me will not die. And everyone who lives and believes in me will never die” (John 11:25–26).

Thus the Apostle, following in the footsteps of his Lord, taught his disciples what he had learned from his master. “We shall not all sleep.” For whoever guards his heart with complete vigilance, watches for Christ’s commandments, and remembers his command when he says, “Watch, because you do not know at what hour the thief will come” (Matt. 24:42), and in another place, “Do not give sleep to your eyes, nor slumber to your eyelids” (Prov. 6:4), so that you may be saved—like a gazelle from bonds and like a bird from snares—will not sleep.

Since, then, some do not sleep—those who always live in Christ and keep watch—it follows that not all sleep. Conversely, all will be changed, not by the change of glory that properly belongs to the saints, but by that change through which this corruptible thing becomes incorruptible, so that it may receive either eternal punishments or eternal rewards.

Even if someone has slept in Christ and fallen asleep in the sleep of negligence, he ought to hear what is written: “Will the one who sleeps not rise again?” (Ps. 40:9).

But whoever does not sleep, rather watches and always lives in Christ, will pass from life to life, or will be caught up in the clouds so as always to be with the Lord.

Lazarus belonged to such sleepers, concerning whom the Lord said, “Lazarus our friend sleeps.” And concerning this sleeper he said to Martha: “Whoever believes in me, even if he has died, will live; and everyone who lives and believes in me will never die” (John 11:11, 25–26).

For whoever trusts in Christ with his whole mind, even if, as a fallen human being, he has died in sin [Note: This is readily understood if he has been entangled in a light sin, but not in a mortal sin, as it is called; Jerome had explained this a little earlier concerning those who will not die an everlasting death. Certain heterodox critics calumniate this passage very foolishly and wretchedly], lives forever through his faith.

Otherwise, this common death is owed equally to believers and unbelievers, and all will rise alike: some to eternal confusion, others, because of what they believe, to everlasting life. Thus it can stand that the one who believes in Christ does not die, and that, even if he has died, he lives forever.

With respect to bodily death, it is clear that this has happened to no one except Enoch and Elijah (Gen. 5; 2 Kings 2).

Those who always live in Christ through the greatness of their faith will neither sleep nor die. They will be imitators of the apostolic life: they lived without any fault under the law of righteousness, and, passing over to faith in the Lord and believing in him who is called life and resurrection, they never slept and never died.

“For the soul that sins, it shall die” (Ezek. 18:4). Thus, just as the soul that sins is dead while the body lives, and on the very day on which it sins sleeps in death, so the soul that has kept Christ’s commandments will live forever, even if the body has died.

[Note: This passage from Ecclesiastes 8:12 is quoted from the ancient translators Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion, who translated the Hebrew verb *maʿat* by ἀπέθανεν, “he died,” whereas the Septuagint rendered it ἀπὸ τότε, “from then on.” Jerome joins both interpretations together in order to draw from them a new and especially elegant sense.]

This, however, should be understood as agreeing better with the truth: “Everyone will indeed sleep, but not everyone will be changed,” especially because what follows says, “The dead will rise incorruptible, and we will be changed.” If everyone is to be changed, according to the other reading, how can it later say, as something special and particular, properly belonging to the Apostles, “and we will be changed”? When he says “we,” he signifies all the saints.

### 8.

You ask how we should understand what is written in the First Epistle to the Thessalonians:

“For this we say to you by the word of the Lord: We who are alive, who remain at the coming of the Lord, shall not precede those who have slept; for the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God; and the dead who are in Christ will rise first; then we who are alive, who remain, will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet Christ in the air; and thus we shall always be with the Lord” (1 Thess. 4:15 ff.).

Although Acacius’s preceding discussion has treated this matter more fully, it is nevertheless necessary to state what others think—namely Theodore, Apollinarius, and Diodorus, who follow one and the same interpretation. Diodorus wrote as follows:

> “Paul the Apostle calls them ‘those who remain’ and ‘the living,’ not because he wishes it to be understood that he and others will be found bodily present at the time of the resurrection, but because he said ‘we’ in the sense of ‘the righteous,’ among whom I too am numbered. They will be caught up to meet Christ, and not sinners.
>
> “We understand ‘the living’ not tropologically, as saints who have not died through sin, but as all those whom Christ, when he comes, will find in the body [Note: The Verona manuscript lacks the negative particle, though not with a different meaning]. What follows—‘We shall not precede those who have slept’—must by no means be referred to sinners; for sinners will not be caught up with the righteous to meet Christ, but those whom death has dissolved [Note: The Benedictine editor again printed ‘but them,’ following the Basel edition; this is neither Latin nor true. The manuscripts and Victorius correct it].
>
> “But why do I investigate these matters and bring an accusation against apostolic words, when he himself most clearly writes, ‘we who remain at the coming of the Lord’? Who those who remain are, we learn from the Savior’s words: ‘As in the days of Noah they were taking wives and marrying, and suddenly the flood came and swept them all away, so will be the coming of the Son of Man’ (Matt. 24; Luke 17). These words establish that at the end of the world many will be alive and still found in their bodies.
>
> “It follows: ‘With a command and with the voice of an archangel, and the dead will rise first.’ Again the Savior says this in the Gospel: ‘At midnight the bridegroom came’ (Matt. 25:6). He will certainly find people living in the body, when ‘two will be in one bed: one will be taken and the other left; and two will be grinding together: one will be taken and the other left’ (Luke 17).
>
> “By these words it is shown that the consummation of the world will come at midnight, when everyone is secure.”

### 9.

In the third volume of Origen’s *Exegetical Works* (ἐξηγητικῶν) on Paul’s First Epistle to the Thessalonians, after discussing many matters in varied and prudent language, he added the following; there is no doubt that Acacius drew much of his material from it:

[Note: Elsewhere Jerome more often mentions Origen’s ἐξηγητικῶν, “exegetical works,” but never ἐξηγηματικῶν, “explanatory works,” as this passage had hitherto been printed. The latter reading was false, although it caused no loss of meaning, and has been corrected with the help of manuscripts.]

> “What, then, is the meaning of what Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy write to the Thessalonians by the word of God: ‘We who are alive, who remain at the coming of the Lord, shall not precede those who have slept’? Who are these living people who speak such things? Surely Paul, who is an Apostle ‘not from men, nor through a man’ (Gal. 1), and his beloved son in the faith, Timothy, and Silvanus, who was joined to them both in affection and in virtues.
>
> “And not only they, but anyone who is like Paul in knowledge and conduct, can say: ‘We who are alive,’ whose body is dead because of sin, but whose spirit lives because of righteousness, and whose members upon the earth have been put to death, so that the flesh no longer desires against the spirit.
>
> “For if the flesh still desires, it lives; and because it lives, it desires; and its members have not been put to death upon the earth. But if they have been put to death, they no longer desire against the spirit, having lost such desire through their mortification.
>
> “Therefore, just as those who have lost the present life and have been transferred to better things live more fully, having laid aside the body of death and all the incentives of vices, so those who carry the mortification of Jesus in their body do not live according to the flesh but according to the spirit. They live in him who is life, and Christ lives in them. Of him it is written: ‘The word of God is living and effective; he is the power of God and the wisdom of God’ (Heb. 4:12).
>
> “They live in those in whom the power of God lives, once all human weakness has been laid aside; in those in whom the wisdom that is hidden in God lives; and in those in whom righteousness lives and works. For Christ has become for us not only righteousness from God, but also wisdom and everything that is virtue (1 Cor. 1).
>
> “If, in the present passage, those who write this Epistle separated themselves from those who sleep and are dead in Christ, the observation would seem [or: seems] superfluous, and a testimony taken from one passage would be ineffective. But now, in the same sense and by the same spirit, he says in the First Epistle to the Corinthians: ‘We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed, in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will rise incorruptible, and we will be changed’ (1 Cor. 15:51–55).
>
> “Compare what is written here, ‘He will descend from heaven at the trumpet of God,’ with what is said to the Corinthians, ‘At the last trumpet; for the trumpet will sound’ (1 Cor. 15:52). Compare with what is read in the Thessalonians, ‘The dead in Christ will rise first’ (1 Thess. 4:15), what is written to the Corinthians, ‘The dead will rise incorruptible.’
>
> [Note: Against the intention of Jerome or Origen, all printed editions add *et cetera*, “and so forth,” as though the words that follow—“the dead will rise incorruptible”—were to be compared together with the preceding sentence, whereas, as the context makes perfectly clear, they belong with the following sentence. The manuscript of Verona showed that they should be deleted. From it we also observe that the word *tuba*, “trumpet,” is consistently omitted after *canet enim*, “for it will sound,” perhaps because the Latin was once rendered from the single Greek word σαλπίσει.]
>
> “What follows, ‘Then we who are alive, who remain,’ corresponds to this: ‘And we will be changed.’ Both statements can be understood in this way: ‘We who are alive, who remain at the coming of the Lord,’ and ‘we who will be changed,’ are not among those called dead, but are alive. Therefore we await the Lord’s presence not in death but in life, because we are of Israel’s race, and from us the remnant has been chosen of which the Lord once spoke: ‘I have left to myself seven thousand men who have not bent the knee to Baal’ (1 Kings 19:18).
>
> “In the Gospel of John also a twofold order of the living and the nonliving is described: ‘Everyone who believes in me, even if he has died, will live; and everyone who lives and believes in me will never die’ (John 11:25–26).
>
> “If we understand ‘the living’ as we have already stated, we shall believe that those who sleep and are dead in Christ are people who, although they wish to live in Christ, have nevertheless died to sin. But if the remnant and election according to grace are called ‘the living,’ then those who do not believe in this way and were not born of Israelite nobility will be called—or are called—sleeping and dead in Christ.”

### 10.

There are some who explain this passage as follows.

The living are those who have never died through sin. Those who have sinned, and have died in the very thing in which they sinned, are afterward converted to repentance and cleanse their former offenses. They are called dead because they sinned, but dead in Christ because they have turned to God with a complete mind.

Those who live and possess the testimony of faith, but have not yet received God’s promise—and who, concerning others, “have provided something better” [Note: From Paul’s passage in Hebrews 11: “And all these, though approved by their faith, did not receive the promise, since God had provided something better for us, that they should not be made perfect apart from us.” From this the sentence is almost verbally taken. Victorius also observed this. It is clear that the reading should be *cogitavit*, “he thought/provided,” referring to God, not *cogitant*, “they think,” which Martianaeus, following Erasmus, wrongly preferred.]—so that they may not be crowned without those who are righteous, possess blessedness in this: they enjoy the good of conscience, they live, and they have been left until the coming of the Lord and Savior.

But because God is merciful and wishes to save even those who have slept and are dead in Christ, they will not precede them, nor will they alone be caught up in the clouds. Rather, following the example of the Gospel parable (Matt. 20), the workers of the eleventh hour and those of the first hour, who were sent into the vineyard, will receive one denarius, one reward, and the price of salvation.

Let no one consider this unjust, that unequal labor should receive one reward. For there is a great difference between those who have been healed after wounds and those who have never seen the terror of death.

[Note: Some manuscripts read “the terror of the mind.” Martianaeus had wrongly read “the error of death,” which makes no sense.]

Of these, I think, it was said: “Who is the person who lives and does not see death? Will he redeem his soul from death?” (Ps. 88:45).

For, as some think, “who” is not taken in the sense of “no one,” but as though he had said, “Who, do you suppose?” as in the passage: “Who is wise and will understand these things?” (Hos. 14:10). And in another place: “Lord, who will dwell in your tabernacle?” (Ps. 14:1). And again: “Who has known the mind of the Lord?” (Rom. 11:34).

Therefore, of those who believe, a few will remain who will see the coming of the Lord, in accordance with what God [Note: Martianaeus, following Erasmus and certain older printed editions, reads “according to what God the Word became,” a reading that Victorius proves at length introduces heresy and an Arian interpretation. He thinks Jerome wrote “according to what God the Word made flesh is,” referring not merely to the Son of God but to the Son already clothed in human flesh, since Jerome immediately adds, “not in the lowliness of flesh, but,” and so forth. Since this conjecture does not seem sufficiently supported by the context, the word *factum*, “made,” which Christian ears reject when spoken of the Word of God, has nevertheless been removed and deleted with the help of ten ancient manuscripts, following Victorius in part, who had already restored the passage in the same way from several Brixian manuscripts.] the Word is, not at all in the lowliness of flesh but in the glory of the triumphant one.

We must consider how he first called them “sleeping,” and then “dead in Christ,” whom the living will not be able to precede.

Whoever does not observe what is written—“Do not give sleep to your eyes, nor slumber to your eyelids, so that you may be saved, like a gazelle from bonds and like a bird from snares” (Prov. 6:4)—will sleep and become numb in culpable slumber. When he has fallen asleep, he will pass into death.

For just as the one who is awake moves, so the one who sleeps lies motionless and grows numb with the likeness of death.

That sleep is followed by death can also be taught by the First Epistle to the Corinthians, in which it is written:

“But now Christ has risen from the dead, the first fruits of those who sleep; for since death came through a human being, through a human being also comes the resurrection of the dead” (1 Cor. 15:20–21).

And shortly afterward:

“We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed, in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will rise incorruptible, and we will be changed” (ibid. 51–52).

Since these things are said about sleep and death, and since we read in the Apostle, “Rise, you who sleep, and rise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you” (Eph. 5:14), let us swear to the Lord and make a vow to the God of Jacob, each saying in his heart:

“If I ascend upon my bed, if I give sleep to my eyes and slumber to my eyelids, until I find a place for the Lord”—that is, without doubt, in his soul, a tabernacle for the God of Jacob (Ps. 131)—so that God may rest in him in an eternal dwelling.

It follows: “For the Lord himself with a command,” and so forth.

For he will descend, sent by the Father, not through a difference of power but through the administration of judgment; and he will descend to those who are below—the Word of God and Wisdom, and Truth and Righteousness.

Although those to whom he deigns to descend are dead, they are nevertheless not alienated from him. They are called dead in Christ.

Those who live have this privilege: they are chosen from among the many.

Nevertheless, both companies—the dead in Christ and the living—will be caught up together in the clouds to meet Christ, so that they will not await him until he descends to earthly things, but will enjoy his presence and companionship in the heights.

How great is Christ’s mercy: for our salvation he not only became flesh, but descended even to the dead, and in death itself possesses the signs of the living. For water and blood came forth from his side (John 19).

The divine Word therefore descends, with the voice of an archangel preceding and preparing a way for him among those who are able to bear his presence.

To understand this, let us learn the mysteries of his first coming.

It is written of John, who was his forerunner, that he said in the wilderness: “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness,” and so forth. What did the voice cry in the wilderness? “Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight” (Matt. 3:3; Luke 3:4; Mark 1:3; John 1:23).

For what reward and recompense? “Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be brought low; crooked places shall become straight, and rough ways smooth; and all flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Isa. 40:3–4).

This is because “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14).

But now it will no longer be the voice of the Prophet in the wilderness. It will be the voice of an archangel preparing the ways, not for one coming in the lowliness of flesh, but for him who is with the Father, the Word who is God.

At that time people went out into the wilderness to hear the forerunner of the assumed human being and to see “a reed shaken by the wind” (Luke 7), from which pipes were made—a musical reed that sounds sweetly in the mouths of children singing in the streets and saying, “We played music for you, and you did not dance” (Matt. 11:17; Luke 7:32).

But now, at the voice of the archangel preceding the Lord as he descends from heaven and at the most resounding trumpet, every believer is summoned either to battle or to priestly ministries.

We read in the Book of Numbers (10:3) about trumpets consecrated to God, which sound before the entrance.

[Note: He compares the trumpets by which the dead will be summoned to judgment with those whose blasts formerly summoned the people of Israel before the entrance of the tabernacle of the covenant. The passage in Numbers should therefore be consulted; it makes perfectly clear that the reading should be “before the entrance,” as restored here, and not “before the sacrifices,” as Martianaeus and others wrongly read from printed editions and manuscripts.]

But if the voice of the angel and the trumpet of the archangel are great, how much greater will be the trumpet of God, which first prepares the ways of those who sleep and of the dead in Christ, and then of those who live, who remain, and await the coming of God’s Word?

Perhaps the sound of the simple trumpet is necessary for those who sleep and are dead in Christ, while the voice of the archangel and the trumpet of God are for those who live and are preserved for God’s presence.

[Note: The words “the voices and the trumpets of God” are absent from the manuscript of Verona.]

Let us see what can be understood by what follows: “We will be caught up together with them.”

By this word, I think, a sudden passage to better things is indicated. For this reason he wished to say “caught up,” so that the speed of the one passing over would exceed the understanding of the one thinking about it.

He marked the same meaning elsewhere by the proper force of the word:

> “I know a man in Christ fourteen years ago—whether in the body I do not know, or outside the body I do not know; God knows—such a one was caught up to the third heaven. And I know that such a man—whether in the body or outside the body I do not know; God knows—was caught up into paradise and heard ineffable words, which it is not permitted to a human being to speak” (2 Cor. 12:2 ff.).

Others, progressing and, so to speak, ascending step by step, grew until they became what is written: “Very great indeed.” We also read of certain people being taken up into heaven.

But Paul, the vessel of election, was caught up and ascended to the third heaven; therefore he heard ineffable words.

How those who are caught up in the clouds are caught up to meet Christ must be considered more carefully.

We know that the Prophets are clouds. God commanded them not to rain upon Israel, when Israel had filled up the measure of its fathers, and when the Law and the Prophets continued until John the Baptist (Matt. 11:13).

And because God placed in the Church, first, Apostles, and second, Prophets (Eph. 4:11), not only the Prophets but also the Apostles are to be understood as clouds.

If, then, someone is caught up to Christ, he ascends above the clouds of the Law and the Gospel, above the Prophets and the Apostles. Taking up the wings of a dove and being lifted by their teaching to the heights, he meets Christ—not below, but in the air and in the spiritual understanding of the Scriptures.

Meeting him in spiritual realities and leaving earthly things behind—whether he is sleeping, dead in Christ, or living and preserved for his presence—he will always be with him and will enjoy the Word of God, Wisdom, Truth, and Righteousness.

### 11.

I have set down these matters in rapid speech, explaining to your wisdom what learned men thought about both passages and by what arguments they wished to establish their positions.

For the authority of my weakness—of one who is nothing and exposed only to the attacks of the envious—is not as great as that of those who preceded us in the Lord.

Nor, in accordance with the disciples of Pythagoras, should the preconceived opinion of a teacher be weighed; rather, the reasoning of the doctrine should be considered.

If someone from the opposing party murmurs, asking why I read the explanations of those whose doctrines I do not accept, let him know that I gladly hear the Apostle’s words: “Test everything; hold fast what is good” (1 Thess. 5:21), and the Savior’s words:

[Note: Martianaeus persuaded himself, by I know not what argument, that this saying of Christ had disappeared from the current Greek and Latin copies of the Gospels. It cannot in any way be proved that it ever existed in them. Jerome does quote it elsewhere, sometimes; in his commentary on Ephesians 4 he says that we should know, like approved money-changers, which coin is genuine and which counterfeit. Origen quotes it frequently, as does Clement in the *Apostolic Constitutions* 2.36 and other writers, especially Greek authors, in whose form it reads: Γίνεστε τραπεζέται δόκιμοι, “Become approved money-changers.” Thus Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* 1, near the end: “Rightly, then, Scripture, wishing us to become such dialecticians, exhorts us in this way: ‘Become approved money-changers,’” and so forth. Cassian, *Conferences* 1.20, says that we should become, according to the Lord’s command, approved money-changers; Origen, volume 19 on John, speaks of those who observe Jesus’ command, “Become approved money-changers”; Ambrose, book 1 on Luke, chapter 1, and others do likewise. It is nevertheless evident that the saying belonged either to Christ or to someone else among the common sayings of the New Testament, sayings drawn from sources other than the four genuine Gospels—perhaps from a good-quality apocryphal Gospel, such as the Gospel of the Nazarenes, or merely from the tradition of the ancients.]

“Be approved money-changers, so that if a coin is counterfeit, and does not bear the image of Caesar, and is not stamped [or: marked] with the public mint, it may be rejected. But the coin that clearly bears the face of Christ should be stored in the purse of our heart.”

For if I wish to know dialectic, or the doctrines of the philosophers, or—to return to our own subject—the knowledge of the Scriptures, I should not question the simple men of the Church, whose gift is of another kind, and each of whom abounds in his own opinion, especially since in the great house of the head of the household there are said to be many kinds of vessels (2 Tim. 2:20).

Rather, I should question those who learned the art from its craftsman and meditate day and night on the Law of the Lord.

From my youth to my old age I have openly acknowledged that Origen and Eusebius of Caesarea were very learned men, but that they erred in the truth of their doctrines.

[Note: We suspect that the words *e contrario* should be replaced by the name of an author whom Jerome had mentioned above. The manuscript of Verona suggested this suspicion, although it reads corruptly, “What concerning the opposite.” Jerome, as we think, wrote: “What can we say concerning Theodore, Diodorus, Acacius, and others?” Then someone excessively ingenious, offended by the similarity of the names Diodorus and Theodore, expelled one of them and inserted *e contrario*. Certainly Jerome had no reason to pass over Diodorus in silence here, since above, in section 3, he had cited him immediately after Theodore, speaking in his own words. There is no doubt that Jerome counted him among the heretics Acacius, Apollinarius, and the others whose writings he approved only for their learning. Meanwhile, all editors who suspect no fault in the printed reading explain *e contrario* as though the Greek were ἐνώπιον, “face to face” or “in contrast.” Victorius devised this interpretation; Martianaeus maintains that the comparison concerns learning between Origen and Eusebius above, and that Theodore, Acacius, and Apollinarius who follow are not regarded as highly learned. No one could persuade us of this, especially concerning Apollinarius, whom Jerome himself once heard and to whom he assigns first place in literary studies, comparing him with Origen and Eusebius as though he were unlearned.]

And yet we can say the opposite about Theodore, Acacius, and Apollinarius; nevertheless, all of them have left us a record of their labor in explaining the Scriptures.

In the earth gold is sought, and shining gravel is brought forth from the beds of rivers. Pactolus is richer in mud than in flowing water.

Why do my friends [Note: Perhaps more correctly, ‘my enemies,’ as two sound manuscripts read] tear me apart, and why do fat swine grunt against one who is silent?

Their entire concern—or rather, the height of their learning—is to criticize what belongs to others, and to defend the faithlessness of the ancients in such a way that they destroy their own faith.

My purpose is to read the ancients, to examine each point, to retain what is good, and not to depart from the faith of the Catholic Church.

### 12.

Wishing to answer other little questions and to dictate immediately either my own thoughts or those of others, I was reminded by my brother Sisinnius that I ought to write a letter both to you and to the other holy brothers who deign to love us [Note: The Verona manuscript reads, ‘that I should write to you and to the other holy brothers,’ omitting the intervening words].

I will therefore restrain my step, and, if life accompanies me, reserve myself for future work, so that I may serve you in parts and so that the fruit and my aged little body may bear a moderate burden.

At the end I briefly remind you of this: the reading found in Latin manuscripts, “We shall all indeed rise again, but we shall not all be changed,” is not found in the Greek books. Instead, they read either, “We shall all sleep, but we shall not all be changed,” or, “We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed.” What the sense of each reading is, we have explained above.

[Note: The Latin Fathers who give and explain this reading should be consulted: Tertullian, *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, chapter 42, and book 5 of *Against Marcion*; Saint Ambrose in his commentary on this passage and elsewhere; Augustine, *On True Religion*, and more explicitly book 20 of *The City of God*, chapter 20, no. 30; and Rufinus, *On the Creed*, no. 43.]

## LETTER 120 [Note: Elsewhere numbered 150. Written in the year 406 or the following year.]

### TO HEDIBIA

[Note: Martianaeus was the first to print this list of chapters from manuscripts in advance, because he thought that it was itself the little commentary sent by Hedibia to Jerome. We have not omitted it solely because all the ancient copies contain it.]

## THE TWELVE CHAPTERS OF HEDIBIA’S QUESTIONS TO SAINT JEROME

[Note: Martianay first printed this list of chapters from manuscripts in advance, believing it to be the little commentary Hedibia had sent to Jerome. It is retained because all the old copies contain it.]

### I.

How can someone be perfect, and how ought a widow who has been left without children to live for God?

[Note: The word ‘God,’ which Jerome does not recognize in his response, is absent from the former Ambrosian manuscript 6 of Saint Columbanus of Bobbio; from it the word ‘with you’ has also been restored in the following question.]

### II.

What is meant by what is written in Matthew: “I will not drink from this fruit of the vine from now on until that day when I drink it new with you in my Father’s kingdom”?

### III.

Why did the Evangelists give different accounts of the Lord’s resurrection and appearances? And why, while Matthew says that the Lord rose in the evening as the Sabbath was dawning toward the first day of the week, does Mark assert that he rose in the morning of the following day?

### IV.

How, according to Matthew, did Mary Magdalene see the risen Lord in the evening of the Sabbath, while the Evangelist John reports that in the morning of the first day of the week she was weeping beside the tomb?

### V.

How, according to Matthew, did Mary Magdalene, together with the other Mary, fall at the Savior’s feet in the evening of the Sabbath, while according to John, in the morning of the first day of the week, she hears the Lord say: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to the Father”?

## VI. How, while a troop of soldiers was keeping watch, Peter and John entered the tomb freely, with none of the guards preventing them.

## VII. How Matthew and Mark write that the Apostles were instructed by the women to go ahead of Jesus into Galilee, and that there they would see him; whereas Luke and John record that he was seen by the Apostles in Jerusalem.

## VIII. What is signified by what is written in the Gospel according to Matthew: “But Jesus, crying out with a loud voice, gave up his spirit; and the veil of the Temple was torn into two parts, from top to bottom,” and what follows.

[Note: The same manuscript, omitting this, substitutes the following passage from Matthew: “The tombs were opened, and many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep arose; and coming out of the tombs after his resurrection, they entered the holy city and appeared to many.” Jerome, however, explains both passages.]

## IX. How the Savior, according to John, breathes the Holy Spirit upon the Apostles, while according to Luke he says that he will send it after his ascension.

[Note: Martianay has “after the Lord’s ascension”; we have removed this final phrase with the help of our manuscripts.]

## X. What is meant by the passage that the Apostle Paul discusses in writing to the Romans: “What therefore shall we say? Is there injustice with God? By no means,” through the place where he says: “Unless the Lord of hosts had left us offspring,” and what follows.

## XI. What is meant by what the Apostle writes to the Corinthians in the Second Epistle: “To some we are the odor of death unto death, and to others the odor of life unto life.”

## XII. What is meant by what is written in the First Epistle to the Thessalonians: “But may the God of peace himself sanctify you completely, and may your spirit and soul and body be preserved blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

Here end the Chapters of the Questions.

# Jerome to Hedibia: On the Twelve Questions

## Preface

Unknown to me in face, but exceedingly well known to me through the ardor of your faith, you send from the furthest boundaries of Gaul, where I lie hidden in the countryside of Bethlehem, a little memorandum requesting answers concerning certain small questions from the holy Scriptures, through Apodemius, a man of God and my son; as though you did not have in your own province eloquent men, accomplished in the Law of God. Unless, perhaps, you are demanding an examination of us more than instruction, and wish to know what we too think about matters you have heard from others.

[Note: The oldest editions read *Commentariolum*, “a little commentary.”]

Your ancestors Patera and Delphidius—one of whom taught rhetoric at Rome before I was born, while the other, when I was already a young man, illuminated all Gaul by his talent in prose and verse—now, though asleep and silent, rightly reproach me for daring to mutter anything concerning the stock of their lineage. Although I readily grant them greatness of eloquence and learning in secular literature, I justly withhold from them knowledge of the Law of God, which no one can receive unless it has been given to him by the Father of lights (James 1), who enlightens every person coming into this world (John 1), and who stands in the midst of believers gathered in his name (Matthew 18).

[Note: This is how the Ambrosian manuscript reads; Martianay wished it corrected from the Cluniac manuscript, whereas all the other printed and handwritten copies read *Paterius*. Jerome also mentions him in the *Chronicle* under the year of Christ 338. There, however, the old parchment manuscripts aspirate the name, *Pather*. The rhetor Patera taught with the greatest glory at Rome; by contrast, Ausonius says in *Commemoration of the Professors of Bordeaux*, poem 4: “And hence for you the names, for you Patera.” Ammianus Marcellinus also mentions Delphidius, whom he calls a most vigorous orator, in Book XVIII, chapter 1; see that passage.]

Therefore I freely confess—and I do not fear that the statement will seem arrogant—that I am writing to you not in learned words of human wisdom, which God will destroy, but in words of faith, “comparing spiritual things with spiritual” (1 Corinthians 2:23), so that the abyss of the Old Testament may call upon the evangelical abyss (Psalm 41), in the voice of the cataracts—that is, of his prophets and apostles—and that the truth of the Lord may reach the clouds, which were commanded not to rain upon unbelieving Israel, but to water the fields of the Gentiles and sweeten the torrent of thorns and the Dead Sea.

Pray, therefore, that the true Elisha may bring life to the barren and dead waters in me, and that he may season my little vegetable dish with the salt of the Apostles, to whom he said, “You are the salt of the earth” (Matthew 5:13), because every sacrifice that is without salt is not offered to the Lord (Leviticus 2:13).

[Note: The very oldest edition reads *meum munusculum*, “my little gift.”]

Nor should you take delight in the brilliance of secular eloquence, which Jesus saw falling from heaven like lightning (Luke 10); instead, look upon him who has “no beauty or appearance,” a man placed among sufferings and acquainted with bearing weakness (Isaiah 53). And whatever I answer concerning the matters proposed, know that I answer not through confidence in my speech, but through faith in him who promised, “Open your mouth, and I will fill it” (Psalm 80:11).

## Chapter One

You ask how someone can be perfect, and how a widow who has been left without children ought to live. A doctor of the Law asks the same thing in the Gospel: “Teacher, what must I do to possess eternal life?” The Lord answered him: “You know the commandments?” He said, “Which ones?” Jesus replied: “You shall not murder, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not steal, you shall not bear false witness; honor your father and mother, and love your neighbor as yourself.” When he said, “I have kept all these things,” the Lord continued: “One thing is lacking to you. If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you possess, and give to the poor; and come, follow me” (Matthew 19:16–21).

Therefore I too will answer you with the words of our Lord: If you wish to be perfect, to take up your cross, to follow the Lord Savior, and to imitate Peter, who says, “Behold, we have left everything and followed you” (Mark 10:28), go and sell everything you possess, give to the poor, and follow the Savior.

He did not say, “Give to your children, give to your brothers, give to your relatives”—for even if you had such persons, the Lord would rightly be preferred to them—but “give to the poor.” Indeed, give to Christ, who is fed in the poor; who, though he was rich, became poor for us; who speaks in the thirty-ninth Psalm: “But I am a beggar and poor, and the Lord is concerned for me” (Psalm 39:18). Immediately the fortieth Psalm begins concerning him: “Blessed is the one who understands concerning the needy and the poor” (Psalm 40:1).

Understanding is necessary, so that after the blessedness of understanding one may know who is needy and poor. It is certainly not the person who is covered with beggary and squalor yet does not depart from vices, but those of whom the Apostle speaks: “Only that we should remember the poor” (Galatians 2:10).

[Note: Martianay reads “with beggary, poverty, and squalor,” inserting these words without informing the reader. Almost all the printed editions omit them, and we found them only in one manuscript.]

For their relief Paul and Barnabas labored in the churches of the Gentiles, so that collections might be made on the first day of the week; and they hastened to carry this offering themselves, not through others, to those who had lost their possessions for Christ, who had suffered persecutions, and who had said to their father and mother, wives and children, “We do not know you” (Deuteronomy 33:9).

These fulfilled the will of the Father and heard the Lord Savior saying, “My mother and my brothers are those who do the will of my Father” (Matthew 12:50; Luke 8:21).

We say this not because we forbid alms from being given to poor Jews or Gentiles, or, in general, to the poor of any nation whatsoever, but because we prefer poor Christians and believers to unbelievers; and even among Christians there is a great distinction according as someone is a sinner or a saint.

[Note: Saint Ambrose, *On Duties*, Book 1, chapter 3: “Perfect generosity is commended by faith, cause, place, and time, so that one may first act toward members of the household of faith.” Jerome explains this same point most elegantly near the end of his *Treatise against Vigilantius*.]

Thus, while approving mercy toward all, the Apostle adds: “Especially toward those who belong to the household of faith” (Galatians 6:10). A member of the household of faith is one who is joined to you by the same religion, whom sins do not separate from the fellowship of brotherhood.

And if we are even commanded concerning our enemies that, if they are hungry, we should give them food, and, if they are thirsty, give them drink—and that by doing so we should heap burning coals upon their heads (Romans 12:20)—how much more concerning those who are not enemies, who are Christians and saints?

Nor should what is said, “For by doing this you will heap burning coals upon his head,” be understood in a bad sense, but in a good one. For when we offer benefits to our enemies, by our goodness we overcome their malice, soften their hardness, and turn their angry spirit toward gentleness and goodwill. Thus we heap coals upon their heads, concerning which it is written: “The sharp arrows of the mighty one, together with burning coals of desolation” (Psalm 119:4).

[Note: The Ambrosian manuscript reads, “we turn the spirit toward affection.”]

Thus, just as a coal taken from the altar by a seraph cleansed the prophet’s lips (Isaiah 6:6–7), so the sins of our enemies may be cleansed; we may overcome evil with good (Romans 12:21), bless those who curse us, and imitate our Father, who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil,

[Note: In one manuscript the concluding words, “and rains upon the just and the unjust,” are absent, as is the pronoun “our.”]

and rains upon the just and the unjust (Matthew 5:45).

Therefore you too, because you do not have a few children, make many friends for yourself from the unrighteous mammon, who may receive you into eternal dwellings (Luke 16:9).

He spoke beautifully of “unrighteous” mammon. For all riches descend from unrighteousness, and unless one person loses, another cannot find.

[Note: Augustine explains this in his commentary on Psalm 48: “either because they were acquired through unrighteousness, or because it is itself an unrighteousness that you possess while another does not possess.”]

Hence that familiar saying seems to me exceedingly true: “Either a rich man is unrighteous, or he is the heir of an unrighteous man.”

When the doctor of the Law had heard this and could not endure it because he had many possessions, the Lord turned to the disciples and said: “How difficult it is for those who have riches to enter the kingdoms of heaven” (Matthew 19:23; Mark 10:23; Luke 18:24).

He did not say “impossible,” but “difficult,” although he supplied an example of impossibility: “It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God.” This, however, is not so much difficult as impossible. It can never happen that a camel passes through the eye of a needle. Therefore a rich person will never be able to enter the kingdoms of heaven.

But a camel is twisted and bent, and weighed down by a heavy burden. Thus we too, when we enter crooked paths, abandon the Lord’s straight way, and are weighed down by the riches of the world or by the burden of sins, are unable to enter the kingdom of God.

If, however, we lay down the heaviest burden and take for ourselves the wings of a dove, we shall fly and rest, and it will be said to us: “If you sleep among the middle sections, the wings of the dove are silvered, and the hinder parts of its back are in the pallor of gold” (Psalm 67:14).

May our back, which was previously misshapen and oppressed by a heavy burden, possess the splendor of gold—which is interpreted as understanding—and silvered wings, which are understood as the utterances of Scripture; then we shall be able to enter the kingdom of God.

The Apostles say that they left everything that had been theirs, and boldly demand a reward for this virtue. The Lord answered them: “Everyone who has left house, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or fields for my name’s sake will receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life” (Matthew 19:29).

O what blessedness—to receive great things for small, eternal things for brief, ever-living things for things that die, and to have the Lord as one’s debtor!

But if a widow has children, especially if she belongs to a noble family, she should not abandon her needy children, but love them impartially;

[Note: Victorius adds from the Brescian codices, “love them”; these two words occur neither in our manuscripts nor in the other printed editions.]

she should remember first her own soul, regard it as one of her children, and distribute her possessions with her children rather than leave everything to them. Indeed, she should make Christ a co-heir with her children.

You will reply: “It is difficult; it is harsh and contrary to nature.” But you will hear the Lord answering you: “Let the one who is able to receive it receive it” (Matthew 19:12). And if you wish to be perfect, he does not impose upon you the yoke of necessity, but grants your will freedom of choice.

Do you wish to be perfect and to stand upon the highest summit of dignity? Do what the Apostles did: sell everything you possess, give to the poor, and follow the Savior, naked and alone; follow the naked and solitary cross.

[Note: Formerly the text read “and the naked one”; then the Ambrosian manuscript has *virtutem*, “virtue,” in place of *crucem*, “cross.”]
