You do not wish to be perfect, but to hold the second rank of virtue? Leave whatever you possess, give to your children, give to your relatives. No one reproaches you if you pursue lower things, provided that you know that the one who chose the first rank is rightly preferred to you.

You will say: “This belongs to the Apostles and to men; but a noble woman cannot sell everything, since she needs many means for this life.”

Hear the Apostle urging you: “Not that there should be relief for others and affliction for you, but that, by equality, your abundance should support their want, so that their abundance also may be a supplement to your want” (2 Corinthians 8:14).

Therefore the Lord says: “Whoever has two tunics should give one to the person who has none” (Luke 3:11).

What if there are the cold spells of Scythia and the snows of the Alps, which are resisted not by two or three tunics, but scarcely by the skins of animals? Whatever, then, can suffice for our body and assist human weakness, with which nature has sent people naked into the world, is to be called one tunic. And whatever is necessary for present nourishment is called one day’s food.

Hence the command is given: “Do not think about tomorrow” (Matthew 6:34)—that is, about a future time. And the Apostle says: “Having food and clothing, let us be content with these” (1 Timothy 6:8). If you have more than is necessary for food and clothing, distribute it, and know that you are indebted in regard to it.

Ananias and Sapphira deserved the judgment of the Apostle because they timidly kept back what was theirs (Acts 5). “Then,” you will say, “is the person who has not given away his possessions to be punished?” Not at all. They were punished because they wished to lie to the Holy Spirit, and, while reserving what was necessary for their sustenance, they pursued empty glory as though they had renounced the world perfectly.

Otherwise, one is freely permitted either to give or not to give. Yet for someone who wishes to be perfect, present poverty ought to be compensated by future riches.

How a widow ought to live the Apostle has summarized in a brief statement: “But the widow who lives in pleasures is dead while she lives” (1 Timothy 5:6). And in the two little books that we wrote to Furia and Salvina, we think that this has been discussed more fully.

[Note: Epistles 54 and 79.]

## Chapter Two

How the Savior’s statement in Matthew is to be understood: “But I say to you: I shall not drink from this fruit of the vine from now on, until that day when I shall drink it new with you in the kingdom of my Father” (Matthew 26:29).

From this passage some construct a story of a thousand years during which they assert that Christ will reign bodily and drink wine which, they say, he has not drunk from that time until the consummation of the world.

Let us instead understand that the bread which the Lord broke and gave to his disciples was the Body of the Lord Savior, since he himself said to them, “Take and eat; this is my body”; and that the cup was the one about which he again said, “Drink from it, all of you; for this is my blood of the New Testament, which will be poured out for many” (Matthew 26:26–28; Mark 14:22–24), and what follows.

This is the cup of which we read in the Prophet: “I will take the cup of salvation” (Psalm 115:4). And elsewhere: “How excellent is your cup, making one drunk!”

[Note: The same manuscript reads, “Your cup,” as Jerome himself corrected it. If desired, see his letter to Sunia and Fretela on the matter. As for Jerome’s interpretation of this passage from Matthew, which is more suitable to the sacred text than any other, most commentators agree with it, especially the Greeks—Origen, Chrysostom, Theophylact, and Euthymius. If only this most lucid testimony from Jerome concerning the real presence of Christ’s Body and Blood in the Eucharist might at some time persuade the heterodox, who stubbornly slander its truth. We do not wish to pursue this matter, since heretics have attacked no dogma of the faith with a more hostile spirit, nor have Catholics defended one with more abundant arguments.]

If, then, the bread that came down from heaven is the Lord’s Body, and the wine that he gave the disciples is his blood of the New Testament, poured out for many for the remission of sins, let us reject Jewish fables and ascend with the Lord into the great, furnished, and cleansed upper room; there let us celebrate the Passover with him, receive from him the cup of the New Testament above, and be made drunk by him with the wine of sobriety.

For the kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness, joy, and peace in the Holy Spirit (Romans 14:17). Nor did Moses give us the true bread, but the Lord Jesus: he himself is both host and feast, himself the one who eats and the one who is eaten.

We drink his blood, and without him we cannot drink. Every day in his sacrifices we tread out red must from the fruit of the true vine, the vine of Sorek—which is interpreted as “chosen”—and from these grapes we drink new wine from the kingdom of the Father, no longer in the oldness of the letter but in the newness of the Spirit. We sing the new song, which no one can sing except in the kingdom of the Church (Revelation 14:3), which is the kingdom of the Father.

The patriarch Jacob also desired to eat this bread, saying: “If the Lord God is with me and gives me bread to eat and clothing to wear” (Genesis 28:20). For as many as are baptized into Christ put on Christ (Galatians 3:27), eat the bread of angels, and hear the Lord proclaiming: “My food is to do the will of him who sent me, the Father, and to complete his work” (John 4:34).

Let us therefore do the will of the Father who sent us and complete his work; and Christ will drink his own blood with us in the kingdom of the Church.

## Chapter Three

Why the Evangelists gave differing accounts of the Lord’s resurrection and appearances.

In the first place you ask why Matthew said, “But in the evening of the Sabbath, as the first day of the week was dawning, the Lord rose” (Matthew, at the end), while Mark records that his resurrection took place in the morning, writing as follows: “When he had risen, on the first day of the week, early in the morning he appeared to Mary Magdalene, from whom he had cast out seven demons. She went and announced it to those who had been with him, as they mourned and wept. And when they heard that he was alive and had been seen by her, they did not believe her” (Mark, at the end, 9–10).

[Note: The old edition and the Ambrosian manuscript omit the negative particle, apparently incorrectly.]

There are two solutions to this question. Either we do not accept Mark’s testimony, since it is reported in only a few Gospels, with almost all the Greek books lacking this chapter at the end, especially since it seems to relate things different from and contrary to the other Evangelists; or we must answer that both told the truth: Matthew said when the Lord rose, in the evening of the Sabbath, whereas Mark said when Mary Magdalene saw him, that is, in the morning of the first day of the week.

The passage should therefore be punctuated as follows: “When he had risen”—with a brief pause in the breath—and then, “on the first day of the week, early in the morning, he appeared to Mary Magdalene.” Thus the one who had risen in the evening of the Sabbath, according to Matthew, appeared in the morning of the first day of the week, according to Mark, to Mary Magdalene. The Evangelist John also indicates this (chapter 20), showing that he was seen in the morning of the following day.

[Note: Gregory of Nyssa likewise bears witness that, in the manuscripts of his own time, the Gospel according to Mark ended at “for they were afraid” in the more accurate copies, *ἐν τοῖς ἀκριβεστέροις τὸ κατὰ Μάρκον εὐαγγέλιον μέχρι τοῦ, ἐφοβοῦντο γὰρ, ἔχει τὸ τέλος*—“in the more accurate copies the Gospel according to Mark has its ending at ‘for they were afraid.’” On the contrary, the Greek and Latin manuscripts that have survived to our time, as well as the ancient translations, almost all contain it; nevertheless, the Fathers who mention it are exceedingly rare. Victor of Antioch and the Anonymous of Toulouse in the Catena on Mark are unaware of this chapter, or of the final twelve verses beginning with verse 9.]

## Chapter Four

How, according to Matthew, Mary Magdalene saw the risen Lord in the evening of the Sabbath, while the Evangelist John reports that she wept beside the tomb in the morning of the first day of the week (John 20).

“The first day of the week” is to be understood as the Lord’s Day, because the whole week is divided into the Sabbath and the first, second, third, fourth, fifth, and sixth days of the Sabbath, which the pagans call by the names of idols and of the elements.

[Note: Namely, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and the elements Sun and Moon; for many examples among ancient writers show that by “elements”—called *στοιχεῖα* in Greek—the Sun and Moon are understood.]

Finally, the Apostle commanded that the money collected for the needy should be gathered on the first day of the week (1 Corinthians 16:2).

We should not suppose that Matthew and John meant different things, but that they called one and the same time—namely, midnight and the crowing of the rooster—by different names.

Matthew writes that “in the evening of the Sabbath,” that is, late—not at the beginning of the night, but when it was already deep and largely past—the Lord appeared to Mary Magdalene. He says “in the evening of the Sabbath as it was dawning toward the first day of the week,” explaining for himself what he meant by “evening of the Sabbath”: namely, as the light of the following day was already approaching.

John likewise did not say simply, “On the first day of the week Mary Magdalene came early to the tomb,” but added, “while it was still dark.” Thus, of the same single time—midnight and the crowing of the rooster—one spoke of the end and the other of the beginning.

It seems to me that the Evangelist Matthew, who composed his Gospel in the Hebrew language,

[Note: This is certainly the most ancient view, confirmed by the testimony of all the Fathers and churches: that Matthew’s Gospel was written *τῇ Ἑβραΐδι διαλέκτῳ*, “in the Hebrew dialect.” Those who maintain that it was first written in Greek do not yet seem to have adequately answered this view. See the observations under the name Matthew in the *Catalogue*.]

did not say so much “in the evening” as “late,” and that the person who translated him, deceived by the ambiguity of the word, did not translate it as “late” but as “in the evening.” Although ordinary human speech maintains that “late” does not mean evening but tardily, we customarily say, “You came late,” that is, tardily, and, “What you ought to have done earlier, do at least late,” that is, tardily.

But if the objection is raised—how can the same Mary who had first seen the risen Lord afterward be reported as weeping at his tomb—we must answer that, both alone and with another woman or with other women, mindful of the benefits that the Lord had bestowed upon her, she often ran to his tomb: at one time worshiping the one whom she saw, at another weeping for the one whom she sought as absent.

Some maintain that there were two Mary Magdalenes from the same town of Magdala: one being the woman who saw him risen in Matthew, and the other the woman who sought him absent in John.

We read in the Gospels that there were four Marys: one the mother of the Lord Savior; another his maternal aunt, who was called Mary of Clopas; a third Mary, the mother of James and Joses; and a fourth, Mary Magdalene. Others, however, maintain that the mother of James and Joses was his maternal aunt.

Some, to free themselves from the difficulty, wish there to be only one of the Marys in Mark, without the surname Magdalene, and claim that through the superfluous error of scribes the surname came to be added, although the first Evangelist did not write it.

Our answer, however, seems simple and clear: the holy women, unable to endure Christ’s absence, ran to the Lord’s tomb throughout the whole night, not once or twice but frequently—especially since the earthquake, the rocks split apart, the fleeing sun, and nature thrown into confusion, and, greater than all these things, the longing for the Savior, had shattered the women’s sleep.

## Chapter Five

How, according to Matthew, Mary Magdalene, together with the other Mary, fell at the Savior’s feet in the evening of the Sabbath, whereas according to John she heard from the Lord in the morning of the Sabbath: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father for you” (John 20:17).

[Note: The two words “in the morning of the Sabbath,” which also occur in the table of chapters, have been supplied here from the manuscripts; they were absent from the printed editions.]

She who had first seen the risen Lord with the other Mary and had fallen at his feet later returned during the night—for she could not remain at home because of her longing for him—and came to the tomb.

When she saw that the stone with which the tomb had been closed had been removed, she ran to Simon Peter and to the other disciple, whom Jesus loved greatly, and said to them: “They have taken the Lord from the tomb, and I do not know where they have put him” (John 20:13).

The woman’s error was joined with devotion. Her devotion lay in her longing for the one whose majesty she knew. Her error lay in saying, “They have taken the Lord from the tomb,” and what follows.

Finally, when Peter and John entered the tomb and saw the linen cloths lying separately, and the napkin that had been wrapped around the Lord’s head placed apart, and believed that he had risen, since they had not found his body in the tomb, Mary stood outside by the tomb, weeping.

When she bent down, she saw two angels in white sitting in the place of the tomb, one at the head and one at the feet, where the body of Jesus had been placed. Thus, under such a distinguished guard, she would not believe that the one guarded by angelic ministers could have been stolen by human beings.

The angels whom she saw said to her: “Woman, why are you weeping?” This recalls what the Lord said to his mother: “Woman, what is that to me and to you? My hour has not yet come” (John 2:4). By calling her “woman,” they reproved her for weeping without cause and said, “Why are you weeping?”

Mary Magdalene, however, had become so stunned and numb, possessing faith as though in darkness because she was terrified by the miracles, that she did not even perceive the presence of the angels. She answered in a womanly manner and said: “I am weeping because they have taken away my Lord, and I do not know where they have put him.”

O Mary, if you believe him to be the Lord, and your Lord, how do you suppose that human beings have taken him away?

“I do not know,” she said, “where they have put him.”

How do you not know the one whom you worshiped a little earlier? When she saw the angels, but did not recognize those whom she saw, terrified by astonishment she turned her face this way and that, desiring nothing other than to see the Lord. Then, turning around, she saw Jesus standing there, but did not know that it was Jesus.

This was not because, as Mani and other heretics claim, the Lord had changed his form and appearance so that he might seem different and various according to his will. Rather, because Mary was stunned by the miracle, she thought the one whom she was seeking with such devotion was the gardener.

Therefore the Lord spoke to her in the same words as the angels: “Woman, why are you weeping?” He added of his own: “Whom are you seeking?”

She answered: “Lord, if you have carried him away, tell me where you have put him, and I will take him away.”

Here she does not call the Lord “Savior” as a confession of true faith, but out of humility and fear she offers the gardener her service.

And observe how great her ignorance is. The one whom a cohort of soldiers guarded, whose tomb was presided over by angels, she supposes has been carried away by a single gardener. Unaware of feminine weakness, she promises herself strength enough to carry a man’s body at the prime of life—a body that, to say nothing of other considerations, had been anointed with a hundred pounds of myrrh—and believes that one frightened woman could carry it.

When Jesus called her and said, “Mary,” so that she might recognize by his voice the one whom she had not recognized by his face, she persisted in her error and called him not “Lord,” but “Rabboni,”

[Note: This is how the ancient parchment manuscripts read, in agreement with the Vulgate and the Greek. The printed editions read *Rabbi*.]

that is, “Teacher.”

Observe the extent of her confusion: she had called him “Lord” while thinking him a gardener, but now calls the risen Son of God “Teacher.”

Thus the Lord speaks to her, who was seeking the living among the dead, who in feminine error and womanly weakness was running here and there, seeking the body of the slain one, whose feet she had held while he was alive, and says: “Do not touch me,

[Note: It is not falsely read, as Victorius maintains, “For I have not yet ascended to my Father for you,” and so forth. The following context requires the present reading, and the agreement of all the manuscripts and printed editions confirms it, with the sole exceptions of Victorius’s edition and another old edition, which, omitting the word *tibi* (“for you”), read “for I have not yet ascended,” and so forth. Jerome himself is also the defender and guarantor of his reading in his letter to Marcella concerning certain questions of the New Testament, question 4: “You do not deserve to hold the feet of the one whom you do not believe to have risen. For I have not yet ascended to my Father.”]

for I have not yet ascended to my Father for you.”

The sense is: “You are not worthy to touch as living the one whom you seek as dead. If you still think that I have not ascended to the Father but have been carried away through human fraud, you are unworthy of my touch.”

He said this not to blunt the zeal of the one who was seeking him, but so that she might know that the dispensation of the assumed flesh had been changed into the glory of divinity, and might no longer wish to be with the Lord bodily, but should believe him to reign spiritually with the Father.

Hence the Apostles possess greater faith: without seeing angels and without seeing the Savior himself, after they had not found his body in the tomb, they believed that he had risen from the dead.

Others think that the order narrated by John came first: Mary Magdalene came to the tomb, saw that the stone had been rolled away from the tomb, and afterward returned with the Apostles Peter and John. She then remained alone at the tomb and, still unbelieving, was rebuked by the Lord. Having returned home, she came again to the tomb with Mary; instructed by the angel, she went out from the tomb, worshiped the Lord, and held his feet, when they both heard from him: “Greetings.” “And they approached, held his feet, and worshiped him.”

They progressed so far that they were sent to the Apostles and heard, first, “Do not be afraid,” and, second, “Go and announce to my brothers that they should go to Galilee; there they will see me.”

## CHAPTER VI

How, while the troop of soldiers was guarding the tomb, Peter and John entered it freely, with none of the guards offering any resistance (Matt. 22; John 20).

This was evidently because, on the evening of the Sabbath, which dawned into the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary came to see the tomb. And behold, there was a great earthquake. An angel of the Lord also descended from heaven and, approaching, rolled away the stone and sat upon it. His appearance was like lightning, and his clothing like snow. Out of fear of him the guards were terrified and became like dead men.

Therefore, those who had been so terrified that they seemed dead must either be believed to have abandoned the tomb and fled, or to have become so numb in body and mind that they did not dare to prevent not merely men, but even women, from wishing to enter the tomb. For great fear had frightened them when they saw the stone rolled away and the earthquake—not one of the ordinary kind, but so great that it shook everything and threatened the utter overturning of the earth—together with the angel’s descent from heaven, whose face was so brilliant that it imitated not a lamp or a light kindled by human skill, but the lightning of heaven by which all things are illumined. Hence they were able to see even in the darkness.

Thus they entered freely. Mary Magdalene, who had told them, had seen that the stone was rolled away and that the Lord’s body had been taken from the tomb. But we should not think that the angel came for the purpose of opening the tomb for the Lord as he rose and rolling away the stone. Rather, after the Lord had risen at the hour he himself willed—an hour known to no mortal—the angel made known what had happened, and by rolling away the stone and by his own presence showed that the tomb was empty. All these things were visible because the radiance of his face overcame the horror of the darkness with the brightness of its lightning.

## CHAPTER VII

How Matthew and Mark write that the women were commissioned to tell the Apostles to go to Galilee to see the Lord again (Matt. 26 and 28; Mark 16), whereas Luke (chap. 24) and John (chaps. 20 and 21) testify that he was seen by them in Jerusalem.

It is one thing for him to present himself to the eleven disciples, who had hidden themselves out of fear of the Jews, when he entered to them through closed doors and, while they thought they were seeing a spirit, displayed his hands and side, wounded by nails and a spear. It is another thing when, according to Luke, he presented himself to them by many proofs over forty days, appearing to them and speaking about the kingdom of God; and, while eating with them, commanded them not to depart from Jerusalem (Acts 1:4).

[Note: Some codices read: “and, having conversed with them, he commanded,” etc. Victorius then adds, “But that they should await the promise of the Father,” which Jerome’s exemplars nevertheless do not have.]

In the former case he appeared for the consolation of those who were afraid, and appeared only briefly, then again vanished from their sight. In the latter there was such familiarity and persistence that he ate together with them. Hence the Apostle Paul also reports that he appeared to more than five hundred disciples at once. And in John we read that, while the Apostles were fishing, he stood on the shore and ate part of a broiled fish and a honeycomb—proofs of a true resurrection. In Jerusalem, however, he is not reported to have done any of these things.

[Note: Not in a different sense, but in the same words which Ambrosianus reads in the little register: “that they should go before the Savior into Galilee, and there see him”; but Luke and John, etc.]

## CHAPTER VIII

What is signified by what is written in the Gospel of Matthew: “But Jesus, crying out with a loud voice, gave up his spirit. And the veil of the Temple was torn in two, from top to bottom; and the earth was shaken, and the rocks were split, and the tombs were opened. And many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep rose. And coming out of the tombs after his resurrection, they entered the holy city and appeared to many” (Matt. 27:50 ff.).

We discussed this passage in the same Commentaries on Matthew. First, it must be said that it is a sign of divine power to lay down the soul when he wills and to take it up again when he wills.

[Note: Two manuscripts read: “that it is a sign of divine power to lay down,” etc.]

Finally, when the centurion heard him say to the Father, “Into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke 23:46), and immediately give up his spirit voluntarily, moved by the greatness of the sign, he said: “Truly this was the Son of God.” The veil of the Temple also was torn in two, so that what Josephus reports the guardians of the Temple to have said might be fulfilled: “Let us depart from these dwelling places.”

[Note: See what we have noted concerning this saying in Letter XVIII to Damasus, no. 9.]

In the Gospel written in Hebrew letters—the Gospel of the Nazarenes—we read not that the veil of the Temple was torn, but that the lintel of the Temple of extraordinary size collapsed.

[Note: The Gospel of the Nazarenes.]

“The earth,” it says, “was shaken, unable to bear its Lord hanging upon it; and the rocks were split, to indicate the hardness of the Jews, who refused to understand the Son of God present among them; and the tombs were opened as a sign of the future resurrection. And many bodies of the saints, coming out of the tombs, entered the holy city and appeared to many.”

We must understand the holy city to be Jerusalem, in distinction from all the cities that at that time served idols.

[Note: Compare what we said in Letter LX to Heliodorus, no. 3, and in Letter XLVI, no. 7.]

For in Jerusalem alone there was a Temple, the worship of the one God, and true religion. And they did not appear to everyone, but to many who received the risen Lord.

### 2

Next, according to the allegorical interpretation, it must be said that, when Jesus cried out and gave up his spirit, the veil of the Temple was torn in two from top to bottom, and all the mysteries of the Law were disclosed, so that what had previously been kept hidden might be revealed to all the nations.

It was torn in two: into the Old and the New Testament. And from top to bottom: from the beginning of the world, when man was created, and through all the intervening events which sacred history recounts, to the consummation of the world.

We must ask whether the veil of the Temple was torn on the outside or on the inside.

[Note: Martianus reads *nisi forte* incorrectly—unless this is a typographical error—as *an anterius*. It is moreover known from Josephus, *The Jewish War* 6.14, that there were two veils in the Temple: one before the Holy of Holies, the other at the entrance to the Tabernacle. Jerome, who thinks that this veil was torn on the outside, followed Origen; most other interpreters understand the other veil, the inner one.]

It seems to me that, during the Lord’s Passion, the veil that had been placed outside in the Tabernacle and in the Temple was torn; it was called the outer veil. For now we see in part and know in part. But when that which is perfect has come (1 Cor. 13:9–10), then the inner veil also must be torn, so that we may see all the mysteries of the house of God which are now hidden from us. We shall see what the two cherubim signify, what the Oracle signifies, and what the golden vessel signifies in which the manna was stored.

For now we see through a mirror, in an enigma (ibid. 12). And although the veil of the historical narrative has been torn for us, so that we may enter the court of God, we cannot know his secrets and all his mysteries, which are kept closed in the heavenly Jerusalem.

At the Lord’s Passion, therefore, the earth was shaken, according to what is written in Haggai: “Yet once more, and I will shake heaven and earth: and the Desired One of all nations will come” (Hag. 2:7–8), so that people may come from east and west and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (Matt. 8:11).

And the rocks were split—that is, the hard hearts of the Gentiles—or the rocks, meaning all the prophecies of the prophets, who themselves, from the Rock—that is, from Christ—received with the Apostles the name “rocks.”

[Note: Victorius reads “from the Rock, Christ.”]

Thus whatever in them had been enclosed by the hard veil of the Law might be split open and revealed to the nations.

The tombs also, of which it is written, “You are like whitewashed tombs outwardly, which within are full of dead men’s bones” (Matt. 23:27), were opened so that those who had previously been dead in unbelief might come out of them and, together with Christ who had risen and was alive, might live (Eph. 2), enter the heavenly Jerusalem, and possess citizenship—not on earth, but in heaven. Dying with the earthly Adam, they might rise with the heavenly Adam.

According to the literal sense, however, no one should find it forced that Jerusalem is called the holy city after the Savior’s death, since the Apostles continued to enter the Temple until its destruction and, out of consideration for those who had believed from among the Jews, continued to observe the ceremonies of the Law.

The Lord loved Jerusalem so greatly that he wept and mourned over it (Luke 19:41), and while hanging on the cross said: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (ibid. 23:34). Thus he obtained what he had asked: many thousands of Jews immediately believed, and a period for repentance was granted to it until the forty-second year.

[Note: We have added *ei* from Victorius. Shortly afterward the manuscript copies read *in malitia* (“in wickedness”) instead of *in blasphemia* (“in blasphemy”). It should also be noted that, in the history of Elisha in 2 Kings, when he went up to Bethel, “little boys came out of the city and mocked him, saying, ‘Go up, baldhead; go up, baldhead.’ When he looked back and saw them, he cursed them in the name of the Lord; and two bears came out of the forest and tore forty-two of the boys.”]

After this, while they persisted in wickedness, two bears came out of the forests of the Roman Gentiles, Vespasian and Titus; and they killed and mangled the blaspheming boys who, with one voice, mocked Elisha as he ascended into the house of God—for this is what *Bethel* means (2 Kings 2).

From that time Jerusalem is no longer called the holy city. Having lost its holiness and its former name, it is spiritually called Sodom and Egypt, so that in its place a new city may be built, the city made glad by the rush of the river (Ps. 45:5), and from whose midst proceeds a fountain that has mitigated the bitterness of the whole world.

[Note: The Ambrosian manuscript reads “the bitterness of the whole city.”]

Thus wretched Israel may mourn the ruins of the Temple with bared arms, while the crowd of believers in Christ daily sees the new buildings of the Church rising and says to Zion: “The place is too narrow for me” (Isa. 49:20). And what is written in Isaiah may be fulfilled: “And his tomb shall be glorious” (ibid. 11:10).

## CHAPTER IX

How, according to John (John 20), the Savior breathed the Holy Spirit into the holy Apostles, while according to Luke he promises that he will send him after the Ascension.

The solution to this question is very easy if, instructed by the Apostle Paul, we recognize the different gifts of the Holy Spirit. For he writes in the First Epistle to the Corinthians:

“There are divisions of gifts, but the same Spirit; and there are divisions of ministries, but the same Lord; and there are divisions of activities, but the same God, who works all things in all. To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for what is beneficial. To one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another the grace of healings in one Spirit; to another faith in the same Spirit; to another the working of miracles; to another prophecy; to another the discernment of spirits; to another kinds of tongues; and to another the interpretation of tongues. But one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each one as he wills” (1 Cor. 12:4 ff.).

[Note: Martianus reads “for usefulness,” in accordance with the Vulgate.]

Therefore, the Lord, who after his resurrection, according to Luke’s Gospel, had said: “Behold, I will send the promise of my Father upon you; but you remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” (Luke 24:49), and who, according to the same evangelist in the Acts of the Apostles, said: “He commanded them not to depart from Jerusalem, but to await the promise of the Father, which you have heard, he said, from my mouth: for John indeed baptized with water, but you shall be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now” (Acts 1:4–5)—is again reported, at the end of the Gospel according to John, on the day on which he had risen, that is, on the Lord’s Day, to have entered to the Apostles through closed doors and said to them a second time, “Peace be with you.” Then he added: “As the Father sent me, so I send you.” When he had said this, he breathed upon them and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them, and whose you retain are retained” (John 20:21 ff.).

On the first day of the resurrection, therefore, they received the grace of the Holy Spirit by which they were to forgive sins, baptize, make people children of God, and bestow the spirit of adoption upon believers. The Savior himself said: “Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them, and whose you retain are retained.”

On the day of Pentecost, however, a fuller promise was made to them: that they would be baptized with the Holy Spirit and clothed with power from on high, by which they would preach the Gospel of Christ to all nations, according to what we read in the sixty-seventh Psalm: “The Lord will give the word to those who evangelize with great power.”

[Note: The same person had incorrectly read *in the sixtieth Psalm*.]

Thus they would possess the working of miracles and the grace of healings; and, since they were going to preach to many nations, they would receive kinds of tongues, so that it might already then be known which of the Apostles ought to announce the Gospel to which nations.

Finally, the Apostle Paul, who preached from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum and from there hastened to go through Rome to Spain (Rom. 15), gives thanks to God that he speaks in tongues more than all the Apostles (1 Cor. 14).

[Note: This is how the Greek text, the Greek Fathers, and the Syriac read; but most other Latin writers omit *magis*, “more.”]

For he who was going to announce the Gospel to many nations had received the grace of many languages.

This promise of the Holy Spirit was fulfilled on the tenth day after the Savior’s Ascension. Luke reports it, writing:

“When the days of Pentecost were fulfilled, they were all together in the same place. And suddenly there came from heaven a sound as of a rushing mighty Spirit, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting. And divided tongues as of fire appeared to them, and one rested upon each of them. And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in various languages, as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance” (Acts 2:1 ff.).

[Note: Victorius preferred “to speak in other languages,” according to the Greek *heterais* (ἑτέραις). The Ambrosian manuscript, however, has only “to speak in languages.”]

Then what is read in Joel was fulfilled:

“And it shall be in the last days, says the Lord: I will pour out from my Spirit upon all flesh; and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy; your old men shall dream dreams, and your young men shall see visions” (Joel 2:18).

The word “pouring out” signifies the generosity of grace, and means the same as what the Lord promised: “You shall be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now” (Acts 1:5).

They were baptized with the Holy Spirit to such an extent that the whole house where they were sitting was filled, and the fire of the Holy Spirit found in them a dwelling it desired, divided their tongues, and, according to Isaiah—who had said that he possessed unclean lips—purified their lips, so that they might preach the Gospel of Christ more purely.

In Isaiah (chap. 6), the lintel of the Temple is said to have been shaken, and the whole house was filled with smoke—that is, with error, darkness, and ignorance of the truth. At the beginning of the Gospel, however, the Church is filled with the Holy Spirit, so that by his grace and ardor the sins of all believers may be purified, and the tongue that preaches Christ may be healed by the fire of the Holy Spirit, which the Lord had said he would send.

John and Luke, therefore, are not in disagreement, so that what one indicates was given on the first day of the resurrection the other describes as having come on the fiftieth day. Rather, there was an apostolic advancement: those who had first received the grace of forgiving sins later received the working of miracles and all the kinds of gifts which we have recalled as described by the Apostle—and, what was more necessary, the diversity of the languages of all nations, so that, when they were going to announce Christ, they would need no interpreter.

[Note: Compare Basil, *On the Holy Spirit*, ch. 16; Ambrose, on Psalm 118, sermon 10; and, not to mention others, Cyril, Leontius, and Euthymius, who especially support Jerome’s interpretation.]

Hence, when the Lycaonians heard Paul and Barnabas speaking in their own languages, they thought that gods had come down in human form (Acts 14).

And truly, the clothing of power is the grace of the Holy Spirit. Possessing it, they did not fear the tribunals of judges or the purple robes of kings. For before he suffered, the Lord had promised and said:

“When they hand you over, do not worry about how or what you are to speak; for it will be given to you in that hour what you are to speak. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. 10:19).

I declare boldly and with complete freedom that, from the time when the Apostles believed in the Lord, they always possessed the Holy Spirit, and that they could not perform signs without the grace of the Holy Spirit—but according to its measure and proportion.

Hence the Savior cried out in the Temple, saying:

“Let the one who thirsts come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly.”

He said this about the Spirit whom those who believed in him were going to receive (John 7:37–38). And in the same passage he adds:

“For the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (ibid. 39).

This does not mean that the Holy Spirit did not exist, since the Lord and Savior says: “But if I cast out demons by the Holy Spirit, by whom do your sons cast them out?” (Matt. 12:28).

[Note: In Victorius, the words “by whom do they cast them out?” are absent.]

Rather, the Spirit was in the Lord, but did not yet dwell completely in the Apostles. For this reason they were terrified at his Passion, denied him, and swore that they did not know Christ.

But after they were baptized in the Holy Spirit and the grace of the Holy Spirit was poured into them, they spoke freely to the rulers of the Jews:

[Note: The Ambrosian manuscript more correctly reads, “to the chief priests.”]

“We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29). They raised the dead, rejoiced amid scourging, poured out their blood for Christ, and were crowned by their punishments.

The Spirit, therefore, was not yet in the Apostles, nor did spiritual graces flow from their belly, because the Lord had not yet been glorified.

What this glory is, he himself explains in the Gospel: “Father, glorify me with the glory which I had with you before the world existed.” The glory of the Savior is the triumphal cross. He is crucified as a human being; he is glorified as God.

Finally, the sun was darkened, the moon was changed into blood, the earth trembled with an extraordinary earthquake, the underworld was opened, the dead walked, and the rocks were split. This is the glory of which he spoke in the Psalm: “Awake, my glory; awake, psaltery and harp” (Ps. 57:9).

And glory itself, together with the dispensation of the flesh he had assumed, answered concerning itself: “I shall rise at dawn,” so that the title of the twenty-first Psalm might be fulfilled, “for the assumption at dawn.”

We say these things not because we believe that there is one God and another human being, or make two persons in the one Son of God, as the new heresy falsely accuses us of doing.

[Note: Thus, even before Nestorius’s installation as bishop of Constantinople in 428—the date assigned as the beginning of his impious heresy—there were those who foreshadowed the perfidy which he revived twenty years later. Perhaps this was the teaching of Theodore of Mopsuestia and his disciples; according to Evagrius, *Ecclesiastical History* 1.2, Nestorius suffered shipwreck of piety as soon as he adopted it. See Liberatus the Deacon, *Breviary*.]

Rather, the one and same person is both Son of God and Son of man; and whatever he says, we refer one part to his divine glory and another to our salvation.

For our sake “he did not regard equality with God as a thing to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, becoming obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. 2). “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14).

I am astonished at Montanus and his deranged women, abortive prophets, who, although the Lord promised and said, “I will go and send you another Paraclete” (John 14:16), and although afterward the evangelist Luke relates (Acts 1 and 2) that the Apostles received what had been promised, claim that this was fulfilled in themselves only much later.

For the promise was made to the Apostles: “I will send the promise of my Father upon you; and you shall remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” (Luke 24:49). After rising, he breathed upon the Apostles—not upon Montanus, Priscilla, and Maximilla—and said to them, that is, to the Apostles: “Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them, and whose you retain are retained.”

[Note: Two manuscripts read “he breathed upon the face of the Apostles.” Elsewhere, in the catalogue, chapters 39 and 40, Priscas is written rather than Priscilla.]

I repeat: he commanded the Apostles not to depart from Jerusalem, but to await the promise of the Father. And afterward we read that what had been promised was fulfilled: “They were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in various languages, as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance” (Acts 2:4).

For the Holy Spirit breathes where he wills (John 3:8). And when the Lord says, “I will send you another Paraclete,” he shows that he himself is also the Paraclete, who is called the Comforter.

Hence God the Father is also designated by this name: “the God of mercies and of all consolation” (2 Cor. 1:3). If, then, the Father is Comforter, the Son is Comforter, and the Holy Spirit is Comforter; and believers are baptized in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—what is understood as the name of God—and there is one name of the Godhead and of the Comforter, then they also have one nature.

This Holy Spirit was not only in the Apostles, but also in the prophets. David prayed concerning him, saying: “Do not take your Holy Spirit from me” (Ps. 50:13). Daniel is also said to have possessed the Spirit of God. And David speaks in the Spirit when he says that the Lord said to his Lord: “Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet” (Ps. 109).

The prophets did not prophesy without the Holy Spirit. “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their power.” Whatever belongs to the Father and the Son belongs likewise to the Holy Spirit. And when the Holy Spirit himself is sent, he is sent by the Father and the Son. In different passages he is called the Spirit of God the Father and the Spirit of Christ.

[Note: The old edition and the Milanese manuscript incorrectly read: “and the Spirit is sent by the Father, and comes in place of the Son,” in one passage and another.]

Thus, in the Acts of the Apostles, those who had been baptized with the baptism of John and believed in God the Father and Christ—but did not know the Holy Spirit—are baptized again; indeed, it is then that they receive true baptism.

For without the Holy Spirit the mystery of the Trinity is incomplete.

And in the same book Peter is reported to have said to Ananias and Sapphira that, by lying to the Holy Spirit, they had not lied to human beings but to God (Acts 5).

## CHAPTER X

What does the passage mean that the Apostle Paul discusses when writing to the Romans: “What then shall we say? Is there injustice with God? By no means” (Rom. 9:14), up to the place where he says: “Unless the Lord Sabaoth had left us offspring, we would have become like Sodom, and we would have been made like Gomorrah” (ibid. 29)?

The whole Epistle to the Romans requires interpretation and is enveloped in such great obscurities that, in order to understand it, we need the assistance of the Holy Spirit, who dictated these very words through the Apostle. But this passage especially has caused difficulty. Some, wishing to preserve God’s justice, say on the basis of the preceding arguments that Jacob was chosen in Rebecca’s womb and Esau rejected (Gen. 25), just as Jeremiah and John the Baptist are chosen in the womb (Jer. 1; Luke 1), and the Apostle Paul himself is predestined for the Gospel before he is born.

For our part, we approve nothing except what is ecclesiastical and what we do not fear to say publicly in the church, lest, in accordance with Pythagoras, Plato, and their disciples—who introduce pagan doctrine under the Christian name [Note: [Col. 0998] See Philo, *On Allegories*; and a little below, on the Manichaean heresy, Augustine, *Enchiridion*, ch. 99, and Question 68 among the Eighty-Three.]—we should say that souls fell from heaven and, according to the diversity of their merits, suffer punishment for their former sins in these or those bodies. It is much better simply to confess our ignorance and, among the many things we do not know, to avoid the obscurity of this passage [Note: [Col. 0998] We explain these matters at greater length in the Letter to Desiderius, which serves as the preface to the Pentateuch. By “Iberian fables” he means the fantasies of the apocryphal *Ascension of Isaiah* and the dreams of the *Apocalypse of Elijah*, by which Marcus the Egyptian, a disciple of Basilides, deceived and took possession of many people in Spain. He also calls them “Egyptian portents” from Marcus’s native land, Egypt. See the Commentary on Isaiah, chapter 64, and our notes there.] rather than, while wishing to vindicate God’s justice, defend the heresy of Basilides and Mani, and pursue Iberian fables and Egyptian portents. [Note: [Col. 0997] The old edition and the Milan manuscript incorrectly read: “that the Spirit is sent by the Father and comes in place of the Son,” and so forth, in another and another passage.]

Let us therefore speak as we can, following the traces of the Apostle’s intention, and not depart from his opinions by even a point—or, as the saying goes, by a fingernail’s breadth.

He had earlier lamented and summoned the Holy Spirit as witness to his sorrow and conscience, because his brothers and kinsmen according to the flesh—that is, the Israelites—had not received the Son of God. “Their adoption,” he says, “and the glory, and the covenants, and the giving of the law” [Note: [Col. 0998] The Ambrosian manuscript adds “and the service”], “and the worship, and the promises; from them also Christ, according to the flesh, was generated from Mary the Virgin.” And he is so continuously tormented by the grief of his heart that he himself wishes to be anathema from Christ—that is, to perish alone—so that the entire Israelite race might not perish (Rom. 9).

Because he had said this, he immediately foresaw the question that would arise from the opposite side: “What then are you saying? Did all who are from Israel perish? And how have you yourself, and the other Apostles, and the countless multitude of the Jewish people received Christ, the Son of God?”

He resolves the question in this way: In the holy Scriptures Israel is called by two names and is divided into two sons: one according to the flesh and the other according to promise and spirit. Abraham had two sons, Ishmael and Isaac. Ishmael, who was born according to the flesh, did not receive his father’s inheritance. Isaac, who was begotten from Sarah according to the promise, is called the seed of God. For it is written: “In Isaac shall your offspring be called”—that is, “It is not the children of the flesh who are children of God, but the children of the promise are regarded as offspring” [Note: [Col. 0998] Victorius argues that the reading should be “are considered” (*aestimantur*).]

And we prove that this did not occur only in Ishmael and Isaac, but also in Rebecca’s two sons, Esau and Jacob, of whom one was rejected and the other chosen. He says all this in order to indicate, through the two earlier brothers, Ishmael and Esau, that the Jewish people was rejected, and through the later ones, namely Isaac and Jacob, that the people of the Gentiles was chosen—or those Jews who were going to believe in Christ.

Since he wished to establish this, he had proposed the testimony concerning the twins Esau and Jacob, about whom it is written: “The elder shall serve the younger” (Gen. 25); and in Malachi we read: “I loved Jacob, but I hated Esau” (Mal. 1:2–3). He then, as is his custom, proposes and discusses the question that comes in from the side, and, once it has been resolved, returns to the matter with which he had begun.

“If Esau and Jacob had not yet been born, and had done nothing good or evil by which they might either please God or offend him; and if their election and rejection displayed not the merits of each individual but the will of the one who chooses and rejects, what then shall we say? Is God unjust?”

He bases the question on the example in which God speaks to Moses: “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will show compassion to whom I show compassion” (Rom. 9:15). If we accept this, he says, namely, that God does whatever he wishes and, without regard to merit or works, either chooses or condemns someone, then “it is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who has mercy.” This is especially so since the same Scripture—that is, the same God—speaks to Pharaoh: “For this very purpose I raised you up, that I might show my power in you and that my name might be proclaimed throughout the whole earth.”

If this is so, and if God has mercy on Israel according to his will and hardens Pharaoh, then it is useless for him to accuse and blame us for having either failed to do good or done evil, since it lies within his power and will, apart from good or evil works, either to choose someone or reject him—especially since human frailty cannot resist his will.

The Apostle dissolves this powerful question, woven together from the reasoning of Scripture and almost incapable of solution, in a brief statement: “O man, who are you to answer back to God?” The sense is this: In answering God and bringing accusations, and in searching so deeply through the Scriptures that you speak against God and reproach [al. investigate] the justice of his will, you show that you possess free choice and can do what you wish, whether to remain silent or to speak.

For if you think that you were created by God like a clay vessel and cannot resist his will, consider this: A clay vessel does not say to the potter, “Why have you made me this way?” For the potter has power from the same clay, or from the same lump, to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor. God, however, created all people with an equal lot and gave them freedom of choice, so that each person may do what he wishes, whether good or evil.

He gave everyone such power that an impious voice argues against its Creator and searches out the reasons for his will. But if God, wishing to display his wrath and make his power known, endured with much patience vessels of wrath, prepared for destruction, in order to show the riches of his glory in vessels of mercy that he prepared for glory—those whom he also called, not only from the Jews but also from the Gentiles, as he says in Hosea (chap. 2:24): “I will call the one who was not my people, my people;” and “the one who was not loved, loved”—“and it shall be in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ there they shall be called sons of the living God” (Rom. 9:22 ff.)—

If, he says, God’s patience hardened Pharaoh and postponed punishment for Israel over a long period so that he might condemn more justly those whom he had endured for so long, then it is not God’s patience and boundless mercy that should be blamed, but the hardness of those who abused God’s goodness to their own destruction.

Otherwise, the heat of the sun is one and the same, yet according to the substances beneath it, it melts some things, hardens others, dissolves others, and constricts others. Wax is melted and clay hardened, yet the nature of the heat is not different. So too the goodness and mercy of God harden the vessels of wrath that are prepared for destruction—that is, the people of Israel. But the vessels of mercy, which he prepared for glory and called—that is, us, who are not only from the Jews but also from the Gentiles—he saves neither irrationally nor without the truth of judgment, but according to preceding causes: some did not receive the Son of God, while others willingly chose to receive him.

These vessels of mercy are not only the people of the Gentiles, but also those Jews who wished to believe; and the one people of believers was formed from both. From this it is shown that it is not the Gentiles who are chosen, but human wills. Thus what was said in Hosea was fulfilled: “I will call the one who was not my people, my people”—that is, the people of the Gentiles—and those to whom it was formerly said, “You are not my people,” shall now be called [al. “are called”] sons of the living God.

And lest he should seem to say this only of the Gentiles, he also calls those who believed from the multitude of Israel vessels of mercy and election. For Isaiah cries out concerning Israel: “Though the number of the children of Israel be like the sand of the sea, a remnant shall be saved” (Rom. 9:27)—that is, even if the multitude does not believe, a few nevertheless will believe.

For God weighed his completed and abbreviated word in his justice, so that through the humility and incarnation of Christ he might save those who wished to believe in him. Isaiah said the same thing elsewhere: “Unless the Lord Sabaoth had left us offspring, we would have become like Sodom, and we would have been made like Gomorrah” (Isa. 1:9).

After presenting the testimonies in which a twofold calling is foretold, of both the Gentiles and the Jewish people, he moves on to the connected argument. He therefore says that the Gentiles, who were not pursuing righteousness, attained righteousness because they did not become proud but believed in Christ. But the greater part of Israel fell because it stumbled over the stone of stumbling and the rock of offense, and did not know the righteousness of God; seeking to establish its own righteousness, it refused to submit to the righteousness of God, which is Christ.

I have read in the Commentary of a certain writer that the Apostle answered in such a way as to entangle the question more than to resolve it. For, in response to what he had proposed—“What then shall we say? Is there injustice with God?”; “It is not of the one who wills or runs, but of God who has mercy”; “He has mercy on whom he wishes, and he hardens whom he wishes”; “Who can resist his will?”—the Apostle is said to have answered thus:

“O man, who are earth and ashes, do you dare to raise a question with God? Do you, a fragile and earthen vessel, rebel against your potter? Can a thing fashioned say to the one who fashioned it, ‘Why have you made me this way’? Or does the potter not have power over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor? Be silent, then, in eternal silence; recognize your frailty, and do not raise a question against God, who has done what he wished, so that he might be merciful toward some and severe toward others.”

What does the Apostle mean when he writes in the Second Epistle to the Corinthians: “To some we are the odor of death unto death, but to others the odor of life unto life; and who is sufficient for these things?” (2 Cor. 2:16)?

Let us set forth the entire passage, so that from what precedes and follows the middle portions may be understood, since they are woven together from both contexts.

“When I came to Troas,” he says, “for the Gospel of Christ, and a door had been opened to me in the Lord, I had no rest for my spirit, because I did not find Titus my brother. But, taking leave of them, I departed for Macedonia. But thanks be to God, who always leads us in triumph in Christ Jesus and manifests through us the fragrance of his knowledge in every place. For we are the good fragrance of Christ to God among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing: to some indeed the odor of death unto death, but to others the odor of life unto life. And who is sufficient for these things? For we are not like the many, selling the word of God [Note: [Col. 1001] Following the Greek *kapēleuontes* (καπηλεύοντες), Martianaeus and our older manuscripts read this way; others, however, prefer *adulterantes*, with the Vulgate edition, a reading approved by Victorius. In reality Chrysostom, whom others generally follow, approves the latter interpretation: they explain *kapēleuontes* as ‘mixing their own things with the divine.’]; but from sincerity, but as from God, before God, we speak in Christ.”

He tells the Corinthians what he did, what he suffered, and how he gives thanks to God in all things, in order to urge them, by his own example, to strive.

“I came,” he says, “to Troas, which was formerly called Troy, in order to preach the Gospel of Christ in Asia. And when a door had been opened to me in the Lord—that is, when many had believed, either through the signs and wonders that God worked through me, or because there was hope of a faith being born and growing in the Lord—I had no rest for my spirit; that is, I could not find the consolation I had hoped for, because I had not found my brother Titus, whether he was someone whom I thought I would find there, someone I had heard was staying there, or someone who had said that he would come there.”

What was this great consolation, and what rest for his spirit was there in Titus’s presence, since, because he did not find him, he took leave of them and departed for Macedonia?

We have often said that the Apostle Paul was a very learned man, educated at the feet of Gamaliel (Acts 22:3), who preaches in the Acts of the Apostles and says: “What do you have to do with these men? For if it is from God, it will stand; but if it is from men, it will be destroyed” (ibid. 5:38–39).

Since he possessed knowledge of the holy Scriptures and the gift of speech in various languages [Col. 1002]—which is why he boasts in the Lord and says, “I thank God that I speak in tongues more than all of you” (1 Cor. 14:18)—he could not express the majesty of divine meanings in language worthy of them through Greek eloquence.

[Note: [Col. 1002] Jerome repeatedly admires and praises the Apostle for his learning. But when he denies him Greek eloquence here, and does so even more explicitly in the following Letter to Algasia, Question 10, this should not be attributed, as most do, to a contradiction in Jerome. It should instead be understood in this sense: although he called him most eloquent in force and energy of speech, he considered him inferior to the more distinguished rhetoricians in polish and elegance of wording. As Jerome himself explains in his work against Rufinus, he either despised Greek eloquence or, certainly out of humility, concealed it. Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine* 4.7.11: “Just as we do not say that the Apostle followed the precepts of eloquence, so we do not deny that eloquence followed his wisdom.”]

He therefore had Titus as his interpreter, just as blessed Peter had Mark, whose Gospel was composed with Peter relating it and Mark writing it. Indeed, the two Epistles attributed to Peter differ from one another in style, character, and structure of wording. From this we understand that, according to the needs of circumstances, he used different interpreters.

Thus the Apostle Paul is also saddened because he had not found, for the present, the pipe and instrument of his preaching through which he might sing for Christ. He proceeded to Macedonia, for a Macedonian man had appeared to him saying: “Cross over and help us.” He went there to find Titus and visit the brothers—or to be tested by persecutions. For this is what he says: “But thanks be to God, who always triumphs over us in Christ Jesus and spreads the fragrance of his knowledge in every place.”

“Triumphs over us” means “triumphs concerning us,” or “celebrates his triumph through us.” Elsewhere he had said: “We have become a spectacle to the world, to angels, and to men” (1 Cor. 4).

Finally, he relates what follows: “For when we came into Macedonia, our flesh had no rest, but we suffered every affliction: conflicts outside, fears within. But God, who comforts the humble, comforted us by the arrival of Titus.” Not only by his arrival, but also by his consolation [al. “comfort”].

Therefore, after taking leave of the Trojans or people of Troas, he departed for Macedonia in order to find Titus there and have the consolation of interpretation and of the Gospel. We understand that Titus was not found there immediately, but arrived after the Apostle’s tribulations and persecutions.

Before Titus came, therefore, after enduring many hardships, Paul gave thanks to God in Christ Jesus, whom he preached to the Gentiles, because God had chosen him as one in whom he would celebrate the triumph of his Son.

God’s triumph is the suffering of the martyrs, the shedding of blood for Christ’s name, and joy amid torments. For when someone sees the martyrs standing with such perseverance, being tortured, and glorying in their sufferings, the fragrance of the knowledge of God is spread among the nations, and the silent thought arises that, unless the Gospel were true, it would never be defended with blood.

For confession is not delicate, devoted to wealth, and secure, but exists in prisons, wounds, persecutions, hunger, nakedness, and thirst. This is God’s triumph and the victory of the Apostles.

But someone hearing this could reply: “How, then, did not everyone believe?”

Before he is questioned, Paul resolves the *anthypophora* (ἀνθυποφορά, “counter-objection”) and, according to his custom, explains in advance whatever another person might object before it is raised.

The sense is this: “We are the good fragrance of Christ’s name to God in every place, and the fragrance of our preaching breathes far and wide. But because human beings have been left to their own free choice—for they do not do good by necessity but by will, so that believers may receive a crown and unbelievers be handed over to punishments—therefore our fragrance, which is good in itself, passes into life or death according to the power and fault of those who receive or do not receive it. Thus those who believe are saved, while those who do not believe perish.”

Nor is this remarkable in the case of the Apostle, since we also read it concerning the Lord: “Behold, this one is appointed for the fall and resurrection of many in Israel, and as a sign that will be opposed [Note: [Col. 1003] Other manuscripts and printed editions have the contrary reading, which the Benedictine editor preferred. The Greek is ἀντιλέγομεν, “we oppose” or “speak against.”]” (Luke 2:34).

The rays of the sun shine equally upon clean and unclean places, and shine upon flowers as they do upon dung, yet the rays of the sun are not polluted. So too the good fragrance of Christ, which can never be changed or lose its nature, is life to believers and death to unbelievers.

This death is not the common death, since we die along with beasts and animals, but the death of which it is written: “The soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezek. 18:4).

Accordingly, life too should be understood as not the life by which we breathe, walk, and run here and there, but the life of which David speaks: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. 26:13) [Note: [Col. 1003] Some manuscripts read “in the region of the living.”]. For God is God of the living and not of the dead (Matt. 22:23), and “our life is hidden with Christ in God. When Christ, our life, appears, then we too shall appear with him in glory” (Col. 3:3–4).

“Nor should it seem insignificant to you, Corinthians, if, while we preach the truth, some believe and others do not; if some die the true death while others live by that life which says, ‘I am life.’ For unless we had spoken, neither death would follow unbelievers nor life believers, since it is difficult to find a preacher worthy of Christ’s virtues who, in proclaiming them, seeks not his own glory but the glory of the one whom he preaches.”

In saying that he is not like the many who sell the word of God, he shows that there are very many who consider piety a source of profit and do everything for the sake of shameful gain—those who devour widows’ houses (Luke 20). He, however, speaks from sincerity, as one sent by God and in the presence of the one who sent him, speaking everything in Christ and for Christ, so that the cause of the preaching, the triumph of Christ, and the glory may belong to God.

It should also be noted that at the end of this chapter he indicates the mystery of the Trinity. He speaks from God, in the Holy Spirit, before God the Father, in Christ.

To establish that he went from Troas to Macedonia, I shall cite testimony from the Acts of the Apostles:

“When they had passed through Mysia, they went down to Troas. And a vision appeared to Paul during the night: a certain Macedonian man was standing and pleading with him and saying, ‘Cross over into Macedonia and help us.’ And when he had seen the vision, immediately we sought to depart for Macedonia, having been assured that God had called us to evangelize them” (Acts 16:8 ff.).

## CHAPTER XII

What does the Apostle mean when he writes in the First Epistle to the Thessalonians: “May the God of peace himself sanctify you completely, so that your spirit and soul and body may be preserved whole and blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Thess. 5:23)?

It is a famous question, but it must be treated briefly. Earlier he had said: “Do not extinguish the Spirit” (ibid. 19). Once this has been understood, we shall immediately know what sort of spirit it is that is to be preserved, together with soul and body, on the day of the Lord’s coming.

For who could believe that the Holy Spirit is extinguished like a flame, which ceases to be what it was when it is extinguished, and that he who once existed in Israel should suffer his own abolition—he who could speak through Isaiah, Jeremiah, and each of the Prophets, saying, “Thus says the Lord,” and who now speaks in the Church through Agabus, “Thus says the Holy Spirit”?

“There are divisions of gifts, but the same Spirit; divisions of ministries, but the same Lord; and divisions of activities, but the same God, who works all things in all. To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for what is beneficial. To one is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom, to another a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another faith in the same Spirit; to another the working of miracles; to another gifts of healings in one Spirit; to another prophecy; to another discernment of spirits. But all these things are worked by one and the same Spirit, distributing to each as he wills” (1 Cor. 12:4 ff.).

David prayed concerning this Spirit that he not be taken away from him, saying: “Do not take your Holy Spirit from me” (Ps. 50:13). When he is taken away, he is extinguished not in his own substance but in the person from whom he is taken [Note: [Col. 1004] Victorius argues that the more accurate reading is “not in his substance,” which he derived from the Brixian manuscripts.].

I think that “Do not extinguish the Spirit” (1 Thess. 5:19) means the same thing as what he writes elsewhere: “Be fervent in spirit” (Rom. 12:11). For when the fervor of the spirit does not grow lukewarm through multiplied iniquity and the cooling of charity, the spirit is by no means extinguished.

Therefore, “May the God of peace sanctify you completely”—or “in all things,” or “full and perfect”; for this is more exactly expressed by the Greek word *holoteleis* (ὁλοτελεῖς).

God is called the God of peace because through Christ we have been reconciled to him. Christ is our peace, who made both one (Eph. 2:14). He is also called, elsewhere, “the peace of God which surpasses all understanding,” which guards the hearts and thoughts of the saints.

Whoever is sanctified, or perfect in all things, has spirit, soul, and body preserved in this condition on the day of the Lord.

The body is whole if each of its members performs its functions—for example, if the hand works, the foot walks, the eye sees, the ear hears, the teeth grind food, the stomach cooks it, and the intestines digest it—or if it has not been mutilated in any part.

But can anyone believe that the Apostle prays for believers so that, on the day of judgment, Christ may find their entire bodies intact, when everyone’s bodies have either been dissolved by death or, if they are found still breathing, as some maintain, still bear their infirmities [Col. 1005] [al. “still possess their infirmities”], especially the bodies of martyrs and of those who, for Christ’s name, have had their eyes torn out, their noses cut off, or their hands severed?

Therefore, the whole body is that of which we spoke in another question: it holds the head, from whom the entire body, joined and compacted together, receives [al. “receives”] its growth [Note: [Col. 1005] Following the older and more accurate books, we read this with Victorius, in accordance with the Greek *epichorēgias* (ἐπιχορηγίας). Martianaeus reads “for the building up.”] for the functioning of the body of Christ. This body is the Church.

Whoever holds fast to the head of this body and preserves the remaining members will have a whole body, insofar as human nature can receive wholeness.

In the same way, the integrity of the soul must be preserved. It can say: “Bless the Lord, O my soul, who heals all your diseases” (Ps. 102:1, 3). Of the soul it is written: “He sent his word and healed them” (Ps. 106:20).

The spirit within us is also preserved whole when we do not err in spiritual matters, but live in the spirit, submit to the spirit, and put to death the works of the flesh by the spirit, bringing forth all its fruits: charity, joy, peace, and the rest.

### Another Interpretation

Solomon commands us: “Write these things for yourself three times, in counsel and knowledge, so that you may answer with words of truth those who propose questions to you” (Prov. 22:20–21) [Note: [Col. 1005] Martianaeus, following Erasmus throughout, here also reads the singular *verbum* (“word”) instead of *verba* (“words”), as do all the ancient books and both textual traditions; Victorius himself corrects the reading. Immediately afterward, for the sense to be clear—or at least more harmonious—it seems that the following clause should be connected with Solomon’s words as “by one spirit,” with the final little word removed, so that the threefold description itself and the rule may be understood as being prescribed.].

There is a threefold inscription and rule of the Scriptures in our heart.

First, we are to understand them according to history.

Second, according to tropology.

Third, according to spiritual understanding.

In history, the order of the things written is preserved. In tropology, we rise from the letter to greater things, and whatever was done carnally among the earlier people, we interpret according to the moral sense and turn it toward the benefit of our soul. In spiritual *theōria* (θεωρία), we pass on to higher things, leave earthly matters behind, and discuss the blessedness of the future and heavenly things, so that meditation on the present life may be the shadow of future blessedness.

If Christ finds people of such a kind that they are preserved whole in body, soul, and spirit and possess within themselves the perfect truth of this threefold knowledge, he will sanctify them with his peace and make them perfect.

Many understand this passage simply of the resurrection, so that spirit, soul, and body may be preserved whole at the Lord’s coming.

[Note: [Col. 1005] Tatian devised and defended this other explanation or opinion. He distinguishes the soul from body and spirit in such a way that the soul is, as it were, a substance intermediate between spirit and body: it governs the body, but is itself governed by the spirit, which he calls the divine light and the image and likeness of God. See his *Oration to the Greeks*.]

Others wish to establish from this passage a threefold substance in the human being: the spirit, by which we perceive; the soul, by which we live; and the body, by which we walk.

There are those who argue that a human being consists only of soul and body and wish the third element, spirit, to be understood not as a substance but as an activity, by which the mind, sense, thought, and disposition within us are named; naturally, there are not as many substances as there are names.

When the passage is brought against them, “Bless the Lord, spirits and souls of the righteous” (Dan. 3:86), they do not accept the Scripture, saying that it is not found in the Hebrew.

But in the present passage, as we said above, by the “spirit” that is preserved whole together with soul and body, we do not understand the substance of the Holy Spirit, which cannot perish, but his gifts and bestowals [Note: [Col. 1006] Theodoret is entirely correct in calling the Spirit the gift itself—“he called the Spirit the gift” (Πνεῦμα τὸ χάρισμα κέκληκε). Irenaeus, Clement of Alexandria, and Chrysostom also have similar interpretations of this passage.] which, according to our virtue or fault, are both kindled and extinguished within us.

## LETTER CXXI

[Note: [Col. 1006] Otherwise numbered 151. Written in the same year as the preceding letter.]

### TO ALGASIA

## TABLE OF CONTENTS

[Note: [Col. 1006] We have likewise printed these chapters of the Questions of Algasia in advance, for the same reasons mentioned above concerning the material drawn from the little Commentary of Hedibia.]

### ELEVEN QUESTIONS OF ALGASIA TO SAINT JEROME

**I.** Why does John send his disciples to the Lord to ask him, “Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect another?” when he himself had previously said of him: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold the one who takes away the sins of the world”?

**II.** What does it signify that it is written in Matthew: “He will not break a bruised reed, and he will not extinguish smoking flax”?

**III.** What sense does the statement in the Gospel of Matthew have: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself”? What is self-denial, or how does someone who follows the Savior deny himself?

**IV.** What does the statement in the same Matthew signify: “Woe to those who are pregnant and to those who are nursing in those days”; and, “Pray that your flight may not occur in winter or on the Sabbath”?

**V.** What does the statement in the Gospel according to Luke mean: “They did not receive him, because his face was set toward Jerusalem”?

**VI.** Who is the steward of iniquity, who was praised by the Lord’s voice?

**VII.** In what sense should we understand what we read in the Epistle to the Romans: “Hardly anyone dies for a righteous person; perhaps someone might dare to die for a good person” (Rom. 5:7)?

**VIII.** What does the Apostle mean when he writes to the Romans: “Taking occasion, sin worked in me through the commandment every kind of covetous desire”?

**IX.** Why does the Apostle Paul write in the same Epistle to the Romans: “I myself was wishing to be anathema from Christ for the sake of my brothers,” and the rest?

**X.** What does the same Apostle mean when he writes to the Colossians: “Let no one prevail over you, wishing to do so through humility of mind and the worship of angels,” and the rest?

**XI.** What does the same Apostle mean when he writes to the Thessalonians: “Unless the rebellion comes first and the man of sin is revealed,” and the rest?

[Col. 1007] Here end the chapters.

## JEROME TO ALGASIA

### On the Eleven Questions
## Preface

My son Apod[e]mius, who, in accordance with the interpretation of his name [Note: [Col. 1007] Namely, *ἀπόδημος*, from which *Apod[e]mius* is derived in Latin, from the Greek verb *ἀποδημέω*, means “abroad” or “a traveler.” In Mark 13:34, *ὡς ἄνθρωπος ἀπόδημος* means “like a man who has gone abroad,” etc. Soon afterward he also alludes to the meaning of Bethlehem, which is interpreted as “house of bread.”], marked his arrival to us by a long voyage, and, coming from the shore of the Ocean and the furthest regions of Gaul, passing Rome, sought Bethlehem, in order to find in it the heavenly bread, and, having been satisfied, to pour forth praise in the Lord and say: “My heart has uttered a good word; I speak of my works to the king” (Ps. 44:1). He brought me on a small sheet of paper very great questions, which he said had been given by you to be handed over to me.

When I read them, I understood that the zeal of the Queen of Sheba had been fulfilled in you: she came from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon’s wisdom (3 Kings 10:4; Matt. 12:42). I am certainly not Solomon, who is preferred in wisdom to all people both before and after him; but you must be called the Queen of Sheba [or: “from Sheba”], in whose mortal body sin does not reign, and who, having turned with your whole mind to the Lord, will hear him say: “Turn, turn, O Shulammite” (Song 6:12). For *Sheba* in our language signifies “turning.”

At the same time I have observed that the fact that your little questions have been proposed only from the Gospel and the Apostle indicates that you either do not read the Old Scripture sufficiently or do not understand it sufficiently. It is wrapped in such great obscurities and types of future things that it requires interpretation throughout. The eastern gate, from which the true light rises and through which the High Priest enters and departs, is always closed (Ezek. 43:1–2; 44:1) and is open only to Christ (Rev. 5), who possesses the key of David—he opens, and no one shuts; he shuts, and no one opens—so that, when he unlocks it, you may enter his chamber and say: “The king has brought me into his chamber” (Song 1:3).

Moreover, I have wondered greatly why, abandoning the nearby stream of the purest spring, you have sought the waters of our little rivulets so far away, and, leaving aside the waters of Shiloah, which flow silently (Isa. 8), desired [or: desire] the waters of Sihor (the Nile), which are befouled by the turbid vices of this age.
