You have there the holy man Alethius the Presbyter [Note: [Col. 1007] He appears to be that Alethius to whom Saint Paulinus’s thirty-third letter is addressed, the brother of Florentius and his successor in the bishopric of Cahors; concerning him, see Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, book 2, chapter 13. Algasia, moreover, was from this same region of Gaul.], who, as they say, with living speech and prudent, eloquent discourse, can resolve what you ask—unless perhaps you desire foreign wares and, for variety of taste, are also pleased by the seasonings of our country.

Some prefer sweet things; some enjoy things slightly bitter. Sour flavors refresh the stomachs of some, while salty foods sustain those of others. I myself have often seen nausea and dizziness cured by the antidote called *πικρά* [“bitter”] [Note: [Col. 1007] See Letter 78 to Fabiola, section V; Pliny, book 22, chapter 22.], and, according to Hippocrates, opposites are the remedies of opposites.

Therefore cure our bitterness with his nectar-like honey, and place the wood of the cross in Marah; restrain the phlegm of old age with youthful austerity, so that you may joyfully sing: “How sweet are your words to my throat, sweeter than honey to my mouth” (Ps. 118:103).

## Chapter One

### Why does John send his disciples to the Lord to ask him, “Are you the one who is to come, or are we to expect another?” (Matt. 11:3; Luke 7:20), when he had previously said of him, “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1:29)?

We have spoken more fully about this question in the *Commentaries on Matthew*. From this it is clear that, although you ask these questions, you do not possess those volumes. Nevertheless, we must touch on the matter briefly, lest we appear to have been entirely silent.

John sent his disciples while he was in prison, seeking information for himself but learning for them; and, as he was about to be beheaded, he taught them that they must follow the one whom, through his question, he acknowledged as the teacher of all. For he could not be ignorant of the one whom he had previously pointed out to those who did not know him, and of whom he had said: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom” (ibid. 3:29); and, “I am not worthy to carry his sandal” (Matt. 3:11); and, “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 1:27).

He had also heard God the Father thunder: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I have been well pleased” (ibid. 3:30) [Note: [Col. 1008] Victorius, on the basis of the Brixian manuscripts, reads “in whom I have been well pleased,” seeking to confirm this wording from the Greek *εὐδόκησα*.].

But when he says, “Are you the one who is to come, or are we to expect another?” (Matt. 3:17), this meaning too may be intended: “I know that you are the one who came to take away the sins of the world; but because I am going to descend to the underworld, I also ask this: will you yourself descend there as well, or would it be impious to believe this of the Son of God, and will you send another? This is what I desire to know: since I announced you to human beings on earth, may I also announce you to the dead, if you are indeed going to come. For you are the one who came to release captivity and set free those who were held in bonds.”

Understanding his inquiry, the Lord answers by works rather than by words, and commands that it be reported to John that the blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead rise, and—what is greater than these—the poor are evangelized (Matt. 11; Luke 7). The poor means either those poor in humility or those poor in wealth, so that there is no difference in salvation between rich and poor, but all are called equally.

And when he adds, “Blessed is the one who is not scandalized by me” (Matt. 11:6), he is striking not John but his disciples, who had earlier approached him and said: “Why do we and the Pharisees fast frequently, but your disciples do not fast?” (Mark 18; Luke 5:33). They had also said to John: “Teacher, the one to whom you bore witness beside the Jordan—behold, his disciples are baptizing, and everyone is coming to him” (John 3:26).

By these words they reveal jealousy concerning the greatness of his signs, arising from the sharpness of envy: why, after being baptized by John, he dared to baptize himself, and why a much greater crowd flocked to him than had previously come to John.

And lest the people, who did not understand, should suppose that John was being reproached by these words, he concludes with praise of him. He began to say to the crowds standing around: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind? But what did you go out into the wilderness to see? A man clothed in soft garments?” (Matt. 11:7–8; Luke 7:24–25), and so forth.

The meaning of this statement is: “Did you go out into the desert for this purpose—to see a man, like a reed, bending in different directions under the breath of the winds? So that the one whom he had previously praised would now doubt him, and the one of whom he had earlier said, ‘Behold the Lamb of God,’ would now ask whether he or another was the one who had come or was to come?”

And because every false preaching pursues profits and seeks human glory, so that advantages may be born from glory, he declares that John, clothed in camel’s hair, could yield to no flattery. Since he ate locusts and wild honey (Matt. 3:4), he sought neither wealth nor other earthly delights; he lived a severe and austere life and avoided the halls of the palace, which are sought by those who dress in purple, linen, silk, and soft garments [Note: [Col. 1009] Older printed editions add: “who are in the houses of kings.” Shortly afterward, *monstrat* was read instead of *monstravit*.].

He says that John was not merely a prophet, who customarily foretells future things, but more than a prophet: for the one whom the prophets had said would come, John showed to have come, saying: “Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1:29).

This is especially so because the Baptist received a privilege surpassing that of the prophets: although he had said, “I ought to be baptized by you” (Matt. 3:14), he himself baptized Christ—not through the presumption of one greater, but through the obedience of a disciple and the fear of a servant.

And when he declares that among those born of women none greater than John has arisen (Matt. 11:11), he recalls that he himself, who was born of a Virgin, is greater—or that the least angel in heaven surpasses all human beings on earth. For we advance toward the angels, and the angels do not advance toward us [Note: [Col. 1009] Origen taught this, as Epiphanius testifies, *Against Heresies* 64.4 and 33: namely, that all human souls had been angels and would become so again. He speculates particularly about the Forerunner, whom he suspects had formerly been an angel. In *Commentary on John*, book 5, he says: “Nor is it at all remarkable that, when the firstborn of all creation was embodied through benevolence, certain zealous followers and imitators of Christ arose, who loved to serve his kindness toward human beings through the body.” See also his *Letter to Avitus*, chapter 1, and his *Commentary on Haggai*, book 1. Such heretics are called “Psychopneumones” by the author of the *Praedestinatus*.], just as some people, snoring, dream in a very deep sleep.

Nor is this sufficient for John’s praise unless it is also reported that, while preaching the baptism of repentance, he first said: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. 3:1). From the days of his preaching, therefore, the kingdom of heaven suffers violence (ibid. 11:12), so that the human being who was born as a human being desires to be an angel, and the earthly animal seeks a heavenly dwelling.

“For the Law and the Prophets prophesied until John” (ibid. 11:13)—not because John is the end of the Prophets and the Law, but because the one whom John’s testimony proclaimed is their end.

According to the mystery written in Malachi (chapter 4, verse 5), John is “Elijah, who is to come” (Matt. 11:14). This does not mean that the same soul was in Elijah and in John, as the heretics suppose, but that John possessed the same grace of the Holy Spirit: he was girded with a belt like Elijah, lived in the wilderness like Elijah, and suffered persecution from Herodias as Elijah suffered from Jezebel. Just as Elijah is the forerunner of the second coming, so John greeted the Lord and Savior, who was to come in the flesh, not only in the wilderness but also in his mother’s womb, and announced him through the movement of his body.

## Chapter Two

### What does the statement written in Matthew mean: “He will not break a bruised reed, and he will not extinguish a smoldering wick” (Matt. 12:20)?

For the exposition of this passage, the whole testimony that Matthew takes from the prophet Isaiah must be set out, together with Isaiah’s own words—according to the Septuagint interpreters, and also the Hebrew text, to which Theodotion, Aquila, and Symmachus agree.

Thus, of the four Evangelists, Matthew alone wrote:

> “But Jesus, knowing this, withdrew from there. And many followed him, and he healed them all. And he charged them not to make him known, so that what had been spoken through Isaiah the prophet might be fulfilled (chapter 42, verses 1 and following), saying:
>
> ‘Behold my servant whom I have chosen, my beloved, in whom my soul has been well pleased. I will put my Spirit upon him, and he will announce judgment to the nations. He will not contend or cry out, nor will anyone hear his voice in the streets. He will not break a bruised reed, and he will not extinguish a smoldering wick, until he brings judgment forth to victory; and in his name the nations will hope’” (Matt. 12:15 and following).

In Isaiah, according to the Septuagint interpreters, it is written as follows:

> “Jacob is my servant; I will receive him. Israel is my chosen one; my soul has received him. I have placed my Spirit upon him; he will bring forth judgment to the nations. He will not cry out, nor will he let go, nor will his voice be heard outside. He will not crush a broken reed, and he will not extinguish a smoldering wick; but in truth he will bring forth judgment. He will shine, and he will not be shaken, until he establishes judgment upon the earth; and in his name the nations will hope.”

But from the Hebrew we have translated it in this way:

> “Behold my servant [or: slave]; I will receive him. My chosen one, my soul has been pleased with him. I have placed my Spirit upon him; he will bring forth judgment to the nations. He will not cry out, nor will he accept a person’s status, nor will his voice be heard outside. He will not crush a bruised reed, and he will not extinguish a smoldering wick. In truth he will bring forth judgment. He will not be sad or turbulent, until he establishes judgment on the earth; and the islands will await his law.”

From this it is clear that Matthew the Evangelist, not bound by the authority of the old translation, did not abandon the Hebrew Truth but, as a Hebrew from the Hebrews and one most learned in the Law of the Lord, presented to the nations what he had read in Hebrew.

For if the passage is to be understood as the Septuagint interpreters rendered it—“Jacob is my servant; I will receive him. Israel is my chosen one; my soul has received him”—how do we understand that what is written about Jacob and Israel has been fulfilled in Jesus? [Note: [Col. 1011] One should recall what he says in the *Commentaries on Isaiah*: “Jacob and Israel are not found in the present chapter, since the Evangelist Matthew also did not include them, following the Hebrew Truth.” We say this in reproach of those who despise our work. The matter has been discussed more fully in the brief *Commentaries on Matthew* and in the book recently written to Algasia.]

We read that blessed Matthew did the same not only in this testimony but also elsewhere: “Out of Egypt I called my son” (Hos. 11:2), whereas the Septuagint translated: “Out of Egypt I called his sons.” Unless we follow the Hebrew Truth, it is plainly impossible for this to refer to the Lord and Savior. For what follows is: “But they sacrificed to the Baals.”

As for what is lacking in the testimony adopted by the Gospel—“He will shine, and he will not be shaken, until he establishes judgment upon the earth”—it seems to me to have resulted from an error by the first copyist. Reading the preceding sentence as ending with the word “judgment,” he thought that the final word of the following sentence was also “judgment,” and omitted the few words that stood between the two occurrences of “judgment.”

Again, where the Hebrew reads, “And the islands will hope in his law,” Matthew, interpreting the meaning rather than the words, put “name” and “nations” in place of “law” and “islands.” This should be carefully observed not only in the present passage but wherever the Evangelists and Apostles have brought forward testimonies from the Old Testament: they followed not the words but the meaning; and wherever the Septuagint differs from the Hebrew, they expressed the Hebrew meaning in their own language.

The servant, therefore, of the almighty God, according to the dispensation of the assumed flesh by which he was sent to us, was called the Savior. To him the Father also says in another passage: “It is a great thing for you to be called my servant, so that you may gather the tribes of Jacob” (Isa. 49:3).

This is the vine of Sorek, which is interpreted as “chosen.” This is the most beloved Son, in whom the soul of God was well pleased—not because God has a soul, but because every affection of God is displayed in the soul.

Nor is it surprising if a soul is named in relation to God, since all the members of the human body are said, according to the laws of figurative interpretation and the various senses of Scripture, to belong to him.

He also placed his Spirit upon him: the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and strength, the Spirit of wisdom and piety, and the fear of the Lord (Isa. 11). This Spirit descended upon him in the form of a dove. Concerning him John the Baptist also reports that he heard from God the Father: “Upon whomever you see the Holy Spirit descending and remaining upon him, he is the one” (John 1:33).

“And he will announce judgment to the nations.” Concerning this we read also in the Psalms: “Give the king your judgment, O God, and your righteousness to the king’s son” (Ps. 71:1). He himself says in the Gospel: “For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5:22).

“He will not contend,” just as a lamb is led to the sacrifice; he will not contend in the destruction of those who hear. “He will not cry out,” in accordance with what the Apostle Paul writes: “Let all clamor, anger, and bitterness be taken away from you” (Eph. 4:31).

“He will not cry out,” because Israel did not execute judgment but produced a cry. Nor will anyone hear his voice in the streets, that is, outside. For “all the glory of the king’s daughter is within” (Ps. 44:14), and “the way that leads to life is narrow and constricted” (Matt. 7:14).

Therefore his voice is not heard in the streets, where Wisdom acts confidently, neither entering the broad and spacious way nor failing to rebuke and condemn it. For this reason he spoke to those who were outside, not in his own voice but through parables.

“He will not break,” he says, “a bruised reed,” or, as the Septuagint translated it, “he will not crush a broken reed.” The broken reed, which was formerly vocal and sang praises to the Lord, should be understood as Israel. Because Israel struck against the cornerstone, fell upon it, and was broken upon it, it is said of Israel: “Rebuke the beasts of the reed” (Ps. 67:31).

In the book of Jesus, a torrent of reeds—that is, of canes—is mentioned. It has turbid waters, which Israel chose while scorning the purest streams of the Jordan. Turning back in mind toward Egypt and desiring the muddy, marshy region, melons, onions, garlic, cucumbers, and pots of Egyptian meat, Israel is rightly called by Isaiah a broken reed. Whoever wishes to lean upon it will have his hand pierced.

For whoever, after the coming of the Lord and Savior, abandons the spirit of the Gospel’s interpretation and rests in the death of the Jewish letter has all his works wounded.

Nor will he extinguish a smoldering wick: this means the people gathered from the nations, who, after the heat of the natural law had been extinguished, were enveloped in the most bitter smoke—which is harmful to the eyes—and in the errors of dark obscurity.

He not only did not quench this people and reduce it to ashes; on the contrary, from a small and almost dying spark he raised up the greatest fires, so that the whole world might burn with the fire of the Lord and Savior, which he came to cast upon the earth and desired to see burning everywhere (Luke 12:49).

According to the figurative interpretation, we briefly noted in the *Commentaries on Matthew* what we thought about this passage [Note: [Col. 1012] The note is as follows, book 2, chapter 12: “Whoever does not extend a hand to the sinner and does not carry the burden of his brother breaks a bruised reed. And whoever despises the small spark of faith in little ones extinguishes a smoldering wick. Christ did neither of these things; for he came to save what had perished.”].

But he who did not break the bruised reed or extinguish the smoldering wick also brought judgment forth to victory (Isa. 42:3). His judgments are true, justified in themselves (Ps. 18), so that he may be justified in his words and prevail when he is judged (Ps. 50). The light of his preaching will shine in the world for so long, and will be crushed by no one and overcome by no stratagem, until he establishes judgment on the earth and what is written is fulfilled: “May your will be done, as in heaven so also on earth” (Matt. 6:10).

“And in his name the nations will hope” (Isa. 11:10), or, “the islands will hope in his law” (ibid. 42:4). For just as islands are indeed struck by whirlwinds, blasts of wind, and frequent storms, but are not overturned, as an example of the Gospel house founded with a solid mass upon the rock (Matt. 7; Luke 6), so the churches that hope in the law and in the name of the Lord and Savior speak through Isaiah:

> “I am a fortified city, a city that is not besieged” (Isa. 27:3, according to the Septuagint) [Note: [Col. 1013] Most printed editions and manuscripts have the negative particle, and this reading is not disputed, just as it is quoted in the letter to Paula concerning the Hebrew alphabet. The meaning in both passages is the same: it should be understood and explained as “not besieged.” Martianaeus, however, preferred, on the basis of other manuscripts and perhaps also the Greek text, *a city being besieged* (*πόλις πολιορκουμένη*), meaning “a city that is besieged.”].

## Chapter Three

### What meaning does the statement written in the Gospel of Matthew have: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself” (Matt. 16:24)? What is self-denial, or how does the one who follows the Savior deny himself?

In the third book of the *Commentaries on the same Matthew*, I spoke briefly as follows:

> Whoever lays aside the old human being with his works denies himself, saying: “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2:20); he takes up his cross and is crucified to the world. But for the one to whom the world has been crucified, the crucified Lord is the one he follows.

To this we may now add the following. After showing his disciples that he had to go to Jerusalem and suffer many things from the priests, scribes, and chief priests, and be killed, Peter took him aside and began to rebuke him, saying: “Far be it from you, Lord; this shall never happen to you.” Turning, he said to Peter: “Get behind me, Satan; you are a stumbling block to me, because you do not understand the things of God but those of human beings” (Matt. 16:23).

Terrified by human fear, Peter dreaded the Lord’s passion. And just as, hearing that he would suffer many things and be killed, he was afraid, so, hearing that he would rise again on the third day [Note: [Col. 1013] Earlier editions read “will rise again.”], he ought to have rejoiced and softened the sorrow of the passion by the glory of the resurrection.

Therefore, after rebuking him for his fear, the Lord spoke to all the disciples—or, as Mark has it, summoned the crowd together with his disciples—or, according to Luke, said to everyone:

> “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Luke 9:23).

The meaning of this exhortation is: There is no delicate or carefree confession of faith in God. Whoever believes in me must shed his own blood. “Whoever loses his life in the present will gain it in the future” (Matt. 10:39).

Every day, the believer in Christ takes up his cross and denies himself. Whoever was unchaste, turning toward chastity, denies lust through self-control. Whoever was fearful and timid, having taken up the strength of courage, no longer recognizes his former self. If an unjust person follows righteousness, he denies injustice. If a foolish person confesses Christ as the power and wisdom of God, he denies foolishness (1 Cor. 1).

Knowing this, let us deny not only during persecution and the necessity of martyrdom but in our entire way of life, in our deeds, thoughts, and speech, the selves we formerly were; and let us confess those whom we have become through rebirth in Christ.

For this reason the Lord was crucified: so that we, who believe in him and have died to sin, might also be crucified with him, and say what the Apostle Paul taught: “I have been crucified with Christ” (Gal. 2:19). And: “For me, may it never be that I should boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. 6:14).

Let the one who has been crucified with Christ strip the principalities and powers and triumph over them on the wood. Therefore, in the Gospel according to Matthew [Note: [Col. 1014] Nine Brixian manuscripts belonging to Victorius and two others in our possession, one of them printed, cite the Gospel according to John here, not Matthew. From Jerome’s context and manner of expression it seems quite clear, in our judgment, that he did not intend to cite Matthew. For since what he has explained thus far has been drawn from various passages of that Gospel, why would he say, as though referring to testimony previously introduced nowhere, “Therefore also in the Gospel according to Matthew”? If John is substituted on the basis of the manuscripts, however, the truth of the sentence still does not become clear. Of all the Evangelists who unanimously testify that Jesus’ cross was carried by Simon of Cyrene, John alone explicitly asserts that Christ had previously taken it up himself. Accordingly, in the sense which I have no doubt was also intended by the holy Doctor, the passage would still need to be emended conjecturally after the manuscript reading, with the name of John substituted and the order of the words changed approximately as follows: “The cross which, according to the other Evangelists, Simon of Cyrene carries, he himself carried first.” But because the manuscripts support us only in the former point, we have changed nothing from the printed reading, which the other editors also scrupulously preserve.], as a type of those who were to believe in the Lord and be crucified with him, Simon of Cyrene carries his cross—which, according to the other Evangelists, he himself carried first.

## Chapter Four

### What does the statement written in the same Matthew mean: “Woe to those who are pregnant and to those who nurse infants in those days. And pray that your flight may not be in winter or on the Sabbath” (Matt. 24:19–20)?

It is clear that this depends on what precedes. When the Gospel of Christ has been preached to all nations and the end has come, and they have seen “the abomination of desolation,” spoken of by the prophet Daniel, standing in the holy place (Mark 13), then those who are in Judea are commanded to flee to the mountains; the one who is on the roof is told not to descend to take anything from his house; and the one who is in the field is told not to return to take his cloak.

We have discussed these matters more fully in the *Commentaries on the same Matthew*. Immediately afterward it is joined to them: “Woe to those who are pregnant and to those who nurse infants in those days.” In which days? When the abomination of desolation has stood in the holy place.

No one doubts that, according to the literal sense, this is proclaimed concerning the coming of Antichrist, when the magnitude of the persecution compels flight, and pregnant women and nursing infants delay the escape. Some, however, wish it to signify the war of Titus and Vespasian against the Jews, especially the siege and battle against Jerusalem.

They interpret winter and the Sabbath in this way as well: the command is that they not be compelled to flee at a time when the harshness of the cold in the fields and deserted places prevents fugitives from hiding; and that observance of the Sabbath would either make them transgressors if they fled, or expose them to the swords of their enemies if, by observing the Sabbath rest and commandments, they remained still.

But when we hear the Lord and Savior command those who are in Judea to flee to the mountains, let us also lift our eyes toward the mountains, concerning which it is written: “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from which my help will come” (Ps. 120:1). And in another place: “Its foundations are in the holy mountains” (Ps. 86:1); and, “The mountains surround it, and the Lord surrounds his people” (Ps. 124); and, “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matt. 5:14) [Note: [Col. 1015] Victorius, on the basis of the Vulgate edition, certain Florentine manuscripts, and other Brixian manuscripts, reads *cannot be hidden*, a reading supported also by the Greek *κρυβῆναι*.].

Let us also strip off the skin of the letter and, with bare feet, ascend the mountain with Moses [Note: [Col. 1015] Others add “Sinai,” which is the name of that mountain.], saying: “I will pass over and see this great vision” (Exod. 3:3), so that we may understand pregnant souls—those which have conceived the beginnings of faith from the seed of teaching and the word of God—and may say with Isaiah: “Because of your fear, O Lord, we conceived, and we labored, and we gave birth to the spirit of your salvation, which you made upon the earth” (Isa. 26:14).

For just as seeds are gradually formed in the wombs and a human being is not considered [or: “reckoned”] to exist until the confused elements receive their own shapes and limbs [Note: [Col. 1015] All editions before Martianaeus read thus, as both the argument and the sense require. Yet he, on the basis of certain corrupted manuscripts, read “homicide” in place of “a human being”; this reading is irrelevant and, even from his explanation, contains unsound doctrine. He also invents in the margin a reference to Exodus 21:22, which has nothing whatever to do with Jerome’s meaning.], so a meaning conceived by reason, unless it breaks forth into action, is still retained in the womb; and it quickly perishes through miscarriage when it sees “the abomination of desolation” standing in the Church (Dan. 9:27; Matt. 24:15; Mark 13:14), and Satan transformed into an angel of light (2 Cor. 11:14).

Paul speaks of such embryos when he says: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Gal. 4:10).

Therefore I think that, according to the mystical interpretations, these are the women about whom the same Apostle writes: “The woman, having been deceived, came into transgression. But she will be saved through the bearing of children, if they remain in faith, love, and holiness with modesty” (1 Tim. 2:14–15).

If she has at some time given birth from the divine word, it is necessary that what has been born should grow, first receiving the milk of infancy (1 Cor. 3:2), until it reaches solid food and the mature age of the fullness of Christ (Eph. 4:13). For everyone who is nourished on milk is inexperienced in the word of righteousness; he is a child.

These souls, then, which have not yet given birth, or which have not yet been able to nourish what has been born, are quickly scandalized and perish when they see heretical speech standing in the Church. They cannot endure in storm and persecution, especially if they have been idle in good works and have not walked in the way that is Christ (John 14:6).

Concerning this abomination of heretical and perverse doctrine, the Apostle said that the human being of iniquity and the adversary exalts himself against everything called God or regarded as sacred, so that he dares to stand in the temple of God and display himself as though he were God (2 Thess. 2:4). His coming operates according to the activity of Satan; it causes what has been conceived to perish by miscarriage and prevents what has been born from reaching either childhood or full maturity.

Therefore the Lord must be entreated lest winter arise at the beginning of faith and during its growth, concerning which it is written: “Winter has passed; the rain has gone away” (Song 2:11). Let us not grow sluggish through idleness; rather, when shipwreck threatens, let us awaken the sleeping Lord and say: “Teacher, save us; we are perishing” (Matt. 8:25).

## Chapter V

What is meant by what is written in the Gospel according to Luke: “And they did not receive him, because his face was [Note: Victorius reads *obfirmata vadens* (“set toward going”), although the word *obfirmata* is absent from all the manuscripts, I think even those collated by Martianaeus, though he hardly alerts the reader to this. Indeed, it is also absent from the Greek manuscript, where there is only ὅτι τὸ πρόσωπον αὐτοῦ ἦν πορευόμενον (“because his face was going”), and from the Vulgate translator himself: “because his face was going,” etc. Nevertheless, the Reatinus interpreter insists that it must absolutely be retained, since this is clear from Jerome’s interpretation appended below: for he adds, “For firmness and courage are necessary,” and other similar expressions below. Yet we are very much afraid that he and the other editors have not sufficiently attended to the fact that Jerome is repeating the entire preceding narrative from the Gospel in order to serve his explanation, and that the words “he set his face to go to Jerusalem” belong to the preceding verse of the Gospel. The whole passage in which St. Doctor here introduces the mention of firmness must therefore be referred to that verse, not at all to this fifty-third verse, which, when he quotes it again a little below, he consistently reads without adding that word.] going to Jerusalem” (Luke 9:53).

The Lord was hastening to proceed to Jerusalem, so that the days of his assumption might be fulfilled and he might celebrate the Passover, of which he had said, “With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer” (ibid. 22:15), and drink the cup of which he says, “The cup which the Father has given me, shall I not drink it?” (John 18:11); and so that he might strengthen all his teaching by the cross, in accordance with what is written: “And I, when I have been lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself” (ibid. 12:32). He set his face to go to Jerusalem. For firmness and courage are necessary for one who willingly hastens toward suffering.

Thus also to Ezekiel, to whom God had said, “Son of man, you dwell in the midst of scorpions, and do not fear them,” he says: “I have set your face firm, and I have given you a bronze face and an iron forehead” (Ezek. 2:6; 3:9). Thus, if perhaps the hammer of the whole earth should rise against him, he might resist like an exceedingly hard anvil and shatter the hammer, concerning which it is written: “How the hammer of the whole earth has been broken and shattered” (Jer. 50:23).

“And he sent messengers”—that is, angels—“before his face” (Luke 9:52). For it was just that angels should minister to the Son of God. Or he calls the Apostles “angels,” since John, the Lord’s forerunner, was also called an angel (Mal. 3; Matt. 11). [Note: Victorius likewise reads: “He set firm,” etc.]

And when they had entered a village of Samaria to prepare for him, they did not receive him, because his face was going to Jerusalem. The Samaritans and the Jews were at odds with one another through hostile hatred; and although all nations hate one another, they rage against each other with a particular fury, since both contend over possession of the Law. They persecute one another so intensely that, after the Jews had returned from Babylonia, the Samaritans continually obstructed the rebuilding of the Temple. When they themselves wished to build the Temple together with them, the Jews replied: “It is not permitted for us and you to build a house for our God” (1 Esdras 4).

Finally, as the height of insult, the Pharisees reproached the Lord: “Are we not right in saying that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?” (John 8:48). And in the parable of the man descending from Jerusalem to Jericho, the Samaritan is introduced as a sign and wonder: that an evil person should do good (Luke 10). And concerning the Samaritan woman at the well it is written: “For Jews do not associate with Samaritans” (John 4:9).

When the Samaritans therefore saw the Lord going to Jerusalem—that is, to their enemies—they learned from his disciples, who had come to prepare lodging for him, that he was a Jew. And, regarding him as a Jew and an outsider, and as one who was going to his enemies, they refused to receive him.

Although another interpretation is also offered to us: that it was the Lord’s will not to be received by the Samaritans, because he was hastening to go to Jerusalem and suffer there and shed his blood, lest, occupied with Samaritan hospitality and with teaching that people, he postpone the day of his passion, which he had come to endure. Hence elsewhere he says: “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. 15:24). And he commanded the Apostles: “You shall not enter a city of the Samaritans” (ibid. 10:5), wishing to remove every occasion for Jewish persecution, lest they later say, “We crucified him because he had joined himself to our enemies and adversaries.”

His face, therefore, was that of one going to Jerusalem. And for this reason, according to the other interpretation, the Samaritans did not receive him because he was hastening to enter Jerusalem. Yet his not being received was the Lord’s will. Finally, the Apostles, trained in the Law, in which they had known only justice, attempted to avenge the injury according to “an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth,” and to imitate Elijah, at whose word fire had consumed two captains of fifty soldiers. They said to the Lord: “Do you wish us to command fire to come down from heaven and consume them?” (Luke 9:51). [Note: Thus also Ambrose and Theophylact appear to understand this passage, although others reject this interpretation—not without reason—and contend that it conflicts with the sacred text. For if the Samaritans could not retain Christ because he was hastening to Jerusalem, and if he himself did not wish to be received by those who wanted to receive him, what reason was there for his disciples James and John to ask the Lord that fire descend from heaven and burn the Samaritans, in order to avenge the injury they had received from them?]

Beautifully they say, “Do you wish us to command it?” For Elijah too had said: “If I am a man of God, let fire come down from heaven upon you” (4 Kings 1:10). Therefore, in order that the Apostles’ speech might have effect, it depends upon the Lord’s will. Unless he gives the command, the Apostles say in vain that fire should descend upon them; in a certain sense they express this in other words. If, in response to an injury done to Elijah, fire descended from heaven, and the conflagration consumed not Samaritans but Jews, how much more, in contempt of the Son of God, ought the flame to rage against impious Samaritans?

By contrast, the Lord, who had come not to judge but to save—not in power but in humility, not in the glory of the Father but in the lowliness of a human being—rebuked them because they did not remember his teaching and the goodness of the Gospel, in which he had said: “To him who strikes you on the cheek, offer the other also” (Matt. 5:39). [Note: The manuscripts and printed editions agree in reading this way. The Vulgate adds *dexteram* (“right”) and *tuam* (“your”), of which the former word is also absent from the more ancient Greek manuscripts. Both words were easily absent from the old Latin translation, for Tertullian too, *On Patience*, chapter 7, has: “To him who strikes you in the face, turn the other cheek also.”] And: “Love your enemies” (Luke 6:35).

## Chapter VI

You proposed another little question from the Gospel of Luke (chapter 16, verse 1 and following): who is the unjust steward, commended by the Lord’s voice? Wishing to know the reason for this and from what source it arose, I reread the Gospel volume and found, among other things, that when tax collectors and sinners were drawing near to the Savior to hear him, the Pharisees and scribes murmured, saying: “Why does this man receive sinners and eat with them?” (Luke 15:2).

He addressed to them the parable of the hundred sheep and the one that was lost, which, once found, was carried back on the shepherd’s shoulders. And immediately he explained why it had been proposed: “I tell you, so there will be joy in heaven over one sinner who repents, more than over ninety-nine righteous persons who have no need of repentance.” He also proposed another parable about ten drachmas, one of which was lost and then found, and concluded it with a similar ending: “So I tell you, there will be joy before the angels of God over one sinner who repents.”

He also proposed a third parable, about a man who had two sons and divided his property between them. When the younger son had squandered his resources, begun to suffer want, and was eating carob pods, the food of pigs, he returned to his father and was received by him. His elder brother, in his envy, was also rebuked by the father, because he ought to have rejoiced and been glad that his brother, who had been dead, had come to life again, and who had been lost had been found.

He spoke these three parables against the Pharisees and scribes, who were unwilling to receive the repentance of sinners and the salvation of tax collectors. “But he was also saying,” it says, “to his disciples” (ibid. 16:1)—with no doubt that he was speaking a parable, just as earlier to the scribes and Pharisees—so that by this parable he might exhort the disciples to clemency, saying in other words: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven” (Luke 6:37), so that with open confidence you may ask in the Lord’s Prayer: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6:12).

What, then, is the parable by which he exhorts the disciples to clemency? “There was a certain rich man who had a steward” (Luke 16:1), or administrator, for this is what οἰκονόμος signifies. A *villicus* properly means the governor of an estate, and therefore the name *villicus* is derived from *villa*. But an οἰκονόμος is an administrator both of money and of crops and of everything that the master possesses. Hence Xenophon’s *Oeconomicus* is a very beautiful book, which, as Cicero translates it, signifies not the management of an estate but the administration of an entire household.

This administrator was accused before his master of squandering his property. When he had been summoned, he said: “What is this I hear about you? Give an account of your administration, for you will no longer be able to administer my affairs.” What did he say within himself? “What shall I do, since my master is taking the administration away from me? I cannot dig; I am ashamed to beg. I know what I shall do, so that, when the administration has been taken from me, they may receive me into their houses.”

So he summoned each of his master’s debtors and said to the first: “How much do you owe my master?” He replied: “A hundred bats of oil.” He said to him: “Take your bond, sit down quickly, and write fifty.” Then he said to another: “And how much do you owe?” He replied: “A hundred cors of wheat.” He said to him: “Take your bond and write eighty.”

And the master praised the unjust steward, or administrator, because he had acted prudently: “For the children of this age are more prudent in their generation than the children of light.” And I say to you: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that when you fail, they may receive you into eternal dwellings. The one who is faithful in little is faithful also in much; and the one who is unjust in the least is unjust also in much. If therefore you have not been faithful in unjust mammon, who will entrust to you what is true? And if you have not been faithful in what belongs to another, who will give you what is yours? No servant can serve two masters; for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will attend to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and mammon.”

The Pharisees, who were lovers of money, were hearing all these things and scoffing at him.

I have set out the entire text of this parable so that we may not seek its meaning from elsewhere or strive to discover particular persons in the parable, but interpret it as a parable—that is, as a likeness—which is called by this name because it is *paraballetai* (παραβάλλεται), that is, “compared” or “made similar” to something else, and is like a shadow preceding the truth.

If, therefore, the steward of unjust mammon is praised by the Lord’s voice because he prepared righteousness for himself from an unjust possession; and if the master, having suffered loss, praises the steward’s prudence because he acted fraudulently against his master but prudently for himself—how much more will Christ, who can suffer no loss and is inclined toward clemency, praise his disciples if they are merciful toward those who are going to believe in him [or: who have been entrusted to him]?

Finally, after the parable he added: “And I say to you, make friends for yourselves from the unjust mammon.” Mammon is called “wealth” not in the language of the Hebrews but of the Syrians. [Note: He evidently thought the word a compound, and perhaps derived it from [two Hebrew words lacking in the supplied text], *minavon* (“from iniquity”), since *avon* signifies vanity and iniquity. St. Irenaeus himself, in book 3, chapter 8, found some sort of addition and compound in this word, but the passage rests upon an error. Meanwhile, in Chaldean and Syriac there is one word, [a Syriac term lacking in the supplied text], by which Jews using the idiom of that period called riches, especially those lent to another at interest. Hence, after the various opinions of learned men, we think the true etymology of the name is none other than that derived from the Hebrew word meaning “he believed” [the original term is lacking in the supplied text], from which comes *creditum*, a loan, which in Greek is δάνεισμα, or interest. How remarkably this interpretation fits the Gospel passages!]

These riches have been gathered from iniquity. If, therefore, iniquity, when properly administered, is turned into righteousness, how much more will the divine word—in which there is no iniquity, and which was entrusted also to the Apostles—raise its administrators to heaven if it has been properly administered?

Therefore it follows: “The one who is faithful in the least”—that is, in bodily or material things—“will also be faithful in much”—that is, in spiritual things. But the one who is unjust in little, refusing to give his brothers for their use what God created for all, will also be unjust in distributing spiritual money, dividing the Lord’s teaching according not to need but to persons.

“If, then,” he says, “you have not properly administered material riches, which pass away, who will entrust to you the true and eternal riches of the teaching of God? And if you were unfaithful in what is another’s”—for everything belonging to this age is foreign to us—“who will be able to entrust to you what is yours, what has been specifically assigned to a human being?”

Thus he rebukes avarice and says that the one who loves money cannot love God. Therefore, if the Apostles wish to love God, they too must despise money.

Hence the scribes and Pharisees, who were avaricious, understood that the parable had been spoken against them and scoffed at him, preferring material things, as certain and present, to spiritual and future things, as though they were uncertain.

Theophilus, seventh bishop of the Church of Antioch after the Apostle Peter, [Note: Elsewhere, in the *Catalogue*, he calls him the sixth bishop of the Church of Antioch. Thus the title of Theophilus’ work *To Autolycus* reads: Θεοφίλου Πατριάρχου ἕκτου Ἀντιοχίας, “of Theophilus, sixth patriarch of Antioch.” Peter is evidently not counted, as often happens when the Apostles are either placed before episcopal lists on account of their apostolic authority or excluded from them.] who joined together the sayings of the four Evangelists into a single work and left us a memorial of his talent [or: “left behind”], spoke as follows about this parable in his *Commentaries*:

> “The rich man who had a steward, or administrator, is Almighty God, than whom nothing is richer. His administrator is Paul, who learned the sacred Scriptures at the feet of Gamaliel (Acts 22:3) and had received the Law to administer. When he began to persecute, bind, and kill those who believed in Christ, and to squander all the substance of his master, he was rebuked by the Lord: ‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? It is hard for you to kick against the goad’ (Acts 9:4–5).
>
> “And he said in his heart: ‘What shall I do? For although I was a teacher and steward, I am compelled to become a disciple and a laborer. I cannot dig.’ For I see that all the commandments of the Law, which rested upon the earth, have been destroyed, and that the Law and the Prophets have come to an end as far as John the Baptist.
>
> “‘I am ashamed to beg,’ since, although I had been a teacher of the Jews, I am compelled to beg from the Gentiles and from the disciple Ananias the teaching of salvation and faith. I shall therefore do what I understand to be useful for me, so that, after I have been expelled from my stewardship, Christians may receive me into their houses.
>
> “And he began to teach those who had previously lived in the Law and had believed in Christ in such a way [Note: From an older printed edition and one manuscript we read *ut*, as the sequence of the sentence and the preceding words seem to require. Previously it had *ne arbitrarentur* (“lest they should think”), which gives the opposite and erroneous sense.] that they should understand that they were not to be justified in the Law: that the Law had been abolished [Note: Most other printed editions read “the Prophets”], that the prophecies had passed away, and that what had previously been gain was to be regarded as refuse (Phil. 3:8).
>
> “He therefore summoned two of the many debtors. First, the one who owed a hundred bats of oil—namely, those who had been gathered from the Gentiles and greatly needed the mercy of God. From the number one hundred, which is full and perfect, he made them write fifty, the number especially belonging to penitents, in accordance with the jubilee and that parable in the Gospel in which five hundred denarii are forgiven to one person and fifty to another.
>
> “Then he summoned the Jewish people, who had been nourished by the wheat of God’s commandments and owed the number one hundred. He compelled them to make eighty out of one hundred—that is, to believe in the Lord’s resurrection, which is contained in the number of the eighth day and is completed by eight decades—so that they might pass from the Sabbath of the Law to the first day of the week.
>
> “For this reason he is praised by the Lord, because he acted well and, for the sake of his salvation, was changed from the severity of the Law into the clemency of the Gospel. [Note: Some editions corruptly read *mutuatus sit*.]
>
> “If you ask why he is called the steward of iniquity, although the Law belongs to God: in the Law the steward was unjust because he offered rightly but did not divide rightly—believing in the Father but persecuting the Son; possessing Almighty God but denying the Holy Spirit.
>
> “The Apostle Paul was therefore more prudent, in transgressing the Law, than the former children of light, who, occupied with observing the Law, lost Christ, who is the true light of God the Father.”

What Ambrose, bishop of Milan, thought about this passage you will be able to read in his *Commentaries*. I have not been able to find Origen’s or Didymus’ explanation of this parable. Whether it has been destroyed by the passage of time or they themselves did not write it, I do not know.

To me, in accordance with the earlier interpretation, it seems that we ought to make friends for ourselves from the unjust mammon—not just any poor people, but those who can receive us into their houses and into eternal dwellings—so that, when we have provided them with small things, we may receive great things from them; and, giving what belongs to another, may receive what is ours; and sow in blessing, so that we may reap blessing. For “the one who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly.”

## Chapter VII

In what sense should we understand what we read in the Epistle to the Romans: “For scarcely does anyone die for a righteous person; for perhaps someone might even dare to die for a good person” (Rom. 5:7)?

Two heresies, taking occasion from this testimony, which they do not understand, blaspheme with different errors but equal impiety.

Marcion, who makes the just God the Creator of the Law and the Prophets, but the good God the author of the Gospels and the Apostles, whose Son he wishes Christ to be, introduces two gods: one just and the other good. He maintains that for the just one either no one or very few have undergone death, but that for the good one—that is, Christ—innumerable martyrs have appeared.

Arius, on the other hand, refers “just” to Christ, concerning whom it is said: “Give the king your judgments, O God, and your righteousness to the king’s son” (Ps. 71:1); and he himself says in the Gospel: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5:22); and, “As I hear, I judge” (ibid. 30).

He refers “good” to God the Father, concerning whom the Son himself confesses: “Why do you call me good? No one is good except one, God the Father” (Luke 18:19).

Although up to this point he has been able to find the crooked paths of his blasphemy, in what follows he stumbles and falls. For how can anyone dare to die for the Father, while scarcely dying for the Son, when so much martyr blood has been poured out for the name of Christ?

One who explains this passage simply may say that in the Old Law, in which there is justice, scarcely a few were found who poured out their blood for it. But in the New Testament, in which there is goodness and clemency, innumerable martyrs appeared.

Yet by adding “perhaps someone might even dare to die”—[Note: The Greek has καὶ, “even”; this word is absent from the Latin manuscripts.] and by tempering the statement with a hesitant expression—he shows that some might indeed be found who would dare to die for the Gospel. The passage must therefore not be understood in this way, but its meaning must be considered from what precedes and follows.

For when Paul says that he glories in tribulations, “because tribulation produces endurance; endurance, proven character; and proven character, hope; and hope does not disappoint” (Rom. 5:4–5), which possesses a firm promise because “the love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (ibid.), in accordance with what God had said through the Prophet: “I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh” (Joel 2:28), he marvels at Christ’s goodness: that he was willing to die for the impious, the weak, and sinners, and to die at the proper time, concerning which he himself says: “At the acceptable time I heard you, and on the day of salvation I helped you” (Isa. 49:8). And again: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Cor. 6:2).

When all had sinned and together become worthless, there was no one who did good, not even one (Ps. 13:1). It is therefore an incredible goodness and unheard-of clemency to die for the impious. For scarcely would anyone shed his blood for a righteous person, and even for a good person—[Note: Older printed editions add *contingit*, “it happens.”] since fear of death terrifies all things.

Sometimes, however, it can happen that someone dares to die for a just and good cause. But God’s love, which he had for us, is shown above all by this: that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us, and “his life was taken from the earth”; “for the sins of the people he was led to death”; “he bore our sins”; “his soul was handed over to death”; and “he was numbered with the transgressors” (Isa. 53), so that he might make us, the impious, weak, and sinful, pious, strong, and righteous.

Some interpret the passage in this way: If he died for us, the impious and sinful, how much more ought we, without hesitation, to die for Christ, who is righteous and good?

But we should not think that “righteous” and “good” are different, or that they specifically signify some particular person. Rather, they signify absolutely a righteous and good cause, for which it is difficult—though sometimes someone may be found—to pour out his blood.

## CHAPTER VIII

What does the Apostle mean when he writes to the Romans: “Taking occasion, sin through the commandment worked in me every kind of covetous desire” (Rom. 7:7)? Let us set out the whole passage and, discussing each point with Christ’s help, state simply what seems to us to be its meaning, without prejudging your understanding of what you wish to take it as meaning, but briefly explaining our own view.

What, then, shall we say? Is the Law sin? By no means. But I did not know sin except through the Law. For I would not have known covetous desire unless the Law had said, “You shall not covet.” But, taking occasion, sin through the commandment worked in me every kind of covetous desire. For without the Law sin was dead. I was once alive without the Law; but when the commandment came, sin revived. I died, and the commandment that was meant for life was found by me to be for death. For sin, taking occasion through the commandment, deceived me and through it killed me. Thus the Law indeed is holy, and the commandment holy, just, and good.

What, then, is good—did it become death to me? [Note: Greek: “to me, death,” although others, together with the Latin texts, add γέγονε, “became.”] By no means. But, so that sin might appear to be sin, through what was good it worked death in me, so that through the commandment sin might become sinful beyond measure. For we know that the Law is spiritual, but I am carnal, sold under sin. For I do not understand what I do [variant: “I do not comprehend it”]. For I do not do what I want, but I do what I hate.

[Note: Thus the better Latin manuscripts and the Greek textual exemplars read. The Vulgate edition, however, adds *good* here and, in the contrasting clause that follows, *evil*: “For I do not do the good that I want, but I do the evil that I hate.”]

But if I do what I do not want, I agree with the Law, that it is good. Now, however, it is no longer I who do it, but sin dwelling in me. For I know that good does not dwell in me—that is, in my flesh. For the willing is present to me, but I do not find the performance of the good.

[Note: Two manuscripts, without the verb “to find,” have only “not at all.” Likewise, quite a few Greek manuscripts have οὐ (“not”) rather than οὐχ εὑρίσκω (“I do not find”).]

For I do not do the good that I want, but the evil that I do not want—that I do. But if I do what I do not want, it is no longer I who do it, but sin dwelling in me. I discover, therefore, this law: when I wish to do good, evil is present with me. For I delight in the law of God according to the inner man. But I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin, which is in my members. Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God [Note: Most Latin manuscripts and the Fathers read “the grace of God”; but the Greek exemplars followed by Jerome have εὐχαριστῶ τῷ θεῷ or χάρις δὲ τῷ θεῷ, “I give thanks to God” or “but thanks be to God,” which Lucas Brugensis thinks may once have stood in the Vulgate itself.] through Jesus Christ our Lord.

Just as medicine is not the cause of death if it reveals deadly poisons, although evil people misuse them for death, either killing themselves or plotting against their enemies, so the Law was given to display the poisons of sins. It restrains by the bridle of the Law the person who wrongly abuses his freedom, who previously was carried along heedlessly and was slipping over precipices, and teaches him to walk with ordered steps, so that we may serve in newness of spirit and not in the oldness of the letter—that is, that we may live under a commandment, whereas previously we used to say like irrational animals: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die” (1 Cor. 15:32).

But if, when the Law enters—teaching what we ought to do and forbidding what we ought not to do—we are driven by our own vice and lack of self-control against the legal ordinances, the Law seems to be the cause of sin, since, by forbidding covetous desire, it is understood in a certain way to inflame it. There is a common saying among the Greeks: “Whatever is permitted is desired less.” Therefore, conversely, whatever is not permitted receives fuel for desire. For this reason Cicero denies that Solon wrote among the Athenians concerning the punishments of parricides, lest he should seem not so much to prohibit the crime as to call it to mind.

Thus the Law seems to be an occasion of offenses for those who despise it and trample upon its commands, since, by forbidding what it does not want to be done, it binds them with the bonds of commandments—although previously they sinned without the Law and were not held by legal charges. We have said this understanding the Law that was given through Moses.

But because in what follows “the law of God,” “the law of the flesh,” and “the law of the members” are written—the latter warring against the law of our mind and taking us captive under the law of sin—and because I recognize that four laws fighting against one another are written together in one place, I think it not beside the point to inquire how many kinds of law are mentioned in the Holy Scriptures.

[Note: This discussion of the various meanings of “Law” is taken almost word for word from Origen, volume IX, on the Epistle to the Romans: “That the word *law* does not signify one and the same thing, but has been fashioned to signify many things . . . . It is said in the Epistle to the Galatians: ‘For as many as are of the works of the law,’ etc., etc.” The same traces are followed exactly by Jerome. Then: “The history recorded by Moses is also signified by the word *law*, as may be taken from the same Epistle, from ‘Tell me,’ etc. I also know that the Psalms are called *law*, as is clear from ‘That it might be fulfilled,’ etc. But the prophecy of Isaiah is also called *law* by the Apostle, who says, ‘In the law it is written . . . .’ For I found expressions equivalent to this wording in the version of Aquila, where it reads, ‘Law is also called the more mystical and divine understanding of the Law,’ as in ‘For we know that the Law is spiritual.’ In addition to these, the law implanted in the soul according to common notions is called *law*,” and so forth. It will be worthwhile to compare the rest.]

The Law given through Moses is called “Law,” according to what is written to the Galatians: “As many as are of the works of the Law are under a curse. For it is written: ‘Cursed is everyone who does not remain in all the things written in the book of the Law, to do them’” (Gal. 3:10).

And again, in the same Epistle: “The Law was established because of transgressions, until the offspring should come to whom the promise was made, having been arranged through angels in the hand of a mediator” (Gal. 3:19). And again: “Thus the Law was our tutor in Christ, so that we might be justified by faith. But after faith came, we are no longer under a tutor. For you are all sons of God through faith, which is in Christ Jesus” (Gal. 3:24 and following).

The history, too, which contains no commandments but reports what happened, is called “Law” by the Apostle. “Tell me,” he says, “you who wish to be under the Law, have you not read the Law? For it is written that Abraham had two sons, one by a slave woman and the other by a free woman. But the one who was by the slave woman was born according to the flesh, while the one by the free woman was born through the promise” (ibid. 4:22–23).

The Psalms, too, are called “Law”: “That the word written in their Law might be fulfilled: ‘They hated me without cause’” (Ps. 68:5). The Apostle likewise calls the prophecy of Isaiah “Law” (1 Cor. 14:21): “It is written in the Law: ‘In other tongues and with other lips I shall speak to this people, and even so they will not listen to me, says the Lord’” (Isa. 28:11). I found this written in Isaiah according to the Hebrew and according to Aquila.

The mystical understanding of the Scriptures is also called “Law”: “We know that the Law is spiritual” (Rom. 7:14). And, beyond all these, the same Apostle teaches that the natural law is written in our hearts. “For when the Gentiles, who do not have the Law, by nature do the things of the Law, these, though they do not have the Law, are a law to themselves. They show the work of the Law written in their hearts, their conscience bearing witness” (ibid. 2:14–15).

This law written in the heart embraces all nations, and there is no human being who does not know it. Hence the whole world is under sin, and all human beings are transgressors of the law. Therefore God’s judgment is just when he writes in the heart of the human race: “What you do not want to be done to you, do not do to another.” For who does not know that murder, adultery, theft, and every kind of covetous desire are evil, from the fact that he does not want them done to himself? If he did not know that they were evil, he would certainly not be grieved when they were inflicted upon him.

Through this natural law Cain also recognized his sin, saying: “My guilt is greater than that I should be forgiven.” Adam and Eve likewise recognized their sin and therefore hid themselves under the tree of life. Pharaoh too, before the Law was given through Moses, stirred by the law of nature, confesses his crimes and says: “The Lord is righteous, but I and my people are impious” (Exod. 9:27).

[Note: This explanation too is taken from Origen. Through Rufinus as interpreter, his view is as follows: Paul’s words indicate a human being in infancy, who is ignorant of the Law for as long as, with the progress of age, he learns to distinguish between good and evil and hears from his conscience, “You shall not covet.” But most other Fathers interpret human nature as a whole as represented in Paul’s person—at first free, and afterward constrained by the Law. See Chrysostom, and especially Augustine, book 1, *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*.]

Childhood does not know this law; infancy is ignorant of it; and one who sins without a commandment is not held under the law of sin. He curses his father and mother and beats his parents; and because he has not yet received the law of wisdom, sin is dead in him. But when the commandment comes—that is, the time of understanding, when one desires good things and avoids evil—then sin begins to revive, and he begins to die and to become liable for sin.

Thus it happens that the time of understanding, through which we come to know God’s commandments so that we may attain life, works death in us if we act carelessly, and if the occasion for wisdom deceives and trips us up and leads us to death. This is not because understanding is sin—for the law of understanding is holy, just, and good—but through understanding of sins and virtues sin is born in me, whereas before I understood that it was sin, I did not know it to be sin.

Thus what was given to me as a good is changed by my fault into evil. And, to speak hyperbolically and to use a new word in explaining my meaning: sin, which before I possessed understanding was “without sin,” begins through transgression of the commandment to be for me, a sinner, “more sinful.”

First let us ask what this covetous desire is of which the Law says: “You shall not covet.” Some think that the commandment written in the Decalogue is meant: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s property” (Deut. 5:21). We, however, think that by “covetous desire” all the disturbances of the soul are signified, through which we grieve and rejoice, fear and desire.

And this the Apostle, the vessel of election, whose body was a temple of the Holy Spirit, also says—he who declared: “Do you seek proof of Christ speaking in me?” (2 Cor. 13:3); and elsewhere: “Christ redeemed us” (Gal. 3:13); and again: “I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me” (ibid. 2:20). He is not speaking about himself, but about the person who wishes to do penance after sins; and under his own person he describes the weakness of human condition, which suffers the continual conflicts of two human beings, the inner and the outer, fighting against each other.

The inner man agrees with both the written and the natural law, because it is good, holy, just, and spiritual. The outer man says: “I am carnal, sold under sin. For what I do I do not understand, and I do not do what I want, but what I hate” (Rom. 7:14).

But if the outer man does what he does not want and performs what he hates, he shows that the commandment is good and that he is not himself doing what is evil, but that sin dwelling in his flesh is doing it. This means the vices of the body and the desires of pleasure, which have been implanted in human bodies for the sake of descendants and offspring; and if they pass beyond their proper limits, they are turned into sin.

Let each person examine himself and, acting as his own accuser, consider the incitements of vice: how often, in speech, thought, and bodily heat, he speaks, thinks, and suffers what he does not want. I do not say “does,” lest I seem to accuse holy men, of whom it is written: “That man was true and blameless, righteous, a worshiper of God, withdrawing from every evil work” (Job 1:1). And of Zechariah and Elizabeth: “They were both righteous before God, walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord without blame” (Luke 1:6). The Apostles too are commanded: “Be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect” (Matt. 5:48). He would never have commanded this of the Apostles unless he knew that a human being could be perfect.

[Note: You see that the preceding statements are proposed tentatively, not established as certainties; for immediately afterward, as though reconsidering them, he explains how that view concerning human perfection is to be understood. When the Pelagians attempted to draw such passages and examples into their heresy, he defended them and freed them from their slanders in three complete books, *Letter to Ctesiphon*, no. XIII: “But since many righteous people are called righteous in the Holy Scriptures, such as Zechariah and Elizabeth . . . and many others whose names are woven into the fabric of Holy Scripture . . . it is enough briefly to touch upon this: they are called righteous not because they are free from every fault, but because they are commended for the greater part of their virtues.”]

Unless perhaps we should say that “withdrawing from every evil” signifies amendment: a passage from the errors of childhood and the vices of a wanton age to correction and virtue; and that the righteousness praised in Zechariah and Elizabeth is outward, whereas the covetous desire now said to dwell in our members operates inwardly. The command is also given to Apostles, not to children but to those already of mature age, that they should take on perfection—which we too confess to exist in a perfected age.

In saying these things we do not flatter vices; rather, we follow the authority of the Scriptures, which says that no human being is without sin, but that God has enclosed all under sin so that he might have mercy upon all (Gal. 3:22)—apart from the one who committed no sin, and in whose mouth no deceit was found (Isa. 53).

Hence it is also said through Solomon that the serpent’s tracks are not found upon the rock (Prov. 30). And the Lord himself says of himself: “Behold, the ruler of this world is coming, and he found nothing in me” (John 14:30)—that is, nothing of his work or trace.

For this reason we are commanded not to reproach a person returning from his sins and not to abhor the Egyptian, because we too were once in Egypt, and from mud and bricks we built cities for Pharaoh (Deut. 23); and because we were led captive into Babylon under the law of sin that dwelt in our members.

When the situation seemed to have reached utter despair—indeed, an open confession that every human being is entangled in the devil’s snares—the Apostle, or rather the human being under whose person the Apostle speaks, turns back to himself and gives thanks to the Savior, because he has been redeemed by his blood, laid aside his filth in baptism, put on the new garment of Christ, and, with the old man dead, has been born as a new man who says: “Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7:24). “I give thanks to God through Jesus Christ our Lord, who freed me from the body of death.”

If anyone does not think that the Apostle is saying this about others under his own person, let him explain how Daniel, whom we know to have been righteous, speaks as though about himself when he prays on behalf of others:

“We have sinned, we have acted wickedly, we have behaved unjustly, we have acted impiously, and we have departed and turned aside from your commandments and judgments. We have not listened to your servants the prophets, who spoke in your name to our kings, rulers, fathers, and to all the people of the land. To you, Lord, belongs righteousness, but to us confusion” (Dan. 3:29 and following).

[Note: In his Commentary on this passage he says: “Certainly the three youths had not sinned, nor were they of such an age when they were led into Babylon that they were being punished for their own vices. Therefore, just as these speak in the person of the people, so that statement of the Apostle must be read: ‘For I do not do what I want, but I perform what I do not want.’”]

Likewise, what is said in Psalm 31: “I made my sin known to you, and I did not hide my iniquity. I said: ‘I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord’; and you forgave the impiety of my sin. For this every holy person shall pray to you at an opportune time” (Ps. 31:5 and following)—this does not suit David and a righteous man, or, to speak simply, the Prophet whose words are being reported, but suits a sinner.

When the righteous man had poured out such words under the person of the penitent, he deserved to hear from God: “I will give you understanding and teach you in the way in which you shall walk; I will establish my eyes upon you” (ibid. 8).

In Psalm 37, whose title is “For a memorial,” teaching us that we must always remember our sins and do penance, we likewise read:

“There is no peace in my bones because of my sins. For my iniquities have risen above my head; like a heavy burden they have weighed heavily upon me. My wounds have become corrupt and have festered because of my foolishness. I am afflicted and bowed down to the end” (Ps. 37:4 and following).

This entire passage of the Apostle, both in what precedes and in what follows—in fact, his whole Epistle to the Romans—is wrapped in extreme obscurity. If I wished to discuss everything, one book would certainly not be enough for me; rather, great and numerous volumes would have to be written.

## CHAPTER IX

Why does the Apostle Paul write in the same Epistle to the Romans: “I myself was wishing to be anathema from Christ for the sake of my brothers and my kinsmen according to the flesh, who are Israelites, to whom belong adoption and glory and covenants and legislation and worship and promises; to whom belong the fathers, and from whom Christ is according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed forever. Amen” (Rom. 9:3 and following)?

The question is truly substantial: how can the Apostle, who had said above, “Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword?” (ibid. 8:35), and again, “I am confident that neither death nor life, nor angels nor principalities, nor things present nor things to come, nor powers, nor heights nor depths, nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God that we have in Christ Jesus our Lord” (ibid. 38–39), now confirm under oath and say:

“I speak the truth in Christ; I do not lie; my conscience bears witness with me in the Holy Spirit: I have great sorrow and continual pain in my heart. For I was wishing to be anathema from Christ for the sake of my brothers and my kinsmen according to the flesh,” and so forth.

For if his love for God is so great that neither fear of death, nor hope of life, nor persecution, nor famine, nor nakedness, nor danger, nor the sword can separate him from his love; and if angels and powers, things present or future, all the forces of heaven, heights and depths alike, and every creature together should rush upon him—which cannot happen—yet he would not be separated from the love of God that he has in Christ Jesus, what is this tremendous change, or rather this unheard-of wisdom, by which, for the love of Christ, he does not wish to have Christ?

And lest we perhaps fail to believe him, he swears and confirms it in Christ, and calls the Holy Spirit as witness to his conscience that he has sorrow—not slight or accidental, but great and incredible—and that he has pain in his heart, not pain that pricks and passes in an hour, but pain that remains continually in his heart.

What is the purpose of this sorrow? What does this unceasing pain accomplish? He wishes to be anathema from Christ and to perish so that others may be saved.

But if we consider the words of Moses, who pleaded with God for the Jewish people and said, “If you forgive them their sin, forgive it; but if you will not, erase me from the book you have written” (Exod. 32:31–32), we shall perceive the same disposition in Moses and Paul toward the flock entrusted to them. “The good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep. But the hired man, when he sees the wolf coming, flees, because the sheep are not his” (John 10:11–12).

And this is precisely what it means to say: “I wished to be anathema from Christ,” and “Erase me from the book you have written.” For those who are erased from the book of the living and are not written with the righteous become accursed by the Lord.

At the same time, observe how great the Apostle’s love for Christ is: he desires to die for him and to perish alone, provided that the entire human race should believe in him. To perish, however, means not forever but for the present. For “whoever loses his life for Christ will save it” (Matt. 10:39).

Therefore he also takes an example from Psalm 43: “For your sake we are put to death all day long; we have been counted as sheep for slaughter” (Ps. 43:22). The Apostle therefore wishes to perish in the flesh so that others may be saved in the spirit; to pour out his blood so that the souls of many may be preserved.

That “anathema” can sometimes signify slaughter may be proved by many testimonies of the Old Testament. And lest we think that his sorrow is slight and the cause of his pain insignificant, he adds and says: “For the sake of my brothers and my kinsmen according to the flesh.”

When he calls them kinsmen and brothers according to the flesh, he shows that in the spirit they are alien to him. “To whom,” he says, “belongs adoption”—which in Greek is more significantly called ὑιοθεσία (*huiothesia*, adoption as sons). Of them the Lord once spoke: “Israel is my firstborn son,” and “I have begotten and exalted sons” (Isa. 1:2); but now he says: “Foreign sons have lied to me” (Ps. 17:46).

And “to whom belongs glory,” because they were chosen from all the nations as God’s special people. “And to whom belong covenants” [Note: In addition to the Greek exemplars, Augustine and Ambrose also read the plural. But Jerome’s interpretation of the old and new “Instrument” or covenant, although it has many ancient authorities as guarantors, seems to some not to accord with the Apostle’s meaning, since he is enumerating the privileges of the old people, or Synagogue, not of the Church.]: one in the letter, the other in the spirit; so that those who had formerly served in the flesh through the ceremonies of the abolished Law might afterward serve in the spirit through the commandments of the eternal Gospel.

“And legislation” corresponds to both the new and the Old Instrument. “And worship,” that is, true religion. “And promises,” so that whatever was promised to the fathers might be fulfilled in their children. And—what is greater than all—from them Christ was born of the Virgin Mary.

And so that we might know who this Christ is, he gathers the causes of his sorrow into one expression: “who is God over all, blessed forever. Amen.” And this one so great and so exalted is not received by those from whose stock he was born.

Nevertheless, he praises the truth of the judgment, lest God’s sentence against his kinsmen and brothers seem displeasing, either harsh or excessive. In those who possessed such great blessings, he grieves that there are now such great evils.

## CHAPTER X

What the same Apostle intends when he writes to the Colossians: “Let no one deprive you of your prize, wishing to do so through humility of mind and the worship of angels, walking in things which he has not seen, vainly puffed up by the perception of his flesh, and not holding fast to the head, from whom the whole body, supplied and joined together through its ligaments and connections, grows with the increase of God” (Colossians 2:18–19), and what follows.
