We now approve once again the interpretation we have often stated: “And although unskilled in speech, yet not in knowledge” (2 Corinthians 11:6)—namely, that Paul was speaking not about humility, [Note: [Col. 1029] See the preceding Letter to Hedibia, Question XI, note b.] but about the truth of his conscience. For the tongue does not express profound and hidden thoughts. And when a person himself understands what he is saying, he cannot transfer it in pure language to the ears of others. Although Paul was most eloquent in his native language—for he was “a Hebrew of Hebrews” and educated at the feet of Gamaliel, a man most learned in the Law—when he wishes to interpret himself, he becomes entangled. If this happened to him in the Greek language, which he had absorbed from childhood while being raised at Tarsus in Cilicia, what must be said of the Latins, who, trying to express word for word, make his sentences more obscure and, like weeds that grow up, choke the fertility of the crops?

We shall therefore attempt to unfold his meaning παραφραστικῶς, that is, by paraphrase, and restore the tangles of his involved expression to their proper order and structure, so that the threads of his words may run on a simple warp and the texture of the Apostle’s speech may grow upon a pure weft.

“Let no one deprive you of your prize”: that is, let no one obtain the prize against you. For this is what the Greek καταβραβευέτω means: when someone engaged in a contest loses the βραβεῖον, the prize and palm due to him, through the injustice of the contest-official or through the tricks of the judges.

There are many expressions which the Apostle uses more familiarly according to the custom of his city and province. A few of them may be given by way of example. “But it is of little concern to me to be judged by a human day” (1 Corinthians 1), that is, ἀπὸ ἀνθρωπίνης ἡμέρας, “by a human day.” And, “I speak humanly” (Romans 6), that is, ἀνθρώπινον λέγω, “I speak in human terms.” And, οὐ κατενάρκησα ὑμᾶς, that is, “I did not burden you” (2 Corinthians 12). And what is said here, μηδεὶς ὑμᾶς καταβραβευέτω, means, “Let no one obtain the prize against you.” The Cilicians continue to use these and many other expressions to this day.

Nor should we be surprised if the Apostle uses the customary language of the tongue in which he was born and raised, since Virgil—our second Homer—following the custom of his native land, calls cold “criminal” or “guilty” cold (Georgics 2).

Therefore, let no one deprive you of your prize and defeat you, wishing to follow the humility of the letter and the worship and veneration of angels [Note: [Col. 1030] Compare the Commentary on Matthew, chapter 5; and, on Jewish worship of angels, Porphyry, On Abstinence, book 4; Origen, Against Celsus, book 5; and Tertullian, On Prescription, chapter 43, on Simon and Cerinthus. Most explicitly, Clement of Alexandria, Stromata, book 6, says of the Jews: “Thinking that they alone know God, they do not understand that they worship angels and archangels,” etc.], so that you may not serve spiritual understanding but the patterns of future things—which the one who desires to deprive you of your prize has not himself seen, or sees [Note: [Col. 1030] The editor of Reate explains this from the fact that the Greek word ἐώρακεν expresses both tenses, although it is a perfect tense. Consider whether we may have grasped its force and perhaps Jerome’s meaning more closely; for we have never known ἐώρακεν to signify anything other than past time, and certainly not to be used for the present. We think that two readings of the Pauline passage are indicated, arising nevertheless from the same letters: one, the reading preferred by the manuscripts of today, ἐώρακεν ἐμβατεύων, “he has seen, walking”; the other, ἐώρα κενεμβατεύων, with only a different division of the syllables: “he sees, walking vainly.” The former plainly means “he has seen,” no one denying it; the latter means “he sees,” from the imperfect tense, which can also have the force of the present. For κὲν, meaning “vainly,” from κενὸν, joined with ἐμβατεύων according to the character of the Greek language, is equivalent to “walking puffed up,” that is, “walking in empty glory.” Thus it may most truthfully be affirmed that both tenses are found in the Greek. We do not conceal that Augustine, Letter 149 to Paulinus, section 28, reports that in certain manuscripts the negative particle is omitted and the text reads “the things which he saw.” We also know that some Latin and Greek manuscripts of this kind exist, nor do we deny that Jerome may have alluded to the same reading, so that where he has “sees,” “has seen” should be read. But since he calls the Greek expression a single one and does not seem to note so great a variation as that between denial and affirmation—and since, finally, the text should not be rashly tampered with—we conjecture that ἐώρα, or rather ὀρᾶ, with the augment easily introduced by copyists removed, and κενεμβατεύων are intended. Certainly Erasmus is least of all to be followed, since, failing to understand the holy Doctor’s meaning, he read a text of his own invention, “or heard.”]

—or, since both are found in the Greek, sees—especially since he walks swelling with pride and advances puffed up, displaying the arrogance of his mind in the gesture of his body. For this is what ἐμβατεύων means.

But he is vainly inflated and swollen with the perception of his flesh, understanding everything carnally, investigating the ravings of Jewish traditions, and not holding fast to the head of all the Scriptures, of whom it is written: “The head of the man is Christ” (1 Corinthians 2:3; Ephesians 1, 4, and 5; Colossians 1).

He is the head and beginning of the whole body, and of those who believe, and of all spiritual understanding. From this head the body of the Church receives, through its joints and connections, the life-giving sap of heavenly teaching, so that all its members are gradually invigorated; and through the hidden passages of the veins the purified blood of nourishment is poured out, supplied and increased—or rather, the body’s balance is maintained—so that, watered from the fountain of the head, the limbs may grow toward the perfection of God, and the Savior’s prayer may be fulfilled: “Father, I will that, as I and you are one, so these also may be one in us” (John 17:21); so that, after Christ has handed us over to the Father, “God may be all in all” (1 Corinthians 15:28).

He writes something similar, though in exceedingly obscure fashion, both in words and in meaning and in manner of expression, to the Ephesians: “But speaking the truth in love, let us grow in all things into him who is the head, Christ, from whom the whole body, compacted and joined together through every supporting joint, according to the working in the measure [or: according to the measure] of each individual member, makes the body grow for its own building up in love” (Ephesians 4:25, 16). We have spoken about this more fully in our Commentary on the same Epistle.

He is speaking throughout against those who, having believed in the Lord and Savior as Jews, wished to observe Jewish ceremonies. On this matter a considerable dispute was also stirred up in the Acts of the Apostles (chapter 15). Hence Paul says above concerning those who boast that they are teachers of the Law: “Let no one judge you in food or drink” (Colossians 2:16), as though some things were clean and others unclean; or concerning a portion of a feast day, as though they considered some days festive and others not festive. [Note: [Col. 1031] Origen proves this at length in the eighth book Against Celsus: “The perfect person … is always in his days, and always celebrates the Lord’s days,” and shortly afterward, “his whole life is in a complete and uninterrupted festival,” together with other statements of this kind.]

For us who believe that Christ rose again, there is perpetual and eternal festivity. Or concerning a portion of the new moon, that is, of the Kalends and the new month, when the waning moon comes to an end and is covered by the shadows of night. For the light of Christians is eternal, and they are always illumined by the rays of the Sun of righteousness. Or concerning a portion of the sabbaths, so that they do not perform servile work and do not carry burdens, because we have been granted freedom through Christ and have ceased to carry the burdens of sins.

“All these things,” he says, “are a shadow of things to come,” and images of future happiness. Thus, while the Jews remain entangled in them according to the letter and are held fast upon the earth, we, according to the spirit, pass over to Christ, who, in contrast with shadows, is now called the body.

For just as truth is in the body and falsehood in the body’s shadow, so, in spiritual understanding, the whole world’s food and drink, the entire festivity, perpetual Kalends, and eternal rest are to be awaited. [Note: [Col. 1031] Tertullian, Against Marcion, book 5, chapter 19. He censures certain people who said, on the basis of visions of angels, that one must abstain from foods.]

We ask what he intended by “humility and worship of angels,” or what meaning it bears. Ever since the Lord said to the disciples, “Rise, let us go from here” (John 14:31), and, “Your house shall be left to you desolate” (Matthew 23:38), and since the place where the Lord was crucified is spiritually called Egypt and Sodom (Revelation 11:8), the entire practice of Jewish observances has been destroyed. Whatever victims they offer, they offer not to God but to rebellious angels and unclean spirits.

Nor is it surprising that they do this after the Lord’s Passion, since through the prophet Amos it is also said to them: “Did you offer me sacrifices and offerings for forty years in the wilderness, house of Israel? And you took up the tabernacle of Moloch and the star of your god Rempham, the images that you made in order to worship them” (Amos 5:25–26).

The martyr Stephen, explaining this more fully in his Jewish assembly and reviewing the ancient history, spoke as follows: “And they made a calf in those days, and offered sacrifice to an idol, and rejoiced in the works of their hands. But God turned and delivered them over to worship the host of heaven, as it is written in the book of the Prophets” (Acts 7:41–42).

The host of heaven [Note: [Col. 1032] Hebrew teachers held that the heavenly spheres were endowed with soul and intelligence, as David Kimhi explains Psalm 19 from Rabbi Moses. The Jewish worshipers of heaven are also well known, concerning whom see the Theodosian Code. Recall the preceding note.] is not merely the sun, moon, and shining stars, but also the whole multitude of angels and their army, which in Hebrew is called SABAOTH, that is, “of powers,” or “of armies.” Hence we read in the Gospel according to Luke: “And suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly army, praising God and saying: Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace among people of good will” (Luke 2:13–14).

For God makes his angels spirits and his ministers a burning fire (Psalm 103).

And so that we may know that those who worshiped idols, even when they appeared to offer sacrifices in the Temple, did not offer them to God but to angels, we learn more fully through Ezekiel: “I gave them statutes that were not good and ordinances that were not good” (Ezekiel 20:25).

For God does not seek the blood of goats or bulls; rather, a sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit, and God does not despise a broken and humbled heart (Psalm 50).

Therefore, those who had made the calf at Horeb and worshiped the star of their god Rempham, about which we have discussed more fully in our commentary on the prophet Amos, worshiped the images that they themselves had made. And God delivered them over to serve the host of heaven, which the Apostle now calls “the worship of angels.”

For “humility” the Greek reads ταπεινοφροσύνη, that is, humility of mind or understanding. Truly humble understanding—and pitiable superstition—is to believe that God takes pleasure in the blood of goats and bulls and in the odor of incense, from which human beings often turn away.

What follows—“If you have died with Christ to the elements of the world, why, as though living in the world, do you submit to regulations: Do not touch, do not taste, do not handle”—all of which perish through use, according to the commandments and doctrines of human beings, which have indeed an appearance of wisdom in superstition, humility, and the refusal to spare the body [Note: [Col. 1032] Alternatively, “and not sparing,” according to the Vulgate.]; but have no honor in satisfying the flesh (Colossians 2:20 and following)—seems to us to have this meaning.

Let us run through each point, and, with Christ unlocking the meaning, disclose the obscurity of the thoughts and words.

If you have been baptized in Christ and buried with Christ in baptism, and have died to the elements of this world—for the text says “to the elements”—why do you not say with me: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Galatians 6:14)?

Have you not also heard the Lord saying to the Father: “They are not of the world, just as I am not of the world; and the world hates them because they are not of the world, just as I am not of the world” (John 17:16; 15:19)?

Yet, on the contrary, as though living in the world, you impose regulations: “Do not touch” the body of a dead person, or a garment, or the stool on which a menstruating woman has sat; “do not taste” the flesh of pigs, hares, cuttlefish, squid, moray eels, eels, or any fish that does not have scales and fins—all things which through use pass into corruption and destruction and are digested into excrement.

“For food is for the stomach, and the stomach for foods,” and, “Whatever enters through the mouth does not defile a person, but the things that come out of us” (Matthew 15:11; Mark 7:15).

“According to the commandments,” he says, “and doctrines of human beings,” in accordance with what Isaiah says: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isaiah 29:13). “In vain they worship me, teaching doctrines and commandments of human beings” (Matthew 15:8–9).

Hence the Lord also rebukes the Pharisees, saying: “You have made the commandment of God void in order to establish your traditions. For God said: Honor your father and mother, and whoever curses father or mother, let him die the death. But you say, Whoever says to his father or mother, ‘Whatever gift is from me will benefit you,’ and does not honor his father or mother,” and so forth. Then he adds: “And you have made the commandment of God void because of your traditions” (ibid., verses 4–6).

I cannot unfold how numerous the traditions of the Pharisees are—traditions which they now call δευτερώσεις. [Note: [Col. 1033] The older printed editions had erroneously read δευτερονόμους. The Hebrew term is מִשְׁנָיוֹת, Mishnayot, the title of the book in which the Pharisees had already collected their empty traditions; its Greek equivalent is δευτερώσεις, as it is also called in Justinian’s Novella 146.] Nor can I recount how childish their tales are. For the size of the book does not permit it, and many of them are so shameful that I blush to mention them.

Nevertheless, I shall mention one, to the disgrace of the hostile nation. They appoint the wisest men over the synagogues and assign them to a filthy task: if they cannot distinguish by sight whether the blood of a virgin or of a menstruating woman is clean or unclean, they test it by taste [or: taste a sample of it].

Furthermore, because it was commanded that on sabbath days each person should sit in his own house and not go out (Exodus 16:29), nor walk from the place where he lives, whenever we try to press them according to the letter—so that they may neither lie down, walk, nor stand, but only sit, if they wish to observe the commandments—they customarily answer and say: [Note: [Col. 1033–1034] Victorius, after Erasmus, reads “Rab Achiba, Simeon, and Hillel”; Martianay particularly insists that the first name is erroneous. But he fails to observe that ancient writers use both Bar Achiban and Rabakiban interchangeably. Indeed, Agobard, quoting this very passage of Jerome in Against Felix, chapter 10, reads “Rab Achibam,” although Masson printed “Rarachiam.” Saint Epiphanius calls him βαρακιβὰν and ῥαββιακιβὰν, and even simply ἀκιβὰν; see Heresies 15, 12, and 33, where statements about him may profitably be compared with these. Nor did Jerome do otherwise: in his Commentary on Isaiah, book 3, chapter 8, he simply calls him Akibas: “Samai and Hillel, from whom arose the scribes and Pharisees, whose school Akibas inherited; they say that he was the teacher of Aquila the proselyte.” At that passage we have collected further material on the other two teachers, Simeon and Hillel. Meanwhile Martianay himself errs more seriously by substituting Helles for the reading which we corrected from manuscripts and ancient testimonies to be cited elsewhere.]

“Barachibas, Simeon, and Hellel, our teachers, handed down to us that we may walk two thousand [Note: [Col. 1034] Understand “two thousand paces.” According to the opinion of the Hebrews—which Origen also cites in book 4, On First Principles—two thousand cubits, δισχιλίους πήχεις, or, as Rufinus translates it, “two thousand forearms,” comprise the sabbath journey. Hence, for most people the shorter pace and the cubit are treated as equivalent; Jerome, however, interprets the cubits themselves as feet. It is also worth adding that the definition of this measure is derived from Joshua 3:4, where an interval of two thousand cubits is prescribed between the Ark and the people. From this, some of the rabbis explain the tradition concerning the sabbath journey, namely, that on that day one was permitted to approach the Ark only that distance.] feet on the sabbath,” and other things of this kind, preferring human doctrines to the doctrine of God.

We do not mean that one must always sit on the sabbath and never depart at all from the place in which one happens to be occupied [Note: [Col. 1034] The word penitus, “at all,” was missing; we supplied it from manuscripts and an older edition.]. Rather, what is impossible for the Law, in which it is weakened through the flesh, must be fulfilled through spiritual observance.

The text continues: “Which indeed have an appearance of wisdom.” Here “indeed” is a superfluous conjunction, as we find the Apostle doing in many places through ignorance of grammatical technique. For there is no “but,” or another conjunction, following, as ordinarily responds to the particle “indeed” wherever it is placed.

Jewish observances therefore appear to the uneducated and the common people to possess an appearance of rationality and human wisdom. Hence their teachers are called σοφοὶ, that is, “wise.” And whenever they expound their traditions on appointed days, they customarily say to their disciples, οἱ σοφοὶ δευτερῶσιν, that is, “the wise teach the traditions.” [Note: [Col. 1034] This is the familiar formula which in Hebrew they call “the wise hand down”; hence the Greek δευτεροῦσιν or δευτερῶσιν. Erasmus read δευτερώσεις very badly.]

In place of “superstition,” the Greek has ἐθελοθρησκεία, that is, false worship. And in place of “humility” it has ταπεινοφροσύνη, which generally signifies a virtue rather than a vice. Here ταπεινοφρονεῖν must be understood as meaning that they think lowly and earthly thoughts.

Ἀφειδία δὲ σώματος, whose name Latin speech does not express, is rendered among us “the refusal to spare the body.” The Jews do not spare their bodies in the taking of food, sometimes rejecting what they possess and seeking what they do not possess. From this necessity they sometimes contract weakness and disease. Nor do they honor themselves, since “all things are clean to the clean” (Titus 1:15), and nothing can be polluted that is received with thanksgiving and was created by the Lord for the purpose of invigorating and sustaining human limbs through the nourishment and filling of the flesh.

But by “the elements of the world,” to which we are dead—or rather, to which we have died [Note: [Col. 1035] The older printed editions incorrectly read “from which we have been buried,” but the correct reading is “to which we have died.”]—the Law of Moses and the whole Old Testament are to be understood. By these elements, as by the beginnings of religion, we learn about God.

For just as letters are called elements, because by them we join syllables and words and proceed, after prolonged reflection, to weave speech; and just as the art of music has its elements, and geometry begins from the elements of lines, and dialectic and medicine have their εἰσαγωγαί, their introductions; so, through the elements of the Old Testament, the infancy of the holy man is educated in order to arrive at the fullness of the Gospel.

Hence Psalm 118, and all the other psalms marked by letters, lead us through ethics to theoretical contemplation, and from the elements of the written letter, which is passing away, they cause us to cross over to the life-giving spirit. [Note: [Col. 1035] Jerome taught elsewhere, especially in his Letter to Paula on the Hebrew Alphabet, that we are led through ethics to θεωρία, or from the moral discipline to the contemplative, which is concerned solely with contemplation. There he states, against the common error and on the testimony of Origen, that among the ancients there were “three general disciplines by which one reaches knowledge of things, which the Greeks called Ethics, Physics, and Theoretical contemplation. We may call them Moral, Natural, and Contemplative; through the latter we rise above visible things and contemplate something divine and heavenly, perceiving it with the mind alone.” Meanwhile, in this passage all the printed books had read “theology” instead of “theoretical contemplation.” We did not hesitate to correct this error even without the support of manuscripts, on the basis of Jerome’s meaning, which he explains more fully in the Letter to Paula just mentioned and elsewhere. If desired, compare also the Commentary on Ecclesiastes, chapter 1.]

Therefore, since we have died to the world and to its elements, we ought not to observe the things that belong to the world, because in one there is a beginning, while in the other there is perfection.

## CHAPTER XI

What is meant by the statement that the same Apostle writes to the Thessalonians: “Unless the apostasy comes first and the man of sin is revealed” (2 Thessalonians 2:3), and what follows.

In his First Epistle to the Thessalonians he had written: “But concerning the times and moments, brothers, you have no need that we write to you. For you yourselves know accurately that the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night. When they say, ‘Peace and security,’ then sudden destruction will come upon them, like labor-pain upon a woman with child, and they will not escape” (1 Thessalonians 5:1 and following).

Earlier he had written to them: “This we say to you by the word of the Lord: we who are alive, who remain until the coming of the Lord, shall not precede those who have fallen asleep. For the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God; and the dead who are in Christ will rise first. Then we who are alive, who are left, will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet Christ in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord. Therefore comfort one another with these words” (ibid. 4:14 and following).

When the Macedonians heard this, they did not understand whom the Apostle meant by “we,” who would be living together with him, nor who were called “those who remain,” who would be caught up with him in the clouds to meet the Lord. Instead, they imagined that, while they were still in the body and before they had tasted death, Christ would come in his majesty.

When the Apostle heard this, he begged and adjured them by the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ not to be quickly shaken, whether by spirit, by word, or by a letter supposedly written by him, as though the day of the Lord were imminent.

Both the volumes of the Prophets and the faith of the Gospels teach that there will be two comings of the Lord and Savior: that he first came in humility and afterward will come in glory. The Lord himself declares what will occur before the consummation of the world and how the Antichrist will come, when he says to the Apostles:

“When you see the abomination of desolation, spoken of by Daniel the prophet, standing in the holy place—let the reader understand—then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains, and let the one who is on the roof not come down to take anything from his house” (Matthew 24:15 and following, an. D 9). [Note: [Col. 1036] Victorius adds from Brixian manuscripts: “and let the one who is in the field not return to take his tunic.”]

And again: “Then if anyone says to you, ‘Behold, here is the Christ,’ or, ‘There,’ do not believe it. For false Christs and false prophets will arise and give great signs and wonders, so that, if possible, even the elect may be led astray. Behold, I have foretold it to you. Therefore, if they say to you, ‘Behold, he is in the wilderness,’ do not go out; ‘Behold, he is in the inner rooms,’ do not believe it. For as lightning comes out from the east and appears even to the west, so will be the coming of the Son of Man.”

And afterward: “Then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven, [Note: [Col. 1036] Again, from the same manuscripts and from the text of the Gospel, Victorius adds: “and then all the tribes of the earth will mourn,” which our manuscripts omit.] and they will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds of heaven with great power and majesty. And he will send his angels with a trumpet and a loud voice, and they will gather his elect from the four winds, from the highest heavens to their farthest boundaries” (ibid. 23 and following).

Again, speaking to the Jews about the Antichrist, he says: “I have come in my Father’s name, and you have not received me. If another comes in his own name, him you will receive” (John 7:43).

The minds of the Thessalonians had therefore been disturbed and thrown into confusion either by the occasion of an Epistle they had not understood, or by a fabricated revelation that had deceived them while asleep in a dream, or by the conjecture of certain people who interpreted the words of Isaiah, Daniel, and the Gospels that foretold the Antichrist as referring to that time. Thus they hoped that Christ would then come in his majesty.

The Apostle remedies this error and explains what they must expect before Christ’s coming, so that, when they see these things happen, they may know that the Antichrist—that is, the man of sin and son of perdition, who opposes and exalts himself above everything called God or worshiped—will come, so that he will sit in the Temple of God.

“Unless,” he says, “the apostasy comes first,” which in Greek is called ἀποστασία, so that all the nations subject to the Roman Empire may withdraw from it, “and the man of sin is revealed,” that is, shown forth—the one whom all the words of the Prophets foretell—the man of sin, in whom is the source of every sin; “and the son of perdition,” that is, of the devil. [Note: [Col. 1036] In the Commentary on Daniel, chapter 7: “We should not, according to the opinion of some, think that he is either the Devil or a demon, but one of human beings, in whom Satan will dwell bodily in his entirety.”]

He himself is the destruction of all, who opposes Christ and is therefore called Antichrist. He exalts himself above everything called God, so that he may trample under his foot the gods of all nations, or every tested and true religion. And he will sit in the Temple of God, or in Jerusalem, as some think, or in the Church, as we more correctly believe [Note: [Col. 1037] Theophylact aptly expresses Jerome’s view: “Not specifically in the temple at Jerusalem, but in churches generally, and in every divine temple.”], showing himself as though he himself were Christ and the Son of God.

“Unless,” he says, “the Roman Empire has first been desolated and the Antichrist has come beforehand, Christ will not come”—for he will come for the very purpose of destroying the Antichrist.

“Do you remember,” he says, “that when I was with you I used to tell you these very things in person, which I am now writing in my Epistle? I told you that Christ would not come unless the Antichrist came first. And now you know what restrains him, so that he may be revealed in his own time.” That is, you know very well what prevents the Antichrist from coming at present.

He does not wish to say openly that the Roman Empire must be destroyed, because those who rule it themselves consider it eternal. Hence, according to the Apocalypse of John, on the forehead of the purple-clad harlot is written the name of blasphemy, that is, “Eternal Rome.”

For if he had openly and boldly said, “The Antichrist will not come unless the Roman Empire is first destroyed,” there would have seemed to be a just cause for persecution to arise against the Church in the East. [Note: [Col. 1037] Chrysostom likewise writes: “But when he says this concerning the Roman authority, he has reasonably hinted at it and for the present speaks in veiled terms. For he did not wish to incur unnecessary enmities and useless dangers.” Augustine also writes, City of God, book 20, chapter 19, section 3: “Some think … that the Apostle Paul did not wish to write this openly, lest he should incur the accusation of having wished evil upon the Roman Empire, since it was hoped that it would be eternal.”]

The statement that follows—“For the mystery of iniquity is already at work; only let the one who now restrains hold fast, until he is removed from the midst, and then the lawless one will be revealed”—has this meaning:

The advent of the Antichrist is being brought to birth through the many evils and sins with which Nero, the most impure of emperors, oppresses the world. [Note: [Col. 1037] Compare the Commentary on Daniel, chapter 11, where Jerome says: “Many of our people think, because of the magnitude of his cruelty and depravity, that Domitius Nero will be the Antichrist.” See also Augustine, City of God, at the place cited above, Suetonius’ Nero, and Tacitus, Histories, book 2.] What he will later accomplish is already partly fulfilled in Nero, provided that the Roman Empire, which now holds all nations in its power, withdraws and is removed from the midst. Then the Antichrist will come, the source of iniquity, whom the Lord Jesus will kill with the breath of his mouth—that is, by divine power and the authority of his majesty, for with him to command is to accomplish.

He will not be destroyed through a multitude of armies, military strength, or angelic assistance. As soon as he arrives, the Antichrist will be killed. And just as darkness is driven away by the coming of the sun, so the Lord will destroy and abolish him by the radiance of his coming.

His works are the works of Satan. And just as the fullness of divinity dwelt bodily in Christ (Colossians 2:9), so in the Antichrist there will be all kinds of power, signs, and wonders—but all of them lies.

For just as the magicians opposed the signs of God that he performed through Moses with their own lies, and Moses’ staff swallowed their staffs (Exodus 7), so the truth of Christ will swallow the Antichrist’s falsehood. [Note: [Col. 1037] The Fathers commonly compare the false miracles of Antichrist with the magical deceptions opposed to Moses; Theodoret calls them “things that will be, but not true miracles,” etc. Augustine, Eighty-Three Questions, question 79, sections 3–4, should nevertheless be consulted.]

Those who are prepared for destruction will be deceived by his lie. And because a silent question might arise—why did God permit him to possess such power, signs, and wonders, by which, if possible, even God’s elect might be led astray?—the Apostle anticipates the question with its answer and resolves the objection before it is raised.

He will do all these things, he says, not by his own power but by God’s permission, on account of the Jews [Note: [Col. 1038] Some older printed editions read ait qui; but ut is to be understood in the sense of utpote, “inasmuch as.”], who refused to receive the love of truth—that is, the Spirit of God through Christ—for “the love of God has been poured into the hearts of believers” (Romans 5:5). And Christ himself says, “I am the truth” (John 14:6), concerning whom it is written in the Psalms: “Truth has sprung up from the earth” (Psalm 84:12).

Therefore, because they did not receive love and truth so that they might be saved by accepting the Savior, God will send them not an agent but the operation itself—that is, the source of error—so that they may believe the lie. For “he is a liar, and the father of it.”

If the Antichrist had been born of a virgin and had come into the world first, the Jews could have had an excuse and could have said that they had thought him to be the truth and had therefore accepted falsehood in place of truth. But now they will be judged, indeed unquestionably condemned, because, having rejected the truth of Christ, they will afterward accept falsehood—that is, the Antichrist.

## LETTER CXXII

[Note: [Col. 1038] Elsewhere numbered 46. Written around A.D. 408.]

### TO RUSTICUS

[Note: [Col. 1038] Erasmus thinks that Jerome deliberately omitted the name of the person to whom this letter was sent, so as not to mark his reputation, and that consequently it was addressed “to Rusticus” by someone else. We, however, do not doubt that the name consistently preferred by the manuscripts is the man’s genuine name.]

**On Repentance**

Rusticus, who had broken the continence he had promised together with his wife Artemia, is urged toward repentance and, following his wife’s example, to visit the holy places.

### 1.

That I, an unknown man, dare to write to an unknown man [Note: I truly do not see why this Letter should not seem to bear the style of Jerome rather than that of Rufinus.] was brought about by the entreaty of the holy handmaid of Christ Hedibia and of my daughter, your wife Artemia—rather, your sister through your wife and your fellow-servant. Not content in any way with her own salvation, she first sought yours in your homeland and now seeks it in the holy places, wishing to imitate the goodwill of the Apostles Andrew and Philip. Each of them, after being found by Christ, desired to find his brother Simon and his friend Nathanael, so that one of them might deserve to hear: “You are Simon, son of [Note: The older Vulgate manuscripts read “son of Johanna”; others, with the Vulgate edition, “son of Jona.”] John; you shall be called Cephas,” which is translated “Peter.” The other, “God’s gift”—for this is what Nathanael means in our language—was exalted by the testimony of Christ speaking to him: “Behold, truly an Israelite, in whom there is no deceit” (John 1).

Long ago Lot also wished to save his wife together with his daughters and, escaping almost half-burned from the conflagration of Sodom and Gomorrah, to lead out the woman who was held fast by her former vices. But she, trembling in despair and looking back behind her, was condemned with an everlasting mark of unbelief. Yet ardent faith, for the sake of one woman who was lost, freed the whole city of Segor. Finally, after abandoning the valleys and darkness of Sodom and climbing into the mountains, the sun rose upon him in Segor, which means “little,” so that Lot’s small faith, since he could not attain greater things, might at least preserve lesser ones. For the former inhabitant of Gomorrah and of error could not immediately reach the south, where Abraham, the friend of the Lord, received God with the angels.

Joseph also feeds his brothers in Egypt, and the bridegroom hears from the bride: “Where do you lie? Where do you feed at midday?” (Song of Songs 1:6). Samuel once wept for Saul (1 Samuel 15), because he did not heal the wounds of pride with the medicine of repentance. And Paul mourned for the Corinthians, who were unwilling to wipe away the stains of fornication with tears (1 Corinthians 5:2; 2 Corinthians 2:1). Hence Ezekiel also devours a scroll written within and without, with “song, lamentation, and woe” (Ezekiel 2:9; 3:1): song concerning the praise of the righteous; lamentation concerning penitents; woe concerning those of whom it is written: “When the wicked has come into the depths of evils, he despises” (Proverbs 18:3).

Isaiah points them out when he says: “The Lord of hosts called on that day for weeping and lamentation, for baldness and the girding-on of sackcloth; but they made rejoicing and gladness, slaughtering calves and killing sheep so that they might eat flesh” [Note: Gravius adds “and drink wine,” completing the sacred context.] and saying: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die” (Isaiah 22:12–13).

Ezekiel also speaks of them: “And you, son of man, say to the house of Israel: Thus you have spoken, saying, ‘Our errors and our iniquities are upon us, and in them we waste away; how then can we be saved?’ Say to them: ‘As I live, says the Lord, I do not desire the death of the wicked, but that he turn from his way.’” And again: “Return, you who are turning away, from your ways; why will you die, O house of Israel?” (Ezekiel 33:11).

Nothing so offends God as clinging to worse things out of despair of better ones [or: former things], although despair itself is also an indication of unbelief. For whoever despairs of salvation does not think that judgment will come. If he feared it, he would surely prepare himself for the Judge by good works.

Let us hear God speaking through Jeremiah: “Turn your foot away from the rough way, and your throat from thirst” (Jeremiah 2:25). And again: “Does he who falls not rise again? Or will he who has turned away not return?” And through Isaiah: “When you have turned and groaned, then you will be saved, and you will know where you have been” (Isaiah 30:15). [Note: You will seek this passage in vain in the Vulgate translator, who reads it differently: “If you return and keep quiet, you will be saved.” It is from the old Latin version of Isaiah 30:15 according to the Septuagint, and is presented in this form by Saint Cyprian in *On the Lapsed* and in Letter 28 of the final edition, and likewise by Saint Gaudentius of Brescia near the end of Sermon 1, and again by Jerome himself in his Letter to Sabinianus, around the middle.]

We cannot know the evils of illness until health has followed. And the amount of good virtue possesses is shown by vices; light becomes clearer by comparison with darkness.

Ezekiel likewise, in the same words because by the same Spirit, says: “Turn and return from your iniquities, O house of Israel, and your impieties will not be a torment to you. Cast away from yourselves all your impieties by which you have acted impiously against me, and make yourselves a new heart and a new spirit. And why will you die, O house of Israel? For I do not desire the death of the sinner, says the Lord” (Ezekiel 18:30–31; 33:11; 18:32).

Hence in what follows he says: “As I live, says the Lord, I do not desire the death of the sinner, except that he return from his way and live” [or: “nor that he should die”], lest an unbelieving mind despair of the promise of good things, and a spirit once given over to destruction fail to apply a remedy to its wound because it thinks that wound cannot be healed.

For this reason he says that he swears, so that, if we do not believe God when he makes a promise, we may at least believe him when he swears for the sake of our salvation.

For this reason the righteous man prays and says: “Restore us, O God our Savior, and turn away your anger from us” (Psalm 84:4). And again: “Lord, in your favor you gave strength to my beauty. You turned your face away from me, and I became troubled” (Psalm 29:8). For after I changed the ugliness of my sins into the beauty of virtues, you strengthened my weakness by your grace.

Behold, I hear him promising: “I will pursue my enemies and overtake them, and I will not turn back [or: return] until they fail” (Psalm 17:38)—so that I, who once fled from you and was your enemy, may be overtaken by your hand. Do not cease pursuing me until I cease from my worst way and return to my former husband, who will give me my linens, oil, and fine flour and feed me with the richest foods.

He therefore hedged in and blocked my worst ways so that I might find that way which says in the Gospel: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John 14:6).

Hear the Prophet speaking: “Those who sow in tears shall reap in joy. Going forth, they went and wept, carrying their seeds; but coming, they shall come with exultation, carrying their sheaves” (Psalm 125:6–7). And speak with him: “Every night I will wash my bed; I will water my couch with my tears” (Psalm 6:7).

And again: “As the deer longs for springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God. My soul thirsted for you, the living fountain, when shall I come and appear before the face of God? My tears have become my bread by day and by night” (Psalm 41:1ff.). [Note: This is how the printed editions and manuscripts read, whereas the Vulgate translator has *fortem* (“strong”) from the Greek τὸν ἰσχυρόν, which is found in the Complutensian manuscript. All the others, following the Hebrew, have πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν τὸν ζῶντα, “to the living God,” a reading also approved by Ambrose, Augustine, and most other versions. But *fontem* (“fountain”) once also prevailed in editions of the Vulgate until it was corrected in the Clementine recension; the so-called Ambrosian Psalter also reads it. There seems no doubt that it arose from the ingenuity of Latin critics; but here, in Jerome, we were not permitted to alter it.]

And in another place: “O God, my God, to you I keep vigil from the light. My soul thirsted for you; how manifoldly my flesh longs for you. In a desert and trackless and waterless land, so I appeared to you in the sanctuary” (Psalm 62:2–3). Although my soul has thirsted for you, nevertheless I have sought you much more through the labor of my flesh, and I could not appear to you, the Holy One, unless I first dwelt in a land deserted of vices, trackless to hostile powers, and without the moisture and flow of any lust.

The Lord also wept over the city of Jerusalem because they had not repented (Luke 19:41), and Peter washed away his threefold denial in the bitterness of tears (Matthew 26:75), fulfilling the prophetic saying: “Streams of waters have run down from my eyes” (Psalm 118:136).

Jeremiah also mourns the people who do not repent, saying: “Who will give water to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes, so that I may weep for this people day and night?” (Jeremiah 9:1). Why he mourns and laments, he demonstrates in the following words: “Do not weep for the dead, nor mourn him. Weep with the weeping of him who goes forth, because he will not return again.”

Therefore the Gentile and the Jew who were not in the Church and died once are not to be mourned—of them the Savior says, “Let the dead bury their dead” (Matthew 8)—but mourn those who through crimes and sins go out from the Church and, condemned by their vices, do not wish to return to it.

Hence the prophetic word speaks also to ecclesiastical men, who are called the walls and towers of the Church, saying: “Walls of Zion, bring forth tears” (Lamentations 2:18), fulfilling the Apostle’s command: “Rejoice with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep” (Romans 12:15), so that by your tears you may stir the hard hearts of sinners to weeping, lest, persevering in wickedness, they hear: “I planted you as a fruitful vine, wholly true seed; how have you been turned into the bitterness of a foreign vine?” (Jeremiah 2:21).

And again: “They said to wood, ‘You are my father’; and to a stone, ‘You begot me.’ And they turned their backs to me and not their faces” (Jeremiah 2:27). The meaning is: They did not wish to turn back to me and repent, but through hardness of heart they turned their backs against me as an insult.

Therefore the Lord also speaks to Jeremiah: “Have you seen what they have done to me, the dwelling-place of Israel? They have gone up upon every high mountain and under every leafy tree, and there they have committed fornication. And I said, after she committed fornication and did all these things, ‘Return to me’; but she did not return” (Jeremiah 3; Isaiah 57).

### 2.

O God’s mercy! O our hardness! Even after such great crimes he urges us toward salvation. And yet we still do not wish to turn toward better things. “If,” he says, “a wife leaves her husband, marries another, and afterward wishes to return to him, will he receive her and not reject her?” (Jeremiah 2:1). [Note: Other Hebrew and Greek texts, as well as the Vulgate Latin itself, have the opposite: “If a man dismisses his wife, and she departs from him and marries another man, will he return to her again? Will that woman not be polluted and defiled?”—or, as in the Hebrew, “that land.” But the part of the verse more suited to the purpose, namely, “And you have fornicated with many lovers; nevertheless, return to me, says the Lord,” has here been lost through the carelessness of copyists and must be supplied, so that it may be clear in whose place the words found in the Hebrew are being used, while they are absent from the Greek and Latin manuscripts. Once this has been done, a very serious difficulty still remains to be explained. For what he says here is found in the Hebrew—“And you have abandoned me; nevertheless, turn back, and I will receive you, says the Lord”—but it is not found in present copies; they have only, “And you have fornicated with many lovers; nevertheless, return to me, says the Lord,” just as all books, and even Jerome’s own translation from the Hebrew, present it. One who asserts that it fell out of the older books because of the similarity of the letters would be speaking rashly and without authority. Nevertheless, from this testimony of the holy Doctor it is necessary to suspect some lacuna in the Hebrew archetype. This is also suggested by manuscripts of the same translation from the Hebrew, in which either in the text or in the margin of the verse are added the words, “and I will receive you.” Martianaeus considers this a gloss and relegated it to the end of the book, but it truly proceeded from Jerome’s pen. For in his Commentary on the same passage he says: “In the Hebrew, even after fornication, he receives the penitent and urges her to return to him; but in the Septuagint he does not call her to repentance,” and so forth. See what we have explained more fully on this subject there and in the *Divine Library*.]

In its place, according to the Hebrew Truth, it is written—though it is not found in the Greek and Latin books: “And you have abandoned me; nevertheless, turn back, and I will receive you, says the Lord.”

Isaiah also speaks in almost the same words and to the same effect: “Turn back, you who devise deep counsel and iniquity, O children of Israel; return to me, and I will redeem you. I am God, and there is no other besides me, just and savior; there is none besides me. Return to me, and you will be saved, you who are at the ends of the earth. Remember these things, groan, and repent, you who wander. Turn back in your heart, and remember the former things from of old, for I am God, and there is no other besides me” (Isaiah 21, 31, and 45).

Joel also writes: “Turn back to me with all your heart, in fasting and weeping and mourning. Tear your hearts and not your garments. For the Lord is merciful and compassionate, and repentant concerning evils” (Joel 2).

How great his mercy is, and how—if I may put it so—immeasurable and unspeakable his clemency, the Prophet Hosea teaches us. Through him God speaks: “What shall I do for you, Ephraim? How shall I protect you, Israel? What, I ask, shall I do for you? I shall make you like Adama and like Seboim. My heart has been turned within me, and my repentance is stirred. I will by no means act according to the anger of my fury” (Hosea 6).

Hence David also says in the Psalm: “There is none who remembers you in death; and in hell, who will confess to you?” (Psalm 6). And in another place: “I made my sin known, and I did not hide my iniquity. I said, ‘I will declare my iniquity against myself to the Lord’; and you forgave the impiety [or: sin] of my heart. For this every holy person will pray to you at a suitable time. Yet in the flood of many waters they will not approach him” (Psalm 31).

### 3.

See how great the abundance of tears must be, since it is compared with a flood of waters. Whoever possesses them and says with Jeremiah, “Let not the pupil of my eye cease” (Lamentations 2:18), will immediately have fulfilled in him: “Mercy and truth have met one another; justice and peace have kissed” (Psalm 48). [Note: Formerly the reading was: “so that there may be justice and truth, which preserve, and mercy and peace, which call to salvation.”] Thus, if justice and truth have terrified you, mercy and peace may summon you to salvation.

The fiftieth Psalm displays the whole repentance of the sinner. When David went in to Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah the Hittite, and was rebuked by the prophet Nathan, he replied: “I have sinned.” Immediately he deserved to hear: “And the Lord has taken away your sin” (2 Samuel 11).

For he had joined murder to adultery; yet, turning to tears, he said: “Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy; and according to the multitude of your mercies, blot out my iniquity” (Psalm 50). For a great sin required great mercy.

Hence he adds: “Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin. For I acknowledge my iniquity, and my sin is always before me. Against you alone I have sinned”—for I was king and feared no other [or: “for he was and feared another”]—“and I have done evil in your sight, so that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged.”

For God confined all things under sin so that he might have mercy on all (Romans 11:32). And David made such progress that, though previously a sinner and penitent, he passed over into being a teacher and said: “I will teach transgressors your ways, and the ungodly shall turn back to you” (Psalm 50).

For confession and beauty are before him, so that whoever confesses his sins and says, “My wounds have become foul and putrid because of my foolishness” (Psalm 37:6), may have the ugliness of his wounds changed into the beauty of health. “Whoever hides his iniquity will not prosper” (Proverbs 28).

Ahab, the most impious king, possessed Naboth’s vineyard through bloodshed (1 Kings 21). When he was rebuked by Elijah, together with Jezebel—joined to him not so much by marriage as by cruelty—he heard: “Thus says the Lord: You have killed and taken possession.” And again: “In the place where the dogs licked Naboth’s blood, they shall lick your blood; and the dogs shall eat Jezebel before the walls of Jezreel.”

When Ahab heard this, he tore his garments, put sackcloth upon his flesh, fasted, and slept in sackcloth. Then the word of the Lord came to Elijah, saying: [Note: Older printed editions read differently: “Because Ahab has returned to my humility’s account, I will not bring evil in his days, but upon his sons. For although Ahab and Jezebel committed one crime, nevertheless,” and so forth. We have supplied the word “God” from the manuscripts.]

“Because Ahab has feared my face, I will not bring evil in his days.” Ahab and Jezebel committed one crime; yet when Ahab turned to repentance, punishment was deferred to his descendants, while Jezebel, persisting in her crime, was condemned by a judgment in the present.

The Lord also speaks in the Gospel: “The men of Nineveh will rise in judgment with this generation and condemn it, because they repented at the preaching of Jonah” (Matthew 12). And again: “For I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance” (Matthew 9:13).

The drachma is lost, yet it is found in the filth (Luke 5). The ninety-nine sheep are left in the wilderness, and the one sheep that had gone astray is carried back on the shepherd’s shoulders (Luke 15). Hence there is joy among the angels over one sinner who repents.

What blessedness it is that the heavenly beings rejoice over our salvation! Of them it is said: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near.” There is no interval between them. Death and life are opposites, yet through repentance they are joined.

The prodigal son had squandered his whole inheritance and, far from his father, barely sustained his hunger on the food of pigs. He returns to his parent, and the fattened calf is slaughtered for him; he receives a robe and a ring (Luke 15), so that he may receive Christ’s garment, which he had earlier polluted, and deserve to hear: “Let your garments always be white” (Ecclesiastes 9).

Having received again God’s seal, let him proclaim to the Lord: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you.” And reconciled by the kiss, let him say to him: “The light of your face, O Lord, has been marked upon us” (Psalm 4).

“The justice of the just will not deliver him on whatever day he sins; and the iniquity of the wicked will not harm him on whatever day he turns back” (Ezekiel 33:12). [Note: This is a famous saying, as though reported as a saying of the Savior by Justin Martyr in the *Dialogue with Trypho*: ἐν οἷς ἂν ὑμᾶς καταλάβω, ἐν τούτοις καὶ κρινῶ—“In whatever state I find you, in that I will also judge you.” Different writers attribute it to different persons.]

God judges each person as he finds him. He does not consider past things, but present ones—provided that old crimes are changed by a new conversion. [Note: Victorius has “The righteous falls seven times in a day,” but the two words “in a day” are found neither in the manuscripts nor in the Hebrew text or in any version of Scripture. We have therefore removed them here and below, following Erasmus and other older editions. Consult what we note in Jerome, *Against the Pelagians*, book 3, chapter 1.]

“The righteous falls seven times and rises again” (Proverbs 24). If he falls, how is he righteous? If he is righteous, how does he fall? But he does not lose the name “righteous,” because through repentance he always rises again.

And not only seven times, but even if someone sins seventy times seven times, if he turns to repentance, his sins are forgiven (Matthew 18). “The one to whom more is forgiven loves more.”

The prostitute washes the Savior’s feet with her tears and wipes them with her hair. As a type of the Church gathered from the Gentiles, she deserves to hear: “Your sins are forgiven” (Luke 7). The righteousness of the Pharisees perishes through pride, while the humility of the publican is saved through confession (Luke 18).

Through Jeremiah God solemnly declares: “At one moment I shall speak against a nation and against a kingdom, to uproot and destroy and ruin it. If that nation repents of its evil against which I have spoken, I too will repent of the evil which I had thought to do to it. And at another moment I shall speak concerning a nation and a kingdom, to build and plant it. If it does evil in my sight, so that it does not hear my voice, I will repent concerning the good which I had spoken of doing to it.”

Immediately he adds: “Behold, I am fashioning evil against you and devising a plan against you. Let each person turn back from his evil way and set your ways and your purposes straight.” They said: “We have despaired; for we shall follow our own thoughts, and each of us shall do evil according to the perversity of his heart” [Note: Here Gravius has *mali* (“of evil”), from the Greek of the Septuagint.] (Jeremiah 18).

Simeon the righteous says in the Gospel: “Behold, this one is appointed for the fall and resurrection of many” (Luke 2)—for the fall, namely, of sinners, and for the resurrection of those who repent.

The Apostle writes to the Corinthians: “Fornication is heard of among you, and such fornication as is not even among the Gentiles, so that someone has his father’s wife. And you are puffed up, and have not rather mourned, so that he who did this deed might be removed from your midst” (1 Corinthians 5).

And in his second Letter to them, “lest he who is such should be swallowed up by excessive sorrow” (2 Corinthians 2:7), he recalls him and pleads that they confirm their love toward him, so that the man who had perished through incest might be preserved by repentance.

No one is free from sin—not even if his life should last a single day; but the years of his life are countable (Job 15 and 25). [Note: Other printed editions and manuscripts have: “How much less will the years of his life be numerous,” or “if they are countable,” or “if the years are many.”] Even the stars are not clean in his sight, and he devised something perverse against his angels (Job 4:18).

If there is sin in heaven, how much more on earth? If there is transgression among those who lack bodily temptation, how much more among us, who are surrounded by fragile flesh and say with the Apostle: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the body of this death?” (Romans 7:24).

For good does not dwell in our flesh; nor do we do what we wish, but what we do not wish, so that the soul desires one thing while the flesh is compelled to do another.

If some are called righteous in the Scriptures—and not merely righteous, but righteous in the sight of God—they are called righteous according to that righteousness of which it was said above: “The righteous falls seven times and rises again” (Proverbs 24). And according to the saying that the iniquity of the wicked will not harm him on whatever day he turns back (Ezekiel 33:12). [Note: Older Vulgate editions add under an interrogative mark: “Who, then, should despair?”]

Finally, Zechariah, the father of John, who is described as righteous, sinned by not believing, and was immediately condemned to silence (Luke 1). Job also, who at the beginning of his book is described as righteous, blameless, and without complaint, is later proved a sinner both by God’s speech and by his own confession.

If Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; if the Prophets and Apostles likewise were by no means without sin; if the purest wheat contained mixed chaff, what can be said of us, concerning whom it is written: “What has straw to do with grain? says the Lord” (Jeremiah 23)?

Yet the chaff is reserved for the future burning, and the weeds are at present mixed with the crops of wheat, until he comes who has the winnowing fork in his hand and cleanses his threshing floor, gathering the wheat into his barns and burning the refuse in the fire of Gehenna.

### 4.

After running, as it were, through all these things across the beautiful meadows of the Scriptures, I wished to gather them into one place and weave for you, from the fairest flowers, a crown of repentance to place upon your head. Then you may take up the wings of a dove, fly, and rest (Psalm 54), and be reconciled to the most merciful Father.

Your former wife, now your sister and fellow-servant, told me that, in accordance with the Apostle’s command, you both abstained by mutual consent from marital relations so that you might devote yourselves to prayer; but afterward your steps, as though set upon the sea, began to waver—or rather, to speak more plainly, you fell.

She, however, heard from the Lord, together with Moses: “But stand here with me” (Exodus 33), and said of the Lord: “He set my feet upon a rock” (Psalm 39).

Your house, which did not possess solid foundations of faith, afterward collapsed in the whirlwind of the devil. Yet she remains steadfast in the Lord and does not deny you her hospitality, so that you, who were once joined to her in body, may now be joined in spirit. “Whoever clings to the Lord is one spirit with him” (1 Corinthians 6:17).

When the fury of the barbarians and the impending captivity separated you, you promised under the testimony of an oath [or: “you promised”] that, when she departed for the holy places, you would follow her either immediately or later and save your soul, which you appeared to have lost through negligence.

Therefore repay what you promised in the presence of God. The life of mortals is uncertain. Do not let yourself be snatched away before you fulfill your promise; imitate her whom you ought to have taught.

Shame! The weaker sex conquers the world, while the stronger is overcome by the world. “A woman was the leader of so great a deed” (from Virgil); and you will not follow her for whose salvation you have been enrolled as a candidate of faith?

But if the remnants of your property hold you back, so that you may see both the deaths of friends and fellow citizens and the ruins of cities and villages, then, amid the evils of captivity, the fierce faces of enemies, and the boundless shipwreck of your province, at least hold fast to the plank of repentance. Remember your fellow-servant, who sighs for you daily and does not despair of your salvation.

You wander in your homeland—or rather, it is no homeland, because you have lost your homeland. She, for your sake, in the venerable places of the Resurrection and the Cross and of the Lord Savior’s infancy, where he cried as a little child, remembers your name and draws you to herself by her prayers, so that, if not by your own merit, at least by her faith you may be saved.

Once a paralytic lay on a bed and was so disabled in all his limbs that he could neither use his feet to walk nor move his hands to pray. Yet he was carried by others and restored to his former health, so that he carried the bed (Mark 2; John 5), whereas previously he had been carried by the bed.

And so, though absent in body, present in faith, your fellow-servant offers you to the Lord Savior and says with the Canaanite woman: “My daughter is grievously tormented by a demon” (Matthew 15:22).

For I shall rightly call your soul the daughter of her soul, since she recognizes no distinction of sex. Like a little child and nursing infant, not yet able to take solid food, she invites you to the milk of infancy and shows you the nourishment of a nurse, so that you may say with the Prophet: “I have gone astray like a sheep that is lost; seek your servant, for I have not forgotten your commandments” (Psalm 118:176).

---

## Letter CXXIII [Note: Formerly 11. Written in the year 409.]  
### To Ageruchia [Note: As others have also noted, manuscript copies vary: some read *Geruntia* or *Gerontia*, others *Agerusia*, *Acherusia*, or finally *Acherundia*. The true reading, however, is shown by Jerome’s allusion to be *Agerochia*, not, as Martianaeus thought, from ἄγηρως, a word meaning “immortal” or “not experiencing old age”; nor, as Victorius thinks, from ἀγείρω, “to gather,” with the name derived prophetically from the future—that her grandmother, mother, and aunt, women approved in Christ, would be surrounded by a crowd. Rather, it comes from vigor, steadfastness of spirit, and courage, as the Greek name ἀγερωχία, *Agerochia*, signifies. In this sense the name is used by Gregory Nazianzen concerning Nona, and by Philostratus in book 2 of the *Life of Apollonius*, as well as by others; and Jerome here marks this meaning, as it were, with his finger. An unpublished Greek lexicon of remarkable antiquity, a copy of which we possess, is entitled κατὰ Ὠρίωνα τὸν Θηβαῖον, “according to Orion of Thebes,” that celebrated and much-desired authority. It interprets Ἀγέρωχος as ὁ ἃγαν αὐχῶν, “one who boasts exceedingly,” an etymology which is not unsuited to our purpose. As for Victorius calling Ageruchia a virgin, he seems to have done so through a lapse of memory.]  
### On Monogamy

He dissuades the young widow Ageruchia from a second marriage, rejecting the arguments that seemed to favor it and also setting before her eyes, for the same purpose, the calamities of the world.

### 1.

On an old road we seek a new path, and in ancient, worn-out material we devise the fresh elegance of art, so that the things may not be the same, and yet may be the same. There is one road, but many shortcuts to the place you desire to reach.

We have often written to widows, and, in exhorting them, have repeatedly drawn many examples from the Holy Scriptures, weaving various flowers of testimony into a single crown of chastity.

Now our discourse is addressed to Ageruchia, who received her name through a kind of prophecy of future things and through the assistance of God who presides. A noble company surrounds her: her grandmother, mother, and aunt, women approved in Christ.

Her grandmother Metronia, having persevered as a widow for forty years, has brought before us Anna, the daughter of Phanuel, from the Gospel (Luke 2:36). Her mother Benigna, completing her fourteenth year of widowhood, is surrounded by a choir of a hundred virgins. [Note: Gravius prefers: “Agerochia, sister of Celerinus the father of Ageruchia,” so that the aunt too is called Agerochia, sister of Celerinus the father.]

The sister of Celerinus, Ageruchia’s father, who raised the little infant and received her, born into the world, in her own lap, deprived of her husband’s companionship for twenty years, instructs her niece, teaching her what she learned from her mother.

### 2.

I have touched on these matters briefly to show that my young woman does not merely preserve monogamy for her family, but returns it to them; and that she is not so much to be praised if she grants it as to be execrated by all if she attempts to refuse it—especially since her posthumous son Simplicius bears his father’s name, and there is no excuse based on an abandoned and heirless household. Under the protection of such excuses, lust sometimes flatters itself, so that what women do because of their own intemperance may appear to be done from a desire for children.

But why do I speak as though addressing someone who resists, when I hear that she avoids many suitors of the Palace [Note: Victorius, followed by Martianaeus, reads “nobles,” a reading insufficiently appropriate. The reading *procos* (“suitors”), which we have adopted, is supported by the Verona manuscript and all the older printed books, and above all suits Jerome’s intention if one attends to the context.], whom the devil inflames in rivalry so that they may test our widow’s chastity—a chastity made desirable to everyone by her nobility, beauty, age, and wealth? Thus, the more numerous the things that attack her modesty, the greater may be the rewards of her victory.

### 3.

Since, as we leave the harbor, a certain rock is set before us, preventing us from running safely out into the open sea, and the authority of the Apostle Paul, writing to Timothy, is brought forward—where, discussing widows, he says: “But I desire that younger women marry, bear children, manage households, giving the adversary no occasion for reproach. For some have already turned aside after Satan” (1 Timothy 5:14–15)—we must first examine the meaning of the command and investigate the whole context of the passage, or the entire connection of the discourse, and then, following the Apostle’s footsteps, not deviate even, as the saying goes, by a fingernail toward the other side.

Above he had written what kind of widow she ought to be: “The wife of one husband, having brought up children, having testimony in good works, having supplied from her modest means to the needs of the afflicted” (1 Timothy 5:9–10), whose hope is in God and who remains in supplication and prayers night and day (1 Timothy 5:5).

After this he joins the opposing case: “But she who lives in luxury is dead while she lives.” Immediately he adds, to fortify his disciple with every device of instruction: “But avoid younger widows, for when they have grown wanton against Christ, they wish to marry, having condemnation because they have annulled their first faith” (1 Timothy 5:11–12).

Therefore, because of these women who have committed fornication to the injury of their husband Christ—for this is what the Greek word καταστρηνιάσωσι signifies—[Note: Almost all interpreters understand καταστρηνιάσασθαι loosely as “to behave wantonly,” “to act softly or delicately,” “to live in luxury,” “to grow wanton,” or something similar. Jerome’s explanation, “to fornicate to the injury of Christ,” seems to require a broader sense.] the Apostle wishes a second marriage, preferring bigamy to fornication: only by way of indulgence, not by way of command.

### 4.

At the same time, each word of the testimony must be examined. “I desire,” he says, “that the younger women marry.” Why, I ask? Because I do not want them to fornicate.

“Bear children.” For what reason? So that, through fear of giving birth to children conceived in adultery, they may not be compelled to kill them.

“Be household managers.” Why, I ask? Because it is far more tolerable to be twice-married than to be a prostitute, and to have a second husband than several adulterers. In the one case there is consolation amid miseries; in the other, punishment for sin.

He continues: “Giving the adversary no occasion for reproach.” This brief and tightly framed command contains many admonitions at once:

Let not the widow’s chosen adornment bring her reputation into disgrace.

Let her not draw after her, through glances of the eyes and the cheerfulness of her expression, crowds of young men.

Let her not promise one thing by word and another by her dress, so that the familiar verse may apply to her:

> She smiled, and with her speaking eye promised something.  
> *(Ovid, Amatory Elegies, book 3, elegy 22)*
And, to summarize all the reasons for marriage in a brief statement, he showed why he had given this instruction, saying: “For some have already turned back after Satan.” Therefore he opens a second marriage, and, if necessary, a third, to those who lack self-control, so that he may draw them away from Satan, so that he may make a woman joined to any man whatsoever rather than to the devil. But to the Corinthians also he says something similar: “But I say to the unmarried and to widows: it is good for them if they remain as I am. But if they do not exercise self-control, let them marry. For it is better to marry than to burn” (1 Cor. 7:8–9). Why, Apostle? He immediately added: because it is worse to burn [Note: Gravius wishes these two words, “than to burn,” to be deleted in this context, in accordance with the authority of the older manuscript and the sequence of the argument.].

### 5

Otherwise, being what the Apostle is—that is, released, not bound; not a slave but free; thinking about the things that belong to God, not those that belong to a wife—is an absolute good, without comparison with anything worse. And immediately afterward: “A woman,” he says, “is bound to her husband as long as her husband lives; but if her husband has died, she is free: let her marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord. But she will be happier if she remains as she is, according to my advice. Yet I think that I also have the Spirit of God” (ibid. 39). Here too the meaning is the same, because the Spirit is the same; [903] the letters are different, but there is one author of the letters.

While her husband lives, a woman is bound; when he has died, she is released. Marriage, therefore, is a bond, and widowhood a release. A wife is bound to her husband, and the husband is bound to his wife, to such an extent that they do not have authority over their own bodies but must render the marital debt to one another. Nor can those who serve the rule of marriage possess the freedom of chastity.

And what he added—“only in the Lord”—cuts off marriages with pagans, about which he had said elsewhere: “Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers. For what partnership has righteousness with lawlessness? Or what fellowship has light with darkness? What agreement has Christ with Belial? Or what portion has a believer with an unbeliever? What agreement has the temple of God with idols?” (2 Cor. 6:14 ff.). This is so that we do not plow with an ox and an ass (Deut. 22:10), and so that the wedding garment is not woven with threads of different kinds.

At once he withdraws what he had granted, and, as though repenting of his judgment, retracts it: “She will be happier if she remains as she is”; and he says that this is more properly his advice [Note: Here we have restored the word *dicit* (“he says”), and above and below have made several other corrections of lesser importance.]. And lest this be disregarded as merely human counsel, he confirms it by the authority of the Holy Spirit, so that it is not a man indulging the weakness of human flesh whom we hear, but the Holy Spirit giving instruction through the Apostle.

A widow ought not flatter herself in this matter on account of her youthful years, since he commands that no one be enrolled who is less than sixty years old (1 Tim. 5:9). For he does not compel unmarried women or young women to marry, since he also speaks of married women: “The time is short. From now on, let those who have wives live as though they had none” (1 Cor. 7:29). Rather, he is discussing those widows who are supported by the resources of their own households, who are imposed upon the necks of their children and grandchildren. He commands them to learn to manage their own household, to repay their parents, and to provide them with sufficient support, so that the Church may not be burdened and may be able to minister to genuine widows.

Of these it is written: “Honor widows who are truly widows” (1 Tim. 5:3)—that is, those deprived of all assistance from their family, who cannot work with their hands, whom poverty weakens and age consumes; those whose hope is God and whose entire work is prayer. From this it may be understood that young widows, except those whom infirmity excuses, are to be assigned either to their own labor or to the service of their children [904] and relatives.

“Honor” here is understood either as almsgiving or as a benefaction, as in the statement: “Let the presbyters be considered worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in word and teaching” (1 Tim. 5:17). In the Gospel also the Lord explains the commandment of the Law in which it is said, “Honor your father and your mother” (Exod. 20:21). This is not to be understood as mere verbal expression—which can frustrate the poverty of parents through empty flattery—but as the provision of what is necessary for their sustenance.

For when the Lord commanded that children should feed their impoverished parents and repay the old for the benefits they had received as little ones, the scribes and Pharisees taught the opposite: that children should say to their parents, “Corban,” that is, “a gift”: “What I have promised to the altar, and what I have vowed among the temple gifts [Note: I would more willingly read, “even if you have not received it from me,” as Victor also conjectured. This is the sense intended by Jerome: even if I do not give it to you for the temple, the gift will nevertheless be turned to your relief. The authority of the ancient manuscripts, as well as the interpretations of Origen and Jerome on Matthew, more strongly supports our judgment.]—if you receive food from me, it will be turned to your relief.” Thus it happened that, while their father and mother were in need, the children offered a sacrifice, which the priests and scribes consumed.

If, therefore, the Apostle compels poor widows—those, however, who are young and not broken by any infirmity—to work with their own hands, so that the Church may not be burdened and may be able to support elderly widows, what excuse will she use who abounds in the wealth of the world, who can even minister to others and make friends for herself from the unrighteous mammon, friends who may receive her into eternal dwellings?

At the same time, consider that a widow is enrolled only if she has been the wife of one husband. And we think [Note: The Benedictine editor, contrary to Jerome’s meaning, had read, “And we think.” Reatinus read somewhat more correctly, “we thought”; but we do not find this reading satisfactory either, and we believe that it should be read, “and it must not be thought.”] that this is merely a privilege of priests, so that no one is admitted to the altar unless he has had one wife. For not only is a digamist excluded from the office of priesthood; he is also excluded from the Church’s alms, since she is considered unworthy of support who has proceeded to a second marriage.

Although, according to priestly law [Note: The argument is taken from Tertullian’s *On the Exhortation to Chastity*, where he establishes the necessity of monogamy as follows: “God wishes us all to be so ordered that everywhere we may be fit to perform his sacraments. One God, one faith, and one discipline. Indeed, unless laymen also observe those practices by which presbyters are chosen, how will those be presbyters who are chosen from among the laymen?”], even a layman is bound by this rule, since he must present himself in such a way that he may be eligible for priesthood. For he is not chosen if he has been a digamist. Moreover, priests are chosen from among the laity. Therefore the layman too is bound by the command through which one reaches the priesthood.

### 7

The Apostle’s actual desire is one thing; what he is compelled to desire is another. That he grants second marriages is due to my lack of self-control, not to his own will. He wishes everyone to be as he himself is, to think about the things that belong to God, and, once released, never again to be bound. But if he sees those who are slipping through lack of self-control and approaching the abyss of fornication, he extends a hand to digamy, so that they may wallow with one woman rather than with many.

Let the second-married man not hear this as though it were spoken affectionately or contrary to the Apostle’s rule. For the Apostle has two wills: one by which he commands, “But I say to the unmarried and to widows: it is good for them if they remain as I am”; the other by which he indulges them: “But if they do not exercise self-control, let them marry. For it is better to marry than to burn.” First he shows what he wants; then what he is compelled to want. He wishes us to remain after marriage as he himself is, and he sets before us the Apostolic example of blessedness. But if he sees that we are unwilling to desire what he desires, he grants indulgence to our lack of self-control.

Which of the two wills do we choose—the one he wants more, and which is good in itself, or the one that is made lighter by comparison with evil and is, in a certain sense, not even good, because it is preferred to evil?
