Therefore, if we choose what the Apostle does not want but is compelled to want—indeed, what he concedes to those who desire worse things—we are doing not the Apostle’s will but our own [Note: With the support of an ancient codex, Gravius restored this passage, which he considered corrupt, as follows: “We read in the Old Testament that the high priests were married once, and that the daughters of priests, if they had become widows, etc.” To this he adds the passage from Leviticus: “If a priest’s daughter has been married to any of the people, she shall not eat of the consecrated things or of the firstfruits. But if she has become a widow, or has been divorced and returned without children to her father’s house, as when she was a girl, she shall be fed from her father’s food.”].

“We read in the Old Testament” (Lev. 22; and Ezek. 44): that the daughters of priests who had been married once, if they became widows, were to eat of the priestly foods; and, when they died, funeral rites were to be performed for them as for a father and mother [Note: Victor: “and when they have died, the duty of burial is to be performed by the father,” etc.]. But if they had taken other husbands, they were to become strangers both to their father and to the sacrifices, and were to be reckoned among outsiders.

### 8

This is observed even among the Gentiles, to our condemnation, if the truth does not offer Christ what falsehood attributes to the devil [Note: From Tertullian, *On the Exhortation to Chastity*, as noted by Gravius: “After lust, the devil discovered chastity as something destructive, so that the Christian would be guilty if he refused to preserve chastity, which is protective.”]—the devil who also discovered chastity as something destructive.

Among the Athenians the Hierophant renounces intercourse with a man and becomes chaste through perpetual incapacity [Note: Martianaeus and some printed editions read *eviratur* (“is castrated”), falsely, in place of the two words *ejurat virum* (“renounces a man”); or, as other manuscripts have it, *ejerat virum*. This reading has been restored by us and is the only true one, in accordance with the manuscripts. For the Hierophant was not castrated at Athens, but renounced a man. *Ejerare*, or *ejurare*, means to renounce or repudiate; thus *virum ejerare* is equivalent to abstaining from all generation. Sextus Pompeius says: “He renounces what he swears he cannot provide.” Petronius likewise writes in the *Satyricon*: “If you renounce today’s bile, we shall dine together.” Tacitus used *ejurare* of renouncing the consulship and empire. Finally, Seneca, in the *Suasoria* concerning M. Tullius of Asinius Pollio, writes: “Nor was there any delay before he renounced those speeches which he had poured forth with the greatest eagerness.” Concerning the Hierophants, Julian says in Oration 5: “Thus also among the Athenians, those who touch the sacred mysteries live in complete purity, and the one who presides over them, the Hierophant, abstains entirely from generation.” From this it is perfectly clear how wrongly learned men expel this word *ejurandi* from Jerome, contrary to the testimony of the manuscripts that they themselves produce.].

A flamen who has had one wife is admitted to the priesthood. The flaminica likewise is chosen who has had one husband. A man married once is admitted to the rites of the Egyptian bull. I say nothing of the virgins of Vesta, Apollo, Juno, [Note: Tertullian, *To His Wife* 1.6: “At Aegium, in the city of Achaea, a virgin is chosen by lot for Juno.” Erasmus thought that *Argivae* should be read instead of *Achivae*, but this is not convincing; others prefer *Achaicae*, as Tertullian has it elsewhere in *On the Exhortation to Chastity*.] Diana, and Minerva, who waste away in perpetual virginity of priesthood.

I shall briefly mention the queen of Carthage, who preferred to burn rather than marry King Hiarbas; and Hasdrubal’s wife, who seized her children with both hands and threw herself into the fire beneath her, so as not to suffer the loss of chastity; and Lucretia, who, having lost the glory of chastity, refused to survive with a polluted conscience.

And, not to weave together too many examples in a lengthy discourse—examples that you can take for your edification from the first book against Jovinian—I shall repeat only one event that occurred in your own homeland, so that you may know that chastity is held in honor even among barbarous, savage, and bloodthirsty peoples.

The people of the Teutons [Note: Martianus, following Erasmus, reads “from the farthest shores of Gaul by the Ocean and of Germany.” See Valerius Maximus, book 6, chapter 1.] came from the remotest shores of the Ocean and Germany and flooded all Gaul. After repeatedly defeating Roman armies, they were overcome at Aquae Sextiae while Marius was fighting.

When three hundred of their matrons learned that they were to be handed over, together with the other women, to other men as the condition of captivity, they first begged the consul to hand them over as slaves to the temple of Ceres and Venus. When they did not obtain this request, and the lictor was driving them away, they killed their young children; in the morning they were found dead, their throats strangled with nooses, holding one another in mutual embraces.

### 9

What captivity could not inflict upon barbarian chastity—will a noble matron do this? Will she try a second husband, after either losing a good first husband or experiencing a bad one, and thus attempt again to act contrary to God’s judgment? What if she immediately loses the second as well? Will she obtain a third [or: be joined to a third]? And if he dies, will she proceed to a fourth and a fifth, so that there is nothing by which she differs from prostitutes?

Every precaution must be taken for a widow, lest she exceed the first boundaries of chastity. If she exceeds them and breaks through a matron’s modesty, she will rage through every kind of luxury, so that she deserves to hear the Prophet saying: “You have the face of a prostitute; you have no shame” (Jer. 3:3).

What then? Do we condemn second marriages? Certainly not; but we praise first marriages. Do we cast digamists out of the Church? Far from it; but we urge monogamists toward continence.

In Noah’s Ark there were not only clean animals but also unclean ones. It contained human beings, and it contained serpents. In a great house also there are various vessels, some for honor and others for dishonor (2 Tim. 2:20). There is a cup for drinking, and there is also a chamber pot for the more private functions of nature.

For when the Gospels teach that in the good soil there is a hundredfold, a sixtyfold, and a thirtyfold harvest (Matt. 13:8)—the hundredfold holding first place as the crown of virginity, the sixtyfold occupying the second rank for the labor of widows, and the thirtyfold testifying to the bond of marriage through the joining of the fingers [Note: He refers to the ancient practice of counting on the fingers, about which we shall have more to say in book 1 against Jovinian. Here it will be useful to recall one or two passages from Bede: “When you wish to signify thirty,” he says, “you join the nails of the index finger and thumb in a gentle embrace. When you say sixty, you carefully encircle the bent thumb with the curved index finger from the front.”]—in what number will digamy be found? Rather, outside the number. Certainly it does not arise in good soil but among the thorns and briars of foxes, who are compared with the most impious Herod, so that a woman considers herself praiseworthy if she is better than prostitutes: if she surpasses the victims of public lust; if she has prostituted herself to one man rather than to many.

### 10

I shall relate something incredible, but supported by the testimony of many. Many years ago, when I was assisting Damasus, bishop of the city of Rome, with the Church archives and replying to synodical consultations from East and West, I saw two people of equal standing, a matched pair drawn from the lowest ranks of the common people: a man who had buried twenty wives and a woman who had had twenty-two husbands, joined to one another in what they themselves regarded as their final marriage.

Everyone—men and women alike—waited eagerly to see, after so many marriage contests, which of the two would carry the other out first. The husband won. With the whole population of the city streaming together, he was crowned and held the palm; while the people shouted their acclamations individually [Note: We would prefer *adoreasque per singulas subclamante*, “with each one shouting his acclamations,” a reading formed with the slightest alteration from the manuscripts, where the reading is *adoreasque per singula subclamantes*.], and he preceded the bier of his multiply married wife.

What shall we say to such a woman? Surely what the Lord said to the Samaritan woman: “You have had twenty-two husbands, and the one by whom you are now being buried is not your husband” (John 4).

### 11

Therefore I beg you, religious daughter in Christ, not to acquaint yourself with these testimonies, by which assistance is offered to those who lack self-control and are wretched; but rather to read those by which chastity is crowned.

It is enough for you that you lost the first rank of virginity and came by the third to the second—that is, through the duty of marriage to the continence of widowhood. Do not think about what is last, or rather what is degraded; do not seek examples that are alien and far removed. You have a grandmother, a mother, and an aunt, whose abundant example and instruction, and whose rules for living, are a pattern of virtue for you.

For if many women in marriage, while their husbands are still alive, understand the Apostle’s saying, “All things are lawful, but not all things are beneficial” (1 Cor. 6:12), and “make themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven,” either by mutual agreement after the second birth in baptism or, after marriage, through the fervor of faith, why should a widow—who by God’s judgment has ceased to have a husband—not joyfully repeat the words, “The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away” (Job 1), and seize the opportunity of freedom, so that she may have authority over her own body and not again become a man’s slave?

Certainly it is far more burdensome not to enjoy what one possesses than to desire what one has lost. Hence virginity is easier in this respect, because it does not know the incentives of the flesh; widowhood is more anxious in this respect, because it recalls former pleasures in the mind—especially if she thinks that she has lost a husband rather than sent him ahead: one of these belongs to grief, the other to joy.

### 12

The creation of the first man teaches us to reject multiple marriages. There was one Adam and one Eve; indeed, one rib was separated from him into a woman. Again, what had been divided was joined together in marriage, as Scripture says: “The two shall become one flesh”—not two, nor three. “Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and cling to his wife” (Gen. 2:24)—certainly not to his wives.

Explaining this testimony, Paul refers it to Christ and to the Church (1 Cor. 6:16 ff.), so that, as the first Adam was monogamous in the flesh, the second might be monogamous in the spirit [Note: Gravius orders that this be read: “one,” etc.].

Let there be one Eve, mother of all the living, and one Church, parent of all Christians. Just as accursed Lamech divided the former among two wives, so heretics tear the latter into multiple churches, which, according to John’s Apocalypse, ought rather to be called “the synagogue of Satan” (Rev. 2:9) than assemblies of Christ.

We read in the book of the Song of Songs: “There are sixty queens, and eighty concubines, and young women without number. My dove, my perfect one, is one; she is the only one of her mother, the chosen one of her who bore her” (Song 6). To her the same John writes his letter: “The elder to the elect lady and her children” (2 John 1) [Note: Jerome interprets the name “Elect” here and often elsewhere as a proper name.].

And in the Ark, which the Apostle Peter interprets symbolically as the Church (1 Pet. 3), Noah brought in, with his three sons, one wife for each, not two (Gen. 6). Even of the unclean animals, pairs were taken, male and female, so that not even among beasts, serpents, crocodiles, and lizards would digamy have a place.

But if seven of the clean animals were brought in—that is, an odd number—here too the palm of virginity is displayed. For after leaving the Ark Noah offered victims to God, not from an even number but from an odd one, because one group was prepared for offspring and marriage, the other for sacrifice.

### 13

But the patriarchs did not each have only one wife; indeed, they had many concubines. And, as though this were not enough, David had many wives, and Solomon had innumerable ones. Judah enters in to Tamar as though she were a prostitute. And, according to the Western letter, the prophet Hosea is joined not only to a prostitute but also to an adulterous woman (Hos. 1).

If this too is lawfully granted to us, let us neigh after every woman, and, like Sodom and Gomorrah, let us be found on the last day buying and selling, marrying and giving in marriage (Matt. 24:38); and let marriage have its end only when life itself ends.

Even if this opinion prevailed after the Flood and before the Flood—“Be fruitful and multiply, and fill the earth” (Gen. 1:28)—what does it have to do with us, upon whom the ends of the ages have come, to whom it is said, “The time is short” (1 Cor. 7:29), and, “Already the axe is laid at the roots of the trees,” to cut down the forest of the Law and of marriage with evangelical chastity?

“There is a time for embracing, and a time to refrain from embracing” (Eccl. 3:5). Jeremiah, with captivity near at hand, is forbidden to take a wife. Ezekiel, in Babylon, says: “My wife has died, and my mouth has been opened” (Ezek. 24:28).

Neither the man who is about to marry nor the man who has married can prophesy freely in the work of marriage. Formerly it was a glory to hear the verse: “Your children are like olive shoots around your table; and may you see your children’s children” (Ps. 127). Now it is said of those who practice continence: “The one who clings to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Cor. 6:17); and, “My soul clung to you; your right hand upheld me” (Ps. 62:9).

At that time it was “an eye for an eye”; now we offer the other cheek to the one who strikes. At that time warriors were told: “Gird your sword upon your thigh, O mighty one” (Ps. 44:4); now Peter hears: “Put your sword into its sheath. For everyone who takes the sword will perish by the sword” (Matt. 26:52).

We say these things not by separating the Law and the Gospel, as Marcion slanders us, but by accepting one and the same God, who, according to the variety of times and circumstances, is both beginning and end; who sows in order to reap, plants in order to have something to cut down, and lays a foundation in order to place a summit upon the building when the age has been brought to completion.

Otherwise, if we come to the sacraments and consider the types of future things—not according to our own judgment, but as the Apostle explains them [Note: We have restored this word, which was absent, from older printed editions.]—Hagar and Sarah, or Mount Sinai and Zion, signify the two Testaments. Leah, with her dim eyes, and Rachel, whom Jacob loved most (Gen. 29), bear witness to the Synagogue and the Church. Hence Anna, previously barren, becomes more fruitful than Peninnah in abundance (1 Sam. 1).

Monogamy also preceded us in Isaac and Rebekah, whose pregnancy alone received a revelation from the Lord. No other woman consulted God on her own behalf.

What shall I say of Tamar, who gave birth to the twin infants Zerah and Perez? At their birth, the divided wall separated two peoples; and the hand bound with scarlet already sprinkled the conscience of the Jews with the passion of Christ [Note: Through a shameful error, which the earlier Reatinus editor had corrected, the Benedictine editor, following Erasmus, read *Ezron* instead of *Zaram*. See Genesis 38:29–30. The statement that two separated peoples—Jews and Gentiles—are signified in their birth derives from the interpretation of the ancient Fathers, which Jerome explains more fully in his commentary on Micah, chapter 2.].

And concerning the prophetic prostitute, whose likeness signifies either the Church gathered from the Gentiles or—which better suits the passage itself—the Synagogue, first taken from idolaters through Abraham and Moses, then, after the adultery and rejection of the Savior, sitting for a long time without altar, priests, or prophets and awaiting the companionship of her former husband, so that, after the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, all Israel may be saved (Rom. 11).

### 14

As though on a small tablet I wished to display the broadest regions of the earth, so that I might proceed to other little questions, the first of which concerns Anna’s decision:

“Were you alone to waste away your youth in perpetual grief?

Were you never to know sweet children, nor the rewards of Venus?

Do you think that ashes or buried spirits care about this?”

She herself, who endured these things, might briefly answer:

“You were overcome by my tears; you first, my sister, load the raging one with these misfortunes and thrust me before the enemy.

I was not permitted to live without blame, deprived of the marriage chamber, like a wild creature, nor to avoid such cares.

The fidelity promised to the ashes of Sichaeus was not preserved” (Aeneid 4).

You set before me the joys of marriage; I shall set against them the funeral pyre, the sword, and the fire. Marriage does not contain as much good as we hope for as it contains evil that can happen and must be feared.

LUST, ONCE SATISFIED, always leaves regret behind. It is never satisfied, and when extinguished it is rekindled. It grows through use and diminishes through use; it does not obey reason, since it is driven by impulse.

But you will say: “Great wealth and the management of household affairs require a man’s authority.” Clearly, then, the households of celibates have perished, and unless you serve together with your own servants, you will be unable to rule your household. Are your grandmother, mother, and aunt not possessed of greater authority and honor than before, while both the whole province and the leaders of the Churches look up to them?

Therefore [Note: In former times soldiers were forbidden by law to take wives, as Dio very clearly testifies at the beginning of book 60, where, speaking of Claudius, he says that he granted the rights of husbands “to those serving in the army, since by the laws they were unable to have wives.” The passage noted by Gravius is also expressed in Tertullian’s *On the Exhortation to Chastity*: “Clearly, only the households of married men are prosperous; the families of celibates, eunuchs, soldiers, or travelers without wives have perished.”] do soldiers and travelers without wives not manage their little lodgings? Do they neither invite people to banquets nor receive invitations? As though you could not have servants or freedmen of suitable age, in whose hands you were raised, who could preside over the household, answer for public obligations, pay taxes, look up to you as their patroness, love you as their foster-mother, and revere you as a holy woman.

“Seek first the kingdom of God, and all these things will be added to you” (Matt. 6:33). If you think about clothing, the lilies are set before you in the Gospel. If about food, you are referred to the birds, which neither sow nor reap, and your heavenly Father feeds them.

How many virgins and widows have managed their modest property without any stain of scandal? [912]

### 15

Take care not to attach yourself to young women; do not cling to those on account of whom the Apostle grants second marriages, and suffer shipwreck in the midst of tranquility. If Timothy is told, “Avoid younger widows,” and again, “Treat older women as mothers, younger women as sisters, with complete chastity,” why do you not listen when I warn you?

Avoid persons in whom there may be suspicion of bad conduct, and do not have ready that saying from the street: “My conscience is sufficient for me; I do not care what people say about me.” Certainly the Apostle took care to do what was honorable not only before God but also before human beings (Rom. 12), lest through him the name of God be blasphemed among the Gentiles (ibid. 2:24).

He certainly had the authority to take a woman who was a sister with him on his journeys, but he did not want to be judged by an unbelieving conscience [Note: He seems to have read *ab infideli conscientia* (“by an unbelieving conscience”) in 1 Corinthians 10:29, instead of *ab aliena* (“by another’s conscience”). Several Latin manuscripts preserve this reading, as do the author *On the Singular Life of Clerics*, among the works of Cyprian, and Primasius. The Greek terms *allos* and *allotrios* are also sometimes used for “unbelieving.”].

And although he could live from the Gospel, he labored with his hands day and night so as not to burden any of the believers. “If food,” he says, “causes my brother to stumble, I will never eat meat” (1 Cor. 8:13). Let us say the same: if a sister or brother causes scandal—not to one or another person, but to the entire Church—I will see neither sister nor brother.

It is better for one’s household resources to be diminished than for the soul’s salvation to perish. It is better to lose what, whether we wish it or not, will one day perish. It is better to give it up voluntarily than to lose what requires everything else to be given up.

Who among us, not to mention a cubit, which would be excessive, can add even a tenth of a tiny inch to his stature? Yet we are anxious about what we shall eat or drink. Let us not think about tomorrow: “Sufficient for the day is its own trouble” (Matt. 6:34).

Fleeing from his brother, Jacob left great wealth behind in his father’s house and went naked to Mesopotamia [or: fled there]. And, to give us an example of his courage, he placed a stone beneath his head, saw a ladder erected as far as heaven, and the Lord leaning upon it; angels were ascending and descending by it (Gen. 28:5). Thus neither should the sinner despair of salvation nor should the righteous be secure in his own strength [Note: Gravius easily persuades himself that Jerome wrote “with Moses,” based on other passages of Jerome, as in his commentary on Ecclesiastes 12: “If it is said to Moses, ‘I will place you in the cleft of the rock,’ etc.”; and in his commentary on Isaiah 2: Moses too is placed in the cleft of the rock, etc. Elijah, however, stood at the entrance of the cave, 1 Kings 19, etc.].

And, to pass over many things—for there is no time to explain everything in the testimony we have undertaken—after twenty years, a wealthy master and a still wealthier father [or: richer than his father], who shortly before had crossed the Jordan with only a staff, returned to his homeland with three herds.

The Apostles, travelers throughout the whole world, had neither bronze in their belts nor a staff in their hand nor sandals on their feet, and yet they could say: “As having nothing, yet possessing everything” (2 Cor. 6:10). And: “We have neither gold nor silver, but what we have we give you: in the name of Jesus Christ the Nazarene, rise and walk” (Acts 3:6).

For they were not weighed down by a burden of riches. And therefore, standing with Elijah in the cleft of the rock, they could pass through the narrow opening of a needle and contemplate the Lord’s back [Note: Gravius readily persuades himself that Jerome wrote “with Moses,” from other passages of Jerome, as in Ecclesiastes 12 and Isaiah 2. Elijah, however, stood at the entrance of the cave, 1 Kings 19, etc.].

But we burn with greed, and while arguing against money we spread out our lap to receive gold; nothing is ever enough for us. And what is said about the Megarians can rightly be applied to wretched people: “They build as though they would live forever; they live as though they would die tomorrow.”

We do these things because we do not believe the Lord’s words, and because the age desired by everyone promises us not the nearness of death, which is owed to mortals by the law of nature, but stretches of years through an empty hope. No one is so broken in strength or so decrepit with age that he does not think he will live one more year. Hence forgetfulness of his condition creeps in, so that an earthly creature, already on the point of being dissolved, rises into pride and holds heaven in his mind.

### 16

But what am I doing? With the ship broken, I am discussing the cargo. “The one who restrains” is removed from the midst, and we do not understand that the Antichrist is drawing near, whom the Lord Jesus Christ will kill with the breath of his mouth (2 Thess. 2:8) [Note: From the Apostle, 2 Thessalonians 2:7, where he signifies the end of the Roman Empire before the coming of the Antichrist. This was a familiar complaint among ancient writers: amid the most grievous calamities of their times, they believed that the Antichrist was approaching. Hilary, *Against Auxentius* 5, says, because of the violence of the Arians: “It is necessary that we have fallen into the very age of the Antichrist.” Basil, Letter 71; Ambrose, book 10 on Luke, chapter 1, and his *Oration on the Death of His Brother Satyrus*; Sulpicius Severus, *Dialogues* 2; Chrysostom, Homily 33 on Jonah; and especially Gregory the Great in several places make similar statements, to omit later writers.].

“Woe to those who are pregnant and to those who nurse in that day” (Mark 13:17; and Luke 21)—both conditions arising from the fruits of marriage.

I shall briefly pass over the present miseries. The fact that a few of us have remained here until now is due not to our merit but to the Lord’s mercy. Innumerable and exceedingly savage nations have occupied all Gaul. Whatever lies between the Alps and the Pyrenees, whatever is enclosed by the Ocean and the Rhine, the Quadi, Vandals, Sarmatians, Alans, [Note: The Gesipedes, in a certain Worms Chronicle.] Gepids, Heruli, Saxons, Burgundians, Alemanni, and—O mournful state!—Pannonian enemies have devastated.

“For Assur has come with them” (Ps. 82:9). Mainz [or: Mogontiacum], once a distinguished city, has been captured and destroyed, and many thousands of people have been slaughtered in the church. [Col. 1058] The Vangiones have been wiped out by a long siege. The powerful city of the Remi, Ambiani, Atrebates, [Note: This half-line is Virgilian, from Aeneid 9: “And the Morini, the most remote of men, and the two-horned Rhine.” Some manuscripts add the more recent name of the city beside the name of the Nemetae, namely Spira.] the most distant Morini, Tournai, the Nemetae, and Strasbourg have been transferred into Germany.

The provinces of Aquitaine, the Nine Peoples, Lugdunensis, and Narbonensis have been wholly devastated except for a few cities. Even these are ravaged from outside by the sword and from within by famine.

I cannot mention Toulouse without tears: the merits of the holy bishop Exuperius have so far prevented its collapse. Spain itself, already on the point of perishing, trembles daily, remembering the invasion of the Cimbri [Note: Cited from the Worms Chronicle concerning the invasion of Africa.] and enduring perpetually in fear whatever others suffered only once.

### 17

I say nothing further, lest I seem to despair of God’s mercy. Once, from the Pontic Sea to the Julian Alps, the territories that are now ours were not ours. For thirty years, after the Danube frontier had been broken, fighting took place in the very heart of the Roman Empire. Through age, tears have dried up. Except for a few old men, everyone was born in captivity and under siege; they did not long for a freedom they had never known.

Who will believe this? What history could encompass it in language worthy of the subject? That Rome should fight within her own embrace, not for glory but for safety—or rather, that she should not even fight, but redeem her life with gold and all her possessions? This happened not through the fault of the emperors [Col. 1058]—Arcadius and Honorius, who are among the most religious—but through the crime of a half-barbarian traitor [Col. 1058]—Stilicho, related to the Vandals—who armed our enemies against us with our own resources.

The Roman Empire once labored under an everlasting disgrace: when the Gauls were devastating everything and the army had been routed at the Allia, Brennus entered Rome. It could not erase that former dishonor until it had subjected to its rule both Gaul, the native land of the Gauls, and Gallograecia, where the conquerors of East and West had settled.

Hannibal, the storm that arose from the borders of Spain, after laying waste to Italy, saw the city but did not dare to besiege it. Pyrrhus was held by so great a reverence for the Roman name that, after destroying everything, he withdrew from the vicinity; as a victor, he did not dare look upon the city of kings that he had learned about.

And yet, for this injury—not, I will not say, arrogance—which had a good outcome, one of them [Col. 1058]—Hannibal—became a fugitive throughout the whole world and at last found death by poison in Bithynia; the other [Col. 1058]—Pyrrhus—returned to his homeland and fell in his own kingdom. The peoples of both provinces are tributary to the Roman people.

Now, even if everything should turn out favorably, apart from the possessions we have lost we have nothing to take from our defeated enemies. The fiery Poet, describing the power of the city of Rome, says:

> What is enough, if Rome is too little?  
> *(Lucan, Pharsalia 5)*

Let us alter this into another expression:

> What remains safe, if Rome perishes?

> Not though I had a hundred tongues and a hundred mouths,  
> an iron voice, could I recount all the sufferings of captives,  
> or run through all the names of those who were slain.  
> *(Virgil, Aeneid 6)*

And even these words that I have spoken are dangerous both to those who utter them and to those who hear them, so that not even a groan is free for us, unwilling—or rather, not daring—to weep for what we suffer.

### 18

Tell me, dearest daughter in Christ: are you going to marry amid these circumstances? What sort of husband will you take, pray tell—a man who will flee, or one who will fight? You understand what follows in either case.

In place of the wedding song [Col. 1059]—the nuptial song—a terrifying trumpet will blare for you with hoarse sound, so that the women you have as bridesmaids may perhaps become mourners. Or with what pleasures can you abound, when you have lost the revenues from your estates and see your little household, under siege, wasting away through sickness and hunger?

But far be it from me to think such things of you, or to suspect anything unfavorable concerning one who has consecrated her soul to the Lord. I have spoken not so much to you as, under your name, to others: women who, idle, inquisitive, and talkative, go around the houses of married women; women whose god is their belly and whose glory is in their shame (Philippians 3). They know nothing from the Scriptures except the precepts concerning remarriage; they console their own desires in another woman’s body, so that they may see others doing what they themselves have done and may be caressed by the companionship of the wicked.

When you have crushed their shamelessness and arguments by interpreting the apostolic pronouncements, read how you should live in order to preserve your widowhood: the book addressed to Eustochium, *On Preserving Virginity* (Letter 22 to Eustochium), and the others addressed to Furia and Salvina (Letter 54 to Furia and Letter 79 to Salvina). One of these women was the daughter-in-law of the former consul Probus; the other was the daughter of Gildo, who held Africa.

This little book, *On Monogamy*, will bear a title under your name.

## LETTER 124 [Col. 1059]

Formerly Letter 59. Written in the year 410.

### To Avitus [Col. 1059]

This Avitus seems to be the same man who prompted Jerome to write to Salvina, and whom Jerome himself mentions elsewhere, as does Gennadius in chapter 47. Huet distinguishes two Spanish Avituses infected with Origenist corruption and holds that this is the one to whom Jerome’s letter was sent.

### What Must Be Guarded Against in the Books *Περὶ ἀρχῶν* (*On First Principles*)

Origen’s book *Περὶ ἀρχῶν* (*On First Principles*), which Rufinus had previously translated into Latin with little faithfulness, adding and cutting certain passages, Jerome translated anew at the request of Pammachius. He changed nothing in such a way as to make it readable without danger to the faith; rather, he showed what had been said impiously in it and what must be avoided as heretical.

### 1

About ten years ago [Col. 1059]—recall Letter 83, Pammachius to Jerome, especially this passage: “We ask your Eminence to make known in your own language the aforesaid book of Origen faithfully, just as it was published by its author, and to disclose what has been interpolated by its defender, and so forth”—the holy man Pammachius sent me certain sheets containing volumes of Origen’s *Περὶ ἀρχῶν*, translated—or rather corrupted. He earnestly requested that the Latin translation preserve the Greek truth, and that, whether the author had spoken rightly or wrongly on either side [Col. 1060]—Origen, not Rufinus, as Victorius wrongly thinks—the Roman-speaking world should recognize it without the translator’s advocacy.

I did as he wished and sent him the books. When he had read them, he was horrified and locked them away in a chest, lest, if they were brought before the public, they should wound the minds of many. A certain brother who possessed zeal for God, but not according to knowledge, asked him to hand them over for reading, promising to return them immediately and claiming that he had little time. He could not suspect the fraud. The man who had received them for reading summoned scribes and copied out the entire work, returning the codex much sooner than he had promised.

With the same recklessness—or, to put it more mildly, stupidity—he entrusted to others what he had stolen badly. Earlier the text read “to another”; shortly afterward, the Regius manuscript 490 reads “large books, and concerning matters … can preserve,” etc. Since large books discussing mystical matters can scarcely preserve the abbreviations of notes, especially when they are dictated furtively and rapidly, everything in them became confused, so that in many places they lack both order and meaning.

For this reason, dearest Avitus, you ask me to send you the very copy that I once translated and gave to no one else, but which the aforementioned brother published in a perverse form.

### 2

Receive, then, what you have requested, but in such a way that you know that there is very much in it that you must detest and that, according to the Lord’s saying, you must walk among scorpions and serpents (Luke 10). For example, at the very beginning of the first book. Nothing of this sort is found in Rufinus’s sole surviving translation of that book. Nevertheless, there is much reason to suspect that Origen did not think correctly about Christ’s birth, or at least did not express a sound opinion in sufficiently sound terms. He is repeatedly charged with having believed that Christ’s body was by no means born from Mary, but brought down from heaven—an insanity drawn from the polluted pools of the Marcionites. Gennadius of Marseilles likewise attributes this error to him in *On Dogmas*, chapter 2, and Zonaras, book 2, reports similar things of him. We have considered elsewhere the remaining claims concerning the Father’s invisibility and his superiority over the Son; see also *On First Principles*, chapter 2, on Christ.

Christ the Son of God was not born but made. God the Father, because of his invisible nature, is not seen even by the Son. The Son, who is the image of the invisible Father, is not truth when compared with the Father; but among us, who cannot apprehend the truth of almighty God, he appears to be an imaginary truth, so that the majesty and greatness of the greater one may be perceived as somehow circumscribed in the Son.

God the Father is an incomprehensible light. In comparison with the Father, Christ is a very small radiance, which appears great among us because of our weakness. He gives the example of two statues, one large and one small: one that fills the world and is, in a sense, invisible because of its size, and another that falls beneath the eyes; he compares the Father to the former and the Son to the latter.

He calls God the almighty Father good and of perfect goodness. He says that the Son is not good, but a kind of breath and image of goodness, so that he is not called absolutely good, but with an added qualification—“the good shepherd,” and so forth.

In dignity and honor, he places the Holy Spirit third after the Father and the Son. Although he says that he does not know whether the Spirit is made or unmade, he later expressed his view of him, affirming that nothing except God the Father alone is unmade.

Rufinus translates this as “whether born or unborn.” Adamantius, however, may have written γενητὸς ἢ ἀγένητος. See Rufinus, *On the Adulteration of Origen’s Books*, for a notable passage on this subject. Huet has observed that, if ἀγένητον is taken to mean “not created” or “not generated,” it can apply to the Holy Spirit; it cannot do so if it is used of what has no beginning. For this reason the ancient Fathers order that this designation be removed from the Holy Spirit: Basil, *Homily 17 against Sabellius*, and Theodoret, *Dialogue 3*. Some Latin Fathers explain ἀγέννητον as “uncreated,” “inoperative,” or “without origin.” It must be observed that γενητὸν and γεννητὸν are different words: one comes from γεννάω, “to beget,” the other from γίγνομαι, “to become, to exist.” Thus Catholics used ἀγένητος of the Son, but not ἀγέννητος. Hence, when Origen says that he doubts whether the Holy Spirit is γενητός or ἀγένητος, this must be understood in the former sense, “whether generated or ungenerated,” as is clear from what follows. He says this according to the customary judgment of Greek writers, which Athanasius cites in *Oration 2 against the Arians*: ἓν τὸ ἀγένητον ὁ Πατὴρ—“The Father is the one uncreated thing.”

The Greek words of Adamantius are quoted by Justinian in his letter to Menas at the end:

> God and Father, while holding all things together, reaches every existing thing, imparting to each from his own being—for he himself exists. The Son, however, is lesser in relation to the Father, reaching only rational beings; for he is second to the Father. The Holy Spirit is still lesser, being shown among the saints alone. Accordingly, the Father’s power is greater than that of the Son and the Holy Spirit; the Son’s power is greater than that of the Holy Spirit; and, again, the power of the Holy Spirit more fully pervades the other things called holy.

He also says that the Son is less than the Father because he is second to him, and that the Holy Spirit is inferior to the Son because he is present among the saints. In this order, therefore, the Father’s strength is greater than that of the Son and the Holy Spirit; the Son’s strength is greater than that of the Holy Spirit; and, correspondingly, the virtue of the Holy Spirit is greater than that of all other things called holy.

### 3

When he came to rational creatures and said that through negligence [variant: *negligences*] they had descended into earthly bodies, he added this:

> It is a mark of great negligence and sloth for someone to sink and become so emptied that, having come to vices, he can be bound in the gross body of irrational beasts.

Leontius of Byzantium should be consulted, *Scholia on the Acts*, Act 4, where several words on this opinion of Origen were cited above in the note to the *Synodical Letter*. Jerome also treats the subject in his commentary on Jeremiah 29:14.

And afterward [Col. 1061]:

> Moved by these arguments, we suppose that some are voluntarily among the number of the saints and in God’s service, while others, falling from holiness through their own fault, have fallen into such great negligence that they have even been changed into opposing powers.

Compare Rufinus’s translation, Book 1, chapter 5, at the end, to test the reliability—loose and troublesome as it is—of his translation.

Again, he says that a beginning arises from an ending and an ending from a beginning, and that everything changes in such a way that the one who is now a human being can become a demon in another world, while the demon who acts negligently can be sent into grosser bodies—that is, become a human being. Many manuscripts and the oldest edition read *religetur* (“be bound”) instead of *relegetur* (“be sent away”); shortly afterward the Regius manuscript cited above reads, “those who have wavered and, with their feet moved, have by no means altogether fallen, will be subjected to administration,” etc. See Jerome’s Letter to Algasia, question 1, near the end, note b; add Gregory of Nyssa, *On the Making of Man*, chapter 28, which lists this opinion of Origen among Greek fables.

Thus he confuses everything, so that an archangel can become the devil, and the devil can again return to an angel. Those who have wavered but, with their feet in motion, have not altogether fallen will certainly be assigned to Principalities, Powers, Thrones, and Dominions to be administered, governed, and guided toward better things [Col. 1062]. Perhaps the human race will arise from these in one of the worlds, when, according to Isaiah, heaven and earth will become new (Isaiah 65).

But those who have not been worthy to return to their former state through the human race will become the devil and his angels, and the worst demons. In each world they will receive different offices according to the diversity of their merits.

He also says that the demons themselves and the rulers of darkness in some world—or in several worlds—if they should wish to turn toward better things, will become human beings and thus return to their ancient beginning. This will happen only in such a way that, after enduring punishments and torments for either a long or a short time, they will be instructed in human bodies and once again rise to the heights of the angels.

From this, he says, it follows by logical necessity that all rational creatures can arise from human beings—not once and suddenly, but repeatedly. We and the angels can become demons if we act negligently, and demons can again attain angelic dignity if they wish to acquire virtues.

The word “can” has been supplied from the Regius manuscript and certain printed editions. In place of “from human beings,” several manuscripts and editions read “from all things,” which seemed an incongruous reading; for Origen maintained that rational creatures—namely demons and angels—could arise not from all things in the world, but from human beings.

### 4

Compare what we noted on the Synodical Letter, no. 2, note c. Rufinus, on the contrary—or at least following a different Greek copy—translates: “If, at this end, anyone thinks that material, that is, bodily nature will wholly perish, I cannot in any way conceive how so many and such great substances can live and subsist without bodies, since it is proper to the nature of God alone—that is, of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—to be understood as subsisting without material substance and without any association with bodily addition. Another perhaps will say that, at that end, every bodily substance will be so pure and cleansed that it may be conceived after the fashion of ether and of a certain heavenly purity and simplicity. Yet God alone knows more certainly what its condition will be,” and so forth.

He also says that bodily substances will entirely dissolve, or at least that at the end of all things bodies will become what the ether and heaven now are, or whatever other body can be conceived as more transparent and purer. Since this is his view, what he thinks about the resurrection is clear.

He also says that the sun, the moon, and the other stars are living beings. Just as we human beings, because of certain sins, have been enclosed in bodies that are dense and sluggish [variant: “fat”], so the heavenly luminaries have received bodies of one kind or another, so that they shine more or less brightly. Demons, because of greater offenses, are clothed in an aerial body.

According to the Apostle, every creature has been subjected to futility and will be liberated into the revelation of the children of God (Romans 8:19–20). And lest anyone suppose that what we are saying is our own, let us quote his words:

> At the end and consummation of the world, when souls and rational creatures have been released by the Lord from what are, as it were, certain barriers and prisons, some of them will move more slowly because of sluggishness, while others will fly with swift course because of diligence. Since all possess free choice and can voluntarily acquire either virtues or vices, the former will be in a much worse condition than they are now. The latter will reach a better state. For diverse movements and varied wills will receive different conditions in either direction: they will become angels, human beings, or demons, and again from these human beings or angels.

After treating all these matters in various ways, and asserting that the devil is not incapable of virtue but nevertheless does not yet wish to acquire it, he conducted a very lengthy discussion to the effect that an angel, a soul, or certainly a demon—whom he declares to possess one and the same nature but different wills—can, according to the magnitude of negligence and folly, become a beast of burden, and, because of the pain of punishments and the heat of fire, may prefer to be a brute animal and live in waters and waves, assuming the body of one beast or another. Thus, he says, we must fear not only the bodies of quadrupeds but also those of fish. He indeed thought that the bodies with which we shall be clothed at the resurrection will be tortured more severely, since they are subtler and aerial.

Rufinus’s Book 1, chapter 8, allows one to infer that Adamantius said that the Devil, before his fall, was capable of virtue, but not that, because he could receive the good, he therefore wished to receive it. Justinian also quotes certain Greek words of Origen concerning *μετεμψύχωσις* at the end of his letter to Menas; they agree entirely with Jerome’s interpretation.

Finally, lest he be held guilty of the Pythagorean doctrine that asserts *μετεμψύχωσις*—“transanimation,” or the transmigration of the soul from body to body—after this unspeakable discussion, by which he wounded the reader’s mind, he said:

> These propositions, according to our view, are not doctrines but merely questions and conjectures, so that they might not appear to have been left entirely untreated.

At the end of the second book, while discussing our perfection, he added:

> When we have advanced so far that we are no longer flesh and bodies—or perhaps not even souls—but mind and perception brought to perfection, with no cloud of disturbances obscuring us, we shall behold rational and intelligible substances face to face.

The manuscripts and older printed editions have “we shall behold”; the context perhaps favors “we shall behold” in the plural.

### 5. CHAPTER II

In the second book he asserts that there are innumerable worlds—not, as Epicurus held, many worlds existing simultaneously and resembling one another, but one beginning after the end of another. Before this present world, he says, there was another world; after this one, another will exist, and after that one, another; and so on, each following the next.

He doubts whether a future world will be so similar in every respect [variant: “in some respect”] to another world that they will appear to differ from one another in no detail [Col. 1063], or whether one world will never be entirely undistinguished from and similar to another.

The older edition, often cited, adds *articulo*, “in no detail”; this reading is more polished and is preferable. It also has “or perhaps” where the printed text reads “or certainly.”

The Regius manuscripts offer the opposite sense: “whether it will be entirely distinct and dissimilar.” But the printed reading is more likely, for from the words of Origen that Jerome soon quotes, it is clear that Origen asserted that worlds always had been and would be dissimilar:

> For this reason I think that different worlds are made according to the diversity of causes, and that the errors of those who maintain that worlds resemble one another are refuted.

Justinian likewise reports in his letter to Menas:

> Ὑποτίθεται δὲ καὶ διαφόρους κόσμους συστῆναί τε καὶ συνίστασθαι, τοῦτο μὲν παρελθόντας, τοῦτο δὲ μέλλοντας.

> “He holds that different worlds both have existed and exist, some belonging to the past and others to the future.”

See below, Jerome §8, and also Book 3 of *On First Principles*, where Origen makes the same assertion.

Again, shortly afterward:

> If all things, as the order of the argument itself compels us, should live without a body, all bodily nature will be consumed and reduced to nothing, although it was once made from nothing; and there will be a time when its use will again be necessary.

And afterward:

> But if, as reason and the authority of Scripture demonstrate, this corruptible nature shall put on incorruption and this mortal nature shall put on immortality (1 Corinthians 15), death will be swallowed up in victory, corruption in incorruption, and perhaps all bodily nature will be removed from the midst, since death can operate only in it.

Rufinus, Book 2, chapter 3, translates the passage differently:

> If anyone can live without a body, all things can also exist without a body, for the preceding discussion has taught that all things tend toward one end. But if all things can do without bodies, there will undoubtedly be no bodily substance whose use exists.

And shortly afterward:

> If it is true that this corruptible nature shall put on incorruption, this mortal nature shall put on immortality, and death shall be swallowed up at the end, this declares nothing other than that material nature is to be destroyed, in which death could operate.

And a little later:

> If these conclusions seem to follow, it remains that our state must at some time be believed to become incorporeal. If this is accepted, and all are said to be subject to Christ, it is necessary that this too be granted to all in whom Christ’s subjection has been accomplished.

It is tedious to copy out the rest, but it will be worthwhile to compare it, so that one may see how much Rufinus claimed for himself in translating.

And a little later:

> If these things are not contrary to the faith, perhaps we shall at some time live without bodies. But if the one who is perfectly subject to Christ is understood to be without a body, and all are to be subjected to Christ, then we too shall be without bodies when we have been perfectly subjected to him.

And in the same place:

> If all are subjected to God, all will lay aside their bodies, and then the whole nature of bodily things will be dissolved into nothing. If necessity should demand it a second time, it will exist again because of the fall of rational creatures. For God left souls to struggle and contend, so that they might understand that they had achieved complete and consummated victory not by their own strength but by God’s grace. For this reason I think that different worlds are made according to the diversity of causes, and that the errors of those who maintain that worlds resemble one another are refuted.

And again:

> Three possibilities concerning the end are therefore suggested to us; the reader must investigate which is true and better. Either we shall live without bodies when, subjected to Christ, we are subjected to God and God is all in all; or, just as all things are subjected to Christ, they will be subjected with Christ to God and bound together in one covenant, so that every substance will be reduced to the best quality and dissolved into ether, which is of a purer and simpler nature; or else that sphere which we called above the ἀπλανής, “the fixed sphere,” and whatever is contained within its circle, will be dissolved into nothing. But the sphere held and enclosed by what is called αἰτιζώνη [the reading is uncertain] will be called the good earth. Another sphere, which surrounds this earth itself in its revolution and is called heaven, will be preserved as the dwelling-place of the saints.

[Note: [Col. 1064] The manuscripts usually give this Greek word and the one immediately following in the forms ΑΝΑΙωΝΗΝ and ΑΝΑΙωΝΗ. Rufinus’s translation confirms the printed reading; we append it here because it also sheds light on this passage:

> “When all corruptibility has been shaken off and purged away, and the entire condition of this world, which is called the sphere of the ἀκηράτων (‘unmixed’ or ‘untainted’ things), has been surpassed and overcome, the dwelling of the pious and blessed is placed above the sphere called Apianes, as though in a good land and in the land of the living.”

And so forth; consulting the remainder will not cause regret. See Letter 55 to Amandus, no. 5.]

### 6

When he says these things, does he not most clearly follow the error of the pagans and introduce the ravings of philosophers into Christian simplicity? And in the same book:

> It remains that God is invisible. But if he is invisible by nature, he will not be visible even to the Savior.

And farther on:

> No other soul that descended into a human body expressed in itself the pure and genuine likeness of the prior sign, except the one of which the Savior speaks: “No one will take my soul from me, but I lay it down of myself” (John 10).

And elsewhere:

> Therefore the matter must be treated with the utmost caution, lest, when souls have attained salvation and reached blessed life, they cease to be souls.

The same words are also found in Greek at the end of Justinian’s letter to Menas:

> Just as the Savior came to save what was lost, and when what was lost is saved it is no longer lost, so the soul that he came to save as what was lost does not remain a soul when it has been saved. Nor is what was lost to be tormented forever; just as what was lost existed when it was not lost, and there will be a time when it will not be lost, so the soul existed when it was not a soul, and there will be a time when it will not be a soul.

After discussing the soul at length, he added:

> νοῦς, that is, a mind falling, became a soul; and again, a soul furnished with virtues will become mind.

We can discover the same concerning Esau’s soul when we investigate it: because of ancient sins, he was condemned to a worse life.

Concerning the heavenly bodies, too, we must inquire whether the soul of the sun—or whatever it ought to be called—began to exist not at the time when the world was made, but before it entered that luminous and fiery body. Let us think similarly about the moon and the stars: because of preceding causes, although unwillingly, they were compelled to be subjected to futility, on account of future rewards, not to do their own will but that of the Creator, by whom they were assigned to these offices.

### 7

He also says that the fire of Gehenna and the torments with which Holy Scripture threatens sinners “are not located in external punishments, but in the consciousness of sins,” when by God’s power and might the memory of all our offenses is set before our eyes. And as though from certain seeds left in the soul, the entire harvest of vices springs forth; and whatever shameful or impious thing we have done in life, the whole picture of those deeds is depicted before our eyes. As the mind looks upon past pleasures, it is punished by the burning of conscience and pierced by the goads of repentance.”

Martianaeus reads “fires,” while Victorius reads “fire”; shortly afterward Victorius has “does not punish” instead of “does not place,” an obvious error. The passage Jerome attacks is found in Origen, Book 2, chapter 11, where, after quoting Isaiah 50:11, “Walk in the light of your fire and in the flame that you have kindled,” he says:

> These words seem to indicate that the sinner himself kindles for himself the flame of his own fire, rather than being plunged into a fire previously kindled by another or existing before him.

Jerome returns to the matter in Book 3 of his commentary on Ephesians 5:6:

> Since there are many who say that punishments for sins are not future, and that torments are not applied from outside, but that sin itself and consciousness of the offense serve as the punishment, and so forth.

Origen continues:

> Unless perhaps this fat and earthly body ought to be called gloom and darkness, through which, when this world has been brought to completion and it becomes necessary to pass into another world, one will again take up the beginnings of being born.

By saying this, he plainly defends the *μετεμψύχωσις* of Pythagoras and Plato [Col. 1066].

At the end of the second book, while discussing our perfection, he added [the final chapter of Book 2, which Rufinus corrupts]:

> When we have advanced so far that we are no longer flesh and bodies—or perhaps not even souls—but mind and perception brought to perfection, with no cloud of disturbances obscuring us, we shall behold rational and intelligible substances face to face.

### 8. CHAPTER III

The third book, too, contains the following errors:

> If we once accept that, on the basis of preceding causes, one vessel was created for honor and another for dishonor, why should we not return to the soul’s secret history and understand that it acted in ancient times in such a way that one was loved and another hated (Malachi 1:2), before it supplanted in Jacob’s body and, in Esau, was held by its brother at the sole of the foot (Genesis 25:25)?

And again:

> For some souls to become vessels of honor and others vessels of dishonor, the merits of their materials and causes preceded them.

And in the same place:

> According to our view, on the basis of preceding merits, a vessel fashioned for honor, if it does not perform a work worthy of its name, will become a vessel of dishonor in another age. Conversely, that vessel which, because of an earlier fault, had received the name of dishonor, if it wishes to be corrected in the present life, will become in the new creation a sanctified vessel, useful to the Lord and prepared for every good work.

He immediately adds:

> I think that some human beings, beginning with small vices, can reach such great wickedness—if they do not wish to turn toward better things and correct their sins through repentance—that they even become opposing powers. Conversely, from hostile and opposing virtues, some can, over a long period, apply medicine to their wounds, restrain the sins that previously flowed forth, and pass over to the place of the best.

We have often said that, throughout infinite and everlasting ages in which the soul subsists and lives, some souls fall into worse things until they occupy the lowest place of wickedness, while others make progress until they come from the lowest degree of wickedness to perfect and complete virtue.

By these statements he attempts to show that human beings—that is, souls—can become demons, and that demons can again be restored to angelic dignity.

In the same volume he says:

> But this too must be investigated: why is the human soul now moved toward different things by one set of virtues and now by another?

He thinks that the merits of some souls preceded them before they came into bodies. The earlier editions read “before they came into the body”; the wording has been emended here. He cites the case of John, who leaped in his mother’s womb when Elizabeth, at the sound of Mary’s greeting, confessed herself unworthy of her conversation.

He immediately adds:

> Conversely, infants, even those still almost nursing, are filled with evil spirits and are inspired to become diviners and soothsayers. Indeed, a Pythonic demon can possess some from their earliest age. To say that such children have been abandoned by God’s providence, although they have done nothing to deserve suffering such madness, is not compatible with one who wishes nothing to happen without God and believes that everything is governed by his justice.

The Greeks call the spirits that foretell the future *Pythons*.

### 9.

Again, concerning the world:

> “It is our opinion that another world existed before this world, and that another will exist after it. Do you wish to learn that another world will exist after the dissolution of this world? Hear Isaiah speaking: ‘There will be a new heaven and a new earth, which I make to remain in my sight’ (ch. 66:22). Do you wish to know that other worlds existed in the past before the making of this world? Listen to Ecclesiastes: ‘What is that which has been? The very thing that will be. And what is that which has been made? The very thing that will be made. And there is nothing new under the sun, of which one may speak and say, “Behold, this is new.” It has already existed in the ages that were before us’ (Eccl. 1:9–10).”

This testimony declares not only that worlds have existed, but that worlds will exist: not that they all come into being simultaneously and together, but one after another. He immediately adds:

> “I understand the dwelling-place of Divinity and the true rest to be above, in which rational creatures dwelt before they descended to lower regions and migrated from invisible things to visible things. As they fell toward the earth and required dense bodies, they enjoyed their ancient blessedness. Therefore God the Creator made bodies suitable for them in their humble places and fashioned this visible world. For the salvation and correction of those who had fallen, he sent ministers into the world: some of them were to obtain particular places and obey the necessities of the world; others were to attend diligently to the duties assigned to them at their respective times, which God the Craftsman knows. And from among these the higher places of the world—sun, moon, and stars, which the Apostle calls ‘creation’—received their inhabitants. This creation has been subjected to vanity (Rom. 8), because it is surrounded by dense bodies and is exposed to sight. Yet it was not subjected to vanity willingly, but because of the will of him who subjected it in hope. And again: others serve as administrators of the world in particular places and at particular times, which the Craftsman alone knows; we believe these to be his angels.”

[Note: [Col. 1067] We have restored the passage with the aid of the Regius manuscript, since all earlier editions had it incorrectly as “the dwelling-place of Divinity.” The words “dwelling there,” although the sense remains complete, are also absent from that manuscript. In any case, one should not establish Origen’s true meaning from Rufinus’s translation. Compare what follows from here to the next section.]

And a little later:

> “The providence of the whole world governs this order of things, while some powers fall from higher regions and others gradually sink toward the earth. These descend voluntarily; others are precipitated against their will. The former willingly undertake ministries, so as to extend a hand to those who are falling; the latter are compelled, unwillingly, to persist for so long a time in the office they have undertaken.”

[Note: [Col. 1067] The same Regius manuscript, partly supported by the old edition, reads: “and they persist for so long or so long a time in the office undertaken,” and so forth.]

And again:

> “From this it follows that, because of varying movements, various worlds are also created, and that after this world which we inhabit another world, very different from it, will come into being. No one else can distribute, according to different circumstances, advances, and either the rewards of virtues or the punishments of vices, both in the present and in the future, and in all times, both past and subsequent, nor bring all things again to a single end, except the one God, Creator of all. He knows the reasons why he permits some to enjoy their own will and gradually descend from higher things to the lowest, while he begins to visit others and, as it were, gradually draws them back by an offered hand to their former state and places them in the heights.”

[Note: [Col. 1068] Martianaeus has the earlier reading, which we corrected from Victorius’s edition; this edition, however, seems mistaken here in reading *merito* for *merita*. A little below, we supplied the word “gradually” (*paulatim*) from the manuscripts and the old edition.]

[Note: [Col. 1068] Other editions read “in [the] Holy One”; but, with a particle deleted, we supplied the following word from the manuscripts for clarity of sense.]

### 9.

When he began to discuss the end, he introduced the following:

> “Since, as we have frequently said, the beginning is again generated from the end, the question arises whether bodies will also exist at that time, or whether at some point we shall live without bodies, after they have been reduced to nothing, and whether the life of incorporeal beings is to be believed incorporeal, like that which we know God to possess. There is no doubt that, if all bodies belong to this sensible world, which the Apostle calls ‘visible’ (Rom. 1), the future life of incorporeal beings will be incorporeal.”

And shortly afterward:

> “We understand what is also said by the same Apostle—‘Every creature will be liberated from slavery to corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God’ (Rom. 8:21)—as follows: we call the first creation rational and incorporeal, since it is not subject to corruption, because it is not clothed with bodies; and wherever bodies exist, corruption immediately follows. It will afterward be liberated from slavery to corruption when they receive the glory of the children [or: child] of God, and God is all in all.”

And in the same place:

> “That we should believe the end of all things to be incorporeal is prompted by the Savior’s prayer, in which he says: ‘That just as I and you are one, so these also may be one in us.’ For we must understand what God is, what the Savior will be at the end, and how the likeness of the Father and the Son has been promised in the saints, so that just as they are one in themselves, so these also may be one in them. Either we must accept that the God of the universe is clothed with a body, and that just as we are surrounded by flesh, so he is surrounded by some kind of matter, so that at the end the likeness of God’s life may be attained by the saints; or, if this is improper—especially among those who desire to perceive, even in the smallest measure, the majesty of God and to form some conception of the glory of his unbegotten nature, which surpasses all things—we are compelled to accept one of two alternatives: either to despair of likeness to God if we are always to have these same bodies, or, if the blessedness of a life identical with God’s is promised to us, to live under the same condition by which God lives.”

### 10.

From all these statements it is established what he thinks concerning the resurrection, and that he affirms that all bodies will perish, so that we shall exist without bodies, as we did previously, before we were clothed with dense bodies.

Again, while discussing the variety of worlds and asserting that angels may become demons, demons angels, or human beings, and, conversely, that human beings may become demons, and that everything may arise from everything, he confirms his opinion with the following conclusion:

> “There is no doubt that, after certain intervals of time, matter will again exist, bodies will be formed, and a diversity of worlds will be constructed because of the various wills of rational creatures. After perfect blessedness, they gradually declined toward lower things until the end of all things and received such great wickedness that they were changed into the opposite, because they did not wish to preserve their beginning and possess incorruptible blessedness. Nor should this be ignored: many rational creatures will preserve their beginning through the second, third, and fourth world, and will not allow change any place within themselves. Others will lose so little of their former state that they will seem almost to have lost nothing; while some will be hurled down by a great ruin into the final abyss. God, the administrator of all things, knows how to make use of each one according to its merit in the ordering of the worlds, and knows the opportunities and causes by which the governments of the worlds are sustained and initiated. Thus the one who has overcome all others in wickedness and has made himself entirely equal to the earth will become the devil in another world, which is to be fashioned afterward—the beginning of the Lord’s creation—so that he may be mocked by angels who have lost the virtue of their beginning.”

[Note: [Col. 1069] Let this passage finally serve as an example of how skillfully Rufinus concealed Origen’s errors: for he attributes this very widely known opinion of Origen concerning the fall of the blessed to his own translation elsewhere, in book 3, chapter 6: “But some think that this perfection and blessedness of rational creatures, or natures, can remain permanently in the state described above—that is, if they possess God as all things and God is all things to them—provided that no fellowship with bodily nature brings them into contact with it. Otherwise, they believe that the glory of supreme blessedness would be impeded if an admixture of material substance were introduced.” Indeed, shortly afterward he even introduces Origen refuting this: “In this state of blessedness also we must believe that they will remain forever and immutably by the Creator’s will, with the Apostle’s statement confirming the matter: ‘We have a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens.’”]

After saying this, what else is he trying to show except that sinful human beings in this world can become the devil and demons in another world, and that demons now can in another world be produced either as angels or as human beings?

After a very lengthy discussion in which he says that every bodily creature must be changed into spiritual and tenuous bodies, and that the whole substance must be converted into one body, most pure and purer than every splendor, and of a kind that the human mind can now scarcely imagine, he finally adds:

> “And God will be all in all, so that the whole bodily nature may be reduced to that substance which is better than all others—namely, the divine substance, than which none is better.”

### 11. Chapter IV

In the fourth book as well, which is the final book of his work, he inserts the following statements, which must be condemned by the Church of Christ:

> “Perhaps, just as in this world those who die through the separation of flesh and soul obtain different places among the dead according to the difference of their works, so those who die from the administration of the heavenly Jerusalem, so to speak, descend to the underworld of our world, in order to possess different places on earth according to the quality of their merits.”

And again:

> “Since we have compared the souls departing from this world to the underworld with those souls that, arriving from the higher heaven at our dwellings, have in a certain manner died, we must investigate carefully whether we can also say this concerning the birth of individuals: just as the souls born on this earth of ours either come from the underworld, desiring better things, and ascend to higher regions and assume a human body, or descend to us from better places, so also those regions above, in the firmament, may be possessed by other souls—some progressing from our abodes toward better things, others having fallen from heavenly places only as far as the firmament, because they had not committed so great a sin that they should be thrust down to the places we inhabit.”

[Note: [Col. 1070] The Regius manuscript reads: “nor had they committed so great a sin that they should be thrust down to the lower places we inhabit,” and so forth.]

By these statements he attempts to establish that the firmament—that is, heaven—is, in comparison with the higher heaven, an underworld; that this earth we inhabit is called an underworld in comparison with the firmament; and that, conversely, in comparison with the underworld beneath us, we are called heaven—so that what is an underworld for some is heaven for others.

Nor content with this discussion, he says:

> “At the end of all things, when we are to return to the heavenly Jerusalem, the wars of the adversaries of the Powers will rise up against the people of God, so that the Powers’ strength may not remain idle, but that they may be trained for warfare and have material for developing their strength—something they cannot attain unless they first resist their adversaries.”

[Note: [Col. 1070] From this one can easily understand what Theophilus meant in his first Paschal letter when he said that Origen dreamed of souls ascending to heaven and descending from it, now progressing and now falling to lower regions.]

[Note: [Col. 1070] Thus we have restored the text from the manuscripts and other editions; Martianaeus has “than that they may attain,” and shortly afterward, “they may press on.”]

These adversaries, we read, were overcome by reason, order, and skill in resistance in the Book of Numbers (Num. 10:26, 33).

### 12.

When he had said, in accordance with John’s Apocalypse (ch. 4:6), that the everlasting Gospel—that is, the Gospel that is to come in heaven—surpasses our Gospel to the same extent that Christ’s preaching surpasses the mysteries of the old Law, he finally added—and it is sacrilegious even to have conceived this—that Christ would suffer in the air and in the heavenly regions for the salvation of demons.

Although he did not say this explicitly, it is understood as the consequence: just as he became human for human beings in order to deliver human beings, so, for the salvation of demons, God would become what these beings are, in order to come to deliver them.

Lest we seem to assert this from our own interpretation, his own words must be presented:

> “For just as through the shadow of the Gospel he fulfilled the shadow of the Law, so, since every law is an example and shadow of the heavenly ceremonies, we must inquire more carefully whether we rightly understand that the heavenly Law and the ceremonies of the higher worship likewise do not possess fullness, but require the truth of the Gospel. In John’s Apocalypse we read that this is the everlasting Gospel, evidently in comparison with our Gospel, which is temporal and was preached in a world and age that is passing away. Even if we wish to investigate this as far as the passion of the Lord and Savior, although it would be bold and rash to seek his passion in heaven, nevertheless, if spiritual forces of wickedness are in the heavenly places, and we are not ashamed to confess the Lord’s cross because of the destruction of those things that he destroyed through his passion, why should we fear even in the higher regions, at the consummation of the ages, to suspect something similar, so that the nations of every region may be saved through his passion?”

[Note: [Col. 1070–1071] Justinian, in his letter to Menas, represents this passage from the Greek text of book 4 of *On First Principles* as follows; and this is how it is commonly printed:

> “And even if someone should investigate as far as the passion, he will seem to be acting boldly if he seeks the same thing concerning the heavenly regions. But if there are spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places, then, just as here we are not ashamed to confess him crucified for the destruction of those things which he destroyed by suffering, so, granting that something similar happens there as well, we shall not fear to say so, even until the consummation of the whole age.”

### 13.

Again, blaspheming concerning the Son, he spoke as follows:

> “For if the Son knows the Father, he appears, by knowing the Father, to be able to comprehend him—just as we might say that the mind of an artisan knows the measure of his art. There is no doubt that, if the Father is in the Son, he is comprehended by the one in whom he is. But if we call comprehension not merely the act by which someone comprehends through sense and wisdom, but also the act by which he holds all things through virtue and power, then we cannot say that the Son comprehends the Father; the Father, however, comprehends all things. Among all things, moreover, is the Son; therefore he also comprehends the Son.”

And so that we might know the reasons why the Father comprehends the Son, whereas the Son cannot comprehend the Father, he adds these words:

> “Let the curious reader inquire whether the Father knows himself in the same way as he is known by the Son. And knowing what is written—‘The Father who sent me is greater than I in all things’ (John 14:28)—he will maintain [perhaps: concede] that it is true to say that the Father is greater than the Son even in knowledge, since he is known more perfectly and purely by himself than by the Son.”

[Note: [Col. 1071] The Regius manuscript does not recognize the little word “if.”]

[Note: [Col. 1071] Martianaeus, following a corrupted ancient reading, has “greater than all,” which is written nowhere. We have printed what we believe to be the true reading from the Regius manuscript and the edition of Victorius.]

[Note: [Col. 1071] Gravius reads this differently. Here too he is convicted of agreeing with metempsychosis (*metempsychosis*, μετεμψύχωσις) and the abolition of bodies.]

### 14.

He is likewise shown by the following to hold *metempsychosis* (μετεμψύχωσις) and the abolition of bodies:

> “If anyone is able to show that an incorporeal and rational nature, after stripping off its body, lives by itself, and that it is in a worse condition when clothed with bodies and in a better condition when it lays them aside, no one can doubt that bodies do not subsist primarily, but come into being intermittently and because of the various movements of rational creatures, so that those who need them may be clothed with them; and again, when through the corruption of their falls they have corrected themselves toward better things, bodies are dissolved into nothing, and the succession continually varies in this way.”

[Note: [Col. 1071] Victorius maintains that “fallen” (*lapsos*) ought to be read, but this does not seem satisfactory to us.]
