And lest we should think the impiety of what he had said earlier insignificant, at the end of the same volume he joins it to the following claim: all rational natures—namely, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; angels, powers, dominions, and the other virtues; and the human being himself according to the dignity of his soul—are of one substance.

> “God,” he says, “and his only-begotten Son and the Holy Spirit perceive an intellectual and rational nature; angels, powers, and the other virtues perceive it; and the inner human being, who was created in the image and likeness of God, perceives it. From this it follows that God and these beings are, in a certain manner, of one substance.”

[Note: [Col. 1072] Elsewhere, in his book against John of Jerusalem addressed to Pammachius, chapters 5 and 6, he says that it was the madness of the Manichaeans, not of Origen, to claim that human souls were part of God’s nature or of God’s substance. Hence Augustine, *City of God*, book 11, chapter 23: “They say that souls are not indeed parts of God, but, having been made by God, sinned by departing from their Creator and, through various progressions corresponding to the variety of their sins, earned different bodies as bonds, from heaven even to earth . . . For this reason Origen is rightly blamed; for in the books which they call *On First Principles* he held and wrote this.” Moreover, Jerome himself says again in his forthcoming letter 126 to Marcellinus and Anapsychia: “Concerning the state of the soul, whether it has fallen from heaven, as the philosopher Pythagoras, all the Platonists, and Origen think, or whether it is from God’s own substance, as the Stoics, Manichaeus, and the Spanish heresy of Priscillian suspect,” and so forth. Nevertheless, Justinian, in his letter to the Fifth Synod, echoes the charge brought against Adamantius when he reproaches the Origenists for saying that there is “a unity of all rational beings through identity of substance, operation, and power in relation to God, as well as through union and knowledge”—that is: “the unity of all rational beings, since they are identical in substance, operation, and in the power that exists with God the Word, and also in union and recognition.”]

He adds the single word “in a certain manner,” so that he might escape the charge of so great a sacrilege. Yet he who elsewhere does not wish the Son and the Holy Spirit to be of the Father’s substance, lest he appear to divide the divinity into parts, here grants the nature of almighty God to angels and human beings.

### 15.

Since these things are so, what madness is it to alter a few statements concerning the Son and the Holy Spirit, which plainly displayed blasphemy, while bringing forward all the rest exactly as it was written and praising it with an impious voice—when both those statements and these proceeded from the same source of impiety?

To write against everything is not possible at this time; and all those who wrote against Arius, Eunomius, Manichaeus, and the various heresies must be believed to have answered these impieties as well.

Whoever, therefore, wishes to read these books and to proceed with shod feet toward the promised land, lest he be bitten anywhere by serpents or struck by the curved wound of the scorpion, should first read this book and learn, before entering upon the road, what he must avoid.

## Letter 125

[Note: [Col. 1072] Also numbered 4. Written in the year 411.]

### To Rusticus the Monk

He explains how one ought to order a life worthy of the name “monk,” and urges above all that the companionship of suspect women must be avoided. He also says that it is safer for a young man to live in a monastery than in solitude. One should come late to teaching and to writing books; the companionship of detractors must be avoided in every way.

### 1.

Nothing is happier than a Christian, to whom the kingdom of heaven is promised. Nothing is more laborious than the Christian, who is daily in danger of his life. Nothing is stronger than the one who conquers the devil. Nothing is weaker than the one who is overcome by the flesh.

There are very many examples of both conditions. The thief believes on the cross and immediately merits hearing: “Truly I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43). Judas falls from the height of apostleship into the Tartarus of destruction and is not broken either by the intimacy of the meal, the dipping of the morsel, or the grace of the kiss, lest he betray as a mere man the one whom he knew to be the Son of God.

What was more insignificant than the Samaritan woman? Not only did she herself believe and, after six husbands, find one Lord and recognize the Messiah at the well whom the Jewish people did not recognize in the Temple; she also became the author of the salvation of many. While the Apostles were buying food, she refreshed the hungry man and supported the weary one (John 4).

What was wiser than Solomon? Yet he was made foolish by love for women (1 Kings 11:1). Salt is good, and no sacrifice is accepted without its sprinkling (Lev. 2). Hence the Apostle also commanded: “Let your speech always be seasoned with grace, with salt” (Col. 4:6). But if it becomes tasteless, it is thrown outside (Mark 8), and it loses the dignity of its name to such an extent that it is not even useful for the dunghill, with which people customarily fertilize the fields of believers and enrich the barren soil of souls.

We say these things so that at the very outset, my son Rusticus, we may teach you that you have undertaken great things and are pursuing lofty ones; that, trampling underfoot the incentives of adolescence—or rather, of puberty—you are climbing toward the rank of mature age; but that the path on which you are entering is slippery, and that not so much glory follows victory as disgrace follows a fall.

### 2.

I do not now need to lead a little stream through the meadows of virtues, nor labor to show you the beauty of various flowers: what purity the lilies contain, what modesty the rose possesses, what purple the violet promises in the kingdom, or what the gleaming colors of gems pledge.

For now, by the Lord’s favor, you hold the plow. You have already climbed with the Apostle Peter onto the roof and the upper room. Hungry among the Jews, he is filled by Cornelius’s faith; and he quenches their hunger caused by unbelief through the conversion of the Gentiles. In the quadrangular vessel of the Gospels, which descended from heaven to earth, he is taught and learns that all human beings can be saved.

Again, what he had seen in the form of the whitest linen cloth is transferred above, and he carries the believing crowd from earth to heaven, so that the Lord’s promise may be fulfilled: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8).

Everything I wish to convey to you by taking you by the hand—like a learned sailor trying, after many shipwrecks, to instruct an inexperienced passenger—is this: you must know on which shore of chastity there is a pirate; where Charybdis is, namely greed, the root of all evils; where are the Scyllaean dogs of detractors, about whom the Apostle speaks: “If you bite and devour one another, take care that you are not consumed by one another” (Gal. 5:15); how, in the midst of calm, we may sometimes be overwhelmed by the Libyan Syrtes of vices; and what kinds of poisonous creatures the desert of this age nourishes.

### 3.

Those sailing across the Red Sea—where we ought to wish that the true Pharaoh might be drowned with his army—arrive, amid many difficulties and dangers, at the city of Auxuma.

[Note: [Col. 1074] Ancient copyists, not understanding what the word “Auxuma” meant, substituted “Maxima” through an easy alteration of letters. This corrupted passage has nevertheless perplexed the editors of Jerome before us, who have offered various speculations and attempted, by guesswork, to explain what city “Maxima” might be. Martianaeus interprets it as Ailath, since the following is written under that word in the *Book of Places*: “The Red Sea, from which one sails from Egypt to India.” Others, with a less fortunate conjecture, understand Rabbath, because, according to Jerome’s testimony in Ezekiel 25, this city is properly called by that name on account of its size—for Rabbath means “the greatest.”

“We, perceiving that the corruption lay in the word itself, judged that ‘Auxuma’ should be restored, having learned that our conjecture was confirmed by the notes of the distinguished Lucas Holstenius on Stephanus of Byzantium, so that we no longer hesitated to restore the true reading on his authority. For Axuma, or Auxuma—Greek Αὐξούμη or Αὐξωμις—was once the royal city of the Abyssinians and the capital of the entire kingdom, as Nonnosus says in the *Bibliotheca* of Photius, chapter 3: ‘Auxumis is a very great city and, so to speak, the metropolis of all Ethiopia.’ Job Ludolphus testifies that it lies at fourteen and a half degrees north latitude and is only forty-five Portuguese leagues from the Red Sea. Arrian, in his *Periplus of the Erythraean Sea*, reports that it was a notable market, so that the difficulty should not be considered decisive merely because it lies at this distance from the sea, since all the other details mentioned here fit it extremely well.”]

[Note: [Col. 1074] We would prefer “guide,” or, as Victorius reads, “skilled lookout,” but the manuscripts resist these readings.]

On either shore live wandering peoples, or rather, exceedingly savage beasts. Always anxious, always armed, they carry provisions for the entire year. Everything is filled with hidden rocks and extremely hard shallows, so that the lookout and the skilled pilot must sit at the very top of the mast and from there give instructions for steering and turning the ship.

The voyage is fortunate if, after six months, they reach the harbor of the aforementioned city, from which the Ocean begins to open. Through it one can scarcely reach India in an entire year, and the river Ganges—which Holy Scripture calls the Phison and says surrounds the whole land of Havilah—is said to carry many kinds of spices from the fountain of paradise.

There the carbuncle and emerald are born, along with shining pearls and “unions,” which inflame the ambition of noblewomen; and there are golden mountains which, because of griffins, dragons, and monsters of immense bodies, it is impossible for human beings to approach. Thus we are shown what kind of guardians greed has.

### 4.

Why do I say these things? It is clear: if merchants of this world endure so much in order to reach uncertain and perishable riches, and preserve, at the risk of their souls, what they acquired through many dangers, what must the merchant of Christ do, who sells everything to seek the most precious pearl? What must he do who, with all the resources of his property, buys a field in which he may find a treasure that no thief can dig up and no robber carry away?

### 5.

I know that I shall offend very many people who apply a general discussion of vices to their own insult; and while they are angry with me, they reveal their own conscience. They judge themselves much more harshly than they judge me.

I shall name no one, nor, with the license of Old Comedy, shall I select and lash particular persons. It is the mark of a prudent man—and of prudent women—to conceal, or rather to correct, what they recognize in themselves, and to be indignant with themselves rather than with me; they should not heap insults upon the one who warns them.

Even if such a person is held by the same crimes, he is certainly better in this respect: his own evils do not please him.

### 6.

I hear that you have a devout mother, a widow of many years, who raised and educated you as a child. After your studies in Gaul, which are among the most flourishing, she sent you to Rome, sparing no expense and sustaining the absence of her son with hope for the future, so that the richness and polish of Gallic speech might be seasoned by Roman gravity.

She did not use spurs upon you, but reins. We read the same of the most eloquent men of Greece:

[Note: [Col. 1075] Recall the examples in Quintilian, book 12, chapter 10, including Cicero in the *Orator*.]

They dried the Asiatic swelling with Attic salt and restrained luxuriant vines with pruning hooks, so that the winepresses of eloquence might overflow not with clusters of words but with the expression of meanings, as of grapes.

Honor her as a parent; love her as a nurse; venerate her as a holy woman. Do not imitate the example of others who abandon their own mothers and seek those of others. Their disgrace is openly visible: under the names of piety they seek suspect associations.

[Note: [Col. 1075] He sharply mocks the Agapetae, that most disgraceful class of people who, under the pretext of charity or piety, disguised illicit cohabitation with women. In Letter 22 to Eustochium, Nazianzenus calls them “the plague of the Agapetae”:

> “Your love—and this revered name—  
> alas, alas, may it not contain something of impure love.”

And the author of the book *On the Singularity of Clerics* says: “They cover naked disgrace with the veil of a good name, while among them true affection is violated under the false name of love.”]

I know some women of already mature age, and many of them, who delight in young men of the freedman class and seek spiritual sons. Gradually overcoming shame, they break out into marital license under the fictitious names of mothers.

Others abandon their virgin sisters and attach themselves to unrelated widows. Some hate their own relations and are caressed by the affection of those who are not theirs. Their impatience, the indication of their character, admits no excuse; it tears apart the empty veils of immodesty like threads of spiders.

You may see some with girded loins, dark tunics, and long beards, unable to leave women, remaining under the same roof, sharing meals, keeping young maidservants in their service, and—apart from the word “marriage”—having everything that belongs to marriage.

This is not the fault of the Christian name when a pretender to religion is living in vice. Indeed, it is a source of confusion to the Gentiles when they see that what displeases all good people also displeases the Churches.

### 7. The Duty of a Good Monk

But if you wish to be a monk, not merely to appear one, care for your soul, not for the household property which, by renouncing it, you began to be a monk.

Let dirty clothes be signs of a pure mind; let a cheap tunic demonstrate contempt for the world—but only so that your spirit does not become swollen with pride and your dress and speech do not disagree.

Let the one who wishes to extinguish the heat of the body in the cold of fasting not seek the warm baths. The fasts themselves should be moderate, lest excessive austerity weaken the stomach and, by demanding greater nourishment, break out into belching, which is the parent of lust.

Moderate and temperate food is beneficial both to body and soul.

Look upon your mother in such a way that through her you are not compelled to look upon other women, whose faces may cling to your heart:

> “And let a silent wound live beneath the breast”  
> (*Aeneid* 4).

Know that the maidservants who attend her are lying in wait for you; for the lower their condition, the easier the fall.

John the Baptist had a holy mother and was the son of a priest. Yet he was not overcome either by his mother’s affection or by his father’s wealth, so as to live in his parents’ house at the risk of his chastity. He lived in the wilderness (Luke 1), and with eyes longing for Christ he deemed nothing else worthy of seeing.

Rough clothing, a leather belt, locusts for food, and wild honey (Mark 1): everything was prepared for virtue and self-restraint.

The sons of the prophets—whom we read of as monks in the Old Testament—built themselves huts beside the streams of the Jordan. Having abandoned the crowds of the cities, they lived on coarse meal and wild herbs (2 Kings 6).

As long as you are in your homeland, make your cell a paradise. Pluck the varied fruits of Scripture. Use these as your delights; enjoy their embrace.

If your eye, foot, or hand causes you to stumble, cast it away (Matt. 5). Spare no one, so that you may spare your soul alone.

The Lord says: “Whoever looks upon a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.” Who can boast that he has a pure heart (Prov. 20:9)?

The stars are not clean in the Lord’s sight; how much less human beings (Job 25:5–6), whose life is a time of testing?

Woe to us: as often as we desire, so often do we commit fornication.

He says: “My sword is drunk in heaven” (Isa. 34:5)—much more so on earth, which produces thorns and thistles.

The chosen vessel, from whose mouth Christ resounded, disciplines his body and brings it into subjection (1 Cor. 9:27). Yet he sees the natural heat of the flesh resisting his judgment, so that he is compelled to do what he does not wish; and, as though suffering violence, he cries out and says: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the body of this death?” (Rom. 7:24).

And do you imagine that you can pass without falling or being wounded unless you guard your heart with every vigilance and say with the Savior: “My mother and my brothers are these who do the will of my Father” (Matt. 12:50; Mark 3:35)?

This cruelty is piety. Indeed, what is so pious as for a holy mother to safeguard a holy son?

She also wishes you to live and, for a time, not to see you, so that she may see you forever with Christ.

Hannah gave birth to Samuel not for herself but for the Tabernacle (1 Sam. 2).

The sons of Jonadab, who did not drink wine or strong drink, who lived in tents and had dwellings wherever night compelled them to stay, are written about in the Psalm (Ps. 70 according to the Septuagint) as having been the first to endure captivity, since they were forced to enter the cities by the Chaldean army devastating Judaea.

[Note: [Col. 1076] He refers to the title of Psalm 70 according to the Septuagint, which bears the inscription: “For the sons of Jonadab and of those first taken captive.” In the Vulgate: “For the sons of Jonadab and the first captives.” See Letter 58 to Paulinus, near the end.]

### 8.

Let others see what they think. For each person is led by his own judgment. For me, the town is a prison, and solitude is paradise. Why do we desire the crowds of cities, when we are counted among those who live apart? Moses was trained for forty years in the wilderness so that he might preside over the Jewish people (Exod. 3); he became a shepherd of human beings from being a shepherd of sheep (Luke 5:10). The Apostles passed from fishing in the lake of Gennesaret to fishing for human beings. Then—according to another reading, “those who then had”—a father, a net, and a little boat, they followed the Lord and immediately abandoned everything, carrying their cross daily and not even having a staff in their hands.[^c0122-1]

I say this so that, even if the desire for the clerical state tempts you, you may learn what you can teach and offer Christ a reasonable sacrifice: do not be a soldier before you have been a recruit, nor a teacher before you have been a disciple. It is not for me, nor within my competence, to judge the clergy or to say anything unfavorable about the ministers of the churches. Let them have their order and rank; if you maintain that rank, the book addressed to Nepotianus (Epistle 52) can teach you how you ought to live in it. For now we are examining the beginnings and practices of the monk—and of a monk who, educated in the liberal arts during adolescence, placed the yoke of Christ upon his neck.

### 9. Praise of the Coenobitic Life

The first matter to consider is whether you ought to live alone or with others in a monastery. For my part, I approve your having the companionship of holy men, and that you should not teach yourself or enter without a guide[^c0122-26] upon a road you have never traveled. Otherwise you may immediately turn aside in one direction or another, become exposed to error, and walk more or less than necessary—either exhausting yourself by running or falling asleep because of delay.

In solitude pride quickly creeps in. If someone fasts for a little while and sees no human being, he thinks himself a person of importance. Forgetful of himself, he wanders inwardly in his heart and outwardly with his tongue, forgetting both where he came from and where he is going. Against the Apostle’s will, he judges other people’s servants; he stretches out his hand wherever gluttony directs; he sleeps as long as he wishes; he respects no one and does whatever he wishes; he considers everyone beneath him. More often he is in the cities than in his cell, and among the crowds of the streets he is battered, though among the brothers he pretends modesty.

What, then? Do we condemn the solitary life? Certainly not, since we have often praised it. But we wish soldiers of this kind to emerge from the training ground of monasteries—men whom the harsh beginnings of the wilderness do not frighten; who have given a long demonstration of their way of life; who have been the least of all so that they might become the first of all; whom neither hunger nor satiety has ever overcome; who rejoice in poverty; whose clothing, speech, face, gait, and instruction are lessons in virtue; who, unlike certain foolish men, do not invent fantastic stories about demons fighting against them, in order to make themselves seem miraculous to the ignorant and the common people and then pursue profits from it.

### 10.

Recently we saw—and mourned—the wealth of a Croesus exposed by the death of a single man: the city’s contributions, gathered as though for the use of the poor, left behind for his family and descendants.[^c0122-2] Then the iron that lay hidden in the depths floated to the surface of the water, and the bitterness of Merrha was revealed among the palm trees.[^c0122-3] Nor is this surprising: he had such a companion and teacher, one who made the hunger of the needy his own wealth and reserved what had been abandoned to the wretched for his own misery. Their cry at last reached heaven and overcame the long-suffering ears of God, so that an evil angel, sent to Nabal of Carmel, said: “Fool, this night they will take your life from you; and the things you have prepared—whose will they be?” (Luke 12:2).

### 11.

I therefore want you, for the reasons I explained above, not to live with your mother—especially so that you do not either grieve her by refusing the delicate foods she offers or, if you accept them, add fuel to the fire; and so that, amid the company of girls, you do not see by day what you will think about at night.

Let a book never leave your hands or your eyes. Learn the Psalter word for word; pray without ceasing; keep your mind vigilant and closed to empty thoughts. Let body and soul alike be directed toward the Lord. Conquer anger through patience. Love knowledge of the Scriptures, and you will not love the vices of the flesh. Do not let your mind lie open to various disturbances; if they settle in your breast, they will rule you and lead you into the greatest sin.[^c0122-5]

Do some work, so that the devil may always find you occupied. If the Apostles, though they had the power to live from the Gospel,[^c0122-27] worked with their hands so as not to burden anyone, and gave relief to others from whom they ought to have reaped material things in return for spiritual things (1 Cor. 9:11), why do you not prepare something that will serve your own needs? Weave either a little basket from rushes, or plait a basket from supple willow branches. Let the ground be dug; let the garden beds be divided by an even boundary. When seeds of vegetables have been sown in them, or plants set out in rows, let channels of water be led through them, so that you may stand as a spectator of the most beautiful verses:

> Behold, from the brow of the sloping path she draws  
> A stream of water; as it falls, it raises a hoarse murmur  
> Over the smooth rocks and tempers the parched fields with its springs.  
> *(Georgics 3)*

Graft unfruitful trees with buds or shoots,[^c0122-7] so that after a short time you may gather the sweet fruit of your labor. Build hives for bees, to which Solomon’s Proverbs send you (Prov. 6:8, according to the Septuagint), and learn in their tiny bodies the order of monasteries and the discipline of a kingdom. Let linen nets also be woven for catching fish; let books be written, so that the hand may produce food and the mind be filled with reading.[^c0122-6] “Every idle person is in desires” (Prov. 13:14, according to the Septuagint).

The monasteries of the Egyptians observe this practice: they receive no one without the labor of work—not so much because of the need for food as because of the salvation of the soul. The mind must not wander through destructive thoughts and, like Jerusalem the prostitute, spread its legs to every passerby (Ezek. 17:23).

### 12.

When I was young and the deserts of solitude enclosed me, I could not endure the incentives of vice and the heat of nature. Although I broke them through frequent fasts, my mind still seethed with thoughts. To subdue it, I placed myself under the discipline of a certain brother who had believed as one of the Hebrews, so that after the refinements of Quintilian, the torrents of Cicero, the gravity of Fronto, and the elegance of Pliny, I might learn the alphabet and practice harsh, breathy words.

My conscience bears witness to how much labor I expended there, what difficulty I endured, how often I despaired, how often I stopped, and how, through the struggle to learn, I began again—my conscience, both mine, who suffered these things, and that of those who shared my life. I give thanks to the Lord that from the bitter seed of literature I am now harvesting sweet fruits.

### 13.

I will also mention something else that I saw in Egypt. There was a Greek youth in a coenobium who could extinguish the flame of the flesh by no abstinence and no amount of work.[^c0122-8] The father of the monastery saved this endangered youth by the following device: he ordered a serious man to attack him with quarrels and insults and, after inflicting the injury, to be the first to come forward with a complaint. Witnesses were summoned, and they spoke in favor of the man who had committed the insult.[^c0122-9]

The youth began to weep against the lie, because no one believed the truth. Only the father cunningly put forward his defense, lest the brother be swallowed up by excessive grief. What more need be said? A year passed in this way. When it was over, the youth was asked whether he still suffered any trouble from his former thoughts. “Good heavens,” he replied, “I am not allowed to live—and to fornicate?” If he had been alone, with whose help would he have overcome it?

### 14.

The philosophers of the world commonly drive out an old love by means of a new love, as though driving out a nail with another nail.[^c0122-10] The seven leading Persians did the same for King Ahasuerus, suppressing his desire for Queen Vashti through love of other girls (Esth. 2:3). They cure vice with vice and sin with sin; we should overcome vices through love of virtues.

“Turn away from evil,” he says, “and do good” (Ps. 36:37); “Seek peace and pursue it.” Unless we hate evil, we cannot love the good. Rather, good must be done so that we may turn away from evil. Peace must be sought so that we may flee wars. Nor is it enough to seek it unless, once found and fleeing from us, we pursue it with every effort—peace that surpasses all understanding. In it is the dwelling of God, as the Prophet says: “His dwelling has become in peace” (Ps. 75:2).

The pursuit of peace is beautifully expressed, in accordance with the Apostle’s words, “pursuing hospitality” (Rom. 12:13): we are not to invite guests with a light and customary phrase, merely with the tips of our lips, but to hold them with the full ardor of our minds, as though they were taking away with them something from our profit and gain.[^c0122-11]

### 15.

No art is learned without a teacher. Even mute animals and herds of wild beasts follow their leaders. Among bees there are rulers; cranes follow one leader in an ordered, letter-shaped formation.[^c0122-12] There is one emperor and one judge for a province. From the time it was founded, Rome could not have two brothers as kings at once, and it dedicated itself to parricide. In Rebecca’s womb Esau and Jacob waged war (Gen. 25:22).

Each church has its own bishop; each has its own archpriest and archdeacon. Every ecclesiastical order rests upon its own leaders. In a ship there is one helmsman; in a house one master; in however large an army, the sign of one commander is awaited. And lest I weary the reader by repeating more examples, the whole argument tends toward this: I wish to teach you that you must not be left to your own judgment, but must live in a monastery under the discipline of one father and in the fellowship of many, so that you may learn humility from one person and patience from another; one may teach you silence, another gentleness.

Do not do what you wish. Eat what you are ordered to eat; wear what you are given; discharge the task assigned to you; submit to someone to whom you do not wish to submit; come to bed exhausted; walk while you sleep; and, before your sleep is completed—or, according to another reading, only then—be compelled to rise. Say the Psalm in your proper order.[^c0122-13] In this, not sweetness of voice but affection of mind is sought, as the Apostle says: “I will sing with the spirit, and I will sing with the mind” (1 Cor. 14:15), and, “Singing in your hearts to the Lord.” For he had read that the command was: “Sing wisely.”

Serve the brothers; wash the feet of guests. When you have suffered an injury, remain silent. Fear the superior of the monastery as a lord, and love him as a parent. Believe that whatever he commands you is for your salvation. Do not judge the decision of your superiors, since your duty is to obey and fulfill what has been ordered. Moses says: “Hear, Israel, and be silent” (Deut. 27:9, according to the Septuagint).

Occupied with so many tasks, you will have no leisure for empty thoughts. As you pass from one activity to another and one task succeeds another, you will keep in mind only what you are compelled to do.

### 16. False Monks

I myself have seen certain men who, after renouncing the world, changed nothing of their former way of life except their clothing and the profession of their voice, not their deeds. Their household property was increased rather than diminished. The same services of slaves, the same preparation for banquets. Gold is eaten from glass and earthenware, and amid crowds and swarms of servants they claim for themselves the name of solitaries.

Those who are poor and possess only a small amount of property, yet consider themselves clever, proceed into public resembling the bearers of ceremonial vessels, so that they may practice a doglike eloquence.[^c0122-14] Others, with their shoulders raised high, muttering something or other within themselves, and with their eyes fixed in amazement upon the ground, weigh their swollen words—as though, if you added a herald, you would think a prefecture was marching by.[^c0122-15]

Some, through the dampness of their cells, excessive fasts, weariness of solitude, and excessive reading—while their ears ring day and night—turn melancholic and need the remedies of Hippocrates more than our admonitions.

Most cannot give up their former trades and business dealings. Changing only the names of their shops, they carry on the same commerce, pursuing not the food and clothing prescribed by the Apostle (2 Tim. 6), but profits greater than those of worldly people. Formerly the aediles, whom the Greeks call *agoranomoi*, restrained the frenzy of sellers, and wrongdoing did not go unpunished. Now unjust profits—or, according to another reading, unjust commercial dealings—are conducted under the title of religion, and the honor of the Christian name produces fraud more than it endures.

And what one is ashamed to say, but must say so that at least in this way we may blush for our disgrace: publicly extending our hands, we cover gold with rags; and contrary to everyone’s expectation, we die rich, with full purses, though we lived as though poor.

When you are in a monastery, you will not be permitted to do these things. As the habit gradually grows upon you, what at first you were compelled to do you will begin to do willingly, and your labor will delight you. Forgetting the past, you will always pursue what lies ahead, considering not what evil others are doing but what good you ought to do.

### 17. Praise of the Clergy

Do not let the multitude of sinners lead you astray, nor let the crowd of those who are perishing trouble you, so that you silently think: “What, then? Will everyone who lives in the cities perish?” Look: they enjoy their possessions, serve the churches, go to the baths, and do not reject perfumes; yet they are on everyone’s lips.

I have already answered this, and now I answer briefly: in this little work I am not discussing the clergy but instructing a monk. The clergy are holy, and the life of all of them is worthy of praise. Therefore act and live in the monastery so that you may deserve to become a cleric; so that you do not stain your adolescence with any defilement; so that you may proceed to Christ’s altar like a virgin from her bridal chamber; and so that you may have a good reputation among outsiders—so that women may know your name but not know your face.

When you reach mature age, if your life has accompanied you faithfully, and either the people or the bishop of the city chooses you for the clergy, perform the duties of a cleric and, among the clergy themselves, follow the better men. For in every condition and rank the best are mixed with the worst.

### 18. What Must Be Avoided

Do not rush forward to write, and do not be led by a light madness. Learn for a long time what you are going to teach. Do not believe your flatterers; indeed, do not willingly lend an ear to your mockers. When they have warmed you with flatteries and, so to speak, made you incapable of self-control, if you suddenly look behind you, you will discover either the necks of storks bent behind you, or a hand waving donkey’s ears, or the tongue of a panting dog thrust out.[^c0122-17]

Do not disparage anyone, and do not think yourself holy because you tear others apart. We often accuse others of what we ourselves do; eloquent against ourselves, we attack our own vices and, while mute, judge the eloquent.

Grunnius proceeded with a tortoise-like pace when he spoke, plucking out only a few words at intervals, so that you would think he was hiccupping rather than speaking. Yet when the table had been set and he had displayed a heap of books, with raised eyebrows, contracted nostrils, and wrinkled forehead, he snapped his fingers as a signal inviting his pupils to listen. Then he poured forth mere nonsense and declaimed against individuals. You would have said that he was a Longinus in criticism and a censor of Roman eloquence, marking anyone he wished and excluding him from the senate of learned men.[^c0122-18]

This man, who was well supplied with money, was more welcome at dinners.[^c0122-19] Nor is it surprising: one who was accustomed to bait many people, surrounded by a crowd of noisy chatterers, proceeded into public—Nero within, Cato without. He was wholly ambiguous, so that you would have said one monster and one new beast had been formed from contrary and differing natures, in accordance with the poetic line:

> In front a lion, behind a dragon, and in the middle a chimera.[^c0122-20]

### 19.

Therefore never look upon such men, associate yourself with people of this sort, or incline your heart to words of wickedness. Do not hear: “You sat and spoke against your brother, and you placed a stumbling-block against the son of your mother.” And again: “The sons of men—their teeth are weapons and arrows” (Ps. 56:5). And elsewhere: “His words are softer than oil, yet they are darts” (Ps. 54:22). And more plainly in Ecclesiastes: “As a serpent bites in silence, so does one who secretly slanders his brother” (Eccl. 10:11).

But you will say: “I do not slander him myself. What can I do when others are speaking?” We use such excuses “to make excuses for sins” (Ps. 140:4). Christ is not deceived by cleverness. It is not my judgment but the Apostle’s: “Do not be deceived: God is not mocked” (Gal. 6:7). He sees the heart; we see the face.

Solomon says in Proverbs: “The north wind drives away clouds, and a sad face the tongues of slanderers” (Prov. 25:23). For just as an arrow, if shot against hard material, sometimes rebounds upon the one who shot it and wounds the wounding hand, so the saying is fulfilled: “They became for me a crooked bow” (Ps. 77:57). And elsewhere: “Whoever throws a stone upward will have it fall upon his own head” (Eccl. 27:28).

So also, when a slanderer sees a sad face in the listener—or rather, not even a listener, but someone stopping up his ears so as not to hear the judgment of blood—he immediately falls silent. His face grows pale, his lips stick together, and his saliva dries up. Hence the same wise man says: “Do not associate with slanderers, because their destruction will come suddenly; and who knows the ruin of both?” (Prov. 24:21)—that is, both of the one who speaks and of the one who listens to the speaker.

Truth does not love corners, nor does it seek whisperers. Timothy is told: “Do not quickly receive an accusation against an elder.”[^c0122-28] But “those who are sinning rebuke before everyone, so that the others may have fear” (1 Tim. 5:19–20). It is not easy to believe accusations against advanced age, which is defended both by its past life and by the honorable name of its dignity. Yet because we are human and sometimes fall into the vices of children despite the maturity of our years, if you wish to correct me when I have done wrong, rebuke me openly—only do not bite me in secret.

“Let the righteous rebuke me in mercy and reprove me; but let the oil of the sinner not make my head fat” (Ps. 140:5). “The Lord chastises the one whom he loves, and he scourges every son whom he receives” (Prov. 3:12). Through Isaiah the Lord cries out: “My people, those who call you blessed deceive you and overturn the paths of your feet” (Isa. 3:11).

What benefit is it to me if you report my faults to others? If, while I am unaware, you wound someone else with my sins—or rather, with your slanders—and, while telling everyone in turn, speak to each person as though you had told no one else? This is not to correct me; it is to satisfy your own vice.

The Lord commands that sinners be rebuked to their face, privately or with a witness present; and if they refuse to listen, that the matter be reported to the church, and that those who persist in evil be treated as pagans and tax collectors (Matt. 18).

### 20.

I speak more explicitly about these things so that I may free my young man from the itch of the tongue and the ears, and present him, reborn in Christ, without wrinkle or stain, like a chaste virgin, pure in mind as well as in body. Let him not boast merely in name and, with the lamp of good works extinguished, be shut out from the bridegroom for lack of oil.

You have there the holy and most learned bishop Proculus,[^c0122-21] who by his living and present voice surpasses my little writings and can direct your journey through daily discourses. He will not allow you, by turning aside in another direction, to abandon the royal road by which Israel, hurrying toward the promised land, promises that it will pass.

Would that the voice of the Church making its plea might be heard: “Lord, give us peace; for you have given us all things” (Isa. 16, according to the Septuagint).[^c0122-29] Would that our renunciation of the world were a matter of will rather than necessity, and that poverty possessed the glory of being sought rather than the torment of being imposed.

In view of the miseries of this age and the swords raging everywhere, the man who does not lack bread is rich enough. He is powerful enough who is not compelled to serve.

The holy Exuperius, bishop of Toulouse, an imitator of the widow of Zarephath, feeds others while hungry. With a face pale from fasting, he is tormented by another’s hunger, and he has distributed all his substance among the members of Christ. No one is richer than the man who carries the Lord’s—or, according to another reading, Christ’s—Body in a wicker basket and the Blood in a glass.[^c0122-22]

He drove avarice from the Temple; without a whip and without rebuke, he overturned the seats of those selling doves—that is, the gifts of the Holy Spirit—and the tables of mammon, and scattered the money-changers’ coins, so that the house of God might be called a house of prayer and not a den of thieves.

Follow his footsteps at close hand, and those of the others who resemble him in virtue—men whom the priesthood makes both humbler and poorer. Or, if you desire perfection, go out with Abraham from your country and your kindred, and go where you do not know. If you have possessions, sell them and give to the poor. If you have none, you have been freed from a great burden: follow the naked Christ naked. It is hard, great, difficult—but the rewards are great.

## Epistle 126[^c0122-23]

### To Marcellinus and Anapsychia[^c0122-30]

He explains differing opinions concerning the origin of the soul, urging them to seek the rest from Augustine and indicating the studies with which he himself is occupied.

To my truly holy lords and sons, venerable for every expression of affection and service, Marcellinus and Anapsychia, Jerome sends greetings in Christ.

### 1.

At last I received from your Africa a letter expressing your mutual affection. I do not regret the boldness with which, although you remained silent,[^c0122-31] I repeatedly thrust my letters upon you, so that I might deserve a reply and learn that you were safe—not through reports from others, but chiefly through your own words.

I remember your little question concerning the state of the soul—or rather, a question of the greatest ecclesiastical importance: Did the soul fall from heaven, as the philosopher Pythagoras, all the Platonists, and Origen believe? Or does it come from God’s own substance, as the Stoics, Mani, and the Spanish heresy of Priscillian suspect? Or are souls held in God’s treasury, created long ago, as certain churchmen foolishly persuade themselves?[^c0122-24] Or are they made daily by God and sent into bodies, according to what is written in the Gospel: “My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John 5:17)? Or, certainly, do they arise by transmission, as Tertullian, Apollinaris, and the greater part of the Westerners maintain—so that, just as body comes from body, soul is born from soul and exists under a condition like that of irrational animals?[^c0122-25]

I know that I wrote what I thought about this in the works composed against Rufinus, in the book[^c0122-32] that he gave—or, according to another reading, published—for the holy memory of Anastasius, bishop of the Roman Church. In it, while attempting through a slippery and deceitful—or rather foolish—confession to mock the simplicity of his hearers, he mocked his own faith, or rather his own faithlessness. I think your holy father Oceanus possesses those books. They were published long ago, replying to many of Rufinus’s books against his accusers.

Certainly you have there the holy and learned bishop Augustine, who, as they say, can teach you by his living voice and explain both his own position and, indeed, our position through himself.

[^c0122-1]: The note argues that *daily* (*quotidie*) is supported by ancient manuscripts. Jerome himself makes this point in the immediately following Epistle 127 to Principia. The reference seems to be Luke 9:23, where most Greek manuscripts omit “daily,” while the Latin and other interpreters include it. Others refer the addition to Matthew 16:24 or Luke 14:27.

[^c0122-2]: The note says that the passage elegantly alludes to the story of Elisha, whose intervention caused the iron lost by one of the sons of the prophets while cutting wood to rise to the surface of the water. It further explains that the reading *Merrhae* has been restored by conjecture, since all printed editions and manuscripts previously had *Myrrhae*. See Exodus 15:23ff. Earlier copyists, unfamiliar with the name of the spring Merrha—or Mara in the Vulgate—easily confused it with *Myrrha* because of the similarity of the name and the association with bitterness. Jerome and other Latin books are consequently often corrupt where they allude to this passage.

[^c0122-3]: The note explains that the Verona manuscript places *sicut* before *Nabal Carmelio*, and that Jerome compares Nabal, who refused food to David and his companions and was struck by an angel, learnedly with the rich man in the Gospel. The two stories are indicated by a single expression. For *auferent*, another reading has *repetent*, in accordance with the Vulgate.

[^c0122-4]: The biblical wording is drawn from Luke 12:20; the note observes that one manuscript reads “they will take your life from you,” and that the passage combines Nabal’s story with that of the rich fool.

[^c0122-5]: The note says that Jerome calls an evil thought carried out in deed the greatest sin, as in Epistle 130 to Demetrias and in his commentary on Ecclesiastes 10, deriving the point from Psalm 18: “If they have not ruled over me, then I shall be blameless and cleansed from the greatest sin.”

[^c0122-6]: The note cites Stephen’s Rule, chapter 38, and attributes the maxim to Solomon: “Since a monk who is idle in body can never be idle in mind from sordid thoughts, Solomon says: ‘In desires is every idle person.’” The wording occurs only in the Greek Septuagint: “Every idle person is in desires” (Prov. 13:4). Cassian also cites it in *Conferences* 24.11. Elsewhere, in his commentary on Ezekiel 16, Jerome has “every idle soul” instead of “every idle person.”

[^c0122-7]: The note refers to Trithemius, *On the Praise of Manual Writing*, chapter 5, and to the Rule of Saint Ferriolus, chapter 28: “Let the one who does not mark the page with his finger mark the earth with the plow; for whoever cannot practice agriculture can read and write—which is the chief work—and can also arrange the catching of fish and perform similar tasks.” It also refers to Sulpicius Severus’s *Life of Saint Martin* and Palladius’s *Lausiac History*, chapter 86.

[^c0122-8]: Another reading has *continentia*, “self-restraint,” instead of *abstinentia*, “abstinence.”

[^c0122-9]: The note says that Martianus found the wording “he began to weep against the lie” objectionable because no one would believe the truth, and therefore tried to add two words, “began” and “tried.” Most manuscripts, however, omit both or retain only one. The Verona manuscript, among others, omits them; those who know Latin understand the intended sense more elegantly without them, contrary to Martianus, who thought the sense was lost and the passage became full of solecisms.

[^c0122-10]: The note cites Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* 4.35: “Some people think that an old love must be driven out by a new love, as a nail is driven out by a nail,” and Ovid, *Remedies for Love*: “One love takes away the strength of another.”

[^c0122-11]: The note says that the earlier text read “as though displaying themselves with profit.” The Verona manuscript offers the preferable reading: “as though taking away with them something from our profit,” since guests should be retained not as though they offered themselves, but as though they took away our profit and therefore must be held with the full ardor of the mind.

[^c0122-12]: The note cites Pliny, *Natural History* 10.23, on the order of cranes in flight: “The formation stretches out behind, gradually widening into a wedge. Arranged in this order, they represent the letter Y, whose point is formed by the leader; hence they are commonly called the birds of Palamedes.” Claudian likewise writes:

> Through the clouds a letter is woven by wings in varied ranks,  
> And the air is inscribed with the marks of feathers.

[^c0122-13]: The note observes that this differs from contemporary practice, in which one person begins or leads and many others sing whole psalms responsively. In many churches formerly, monks or clergy did not all sing together: one sang while the others listened attentively and did not respond. For Jerome and later authorities, to say a Psalm “in one’s order” means to say it individually, according to one’s assigned order. Jerome wrote in the preface to the Rule of Saint Pachomius: “Whoever first enters the monastery sits first, walks first, and says the Psalm first.” Similar practices are confirmed in the rules of Macarius, Saint Fructuosus, and Saint Benedict. The custom came from the Egyptian monks, among whom it especially flourished. Cassian writes that one person rises in the midst to sing the psalms while all sit, and that such silence prevails that, apart from the one singing, no human being seems to be present.

[^c0122-14]: The note derives the image from Cicero, *On Duties* 1.36: “Care must be taken not to use a slower pace in walking so that we may seem like the bearers of ceremonial dishes.” Such vessels were carried in processions containing images of the gods, spoils of enemies, and similar objects. The reference to doglike eloquence or the malicious speech of Appius was explained above from Quintilian. The final image also echoes Persius:

> With head bent forward and eyes fixed upon the ground,  
> They weigh their words with an outstretched lip.  
> “I do not know what weighty thing you are muttering with me, fool.”

[^c0122-15]: The note cites Symmachus, *Letters* 1, where a herald announced everywhere the arrival of the prefecture, and Cassiodorus, *Divine Institutions* 2 and *Variae* 6, in the formula of the Praetorian Prefecture: “Even today the herald’s voice resounds, instructing the judge not to allow himself to be unlike it.”

[^c0122-16]: The note says that the Verona manuscript has the reading “unjust profits,” while another reading has “unjust commercial dealings.”

[^c0122-17]: The note derives the three modes of mockery from Persius, *Satires* 1:

> O Janus, whom no stork has pecked from behind,  
> Whose mobile hand has not imitated white ears,  
> And whose tongue is not so thirsty as that of an Apulian dog.

[^c0122-18]: The note says that *Creticus* was corrupt and has been emended on contextual grounds and on the authority of Latinius. Longinus was not a Cretan but perhaps an Emesene, and there would be no reason here to mention his homeland. By contrast, just as Aristarchus was a famous name among ancient critics, so was Longinus; he was especially renowned as an extremely exact critic. The proverbial expression “not to judge according to Longinus” means to judge rashly. Another reading proposed by Gravius is *Censorium*, “censorial,” instead of *Censoremque*.

[^c0122-19]: Another manuscript reading is “That one pleased him more,” with reference to lunches or dinner parties.

[^c0122-20]: The note identifies the verse as adapted from Hesiod’s *Theogony* 323 or Homer’s *Iliad* 6.181:

> In front a lion, behind a dragon, and in the middle a she-goat.

The note adds that the Latin image is also found in Lucretius, book 5.

[^c0122-21]: The note identifies Proculus as the bishop of Marseille. He had acquired a considerable reputation for holiness, and the Council of Turin had granted him the privilege of presiding over bishops whom he claimed to have ordained, as a father over his sons. Later, however, he incurred great hostility by assuming metropolitan authority and was condemned by Pope Zosimus. See the three papal letters to Patroclus, bishop of Arles.

[^c0122-22]: The note praises Exuperius similarly in the preceding Epistle 123 to Ageruchia, where Jerome complains of the barbarian invasions in comparable terms. Pope Innocent’s notable letter beginning “Consulting you” was addressed to him.

[^c0122-23]: Another numbering is 82. The letter was written in 411.

[^c0122-24]: The note identifies possible proponents of the view that souls were created long ago and stored in God’s treasury: Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* 2 and 3; Pierius of Alexandria, as reported by Photius, codex 119; Nemesius, *On the Nature of Man* 2–3; Gregory of Nyssa, *On the Making of Man* 28; and others. Rufinus attempted to draw Jerome into this view from several passages in his commentary on Ephesians. Jerome responds in books 2 and 3 of his *Apology*, turning the accusation back against Rufinus. See Allatius’s notes to Methodius, p. 389ff.

[^c0122-25]: The note says that Nemesius, chapter 2, reports that Apollinaris held that souls are generated from souls just as bodies are generated from bodies. Compare Athanasius, *On the Incarnation of Christ*, against Apollinaris, and Augustine’s following Epistle 131 to Jerome, concerning the origin of the soul.

[^c0122-26]: The earlier text read *doctore* (“teacher”); Gravius aptly proposed *ductore* (“guide”).

[^c0122-27]: Isidore in his *Rule*, and certain others, report that the Apostles practised their trades while preaching; Augustine, however, rules otherwise in *On the Work of Monks* 20, where he says that only Paul and Barnabas worked with their hands.

[^c0122-28]: The editor does not know in which manuscripts this reading occurs. Earlier witnesses read “an accusation against an elder” without *do not quickly receive*; Cyprian, Ambrosiaster (Hilary the Deacon), Primasius, and others read similarly. The present editor holds that the concluding words, “do not receive it except on the testimony of two or three witnesses,” should be supplied. Although the Greek text and the Vulgate retain them, some recent writers consider them superfluous; this textual prompt nevertheless lends the reading some support.

[^c0122-29]: Gravius prefers *reddidisti* (“you have rendered”), following the Greek *apédōkas*, in place of *dedisti* (“you have given”).

[^c0122-30]: This Marcellinus was the tribune and notary sent by Honorius to Africa to serve as arbitrator and judge at the Conference of Carthage. Having pronounced judgment against the Donatists, he became the target of their hostility and, though innocent, fell under the suspicion connected with Heraclianus’s tyranny. Jerome laments this at the end of book 3 against the Pelagians.

[^c0122-31]: Letters of this kind have been lost; neither the surviving record nor the age of Marcellinus and Anapsychia preserves the letter to which Jerome now replies concerning the state of the soul.

[^c0122-32]: This is the work beginning “I have heard certain persons …”; it will be printed in its proper place in the following volume, and Jerome answers it at the beginning of the second *Apology*.

## 2.

Long ago I wanted to undertake the volume of Ezekiel and to fulfill my frequent promise to diligent readers; but at the very beginning of dictation my mind was so confounded by the devastation of the provinces of the West, and especially of the city of Rome [or: Roman], that, according to the common proverb, I did not even know the proper word for anything; and for a long time I remained silent, knowing that it was a time for tears.

This year, however, after I had explained three books, a sudden onslaught of the barbarians—of whom your Virgil says, “the Barcaeans roaming far and wide” (*Aeneid* 4)—and of whom Holy Scripture says concerning Ishmael, “He shall dwell in the presence of all his brethren” (Gen. 16:12), swept along like a torrent over the borders of Egypt, Palestine, Phoenicia, and Syria, dragging everything with it, so that we scarcely escaped their hands through the mercy of Christ.

And if, according to the famous orator, “the laws are silent amid arms” (Cicero, *Pro Milone*), how much more the study of the Scriptures? It requires both an abundance of books and silence, the diligence of scribes, and—what is especially necessary—security and leisure for those dictating.

I have therefore sent two books to my holy daughter Fabiola [Note: May I see this same woman—the one to whom Augustine writes in Letter 267—certainly different from the one to whom our Author gave those letters on Priestly Dress and on the Mansions. Yet it is remarkable that Oceanus, so indispensable to this Fabiola, is mentioned in the following section of this letter.] You may borrow copies from her if you wish. Because of the pressure of time, I could not have others copied [or: other exemplars]. When you have read them and seen the vestibules, it will be easy to conjecture what the house itself will be like.

But I trust in the mercy of God, who helped us at the very difficult beginning of the work mentioned above, that he will also help us in the penultimate parts of the Prophet, where the wars of Gog and Magog are related, and in the final parts, where the construction, variety, and measurements of the most holy and inexplicable temple are described.

## 3.

Our holy brother Oceanus, to whose good offices you wish to be commended, is so great and so distinguished, and so learned in the Law of the Lord, that without any request from us he can instruct you and explain, according to the measure of our common understanding, our judgment on all the questions of Scripture.

May Christ our God almighty protect you unharmed and flourishing through a long life, truly holy servants of the Lord.

# LETTER CXXVII

[Note: Alternatively numbered 16. Written in A.D. 412.]

## TO THE VIRGIN PRINCIPIA, OR THE EPITAPH OF THE WIDOW MARCELLA

He praises Marcella, a woman of the highest nobility, who, widowed in the seventh month after her marriage, afterward rejected the consul Cerealis, who sought her hand, and was the first among noblewomen at Rome to profess the monastic life, drawing many others to the same way of life. Then, from Jerome himself, she learned the divine Scriptures most diligently at Rome. She often wrote to him when he was absent; and finally, through her efforts, the party of the Origenists—which had begun to gain strength in the city—was exposed and extinguished. She died a few days after the city had been plundered by the Goths.

## 1.

You often and earnestly demand, O virgin of Christ Principia, that I recall in writing the memory of the holy woman Marcella [Note: He calls her “the unique example of widowhood and Roman holiness” in the prologue to his *Commentary on Ephesians* and in the preface to *Daniel*. He calls her Pammachius’ cousin in Letter 48 to Pammachius; he also praises her at length in the preface to *Galatians* and in the preface to his commentary on Ezekiel.] and describe for the knowledge and imitation of others the good which we enjoyed for so long.

I am sufficiently grieved that you urge one who is running of his own accord, and think that I need prayers—although in love for her I shall not yield even to you, and in remembering such virtues shall receive far more benefit than I bestow. For the fact that I have remained silent until now and passed over two years in silence was not, as you wrongly suppose, dissimulation, but inconceivable grief, which so overwhelmed my mind that I judged it better for the moment to remain silent than to say nothing worthy of her praises.

Nor shall I praise your Marcella—rather mine, or, more truly, ours and that of all the saints, the illustrious glory of Rome itself—according to the rules of rhetoricians, by displaying the splendor of her family, the distinction of her ancient blood, and the genealogies extending through consuls and prefects of the praetorium [Note: Victorius reads “through proconsuls.” The consular robes themselves were, of course, especially well known in the family of Marcella.]. I shall praise nothing in her except what is her own, and what became more noble because, despising wealth and nobility, she became more noble through poverty and humility.

## 2.

She was deprived of her father by death, and after her marriage she was also deprived of her husband in the seventh month. When Cerealis [Note: Neratius Cerealis, who was consul with Datianus in the year 358—not, as Baronius thought, the brother of Justin, but of Galla, who was the mother of Gallus Caesar. Hence the ancient author of the letter to Marcella encouraging her to endure adversity, which we shall present in the final volume, says that he saw her at the time when the relationship with Regalius was seeking her hand. See Ammianus, Book XIV, chapter 11.]—whose name is illustrious among the consuls—sought her with particular eagerness because of her age, the antiquity of her family, and the notable beauty of her body, which men especially tend to admire, as well as the moderation of her character, and, being already old, promised her his long-preserved wealth, wishing to transfer it to her not as to a wife but as to a daughter; and when her mother Albina eagerly desired so distinguished a support for her widowed household, Marcella replied:

“If I wished to marry, and did not desire to dedicate myself to perpetual chastity, I would certainly seek a husband, not an inheritance.”

When he sent word that old men too could live a long time, while young men could die quickly, she made this elegant jest:

“A young man indeed can die quickly; but an old man cannot live long.”

Rejected by this reply, he became an example to the others, so that they despaired of obtaining her in marriage.

We read in the Gospel according to Luke:

“There was Anna, a prophetess, the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher. She was advanced in age, having lived with her husband seven years from her virginity, and she was a widow for eighty-four years; she did not depart from the Temple, serving God with fasting and prayers night and day” (Luke 2:36–37).

It is no wonder that she deserved to see the Savior, whom she sought with such great labor.

Let us compare seven years with seven months: to hope for Christ and to possess him; to confess him as born and to believe in him as crucified; not to deny him as a little child and to rejoice in him as a man reigning.

I make no distinction among holy women, as some have foolishly been accustomed to do among holy men and leaders of the churches; but my argument tends toward this end: that since their labor is one, their reward also may be one.

## 3.

It is difficult, in a malicious city and in a city whose people were once the people of the world, not to incur some tale of sinister rumor when they attack the honorable and stain what is pure and clean. Therefore the Prophet, as though desiring something exceedingly difficult and almost impossible, rather than confidently expecting it, says:

“Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord” (Ps. 118:1).

He calls “undefiled in the way of this world” those whom no breath of obscene rumor has stained, who have not received reproach against their neighbors. Concerning such people the Savior says in the Gospel:

“Be well disposed,” or “think favorably,” “toward your adversary while you are with him on the way” (Matt. 5:25).

Who ever heard anything displeasing about this woman, so as to believe it? Who believed anything, without rather condemning himself for malice and defamation?

Through her the pagan world was first confounded, when it became evident to all what Christian widowhood was, since she proclaimed it both by her conscience and by her dress. Pagan women customarily paint their faces with red pigment and white lead, shine in silken garments, glitter with jewels, wear gold around their necks and in their pierced ears, hang from themselves the most precious pearls of the Red Sea [Note: Tertullian, in *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, calls them “the shining grains of the Red Sea.” But soon afterward Victorius and Bollandus read *fragrare musco mure*—“to smell fragrant with musk and civet”—which the latter thinks has the added word *mure* to distinguish it from ordinary musk that clings to rocks and trees. In fact, however, the word is absent here. In *Against Jovinianus*, Book II: “musk and the skin of the foreign civet.”], smell of civet, and mourn their husbands in such a way that in the end they rejoice to have been freed from their domination and seek others—not men whom, according to God’s judgment, they may serve, but men whom they may rule.

For this reason they also choose poor men, so that they may merely seem to have husbands, men who patiently endure their rivals; if they mutter, they are immediately to be cast out.

Our widow used such garments as would keep out the cold, not expose her limbs. She rejected gold except for the seal-ring on her finger, and stored it more in the stomachs of the needy than in purses.

She was never without her mother. She saw no cleric or monk—although the needs of a large household sometimes required their presence—without witnesses. She always had virgins and widows in her company, and those women themselves were of serious character, knowing that the behavior of mistresses is often judged from the wantonness of their girls, and that each person’s character is shown by the company in which she delights.

## 4.

Her zeal for the divine Scriptures was extraordinary, and she was always singing:

“I have hidden your words in my heart, that I may not sin against you” (Ps. 118:11),

and this concerning the perfect man:

“His delight is in the law of the Lord, and on his law he will meditate day and night” (Ps. 1:2).

She understood meditation on the law not as repeating what has been written, as the Pharisees among the Jews suppose, but as putting it into practice, according to the apostolic saying:

“Whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do everything for the glory of the Lord” (1 Cor. 10).

And according to the Prophet’s words:

“From your commandments I have gained understanding” (Ps. 118:104),

so that, after she had fulfilled the commandments, she might know that she deserved understanding of the Scriptures.

We also read elsewhere:

“Jesus began both to do and to teach” (Acts 1:1).

For any distinguished teaching blushes when one’s own conscience condemns it; and in vain does his tongue proclaim poverty and teach almsgiving if he swells with the riches of Croesus, or, covered in a cheap cloak, wages war against moths in silken garments.

Her fasts were moderate, and she abstained from meat. She smelled wine more often than she tasted it, because of her stomach and frequent illnesses (1 Tim. 5) [Note: Alternatively: “moderate fasts,” or “moderate for her,” and so forth.].

She rarely went out in public, and especially avoided the houses of noble matrons, lest she be forced to see what she had despised. She celebrated the basilicas of the Apostles and Martyrs with private prayers, avoiding the crowds of the people.

She was so obedient to her mother that she sometimes did what she did not wish to do. For when her mother neglected her own blood relatives and wished to transfer everything to the children of her brother, Marcella chose the poor, yet could not oppose her mother. She gave necklaces and whatever household goods she possessed to the rich, who would soon lose them, preferring to lose money rather than grieve her parent’s heart.

## 5.

At that time no noblewoman at Rome knew the way of life of the monks, nor did any dare, because of the novelty of the matter, to assume a name considered then disgraceful [Note: Ancient copies, Gravius notes, agree with this reading: “considered then disgraceful,” or “to assume the name of the veiled woman”; but the latter reading does not please him.] and lowly among the people.

From the Alexandrian priests [Note: Victorius reads: “From the Alexandrian priests first.” When Athanasius first came to Rome, around the year 340, there was with him Peter, a presbyter of the Alexandrian Church, who later succeeded Athanasius in the episcopate. Since he was at Rome in 373 or 374, Marcella more probably had him as her teacher of monastic life and followed his practices. Before that, she could have learned examples of monks from Athanasius only by hearsay. Augustine, moreover, in *On the Customs of the Catholic Church*, chapter 33, says: “At Rome he knew several monasteries, in which men distinguished by seriousness, prudence, and divine knowledge presided over the others living with them, who lived in Christian charity, holiness, and freedom.”] and from Pope Athanasius, and afterward from Peter, who, fleeing the persecution of the Arian heresy, had taken refuge at Rome as though at the safest harbor of their communion, she learned the life of the blessed Antony, who was still living at that time, and the discipline of the monasteries in the Thebaid, of Pachomius, and of virgins and widows.

She was not ashamed to profess what she had learned to be pleasing to Christ. Many years later Sophronia [or: Sophronius] and others imitated her; to them Ennius’ saying can be applied most appropriately:

“Would that it had never fallen in the Pelian forest.”

[Note: These words are from the surviving fragments of Ennius’ *Medea*. They are the words of the Nurse, earnestly wishing that the Argonauts had never landed on the shores of Colchis:

“Would that in the Pelian forest, by axes cut down,

the firwood beam had not fallen to the ground;

nor from it had begun the building of the ship

which is now called by the name

Argo, in which the Argive heroes sailed, delightful …”

The opening words, “Would that in the Pelian forest,” although not a complete sentence, passed into a proverb. Cicero used it in *On Ends* I and in the speech *For Caelius*, as did Quintilian, Book V, and others, when lamenting the cause of some misfortune. When Jerome says that Ennius’ words can be applied most appropriately to Sophronia and the others in the Roman monastery, either certain faults had indeed crept in at that time, or he says that the words could be applied by those to whom the institutions of the monks were distasteful—unless one prefers to understand that the proverb can be applied most appropriately, but in another and opposite sense.]

The venerable Paula enjoyed her friendship. Eustochium, the glory of virginity, was raised in her chamber. Thus one can easily judge what sort of teacher she was, when her disciples were such as these.

Perhaps an unbelieving reader will laugh at my lingering over the praises of little women. But if he recalls the holy women, companions of the Lord and Savior, who ministered to him from their possessions, and the three Marys standing before the cross, especially Mary Magdalene, who because of her devotion and ardor of faith received the name “towered one” and was the first among the Apostles to deserve to see Christ risen, he will condemn himself for pride rather than condemn us for foolishness.

We judge virtues not by sex but by character; and we regard despised nobility and wealth as bringing greater glory.

For this reason Jesus also loved John the Evangelist exceedingly, who, because of the nobility of his birth, was known to the high priest and did not fear the plots of the Jews. Thus he introduced Peter into the courtyard, and alone among the Apostles stood before the cross; and the virgin Son received the virgin mother of the Savior into his own [Note: Many manuscript codices read “into his own mother,” in accordance with the Vulgate edition; but more and better copies, following the Greek εἰς τὰ ἴδια, read “into his own possessions,” that is, among the things belonging to him.].

And the Son, a virgin, received the virgin mother as the inheritance of the Lord’s virgin; [and] the virgin mother was received by her virgin son.

## 6.

For many years, therefore, she passed her life in such a way that she saw herself growing old before she could remember having been young, praising that Platonic saying which called philosophy meditation on death.

Hence also our Apostle says:

“Every day I die, for your salvation” (1 Cor. 15:31).

And the Lord, according to ancient copies:

“Unless someone takes up his cross daily and follows me, he cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14:27) [Note: Victorius reports that some think, falsely, that these words have been transposed here in the ancient copies and ought to precede “and the Lord,” so that they would refer to the preceding passage of Paul, which Jerome cited differently from the form current among the Greeks at that time. For present copies have *glory* (*καύχησιν*) instead of “salvation.” This conjecture is not at all attractive; see what we observe in the note on section 19 of the preceding letter to Rusticus.].

And long before, through the Prophet, the Holy Spirit had said:

“For your sake we are put to death all day long; we are regarded as sheep for slaughter” (Rom. 8:36).

And after many generations came the saying:

“Remember the day of death always, and you will never sin” (Ecclesiasticus 7).

And the very eloquent precept of the satirist:

“Live mindful of death; the hour flies; this very thing that I say is already in the past.”

[Note: From Persius, *Satire* 5. Martianus read *laeti* incorrectly, and shortly afterward omitted the word *se* before *hostiam*.]

Thus, as we had begun to say, she led her life and lived as though she always believed herself about to die. She dressed herself in such a way that she remembered the grave, offering herself as a rational, living, and pleasing sacrifice to God.

## 7. When she came to Rome

Finally, when necessity had drawn me to Rome with the holy bishops Paulinus and Epiphanius—the one governing the Church of Antioch in Syria, the other that of Salamis in Cyprus—and I modestly avoided the eyes of noblewomen, she acted, according to the Apostle, “in season and out of season” (2 Tim. 4), so that by her persistence she overcame my modesty.

Because I was then thought to possess some reputation for my study of Scripture, she never met me without asking something about the Scriptures—not so that she might immediately accept my answer, but so that, on the contrary, she might raise questions; not in order to argue, but by asking to learn the solutions to the questions which she understood could be raised.

What virtues, what intelligence, what holiness, what purity I found in her, I fear to say, lest I exceed the credibility of belief and inflict greater sorrow on you as you remember how great a good you have lost.

I shall say only this: whatever had been gathered in us through long study and transformed, as it were, into nature through prolonged meditation—this she sampled, learned, and possessed, so that after our departure, if a dispute arose over some testimony of Scripture, people went to her as judge.

Because she was very wise and knew what philosophers call τὸ πρέπον (*to prepon*), that is, “what is fitting to do,” she answered questions in such a way that she called her own words not her own, but either mine or someone else’s, thereby confessing herself a disciple even in the very thing she was teaching.

For she knew the Apostle’s saying:

“I do not permit a woman to teach” (1 Tim. 2:12) [Note: In a more ancient manuscript this passage is read as follows, and Gravius testifies that the next sentence is joined to it: “Therefore, lest she seem to do an injustice to the male sex, and sometimes to priests asking about obscure and ambiguous matters, she immediately urged them to go to our place. We have heard you …” This reading does not please us, but it should nevertheless be examined more carefully.],

lest she seem to do an injustice to the male sex and, sometimes, to priests who asked about obscure and ambiguous matters.

## 8.

Immediately afterward, we heard that you had attached yourself to her companionship and had never withdrawn from her even by a finger’s breadth, as the saying goes. You shared the same house and the same chamber [Note: Some copies consulted by Victorius read “having used the same bedchamber,” and others, “having used the same room, one bed.”], so that it became known throughout the famous city that you had found in her a mother and she in you a daughter.

The countryside outside the city was your monastery, and the country was chosen as your solitude. You lived in this way for so long that, through your example, we rejoiced that Rome had become Jerusalem by the conversion of many [Note: Victorius prefers “and by the conversion.” Bollandus follows him.].

There were frequent monasteries of virgins and an innumerable multitude of monks, so that, because of the number of those serving God, what had previously been a disgrace afterward became a glory.

Meanwhile we consoled our absence with mutual conversations and returned in spirit what we could not give in the body: always meeting one another through letters, surpassing one another in attentions, and anticipating one another in greetings. Absence lost little when we were joined by constant correspondence.

## 9. The Origenists

In this tranquility and service of the Lord, a heretical storm arose in these provinces and threw everything into confusion. It was stirred to such madness that it spared neither itself nor any good person.

And as though it were not enough to have disturbed everything here, it brought a ship full of blasphemies into the Roman harbor [Note: This refers to the arrival of Rufinus at Rome; he is mentioned again in the second *Apology*.].

It immediately found a pot its lid, and muddy footprints mixed the purest spring of the Roman faith with filth.

It is no wonder if, in the streets and in the marketplace of things for sale, a counterfeit fortune-teller beats the buttocks of fools and shakes the teeth of those who bite, using a twisted staff [Note: The Reatine editor reads *Nares*, and elsewhere the Benedictine editor himself, in *Apology* I, chapter 4, says: “I believe that a counterfeit fortune-teller or mountebank, to make the crowd laugh, was striking the buttocks of some fool, and that, if he wished to bite, he sometimes shook his teeth with a twisted cudgel.” Something similar can be found in Lucian’s *Death of Peregrinus*: “striking and being struck on the buttocks with a fennel stalk, and performing many other youthful tricks.”] when it has found in Rome people whom it could infect with its poisonous and filthy teaching.

Then came the infamous interpretation of the books *On First Principles* (περὶ ἀρχῶν). Then the disciple “Blessed” (ὄλβιος), truly blessed in name, if he had not stumbled upon such a teacher [Note: He alludes to Macarius, a disciple of Rufinus; the name is synonymous in Greek with ὄλβιος, “blessed,” since Rufinus dedicated his translation of *On First Principles* to him.].

Then came the divided opposition of our party [Note: Victorius read in his manuscripts διδακτικῶν, “of teachers,” and following that reading says that he found other copies which had the Greek ἀντίφασις, “contradiction,” in place of the Latin word. Martianus rightly emended the reading to διάλυτος, “dissolved.”], and the school of the Pharisees was thrown into confusion [Note: Perhaps this name alludes to the Roman clergy. Compare the preface to Didymus’ *On the Holy Spirit*.].
