Then holy Marcella, who had long restrained herself lest she seem to act out of rivalry, after she perceived that the faith praised by the apostolic mouth (Rom. 1:18) was being violated in many respects, and that it was drawing even priests, some monks, and especially worldly people into agreement with itself while mocking the simplicity of the bishop [Note: Siricius. See Book III of the *Apology*.], who judged others by his own intelligence, openly resisted it, preferring to please God rather than human beings.

## 10.

The Savior praises the unjust steward in the Gospel because, although he acted fraudulently toward his master, he acted prudently for himself (Luke 16:10).

When the heretics saw that great conflagrations were being kindled from a small spark, and that the fire long kept hidden had already reached the heights, and that what had deceived many could no longer remain concealed, they requested and obtained ecclesiastical letters, so that they might appear to have departed while remaining in communion with the Church.

Not much time passed before the distinguished man Anastasius succeeded to the pontificate. Rome did not deserve to possess him for long, lest the head of the world should be crippled under such a bishop [Note: He held the Roman see for three years and a few days; and the head of the world—that is, Rome—was mutilated under his successor Innocent, or rather Rome was captured by the Goths.].

Indeed, he was taken away and transferred for this reason: so that, once the judgment had been issued, he would not try to bend it by his prayers. For the Lord says to Jeremiah:

“Do not pray for this people, nor ask for their good. For if they fast, I will not hear their prayers; and if they offer burnt offerings and sacrifices, I will not accept them. For by sword, famine, and pestilence I will consume them” (Jer. 14:11–12).

You may ask what this has to do with the praise of Marcella.

This was the beginning of the condemnation of the heretics: she brought forward witnesses who had first been instructed by them and afterward had been corrected from heretical error; she displayed the multitude of those deceived; she produced the impious volumes *On First Principles*, which were shown corrected by the hand of a scorpion; and, although the heretics were summoned by repeated letters to defend themselves, they did not dare to come.

Such was the force of conscience that they preferred to be condemned in their absence rather than be convicted in person [Note: Victorius omits “more,” which is a pleonasm not uncommon among Latin writers. Some therefore confidently infer that Rufinus was not merely accused and summoned to Rome, but also condemned by the judgment of Pope Anastasius. In Book II of his *Apology*, the holy Doctor presses the same letters of the Roman pontiff upon Rufinus, saying, “If you do not wish to hear your brother, hear the bishop condemning you.” These words can, however, be understood conveniently in light of other testimonies of Jerome: he said that Rufinus was condemned only insofar as, when Origen was condemned, those who were entangled in the same errors were regarded as condemned with him. Certainly the letter of Anastasius itself to John of Jerusalem does not strike Rufinus with an anathema, nor is such a thing reported in other ancient documents. Indeed, Rufinus maintained friendship until death with the holiest men—Paulinus of Nola, Chromatius of Aquileia, Gaudentius of Brescia, and others—and it is hardly reasonable to believe that he could have enjoyed their intimacy if he had been bound by the chains of condemnation.].

The origin of this glorious victory was Marcella. You, the head and cause of these good things, know that I am telling the truth. You know that I am saying scarcely a few things out of many, lest an odious repetition weary the reader, and lest I seem, under the pretext of praising another, to be digesting my own anger before hostile people.

I shall proceed to the rest.

## 11.

From the regions of the West the storm crossed over into the East and threatened many with great shipwrecks. Then the saying was fulfilled:

“When the Son of Man comes, do you think he will find faith upon the earth?” (Luke 18:8).

As the love of many grew cold, the few who loved the truth of the faith joined our side. Their heads were publicly demanded; all resources were prepared against them, so that even Barnabas was drawn into that pretense, or rather into the open crime of parricide, which he committed not by physical strength but by will [Note: It is difficult to determine whether under the name Barnabas he means Rufinus or John of Jerusalem. Certainly he suggests a formerly very dear friend who afterward separated from him as Barnabas separated from Paul; this fits Rufinus especially well. He also hints at an attempt on his life, which likewise suits Rufinus, concerning whom he says in his third book of the *Apology*: “You threaten me with death unless I remain silent.” But John too had threatened Jerome with such violence, as is clear from the book to Pammachius and from Letter 82 to Theophilus against him. What follows below can very well refer to the same man. Huetius, *Origeniana* II, section 2, thinks that John Chrysostom is obscurely attacked under the name Barnabas: when he had kindly received the fifty Origenists expelled by Theophilus, he also supported them by his influence with Arcadius and Eudoxia against the envoys of Theophilus, who, convicted of slander and severely beaten, were thrust into prison and shortly afterward deported to the island of Proconnesus, as Palladius relates.].

And behold, the whole storm was destroyed when the Lord blew upon it, and the prophetic oracle was fulfilled:

“You will take away their spirit, and they will fail and return to their dust” (Ps. 103:29).

“On that day all their thoughts will perish” (Ps. 145:4).

And the Gospel saying:

“Fool, this night your soul will be taken from you; and whose will those things be which you have prepared?” (Luke 12:20).

## 12.

While these things were happening in Jebus—that is, Jerusalem—a terrible report came from the West: Rome was under siege [Note: Namely, in the year 409, by Alaric, king of the Goths. The Roman people had redeemed their safety from him, though he could have invaded and plundered the city, with an immense quantity of gold and silver. But the following year, when Honorius rejected the terms of peace offered by Alaric, he again besieged Rome and plundered it. See the preceding letters 123 to Ageruchia and 125 to Rusticus, among others.], and the safety of the citizens had been bought with gold, while those already stripped of their possessions were once again surrounded, so that after their property they might lose their lives as well.

My voice sticks, and sobs interrupt the words of the one dictating. The City is captured which had captured the whole world; indeed, it perishes from hunger before the sword, and scarcely a few are found to be taken captive.

The fury of the starving broke out into unspeakable foods, and they tore one another’s limbs, while a mother did not spare her nursing infant and received back into her womb the child whom she had shortly before brought forth [or: “and received her own child back.”].

At night Moab was captured; at night its wall fell (Isa. 15:1).

“O God, the nations have entered your inheritance; they have defiled your holy temple. They have made Jerusalem into a place for keeping fruit. They have given the corpses of your servants as food to the birds of heaven, and the flesh of your holy ones to the beasts of the earth. They have poured out their blood like water around Jerusalem, and there was no one to bury them” (Ps. 78:1ff.).

> Who could tell the disaster of that night, who could express its deaths in words,
>
> or match the grief with tears?
>
> The ancient city falls, which ruled for many years;
>
> countless inert bodies are scattered everywhere through the streets,
>
> through the houses, and everywhere is the image of death.
>
> —Virgil, *Aeneid* II

## 13.

Meanwhile, amid such a confusion of affairs, the bloodstained victor also entered Marcella’s house.

May I be permitted to speak of what I have heard (*Virgil, Aeneid* VI)—indeed, to relate what holy men saw, who were present there and say that you too shared her danger. She is said to have received those who entered with an unafraid face. When they demanded gold, and she pleaded that her wealth had been buried, using her shabby tunic as an excuse, she nevertheless failed to convince them of her voluntary poverty.

They say that, beaten with clubs and scourges, she did not feel the tortures; but she did feel them when, in tears, she threw herself at their feet and begged them not to separate you from her company, lest youth endure what old age could not fear.

Christ softened their hard hearts, and compassion found a place among bloodstained swords.

When the barbarians had led both her and you to the basilica of the Apostle Paul [Note: Orosius relates this, Book VII, chapter 39. Alaric ordered, after the capture of the city, “that if anyone had fled to holy places, especially to the basilicas of the holy Apostles Peter and Paul, they should above all allow them to remain unharmed and safe.” Sozomen likewise relates, Book IX, chapter 10, that a certain woman was brought by a soldier to the basilica of Saint Peter so that her modesty might be spared.], either to show you safety or a tomb, she is said to have burst into such joy that she gave thanks to God: because he had preserved you safe for her; because captivity had not made that poor woman poor, but had found her already so; because she needed her daily food; because, filled with Christ, she did not feel hunger; because in word and deed she said:

“Naked I came from my mother’s womb, and naked I shall return. As it has pleased the Lord, so it has happened. Blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1:21).

## 14.

After a few days, with her little body sound, whole, and vigorous, she fell asleep in the Lord. She left you as heir to her little poverty—or rather, through you, the poor—closing her eyes in your hands and giving up her spirit amid your kisses. While you wept, she smiled because of the consciousness of a good life and of future rewards [Note: Martianus reads “she saw”; this is incorrect, unless it is a printer’s error.].

These things I have dictated for you, venerable Marcella, and for you, daughter Principia, in a single brief nocturnal labor, desiring to please both God and readers not by elegance of speech but by the goodwill of a most grateful spirit toward you.

# LETTER CXXVIII

[Note: Alternatively numbered 12. Written around A.D. 413.]

## TO GAUDENTIUS

### On the education of the little girl Pacatula

He teaches by what elementary exercises the untutored age of a girl destined for virginity should be formed, before she has learned to distinguish good from evil.

1. It is a difficult task to write to a little girl who does not understand what you are saying, whose mind you do not know, and whose wishes you would dangerously promise to satisfy, so that, in the words of the celebrated Orator, the conclusion [exodium] may be more praiseworthy in her than the substance. For what would you exhort to continence one who longs for pastries, who babbles in her mother’s lap with a prattling voice, and to whom honey is sweeter than words? Would she hear the profound teachings of the Apostle, when she is more delighted by old women’s tales? Would she grasp the riddles of the prophets, when a nurse’s stern face frightens her more? Would she understand the majesty of the Gospel, before whose flashes every human understanding grows dull? Should I exhort her to submit to her parent, when with her tender hand she strikes her laughing mother?

[Note: Martianus, following Erasmus, incorrectly inserts *exordium* after *Orator*. It is well known, moreover, that *exodia* means sententious conclusions, the term being taken from the ancient stage, where such passages—often used as exchanges of dialogue—were appended to tragedies to turn the spectators from tragic emotions toward cheerfulness. Euripides attached something of this kind to nearly all his tragedies, as in the line, “Many are the forms of the divine,” which he repeats in *Alcestis* and *Andromache*. See Letter 130 to Demetrias, §1, where we indicate Cicero’s passage from *On the Republic*.]

Therefore let our little Pacatula receive this brief letter after she has learned to read. For the present, let her merely recognize the letters, join syllables, learn words, and combine them into sentences. And so that she may practice these things in her little ringing voice, let little cakes be set before her as rewards sweetened with mulsum, along with whatever is pleasant to the taste. Let her eagerly accept whatever blooms in flowers, glitters in gems, or charms in dolls. Meanwhile, let her also try with her tender thumb to draw out threads; let her often break the warp, so that one day she may not break it. After her work, let her delight in play; let her hang upon her mother’s neck; let her snatch kisses from her relatives; let her recite psalms in return for a reward; let her love what she is compelled to learn, so that it may be not a task but a pleasure, not compulsion but willingness.

[Note: Some manuscripts read *mulsiprema*, a reading which the Benedictine editor relegated to the margin of the book. It can appropriately be referred to the cake itself, pressed and seasoned with mulsum. The wording is taken from Horace:

> … as fond nurses once gave little cakes to children.

“... as kindly teachers give little cakes to children, so that they may wish to learn their first elements.”]

2. When some women have promised a girl as a future virgin, they customarily dress her in a dark tunic, cover her with a dusky cloak [variant: tawny], remove her linen garments, and permit no gold on her neck or head. This is indeed sound advice, lest she learn in childhood to possess what she will later be forced to lay aside.

Others, however, think the opposite. “What does it matter,” they say, “if she herself does not possess such things, so long as she sees others who do? The female sex is fond of adornment [*philókosmon*]; and we know that many women of remarkable chastity, although they adorn themselves for no man, nevertheless gladly adorn themselves for their own sake.”

[Note: For the Greek word *philókosmon*, older printed editions have “eager for trifles, necklaces, and ornaments” (I would read “small caps”); whatever the case, this gloss seems inept to us. For *philókosmon* to be feminine is equivalent to saying “eager for and devoted to adornment.”]

Let her rather become satiated by having such things, and let her see other girls praised who do not possess them. It is better for her to despise them once she is satisfied than, because she has not had them, to desire to possess them. [Note: The older edition which we often use, and Victor, insert *vides* (“you see”); a little below, in place of *prius* (“earlier”), they read *reperies* (“you will find”), with an equally good sense, but we have not found these readings in the manuscripts.]

The Lord did something similar for the Israelite people: when they craved Egyptian meat, he supplied quail until they were nauseated and vomited. Many people of the world, too, have found it easier to do without bodily pleasure after experiencing it than those who have been ignorant of lust from childhood. Some tread upon what they know; others desire what they do not know. The former avoid, through repentance, the snares of pleasure they have escaped; the latter discover that the allurements of the flesh, which flatter the body with a sweet tickling, are deadly poisons while they think them honey.

“For the lips of a prostitute drip honey” (Proverbs 5, according to the Septuagint), which for a time fattens the throats of those who consume it but afterward proves more bitter than gall. Hence, too, honey is not offered in the Lord’s sacrifices; and wax, which is honey’s dwelling place, is rejected, while oil is kindled in the temple of God (Leviticus 2)—oil pressed from bitter olives. The Passover also is eaten with bitter things (Exodus 12), with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth (1 Corinthians 5:8), and whoever possesses these will suffer persecution in the world. Hence the Prophet sings mystically:

> I sat alone, because I was filled with bitterness.  
> (Jeremiah 15:17)

3. What then? Should one indulge in youth so that afterward indulgence may be despised more forcefully? “By no means,” they reply. “Let each person remain in the calling in which he was called” (1 Corinthians 7:24).

If someone was called circumcised—that is, as a virgin—let her not bring upon herself a foreskin; that is, let her not seek the leather tunics of marriage with which Adam, expelled from the paradise of virginity, was clothed. If someone was called in uncircumcision—that is, possessing a wife and clothed in the skin of marriage—let her not seek the nakedness of virginity and eternal chastity, which she once ceased to possess. Rather, let her use her own vessel in sanctification and chastity (1 Thessalonians 4:4), and let her drink from her own fountains; let her not seek the broken cisterns of brothels, which cannot contain the purest waters of chastity (Proverbs 5).

Therefore Paul, discussing virginity and marriage in the same chapter, calls those established in marriage slaves of the flesh, and calls free those who, without the yoke of marriage, serve the Lord with complete freedom. What we are saying is not being said universally, but is being treated in part; nor are we speaking about everyone, but about some. Our discourse is directed to both sexes, not only to the weaker vessel.

You are a virgin: what pleasure do you take in the companionship of a woman? Why entrust a frail, stitched vessel to great waves, and confidently embark upon the great danger of an uncertain voyage?

[Note: The same edition and Victor read *subtilem* (“slender”), not very well and against the manuscripts. Vergil, *Aeneid* VI: “the patched boat groaned under the weight,” etc.]

You do not know what you desire, yet you join yourself to her as though you had either desired it before or—as I put it most gently—were going to desire it afterward.

[Note: Martianus, following Erasmus, has *eis*, as though Victor had not already restored *ei*, that is, “to the woman,” whose companionship he has just condemned. Shortly afterward he also has *erat*, whereas we have corrected the text, on the authority of the larger Verona manuscript and Victor, to *eris*, “you will desire.”]

But this sex is more suited to ministry. Choose, then, an ugly old woman; choose one whose continence in the Lord has been tested. Why does a young woman, why beauty, why luxury delight you? You use the baths, walk about with shining skin and ruddy cheeks, eat meat, abound in riches, and are surrounded by costly clothing, yet you think you can safely sleep beside a deadly serpent?

“But you do not live in the same lodging”—except at night, perhaps. Yet you spend whole days in conversation with her. Why do you sit alone with a woman alone, without witnesses, so that, even if you yourself do not sin, you may appear to others to be sinning, and so that you may become an example to wretched people who will offend by relying on the authority of your name? You too, whether virgin or widow, why are you detained in such a lengthy conversation with a man? Why, when left alone with him, are you not afraid? At least let the necessity of your bowels or bladder compel you to go outside and leave him in this matter—the man with whom you have behaved more freely than with a brother and far more shamelessly than with a husband.

“But you ask something from the Holy Scriptures.” Ask publicly. Let your serving girls hear; let your companions hear. “Everything that is made manifest is light” (Ephesians 5:13). A good discourse seeks no secrecy; rather, it delights in its own praises and in the testimony of many. Yet this outstanding teacher despises men, looks down on brothers, and labors over the secret instruction of a single little woman.

[Note: The same reading occurs in the following Letter 130 to Demetrias.]

3. I have digressed briefly from my subject because of others; and while instructing, or rather nourishing, the infant Pacatula, I have suddenly taken up a battle against many women who are badly pacified. I shall return to my subject.

Let the female sex associate with its own sex. Let her not know—indeed, let her fear—to play with boys. Let her know no indecent word; and if by chance she hears something amid the commotion of a busy household, let her not understand it. Let her regard her mother’s gesture as words and instruction, and as a command. Let her love her as a parent, submit to her as a mistress, and fear her as a teacher.

When the seventh year of age has received the inexperienced little girl, still toothless, and she has begun to blush, to know what she should keep silent about, and to hesitate over what she should say, let her learn the Psalter by heart; and until the years of puberty, let her make the books of Solomon, the Gospels, the Apostles, and the Prophets the treasure of her heart. Let her not go out too freely in public, nor constantly seek the crowds of churches. Let her have all her pleasures in her bedroom. Let her never see young men, never see young men with curled hair, whose sweet voices wound the soul through the ear; and let her repel the wantonness of girls. The more freely such persons approach, the more difficult they are to avoid; and what they have learned they teach in secret, violating the secluded Danae through the talk of the crowd.

Let her have as teacher a companion, as tutor a guardian—one not devoted to much wine, not, in the Apostle’s words, idle and talkative, but sober, dignified, skilled in wool-working, and speaking only those things that train a girl’s mind toward virtue. For just as water in a garden bed follows the finger that leads it, so an age that is soft and tender is pliable in either direction and is drawn wherever you lead it.

Licentious and fashionably dressed young men commonly seek access for themselves through flattering words, affability, and little gifts, by means of nurses or foster-daughters. Once they have entered with apparent gentleness, they kindle fires from sparks and gradually advance toward shamelessness; and they cannot be prevented at all, proving the truth of the verse:

> It is hard to rebuke what you allow to become habitual.

[Note: Alternatively, *comatulis*, “long-haired”; likewise, a little later, other books read “by blandishments, affability; by little gifts, access,” etc.]

I am ashamed to say it, yet it must be said: noble women, who have rejected more noble suitors, are joined to men of the lowest condition and to little slaves. Under the name of religion and the shadow of continence, they sometimes abandon their husbands, follow Helen’s Alexanders, and do not fear the Menelauses.

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “Noble women, intending to have nobler suitors,” and shortly afterward omit the particle *nec* before “Menelauses.”]

These things are seen, lamented, and not punished, because the multitude of sinners supplies permission to sin.

[Col. 1099]

4. Oh the outrage! The whole world is collapsing, yet our sins do not collapse. The famous city, the capital of the Roman Empire, has been swallowed up by a single fire. There is no region that does not contain Roman exiles. Sacred churches once fell into ashes and embers, yet we are devoted to avarice.

[Note: A very similar sentiment is expressed concerning the Megarensians in Letter 123 to Ageruchia, §15: that they built as though they would always live, and lived as though they would die the next day. Something similar is also found in an epigram of Lucian, who himself took it from Socrates:

> Enjoy your possessions as one who is going to die;  
> but spare your goods as one who is going to live.]

We live as though we would die tomorrow, and we build as though we would live forever in this world. Our walls are gold, our ceilings are gold, the capitals of our columns glitter with gold, while Christ, naked and hungry, dies before our doors in the person of the poor.

We read that Aaron the high priest went out to meet the raging flames and, with a censer kindled, restrained God’s anger (Numbers 16). The great priest stood between death and life, and the fire did not dare advance beyond his footprints.

God says to Moses: “Let me alone, and I will destroy this people” (Exodus 32:10). When he says, “Let me alone,” he shows that he can be restrained from doing what he has threatened; for the prayers of a servant were hindering the power of God.

Who, do you think, is that man under heaven who could now confront God’s anger, meet the flames, and say with the Apostle, “I could wish that I myself were accursed for my brothers” (Romans 9:3)? Flocks perish with their shepherds, because as the people are, so is the priest.

Moses spoke from a feeling of compassion: “If you forgive this people, forgive them; but if not, erase me from your book” (Exodus 32:31–32). He wishes to perish with those who are perishing and is not satisfied with his own salvation. For “the glory of a king is a multitude of people” (Proverbs 14).

Our Pacatula was born in such times. Amid these rattles she passes through the first stage of life, destined to know tears before laughter and to experience weeping before joy. She has not yet entered, and already there is departure. Let her always think that the world has been such as it is now. Let her not know the past, flee the present, and desire the future.

Your affection, brother Gaudentius, moved me to dictate these things in a hasty discourse and, after the deaths of friends and perpetual mourning, to write to an infant in my old age after so long an interval. I preferred to give a little rather than nothing at all to one who was asking: in the one case the will is crushed by grief; in the other, there is a dissimulation of friendship.

## Letter CXXIX

[Note: Also numbered 129. Written around the year 414.]

### To Dardanus

#### On the Promised Land

The Promised Land is not the land possessed by the Jews; rather, another heavenly land is to be understood, namely, the land of the living promised in the Gospel to the meek. The only cause of the Jews’ miseries and everlasting captivity is the blood of Christ that was shed and the execrable crime by which they did not fear to inflict death upon him.

[Note: This is Claudianus Postumus Dardanus, *vir illustris* and of patrician rank, as the old inscription has it, cited by Sirmond and Gothofred.]

1. You ask, Dardanus—most noble among Christians, and most Christian among the noble—what is the Promised Land that the Jews possessed when they returned from Egypt, although it had already been possessed by their ancestors and therefore was not promised but restored. You use these words at the end of your letter.

[Note: These two words, “most Christian of the noble,” are absent from the oldest manuscript, the Regina codex 215. They nevertheless belong to Jerome’s style: he addresses Pammachius in Letter 61 as “most noble of Christians” and “most Christian of the noble.” We are not troubled by the contrary testimony of Sidonius Apollinaris, who in Book 5, Letter 9, makes this Dardanus a most wicked man, in whom others condemned every crime at once.]

By asking this question, you seem to hold the view preferred by many of our people: that another promised land must be sought, of which David also speaks in the psalm: “I believe that I shall see the goodness of the Lord in the land of the living” (Psalm 26:13); and the Lord in the Gospel: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the land” (Matthew 5:4).

Certainly, when David sang these words in the Spirit, he was in the Promised Land; and he was not merely dwelling within the boundaries of Judea, but had become victor over many surrounding nations extending from the Torrent of Egypt, which is Rhinocorura, to the Euphrates River. In another place he says: “Upon Edom I will cast my sandal; to me the foreigners will serve” (Psalm 59:9).

[Note: The word “will serve” corresponds neither to the Hebrew and Greek sources nor to any ancient Latin version. See Letter 106 to Sunnia and Fretela, §69. Perhaps some Greek manuscript once had *hypetagēsontai* instead of *hypetagēsan*.]

How, then, could he believe that he was going to receive what he already possessed by victory? And lest he leave Jewish readers uncertain about which land he desired to see, he demonstrates it in the very same statement, saying: “I believe that I shall see the goodness of the Lord in the land of the living.”

Therefore the land of Judea, which was under his rule, is not the land of the living—that is, the land of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, concerning whom the Lord says in the question of the Resurrection, “He is not God of the dead, but of the living” (Matthew 22:32). Rather, it is the land and region of the dead, concerning whom Ezekiel says: “The soul that sins, it shall die” (Ezekiel 18:4).

And again: “The dead shall not praise you, Lord, but we who live” (Psalms 113:17–18)—we who at the resurrection will meet the Lord Savior, as the Apostle says: “For this we say to you by the word of the Lord: we who are alive, who remain until the coming of the Lord, shall not precede those who sleep” (1 Thessalonians 4:15).

[Note: Erasmus and Victor add “we bless the Lord,” words which the manuscript books do not recognize. A little later they read *sumus* (“we are”) for *sunt* (“are”).]

Jeremiah also speaks of them: “Those who forsake you shall be written upon the earth” (Jeremiah 17:13).

And when David promises, “I believe that I shall see the goodness of the Lord,” he plainly draws us toward a spiritual understanding. What other goods could the king have sought, or what did he lack, since he possessed such power that his son Solomon—richer than anyone in the world—was content with the wealth acquired through him? Yet in the land of the living he was seeking those goods “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor entered into the heart of man,” which God has prepared for those who love him.

As for the Gospel saying, “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the land” (Matthew 5:4), it appears, according to the literal sense, to contradict itself. Possession of the land does not seem to belong to the gentle and meek, who often lose even what their parents left them because of their meekness, but to strong and violent men, who are most ready for war.

Thus, in the forty-fourth psalm, which under Solomon’s name refers to the mystery of Christ and his Church, it is written:

> Gird your sword upon your thigh, O most mighty.  
> In your beauty and your splendor, advance, prosper, and reign.  
> Because of meekness, justice, and truth, your right hand shall lead you wonderfully.

This is the one who also spoke in another psalm:

> Remember, Lord, David and all his meekness.  
> (Psalm 131:1)

And again:

> The Lord lifts up the meek.  
> (Psalm 146:6)

And more openly in the Gospel:

> Learn from me, because I am humble and meek of heart.  
> (Matthew 11:29)

Moses is also written as the meekest of all human beings who were upon the earth, as a type of him (Numbers 12:3).

2. This, as we have said, is the land of the living, in which the goods of the Lord are prepared for holy and meek men. Before the coming of the Lord Savior in the flesh, neither Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, nor the Prophets and other righteous men could attain it.

Thus Abraham, although in different regions, is seen with Lazarus among the dead (Luke 16); and Jacob, a righteous man, says: “Mourning and lamenting, I shall descend to the underworld” (Genesis 37:35).

The blood of Christ is the key of paradise. He said to the thief: “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43).

This is, as we have said, the land of the living, the land of God’s riches and goodness, which the first Adam lost and the second Adam found—or rather, which the second restored after it had been lost by the first. The Apostle says: “Death reigned from Adam to Moses”—under whose person the Law is understood—“in the likeness of Adam’s transgression, who is a type of the one to come” (Romans 5:14).

If we wish to know more clearly what this land is, let us read in Malachi: “All will call you blessed, says the Lord, because you will be a desirable land” (Malachi 3:12).

[Note: The Greek or Hebrew text of Malachi does not have “in the land,” but simply *land* in the nominative.]

It is more significantly called in Greek *thelētē*, meaning either the land desired by the saints or the land pleasing to God.

Isaiah also agrees with this meaning, saying: “A man will be hidden, concealing his words, and he will appear in the land of Zion like a glorious river in a thirsty land” (Isaiah 32:2, according to the Septuagint).

What is the land of Zion in which the glorious river will appear? It is evidently that of which David sings in another psalm:

> Glorious things are spoken of you, city of God.  
> (Psalm 86:3)

And again:

> The Lord loves the gates of Zion above all the tents of Jacob.  
> (Psalm 86:2)

Does God love those gates which we see transformed into ashes and embers? This cannot be persuaded even to the wise—not even to the foolish.

I think that the passage we read in Psalm 64 also accords with this meaning:

> You visited the earth and watered it abundantly;  
> you enriched it greatly.  
> The river of God is filled with waters;  
> you prepared their food, for thus is your preparation.  
> Water its furrows; multiply its offspring.  
> In its showers it will rejoice as it germinates.

That land is visited daily by God and watered, and it is filled with every kind of wealth. From it proceeds the river of God, of which it is written:

> The river’s streams make glad the city of God.  
> (Psalm 45:5)

This river is also described in mystical language in Ezekiel’s account of the Temple (Ezekiel 47); along its banks are trees, on both sides, abounding each month in new fruits.

Concerning this land the wisest of men also wrote in Proverbs:

> Whoever cultivates his own land will be filled with bread.  
> (Proverbs 12:11)

If someone thinks this must be understood of the land we see, which is possessed more by sinners and of which it is written, “Cursed is the earth in your works” (Genesis 3:17), let him explain how this statement can stand: “Whoever cultivates his own land will be filled with bread.” How many cultivate the earth and work it with the plow, yet, because of many hindering circumstances, are consumed by want and poverty?

We must consider what Scripture says: “Whoever cultivates his own land”—that is, land properly belonging to him, from which he can never be expelled. In this sense it is also written: “The redemption of a man’s soul is his own wealth” (Proverbs 13:8).

This cannot be understood according to the literal sense. How many are redeemed with the money of strangers and friends?

The cultivators and farmers of this land are the Apostles, to whom it is said: “You are the salt of the earth” (Matthew 5:13). And elsewhere: “In your patience you will possess your souls” (Luke 21:19). One of them, the vessel of election, spoke with complete confidence:

> We are God’s fellow workers; you are God’s agriculture, God’s building.  
> (1 Corinthians 3:9)

There are many other passages, which I do not repeat lest I seem to dull the reader’s understanding and distrust his memory.

3. Let us also examine this carefully, and let the authority of the Scriptures teach us that the saints of this land—which the Jews call the Promised Land—are not inhabitants but resident aliens and pilgrims.

We read from the person of a righteous man:

> I am a stranger and a sojourner, as all my fathers were.  
> (Psalm 38:13)

When he had long dwelt amid the darkness of this land, he groans plaintively and says:

> Woe is me, for my sojourning has been prolonged;  
> I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Kedar;  
> my soul has been a long-time resident.  
> (Psalm 119:5)

[Note: The Regina manuscript gives the older reading, “my sojourning has been made far away,” to which Augustine’s reading, “has been made distant,” is nearly identical; the Vulgate has “was an inhabitant,” as do the earlier printed editions and most manuscripts.]

Wherever an inhabitant of the earth is mentioned, let us examine the beginning, middle, and end, and the rule of Scripture can clearly be shown to be that the inhabitants of the earth are always called sinners. Concerning them there is this example in the Apocalypse of John:

> Woe to the inhabitants of the earth!  
> (Revelation 8:13)

Abraham was the first to receive the promise, when the Lord said, “To you I will give this land and to your descendants” (Genesis 12:7). Yet according to the sermon of Stephen, the first martyr in Christ, he is said not to have received even a footprint of this land.

For it is written:

> Then he came out from the land of the Chaldeans and lived in Carran; and from there, after his father died, he migrated into this land in which you now dwell. He gave him no inheritance in it, not even a footprint, although he promised to give it to him as a possession and to his descendants after him.  
> (Acts 7:4 and following)

And lest the reader’s silent thought perhaps lead him to the interpretation that what was not given to the parent was restored to his descendants, the vessel of election speaks to the Hebrews:

> By faith Abraham, when he was called, obeyed by going out to the place he was to receive as an inheritance; and he went out, not knowing where he was going. By faith he dwelt as a stranger in the land of promise, as in a foreign land, living in tents with Isaac and Jacob, heirs with him of the same promise. For he awaited the city having foundations, whose architect and creator is God.  
> (Hebrews 11:8 and following)

And again, after speaking of Abel, Enoch, Noah, and Sarah, he adds:

> In accordance with faith all these died without receiving the promises, but seeing and greeting them from afar and confessing that they were strangers and resident aliens upon the earth. For those who say such things show that they are seeking a homeland. And if they had remembered the one from which they had departed, they had time to return; but now they desire a better one, that is, a heavenly one.  
> (Hebrews 11:13 and following)

After mentioning many saints in the intervening passage, he concludes:

> And all these, having received testimony through faith, did not receive the promise, since God had provided something better for us, so that they might not be perfected without us.  
> (Hebrews 11:39 and following)

For we have approached Mount Zion and the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and countless thousands of angels in solemn assembly, and the Church of the firstborn who are written in heaven (Hebrews 12:22–23).

[Note: Martianus admits that nearly all manuscripts read in this manner, although he did not wish to follow their testimony and instead read, with the printed editions, “the gathering of many thousands of angels.” We are not permitted to depart from our manuscripts, especially since these words are quoted from an old Latin translation and adhere more closely to the Greek text: “You have approached Zion, the mountain … and a festal gathering of myriads of angels, and the assembly,” and so forth.]

I am not unaware that the unbelief of the Jews rejects these testimonies, which are certainly confirmed by the authority of the Old Testament. We must say to our own people that this letter entitled “To the Hebrews” is received not only by the churches of the East but by all the ecclesiastical writers of the Greek language from earliest times as the work of the Apostle Paul, although most consider it to belong either to Barnabas or to Clement. It makes no difference whose it is, since it is the work of an ecclesiastical man and is celebrated daily in the reading of the churches.

[Note: Victor reads “by the Churches,” and the Greek writers likewise; shortly afterward and elsewhere Jerome admits that it had long not been accepted among the canonical books by the Latin churches, especially the Roman church. In his commentary on Isaiah, Book 3, he says, “Latin custom does not receive it,” and in *On Illustrious Men*, under Caius, “Among the Romans it is still not regarded as belonging to the Apostle Paul.” He says similar things concerning Zechariah 8, Matthew 26, his letter to Evangelus, his letter to Paulinus, and elsewhere. We have not altered Martianus’s reading, which is supported by some of our manuscripts, “by the ecclesiastical writers,” without the conjunction. Nevertheless the reading preferred by other, and indeed older, manuscripts is equally sound: “by the Greek ecclesiastical writers from earliest times”; a few of these omit *retro*. See also Augustine, *City of God* Book 16 and *On Christian Doctrine* Book 2, chapter 8. It would scarcely be worthwhile here to cite the Greek Fathers merely by name, since they quote testimonies from this letter. Theodoret may be consulted as one example, in his preface to this very letter.]

If Latin custom does not receive it among the canonical Scriptures, neither do the Greek churches receive the Apocalypse of John with the same freedom. Yet we accept both, following not the custom of our own time but the authority of the ancient writers, who generally make use of the testimonies of both books—not as they sometimes do with apocryphal writings, since they rarely use examples from pagan literature either, but as though they were canonical and ecclesiastical.

4.

[Note: Bishop Eucherius, in a letter to Faustus preserved by Labbe in the *New Bibliotheca of Manuscripts*, volume 1, page 765, writes: “Accordingly, Saint Jerome determined the length and also the breadth of Judea in a certain letter to Dardanus. From it we have extracted for this work whatever seemed necessary; in it, while arguing against the Jews about the Promised Land, he also added the following: ‘Let those who think that this land …’” The quotation continues through this and the following chapter, where he reads certain passages from a better manuscript.]

Let those who think that this land—which has now become the Promised Land for us through Christ’s Passion and Resurrection—was possessed by the Jewish people after their return from Egypt answer me: how much did they possess? Certainly from Dan to Beersheba, a distance scarcely one hundred and sixty miles in length.

For Scripture does not testify that David and Solomon, the most powerful kings, possessed more, apart from those whom they received into friendship after their victory (2 Samuel 17).

[Note: From Eucherius’s letter: “apart from those,” not “these,” which appears to be the more correct reading. Above: “through Christ’s Passion and Resurrection.”]

I say this while leaving aside the five cities of Palestine—Gaza, Ascalon, Gath, Ekron, and Azotus—as well as the Idumeans, scarcely seventy-five miles from Jerusalem on the southern side, and the Arabs and Hagarenes, now called Saracens, in the vicinity of the city of Jerusalem.

[Note: Ducaeus restores “on the southern side” from several books, producing a more coherent text.]

[Note: Both our manuscripts and Martianus’s manuscripts generally read “twenty-five miles from Jerusalem,” etc.]

I am ashamed to speak of the breadth of the Promised Land, lest I seem to provide the pagans with an occasion for blasphemy. From Joppa to our little village of Bethlehem there are forty-six miles; beyond it stretches a vast wilderness, full of savage barbarians, of whom it is said:

> He will dwell opposite all his brothers.  
> (Genesis 16:12)

And of whom the most eloquent Poet makes mention:

> And the Barcaeans, wandering far and wide,  
> from the town of Barca, which lies in the wilderness;  
> whom the Africans now call, in corrupted speech, Baricians.

[Note: The old edition and the Regina manuscript read, “He will dwell opposite all his brothers.” Virgil’s manuscripts have *furentes*, “raging,” rather than *vagantes*, “wandering.” Jerome also uses this half-line in his preceding letter to Marcellinus and Anapsychia. Bochart does not think it likely that a single people was spread over so wide an area, as Jerome indicates here. He merely means that, just as the region of Marmarica is now called the desert of Barca, so the Barcaeans of old were the same as the Libyans and Marmaric peoples who lived around Cyrene. Jerome appropriately notes that they are called by different names according to the character of the places they occupy.]

These are the peoples who, according to the character of the regions, are called by different names; and they extend from Mauretania through Africa, Egypt, Palestine, Phoenicia, Coele-Syria, Osrhoene, Mesopotamia, and Persia as far as India.

This, Jew, is the length and breadth of your lands. In these you glory; over these you boast before people throughout the various provinces who know nothing of you.

> Wear your trappings for the people; I know you within and to the skin.  
> (Persius, *Satires* 3)

### 5

[Note: [Col. 1104] This passage is cited again in Eucherius’s letter. “But if someone should object that these things do not fit very well with what follows, I too shall admit as much to you.”]

But if you object that the land of promise is the territory described in the Book of Numbers (chapter 34)—from the southern end of the Salt Sea, through [Note: [Col. 1105] So the printed editions and manuscripts read, and Eucherius himself reads *Sina*. But Relandus insists that *Sina* should be corrected and replaced by *Sin*, for Sinai has no relevance here; and it is clear from Numbers 34:4 that *Sin* must be read. I myself would rather replace *Sina* with *Senna*, from the same passage in Numbers. For from the south of the very salty sea, or Salt Sea, one passes through Senna and Kadesh-barnea, and so forth. Consult the map. Jerome, explaining this passage from Numbers in the same words in his commentary on Ezekiel 47, writes: “From the wilderness of Sin, which is beside Edom … through the ascent of Akrabbim, and through Senna and Kadesh-barnea … one arrives at the Brook of Egypt, which flows into the sea near the city of Rhinocolura.”] Sin and Kadesh-barnea as far as the Brook of Egypt, which flows into the Great Sea near Rhinocolura; and [p. 973] from the west, the sea itself, which stretches along Palestine, Phoenicia, Coele-Syria, and Cilicia [Note: [Col. 1105] Martianus corrupts the good reading of the earlier editors by reading *Phoenicis* and *pertenditur*. The text is restored from our manuscripts, and even from the Cluniac manuscript cited by him, as well as from the letter to Faustus mentioned above.]; from the north, Mount Taurus and Zephyrium as far as Hamath, which is called Epiphanea of Syria; but to the east, through Antioch, Lake Chinnereth, now called Tiberias, and the Jordan, which flows into the Salt Sea, now called the Dead Sea; beyond the Jordan, however, lies the possession of two and a half tribes: Reuben and Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh.

I too shall admit that these things were promised to you, not handed over to you—if you had observed God’s commandments and walked in his ordinances; if you had not worshiped Beel-phegor and [Note: [Col. 1105] The older printed editions read *Baal*.] the Baals instead of the Almighty God, Beelzebub and Chemosh. Because you preferred them to God, you lost everything that had been promised to you.

The kingdoms of heaven are also promised to me in the Gospel, though the Old Scripture nowhere names them. But if I do not do what has been commanded, the fault will certainly not lie with the one who made the promise, but with me, who was not worthy to receive what was promised. For when a choice is offered for one to make, if you refuse to act, you desire in vain what has been promised.

Read the Book of Joshua and the Book of Judges, and you will understand by how many narrow limits of possession you have been confined. Why should I mention the foreigners in the various cities, whom the Jewish people were unable to drive out from their cities and settlements, when your own capital—first Jebus, then Salem, third Jerusalem, and now Aelia—was unable to drive out the Jebusites, but remained with them as a scandal and an example to its neighbors? So much so that your temple was built there where the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite had been, and that the temple itself was constructed by seventy thousand [Note: [Col. 1105] Scripture, including Jerome’s version, gives the number of laborers in the reverse order: “seventy thousand of those who carried burdens, and eighty thousand stonecutters.”] stonecutters and eighty thousand carriers—that is, one hundred and fifty thousand men, besides the overseers of the works—because of the great number of uncircumcised foreigners living among you.

### 6

Nor do I say this to insult the land of Judea, as the heretical slanderer falsely claims, or to abolish the truth of the history, which is the foundation of spiritual understanding. I say it to strike down the arrogance of the Jews, who prefer the narrowness of the synagogue to the breadth of the Church.

For if they follow only the killing letter, and not the life-giving Spirit, [p. 974] let them show the land of promise flowing with milk and honey. But if they understand it tropologically—that is, as signifying the abundance of all things—we shall prefer the land of confession and the land of the living to a land of thorns, since the Lord says to Moses concerning Israel’s rejection and the calling of the nations: “Let me go, that I may destroy this people and make you into a great nation” (Exod. 32:10).

And the same Father says to the Son: “Ask of me, and I will give you your inheritance, and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Ps. 2:8). And more plainly through Isaiah: “It is too little for you to be my servant, to raise up the tribes of Jacob and to gather the dregs—or the remnant—of Israel. I have given you as a light to all the nations, that you may be the savior of the whole earth” (Isa. 49:6).

From this it is plainly demonstrated that all the things belonging to that people came beforehand in shadow, type, and image, but were written for us, upon whom the ends of the ages have come.

### 7

You have committed many crimes, Jew, and have served all the nations around you. Why did this happen? Certainly because of idolatry. And whenever you had served them, God took pity on you and sent judges and deliverers, who freed you from servitude to the Moabites and Ammonites, the Philistines, and various other nations.

At last, under the kings, you offended God, and your entire province was destroyed when the Babylonian nation [Note: [Col. 1106] Some ancient copies in Martianus read “the Babylonian people” instead of “the Babylonian nation.”] ravaged it. For seventy years the temple remained desolate. The captivity was released by Cyrus, king of the Persians. Ezra and Nehemiah report this most clearly.

The temple was rebuilt under Darius, king of the Persians and Medes, by Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and Jeshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest. I shall not enumerate what you suffered from the Medes, Egyptians, and Macedonians. Nor shall I bring back to your memory Antiochus Epiphanes, the most savage of all tyrants; nor shall I rehearse Gnaeus Pompey, Gabinius, Scaurus, Varus, Cassius, and Sosius, who insulted your cities, and Jerusalem above all.

Finally, under Vespasian and Titus, the city was captured and the temple overturned. Thereafter the remnants of the city remained for fifty years, down to the emperor Hadrian. After the destruction of the Temple, the ruins of both city and temple remained for somewhat less than four hundred [p. 975] years.

For what such enormous crime? Certainly you do not worship idols—but even while serving Persians and Romans and being weighed down under the yoke of captivity, you do not know foreign gods. How is it that the once most merciful God, who never forgot you, is now not moved by your misery through so long a span of time—so as to release your captivity, or, to speak more accurately, send you the Antichrist whom you await?

For what crime, I ask, and such execrable wickedness, has he turned his eyes away from you? Do you not know? Remember the words of your parents: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27:25). And: “Come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours” (ibid. 21:8). And: “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19:15).

You have what you chose. You will serve Caesar until the end of the world, until the fullness of the nations enters, and thus all Israel is saved, so that the one who was once the head may be turned into the tail.

### 8

[Note: [Col. 1106] He had been Praetorian Prefect of Gaul twice. His first prefecture fell in the year 409, as Gothofredus has very properly established from Law 171, title 1, *On Centurions*; the second was in 413, as can be inferred from Olympiodorus in Photius’s account of that year and from the Chronicle of Tiro Prosper. Augustine also wrote this letter to the same Dardanus.]

These things I have hastily and briefly composed for you, most eloquent man, now that you have completed the honor of a double prefecture [Col. 1107], and are more honored in Christ, lest I seem altogether to remain silent.

For at the same time—indeed, on the same day—your letter was delivered to me and the letter you requested of me [Note: [Col. 1107] The copy of the Regina manuscript perhaps more correctly reads *et meae expeditae*, that is, “written” or “completed.”]. Thus I had either to remain silent or to answer in unpolished language: the one course belongs to modesty, the other to affection.

## LETTER CXXX

[Note: [Col. 1107] Otherwise Letter 8. Written in the same year, 414.]

### TO DEMETRIAS  
### On Preserving Virginity

He praises Demetrias, a virgin, daughter of Juliana and granddaughter of Proba, because she has consecrated herself to Christ; he exhorts her to persevere and immediately to resist the promptings of the devil, who urges her toward shameful things. He gives instructions concerning diligence, fasting, obedience, the avoidance of jokes, and the other matters relevant to the discipline of a virgin.

### 1

Of all the subjects on which I have written from adolescence to the present age, whether by my own hand or that of my secretaries, nothing has been more difficult [p. 976] than the present work. For in writing to Demetrias, a virgin of Christ who is first in the Roman world both in nobility and in wealth, if I say everything that accords with her virtues, I shall be thought to flatter; but if I hold back certain things lest they seem incredible, my modesty will do harm to her praises.

What, then, shall I do? I do not dare deny what I cannot fulfill. Such is the authority of her grandmother and mother, distinguished women, in commanding; such their confidence in asking; such their persistence in obtaining. For they do not demand from me something new and extraordinary, since my talent has often been worn smooth by subjects of this kind. They ask only that, so far as my ability permits, the testimony of my voice not be lacking in unfolding the virtues of one of whom, to use the saying of the illustrious orator, [Note: [Col. 1107] Servius says in his commentary on Aeneid 6 that this was Cicero’s maxim in the *Dialogue on the Republic*, and quotes it in these words: “O Fannius, the task is difficult: to praise a boy, for it is not the thing itself that must be praised, but the hope.” It is also cited by Quintilian, book 10, chapter 3. See the beginning of the preceding letter to Gaudentius.] “The hope is more worthy of praise than the reality.”

Although she has surpassed her maiden years in the ardor of faith, and has begun at the point where others have ceased, this is the mark of perfect and consummate virtue.

### 2

Far be detraction [Variant: “let it be far”]; let envy depart. Let there be no fault of ambition. We are writing from an unknown person to one unknown, at least as regards bodily appearance. Otherwise, the inner person is well known to herself by that knowledge through which the apostle Paul also knew the Colossians and many believers whom he had not previously seen.

How great, indeed how miraculous, is the merit of our virgin may be judged from this: while occupied with my exposition of the Temple of Ezekiel, a work that is among the most difficult in all the Holy Scriptures, and while treating that part of the sanctuary in which the Holy of Holies and the altar of incense are described, I preferred for a little while to take this side path, so that from altar I might pass to altar and consecrate to eternal chastity a living sacrifice, pleasing to God and without any blemish.

I know that, at the bishop’s invocation, [Note: [Col. 1108] Understand Aurelius, bishop of Carthage. A little later, in Martianus, the reading was *operuit*.] the sacred bridal veil covered her virgin head, and that celebrated saying of the apostolic voice was fulfilled: “But I desire to present you all as a chaste virgin to Christ.”

“When the queen stood at his right hand, clothed in gold, surrounded by varied adornment.” In that embroidered garment, woven from a diversity of many [p. 977] virtues, Joseph too was clothed, and the daughters of kings once wore such garments. Hence the bride herself rejoices and says: “The king brought me into his chamber” (Song 1:3). And the chorus of her companions replies: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within” (Ps. 44:14).

But our prayer too will provide some benefit. Horses run more swiftly when encouraged by applause. The strength of boxers is spurred on by shouting. Armies ready for battle and drawn swords are set ablaze by the emperor’s speech. Thus, in the present work, the grandmother and mother planted, but we shall water, and the Lord will give the growth.

### 3

It is the discipline of rhetoricians to adorn the person one praises with ancestors, forefathers, and all the nobility of the past, so that a fruitful root may compensate for the sterility of its branches, and one may admire in the trunk what one does not find in the fruit.

Must I now recall the illustrious names of the Probi and Olybrii, and the distinguished lineage of the Anician blood, in which either no one, or only a rare person, has failed to deserve the consulship? Or must I bring forward [Note: [Col. 1108] Some copies read “whom he praises,” or “whom you praise.”] Olybrius, the father of our virgin, whom Rome mourned when he was taken away by an untimely death?

I fear saying more, lest I reopen the wound of her holy mother and the remembrance of her virtues become a renewal of grief. He was a dutiful son, an amiable man, a kindly master, an approachable citizen, consul indeed in his youth, but more distinguished as a senator through the goodness of his character.

Happy in his death, since he did not see his country collapsing; happier in his offspring, since the perpetual chastity of Demetrias his daughter made the nobility of Demetrias her great-grandmother more illustrious.

### 4

But what am I doing? Forgetting my purpose, while admiring the young woman I have praised certain worldly advantages, when what ought to be praised in our virgin is precisely that she despised them all, that she considered herself not noble, not preeminent in wealth, but simply a human being.

What incredible strength of soul—to seek the labor of fasts, the harshness of clothing, and restraint in food amid gems and silk; amid crowds of eunuchs and girls; amid the flattery and services of a loudly bustling household; amid the sumptuous meals supplied by the abundance of a great house!

For she had read the words [p. 978] of the Lord: “Those who wear soft clothing are in the houses of kings” (Matt. 11:8). She marveled at the way of life of Elijah and John the Baptist, each of whom girded and mortified his loins with a leather belt. One of them is said to have come in the spirit and power of Elijah—the forerunner of the Lord—prophesying while still in his mother’s womb, and praised by the voice of the Judge before the day of judgment. [Note: [Col. 1109] Graven and Cyprian, in the book *On Almsgiving*, comment: “Very blessed and glorious is the woman who deserved to be praised by the voice of the Judge even before the day of judgment.”]

She marveled at the ardor of Anna, daughter of Phanuel, who served the Lord in the temple with prayers and fasts into extreme old age. She longed for the company of Philip’s four virgin daughters and wished to be one of them, those who obtained the grace of prophecy through virgin chastity.

With these and similar thoughts she nourished her spirit, fearing nothing so much as offending her grandmother and mother. [Note: [Col. 1109] Some manuscripts read “to show her grandmother and mother,” from which a more accurate and harmonious sense may perhaps arise if one reads “her grandmother and mother.” That is, Demetrias avoided their sight lest she be deterred from her purpose of a stricter life, and she poured out prayers to God that he would soften the minds of her grandmother and mother, as is made clearer below.]

Although she was stirred by their example, she was frightened by their wishes and ambitions—not because they disapproved of her holy purpose, but because, considering the greatness of the undertaking, they did not dare to hope for or desire it.

The young recruit of Christ was in turmoil. She hated her adornment and spoke to the Lord with Esther: “You know that I hated the insignia of my head”—that is, the diadem which she wore like a queen—“and regarded it as unclean as a menstrual cloth” (Esther 14:16).

Holy and noble women who saw her and knew her—women whom a savage storm had driven from the shores of Gaul to the habitation of the holy places in Africa—say that she never used linen, never the softness of feathers, but had a little haircloth as her bed on the bare ground; that she continually drenched her face with tears, mentally prostrate at the Savior’s knees, asking him to accept her purpose, fulfill her desire, and soften the heart of her grandmother and mother.

### 5

Why do I delay any longer? When the day of the wedding was already approaching and the bridal chamber was being prepared for the marriage to come, she is said to have armed herself with the following reflections, privately and without witnesses, taking the night as her companion:

“What are you doing, Demetrias? Why do you defend your chastity with such fear? You need freedom and courage. If you [p. 979] fear such things in peacetime, what would you do when enduring martyrdom? If you cannot bear the faces of your own family, how would you withstand the tribunals of persecutors?

If examples of men do not move you, let blessed Agnes the martyr encourage you and make you fearless—she who overcame both her age and the tyrant, and consecrated the title of chastity through martyrdom.

“Wretched girl, you do not know—you do not know to whom you owe your virginity. Not long ago you trembled amid barbarian hands, and were sheltered in the lap and under the cloaks of your grandmother and mother. You saw yourself captive, and your chastity not under your own control. You shuddered at the fierce faces of the enemy; you silently watched God’s virgins being carried away.

“Your city, once the capital of the world, is the tomb of the Roman people; and you, on the Libyan shore, will receive an exiled husband, yourself an exile? What woman will serve as your matron of honor? In what procession will you be led? The shameless Fescennine songs of Punic speech will be sung for you. [Note: [Col. 1109] It is well known how licentious and lascivious were the Fescennine songs sung at weddings. Prudentius, in *Hamartigenia*, calls them “the convivial song of heated wickedness.”]

“Break through every delay. ‘Perfect love casts out fear’ (1 John 4:18). Take up the shield of faith, the breastplate of righteousness, and the helmet of salvation; go forth to battle. Preserved chastity too has its martyrdom.

“What do you fear from your grandmother? What do you fear from your mother? Perhaps they themselves desire what they do not believe you desire.”

Inflamed by these and many other goads, she cast off all bodily adornment and worldly dress as impediments to her purpose. Precious necklaces, pearls heavy with their price, and blazing gems were returned to their chests. She put on a cheap tunic and covered herself with a cheaper cloak. Then, unexpectedly, she suddenly fell at her grandmother’s knees and revealed who she was only through her weeping and lamentation.

The holy and dignified woman was stunned to see unfamiliar clothing on her granddaughter. Her mother stood astonished with joy. Neither of them could believe what they longed to be true. Their voices stuck in their throats, and amid blushing and pallor, fear and joy, various thoughts wavered.

### 6

I must yield to this point, and I shall not [perhaps: “lest I”] attempt to narrate what I would diminish by narrating. To explain the greatness of such incredible joy, even the stream of Tullian eloquence would run dry, and the twisted and flashing sentences of Demosthenes would move more slowly and weakly.

Whatever the mind can imagine, whatever [p. 980] speech can express—or cannot express—took place at that moment. Granddaughter and daughter, mother and grandmother, rushed together for kisses. They wept copiously for joy, raised her from the ground with their hands, and anxiously embraced her. They recognized their own spirit in her purpose and rejoiced that a virgin was making a noble family more noble through her virginity.

They found in her something that surpassed her lineage and that softened the ashes of the Roman city. Good Jesus, what rejoicing there was throughout the entire household! As from a fertile root, many virgins sprang up together, and a crowd of clients and servants followed the example of their patroness and mistress.

Throughout every household the profession of virginity was fervent. Although their condition in the flesh was unequal, the reward of chastity was one. I am saying too little. All the Churches throughout Africa rejoiced in a kind of triumph. The famous report penetrated not only to cities, towns, and villages, but even to the isolated farmsteads. [Variant: *mapalia* rather than *magalia*.] All the islands between Africa and Italy were filled [Variant: “refilled”] with this rumor, and joy ran farther with unhindered step.

Then Italy changed its mourning garments, and the half-ruined walls of the city of Rome recovered some of their former splendor, believing that God had shown them favor in the conversion of their foster daughter.

You might have thought that the hand of the Goths had been destroyed, and that the mass of fugitives and slaves had been struck down by the thunderbolt of the Lord from above. It was not so after Trebia, Trasimene, and Cannae, where thousands of Roman soldiers were slaughtered; after the first battle of Marcellus at Nola, the Roman people raised themselves up. [Note: [Col. 1110] Cicero says in the *Brutus* that after that disaster at Cannae the Roman people first recovered their courage in Marcellus’s battle at Nola. Gravius.]

With less joy, previously, the Roman people had seen the ranks of Gauls laid low, the nobility ransomed with gold, and the seedbed of the Roman race preserved in the citadel. This report reached the shores of the East, and the triumph of Christian glory was heard even in inland cities.

Which virgin of Christ did not boast of belonging to this company? Which mother did not proclaim your womb blessed, Juliana? Let the rewards of the future be uncertain among unbelievers. In the meantime, virgin, you have received more than you offered. One province alone had known you as a man’s bride; the whole world has heard of you as Christ’s virgin.

Wretched parents, and Christians whose faith is incomplete, [p. 981] commonly give to virginity daughters who are deformed or disabled in some limb because they cannot find sons-in-law worthy of them. “Glass is valued,” as the saying goes, “as highly as a pearl.” [Note: [Col. 1111] This is a very common proverb in our author, who by “glass” understands glass gems made to imitate genuine ones. Tertullian says similarly in chapter 3 of *To the Martyrs*: “Who values glass as highly as a true pearl? Who would not most willingly spend as much for a genuine one as others spend for a false one?” From Anastasius’s *Lives of the Popes* we also learn that glass gems were held in some esteem.]

Certainly those who consider themselves more religious give to virgins only a small amount, scarcely enough for food, while bestowing their entire wealth in both sexes upon secular children.

This is what a certain wealthy presbyter recently did in this city: he left two daughters poor in their virginal calling, while providing abundance for the luxury and pleasures of the children of others. Many women of our calling have done this, alas! Would that the example were rare. For the more common it is, the happier are those who have not followed even the examples of the majority.

### 7

It is reported, and celebrated with the praise of all Christians, that whatever had been prepared for the wedding was handed over to the virgin by the holy Christian *synoris*—her grandmother and mother—, [Note: [Col. 1111] Understand the grandmother and mother. Thus the pair is called in Greek *synoris* or *synōris*, as in “the pair of brothers.” We preferred to restore the Latinized form *Synoride*, as it appears in the manuscripts and in other printed copies, rather than *sinoride*, the corrupt form found in Martianus.] so that no injustice might be done to the bridegroom; indeed, so that she might come to the bridegroom endowed with her former wealth, and so that what was destined to perish in worldly affairs might support the poverty of God’s household.

Who could believe this? [Note: [Col. 1111] Anicia Faltonia Proba was the wife of Sextus Anicius Petronius Probus, consul in 371; she was the grandmother of the virgin Demetrias and not the actual mother of Juliana, but her mother-in-law, as can be gathered from Augustine, *On the Gift of Widowhood*, chapter 19. She bore three sons: the first, Anicius Hermogenianus Olybrius, husband of Juliana and father of Demetrias, consul in 395; the second, Anicius Probinus, consul in the same year; the third, Anicius Probus, consul in 406. Some wrongly confuse our Proba, the grandmother of Demetrias, with Proba Falconia, who composed the highly praised *Virgilian Cento on Christ*.]

That Proba, the most illustrious name of every dignity and of all nobility in the Roman world, whose holiness and goodness poured out upon everyone made her venerable even among barbarians; whom the ordinary consulships of her three sons—Probinus, Olybrius, and Probus—did not exhaust; now, when everything in the City had been burned and plundered and captivity had come, is said to have sold her ancestral possessions and made friends for herself from unrighteous mammon, so that they might receive her into eternal dwellings.

Let every rank of ecclesiastical ministry blush, and let the empty titles of monks blush, when they purchase estates while such nobility is selling them.

She had scarcely escaped the hands of the barbarians and mourned the virgins torn from her embrace when suddenly she was [p. 982] struck by the bereavement of her beloved son, something intolerable that she had never feared. [Note: [Col. 1112] Namely, the death of Olybrius, who was the father of Demetrias and died around 409.] And, as the future grandmother of Christ’s virgin, she received in hope of what was to come a deadly wound—proving in herself the truth of what is said in the lyric poem in praise of the just man:

“If the world, shattered, should fall,

Its ruins will strike the fearless man.”  
(Horace, Book 3 of the *Odes*, Ode 3.)

We read in the Book of Job: “While he was still speaking, another messenger came” (Job 1:16). And in the same book: “The life of a human being upon earth is a temptation—or, as it is better rendered in Hebrew, a military service” (Job 7:1). For this we labor and are tested in the warfare of this age, so that we may be crowned in the age to come.

Nor is it surprising to believe this of human beings, since the Lord himself was tempted (Matt. 4), and Scripture testifies of Abraham that God tested him (Gen. 22). For this reason the Apostle also says: “Rejoicing in tribulation”; and: “Knowing that tribulation produces perseverance, perseverance produces proven character, and proven character produces hope; and hope does not disappoint” (Rom. 5 and following).

And elsewhere: “Who will separate us from the love of God [Variant: Christ]? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword? As it is written: ‘For your sake we are put to death all day long; we are regarded as sheep for slaughter’” (Rom. 8:35–36).

Isaiah also exhorts such people, saying: “You who have been weaned from milk, who have been torn away from the breast, await tribulation upon tribulation, hope upon hope” (Isa. 28:7, 10). “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Rom. 8:18).

Why have I recounted these things? The following discourse will show. She had seen her homeland smoking across the middle of the sea and had entrusted her own safety and that of her family to a fragile boat; but she found the shores of Africa more cruel.

For she was received by one of whom you would not know whether he was more greedy or more cruel, [Note: [Col. 1112] Heraclianus, Count of Africa.] a man for whom nothing was sweet except wine and money, and who, under the pretext of acting on behalf of the most merciful emperor [Note: [Col. 1112] Honorius.], proved the fiercest of all tyrants.

And—to say something from the fables of the poets—like Orcus in Tartarus, he had not a three-headed Cerberus but one with many [p. 983] heads, who dragged away and tore everything apart. [Note: [Col. 1112] Sabinus, Heraclianus’s son-in-law.] This man tore promised brides from their mothers’ laps and sold the marriages of noble girls to merchants and to the Syrians, the most greedy of mortals. He spared neither the poverty of orphan girls, widows, nor Christ’s virgins, and looked more at the hands of those begging than at their faces.

Fleeing from barbarians, the matron endured this savage Charybdis and Scylla girded with many dogs—he who spared neither shipwrecks nor captivity.

At least imitate the cruel enemy of the Roman Empire. [Col. 1113] [Note: [Col. 1113] Understand Alaric, king of the Goths, whom he compares with Brennus, leader of the Gauls, because both were enemies of the Roman people, both besieged Rome, and both were given silver by the Roman people to lift their sieges. He makes Heraclianus worse because Heraclianus despoiled even the refugees, who had lost everything, out of infamous greed.]

“Brennus of our own time took only what he found; you search for what you do not find.” And his rivals wonder—for virtue is always exposed to envy—why she should have earned such chastity for herself through a silent proscription, since even the man who could have taken everything deemed it worthy to accept a portion; and why she, who understood that she was serving a tyrant under the title of private dignity, would not have dared to refuse something to the Count.

I sense that I am exposed to the bites of my enemies, since I may seem to flatter a most distinguished and noble woman. They will not be able to accuse me if they know that I have remained silent until now. For I have never praised in her the antiquity of her family, the greatness of her wealth and power, whether her husband was alive or dead—things which others may perhaps have praised in a mercenary speech.

My purpose is, in ecclesiastical style, to praise the grandmother of my virgin and to give thanks that she assisted her will with her own will. Otherwise, a monastery cell, humble food, a despised garment, an age already near death, and a short provision for the journey have no trace of flattery.

Finally, in the remaining sections my entire discourse will be addressed to the virgin—and to a noble virgin, noble no less in holiness than in lineage—whose ascent is more exalted and whose fall is therefore more dangerous.

[Note: [Col. 1113] From Virgil’s *Aeneid*, book 3, where he has “daughter of a goddess.” Some manuscripts of Jerome alter the first verse, or even omit it, through scribal error. “That one thing, born for God, for which you abandoned everything, I shall proclaim,” and so forth. In the form in which we have printed it, the passage was also read long ago by the Council of Aachen in 816 under Louis the Pious, which copied most of the remainder of this letter from this passage; hence a better reading is sometimes restored.]

“That one thing alone, born for God: above all, one thing alone,

I shall proclaim, and repeating it, again and again I shall urge you: occupy your mind [p. 984] with love of sacred reading. Do not let the good soil of your heart receive the seed of darnel and oats, lest, while the master of the house sleeps—the master who is the *nous* (νοῦς), that is, the mind, always clinging to God—the enemy sow weeds over it.

But always say: “At night I sought him whom my soul loved” (Song 3:1), and “Where do you pasture, where do you lie down at noon?” (ibid. 1:6). And: “My soul has clung to you; your right hand has received me” (Ps. 62:9).

And that saying of Jeremiah: “I have not labored by following you; for there is no grief in Jacob, nor labor in Israel” (Jer. 17).

When you were in the world, you loved the things that belonged to the world: to polish your face with rouge and paint your cheeks with white lead; to adorn your hair and build up your head into a tower with other people’s hair.

I say nothing of the price of earrings, the whiteness of pearls that testify to the depths of the Red Sea, the green of emeralds, the flames of thunderstones, and the sea-like hue of hyacinths—objects toward which the passions of matrons burn and rage.

But now that you have abandoned the world and, in the second stage after baptism, have entered into a covenant with your adversary, saying to him, “I renounce you, devil, and your world, and your pomp, and your works [Variant: riches],” keep the agreement you made and remain in accord with your adversary, preserving the covenant while you are on the road of this world.

[Col. 1114] Otherwise, he may hand you over to the judge and prove that you have appropriated something of his; you may be handed over to the officer—who is himself both enemy and avenger—and sent into prison (Matt. 5), into the outer darkness, which surrounds us with the greater horror the farther it is separated from Christ, the true light.

You will not come out from there until you have paid the last farthing—that is, every smallest offense—because we shall also give an account for every idle word on the day of judgment (ibid. 12:36).

### 8
