Let these words be spoken, not as an ill-omened prophecy against you, [Note: Two manuscripts read: “but certainly in the anxious duty of an admonisher.”] but in the anxious and cautious duty of one who fears even what is safe for you. “If the spirit of one who has authority rises up against you, do not abandon your place” (Ecclesiastes 10:4). We always stand as though in battle array and on the front line, ready for combat. The enemy wants to dislodge us from our position and make us leave our footing; but our steps must be made firm, and we must say: “He set my feet upon a rock” (Psalm 39:3); and, “The rock is a refuge for the rabbits” (Psalm 103:18), although many read “hedgehogs” instead.

The hedgehog is a small, swift animal, weighed down by thickets of thorns. But for this reason Jesus was crowned with thorns, bore our sins, and suffered for us, so that from the thorns and tribulations of women—of whom it is said, “In anxieties and pains you shall give birth, woman, and your turning shall be toward your husband, and he himself shall rule over you” (Genesis 3)—there might arise roses of virginity and lilies of chastity. Hence the bridegroom feeds among lilies, and among those who have not defiled their garments, for they remained virgins and heard the command: “Let your garments always be white” (Ecclesiastes 9:8). And as the author and prince of virginity he speaks confidently: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (Song of Songs 2:1).

The rock, then, is the refuge of the rabbits—those who flee from city to city during persecutions—and they do not fear that prophetic saying: “Flight has perished from me” (Psalm 141:5). The high mountains, however, belong to the stags, whose food is serpents; a little child brings them out from their hole, when the leopard and the kid lie down together, and the ox and the lion eat straw, so that the ox may no longer learn savageness, but the lion may be taught gentleness.

Let us return to the testimony under discussion: “If the spirit of one who has authority rises up against you, do not abandon your place.” What follows is: “For healing makes the greatest sins cease.” The verse has this meaning: If a serpent climbs into your thoughts, guard your heart with every care, and sing with David: “Cleanse me from my secret faults, O Lord, and spare your servant from those belonging to others” (Psalm 18:13). Thus you will never reach the greatest sin, which is committed in deed; rather, you will immediately cut down the incentives to vice in your mind and dash the little ones of Babylon against the rock, where no trace of the serpent is found. With caution you will promise the Lord: “If they do not rule over me, then I shall be blameless and cleansed from the greatest sin” (Psalm 18:14).

This is what Scripture elsewhere attests: “I will repay the sins of the fathers upon the children to the third and fourth generation” (Numbers 14:18)—that is, he does not immediately punish our thoughts and the decision of the mind, but repays them in later generations, namely, in evil deeds and perseverance in sins. For through Amos he says: “For three and four wickednesses of him and of that city, shall I not reject it?” (Amos 1:3; 2:4).

### 9

Let this suffice as though I had hastily gathered a few small flowers from the most beautiful meadow of the holy Scriptures, as a warning for you: close the chamber of your heart and frequently fortify your forehead with the sign of the cross, lest the destroyer of Egypt find a place in you. Rather, let the firstborn who perish among the Egyptians be saved in your mind, and say with the Prophet: “My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready; I will sing and make melody. Awake, my glory; awake, psaltery and lyre” (Psalm 107:1–2).

Tyre too is commanded to take up this psaltery, pierced through with many wounds of sin, so that it may repent and wash away the stains of its former foulness with bitter tears, together with Peter. [Note: The Cistercian manuscript adds the negative particle: “But let us not know repentance,” etc. We do not approve this reading, since it is not Jerome’s meaning.] But let us not know repentance, so that we may not sin easily. For repentance is like a second plank after shipwreck for the wretched; in a virgin, the ship should be preserved intact. It is one thing to seek what you have lost; it is another to possess what you have never lost.

Hence the Apostle chastised his body and brought it into servitude, lest, while preaching to others, he himself should be found disqualified. Burning with the passions of the human race, he said: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?” (Romans 7:24). And again: “I know that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh. For to will is present with me, but to perform the good is not. For I do not do the good that I will, but the evil that I do not will—this I do” (Romans 7:18–19). And again: “Those who are in the flesh cannot please God. But you are not in the flesh but in the spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you” (Romans 8:8–9).

### 10

After the most diligent guarding of your thoughts, you must take up the weapons of fasting and sing with David: “I humbled my soul with fasting” (Psalm 68:11); and, “I ate ashes like bread” (Psalm 101:10); and, “When they troubled me, I clothed myself in sackcloth” (Psalm 34:13).

Eve was expelled from paradise through food. Elijah, exercised by a forty-day fast, was carried into heaven in a fiery chariot (3 Kings 19). Moses, for forty days and nights, was nourished by intimacy and speech with God (Exodus 24 and 34), proving in himself the truth of what is said: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Matthew 4:4).

The Savior of the human race, who left us an example of his virtues and way of life, [Note: We have restored the words “by the Spirit” from other printed copies and manuscripts, whose authority we follow shortly afterward as well in the Apostle’s words, where we read “under your feet,” in accordance with the Greek and the Vulgate, whereas previously our copies had a different reading.] immediately after his baptism is taken up by the Spirit [Col. 1116] to fight against the devil, and, after he has been crushed and overthrown, to hand him over to the disciples to trample underfoot. Hence the Apostle says: “The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet” (Romans 16:20).

Yet the ancient enemy, after a forty-day fast, attempts his ambush through food and says: “If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become loaves of bread” (Matthew 4:3). In the Law, in the seventh month, after the blast of the trumpets, on the tenth day of the month there is a fast for the whole Hebrew people; and that person is exterminated from his people who prefers satiety to self-restraint.

In Job it is written of the dragon: “His strength is in his loins, and his power is over the navel of his belly” (Job 38). Our enemy exploits young men and girls through the ardor of their age; he inflames the wheel of our birth and fulfills the saying of Hosea: “They are all adulterers; their hearts are like an oven” (Hosea 7:4). These passions are extinguished by God’s mercy and by the rigor [or: coldness] of fasting.

These are the fiery arrows of the devil, which both wound and inflame at once. Three youths are made ready by the Babylonian king, who kindled a furnace forty-nine cubits high, himself also possessing seven weeks for destruction—weeks which the Lord had commanded to be observed for salvation. But just as there the fourth figure, having the appearance of a son of man, mitigated the immense heat and taught the flames to lose their burning power amid the blazing furnace, making the fire appear one thing to the eyes and offer another to the touch, so also in a virgin’s soul the heat of girlhood is extinguished by heavenly dew and the rigor [or: coldness] of fasting, and the companionship of angels is obtained within a human body.

For this reason the chosen vessel says that he has no command from the Lord concerning virgins (1 Corinthians 7), because it is against nature—indeed, beyond nature—not to exercise what one has been born for: to kill one’s own root within oneself, to pluck only the fruits of virginity, not to know the marriage bed, to shudder at every contact with men, and to live in the body as though without a body.

### 11

We do not, however, command you to undertake immoderate fasts or an excessive abstinence from food, by which delicate bodies are immediately broken and begin to fall ill before they have begun to lay the foundations of holy conduct. The philosophers too hold that “moderations are virtues, excesses are vices”—μεσότητες ἀρεταί, ὑπερβολαὶ κακίαι εἶναι—which may be rendered in Latin: “Moderate things are virtues; things exceeding measure and limit are counted among vices” [or: “assigned to vices”].

Hence one of the seven sages said: “Nothing in excess.” This became so famous that it was expressed even in a comic verse. [Note: See the Greek saying repeated in Paula’s Epitaph, or Letter 108, no. 20. The one whom Jerome mentions without naming as one of the seven sages is identified by Diogenes Laertius as Solon. His Greek words, μηδὲν ἄγαν, or ὦναι μηδὲν ἄγαν—“nothing in excess”—are inserted by all printed books, with the exception of the Benedictine edition, and by the manuscripts, none of which we found that omitted them.]

You should fast in such a way that you do not stagger, scarcely breathe, or have to be carried or dragged by the hands of your companions, but so that, although the body’s appetite has been weakened, you do nothing less than usual in reading, in the Psalms, or in vigils. Fasting is not perfect virtue but the foundation of the other virtues; and sanctification and chastity, without which no one will see God, provide a step for those ascending to the heights, though, if they stand alone, they cannot crown a virgin.

Let us read the Gospel concerning the wise and foolish virgins. Some of them enter the bridegroom’s chamber; others, having no oil of good works, are shut out when their lamps have gone out (Matthew 25). The field of fasting is broad. We too have often run through it, and many have written books devoted to it. We refer you to their reading, so that you may learn what good self-restraint possesses and what evil, by contrast, satiety possesses.

### 12

Imitate your bridegroom [Note: Namely, Christ, of whom it is related in Luke that he was subject to Mary and Joseph.] and be subject to your grandmother and mother. Do not see any man, especially any young man, except in their company. Know no one whom they do not know.

There is also a secular saying: “To want the same things and to reject the same things—this at last is firm friendship.” [Note: The saying is taken from Catiline’s speech in Sallust, chapter 20. Jerome quotes it elsewhere, including in Against Rufinus 2. Our Zeno of Verona, among others, also says in his Sermon on Patience: “You taught that friendship consists in willing the same things and rejecting the same things.”]

Their examples taught you to desire virginity, to know Christ’s commandments, and to understand what was good for you and what you ought to choose [or: love]. Holy conduct at home instructed you. Therefore do not think that what is yours belongs only to you, but also to them who displayed their chastity in you and brought forth in you the most precious flower of honorable marriage and an undefiled marriage-bed. This flower will produce perfect fruits if you humble yourself under the powerful hand of God and always remember what is written: “God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6).

Where there is grace, there is not a recompense for works but the generosity of the giver, so that the Apostle’s saying may be fulfilled: “It is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Romans 9:16). Yet willing and refusing belong to us; and even what belongs to us does not belong to us without God’s mercy.

### 13

Let the character of eunuchs, girls, and servants be preferred by you to elegance of appearance, because in every sex and age—even in the forced chastity of mutilated bodies—the soul must be considered. Such chastity cannot be cut away except through fear of Christ.

Coarseness and wantonness must have no place in your presence. Never hear an indecent word; or, if you hear one, do not be angry. [Note: Most manuscripts, agreeing with the older printed editions, read non irascaris (“do not be angry”) instead of inesceris. Shortly afterward Victorius thought mentes hominum should be corrected to mentis homines; we adopt the latter from the reading of the Synod of Aachen and one or two manuscripts.] Men of depraved mind frequently test the barriers of chastity with one light and passing remark. Leave laughter and the desire to be laughed at to worldly people. Seriousness suits your character.

Cato also [Note: Jerome elsewhere relates from Lucilius—or more accurately from Cicero, who in Book 5 of On Ends reports it from Lucilius—that Marcus Crassus laughed only once in his life. I do not know of the same thing being recorded about Cato. Since, however, this passage applies the same testimony to both, I suspect that the reading is corrupt, especially the word “also,” in whose place perhaps “know” or “imitate,” or something similar, should be read. The ancient manuscripts too add a relative pronoun after Marcus Crassus, and if it is added, the sense becomes clearer.]—I mean Cato the Censor, once the leader of your city—although in old age he learned Greek literature, neither ashamed as censor nor despairing as an old man of learning it; and Lucilius writes that Marcus Crassus laughed once in his life.

Perhaps that was affected severity, seeking glory and popular favor. But, as long as we dwell in this body’s tent and are surrounded by fragile flesh, we can moderate and govern our emotions and disturbances; we cannot cut them out entirely. Hence the Psalmist says: “Be angry, and do not sin” (Psalm 4:5). Explaining this, the Apostle says: “Let not the sun go down upon your anger” (Ephesians 4:26). For to become angry is human, but to put an end to anger is Christian.

### 14

I consider it unnecessary to warn you against greed, since it is characteristic of your family both to possess and to trample riches, and since the Apostle teaches that greed is the worship of idols (Ephesians 5:5). The Lord also answers the one who asks, “Good Teacher, what good thing shall I do to possess eternal life?”: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come, follow me” (Matthew 19:16, 21).

It belongs to apostolic eminence and perfect virtue to sell everything, distribute it to the poor, and thus, light and unencumbered, fly upward with Christ to heavenly things. To us—or rather, to you—a careful stewardship has been entrusted, although in this matter freedom of choice has been left to every age and every person. “If you wish to be perfect,” he says. “I do not compel you; I do not command you. I set before you the palm of victory and show you the rewards. It is yours to choose, if you wish to be crowned in the contest and struggle.”

Let us consider how wisely Wisdom has spoken: “Sell what you have.” To whom is this commanded? To the one to whom it was said: “If you wish to be perfect.” He does not say, “Sell part of your possessions,” but “all.” And when you have sold them, what follows? “Give to the poor.” Not to the rich, not to relatives, not for luxury, but for necessity. Whether the person is a priest, a relative, or a kinsman, consider nothing else in him but his poverty. Let the entrails of the hungry praise you, not the lavish banquets of those who belch from fullness.

In the Acts of the Apostles (chapter 4, verse 5), when the blood of our Lord was still warm and faith was freshly burning among believers, everyone sold his possessions and brought their prices to the Apostles’ feet, to show that money was to be trampled underfoot. It was distributed to each according to his need.

Ananias and Sapphira were timid stewards—rather, double-hearted—and were condemned because, after making their vow, they offered what was supposedly their own and not the property of the one to whom they had once vowed it. They reserved part of another’s substance for themselves, fearing hunger, which true faith does not fear, and thereby deserved immediate punishment—not through the cruelty of the sentence, but as an example of correction.

Finally, the Apostle Peter does not curse them with death, as the foolish Porphyry slanderously claims; rather, by the prophetic Spirit he announces God’s judgment, so that the punishment of two people might become instruction for many.

From the time when you were consecrated to perpetual virginity, your possessions are not yours—or rather, they are truly yours, because they have begun to belong to Christ—and, while your grandmother or mother lives, they are to be distributed according to their judgment. But if they die and rest in the sleep of the saints (for I know that they too desire to have you survive them), then, when your age is more mature, your will more serious, and your decision firmer, you will do what seems right to you—or rather, what the Lord commands [or: commands you]—knowing that you will possess nothing except what you have distributed in good works.

Some build churches and clothe their walls with slabs of marble; they transport massive columns and gild their capitals, which feel nothing of their precious adornment; they adorn doors with ivory and silver and distinguish gilded altars with gems. I do not criticize or reject this. Let each person abound in his own judgment. It is better to do this than to lie upon hoarded wealth.

But you have another purpose: to clothe Christ in the poor, visit him in the sick, feed him in the hungry, receive him in those who need shelter, and especially, among the household of faith, to nourish monasteries of virgins and care for servants of God and the poor in spirit, who serve your Lord day and night. Placed on earth, they imitate the life of angels and speak of nothing except what pertains to the praise of God. Having food and clothing, [Note: Some manuscripts add: “They are content with these.” A little earlier, instead of “to nourish monasteries of virgins,” there was “to nourish a virgin.” We have corrected such faults throughout, even without burdening the reader.] they rejoice in these riches and do not wish to have more—provided they preserve their chosen way of life. Otherwise, if they desire more, they are judged unworthy even of what is necessary.

I have spoken these things to a rich virgin and a noble virgin.

### 15

Now I shall speak only to a virgin, considering only what is within you, not what is outside you. Besides the order of psalms and prayer, which you must always perform at the Third, Sixth, and Ninth Hours, at Vespers, at midnight, and in the morning, determine how many hours you ought to spend learning Holy Scripture by heart, and how much time reading—not as a burden, but for the delight and instruction of your soul.

When you have completed these periods, and concern for your soul has frequently roused you to bend your knees, always keep wool in your hands. Draw out the threads of the warp with your thumb, or let the spindles turn in the baskets for twisting the weft. Gather the spun threads of others into a ball, or arrange them for weaving. Inspect what has been woven; correct what is defective; determine what must be done.

If you are occupied with such a variety of tasks, your days will never seem long. Even though they are stretched out by the summer sun, they will appear short when some work has been omitted. [Note: Victorius, together with most other printed copies, gives a false and contrary meaning by reading “in which no work has been omitted.”]

By observing these things, you will save yourself and others, and you will become a teacher of holy conduct, making the chastity of many your gain. Scripture says: “Every idle soul is in desires.” You must not therefore cease from work because, by God’s favor, you lack nothing. Rather, you must work with everyone so that, through the opportunity of work, you may think of nothing except what belongs to the service of the Lord.

I shall speak plainly. Even if you distribute all your wealth among the poor, nothing will be more precious before Christ than what you yourself have made with your hands, either for your own use, as an example to other virgins, or to offer to your grandmother and mother, from whom you will receive greater compensation for the support of the poor.

### 16

I almost passed over what is perhaps most important. When you were a little child, and Anastasius, bishop of holy and blessed memory, governed the Roman Church, a savage storm of heretics from the eastern regions attempted to pollute and shake the simplicity of the faith praised by the Apostle’s voice. But that man of richest poverty and apostolic concern immediately struck down the harmful head and silenced the hissing mouths of the hydra.

Because I fear—or rather, because I have learned by report—that poisonous nurseries still live and grow in certain places, I think I should warn you with devoted affection to hold fast to the faith of holy Innocent, who is both successor and son of the aforementioned man in the apostolic see. Do not accept a foreign doctrine, even if you appear prudent and clever. [Note: Martianaeus and a few other printed books and manuscripts read “you appear,” referring this to the doctrine. The majority reading, which we approve, is also more harmonious.]

Such people customarily mutter in corners and seem to seek what they call God’s justice. “Why was that soul born in that province? What reason was there for some to be born of Christian parents and others among savage and most ferocious nations, where there is no knowledge of God?” When they have struck the simple with this scorpion’s sting and made a place for themselves through a piped wound, they spread their poisons.

Do you suppose it is without reason that a tiny infant, who can scarcely recognize his mother by her smile and cheerful expression, who has done neither good nor evil, is overwhelmed by a severe illness [the printed reading is uncertain] and suffers what we see ungodly people escape and servants of God endure? [Note: This is drawn from Virgil, Eclogue 4: “Begin, little boy, to recognize your mother by her smile.” Gravius objects. The thought is otherwise taken from Cicero’s speech for Sextius: speaking of Solon, who had established no punishment for parricide, Cicero says that he did not wish to seem so much to prohibit it as to suggest it.]

“But if the judgments of the Lord are true,” they say, “and justified in themselves” (Psalm 18), and if there is nothing unjust with God, reason itself compels us to believe that souls existed in heavenly places and, because of certain ancient sins, were condemned into human bodies and, so to speak, buried in them, and that we pay in this valley of tears the penalties for ancient sins.

Hence the Prophet says: “Before I was humbled, I sinned” (Psalm 118:67); and, “Bring my soul out of prison” (Psalm 141:8); and, “Did this man sin, or did his parents, that he should be born blind from the womb?” (John 9:2), along with other things of the same kind.

This impious and criminal doctrine once circulated in Egypt and the eastern regions, and now it lurks secretly, as if in vipers’ pits, among many people. It pollutes the purity of those regions and, like an inherited evil, creeps through a few in order to reach many. I am certain that, if you hear it, you will not accept it.

For you have teachers before God whose faith is the standard of doctrine. You understand what I mean. God will give you understanding in all things.

Do not immediately demand a human reply against this most savage heresy, and against things much worse than those I have mentioned, lest I seem less to prohibit than to admonish. [Note: An old edition read Ordinis instead of hominis, but neither reading is really satisfactory. The work offered to Demetrias appears to be none other than Letter 124 to Avitus, in which he exposes the deceptions of Origenist books, *On First Principles* (Περὶ Ἀρχῶν).] The purpose of the present work is to form [or: instruct] a virgin, not to answer heretics.

As for all their frauds and the underground passages by which they attempt to overthrow the truth, with God’s help we have overthrown them in another work. If you wish, we shall readily and gladly send it to you. For, as they say, “Goods offered freely become cheap, and prices decline through ease of acquisition” [or: “become lower”], whereas things that are rare are always more valuable.

### 17

There is commonly a dispute among many people whether a solitary life or life with others is better. The former is indeed preferred to the latter; but if solitude is dangerous for men, lest, withdrawn from human company, they become exposed to filthy and impious thoughts, and, filled with arrogance and pride, despise everyone and arm their tongues by slandering clergy or other monks—of whom it is rightly said, “The teeth of the children of men are weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword” (Psalm 56:5)—how much more dangerous is it for women, whose changeable and wavering judgment, if left to itself, quickly slips toward worse things?

I have known people of both sexes whose mental health was disturbed by excessive abstinence, especially those who lived in damp and cold cells, so that they did not know what they were doing or where to turn, what they ought to say or what they ought to keep silent about.

Certainly, if people inexperienced in secular literature read something from the works of eloquent men, they learn only verbal fluency without knowledge of the Scriptures. According to the old saying, “When they do not know how to speak, they cannot keep silent.” They teach Scriptures they do not understand, and once they have persuaded others, they assume the arrogance of the learned: teachers of the ignorant before becoming disciples of the educated.

It is therefore good to obey one’s elders, submit to superiors [or: to the perfect], and, after the rules of Scripture, learn the course of one’s life from others, rather than use as one’s teacher the worst instructor of all—one’s own presumption.

The Apostle also speaks of such women: “They are carried about by every wind of doctrine” (Ephesians 4:14), “always learning and never arriving at a knowledge of the truth” (2 Timothy 3:7).

### 18. The company of worldly people must be avoided

Avoid the company of married women who serve their husbands and the world, lest your mind become agitated and you hear what either husband has said to wife or wife to husband. Conversations of this kind are poisonous. In condemning them, the Apostle took up a worldly verse and made it ecclesiastical: “Evil conversations corrupt good morals” (1 Corinthians 15:33). [Note: The saying is from Menander, as has been noted elsewhere: φθείρουσιν ἤθη χρηστὰ ὁμιλίαι κακαί—“evil conversations corrupt good character.” The meter of the iambic verse was not reproduced in the Latin translation, which translated word for word. As Victorius observed, it could have been rendered: “Evil conversations corrupt good morals,” preserving the meter.]

Choose serious women as your companions, especially widows and virgins, women whose conduct has been tested, whose speech is restrained, and whose modesty is holy.

Flee the wantonness of girls who adorn their heads, let their hair fall over their foreheads, pluck their skin, use cosmetics, wear tightly fastened sleeves, wrinkle-free garments, and curling slippers, so that, under the name of virginity, they may perish—or: appear—more saleably. For the character and pursuits of mistresses are generally judged from the character of their maidservants and companions.

Let the woman be beautiful to you, lovable to you, and worthy to be counted among your companions who does not know herself to be beautiful, who neglects the advantage of her appearance, and, when she goes out in public, does not bare her chest and neck or expose her throat by turning back her cloak, but conceals her face and enters with scarcely one eye visible—the one needed to see the road.

### 19. What must be avoided

I hesitate to speak, but whether I wish to or not, because this occurs frequently, it must be said—not because I ought to fear these things in you, since perhaps you do not know them and have never heard of them, but so that, through the occasion of speaking to you, the others may be warned.

A virgin must avoid boys with curled hair and artificially waved locks, boys smelling of foreign mouse skins, concerning whom there is the saying of Arbiter: “He does not smell good who always smells good,” [Note: Victorius preferred “a little pelt,” since the expression should refer not to those who smell but rather to the boys. Yet the verb “to smell” is more elegantly joined with the accusative. Jornandes reports in his Gothic History that these mouse skins, whose use Jerome also sharply criticizes elsewhere and in Book 2 of Against Jovinian, were brought into the Roman world by the Hunuguri, a Hunnic people. See above, Letter 127, no. 1. The verse is in Martial, Book 2, epigram; I do not find it in Petronius Arbiter, though some of his books are known to be missing, and either author could easily have used the same saying. I would rather consider the Cistercian manuscript’s reading trivii (“of the crossroads”), properly said of a proverb in common popular circulation, such as this seems to have been.] as though she were to avoid certain plagues and poisons of chastity.

I say nothing of the others whose intrusive visits disgrace both themselves and others, even if no evil is committed. Nevertheless, this itself is perhaps the greatest evil: to lie needlessly exposed to the slanders and attacks of pagans. We do not say this of everyone, but of those whom the Church itself reproves, whom it sometimes expels, and against whom the judgment of bishops and presbyters occasionally rages. Thus it is almost more dangerous for wanton girls to go to places of religion than to go out in public.

Those who live in a monastery, and who are present together in a large number, must never go out alone or without their mother. From a flock of doves a hawk often separates one, which it immediately attacks and tears apart, satisfying itself with her flesh and blood. Sick sheep leave their flock and are devoured by wolves.

I know holy virgins who, on feast days, because of the crowds of people, keep their feet at home. They do not go out precisely when greater vigilance is required and public places must be entirely avoided.

About thirty years ago I published a book on preserving virginity (Letter 22, Book 1, to Eustochium), in which I had to attack vices and, for the instruction of the virgin whom I was admonishing, expose the devil’s snares. That discourse offended many people: each one, recognizing in himself what was being said, did not willingly listen to an admonisher but rejected him as though he were an accuser of his conduct.

Yet what did it accomplish to arm an army of protesters and reveal the wound of conscience by causing pain? The book remains; the people have passed away.

I also wrote to many virgins and widows [Note: We follow the old handwritten books, in nearly all of which ΚΠΟΥΔΑΚΜΑΤΙΑ appears, not σπουδάσματα, as in other printed editions. It is a diminutive word, meaning approximately the same as σπουδάσματα, “little works,” but somewhat shorter, in accordance with the character and analogy of the Greek language, although it does not occur in Greek authors or lexicographers.] σπουδασμάτια, “little treatises,” and everything that could be said was culled in those small works, so that either we repeat the same things unnecessarily or, if now omitted, cause great harm.

Certainly blessed Cyprian published an excellent volume on virginity, as did many others, in both Latin and Greek. In the literature and languages of all nations, especially in the Churches, a chaste life—ἀγνὴ ζωή, “a life pure from sexual things”—has been praised. [Note: The word “especially,” absent from the Benedictine edition, has been supplied from all the other books. But the editions published hitherto were immediately burdened by a more serious error: they read “the life of Agnes,” from which I had conjecturally understood “the life of blessed Agnes” above, at no. 5. Yet that work was not celebrated in the literature and languages of all nations, but only in the Churches, perhaps not even among pagans but only among the faithful. Her martyrdom is praised more than her life, which, according to Ambrose, is said to have lasted thirteen years; nor does she appear to be put forward as the singular model of virginity, since at that age it had scarcely begun to be tested, while her martyrdom was far more glorious. We therefore correct the text by reading the Greek ἀγνή, agnē, “chaste” or “unmarried,” and βίος ἁγνὸς τῶν ἀφροδισίων, “a life pure from sexual relations,” which is clearly what Jerome intended throughout the context.]

But this concerns those who have not yet chosen virginity and need exhortation, so that they may know what it is they ought to choose. We must preserve what has been chosen and walk, as it were, among scorpions and serpents. With our loins girded, our feet shod, and staffs grasped in our hands, we must make our way amid the ambushes of this world and among its poisons, so that we may reach the sweet waters of the Jordan, enter the promised land, ascend to the house of God, and say with the Prophet: “Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house and the place where your glory dwells” (Psalm 25:8). And: “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I shall seek: to dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life” (Psalm 26:7).

Happy is that conscience, and blessed is that virginity, in whose heart no love dwells except the love of Christ, who is wisdom, chastity, patience, and justice, together with the other virtues. Such a woman does not sigh even once at the recollection of a man, nor desire to see one whom, once seen, she would be unwilling to release.

The holy purpose of virgins and the glory of the heavenly family of angels are discredited by the reputation of certain women who do not conduct themselves well. They must be told plainly either to marry if they cannot remain continent, or to remain continent if they do not wish to marry.

It is a matter for laughter—or rather for mourning—that, when mistresses walk out, a virgin maidservant proceeds more splendidly adorned, so that, because of excessive familiarity, you would suppose that the woman you see unkempt is the mistress.

Some women seek lodgings apart and without witnesses so that they may live more freely, use the baths, do what they wish, and avoid the consciences of many others. We see and endure these things, and if a gold coin shines forth, we count them among good works.

20. I join the end to the beginning; nor am I content to have warned you only once. Love the holy Scriptures, and wisdom will love you; cherish her, and she will preserve you; honor her, and she will embrace you. Let these jewels hang upon your breast and in your ears. Let your tongue know nothing other than Christ. Let it be able to sound forth nothing except what is holy. May the sweetness of your grandmother and mother always dwell upon your lips; their imitation is a model of virtue.

# LETTER

[Note: Concerning this and the following letter of Augustine to Jerome, the author himself speaks as follows in *Retractations* 2.45: “I also wrote two books to Jerome the presbyter, residing at Bethlehem: one ‘On the Origin of the Human Soul’; the other ‘On the Statement of the Apostle James,’ where he says, ‘Whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles in one point has become guilty of all of it,’ consulting him about both. In the former, however, I myself did not solve the question which I had proposed; in the latter, I did not keep silent about what seemed to me a solution of it, but consulted him as to whether he too approved this. He replied, praising my consultation, but answered that he did not have leisure to respond. While he was still alive, I did not wish to publish these books, lest perhaps he should sometime reply and they should be published together with his response. After his death, however, I published the former so that the reader might be warned either not to ask at all how the soul is given to those being born, or at least to accept concerning this obscure question a solution that is not contrary to the clearest truths known to the Catholic faith concerning original sin: namely, that infants are without doubt condemned unless they are regenerated in Christ. I published the latter so that the solution of the question discussed there, as it appeared to us, might also be known. This work begins: ‘Our God, who has called us …’”]

131 [Note: Not counted among the letters to Jerome elsewhere. Written in the spring of 415.] AUGUSTINE TO JEROME, OR A BOOK [Note: In the very old Ambrosian manuscript 212 it is entitled: “The Consultation of Aurelius Augustine to Jerome the Presbyter concerning the Origin of Souls.”] ON THE ORIGIN OF THE HUMAN SOUL.

He reviews various opinions concerning the origin of the soul and wishes to be taught which one ought especially to be maintained, and how that opinion can be defended against the doctrine of the Pelagians which Jerome seems, in the preceding Letter 126, almost to have indicated as his own: “that individual souls are newly made for those being born.”

## 1

“May our God, who has called us into his kingdom and glory, whom I both asked and now ask, grant that what I write to you, holy brother Jerome, consulting you about matters I do not know, may prove fruitful for us [or: may you wish it to be fruitful for us]. Although you are much older in years than I am, I too, now an old man, am consulting you. Yet for learning what is necessary, no age can seem late to me; for although old men are more suited to teaching than to learning, it is still better for them to learn than to be ignorant of what they should teach.

“Nothing do I endure more painfully, amid all the anxieties that I suffer in difficult questions, than the absence of your affection at so great a distance, so that I can scarcely give or receive your letters, at intervals not of days or months but of several years; whereas, if it were possible, I would wish to have you present every day, so that I might speak with you about whatever I wished. Nevertheless, I ought not for that reason to have failed to do what I could, even if I could not do everything I wished.”

[Note: The same Ambrosian manuscript reads: “I could scarcely receive.”]

## 2

“Behold, there has come to me a devout young man, a brother in Catholic peace, a son in age, and our fellow presbyter in honor, Orosius: watchful in intellect, ready in speech, burning with zeal, and desiring to be a useful vessel in the house of the Lord, for refuting the false and pernicious doctrines that have slaughtered the souls of the Spaniards far more unhappily than the barbarian sword has slaughtered their bodies.

“For from the shores of the ocean he hastened to us, summoned by the report that from me he could hear whatever he wished to know about the matters he desired to learn. Nor did his arrival bear no fruit. First, I prevented him from believing too much of the reports about me. Then I taught the man what I could; and what I could not, I indicated where he might learn it, and I urged him to go to you. Since he willingly and obediently accepted my advice—or command—I asked him, when he came away from you, to return through us to his own country.

“Holding fast to this promise of his, I believed that an opportunity had been granted me by the Lord to write to you about the matters which I desire to know through you. For I had been seeking someone to send to you, and it was not easy for me to find a person suitable both in faithfulness of conduct, eagerness to obey, and experience of travel. When, therefore, I had tested this young man and found him to be precisely the sort of person I was asking from the Lord, I could not doubt that he was the man himself.”

## 3

“Receive, then, what I ask you not to disdain to disclose and discuss for me. The question concerning the soul has moved many people, among whom I confess myself to be one. I will not conceal what I hold most firmly about the soul; afterward I shall add what I still wish to have clarified.

“The human soul is immortal, in a certain mode proper to it. For it is not immortal in every respect as God is, of whom it is said, ‘who alone possesses immortality’ (1 Timothy 6:15). Holy Scripture mentions many deaths of the soul; hence the statement, ‘Let the dead bury their own dead’ (Matthew 8:22).

“But because the soul dies in such a way that, although alienated from the life of God, it nevertheless does not altogether cease to live according to its own nature, it is found to be mortal for some reason and is also, not without reason, called immortal.

“The soul is not a part of God. For if it were, it would be wholly immutable and incorruptible. If it were so, it would neither decline for the worse nor advance for the better; nor, insofar as its own affections are concerned, would it either begin to possess something that it had not possessed or cease to possess something that it had possessed. But it is unnecessary to seek external testimony concerning how differently it is constituted; anyone who attends to himself recognizes this.

“It is useless, however, for those who wish the soul to be a part of God to say that the stain and disgrace which we see in the most wicked people, and finally the weakness and sickness which we feel in all human beings, do not arise from the soul itself but from the body. What difference does it make from what source that which is sick becomes sick, if it were immutable and therefore could not become sick from any source? For what is truly immutable and incorruptible cannot be changed or corrupted by the accession of anything else. Otherwise, not merely the body of Achilles, as the stories relate, but every fleshly body would be invulnerable if no accident could happen to it.

“Therefore a nature that is mutable in some way, for some reason, and in some part, is not immutable. But it is impious to believe God to be anything other than truly and supremely immutable. The soul, therefore, is not a part of God.”

[Note: Erasmus and Martianay add “in some way,” and shortly afterward read “happened” where the text has “would happen.”]

## 4. The soul is incorporeal

“I also confess that I am persuaded that the soul is incorporeal, although it may be difficult to convince those who are slower to understand. But lest I either unnecessarily create or deservedly suffer a dispute about a word—for when there is agreement about the matter, there is no need to quarrel over the name—if every substance or essence is called a body, or if whatever is more suitably named ‘body’ is that which exists in some way in itself, then the soul is a body.

“Likewise, if one wishes to call only that nature incorporeal which is supremely immutable and wholly present everywhere, then the soul is a body, since it is not such a thing.

“Furthermore, if a body is only that which, through the extension of place, is established or moved with length, breadth, and height in such a way that the greater part of it occupies a greater place, the smaller part a smaller place, and it is less in a part than in the whole, then the soul is not a body. For it extends throughout the whole body which it animates, not by local diffusion but by a certain vital activity. It is wholly present at once in all its parts; it is not less in smaller parts and greater in larger ones, but is more intensely present in some places and less intensely in others, while it is wholly present both in all parts together and in each part individually.

“For otherwise, even when something is perceived in only part of the body, it would not be wholly perceived. When something touches a tiny point in living flesh, although that place is not merely less than the whole body but scarcely visible as part of the body, the whole soul is nevertheless aware of it. What is perceived does not travel through all the parts of the body; it is perceived only where it occurs.

“How, then, does what occurs not throughout the body immediately reach the whole soul, unless the soul is wholly present where the event occurs, without abandoning the other places in order to be wholly there? For those other places live in its presence, although nothing of that kind has occurred there. If such an event occurred there too, and both happened at once, the whole soul would be equally unaware of neither but would perceive both simultaneously.

“Accordingly, the soul could not be wholly present at once in all the parts and in each individual part of its body if it were diffused through them in the way we see bodies diffused through spatial regions, occupying smaller spaces with their smaller parts and larger spaces with their larger parts.

“Therefore, if the soul is to be called a body, it is certainly not a body like an earthly body, nor like a fluid, aerial, or ethereal body. All such things are greater in larger places and smaller in smaller places, and none of them is wholly present in any one of its parts; rather, just as places have parts, so bodies occupy them with their parts.

“From this it is understood that the soul—whether it should be called corporeal or incorporeal—has a nature of its own, created with a substance superior to all these elements of the world’s mass. It cannot truly be conceived in any image of corporeal things of the kind that we perceive through the senses of the flesh; it must instead be understood by the mind and experienced as life.

“I do not speak this way to teach you what is already known to you, but to make clear what I hold most firmly about the soul, lest anyone suppose, when I come to the matters I am asking about, that I possess no knowledge or faith concerning the soul.”

[Note: Erasmus and Martianay read “similarly” where the text has “therefore,” and shortly afterward “may I hold” where the text has “I hold.”]

## 5. The soul fell through its own fault and is freed solely by God’s mercy

“I am also certain that the soul fell into sin by no fault of God, by no necessity imposed by God or by itself, but by its own will; and that it cannot be freed from this body of death either by the power of its own will, as though that were sufficient for the purpose, or by the death of the body itself, but only by the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord.

“Nor is there any soul in the human race for which the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, is not necessary for liberation. Every soul that departs from the body without the grace of the mediator and his sacrament, at whatever age of the body, will be received into future punishment and, at the final judgment, will receive its body for punishment.

“But if, after the human generation that came from Adam, souls are regenerated in Christ and brought into fellowship with him, they will receive rest after the death of the body and will receive the body for glory. These are the things I hold most firmly about the soul.”

## 6. From where the soul’s guilt arises

“Now receive, I ask, what I am seeking, and do not despise me—so may he who for our sake deigned to be despised not despise you. I ask where the soul contracted the guilt by which it is dragged into condemnation, even when death overtakes an infant, if the grace of Christ does not come to its aid through the sacrament by which infants too are baptized.

“For you are not one of those who have lately begun to chatter certain novelties, saying that no guilt was drawn from Adam which is released in the infant through baptism. If I knew that this was your opinion—or rather, unless I knew that it was not your opinion—I would never ask this of you or think it ought to be asked.

“But because we hold your view on this matter to be in harmony with the deeply founded Catholic faith, since, when refuting Jovinian’s empty talk, you cited the testimony from the Book of Job, ‘No one is clean in your sight, not even an infant whose life upon the earth is but one day’ (Job 15:4 according to the Septuagint), and then added, ‘We are held guilty in likeness to Adam’s transgression’; and since your book on the prophet Jonah makes this sufficiently and most clearly evident, where you said that infants were rightly compelled to fast on account of original sin, I not unreasonably ask you where the soul contracted this guilt, from which it must be freed even at that age through the sacrament of Christian grace.”

## 7

“Several years ago, when I was writing certain books on free will that have circulated into the hands of many and are now possessed by very many people, I thought that four opinions concerning the soul’s embodiment ought to be treated in such a way that, whichever of them were true, it would not impede my purpose. At that time I was opposing with all the strength I could those who endeavor to introduce against God a nature of evil endowed with its own principle—that is, the Manichaeans.

“For I had not yet heard anything about the Priscillianists, who invent blasphemies not greatly different from theirs. I therefore did not add a fifth opinion, which you mentioned among the others in your letter, when you replied to Marcellinus, a man of religious memory and most dear to us in the love of Christ, that the soul is not a part of God.

“First, because in asking this question one is not asking about its embodiment but about its nature. Second, because this is the view held by those against whom I was arguing, and I was arguing chiefly in order to separate the blameless and inviolable nature of the Creator from the faults and stain of the creature. They maintain that the very substance of the good God has been corrupted and oppressed in the part in which it has been captured by the substance of evil, to which they assign its own principle and rulers, and that it has been driven into the necessity of sinning.

“Setting aside, therefore, this error of heretical opinion, I desire to know which of the remaining four opinions ought to be chosen. For whichever must be chosen, far be it from attacking this faith of ours, of which we are certain: that every soul, even that of an infant, needs liberation from the bondage of sin, and that this liberation exists only through Jesus Christ, and him crucified.”

[Note: In the Louvain edition, as the Benedictines note, the reading was “had been published.”]

[Note: Six manuscripts among those consulted by the Benedictines read: “which has been captured,” and so forth.]

[Note: The negative particle, which the printed editions and the Ambrosian manuscript preserve, has been restored by the Benedictines after having been deleted. Jerome had evidently written this reply to Marcellinus against the Manichaean opinion that the soul is a part of God.]

## 8

“Therefore, not to make this lengthy, you certainly hold that God even now makes individual souls for each individual person being born. To prevent the objection that God completed all creatures on the sixth day and rested on the seventh day, you cite the testimony from the Gospel, ‘My Father is working until now’ (John 5:17).

“Thus you wrote to Marcellinus—in that letter you also most kindly deigned to mention me, saying that he had me here in Africa, so that I could more easily explain the opinion to him. If I had been able to do so, he would not have inquired of you, so far away; assuming, that is, that he wrote to you from Africa.

“I do not know when he wrote. I know only that he had learned well of my hesitation concerning this matter; and for that reason he wished to act without consulting me. Even if he had consulted me, however, I would rather have encouraged him and given thanks for whatever you could contribute to all of us, if only you had preferred to write a brief reply rather than to give a full answer.

“I suppose you did not wish to undertake unnecessary labor when I was there, whom you thought to know best what he had asked. Behold, I wish that this opinion might also be mine, but I do not yet affirm that it is.”

[Note: Martianay, after Erasmus, adds “and I work,” an addition with which the passage appears in Jerome’s Letter 126 to Marcellinus, which Augustine is now examining.]

## 9

“You have sent me disciples to teach them what I myself have not yet learned. Teach me, then, what I am to teach. For many demand that I teach them, and I confess that I am ignorant of this matter just as of many others. Perhaps, although they are ashamed to say so to my face, they nevertheless say among themselves, ‘You are the teacher of Israel, and you do not know these things?’ (John 3:10).

“The Lord said this to one of those who delighted in being called ‘Rabbi.’ For this reason he had also come by night to the true teacher, perhaps because he was ashamed to learn, having been accustomed to teach.

“As for me, I take greater pleasure in hearing a teacher than in being heard as though I were a teacher. For I remember what he said to those whom he chose above the others: ‘But you are not to be called Rabbi by human beings, for one is your teacher, Christ’ (Matthew 23:8).

“Nor was it another who taught Moses, even through Jethro; nor another who taught Cornelius, even through the earlier Peter; nor another who taught Peter, even through the later Paul. For truth is spoken by whomever he grants it, who is himself the truth.

“And if we still do not know these things, and have been unable to discover them by praying, reading, thinking, and reasoning, is this perhaps so that we may prove not only with what love we should teach the unlearned, but also with what humility we should learn from the learned?”

[Note: The same reading as Erasmus adds “Jesus”; shortly afterward it also omits the adverb at the first occurrence.]

## 10

“Teach me, then, I ask, what I am to teach; teach me what I am to hold; and tell me this: if souls are made individually for individual people being born even now, where do they sin in infants, so that they need the remission of sin in Christ’s sacrament, sinning in Adam, from whom the flesh of sin has been propagated?

“Or, if they do not sin, by what justice of the Creator are they so bound by another’s sin when they are inserted into mortal members propagated from him, so that condemnation overtakes them unless the Church comes to their aid, although it is not within their power to arrange that the grace of baptism should come to their aid?

“By what justice, then, are so many thousands of souls, which depart from their bodies in the deaths of infants without the indulgence of the Christian sacrament, condemned, if they were newly created, with no preceding sin of their own, and by the Creator’s will individually attached to individual persons being born—he who created and gave them to animate those persons, and who certainly knew that each one of these souls would depart from the body without Christ’s baptism through no fault of its own?

“Since, therefore, we cannot say of God either that he compels souls to become sinful or that he punishes the innocent, and since we are not permitted to deny that those who depart from their bodies without Christ’s sacrament, even infants, are drawn into condemnation, I beg you: how is this opinion defended, according to which souls are believed not all to be made from that one soul of the first human being, but just as that one soul was made for one person, so individual souls are made for individual people?”

[Note: The Benedictines note that in not a few manuscripts there is the reading “of the new creature.”]

## 11

“As for the other arguments brought against this opinion, I think I can easily refute them. One is the argument by which some think they press the matter: how did God complete all his works on the sixth day and rest on the seventh (Genesis 2:2), if he still creates new souls?

“If we reply to them with the statement you placed in the aforementioned letter from the Gospel, ‘My Father is working until now’ (John 5:17), they answer that ‘he is working’ means that he administers the creatures he established, not that he establishes new natures, lest contradiction be introduced into the text of Genesis, where it is stated most openly that God completed all his works.

“And when Scripture says that he rested, this must certainly be understood as meaning that he rested from creating creatures for us, not from governing them. For then he made those things that did not exist, and from making them he rested, because he had completed everything that, before it existed, he had seen needed to be made. Thereafter he would not create things that did not exist, but from things that already existed he would create and make whatever he might make.

“Thus both statements are shown to be true: ‘He rested from his works,’ and ‘He is working until now,’ since the Gospel cannot be contrary to Genesis.”

## 12

“But to those who say these things in order that God may not be believed to make new souls now, as he made that one soul, which did not exist, but rather to create them from that one which already existed, or to send them from some spring or treasury which he made at that time, the answer is easy.

“During those six days too God created many things from natures that he had already created: birds and fish from the waters, and trees, grass, and animals from the earth. Yet it is clear that at that time he made things that did not exist. For there was no bird, no fish, no tree, and no animal. It is rightly understood that he rested from creating these things, which did not exist and were created—that is, he ceased creating things that did not exist.

“But now, when it is said that he does not send souls already existing in some unknown source, nor sprinkle them from himself as though they were his particles, nor draw them originally from that one soul, nor fetter them with bodily bonds on account of sins committed before the flesh, but creates new souls individually for each person being born, this is not said to involve his doing something he had not done before.

“For on the sixth day he had already made human beings in his image, which is certainly understood to have been done with respect to the rational soul. He does this now too, not instituting what did not exist, but multiplying what did exist.

“Hence it is true both that he rested from instituting things that did not exist, and that he continues working until now, not merely by governing what he made, but also by creating in greater number something not yet created but something he had already created.

“Thus, whether in this way or in any other, we escape the objection concerning God’s rest from his works, so that we need not on that account refuse to believe that new souls are still being made—not from that one soul, but in the same way as that one.”

[Note: Martianay reads somewhat differently: “not sending souls already existing from some unknown source.”]

[Note: Five Vatican manuscripts and six Gallican manuscripts consulted by the Benedictines add the following: “Finally, after a lengthy discussion, you confirmed the ecclesiastical opinion.” I have no doubt that this was the marginal note of a diligent reader, later and improperly introduced into the text.]

## 13

[Col. 1131]

“For when it is asked, ‘Why does he make souls for those whom he knows will soon die?’ we can answer that the sins of the parents are thereby either exposed or chastised.

“We can also rightly leave these matters to the governance of the one whom we know to give to all things that pass away in time—including the births and deaths of animals—a course of the greatest beauty and order, although we are unable to perceive these things; if we could perceive them, we would be soothed by ineffable delight.

“For it was not without reason that the prophet, who had learned these things by divine inspiration, said of God, ‘He brings out the age in ordered number’ (Isaiah 40:26).”

[Note: From the Septuagint: ὁ ἐκφέρων κατ’ ἀριθμὸν τὸν κόσμον αὐτοῦ, “who brings out his world according to number.” The Vulgate has: “who brings out their host in number.”]

“Hence music—that is, the knowledge or sense of good modulation—was granted by God’s generosity even to mortal rational beings as a reminder of a great matter.

“If a human craftsman who composes a song knows what durations to assign to which sounds, so that what is sung may proceed and pass most beautifully as sounds come and go, how much more does God, whose wisdom, through which he made all things, is far superior to every art, permit no intervals of time in things coming into being and passing away—intervals that belong, like syllables and words, to the parts of this age—to pass in this moving world’s marvelous song either more briefly or more slowly than the pre-known and predetermined modulation requires?

“When I say this even about the leaf of a tree and the number of hairs on our heads, how much more should I say it about the birth and death of a human being, whose temporal life is not prolonged or shortened beyond what God, the arranger of times, knows to harmonize with the governance of the universe?”

## 14

“That argument too does not move our faith: namely, the claim that everything that begins to exist in time cannot be immortal, because everything that is born dies and everything that grows grows old, and that therefore the human soul must be believed immortal because it was created before all times.

“To say nothing of other matters, the immortality of Christ’s flesh began in time, and yet it no longer dies, and death will no longer rule over it (Romans 6:9).”

## 15

“But what you wrote in your book against Rufinus, book 3, at the very end [Note: Rufinus was pressing precisely this argument: ‘And where is God’s justice, if he grants souls to those born from adultery and incest?’ This comes, of course, from Origen, *Περὶ ἀρχῶν* (*On First Principles*) 3.3: ‘It will not otherwise be possible to answer in such a way that providence may be shown to be free of every charge of injustice, unless it is said that certain prior causes existed for them, through which, before their souls were born in a body, they contracted some fault in their perceptions or movements.’ Shortly afterward the Benedictines read *huiusmodi*, “of this kind,” instead of *huius mundi*, “of this world.”], namely, that some people slander this opinion because it seems unworthy of God to give souls to conceptions arising from adultery, and therefore endeavor to establish that, on account of deeds meriting punishment committed during a life before the flesh, souls may justly be brought into the prison of this world—I am not moved by this, since I can think of many arguments by which the slander could be refuted.

“Your own answer is also an elegant comparison: the seed in wheat that is said to have been stolen is not defective; the fault lies in the one who stole the grain. Nor, because the sower cast it with an unclean hand, ought the earth therefore not to cherish the seed in its womb.

“Even before I read this, the objection concerning offspring begotten in adultery caused me no difficulty in this question, since I considered generally how many good things God makes even from our evils and our sins.

“The creation of any animal, if it has a pious and prudent observer, arouses ineffable praise of the Creator; how much more the creation not of just any animal but of a human being?

“If the reason for creating is sought, no answer is given more quickly or more suitably than this: every creature of God is good. And what is more worthy than that the good God should make good things, which no one can make except God?”

## 16

“These and other arguments, insofar as I can, I offer against those who try to weaken this opinion, according to which souls are made individually for individual people in the same way as that one soul was made.

“But when we come to the punishments of infants, believe me, I am pressed by great difficulties and find absolutely no answer. I am speaking not only of those punishments which that condemnation has after this life, into which they must be drawn if they depart from the body without the sacrament of Christian grace, but also of the very sufferings which, while we grieve, are before our eyes in this life. If I wished to enumerate them, time would run out before examples did.

“They waste away through illnesses, are tormented by pains, tortured by hunger and thirst, weakened in their limbs, deprived of their senses, and harassed by unclean spirits.

“It must certainly be demonstrated how they can justly suffer these things without any evil cause of their own. For it is not permissible to say either that these things occur without God’s knowledge, or that he is unable to resist those who cause them, or that he either does or permits them unjustly.

“Can we rightly say that, just as irrational animals are given for the use of superior natures, even vicious ones—as we see most clearly in the Gospel, where pigs are granted to the demons for their desired use (Matthew 8:22)—the same may rightly be said of a human being?

“He is indeed an animal, but a rational one, although mortal. A rational soul is present in those members that pay the penalty through such great afflictions. God is good, God is just, God is omnipotent; to doubt this at all would be sheer madness.

“Let a just cause, then, be stated for so many evils that occur to infants. When adults suffer such things, we usually say either that their merits are being tested, as in Job, or that sins are being punished, as in Herod. Concerning certain examples that God wished to make clear, human beings are permitted to conjecture other things that are obscure—but this applies to adults.

“As for infants, explain what we are to answer if no sins in them are being punished by such great sufferings. For certainly at those ages there is no justice to be tested.”

[Note: Erasmus and Martianay add “therefore.”]

[Note: The same editors have “human conjectures are permitted,” though this is erroneous.]

## 17

“What shall I say about the diversity—or rather the absurdity—of intellects? It lies hidden in infants but, derived from their very natural beginnings, becomes apparent in adults. Some are so slow and forgetful that they have not been able to learn even the first elements of letters; others are so foolish that they differ little from cattle. Such people are commonly called simpletons.

“Perhaps the answer is that bodies cause this. But according to the opinion we wish to defend, did the soul choose a body for itself and, deceived in its choice, make a mistake? Or, when it was compelled to enter a body by the necessity of birth, did it find no other body because crowds of souls had taken possession of the others, and, like someone seeking a place in a theater, occupy not the flesh it wished for but the flesh it was able to obtain?

“Can we either say or believe such things? Teach me, then, what we ought to believe and what we ought to say, so that we may have an account of newly made souls, each individually made for each individual body.”

[Note: The Benedictines note that some printed editions and manuscripts omit *imo absurditate*, “or rather the absurdity.”]

[Note: We have not adopted Martianay’s reading after Erasmus, since it has the contrary sense; it is false, as is clear from the preceding context.]

[Note: Another reading is “individually and separately made for individual bodies.”]

## 18

“As for myself, I did say something in those books on free will—not about intellects, but at least about the punishments of infants that they suffer in this life (book 3.23.67). I shall explain what it was and why it is not sufficient for me in the question now before us, and I shall insert in this letter the passage itself, excerpted from the third book. It reads as follows:

“‘As for the bodily sufferings by which infants are afflicted, although they have no sins because of their age, if the souls by which they are animated did not begin to exist before the human beings themselves began to exist, a greater complaint and, as it were, a compassionate protest is usually raised: “What evil have they done, that they should suffer these things?” It is as though there could be a merit of innocence before anyone is capable of doing harm.

“‘But when God does something good in correcting adults, when they are chastised through the pains and deaths of their children, who are dear to them, why should these things not happen, since, once they have passed away, they will count as though they had not happened for those in whom they occurred? Those for whose sake they occurred will either become better, if, corrected by temporal troubles, they choose to live more rightly; or they will have no excuse at the punishment of the future judgment if, through the anguish of this life, they refuse to turn their desire toward eternal life.

“‘But who knows what God reserves in the secrecy of his judgments as a good recompense for the infants whose sufferings crush the hardness of adults, exercise their faith, or test their compassion? Who, I say, knows what he reserves for the infants themselves? For although they have done nothing rightly, nevertheless they have suffered these things without having committed any sin.

“‘For it is not without reason that the Church also commends those infants who were killed when our Lord Jesus Christ was being sought by Herod for execution, receiving them into the honor of the martyrs.’”

[Note: The Benedictines read, “Who, then, knows …”; others read, “Who, I say, then, knows …”]

## 19

“I said these things at the time when I wished to strengthen this very opinion that is now under discussion. As I mentioned shortly before, whichever of the four opinions concerning the soul’s embodiment were true, I was striving to show that the substance of the Creator was blameless and as far removed as possible from participation in our sins.

“Therefore, whichever of those opinions could be refuted and rejected did not affect the purpose I then had. For when all of them had been examined in a sufficiently careful discussion, whichever one rightly defeated the others would leave me completely secure, since I was showing that, according to every one of them, the point I was arguing remained invincible.

“Now, however, I wish, if I can, to choose one of them by sound reasoning. For that reason, when I look more attentively at my words in the passages I have cited from that book in defense of the very opinion we are now discussing, I do not see that its defense is strong and secure.”

20. “For the foundation of that argument of mine is what I said there: ‘But who knows what God reserves in the hidden counsels of his judgments as a fitting recompense for those little ones whose sufferings crush the hardness of adults, exercise faith, or test mercy?’ [Note: Erasmus and Martianay add here also, from the same book: ‘For although they did nothing right, nevertheless they suffered these things without having sinned.’] Yet I see that this can rightly be said of those who either suffer something of this kind for Christ’s name and the true religion, even without knowing it, or have already been imbued with Christ’s sacrament, since they cannot be freed from condemnation without sharing in the one Mediator, so that this recompense may be granted to them even for those evils which they endured here amid various afflictions. But since this question cannot be resolved unless an answer is also given concerning those little ones who, after the most grievous sufferings, die without the sacrament of Christian fellowship, what recompense is to be conceived for them, when condemnation has moreover been prepared for them? In the same book I did give some sort of answer concerning the baptism of little children—not indeed sufficiently, but insofar as seemed adequate for that work—that it benefits even those who are unaware and do not yet possess their own faith. Yet I did not then think that anything needed to be said about the condemnation of those little ones who depart this life without it, because the issue now under discussion was not then being discussed.

21. But, setting aside and disregarding the things they suffer for a brief time, which cannot be undone once past, can we similarly disregard the fact that ‘through one man there is death, and through one man the resurrection of the dead’? For just as all die in Adam, so also all will be made alive in Christ (1 Cor. 15:21–22). Through this apostolic, divine, and clear pronouncement it is sufficiently evident that no one goes into death except through Adam, and no one goes into eternal life except through Christ. For this is what ‘all’ and ‘all’ mean: just as all human beings belong to Adam through the first, that is, carnal, generation, so all human beings come to the second, that is, spiritual [Note: The same editors: ‘spiritual regeneration.’] generation who come to Christ. Therefore it is said ‘all’ in both places, because just as all who die die only in Adam, so all who will be made alive will be made alive only in Christ.

Accordingly, whoever tells us that anyone can be made alive in the resurrection of the dead except in Christ is to be detested as a common enemy of the faith [Note: In the Codex Thuaneus, in the Benedictines’ possession: ‘a common plague.’]. Likewise, whoever says that even those little ones who leave this life without sharing in his sacrament will be made alive in Christ is plainly acting against apostolic preaching and condemning the whole Church. For this is why the Church hastens and runs to have little ones baptized: because it undoubtedly believes that they cannot possibly be made alive in Christ in any other way.

But whoever is not made alive in Christ must remain in that condemnation [al. ‘the same condemnation’] of which the Apostle says: ‘Through one trespass there was condemnation for all people’ (Rom. 5:18). The whole Church believes that little ones are born subject to this trespass; and you yourself, when already arguing against Jovinian and expounding the prophet Jonah, as I recalled shortly before, affirmed this with the most truthful faith. I believe you have done so also in other places in your works, which I have either not read or do not presently remember.

I therefore ask what is the cause of this condemnation in the case of little ones, since, if souls are newly created one for each individual birth, I see no sin in them at that age, nor do I believe that God condemns any soul whom he sees to possess no sin.”

22. “Or should it perhaps be said that in the little one the flesh alone is the cause of sin, while a new soul is made for him, and that, by living according to God’s commands with the help of Christ’s grace [Note: Martianay, following Erasmus, incorrectly has ‘the grace of God’], and with the flesh itself subdued and brought under control [Note: the same reading has ‘subjected’ for ‘subjugated’], it can acquire the merit of incorruption? But because the soul in a little one cannot yet do this unless it has received Christ’s sacrament, through this grace the flesh acquires what the soul could not yet acquire through its conduct. If, however, the soul of the little one departs without that sacrament, it will itself indeed be in eternal life, from which no sin could separate it; but will its flesh not rise in Christ because it did not receive the sacrament before death?” [Note: The same editors, along with other printed editions, read accesserit.]

23. “I have never heard or read this opinion. But I have plainly heard and believed the following, and therefore have spoken: ‘The hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice, and will come forth—those who have done good, to the resurrection of life’ (John 5:28–29). [Note: Martianay, following Erasmus, reads veniet (‘will come’), and shortly afterward bona (‘good things’) for bene (‘well’), the latter closer to the Greek.] This is the resurrection of which it is said, ‘through one man, the resurrection of the dead’ (1 Cor. 15:21); this is the resurrection in which all will be made alive in Christ. ‘Those who have done evil,’ however, will rise ‘to the resurrection of judgment.’

What, then, are we to understand here concerning those infants who, before they could do either good or evil, were deprived of their bodies without baptism? Nothing is said here about such persons. But if their flesh will not rise for the reason that they did neither good nor evil, then neither will the flesh of those rise who died at that age after receiving the grace of baptism, at which they could do nothing either good or evil.

If, however, the latter will rise among the saints—that is, among those who did good—among whom will the former rise, unless among those who did evil? Otherwise we would have to believe that certain human souls will not receive their bodies, whether in the resurrection of life or in the resurrection of judgment. Even before it is refuted, this view is already displeasing because of its novelty. Moreover, who could tolerate the thought that those who hurry with their little ones to baptism believe they are hurrying for the sake of their flesh [al. ‘flesh’], not their souls?

Blessed Cyprian, indeed [Note: Epistle 59 to Fidus, from which Jerome and Augustine elsewhere draw arguments against the Pelagians.], while not issuing a new decree but preserving the Church’s most firmly established [al. ‘firmest’] faith, said—against those who thought that a little one should not be baptized before the eighth day after birth—not that the flesh, but that the soul, must not be lost; and he judged, together with certain fellow bishops, that a child could properly be baptized immediately after birth.”

24. “Let anyone think what he wishes against some opinion of Cyprian, where perhaps he failed to see what needed to be seen; only let no one think anything against the most unmistakable apostolic faith [Note: With Erasmus, Martianay has: ‘which proclaims that through the trespass of one all people are brought into condemnation,’ and so forth.], which proclaims that through the trespass of one all are brought into condemnation, and that no one is freed from this condemnation except by the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord, in whom alone all are made alive—whoever are made alive.

Let no one think anything against the Church’s foundational practice: if people ran to baptism for the sake of the little ones’ bodies alone, the candidates for baptism would be brought forward dead.”

25. “Since this is so, the cause must be sought and explained why souls that are newly created for each individual at birth are condemned [al. ‘are being condemned’] if the little ones die apart from Christ’s sacrament. That they are condemned if they depart from the body in this condition is attested both by Holy Scripture and by the holy Church.
