Therefore, if the opinion concerning the creation of new souls does not oppose this most firmly established faith, let it be mine also; but if it opposes it, let it not be yours.”

26. “I do not want anyone to tell me that this opinion should be supported by what is written: ‘He who formed the spirit of man within him’ (Zech. 12:1), and ‘He who formed their hearts one by one’ (Ps. 32:15). Something utterly strong and invincible must be sought—something that does not force us to believe that God condemns any souls without some fault.

For ‘to create’ perhaps means as much as, or even more than, ‘to form’; yet it is written: ‘Create in me a clean heart, O God’ (Ps. 50:12). Nor can it therefore be supposed that the soul is asking here to be made before it existed in any way. Thus, just as an already existing soul is created through the renewal of righteousness, so an already existing soul is formed through conformity to teaching. [Note: The same editors again give incorrectly: ‘formed through confirmation of doctrine.’]

Nor does the statement written in Ecclesiastes confirm the opinion we wish to make ours: ‘Then the dust will return to the earth as it was, and the spirit will return to God who gave it’ (Eccl. 12:7). Indeed, this supports more strongly those who think that all souls derive from one.

‘For,’ they say, ‘just as the dust returns to the earth as it was, although the flesh of which this was said does not return to the man from whom it was propagated, but to the earth from which the first man was made, so too the spirit, propagated from that one man’s spirit, does not return to him, but to the Lord by whom it was given to him.’

But since this testimony sounds so much in their favor that it does not appear wholly opposed to the opinion I wish to defend, I thought it sufficient to draw your prudence’s attention to it, lest you try to rescue me from these difficulties by means of such testimonies. For although no one can make what is not true become true merely by wishing it, nevertheless, if it could be so, I would wish this opinion to be true, just as I wish that, if it is true, you would defend it with the utmost clarity and invincibility.”

27. “This difficulty also confronts those who think that souls already exist elsewhere, prepared from the beginning of God’s works, and are sent by God into bodies. They too must answer the same question: if innocent souls come obediently to the bodies to which they are sent, why are they punished in little ones if they end this life without baptism?

The difficulty is precisely the same in both opinions. Those who assert that souls are joined individually to individual bodies according to the merits of a former life seem to themselves to escape this question more easily. For they think that ‘to die in Adam’ means to suffer punishment in the flesh propagated from Adam, from which guilt, they say, Christ’s grace frees the little along with the great.

This is right, true, and excellent: Christ’s grace frees the little along with the great from the guilt of sins. But that souls sinned in another, earlier life and were then cast into prisons of flesh—I do not believe, accept, or agree to this [Note: The Benedictines have: ‘First, because, I do not know by what circuits they say this comes about,’ and so forth.].

First, I do not know what circuits they claim bring this about, so that after I know not how many cycles of the ages one must return again to this corruptible [al. ‘corruptible’ in the genitive] burden of flesh and undergo punishment. I do not know what could be imagined more horrifying than this opinion.

Further, what righteous person has ever died concerning whom we should not be anxious—if they speak truly—not lest, while sinning in Abraham’s bosom, he be cast into the flames of that rich man? For why should it not be possible to sin after this body, if it was possible before it?

Finally, it is one thing to have sinned in Adam, whence the Apostle says, ‘in whom all sinned’ (Rom. 5:12), and another thing to have sinned outside Adam, somewhere unknown, and therefore to be thrust into Adam—that is, into the flesh propagated from Adam—as into a prison.

As for the opinion that all souls derive from one, I do not wish even to discuss it unless necessity requires. And would that the opinion we are now discussing, if it is true, were defended by you in such a way that this would no longer be necessary.”

28. “Although I desire, ask, ardently pray for, and long that through you the Lord may remove my ignorance of this matter [Note: Among the Benedictines: ‘and await.’], nevertheless, if—which God forbid—I have not deserved this, I shall ask our Lord God for patience. If we believe in him, then, even if he does not reveal certain things to us when we knock, we must in no way murmur against him. [Note: Martianay, following Erasmus, has: ‘Let us remember that it was said to the Apostles themselves,’ as in thirteen Benedictine manuscripts.]

I remember that it was said previously even to the Apostles: ‘I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now’ (John 16:12). As far as I am concerned, I would count this matter among them. Nor should I be indignant that I do not know it, lest by this very fact I prove myself even less worthy. For there are many other things that I likewise do not know, which I cannot recall or enumerate.

I would bear this ignorance tolerably enough if I did not fear that some of these opinions might creep unwarily into minds, contrary to what we hold with the firmest faith. But before I know which of them ought rather to be chosen, I openly profess that I do not rashly believe that the opinion which is true is opposed to that most strong and firmly founded faith by which Christ’s Church believes that even newly born little human beings cannot be freed from condemnation except through the grace of Christ’s name, which he has commended in his sacraments.”

EPISTLE 132 [Note: Not counted among Jerome’s epistles elsewhere. Written at the same time as the preceding one.] OF AUGUSTINE TO JEROME, OR THE BOOK ON THE MEANING OF JAMES

He asks about the passage from James 2:10, ‘Whoever keeps the whole Law but stumbles in one point has become guilty of all.’ He brings in much concerning the Stoics, who taught that all sins were equal; that whoever possessed one virtue possessed them all; and that whoever lacked one possessed none.

1. What I wrote to you, my honored brother in Christ, Jerome, when I was asking about the human soul—whether, as new souls are now made individually for each person being born, they incur the bond of sin that, as we do not doubt, must be loosed even in newly born infants through the sacrament of Christ’s grace—was becoming a work of no small length. I did not wish to burden it with any other question; but what presses more urgently must still less be neglected.

Therefore I ask, and beseech you by God, to explain something which I think would benefit many—or, if you already have an explanation from yourself or someone else, to send it to us: how are we to understand what is written in the epistle of the Apostle James? ‘For whoever keeps the whole Law but stumbles in one point has become guilty of all’ (James 2:10). The matter is of such importance and magnitude that I greatly regret not having written to you about it long ago. [Note: The same editor has: ‘Therefore I ask,’ and so forth.]

For this question concerns how we are to conduct our present life so as to attain eternal life, not the investigation of a past life that oblivion has utterly submerged—as is the question I thought should be asked about the soul.

A witty story is reported that fits this matter very well. When someone had fallen into a well where the water was so deep that it held him up so that he did not die, rather than suffocating him so that he could not speak, another man approached and, seeing him, asked in amazement, ‘How did you fall in here?’ [Note: Ten manuscripts cited by the Benedictines read, ‘having pity, he said.’] The man replied, ‘Please think about how you can get me out of here; do not ask how I fell in.’

So, since we confess and hold by Catholic faith that the soul even of a little infant must be freed by Christ’s grace from the guilt of sin as from a well, it is enough for us to know the manner in which it is saved, even if we never learn how it came into that evil. Yet I thought the question should be asked lest we perhaps unwisely hold one of the opinions concerning the soul’s incarnation that entirely denies that the little one’s soul needs to be freed, by denying that it is in this evil condition.

Let this therefore be held most firmly: the soul of the little one must be freed from the guilt of sin, and it can be freed in no other way than by the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord. If we can also know the cause and origin of this evil itself, we shall be better and more fully equipped to resist not merely empty talkers but contentious disputants. If we cannot, however, the fact that the beginning of misery lies hidden must not make the work of mercy grow sluggish.

Against those who think they know what they do not know, we are safer because we are not ignorant of our own ignorance. For one thing is not knowing what it is harmful not to know; another is something that either cannot be known, or need not be known, or is irrelevant to the life we seek. But what I now ask concerning the Apostle James’s words concerns precisely the activity in which we live and by which we strive to please God so that we may live forever.

2. How, then, I ask you, are we to understand: ‘Whoever keeps the whole Law but stumbles in one point has become guilty of all’ (James 2:10)? Does this mean that someone who commits theft—or rather, someone who says to a rich man, ‘Sit here,’ but to a poor man, ‘Stand there’—is guilty of murder, adultery, and sacrilege as well?

If not, how has the one who stumbles in a single point become guilty of all? Or does what he said about the rich and poor not pertain to these matters, while anyone who stumbles in one of these becomes guilty of all? But we must recall where that statement came from, what preceded it, and to what connected argument it belongs.

‘My brothers,’ he says, ‘do not hold the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory, with partiality. For if a man wearing a gold ring in splendid clothing enters your assembly, and a poor man in filthy clothing also enters, and you look upon the one wearing splendid clothing and say to him, “You sit here in a good place,” but say to the poor man, “You stand there,” or, “Sit beneath my footstool,” are you not judging among yourselves and becoming judges with evil thoughts?

‘Listen, my beloved brothers’ [Note: Erasmus and Martianay have: ‘My most beloved brothers.’], ‘has not God chosen the poor in this world to be rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom that God promised to those who love him? But you have dishonored the poor man’—the one, that is, to whom it was said, ‘You stand there,’ while the man with the gold ring was told, ‘You sit here in a good place.’

Then he continues, expanding and explaining the same point: ‘Do not the rich oppress you by their power and drag you before the courts? Do they not blaspheme the good name that has been invoked over you? If you fulfill the royal law according to Scripture, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself,” you do well. But if you show partiality, you commit sin, being convicted by the Law as transgressors.’

See how he calls those who say to the rich man, ‘Sit here,’ and to the poor man, ‘Stand there,’ transgressors of the Law. [Note: In the Benedictines: ‘See,’ apparently a typographical error.] Therefore, lest they think that transgressing the Law in this one matter was a contemptible sin, he immediately added: ‘Whoever keeps the whole Law but stumbles in one point has become guilty of all. For he who said, “You shall not commit adultery,” also said, “You shall not kill.” Now if you do not commit adultery but do kill, you have become a transgressor of the Law’—referring to what he had said: ‘being convicted by the Law as transgressors.’

Since this is so, it appears to follow—unless another interpretation is demonstrated—that whoever says to the rich man, ‘Sit here,’ and to the poor man, ‘Stand there,’ while not rendering the latter the honor that he renders to the former [Note: Jerome’s editors have: ‘showing greater honor to this one than to that one.’ They should at least have written the order inversely: ‘showing greater honor to that one than to this one,’ and so forth.], must be judged guilty of idolatry, blasphemy, adultery, murder, and—as it would take too long to enumerate everything—of every crime. For by stumbling in one point, he has become guilty of all.

3. But, someone may object, whoever has one virtue has them all, and whoever lacks one has none. If this is true, it confirms this interpretation. But I wish it to be explained, not confirmed, since for us it is firmer in itself than all the authority of the philosophers.

As for the matter of virtues and vices, even if it is stated truly, it does not follow that all sins are therefore equal. The inseparability of the virtues, unless I am mistaken—and if I remember correctly, though I scarcely remember it—was accepted by all philosophers who said that these same virtues were necessary for the conduct of life. [Note: The Benedictines add: ‘although perhaps,’ and so forth.]

But only the Stoics dared to argue that sins were equal, against the universal judgment of the human race. You exposed their folly with the greatest clarity from the Holy Scriptures in that Jovinian, who was a Stoic in this opinion but an Epicurean in pursuing and defending pleasures (Against Jovinian, book 2). In that delightful and distinguished discussion of yours it became sufficiently clear that the authors of our faith—or rather, the truth that spoke through them—did not approve the view that all sins are equal.

I shall try, with the Lord’s help, to explain as far as I can how it is possible that, even if the statement about virtues is true, we are nevertheless not compelled to admit that all sins are equal. If I succeed, you will approve it; but wherever I fall short in the argument, you will supply what is lacking.

4. The chain of virtues.—Certainly those who say that whoever has one virtue has them all, and that all are absent from anyone who lacks one, derive their conviction from this: prudence cannot be cowardly, unjust, or intemperate; for if it were any of these things, it would not be prudence. Moreover, prudence exists only if it is also courageous, just, and temperate; therefore, wherever prudence exists, it brings the others with it.

Likewise, courage cannot be imprudent, intemperate, or unjust. Temperance, too, must be prudent, courageous, and just. Justice is not justice unless it is prudent, courageous, and temperate. Thus, wherever any one of these is true, the others are likewise present. [Note: The Benedictines have: ‘Thus, wherever any one of them is true, and so forth,’ and shortly afterward, ‘that true virtue is not.’] But where the others are absent, that one is not true either, even if in some way it may appear similar.

5. Manifest and disguised vices.—For, as you know, some vices are plainly opposed to virtues, such as imprudence to prudence. Others are opposed simply because they are vices, yet are similar in a deceptive guise—for example, not imprudence but cunning to the same prudence.

By ‘cunning’ I mean here what is more commonly understood and called cunning among malicious people, not what our Scriptures customarily mean by cunning, since they often use it in a good sense: ‘Be cunning as serpents’ (Matt. 10:16), and, ‘To give cunning to the simple’ (Prov. 1:4). Indeed, the most eloquent writer in the Roman language among them also said: ‘Nor did deceit or cunning fail him for taking precautions,’ placing cunning in a good sense. But this is very rare among them and very common among us.

Likewise, among the parts of temperance, the most plainly opposed vice is extravagance, which is opposed to thrift. What is commonly called miserliness is indeed a vice, but it resembles thrift not in nature, but in a most deceptive appearance.

In the same way, injustice is manifestly opposed to justice. Yet the desire for revenge often imitates justice, although it is a vice. Cowardice is plainly opposed to courage; hardness, however, differs from courage in nature but deceives by its resemblance.

Constancy is a part of virtue; inconstancy is far removed from it and plainly opposed to it. But obstinacy seeks to be called constancy and is not, because the former is a virtue while the latter is a vice.

6. Therefore, so that we do not need to repeat these matters again, let us take an example from which the rest may be understood. Catiline, according to those who were able to know him [Note: The same editors, On Catiline, chapter 5: ‘His body endured hunger, vigils, and cold beyond what anyone could believe,’ and so forth.], could endure cold, thirst, and hunger; he was more capable of enduring hunger, cold, and sleeplessness than anyone could believe. Thus he appeared to possess great courage, both for himself and for his followers.

But this courage was not prudent, for he chose evil things over good. He was not temperate, for he was defiled by the most shameful corruptions. He was not just, for he had conspired against his country. Therefore it was not courage either; rather, hardness assumed the name of courage in order to deceive fools. For if it had been courage, it would have been a virtue, not a vice. And if it had been a virtue, it would never have been abandoned by the other virtues as inseparable companions.

7. Therefore, when the question is asked whether vices likewise are all present wherever one is present, or none are present wherever one is absent, it is difficult to demonstrate this. The reason is that two vices are usually opposed to one virtue: the one that is openly contrary and the one that is veiled beneath the appearance of similarity.

Thus it was easier to see what Catiline possessed, since it was not courage, when he did not possess the other virtues either. But it is difficult to persuade people that cowardice was present where there was an ability to practice and endure the most severe hardships beyond anything anyone could believe. Perhaps, however, to those who look more sharply, that very hardness appears to be cowardice, because he had neglected the labor of good pursuits by which true courage is acquired.

Nevertheless, because there are bold people who are not timid, and again timid people who lack boldness, although both are vices—for one who is courageous with true courage neither acts rashly nor fears thoughtlessly—we are compelled to admit that there are more vices than virtues.

8. Hence sometimes one vice is removed by another, as love of money by love of praise. Sometimes one vice gives way so that several others may take its place, as when a drunkard drinks moderately and learns both miserliness and ambition. Vices, therefore, can give way to vices that succeed them, not to virtues, and for that reason they are numerous.

But wherever one virtue enters, since it brings the others with it, all the vices that were present must certainly give way. For they were not all present: sometimes an equal number succeeded one another, sometimes more replaced fewer, or fewer replaced more.

9. Whether matters really stand this way must be investigated more carefully. For this too is not a divine pronouncement—the statement that whoever has one virtue has them all, and that no virtue exists in anyone who lacks one—but an opinion formed by human beings, certainly ingenious and diligent, but still human beings.

I do not know how to put the matter. I will not speak of a man from whom virtue is said to receive its name, but even of a woman who preserves fidelity to her husband’s marriage bed—if she does so because of a command and promise, and is first of all faithful to him [Note: The same editors, along with many other printed editions, have ‘and which.’ The Benedictines restore the printed reading from two manuscripts, noting that it is likewise found in three other Vatican manuscripts: ‘and to whom,’ namely, God.]—I do not know how to say that she lacks chastity, or that chastity is no virtue or only a slight virtue. The same applies to a husband who observes this toward his wife.

And yet there are many such people, of whom I would not say that any one is without some sin; and certainly that sin, whatever its character, proceeds from some vice. Therefore conjugal chastity in religious men and women, although it is undoubtedly a virtue—for it is neither nothing nor a vice—does not nevertheless bring all the virtues with it.

For if all were present there, no vice would exist; if no vice existed, there would be no sin at all. But who is without some sin? Who, then, is without some vice—that is, some fuel or kind of root of sin—when the one who reclined upon the Lord’s breast cries out, ‘If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us’ (1 John 1:8)?

This does not need to be argued with you at greater length; I say it for the sake of others who may perhaps read this. For you yourself, in that distinguished work of yours Against Jovinian, also carefully proved this from the Holy Scriptures. There you included, from this very epistle whose words we are now seeking to understand, the statement: ‘For we all stumble in many ways’ (James 3:2). The Apostle does not say, ‘You stumble,’ but ‘we all stumble,’ although he was speaking as Christ’s Apostle; and in the present passage he says: ‘Whoever keeps the whole Law but stumbles in one point has become guilty of all’ (James 2:10). There he says that not merely some, but all, stumble—not in one matter, but in many.

10. Yet far be it from any believer to think that the many thousands of Christ’s servants who truthfully say that they have sin, lest they deceive themselves and the truth not be in them, possess no virtue—when wisdom itself is a great virtue.

Wisdom itself said to the human being, ‘Behold, piety is wisdom’ (Job 28:28, according to the Septuagint). Far be it, then, that we should say that so many faithful and devout people do not possess piety toward God, which the Greeks call either εὐσέβεια (eusebeia) or, more explicitly and fully, θεοσέβεια (theosebeia). But what is piety except the worship of God? And how is he worshiped except through love?

Love, therefore, proceeding from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith, is a great and true virtue, because it is the fulfillment of the commandment. It is rightly called strong, ‘as death’ (Song 2:6): either because no one conquers it, just as no one conquers death; or because in this life the measure of love extends to death, as the Lord says, ‘Greater love has no one than this, that someone should lay down his life for his friends’ (John 15:13); or rather because, just as death tears the soul away from the senses of the flesh, so love tears it away from carnal desires.

Knowledge serves love when it is useful, for without love it puffs up. Whatever love has fulfilled by building up, knowledge will find nothing empty there to inflate it. He demonstrated the usefulness of knowledge by defining it: after saying, ‘Behold, piety is wisdom,’ he immediately added, ‘To abstain from evil is knowledge’ (Job 28:28).

Why, then, should we not say that whoever possesses this virtue possesses all virtues, since ‘love is the fulfillment of the Law’ (Rom. 13:10)? Or is it rather the case that the more love there is in a person, the more virtue that person possesses, while the less love there is, the less virtue is present, because love itself is virtue—and the less virtue there is, the greater the vice? [Note: Again the same editors: ‘the less faith, the less virtue.’] Wherever love is full and perfect, therefore, nothing of vice will remain.

11. Accordingly, the Stoics seem to me to be mistaken because they refuse to allow a person who is progressing in wisdom to possess wisdom at all. They say that a person possesses it only when he has become wholly perfect in it—not because they deny that he has advanced, but because unless he suddenly emerges from some deep abyss into the free air of wisdom, he is wise in no respect.

For, just as it makes no difference to suffocate a person whether the water above him is many stadia deep, a palm’s breadth, or a finger’s breadth, so they say that those who are striving toward wisdom do make progress, as though rising from the bottom of a whirlpool into the air; but unless by progressing, as though emerging, they escape all folly—the water pressing upon them—they do not possess virtue and are not wise. Once they have escaped, however, they immediately possess it all, and no folly remains from which any sin at all could arise.

12. “This comparison, in which folly is represented as water and wisdom as air, so that the mind, emerging into wisdom as though from the suffocation of folly, suddenly breathes again, does not seem to me sufficiently suited to the authority of our Scriptures. Rather, vice or folly should be compared with darkness, and virtue and wisdom with light, insofar as such bodily likenesses can be transferred to intelligible realities.

It is not, therefore, like rising from water into air, where, once one has passed above the surface, one suddenly inhales as much as is needed. It is rather like proceeding from darkness into light: as one advances gradually, one is gradually illuminated. Until this happens in the fullest measure, we nevertheless already say that the person is like someone emerging from the deepest cave, touched by the nearness of the light—more so the closer he comes to the exit. [Note: Some have corruptly ‘having emerged.’]

Whatever shines in him comes from the light toward which he is advancing; whatever remains dark comes from the darkness out of which he is emerging.

Thus it is true both that ‘no living person will be justified in your sight’ (Ps. 142:2), and that ‘the just person lives by faith’ (Hab. 2:4). The saints are clothed with righteousness (Job 29:14), one more and another less. No one here lives without sin, and in this respect too one has more and another less. But the best person is the one who has the least.”

14. “But why have I, as though forgetful of whom I am addressing, assumed the role of a teacher, when I had proposed that I wished to learn from you? Yet since, concerning the equality of sins—the subject from which the question at hand arose—I had decided to set forth my opinion for your examination, I shall at last bring it to a conclusion.

“For even if it is true that the person who possesses one virtue possesses all the virtues, and that the person who lacks one possesses none, sins are not thereby equal. For where there is no virtue, nothing indeed is right; yet it does not follow that one thing is not more wrong than another, or one distortion more distorted than another.

“But if, as I consider more true and more consistent with the sacred Scriptures, the movements of the soul are like the members of the body—not in their apparent location, but in their felt dispositions—and if some are more greatly illuminated, others less, while another entirely lacks light and is overshadowed by a dark obstacle, then surely, just as anyone who is affected by the illumination of devout love is affected more in one action, less in another, and not at all in some, [1022] so he may be said to possess one virtue and not possess another, to possess one more and another less.

“For we may rightly say that charity is greater in this person than in that one; and that, with respect to the charity which is piety, there is some charity in this person and none in that one. Even in the same individual, one may possess greater chastity than patience, and greater chastity today than yesterday, if he is making progress; he may still lack continence, while possessing no small measure of mercy.”

[Note: [Col. 1144] Erasmus and Martianay read: “which pertains to piety.”]

15. “To state briefly and generally what conception I have of virtue, insofar as it concerns right living: VIRTUE IS CHARITY, by which what ought to be loved is loved. In some it is greater, in others less, and in others it is absent altogether. Yet the fullest charity, which cannot be increased so long as a person lives here, exists in no one. And so long as it can be increased, whatever is less than it ought to be arises from fault.

“Because of this fault, there is no just person on earth who does good and does not sin. Because of this fault, no living person will be justified in God’s sight. Because of this fault, ‘if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us’ (1 John 1:8). Because of this also, however far we may have advanced, it is necessary for us to say, ‘Forgive us our debts’ (Matt. 6:12), even though all things said, done, and thought have already been forgiven in baptism.

[Col. 1145] [Note: The same writers also place a question mark at the end: “What, then, does the person who sees rightly see—where, and when,” and so forth.]

“Therefore the person who sees rightly sees where, when, and in what way that perfection is to be hoped for to which nothing can be added.” If there were no commandments, there would certainly be no place where a person could examine himself more surely and see from what he should turn away, toward what he should strive, for what he should give thanks, and what he should ask for. The commandments are therefore greatly useful, provided that free will is granted only so much that God’s grace may be honored more greatly.”

16. Resolution of the question.—“If these things are so, how does the person who has kept the whole Law become guilty of all if he offends in one matter? Or is it perhaps because ‘the fullness of the Law is charity’ (Rom. 13:10), by which God and one’s neighbor are loved, and because the whole Law and the Prophets depend upon these commandments of charity (Matt. 22:40)? Accordingly, the person who acts against that charity on which everything depends rightly becomes guilty of all.

“No one sins except by acting against it. For ‘you shall not commit adultery, you shall not murder, you shall not steal, you shall not covet,’ and if there is any other commandment, it is summed up in this saying: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’ Love does no harm to one’s neighbor. Therefore charity is the fullness of the Law (Rom. 13:9–10).

“No one loves his neighbor without loving God; and he should extend to his neighbor, whom he loves as himself, as much of this love as he can, [1023] so that his neighbor too may love God. If he does not love God, he loves neither himself nor his neighbor.

“Thus the person who has kept the whole Law, if he offends in one matter, becomes guilty of all, because he acts against charity, upon which the whole Law depends. He therefore becomes guilty of all by acting against that on which everything depends.”

17. “Why, then, are sins not said to be equal? Is it perhaps because the person who sins more gravely acts more against charity, while the person who sins less gravely acts less against it? By the very fact that he commits a sin, he becomes guilty of all; but the person who sins more gravely, or sins in more matters, is more guilty, while the person who sins less gravely, or in fewer matters, is less guilty—guilty in greater measure according as he has sinned more, and in lesser measure according as he has sinned less. Yet even if he offends in one matter, he is guilty of all, because he acts against that on which everything depends.

“If these things are true, the statement made by the man who also possessed apostolic grace is resolved in the same way: ‘For we all offend in many things’ (James 3:2). We all offend, but one person more gravely and another less gravely. According to how gravely or lightly each person sins, he is greater in committing sin insofar as he is lesser in loving God and neighbor. Conversely, he is lesser in committing sin insofar as he is greater in loving God and neighbor.

“Thus he is fuller of iniquity insofar as he is emptier of charity. And we are perfect in charity when nothing remains of weakness.”

[Col. 1146]

18. “Nor, in my opinion, should the sin of showing partiality be considered trivial, if we understand the distinction between sitting and standing as referring to ecclesiastical honors. For who could tolerate a rich man being chosen for the seat of honor in the Church while a poorer man, more learned and holier, is disregarded?

“But if he is speaking of ordinary gatherings, who does not sin in this respect—if indeed he sins—unless he judges inwardly in such a way that the richer man seems to him better than the poorer precisely because he is richer? For this is what he appears to have signified when he says: ‘Are you not judging among yourselves, and have you not become judges with evil thoughts?’ (James 2:4).”

19. “The law of liberty, therefore, is the law of charity, of which he says:

“‘If you fulfill the royal law according to the Scriptures, “You shall love your neighbor [or: your neighbor] as yourself,” you do well. But if you show partiality, you commit sin, being convicted by the Law as transgressors.’

“And after that most difficult statement to understand, concerning which I have said enough of what I thought ought to be said, he recalls the same law of liberty:

“‘So speak and so act as those who are beginning to be judged through the law of liberty’ [1024] (James 2:12).

“And since he knows what he said shortly before—‘For we all offend in many things’—he suggests the Lord’s medicine as something daily for daily wounds, though they may be lighter:

“‘For judgment without mercy,’ he says, ‘will be upon the person who has not shown mercy’ (ibid. 13).

“Hence also the Lord says: ‘Forgive, and you will be forgiven; give, and it will be given to you’ (Luke 6:37).

[Note: In Greek, κατακαυχεῖται. After Erasmus, Martianay renders it here and below as *superexaltat* (‘exalts above’); shortly afterward he also reads *judicium* for *judicio*, as below.]

“‘Mercy exults over judgment’ (James 2:13). It does not say, ‘Mercy defeats judgment,’ for mercy is not opposed to judgment, but it ‘exults over’ it, because many are gathered through mercy—but they are those who have shown mercy. For ‘blessed are the merciful, because God will have mercy on them’ (Matt. 5:7).”

20. “And this is certainly just: that those who have forgiven should be forgiven, and that those who have given should be given to. For God possesses both mercy when judging and judgment when showing mercy; therefore it is said to him: ‘I will sing of mercy and judgment to you, Lord’ (Ps. 100:1).

“For whoever, as though excessively righteous, confidently awaits judgment without mercy provokes the most righteous anger, fearing which that person said: ‘Do not enter into judgment with your servant’ (Ps. 142:2). Hence it is said to a rebellious people: ‘Why do you contend with me in judgment?’ (Jer. 2:29).

“For when the just king sits upon his throne, who will boast that he has a pure heart? Or who will boast that he is clean from sin? (Prov. 20:8–9). What hope, then, is there, unless mercy triumphs over judgment? But this is true of those who have shown mercy, saying truthfully, ‘Forgive us,’ [Note: The Benedictines add, ‘our debts.’] ‘as we also forgive’ (Matt. 6:12), and giving without complaint; for ‘God loves a cheerful giver’ (2 Cor. 9:7). [Col. 1147]

“Finally, Saint James from this very point speaks of works of mercy, so that he may console those whom that severe statement had greatly frightened. He reminds them how even daily sins, without which no one lives here, are expiated by daily remedies, lest a person who, when he has offended in one matter, becomes guilty of all (James 5:16), by offending in many things—for ‘we all offend in many things’—should, because of the great heap of his guilt collected bit by bit, reach the tribunal of so great a judge and fail to find the mercy he did not show. Rather, by forgiving and giving, let him deserve to have his sins forgiven and the promises restored to him.”

21. “I have said much, perhaps causing you weariness, although you do not expect to learn from me these things which you approve and which you are accustomed to teach. But if there is anything in them, insofar as the matter itself is concerned—for I am not greatly concerned with the eloquence in which it has been expressed—[1025] if there is anything that offends your learning, I ask you to warn me by writing back and not to consider it burdensome to correct me.

“Unhappy is the person who neither honors worthily the great and holy labors of your studies nor gives thanks for them to our Lord God, by whose gift you are such a person. Since I ought more willingly to learn from anyone what I ignorantly fail to know than readily to teach anyone what I do know, how much more rightly do I demand this debt of charity from you, by whose teaching, in the name and with the help of the Lord, ecclesiastical literature in the Latin language has been aided as greatly as it never before could be?

“Above all, however, concerning this statement—‘Whoever keeps the whole Law but offends in one matter has become guilty of all’ (James 2:10)—if your affection knows some other way in which it can be better explained, I beg you by the Lord to be willing to share it with us.”

---

## LETTER CXXXIII [Note: In some copies it lacks a number. Written in the same year, 415.] TO [Note: In certain manuscripts and early editions, including the former Vatican manuscript of Queen Christina of Sweden, no. 286, it is headed “To Ctesiphon Urbicus”; in others, “To Atesiphon” or “To Tesiphon Urbicus.” Orosius simply calls him Ctesiphon. It seems beyond doubt that *Urbicus* was a surname derived from the city of Rome, just as Pope Zephyrinus is called *Urbicus* by Optatus in book 1, and Siricius by Paulinus in Letter 1 to Severus—not to mention Paula *Urbica*, as Jerome calls her, and several others.] CTESIPHON. Against Pelagius.

He refutes, at the request of Ctesiphon, the madness of the Pelagian teaching, especially *apatheia* (ἀπάθεια) and *anamartēsia* (ἀναμαρτησία), that is, freedom from the disturbances of the soul and impeccancy. He shows from what foul sources they flowed. He then rebukes Rufinus, who translated into Latin a book by Xystus the Pythagorean, redolent of the Pelagian error, under the name of Xystus the martyr and Roman Pontiff, and who also passed off another work by Eusebius Pamphilus as if it had been written by the martyr Pamphilus. Finally, he promises that, when leisure permits, he will answer the Pelagian teaching in a substantial volume.

### 1.

You have acted neither rashly, as you falsely suppose, but lovingly and diligently, in sending me from an old source a new question [Col. 1148] which, even before your letter, had deceived many in the East: namely, that through feigned humility they might learn pride and say with the devil, “I will ascend into heaven; above the stars of heaven I will set my throne, and I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14:13).

“For what greater rashness can there be than to claim for oneself not merely likeness to God, but equality with God, and in a brief assertion [1026] to embrace all the poisons of the heretics, which flowed from the source of the philosophers, especially Pythagoras and Zeno, the leader of the Stoics?

“For they assert that what the Greeks call *pathē* (πάθη), which we may call disturbances, namely distress and joy, hope and fear—two of them concerned with the present and two with the future—can be eradicated from the mind, and that no fiber or root of vices can remain at all in a human being through meditation and constant practice of the virtues.

“Against them the Peripatetics, who descend from the source of Aristotle, argue with great force; so do the later Academics, whom Cicero follows. These philosophers overturn, in their case, not realities—for there are none—but shadows and wishes.

“For this is to remove the human being from the human being, and to make him exist as a being without a body. It is to desire rather than to teach, when the Apostle says: ‘Wretched man that I am, who will free me from this body of death?’ (Rom. 7:24).

“And because the brevity of a letter cannot contain everything, I shall briefly set out for you what must be avoided. Hence also comes that line of Virgil:

> Hence they fear and desire, grieve and rejoice, nor look back upon the breezes,  
> Shut in by darkness and a blind prison.  
> (Aeneid 6)

“For who can either not exult with joy, or not be contracted by sorrow, or not be lifted up by hope, or not be terrified by fear? Therefore the very weighty poet Flaccus also wrote in a satire:

> For no one is born without faults; the best person is the one  
> Oppressed by the fewest.  
> (Horace, *Satires* 1.3)

### 2.

“Beautifully one of our writers said: ‘Philosophers are the patriarchs of heretics.’ Through perverse teaching they have stained the purity of the Church, so that they do not know the saying concerning human frailty: ‘What does earth and ashes boast of?’ (Ecclus. 10:49).

[Note: The text is corrupt in Martianay’s edition, and the manuscripts resist the reading adopted by Erasmus: “when the same Apostle says concerning them,” etc.]

“This is especially so since the same Apostle says: [Col. 1148] ‘I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and leading me captive’ (Rom. 7:23). And again: ‘For I do not do the good that I want, but the evil that I do not want, that I practice’ (ibid. 19).

“If he does what he does not want, how can the statement stand that a person can be without sin if he wishes? How can he do what he wishes when the Apostle asserts that he cannot accomplish what he desires? [1027] [Col. 1149]

“When we ask them who those people are whom they consider without sin, they try to evade the truth by a new trick: they say that they do not mean those who are or have been without sin, but those who can be so. These excellent teachers say that something can exist which they demonstrate has never existed, although Scripture says: ‘Whatever is to be, has already been in former time’ (Eccles. 1:9).

“Nor is it now necessary for me to go through each of the saints and, as upon a beautiful body, point out certain moles and spots. Most of our people do this straightforwardly, although with a few brief statements of Scripture the arguments of the heretics—and through them those of the philosophers—can be refuted.

“For what does the chosen vessel say? ‘God has enclosed all under sin, so that he may have mercy on all’ (Rom. 11:32). And elsewhere: ‘For all have sinned and lack the glory of God’ (ibid. 3:23).

“Ecclesiastes too, through whom Wisdom itself sang, openly declares and says: ‘For there is no just person upon earth who does good and does not sin’ (Eccles. 7:21). And again: ‘If your people sin—for there is no human being who does not sin’ (ibid.). And: ‘Who will boast that he has a pure heart?’ (Prov. 20:9). And: ‘No one is clean from defilement, not even if his life upon earth has been for a single day.’

“Hence David also says: ‘For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother conceived me’ (Ps. 50:7). And in another psalm: ‘No living person will be justified in your sight’ (Ps. 142:2).

“They evade this testimony through a new argument under the guise of piety. They say that no one is perfect in comparison with God, as though Scripture had said this. For it does not say, ‘No living person will be justified in comparison with you,’ but, ‘No living person will be justified in your sight.’

“When it says ‘in your sight,’ it wishes this to be understood: even those who appear holy to human beings are not holy before God’s knowledge and awareness. For a human being [1028] sees the face, but God sees the heart.

“If, with God examining and contemplating all things—and the secrets of the heart cannot deceive him—there is no just person, it is clearly shown that the heretics do not exalt the human being to a lofty height but detract from God’s power. I could gather many other such passages from the sacred Scriptures; if I wished to do so, I would exceed not merely the length of a letter but even that of a volume.”

### 3.

“Those who, in this kind of self-applauding faithlessness, deceive the simple and unlearned assert nothing new; but they cannot deceive ecclesiastical men who meditate on God’s law day and night.

“Let them therefore be ashamed of their leaders and associates, who say that a person can be without sin if he wishes—what the Greeks call *anamartētos* (ἀναμάρτητος).

[Note: Among the Greeks that opinion was common according to which God alone was said to be without sin: ὁ μόνος ἀναμάρτητος, “the only one without sin.” See Clement of Alexandria.]

“And because the ears of the Churches throughout the East cannot bear this, they pretend that they do indeed say ‘without sin,’ but do not dare to say *anamartētos*. [Note: Huet and other learned men think Jerome himself mistaken in identifying *anamartētos* with ‘without sin,’ since according to their view it rather signifies ‘incapable of sinning.’ Nor did Pelagius wish the perfect to be incapable of sin, but only able to be free from sin; because he maintained that this could be achieved by the powers of free will, he was gravely mistaken in faith. They say the same concerning *anamartēsia*, which Jerome generally renders as ‘impeccancy,’ or ‘not sinning’; they, on the contrary, render it ‘impeccability,’ or ‘the inability to sin.’ Since we are reluctant to dwell longer on these matters, we maintain that Jerome’s interpretation and meaning can be defended by one or two examples. When the Lord Christ wished to drive away the troublesome accusers of the adulterous woman, he said, ‘Let the one among you who is without sin first,’ and so forth. In that passage it is perfectly clear that *anamartētos* does not mean ‘incapable of sinning,’ but simply ‘without sin,’ as the Vulgate translator renders it, and as it must necessarily be translated. In the same way Herodotus, book 5, chapter 39, says of Anaxandrides, who refused to dismiss γυναῖκα ἐοῦσαν ἀναμάρτητον, that is, “a woman who had not sinned”; he certainly did not understand the word as meaning “incapable of sin,” or “one who could not have sinned.”]

[Col. 1150]

“Thus they act as though ‘without sin’ were one thing and *anamartētos* another, and as though the Greek expression used among them had been expressed in Latin by two words.

“If you say ‘without sin’ and deny that you say *anamartētos*, then condemn those who proclaim you *anamartētos*. But you do not do so. For you know what you teach your disciples inwardly, mentioning one thing with your mouth while concealing another in your conscience. You speak to us outsiders and the unlearned through parables, but to your own people you confess the mysteries. You even boast that you do this according to Scripture, because it is said: ‘Jesus spoke to the crowds in parables’ (Luke 8:20); and to the disciples in the house he says: ‘To you it has been given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, but to them it has not been given’ (Matt. 13:11).

“But, as I began to say, I shall briefly set out the names of your leaders and associates, so that you may observe the sort of company in which you glory.

“Manichaeus says that his elect, whom he places among Plato’s *apsides* (ἀψῖδες) [1029] in the heavens, are entirely without sin and cannot sin even if they wish. For he says that they have risen to such heights of virtue that they mock the works of the flesh.

[Note: Formerly the phrase was understood to refer to the souls, or among the ideas and forms, of Plato. The printed reading restored by the Benedictines is confirmed by a large number of our manuscripts, although they more often give the Latin forms *absidas*, as in Ambrosian manuscript S. 42, or *apsidas*. Tertullian explains the matter in *De anima*, chapter 54, where he says: “According to Plato, wise souls are raised into the ether; according to Arius, into the air; according to the Stoics, beneath the moon.” Thus one may understand that Plato intended the ether by *apsides*, or ἀψῖδες. Pliny, book 2, chapter 15, reports that the Greeks called the circles of the stars *apsides*.]

“Priscillian, in Spain, a branch of Manichaeus—concerning whose depravity your disciples love you greatly—rashly claiming for yourselves the word of perfection and knowledge, shut themselves away alone with women, and during sexual intercourse and embraces sing this verse to them:

> Then the almighty Father descended in fertile rains  
> Into the lap of his joyful spouse; and, mingled  
> With the great body, the Great One nourishes all offspring.  
> (Virgil, *Georgics* 2)

“They have a share in the Gnostic heresy, which proceeds from the impiety of Basilides. Hence you also assert that those who lack knowledge of the Law cannot avoid sins.

“What should I say about Priscillian, who was condemned both by the sword of the state and by the authority of the whole world?

[Note: He was condemned to death by the Emperor Maximus after the anathemas of two councils, in the year 385.]

“Evagrius Ponticus [Note: Other manuscripts have *Iborita*, as does the Ambrosian manuscript, but nearly all have *Hyperiboritam* or *Hyperiberitam*. Some learned men think this is a designation of his homeland twisted into a term of abuse, as though he were said to be beyond the Iberians, an Iberian worse than Iberians. For the Iberians and the other peoples of Pontus had a bad reputation, as Tertullian especially testifies at the beginning of book 8 against Marcion. We would prefer *Iberipolitam*, introduced by the slightest alteration of the letters. If anyone thinks we are guessing, let him consider that Evagrius is called by this very expression, Ἰβήρων πολίτης, “a citizen of the Iberians,” by Sozomen, book 6, chapter 30: ἐγένετο δὲ μὲν γένει, Ἰβήρων πολίτης πρὸς τῷ καλουμένῳ Εὐξείνῳ πόντῳ, “He was by birth an Iberopolite, or a citizen of Ibera or Ibora, on the Euxine Sea.” Whatever Valesius may think, this reading alone is genuine and most correct. Palladius, cited by the same author, chapter 86, says: οὗτος (Evagrius) τῷ μὲν γένει Ποντικός ἦν, πόλεος Ἰβήρων, “This man, Evagrius, was by birth a Pontic, from the city of Ibera”; he did not say γένει Ἰβήρων πόλεως. This city is known from the subscriptions of several bishops at the Councils of Chalcedon and Constantinople, in Greek lists edited by Schelestratus, and from Constantine Porphyrogenitus, book 1 *On the Themes*. Other manuscripts incorrectly call him an *Hebionite*. Concerning Evagrius himself, his character, writings, and philosophical institutions, see Sozomen in the cited passage.]

“—who writes to virgins, writes to monks, and writes to the woman whose name bears witness to the darkness of her faithlessness—

[Note: Melania: in Greek μελανία means “blackness” in Latin.]

“—published a book and *Sentences*, *On Impassibility* (περὶ ἀπαθείας), [Note: Gennadius, who lists and translates the books of Evagrius’ sayings, makes no mention at all of this title. Nevertheless, a book *On Impassibility*, περὶ ἀπαθείας, is said to have been published by Holstenius, although we have not been able to see it. There is also an ancient controversy concerning the meaning of this word, which Jerome interprets as “impassibility” or “freedom from disturbance.” Seneca, Letter 9, says: “We fall into ambiguity if we wish to express *apatheia* elegantly in a single word and say *impatientia*. For it may be understood as the opposite of what we intend. We do not mean one who rejects all experience of evil; that would mean one who can endure no evil. Consider, then, whether it is better to say ‘an invulnerable mind’ or ‘a mind placed beyond suffering.’” See the preface to book 4 of the *Commentary on Jeremiah*.] which we may call impassibility or freedom from disturbance, since the mind is never stirred by any disturbance of passion. To put it simply, such a person is either a stone or God.

“His Greek books are read throughout the East, and, through the translation of his disciple Rufinus, his Latin books are read by many in the West. [Col. 1151] Rufinus also wrote a book ostensibly about monks and enumerates many people in it [1030] [Note: Who could believe that Rufinus listed people who never existed? Jerome therefore wishes this to be understood as saying that Rufinus wrote a book *quasi* about monks—‘as if’ about monks—who nevertheless were never monks, but either coenobites or ascetics of another institution. Elsewhere, in denying that the *Apology for Origen* was written by the martyr Pamphilus, Jerome says: “You preface it as though it were the book of a martyr.” This passage had long perplexed learned men who did not understand the expression properly, so that they considered Jerome to be exaggerating or nearly lying, although the meaning of the word is almost self-evident. The three who follow were well-known among the Origenists and were commonly called the “Tall Brothers.”]—whom he describes as Origenists and who were condemned by bishops; namely, Ammonius, Eusebius, Euthymius, Evagrius himself, Or, Isidore, and many others whom it is tedious to enumerate.

“And, in accordance with that verse of Lucretius:

> Just as physicians, when they try to give bitter wormwood  
> To children, first touch the rims of the cups  
> With the sweet yellow liquid of honey.  
> (Lucretius, book 4, *On the Nature of Things*)

“Thus he placed one John at the very beginning of his book [Note: What Victor formerly supposed, Martianay, through an egregious error, asserts: namely, that this was John Chrysostom, whom Jerome praises as Catholic and holy. In fact, this was John the Egyptian, who lived in the desert near the city of Lycus, in a certain crag of a lofty mountain; he is commonly called Lycopolitan or Lycopolite.] [Col. 1152]—and there is no doubt that this man was Catholic and holy—in order, through his inclusion, to introduce into the Church the other men whom he had listed as heretics.

“Who could describe in language worthy of it the rashness, or rather madness, of that man, who placed at the head of a book by Xystus the Pythagorean, a man without Christ and a pagan, the altered name of Sixtus the Martyr and Bishop of the Roman Church? [Note: Manuscripts and printed editions vary: some prefer *Sextus* or *Xestus*, others *Syxtus*. Elsewhere, especially in chapter 22 on Jeremiah and chapter 18 on Ezekiel, Jerome frequently attacks Rufinus for passing off Xystus the Pythagorean as Xystus the Pontiff and martyr. Rufinus nevertheless declares in the preface which he placed before these sayings that he had received this attribution from others; and Saint Augustine too, in *Retractations* 2.42, corrects his earlier belief that the book belonged to Sixtus, the Roman bishop, after later reading that it belonged to Sixtus the philosopher.]

“In that book, according to the doctrine of the Pythagoreans, who make man equal to God and say that he is of God’s substance, much is said about perfection, so that those who do not know the philosopher’s volume may drink from Babylon’s golden cup under the name of a martyr.

“Finally, in that entire volume [1031] there is no mention of any prophet, patriarch, apostle, or Christ, so that he might assert that a bishop and martyr existed without faith in Christ.

“Hence you too appropriate many testimonies against the Church. He had done this also under the name of the holy martyr Pamphilus: he gave the first book of the six books defending Origen, written by Eusebius of Caesarea—whom no one is unaware was an Arian—the title of a work by Pamphilus the martyr, so that he might pour those distinguished four volumes of Origen’s *On First Principles* (περὶ Ἀρχῶν) into Latin ears.

“Do you still wish to know another originator of your error? Your teaching is a little branch of Origen. For in the psalm where it is written—leaving aside the other passages—‘Indeed, even through the night my kidneys instructed me’ (Ps. 15:7), he asserts that the holy man—of whose number you too are—when he has reached the summit of the virtues, does not even at night suffer what belongs to human beings, nor experience the slightest tickling from any thought of vice.

[Note: Erasmus talks nonsense in his annotations, insisting that this opinion is not rightly marked by Jerome as an error.]

“Do not be ashamed of the company of such people while rejecting their names, when you are joined to them in their blasphemies. Jovinian’s second proposition is a discipline of your own mind. Whatever answer was made to him, consider it an answer to you. Nor can the outcome of those whose opinion is one be different.”

[Note: Jovinian’s and the Pelagians’ opinion and manner of speaking were indeed different, but their error was the same insofar as *apatheia* was concerned. His second proposition was: “Those who have been baptized are not subject to the temptations of the devil.”]

### 4.

“If these things are so, what do the wretched women burdened with sins want—women who are carried about by every wind of doctrine, always learning and never arriving at knowledge of the truth (2 Tim. 3:6–7)—and what do the other companions of these women want, itching in their ears and ignorant of what they hear and what they say? They take up ancient mud as though it were a new mixture:

[Col. 1153]

“According to Ezekiel, they plaster a wall without mortar, and when the rain of truth comes upon it, they are scattered.

“Simon Magus founded a heresy with the assistance of the prostitute Helena. Nicolas of Antioch, the discoverer of every impurity, led bands of women. Marcion sent a woman ahead to Rome to prepare minds for him to deceive. Apelles had Philumene [or: Philomene] as a companion of his teachings. Montanus, a preacher of the unclean spirit, first corrupted many Churches [1032] through Prisca and Maximilla, noble and wealthy women, with gold; then he polluted them with heresy.

“I shall leave the ancient examples and pass to those nearer our own time. Arius, in order to deceive the world, first deceived the ruler’s sister. Donatus, throughout Africa, was aided by Lucilla’s resources in order to pollute the unfortunate with his foul waters. In Spain Agape led Elpidius—a woman leading a man, and a blind woman leading a blind man into a pit—and Elpidius had as his successor Priscillian, a most devoted student of the magus Zoroaster and, from a magician, a bishop. Galla, joined to him not by race but by name, left as heir a sister running here and there between one heresy and its neighboring counterpart.

“Even now the mystery of iniquity is at work. Each sex overthrows the other, so that we are compelled to adopt that prophetic saying:

> The partridge called out; it gathered what it did not hatch,  
> Making its riches not with judgment.  
> In the middle of its days [Note: Three manuscripts read ‘they will abandon him,’ in accordance with the Greek ἐγκαταλείψουσιν αὐτόν.] it will abandon them,  
> And at its end it will be a fool.  
> (Jer. 17:11)”

### 5

But what they later fitted to this opinion in order to deceive people—“Not without the grace of God”—although it deceives readers at first glance, cannot deceive anyone who examines and carefully weighs it. For they place God’s grace in such a way that we do not rely upon and are not governed by its help in each individual work; rather, they refer it to free choice, and, applying it to the precepts of the Law, they introduce the saying of Isaiah: “For God placed the Law as an aid” (Isaiah 8, according to the Septuagint), so that thanks are to be given to God for having created us such that, by our own choice, we can both choose good and avoid evil.

And they do not understand, when they say these things, that through their mouths the devil is hissing an intolerable blasphemy. For if God’s grace consists only in the fact that he created us with our own will, and we are satisfied with free choice and no longer need his help—lest, if we should need it, free choice be broken—then we ought never again to pray, nor to bend his mercy by our prayers, so that we may receive daily what, once received, lies within our own power. Such men abolish prayer and boast that, through free choice, they have been made not men of their own will but of God’s power, needing no one’s assistance.

[Note: Pelagians continually asserted that the necessity of divine grace for pious works harmed free choice; for, they argued, a person could not truly do anything, or be truly free to do anything, if he could not do it independently and without God’s help. Augustine often refutes this calumny with the same arguments as Jerome, especially because they contradicted our prayers.]

[Note: This refers, we understand, to Caelestius, whose *Definitions* and *Syllogisms* are extant; against them St Augustine wrote his book *On the Perfection of Righteousness*. Although in other words, they contain the matters Jerome recounts here.]

Let fasting and every form of self-restraint be abolished as well. For why must I labor in order to obtain through diligence what has once been placed within my power? What I am saying is not my own argument. One of his disciples—or rather, already his teacher and leader of the entire army, and, contrary to the Apostle, a vessel of destruction—running through a thicket of solecisms, not, as they boast, of syllogisms, philosophizes and argues as follows:

> “If I do nothing without God’s help, and if everything I accomplish in each individual work belongs to him, then it is not I who labor who will be crowned, but God’s help within me; and he gave me the power of choice in vain, since I cannot exercise it unless he is continually helping me. For the will that needs another’s assistance is destroyed. But God gave free choice, which will not otherwise be free unless I do what I wish. Therefore,” he says, “either I make use of the power once given to me, so that free choice may be preserved; or, if I need another’s help, the freedom of choice will be destroyed in me.”

### 6

What blasphemy does the man who says these things not surpass? What poisons of heretics does he not exceed? They assert that, through freedom of choice, they no longer need God at all, and they do not know what is written: “What do you have that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Corinthians 4:7).

He gives great thanks to God who, through freedom of choice, is rebellious against God.

[Note: Another Vatican manuscript (4945) reads, “we have gladly received and embraced.” This, moreover, is what Augustine, and Jerome below, call the common doctrine, with the necessity of assistance for salutary works added.]

We gladly embrace free choice, provided only that we always give thanks to its giver, and know that we are nothing except what he himself has preserved in us after granting it, as the Apostle says: “It is not of him who wills or of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Romans 9:16).

To will and to run are mine; but this very “mine” will not be mine without God’s constant help. For the same Apostle says: “God is the one who works in us both to will and to accomplish” (Philippians 2:13). And the Savior says in the Gospel: “My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John 5:17). He is always the giver, always the one who grants. What he has given once is not enough for me unless he continues to give it. I ask in order to receive; and when I have received, I ask again. I am greedy in receiving God’s benefits: he does not grow weary in giving, nor am I satisfied in receiving.

The more I drink, the more I thirst. For I have read that the Psalmist sings: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Psalm 33:9). Everything good that we have is a taste of the Lord. When I think that I have reached the end of the virtues, then I shall have their beginning. For “the beginning of wisdom is fear of the Lord” (Psalm 110:10), which is expelled and destroyed by love.

This alone is perfection for human beings: to know that they are imperfect. And you, he says, “when you have done everything, say: We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we were obliged to do” (Luke 17:10). If the person who has done everything is unprofitable, what should be said of the one who has not been able to fulfill everything?

Therefore the Apostle says that he has received in part and understood in part, and that he is not yet perfect; he forgets what lies behind and stretches forward toward what lies ahead (1 Corinthians 13:10; Philippians 3:13). Whoever always forgets the past and desires the future shows that he is not content with the present.

As for what they loudly proclaim above and below—that free choice is destroyed by us—let them hear, on the contrary, that those destroy the freedom of choice who misuse it against the beneficence of its giver. Who destroys choice: the person who always gives thanks to God and refers whatever flows in his little stream back to its spring, or the one who says, “Keep away from me, for I am clean” (Isaiah 65:5), “I have no need of you”? “You gave me freedom of choice once, so that I might do what I wished. Why do you intrude again, so that I can do nothing unless you complete your gifts in me?”

You deceitfully invoke God’s grace in order to reduce it to a condition of human nature and not require God’s help in each individual work, lest you appear to lose free choice; and, while you despise God’s assistance, you seek the assistance of human beings.

[Note: Formerly the particle *ut* was incorrectly prefixed: “so that they may reduce God’s grace to the condition …” Other similar readings will be corrected below from the manuscripts.]

### 7

Listen, I ask you—listen to the sacrilegious man.

[Note: Compare Augustine, *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, to this effect.]

> “If,” he says, “I want to bend a finger, move a hand, sit, stand, walk, run about, spit, brush the dirt from my nostrils with two little fingers, relieve my bowels, or pass urine, will I always need God’s help?”

Listen, ungrateful—or rather sacrilegious—man, to the Apostle preaching: “Whether you eat or drink, or do anything else, do everything in the name of God” (1 Corinthians 10:31).

And hear also James:

> “Come now, you who say, ‘Today or tomorrow we will go to that city, spend a year there, conduct business, and make a profit,’ you who do not know what tomorrow will bring. For what is your life? It is a vapor, appearing for a little while and then vanishing; instead, you ought to say, ‘If the Lord wills and we live, we shall do this or that.’ But now you exult in your arrogance; all such boasting is evil” (James 4:13 and following).

Do you think that an injury is done to you and that the freedom of choice is destroyed if you always turn to God as its author, depend upon his will, and say: “My eyes are always toward the Lord, for he himself will draw my feet out of the snare” (Psalm 24:15)?

How then do you dare to utter with a presumptuous tongue that each person is governed by his own choice? If he is governed by his own choice, where is God’s help? If he does not need Christ as his guide, how does Jeremiah write: “A person’s way is not his own,” and, “The steps of a person are directed by the Lord” (Jeremiah 10:23)?

You say that God’s commandments are easy, yet you cannot produce a single person who has fulfilled them all. Answer me: are they easy or difficult? If they are easy, produce the person who has fulfilled them, and explain why David sings in the Psalm: “You fashioned labor into the commandment” (Psalm 93:20). And again: “Because of the words of your lips, I have kept to difficult paths” (Psalm 16:4). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “Enter through the narrow gate” (Matthew 7:13), and, “Love your enemies” (Luke 6:35), and, “Pray for those who persecute you” (Matthew 5:44).

But if they are difficult, why did you dare to say that God’s commandments are easy, when no one has fulfilled them? Do you not understand that your opinions contradict one another? Either they are easy, and there is an innumerable multitude of people who have fulfilled them; or they are difficult, and you rashly called easy what is difficult.

### 8

You also customarily say that the commandments are either possible and therefore rightly given by God, or impossible, in which case the fault lies not with those who receive the commandments but with the one who gave impossible commandments.

Did God command me to be what God is; to have nothing between myself and the Lord Creator; to be higher than the rank of the angels; or to possess what the angels do not possess? Of Christ it is written as something proper to him: “He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (Isaiah 53:9).

[Note: Augustine does not approve this argument against the heretic in his book *On Nature and Grace against Pelagius*, chapter 33. “Far be it,” he says, “from us to tell him what you say some people allege against you: that, if a human being is asserted to be without sin, he is thereby compared with God—as though an angel, because he is without sin, were thereby compared with God. I hold this view: even when there is in us such great righteousness that absolutely nothing can be added to it, the creature will not be equal to the Creator. But if some think that our progress will one day be so great that we shall be changed into God’s substance and become exactly what he is, let them see how they support their opinion. I confess that I am not persuaded of this.”]

If this too is something I share with Christ, what did he possess uniquely? Otherwise your own position will destroy itself. You assert that a human being can be without sin if he wishes; and then, after this grave slumber, you vainly attempt to add, in order to deceive inexperienced souls, “Not without the grace of God.”

For if a human being can once be without sin by himself, what need is there for God’s grace? But if he can do nothing without God’s grace, why was it necessary to say that he can do what he cannot?

“He can,” you say, “be without sin; he can be perfect, if he wishes.” What Christian does not wish to be without sin, or who refuses perfection if merely wishing is enough for him, and the ability immediately follows if the wish comes first? There is no Christian who does not wish to be without sin. Therefore all will be without sin, since certainly all desire to be without sin.

[Note: Formerly *ingratus* was printed incorrectly. But *ingratis*, or *ingratiis*, as everyone knows, means the same as *invito* (“unwillingly”). Jerome uses it thus in book 1 of the *Dialogue*: “You must confess unwillingly”; and shortly below, “against your will you will be held …,” as you boast that what is possible can be done.]

And in this you will be held fast against your will, since you can produce no one—or scarcely anyone—without sin, yet confess that everyone can be without sin. “God gave possible commandments,” you say. And who denies this? But the one appointed vessel of election teaches most clearly how this statement is to be understood. He says:

> “What was impossible for the Law, because it was weakened through the flesh, God did by sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and on account of sin condemned sin in the flesh” (Romans 8:3).

And again:

> “By works of the Law no flesh will be justified” (Romans 3:30).

Lest you think that this was said only of the Law of Moses and not of all the commandments included under the single name “Law,” the same Apostle writes:

> “I agree with the Law of God according to the inner person; but I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive in the law of sin which is in my members. Wretched man that I am, who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God, through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Romans 7:22 and following).

Why he said this, he demonstrates elsewhere:

> “We know that the Law is spiritual, but I am carnal, sold under sin. For I do not understand what I am doing. For I do not do what I wish, but I do what I hate. But if I do what I do not wish, I agree with the Law, that it is good. Now, however, it is no longer I who do it, but sin dwelling in me. For I know that good does not dwell in me—that is, in my flesh. For to will is present with me, but to accomplish the good I do not find. For I do not do the good that I wish, but the evil that I do not wish, that I do. But if I do what I do not wish, it is no longer I who do it, but sin dwelling in me” (Romans 7:14 and following).

### 9

You will object and say that we follow the doctrine of the Manichaeans and of those who stir up wars in the Church over different natures, asserting that a nature which cannot in any way be changed is evil.

[Note: It was customary for the Pelagians to accuse Catholics of Manichaeism; Augustine clears them of this calumny in many places.]

Attribute this not to me but to the Apostle, who knows that God is one thing and a human being another, the weakness of the flesh one thing and the strength of the spirit another. “For the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh; and these oppose one another, so that you do not do the things you wish” (Galatians 5:17).

You will never hear me say that nature is evil. But let us learn from the very author of these words, who teaches how the weakness of the flesh is to be explained. Ask him why he said: “I do not do the good that I wish, but I do the evil that I hate.” What necessity hinders his will? What such force commands him to do what deserves hatred, so that he is compelled to do what he does not wish, what he hates?

He will answer you:

> “O man, who are you to answer back to God? Does the molded object say to the molder, ‘Why did you make me so?’ Or does the potter not have authority over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?” (Romans 9:20–21).

Bring an even stronger charge against the powerful God: why, while Esau and Jacob were still in the womb, did he say, “I loved Jacob, but I hated Esau” (Malachi 1:3)?

Accuse him of injustice: why did Achan, son of Carmi, steal something from the spoils of Jericho, and why were so many thousands of people slaughtered because of his offense (Joshua 7)? Why did the sons of Eli sin, and nearly the entire people perish, while the ark was captured? David sinned by numbering the people; why, then, were so many thousands of people killed throughout Israel (1 Kingdoms 2 and following)?

And finally—an objection which your companion Porphyry habitually makes—why did the merciful and compassionate God allow all the nations, from Adam to Moses and from Moses to Christ’s coming, to perish in ignorance of the Law and the commandments of God?

[Note: See Augustine, Letter 102 to the Presbyter Deogratias. There, in answering six questions from pagans, he refutes this objection from Porphyry with strong arguments in the second question.]

For neither fertile Britain, a province of tyrants, nor the peoples of the Scots, nor all the barbarian nations around the Ocean had known Moses and the Prophets.

[Note: Quite a few manuscripts, with the older editions, read “the Scythian peoples”; but Jerome plainly preferred to reproach Pelagius, who came from Albion in Scotland, with his homeland and the barbarous customs of its province.]

Why was it necessary for him to come at the end of time, and not before an innumerable multitude of people perished?

The blessed Apostle, writing to the Romans, most wisely examines this question, acknowledging his ignorance of these things and leaving them to God’s knowledge. Therefore, you too should consent to be ignorant of what you ask. Grant God the power over his own affairs; he has no need of you as his defender.

I am wretched, awaiting your insults, while I constantly read: “By grace you have been saved” (Ephesians 2:8), and, “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven and whose sins have been covered” (Psalm 31:1).

Speaking of my own weakness, I know that I often wish for many things that ought to be done, and yet I cannot fulfill them. For the strength of the spirit leads to life, but the weakness of the flesh leads to death. And I hear the Lord warning: “Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation. The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matthew 26:41; Mark 14:38).

### 10

In vain do you blaspheme and thrust into the ears of the ignorant the claim that we condemn free choice. Let the person who condemns it be condemned. For the reason we differ from brute animals is not simply that we were created with free choice; rather, free choice itself, as we have said, depends upon God’s help and needs his assistance in each individual act—something you do not want. What you want is that whoever once possesses free choice should no longer need God’s help.

Free choice grants a free will, but a human being does not act immediately by free choice alone; he acts with the Lord’s help, who himself needs no one’s assistance.

You yourself, who boast that human beings possess a perfect righteousness equal to God’s, and who confess that you are a sinner, answer me: do you wish, or do you not wish, to be free from sin? If you wish it, why, according to your own position, do you not fulfill what you desire? But if you do not wish it, you show yourself to be a despiser of God’s commandments. If you are a despiser, then you are also a sinner.

If you are a sinner, hear Scripture speaking to you:

> “God said to the sinner: ‘Why do you recite my ordinances and take up my covenant in your mouth? But you hate discipline and cast my words behind you’” (Psalm 49:16).

By refusing to do God’s words, you cast them behind your back. And you, a new apostle, decree for the whole world what must and must not be done.

But it is not as you say; something else is moving in your mind. When you call yourself a sinner and say that a human being can be without sin if he wishes, you want it understood that you are holy and free from every sin, but that, out of humility, you assume the name of “sinner,” so that you may praise others and disparage yourself.

### 11

Who could endure this argument of yours? You put it in these words:

> “It is one thing to be, and another to be able to be. Being is not placed within our power; being able, however, is stated generally: although no one has been what he could be, nevertheless anyone who wishes to be can be.”

[Note: The printed editions read “although on other occasions there has not been”; we had conjectured that *alius* should be read for *alias*, until a Vatican manuscript showed that *aliquis* (“anyone”) must be restored. Although dialecticians’ followers may think otherwise, Jerome argues most correctly: it is incredible that no person has ever done, or will do, what each person can do independently and without another’s help, if he wishes.]

I ask: what sort of argument is this—that something can exist which has never existed; that something can be done which you testify no one has ever done; that you attribute it to anyone, although you do not know whether he will ever exist; and that you grant to some unknown person what you cannot prove existed among the Patriarchs, Prophets, or Apostles?
