Listen to ecclesiastical simplicity—or rusticity, or ignorance, as it seems to you. Speak what you believe; publicly preach what you say privately to your disciples. If you claim to possess freedom of choice, why do you not freely speak what you think?

The secrets of your bedrooms hear one thing; the crowds in the public places hear another.

[Note: Victor thinks that those who appear before the public tribunals and in the streets are meant. The manuscripts, however, generally read “the people of our platforms.”]

For the uneducated crowd cannot bear the burdens of your secrets, nor take solid food, being content with the milk of infancy.

I have not yet written, and you threaten me with the thunderbolts of your replies, so that, terrified by this fear, I might not dare to open my mouth. You do not notice that we write precisely so that you will be compelled to answer and at last openly say what, according to the time, the persons, and the places, you either speak or keep silent about.

I do not want it to be open to you to deny what you have once written. The Church’s victory consists in your openly saying what you think. For either you will give the same answer as we give and will in no way be our opponents but our friends; or, if you say what contradicts our doctrine, we shall win in this respect: all the churches will learn what you think. To expose your opinions is to overcome you.

The blasphemy is obvious at first glance. What is blasphemous by its own profession does not need to be proved so.

You threaten us with a reply which no one can avoid except one who does not write at all. How do you know what we are going to say, so that you can prepare a reply? Perhaps we shall say what you say, and you will sharpen your pen in vain.

The Eunomians, Arians, and Macedonians, distinct in name but united in impiety, cause us no trouble. They say what they think. This is the only heresy that is ashamed to say publicly what it does not fear to teach privately.

The fury of the disciples reveals the silence of their teachers. What they heard in their bedrooms they preach from the rooftops: if their hearers approve what they say, it is reported to the glory of their teachers; if it displeases them, the fault belongs to the disciple, not the teacher.

That is why your heresy has grown and you have deceived many, especially those who attach themselves to women and know that they cannot sin. For you are always teaching and always denying, and you deserve to hear the prophetic word:

> “Give them, Lord—what will you give them? A barren womb and dry breasts” (Hosea 11 and 14, according to the Septuagint.)

My spirit is aflame, and I cannot restrain my words. The narrow limits of a letter do not permit the magnitude of a lengthy work. No one’s name is expressly attacked in this little work. We have spoken against the teacher of a perverse doctrine. If he becomes angry and sends a reply, he will expose himself, like a mouse, by his own evidence, and will receive greater wounds in the true contest.

### 12

Many years have passed since, from adolescence to my present age, I wrote various little works. I have always made it my practice to speak to my hearers about what I had learned publicly in the Church, not to follow the arguments of philosophers but to rest in the simplicity of the Apostles, knowing what is written:

> “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and reject the understanding of the intelligent” (Isaiah 29:14; 1 Corinthians 1:19).

And:

> “The foolishness of God is wiser than human beings” (1 Corinthians 1:25).

Since these things are so, I challenge my opponents to examine all my earlier writings thoroughly and, if they find any fault in my small talent, to bring it into the open. Either the writings will be sound, and I shall refute their calumny; or they will be open to criticism, and I shall confess my error, preferring to correct myself rather than persist in a perverse opinion.

And so, distinguished teacher, either defend what you have said and support the acuteness of your opinions with the eloquence that follows, lest, whenever it suits you, you deny what you have said; or, if you truly have erred, freely confess it as a human being and restore agreement among those who disagree.

Let it come to your mind that even the soldiers did not tear apart the Savior’s tunic. You see quarrels among brothers and laugh and rejoice because some are called by your name and others by the name of Christ.

Imitate Jonah and say: “If this storm is because of me, take me up and throw me into the sea” (Jonah 1:12). He was cast down into the depths in humility so that, as a type of the Lord, he might rise again in glory. You are lifted to the stars through pride, so that Jesus may say of you: “I saw Satan falling like lightning from heaven” (Luke 10:18).

### 13

As many righteous people are called righteous in the Holy Scriptures—Zachariah and Elizabeth, Job, Jehoshaphat and Josiah, and many others whose names make up the fabric of sacred Scripture—although I shall speak of this more fully in the promised work, if the Lord grants me grace, it is enough for the present letter to touch briefly upon this point: they are called righteous not because they are free from every fault, but because they are commended for the greater part of their virtues.

[Note: Alternative reading: “although I shall speak” (*dicturus sum*).]

[Note: Recall Letter 121 to Algasia, question 8, page 1026, and what we noted there.]

Indeed, Zachariah is condemned to silence (Luke 1), Job is reproved in the course of the narrative, and Jehoshaphat and Josiah—who are unquestionably called righteous—are reported to have done things displeasing to the Lord. One of them gave assistance to an impious man (3 Kingdoms 22) and was rebuked by a prophet; the other, contrary to the Lord’s command spoken through Jeremiah, went out to meet Necho, king of Egypt, and was killed (4 Kingdoms 23; 2 Chronicles 35). Yet both are called righteous.

[Note: Another manuscript reads, “but because they possessed a greater share of virtues.” Compare, if desired, Augustine’s response to these examples in almost the same manner as Jerome.]

It is not the time to write about the others. For you asked me not for a book but for a letter, which must be dictated in leisure, and all their objections must be destroyed with Christ’s help. This we must establish by the testimonies of the Holy Scriptures, through which God speaks daily to believers.

I beg and admonish, through you, that the congregation of that holy and distinguished household not receive, because of one person—or at most three insignificant men—the filth of such great heresies, or, to put it mildly, their infamy; so that where virtue and holiness were once praised, the disgrace of a most sordid association may not take its place.

[Note: Formerly the text read, “And I beg you through the holy…,” a reading rejected by Victor. Other printed editions have “through you and the holy,” which may perhaps be the genuine reading. This distinguished household seems to be the same one mentioned in the letter to Apronius: “I grieve that a noble household has been utterly overthrown… although in part we may deserve God’s displeasure, because we have sheltered the Lord’s enemies.”]

Let those who supply wealth to such men know that they are gathering a multitude of heretics, making them enemies of Christ, and nourishing his adversaries. They vainly profess one thing with their tongue, while their hand—or, according to another reading, their intention—proves that they think something else.

## LETTER 134

[Note: Otherwise numbered 94. Written in the year 416.]

### TO AUGUSTINE

He indicates that he received from Orosius two books addressed to him, or Augustine’s two preceding letters, 131 and 132, and explains why he did not reply to them.

To the truly holy Lord and father, venerable to me with every affection, Pope AUGUSTINE, Jerome sends greetings in Christ.

### 1

I received my honorable brother, the Presbyter Orosius, a son of your gracious favor, both because of his own merit and at your command.

[Note: Martianay wrongly begins the passage here; the error is corrected from other editions and the very ancient Ambrosian manuscript 212. Orosius, sent by Augustine to Palestine to consult Jerome about the origin of souls, arrived at a most difficult time: Jerome, occupied with other works, could not answer this question.]

But he arrived at a most difficult time, when it was better for me to keep silent than to speak, so that our studies ceased and, in the words of Appius, canine eloquence was being practiced.

[Note: In Augustine’s letter to Optatus, recently published at Vienna, where this entire chapter is quoted, the reading is “according to Appius,” rather than “and.” We have discussed that saying elsewhere, especially Letter 125 to Rusticus, section 16.]

Therefore I was unable at that time to reply to your two little books, which you dedicated in my name, works of great learning and shining with every splendor of eloquence. This was not because I thought there was anything to criticize in them, but because, according to the Apostle, “let each person abound in his own understanding: one indeed in this way, another in that” (Romans 14:5).

[Note: The Ambrosian manuscript reads “according to the blessed Apostle,” as in the letter to Optatus; it also has *abundat* where the printed text has *abundet*.]

Certainly, whatever could be said, and whatever could be drawn from the fountains of the Holy Scriptures by a lofty intellect, has been set forth and explained by you. But I ask your reverence to allow me for a moment to praise your intellect. We discuss these matters among ourselves for the sake of learning. But rivals, and especially heretics, will accuse us of proceeding from bitterness of spirit if they see that we hold different opinions.

For my part, I have resolved to love you, honor you, revere you, admire you, and defend your words as though they were my own. Certainly, in the dialogue that I recently published, I remembered your blessedness as was fitting.

Let us rather devote ourselves to removing from the churches the most pernicious heresy, that of the Pelagians.

[Note: “Of the Pelagians.”]

It continually pretends repentance in order to obtain the power to teach in the churches; for if it reveals itself in the clear light of day, it will be driven out and perish.

[Note: Alternatively, it conceals and disavows its errors, as at the Synod of Diospolis, which Jerome calls pitiable because it acquitted Pelagius after being deceived by this strategy.]

### 2

Your holy and venerable daughters Eustochium and Paula the Younger proceed worthily, both by their birth and by your exhortation, and they especially salute your blessedness. So does all the brotherhood that strives with us to serve the Lord and Savior.

Last year we sent the holy Presbyter Firmus to Ravenna, and from there to Africa and Sicily, on their business. We think that he is now staying somewhere in Africa. Please greet, as a service to me, the holy men who remain at your side.

I also sent a letter of mine to the holy Presbyter Firmus. If it reaches you, do not hesitate to forward it to him.

[Note: The venerable Ambrosian manuscript mentioned above reads *librum dirigere* (“to send the book”) instead of *direxi* (“I sent”), omitting what follows here: “If it reaches you, do not hesitate to forward it to him.” These words from the holy Father’s letter to Firmus have evidently dropped out.]

May Christ the Lord preserve you unharmed and mindful of me, truly holy and most blessed father.

[Note: The Ambrosian manuscript does not contain what follows to the end, and many printed editions also omit it.]

And below:

We suffer in this province from a severe shortage of scribes skilled in the Latin language; for this reason we cannot comply with your instructions, especially in the edition of the Septuagint, which is marked with asterisks and obeli. We have lost most of the earlier work through the dishonesty of someone.

## LETTER 135

[Note: We have transferred here, from Constantius’s edition of the letters of the Roman Pontiffs, the three letters that follow. They were first published from an old Vatican-library manuscript and later reprinted by Baronius, who compared them with another manuscript, under the year 416. Their background is made clear by what Augustine relates at the end of his book *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*: “As for the things said to have been perpetrated after that judgment there [at Diospolis] by some band of wicked men, who are reported to support Pelagius with great perversity, with incredible boldness—so that servants and handmaids of God associated with the care of Saint Jerome were subjected to a most criminal slaughter, a deacon was killed, and the buildings of monasteries were burned—I think that we should rather keep silent and await what our brother bishops there judge ought to be done about such great evils, since who could believe that they can overlook them?” See also what we have said about these matters in the special preface to this volume.]

### OF POPE INNOCENT TO AURELIUS

Innocent sends Aurelius a letter to be delivered to Jerome.

To his dearest brother AURELIUS, INNOCENT sends greetings.

[Note: Bishop of Carthage, very well known in the proceedings against the Pelagians.]

Our fellow presbyter Jerome has duly commended to us your most devout desire to come to us. We sympathize with a member of our flock, and we have quickly carried out what we judged should be done, or what we were able to do. Let your Brotherhood, dearest brother, hasten to deliver the letter to the person mentioned.

[Note: We interpret the passage in this way: Jerome persuaded Aurelius to travel as far as Rome, so that he might personally inform the Roman Pontiff about the crimes of the Pelagians; since Aurelius could not accomplish this, Innocent nevertheless praises Jerome’s position. But perhaps, as has not yet occurred to us, the reading is corrupt, and *reddidit* (“he reported” or “he indicated”) should be restored.]

## LETTER 136

[Note: Otherwise not numbered among the Jerome letters. Written at the same time as the preceding one.]

### OF INNOCENT TO JEROME

Innocent consoles Jerome for what he has suffered and explains what he judged should be done at the time and what he has already done.

To his dearest son, the Presbyter JEROME, INNOCENT sends greetings.

The Apostle testifies that contention has never accomplished anything good in the Church (Tit. 3:10); and therefore he commands that heretics first be corrected rather than subjected to a prolonged disputation. [Note: Constantius restored this reading from the examination of the Vatican archetype; previously the text was corrupt and read “and more prolonged.”] When this rule is carelessly disregarded, the evil that ought to be avoided is not avoided but increased. [Note: Baronius reads “is accepted,” after rejecting the reading “is looked at in the white of the book.”]

Nevertheless, since your grief and lamentation have so affected our inmost being [Note: If one may supply what appears to be missing from the mutilated sentence, I would read: “so that no method of dealing with the matter or of giving counsel should be left untried.” If one prefers to explain it, the passage is not without a reasonable sense: one might understand it to say that grief itself has closed off every counsel. In the Vatican manuscript, however, the word *ratio* is missing.] that there is no room for discussion or counsel, I first address the faithfulness of your steadfastness. For truth’s sake, you have often told many that anyone who is struck by injustice—or, as you say, by danger—should await blessedness; and we remind you that you yourself remember your preaching well. [Note: *Libens*, or something similar, must certainly be supplied before *quisque*; then the sense immediately becomes perfectly clear.] Thus, stirred by so great a spectacle of evils, we hastened to exercise the authority of the Apostolic See in order to suppress every outrage. But we have read neither against whom we should rise—for no one is named—nor any definite charge brought against him. Therefore, whatever we can do, we grieve with you.

If, however, you submit an open and explicit accusation against certain persons, I shall either appoint competent judges, or, if something more urgent and careful can be done by us, I shall not delay, dearest son. Yet I have written to my brother Bishop John that he should act more cautiously, lest anything of this kind occur again around the Church entrusted to him—something which it would be both his duty and his greatest burden afterward to have foreseen and prevented, or at least to prevent if it should occur. [Note: The passage would be more complete if *et* were supplied here, or if one read *si accidat*—“if it should occur”—in place of *vel ne accidat*, “or lest it occur.”]

## LETTER CXXXVII [Note: Elsewhere not counted among the Hieronymian letters. Written at the same time as the preceding letter.] INNOCENTIUS TO JOHN

John of Jerusalem ought to have taken care that Jerome, Eustochium, and Paula were not overwhelmed by the many and great evils by which they were afflicted; and unless these matters are henceforth corrected or restrained, he will be required to render an account of them.

To his dearest brother John, Innocentius.

The most noble and holy virgins Eustochium and Paula, with the utmost clemency, lamented that the Devil had perpetrated pillage, slaughter, fires, and every outrage in the places belonging to their church. [Note: Baronius and the edition of the Councils read *dementiae*—“of madness”—and refer that reading to the outrage of the Pelagians. But P. Constantius more correctly judged that the passage instead praises the holy virgins for their extreme clemency, because they concealed the man’s name and the charge against him; the Roman edition prefers this reading.]

For although it is not uncertain by whom the deed was committed [Note: Namely, Pelagius, upon whom suspicion of the crime fell], your brotherly care ought nevertheless to have guarded more attentively and provided for that flock of his, lest anything of this kind arise. Yet, while the dangers of others provoke your negligence, we have heard that you have admitted into the Lord’s flock such ewes as were left naked and helpless by fire, weapons, and persecution, after the slaughter and deaths of their own people, and could scarcely remain alive. [Note: Baronius emended the earlier reading, which had *amittere gregem*—“to lose the flock”—a customary error in old books, where *amittere* is written for *admittere*. But, as the Benedictine editor soon observes, Baronius himself errs more seriously when he reads “and such lambs, whom you strip naked by fire …,” as though this were the second-person form of the verb *nudo*, making John himself the author of the crime.]

Does that priestly piety of yours feel no compunction at such great power of the Devil being admitted against you and your people? Against you, I say: for such an outrage being completed in the Church utterly condemns the dignity of a priest. Where were your precautions? Where, certainly, if these events had occurred, were your assistance or consolations, when they say that they still fear more than they complain of having suffered? I would judge the matter more severely if they had spoken more openly with me about it. See, brother, the snares of the ancient enemy, and keep vigilant with the spirit of a good ruler, so that these things, which have been reported to us as manifest more by rumor than by accusation, may either be corrected or restrained; lest ecclesiastical law, concerning causes that have been undermined, compel the one who failed to defend them to answer for them. [Note: Formerly the text read *causis*; the Benedictine editor restored *causas* from the examination of the Vatican archetype, since *jus ecclesiasticum* is the subject of the sentence.]

## LETTER CXXXVIII [Note: Elsewhere 55. Written around A.D. 417.] TO RIPARIUS

[Note: Some manuscripts, agreeing with the old edition, read: “To the truly holy Lord, and Riparius, venerable in every affection, Jerome sends greetings in Christ.”]

He explains to the presbyter Riparius how the Pelagian doctrines were rejected, how their disseminator was expelled like another Catiline, and what happened to him in that affair.

### 1

I have learned, both from your letters and from the report of many, that you are waging the wars of the Catholic faith against the enemies of Christ, and that the winds are contrary, while those who ought to be defenders of the age are supporters of perdition and allies in mutual destruction. Yet you should know that in this province he was driven out, not by any human assistance but specifically by the judgment of Christ—not only from the city but also from the borders of Palestine—like Catiline. [Note: As is well known from Sallust, when Catiline escaped from Rome by night, he left P. Cornelius Lentulus in the city to strengthen the conspirators in their treachery; Jerome alludes to this. It is difficult to understand anyone else here under the name of Catiline than Pelagius and his followers. Ruffinus, whom the interpreters of Jerome commonly suppose to be meant, had already departed from Palestine in 397, willingly and reconciled with Jerome.]

And we greatly grieve that, although many associates of the conspiracy remained with Lentulus, they are lingering in Joppa. We thought it better to change our place than the truth of the faith, and to lose the pleasantness of our buildings and dwelling rather than stain it by communion with those with whom, for the present, we either had to yield or else fight daily—not with words but with swords. [Note: It was noted above, in the note to Letter 135, that Augustine, in *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, says at the end that “by some band of wretched men, who were said to support Pelagius most perversely,” among the other deeds carried out with incredible audacity against Saint Jerome, his monasteries’ buildings were also burned, so that scarcely even a fortified tower could protect him from the assault and attack of the impious except by God’s mercy.]

I think you have learned through widespread report how much we suffered and how the exalted hand of Christ raged on our behalf against the enemy. [Note: I would prefer *omnia*, “everything.” Shortly afterward the old edition reads, “certainly each person knows that,” and so forth.] I therefore ask you to complete the work you have undertaken, and do not allow Christ’s Church, while you are present, to lack a defender. Certainly everyone knows what is sufficient for you according to your ability: for the battle is not to be fought with bodily strength but with the love of the soul, which can never be overcome.

The holy brothers who are with our lowliness greet you warmly. I also think that our holy brother the deacon Alentius will faithfully recount everything to your graciousness. May Christ our Lord and almighty God preserve you unharmed and mindful of me, truly holy lord and worthy brother.

## LETTER CXXXIX [Note: Elsewhere 56. Written around A.D. 417.] [Note: The sequence of matters treated in this letter and the whole composition prove Jerome to be its author, contrary to Victorius, who does not think it bears the style of the holy Father and believes it was written by one of his associates.] TO APRONIUS

He praises Apronius because he remained steadfast in the faith against the Pelagians, and urges him to visit the holy places of Jerusalem.

### 1

I do not know by what temptation of the Devil it has happened that neither your labor, nor the diligence of the presbyter Saint Innocentius, nor our longing seems at present to have any effect. Thanks be to God that I have learned that you are safe and burning with the ardor of faith amid the very trials of the Devil. [Note: This appears to be that Innocentius to whom Jerome gave letters concerning holy Bethlehem, to be carried westward to Alypius and Augustine; Jerome himself testifies to this at the beginning and again at the end of the following Letter 143.]

This is my joy, whenever I hear that my children are fighting in Christ; and may he himself, in whom we believe, strengthen this zeal in us, so that we may willingly shed our blood for his faith. [Note: See the end of Letter 133, to Ctesiphon, where he complains about a distinguished household that supported heretics and which may appear to have been overthrown in the same manner as the present one.]

I grieve that the noble household has been utterly destroyed, and yet I could not discover what the cause was. For the bearer of the letter said that he did not know. Thus we can grieve for our common friends and implore the clemency of Christ, who alone is powerful and Lord. [Note: The older editions place the words differently: “and his clemency,” so that the name of Christ refers to the friends.] Although, on God’s side, we may deserve offense because we have sheltered the Lord’s enemies.

You will do best, however, if, leaving everything else aside, you seek the East and especially the holy places; for everything here is peaceful. Although they have not cast off the poisons in their hearts, they do not dare to open the mouth of impiety. They are like deaf adders, stopping their ears (Ps. 57:5).

Greet the holy brothers. Our household, though utterly ruined in its worldly possessions by the persecutions of heretics, is, by Christ’s favor, full of spiritual riches. For it is better to eat bread than to lose the faith.

## LETTER CXL [Note: Elsewhere 139. Written around A.D. 418.] TO THE PRESBYTER CYPRIAN

He piously and eloquently expounds Psalm 89, whose beginning is “Lord, you have been our refuge,” according to the truth of the Hebrew text, after the Septuagint and the Vulgate edition.

### 1

Previously I knew you, Cyprian, most devoted of presbyters, only through letters—as one of the number of those concerning whom Moses heard: “Choose presbyters whom you yourself know to be presbyters” (Exod. 12)—and as one who had obtained the title of the blessed man who meditates on the Law of God day and night (Ps. 1).

But now, since we have also come to know one another’s outward persons, and after the greeting and the sweet embraces by which friendship is joined, you immediately ask me, to prove that what you had heard was true, to explain for you the very difficult psalm that is numbered eighty-ninth among the Greeks and Latins—not in a polished arrangement of words and popular applause, which usually deceives and flatters the ears of the unlearned, but in simple speech and the truth of ecclesiastical eloquence. Our interpretation, then, should require no other interpreter, as often happens with those who are excessively eloquent, whose explanations are more difficult to understand than the things they attempt to explain.

I shall undertake this very difficult work, supported by the help of your holy prayers, and I shall remember that verse: “The Lord will give the word to those who proclaim the gospel with great power” (Ps. 67:12).

### 2

First, it must be known that, according to the Hebrew, the title of this psalm is “A Prayer of Moses, the man of God”; according to the Septuagint, “A Prayer of Moses, a man of God.” Let Holy Scripture teach us what difference there is between *man* and *male* or *husband*. The captain of fifty speaks to Elijah: “Man of God, the king calls you.” He replied: “If I am a man of God, let fire come down from heaven and consume you and your fifty men” (4 Kgs. 1:9–10). The Apostle also writes to Timothy: “But you, O man of God, flee these things” (1 Tim. 6:11).

Regarding the man or husband of God, the same Apostle instructs us: “I want you to know that the head of every man is Christ; the head of a woman is man; and the head of Christ is God” (1 Cor. 11:3). This is the man who ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God, and who prays daily, saying: “But we all, with unveiled face beholding the glory of the Lord, are transformed into the same image, from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord” (2 Cor. 3:18). And elsewhere: “Until we all arrive at the perfect man, at the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ” (Eph. 4:13).

Thus, whether the holy man is called *man* or *male*, the designation suits him who saw God face to face and whose soul was saved. From his mouth we learned the creation of the world—at least of those things that are visible—the formation of man, and the truth of all earlier history. He not only left us five books: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy, but also eleven psalms, from the eighty-ninth, whose beginning is “Lord, you have been our refuge,” up to the ninety-ninth, entitled “A Psalm of thanksgiving.”

Although in most copies the ninety-eighth bears the title “A Psalm of David,” this is not found in the Hebrew. Holy Scripture has the custom that psalms which do not name their authors in their titles are assigned to those whose names occur in the preceding psalms. [Note: See the preface to the Commentaries on Malachi. It was an accepted opinion among the ancient Fathers, approved by Origen, Eusebius, Hilary, Athanasius, and others, although some later writers disagree, that all psalms without authors’ titles are assigned to the author named previously.]

[Note: Augustine disagrees in his exposition of Psalm 89. He prefers to attribute the entire Psalter to David. Regarding this particular psalm he says: “It must not be believed that this psalm was composed entirely by Moses himself, since it is not included among any of his writings in which his songs are recorded; rather, the name of a servant of God of some significance and great merit was applied for the sake of directing the attention of the reader or hearer.” Jerome, however, arguing again from Origen’s position against Ruffinus, attributes it to Moses according to the exposition of the Hebrew patriarch Huillius—more correctly, Julius. Origen mentions this Jewish patriarch elsewhere and says that he met with him. Recall his passage near the beginning of the selected material on the Psalms, volume 2 of the works, p. 514. John Malalas should also be consulted; among Moses’ *commentaries* (*hypomnēmata*, ὑπομνήματα) he praises him on p. 294, as does Cosmas Indicopleustes in Book V of his *Cosmography*, who thinks that the author of the psalm was not the ancient legislator Moses but another, younger Moses of the same name who lived in David’s time.]

### 3

There are four psalms that bear the title “Prayer.” The sixteenth is entitled “A Prayer of David” and begins, “Hear, Lord, my righteousness.” The eighty-fifth begins, “Incline, Lord.” The eighty-ninth, which we now have in hand, begins, “Lord, you have been our refuge.” The hundred-and-first bears the title “A Prayer of the poor man when he is anxious and pours out his prayer before the Lord.”

David and the poor man—who, although he was rich, became poor for our sake—refer to Christ, who sat upon the foal of a donkey, according to Zechariah (chap. 9:9), poor and gentle.

Moses, through whom the Lord gave the Law, and from whose mouth we heard God say, “Let us make man according to our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:26), immediately adds: “And God made man according to his image; according to the image of God he made him; male and female he made them.” [Note: Martianay’s edition lacked the words “according to his image”; we restored them from other printed editions and manuscripts. Some copies have “created” instead of “made.”]

From the beginning of the creation of man to his death and resurrection, Moses explains everything: how man was created, how long he lives, what he does in the world, what fruit of life he possesses, why he labors, and where he strives to go. And since the very person who writes these things is a human being, he bears witness in his own person concerning the condition of the whole human race.

Some refer this psalm, or prayer, to the people of Israel: how they offended God and fell in the wilderness and did not deserve to enter the Promised Land; how their sons entered in place of their fathers; and how they again await God’s reconciliation, which is fulfilled in the coming of Christ.

### 4. What “prayer” means in Scripture

Among grammarians, *prayer* (*oratio*) means every speech of those who speak, and they express its etymology in this way: *oratio* is “the reasoning of the mouth” (*oris ratio*). In the Holy Scriptures, however, we rarely read *prayer* in this sense; rather, we read of prayer that pertains to petitions and supplications.

The Hebrews say that the single volume of the Psalms contains five books: from the first to the fortieth; from the forty-first to the seventy-first; from the seventy-second to the eighty-eighth; from the eighty-ninth—which is the beginning of the fourth book and which we are now discussing—to the hundred-and-fifth; and from the hundred-and-sixth to the end. At the end of all these books a double “Amen” is placed, which the Septuagint translates as “May it be, may it be.” Like the Twelve Prophets, who, although they issued books [or: booklets] of their own, are comprised under the title of a single volume. [Note: See the preface to the Book of Psalms according to the Hebrew truth addressed to Sophronius. Also see Saint Hilary’s Prologue and Augustine on Psalm 150, among many others. Cassiodorus is plainly mistaken on this point: in his preface to the Psalter, while defining it as a single book of Psalms, he nevertheless attributes the division into five books to Jerome, although no one rejects that division more strongly. The division was accepted not only among the Hebrews but also among some Greeks, by whom the Psalter is called a *Pentateuch* (Πεντάτευχον).]

I nearly passed over this point when I said that, among the eleven psalms of Moses, the ninety-eighth is also included. It contains: “Exalt the Lord our God, and worship the footstool of his feet, for he is holy. Moses and Aaron among his priests, and Samuel among those who call upon his name.” This appears to contradict our position: how can it be Moses’ psalm if it mentions Samuel, whom we know lived many ages later?

The question has an easy solution. The name Samuel was prophetically mentioned because he possessed such great merit that he was placed alongside Moses in Jeremiah: “If Moses and Samuel were to stand” (Jer. 15:1). The same kind of example occurs when the man of God speaks in Samaria: “Altar, altar, thus says the Lord: Behold, a son shall be born to the house of David, Josiah shall be his name” (4 Kgs. 13:2).

We should also know that those are mistaken who hold that all the psalms are David’s, rather than the works of those in whose names they are inscribed. [Note: One of these was Philastrius, *Heresy* 127: “There are others,” he says, “heretics who suffer no small error concerning the inequality of the Psalter, believing that the whole Book of Psalms is not David’s.” Yet this opinion is so far from being heretical, as Philastrius thinks, that it is entirely true and is commonly approved, with Jerome, by the Fathers of the Catholic Church.]

Thus they want this psalm, although it bears Moses’ name, to have been composed by David: namely, that the Lawgiver should describe with sacred lips the common offense and calamity of the human race and then its expectation of salvation.

### 5. “Lord, you have become our dwelling place, from generation to generation”

The Septuagint reads: “Lord, you have become our refuge, in every generation and generation.”

In place of “dwelling” and “refuge,” the Hebrew has *MAON*, which more properly means “dwelling” than “refuge.” Since he is about to recount sad things and lament the human race, he begins with praise of God, so that whatever adversity afterward befalls man may appear to have occurred not through the Creator’s harshness but through the fault of the one who was created.

One who endures a storm seeks refuge either in a rock or under a roof. One pursued by an enemy flees to the walls of cities. A traveler tired by sun and dust seeks the comfort of shade. If a savage beast thirsts for human blood, a person wishes and strives, by whatever means he can, to avoid the immediate danger.

So too man, from the beginning of his creation, uses God as his helper. Since it is by God’s grace that he was created, and by God’s mercy that he subsists and lives, he can perform no good work without him who granted free will in such a way that he would not deny his grace in each individual act. This was so that the freedom of the will would not turn into an injury to the Creator or into defiance of the one who was created free for the very purpose of knowing that, without God, he is nothing.

When he says “from generation to generation,” he signifies all times: both before the Law, under the Law, and in the grace of the Gospel. Thus the Apostle says: “You have been saved by grace through faith, and this is not from yourselves, but is the gift of God” (Eph. 2:8). All his Epistles likewise, at the beginning of their greetings, do not first have peace and then grace; rather, they have grace first and then peace, so that, once our sins have been forgiven, we may obtain the peace of the Lord.

### 6. “Before the mountains were born and the earth and the world were brought forth, from everlasting to everlasting you are God”

The Septuagint reads: “Before the mountains were established and the earth and the world were formed, from age and even to age you are God.” [Note: Recall Letter 106 to Sunia and Fretela, §58: “And you say that the Greek does not have ‘God,’ which is plainly absent from their copies; for the Hebrew has it, as do all the other interpreters, and likewise the Septuagint,” and so forth. We have observed that the word survives in no Greek copy. If it is admitted here, the following verse becomes disjointed: “Do not turn man away,” unless one supposes that the Hebrew word once appeared twice under different readings—first *El*, “God,” and then *al*, “do not.”]

Some overturn this passage by an incorrect punctuation, especially those who want souls to have existed before man was formed on the sixth day. They read and punctuate it in this way: “Lord, you have become our refuge from generation to generation, before the mountains were established and the earth and the world were formed”; so that what follows is understood afterward: “from age and even to age you are God.”

[Note: The spurious Jerome, in the *Brief Commentary on the Psalms*, has a similar passage, which we judge should be transcribed here, because comparison of the two makes the sense easier to grasp and shows what was taken from this passage. “A heresy,” he says, “crept in at this point: If he became our refuge before things were made and the world formed, then souls existed before the world was made.” For what does Scripture say? “Lord, you have been our refuge, in generation,” it says, “and generation.” From the beginning of the world: before the beginning of the world [lacuna]. But if he was our refuge before the world was made, souls therefore existed before the world was made. You punctuate wrongly, heresy. Why do you calumniate the Holy Spirit? Speak as the Holy Spirit spoke. It should therefore be read: “Lord, you have been our refuge, in generation and generation.” And thus far is the punctuation. Again, another beginning: “Before the mountains were made and the earth and world formed, from age and to age you are God.” You are God before the mountains were made; you are God before the earth was formed.]

This is how they explain it: If the Lord was the refuge of human beings before the mountains were established and the earth and the world were formed, then souls existed in heaven before human bodies were fashioned.

We, however, as we proposed, must punctuate the reading in this way: “Before the mountains were established and the earth and the world were formed, from everlasting to everlasting you are God.” Thus God was not our refuge before the creation of the world, when we did not yet exist; rather, God is eternally and forever God.

In place of what the Latin interpreter rendered “from age to age,” and what is said in Hebrew as *OLAM*, we should more accurately translate “from everlasting to everlasting.”

A similar passage is read in Proverbs in the person of Wisdom, who is Christ: “The Lord created me at the beginning of his ways, for his works; he established me before the ages, in the beginning, before he made the earth and the abysses, before the springs of waters came forth [or: were produced], before the mountains were established; before all the hills he begot me” (Prov. 8:22 ff.). [Note: Some old editions have “in the beginning of his ways,” with the preposition *in* at the beginning.]

No one should be troubled by the word “creation,” since in Hebrew the word translated “creation” is not present but *BARA*, “possession.” For it is written: *ADONAI CANANI BRESITH DERCHO*, which in our language is expressed: “The Lord possessed me at the beginning of his ways.” [Note: Perhaps the word was *Briah* or *Beriah*, based on what Jerome had read; *Bara* means “he created,” not “creation.” As for *Bresith*, shortly below he has it without the preposition, reading the Hebrew *resith*. Martianay attributes that reading to Jerome’s copy. Yet the old editions, which are not without manuscript authority, have the simple *resith*. From this, and from the ancient Greek interpreters and Jerome himself, whose appended interpretation expresses the phrase without the preposition, one may infer that they too read *resith*. Let no one object that the Hebrew differs from the Septuagint in the verb “to create”: the Targum, Syriac, and Arabic agree with the Septuagint. Nevertheless, the meaning of the word should still matter, since among the ancients even generation was called creation. The well-known line of Virgil says, “Four youths, created by Sulmo” (*Aeneid* 10); and Cicero, *On the Republic* 1, says: “The fatherland is an older parent than he who, as they say, created him.” I say nothing of the fact that among the Greeks the terms *ktisis* (κτίσις) and *ktēsis* (κτῆσις) are easily exchanged. The words that follow are Hebrew. See the Commentaries on Isaiah 26, Micah 4, and Ephesians 2, where the holy Father himself proves from the Hebrew that *possessed* means *created*.]

There is a great difference between possession and creation. Possession signifies that the Son has always been in the Father and the Father in the Son. Creation, however, signifies the beginning of the condition of one who previously did not exist.

According to the laws of allegorical interpretation, the words “before the mountains were established and the earth and the world were formed” may mean that, before the sublime doctrines were established in our soul and before the earth of our body was formed or stabilized by God—and before the world, which in Hebrew is called *THEBEL* and in Greek, more significantly, *oikoumenē* (οἰκουμένη), which we may translate as “inhabited,” was established or stabilized—God was always our refuge.

The soul is inhabited, not deserted, when it deserves to have God as its guest, as the Savior says: “I and the Father will come, and we will make our dwelling with him” (John 14:23).

The Hebrew and all the other interpreters also have: “Before the mountains were born and the earth was brought forth.” This plainly draws us toward allegory. Mountains and earth do not literally receive birth and labor; rather, they receive formation. From this it is clearly demonstrated that holy and exalted virtues too are always brought forth by God’s mercy.

### 7. “You will turn man to destruction, and you will say, ‘Return, children of Adam’”

The Septuagint reads: “Do not turn man toward humiliation, and you said: ‘Turn back, children of men.’”

According to the Hebrew, the sense is this: O God, who created man and from his beginning have been his refuge and dwelling, you will turn him toward destruction. You made and formed him so that he would be crushed in death and that your vessel would be broken at the end of his life. Since this is his condition—that what is born should perish, and that, however long he may live, he should nevertheless be dissolved at the final end—you speak to him daily through the Prophets: “Return, children of Adam,” who by your own fault offended God and were changed from immortal beings into mortals. [Note: Martianay’s edition corruptly reads “from immortalities.”]

For you did not wish to hear the command of the one who gave the order: “You may eat from every tree that is in paradise; but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat. For on whatever day you taste of it, you shall surely die” (Gen. 2:17).

But the words translated by the Septuagint—“Do not turn man toward humiliation, and you said: ‘Turn back, children of men’”—have this meaning: I ask you not to humble forever through sin the man whom you created according to your image and likeness, and whom you deigned to honor so greatly that you called a servant your son; do not let the ancient sentence prevail over him: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. 3:19).

For you promised us repentance, saying: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but only that he should turn back and live” (Ezek. 18:23). You said, through the utterance of all your saints: “Turn back,” or “Return,” children of men, to the most merciful Father, who runs out to meet those who come, offers the sign that they lost through their own fault, and grants the ancient robe of incorruption.

### 8.

For a thousand years in your sight are like yesterday, which has passed, [Note: We restore from Victorius and manuscript codices the genuine reading, which after Erasmus the Benedictine editor presents as *which has passed, has gone by like a night watch*, contrary to the text of the Psalm itself in Hebrew and Greek, where the verb διῆλθε (*passed through*) is not repeated. Accordingly, it is clear that *has gone by* belongs not to the text but to Jerome’s interpretation, and that the particle *as* must in any event precede it.] or has gone by, and like a night watch, or during the night.

You who always summon us to repentance through the Prophets, saying, “Return, sons of men,” we ask—as I have already said—that you not allow a human being to be held forever in humiliation. For we do not think that what you promise us is long delayed: salvation is to be granted us after many ages. Compared with eternity, the length of all times is short. For in your sight a thousand years are reckoned as one day.

And immediately he corrects himself: “I have spoken wrongly in saying one day, and in reckoning the length of a thousand years with you as the span of one day, when rather I ought to have said that the span of one watch has the length of a thousand years.” The night is divided into four watches, each reckoned as three hours. Hence the Lord came to the Apostles who were sailing in the fourth watch (Matt. 14; Mark 6). Thus, just as one watch of the night passes quickly—especially for those wearied by the labor of keeping watch—so the spans of a thousand years are reckoned by you, who always are, and are to be, and have been, as a very brief time.

And when he adds, “Like yesterday, which has passed,” let us understand it according to what the Apostle writes to the Hebrews: “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever” (Heb. 13:8). Therefore, I think that from this passage and from the Epistle inscribed under the name of the Apostle Peter [Note: He means the Second Epistle of Peter, which in the earliest centuries of the Church was not accepted as canonical by all the churches. Thus, in the *Catalogue*, he says: “The second is denied by most to be his, because its style differs from the first.” From the passage indicated in that Epistle, not a few of the ancients concluded that the entire duration of the present age was contained within six thousand years. See Irenaeus, book 5, chapter 28; Origen, book 2 *Against Celsus*; Lactantius, book 7, chapter 14; and Augustine, *City of God*, book 20, chapter 7—although in his exposition of this passage of the Psalm he does not at all approve the opinion that he had earlier called probable; also Gregory of Nyssa, exposition of Psalm 6, and others.] I judge that a thousand years are customarily called one day: namely, because the world was fashioned in six days, it is believed to subsist for only six thousand years; afterward comes the number seven and the number eight, in which the true Sabbath-rest is practiced and the purity of circumcision is restored. Hence also rewards for good works are promised in eight beatitudes.

Peter writes in this way: “Let this one thing not escape you, beloved: that one day with the Lord is like a thousand years, and a thousand years like one day. The Lord is not delaying his promise, as some consider delay” (2 Pet. 3:8–9).

### 9.

When you strike them, they will be a dream; in the morning, like grass that passes away. In the morning it blossoms and departs; toward evening it will be cut down and withered.

The Septuagint: “Their years will be as things counted for nothing. In the morning may it pass away like grass; in the morning may it blossom and pass away; in the evening may it fall, grow hard, and wither.”

According to the Hebrew, the sense is this: Our conversion and salvation have been greatly aided by the fact that the whole life of mortals, contracted by swift death, is like a dream; it dries up and perishes at almost the same moment, in the likeness of flowers and hay. “When you strike them,” he says—that is, human beings—and when that saying has been fulfilled: “Fool, this night they are demanding your soul from you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?” (Luke 12:20), every human condition will be compared to a dream.

For just as grass, green in the morning and blooming with its flowers, delights the eyes of those who look upon it, but gradually withers, loses its beauty, and is changed into hay to be trampled down, so the whole appearance of humanity is fresh in little children, blossoms in young men, and is vigorous in men of mature age. Then suddenly, before he knows it, the head grows white, the face becomes wrinkled, and the skin, formerly stretched smooth, contracts. At the final stage, which is here called evening—that is, old age—he can scarcely move, so that one cannot recognize who he formerly was, but he is almost changed into another person.

Why speak of the stages from infancy to extreme and decrepit old age, when illness and the misery of hunger also bring this about—so that a woman’s face, formerly most beautiful, changes into such ugliness that love is transformed into hatred? Isaiah too speaks of this condition of mortals: “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass. The grass withers, the flower falls” (Isa. 40:6).

The passage should likewise be explained according to the Septuagint. Everything that seems long in this age is brief with you, O God. For the days and years by which human life is measured, if compared with eternity, will be counted as nothing. Just as grass grows and blossoms in the morning, dries up, and toward evening becomes hard and perishes, so will all human beauty be.

### 10.

For we have been consumed in your anger, and in your indignation we have been troubled.

The Septuagint: “For we have failed in your anger, and in your fury we have been troubled.”

For what we have rendered, “we have been troubled,” Symmachus and Aquila translated “we hastened.” [Note: Eusebius, however, cites Symmachus’s version, which is similar to that of the Septuagint: ἐταράχθημεν (*we were troubled*). See the *Hexapla*.]

This signifies the brevity of human life. And when he adds, “in your anger and in your fury,” he displays the persistence of God’s sentence, to which all human beings are subject—namely: “You are dust, and to dust you shall return.” Beautifully, therefore, it does not say, as in the Septuagint, “we have been troubled,” but, according to the Hebrew, “we have hastened,” so that although human life may seem long, it is short in comparison with eternity.

The illustrious Poet also testifies to this, saying:

> But meanwhile time flees, irretrievable time flees.  
> (*Georgics*, book 3)

And again:

> O Rhoebus, long—if anything is long for mortals—  
> we lived.  
> (*Aeneid*, book 10)

### 11.

You have set our iniquities before you, our negligences in the light of your countenance.

The Septuagint: “You have set our iniquities in your sight, our age in the illumination of your countenance.”

Where we, according to the Hebrew and Symmachus, have rendered “our negligences,” for which the Septuagint translated “our age,” the Hebrew has *ALOMENU*, which the Fifth Edition interprets as “youth”; Aquila has παροράσεις (*oversights*); and we may translate it into our language as “errors” or “ignorances.” Hence he says elsewhere: “Do not remember the sins of my youth and my ignorances” (Ps. 24:7). And again: “Who understands sins?” and: “Cleanse me, Lord, from my secret faults, and spare your servant from those of others” (Ps. 18:13).

Vices are “those of others” for us when we commit them sometimes willingly, sometimes through ignorance and error; yet even when there is no will in the crime, there is error in the fault.

I wonder, however, why the Septuagint wished to say “our age” instead of “youth,” “errors,” or “ignorances,” unless perhaps because vices are committed in this age and during the period of this life. [Note: It is more reasonable to suppose that the Septuagint took this from a form written with a *vav*, and that it was at times written without a *vav*, as Jerome himself testifies; thus they translated “our age” very appropriately in that sense. But Martianaeus had not written it correctly according to the Hebrew exemplar.]

And when he adds, “in the illumination,” or “in the light of your countenance,” the meaning is this: Nothing of our sins has escaped you; your eye has examined even our secrets, according to what is written: “Darkness will not be hidden [or: darkened] from you” (Ps. 138:12); and, “God searches hearts and kidneys” (Ps. 7:10); and again: “As is his darkness, so also is his light” (Ps. 138:12). A human being sees in the face, but God sees in the heart.

### 12.

For all our days have passed away, and we have consumed our years in your fury, like a word being spoken.

The Septuagint: “For our days have failed, and in your anger we have failed. Our years have been meditated like a spider.”

He now compares the brevity of human life—which until this point has been subject to God’s sentence and which he compared in the preceding verse to a dream, saying, “When you strike them, they will be a dream”—to the speech of those who speak. For just as a word that is on the lips is interrupted as it is uttered and ceases to exist, so our whole life passes away and ceases; and this happens in the anger and fury of God, to which we are deservedly subject, since God’s sentence, as we said above, lives within us.

What the anger and fury of God are, we have explained frequently: not that God takes vengeance in anger, but that he appears angry to those who suffer punishments. For what descends upon us from disturbance is in him the truth of judgment. [Note: Older printed editions read: “In him it is from judgment and from truth.”]

[Note: In the Hebrew there is only [a word omitted in the supplied text], meaning “as one uttering” or “as one meditating”; therefore I readily agree with those persuaded that the word “spider” has fallen out of the Hebrew archetype.]

Instead of “like a speaking word,” the Septuagint translated “the meditation of a spider.” For just as the speech of one speaking flies past, so the spider’s work is woven in vain. Of this it is written in Isaiah concerning the person of heretics: “They weave spiders’ webs” (Isa. 59:5). Such a web can catch only small and weak creatures, such as flies, gnats, and things of that kind; stronger creatures tear it apart. It is like the simple and weak members in the Church who are deceived by their errors, since they cannot ensnare men strong in the truth of the faith.

### 10.

The days of our years are seventy years in themselves; and, if they are much, eighty years; and what is beyond that is labor and pain.

The Septuagint: “The days of our years are seventy years. But if they are in strength, eighty years; and what is beyond them is labor and pain.”

For what we have set as “in themselves,” and what is found in Hebrew as *BAEM*, Symmachus translated more significantly as ὁλόκληροι (*whole, complete*), which we can render according to the sense rather than literally as “all together.” [Note: That is, all our years are seventy years; but what he translated below as “against expectation” is, in Hebrew, a term meaning “in the strong,” while the Septuagint has, as far as possible, “the greater part.”]

Whatever, therefore, we live, and in whatever human life is delightful, is contained within the span of seventy years. But if it is much, and, as Symmachus translated it, “against expectation,” there are eighty years; whatever is beyond this is spent in illnesses and weakness, which accompany old age: eyes growing dim, teeth that were formerly very hard aching or falling out. The divine word describes this more fully in Ecclesiastes:

> The days of evil will come, and the days in which we shall say, “We have no pleasure in them”; when the sun, moon, and stars will be darkened, and the clouds will return after the rain. On the day when the guardians of the house will tremble and the men of strength will be overthrown; the grinders will cease because they have become few; those who look through the openings will grow dark, and the doors in the marketplace will be closed; when the sound of the grinding will be weakened, and one will rise at the sound of a bird, and all the daughters of song will be humbled; and they will look down from on high, and there will be terrors on the road; and the almond tree will blossom, and the locust will grow fat, and the caper-berry will split. For the human being will go to his eternal house, and those who mourn will go about in the marketplace until the silver cord is not struck and the golden ornament is crushed, the jar at the spring is broken, the wheel at the cistern is hindered, the dust returns to the earth as it was, and the spirit returns to God, who gave it. “Vanity of vanities,” says Ecclesiastes, “and all is vanity.”

All these things encompass the miseries of human life, and especially of old age. What meaning they have, we have discussed in its proper place. [Note: In the commentary on Ecclesiastes, chapter 12.]

There are some who interpret this passage allegorically and refer it to the mystery of the Sabbath and circumcision: that first we rest in the Law, and afterward the sacraments of true circumcision in the Gospel take hold of us. They also call to mind: “Give a portion to seven, and also to eight.” And they refer to the seventy thousand and eighty thousand men by whom the Temple was constructed under Solomon.

But what has this to do with the present passage, for which a simple and pure explanation is sufficient—one that should seek not the glory of doctrine through multiplying words, but the reader’s understanding?

### 14.

For we have passed quickly and flown away.

The Septuagint: “For gentleness has come upon us, and we shall be disciplined.”

The Greek has παιδευθησόμεθα (*we shall be disciplined*), an ambiguous verb signifying both correction and education or instruction. “Whom the Lord loves, he corrects,” or “educates,” “and he scourges every son whom he receives.”

Symmachus translated the passage in this way: “For we have been cut down suddenly, and we fly away.”

The Fifth Edition has: “For we have passed quickly and are dissolved.”

The sense is this: After seventy years—or, at most, eighty, in which human life is spent—when the soul has been separated from the body, we fly away like the wind. Or, because above he compares a human being to green grass and the beauty of flowers, and to their dryness toward evening, he now places the cutting down of flowers in the position of evening’s dryness. When everything we live through has passed away, he says, we are dissolved by sudden death.

But what the Septuagint said, “For gentleness will come upon us” [or: “has come upon us”], has this meaning: After seventy or eighty years, when the gentleness of the Lord has come and the day of death has overtaken us, we shall not be judged according to merit but according to mercy; and what is thought to be correction is education and instruction.

We are sufficiently astonished that the Septuagint, Theodotion, and the Sixth Edition wished to translate the Hebrew word *AIS* as “gentleness,” since Aquila, Symmachus, and the Fifth Edition translated it as “haste,” “suddenly,” or “quickly.” [Note: Aquila, however, seems to have read the Hebrew text differently from the others, and also differently from what Jerome asserts—that he did not translate “haste” or “quickness”—if the version cited by Drusius is genuinely his: ὅτι διεπέλασεν ἀνήρ, “for a man passed by.” He apparently read, with a slight alteration, a word meaning “man” in place of the Hebrew term.]

### 15.

Who knows the strength of your anger, and, according to your fear, your indignation?

The Septuagint: “Who knows the power of your anger, and who can count your anger because of your fear?”

There is a different division of the sentence in the Hebrew and in the Septuagint. The Septuagint joins the counting to the fear and fury of the Lord. The Hebrew, on the other hand, connects it with the following verse, so that it reads: “So that our days may be numbered, make it known, and we shall come with a wise heart.”

This seems briefly to require the following explanation. Who can know how long your anger will endure—the anger from which the human race derives fear—unless you teach us, since you are God? Therefore I ask you to make known to us the time of our life, so that with a wise heart we may prepare ourselves for your judgment.

When he says, “Who knows the strength,” or “power,” “of your anger, and, according to your fear, your indignation?” he shows that it is difficult to know the secret and reason of God’s anger, fear, and indignation. Hence the Prophet mournfully prays: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor correct me in your fury” (Ps. 6:1). For he does not correct in order to kill and destroy, but to correct and amend.

Therefore in Hosea (4:14), speaking to the Jewish people, with whom he was greatly angry, he says that he will not be angry and will not visit their daughters-in-law when they commit adultery. And through Ezekiel he speaks to Jerusalem: “Now I will no longer be angry with you, and my jealousy has departed from you” (Ezek. 16:42). And in the Books of Days it is said that Israel goes into battle against its enemies “with a peaceful heart.” [Note: Corresponding to the Greek ἐν ψυχῇ εἰρηνικῇ, “with a peaceful soul.”]

### 16.

So make it known that our days may be numbered, and we shall come with a wise heart.

The Septuagint: “Make your right hand known in this way, and those instructed in wisdom in heart.”

Aquila, Symmachus, and the Fifth Edition translated it thus: “Make our days known in this way, and we shall come with a wise heart.”

The reason for the Septuagint’s saying “right hand” instead of “days” is clear. *JAMENU* is a compound word signifying “our days.” If it is written in the singular, the final letter, called *nun*, expresses “right hand,” as in the name Benjamin, which means “son of the right hand.” But if it has *mem*, it denotes “day” or “days.”

The sense is this: Make known to us the number of our years and days, in which you have appointed us to live in this age, so that we may prepare ourselves for your coming; and, having despised the error of mortals, hasten to go to you, desire your presence, and hasten to you with a wise heart.

Nothing deceives the human race so much as this: while people are ignorant of the span of their life, they promise themselves a longer possession of this age. Hence that excellent saying: “No one is so old, and of such decrepit age, that he does not suppose he will live one more year.” [Note: Presumably from Cicero, *On Old Age*: “For no one is so old that he does not think he can live one more year.”]

This also belongs to the meaning of: “Remember your death, and you will not sin” (Eccl. 7:40). For whoever remembers daily that he is going to die despises present things and hastens toward those to come.

This is what David prays for elsewhere, saying: “Do not take me away in the middle of my days, before I depart and cease to be” (Ps. 101:25; Ps. 38:14). It is explained in this way: “Do not cause me to die at a time when I still thought I would live, so that I might correct my sins through repentance.” For if you do this, I shall cease to be found in my sins—not because he denies the hope of resurrection, but because he denies that he can stand before the one before whom all who persevere in vices are counted as nothing [or: reckoned as nothing].

Where we translated “instructed in heart in wisdom” [more correctly, “with a wise heart”], others translated “shackled,” deceived by the ambiguity of the word. For if you say πεπεδημένους, it means “shackled.” [Note: Older printed editions add: “and, apart from the Florentine manuscript, certain other manuscripts. But if you say πεπαιδευμένους, it means ‘instructed.’ The ancient Latin translator was misled by a Greek scribe who wrote πεπεδημένους, ‘shackled,’ in place of πεπαιδευμένους, ‘instructed.’ Jerome is mistaken in the *Breviary*: ‘In some codices it is said “instructed,” in others “shackled.”’]

### 17.

Return, Lord—how long? And be gracious toward your servants.

The Septuagint has the same.

Because we are doing penance, and, knowing the brevity of our life, wish to reach you with a wise heart, do you, Lord, return to us. For you had withdrawn far away because of our sins and had abandoned us, so that we might walk according to our own will and thoughts.

The addition “how long?” has the same meaning as what we read in Psalm 12: “How long, Lord, will you forget me forever?” [Note: Some printed editions and manuscripts read “we have said,” which can suitably refer to the exposition of Psalm 12 that Jerome had composed among those works which, as he himself testifies in the *Catalogue*, included seven treatises from Psalm 10 through Psalm 16; these have been lost.]

For one who is placed in distress, God’s help seems late; therefore he prays more earnestly to feel the Lord [or: God] as helper quickly, and to find him not an angry judge but a reconciled one.

### 18.

Fill us in the morning with your mercy, and we shall praise and rejoice throughout all our days.

The Septuagint: “We have been filled in the morning with your mercy, and we have rejoiced and delighted in all our days.”

In almost all passages the Septuagint has this practice: what is expressed among the Hebrews in the future, they report as though it had already happened and were past. Here, therefore, they do not mean—as they wished—that they have been filled with the morning mercy of God and have rejoiced. Otherwise, if this had happened, how could they later pray and say, “Look upon your servants and upon your works”? Rather, they pray for everything they request so that they may deserve his morning mercy; when they have obtained it, they will praise God and rejoice throughout all the days of their life. [Note: Earlier it stood in the singular number, and seems not sufficiently coherent with what precedes, reading “and saying”; then the preposition *in* was absent, and, in another sense, the conjunction *and* was added after “hope of the resurrection.”]

It seems to me that they are praying for the rewards of eternal life in the hope of the resurrection, saying, “Fill us with your morning mercy.” This is also signified by the title of Psalm 21, which properly concerns the mystery of the Lord and his resurrection and is inscribed, “For the assumption of the morning.”

### 19.

Make us glad for the days in which you afflicted us, and for the years in which we saw evils.

The Septuagint: “We rejoiced for the days in which you humbled us, and for the years in which we saw evils.”

And Lazarus, who had received evil things in his life, rests in eternal joy in Abraham’s bosom (Luke 16). He calls “evils” not those things that are contrary to good, but affliction and distress. Sarah also afflicted Hagar her maidservant with such evils; and of these it is written in the Gospel: “Sufficient for the day is its own evil” (Matt. 6:34).

Therefore, the more we have been afflicted in this age by persecutions, poverty, the power of enemies, or the torments of illnesses, the greater rewards we shall obtain in the future after the resurrection.

Beautifully, he does not say, “We endured evils,” but “We saw them.” For who is the human being who lives and does not see death? (Ps. 88:49). This should refer not so much to the dissolution of the body as to the multitude of sins, according to which it is said: “The soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezek. 18).

### 20.

Let your work appear to your servants, and your glory upon their children.

The Septuagint: “Look upon your servants and upon your works, and direct their children.” [Note: Martianaeus, following Erasmus without informing the reader, omitted this verse according to the Septuagint; Victorius restored it from the Brixian manuscripts. It could indeed be absent without loss to the interpretation that follows. Yet, apart from the testimony of other manuscripts in which it is often found, Jerome’s established and firm rule and practice should be considered: in the exposition of this Psalm, as elsewhere in his exposition of other Scriptures, he regularly joins the Septuagint version and, even when the wording is not otherwise found among them, at least informs the reader of it.]

Therefore the Lord himself works his work in his servants. And the one who asks is not content with his own salvation, but seeks the glory of his children—that is, of the servants of God.

We should understand “children” not so much as those born from their stock, but as disciples, concerning whom Paul also spoke: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor” (Gal. 4:19). Hence the Apostle John writes according to the merits of his children and the progress of each one’s works: he writes to little children, to young men, and to fathers.

### 21.

And may the beauty of the Lord our God be upon us, and establish the work of our hands upon us; and confirm the work of our hands.

The Septuagint: “And may the splendor of the Lord our God be upon us; and direct the works of our hands upon us; and direct the work of our hands.” [Note: This second addition, “and direct the works of our hands,” is absent from several older Latin Psalters and from certain Greek manuscripts, as well as from the Roman edition. Augustine notes that in the most carefully corrected manuscripts it is marked with an asterisk, indicating that it should be supplied from the Hebrew.]

And where are those who boast in the power of free will and think that they have obtained the grace of God if they possess the power to do or not to do good or evil? Behold, blessed Moses, after the resurrection he had requested by saying, “Fill us with your morning mercy, and we shall praise and rejoice throughout all our days,” is not content merely to have risen and obtained the rewards of eternal life. Rather, he asks that the beauty of the Lord his God be upon those who have risen and shine in the souls and hearts of the saints; and that he himself direct the works of their hands and make them everlasting; and that he himself confirm whatever good appears in the saints.

For just as the humility of the one who prays merits rewards, so the pride of the one who despises [or: trusts in himself] will be abandoned by the help of God.

## EPISTLE 141

[Note: Alternatively numbered 80. Possibly written in A.D. 418.] [Note: This Epistle is appended immediately to the preceding one in two manuscripts of the monastery of Vendôme, as reported by the Benedictines, with only these three intervening words: “Now after the superscription. Many limp with both feet,” etc. This connection with the first Epistle seems especially plausible to us, since it is scarcely credible that Jerome could have written separately to Augustine so brief a composition reporting only one or two riddles. Moreover, its style and sequence prove it to be, as it were, an appendix to the preceding Epistle. But since all printed editions hitherto divide them into two, and the editors of St. Augustine himself, who had examined the evidence of their manuscripts, separate this one from the other not merely in some fashion but by an interval of eight years, it did not seem right to oppose ancient authority. Nevertheless, we place it here in its proper position, in order, insofar as possible, to preserve the native order.]

### TO AUGUSTINE

He congratulates Augustine on his zeal, by which he resisted the factions of the heretics, and in this matter also testifies to his own devotion.

To the holy and most blessed Pope Augustine, Jerome.

At all times I have venerated your Blessedness with the honor that is fitting, and I have loved the Lord and Savior dwelling in you. But now, if it is possible, we add something to the fullness of this and complete it entirely, so that we do not allow even a single hour to pass without mentioning your name—you who have stood firm against the blowing winds through the ardor of faith.

You preferred, insofar as it lay within you, to be saved alone from Sodom rather than to remain among those who were perishing. Your prudence knows what I mean. Well done for your courage: you are celebrated throughout the world [or: in the city]. Catholics venerate and honor you as the restorer of the ancient faith; and, what is a sign of greater glory, all heretics detest you. They persecute me with the same hatred, so that those whom they cannot kill with swords they may kill by their wish.

May the mercy of Christ the Lord preserve you unharmed and mindful of me, venerable and most blessed Pope.

## EPISTLE 142

[Note: Alternatively numbered 81. Written at the same time.]

### TO AUGUSTINE

He indicates that the condemned heresies are still secretly and indirectly plotting, and that there is someone powerful who covertly favors them.

To the holy and most blessed Pope Augustine, Jerome.

Many limp with both feet; and even with their necks broken they do not bow, retaining an affection for their former error although they no longer possess the freedom to preach it.

The holy brothers who are with our small community, especially your holy and venerable daughters, earnestly salute you. I ask you to salute in my name your brothers, my lords Alypius and Evodius—your crown. [Note: He says this because African bishops wore their hair cut in the form of a crown. Thus the expression means: “I entreat your head,” or “your dignity.” Many other similar examples can be found.]

Jerusalem is held captive by Nebuchadnezzar and refuses to listen to Jeremiah’s counsels. Rather, it longs for Egypt, so that it may die at Taphnes and perish there in everlasting slavery. [Note: Some think that by the names Jerusalem and Nebuchadnezzar Rome and Alaric, who captured it, are signified. Others, with Victorius, understand John of Jerusalem: he was still attempting secretly and indirectly to defend his errors, or heresies already condemned—namely, those of the Pelagians—and by his authority and faction was keeping Jerusalem itself oppressed, lest it recover its senses.]

## EPISTLE 143

[Note: Alternatively numbered 79. Written toward the end of A.D. 419.]

### TO ALYPIUS AND AUGUSTINE

He congratulates Alypius and Augustine, through whose efforts the Celestian heresy has been destroyed; at the same time he excuses himself for not yet having written against the books of Annianus, the Pelagian deacon.

To the truly holy lords Alypius and Augustine, bishops worthy of veneration with every affection and by every right, Jerome sends greeting in Christ.

The holy Presbyter Innocentius, who is the bearer of this letter, last year, when he seemed unlikely ever to return to Africa, did not take with him my letter to your Dignities. Yet we give thanks to God that it happened in such a way that you overcame my silence with your letters.

Every opportunity by which I write to your Reverence is most welcome to me. I call God as witness that, if it were possible, I would take wings like a dove and entwine myself in your embraces—always, indeed, because of the merit of your virtues, but now especially because through you, as fellow workers and authors, the Celestian heresy has been slaughtered. This heresy infected the hearts of many so deeply that, even while they recognize themselves to have been overcome and condemned, they do not abandon [perhaps: do not lose] the poisons of their minds. And the only thing they can do is hate us, through whom they think they have lost the freedom to teach their heresy.

2. As for your question whether I have written a reply against the books of Annianus [elsewhere Amandus], the pseudo-deacon Celedensis [Note: [Col. 1181] Some wish to read *Teledensis*, from Teledan, a town of not unknown name in the region of Chalcis, of which he seems to have been a native, as also was that Marcus to whom Jerome wrote Letter 17. Others, with Baronius but on very weak arguments, prefer *Cenedensis* and *Valerianus* in place of *Anianus*. Most, however, make him a Campanian by birth and deacon of Celennae; yet he is commonly called *Celedensis*, even in the manuscripts. He seems, moreover, to be the man whom Orosius calls Goliath, or Pelagius’s armour-bearer: “Goliath, most monstrous in pride, stands . . . having behind him his armour-bearer, who, although he does not himself fight, nevertheless supplies every assistance of bronze and iron.” That is, Pelagius made use of his work and writings; several homilies of St John Chrysostom, rendered into Latin by him in a Pelagian sense and spirit and dedicated to Orontius, a Pelagian bishop, survive.], who feeds most abundantly [Note: That is, on the Pelagian heresy. Augustine says something similar about Julian in *Unfinished Work* 2.51: “You idly feed on deceived wretches.”]—so that he may supply the frivolous words of another’s blasphemy, you should know that I received the books themselves, sent in notebooks by our holy brother Eusebius the Priest, not long ago. From that time onward, either because of the onset of illness or because of the falling asleep of your holy and venerable daughter Eustochium, I have grieved so deeply that I almost thought the books should be disregarded.

For he remains stuck in the same mud, and, apart from his tinkling and beggarly expressions, says nothing else. Nevertheless, we have taken considerable pains: while attempting to answer my letter, he has exposed himself more openly and made his blasphemies plain to everyone. Whatever he denies having said at that wretched Council of Diospolis, he confesses in this work [Col. 1182]; and it is no great task to answer the most foolish of his laments.
