If, however, the Lord grants me life and we have a sufficient supply of copyists, I shall answer in a few little night-time works—not in order to refute a heresy that has already died [elsewhere, “is dead”], but to confute his ignorance and blasphemy with our own arguments. Your Holiness would do this better, lest we be compelled to praise our own work against a heretic.

Our holy sons Albina, Pinianus, and Melania send you many greetings [Note: Formerly, in Martianaeus and Victor, the names were *Albinus* and *Apinianus*. It is well known that Albina is meant here: the daughter of the elder Melania and the mother of the younger Melania, who married Pinianus. Baroncius long ago therefore suggested that *Albina* should be read instead of *Albinus*, just as Baluzius found it written in three very ancient manuscripts of the Colbert Library. In the same library’s manuscript, Baluzius also reports that, in the catalogue of Augustine’s works, where his writings against the Pelagians are listed, he read *to Albina*, while Ulimmerius’s edition has *Albinianum*, other editions *Albinum*, and Chiffletius notes that the excerpts from the Jura manuscript read *Albinam*. In our third letter to Rufinus we said, following the opinion of others, that the names of distinguished women were sometimes given masculine inflections by the ancients, whence *Melanius* might stand for *Melania* and *Albinus* for *Albina*. We now wish to correct that view and instead maintain that women’s names ending in *-a* were sometimes rendered diminutively with an ending in *-ium*: thus *Melanium*, not *Melanius*; *Eubolium* for *Eubole*; *Gregorium* for *Gregoria*; *Glycerium*, *Erotium*, *Philomathium*, *Adelphasium*, and others similarly formed. The same may perhaps be said of the present *Albina*, which may have been called *Albinium* or *Albinum*. Yet although many Greek feminine names are pronounced in Latin with an ending in *-ium*, in accordance with the Greek tendency toward diminutive forms, I nowhere find this in a Roman name such as *Albina*. Nor, according to the analogy of this language, should it be *Albinium*, but *Albinula*. Conversely, the manuscripts consistently have *Albino* or *Albinum*, and in the vocative *Albine*, with a masculine ending, both here and elsewhere in Augustine, although in his Letter 124 one Corbie manuscript has restored *Albinae*. We have therefore adopted the same decision here, writing *Albina* for the sake of brevity in the notes. We have also restored *Pinianus* in place of *Apinianus*, since we find him called this in hundreds of places in Augustine. The older printed editions, however, consistently call him *Apinianus*; even Jerome, the author of the Life of Saint Melania, in Surius under 31 January, writes: “He was twenty-four years old, Apinianus.” Furthermore, *Melanium* rather than *Melania* seems to be required in the nominative.].

I have given this letter from holy Bethlehem to the holy Priest Innocentius to deliver. Your niece Paula [Note: Recently published for the first time at Vienna. Apparently written in the year 420.] earnestly begs that you remember her, and sends you many greetings. May the clemency of our Lord Jesus Christ preserve you unharmed and mindful of me, O truly holy lords and fathers, truly holy and venerable in the affection of all.

## LETTER CXLIV [Note: [Col. 1182] Understand Paula the Younger, daughter of Laeta and Toxotius, niece of Eustochium.]. ST AUGUSTINE TO OPTATUS, BISHOP OF MILEVIS

### On the Nature and Origin of the Soul

He says that he has not yet received from Jerome an answer to his Letter 131 here, on the origin of the soul, and does not approve meanwhile of publishing that consultation.

To the most blessed, most sincerely beloved, and most longed-for lord, brother, and fellow bishop OPTATUS, AUGUSTINE sends greeting in the Lord.

1. “Through the devout priest Saturninus [Note: [Col. 1182] This is the ‘second letter of St Augustine to Optatus of Milevis on the Nature and Origin of the Soul,’ namely one of those which he wrote to him on this matter.] I received the letter of your Reverence [Col. 1183], demanding with great eagerness something from me which I do not yet possess. But you disclosed to me why you did this: namely, because you believe that an answer has already been given to my consultation on this matter. Would that it were so! Far be it from me to deprive you, whose most eager expectation I know, of a share in this gift. But, if you will believe me, dearest brother, nearly five years have now elapsed since I sent to the East [Note: [Col. 1183] Letter 131 in this recension, written in the year 415.] the book, not of my presumption but of my consultation; and I have not yet merited a reply which might unravel for me this question, on which you want me to bring you a definite judgment. I should have sent both, if I had both. But what I have, without the other thing which I do not yet have, I do not think I ought now to send or publish for anyone, lest he who may perhaps answer me, as I desire, should rightly be offended that my question, worked out in a most laborious discussion, is circulated through people’s hands and knowledge without his reply—which is not yet to be despaired of—and should judge that I acted more boastfully than usefully, as though I could ask what he could not unravel, though perhaps he can, and, while he is doing it, must be awaited. For I know rather that he is occupied with matters which are by no means to be deferred and are of greater importance. That your Holiness may know this too, attend briefly to what he wrote to me the following year [Note: [Col. 1183] That is, through Orosius. This is Jerome’s Letter 144, written in 416, which is transferred here for the greater part.] by the returning bearer through whom I had written. For I transferred this from his letter into this one.”

“A most difficult time,” he says, “occurred, when it was better for me to be silent than to speak, so that our studies ceased [Note: [Col. 1183] Previously *et* stood for *ne*, which reverses the sense of the sentence.], lest, in Appius’s words, a dog-like eloquence be exercised. Thus I could not for the present answer your two little books, dedicated to my name, most learned and shining with every splendour of eloquence. Not because I think anything in them deserving of censure, but because, according to the Apostle, ‘let each be fully assured in his own mind’ [Note: [Col. 1183] According to the Greek, πληροφορείσθω. The manuscript has *abundet*.]: one indeed thus, another otherwise (Rom. 14:5). Certainly, whatever could be said and drawn by sublime talent from the fountains of the holy Scriptures has been set forth and discussed by you. But I ask your Reverence to suffer me briefly to praise your talent. For we discuss learning among ourselves. But rivals, and especially heretics, if they see differing opinions among us, will maliciously allege that they arise from bitterness of spirit. But I have resolved to love you, to esteem, honour, and admire you, and to defend your sayings as though they were my own. Certainly, in the Dialogue which I published recently, I mentioned your Blessedness as was fitting. Let us rather strive that the most pernicious heresy be removed from the Churches, which always feigns penitence, in order that it may have freedom to teach in the Churches [Note: [Col. 1183] From the cited letter of Jerome to Augustine, the principal editor, Gottivv, appends the following words of Jerome:] [Col. 1184] lest, if it revealed itself in open daylight, it should be cast out and die.” [Note: Manuscript: *to receive you*, which is not disapproved. Appropriate to the matter: “When they perceive that they have been overcome and condemned, they nevertheless do not abandon the poisons of their minds, and, so far as they can, hate us, through whom they have lost the liberty of teaching heresy,” etc.]

2. “You see, then, venerable brother, that these words of my dearest friend, given in answer to my inquiry, did not deny an answer to it but excused the time, because he was compelled to devote care to other, more pressing matters. You see also how kindly disposed he is toward me, and what he warns: namely, that our rivals, and especially heretics, should not maliciously allege that what we do between ourselves, with charity and the sincerity of friendship certainly preserved, for the sake of learning, arises from bitterness of spirit. Therefore, if people read both our works—where I inquired and where he himself answered the inquiries—as they should, then, if the same question has been sufficiently explained according to his judgment, I shall give thanks that I have been instructed. There will be no small benefit when this comes to the knowledge of many: our juniors will not only know what they ought to think on this matter, discussed between us in careful debate, but will also learn from our example, through God’s mercy and favour, how among dearest brothers there may be reciprocal discussion for the sake of inquiry, while love nevertheless remains inviolate.”

3. “But if my writing, in which a most obscure matter is read merely as inquired into, is published without his reply, in which perhaps the discovery will appear, and circulates more widely, reaching also those who, as the Apostle says, ‘comparing themselves with themselves, do not understand,’ they will not understand in what spirit we act, since they themselves do not know how to act in that spirit. They will interpret my will toward a friend most beloved and deserving of honour for his great merits not as they see it—for they do not see it—but as pleases them and as they suspect at the prompting of their hatred. This, certainly, so far as lies in us, we ought to avoid. But if perhaps what we do not wish to become known through us becomes known, even against our will, to those to whom we do not wish it known, what remains except to bear the Lord’s will with equanimity? For I ought not to write this to anyone if I wished it always to remain hidden. For if—God forbid—he should never reply through some accident or necessity, our consultation which we sent to him will undoubtedly sometime become known. Nor will it be useless to readers: even if they do not find what they seek, they will at least find how matters unknown ought to be investigated and not rashly affirmed. And while they themselves take care, with diligent charity rather than contentious strife, to consult whom they can about what they read there, they will either find what they seek or exercise the mind’s edge by inquiry itself, so as to recognize that inquiry ought not to proceed further. Yet for the present, as long as an answer from the friend already consulted is not to be despaired of, I think I have persuaded your affection that our consultation should not be published, so far as lies in us. Besides, you yourself requested not that alone, but desired that the answer of the man whom I consulted be sent to you joined with it [Col. 1185], which I would certainly do if I had it. But if, to use the words of your Holiness which you set down in your letter, by ‘the lucid demonstration of my wisdom, which, as you write, the author of light has attributed to me according to the merit of my life,’ you mean not the consultation and inquiry itself but suppose that I have already found the thing for which I asked, and request that discovery rather be sent, I would do so if things were as you think. For I confess that I have not yet found how the soul both derives sin from Adam—which it is not lawful to doubt—and is itself not derived from Adam. This must be investigated by me more carefully than asserted inconsiderately.”

4. “Your letter mentions I know not how many old men and men instructed by learned priests, whom you could not recall to the understanding and assertion, most full of truth, of your Moderation; yet you do not state what that assertion, most full of truth, is, to which you could not recall the old men and men instructed by learned priests. For if these old men held or hold what they received from learned priests, how could a rustic and insufficiently instructed crowd of clerics trouble you in matters in which they had been instructed by learned priests? But if those old men or the crowd of clerics had perversely departed from what they received from learned priests, they ought rather to have been corrected by those men’s authority and restrained from their most contentious tumult. But again, when you say that you, a new and untrained teacher, feared to corrupt the traditions of so many and such bishops, and feared to turn people to the better side because of injury to the dead, what do you suggest except that those whom you wished to correct refused to acquiesce in a new and untrained teacher because they were unwilling to abandon the traditions of learned and great bishops already deceased? On that point I say nothing for the present about them; but I very much desire to know your assertion, which you say is most full of truth—not the opinion itself, I mean, but its proof.”

5. “For you have sufficiently made known to us that you disapprove those who affirm that all human souls are propagated and transmitted from that one soul given to the first-created man through the succession of generations. But, because your letter does not contain the reasoning or testimonies of the divine Scriptures by which you have shown this to be false, we do not know them. Further, what you yourself maintain in place of what you disapprove is not clearly apparent to one reading either the letter you formerly sent to the brethren of Caesarea or the one you have most recently directed to me [Note: [Col. 1185] Augustine speaks of these letters sent by Optatus to the Caesareans in Letter 190 to Optatus: “Although I have received no letters of your Holiness addressed to me personally, yet because those which you sent to Caesarea in Mauretania arrived while I was present at Caesarea . . . it came about that I too read what you wrote,” etc.], except that I see you believe, as you write, that God made human beings, makes them, and will make them, and that nothing exists in heaven or on earth which has not been and is not established by him as author. This is indeed so true that no one ought to doubt it [Col. 1186]. But you must still state from what God makes the souls which you deny are produced by propagation: from something else? And if so, what is that; or altogether from nothing? But far be it from you to hold the opinion of Origen and Priscillian, or of any others who think anything similar: that souls are thrust into earthly and mortal bodies for the merits of a prior life [Note: [Col. 1186] Previously *contradantur* stood here, wrongly, as also the following word *an* in the archetype for *in*, which we correct.]. For apostolic authority wholly contradicts that opinion, saying that Esau and Jacob, before they were born, had done nothing good or evil. Therefore your opinion on this matter is known to us not wholly but only in part; its proof—that is, by what it is taught that what you think is true—remains altogether unknown to us. For that reason I asked in my earlier letter that you would deign to send me the little book on Faith which you mention having written, and to which you complain that I know not what priest falsely subscribed; and I ask now as well what divine testimonies you were able to apply to the resolution of this question [Note: [Col. 1186] The editor Gottivv notes that perhaps *quidquid* should be read.]. For in your letter to the Caesareans you say that it pleased you that even secular judges should know every proof of truth; and that, as they sat at the common request and examined everything with a view to faith, the Divinity, as you write, granted by the infusion of his mercy that they should offer a stronger confirmation and proof for their opinions than your own Moderation was maintaining against them with the authorities of weighty testimonies. I therefore desire with great eagerness to know these authorities of weighty testimonies. For you seem to have followed only one ground on which to refute your opponents: namely, that they denied our souls to be God’s work. If they think this, their opinion is rightly judged condemnable. For if they said this of bodies themselves, they would undoubtedly have to be corrected or denounced. For what Christian denies that the bodies of every individual born are God’s works? Yet we do not therefore deny that they are begotten by parents because we confess that they are fashioned by God. Therefore, when it is said that certain incorporeal seeds of their own kind are likewise drawn from parents and that souls are nevertheless made from them by God’s work, divine Scripture, not human conjecture, must be produced as witness to refute this. For from the holy books of canonical authority we may have an abundance of testimonies proving that God makes souls; but such testimonies refute those who deny that every individual soul in human beings who are born is God’s work, not those who confess this and nevertheless contend that souls, like bodies, are formed indeed with God at work but from parental propagation. To refute these, you must seek definite divine testimonies; or, if you have already found them, send them in mutual love to us, who, so far as we can, are most earnestly seeking but have not yet found them [Col. 1187]. For your brief consultation, placed last in the letter which you sent to the Caesarean brethren, reads as follows: ‘I beg that you instruct me, your son and disciple, newly and only recently coming to these mysteries with God’s help, by the instruction which you ought, which is fitting, and which prudent priests ought to give in answer: whether that opinion should rather be held which says that the soul is from propagation and that, through a certain hidden origin and secret order, the other souls flow into the whole human race by transmission from Adam, the first-created man; or rather whether the definition, and the belief to be retained, which all your brethren and priests established here maintain and affirm should be chosen—the belief which testifies and believes that God is and was and will be the author of all things and of all human beings.’”

6. “Of these two alternatives, then, which you proposed in asking advice, you wish one or the other to be chosen and answered to you. That should be done by those who know, if these two were contrary to each other, so that, once one was chosen, the other would consequently be rejected. But now if someone chooses not one of these two but answers that both are true—that the other souls flow into the whole human race through transmission from Adam, the first-created man, and nevertheless believes and says that God is and was and will be the author of all things and all human beings—what do you think should be said against him? Shall we perhaps say: ‘If souls are propagated from parents, God is not the author of all things because he does not make souls’? For if we say this, the answer will be: ‘Therefore, because bodies are propagated from parents, God is not the author of all things, if for that reason he must be said not to make bodies.’ But who would deny that God is the author of all human bodies, while saying that he is creator only of that one which he first fashioned from earth, or perhaps also of that man’s wife, because he himself formed her from his side, but not of the rest, because we cannot deny that all other human bodies flowed from them?”

7. “Accordingly, if those with whom you are in conflict on this question assert the propagation of souls by derivation from that one soul in such a way that they now deny that God makes and forms them, persist in refuting, convicting, and correcting them as far as, with the Lord’s help, you can. But if they affirm that certain beginnings are drawn from that one and thereafter from parents, and yet that each individual soul in each individual human being is created and formed by God, the author of all things, seek from the most holy Scriptures what may be answered to them—something unambiguous and incapable of another interpretation—or, if you have already found it, send it also to us, as I requested above. But if this is still unknown to you as it is to me, persist with all your strength in refuting those who say that souls are not from divine work; you said that they muttered this among their more secret tales in your first letter, and then, because of this foolish and impious opinion, withdrew from your fellowship and the service of the Church. And defend and uphold by every means against them what you put in that same letter: that God made souls, makes them, and will make them, and that nothing exists in heaven or on earth which has not been or is not established by him as author [Col. 1188]. For this is believed, said, defended, and proved most truly and rightly concerning every kind whatsoever of creature. For God was, is, and will be the author of all things and all human beings, as you put in your final Consultation to our fellow bishops of the Province of Caesarea, and as you in some way urged them to choose rather, following the example of all the brethren and fellow priests among you who maintain it. But one question is whether God is author and maker of all souls and bodies—which truth holds—or whether some natural being arises which he does not make, an opinion wholly erroneous; another question is whether God makes human souls from propagation or without propagation, though it is not lawful to doubt that they are made by him. I want you to be sober and watchful in this question [Note: [Col. 1188] The archetype has *nec*. If one wishes to retain it, says the editor Gottivv, different punctuation is necessary: ‘I want you to be watchful, nor is it . . .’; but this is less satisfactory.], lest, while you destroy the propagation of souls, you unwittingly fall into the Pelagian heresy. For if we say—and say truly—that God is creator of human bodies, whose propagation is known to all, not merely of that first man and the first married pair but of all propagated from them, I think it is easy to understand that those who defend propagation of souls do not wish us to destroy on this ground [Note: [Col. 1188] Perhaps something is missing: ‘that souls are made by God.’] the fact that God makes souls, since he also makes bodies, which we cannot deny are made by propagation. Rather, other proofs must be sought by which those who think souls are propagated may be repelled, if truth declares them in error. On this matter those men ought, if possible, rather to have been questioned, because of injury to the dead [Note: [Col. 1188] Again the editor says: the words are corrupt and displaced.], as you write in the letter you sent me later [Note: [Col. 1188] This letter too has been lost; compare the recently cited Augustine, no. 22.], you feared to turn people to the better side. For you said that these deceased bishops were so distinguished, so great, and so learned that you, a new and untrained teacher, feared to wish to corrupt their traditions. Thus, if I could know that men so distinguished, so great, and so learned asserted this opinion of the propagation of souls, by what testimonies [Note: [Col. 1188] That is, ‘at least’; for I do not see why that word or particle, which was in the archetype, should have been relegated to the margin in the edition. The period in this very line needs a healing hand, being defective and gaping: perhaps *I would consider* or *I would judge*, or something similar, should be supplied after *asserted*. In the immediately preceding place, where it says, ‘Thus, if I could know,’ the editor Gottivv thinks *I would wish* is missing, that is, ‘I would wish, if I could know,’ etc. He considers the following words should be reconstructed thus: ‘what kind of testimonies, or rather by what reasoning and what testimonies,’ etc.]—yet in the letter sent to the Caesareans, without any regard for their authority, you said it was a new invention and unheard-of doctrine—although, even if it is an error, we know it is not new but very old and ancient.”

8. “When some reasons rightly compel us to doubt in a question, we ought not on that account also to doubt whether we ought to doubt [Col. 1189]. For concerning doubtful matters we must doubt without doubt. You see how the Apostle does not doubt that he doubts concerning himself whether he was caught up into the third heaven in the body or outside the body: ‘whether this or that, I do not know; God knows’ (2 Cor. 12:2–3). Why then, so long as I do not know, should I not be allowed to doubt whether my soul came into this life by propagation or without propagation, when I do not doubt that it was made in either way by the highest and true God? Why should it not be lawful for me to say: ‘I know that my soul exists from God’s work and is altogether God’s work; whether by propagation, like the body, or outside propagation, like that which was given to the first man, I do not know; God knows’ [Note: [Col. 1189] The editor Gottivv, following his archetype, has *whether*; he next directs the reader to consult the final chapter of the book Against the Priscillianists.]? You want me to establish one of these? I could, if I knew it. But if you know it yourself, see: you have me more eager to learn what I do not know than to teach what I know. If you do not know, as I do not, pray as I do, that whether through any servant of his or through himself, that Teacher may teach us who said to his disciples: ‘Do not wish to be called Rabbi by men; for one is your Teacher, Christ’ (Matt. 23:8). Provided, however, that he knows it expedient for us to know such things; for he knows not only what to teach, but also what it is expedient for us to learn. For I confess my desire to your affection: I do indeed desire to know also what you ask, but much more I would desire, if possible, to know when he who is desired by all nations will appear [Note: [Col. 1189] Read, says the editor Gottivv, *will appear*; for this he adduces testimonies from Book XI of the Confessions.] and when the kingdom of the Saints will be, rather than from what source I began to come into this earth. Yet when his disciples, our Apostles, asked him who knows all things about that, they received the answer: ‘It is not for you to know the time or seasons which God has placed in his own power’ (Acts 1:7). What if he also knows that this is not ours to know, he who certainly knows what it is useful for us to know? Through him I do know that it is not ours to know the times which the Father has placed in his own power; but whether it is ours to know the origin of souls, which I do not yet know—that is, whether knowing it belongs to us—even this I do not know. For if I knew at least this, that it is not ours to know it, I would cease not only from affirming it while I do not know, but even from seeking it. But now, although it is so obscure and deep that there I fear rashness in teaching more than I have desire in learning [1077], I still wish to know this too, if I can. And although what that saint says is much more necessary: ‘Make known to me, Lord, my end’ (Ps. 38:5)—for he does not say, ‘my beginning’—I would wish that what concerns this question were not hidden from me [Note: [Col. 1189] Eugyppius seems to cite this passage, where he read ‘I would wish, however,’ not ‘my beginning.’ The editor Gottivv prefers, for the following context, ‘I would wish that what concerns this question were not hidden from me.’].”

9. “Yet concerning my beginning itself, I am not ungrateful to my Teacher, because I know that the human soul is spirit, not body, and is rational or intellectual; that it is not God’s nature but rather a creature in some respect mortal, insofar as it can be changed for the worse and alienated from God’s life, by participation in which it is blessed; and in some respect immortal, because it cannot lose the sense by which it is well or ill after this life [Col. 1190; Note: Consult, says the editor Gottivv, Against the Priscillianists 1.1 and Against Maximinus 2.12.2.]. I know also that it did not merit to be enclosed in flesh for acts done before the flesh, but that it is not therefore in a human being without the stain of sin, even if its life upon earth has been but one day, as it is written (Job 14:5, according to the Septuagint). And so I know that no one is born from Adam through the succession of generation without sin, whence even infants must be reborn in Christ through the grace of regeneration. I rejoice that I have learned, and affirm that I know, these many and not small things about the beginning or origin of our souls, in which there are several points belonging to that knowledge which stand by faith. Therefore, if I do not know, concerning the origin of souls, whether God makes them for human beings from propagation or without propagation, though I do not doubt that they are made by him, I do indeed choose rather to know this also than not to know it; but as long as I cannot, I do better to doubt on this point than rashly dare to affirm as certain something which may perhaps be contrary to the matter about which I ought not to doubt.

10. “Therefore, my good brother, since you consult me and want me to decide one of these: whether the other souls are made, each for each individual, from that one man through propagation like bodies, or without propagation like that one man’s soul from the Creator—for we do not deny that they are made by him, whether in this way or that—allow me also to inquire how the soul derives original sin from that from which it is not itself originally derived. For we likewise do not deny that all souls derive original sin from Adam, lest we fall into the detestable Pelagian heresy. If you do not know what I ask, as I do not, patiently endure with me that we do not know either what you ask or what I ask. But if you now know what I ask, when you have taught me this also, then I shall answer what you want me to answer, fearing nothing there any longer [Note: [Col. 1190] The passage is restored from Eugyppius, where it previously stood corruptly as *intuens*. The editor Gottivv would prefer to restore: ‘answer, now seeing no evil.’]. I ask, therefore, that you not be angry because I could not establish what you ask, but could show what you are asking, so that when you have found it, you will not doubt to establish what you were seeking. I thought this should be written to your Holiness, who already thinks, as though certain, that the propagation of souls must be disapproved. But if an answer had to be written to those who affirm it, I might perhaps show how they do not know what they think they know, and how greatly they ought to fear to dare affirm it. Certainly, in the friend’s reply which I inserted into this Letter, do not let it move you that he mentioned two books sent by me, to which he replied that he had not had leisure to answer. Only one, not both, concerns this question; in the other I asked and examined another matter in consulting him [Note: [Col. 1190] We restore this again from conjectures, since the exemplar [Col. 1191] had *that* for *another*, confusing the sense. The other matter which he indicates he consulted in another letter is Jacob’s opinion. Before us the editor Gottivv corrected this, which we only now recognize while using his edition.]. But when he warns and urges us rather to strive that the most pernicious heresy be removed from the Churches, he means that very Pelagian heresy. I warn you, brother, as earnestly as I can, to avoid it most carefully when you either consider or already discuss the origin of souls: do not let it creep in that one ought to believe that absolutely no soul, except that of the one Mediator, fails to derive from Adam original sin bound by generation and to be loosed by regeneration [Col. 1192; Note: The same editor rightly directs that *subrepat* be written, and confirms this with several examples of such phrasing.].

## FIFTH CLASS, CONTAINING THREE LETTERS WHOSE DATE IS LESS WELL ESTABLISHED; TO WHICH ARE ADDED THREE OTHERS OF UNCERTAIN AUTHORSHIP

[Col. 1191]

## LETTER CXLV [Note: [Col. 1191] Elsewhere 39. Written in an uncertain year.]. TO EXUPERANTIUS [Note: [Col. 1191] This Exuperantius seems to be the man whom Palladius, in the Paradise of Heraclides, maliciously reports to have been compelled by jealousy and envy of St Jerome to leave his Bethlehemitic retreat. See the chronological arguments. In the Verona manuscript it is entitled ‘To Exuperantius on penitence.’]

[Col. 1191]

He exhorts Exuperantius, after leaving military service, to devote himself to the perfect Christian life and to move to Bethlehem together with his brother Quintilianus.

1. Among all the benefits that the friendship of the holy brother Quintilianus has conferred upon me, this is perhaps the greatest: that although unknown to me in body, he has joined you to me in mind. [Note: The Verona manuscript reads “Quintianus,” but at the end of the letter calls him “Quintilianus,” as do the printed editions.] For who would not love one who, beneath a military cloak and in military dress, performs the works of the Prophets and conquers the outward man, who promises one thing, by the inward man, who has been formed in the image of the Creator? [Note: The same manuscript reads “conformed.”] Hence I am the first to invite you to the duty of correspondence, and I beg you to give me occasion to write back more often, so that thereafter I may write more boldly.

It is enough briefly to have indicated this to your prudence: remember the apostolic judgment, “Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek release. Are you released from a wife? Do not seek a wife” (1 Cor. 7:27)—that is, a bond, which is contrary to release. Therefore, whoever serves the obligations of marriage is bound; whoever is bound is a servant; but whoever is released is free.

Since, then, you rejoice in the freedom of Christ, yet do one thing and promise another, and are practically established on the housetop, you must not descend from the roof to retrieve your tunic (Luke 17), nor look back, nor release the plow-handle once you have taken hold of the plow (Luke 9:62). Rather, if it can be done, imitate Joseph and leave the Egyptian mistress’s cloak behind, so that naked you may follow the Lord and Savior, who says in the Gospel: “Unless someone renounces everything, takes up his cross, and follows me, he cannot be my disciple” (Matt. 10:38). [Note: This clause, “renounces everything,” is absent from two Verona manuscripts; nor does Matthew have it in this place, though it suits Jerome’s context.]

Throw off the burden of the world; do not seek riches, which are compared with the crookedness of camels (Matt. 19:24). Naked and light, fly up to heaven, lest the weights of gold depress the wings of your virtues.

I say this not because I have learned that you are greedy, but because I understand that you are still devoting yourself to military service for this reason: to fill the purse that the Lord commanded to be emptied. [Note: The same manuscripts read “but let me understand,” whereas the printed editions have “but I understand.”]

If, then, those who possess estates and riches are commanded to sell everything, give it to the poor, and thus follow the Savior, your distinction must either be wealthy, and therefore do what has been commanded, or still be poor, and therefore ought not to seek what it will later distribute. Certainly Christ reckons everything according to the will of the soul.

No one was poorer than the Apostles, and no one abandoned so much for the Lord. That poor widow in the Gospel who put two small coins into the treasury is preferred to all the wealthy, because she gave everything she had (Luke 21). Therefore, do not seek what you may distribute; distribute what you have already sought, so that Christ may recognize you as his bravest recruit; so that the Father may joyfully go out to meet you when you come from a very distant land; so that he may give you a robe, bestow a ring, and sacrifice a fattened calf for you (Luke 15); so that he may quickly make you sail to us, unencumbered, together with your holy brother Quintilianus.

I have knocked at the doors of friendship. If you open them, you will often have us as your guests.

## Letter 146

[Note: Formerly numbered 85. Written at an uncertain time.]

### To Evangelus

[Note: This concerns the necessity of the episcopate and its superiority over the presbyterate. Some have thought that Jerome expressed an opposing view in this letter, although many learned writers have treated the matter in various dissertations and, by comparison with other passages, have set forth the Doctor’s genuine—and Catholic—meaning. We think it better to refer the reader to them than to delay him here. Jerome himself may readily be compared with the letter to Heliodorus, Letter 52 to Nepotianus, Letter 22 to Eustochium, and another to Theophilus; also with his Commentaries on Micah 7 and Isaiah 60, and with the *Dialogue against the Luciferians* and *Against Jovinianus*, book 1, together with other passages that we carefully note in the index. As for the Evangelus mentioned here, he seems to be the same person to whom, in our recension, Jerome addressed Letter 73 concerning Melchizedek. Nor is it an empty conjecture that this is the presbyter Evangelus to whom Anianus of Celeda dedicated seven homilies of Chrysostom translated by him into Latin. The person who equated deacons with presbyters, or even placed them ahead of presbyters, and defended the ambition of the deacons of the Roman Church, is said by some to have been a certain Falcidius, generally regarded as an author older than Jerome himself and Augustine. Certainly the whole of Question 101 in the collection entitled *Questions from Both Testaments Mixed Together*, in the Appendix to the Works of St. Augustine, volume 3, is drawn from this letter; it will be very useful to compare it closely. To establish the correct spelling of the name, we previously cited Evangelus from Macrobius. More relevant to our subject is Evangelus, bishop of the Church of Assura, who is mentioned in the Acts of the Conference of Carthage and who took part in the councils held at Carthage in 397 and 401, as is known from the Book of Canons of the African Church. In the two Verona manuscripts, the title reads: “To Evangelus the Presbyter, on the Order of the Priesthood.”]

He refutes the error of those who placed a deacon on the same level as a presbyter, showing what distinction exists among a bishop, a presbyter, and a deacon.

### 1

We read in Isaiah: “A fool will speak foolish things” (Isa. 32:6). I hear that someone has burst into such madness that he places deacons above presbyters, that is, above bishops. For although the Apostle clearly teaches that presbyters and bishops are the same, what afflicts this minister of tables and widows, that he should arrogantly exalt himself above those at whose prayers the Body and Blood of Christ are made? [Note: Thus read the older printed books and manuscripts, among them the two most excellent Verona manuscripts. Formerly the text read, in a different and insufficiently coherent sense, “Who can endure it?” Here Jerome uses *pati* in the sense of being afflicted or distressed by some malady, as though he had said, “With what disease or madness is he vexed?” In the same sense, in Letter 109 to Riparius, on Vigilantius, §5: “What did the Apostles suffer, that they should precede the unclean body of Stephen with such funeral pomp?” Plautus, at the beginning of the *Mostellaria*: “What evil shouting is this before the house?”]

Do you seek authority? Hear the testimony: “Paul and Timothy, servants of Jesus Christ, to all the saints in Christ Jesus who are at Philippi, with the bishops and deacons” (Phil. 1:1).

Do you want another example? In the Acts of the Apostles Paul speaks thus to the priests of one Church: “Take heed to yourselves and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has appointed you bishops, to govern the Church of the Lord, which he acquired with his own blood” (Acts 20:18).

And lest anyone contentiously insist that there were several bishops in one Church, hear another testimony, in which it is most plainly demonstrated that bishop and presbyter are the same: “For this reason I left you in Crete, that you might correct what was lacking and appoint presbyters in every city, as I commanded you. If anyone is blameless, the husband of one wife, having believing children, not accused of debauchery or disobedient—for a bishop must be blameless, as God’s steward” (Titus 1:5 ff.).

And to Timothy: “Do not neglect the grace that is in you, which was given to you through prophecy, by the laying on of the hands of the presbyterate” (1 Tim. 4:14). [Note: The same books, as well as Gratian, who quotes this entire letter, omit the words “which is in you,” despite the Greek text.]

Peter likewise says in his First Epistle: “I exhort the presbyters among you, as a fellow presbyter and a witness of the sufferings of Christ, and a participant in the glory that is to be revealed: shepherd the flock of Christ and exercise oversight, not under compulsion but willingly, according to God” (1 Pet. 5). This is expressed more significantly in Greek as ἐπισκοποῦντες, that is, “exercising oversight,” from which the name “bishop” (*episcopus*) is derived. [Note: I think the interpretation of the Greek word—namely, “overseeing”—is more accurate. Our oldest manuscripts do not contain it, although they too read the Greek word.]

Do the testimonies of such great men seem insufficient to you? Let the Gospel trumpet sound—the son of thunder, whom Jesus loved greatly, who drank the streams of doctrine from the Savior’s breast (John 21): “The presbyter to the chosen Lady and her children, whom I love in truth” (2 John 1). And in another letter: “The presbyter to Gaius, the beloved, whom I love in truth” (3 John 1).

The fact that afterward one man was chosen to be placed over the others was done as a remedy for schism, lest each person, drawing Christ’s Church to himself, should rend it. Indeed, in Alexandria, from Mark the Evangelist until the bishops Heraclas and Dionysius, the presbyters always chose one from among themselves, placed him in a higher rank, and called him bishop—just as if an army were to make one of its number emperor, or deacons were to choose from among themselves someone whom they knew to be capable and call him archdeacon.

For what does a bishop do, apart from ordination, that a presbyter does not do? [Note: In the *Dialogue against the Luciferians* Jerome also attributes to bishops alone the power to confer Confirmation. What he says there should be consulted. Meanwhile, Chrysostom agrees with Jerome when he writes concerning bishops in Homily 11 on the First Epistle to Timothy: “They are superior by ordination alone, and seem to possess only this more than presbyters.”]

Nor should one Church of the city of Rome be considered one thing and the Church of the whole world another. Gaul, Britain, Africa, Persia, the East, India, and all the barbarian nations worship one Christ and observe one rule of truth. If authority is sought, the world is greater than the city.

Wherever there is a bishop—whether in Rome, Eugubium, Constantinople, Rhegium, Alexandria, or Tanis—he has the same merit and the same priesthood. [Note: The separate Lyon edition of this letter, from 1510, adds “or Thebes,” and further adds “or Guarmatia, or Wormatia.” The latter name was also formerly read by Gratian. As Victorius conjectures, it was inserted from Burchard of Worms, who drew extensively from this passage.]

The power of riches or the humility of poverty does not make one bishop higher or another lower. [Note: The older printed editions and even the better manuscripts reject the negative particle, so that the meaning is that, because of the greatness of cities, some bishops are called higher and others lower because of poverty—not with respect to the character of their dignity, but with respect to precedence and governance. This seems also to have been the meaning expressed by the author of the aforementioned *Questions from Both Testaments Mixed Together*. Jerome’s text is more elegant, especially in view of the following clause, “but all,” although the recent edition of Gratian has “of the others” and refers the phrase to the Apostles.] Nevertheless, all are successors of the Apostles.

### 2

But you will say: How is it that at Rome a presbyter is ordained at the testimony of a deacon? What are you offering me—the custom of one city? Why do you claim as laws of the Church a small number, from which arrogance has arisen? Everything rare is more eagerly sought. Among the Indians, pennyroyal is more valuable than pepper. The scarcity of deacons makes them honorable; the multitude of presbyters makes them contemptible.

Nevertheless, even in the Church of Rome, the presbyters sit and the deacons stand. Although, as vices gradually increased, I have seen a deacon sit among the presbyters in the bishop’s absence and give blessings at domestic banquets. [Note: The larger Verona manuscript reads “I have heard” rather than “I have seen”; this is especially worth noting. Gratian soon has “blessings before the presbyters,” a reading Victorius praises: “For it is both foolish to think and erroneous to believe that deacons should bless presbyters.”]

Let those who do this learn that they are not acting rightly, and let them hear the Apostles: “It is not right for us to leave the word of God and serve tables” (Acts 6:2). Let them know why deacons were instituted. Let them read the Acts of the Apostles and remember their condition.

“Presbyter” and “bishop” are different names for age and dignity. Hence, in the passages to Titus and Timothy concerning the ordination of a bishop and a deacon (Titus 1; 1 Tim. 3), presbyters are not mentioned at all, because the presbyter is contained in the bishop. Whoever is promoted advances from the lesser to the greater.

Therefore, either let a deacon be ordained from a presbyter, so that the presbyter may be shown to be inferior to the deacon into whom he grows from a lesser position; or, if a presbyter is ordained from a deacon, let him know that he is inferior in financial advantages but superior in priesthood.

And so that we may know that the Apostolic traditions were taken from the Old Testament—that Aaron, his sons, and the Levites served in the Temple—let bishops, presbyters, and deacons claim these roles for themselves in the Church.

## Letter 147

[Note: Formerly numbered 48. Written at an uncertain time.]

### To Sabinianus, Who Fell

[Note: In one Verona manuscript of astonishing antiquity, the title reads “To Sabinianus, an exhortation concerning penance.” It begins with the conjunction *et* (“and”), followed by “Samuel,” and so forth, emphatically.]

Sabinianus, a deacon who, after committing adultery, had fled to Bethlehem and had been commended to Jerome by a letter from his bishop, remained in the holy places and performed the office of deacon. He had solicited a certain consecrated virgin to sexual violation and flight. After being discovered, Jerome rebukes him and urges him to repent in a monastery.

### 1

Samuel once mourned Saul, because “the Lord repented that he had made him king over Israel” (1 Sam. 16). Paul likewise reminded the Corinthians, among whom fornication was being heard of—such fornication as did not even exist among the Gentiles—in a mournful voice, saying: “Lest, when I come again, God humble me among you, and I mourn over many of those who previously sinned and have not repented of the uncleanness, impurity, and fornication that they have committed” (1 Cor. 12, at the end). [Note: The former reading was “such as not even among the Gentiles, and indeed in a mournful voice,” an awkward and obscure sense, which we have corrected from the same Verona archetype.]

If the Prophet and the Apostle, themselves stained by no fault, acted with a merciful disposition toward everyone, how much more ought I, myself a sinner, to act toward you, a sinner, when you refuse to rise after your fall and do not lift your eyes to heaven. [Note: Formerly the text had “a sinner,” and shortly afterward “to raise,” instead of “you raise”; the two Verona manuscripts correct both.]

Rather, after squandering the Father’s substance, you take pleasure in the husks of swine (Luke 15), and, climbing the precipitous heights of pride, plunge headlong into the abyss. [Note: Several manuscripts read “scattered”; among the printed editions some have “lost,” others “betrayed.” The printed reading found in Verona is supported by a very similar passage in Tertullian, *On Modesty*, chapter 8: “The younger son, having squandered his substance, begs in a foreign land.” Jerome likewise writes in his Commentary on Jonah 3: “After the substance had been squandered,” and so forth.]

You want to have your belly as God instead of Christ; you serve lust; you glory in your flesh and your shame; and, like a fattened victim, you are fattened for your own death. You imitate the life of those whose torments you do not fear, ignorant that the kindness of God urges you to repentance. “But according to your hardness and impenitent heart, you store up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath” (Rom. 2:5). [Note: The Verona manuscript reads “you glory in your shame,” omitting “and your flesh”; shortly afterward it has “their vices” for “their life,” and finally “because goodness” for “because the kindness.”]

Is your heart hardened, like Pharaoh’s, for this reason: because you are not immediately struck and are being delayed for punishment for a long time? [Note: Again, we have followed Verona, which has “although you are long delayed for punishment,” whereas the former reading was “although you are delayed for a long time.”]

He too was delayed, and endured the ten plagues not as if from an angry God but as if from a father giving warning, until, having turned his repentance toward perversity, he followed through the wilderness the people whom he had released and dared to enter the seas—through which alone he could learn that the one whom even the elements obey must be feared. [Note: The word “even” was missing and has been supplied from the manuscripts; shortly afterward they read “they serve” instead of “they would serve.”]

He too had said, “I do not know the Lord, nor will I release Israel.” Imitating him, you say: “The vision that he sees is for many days, and he prophesies for distant times” (Ezek. 12:27). Therefore the same Prophet says: “Thus says the Lord God: None of my words shall be prolonged any further, whatever words I speak. I will speak the word, and I will perform it” (ibid. v. 28). [Note: In the Verona manuscript the words “the same Prophet: Thus says” are omitted. This passage from Ezekiel follows the Greek text, from which the Latin translator differs somewhat.]

Holy David speaks of the impious and wicked—of whom you are not merely a considerable part but the leader—and says that they enjoyed worldly prosperity and said: “How does God know, and is there knowledge in the Most High? Behold, these sinners and those who abound in the world have acquired riches” (Ps. 72:11–12). With his foot almost slipping and his step wavering, he complained, saying: “Then I have justified my heart without cause, and washed my hands among the innocent” (ibid. v. 13).

For he had previously said: “Because I was jealous of those who act wickedly, seeing the peace of sinners: for there is no regard for their death, and their wound is not solid in their afflictions. They are not in the labors of men, and they will not be scourged with men. Therefore pride took possession of them; they are surrounded by their iniquity and impiety. Their iniquity will go forth as though from fatness; they have passed into the desire of their heart. They have thought and spoken evil; they have spoken iniquity on high. They have set their mouth against heaven, and their tongue has traversed the earth” (ibid. vv. 3 ff.).

### 2

Does it not seem to you that this entire Psalm was composed about you? Your body is vigorous, and, as a new apostle of Antichrist, once you have become known in one city, you pass over to another. You do not lack resources; you are not struck by a severe blow; and, unlike men who are not like you, like irrational beasts, you do not deserve to be punished with them.

Therefore you have been lifted up in pride, and your garment has become luxury. As though belching forth deadly words from rich grease and a certain fatness, you do not consider that you will die, nor are you ever bitten by repentance after your lust has been satisfied. [Note: The Cistercian manuscript and another Verona manuscript read “your garment has become foul with luxury”; otherwise the printed editions have “has become luxury,” and the latest edition has “has become fetid with luxury.”]

You have passed into the desire of your heart. And lest you seem to yourself to have erred alone, you invent abominations about the servants of God, not knowing that you speak iniquity on high and set your mouth against heaven. Nor is it surprising that you blaspheme whatever servants of God you can, since your fathers called the master of the household Beelzebub. “The disciple is not above his teacher, nor the servant above his lord.” If they did such things to the green wood, what will you do to me, the dry wood (Luke 23:31)?

The scandalized people of believers in Malachi likewise speak from your heart: [Note: The printed editions read “from your mouth”; below we correct various other minor readings from the Verona manuscripts.] “They have said, ‘He is useless who serves God.’ And what more? ‘Because we have kept his commandments, and because we have gone supplicating before the face of the Lord Almighty. And now we call outsiders blessed. Those who do iniquity are rebuilt. They have opposed God and have been saved’” (Mal. 3:14–15, according to the Septuagint). Afterward the Lord threatens them with the day of judgment and, announcing long beforehand what will occur between the just and the unjust, says: “And turn back, and you shall see what is between the just and the unjust, between the one who serves the Lord and the one who does not serve him” (ibid., at the end).

### 3

These things may perhaps seem ridiculous to you, since you take pleasure in comic poets, lyric writers, and the mimes of Lentulus. [Note: Martianus reads “mimes and Lentuli” and adds a note: “Lentulus was a famous writer of mimes.” This also fits correctly. (N. E.)] Yet, because of your excessive dullness of mind, I would not grant that even these things are intelligible to you.

You will despise the words of the Prophets; but Amos will answer you: “For three and for four impieties, shall I not reject him, says the Lord?” (Amos 1:3, according to the Septuagint).

Because Damascus, Gaza, Tyre, Edom, the Ammonites, and the Moabites, as well as the Jews and Israel, repeatedly refused to listen when God’s prophecy was directed to them so that they might finally repent, the Lord gives the most just grounds for the wrath he is about to bring, saying: “For three and four impieties, shall I not reject them?” [Note: An important passage of Jerome on Amos 1 should be recalled: “The first sin is to have thought what is evil; the second is to have assented to wicked thoughts; the third is to have completed in deed what one had resolved in mind; the fourth, after sinning, is not to repent and to take pleasure in one’s offense.” These are the stages that Jerome reproaches Sabinianus with here.]

“Thinking evil is criminal,” he says; “I have conceded that. It is worse to wish to carry out what has been wrongly thought, and in my mercy I have generously pardoned this. Was the sin also to be fulfilled in deed, and my mercy to be trampled upon arrogantly? Nevertheless, even after the deed—because I desire the sinner’s repentance rather than his death; for ‘the healthy have no need of a physician, but those who are sick’ (Luke 5:31)—I extend my hand to the one lying there, and exhort the one covered in his own blood to wash himself with his own tears.

“But if even then he refuses to repent, and, when the ship is broken, does not hold on to the plank by which he could have been saved, I am forced to say: ‘For three and four impieties, shall I not reject him, says the Lord?’ I regard rejection as punishment, while the sinner is abandoned to his own will.” [Note: We have restored this reading from Verona and the Cistercian manuscripts, with partial support from the older printed editions, which have “leading” rather than the less suitable “saying” in the sense of punishment.]

This is why he repays the sins of the fathers to the third and fourth generation (Exod. 20): he does not wish to punish sinners immediately, but, forgiving the first generations, condemns the last. Otherwise, if he immediately appeared as an avenger of crimes, many others—and certainly the Apostle Paul—would not have become members of the Church.

The Prophet Ezekiel, whom we mentioned above, reporting the word of God spoken to him, says: “Open your mouth and eat what I shall give you.” And I saw, he says, and behold, a hand extended toward me, and in it a scroll of a book. And he unrolled it before me, and in it was written, on the front and on the back, lamentation, a song, and woe (Ezek. 2:8 ff.).

The first writing concerns you, if only you are willing to repent after your offense. The second concerns the saints, who are summoned to God’s song. For praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner. The third concerns those like you, who, despairing of themselves, have given themselves over to uncleanness, fornication, the belly, and the things beneath the belly; who think that everything ends in death, that nothing exists after death, and say: “When the storm has passed, it will not come upon us” (Isa. 28:15).

The scroll that the Prophet devours is the entire sequence of the Scriptures. In them the penitent is mourned, the just person is sung, and the one who despairs is cursed. [Note: Some manuscripts have “the one despairing” rather than “the one who has despaired.”]

Nothing is so opposed to God as an impenitent heart. It is the one crime that cannot obtain pardon. For if forgiveness is granted after sin to the one who ceases to sin, and if the one who begs bends the judge, every impenitent person provokes the judge to anger. The only crime that cannot be healed is the crime of despair.

Moreover, so that you may know that God daily summons sinners to repentance—and that, if they persist in hardness, they make him severe and savage instead of merciful—hear the words of Isaiah, who says: “And the Lord of hosts will call on that day to weeping, great mourning, shaving of the head, and girding with sackcloth.” But they made for themselves joy and gladness, slaughtering calves and sacrificing sheep, so that they might eat meat and drink wine, saying: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die” (Isa. 22:12 ff.). [Note: More accurately, at least according to the Greek text, the two excellent manuscripts of our collection read “on that day weeping, mourning, and shaving of the head,” without the preposition *to* and without the word “great.”]

After these words and the audacity of a ruined mind, Scripture records the following: “And these things were revealed in the ears of the Lord of hosts: This sin shall not be forgiven you until you die” (ibid. v. 14). For if they die to sin, then their sin will be forgiven them. As long as they live in sin, it is not forgiven.

### 4

Spare your own soul, I beg you. [Note: The printed editions read: “Believe that the Son of God will be the judge. Remember by which bishop,” and so forth. We have preferred to follow the Verona manuscript, on whose authority we have corrected several other minor matters.]

Believe that there will be a judgment of God. Remember by what kind of bishop you were ordained a deacon. Nor is it surprising that even a holy man could have been deceived in choosing a person, since God himself repented that he had anointed Saul king (1 Sam. 15), and among the twelve Apostles Judas was found to be a traitor. It is also reported that Nicolaus of Antioch, once a member of your order, became the author of every kind of impurity and the founder of the heresy of the Nicolaitans. [Note: Jerome consistently attributes the heresy of the Nicolaitans to Nicolaus of Antioch, one of the first seven deacons; Tertullian, *On the Prescription against Heretics*, chapter 46, Irenaeus, book 1, chapter 27, Epiphanius, *Heresy* 25, and others agree with him. Ignatius, in his *Letter to the Trallians*, Clement of Alexandria in book 1 of the *Stromata*, Eusebius in book 3 of his *History*, Theodoret, and others report that he was indeed claimed by the Nicolaitans as their founder, but falsely. Here, however, it is worth observing that the manuscripts, with broad agreement, have “Neophytes” in place of “Nicolaitans.” I would prefer the reading of the Verona archetype, “Ophites.” As we noted elsewhere, in Letter 14 to Heliodorus, St. Epiphanius, the author of the *Catalogue of Heresies* attributed to Jerome, and St. Augustine in *Heresy* 17 derive the Ophites from the Nicolaitans: “Through their fabulous inventions they proceeded to the worship of the serpent.”]

I am not repeating those things to you now: that you are said to have violated many virgins; that, by you, the marriages of noblewomen were publicly struck down with the sword; that you ran through brothels, impure and gluttonous. These are indeed grave matters in themselves, but they become lighter by comparison with what I am about to bring against you.

I ask: how great a crime is it when fornication and adultery are a small matter? Most wretched of mortals, you enter that cave in which the Son of God was born, in which Truth arose from the earth and the earth gave its fruit, in order to arrange a sexual encounter. Are you not afraid that the infant may cry from the manger, that the Virgin who has given birth may see you, that the mother of the Lord may look upon you?

Angels cry out, shepherds run, the star shines from above, the Magi worship, Herod is terrified, Jerusalem is troubled—and you creep into the Virgin’s chamber in order to deceive a virgin?

I tremble, wretched man, and shudder in mind and body, wishing to place your deed before your eyes. The whole Church resounded with hymns to Christ the Lord during the night watches, and in the languages of diverse nations one Spirit joined in the praises of God. You were propping up love letters between the doorposts of the Lord’s former manger, now his altar—letters that the wretched woman later found and read, as though she were about to worship on bended knee. Then you stood in the choir of those singing psalms and spoke to her with immodest nods.

### 5

Shame upon the crime! I cannot go on. [Note: The former reading was “Tears burst forth before,” and so forth, but the manuscripts reject it.] Sobs break forth before words, and through indignation and grief alike my breath is constricted in my throat.

Where now is that sea of Ciceronian eloquence? Where is the rushing river of Demosthenes?

Now, surely, both of you would be mute, and your tongues would grow numb. A deed has been discovered that no eloquence could explain. A crime has been found that no mime could invent, no buffoon make sport of, and no Atellan actor express.

It is customary in the monasteries of Egypt and Syria that both the virgin and the widow who have vowed themselves to God, renounced the world, and trampled underfoot all the world’s pleasures, offer the hair of their heads to the mothers of the monasteries to be cut off, thereafter wearing it not uncovered, contrary to the Apostle’s command, but bound up and veiled. [Note: Another reading is: “According to the Apostle’s will, wearing the head uncovered.” Concerning the “mothers of the monasteries,” as he calls them, see the *Book against Vigilantius* near the end and our notes on that passage. For the custom of cutting the hair of women who professed virginity, see Menardus, notes on the *Gregorian Sacramentary*, p. 212, and *The Monastic History of the East*, book 1, chapter 12. In the Acts of St. Saturninus and his companions, St. Victoria is said to have “preserved, with unshaken modesty, the most sacred hair of her head, consecrated and dedicated to God, in perpetual virginity,” so that one may understand that in at least some Western churches another custom prevailed, namely, that they did not cut off their hair. This is demonstrated more fully by Optatus, book 6, and by St. Ambrose, *To the Fallen Virgin*, chapter 8.]

No one knows this except those who cut the hair and those whose hair is cut—except that, because everyone does it, almost everyone knows about it. This practice has become, through custom, a second nature for two reasons: either because they do not go to the baths, or because they know neither oil for the head nor ointment for the face, lest they be overwhelmed by the small creatures that ordinarily breed between skin and hair and by accumulated filth. [Note: Perhaps the more accurate reading in the Verona manuscript is “among the unkempt hair.”]

### 6

Let us see, then, good man, what you have done amid all this. You accept the hair as a kind of pledge of a future marriage in that venerable cave; you carry away the unhappy woman’s handkerchiefs and the belt, the pledge of the dowry, swearing to her that you will love no other in the same way. Then you run to the place of the shepherds, and, while the sound of the Angels resounds above, you make the same declaration.

I say nothing further about your rushing to kisses and embracing her. Everything may indeed be believed of you, but reverence for the manger and the place does not allow me to believe that you fell further than in will and intention.

Wretched man! When you began to stand with the virgin in the cave, did not your eyes grow dim, your tongue grow numb, your arms collapse, your breast tremble, and your step falter? [Note: The printed editions add “your eyes.” A very similar passage may be found in Cyprian, *On the Lapsed*: “The step faltered, the sight grew dim, the bowels trembled, the arms collapsed, the senses were stunned, speech stuck, and the tongue failed.”]

After the Basilica of the Apostle Peter, in which she had been consecrated with Christ’s bridal veil; after the mysteries of the Lord’s Cross, Resurrection, and Ascension, by which she had once again promised that she would live in the monastery, do you dare to take with you at night the hair that she had cut for Christ in the cave, so that she might sleep with you?

Then, from evening until morning, you sit at her window. And because, on account of its height, you could not cling closely to one another, by means of a cord you either receive something or send something back.

See how great was the care of the Lady, so that you should never see the virgin except in church; and since both of you had such a desire, you had no opportunity to converse except through the window at night. [Note: The commonly printed text corruptly has “the care of the Lord”; the Verona manuscript, together with the Cistercian manuscript, corrects it. “Lady” is a title of honor for the woman who presided over the other sisters in the monastery. We have also deleted the word “at home” after “never,” following the Verona manuscript, since it somewhat disturbed the sense.]

The sun rose for you, as I later learned, against your will. Bloodless, withered, and pale, so as to avoid all suspicion, you repeatedly read Christ’s Gospel as though you were a deacon. We thought your pallor came from fasting, and we admired your bloodless face as though it had been worn down by vigils, contrary to your habitual rule and custom.

Already ladders were being prepared for you, by which you might lower the wretched woman; already the journey had been arranged, ships ordered, the day agreed upon, and flight planned in your mind. And behold, that angel—the doorkeeper of Mary’s chamber, the guardian of the Lord’s cradle, and the bearer of the infant Christ—before whom you were doing all these things, himself betrayed you.

### 7

O my accursed eyes! O that day, deserving every curse, on which, with a mind thrown into confusion, I read those letters of yours that we still possess! What obscenities were there! What flatteries! What rejoicing over the arranged sexual encounter!

Could a deacon—not merely speak such things, but even know them? [Note: The Cistercian manuscript reads: “This—is it a deacon speaking, or rather the Devil?” and so forth. Its reading is neither without probability nor elegance.]

Wretched man, where did you learn such things, when you boasted that you had been raised in the Church? Unless it is that, in those same letters, you swear that you were never chaste and were never a deacon. If you wish to deny it, your own hand will refute you; the very letters will cry out: “Keep for the moment the profit of your crime. I cannot force upon you what you yourself have written.”

### 8

Thus you lie prostrate, clasping my knees, and, to use your own words, you beg for a half-sextarius of blood. And, O wretched man, disregarding God’s judgment, you fear me alone as though I were an avenger! I confess that I forgave you; for what else can I, as a Christian, do to you? I urged you to do penance, to roll about in sackcloth and ashes, to seek solitude, to live in a monastery, and to implore God’s mercy with continual tears.

[Note: [Col. 1201] It seems that *heminam* should be read here on the authority of the Verona manuscript, rather than *misericordiam*, which has prevailed hitherto in the common editions. A *hemina* is a measure, almost the smallest of all, being half a *sextarius*. Sabinianus—also called above “withered,” “pale,” and “bloodless”—compares his blood, in order to move Jerome to pity, to a *hemina*, the very small price of life. A similar expression occurs in Scripture: “a leaf carried away by the wind,” and so forth. The critics corrupted the more obscure or less familiar word.]

But you, “the pillar of good hope,” inflamed by the goadings of the viper, have become for me a twisted bow, and shoot against me arrows of abuse. I have become your enemy by speaking the truth. I shall not grieve over your curses; for who does not know that nothing except what is disgraceful is praised by your mouth?

[Note: [Col. 1201] The Cistercian manuscript has *coluber* (“serpent”), a term that seemed to fit the following context better, unless it is said ironically, as in *Paschal* 2.7. Origen is called “a pillar of truth.”]

This is what I lament: that you do not lament yourself, that you do not realize that you are dead; that, like a gladiator prepared for the funeral games, you adorn yourself for your own burial.

[Note: [Col. 1201] Some manuscripts incorrectly read *libidine* (“lust”). The reference is to the funeral games at which gladiators formerly used to fight at the funerals of eminent men; Cicero calls them *bustuarii*.]

You clothe yourself in linen, load your fingers with rings, polish your teeth with powder, and arrange your sparse hairs over a reddish bald skull. Your bull-like neck, swelling with fatty folds, bends—not because it has been broken by lust.

[Note: [Col. 1201] These two words are absent because of the mention of lust from the Cistercian manuscript, which shortly afterward reads *unguentis* for *unguenta*.]

Moreover, you smell of perfumes, change baths, and fight against your growing hair; through the forum and streets you walk as a shining, polished lover. You have acquired the face of a prostitute and do not know how to blush.

Turn, wretched man, to the Lord, so that the Lord may turn to you. Do penance, so that he too may repent of all the evils that he has said he would do to you.

### 9

Why, neglecting your own wound, do you strive to defame others? Why do you tear me with your bite like a madman, when I am advising you well and diligently? Suppose that I am disgraceful, as you loudly proclaim: at least do penance with me. Suppose that I am criminal, as you pretend: imitate the tears of a criminal.

[Note: [Col. 1201] The same manuscript has *Criminosus sum* (“I am criminal”), as you accuse me.]

Are my sins your virtues? Or do you think it a consolation for your own evils if you have many people like yourself? Let tears flow for a little from your eyes between the silken and linen garments in which you imagine yourself radiant and handsome; understand that you are naked, torn, soiled, and begging.

[Note: [Col. 1201] Cyprian, *Epistle to Demetrianus*: “For one who still remains in this world, no penance is ever too late.”]

Penance is never too late.

[Col. 1202] Even if you have come down from Jerusalem and have been wounded on the road, the Samaritan will take you from there, place you upon his beast, and carry you to the inn to be cared for. And even if you lie dead in the tomb, the Lord will nevertheless raise you, foul-smelling though you are.

At least imitate those blind men for whose sake the Savior, leaving his own home and inheritance, came to Jericho. Light arose for those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death. When they recognized that the Lord was passing by, they began to cry out, saying: “Son of David, have mercy on us.” You too will be able to see if you cry out, and if, summoned by him, you throw off your filthy garments.

[Note: [Col. 1202] Recall what we said about this passage from Isaiah in *Epistle* 122 to Rusticus.]

When you have turned and groaned, then you will be saved, and then you will know where you had been (Isa. 30:15). Let him now touch your scars and examine the traces of your former eyes. Even if you were born thus from the womb, and your mother conceived you in sins, he will sprinkle you with hyssop and you will be cleansed; he will wash you, and you will become whiter than snow.

Why do you cling bent over to the earth and lie wholly in the mud? The woman whom Satan had bound for eighteen years, after she was healed by the Savior, stood upright and looked toward heaven.

Consider the words spoken to Cain to have been spoken to you: “You have sinned; be quiet” (Gen. 4:13).

[Note: [Col. 1202] See above, *Epistle* under number C, where our annotation concerns this passage of Scripture.]

Why do you withdraw farther from the presence of God and dwell in the land of Naid?

[Note: [Col. 1202] This is what the land where Cain dwelt after departing from the presence of the Lord is called in Greek. Jerome, on Ezekiel 16: “Cast out from the paradise of steadfastness, they dwell in the region of Naid, which is interpreted as ‘wandering,’” and so forth. Formerly the text incorrectly read *Naim*.]

Why do you drift wholly upon the sea and never set your foot upon the rock?

Beware lest Phinehas pierce you, fornicating with the Midianite woman, with a *seiromastes*.

[Note: [Col. 1202] Most printed editions have *sua hasia*, others *sero hasta*. The critics corrupted the rarer word *seiromastes*, which they scarcely understood. We have corrected the text on the basis of a Verona manuscript; moreover, it is established that the Septuagint calls *σειρομάστης* the spear with which Phinehas pierced through the Midianite prostitute. See *Epistle* 109.3. The reading is “Phinehas with a *seiromastes*.” Soon afterward, the common editions likewise incorrectly read *Qui plus quam Thamar* (“who more than Tamar”) instead of *Quid postquam* (“What, after”), as the Verona manuscript corrects it.]

What, after you have polluted Tamar, a virgin who was your sister and kinswoman, do you now, having become Absalom, desire to kill the man who laments you while you rebel and lie dead?

The blood of Naboth cries out against you, and the vineyard of Jezreel—that is, “of the seed of God”—which you have turned into a garden of pleasure and vegetables of wantonness, demands a fitting vengeance upon you. Elijah is sent to you, announcing torment and destruction. Bend down and clothe yourself in sackcloth for a while, and God will be able to say of you: “Have you seen how Ahab has humbled himself before me? Because he has humbled himself before me, I will not bring the evil in his days” (3 Kings 21:29).

### 10

But perhaps you flatter yourself because you were ordained deacon by such a bishop. I have already said above that neither the father is punished for the son, nor the son for the father. “The soul that sins, it shall die” (Ezek. 18:4).

Samuel too had sons who departed from the fear of God and went after avarice and iniquity. Eli also was a holy priest, but he had sons who, as we read in the Hebrew volume, fornicating with women in the tabernacle of God, shamelessly claimed for themselves the ministry of God, after your likeness (1 Sam. 8).

[Note: [Col. 1202] Previously the reading was *voluminibus* (“volumes”). But lest you think that the author is inventing some apocryphal matter, he appeals to the authority of “the Hebrews,” because these matters concerning the fornication of Eli’s sons were not found in the Greek books or in the Latin works translated from them.]

Therefore the place of the tabernacle itself was overturned, and because of the priests’ vices the sanctuary was abandoned—or destroyed.

[Note: [Col. 1203] The alternative reading is *destructum* (“destroyed”).]

Although Eli himself, by being excessively lenient toward his sons, offended God, it is so far from being possible for your bishop’s righteousness to free you that it must be feared that, because of you, he may fall from his throne and perish by an incurable backward contraction of the neck.

[Note: [Col. 1203] We have supplied from a single Verona manuscript the Greek word, previously unknown in the printed and manuscript books but necessary to the context. In that manuscript, however, the copyist had written ΕΠΙϹΤΑΤΟΝΩ, which we have corrected. The word *Heli* also needed to be inserted, since the history to which Jerome alludes says that Eli fell backward from his seat, *ὀπισθίως*. The term actually used here by Jerome, *ὀπισθότονος*, denotes the affliction of the neck itself, when the head of someone who has fallen backward is drawn toward the shoulders. Hence we have also corrected *insanabili* to *insanabilem*, and supplied the preposition *si* from the same Verona manuscript.]

If Uzzah, a Levite, wished to support the Ark of the Lord, which he himself ought to have carried, as though it were falling, and was struck down, what do you think will happen to you, who have attempted to overturn the standing Ark of the Lord?

The more worthy of approval the bishop who ordained you is, the more detestable you are, because you deceived such a man. We are accustomed to be the last to know the evils of our household, and, while our neighbors sing them aloud, to remain unaware of the vices of our children and wives.

All Italy knew you. Everyone groaned to see you standing before the altar of Christ. Nor were you so clever as to conceal your vices prudently. You burned with such heat, and pleasure carried you here and there in such a state of arousal and wantonness, that, as though celebrating certain triumphs and raising the palm of victory, you lifted it over your consummated lusts.

### 11

Finally, amid barbarian swords, barbarian husbands, and the guards of a powerful husband, the flame of impurity swept you away.
