[Note: [Col. 1203] We have restored the words *et barbari* from the Verona manuscript; they may perhaps designate some Gothic soldier.]

You were not afraid to commit adultery in that house where the injured husband could avenge himself without a judge. You were led to gardens and dragged off to suburban estates; you behaved so freely and madly that, while the husband was absent, you imagined that you had a wife, not an adulteress.

From there, while she was being kept under guard, you escaped through certain tunnels. You entered Rome secretly and hid among Samnite bandits; and at the first message from the husband—that a new Hannibal had descended upon you from the Alps—you entrusted yourself to a ship, believing yourself safe. Your flight was so swift that you considered a storm at sea safer than the land.

You arrived somehow in Syria and declared that you wished to proceed from there to Jerusalem and serve the Lord. Who would not receive a man who professed himself a monk, especially one ignorant of your tragedies and reading the commendatory letters of your bishop to the other priests?

But you, wretched man, transformed yourself into an angel of light, and, as a minister of Satan, pretended to be a minister of righteousness. Beneath the clothing of sheep you concealed a wolf; and after being an adulterer against a man, you wished to become an adulterer against Christ.

### 12

I have recounted these things in order to paint for you, as it were upon a small tablet, the entire scene of your deeds, and to place your actions before your eyes, lest you regard the Lord’s mercy and excessive clemency as an opportunity for sins, crucifying the Son of God again for yourself, making a spectacle of him, and failing to read what follows:

“For the earth, often drinking in the rain that falls upon it and producing suitable vegetation for those by whom it is cultivated, receives a blessing from God. But producing thorns and thistles, it is rejected and near to a curse; its end is burning” (Heb. 6:7–8).

## Epistle CXLVIII

[Note: [Col. 1204] That this is not an epistle of Jerome is acknowledged not only by all editors and critics after Erasmus, but also much earlier. Toward the end of the eleventh century, Saint Guigo, abbot, included it among the spurious writings in his fourth epistle to the brothers of Durbon. He says: “To Celantia, beginning in this way: ‘It is a celebrated saying of the Old Scripture.’ It is written in a somewhat nobler style, but even so it is not worthy of Jerome.”

Erasmus, Victorius, and others think that it may somehow be attributed to Paulinus; Martianaeus establishes this as certain. But the recent editor of Saint Paulinus, in declining to assign it to him, cites the dissimilarity of style, which is too far removed from the energy and fluency of Paulinus, as well as the markedly different manner of expressing passages of Holy Scripture. He nevertheless does not decide to whom it should rightly be attributed, since everything else indicated in the epistle—such as the period when paganism had not yet been entirely abolished, the mention of the heretic Jovinianus, and a certain sweetness in its expression—is not inconsistent with Paulinus.

For my part, unless this conjecture is bolder than to deserve pardon if I am mistaken, I am inclined to attribute it to Sulpicius Severus. The same elegance and gravity of composition seem to belong to him and to our author; the same expression of Scripture, as far as we have been able to understand from comparing several passages; plainly the same intellect. It is established from Gennadius, chapter 19, that Sulpicius wrote “many epistles urging the love of God and contempt for the world,” besides those which he gave to his sister Claudia.

The chronology also fits well, for he lived in the same age as Jerome and Sulpicius, with whom he was also joined in friendship. We have therefore wished to print this epistle under a different type, if indeed it is his, but certainly not Jerome’s or Paulinus’s, because it has hitherto held a place among the works of Jerome and did not seem fit to be relegated to the final volume.]

[Note: [Col. 1204] Elsewhere numbered 14.]

### To Celantia, a Matron

#### On the manner of living piously

*(C, G)*

He teaches the noble matron Celantia how, amid the honors and riches of the world and the burdens of marriage, she may lead her life in holiness and devotion. First he urges her to read divine Scripture; then he teaches her not to be proud of the nobility of her lineage and explains in what true nobility consists. Finally, he sharply reproves her because, several years earlier, she had resolved to practice continence without an agreement with or the consent of her husband, and he shows her what she owes to her husband.

### 1

“It is a celebrated saying of Scripture that there is a shame which brings glory and grace, and again a shame which is accustomed to produce sin.” Although the truth of this saying, by its own light, shines clearly enough for everyone’s understanding, somehow it has become more fully known to me in the present case.

Provoked to write by your letters, which with extraordinary entreaties demanded this from me, I confess that I long hesitated about replying, modesty commanding me to remain silent. Yet the faithful earnestness of your prayers resisted it most strongly and did violence to it. The humility of the petitioner fought fiercely against my hesitation, and with a great force of faith knocked upon the barriers of my mouth.

While different thoughts thus weighed upon a mind wavering between the two alternatives, shame almost excluded duty. But the wise saying I have cited above armed me to drive away useless modesty and dissolve harmful silence, since I saw that the very reason for writing was so honorable and so holy that I would believe myself to be sinning if I remained silent. I kept in mind that saying of Scripture: “There is a time to keep silence, and a time to speak” (Eccl. 3:7). And again: “Do not withhold a word in the time of salvation” (Ecclus. 4:28). And that saying of blessed Peter: “Always ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you for a reason” (1 Pet. 3:15).

[Col. 1205]

### 2

For you ask—and ask earnestly and insistently—that we establish for you from the holy Scriptures a definite rule by which you may order the course of your life, so that, having learned the Lord’s will, amid the honors of the world and the attractions of wealth you may love the adornment of character more than possessions, and, although established in marriage, may please not only your husband but also him who granted you marriage.

Not to satisfy such a holy request and so devout a desire: what else is that than not loving another’s progress? I shall therefore obey your prayers and strive to spur you, ready as you are to fulfill the Lord’s will, by his own sayings. For the true Lord and teacher of all is the same one who commands us to please him and teaches how we may please him.

Let him himself shape you; let him himself teach you—the one who, when the young man in the Gospel asked what he should do to deserve eternal life, immediately set forth the divine commandments (Matt. 19), showing us that we must do the will of the one from whom we hope also to receive rewards.

For this reason he testifies elsewhere: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven will enter the kingdom of heaven” (ibid. 7:21). This plainly shows that we do not earn the greatness of so great a reward by confessing God alone, unless works of faith and righteousness are joined to it.

### 3

For what sort of confession is that which believes in God in such a way that it counts his command as nothing?

[Note: [Col. 1205] The Cistercian manuscripts, formerly the two Nonantulan manuscripts, omit the question mark: “Do we not sincerely say,” and so forth.]

Or how do we say sincerely and truly, “Lord, Lord,” if we despise the commands of the one whom we confess to be Lord? Hence he himself says in the Gospel: “Why do you call me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ and do not do what I say?” (Luke 6:46). And again: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Matt. 15:8; Isa. 29:13).

And again he speaks through the Prophet: “A son honors his father, and a servant fears his master. And if I am a father, where is my honor? And if I am Lord, where is my fear?” (Mal. 1:6). From this it is clear that the Lord is neither honored nor feared by those who do not do his commands.

And to David, who had committed sin, it is said more explicitly: “You have counted the Lord as nothing” (2 Sam. 12).

[Note: [Col. 1205] We have restored *Dominum* (“the Lord”) from these same manuscripts, in accordance with the Greek, where previously *Deum* (“God”) was read.]

And the word of the Lord is addressed to Eli: “Those who honor me I will honor, but those who count me as nothing will be reduced to nothing” (1 Sam. 2:30).

### 4

And are we secure and confident when, through each and every commandment, dishonoring the most merciful Lord God, we provoke him to anger and, by arrogantly despising his command, commit an offense against such great majesty?

[Note: [Col. 1205] Other manuscripts read *per singula quaeque peccata* (“through each and every sin”). [Col. 1206] Shortly afterward we restored the word *Dominum* (“the Lord”) from two manuscripts and certain printed editions.]

For what could ever appear so proud, or indeed so ungrateful, as to live contrary to the will of the one from whom you have received life itself? What could be more so than to despise the commands of the one who commands something for the very purpose of having grounds to reward?

For God does not need our obedience; we need his command. “His commandments are more desirable than gold and precious stone, and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb; for in keeping them there is great reward” (Ps. 18:11–12).

And therefore he is angry with us; therefore that immeasurable goodness of God is more deeply offended, because we despise it even at the cost of losing so great a reward, and count as nothing not only what he commands but also what he promises.

[Note: [Col. 1206] The Cistercian manuscript has *cognovimus* (“we have known”), with a different meaning. Then, in place of *imperata* (“commands”), other books read *imperia* (“orders”).]

Hence that saying of the Lord must often—indeed always—be turned over in our minds: “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments” (Matt. 19:17). For this is the concern of the whole Law with us; this is what the Prophets teach; this is what the Apostles teach; this is what both the voice of Christ and his blood demand from us—he who died for all in order that those who live might no longer live for themselves but for him who died for them (2 Cor. 5:15).

To live for him means nothing other than to keep his commands, which he entrusted to us for observance as a definite pledge of his love. “If you love me,” he says, “keep my commandments” (John 14:15). And: “The one who has my commandments and keeps them is the one who loves me.”

And again: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him. Whoever does not love me does not keep my words” (ibid. vv. 21, 23–24).

True love possesses great force. The one who is perfectly loved claims for himself the whole will of the lover. Nothing is more commanding than love. If we truly love Christ, if we remember that we have been redeemed by his blood, we ought neither to wish nor to do anything more than what we know him to wish.

### 5

There are two kinds of commandments, in which the whole of righteousness is contained. One consists in prohibitions, the other in commands. Just as evils are prohibited, so good things are commanded. There, idleness is commanded; here, zeal.

[Note: [Col. 1206] Martianaeus, after Erasmus, incorrectly reads *operatur* (“works”) for *imperatur* (“is commanded”). In place of *otium* (“idleness”), which appears in all the books, I would readily substitute *odium* (“hatred”), on the basis of the sequence and meaning of the passage, especially the Apostle’s immediately connected words, “hating evil, clinging to what is good.” From this it is clear that hatred of evil and devotion to good are commanded.]

There the mind is restrained; here it is urged forward. There it is culpable to have done something; here it is culpable not to have done something.

[Note: [Col. 1206] Previously the text read: “Here, to have done; there, not to have done.” Our reading, taken from one manuscript, is more harmonious with what precedes: “There and here.”]

Hence the Prophet says: “Who is the man who desires life and longs to see good days? Keep your tongue from evil and your lips from speaking deceit. Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. 33:13–15). And the blessed Apostle says: “Hating evil, clinging to what is good” (Rom. 12:9).

This twofold and distinct commandment, namely, the commandment to prohibit and the commandment to order, has been imposed equally upon everyone. No virgin, no widow, no married woman is free from this command. In every calling, in every rank, it is an equal sin either to commit what is prohibited or not to do what is commanded.

Nor should you be misled by the error of those who, according to their own choice, select which commandments of God they will do and despise others as though they were worthless and insignificant. They do not fear that, according to the divine saying, by despising what is least they may gradually fall away (Ecclus. 19:1).

[Note: [Col. 1207] With Erasmus, Martianaeus incorrectly reads *contemnant* (“they despise”) for *faciant* (“they do”), which we have corrected from all the manuscripts and most printed editions.]

### 6

[Note: [Col. 1207] Compare the genuine Jerome in the second book *Against Jovinianus*, where he refutes this Stoic doctrine at greater length. See also his commentary on Ezekiel, chapter 9, and Cyprian, *Epistle* 55 to Antonianus: “The Stoics, who say that all sins are equal,” and so forth.]

It is indeed a Stoic doctrine to abolish distinctions among sins and to judge all offenses equal, making no difference between a crime and an error. We, however, although we believe that sins differ greatly from one another, because we also read this in Scripture, nevertheless say that it is useful for caution to guard against even the smallest sins as though they were the greatest.

For we abstain from any offense all the more easily the more we fear it. The one who fears even small sins does not quickly advance to greater ones. And truly, I do not know whether we can call any sin light when it is committed in contempt of God.

The wisest person is the one who considers not so much what has been commanded as the one who commanded it; who thinks not of the extent of the command but of the dignity of the commander.

### 7

As you build a spiritual house—not upon the lightness of sand but upon the solidity of rock—let the foundation of innocence first be laid, upon which you may more easily raise the lofty summit of righteousness.

[Note: [Col. 1207] Some manuscripts read: “upon which the lofty summit of righteousness may rise more easily.”]

For the greater part of equity has been fulfilled by the one who has harmed no one. Blessed is the one who can say with holy Job: “I have harmed no human being; I have lived justly with everyone” (Job 27:6).

Therefore he spoke boldly and simply to the Lord: “Who is he who will be judged with me?” (Job 13:19).

[Note: [Col. 1207] The Cistercian manuscript reads: “Who can call for your judgment against me?”]

That is: Who can invoke your judgment against me in order to prove that he has been injured by me?

It belongs to the purest conscience to sing confidently with the Prophet: “I walked in the innocence of my heart, in the midst of my house” (Ps. 100:3).

[Note: [Col. 1207] Previously the reading was *domus tuae* (“your house”), which we did not hesitate to change, on the basis of two manuscripts, to *domus meae* (“my house”), in accordance with the Greek and the Vulgate. At the end of this epistle the author repeats this same verse, and we have kept the reading consistent.]

Hence the same person says elsewhere: “God did not deprive those who walk in innocence of good things” (Ps. 83:13).

[Note: [Col. 1207] There is no doubt that the future tense *fraudabit* (“will deprive”) should be read. Yet in this passage our author uses a distinctive version, and I do not know whether anyone ever read or translated it in this way. The Greek is Κύριος οὐχ ὑστερήσει τὰ ἀγαθά, “The Lord will not withhold good things.”]

Therefore the Christian soul must drive away from itself malice, hatred, and envy, which are either the greatest or the only seeds of harm; it must guard innocence not only with hand and tongue but also in the heart, and fear to harm not only by deed but also by intention. For, as far as the nature of sin is concerned, the one who intended to harm has also done harm.

Many among us define the one as absolutely and completely innocent who harms no one even in the matter in which he ceases to be beneficial.

[Note: [Col. 1208] We have read and corrected this from the Cistercian manuscript. Previously all the printed books, with a solecism and corrupted sense, had *Multi nomen illud absolute* (“many [define] that name absolutely”). The sentence is taken from Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* 3: “Innocence is such a disposition of mind as harms no one”; Cicero has similar wording in *Against Piso*.]

If this is true, then rejoice in the testimony of innocence only if, when you are able to help, you do not cease to do so. But if these things are divided and distinguished from one another—if not harming, which you can always do, is one thing; helping when you are able is another; not doing evil is one thing; doing good is another—then let this return to your mind: it is not enough for a Christian to fulfill one part of righteousness, when both parts are commanded to him.

[Note: [Col. 1208] From the same manuscript we read *utrumque* (“both”), whereas previously the text had *utrum*. Shortly afterward, in place of *debemus* (“we ought”), some printed editions and manuscripts have *decet* (“it is fitting”). One manuscript reads: “Nor ought we to look to the life of the wicked multitude, which…”]

### 8

For we ought not to look to the examples of the multitude. It follows no discipline of character and observes no order of life; it is guided not so much by reason as carried along by a kind of impulse.

Nor should we imitate those who, under the Christian name, lead a pagan life and bear witness to one thing by their profession and another by their conduct; who, as the Apostle says, “profess that they know God, but deny him by their deeds” (Tit. 1:13).

It is not faith alone that ought to distinguish a Christian from a pagan, but life as well; different religion must be shown through different works. “Do not,” says the Apostle, “be yoked together with unbelievers. For what partnership has righteousness with iniquity? Or what fellowship has light with darkness? What agreement has Christ with Belial? Or what portion has the believer with the unbeliever? What agreement has the temple of God with idols?” (2 Cor. 6:14ff.).

[Note: [Col. 1208] Most manuscripts read *ad hunc modum* (“in this manner”), in accordance with the Greek and the Vulgate; almost all printed editions have *lucis* (“of light”). The Cistercian manuscript omits the clause “What agreement has Christ with Belial?” Our author must have read *Beliar*.]

### 9

Let there therefore be the greatest separation between us and them. Error and truth are divided by a definite distinction. Let those who do not possess the promises of heaven be concerned with earthly things. Let those who do not know eternal life entangle themselves wholly in this brief life. Let those who believe that sins go unpunished not fear to sin. Let those who do not hope for future rewards serve their vices.

But we, who confess with the purest faith that every human being must be revealed before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive what belongs to his body according to what he has done, whether good or evil (2 Cor. 5:10), ought to be far from vices, since the Apostle says: “Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires” (Gal. 5:24).

Let those who profess themselves disciples of the truth not follow the wandering crowd.

### 10

Certainly, in the Gospel the Savior shows two ways of life and paths of living that diverge in opposite directions. “How broad,” he says, “is the way that leads to destruction, and many are those who enter through it.” And again: “How narrow and constricted is the way that leads to life, and few are those who find it” (Matt. 7:13–14).

[Col. 1209]

See how great the separation between these ways is, and how great the difference. The one leads to death; the other tends toward life. The one is celebrated and worn down by many; the other is scarcely found by a few.

[Note: [Col. 1209] Other manuscripts read: “The one is celebrated by many and followed by many.”]

For, through the habit of vices, the one—being more downward-sloping and softer, and made pleasant, as it were, by certain flowers of pleasure—easily draws to itself the multitude of passersby. The other, on an unfamiliar path, is more gloomy and rough because of the virtues; it is chosen only by those who care less for the pleasure of the journey than for the usefulness of the dwelling-place.

Excessive habit of vices makes the path of virtues rough and unpleasant for us. If that habit is transferred to the other side, the path of righteousness will be found, as Scripture says, to be smooth (Prov. 2:20, according to the Septuagint).

[Note: [Col. 1209] The Septuagint has εὕρησαν ἂν τρίβους δικαιοσύνης λείας, “they would indeed have found smooth paths of righteousness.” Some early printed editions read: “You will find the path of righteousness smooth.”]

Let us therefore now examine the pattern of our life and learn, with conscience as our witness, along which road we are chiefly walking. Everything we do and everything we say belongs either to the broad way or to the narrow way.

If, with the few, we find the narrow road and a certain slender path, we are tending toward life. But if we accompany the way of the many, according to the Lord’s judgment, we are going toward death.

### 11

If, then, we are possessed by hatred and envy; if we yield to greed and avarice; if we prefer present advantages to future ones, we are walking along the broad way. We have a multitude of companions in these things, and are surrounded on every side by dense ranks of people like ourselves.

If we wish to satisfy anger and lust; if we avenge an injury; if we return curses for curses and are hostile in spirit toward an enemy, we are likewise carried along with many others.

If we flatter someone ourselves or gladly listen to a flatterer; if favor prevents us from speaking the truth and we fear offending people’s feelings more than failing to speak sincerely, we too belong to the way of the many.

[Note: [Col. 1209] Two Cistercian manuscripts and two printed editions read: “If, however, we show favor and do so more,” and so forth.]

As many as are strangers to the truth are our companions. But, on the other hand:

[Note: [Col. 1209] Martianaeus omitted the word *his* (“these”). One manuscript reads *vacui sumus* (“we are empty”) instead of *sumus extranei* (“we are strangers”).]

If we are strangers to all these vices; if we present a pure and free spirit; if, having trampled down every desire, we strive to be rich only in virtues, we are pressing along the narrow way. Such a life belongs to few. It is exceedingly rare and difficult to find suitable companions for this journey.

Indeed, many pretend to walk along this road, but through various side paths of error they return to the road of the multitude. Therefore it must be feared that those whom we believe we have as guides on this right path may prove to be companions in error.

### 12

If, then, examples are found that lead us along this way and keep to the straight path of the Gospel, they should be followed. But if such examples are lacking, or are thought to be lacking, the pattern of the Apostles has been set before everyone.

Paul, the chosen vessel, cries out and, calling us as it were to this narrow path, says: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (1 Cor. 11:1).

Certainly, greater than all other examples, the example of the Lord himself shines forth. In the Gospel he says: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matt. 11:28–29).

[Note: [Col. 1210] Other printed editions read: “I will refresh you.”]

If it is dangerous to imitate those of whom you doubt whether they should be imitated, then it is most safe to imitate this one and follow the footsteps of him who said: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). For the one who follows the truth never goes astray.

Hence the Apostle John also says: “The one who says that he remains in Christ ought himself to walk as he walked” (1 John 2:6).

And blessed Peter says: “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example so that you might follow his footsteps. He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth. When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but entrusted himself to the one who judges unjustly. He himself bore our sins in his body upon the tree, so that, having died to sins, we might live for righteousness” (1 Pet. 2:21ff.).

### 15

Let every excuse for errors cease; let the shameful consolations of sinning be removed. We achieve absolutely nothing by defending ourselves through the examples of the multitude and, often reckoning up the faults of others for our consolation, saying that those whom we ought to follow are lacking to us. We are sent to the example of him whom we all confess should be imitated. Therefore let your chief care be to know the divine law, through which

[Note: [Col. 1210] For *possis*, the Cistercian parchment has *putes* (“you may suppose”).]

you may, as though seeing them present, behold the examples of the saints. Learn from its counsel what must be done and what avoided [variant: *disce*, “learn”; alternatively, *discere*, “to learn”]. For the greatest aid toward righteousness is to fill the mind with divine utterances and always to meditate in the heart upon what you desire to carry out in deed.

The Lord commands through Moses a people still untaught and persons unaccustomed to obedience that, as a memorial sign by which they may remember the Lord’s commandments,

[Note: [Col. 1210] For *cocco*, the Cistercian manuscript has *toto*; others have *tota* or *torta*. All are corrupt, in my opinion; for what relevance has scarlet, to speak only of this word, which all the printed editions prefer? But, to understand that this entire passage is corrupt, there are not even two manuscript copies that read it in precisely the same words. I give the Cistercian reading alone: “Let them have fringes at the edges of their garments, and mark them with emblems wholly of hyacinth-blue color.” Although I much prefer the first clause of this reading to the printed editions, I would emend the second by conjecture thus: “and let them mark them with a tassel of hyacinth-blue color.” For it is well known that from the four corners of the fringe, which ran around the outer edge of the cloak, hyacinth-blue tassels hung—a practice the Jews retain to this day.]

they should have on each fringe of their garments emblems of hyacinth-blue color with scarlet, so that even when their eyes chance to look this way and that, remembrance of the heavenly commandments may arise. On account of these fringes the Pharisees are rebuked by the Lord (Matthew 23:5), [1103] because, through a perverse use, they began to wear them not as a reminder of God’s precepts but for display of themselves, so that they might be judged holy by the people as though for greater diligence in observance.

### 14

But for you, who observe no longer the precepts of the letter but of the spirit, the remembrance of the divine commandments must be cultivated spiritually. You must not remember the Lord’s commandments so much frequently as think upon them always. Let the divine Scriptures always be in your hands and continually turned over in your mind. Nor should you think it enough [Col. 1211] to retain God’s commandments in memory while forgetting them in your deeds. Learn them precisely in order to do whatever you have learned must be done. “For not the hearers of the law are righteous before God, but the doers of the law shall be justified” (Romans 2:31).

The broad and boundless field of the divine law extends widely. Flourishing with diverse testimonies of truth, like certain heavenly flowers, it feeds and refreshes the reader’s mind with marvelous delight. Always to know and ponder all these things is a great benefit for preserving righteousness. But, as a kind of concise reminder,

[Note: [Col. 1211] Erasmus and Martianay have: “as a kind of concise place, a reminder,” etc.]

you should choose for yourself and inscribe upon your heart that saying of the Gospel which the Lord utters as a summary of all righteousness: “All things whatsoever you wish people to do to you, do these things also to them; for this is the Law and the Prophets” (Matthew 7:12). For the kinds and parts of righteousness are infinite: it is most difficult not only to pursue them with a pen, but even to grasp them in thought. All of them are comprehended by this one brief saying, which by the secret judgment of the mind either acquits or condemns the hidden conscience of humankind.

### 15

Let every action, every word, and even every thought be measured against this saying. Let it stand before you like a mirror, always ready and at hand, showing the quality of your will; let it either rebuke you for an unjust deed or gladden you for a just one. Whenever you bear toward another the same disposition that you wish another to maintain toward you, you are following the path of equity. But whenever you behave toward another in a way that you do not want anyone to behave toward you, you have abandoned the road of justice.

Behold the whole arduous and difficult burden of the divine law! Behold why we complain against the Lord’s stern commands and say that we are oppressed by the difficulty or impossibility of the commandments. It is not enough that we fail to do what is commanded unless we also declare the one who commands unjust—complaining that the very author of equity has commanded not merely difficult and arduous things, but even impossible ones.

“He says: Whatever you wish people to do to you, do the same to them.” He wishes love to join and bind us together through mutual acts of kindness. He wishes all people to be united with one another by reciprocal love, so that each person may render to another what he wishes all people to render to him; thus the whole of justice, and this commandment of God, may become the common benefit of humanity.

And O the Lord’s marvelous clemency! O God’s ineffable goodness! He promises us a reward if we love one another—that is, if we mutually provide one another with those things of which we in turn have need. Yet we, with an attitude at once proud and ungrateful, resist his will, even though his command itself is a benefit.

### 16

Never speak ill of anyone, and do not wish to appear praiseworthy by criticizing others. Learn rather to adorn your own life than to attack another’s.

[Note: Most manuscripts and printed editions have *ordinare* (“to order,” “to arrange”); Martianay, following Erasmus, has *ornare* (“to adorn”). The following passage was read by our author from the Greek. The Vulgate translator, according to the Hebrew truth, has: “Do not love sleep, lest poverty overwhelm you.” The explanation of so great a difference must be sought in the homonymy of the Hebrew words, which is not the place to discuss. We merely note that, instead of *ne eradiceris* (“lest you be uprooted”), ancient Latin writers who quote this passage from the Septuagint usually read *ne extollaris* (“lest you be exalted”), which should be understood as though it said, “lest you be removed from the midst.”]

And always remember Scripture, which says: “Do not love slander, lest you be uprooted” (Proverbs 20:13, according to the Septuagint).

Very few renounce this vice, and you will rarely find someone willing to make his own life so irreproachable that he does not gladly criticize another’s. So great a passion for this evil has seized people’s minds that even those who have withdrawn far from other vices nevertheless fall into this one, as into the devil’s final snare.

You, however, must flee this evil so completely that you not only refrain from slandering anyone yourself, but do not at any time believe another who slanders. Do not lend authority to slanderers by agreeing with them, lest you nourish their vice by your assent.

Scripture says: “Do not be an accomplice with those who disparage your neighbor, and you will not take sin upon him.”

[Note: Two old printed editions have: “and you will not take sin upon him through them.” Two manuscripts have: “against them.”]

And elsewhere: “Hedge your ears with thorns, and do not listen to an evil tongue” (Ecclesiasticus 28:28).

Therefore blessed David, enumerating various forms of innocence and justice, did not remain silent about this virtue either, saying: “And he has not accepted reproach against his neighbors” (Psalm 14:4), because he not only opposes but also pursues the slanderer. For he says: “The one who secretly slanders his neighbor, him I will pursue” (Psalm 100:5).

This is certainly a vice that must be extinguished above all and entirely excluded by those who wish to train themselves in holiness. Nothing so disturbs the mind, nothing makes the spirit so changeable and fickle, as readily believing everything and following the words of slanderers with rash assent of mind. From this arise frequent disagreements; from this, unjust hatreds. This is what often turns even close friends into enemies, when a malicious tongue separates souls that are indeed harmonious but too credulous.

By contrast, there is great peace of mind and great steadiness of character in not rashly hearing anything sinister about anyone. Blessed is the person who has armed himself so thoroughly against this vice that no one dares to slander in his presence. If only we were this careful—not to believe slanderers indiscriminately—then everyone would fear slandering, lest by slandering they make not others so much as themselves contemptible. But this evil is so widespread, and this vice burns so fiercely in many, because it is gladly heard by almost everyone.

### 17

Flee also the flatteries of flatterers and the harmful, deceitful blandishments of false praise, as though they were plagues of the soul. Nothing corrupts people’s minds so easily; nothing wounds the spirit with so sweet and gentle a blow.

Hence a certain wise man says: “The words of flatterers are smooth, but they strike the innermost parts of the belly” (Proverbs 26:22).

And the Lord speaks through the Prophet: “My people, those who call you blessed lead you astray and destroy the paths of your feet” (Isaiah 3:12, according to the Septuagint).

In many people, especially in the present age, this vice holds sway, and it is regarded as a form of humility and goodwill. Consequently, anyone who does not know how to flatter is considered either envious or proud.

It is indeed a great and subtle art to praise another in order to commend oneself, and, by deceiving someone, to make the deceived person beholden to oneself. This vice is commonly practiced by selling fabricated praise at a fixed price.

What great fickleness of mind, what great vanity, is it to abandon one’s own conscience and follow another person’s opinion—and one that is fabricated and feigned? To be carried away by the wind of false praise, to rejoice in one’s own deception, and to accept mockery as a benefit?

Therefore, if you truly wish to be praiseworthy, do not seek human praise. Prepare your conscience for the one who “will bring to light the hidden things of darkness and disclose the purposes of hearts,” and “then praise will come to you from God” (1 Corinthians 4:5).

[Note: The Cistercian manuscript has *unicuique* (“to each person”) instead of *tibi* (“to you”).]

### 18

Let your mind be attentive and watchful, and always armed against sins. Let your speech in every respect be measured and sparing, indicating more the necessity of speaking than the desire to speak.

[Note: The same Cistercian manuscript has: “Let modesty adorn prudence.”]

Let modesty adorn prudence, and—what has always been especially characteristic of women—let modesty surpass all virtues in you. Consider well in advance what ought to be said; while still silent, take care that you do not later regret having said something. Let thought weigh your words, and let the balance of your mind regulate the office of your tongue.

Hence Scripture says: “Melt down your silver and your gold, make a balance for your words, and straight bridles for your mouth; and take care lest you slip with your tongue” (Ecclesiasticus 28).

[Note: Together with the Cistercian manuscript just mentioned, most manuscripts read: “Never let a curse come from your mouth,” while other books have “a malediction.”]

Never let an evil word proceed from your mouth, for you are commanded, as the culmination of kindness, even to bless those who curse you. “Be merciful, modest, humble, not returning evil for evil or cursing for cursing, but on the contrary blessing” (1 Peter 3:9).

### 19

Let your tongue be entirely unacquainted with lying and swearing. Let your love of truth be so great that, whatever you say, you may regard it as sworn.

[Note: Manuscript copies have “love of truth,” and shortly afterward one Cistercian manuscript has “you may regard the oath.”]

Concerning this the Savior says to his disciples: “But I say to you, do not swear at all.” And shortly afterward: “Let your speech be: Yes, yes; no, no. Whatever is more than these is from evil” (Matthew 5:34, 37).

Therefore, in every action and word, let a quiet and peaceful mind be preserved; let the presence of God always meet your thoughts. Let your mind be humble and gentle, raised up against vices alone. Let neither pride elevate it, nor greed bend it, nor anger plunge it headlong.

Nothing should be quieter, nothing purer, nothing finally more beautiful than the mind that is to be prepared as God’s dwelling. He is not pleased by temples shining with gold or altars adorned with gems, but by a soul adorned with virtues.

Therefore the hearts of the saints are called the temple of God, as the Apostle affirms when he says: “If anyone violates the temple of God, God will destroy him. For the temple of God is holy, and you are that temple” (1 Corinthians 3:17).

### 20

Have nothing more excellent than humility, and nothing more lovable. It is the chief preserver and, as it were, guardian of all virtues. Nothing makes us so acceptable to human beings and to God as being great in the merit of our life yet lowly in humility.

For this reason Scripture says: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things, and you will find grace before God” (Ecclesiasticus 3:20).

And the Lord speaks through the Prophet: “Upon whom shall I rest, if not upon the humble, the quiet, and the one who trembles at my words?” (Isaiah 66:2).

[Note: This is how we read it from our manuscripts, whereas all previously printed editions had: “Nevertheless, with humility …”]

But follow that humility which is expressed not displayed and feigned through bodily gesture or a broken tone of voice, but manifested by a pure disposition of heart. It is one thing to possess a virtue and another to possess the likeness of a virtue; one thing to follow the shadow of things and another to follow the truth.

Much more disfigured is the pride that hides beneath certain signs of humility. I do not know how it is that vices concealed under the appearance of virtues are more shameful.

### 21

Never set yourself above anyone on account of noble birth, and do not consider those born in obscurer or lower circumstances inferior to you. Our religion does not know how to show partiality to persons; it examines not people’s conditions but the disposition of each individual. It judges slave and noble according to their character.

The only freedom before God is not to serve sins. The highest nobility before God is to be distinguished by virtues.

Who among men was nobler before God than Peter, who was a fisherman and poor?

[Note: The Cistercian manuscript lacks “who was a fisherman and poor.” Shortly afterward, for *creduntur*, other manuscript copies have *donantur* (“are given”).]

And among women, who was more illustrious than blessed Mary, who is described as the wife of a craftsman? Yet to that fisherman and poor man Christ entrusted the keys of the heavenly kingdom. This wife of a craftsman deserved to be the mother of the one by whom those very keys were given.

For God chooses “the base and despised things of this world” (1 Corinthians 1:27), so that he may bring the powerful and noble more easily to humility.

Besides, anyone else boasts of noble birth in vain, since all who have been redeemed by the one blood of Christ possess equal honor and the same worth before God. Nor does it matter in what condition someone was born, since we are all reborn equally in Christ. Even if we forget that we were all generated from one ancestor, we must at least always remember that through one person we are all regenerated.

### 22

Take care that, if you begin to fast or abstain, you do not suppose that you are already holy. This virtue is an aid, not the perfection of holiness. Rather, you must ensure that, while you despise what is lawful, this practice does not give you a certain security regarding what is unlawful.

Whatever is offered to God beyond justice must not hinder justice but assist it. What benefit is it to make the body thin through abstinence if the mind swells with pride? What praise will we deserve for the pallor of fasting if we are livid with envy? What virtue is there in not drinking wine while becoming drunk with anger and hatred?

Then, I say, abstinence is excellent; then the chastisement of the body is beautiful and magnificent, when the mind is fasting from vices.

Indeed, those who practice abstinence reasonably and knowledgeably afflict their flesh precisely so that they may break the pride of the soul: so that, as though descending from some height of self-contempt and arrogance, they may come down to fulfill the Lord’s will, which is perfected above all in humility.

[Note: The Benedictine editor wrongly followed the reading of Erasmus, *fastidio* (“disdain”). He said, as Victorius notes, *contemptus sui* (“contempt of himself”), by which he despises others, not himself.]

For this reason they withdraw the mind from various desires for food, so that they may devote all its strength to the desire for virtues. The flesh now feels the labor of fasting and abstinence less, while the soul hungers for justice.

Even Paul, the chosen vessel, while chastising his body and bringing it into servitude, lest after preaching to others he himself should be found reprobate (1 Corinthians 9:27), does not do this—as some inexperienced people think—only for chastity. Abstinence does not assist chastity alone but all virtues without exception.

Nor is the Apostle’s great or complete glory simply that he does not fornicate. Rather, he does this so that through chastising the body the mind may be trained; and the less it desires anything from pleasures, the more it may be able to think about virtues. Thus the teacher of perfection may not show himself imperfect in anything; the imitator of Christ may do nothing outside Christ’s command or will; and he may teach by example no less than by word, lest, after preaching to others, he himself be rejected.

[Note: The Cistercian manuscript, together with certain printed editions, adds “by the Lord.”]

Let him hear also the words addressed to the Pharisees: “For they say and do not do” (Matthew 23:3).

### 23

It is both an apostolic command and an example that we should take account not only of conscience but also of reputation (Romans 12:17). The teacher of the nations does not teach this point superfluously or without fruit. He wishes outsiders also to advance toward faith through the works of believers, so that the discipline of religion may commend religion itself.

Therefore he commands us to shine like lights in the world amid a crooked and perverse nation, so that the unbelieving minds of those who err may discern the darkness of their ignorance by the light of our actions.

Hence he himself says to the Romans: “Providing what is good not only before God but also before human beings” (Romans 12:17). And elsewhere: “Be without offense to Jews and Gentiles and the Church of God, just as I please everyone in all things, not seeking what is useful for myself but what is useful for many” (1 Corinthians 10:32–33).

Blessed is the person who has ordered his life so holily and gravely that nothing sinister can even be fabricated about him; for the greatness of his merit contends against the desire of slanderers, and no one dares to invent what he thinks no one would believe.

But if attaining this is difficult and exceedingly arduous, let us at least exercise such care over our lives that evil minds find no opportunity to slander. Let no spark proceed from us by which the flame of an evil reputation may be kindled against us.

Otherwise, we are angry with our slanderers in vain if we ourselves provide them with material for slander.

[Note: The manuscript had *eisipsis* in a single word, incorrectly. Shortly afterward other manuscript copies have *materias* (“materials”).]

But if we carefully and diligently provide for everything honorable in us, and place the fear of God before all our actions, yet they still rage against us, let our conscience console us. It is then most secure and safest, when it has not even given anyone an opportunity to think badly of it.

Through the Prophet, woe is pronounced upon those who call good evil, who call light darkness, and who call what is sweet bitter (Isaiah 5:20, according to the Septuagint).

The Savior’s saying will therefore apply to us: “Blessed are you when people curse you, lying” (Matthew 5:11). Let us act in such a way that no one can speak evil of us without lying.

### 24

Manage the household with such care that you nevertheless grant your soul some leisure. Choose for yourself a suitable place, somewhat removed from the noise of the household, to which you may withdraw as into a harbor, as though from a great storm of anxieties, and there calm the waves of thoughts stirred up outside through the tranquility of solitude.

Let the study of divine reading be so constant there, the turns of prayer so frequent, and the meditation on future things so steady and concentrated, that you may easily compensate by this retreat for all the occupations of the remaining time.

We do not say this in order to draw you away from your own people. Rather, we do it so that there you may learn and meditate what sort of person you ought to present yourself as to them.

### 25

Rule and cherish your household in such a way that you wish to appear more the mother of your people than their mistress. Demand their respect by kindness rather than severity. Obedience that proceeds from love is always more faithful and more pleasing than that which proceeds from fear.

Above all, in honorable and undefiled marriage, let the order of apostolic discipline be maintained.

### 26

First of all, let the husband retain his authority, and let the whole household learn from you how much honor it owes him. Show him to be lord through your obedience; show him to be great through your humility. You will yourself become more honored the more you honor him.

For, as the Apostle says, “the husband is the head of the woman” (Ephesians 5:23), and the rest of the body is adorned by nothing more than by the dignity of the head.

Hence the same Apostle says elsewhere: “Wives, be subject to your husbands, as is fitting in the Lord” (Colossians 3:18).

Blessed Peter the Apostle also says: “Likewise, let women be subject to their husbands, so that even if some do not believe the word, they may be won without a word through the conduct of their wives” (1 Peter 3:1).

If, therefore, honor is owed by right of marriage even to unbelieving husbands, how much more must it be rendered to Christian husbands.

### 27

And to show with what ornaments women joined to men ought also to be adorned, he says: “Let their adornment not be external, the braiding of hair, the wearing of gold, or the putting on of clothing, but the hidden person of the heart in the incorruptibility of a quiet and modest spirit, which is rich in the sight of God. For thus formerly the holy women who hoped in God adorned themselves, being subject to their own husbands, as Sarah obeyed Abraham, calling him her lord” (ibid. 3 and following).

[Note: We preferred this reading with the manuscript books to the printed reading *squalore, sordibus* (“with squalor and filth”).]

In giving this command he does not order them to be filthy or to cover themselves with repulsive scraps of cloth. Rather, he forbids excessive adornment and overly elaborate finery, and commends simple decoration and dress.

Concerning this the chosen vessel also says: “Likewise, women should adorn themselves in suitable clothing, with modesty and sobriety, not with braided hair, gold, pearls, or expensive clothing, but—as is proper for women professing chastity through good works” (1 Timothy 2:9–10).

### 28

I find that, inflamed with a remarkable ardor of faith, you adopted continence several years ago and consecrated the remainder of your life to chastity.

This is a sign of great courage and an indication of perfect virtue: suddenly to renounce pleasure once experienced, to flee the familiar enticements of the flesh, and to extinguish the flames of still-heated youth through love of faith.

But I have also learned something else, which troubles and pains me considerably: namely, that you began to preserve this great good without the consent and agreement of your husband, although apostolic authority absolutely forbids this. In this particular matter it subjects not only the wife to the husband’s authority but also the husband to that of the wife.

“The wife,” it says, “does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does. Likewise, the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does” (1 Corinthians 7:4).

Yet, as though forgetful of the marriage covenant and mindful neither of this agreement nor of this right, you vowed chastity to the Lord without consulting your husband.

But what still lies under another person’s authority is promised at one’s peril. And I do not know how pleasing a gift can be if one person offers what belongs to two.

[Note: Compare Saint Augustine, Letter 262, to Ecdicia.]

Through such ignorance we have already both heard and seen many marriages torn apart, and—what is painful to recall—adultery committed on the pretext of chastity. For while one party abstained even from what was lawful, the other fell into what was unlawful.

In such a case I do not know who should be accused more or blamed more: the man who, rejected by his wife, commits fornication, or the woman who, rejecting her husband, in a sense thrusts him into fornication.

To make you recognize what truth teaches about this matter, I must set before you a few passages from divine authority. The rule of apostolic teaching neither equates the practice of continence with marriage, as Jovinian did, nor condemns marriage, as Manichaeus did.

Thus the chosen vessel and teacher of the nations proceeds between the two, maintaining a middle course, so that he grants a remedy for lack of continence while inviting people to the reward of continence. His entire meaning in this matter is that chastity should be proposed by the decision of both parties, or at least that the common marital obligation should be discharged by both.

### 29

Let us now set down the Apostle’s own words and reconsider the entire matter from its beginning. He speaks to the Corinthians:

“Concerning the matters about which you wrote to me: It is good for a man not to touch a woman” (1 Corinthians 7:1).

Although he praised chastity here, nevertheless, lest anyone seem to think that he was forbidding marriage, he adds: “But because of fornication, let each man have his own wife.”

[Note: Victorius and a few other printed editions add, “and let each woman have her own husband,” but this is not found in the manuscripts.]

“Let the husband render the wife her due; likewise also the wife to the husband. The woman does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does. And the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the woman does. Do not defraud one another” (ibid. and following).

And again, lest by speaking so much in favor of marriage he appear to exclude chastity, he continues: “Unless perhaps by mutual consent for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer.”

Immediately afterward he seems to retract the limitation “for a time,” lest he appear to teach not perpetual but only temporary and brief continence. For he says: “Because of your lack of self-control. But I say this by concession, not by command.”

By saying “for a time,” therefore, he teaches that chastity should be tested, so that at fixed intervals, as though they had examined the strength of their continence, both parties may promise each other without danger what must always be maintained by both.

But what he wants absolutely, he states openly: “I wish all people to be as I myself am”—that is, to live in continual and perpetual chastity.

### 30

Do you see how cautiously, prudently, and without giving any occasion for scandal the teacher established his judgment concerning chastity? He did not wish so great a good to rest on the rashness of one person when it ought to be bound and confirmed by the consent of both.

And truly, what is firmer or safer than that chastity which begins with the decision of two people and is maintained by both as a common possession? Neither party is concerned only for himself or herself; rather, each mutually encourages the other to persevere in virtue.

For this, like other good things, is praiseworthy not merely when begun but when brought to completion.

As you understand, the discourse has long been moving through a rocky and difficult place. It dares not incline toward either side, fearing both equally. From our own difficulty recognize your danger: we preferred perhaps to grieve you by telling the truth rather than deceive you with fabricated flattery.

[Note: The reading of Erasmus, which Martianay copies, has *ducere* (“to lead”) instead of *decipere* (“to deceive”).]

As you see, the evil is double, and the danger equal and uncertain: you are constrained from both sides and bound from both sides.

To despise and reject your husband altogether is openly contrary to the Apostle’s judgment.

[Note: The Benedictine editor again followed Erasmus incorrectly, reading “betray the husband.”]

But to abandon the chastity you have maintained for so long and fail to give back to God what you promised is something to fear and dread.

As the common saying goes: “You will easily turn a friend into an enemy if you do not return what you have promised him.”

[Note: Erasmus and Martianay have *sicut* (“just as”) instead of *sic* (“thus”). Shortly afterward they have *erit enim* (“for it will be”) instead of *et erit tibi* (“and it will be for you”).]

For Scripture says: “If you make a vow to the Lord your God, do not delay fulfilling it, because the Lord your God will surely require it of you, and it will be counted as sin for you” (Deuteronomy 23:21, according to the Septuagint, and Ecclesiastes 5:3).

Therefore he says: “Show your husband the honor he is owed, so that through both of you you may be able to fulfill to the Lord what you have vowed.”

We would not distrust his conscience if you had waited a little—not because we are drawing you away from the good of chastity, but because we wish to urge his mind with all our strength toward the oracle of chastity, so that he may offer God a voluntary sacrifice as a sweet fragrance; so that, freed from all worldly restraints and bodily pleasures, his mind may be able to cling more fully to the Lord’s commandments.

[Note: A certain old edition has *vacat* (“it is empty”) instead of *sit* (“may it be”); omitting the words, the reading is equally sound.]

Nevertheless, lest you suppose that we have spoken carelessly about this, we have instructed you by the testimonies of the divine Scriptures, just as the Apostle also says: “The two will become one flesh” (1 Corinthians 6:16–17); “no longer one flesh” (Matthew 19:6), but “one spirit” (1 Corinthians 6:17).

### 31

This sacrament is great, and the road of chastity is arduous. But great are its rewards, and the Lord calls us in the Gospel, saying: “Come, you blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 25:34).

The same Lord says: “Come to me, all who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls; for my yoke is easy and my burden light.”

The same Lord says to those who will be on his left: “Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire prepared by my Father for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25:41): “I do not know you, workers of iniquity.”

There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. All those who entangle themselves in the cares of the present life so completely that they forget the future will weep and mourn there. The Lord’s coming will overtake them as they are overwhelmed by the waves of ignorance and evil security, as though by a kind of sleep.

Therefore he himself says in the Gospel: “Take heed to yourselves, lest your hearts be weighed down with gluttony, drunkenness, and the cares of this life, and that day come upon you suddenly. For it will come like a snare upon all who sit upon the face of the whole earth” (Luke 21:34–35).

And again: “Watch and pray, for you do not know when the time will be” (Matthew 24:42; 25:13).

### 32

Blessed are those who await and watch for that day in such a way that they prepare themselves for it every day, not flattering themselves on the basis of past righteousness but, according to the Apostle, being renewed in virtue day by day (2 Corinthians 4:16).

For the righteousness of a righteous person will not benefit him from the day on which he ceases to be righteous. Likewise, the wickedness of a wicked person will not harm him from the day on which he turns away from wickedness (Ezekiel 18:24).

Therefore the holy person must not be secure so long as he remains engaged in the struggle of this life; nor should the sinner despair, since, according to the Prophet’s statement cited above, he can make himself righteous in a single day.

The whole span of your life is available for you to pursue and complete righteousness. Do not become more lax by trusting in past righteousness. Rather, as the Apostle says: “Forgetting what lies behind and reaching forward to what lies ahead, I pursue the appointed prize of the heavenly calling,” knowing that God examines the heart (Philippians 3:15; Proverbs 24:12).

For this reason he strives to keep his soul free from sin. Hence it is written: “Guard your heart with all vigilance” (Proverbs 4:23). And again: “The Lord loves pure hearts; and all the blameless are acceptable to him” (Proverbs 11:20, according to the Septuagint).

Therefore act so that you may order the remainder of your life without offense, so that you may safely sing with the Prophet: “I will walk in the innocence of my heart, in the midst of my house” (Psalm 100:2).

And again: “I will enter the altar of God, to God, who gladdens my youth” (Psalm 42:4).

For it is not enough to have begun; to have completed is righteousness.

## LETTER CXLIX

[Note: Alternatively, unpublished.]

**Saint Jerome. (C, G)**

[Note: This letter now appears for the first time from Vatican Codex 642, folio 89. It is attributed to Jerome, but falsely, as will become clear to us from the mere reading of the text, even without further comment. It seems that the person who falsely claimed Jerome as author also falsely named Damasus as the person to whom it was addressed, as can be inferred from the closing, since no name is attached in the heading. We have published it both for other reasons and especially because of its novelty, merely noting that we have removed innumerable errors from it, of which we will mention only a few as examples, lest we appear to be advertising our own work.]

### On the Solemnities of Easter

He explains the feast days of the Hebrews and teaches that they ought by no means to be observed after the Gospel.

1. Concerning the solemnities and Sabbaths, the New Moons which are commanded by the Lord in the Law to be observed: compelled by the command of your charity to declare what ought to be rejected according to the letter, and what ought to be observed spiritually, we are first obliged to answer the lovers of the letter and the adversaries of truth. Although I could, with good right, strike them back—[Note: The manuscript had *cum eo in se*, which makes no sense. The genuine Jerome, in his letter to Marcella, has: “whom I could despise with good right; for a lyre sings uselessly to an ass; nevertheless, lest we,” etc.]—I prefer to address them more gently and mildly, desiring that they come to recognition of the truth. For although they wish to chew the bitter bark of the roots, they spit out the fruits; and while they admire the dust of gold, they despise the fashioned metals. Even if they insist that everything in the Law must be observed according to the letter, with the veil placed over the face of Moses they cannot be illumined by the light of the Spirit of truth. [Note: What follows from here is badly corrupted and disordered; if we wished to restore it by conjecture, far too much would have to be changed.] And even if they do not yield to the truth, nevertheless, like a scapegoat, they are ready—upon the shoulder of our patience—to give an answer concerning the faith that is in us (1 Peter 3:15), and to go into the wilderness of their destruction, and afterward wash their garments, lest they remain polluted by the contagion of heretical thinking. We, however, taught at the beginning of this little work by the example of Jeremiah, propose first to uproot and destroy, and afterward to plant and build.

2. Desiring first to show from the Scriptures how these feasts of the Lord, which are commanded to be observed in the Law, are celebrated not by shadow but by spiritual observance: if some should wish to make light of the authority of our weakness, let them hear the Prophets, who, with provident protection, openly foretold the rejection of these things in the time of the Gospel. Indeed, with the Lord speaking through them:

> “Your feast days, and your New Moons, and your Sabbaths, my soul hears.”

And the Lord declares that he did not command these things, although it is clear that he himself commanded them in the Law. What else is shown by these words except that, when the end of the Law arrived with Christ, he did not command them to be kept according to the letter?

Concerning sacrifices he speaks through another Prophet:

> “I will not rebuke you because of your sacrifices. Your burnt offerings are always before me,” [Note: Supply: “I will not take calves from your house,” which the hurried copyist omitted.] “nor goats from your flocks,”

and the rest, up to:

> “or drink the blood of goats.”

Filled with the same Spirit, the Apostle, agreeing with this, says:

> “Let no one deceive you in food or drink, or with regard to a festival day, or a New Moon, or a Sabbath, which are a shadow of things to come,”

and the rest. By these words he makes perfectly clear that, whether in the temporal observance of days or in the observance of bodily foods, one can find nothing except a most vain shadow and the sedition of error [another reading: “that nothing else can be found”].

The Lord Jesus Christ also declared in the Gospel that he dissolved the Sabbath, when he commanded the paralytic:

> “Take up your pallet,”

which was plainly forbidden by the Law, namely, to carry burdens on the Sabbath. He also dissolved the Feast of Tabernacles when he said:

> “I will not go up to this feast,”

as though he had said: “In this observance of this feast the glory of my honor will not ascend.”

3. Concerning Passover, as the greatest sacrament of our salvation, I shall say somewhat more at length. Although it is not appropriate to discuss everything at this time, I first wish to show by what and how many considerations the Lord’s Passover is commanded to be observed.

In the first month, on the tenth day of the month, the Lord commanded through Moses that a year-old, spotless lamb be set apart and kept until the thirteenth and fourteenth days, and that it be killed by the entire assembly of the children of Israel in the evening. When the true Lamb, the Lord himself, advanced toward the evening Passover, he wished some of these considerations to remain and changed others because he did not wish them to be observed. Although he graciously allowed himself to be sacrificed in the first month according to the command of the Law, he in no way permitted the time of his Passion to be anticipated before the thirteenth day.

Nevertheless, the Gospel relates that he did something contrary to the figure: when he was betrayed by Judas to the Jews, he was seized on the eleventh day of the first month. [Note: Thus in the copy, which a later hand corrected to “on the tenth.” The author’s hallucinations are by no means slight; the diligent reader may correct them from the writings of the ancient Fathers.] And when he graciously gave the sacrament of his body and blood during his lifetime to his disciples, this too is shown to have been contrary to the figure.

When that lamb, therefore, was commanded to be killed in the type of Christ, roasted by fire with its head and feet, and its entrails consumed by the people after its slaughter, the Lord is understood, as I think, to have done this for two reasonable causes. First, so that, when he ate the Passover with his disciples, they would not believe that it ought to be observed afterward in the same way, unless he had subsequently changed the sacrifice by saying:

> “This is my body” (Matthew 26:26).

The second cause, as I suppose, was that they might see the Lord’s body whole and containing his own blood within it before the Passion, and believe that they were spiritually nourished by this body; and thus it ought also now to be believed by us.

We must also observe that it was not on the fourteenth day in the evening, as the Law commands, that the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world, our Passover, was sacrificed—Christ (2 Corinthians 5)—but on the fifteenth day. It is therefore clear that the Jewish feast, together with its sacrifice, was dissolved by the Lord. [Col. 1222]

But what are we to understand from this: that he first eats the flesh of the lamb figured beforehand, afterward nourishes our Apostles with the food of his own body, and Christ is sacrificed after the Jews’ typological Passover? This, as I suppose, means not that the reality should precede the figure, but that the figure should precede the reality; for not first what is spiritual, but what is natural, and afterward what is spiritual—

[Note: The manuscript incorrectly reads: “and afterward what is natural, the chosen wife.”]

—from which the universal Church, the chosen and beloved bride of Christ, anathematizes those who determine that Passover should be celebrated with the Jews on the fourteenth day, as well as the Sabbaths and the other observances of this shadowy practice.

The Church has judged worthy of observing only this: that in the first month, after the fourteenth day, the Paschal feast should be celebrated on the first day of the week, without any ambiguity. Even in this matter, however, disagreement arose in the Church: some thought it sufficient not to celebrate Passover with the Jews on the fourteenth day; others carefully and firmly observed that they should not dare to celebrate the sacrifice of the true Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world, before the fourteenth day, according to that legal command which the Lord, coming to his Passion, by no means despised:

> “You shall keep it until the fourteenth day” (Exodus 13:6).

The Church now chiefly observes this practice, following the authority of the Apostolic See.

But leaving these matters aside—for it is not the time to examine them individually—we turn the attention of our minds to spiritual understanding. We are commanded, on the fourteenth day of the month of new things, the Paschal month, to eat the flesh of the lamb, so that, when we who are being born have completed the words of the Decalogue through the fruits of good works, and stand in the perfection of the Gospel according to the number four, we may eat the flesh of our Lamb at the evening of the world, when the end of the ages has arrived—not with hearts darkened, but with the Holy Spirit illuminating our night.

4. Concerning the Sabbath: we are commanded to work for six days; but on the seventh, that is, the Sabbath, we are forbidden every servile work. By the number six the perfection of works is signified, because the Lord made heaven and earth in six days. On the Sabbath we are forbidden to perform every servile work—that is, sin—because “whoever commits sin is the slave of sin” (John 8:34). Thus, when in the present age we have completed the perfection of works, and do not harden our hearts, may we deserve to reach the true rest, which is denied to the rebellious, with the Lord speaking through David:

> “If they shall enter into my rest” (Psalm 49:11).

The Law commands us to count, from the day after the Sabbath, seven complete weeks until the day after the completion of the seventh week—that is, the fiftieth day, on which the first fruits are offered. I think that this complete reckoning of perfection through the number seven, and through fifteen and five times ten, signifies that, by the number fifty, which contains remission within itself, through charity—which has been poured into our hearts by the sevenfold Spirit of grace—we should have the five senses of our body subject to the Law of God.

These words contain the Decalogue; and through charity, as I said, “charity covers a multitude of sins” (1 Peter 4:8). Thus we offer a new sacrifice to the Lord from all our dwellings, yielding ourselves for the use of our Priest together with our peace offerings, if we have made peace with the Lord and offer spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ.

The High Priest, who has entered heaven and can sympathize with our weaknesses, eats the loaves of the first fruits of our land, although they are leavened, yet consecrated to him. And since we have an advocate with the Father, when works fermented by the leaven of our weakness, raised by the hand of prayer for the use of this Priest, are offered, he devours them through the bowels of mercy. They provide a pleasing fragrance to God, but they demand forgiveness all the more.

5. Concerning the Feast of Tabernacles and the end of the solar year among the Hebrews: in that same seventh month, when the fruits are gathered into the granaries or storehouses, the Law commands that solemnities be celebrated. That is, the Sabbath is to be celebrated on the first day of the month of trumpets, on the tenth day of atonements, and on the fifteenth day for seven days, until they are completed; the eighth day is commanded to be the feast of tabernacles.

These things may perhaps signify that, because at the end of the age we have been consecrated by the sacrament of the threefold invocation, we do not cease to proclaim the trumpet of faith in the preaching of the Gospel and the sprinkling of the blood of Jesus Christ, in which true propitiation exists, when the time of the Law has ended. Having gathered the fruits of good works, and resting from every evil work through the grace of the sevenfold Spirit amid sustained persecution, may we deserve to reach the number of the eighth blessedness.

There is no doubt that this is accomplished through the labor of fasting and prayer, because the Law also commands that souls be afflicted.

6. Concerning the New Moons: on the New Moon, that is, the new month, we are commanded to blow the trumpet. Whoever has been illuminated by the light of knowledge ought not to cease preaching to others. Paul, illuminated by the splendor of the knowledge of Christ, by preaching in the synagogues did not disdain to observe this command.

I had decided to say only a few things, [Note: It seems necessary to supply “concerning sacrifices also,” or something similar, unless the preceding words are defective through an ugly transposition.] which, since they contain within themselves the figure of the sacrifices of the true High Priest, must also be offered spiritually by us to the Lord.

By the calf is understood our labor; by the sheep, innocence; by the goat, the mortification of fornicatory pleasure; by the she-goat, which feeds in high places, the contemplative life; by the ram—[Note: Read “fruitfulness,” or something similar. Shortly afterward, for *stis*, read, in my judgment, “through the virtue of chastity, chastity through the turtledove.”]—preaching, which produces lambs for the good Shepherd; by the virtue of solitary chastity, the mind joined to no one except Christ; by the dove, penetrating insight into the mysteries; by the bread, firmness in the commandments; by fine flour, sincerity of life; by wine and salt, the truth of preaching.

The Law commands all these things, whether feasts or sacrifices, to be celebrated and offered in one place, because everything is beneficial when it is carried out in the unity of the Church, without any error of schism.

Discussing these few things from the abyss of the many commandments of the Law, [Note: The copy had *deserens* corruptly; shortly afterward, by the usual scribal lapse, it had *cibi* instead of *civi*.] I did not fear to offer this little bowl—poor to the rich, a stranger to a citizen. “Perfect love casts out fear” (1 John 4:8). I also believe this, venerable Pope: that obedience with faith is worth more than the capacity of human ingenuity.

These things were requested by you and spoken by me on account of those who, although they appear Christians on the surface, do not fear to tear apart the body of Christ, the Church, by their schisms through the impiety of Jewish thinking.

We have passed over these matters briefly. If they were treated in their entirety, they would demand a large volume, which [Note: Read *majoris* instead of *in hujus*, which is certainly a *σφάλμα*—an error.] would require the leisure of a longer time.

Pray for me, venerable Pope.

## Letter 150. Procopius to Jerome (G)

### Procopius to Jerome

[Note: Procopius of Gaza, evidently. This is Letter 26 of his sixty letters. Jerome, however, is certainly not our Jerome of Stridon, but his Egyptian namesake, or someone who lived in the regions of Egypt. It is remarkable what fabrications Isaac Vossius has imposed on this passage concerning Saint Jerome: that he had either fallen into the hands of Arab brigands or at least been exposed to great danger; hence Procopius supposedly warns him that, if he should again pass through Elusa and encounter the Saracens, he would not escape so easily, and would call in vain upon the “golden rain” of the wealthy matrons with whom he associated. He also accuses the holy Doctor of pride, although Jerome charged other Greek writers with the same vice, and said of Saint Basil in the Chronicle under the year 2392 that he had “lost many good qualities of continence and intellect through the single fault of pride.” This is a most foul calumny and a lie of outrageous audacity, since no one is unaware that the closing remark refers to Photinus, not to Basil. There is no time to refute the rest, since Procopius, a Christian sophist under Justin the Thracian, was a full century later than our Jerome, and no sane person can believe that he could have written letters to our holy Doctor. We reprint this letter itself—not because it has any relevance to our edition, but because it appeared in the Benedictine edition, so that nothing from it might be lacking in ours—and also because its notable errors had to be corrected and restored from the madness of a heretical man.]

> “Egypt again, and softness, while we poor men are nothing to you and there is no account taken of those who are absent. This is nothing—just laugh while gazing upon the Nile flowing with gold. Even if you raise your brow still higher, we shall endure your contempt entirely. For there will be a time when you see Elusa again and lament the sand scattered by the winds and laying waste to the vine down to its root. [Note: In the Greek text of this letter there is a gap involving several words, namely those corresponding to the passage enclosed in brackets in the Latin text. They are: *ἄμπελον· ἔνθα καὶ Νύμφαι ξέναι τινὲς καὶ θαλάττιαι καὶ Ζεὺς*—‘the vine; where also are certain foreign and sea-born Nymphs, and Zeus.’] There will be no rain-bringing Jupiter there. Then I myself shall laugh and mock fortune. You, however, will think me now cast down, but then blessed.

> “Nevertheless, while the Nile permits you to live in luxury, write at least, and call us ‘little ones,’ like creatures creeping out of the earth. Thus we shall enjoy your writing, and shall bear your pride more gently in expectation of what is to come.”

# Notes of Dom Jean Martianay, Benedictine monk of the Congregation of Saint-Maur, on all the letters of Saint Jerome

**N.B.** The column numbers indicated by us are taken from the Benedictine edition. They refer to the numerical notes that we inserted throughout the work and distinguished by heavier type: thus number 3 corresponds to column 327 of our edition, number 5 to column 328, number 7 to column 331, where they may be found; and similarly for the rest.

## Letter 1. To Innocent

### “Who had not yet handled the boat-hook”

In manuscript codices there are various readings of this kind: “who had not yet handled the helm in the lake”; or “who had not yet handled the *scalfum*,” etc.; or “who had not yet handled the *capha* in the lake.” One manuscript has *scalnum*. | 3 |

### “Therefore, Vercellae of the Ligurians”

Here too the manuscripts vary: “Therefore, the city of the Vergellani”; or “Therefore, the city of Vercellae of the Ligurians”; “Therefore, the city of the Vercellani.” | Ibid. |
