### “A little blood from the scratch”

In several ancient manuscript codices the passage reads:

> “And lightly grazing the skin, he sprinkled it with a little blood from the scratch. The striker, unwarlike and without a battle, was frightened at the blow of an unarmed hand; and, angry at his defeated right hand, he turns it toward a second attack with his sword already growing weak.”

| 5 |

### “The third blow had frustrated the sacrament”

The older manuscript codices read in this way. The printed editions read otherwise: “and the third blow had frustrated the sacrament of the Trinity.” The learned Gravius decided that it should be read: “and the third blow, having frustrated it, was the sacrament of the Trinity.” | Ibid. |

### “May it enter the minds of all”

The manuscript copies read: “May it enter the minds of all.” | Ibid. |

### “Lying at Milan”

Marianus charged this reading with error, but without justification, as learned men know, who correctly interpret the word “lying.” | 7 |

## Letter 3. To Rufinus

### “Who sufficiently desires the vows through boldness”

The printed editions read: “who, I thought, wanted it sufficiently to be accomplished through boldness,” etc. | 9 |

### “To the Egyptian Confessors”

These Egyptian Confessors are, according to recent writers, those whom the Emperor Valens sent into exile in 371 because of their confession of the divinity of Christ. But this conflicts with the arrival of Rufinus and Melania in Egypt. For from Palladius, *Lausiac History*, chapter 33, we know with certainty that Melania reached Alexandria at the very beginning of Valens’s reign, that is, in the year of Christ 364 or 365. We assign this letter of Jerome to Rufinus the monk to that period. | 10 |

### “The servant of holy Melania”

Do not read, with Erasmus and Marianus, “of holy Melanius,” but “of holy Melanii,” or “of holy Melania,” as some manuscript codices read. | 11 |

### “With no pleasantness of channels”

The ancients had pipes and channels in their gardens, constructed in such a way that water flowed and flowed back in wondrous turns, modeled on the channel of the sea, from which they took the name *Euripi*. | Ibid. |

### “Let anyone shine with gold”

We have followed the Cluniac manuscript and others here. The printed editions alter the reading as follows:

> “Let him shine—whomever you please—with gold, and let metals glitter from his baggage in pompous dishes.”

But this makes no sense, nor is such a construction free from solecism. | 13 |

## Letter 4. To Florentius

A great many manuscript codices entitle the Second Letter “On the Origin of Friendship,” that is: “Here begins the letter of Jerome to Florentius, on the Origin of Friendship.” | Ibid. |

### “In which you sustained Christ”

The Cluniac manuscript, of excellent quality, reads: “in sustaining whom you clothed Christ,” etc. | Ibid. |

### “Even the mouths of the mute can”

The same manuscript reads “of the mute”; others read “of the many.” | Ibid. |

### “I, that most sluggish man”

Apart from the same Cluniac manuscript, ten other manuscripts read with the opposite meaning: “I, that most ardent man, whom intolerable languor afflicted.” | Ibid. |

### “By a gesture and vow of charity”

We followed the Cluniac copy. The other manuscript codices preserve various readings of this kind: “by a certain vow of charity”; or “by a charter of charity and a vow.” | Ibid. |

## Letter 5. To Florentius

### “I have pupils who serve the antiquarian art”

The passage is extremely corrupt in many manuscript copies, where we read: “who instruct me in an ancient art.” | 15 |

## Letter 6. To Julian

In the ancient manuscript books it is entitled “To Julian, Deacon of Aquileia.” Yet there was a deacon in Saint Jerome’s homeland, that is, in Stridon, and not in Aquileia. | 16 |

### “The Iberian serpent”

This serpent, or hydra, was the priest Lupicinus, a hireling and useless shepherd, who had perhaps shared in the misfortune and fault of Jerome’s sister and afterward slandered her brother. | 17 |

## Letter 8. To Niceas

### “Turpilius the comic poet”

Eusebius testifies that this comic poet lived in the time of Pompey; but no monument of this author survives today. | 21 |

### “In a matter that is not true”

“In a matter that is not true,” that is, in his comedy. For comedy is a fictitious affair, though it contains true sentiments. | Ibid. |

### “Whom Ennius calls *Casci*”

In the language of the Sabines, *cascus* meant “old” and “ancient.” Hence Erasmus’s proverb in his *Chiliads*: “An old man takes an old woman [in marriage],” that is, “an aged man [takes] an aged woman.” Thus the *Casci* sought their food in the manner of beasts, because they lived on acorns. | Ibid. |

### “Laelius in Cicero”

Marcus Tullius records this in the book entitled *Laelius*, where he teaches that a relationship should be loosened, not violently severed, if we happen to enter into a friendship that is unsuitable for us. | Ibid. |

## Letter 9. To Chrysogonus

The manuscript codices call him “Chrysocomas.” | Ibid. |

## Letter 10. To Paul

### “White in the likeness of Christ”

Jerome has the following in his commentary on Ecclesiastes 10:

> “Read Daniel: you will find there the Ancient of Days, God. Read the Apocalypse of John, and you will find the head of the Savior white as snow and, as it were, white wool.” | 24 |

## Letter 12. To Anthony the Monk

Twelve manuscript copies entitle this letter in the following way; one, belonging to the College of Navarre, has “To Ammonius the Monk”; another, from the monastery of Saint Cygiranus, has “To Chrysocomas, Monk of Aquileia.”

One very ancient codex of the Royal Library and another from Saint-Martin-des-Champs preserve this reading:

> “Here begins the letter to Anthony, Monk of Hemona,” that is, Hermona.

That monk therefore lived where the Virgins of Hermona were. | 26 |

### “Since you do not utter even a mu”

Concerning this syllable *μῦ* (*mu*), which mutes commonly pronounce, we spoke in our notes on the Letter to Philemon. See Jerome’s commentary on Isaiah, chapter 3. Instead of “not even a nod,” I would prefer to restore “not even a mu,” because that expression was very familiar to Jerome. | 27 |

## Letter 14. To Heliodorus

We read: “pleasure smiles upon Scylleus.” Erasmus reads: “pleasure smiles upon Scyllacaeus,” etc.

The manuscript codices contain diverse and varying titles for this letter, namely: “Here begins Jerome’s letter to Heliodorus the Presbyter”; or “to Heliodorus the Bishop”; others read “to Heliodorus the Monk.” One very ancient codex, however, has: “To Heliodorus the Monk, afterward Bishop.” I recognize this as the genuine title. | 28 |

### “I do not want you to remember former necessities”

The printed editions read: “I do not want you to remember former relationships.” But all the manuscript codices object, retaining “necessities.” The truth of this reading can be confirmed from the first letter to Florentius, where Jerome said:

> “The necessity of your assistance to the brother Heliodorus can even loosen the mouths of the mute. With what thanks, with what praise, he reported that the hardships of his journey had been relieved by you!”

It is these necessities, and the hardships of the ancient journey, that Saint Jerome is discussing here. | 29 |

### “Let him not confess fraud to be idolatry”

Some manuscript copies read:

> “Let him not confess idolaters, but those like them,”

or:

> “Let him not confess those who hate idols only, but those like them.” | 32 |

### “Lust, smiling like Scylla, flatters”

In very many manuscript codices. |

[Col. 1227] | 32 |

### “Let the cross be fixed as a mast”

Other manuscript codices, together with the printed editions, read: “Let the cross be fixed as a mast,” etc. | 33 |

### “The heresy of the Nicolaitans”

For curious readers I transcribe a marginal annotation found in an ancient Cluniac manuscript of the letters of Saint Jerome. It is placed opposite the word “Neophytes,” which that manuscript reads in place of “Nicolaitans”:

> “Neophytes were called heretics, that is, newcomers. The heresy arose from Nicolaus. For when he had a very beautiful wife whom he guarded with excessive jealousy, and when they reproached him excessively for being jealous, he brought her out publicly, saying: ‘Whoever wishes may abuse this wife of mine.’ He said this simply; nevertheless, from it a heresy arose, so that wives would be common to everyone. On account of this evil he consequently fell into other crimes.” | 35 |

### “And so that it may happen for him to be present at these things”

Here we followed the Cluniac codex, because it supplies the genuine meaning. It is difficult to find this in the others, except in another manuscript from Saint-Martin-des-Champs, which reads in the same way. | 39 |

## Letters 15 and 16. To Damasus

### “From a priest, a victim, greetings”

All the manuscripts read: “From a priest, a victim, greetings; from a shepherd,” etc. The printed editions, however, read: “a victim of salvation.” | Ibid. |

### “He determines it by the boundary”

The printed editions have “he separates it,” but all the manuscript codices read “he determines it.” The ancients called the Eucharist the holy thing of the Lord; they sent it to one another as a sign of Catholic communion. | 39 |

### “From the leader of the Arians”

In several manuscript codices we read: “from the offspring of the Arians, the Campenses,” etc. | Ibid. |

### “The crucified salvation of the world”

Here too the oldest copies read: “through the crucified salvation of the world, through the consubstantial Trinity.” | 41 |

### “Lest the obscurity of the place where I dwell deceive the bearers”

The printed editions altered the excellent reading of the manuscript codices in this way:

> “Lest the obscurity of the place where I dwell deceive you through the carriers of letters,” etc.

| Ibid. |

### “Through the necessary ornament of faith”

Thus the manuscript copies read, except for the ancient Cluniac codex, which retains the following reading:

> “Through the necessary ornament of the sufferings of our faith; thus you who follow the Apostles in honor,” etc. | 43 |

## Letter 17. To Marcus

In very many manuscript codices this letter is entitled “To Marcus, Presbyter of Chalcis”; in the ancient Cluniac manuscript already mentioned, “To Marcus, Bishop of Chalcis.”

The printed books therefore wrongly called him a presbyter of Caleda or Teleda, both in Latin and in French. Marcus was a presbyter or bishop of the city or region of Chalcis, to whom belonged the responsibility of recognizing the faith of the monks of the desert of Chalcis. | Ibid. |

## Letter 18. To Damasus

### “Although they are most learned”

He means Origen, concerning whom the letter to Pammachius and Oceanus says:

> “In his interpretation of Isaiah, where two Seraphim are described crying out, when he interpreted one as the Son and the other as the Holy Spirit, did I not change his detestable interpretation into the two Testaments? A book published twenty years ago is in people’s hands,” etc. | 48 |

### “Jod he, jod he”

I am astonished by the silence of Erasmus and Marianus concerning Jerome’s more obscure passages. I could find nothing about the Tetragrammaton, the four-letter Name of God, in such editors, although they often embellish trivial matters with scholia and notes.

The curious reader should know that Jerome is referring here to the ineffable name of God as it was read in Greek books, where it was customarily written in this form: *IIIIII*. From this manner of writing and reading that name Jerome could say that the ineffable name of God, the Tetragrammaton, was written as JOD HE, JOD HE, or as a double IA.

Consult what I said in the third Prolegomenon, number 6, in Volume I, and afterward in Volume II, column 281. See also the Letter to Marcella, column 705 of the same Volume II of our edition. | 52 |

### “The Septuagint: ‘And it was sent’”

This part of the exposition of Isaiah’s vision was written at the same time and in the same place as the preceding exposition, which Jerome did not complete in one continuous sitting because of pain in his eyes, and because the secretary who was recording the dictated words on wax tablets had scraped away the wax when the explanation had already reached the following verse:

> “And it was sent to me,” etc.

Thus it must be acknowledged as one letter, or brief treatise, consisting of two parts dictated at different intervals. Hence in the manuscript codex of the Dominican convent of Saint Dominic at Toulouse this entire treatise is found arranged in its proper order without division, under the same number, as though it were one single letter. | 59 |

### “Symmachus”

The printed books omit Symmachus’s reading, which all the manuscript codices retain; Jerome himself mentions it shortly afterward. | Ibid. |

## Letter 19. Of Damasus

### “It belongs to your affection”

Several manuscript codices read after the word “they bring forth”:

> “Therefore I ask for the devotion of your affection, so that, being ardent,” etc. | 63 |

### “And with deceptive ambiguities”

The printed books substitute *scrupulous* for *deceptive*, that is, “and with scrupulous ambiguities.” | Ibid. |

## Letter 20. To Damasus

### “He says that the Ain had been elided”

He says that the sound of the Jod was represented by the same Ain in this word.

### “PHEDUTH is interpreted”

In all the manuscript copies this name has been changed into the word *EPHOD*, partly because of a certain similarity between the words and partly through the ignorance of ancient copyists, to whom the word *Ephod* was more familiar than *Pheduth*, which they did not understand. | 64 |

### “Let the reader find”

Thus we read in all the manuscript codices. The printed editions insert between “reader” and “find” the addition: “what follows.” | 65 |

### “ANNA ADONAI”

In the Hebrew text as it is read today, we find this in Psalm 117, verse 25. In the time of Saint Jerome, however, the first and second occurrences of *Anna* were read with a *he* at the end; the third, which occurs before the word *Baruch*, was read with a *he* at the beginning and at the end. For the *he* in the word *Aslianna* was not paragogic among the ancient Hebrews, but the first element of the word *Anna*, which was regarded as a conjunction or interjection, like *δὴ* among the Greeks in *σῶσον δὴ* (“save, I pray”) and *εὐόδωσον δή* (“prosper, I pray”).

This passage is so corrupt in the ancient editions that Jerome’s meaning can scarcely be perceived or understood from them. Through careful reading and with the assistance of manuscript codices, we have restored the Hebrew, Greek, and Latin words to their former integrity. Whoever wishes may compare the new readings with the old, so that he may more easily appreciate the fruit of our labor. | Ibid. |

### “Lest we seem to change it in Latin”

That is, in transferring it into the Latin language, lest we seem to change the words of the Greek interpreters—Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion, and the Fifth Edition. The ancient editors, who did not understand this, printed “in the Latin” and “in the feminine Latin.” | Ibid. |

### “The word *δή* is placed”

We have restored this passage according to the authority of the manuscript copies, especially that of the outstanding codex of the monastery of Saint Cygiranus. Since Erasmus and Marianus did not understand Jerome’s text here, Erasmus himself must be heard in his scholia:

> “This passage,” he says, “is so corrupted in all the copies that I cannot conjecture its meaning with certainty. Nevertheless, from the traces of the letters I think it should be read: *Δεήσεως ὡς ἄνα*, that is, ‘of supplication,’ with *ἄνα*—a word that among the Greeks sometimes belongs to one who is entreating, especially among the poets. But let whoever finds something more probable immediately reject my conjecture.”

Someone had added after the word “is placed” the term *σχετλιαστικῶς*, “in a lamenting manner,” relying, as I think, more on his own conjecture than on the copies. This is what Erasmus says. If Marianus had wished to imitate him, he would immediately have rejected the word *σχετλιαστικῶς*. But he was not a sufficiently careful editor, and so he thrust upon us the futile conjecture of some unknown person as though it were Jerome’s genuine text. | 66 |

### “The Hebrew interjection *Anna*”

The Hebrew interjection *Anna*, whether it begins with an *aleph*, is not expressed in the Latin language of the Vulgate edition of the Psalms. Jerome, however, expressed it in his Latin Psalter derived from the Hebrew source, for he has:

> “I beseech you, Lord; save, I beseech you; I beseech you, Lord, prosper, I beseech you.”

Here *Anna* is rendered four times by *obsecro*, “I beseech.” Consequently, in Jerome’s time it was written four times in the Hebrew books, as it still exists today in the Masoretic copies.

Jerome therefore compared the Hebrew text of the Psalms more carefully when he prepared the Latin translation than when, still a younger man, he wrote to Pope Damasus. Unless we say in his defense that there were different readings among Hebrew codices at that time—which I would readily believe. | 67 |

### “This has been done by the Lord”

The Cluniac manuscript codices, especially the one we followed, preserve this entire passage in a most beautiful and genuine form. We have added only *sith* from another codex, since others read *si*. The books printed before ours corruptly read as follows:

> “And when we wish to impose silence, we constrict and force the breath with clenched teeth, producing, as it were, a hissing sound; so also the Hebrews,” etc.

| Ibid. |

### “The last letter of the preceding word”

The ancient editors change this genuine passage of Jerome into another, false and ignorant form. Contrary to the testimony of all the manuscript copies, they read:

> “For the letter Aleph, the first letter of the following word, when it encounters the final letter Jod of the preceding word, excludes it.”

But in *Hosiach anna*, the letter Jod is not the final letter of the preceding word; it is the letter Ain, as all the manuscript codices consistently retain. The error arose because Erasmus and Marianus did not pay attention to Jerome’s practice of treating Aleph and Ain as vowels. Thus in *OSI*—

[Col. 1229] | 68 |

### “OSANNA BARRAMA”

Although Jerome reads it with elision as *Osana Barrama*, nevertheless in Matthew it was read as in the Psalm: *hosiah anna*.

He reads *barrama* according to the rules of modern grammarians, who teach that the emphatic *he*, or article, takes *pataḥ*, that is, a vowel, followed by *dagesh*, as in *haddabar*, “the word.” They teach that this article is frequently excluded by servile letters, which take its pointing—for example, *hacchoben* instead of *hehacchoben*.

Thus Jerome read *OSANNA BARRAMA* instead of *bebarama*. Above, however, he read *basem* with an *a*, but did not double the letter *s* according to the modern form *bassem*. If this had been clear to the ignorant John Clericus, he would not have been the foolish defender of the ignorance of others who, in the *Hebrew Questions of Saint Jerome on Genesis*, printed *beben*, “in the son,” instead of the true and genuine *baben*. | Ibid. |

### “To report a fabricated judgment”

In many manuscript codices we read:

> “To report a judgment fabricated from another language, elsewhere false.”

Hence the printed books have the double reading: “to report a fabricated and false judgment.” | Ibid. |

## Letter 21. To Damasus

### “Why does he receive sinners here?”

All the manuscript codices read this way. Marianus may not change the reading without the authority of manuscript copies, even though the Vulgate has: “Because he receives sinners here,” etc. | 69 |

### “Mark also in the same passage”

The edition of Erasmus adds here: “to repentance.” This addition was found in copies of the Italian Version, as may be seen in our Italian version, the old Latin Vulgate which I recently published. | 70 |
Source/review notes: Latin and transliterated apparatus lemmata are retained with English glosses. Corrupt Greek remains marked as corrupt. Hebrew characters absent from the visible supplied source are identified as absent rather than reconstructed.

*Pendens ex Israel* [“Hanging from Israel [a fragmentary lemma]”]. I find nothing else in the manuscript copies of this Epistle; therefore I do not approve of Marianus, who added the word “sons,” since Tertullian, in *On Modesty*, chapter 9, read from this passage of Deuteronomy: “You shall not be a hanging thing from the sons of Israel.” | 71 |

Famis autem μεταφορικῶς [“But famine,” metaphorically]. Erasmus did not restore this passage, as he supposed, but published it in a corrupted form both in the text and in the scholia. Marianus, no more diligent than Erasmus and no more fortunate in his new corruption, emends it as follows: “But famine μετὰ ἐκτάσεως ἰσχυροῦ [reading uncertain].” Ἔκτασις means “production” or “extension.” Previously ἐκστάσεως was read, but incorrectly. The meaning is that it was not merely said that a famine had occurred, but that a severe famine had also occurred, and this was written “with a certain extension.” Thus far Marianus.

Good heavens, what sort of Jerome do we possess in the old editions! Nothing in them is certainly genuine, and nothing is consistently Jerome’s; most things are fabricated and false, as may become clear from the present passage, which I have restored with the assistance of ten manuscript copies. | 74 |

## EPISTLE XXII. TO EUSTOCHIUM

Persius, *Satires* 3:

> “And like the sons of kings, you ask for tiny pap;  
> and, angry, refuse to lisp ‘mamma.’”

Here *pappare minutum* signifies children’s porridge, which we too call *papet*, as learned men before us have observed in Calpinus. Just as that ancient food was made from flour, water, honey or cheese, and a cooked egg, so the porridges of old men could be prepared from flour and the gravies of poultry and other meats. Hence the troublesome old man was accustomed to approve his dinner and such porridge by its smells of poultry and meat.

The other manuscript copies support this reading and meaning; for they all read the accusative forms *opopan* and *pepan* in this way: “He approves the dinner by its smells, and the poultry is commonly called *papizo*”; or, “and the poultry, by the term *pepa*, is commonly called *papizo*”; or finally, “and the poultry, by the term *geronepepan*, is commonly called *papizo*.” The Cluniacensis Codex, which we followed, adds after *pappezo*: “or *papio*.”

I could readily have supplied another reading, had I wished to alter anything in the ancient readings. I would instead conjecture that it should be read, while preserving the preceding reading: “He approves the dinner by its smells, like a poultry-bird *geronepopa*, which is commonly called *pappezo*.”

For it is certain and established in my experience from youth that the hoopoe, a most filthy little bird, which delights in cow dung and excrement, approves its dinner by its smells and flies on swift wings over those meadows which are fouled with bovine dung and excrement. Jerome could therefore have called the old man, for whom chastity and fasting were alike enemies, a *geronepupa* or *geronepepan*, one who approved his dinner by its smells, in imitation of ancient hoopoes that delighted in smells and dung.

If we wish to resort to Greek words and seek assistance from a foreign language, it must be read in a third and different way: “He approves his dinner by its smells, and the poultry γέρων ὁ τόππα [‘the old man, the *toppa*’; the second noun is uncertain or corrupt]; it is commonly called *pappizo*.” That is: that old man, a *popa* of the belly, gluttonous and insatiable, approves poultry and his dinner by the smells of meat and smoke, and gladly hastens to tavern delicacies.

These are, unless I am mistaken, the possibilities that can be devised for restoring this passage. From this you may see how fruitlessly those men labored who tried, through “younger cranes,” to restore and interpret this passage with many words.

Moreover, the hoopoe, which according to the second restoration was commonly called *pappezo* among the Romans, is now called *la plupe* by the Basques; for they call birds with feathered crests *aves plupades*. Hunters pursue them because they are plump and fat, and they are caught at the end of summer, together with fig-peckers and other little birds that become very fat at that season.

So that nothing may be lacking after our long meditation and strenuous labor, let us add a fourth reading of this kind, which has excellent sense: “He approves his dinner by its smells and the poultry; he is commonly called *papezo*.” He was commonly called *pappezo*, that is, *pappedo*, which we would say in French, *vieux gourmand*, or *père-gourmand*, just as in proverbial expressions we say *un vieux singe*, *un vieux barbon*, *un vieil ivrogne*, or *un maître ivrogne*.

If anyone discovers a better and truer restoration, we shall gladly accept it, provided that he demonstrates it rather than merely disparaging others. It is also worth remembering that this last reading belongs to Colbertinus Codex no. 2397. Since it omits the word *geronepopan*, it seems somewhat corrupt, although elsewhere it is an excellent and ancient copy.

Nevertheless, after inextricable difficulties, I believe it should be read from the same manuscript in this way: “He approves his dinner by its smells and the poultry, γέρων ὁ πάππας, and is commonly called *pappezo*.” There is no reading so easy and straightforward, either in words or in sense. For that cleric was an old man who approved his dinner and poultry by their smells; hence he is called *geron ho pappas* (‘the old man, the papa’), in French *ce vieux papa*, and was also commonly called *papezo* as a joke and term of contempt, just as an infant is called *pusio* among the ancient Latins.

*Concerning the clothing and footwear of the brothers:* “Let everything necessary be given by the abbot … so that every excuse based on necessity may be removed.”

*Super humeros hyacinthina laena* [“A hyacinth-colored cloak over the shoulders”]. This passage is altogether corrupt in the printed books, which read: “And across the shoulders, a hyacinth-colored cloak perhaps flying,” or, “And across the shoulders, a hyacinth-colored cloak flying in the manner of Mars.” Nothing concerning a hyacinth-colored cloak exists in the manuscript copies; these words were fabricated by those who did not understand the text.

It should therefore be read: “And flying over the shoulders, a *Maforte*.” *Maforte*, or rather *Marphote*, is a thin silk veil, which we now call *la coeffe*, and which in Vasconia is called *la Marsovile*. Among maidens this veil is white, among other women black. It often floats over the shoulders when the head has been tied rather loosely.

I have no doubt that this name derives from the Greek word μορφή, which signifies form and beauty of face. For this ornament is used to arrange and adorn the faces of women and maidens. Those who wish to make *Maforte* an Egyptian word have not paid sufficient attention to the fact that Jerome wrote this little work at Rome and was speaking of Roman maidens, not Egyptian monks. | 97 |

*Humilis sedeas* [“You should sit low down”]. In the Cluniacensis manuscript it is read: “Sit in a low place, with a stool for you,” etc. Quite a few others read: “Sit on the ground, with a stool for you,” etc. | 111 |

Et nudi impatientia [“And bare [feet], [able to endure] cold”]. Three or four manuscript copies read: “And bare feet exposed to the endurance of cold.” | 112 |

*Probat, et altilis geronepopam* [“He approves [it], and the poultry *geronepopam* [the final form is corrupt or coined]”]. This passage is exceedingly obscure and can scarcely be restored except with the assistance of the old manuscript books. Nevertheless, I would not hesitate to regard the reading of the Cluniacensis Codex as genuine, if it is correct in the ancient copies. For the sense of this reading represents Jerome’s thought to us, and the sequence of his discourse seems clear to me.

“He approves,” he says, “his dinner by its smells, and the poultry *geronepopam*, which is commonly called *pappezo*.” Certainly, if *geronepopa*, or *gerontopopa*, was a porridge or food of old men made from the juice of a fat fowl and wheat flour, commonly called *pappezo*, the ancient and excellent Cluniacensis Codex preserves nearly what Jerome had published.

And who does not know that *pappa* is children’s food or porridge, and that *pappare* means the same as to take food?

[Col. 1230]

112

*Quod Remoboth dicunt* [“What they call Remoboth”]. In the manuscript copies this word is written in more than one way. In very many we read *Ronnuoth*; in others, *Remnevoth* or *Remnoth*. Our holy father Benedict calls this the third kind of monks, *Sarabaites*, and adds a fourth kind, calling it *gyrovagi*, in chapter 1 of the Rule. Let anyone who wishes consult Cassian, *Conferences* 18, which is Priam’s, chapter 4, and chapter 7, where these monks are discussed.

As for what follows, “in our province,” do not understand this as Pannonia, Jerome’s homeland, or Italy, but Syria or Palestine, where Jerome first professed the monastic life. Consult Sulpicius Severus speaking about Jerome in the *Dialogue*. | 118 |

*Ut nemo dehabeat* [“So that no one may lack”]. All the manuscript copies, without exception, retain this reading. Ancient writers likewise use the word *dehabere*, in book 3 of *The Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 20: “Especially if they lack things and are needier.” Here you see that *dehabere* means “to have less” or “not to have sufficiently,” contrary to Marianus’s opinion.

Jerome’s meaning, therefore, is this: the steward so regulates everything in the monastery that no one lacks necessary things, no one asks for anything, and no one has less than is necessary. Saint Benedict, who seems to have composed several chapters of his Rule from this passage, says in chapter 55, “Of …”

[Col. 1231]

120

*Novem mensibus* [“For nine months”]. In the Cluniacensis manuscript a later hand wrote *novem* in place of *decem*; but the first scribe’s hand had written *decem*, which all the other ancient copies retain. Concerning the nine or ten months during which infants are customarily carried in the womb, consult physicians and writers on natural science. | 123 |

*Pone me sicut umbraculum in corde tuo* [“Set me like a shelter in your heart”]. The manuscript of the library of the eminent Cardinal Chigi appended much material after this, but since it is plainly spurious, we have disregarded it. | 126 |

## EPISTLE XXIII. TO MARCELLA

*De suis socculis detrahentem* [“Pulling her down by her slippers—that is, treating her with contempt”]. The printed books substitute a false reading here, while placing the true one in the margin or notes. For what does it mean to say “the designated consul detracting from his *socculi*,” or “detracting from his *socculi*”? The reading of the ancient copies must therefore be restored:

“Third, that we may show that the designated consul, who had treated her with contempt, is in hell.”

For Jerome was showing three things concerning holy Lea. First, that she should be accompanied by the rejoicing of all, since she had already received in heaven the crown of her virtues. Second, her life had briefly to be explained. Third, he was teaching that the designated consul Praetextatus, who had once treated Lea with contempt, was in hell, while she enjoyed eternal blessedness. | 127 |

## EPISTLE XXV. TO THE SAME WOMAN

*Interpretantur ἱκανὸν* [“They translate it as ἱκανόν, ‘sufficient’ or ‘mighty’”]. In place of this word Erasmus and Marianus inserted another word fabricated by themselves, namely ἅλκιμον (‘strong’ or ‘valiant’), of which there is no trace in the manuscript copies. These consistently read ἰκανόν, although in very many they are somewhat corrupt, where the corrupt forms ἂπανον and ἄκανον have also been falsely added. | 130 |

*ELOIM AND ELOE* [“Eloim and Eloe [divine names]”]. Johannes Drusius, in his notes on the book *On the Name Elohim*, rightly censures the old editions of Erasmus and Marianus in these words:

“Those who added Hebrew words to Jerome wrote Elohe, and, with excessive ignorance and ineptitude, Eloe, just as Manoa becomes Monoe, Noa Noe, Hosea Hoseae.”

But the learned man seems mistaken to me when he is surprised that Jerome placed *Elohim* and *Eloe* as two different names, because they truly are different, whether one calls *Eloe* Chaldean or Hebrew. | Ibid. |

*Aquila exercituum* [“Aquila: ‘of hosts’”]. The Cluniacensis manuscript reads: “Aquila and Theodotion translated it, ‘of armies.’” | 131 |

*ESER IEJE* [“Eser Ieje [a supplied divine-name form; no meaning is given here]”]. The same codex reads here *ASER IEJE*. Consult our notes above, column 271 and following, where the ten Names of God are discussed more fully. | Ibid. |

*Nonum τετράγραμμον* [“The ninth [name is] the τετράγραμμον, the four-letter Name”]. Quite a number of manuscript copies have *tetragramum*. | Ibid. |

*Non interpretatum ponitur* [“It is set down untranslated”]. Here we corrected an error in both the manuscripts and the printed books. In them it had previously been falsely read without the negative particle: “And in Ezekiel it is placed translated.” It should read: “It is placed untranslated,” namely in Ezekiel, chapter 10, verse 5: ὡς φωνὴ Θεοῦ Σαδδαί λαλοῦντος, “as the voice of God Saddai speaking.”

Symmachus and Theodotion render this as βροντὴ Θεοῦ ἱκανοῦ, “the thunder of the mighty God.” Hence it is clear that *Saddai* was translated as ἱκανὸν, “mighty,” not ἂλκιμον, as Erasmus and Marianus fabricate above. | Ibid. |

*Athenas, Thebas, Salonas* [“Athens, Thebes, Salona”]. In almost all the manuscript copies these are incorrectly written in Greek letters as ΑΙΘΕΝΑϹ ΘΕΒΑϹ ϹΑΔΟΝΑϹ [corrupt Greek spellings of ‘Athens, Thebes, Salona’]. | Ibid. |

## EPISTLE XXVI. TO THE SAME WOMAN

*Hebraeos, legitur* [“It is read in Hebrew [a fragmentary lemma]”]. These are the Hebrew words: in the previously printed books they were read as *halleluia chi tob samra*, with the *zayin* read most incorrectly as *z*. In Jerome’s Hebrew copy it seems to have been written *zammer*, not *zamera*, as it is read today. | 132 |

*Pro EJELETH* [“For, or in place of, Ajeleth”]. This is the title of Psalm 22, which has been discussed more fully in its proper place, in the notes on the *Canon of Hebrew Truth*. Consult the *Divine Library of Saint Jerome*, edited by us. It should be noted, however, that in place of *Ajeleth* all the manuscript copies ordinarily read *meleth*, because ancient scribes easily confused the letter *m* and the diphthong *ai*. | 133 |

*Ultroneas putere merces* [“That unsolicited wares stink”]. Horace, *Epistles* 2.2, to Julius Florus:

> “Many promises weaken trust, when he praises beyond measure  
> the merchandise he wishes to force upon buyers.”

| Ibid. |

## EPISTLE XXVII. TO THE SAME WOMAN

Jerome refers here to the account given by Livy, *Decades* III, book 5, concerning Jubellius Taurea, a Campanian knight, and Claudius Asellus, a Roman knight. From this, they say, arose the rustic proverb, “A gelding in a ditch.” Some think that Palladius the Galatian is being indicated here, because he deliberately disparaged Jerome on account of his new translation of Scripture.

Certainly, in some ancient manuscript copies I found something similar, namely this annotation, either in the text itself or after the text: “For he was a Gaul who had detracted from the translation.” Consult what we said in volume III, in chapter 4 of the Prophet Jonah, where the gelding rebukes Jerome.

In this passage, however, I think that some follower of Montanus is being subtly indicated, rather than Palladius the Galatian, a Greek who was scarcely known to Jerome at this time. See Epistle XXVI, concerning the half-men and the emasculated.

*Gallicis Cantheriis* [“Than Gallic geldings [a fragmentary lemma]”]. Plautus, in the *Aulularia*: “Let them be cheaper than Gallic geldings.” A *cantherius* is a gelded horse, so called because it lacks seed. I do not know whether he had in mind …

[Col. 1232]

135

## EPISTLE XXVIII. TO THE SAME WOMAN

*Quid prodest ad ἐργοδιώκτην* [“What good does it do for the ἐργοδιώκτης, the taskmaster or work-driver?”]. We have restored this passage, which was thoroughly corrupted, chiefly with the help of two manuscript copies, one Cluniacensis and the other Sancygirannus. These preserve the pure and complete word ἐργοδιώκτην, which Erasmus had altered by conjecture to ἐπισιωπᾶν με.

An *ergodioctes* is one who drives on work, just as Marcella pressed Jerome’s labors. Consult the Greek edition of the Septuagint translators at Exodus 1:11 and 3, and the *Epitaph of Nepotianus*, whom Jerome called an ἐργοδιώκτην. Origen likewise calls Ambrose this in one of his Epistles, because Ambrose demanded work from Origen every day with incredible zeal. See the *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers* under Hippolytus. | Ibid. |

*Saepe quaerens causas* [“Often asking the reasons”]. From this passage we identified a well-known and unmistakable Epistle of Origen that has not yet been published. It is found copied, together with various short works on the Psalms, in a very ancient Greek manuscript of the Royal Library, but without a title or the author’s name. One of our scholars will perhaps publish this work of Origen at some time. | 137 |

*Post AMUDA* [“After *amuda*”]. Origen, in the work mentioned above, has μετὰ τοῦ ἀμοῦδα, that is, “after *amuda*”; and all Jerome’s manuscript copies likewise read this without exception. From this we observed that all the Hebrew words are read in corrupted form in Erasmus and Marianus, who foist the Masoretes upon us in place of Origen and Jerome, reading *ammudeia*. | 138 |

*Pro quo apud Aquilam* [“In place of this, according to Aquila”]. The Erasmus edition incorrectly reads, “in place of which Aquila.” For, besides the fact that Jerome’s manuscript copies retain “in place of which, according to Aquila,” Origen himself has it this way:

> Ἀντὶ δὲ τούτου παρὰ μὲν Ἀκύλα, μετὰ θυρεὸν, καὶ πόλεμον, καὶ μάχαιραν, τὸ αἰεί

That is: “In place of this, according to Aquila, ‘after shield, and war, and sword,’ always.” | Ibid. |

*Post UMALAMA* [“After *umalama*”]. The Latin copies have *omalama* or *omalaama*, because the ancients indiscriminately took and read *ou* for *o*, and *o* for *ou*. In the Greek of Origen we read ὀυμάλομα, *umalama*, as I restored it. Erasmus and Marianus have the thoroughly corrupt *umilhama*. | Ibid. |

*ANIE ARES* [“Anie ares [‘the meek of the earth,’ as explained below]”]. In Origen’s Greek: κατὰ τὸ ἀνίη αρς· ὅ ἕστι, πραεῖς τῆς γῆς, τὸ σολ, that is: “after *anie ars*, that is, ‘the meek of the earth,’ *sela*.” Jerome’s Latin copies likewise retain *anie ares*, *annie ares*, or *aniares*. Hence we know with certainty that the ancient writers read in the Hebrew text [Hebrew form absent in the supplied source], and not *aneve erez*, as Erasmus and Marianus falsely read. | 139 |

*Cujus nos maluimus* [“Whose [reading] we preferred [a fragmentary lemma]”]. Erasmus suspects that this passage should be read: “Whose prudent ignorance we preferred to follow in this discussion alone, rather than to possess the foolish knowledge of those who do not know.” The Cluniacensis manuscript retains what we published; several others have *peritiam sequi*, as did the previously printed books. | Ibid. |

## EPISTLE XXIX. TO THE SAME WOMAN

*altissimum nepotum gurgitem vocat* [“he calls it the deepest whirlpool of descendants”]. Juvenal also mentions this. Since a little earlier Jerome compared conversation conducted through letters with a banquet, he now, remembering the metaphor, calls the reader a fastidious guest, whose palate finds nothing tasty unless it is highly refined and seasoned with various condiments of eloquence. The subject itself is like food; verbal ornament is the seasoning.

So far Erasmus. I add briefly that among the thirteen or fourteen manuscript copies I collated, not one fails to read distinctly what we published. These manuscripts are two Vatican copies, two Remigian copies, two Sorbonic copies, one Royal, one Colbertine, one Cluniacensis, one Sangermanensis, one from the convent of Saint Dominic at Toulouse, one Sancygirannus, and another from the College of Navarre. None of these supports Erasmus’s conjectures in any way. Therefore, rather than impose Erasmus upon the reader in place of Jerome, we preferred to leave the text as it is found in the oldest copies.

He says: “It is remarkable how corrupted this passage is in all the copies. I think it should be read in the following way, so that I may not torment the reader as long as I myself was tormented. Aquila, however, called what they called ἱμάτιον and ἐπίρραμμα, that is, ‘garment’ and ‘undergarment,’ ἕνδυμα and ἐπένδυμα, which is a tunic worn underneath; and what in Hebrew is called *mail*, [Hebrew term absent in the supplied source], ἐπένδυμα, that is, an upper tunic. Ἐπωμίς, however, which in Hebrew is called *ephod*, although it signifies an upper cloak,” etc.

Marianus Victorius shows that this emendation is defective in many respects. But he himself was no more successful in restoring this passage, since he often imitates Erasmus and leaves the reader uncertain about Jerome’s genuine reading. With the assistance of fifteen manuscript copies, we present the pure text—not, however, with how much labor, lest I seem to exalt myself insolently before my rivals. | Ibid. |

The Cluniacensis Codex falsely entitles this Epistle “To Bishop Damasus,” and in the text adjusts certain words to the fictitious title, for example, *Verum totus in* instead of *Verum tota in*. | Ibid. |

*Tale convivium doctrinae* [“Such a banquet of learning”]. The same manuscript and several others read, “such a banquet of your conversation”; consequently, many also read it in this way: “But you are wholly occupied with treatises … and compel people to read the Scriptures.” | Ibid. |

*Non sunt suaves epulae* [“The dishes are not pleasant”]. To make the meaning of this passage easier to understand, I shall transcribe the entire Erasmian scholion:

> “‘The dishes are not pleasant.’ This passage was found variously corrupted in almost all the copies. Some had it written this way: ‘Which do not please and smell sweet.’ When I compare the traces of the ancient copies, it seems to me that it should be read: ‘The dishes are not pleasant if they do not smell of *placenta*, if Apicius has not seasoned them, and if nothing from the masters of our time fumes in them.’ I do not know whether, instead of *magistrorum*, one should read *magirorum*, that is, cooks.
>
> “*Placenta* is a type of food once regarded as a delicacy. Apicius earned distinction through his skill in culinary matters. Some of his commentaries on cooking and seasoning foods are still extant. Pliny …”

[Col. 1233]

140

*Sed quia vector* [“But because [he is] a traveler or carrier [a fragmentary lemma]”]. In some manuscript copies: “traveler and intermediary.” | Ibid. |

*Si eloquentiam quaeris* [“If you seek eloquence”]. Likewise, some copies read: “if we seek eloquence.” | Ibid. |

*Et Samuel* [“And Samuel”]. Let the reader observe that Jerome is quoting Scripture according to the version of the Septuagint translators; he had not yet published a new edition from the Hebrew sources. | Ibid. |

Doec Syrus mortificavit [“Doeg the Syrian killed him”]. Vaticanus 342 reads: “Doeg the Idumean killed the Syrian.” | Ibid. |

*Abimelech filii Achitoh* [“Abimelech, son of Achitoh”]. Some manuscript copies read *Abimelech*, which I likewise find written in the Septuagint. | 141 |

*Esse non possit* [“It cannot be”]. The Royal manuscript reads: “cannot be a garment”; several others: “cannot be a type of garment.” | Ibid. |

*Et fuit in domo Michae* [“And it was in the house of Micha”]. Marianus, against Erasmus, wished to alter this thoroughly corrupted passage, which was devoid of all sense. He censures Erasmus in the following annotation:

> “This passage was previously exceedingly corrupt and entirely without meaning. It has now been restored with the help of the Septuagint version from which it was taken. Thus they read in Judges 17, where this story is found: καὶ ὁ οἶκος Μιχα, αὐτῷ οἶκος Θεοῦ, that is, ‘Micha consecrated and dedicated his house to that God’ …”

Previously, however, through Erasmus’s corruption rather than correction, it was read: “He made that carved and molten image which was in the house of Micha; and the man Micha, and his house, of God.” What this was supposed to mean would have been for him himself to explain.

But all the Hebrew, Greek, and Latin books show that Erasmus was unjustly censured by Marianus. For although the Marian reading is found in the Roman edition of the Septuagint, Erasmus’s genuine Jerome text is found in the Alexandrian manuscript.

We therefore read it written as follows:

> Καὶ ἐγένετο ἐν τῷ οἴκῳ Μειχά. Καὶ ὁ ἀνὴρ Μειχά, αὐτῷ οἶκος Θεοῦ.

That is: “And it came to pass in the house of Micha. And the man Micha, for him a house of God.”

The Chaldean Paraphrast explains the passage by saying: “And the man Micha, for him a house of error.” But the Syriac Interpreter makes it clearer still: “For that man Micha had a shrine of gods.”

Finally, in the Hebrew source it is written [Hebrew form absent in the supplied source], *Ve’isch Micha, lo beth Elohim*, that is: “And the man Micha, for him a house of God”—as if it were said: “And the man Micha was the man in whose house there was a house of an idol.”

Surely this could not have been wholly unknown to Erasmus’s harsh critic and false restorer of Jerome’s passage. Moreover, all the Latin manuscript copies favor Erasmus; none favors the restoration of Marianus Victorius. It was my concern to award victory to the truth and to inform the reader of it. | Ibid. |

*Coarguit igitur eorum opinionem* [“Therefore he refutes their opinion”]. Several manuscripts read in the opposite sense: “Their opinion is refuted, for those who wished to make the question insoluble,” etc. But the reading of the others must be retained, whatever Marianus may wish against Erasmus. For the question becomes insoluble if, with the ancient Greeks and Latins, we say that the *ephod* was made of silver, since Scripture consistently says that the *ephod* was woven from linen, or from gold, hyacinth, purple, scarlet, and fine linen—not from silver, as those thought who made the question insoluble. | 142 |

Et Sacerdotes Nobe hoc dignitatis suae insigne portabant [“And the priests of Nob wore this badge of their rank”]. In Erasmus we falsely read here: “And the priests of Nob, *bad*, that is, carried the emblem of their dignity.” | Ibid. |

*Et vestivit eum ὑποδύτην* [“And he clothed him in a ὑποδύτης, an undergarment”]. The printed books read ὑποδύτην, following the Septuagint translators of the Roman edition. But among fifteen manuscript copies there is not one that does not retain ἐπενδύτην or ὑπενδύτην. The manuscript of the monastery of Sancygirannus reads ΕΠΗΝΔΙΤΗΝ; others read ΥΠΕΝΔΙΤΗ or ΥΠΕΝΔΥΤΗΝ. I also find this reading, Ἐπενδύτην, in the Alexandrian manuscript of the Septuagint translators.

I therefore believe it should by no means be changed, even though ὑποδύτην better corresponds to Jerome’s explanation, “a garment worn under the tunic,” and although below it is said that the Septuagint translators used ὑποδύτην and ἐπωμίδα. Nor does it matter that the manuscript copies read ὑπενδύτην, since ancient inexperienced scribes change *e* into *y*, as in *ypenduma* for *ependuma*. | 143 |

*Quod illi ὑποδύτην et ἐπωμίδα dixerunt* [“What they called a ὑποδύτης, ‘undergarment,’ and an ἐπωμίς, ‘shoulder garment’”]. How greatly this passage troubled Erasmus’s diligence is plainly shown in the scholia.

[Col. 1234]

Ibid.

*Audiens bar* [“Hearing *bar* [a fragmentary lemma]”]. Saint Jerome recalls this error in book 3 of his *Commentary on Zechariah*, chapter 12. Saint Augustine, however, reads *Bar* or *Bad* in Question 12 on Judges. Consult those passages if you wish. | 144 |

*PHESTHA significantius exprimatur* [“Let *phestha* be expressed more precisely”]. The manuscripts do not read *pistha*, but *effertim* and *efferth*, or *efferthain*. The Cluniacensis reads: “*effertain* may be expressed more significantly”; the Sancygirannus: “*restam* may be expressed more significantly.”

From so many and such great corruptions of the Hebrew word, it is sufficiently clear that the reading must be *phesta* in the singular, [Hebrew form absent in the supplied source], which today they read *pistha*; or certainly in the plural, [Hebrew form absent in the supplied source], *phesthim*, corresponding to the plural forms *effertim* and *efferthain* in the manuscript copies. | Ibid. |

*Quia ubicumque cum hac littera scribitur* [“Because wherever it is written with this letter”]. From this observation of Jerome we learn that many things in the ancient Hebrew copies differed from what is read in the present Masoretic text. For the name *Cherubim*, which in Ezekiel chapter 10 signifies living creatures, is very often written without *vau* in this form [Hebrew form absent in the supplied source].

We mention this so that the prudent reader may know that the Hebrew words in Jerome’s works should by no means be restored according to the reading and vowel-pointing of the present Masoretic tradition. | 145 |

*Quam vellem nunc tibi* [“How I would wish [it] for you now”]. He fulfilled that wish in the preceding Epistle to Fabiola, concerning the dress of the priest. | Ibid. |

Praesens percontator praesentem [“Let one who is present question one who is present”]. The manuscripts read: “question the present [person] in person.” There is no change of meaning, although the final letter *r* of the imperative verb has been omitted.

Moreover, both the printed books and many manuscript copies omit the entire clause, “Common mother,” etc. It is, however, very familiar to Jerome, as in Epistle 74: “I wish our common mother Albina well,” etc. | 146 |

*Juxta Aesopici canis fabulam* [“According to the fable of Aesop’s dog”]. Several manuscript copies read: “according to the Aesopian fable,” or “according to the fable of Aesop.” There is also a fable about a dog who, when he saw a larger shadow in the water and gaped at it with open jaws, lost the piece of meat that he was holding in his mouth. | Ibid. |

## EPISTLE XXX. TO PAULA

Some manuscript copies entitle this Epistle “To Marcella,” but this is plainly a scribal error arising from ignorance, since Jerome declared in the book of Hebrew Names that he had written this Epistle to Paula. See above, column 51, line 16, and the conclusion of the Epistle itself. | Ibid. |

*Theologicen sibi vendicant* [“They claim theology for themselves”]. All the manuscript copies read this, except the Cluniacensis, which has *Theologicam*. The previously printed books therefore read *theoricem* incorrectly. The reading of our manuscript copies is confirmed by Henricus Valesius in his notes on book 1 of Eusebius Pamphilus’s *Ecclesiastical History*. | 147 |

*Tres versiculos qui sibi* [“Three little verses which to themselves … [incomplete lemma]”]. One manuscript from our monastery of Saint Andrew near Avignon reads in this way: “three verses which are appended,” etc. | Ibid. |

*Nisi Ethicae* [“Unless [from] the Ethics”]. The same manuscript, as well as the Cluniacensis, retains the reading of the printed books. Another from Saint Remigius has: “unless from the Ethics themselves,” etc. The Sancygirannus has: “unless from the very beginnings of the Ethics, according to the second …” A few copies agree with the printed books: “unless we have taken it from Ethics,” etc. | 148 |

*Conterat Satanam* [“May he crush Satan”]. The same wording occurs in the *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*, chapter 3, verse 15: “And the Lord will swiftly crush Satan beneath our feet.” | 150 |

## EPISTLE XXXI. TO EUSTOCHIUM

*Velle honorare Martyrem* [“To wish to honor the Martyr”]. I find that the learned man was greatly mistaken here when he thought that Jerome meant Peter of Alexandria, whose feast day is celebrated on the seventh day before the Kalends of December. Certainly cherries do not grow in Rome in November, but in June, around the time of the feast of blessed Peter the Apostle, on which day they were sent by Eustochium together with other little gifts.

Here, therefore, understand “the Martyr” and “the Apostle” to mean Peter, who suffered martyrdom at Rome. | 125 |

## EPISTLE XXXII. TO MARCELLA

The beginning is: “The day before yesterday,” etc. For this reason, in many manuscript copies it is entitled “To Marcella,” as was noted in its proper place in volume II of our edition. The preceding Epistle, however, is addressed to Eustochium and concerns the little gifts.

Two Epistles. One of those two Epistles was the same as the one written to Paula concerning the Hebrew alphabet, of which …

[Col. 1235]

152

## EPISTLE XXXIII. TO PAULA

*Damnatur a Demetrio* [“He is condemned by Demetrius”]. Jerome mentions this Epistle in the *Book of Ecclesiastical Writers*, under Origen, where he observes that Bishop Demetrius raged against Origen with such madness that he wrote throughout the whole world concerning his name. Whoever wishes may consult the passage, and Eusebius of Caesarea’s *Ecclesiastical History*, book VI, etc. | 154 |

*Urbe Romana* [“At Rome”]. Rufinus, in book 2 of his invectives against Jerome, rejoices that he has found in these words an occasion for calumny; but with unhappy judgment he turns them against his own author, as may be seen below in the *Apology of the Holy Doctor against His Accuser*. | Ibid. |

## EPISTLE XXXIV. TO MARCELLA

*Acacius dehinc* [“Acacius thereafter”]. Concerning the same man, in the *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*: “As a young man,” he says, “he was educated at Caesarea; and afterwards, as bishop of that same city, he attempted with much labor to restore on parchment the corrupted library of Origen and Pamphilus.” | 155 |

*Et PHE* [“And PHE”]. This passage seems to indicate that Origen published treatises on the letters of the Hebrew alphabet. The manuscripts consistently read not *Phe* but *Fe*. | Ibid. |

Τῶν δίαπονημάτων [“Of the labors”]. The previously printed books omit the article τῶν, which I have nevertheless found in all the manuscript copies. The same copies subsequently read κακαπαθούμενον [“suffering hardship”]. | Ibid. |

*Reprehendere non audeo* [“I do not dare to censure”]. To prove that I do not serve my own resentment at all, but rather take every precaution not to injure anyone, I pass over certain scholia in Hilary’s commentary on Psalm 126 that are wholly inconsistent with the truth. It is enough to have said that the author of such scholia was greatly mistaken, and that, merely by comparing this Epistle with the aforementioned commentaries of Saint Hilary on Psalm 126, whatever he wrote against Jerome is found to be false without any effort. | 156 |

*Executus est* [“He carried it out”]. Some manuscript copies read: “and he was more fully excused for another’s error.” | Ibid. |

*Sexta ὰκὀνεος νοῦ* [“The sixth [book or work] of a sharpened mind [the Greek is corrupt]”]. Thus reads the Royal manuscript, which is corrupt in almost all other places. The other manuscript copies likewise retain the same Greek word, though slightly corrupted in its letters: for instead of ἀκόνεος (‘sharpened’) they read the corrupt forms ΕΚΟΝΗΟΣ, ΕΚΩΝΗΟΣ, or ΕΚΟΝΕΟΣ. Now ἀκονὴς means “sharp” or “sharpened,” just as in Hesychius νεηκονὴς means “newly sharp.” From this you may understand how false is Marianus’s annotation on the present passage, where he rebukes Erasmus in these words: “Sexta ἡκονηθέντος νοῦ. That is, ‘of a keen mind,’ as he himself explains; and all the manuscript copies have it thus. Therefore there is no need for Erasmus, at his own pleasure, to substitute ὠξηκονήμενοι, that is, ‘sharpened.’” Certainly, if Marianus were alive in our time, I would confidently challenge him to produce Jerome’s manuscript copies, knowing that there is absolutely none in which ἠκονηθέντους νοῦ [intended sense: ‘of a sharpened mind’] is read, whereas all retain what I have just observed. | 157 |

*Cujusdam librum* [“A certain person’s book”]. Saint Athanasius has almost the same words in volume I of the new edition, column 1224. Thus the above-mentioned scholiast of Hilary is shown to be mistaken, for he thought that this elegant thought had been taken from Hilary. | Ibid. |

*CHAPHACH* [“Chaphach [a supplied Hebrew form; no meaning is given here]”]. The books previously printed read *Caphecha*, in accordance with current usage; so that from first to last there is not a single Hebrew word which they have not corrupted in all the works of Saint Jerome. | 158 |

## EPISTLE XXXVI. OF DAMASUS

The sense seems to require “while they were disputing,” contrary to Marianus’s opinion.

*Excitare disposui* [“I resolved to stir up”]. Two manuscript copies read *excitare debui*. | Ibid. |

*Et heri tabellario* [“And yesterday, by the courier [a fragmentary lemma]”]. Marianus altered this passage and maintained that it should be read: “because, when the courier Etherius had been sent back to me.” Baronius likewise considered this reading genuine in his *Ecclesiastical Annals* for the year of Christ 378. There the learned man asserts that Jerome was staying in Jerusalem when Damasus wrote the present Epistle to him. But above, in the Prolegomena to this second volume, I demonstrated the contrary view by chronological arguments. | Ibid. |

*Noctium operis* [“Of the work of nights”]. Very many manuscript copies read “by stolen labors of the nights”; two others, “in the hours of the night.” | 159 |

*Etiam si negasses* [“Even if you had refused”]. Marianus’s edition, and quite a few manuscript copies, read: “what I had wished to ask, even if you had refused.” | Ibid. |

*Lactantii dederas libros* [“You had given the books of Lactantius”]. In two manuscript copies *lectitanti* is corruptly written for *Lactantii*. | Ibid. |

*Ejus usque* [“Of it, up to … [incomplete lemma]”]. Previously printed books read “and most of the Epistles in them, up to …”; but all the manuscripts retain the text printed here. | Ibid. |

*Philosophis disputantibus* [“While the philosophers were disputing”]. Both the printed and manuscript books vary in this word: most have *disputandis*, others *disputantia*.

[Col. 1236]

159

## EPISTLE XXXVI. TO DAMASUS

—since Jerome wrote φενόλην (‘cloak’ or *paenula*) in Greek, or *Phenolen* in Latin letters.

*Interim jam et ego linguam* [“Meanwhile, now I too [my] tongue … [incomplete lemma]”]. The printed books read: “Meanwhile, however, I too [my] tongue.” | 160 |

*Verum quia heri diacono* [“But because yesterday, by a deacon [a fragmentary lemma]”]. This is the same difficulty as above in Damasus’s Epistle to Jerome, and Marianus Victorius did not weigh it sufficiently. For the very sequence of the Epistles, together with the older and better manuscript copies, teaches that it should be read: “because yesterday, when a deacon had been sent to me.” But we have discussed these matters at length in our Prolegomena. | Ibid. |
## “I drafted these things for you.”

This passage is extremely corrupt in the Erasmian edition, which Marianus therefore rightly corrects in these words: “This passage was especially corrupted in Erasmus; for it read *αὐτοσχεδιαστὶ*, and ‘I discussed food immediately’ (*et cibi confestim discussi*), that is, ‘discussed extemporaneously and without prior preparation.’” But apart from the fact that what Hieronymus had worked out was missing here—namely, the case which grammarians call the accusative—the verb had no case to follow it, and the word *et* was also superfluous. The error arose because someone knowledgeable in Greek first translated *ταῦτά σοι ἐσχεδίασα* as *haec tibi confestim discussi*, “I discussed these things with you extemporaneously”; then the translation was inserted into the manuscript, and *haec* was substituted for it, since the Greek verb had been explained in Latin. Thus one error continually gives birth to another, and so forth. | Ibid. |

### Our Tertullian, that is

The Morbacensis manuscript, eight hundred years old, reads without the pronoun: “Tertullian and Novatian have been published in the Latin language.” | Ibid. |

### In the volume of the Expositions

One of the Colbertine manuscripts reads: “in the volume of the expository works on Romans.” | 161 |

### Comparing with the Hebrew language

Five manuscripts read: “let us arrange it together with the Hebrew itself.” | Ibid. |

### “VAYOMAR LO ADONAI,” etc.

All the manuscripts read this way. In modern Hebrew we read: *Vaiomer lo Adonai lachen kol horeg Cain shivathaim juqqam*. The modern Hebrew text does not add a paragogic *vav* in the final word, unlike Hieronymus’s Hebrew exemplars, which he seems to have read as *jucccamo* or *joccamo*. This is a Hophal future with a paragogic affix, as though it were said: “He himself shall be punished,” or “He shall be avenged.” | Ibid. |

### *Hebdomas*

Through the ignorance of ancient copyists, *hebdomadas* was substituted for *hebdomas*, that is, “the seventh.” Nor is the Erasmian reading *hebdomada* any better. In Greek, *ἔβδομος* means “seventh”; and, if I am not mistaken, Hieronymus wrote *hebdomos*, not *hebdomas*, because *ἐβδομάς* is the number seven, not “the seventh,” as Hieronymus interprets it. | Ibid. |

### To bear the very light

The word *tremebundus* is omitted in many manuscript copies. | 162 |

### And by the agitation of a maddened mind

Very many manuscripts read: “and will understand that he is driven by a maddened mind”; or: “and understands that he is driven by a maddened mind”; or: “he understands that he himself is driven.” | Ibid. |

### To end the torments of death

They similarly read here: “to end the torments of a shortened death.” | Ibid. |

### “Let the slayer release”

Two or three manuscripts read: “let him release the slain.” As many read: “let him acquit by the killing.” | Ibid. |

### Enoch begot Irad

The Morbacensis manuscript reads: “Enoch begot Gaidad,” in accordance with the faulty reading of the Greeks. See J. Drusius, *Henoch*, chapter 4. | 163 |

### “Or in some Hebrew [book]”

Hieronymus acknowledges twice in this response the apocryphal books of the Hebrews; whether they still survive, I truly do not know. | Ibid. |

### “He has given himself over to his crime”

Five manuscripts read: “he has given himself over to his crimes.” | Ibid. |

### “He continued through the Flood”

Several manuscript copies read: “he continued through the waters of the Flood,” and so forth. | 164 |

### Through the longevity of grief

Several manuscripts read: “compelled by grief over a long life.” | Ibid. |

### “Consecrated,” in the Gospel

Six handwritten copies have: “he consecrates the debtor placed in the Gospel.” | 165 |

### About eight

Not “about eighteen,” but “about sixteen,” is found in a great many manuscripts. | Ibid. |

### To Phinehas

Six or seven manuscripts read here: “from Amram and to Phinehas.” | 166 |

### He calls it *Φενόλην* according to some

Grammarians and interpreters of Holy Scripture dispute the word *φελόνης* or *φενόλης*, which is read at 2 Timothy 4:13 and which Edward Leigh discusses at length in his *Sacred Criticism*, page 343. But here we ought to present only what is peculiar to Hieronymus.

Accordingly, eight manuscript codices, which I carefully examined with attentive eyes, read the previously mentioned word as follows: “which Paul calls *Phenolem*”; or, “which Paul calls *Poenolon* or *Penolem”; one manuscript of the monastery of Saint Cygirannus reads, “which Paul calls the *penula*.” Erasmus and Marianus therefore read falsely when they print *αἰλόνην* and *φαλόνην*. | [Col. 1237] | 167 |

### “VAMUSIM ALU”

The Hebrew which they read in Hieronymus is: *Vahamusim alu bene Israel meerez Mizraim*. | Ibid. |

### “AMESA DOR”

This passage was altogether corrupted in the books previously published. For instead of *Amesa dor*, as Hieronymus wrote it, they changed the gender and the order of the words, reading *Dor amisi*, in the masculine, contrary to the testimony of all the manuscript copies of the Epistle to Damasus. | Ibid. |

### In the priesthood of God

Almost all the manuscripts read as follows: “numbered with Moses in the Psalter,” and so forth. This refers, of course, to Psalm 98:6: “Moses and Aaron among his priests, and Samuel among those who call upon his name.” Samuel is also numbered with Moses in Jeremiah 15:1: “Though Moses and Samuel stood before me,” and so forth. | 168 |

### Always ignorant

The printed books read: “And, ignorant through each of his seven sons.” In several manuscripts the continuation reads: “He does not know up to David.” | 169 |

### He could kill

Here, too, Erasmus and Marianus read: “and the one who afterward, if he could, would kill his brother.” | Ibid. |

### “The voice, indeed”

Some manuscript copies read: “This voice is the voice of Jacob.” Others: “The voice—the voice of Jacob is.” | Ibid. |

### Tender and good

The previously printed books read: “it signifies teachable and innocent souls.” The cloak or garment of Esau, and so forth. But all our Vatican, Gallican, and German manuscripts consistently retain what we have printed. The verb *sunt*—“are”—or *significantur*—“are signified”—is therefore understood. For, in the allegorical sense, the tender and good kids signify teachable and innocent souls. | 170 |

### The power of the resurrection

Quite a few very ancient and excellent manuscripts read: “he enjoys the fragrance”; and: “a clear proclamation of resurrection and kingdom.” | Ibid. |

### “The days of my father’s passion are drawing near”

All the manuscripts read in this way: “may they draw near,” and so forth. None reads “they are drawing near,” in accordance with Marianus’s alteration. | Ibid. |

## EPISTLE XXXVII. TO MARCELLA

### Of Rheticius, Bishop of Autun

He mentions this Rheticius in the *Catalogue of Illustrious Men* and in the second Epistle to Florentius, in these words: “I earnestly ask you to prevail upon the blessed Rheticius, Bishop of Autun, to lend you his commentaries for copying, in which he expounded the Song of Songs in a more sublime sense.” | 171 |

### To be a homonymous word

Erasmus reads: “to be a homonymous word.” *ὑμώνυμον*, moreover, means “equivocal,” since the same word signifies different things; thus the name Tharsis used here signifies a region of India, a precious stone, and the sea itself. | 172 |

### With the letter *tau* changed

The editions of this passage differ. The Erasmian edition reads: “Although Josephus thinks that, with *tau* changed into the letter *theta*, the Greeks call it Tarsus instead of Tharsis.” Marianus has it differently: “Although Josephus thinks that, with the letter changed, the Greeks,” and so forth.

Josephus himself, in *Antiquities*, book 1, chapter 7, says the following about the same word: *τὸ ταῦ πρὸς τὴν κλῆσιν, ἀντὶ τοῦ θῆτα μεταβαλλόντων*, that is, “with *tau* changed into *theta* for the designation.” These words undoubtedly show the genuine reading, which we have restored on the authority of the manuscript copies. | 173 |

### Flowing in the high buskin

A lofty manner of speaking is called *cothurnus*, “buskin,” and was used among tragic poets. Hence Virgil’s line in the Eclogue: “Your songs alone are worthy of Sophoclean buskins.” In his Epistle to Florentius, Hieronymus appears to favor this interpretation, for he says that the Song of Songs was expounded by Rheticius of Autun in a more sublime sense. | Ibid. |

### So that no one could

The Cluniacensis manuscript adds: “of his descendants.” | Ibid. |

## EPISTLE XXXVIII. TO THE SAME

This Epistle is entitled in the manuscript books *On the Conversion of Blesilla*. This is rightly said, since in this Epistle Hieronymus wrote both about Blesilla’s illness and about her conversion. | Ibid. |

### “Which, finally”

We previously restored this passage in the commentaries of the same Saint Hieronymus on chapter 2 of the Epistle to Titus, where we said that it should be read as follows: “Although there are very many who are not ashamed of their gray hair and, trembling before a crowd of grandchildren, adorn themselves like little girls.”

If the particle *ut*—“so that” or “as”—is added here, the meaning is clear: although old women trembling before a crowd of grandchildren, they nevertheless adorn and beautify themselves like little girls. Without that particle, the phrase is presented ironically: “trembling little girls,” as though he were saying that the little girls whom they imitate are trembling from old age. | 175 |

## EPISTLE XXXIX. TO PAULA

### Notes

The others, together with the printed books, omit *sentiens*—“perceiving”—and everything up to *Confidimus*—“We trust.” Some also read: “We trust, approving what we say. Conversion is never too late.”

### Half-alive on the little bed

In other manuscript codices we read, with the same meaning: “would surround the half-alive man on his little bed,” and so forth. | 177 |

### Be secure

The Cluniacensis codex of excellent [reading incomplete in the source] reads in this way. | [Col. 1238] | 177 |

## EPISTLE XL. TO MARCELLA

I am astonished that Erasmus, and especially Marianus, wished to change the title and inscription of this Epistle. In all the manuscript codices—namely, in twenty or more which I have seen—it is entitled not “To Bonasus,” but “To Marcella about Onasus,” in this form: “Hieronymus to Marcella concerning Onasus.” Or in another form: “Here begins [the Epistle] about Onasus to Marcella,” or something similar.

They then falsely changed the name *Onasus* to *Bonasus*, although there is no manuscript exemplar in which we do not read “concerning Onasus,” and Onasus Segestanus in the body of the Epistle. But Onasus was called by an auspicious name, namely *Onasus*, that is, *Onasimus* or *Onesimus*, which in the Book of Hebrew Names is understood as “useful,” “comely,” or “corresponding.” It did not come from *Naso*, “Bonasus,” as the ancient editors absurdly supposed, since they failed to notice that a man called by an auspicious name was mocked by Hieronymus with laughter because of his enormous nose, or the ugliness of that nose: “Let not the Nose appear in the face,” and so forth. | 186 |

### Onasus of Segesta

This is how we read it in all the manuscript copies, and I do not think Marianus ever saw one in which *Bonasus* was written. Onasus was from Egesta, or Segesta, a city of Sicily, where there is an Egestan or Segestan market. | 187 |

### Because you are called by an auspicious name

I said above that this auspicious name was *Onasus*, a shortened and abbreviated form of *Onasimus* or *Onesimus*, a name meaning “honorable” in the Book of Hebrew Names. | Ibid. |

### May the king and queen desire you as a son-in-law

The manuscript codices read: “May the king and queen, the girl, and so forth, desire you as a handsome son-in-law.” | Ibid. |

## EPISTLE XLI. TO THE SAME

### In agreement with us throughout the world

I do not wish to accuse Erasmus of deliberate deception in this corruption of Hieronymus’s text. But I can scarcely refrain from censuring Marianus Victor, who did not know how to correct Erasmus here, despite the authority and agreement of the ancient codices. For they read: “with the whole world agreeing with us,” and not: “with the time of year agreeing with us.” Thus the entire world agreed with us in observing Lent. | 189 |

### And a half-man

He calls him mutilated and a half-man because Montanus was from Phrygia, where the priests of Cybele were accustomed to be castrated. | 190 |

## EPISTLE XLIII. TO THE SAME

### I will not buy firewood

There was no need to buy firewood to ward off the cold, because the forest near Bethlehem abundantly supplied firewood; and if it had to be purchased, it could have been obtained at a lower price. | 194 |

### On earth. Farewell.

What follows in the printed books is not found in the manuscript codices. There is no doubt that it was transferred here by incompetent scribes from the preceding Epistle of Paula and Eustochium. | Ibid. |

## EPISTLE XLVI. OF PAULA AND EUSTOCHIUM TO THE SAME

### Certainly, even if

Cicero, *Against Verres*, in the *Divinatio*: “If from childhood you had devoted yourself to the best disciplines and arts, and had labored in them; if you had learned Greek literature at Athens, not Lilybaeum, and Latin at Rome, not in Sicily.” | 206 |

## EPISTLE XLVIII. TO PAMMACHIUS

### “It is said against those things which the pagans say”

We retain what we read in eight manuscript copies.

In very many manuscript copies this Apology has another title, namely: “Here begins the Apologetic Book to Pammachius”; or: “The Apologetic Epistle of Saint Hieronymus to Pammachius.” In the preface to his Commentaries on Jonah, Hieronymus calls it an *Apologeticum*; and in the preface to Book I on Jeremiah, he calls it an *Apologia*. “Let him read the Apology of the same work which Rome joyfully received many years ago against his teacher; and then he will observe,” and so forth. | 211 |

### Your Tullius

M. Antonius in Cicero, *On the Orator*, book 1, and *For Aulus Cluentius*. The printed books and many manuscript codices consistently read: “to be the first cause of victory,” and so forth. | 212 |

### Rome could not hear

The older manuscript codices read this way. Others, together with the printed books, add the name Victorinus, or “Victorinus the Martyr,” but falsely. | Ibid. |

### As fellow heirs

Marianus corrupts this passage under the pretext of the Latin Vulgate, for against the agreement of all the manuscript codices he reads: “as stewards,” and so forth. | 215 |

### “We have read, most learned man”

One manuscript codex reads in the singular: “We have read, most learned man,” and so forth, as though Hieronymus were addressing Pammachius alone. But what follows contradicts this interpretation: “Read Tullius,” and so forth. | 222 |

### The devil’s problems

Several manuscript codices read as follows: “Consider by what arguments, and how slippery, the problems of the devil, woven by his spirit, are overthrown.”

The printed books consequently alter Hieronymus’s text: “But what is necessary—” | [Col. 1239] | 223 |

### Of whom Cyprian

The editions of Erasmus and Marianus thrust Hilary upon us in place of Cyprian without any authority. All the manuscript codices, without exception, preserve the true and genuine reading: “Of whom Cyprian [speaks] concerning the number seven,” and so forth. Marianus’s error is refuted in the preface to the works of Saint Hilary of Poitiers, recently published by our master, Dom Pierre Coustant. | 232 |

## EPISTLE XLIX. TO PAMMACHIUS

### *Προσεφώνησα*

Erasmus and Marianus fabricate another context, reading words which are found in no manuscript exemplar: “I sent you the Apologetic work itself, and the one whom I addressed, and I published it at your request. Whom,” and so forth. | |

### Between the truth

Hieronymus says this only about the mutilated and corrupted book of Job in the old translation, not about the other books of the Old Testament, as Erasmus incompetently notes. His notes on this Epistle of Hieronymus are full of errors. | Ibid. |

## EPISTLE L. TO DOMNIO

### “All writers received the censor’s mark”

This monk, the critic of the books *Against Jovinianus*, has taken the censor’s rod against all writers: “None of us deserves to be called writers,” under this novel Attilius as censor and judge, because, as is said below, there is no one on earth whose eloquence does not displease him.

### A monk who carries tales

This monk is not Ruffinus, nor does he betray his own identity, as many suppose from the second book of his *Invectives against Hieronymus*, where we read:

“When I had criticized the little books which he wrote against Jovinianus, he himself replied in defense of them to a certain Domnio of blessed memory, an old man who had reported this very matter to him, and he said that it was impossible that he could have been in error in any way—a man who possessed knowledge of everything. After he had listed the kinds of syllogisms, or the arts of speaking and writing which the man who criticized him evidently did not know, he immediately added this: ‘Foolish is the man who thinks that I could not know this without the philosophers,’” and so forth.

Do not read, with incompetent copyists, *reprehendissem*—“when I had criticized”—in the first person, but in the third: “when someone had criticized him”; “to Domnio of blessed memory,” and so forth. Ruffinus is speaking about someone else, not about himself, as is clear from the words that follow. | 236 |

### *Ἀσυλλογίστους*

After the word *syllogismos*, Erasmus read in his manuscript *osanoistois*. He therefore noted in his scholia that perhaps one should read “to weave horned syllogisms,” *syllogismos κερατίνους*, that is, “horned” syllogisms.

Marianus says that he found *δυσφύκτους* in certain manuscript exemplars, that is, “indissoluble syllogisms.” To avoid detracting from anyone, it is enough to inform the reader that among our copies there is no manuscript exemplar in which the word *δυσφύκτους* is read.

In the manuscript of Saint Cygirannus, written in Latin letters, we read: *syllogismis usianusitois texere*; and in many others the Greek word appears, but its traces say nothing of Marianus’s *δυσφύκτους*. At last I found a Cluniacensis manuscript in which the genuine reading is preserved: *syllogismos ἀσυλλογίστους*, “non-concluding syllogisms.” See Synesius, Epistle 154. | Ibid. |

### *Καὶ αὐτοδίδακτος*

Here the Greek word *ἔνθεος* has been wrongly added; it appears in no manuscript exemplar. | 237 |

### To make our religion a contest

The codex of Saint Theodoric near Rheims reads: “and to wage war against our religion.” The printed books read: “and to make our religion pagan.” | 238 |

### *ἀπελογισάμην*

The ancient exemplars retain the Greek word, especially the Cluniacensis and another from the monastery of Saint Theodoric. One Sorbonne codex reads only the Latin translation: “to which I replied as best I could.”

Erasmus and Marianus follow this reading. Hence I infer that they used more recent manuscript exemplars, and very few of them, or at least that they compared them carelessly with the earlier editions of Hieronymus’s Epistles. Whoever reads the Greek words restored by us in this Epistle alone will certainly notice how great is the difference between truth and falsehood, and between a careful edition and one produced hastily or negligently. | Ibid. |

### *Πάντες οὐ συγγραφεῖς*

Erasmus sweated considerably over restoring this passage, which he arranged for himself from the most reliable traces of the letters: *πάντας συγγραφεῖς pellamus*, “let us drive out all writers,” under Attilius as judge.

But if he had had access to manuscript codices, it would have been easy to find what he was seeking, for the more recent copies retain the reading in Latin. Such is the Sorbonne codex, which reads: “Let us drive out all writers under Attilius as judge.”

This reading, however, is corrupt and defective. We must retain the one which we have restored from the agreement of the ancient manuscript codices.
