For all read: *πάντες οὐ συγγραφεῖς*; but they vary in the final words, some reading *appellamus*—“we call”—instead of *appellamur*—“we are called”—and *a tali judice*—“by such a judge”—instead of *Attilio judice*—“with Attilius as judge.”

The older and better Cluniacensis codex retains *appellamur* and originally had *Atalu judice* in the first hand; now, however, it reads *A tali judice*. All these witnesses taught us the genuine reading of Hieronymus: *πάντες οὐ συγγραφεῖς appellamur Attilio judice*, that is, “we are all called ‘not writers’ by Attilius as judge,” if in— | [Col. 1240] | 239 |

### Let them be called Gnathonic or Phormionic

Gnatho was a celebrated flatterer, and Phormio an shameless parasite. The censoring monk, chattering through houses and physicians’ shops, was worthy of such disciples. | Ibid. |

### Always ready for lawsuits

Here some word seems to be missing in the manuscripts. All except the Sorbonne codex read: “It belongs to buffoons and parasites always to be ready for lawsuits.”

The Sorbonne codex preserves a complete sense: “It belongs to buffoons and those prepared always for lawsuits.” The Cluniacensis deletes the middle letters *s* and *i* from *parasitorum*, producing *paratorum ad lites*, “of those prepared for lawsuits.” Saint Cygirannus, on the contrary, adds the same letters, *s* and *i*, to *paratorum*, so that it reads *parasitorum*.

Amid such variety of readings, we retain *paratorum semper ad lites*—“of those always prepared for lawsuits”—because this is the nature of buffoons, not parasites, whose interests more often require them not to quarrel. | 240 |

## EPISTLE LII. TO NEPOTIAN

### Dearest Nepotian

Of the twenty manuscript codices which I had for collating this Epistle, two read as follows: “You ask, dearest Nepotian, in transmarine letters, and you frequently ask me, to write for you in a short volume,” and so forth. | 254 |

### Or the games of the Atellanae

Atella is a town of Campania, from which the Atellan games take their name. It had an outstanding amphitheater. So says Stephanus.

We find the same note in the margin of several manuscript codices. In one exemplar of the Colbertine Library, no. 28.7, and in another of the College of Navarre, I found it written as follows: “Atella is a town of Campania, from which the Atellans were named”; or: “from there came the Atellans.”

The *Atellana* is a type of rather obscene and lascivious comedy, so called from Atella, a city of the Oscans, as Livy testifies in book 7. Saint Hieronymus likewise says below, to Sabinian: “A deed was discovered which neither one could devise more subtly, nor a buffoon enact, nor an Atellan utter.” | 255 |

### *Chameuniae*, etc.

*Chameuniae* means lying down on the ground. Hieronymus retains this Greek word elsewhere as well, because it cannot be rendered very conveniently in Latin. For *χαμαί* means “on the ground,” and *εὐνή* means “a bed.” Hence *χαμευνία* means lying on bare ground. | 256 |

### They will not profit them

After the words “they will not profit them,” the printed books retain the following addition:

“For some monks are richer than they were when they were laymen, and there are clerics who possess wealth under the poor Christ which they had not possessed under the wealthy and deceitful devil, so that the Church sighs for those whom the world previously held as beggars, now rich.”

We read nothing similar in twenty manuscript codices, except in an old manuscript of the Colbertine Library, no. 635. It contains the addition not within the text, but in the lower margin, and not in the first hand. It could therefore have passed into more recent copies, and from there into the printed books. It was taken, however, from the following Epistle. | 259 |

### A worn brow

Here too some add words, reading: “a worn brow, which loves markets and forums,” and so forth. | Ibid. |

### To provide for poverty

Twelve or fifteen manuscript codices read with Erasmus: “to provide for the resources of the poor.” | 261 |

### That saying of Domitius

All the manuscript codices retain the name Domitius. Cicero, however, Valerius Maximus, and Fabius in book 6, chapter 3, attribute the saying to L. Crassus:

“Should I regard you as consul, when you do not regard me as a senator?”

For Domitius, see Eusebius in the *Chronicle*, in the year of Our Lord 46, and Fabius, book 12, chapter 11. | 262 |

### Quintus Gallius

Some manuscripts read *Gallo* instead of *Gallio*, but the older ones retain *Gallium*. | 263 |

### How much better it would have been

The order of this passage is completely reversed in almost all the manuscript codices. For in them we read:

“And, with conscience resisting, to be surrounded by Pharisaic ambition. From this depends the Gospel; from this, the Cross and the Prophets. Faithful reader, you understand with me what I am silent about and what I speak more forcefully by keeping silent. As many rules as there are forms of glory. How much better it would have been to carry these things not on the body but in the heart, to have the Lord as one’s patron, not the gaze of men. Do you wish to know?” | 267 |

### From this, the Cross and the Prophets

In the printed books of Erasmus and Marianus: “from this, the Law and the Prophets.” But this is false, for all our manuscripts—more than twenty—retain the word *Cross*.

That word suits the meaning of the passage, in which the subject is the Gospel, or apostolic teaching, as Hieronymus himself interprets it. Moreover, the image of the Lord’s Cross could have been represented on the fringes and phylacteries of the priests. The passage should therefore be read in the best sense: “From this depends the Gospel; from this, the Cross and the Prophets,” that is, the sacred apostolic teaching, which is wholly concerned with the Cross of the Lord. | Ibid. |

## EPISTLE LIII. TO PAULINUS

### Herod, book 3, *Thalia*

Valerius Maximus, book 4, chapter 1. John of Salisbury, in his Epistle to Count Henry. Rhodiginus, book 29, chapter 4.

### The most famous Table of the Sun

Concerning the most famous Table of the Sun. | [Col. 1241] | 271 |

### Nevertheless, *τῇ δυνάμει*

The manuscripts retain this Greek phrase. The printed books read: “nevertheless, he is wholly so in power.” | 272 |

### He writes to Timothy

Almost all the manuscript codices read without the preposition *ad*—“to”: “He writes Timothy,” and so forth. | Ibid. |

### *Τὸ δόγμα, τὴν μέθοδον*

In many manuscript codices these are Greek words mixed with Latin: “the doctrine, *τὸ δόγμα*, is divided into method and use.” | 275 |

### Scripture alone

Contrary to the reading *lege*—“law”—found in all the manuscript copies, the books published before ours retain the word *lingua*—“language.” | Ibid. |

## EPISTLE LIV. TO FURIA

### The genuine [envy] inflicts

Two manuscript codices read: “genuine envy inflicts”; two others: “genuine speech inflicts”; the remaining six or eight retain the reading of the printed books. | 283 |

### Wherever they see a Christian

This is Hieronymus’s genuine reading, as we have established from Epistle 19, otherwise numbered 23, where the same proverb is rendered in Latin: “He is an impostor and a Greek.” Compare the two Epistles, since you will find many similar statements in them concerning women’s adornment, and so forth.

The printed books falsely added after “Greek”: “they call him an impostor,” and removed the rest. Nothing of the kind is found in the manuscript codices. | 284 |

### Rumor emerges from falsehood

Several manuscript exemplars read: “Infamy emerges,” and so forth. | Ibid. |

### In viper-like coils

Here too they read: “in viper-like colors.” | Ibid. |

### I remove the incentives to pleasures

Very many manuscript codices read: “I assert the incentives to pleasures.” | 287 |

### The fool will be wiser

Marianus reads: “The fool will be wiser.” Several manuscript codices also read this. But from the meaning of Hieronymus’s words, we retain the Erasmian reading. | 290 |

### Which is more august than the city of Rome

This is a formula customary with Hieronymus, who calls Bethlehem more august than Rome because of Christ, our Leader and Emperor. See the preface to the Commentary on Ecclesiastes, the preface to Didymus’s book *On the Holy Spirit*, and elsewhere. | 291 |

### So that, as a poisoner, etc.

Marianus has a different order of these words, but without the authority of manuscript codices. | 292 |

### Someone incompetently

Among others, Saint Ambrose, in his book *On Widows*. | 293 |

## EPISTLE LV. TO AMANDUS

### I found it joined to the Epistle

I do not see on what authority Erasmus and Marianus wished to change the order and sequence of the text of this Epistle. All the manuscript codices retain the continuous and consistent sequence: “I found it joined,” and so forth; and below, the third question, or final proposition, concerning the resurrection. | 297 |

### Whether the woman, having been abandoned

This may perhaps be understood of Fabiola, about whom we shall speak in the proper place. | Ibid. |

## EPISTLE LVI. OF AUGUSTINE

### “Augustine to his brother and fellow presbyter Hieronymus”

All the manuscript codices retain this salutation. But our Corbeiensis codex, no. 675, adds the word *Presbyter* at the end. And indeed at that time Saint Augustine was not a bishop, but only a presbyter. | 300 |

## EPISTLE LVII. TO PAMMACHIUS

### *Λογοδαίδαλοι*

In the manuscript codices this is written in Latin letters as *logodedali*. The copyist of the codex of Saint Theodoric, ignorant of this expression, fabricated another word which he understood: “Let the teachers and the fastidious answer,” and so forth.

They are *logodaedali*, as it were, craftsmen and makers of words. See Cicero, *On the Orator*, and Plato, *Phaedrus*.

### *Αἰδεσιμώτατον Πάππαν*

Erasmus may in some measure be excused for thrusting a false Greek and Latin text into this passage of Hieronymus. For certain manuscript codices gave him the opportunity for the error by reading as follows: *αἰδέσιμον ὤτων πάντων*, which they translate into Latin as “honorable to the ears of all.”

Erasmus therefore wished to restore the same words and meaning according to the rules of Greek. For this reason he published the following without scholia: *αἰδέσιμον ὠσὶν ἁπάντων*, that is, “revered by the ears of all,” refusing to translate it. We find the same reading in Marianus Victor: “The learned Gravius, however, in his annotations, indicates the following reading from an ancient exemplar: *αἰδέσιμον ὤτων ἀπάντων*.”

But not to prolong the matter, readings of this kind are false and corrupted. The true and genuine reading is the one which we restored from five or six ancient manuscript exemplars.

The preceding words also seem to indicate it: “instead of saying ‘honorable,’ [he said] ‘dearest’; and through a malicious interpretation—which it would be impious to say—[he] refused to translate *αἰδεσιμώτατον πάππαν*.”

They therefore accused Hieronymus of refusing to translate words spoken as a mark of honor to John of Jerusalem—namely, “honorable and most revered Father.” | 306 |

### “They pretend to understand”

These words are taken from Terence’s Prologue to the *Andria* and mean in the Gallic language: “They act as though they understand everything, but understand nothing.” Some write *nae* with a diphthong; but in the manuscript codices I find it written *ne*. | 308 |

| [Col. 1242] | 312 |

### “ELI, ELI”

Because in Matthew 27:46 we read: “Eli, Eli, lama sabacthani,” from the Chaldaic *sebacthani*, some copyists wrote in this Epistle *lama sabactani* instead of the Hebrew and Hieronymian *lama azabtham*.

But the better reading of the more numerous manuscript codices must be retained, where we read *azabctani*, as in Psalm 21, not *sabacthani*, which is Chaldaic. | 315 |

### Yet rightly

Marianus thought that one should read: “he obtained strength.” But in vain, for the manuscripts retain: “he obtained it rightly.” Conversely, of Aquila’s version it is said: “it is rightly rejected by us.” | 316 |

### For who

This passage was printed in an extremely corrupt form by Erasmus and Marianus. The learned Gravius was the first to restore it—not with the rash presumption customary among the shallow scholars of our own time, but with the assistance of ancient manuscript codices, which he used conscientiously and prudently.

Following this writer’s reliability and diligence, I shall undertake to supplement certain things omitted or altered by him in the same restoration. Thus we restore the entire passage from nine manuscript codices:

“For who, in place of grain, wine, and oil, could either read or understand *χεῦμα ὁπωρισμὸν, σιλπνότητα*, which we can call ‘a pouring, fruitfulness, and brightness’? Or because the Hebrews have not only *ἄρθρα*—articles—but also *πρόαρθρα*—pre-articles, that man, in an affected manner, interprets syllables and letters, and says *σὺν τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ σὺν τὴν γῆν*—a thing which neither Greek nor Latin admits at all. We can take an example of this matter from our own language,” and so forth.

Whoever compares these words with the older editions will clearly see that neither Hieronymus’s words nor his meaning had been preserved in them.

The holy Doctor therefore says: “Because the Hebrews in their language possess not only articles but also attachments of letters, ought Aquila, a proselyte and contentious translator, to render those articles and pre-articles? And in place of the Hebrew words *eth hasshamayim ve-eth ha-aretz*, should he say in Greek *σὺν τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ σὺν τὴν γῆν*?”

Here you see that *eth* was called a syllable and an article, while *be* was called a letter and a pre-article, or a connection and joining. All experts in the Hebrew language acknowledge that these observations are sound and learned. | Ibid. |

### He said *οἰήματι*

I do not know why Erasmus and Marianus wished to corrupt Hieronymus’s text here as well, reading *οἰδήματι* rather than *οἰήματι*, since all the manuscript exemplars read the latter. *Οἴημα* generally refers to an arrogant and foolish opinion which someone has formed about himself. | 317 |

### To the *ceroma*

*Ceroma* is an ointment with which athletes anointed themselves for the wrestling school, a contest for which an ox is utterly unsuitable. | Ibid. |

### Of Melanius, his teachers

The Cluniacensis codex reads this way; others have *Melaniae*, as was already noted above in the First Epistle. | Ibid. |

### In which there is speech, etc.

Erasmus illustrated this sentence, badly edited, with an even worse scholion. All the manuscripts preserve Hieronymus’s true meaning and words.

For the rest, we omit many things without scholia or notes, lest we seem to distrust the memory and diligence of the learned reader. | 318 |

## EPISTLE LVIII. TO PAULINUS

### While you are still gray

All the manuscript codices preserve this genuine reading. The printed books read: “while you are not yet gray,” and so forth.

### A good man

In ten or twelve manuscript exemplars this Epistle has the following title and heading:

“Here begins the Epistle of Saint Hieronymus to Paulinus the Presbyter, concerning the instruction of clerics or monks, and concerning various expositions of sacred history.” | Ibid. |

### “Rise; let us depart”

That Christ was in the upper room when he spoke these words is plainly proved by the Gospel history. But since Hieronymus was discussing the Jews abandoned by God and joins together two testimonies in proof—one of which was undoubtedly spoken in the Temple, from Matthew 24:1—he could consequently say that Christ spoke these words in the Temple to the disciples and to the Jews who trusted in the Temple.

But if anyone does not like this interpretation and wishes to read “in the upper room,” let him also show how Christ could have said to the Jews in the upper room: “Your house shall be left to you desolate.”

From this passage I can easily defend our brief annotation in the first chapter of the Commentary on Isaiah, which the curious reader may examine in the apologetic appendices of volume IV of this work. | 320 |

### To live abroad

This is the reading of all the manuscript codices, which Marianus, not understanding it, changed to “to live more dangerously.”

But to live *peraegrē* means to live with distraction of mind because of association and conversation with worldly people. | 324 |

| [Col. 1243] | 326 |

## EPISTLE LX. TO HELIODORUS

### The heavenly Jerusalem

That the bodies of the saints were seen in the heavenly Jerusalem after Christ’s resurrection, Hieronymus affirms by following the common opinion: we believe that Christ brought into heaven the saints who had risen with him, when, according to Matthew 27, many bodies of saints who had fallen asleep were seen in the holy city and appeared to many.

Nevertheless, in the Epistle of Paula and Eustochium to Marcella, the same matter seems by no means to be approved. They say: “Nor is the heavenly Jerusalem immediately understood in this passage, as many absurdly suppose, since there could have been no sign among men of the Lord’s resurrection if the bodies of the saints were seen in the heavenly Jerusalem.” | 333 |

### How varied in languages

He brought these words from the eighth book of Virgil’s *Aeneid*: “The conquered nations advance in long procession.” | |

### As varied in languages and appearance, so in clothing and arms

| Ibid. |

### Which nations of faith

The older manuscript codices read in this way. Others, together with the printed books, read: “Which nations he dedicated under the title of the Cross.” | 334 |

### The savagery of the Bessi

The learned Gravius did not establish who the Bessi and the Pelliti peoples were. I, however, would have no doubt that they were peoples of Thrace, about whom Ovidius writes in Book 6 of the *Tristia*:

To live—how miserable it is among the Bessi and Getae. | |

Then, in Book Four of *Ex Ponto*, Elegy 10, he calls the Getae “fur-clad” because they were covered with skins to ward off the cold, as northern peoples are still today. The savagery of the Bessi is also better known to us from Diomedes, king of Thrace, who, having fed his horses human flesh, was defeated by Hercules and thrown to his own horses as fodder. See the same Ovid in *Ibis* and *Metamorphoses* 9. “Funeral offerings” (*inferiae*) for the dead, says Servius, are rites of the dead that are paid to the infernal gods. Hence Virgil, *Aeneid* 10:

> He seizes the living, whom he may sacrifice to the shades as funeral offerings. | |

Ovid likewise said “to give funeral offerings to the spirits” in *Fasti* 5, and “to send funeral offerings to someone deceased” in *Metamorphoses* 11; Statius, Book 3, says “to consecrate eternal funeral offerings to the shades.” Funeral offerings, therefore, were rites of the dead, called *inferiae* from the infernal gods. “It was indeed the custom,” says the same Servius, “for captives to be killed at the tombs of the brave. When this came to be regarded as cruel, it was decided that gladiators should fight before the tombs; they were called *bustiarii* from the funeral pyres (*busta*).” Instead of “spirits” and “shades,” Jerome appears here to have taken *inferiae* in the sense of victims. Virgil uses it of victims in *Aeneid* 11:

> He had bound their hands behind their backs, to send them to the shades  
> As funeral offerings, that they might sprinkle the flames with the blood of the slain. | Ibid. |

Wherever he. In certain copies, the correctors of the manuscript codices inserted: “Wherever you might seek him, you would find him in the Church.” Erasmus followed this reading, and after him Marianus Victorius. | 340 |

Rather less to the king than to the bishop. This is the genuine reading in all the old manuscript copies. In the Cluniacensis, a later hand altered the order of the words to: “rather less to the bishop than to the king.” But the first reading is true and authentic, as can clearly be demonstrated from the words that follow. The printed editions retain the falsified reading. | 342 |

Here he is given over to slavery. Several manuscript codices read here: “Here he rules by servitude.” | Ibid. |

## EPISTLE LXI. TO VIGILANTIUS

An ἀσυνάρτητον (*asynartēton*) discourse. This word does not mean disordered or uncomposed, but unconnected, incoherent, or, more precisely, inept and inappropriate. It derives from the root ἀρτάω or from the verb ἄρω, not from ἀρτίζω, as Erasmus teaches in his notes.

It would indeed have been right. I find very many additions in the Cluniacensis manuscript, beginning here at once with: “It would indeed have been useful and right,” etc. Below, it retains interpretations of the Greek words that do not appear in the other copies. | 347 |

Τῷ σοφωτάτῳ κρανίῳ (*tō sophōtatō kraniō*). The Cluniacensis Codex adds an interpretation of the Greek words in this form: “You alone are permitted, with your most sagacious brain (*sapientissimo cerebro*), to speak about everything,” etc. | 349 |

Πᾶσαν τὴν ἀριστείαν σου (*pasan tēn aristeian sou*). Here the printed editions omit the Latin words “also sung by the voice of little children,” although they are found in all the manuscript copies. The Cluniacensis Codex, however, preserves the entire passage partly in Greek letters in this form:

> Otherwise I would prefer ΠΑϹΑΝ ΤΗΝ ΑΡΙϹΤΙΑΝ ϹΟΥ ΚΑΙ ΤΡΟΠΕΟΦΟΡΟΝ—“all your battles and your trophy,” carried even on the shoulder of little children and sung by their voice.

But, etc. This alone has the passage corrupted in this way; nearly all the others read τροπενοφόρον, perhaps for τροπαιοφόρος, that is, “bearing a trophy.” One Colbertinus reads τροπηοφορίαν for τροπαιοφορίαν, the reading retained by us. Jerome’s meaning is this: “I am restrained by Christian modesty from displaying your brilliant deeds and the pomp of your trophies, as little children sing of the exploits of the bravest men.” The holy man said this ironically, lest he be forced to call the disgraceful deeds of a tavern-keeper by their proper names. | Ibid. |

| |

[Col. 1244] |

350 |

The proverb ὂνῳ λύρα (*onō lyra*). The older editions wrongly alter the Greek proverb here, where they read ὂνος πρός λύραν (*onos pros luran*), “an ass to the lyre.” The true and genuine reading is therefore retained in all the manuscript codices, namely ὀνω λύρα or ὂνος λύρα. But from Jerome himself the earlier reading is to be retained: ὅσω λύρα, “a lyre for an ass”—that is, “he sings uselessly,” as Jerome has it in his Epistle to Marcella: “Although I could rightly despise them—for a lyre sings uselessly to an ass—nevertheless, lest we [be accused] of arrogance,” etc. The Cluniacensis Codex reads: “It is truly a Greek proverb, ‘a lyre sings uselessly to an ass,’ ΟΝΩϹΛϹΥΡΑ.” Jerome therefore says that this Greek proverb fits Vigilantius most aptly; his name too had been imposed by antiphrasis, since he ought rather to have been called “Dormitantius” than “Vigilantius.” We have much about this proverb in Erasmus’s *Chiliades*, or *Adages*. Let whoever wishes consult it. | Ibid. |

## EPISTLE LXIV. TO FABIOLA

Aquila’s ἐπένδυμα (*ependuma*). The printed editions corruptly read ἐπίραμμα (*epirrhama*) instead of ἐπένδυμα, that is, “an overgarment.”

The order of the Epistles to Fabiola was reversed in the books previously published. For the one concerning the forty-two stations of the children of Israel in the wilderness is printed first in them, although it is later both in chronological order and in the nature of its subject—specifically, in relation to the Mosaic volumes, whose sequence we imitate in arranging these Critical Epistles on the Old Testament. Since, therefore, the Book of Exodus, in which Moses speaks about the priests’ vestments, precedes the Book of Numbers, whose final part Jerome explains in the Epistle concerning the Forty-Two Stations, we judged it right to publish first the epistle that was written first by the author and that carefully treats the matters read in Exodus. Moreover, he himself taught that this order should be followed in the *Epitaph of Fabiola* to Oceanus. | 354 |

On the chest and belly. The printed editions read “on the little chest and belly”; the Regius manuscript 3993 and another celebrated manuscript of the Abbey of Cluny read: “[uncertain: on the right shoulder, foot, and belly].” | Ibid. |

Ἐπιθέματος (*epithematοs*). In all the manuscript codices it is called ἐπιθέματος, that is, “of an addition.” The Greek word and its unchanged grammatical case have been preserved in accordance with the writing of the Septuagint translators: “the little chest of the addition,” etc. | 355 |

Pierced through. The manuscript copies vary in this word: some read “fixed through,” several “buried,” and the rest “pierced through.” Correspondingly, they also read “we care” and “we run.” | Ibid. |

Let them be sluggish. The edition of Marianus and several manuscripts read “let them be distinguished.” Later, two Roman or Vatican manuscripts, 342 and 343, read “half-nostrils.” | 356 |

The price is offered equally. Very many manuscript codices read with the same meaning: “all offer the price equally.” | 357 |

Christ their God is upon him. The printed editions omit the name “Christ,” although it is found in all our manuscript copies. | 358 |

Bowls. One manuscript codex of Saint-Thierry near Rheims reads “cups, goblets.” | 360 |

The ornament will have been exposed. The printed editions and several manuscripts read simply “the ornament.” Correspondingly, some also read “with breeches” and “modesty” instead of “the private parts.” | Ibid. |

By directing the spear. Several manuscript copies, together with the printed editions, retain here: “to direct spears, to hold the shield, to balance the sword.” | 361 |

They call it HEMIAN. All the manuscript codices read this way; the printed editions, however, read as in the Chaldean paraphrase, *heinejanim*. They should have read, as in the Polyglots, *hemjanin*, Exodus 28:40. How far Erasmus and Marianus are from the truth is clear and certain from this passage: they do not investigate the proper origin at all, but trace the matter to foreign works, here to the Targum of Onkelos, when they should have returned to Josephus.

I know that the Chaldeans call a girdle *hemjan*; nevertheless, I do not wish to derive the true reading of Jerome’s text from them, but from Josephus, the author of the *Jewish Antiquities*, from whom it was transferred into Jerome’s present little work. Josephus, therefore, speaking in Book 3 of the *Jewish Antiquities*, chapter 8, about the pontifical and priestly vestments, teaches us the following about the girdle:

> Moses called it ἀβανήφ (*abanēph*), but we, having learned from the Babylonians, call it ἐμίαν (*emian*); for that is what it is called among them.

All the manuscripts agree with Josephus, for they read *Emian*, and *Hemian* with aspiration. What Jerome means here when he calls it a new Babylonian word will be explained more suitably elsewhere. | 362 |

The Hebrews call it MISNEPHET. Several manuscript codices omit these words, “the Hebrews call it Misnephet.” | Ibid. |

| |

[Col. 1245] |

I remember having written the Epistle. See below the Epistle to Marcella, which begins “The office of an epistle”; in the books previously published it is numbered 130. | Ibid. |

I could not find *lyncurium*. Erasmus notes in his scholia or annotations that the reading is *ligurius*. There can be no doubt that *lyngurius* should be read. Jerome frankly admits that he was unable to find this gem in the authors who wrote about it; nor is it surprising that such a small stone escaped the man, since at times we fail to see even what we stumble upon.

Theophrastus nevertheless mentions *lyngurius* in his little book Περὶ τῶν λίθων (*Peri tōn lithōn*, “On Stones”), and Pliny followed him in Book 37, chapter 4. They say that it is produced from the urine of a lynx, from which it also gets its name: λύγξ (*lynx*) is the animal, and οὖρος (*ouros*) is urine. It immediately hardens into a gem. But the jealous animal promptly covers its excreted urine with earth so that it cannot be found by a human being. It is effective for many medicines, for it is said to draw out bladder stones and to be beneficial against jaundice if worn or drunk in wine. It resembles amber, or *succinum*. For it not only attracts pieces of straw and wood but also iron, if it is genuine. Theophrastus cites Diocles as his authority for this. Pliny, however, trusts neither of them in this matter and denies that he has ever seen a gem called by this name. | 365 |

with the Epistle to the Virgin Principia. Indeed, there are five at once in Job, chapter 28: the first, common to every kind of gold, is *zahar*, verses 1 and 6. The second name is *Segor*, verse 15. The third, *Chethem Ophir*, verse 16. The fourth, *Phaz*, verse 17. The fifth, *Chethem tahor*, verse 19. If you add the name *harus*, Job 41:21, and *Ophaz*, Jeremiah 10:9, the number of seven names by which gold is called among the Hebrews will be complete. HALOTH is read. The manuscript codices read *Aloth* and *Heloth*. Either can be read from Jerome himself. For above, in his *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*, he taught that it is a feature of the Hebrew language to write with *he* and read with *a*, just as conversely the letter *a* is pronounced as *he*. Thus *haloth* is very correctly read according to that Hebrew idiom, or, in the customary manner, *Aaloth* or *Ahaloth*. | 385 |

Σύγκοιτον, that is, etc. Marianus illuminates the passage in the following note: “For this Aquila has σῦγκοίτιν, that is, ‘concubine.’ συγκσίτην was previously read incorrectly, for that word is masculine.” But the manuscript codices read neither συγκοίτην nor σύγκοιτιν; they all consistently retain the genuine word σύγκοιτον. The word σύγκοιτος is used of a husband and wife and is more generally taken to mean a male or female bedfellow. | Ibid. |

For there are seven. In Book 2 of his *Commentary on Jeremiah*, chapter 10, he likewise says: “Among the Hebrews gold is called by seven names; one of them is called *Ophaz*, which we may call *abrizum*.” John Drusius discusses this in Book 4, chapter 15, of his *Observations*:

> Jerome notes that gold is called by seven names among the Hebrews, in Jeremiah 10 and in the Epistle to Principia; but what those names are, neither does he himself ever record, nor, so far as I know, has anyone yet recorded them. Since I have devoted some time and effort to seeking them and, unless I am mistaken, have found them, I shall be doing something worthwhile if I list them here and candidly share them with students of these letters.

The first name, then, is *Zahab*, common to every kind of gold. The second is *Phaz*, or *Ophaz*, the kind of gold that the Greeks call κιρρόν (*kirrhon*, “yellow” or “tawny”), as Jerome says. The third is *Harus*, so called because it is cut or dug out of the earth, for *haras* means “to cut out.” The fourth is *Chethem*, which Aquila nevertheless rendered in David as σπίλωμα (*spilōma*, “stain” or “blemish”). The fifth is *Ophir*, named from the place from which it was brought; from this comes *obrysum*, as though *Ophyrisum*, if we believe Jerome. The sixth is *haser*, Job 22:24. The seventh is *Segor*, which Camius interprets by saying that it is pure, unalloyed gold.

Thus far Drusius, followed by the author of *Sacred Criticism*, Part 1, page 53—that is, Waserius, *On the Ancient Coins of the Hebrews*, Book 1, chapter 4. But it must be noted that the sixth name, *baser*, Job 22:24, was by no means expressed as “pure” by Jerome; another name must therefore be sought if seven names for gold are to be found. IDIDIA. The name is somewhat corrupted in the printed editions, where we read *Jedidia*. In almost all the manuscripts it is written *Idida* or *Iddida*, with the final *i* elided. During the interregnums. Everyone altered and restored this very confused passage according to his own interpretation: Marianus after Erasmus, and Fronto Ducaeus after Marianus. The Erasmian reading is:

> “But either because of the seditions of the people, or because of certain kingdoms at odds among themselves—that is, with Judah and Samaria in conflict—or certainly because of the evils pressing upon them and arising here and there,” etc.

Marianus Victorius corrected this with the help, as he says, of the Florentine codices, especially:

> “But either because of the seditions of the people, or because of certain interregnums, or certainly because of the evils pressing upon them,” etc.

Finally, Ducaeus, finding interregnums entirely unacceptable in Jerome’s text, judged that the passage should be restored as follows:

> “A son had been appointed to the rule; but either because of certain internal seditions of the people, or because of evils pressing from outside and wars arising here and there.”

The passage is explained well and clearly, but it has no manuscript witness in its support. Therefore the reading of Marianus must be retained, since it is supported by the authority and reliability of the most ancient copies of Saint Jerome. We note, however, that the interregnums discussed here are to be attributed not to Jerome but to the Jew who was telling the story, whether or not such interregnums actually existed. | Ibid. |

## EPISTLE LXXIII. TO EVANGELUS

That great Eustathius, the most vigorous defender, bishop of the Church of Antioch, who at the Council of Nicaea spoke out against Arius and in his little works sounded the trumpet of war with the clearest voice, was exceedingly energetic. The name of Eustathius, however, is thoroughly corrupted in many manuscript copies, where he is called Eustatius, Eustachius, and Eustochius. Finally, in the manuscript codex of the Monastery of Saint Cygiranus, I find it written as follows: “Apollinaris the martyr also, and our Eustasius.” Some codices consistently have: “who earlier . . . was bishop and [spoke] against Arius,” etc.

The printed books placed *Evagrius* rather than *Evangelus*. All the manuscript codices, however, retain *Evangelus* or *Evangelium*. An Illyrian bishop was later called by the same name. See Baronius under the year 516. Moreover, the little work sent by Evangelus still survives in the Appendix to Volume 3 of the new edition of the works of Saint Augustine. | 440 |

Ἀνώνυμον (*anōnymon*). We have found no manuscript copy in which the connective particle καὶ (*kai*) is read. It therefore seems clear to us that Erasmus and Marianus added ἀνώνυμον ἀδέσποτον (*anōnymon adēspoton*), “anonymous and without an owner.” | Ibid. |

And he attempts to mix [it] into a φιλεγκλήμονι treatise. The manuscript codices certainly offer Erasmus no support, for they retain Marianus’s reading and restoration. A φιλεγκλήμων treatise is one that loves complaints, or is querulous, because it provides an occasion for offense and controversy. | Ibid. |

The greatest Doctor of the Catholic Church could not have called a heretical man “our man” or spoken of him in that way. We therefore understand “our man” of Eustathius, because he was a man of the Catholic faith. |

The priest of the Son of God. Several manuscripts read: “to have gone before as a type of the priesthood of the Son of God.” | 442 |
