**Fleas.** The editions of Erasmus and Marianus have *vermiculi et culices* (“worms and gnats”); but the testimony of all the manuscript codices contradicts this. Quite a few of them also read, in what follows, *scientiam inscientiae* (“knowledge of ignorance”). | Ibid. |

**UMELCHISEDECH, etc.** There is scarcely a word in this quoted passage that has not been corrupted in Erasmus and Marianus and set down contrary to the practice of the ancient Fathers. For they do not make it their aim to follow Jerome’s manuscript copies, but rather the rules of the modern grammarians, which differ greatly from the usage of the ancient Hebrews and ecclesiastical writers. Accordingly, they wished Jerome to have read as follows:

> “And Melchizedek, king of Salem, brought out bread and wine, and he was priest of God Most High; and he blessed him and said: Blessed is Abraham by God Most High, who made heaven and earth; and blessed is God Most High, who delivered your enemies into your hand; and he gave him a tithe of everything.”

Whoever compares this with our edition will everywhere detect that Erasmus and Marianus’ text is false, and that Jerome was entirely ignorant of the Hebrew language—inasmuch as they read *zadecho*, with *daleth* in place of *resh*, and interpret this word as “your enemies,” although it more properly signifies “your sides.” Jerome therefore read *sarach* and *biadach* in the Chaldean manner; for the Targum of Onkelos renders this passage of Genesis 14:20 as *sarach* and *bidach*, “your enemies in your hand.” See below a similar reading in the Letter to Sunnia and Fretela.

In the current Hebrew text, however, the Hebrew words cited by Jerome are read as follows:

> “Umalchi thsedec, king of Salem, brought out bread and wine; and he was priest of God Most High, and he blessed him and said: Blessed is Abram by God Most High, possessor of heaven and earth; and blessed is God Most High, who delivered your enemies into your hand, and he gave him a tithe of everything.”

| Ibid. |

**Thirty-five years.** Erasmus falsely printed “forty” in place of “thirty-five,” as is immediately apparent from the calculation. | 444 |

**Ignorance produces confidence.** This is a saying of Thucydides: *ἀμαθία μὲν θράσος, λογισμὸς δὲ ὄκνον φέρει*—that is, “lack of understanding produces boldness, while reflection brings hesitation.” Thucydides, book 3. | 446 |

## LETTER LXXIV. TO RUFINUS

They read thus; others have *genuerit* (“has begotten”), which is more strongly supported by Marianus.

I found this Letter bearing different titles in the manuscript copies, but all consistently retain the words “to Rufinus, Priest at Rome.” From this it is most clearly established that this Rufinus was a Roman priest, not an Aquileian, and ultimately Jerome’s most bitter enemy. Concerning this same Roman Rufinus Jerome writes to the Aquileian in Letter 66, now numbered 66:

> “We also sent the holy priest Rufinus from Rome to Milan for a certain reason,” etc.

The title of the manuscript codices, which encompasses all the others, is this:

> “Letter of Saint Jerome to Rufinus, Priest at Rome, concerning Solomon’s judgment in the case of the child.”

| 447 |

**By a false report.** Several manuscripts have *falsorum ore concelebrat* (“he celebrates by the mouth of false men”); an easy error, but one plainly contradicted by all the others. | Ibid. |

**Concerning us.** Eight or ten manuscript codices, together with Erasmus, read thus. Marianus, often unfair to Erasmus, reads *ad correptionem nostram* (“for our correction”). | Ibid. |

**He begot children of fornication.** Very many manuscript codices … |

[Col. 1251] |

448 |

**A cord and I fed the flock.** Here too, [some manuscripts read] *funiculos* (“cords”); a few, together with Marianus, retain *funiculum* (“a cord”). | Ibid. |

**Which conceived me.** Almost all the manuscript copies have *quae concepit me* (“which conceived me”); the printed editions have *quae me genuit* (“which begot me”). | 449 |

**If I should run through them one by one.** The printed editions have *si velim singula percurrere* (“if I should run through them individually”). | 450 |

**Again, what I have read.** This phrase is from Horace; for Horace has the following in Book One, Satire Ten:

> “Often turn your stylus again, when you are about to write  
> what deserves to be read again; nor labor to win the crowd’s admiration.”

| 451 |

**I was glad to see Caninus.** Five manuscript codices read *Caninum* rather than *Caninium*. | Ibid. |

## LETTER LXXV. TO THEODORA

**In no way accepting.** Concerning these portentous names, see Jerome *Against Vigilantius*, and also his commentaries on Isaiah 64, Amos 3, Nahum, and his Letter to Hedibia. The manuscript codices consistently read *Armazet* rather than *Armagil*. | 453 |

## LETTER LXXVI. TO ABIGAUS

**Finally, certain people, etc.** Understand Democritus and his disciple Metrodorus. Cicero, Book V of *On Ends* and Book V of the *Tusculan Disputations*; Jerome, Book II *Against Jovinian*; Tertullian, *Apology*. | 456 |

## LETTER LXXVIII. TO FABIOLA

A manuscript copy has *purulentias Aegyptiorum* (“the purulences of the Egyptians”), and then, together with all the others, *qui sunt magnarum carnium* (“who are of great flesh”); in the margin, written by a more recent hand, it retains *virulentias* (“the poisonous things”). Jerome recalls the words of Ezekiel 16:26:

> “And you fornicated with the sons of Egypt, your neighbors, who are of great flesh.”

The same author writes in Book I of his Commentary on Hosea, chapter 1:

> “She followed the Chaldeans, Assyrians, and Egyptians, who are of great flesh.”

If the editors of the ancient editions had paid closer attention to this, they would never have inserted a ridiculous reading into Jerome’s text. For they foolishly wished to read: “Nor here the poisonous things of the Egyptians, which are the songs of poets,” etc.

**They encamped.** Several manuscripts have *Hihim*, with the aspiration.

Very many manuscript codices bear the following title:

> “Here begins [the work] concerning the Stations of the Israelite people.”

One more recent Colbertinus has:

> “Here begins the little book of Saint Jerome concerning the forty-two Stations of the Israelite people, composed in memory of Fabiola.”

The very ancient Corbeiensis, which will frequently be praised below, has:

> “Treatise concerning the forty-two Stations of the children of Israel.”

| 467 |

**But we more truly, etc.** Consult above the *Apology for Jerome’s Learning in the Hebrew Language*, chapter 2 of the Commentary on the Book of Hebrew Names. | 468 |

**From eating out, etc.** The earlier editions incorrectly read *et excedente* (“and exceeding”). But, unless I am mistaken, Erasmus and Marianus printed *exedente* (“eating out”); ignorant typesetters produced *excedente*. Several manuscripts have *et comedente* (“and eating”), etc. | 470 |

**They thought it was thunder.** This was not at the Savior’s baptism, but when he himself asked the Father to glorify his name, John 12:29:

> “The crowd that stood there and heard it said that thunder had occurred,” etc.

Perhaps, however, Jerome here recalled some apocryphal Gospel in which this was written, just as one copy of the Itala Version explicitly mentions a great light appearing at the Savior’s baptism. See my edition of the Gospel according to Matthew, and, among Cyprian’s works, a little work by an anonymous author, in the *Observations* of Rigault, p. 139. | Ibid. |

**With the thunder of joy, etc.** Other copies read with the same meaning, *tonitrui gaudio* (“with the joy of thunder”). | Ibid. |

**May it have a protector.** The editions printed before ours add: “and may the night also have fire,” etc. | 472 |

**Dangers confront [them] again.** Erasmus and Marianus likewise print here: “The Egyptians and Pharaoh confront [them] again.” | 473 |

**Instruction, etc.** The same Erasmus and Marianus read: “Evangelical doctrine.” | Ibid. |

**Adhesion.** Contrary to the testimony of all the manuscript codices, and of the *Book of Hebrew Names*, they alter the genuine reading here as well, substituting *retentionem* (“retention”) for *remissionem* (“remission”). See our annotation above, column 19. | 476 |

**If the middle word is written with the letter BETH.** *Debehca*, from *dabac*, signifies “joined” and “adhering”; *dephca*, however, from *daephac*, is understood by the grammarians, in accordance with Jerome’s observation, as “a striking” or “struck.” | Ibid. |

**Concerning things wrongly translated.** He means the Greek edition of the Septuagint, where we read *ῥαφακὰ* (*raphaka*) in place of *Dephca*—that is, *resh* in place of *daleth*, letters distinguished only by a small stroke, as follows: *daleth*, *resh*. | Ibid. |

**ABEN EZER.** The earlier printed books falsely have *haben haaser*, as though it were written with *samech* or *sin* in the Hebrew text. For if we say it is written with these letters, *abon haaser* by no means signifies “stone of help.” | 477 |

**They encamped.** In some manuscripts and in the printed editions one reads, “they set up camp.” | 478 |

**In one hundred and twenty of the Mosaic [age], etc.** The manuscript copies consistently retain this reading, which the printed editions altered as follows:

> “And also upon the Apostles and those who were with them, established at the number one hundred and twenty of the Mosaic age,” etc.

| Ibid. |

**The bramble.** The very ancient Corbeiensis manuscript, written in uncial letters on parchment about a thousand years ago … |

[Col. 1252] |

480 |

**Ἀρκευθον among the Greeks.** This word is transcribed into Latin in several manuscript copies as *arceuthon*. | 481 |

**Malachi, bricks, etc.** Either Jerome’s memory failed, or he was using different copies of Malachi, or perhaps ignorant copyists wrote “Malachi” in place of “Isaiah,” just as elsewhere they wrote “Jeremiah” in place of “Zechariah.” In Isaiah chapter 9, verse 10, we therefore read what the holy Doctor notes here; but the Idumeans are not involved in this passage, for those who seek to replace destroyed bricks with dressed stones are mentioned. The cited verse reads:

> “The bricks have fallen, but we will build with dressed stones.”

These are the words of the people of Ephraim and the inhabitants of Samaria, not of the Idumeans. | 482 |

**This word, etc.** The word meaning “bridles,” namely *resen*, occurs several times in another form. Jerome therefore taught us many things here:

1. That the word *Ressa* or *Rissa* is found only among the Hebrews, in Numbers 33:21–22.
2. That in ancient times there was an apocryphal book in which the word *Ressa* occurred and was used there for “a stadium.”
3. Finally, that this book was called by the Greeks *λεπτή*—that is, “the little Genesis.”

Why Erasmus and Marianus should have invented the Greek word *μικρογένεσις* on their own, removing both the name used by Jerome and its interpretation, contrary to the testimony of all the manuscript codices, is not for me to say, but for those who wish to flatter manifest errors. | 483 |

**He wounded the prince of Tyre.** Concerning the prince of Tyre, see Ezekiel chapter 28, where you have an image of the proud Angel wounded by Christ. | Ibid. |

**In the aforementioned apocryphal volume of Genesis.** Here, as above, Jerome continues the allegory of the apocryphal book. It should also be noted that the etymology of the name *Thare*, given in the *Book of Hebrew Names*, is rejected by Jerome himself in this Station:

> “And they would not err,” he says, “if it were written with the letter *ain*,” etc.

For in fact *Thare* or *Thara*, with *ain*, signifies “wickedness,” or “feeding,” or “pasture”; but with *heth* and a double aspiration, *Thare* is expressed, according to the apocryphal book, as “one who drives away” or “one who repels.” | 485 |

**He does not permit it to be devoured.** See Genesis 25:11, where Abraham drives the birds away from the parts and limbs of the divided sacrifice. | Ibid. |

**Moseroth.** In the very ancient Corbeiensis manuscript previously mentioned, it is written not *Moseroth* but *Museroth*. | 486 |

**The desolations of a man.** Several very ancient and more recent manuscripts read *dedolationis hominis* (“the desolation of a man”). Then, in the Corbeiensis, written in Greek letters, we find *ξυλοκισμοὶ ἀνδρὸς* (“timber-cuttings of a man”); from traces of other copies we find that this too should be read, as Erasmus admitted in his scholia—although Marianus unjustly censured him here, wishing to read *ξυλακισμοφόρος*, a word wholly uncharacteristic of Jerome.

For the Hebrew name *Asion* or *Etsion-gaber* is more meaningfully expressed in Greek by *ξυλισμός*, that is, “woodcutting,” or *ξυλοκισμοὶ ἀνδρός*, “the timber-cuttings of a man,” than by *ξυλακισμοφόρος*, “bearing wood.” Jerome’s following words clearly establish this:

> “They can signify the timber-cuttings of a man; the kinds of forests and of all trees …”

| 488 |

**By Gimet.** The Greeks read *Gasion Gaber*, because the Septuagint translators often rendered the Hebrew *ayin* by the Greek gamma, as in *Gomorrha* for *Amorrha*. | 489 |

**And they would not err.** From this passage we can learn Jerome’s diligence in Hebrew matters and in investigating the etymologies of names, and how often by a single observation he corrected the errors of Greeks and Latins. | 490 |

**It is called diminutively.** *Ὑποκοριστικῶς* means “diminutively.” The two diminutives are *Selmona*, that is, “a little image,” and *Phinon*, that is, “a little mouth”; or, if one may abuse a new word, “a little mouth.” Unless I should rather say, with Virgil and Columella, *oscillum*, “a little mask” or “swinging image.” | 491 |

**According to the words of Elihu.** The printed editions retain the name *Helui* here. I find no annotation by Marianus or Erasmus that tells me who this Helui was, according to whose words *Oboth* signifies “large bottles.” But they should have remembered Elihu’s words in Job 32:19:

> “Behold, my belly is like fermenting wine without an opening, which bursts new bottles.”

Here *Oboth* signifies “bottles,” according to Elihu, unknown in the ancient editions of Jerome. | 492 |

[Col. 1253] |

492 |

**Deblathaim.** Whether Jerome wished it or not, Erasmus and Marianus always read the Hebrew words according to the vowel-points of the Masoretes and other grammatical intricacies: thus above *Phunon* for *Phinon*, and here *Diblathajema* for *Diblathaim*. It should be observed, however, that in the Hebrew text of the Samaritans and in the Syriac version *Phinon* has been retained, and likewise *Deblathaim* among the Syrians. | 494 |

**The people are counted again.** The earlier printed books add: “and the Levites are counted.” They consequently read as follows:

> “And they receive an inheritance by the judgment of the Lord, so that even the female sex may not be excluded from God’s possession among their brothers.”

| 495 |

**He ought to offer.** Quite a few manuscript codices have *ferre* (“to bear”) and *afferre* (“to bring”) in place of *offerre* (“to offer”). | Ibid. |

**A preparation of the Gospel.** The manuscript copies differ in this word, since very many read *mediatorium* rather than *meditatorium*. But the latter reading should be retained, as Jerome’s meaning requires: he teaches that Deuteronomy is, as it were, a preparation for a second Law and represents within itself the Gospel that was to come. | 496 |

## LETTER LXXIX. TO SALVINA

In the manuscript codices: “Here begins the consolatory letter to Salvina concerning Nebridius and the preservation of widowhood.” In some copies I read: “Concerning the death of Nebridius and the preservation of widowhood.” | 497 |

**Not of men, etc.** Four manuscript copies retain the following reading:

> “For each thing must be judged not by the weight of men but by the weight of matters.”

| 498 |

## LETTER LXXXII. TO THEOPHILUS

**An ancient saying.** The Erasmian edition adds the proper name of this ancient monastery and reads:

> “For the monastery of Saint Pope Epiphanius was formerly called by this name.”

But I cannot know which reading is genuine, because in this Letter I lack the assistance of manuscript codices. | 518 |

## LETTER LXXXIV. TO PAMMACHIUS AND O—

**He introduced a divided economy of Christ.** He called Christ’s economy “divided” because Apollinaris held that the Word assumed flesh alone, and not a soul. Consequently, Eusebius of Caesarea is called an unmistakable defender of Arius, although some appear to deny this. | 523 |

**Bar-aninas our teacher, etc.** *Bar-anina* was the name of Jerome’s Jewish teacher, not *Barrahanus*, as it is falsely read in the ancient editions. Because of his ignorance, Rufinus foolishly misused this name in his books of invective. | 524 |

**A thousand and more treatises.** The Sancygirannus Codex reads:

> “I read a thousand and more treatises which he delivered in the Church. In addition, he published innumerable Commentaries,” etc.

Marianus Victorius has:

> “He delivered a thousand and more treatises in the Church. He published,” etc.

| 530 |

**Εὐρεσιλογοῦσιν.** Do not read, with Erasmus, *αἰτιαλογοῦσιν*, that is, “they make accusations”; nor, with Marianus in the Notes, *ἀντιολογοῦσιν*. I am astonished that Marianus rejected the Greek word *εὐρεσιλογοῦσιν*, saying that it was incorrectly written in certain manuscript codices, when it is certain that this is Saint Jerome’s genuine reading, both from the sense of the words and from the testimony of the manuscript copies, in which it appears either as *εὑρελογοῦσιν* or *εὑρεσιλογοῦσιν*.

*Εὑρεσιλογέω* means “I speak eloquently and elaborately,” or “I speak copiously and readily.” Thus Rufinus and the other supporters of Origen defended with elaborate falsehoods and at length the claim that the passages displeasing to Catholics were not Origen’s in his books. Hence Jerome says:

> “Since Origen himself, in his Letter to Fabianus, does penance for having written such things, why do you still say, with your foolish abundance of words, that the things which displease are not his?”

| 532 |

## LETTER LXXXV. TO PAULINUS

**They accuse the ἀκαιροσπουδασταί.** The learned Reader will scarcely believe with what rashness this passage has been altered and corrupted in Erasmus, Marianus, and the other ancient editors of Jerome. For, in place of the Greek compound formed from *ἄκαιρος* and *σπουδαστής*—that is, in place of *ἀκαιροσπουδασταί*—all those before us inserted the fabricated words: “what he accuses me of.”

**CALPHURNIUS LANARIUS AND HIS DISCIPLES.** It was not enough for them to remove Origen’s *acairospoudastae*, that is, his “untimely and excessive enthusiasts and supporters,” unless they also substituted Rufinus and his disciples for Origen. Let everyone reread the entire passage of Jerome, so that he may immediately congratulate himself on possessing from us a new and true edition of the works of the holy Doctor. Erasmus was so blind in reading the manuscript codices that, in place of ΑΚΑΙΡΟΚΠΟΥΔΑΚΤΑΙ, he read ΥΠΕΡΑΚΠΙΚΤΑΙ in them. | 534 |

## LETTER XCVII. TO PAMMACHIUS AND MARCELLA

The three Paschal books of Theophilus, which Jerome sent to Pammachius and Marcella. We too have followed this order and arranged for these same books, translated from Greek into Latin by Jerome, to be published here, so that the proper order of subjects and dates might be maintained in our edition.

**May they die.** In the ancient codex of Saint Theodoric near Rheims, after Jerome’s Letter there follow in due order … |

[Col. 1254] |

583 |

## LETTER XCVIII

In the same manuscript codex of Saint Theodoric, after Jerome’s Letter to Pammachius and Marcella, the following is appended:

> “The Preface ends. Here begins the first Paschal Letter of Theophilus, Bishop of the city of Alexandria, to all the bishops of Egypt, translated from Greek into Latin by the blessed Jerome.”

| Ibid. |

## LETTER CIV. OF AUGUSTINE

**By those inflaming the accusation, etc.** In all the copies that I examined with the greatest care in order to understand this passage, I found written not *inclamantibus* (“those crying out”), but *inflammantibus calumniam falsitatis* (“those inflaming the accusation of falsehood”). Nevertheless, I did not wish to change the ancient reading, lest I should seem to oppose so many learned men.

The words that follow, in parentheses—“for it was a city of the Jews”—are to be read in this way, as the context of Augustine’s discourse itself teaches. The agreement of all the manuscript codices confirms this as well. I therefore marvel that the parent and defender of false antiquities wished, without the support of the copies, to disturb such an authentic reading and impose on us a text of his own: “for it was the city of Oea.”

Certainly Jerome asserts below, in Letter 70, elsewhere numbered 99, that it was a small town. Oea, however, or Tripolis, was not a small town crowded with Jews and other peoples, but a large city of Africa, one of those which, according to Solinus, favored the Romans. Even now Tripolis is a large and fortified city, the capital of the kingdom of Tripoli, with a harbor on the coast of the Mediterranean Sea.

Finally, the very learned French interpreter of Augustine, following the reading and punctuation of this present edition, explained the passage twice as follows:

> “The bishop was compelled to consult the Jews, for it is a city in which there are some,” etc.

Therefore I am compelled to cry out: “Happy are the arts, if only their practitioners judged them; then we should have no shoemakers beyond their shoes”—that is, no one judging matters beyond his competence. | 637 |

## LETTER CVI. TO SUNNIA AND FRETELA

He condemned [the spurious verses] by placing small spits before them; but the genuine and distinguished verses, possessing the Homeric vein, he marked and illuminated with *ἀστερίσκοις*, that is, little stars. Origen therefore transferred these signs into the sacred books, as Epiphanius testifies in his book *On Weights and Measures*, and Jerome in this Letter to Sunnia and Fretela and in nearly all the Prefaces to the divine Scriptures.

From this established practice those who judge books are called Aristarchi. Hence Horace, in the *Art of Poetry*, writes:

> “The good and prudent man will condemn sluggish verses;  
> he will censure the harsh; upon the unpolished he will draw  
> a black mark with his crosswise pen; he will cut away  
> ambitious ornaments; he will compel clarity to be given  
> to what is too obscure; he will criticize ambiguous speech;  
> he will mark what must be changed; he will become an Aristarchus,” etc.

What Horace calls the “black mark with a crosswise pen,” Jerome calls a “transverse rod,” or “a line lying across,” in his Preface to Chronicles according to the Septuagint and in the books of Solomon, which he himself distinguished with asterisks and obeli. Erasmus and Marianus, although the Roman and Gallican manuscript codices consistently retain it.

**To the most beloved brothers Sunnia, etc.** All the manuscript codices, without exception, read this way. Since this epistolary salutation had been removed by Erasmus and Marianus, it gave the father of the history of Old Testament criticism the opportunity for his error: he persuaded himself that Sunnia and Fretela were women learned in Greek and Hebrew. Consult below our annotations placed at the end of this Letter. | 641 |

**Κοινήν.** Several manuscripts corruptly retain *ΚΟΙΝΑ* and *Coine* here; consequently they also have *Luciani* and *Lucianos*. | 642 |

**Jerusalem, etc.** It should be observed, contrary to the opinion of the superficial scholars of our time, that the edition of the Septuagint which did not differ from the Hebrew source was chanted in Jerusalem and in the churches of the East; whereas another edition, not conforming to its source, was rejected and cast aside. | Ibid. |

**Writing in common, I reply.** Codex Vaticanus 344 has: “The person who delivered your Letter to me, I reply by writing to two”; and shortly afterward: “And the truth must be sought among the copies; we return,” etc. | Ibid. |

**Protagoras of Plato.** In the more ancient manuscripts of Saint Jerome’s works I always find *Pythagoram* in place of *Protagora*. This was certainly an easy mistake by ancient copyists, who retained the familiar and better-known name and rejected the unfamiliar one. Consult the Preface to Genesis in Volume 1 of our edition, where Xenophon’s *Oeconomicus* is cited. | 643 |

**OSER, etc.** How false this kind of Hebrew reading is in the Marian edition is clear even to the unlearned. Who has ever read *hajesar* with a consonantal *yod* and a full *ḥolem*? Concerning this corrupt reading, see what is said in our annotations. | 644 |

**Not while we were praying, etc.** We have restored several less important variant readings merely to fill vacant spaces in the column of the old edition, not because they were intended to teach us anything remarkable. | Ibid. |

**It has MOD.** Concerning this and the following false Hebrew reading in Erasmus and Marianus, see our annotations after the text of the Letter. | Ibid. |

**That is, a star.** Let learned men learn the use of asterisks and obeli from Jerome, who had Origen’s Hexapla constantly in his hands—not from certain ignorant writers of our own age, taught not by daily experience of the subject but by the presumption of foolish disputation. Whatever Jerome says concerning the signs of the obelus and asterisk in the Book of Psalms, the Reader will find in full in the second part of the same Saint Jerome’s *Divine Library*, recently published by us. | 645 |

**They are found in poems.** Aristarchus the grammarian, who collected Homer’s poems into a corpus and arranged them into books, marked spurious, adulterated, and interpolated verses with obelisks—that is … |

[Col. 1255] |

645 |

**With two verses inserted.** Consult our annotations below on this passage. | 646 |

**Ὡσεὶ ἒλαφου.** The Cluniacensis manuscript has *ὡς ἐλάφου*, that is, “as of a deer,” etc. | Ibid. |

**Ἀπὸ κοινοῦ.** Very many manuscripts omit these Greek words, but the extremely ancient Cluniacensis did not omit them; from it we restored them in the present edition. | 647 |

**For briefly.** All the older and better manuscripts read thus. One more recent Regius manuscript, written in Florence, retains the reading of Erasmus and Marianus, by which it is most clearly proved that they used only corrupt and recent handwritten copies for their edition of Jerome’s Letters. For, among other corruptions, that same Regius manuscript, no. 3629, consistently retains all the Greek verses [lacuna] from the Septuagint interpreters exactly as they appear in Erasmus and Marianus. | Ibid. |

**Concerning the Hebrew, etc.** These emendations of Jerome are present in the two Psalters, the Roman and the Gallican, published in the second part of the *Divine Library*, that is, in Volume One of our new edition of the works of Saint Jerome. | 649 |

**And the sixth edition.** The word “edition” is omitted in almost all the manuscript copies. | Ibid. |

**Πρόσχες.** In the Regius Florentine manuscript mentioned above, we read *ἐπίβλεπε* with two accents in place of *πρόσχες*. | 650 |

**I found it written.** No trace of the Hebrew reading exists in the older manuscripts, but only in the Regius Florentine, in which there is an erased blank space sufficient for writing the Hebrew words. You should therefore not be surprised that so many adulterated sentences occur in Erasmus and Marianus, since recent codices interpolated and corrupted by ignorant men supplied the cause of their error. | 651 |

**And concerning the preceding third verse.** Consult our Observations below on this most false reading. | 652 |

**What we have translated.** The Gallican Psalter, which was completed with greater care than the Roman Psalter, translated the word “earth” as *tulit* (“took away”). See this in the second part of Volume I of our new edition. | Ibid. |

**Εὐθεῖς.** All the most ancient and best manuscripts read thus. The Regius Florentine, copied by a most ignorant and reckless man, retains *εὐθείων*, because in the Vulgate we read *justorum* (“of the just”) in the plural, although the genuine reading is *εὐθοῦς*, “just” or “upright.” We can learn this from Theodoret and other Greek writers, for, in conformity with the Hebrew, they read:

> *οὐχὶ αὐτὸ γέγραπται* or *τοῦτο γεγραμμένον ἐπὶ βιβλίου τοῦ εὐθοῦς*,

that is:

> “Is this not written in the book of the upright?”

All the Latin manuscripts must therefore be emended on the basis of Theodoret, *Questions* 13 on this passage in Joshua, and on the basis of other copies of the Septuagint translators, which retain this clause. | Ibid. |

**Πάτερ δόξασον, etc.** Here too the Regius Florentine codex is exceedingly corrupt, for it omits all the Greek words except *Πάτερ δόξασον με* (“Father, glorify me”). Erasmus and Marianus supply the rest from the Greek Gospel that is in everyone’s hands. See our annotations below on the Greek words of this Letter. | 654 |

**MERUA.** In the manuscript codices it is written *Merucha* and *Meruha*, but Jerome’s true and genuine reading is *Merua*, because in six hundred passages he himself reads the Hebrew as *Rua*. | Ibid. |

**And of the ends of the earth.** Reader, do not be surprised by the many and extensive additions of Greek verses and words found in the Erasmian and Marian editions. They followed exceedingly corrupt recent copies, in which some reckless person polluted and confused the entire text of Jerome with these additions. The Regius Florentine codex mentioned so often above retains the same spurious additions. | 655 |

**For which it is better, etc.** They omitted this entire passage … |

[Col. 1256] |

656 |

**CATOROT ELIM.** All the manuscript codices read in this way, although the Hebrew has *Cetoreth* in the singular form. I do not know whether *Cetoroth* may have been written in Jerome’s Hebrew volumes. | Ibid. |

**It has written MALOCHOTACH.** Consult our annotations below on this passage. | 659 |

**And yet it must be understood.** This is a notable passage for blunting the ignorance of certain writers of our time, who chatter much against the Hebrew Truth whenever they see that certain things have been adopted in the Church from the Septuagint translators because of their antiquity. Let them therefore hear the most learned Jerome and learn from him to give the source its proper honor without denying the stream its own. | 660 |

**He interpreted it as waters.** The Regius manuscript and the old editions of Erasmus and Marianus thrust upon us an entirely corrupt Greek text, of which not a trace exists in the other manuscript copies. | Ibid. |

**Of my psalms in the night, etc.** Erasmus and Marianus, following the Regius Florentine codex, corruptly read *tuorum* (“of your psalms”). May I be permitted to curse that codex because of how gnawed, mutilated, defiled, interpolated, and contaminated with every filth of corruption it is in the work of Saint Jerome. | 661 |

**JASAPHPHERU.** All the older and more recent manuscript codices of no inferior quality read thus. The printed editions therefore wrongly add the conjunction *vau* and substitute the letter *p* for the double *ph* in the middle. | Ibid. |

**Ὅ ἐκτήσατο.** The execrable Florentine codex adds still other notable corruptions, namely: *αὐτὴ ἡ ἐκτήσατο ἡ δεξία αὐτοῦ*. Consult our annotations below on these Greek words and on those immediately following. | 662 |

**The interpreter of that time.** He seems to attack Rufinus, who in Jerome’s time was considered by the ignorant to be a most eloquent interpreter. Elsewhere Jerome teaches that Rufinus was inept in the Latin language. | 665 |

**BOS is written.** All the most ancient and more recent manuscript codices read thus. See our annotations below on this variant Hebrew reading. | 667 |

**AFAR is given.** Reader, do not be surprised if the Hebrew word is read here with *f* in the middle, *AFAR*, and not *APHAR*, because Jerome often represents the Hebrew letter [with] the Latin *f*, as can be seen in the *Book of Hebrew Names and Places*. | 668 |

**So that you may bring bread out of the earth.** He resumes the preceding verses of the Psalm, since they appear to have been arranged in this way in Sunnia and Fretela’s memorandum. | 669 |

**The fir is the house of the kite.** Jerome thus translated it from Hebrew into Latin. Consult the Book of Psalms in the Canon of the Hebrew Truth, or Volume I of our edition. | 670 |

**EPHSAU.** This is an utterly obvious falsehood in Erasmus and Marianus, who have *hephzi*, etc. They attribute such profound ignorance of the Hebrew language to Jerome that they make him confuse the first-person affix with the affix, or pronoun, of the third person: “my” with “his” or “her.” See our annotations below. | 672 |

**Thus we translate from the Hebrew.** He calls his Latin translation of the Psalms “Hebrew” here because it had been drawn from Hebrew volumes. This is so, however, only if the reading of the manuscript codices in *Hebraeo* is genuine; for it seems somewhat suspect to me, especially since it has been corrected to *in* and changed to *de* in the Cluniacensis copy. | 674 |

## OTHER ANNOTATIONS ON THE SAME LETTER

### Concerning the Subject and Title of this Letter

The subject of this Letter was the correction of the Psalter according to the Hebrew Truth. The manuscript codices state this explicitly in the title of the work itself. The Colbertinus manuscript, no. 455, also indicates this clearly, where we read:

> “Concerning the Psalter: what has been corrupted from the edition of the Septuagint translators.”

For the variant readings of the Latin and Greek books, which Sunnia and Fretela had arranged in order in a memorandum, publicly exposed the corrupted and contaminated interpretation of the Psalms. As Jerome most excellently says to Damasus in the Preface to the Four Gospels:

> “That something is not true because it varies is proved even by the testimony of slanderers.”

The emendation had to be made according to the testimony of the Hebrew codices. Sunnia and Fretela were seeking precisely this, and Jerome consistently teaches it, saying:

> “In the Old Testament, whenever there is a difference between the Greeks and the Latins, we must flee to the Hebrew Truth, so that whatever proceeds from the source, we may seek in the streams.”

The correction of the Psalms could also have been carried out according to that edition of the Seventy Elders which was preserved in Origen’s *Hexapla* and retained in the books of learned men. Concerning that translation of the Septuagint Jerome himself declares:

> “Whatever, therefore, differs from it, no one can doubt that it likewise disagrees with the authority of the Hebrews.”

| [Col. 1257] |

Moreover, some learned writers assert that Sunnia and Fretela were women of rank, distinguished not only by knowledge of Latin and Greek but also of Hebrew. This twofold error is refuted both by the title of the Letter and by its entire context.

First, in all the handwritten books and in the old Venetian edition, this Letter is addressed to *fratres* (“brothers”), not *sorores* or *filiae* (“sisters” or “daughters”), that is, to men and not to women. Thus I found it written in the manuscript codices:

> “To the most beloved brothers Sunnia and Fretela, and to the others who serve the Lord together with you, Jerome.”

Then the holy Doctor congratulates Sunnia and Fretela because their hands and fingers, “formerly hardened by holding the hilt and more suited to handling arrows, are softening for the stylus and pen, and their warlike hearts are being turned toward Christian gentleness.”

It is therefore entirely clear from the words of this Letter that Sunnia and Fretela were men, indeed of Gothic origin, but highly distinguished by the religion of Christ and by their study of the divine Scriptures.

To this may be added that *Fritilas*, *Suinthila* or *Svvintlas*, *Attila*, *Totila*, and *Agila* were masculine names among the Goths. *Fritilas* differs in no way from *Fretela* or *Fritelas*; and *Suinthila* does not differ so greatly from *Sunnia* that the latter could not have been derived from it by adding or changing certain letters.

Moreover, we know that those men, although devoted to the study of sacred books, were nevertheless ignorant of the Hebrew language; for Hieronymus teaches them the letters and syllables of the Hebrew Truth in his Epistle. Thus, in Psalm VII he makes this observation:

> “In Hebrew it has **SEDECI**, which means ‘my righteousness,’ and not **SEDECACH**, which signifies ‘your righteousness.’”

Likewise, in Psalm XXII Hieronymus writes:

> “Moreover, both the Septuagint and the Hebrews, and all interpreters, have ‘my cup’; in Hebrew it is **CHOSI**. Otherwise, if it were ‘your cup,’ it would be said **CHOSACH**.”

Hieronymus certainly would not have taught this to men who had only the slightest acquaintance with Hebrew letters. Finally, Sunnia and Fretela ask the holy Doctor to indicate, among the variant Greek and Latin readings of the Psalms, what agrees best with the Hebrew. They might have managed to pursue that study by their own efforts, unless they were altogether unskilled in Hebrew matters.

### On the date of this writing

Several considerations persuade us that the Epistle of Saint Hieronymus to Sunnia and Fretela was written in the year 405 after Christ. Our first conjecture arises from the journey of the presbyter Firmus, who was the bearer of this work, that is, of the Epistle, as Hieronymus himself testifies in his reply. In that year, 405, the presbyter Firmus brought from Palestine to Africa Hieronymus’s Epistle, now numbered XCVI, written to Augustine. This is established in the chronological notes of the new edition of Saint Augustine. Firmus could therefore have received from Hieronymus this Epistle to Sunnia and Fretela, either to return it or to deliver it.

We may draw the same conclusion from the controversies among the Greeks at that time, which Hieronymus alludes to plainly enough in these words at the beginning of the Epistle:

> “Who would believe,” he says, “that the barbarous language of the Getae was seeking the Hebrew truth, and that, while the Greeks were sleeping—or rather disputing—Germany itself was examining the utterances of the Holy Spirit?”

If these words are understood of the rival factions among the Greeks in the affair of Theophilus and Saint Chrysostom, it is necessary to affirm that this Epistle was written by Hieronymus in 405, or in the preceding year, 404.

It is certain that he did not write to Sunnia and Fretela before 392, when Hieronymus’s Latin translation of the Psalms from the Hebrew source had been completed and was circulating. The Epistle frequently contains readings from this translation and statements cited by Hieronymus himself. Moreover, Hieronymus would hardly have failed to mention the Epistle to Sunnia and Fretela in his books of Apology against Ruffinus if he had written it before 402, the date at which the later Apology is thought to have been composed. In that splendid work the Septuagint Interpreters are everywhere treated with honor; this could have been a powerful means of blunting Ruffinus’s slander, by which he sought to persuade everyone that Hieronymus had undertaken and composed a new translation of the Old Testament in order to disparage the Seventy Elders.

Finally, in my judgment, Hieronymus also mocks Ruffinus when, writing ironically to Sunnia and Fretela about a certain interpreter of that period, he says:

> “Unless perhaps you suppose that **ἐξουδένωσας** should not be translated ‘you despised,’ but, according to the most eloquent interpreter of that age, ‘you annihilated,’ or ‘you annulled,’ or ‘you nullified’; and whatever other monstrosities of words may be found among the unlearned.”

At that time Ruffinus was regarded by some as a distinguished interpreter. He claimed so much authority for himself that he would correct Latin copies of the divine Scriptures from the Greek manuscripts. “You will correct the Latin Scriptures from the Greek,” Hieronymus says in the final Apology, “and will give the churches something different to read from what they once received from the Apostles; but I shall not be permitted to do so,” and so forth. From this we may understand—if there is room for conjecture—that Ruffinus perhaps rendered the Greek **ἐξουδένωσας**, and the Latin *despexisti*, somewhere as “you annihilated” or “you nullified,” the monstrous expressions which Hieronymus calls the words of unlearned men.

Ruffinus is believed to have departed this life around 410 after Christ. I know, certainly, that because of the affair involving Eustochium and the younger Paula, Hieronymus sent the presbyter Firmus to Ravenna, and from there to Africa and Sicily, in the year 415; Firmus could therefore have undertaken to carry Hieronymus’s Epistle to Sunnia and Fretela along with others. Yet the considerations noted concerning the controversies of the Greeks by no means allow the writing of the Epistle to be postponed to so late a date.

### On some obscure passages and variant readings

Concerning this matter my holy son Avitus had often inquired.

Together with three other editions—those of Aquila, Theodotion, and Symmachus—he removed all the errors that had crept into the edition of the Seventy Elders and caused the stream of the Greek translation to return, as it were, from its channel to its source and spring. He himself testifies to this in the eighth Treatise on Matthew, in these words:

> “In the copies of the Old Testament, whatever inconsistencies there were, we were able, God assisting, to reconcile, using the judgment of the other editions. For those things that appeared doubtful in the Septuagint because of the agreement of the copies, we made a judgment from the remaining editions and preserved what was consistent.”

Hence such agreement arose between the Hebrew and Greek books of the Hexapla, although otherwise the copies of the Seventy Elders themselves differed in many respects from those found in the books of the Hebrews. The same Hieronymus teaches this, and here discusses the matter at greater length.

If the holy Doctor were to rise again today, how many annotations would he find inserted by scribes into the body of his writings—annotations that he had added in the margin for the instruction of the reader? Through the willfulness of copyists, everything has been confused and thrown into disorder in many handwritten books and printed editions. Unless the abundance of numerous manuscripts of the highest quality had come to our aid, I would have despaired of restoring the works of Saint Hieronymus in their entirety.

In ancient manuscripts I found so great an admixture of such annotations in the text of the Latin Psalms that, because of the frequency of these corruptions, I was terrified as I read. Who would believe that, in the text of Psalm LXVII alone, nine anonymous annotations had been placed in the margin—annotations that the excellent manuscript codices of the Church of Carcassonne and our San-Germain manuscript display beside the verses? If I had not fortunately obtained these books, how could I have recognized the annotations introduced into the text by scribes in Hieronymus’s Latin Psalter, rendered from the Hebrew source? These annotations often come closer to the meaning of the Hebrew words than do other words in the text itself.

Certainly, the reliability of the printed books would have seemed suspect to me in the Psalms because of the variant readings of certain manuscripts; and, unaware of the ignorance of ancient scribes, I might have written as uncorrected what had actually been corrected, unless the use of the oldest books already praised had most fortunately been available to me.

I have not yet established whether this Avitus is the man who, in the year 415 after Christ, published in the Latin language for the peoples of the West, through Orosius, the little work of the presbyter Lucian on the discovery of the relics of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr. Four or five contemporaries named Avitus are, moreover, distinguishable from the letters of Hieronymus and Augustine.

The first is the very man whom the holy Doctor now mentions in the Epistle to Sunnia and Fretela:

> “Concerning this matter also my holy son Avitus had often inquired.”

And again at the end:

> “For this reason also, concerning what you ask at the end of your note, and what my holy son Avitus frequently requests,” and so forth.

Of another Avitus the same Hieronymus wrote in Epistle IX to Salvina:

> “The final reason,” he says, “and the stronger one, is that I could deny nothing to my son Avitus when he asked. By frequent letters he overcame the resistance of a harsh judge, and by setting before me examples of many to whom I had written on the same subject, he so overwhelmed the shame of refusal that I considered more what he desired than what it was fitting for me to do.”

Thus in both Epistles Avitus is called a son by Hieronymus; in both he repeatedly requests something, and in frequent letters asks much of him. It remains to suppose that this Avitus was African by birth and a fellow countryman of Salvina, the daughter of Gildo, the tyrant who at that time occupied Africa. If we accept this, I readily persuade myself that the Avitus of both Epistles—IX and CXXXV—is one and the same man: he had often asked Hieronymus both for discussions of variant readings in the Psalms on his own behalf and for exhortatory letters to Salvina concerning the holy preservation of widowhood.

| 642 |

These facts plainly agree with what we brought forward above concerning the presbyter Firmus returning from Palestine to Africa in the year 405. Hieronymus replied to his son Avitus on the occasion of the presbyter Firmus:

> “Concerning this matter also my holy son Avitus had often inquired. And since the occasion of our brother Firmus the presbyter presented itself—he who brought me your Epistle from you—I am writing a general reply and freeing myself from a great debt of friendship.”

But if the elder Avitus of Spain is to be understood here, he could have been present in Jerusalem when these words were written by Hieronymus. From what Baronius records under the year 415, he appears to have spent sufficient time in Palestine. That elder Avitus himself writes to the Church of Braga.

Nor is he one of the two Aviti who are spoken of unfavorably in Orosius’s consultation or memorandum to Augustine. Orosius himself would surely have avoided him altogether as a heretical Origenist, after writing the following about those two fellow citizens of his:

> “Then two fellow citizens of mine, Avitus and another Avitus, [lacuna] went abroad. One departed for Jerusalem, the other for Rome. When they returned, one brought back Origen, the other Victorinus.”

And again:

> “These two Aviti, and with them the holy Greek Basil, who taught these things most blessedly, nevertheless handed down certain matters from Origen’s books incorrectly, as I have recently come to understand.”

The Avitus who went to Jerusalem and brought Origen back among the Spaniards is the man to whom Hieronymus’s Epistle 59 is recorded as having been written. We shall speak of these matters in their proper place.

And, according to the intention of the scribes, the old edition is corrupt. All the manuscripts read this way, and the context itself urges that it should be read so: for the **Κοινὴ** Edition is said to be corrupt in different places and periods, which would not be the case if it were thought to have been corrupted only through the negligence and ignorance of ancient scribes.

| 643 |

Whatever therefore differs from this is without doubt also at variance with the authority of the Hebrews. Nor should it seem surprising that the Greek copies of the Seventy Interpreters in Origen’s Hexapla agree so well with the authority of the Hebrew books, because Origen himself, after comparing copies of the Seventy Elders partly with the Hebrew text and partly—

[Column 1259]

| 643 |

And you ask why the Greek does not have this verse a second time, with two verses inserted between. This is an altogether remarkable passage for recalling antiquity, from which we learn that among the ancients the order of the verses in the Psalms was arranged differently and that their sequence was counted differently. For the verses of the Psalms, once copied separately and continuously, were formerly separated by spaces so large that the verse which among us is numbered Psalm XVII, verse 14, is found in the books of ancient writers as verse 35 or 36; and our single verse 14 was divided by them into three.

Saint Hieronymus demonstrates this most clearly when he says that two verses had been inserted after the first verse:

> “Hail and coals of fire.”

Accordingly, this passage of Psalm XVII was written in Hieronymus’s copies in the following form:

> Hail and coals of fire.  
>   
> And the Lord thundered from the heavens.  
>   
> And the Most High gave his voice.  
>   
> Hail and coals of fire.

In the very ancient manuscript codex of the Church of Carcassonne, in which Hieronymus’s Psalter, translated from the Hebrew into Latin, is written *stichērōs*—that is, in verse-by-verse form—the same order and numbering of the verses would have been preserved, had not, through the fault of the first scribe, three verses in the text of the Psalm been omitted after the verse “Hail and coals of fire.” He later placed them at the lower margin of the book in this form:

> And the Lord thundered from the heavens,  
>   
> and the Most High gave his voice; hail and  
>   
> coals of fire.

These verses, being set out separately rather than copied continuously, would have occupied almost the entire lower edge of the parchment; therefore two verses necessarily coalesced into one there. If this were not so, the passage in the manuscript codices would have to be corrected on the basis of the very words of Hieronymus just cited. See the *Canon of the Hebrew Truth*, volume I of our edition.

| 646 |

An addition was made concerning the preceding verse, in which one reads: “Gird your sword upon your thigh, O most mighty one.” Here the reliability of the editions of Erasmus and Marianus fails completely. Lacking an adequate supply of manuscript copies for correcting Hieronymus, those editors adhered to the most corrupt and most recent copies of the lowest quality.

Their correctors therefore read, after the copyist of the Florentine Royal Codex:

> “An addition was made concerning the preceding third verse,” and so forth.

This is as though, in Hieronymus’s time, the verse of Psalm 44, “Gird your sword upon your thigh, O most mighty one,” had been numbered and written as the third verse, as is now customary among us in the Latin Vulgate and in the Greek translation of the Seventy Interpreters. In Hieronymus it was not written as the third verse, but as the sixth, or even the ninth if the title of the Psalm is counted among the verses. This is confirmed by the manuscript codices of the Psalms: the Carcassonne manuscript mentioned above, the San-Germain manuscript, and the Memmian manuscript, of which we have spoken elsewhere.

| 652 |

For what the Septuagint translated should, because of its antiquity, be sung in the churches; and the other translation should be known by the learned for knowledge of the Scriptures. This statement deserves to be weighed in gold. Would that the recent defenders of the chronology of the Seventy Interpreters had weighed such golden words more carefully! They hear the ages of the world, from its creation to the birth of Christ, reckoned according to the calculation of the Seventy Elders once each year in the churches, when the Martyrology is read in choir; and immediately they pronounce the chronology of the Hebrew source and of the Latin Vulgate Edition corrupt, indeed rejected by the Church of Christ’s sound judgment.

They do not understand that, because of its antiquity, the Eusebian Chronicle is still used in the Roman Church; whereas knowledge of the Scriptures is to be obtained only from the authoritative books, namely, the Hebrew and Latin copies.

| 660 |

Therefore, if anything was added in the margin for the sake of study, it ought not to be placed in the body of the text, lest it disturb the earlier translation according to the will of the scribes. Because of a single annotation of Hieronymus, rashly placed by someone in the body of the translation from the margin, a question formerly arose among many—

[Column 1260]

“And I do not know what, which is not said, seems to have been founded upon the earth.” Erasmus and Marianus read this with the opposite meaning:

> “And I do not know what, which is said, seems to have been founded upon the earth.”

That this is false is apparent even to those paying little attention. We pass over the remaining matters in which the old editions contain a perverse order, fabricated interpretations, lacunae in the principal subjects, and passages interpolated with many verses, because these things are made clear simply by reading the Epistle and comparing the editions. Nevertheless, it must not be omitted that many faults remain in the commonly circulated Latin copies of the Psalms—faults that Hieronymus himself had removed and that he wished us to cut away as either superfluous or false. See Psalms 43 and 47, and so forth.

### On the Greek variant readings of this Epistle

Thus Hieronymus would flow entirely through muddy water. In reciting the words of this Doctor, Nobilius relied on Marianus; hence it happened that he sprinkled innumerable errors throughout his critical notes, since he generally reports variant readings from thoroughly corrupt books.

“That Saint Hieronymus,” he says at this point, “testifies that the Septuagint said **τὰ ἐπαγγέλματα σου**, ‘your proclamations’—which the Vulgate has—or ‘your promises’; but Aquila had **ἀγγέλους σου**, ‘your angels and messengers.’”

It was worthwhile to warn the reader that Nobilius is thoroughly corrupt in his notes on this passage, lest thereafter he happen to sit in an unreliable seat and cling to false readings cited from the corrupted Hieronymus in Marianus.

**Κατεύθυνον ἐνόπιον σου ὁδόν μου** — “Direct my way before you.” Formerly only the **Κοινὴ** Edition preferred this reading, as Hieronymus testifies here. The Roman Edition of the Seventy Elders now has the same reading. How closely it approaches the **Κοινὴ** and the edition called Lucian’s can easily be proved from several passages of this Epistle. We shall henceforth refer readers to such agreements, lest the excessive length of our observations discourage their study.

| 644 |

**Ἐν τῷ στόματι αὐτοῦ δόλος** — “In his mouth there is deceit.” The old editions add **οὐδὲ ἐστίν**, “and there is not,” and in Latin, *neque est*, “nor is there.”

On the following page, moreover, instead of the single Greek word **σπεῦσον**, “hasten,” Erasmus and Marianus recite the entire verse of Psalm XXXIX. Throughout the Epistle they similarly insert complete verses from Greek copies of the Seventy, as though Hieronymus himself had placed them there, although he reports only a very few words suitable for resolving the questions—and in many other places merely cites Latin words. The comparison of the new and old editions alone makes this clear; we therefore do not linger over these matters.

| 649 |

**Πάτερ δοξασόν με**, etc. — “Father, glorify me,” etc. The Greek reading of the Gospel text, varying in so many words, clearly shows that the editions of Erasmus and Marianus are not trustworthy. In correcting Hieronymus, they consistently use not ancient manuscript codices of Hieronymus but Bibles of the Plautine type or the Roman edition, as though Hieronymus had possessed one single and identical text of Hebrew, Greek, and Latin Scripture, the same as our present arrangement of the sacred books.

| 654 |

Aquila translated it **ἀγγελίας**, that is, “your messengers”; the Septuagint translated it **τὰς ἐπαγγελίας σου**, that is, “your proclamations,” or “your promises.”

Not Hieronymus alone, but also Aquila as cited by Hieronymus, together with the Septuagint and the other interpreters, have been corrupted very ineptly by certain recent manuscripts and old editions. In this passage they teach that Aquila translated **ἀγγέλους σου**, “your angels,” and that the Septuagint had **τὰ ἐπαγγελματα σου**. Both statements are proved false, both by the one reading found in all the manuscript codices and by the absurd meaning that Aquila would have produced if he had rendered it **ἀγγέλους σου** here.

For who does not know that this reading is absurd and alien to the sense of Scripture?

> “But for me it is good to cling to God, to place my hope in the Lord, so that I may announce all your angels at the gates of the daughter of Zion.”

Messengers and angels are not themselves announced; rather, they are the ones who announce and proclaim the great works of God to others. The Prophet therefore wishes neither to proclaim himself nor to announce any messengers, but to proclaim the **ἀγγελίας** and **ἐπαγγελίας** of his God—that is, his proclamations, praises, and promises—at the gates of the daughter of Zion.

Let the reader take note, in the Greek and Latin observations with which Nobilius illustrated the Roman Edition of the Seventy Elders—

| 669 |

**Ἐνεπύρισαν πάσας τὰς συναγωγὰς τοῦ Θεοῦ** — “They burned all the assemblies of God.” The corruption of Hieronymus in Marianus and Nobilius is demonstrated here with the greatest clarity. Since the holy Doctor testified that Aquila and Symmachus translated as I have already written, **ἐνεπύρισαν**, and so forth, those editors, if I am not mistaken, produce this reading fabricated from several interpreters:

The scholiast in Nobilius also departs from Hieronymus concerning Aquila and Theodotion. But leaving all these matters aside, it is preferable to follow the writer who recited the Greek interpretations according to the authority of Origen’s Hexapla.

Aquila translated **ἐν λιπαροῖς αὐτῶν**, “among their rich places”; Symmachus, **εὐπώροις τοὺς λιπαρωτέρους αὐτῶν**, “in prosperous places, their more prosperous ones.” The scholiast in Nobilius’s notes on Psalm LXXVII also testifies that Aquila and Symmachus translated in this way. From whatever source Erasmus and Marianus borrowed **εὐπώροις αὐτῶν**, **τοῖς εὐπορωτέροις**, and consequently **πληρέσιν**, “full,” and **ἐψεύσαντο αὐτὸν**, “they lied to him,” it is clear that Hieronymus was falsified by them.

**Ὃρος τοῦτο ἐκτήσατο ἡ δεξιὰ αὐτοῦ**, “This mountain his right hand acquired,” not, as you suppose, **ὃ ἐκτήσατο**, “which he acquired.” The correctors whom we have so often criticized overturn here the authority, words, and meaning of Hieronymus from the foundations.

Hieronymus acknowledges that the Septuagint has **ὄρος τοῦτο**, that is, “this mountain,” but denies that the following **ὅ** was present, as Sunnia and Fretela supposed. From the **Κοινή** they were reading in Latin, “this mountain which he acquired,” and so forth. This reading is also found today in the Roman Edition of the Seventy.

Symmachus therefore interpreted the passage more correctly according to the Hebrew idiom. In place of the Septuagint’s **τοῦτο ἐκτήσατο**, he wrote **ὃ ἐκτήσατο**, with Hieronymus’s approval; Hieronymus was exceptionally well versed in the meaning and idiom of the Hebrew language.

It would be surprising to discover anything elsewhere in Erasmus and Marianus that was not recent and fabricated from the old Hieronymus. Here they read the Greek from modern copies and impose upon us the feminine **ἤ** in place of the neuter article **ὅ**.

The Cluniac manuscript also retains this reading. The Sorbonne manuscript, however, does have **λιθόριον**, but, together with the other more ancient copies, reads **ὡς ὀπωροφηλάκιον**.

Among these variant readings, I now prefer **εἰς** and **λιθύριον** to **ὡς** and **λιθαόριον**, although the latter have already been printed in the context of the preceding Epistle.

They wish Hieronymus to have testified that all the interpreters translated the Hebrew expression **LAASIDACH** as **τοῖς ἀγίοις σου**, “to your holy ones,” although it is certain from the same uncorrupted Hieronymus that none of the Greek interpreters had **ἀγίοις**, but that all rendered it **ὁσίοις**.

### On the Hebrew words of the same Epistle

The following is written concerning the same element in Hieronymus’s book *On Hebrew Places*:

> “Up to this point,” he says, “we must read through the letter C, that is, the Greek kappa. From there onward it must be written and read through the element chi, which contains an aspiration and is not found among the Latins.”

Since these words were misunderstood by scribes, they could easily pronounce and write *chi* as *ch*.

The holy Hieronymus read the following verse of Psalm V, apart from the vowel points, as it is in the Hebrew:

> **oser laphanai darchach**, that is, “direct your way before me.”

All the ancient interpreters translated it with a similar wording, although in the common Edition and in the Vulgate of the Seventy Elders it appears to have been read:

> **oser laphanach darchi**, that is, “direct my way before you.”

The many corruptions of this passage demonstrate how greatly Hieronymus’s Hebrew words have been corrupted and how incorrectly they are read in Erasmus and Marianus. Nor do they wish to read with the holy Doctor **oser laphanai darchach**, but rather, with the Masoretes or modern grammarians, **haiesar lephanai darchecha**.

It is as though Hieronymus’s Hebrew readings had to be adapted to the complications of the Masoretic *qere* and *ketiv* or to the rules of the grammarians, rather than the punctuation and critical signs of the Masoretes being corrected on the basis of Hieronymus, who is greatly superior to all of them.

The holy Doctor therefore read **oser** instead of the modern **haiesar**; following the usage of the ancients, he read **laphanai** instead of **lephanai**; and, in the Chaldean manner, **darchach** instead of **darchecha**.

He has **MALACHOTACH** written in Hebrew. The manuscript codices seem to have a somewhat corrupt reading here, where we read **malochochach**. This arose readily through the scribes’ tendency to write *eh* instead of *lh*; and, according to each person’s whim, they add or remove *h* and *c*. From this, without doubt, **malochochach** arose in place of **malochothach**.

Yet this passage is not free from difficulty if **malochochach** is examined more carefully. Certainly, in Nahum, chapter 2, verse 14, we read a form which, with the vowels supplied, appears to be the **malochochach** of the manuscript codices, especially since it has the same meaning as **malochochah** or **malachechech**, and **malachecha**.

[The preceding words are textually incomplete:] “by the holy Doctor, ‘of his will.’” This is a shameful error, one that cannot be excused in the correctors of Hieronymus, since it imputes profound ignorance to a thoroughly learned man and completely destroys the sense of Scripture and of the interpreters.

For who among the Hebrews does not know that **Hephzi** means “my will,” and not “his will” or “the will of him”? The reading of all the manuscripts is therefore true and genuine, while the reading in the previously printed books is depraved and utterly corrupt.

**OSER LAPHANAI DARCHACH.** This is how I read it in all the manuscript books and in the Venetian edition of Andrea de Toresanis. They add only an *i* at the end of **darchach**, reading **darchachi**. Many manuscripts retain the same form below in **cosachi**, in place of **chosach**. This is plainly a scribal error in which the name of the element was put in place of the element itself: **CHI** for **CII**, just as elsewhere **QU** is used for **Q**, as will be clear at the place where *liquebit* or *lice bit* is involved.

[Column 1262]

| 644 |

In Hebrew it has **MOD**, that is, “very greatly.” Hieronymus was unfamiliar with the grammarians’ *sheva* of his time; therefore he habitually wrote **mod**, not **meod** as they did. In the Florentine Royal Manuscript and in the Venetian Edition, in place of the Hebrew **mod**, we read the Latin word *modum*. The authors and ancient copyists of this edition were so unskilled in Hebrew that, since Hebrew **mod** or **meod** means “very greatly,” they added *um* to **mod**, making *modum* function adverbially for *admodum*, “very greatly.”

From this the reader may observe the foolish presumption of many superficial scholars who, once they have been dipped in Latin or Greek letters, dare anything in restoring the writings of ancient authors, swollen, naturally, with an excessive love of praise.

| Same place |

**SEDECI HABEТ.** This passage has been corrupted in more than one way by Erasmus and Marianus, who read **zideki**, contrary to the practice of Hieronymus. His words in the book *On Hebrew Names* are these:

> “What we said at the beginning should be observed in the vowel letters . . . must now also be understood concerning the letter *s*. Among them there are three letters *s*: one called *samech*, which is read simply, as though it were represented by our letter; another, *sin*, in which a certain hissing sound of a kind not found in our language is heard; and a third, *sade*, which our ears utterly dread,” and so forth.

Below he also wished us to observe the following concerning several letters:

> “The letter *h*,” he says, “is considered by most people to be an aspiration, not a letter. There is no need to mention *k*, since among the Latins also, except in *kalends*, it is judged superfluous.”

Hieronymus would therefore be inconsistent with himself unless he read **sedeci** here, and not **zideki** with his correctors, who consequently also change the form **sedechach** into **zidekathecha**.

| Same place |

**BIOM**, that is, “on the day.” Thus Hieronymus read it in place of the modern **beiom**, and below **brucho**, **sphannim**, and **idaim**, instead of **berucho**, **sephannim**, and **jedaim**.

The reason for this kind of reading is clear among ancient writers, who often used the elements in place of the sounds of letters: *b* for *be*, hence *krus* for *karus*; *qi*, *qae*, and *qid* for *qui*, *quae*, and *quid*, and so forth.

| 647 |

**SCRIBERETUR BAFFIO.** In the manuscripts we read **bafficho**, as was customary among ancient copyists. They placed dense aspirations between two vowels: *michi*, *nichil*, *bafficho*, *merucha*, *merechim*, and many similar forms.

| 649 |

**SCRIPTUM EST, BATTHOCH MEAI.** The Florentine Codex and the Venetian Edition provoke laughter here. In place of **batthoc meai**, we read **batthos meae**, as though “belly” in Hebrew were *bas* or *bantos*, and had a feminine genitive.

The passage concerns the words “in the middle of my belly.” The unlearned, having no acquaintance with Hebrew letters from elsewhere, supposed that the *c* of **batthoc** was the Greek sigma and that **meai** was a first-person possessive pronoun put in place of *meae*, just as **aulai** and **musai** are used instead of *aulae* and *musae*.

Thus, attending to the Latin translation, “of my belly,” they very ineptly thrust upon us certain barbarous and, so to speak, Sarmatian words, previously unheard among Hebrews, Greeks, or Latins. Let our superficial scholars now see how dangerous the presumption of men like themselves has always been—men who did not hesitate to lay unlearned hands upon the learned Hieronymus. Let them be ashamed of that futile loquacity which, with such contempt, pours out its abuse against students of the Hebrew codices.

[Column 1263]

| 659 |

**SARPHU CHOL MOEDAU EL BAARES.** It plainly appears that Hieronymus read **moedau** or **moedav** in his Hebrew copy in place of the modern **moade**. Whether one calls this a pleonasm or the paragoge of the attached *vau*, a variant Hebrew reading arises here, one that, as far as I know, no one has yet observed in this Psalm.

| 660 |

**HABETUR BATHABUNOTH.** The manuscript books do not read **bathabunoth**, but all read **Athacunuth**. In this form the preposition *b* of the Hebrew text is omitted, *c* is written in the middle in place of *b*, and at the end **uth** is written instead of **oth**.

Many will therefore suppose that this reading in the manuscripts has been turned into something worse and has been contaminated and corrupted on every side. But anyone who pays attention to the habits and usage of ancient copyists will readily see that **Athachunut** can pass into **Batcabunoth**.

We can readily establish this from a single manuscript in the Royal Library. The Royal manuscript book of the Epistles of Saint Hieronymus, number 3999, uses the following forms of Greek letters in the Epistle to Evangelus concerning Melchizedek: **Bpb)-(.** Abram reads this, with Latin letters supplied and a line drawn above it, as **Bhpcheu**; similarly **Barcheu**, and **cbp θh**, **Sarath**.

These examples clearly show that ancient scribes used the letter *h* when writing Hebrew words in place of the vowel *a*. Moreover, *B* and *C*, or *k*, were used interchangeably among them because of the similarity in the shape of the two elements. For the *B* written in this way in the manuscripts appears to be the letter *K* itself.

Finally, it is universally acknowledged among students that *o* was frequently changed into *u*: hence *epistulam*, *sosunde*, and *praestu* instead of *epistolam*, *sosonde*, and *praesto*.

Thus **bathabunoth** may originally have been written with these letters as **bθakunuθh**. From this one person could read **Athacunuth**, while another could read **bthabunoth**. However the scribes may have written it, there is no doubt that Hieronymus read **bathabunoth**, since everywhere he interpreted this word as “in understandings.”

I know that the Chaldean, the Syriac, and others read it in the singular, as though it were **bathabunuth**, “in prudence” and “in understanding.” But our present discussion concerns the reading of Hieronymus.

| 663 |

**LIIN IS WRITTEN.** Thus in Micah, chapter 3, verse 12, we read the same meaning, although **liim** may also be read here, because scribes very often change *m* into *n*, as in *Cherubin* and *Seraphin*.

| Same place |

**LAASIDACH IS FOUND.** In modern Hebrew it is written **labasidecha**, without the superfluous *iod* at the end. Pagninus or Arias Montanus translates it as “to your merciful one.” Hieronymus and all the ancient interpreters oppose this reading; they likewise render it in the plural as “your sons,” “your holy ones,” or “your righteous ones.”

The authority for this reading may be found in the Chaldean Paraphrase, where it is read in the plural as **lahasidaich**, or Hieronymus’s **laasidach**.

| 664 |

**MEOLAM AD OLAM ATH EL.** No one has observed this variant reading of the Hebrew text of Psalm LXXXIX, verse 12, although grammarians teach in several passages that it is put in place of another form [the precise omitted reference is uncertain].

The word BOS is written. We therefore read Cos, as it was read today in all the copies of the Ancients—unless we suppose that Jerome was misled by the similarity of the letters beth and caph; or, at any rate, that K was changed into B, that is, C into B, as was noted a little earlier. But when the meaning of this word Bos is carefully examined, the Arabic word baz, or boz, immediately presents itself; among the Arabs it is read bisi and signifies a falcon, a hawk, and other birds of prey. The Rabbis also call the owl and the horned owl bua. No one, surely, will deny that this strongly supports the reading Bos in this passage—especially because Jerome himself, following the Sixth Edition, translated Bos into Latin as *noctua* (“owl”), and testifies that many had contentiously interpreted the same word as *bubo* (“horned owl”). It makes no difference whether we read *bas* or *boz*, since among Eastern peoples, and especially among the Arabs, quiescent letters, as well as letters produced by the same organ, frequently interchange. But concerning Bos or Cos, let the judgment here belong to the learned. | 666 |

He does not have EPHSAV. In place of *ephsav*, Erasmus and Marianus read *hephzi*. And they say that this word *hephzi* was interpreted by a—

667

It is called BACHAFFI. I once suspected that Jerome had read not *bachaffi* but *bachaffai* in the plural. But when I examined the Latin interpretation of the Psalms from the Hebrew, I learned from Jerome himself that *bachaffi* is the correct reading. For in Psalm 118, verse 109, he renders it in Latin in this way: “My soul is continually in my hand.” No one should be troubled by the fact that in this Letter we read “in my hands,” for, since the sense of Scripture is one, he followed here the custom of the ancient interpreters. On this matter he warned the Reader in more than one place: “But in this too there is no change in meaning, and, following the ancient interpretation, we did not wish to change what caused no harm.” | 672 |

Moreover, the diligent Reader should apparently be warned that we have removed certain letters, or the aspirations H and CH, from some Hebrew words, wherever we were fully certain that they had been written and introduced through the practice of ancient scribes. But everything remains untouched and complete when Jerome’s reading appeared uncertain and doubtful, as in *Brucho*, etc., or when it does not harm the sense of the words, as in *Hod* and *Lahed*. But enough concerning Hebrew matters and the Letter to Sunnia and Fretela. | 674 |

EPISTLE 107, TO LAETA

Very many manuscript copies read, “The Letter of Saint Jerome to Aleta”; but the older copies retain *Laeta*. | 677 |

“Is it not the cave of Mithras?” This is a notable passage, both because of the commentaries of learned men and because of the various corruptions of the text in printed books and in the editors’ annotations. Readers encounter it in this form: “To whom Corax, Niphus, Miles, Leo, Perses, Helios, Bromius the Father are initiated; he overturned, broke, and shook.” We read nothing in the manuscript copies about the words *Helios* and *Bromios pater*. These are false names, fabricated by the editors. In all our copies I read as follows: “Perses Heliodromos likewise are initiated,” or “were being initiated”; and afterward, “he overturned, broke, and shook.”

Moreover, this passage was not, in my view, so tangled and difficult that it should have been handed down to us as unintelligible and inexplicable after the efforts of so many men. We can therefore explain the present passage in this way. Porphyry, in his account drawn from Eubulus, reports that among the Persians Zoroaster first consecrated, in honor of Mithras, the creator and father of all things, a cave naturally formed in the mountains of Persia, so that by means of the cave he might signify that the world had been created by Mithras. To this refer what is said by Socrates in Book 3, chapter 12, and by Sozomen, who says: “In a Mithraeum certain images and instruments of unknown sort were found; but they appeared exceedingly ridiculous and strange.”

When Rome had become the teacher of falsehood and served the errors of all nations, she seemed to herself to have assumed a great religion if she possessed a cave of Mithras along with the other temples of idols. This cave of Mithras, therefore, the urban prefect Gracchus overturned before he was initiated into the mysteries of Christ. In the cave of Mithras there were symbols of the stars and planets, and consequently images of the heavenly bodies listed by Jerome. For who does not know that there is a constellation called the Raven (*Corax*), as well as the Nymph—that is, the Nymph and the Virgin—and the Soldier, or Warrior, and the Giant, the Lion, Perses or Perseus, and the other signs of the Zodiac, which are properly represented in *Heliodromos*? For *Heliodromos* means the course or path of the sun as it completes its circuit. Whoever wishes may consult L. Coelius Rhodiginus’s *Ancient Readings*, the pagan Proclus, and C. Julius Hyginus. | 678 |

“The letter, when it leads to a crossroads.” Consult what we have said about the Pythagorean letter Υ in the Commentaries on Ecclesiastes, vol. II, col. 770. | 684 |

EPISTLE 108, TO EUSTOCHIUM V

“The Letter.” When he says that some copies read *vau*, he must necessarily mean printed copies, since there is no manuscript copy that does not read *zop* or *zod*. Moreover, *zo*, or *zu*, is now a common demonstrative pronoun among grammarians, meaning “this man” or “this woman.” Then *zolk*, feminine, is often used among the Hebrews with neuter gender. Paula could therefore have taken these Hebrew pronouns and suffixes indiscriminately, so as to refer the Psalmist’s words to Christ himself: “Behold, we have heard him; we have found him.” The Syriac translator into Latin also seems to have done the same, saying: “Behold, we heard this in Ephratha, and found it in the fields.” Certainly, in the present Hebrew text we do not read *schemaanuba*, “we found him,” but *schemaanuha*, “we found her.” Thus Paula seems to say here that the feminine suffix can be understood as masculine because of the context, in which the suffixes are masculine: “We shall enter into his tabernacle. We shall worship where his feet stood.”

“[She] reached Acco.” In place of *Acco*, or *Accho*, ancient scribes wrote *ad Coth*. But there is no such place as Coth, especially not one called Ptolemais. There is indeed Cotta, or Κουθὰ, in the tribe of Zebulun, a city assigned to the Levites according to Eusebius and Jerome in the *Book of Hebrew Places*. But it is called *Cateth* in the Vulgate, and was never called Ptolemais. In the Cluniac manuscript a second hand wrote *ad Choum*; but in vain, since Chous is not in Galilee. | 696 |

“Thus *zo* is a Hebrew word.” This passage has been variously corrupted through ignorance of both Greek and Hebrew, as Desiderius Erasmus taught before us in his scholia on this—

“Is reserved for Christ’s flame-colored veil.” The *flammeum* was a garment, or veil, of flame-colored fabric, proper to virgins consecrated to God. | 720 |

“Sleeping,” in the Hebrew, Greek, etc. The word “Hebrew” is absent from the manuscripts; in the Cluniac copies this word is placed in the margin. | 723 |

We have placed the Letter to Riparius of Tarragona here in the Cluniac codex, not in chronological order, but because of the subject of the Letter and the immediately following work against Vigilantius, which had to be published among the polemical works, following the practice of the ancient editions. | 725 |
