EPISTLE 112, TO AUGUSTINE

“And Apollinaris of Laodicea.” This is how the old Cluniac codex reads; others omit *Apollinaris*, reading only “and of Laodicea.” | 739 |

“To him who previously, etc.” Very many manuscript copies read: “With whom the Testament had not previously existed.” This is the best reading and should not be rejected. | 748 |

“Made from a woman.” Jerome often reads this in accordance with the Greek. The printed editions read, “born of a woman.” | Ibid. |

“But whether they did it through ignorance.” The old Cluniac codex, corrected by the hand of the scribe himself, reads as follows: “But whether they did it through ignorance or malice, I do not know. But they answered that in the Hebrew copies it was this, etc.” Here the sense is complete and perfect, whereas in the other copies it appears somewhat suspended. | 754 |

“Cornelius and Asinius Pollio of that time.” In our own times this Cornelius and Asinius Pollio have sprouted again in Voffius and Pezron, defenders of the Septuagint translators. Both this *akairospoudastes* of the Septuagint and this “cucurbitarian” are refuted by my repeated *Defense of the Hebrew Copies and the Latin Vulgate Edition of the Bible*. I think I should refer the prudent Reader to that work, so that he may marvel especially at the prudence of the author of the *Defense of the Antiquity of the Times*, who, in pursuing the rivulets of a heretical man’s opinions, while neglecting the fountain of the Bible and of truth, renews his attacks against a Doctor of the Church and the greatest interpreter in explaining the canonical Scriptures. He would apparently have thought it insufficient merely to despise the decree of the Council of Trent, by which one is bound to adhere to the Vulgate edition—that is, to Jerome—unless he had also presented himself as a judge of the Hebrew learning of that most holy Doctor, although he himself is scarcely imbued with the first elements of Hebrew. But this should not seem strange in him, according to that familiar proverb: “Ignorance creates confidence; learning creates fear.” | Ibid. |

“The Syrians call [it] CICEJAN.” Here, as in the Commentaries on the Prophet Jonah, Jerome, Erasmus, and Marianus published a corrupt text, putting *elceroa* in place of *ciceia*, which is retained by all the manuscript copies. On our restoration of the reading, see our brief annotations on the fourth chapter of Jonah. But there, in place of *Cantherius*, Cornelius should apparently be restored on the basis of this Letter of Jerome, in which *Cornelius and Asinius Pollio* is consistently retained. Let each person’s judgment be free in a matter plausible on both sides. | 755 |

EPISTLES 113 AND 114, TO THEOPHILUS

“The Letter, etc.” From this we understand that it was written after the year 404 and after the death of Saint Epiphanius, whom Jerome himself here calls “a man of holy memory, a man of God.” Nor should anyone wonder that Saint Jerome attacks Saint Chrysostom with unusual severity, since at that time Chrysostom’s innocence and holiness lay hidden beneath the crimes and accusations of his enemies, were manifest only to God, and were defended by only a few. Nor could Jerome be persuaded that the mind and judgment of the Council of thirty-six bishops and of the patriarchs of the entire East had faltered in condemning John Chrysostom, especially since it was known to everyone that John had offended Saint Epiphanius because he had received the Origenists and refused to condemn Origen. Who, at that time, would not have regarded Chrysostom as guilty and the judgment of the Eastern bishops as true?

Certainly, a monk wholly devoted to God in solitude, together with a few brothers, could not investigate such intricate causes of dissension among the bishops and bring them to the light of truth without being deceived, as were many who were forced to judge difficult episcopal cases from hearsay and the outcome of events, rather than through divine inspiration. Moreover, the learned Valesius thought that the greater and earlier part of this Letter should be attributed to Theophilus of Alexandria, up to the words “Lest the delay of Your Blessedness,” etc., and that Jerome’s Letter to Theophilus should begin with those words. But, lest we admit anything contrary to the truth, we fear adhering to the judgment of this most learned man, since the Letter has a single continuous text in both the printed and manuscript books.

Furthermore, the sense is clear if Jerome’s words are correctly understood. For he says: “Knowing, therefore, that it was said by the Savior, ‘Do not judge according to appearance, but judge a just judgment, lest in any way,’ etc.” He seems to be saying to Theophilus: “The many obstacles that caused me to send your Book to you so late did not arise, as you suppose, from your judgment against John—which I consider a just judgment—although John’s reputation for holiness may seem to indicate that it was not true, but was made only according to outward appearance.”

Or we may understand it in another way, and indeed in a way that is more straightforward and clearer: “Do not judge by appearances, and do not accuse me of idleness and delay because the Latin translation of your Book was postponed. I warn you that these were the obstacles that caused me to return it to you later than I should have: namely, the sudden incursion of the Isaurians,” etc. If anyone can find a better meaning in this passage, we shall receive it with grateful acknowledgment.

Perhaps a word is missing, which I could easily have supplied if I had not been unusually deprived of a supply of manuscript copies and had not published the Letter from a single exemplar. Therefore, lest we too judge the matter and Jerome’s criticism by appearances, let us remember the time at which the preceding Letter to Theophilus was written; and then at last, as it were, let the light of our judgment go forth.

I transcribed this Letter of Jerome from the previously mentioned ancient codex of Saint Theodoric, where it is found at the end, after the Letter to Pammachius and Marcella, after the three Books or Paschal Letters of Theophilus, and after the Letter of Epiphanius to Saint Jerome, which begins, “General—”

“Of canine eloquence.” He calls the speeches of forensic advocates and litigants “canine eloquence.” Among rhetoricians, canine eloquence is that which is exercised in accusing others and of which abuse constitutes a large part. Quintilian speaks of canine eloquence in Book 12, chapter 9. Minervius and Alexander therefore seem to have been rhetoricians or advocates before they embraced the monastic life. | 800 |

“Be approved, etc.” The Greek Fathers often quote this verse: δόκιμοι τραπεζίται γίνεσθε, “become approved bankers”; but these words have dropped out of the present-day Greek and Latin copies. | 815 |

EPISTLE 120, TO HEDIBIA

“Concerning the same Hedibia, the servant of Christ.” Jerome mentions this Hedibia when writing to a certain man of Gallic origin whom he calls Rusticus in the heading of the Letter written to him concerning repentance. See that Letter below in its proper place. | 817 |

“Sending a memorandum.” The printed editions corruptly read, “sending commentaries,” contrary to the testimony of all the manuscript copies and to the manifest sense of Saint Jerome. | 818 |

“Patera and—” In all printed and manuscript copies *Paterius* is incorrectly read, except in one Cluniac codex, which retains the name *Patero*. This is the same as *Patera*, since the Ancients use *o* and *a* interchangeably. Who Patera was, and where he derived his name, Ausonius explains in *The Rhetors*, or *Commemoration of the Professors of Bordeaux*, chapter 4:

> You, Bagocassis, born of the stock of the Druids,  
> If fame does not betray the truth,  
> You lead a race consecrated to the temple of Belenus,  
> And from this come your names:  
> For you, the Paterae: thus they name the ministers  
> Of mystical Apollo, etc.

*Patera*, therefore, in the Gallic language means “priest of Apollo,” whom the Gauls called Belenus. Patera and Delphidius derived their lineage from these priests. See the later book of Eusebius’s *Chronicle*, under the year of Christ 337. | Ibid. |

“You do not have a few sons.” This is the genuine and correct reading of the passage, retained by three manuscript copies: one, namely, our Sangermanensis, which we followed; another, the Cluniac; and a third from the monastery of Saint Cygirannus. In the last of these we read: “Therefore, since you do not have children, make many friends for yourself from,” etc. In the Cluniac it is written in the same sense: “Therefore, since you, having not even a few sons, have many, make friends for yourself from,” etc.

The printed editions incorrectly remove the negative particle, reading: “Since you have a few sons, make many friends for yourself,” etc. This is absurd and false in view of the first question of Hedibia, where she is said to have been left without children. Jerome rightly said to the wealthy Hedibia: “Therefore, since you do not have even a few sons, make many friends for yourself from the mammon of iniquity, so that,” etc. | 821 |

“The Doctor had heard.” We read that this rich man was a young man, not a Doctor of the Law—unless *Princeps* in Luke is meant by this. | Ibid. |

Consult our annotations on that Commentary of Jerome, which we restored, just as here we restore the name *Barachibas* in place of the exceedingly corrupt reading of Erasmus and Marianus, who wrote: “They usually answer and say, Rab Akiba, and Simeon, and Hillel, the teachers.” | 884 |

EPISTLE 123, TO AGERUCHIA

“Now to Ageruchia.” The name of this widow is exceedingly corrupt both in the printed books and in the manuscript copies. In some it is read *Gerontia*, *Acheruchia*, *Agerundia*, and *Acherusia*. For us the true and genuine reading is *Ageruchia*, or *Agerochia*, for ἄγηρως means “immortal,” or “not experiencing old age.” Jerome’s words draw us toward this meaning when he indicates that monogamy and widowhood are, in a certain sense, immortal in Ageruchia’s family, since her grandmother, mother, and aunt remained widows for many years. Thus, by a kind of prophecy of future events, Ageruchia received this name, and she too was destined to become a widow. | 900 |

“At Athens the eunuch is made.” In the ancient copies: “The Hierophant at Athens castrates the man.” See Book 2 Against Jovinianus, and then Tertullian’s Book On the Exhortation to Chastity, his Book On Monogamy, and Book 1 To His Wife. | 905 |

“The nation of the Teutons.” Erasmus and Marianus falsely add the name “Gauls” here. You will find histories of this kind in Florus and Plutarch’s Life of Marius, and in Valerius’s chapter On Chastity. | 906 |

“And offering the *adorea*, etc.” The manuscript copies read: “and worshiping, shouting one by one,” etc. *Adorea* is used for glory and praise, as Pliny and Festus testify. It is used of a portion of grain and the soldiers’ pay after victory in Plautus. | 907 |

EPISTLE 124, TO AVITUS

“Dearest Avitus, you ask.” Jerome mentions this Avitus above in the Letter to Salvina. | 916 |

“The Greatest City.” Concerning the same matter, see the Letter to Fabiola on the forty-two stopping places, and then chapter 7 of Amos. These words are read in the *Book of Places* under the entry *Ailath*: “the Red Sea, from which one sails from Egypt to India and from there back to Egypt.” | 934 |

“He began to weep, etc.” The older editions of Erasmus and Marianus read this entire passage without sense, though not without solecisms, as follows: “He wept against the lie. No one else believed the truth; the father alone skillfully opposed his defense, lest the brother be swallowed up by excessive sadness.” Here you can see that words are missing from each clause. I supplied them from ten manuscript copies and from the *Lives of the Fathers* by Rufinus, Book 3, no. 220, for there we read: “But he began to weep against the lie: groans every day,” etc. | 941 |

EPISTLE 127, TO PRINCIPIA

“Διάλυτος contradiction.” Seven manuscript copies read this way, and Marianus Victorius will never persuade me that all the copies of this Letter read, “Then the contradiction of our διδακτικῶν,” since all our very ancient and excellent copies retain “the contradiction of our ΔΙΑΛΙΡΟϹ,” or “the contradiction of our insane *dyaletos*,” or “the contradiction of our ΔΙΑΛΥΡΟΚ.” This reading has a very fine sense and suits the following clause. Concerning Marianus’s *ἀντίφασις*, the scribes of Jerome are entirely silent. | 957 |

EPISTLE 129, TO DARDANUS

“Divided into portions.”

“Returning from Egypt, they took possession.” The Cluniac manuscript, like all the others, initially read *redeuntes* (“returning”); but after being corrected it retained *exeuntes* (“going out”). | 966 |

“Who also at the resurrection, etc.” The earlier printed books add, “we bless the Lord,” and consequently read in the first person *sumus* (“we are”) instead of the third-person *sunt* (“they are”). | 967 |

“They sleep.” Nearly all the manuscript copies read this way; some, along with the printed editions, retain *dormierunt* (“they slept”). | Ibid. |

“By the resources acquired through him.” Several manuscript copies read *paratis* (“acquired,” or “prepared”)—

[Col. 1269]

967

“Which the first Adam lost.” Some manuscript copies, together with the printed books, refer this to the earth. Hence they read: “which the first Adam lost . . . indeed, having been lost,” etc. Shortly afterward: “We wish to know more clearly what this earth is; let us read Malachi.” | 968 |

“Θελητή.” Erasmus thinks that τέμπη should be read, meaning “pleasurable.” Marianus, unable to tolerate this, rebukes him rather harshly. Yet he himself reads *voluptaria* (“pleasurable”) in Latin instead of *voluntaria* (“desired,” or “willing”), although in Malachi 3:12 we read θελητή interpreted as “accepted,” while Jerome has “the desirable land.” | Ibid. |

“Are these gates not, etc.?” Several manuscript copies omit *Numquid* (“Are … not?”). | Ibid. |

“My soul was very much a sojourner.” Here some copies retain the Vulgate reading, “was a dweller.” | 970 |

“And many thousands of angels, etc.” Nearly all the manuscript copies read: “many thousands of angels of solemnity, and the Church,” etc. | Ibid. |

“Not only from the Churches of the East.” From this passage of Jerome the Heterodox should be pressed either to accept the Deuterocanonical books or to reject those which they admit into their canon. See this question in the second volume of my Treatises On the Truth and Knowledge of the Sacred Scriptures. | 971 |

“Writers in the Greek language of the Church.” The manuscript copies retain divergent readings here. Some read without *retro*: “but by all the writers of the Greek-speaking Church”; others: “but by all the churches behind,” etc. Marianus reads: “but by all the churches behind, and of the Greeks,” etc. | Ibid. |

“Seventy-five thousand miles, etc.” Very many manuscripts read “barely twenty-five thousand”; but the Cluniac, of excellent quality and carefully corrected, reads: “separated from Jerusalem by seventy-five miles toward the southern region.” | 972 |

“The most eloquent poet mentions.” Virgil, in Book 4 of the *Aeneid*:

> Hence the region, deserted by thirst, and the Barcaeans  
> raging far and wide.

They were called Barcaeans from the town Barca, or Barce, as Erasmus and Marianus read. See Strabo and Servius concerning the city of Barce, which was called Ptolemais. | Ibid. |

“Coele-Syria and Osrhoene.” Some ignorant scribes omit *Osrhoene*. | Ibid. |

“To the people, the ornaments.” Thus Persius in Satire 3. This means: “Among the ignorant crowd, boast and sell smoke about yourself; before me, who know you completely, you will have done this in vain.” *Praetenditur* (“is extended before”) is the reading. Marianus has *protenditur* (“is stretched forward”); the Cluniac codex reads: “It extends before Phoenicia, Coele-Syria, and Cilicia.” | 973 |

“Baalim.” The printed editions read the singular *Baal*, but all the manuscripts I examined retain the plural *Baalim*. | Ibid. |

“An example of neighbors.” The ancient scribes did not place here what they had found, but what they understood; for quite a few copies read “as an example of vices.” We have omitted the remaining matters as being of lesser importance. | 974 |

“You would have served repeatedly.” In very many manuscript copies: “and whenever you served repeatedly,” etc. | Ibid. |

“With Babylon laying waste.” One very ancient manuscript reads: “It was destroyed while Babylon was laying waste.” The two Vatican copies, 342 and 343, read in the same way. | Ibid. |

“After the completion.” Many copies here read: “after the honor of the dual prefecture had been completed.” | 975 |

EPISTLE 130, TO DEMETRIAS

“From the holy company of Christ.” He calls a pair of holy women—the mothers of Demetrias, Proba and Juliana—a *synoris*. In the same way Gregory of Nazianzus and Basil were a *synoris*, that is, a pair of friends joined by an indissoluble bond of charity. Likewise, *συνωρίς* or *ξυνωρίς* is used for a team of two and for a pair by Eusebius, Chrysostom, and Synesius. In the Corbie manuscript, written nine hundred years ago, we read ΚΥΝΩΡΙΔΕ; in others, in Latin, *Synoride*. | 981 |

“Whether he was more greedy.” Here Jerome attacks the exceedingly cruel count Heraclianus and his son-in-law Sabinus. You may see their history in Prosper’s *Chronicle*, in Orosius, Book 7, chapter 42, and in the *Chronicle* of Marcellinus Comes. | 982 |

EPISTLE 133, TO CTESIPHON

“Shall I use [it], a vault? Or, at any rate, etc.” The Manichaean therefore, just as he placed Christ in the tabernacle of the sun, likewise placed his elect—that is, the twelve perfect ones—among the celestial vaults or circles of the planets and stars. John Chrysostom attributes this summit of perfection to almsgiving in Homily 9 On Repentance: Λέγω δὲ, τὴν ἐλεημοσύνην τὴν βασιλίδα τῶν ἀρετῶν τὴν ταχέως ἀνάγουσαν εἰς τὰς ἀψίδας τῶν οὐρανῶν τοὺς ἀνθρώπους, that is: “I say that almsgiving is the queen of virtues, quickly raising human beings to the vaults of heaven,” that is, “to the highest degree of perfection,” or “to the heavenly heights and circles of heaven.” In the same sense, the Manichaean placed his elect among the vaults in the heavens because of the perfection supposedly possessed by them and falsely attributed to them.

“Among whom [were] ἀψῖδας.” Up to this point the genuine and Jerome’s reading of the passage had been unknown, because the ancient editors, mocking readers in their customary manner, inserted “the souls of Plato” instead of ἀψῖδας, which all the manuscript copies retain, either in Greek as ΑΨΙΔΑΚ or in Latin as *absidas*, with *b* for *p*. What Plato’s—or rather Pliny’s—vaults are in the heavens may be inferred from another passage of Jerome. For, in explaining the fourth chapter of the Letter to the Ephesians, he says this concerning verse 10, “He who descended is himself,” etc.: “Did he not, passing bodily through all the heavens and every height, and through the circles of heaven—which philosophers call spheres—and transcending them, stand at the summit of the heavenly vault, and, by the very word—”

[Col. 1270]

1028

“Hiberite, etc.” The smaller Corbie codex indicates that this should be read in accordance with the following Prologue, where Evagrius Ponticus is called *Hiberite*, not *Hyperborite*. | 1029 |

“The name of blackness.” He means Melania, who was first called beautiful and holy because of her virtue, almsgiving, and pilgrimages; but afterward black and foul because of the stain of heresy with which Rufinus, having become an Origenist, polluted her. | Ibid. |

“Or also, etc.” All the manuscript copies read *Or*. | 1030 |

“John, etc.” This is the most holy John Chrysostom, whom Jerome here proclaims holy and catholic, despite Theophilus and Cyril of Alexandria, among whom Chrysostom had a bad reputation. | Ibid. |

“Of Xystus the Pythagorean.” The larger Corbie codex reads: “which is the Book of Sextus the Pythagorean,” and afterward, “with the name of Xystus the Martyr changed.” | Ibid. |

EPISTLE 140, TO CYPRIAN

“He makes him speak in this way to his horse, which he called Rhoebus:

> Rhoebus, we have lived long—if anything among mortals is long-lived—  
> or today you will return victorious with those bloody spoils  
> and the head of Aeneas,” etc.

“May they proceed with a perfect spirit and peaceful mind.”

“Choose presbyters.” Jerome has given the sense of Scripture, not its words, in this passage—unless he read them from some old copy in which the Ancients read: “Choose presbyters whom you yourself know to be the presbyters of Israel, whom you yourself know, because these are the presbyters.” This passage was corrupted by Erasmus and Marianus, who read: “Choose presbyters whom you yourself know to be worthy,” and falsely cited Exodus, chapter 17, verse 18, although it is manifestly a sentence borrowed from the Book of Numbers. | 1048 |

“He speaks while praying.” In the earlier printed editions and in the exceedingly corrupt Florentine manuscript, Paul’s name is forced into the text: “Paul speaks every day.” | 1049 |

“So that all, etc.” He teaches the same thing in the Preface to the Commentaries on Malachi, saying: “The time and the title also agree; as we said in the Psalms, those that have no titles should be believed to belong to those whose names appear at the head of the preceding Psalms.” | 1050 |

“And God made.” Erasmus: “And God made man in his own image; in the image of God he made him; male and female he created them.” | Ibid. |

OLAM. The earlier printed books falsely force upon us Hebrew words here. | 1053 |

“At the beginning of the ways.” Several manuscripts read *initiarium viarum suarum* (“the initiation of his ways”); Erasmus, however, reads *in initio viarum suarum* (“at the beginning of his ways”). We shall speak about this shortly. | Ibid. |

BRESITH. All the manuscript copies read *Bresith*, and not *Resith*, as the earlier printed books do. I have no doubt that Jerome read in Hebrew *Adonai canani Bresith dercho*, since in his Latin Translation of Proverbs he rendered the present passage as follows: “The Lord possessed me at the beginning of his ways, or in the beginning of his ways,” according to the Vulgate edition.

Moreover, the Chaldean and Syriac translators read in their Hebrew copies the preposition *be*, that is, *Bresith*, “in the beginning,” not *initium*, “beginning.” This clearly shows that the very ancient Hebrew copies differed from the one which the Septuagint translators found, in which the name *Resith* appeared without a preposition, as it is read today; while the Chaldean, Syriac, and Jerome read the same word with the prefixed particle, *Bresith*. | 1054 |

“Beginning of the ways.” In the first volume of the new edition of Saint Jerome’s works I previously presented this differently, namely: “The Lord possessed me, the beginning of his ways.” At that time, however, I quoted the verse from Marianus’s edition, which is corrupt here, as I have now shown by restoring the Hebrew text. Let the curious Reader consult the third Prolegomenon, no. 3, in Saint Jerome’s *Divine Library*, where he discusses this verse of Proverbs more fully. | Ibid. |

“He passed by, etc.” We followed Erasmus and the manuscript copies. Marianus reads: “which passed by, or went across, and like a night watch.” | 1055 |

“The poet bears witness.” This illustrious poet is Virgil, who in the middle of Book 3 of the *Georgics* has the following:

> But meanwhile time flees, irretrievable time,
Each of us, while we are carried along, captive to love. And again, near the end of Book Ten of the *Aeneid*, concerning Mezentius—

[Col. 1271]

1058

**“They will be hidden from you.”** All the manuscript codices read this way. Marianus ought not to have altered their reading in order to make it conform to the Latin Vulgate text of the Psalm. | Same page |

**“It is from judgment,” etc.** In the earlier editions we read: “In him there is judgment and truth.” | 1059 |

**BAEM.** Some manuscript codices read *bahem*, because ancient scribes inserted an aspiration between two vowels; hence, following Servius, they also wrote *incoho* for *inchoo*. | Same page |

**“Until it is not struck,” etc.** Marianus advises that the passage should, in the opposite sense, be read without the negative particle: “until the silver cord is struck.” But he would immediately have changed his opinion if he had remembered that Jerome recites this entire passage from the edition of the Seventy Translators, among whom we read, with the negation, ἕως ὅτου μὴ ἀνατραπῇ—that is, “until it is not overturned.” Moreover, I have collated no manuscript exemplar that does not read, as Erasmus does, “until the silver cord is not struck.” Marianus Victor therefore acted wrongly when, on the basis of our Vulgate edition, he attempted to restore everything. | 1060 |

**“In its proper place,” etc.** He means the book of *Commentaries on Ecclesiastes*, which follows immediately afterward in our edition, after the Critical Epistles. | Same page |

**“Thousands, and eighty,” etc.** Here too Marianus altered the reading of the manuscript codices according to his usual practice. For he reads as follows: “And multitudes of seventy thousand and eighty thousand men.” | Same page |

**AIS.** The old editions of this epistle remove Jerome’s reading and, in place of the single word *AIS*, substitute the Hebrew words *gas his*. | 1061 |

**“When he proceeds,” etc.** This is an obscure passage. For its interpretation, considerable assistance is provided by the epistle of that same Jerome written to Augustine, namely Epistle 89 in Marianus’s edition. There it is written:

> “And in the Book of Chronicles we read that the children of Israel went forth to battle with a peaceful mind; even amid swords and the shedding of blood, and the corpses of the fallen, they were thinking not of victory for themselves but of victory for peace.”

These words are taken from 1 Chronicles 12:38. For among the Seventy we read as follows: “All these men were warriors, arraying the battle line with a peaceful mind,” ἐν ψυχῇ εἰρηνικῇ. This is rendered in the Latin Vulgate as “with a perfect heart,” because the Hebrew expression *belebab salem*, or *belevav scalem*, may be rendered in Latin as “with a perfect heart,” or “with a peaceful mind,” or even “with a peaceful intention.” These words in the Books of Days—that is, in the Book of Chronicles—may therefore mean that God does not strike in order to kill and destroy, but in order to correct and amend, since human beings, too, sometimes against enemies—

[Col. 1272]

1062

**“No one so weak,” etc.** The same point is repeated in the epistle to Ageruchia on monogamy:

> “For no one,” he says, “is so broken in strength and so advanced in old age that he does not think he will live for at least one more year. Hence forgetfulness of his condition steals upon him,” etc.

This is Cicero’s thought; in his book *On Old Age* he says:

> “For no one is so old that he does not think he can live for one year.”

Seneca likewise says in Letter 12 of Book 1:

> “No one is so old that he does not improperly hope for one day.”

| Same page |

**“DAILY,” etc.** Likewise in Epistle 103 to Paulinus:

> “He easily despises everything who constantly thinks that he is going to die.”

| Same page |

**“He means those bound in fetters.”** The previously published books add, after the Florentine manuscript codex:

> “But if it means πεπαιδευμένους, it means the educated.”

But these words are not found in the more ancient manuscript exemplars. I therefore infer that they are not Jerome’s words, but those of the person who is demonstrably responsible for corrupting the Florentine exemplar with numerous additions. | 1063 |

**“We read.”** This is a notable passage and one in which readers can easily err if we retain the reading found in many manuscripts and printed books, where, in place of *we read*, one finds *we said*. It would seem that Jerome intended by the word *we said* to indicate that he had himself composed certain commentaries on the twelfth Psalm. But the Cluniac manuscript resolves this difficulty: after correction by an ancient hand, it retains the word *we read*, not *we said*. Yet I am not unaware that Jerome wrote seven treatises on the Psalms, from the tenth through the sixteenth; this most clearly confirms the truth of the reading *we said*. | Same page |

## EPISTLE 146. TO EVANGELUS

**“We read in Isaiah.”** The old editions incorrectly title this epistle “To Evagrius,” whereas all the manuscript codices I have seen retain *Evangelus*, or *Evangelium*, as I have already observed in the second volume, in the epistle to the same man concerning Melchizedek. Evangelus was, moreover, a presbyter to whom Annianus the Pelagian wrote. He was the translator of the homilies of St. Chrysostom on the Epistles of Blessed Paul. See Volume VI of Bede’s works, at the end. This foolish man, who preferred deacons to presbyters, is called Falcidius in the Appendix to Volume III of our edition of St. Augustine, in the *Questions Mixed from Both Authors*, Question 101. | 1080 |

## EPISTLE 150. OF PROCOPIUS

The ignorance of a heretical man raging against Jerome was the cause of the preceding epistle of Procopius, published by Vossius, who did not know that St. Jerome had never lived in Egypt and had never been a captive among the Saracens. From the same source of error and envy sprang the golden rain of matrons, which never watered the fields of the most holy Doctor, who says: “Whose bronze ever sounded in my hand?” Finally, Vossius wrongly attributed the pride of Photinus to Basil, as is clear to the learned from the *Chronicles*. | 1119 |

## ORDER OF THE EPISTLES OF SAINT JEROME, COMPARED WITH THE ANCIENT EDITIONS AND THE BENEDICTINE EDITION

[Note: This index refers to the *Epistles of St. Jerome* between columns 325 and 1224 of this volume.]

The epistle that appears as no. 40 in the old editions is not included here among the Hieronymian epistles, since it mentions the city of Leges and other matters belonging to a later age; it has therefore been placed among the spurious works in the final volume.
