# INDEX OF THE MATTERS CONTAINED IN THIS VOLUME
Epistle of Dedication by Dominicus Vallarsius to Clement XII, Supreme Pontiff. V–VI. General Preface. VII–VIII. 1. The excellence of Jerome’s works. Ibid. 2. The necessity of a new edition. Ibid. 3. The reasons for undertaking a new edition. IX–X. 4. The threefold division of this preface. Ibid. The first part, in which the manuscripts and published collections are discussed individually. Ibid. 5. Manuscript collections of Jerome’s works. Ibid. 6. The first edition, Rome. XI–XII. 7. Ancient editions of the Commentaries and other works. XIII–XIV. 8. All of them incomplete. Ibid. 9. The edition of Desiderius Erasmus. Ibid. 10. The edition of Marianus Victorius. XV–XVI. 11. The same edition enriched by additions from several learned men. Ibid. 12. Nevertheless, it is erroneous, especially in Hebrew matters. Ibid. 13. The edition of the Benedictine Fathers, or that of Dom Jean Martianay. Ibid. 14. The chief defects of that edition. XVII–XVIII. The second part, in which, after explaining the character of Jerome’s works, those works which have perished or are thought to have perished are discussed. Ibid. 15. The two kinds of Jerome’s works. Ibid. 16. The second kind. XIX–XX. 17. An account of works no longer extant, beginning with the correction of the Scriptures from the Greek. Ibid. 18. The Gospel according to the Hebrews. XXI–XXII. 19. What Theodore of Mopsuestia alleged against that translation. Ibid. 20. A specimen of the Commentary on Obadiah. Ibid. 21. Seven treatises on the Psalms. XXIII–XXIV. 22. Whether they were translated from Origen into Latin. Ibid. 23. An exposition of Psalm 93. XXV–XXVI. 24. Short commentaries on the Psalms. Ibid. 25. A translation of the book *On First Principles* (*περὶ ἀρχῶν*). XXVII–XXVIII. 26. A translation of the book against John Chrysostom. Ibid. 27. Several lost letters. Ibid. 28. Hebrew Questions on the Old Testament. XXXI–XXXII. 29. Shorter commentaries on the Twelve Prophets. Ibid. 30. Fourteen books on Jeremiah. XXXIII–XXXIV. 31. A Latin translation of the commentaries of Alexander of Aphrodisias. XXXV–XXXVI. 32. The book addressed to Abundantius. Ibid. 33. Two books against Helvidius. XXXVII–XXXVIII. The third part, in which what has been accomplished in this new edition is explained. Ibid. 34. The division of the works. Ibid. 35. The libraries and manuscripts that we use, and how we use them. XXXIX–XL. 36. The method by which the text has been corrected. Ibid. 37. Variant readings. Ibid. [Col. 1284] 38. Observations and notes. XLI–XLII. 39. The notes of others, especially those of the Benedictines, at the end of the volume. Ibid. 40. Praise of the men named. Ibid.

Preface to this volume. XLIII–XLIV. 1. The qualities of the letters of Saint Jerome. Ibid. 2. The confusion of the ancient editions in arranging them. Ibid. 3. The necessity and rationale of a new order. Ibid. 4. Treatises and minor works, together with the prefaces to other works, are excluded. XLV–XLVI. 5. Five letters not previously published are added. Ibid. 6. Six others are included here for the first time. XLVII–XLVIII. 7. The five classes of letters, their subjects, chapter-headings, and so forth. Ibid.

The chronological order of the letters demonstrated by their subjects. XLIX–L. The letters of the first class, which Jerome wrote chiefly from the desert of Chalcis, from the year 370 to 380. Ibid. The letters of the second class, which Jerome wrote at Rome for nearly three years, from the end of 382 to the middle of 385. LIII–LIV. The letters of the third class, which Jerome wrote from the monastery at Bethlehem from the year 386 until the end of the fourth century and the condemnation of Origen at the Alexandrian synod in the year 400. LIX–LX. The letters of the fourth class, which Jerome wrote from the beginning of 401 until 420, that is, until the end of his life. LXXVII–LXXVIII.

The Life of Saint Eusebius Jerome of Stridon, Priest, compiled chiefly from his own writings, addressed to the Most Eminent Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, Dominicus Riviera. 5–6.

CHAPTER I.—I. Jerome’s birthplace. II. The year of his birth. III. His name. IV. His parents and relatives. 5.

CHAPTER II.—I. Properly educated at home together with Bonosus, he is sent to Rome to learn literature. II. He attends the schools of grammarians, rhetoricians, and philosophers. III. In boyhood he falls into certain vices. 14.

CHAPTER III.—I. He receives baptism at Rome. II. Under Pope Liberius, at approximately twenty years of age. 16.

CHAPTER IV.—I. After his Roman studies he returns home. II. He remains for a short time at Aquileia. III. He sets out for Gaul. 18.

CHAPTER V.—I. From Gaul he returns to Stridon and Aquileia. II. He writes to Innocentius concerning a woman struck seven times. 20.

CHAPTER VI.—I. At Aquileia he incurs various enmities. II. Suddenly torn away from there, he sails to the East. 22.

CHAPTER VII.—I. The journey of the holy Father is described. II. Whether he then visited Jerusalem. III. He stopped at Antioch. 24.

CHAPTER VIII.—I. He stays at Antioch, where he considers with himself the undertaking of the solitary life. II. On this subject he writes letters to his friends. III. He listens to Apollinarius of Laodicea and avoids his heresy. IV. While staying at Maronia, he hears from Malchus’s own mouth the story of the monk Malchus. 27.

CHAPTER IX.—I. He withdraws into the desert of Chalcis and devotes himself to penance. II. He gives himself wholly to the study of the Hebrew language, in order to master the flesh more completely. III. Whether he also learned Greek. IV. Warned in a dream, he dismisses profane authors. 28.

CHAPTER X.—I. He writes the Life of Saint Paul the Hermit. II. Also letters to various people. III. And an exhortation to Heliodorus. 32.

CHAPTER XI.—I. The Church of Antioch is disturbed by the factions of three bishops at once. II. Each of them strives to draw Jerome to his side. III. The Meletians among them demand from him a profession of the three hypostases. IV. He writes to Damasus once and again on this matter. V. Compelled to yield to the arrogance of the factions, the holy young man considers abandoning the desert. VII. He writes to Marcus. 34.

CHAPTER XII.—I. He leaves the desert and returns to Antioch. II. He writes the Dialogue between a Luciferian and an Orthodox Christian. III. He is ordained priest by Paulinus. IV. The date of his ordination is established. 39.

CHAPTER XIII.—I. From Antioch he travels to Constantinople, where he listens to Gregory of Nazianzus. II. There he translates the Chronicle of Eusebius into Latin and continues it. III. He also translates twenty-eight homilies of Origen. IV. He likewise writes a treatise on the Seraphim. 43.

CHAPTER XIV.—I. From Constantinople he sets out for Rome for the synod. II. There he is chosen by Damasus as secretary for correspondence, and in his name replies to consultations from East and West. III. Whether he was a cardinal priest. IV. He resolves for Damasus questions concerning *Hosanna* and the two sons, the dutiful and the profligate. V. At his request he renders the Gospels according to the Greek text. VI. He also hastily corrects the Psalter according to the Septuagint. 46.

CHAPTER XV.—I. He is compelled to instruct several virgins and matrons at Rome in the sacred writings. II. To them he writes several letters. III. A separate account of that celebrated letter to Eustochium. IV. Questioned by Damasus about five matters, he replies. V. He compares Aquila’s edition with the Hebrew copy and also translates Origen’s homilies on the Song of Songs. VI. He writes against Helvidius. VII. Certain other writings and deeds of his. 49.

CHAPTER XVI.—I. Damasus dies and is succeeded by Siricius, who was not especially devoted to Jerome. II. Jerome then incurs the hostility of many. III. He is freed from a very serious criminal accusation. IV. He resolves to leave Rome. V. He writes to Asella. 53.

CHAPTER XVII.—I. Jerome sails to the East. II. Saint Paula and Eustochium also set out for there. III. Together they visit all Palestine and the holy places. IV. They also tour Egypt and the monasteries of Nitria. V. They withdraw to Bethlehem and establish their residence there. 58.

CHAPTER XVIII.—I. What was Jerome’s manner of life at Bethlehem. II. Whether he was rector of its church, as Sulpicius says. III. He writes commentaries on four of Paul’s letters. IV. Whether he also expounded all the others. V. The general character of his writing according to Jerome’s own understanding. 63.

CHAPTER XIX.—I. He writes commentaries on Ecclesiastes. II. Also Hebrew Questions on Genesis, and separate books on places and on Hebrew names. III. He translates Didymus’s book on the Holy Spirit into Latin. IV. He also translates thirty-nine homilies of Origen on Luke. V. He writes seven treatises on the Psalms, from the tenth through the sixteenth. VI. Finally, the Life of Malchus the Captive Monk and that of Blessed Hilarion. 70.

CHAPTER XX.—I. The corrections that Jerome made in the then-current Latin edition from the copy of the Septuagint (*τῶν LXX*) are reviewed. II. The books that now survive from that labor. 74.

CHAPTER XXI.—I. He translates the Old Testament from the Hebrew. II. In an inverted order, beginning with the books of Kings, he published the greater part of this translation before the year 392. III. He kept a certain portion by him for some time. IV. In later years he completed the remainder of the Hebrew canon. 77.

CHAPTER XXII.—I. Meanwhile Jerome writes various letters to Paula and Eustochium. II. He also writes commentaries on Micah, Zephaniah, Nahum, Habakkuk, and Haggai. III. Whether he had previously expounded Jonah, and whether he had composed shorter commentaries on each of the twelve Minor Prophets. IV. He continues the same work of illuminating the other Prophets. V. He publishes the book *On Illustrious Men*. 83.

CHAPTER XXIII.—I. The holy Father attacks Jovinian’s heresy in two books. II. In exalting virginity, he appeared to disparage marriage. III. Accordingly he writes an Apology for those same books to Pammachius. IV. Likewise to Domnion on the same subject. V. He also replies to Desiderius’s letters and to the questions put to him by Amandus. 87.

CHAPTER XXIV.—I. He temporarily withdraws from his friendship with Rufinus through a certain declaration of his concerning Origen. II. This develops into open hostility on the occasion of the arrival of Saint Epiphanius at Jerusalem. [Col. 1286] III. Hence the beginnings of the Jerusalem schism, whose history is briefly outlined. IV. Our author takes his stand with Epiphanius against the Origenists, while Rufinus adheres to John of Jerusalem. V. The opportunity for dissension is increased by Epiphanius’s ordination of Paulinianus, Jerome’s brother. VI. Likewise, the dispute grows more bitter because of Epiphanius’s letter to John, written in Greek and translated into Latin by Jerome, and because of another letter to Pammachius in which he defends it. 92.

CHAPTER XXV.—I. Count Archelaus unsuccessfully attempts to reconcile the dissenting parties. II. Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, also vainly attempts to do so. III. This is chiefly due to the fault of Isidore the presbyter, an Origenist, whom he had sent as his representative for that purpose. IV. Hence Theophilus’s goodwill toward Jerome cools. V. Nevertheless the holy Father writes to him repeatedly. VI. Also to Marcella, and the Epitaph of Nepotianus. VII. Also commentaries on Jonah. VIII. Then other letters to various persons, in which there is some discussion of the Origenist controversy. 101.

CHAPTER XXVI.—I. As Rufinus is about to return to the West, he is reconciled with Jerome in the church of the Anastasis, in accordance with their former friendship. II. The year in which this occurred is established by new arguments. III. Whether at this time, chiefly through the efforts of Rufinus and Melania, the Jerusalem schism was completely extinguished and peace restored between John and the remaining monks. IV. Arguments on behalf of those who assert this are answered, and others are brought forward that deny it. Some incidental remarks about Palladius. VI. Meanwhile the holy Father falls ill and suffers from fever for three months. VII. Nevertheless he writes certain works, which are listed. VIII. Among them are the Commentaries on Matthew. IX. Also the work against John, addressed to Pammachius and to Theophilus. X. The date of these writings is established and defended. XI. Finally, after peace has been restored among all, he writes to Fabiola about the priestly vestment. 111.

CHAPTER XXVII.—I. A new dispute arises with Rufinus because he translated Origen’s book *On First Principles* (*Περὶ ἀρχῶν*) and praised Jerome in the preface. II. Pammachius and Oceanus urge Jerome to answer Rufinus. III. Our author writes to Rufinus on this matter in a friendly spirit of complaint. IV. But in a brilliant letter addressed to them he clears himself, sending with it his own faithful translation of *On First Principles*. V. He also writes various letters on various subjects, which are listed. VI. Meanwhile Theophilus condemns Origen and his followers, and writes to Jerome and to Pope Anastasius about the matter. VII. The latter likewise condemns the blasphemies extracted from that book of Origen and writes on the matter to Simplicianus, bishop of Milan. VIII. He also summons Rufinus to Rome to plead his case. IX. At the same time Rufinus writes against Jerome an Apology, or books of invective. 122.

CHAPTER XXVIII.—I. Theophilus attacks the Origenists in a Paschal Letter. II. Then, after convening a synod concerning the monasteries of Nitria, he expels them from there. III. He also writes a synodical, or general, letter against them. IV. Other writings by him and by others on the matter. V. Jerome translates all of these into Latin. VI. Beginning with the Paschal Letter of the seventh year. VII and VIII. From this the chronological order of his other translations is restored. IX. The genuineness of Jerome’s work in these translations is established. 133.

CHAPTER XXIX.—I. He translates Theophilus’s second Paschal Letter. II. Then he replies to a summary of Rufinus’s books against him. III. At this time he builds a guesthouse beside the monastery. IV. Rufinus sends him a complete copy of his books of invective. V. At the same time he sends a letter, now lost, in which he treats Jerome and his books most harshly. VI. Against him our author composes a third book of his Apology. VII. Although he had been asked by Saint Chromatius, bishop of Aquileia, to refrain from writing against Rufinus. VIII. Concerning a forged letter to the Africans, published under his name. IX. He writes letters to various people, which are listed. 141.

CHAPTER XXX.—I. A dispute arises between Jerome and Augustine. II. Letters are sent back and forth on this matter. III. The Commentary on Obadiah is assigned to this period. IV. Saint Paula dies, and the holy Father celebrates her praises in a letter to Eustochium. V. He then translates Theophilus’s Paschal Letter for that year into Latin. VI. Likewise the Rule of Saint Pachomius, together with his and Theodore’s letters and mystical sayings. VII. He again argues against Augustine. VIII. Their letters on this matter. IX. Certain other writings of the holy Father that belong here. 149.

CHAPTER XXXI.—I. He translates from Greek Theophilus’s book against Saint John Chrysostom. II. He composes commentaries on the prophets Zechariah and Malachi, and also on Hosea, Joel, and Amos. III. He writes a book against Vigilantius. IV. Then, to Minervius and Alexander, concerning the Apostle’s words, “We shall all indeed sleep,” and so forth. V. Also a Commentary on Daniel. VI. On this occasion he undergoes a very serious accusation. VII. Letters of the same author to various persons. VIII. Finally, a Commentary on Isaiah. 157.

[Col. 1287]

CHAPTER XXXII.—I. Overwhelmed by the report that Rome had been captured and by Marcella’s death, he loses heart. II. Nevertheless he later resumes the Commentaries on Ezekiel, which he had begun. III. In reply to Marcellinus, he complains about the invasion of the Saracens, from whom he barely escaped alive. IV. He then writes to Principia the Epitaph of Marcella. V. Also letters to Rusticus and to Gaudentius. VI. He completes the Commentaries on Ezekiel. VII. He writes to Demetrias and to Dardanus. VIII. Certain other writings and actions of his. 164.

CHAPTER XXXIII.—I. Pelagius introduces his heresy into Palestine. II. Jerome attacks him while writing on Jeremiah. III. Soon afterward he opposes him in a letter addressed to Ctesiphon. IV. Also in the second and third prefaces to Jeremiah. V. Then in a work of his own, namely, three books of Dialogues. VI. He returns again to the Commentaries, but leaves this work unfinished. VII. He is badly treated by the Pelagians, who attack his monastery with fire and slaughter. VIII. He receives a letter of consolation on this matter from Pope Innocent. IX. He changes his residence, but does not cease to oppose the heresy. X. Eustochium dies. XI. The holy Father himself also dies. 169.

HERE BEGINS THE LIFE OF SAINT JEROME THE PRIEST. 175–176.

The life of Saint Eusebius Jerome, incomparable Doctor of the Church of Christ and a man of outstanding holiness, collected chiefly from his own writings and also from treatises by Saints Augustine, Damasus, Gregory, Gelasius, and several others. 183–184.

THE LIFE OF THE DIVINE JEROME, BY AN UNKNOWN AUTHOR. 201–202.

Selected ancient testimonies concerning Jerome and his writings. 213–214.

The oration of Peter Paul Vergerius of Justinopolis on the divine Jerome. 231–232.

From an ancient Ambrosian Library manuscript preserved at Milan, no. 173. 235–236.

From another Ambrosian manuscript, I. LIII: the translation of the body of Saint Jerome. How the body of the Lord Jerome was brought to Rome and placed in the basilica of the Blessed Virgin. 237–238.

Notice concerning the following short work. Eusebius on the death of Jerome, to Damasus. 239.

Notice: Augustine, bishop of Hippo, to Cyril, bishop of Jerusalem, concerning the magnificence of blessed Jerome. 281.

Cyril, bishop of Jerusalem, on Jerome’s miracles, to Saint Augustine, bishop of Hippo. 289.

The letters of Saint Jerome, arranged with exactness according to chronological order and divided into four classes. 325–326.

The first class, comprising chiefly the letters written from the desert of Chalcis, from the year of Christ 370 to 380. Ibid.

LETTER ONE. To Innocentius, concerning a woman struck seven times.

At the request of Innocentius, Jerome relates the history of a certain miracle that occurred at Vercellae in Liguria during his own lifetime. A woman falsely accused of adultery and a young man denounced together with her are tortured in order to elicit the truth. The young man, confessing under the pain something he had not done, is killed; but the woman, struck repeatedly, does not die. At last, when she seemed to have succumbed, she revives; and when she is again demanded for execution, Evagrius obtains pardon for her from the Emperor. 325.

LETTER II. To Theodosius and the other anchorites, whom he asks to obtain from God that he may wish and be able to live in the desert. 331.

LETTER III. To Rufinus the monk.

He ardently desires to see and speak with Rufinus of Aquileia, whom he had heard had gone to Egypt, and informs him about his own condition and about Bonosus, his dearest companion, who had withdrawn to a certain island in order to complete his penance. Finally, he begs him to persevere in mutual affection. 332.

LETTER IV. To Florentius.

He joins the preceding letter, which is to be delivered to Rufinus, to this letter for Florentius, and praises Florentius highly, since he was living at Jerusalem and relieving the needs of many poor people. He then adds praises of Rufinus. 335.

LETTER V. To Florentius.

He replies to Florentius and informs him that he has now seized upon the solitude adjoining Syria and the Saracens. He then asks him for certain books and offers him others of which he had an abundance. 336.

LETTER VI. To Julian, deacon of Aquileia.

He excuses himself to Julian for his silence in correspondence; and, having learned from Julian, who was the first to report it, that his sister was persevering in what she had begun, he asks him to make him happier by writing frequently about her purpose. Meanwhile he adds that he despises his detractor. 337.

LETTER VII. To Chromatius, Jovinus, and Eusebius.

He sends greetings to the brothers Chromatius and Eusebius, who were living a holy life in the same house with their friend Jovinus, as well as with their mother and their virgin sisters, and praises their shared life. He then adds praises of Bonosus, about whom they had written to him. Finally, he commends to them his sister, who had no good teachers of life in her native country. 338.

LETTER VIII. To Niceas, subdeacon of Aquileia.

He urges Niceas, his old companion and fellow traveler, now returned to his homeland, to write to him sometime, following the example of the brothers Chromatius and Eusebius. 341.

LETTER IX. To Chrysogonus, monk of Aquileia.

He reproaches Chrysogonus, a recent friend, because he has written nothing to him. 342.

LETTER X. To Paul the Elder of Concordia.

He praises Paul, who was living through his hundredth year yet retained a sound and flourishing body, and asks him for several books. Meanwhile he sends him the Life of Paul the Hermit, which he had recently prepared. 343.

LETTER XI. To the Virgins of Aemona.

He complains that the virgins living at Aemona on the borders of Italy, though often prompted by his letters, have never replied. He shows that his detractors should not be believed. 344.

LETTER XII. To Antony the monk.

He reproves Antony because, although asked so many times, he has never replied; and again urges him to love one who is diligent and to answer one who writes. 345.

LETTER XIII. To Castorina, his maternal aunt.

He urges Castorina, his maternal aunt, with whom he had had some disagreement, toward peace and harmony, as he had also done in other letters. 346.

LETTER XIV. To Heliodorus the monk.

He writes to Heliodorus, his companion on the journey, whom he had vainly attempted to keep with him in the desert as a partner in his way of life. As he had promised when Heliodorus departed, he invites him back and praises the blessedness of the eremitical life. 347.

LETTER XV. To Pope Damasus.

He asks him to inform him whether three hypostases should be spoken of in God or left unmentioned, and with whom he ought to enter into communion at Antioch. 355.

LETTER XVI. To Pope Damasus.

He again solemnly begs him to inform him with which of the three parties dividing the Church of Antioch he ought to communicate. 358.

LETTER XVII. To Marcus the presbyter.

He sets forth to Marcus his profession of faith concerning the Trinity, agreeing with the Roman and Alexandrian Churches. He deeply regrets that the faction of the Arians has forced his friends to leave the desert, and that he himself is daily being urged to abandon those places. 359.

LETTER XVIII. To Pope Damasus. On the Seraphim and the Coal.

He explains the vision in the sixth chapter of the prophet Isaiah; and, after some remarks on the history and death of King Uzziah, treats learnedly, in his customary manner, of the Seraphim and the Trisagion. 361.

The second class, comprising the letters that Jerome wrote at Rome for nearly three years, from the end of the year of Christ 382 until after the middle of 385. 375–376.

LETTER XIX. Pope Damasus to Jerome.

He asks Jerome to explain clearly what *Hosanna* means among the Hebrews. 375.

LETTER XX. Or, Jerome’s reply to Damasus.

He explains what the word *Hosanna* means according to the Hebrew source, and why this Hebrew word, preserved among the Hebrews in its original form, has been retained in all languages. Ibid.

LETTER XXI. To Damasus.

At Damasus’s request, he interprets in the form of a commentary the Gospel parable found in Luke concerning the prodigal son and the dutiful son. 379.

LETTER XXII. To Eustochium, daughter of Paula.

He teaches the virgin Eustochium how she ought to preserve the virginity she had professed, and vehemently attacks those who, under the appearance of chastity, serve their belly and their greed. 394.

LETTER XXIII. To Marcella.

He compares the death of Lea, a most religious woman, with the death of a consul-designate who died at about the same time, showing how great the difference is between the ends of saints and of pagans. 425.

LETTER XXIV. To the same Marcella.

He praises to Marcella the virgin Asella, who lived at Rome like a solitary in the desert and led a most holy life; Marcella had informed him of her holiness. 427.

LETTER XXV. To the same Marcella.

At Marcella’s request, he explains the ten names by which God is called among the Hebrews. 428.

LETTER XXVI. To the same Marcella.

He explains why certain Hebrew names have remained without interpretation in translations of the Scriptures, and what they mean. 430.

LETTER XXVII. To the same Marcella.

He replies to those who criticized him because he had altered certain passages already accepted from the New Testament and had censured the association of virgins with men. 431.

LETTER XXVIII. To the same Marcella.

He explains what *Sela*, or *Diapsalma*, means. Then he presents Origen’s letter in Latin, so that Marcella may learn more fully what he thought about the question under discussion. 433.

LETTER XXIX.—To the same Marcella.

When Marcella asks him to explain what *Ephod Bad* means in the First Book of Kings, he satisfies her request and also adds what *Teraphim* means in the Book of Judges. 435.

LETTER XXX. To Paula.

He teaches the holy Paula the etymologies and interpretations of the Hebrew letters and briefly explains how great the divine mysteries are in the combination of these same elements. 441.

LETTER XXXI. To Eustochium.

He applies by mystical interpretation to the formation of character certain small gifts that Eustochium had sent him on the feast of Saint Peter. 445.

LETTER XXXII. To Marcella.

He excuses himself for writing briefly, since he was occupied in comparing Hebrew volumes with Aquila’s translation. He compensates for the brevity of this letter with the two preceding letters addressed to Paula and Eustochium, which he sends to Marcella to read. 446.

LETTER XXXIII. To Paula, part of a letter.

Comparing a catalogue of Origen’s works with the works of Varro, he shows that the Church of Christ had a writer who surpassed all Greeks and Latins even in the multitude of books he published. Ibid.

LETTER XXXIV. To Marcella.

He elegantly explains what the “bread of sorrows” and the “sons of the banished” mean in Psalm 126, while excusing Saint Hilary for not having correctly understood the word “banished,” since he had been misled by the presbyter Heliodorus. 448.

LETTER XXXV. Pope Damasus to Jerome.

Damasus, who professes that he reads many of Jerome’s writings eagerly, earnestly asks him to answer the five questions appended from the Old Testament. 451.

LETTER XXXVI. Or, Jerome’s reply to Damasus.

After prefacing an excuse for the delay, and passing over only two of the questions—the second and fourth, which had been discussed by Tertullian, Novatian, and Origen—he answers the remaining three at length. 452.

LETTER XXXVII. To Marcella.

He refutes Saint Rheticius, bishop of Autun, because in his commentaries on the Song of Songs he had understood *Tarshish* as Tarsus of Cilicia, and the gold of Ophaz as Peter, chief of the Apostles, in a most inept manner. 461.

LETTER XXXVIII. To Marcella.

He praises Blaesilla, Paula’s daughter, who, after her husband’s death and after being visited by a severe fever, had turned wholly to Christ and begun to profess the monastic life; he also replies to her detractors. 463.

LETTER XXXIX. To Paula.

Jerome consoles Paula, Blaesilla’s mother, over Blaesilla, who had died shortly after her husband’s death and her own conversion. He rebukes Paula’s excessive grief and meanwhile adds an account of Blaesilla’s virtues and life. 465.

LETTER XL.

He observes a certain detractor named Onasus, who thought that what Jerome had written against vices in his books was directed as an insult against himself. 473.

LETTER XLI.

He refutes the doctrines of the heretic Montanus and shows what difference there is between his errors and the teaching of the Church. 474.

LETTER XLII. To Marcella.

When Marcella asks what the word against the Holy Spirit means, he replies, showing that Novatian’s interpretation is false. 477.

LETTER XLIII. To Marcella.

He urges her to leave Rome and withdraw to the countryside, demonstrating by comparison both how many troubles Rome contains and how many advantages solitude offers. 478.

LETTER XLIV. To Marcella.

He interprets jokingly and allegorically the small gifts sent by Marcella to himself, Paula, and her daughter Eustochium. 480.

LETTER XLV. To Asella.

As he boards a ship to depart from Rome, he clears himself of the calumnies of his detractors, among whom he had incurred great hatred because he had drawn Paula and Eustochium, women of the highest rank, into the monastic way of life. Ibid.

THE THIRD CLASS, comprising the letters written from the monastery at Bethlehem from the year 386 until the end of the fourth century and the condemnation of Origen at the Alexandrian synod in the year 400. 483–484.

LETTER XLVI. Paula and Eustochium to Marcella.

When Paula and her daughter Eustochium had reached the holy places, they urge Marcella to leave Rome and move to them at Bethlehem, where she would enjoy all the memorials of Christ, in the places where most of the mysteries of our religion had been enacted. 483.

LETTER XLVII. To Desiderius.

He commends Desiderius and his sister Serenilla, from whom he had received a letter, beginning with an explanation drawn from the etymology of their names. He urges them to come to the holy places and fulfill their purpose, and explains why he does not meanwhile send them any of his works. 492.

LETTER XLVIII. Or, an Apologetic Book to Pammachius.

He defends his books against Jovinian, which Pammachius had received and which Jerome’s detractors maliciously represented as excessively favorable to the praise of virginity and, conversely, unfair toward marriage.

LETTER XLIX. To Pammachius.

He sends Pammachius the preceding Apologetic Letter and congratulates him on being considered worthy by all of the priesthood. Finally, he invites him to read his translations from the Hebrew and his other minor works. 511.

LETTER L. To Domnion.

Having been informed by Saint Domnion about the insults with which many people at Rome were attacking his books against Jovinian—especially a certain young monk, a gossip—he harasses this man extraordinarily, rebukes his ignorance, and challenges him to write. 512.

LETTER LI. Saint Epiphanius’s letter to John, bishop of Jerusalem, translated into Latin by Jerome.

Epiphanius, bishop of Salamis in Cyprus, excuses himself to John, bishop of Jerusalem, for having ordained the presbyter Paulinianus without consulting him. He then warns him to abstain from the errors of Origen. 517.

LETTER LII. To Nepotianus.

He prescribes for Nepotianus, the nephew of Heliodorus through his sister, the form of life that clerics and monks ought to follow, setting forth in an exhortation highly salutary precepts concerning each of the virtues relevant to their life. 527.

LETTER LIII. To Paulinus.

By the examples of all wise men he urges the study of sacred literature and shows how much difficulty it contains. Then, to inflame him more strongly toward that study, he briefly commends the individual books, authors, and subjects with various praises. Finally, he urges him to free himself completely from worldly affairs. 540.

LETTER LIV. To Furia.

He urges Furia, a widow and daughter of Titiana, to persevere in widowhood and not to marry again. Since she was still in the flower of youth, he instructs her how she should preserve both chastity and reputation. 530.

LETTER LV. To Amandus.

He replies point by point to the presbyter Amandus, who had proposed three questions to him in writing and had also asked his advice concerning the condition of a certain sister. 560.

LETTER LVI. Augustine to Jerome.

Augustine remonstrates with Jerome concerning his new translation of the Old Testament after the Septuagint and concerning Peter’s being rebuked by Paul in Galatians 2, accusing him of having undertaken the defense of a useful lie. 565.

LETTER LVII. To Pammachius.

Rufinus had quibbled that Jerome had translated incorrectly the preceding Letter LI of Epiphanius to John, bishop of Jerusalem. After complaining that someone had stolen from his files, without his knowledge, a letter not yet fully corrected, Jerome demonstrates by the testimony both of all ancient learned men and of the sacred Scriptures what is the best kind of translation. He shows that it is the method he himself used in translating the letter: transferring sense from sense, not word from word. 568.

LETTER LVIII. To Paulinus.

Out of Christian humility he declines Paulinus’s praises, while repaying praises with praises in return for Paulinus’s eloquence and upright character. He urges him to the study of the divine Scriptures and proposes to him a rule for living a holy and chaste life. 579.

LETTER LIX. To Marcella.

He answers each of the five questions that Marcella had put to him. 586.

LETTER LX. To Heliodorus.

He consoles Heliodorus, the uncle of the presbyter Nepotianus, concerning Nepotianus’s death. He shows that death, which has been conquered by Christ, is not to be feared. Then, presenting many examples from the ancient pagans, he elaborates Nepotianus’s praises and finally, in view of the needs of those times, urges contempt for life. 589.

LETTER LXI. To Vigilantius.

He rebukes Vigilantius, who, after returning to the West, was defaming Jerome’s name and his friends. He urges him at last to come to his senses and stop slandering, sharply refuting his blasphemies at the end. 602.

LETTER LXII. To Tranquillinus.

He teaches to what extent Origen ought to be embraced and read. 606.

LETTER LXIII. To Theophilus.

In reply to Theophilus, he declares that nothing is more important to him than preserving the rights of Christ. Meanwhile he gives thanks for Theophilus’s admonition concerning the ecclesiastical Canons, though he does not approve his more lenient conduct in the case of the Origenists. 607.

LETTER LXIV. To Fabiola.

To Fabiola, who had gone to Bethlehem intending to live there with Paula and Eustochium but, because of the sudden invasion of the barbarians, had been compelled suddenly to return to Rome, he explains the mystery contained in the clothing of priests and Levites. He adds, as an appendix, an account of the ritual and ceremonies of sacred worship and of the vessels of the Temple. He modestly invites her to return to her former fellowship, since the region of Bethlehem had now become peaceful. 608.

LETTER LXV. To Principia the Virgin.

He interprets for the Roman virgin Principia Psalm 44, which begins, “My heart has poured forth a good word,” and in which the wedding song of Christ the Bridegroom and the Church his Bride is sung. He does so after defending himself against calumnies and defending the female sex, which in the interpretation of the Scriptures he sometimes placed before men. 622.

LETTER LXVI. To Pammachius.

He praises Paulina, Paula’s daughter, who had married Pammachius, a young man especially learned and noble, and who had died. He urges Pammachius, who immediately after her death had adopted the monastic life and distributed his wealth for the support of the poor, to persevere in his holy purpose. 639.

LETTER LXVII. Augustine to Jerome.

Augustine asks Jerome about the title of the book on ecclesiastical writers that Jerome himself had published, and again asks about Peter’s being rebuked by Paul—not falsely—as he had also asked in the preceding Letter 56. Finally, he asks Jerome to indicate to him the errors of Origen and of the other heretics. 647.

LETTER LXVIII. To Castrucius.

He thanks Castrucius of Pannonia, who had decided to sail in order to visit Jerome, and consoles him concerning the blindness of his eyes, teaching that such blindness is sometimes inflicted by a merciful God. 651.

LETTER.

### LXIX. To Oceanus

He defends the ordination of Carterius, a Spanish bishop who had married one wife before baptism and, after her death, another after baptism, so that he should not be judged a bigamist, contrary to Oceanus’s view. Taking this as his occasion, he discusses the Apostle’s words, “the husband of one wife,” and the virtues especially required in a bishop. 653

### EPISTLE LXX. To Magnus, the Orator of the City of Rome

To a certain Roman rhetorician named Magnus, whom Rufinus had prompted to ask Jerome why he inserted examples from secular literature in his little works, he gives an explanation and shows to what extent this is permissible and whose example he follows in doing so. 664

### EPISTLE LXXI. To Lucinius

He urges Lucinius, a native of Baetica, who was leading a chaste life with his wife Theodora and had decided to sail to Jerusalem, to persevere in his purpose and to make the voyage. Meanwhile he sends him certain of his works, which Lucinius had requested, together with four little haircloth garments and a copy of Isaiah. He then discusses fasts, reception of the Eucharist, and ecclesiastical traditions. 669

### EPISTLE LXXII. To Vitalis the Presbyter

Replying to another letter from Vitalis, he teaches that it should be believed as true that Solomon and Ahaz fathered sons in the eleventh year of their age. Scripture, however, which asserts this, can be explained in another way; nevertheless, he dissuades him from anxiously investigating questions of this kind. 673

### EPISTLE LXXIII. To Evangelus the Presbyter

He refutes, by appealing to the opinions of the ancient Christians, a book by an anonymous author who asserted that Melchizedek was not a man but the Holy Spirit. He shows that Melchizedek was in fact a man of Canaanite origin—or, if the Jews are to be believed, Shem, the first son of the patriarch Noah. 676

### EPISTLE LXXIV. To the Presbyter Rufinus

After briefly recalling the duties of his recent friendship with Rufinus, he interprets allegorically the quarrel of the two prostitutes as referring to the Church gathered from the Gentiles and the Synagogue of the Jews. 682

### EPISTLE LXXV. To Theodora, a Widow

He consoles Theodora, Lucinius’s widow, over the death of her husband, whose virtues—and especially his chastity—he praises. 685

### EPISTLE LXXVI. To Abigaus

He excuses himself to the presbyter Abigaus for not having written, and consoles him so that he will not grieve over bodily blindness, since he sees with his mind. Finally, he praises his integrity and commends to him Theodora, Lucinius’s widow. 689

### EPISTLE LXXVII. To Oceanus

He praises the noblewoman Fabiola because, after her fall, she turned to Christ, led a most holy and truly Christian life, and attained a glorious end. He then joins to it another letter concerning the forty-two encampments and dedicates it to her memory. 690

### EPISTLE LXXVIII. Or, an Exegetical Book to Fabiola

After teaching that the history of the Hebrews’ departure from Egypt and their long journey should be understood spiritually, he continues the sequence of the encampments, explaining each one according to tropology. In this way he dedicates to Fabiola’s memory the work that he had promised her while she was alive. 698

### EPISTLE LXXIX. To Salvina

He consoles Salvina, a most noble woman, over the death of her husband Nebridius. After praising her deceased husband, he teaches her how she ought to raise the children surviving him and what kind of life she herself should lead, and he dissuades her from a second marriage. 724

### EPISTLE LXXX. Or, Rufinus’s Preface to Origen’s Books *On First Principles* (*περὶ ἀρχῶν*)

In order to impose Origen on everyone as though cleansed of the errors attributed to him and fit for universal reading, Rufinus praises Jerome as an ally of his own opinion and falsely claims him as a supporter of Origenist views. This produced the greatest dispute between the two men. 733

### EPISTLE LXXXI. To Rufinus

When he was being drawn under suspicion of Origenist heresy because of Rufinus’s indirect praises, [Col. 1292] with his friends also urging him on, he replies to the preceding letter and warns Rufinus not to praise him in that manner again. 735

### EPISTLE LXXXII. To Theophilus

Theophilus, Bishop of Alexandria, had sent letters to Jerome and to the monks living with him in order to reconcile peace between them and John, Bishop of Jerusalem. Jerome replies that he has nothing more at heart than that the dispute be settled and the peace of Christ restored between both parties. He then defends his Latin translations of Origen and the ordination of his brother Paulinianus against the complaints of that same John. 736

### EPISTLE LXXXIII

Pammachius and Oceanus urge Jerome to translate the book *On First Principles* (*περὶ ἀρχῶν*) accurately into Latin, to clear himself of Rufinus’s accusations and of people’s suspicions, and to show that he is alien to the errors of the Origenists. 743

### EPISTLE LXXXIV

Replying to the preceding letter, he explains with what intention he read and praised Origen, whom he would like everyone to read, if this could be done without danger to piety. He refutes the slanders of his rivals and dispels people’s suspicions. Forced to do so, he exposes the errors of Origen, which those who sought to defend their own heresy under Origen’s pretext were vainly attempting to defend. 744

### EPISTLE LXXXV. To Paulinus

He replies briefly to the second of the two questions proposed to him by Paulinus. He omits the first, since it is elucidated in the books *On First Principles* (*περὶ ἀρχῶν*) that he had recently translated into Latin. He then explains with what intention he read Origen. 752

### EPISTLE LXXXVI. To Theophilus

He praises the prudence of Theophilus, through whose efforts the faction of the Origenists was defeated. 754

### EPISTLE LXXXVIII. To Theophilus

He replies to the preceding letter and praises Theophilus, through whom not only Egypt and Syria but all Italy was liberated from heresy. 755

### EPISTLE LXXXIX. Theophilus to Jerome

He urges Jerome, now that the Origenists have been rejected, to pursue any who may be concealing themselves in Palestine. 756

### EPISTLE XC. Theophilus to Epiphanius

He urges Epiphanius to make every effort so that, once a synod has been convened, the heresy of the Origenists may be condemned by public authority. At the same time, he sends him the Synodical Letter that he himself had written. Ibid.

### EPISTLE XCI. Epiphanius to Jerome

He announces that, through the efforts of Theophilus, the faction of the Origenists has been condemned. Sending Jerome a copy of the Synodical Letter, he urges him to publish the books he had written against that heresy. 757

### EPISTLE XCII

Or, the Synodical Letter of Theophilus to the Palestinian and Cypriot bishops. 758

### EPISTLE XCIII

Or, the response of the Jerusalem Synod to the preceding letter of Theophilus, apparently translated by Saint Jerome.

The Fathers of the Synod reply that Palestine is free from the Origenist heresy, which they repeatedly curse. Nevertheless, they declare that they condemn the doctrines and persons whom Theophilus had condemned in his preceding Synodical Letter. 769

### EPISTLE XCIV. Dionysius to Theophilus, apparently rendered into Latin by Saint Jerome

He promptly praises Theophilus because through his efforts the Origenist heresy has been condemned, and earnestly urges him not to cease pursuing it to the end. 771

### EPISTLE XCV. Pope Anastasius to Simplicianus

He praises the zeal and vigilance of Theophilus. Informed by Theophilus’s letter, he declares to Simplicianus, Bishop of Milan, that he too has pronounced an anathema against the Origenist heresy. 772

### Fourth Class

Containing the letters from the beginning of the year 401 through 420, that is, to the end of Jerome’s life. 773–774

### EPISTLE XCVI

Or, the Paschal Letter of Theophilus, Bishop of Alexandria, for the year 401, to all the bishops of Egypt, rendered into Latin by Saint Jerome.

The divinity of Christ is asserted especially against Apollinaris. Most of Origen’s errors are then set out individually and refuted. Finally, love for one’s neighbors, necessary for celebrating the Lord’s Pascha properly, is praised as the chief virtue. 773

### EPISTLE XCVII. To Pammachius and Marcella

He sends them another Paschal Letter of Theophilus, which he had rendered into Latin against Origen. Because the Origenists had accused him of altering the preceding letter, he once again appends the Greek copy to his translation that year and attacks the heretics briefly. 790

### EPISTLE XCVIII

Or, the second Paschal Letter of Theophilus, Bishop of Alexandria, for the year 402, to all the bishops of Egypt, with Saint Jerome as translator.

First he urges the believers to celebrate the Lord’s Pascha. Next he attacks and destroys the errors of Apollinaris and, third, those of Origen. Finally, he exhorts the heretics to repentance. 792

### EPISTLE XCIX. To Theophilus

He excuses himself to Theophilus for having translated his appended Paschal Letter late, being hindered partly by Paula’s death and partly by his own illness. 812

### EPISTLE C

Or, the Paschal Letter of Theophilus, Bishop of Alexandria, for the year 404, to all the [Col. 1293] bishops of Egypt, with the Lord Jerome as translator.

People must cease from sins and adopt a habitual practice of virtues by which their souls may prepare to celebrate Pascha. The holy observance of the Lenten fasts and right faith in God are set forth. Origen’s errors, which ought to be execrated before the Lord’s Pascha, are also set forth. Moreover, avarice must be trampled down, and love of one’s neighbors must be joined to love of God. 813

### EPISTLE CI. Augustine to Jerome

He denies that he wrote a book against Jerome, though he is mistaken in this because someone had called a lengthy letter a book. 829

### EPISTLE CII. Jerome to Augustine

After receiving Augustine’s letters containing a question about a well-intentioned lie, and still uncertain whether the letter was Augustine’s, Jerome says that he will not reply until he is more certain of its author. He also mentions Rufinus under an assumed name. 830

### EPISTLE CIII. To Augustine

He commends Praesidius to Augustine and sends greetings to Alypius. 831

### EPISTLE CIV. Augustine to Jerome

Augustine dissuades Jerome from translating the books of the Old Testament from Hebrew. Rather, he advises him to restore the Septuagint version, which has been remarkably corrupted and made inconsistent, to conformity with its truth. He approves Jerome’s correction of the New Testament. 832

### EPISTLE CV. To Augustine

He protests against Augustine’s letter, circulated throughout Italy, in which Augustine criticized a passage that Jerome had not correctly expounded in his Letter to the Galatians. 834

### EPISTLE CVI. To Sunnia and Fretela

After congratulating Sunnia and Fretela—men of Gothic origin, it is true, but distinguished by their study of the divine Scriptures—he replies to the questions they had proposed concerning the Psalms and resolves all their difficulties. He shows which readings among the Greek and Latin texts should be preferred and which comes closer to the Hebrew source. 837

### EPISTLE CVII. To Laeta

He urges Laeta to train her daughter in Christian piety from her earliest infancy. For this purpose he offers very sound instructions concerning dress, food, the proper education of adolescence, study of the Scriptures, and avoidance of apocryphal writings. 867

### EPISTLE CVIII. To the Virgin Eustochium

He narrates Paula’s life, praising her first for the nobility of her lineage and then, above all, for the virtue of her character: after the death of her husband Toxotius, she devoted herself entirely to God and lived for a long time in Rome according to her holy purpose.

He then describes her journey in the greatest detail. After visiting the holy places of Judaea and traveling through Egypt as far as Alexandria, she settled in Bethlehem. There he explains what monasteries for virgins she built and by what examples and instructions she governed them. He praises her humility, patience, contempt for the world, charity toward the poor and sick, knowledge of the Scriptures, purity of faith, and other virtues. Finally, he describes her death and funeral at length. 878

### EPISTLE CIX. To Riparius the Presbyter

After being informed by Riparius’s letter that Vigilantius taught that the ashes of the martyrs should not be venerated, he uses this letter as a kind of skirmish and prelude to battle. He shows that he is ready to refute the man’s error if Riparius sends his books to him. 906

### EPISTLE CX. Augustine to Jerome

Augustine endeavors to soothe Jerome, who had been somewhat offended by his letters. He testifies that he has received Jerome’s defense against Rufinus and laments that discord had arisen between men who had once been such close friends. 909

### EPISTLE CXI. Augustine to Praesidius

Augustine asks Praesidius to ensure that the preceding letter is delivered to Jerome and to appease him on Augustine’s behalf by his own letters as well. 915

### EPISTLE CXXII. Jerome to Augustine

At last Jerome replies to the questions Augustine had proposed in Epistles 66, 67, and 104: concerning the title of the book recounting ecclesiastical writers, Peter’s being reproved by Paul in the Letter to the Galatians, the translation of the Old Testament, and the word “ivy” in Jonah. He vigorously defends his writings and translations against Augustine. 916

### EPISTLE CXIII. Theophilus to Jerome

He testifies that he had always sincerely wished well to John Chrysostom and had not rashly believed his accusers, until, when the judgment of the Council broke forth, John was expelled from his Constantinopolitan see and driven into exile. 931

### EPISTLE CXIV. Jerome to Theophilus

He gives many reasons for the obstacles that caused him to translate only later the book written by Theophilus against John Chrysostom. He then praises the teaching and arguments of that book, asking pardon if at any point he has not rendered the Greek meanings sufficiently well in Latin. 933

### EPISTLE CXV. To Augustine

He returns Augustine’s greeting and excuses himself for having replied too freely. He again mentions the gourd and asks that, once contentious questions have been set aside, they should henceforth discuss matters with one another as friends and proceed calmly in the field of the sacred Scriptures. 935

### [Col. 1294]

### EPISTLE CXVI. Augustine to Jerome

He replies more fully to Jerome’s Epistles 105, 113, and 115 concerning the interpretation of the passage in the Letter to the Galatians, affirming that Peter was rightly and truthfully reproved by Paul. For the rest, he asks pardon if his words were perhaps too careless and offended Jerome’s mind, explaining that the letter, through no fault of his own, had circulated through many hands before reaching the person to whom it had been written. 936

### EPISTLE CXVII. To a Mother and Daughter Living in Gaul

He teaches that widows and virgins must avoid domestic familiarity with those from whom there may arise danger either to chastity or to reputation. 953

### EPISTLE CXVIII. To Julianus

He consoles a certain very wealthy Julianus, who within a few days had lost two daughters and his wife and, because of the incursions of the barbarians, a considerable portion of his property. He does so by comparing him with Job and exhorts him, by the example of Pammachius and Paulinus, to a perfect life—that is, to complete contempt of the world—since fortune itself is also calling him to this. 960

### EPISTLE CXIX. To the Monks Minervius and Alexander

He replies to Minervius and Alexander, who had asked through the monk Sisinnius, son of Saint Exuperius, Bishop of Toulouse, about the Apostle’s words, “We shall all indeed sleep,” and so forth. He postpones to another time the other questions that had been proposed at the same time. 966

### EPISTLE CXX. To Hedibia

He replies to Hedibia, who had questioned him about the following twelve matters:

1. How anyone can be perfect, and how a widow who has been left without children ought to live for God.

2. What is meant by this passage in Matthew: “I will not drink from this fruit of the vine from now on,” and so forth.

3. Why the Evangelists gave differing accounts concerning the resurrection and appearances of the Lord.

4. How, according to Matthew, Mary Magdalene saw the risen Lord on the evening of the Sabbath, while the Evangelist John reports that she was weeping beside the tomb early on the first day of the week.

5. How, according to Matthew, Mary Magdalene, on the evening of the Sabbath, fell at the Savior’s feet with the other Mary, while according to John, early on the first day of the week, she heard the Lord say, “Do not touch me,” and so forth.

6. How Peter and John entered the tomb freely while a crowd of soldiers was guarding it.

7. How Matthew and Mark write that the Apostles were commanded through the women to go ahead to Galilee, where they would see Jesus, while Luke and John record that he was seen by the Apostles in Jerusalem.

8. What is signified by what is read in Matthew: “But Jesus, crying out with a loud voice, gave up his spirit; and the veil of the temple was torn,” and so forth.

9. How, according to John, the Savior breathes the Holy Spirit upon the Apostles, while according to Luke he says that he will send it after the Ascension.

10. What these words of Paul to the Romans mean: “What then shall we say? Is there injustice with God? By no means,” up to the passage where he says: “Unless the Lord of Hosts had left us offspring,” and so forth.

11. What the Apostle’s words to the Corinthians mean: “To some we are the odor of death unto death, and to others the odor of life unto life.”

12. What is meant by this passage from the First Letter to the Thessalonians: “But may the God of peace himself sanctify you completely,” and so forth. 980

### EPISTLE CXXI. To Algasia

He replies to the following eleven questions:

1. Why does John ask the Lord whether he is the one who is to come, when he had said of him, “Behold the Lamb of God,” and so forth?

2. What is meant by what is read in Matthew: “He will not break a bruised reed, and he will not extinguish a smoking wick.”

3. What is meant by these words of Matthew: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself.”

4. What is the meaning of what is read in Matthew: “Woe to those who are pregnant and nursing in those days,” and of this: “Pray that your flight may not take place in winter or on the Sabbath.”

5. What is signified by these words in the Gospel according to Luke: “And they did not receive him, because his face was set toward Jerusalem.”

6. Who is the unjust steward whom the Lord’s voice praised.

7. In what sense should we understand what we read in the Letter to the Romans: “For scarcely does anyone die for a righteous person; perhaps someone might dare to die for a good person.”

8. What is meant by what the Apostle writes to the Romans: “Taking occasion, sin worked in me through the commandment every kind of covetousness.”

9. Why the Apostle writes to the Romans: “I myself was wishing to be accursed from Christ for the sake of my brothers,” and so forth.

10. What is meant by what Paul writes to the Colossians: “Let no one take advantage of you, taking delight in humility of mind and the worship of angels,” and so forth.

11. What is meant by what the same Apostle writes to the Thessalonians: “Unless the falling away comes first and the man of sin is revealed,” and so forth. 1006

### EPISTLE CXXII. To Rusticus

Because Rusticus had broken the continence he had promised together with his wife Artemia, he invites him to repentance and to holy places, urging him by the example of his wife. 1038

### EPISTLE CXXIII. To Ageruchia

He dissuades the young widow Ageruchia from a second marriage, rejecting the arguments that seemed to favor the contrary position and also placing before [Col. 1295] her eyes, for the same purpose, the calamities of the world. 1046

### EPISTLE CXXIV. To Avitus

After being asked by Pammachius to translate again Origen’s book *On First Principles* (*περὶ ἀρχῶν*), which Rufinus had previously rendered into Latin in bad faith, adding and cutting out certain things, Jerome translates it without alteration so that it may be read without danger to the faith. He shows what statements in it are impious and must be avoided as heretical. 1059

### EPISTLE CXXV. To the Monk Rusticus

He teaches how one ought to establish a life worthy of the name of monk and warns above all that one must avoid the company of suspect women. It is safer, however, for a young man to live in a coenobium than in solitude. He then teaches that one should come late to teaching and writing books and that the intimacy of detractors must be avoided in every way. 1072

### EPISTLE CXXVI. To Marcellinus and Anapsychia

He sets out the various opinions concerning the origin of the soul, urging them to seek the remaining answers from Augustine and indicating the studies with which he himself is occupied. 1085

### EPISTLE CXXVII. To the Virgin Principia, or the Epitaph of the Widow Marcella

He praises Marcella, a woman of the highest nobility, who, widowed seven months after her marriage, later rejected the consul Cerealis, who sought her hand, and was the first noblewoman in Rome to venture to profess the monastic life, drawing many others into the same way of life. She also learned the divine Scriptures most diligently in Rome from Jerome himself, often wrote to him when he was absent, and finally, through her efforts, exposed and destroyed the faction of the Origenists, which had begun to grow powerful in the city. She died a few days after the city had been sacked by the Goths. 1087

### EPISTLE CXXVIII. To Gaudentius

He teaches by what elementary instruction a girl of tender age, destined for virginity, should be trained before she knows the distinction between good and evil. 1095

### EPISTLE CXXIX. To Dardanus

He teaches that the promised land is not the land possessed by the Jews but another, heavenly land: namely, the land of the living promised in the Gospel to the meek. He also teaches that the only cause of the Jews’ miseries and eternal captivity is the blood of Christ that was shed and the accursed crime by which they did not fear to inflict death upon him. 1097

### EPISTLE CXXX. To Demetrias

He praises the virgin Demetrias, daughter of Juliana and granddaughter of Proba, because she consecrated herself to Christ. He urges her to persevere and immediately to resist the promptings of the devil, who solicits her to shameful things. He gives instructions concerning study, fasting, obedience, avoidance of jokes, and the other matters relevant to the discipline of a virgin. 1105

### EPISTLE CXXXI. Augustine to Jerome, or a Book on the Origin of the Human Soul

After reviewing various opinions concerning the origin of the soul, Augustine wishes to be taught which should chiefly be held and how the position that Jerome almost indicated as his own in the preceding Epistle 126—that individual souls are newly created for those being born—can be defended against the doctrine of the Pelagians. 1122

### EPISTLE CXXXII. Augustine to Jerome, or a Book on the Saying of James

He asks about the passage from James 2:10: “Whoever offends in one point has become guilty of all.” He also introduces much concerning the Stoics, who taught that all sins are equal, that whoever possessed one virtue possessed them all, and that whoever lacked one possessed none. 1138

### EPISTLE CXXXIII. To Ctesiphon

At Ctesiphon’s request, he refutes the insanity of Pelagian doctrine, especially *apatheia* (*ἀπάθεια*) and *anamartēsia* (*ἀναμαρτησία*), that is, freedom from disturbances of the soul and sinlessness. He shows from what foul sources they flowed.

He then rebukes Rufinus, who translated into Latin a book by Xystus the Pythagorean under the name of Sixtus the martyr and Roman pontiff, although the book contained an odor of Pelagian error, and who passed off another book by Eusebius Pamphilus as the work of Pamphilus the martyr.

Finally, he promises that, when leisure permits, he will respond to Pelagian doctrine in a substantial volume. 1147

### EPISTLE CXXXIV. To Augustine

He states that he received from Orosius two books addressed to him—namely, [Col. 1296] Augustine’s two preceding Epistles 131 and 132—and explains why he did not reply to them. 1161

### EPISTLE CXXXV. Pope Innocent to Aurelius

Innocent sends Aurelius a letter to be delivered to Jerome. 1162

### EPISTLE CXXXVI. Innocent to Jerome

Innocent consoles Jerome for what he has suffered and declares what he has thought should be done for the time being and what he has already done. 1163

### EPISTLE CXXXVII. Innocent to John

He says that John of Jerusalem ought to have seen to it that Jerome, Eustochium, and Paula were not overwhelmed by the many and great evils afflicting them. Unless these matters are henceforth corrected or checked, John will have to give an account of them. Ibid.

### EPISTLE CXXXVIII. To Riparius

He tells the presbyter Riparius how the Pelagian doctrines were rejected and their disseminator, like another Catiline, expelled, and what happened to him in that affair. 1164

### EPISTLE CXXXIX. To Apronius

He praises Apronius for remaining steadfast in the faith against the Pelagians and urges him to visit the holy places of Jerusalem. 1165

### EPISTLE CXL. To the Presbyter Cyprian

To Cyprian the presbyter he expounds Psalm 89, whose beginning is “Lord, you have been our refuge,” piously and eloquently according to the truth of the Hebrew, after the Septuagint and the Vulgate editions. 1166

### EPISTLE CXLI. To Augustine

He congratulates Augustine on his diligence, through which he resisted the factions of the heretics, and in this matter he also gives evidence of his own zeal. 1179

### EPISTLE CXLII. To Augustine

He indicates that the condemned heresies are still secretly and indirectly at work and that there is someone powerful who covertly favors them. 1180

### EPISTLE CXLIII. To Alypius and Augustine

He congratulates Alypius and Augustine, through whose efforts the Coelestian heresy has been extinguished. At the same time, he excuses himself for not yet having written against the books of Annianus, the Pelagian deacon. 1181

### EPISTLE CXLIV. Saint Augustine to Optatus, Bishop of Milevis

He says that he has not yet received from Jerome a reply to his Epistle 131 concerning the origin of the soul, nor does he approve of that inquiry being published to the general public in the meantime. 1182

### Fifth Class

Containing three letters whose dates are less certain, followed by three others whose authorship is uncertain. 1191–1192

### EPISTLE CXLV. To Exuperantius

He urges Exuperantius to abandon military service, devote himself to the perfect Christian life, and move to Bethlehem together with his brother Quintilianus. 1191

### EPISTLE CXLVI. To Evangelus

He refutes the error of those who equated the deacon with the presbyter, showing what distinction there is among a bishop, a presbyter, and a deacon. 1192

### EPISTLE CXLVII. To the Fallen Sabinianus

He rebukes the deacon Sabinianus, who, after committing adultery, had fled to Bethlehem, where he had been commended to Jerome by a letter from his bishop. Remaining in the holy places and exercising the office of deacon, Sabinianus had solicited a consecrated virgin to sexual violation and flight. Jerome urges him to repent in a monastery. 1195

### EPISTLE CXLVIII. To the Matron Celantia

He teaches the noble matron Celantia how to lead her life in a holy and religious manner amid the honors and riches of the world and the burdens of marriage. First he urges her to read the divine Scripture; then he teaches her not to be proud of the nobility of her lineage and where true nobility lies. Finally, he sharply rebukes her for having resolved some years earlier to practice continence without any agreement or consent from her husband, and he shows what she owes her husband. 1204

### EPISTLE CXLIX

Jerome explains the feast days of the Hebrews and teaches that they should by no means be observed after the Gospel. 1220

### EPISTLE CL. Procopius to Jerome

1224

### Notes of Jean Martianay on All the Epistles of Saint Jerome

1225–1226
**END OF THE FIRST VOLUME OF SAINT JEROME.**
